chunks.text: The Authority is, within the scope of its jurisdiction, deemed to be a commission of inquiry under the Commissions of Inquiry Act 1908. The provisions of that Act, except sections 2, 10, 11, and 12, apply accordingly, subject to the provisions of this Act.

chunks.title: 13 Contempt of authority
chunks.text: A person commits an offence if the person— wilfully insults or obstructs the authority or any member of it, a witness, or an officer of the authority during a sitting of the authority or while a member, a witness, or an officer is going to, or returning from, a sitting of the authority; or wilfully insults or obstructs any person in attendance at a sitting of the authority; or wilfully interrupts, or otherwise misbehaves at, a sitting of the authority; or wilfully and without lawful excuse disobeys any order or direction of the authority in the course of the hearing of any appeal. A person who commits an offence against subclause (1) is liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $1,000. The authority may order the exclusion from a sitting of the authority of any person whose behaviour, in the opinion of the authority, constitutes an offence against subclause (1), whether or not the person is charged with the offence; and any officer of the authority or constable may take any steps that are reasonably necessary to enforce the exclusion.

chunks.title: 1 Establishment and membership
chunks.text: A medical board consists of 3 members appointed— by the chief executive; and for the particular purpose. A person is ineligible for appointment as a member unless the person is— a medical practitioner; or a rehabilitation professional (see subclause (3)); or a person who has appropriate expertise in the fields of vocational training or vocational support for persons with health conditions, injury, or disability. In subclause (2)﻿(b), rehabilitation professional means a person who is— a person professionally engaged in the rehabilitation of persons from sickness or accident or with disabilities; or a nurse; or an occupational therapist; or a physiotherapist; or a psychologist. In subclause (3)﻿(b), nurse means a health practitioner who is, or is deemed to be, registered with the Nursing Council of New Zealand continued by section 114(1)﻿(a) of the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003 as a practitioner of the profession of nursing whose scope of practice permits the performance of general nursing functions. In subclause (3)﻿(c), occupational therapist means a health practitioner who is, or is deemed to be, registered with the Occupational Therapy Board continued by section 114(1)﻿(a) of the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003 as a practitioner of the profession of occupational therapy. In subclause (3)﻿(d), physiotherapist means a health practitioner who is, or is deemed to be, registered with the Physiotherapy Board continued by section 114(1)﻿(a) of the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003 as a practitioner of the profession of physiotherapy. In subclause (3)﻿(e), psychologist means a health practitioner who is, or is deemed to be, registered with the Psychologists Board continued by section 114(1)﻿(a) of the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003 as a practitioner of the profession of psychology.

chunks.title: 2 Members’ terms and conditions of office
chunks.text: Each member holds office on terms and conditions that— are not inconsistent with this Act; and the chief executive thinks fit. Each member— may be paid remuneration at a rate and of a kind determined by the chief executive; and is entitled to be reimbursed for actual and reasonable travelling and other expenses determined by the chief executive. No member is, just because of membership of a board, to be treated as employed in the service of the Crown for the purposes of— the Public Service Act 2020; or the Government Superannuation Fund Act 1956.

chunks.title: 3 Secretarial and administrative services
chunks.text: MSD must meet the costs of all secretarial and administrative services required for a board’s purposes.

chunks.title: 4 Quorum, and board’s decision, at meetings
chunks.text: At any meeting of a board,— the quorum is that board’s total membership; and the decision of any 2 members of that board is that board’s decision.

chunks.title: 31 References to Child Welfare Officer to be read as references to social workers, etc
chunks.text: Every reference in this Act and its amendments, as in force on or after 1 April 1972, to a Child Welfare Officer must be read as a reference to a social worker. Subsection (1) applies— subject to the amendments made by section 23(1) to (3) of the Department of Social Welfare Act 1971; and unless the context otherwise requires. This section does not affect the operation of section 23(4)﻿(a) of the Department of Social Welfare Act 1971 (which required references to the Superintendent of Child Welfare to be read as references to the Director-General of Social Welfare under that Act) at any time or times— on or after 1 April 1972; and before its repeal, on 1 April 1990, by section 36(6) of the Social Welfare (Transitional Provisions) Act 1990.

chunks.title: 101B Power to issue deduction notices under Social Security Act 2018
chunks.text: This section applies to a payment— under a maintenance order; and that is in arrear and unpaid. The chief executive of the department for the time being responsible for the administration of the Social Security Act 2018 may issue a deduction notice under regulations made under section 444 of that Act to a person as if the payment in arrear and unpaid were a debt due to the Crown under that Act. However, the deduction notice cannot be issued to the employer of, acting in the capacity of the employer of, the person against whom the order was made. This section does not limit section 101 or section 110 (as saved by section 259(1) of the Child Support Act 1991).

chunks.title: 34 Effect on other benefits
chunks.text: A person being paid a benefit under section 31 is not entitled to receive any assistance under the Social Security Act 2018 or under a programme approved under section 100 or 101 of that Act.

chunks.title: 39 Right to benefits
chunks.text: A resident is not disentitled from obtaining a benefit (as defined in Schedule 2 of the Social Security Act 2018). For the purpose of calculating the benefit, the resident is taken to be a patient in a hospital (within the meaning of, as the case requires, sections 206 and 207 and Schedule 2 of that Act, or section 19(1) of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001) for more than 13 weeks.

chunks.title: 9 Hearing and disposal of appeal
chunks.text: Sections 400, 401(3) and (4), 403, 404, and 405 to 410, and Schedule 8, and regulations made under section 451, of the Social Security Act 2018 apply to the hearing and disposal of the appeal (including matters relating to procedure) with the following, and all other necessary, modifications: a reference in any of those provisions to the chief executive is a reference to the agency: a reference in any of those provisions to a decision is a reference to a decision, determination, or assessment of the agency. Appeals under regulation 8 that are not completed on the repeal of the Social Security Act 1964 continue under this regulation as inserted on that repeal.

chunks.title: Amount of reimbursement — community services card
chunks.text:
## Amount of reimbursement
The following amounts can be reimbursed when the client has applied for a Community Services Card, High Use Health Card or Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card, but are yet to be issued with one of these cards.
## Health practitioners costs
Consultation fees vary so it is very important to know the amount the general practice would usually charge without a Community Services Card or High Use Health Card before the amount to be reimbursed is calculated.
The following amounts are the maximum reimbursement payment:
Child aged 14-18 years (if under caregiver's card)
$20.00
Adult
$15.00
Note MSD does not reimburse claims for children under 14 years of age. All children in this age group are entitled to subsidised fees for medical practitioner and nurse practitioner consultations. However, there may be additional charges that are not subsidised, which must be paid by the parent or carer.
## Prescriptions
MSD reimburses the difference between what the client actually paid and what they would have paid if they had their card with them.
There is no $5.00 co-payment for fully subsidised prescription items from publicly funded health providers for people:
- under 14 or
- holding a Community Services Card (and their dependents aged 14-17 years old) or
- 65 years or older
If someone in one of the above groups is prescribed items from a publicly funded health provider, they may still have to pay a fee.
For example, if they are prescribed partially subsidised and non-subsidised prescription items.
For example:

$10.00

Note there is no government prescription charge on items for children under 14. There may still be a part-charge or pharmacy fees for services such as packaging and faxes that families pay.

chunks.title: Health practitioner visits — community services card
chunks.text: When a client has a Community Services Card they can get a subsidy for visits to a health practitioner outside their Primary Health Organisation (PHO), as well as reduced fees for after-hours health practitioner visits. The current subsidy levels for each visit are: Adult 18 years or over $15.00 Children 14-17 years $20.00 Most enrolled children under 14 will not be charged standard health practitioner's fees - with or without a Community Services Card. Example if a health practitioner's normal charge is $60.00 per visit, it will cost $45.00 for an adult or $40.00 for a child aged 14-17 years old. The Community Services Card does not subsidise visits to privately funded health practitioners including specialists, osteopaths, podiatrists and dietitians.

chunks.title: Prescription charges — community services card
chunks.text: The amount paid for prescriptions will depend on what prescription item is needed, whether it was prescribed by a publicly funded health provider or a privately funded health provider, and if the person holds a Community Services Card, Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card and/or High Use Health Card. From 1 February 2026, prescribers can issue prescriptions for up to 12 months in some cases. Any co-payment charged is per prescription, rather than each time it is dispensed. This means clients may only have to pay for one $5.00 co-payment within a 12-month period. Anyone getting a prescription may have to pay other pharmacy fees that are not subsidised (e.g. packaging, printing and faxing).

chunks.title: Publicly funded providers — community services card
chunks.text: Fully subsidised prescription items from publicly funded health providers (including public specialists) are free for people: - under 14 or - holding a Community Services Card (and their dependents aged 14-17 years old) or - 65 years or older (from 1 July 2024) If a someone in one of the above groups is prescribed items from a publicly funded health provider, they may still have to pay a fee. For example, if they are prescribed partially subsidised and non-subsidised prescription items. This includes clients who hold a Community Services Card, Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card and/or High Use Health Card. Example 1 - client is not in a subsidised group George has asthma that has been stable for 10 years. He visits a publicly funded specialist for his inhaler. He requests to change from one of the partially subsidised inhalers to a fully subsidised inhaler. His doctor notes that both inhalers do the same thing. At the pharmacy George pays a $5.00 co-payment for his initial inhaler as he does not fall into one of the subsidised groups, and any extra inhalers needed in that 12-month period will not have another co-payment. Example 2 - client is in a subsidised group Tina visits her general practitioner (GP). They prescribe her the medication she needs for her ongoing disability. The medication prescribed is fully subsidised. At the pharmacy Tina does not have to pay anything for her medication as she has a Community Services Card.

chunks.title: Privately funded providers — community services card
chunks.text: When prescriptions are prescribed by privately funded health providers (including private specialists) there is a cost. This includes fully subsidised, partially subsidised and non-subsidised prescription items. Prescriptions from privately funded health providers have a: - $10.00 co-payment for people aged 14-17 years old or - $15.00 co-payment for people aged 18 years and older Example Sarah has an ongoing skin condition and visits her private specialist. She is prescribed a fully subsidised prescription cream. As Sarah is over 18 years old, she is charged a $15.00 co-payment for her medicine at the pharmacy.

chunks.title: Public transport — community services card
chunks.text: Community Connect is a transport initiative led by the Ministry of Transport allowing Community Services Card holders to get a 50% discount on public transport fares.

chunks.title: Authorised use for health services — community services card
chunks.text:
## Authorised use for health services
A client who is issued a Community Services Card may use the card to:
- provide evidence that they have been issued with the card and as proof of their client number
- provide evidence to the Ministry of Health, health practice, specialist, pharmacist or hospital that:
- they are eligible for a Community Services Card and
- they and their dependent children are eligible for services provided by the Ministry of Health, any exemptions for those services and the maximum charge payable
A person can temporarily loan their Community Services Card to:
- their dependent child or a person looking after their dependent child to obtain services from the Ministry of Health or
- to another person to obtain services from the Ministry of Health for the cardholder
## Authorised use for public transport
A person who is issued a Community Services Card may use the card to:
- provide evidence to an authorised person collecting public transport fares, issuing public transport tickets or operating a public transport service or anyone that is carrying out work specified for those services that:
- they are a Community Services Card holder and
- confirm eligibility for a discount on public transport fares

chunks.title: Card History Letters and Special Plastic Cards — community services card
chunks.text:
## Card History Letters and Special Plastic Cards
Because a physical card cannot be issued for short-term clients who qualify, a Card History Letter can be issued:
- where a benefit has been granted for 4 weeks or less (for example a short-term Jobseeker Support) or
- if a card is lost, stolen or destroyed within 4 weeks of the expiry date.
Note a Card History Letter can only be issued by the Senior Support Centre.
## Special Plastic Cards
Special Plastic Cards are issued for clients in the following situations:
- clients on a portable pension
- clients who have a name that is longer than 27 characters or
- clients who would normally have a card history letter issued but have specifically requested a plastic card.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — community services card
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
Community Services Cards can be reissued if they are lost, damaged or stolen. A client can be reimbursed if they are charged the full amount for health services because they had forgotten their card.
A client can review any decisions made.
For more information see:
- Death of a client
- Lost, stolen, damaged destroyed or forgotten cards
- Reimbursement of medical fees
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals

chunks.title: Child not living at home — community services card
chunks.text:
## Child not living at home
The child doesn't have to be living with the client to be a dependent child. MSD should consider the following:
- why the child is living away from home and
- how permanent the arrangement is and
- what payments the client makes towards the child's care and everyday living expenses
Here are some examples where the child does not live at home, but would be considered a dependent child.
## Child attending a boarding school
Generally, the client should pay for some of the costs of the child attending a boarding school, including school fees, pocket money, clothing or travel. In addition to this the child should return to the client for some of the school holidays.
Note the client may not be paying boarding fees for the child when the child is getting a scholarship.
## Child overseas on American Field Scholarship or other exchange student programme
The client must pay for some of the costs.
## Child attending a specialist school
The client must pay for some of the costs of a child attending a specialist school.
## Away From Home Allowance
When a 16-17 year old dependent child has needed to or chosen to move away from home to undertake tertiary study or employment related training, the client can receive an Away From Home Allowance to help pay the 16-17 year olds accommodation costs. See:
- Away From Home Allowance

chunks.title: Child temporarily with another person — community services card
chunks.text:
## Child temporarily with another person
If a child is living temporarily with another person but is still dependent on their parents, they are still considered to be part of the parents' family unit and can access services under their parents' Community Services Card. The parent is responsible for providing a copy of the card information to the temporary carer.
If the parents do not qualify for a Community Services Card, the child cannot access services even if the temporary carer has a Community Services Card.

chunks.title: Children — community services card
chunks.text:
## Children
The Community Services Card is issued to each adult in a family. Dependent children are not issued with their own card but can access services through their parent's card. The names of the children are not printed on the card.
For a child whose parent or carer is getting on their behalf:
- Orphans Benefit
- Unsupported Child's Benefit
- Child Disability Allowance
The card is issued in the child's name but is sent to the parent or carer.
If the child is too young or unable to sign the back of the card, the parent or carer may sign it on the child's behalf.
For more information see:
- In the care of Oranga Tamariki
## 16 or 17 year olds in tertiary study
16 and 17 years olds who are undertaking tertiary study may be able to get a Community Services Card in their own right. For more information see:
- Students
If the child is still dependent, they can be included in the parent or caregiver's family unit when deciding eligibility for Community Services Card (whether or not the 16 or 17 year old qualifies for a card in their own right). For more information see:
- Family unit

chunks.title: Clients excluded from a Community Services Card — community services card
chunks.text:
## Clients excluded from a Community Services Card
The following clients cannot get a Community Services Card:
- a person who is unlawfully present in New Zealand
- a person who is lawfully resident or present in New Zealand but only by virtue of a: temporary entry class visa or transit visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009temporary permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987 (such as a visitor, work or student)
- temporary entry class visa or transit visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009
- temporary permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987 (such as a visitor, work or student)
Note children of these people are also excluded from receiving a Community Services Card
- children of diplomats
- overseas students and
- prison inmates (health needs are met by the Ministry of Justice)

chunks.title: Commencement date — community services card
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
The commencement date for the Community Services Card is:
- the date the client became eligible for a benefit
- for clients with children, 3 months before the date on which the application for the card was received
- for low income earners without dependent children, New Zealand superannuation clients and students: 28 days before the application was received orthe date the client became eligible to receive the card
- 28 days before the application was received or
- the date the client became eligible to receive the card
whichever is the later date
- for clients in residential care: the date the client commenced receiving residential care disability services
Clients can make a verbal application for the Community Services Card but will need to formalise this within 20 working days by completing a Community Services Card Application form.
For more information see:
- Application for assistance

chunks.title: Death of a client — community services card
chunks.text:
## Death of a client
When a client receiving any assistance dies, the Community Services Card must be cancelled before date of death details can be added to the client’s record.
## Children of a deceased client
Children may access health services through the Community Services Card of the surviving spouse or partner.
If the deceased has no surviving spouse or partner, the person who is appointed the dependent child's carer may apply for a card and include the child in their application.
Note if a client is granted Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphans Benefit for a child, the child is issued a card in their own right. The child is not included in their carer's application for a Community Services Card, they are not considered a dependent child for the Community Services Card.

chunks.title: Deduction of child support — community services card
chunks.text:
## Deduction of child support
Clients with dependent children who also pay child support can deduct this amount from their income for Community Services Card assessment purposes.

chunks.title: Definition of income — community services card
chunks.text:
## Definition of income
There are 3 definitions of income used to determine eligibility for the Community Services Card, depending on the circumstances of the client.
1. Income as defined in dictionary schedule 2 of the Social Security Act 2018.
This definition is used to assess low income earners who do not have dependent children, i.e. income received from any source as well as the value of goods and services received instead of money.
2. 'Net Income' as defined in section YA1 of the Income Tax Act 2007 and regulation 2 of the Health Entitlement Card Regulations 1993.
This definition is used to assess New Zealand Superannuitants, i.e. taxable income plus 50% of private pensions or annuities received.
3. Family Credit Income as defined in subpart MB of the Income Tax Act 2007 and regulation 2 of the Health Entitlement Card Regulations 1993. This definition is used to assess low income earners with dependent children, i.e. taxable income plus Working for Families Tax Credits entitlements from Inland Revenue.
Note assessed income is rounded down to the nearest complete dollar, eg: $65,273.72 is rounded down to $65,273.00.
## Child Support income
Child Support must be considered under the general definition of income for Community Services Card purposes.
Clients must declare all Child Support income they get (including any payments that have been notified to MSD through the information share with Inland Revenue).
Generally, this income is charged over the period it is earned in or relates to.
Child Support income is treated this way for all low income earners and New Zealand Superannuitants, regardless of whether the client has a dependent child in their care or not.
For more information about income see:
- Core Policy Income

chunks.title: Dependent children — community services card
chunks.text:
## Dependent children
A dependent child for a Community Services Card is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- maintained as a member of their family
- financially dependent on the client or
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for a Community Services Card does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples) or
- child for whom an Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid
In some situations a child may not be living at home but is still considered to be a dependent child.
## 16 - 17 year olds in tertiary study
16 and 17 years olds who are undertaking tertiary study may be able to get a Community Services Card in their own right.
If the child is still dependent, they can be included in the parent or caregiver's family unit when deciding eligibility for Community Services Card (whether or not the 16-17 year old qualifies for a card in their own right).
## Care and protection concerns
If MSD believes any child has been, or is likely to be harmed (physically, emotionally or sexually), ill-treated, abused, neglected, deprived or MSD has concerns about the wellbeing of the child, the case must be referred to Oranga Tamariki.

chunks.title: Family unit — community services card
chunks.text:
## Family unit
A family is defined as a group of persons who live together in the same household that comprises either:
- 1 adult who cares for one or more dependent children who are part of that group or
- 2 adults who care for one or more dependent children who are part of that group
Where other members of the extended family, for example, a grandparent or an adult sibling, lives with the family, they cannot be included as part of the family unit and must establish eligibility in their own right.
The income limits for a family unit, at 1 April 2026, are:
Family of 2: 1 adult + 1 child
$67,791 per annum
Family of 3
$83,444 per annum
Family of 4
$96,266 per annum
Family of 5
$108,860 per annum
Family of 6
$122,724 per annum
Family of 7 or more add $12,440 for each extra child
For the income limits for all clients see:
- Deskfile Income cut-out points

chunks.title: Fees for completing tax returns — community services card
chunks.text:
## Fees for completing tax returns
Clients who receive New Zealand Superannuation and have their income tax returns prepared by an accountant or other agency are able to deduct the cost of preparation from their return.
These clients can deduct this cost in the same way as for their tax return when determining income for the Community Services Card.

chunks.title: In the care of Oranga Tamariki — community services card
chunks.text:
## In the care of Oranga Tamariki
The Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki is responsible for meeting the medical costs of the children placed in their care.
Children in the care of Oranga Tamariki must pay full costs for services that are covered by a Community Services Card.
An individual child in care may qualify for a High Use Health Card under the same criteria as any other person.
For more information see:
- High Use Health Card.
Carers have the following choices when paying for health services on behalf of the child:
- have the service provider send the account to the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki
- meet the expenses and send the relevant receipts to their social worker who arranges for the expenses to be refunded
- if the child has a personal High Use Health Card then the caregiver should use this to obtain the lower health charges. No refund would be claimable through Oranga Tamariki as the child's care allowance is intended to cover these minor expenses. However, if prescription co-payments (for fully subsidised, partially subsidised or non-subsidised prescription items) are incurred, then Oranga Tamariki will consider reimbursement when they determine it is appropriate
- the only time MSD is involved in reimbursement for High Use Health Card holders is when: charges were incurred before the client got their card or when a full charge was made because the carer did not have the entitlement card
- charges were incurred before the client got their card or
- when a full charge was made because the carer did not have the entitlement card

chunks.title: Income test — community services card
chunks.text:
## Income test
A client doesn't need to be income tested to get a Community Services Card if they:
- are tenants of social housing or
- are getting an Accommodation Supplement or
- are getting an income-tested benefit or
- receive a Veteran's Pension
Otherwise, clients must meet an income test to qualify for a Community Services Card. The income limit for a Community Services Card depends on the client's relationship status and living situation.
Note a New Zealand Superannuation client whose partner is getting an income-tested benefit automatically qualifies for a Community Services Card, and is not income tested separately.

chunks.title: Introduction — community services card
chunks.text:
## Introduction
A Community Services Card is available to low or middle income earners to enable them and their family to access subsidised health services. Community Services Card holders can also get a 50% discount on public transport fares for themselves.
The Senior Support Centre is responsible for deciding if a client qualifies for a Community Services Card.

chunks.title: Lost, stolen, damaged, destroyed or forgotten cards — community services card
chunks.text:
## Lost, stolen, damaged, destroyed or forgotten cards
Clients whose cards are lost, stolen, damaged or destroyed should contact the Senior Support Centre to request a replacement card.
The replacement card will have the same expiry date as the original. Replacement cards cannot administratively be issued if the card is due to expire within a month, instead a card history letter will be issued. For more information see:
- Card history letter
If a client has forgotten or no longer has their card and cannot be charged the subsidised rate for health services, they may apply to have the difference reimbursed once they receive their replacement card.
For more information see:
- Reimbursement of medical fees

chunks.title: Married, civil union or de facto couple without children — community services card
chunks.text:
## Married, civil union or de facto couple without children
If a client is married, in a civil union, or in a de facto relationship with a person of the same or different sex, both the client and partner's income is assessed.
The current income limit for a married, civil union or de facto couple as at 1 April 2026 is:
Married, civil union or de facto couple, not entitled to New Zealand Superannuation (at 1 April 2026)
$55,501 per annum (gross)
Married, civil union or de facto couple, entitled to New Zealand Superannuation (at 1 April 2026)
$59,694 per annum (gross)
Note a New Zealand Superannuation client whose partner is getting an income tested benefit automatically qualifies for a Community Services Card, and is not income tested separately.
For the income limits for all clients see:
- Deskfile Income cut-out points

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation — community services card
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation
New Zealand Superannuation clients must meet the income test to qualify for a Community Service Card unless they:
- are getting Accommodation Supplement or
- are tenants of social housing or
- their partner is getting an income tested benefit
There is no residence test for New Zealand Superannuation clients to get a Community Services Card because they have already met the residence requirement for their superannuation.
If a grandparented non-qualified partner was included, both clients are considered New Zealand Superannuation clients.
Partners of clients getting Residential Care Subsidy have to apply and qualify for a Community Services Card in their own right.
When one partner is living in a rest home but does not qualify for Residential Care Subsidy, you must consider eligibility for the card as a family unit.

chunks.title: Obligations — community services card
chunks.text:
## Obligations
People who are issued a Community Services Card have the following obligations:
- may at any time return the card to the Ministry of Social Development and ask for it to be cancelled.
- must return their card to the Ministry if requested in writing
If a client fails to meet their obligations, you can ask, in writing for the Community Services Card to be returned. The cardholder can be fined up to $1,000 for misuse of the card.
For more information see:
- Authorised uses
- Unauthorised uses

chunks.title: Other health services — community services card
chunks.text:
## Other health services
There may be other types of help available to Community Services Card holders. Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora has contracts with community organisations to provide health care and assistance.
Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora rules vary depending on which region you are in, so it is important the card holder makes direct contact with their local hospital or health professional to find out what services are available in their area.
## Dentists
Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora has contracts to provide Emergency Dental Services with some dentists across New Zealand.
To get this help, people must have a current Community Services Card and must not qualify for assistance from MSD, for example a Special Needs Grant to help pay for the treatment.
The card holder needs to bring in a quote from the dentist and have their entitlement assessed by MSD.
If there is no entitlement, written confirmation will be provided, and the dentist can start treatment.
## Home Help
People who hold current Community Services Cards can apply for home help assistance from Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora or their agent. This can include:
- Home help
- Personal care
- Carer Relief (home help, personal care, day care, 'in-home' respite care and residential respite care).
## Travel and Accommodation
Cardholders who need hospital treatment outside of their local area can get help with travel and accommodation. They need to let their local hospital know before they make their own travel arrangements.
## Spectacles Subsidy for children
The Spectacles Subsidy, paid for by Whaikaha – Ministry for Disabled People, is for children aged 15 and under, if:
- the child or their caregiver has a current Community Services Card, or
- the child has a current high use health card.
Clients who want to find out more about this subsidy should call 0800 171 981 to find an assessor.
A child needs to have an assessment by an optometrist or eye specialist who is registered as an assessor for the subsidy.
The subsidy covers:
- examination
- lenses
- frames
- eye patches
If the subsidy does not cover the full cost, the caregiver is required to pay the balance. They may be eligible for recoverable assistance to help with the cost.

chunks.title: High Use Health Card — community services card
chunks.text:
## High Use Health Card
High users of a health practitioner's services may qualify for a High Use Health Card. To get this card, the person and the health practitioner must apply together to Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora.
This card is valid for the person only (i.e. not other family members). A person must have made 12 visits in the past 12 months for one or more on-going health conditions. The card will start on the day after the person's 12th visit and will expire on the same date in the following year.
## Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card
An individual or family unit pays the co-payment for the first 20 prescription items that are prescribed in any "pharmaceutical year" (defined as 1 February to 31 January).
Note this applies to every new prescription and does not apply to repeat supplies on the same prescription.
After 20 pharmaceutical items have been purchased by an individual or family unit from the same pharmacy, the pharmacist issues a Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card.
Once a Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card is issued that individual or family unit will not have to pay the co-payment for the rest of the pharmaceutical year.
There may be other charges that people must pay, including those who hold a Community Services Card, Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card and/or High Use Health Card. These charges could include:
- a part-charge, if the cost to manufacture the item is more than the government subsidy
- pharmacy fees that are not subsidised (e.g. packaging, printing and faxing)
Note the Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card is also known as a Prescription Subsidy Card.

chunks.title: Overseas students — community services card
chunks.text:
## Overseas students
Overseas students studying in New Zealand under assistance or exchange programmes approved by the New Zealand Government generally cannot receive a Community Services Card (this includes students who are exempt from paying student fees) because they are not ordinarily resident in New Zealand.
This includes:
- students fully funded by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade
- students who are partly funded by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (including those who have only their tuition fees paid for by the Ministry)
- students on exchange programmes

chunks.title: Partners — community services card
chunks.text:
## Partners
Partners of clients getting Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy are treated as single, and need to apply and qualify for a card in their own right.
Partners of clients who are tenants of social housing or are getting an Accommodation Supplement may get a card if they meet the residence criteria.
A New Zealand Superannuation client whose partner gets an income tested benefit is automatically entitled to a Community Services Card, and is not income tested separately.
If a client is entitled to a card and has a partner, their partner can also get a Community Services Card if they meet the residence criteria and are ordinarily resident in New Zealand.
Partners of clients who get weekly income compensation from Veteran's Affairs will have to apply for a card in their own right.
The partner's income is included in the client's family unit, unless either partner is getting Residential Care Subsidy.

chunks.title: Period of assessment — community services card
chunks.text:
## Period of assessment
Assessment of income should be based on the client's (and any partner's) yearly income at the time of application. However, there is discretion to assess a client's income from another 12-month period other than the expiry and issue date of a card but not more than 2 years before the date of issue.
A different income period may be appropriate where:
- a client does not qualify immediately, but will in the near future
- the client made an error when filling out their application form
- the client's estimated income in the next 12 months is lower than the previous 12 months or
- the client is self employed
If you feel that a different income period should be used, you should discuss the case with your manager client service delivery.
For self-employed clients you should ask to see their most recent set of business accounts if their current income is unavailable.
When deciding a client's income for the purpose of the Community Services Card, you should round down the amount calculated to the nearest whole dollar.

chunks.title: Primary Health Organisations — community services card
chunks.text:
## Primary Health Organisations
When family members are enrolled patients of a health practitioner who belongs to a Primary Health Organisation they do not need a Community Services Card to get reduced fees for health practitioner's consultations and prescription items.
However, they do need a current Community Services Card if they visit a different health practice after hours or on the weekend, or if they go to a health practice when they are out of town.
For example, if a client is visiting family members in another part of the country, and gets sick and needs to go to a health practice, they will be charged a higher fee unless they can produce a current Community Services Card.
For more information see
- Other health services
- Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora Primary health organisations

chunks.title: Public transport (Community Connect) — community services card
chunks.text:
## Public transport (Community Connect)
Community Connect is a transport initiative led by the Ministry of Transport that allows Community Services Card holders to get a 50% discount on public transport fares.
The 50% discount applies to single adult smartcard fares during any time of the day or night. Public transport agencies may apply the discount to other fare types (e.g. monthly pass) or cash fares, at their discretion.
Clients using public transport can use their Community Services Card to confirm their entitlement to the Community Connect 50% discount.
In regions where travel smartcards are used, clients may get a free smartcard when they apply to a public transport provider for the 50% Community Connect discount for the first time.
Clients should contact their local public transport provider for more information about travel smartcards and Community Connect discounted fares.
Public transport agencies that are eligible to take part in the Community Connect initiative are those whose services are contracted under the Public Transport Operating Model and the Metropolitan Rail Operating Model, the Capital Connection Rail Service and Hokianga Ferry Service.

chunks.title: Qualifications — community services card
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for a Community Services Card, a client must:
- be getting an income tested benefit or
- be a child for whom an Orphan's Benefit, an Unsupported Child's Benefit or a Child Disability Allowance is paid or
- receive a Residential Care Subsidy or
- receive a Residential Support Subsidy or
- receive New Zealand Superannuation (including a grandparented non-qualified partner) and meet an income test or
- receive Veteran's Pension (including a grandparented non-qualified partner) or
- receive weekly income compensation (paid by Veterans' Affairs) or
- receive weekly compensation (paid by Veterans' Affairs) or
- receive Accommodation Supplement or
- be a tenant of social housing or
- be a full-time student, generally be ordinarily resident and meet an income test or
- for people with dependent children meet an income test andgenerally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand orbe eligible to get Working for Families Tax Credits (where Inland Revenue applies a Residency test)
- meet an income test and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand or
- be eligible to get Working for Families Tax Credits (where Inland Revenue applies a Residency test)
- for people with no children: meet an income test andgenerally be ordinarily resident andbe aged over 16 years old, but not be a dependent child
- meet an income test and
- generally be ordinarily resident and
- be aged over 16 years old, but not be a dependent child

chunks.title: Reimbursement of medical fees — community services card
chunks.text:
## Reimbursement of medical fees
Clients who have applied for a Community Services Card, High Use Health Card or Pharmaceutical (Prescription) Subsidy Card, can be reimbursed for the extra costs paid for medical practitioner or nurse practitioner consultations and prescriptions before getting their card.
When a Community Services Card is granted it is backdated either 28 days or 3 months. The backdating period is based on whether the client has dependent children.
Because the grant of a Community Services Card is backdated, the client was eligible for a subsidy during that period but they did not have a physical card.
If they made full payment for general practice visits during their entitlement period, the extra charge can be reimbursed.
We do not reimburse claims from clients who have not paid their general practitioner consultation fee or prescription charges.
Note only medical practitioner and nurse practitioner consultation fees and some prescription charges may be reimbursed. All other expenses are not eligible for reimbursement.
For more information see:
- Amount of reimbursement
- Verification.
## Expenses not reimbursed
Only medical practitioner and nurse practitioner consultation fees and prescription charges may be reimbursed. All other expenses are not eligible for reimbursement.
Examples of services that are not reimbursed include:
- ACC related treatment
- counselling services
- dental treatment
- registered nurse consultations
- physiotherapy
- psychiatric services
- glasses
- spectacles
- x-rays and other scans.

chunks.title: Residence — community services card
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get a Community Services Card, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- have a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
Note for a Community Services Card no period of residence is required.
If a client is getting a benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Working for Families Tax Credits, they are automatically considered to meet the residence criteria.
## Clients without citizenship or a residence class visa
People who are in New Zealand unlawfully or here on a temporary entry class visa generally do not qualify for a Community Services Card.
If a client does not have New Zealand citizenship or a residence class visa, they can only get a Community Services Card if they are awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protected person status.

chunks.title: Residents of rest homes and hospitals — community services card
chunks.text:
## Residents of rest homes and hospitals
All residents of rest homes and hospitals who get either a Residential Care Subsidy or an income tested benefit qualify for a Community Services Card automatically.
Rest home residents who are not getting a Residential Care Subsidy or a main benefit must meet the Community Services Card qualifications to receive the card.
When a client applies for a Community Services Card and their partner is in a rest home or hospital and is getting a Residential Care Subsidy, the client is assessed against the single person qualifications. When the partner in the rest home does not qualify for a Residential Care Subsidy, you must consider eligibility for the card as a family unit.

chunks.title: Self-employed clients — community services card
chunks.text:
## Self-employed clients
Self-employed clients are required to submit their latest full set of accounts with their application.
If the business is in the first year of trading and no profit and loss accounts have yet been prepared, the client must provide an estimate of their expected profit or loss for the business in the first year. This estimate can be provided in two ways:
- if the client has already had an estimate completed by an accountant, they should provide a copy of this. Estimates of profit and loss accounts are usually required by financial institutions if an application for a loan is being sought to establish a business
- in the absence of estimates, the client must complete a declaration stating what they expect the profit or loss to be in the next 12 months

chunks.title: Single living alone — community services card
chunks.text:
## Single living alone
A person is considered to be single, living alone if they are living by themselves in one of the following situations:
- a house or a flat which they rent or own
- a hotel or motel
- a caravan park or
- a granny flat which they own and pay the rates for, or pay rent for at the full market rate and where they live independently of the people in the main house
- a boarding house
- a self-contained mobile home
The client must live in one of the above types of accommodation for most of the time and not be in shared accommodation with another adult.
New Zealand Superannuation clients do not have to be getting the single living alone rate to be considered as living alone for Community Services Card assessments.
The current income limit for clients who are single and living alone is:
Single living alone, not entitled to New Zealand Superannuation (as at 1 April 2026)
$37,116 per annum (gross)
Single living alone, entitled to New Zealand Superannuation (as at 1 April 2026)
$39,796 per annum (gross)
## For the income limits for all clients see:
- Deskfile Income cut-out points

chunks.title: Single sharing — community services card
chunks.text:
## Single sharing
A client is single, sharing accommodation if they are living in one of the following situations:
- accommodation with other adults
- private boarding accommodation
- a rest home or hospital
- a granny flat where they share accommodation expenses with the people in the main house or
- a hall of residence.
The current income threshold for single clients sharing accommodation is:
Single sharing, not entitled to New Zealand Superannuation (as at 1 April 2026)
$34,974 per annum
Single sharing, entitled to New Zealand Superannuation (as at 1 April 2026)
$37,372 per annum
## For the income limits for all clients see:
- Deskfile Income cut-out points.

chunks.title: Split or shared care — community services card
chunks.text:
## Split or shared care
Whether a child can receive services depends on whether their primary carer qualifies for a Community Services Card.
A child can receive services if their primary carer has a Community Services Card. It makes no difference whether or not the other family member has a card.
A client would usually be considered as the primary carer if the child is included in the client's benefit. If not, then the primary carer is considered to be the person who is the principal provider of on-going day-to-day care for the child.
## Guidelines for determining who is the primary carer
The parent with greater responsibility is usually the caregiver. If a parent has the child for at least 60% of the time they have the primary responsibility.
Where parents have equal time, to help you decide which parent has greater responsibility, consider the following:
- who pays for the child's material support (furniture, clothes etc)
- who decides about the child's daily activities
- who takes them to and from school and supervises leisure activities
- who makes decisions about their education and health, who pays for which expenses
If it is not clear who has greater responsibility or the parents share the responsibility equally, the parent who was mainly responsible for the day-to-day care of the child before their separation would be considered the primary carer.

chunks.title: Students — community services card
chunks.text:
## Students
A student can qualify for a Community Services Card if they:
- meet the income test
- are ordinarily resident in New Zealand and
- are undertaking a recognised course of study in a full-time course at a tertiary institution that qualifies for a Student Allowance
For more information see:
- Income test
- Residence
Secondary school students cannot get a Community Services Card.
A student may get a Community Services Card automatically if they meet the following criteria:
- Student Allowance status in SAL is either "partially approved" or "approved"
- they are single or they have a dependent partner and
- their client information in SAL and CMS matches
Community Services Cards for students are valid for 12 months. If a student continues their course of study and meets the criteria, their card will automatically be renewed.
## Working partners or getting Student Loan only
Students who have a working partner, or who only get a Student Loan, need to apply for a Community Services Card.
## Income
Students must declare the value of any:
- Student Allowance
- Child Support received
- bursaries/scholarships
- vacation work and
- any other goods or services received, including board and lodgings
## 16 or 17 year olds
16 or 17 year old students can still be included in their parent/caregiver's family unit when deciding eligibility for their card, whether or not the 16 or 17 year old qualifies for a card in their own right.

chunks.title: Unauthorised uses — community services card
chunks.text:
## Unauthorised uses
A cardholder cannot:
- assign, transfer, lend, bail, gift, sell, pledge, or mortgage the card to any person or deal with the card in a manner that allows any person to make an unauthorised use of the card or
- use the card after being asked for its return in writing by MSD
No person can:
- accept any Community Services Card by way of assignment, transfer, loan, bailment, gift, sale, pledge or mortgage
- use another person's Community Services Card or
- use any Community Services Card not issued to that person in any other way
If a client uses their Community Services Card in an unauthorised way, you can ask in writing for the Community Services Card to be returned. The client can also be fined up to $1,000.
## Unauthorised use for health services
No person other than employees of MSD, or a service provider authorised by the Ministry of Health or a Pharmacist demand or request the Community Services Card as identification or to confirm that the client is eligible for the card.
If a client cannot produce their Community Services Card as evidence for MSD, or a service provider authorised by the Ministry of Health, they may be treated as if they are not the holder of a Community Services Card. In these situations, a client may be reimbursed if they are charged for medical fees.
## Unauthorised uses for public transport
No person other than an authorised person collecting public transport fares, issuing public transport tickets or operating or working in a public transport service can request or demand a Community Services Card as evidence to confirm a person is eligible for the card and the 50% discount on public transport fares.
If a person does not provide their Community Services Card to an authorised person when it is requested, the person may be treated as if they are not a holder of the card and may need to pay a full price fare.
Note that the person cannot be reimbursed if they must pay a full price fare.

chunks.title: Verification — community services card
chunks.text:
## Verification
A claim for reimbursement will not be processed unless the following items are received:
- a completed Application for reimbursement of health overcharges form (C04)
- verification of bank account if the client is not receiving a current benefit or New Zealand Superannuation Verification can either be a pre-printed deposit slip or bank statement or the bank can complete the panel on the claim form.
- Verification can either be a pre-printed deposit slip or bank statement or the bank can complete the panel on the claim form.
- original itemised receipts from the general practice or pharmacy including proof that the client has paid full the cost for the consultation or prescription item
All original receipts are returned to the client once the Reimbursement Processing Officer has stamped them. This prevents the same receipts from being sent in more than once.

chunks.title: Assistance provided — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Assistance provided
The SuperGold Card provides easy access to government concessions and discounts for everyday goods and services.
Information about the types of concessions and discounts available to card holders is available on the SuperGold Card website.
Cardholders who do not have access to the internet at home and/or are not able to use this medium can:
- visit a service centre and either use the self-service computer kiosks (at no charge), or ask a staff member to print out their local listings for them or
- call the Seniors Support Centre on 0800 25 45 65 to ask them to print and post out their local listings to them
For more information see:
- SuperGold Card website
- Concessions

chunks.title: Authorised uses — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Authorised uses
A client issued a SuperGold Card may use the card to:
- provide evidence to the Ministry of Social Development that they have been issued with the card and as proof of their client number
- show concession providers that they are entitled to a concession provided to SuperGold Card holders

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client can review any decisions made regarding the SuperGold Card.
For more information on changes and review actions see:
- Death of a client
- Lost, stolen, damaged, destroyed or forgotten cards
- Other Subsidy cards
- Special Card requests
- Core Policy Reviews and Appeals
- Reviews and appeals

chunks.title: Clients excluded from a SuperGold Card — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Clients excluded from a SuperGold Card
The following people cannot get a SuperGold Card:
- a person who is unlawfully present in New Zealand
- a person who is not ordinarily resident in New Zealand
- a person who is lawfully resident or present in New Zealand but only by virtue of: a temporary entry class visa issued under the Immigration Act 2009a temporary permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987 (such as a visitor permit, work permit or a student permit)
- a temporary entry class visa issued under the Immigration Act 2009
- a temporary permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987 (such as a visitor permit, work permit or a student permit)
- the partner of a New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client who is no longer included as a grandparented non-qualified partner

chunks.title: Concessions — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Concessions
The directory is available online.
Cardholders who do not have access to the internet at home and/or are not able to use this medium can:
- visit a service centre and either use the self-service computer kiosks (at no charge), or ask a staff member to print out their local listings for them or
- call the Seniors Support Centre on 0800 25 45 65 to ask them to print and post out their local listings to them
Business owners who are interested in joining the program and want to be listed in the concession directory can call the SuperGold Card business freephone on 0508 65 00 00 or visit the SuperGold Card website.

chunks.title: Death of a client — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Death of a client
When a client receiving a main income tested benefit or pension dies, their SuperGold Card must be cancelled before the death details can be added to the Client Details field in CMS.
This prevents further cards or renewal forms being sent to the deceased or their family.
Contact the Senior Support Centre by phone or email to request cancellation of the card.

chunks.title: Introduction — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The SuperGold Card is a discount and concession card for all New Zealanders aged 65 and over, and those who qualify for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension.
It provides access to government concessions and discounts for everyday goods and services.
The Senior Support Centre is responsible for deciding if a client qualifies for a SuperGold Card.
For more information see:
- Assistance provided
- Qualifications
- Obligations
- Changes and reviews
Clients may also be able to get a Community Services Card, High Use Health Card and/or a Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card from the Ministry of Health.
SuperGold Card holders who also qualify for a Community Services Card can get the Community Connect 50% discount for travel on public transport at peak times.

chunks.title: Lost, stolen, damaged, destroyed or forgotten cards — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Lost, stolen, damaged, destroyed or forgotten cards
If a client's SuperGold Card has been lost, stolen, damaged or destroyed they should contact the Senior Support Centre to request a replacement card.
Where the client has a SuperGold Card with Community Services Card entitlement included, the replacement card will have the same start and expiry dates as the original.
Replacement plastic cards cannot be issued if the current card is due to expire within a month. Instead a card history letter may be issued.
If a client with combined SuperGold Card and Community Services Card entitlement has forgotten or lost their card and cannot be charged the subsidised rate for health services, they may apply to have the difference reimbursed once they receive a replacement card.
For more information see:
- Community Services Card Lost, stolen, damaged, destroyed or forgotten cards
- Community Services Card Reimbursement of medical fees

chunks.title: Main benefit clients — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Main benefit clients
Main benefit clients transferring to New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension, will get their SuperGold Card automatically about 3 weeks after grant date. Clients are encouraged to contact us if they have a question or concerns about not receiving a SuperGold card on the day they turn 65.
As an exception we can generate a manual card before they turn 65. An email should be sent to the Seniors Support Centre to advise that an interim card needs to be sent. These cards are only approved when there is an urgent need.

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation clients — supergold card
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation clients
New Zealand Superannuation clients are issued a SuperGold Card automatically when they are granted New Zealand Superannuation.
Grandparented non-qualified partner
If a grandparented non-qualified partner was included in New Zealand Superannuation, both clients are considered New Zealand Superannuation clients and both were issued a SuperGold Card.
Partner not included in New Zealand Superannuation
If a New Zealand Superannuation client has a partner who is not included in their New Zealand Superannuation, the partner will not be issued a SuperGold Card unless they are eligible in their own right.
Income test
New Zealand Superannuation clients must meet the income test to qualify for a Community Service Card. If they apply and are entitled to a Community Services Card, this information (start date and expiry date) is printed on their SuperGold Card.
Card issued
Note The SuperGold Card is issued at least 15 days after the grant of New Zealand Superannuation is processed.

chunks.title: Obligations — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Obligations
A client must return their SuperGold Card to the Ministry if they are asked in writing.
If a client fails to meet their obligations to the Ministry of Social Development, the client can be fined up to $1000 for misuse of the card.
The Ministry must cancel a SuperGold Card if requested by the client.
If a grandparented non-qualified New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension partner is no longer included in the partner's payments, they must return their SuperGold card. A written request must be made by the Ministry for the card to be returned.

chunks.title: Community Services Card — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Community Services Card
The Community Services Card is used to access health subsidies when the holder needs to visit:
- a health practitioner who is not registered with a Primary Health Organisation (PHO) or
- outside the patients PHO area or
- a health practitioner after hours
Clients who hold a Community Services Card (and their dependants aged 14-17 years old) do not have to pay the $5.00 co-payment on fully subsidised prescriptions from publicly funded health providers.
It can also be used to get the Community Connect 50% discount for travel on public transport.
## High Use Health Card
High users of a health practitioner's services may qualify for a High Use Health Card. To get this card, the person and the health practitioner must apply together to Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora.
This card is valid for the holder only (i.e. not for other family members). The person must have made 12 visits in the past 12 months for 1 or more ongoing conditions. The card will start on the day after the person's 12th visit and expires on the same date in the following year.
## Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card
An individual or family unit pays the co-payment for the first 20 prescription items that are prescribed in any "pharmaceutical year" (defined as 1 February to 31 January).
Note this applies to every new prescription and does not apply to repeat supplies on the same prescription.
After 20 pharmaceutical items have been purchased by an individual or family unit from the same pharmacy, the pharmacist issues a Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card. Once a Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card is issued that individual or family unit will not have to pay the co-payment for the rest of the pharmaceutical year.
There may also be scenarios where a Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card reduces prescription fees instead of removing them completely.
- a part-charge to pay if the cost to manufacture the item is more than the government subsidy
- pharmacy fees that are not subsidised (such as packaging, printing and faxing)
Note the Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card is also known as a Prescription Subsidy Card.

chunks.title: Partners — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Partners
A partner is a spouse, a civil union partner, or a person of the same or opposite sex with whom a client has a de facto relationship.
If a client has a partner, they may also receive a SuperGold Card if they are:
- aged 65 years or older or
- included as a grandparented non-qualified partner for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension and
- generally ordinarily resident in New Zealand

chunks.title: Qualifications — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To get a SuperGold Card, a client must be:
- 65 years old or
- getting New Zealand Superannuation or
- getting Veteran's Pension or
- included as the grandparented non-qualified partner of a client getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
and
- residentially qualified for the card
For more information see:
- Residence
- Partners
- New Zealand Superannuation clients
- Veterans Pension clients
- Main benefit clients
- Clients excluded from a SuperGold Card
- Residents of rest homes and hospitals

chunks.title: Recognised Service — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Recognised Service
Clients who believe they are eligible for a Veteran SuperGold Card, or who have a SuperGold Card and prefer the veteran (poppy card) version, can request this card by contacting the Senior Support Centre.
Please advise clients that when they call the Senior Support Centre, they should have the following information available:
- their SuperGold Card client number (detailed on the back of their SuperGold Card)
- their New Zealand Armed Forces Service Number and the service they served with and
- the service, war, emergency or peace keeping operation(s), they were deployed to
Once this information is verified and confirmed with Veterans' Affairs, a Veteran SuperGold Card will be issued within 3 weeks.

chunks.title: Residence — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get a SuperGold Card, a client must be:
- a New Zealand citizen or
- have a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
Note for a SuperGold Card no period of residence is required.
People who are in New Zealand unlawfully or here on a temporary entry class visa do not qualify for a SuperGold Card.
## Extended travelling holiday
Clients who intend to travel overseas for any length of time, and who are ordinarily resident in New Zealand are still entitled to a SuperGold Card.
These clients have advised New Zealand is where they ordinarily live when they are not travelling.
## Moving overseas
Clients who move overseas to live are not considered ordinarily resident in New Zealand and are not eligible for a SuperGold Card.

chunks.title: Residents of rest homes and hospitals — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Residents of rest homes and hospitals
All residents of rest homes and hospitals aged 65 and over who receive New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran's Pension, Residential Care Subsidy or an income tested benefit qualify for a SuperGold Card automatically.
Rest home and hospital residents who do not receive a current service from the Ministry of Social Development must meet the SuperGold Card qualifications and make an application in order to receive the card.

chunks.title: Reviews and appeals — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Reviews and appeals
If a client does not agree with any decision made, they can ask for the decision to be reviewed if they apply within 3 months from the date the letter detailing the decision was sent.
If the client still does not agree after the review is decided, they can appeal.
Note a review must be completed before the client can take the decision to a Benefit Review Committee.

chunks.title: Special Card requests — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Special Card requests
Special Card requests can be made when a SuperGold Card needs to be issued to a client who is unable to be issued a card using the Ministry of Social Development systems.
Special Card requests can be made for clients in the following situations:
- clients who have a name that is longer than 27 characters or
- clients who would normally have a card history letter issued but have specifically requested a plastic card
Clients who have lost their SuperGold Card should be directed to the Senior Support Centre to arrange for a replacement card to be issued.

chunks.title: Unauthorised uses — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Unauthorised uses
A cardholder cannot:
- assign, transfer, lend, bail, gift, sell, pledge, or mortgage the card to any person or deal with the card in a manner that allows any person to make an unauthorised use of the card or
- use another person's SuperGold Card or
- use the card after being asked for its return in writing by the Ministry of Social Development
No person can:
- accept any SuperGold Card by way of assignment, transfer, loan, bailment, gift, sale, pledge or mortgage
- use any SuperGold Card not issued to that person in any way
If a client uses their SuperGold Card in an unauthorised way, you can ask in writing for the SuperGold Card to be returned. The client can also be fined up to $1,000.

chunks.title: Veteran's Pension clients — supergold card
chunks.text:
## Veteran's Pension clients
The Veteran SuperGold Card is a specially branded (poppy card) version of the SuperGold Card. It is available for those who have served in the New Zealand Armed Forces in a recognised service including war, emergency or peace keeping operation(s).
Recognised service is verified by Veterans' Affairs.
People with recognised service who get Veteran's Pension are issued a Veteran SuperGold Card automatically.
Where both client and partner are entitled to a Veteran's Pension in their own right, they will both be issued with a Veterans SuperGold Card.
Grandparented non-qualified partner
If a grandparented non-qualified partner was included in the Veteran's Pension, both clients are considered New Zealand Veteran's Pension clients and both were issued cards. The veteran with recognised service was issued a Veteran branded SuperGold Card. Their partner received an ordinary SuperGold Card.
Partner not included in Veteran's Pension
If a Veteran's Pension client has a partner who was not included in their pension, the partner will not be issued a SuperGold Card unless they are eligible in their own right.
For more information see:
- Veterans Pension Recognised Service
- Community Services Card

chunks.title: 12-month period
chunks.text:
## 12-month period
The 12-month period makes sure a client's rent cannot be increased within 12 months of the day after the:
- day the rent last increased or
- day the tenancy started
Any rent increase will be effective from the day after the 12-month period is up and only applies when the 60-day notice period is being used (that is, when the change is not related to a change in household circumstances).
There are some situations where rent can be increased inside the 12-month period, these must be by agreement or under application by the landlord who get a Tribunal order such as when the:
- landlord has made significant improvements to a property (including improvements to facilities or services)
- landlord incurred unforeseen expenses in relation to the property or
- tenancy agreement has been varied and benefits the tenant

chunks.title: 14-day notice period
chunks.text:
## 14-day notice period
Housing providers must give tenants at least 14 calendar days' notice of any increase in their rate of Income Related Rent due to a change in their circumstances. This is to ensure that the tenant has time to adjust their circumstances to pay the higher rate of rent.
The 14-day notice must be given before the effective date. It could be within the 61-day period, or in addition to it, depending on when the change of circumstance was notified or discovered.
The 14-day notice period starts from the date the notice is deemed to have been given to the tenant. In other words, it is in addition to the service period that applies (the length of the service period depends on the method of delivery).
The 14-day notice period is counted in calendar days.
Example
On 16 March 2022, the Ministry reviews the rate of a client’s Income Related Rent and needs to let them know their rate is changing.
The service period will run from 17 March 2022 to 22 March 2022 (5 days).
The 14-day notice period takes place after the service period has finished so will occur from 23 March to 6 April 2022.

chunks.title: 26-week period
chunks.text:
## 26-week period
A 26-week period, in relation to a Special Needs Grant, means the 26 weeks immediately preceding the date of application for the Grant.

chunks.title: 31 days or more
chunks.text:
## 31 days or more
When calculating the number of days that a client has been in prison or held on remand, you should include the date the client:
- enters prison or held on remand and
- leaves prison or is released from remand

chunks.title: Employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Employment and work readiness assistance
A 52-week period means a period of 52 weeks commencing on the date on which a payment of employment and work readiness assistance is made to or in respect of a client.
## Special Needs Grant
A 52-week period, in relation to a Special Needs Grant, means the 52 weeks immediately preceding the date of application for the Grant.

chunks.title: 60-day notice period
chunks.text:
## 60-day notice period
The 60-day notice period ensures that a client gets at least 60 days' notice of an increase in their rent. The 60-day notice period will apply to all increases of rent where the 61-day period is not applicable.
This happens:
- following the annual review of the rate of Income Related Rent where the rate has been increased due to the annual general adjustment to the rates of the Ministry of Social Development financial assistance
- when an applicable person has not completed an annual review form or provided sufficient information to process an annual review
- when a client has had a change in circumstances, but has not provided sufficient information to process the review within 10 working days of the information being requested
- when the tenant is paying rent at the market rent rate and the housing provider increases the rate of market rent
This includes when the client does not provide sufficient information to the Ministry of Social Development to calculate or review the rate of Income Related Rent and generally their rent is to be increased to market rent.
Where the 60-day notice period applies, the 12-month period also applies. The 12-month period makes sure a client's rent cannot be increased within 12 months of the day after:
- the day the rent last increased or
- the day the tenancy started
The 60-day notice period means the rent will not be increased until at least 60 days after the date the notice is deemed to have been given to the client.
Note in some situations, the 60-day notice period (and service period) can be within the 12-month period.
The 60-day notice period is counted in calendar days.
Example
On 14 January 2021, the Ministry reviews the rate of a client's Income Related Rent and needs to let them know their rate is changing.
The service period will run from 15 January 2021 - 20 January 2021 (5 days).
The 60-day notice period takes place after the service period has finished so will occur from 21 January 2021 - 22 March 2022.

chunks.title: 61 day period
chunks.text:
## 61 day period
The 61-day period ensures, when a tenant has a change of circumstance, any increase in their Income Related Rent cannot take effect until at least 61 days after the date that the change in circumstances occurred (regardless of when the change of circumstance was notified or discovered). The 61-day period is counted from the day after the day that the change of circumstances occurred, and the 14-day notice period is being used.
While housing providers are responsible for the 61-day period, MSD must take into account when calculating debt in situations of late notification/discovery of a tenant's change in circumstances, and it is also relevant to MSD's calculation of Income Related Rent subsidy payable to housing providers.
The 61-day period is counted in calendar days.
Example
A client had a change of circumstances on 22 February 2024, so MSD reviews their Income Related Rent.
As this means an increase to their rate, the client must be given 61 days' notice. This will run from 22 February 2024 to 22 April 2024.

chunks.title: academic year
chunks.text:
## academic year
To determine eligibility for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, tertiary study, Student Allowance and Student Loan, “academic year” means:
- the study year of the full time course forming part of a recognised programme that the student is enrolled in
Note this does not need to align with the calendar year.
For example, a 1-year course starts in July and finishes in May the following year. The academic year is July to May.

chunks.title: accommodation costs
chunks.text:
## accommodation costs
Regular and repeated costs that the client must pay for their accommodation. This can include any costs paid as a lump sum that are intended to act as regular and repeated costs for accommodation.
For clients in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to, service costs can be included when they cannot be separated from the rest of the payment.
For clients in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to, accommodation costs means rent.

chunks.title: Accommodation deduction
chunks.text:
## Accommodation deduction
For the purposes of calculating accommodation costs for Temporary Additional Support, an amount of $34.13 (as at 1 April 2026) is deducted from the total amount of weekly allowable accommodation costs.
Example a client who has allowable accommodation costs of $250 per week will have $215.87 per week (as at 1 April 2026) included in their assessment for Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: accommodation income
chunks.text:
## accommodation income
Accommodation income is rent, board or additional occupant contribution payments a client gets from someone living in the same premises.
