Accommodation income is deducted from a client's accommodation costs when calculating a client's weekly qualifying accommodation cost.
Accommodation income includes:
- rent a client gets from another person (not being additional occupants or boarders) residing in the same premises, except where the person paying the rent is in a self-contained part of the premises or the rent payment is part of the income of a business on the premises
- 62% of payments for board a client gets from another person residing in the same premises, except where the board payment is part of the income of a business on the premises
- 62% of contributions a client gets from an additional occupant residing in the same premises.
Note when accommodation income is more than the client's accommodation costs (after the deduction of the cost of any part of the property not being lived in by the client), the excess amount is income and must be charged against any financial assistance the client gets. In this case, the client will have no weekly qualifying accommodation costs.
For more information see:
- Rent and board payments
- Weekly qualifying accommodation costs

chunks.title: accommodation supplier
chunks.text:
## accommodation supplier
A person who provides accommodation to a client. An accommodation supplier can include:
- a landlord as defined in the Residential Tenancies Act 1986
- a person, organisation or company that provides accommodation
- the agent of the accommodation supplier
- a head tenant of the property that the client is staying in as a subletter

chunks.title: accommodation
chunks.text:
## accommodation
Accommodation for Housing Support Products means the premises that a client occupies or intends to occupy as a home for the purpose of accommodation.
A premises is considered accommodation regardless of whether or not the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies, but does not include the following:
- premises owned in part or fully by the applicant or their spouse or partner
- tents, including tents adjoined to vehicles
- homeless shelters
- prisons and correctional facilities
- premises used to provide emergency or transitional accommodation for which— an Emergency Housing Grant has been made to the applicant or their spouse or partner; orany other payment has been made by a government department for the provision of emergency or transitional accommodation to people in need of housing
- an Emergency Housing Grant has been made to the applicant or their spouse or partner; or
- any other payment has been made by a government department for the provision of emergency or transitional accommodation to people in need of housing

chunks.title: Active Tenancy Costs Cover
chunks.text:
## Active Tenancy Costs Cover
Active Tenancy Costs Cover means a Tenancy Costs Cover that has been conditionally granted to a client or their partner (if any) and not yet paid but could still be paid because all the conditions for that Tenancy Costs Cover could still be met.
Tenancy costs cover: Eligibility clause 33 Housing Support Programme

chunks.title: activity
chunks.text:
## activity
Activity for Childcare Assistance includes:
- paid employment (including full-time, part-time, temporary or casual)
- an approved rehabilitation programme (Childcare Subsidy only)
- an employment-related training course offered by a course provider accredited by the New Zealand Qualifications Authority
- any other employment-related training course approved by MSD (Childcare Subsidy only)
- a course of study at a secondary school or tertiary educational institute
- suitable activities under section 146 or section 324 of the Social Security Act 2018

chunks.title: addiction medicine specialist
chunks.text:
## addiction medicine specialist
An addiction medicine specialist is a medical practitioner who focuses on the evaluation and treatment of individuals with alcohol, drug or other substance-related disorders and of individuals with the dual diagnosis of substance related and other psychiatric disorders.

chunks.title: Afghan evacuee
chunks.text:
## Afghan evacuee
A person evacuated to New Zealand from Afghanistan due to the deteriorating political and security situation after the withdrawal of international forces in 2021, who either:
- holds or has applied for an Afghan emergency resettlement visa (a residence class visa issued under the Immigration Act 2009) or
- holds another residence class visa issued under the Immigration Act 2009, or is a New Zealand citizen and
- would have been eligible for an Afghan emergency resettlement visa if they did not already hold a residence class visa, or were not a New Zealand citizen

chunks.title: Afghan interpreter
chunks.text:
## Afghan interpreter
A person who worked with the New Zealand Defence Force, the New Zealand Police or the New Zealand Special Air Service in Afghanistan and has been granted a residence class visa by the Minister of Immigration as an exception to residence instructions under section 72(3) of the Immigration Act 2009.

chunks.title: all benefit types
chunks.text:
## all benefit types
The severe disablement exemption applies to:
- all main benefits including New Zealand Superannuation, Veterans Pension, Unsupported Childs Benefit and Orphans Benefit
- Employment Transition Payment
- Accommodation Supplement
- Childcare assistance
- Disability Allowance
- Special Benefit and
- Temporary Additional Support
For Unsupported Childs Benefit and Orphans Benefit, the income must be received by the child from their own personal effort, not the caregiver.

chunks.title: all tertiary study
chunks.text:
## all tertiary study
The EFTS for all courses that are approved for Student Loans are counted regardless of whether or not the student was able to access a Student Loan for their course.

chunks.title: allergist or immunologist
chunks.text:
## allergist or immunologist
An allergist/immunologist is a medical specialist with expertise in the evaluation, physical and laboratory diagnosis, and management of disorders potentially involving the immune system.
Selected examples of such conditions include asthma, anaphylaxis, eczema and adverse reactions to drugs, foods, and insect stings as well as immune deficiency diseases (both acquired and congenital).

chunks.title: Alternative housing (Housing Support Products)
chunks.text:
## Alternative housing (Housing Support Products)
Alternative housing for Housing Support Products is a residential premises in New Zealand an applicant occupies, or occupied or intends to occupy as a tenant under a tenancy agreement (excluding social housing).

chunks.title: alternative housing
chunks.text:
## alternative housing
Alternative housing means housing located in New Zealand other than social housing and includes:
- private rentals
- owner-occupier housing
- housing offered by non-government organisations (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes)
- local government housing
- boarding
- flatting (not on a tenancy agreement)

chunks.title: annual benefits
chunks.text:
## annual benefits
For the purposes of determining renewal codes, annual benefits are:
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Orphans and Unsupported Child's Benefit

chunks.title: annuity
chunks.text:
## annuity
An annual payment that is made to a person for life or for a fixed number of years.

chunks.title: AOD practitioner
chunks.text:
## AOD practitioner
AOD practitioners are alcohol and other drug practitioners who are Registered Practitioners and members of DAPAANZ.
They complete assessments to help determine drug dependency.
Note there are AOD counsellors who are not registered AOD practitioners. AOD counsellors do not complete dependency assessments.

chunks.title: applicable people
chunks.text:
## applicable people
Applicable people are:
- persons applying for social housing with the intention of being signatories to the tenancy agreement or
- persons in social housing and on the tenancy agreement
and
- any partner of those persons, regardless of whether they are a signatory to the tenancy agreement for social housing

chunks.title: applicable person
chunks.text:
## applicable person
An applicable person is:
- a person applying for social housing with the intention of being a signatory to the tenancy agreement or
- a person in social housing and on the tenancy agreement
and
- any partner of that person, regardless of whether they are a signatory to the tenancy agreement for social housing

chunks.title: Assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early
chunks.text:
## Assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early
If a landlord incurs actual and reasonable costs from assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early, they can recover the costs from the tenant.
- Assignment is when an existing tenant is replaced by a new tenant and that person takes over all the old tenant's responsibilities.
- Subletting is usually where the existing tenant moves out of the premises they are renting, and then rents it to a new tenant. The new tenant generally signs a tenancy agreement with the existing tenant. The existing tenant then becomes the new tenant's landlord. In some cases, only a part of the premises is sublet and the new tenant has exclusive rights to that part (ie they will not share the facilities, like flatmates do).
- Ending a tenancy early can occur when both the landlord and the tenant agree to end a tenancy before the expiry, or for a periodic tenancy before the end of the appropriate notice period.

chunks.title: Automated
chunks.text:
## Automated
The use of systems or components of systems to replace repeatable processes to reduce dependency on manual actions or interventions.

chunks.title: Average Wage Growth
chunks.text:
## Average Wage Growth
Average wage growth is the increase of full time equivalent net Average Ordinary Time Weekly Wage between each financial year.
This is calculated by Statistics New Zealand by deducting tax and ACC levies from the full time equivalent of gross Average Ordinary Time Weekly Wage.

chunks.title: B2B
chunks.text:
## B2B
B2B is the exchange of services or information directly between businesses, rather than between businesses and customers.
B2B technology supports the efficient exchange of information to or from the Ministry of Social Development and another agency or provider.

chunks.title: barriers
chunks.text:
## barriers
Barriers are any:
- features of the clients individual circumstances (for example - parenting responsibilities) that may affect their ability to earn a sufficient livelihood
- specific constraints arising from those circumstances or responsibilities that your client may have in obtaining and sustaining employment
- lack of skills and experience (including unpaid work) that are relevant to facilitating the most effective path to enable them to obtain sustainable employment and
- practical assistance that they require to enable them to support themselves (and any dependent family) through employment

chunks.title: benefit
chunks.text:
## benefit
A 'benefit' as defined in schedule 2 of the Social Security Act 2018 includes the following main benefits and extra help:
- Emergency Benefit
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance
- Jobseeker Support
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment (caring for a person)
- Supported Living Payment (restricted work capacity due to health condition, injury, disability or total blindness)
- Orphan's Benefit
- Unsupported Child's Benefit
- Youth Payment
- Young Parent Payment
- New Zealand Superannuation
- Veteran's Pension
- Accommodation Supplement
- Childcare Assistance (including Childcare Subsidy and OSCAR Subsidy)
- Child Disability Allowance
- Disability Allowance
- Special Disability Allowance
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit
- Winter Energy Payment

chunks.title: biosecurity event
chunks.text:
## biosecurity event
A biosecurity event is the arrival of an organism (pest or disease) within New Zealand, after it is has crossed the border.

chunks.title: Board
chunks.text:
## Board
Board is an arrangement where a person pays a set amount that includes the cost of residing at the premises along with food and may include other costs such as power, water, and internet.
When a person pays board, 62% of their total payment is considered to be their allowable accommodation cost.
A person is considered to be a boarder when they are:
- making payments for their accommodation and food for residing at the premises and
- the accommodation cost can't be separately identified as part of the amount they pay
or
- living in a commercial boarding house and the amount they pay for residing at the premises includes accommodation and food costs
## Additional occupant living in a social housing property
Additional occupants may pay a contribution towards accommodation costs while living in the social housing property.
The contribution amount may include food and sometimes other costs. Whether it includes food (and/or other costs ) or not, only 62% of the contribution can be considered as their allowable accommodation cost. This means they are treated the same as a boarder.

chunks.title: boarding house
chunks.text:
## boarding house
A boarding house is a residential premises containing 1 or more boarding rooms along with facilities for communal use by the tenants of the boarding house; and occupied, or intended by the landlord to be occupied, by at least 6 tenants at any one time.
Facilities means the facilities provided by the landlord of a boarding house for the shared use by tenants of the boarding house, such as:
- toilet and bathroom facilities
- cooking facilities
- general living, dining or recreational areas
- laundry facilities
- lifts and stairways
- rubbish storage and rubbish disposal facilities
- appliances for heating or cooling premises
- communication facilities
- lawns, gardens and outhouses
- any land or buildings intended for use for storage space or for the parking of motor vehicles

chunks.title: broken rent
chunks.text:
## broken rent
The rent paid between the start date of the tenancy and the first rent charge date (where the start date and the rent charge date are not aligned), worked out as a daily portion of the weekly rent. For example if a client moves in on a Monday, but their rent charge date is not until Friday. They would have to pay four days rent.
Normally the broken rent is paid as part of the Rent in Advance.

chunks.title: business day
chunks.text:
## business day
A day of the week other than:
- a Saturday, a Sunday, Waitangi Day, Good Friday, Easter Monday, Anzac Day, the Sovereign's birthday, Te Rā Aro o Matariki/Matariki Observance Day, and Labour Day and
- if Waitangi Day or Anzac Day falls on a Saturday or a Sunday, the following Monday and
- Christmas Day, Boxing Day, New Years Day, 2 January and
- if Christmas Day or 1 January falls on a Friday, the following Monday and
- if Christmas Day or 1 January falls on a Saturday or a Sunday, the following Monday and Tuesday

chunks.title: business
chunks.text:
## business
Generally a person is in business when they:
- start charging others for the goods/services that they provide
- supply goods/services on a regular basis
- intend to make a profit from doing so
To decide whether a person is in business Inland Revenue will take into consideration:
- the nature of the activity
- how much time, money, and effort is put into the activity
- how long has the person been doing the activity and the future plans for the activity
- how much is made from the activity
- whether the activity is run in a similar way to most businesses in the same trade
- if the person intends to make a profit

chunks.title: Canadian creditable periods
chunks.text:
## Canadian creditable periods
'Canadian creditable period' means a period of residence or contributions which can be used to acquire the right to a benefit under the legislation of Canada, and includes a period during which a disability pension is payable under the Canada Pension Plan.
Note that Canadian creditable periods accumulated under the Old Age Security Act which coincide with creditable periods accumulated under the Canadian Pension Plan shall only be taken into account once.

chunks.title: capital account
chunks.text:
## capital account
The capital account is a component of financial statements. This account contains the capital invested in assets by the owners of a business (for example, real estate, machinery, savings), but excludes current or operating expenses.
A capital account should be distinguished from a revenue account. Payments received on a revenue account are income and generally taxable. For example, in cases when the shares are held in the revenue account and the shares have a market value that is higher than the market value on the date received, they will be taxed on the difference between these two values and this amount would be parental income.
The use of a capital account ensures that where a parent uses income to purchase an asset, when this asset is sold, the original purchase amount is not counted as income.

A carer is a person who is the principal provider of ongoing daily care for a child, or someone who shares the ongoing care of a child substantially equally with another person (for at least 40% of the time).

chunks.title: child tax credit
chunks.text:
## child tax credit
Child tax credit is a payment that was made by Inland Revenue once a family's income went below a certain amount. Clients receiving a benefit or Student Allowance from Work and Income couldn't receive the child tax credit.
The in-work tax credit (formerly in-work payment) replaced the child tax credit from 1 April 2006. Clients who were receiving this payment prior to 1 April 2006 can continue to receive payments of the child tax credit until they become ineligible.
This amount paid is dependent on the family's total earnings and the number of children.
Contact Inland Revenue for more information.

A child is a single person under the age of 18 years, other than a person who is:

In some cases, a child may also include a person who is 18 years old for a limited period, if they are:

chunks.text:
## chiropractor
A chiropractor is a health practitioner who registered with the New Zealand Chiropractic Board and specialises in detecting and correcting by manual or mechanical means structural imbalance, distortion or subluxations in the human body for the purpose of removing nerve interference.
They use joint adjustments to correct structural or mechanical imbalances.

chunks.title: cliff face threshold
chunks.text:
## cliff face threshold
A 'cliff face' threshold means that if a student's gross income per week is more than the personal income threshold, there is no entitlement to Student Allowance.
This differs from an 'abatement threshold', where entitlement to Student Allowance is reduced by a certain percentage when a student's gross income per week is more than the personal income threshold.

## closely-held company

or
If market value circumstances exists for the company, there are 5 or fewer people whose market value interests in the company is more than 50%.

chunks.text:

This is effective from 1 January 2020.

chunks.title: compelled
chunks.text:
## compelled
It is not possible to detail the circumstances under which this may occur. However, there must be very strong and compelling reasons why the client is unable to return to their country of origin.
Lack of funds should not be regarded as a reason for not being able to return. When the client originally arrived in New Zealand, a condition of entry would have required a return air ticket to their country of origin.

Compensation payments do not include payments made because of:
- an employment relationship or
- a contract to provide goods or services

chunks.title: complying superannuation fund
chunks.text:
## complying superannuation fund
A complying superannuation fund is a superannuation scheme that has membership criteria similar to KiwiSaver, such as the savings being locked in until the age of eligibility for New Zealand Superannuation.
A complying superannuation fund distribution is generally distributed as a lump sum payment. Alternatively, the payments may be returned as an annuity (a regular ongoing payment).
For more information see:
- Inland Revenue KiwiSaver

chunks.title: concurrent
chunks.text:
## concurrent
Concurrent study occurs when a student undertakes study at two education providers that will be credited towards a qualification at one of the education providers.
A programme of study that involves concurrent enrolment must have approval by the Tertiary Education Commission to be treated as a single programme for Student Allowance purposes. This approval verifies that:
- the student has approval to complete papers at two separate education providers simultaneously
- the papers (from both education providers) will be credited towards one recognised programme
One education provider is responsible for ensuring that the concurrent programme is approved by the Tertiary Education Commission.
Both education providers submit a VoS response with the same PC Code and appropriate EFTS value for the course.

chunks.title: conjoint
chunks.text:
## conjoint
Conjoint study occurs where a student undertakes two qualifications at the same time.
This can include situations where two qualifications are combined under one programme code.
The following examples describe conjoint study programmes:
- where there are special concessions (such as exemptions or cross credits) included in programme regulations that permit a student to pursue two qualifications at the same time and qualify for both by passing fewer than the number of units or subjects required when the programmes are taken individually.
- where study programmes are combined, such as BA and LLB, with a special relationship or relevance to each other
The education provider must submit a VoS with a unique code which signifies that the study being undertaken is conjoint study. SAL will then treat the study as being combined under one programme for Student Allowance purposes.

chunks.text:
## Continuous entry

For more information see:

chunks.title: Contracted emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Contracted emergency housing
Contracted emergency housing is an emergency housing pilot currently operating in Rotorua.
Contracted emergency housing is funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development and provides temporary accommodation in specific motels for people with an emergency housing need.
Contracted emergency housing is managed by accommodation providers and support service providers contracted by or on behalf of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development.
## Accommodation providers
The accommodation provider's role is to manage the operation of the accommodation.
## Support service providers
The support service provider’s role is to help facilitate the relationships between the accommodation provider, the client, and the Ministry of Social Development, as well as provide wrap around services to support the client into sustainable housing.
## Residential Tenancies Act 1986
The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to contracted emergency housing as it is used to provide emergency accommodation and is funded by a government department (the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development).

The date a client first contacts us to request financial assistance is their date of first contact. A client may contact the Ministry of Social Development at any time, through various methods e.g. at reception in a service centre, via telephone through one of the contact centres, or in writing.

chunks.text:
## dependent child
A dependent child is a child who is:

- financially dependent on that client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child does not include a:

## Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit being paid for the child

## Child turns 18
When a child turns 18, they may be considered a dependent child for a limited period, if they are a child who is:
- continuing in education and
- not financially independent

chunks.title: dependent children
chunks.text:
## dependent children
A dependent child is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- maintained as a member of that family

- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care

In relation to an applicant, means a spouse, civil union or de facto partner who is not entitled to a working-age benefit in their own right and whose weekly income, when combined with the weekly income of the applicant, is not more than the combined weekly income amount in clause 1(1) of Schedule 2 of the Student Allowances Regulations 1998.

## dermatologist
A dermatologist is a medical practitioner who has expertise in the diagnosis and treatment of skin cancers, melanomas, moles and other tumours of the skin, contact dermatitis, and other allergic and non allergic disorders, and in the recognition of the skin manifestations of systemic and infectious diseases.

chunks.title: digital signature
chunks.text:
## digital signature
A digital signature is a secure form of electronic signature which is produced using identity verification embedded into the document or form with encryption.
It is the most secure form of electronic signature.

chunks.title: Disability Allowance costs
chunks.text:
## Disability Allowance costs
For the purposes of Temporary Additional Support, Disability Allowance costs are any health and disability costs that could be included in a Disability Allowance.
However, these costs do not include any counselling or transport costs to attend counselling sessions that are in excess of the Disability Allowance paid, if any.

chunks.title: Discretion
chunks.text:
## Discretion
Discretion is often expressed in law by the use of the word "may" as opposed to the use of "shall" or "must".
Exercising discretion involves the use of reason and judgement to make a decision within a "range" of decisions that are potentially available to the decision maker.
The extent of the discretion available to the decision maker depends on the particular provision.
Discretion involves:
- a good knowledge and understanding of the authority for the discretion (e.g. the particular provision within the Student Allowances Regulations), including; the purpose and intent of the authority, the actual wording of the provision and how that wording limits the extent of the discretion available to the decision maker
- identification of what information is needed, and why, including what information or advice is relevant, in order to exercise the discretion
- examination of the relevant information and then weighing up the importance, relevance and validity of that information in order to make a decision
- not taking into account any irrelevant considerations
Discretion involves exercising good judgement based on experience to ensure any decisions are lawful, right and consistent with the purpose and intent of the programme or schedule.
It is important to document any exercise of discretion in a way that enables the decision-making process (and the information used) to be clear, transparent and reviewable.

chunks.title: discretionary benefit
chunks.text:
## discretionary benefit
For the purposes of the review of circumstances when a child turns 18 or an 18-year-old child is no longer considered a dependent child and is excluded from a parent or caregiver's benefit, the following are discretionary benefits:
- Emergency Benefit
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance
- Jobseeker Support Hardship
- Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
- Special Benefit
- Community Costs
Parents and caregivers must respond to the notice and complete the review of circumstances when a dependent child turns 18 or their discretionary benefit will suspend.

chunks.title: disqualifying rate
chunks.text:
## disqualifying rate
When the level of income the client receives is high enough (when charged against the benefit) to reduce the benefit to a nil rate of payment.

chunks.title: drug test provider
chunks.text:
## drug test provider
The term drug test provider includes drug testing companies, and accredited laboratories.

chunks.title: Early Leaving Exemption
chunks.text:
## Early Leaving Exemption
Parents may apply for permission for a student to leave school at the age of 15. The application must be based on the student's educational problems or conduct, or the estimated benefit of their staying at school. Students granted Early Leaving Exemptions take up training courses, or enter polytechnic, university, or full-time employment.

chunks.title: EFTS
chunks.text:
## EFTS
Equivalent Full-time Student.
The EFTS value is a measure of the amount of study or workload involved in undertaking a course.
The Tertiary Education Commission confirms the EFTS value of each course as part of approving access to government funding.

chunks.title: electronic signature
chunks.text:
## electronic signature
An electronic signatutre is an electronic means of identifying someone.
It is also known as an 'e-signature'.
There are many different forms of electronic signature, including:
- a scanned image of a signature
- a signature signed using a stylus andagreeing to the terms and conditions of a contract by ticking a box on an online form (which specifically states that by ticking the box you agree to be bound by all the relevant terms) or
- a digital signature

chunks.title: emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing security deposit
chunks.text:
## emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing security deposit
The emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing security deposit means, any sum of money required by the supplier of emergency accommodation funded by the Emergency Housing Grant, or the provider of transitional or contracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, as security against any loss arising from:
- damage or
- a failure by the applicant to observe and perform the applicant's obligations under the agreement for the provision of the emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing

chunks.title: Employer
chunks.text:
## Employer
An employer is a person or business registered with the Inland Revenue Department who employs an employee or engages with a self-employed contractor.

chunks.title: employment agreement
chunks.text:
## employment agreement
A signed agreement between an employer and employee outlining the terms and conditions of employment for both parties.

chunks.title: employment workshops
chunks.text:
## employment workshops
A group based activity designed to help job seekers with their job searching in a supported and structured environment.
Job Seekers are required to attend the workshops once a week for a one hour period. A trained facilitator talks to modular based topics, such as CV preparation, and then helps the group with self-directed job search activities.

chunks.title: employment
chunks.text:
## employment
For family tax credit income from employment is defined by Inland Revenue under the Income Tax 2007 and includes income from (but not fully listed):
- benefits and pensions
- salary or wages
- self employment
- ACC
- employment related earnings including bonus, commission, extra salary, gratuity, overtime pay or other remuneration
- basic grants and independent circumstances grants
- periodic payments of a pension, retiring allowance, superannuation or other allowance or annuity
- parental leave payments

chunks.title: enquiries
chunks.text:
## enquiries
Inland Revenue has a dedicated phone line for Work and Income staff to enquire about Working for Families Tax Credits. The number is 0800 473 383.
This phone number is only available for Work and Income staff, and must not be given to clients.

chunks.title: error
chunks.text:
## error
Error is defined in regulation 208 of the Social Security Regulations 2018, as:
- the provision of incorrect information by MSD
- any erroneous act or omission by MSD that occurs when inquiring into a claim for a benefit under section 298 of the Social Security Act 2018
- any other erroneous act or omission by MSD
but
does not include the simple act of making a payment to which the recipient is not entitled if that act is not caused, wholly or partly, by any erroneous act or omission by MSD.

chunks.title: Student and parent estranged
chunks.text:
## Student and parent estranged
The relationship has broken down. There is no support, trust or mutual respect between the student and their parent.
## Couple estranged
No longer living with and no longer having a relationship of mutual love and affection for a spouse or partner.

chunks.title: ex gratia
chunks.text:
## ex gratia
Ex gratia payments are made:
- in recognition of harm experienced by the client and
- without legal obligation or acceptance of liability

chunks.title: Expected date of the next in-cycle payment
chunks.text:
## Expected date of the next in-cycle payment
The date when MSD expects the client to get their next in-cycle payment of Child Support.
The expected date of the next in-cycle payment is 3 business days after the 19th of the following month.

chunks.title: extended care services
chunks.text:
## extended care services
Extended care is the level of care provided for the care and attention of a child or young person where the extent of their disability is such that suitable care can be provided only by an approved organisation or body. In some cases, the extended care arrangement may be an approved foster care placement.
This kind of care is facilitated by Oranga Tamariki through a Family Group Conference under section 141 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989.

chunks.title: extramural student
chunks.text:
## extramural student
Extramural students are students who are not completing their studies onsite at an education provider e.g. they are using correspondence school or distance learning.
For these students the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit is based on their residential address.
Example
Mahesh lives in Timaru and studies by distance at Canterbury University. Mahesh gets the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit based on his Timaru address (not the education provider's address).

chunks.title: faith-based institutions
chunks.text:
## faith-based institutions
A faith-based institution means an organisation whose purpose or activity is connected to any religious or spiritual belief system, regardless of whether the organisation relates to a particular faith, religion or denomination. This could include organisations such as:
- The Catholic Church of New Zealand
- Empower Ministries
- Nazareth House Care Facility
- The Salvation Army

chunks.title: Family Assistance
chunks.text:
## Family Assistance
Family Assistance was financial help that Inland Revenue paid to qualifying families with dependent children.
Working for Families Tax Credits replaced Family Assistance from 1 April 2007.
Contact Inland Revenue for more information.

chunks.title: Family member (affected person)
chunks.text:
## Family member (affected person)
Family member (affected person) includes:
- partner
- child
- grandchild
- parent
- grandparent
- sibling
- aunt
- uncle
- niece
- nephew
- first cousin (i.e. a child of an aunt or uncle)
- parent-in-law
- sibling-in-law
- child-in-law
- step-child
- step-parent or
- step-sibling
either through birth, marriage or adoption.

chunks.title: family tax credit threshold
chunks.text:
## family tax credit threshold
For the current (and some previous) family tax credit thresholds, see:
- Inland Revenue Can I get Working for Families?
For thresholds for other periods, contact Inland Revenue.

chunks.title: family
chunks.text:
## family
For the purposes of Temporary Additional Support, a family includes the client, their spouse or partner, and any dependent children of the client or the client's spouse or partner.

chunks.title: financial assistance
chunks.text:
## financial assistance
Accommodation Supplement - the amount that the client would be entitled to, based on the market rent for properties in the area where the client needs to live
Temporary Additional Support - the amount that the client may be entitled to, based on their income and assets, and the actual costs of the alternative housing.

chunks.title: financially interdependent
chunks.text:
## financially interdependent
Physical evidence of joint finances sufficient to indicate that a couple is financially interdependent could include:
- joint hire purchases
- joint loans or credit
- joint bank accounts
- jointly owned properties
- do both partners contribute to the household expenses

chunks.title: formal notification
chunks.text:
## formal notification
Formal notification is:
- a letter
- an action in SWIFTT to grant, decline or review the rate of payment
- a written decision on the benefit application form or
- a written decision on social housing assessment or the outcome of an Income Related Rent calculation or review

chunks.title: Formula assessment
chunks.text:
## Formula assessment
Child Support where Inland Revenue works out who pays and how much. Inland Revenue collects the money from the liable parent and pays it to the receiving carer.

chunks.title: foster child
chunks.text:
## foster child
For the purposes of exemptions from work or work preparation obligations for:
- home schooling
- caring for a child under 5 who is not their dependent child and
- caring for a child with special needs
a foster child means a child placed in a person's charge under section 362 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989.

chunks.title: fringe benefits
chunks.text:
## fringe benefits
The fringe benefit must be attributed to the parent under section RD 47 of the Income Tax Act 2007.

chunks.title: full-time employment
chunks.text:
## full-time employment
Full-time employment is paid employment for 30 hours or more each week. This includes temporary or casual employment during any week that a person works for 30 hours or more.

chunks.title: full-time student
chunks.text:
## full-time student
A person enrolled:
- in a full time course or
- was enrolled in the semester or academic year just ended and
- who is or intends to be enrolled in a full time course in the next academic year

chunks.title: funeral costs
chunks.text:
## funeral costs
For the interest and/or dividends to be exempt from the parental income test under funeral costs, the sole purpose of the funds must be for:
- employees of an employer or
- partner's or dependents of employees of the employer and
- the employer must have at least 10 employees and
- all people eligible for benefits from the fund are eligible equally for all benefits from the fund and
- no contributions are made to the fund by persons that are not the employer or an employee of an employer and
- the fund must be approved by the Commissioner of Inland Revenue

chunks.title: general practitioner
chunks.text:
## general practitioner
A general practitioner is a medical practitioner who has general training in all areas of medicine, including psychiatry. General practitioners manage your general health care.

chunks.title: general surgeon
chunks.text:
## general surgeon
A general surgeon is a medical specialist prepared to manage a broad spectrum of surgical conditions affecting almost any area of the body.

chunks.title: Graduate-entry
chunks.text:
## Graduate-entry
A graduate-entry student is a student who starts a long undergraduate qualification after completing a bachelor degree or higher level qualification first.

chunks.title: grandparented clients
chunks.text:
## grandparented clients
A grandparented client for Jobseeker Support means a client who was transferred to Jobseeker Support on 15 July 2013 from one of the following benefits:
- Domestic Purposes Benefit - Women Alone or
- Widows Benefit (with no children or their youngest child was 14 years or older)
These clients continue to have their income charged using the part-time income test.
They must remain in continuous receipt of Jobseeker Support from 15 July 2013 to continue being considered a grandparented client.

chunks.title: grandparented non-qualified partner
chunks.text:
## grandparented non-qualified partner
A grandparented non-qualified partner is any person who was included in a New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension as a non-qualified partner before 9 November 2020 and is still included after 9 November 2020.
## Non-qualified partner - before 9 November 2020
A non-qualified partner is the partner of a New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client who did not qualify for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension in their own right before 9 November 2020.

chunks.title: grant date
chunks.text:
## grant date
A grant date is a single day on which a client is paid one or more Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit, or Recoverable Assistance Payments (excluding payments in specific circumstances and payments for driver licences).
The number of grant dates is based on the number of dates in the previous 12 months (from 27 September 2010) when a client received payments, e.g. if a client is applying for assistance after receiving payments on two different dates in the past 12 months, this will be their third grant date.
The number of grant dates is recorded in CMS under the SNG/Advance tab.
Note payments made on two consecutive days count as two grant dates.
Note each person within a couple will have their grant dates counted individually.

chunks.title: harm
chunks.text:
## harm
Harm, in relation to ex gratia or compensation payments:
- means illness, injury, or both, includes physical harmmental harm andhumiliation, loss of dignity, and injury to feelings of the aggrieved person
- physical harm
- mental harm and
- humiliation, loss of dignity, and injury to feelings of the aggrieved person
Harm does not include:
- economic loss, for example loss of wages
- loss or reduction of property or
- loss of employment, or loss of office

chunks.title: health agency
chunks.text:
## health agency
Health agency means any of:
- the Minister of Health
- the Ministry of Health
- a funder within the meaning of the Health and Disability Services Act 1993 or
- a Hospital and Health service within the meaning of that Act or the
- the Accident Compensation Corporation
- an insurer within the meaning of the Accident Insurance Act 1998 or
- the General Manager of Veterans' Affairs New Zealand in respect of grants or subsidies for a Hospital and Health Service within the meaning of that Act. Disability Services made under the Veterans. Support Act 2014 or regulations made under that Act

chunks.title: health practitioner
chunks.text:
## health practitioner
A health practitioner is a person who is registered with an authority as a practitioner of a particular health profession under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003. All health practitioners have a unique identifying number called a Health Practitioners Index number (HPI number).
MSD may require information from a registered health practitioner to help determine a person's eligibility for some types of financial assistance.
Note unless specifically mentioned otherwise, most medical certificates must be completed by medical practitioners and nurse practitioners.
The full list of health practitioners includes:
- Anaesthetic Technician
- Chinese Medicine Services
- Chiropractor
- Clinical Dental Technician
- Dental Hygienist
- Dental Technician
- Dental Therapist
- Dentist
- Dietician
- Dispensing Optician
- Medical Laboratory Technologist
- Medical Practitioner
- Medical Radiation Technologist
- Midwife
- Nurse
- Nurse Practitioner
- Occupational Therapist
- Optometrist
- Osteopath
- Paramedic
- Pharmacist
- Physiotherapist
- Podiatrist
- Psychologist
- Psychotherapist
These professions are recognised through registration with the appropriate authority under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003 for their scope of practice.

chunks.title: high level of care
chunks.text:
## high level of care
A client is considered to have received a high level of care when they have received care from a caregiver who was living with them and that care delayed their entry into residential care.

chunks.title: Holiday pay
chunks.text:
## Holiday pay
All employees in New Zealand are entitled to at least 4 weeks paid annual holidays after 12 months employment. When an employee takes an annual holiday day (also known as annual leave), they are paid holiday pay instead of their regular wages or salary.
Casual workers and people on fixed-term contracts are not always paid holiday pay the same as permanent employees. These people may either have their holiday pay:
- included in their regular salary or wages or
- paid as a lump sum at the end of their contract
Holiday pay also includes:
- pay for a public holiday that an employee would normally work but does not as it is a public holiday and
- alternative holidays, where an employee gets a days paid leave in return for working on a public holiday (also known as a day in lieu)
Sometimes the term annual leave is used instead of holiday pay. Annual leave and holiday pay mean the same thing.

chunks.title: hospital care
chunks.text:
## hospital care
Hospital care is the level of care provided by a non-government organisation (NGO) or District Health Board (DHB) as an in-patient or residential hospital care, including geriatric hospital-level care.
Hospital care is more than the level of care provided if a person is solely seeing a hospital specialist or receiving out-patient care.

chunks.title: hospital
chunks.text:
## hospital
An institution that provides hospital care (which is; children's health services, geriatric services, maternity services, medical services, mental health services, or surgical services), and:
- the premises can accommodate 2 or more of the people for whom the services are provided for continuous periods of 24 hours or longer and
- payment is made by the Crown, the person receiving care, or any other person

chunks.title: housing need
chunks.text:
## housing need
Housing need refers to households lacking their own housing or living in housing which is inadequate, unsuitable or unaffordable, and who are unable to meet their housing needs (property requirements) without assistance.
Note to be eligible to be allocated social housing a client must be assessed as being at risk (A priority) or have a serious housing need (B priority).

chunks.title: housing needs
chunks.text:
## housing needs
Housing needs describe the property requirements (which include particular types of houses or areas) the prospective tenant requires for their household circumstances. This may include:
- size of house for example, requires more or less bedrooms
- letting area the prospective tenant requires to be for example, to be closer to health practitioners, family, special schools, employment opportunities or be away from certain neighbourhood influences
- features or functionality of the house for example, for health or disability reasons requires a ramp, single storey building or an accessible bathroom

chunks.title: ICA
chunks.text:
## ICA
Independent Circumstances Allowance - ICA
Students between the ages of 16-24 are able to apply for this if they are unable to, or it is unreasonable to expect them to, rely on their parents for financial support.

chunks.title: immediate emergency housing need
chunks.text:
## immediate emergency housing need
A client would be assessed as having an immediate emergency housing need if, on the date they apply or during some or all of the next 7 days, they:
- cannot remain in their usual place of residence (if any) and
- will not have access to other accommodation that is adequate for the needs of the client and their immediate family

chunks.title: immediate family for Flexible Funding Assistance
chunks.text:
## immediate family for Flexible Funding Assistance
For a client getting Flexible Funding Assistance immediate family means an applicant's:
- dependent children and
- partner (if any)
who are staying with the applicant in the same emergency housing.

chunks.title: Immediate family member of a refugee or protected person
chunks.text:
## Immediate family member of a refugee or protected person
An immediate family member of a refugee or protected person is:
- the partner or child, of the refugee or protected person or
- if the refugee or protected person is a dependent child, their parent(s) or sibling(s)
Note Immigration New Zealand determines who is a dependent child under the Immigration Act 2009 and its regulations.

chunks.title: immediate family
chunks.text:
## immediate family
For the purposes of a Special Needs Grant, immediate family means:
- in the case of a person in a relationship; that person, their partner, and their dependent children (if any)
- in the case of a sole parent; that person and their dependent children
- in the case of a dependent child; that child, their parent, and any other dependent children of that parent
For the purposes of Relocate for Work Support, immediate family means the client's spouse or partner and their dependent children.

chunks.title: immediate need
chunks.text:
## immediate need
An immediate need for Flexible Funding Assistance is a need that must be met while the client and their immediate family (the applicant, their dependent children and partner (if any)) are in emergency housing, generally within the next 7 days, to meet the expenses of the client or their immediate family.

chunks.title: In-cycle payment
chunks.text:
## In-cycle payment
An information share Child Support payment that is paid by Inland Revenue to a receiving carer on the second business day after the 19th of a month.
These payments generally relate to ‘on-time’ Child Support liability for the previous month, but could also be ‘late’ payments of Child Support for any period of liability in the past that are paid on the same day as an in-cycle payment.

chunks.title: in-work payment
chunks.text:
## in-work payment
The in-work payment was renamed the in-work tax credit on 1 April 2007.
It replaced the Child Tax Credit from 1 April 2006, though clients who were getting the Child Tax Credit before 1 April 2006 could continue to get this until they became ineligible.

chunks.title: INCMA
chunks.text:
## INCMA
Income add screen.
Use this screen to add income and/or assets to a client's and/or partner's record from the date you wish the income to be charged.

chunks.title: INCMH
chunks.text:
## INCMH
Income history screen.
Use this screen to see a client's income history. You can select an income period to add to, or you can change the effective date.

chunks.title: income-tested benefit
chunks.text:
## income-tested benefit
Income-tested benefit means any of the following benefits:
- Emergency Benefit
- Jobseeker Support
- Orphan's Benefit
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Unsupported Child's Benefit
- New Zealand Superannuation - non-qualified partner included
- Veterans Pension - non-qualified partner included
- Young Parent Payment
- Youth Payment

chunks.title: income
chunks.text:
## income
Any money a client receives that is used to support themselves and their dependants.

chunks.title: incorporated societies
chunks.text:
## incorporated societies
An incorporated society is a group or organisation that has been registered under the Incorporated Societies Act 1908 and is authorised to run its affairs as though it were an individual person. This means members are not personally liable for the society’s debts, contracts or other obligations and do not have any personal interest in property or assets owned by the society.
There are a wide range of incorporated societies including sports clubs, social clubs, music and cultural groups, special interest and activist organisations, for example:
- Age Concern
- Care Association New Zealand
- Health and Safety Association of New Zealand
- Sports and Exercise Physiotherapy New Zealand

chunks.title: institution
chunks.text:
## institution
A facility that provides hospital care (which is: children's health services, geriatric services, maternity services, medical services, mental health services, or surgical services), or residential disability type care, and:
- the premises can accommodate 2 or more of the people for whom the services are provided for continuous periods of 24 hours or longer and
- payment is made by the Crown, the person receiving the care, or any other person

chunks.title: intellectual disability
chunks.text:
## intellectual disability
A person with an intellectual disability has intellectual functioning significantly below average. They may also have limitations with their behaviour (either behavioural problems or difficulty with managing day to day tasks or both).
An intellectual disability is not an illness or a disease and there may be various causes, for example; genetic, chromosomal abnormality or injury. One example of intellectual disability is Down Syndrome.

chunks.title: International Services
chunks.text:
## International Services
The contact details for International Services are:
From New Zealand 0800 777 227 (free calling within New Zealand only)
From Australia 1800 150 479
From other countries +64 4 978 1180
Email international_services@msd.govt.nz
Postal
International ServicesMinistry of Social DevelopmentPO Box 27178Wellington 6141New Zealand
Fax 04 918 0159
Note when calling from overseas replace the '+' with the international direct dial prefix for the country you are in.

chunks.title: intramural student
chunks.text:
## intramural student
Intramural students are students completing their studies onsite at an education provider.
The standard rate of Accommodation Benefit is based on the location of their education provider, not their residential address.
Generally students will be living and studying on or near their providers location.
Example
Sara lives in Upper Hutt and attends Victoria University of Wellington - Te Herenga Waka.
As Sara is studying onsite, she is getting the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit for Victoria University - Te Herenga Waka, Wellington City location.

chunks.title: Jersey and Guernsey
chunks.text:
## Jersey and Guernsey
'Jersey' means the Island of Jersey, and 'Guernsey' means the Islands of Guernsey, Alderney, Herm and Jethro.

chunks.title: Job Search Service
chunks.text:
## Job Search Service
A service that provides appropriate, work focused services to all job seekers to support them back into work as quickly as possible.
There are two main services that are provided to job seekers dependent on the level of support they require. They are:
- Self Directed:a service provided by Job Connect for more skilled, qualified and experienced job seekers who can undertake independent job searching
- Central Service:a service that gives job seekers access to employment related activities such as Target 20 and employment workshops

chunks.title: joint tenancy
chunks.text:
## joint tenancy
Each owner has an undivided share of the property, which they cannot deal with independently of the other owner(s).

chunks.title: Kāinga Ora energy subsidy
chunks.text:
## Kāinga Ora energy subsidy
Kāinga Ora energy subsidy (also known as Winter Energy Study subsidy) is a subsidy paid by Kāinga Ora to an energy retailer for the supply of electricity to a person living in Kāinga Ora housing.
This subsidy is not included as:
- income under the Social Security Act 2018
- a student's personal income, or the income of their spouse or partner, when assessing the student's eligibility for Student Allowance

chunks.title: Kaupapa Māori pathway grants
chunks.text:
## Kaupapa Māori pathway grants
People who have been affected by a severe weather event whose property has been designated as category 3 may get a Kaupapa Māori Pathway grant from the Crown or local authority.
This grant allows people to move from their category 3 property while retaining ownership of their property.
Category 3 means the Crown or local authority considers the land is exposed to an unacceptable risk from future severe weather events that cannot be sufficiently mitigated.

chunks.title: KiwiSaver schemes
chunks.text:
## KiwiSaver schemes
A KiwiSaver scheme is an investment scheme where your savings are invested and locked in until the age of 65, though there are some exceptions for early withdrawals for people:
- suffering from significant financial hardship or a serious illness
- moving overseas permanently
- buying their first home
All KiwiSaver schemes must be registered with the Financial Markets Authority and offered and managed by KiwiSaver providers.
KiwiSaver distributions are generally distributed as a lump sum payment. Alternatively, the payments may be returned as an annuity (a regular ongoing payment).
For more information see:
- Inland Revenue KiwiSaver

chunks.title: lapse
chunks.text:
## lapse
"Lapse" means that the application process is not complete within 20 working days of the date of first contact. A benefit cannot be granted until a new application is completed.

chunks.title: LEA - Loan Entitlement Advice
chunks.text:
## LEA - Loan Entitlement Advice
Loan Entitlement Advice
This is the letter sent to students who apply for a Student Loan.
The letter sets out the details of their Student Loan, including how much they can borrow and when they can access the money.
A new LEA will be issued if there is a change in a students entitlement to a Student Loan.

chunks.title: lender
chunks.text:
## lender
Lender means MSD being responsible for the administration of the Social Security Act 2018.

chunks.title: LET - Loan Entry Threshold
chunks.text:
## LET - Loan Entry Threshold
Loan Entry Threshold
This is the minimum number of EFTS that is required for a student to be considered as studying full-time.

chunks.title: Liability period
chunks.text:
## Liability period
A specified period of time in which a liable parent is required to pay Child Support to a receiving carer.

chunks.title: Liable parent
chunks.text:
## Liable parent
A person who must pay Child Support to Inland Revenue in respect of a qualifying child.
They may or may not also be a caregiver of that child. For example, they may be a caregiver of the qualifying child in a shared care situation, as well as being the liable parent.

chunks.title: life interest or lease for life
chunks.text:
## life interest or lease for life
Life interest or lease for life is a freehold estate that gives the person or persons, known as the life tenant or tenants, full rights of occupation and enjoyment of the land.
The life interest or lease for life can be transferred or disposed of by the life tenant as they choose but ceases upon the death of the life tenant and it cannot be disposed of by will.
A life interest (or lease for life) arises from a will or is obtained as a condition of the selling or gifting of an asset, in most cases to a trust.

chunks.title: Loan manager
chunks.text:
## Loan manager
The Loan Manager is the person appointed by the lender as set out in section 4(1) of the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011 to make, charge, and administer loan advances under the Student Loan Scheme.
In 2000 MSD appointed the Operations Manager at the Student Support Centre as the Loan Manager.

chunks.title: Loans for Major Repairs Advances to Homes
chunks.text:
## Loans for Major Repairs Advances to Homes
The "Loans for Major Repairs Advances to Homes" programme was abolished from 1 July 1996.
The loans were available to beneficiaries to carry out essential repairs and maintenance to their home, to provide essential services, or to provide essential, permanently installed appliances.
The maximum loan was $2,652, and was charged against the property and registered under the Statutory Land Charges Registration Act 1928.

chunks.title: local authority
chunks.text:
## local authority
Means a local authority as defined in section YA 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007.

chunks.title: long-acting reversible contraception
chunks.text:
## long-acting reversible contraception
Long-acting reversible contraception means a substance, device or technique intended to prevent a person conceiving, or, if conception has occurred, implantation of the foetus in the person's uterus, and that are:
- effective for an extended period of time without any action on the part of the person and
- can be removed or discontinued
Examples of long-acting reversible contraception include:
- contraceptive injections - ie Depo-Provera
- contraceptive implants
- intra uterine device (IUD)

chunks.title: long-term residential care
chunks.text:
## long-term residential care
A client is considered to be in long-term residential care in a rest home or hospital when it is likely they will remain in care for more than 26 weeks.

chunks.title: lower quartile private rent
chunks.text:
## lower quartile private rent
Lower quartile private rent is the weekly rent at 25% of all market rents, when all are placed in order of value.

chunks.title: LSUM
chunks.text:
## LSUM
Letter Summary
Use this screen to:
- see a summary of all automatic letters produced by this action
- check the contents of the letter before sending to the client
- decide whether the letter is to be produced now or generated overnight
- identify how or if contact was made between region and client prior to the resulting letter

chunks.title: lump sum
chunks.text:
## lump sum
A lump sum payment is a one-time or single payment. It does not include a series of payments that have been added together to make a single "lump sum" payment.
example a payment of arrears in a "lump sum" that represents a number of payments that would ordinarily have been made individually.
Any interest received from investing lumps sums must be declared and the interest will be counted as personal income.

chunks.title: main benefit
chunks.text:
## main benefit
A main benefit means one of the following:
- Emergency Benefit
- Jobseeker Support
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury, disability, or total blindness
- Supported Living Payment - caring for a person
- Youth Payment
- Young Parent Payment

chunks.title: income equalisation scheme
chunks.text:
## income equalisation scheme
Income equalisation and environmental restoration schemes are a way for some types of businesses to even out income fluctuations by spreading their gross income from year to year.
This includes income from:
- farming
- fishing
- forestry
- testing, construction and mining (when related to environmental restoration)
Businesses pay the income into a special account which earns interest at 3% on amounts left on deposit for more than 12 months. The interest paid becomes part of the deposit for tax purposes.
Inland Revenue holds the deposit for up to 5 years. It's tax deductible in the year for which it is made. Any withdrawals (including interest) are generally assessable (counted as taxable income) in the year businesses apply to withdraw them.
In normal circumstances an amount cannot be withdrawn unless it's been on deposit for at least 12 months.

chunks.title: Mana in Mahi
chunks.text:
## Mana in Mahi
Mana in Mahi (Strength in Work) is provided by the Ministry of Social Development to support people who are at risk of long-term benefit receipt to get an apprenticeship or formal industry qualification to gain sustainable employment.
Employers get support to recruit people and to then support those people through an industry training pathway.
The Ministry:
- pays a wage subsidy to the employer and
- provides clients with incentive payments and ongoing support (along with a range of other supports)

chunks.title: Medical coverage (Jobseeker Support)
chunks.text:
## Medical coverage (Jobseeker Support)
Medical coverage is the period of time a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, dentist or midwife (where relevant) has medically determined a client is unable to work, due to their health condition, injury or disability.
The medical coverage should also tell MSD when the client will:
- next be clinically reassessed or
- be able to return to full-time work
One of the registered health practitioners listed above will indicate the period of a client's medical coverage on a Work Capacity Medical Certificate, or another type of a medical certificate provided it contains all the information needed.

chunks.title: medical practitioner
chunks.text:
## medical practitioner
A medical practitioner is commonly referred to as a doctor. Medical practitioners are health practitioners who are registered with the Medical Council of New Zealand as practitioners of the profession of medicine and hold a current practising certificate.
All medical practitioners have a unique identifying number called a Health Practitioners Index number (HPI number).
Medical practitioners don't need to have completed their training in New Zealand but must be registered with the New Zealand Medical Council and hold a current practising certificate.
A medical practitioner is a person trained to understand the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of disease. Specialists concentrate on certain body organ systems, specific age groups, or on complex scientific techniques developed to diagnose or treat certain types of disorders (for example an oncologist treats cancer). General practitioners are specialists in primary care, and usually work in the community as opposed to in hospital settings.
Examples of medical practitioners can include:
- addiction medicine specialist
- allergist or immunologist
- dermatologist
- general practitioner
- general surgeon
- neurologist
- oncologist
- ophthalmologist
- paediatrician
- psychiatrist

chunks.title: MedicAlert
chunks.text:
## MedicAlert
MedicAlert provides medical information in emergency situations. Clients pay a one-off enrolment fee to join (which includes the basic MedicAlert bracelet or pendant). They must also pay an ongoing membership fee for the basic package.
Clients may also choose to pay for an additional bracelet or pendant, or to upgrade their bracelet or pendant to another material (eg gold or titanium).
MedicAlert Foundation is the name of the organisation that provides the MedicAlert service described above.

chunks.title: midwife
chunks.text:
## midwife
A midwife is a health practitioner who is registered with the Midwifery Council of New Zealand and trained to provide necessary support, care and advice during pregnancy, labour and the postpartum period up to 6 weeks, to facilitate births and to provide care for the newborn.
Midwives can only sign medical certificates for pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions within the range of the midwives' profession.
This includes signing medical certificates for complications associated with pregnancies that occur before the 27th week of pregnancy.

chunks.title: minimum family tax credit
chunks.text:
## minimum family tax credit
The minimum family tax credit tops up a family's total income to a guaranteed level.
To qualify:
- at least one parent must work for wages or salary
- sole parents must work for at least 20 hours a week
- couples with dependent children must work for a combined total of at least 30 hours a week
The minimum family tax credit was known as the Family Tax Credit before 1 April 2007.
Contact Inland Revenue for more information.

chunks.title: Ministry of Health contracted provider
chunks.text:
## Ministry of Health contracted provider
The contracted provider provides funding on behalf of the Ministry of Health for vehicle and house modifications.
If you live in Auckland or Northland, the contracted provider is Accessable 0508 001 002.
For the rest of New Zealand, the contracted provider is Enable New Zealand 0800 362 253.

chunks.title: Ministry of Social Development debt
chunks.text:
## Ministry of Social Development debt
Ministry of Social Development debt is any debt that an individual owes to the Ministry of Social Development.
This may include, but is not limited to:
- Advance Payment of Benefits
- Benefit debt - including shared debts
- Child Maintenance debt
- Liable Parent Contribution debt
- Major Repair Advances
- Recoverable Assistance payments
- recoverable Special Needs Grants payments
- Student Allowance debt
- Student Loan MSD debt
For more information regarding shared debts see:
- Relationship debt sharing

chunks.title: minor
chunks.text:
## minor
Minor means a person who has not attained the age of 18 years.

chunks.title: Mixed Child Support payment
chunks.text:
## Mixed Child Support payment
Child Support paid to a receiving carer who is entitled to both Unsupported Child’s Benefit excess payments and other Child Support from Inland Revenue.
The payment is a mixed Child Support payment when it is paid to the receiving carer by the same liable parent in respect of multiple children.

chunks.title: mortgage security
chunks.text:
## mortgage security
Mortgage security includes:
- a deferred payment disposition and the balance of the purchase price required to be paid to the vendor of the premises under that disposition
- money secured over a person's share or shares in any flat owning company within the meaning of Subpart 6 of the Land Transfer Act 2017
- money payable under and secured by a deferred payment licence under the Land Act 1948

chunks.title: MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier
chunks.text:
## MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier
An MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier is a medical alarm supplier who has been accredited by the Ministry of Social Development for the purposes of providing medical alarm services, to people seeking assistance with the cost of a medical alarm service through Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: NCEA
chunks.text:
## NCEA
National Certificates of Educational Achievement
New Zealand's National Certificates of Educational Achievement (NCEA) are national qualifications for senior secondary students.

chunks.title: net equity
chunks.text:
## net equity
The net equity in a property is:
- house and/or land value
minus
- outstanding mortgage only (no interest)
Net equity in a vehicle/caravan/boat is the amount of money the client would have if they sold their vehicle/caravan/boat after they had paid any debts owing on it.
For example, the client has a boat that has a market value of $4,000. They still owe the bank $1,500, so the net equity would be $2,500. This is the amount the client would get if they sold the boat at market value and paid the bank what it was owed.

chunks.title: Net payment
chunks.text:
## Net payment
Net payment means the total of all financial assistance payable by the Ministry of Social Development to the client and their partner (if any) under the:
- Social Security Act 2018
- Social Security Regulations 2018
- New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001
- Veteran's Support Act 2014
- Student Allowances Regulations 1998
- Christchurch Mosques Attack Welfare Programme 2019
but excludes special assistance under a welfare programme (except for special assistance under the Christchurch Mosques Attack Welfare Programme 2019).

chunks.title: net rate
chunks.text:
## net rate
For the purposes of Temporary Additional Support, the net rate in relation to any benefit means the appropriate rate from the appropriate Schedule.
For New Zealand Superannuation it means the appropriate rate set out in Schedule 1 of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001 after the deduction of standard tax.
For Veteran's Pension it means the appropriate rate set out in Regulation 42 of the Veterans' Support Regulations 2014 after the deduction of standard tax.

chunks.title: neurologist
chunks.text:
## neurologist
A neurologist is a medical specialist concerned with the diagnosis and treatment of all categories of disease or impaired function of the brain, spinal cord, peripheral nerves, muscles, and automatic nervous system, and the blood vessels that relate to these structures.

chunks.title: New Zealand citizen
chunks.text:
## New Zealand citizen
A person can be a New Zealand citizen by either:
- birth
- grant or
- descent
For New Zealand citizenship, New Zealand includes the self-governing states of:
- the Cook Islands
- Niue and
- Tokelau
Citizenship is granted by the Department of Internal Affairs.
Note people born in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau may not automatically be New Zealand citizens. To be considered a New Zealand citizen from birth, a person born on or after 1 January 2006 must have:
- been born in New Zealand, Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau, and
- at least one parent who at the time of the person's birth was a New Zealand citizen or entitled to reside indefinitely in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau

chunks.title: New Zealand
chunks.text:
## New Zealand
'New Zealand' means New Zealand only.
It does not include the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau.

chunks.title: No Asset Procedure
chunks.text:
## No Asset Procedure
No Asset Procedure is for a client who has no realisable assets and has unsecured debts of between $1000-$40,000, which they are unable to repay.

chunks.title: non-core family member
chunks.text:
## non-core family member
For the purposes of Residential Care Subsidy, a non-core-family member includes:
- siblings
- single adult offspring
- joint owners of the home
- other occupiers of the home
A spouse, civil union or de facto partner, or dependent child is considered a core family member.

chunks.title: non-current debt
chunks.text:
## non-current debt
Where a client is no longer receiving Work and Income benefit or pension entitlement, and has received:
- payment above their entitlement
- an advance or
- a recoverable grant of special assistance
the debts are held on the Debt Management System.

chunks.title: non-entitlement period
chunks.text:
## non-entitlement period
A non-entitlement period is a 13 week period when the client or their spouse or partner is not entitled to a benefit because they:
- became voluntarily unemployed without a good and sufficient reason
- lost their job because of misconduct
- have a Grade 3 sanction imposed or
- have refused an offer of suitable employment

chunks.title: non work-obligated
chunks.text:
## non work-obligated
For the purposes of Activity in the Community and Work Experience, non work-obligated means clients receiving the following benefits:
- Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability with work preparation obligations
- Sole Parent Support with a youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
- Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
and
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance and Emergency Benefit (equivalent to the benefits listed above)
and
- partners of clients whose youngest dependent child is under 3 years

chunks.title: notice period
chunks.text:
## notice period
For the purposes of the reapplication process the notice period starts 20 working days before the expiry date and ends the day before the expiry date.
An initial notice to reapply letter is sent to the client 25 working days before the expiry date.

chunks.title: notification
chunks.text:
## notification
The Commissioner of Inland Revenue must notify a borrower in writing if a loan advance debt that belongs to that borrower is transferred to the Commissioner.
The notification must:
- specify the period to which it applies, which must not be greater than 6 months and
- set out the details of all loan advances that have been made or charged to the borrower during that period and
- specify the borrowers consolidated loan balance on the first and last days of the period to which it applies and
- set out the borrowers right to object to the details of a loan advance set out in the notification and
- state the date on or before which an objection by the borrower must be received by the Loan Manager, which must be at least 31 days after the date on which the borrower is notified in accordance with this section and
- provide any other information that the Commissioner considers appropriate

chunks.title: notional pension rate
chunks.text:
## notional pension rate
The Australian notional pension rate is the rate Australia assesses before taking into account the third country pension for income purposes.

chunks.title: nurse practitioner
chunks.text:
## nurse practitioner
Nurse practitioners are health practitioners who are registered with the Nursing Council of New Zealand and hold a current annual practising certificate.
Nurse practitioners are expert or specialist nurses with advanced education, clinical training and experience. They have demonstrated clinical competence and have the legal authority to practice as independent healthcare providers.
All nurse practitioners have a unique identifying number called a Health Practitioners Index number (HPI number).
Some nurse practitioners have specialised in primary health care, hospital settings or specialities. They can practice in an expanded nursing role in clinical settings. This can include prescribing certain medications and completing certain medical certificates and examinations.
Note nurse practitioners should not be confused with registered or enrolled nurses or Nurse prescribers who do not have the necessary scope of practice to complete medical certificates.

chunks.title: occupational therapist
chunks.text:
## occupational therapist
An occupational therapist is health practitioner who is registered with the Occupational Therapy Board of New Zealand and trained to help people manage the daily activities of living, such as dressing, grooming or cooking, and regaining vocational skills.
They work with individuals who have conditions that are mentally, physically, developmentally, or emotionally disabling.

chunks.title: Official Assignee
chunks.text:
## Official Assignee
The Official Assignee is an employee of the Insolvency and Trustee Service whose function is to fairly and independently administer the affairs of people who become bankrupt.

chunks.title: Offset Child Support
chunks.text:
## Offset Child Support
An amount of formula assessed or voluntary agreement Child Support that a liable parent is liable to pay to a receiving carer, but is not required to be paid in cash because the amount of Child Support is offset under section 152B of the CSA.
i.e. where two parents are each liable to pay the other a regular amount of Child Support and Inland Revenue offsets one liability against the other.

chunks.title: oncologist
chunks.text:
## oncologist
An oncologist is a medial practitioner who specialises in the diagnosis and treatment of all types of cancer and other benign and malignant tumours.

chunks.title: open employment
chunks.text:
## open employment
A job available to anyone in the community and meets the minimum terms and conditions of employment.

chunks.title: ophthalmologist
chunks.text:
## ophthalmologist
An ophthalmologist is medical specialist who deals with the diseases and surgery of the visual pathways, including the eye, brain, and areas surrounding the eye.

chunks.title: optometrist
chunks.text:
## optometrist
An optometrist is a health practitioner who specialises in vision care and is trained to detect, measure and correct vision problems.

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
chunks.text:
## Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
The Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 is also known as the Children's and Young People's Well-being Act 1989. It was previously known as the:
- Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Act 1989, or
- CYP and F Act 1989

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki
chunks.text:
## Oranga Tamariki
