chunks.title: sensitive claim
chunks.text:
## sensitive claim
A claim for physical and/or mental injury suffered as a result of sexual abuse or sexual assault.

chunks.title: Service costs
chunks.text:
## Service costs
Service Costs means the cost as reasonably determined by MSD of any services (for example, electricity supply, gas supply, telephone network connection, or broadband Internet connection) provided to or in connection with the premises for consumption or use by the occupants of the premises. Service costs do not include the cost of water supplied to the premises.

chunks.title: settlor
chunks.text:
## settlor
A settlor of a trust is a person who:
- transfers assets or income to the trust or
- transfers assets or income for the benefit of the trust or
- transfers assets or income on terms of the trust or
- provides financial assistance to the trust or for the benefit of the trust with an obligation to pay on demand, and the right to demand payments not exercised or is deferred or
- can be treated as a settlor by virtue of being a person who: declines to act for the purpose of defeating trust ruleshas a 10% or more control interest in a foreign controlled company who settles an amount on a trust or who settles to a sub-trust oracquires rights or powers requiring the trustees to treat them as a beneficiary
- declines to act for the purpose of defeating trust rules
- has a 10% or more control interest in a foreign controlled company who settles an amount on a trust or who settles to a sub-trust or
- acquires rights or powers requiring the trustees to treat them as a beneficiary
From the 2014/2015 tax year onwards, a person who makes a contribution to a trust that is a foreign superannuation scheme is not a settlor of the trust.

chunks.title: Severe weather event buyout payments
chunks.text:
## Severe weather event buyout payments
People affected by a severe weather event whose property has been designated as category 3 may accept an offer from the Crown or local authority to purchase their home and/or land.
When the offer is accepted the Crown or local authority pays the purchase price of their home and/or land.
Category 3 means the Crown or local authority considers the land is exposed to an unacceptable risk from future severe weather events that cannot be sufficiently mitigated.

chunks.title: Severe weather event donations
chunks.text:
## Severe weather event donations
People may get financial donations because they have been affected by a severe weather event.
Donations may come from a range of sources including (but not limited to):
- New Zealand Disaster Relief Fund (Red Cross)
- Cyclone Appeal
- New Zealand Lotteries Commission
- donations made through crowdfunding websites such as www.givealittle.co.nz
- businesses
- employers
- individuals
People may use these donations for various reasons such as replacing belongings or repairing their property.

chunks.title: Severe weather event insurance payments
chunks.text:
## Severe weather event insurance payments
People who have been affected by a severe weather event may get one or more insurance payments to cover the costs of:
- repairing, replacing, or rebuilding their home that was damaged by a severe weather event
- temporary accommodation needed by the person, and any members of their family who usually live with them, because of a severe weather event – these payments may be a lump sum or periodic.

chunks.title: severely restricted
chunks.text:
## severely restricted
To be severely restricted in their capacity for work, the Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied the client is incapable of regularly working 15 or more hours a week in open employment.
For more information see:
- Supported Living Payment Sheltered employment
The features of the client's working environment in relation to the client's health condition, illness or disability need to be considered on a case by case by basis.

chunks.title: SEXPI
chunks.text:
## SEXPI
SWIFFT Expiries Inquiry screen.
Use this screen to see all unactioned and actioned expiries for a client, and to select an unactioned user-created expiry or an actioned expiry to be deleted.

chunks.title: shared accommodation
chunks.text:
## shared accommodation
Accommodation with 2 or more occupants who are named on the accommodation agreement where at least one of those occupants is not the client’s partner.

chunks.title: shared housing
chunks.text:
## shared housing
Shared housing is where a client is living in a bedroom in a social housing provider property. Each bedroom will have its own bathroom, but the client may be required to share kitchen, lounge and other facilities with the other tenants.
A shared property can only have five or less tenants living at the property at any one time.
Tenants other than social housing clients can live in the property.

chunks.title: Shared tenancy
chunks.text:
## Shared tenancy
Shared tenancy means a tenancy with 2 or more tenants who are not in a relationship with each other.

chunks.title: short-term charge facility
chunks.text:
## short-term charge facility
A short-term charge facility allows a person to buy, hire or charge goods or services. Some examples of this occurring are that:
- an employer provides vouchers as a payment for work done or as a reward or bonus
- an employer's business charge account is used with a supplier for a person's own private purchases
- a business credit card for private purchases
Note this income is only considered parental income where the parent is not required to pay all the costs associated with the purchase, including any interest and fees.

chunks.title: Short-term training course
chunks.text:
## Short-term training course
Short-term training means training of 12 weeks or less that is not provided under the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF). This includes pre-employment, on-the-job, and external training eg a course or programme through a provider.

chunks.title: shorter fixed period
chunks.text:
## shorter fixed period
For the purposes of Temporary Additional Support, a shorter fixed period is where Temporary Additional Support will end earlier than the standard 13 week period.

chunks.title: signatory
chunks.text:
## signatory
A signatory is a person who signs the tenancy agreement. They are also referred to as the "tenant".
The only people who have security of tenure at the property are the signatories. Any other people living at the property have no rights to the tenancy.

chunks.title: SINCC
chunks.text:
## SINCC
Incapacity Add/Change.
Use this screen to add or change details of a client's incapacity for:
- Emergency Benefit
- Jobseeker Support
- Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
- Young Parent Payment and
- Youth Payment
You also use this screen to link clients to designated health practitioner and health practitioner.

chunks.title: single
chunks.text:
## single
Single includes having a spouse or civil union partner when:
- either spouse / partner is under 25 years old (or under 24 years old on or after 1 January 2009) and
- neither spouse / partner has a dependent child

chunks.title: SNORI
chunks.text:
## SNORI
SWIFTT Notional Rate Inquiry screen - allows authorised users to view a history of the annual Australian Notional rates for a client.

chunks.title: SNSRA
chunks.text:
## SNSRA
SWIFTT Non Standard Rate Add/change.
Use this screen to add or change a non-standard rate of parent benefit or pension or family tax credit (formerly Family Support).

chunks.title: social housing provider
chunks.text:
## social housing provider
Social housing providers are housing providers, which include Housing New Zealand and community housing providers.
Community housing providers are approved, registered and regulated by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment.
A social housing provider can provide properties for tenants who are eligible for social housing and for subsided rent through Income Related Rent.

chunks.title: SOFSI
chunks.text:
## SOFSI
Offset inquiry.
Use this screen to see details of existing offsets or select an offset to be changed.

chunks.title: sole parent carer
chunks.text:
## sole parent carer
Sole parents getting a sole parent rate of the following benefits:
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment - restricted in their capacity to work due to a health condition, injury, disability, or totally blind
- Jobseeker Support (except Jobseeker Support Student Hardship)
- Young Parent Payment
- Emergency Benefit
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance

chunks.title: sole parent
chunks.text:
## sole parent
Sole parent means a person who is the principal caregiver in respect of a dependent child and who is:
- married or in a civil union but living apart from their spouse or partner or
- not married or in a civil union and not living in a de facto relationship

chunks.title: SOPDA
chunks.text:
## SOPDA
SWIFTT Overseas Pensions Details Add/Change screen.
Use this screen to inquire on or add details of a client's Overseas Pension.

chunks.title: SOPHC
chunks.text:
## SOPHC
SWIFTT Overseas Pensions Change screen.
Use this screen to change a client's Overseas Pension.

chunks.title: SOPHI
chunks.text:
## SOPHI
SWIFTT Overseas Pensions History Inquiry screen.
Use this screen to view a client's Overseas Pension history.

chunks.title: SPBR
chunks.text:
## SPBR
Parent benefit/pension re-assessment.
Use this screen to re-assess the benefit record following - any changes made on screens SDT1A (Data add/change weekly benefits) and SDT2A (Data add/change 2 weekly benefits), or after extending a medical certificate on an expired record.

chunks.title: Special Banking Option
chunks.text:
## Special Banking Option
When a client is receiving a pension from Ireland, Australia, the United Kingdom or the Netherlands they can choose to have it paid into a Special Banking Option account.
The overseas social security authority pays the pension into this account instead of into the clients own bank account.
The client will then receive the full rate of their New Zealand benefit. The account is only able to be accessed by Work and Income and is administered by International Services.

chunks.title: special circumstances
chunks.text:
## special circumstances
Special circumstances are circumstances that are unusual and are specific to the person and/or situation and therefore would not otherwise occur.

chunks.title: special portability arrangement
chunks.text:
## special portability arrangement
In some instances New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension can be paid to clients who are leaving New Zealand for more than 52 weeks to live in certain Pacific countries.
Client's can receive up to 100% depending on their years of New Zealand residence.

chunks.title: specialist school
chunks.text:
## specialist school
A specialist school is a school that offers special education to students in any of years 1-13.
Special education is education for children who require educational services beyond that normally obtained in an ordinary class in a state school.
This includes residential and day schools supporting students who:
- are hearing or vision impaired or
- have severe behavioural needs or
- have educational, social and emotional needs together with a slow rate of learning
Specialist schools also include regional health schools that provide teachers for children who are unwell.

chunks.title: specified beneficiary
chunks.text:
## specified beneficiary
A specified beneficiary is a person who is in a relationship, and is getting in their own right one of the following benefits:
- Emergency Benefit
- Jobseeker Support
- Supported Living Payment - health condition, illness, disability or totally blind
- New Zealand Superannuation
- Veterans Pension

chunks.title: specified benefit
chunks.text:
## specified benefit
The direct deduction of ACC weekly compensation applies to specified benefits only.
Specified benefit means one of the following:
- Main benefit
- Orphans Benefit
- Unsupported Childs Benefit
- Veterans Pension that is subject to abatement

chunks.title: Specified payment - Transitional Assistance Payment - Benefit Rate Increase
chunks.text:
## Specified payment - Transitional Assistance Payment - Benefit Rate Increase
To get Transitional Assistance Payment - Benefit Rate Increase for being financially disadvantaged on 1 July 2021 as an unintended consequence of either the:
- increase to main benefit rates, or
- change to the calculation of the disability exception amount in the Temporary Additional Support formula
the client must have been getting a specified payment on 30 June 2021. The specified payments are:
- Temporary Additional Support
- Christchurch Mosques Attack special assistance

chunks.title: specified student
chunks.text:
## specified student
A person awarded a student allowance (other than a person who has lost eligibility to that allowance or a person whose allowance is suspended under any of regulations 28 to 31 of the regulations), whether or not that allowance was payable because of income.

chunks.title: specified supplementary assistance
chunks.text:
## specified supplementary assistance
Specified supplementary assistance that must be reviewed when a backdated ACC weekly compensation payment reduces the specified benefit to zero means any of the following:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Winter Energy Payment
- Disability Allowance
- Special Disability Allowance
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit
- Temporary GST Assistance

chunks.title: SPINC
chunks.text:
## SPINC
SWIFTT Partner Inclusion screen.
Use this screen to include a partner in a client's current benefit.

chunks.title: SREG
chunks.text:
## SREG
Register benefit/pension screen.
Use this screen to register an application for a parent benefit or pension. Before you enter this screen you must select the client.

chunks.title: SSBOA
chunks.text:
## SSBOA
SWIFTT Special Banking Option Add screen.
Use this screen to add the special banking option to a client's record.

chunks.title: SSNAR
chunks.text:
## SSNAR
Special Needs Grant/advance/lump sum recommend/decline.
Use this screen to recommend or decline a:
- Advance Payment of Benefit
- benefit due payment
- Civil Defence payment
- Course Participation Assistance
- Funeral Grant
- Special Benefit lump sum
- Special Needs Grant
- Training Incentive Allowance pre-enrolment fee
- Transition to Work Grant
- Veterans Pension Lump Sum

chunks.title: SSPBA
chunks.text:
## SSPBA
Special Benefit register/grant/decline.
Use this screen to assess a client's entitlement to Special Benefit. You can register, grant and decline.

chunks.title: SSPWA
chunks.text:
## SSPWA
Special Benefit weekly costs.
Use this screen to add or delete details of a client's weekly costs due to their special circumstances.

chunks.title: SSTAI
chunks.text:
## SSTAI
SWIFTT Status Inquiry
Use this screen to see a clients latest benefit/pension details:
- benefit/pension status
- rate of payment
- extra help payable (supplementary allowances)
- bank account

chunks.title: standard period
chunks.text:
## standard period
For the purposes of Temporary Additional Support, the standard period of payment is 13 weeks. This is the maximum period that Temporary Additional Support can be paid.

chunks.title: start date of the tenancy
chunks.text:
## start date of the tenancy
The start date is the date of commencement of the tenancy as stated in the tenancy agreement. This is usually the same date the client moves in or takes possession of the property.
There may be situations where the client is unable to take possession of the property straight away. In this situation the housing provider is responsible for providing alternative accommodation for the client.
The rate of the Income Related Rent Subsidy that can be claimed by the housing provider would be based on the property to which the client has been matched, not the alternative accommodation, and the client is still liable for paying rent at the matched property.

chunks.title: state-integrated schools or kura
chunks.text:
## state-integrated schools or kura
State-integrated schools are schools with a 'special character'. This means they may be run by a particular religious faith, eg Catholic, or use specialist education methods, like Steiner and Montessori schools.
Education in state integrated schools is also funded by the government, but they usually charge compulsory fees - also known as 'attendance dues' - to help maintain their facilities.

chunks.title: STAXQ
chunks.text:
## STAXQ
SWIFTT Tax Query.
Use this screen to view a client's current monthly tax details.

chunks.title: STRFB
chunks.text:
## STRFB
SWIFTT Transfer Benefit screen
Use this screen to transfer a client from one benefit type to another.

chunks.title: Student Component Funding
chunks.text:
## Student Component Funding
Student Component Funding is a tuition fee subsidy, paid by the government to tertiary institutions for students undertaking courses which are contained in particular qualifications.

chunks.title: substantial degree of care
chunks.text:
## substantial degree of care
Substantial degree of care means a level and type of personal care and support that enables the parent(s) to remain living in their own home or living with a family member. It involves more than simply providing accommodation.

chunks.title: suitable employment
chunks.text:
## suitable employment
Suitable employment varies between clients depending on their individual circumstances. What is suitable for one client may not be for another.
When deciding on whether a job is suitable for a client, MSD must consider the following (but is not limited to):
- appropriate hours of employment e.g. hours are not excessive
- number of hours is within the appropriate range for the client's obligations
- access to childcare
- family commitments
- religious commitments
- jobs which offend strongly held views
- days of the week
- type of employment
- skills required
- experience
- location of the job
- wages

chunks.title: SUKH
chunks.text:
## SUKH
SWIFTT United Kingdom Payments History screen.
Use this screen to inquire on a client's history of United Kingdom payments received.

chunks.title: supervised
chunks.text:
## supervised
In Disability Allowance, supervised by a registered health practitioner means the health practitioner continues to actively manage the client's care and reviews their condition from time to time throughout the year.
This is to ensure the treatment the client is getting is beneficial and of therapeutic value for the client and is directly related to their disability.
Treatment that is beneficial and therapeutic means that the treatment provided may:
- improve the client's condition or
- maintain the client's condition or
- prevent the clients condition from getting worse

chunks.title: Supplementary beneficiary assistance payments
chunks.text:
## Supplementary beneficiary assistance payments
Supplementary beneficiary assistance payments are payments made under the Social Security Act 2018, but do not include main benefits. These payments are also known as Extra help.
These payments include, but are not limited to:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Child Disability Allowance
- Childcare Subsidy
- OSCAR subsidy
- Disability Allowance
- Funeral Grants
- Home Help
- Special Benefit
- Temporary Accommodation Assistance (ended 30 June 2025)
- Temporary Additional Support
- Winter Energy Payment
- Work Bonus
- Orphan's Benefit
- Unsupported Child's Benefit
- Establishment Grants and/or a School and Year Start up payment paid to Unsupported Child's Benefit and Orphans Benefit recipients

chunks.title: supported care
chunks.text:
## supported care
Supported care is where a client is not living with their parent, guardian, or usual caregiver, and care is provided by Oranga Tamariki or one of the following under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989:
- an iwi social service
- a cultural social service
- a child and family support service

chunks.title: sustainable employment
chunks.text:
## sustainable employment
For the purposes of employment and work readiness assistance, sustainable employment means:
- a period of employment that results in a person not receiving a main benefit under the Act for a period of 91 days or longer and
- for a person getting a main benefit who is unable to engage in full-time employment because of a health condition, injury, or disability, includes employment that results in the reduction of benefit payments to the person
For the purposes of Relocate for Work Support, sustainable employment means:
- permanent employment or
- employment under a fixed-term contract of at least 12 months

chunks.title: tailored tax code
chunks.text:
## tailored tax code
New Zealand Superannuation and Veterans Pension clients are the most likely to use a tailored tax code.
Inland Revenue will contact people who may be better off using a tailored tax code.
'Tailored tax codes' replaced 'special tax code' on 1 April 2019.

chunks.title: tamaiti whāngai
chunks.text:
## tamaiti whāngai
This is similar to a foster or adopted child. In cultural terms, it is a child who has been or is being looked after by someone other than the parent.
If this term is used, the legal relationship with the child must be clarified.

chunks.title: tax year
chunks.text:
## tax year
A tax year is a financial year for taxation purposes and covers the period from 1 April of one year to 31 March of the following year.

chunks.title: temporary entry class visa
chunks.text:
## temporary entry class visa
Temporary entry class visas are issued to people who have arrived in New Zealand legally, but are only allowed to stay for a temporary period for the duration and purposes indicated on the visa.
A temporary entry class visa means:
- a temporary visa (such as a student visa, visitor visa, work visa) or
- a limited visa or
- an interim visa

chunks.title: temporary permit
chunks.text:
## temporary permit
Temporary permits were granted before 29 November 2010 for visits, work or study. A temporary permit only allows a person to stay legally in New Zealand for the duration and purposes indicated on the permit.
Temporary permits granted under the Immigration Act 1987 continue to be valid until their expiry date.

chunks.title: tenancy end date
chunks.text:
## tenancy end date
The tenancy end date is the date:
- at the end of the notice period given by either the: tenant orhousing provider or
- tenant or
- housing provider or
- the date specified in the termination order from the Tenancy Tribunal
Generally, the tenancy end date should align with the last rent charge date, however in some cases the last rent payment may be for a partial period.
We must have confirmation from the housing provider that a tenancy has ended before the Ministry of Social Development can stop paying the Income Related Rent Subsidy.
The tenant is responsible for rent payments until the end of the notice period.

chunks.title: tenancy in common
chunks.text:
## tenancy in common
Each owner has a defined share in the property, which they can deal with independently of the other owner(s). The title will specify the exact share held by each owner.

chunks.title: tertiary provider
chunks.text:
## tertiary provider
Includes:
- an institution - such as a University, Wananga or NZIST (NZ Institute of Skills and Training and its subsidiaries that provide education or training)
- a registered establishment – a Private Training Establishment (PTE) registered by NZQA
- a government training establishment – a crown entity or government agency approved to deliver training, the Defence Force, and the NZ Police
- any other organisation that is funded by the government to provide tertiary education
This would also require checking where that term is currently used and linking to it as appropriate.

chunks.title: third party
chunks.text:
## third party
A third party is any organisation or person that has information that we may require to determine a student's entitlement to a Student Allowance or Student Loan.
This person:
- can include any person who is acting in their official capacity as an officer or employee of a department of state or public body
- does not include a person acting in their capacity as an officer of a court

chunks.title: TRACE
chunks.text:
## TRACE
TRACE is the Tracking Recovery And Collection Enforcement computer system.
It is an information system that facilitates the Investigation Unit processes, debt management and is used for a number of other facilities including Cash Receipting and Suspensory Loans.

chunks.title: Transaction date
chunks.text:
## Transaction date
The business day Inland Revenue releases an information share Child Support payment to the bank.

chunks.title: Transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development
chunks.text:
## Transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development
Transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development provides short-term accommodation for people with an immediate housing need.
Transitional housing is generally for up to 12 weeks, while support is put in place to transition them into sustainable housing.
Transitional housing may be extended for more than 12 weeks if needed.
Transitional housing is managed by providers contracted by or on behalf of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development.
Transitional housing may be in a house or a motel. Clients receive wraparound services from a support services provider. The provider's role is to refer clients to agencies to make sure they are getting the appropriate support, eg a budgeting service or referral to health services.
The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to transitional housing funded by a government department, including where the transitional housing is funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development.
## Support service providers
Clients in transitional housing get wraparound services from a support services provider.
The support services provider's role is to refer clients to agencies to make sure they are getting the appropriate support, eg a budgeting service or referral to health services.
## Residential Tenancies Act 1986
The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development.
Note transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development was previously called contracted emergency housing.

chunks.title: Transitional resident
chunks.text:
## Transitional resident
A transitional resident is usually a migrant or returning New Zealander who is temporarily exempt from paying tax on most of their overseas income.
For more information see:
- Inland Revenue New Zealand Tax Residents Exemption

chunks.title: United Kingdom
chunks.text:
## United Kingdom
"United Kingdom" means England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland and the Isle of Man.
It does not include the Channel Islands (Jersey or Guernsey) or the Republic of Ireland: these are covered under separate Reciprocal Agreements.

chunks.title: unlawfully resident
chunks.text:
## unlawfully resident
People who do not have a valid visa (or permit, if granted before 29 November 2010) to stay in New Zealand are unlawfully resident. They are not meant to be living in New Zealand.
They will usually have a temporary entry class visa which has now expired. They are commonly known as "overstayers".

chunks.title: unsuitable business
chunks.text:
## unsuitable business
The kind of employment that is deemed unsuitable employment will include:
- sex workers and operators of brothels
- strippers
- lap-dancers
- people working in or on pornographic films
Note this is not an exhaustive list, if you are unsure contact Helpline.

chunks.title: usual living expenses
chunks.text:
## usual living expenses
These are payments received that are used for something the family would otherwise have paid for themselves.

chunks.title: Veteran's Pension Centre
chunks.text:
## Veteran's Pension Centre
Veterans Pensions are administered by the Veteran's Pension Centre.
Call free on
0800 650 656
Fax
0800 999 996
Email
veteranspension@msd.govt.nz
Postal Address
Veteran's Pension Centre PO Box 5515 Wellington 6011 New Zealand

chunks.title: Violence
chunks.text:
## Violence
Section 9 of the Family Violence Act 2018 is used to define violence, when considering an exemption for applying for Child Support.
Violence means:
- physical abuse
- sexual abuse or
- psychological abuse

chunks.title: Voluntary agreement
chunks.text:
## Voluntary agreement
Child Support where parents agree who pays and how much. Parents register their arrangements with Inland Revenue, who collects and passes the money from the liable parent to the receiving carer.

chunks.title: volunteer
chunks.text:
## volunteer
A volunteer worker does not expect payment and does not receive payment for work done.
They are not considered an employee and employment law does not apply to them (with the exception of Health and Safety law).

chunks.title: VoS - Verification of Study
chunks.text:
## VoS - Verification of Study
Verification of Study
This is the process StudyLink uses to confirm a student's study details they get from the student's Education Provider.
The VoS confirms the:
- student is enrolled at the education provider they've stated on their application form
- student is undertaking an approved course of study
- programme code for the student's study programme
- EFTS value of the student's course (tertiary study only)
- start and end dates of the course of study
## Legal authority
VoS is an authorised information matching programme under the Privacy Act 2020.
It is authorised by Clause 8 of Schedule 9 of the Education and Training Act 2020, and must comply with the requirements set out in Subpart 4 of Part 7, and Schedule 6 of the Privacy Act 2020.

chunks.title: war pension
chunks.text:
## war pension
A war pension is any pension or allowance that is available under the Veterans' Support Act 2014 or from Commonwealth countries for war service.
A war pension includes:
- any pension or allowance under the Veterans' Support Act 2014 received by any person by reason of their own disablement
- any pension received under the Veterans' Support Act 2014 by the surviving spouse or civil union partner of a deceased member of the New Zealand or any other Commonwealth forces, or the Emergency Reserve Corps, or the New Zealand mercantile marine in respect of the death of that member
- any pension or other periodical allowance or any part thereof received by any person from the Government of any Commonwealth country (other than New Zealand) which MSD determines is equivalent to a pension or allowance specified in either of the 2 paragraphs above

chunks.title: Which Course Where
chunks.text:
## Which Course Where
The "Which Course Where" resource is a database that is maintained and updated by the Tertiary Education Commission (TEC). It contains reference to Student Achievement Component funded education providers and programmes and supplies information such as:
- qualification title
- qualification code
- qualification level
- EFTS value
- minimum completion time
- entry requirements
- aim of qualification
- mode of delivery
- Student Allowance/Student Loan funding approval information
This resource is able to be accessed on the internet via www.whichcoursewhere.govt.nz.

chunks.title: Winter Energy Payments
chunks.text:
## Winter Energy Payments
For Winter Energy Payment the winter payment period is 22 weeks, starting on 1 May and finishing 1 October each year.

chunks.title: work ability
chunks.text:
## work ability
A client's work ability takes into account a number of things, including:
- the skills and attributes they can bring to the work place
- the type of work they can do now and in the future
- the things they do at work
- the number of hours they can work
- their motivation and confidence to work

chunks.title: Work Capacity Medical Certificate
chunks.text:
## Work Capacity Medical Certificate
A Work Capacity Medical Certificate provides information to help determine a person's eligibility for a benefit.
Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability requires a Work Capacity Medical Certificate, or other medical certificate with equivalent information, to determine eligibility and activity obligations.
This medical certificate can also be used to determine if people on other benefits are unable to meet work related obligations or to determine eligibility to Supported Living Payment on the ground of having a health condition, injury or disability or being totally blind.
The Work Capacity Medical Certificate contains information about the person's medical conditions, capacity for work, duration they are expected to be unable to work and their ability to undertake work related activities.
The Work Capacity Medical Certificate is available in hard copy and most general practitioners and nurse practitioners have an electronic version in their Patient Management System to complete and print for their client or submit to Work and Income through e-Lodgement.
The completed electronic medical certificate will present information in a different format.

chunks.title: working-age
chunks.text:
## working-age
For the purposes of employment and work readiness assistance, working-age means a person aged:
- 18 to 64 years inclusive or
- 65 years or older if they are not qualified to receive New Zealand Superannuation
For the purposes of Relocate for Work Support, working-age means a person aged:
- 18 to 64 years inclusive or
- 65 years or older if they are not qualified to receive New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: working day
chunks.text:
## working day
Any day of the week other than:
- Saturday, Sunday, Waitangi Day, Good Friday, Easter Monday, Anzac Day, the Sovereign's birthday, Te Rā Aro ki a Matariki/Matariki Observance Day, Labour Day and
- is not a day in the period starting with the 25th day of December in any year and ending with the 15th day of January in the following year and
- the anniversary day observed in the appropriate province

chunks.title: Working for Families assistance
chunks.text:
## Working for Families assistance
Working for Families is a package designed to help make it easier to work and raise a family. It is delivered by Inland Revenue and the Ministry of Social Development.
Working for Families assistance includes:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Childcare Assistance and
- Working for Families Tax Credits
Working for Families Tax Credits include:
- Best Start tax credit
- family tax credit
- in-work tax credit
- minimum family tax credit
Note Best Start tax credit replaced the Parental Tax Credit from 1 July 2018 for children born on or after 1 July 2018. Some Parental Tax Credit payments continued after 1 July 2018 for children born before 1 July 2018.

chunks.title: Working for Families Tax Credits
chunks.text:
## Working for Families Tax Credits
Working for Families Tax Credits is financial help that Inland Revenue pays to qualifying families with dependent children. It includes:
- Best Start tax credit - replaced Parental Tax Credit from 1 July 2018 for children due or born, on or after that date
- family tax credit
- in-work tax credit
- minimum family tax credit
For more information contact Inland Revenue

chunks.title: young person
chunks.text:
## young person
For clients not participating in the youth service, a young person means a person aged at least 16 year but under the age of 20 years.
For clients participating in the youth service, a young person means a person aged at least 15 years but under the age of 18 years.

chunks.title: youth support payments
chunks.text:
## youth support payments
Youth support payments are:
- Young Parent Payment
- Youth Payment

chunks.title: YSSU
chunks.text:
## YSSU
The Youth Service Support Unit (YSSU) is responsible for making decisions on behalf of Work and Income and for the general administration of Young Parent Payment and Youth Payment.

chunks.title: Employment and training
chunks.text:
## Employment and training
Work and Income provides a range of employment and work readiness assistance to help clients move toward and remain in unsubsidised work.
The types of assistance available are targeted to improve client employment and social independence in the community and focuses on those at risk of long term benefit receipt.
There are two types of assistance available:
- Specific employment-related assistance
- Employment and work readiness assistance
To help clients to move into or remain in unsubsidised work a combination of these products and services can be used.

chunks.title: Actual and reasonable costs — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Actual and reasonable costs
Actual and reasonable costs are those costs for items or services a client incurs to undertake an activity or to enable the client to transition into employment. These costs can be 'one-off' or 'ongoing'.
When assessing the actual and reasonable costs a client may incur, consider the following:
- what activity is the client going to undertake
- what item or service is the client purchasing
- does the client already have the item or service, if so, why is this item or service being purchased again
- does the client have the ability to fund the item or service from their own resources
- can the item or service be funded from another source
- if the item or service is not funded, will the client be able to undertake the activity or transition into employment
- what is the least amount for the item or service being purchased
Discuss with the client their needs and responses to the above questions to assess the appropriate amount of assistance required to meet their needs and document these discussions.
In addition consider:
- is the employer responsible for providing the items (for example safety equipment, and uniforms)
- has Ministry of Social Development assistance previously been used to pay for the item

chunks.title: Additional educational support costs for Mana in Mahi — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Additional educational support costs for Mana in Mahi
Additional financial assistance is available to assist a Mana in Mahi participant with additional educational support costs.
These costs include (but are not limited to):
- literacy and numeracy training eg the cost of tutors
- equipment relevant to their work or course that would allow them to work from home eg modem, desk chair, desk, school books, stationery etc
## Payment
The actual and reasonable costs of the additional educational support costs can be paid, but not more than $2,000 (including GST) in total over 1 year.

chunks.title: Asset limit — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Asset limit
Clients applying for some types of employment and work readiness assistance may need to have assets below certain limits.
For more detailed information see:
- Cash assets
- Deskfile Employment and Training information

chunks.title: Assistance to enter self-employment — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Assistance to enter self-employment
Assistance to enter self-employment supports eligible clients to investigate or enter self-employment by providing two types of assistance.
## Business advice and reporting
Financial assistance to assist a client to investigate or enter self-employment by meeting the costs of:
- business skills training
- developing a business plan
- obtaining business advice before and during the start-up period of the person's business
- obtaining an independent vetting report and
- obtaining a post business start-up financial report
## Business start-up costs
Financial assistance to assist a client who is entering self-employment to meet essential business start-up costs of (but not limited to):
- leasing premises
- purchasing or leasing plant or equipment (including legal fees) and
- obtaining insurance
## Flexi-wage self-employment
Flexi-wage self-employment provides a short-term wage subsidy to clients who want to start up their own business and need financial support while they get started.
Flexi-wage self-employment is not included in the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme.
## Payment
Business advice and reporting
Business training and advice grant can pay the costs for a client to investigate or enter self-employment. A client can make more than one application for assistance, but the total amount cannot be more than $5,000 in a 52-week period.
Business start-up costs
Clients entering self-employment can get up to $10,000 in a 52-week period to meet essential business start-up costs. The total business start-up costs cannot be used to pay for any living costs or costs covered by the business training and advice grant.

chunks.title: Assistance to transition into employment — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text: Assistance to transition into employment provides assistance to clients to meet the costs of moving into employment or to move from one job to another. Assistance to transition into employment can include actual and reasonable costs for (but not limited to): - the cost of any uniform, clothing, equipment, or special footwear reasonably required for the client to start employment that are not met by the employer clothing, footwear, or equipment the employer is required to supply to comply with the employer's obligations under the Health and Safety in Employment Act 1992 cannot be considered for payment - the costs of participating in an employment interview - bridging finance to cover the client's living costs for up to 4 weeks between: the ending of the main benefit and the first payment of wages or salary from the employment ortheir last payment of wages or salary in their previous job and their first payment of wages or salary in their new job (when the gap between jobs is 4 weeks or less) - the ending of the main benefit and the first payment of wages or salary from the employment or - their last payment of wages or salary in their previous job and their first payment of wages or salary in their new job (when the gap between jobs is 4 weeks or less) full-time students undertaking employment during the period between the end of an academic year and the start of the next academic year are not eligible for bridging finance - the cost of an interpreter - the cost of tattoo removal if the applicant is referred to a tattoo removal service by a registered health practitioner - job placement expenses that a client needs to: - enter employment (other than training costs) - relocate their place of residence to take up employment. Assistance to transition into employment may be paid to clients seeking work or working less than 30 hours per week for job placement and transport to job interview costs where it is reasonable and appropriate.

chunks.title: Income and asset test — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text: Clients applying for assistance to transition into employment may need to have income and assets below certain limits. For more information see: - Income limit - Asset limit Work Bonus reduces the amount of bridging finance payable under assistance to transition into employment dollar-for-dollar. For more information see: - Bridging finance and Work Bonus

chunks.title: Payment — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text: Assistance to transition into employment can pay for the actual and reasonable costs to enter employment, but not more than $1,500 in total during a 52-week period. For more information see: - Actual and reasonable costs - Work Bonus - Qualifications - Commencement date - Changes and reviews - Deskfile Transition to Work Grant rates - Transition to Work [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Assistance when caring for another person — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Assistance when caring for another person
When a client is a carer, they may be able to get financial assistance to help pay for a care-provider, and any associated costs, so the client can:
- get or stay in employment
- participate in education or
- attend employment-related training
Education or employment-related training must be level 7 or below on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework.
This assistance is available for:
- childcare
- the care of an elderly person or
- the care of a person with a health condition, injury or disability
and
- any associated costs (eg transport to the care-provider)
## Payment
This financial assistance helps pay for the actual and reasonable costs to care for another person that exceed any financial assistance provided by any other publicly funded source (eg transport to the care-provider).

chunks.title: Bridging finance and work bonus — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Bridging finance and work bonus
Work Bonus will reduce the amount of bridging finance payable under assistance to transition into employment dollar-for-dollar. Both payments provide non-recoverable assistance for a transitional period when the client leaves a main benefit to move into employment.
Bridging finance cannot be paid if the total Work Bonus payable for the first 2 weeks following the date of the last payment of the main benefit is equal to or more than $500.
If the Work Bonus payments are less than $500 over the fortnight, the amount of bridging finance payable in respect of a week is reduced by each whole dollar amount of Work Bonus payable in that week.
For more information see:
- Actual and reasonable costs
- Specific employment related assistance Work Bonus
- Specific employment related assistance Work Bonus and Transition to Work Grant
- Qualifications
- Commencement date
- Changes and reviews
- Transition to Work [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Career guidance and information services — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Career guidance and information services
Career guidance and information services are services contracted to assist clients to make informed educational, work, and career-related choices.
The types of programmes and services that can be contracted are:
- career and education guidance
- curriculum preparation
- improving interview skills
## Payment
Payment for career guidance and information services is the contract price of the services agreed with the provider (GST inclusive).
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Commencement date
- Work readiness assistance
- Changes and reviews
- Career Guidance [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Cash assets — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Cash assets
Cash assets mean the assets of the client and their partner (if any) and, if applicable, the person or persons upon whom a dependent child is reliant on for financial support. A cash asset is an asset that can be easily converted into cash.
## Cash assets include
- bills of exchange or promissory notes
- building society shares
- money in bank accounts, including fixed term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society
- money invested with or lent to any bank, other financial institution or person
- money withdrawn from a KiwiSaver scheme
- mortgage investments and other long term loans
- shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds and other bonds
- the applicant's share in any partnership and
- the net equity held in any property or land not used as the person's home
## Cash assets do not include
- a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity of less than $2,000 or which is used by the client or a member of their family for day to day accommodation
- a home property and land on which it is situated
- a motor vehicle principally used by the client for private use
- Christchurch mosques attack support payments
- Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments
- ex-gratia payments made to a client or their partner infected with Hepatitis C through the New Zealand blood supply, for the first 12 months following the date the client received the payment
- Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income
- funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts
- MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to a system processing error from 1993 to 2014
- Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after payment is made
- Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after payment is made
- personal effects
- Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- specified Ex gratia and compensation payments
- FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received
Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or a resource available to a client.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — employment and work readiness assistance > changes and reviews employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client must advise Work and Income of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their eligibility to employment and work readiness assistance.
You may also check their eligibility to employment and work readiness assistance at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.
For more information see:
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit
- Core policy Reviews and appeals
- Imprisonment

chunks.title: Definition of imprisonment — employment and work readiness assistance > changes and reviews employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Definition of imprisonment
A person is regarded as serving a sentence of imprisonment if they are detained in any of the following:
- a prison
- a police jail
- remand prison
Note a prisoner who has escaped from custody is considered to be serving a sentence of imprisonment.
They may be serving a term of:
- imprisonment
- preventive detention or
- corrective training
Note people remanded in custody or serving a term of imprisonment who are temporarily hospitalised for treatment of an injury or illness are still considered to be in prison. However, where a prisoner serving a sentence of imprisonment is detained in or transferred to, a psychiatric hospital they may qualify for financial assistance from Work and Income.
For more information see:
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals

chunks.title: Imprisonment — employment and work readiness assistance > changes and reviews employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Imprisonment
Generally, when client is imprisoned or in custody, they are no longer entitled to get employment and work readiness assistance.
The employment and work readiness assistance should stop from the day following the date of imprisonment or remanded in custody.
MSD must decide whether to temporarily stop or cancel the employment and work readiness assistance considering the likely period in prison (including when the client is being held on remand).
## Release from prison or on bail
A client may be entitled to employment and work readiness assistance when they are released from prison or on bail if they meet the qualifications. If a client was receiving employment and work readiness assistance prior to their imprisonment, the date to recommence payment will be the same date as the client returned to their subsidised employment.
## Care and protection concerns
If a sole caregiver is remanded in custody and/or sentenced to a term of imprisonment, the case must be referred to Oranga Tamariki.
In other situations, if MSD believes any child has been, or is likely to be, harmed (physically, emotionally or sexually), ill-treated, abused, neglected, deprived or MSD has concerns about the wellbeing of the child, the case must be referred to Oranga Tamariki.

chunks.title: Clients who have a health condition, injury or disability — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Clients who have a health condition, injury or disability
Clients who have a health condition, injury or disability can receive extra or specialist assistance by way of purchasing services or wage subsidy (or both) to assist them to:
- take up paid employment or self-employment
- return to paid employment or self-employment
- retain paid employment or self-employment
There are two types of assistance a client may receive. These are purchase of services and a wage subsidy.
## Purchase of services
Purchase of services provides extra or specialist assistance and includes (but not limited to):
- health services
- disability services
- modifications to the workplace or equipment
- additional transport costs
- mentoring
- workplace support
## Wage subsidy
Wage subsidy is the purchase of an employment placement for a client with a health condition, injury, or disability to gain employment skills and to obtain unsubsidised employment
Note a client can receive both the purchase of services and a wage subsidy.
## Payment
The type of assistance a client is receiving will determine how this assistance is paid.
## Purchase of services
The amount paid for actual and reasonable costs for the purchase of services is generally reduced dollar for dollar by any amount of publicly funded assistance for the same or a similar purpose available to the client.
## Wage subsidy
The amount paid as a wage subsidy is a weekly amount of not more than the amount of the person's wage or salary calculated on a weekly basis before the deduction of income tax.
Note all amounts paid to purchase services and wage subsidies are GST inclusive.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Commencement date
- Changes and reviews
For more information programmes and services see:
- Job Support - Overview [no link find out why]
- Mainstream Employment Programme [no link find out why] procedures
- Mainstream Internship [no link find out why] procedures
- Modification Grant - Overview [no link find out why]
- Providing Access to Health Solutions (PATHS) [no link find out why] procedures
- Support Funds [no link find out why]
- Targeted Health Interventions (THI) [no link find out why] procedures
- Training Support - Overview [no link find out why]
- Vocational Services for People with Disabilities [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Commencement date — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
The commencement date of employment and work readiness assistance will vary depending on the type of programme or service provided.
Generally, the commencement date is the date:
- the client's wage subsidy starts (normally the date the client starts subsidised employment)
- the client starts attending their employment-related training
Note a lump sum payment for course fees can be made prior to the client attending the course to ensure their placement. Ongoing costs can only start from the date the client starts attending their course.
or
- the client starts attending the programme or service
Note some types of assistance do not have a commencement date as they are one-off payments and can be considered before the programmes and services start.
## Example
Client is to start a course at the local polytechnic. They have been accepted onto the course, subject to the tuition fees being paid. An assessment is completed with two lump sum payments made for fees and books. An ongoing payment for transport is also assessed.
In this situation, the start date is in 2 weeks (the date the course commences) but two lump sum payments for fees and books can be paid before the course start date.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Employment and Work Readiness Assistance
- Changes and reviews

chunks.title: Costs for work, study, or employment-related training — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Costs for work, study, or employment-related training
Support for work, study, or employment-related training provides financial assistance for additional costs to support clients, for a specified period, participating in the following activities:
- employment
- study in an education course
- employment-related training or
- an activity we think is likely to improve the person's work readiness
Financial assistance for longer education and training courses are only for level 3 courses or below on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework.
The type of assistance provided will depend on the activity the client is undertaking. For the types of assistance see:
- Longer term education or training courses Training Incentive Allowance
- Short-term training Course Participation Assistance [no link find out why] procedures
Income and assets
Clients applying for some types of assistance may need to have income and assets below certain limits. For more information see: Income limit and Asset limit

chunks.title: Education and employment-related training — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text: The aim of education and employment-related training is to purchase, for clients with specific employment skills deficits, a place in either an educational or an employment-related course.

chunks.title: Short-term training course — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text: A placement in a short-term training course can be purchased for a client who has specific employment skills deficits. The short-term training course must be: - employment-related and - no longer than 12 weeks duration Clients participating in a short-term course may apply for assistance to help with some of the costs they may have to attend the course. Currently only Course Participation Assistance is approved to provide assistance for short-term training courses.

chunks.title: Longer education or training courses — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text: Clients undertaking a longer education or training course may be eligible for Training Incentive Allowance to cover the actual costs they have from attending to attend their course of study. Whether the client meets the eligibility depends on their specific circumstances and benefit type. The longer education or training course must: - improve the client's skills for employment and future employment opportunities and - be a level 7 course or below on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework and - be a recognised course of study For more information see: - Training Incentive Allowance

chunks.title: Education or training courses for Mana in Mahi participants — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text: A placement for a Mana in Mahi participant can be purchased on an educational course or an employment-related training course. The placement must be for an education or training programme that is Level 7 or below on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (or an equivalent international qualification).

chunks.title: Income and assets — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text: Clients applying for education and employment-related training assistance may need to have income and assets below certain limits. For more information see: - Income limit - Asset limit

chunks.title: Payment — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text: Short term course The actual and reasonable fees charged by a training provider up to $1,000 in a 52-week period. Longer education or training courses Training Incentive Allowance is paid for the actual costs a client has from attending a course up to a maximum of $143.08 (as at 1 April 2026) per week of the course, (maximum $5,723.20 a year as at 1 April 2026). These payments are not income and asset tested. Education or training courses for Mana in Mahi participants Payment towards course fees charged by the provider of up to $8,000 (plus GST) over 1 year. Note the total payment does not need to be reduced by any payment made under Additional educational support costs associated with Mana in Mahi.

chunks.title: Employment and work readiness assistance — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Employment and work readiness assistance
Employment and work readiness assistance is discretionary and aims to improve client outcomes (employment and social) by moving clients and their partners (if any) closer to independence.
This assistance primarily focuses on those at risk of receiving a benefit long term by granting special assistance to help:
- a client or partner become ready for work by reducing barriers to their employment
or
- a client or partner who is ready for work, facilitate their transition into, and retention of sustainable employment

chunks.title: Employment assistance — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Employment assistance
Employment Assistance is discretionary and aims to improve client outcomes (employment and social) by moving clients and partners (if any) closer to independence.
This assistance primarily focuses on those at risk of receiving a benefit long term by granting special assistance to help a client or partner facilitate transition into, and to retain sustainable employment.
## Income and assets
Clients applying for some types of assistance may need to have income and assets below certain limits. See: Income limit and Asset limit
For more information see:
- Assistance when caring for another person
- Assistance to enter self-employment
- Assistance to transition into employment
- Clients who have a health condition, injury or disability
- Incentive payments
- Job search assistance, employment placement, and in-work support services
- Wage subsidy
- Qualifications
- Commencement date
- Specific employment-related assistance
- Changes and reviews

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances
Generally, payments for work confidence, motivational assistance and wage subsidies cannot be more than the maximum amount.
If a client has exceptional circumstances and needs additional assistance, the maximum amount of assistance can be exceeded for:
- work confidence and motivation assistance
- wage subsidies
When determining if a client has exceptional circumstances you may consider (but are not limited to):
What activity is the client going to undertake
Does the client have the ability to undertake employment now without any further work confidence or motivational assistance, or wage subsidy
Does the client have the ability to fund the item or service from their own resources
Can the item or service be funded from another source
If the work confidence and motivation assistance or wage subsidy is not funded will the client be able to undertake the activity or transition into employment
What is the least amount for the item or service being purchased
Has the Ministry of Social Development assistance previously been used to pay for the item? If yes, what circumstances does the client have that requires MSD to fund this again?
Note any payment for work confidence or motivational assistance or a wage subsidy in excess of the maximum amounts payable within a 52-week period, must be approved by your manager client service delivery or higher.

chunks.title: How to make a decision on programmes and services — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## How to make a decision on programmes and services
When making a decision on the programmes and services that may be appropriate for a client and taking into account the matters to be considered when providing programmes and services and the needs of a client, you will need to document the following:
- is the client in a target group identified for support
- given the skills and experience of the client, is this assistance effective in gaining employment outcomes
- how much employment and training assistance has the client received in the past
- what is the client's risk or likelihood of long term benefit receipt [no link find out why]
- without this assistance would the client be able to find work
- what other factors are relevant (eg prison record, tattoos)
- is the programme or service available
For more information see:
- Matters to consider when providing programmes and services

chunks.title: Incentive payments — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Incentive payments
Incentive payments are approved programmes or services relating to employment and work readiness assistance. There is currently 1 type of incentive payment available.
## Mana in Mahi
Mana in Mahi (Strength in Work) is a wage subsidy and provides other assistance to support people who are disadvantaged in the labour market. People getting Mana in Mahi can get an incentive payment specifically for them.

chunks.title: Incentive payments for Mana in Mahi — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Incentive payments for Mana in Mahi
Incentive payments can be made to a Mana in Mahi participant to encourage them to continue in the programme.
## Payment
Incentive payments are paid in 3 instalments of $1,000 over 1 year when the participant achieves attendance or training milestones, (up to a maximum of $3,000 in total over 1 year).

chunks.title: Income limit — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Income limit
Clients applying for some types of employment and work readiness assistance may need to have income below certain limits.
Income includes:
- the client's income
- the income of any partner
If a client is currently receiving a benefit, they would usually qualify under the existing benefit income test.
For more information about what income includes and does not include see:
- Core Policy Definition of income

chunks.title: Job search, employment and in-work support services — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Job search, employment and in-work support services
Job search assistance, employment placement and in-work support services are programmes and services designed for clients at risk of long-term benefit dependency to support their pre-employment and post-employment placement. For more information see:
- Likelihood of long term benefit receipt (LLTBR) [no link find out why]
## Payment
Job search assistance, employment placement and in-work support services payment is the contract price for the relevant services as agreed with service providers.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Commencement date
- Changes and reviews
For more details on programmes and services available see:
- Enhanced Taskforce Green [no link find out why]
- Skills for Industry [no link find out why]
Note Skills for Industry includes Training for Work and industry partnerships.

chunks.title: Matters to consider when providing programmes and services — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text: When the Ministry of Social Development provides programmes and services through the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme, some matters must be considered to determine the need for the programmes and services. Matters that need to be considered are: - paid employment offers the best opportunity for clients to achieve social and economic well-being - the priority for clients of working age should be to find and retain work - clients for whom work may not currently be an appropriate outcome should be assisted to prepare for work in the future and develop employment focused skills - clients for whom work is not appropriate should be supported by the Ministry of Social Development - any key result areas and performance targets - the principle that employment and work readiness assistance: is available to all people within New Zealand's working-age population, or young persons at risk of long-term benefit receipt, and prioritised for those at greatest riskwill be monitored, evaluated, and where practicable, based on evidence of 'what works'resources will be allocated where the potential benefits are greatestshould minimise adverse impacts on the labour market and should not substitute or displace people within New Zealand's workforce - is available to all people within New Zealand's working-age population, or young persons at risk of long-term benefit receipt, and prioritised for those at greatest risk - will be monitored, evaluated, and where practicable, based on evidence of 'what works' - resources will be allocated where the potential benefits are greatest - should minimise adverse impacts on the labour market and should not substitute or displace people within New Zealand's workforce - any policy of the Government relating to employment and work readiness assistance or a specified kind of employment and work readiness assistance - the client or their partners work-related obligations (if any) depending on whether the client or their partner has been granted a main benefit or has a stand-down period and have: full-time work-test obligations orpart-time work-test orwork preparation obligations - full-time work-test obligations or - part-time work-test or - work preparation obligations - whether the client left their employment voluntarily or lost employment due to misconduct and - whether the client is or may be entitled to any other publicly funded assistance for the same or a similar purpose from the Ministry of Social Development or any other agency Note when considering the matters above, your decision must be recorded. For more information see: - How to make a decision on programmes and services

chunks.title: Income and assets — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text: Clients applying for some types of assistance may need to have income and assets below the relevant limits. For more information see: Income limits and Asset limits For more information see: - Employment and Work Readiness Assistance - Qualifications - Commencement date - Employment assistance - Work readiness assistance - How to make a decision on programmes and services - Likelihood of long term benefit receipt [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Participation allowance — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Participation allowance
Clients receiving a benefit and participating in an activity in the community project may receive a non-taxable allowance to cover participation-related expenses. This allowance is not regarded as income for benefit purposes and therefore will not affect any benefit that a client may be receiving.
Participation allowance is paid at the same rate for both full-time and part-time activity in the community projects.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Commencement date
- Payment calculations
- Actual and reasonable costs
- Work readiness assistance
- Changes and reviews
- Activity in the Community payments Participation Allowance [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Payment calculations — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Payment calculations
A deduction for absence is only applied in the case of non-attendance for a full day.
Examples for non-attendance include (but are not limited to):
- health condition
- leave
- holidays
- bereavement
A deduction is not made if the client makes up the time missed with the sponsor.
## Calculation
Participation Allowance is paid to reimburse a client for expenses incurred while undertaking an activity in the community project they have chosen. The amount of Participation Allowance payable is calculated on a daily basis.
Whenever a client is absent, payment should be calculated using the table below. The amounts shown in the table are those that the client will receive. For example, where the project is for 3 days per week and the client did not attend 2 days, the amount payable is $7.00.
