chunks.title: Qualifications — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for employment and work readiness assistance, clients must:
- be a young person or of working-age
- meet the residence requirements
- not have received the maximum amount payable for any particular kind of employment and work readiness assistance, unless, for that assistance (where applicable), exceptional circumstances exist
Clients are also required to:
- be receiving a main benefit or
- be the partner of another client getting a main benefit or
- have applied for and been assessed as eligible for a main benefit or
- have been receiving a main benefit that has been cancelled because they have moved into employment or
- have applied for a main benefit but need to complete a pre-benefit activity or
- have contacted the Ministry of Social Development or a contracted service provider seeking assistance to obtain or retain employment or
- be applying for Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury, or disability, or total blindness) or
- not currently getting Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) as the client is working in an employment trial, for a period of time agreed with the Ministry of Social Development or
- be receiving New Zealand Superannuation or a Veteran's Pension as a grandparented non-qualified partner
Clients may also need to:
- meet other eligibility criteria specified in: the schedule to the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme andoperational guidelines
- the schedule to the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme and
- operational guidelines
- have income and assets under the relevant limits for some assistance
- be at risk of long-term benefit receipt
Any employment and work readiness assistance must not be granted for any employment, training, activity, or service located or provided outside New Zealand.

chunks.title: Residence — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Residence
To be granted employment and work readiness assistance, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or be a deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 that allows the client or partner to work in New Zealand
or
- be recognised as a refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009
or
- hold a temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 that permits the person to work in New Zealand and who is: awaiting the outcome of their claim for recognition as a refugee or a protected person ora person applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 who is compelled to remain in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances
- awaiting the outcome of their claim for recognition as a refugee or a protected person or
- a person applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 who is compelled to remain in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances
and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit
Note clients who have a residence class visa as they have been sponsored, may need to provide proof that their sponsor cannot provide employment and work readiness assistance.

chunks.title: Wage subsidy — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Wage subsidy
Wage subsidies are paid to an employer on behalf of an eligible client assessed to be at risk of long-term benefit dependency.
The subsidy amount and duration offered to employers will reflect the level of assistance required to support the client to develop the skills required to obtain, or retain unsubsidised employment.
These include:
- Flexi-wage subsidy
- Flexi-wage Self-employment
## Payment
The weekly amount of a Flexi-wage wage subsidy cannot be more than the amount payable for 30 hours of employment at the minimum rate of wage payable to an adult worker paid by the hour (GST inclusive), unless exceptional circumstances exist.

chunks.title: Work confidence and motivation assistance — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Work confidence and motivation assistance
Work confidence and Motivation assistance programmes are contracts with providers designed to help clients who are at risk of long-term benefit dependency [no link find out why] . The aim of these programmes and services are to increase a client's:
- motivation
- confidence
- job searching skills or
- for overcoming factors that impede their entering or continuing employment, or both, including domestic and social circumstances or drug or alcohol use
## Payment
The total amount to purchase services providing work confidence or motivation assistance cannot exceed $10,000 (GST included) within a 52-week period unless exceptional circumstances exist.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Commencement date
- Exceptional circumstances
- Work readiness assistance
- Changes and reviews
- Client Self Help [no link find out why] procedures
- Limited Service Volunteer (LSV) [no link find out why] procedures
- Outward Bound [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Work experience, activity in the community, and voluntary work — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Work experience, activity in the community, and voluntary work
Work experience, activity in the community and voluntary work provides activities for clients to participate that develop work skills, increase self-confidence and social skills, or find out what they may be good at.
The activities a client can undertake can include an activity in the community.
## Payment
Payment of assistance is limited to the actual and reasonable costs of purchasing the opportunity to gain work experience, participate in an activity in the community or voluntary work.
To assist a client with childcare and transport costs a client may be able to get a small weekly allowance depending on the activity. For more information see: Participation allowance

chunks.title: Work readiness assistance — employment and work readiness assistance
chunks.text:
## Work readiness assistance
Work readiness assistance is discretionary and aims to improve client outcomes (employment and social) by getting clients and their partners (if any) work ready and closer to independence.
This assistance primarily focuses on those at risk of receiving a benefit long term by granting special assistance to help a client or partner:
- to staircase to employment and
- transition into, and retain sustainable employment
Income and assets
Clients applying for some types of assistance may need to have income and assets below certain limits. See: Income limit and Asset limit
For more information see:
- Costs for work, study, or employment-related training
- Career guidance and information services
- Education and employment-related training
- Work confidence and motivation assistance
- Work experience, activity in the community and voluntary work
- Qualifications
- Commencement date
- Employment assistance
- Specific employment-related assistance
- Change and reviews

chunks.title: Specific employment-related assistance — specific employment related assistance
chunks.text:
## Specific employment-related assistance
Specific employment-related assistance are products and services targeted towards moving clients into or to help support clients stay in employment.
Specific employment-related assistance can be provided to clients in specific situations.
## Historical assistance
The assistance listed below is no longer available:
- COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme
- COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme
- COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment
- COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified)
- COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension
- COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021)
- COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021)

chunks.title: Applications for assistance — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Applications for assistance
Employers must apply for Apprenticeship Boost through the Work and Income website. Applications can be made for existing apprentices in their first 12 months of study, and any new apprentices who start study, while the programme is available.
Before any payments are made, the employer and the apprentice must consent to their information being shared with other government agencies so their eligibility can be assessed. For the employer, this includes MSD providing information about the employer (legal name, trading name, IRD number and email address) to Inland Revenue for verification.
Before any payments are made:
- an application must be completed, and any necessary supporting evidence received (including a signed consent form from each apprentice) and
- the Tertiary Education Commission must confirm the apprentice eligibility criteria are met
## Application date
The application date is either the date the employer:
- submits their completed online application or
- first creates their online account (and they submit their completed online application and supporting evidence within 20 working days from this date)

chunks.title: Apprentice also gets a benefit or extra help — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Apprentice also gets a benefit or extra help
Some apprentices and their families may be getting financial assistance from MSD (main benefit, extra help etc).
Apprenticeship Boost payments are paid to the apprentice's employer and are not chargeable income for the client's (or their partner's, if any) main benefit, extra help or any other assistance paid under the Social Security Act 2018.

chunks.title: Apprentice changes employer — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Apprentice changes employer
If an eligible apprentice changes employer and their previous employer was getting Apprenticeship Boost payments for them, their new employer can also get Apprenticeship Boost payments for them from the date the new employer and apprentice are both eligible.
This means there may be an overlapping period of eligibility, if there are eligible days for both employers within a single month. When this occurs, payments can be made to both employers for that overlapping month of study or payment period.

chunks.title: Apprentice changes provider — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Apprentice changes provider
If an apprentice changes their provider their eligibility to Apprenticeship Boost will be re-assessed by the Tertiary Education Commission.
This includes a change of provider resulting from the Reform of Vocational Education.
A provider is:
- a Transitional Industry Training Organisation or
- Te Pūkenga - New Zealand Institute of Skills and Technology, including one of its subsidiaries or
- a Wānanga or
- a Private Training Establishment
Any changes will take effect from the next scheduled monthly payment of Apprenticeship Boost.

chunks.title: Apprentice eligibility — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Apprentice eligibility
To be eligible for Apprenticeship Boost, the apprentice must:
- be enrolled and engaged in an apprenticeship programme that is: delivered or arranged by a provider andapproved by the Tertiary Education Commission as a New Zealand Apprenticeship or Managed Apprenticeship anda programme of study in at least one eligible New Zealand Standard Classification of Education (NZSCED) narrow field and
- delivered or arranged by a provider and
- approved by the Tertiary Education Commission as a New Zealand Apprenticeship or Managed Apprenticeship and
- a programme of study in at least one eligible New Zealand Standard Classification of Education (NZSCED) narrow field and
- have not completed more than 12 months of their apprenticeship programme and
- not have had their enrolment withdrawn or put on hold and
- be in paid employment or a paid contracting arrangement with the employer (applicant)
## Providers
A provider is:
- a Transitional Industry Training Organisation or
- Te Pūkenga - New Zealand Institute of Skills and Technology including one of its subsidiaries or
- a Wānanga or
- a Private Training Establishment

## Confirming apprentice eligibility
The Tertiary Education Commission will tell MSD whether an apprentice meets the eligibility criteria to get the Apprenticeship Boost payment including:
- what month of study the apprentice is in, both at the time of the application and on an ongoing basis and
- if there are any subsequent changes to the month of study and
- whether an apprentice's study includes any earlier apprenticeships that are the same or similar

chunks.title: Apprentice withdraws their consent to share information — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Apprentice withdraws their consent to share information
Employers must tell MSD if their apprentice withdraws their consent to share their information for the Apprenticeship Boost Initiative.
Any payments for the apprentice will be stopped from the next scheduled payment as eligibility cannot be established.

chunks.title: Changes in circumstances — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Changes in circumstances
Employers need to tell us about changes in their circumstances that may affect their eligibility to Apprenticeship Boost payments.
These changes could include (but are not limited to) the apprentice:
- leaving their employment
- remaining employed with the same employer but not actively studying towards their qualification e.g. extended/unpaid leave
- changing to another apprenticeship

chunks.title: Commencement date — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
Commencement date is the later of the:
- application date or
- eligibility date
The application date is either the:
- date the employer submits their completed online application or
- date the employer first creates their online account (and they submit their completed application and supporting evidence within 20 working days from this date)
The eligibility date is the date the employer and their apprentice meet the eligibility criteria for Apprenticeship Boost.

chunks.title: Contractor relationship — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Contractor relationship
An apprentice may be a self-employed contractor working under an arrangement with an organisation. The organisation must have a training agreement with the apprentice and provider.
Apprenticeship Boost may be paid to the organisation contracting an eligible apprentice.

chunks.title: Effective date of a change in circumstances — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Effective date of a change in circumstances
When an employer advises MSD of a change in circumstances that means they or their apprentice no longer meet the eligibility criteria for Apprenticeship Boost, no further payment(s) for the employer and/or apprentice will be made for any payment period starting on or after the date of change.
## Change during a payment period
When an employer or apprentice has a change of circumstances that occurs during a particular payment period, the change will take effect from the start of the employer's next payment period.
Example
An employer completes the declaration for their payment period from 8 September to 7 October and gets a monthly payment. The apprentice finishes employment with the employer on 18 September.
The employer is still entitled to their payment for the apprentice for the payment period from 8 September to 7 October because the apprentice was still employed by them for some of the payment period.
The employer is not eligible for payment for the apprentice in the next payment period from (8 October to 7 November).
## No longer eligible but will be eligible again in the future
When an employer declares that an apprentice will no longer be eligible, they can become eligible again in the future.
Example
An employer completes a declaration for their payment period from 5 January to 4 February. The employer then tells MSD one of their apprentices included will be on unpaid leave from 13 January for 8 weeks. Payment of Apprenticeship Boost will stop for this apprentice from the next payment period, starting 4 February.
On 28 February, the employer tells MSD the apprentice will be back at work from 10 March to resume their apprenticeship. The apprentice can be included in the next payment period that includes 10 March (5 March to 4 April).

chunks.title: Employer eligibility and obligations — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Employer eligibility and obligations
To be eligible for Apprenticeship Boost an employer must:
- apply for assistance, including the provision of any supporting evidence required by MSD and
- be a person or registered business who employs a person, or engages a self-employed contractor, who is an eligible apprentice
Employers must also agree to the conditions set out in the online declaration, including that they will:
- support their apprentice's continued employment and training
- comply with their obligations under the Minimum Wage Act 1983 for the apprentice
- tell MSD of any change in circumstance for themselves or their eligible apprentices
## Employers that are not eligible
An employer is not eligible for Apprenticeship Boost if they are a state sector employer.
For a list see:
- Te Kawa Mataaho | Public Service Commission Central government organisations
An employer is also not eligible for Apprenticeship Boost if:
- they are getting a specified wage subsidy for an eligible apprentice for the same period or
- their apprentice is a volunteer, undertaking unpaid work experience, on a short-term work trial, or in an unpaid internship

chunks.title: Employers getting specified wage subsidy for an apprentice for the same period — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Employers getting specified wage subsidy for an apprentice for the same period
Employers getting a specified wage subsidy for the apprentice will not be eligible for Apprenticeship Boost payments for the same period.
Specified wage subsidies are:
- Mana in Mahi assistance paid under the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme
- Regional Apprenticeships
- assistance paid under the Flexi-wage subsidy
- wage subsidy component of the Māori Trades and Training Fund
## Change of employer
If an employer is getting a specified wage subsidy (e.g. Mana in Mahi) for an apprentice and the apprentice changes employers, the new employer may still apply for, and get, Apprenticeship Boost for the apprentice.
In this situation, there may be an overlap between the former employer's final payment period for the Mana in Mahi wage subsidy and the new employer's payment period for Apprenticeship Boost.
An overlap in payment periods is allowed when an apprentice has changed their employer.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Apprenticeship Boost helps employers with the costs of keeping their current apprentices or hiring new ones for up to 12 months of their programme of study. This payment helps apprentices to stay in their jobs so they can earn and progress towards their level 4 qualifications. This helps train and provide a more skilled workforce.
The Apprenticeship Boost Initiative is an education programme administered by MSD with support from the Tertiary Education Commission.

chunks.title: Monthly declarations — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Monthly declarations
Each month employers make a declaration that they are eligible to get payments for their eligible apprentices.
Payments will not be made until a declaration has been received.
Most employers complete a declaration each month. If an employer does not do this for any month, any outstanding payments will only be made after the relevant declaration has been received.

chunks.title: Monthly payment instalments — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Monthly payment instalments
Apprenticeship Boost payments are paid 1 month in advance in full amounts ($500 - excluding GST per apprentice).
Before payments can be made, employers need to confirm they and their apprentice are still eligible (through the monthly declaration). Provided the employer completes their monthly declaration on time, payments will normally be made on the same day every month (based on the commencement date).
## Hiring additional apprentices
Employers may already get Apprenticeship Boost payments and then hire more apprentices. When a new apprentice(s) is included, the employer will get a one-off monthly payment (of $500 excluding GST) then the new apprentice(s) will be added to the employer's existing payment schedule date.
For example an employer applies for Apprenticeship Boost for 7 apprentices on 3 January 2025 and gets paid $3,500 excluding GST (7 x $500) for the payment period from 3 January to 2 February.
They add another apprentice to their account on 10 January and are paid a one-off payment of $500 for the new apprentice. The employer's next payment period is from 3 February to 2 March, which includes a monthly payment for all 8 of their apprentices (8 x $500).
Note if the Apprenticeship Boost commencement date starts on the 29th, 30th or 31st of a month, the payment period start will be moved to the 28th of the next month.

chunks.title: Overpayments of Apprenticeship Boost — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Overpayments of Apprenticeship Boost
Every month employers will need to confirm they meet the eligibility to get Apprenticeship Boost.
If an employer gives MSD incorrect information on the declaration and they do not meet the eligibility criteria, MSD will review their payments and a debt will be created for payments the employer was not eligible for.

chunks.title: Payments — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Payments
Payment is based on the apprentice's month of study under the apprenticeship programme as at the employer's declaration point.
From 1 January 2025, the rate of payment is:
- $500 per month (excluding GST) / $575 (including GST) for apprentices in their first 12 months of training (1 - 12 months inclusive)
This rate applies to any payment period starting on or after 1 January 2025.
GST is added to Apprenticeship Boost payments for GST registered employers.
## Employer has changes that affects their next payment
If an employer has a change of circumstances that affects their eligibility, they need to tell MSD on or before the declaration for their next payment.
This will ensure the payments of Apprenticeship Boost they have already received will not be affected and their next payment can be changed or stopped.
There are no partial payments in this scheme.
## Payment periods that started before 5 August 2022
Before 5 August 2022, the rate of payment for Apprenticeship Boost was based on the apprentice's year of study under the apprenticeship programme as at the employer's declaration point.
These rates were:
- $1,000 per month (excluding GST) / $1,150 (including GST) for apprentices in their first year of training (1 - 12 months inclusive)
- $500 per month (excluding GST) / $575 (including GST) for apprentices in their second year of training (13 - 24 months inclusive)
The above rates apply to any monthly payment periods that start before 5 August 2022.
Example
An employer's monthly payment period is from 4 August 2022 to 3 September 2022. For this payment period, the employer will be paid:
- $1,000 (excluding GST) per month for any eligible apprentices in their first year of training and
- $500 (excluding GST) per month for any eligible apprentices in their second year of training
The employer's next monthly payment period is from 4 September 2022 to 3 October 2022. For this payment period, the employer will be paid $500 (excluding GST) per month for each eligible apprentice in either their first or second year of training.

chunks.title: Review and Appeal rights — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Review and Appeal rights
Employers have review and appeal rights under the Social Security Act 2018.
MSD relies on information from the Tertiary Education Commission to determine apprentice eligibility. If there are any concerns about apprentice eligibility, MSD will refer it back to the Tertiary Education Commission for review.
If the incorrect information was given to MSD, we will reconsider the decision based on updated information from the Tertiary Education Commission.

chunks.title: Specific employment situations — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Specific employment situations
An apprentice's employment situation and status in New Zealand may vary, this may affect whether they are eligible to get Apprenticeship Boost payments.

chunks.title: Standard employment relationship — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Standard employment relationship
An apprentice must be in paid employment to be eligible for Apprenticeship Boost. The apprentice does not have to be full-time to get Apprenticeship Boost but they need to meet all the eligibility criteria.
Employers need to submit monthly declarations and once this has been done, the Apprenticeship Boost payment will be made to employers who are eligible.

chunks.title: Training Agreement — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Training Agreement
Tertiary Education Commission funded and approved New Zealand Apprenticeships and Managed Apprenticeships require there to be a signed training agreement in place between the provider, apprentice and employer.
If an apprentice withdraws from their training agreement, they will no longer be eligible for Apprenticeship Boost payments, until their training agreement is reinstated.

chunks.title: Voluntary work — specific employment related assistance > apprenticeship boost
chunks.text:
## Voluntary work
An apprenticeship may involve volunteering in New Zealand under an arrangement with an organisation (e.g. Habitat for Humanity).
The Apprenticeship Boost payment is not available to volunteer apprentices as the organisation is not keeping the apprentice in paid employment.
This also applies to anyone undertaking unpaid work experience, short-term work trials and unpaid internships.

chunks.title: Affected groups — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Applications for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme closed after 11.59pm on 10 October 2023. An employee was in an affected group if they could not go to work and were unable to work from home because they: - were required to self-isolate in line with public health guidance because they had COVID-19 or - are a parent or caregiver of a dependant who was required to self-isolate in line with public health guidance because they had COVID-19 or - a member of their household was in the category of people who were at 'higher risk' of severe illness from COVID-19 (as defined in public health guidance) and had been advised to self-isolate by a medical practitioner

chunks.title: Public health guidance — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Public health guidance determines who is required to self-isolate and the duration of their self-isolation. Public health guidance changes frequently. Phase 1 Under Phase 1 of the Government's Omicron plan, from 26 January 2022 to 11.59pm 15 February 2022, public health guidance required people to self-isolate if they: - had COVID-19 (required to self-isolate for 14 days) - were a close contact of a person who has COVID-19 (required to self-isolate for 10 days) Phase 2 Under Phase 2 of the Government's Omicron plan, from 16 February 2022 to 11.59pm 24 February 2022, public health guidance required people to self-isolate if they: - had COVID-19 (required to self-isolate for 10 days) - were a household contact of someone who had COVID-19 (required to self-isolate for 10 days) - were a close contact, but not a household contact, of someone who had COVID-19 (required to self-isolate for 7 days) Phase 3 Under Phase 3 of the Government's Omicron plan from 25 February 2022 to 11.59pm 12 September 2022, public health guidance required people to self-isolate if they: - had COVID-19 (required to isolate for 7 days) - were a household contact of someone who had COVID-19 (required to self-isolate for 7 days). Test Day 3 and Day 7 of the case's isolation, or if symptomatic Close contacts were no longer required to self-isolate from 25 February 2022. September 2022 - Changes to self-isolation requirement The public health guidance on COVID-19 and self-isolation requirements have changed and from 11.59pm 12 September 2022 household contacts are no longer required to self-isolate. Public health guidance requirements for self-isolation from 11.59pm 12 September 2022 are that people who have COVID-19 were required to self-isolate for 7 days. Also see: - COVID-19 Manatū Hauora - Ministry of Health NZ An employee (or their dependants) could have been required to self-isolate by the Director-General of Health, or the Minister of Health under the COVID-19 Public Health Response Act 2020 or a medical officer of health under the Health Act 1956.

chunks.title: Public health guidance — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Note the requirement to isolate by the Director-General of Health, or the Minister of Health is not used often. Public health guidelines are the main way of deciding if a person needs to self-isolate. August 2023 - Removal of public health requirements for self-isolation From 12.01am 15 August 2023 people were no longer required to self-isolate due to COVID-19. Applications for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme closed after 15.59pm on 10 October 2023. This was 8-weeks after the mandatory requirement to self-isolate due to COVID-19 was removed. For more information see:

chunks.title: Some businesses cannot get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Applications for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme closed after 11.59pm on 10 October 2023. Businesses can no longer get financial assistance under this scheme. The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme could not be paid to businesses for their employees who: - were a household contact of a person who had COVID-19 if the employee was not required to self-isolate in line with public health guidance - were a contact of a person who had COVID-19 if the employee was not required to self-isolate in line with public health guidance - had COVID-19-like symptoms and were staying home while waiting for a test result, but could return to work if the test result was negative - are New Zealanders who were overseas - were voluntarily choosing to self-isolate but were not required to under public health guidance or as advised by a medical practitioner - were unable to work for any other reason, for example, bereavement or because day-care was not available for an employee's children

chunks.title: Must retain employees and follow employment law when paying wages or salary — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Businesses who got the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme must have kept the employees (for whom they received the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme) in their jobs for the period of the subsidy (unless the employee voluntarily ended the employment relationship). They could not make changes to the employment agreement without the written agreement of the employee. To meet the eligibility criteria and obligations for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme businesses must have made their best efforts to pay at least 80% of each named employees' ordinary wages or salary for the period of the subsidy, as per their employment agreement at the date the business applied for the subsidy. Businesses must have followed employment law. When the employee was earning less than the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme rate, the business must have paid their ordinary wages or salary while they were off work. Any difference should have been used to pay other affected employees. When there were no other affected employees to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other affected employees were already being paid their ordinary or average wages or salary, the business must have told MSD and repaid the remaining subsidy as it was not able to be used for wages. If a person is self-employed and their regular income from their business was less than the subsidy amount they received, they must have repaid any surplus to MSD. If businesses have questions about their obligations under employment law, they should contact Employment New Zealand. For more information see: - Employment New Zealand - Coronavirus (COVID-19) and the workplace

chunks.title: Businesses must meet their obligations under other laws — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Businesses must have met their obligations under existing employment law, including continuing to have: - paid the employee's lawful entitlements and - complied with the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015

chunks.title: Amount a business must pay an employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Amount a business must pay an employee
The amount the business (including self-employed people) must pay an employee, depends on whether the employee's ordinary or average wages or salary are under, or over the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme rate applied for them, and any obligations they have under employment law.
To meet the obligations of the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, a business must pay at least the subsidy rate, when the employee's ordinary or agreed average wages or salary is more than the rate of subsidy paid to the business for them.
An employee who earns less than the subsidy paid to the business for them must be paid their ordinary or average wages or salary.
Note this does not affect the obligations a business has under employment law.
## Calculating employees' pay
Step 1 - Calculate pay based on actual hours
Calculate the employee's pay based on the actual number of hours in their employment agreement.
Actual hours x hourly rate
Amount A = $
Step 2 - Calculate pay based on average hours
Calculate the employee's pay based on the agreed average number of hours the employee has worked each week.
Average hours x hourly rate
Amount B = $
Step 3 - Compare actual and average pay
Compare the employee's pay based on the number of hours in their employment agreement (Amount A) against their pay based on the agreed average hours (Amount B) to identify the higher amount.
Actual hours x hourly rate
Average hours x hourly rate
Amount A = $
Amount B = $
Step 4 - Compare actual or average pay against subsidy rate
The higher amount from Step 3, either Amount A or Amount B, is compared against the amount of the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme paid to the business for the employee to identify the lower amount.
Step 5 - Calculate the amount of subsidy to be paid
If the employee's pay based on either actual or agreed hours (whichever is applicable) is lower than the subsidy rate paid to the business for them, this is the amount the business must pay their employee.
The business must use the remaining subsidy amount to pay other employees' wages or the business must repay this amount to the Ministry of Social Development if they have no other employees.
If the employee's pay is equal to or higher than the subsidy rate paid to the business for them, the business must pay the full amount of the subsidy to their employee.

chunks.title: Applications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Applications for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme closed after 11.59pm on 10 October 2023. At 12.01am 15 August 2023 the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme public health guidelines no longer required mandatory self-isolation due to COVID-19. The standard 8-week period for applications remained open for employees (or self-employed people) who were advised or required to self-isolate in line with public health guidelines before 12.01am 15 August 2023. This period has now ended, and no new applications will be accepted. People who began self-isolation for the period between 11.59pm on 12 August 2023 and 12.01am 15 August 2023 will not have self-isolated for 4 consecutive days. However, depending on when the employer applied they may have been entitled to COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme assistance. Employees (or self-employed people) advised or required to self-isolate after 11.59pm 12 August 2023 whose employer applied for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme before 12.01am 15 August 2023 qualified for the assistance, if they met all other eligibility criteria and complied with their obligations. This is because when the application was made the employer was declaring the employee's eligibility to the best of their knowledge. Note employees did not qualify if applications were made after 11.59pm 15 August 2023 for employees (or self-employed people) who were advised or required to self-isolate in line with public health guidelines for less than 4 consecutive days. As the mandatory requirement to self-isolate stopped from 12.01am 15 August 2023, 15 August is included as a whole day of isolation when considering the number of consecutive days a person has isolated for. Businesses (including self-employed people) must have applied online for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme. Payments were made as a lump sum to the business for each named employee (including self-employed people) who was self-isolating in line with public health guidance. A business may have been eligible for multiple payments of the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme (based on the self-isolation period of the affected employee) the employer must have applied for each payment as the previous payment ends. Each payment covered the number of consecutive days an employee could not work (rounded to the nearest 7 days).

chunks.title: Applications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Note applications for eligible employees made from 14 March 2022 for self-isolation periods ending before this date were accepted while the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is operating. Now that the scheme has closed, these applications are no longer accepted. Example 1 Bronson worked in a hotel as a concierge he got COVID-19 on 13 August 2023. Bronson began self-isolating. He immediately let his employer know and his employer applied for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme on 13 August 2023 to make sure that Bronson was financially supported for his 7-day self-isolation period. On 14 August 2023 it was announced that from 12.01am 15 August 2023 public health guidelines no longer required mandatory self-isolation due to COVID-19 so on 15 August 2023 Bronson returned to work because he was no longer symptomatic. Bronson's employer was granted the full COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme subsidy for Bronson because the application was made in good faith before any changes had been announced. Example 2 Paula worked full-time at a bar and could not work from home. She got COVID-19 on 13 August 2023. Paula began her 7 days of self-isolation and immediately let her employer know. On 14 August 2023, it was announced that from 12.01am 15 August 2023 public health guidelines no longer required mandatory self-isolation due to COVID-19. Paula stayed home on 15 August as she was still unwell. Paula felt better on 16 August. Paula's employer applied for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme on 16 August 2023 to cover the 3 days Paula was required to self-isolate. Although the application is made within 8-weeks from the end of Paula's self-isolation period, it was declined because Paula didn't meet the eligibility criteria of needing to self-isolate for at least 4 days. Note because the mandatory requirement to self-isolate stopped from 12.01am 15 August 2023, 15 August was included as a whole day of isolation when considering the number of consecutive days a person has isolated for. Example 3 Rita worked full-time in retail and could not work from home. She got COVID-19 on 13 August 2023. Rita began her self-isolation.

chunks.title: Applications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: On 14 August 2023 Rita told her employer she was self-isolating with COVID-19. Later that day, it was announced that from 12.01am 15 August 2023 public health guidelines no longer required mandatory self-isolation due to COVID-19 so on 15 August 2023 Rita returned to work because she was not symptomatic. Rita's employer applied for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme nearly a month later on 8 September 2023 to cover the 3 days that Rita was self-isolating. Although the application was made within 8-weeks from the end of Rita's self-isolation period, it was declined because Rita did not meet the eligibility criteria of needing to self-isolate for at least 4 days. Note because the mandatory requirement to self-isolate stopped from 12.01am 15 August 2023, 15 August was included as a whole day of isolation when considering the number of consecutive days a person has isolated for.

chunks.title: Business advised by employee they are in an affected group — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Business advised by employee they are in an affected group
Applications for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme closed after 11.59pm on 10 October 2023.
To be eligible for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, the business (or the self-employed person) must have declared they were advised by their employee they were in an affected group.
Note an employee (or self-employed person) must have been considered in an affected group on or before 12.01am 15 August 2023.
For more information see:
## Businesses required to prepare and retain evidence
Businesses were required to prepare and retain evidence in support of applications demonstrating their employees (or themselves if they are self-employed) were self-isolating for at least 4 consecutive days because they could not work from home and are in an affected group. MSD may request this evidence.
Examples of evidence that may be requested from businesses are, but are not limited to:
- employee leave records (to demonstrate employees were not working at that time)
- communications to customers from self-employed persons to advise them they are self-isolating and are not operating their business at this time
- notifications from an official source (eg Ministry of Health) that a self-employed person was required to self-isolate
- other information that a self-employed person has available to demonstrate they were advised to self-isolate (eg medical certificate from their GP)
## Employees staying home waiting for a COVID-19 test result
Businesses with employees who were staying home waiting for a COVID-19 Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) test result were not eligible to get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for those employees.
If the employee's test result was positive the employer could then apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme.

chunks.title: Business dismisses employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Business dismisses employee
Businesses must agree when they get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.
If a business decides to dismiss an employee for reasons other than redundancy, for example, because of serious or repeated misconduct, for performance issues, or if the employee abandons their employment, the business is no longer eligible for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme subsidy for this employee.
The business does not have to repay the subsidy already paid but they must use the balance towards paying the wages or salary of other affected employees.
If the business has no other affected employees for whom to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other affected employees are already being paid their ordinary wages or salary, the business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining subsidy that could not be used for wages or salary.
The business must follow existing employment law for dismissing an employee.
## Example
Fahima employs 5 staff at her cafe. One of her employees has underlying health conditions and the employee's doctor has advised them to self-isolate for 10 days. The employee cannot work from home. Fahima applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme to continue paying this employee while they are in self-isolation.
The employee was going through a disciplinary process at the time they were advised to self-isolate, and the process concludes while the employee is still in self-isolation. Fahima decides to dismiss the employee based on their repeated misconduct, with the dismissal effective immediately.
As Fahima got the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for this employee, Fahima uses the remaining funds to contribute to the wage costs of her other affected staff.

chunks.title: Business is registered and operating in New Zealand — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Business is registered and operating in New Zealand
A business is registered and operating in New Zealand when they are:
- registered with the New Zealand Companies Office and
- physically located in New Zealand and
- their employees legally work in New Zealand
## Sole traders and self-employed people
Sole traders and self-employed people are not required to be registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, but must have:
- a personal or business Inland Revenue number for paying income tax and/or GST and
- government licences and permits for their business needs where appropriate and
- qualifications or registrations required for their trade or profession
Sole traders and self-employed people must still meet the requirements to be physically located and are employed in New Zealand.
The Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed before paying the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme.

chunks.title: Business makes employee redundant — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Business makes employee redundant
If a business makes an employee redundant during the period they are getting the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for that employee, and the employee will remain employed until the end of the subsidy period, the business can use the subsidy to pay the employee until the end of the subsidy period.
However, if the employee does not remain employed until the end of the subsidy period, the business can use the subsidy to pay the person until the end of their employment but must repay the remaining subsidy back to the Ministry of Social Development.
The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme cannot be used to pay for notice periods extending beyond the subsidy period for that employee. In addition, it cannot be used to pay any other redundancy payments under the employee's employment contract (including any leave payments) or beyond the confirmed redundancy date if that date is extended.
The employee is not required to pay any subsidy back to the business that they have already received.
Businesses who have given their employees notice of redundancy before they apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme are not eligible to get the subsidy for those employees unless the redundancy notice is withdrawn.

chunks.title: Businesses must follow employment law when paying wages or salary — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Businesses must follow employment law when paying wages or salary
The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme must be used by businesses to support the cost of wages or salary for the employees named in their application, for the duration of the subsidy period.
Businesses must pay their employees any amount required by the employment agreement and employment legislation. The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme requirements do not remove or reduce this obligation.
Businesses may agree with their employees to reduce hours or to reduce their hourly rate during this period (but not lower than the minimum wage). However, businesses must follow current employment law when reducing an employee's wages or salary or changing the hours they work.
No business can make a blanket rule that employees take annual leave during the COVID-19 public health restrictions, but the business and employee can agree for the employee to take annual leave.
In this situation the employee should be paid their ordinary wages or salary for their normal hours of work and the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme will help businesses pay for the annual leave taken.
Businesses must follow due process.
## If businesses need more information see:
- Employment New Zealand Coronavirus (COVID-19) and the workplace

chunks.title: Business must meet their obligations under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Business must meet their obligations under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015
Businesses must continue to meet their obligations under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 during the COVID-19 Protection Framework. This means businesses must eliminate work, health and safety risks, and if they cannot eliminate them, minimise as much risk as reasonably practical.
For an employee who has identified themselves as being at high risk by public health guidance if they carry out their work, the business needs to eliminate the risk for the employee where they can, for example by having the employee work from home, or in a way that does not bring them into contact with others.
The business should discuss the controls they put in place with their affected employees and Health and Safety representatives. If the business does nothing to eliminate or minimise the risk to these employees, they may be found in breach of their duties under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015.
A business cannot be paid the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for people who choose not to go to work because they are concerned adequate steps have not been taken to protect them from the risk of becoming infected with COVID-19.
However, the employee may be eligible for this assistance if they are in one of the affected groups (ie they are considered 'higher risk' of severe illness if they get COVID-19, or their household members are considered 'higher risk', and are advised to self-isolate for at least 4 consecutive days by a medical practitioner).

chunks.title: Business not entitled but has been paid — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: If a business (including self-employed people) applied for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, and then they have a change in circumstance within the payment period, they may not be entitled to keep the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme payment they got for an employee named in their application. Change of circumstances Employee voluntarily resigns. The business should use the balance of any of the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme to pay other affected employees named in their application. When there are no other affected employees, the business must contact the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy for this employee as it cannot be used for wages or salary. Employee has been made redundant. The business must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme remaining for the employee. The subsidy can be used to pay the notice period but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract and cannot be used to support other employees. Employee has been dismissed. The business should use the balance of any of the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme to pay other affected employees named in their application. When there are no other affected employees, the business should contact the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining subsidy for this employee as it was not able to be used for wages. Business has closed. The business must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme remaining for the employee. The subsidy can be used to pay the notice period but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract and cannot be used to support other employees. Employee is on fixed-term contract that ends during the period that the business is getting the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for them. The business must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme remaining for the employee at the end of the fixed-term contract. The business can use the subsidy to pay out any notice period, but it cannot be used to pay other entitlements or the wages of other employees. The business applied for the wrong type of COVID-19 scheme for their employee (eg applied for the Wage Subsidy in error). The business must repay any amount they got for the incorrect application and re-apply for the correct scheme they are entitled to. The business applied for the wrong type of COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme rate for their employee, eg applies for full-time when the person was part-time.

chunks.title: Business not entitled but has been paid — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: The business must repay the difference between the full-time rate they got and the part-time rate to which they were entitled. Employer is a state sector organisation who did not have an exception approved by the Minister of Finance to apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme but applied and received the funds. Note this also applied to State-Owned Enterprises and Mixed Ownership Model companies before 14 March 2022. From this date onwards they did not need an exception The business is not entitled to the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme and must repay it in full. Any state sector employers who disagree with the decision should consult with their monitoring agency. Business gets payment they are not entitled to due to a Ministry of Social Development office error (eg their application might have been paid twice or accidentally approved instead of declined). The business is not entitled to the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme and must repay it to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Business requires assistance for same employee for multiple weeks — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Business requires assistance for same employee for multiple weeks
If the business requires assistance for the same employee after the payment period, the business can apply again.
They can apply again when both the business and the employee for whom they are applying continue to meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations, and the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is still available.
## Example
Tana has been advised to self-isolate for 8 days by his doctor while he is recovering from chemotherapy. The business requires assistance to help fund Tana's wages while he remains at home.
The business gets one payment for Tana.
However, Tana's doctor changes the advice to self-isolate to 16 days because Tana is still recovering. The business applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme again and is granted another payment based on the number of days he needs to self-isolate.

chunks.title: Deciding if someone is self-employed — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Deciding if someone is self-employed
A person is likely to be self-employed when they carry out business activities on their own, including contracting, working as a sole trader or owning a small business.
A self-employed person is likely to:
- support the business with their own money (eg providing all the equipment or tools they needed for their job)
- decide or control how they work (eg when, where and what hours they work)
- decide how much they get paid and how
- pay their own income tax (unless they are a young person earning under the tax threshold)
- be responsible for investment decisions and any losses
- be able to sell the business if they wanted to
The above list is not a full list. There may be other things that can be considered.
Self-employed people may apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, provided they meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations.

chunks.title: Dependant required to self-isolate and needs support — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Dependant required to self-isolate and needs support
Applications for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme closed after 11.59pm on 10 October 2023.
From 12.01am 15 August 2023 the public health guidelines no longer required mandatory self-isolation due to COVID-19.
Parents or caregivers of a dependent who were required to self-isolate for at least 4 consecutive days may have needed to help their dependent to self-isolate safely.
For the purposes of the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, a dependent is someone who is primarily the responsibility of the employee and needed support to self-isolate. This includes a dependent child or another person who needed support to self-isolate for reasons such as disability, illness or advanced age.
Businesses who were advised by their employee they were in this group could apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme if the employee could not work from home, and the business met the other eligibility criteria and complied with their obligations.

chunks.title: Eligible businesses — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Eligible businesses
The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is available across all sectors and industries in New Zealand for businesses, with eligible employees, including:
- businesses using any or multiple employment types including full-time, part-time, casual, fixed-term, sole trading and self-employment, including those businesses with employees getting the minimum wage exemption and disabled people who employ people through individualised funding arrangement
- registered charities, incorporated societies, local government organisations (eg local councils), non-government organisations and post-settlement governance entities
- State-Owned Enterprises and Mixed Ownership Model companies (from 14 March 2022)
## State-Owned Enterprises and Mixed Ownership Model companies
From 14 March 2022, State-Owned Enterprises and Mixed Ownership Model companies can access the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme without the need to seek an exception from the Minister of Finance.
State-Owned Enterprises are:
- Airways Corporation of New Zealand Ltd
- Animal Control Products Ltd
- AsureQuality Ltd
- Electricity Corporation of New Zealand Ltd
- KiwiRail Holdings Ltd
- Kordia Group Ltd
- Landcorp Farming Ltd
- Meteorological Service of New Zealand Ltd
- New Zealand Post Ltd
- New Zealand Railways Corporation
- Quotable Value Ltd
- Transpower New Zealand Ltd
Mixed Ownership Model companies are:
- Genesis Energy Ltd
- Mercury NZ Ltd
- Meridian Energy Ltd
## Other state sector organisations
Other state sector organisations are generally not eligible to get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for their employees.
Exceptions for state sector organisations are considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, through the relevant monitoring agency.
Some state sector organisations have been granted an exception by the Minister of Finance and can apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme.

chunks.title: Employee is required to self-isolate — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Employee is required to self-isolate
Applications for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme closed after 11.59pm on 10 October 2023. From 12.01am 15 August 2023 the public health guidelines no longer required mandatory self-isolation due to COVID-19.
The standard 8-week period for applications was open for people who were required to self-isolate under public health guidance on or before 12.01am 15 August 2023. This period has now ended.
People who were COVID-19 cases and were required to self-isolate after 11.59pm 12 August 2023 whose employer applied for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme before 12.01am 15 August qualified for the assistance, if they met all other eligibility criteria and complied with their obligations.
This is because when the application was made the employer was declaring the employee's eligibility to the best of their knowledge.
Note applications made after 11.59pm 15 August 2023 for employees who were required to self-isolate in line with public health guidelines for less than 4 consecutive days were not accepted.
## Previous Settings - Household contacts
Employees who were identified as a contact of someone who has COVID-19 were required to self-isolate for a period in line with public health guidance to limit the spread of COVID-19. They could have been referred to as a household and/or close contact, depending on the public health settings at the time.
Some employees who were contacts may have been required to self-isolate without getting a test (i.e. they are a probable case), or may have been told to get a test and continue self-isolating even if they return a negative test result.
Businesses who were advised by their employee that they were in this group can apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme if the employee:
- could not work from home or
- was required in line with public health guidance or
- was advised by a medical practitioner to self-isolate for at least 4 consecutive days and
- the business met the other eligibility criteria and complied with their obligations
Note public health guidance determines who is required to self-isolate including the duration of their self-isolation and is subject to change. At times contacts may have been told to self-monitor for symptoms rather than self-isolate, so will not be eligible for the scheme.

chunks.title: Employee (or someone in their household) at 'higher risk' of severe illness from COVID-19 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Employee (or someone in their household) at 'higher risk' of severe illness from COVID-19
Applications for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme closed after 11.59pm on 10 October 2023.
From 12.01am 15 August 2023 the public health guidelines no longer required mandatory self-isolation due to COVID-19. Therefore new applications for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for those advised to self-isolate were no longer available.
Public health guidelines provided advice on the groups who are at 'higher risk' of severe illness if they get COVID-19.
The groups who are at 'higher risk' include:
- people with underlying medical conditions
- people aged 70 years or older
- pregnant women
Businesses and employees should check the public health guidelines at COVID-19.govt.nz for more detail. An employee may have been eligible if they had been advised to self-isolate by a medical practitioner.
If their medical practitioner advised the employee to self-isolate before 12.01am 15 August 2023, for a period of at least 4 consecutive days because they are at 'higher risk' of severe illness if they get COVID-19 (in line with public health guidelines), the business could apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme if the business and employee met the other eligibility criteria and the business complies with their obligations.
Note even if a medical practitioner has advised continued self-isolation after 12.01am 15 August 2023 the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme was no longer be available for ongoing self-isolation after this date.
For more information see:
## Someone in their household
To be eligible for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme the person who is at 'higher risk' of severe illness if they get COVID-19 must have lived in the same household as the employee.
Businesses who were advised by their employee that a person who they live with is at 'higher risk' of severe illness if they get COVID-19 (in line with public health guidelines), and they had been advised by a medical practitioner to self-isolate for a period of at least 4 consecutive days, were eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme if the employee could not work from home, and the business meets the other eligibility criteria and complied with their obligations.

chunks.title: Employee voluntarily leaves — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Employee voluntarily leaves
Businesses must agree, when they get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.
If an employee voluntarily leaves their employment, the business must advise the Ministry of Social Development, and the business cannot get any more COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme payments for this employee.
The business does not have to repay the subsidy already paid but they must use the balance towards paying the wages or salary of other affected employees.
If the business has no other employees for whom to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other affected employees are already being paid their ordinary wages or salary, the business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme subsidy that could not be used for wages or salary.

chunks.title: Employee's ordinary wages or salary less than the subsidy rate — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Employee's ordinary wages or salary less than the subsidy rate
If the employee's ordinary wages or salary were less than the subsidy rate when the business applied for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, the business must keep paying their ordinary wages or salary for the duration of the subsidy period.
Businesses must use the remaining support towards topping up the wages or salary of other affected employees, so that they are being paid their ordinary wages or salary.
When there are no other affected employees to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other affected employees are already being paid their ordinary wages or salary, the business must repay the remaining COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme back to the Ministry of Social Development as it could not be used for wages or salary.
If the person is self-employed, and their wages or salary from their business is less than the amount they got from the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example
Miri was required to self-isolate for 7 days when she got COVID-19 (before 12.01am 15 August 2023). Miri usually earns $220 (gross) per week.
Her employer gets the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme rate of $359 (gross) per week.
Because Miri usually earns under the subsidy rate, the employer must pay her wages or salary for 1 week at the rate they would have been paid before she went into self-isolation. That is, her wages of $220 (gross) per week (less any usual wage deductions).
Miri's employer can use the remainder of the support to pay wages of other affected employees their ordinary wages.
When there are no other affected employees, or the other affected employees are already getting their ordinary wages, the business must repay the remainder back to the Ministry of Social Development as it was not used for wages.

chunks.title: Employee's ordinary wages or salary more than the subsidy rate — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Businesses who get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme must make their best efforts to pay employees their ordinary wages or salary, or at least 80% of each named employee's ordinary wages or salary for the period of the subsidy. If paying 80% of ordinary wages or salary is not possible and the employee was usually earning over the subsidy rate applied for, the business must pay the full weekly amount of the subsidy (less any usual wage deductions) to the employee. Any reduction in their pay to the subsidy rate requires good faith consultation and written agreement in line with existing employment law. However, given the short period that the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is intended to cover, it is unlikely there will be adequate time for most businesses to engage with employees to alter employment agreements. As such, most businesses would generally pay 100% of their employee's wages or salary for the duration of the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: John usually earns $956 (gross) per week. His employer can continue to pay 80% of his earnings ($764.80) while John is at home after being advised to self-isolate for 21 days because he is at 'higher risk' of severe illness if he gets COVID-19, and he cannot work from home. John and his employer agree in writing to reduce his wages for the period he cannot work. The business gets the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme rate of $600.00 (gross) per week and pays John $764.80 (gross) per week (less any usual wage deductions) for 1 week and the employer will be eligible to apply for a second payment based on the period of self-isolation.

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Mandy usually earns $1,000 (gross) per week but she is required to self-isolate for 7 days as she has COVID-19. Mandy cannot work from home and the business employing her is unable to pay 80% of her wages ($800) as well as covering the cost of a replacement employee while Mandy is self-isolating. The business and Mandy agree in writing to reduce her wages while she is self-isolating, and the business applies for a COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme payment. The business gets $600 (gross) per week for Mandy and because she usually earns over this amount, and the business cannot afford to pay anything more, the business pays Mandy the full amount (less any usual wage deductions) of the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme.

chunks.title: Employee's weekly hours more than employment agreement — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Employee's weekly hours more than employment agreement
Businesses with employees who have a set number of working hours in their employment agreement and work more hours should generally compare the average weekly wages or salary (gross) to the relevant subsidy rate (part or full-time) and are required to pay the lower amount.
The business must also consider what legal obligations they have under employment law to pay employees while they are not working. The business must make sure those obligations are met which may mean the employer needs to pay more than the subsidy amount.
## Example 1 - average weekly hours more than employment agreement
Mana works at an Early Childhood Centre they are self-isolating because they got COVID-19 and cannot work from home. Their employer intends to apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for Mana and must work out the rate they can apply for.
The number of hours Mana is required to work stated in their employment agreement is 15 per week but they have been working for more than 20 hours per week for almost a year.
Mana's manager calculates the average weekly hours Mana has worked over the last 12 months. Mana and their manager agree in writing that they have been working an average of 27 hours per week over that period.
The business gets a COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme payment at the full-time rate of $600. They must calculate how much of the COVID-19 Leave Support Payment (the subsidy) should be paid to Mana when paying wages.
1
Actual weekly hours x hourly rate = Amount A
15 x $31 = $465 (A)
2
Average weekly hours x hourly rate = Amount B
27 x $31 = $837 (B)
3
Compare Amount A against Amount B to identify the higher amount
$465 (A) - $837 (B)
4
Compare Amount B to the subsidy rate paid to identify the lower amount
(B) $837 or (subsidy) $600
5
The business must pay at least the full amount of the subsidy to Mana because their average weekly wage is higher than the subsidy rate.
(subsidy) $600

chunks.title: Employees with no set hours — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Businesses with employees who have no set hours in their employment agreement (ie casual workers) should calculate average weekly hours and compare this total (gross) to the relevant subsidy rate (part or full-time), and are required to pay the lower amount. The business must also consider what legal obligations they have under employment law to pay employees while they are not working. The business must make sure those obligations are met which may mean the employer needs to pay more than the subsidy amount.

chunks.title: Example 1 - Casual worker average wages more than subsidy — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Cara is a casual worker at a cafe', she only works when the business needs her during busy periods or when other employees are on leave. Cara gets COVID-19 and is required to self-isolate. Since Cara started her job two years ago, she has worked between 5 and 28 hours a week. The business calculates the average weekly hours Cara has worked over the last 12 months. Cara and her manager agree in writing that she has been working an average of 18 hours a week over that period. The business gets a COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme payment at the part-time rate of $359. 1 Actual weekly hours x hourly rate = Amount A 0 x $22 = $0 (A) 2 Average weekly hours x hourly rate = Amount B 18 x $22 = $396 (B) 3 Compare Amount A against Amount B to identify the higher amount $0 (A) - $396 (B) 4 Compare Amount B to the subsidy rate paid to identify the lower amount (B) $396 or (subsidy) $359 5 The business must pay at least the full amount of the subsidy to Cara because their average weekly wage is higher than the subsidy rate. (subsidy) $359

chunks.title: Example 2 - Casual worker average wage less than subsidy — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Jono is a casual worker at a pub, he only works when the is business is busy or when other employees are on leave. Since Jono started his job 8 weeks ago, he has worked between 5 and 13 hours a week. Jono gets COVID-19 and must self-isolate for 7 days. His manager calculates the average weekly hours Jono has worked over the last 8 weeks. Jono and his manager agree in writing that he has been working an average of 9 hours a week over that period. The business gets a COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme payment at the part-time rate of $359. 1 Actual weekly hours x hourly rate = Amount A 0 x $22 = $0 (A) 2 Average weekly hours x hourly rate = Amount B 9 x $22 = $198 (B) 3 Compare Amount A against Amount B to identify the higher amount $0 (A) - $198 (B) 4 Compare Amount B to the subsidy rate paid to identify the lower amount (B) $198 or (subsidy) $359 5 The business must pay the average wages to Jono because their average weekly wage is lower than the subsidy rate. The business can use the rest of the subsidy to pay the wages or salary of other affected employees. (B) $198

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Ailee works 10 hours per week at $22 per hour ($220 gross per week) at the supermarket while she is a student. Ailee is at 'high risk' of severe illness if she gets COVID-19 as she has a heart condition, and her doctor has advised her to self-isolate for 28 days. Ailee cannot work from home. The business is not able to cover the cost of Ailee's leave, as well as the additional cost of hiring replacement staff, so applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for her. Because Ailee's usual earnings are less than $359 (gross) per week, the business uses the subsidy to pay her ordinary wage of $220 (gross) per week for the payment period (less any usual wage deductions). The business must use the remaining COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme subsidy to contribute to the ordinary wages of other affected employees, and when there are no other employees, or the other employees are already being paid their ordinary wages, the business must repay the remaining subsidy back to the Ministry of Social Development

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Felix works 40 hours for a food wholesale warehouse. He has a medical condition that puts him at 'higher risk' of severe illness if he gets COVID-19 and his doctor has advised him to self-isolate for 14 days. He cannot work from home. He usually gets $756 (gross) per week. The business needs support to pay for COVID-19 related leave and provide cover for Felix while he is self-isolating. The business applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme and agrees in writing with Felix to reduce his pay to 80% of his ordinary wages ($604.80) during this period. The business gets the subsidy rate of $600 (gross) per week per application and tops the payment to Felix up to $604.80 (gross) per week (less usual wage deductions).

chunks.title: Example 3 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Stuart works 35 hours a week providing in-home care to allow elderly people to live in their homes. However, Stuart gets COVID-19 and is required to self-isolate for 7 days in line with public health guidance. Stuart cannot work from home. The business needs support to pay for COVID-19 related leave and pay someone else to care for Stuart's clients in his absence and applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme. Even with the support, the business is unable to pay Stuart his ordinary wages of $875 (gross) per week. The business and Stuart agree in writing to reduce his wages to the subsidy rate of $600 (gross) (less any usual wage deductions).

chunks.title: Example 4 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Hiria works 22 hours per week at a local cafe and usually earns $440 (gross) per week. Hiria's daughter is at 'higher risk' of severe illness if she gets COVID-19 as she has Type 1 diabetes that is not well controlled. Hiria is advised by her doctor that her daughter must self-isolate for 14 days. Hiria cannot work from home and the cafe cannot afford to pay her leave. They have other employees who are self-isolating, and cannot cover the cost of replacement employees. The business applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme to continue paying Hiria her ordinary wages of $440 (gross) per week.
