Her employer uses the remaining $160 of the weekly subsidy amount towards the cost of wages for another full-time affected staff member who earns more than the full-time COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme rate.

chunks.title: Fixed-term contract ends within payment period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is open to existing and newly hired employees, including employees on fixed-term contracts. To get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, businesses must agree to retain the employees named in their application for the duration of the subsidy period. Businesses can include employees on fixed-term contracts in their COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme application, even if the employee's contract is scheduled to end during the period that the business would be getting the subsidy for them (ie in the subsidy period from the date of application). However, if an employee's fixed-term contract ends during the payment period, the business will not have met their obligation to retain the employees named in their application. In these circumstances, the business can use the subsidy to pay out any agreed notice period for that employee, but the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme cannot be used to pay any other entitlements and it cannot be used to support the wages or salary of other employees. If the notice period is extended the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme cannot be used to pay the extended notice period. The business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and repay any remaining subsidy for this employee. The business and employee may agree to extend the contract to the end of the subsidy period in order to meet their obligations for the period they get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Anaru is on a fixed-term contract scheduled to end on 22 December 2021. His employer applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme on 18 December 2021 to continue paying Anaru as he has severe asthma and his doctor has advised him to self-isolate for 10 days. Anaru cannot work from home. The employer agrees with Anaru to extend his contract to 25 December 2021 to meet their obligations for the period they get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme. Anaru's employer is eligible to get the full COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme subsidy for Anaru.

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Sacha is on a fixed-term contract scheduled to end on 20 March 2022. Sacha lives with her 82-year old kuia (grandmother) who is considered 'higher risk' of severe illness if she gets COVID-19. Sacha's doctor has advised her to self-isolate for 21 days while cases of COVID-19 are widespread to reduce the risk to her kuia. Sacha cannot work from home. Sacha's employer applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme on 16 March 2022 and includes her in the application. When Sacha's contract ends on 20 March 2022, the employer returns the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Health and disability funded workforce — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Health and disability funded workforce
Health and disability funded workforces (such as businesses that provide community health care) not employed by the state sector are eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme if they meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations.
Health and disability funded workforces not employed by the state sector includes organisations that are contracted to, or funded in whole or part, by organisations in the state sector.
Examples include:
- in-home care workers
- employees in Primary Health Organisations
- nurses and other staff in rest homes or other residential care facilities (eg cooks, cleaners, support staff)
- health and disability facilities or services or get funding from the Ministry of Health, District Health Boards, or the Ministry of Social Development

chunks.title: Instruction to self-isolate — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Instruction to self-isolate
Applications for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme closed after 11.59pm on 10 October 2023.
From 12.01am 15 August 2023 the public health guidelines no longer required mandatory self-isolation due to COVID-19.
For a business to be eligible for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, the employee must have been in an affected group and were required or advised to self-isolate for at least 4 consecutive days and met the other eligibility criteria.
The requirement to self-isolate may have come from:
- public health guidelines
- a direction made under the Health Act 1956 or orders made under the COVID-19 Public Health Response Act 2020
- advice by a medical practitioner (for example, a GP) (as defined in the Health Act 1956)
## Instructions to self-isolate before 16 February 2022
Before 16 February 2022 the instruction to self-isolate for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme had to come from one of the following:
- National Investigation Tracing Centre or
- a medical practitioner (as defined in the Health Act 1956) or
- Director General of Health or the Minister of Health under the COVID-19 Health Response Act 2020 or
- a medical officer of health under the Health Act 1956
How an employee is notified of the requirement to self-isolate is no longer relevant for the purposes of eligibility for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme.
## Evidence
MSD may request the information businesses are required to prepare and retain in support of their applications demonstrating employees (or themselves if they are self-employed) were not working because they, or their dependents were self-isolating, for at least 4 consecutive days.

chunks.title: Other COVID-19 wage subsidy schemes — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Before 14 March 2022 a business could not get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, and any other COVID-19 subsidy (eg Wage Subsidy Support) for the same employee for the same period. The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment is available for businesses whose employees cannot work from home and need to miss work while staying home waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result, in line with public health guidance. This scheme is aimed at people who only need to be away from work while waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result. The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment ended on 17 October 2022. Any COVID-19 PCR tests taken on or before 22 August 2022 may still qualify for this assistance until the closure if all other eligibility criteria are met and obligations complied with. Businesses could not get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme and the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for the same employee at the same time. However, some businesses that got the Short-Term Absence Payment may subsequently apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme if their employee has COVID-19 and was required to self-isolate for a period of at least 4 consecutive days, including the days the employee was required to stay home (and could not work) while waiting for their test results. Businesses will need to ensure they meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations for the specific scheme they are applying for. Example 1 Hana is a landscaper and got a COVID-19 PCR test when she developed symptoms, her test was taken on 17 August 2022. The Unite against COVID-19 website stated that people in her situation should stay home while waiting for their test results, so Hana had to miss 2 days of work while staying at home. The business that employs her applied for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment and the payment was granted. Hana got a positive test result and was required to self-isolate for a further 7 days. The business that employs Hana can apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, if they meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations. The business is eligible for both schemes. For more information see:

chunks.title: Flexi-wage, Flexi-Wage Self-Employment and Mana in Mahi — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: If a business is currently getting the Flexi-Wage, Flexi-Wage Self-Employment, or Mana in Mahi subsidy for their employees, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, if they meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations. All wage subsidies the business is getting must be paid to their employees. For more information see:

chunks.title: Apprenticeship Boost — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Apprenticeship Boost helps businesses with the costs of keeping their current apprentices or hiring new ones for their first 12 months of their programme of study. If a business is currently getting Apprenticeship Boost for their employees, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for those employees, where appropriate. For more information see:

chunks.title: Main benefit and other support — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: If a self-employed person is currently getting a main benefit or other extra help from the Ministry of Social Development, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme. All Ministry of Social Development clients must meet their obligations in relation to the financial assistance they are getting, including declaring any income they get (if appropriate). When assessing an application staff must not check if an applicant for the subsidy is getting other financial assistance from the Ministry of Social Development, as this is a breach of Privacy.

chunks.title: Financial support from other agencies — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: There is a range of financial support available from other agencies for businesses who have been negatively impacted by the COVID-19 financial crisis. These schemes are separate to Work and Income support and have their own eligibility criteria. Businesses who meet the necessary eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations can apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme as well as these other schemes. Applicants need to ensure they meet the eligibility criteria and comply with the obligations for any schemes they apply for.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Applications for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme closed after 11.59pm on 10 October 2023.
The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme provided financial assistance from 28 April 2020 to businesses (including self-employed people) who were required to self-isolate due to COVID-19 public health restrictions.
From 12.01am 15 August 2023 the public health guidelines no longer required mandatory self-isolation due to COVID-19. The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme ended from 12.01am, 15 August 2023.
Businesses (or self-employed people) must have applied for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme within 8-weeks of the last day of their mandatory COVID-19 self-isolation that began before 12.01am on 15 August 2023. The last day applications could be accepted was 10 October 2023 (inclusive).
The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme provided financial assistance to businesses (including self-employed people) during the COVID-19 public health restrictions to:
- encourage employees to self-isolate (stay at home) when they needed to in line with public health guidelines and
- support employees unable to work from home, with an income while they could not work
The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme replaced the COVID-19 Essential Workers Leave Support Scheme and supported all businesses and employees who met the eligibility criteria and complied with their obligations at all settings under the COVID-19 Protection Framework and existing public health measures.
Businesses must have applied online. Payments were made as a lump sum to eligible businesses for each named employee (including self-employed people) who was self-isolating for at least 4 consecutive days, in line with public health guidance or as advised by a medical practitioner.
Applications for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for employees whose self-isolation period ended after 14 March 2022 must have been made within 8-weeks.

chunks.title: Legally working in New Zealand — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Legally working in New Zealand
Legally working in New Zealand means a person is both working in New Zealand and is legally entitled to work in New Zealand.
A person cannot be employed if they cannot legally work in New Zealand in that job.
It is the responsibility of the business to make sure that an employee can work for them legally.

chunks.title: Newly hired employees — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Newly hired employees
The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is open for eligible businesses to apply for any newly hired employees, and previous employees who have been re-hired before the business applies for the subsidy.
## Example 1
Charlie was due to start work in a restaurant but 2 days before his start date he gets COVID-19.
Charlie is required to self-isolate for 7 days, which means he cannot start work.
His employer applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme and is eligible for a payment for Charlie.
## Example 2
Deepa owns a clothing store and needs to hire a new employee. Deepa has completed interviews and the successful candidate is due to start work on Monday the following week.
On Sunday the new employee tells Deepa their dependent child has COVID-19 and is required to self-isolate for 7 days.
The new employee needs to stay home to care for their child, until the child's self-isolation period has ended.
Deepa applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme and is eligible for a payment for the employee until they can start their role.

chunks.title: Ordinary wages or salary — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Ordinary wages or salary
For employees, their ordinary wages or salary are specified in their employment agreement at the date the business applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for them. This includes any statutory obligations that the business must pay their employees (ie public holidays the employee would otherwise have been paid).
Self-employed people can determine their ordinary wages or salary by calculating the regular amount that is left over after they meet their business costs (as at the date that they apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme). This is the amount they regularly pay themselves as wages or salary from the business.
If the person is self-employed and the wages or salary from their business is less than the amount they got from the subsidy, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.
The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme can be used to support the costs of wages or salary, but cannot be used towards other business costs.

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is paid as a lump sum payment at the appropriate weekly subsidy rate for eligible employees who usually: - work 20 hours or more or - work under 20 hours The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is paid at a flat rate based on each named employee's contracted or average hours of paid employment: - $600 (gross) for 20 hours or more per week or - $359 (gross) for less than 20 hours per week A business can access the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for each eligible employee (commencing on the date of application) and can get further payments depending on the period of self-isolation for that employee (while the scheme is still open). They can also apply for other eligible employees at any point during the period the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is operating. Note from 12.01am 15 August 2023 the public health guidelines no longer require mandatory self-isolation due to COVID-19.

chunks.title: Example — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: A business accessed the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for an employee who was advised to self-isolate for 14 days and cannot work for this period. They are granted a payment and are eligible to apply for a second week based on the period of self-isolation. If the same business had a different employee needing support, they can apply for that employee too and get a payment for that employee as well, if they meet the eligibility criteria. The business may be eligible for further weekly payments for those employees, depending on the duration of the self-isolation period.

chunks.title: Calculating variable hours — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: For a self-employed person, or a business who has employees working variable hours, an average over a relevant period can be used to work out which rate to apply for. A relevant period for an employee who has been working for a year, would be an average over this period. For new employees or a person who has been self-employed for less than 1 year, generally an average over 8 weeks is appropriate, but the business can use another time period if it is more appropriate. For example, if using the period that the employee has been employed for would give a better representation of the employee's normal hours, then the business can use this time period instead. It is up to the business to agree with their employees in writing that the calculation of the employee's average hours is correct, to determine the appropriate COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme rate to apply for.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Mana works at an Early Childhood Centre, they are self-isolating because they got COVID-19 and cannot work from home. Their employer intends to apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for Mana and must work out the rate they can apply for. The number of hours Mana is required to work (stated in their employment agreement) is 15 hours per week but they have been working for more than 20 hours per week for almost a year. Mana's manager calculates the average weekly hours Mana has worked over the last 12 months. Mana and their manager agree in writing that they have been working an average of 27 hours per week over that period. The business applies for the full-time rate of the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for Mana.

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: Cara is a casual worker at a cafe', she only works when the business needs her during busy periods or when other employees are on leave. Cara gets COVID-19 and is required to self-isolate. Since Cara started her job two years ago, she has worked between 5 and 28 hours a week. Cara's manager calculates the average weekly hours Cara has worked over the last 12 months. Cara and her manager agree in writing that she has been working an average of 18 hours a week over that period. The business applies for the part-time rate of the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for Cara.

chunks.title: Maximum payment for a business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: There is no cap on the total amount of COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme payments a business can get, it is based on the number of employees they have, and whether they normally work 20 hours or more, or under 20 hours, and the duration of employees' self-isolation period.

chunks.title: August 2021 rate increase — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: On 24 August 2021, the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme rates increased from $585.80 to $600 per week for full-time employees, and from $350 to $359 per week for part-time employees. The increased rates apply for all applications made on or after 24 August 2021. equanimity

chunks.title: People on casual contracts — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## People on casual contracts
Businesses can apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for employees who are on casual contracts, but they must keep them employed for the subsidy period.
Businesses can apply for the Leave Support Scheme for the hours the employee is usually employed. Businesses need to agree with their employees what their hours would usually be during this period, to determine the appropriate COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme rate to apply for.
If an employee's casual work ends during the subsidy period, then the business will not have met their obligation to retain the employees named in their application.
The business must notify the Ministry of Social Development and repay any remaining subsidy for this employee.

chunks.title: People on fixed-term contracts — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## People on fixed-term contracts
Businesses can apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for their employees who are on fixed-term contracts as long as they keep them employed for the subsidy period.
If an employees fixed-term contract ends during the subsidy period, the business will not have met their obligation to retain the employees named in their application. The business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy for this employee.

chunks.title: People getting income from a property business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## People getting income from a property business
Some people are paid a wage or salary from a property business, such as private rentals, Airbnb's and homestay operations.
These businesses are eligible to get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme if they meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations, including being registered and/or operating in New Zealand.
For self-employed people who are not registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, the Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed before paying the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme.
Note the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is paid to support employers to retain their employees or offset a loss of earnings (for self-employed people) and can only be used to support the cost of wages or salary. Self-employed people who apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for a property business must be able to declare that they receive wages or a salary for this work.
## Example
Anthony owns several holiday homes, which he rents out to supplement his income. He works an average of 10 hours per week on the properties, greeting guests and cleaning the property in between guests.
Usually this would be a very busy time of year for his business, but most of his future bookings were cancelled due to the impacts of COVID-19 public health restrictions in the latter part of 2021. In the last month his bookings have been picking up again. However, he needs to self-isolate because he tests positive for COVID-19 and is unable to work from home.
Anthony needs to hire someone to temporarily take over his work for the business while he self-isolates, so applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme to cover the cost of his wages while he cannot work. The Ministry of Social Development is able to verify his self-employment status with Inland Revenue and his application is approved.

chunks.title: People getting weekly compensation from ACC — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## People getting weekly compensation from ACC
Businesses (including self-employed people) may have employees who are unable to work and getting weekly compensation from Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC).
## Employee already getting ACC
If the employee was already getting ACC compensation when the business applied for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, the business is not able to include this person in their application.
If they do include the person in error and the application is approved, the business will have got funds they are not eligible for and must repay the subsidy for this person to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Employee goes on ACC during subsidy period
If the employee is injured and starts getting ACC compensation after the business applies for and/or got the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, the person gets both the subsidy and ACC compensation.
However, the employee must declare their wages from the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme to ACC as income and their weekly compensation may be abated (reduced) accordingly.
## Employee due to finish getting ACC during subsidy period
If the employee was getting ACC compensation at the time the business applied for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for their other employees, but the person is no longer getting the ACC payments, the business can submit a new application for this employee.

chunks.title: People working multiple jobs — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## People working multiple jobs
Businesses may have employees who work for them, and another business. They may work more than 20 hours for one business, and less than 20 hours for the other.
If both businesses meet the criteria, they can each apply for COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for the same employee.

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
Applications for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme closed after 11.59pm on 10 October 2023. To be eligible for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, businesses (including self-employed people) must have met all the eligibility criteria and complied with their obligations in the declaration.
The following eligibility criteria must have been met:
- the business was advised by their employee they (or they are a self-employed person who is): were in one of the affected groups andcould not work andwere required or had been advised to self-isolate for a period of at least 4 consecutive days (including public holidays and days the employee was not due to work e.g. days they were on annual leave)
- were in one of the affected groups and
- could not work and
- were required or had been advised to self-isolate for a period of at least 4 consecutive days (including public holidays and days the employee was not due to work e.g. days they were on annual leave)
- the employee could not work for the business from home (i.e. their work cannot be done from home, e.g. barista at a cafe', or they had COVID-19 and were too unwell to work during their self-isolation period)
- the business was registered (except for sole traders, self-employed people and contractors) and operating in New Zealand
- the employee was legally working in New Zealand and employed by the business as of the date of their application
Note an employee (or self-employed person) must have qualified before 12.01am 15 August 2023 to get this assistance.

chunks.title: Reasonable belief continued working harmful to mental health — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Reasonable belief continued working harmful to mental health
Businesses cannot apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme when an employee decides they want to stop working because COVID-19 is affecting the employee's mental health.
Businesses must still meet obligations under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 and other employment laws.
The employee should tell their employer when their mental health is being affected by COVID-19. The business should work with them to try and eliminate or minimise the problem which is impacting on the employee's mental health. This could include moving to other roles that might decrease the risk of coming into contact with COVID-19.
As well as obligations under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 an employer must also continue to meet their employment law obligations. These obligations include:
- treating the employee in good faith
- offering on-going support
- complying with statutory obligations in relation to sick leave
- not discriminating against the employee and
- maintaining confidentiality
Businesses and their employee can both agree to use another form of paid leave (eg annual leave, sick leave) to cover the period they cannot work.

chunks.title: Receivership or liquidation within payment period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Receivership or liquidation within payment period
In some circumstances, businesses (including self-employed people) who have received the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme may go into receivership or liquidation and may have to sell or close their business permanently.
Note receivership and liquidation processes can be complicated. Please seek legal advice as required.
## Business keeps operating under receivership or liquidation
A business that is currently operating under receivership or liquidation can apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, if they meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations, including retaining the employees named in their application for the subsidy period.
The business (or receiver/liquidator) can continue to use the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme to support the cost of wages or salary for affected employees named in their application as long as they continue to operate.
If the business recovers, or the receiver/liquidator sells the business during the subsidy period and the new owners take on the employees named in the application, then the business can continue to use the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for these employees.
Example
A business goes into receivership after getting the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for their employees who are self-isolating for 7 days after getting COVID-19.
The receiver takes over the business and manages to sell the business to new owners.
The new owners keep all the previous staff and apply for a COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme payment within 8 weeks of their self-isolation periods ending to continue paying these employees.
## Business closes under receivership or liquidation
If the business is liquidated (and permanently closed), or the receiver/liquidator sells the business during the subsidy period, and the new owners do not take on the employees named in the subsidy application, then the business will not have met their obligation to retain the employees named in their application and they must repay any remaining subsidy for these employees.
Where employees are made redundant, the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme can be used to pay the person until the end of their employment. The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme cannot be used to pay for notice periods extending beyond the subsidy period for that employee. In addition, it cannot be used to pay any other redundancy payments under the employee's employment contract (including any leave payments).

chunks.title: Repaying unused funds after the payment period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Repaying unused funds after the payment period
The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is paid in a lump sum to the business to support the cost of wages for a 4 to 10 day period of self-isolation.
If the business does not need the full payment for their employees, any difference should be used for the wages of other affected employees, eg because an employee's ordinary wages are less than the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme rate.
If there are any unused funds at the end of the payment period, the business must repay the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development. The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme cannot be used beyond the payment period.

chunks.title: Retain employees named in their application — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Retain employees named in their application
Businesses must agree, when they get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, to keep all the employees for whom they got support, for the duration of the payment period.

chunks.title: Reviewing decisions to decline the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Reviewing decisions to decline the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme
Decisions to decline the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme are not made under the Social Security Act 2018 and are not covered by the usual Review of Decision guidelines.
If a business’ application (including that of a self-employed person) is declined, MSD must advise them of their right to request MSD to reconsider the decision. This should be based on the following:
- whether all relevant information was obtained and
- whether the appropriate options and implications were considered and
- whether the decision was made at the appropriate level of delegation
If the decision to decline the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is confirmed to be correct, the business can ask the Ombudsman to undertake their own review.

chunks.title: Seasonal work ends within payment period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Seasonal work ends within payment period
Some seasonal workers will have had their work affected by COVID-19 (ie season finished earlier than expected and/or not able to pick up new work due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions).
If the business got the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for any of their employees, but can no longer offer them employment, then the business will not have met their obligation to retain the employees named in their application and must return any remaining subsidy for these employees to the Ministry of Social Development.
If the seasonal workers are casual employees or on fixed-term contracts, then the business can apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme to continue paying them, as long as they keep them employed for the subsidy period and meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations.
## Example 1
Rowan usually picks grapes over the summer months, but he is not able to go into work because his partner Joey has been advised to self-isolate by his doctor for 10 days because Joey has underlying medical conditions which means he is at 'higher risk' of severe illness if he got COVID-19.
The business employing Rowan got the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for him, but soon after, decides to close the harvesting season early. As the business can no longer offer Rowan employment, the business returns the remaining amount of the subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example 2
Tracey employs 30 casual employees on her kiwifruit orchard and is continuing to operate under the red setting of the COVID-19 Protection Framework.
Tracey has an employee who has tested positive for COVID-19 and is required to self-isolate for 7 days, so she applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for this employee.
Tracey calculates the average hours the casual employee would have worked at this time last year, to determine the correct rate to apply for.
Tracey and the employee agree the average hours in writing and she applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme to continue paying this employee.

chunks.title: Seasonal workers — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Seasonal workers
There are a variety of employment arrangements for seasonal workers (eg fixed-term contract or casual employment contract).
Businesses can apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for their seasonal workers, but they must keep them employed for the subsidy period.
If an employee's contract ends during the subsidy period, then the business will not have met their obligation to retain the employees named in their application.
The business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining subsidy for this employee.

chunks.title: Self-employed person is also an employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Self-employed person is also an employee
A person may be self-employed for some of their income, and also be employed by a business or other organisation.
If the self-employed person is eligible, they can apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme for their own business.
Also, if their employer is eligible, they can get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme to continue paying the person (as an employee).

chunks.title: Self-isolation period and rounding — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Self-isolation period and rounding
The payment of the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is a lump sum payment covering a self-isolation period for the number of consecutive days an employee cannot work (rounded to the nearest 7 days).
The employer may be eligible for subsequent payments, but this will depend on the number of calendar days the employee cannot work due to their required or advised self-isolation.
The number of days that an employee cannot work due to their required or advised self-isolation is rounded to the nearest 7 days.
The rounding rule means that, an eligible employer (or a self-employed person) may apply for:
- one payment for an eligible employee who, needs to miss work for a period of at least four consecutive days and up to and including 10 consecutive days
- a second payment for an eligible employee who needs to miss work for a period of 11 consecutive days and up to and including 17 consecutive days
- a third payment (and subsequent payments) can be applied for an eligible employee, who is needs to miss work for a period of 18 consecutive days, and each further consecutive 7-day period of self-isolation beyond 18 days (for example at least 25 days and so on)

chunks.title: Specific employment situations — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text:
## Specific employment situations
People's work situations in New Zealand may vary, and eligibility for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme can sometimes differ.

chunks.title: State sector organisations generally not eligible — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: State sector organisations are generally not eligible to get the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme. State sector organisations are listed on the Public Service Commission website. See: - New Zealand's central government organisations Te Kawa Mataaho Public Service Commission State sector organisations can request an exception to allow them to apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme. Exceptions for state sector organisations are considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, through the relevant monitoring agency. If an exception has already been granted for a COVID-19 Wage Subsidy, the State sector organisation does not need to get another exception to apply for COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme. State sector organisations that have been granted an exception are: - New Zealand Post Limited - Television New Zealand Limited - KiwiRail Holdings Limited - Crown Research Institutes (CRIs): AgResearch LimitedInstitute of Environmental Science and Research LimitedInstitute of Geological and Nuclear Sciences LimitedLandcare Research New Zealand LimitedNational Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research LimitedNew Zealand Forest Research Institute LimitedThe New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research Limited - AgResearch Limited - Institute of Environmental Science and Research Limited - Institute of Geological and Nuclear Sciences Limited - Landcare Research New Zealand Limited - National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research Limited - New Zealand Forest Research Institute Limited - The New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research Limited Note that the above list includes some State-Owned Enterprises and Mixed Ownership Model companies. From 14 March all State-Owned Enterprises and Mixed Ownership Model companies can apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme without the need to seek an exception. State sector organisations in the list above can apply but they must meet all the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations. No other state sector organisations are permitted to apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme.

chunks.title: Other state sector organisations cannot apply — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 leave support scheme
chunks.text: None of the other organisations described on Te Kawa Mataaho Public Service Commission website are permitted to apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme. This includes: - state schools, state-integrated schools and special institutions (each being Boards of Trustees that are bodies corporate constituted under subpart 5 of Part 3 of the Education and Training Act 2020 (including distance schools)) - Crown entity subsidiaries (being companies incorporated under the Companies Act 1993 that are controlled by Crown entities): for a state school, state integrated school or special institution, Crown entity subsidiaries can include separate legal entities providing, for example, after-school care programmes, hostels, shopfor District Health Boards, Crown entity subsidiaries can include separate legal entities providing, for example, laundry services - for a state school, state integrated school or special institution, Crown entity subsidiaries can include separate legal entities providing, for example, after-school care programmes, hostels, shop - for District Health Boards, Crown entity subsidiaries can include separate legal entities providing, for example, laundry services Crown entities should ensure their subsidiaries do not apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme. Note Local government organisations are not state sector organisations.

chunks.title: Amount employer must pay employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: The amount the employer must pay to the employee depends on whether the employee usually earns under, or over the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme rate applied for them.

chunks.title: Employer can pay at least 80% — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: Employers who get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme must use their best endeavours to pay at least 80% of each named employees' wages or salary for the period of the subsidy, at the rate they would have been paid before the business was impacted by the COVID-19 public health restrictions. When the employee was earning less than the subsidy rate, the employer must keep paying their usual wages, even if they are working less hours during the COVID-19 public health restrictions. The employer must use the remaining support towards topping up the wages of other affected staff. When there are no other employees, or the other employees are already being paid their usual wages, the employer must repay the remaining subsidy back to the Ministry of Social Development as it could not be used for wages. If the individual is self-employed and the income they regularly draw from their business is less than the amount they got from the subsidy, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development. Example 1 John earns $956 gross per week. His employer can commit to paying 80% of this ($764.80) while John is at home and there is no work for him. The employer gets the subsidy rate of $585.80 gross per week and continues to pay John $764.80 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions) for the subsidy period. When the business reopens, John goes back to working his normal hours. The employer uses the subsidy to help fund John's normal wages of $956 gross per week. Example 2 Miri earns $220 gross per week. Her employer can continue paying 80% of her earnings ($176) while Miri is at home and there is no work for her. The employer gets the subsidy rate of $350 gross per week, but because Miri earns under the subsidy rate the employer must continue to pay her wages or salary at the rate they would have been paid before the business was impacted by the COVID-19 public health restrictions (ie $220 gross per week). When her employer re-opens, the business starts slowly and Miri is only offered half of her hours. Her employer must pay her for these hours and because she earned under the subsidy rate, her employer must continue to pay her usual wages for the subsidy period (ie $220 gross per week).

chunks.title: Not possible for employer to pay at least 80% — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: If paying 80% of their pre COVID-19 impact wages or salary is not possible, and the employee was usually earning over the subsidy rate applied for, the employer must pass on the full weekly amount of support (less any usual wage deductions) to the employee. When the employee was earning less than the subsidy rate, the employer must keep paying their usual wages, even if they are working less hours during the COVID-19 public health restrictions. The employer must use the remaining support towards topping up the wages of other affected staff. When there are no other employees, or the other employees are already being paid their usual wages, the employer must repay the remaining subsidy back to the Ministry of Social Development as it could not be used for wages. Example 1 Mandy usually earns $1,000 gross per week. Her employer is unable to continue paying 80% of her wages during the time while she is at home, and there is no work for her to do. The employer gets the subsidy rate of $585.80 gross per week, and because she usually earns over this amount, must pass on this amount to Mandy as wages. She gets $585.80 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions) during this period. Mandy can go back to work when her employer begins operating again and continues working her usual hours. The employer uses the subsidy to help to pay her normal wages for the remainder of the subsidy period (ie $1000 gross per week). Example 2 Tane usually earns $450 gross per week for 25 hours and his employer gets the full-time subsidy rate of $585.80 gross per week for him. Because he usually earns under this amount, Tane continues to be paid his usually wages of $450 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions). When Tane goes back to work, his employer only needs him for 15 hours to start with. The employer must continue paying Tane his usual wages of $450 gross per week as the employer has been paid for the full-time subsidy rate. Tane's employer can use the remainder of the support to pay wages of other affected employees. When there are no other affected employees, the employer must repay the remainder back to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Assessing 40% revenue loss due to COVID-19 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Assessing 40% revenue loss due to COVID-19
When deciding if the employer has had a decline in revenue due to COVID-19, the Ministry of Social Development considers:
- the type of work the business does, eg retail, manufacturing, sales, construction, driving etc and
- whether (or to the extent) the business was able to operate in the higher COVID-19 Alert Levels (eg was it an essential business or not, what changes did the business need to make due to the public health restrictions) and
- whether the estimated loss of revenue makes sense (based on the business circumstances)
Note that in most cases verification of the revenue decline is not required. However, the Ministry of Social Development may ask for verification in some cases.
## Employer cannot open due to COVID-19 public health restrictions
Generally, where a business cannot operate due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions, the Ministry of Social Development would usually accept the employer's statement that they have had a 40% revenue decrease due to COVID-19.
## Employer has been open during COVID-19 public health restrictions
Some businesses have been able to operate during the higher COVID- 19 Alert Levels, for example, firms defined as essential businesses or firms operating outside of a regional lockdown that form part of a wider supply chain, or providing click and collect and takeaway options.
For businesses that have been able to operate, when deciding if they have had a decline in revenue, the Ministry of Social Development considers the reasons given for the decline in revenue and whether these are reasonable given the type of work the business does and where the business is located.
Being open for business does not protect a business from having a 40% reduction in revenue, but further consideration needs to be given to their circumstances.
Example a business has remained open or open in some online capacity, and may not be able to sell the same level of product, due to reduced demand from other businesses (eg frozen food which they used to provide to fast food or other restaurants).
For these employers, the Ministry of Social Development will consider their individual situations and make decisions based on the facts of their application when considering if the business has had a decline 40% in revenue due to COVID-19.

chunks.title: Sole traders — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Sole traders
Sole traders are not required to be registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, but must have:
- a personal Inland Revenue number for paying income tax and/or GST and
- government licences and permits for their business needs and
- qualifications or registrations for their trade or profession
Sole traders must still meet the requirements to be physically located and legally working in New Zealand.
The Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed before paying the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme.

chunks.title: Businesses operating for less than a year (or a high growth firm) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Businesses operating for less than a year (or a high growth firm)
When a business has been operating for less than a year or is a high growth firm (eg a business that had a significant increase in revenue), they must compare their revenue against a more recent comparison time period that gives the best estimation of the revenue decline related to COVID-19.
Example 40% loss of revenue attributable to COVID-19 comparing 12 August 2020 – 26 August 2020 to 14 – 28 January 2020.

chunks.title: Businesses who get insurance payments to cover revenue loss — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Businesses who get insurance payments to cover revenue loss
Some businesses have received insurance payments, such as business interruption insurance, to cover their loss of revenue during the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
If the insurance payment does not cover their losses and the business has still experienced a 40% decline in revenue over a 14-day consecutive period between 2 August 2020 to 10 September 2020, then the business will be eligible for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme. If the employer has already got the subsidy and still has a decline in revenue, then they can continue using the payment to pay their employees.
If the insurance payment means that the business has not had a 40% decline in revenue in a 14-day consecutive period between 2 August 2020 to 10 September 2020, then the business will not qualify for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme.
If the employer has already got the subsidy, then they will have received funds they are not eligible for and must repay the subsidy in full to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Businesses who had not started operating before the COVID-19 public health restrictions — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Businesses who had not started operating before the COVID-19 public health restrictions
Some self-employed people or employers may have had their plans to start their business affected by the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
To qualify for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, the employer must have had a 40% decline in revenue over a 14-day consecutive period between 12 August 2020 to 10 September 2020.
To determine the decline, the business needs to compare their revenue to a similar 14-day period in 2019 (or using a more recent comparison 14-day period, if the business has been operating for less than a year or is a high growth firm).
This means the business must have been operating for at least 14 days to determine the decline in revenue.
## Example
A chiropractor was moving from employment to start their own business but did not begin trading before the COVID-19 public health restrictions came into effect. They are unable to open until the public health restrictions ease.
When the chiropractor is able to start and has been trading for 14 days, they will be able to apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, provided they meet the other qualifications.

chunks.title: Comparison period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Comparison period
To determine a decline in revenue, the business or self-employed person must compare the revenue of a 14-day period between 12 August 2020 and 10 September 2020 to a similar period in 2019.
Generally, businesses would compare the same 14-day period in 2019, for example 12 August – 26 August 2020 compared with 12 August – 26 August 2019.
However, in some cases this might not give the best indication of what the business would have been expecting to earn now.
This may be because the business:
- has been operating for less than a year
- is a high growth firm or
- experience an event that caused their revenue to decrease at this time last year.
In other cases, the same 14-day period in 2019 may include weekends or dates that are otherwise difficult for the business to calculate their revenue for.
In these situations, the Ministry of Social Development will consider another similar 14-day period that will reflect what the business would have expected to earn now. This comparison period could be any 14-day period from January 2019 to the date of application. For example, 12 August 2020 – 26 August 2020 compared to 1 September 2019 - 14 September 2019.The revenue of the 14-day period must be at least 40% less than it was in the 14-day period it was compared against.

chunks.title: Decline in revenue for separate legal entities and business units — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Decline in revenue for separate legal entities and business units
A 40% decline in total revenue must be experienced across all units of a business.
Business units within a single corporate entity are not eligible to apply individually. This includes Councils and other business structures who may have different programmes, branches, or divisions that are differently affected by COVID-19, but who employ all their workers under one corporate entity.
Consolidated tax groups (made up of legally separate companies) cannot apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme. The separate companies can apply individually for the subsidy, if they meet the qualifications.
Example 1
A Local Council in Christchurch cannot open their public pools because of the COVID-19 public health restrictions and this part of the business has had a 100% decline in revenue in the last 14-days. However, the Council does not qualify for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme because the rest of the business can operate normally, and the Council has not experienced a 40% decline in revenue overall.
Example 2
A clothing store in Wellington cannot open during the regional public health restrictions. The store can trade online, but their revenue is down more than 40% compared to the same time last year. However, the store is part of a larger company with locations around the country, and the business as a whole has not been significantly impacted by regional restrictions. The store does not qualify for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy because the rest of the business has not experienced a 40% decline in revenue overall.
Example 3
Giani’s Pizza Franchise has locations around the country, however the stores in Auckland cannot open because of the COVID-19 public health restrictions. Although the wider company is able to operate, the stores in Auckland are individually owned as separate legal entities, and they can individually apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy, if they meet the qualifications.

chunks.title: Decline in revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Decline in revenue
To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension the employer or self-employed person must have had a 40% decline in revenue.
This means they have had a 40% decline in:
- actual revenue or
- predicted revenue (eg when a business has had a reduction in bookings such as accommodation providers) and
- the decline is due to the impacts of COVID-19, including the impact of the public health restrictions
The business must experience this decline over a 14-day consecutive period between 12 August 2020 and 10 September 2020.
This 14-day period must be compared to a similar 14-day period in 2019 (or using a more recent comparison time period if the business has been operating for less than a year or is a high growth firm).
Businesses can use a combination of both actual and predicted revenue loss in order to qualify for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme.
However, if the business or self-employed person predicted a 40% decline in revenue but does not experience this, then the business or self-employed person must repay the subsidy.
Example
An employer applies for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme on 2 September 2020. Their actual revenue was more than 40% down last week (24 – 30 August 2020) and they predict that their revenue will be down again this week (31 August – 6 September 2020). They apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme using a combination of actual and predicted revenue.

chunks.title: Definition of revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Definition of revenue
Revenue means the total amount of money a business has earned from its normal business activities, before expenses are deducted.
Some pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses can include a fall in projected capital income when determining a 40% decrease in revenue.

chunks.title: Determining a decline in revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Determining a decline in revenue
To determine a decline in revenue, the employer or self-employed person must compare the revenue of a 14-day period between 12 August 2020 to 10 September 2020 to a similar period in 2019.
Example 12 August – 26 August 2020 compared with 12 August – 26 August 2019.
The revenue of the 14-day period must be at least 40% less than it was in the 14-day period it was compared against.
The decline in revenue must be experienced across all parts of the business as a 40% decline in total revenue. This includes Councils and other business structures who may have different programmes or branches that are differently affected by COVID-19, but who employ all their workers under one business.

chunks.title: Determining if someone is self-employed — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Determining if someone is self-employed
A person is likely to be self-employed when they carry out business activities on their own, including contracting, working as a sole trader or owning a small business.
A self-employed person is likely to:
- support the business with their own money (eg providing all the working equipment needed for their job)
- decide or control how they work (eg when, where and what hours they work)
- decide how much they get paid and how
- pay their own income tax (unless they are a young person earning under the tax threshold)
- be responsible for investment decisions and any losses
- be able to sell the business if they wanted to
The above list is not a full list. There may be other things that can be considered.
Self-employed people are eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, if they meet the qualifications.

chunks.title: Eligible employers — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Eligible employers
The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme is available for:
- businesses using all employment types including full-time, part-time, casual, fixed-term, sole trading and self-employment, including those employers with employees getting the minimum wage exemption
- across all sectors and industries in New Zealand
- includes registered charities, incorporated societies, non-government organisations and post-settlement governance entities (eg Māori authorities)
State Sector organisations are generally not eligible to get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme.
Exceptions for State Sector employers are considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, through the relevant monitoring agency.

chunks.title: Employee is legally entitled to work in New Zealand — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Employee is legally entitled to work in New Zealand
Legally working in New Zealand means a person is both working in New Zealand, and is legally entitled to work in New Zealand.
A person is legally entitled to work in New Zealand if they:
- are a New Zealand or Australian citizen (including a person born in the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau) or
- have a New Zealand residence class visa or
- have a New Zealand work visa, or a condition on their New Zealand temporary visa that allows them to work in New Zealand

chunks.title: Employee temporarily overseas and cannot return due to COVID-19 restrictions — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Employee temporarily overseas and cannot return due to COVID-19 restrictions
Employees who are currently overseas can be named as an employee in the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme application if:
- they were legally working in New Zealand before leaving and
- their absence was intended to be temporary (eg a holiday or a work business trip) and
- they maintain their employment status (that is, they are still employed by the employer) and intended to return to work on a specific date but cannot start on that date because of the COVID-19 travel restrictions

chunks.title: Employee voluntarily leaves — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Employee voluntarily leaves
Employers must agree when they get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.
If an employee voluntarily leaves their employment for another job opportunity, the employer must advise the Ministry of Social Development, and the subsidy can no longer be claimed for that person. The employer does not have to repay the subsidy already paid but they must use the balance towards topping up the wages of other affected employees.
If the employer has no other employees to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other employees are already being paid their usual wages, the employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy as it was not able to be used for wages.

chunks.title: Employer dismisses employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Employer dismisses employee
Employers must agree when they get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.
If an employer decides to dismiss an employee for reasons other than redundancy, for example, because of serious or repeated misconduct, for performance issues, or if the employee abandons their employment, the subsidy can no longer be claimed for that person.
The employer does not have to repay the subsidy already paid but they must use the balance towards topping up the wages of any other remaining affected employees.
If the employer has no other employees to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other employees are already being paid their usual wages, the employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy as it was not able to be used for wages.
The employer must follow existing employment law for dismissing an employee.
## Example
Fahima employees 5 staff at her cafe' but the COVID-19 public health restrictions have significantly impacted her business and she applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension to continue paying her staff.
One of Fahima's employees is caught taking money from the till and this employee is already on notice for similar behaviour in the past. After going through a disciplinary process, Fahima decides to dismiss the employee based on their repeated misconduct.
As Fahima got the subsidy for this employee, Fahima uses the remaining funds to contribute to the wage costs of her other staff. Fahima manages to hire a replacement employee quickly and reapplies for the subsidy for the new employee.
At the end of the subsidy period Fahima has not used all the funds she received, so repays the remaining amount to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Employer makes employee redundant — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Employer makes employee redundant
Employers must agree when they get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid, for the duration of the subsidy period.
If an employer makes the employee redundant, the employer will not have met their obligations to retain affected staff and must repay the remaining subsidy for that person.
The employer cannot keep the remainder of the subsidy to support other remaining affected employees. Other enforcement action may be taken against these employers.
The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme can be used to pay the notice period but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract.
The employee is not required to pay the subsidy back to the employer.
Employers who have given their employees notice of redundancy before they apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme are not eligible to get the subsidy for those employees unless the redundancy notice is withdrawn.

chunks.title: Employer not entitled but has been paid — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: If an employer applied for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, and then they have a change in circumstance within the 2-week period, they may not be entitled to keep the subsidy payment they got for an employee. Change of circumstances Employer action Employee voluntarily resigns. The employer should use the balance of any of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme to pay other affected staff. When no other employees need it, the employer should contact the Ministry of Social Development and must refund the remaining subsidy for this employee as it was not able to be used for wages. Employee has been made redundant. The employer must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme remaining for the employee. The subsidy can be used to pay the notice period, but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract, and cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees. Employee has been dismissed. The employer should use the balance of any of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme to pay other affected staff. When no other employees need it, the employer should contact the Ministry of Social Development and must refund the remaining subsidy for this employee as it was not able to be used for wages. Business has closed. The employer must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme remaining for their employee(s). The subsidy can be used to pay the notice period, but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract and cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees. Employee is on fixed-term contract that ends during the period that the employer is getting the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for them. The employer must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme remaining for the employee at the end of the fixed-term contract. The subsidy cannot be used to meet any entitlements owed under contract and cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees. The employer applied for the wrong type of COVID-19 scheme for their employee (eg applied for the Leave Support Scheme in error). The employer must repay any amount received for the incorrect application and re-apply for the correct scheme that they are entitled to. The employer applied for the wrong type of COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme rate for their employee, eg applies for full-time, when the person was part-time.

chunks.title: Employer not entitled but has been paid — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: The employer must repay the difference between the full-time rate received and the part-time rate they are entitled to. The employer applied for COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme based on a predicted 40% decline in revenue, but the decline did not occur. The employer is not entitled to the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme and must repay it in full. Employer is a State Sector organisation who did not have an exception approved by the Minister of Finance to apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme but applied and got the funds. The employer is not entitled to the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme and must repay it in full. Any State Sector employers who disagree with the decision should consult with their monitoring agency. Employer gets a payment they are not entitled to due to an office error (eg their application might have been paid twice or accidentally approved instead of declined). The employer is not entitled to the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme and must repay it in full. Employer gets an insurance payment that covers their loss in revenue, so they have no longer experienced a 40% decline in revenue between 2 August 2020 to 10 September 2020. The employer is not entitled to the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme and must repay it in full. If an employer applies for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme while the employee is also getting the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme or the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, their application will be declined.

chunks.title: Example — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: A courier company applies for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme as their business has been slower than normal during the COVID-19 public health restrictions. Their accounts for the last 14 days have not yet been finalised, but they predict they will have experienced a 40% decline in revenue, when compared with the same 14 day period last year. They apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy for their employees. When they do finalise their accounts, the company has only experienced a 35% decline in revenue. The company got funds they were not entitled to, so they contact the Ministry of Social Development to repay the subsidy in full.

chunks.title: Employer obligations — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme is being administered under a high trust model, and employers will not be asked for evidence to support some criteria before the subsidy is approved. However, some details will be verified with Inland Revenue before payment. The Ministry of Social Development may also check applications and verify information at a later date. When false or misleading information has been provided by the employer to the Ministry of Social Development, employers can be investigated which may result in civil recovery of any amount paid and/or criminal prosecution. To get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, the employer must agree: - that they meet the following subsidy eligibility criteria: the business has had a minimum 40% revenue drop over a 14-day consecutive period between 12 August 2020 and 10 September 2020, due to the COVID-19 outbreakthe employer is registered and operating in New Zealandthey have taken active steps to mitigate the financial impact of COVID-19 on their business activities, including proactively engaging with their bank and calling on their internal cash reserves (where appropriate)the employees are legally employed by their business and have not been given notice of redundancy at the date they applythey are not currently getting a COVID-19 Wage Subsidy, Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, or Leave Support that was available before 21 August 2020 for the named employees - the business has had a minimum 40% revenue drop over a 14-day consecutive period between 12 August 2020 and 10 September 2020, due to the COVID-19 outbreak - the employer is registered and operating in New Zealand - they have taken active steps to mitigate the financial impact of COVID-19 on their business activities, including proactively engaging with their bank and calling on their internal cash reserves (where appropriate) - the employees are legally employed by their business and have not been given notice of redundancy at the date they apply - they are not currently getting a COVID-19 Wage Subsidy, Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, or Leave Support that was available before 21 August 2020 for the named employees

chunks.title: Employer obligations — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
