chunks.title: Employers mitigating the impact of COVID-19 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Employers mitigating the impact of COVID-19
Before applying for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, a business must have taken measures to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 on their business.
These might include (but are not limited to):
- activating their business continuity plan
- where appropriate, look to their own cash reserves to assist paying staff, eg where they have enough funds, and it won't cause the business to fail if they use it
- proactively engaging with their bank
- seeking advice from the Chamber of Commerce, a relevant industry association, or the Regional Business Partner programme

chunks.title: Employers must follow employment law when paying wages — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Employers must follow employment law when paying wages
Employers must still follow relevant employment laws when reducing an employee's wages to 80% of their income, or to the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme rate. This relationship is between the employer and the employee.
An employer is required to pay their employee ordinary wages in line with their employment agreement, and the subsidy can be used to help with that. The effect of the Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme is that if an employee's hours have had to change, the employer must try to pay at least 80% of their wages, and the minimum amount the employee will get if their hours drop further is the subsidy rate (subject to usual deductions eg PAYE, KiwiSaver, Student Loan etc). But if they usually earned less than the subsidy amount claimed (pre COVID-19 impact), the employer would continue to pay them their usual wages.
Under employment law, employees must be paid for each and every hour that they work at their agreed wage rate. The employer may agree with the employee to reduce hours or to reduce their hourly rate during this period (but not lower than the minimum wage) and this subsidy will help employers to pay this wage. Any change to their wage rate requires good faith consultation and written agreement in line with existing employment law.
No employer can make a blanket rule that employees take annual leave during the COVID-19 public health restrictions, but the employer and employee can agree for the employee to take annual leave. In this situation the employee should be paid their normal wage rate for their normal hours of work, and the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme will help employers pay for the annual leave taken.
When the employer and employee are unable to agree on where the employee will take annual holidays, the employer could direct the employee to take annual holidays, but they must give the employee at least 14 days notice.
Employers must follow the correct employment process. If employers have questions about their obligations under employment law, they should contact Employment New Zealand for advice and assistance.
## If employers need more information, see:
- Employment New Zealand Coronavirus (COVID-19) and the workplace

chunks.title: Examples of deciding 40% revenue decline for employers open during COVID-19 public health restrictions — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Examples of deciding 40% revenue decline for employers open during COVID-19 public health restrictions
The examples below are not exhaustive.
## Manufacturer of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
It may be considered unreasonable to expect that a business who makes PPE would have had a 40% decline in revenue, as they are able to operate at a time of high demand.
However, if that business provided a reason for the decline in revenue that was reasonable when considering their situation, then the Ministry of Social Development can accept there has been a decline.
Example the PPE business was fully staffed by sole parents who could no longer work because they had to stay at home as schools were closed, or they were unable to source enough raw materials because of border closures to make the product.
## Food outlet
Generally, it would be unreasonable to expect that an essential business of this type would have had a 40% revenue drop as they are able to operate at a time of high demand.
However, if that business provided a reason for the decline in revenue that was reasonable when considering their situation, then the Ministry of Social Development would accept there had been a decline.
Example a grocery store in the middle of the Central Business District (CBD), whose main trade was CBD workers and many people are still working from home or choosing not to eat out, or a supermarket in a small town reliant on tourists who have now left. In both these cases, the business remains open and can operate but it would be reasonable that there could have been a 40% decline in their revenue.
## Business outside of regional lockdown
Generally, it would be unreasonable to expect that a business operating outside of a regional lockdown would have had a 40% revenue drop as they are able to operate with minimal restrictions placed on their business.
However, if that business provided a reason for the decline in revenue that was reasonable when considering their situation, then the Ministry of Social Development would accept there had been a decline.
Example 1
A florist in Canterbury who supplies markets around the country. With Alert Level 3 public health restrictions in the Auckland region, the florist is unable to sell their stock to their largest market.
Example 2
A backpackers in Queenstown has seen a reduction in bookings since the Auckland region was placed into Alert Level 3. A number of bookings from Auckland holiday-makers have been cancelled, and although reservations were starting to increase again, numbers have now dropped off.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Example 1
Ailee works 10 hours per week at minimum wage ($189 gross per week) while she is a student. Her employer has experienced a decline in revenue due to the impact of the last COVID-19 public health restrictions, so the employer applies for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme to continue paying her.
Because her usual earnings are less than the subsidy rate of $350 gross per week, the employer must use the subsidy to continue paying her usual wage of $189 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions).
The employer must use the difference to contribute to the wages of their other affected staff and when there are no other employees, must refund the remainder back to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example 2
Jivan works 40 hours at a workshop as a building labourer. He usually gets $756 gross per week. He cannot do any work from home during the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
The employer has a highly skilled and reliable workforce and is using the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme to continue to pay Jivan 80% of his usual wages during this period. If the employer was not able to do this, they would be required to pay Jivan the full-time subsidy rate ($585.80 gross per week).
## Example 3
Stuart is a digger driver. His employer has no revenue coming into the business during the COVID-19 public health restrictions. The employer has many contracts to finish once they can get back to work, so needs to keep their employees over the period of the public health restrictions.
The employer is unable to pay Stuart 80% of his full-time wage over this period, and so his employer pays Stuart the full amount of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme of $585.80 (less any usual wage deductions) over the lockdown period.

chunks.title: Fixed-term contract ends within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Fixed-term contract ends within subsidy period
The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme is open to existing and newly hired employees and this includes employees on fixed-term contracts. To get the subsidy, employers must agree to retain the employees named in their application for the duration of the subsidy period.
Employers can include employees on fixed-term contracts in their COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme application, even if the employee's contract is scheduled to end during the period that their employer would be getting the subsidy for them (ie in the 2 weeks from the date of application).
However, if an employee's fixed-term contract ends during the subsidy period, the employer will not have met their obligation to retain affected staff. In these circumstances, the employer can use the subsidy to pay out any notice period for that employee, but the subsidy cannot be used to pay any other entitlements. It also cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees. The employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy.
The employer and employee may agree to extend the contract to the end of the subsidy period in order to meet their obligation to retain affected staff for the period they get the subsidy.
## Example 1
Anaru is on a fixed-term contract that is scheduled to end on 26 August 2020. His employer applies for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme on 21 August to continue paying his staff during the COVID-19 public health restrictions and includes Anaru in the application.
The employer agrees with Anaru to extend his contract to 4 September 2020 so that Anaru can continue getting wages during this period. Anaru's employer is eligible to get the full 2-week subsidy for Anaru.
## Example 2
Sacha is on a fixed-term contract with that is scheduled to end on 30 August 2020. Her employer applies for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme on 21 August and includes Sacha in the application.
When Sacha's contract ends on 30 August 2020, the employer returns the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Health and disability funded workforce — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Health and disability funded workforce
Health and disability funded workforces (eg businesses that provide community health care) not employed by the State Sector are able to apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme if they meet the qualifications.
Health and disability funded workforces not employed by the State Sector includes organisations contracted to, or funded in whole or part, by organisations in the State Sector (eg the Ministry of Health and District Health Boards).
Examples include:
- in-home care workers
- workers in primary health organisations
- nurses and other staff in rest-homes or other residential care facilities (eg cooks, cleaners, support staff)

chunks.title: Other COVID-19 wage subsidy schemes — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: An employer cannot get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme or any other COVID-19 wage subsidy for the same employee for the same period.

chunks.title: Flexi-wage and Mana in Mahi — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: If an employer is currently getting the Flexi-wage or Mana in Mahi subsidy for their employee(s), they can also apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, if they meet the qualifications. All wage subsidies that the employer is getting must be paid to their employees. For more information see:

chunks.title: Apprenticeship Boost Initiative — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: Apprenticeship Boost helps employers with the costs of keeping their current apprentices or hiring new ones for the first 24 months of their programme of study. If an employer is currently getting Apprenticeship Boost for their employee(s), they can also apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for those employees. However, they cannot apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension while receiving Apprenticeship Boost. For more information see:

chunks.title: Main benefit and other support — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: If an employer or a self-employed individual is currently getting a main benefit or other extra help from the Ministry of Social Development, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for themselves or their employees. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, any individual getting the subsidy as well as other support from the Ministry, must declare the subsidy as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Self-employed person or employee getting Work and Income assistance Interaction with the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension COVID-19 Income Relief Payment Some COVID-19 Income Relief Payment clients may have got the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme before they lost their job or self-employment. These individuals can apply for the COVID-19 Income Relief Payment once their Wage Subsidy payments run out, provided they meet the qualification criteria. Emergency Benefit Some Emergency Benefit clients may be employed or self-employed. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Emergency Benefit clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Emergency Maintenance Assistance Some Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients may be employed or self-employed. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Jobseeker Support Some Jobseeker Support clients may be working part-time (less than 30 hours per week) or getting income that does not reduce the rate of Jobseeker Support to zero. Sole parents and grand-parented Jobseeker Support clients can work full-time for a temporary period provided their income when assessed over a 52-week period doesn't fully reduce the benefit. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Jobseeker Support clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Note the part-time and full-time subsidy rate differs from the definition above. New Zealand Superannuation - Non-qualified partner If a New Zealand Superannuation client includes their partner in their payments, then their New Zealand Superannuation is income-tested. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, New Zealand Superannuation non-qualified partner clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income, and both of their New Zealand Superannuation payments may be abated accordingly. Sole Parent Support

chunks.title: Main benefit and other support — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: Some Sole Parent Support clients will have work obligations and may be employed or self-employed. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Sole Parent Support clients who receive the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Support Living Payment clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly.

chunks.title: Financial support from other agencies — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: There is a range of financial support available from other agencies for employers and individuals who have been negatively impacted by the COVID-19 financial crisis. These schemes, such as the COVID-19 Small Business Cash Flow Loan Scheme, are separate to Work and Income support, and have their own qualification criteria. This means that, provided they meet the necessary qualifications, businesses can apply and get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme as well as these other schemes. Note there are some schemes, such as Ministry of Education's emergency payment for relief teachers, where businesses are not eligible to get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for the same work. Applicants need to ensure they meet the qualification criteria for any schemes they apply for.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme was introduced from 21 August 2020 to 3 September 2020, to support employers impacted by the latest public health restrictions to stay connected to their employees.
The scheme was an addition to previous wage subsidies implemented in response to COVID-19.
Employers who got COVID-19 Wage Subsidy, Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, or Leave Support Scheme payments could apply for the same employees if they meet the qualifications, but only once the period for the previous payment had ended.
## Applications
Employers and self-employed people must apply online for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme through Work and Income.
Applications could be made from 21 August 2020 up to (and including) 3 September 2020. Payments were made as a lump sum to the employer and covered 2 weeks from the date of application.
Applications closed for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme at 11.59pm on 3 September 2020.

chunks.title: Newly hired employees — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Newly hired employees
The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme is open to any newly hired employees, and previous employees who have been re-hired before the employer applies for the subsidy.
## Example 1
Sam was employed full-time as a hairdresser, but their start date was delayed due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
Sam's employer applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for their employees and includes Sam in the application.
The employer pays Sam $585.80 (less any usual wage deductions) until they can start their new role.
## Example 2
Whiti owns a pet store and is getting the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme as her business has experienced a decline in revenue due to COVID-19. One of her employees resigns and she needs to hire a replacement staff member.
Whiti uses the remaining subsidy from the leaving employee to continue paying her other staff, and submits another application for the new employee when they start their role.
## Example 3
Ravi owns a clothing store and has reopened his business after being closed during the COVID-19 public health restrictions. He needs to hire a new employee, but his business is still experiencing more than 40% decline in revenue due to COVID-19.
Ravi is already getting the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for his existing employees, so submits another application for the new employee when they start their role.

chunks.title: Normal wages or salary — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Normal wages or salary
For employees, their normal wages or salary are specified in their employment agreement at the date the employer applies for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme.
Self-employed people can determine their normal wages or drawings by calculating the regular amount that is left over after they meet their business costs. This is the amount that they regularly pay themselves as drawings from the business.
If the individual is self-employed and the income that they regularly draw from their business is less than the amount they got from the subsidy, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.
The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme can be used to support the costs of wages, but cannot be used towards other business costs.

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme is paid at a flat rate based on each named employee's normal (or expected) hours of paid employment before COVID-19 impacted the business: - $585.80 (ie before tax) for 20 hours or more per week, or 40 hours or more per fortnight or - $350.00 (ie before tax) for less than 20 hours per week or less than 40 hours per fortnight The subsidy is paid for a 2-week period as a lump sum payment at the appropriate weekly subsidy rate for: - working 20 hours or more or - working under 20 hours An employer can access the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme more than once in the 2-week period but cannot access it for the same employees in that period. The subsidy covers 2 weeks from the date of application.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: The employer accessed the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for 10 employees as soon as the scheme became available on 21 August 2020. Now the employer needs the subsidy for 20 more employees. The employer can apply for the 20 newly named employees, not the 10 original employees for whom they have already got the subsidy.

chunks.title: Calculating variable hours — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: For a self-employed person, or an employer who has casual employees who work variable hours, an average over a relevant period can be used to work out which subsidy rate to apply. A relevant period for a business or self-employed person who has been working for a year, would be an average over this period. As a guide, for a new business or a person who has been self-employed for less than one year, an average over 8 weeks can be used, unless there is another time period that would be more appropriate. Example if using the period that the individual has been employed for would give a better representation of the employee's usual hours, then the employer can use this time period instead. It is up to employers to agree with their employees what their hours would usually be during this period, to determine the appropriate COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension rate to apply for.

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: Charlotte is a relief teacher for an Early Childhood Education Centre and is called in to provide support as required, but the Centre is closed due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions. The Centre employs Charlotte as a casual staff member and calculates that she has worked an average of 17 hours per week over the last 4 months she has been employed there. The employer applies for a part-time COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme rate to continue paying Charlotte's wages (at a rate of 17 hours per week for the 2-week period). As this is less than the $350 gross per week provided through the subsidy, the employer uses the remaining funds to support the wages of other affected staff.

chunks.title: Maximum payment for an employer — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: There is no cap on the total amount of COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension an employer can get, it is based on the number of employees they have, and whether they are working 20 hours or more, or under 20 hours.

chunks.title: People on fixed-term contracts — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## People on fixed-term contracts
Employers can apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for their employees who are on fixed-term contracts, but they must they keep them employed for the subsidy period.
If an employee's fixed-term contract ends during the subsidy period, then the employer will not have met their obligation to retain affected staff. The employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy.

chunks.title: People getting income from a property business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## People getting income from a property business
Some people are paid a wage, salary or draw an income from a property business, such as private rentals, Airbnb's and homestay operations.
These businesses are eligible to get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme provided they meet the qualification criteria, including being registered and operating in New Zealand.
For sole traders who are not registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, the Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed before paying the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme.
Note the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings and can only be used to support the cost of wages. People who apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for a property business must be able to declare that they draw a wage, salary or income for this work.
## Example
Anthony owns several holiday homes, which he rents out to supplement his income. He works an average of 10 hours per week on the properties, managing the bookings and cleaning the property in between guests.
Usually this would be a very busy time of year for his business, but most of his bookings have been cancelled due to the impacts of COVID-19 public health restrictions. Anthony's income has dropped by more than 40% during this period so applies for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme.
The Ministry is able to verify his self-employment status with Inland Revenue and his application is approved.

chunks.title: People getting paid parental leave — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## People getting paid parental leave
Employers may have employees who are getting paid parental leave.
## Employee already getting paid parental leave
If an employee was already getting paid parental leave when the employer applied for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, the employer is not able to include this employee in their application.
If they do include the employee in error and the application is approved, the employer got funds they are not eligible for and must repay the full amount to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Employee goes on paid parental leave during subsidy period
If an employee starts getting paid parental leave after the employer has made an application and/or received the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, then the employee is not eligible to get both the subsidy and paid parental leave.
The employer must stop using the subsidy for the employee as soon as they go on parental leave.
The remaining funds can be used towards topping up the wages of other affected staff.
If the employer has no other employees to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other employees are already being paid their usual wages, the employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development, and must repay the remaining amount as it was not able to be used for wages.
## Employee due to return from paid parental leave during subsidy period
If the employee was getting paid parental leave at the time of the employer's application for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for their other employees, but has since returned to work, then the employer can make a new application for this employee.
The employer should use the new hours the employee will be working on their return to work to calculate the rate of subsidy to apply for.

chunks.title: People getting weekly compensation from ACC — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## People getting weekly compensation from ACC
Employers may have employees who are unable to work and getting weekly compensation from Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC).
## Employee already getting ACC
If the employee was already getting ACC compensation when the employer applied for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, the employer is not able to include this employee in their application.
If they do include the employee in error and the application is approved, the employer will have got funds they are not eligible for and must repay the full amount to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Employee goes on ACC during subsidy period
If the employee is injured and starts getting ACC compensation after the employer made an application and/or got the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, the employee is eligible to get both the subsidy and ACC compensation.
However, the employee must declare the subsidy to ACC as income and their weekly compensation may be abated accordingly.
## Employee due to finish getting ACC during subsidy period
If the employee was getting ACC compensation at the time of the employer's application for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for their other employees, but is no longer getting the ACC payments, the employer can make a new application for this employee.

chunks.title: People working multiple jobs — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## People working multiple jobs
Employers may have employees who work for them, and another employer. The employee may work more than 20 hours for one employer, and less than 20 hours for the other.
If both employers meet the criteria, they can each apply for COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for the same employee.

chunks.title: Pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses
A small number of pre-revenue research and development ’start-up’ businesses may be eligible to treat a 40% fall in projected capital income as a result of COVID-19, as a fall in revenue for the eligibility of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme.
These employers must:
- be a research and development intensive ‘start-up’ business
- be ‘seed’ or ‘venture’ backed
- be Callaghan Innovation affiliated as of 17 March 2020 and
- have no other revenue other than government support and, seed or venture capital
These employers can apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme if they meet the other qualifications.

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: To qualify for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, businesses must meet the following eligibility criteria: - the business must have experienced or expect to experience a minimum 40% decline in revenue - the decline in revenue must be over a 14-day consecutive period between 12 August 2020 to 10 September 2020 - the 14-day period must be compared with to a similar 14-day period in 2019 (or using a more recent comparison time period, if the business has been operating for less than a year or is a high growth firm) - the decline in revenue must be related to COVID-19 - the business must be registered and operating in New Zealand - their employees must be legally working in New Zealand - before making an application, the employer must have taken active steps to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 - are not currently getting a subsidy for that employee from any previous or current Wage Subsidy or Leave Support Scheme Businesses who have not applied for the previous COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) or Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension can also apply, provided they meet the qualifications. If an employer got a previous COVID-19 wage subsidy or leave payment for their employees, they must wait until the subsidy period for these employees has ended, before they apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme.

chunks.title: Must retain employees and pay at least 80% wages or salary — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: Employers who get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme must keep the employees (for whom they received the wage subsidy) in their jobs for the period of the subsidy (unless the employee voluntarily ends the employment relationship). Employers must endeavour to pay at least 80% of each named employee's wages or salary for the period of the subsidy, at the rate they would have been paid before the business was impacted by the COVID-19 public health restrictions. When the employee was earning less than the subsidy rate, the employer must keep paying their usual wages, even if they are working less hours due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions. Any difference should be used towards topping up the wages of other affected staff. When there are no other employees, or the other employees are already being paid their usual wages, the employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development, and must repay the remaining subsidy as it was not able to be used for wages. If an applicant is self-employed, and the income they regularly draw from their business is less than the subsidy amount they received, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development. Under employment law, employees must be paid for each and every hour that they work at their agreed wage rate. Employers must still adhere to relevant employment laws when reducing an employee's wages or changing the hours they work.

chunks.title: Receivership or liquidation within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Receivership or liquidation within subsidy period
In some circumstances, employers who have received the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme may still go into receivership or liquidation, and may have to sell or close their business permanently.
## Business keeps operating under receivership or liquidation
If the business can continue operating under receivership or for the duration of the liquidation process, then the employer (or the receiver/liquidator) can continue to use the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme to support the cost of wages for employees named in their application.
If the business recovers, or the receiver/liquidator sells the business during the subsidy period and the new owners take on the employees named in the application, then the business can continue to use the subsidy for these employees.
An employer who is currently operating under receivership or liquidation can apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, provided they meet the qualifications and meet their obligations to retain staff for the subsidy period.
Example 1
An employer goes into receivership 2 weeks after getting the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for their employees. The receiver takes over the business and manages to sell the business to new owners. The new owners keep all the previous staff and use the remaining subsidy to continue paying these employees for the duration of the subsidy period.
## Business closes under receivership or liquidation
If the business is liquidated (and permanently closed), or the receiver/liquidator sells the business during the subsidy period, and the new owners do not take on the employees named in the subsidy application, then the business will not have met their obligation to retain affected staff and they must repay the remaining subsidy.
Where employees are made redundant, the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme can be used to pay the notice period but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract, and cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees.
Example 2
A restaurant owner puts their business into liquidation 3 days after getting the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for their employees. The liquidator gives the staff 1 week notice that the business will be closing permanently and uses the subsidy to pay out the notice period for the employees named in the application.
At the end of the notice period, the liquidator repays the remaining 1 week of subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Repaying unused funds after the subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Repaying unused funds after the subsidy period
The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme is paid in one lump sum to the employer to support the cost of wages for 2 weeks.
If the employer does not need the full weekly rate for their employees, because an employee's usual wages are less than the subsidy rate, then any difference should be used for the wages of other affected staff.
If there are any unused funds at the end of the 2-week period, the employer must repay the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development. The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme cannot be used beyond the 2-week period.
If the individual is self-employed and the income that they regularly draw from their business is less than the amount they got from the subsidy, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example
Jason got the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for his only employee who works part-time. The employee was earning under the part-time subsidy rate, so continued getting their normal wages for the duration of the subsidy period.
At the end of the 2 weeks, Jason has not used all the subsidy payment and has some funds remaining.
He contacts the Ministry of Social Development to return the unused subsidy, as the funds were not fully used on wage costs during the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Retain affected staff — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Retain affected staff
Employers must agree when they get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Reviewing decisions to decline the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Reviewing decisions to decline the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme
Decisions to decline the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme are not made under the Social Security Act 2018 and are not covered by the usual Review of Decision guidelines.
If an employer wants a decision to decline the subsidy reviewed, that decision should be reconsidered. This review should be based on whether an informed decision was made and should consider the following:
- whether all relevant information was available and
- whether the appropriate options and implications were considered and
- whether the decision was made at the appropriate level of delegation
If a review of the decision to decline the payment upholds the original decision, the employer can ask the Ombudsman to undertake their own review.

chunks.title: Seasonal work ends within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Seasonal work ends within subsidy period
Some seasonal workers will have had their work affected by COVID-19 (ie season finished earlier than expected and/or not able to pick up new work due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions).
If their employer got the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme but can no longer offer them employment during the subsidy period, then the employer will not be meeting their obligation to retain affected staff and must repay the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.
If the seasonal workers are casual employees or on fixed-term contracts, then the employer can apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme to continue paying them, as long as they keep them employed for the subsidy period.
## Example 1
Rowan usually picks grapes over the summer months, but his employer has closed the harvesting season early due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
Rowan's employer got the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for his employees, but after 1 week he decides to end their contracts as he can no longer offer them employment to return to. The employer uses the subsidy to pay out their notice period and repays any remaining amount to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example 2
Tracey employs 30 casual workers on her kiwifruit orchard, however, the orchard is not able to open due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions and Tracey has no work for these employees.
Tracey calculates the average hours each of her casual employees would have worked at this time last year to determine the correct rate to apply for. Tracey applies for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme to continue paying her employees for the duration of the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Seasonal workers — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Seasonal workers
There are a variety of employment arrangements for seasonal workers (eg fixed-term contract or casual employment contract).
Employers can apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for their employees who are seasonal workers, but they must keep them employed for the subsidy period.
If an employee’s contract ends during the subsidy period, then the employer will not have met their obligation to retain affected staff.
The employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy.

chunks.title: Self-employed person is also an employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Self-employed person is also an employee
A person may be self-employed for some of their income, and also be employed by a business or other organisation.
If the self-employed person qualifies, they can get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for their own business.
Also, if their employer qualifies, they can get the subsidy to continue paying the employee.

chunks.title: Specific employment situations — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text:
## Specific employment situations
People's working situations in New Zealand may vary and eligibility for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme can sometimes differ.

chunks.title: State Sector employers generally not eligible — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: State Sector employers are generally not eligible to get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme. In most situations alternative arrangements have been made to ensure these employers pay their employees in full. Exceptions for State Sector employers are considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, through the relevant monitoring agency. Monitoring agencies will engage with State Sector organisations in their portfolio to understand their financial position and support them to request an exception if appropriate. Example if Airways Corporation of New Zealand Limited believed they met the criteria for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, then they could engage with the Treasury Commercial Operations Team to assess their situation. If appropriate, Treasury will prepare advice for the Minister of Finance asking for an exception on their behalf. If an exception is granted, the monitoring agency will tell the Ministry of Social Development, and advise the State Sector employer to apply for the Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme directly. If an exception has already been granted for an earlier COVID-19 subsidy, the State Sector employer does not need to get another exception to apply for the Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme. State Sector employers include: - Government agencies such as the Ministry of Health, District Health Boards, Inland Revenue, and the Ministry of Social Development - Crown entities such as Kāinga Ora and the Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) - Schools (including state schools, state-integrated schools and their board of trustee members or equivalent) - Tertiary education institutions such as universities, polytechnics, institutes of technology and Wānanga State Sector employers do not include: - Local government such as Regional, City and District Councils, council organisations and council-controlled organisations as stated in the Local Government Act 2002. This includes trusts and other organisations that look after libraries, museums and other operations in partnership with local authorities (note these employers still need to have experienced a 40% decline in revenue and meet the other qualifications to be eligible for the subsidy) - Kindergartens (although kindergarten teachers are State Sector employees, their employers are not, so Ministry of Education is not directly responsible for their payroll) - (note these employers still need to have experienced a 40% decline in revenue and meet the other qualifications to be eligible for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy) - Early childhood centres - Private (or independent) schools, and their board of trustee members or equivalent, proprietors of state-integrated schools and other workers employed by the proprietor (note the proprietor is the owner or leaseholder of the state-integrated school property)

chunks.title: State Sector employers generally not eligible — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: - Non-government organisations - Health and disability funded workforces not employed directly by the State Sector Note businesses contracted to provide services to State Sector employers (eg cleaning, security, managed isolation or quarantine facilities etc) are not State Sector employers, and can apply for the subsidy if they meet the other qualifications.

chunks.title: Transition between previous COVID-19 subsidies and the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Leave Payment ended on 27 March 2020, when it was combined with the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy and became the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified). The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) was replaced by the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension which is available from 10 June to 1 September 2020. The COVID-19 Essential Workers Leave Support Scheme was available from 16 April 2020 and was expanded to the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme from 28 April 2020. Employers who got a previous COVID-19 subsidy are still covered by the obligations they agreed when applying for these subsidies, for the duration of the subsidy period. An employer can apply for the same employees under the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme if they meet the qualifications, but only once the period for the previous payment has ended.

chunks.title: Employer received COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: Between 10 June and 1 September 2020, employers and self-employed people who had a 40% decline in revenue in a 30-day consecutive period in the 40 days before their application date, were eligible to apply for a COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension. The subsidy was intended to support businesses to retain staff and continue to pay them at least 80% of their normal income. Employers can apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme when they meet the criteria and need further assistance but can only apply for employees named in earlier applications once the subsidy period for the previous payment has ended. The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme will only be available for applications between 21 August and 3 September 2020. Example An employer got the original COVID-19 Wage Subsidy for their staff, and when their subsidy period ended, applied again for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension. The employer's Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension ends on 4 September 2020. However, applications for the COVID-19 Resurgent Wage Subsidy Scheme end on 3 September, and the employer is not eligible to apply for the Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme.

chunks.title: Employer received COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension and has funds remaining after the subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: Any unused COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension funds must be repaid to the Ministry of Social Development at the end of the 8-week subsidy period, as the subsidy cannot be used beyond the subsidy period. However, if employers require further assistance between 21 August and 3 September 2020, they can apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, provided they meet the qualification criteria.

chunks.title: Employer applied for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension but not yet granted assistance — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: Unless the employer withdraws their application for this assistance, the employer will be granted the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension and the rules of that scheme will apply.

chunks.title: Employer received COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme was introduced on 28 April 2020 to provide financial assistance to employers during the COVID-19 public health restrictions to: - encourage employees to self-isolate when they need to and - support employees who are unable to work from home to have an income when they cannot work Employers eligible for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme can choose to apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme where it is appropriate for their employee's situation. However, an employer cannot get both the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme and the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for the same period, for the same employee.

chunks.title: Treatment of the subsidy for granting benefits — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: If an employer or a self-employed person is getting a main benefit or extra help from the Ministry of Social Development, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for themselves or their employees. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, any employee or self-employed person getting the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme as well as other support from the Ministry must declare the subsidy as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme should be counted as income over an 2-week period from the date of application for both employees and self-employed people and should not be counted as a cash asset. Any additional income drawn from the business or any other source must also be included in their total income.

chunks.title: Determining a lump sum payment of the subsidy — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: An employee or self-employed person should be paid the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme in the same way their wage or salary is normally paid, eg weekly wages for 2 weeks. However, some employers receiving the subsidy may pass it on to their employees as a lump sum payment. If the employee applies for assistance from the Ministry of Social Development, it is important to determine whether it is a lump sum payment of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme (on top of their regular wages during the subsidy period), or whether it represents a payment for other forms of leave owed to the client. For example, an employer may pay out some of the subsidy to a client to cover their redundancy notice period. This would not be considered a lump sum payment of the subsidy but would instead be pay in lieu of notice, which is a type of termination payment. If the employee is made redundant or the employer has surplus funds remaining at the end of the subsidy period, the employer is required to return any remaining amount of the subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development. However, some employers may pass on the remaining funds directly to the employee. If the employer pays out the remainder of the subsidy (eg once the employee's notice period has ended and they are no longer employed), this would be considered a lump sum payment of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme. If the payment is a lump sum payment of the subsidy, it may affect their eligibility for some types of assistance.

chunks.title: Benefit applications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: As the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme is paid to replace a loss of earnings it should be charged as income for a benefit or extra help, this includes when the subsidy is paid out to the client as a lump sum payment. When a client has received the subsidy as a lump sum payment, the Ministry of Social Development will consider the appropriate period that the payment is intended to represent and will charge it as income for that period. For example, the lump sum payment can be divided by the client's average earnings (using the last 2 weeks if appropriate) to determine how many weeks of income the payment is intended to represent. If the amount of the payment is less than the relevant income cut-out point, the client would qualify for assistance for the period the lump sum payment is charged for. If the amount is higher than the income cut-out point, the client would not qualify until the period the payment represents has finished. Note generally, a lump sum payment of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme (and the previous COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) and Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension) is not considered a termination payment, so does not need to be considered when calculating what date their employment ended. The lump sum would only be considered a termination payment when it is paid in lieu of notice. Example 1 Nate's employer got the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme on 24 August 2020, but 1 week later, decides to close the business and gives his employees notice that they will be made redundant. The business is closed on 31 August 2020, and Nate was paid for the redundancy notice period until that point. The employer decides to pay the balance of the subsidy of 1 week out to Nate as a lump sum. Nate decides to apply for Jobseeker Support and approaches the Ministry of Social Development for assistance on 31 August 2020. Nate's employment ceased date is 31 August 2020 and his commencement date is 1 September 2020. The initial stand-down period has been waived due to COVID-19. As he got a lump sum payment representing 1 week of income, Nate's first week of assistance is abated accordingly. If the lump sum payment is higher than the income cut-out point, Nate will not qualify for assistance until the period the payment represents has passed.

chunks.title: COVID-19 Income Relief Payment applications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 resurgence wage subsidy scheme
chunks.text: A person cannot get the COVID-19 Income Relief Payment if they are currently receiving the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension. If an employee got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension as a lump sum payment from their employer, they would not be eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Income Relief Payment until the appropriate period that the lump sum payment applies to has passed. Example 2 Pania's employer got the Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for her on 21 August 2020, but soon gives her notice of redundancy as their business has been badly affected by COVID-19. Pania gets a lump sum payment from her employer in lieu of working out her notice period. She gets this payment on 26 August 2020. Pania meets the other qualification criteria for the COVID-19 Income Relief Payment but is not eligible to apply for the scheme until the 2 week period the lump sum Wage Subsidy payment represents has passed. If an employer applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, and then they have a change in circumstance within the 2-week period, they may not be entitled to keep the subsidy they got for an employee.

chunks.title: Amount a business must pay an employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: When an employee has an entitlement to be paid as per their employment agreement or the law (eg by taking paid sick leave), the employer will use the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment to pay the employee their ordinary wages or their entitlement under the Holidays Act while they are waiting for the relevant COVID-19 PCR test result. For example, the employer will pay the ordinary wages or salary of each named employees at the same rate they would have been paid before the employee had their COVID-19 PCR test.

chunks.title: Employee has entitlement for paid leave if they are not able to work — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: When an employee has an entitlement to be paid as per their employment agreement or the law (eg by taking paid sick leave), the employer will use the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment to pay the employee their ordinary wages or their entitlement under the Holidays Act while they are waiting for the relevant COVID-19 PCR test result. For example, the employer will pay the ordinary wages or salary of each named employees at the same rate they would have been paid before the employee had their COVID-19 PCR test.

chunks.title: Employee has no entitlement to be paid if they are not able to work — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: When an employee does not have any entitlement to be paid if they are not able to work (eg if an employee has used up their paid sick leave so would be on unpaid leave) and the employer applies for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment, the employer: - should try to pay their employee as if they had worked that day or - if this is not possible, the employer must pay at least the full amount of the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment (minus any usual wage deductions) to the employee, while they are waiting for their COVID-19 PCR test result For example, if a full-time employee would usually earn $500 gross for the period they are at home waiting for their COVID-19 PCR test result and the employer cannot afford to pay them as if they had worked that day, then they must pay them the full COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment of $359 (less any usual wage deductions). Example Jericho is staying home to support his 10 year old daughter, while they are waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result. He normally works as a gym instructor but he needs to miss work for 3 days while they are waiting for his daughter's test result. Jericho's employer applies for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment and uses the $359 to contribute to Jericho's wages. His employer tops up the payment to $450 (less any usual wage deductions) so that Jericho can get his ordinary wages for the time he is staying home waiting for his daughter's test results.

chunks.title: Employee has no entitlement to be paid and would usually have earned less than the payment rate — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: When the employee would have earned equal to or less than the payment rate for the period they are staying home, the business must keep paying their ordinary wages or salary. Employers must use the remaining support to contribute to the wages or salary of other employees. However, when there are no other employees, the employer is not required to repay the surplus to the Ministry of Social Development. If the person is self-employed, and the wages or salary they get from their business is less than the payment rate for the period they are off work, they are not required to repay the surplus to the Ministry of Social Development. Example Harriet works part-time as a tour guide at her local museum. Harriet starts to feel unwell and has COVID-19 like symptoms. Her doctor gets her to take a COVID-19 PCR test, and they tell her that she needs to stay at home until she gets her test result. Harriet has to wait 2 days for her test result and there is no work she can do for her employer from home. Her employer applies for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment and uses the $359 payment to pay Harriet the $220 (less any usual wage deductions) that she would normally have earned during the time she is staying home. Her employer uses the remaining $139 to contribute to the wages of the other staff. If employers have questions about their obligations under employment law, they should contact Employment New Zealand for advice and assistance.

chunks.title: Sole traders and self-employed people — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Sole traders and self-employed people
Sole traders and self-employed people do not have to be registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, but must have:
- a personal Inland Revenue number for paying income tax and/or GST and
- government licences and permits for their business where appropriate and
- qualifications or registrations required for their trade or profession
Sole traders and self-employed people must still meet the requirements to be physically located and employed in New Zealand.
The Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed before paying the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment.

chunks.title: Businesses must follow employment law when paying wages — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Businesses must follow employment law when paying wages
Businesses (including self-employed people) who get the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment must use it to support the cost of wages or salary for the employees named in their application, while they are at home waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result.
Employers must pay their employees any amount required by the employment agreement and employment legislation. The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment requirements do not remove or reduce this obligation.
An employer cannot make employees take annual leave during the COVID-19 public health restrictions, but the employer and employee can agree for the employee to take annual leave.
In this situation the employee should be paid their ordinary wage rate for their ordinary hours of work and the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment will help employers pay for the annual leave taken.
Employers must follow due process.
## If employers need more information see:
- Employment New Zealand Coronavirus (COVID-19) and the workplace

chunks.title: Business not entitled but has been paid — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Business not entitled but has been paid
If a business (including self-employed people) applied for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment, and then they have a change in circumstance, they may not be entitled to keep the payment they got for an employee named in their application.
Change of circumstances
Employer action
The business applied for the wrong type of COVID-19 scheme for their employee, (eg applied for the Short-Term Absence Payment but meant to apply for the Leave Support Scheme).
The business must repay any amount they got for the incorrect application, and re-apply for the correct scheme they are entitled to.
Business is a state sector organisation who did not have an exception approved by the Minister of Finance to apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment but applied and got the funds.
The business is not entitled to the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment and must repay it in full.
Any state sector organisation that disagrees with the decision should consult with their monitoring agency.
Business gets payment they are not entitled to due to an office error (eg their application might have been paid twice or accidentally approved instead of declined).
The business is not entitled to the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment and must repay it to the Ministry of Social Development.
Business gets payment they are not entitled to as their employee does not meet the eligibility criteria (eg employee did not get a COVID-19 PCR test or did not miss any work).
The business is not entitled to the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment and must repay it to the Ministry of Social Development. Other enforcement action may be taken.

chunks.title: COVID-19 PCR test must have been taken — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## COVID-19 PCR test must have been taken
The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment closed at 11.59pm on 17 October 2022.
To qualify for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment the employee must:
- have had a COVID-19 PCR test themselves on or before 22 August 2022 or
- be the parent or caregiver of a dependant who has had a COVID-19 PCR test on or before 22 August 2022, and the employee needs to stay home with them
The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment is only available while an employee is staying at home waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result and is unable to work.
If the employee is told to stay home for a period before the test is taken, they are not eligible for payments until the COVID-19 PCR test has been taken and they are staying at home waiting for the results.

chunks.title: Dependant gets a test — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Dependant gets a test
Parents or caregivers of a dependant who has had a COVID-19 PCR test may need to stay home with them, while waiting for the dependant's test results.
For the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment, a dependant is someone who is primarily the responsibility of the employee and needs support to stay home while waiting for their test results.
This includes a dependent child or other person for reasons such as disability, illness, or advanced age.
Businesses (including self-employed people) told by their employee they have a dependent needing their support are eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment if the employee cannot work from home, and the business meets all the other eligibility criteria and complies with their obligations.
Example
Brooke is a single mother and works full-time as a dog groomer to support her 7 year-old daughter Nicole.
Nicole develops COVID-19 symptoms, so Brooke takes her to a community testing station, where the nurse gives Nicole a COVID-19 PCR test.
The nurse tells Brooke they must stay home until they get Nicole's test results.
Nicole needs support to stay at home safely, but Brooke cannot work from home for her employer.
Brooke's employer applies for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment and uses it to pay her for the time she is off work.

chunks.title: Determining if someone is self-employed — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Determining if someone is self-employed
A person is likely to be self-employed when they carry out business activities on their own, including contracting, working as a sole trader or owning a small business.
A self-employed person is likely to:
- support the business with their own money (eg providing all the equipment and tools needed for their job)
- decide or control how they work (eg when, where and what hours they work)
- decide how much they get paid and how
- pay their own income tax (unless they are a young person earning under the tax threshold)
- be responsible for investment decisions and any losses
- be able to sell the business if they wanted to
Note the above list is not exhaustive. Self-employed people are eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment, if they meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations.

chunks.title: Eligible businesses — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Eligible businesses
The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment is available to businesses with eligible employees across all sectors and industries in New Zealand for:
- businesses using any or multiple employment types including full-time, part-time, casual, fixed-term, sole trading and self-employment, including those businesses with employees getting the minimum wage exemption
- registered charities, incorporated societies, local government organisations (eg local councils), non-government organisations and post-settlement governance entities
- all State-Owned Enterprises and Mixed Ownership Model companies (from 16 March 2022)
## State-Owned Enterprises and Mixed Ownership Model companies
From 16 March 2022, State-Owned Enterprises and Mixed Ownership Model companies can access the COVID-19 Short Term Absence Payment without the need to seek an exception from the Minister of Finance.
State-Owned Enterprises are:
- Airways Corporation of New Zealand Ltd
- Animal Control Products Ltd
- AsureQuality Ltd
- Electricity Corporation of New Zealand Ltd
- KiwiRail Holdings Ltd
- Kordia Group Ltd
- Landcorp Farming Ltd
- Meteorological Service of New Zealand Ltd
- New Zealand Post Ltd
- New Zealand Railways Corporation
- Quotable Value Ltd
- Transpower New Zealand Ltd
Mixed Ownership Model companies are:
- Genesis Energy Ltd
- Mercury NZ Ltd
- Meridian Energy Ltd
## Other state sector organisations
State sector organisations are generally not eligible to get the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for their employees.
Exceptions for state sector employers are considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, through the relevant monitoring agency.

chunks.title: Employee gets a routine or surveillance test — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: Businesses (including self-employed people) whose employees do not have any COVID-19 symptoms and are taking part in routine testing in their workplace, or surveillance testing in the community do not need to stay home while waiting for their test results.

chunks.title: Routine testing in their workplace — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: Some employees are required to undertake routine testing in their workplace because they are at higher risk of exposure to COVID-19. They will not be asked to stay at home while they are waiting for their test results. These employees do not meet the eligibility criteria for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment, including border workers and managed isolation and quarantine (MIQ) workers. Example Mere works at a hotel in Christchurch that is an official MIQ facility. Mere has to get a COVID-19 test every 2 weeks as part of her role at the hotel, but she does not need to stay home while waiting for the results. Her employer is not eligible for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for Mere as the tests are part of routine testing in their workplace.

chunks.title: Surveillance testing in the community — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: Sometimes the Ministry of Health will set up COVID-19 testing sites in the community and members of the public volunteer to get tested at random. These employees will not be told to stay at home while waiting for test results, so do not meet the eligibility criteria for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment.

chunks.title: Employees undertaking routine and surveillance testing who have symptoms — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: However, if the employees undertaking routine or surveillance testing have COVID-19 symptoms and public health guidance requires them to stay home while waiting for their test results (even if the test takes place as part of routine or surveillance testing), then the business can apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for these employees. The business (including self-employed people) and employees in this situation must also meet the other eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations. Example Donna is a self-employed contractor working for New Zealand Customs Services, and is based at Auckland Airport. Donna is classified as a border worker as she interacts with travellers arriving in New Zealand from overseas. As part of this work, Donna and her colleagues are regularly tested for COVID-19. During her routine test on Tuesday, Donna told the nurse that she had developed some mild symptoms of COVID-19. The nurse told her to stay at home while she is waiting for her test result and Donna is away from work for the next 3 days. Although Donna was tested as part of her routine workplace testing, she is eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment as she had COVID-19 symptoms. Donna's self-employed business meets all of the eligibility criteria and obligations and the payment is granted. Donna uses the payment to cover her income for the time she stays at home waiting for her test result.

chunks.title: Air crew members — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: Generally, the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment does not cover air crew members (as defined in the COVID-19 Public Health Response (Required Testing) Order 2020), even if they have COVID-19 symptoms. This includes: - cabin crew who are ordinarily resident in New Zealand and work on an international flight (other than specific flights) on or after 19 October 2020 - other people who are ordinarily resident and are identified as crew members on a crew manifest international flight (other than specific flights) that had an international layover on or after 19 October 2020 These employees must follow different testing and isolation requirements, and other arrangements have been made to make sure these employers support their employees. However, if these employees are the parent or caregiver of a dependant who needs support to stay at home while waiting for their test results, their employer may be eligible for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for them, provided they meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations.

chunks.title: Employee gets a test themselves — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Employee gets a test themselves
Employees who have had a COVID-19 PCR test may need to stay home while waiting for their test results.
Businesses (including self-employed people) who are told by their employee they are in this group can apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment, if the employee cannot work from home and the business meets all the eligibility criteria and complies with their obligations.
Example
Rangi gets an alert through the NZ COVID Tracer application notifying him that a person at his local supermarket has tested positive for COVID-19.
Rangi was shopping for groceries at the same time as the person with COVID-19, and he has COVID-19 like symptoms.
Rangi is an optometrist and cannot work for his employer from home but he does not meet the eligibility criteria for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment until he has had a COVID-19 PCR test.
Rangi and his employer agree for him to take special leave for the time he is off work. The employer applies for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment when Rangi has the COVID-19 PCR test.
The employer continues paying Rangi, while he is waiting for his COVID-19 PCR test results.

chunks.title: Employee must miss work — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: To be eligible for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment, the employee must need to miss work, while staying home waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result. This could mean missing a whole shift or more of work, or just a couple of hours on any day, or a few days when the employee was scheduled to be working. Missing work means that employees must be unable to work because they are staying home waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result, and cannot perform their work from home. However, employees (including self-employed people) must have been scheduled to be working during the time they are staying at home. Note if the employee is told to stay at home for a period before the test is taken and they need to miss work before getting a test they will not be eligible for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment until the COVID-19 PCR test has been taken and they are staying at home waiting for the results. Example 1 Heather is a beautician and lives with her brother Tūmanako who has a learning disability. Heather is Tūmanako's caregiver, but he normally goes to a community day service during the week, while she is at work. Tūmanako gets a COVID-19 PCR test after developing COVID-19 symptoms and the Unite Against COVID-19 website recommends people in his situation stay at home while waiting for test results. Heather left work early on Thursday to take him to get the test and needs to miss her 4 hour shift on Friday to stay home and support him while waiting for the results. There is no work she can do for her employer from home. Tūmanako gets his test results back over the weekend and Heather’s employer applies for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment when she comes back to work on Monday. Her employer meets all of the eligibility criteria and complies with their obligations and uses the payment to pay Heather for the Friday shift that she missed Example 2 Wendy develops COVID-19 symptoms and her doctor tells her to get a COVID-19 PCR test and stay at home while waiting for the results. Wendy works part-time as a cleaner 3 days a week and she cannot do this work from home.

chunks.title: Employee must miss work — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: Wendy is at home for 2 days while waiting for her test results. She is not rostered to be working but her employer calls her on the second day and asks if she can come into work. Wendy has to turn down the extra shift as she is still waiting for her test results. As Wendy did not miss any work that she was expecting to do, she does not meet the eligibility criteria for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment.

chunks.title: Employee taking leave — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: Some employees may take sick leave, unpaid leave or another form of leave while staying at home waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result. The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment is available for businesses (including self-employed people) to pay all eligible employees, regardless of whether they are taking sick leave or have a sick leave balance. An employer cannot unlawfully make any of the employees use their leave entitlements for the period the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment is paid. They must have been planning to work during the time they need to stay home. Note employees who are taking annual leave before they need to stay home are considered to have been planning to work.
