Employees who were already off work, eg employees on long-term unpaid leave, getting compensation from ACC, as well as people on parental leave do not meet the eligibility criteria for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment. This is because they were not planning to be working during the period they need to stay home. Self-employed people do not have any leave entitlements so must need to miss scheduled work to be eligible for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment. Example 1 Che develops COVID-19 symptoms and staff at the community testing station tell them to stay home while waiting for their COVID-19 PCR test results. Che is a bus driver and cannot work for their employer from home. They only have 10 hours of sick leave remaining for the year. Che discusses their situation with their employer and the employer applies for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment to continue paying Che. The employer uses the payment to pay Che their ordinary wages for the time they are at home waiting for their test result, and agrees that Che can take special paid leave. Che gets a negative test result 2 days after their test but they are still not well enough to return to work. Che uses their sick leave for the remaining time they are off work. Note Che has indicated their preferred pronoun is 'they' (rather than he or she) and this is reflected in this example. Example 2 Tākuta is a self-employed electrician from Auckland. While away on holiday in Taupō he is notified through the NZ COVID Tracer application that he went to the same cafe as someone who tested positive for COVID-19. If he gets any symptoms he should get tested and stay home until he gets his test results.

chunks.title: Employee taking leave — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: Over the next couple of days, while he is still away from work, Tākuta develops cold symptoms and decides to get a test. He takes a COVID-19 PCR test and needs to stay at home (or at his holiday accommodation in Taupō) until he gets his test results, but as he was not planning to be working (and is not taking annual leave as he is self-employed), he is not eligible for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment.

chunks.title: Health and disability funded workforce — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Health and disability funded workforce
Health and disability funded workforces (such as businesses that provide community health care) not employed by the state sector are eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment if they meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations.
Health and disability funded workforces not employed by the state sector includes organisations that are contracted to, or funded in whole or part, by organisations in the state sector.
Examples include:
- in-home care workers
- employees in Primary Health Organisations
- nurses and other staff in rest homes or other residential care facilities (eg cooks, cleaners, support staff)
- health and disability facilities or services or get funding from the Ministry of Health, District Health Boards, or the Ministry of Social Development

chunks.title: COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment closed at 11.59pm on 17 October 2022. The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme is available for businesses whose employees (or their dependants) are required or advised to self-isolate in line with public health guidelines. The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme covers people who cannot go to work and cannot work from home because: - they have COVID-19 or - are a contact of someone who has COVID-19 and public health guidance requires them to self-isolate or - they are the caregiver of a dependant who is required to self-isolate or - they or a member of their household is considered at 'higher risk' of severe illness from COVID-19 and a medical practitioner has advised them to self-isolate. Businesses cannot be eligible for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme and the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for the same employee, at the same time. However, some businesses who get the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment may subsequently apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme if their employee's (or their dependants) COVID-19 PCR test result is positive or, is required to self-isolate for a period of at least 4 consecutive days after they get the test results. Other businesses may apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme straight away, regardless of the outcome of their initial test, if their employee is required in line with public health guidance or is advised by a medical practitioner to self-isolate for at least 4 consecutive days, regardless of the outcome of their initial test result. Businesses will need to ensure they meet the eligibility criteria, and comply with the obligations for the specific scheme they are applying for. Example 1 Eru is a builder's apprentice and gets a COVID-19 PCR test after developing symptoms. Eru is required to stay home while waiting for his test results. Eru cannot work from home and misses 2 shifts of work while staying at home. His employer meets the eligibility criteria and obligations for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment, and the payment is granted. Eru gets a positive COVID-19 PCR test result 4 days later and is required to self-isolate in line with public health guidance.

chunks.title: COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: Eru's employer can apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme, provided they meet the eligibility criteria, and comply with their obligations. The eligibility criteria for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme includes that an employee must be self-isolating for a period of at least 4 consecutive days. The number of days Eru has stayed at home waiting for his test result, ie 4 days, can be used towards the total number of days in self-isolation. This is because his COVID-19 PCR test result was positive and Eru is now required to self-isolate for a further 3 days to complete the self-isolation period. Example 2 Fallyn receives a notification through the NZ COVID Tracer application that tells her she was at a local restaurant at the same time as someone with COVID-19. She develops COVID-19 like symptoms and goes to her doctor because she has chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder and is worried about being at higher risk of severe illness if she gets COVID-19. The doctor gets Fallyn to take a COVID-19 PCR test and advises her to self-isolate for 14 days. Fallyn's employer applies for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme as she meets the eligibility criteria of this scheme regardless of the outcome of her COVID-19 test. For more information see:

chunks.title: Flexi-Wage, Flexi-Wage Self-Employment and Mana in Mahi — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: If a business is currently getting the Flexi-Wage, Flexi-Wage Self-Employment or Mana in Mahi subsidy for their employee(s), they can also apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment, provided they meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations. All wage subsidies that the business gets must be used to pay their employees. For more information see:

chunks.title: Apprenticeship Boost Initiative — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: Apprenticeship Boost helps businesses with the costs of keeping their current apprentices or hiring new ones for the first 24 months of their programme of study. If a business is currently getting Apprenticeship Boost for their employee(s), they can also apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for those employees, where appropriate. For more information see:

chunks.title: Main benefit and other support — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: Any individual getting a main benefit or other extra help must declare their wages or salary if they are required to as part of their beneficiary obligations. All Ministry of Social Development clients must meet their obligations in relation to the financial assistance they are getting, including declaring any income they get (if appropriate). When assessing an application staff must not check if an applicant for the subsidy is getting other financial assistance from the Ministry of Social Development, as this is a privacy breach.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment closed at 11.59pm on 17 October 2022.
The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment provided financial assistance from 9 February 2021 to 22 August 2022 for businesses (including self-employed people) during the COVID-19 health response to:
- encourage employees to stay home while waiting for a COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test result (in line with public health guidance) and
- support employees unable to work from home, with an income while they cannot work
This assistance was available to businesses (including self-employed people) as a one-off payment of $359 for each employee who met the eligibility criteria.
Any COVID-19 PCR test taken by an employee on or before 22 August 2022 was still eligible for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment as long as the eligibility criteria were met.
From 23 August 2022 applications for this assistance were still able to be made for COVID-19 PCR tests taken on or before 22 August 2022. These applications must have been made within 8 weeks of the date the COVID-19 PCR test was taken. This means the final date of applications to be made was 17 October 2022.
A business was able apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for an employee once in a 30-day period (unless an exception applied) from the date of application.
## Applications
The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment closed at 11.59pm on 17 October 2022.
Businesses (including self-employed people) must apply online for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment.
An application can be made even if the employee has already got their COVID-19 PCR test results and has returned to work.
Provided the business meets the eligibility criteria and complies with their obligations, an application can be made up to 8 weeks after the relevant COVID-19 test was taken. However, the test must have been taken on or before 22 August 2022.
The last date for an application for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment was 17 October 2022. Any applications made on 17 October 2022 must relate to a COVID-19 PCR test taken on 22 August 2022.

chunks.title: Legally working in New Zealand — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Legally working in New Zealand
Legally working in New Zealand means a person is both working in New Zealand, and legally entitled to work in New Zealand.
A person cannot be employed if they cannot legally work in New Zealand in that job.
It is the responsibility of the business to make sure that an employee can work for them legally.

chunks.title: Newly hired employees — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Newly hired employees
The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment is open for eligible businesses to apply for any newly hired employees, including those who have been unable to start work because they need to stay home while waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result.
The Ministry of Social Development does not require verification such as employment contracts.
Example
Emily was recently hired as a teacher at a local primary school. She was supposed to start work on Monday, but on Saturday she develops COVID-19 symptoms. She goes to a community testing station, takes a COVID-19 PCR test and the staff tell her to stay at home until she gets the test results.
Emily is unable to start work as expected and there is no work she can do for her new employer from home. Emily gets her test results back on Wednesday and her employer applies for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment when she starts work on Thursday.
Her employer meets all of the eligibility criteria and complies with their obligations and uses the payment to pay Emily for the work she missed while staying home waiting for her test results.

chunks.title: One payment in a 30-day period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: Generally, a business (including self-employed people) can only apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment once in any 30-day period for each eligible employee (unless a health official or medical practitioner advises or requires another COVID-19 PCR test to be taken). When a health official or medical practitioner advises or requires an employee or their dependant to get another COVID-19 PCR test within 30 days of a previous COVID-19 PCR test, then the business can apply for another COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment. The Ministry of Social Development considers applications on a case-by-case basis and may contact the applicant for further information to ensure the business meets all of the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations to get a second payment, eg confirming with the employer that the employee did tell them that the employee had been advised by a doctor or other health official they or their dependant needs to get another COVID-19 PCR test, and as a result the employee is staying home while waiting for the results of this COVID-19 PCR test.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: John is a retail assistant for a shoe store. He develops COVID-19 symptoms and Healthline advise him to get a test. John takes a COVID-19 PCR test at a community testing centre and must stay at home until he gets his results. His employer applies for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment. Two weeks later, John's son develops COVID-19 like symptoms and takes a COVID-19 PCR test at their local medical centre. The doctor tells John that his son must stay home while they are waiting for his test results. John must stay at home with his son while waiting for his COVID-19 PCR test results, meaning he has to miss work for a second time within a 30-day period. His employer applies for a second payment of the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment. The business meets the eligibility criteria and obligations, and John's employer uses the payment to contribute to his wages for the time he stays at home.

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: Debbie is a physiotherapist. She develops COVID-19 symptoms and, after getting a COVID-19 PCR test, is told by the community-testing station to stay home while waiting for her test results. She cannot work from home and her employer applies for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment. A couple of weeks later Debbie is unwell again and decides to get another COVID-19 PCR test. The nurse at the testing station recommends she stay home again while waiting for her COVID-19 PCR test results. However, this is the second test Debbie has had in 30 days, and she has not been advised that she needs to get another test by a health official (eg through the National Investigation and Tracing Centre), or by a doctor. Debbie stays home while waiting for her test results but does not meet the criteria for a second payment of the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment within a 30-day period. If the same circumstances had occurred outside of the 30-day period, then Debbie would have been eligible for another payment.

chunks.title: Ordinary wages or salary — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Ordinary wages or salary
For employees, their ordinary wages or salary are specified in their employment agreement at the date their employer applies for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for them.
This includes any statutory obligations that the employer must pay their employees (eg public holidays the employee would otherwise have been paid).
Self-employed people can determine their ordinary wages or salary by calculating the regular amount left over from income generated after they meet their business costs (as at the date that they apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment).
This is the amount they regularly pay themselves from the business.

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment closed at 11.59pm on 17 October 2022. The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment is paid to a business as a one-off payment of $359 per eligible employee. This rate is the same for full-time and part-time employees, and is the same regardless of how long the employee (or self-employed person) needs to stay home while waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result.

chunks.title: Maximum payment for an employer — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: There is no cap on the total amount of COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment an eligible business can get, payments are made based on the eligibility of each employee. Only 1 COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment can be made in a 30-day period for each eligible employee (unless a health official or medical practitioner tells the employee or, their dependant to get another COVID-19 PCR test). See:

chunks.title: Applying retrospectively — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: An application can be made at any point up to 8 weeks after an employee took their COVID-19 PCR test, provided the business meets the qualifications and the employee took their COVID-19 PCR test on or before 22 August 2022. The last day for an application for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment is 17 October 2022. Example 1 Rawiri works part-time as a dental hygienist. He has COVID-19 symptoms on Thursday and decides to get a COVID-19 test that day. Rawiri was supposed to be working on Friday, but at the community testing station after getting his COVID-19 PCR test the nurse tells him he should stay home while waiting for his test results. Rawiri stays home and gets the test results back on Friday afternoon. The test result was negative, so he is able to return to work on Monday. Rawiri's employer applies for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment on Tuesday. Even though Rawiri is already back at work, the business meets all of the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations, and the payment is granted. Example 2 Maria is a self-employed hairdresser and works full-time. She develops COVID-19 symptoms and goes to her doctor for a test. The doctor gets Maria to take a COVID-19 PCR test and tells her she should stay home while waiting for her test results. She cannot work from home and cancels appointments across the 3 days that she is home waiting for her test results. Maria gets her negative test result after 3 days and returns to work the next day. She has a busy couple of weeks and does not get a chance to complete the application for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment until 6 weeks later. Maria meets all the eligibility criteria for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment.

chunks.title: August 2021 rate increase — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: On 24 August 2021, the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence rate increased from $350 to $359. The increased rate applies for all applications made on or after 24 August 2021, even if the relevant test was taken before 24 August 2021.

chunks.title: People getting income from a property business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## People getting income from a property business
Some people are paid a wage or salary from a property business, such as private rental, Airbnb and homestay operations
These businesses can get the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment if they meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations, including being registered (excluding self-employed people) and operating in New Zealand.
Note the payment is paid to support employers to retain their employees, or offset a loss of earnings (for self-employed people) and can only be used to support the cost of wages or salaries. Self-employed people who apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for a property business must be able to declare that they receive wages or salary for this work.
For self-employed people who are not registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, the Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed and cannot perform their work from home before paying the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment.

chunks.title: People working multiple jobs — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## People working multiple jobs
Employers may have employees who work for them, and another employer.
If both employers meet the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations, and the employee misses work for both employers while staying home waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result, they can each apply for COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for the same employee.

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment closed at 11.59pm on 17 October 2022. To be eligible for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment, businesses (including self-employed people) must meet the following eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations: - the business has been told by their employee that a COVID-19 PCR test has been taken for: themselves or their dependant - themselves or their dependant - the employee needs to stay home while waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result, in line with public health guidance - the employee cannot work for the business from home and will miss work when staying at home waiting for the COVID-19 PCR test result - the business is registered (excludes self-employed people) and operating in New Zealand - the employee is legally working in New Zealand and employed by the business as at the date of the application - the business has not already received another COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for the employee in the 30 days before applying (unless the employee meets the exception to get paid more than once in 30 days) Applications can be made for up to 8 weeks after a COVID-19 PCR test is taken. Note before 16 March 2022 the eligibility criteria included that in some circumstances, household members (and other people at the discretion of the Medical Officer of Health) of close contacts may have been told to stay home while waiting for the close contact's COVID-19 test results (people in this category were also known as secondary contacts). This may be because the close contact develops COVID-19 symptoms, or the close contact is at higher risk of having COVID-19. From 16 March 2022 this group is no longer included in the eligibility criteria for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment as this category no longer exists. However, businesses may apply for employees who were staying at home and could not work while waiting for COVID-19 PCR test results before this date, if the application is made within 8 weeks after the date the test was taken.

chunks.title: Applying for more than one payment in any 30-day period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: Generally, a business can only apply once in any 30-day period for each eligible employee. However, if an employee or their dependant is advised or required to get another COVID-19 PCR test within 30 days of a previous test, then the business may be able to apply for another COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for the employee. The employee must have been advised or required (in line with public health guidance) that a second test is needed for the business to get multiple COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payments for an employee within a 30-day period. For more information see:

chunks.title: Some employees cannot get the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment cannot be paid to a business for employees who: - take a COVID-19 Rapid Antigen Test (RAT) unless they take a COVID-19 PCR test to confirm the result of the RAT - do not have COVID-19 symptoms and are taking part in routine testing in their workplace, such as border and Managed Isolation and Quarantine (MIQ) workers - do not have COVID-19 symptoms and are taking part in surveillance testing, or who have not been told to stay home while waiting for test results - are eligible for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme at the date of the relevant COVID-19 test - are employed as an air crew member (as defined in the COVID-19 Public Health Response (Required Testing) Order 2020) and required to comply with any orders made in accordance with the COVID-19 Public Health Response Act 2020 (unless they meet the eligibility criteria for a COVID-19 PCR test for their dependant who must stay home and needs their support to stay home while waiting for their test results). - are a New Zealander who is currently overseas - are required to self-isolate because they have come to New Zealand from overseas

chunks.title: Returning unused funds after the employee gets the test result — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Returning unused funds after the employee gets the test result
The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment is a one-off payment to the business (including self-employed people), to support the cost of wages while the employee is staying home waiting for their COVID-19 PCR test results.
If the business has any unused funds after the employee gets the COVID-19 PCR test results, they can use the remaining amount towards the cost of wages for other employees.
When there are no other employees, the business is not required to repay the remaining amount to the Ministry of Social Development.
Businesses can make voluntary repayments if they would like to.

chunks.title: Reviewing decisions to decline payment — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Reviewing decisions to decline payment
Decisions to decline the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment are not made under the Social Security Act 2018 and are not covered by the usual Review of Decision guidelines.
If a business (including a self-employed person) wants a decision to decline the payment reconsidered, the decision should be reconsidered based on whether an 'informed' decision was made and should consider the following:
- whether all relevant information was obtained and
- whether the appropriate options and implications were considered and
- whether the decision was made at the appropriate level of delegation
If the decision to decline the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment is confirmed to be correct, the business can ask the Ombudsman to undertake their own review.

chunks.title: Self-employed person is also an employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Self-employed person is also an employee
A person may be self-employed for some of their income, and also be employed by a business or other organisation.
If the self-employed person is eligible, and they miss work in their self-employed business while staying home waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result, they can apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for their own business.
Also, if their employer is eligible, and the employee also needs to miss work for their employer while staying home waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result, the employer can also apply for COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for the employee.

chunks.title: Someone else gets a test (in specific circumstances) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: From 16 March 2022 household members (and other people at the discretion of the Medical Officer of Health) of close contacts are no longer required to self-isolate and are not eligible for the COVID-19 Short Term Absence Payment. Businesses (or self-employed people) may be eligible for employees in this group who took a COVID-19 PCR test before 16 March 2022, had to stay home waiting for their test results and could not work from home. However, they must apply within 8 weeks of the date the test was taken.

chunks.title: Guidance before 16 March 2022 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: This guidance is relevant to applications from eligible businesses with eligible employees who took a COVID-19 PCR test before 16 March 2022. People were identified as a close contact of someone who had COVID-19 were advised or directed to self-isolate for a period and get tested for COVID-19 and may have been eligible for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme. In some circumstances, their household members (and other people at the discretion of the Medical Officer of Health) may also have been told to stay home while waiting for the close contact's COVID-19 PCR test results. This may be because the close contact had COVID-19 symptoms, or the close contact was at 'higher risk' if they got COVID-19. If these employees were not considered close contacts themselves, they did not qualify for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme but may have been able to get the Short-Term Absence Payment once the close contact had a COVID-19 PCR test and the employee has also been told to stay home until the close contact gets their test results.

chunks.title: Household member gets a test and the employee is told to stay home — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: People who live with someone who has been identified as a close contact will be told by a medical practitioner or other health officials through the National Contact Tracing process (ie a Public Health Unit, the National Investigation and Tracing Centre or a Ministry of Health-contracted provider) whether they need to stay home while the person in their household is waiting for their test results. This advice may also come from a Medical Officer of Health (as defined in the Health Act 1956). Businesses (including self-employed people) who are told by their employee they are in this group are eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment if the employee cannot work from home and the business meets the other eligibility criteria and complies with their obligations. Example 1 David works as a gondola operator in Queenstown, where he lives with his partner Chris. Chris was identified by the Ministry of Health as a close contact of someone who has COVID-19 and is advised to self-isolate for 14 days and get tested. Although David did not have any contact with the person who has COVID-19, health officials tell him that he should stay at home and wait for the results of Chris' COVID-19 test, which Chris takes 5 days after he starts self-isolating. David is unable to do any work for his employer from home and does not meet the eligibility criteria for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment until Chris has taken the COVID-19 test. David uses annual leave for the time he is off work. After Chris has taken the test, David's employer applies for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment. While they are waiting for the test results, the employer pays David for the time he is home after Chris got the test.

chunks.title: Someone else gets a test and the employee is told to stay home — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: An employee may be told to stay home while waiting for the COVID-19 test results of someone identified as a close contact outside of their household. These employees will be contacted by a medical practitioner or other health officials through the National Contact Tracing process and told to stay home until the close contact returns a negative test result. Whether or not these employees need to stay home is at the discretion of the relevant Medical Officer of Health (as defined in the Health Act 1956). Businesses (including self-employed people) told by their employee they are in this group are eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment if the employee cannot work from home, and the business meets the other eligibility criteria and complies with their obligations. Example 2 Kiri lives with her friend Jo in Wellington. Jo's boyfriend is identified as a close contact of someone who has COVID-19 and is advised to self-isolate for 14 days as a precaution. Jo's boyfriend had been spending a lot of time at Kiri and Jo's house recently and they had all made food together the day after he had contact with the person who has COVID-19. A couple of days after he starts self-isolating, Jo's boyfriend develops COVID-19 symptoms. The National Investigation and Tracing Centre team contacts Kiri and Jo and tells them to stay at home until Jo's boyfriend returns a negative test result. Kiri and Jo both work on the ferry and are unable to work from home for their employers. Their employers apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment and this is used to pay Kiri and Jo for the time they are off work.

chunks.title: Specific employment situations — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Specific employment situations
People's work situations in New Zealand may vary, and eligibility for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment can sometimes differ.

chunks.title: State sector organisations generally not eligible — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: State sector organisations are generally not eligible to get the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment. State sector organisations are listed on the Public Service Commission website. See: - New Zealand's central government organisations Te Kawa Mataaho Public Service Commission State sector organisations can request an exception to allow them to apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment. Exceptions for state sector organisations are considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, through the relevant monitoring agency. If an exception has already been granted for a COVID-19 Wage Subsidy, the state sector organisation does not need to get another exception to apply for COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment.

chunks.title: State sector organisations that can apply — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: As at 17 September 2021, the only state sector organisations that have been granted an exception and can apply for the payment are: - Airways Corporation of New Zealand Limited - New Zealand Post Limited - Television New Zealand Limited - KiwiRail Holdings Limited - Quotable Value Limited - New Zealand Artificial Limb Service - Crown Research Institutes (CRIs): AgResearch LimitedInstitute of Environmental Science and Research LimitedInstitute of Geological and Nuclear Sciences LimitedLandcare Research New Zealand LimitedNational Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research LimitedNew Zealand Forest Research Institute LimitedThe New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research Limited - AgResearch Limited - Institute of Environmental Science and Research Limited - Institute of Geological and Nuclear Sciences Limited - Landcare Research New Zealand Limited - National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research Limited - New Zealand Forest Research Institute Limited - The New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research Limited Note the above list includes some State-Owned Enterprises and Mixed Ownership Model companies. From 16 March all State-Owned Enterprises and Mixed Ownership Model companies can apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment without the need to seek an exception. State sector organisations in the list above can apply but they must meet all the eligibility criteria and comply with their obligations. No other state sector organisations are permitted to apply for the payment.

chunks.title: Other State sector organisations cannot apply — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text: None of the other organisations described on Te Kawa Mataaho Public Service Commission are permitted to apply for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment. This includes: - State schools, state-integrated schools and special institutions (each being Boards of Trustees that are bodies corporate constituted under subpart 5 of Part 3 of the Education and Training Act 2020 (including distance schools)) - Crown entity subsidiaries (being companies incorporated under the Companies Act 1993 that are controlled by Crown entities): for a state school, state integrated school or special institution, Crown entity subsidiaries can include separate legal entities providing, for example, after-school care programmes, hostels, shopfor District Health Boards, Crown entity subsidiaries can include separate legal entities providing, for example, laundry services - for a state school, state integrated school or special institution, Crown entity subsidiaries can include separate legal entities providing, for example, after-school care programmes, hostels, shop - for District Health Boards, Crown entity subsidiaries can include separate legal entities providing, for example, laundry services Crown entities should ensure their subsidiaries do not apply for the payment. Note Local government organisations are not state sector organisations.

chunks.title: Staying at home under public health guidance — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Staying at home under public health guidance
To be eligible for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment the employer must have been told by their employee they are (or they are a self-employed person who is) staying home while waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result, in line with public health guidance.
Whether people need to stay home while waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result will depend on public health guidance at the time the test is taken.
Public health guidance may come from a range of places, including:
- Unite against COVID-19 website
- Healthline
- a doctor or General Practitioner (GP)
- Community-based Assessment Centres or COVID-19 testing clinics
- the National Investigation and Tracing Centre (including push notifications from the COVID-19 Tracer App)
- Medical Officers of Health
- Ministry of Health contracted providers
- Public Health Units
- Media communications such as Ministers' announcements and public briefings
The Ministry of Social Development does not require verification such as a medical certificate or proof of test.

chunks.title: Worker temporarily overseas and cannot return due to COVID-19 restrictions — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 short term absence payment
chunks.text:
## Worker temporarily overseas and cannot return due to COVID-19 restrictions
A person who is legally employed in New Zealand but who is currently overseas is not eligible to be named in a COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment application, as this payment is to support employers to continue paying employees, while the employee is following public health guidance to stay home.
This means that an employer or self-employed person cannot include an employee (or themselves) in their COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment application if they are overseas, even if:
- the employee meets the criteria of needing to miss work to stay home while waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result, in accordance with public health guidance and
- they were legally working in New Zealand before leaving and
- their absence was intended to be temporary (eg a holiday or a work business trip) and
- they maintain their employment status (that is, they are still employed by the employer or their own business), and intended to return to work on a specific date but cannot start on that date because of the COVID-19 travel restrictions
Employers and their employee can both agree to use another form of paid leave (eg annual leave, sick leave) to cover the period they cannot work.

chunks.title: Amount employer must pay employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: The impact of the COVID-19 public health restrictions means that the hours staff work or the amount they are paid (or both) may have to change. That can only be done in accordance with existing employment law. The amount the employer must pay to the employee depends on whether the employee usually earns under, or over the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) rate applied for them.

chunks.title: Employer can pay at least 80% — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: Employers who receive the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) must use their best endeavours to pay at least 80% of each named employees wages or salary for the period of the subsidy, at the rate they would have been paid before the business was impacted by the COVID-19 public health restrictions Note if an employer is not able to continue paying 100% of an employees wages or salary for the duration of the subsidy period, then the employees hours should be adjusted accordingly. When the employee was earning less than the subsidy rate, the employer must keep paying their usual wages, regardless of whether they are working fewer hours during the subsidy period. The employer must use the remaining support to contribute to the wages of other affected staff and where there are no other employees, must repay the remaining subsidy back to the Ministry of Social Development as it was not able to be used for wages. If the person is self-employed and the income that they regularly draw from their business is less than the subsidy amount they received, they can repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development. Example 1 John earns $956 gross per week. His employer can continue paying 80% of this ($764.80) while John is at home and there is no work for him to do. The employer receives the subsidy rate of $585.80 gross per week and continues to pay John $764.80 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions) for the subsidy period. When John goes back to work in Alert Level 3 his employer opens and John goes straight back to working his normal hours. The subsidy is used by the employer to help fund his normal wages of $956 gross per week. Example 2 Miri earns $220 gross per week. Her employer can continue paying 80% of her earnings ($176) while Miri is at home and there is no work for her to do. The employer receives the subsidy rate of $350 gross per week, but because Miri earns under the subsidy rate the employer must continue to pay her wages or salary at the rate they would have been paid before the business was impacted by the COVID-19 public health restrictions. That is her wages of $220 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions).

chunks.title: Employer can pay at least 80% — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: When her employer re-opens, the business starts slowly and Miri is only offered half of her hours. Her employer must pay her for these hours and because she earned under the subsidy rate, her employer must continue to pay her usual wages for the subsidy period ($220 gross per week).

chunks.title: Not possible for employer to pay at least 80% — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: If paying 80% of their pre COVID-19 impact wages or salary is not possible, and the employee was usually earning over the subsidy rate applied for, the employer must pass on the full weekly amount of support (less any usual wage deductions) to the employee. When the employee was earning less than the subsidy rate, the employer must keep paying their usual wages, regardless of whether they are working fewer hours during the subsidy period. The employer must use the remaining support to contribute to the wages of other affected staff and where there are no other employees, must repay the remaining subsidy back to the Ministry of Social Development as it was not able to be used for wages. Example 1 Mandy usually earns $1000 gross per week. Her employer is unable to continue paying 80% of her wages during this time while she is at home, and there is no work for her to do. The employer receives the subsidy rate of $585.80 gross per week, and because she usually earns over this amount, must pass on this amount to Mandy as wages. She receives $585.80 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions) during this period. Mandy can go back to work when her employer begins operating again and continues working her usual hours. The employer uses the subsidy to help to pay her normal wages for the remainder of the subsidy period (ie $1000 gross per week). Example 2 Tane usually earns $450 gross per week for 25 hours and his employer receives the full-time subsidy rate of $585.80 gross per week for him. Because he usually earns under this amount, Tane continues to be paid his usually wages of $450 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions). When Tane goes back to work, his employer only needs him for 15 hours to start with. The employer must continue paying Tane his usual wages of $450 gross per week as the employer has been paid for the full-time subsidy rate. Tane's employer can use the remainder of the support to pay wages of other affected employees. When there are no other affected employees, the employer must refund the remainder back to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Assessing 30% predicted or actual revenue loss — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Assessing 30% predicted or actual revenue loss
When deciding if the employer has had a decline in revenue, the Ministry of Social Development considers:
- the type of work the business does, eg retail, manufacturing, sales, construction, driving and
- whether (or to the extent) the business was able to operate in lockdown (eg was it an essential business or not, what changes did the business have to make due to the Alert Level operating rules) and
- whether the estimated loss of revenue makes sense (based on the business circumstances)?
Note that in most cases verification of the revenue decline is not required. However, the Ministry of Social Development may ask for verification in some cases.
## Employer cannot open due to COVID-19 public health restrictions
Generally, where a business cannot operate due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions, the Ministry of Social Development would usually accept the employer's statement that they have had a 30% revenue decrease, or predicted revenue decrease.
## Employer has been open during COVID-19 public health restrictions
Some businesses have been able to operate during COVID-19 Alert Level 4 and have increased in number at lower Alert Levels (eg Alert Levels 2 and 3). For businesses that have been able to operate, when deciding if they have had a decline in revenue, the Ministry of Social Development considers the reasons given for the decline in revenue, and whether these are reasonable given the type of work the business does.
Being open for business does not protect a business from having a 30% reduction in revenue, but further consideration needs to be given to their circumstances.
For example, a business who has remained open may not be able to sell the same level of product, as they have had reduced demand from other businesses (eg frozen food which they used to provide to fast food or other restaurants).
For these employers, the Ministry needs to consider their individual situations and make decisions based on their facts.

chunks.title: Business is registered and operating in New Zealand — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Business is registered and operating in New Zealand
This means that a business is:
- registered with the New Zealand Companies Office and
- physically located in New Zealand and
- their employees legally work in New Zealand
## Sole traders
Sole traders are not required to be registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, but must have:
- a personal Inland Revenue number for paying income tax and/or GST and
- government licences and permits for their business needs and
- qualifications or registrations for their trade or profession
Sole traders must still meet the requirements to be physically located and legally working in New Zealand.
The Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed before paying the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified).

chunks.title: Businesses operating for less than a year (or a high growth firm) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Businesses operating for less than a year (or a high growth firm)
When a business has been operating for less than a year or is a high growth firm (eg businesses that have had a significant increase in revenue), they can compare their revenue against a previous month or 30 day period that gives the best estimation of the revenue decline related to COVID-19.
Example 30% loss of revenue attributable to COVID-19 comparing January 2020 to March 2020.

chunks.title: Businesses who had not started operating before the COVID-19 public health restrictions — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Businesses who had not started operating before the COVID-19 public health restrictions
Some employers or self-employed people may have had their plans to start their business affected by the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), the employer must have experienced a 30% decline in revenue. To determine this decline, the business needs to be able to compare their actual and predicted revenue against a previous month or 30 day period.
This means that the business must have been operating for at least one month or 30 days to determine the decline in revenue.
## Example
A chiropractor was moving from employment to start their own business but did not begin trading before the COVID-19 public health restrictions came into effect.
When the chiropractor is able to start and has been trading for 30 days, they will be able to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), provided they meet the other qualification criteria.

chunks.title: Businesses who receive insurance payments to cover revenue loss — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Businesses who receive insurance payments to cover revenue loss
Some businesses have received insurance payments, such as business interruption insurance, to cover their loss of revenue during the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
If the insurance payment does not cover their losses and the business has still experienced a minimum 30% decline in actual or predicted revenue over the period of a month or other 30 day period, then the business will be eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified). If the employer has already received the subsidy and still has a decline in revenue, then they can continue using the payment to pay their employees.
If the insurance payment means that the business has not had a 30% decline in revenue over the period of a month or other 30 day period, then the business will not qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified). If the employer has already received the subsidy, then they will have received funds they are not eligible for and must repay the subsidy in full to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Decline in revenue for separate legal entities and business units — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Decline in revenue for separate legal entities and business units
The decline in revenue must be experienced across all units of the business as a 30% decline in total revenue. Business units within a single corporate entity are not eligible to apply individually. This includes Councils and other business structures who may have different programmes, branches, or divisions that are differently affected by COVID-19, but who employ all their workers under one corporate entity.
Consolidated tax groups (made up of legally separate companies) cannot apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified). The separate companies can apply individually for the subsidy, if they meet the qualifications.

chunks.title: Decline in revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Decline in revenue
To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) the employer or self-employed person must have experienced a 30% decline in revenue.
This means they have had a 30% decline in:
- actual revenue or
- predicted revenue (eg when a business has had a reduction in bookings such as accommodation providers) and
- the decline is due to the impacts of COVID-19
The business must experience this decline, or project this decline between January 2020 and 9 June 2020.
If the business or self-employed person predicted a 30% decline in revenue but does not experience this, then the business or self-employed person must repay the subsidy.

chunks.title: Definition of revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Definition of revenue
Revenue means the total amount of money a business has earned from its normal business activities, before expenses are deducted.
Some pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses can include a fall in projected capital income when determining a 30% decrease in revenue.

chunks.title: Determining a decline in revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Determining a decline in revenue
To determine a decline in revenue, the business or self-employed people must compare the actual or predicted revenue of one month or other 30 day period, against the same month or 30 day period in the previous year.
Example February 2020 compared with February 2019.
The revenue of the month or 30 days in the affected period, must be at least 30% less, than it was in the month or 30 day period it was compared against.
For self-employed people with variable monthly income, the decline in revenue should be determined against the previous year's monthly average (ie 30% loss of income due to the impacts of COVID-19 comparing March 2020 to the average monthly income in the period March 2019 to March 2020).

chunks.title: Determining if someone is self-employed — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Determining if someone is self-employed
A person is likely to be self-employed when they carry out business activities on their own, including contracting, working as a sole trader or owning a small business.
A self-employed person is likely to:
- support the business with their own money (eg providing all the working equipment needed for their job)
- decide or control how they work (eg when, where and what hours they work)
- decide how much they get paid and how
- pay their own income tax (unless they are a young person earning under the tax threshold)
- be responsible for investment decisions and any losses
- be able to sell the business if they wanted to
The above list is not exhaustive. Self-employed people are eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), provided they meet the qualifications.

chunks.title: Eligible employers — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Eligible employers
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) is available for:
- businesses using all employment types including full-time, part-time, casual, contracting, fixed-term, sole trading and self-employment, including those employers with employees receiving the minimum wage exemption
- across all business sectors and industries in New Zealand
- includes registered charities, incorporated societies, non-government organisations and post-settlement governance entities (eg Māori authorities)
State Sector organisations are generally not eligible to receive the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for their employees.
From 8 May 2020, exceptions for State Sector employers will be considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, through the relevant monitoring agency.

chunks.title: Employee temporarily overseas and cannot return due to COVID-19 restrictions — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Employee temporarily overseas and cannot return due to COVID-19 restrictions
Employees who are currently overseas are eligible to be named as an employee in the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) application if:
- they were legally working in New Zealand before leaving and
- their absence was intended to be temporary (eg a holiday or a work business trip) and
- they maintained their employment status (that is, they were still employed by the employer) and intended to return to work on a specific date but cannot start on that date because of the COVID-19 travel restrictions

chunks.title: Employee voluntarily leaves — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Employee voluntarily leaves
Employers must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid, for the duration of the subsidy period.
If an employee voluntarily leaves their employment for another job opportunity, the employer must advise the Ministry of Social Development, and no more subsidy can be claimed for that person. The employer does not have to repay the subsidy already paid but they must use the balance to support any other affected employees'.
If the employer has no other employees for whom to use the remainder of any COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) payment, the employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and provide a refund as the money was not able to be used for wages.

chunks.title: Employer dismisses employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Employer dismisses employee
Employers must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.
If an employer decides to dismiss an employee for reasons other than redundancy, for example, because of serious or repeated misconduct, for performance issues, or if the employee abandons their employment, there can be no more subsidy claimed for that person.
The employer does not have to repay the subsidy already paid but they must use the balance to support other remaining affected employees. If the employer has no other employees for whom to use the remainder of any COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) payment, the employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and repay the remaining subsidy as it was not able to be used for wages.
The employer must follow existing employment law for dismissing an employee.
## Example
Fahima employees 5 staff at her cafe but the COVID-19 public health restrictions have significantly impacted her business and she applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) to continue paying her staff.
One of Fahimas employees is caught taking money from the till and this employee is already on notice for similar behaviour in the past. After going through a disciplinary process, Fahima decides to dismiss the employee based on their repeated misconduct.
As Fahima has received the subsidy for this employee, Fahima uses the remaining funds to contribute to the wage costs of her other staff. Fahima manages to hire a replacement employee quickly and reapplies for the subsidy for the new employee.
At the end of the subsidy period Fahima has not used all the funds she received, so repays the remaining amount to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Employer makes employee redundant — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Employer makes employee redundant
Employers must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.
If an employer makes the employee redundant, the employer will not have met their obligations, and must repay the remaining subsidy.
They cannot keep the remainder of the subsidy to support other remaining affected employees. Other enforcement action may be taken against these employers.
Note the original COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (before 27 March 2020) required employers to use their best endeavours to retain employees on at least 80% of their regular income. We consider that making the employee redundant would not be complying with this obligation and the employer may have to refund the remainder of the Wage Subsidy.
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) can be used to pay the notice period but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract.
The employee is not required to pay the Wage Subsidy back to the employer.

chunks.title: Employer not entitled but has been paid — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: If an employer applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), and then they have a change in circumstance within the 12-week period, they may not be entitled to keep the Wage Subsidy payment they received for an employee. Change of circumstances Employer action Employee voluntarily resigns. The employer should use the balance of any of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) to pay other affected staff. When no other employees need it, the employer should contact the Ministry of Social Development and refund the remaining subsidy for this employee as it was not able to be used for wages. Employee has been made redundant. The employer must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) remaining for the employee. It can be used to pay the notice period but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract and cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees. Employee has been dismissed. The employer should use the balance of any of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) to pay other affected staff. When no other employees need it, the employer should contact the Ministry of Social Development and refund the payment remaining for this employee as the remaining funds cannot be used for wages. Business has closed. The employer must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) remaining for their employee(s). The subsidy can be used to pay the notice period but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract and cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees. Employee is on fixed-term contract that ends during the period that the employer is getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for them. The employer must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) remaining for the employee at the end of the fixed-term contract. It cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract and cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees. The employer applied for the wrong type of COVID-19 scheme for their employee, (eg applied for the Leave Payment in error). The employer must repay any amount received for the incorrect application and re-apply for the correct scheme that they are entitled to. The employer applied for the wrong type of COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) rate for their employee, eg applies for full-time, when the person was part-time.

chunks.title: Employer not entitled but has been paid — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: The employer must repay the difference between the full-time rate received and the part-time rate to which they are entitled to. The employer applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) based on a predicted 30% decline in revenue, but the decline did not occur. The employer is not entitled to the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) and must repay it in full. Employer is a State Sector Organisation who did not have an exception approved by the Minister of Finance to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), but applied and received the funds. The employer is not entitled to the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) and must repay it in full. Any State Sector employers who disagree with the decision should consult with their monitoring agency. Employer receives payment they are not entitled to due to an office error (eg their application might have been paid twice or accidentally approved instead of declined). The employer is not entitled to the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) and must repay it in full. If an employer applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) while the employee is also getting the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme or the COVID-19 Essential Workers Leave Support Scheme, their application will be declined.

chunks.title: Employer obligations — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) is being administered under a high trust model, and employers will not be asked for evidence to support some criteria before the subsidy is approved. However, some details will be verified with Inland Revenue before payment. The Ministry of Social Development may also check applications and verify information at a later date. When false or misleading information has been provided by the employer to the Ministry of Social Development, employers can be investigated which may result in civil recovery of any amount paid and potentially criminal prosecution. To receive the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), the employer must agree: - they meet the following subsidy eligibility criteria: the business has had a 30% revenue drop attributable to the COVID-19 outbreakthe employer is registered and operating in New Zealand they have taken active steps to mitigate the financial impact of COVID-19 on their business activities, including proactively engaging with their bank and calling on their internal cash reserves (where appropriate) have taken active steps to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 on their business activitieshave not received a COVID-19 Wage Subsidy that was available before 28 March 2020 for the named employees - the business has had a 30% revenue drop attributable to the COVID-19 outbreak - the employer is registered and operating in New Zealand they have taken active steps to mitigate the financial impact of COVID-19 on their business activities, including proactively engaging with their bank and calling on their internal cash reserves (where appropriate) - they have taken active steps to mitigate the financial impact of COVID-19 on their business activities, including proactively engaging with their bank and calling on their internal cash reserves (where appropriate) - have taken active steps to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 on their business activities - have not received a COVID-19 Wage Subsidy that was available before 28 March 2020 for the named employees

chunks.title: Employers mitigating the impact of COVID-19 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Employers mitigating the impact of COVID-19
Before applying for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), a business must have taken measures to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 on their business.
These might include (but are not limited to):
- activating their business continuity plan
- where appropriate, look to their own cash reserves to assist paying staff, eg where they have enough funds, and it will not cause the business to fail if they use it
- proactively engaging with their bank
- seeking advice from the Chamber of Commerce, a relevant industry association, or the Regional Business Partner programme

chunks.title: Employers must follow employment law when paying wages — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Employers must follow employment law when paying wages
Employers must still adhere to relevant employment laws when reducing an employees wages to 80% of their income, or to the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) rate. This relationship is between the employer and the employee.
An employer is required to pay their employee ordinary wages in line with their employment agreement, and the subsidy can be used to help with that. The effect of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) is that if an employees hours have had to change, the employer must try to pay at least 80% of their wages, and the minimum amount the employee will get if their hours drop further is the subsidy rate (subject to usual deductions eg PAYE, Kiwisaver, Student Loan etc). But if they usually earned less than the subsidy amount claimed (pre COVID-19 impact), the employer would continue to pay them their usual wages.
The employer may agree with the employee to reduce hours or to reduce their hourly rate during this period (but not lower than the minimum wage) and this subsidy will help employers to pay this wage.
No employer can make a blanket rule that employees take annual leave during the COVID-19 public health restrictions, but the employer and employee can agree for the employee to take annual leave. In this situation the employee should be paid their normal wage rate for their normal hours of work, and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) will help employers pay for the annual leave taken.
When the employer and employee are unable to agree on when the employee will take annual holidays, the employer could direct the employee to take annual holidays, but they must give the employee at least 14 days notice.
Employers must follow due process.

chunks.title: Examples of deciding 30% revenue decline for employers who have been open during COVID-19 public health restrictions — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Examples of deciding 30% revenue decline for employers who have been open during COVID-19 public health restrictions
The examples below are not exhaustive.
## Manufacturer of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
It may be considered unreasonable to expect a business who makes PPE would have had a 30% decline in revenue, as they are able to operate at a time of high demand.
However, if that business provided a reason for the decline in revenue that was reasonable when considering their situation, then the Ministry of Social Development would accept there had been a decline.
Example the PPE business was fully staffed by sole parents who could no longer work because they had to stay at home as schools were closed, or they were unable to source enough raw materials because of border closures to make the product.
## Food outlet
Generally, it would be unreasonable to expect that an essential business of this type would have had a 30% revenue drop as they are able to operate at a time of high demand.
However, if that business provided a reason for the decline that was reasonable when considering the situation then we would accept there had been a decline in their revenue.
Example a grocery store in the middle of the Central Business District (CBD), whose main trade was CBD workers and many people are still working from home, or a supermarket in a town reliant on tourists who have now left and the local population is small. In both these cases, they remain open and can operate but it would be reasonable that there could have been a 30% decline in their revenue.
## Courier company
A courier company who is providing contactless delivery of essential goods applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified). Generally it would be unreasonable to expect that an essential business of this type would have had a 30% revenue drop as they are essential and able to operate in a time of high demand.
However, if that business provided a reason for the decline that was reasonable when considering the situation, then the Ministry of Social Development would accept they have had a 30% revenue drop.
Example a courier company whose previous business relied on TradeMe purchases and/or non-essential goods and hasn't picked up any work doing essential deliveries.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Example 1
Ailee works 10 hours per week at minimum wage ($189 gross per week) as she is a student. Her employer has experienced a decline in revenue due to the impact of COVID-19 so the employer applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) to continue paying her.
Because her usual earnings are less than the subsidy rate of $350 gross per week, the employer must use the subsidy to continue paying her usual wage of $189 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions).
The employer must use the difference to contribute to the wages of other affected staff and when there are no other employees, must refund the remainder back to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example 2
Jivan works 40 hours at a workshop as a building labourer. He usually receives $756 gross per week. He cannot do any work from home during the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
The employer has a highly skilled and reliable workforce and is using the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) to continue to pay Jivan 80% of his usual wages during this period. If the employer was not able to do this, they would be required to pay Jivan the fulltime subsidy rate ($585.80 gross per week).
## Example 3
Stuart is a digger driver. His employer has no revenue coming into the business during the COVID-19 public health restrictions. The employer has many contracts to finish once they can get back to work, so needs to keep their employees over the period of the public health restrictions.
The employer is unable to pay Stuart 80% of his full-time wage over this period, and so his employer pays Stuart the full amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) of $585.80 (less any usual wage deductions) over the lockdown period.

chunks.title: Fixed-term contract ends within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Fixed-term contract ends within subsidy period
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) is open to existing and newly hired employees and this includes employees on fixed-term contracts. To receive the Wage Subsidy, employers must agree to retain the employees named in their application for the duration of the subsidy period.
Employers can include employees on fixed-term contracts in their Wage Subsidy application, even if the employee’s contract is scheduled to end during the period that their employer would be getting the Wage Subsidy for them (ie in the 12 weeks from the date of application).
However, if an employee’s fixed-term contract ends during the subsidy period, the employer will not have met their obligation to retain affected staff. In these circumstances, the employer can use the Wage Subsidy to pay out any notice period for that employee, but the subsidy cannot be used to pay any other entitlements, and it cannot be used to support the wages of other affected employees. The employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and repay any remaining funds.
The employer and employee may agree to extend the contract to the end of the subsidy period in order to meet their obligation to retain staff for the period they receive the subsidy.
## Example 1
Anaru is on a fixed-term contract scheduled to end on 25 April 2020. His employer applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy on 10 April to continue paying his staff during the COVID-19 public health restrictions and includes Anaru in the application.
The employer agrees with Anaru to extend his contract to 3 July 2020 so that Anaru can continue getting wages during this period. Anaru's employer is eligible to receive the full 12-week subsidy for Anaru.
## Example 2
Sacha is on a fixed-term contract with her employer that is scheduled to end on 8 May 2020. Her employer applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) on 30 March and includes Sacha in the application.
When Sacha's contract ends on 8 May, the employer returns the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Health and disability funded workforce — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Health and disability funded workforce
Health and disability funded workforces (such as businesses that provide community health care) not employed by the State Sector are able to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) if they meet the qualifications.
Health and disability funded workforces not employed by the State Sector includes organisations that are contracted to, or funded in whole or part, by organisations in the State Sector (for example the Ministry of Health and District Health Boards).
Examples include:
- in-home care workers
- workers in primary health organisations
- nurses and other staff in rest-homes or other residential care facilities (eg cooks, cleaners, support staff)

chunks.title: COVID-19 support schemes — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme was introduced on 28 April 2020 to provide financial assistance to employers during the COVID-19 public health restrictions to: - encourage employees to self-isolate (stay at home) when they need to and - support employees who are unable to work from home to have an income when they cannot work Employers eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) could choose to apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme where it is appropriate for their employee's situation, but they could not receive both the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for the same period, for the same employee. Employers who received a previous COVID-19 subsidy are still covered by the obligations they agreed when applying for these subsidies, for the duration of the subsidy period. An employer who received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) can apply for the same employees under the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension if they meet the qualifications, but only once the period for the previous payment has ended. For more information see:

chunks.title: Flexi-wage subsidy or Mana in Mahi — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: If an employer is currently getting the Flexi-wage subsidy or Mana in Mahi subsidy for their employee(s), they can also apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) if they meet the qualifications.
