All wage subsidies that the employer is getting must be paid to their employees. For more information see:

chunks.title: Main benefit and other support — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: If an employer or a self-employed is currently getting a main benefit or other extra help from the Ministry of Social Development, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for themselves or their employees. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, any individual receiving the subsidy as well as other support from the Ministry must declare the subsidy as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Self-employed person or employee getting Ministry of Social Development assistance Interaction with the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) COVID-19 Income Relief Payment Some COVID-19 Income Relief Payment clients may have received the Wage Subsidy (modified) before they lost their job or self-employment. These people can apply for the COVID-19 Income Relief Payment once their Wage Subsidy payments run out, provided they meet the qualifications. Emergency Benefit Some Emergency Benefit clients may be employed. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Emergency Benefit clients who receive the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Emergency Maintenance Assistance Some Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients may be employed. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients who receive the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Jobseeker Support Some Jobseeker Support clients may be working part-time (less than 30 hours per week) or getting income that does not reduce the rate of Jobseeker Support to zero. Sole parents and grand-parented Jobseeker Support clients can work full-time for a temporary period provided their income when assessed over a 52-week period does not fully reduce the benefit. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Jobseeker Support clients who receive the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Note the part-time and full-time subsidy rate differs from the definition above. New Zealand Superannuation - Non-qualified partner If a New Zealand Superannuation client includes their partner in their payments, then their New Zealand Superannuation is income-tested. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, New Zealand Superannuation non-qualified partner clients who receive the subsidy must declare it as income, and both of their New Zealand Superannuation payments may be abated accordingly. Sole Parent Support Some Sole Parent Support clients will have work obligations and may be employed.

chunks.title: Main benefit and other support — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Sole Parent Support clients who receive the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Supported Living Payment Some Supported Living Payment clients will be working up to 15 hours per week but may not be able to do this on a regular basis. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Support Living Payment clients who receive the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly.

chunks.title: Financial support from other agencies — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: There is a range of financial support available from other agencies for employers and self-employed people who have been negatively impacted by the COVID-19 financial crisis. These schemes, such as the COVID-19 Small Business Cash Flow Loan Scheme, are separate to Work and Income support, and have their own qualification criteria. This means that, provided they meet the necessary qualifications, businesses can apply and receive the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) as well as these other schemes. Note there are some schemes, such as Ministry of Education's emergency payment for relief teachers, where businesses will not be eligible to receive the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for the same work. Applicants will need to ensure they meet the qualification criteria for any schemes they apply for.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) was introduced from 27 March 2020 to 9 June 2020 to support otherwise viable employers to survive the COVID-19 public health restrictions and remain connected to their employees.
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) was replaced by the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension on 10 June 2020.
## Applications
Employers and self-employed people had to apply online for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy through Work and Income.
An application could be made at any point during the time the scheme was available. It was paid in one lump sum to the employer and covered 12 weeks from the date of application.
Applications closed for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) on 9 June 2020.

chunks.title: Newly hired employees — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Newly hired employees
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) is open to any newly hired employees.
## Example 1
Sam was due to start work as a hairdresser, but their start date was delayed due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions. Sam’s employer applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) to pay Sam until they can start their new role.
## Example 2
Whiti owns a pet store and is receiving the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) as her business has experienced a decline in revenue due to COVID-19. One of her employees resigns and she needs to hire a replacement staff member.
Whiti uses the remaining subsidy from the leaving employee to continue paying her other staff and submits another application for the new employee when they start their role.
## Example 3
Ravi owns a clothing store and has reopened his business after being closed during the COVID-19 public health restrictions. He needs to hire a new employee, but his business is still experiencing a significant decline in revenue due to COVID-19.
Ravi is already receiving the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for his existing employees, so submits another application for the new employee when they start their new role.

chunks.title: Normal wages or salary — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Normal wages or salary
For employees, their normal wages or salary are specified in their employment agreement at the date the employer applies for the subsidy.
Self-employed people can determine their normal wages or drawings by calculating the regular amount that is left over after they meet their business costs. This is the amount that they regularly pay themselves as drawings from the business.
If the person is self-employed and the income that they regularly draw from their business is less than the amount they received from the subsidy, they can repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) can be used to support the costs of wages, but cannot be used towards other business costs.

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) is paid at a flat rate based on each named employee's normal (or expected) hours of paid employment before COVID-19 impacted the business: - $585.80 (gross) for 20 hours or more per week, or 40 hours or more per fortnight or - $350.00 (gross) for less than 20 hours per week or less than 40 hours per fortnight The subsidy is paid for a 12-week period as a lump sum payment at the appropriate weekly subsidy rate for: - working 20 hours or more or - working under 20 hours An employer can access the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) more than once in the 12-week period but cannot access it for the same employees in that period. The subsidy covers 12 weeks from the date of application.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: The employer accessed the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy for 10 employees before the COVID-19 Level 4 public health restrictions. Now the employer needs the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for 20 more employees. The employer can apply for the 20 newly named employees, not the 10 original employees for whom they have already received the subsidy.

chunks.title: Calculating variable hours — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: For a self-employed person, or an employer who has casual employees who work variable hours, an average over a relevant period can be used to work out which subsidy rate to apply. A relevant period for a business or self-employed person who has been working for a year, would be an average over this period. For a new business or a person who has been self-employed for less than one year, an average over 8 weeks can be used, unless there is another time period that would be more appropriate. For example, if using the period that the individual has been employed for would give a better representation of the employee's usual hours, then the employer can use this time period instead. The above guidance is intended to support employers in calculating average hours. However, it is up to employers to agree with their employees what their hours would usually be during this period, to determine the appropriate COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) rate to apply for.

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: Charlotte is a relief teacher for an Early Childhood Education Centre and is called in to provide support as required, but the centre is closed due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions. The centre employs Charlotte as a casual staff member and calculates that she has worked an average of 17 hours per week over the last 4 months she has been employed there. The employer applies for a part-time COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) rate to continue paying Charlotte's wages (at a rate of 17 hours per week for the 12-week period). As this is less than the $350 gross per week provided through the subsidy, the employer uses the remaining funds to support the wages of other affected staff.

chunks.title: Maximum payment for an employer — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: There is no cap on the total amount of COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) an employer can receive, it is based on the number of employees they have, and whether they are working 20 hours or more, or under 20 hours.

chunks.title: People on fixed-term contracts — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## People on fixed-term contracts
Employers can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for their employees who are on fixed-term contracts, as long as they keep them employed for the subsidy period.
If an employee's fixed-term contract ends during the subsidy period, then the employer will not have met their obligation to retain affected staff. The employer must notify the Ministry of Social Development and repay the remaining subsidy.

chunks.title: People receiving income from a property business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## People receiving income from a property business
Some people are paid a wage, salary or draw an income from a property business, such as private rentals, Airbnb's and homestay operations.
These businesses are eligible to receive the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) provided they meet the qualification criteria, including being registered and operating in New Zealand.
For sole traders who are not registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, the Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed before paying the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified).
Note the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings and can only be used to support the cost of wages. Individuals who apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for a property business must be able to declare that they draw a wage, salary or income for this work.
## Example
Anthony owns several holiday homes, which he rents out to supplement his income. He works an average of 10 hours per week on the properties, managing the bookings and cleaning the property in between guests.
Usually this would be a very busy time of year for his business, but most of his bookings have been cancelled due the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
Anthony's income has dropped by more than 30% during this period so applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified). The Ministry is able to verify his self-employment status with Inland Revenue and his application is approved.

chunks.title: People receiving paid parental leave — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## People receiving paid parental leave
Employers may have employees who are currently getting paid parental leave.
## Employee already getting paid parental leave
If the employee was already getting paid parental leave when the employer applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), the employer is not able to include this employee in their application.
If they do include the employee in error and the application is approved, the employer will have received funds they are not eligible for and must repay this amount to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Employee goes on paid parental leave during subsidy period
If the employee starts getting paid parental leave after the employer has made an application and/or received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), then the employee is not eligible to receive both the subsidy and paid parental leave.
The employer must finish using the subsidy for the employee as soon as they go on leave, and the remaining funds can be used to support the costs of wages for other affected staff.
If the employer has no other employees to use the remaining subsidy for, the employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and repay the remaining amount as it was not able to be used for wages.
## Employee due to return from paid parental leave during subsidy period
If the employee was getting paid parental leave at the time of the employer's application for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for their other employees, but has since returned to work, then the employer can submit a new application for this employee.
The employer should use the new hours the employee will be working on their return to work to calculate the rate of subsidy to apply for.

chunks.title: People receiving weekly compensation from ACC — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## People receiving weekly compensation from ACC
Employers may have employees who are unable to work and getting weekly compensation from Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC).
## Employee already getting ACC
If the employee was already getting ACC compensation when the employer applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), the employer is not able to include this employee in their application.
If they do include the employee in error and the application is approved, the employer will have received funds they are not eligible for and must repay this amount to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Employee goes on ACC during subsidy period
If the employee is injured and starts getting ACC compensation after the employer made an application and/or received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), the employee is eligible to receive both the subsidy and ACC compensation.
However, the employee must declare the subsidy to ACC as income and their weekly compensation may be abated accordingly.
## Employee due to finish getting ACC during subsidy period
If the employee was getting ACC compensation at the time of the employer’s application for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), but has since finished getting the ACC payments, the employer can submit a new application for this employee.

chunks.title: People working multiple jobs — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## People working multiple jobs
Employers may have employees who work for them, and another employer. They may work more than 20 hours for one employer, and less than 20 hours for the other.
If both employers meet the qualifications, they can each apply for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for the same employee.

chunks.title: Pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses
A small number of pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses have been identified as eligible to treat a 30% fall in in projected capital income as a result of COVID-19, as a fall in revenue for the eligibility of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified).
These employers must:
- be research and development intensive 'start-up' businesses
- be 'seed' or 'venture' backed
- be Callaghan Innovation affiliated as of 17 March 2020 and
- have no other revenue other than government support and seed or venture capital
These employers can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) if they meet the other qualifications.

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), employers must meet the following eligibility criteria:
- the employer or self-employed person must have experienced a minimum 30% decline in actual or predicted revenue over the period of a month or other 30 day period, when compared with the same month or 30 day period last year (or over a shorter period if the business hasn’t been running for a year), and the decline is related to COVID-19
- the business must be registered and operating in New Zealand
- their employees must be legally working in New Zealand
- before making an application, the employer must have taken active steps to mitigate the impact of COVID-19
- have not received (or currently receiving) a subsidy for that employee from the previous Wage Subsidy or Leave Support Scheme
## Must retain employees and pay at least 80% wages or salary
Employers who receive the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) must keep the employees (for whom they received the wage subsidy) in their jobs for the period of the subsidy (unless the employee voluntarily ends the employment relationship).
Employers must endeavour to pay at least 80% of each named employee's wages or salary for the period of the subsidy, at the rate they would have been paid before the business was impacted by the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
When the employee was earning less than the subsidy rate, the employer must keep paying their usual wages. There are other guidelines for when the employer cannot keep paying 80%. Any difference should be used for the wages of other affected staff.
When there are no other employees, the employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and repay the remaining subsidy as it was not able to be used for wages.
If the individual is self-employed and the income they regularly draw from their business is less than the subsidy amount they received, they can repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development if they choose to. This obligation has changed in the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension.

chunks.title: Receivership or liquidation within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Receivership or liquidation within subsidy period
In some circumstances, employers who have received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) may still go into receivership or liquidation and may have to sell or close their business permanently.
## Business keeps operating under receivership or liquidation
If the business can continue operating under receivership or for the duration of the liquidation process, then the employer (or the receiver/liquidator) can continue to use the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) to support the cost of wages for employees named in their application.
If the business recovers, or the receiver/liquidator sells the business during the subsidy period and the new owners take on the employees named in the application, then the business can continue to use the subsidy for these employees.
Example 1
An employer goes into receivership 2 weeks after getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for their employees. The receiver takes over the business and manages to sell the business to new owners. The new owners keep all the previous staff and use the remaining subsidy to continue paying these employees for the duration of the subsidy period.
## Business closes under receivership or liquidation
If the business is liquidated (and permanently closed), or the receiver/liquidator sells the business during the subsidy period, and the new owners do not take on the employees named in the subsidy application, then the business will not have met their obligation to retain staff and they must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) remaining for these employees.
Where employees are made redundant, the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) can be used to pay the notice period but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract and cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees.
Example 2
A restaurant owner puts their business into liquidation 6 weeks after getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for their employees. The liquidator gives the staff 4 weeks notice that the business will be closing permanently and uses the remaining subsidy to pay out the notice period for the employees named in the application. At the end of the notice period, the liquidator returns the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Recent employees re-hired — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Recent employees re-hired
An employer can apply for the COVID-19 wage subsidy (modified) for recently re-hired employees if:
- their employment ended on or after 17 March 2020 as a result of COVID-19 and
- they were re-hired before the employer applies for the subsidy
Note the employer just needs to confirm this as part of the declaration. The Ministry of Social Development does not require verification such as employment contracts.

chunks.title: Retain affected staff — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Retain affected staff
Employers must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Repaying unused funds after the subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Repaying unused funds after the subsidy period
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) is paid in one lump sum to the employer to support the cost of wages for 12 weeks.
If the employer does not require the full weekly rate for their employees, for example, because an employee's usual wages are less than the subsidy rate, then any difference should be used for the wages of other affected staff.
If there are any unused funds at the end of the 12 week period, the employer must return the remaining amount to the Ministry of Social Development. The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) cannot be used beyond the 12-week period.
## Example
Jason received the Wage Subsidy for his 10 part-time employees. All the employees were earning under the part-time subsidy rate, so continued to receive their normal wages for the duration of the subsidy period.
At the end of the 12 weeks, Jason has not used all the subsidy payment and has some funds remaining. He contacts the Ministry of Social Development to repay the unused subsidy as the funds were not used up on wage costs during the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Reviewing decisions to decline the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Reviewing decisions to decline the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified)
Decisions to decline the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) are not made under the Social Security Act 2018 and are not covered by the usual Review of Decision guidelines.
If an employer wants to review the decision to decline the Wage Subsidy reviewed, that decision should be reconsidered. This review should be based on whether an informed decision was made and should consider the following:
- whether all relevant information was obtained and
- whether the appropriate options and implications were considered and
- whether the decision was made at the appropriate level of delegation
If a review of the decision to decline the payment upholds the original decision, the employer can ask the Ombudsman to undertake their own review.

chunks.title: Seasonal work ends within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Seasonal work ends within subsidy period
Some seasonal workers will have had their work affected by COVID-19 (ie season finished earlier than expected and/or not able to pick up new work due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions).
If their employer has received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for the employees, but can no longer offer them employment, then the employer will not have met their obligation to retain affected staff and must repay the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.
If the seasonal workers are casual employees or on fixed-term contracts, then the employer can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) to continue paying them, as long as they keep them employed for the subsidy period.
## Example 1
Rowan usually picks grapes over the summer months, but his employer has closed the harvesting season early due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
Rowan's employer received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for his employees, but after 2 weeks he decides to end their contracts as he can no longer offer them employment to return to. The employer uses the subsidy to pay out their notice period, and repays the remaining amount to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example 2
Tracey employs 30 casual workers on her kiwifruit orchard, however, the orchard is not able to open due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions and Tracey has no work for these employees.
Tracey calculates the average hours each of her casual employees would have worked at this time last year to determine the correct rate to apply for. Tracey applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) to continue paying her employees.

chunks.title: Seasonal workers — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Seasonal workers
There are a variety of employment arrangements for seasonal workers (eg fixed-term contract or casual employment contract).
Employers can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for their employees who are seasonal workers, as long as they keep them employed for the subsidy period.
If an employee's contract ends during the subsidy period, then the employer will not have met their obligation to retain affected staff. The employer must notify the Ministry of Social Development and repay the remaining subsidy.

chunks.title: Self-employed person is also an employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Self-employed person is also an employee
A person may be self-employed for some of their income, and also be employed by a business or other organisation.
If the self-employed person qualifies, they can get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for their own business.
Also, if their employer qualifies, they can get the Wage Subsidy to continue to pay the employee.

chunks.title: Specific employment situations — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text:
## Specific employment situations
People's work situations in New Zealand may vary and eligibility for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) can sometimes differ.

chunks.title: State Sector employers generally not eligible — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: State Sector employers are generally not eligible to receive the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified). In most situations alternative arrangements have been made to ensure these employers pay their employees in full. However, from 8 May 2020 exceptions will be considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, via the relevant monitoring agency. Monitoring agencies will engage with State Sector Organisations in their portfolio to understand their financial position and support them in seeking an exception where appropriate. For example, if Airways Corporation of New Zealand Limited believed they met the criteria for the Wage Subsidy, then they could engage with Treasury Commercial Operations Team to assess their situation, and where appropriate, Treasury would prepare advice for the Minister of Finance seeking an exception on their behalf. If an exception is granted, the monitoring agency will tell the Ministry of Social Development, and will direct the State Sector employer to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) directly. State Sector employers include: - Government agencies such as the Ministry of Health, District Health Boards, Inland Revenue, and the Ministry of Social Development - Crown entities such as Kāinga Ora and the Accident Compensation Corporation - Schools (including state schools, state-integrated schools and their board of trustee members or equivalent) - Tertiary education institutions such as universities, polytechnics, institutes of technology and Wānanga State Sector employers do not include: - Local Government such as Regional, City and District Councils, council organisations and council-controlled organisations as stated in the Local Government Act 2002. This includes trusts and other organisations that look after libraries, museums and other operations in partnership with local authorities (note these employers still need to have experienced a 30% decline in revenue and meet the other qualifications to be eligible for the subsidy) - Kindergartens (although the teachers are state sector employees, their employers are not, so Ministry of Education is not directly responsible for their payroll) - (note these employers still need to have experienced a 30% decline in revenue and meet the other qualifications to be eligible for the subsidy) - Early Childhood Centres - Private (or independent) schools, and their board of trustee members or equivalent, proprietors of state-integrated schools and other workers employed by the proprietor (note the proprietor is the owners or leaseholder of the state-integrated school property) - Non-Government Organisations - Health and disability funded workforces not employed directly by the State Sector

chunks.title: State Sector employers generally not eligible — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: Note businesses contracted to provide services to State Sector employers (eg cleaning, security etc) are not State Sector employers, and can apply for the Wage Subsidy if they meet the other qualifications.

chunks.title: Transition between COVID-19 Wage Subsidy and COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Leave Payment ended on 27 March 2020. The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy was modified from 27 March 2020. Employers who received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy and the COVID-19 Leave Payment are still covered by the obligations they agreed when applying for the subsidies.

chunks.title: Employer received COVID-19 Wage Subsidy before 28 March 2020 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: Before 27 March 2020 employers and self-employed people who had an actual or predicted loss of revenue that was related to COVID-19 of at least 30%, were eligible to apply for a subsidy. The subsidy was intended to support businesses to retain staff and continue to pay them at least 80% of their normal income from employment. Employers could also apply for the COVID-19 Leave Payment, so they were able to keep paying employees who were self-isolating in line with Ministry of Health guidelines. Employers can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) when they meet the criteria and need further assistance but only for named employees they haven’t already applied for a subsidy. Example Employer applied for 10 employees for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Employer applied on 19 March for 22 full-time workers at $585.80 each employee for 12 weeks (total $15,465.12). This was for a subsidy period of 12 weeks. They did not apply for a subsidy for their 22 part-time workers. When the COVID-19 Alert Level 4 came into force, the revenue loss was greater than expected and they had to continue to offset most of the workers wages. On 2 April 2020, the employer applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for the 22 part-time workers. They can receive the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for these 22 part-time workers because they have not received a subsidy for these named employees under the previous scheme.

chunks.title: Employer applied for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy before 26 March 2020, but not yet granted the assistance — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: Unless the employer retracts their application for this assistance, the employer will be granted the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy and the rules of that scheme apply.

chunks.title: Employer received COVID-19 Leave Payment for employee and now needs to apply for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: From 4pm, 27 March 2020, the COVID-19 Leave Payment was no longer available for applications. Employers or self-employed people who applied for this for an employee (or themselves) could not apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) until the period that the Leave Period was paid had passed.

chunks.title: Treatment of the subsidy for granting benefits — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: If an employer or a self-employed person is getting a main benefit or Extra Help from the Ministry of Social Development, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) for themselves or their employees. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, any employee or self-employed person receiving the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) as well as other support from the Ministry must declare the subsidy as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) should be counted as income over a 12-week period from the date of application for both employees and self-employed people and should not be counted as a cash asset. Any additional income drawn from the business or any other source must also be included in their total income.

chunks.title: Determining a lump sum payment of the subsidy — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: An employee or self-employed person should be paid the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) in the same way their wage or salary is normally paid, eg weekly wages for 12 weeks. However, some employers receiving the subsidy may pass it on to their employees as a lump sum payment. If the employee applies for assistance from the Ministry of Social Development, it is important to determine whether it is a lump sum payment of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) - (on top of their regular wages during the subsidy period), or whether it represents a payment for other forms of leave owed to the client. For example, an employer may pay out 4 weeks of the subsidy to a client to cover their redundancy notice period. This would not be considered a lump sum payment of the subsidy but would instead be pay in lieu of notice, which is a type of termination payment. If the employee is made redundant or the employer has surplus funds remaining at the end of the subsidy period, the employer is required to return any remaining amount of the subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development. However, some employers may pass on the remaining funds directly to the employee. If the employer pays out the remainder of the subsidy (eg once the employee's notice period has ended and they are no longer employed), this would be considered a lump sum payment of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified). If the payment is a lump sum payment of the subsidy, it may affect their eligibility for different types of assistance.

chunks.title: Benefit applications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: As the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) is paid to replace a loss of earnings it should be charged as income for the benefit or Extra Help, this includes when the subsidy is paid out to the client as a lump sum payment. When a client has received the subsidy as a lump sum payment, the Ministry of Social Development will consider the appropriate period that the payment is intended to represent and will charge it as income for that period. For example, the lump sum payment can be divided by the client’s average earnings (using the last 4 weeks if appropriate) to determine how many weeks of income the payment is intended to represent. If the amount of the payment is less than the relevant income cut out point, the client would qualify for assistance for the period the lump sum payment is charged for. If the amount is higher than the income cut out point, the client would not qualify until the period the payment represents has finished. Note Generally, a lump sum payment of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) is not considered a termination payment, so does not need to be considered when calculating what date their employment ceased. The lump sum would only be considered a termination payment when it is paid in lieu of notice. Example 1 Nate's employer received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) on 10 April 2020, but 2 weeks later, decides to close the business and gives his employees notice that they will be made redundant. The business is closed on 10 May 2020, and Nate was paid for the redundancy notice period until that point. The employer decides to pay the balance of the subsidy of 8 weeks out to Nate as a lump sum. Nate decides to apply for Jobseeker Support and approaches the Ministry of Social Development for assistance on 11 May 2020. Nate’s employment ceased date is 10 May and his commencement date is 11 May. The initial stand-down period has been waived due to COVID-19. As he has received a lump sum payment representing 8 weeks of income, Nate’s first 8 weeks of assistance are abated accordingly. If the lump sum payment is higher than the income cut out point, Nate will not qualify for assistance until the period the payment represents has passed.

chunks.title: COVID-19 Income Relief Payment applications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy modified
chunks.text: A person is not eligible to receive the COVID-19 Income Relief Payment if they are currently receiving the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified). If an employee receives the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) as a lump sum payment from their employer, they would not be eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Income Relief Payment until the appropriate period that the lump sum payment applies to has passed. Example 2 Pania’s employer was received the Wage Subsidy for her on 15 June 2020, but soon gives her notice of redundancy as their business has been badly affected by COVID-19. Pania receives a lump sum payment from her employer in lieu of working out her 4 week notice period. She receives this payment on 22 June 2020. Pania meets the other qualification criteria for the COVID-19 Income Relief Payment but is not eligible to apply for the scheme until the 4 week period that the lump sum Wage Subsidy payment represents has passed. If an employer applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified), and then they have a change in circumstance within the 12-week period, they may not be entitled to keep the Wage Subsidy payment they received for an employee.

chunks.title: Amount a business must pay an employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Amount a business must pay an employee
The amount the business (including self-employed people) must pay to an employee, depends on whether the employee's ordinary wages or salary are under, or over the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) rate applied for them.
## Employee's ordinary wages or salary less than the subsidy rate
When the employee's ordinary wages or salary were less than the subsidy rate when their business applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), the business must keep paying their ordinary wages for the duration of the subsidy period.
Businesses must use the remaining support towards topping up the wages of other employees, so that they are being paid their ordinary wages. When there are no other employees to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other employees are already being paid their usual wages, the business must repay the remaining subsidy back to the Ministry of Social Development as it could not be used for wages.
If a person is self-employed, and the income they regularly draw from their business is less than the amount they got from the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Employee's ordinary wages or salary more than the subsidy rate
Businesses who receive the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) must use their best endeavours to pay employees their ordinary wages or at least 80% of each named employees ordinary wages or salary for the period of the subsidy.
If paying 80% of ordinary wages or salary isn't possible, and the employee was usually earning over the subsidy rate applied for, the business must pass on the full weekly amount of support (less any usual wage deductions) to the employee.
For example, if a full-time employee was normally earning $1000 gross per week before their employer applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) and the business cannot afford to pay them 80% or $800 gross, then the business must pay them the full-time subsidy rate of $600 (less any usual wage deductions).
If businesses have questions about their obligations under employment law, they should contact Employment New Zealand for advice and assistance.

chunks.title: Assessing 40% revenue loss due to the current escalation in Alert Levels — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Assessing 40% revenue loss due to the current escalation in Alert Levels
When deciding if a business (including self-employed people) has had a decline in revenue due to the current escalation in Alert Levels, the Ministry of Social Development considers:
- the type of work the business does, eg retail, manufacturing, sales, construction, driving etc and
- whether (or to the extent) the business is able to operate while part of the country is in Alert Level 3 or above (eg is it an essential business or not, what changes has the business needed to make due to the public health restrictions) and
- whether the estimated loss of revenue makes sense (based on the business circumstances)
Note businesses are required to prepare and keep evidence of their revenue decline and how it was caused by the current escalation in Alert Levels, and the Ministry of Social Development may ask for verification in some cases.
## Business cannot open due to current escalation in Alert Levels
Generally, where a business cannot operate due to the current escalation in Alert Levels, the Ministry of Social Development would accept the business's statement that they have had a 40% revenue decrease due to the current escalation in Alert Levels.
## Business has been open during current escalation in Alert Levels
Some businesses may be able to operate during the current escalation in Alert Levels, eg in the following circumstances:
- firms defined as essential businesses or
- providing click and collect or
- takeaway options
Note that this is not limited to the above.
For businesses that are able to operate, when deciding if they have had a decline in revenue, the Ministry of Social Development considers the reasons given for the decline in revenue and whether these are reasonable given the type of work the business does and where the business is located.
Being open for business does not protect a business from having a 40% decline in revenue, but further consideration needs to be given to their circumstances.
Example a business has remained open, or is open in some online capacity, and may not be able to sell the same level of product, due to reduced demand from other businesses (eg frozen food which they used to provide to fast food or other restaurants).
For these businesses, the Ministry of Social Development will consider their individual situations and make decisions based on the facts of their application, when considering if the business has had a 40% decline in revenue due to the current escalation in Alert Levels.

chunks.title: Business dismisses employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Business dismisses employee
Businesses must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.
If a business decides to dismiss an employee for reasons other than redundancy, for example, because of serious or repeated misconduct, for performance issues, or if the employee abandons their employment, the business cannot receive any more subsidy payments for this employee.
The business does not have to repay the subsidy already received for this employee, but they must use the balance towards topping up the wages of any other remaining employees named in their application, so they are being paid their ordinary wages.
If the business has no other employees to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other employees are already being paid their ordinary wages, the business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining subsidy that was not able to be used for wages.
The business must follow existing employment law for dismissing an employee.
## Example
Fahima employees 5 staff at her cafe but the COVID-19 public health restrictions have significantly impacted her business and she applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) to continue paying her staff.
One of Fahima's employees is caught taking money from the till and this employee is already on notice for similar behaviour in the past. After going through a disciplinary process, Fahima decides to dismiss the employee based on their repeated misconduct.
As Fahima got the subsidy for this employee, Fahima uses the remaining funds to contribute to the wage costs of her other employees. Fahima manages to hire a replacement employee quickly and reapplies for the subsidy for the new employee.
At the end of the subsidy period Fahima has not used all the funds she received, so repays the remaining amount to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Business gets insurance payments to cover revenue loss — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Business gets insurance payments to cover revenue loss
Some businesses (including self-employed people) have received insurance payments, such as business interruption insurance, to cover their decline in revenue during the current escalation in Alert Levels. Insurance payments are considered revenue for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021).
If the insurance payment does not cover their losses and the business has still experienced at least a 40% decline in revenue during the current revenue test period, then the business is eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021).
If the insurance payment means that the business has not had at least a 40% decline in revenue during the current revenue test period, then the business will not be eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021).
If the business has already got the subsidy, then they will have had funds they are not eligible for, and must repay the subsidy in full to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Business had not started operating before the current escalation in Alert Levels — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Business had not started operating before the current escalation in Alert Levels
Some businesses (including self-employed people) may have had their plans to start their business affected by the current escalation in Alert Levels.
To be eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), the business must have had at least a 40% decline in revenue during the current revenue test period.
To determine the decline, the business needs to compare their revenue using the default comparison period or the seasonal comparison period where it is appropriate.
This means the business must have been operating for at least 14 days (ie generating revenue) during the default comparison period to determine the decline in revenue.
Businesses that have been operating for less than 14 days during the default comparison period are not eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021).

chunks.title: Sole traders, self-employed people, and contractors — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Sole traders, self-employed people, and contractors
Sole traders, self-employed people and contractors are not required to be registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, but must have:
- a personal Inland Revenue number for paying income tax and/or GST and
- government licences and permits for their business needs and
- qualifications or registrations for their trade or profession
Sole traders, self-employed people and contractors must still meet the requirements to be physically located and legally working in New Zealand.
The Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed before paying the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021).

chunks.title: Business makes employee redundant — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Business makes employee redundant
If a business makes an employee redundant during the period they are receiving the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for that employee, and the employee will remain employed until the end of the subsidy period, the business can use the subsidy to pay the employee until the end of the subsidy period.
However, if the employee does not remain employed until the end of the subsidy period, the business can use the subsidy to pay the person until the end of their employment, but must repay the remaining subsidy back to the Ministry of Social Development.
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) cannot be used to pay for notice periods extending beyond the subsidy period for that employee. In addition, it cannot be used to pay any other redundancy payments under the employee’s employment contract (including any leave payments).
The employee is not required to pay any subsidy back to the business that they have already received.
Businesses who have given their employees notice of redundancy before they apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) are not eligible to get the subsidy for those employees unless the redundancy notice is withdrawn.

chunks.title: Business mitigating the impact of the current escalation in Alert Levels — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Business mitigating the impact of the current escalation in Alert Levels
Before applying for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), a business (including self-employed people) must have taken active steps to mitigate the impact of the current escalation in Alert Levels on their business activities.
These might include (but are not limited to):
- where appropriate, look to their own cash reserves to assist paying staff, eg where they have enough funds, and it won't cause the business to fail if they use it
- proactively engaging with their bank
- making an insurance claim

chunks.title: Businesses must follow employment law when paying wages — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) must be used by businesses to support the cost of wages for the employees named in their application, for the duration of the subsidy period. Businesses must still adhere to relevant employment laws when: - reducing an employee's wages to 80% of their ordinary income or - the employee agrees to unpaid leave and being paid the appropriate rate of COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) (when the business cannot afford to pay at least 80% of their ordinary wages or salary) or - advising the employee what leave assistance is available to them This relationship is between the business and the employee.

chunks.title: Agreeing on leave type — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: Businesses and their employees can agree to use any form of paid leave (eg annual leave, sick leave) to cover the period they cannot be at work. However, employees are not required to have used any or all of their paid leave (including sick leave) entitlements before the business can get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) on their behalf. Employees will generally want to use any leave entitlements available to them as this must be paid out to them at the rate outlined in employment law (that is, must be paid out at their ordinary pay amount, and cannot be reduced to 80%). No business can make a blanket rule that employees take annual leave during the current escalation in Alert Levels, but the business and employee can agree for the employee to take annual leave. In this situation the employee should be paid their ordinary wage rate for their usual hours of work and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) will help businesses pay for the annual leave taken.

chunks.title: Unpaid leave — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: Some employees will have agreed with the business to take unpaid leave if they do not have any leave entitlement to cover the current escalation in Alert Levels when there is no work for them. Businesses who get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) should try to continue to pay at least 80% of the employee's income in this situation. But when this is not possible, the business must pass on the full COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) to the employee(s) while they are on unpaid leave (or continue to pay their ordinary wage if it is under the rate applied for). Businesses must follow the correct employment process. If businesses have questions about their obligations under employment law, they should contact Employment New Zealand for advice and assistance.

chunks.title: Business not entitled but has been paid — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: If a business (including self-employed people) applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), and then they had a change in circumstance within the 2-week period, they may not have been entitled to keep the subsidy payment they got for an employee named in their application. Change of circumstances Business action Employee voluntarily resigns The business should use the balance of any of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) to pay other employees named in their application. When no other employees need it, the business should contact the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy for this employee as it was not able to be used for wages. Employee has been made redundant The business must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) remaining for the employee. The subsidy can be used to pay the notice period, but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract, and cannot be used to support other remaining employees named in their application. Employee has been dismissed The business should use the balance of any of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) to pay other employees named in their application. When no other employees need it, the business should contact the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy for this employee as it was not able to be used for wages. Business has closed The business must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) remaining for their employee(s). The subsidy can be used to pay the notice period, but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract and cannot be used to support other remaining employees named in their application. Employee is on fixed-term contract that ends during the period that the business is getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for them. The business must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) remaining for the employee at the end of the fixed-term contract. The subsidy cannot be used to meet any entitlements owed under contract and cannot be used to support other remaining employees named in their application. The business applied for the wrong type of COVID-19 scheme for their employee (eg applied for the Leave Support Scheme in error). The business must repay any amount received for the incorrect application and re-apply for the correct scheme that they are entitled to.

chunks.title: Business not entitled but has been paid — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: The business applied for the wrong type of COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) rate for their employee, eg applies for full-time, when the person was part-time. The business must repay the difference between the full-time rate received and the part-time rate they are entitled to. The business applied for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) based on a predicted 40% decline in revenue, but the decline did not occur. The business is not entitled to the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) and must repay it in full. Employer is a State sector organisation who did not have an exception approved by the Minister of Finance to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) but applied and got the funds. The business is not entitled to the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) and must repay it in full. Any State sector employers who disagree with the decision should consult with their monitoring agency. Business gets payment they are not entitled to due to an office error (eg their application might have been paid twice or accidentally approved instead of declined). The business is not entitled to the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) and must repay it in full. Business gets an insurance payment that covers their loss in revenue, so they have no longer experienced a 40% decline in revenue required to be eligible. The business is not entitled to the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) and must repay it in full. If a business applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) while the employee was getting the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme or the Short-Term Absence Payment, their application was declined.

chunks.title: Example — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: A courier company applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) as their business has been slower than normal during the current escalation in Alert Levels. Their accounts for the last 14 days have not yet been finalised, but they predict they will have experienced a 40% decline in revenue over this period due to the current escalation in Alert Levels, when compared with the default comparison period. They apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for their employees. When they do finalise their accounts, the company has only experienced a 35% decline in revenue. The company got funds they were not entitled to, so they contact the Ministry of Social Development to repay the subsidy in full.

chunks.title: Business units, teams or branches — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Business units, teams or branches
Business units, teams or branches within a single corporate entity cannot apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) individually.
This includes Councils and other business structures who may have different programmes, branches, or divisions that are affected differently by the current escalation in Alert Levels, but who employ all their staff under one corporate entity.
## Example 1
Auckland Council cannot open their public pools because of the current escalation in Alert Levels, and this part of the business has had a 100% decline in revenue in the last 14-days since the current escalation in Alert Levels started.
However, the Council is not eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) scheme because the rest of the business can operate normally, and the Council has not experienced a 40% decline in revenue overall.
## Example 2
A clothing store in Auckland cannot open during the current escalation in Alert Levels.
The store can trade online, but their revenue is down more than 40% compared to a typical 14-day consecutive period in the 6 weeks before the escalation period began.
However, the store is part of a larger company with locations around the country, and the business as a whole has not been significantly impacted by regional restrictions.
The store is not eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) scheme because the rest of the business has not experienced a 40% decline in revenue overall.

chunks.title: Commonly-owned groups with each business a separate legal entity — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Commonly-owned groups with each business a separate legal entity
Some commonly-owned groups consist of a number of separate legal entities and each business within the group employs staff directly and generates revenue.
Businesses who are members of this type of commonly-owned group can each apply individually for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) if they meet the eligibility criteria and obligations in their own right, but they cannot apply as a whole group.
## Example
Giani's Pizza Franchise has locations around the country, however the stores in Auckland cannot open because of the current escalation in Alert Levels.
Although the wider company is able to operate, the stores in Auckland are individually owned as separate legal entities, and they can individually apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) if they meet the eligibility criteria and obligations.

chunks.title: Commonly-owned groups with shared employment functions — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Commonly-owned groups with shared employment functions
Businesses in a commonly-owned group with shared employment functions cannot apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) individually.
This means commonly-owned groups where one business acts as the employer for all employees who work for the other businesses in the group, must apply for the subsidy as a single entity.
The application must be made by the business in the group that carries out the employment function.
## Example
Shipping Enterprises Ltd. is a commonly-owned group, including Fast Truck Company, Big Boat Company, and Hire Right Company. Hire Right employs staff who work across the commonly-owned group, and Fast Truck and Big Boat generate revenue through shipping contracts with various clients.
Shipping Enterprises Ltd. has experienced a decline in revenue because the current escalation in Alert Levels means they cannot deliver to other parts of the country. They have experienced a decline in revenue of more than 40% compared to a typical 14-day consecutive period in the 6 weeks before the escalation period began. Hire Right applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme August 2021) for the staff employed across the group and is granted the subsidy as they meet all the eligibility criteria and obligations.

chunks.title: Commonly-owned groups — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Commonly-owned groups
A commonly-owned group is a group of businesses where each business has the same combination of owners, or the business is part of a larger group of businesses owned by the same entity.
For example, this may include:
- the group has a dominating shareholder or group of shareholders and the businesses operate together as if they were one or
- the group of businesses involves a complex ownership structure where the overall control is centralised and businesses are actually one enterprise

chunks.title: Current escalation in Alert Levels — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Current escalation in Alert Levels
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) was introduced because there was an escalation to Alert Level 3 or above, anywhere in New Zealand, that lasted seven or more consecutive days.
The escalation in Alert Levels for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) refers to the increase to Alert Level 4 that occurred across New Zealand on 17 August 2021.

chunks.title: Current revenue test period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Current revenue test period
The revenue test period for the eighth COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) payment was a period of 14 consecutive days between 23 November 2021 and 6 December 2021.
This applied to all applications made between 9:00am on 26 November 2021 and 11:59pm on 9 December 2021.
Businesses (including self-employed people) cannot use previous revenue test periods [no link find out why] for applications made from 26 November 2021. If a business applied on or after 9:00am on 26 November 2021, they must have used the revenue test period starting on 23 November 2021.

chunks.title: Deciding if someone is self-employed — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Deciding if someone is self-employed
A person is likely to be self-employed when they carry out business activities on their own, including contracting, working as a sole trader or owning a small business.
A self-employed person is likely to:
- support the business with their own money (eg providing all the equipment and tools needed for their job)
- decide or control how they work (eg when, where and what hours they work)
- decide how much they get paid and how
- pay their own income tax (unless they are a young person earning under the tax threshold)
- be responsible for investment decisions and any losses
- be able to sell the business if they wanted to
The above list is not a full list. There may be other things that can be considered.
Self-employed people can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), if they meet the eligibility criteria and obligations.

chunks.title: Decline in revenue for commonly-owned groups — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Decline in revenue for commonly-owned groups
To be eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) as a group entity, the business must be a commonly-owned group with shared employment functions.
The total revenue generated for the group during the current revenue test period must be at least 40% less than the total revenue generated for the group during the relevant comparison period. The decline in revenue test must be met across the group as a whole.
Applicants must use a complete and accurate representation of their business as a whole when assessing whether or not they have had (or will have) at least a 40% decline in revenue.
This means they must use revenue from external business activities, rather than, for example, internal transfers like payments for administration services by one business in the group to others in the group.
Group applicants will generally use the same comparison period across all their businesses. However, if one or more businesses have highly seasonal revenue, they can use the seasonal comparison period for those businesses.
Other businesses within the commonly-owned group that do not have highly seasonal revenue must use the default comparison period.

chunks.title: Decline in revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Decline in revenue
To be eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) the business (or self-employed person) must have had (or expect to have) at least a 40% decline in revenue during the current revenue test period. This is compared to their revenue during the default comparison period or the seasonal comparison period.
This means they have had (or will have) at least a 40% decline in:
- actual revenue or
- predicted revenue (eg when a business has had a reduction in bookings such as accommodation providers) and
- the decline in revenue is due to the effect the current escalation in Alert Levels has had on their business.
Businesses (including self-employed people) can use a combination of both actual and predicted revenue decline in order to be eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021). This will depend on the date they apply for the subsidy and how they are calculating their revenue decline.
However, if the business predicted a 40% decline in revenue but as a result of their actual revenue, they do not experience this, then they must repay the full amount of the subsidy they received.

chunks.title: Default comparison period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Default comparison period
To be eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), a business (including self-employed people) must have experienced (or expect to experience) at least a 40% decline in revenue during the current revenue test period.
Generally, businesses must determine their decline in revenue by comparing the current revenue test period with the typical revenue during a period of 14 consecutive days between 6 July and 17 August 2021, (ie the 6 weeks before the first Alert Level 4 escalation on 17 August 2021). This is called the default comparison period.
When identifying their typical revenue, businesses can choose a period of 14 consecutive days during the default comparison period that best shows the revenue they would normally have earned if their business was not impacted by the current escalation in Alert Levels.
Example
A business applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) on 20 August 2021.
They expect their revenue for the 14-day period from 17 August 2021 will be $5,000.
They compare this against the revenue they received during the 14-day period between 17 and 30 August 2021, which would have been $10,000.
They predict they will experience a decline in revenue of more than 40% and meet the eligibility criteria and obligations for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021).
## Businesses operating for less than a year
All businesses operating for less than a year must use the default comparison period, unless they can demonstrate that using the seasonal comparison period gives a more accurate representation of their revenue decline.

chunks.title: Definition of revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Definition of revenue
Revenue means the total amount of money a business has earned from its normal business activities before expenses are deducted.
Some pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses can include a fall in projected capital income when determining a 40% decrease in revenue.
For the purposes of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), revenue does not include:
- this or any other COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Schemes
- COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment
- COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme
- COVID-19 Essential Workers Leave Support Scheme
- COVID-19 Resurgence Support Payment
- COVID-19 Small Business Cashflow (Loan) Scheme

chunks.title: Determining a decline in revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Determining a decline in revenue
To determine a decline in revenue, the business (including self-employed people) must compare:
- their revenue during the current revenue test period with either: the default comparison period orfor some businesses, the seasonal comparison period
- the default comparison period or
- for some businesses, the seasonal comparison period
To be eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), the revenue of the current revenue test period must be at least 40% less than it was in the period it was compared against, and that revenue decline must have been caused by the effect the current escalation in Alert Levels has had on their business, not COVID-19 generally.

chunks.title: Eligible businesses — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Eligible businesses
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) was available for:
- businesses using all employment types including full-time, part-time, casual, fixed-term, sole trading, and self-employment, including those businesses with employees getting the minimum wage exemption
- across all sectors and industries in New Zealand
- includes registered charities, incorporated societies, non-government organisations and post-settlement governance entities (eg Māori authorities), and commonly-owned groups (in some circumstances)
State sector organisations are generally not eligible to get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for their employees.
Exceptions for State Sector employers are considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, through the relevant monitoring agency.

chunks.title: Employee voluntarily leaves — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Employee voluntarily leaves
Businesses must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.
If an employee voluntarily leaves their employment for another job opportunity, the business must advise the Ministry of Social Development, and the business cannot receive any more subsidy payments for this employee. The business does not have to repay the subsidy already received for this employee, but they must use any remaining balance towards topping up the wages of other employees named in their application so that they are being paid their ordinary wages.
The subsidy can be used to contribute towards the wages of other employees named in their application. If the business has no other employees to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other employees named in their application are already being paid their ordinary wages, the business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining subsidy that was not able to be used for wages.

chunks.title: Manufacturer of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: Generally, it may not be expected that a business who makes PPE would have had a 40% decline in revenue caused by the current escalation in Alert Levels, as they are able to operate at a time of high demand. However, if that business has evidence to support their application, they may be eligible for the subsidy Example 1 The PPE business was fully staffed by sole parents who could no longer work because they had to stay home as schools were closed, due to Alert Level 3 or 4 restrictions. Example 2 The PPE business was unable to source enough raw materials because of shipping delays due to the Alert Level 3 or 4 restrictions and this reduced their production levels.

chunks.title: Food outlet — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: Generally, it may not be expected that a food outlet as an essential business would have had a 40% revenue decline caused by the current escalation in Alert Levels, as they are able to operate at a time of high demand. However, if that business has evidence to support their application, they may be eligible for the subsidy. Example 1 A grocery store in the middle of the Central Business District (CBD), gets most of their trade from CBD workers. Many people are still working from home or choosing not to eat out. Example 2 A supermarket in a small town relies on tourists for a significant amount of their revenue. With the Alert Level restrictions in place, there are now less tourists there.

chunks.title: Business outside of regional Alert Level 3 or 4 lockdown — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: Generally, it might not be expected a business operating outside of a regional Alert Level 3 or 4 lockdown would have had a 40% revenue decline caused by the current escalation in Alert Levels, as they are able to operate with minimal restrictions placed on their business. However, if that business has evidence to support their application and is able to show that the decline in revenue is caused by the Alert Level 3 or 4 restrictions that are in place elsewhere, they may be eligible for the subsidy. Example 1 A florist in Canterbury who supplies markets around the country. With Alert Level 3 or 4 public health restrictions in the Auckland region, the florist is unable to sell their stock to their largest market. Example 2 A backpackers in Queenstown has seen a reduction in bookings since the Auckland region has been in Alert Level 3 or 4.
