A large number of bookings from Auckland holiday-makers have been cancelled, and although reservations were starting to increase again, numbers have now dropped off.

chunks.title: Business outside of regional Alert Level 3 or 4 lockdown, only affected by Alert Level 2 restrictions — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: To be eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), a business' decline in revenue must be caused by the effect the continuation in Alert Levels 3 or 4 from 17 August 2021 has had on their business. If a business in a region at Alert Level 2 has a decline in revenue because of the associated restrictions of Alert Level 2 (and not because of the effect of Alert Levels 3 or 4), they are not eligible for the subsidy even if the decline in revenue is at least 40%. Example Auckland is in Alert Level 4 and the rest of the country is in Alert Level 2. Under ordinary circumstances, a Wellington theatre has a seating capacity of 300 people. However, under Alert Level 2 they can only seat 100 people. The business expects to experience at least a 40% decline in revenue while the Alert Level 2 restrictions are in place. Although the business predicts its revenue will decline by more than 40% it is not eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021). This is because their decline in revenue is caused by the Alert Level 2 restrictions, not the effect that the continuation of Alert Levels 3 or 4 from 17 August 2021 has had on their business.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Example 1
Ailee works 10 hours per week at minimum wage ($200 gross per week, at 1 April 2021) while she is a student. The business that employs her has experienced a decline in revenue due to the current escalation in Alert Levels, so the business applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) to continue paying her.
Because her ordinary wages are less than the subsidy rate of $359 gross per week, the business must use the subsidy to continue paying her ordinary wage of $200 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions).
The business must use the difference to contribute to the wages of their other employees named in the application and when there are no other employees, must refund the remainder back to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example 2
Jivan works 40 hours at a workshop as a building labourer. He usually gets $1000 gross per week. He cannot do any work from home during the current escalation in Alert Levels.
The business has a highly skilled and reliable workforce and is using the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) to continue to pay Jivan 80% of his ordinary wages during this period ($800 gross per week). If the business was not able to do this, they would be required to pay Jivan the full-time subsidy rate ($600 gross per week). Any changes the business makes to his employment agreement (ie to reduce his wages) must be agreed with Jivan in writing.
## Example 3
Stuart is a digger driver. The business that employs him has no revenue coming into the business during current escalation in Alert Levels. The business has many contracts to finish once they can get back to work, so needs to keep their employees during the current escalation in Alert Levels.
The business is unable to pay Stuart 80% of his full-time wage over this period, and so the business pays Stuart the full amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) of $600 (less any usual wage deductions). Any changes the business makes to his employment agreement (ie to reduce his wages) must be agreed with Stuart in writing.

chunks.title: Fixed-term contract ends within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Fixed-term contract ends within subsidy period
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) is open to existing and newly hired employees and this includes employees on fixed-term contracts. To get the subsidy, businesses must agree to retain the employees named in their application for the duration of the subsidy period.
Businesses can include employees on fixed-term contracts in their COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) application, even if the employee's contract is scheduled to end during the period that the business would be getting the subsidy for them.
However, if an employee's fixed-term contract ends during the subsidy period, the business will not have met their obligation to retain the employees named in the application. In these circumstances, the business can use the subsidy to pay out any notice period for that employee, but the subsidy cannot be used to pay any other entitlements. It also cannot be used to support other remaining employees. The business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining subsidy for this employee.
The business and the employee may agree to extend the contract to the end of the subsidy period in order to meet their obligation to retain the employees named in their application for the period they get the subsidy.
## Example 1
Anaru is on a fixed-term contract that is scheduled to end on 27 August 2021. The business that employs Anaru applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) on 23 August 2021 to continue paying its employees during the current escalation in Alert Levels and includes Anaru in the application.
The business agrees with Anaru to extend his contract to 6 September 2021 so that Anaru can continue getting wages during this period. The business is eligible to get the full 2-week subsidy for Anaru.
## Example 2
Sacha is on a fixed-term contract that is scheduled to end on 30 August 2021. The business that employs her applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) on 23 August 2021 and includes Sacha in the application.
When Sacha's contract ends on 30 August 2021, the business returns the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Health and disability funded workforce — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Health and disability funded workforce
Health and disability funded workforces (eg businesses that provide community health care) not employed by the State Sector are able to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) if they meet the eligibility criteria and obligations.
Health and disability funded workforces not employed by the State sector includes organisations contracted to, or funded in whole or part, by organisations in the State sector (eg the Ministry of Health and District Health Boards).
Examples include:
- in-home care workers
- employees in primary health organisations
- nurses and other staff in rest-homes or other residential care facilities (eg cooks, cleaners, support staff)

chunks.title: Flexi-wage, Flexi-Wage Self-Employed and Mana in Mahi — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: If a business is currently getting the Flexi-Wage, Flexi-Wage Self-Employed, or Mana in Mahi subsidy for their employee(s), they can also apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), if they meet the eligibility criteria and obligations. All wage subsidies the business is getting must be paid to their employees. For more information see:

chunks.title: Apprenticeship Boost Initiative — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: Apprenticeship Boost helps businesses with the costs of keeping their current apprentices or hiring new ones for the first 24 months of their programme of study. If a business is currently getting Apprenticeship Boost, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for their employees, if they meet the other eligibility criteria and obligations. For more information see:

chunks.title: Main benefit and other support — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: If a self-employed person is currently getting a main benefit or other extra help from the Ministry of Social Development, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021). All Ministry of Social Development clients must meet their obligations in relation to the financial assistance they are receiving, including declaring any income they receive (if appropriate). When assessing an application staff must not check if an applicant for the subsidy is receiving other financial assistance from the Ministry of Social Development, as this is a breach of Privacy.

chunks.title: Financial support from other agencies — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: There is a range of financial support available from other agencies for businesses who have been negatively impacted by the COVID-19 financial crisis. These schemes, such as the Resurgence Support Payment from Inland Revenue, are separate to Work and Income support, and have their own eligibility criteria. This means that, if they meet the necessary eligibility criteria and obligations, businesses can apply and get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) as well as other schemes. Applicants need to make sure they meet the eligibility criteria for any schemes they apply for. Note the Resurgence Support Payment from Inland Revenue is intended to support businesses to cover fixed costs. It is available to eligible businesses whenever COVID-19 Alert Levels are increased to Level 2 or above for a period of 7 consecutive days. This differs from the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), which is activated after an escalation to Level 3 or above for 7 consecutive days, and is intended to keep businesses (including self-employed people) connected to their employees by supporting businesses with the cost of wages. Businesses can receive the Resurgence Support Payment and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme at the same time.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Applications for the Wage Subsidy Scheme August 2021 closed at 11.59pm on 9 December 2021.
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) was available for 16 weeks, 8 x 2-weekly payments, were made from 20 August 2021, to support businesses impacted by the escalation to Alert Level 4 nationwide on 17 August 2021, to help the businesses stay connected to their workers.
This scheme was the August 2021 addition to previous wage subsidies implemented in response to COVID-19.
Businesses who got previous COVID-19 Wage Subsidy, or Leave Support Scheme payments, or Short-Term Absence Payment could apply for the same employees again, if they met the qualifications, but only once the period for any previous payment had ended
## Applications
Businesses and self-employed people applied online for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021).
Applications could be made from 9.00am, 20 August 2021. Payments were made as a lump sum to the business for each named employee (including self-employed people) and covered a 2-week period from the date of application.

chunks.title: Legally working in New Zealand — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Legally working in New Zealand
Legally working in New Zealand means a person is both working in New Zealand, and is legally entitled to work in New Zealand.
A person cannot be employed if they cannot legally work in New Zealand in that job. It is the responsibility of the business to make sure that their employee can work for them legally.

chunks.title: Newly hired employees — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Newly hired employees
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) was open for eligible businesses to apply for any newly hired employees, and previous employees who were re-hired before the business applied for the subsidy.
## Example 1
Sam was employed full-time as a hairdresser, but their start date was delayed due to the current escalation in Alert Levels.
Sam's employer applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for their employees and includes Sam in the application.
The employer pays Sam $600 (less any usual wage deductions) until they can start their new role.
## Example 2
Whiti owns a pet store and is getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) as her business has experienced a decline in revenue due to the current escalation in Alert Levels.
One of her employees resigns and she needs to hire a replacement.
Whiti uses the remaining subsidy from the leaving employee to continue paying her other staff, and submits another application for the new employee when they start their role.
## Example 3
Ravi owns a clothing store and has reopened his business after being closed during the COVID-19 public health restrictions. He needs to hire a new employee, but his business is still experiencing more than 40% decline in revenue due to the recent escalation in COVID-19 Alert Levels.
Ravi is already getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for his existing employees, so submits another application for the new employee when they start their role.

chunks.title: Ordinary wages or salary — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Ordinary wages or salary
For employees, their ordinary wages or salary are specified in their employment agreement at the date the business applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021).
Self-employed people can determine their ordinary wages or drawings by calculating the regular amount that is left over after they meet their business costs. This is the amount they regularly pay themselves as drawings from the business.
If the individual is self-employed, and the income they regularly draw from their business is less than the amount they got from the subsidy, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) can be used to support the costs of wages, but cannot be used towards other business costs.

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: Applications for the Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) closed at 11.59pm on 9 December 2021. The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) was paid for a 2-week period as a lump sum payment at the appropriate weekly subsidy rate for: - working 20 hours or more or - working under 20 hours The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) was paid at a flat rate based on each named worker's normal (or expected) hours of paid employment: - $600 (before tax) for 20 hours or more per week, or 40 hours or more per fortnight or - $359 (before tax) for less than 20 hours per week, or less than 40 hours per fortnight The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) covered each eligible worker for 2 weeks from the date of application.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: The business accessed the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for 10 employees as soon as the scheme became available on 20 August 2021. Now the business needs the subsidy for 20 more employees. The business can apply for the 20 newly named employees, but not the 10 original employees for whom they have already got the subsidy.

chunks.title: Calculating variable hours — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: For a self-employed person, or a business with casual employees who work variable hours, an average over a relevant period can be used to work out which subsidy rate to apply. A relevant period for a business or self-employed person who has been working for a year, would be an average over this period. As a guide, for a new business or a person who has been self-employed for less than one year, an average over 8 weeks can be used, unless there is another time period that would be more appropriate. Example if using the period that the individual has been employed for would give a better representation of the employee's usual hours, then the business can use this time period instead. It is up to businesses to agree with their employees what their hours would usually be during this period, to determine the appropriate COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) rate to apply for.

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: Charlotte is a relief teacher for an Early Childhood Education Centre and is called in to provide support as required, but the Centre is closed due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions. The Centre employs Charlotte as a casual employee and calculates that she has worked an average of 17 hours per week over the last 4 months she has been employed there. The business applies for a part-time COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (August 2021) rate to continue paying Charlotte's wages (at a rate of 17 hours per week for the 2-week period). As this is less than the $359 gross per week provided through the subsidy, the business uses the remaining subsidy to support the wages of other employees named in the application.

chunks.title: Maximum payment for a business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: There is no cap on the total amount of COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) a business can get. It is based on the number of employees they have, and whether they are working 20 hours or more, or under 20 hours.

chunks.title: People getting income from a property business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## People getting income from a property business
Some people are paid a wage, salary or draw an income from a property business, such as private rentals, Airbnb's and homestay operations.
These businesses were eligible to get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) if they met the qualifications, including being registered and operating in New Zealand.
Note the subsidy was paid to support employers to retain their employees or offset a loss of earnings (for self-employed people) and could only be used to support the cost of wages. People who applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for a property business must be able to declare that they draw a wage, salary, or income for this work.
For self-employed people who are not registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, the Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed before paying the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021).
## Example
Anthony owns several holiday homes, which he rents out to supplement his income. He works an average of 10 hours per week on the properties, managing the bookings and cleaning the property in between guests.
Usually this would be a very busy time of year for his business, but most of his bookings have been cancelled due to the current escalation of COVID-19 Alert Levels. Anthony's income has dropped by more than 40% during this period so he applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021).
The Ministry is able to verify his self-employment status with Inland Revenue and his application is approved.

chunks.title: People getting paid parental leave — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## People getting paid parental leave
Businesses (including self-employed people) may have employees who are getting paid parental leave from Inland Revenue.
## Employee already getting paid parental leave
If an employee was already getting paid parental leave from Inland Revenue when the business applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), the business is not able to include this person in their application.
If they do include the person in error and the application is approved, the business got funds they are not eligible for and must repay the full amount for this person to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Employee goes on paid parental leave during subsidy period
If an employee starts getting paid parental leave from Inland Revenue after the business has made an application and/or received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), then the person is not eligible to get both the subsidy and paid parental leave.
The business must stop using the subsidy for the person as soon as they go on parental leave.
The remaining funds can be used towards topping up the wages of other employees named in their application, so that they are being paid their ordinary wages.
If the business has no other employees to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other employees named in their application are already being paid their ordinary wages, the business must tell the Ministry of Social Development, and must repay any remaining amount that was not able to be used for wages.
## Employee due to return from paid parental leave during subsidy period
If an employee was getting paid parental leave from Inland Revenue at the time of the business's application for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for their other employees, but the employee has since returned to work, then the business can make a new application for them.
The business should use the new hours the employee will be working on their return to work to calculate the rate of subsidy to apply for.

chunks.title: Employee already getting ACC — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Employee already getting ACC
If the employee was already getting ACC compensation when the business applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), the business is not able to include this person in their application.
If they do include the person in error and the application is approved, the business will have got funds they are not eligible for and must repay the subsidy for this person to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Employee goes on ACC during subsidy period
If the employee is injured and starts getting ACC compensation after the business made an application and/or got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), the person can get both the subsidy and ACC compensation.
However, the employee must declare the subsidy to ACC as income and their weekly compensation may be abated (reduced) accordingly.
## Employee due to finish getting ACC during subsidy period
If the employee was getting ACC compensation at the time of the business's application for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for their other employees, but the person is no longer getting the ACC payments, the business can make a new application for them.

chunks.title: People on casual contracts — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## People on casual contracts
Businesses can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for employees who are on casual contracts, but they must keep them employed for the subsidy period.
Businesses can apply for the subsidy for the hours the employee is usually employed. Businesses need to agree with their employees what their hours would usually be during this period, to determine the appropriate COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) rate to apply for.
If an employee's casual contract ends during the subsidy period, then the business will not have met their obligation to retain the employees named in their application.
The business must notify the Ministry of Social Development and repay any remaining subsidy for this employee.

chunks.title: People on fixed-term contracts — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## People on fixed-term contracts
Businesses can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for employees who are on fixed-term contracts, but they must keep them employed for the subsidy period.
If an employee's fixed-term contract ends during the subsidy period, the business will not have met their obligation to retain the employees named in their application. The business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining subsidy for this employee.

chunks.title: People working multiple jobs — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## People working multiple jobs
Businesses may have employees who work for them, and another business. The employee may work more than 20 hours for one business, and less than 20 hours for the other.
If both businesses meet the criteria, they can each apply for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for the same employee.

chunks.title: Pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' business
A small number of pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses may be eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) if they:
- are a research and development intensive start-up business and
- are 'seed' or 'venture backed' and
- are recognised by Callaghan Innovation as a legitimate research and development 'start-up' business and
- have no other revenue other than government funding, and seed or venture capital
Eligible pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses may use projected capital income as their source of revenue when assessing if they meet the revenue decline eligibility criteria. These businesses must determine their decline in revenue using the default comparison period, unless they can show that they meet the criteria for the seasonal comparison period.
These businesses can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) if they meet the other eligibility criteria and obligations.

chunks.title: Initial revenue test period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: The revenue test period for the initial payment of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) was a period of 14 consecutive days between 17 August and 31 August 2021. This applied to all applications made between 9:00am on 20 August 2021 and 11:59pm on 2 September 2021.

chunks.title: Changed revenue test period (17 to 31 August 2021) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: On 26 August 2021, the revenue test period for the initial payment of the subsidy was extended to include 31 August 2021. Businesses had a full day of business on 17 August under Alert Level 1. Some businesses also experienced a surge in revenue due to people stocking up on supplies between the Alert Level 4 announcement, and its activation at 11:59pm on 17 August 2021. The extension of the revenue test period to include 31 August allowed businesses (including self-employed people) who applied for the initial payment to choose whether a revenue test period of 17 August 2021 to 30 August 2021 or 18 August 2021 to 31 August 2021 was appropriate for their business.

chunks.title: Second revenue test period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: The revenue test period for the second payment of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) was a period of 14 consecutive days between 31 August and 13 September 2021. This applied to all applications made between 9:00am on 3 September 2021 and 11:59pm on 16 September 2021. Businesses could use 31 August 2021 to calculate their revenue test period for both the initial and second payments.

chunks.title: Third revenue test period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: The revenue test period for the third payment of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) was a period of 14 consecutive days between 14 September 2021 and 27 September 2021. This applied to all applications made between 9:00am on 17 September 2021 and 11:59pm on 30 September 2021.

chunks.title: Fourth revenue test period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: The revenue test period for the fourth COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) payment was a period of 14 consecutive days between 28 September 2021 and 11 October 2021. This applied to all applications made between 9:00am on 1 October 2021 and 11:59pm on 14 October 2021.

chunks.title: Fifth revenue test period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: The revenue test period for the fifth COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) payment was a period of 14 consecutive days between 12 October 2021 and 25 October 2021. This applied to all applications made between 9:00am 15 October 2021 and 11:59pm on 28 October 2021.

chunks.title: Sixth revenue test period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: The revenue test period for the sixth COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) payment was a period of 14 consecutive days between 26 October 2021 and 8 November 2021. This applied to all applications made between 9:00am 29 October 2021 and 11:59pm on 11 November 2021.

chunks.title: Seventh revenue test period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: The revenue test period for the seventh COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) payment was a period of 14 consecutive days between 9 November 2021 and 22 November 2021. This applied to all applications made between 9:00am 12 November 2021 and 11:59pm on 25 November 2021.

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: Applications for the Wage Subsidy Scheme August 2021 closed at 11.59pm on 9 December 2021. To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), businesses must have met the following eligibility criteria and obligations: - the business must have experienced or expect to experience at least a 40% decline in revenue - the decline in revenue must be during the current revenue test period, when compared to the default comparison period or the seasonal comparison period - the decline in revenue must be caused by the effect the current escalation in Alert Levels has had on their business - the business must be registered and operating in New Zealand - the employees named in their application must be legally working in New Zealand and employed by the business as at the date of application - before making an application, the business must have taken active steps to mitigate the impact of the current escalation in Alert Levels on their business activities - the business must not be currently getting a subsidy for the employees named in their application for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), the Leave Support Scheme or Short-Term Absence Payment If a business is getting a COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme payment or Short-Term Absence Payment for their employees, they must wait until the subsidy period for these employees has ended before they apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for those employees.

chunks.title: Must retain employees and pay at least 80% wages or salary — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: Businesses who get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) must keep the employees (for whom they received the wage subsidy) in employment for the period of the subsidy (unless the employee voluntarily ends the employment relationship). In order to meet the eligibility criteria and obligations for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (August 2021), businesses must try to pay at least 80% of each named employees' ordinary wages or salary for the period of the subsidy, as per their employment agreement at the date the business applies for the subsidy. However, businesses must follow current employment law when reducing an employee's wages or changing the hours they work. When the employee was earning less than the subsidy rate, the business must keep paying their ordinary wages, even if they are working less hours due to the current escalation in Alert Levels. Any difference should be used towards topping up the wages of other employees named in their application. When there are no other employees to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other employees named in their application are already being paid their ordinary wages, the business must tell the Ministry of Social Development, and must repay any remaining subsidy that was not able to be used for wages. If a person is self-employed, and the income they regularly draw from their business is less than the subsidy amount they received, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Receivership or liquidation within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: In some circumstances, businesses (including self-employed people) who have received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) may still go into receivership or liquidation, and may have to sell or close their business permanently. Note receivership and liquidation processes can be complicated. Please seek legal advice as required.

chunks.title: Business operating under receivership or liquidation before applying — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: A business who is currently operating under receivership or liquidation can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), if they meet the eligibility criteria and obligations to retain employees named in their application for the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Business goes into receivership or liquidation but keeps operating — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: If the business can continue operating under receivership or for the duration of the liquidation process, then the business (or the receiver/liquidator) can continue to use the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) to support the cost of wages for employees named in their application. If the business recovers, or the receiver/liquidator sells the business during the subsidy period and the new owners take on the employees named in their application, then the business can continue to use the subsidy for these employees. Example 1 A business goes into receivership 2 weeks after getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for their employees. The receiver takes over the business and manages to sell the business to new owners. The new owners keep all the previous employees and use any remaining subsidy to continue paying these employees for the duration of the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Business closes under receivership or liquidation — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: If the business is liquidated (and permanently closed), or the receiver/liquidator sells the business during the subsidy period, and the new owners do not take on the employees named in the subsidy application, then the business will not have met their obligation to retain employees named in their application and they must repay any remaining subsidy for these employees. Where employees are made redundant, the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) can be used to pay the notice period but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract, and cannot be used to support other remaining employees named in the application. Example 2 A restaurant owner puts their business into liquidation 3 days after getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for their employees. The liquidator gives the employees 1 weeks' notice that the business will be closing permanently and uses the subsidy to pay out the notice period for the employees named in their application. At the end of the notice period, the liquidator repays the remaining 1 week of subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Repaying unused funds after the subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Repaying unused funds after the subsidy period
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) was paid in one lump sum to the business to support the cost of wages for 2 weeks.
If the business does not need the full weekly rate for their employee(s), then any difference should be used for the wages of other employees named in their application.
If there are any unused funds at the end of the 2-week period, the business must repay the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development. The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) cannot be used beyond the 2-week period.
If the person is self-employed and the income that they regularly draw from their business is less than the amount they got from the subsidy, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) cannot be used beyond the 2-week period for which it is paid.
## Example
Jason got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for his only employee who works part-time. The employee was earning under the part-time subsidy rate, so continued getting their ordinary wages for the duration of the subsidy period.
At the end of the 2 weeks, Jason has not used all the subsidy payment and has some funds remaining.
He contacts the Ministry of Social Development to repay the unused subsidy, as the funds were not fully used on wage costs during the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Retain employees named in their application — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Retain employees named in their application
Businesses must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), to retain the employees the subsidy was paid for, for the duration of the subsidy period.
Businesses must agree to retain their employees for the full 2-week period that they receive the subsidy for these employees.

chunks.title: Reviewing decisions to decline the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Reviewing decisions to decline the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021)
Applications for the Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) closed at 11.59pm on 9 December 2021.
Decisions to decline the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) are not made under the Social Security Act 2018 and are not covered by the usual Review of Decision guidelines.
If a business (including a self-employed person) wanted a decision to decline the subsidy reviewed, that decision should be reconsidered. This review should be based on whether an informed decision was made and should consider the following:
- whether all relevant information was available and
- whether the appropriate options and implications were considered and
- whether the decision was made at the appropriate level of delegation
If a review of the decision to decline the payment upholds the original decision, the business can ask the Ombudsman to undertake their own review.

chunks.title: Seasonal comparison period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: To be eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021), a business (including self-employed people) must have experienced (or expect to experience) at least a 40% decline in revenue during the current revenue test period. Generally, businesses must determine their decline in revenue using the default comparison period. However, for businesses who have highly seasonal fluctuations in their revenue, the default comparison period might not give an accurate representation of what the business would have been expecting to earn during the current revenue test period. These businesses can use the seasonal comparison period. The seasonal comparison period is the same period of 14 consecutive days as the current revenue test period, in 2020 or 2019. The business can choose if the period in 2020 or 2019 gives the most accurate representation of what the business would have been expecting to earn during the current revenue test period.

chunks.title: Types of seasonal business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: Some examples of businesses with highly seasonal revenue could be seasonal work such as harvesting fruit and vegetables, music festival or event planners whose peak seasons are during the summer months, or tourism businesses where the season starts on a specific date. For example, the 6 weeks before the COVID-19 Alert Level change (ie the default comparison period) is their seasonal quiet period where they do not usually have any revenue coming in, or their revenue is low, but the 2 weeks after the Alert Level change is where they would have started to have revenue coming in, or increased revenue. If they compare their revenue in the 14 days since the Alert Level change with a period of 14 consecutive days from the 6 weeks prior, it will look like the business has not had a loss of revenue. However, if they compare their revenue to the same 14-day period in 2019, they have clearly had a 40% decline in revenue they can attribute to the seasonal nature of their business. This is the 14-day period since the Alert Level changed, but in 2019.

chunks.title: Evidence — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: If asked, businesses will need to provide evidence to show the basis on which they consider their revenue to be seasonal and how the seasonality makes it harder to meet the decline in revenue with the default comparison period. This could be information about the type of work the business does or financial records showing the fluctuation in their revenue in different seasons. The seasonal comparison period must be a reasonable representation of what the business would have been expecting to earn now if the business was not affected by the current escalation in Alert Levels.

chunks.title: Example — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: Jayne runs a fruit packhouse business and applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) on 20 August 2021. Her business is highly seasonal and their peak season only begins on 23 August 2021. If Jayne used the default comparison period, this would not show her revenue decline as the business did not have much revenue in the 6 weeks before the escalation to Alert Level 4 on 17 August 2021. However, if she uses the seasonal comparison period, this shows what revenue the business would have received at the same time 2 years ago (before the business was impacted by COVID-19 in 2019). Jayne compares what the business would have expected to get between 18 August and 31 August 2021, to the revenue received between 18 and 31 August 2019 and calculates a revenue loss of 40%. Jayne's business meets the eligibility criteria and obligations for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021).

chunks.title: Seasonal work ends within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Seasonal work ends within subsidy period
Some seasonal workers will have had their work affected by the current escalation in Alert Levels (ie season finished earlier than expected and/or not able to pick up new work due to the escalation in Alert Levels).
If the business got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) but can no longer offer them employment during the subsidy period, then the business will not be meeting their obligation to retain the employees named in their application and must repay any remaining subsidy for these employees to the Ministry of Social Development.
If the seasonal workers are casual employees or on fixed-term contracts, then the business can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) to continue paying them, as long as they keep them employed for the subsidy period.
## Example 1
Rowan usually picks grapes over the summer months, but the winery that employs him has closed the harvesting season early due to the current escalation in Alert Levels.
The winery got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for its employees, but after 1 week the winery decides to end their contracts as the business can no longer offer them employment to return to. The business uses the subsidy to pay out the employee's notice period and repays any remaining amount to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example 2
Tracey employs 30 casual employees on her kiwifruit orchard, however, the orchard is not able to open due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions and Tracey has no work for these employees.
Tracey calculates the average hours each of her casual employees would have worked at this time last year to determine the correct rate to apply for. Tracey applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) to continue paying her employees for the duration of the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Seasonal workers — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Seasonal workers
There are a variety of employment arrangements for seasonal workers (eg fixed-term contract or casual employment contract).
Businesses can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for their seasonal workers, but they must keep them employed for the subsidy period.
If an employee's contract ends during the subsidy period, then the business will not have met their obligation to retain the employees named in their application.
The business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining subsidy for this employee.

chunks.title: Self-employed person is also an employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Self-employed person is also an employee
A person may be self-employed for some of their income, and also be employed by a business or other organisation.
If the self-employed person qualifies, they can get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for their own business.
Also, if their employer qualifies, the employer can get the subsidy to continue paying the person as an employee.

chunks.title: Specific employment situations — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Specific employment situations
People's working situations in New Zealand may vary and eligibility for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) can sometimes differ.

chunks.title: State sector organisations generally not eligible — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: State sector organisations are generally not eligible to get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021). State sector organisations are listed on the Public Service Commission website. See: - New Zealand's central government organisations Te Kawa Mataaho Public Service Commission State sector organisations can request an exception to allow them to apply for the subsidy. Exceptions for State sector organisations are considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, through the relevant monitoring agency. If an exception has already been granted for an earlier COVID-19 Wage Subsidy the State sector organisation does not need to get another exception to apply for this or future COVID-19 Wage Subsidy schemes.

chunks.title: State sector organisations that can apply — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: As at 17 September 2021, the only State sector organisations that have been granted an exception and can apply for the subsidy are: - Airways Corporation of New Zealand Limited - New Zealand Post Limited - Television New Zealand Limited - KiwiRail Holdings Limited - Quotable Value Limited - New Zealand Artificial Limb Service - Crown Research Institutes (CRIs): AgResearch LimitedInstitute of Environmental Science and Research LimitedInstitute of Geological and Nuclear Sciences LimitedLandcare Research New Zealand LimitedNational Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research LimitedNew Zealand Forest Research Institute LimitedThe New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research Limited - AgResearch Limited - Institute of Environmental Science and Research Limited - Institute of Geological and Nuclear Sciences Limited - Landcare Research New Zealand Limited - National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research Limited - New Zealand Forest Research Institute Limited - The New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research Limited Note the State sector organisations in the list above can apply but they must meet all the eligibility criteria and obligations. No other State sector organisations are permitted to apply for the subsidy.

chunks.title: Other State sector organisations cannot apply — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text: None of the other organisations described on Te Kawa Mataaho Public Service Commission website are permitted to apply for the subsidy. This includes: - State schools, state-integrated schools and special institutions (each being Boards of Trustees that are bodies corporate constituted under subpart 5 of Part 3 of the Education and Training Act 2020 (including distance schools)) - Crown entity subsidiaries (being companies incorporated under the Companies Act 1993 that are controlled by Crown entities): for a state school, state integrated school or special institution, Crown entity subsidiaries can include separate legal entities providing, for example, after-school care programmes, hostels, shopfor DHBs, Crown entity subsidiaries can include separate legal entities providing, for example, laundry services - for a state school, state integrated school or special institution, Crown entity subsidiaries can include separate legal entities providing, for example, after-school care programmes, hostels, shop - for DHBs, Crown entity subsidiaries can include separate legal entities providing, for example, laundry services Crown entities should ensure their subsidiaries do not apply for the subsidy. Note Local government organisations are not State sector organisations.

chunks.title: Transition between previous COVID-19 subsidies and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Transition between previous COVID-19 subsidies and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021)
A business (including self-employed people) can apply for the same employees under different COVID-19 subsidies if they meet the eligibility criteria and obligations, but only after the period for the previous payment has ended.
## Business got a COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment
Businesses can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) when they meet the criteria, and need other assistance. But they can only apply for employees named in Short-Term Absence Payment after the payment period for the Short-Term Absence Payment has ended.
Example
A business got the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for Maria on Saturday 18 August 2021 and then applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) on 20 August 2021 for the rest of their 15 employees as well.
The business cannot be paid the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for Maria until 21 August 2021. The business can get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for their other staff from 20 August 2021.
## Business got a COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme payment
The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme was introduced on 28 April 2020 to provide financial assistance to businesses during the COVID-19 public health restrictions to:
- encourage employees to self-isolate when they need to and
- support employees who are unable to work from home to have an income when they cannot work
Businesses eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) can choose to apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme when appropriate for their employee's situation.
However, a business cannot get both the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) for the same period, for the same employee.

chunks.title: Worker temporarily overseas and cannot return due to COVID-19 restrictions — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme august 2021
chunks.text:
## Worker temporarily overseas and cannot return due to COVID-19 restrictions
A person who is legally employed in New Zealand but who is currently overseas can be named as an employee in a COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021) application if:
- they were legally working in New Zealand before leaving and
- their absence was intended to be temporary (eg a holiday or a work business trip) and
- they maintain their employment status (that is, they are still employed by the business) and intended to return to work on a specific date but cannot start on that date due to the COVID-19 travel restrictions and
- the business meets the other eligibility criteria and obligations for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (August 2021)

chunks.title: Amount employer must pay employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: The amount the employer must pay to the employee depends on whether the employee usually earns under, or over the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension rate applied for them.

chunks.title: Employer can pay at least 80% — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: Employers who get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension must use their best endeavours to pay at least 80% of each named employees wages or salary for the period of the subsidy, at the rate they would have been paid before the business was impacted by the COVID-19 public health restrictions. When the employee was earning less than the subsidy rate, the employer must keep paying their usual wages, even if they are working less hours during to the COVID-19 public health restrictions. The employer must use the remaining support towards topping up the wages of other affected staff. When there are no other employees, or the other employees are already being paid their usual wages, the employer must repay the remaining subsidy back to the Ministry of Social Development as it could not be used for wages. If the individual is self-employed and the income that they regularly draw from their business is less than the amount they got via the subsidy, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development. Example 1 John earns $956 gross per week. His employer can commit to paying 80% of this ($764.80) while John is at home during the COVID-19 public health restrictions and there is no work for him. The employer gets the subsidy rate of $585.80 gross per week and continues to pay John $764.80 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions) for the subsidy period. When the business reopens, John goes back to working his normal hours. The employer uses the subsidy to help fund John's normal wages of $956 gross per week. Example 2 Miri earns $220 gross per week. Her employer can continue paying 80% of her earnings ($176) while Miri is at home during the COVID-19 public health restrictions and there is no work for her. The employer gets the subsidy rate of $350 gross per week, but because Miri earns under the subsidy rate the employer must continue to pay her wages or salary at the rate they would have been paid before the business was impacted by the COVID-19 public health restrictions (ie $220 gross per week).

chunks.title: Employer can pay at least 80% — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: When her employer re-opens, the business starts slowly and Miri is only offered half of her hours. Her employer must pay her for these hours and because she earned under the subsidy rate, her employer must continue to pay her usual wages for the subsidy period (ie $220 gross per week).

chunks.title: Not possible for employer to pay at least 80% — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: If paying 80% of their pre COVID-19 impact wages or salary is not possible, and the employee was usually earning over the subsidy rate applied for, the employer must pass on the full weekly amount of support (less any usual wage deductions) to the employee. When the employee was earning less than the subsidy rate, the employer must keep paying their usual wages, even if they are working less hours during to the COVID-19 public health restrictions. The employer must use the remaining support towards topping up the wages of other affected staff. When there are no other employees, or the other employees are already being paid their usual wages, must repay the remaining subsidy back to the Ministry of Social Development as it was could not be used for wages. Example 1 Mandy usually earns $1000 gross per week. Her employer is unable to continue paying 80% of her wages during the time while she is at home, and there is no work for her to do. The employer gets the subsidy rate of $585.80 gross per week, and because she usually earns over this amount, must pass on this amount to Mandy as wages. She gets $585.80 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions) during this period. Mandy can go back to work when her employer begins operating again and continues working her usual hours. The employer uses the subsidy to help to pay her normal wages for the remainder of the subsidy period (ie $1000 gross per week). Example 2 Tane usually earns $450 gross per week for 25 hours and his employer receives the full-time subsidy rate of $585.80 gross per week for him. Because he usually earns under this amount, Tane continues to be paid his usually wages of $450 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions). When Tane goes back to work, his employer only needs him for 15 hours to start with. The employer must continue paying Tane his usual wages of $450 gross per week as the employer has been paid for the full-time subsidy rate. Tane's employer can use the remainder of the support to pay wages of other affected employees. When there are no other affected employees, the employer must repay the remainder back to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Assessing 40% revenue loss due to COVID-19 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Assessing 40% revenue loss due to COVID-19
When deciding if the employer has had a decline in revenue due to COVID-19, the Ministry of Social Development considers:
- the type of work the business does, eg retail, manufacturing, sales, construction, driving etc and
- whether (or to the extent) the business was able to operate in the higher COVID-19 Alert Levels (eg was it an essential business or not, what changes did the business need to make due to the public health restrictions) and
- whether the estimated loss of revenue makes sense (based on the business circumstances)?
Note that in most cases verification of the revenue decline is not required. However, the Ministry of Social Development may ask for verification in some cases.
## Employer has been open during COVID-19 public health restrictions
Some businesses have been able to operate during the higher COVID- 19 Alert Levels, for example, firms defined as essential businesses or firms operating outside of a regional lockdown that form part of a wider supply chain, or providing click and collect and takeaway options.
For businesses that have been able to operate, when deciding if they have had a decline in revenue, the Ministry of Social Development considers the reasons given for the decline in revenue and whether these are reasonable given the type of work the business does and where the business is located.
Being open for business does not protect a business from having a 40% reduction in revenue, but further consideration needs to be given to their circumstances.
Example, a business has remained open or open in some online capacity, and may not be able to sell the same level of product, due to reduced demand from other businesses (eg frozen food which they used to provide to fast food or other restaurants).
For these employers, the Ministry of Social Development will consider their individual situations and make decisions based on the facts of their application when considering if the business has had a decline 40% in revenue due to COVID-19.

chunks.title: Sole traders — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Sole traders
Sole traders are not required to be registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, but must have:
- a personal Inland Revenue number for paying income tax and/or GST and
- government licences and permits for their business needs and
- qualifications or registrations for their trade or profession
Sole traders must still meet the requirements to be physically located and legally working in New Zealand.
The Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed before paying the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension.

chunks.title: Businesses operating for less than a year (or a high growth firm) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Businesses operating for less than a year (or a high growth firm)
When a business has been operating for less than a year or is a high growth firm (eg businesses that have had a significant increase in revenue), they must compare their revenue against a more recent comparison time period that gives the best estimation of the revenue decline related to COVID-19.
Example 40% loss of revenue attributable to COVID-19 comparing 11 May 2020 – 9 June 2020 to 1 – 30 January 2020.

chunks.title: Businesses who had not started operating before the COVID-19 public health restrictions — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Businesses who had not started operating before the COVID-19 public health restrictions
Some self-employed people or employers may have had their plans to start their business affected by the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, the employer must have had a 40% decline in revenue over a 30-day consecutive period in the 40 days before the application date (but beginning no earlier than 10 May 2020). To determine this decline, the business needs to compare their revenue against the nearest comparable 30-day period last year (or using a more recent comparison time period if the business has been operating for less than a year or is a high growth firm).
This means the business must have been operating for at least 60 days to determine the decline in revenue.
## Example
A chiropractor was moving from employment to start their own business but did not begin trading before the COVID-19 public health restrictions came into effect. They are unable to open until the public health restrictions ease.
When the chiropractor is able to start and has been trading for 60 days, they will be able to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, provided they meet the other qualification criteria.

chunks.title: Businesses who get insurance payments to cover revenue loss — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Businesses who get insurance payments to cover revenue loss
Some businesses have received insurance payments, such as business interruption insurance, to cover their loss of revenue during the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
If the insurance payment does not cover their losses and the business has still experienced a 40% decline in revenue over a 30-day consecutive period within the 40 days before their application date, then the business will be eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension. If the employer has already received the subsidy and still has a decline in revenue, then they can continue using the payment to pay their employees.
If the insurance payment means that the business has not had a 40% decline in revenue in a 30-day consecutive period within the 40 days before their application, then the business will not qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension.
If the employer has already got the subsidy, then they will have got funds they are not eligible for and must repay the subsidy in full to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Decline in revenue for separate legal entities and business units — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Decline in revenue for separate legal entities and business units
The decline in revenue must be experienced across all units of the business as a 40% decline in total revenue.
Business units within a single corporate entity are not eligible to apply individually. This includes Councils and other business structures who may have different programmes, branches, or divisions that are differently affected by COVID-19, but who employ all their workers under one corporate entity.
Consolidated tax groups (made up of legally separate companies) cannot apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension. The separate companies can apply individually for the subsidy, if they meet the qualifications.
## Example 1
A local Council in Christchurch cannot open their public pools because of the COVID-19 public health restrictions and this part of the business has had a 100% decline in revenue in the last 14-days.
However, the Council does not qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension because the rest of the business can operate normally, and the Council has not experienced a 40% decline in revenue overall.
## Example 2
A clothing store in Wellington cannot open during the regional public health restrictions.
The store can trade online, but their revenue is down more than 40% compared to the same time last year.
However, the store is part of a larger company with locations around the country, and the business as a whole has not been significantly impacted by regional restrictions.
The store does not qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension because the rest of the business has not experienced a 40% decline in revenue overall.
## Example 3
A clothing store in Wellington cannot open during the regional public health restrictions.
The store can trade online, but their revenue is down more than 40% compared to the same time last year. However, the store is part of a larger company with locations around the country, and the business as a whole has not been significantly impacted by regional restrictions.
The store does not qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension because the rest of the business has not experienced a 40% decline in revenue overall.

chunks.title: Decline in revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Decline in revenue
To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension the employer or self-employed person must have had a 40% decline in revenue.
This means they have had a 40% decline in:
- actual revenue and
- the decline is due to the impacts of COVID-19
The business must have this decline over a 30-day consecutive period in the 40 days before the date of application (but beginning no earlier than 10 May 2020).
This 30-day period must be compared with the nearest comparable 30-day period last year (or using a more recent comparison time period if the business has been operating for less than a year, or is a high growth firm).
If the business or self-employed person predicted a 40% decline in revenue but does not experience this, then the business or self-employed person must repay the subsidy.

chunks.title: Definition of revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Definition of revenue
Revenue means the total amount of money a business has earned from its normal business activities, before expenses are deducted.
Some pre-revenue research and development “start-up” businesses can include a fall in projected capital income when determining a 40% decrease in revenue.

chunks.title: Determining a decline in revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Determining a decline in revenue
To determine a decline in revenue, the employer or self-employed person must compare the revenue of a 30-day consecutive period against the nearest comparable period last year. This 30-day period needs to be in the 40 days before the date of application (but beginning no earlier than 10 May 2020).
Example 11 May 2020 - 9 June 2020 compared with 11 May 2019 - 9 June 2019.
The decline in revenue must be calculated from 10 May 2020 onwards. This is to make sure businesses who are still struggling with the impacts of COVID-19 during Alert Levels 1 and 2 can get the support they need.
For businesses calculating a loss of revenue in May 2020, they will need to calculate the decline in revenue for a 30-day period from 10 May 2020 onwards. The comparison period must be to a similar 30-day period last year.
The revenue of the 30-day period must be at least 40% less than it was in the 30-day period it was compared against.
The decline in revenue must be experienced across all parts of the business as a 40% decline in total revenue. This includes Councils and other business structures who may have different programmes or branches that are differently affected by COVID-19, but who employ all their workers under one business.
For self-employed individuals with variable monthly income, the decline in revenue should be determined against the previous year's monthly average (ie 40% loss of income due to the impacts of COVID-19 comparing 11 May 2020 - 9 June 2020 to the average monthly income in the period May 2019 to May 2020).

chunks.title: Determining if someone is self-employed — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Determining if someone is self-employed
A person is likely to be self-employed when they carry out business activities on their own, including contracting, working as a sole trader or owning a small business.
A self-employed person is likely to:
- support the business with their own money (eg providing all the working equipment needed for their job)
- decide or control how they work (eg when, where and what hours they work)
- decide how much they get paid and how
- pay their own income tax (unless they are a young person earning under the tax threshold)
- be responsible for investment decisions and any losses
- be able to sell the business if they wanted to
The above list is not exhaustive. Self-employed people are eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, if they meet the qualifications.

chunks.title: Eligible employers — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Eligible employers
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension is available for:
- businesses using all employment types including full-time, part-time, casual, fixed-term, sole trading and self-employment, including those employers with employees getting the minimum wage exemption
- across all sectors and industries in New Zealand
- includes registered charities, incorporated societies, non-government organisations and post-settlement governance entities (eg Māori authorities)
State Sector organisations are generally not eligible to get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension.
Exceptions for State Sector employers are considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, through the relevant monitoring agency.

chunks.title: Employee temporarily overseas and cannot return due to COVID-19 restrictions — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Employee temporarily overseas and cannot return due to COVID-19 restrictions
Employees who are currently overseas are eligible to be named as an employee in the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension application if:
- they were legally working in New Zealand before leaving and
- their absence was intended to be temporary (eg a holiday or a work business trip) and
- they maintain their employment status (that is, they are still employed by the employer) and intended to return to work on a specific date but cannot start on that date because of the COVID-19 travel restrictions

chunks.title: Employee voluntarily leaves — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Employee voluntarily leaves
Employers must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.
If an employee voluntarily leaves their employment for another job opportunity, the employer must advise the Ministry of Social Development, and the subsidy can no longer be claimed for that person. The employer does not have to repay the subsidy already paid but they must use the balance towards topping up the wages of other affected employees.
If the employer has no other employees for whom to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other employees are already being paid their usual wages, the employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy as it was not able to be used for wages.

chunks.title: Employer dismisses employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Employer dismisses employee
Employers must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.
If an employer decides to dismiss an employee for reasons other than redundancy, for example, because of serious or repeated misconduct, for performance issues, or if the employee abandons their employment, the subsidy can no longer be claimed for that person.
The employer does not have to repay the subsidy already paid but they must use the balance towards topping up the wages of any other remaining affected employees.
If the employer has no other employees for whom to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other employees are already being paid their usual wages, the employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy as it was not able to be used for wages.
The employer must follow existing employment law for dismissing an employee.
## Example
Fahima employees 5 staff at her cafe but the COVID-19 public health restrictions have significantly impacted her business and she applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension to continue paying her staff.
One of Fahima's employees is caught taking money from the till and this employee is already on notice for similar behaviour in the past. After going through a disciplinary process, Fahima decides to dismiss the employee based on their repeated misconduct.
As Fahima has got the subsidy for this employee, Fahima uses the remaining funds to contribute to the wage costs of her other staff. Fahima manages to hire a replacement employee quickly and reapplies for the subsidy for the new employee.
At the end of the subsidy period Fahima has not used all the funds she received, so repays the remaining amount to the Ministry of Social Development

chunks.title: Employer makes employee redundant — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Employer makes employee redundant
Employers must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid, for the duration of the subsidy period for that person.
If an employer makes the employee redundant, the employer will not have met their obligations to retain affected staff and must repay the remaining subsidy.
The employer cannot keep the remainder of the subsidy to support other employees. Other enforcement action may be taken against these employers
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension can be used to pay the notice period but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract.
The employee is not required to pay the subsidy back to the employer.
Employers who have given their employees notice of redundancy before they apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension are not eligible to get the subsidy for those employees unless the redundancy notice is withdrawn.

chunks.title: Employer not entitled but has been paid — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: If an employer applied for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme, and then they have a change in circumstance within the 2-week period, they may not be entitled to keep the subsidy payment they got for an employee. Change of circumstances Employer action Employee voluntarily resigns. The employer should use the balance of any of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme to pay other affected staff. When no other employees need it, the employer should contact the Ministry of Social Development and must refund the remaining subsidy for this employee as it was not able to be used for wages. Employee has been made redundant. The employer must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme remaining for the employee. The subsidy can be used to pay the notice period. But cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract, and cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees. Employee has been dismissed. The employer should use the balance of any of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme to pay other affected staff. When no other employees need it, the employer should contact the Ministry of Social Development and must refund the remaining subsidy for this employee as it was not able to be used for wages. Business has closed. The employer must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme remaining for their employee(s). The subsidy can be used to pay the notice period. But cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract and cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees. Employee is on fixed-term contract that ends during the period that the employer is getting the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for them. The employer must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme remaining for the employee at the end of the fixed-term contract.
