The subsidy cannot be used to meet any entitlements owed under contract and cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees. The employer applied for the wrong type of COVID-19 scheme for their employee (eg applied for the Leave Support Scheme in error). The employer must repay any amount received for the incorrect application and re-apply for the correct scheme that they are entitled to. The employer applied for the wrong type of COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme rate for their employee, eg applies for full-time, when the person was part-time.

chunks.title: Employer not entitled but has been paid — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: The employer must repay the difference between the full-time rate received and the part-time rate they are entitled to. The employer applied for COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme based on a predicted 40% decline in revenue, but the decline did not occur. The employer is not entitled to the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme and must repay it in full. Employer is a State Sector organisation who did not have an exception approved by the Minister of Finance to apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme but applied and received the funds. The employer is not entitled to the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme and must repay it in full. Any State Sector employers who disagree with the decision should consult with their monitoring agency. Employer gets payment they are not entitled to due to an office error (eg their application might have been paid twice or accidentally approved instead of declined). The employer is not entitled to the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme and must repay it in full. Employer gets insurance payment that covers their loss in revenue, so they have no longer experienced a 40% decline in revenue between 2 August 2020 to 10 September 2020. The employer is not entitled to the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme and must repay it in full. If an employer applies for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme while the employee is also getting the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme or the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, their application will be declined.

chunks.title: Example — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: A courier company applies for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme as their business has been slower than normal during the COVID-19 public health restrictions. Their accounts for the last 14 days have not yet been finalised, but they predict they will have experienced a 40% decline in revenue, when compared with the same 14 day period last year. They apply for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy for their employees. When they do finalise their accounts, the company has only experienced a 35% decline in revenue. The company received funds they were not entitled to, so they contact the Ministry of Social Development to repay the subsidy in full.

chunks.title: Employer obligations — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension is being administered under a high trust model, and employers will not be asked for evidence to support some criteria before the subsidy is approved. However, some details will be verified with Inland Revenue before payment. The Ministry of Social Development may also check applications and verify information at a later date. When false or misleading information has been provided by the employer to the Ministry of Social Development, employers can be investigated which may result in civil recovery of any amount paid and/or potentially criminal prosecution. To get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, the employer must agree: - that they meet the following subsidy eligibility criteria: the business has had a minimum 40% revenue drop over a 30-day consecutive period in the 40 days immediately before their application, attributable to the COVID-19 outbreakthe employer is registered and operating in New Zealandthey have taken active steps to mitigate the financial impact of COVID-19 on their business activities, including proactively engaging with their bank and calling on their internal cash reserves (where appropriate)the employees are legally employed by their business and have not been given notice of redundancy at the date they applythey are not currently getting a COVID-19 Wage Subsidy, or Leave Support that was available before 10 June 2020 for the named employees - the business has had a minimum 40% revenue drop over a 30-day consecutive period in the 40 days immediately before their application, attributable to the COVID-19 outbreak - the employer is registered and operating in New Zealand - they have taken active steps to mitigate the financial impact of COVID-19 on their business activities, including proactively engaging with their bank and calling on their internal cash reserves (where appropriate) - the employees are legally employed by their business and have not been given notice of redundancy at the date they apply - they are not currently getting a COVID-19 Wage Subsidy, or Leave Support that was available before 10 June 2020 for the named employees

chunks.title: Employers mitigating the impact of COVID-19 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Employers mitigating the impact of COVID-19
Before applying for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, a business must have taken measures to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 on their business.
These might include (but are not limited to):
- activating their business continuity plan
- where appropriate, look to their own cash reserves to assist paying staff, eg where they have enough funds, and it won’t cause the business to fail if they use it
- proactively engaging with their bank
- seeking advice from the Chamber of Commerce, a relevant industry association, or the Regional Business Partner programme

chunks.title: Employers must follow employment law when paying wages — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Employers must follow employment law when paying wages
Employers must follow the correct employment process. If employers have questions about their obligations under employment law, they should contact Employment New Zealand for advice and assistance.
Under employment law, employees must be paid for each and every hour that they work at their agreed wage rate. The employer may agree with the employee to reduce hours or to reduce their hourly rate during this period (but not lower than the minimum wage) and this subsidy will help employers to pay this wage. Any change to their wage rate requires good faith consultation and written agreement in line with existing employment law.
Employers must still adhere to relevant employment laws when reducing an employee's wages to 80% of their income, or to the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension rate. This relationship is between the employer and the employee.
An employer is required to pay their employee ordinary wages in line with their employment agreement, and the subsidy can be used to help with that. The effect of the Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension is that if an employee's hours have had to change, the employer must try to pay at least 80% of their wages, and the minimum amount the employee will get if their hours drop further is the subsidy rate (subject to usual deductions eg PAYE, Kiwisaver, Student Loan etc). But if they usually earned less than the subsidy amount claimed (pre COVID-19 impact), the employer would continue to pay them their usual wages.
No employer can make a blanket rule that employees take annual leave during the COVID-19 public health restrictions, but the employer and employee can agree for the employee to take annual leave. In this situation the employee should be paid their normal wage rate for their normal hours of work, and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension will help employers pay for the annual leave taken.
When the employer and employee are unable to agree on where the employee will take annual holidays, the employer could direct the employee to take annual holidays, but they must give the employee at least 14 days notice.

chunks.title: Manufacturer of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Manufacturer of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
It may be considered unreasonable to expect that a business who makes PPE would have had a 40% decline in revenue, as they are able to operate at a time of high demand.
However, if that business provided a reason for the decline in revenue that was reasonable when considering their situation, then the Ministry of Social Development would accept there had been a decline.
Example the PPE business was fully staffed by sole parents who could no longer work because they had to stay at home as schools were closed, or they were unable to source enough raw materials because of border closures to make the product.
## Food outlet
Generally, it would be unreasonable to expect that an essential business of this type would have had a 40% revenue drop as they are able to operate at a time of high demand.
However, if that business provided a reason for the decline in revenue that was reasonable when considering their situation, then the Ministry of Social Development would accept there had been a decline.
Example a grocery store in the middle of the Central Business District (CBD), whose main trade was CBD workers and many people are still working from home or choosing not to eat out, or a supermarket in a town reliant on tourists who have now left, and the local population is small. In both these cases, they remain open and can operate but it would be reasonable that there could have been a 40% decline in their revenue.
## Courier company
A courier company who is providing contactless delivery of essential goods applies for the subsidy. Generally, it would be unreasonable to expect that an essential business of this type would have had a 40% revenue drop as they are able to operate in a time of high demand.
However, if that business provided a reason for the decline in revenue that was reasonable when considering their situation, then the Ministry of Social Development would accept there had been a decline.
Example a courier company whose previous business relied on TradeMe purchases and/or non-essential goods and hasn't picked up any work doing essential deliveries.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Example 1
Ailee works 10 hours per week at minimum wage ($189 gross per week) while she is a student. Her employer has experienced a decline in revenue due to the impact of COVID-19 so the employer applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension to continue paying her.
Because her usual earnings are less than the subsidy rate of $350 gross per week, the employer must use the subsidy to continue paying her usual wage of $189 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions).
The employer must use the difference to contribute to the wages of other affected staff and when there are no other employees, must refund the remainder back to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example 2
Jivan works 40 hours at a workshop as a building labourer. He usually gets $756 gross per week. He cannot do any work from home during the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
The employer has a highly skilled and reliable workforce and is using the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension to continue to pay Jivan 80% of his usual wages during this period. If the employer was not able to do this, they would be required to pay Jivan the fulltime subsidy rate ($585.80 gross per week).
## Example 3
Stuart is a digger driver. His employer has no revenue coming into the business during the COVID-19 public health restrictions. The employer has many contracts to finish once they can get back to work, so needs to keep their employees over the period of the public health restrictions.
The employer is unable to pay Stuart 80% of his full-time wage over this period, and so his employer pays Stuart the full amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension of $585.80 (less any usual wage deductions) over the lockdown period.

chunks.title: Fixed-term contract ends within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Fixed-term contract ends within subsidy period
The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme is open to existing and newly hired employees and this includes employees on fixed-term contracts. To get the subsidy, employers must agree to retain the employees named in their application for the duration of the subsidy period.
Employers can include employees on fixed-term contracts in their COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme application, even if the employee's contract is scheduled to end during the period that their employer would be getting the subsidy for them (ie in the 2 weeks from the date of application).
However, if an employee's fixed-term contract ends during the subsidy period, the employer will not have met their obligation to keep their staff employed. In these circumstances, the employer can use the subsidy to pay out any notice period for that employee, but the subsidy cannot be used to pay any other entitlements. It also cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees. The employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy.
The employer and employee may agree to extend the contract to the end of the subsidy period in order to meet their obligation to retain affected staff for the period they get the subsidy.

chunks.title: Health and disability funded workforce — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Health and disability funded workforce
Health and disability funded workforces (such as businesses that provide community health care) not employed by the State Sector are able to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension if they meet the qualifications.
Health and disability funded workforces not employed by the State Sector includes organisations that are contracted to, or funded in whole or part, by organisations in the State Sector (such as the Ministry of Health and District Health Boards).
Examples include:
- in-home care workers
- workers in primary health organisations
- nurses and other staff in rest-homes or other residential care facilities (eg cooks, cleaners, support staff)

chunks.title: Other COVID-19 wage subsidy schemes — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: An employer cannot get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension or any other COVID-19 wage subsidy for the same employee for the same period.

chunks.title: Flexi-wage and Mana in Mahi — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: If an employer is currently getting the Flexi-Wage or Mana in Mahi subsidy for their employee(s), they can also apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, if they meet the qualifications. All wage subsidies that the employer is getting must be paid to their employees. For more information see:

chunks.title: Apprenticeship Boost Initiative — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: Apprenticeship Boost helps employers with the costs of keeping their current apprentices or hiring new ones for the first 24 months of their programme of study. If an employer is currently getting Apprenticeship Boost for their employee(s), they cannot apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for those employees. For more information see:

chunks.title: Main benefit and other support — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: If an employer or a self-employed individual is currently getting a main benefit or other extra help from the Ministry of Social Development, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for themselves or their employees. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, any individual getting the subsidy as well as other support from the Ministry must declare the subsidy as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Self-employed person or employee getting Work and Income assistance Interaction with the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension COVID-19 Income Relief Payment Some COVID-19 Income Relief Payment clients may have got the Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension before they lost their job or self-employment. These individuals can apply for the COVID-19 Income Relief Payment once their Wage Subsidy payments run out, provided they meet the qualification criteria. Emergency Benefit Some Emergency Benefit clients may be employed or self-employed. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Emergency Benefit clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Emergency Maintenance Assistance Some Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients may be employed or self-employed. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Jobseeker Support Some Jobseeker Support clients may be working part-time (less than 30 hours per week) or getting income that does not reduce the rate of Jobseeker Support to zero. Sole parents and grand-parented Jobseeker Support clients can work full-time for a temporary period provided their income when assessed over a 52-week period doesn't fully reduce the benefit. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Jobseeker Support clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Note the part-time and full-time subsidy rate differs from the definition above. New Zealand Superannuation - Non-qualified partner If a New Zealand Superannuation client includes their partner in their payments, then their New Zealand Superannuation is income-tested. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, New Zealand Superannuation non-qualified partner clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and both of their New Zealand Superannuation payments may be abated accordingly. Sole Parent Support

chunks.title: Main benefit and other support — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: Some Sole Parent Support clients will have work obligations and may be employed or self-employed. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Sole Parent Support clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. Supported Living Payment Some Supported Living Payment clients will be working up to 15 hours per week but may not be able to do this on a regular basis. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Support Living Payment clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly.

chunks.title: Financial support from other agencies — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: There is a range of financial support available from other agencies for employers and individuals who have been negatively impacted by the COVID-19 financial crisis. These schemes, such as the COVID-19 Small Business Cash Flow Loan Scheme, are separate to Work and Income support, and have their own qualification criteria. This means that, provided they meet the necessary qualifications, businesses can apply and get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension as well as these other schemes. Note there are some schemes, such as Ministry of Education's emergency payment for relief teachers, where businesses will not be eligible to get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for the same work. Applicants will need to ensure they meet the qualification criteria for any schemes they apply for.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Extension was introduced from 10 June 2020 to 1 September 2020 to support employers still struggling with the impacts of the COVID-19 public health restrictions, to stay connected to their employees.
The scheme was an extension of previous wage subsidies implemented in response to COVID-19.
Employers who got COVID-19 Wage Subsidy or Leave Support Scheme payments could apply for the same employees if they met the qualifications, but only once the period for the previous payment had ended.
Employers who did not apply for the previous COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) could apply.
## Applications
Employers and self-employed people must apply online for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension through Work and Income
Applications could be made at any point that the scheme was available. Payments were made as a lump sum to the employer and covered 8 weeks from the date of application.
Applications closed for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension at 11.59pm on 1 September 2020.

chunks.title: Nearest comparable period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Nearest comparable period
To determine a decline in revenue, the business or self-employed person must compare the revenue of a 30-day consecutive period against the nearest comparable period last year.
Generally, businesses would compare the same 30-day period to the year before, for example, 1 June 2020 - 30 June 2020 compared to 1 June 2019 - 30 June 2019.
However, in some cases this might not give the best indication of what the business would have been expecting to earn now. This may be because the business has been operating:
- for less than a year
- is a high growth firm or
- something happened in the business to cause their revenue to decrease at this time last year
In these situations, the Ministry of Social Development will consider another 30-day comparison period that will reflect what the business would have expected to earn now. This comparison period could be any 30-day period from January 2019 to 40 days before the date of their application.
For example, 1 June 2020 - 30 June 2020 compared to 1 September 2019 - 30 September 2019.
The decline in revenue needs to be for a 30-day period in the 40 days before the application date (but beginning no earlier than 10 May 2020).

chunks.title: Newly hired employees — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Newly hired employees
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension is open to any newly hired employees, and previous employees who have been re-hired before the employer applies for the subsidy.
## Example 1
Sam was employed full-time as a hairdresser, but their start date was delayed due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
Sam's employer applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for their employees and includes Sam in the application.
The employer pays Sam $585.80 (less any usual wage deductions) to pay Sam until they can start their new role.
## Example 2
Whiti owns a pet store and is getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension as her business has experienced a decline in revenue due to COVID-19. One of her employees resigns and she needs to hire a replacement staff member.
Whiti uses the remaining subsidy from the leaving employee to continue paying her other staff and submits another application for the new employee when they start their role.
## Example 3
Ravi owns a clothing store and has reopened his business after being closed during the COVID-19 public health restrictions. He needs to hire a new employee, but his business is still experiencing a significant decline in revenue due to COVID-19.
Ravi is already getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for his existing employees, so submits another application for the new employee when they start their role.

chunks.title: Normal wages or salary — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Normal wages or salary
For employees, their normal wages or salary are specified in their employment agreement at the date the employer applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension.
Self-employed people can determine their normal wages or drawings by calculating the regular amount that is left over after they meet their business costs. This is the amount that they regularly pay themselves as drawings from the business.
If the individual is self-employed and the income that they regularly draw from their business is less than the amount they got from the subsidy, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension can be used to support the costs of wages, but cannot be used towards other business costs.

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension is paid at a flat rate based on each named employee's normal (or expected) hours of paid employment before COVID-19 impacted the business: - $585.80 (gross) for 20 hours or more per week, or 40 hours or more per fortnight or - $350.00 (gross) for less than 20 hours per week or less than 40 hours per fortnight The subsidy is paid for an 8-week period as a lump sum payment at the appropriate weekly subsidy rate for: - working 20 hours or more or - working under 20 hours An employer can access the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension more than once in the 8-week period but cannot access it for the same employees in that period. The subsidy covers 8 weeks from the date of application.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: The employer accessed the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for 10 employees as soon as the scheme became available on 10 June 2020. Now the employer needs the subsidy for 20 more employees. The employer can apply for the 20 newly named employees, but not the 10 original employees for whom they have already received the subsidy.

chunks.title: Calculating variable hours — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: For a self-employed person, or an employer who has casual employees who work variable hours, an average over a relevant period can be used to work out which subsidy rate to apply. A relevant period for a business or self-employed person who has been working for a year, would be an average over this period. As a guide for a new business or a person who has been self-employed for less than one year, an average over 8 weeks can be used, unless there is another time period that would be more appropriate. For example, if using the period that the individual has been employed for would give a better representation of the employee's usual hours, then the employer can use this time period instead. It is up to employers to agree with their employees what their hours would usually be during this period, to determine the appropriate COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension rate to apply for.

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: Charlotte is a relief teacher for an Early Childhood Education Centre and is called in to provide support as required, but the Centre is closed due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions. The Centre employs Charlotte as a casual staff member and calculates that she has worked an average of 17 hours per week over the last 4 months she has been employed there. The employer applies for a part-time COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension rate to continue paying Charlotte's wages (at a rate of 17 hours per week for the 8-week period). As this is less than the $350 gross per week provided through the subsidy, the employer uses the remaining funds to support the wages of other affected staff.

chunks.title: Maximum payment for an employer — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: There is no cap on the total amount of COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension an employer could get, was based on the number of employees they had, and whether they were working 20 hours or more, or under 20 hours.

chunks.title: People on fixed-term contracts — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## People on fixed-term contracts
Employers can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for their employees who are on fixed-term contracts, as long as they keep them employed for the subsidy period.
If an employee's fixed-term contract ends during the subsidy period, then the employer will not have met their obligation to retain affected staff. The employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and repay the remaining subsidy.

chunks.title: People receiving income from a property business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## People receiving income from a property business
Some people are paid a wage, salary or draw an income from a property business, such as private rentals, Airbnb's and homestay operations.
These businesses are eligible to get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension provided they meet the qualification criteria, including being registered and operating in New Zealand.
For sole traders who are not registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, the Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed before paying the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension.
Note the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings and can only be used to support the cost of wages. People who apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for a property business must be able to declare that they draw a wage, salary or income for this work.
## Example
Anthony owns several holiday homes, which he rents out to supplement his income. He works an average of 10 hours per week on the properties, managing the bookings and cleaning the property in between guests.
Usually this would be a very busy time of year for his business, but most of his bookings have been cancelled due to the impacts of COVID-19 public health restrictions. Anthony's income has dropped by more than 40% during this period so applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension.
The Ministry is able to verify his self-employment status with Inland Revenue and his application is approved.

chunks.title: Employee already getting paid parental leave — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Employee already getting paid parental leave
If an employee was already getting paid parental leave when the employer applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, the employer is not able to include this employee in their application.
If they do include the employee in error and the application is approved, the employer got funds they are not eligible for and must repay the full amount to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Employee goes on paid parental leave during subsidy period
If an employee starts getting paid parental leave after the employer has made an application and/or received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, then the employee is not eligible to get both the subsidy and paid parental leave.
The employer must stop using the subsidy for the employee as soon as they go on parental leave.
The remaining funds can be used towards topping up the wages of other affected staff.
If the employer has no other employees to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other employees are already being paid their usual wages, the employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development, and must repay the remaining amount as it was not able to be used for wages.
## Employee due to return from paid parental leave during subsidy period
If the employee was getting paid parental leave at the time of the employer's application for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for their other employees, but has since returned to work, then the employer can make a new application for this employee.
The employer should use the new hours the employee will be working on their return to work to calculate the rate of subsidy to apply for.

chunks.title: Employee already getting ACC — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Employee already getting ACC
If the employee was already getting ACC compensation when the employer applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, the employer is not able to include this employee in their application.
If they do include the employee in error and the application is approved, the employer will have got funds they are not eligible for and must repay this amount to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Employee goes on ACC during subsidy period
If the employee is injured and starts getting ACC compensation after the employer made an application and/or got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, the employee is eligible to get both the subsidy and ACC compensation.
However, the employee must declare the subsidy to ACC as income and their weekly compensation may be abated accordingly.
## Employee due to finish getting ACC during subsidy period
If the employee was getting ACC compensation at the time of the employer's application for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for their other employees, but has since finished getting the ACC payments, the employer can submit a new application for this employee.

chunks.title: People working multiple jobs — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## People working multiple jobs
Employers may have employees who work for them, and another employer. They may work more than 20 hours for one employer, and less than 20 hours for the other.
If both employers meet the criteria, they can each apply for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for the same employee.

chunks.title: Pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses
A small number of pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses may be eligible to treat a 40% fall in projected capital income as a result of COVID-19 as a fall in revenue for the eligibility of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension.
These employers must:
- be research and development intensive 'start-up' businesses
- be 'seed' or 'venture' backed
- be Callaghan Innovation affiliated as of 17 March 2020 and
- have no other revenue other than government support, and seed or venture capital.
These employers can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension if they meet the other qualifications.

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: Businesses who have not applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) or COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme can also apply, provided they meet the qualifications. If an employer got a previous COVID-19 wage subsidy or leave payment for their employees, they must wait until the subsidy period for these employees has ended, before they apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension. To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, businesses must meet the following eligibility criteria: - the business must have experienced a minimum 40% decline in revenue - the decline in revenue must be over a 30-day consecutive period in the 40 days immediately before the application date (but beginning no earlier than 10 May 2020) - the 30-day period must be when compared with the nearest comparable 30-day period last year (or using a more recent comparison time period if the business has been operating for less than a year or is a high growth firm) - the decline in revenue must be related to COVID-19 - the business must be registered and operating in New Zealand - their employees must be legally working in New Zealand - before making an application, the employer must have taken active steps to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 - are not currently getting a subsidy for that employee from any previous or current Wage Subsidy or Leave Support Scheme Businesses who have not applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) or COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme can also apply, provided they meet the qualifications. If an employer got a previous COVID-19 wage subsidy or leave payment for their employees, they must wait until the subsidy period for these employees has ended, before they apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension.

chunks.title: Must retain employees and pay at least 80% wages or salary — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: Employers who get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension must keep the employees (for whom they received the wage subsidy) in their jobs for the period of the subsidy (unless the employee voluntarily ends the employment relationship). Employers must endeavour to pay at least 80% of each named employee's wages or salary for the period of the subsidy, at the rate they would have been paid before the business was impacted by the COVID-19 public health restrictions. When the employee was earning less than the subsidy rate, the employer must keep paying their usual wages, even if they are working less hours due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions. Any difference should be used for topping up the wages of other affected staff. When there are no other employees, or the other employees are already being paid their usual wages, the employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy as it was not able to be used for wages. If an applicant is self-employed and the income they regularly draw from their business is less than the subsidy amount they received, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development. Under employment law, employees must be paid for each and every hour that they work at their agreed wage rate. Employers must still adhere to relevant employment laws when reducing an employee's wages or changing the hours they work.

chunks.title: Business keeps operating under receivership or liquidation — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Business keeps operating under receivership or liquidation
If the business can continue operating under receivership or for the duration of the liquidation process, then the employer (or the receiver/liquidator) can continue to use the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme to support the cost of wages for employees named in their application.
If the business recovers, or the receiver/liquidator sells the business during the subsidy period and the new owners take on the employees named in the application, then the business can continue to use the subsidy for these employees.
An employer who is currently operating under receivership or liquidation can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, provided they meet the qualifications and meet their obligations to retain staff for the subsidy period.
Example 1
An employer goes into receivership 2 weeks after getting the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for their employees. The receiver takes over the business and manages to sell the business to new owners. The new owners keep all the previous staff and use the remaining subsidy to continue paying these employees for the duration of the subsidy period.
## Business closes under receivership or liquidation
If the business is liquidated (and permanently closed), or the receiver / liquidator sells the business during the subsidy period, and the new owners do not take on the employees named in the subsidy application, then the business will not have met their obligation to keep employing affected staff and they must repay the remaining subsidy.
Where employees are made redundant, the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme can be used to pay the notice period but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract, and cannot be used to support other remaining affected employees.
Example 2
A restaurant owner puts their business into liquidation 3 days after getting the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy Scheme for their employees. The liquidator gives the staff 1 weeks' notice that the business will be closing permanently and uses the subsidy to pay out the notice period for the employees named in the application.
At the end of the notice period, the liquidator repays the remaining 1 week of subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Retain affected staff — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Retain affected staff
Employers must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, to retain the employees for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Repaying unused funds after the subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Repaying unused funds after the subsidy period
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension is paid in one lump sum to the employer to support the cost of wages for 8 weeks.
If the employer does not require the full weekly rate for their employees, because an employee's usual wages are less than the subsidy rate, then any difference should be used for the wages of other affected staff.
If there are any unused funds at the end of the 8-week period, the employer must repay the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development. The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension cannot be used beyond the 8-week period.
If the individual is self-employed and the income that they regularly draw from their business is less than the amount they got from the subsidy, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example
Jason got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for his 10 part-time employees. All the employees were earning under the part-time subsidy rate, so continued to receive their normal wages for the duration of the subsidy period.
At the end of the 8 weeks, Jason has not used all the subsidy payment and has some funds remaining. He contacts the Ministry of Social Development to return the unused subsidy, as the funds were not used up on wage costs during the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Reviewing decisions to decline the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Reviewing decisions to decline the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension
Decisions to decline the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension are not made under the Social Security Act 2018 and are not covered by the usual Review of Decision guidelines.
If an employer wants the decision to decline the subsidy reviewed, that decision should be reconsidered. This review should be based on whether an ‘informed’ decision was made and should consider the following:
- whether all relevant information was obtained and
- whether the appropriate options and implications were considered and
- whether the decision was made at the appropriate level of delegation
If a review of the decision to decline the payment upholds the original decision, the employer can ask the Ombudsman to undertake their own review.

chunks.title: Seasonal work ends within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Seasonal work ends within subsidy period
Some seasonal workers will have had their work affected by COVID-19 (ie season finished earlier than expected and/or not able to pick up new work due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions).
If their employer has got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension but can no longer offer them employment during the subsidy period, then the employer will not have met their obligation to retain affected staff and must repay the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.
If the seasonal workers are casual employees or on fixed-term contracts, then the employer can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension to continue paying them, as long as they keep them employed for the subsidy period.
## Example 1
Rowan usually picks grapes over the summer months, but his employer has closed the harvesting season early due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions.
Rowan's employer got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for his employees, but after 2 weeks he decides to end their contracts as he can no longer offer them employment to return to. The employer uses the subsidy to pay out their notice period and repays the remaining amount to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example 2
Tracey employs 30 casual workers on her kiwifruit orchard, however, the orchard is not able to open due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions and Tracey has no work for these employees.
Tracey calculates the average hours each of her casual employees would have worked at this time last year to determine the correct rate to apply for. Tracey applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension to continue paying her employees for the duration of the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Seasonal workers — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Seasonal workers
There are a variety of employment arrangements for seasonal workers (eg fixed-term contract or casual employment contract).
Employers can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for their employees who are seasonal workers, but they must keep them employed for the subsidy period.
If an employee's contract ends during the subsidy period, then the employer will not have met their obligation to retain affected staff.
The employer must tell the Ministry of Social Development, and repay the remaining subsidy.

chunks.title: Self-employed person is also an employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Self-employed person is also an employee
A person may be self-employed for some of their income, and also be employed by a business or other organisation.
If the self-employed person qualifies, they can get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for their own business.
Also, if their employer qualifies, they can get the subsidy to continue paying the employee.

chunks.title: Specific employment situations — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text:
## Specific employment situations
People’s work situations in New Zealand may vary and eligibility for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension can sometimes differ.

chunks.title: State Sector employers generally not eligible — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: State Sector employers are generally not eligible to get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension. In most situations alternative arrangements have been made to ensure these employers pay their employees in full. Exceptions for State Sector employers are considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, through the relevant monitoring agency. Monitoring agencies will engage with State Sector organisations in their portfolio to understand their financial position and support them in seeking an exception if appropriate. Example if Airways Corporation of New Zealand Limited believed they met the criteria for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, then they could engage with Treasury Commercial Operations Team to assess their situation, and if appropriate, Treasury will prepare advice for the Minister of Finance asking for an exception on their behalf. If an exception is granted, the monitoring agency will tell the Ministry of Social Development and will advise the State Sector employer to apply for the Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension directly. If an exception has already been granted for an earlier COVID-19 subsidy, the State Sector employer does not need to get another exception to apply for the Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension State Sector employers include: - Government agencies such as the Ministry of Health, District Health Boards, Inland Revenue, and the Ministry of Social Development - Crown entities such as Kāinga Ora and the Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) - Schools (including state schools, state-integrated schools and their board of trustee members or equivalent) - Tertiary education institutions such as universities, polytechnics, institutes of technology and Wānanga State Sector employers do not include: - Local Government such as Regional, City and District Councils, council organisations and council-controlled organisations as stated in the Local Government Act 2002. This includes trusts and other organisations that look after libraries, museums and other operations in partnership with local authorities (note these employers still need to have experienced a 40% decline in revenue and meet the other qualifications to be eligible for the subsidy) - Kindergartens (although kindergarten teachers are State Sector employees, their employers are not, so Ministry of Education is not directly responsible for their payroll) - (note these employers still need to have experienced a 40% decline in revenue and meet the other qualifications to be eligible for the Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension) - Early childhood centres - Private (or independent) schools, and their board of trustee members or equivalent, proprietors of state-integrated schools and other workers employed by the proprietor (note the proprietor is the owner or leaseholder of the state-integrated school property) - Non-Government organisations

chunks.title: State Sector employers generally not eligible — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: - Health and disability funded workforces not employed directly by the State Sector Note businesses contracted to provide services to State Sector employers (eg cleaning, security, managed isolation or quarantine facilities etc) are not State Sector employers, and can apply for the subsidy if they meet the other qualifications.

chunks.title: Transition between previous COVID-19 subsidies and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Leave Payment ended on 27 March 2020, when it was combined with the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy and became the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified). The COVID-19 Essential Workers Leave Support Scheme was available from 16 April 2020 and was expanded to the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme from 28 April 2020. Employers who got a previous COVID-19 subsidy are still covered by the obligations they agreed when applying for these subsidies, for the duration of the subsidy period. An employer can apply for the same employees under the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension if they meet the qualifications, but only once the period for the previous payment has ended.

chunks.title: Employer received COVID-19 Wage Subsidy before 10 June 2020 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: Before 10 June 2020, employers and self-employed people who had an actual or predicted loss of revenue that was related to COVID-19 of at least 30%, were eligible to apply for a COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified). The subsidy was intended to support businesses to retain staff and continue to pay them at least 80% of their normal income. Employers can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension when they meet the criteria and need further assistance but can only apply for employees named in previous applications once the subsidy period for the initial payment has ended. Employers who applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) on 17 March 2020 will reach the end of their subsidy period on 8 June 2020. The Wage Subsidy will still be available for new applications on 9 June, however, employers who have already received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) are not able to re-apply for the subsidy for the same employees on this date, as the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) can only be claimed once per employee. They can apply for the new COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension on 10 June 2020, if they meet the qualifications.

chunks.title: Employer received COVID-19 Wage Subsidy before 10 June 2020 and has funds remaining after the 12 week subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: Any unused COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) funds must be repaid to the Ministry of Social Development at the end of the 12-week period, as the Wage Subsidy cannot be used beyond the subsidy period. However, if employers require further assistance, they can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, provided they meet the qualifications.

chunks.title: Employer applied for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy before 10 June 2020, and has funds remaining after the 12 week subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: Any unused COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) funds must be repaid to the Ministry of Social Development at the end of the 12-week period, as the Wage Subsidy cannot be used beyond the subsidy period. However, if employers require further assistance, they can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, provided they meet the qualifications.

chunks.title: Employer applied for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy before 10 June 2020, but not yet granted assistance — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: Unless the employer retracts their application for this assistance, the employer will be granted the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) and the rules of that scheme apply.

chunks.title: Employer received COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme before 10 June 2020 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme was introduced on 28 April 2020 to provide financial assistance to employers during the COVID-19 public health restrictions to: - encourage employees to self-isolate (stay at home) when they need to and - support employees who are unable to work from home to have an income when they cannot work Employers eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension can choose to apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme where it is appropriate for their employee's situation, but they cannot get both the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for the same period, for the same employee. When an employer qualifies for both it is recommended that they apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for their employees.

chunks.title: Treatment of the subsidy for granting benefits — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: If an employer or a self-employed person is getting a main benefit or extra help from the Ministry of Social Development, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for themselves or their employees. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, any employee or self-employed person receiving the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension as well as other support from the Ministry must declare the subsidy as income and their benefit may be abated accordingly. The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension should be counted as income over an 8-week period from the date of application for both employees and self-employed people and should not be counted as a cash asset. Any additional income drawn from the business or any other source must also be included in their total income.

chunks.title: Determining a lump sum payment of the subsidy — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: An employee or self-employed person should be paid the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension in the same way their wage or salary is normally paid, eg weekly wages for 8 weeks. However, some employers receiving the subsidy may pass it on to their employees as a lump sum payment. If the employee applies for assistance from the Ministry of Social Development, it is important to determine whether it is a lump sum payment of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension (on top of their regular wages during the subsidy period), or whether it represents a payment for other forms of leave owed to the client. For example, an employer may pay out 4 weeks of the subsidy to a client to cover their redundancy notice period. This would not be considered a lump sum payment of the subsidy but would instead be pay in lieu of notice, which is a type of termination payment. If the employee is made redundant or the employer has surplus funds remaining at the end of the subsidy period, the employer is required to return any remaining amount of the subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development. However, some employers may pass on the remaining funds directly to the employee. If the employer pays out the remainder of the subsidy (eg once the employee's notice period has ended and they are no longer employed), this would be considered a lump sum payment of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension. If the payment is a lump sum payment of the subsidy, it may affect their eligibility for different types of assistance.

chunks.title: Benefit applications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: As the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension is paid to replace a loss of earnings it should be charged as income for the benefit or extra help, this includes when the subsidy is paid out to the client as a lump sum payment. When a client has received the subsidy as a lump sum payment, the Ministry of Social Development will consider the appropriate period that the payment is intended to represent and will charge it as income for that period. For example, the lump sum payment can be divided by the client's average earnings (using the last 4 weeks if appropriate) to determine how many weeks of income the payment is intended to represent. If the amount of the payment is less than the relevant income cut-out point, the client would qualify for assistance for the period the lump sum payment is charged for. If the amount is higher than the income cut out point, the client would not qualify until the period the payment represents has finished. Note generally, a lump sum payment of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension (and the previous COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (modified) Scheme) is not considered a termination payment, so does not need to be considered when calculating what date their employment ceased. The lump sum would only be considered a termination payment when it is paid in lieu of notice. Example 1 Nate's employer got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension on 10 June 2020, but 2 weeks later, decides to close the business and gives his employees notice that they will be made redundant. The business is closed on 10 July 2020, and Nate was paid for the redundancy notice period until that point. The employer decides to pay the balance of the subsidy of 4 weeks out to Nate as a lump sum. Nate decides to apply for Jobseeker Support and approaches the Ministry of Social Development for assistance on 10 July 2020. Nate's employment ceased date is 10 July and his commencement date is 11 July. The initial stand-down period has been waived due to COVID-19. As he has received a lump sum payment representing 4 weeks of income, Nate's first 4 weeks of assistance are abated accordingly. If the lump sum payment is higher than the income cut out point, Nate will not qualify for assistance until the period the payment represents has passed.

chunks.title: COVID-19 Income Relief Payment applications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme extension
chunks.text: A person is not eligible to get the COVID-19 Income Relief Payment if they are currently receiving the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension. If an employee got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension as a lump sum payment from their employer, they would not be eligible to apply for the COVID-19 Income Relief Payment until the appropriate period that the lump sum payment applies to has passed. Example 2 Pania's employer got the Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension for her on 15 June 2020, but soon gives her notice of redundancy as their business has been badly affected by COVID-19. Pania receives a lump sum payment from her employer in lieu of working out her 4 week notice period. She gets this payment on 22 June 2020. Pania meets the other qualification criteria for the COVID-19 Income Relief Payment but is not eligible to apply for the scheme until the 4 week period that the lump sum Wage Subsidy payment represents has passed. If an employer applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme Extension, and then they have a change in circumstance within the 8-week period, they may not be entitled to keep the subsidy they got for an employee.

chunks.title: Amount a business must pay a worker — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Amount a business must pay a worker
The amount the business must pay to the worker, depends on whether the worker's ordinary wages or salary are under, or over the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) rate applied for them.
## Worker's ordinary wages or salary less than the subsidy rate
When the worker's ordinary wages or salary were less than the subsidy rate when their business applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), the business must keep paying their ordinary wages for the duration of the subsidy period.
Businesses must use the remaining support towards topping up the wages of other workers, so that they are being paid their ordinary wages. When there are no other workers to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other workers are already being paid their usual wages, the business must repay the remaining subsidy back to the Ministry of Social Development as it could not be used for wages.
If the worker is self-employed, and the income they regularly draw from their business is less than the amount they got from the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Worker's ordinary wages or salary more than the subsidy rate
Businesses who receive the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) must use their best endeavours to pay workers their ordinary wages or at least 80% of each named workers ordinary wages or salary for the period of the subsidy.
If paying 80% of ordinary wages or salary isn't possible, and the worker was usually earning over the subsidy rate applied for, the business must pass on the full weekly amount of support (less any usual wage deductions) to the worker.
For example, if a full-time worker was normally earning $1000 gross per week before their employer applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) and the business cannot afford to pay them 80% or $800 gross, then the business must pay them the full-time subsidy rate of $585.80 (less any usual wage deductions).
If businesses have questions about their obligations under employment law, they should contact Employment New Zealand for advice and assistance.

chunks.title: Assessing 40% revenue loss due to the current escalation in Alert Levels — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Assessing 40% revenue loss due to the current escalation in Alert Levels
When deciding if the business has had a decline in revenue due to the current escalation in Alert Levels, the Ministry of Social Development considers:
- the type of work the business does, eg retail, manufacturing, sales, construction, driving etc and
- whether (or to the extent) the business is able to operate while part of the country is in Alert Level 3 (eg is it an essential business or not, what changes has the business needed to make due to the public health restrictions) and
- whether the estimated loss of revenue makes sense (based on the business circumstances)
Note businesses are required to prepare and keep evidence of their revenue decline and how it was caused by the current escalation in Alert Levels, and the Ministry of Social Development may ask for verification in some cases.
## Business has been open during current escalation in Alert Levels
Some businesses may be able to operate during the current escalation in Alert Levels, eg in the following circumstances:
- firms defined as essential businesses or
- firms operating outside of a regional lockdown that form part of a wider supply chain or
- providing click and collect or
- takeaway options
Note that this is not limited to the above.
For businesses that are able to operate, when deciding if they have had a decline in revenue, the Ministry of Social Development considers the reasons given for the decline in revenue and whether these are reasonable given the type of work the business does and where the business is located.
Being open for business does not protect a business from having a 40% decline in revenue, but further consideration needs to be given to their circumstances.
Example a business has remained open, or is open in some online capacity, and may not be able to sell the same level of product, due to reduced demand from other businesses (eg frozen food which they used to provide to fast food or other restaurants).
For these businesses, the Ministry of Social Development will consider their individual situations and make decisions based on the facts of their application, when considering if the business has had a 40% decline in revenue due to the current escalation in Alert Levels.

chunks.title: Business dismisses worker — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Business dismisses worker
Businesses must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), to retain the workers for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.
If a business decides to dismiss a worker for reasons other than redundancy, for example, because of serious or repeated misconduct, for performance issues, or if the worker abandons their employment, the business cannot receive any more subsidy payments for this worker.
The business does not have to repay the subsidy already received for this worker, but they must use the balance towards topping up the wages of any other remaining workers named in their application, so they are being paid their ordinary wages.
If the business has no other workers to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other workers are already being paid their ordinary wages, the business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining subsidy that was not able to be used for wages.
The business must follow existing employment law for dismissing a worker.
## Example
Fahima employees 5 staff at her cafe but the COVID-19 public health restrictions have significantly impacted her business and she applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) to continue paying her staff.
One of Fahima's workers is caught taking money from the till and this worker is already on notice for similar behaviour in the past. After going through a disciplinary process, Fahima decides to dismiss the worker based on their repeated misconduct.
As Fahima got the subsidy for this worker, Fahima uses the remaining funds to contribute to the wage costs of her other workers. Fahima manages to hire a replacement worker quickly and reapplies for the subsidy for the new worker.
At the end of the subsidy period Fahima has not used all the funds she received, so repays the remaining amount to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Business gets insurance payments to cover revenue loss — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Business gets insurance payments to cover revenue loss
Some businesses have received insurance payments, such as business interruption insurance, to cover their decline in revenue during the current escalation in Alert Levels. Insurance payments are considered revenue for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021).
If the insurance payment does not cover their losses and the business has still experienced a minimum 40% decline in revenue over a period of 14 consecutive days during the current revenue test period, then the business is eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021).
If the insurance payment means that the business has not had a 40% decline in revenue over a period of 14 consecutive days during the current revenue test period, then the business will not qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021).
If the business has already got the subsidy, then they will have had funds they do not qualify for and must repay the subsidy in full to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Business had not started operating before the current escalation in Alert Levels — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Business had not started operating before the current escalation in Alert Levels
Some businesses may have had their plans to start their business affected by the current escalation in Alert Levels.
To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), the business must have had a minimum 40% decline in revenue over a period of 14 consecutive days during the current revenue test period.
To determine the decline, the businesses needs to compare their revenue using the default comparison period or the seasonal comparison period where it is appropriate.
This means the business must have been operating for at least 14 days during the default comparison period to determine the decline in revenue. The business must have been open and trading (ie generating revenue) for at least 14 consecutive days during this period to qualify.
Businesses that have been operating for less than 14 days during the default comparison period are not eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021).

chunks.title: Business is registered and operating in New Zealand — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Business is registered and operating in New Zealand
A business is registered and operating in New Zealand when they are:
- registered with the New Zealand Companies Office and
- physically located in New Zealand and
- their workers legally work in New Zealand
## Sole traders, self-employed people, and contractors
Sole traders, self-employed people and contractors are not required to be registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, but must have:
- a personal Inland Revenue number for paying income tax and/or GST and
- government licences and permits for their business needs and
- qualifications or registrations for their trade or profession
Sole traders, self-employed people and contractors must still meet the requirements to be physically located and legally working in New Zealand.
The Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed before paying the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021).

chunks.title: Business makes worker redundant — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Business makes worker redundant
Businesses must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), to retain the workers the subsidy was paid for, for the duration of the subsidy period.
If a business makes the worker redundant, the business will not have met their obligations to retain the workers named in their application and must repay any remaining subsidy for this worker.
The business cannot keep the remainder of the subsidy to support other remaining workers. Other enforcement action may be taken against these businesses.
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) can be used to pay the worker's notice period but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract.
The worker is not required to pay the subsidy back to the business.
Businesses who have given their workers notice of redundancy before they apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) are not eligible to get the subsidy for those workers unless the redundancy notice is withdrawn.

chunks.title: Business mitigating the impact of the current escalation in Alert Levels — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Business mitigating the impact of the current escalation in Alert Levels
Before applying for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), a business must have taken active steps to mitigate the impact of the current escalation in Alert Levels on their business activities.
These might include (but are not limited to):
- activating their business continuity plan
- where appropriate, look to their own cash reserves to assist paying staff, eg where they have enough funds, and it won't cause the business to fail if they use it
- proactively engaging with their bank
- making an insurance claim
- seeking advice from the Chamber of Commerce, a relevant industry association, or the Regional Business Partner programme

chunks.title: Businesses must follow employment law when paying wages — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) must be used by businesses to support the cost of wages for the workers named in their application, for duration of the subsidy period. Businesses must still adhere to relevant employment laws when: - reducing a worker's wages to 80% of their ordinary income or - the worker agrees to unpaid leave and being paid the appropriate rate of COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) (when the business cannot afford to pay at least 80% of their ordinary wages or salary) or - advising the worker what leave assistance is available to them This relationship is between the business and the worker.

chunks.title: Agreeing on leave type — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: Businesses and their workers can agree to use any form of paid leave (eg annual leave, sick leave) to cover the period they cannot be at work. However, workers are not required to have used any or all of their paid leave (including sick leave) entitlements before the business can get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) on their behalf. Workers will generally want to use any leave entitlements available to them as this must be paid out to them at the rate outlined in employment law (that is, must be paid out at their ordinary pay amount, and cannot be reduced to 80%). No business can make a blanket rule that workers take annual leave during the current escalation in Alert Levels, but the business and worker can agree for the worker to take annual leave. In this situation the worker should be paid their ordinary wage rate for their usual hours of work and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) will help businesses pay for the annual leave taken.

chunks.title: Unpaid leave — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: Some workers will have agreed with the business to take unpaid leave if they do not have any leave entitlement to cover the current escalation in Alert Levels when there is no work for them. Businesses who get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) should try to continue to pay at least 80% of the worker's income in this situation. But when this is not possible, the business must pass on the full COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) to the worker(s) while they are on unpaid leave (or continue to pay their ordinary wage if it is under the rate applied for). Businesses must follow the correct employment process. If businesses have questions about their obligations under employment law, they should contact Employment New Zealand for advice and assistance.

chunks.title: Business not entitled but has been paid — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: If a business applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), and then they have a change in circumstance within the 2-week period, they may not be entitled to keep the subsidy payment they got for a worker named in their application. Change of circumstances Business action Worker voluntarily resigns The business should use the balance of any of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) to pay other workers named in their application. When no other workers need it, the business should contact the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy for this worker as it was not able to be used for wages. Worker has been made redundant The business must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) remaining for the worker. The subsidy can be used to pay the notice period, but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract, and cannot be used to support other remaining workers named in their application. Worker has been dismissed The business should use the balance of any of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) to pay other workers named in their application. When no other workers need it, the business should contact the Ministry of Social Development and must repay the remaining subsidy for this worker as it was not able to be used for wages. Business has closed The business must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) remaining for their worker(s). The subsidy can be used to pay the notice period, but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract and cannot be used to support other remaining workers named in their application. Worker is on fixed-term contract that ends during the period that the business is getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for them. The business must repay any amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) remaining for the worker at the end of the fixed-term contract. The subsidy cannot be used to meet any entitlements owed under contract and cannot be used to support other remaining workers named in their application. The business applied for the wrong type of COVID-19 scheme for their worker (eg applied for the Leave Support Scheme in error).
