The business must repay any amount received for the incorrect application and re-apply for the correct scheme that they are entitled to.

chunks.title: Business not entitled but has been paid — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: The business applied for the wrong type of COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) rate for their worker, eg applies for full-time, when the person was part-time. The business must repay the difference between the full-time rate received and the part-time rate they are entitled to. The business applied for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) based on a predicted 40% decline in revenue, but the decline did not occur. The business is not entitled to the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) and must repay it in full. Employer is a State Sector organisation who did not have an exception approved by the Minister of Finance to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) but applied and got the funds. The business is not entitled to the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) and must repay it in full. Any State Sector employers who disagree with the decision should consult with their monitoring agency. Business gets payment they are not entitled to due to an office error (eg their application might have been paid twice or accidentally approved instead of declined). The business is not entitled to the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) and must repay it in full. Business gets an insurance payment that covers their loss in revenue, so they have no longer experienced a 40% decline in revenue required to be eligible. The business is not entitled to the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) and must repay it in full. If a business applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) while the worker is also getting the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme or the Short-Term Absence Payment, their application will be declined.

chunks.title: Example — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: A courier company applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) as their business has been slower than normal during the current escalation in Alert Levels. Their accounts for the last 14 days have not yet been finalised, but they predict they will have experienced a 40% decline in revenue over this period due to the current escalation in Alert Levels, when compared with the default comparison period. They apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for their workers. When they do finalise their accounts, the company has only experienced a 35% decline in revenue. The company got funds they were not entitled to, so they contact the Ministry of Social Development to repay the subsidy in full.

chunks.title: Current escalation in Alert Levels — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Current escalation in Alert Levels
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) was introduced because there was an escalation to Alert Level 3 or above, anywhere in New Zealand, that lasted seven or more consecutive days.
The current escalation in Alert Levels for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) refers to the increase to Alert Level 3 that occurred in Auckland on 28 February 2021.
Applications for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) closed at 11.59pm on 21 March 2021.

chunks.title: Current revenue test period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Current revenue test period
For the initial COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), applications were opened early on 4 March 2021 to give businesses certainty of support. Payments were made from 8 March 2021 and applications closed on 21 March 2021. The current revenue test period for this subsidy period is from 28 February to 21 March 2021.
If the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) is extended, the current revenue test period will be a 21-day window that begins seven days before applications open for the subsequent subsidy period. The current revenue test period will end when applications for the subsequent subsidy period close.

chunks.title: Deciding if someone is self-employed — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Deciding if someone is self-employed
A person is likely to be self-employed when they carry out business activities on their own, including contracting, working as a sole trader or owning a small business.
A self-employed person is likely to:
- support the business with their own money (eg providing all the equipment and tools needed for their job)
- decide or control how they work (eg when, where and what hours they work)
- decide how much they get paid and how
- pay their own income tax (unless they are a young person earning under the tax threshold)
- be responsible for investment decisions and any losses
- be able to sell the business if they wanted to
The above list is not a full list. There may be other things that can be considered.
Self-employed people can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), if they meet the qualifications.

chunks.title: Decline in revenue across business as a whole — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Decline in revenue across business as a whole
The decline in revenue must be experienced across all parts of the business as a minimum 40% decline in total revenue.
Business units within a single corporate entity are not eligible to apply individually. This includes Councils and other business structures who may have different programmes, branches, or divisions that are differently affected by the current escalation in Alert Levels, but who employ all their workers under one corporate entity.
Consolidated tax groups (made up of legally separate companies) cannot apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021). The separate companies can apply individually for the subsidy if they meet the qualifications.
## Example 1
Auckland Council cannot open their public pools because of the current escalation in Alert Levels, and this part of the business has had a 100% decline in revenue in the last 14-days since the current escalation in Alert Levels started.
However, the Council does not qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) scheme because the rest of the business can operate normally, and the Council has not experienced a 40% decline in revenue overall.
## Example 2
A clothing store in Auckland cannot open during the current escalation in Alert Levels.
The store can trade online, but their revenue is down more than 40% compared to a typical 14-day consecutive period in the 6 weeks before the escalation period began.
However, the store is part of a larger company with locations around the country, and the business as a whole has not been significantly impacted by regional restrictions.
The store does not qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) scheme because the rest of the business has not experienced a 40% decline in revenue overall.
## Example 3
Giani's Pizza Franchise has locations around the country, however the stores in Auckland cannot open because of the current escalation in Alert Levels.
Although the wider company is able to operate, the stores in Auckland are individually owned as separate legal entities, and they can individually apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) if they meet the qualifications.

chunks.title: Decline in revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Decline in revenue
To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) the business must have had (or expect to have) a minimum 40% decline in revenue over a period of 14 consecutive days during the current revenue test period. This is compared to their revenue during the default comparison period or the seasonal comparison period.
This means they have had (or will have) a minimum 40% decline in:
- actual revenue or
- predicted revenue (eg when a business has had a reduction in bookings such as accommodation providers) and
- the decline is due to the impact of the current escalation in Alert Levels on their business
Businesses can use a combination of both actual and predicted revenue decline in order to qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021). This will depend on the date they apply for the subsidy and how they are calculating their revenue decline.
However, if the business predicted a 40% decline in revenue but as a result of their actual revenue, they do not experience this, then they must repay the full amount of the subsidy they received.
Example
A business applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) on 8 March 2021.
Their actual revenue was more than 40% down last week (28 February to 7 March 2021) and they predict their revenue will be down again this week (8 March to 14 March 2021).
They apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) using a combination of actual and predicted revenue.

chunks.title: Default comparison period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Default comparison period
To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), a business must have experienced (or expect to experience) a minimum 40% decline in revenue over a period of 14 consecutive days during the current revenue test period.
Generally, businesses must determine their decline in revenue by comparing the revenue of a 14-day consecutive period during the current revenue test period with the typical revenue during a period of 14 consecutive days between 4 January and 14 February 2021, (ie the 6 weeks before the first Alert Level 3 escalation on 14 February 2021). This is called the default comparison period.
When identifying their typical revenue, businesses can choose a period of 14 consecutive days during the default comparison period that best shows the revenue they would normally have earned if their business was not impacted by the current escalation in Alert Levels.
Example
A business applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) on 4 March 2021.
They expect their revenue for the 14-day period since 28 February 2021 will be $5,000.
They compare this against the revenue they received during the 14-day period between 18 and 31 January 2021, which would have been $10,000.
They predict they will experience a decline in revenue of more than 40% and meet the qualifications for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021).
## Businesses operating for less than a year and high growth firms
All businesses operating for less than a year or high growth firms (eg a business that has had a significant increase in revenue) must use the default comparison period, unless they can demonstrate that using the seasonal comparison period gives a more accurate representation of their revenue decline.

chunks.title: Definition of revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Definition of revenue
Revenue means the total amount of money a business has earned from its normal business activities before expenses are deducted.
Some pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses can include a fall in projected capital income when determining a 40% decrease in revenue.
For the purposes of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), revenue does not include:
- this or any other COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Schemes
- COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment
- COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme
- COVID-19 Essential Workers Leave Support Scheme
- COVID-19 Resurgence Support Payment
- COVID-19 Small Business Cashflow (Loan) Scheme

chunks.title: Determining a decline in revenue — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Determining a decline in revenue
To determine a decline in revenue, the business or self-employed person must compare:
- the revenue of a period of 14 consecutive days during the current revenue test period with either: the default comparison period orfor some businesses, the seasonal comparison period
- the default comparison period or
- for some businesses, the seasonal comparison period
To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), the revenue of the 14-day period must be at least 40% less than it was in the 14-day period it was compared against.

chunks.title: Eligible businesses — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Eligible businesses
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) is available for:
- businesses using all employment types including full-time, part-time, casual, fixed-term, sole trading, and self-employment, including those businesses with workers getting the minimum wage exemption
- across all sectors and industries in New Zealand
- includes registered charities, incorporated societies, non-government organisations and post-settlement governance entities (eg Māori authorities)
State Sector organisations are generally not eligible to get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for their workers.
Exceptions for State Sector employers are considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, through the relevant monitoring agency.

chunks.title: Examples of deciding 40% revenue decline for businesses open during current escalation in Alert Levels — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Examples of deciding 40% revenue decline for businesses open during current escalation in Alert Levels
The examples below are not exhaustive.
## Food outlet
Generally, it would be unreasonable to expect that an essential business of this type would have had a 40% revenue decline as they are able to operate at a time of high demand.
However, if that business provided a reason for the decline in revenue that was reasonable when considering their situation, then the Ministry of Social Development would accept there had been a decline.
Example a grocery store in the middle of the Central Business District (CBD), whose main trade was CBD workers and many people are still working from home or choosing not to eat out, or a supermarket in a small town reliant on tourists who have now left. In both these cases, the business remains open and can operate but it would be reasonable that there could have been a 40% decline in their revenue.
## Business outside of regional lockdown
Generally, it would be unreasonable to expect that a business operating outside of a regional lockdown would have had a 40% revenue decline as they are able to operate with minimal restrictions placed on their business.
However, if that business provided a reason for the decline in revenue that was reasonable when considering their situation, then the Ministry of Social Development would accept there had been a decline.
Example 1
A florist in Canterbury who supplies markets around the country. With Alert Level 3 public health restrictions in the Auckland region, the florist is unable to sell their stock to their largest market.
Example 2
A backpackers in Queenstown has seen a reduction in bookings since the Auckland region was placed into Alert Level 3. A number of bookings from Auckland holiday-makers have been cancelled, and although reservations were starting to increase again, numbers have now dropped off.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Example 1
Ailee works 10 hours per week at minimum wage ($200 gross per week, at 1 April 2021) while she is a student. The business that employs her has experienced a decline in revenue due to the current escalation in Alert Levels, so the business applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) to continue paying her.
Because her ordinary wages are less than the subsidy rate of $350 gross per week, the business must use the subsidy to continue paying her ordinary wage of $200 gross per week (less any usual wage deductions).
The business must use the difference to contribute to the wages of their other workers named in the application and when there are no other workers, must refund the remainder back to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example 2
Jivan works 40 hours at a workshop as a building labourer. He usually gets $756 gross per week. He cannot do any work from home during the current escalation in Alert Levels.
The business has a highly skilled and reliable workforce and is using the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) to continue to pay Jivan 80% of his ordinary wages during this period ($604.80 gross per week). If the business was not able to do this, they would be required to pay Jivan the full-time subsidy rate ($585.80 gross per week). Any changes the business makes to his employment agreement (i.e. to reduce his wages) must be agreed with Jivan in writing.
## Example 3
Stuart is a digger driver. The business that employs him has no revenue coming into the business during current escalation in Alert Levels. The business has many contracts to finish once they can get back to work, so needs to keep their workers during the current escalation in Alert Levels.
The business is unable to pay Stuart 80% of his full-time wage over this period, and so the business pays Stuart the full amount of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) of $585.80 (less any usual wage deductions). Any changes the business makes to his employment agreement (ie to reduce his wages) must be agreed with Stuart in writing.

chunks.title: Fixed-term contract ends within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Fixed-term contract ends within subsidy period
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) is open to existing and newly hired workers and this includes workers on fixed-term contracts. To get the subsidy, businesses must agree to retain the workers named in their application for the duration of the subsidy period.
Businesses can include workers on fixed-term contracts in their COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) application, even if the worker's contract is scheduled to end during the period that the business would be getting the subsidy for them.
However, if a worker's fixed-term contract ends during the subsidy period, the business will not have met their obligation to retain the workers named in the application. In these circumstances, the business can use the subsidy to pay out any notice period for that worker, but the subsidy cannot be used to pay any other entitlements. It also cannot be used to support other remaining workers. The business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining subsidy for this worker.
The business and the worker may agree to extend the contract to the end of the subsidy period in order to meet their obligation to retain the workers named in their application for the period they get the subsidy.
## Example 1
Anaru is on a fixed-term contract that is scheduled to end on 12 March 2021. The business that employs Anaru applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) on 8 March 2021 to continue paying its workers during the current escalation in Alert Levels and includes Anaru in the application.
The business agrees with Anaru to extend his contract to 19 March 2021 so that Anaru can continue getting wages during this period. The business is eligible to get the full 2-week subsidy for Anaru.
## Example 2
Sacha is on a fixed-term contract that is scheduled to end on 12 March 2021. The business that employs her applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) on 4 March 2021 and includes Sacha in the application.
When Sacha's contract ends on 12 March 2021, the business returns the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Health and disability funded workforce — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Health and disability funded workforce
Health and disability funded workforces (eg businesses that provide community health care) not employed by the state sector are able to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) if they meet the qualifications.
Health and disability funded workforces not employed by the state sector includes organisations contracted to, or funded in whole or part, by organisations in the state sector (eg the Ministry of Health and District Health Boards).
Examples include:
- in-home care workers
- workers in primary health organisations
- nurses and other staff in rest-homes or other residential care facilities (eg cooks, cleaners, support staff)

chunks.title: Flexi-wage, Flexi-Wage Self-Employed and Mana in Mahi — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: If a business is currently getting the Flexi-Wage, Flexi-Wage Self-Employed, or Mana in Mahi subsidy for their worker(s), they can also apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), if they meet the qualifications. All wage subsidies the business is getting must be paid to their workers. For more information see:

chunks.title: Apprenticeship Boost Initiative — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: Apprenticeship Boost helps businesses with the costs of keeping their current apprentices or hiring new ones for the first 24 months of their programme of study. If a business is currently getting Apprenticeship Boost for their workers, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for these workers, if they meet the other qualifications. For more information see:

chunks.title: Main benefit and other support — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: If a self-employed person is currently getting a main benefit or other extra help from the Ministry of Social Development, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021). As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, any person getting the subsidy as well as other support from the Ministry must declare the subsidy as income and their benefit may be reduced accordingly.

chunks.title: Interaction with the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: Emergency Benefit Some Emergency Benefit clients may be employed or self-employed. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Emergency Benefit clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be reduced. Emergency Maintenance Assistance Some Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients may be employed or self-employed. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be reduced. Jobseeker Support Some Jobseeker Support clients may be working part-time (less than 30 hours per week) or getting income that does not reduce the rate of Jobseeker Support to zero. Sole parents and grandparented Jobseeker Support clients can work full-time for a temporary period provided their income when assessed over a 52-week period does not fully reduce the benefit. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Jobseeker Support clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be reduced. Note the part-time and full-time subsidy rate differs from the definition above. New Zealand Superannuation - Non-qualified partner If a New Zealand Superannuation client has included their grandparented non-qualified partner in their payments, their New Zealand Superannuation is income-tested. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, New Zealand Superannuation grandparented non-qualified partner clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income, and both of their New Zealand Superannuation payments may be reduced. Sole Parent Support Some Sole Parent Support clients have work obligations and may be employed or self-employed. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Sole Parent Support clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be reduced. Supported Living Payment Some Supported Living Payment clients will be working up to 15 hours per week but may not be able to do this on a regular basis. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, Support Living Payment clients who get the subsidy must declare it as income and their benefit may be reduced.

chunks.title: Financial support from other agencies — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: There is a range of financial support available from other agencies for businesses who have been negatively impacted by the COVID-19 financial crisis. These schemes, such as the Resurgence Support Payment from Inland Revenue, are separate to Work and Income support, and have their own qualification criteria. This means that, if they meet the necessary qualifications, businesses can apply and get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) as well as other schemes. Applicants need to make sure they meet the qualifications for any schemes they apply for. Note the Resurgence Support Payment from Inland Revenue is intended to support businesses to cover fixed costs. It is available to eligible businesses whenever COVID-19 Alert Levels are increased to Level 2 or above for a period of 7 consecutive days. This differs from the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), which is activated after an escalation to Level 3 or above for 7 consecutive days, and is intended to keep businesses connected to their workers by supporting businesses with the cost of wages. Businesses can receive the Resurgence Support Payment and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme at the same time.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) was introduced from 4 March 2021, to support businesses impacted by the current escalation in Alert Levels, to help the businesses stay connected to their workers.
This scheme was the March 2021 addition to previous wage subsidies implemented in response to COVID-19.
Businesses who got previous COVID-19 Wage Subsidy, or Leave Support Scheme payments, or Short-Term Absence Payment could apply for the same workers again, if they met the qualifications, but only once the period for any previous payment had ended.
## Applications
Businesses and self-employed people must apply online for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021).
Applications could be made from 4 March 2021, with payments commencing from 8 March 2021. Payments were made as a lump sum to the business for each named worker (including self-employed people) and covered a 2-week period from either 8 March 2021 or the date of application (whichever is the later date).
Applications for the current scheme closed at 11.59pm on 21 March 2021.

chunks.title: Newly hired workers — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Newly hired workers
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) is open for eligible businesses to apply for any newly hired workers, and previous workers who were re-hired before the business applies for the subsidy.
## Example 1
Sam was employed full-time as a hairdresser, but their start date was delayed due to the current escalation in Alert Levels.
Sam's employer applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for their workers and includes Sam in the application.
The employer pays Sam $585.80 (less any usual wage deductions) until they can start their new role.
## Example 2
Whiti owns a pet store and is getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) as her business has experienced a decline in revenue due to the current escalation in Alert Levels.
One of her workers resigns and she needs to hire a replacement worker.
Whiti uses the remaining subsidy from the leaving worker to continue paying her other staff, and submits another application for the new worker when they start their role.
## Example 3
Ravi owns a clothing store and has reopened his business after being closed during the COVID-19 public health restrictions. He needs to hire a new worker, but his business is still experiencing more than 40% decline in revenue due to the recent escalation in COVID-19 Alert Levels.
Ravi is already getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for his existing workers, so submits another application for the new worker when they start their role.

chunks.title: Ordinary wages or salary — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Ordinary wages or salary
For workers, their ordinary wages or salary are specified in their employment agreement at the date the business applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021).
Self-employed people can determine their ordinary wages or drawings by calculating the regular amount that is left over after they meet their business costs. This is the amount they regularly pay themselves as drawings from the business.
If the individual is self-employed, and the income they regularly draw from their business is less than the amount they got from the subsidy, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) can be used to support the costs of wages, but cannot be used towards other business costs.

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) is paid at a flat rate based on each named worker's normal (or expected) hours of paid employment: - $585.80 (before tax) for 20 hours or more per week, or 40 hours or more per fortnight or - $350.00 (before tax) for less than 20 hours per week or less than 40 hours per fortnight The subsidy is paid for a 2-week period as a lump sum payment at the appropriate weekly subsidy rate for: - working 20 hours or more or - working under 20 hours The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) covers each eligible worker for 2 weeks from 8 March 2021 or the date of application, whichever is the later date.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: The business accessed the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for 10 workers as soon as the scheme became available on 4 March 2021. Now the business needs the subsidy for 20 more workers. The business can apply for the 20 newly named workers, but not the 10 original workers for whom they have already got the subsidy.

chunks.title: Calculating variable hours — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: For a self-employed person, or a business who has casual workers who work variable hours, an average over a relevant period can be used to work out which subsidy rate to apply. A relevant period for a business or self-employed person who has been working for a year, would be an average over this period. As a guide, for a new business or a person who has been self-employed for less than one year, an average over 8 weeks can be used, unless there is another time period that would be more appropriate. Example if using the period that the individual has been employed for would give a better representation of the worker's usual hours, then the business can use this time period instead. It is up to businesses to agree with their workers what their hours would usually be during this period, to determine the appropriate COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) rate to apply for.

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: Charlotte is a relief teacher for an Early Childhood Education Centre and is called in to provide support as required, but the Centre is closed due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions. The Centre employs Charlotte as a casual worker and calculates that she has worked an average of 17 hours per week over the last 4 months she has been employed there. The business applies for a part-time COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (March 2021) rate to continue paying Charlotte's wages (at a rate of 17 hours per week for the 2-week period). As this is less than the $350 gross per week provided through the subsidy, the business uses the remaining subsidy to support the wages of other workers named in the application.

chunks.title: Maximum payment for a business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: There is no cap on the total amount of COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) a business can get. It is based on the number of workers they have, and whether they are working 20 hours or more, or under 20 hours.

chunks.title: People getting income from a property business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## People getting income from a property business
Some people are paid a wage, salary or draw an income from a property business, such as private rentals, Airbnb's and homestay operations.
These businesses are eligible to get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) if they meet the qualifications, including being registered and operating in New Zealand.
Note the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings and can only be used to support the cost of wages. People who apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for a property business must be able to declare that they draw a wage, salary, or income for this work.
For self-employed people who are not registered with the New Zealand Companies Office, the Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that the person is self-employed before paying the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021).
## Example
Anthony owns several holiday homes, which he rents out to supplement his income. He works an average of 10 hours per week on the properties, managing the bookings and cleaning the property in between guests.
Usually this would be a very busy time of year for his business, but most of his bookings have been cancelled due to the current escalation of COVID-19 Alert Levels. Anthony's income has dropped by more than 40% during this period so he applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021).
The Ministry is able to verify his self-employment status with Inland Revenue and his application is approved.

chunks.title: People getting paid parental leave — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## People getting paid parental leave
Businesses may have workers who are getting paid parental leave.
## Worker already getting paid parental leave
If a worker was already getting paid parental leave when the business applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), the business is not able to include this worker in their application.
If they do include the worker in error and the application is approved, the business got funds they are not eligible for and must repay the full amount for this worker to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Worker goes on paid parental leave during subsidy period
If a worker starts getting paid parental leave after the business has made an application and/or received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), then the worker is not eligible to get both the subsidy and paid parental leave.
The business must stop using the subsidy for the worker as soon as they go on parental leave.
The remaining funds can be used towards topping up the wages of other workers named in their application, so that they are being paid their ordinary wages.
If the business has no other workers to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other workers named in their application are already being paid their ordinary wages, the business must tell the Ministry of Social Development, and must repay any remaining amount that was not able to be used for wages.
## Worker due to return from paid parental leave during subsidy period
If a worker was getting paid parental leave at the time of the business's application for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for their other workers, but the worker has since returned to work, then the business can make a new application for them.
The business should use the new hours the worker will be working on their return to work to calculate the rate of subsidy to apply for.

chunks.title: People getting weekly compensation from ACC — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## People getting weekly compensation from ACC
Businesses may have workers who are unable to work and getting weekly compensation from Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC).
## Worker already getting ACC
If the worker was already getting ACC compensation when the business applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), the business is not able to include this worker in their application.
If they do include the worker in error and the application is approved, the business will have got funds they are not eligible for and must repay the subsidy for this worker to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Worker goes on ACC during subsidy period
If the worker is injured and starts getting ACC compensation after the business made an application and/or got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), the worker is eligible to get both the subsidy and ACC compensation.
However, the worker must declare the subsidy to ACC as income and their weekly compensation may be abated (reduced) accordingly.
## Worker due to finish getting ACC during subsidy period
If a worker was getting ACC compensation at the time of the business's application for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for their other workers, but the worker is no longer getting the ACC payments, the business can make a new application for them.

chunks.title: People on casual contracts — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## People on casual contracts
Businesses can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for workers who are on casual contracts, but they must keep them employed for the subsidy period.
Businesses can apply for the subsidy for the hours the worker is usually employed. Businesses need to agree with their workers what their hours would usually be during this period, to determine the appropriate COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) rate to apply for.
If a worker's casual work ends during the subsidy period, then the business will not have met their obligation to retain the workers named in their application.
The business must notify the Ministry of Social Development and repay any remaining subsidy for this worker.

chunks.title: People on fixed-term contracts — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## People on fixed-term contracts
Businesses can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for workers who are on fixed-term contracts, but they must keep them employed for the subsidy period.
If a worker's fixed-term contract ends during the subsidy period, the business will not have met their obligation to retain the workers named in their application. The business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining subsidy for this worker.

chunks.title: People working multiple jobs — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## People working multiple jobs
Businesses may have workers who work for them, and another business. The worker may work more than 20 hours for one business, and less than 20 hours for the other.
If both businesses meet the criteria, they can each apply for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for the same worker.

chunks.title: Pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' business
A small number of pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses may be eligible to treat a 40% fall in projected capital income as a result of COVID-19, as a fall in revenue for the eligibility of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021).
These businesses must:
- be a research and development intensive start-up business
- be 'seed' or 'venture backed'
- be Callaghan Innovation affiliated as of 28 February 2021 and
- have no other revenue other than government support and, seed or venture capital
Eligible pre-revenue research and development 'start-up' businesses must determine their decline in revenue (ie projected capital income) using the default comparison period, unless they can show that they meet the criteria for the seasonal comparison period.
These businesses can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) if they meet the other qualifications.

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), businesses must meet the following eligibility criteria: - the business must have experienced or expect to experience a minimum 40% decline in revenue - the decline in revenue must be over a period of 14 consecutive days during the current revenue test period, when compared to the default comparison period or the seasonal comparison period - the decline in revenue must be caused by the current escalation in Alert Levels - the business must be registered and operating in New Zealand - the workers named in their application must be legally working in New Zealand and employed by the business as at 8 March 2021 or the date of application, whichever is the later date - before making an application, the business must have taken active steps to mitigate the impact of the current escalation in Alert Levels on their business - the business must not be currently getting a subsidy for the workers named in their application for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), the Leave Support Scheme or Short-Term Absence Payment If a business is getting a COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme payment or Short-Term Absence Payment for their workers, they must wait until the subsidy period for these workers has ended before they apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for those workers.

chunks.title: Must retain workers and pay at least 80% wages or salary — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: Businesses who get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) must keep the workers (for whom they received the wage subsidy) in employment for the period of the subsidy (unless the worker voluntarily ends the employment relationship). In order to meet the qualifications for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (March 2021), businesses must try to pay at least 80% of each named workers’ ordinary wages or salary for the period of the subsidy, as per their employment agreement at the date the business applies for the subsidy. However, businesses must follow current employment law when reducing a worker's wages or changing the hours they work. When the worker was earning less than the subsidy rate, the business must keep paying their ordinary wages, even if they are working less hours due to the current escalation in Alert Levels. Any difference should be used towards topping up the wages of other workers named in their application. When there are no other workers to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other workers named in their application are already being paid their ordinary wages, the business must tell the Ministry of Social Development, and must repay any remaining subsidy that was not able to be used for wages. If a person is self-employed, and the income they regularly draw from their business is less than the subsidy amount they received, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Receivership or liquidation within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: In some circumstances, businesses who have received the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) may still go into receivership or liquidation, and may have to sell or close their business permanently.

chunks.title: Business operating under receivership or liquidation before applying — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: A business who is currently operating under receivership or liquidation can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), if they meet the qualifications and meet their obligations to retain workers for the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Business goes into receivership or liquidation but keeps operating — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: If the business can continue operating under receivership or for the duration of the liquidation process, then the business (or the receiver/liquidator) can continue to use the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) to support the cost of wages for workers named in their application. If the business recovers, or the receiver/liquidator sells the business during the subsidy period and the new owners take on the workers named in their application, then the business can continue to use the subsidy for these workers. Example 1 A business goes into receivership 2 weeks after getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for their workers. The receiver takes over the business and manages to sell the business to new owners. The new owners keep all the previous workers and use any remaining subsidy to continue paying these workers for the duration of the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Business closes under receivership or liquidation — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: If the business is liquidated (and permanently closed), or the receiver/liquidator sells the business during the subsidy period, and the new owners do not take on the workers named in the subsidy application, then the business will not have met their obligation to retain workers named in their application and they must repay any remaining subsidy for these workers. Where workers are made redundant, the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) can be used to pay the notice period but cannot be used to meet any redundancy payments owed under contract, and cannot be used to support other remaining workers named in the application. Example 2 A restaurant owner puts their business into liquidation 3 days after getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for their workers. The liquidator gives the workers 1 week's notice that the business will be closing permanently and uses the subsidy to pay out the notice period for the workers named in their application. At the end of the notice period, the liquidator repays the remaining 1 week of subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: Repaying unused funds after the subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Repaying unused funds after the subsidy period
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) is paid in one lump sum to the business to support the cost of wages for 2 weeks.
If the business does not need the full weekly rate for their worker(s), then any difference should be used for the wages of other workers named in their application.
If there are any unused funds at the end of the 2-week period, the business must repay the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development. The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) cannot be used beyond the 2-week period.
If the person is self-employed and the income that they regularly draw from their business is less than the amount they got from the subsidy, they must repay any surplus to the Ministry of Social Development.
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) cannot be used beyond the 2-week period for which it is paid.
## Example
Jason got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for his only worker who works part-time. The worker was earning under the part-time subsidy rate, so continued getting their ordinary wages for the duration of the subsidy period.
At the end of the 2 weeks, Jason has not used all the subsidy payment and has some funds remaining.
He contacts the Ministry of Social Development to repay the unused subsidy, as the funds were not fully used on wage costs during the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Retain workers named in their application — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Retain workers named in their application
Businesses must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), to retain the workers the subsidy was paid for, for the duration of the subsidy period.
Businesses must agree to retain their workers for the full 2 week period that they receive the subsidy for these workers, ie from 8 March or the date of their application, whichever is the later date.

chunks.title: Reviewing decisions to decline the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Reviewing decisions to decline the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021)
Decisions to decline the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) are not made under the Social Security Act 2018 and are not covered by the usual Review of Decision guidelines.
If a business wants a decision to decline the subsidy reviewed, that decision should be reconsidered. This review should be based on whether an informed decision was made and should consider the following:
- whether all relevant information was available and
- whether the appropriate options and implications were considered and
- whether the decision was made at the appropriate level of delegation
If a review of the decision to decline the payment upholds the original decision, the business can ask the Ombudsman to undertake their own review.

chunks.title: Seasonal comparison period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: To qualify for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), a business must have experienced (or expect to experience) a minimum 40% decline in revenue over a period of 14 consecutive days during the current revenue test period. Generally, businesses must determine their decline in revenue using the default comparison period. However, for businesses who have highly seasonal fluctuations in their revenue, the default comparison period might not give an accurate representation of what the business would have been expecting to earn during the current revenue test period. These businesses can use the seasonal comparison period. The seasonal comparison period is the same period of 14 consecutive days the business chooses during the current revenue test period, in 2020 or 2019. The business can choose if the period in 2020 or 2019 gives the most accurate representation of what the business would have been expecting to earn during the current revenue test period.

chunks.title: Types of seasonal business — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: Some examples of businesses with highly seasonal revenue could be seasonal work such as harvesting fruit and vegetables, music festival or event planners whose peak seasons are during the summer months, or tourism businesses where the season starts on a specific date. For example, the 6 weeks before the COVID-19 Alert Level change (ie the default comparison period) is their seasonal quiet period where they do not usually have any revenue coming in, but the 2 weeks after the Alert Level change is where they would have started to have revenue coming in. If they compare their revenue in the 14 days since the Alert Level change with a period of 14 consecutive days from the 6 weeks prior, it will look like the business has not had a loss of revenue. However, if they compare their revenue to the same 14-day period in 2019, they have clearly had a 40% decline in revenue they can attribute to the seasonal nature of their business.

chunks.title: Example — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: Jayne runs an apple picking business and applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) on 4 March 2021. Her business is highly seasonal and their peak season only began on 1 March 2021. If Jayne used the default comparison period, this would not show her revenue decline as the business did not have much revenue in the six weeks before the first escalation to Alert Level 3 on 14 February 2021. However, if she uses the seasonal comparison period, this shows what revenue the business would have received at the same time two years ago (before the business was impacted by COVID-19 in 2020). Jayne compares what the business would have expected to get between 28 February and 14 March 2021 to the revenue received between 28 February and 14 March 2019 and calculates a revenue loss of 40%. Jayne's business meets the qualifications for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021).

chunks.title: Seasonal work ends within subsidy period — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Seasonal work ends within subsidy period
Some seasonal workers will have had their work affected by the current escalation in Alert Levels (ie season finished earlier than expected and/or not able to pick up new work due to the escalation in Alert Levels).
If the business got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) but can no longer offer them employment during the subsidy period, then the business will not be meeting their obligation to retain the workers named in their application and must repay any remaining subsidy for these workers to the Ministry of Social Development.
If the seasonal workers are casual workers or on fixed-term contracts, then the business can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) to continue paying them, as long as they keep them employed for the subsidy period.
## Example 1
Rowan usually picks grapes over the summer months, but the winery that employs him has closed the harvesting season early due to the current escalation in Alert Levels.
The winery got the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for its workers, but after 1 week the winery decides to end their contracts as the business can no longer offer them employment to return to. The business uses the subsidy to pay out the worker's notice period and repays any remaining amount to the Ministry of Social Development.
## Example 2
Tracey employs 30 casual workers on her kiwifruit orchard, however, the orchard is not able to open due to the COVID-19 public health restrictions and Tracey has no work for these workers.
Tracey calculates the average hours each of her casual workers would have worked at this time last year to determine the correct rate to apply for. Tracey applies for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) to continue paying her workers for the duration of the subsidy period.

chunks.title: Seasonal workers — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Seasonal workers
There are a variety of employment arrangements for seasonal workers (eg fixed-term contract or casual employment contract).
Businesses can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for their seasonal workers, but they must keep them employed for the subsidy period.
If a worker's contract ends during the subsidy period, then the business will not have met their obligation to retain the workers named in their application.
The business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining subsidy for this worker.

chunks.title: Self-employed person is also an employee — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Self-employed person is also an employee
A person may be self-employed for some of their income, and also be employed by a business or other organisation.
If the self-employed person qualifies, they can get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for their own business.
Also, if their employer qualifies, the employer can get the subsidy to continue paying the person as a worker.

chunks.title: Specific employment situations — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Specific employment situations
People's working situations in New Zealand may vary and eligibility for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) can sometimes differ.

chunks.title: State Sector employers generally not eligible — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: State Sector employers, including State Sector organisations and State Owned enterprises, are generally not eligible to get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021). In most situations other arrangements have been made to make sure these employers pay their workers in full. Exceptions for State Sector employers are considered on a case-by-case basis by the Minister of Finance, through the relevant monitoring agency. Monitoring agencies will engage with State Sector employers in their portfolio to understand their financial position and support them to request an exception if appropriate. Example if Airways Corporation of New Zealand Limited believed they met the criteria for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), then they could engage with the Treasury Commercial Operations Team to assess their situation. If appropriate, Treasury would prepare advice for the Minister of Finance asking for an exception on their behalf. If an exception was granted, the monitoring agency would tell the Ministry of Social Development and advise the State Sector employer to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) directly. If an exception has already been granted for an earlier COVID-19 Wage Subsidy or Leave Support Scheme, the State Sector employer does not need to get another exception to apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy (March 2021).

chunks.title: State Sector employers include: — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: - Government agencies such as the Ministry of Health, District Health Boards, Inland Revenue, and the Ministry of Social Development - Crown entities such as Kāinga Ora and the Accident Compensation Corporation - Schools (including state schools, state-integrated schools and their board of trustee members or equivalent) - Tertiary education institutions such as universities, Te Pūkenga - New Zealand Institute of Skills and Technology (including polytechs and institutes of technology), and Wānanga

chunks.title: State Sector employers do not include: — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: - Local government such as Regional, City and District Councils, council organisations and council-controlled organisations as stated in the Local Government Act 2002. This includes trusts and other organisations that look after libraries, museums and other operations in partnership with local authorities (note these employers still need to have a minimum 40% decline in revenue and meet the other qualifications to be eligible for the subsidy) - Kindergartens (although kindergarten teachers are State Sector employees, their employers are not, so Ministry of Education is not directly responsible for their payroll) - (note these employers still need to have a minimum 40% decline in revenue and meet the other qualifications to be eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) - Early childhood centres - Private (or independent) schools, and their board of trustee members or equivalent, proprietors of state-integrated schools and other workers employed by the proprietor (note the proprietor is the owner or leaseholder of the state-integrated school property) - Non-government organisations - Health and disability funded workforces not employed directly by the State Sector Note businesses contracted to provide services to State Sector employers (eg cleaning, security, managed isolation or quarantine facilities etc) are not State Sector employers, and can apply for the subsidy if they meet the other qualifications.

chunks.title: Transition between previous COVID-19 subsidies and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Transition between previous COVID-19 subsidies and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021)
A business can apply for the same workers under different COVID-19 subsidies if they meet the qualifications, but only after the period for the previous payment has ended.
## Business got a COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment
Businesses can apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) when they meet the criteria, and need other assistance. But they can only apply for workers named in Short-Term Absence Payment after the payment period for the Short-Term Absence Payment has ended.
Example
A business got the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment for Maria on Saturday 6 March 2021 and then applied for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) on 8 March 2021 for the rest of their 15 workers as well.
The business cannot be paid the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for Maria until 9 March 2021. The business can get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for their other staff from 8 March 2021.
## Business got a COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme payment
The COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme was introduced on 28 April 2020 to provide financial assistance to businesses during the COVID-19 public health restrictions to:
- encourage workers to self-isolate when they need to and
- support workers who are unable to work from home to have an income when they cannot work
Businesses eligible for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) can choose to apply for the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme when appropriate for their worker's situation.
However, a business cannot get both the COVID-19 Leave Support Scheme and the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for the same period, for the same worker.

chunks.title: Treatment of the subsidy for granting benefits — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: If a worker or a self-employed person is getting a main benefit or extra help from the Ministry of Social Development, they can also apply for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) for themselves or their workers. As the subsidy is paid to replace a loss of earnings, any worker getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) as well as other support from the Ministry must declare the subsidy as income and their benefit may be abated (reduced) accordingly. The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) should be counted as income over a 2-week period from 8 March 2021 or the date of application, whichever is the later date, and should not be counted as a cash asset. Any additional income drawn from the business or any other source must also be included in their total income.

chunks.title: Determining a lump sum payment of the subsidy — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: Workers are paid the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) in the same way their wage or salary is normally paid, eg weekly wages for 2 weeks. However, some businesses receiving the subsidy may pass it on to their workers as a lump sum payment. If the worker applies for assistance from the Ministry of Social Development, it is important to determine whether it is a lump sum payment of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) (on top of their ordinary wages during the subsidy period), or whether it represents a payment for other forms of leave owed to the client. For example, a business may pay out some of the subsidy to a worker to cover their notice period after being made redundant. If the worker then applied for financial assistance from the Ministry of Social Development, this would not be considered a lump sum payment of the subsidy. This would instead be pay in lieu of notice, which is a type of termination payment. If the worker is made redundant or the business has surplus funds at the end of the subsidy period, the business is required to repay the remaining subsidy to the Ministry of Social Development. However, some businesses may pass on the remaining funds directly to the worker. If the business pays out the remainder of the subsidy (eg once the worker's notice period has ended and they are no longer employed), this would be considered a lump sum payment of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021). If the payment is a lump sum payment of the subsidy, it may affect their eligibility for some types of assistance.

chunks.title: Benefit applications — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text: As the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) is paid to replace a loss of earnings it should be charged as income for a benefit or extra help, this includes when the subsidy is paid to the client as a lump sum payment. When a client has received the subsidy as a lump sum payment, the Ministry of Social Development will consider the appropriate period that the payment is intended to represent and will charge it as income for that period. For example, the lump sum payment can be divided by the client's average earnings (using the last 2 weeks if appropriate) to determine how many weeks of income the payment is intended to represent. If the amount of the payment is less than the relevant income cut-out point, the client would qualify for assistance for the period the lump sum payment is charged for. If the amount is higher than the income cut-out point, the client would not qualify until the period the payment represents has finished. Note generally, a lump sum payment of the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) is not considered a termination payment, so does not need to be considered when calculating what date their employment ended. The lump sum would only be considered a termination payment when it is paid in lieu of notice.

chunks.title: Worker is legally working in New Zealand — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Worker is legally working in New Zealand
Legally working in New Zealand means a person is both working in New Zealand, and is legally entitled to work in New Zealand.
A person cannot be employed if they cannot legally work in New Zealand in that job. It is the responsibility of the business to make sure that a worker can work for them legally.

chunks.title: Worker temporarily overseas and cannot return due to COVID-19 restrictions — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Worker temporarily overseas and cannot return due to COVID-19 restrictions
Workers who are legally employed in New Zealand but who are currently overseas can be named as a worker in the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021) application if:
- they were legally working in New Zealand before leaving and
- their absence was intended to be temporary (eg a holiday or a work business trip) and
- they maintain their employment status (that is, they are still employed by the business) and intended to return to work on a specific date but cannot start on that date due to the COVID-19 travel restrictions and
- the business meets the other qualifications for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021)

chunks.title: Worker voluntarily leaves — specific employment related assistance > covid 19 wage subsidy scheme march 2021
chunks.text:
## Worker voluntarily leaves
Businesses must agree when they get the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Scheme (March 2021), to retain the workers for whom the subsidy was paid for the duration of the subsidy period.
If a worker voluntarily leaves their employment for another job opportunity, the business must advise the Ministry of Social Development, and the business cannot receive any more subsidy payments for this worker. The business does not have to repay the subsidy already received for this worker, but they must use any remaining balance towards topping up the wages of other workers named in their application so that they are being paid their ordinary wages.
The subsidy can be used to contribute towards the wages of other workers named in their application. If the business has no other workers to use the remaining subsidy for, or the other workers named in their application are already being paid their ordinary wages, the business must tell the Ministry of Social Development and must repay any remaining subsidy that was not able to be used for wages.

chunks.title: Applications for Employment Transition assistance — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Applications for Employment Transition assistance
All clients who would like to receive this payment should complete a personal details form requesting Employment Transition Assistance.
## Employment trial ends after 1 July 2005
A client has 28 days from the end date of their Sustainable Employment Trial to apply for the Employment Transition Assistance if their Sustainable Employment Trial ends after 1 July 2005.
## Late applications
If an eligible client makes an application for the Employment Transition Assistance outside the allowable dates they cannot be granted the Employment Transition Assistance.
All clients must apply for this assistance within the specified time frames.
## Employment trial ended before 1 July 2005
A client had until 29 August 2005 to apply for Employment Transition Assistance if their Sustainable Employment Trial ended before 1 July 2005.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
Clients (including non-beneficiaries) can be absent from New Zealand and continue getting payment for the first 28 days of any absence in any 52 week period if:
- the absence does not affect the client's qualification for the Employment Transition Assistance and
- the client will continue with their employment immediately on their return to New Zealand
To pay Employment Transition Assistance while the client is absent from New Zealand depends on whether the client is also getting a main benefit.
## Clients getting a main benefit
All clients getting a main benefit must tell the Ministry of Social Development before they leave New Zealand. If the client or partner does not tell the Ministry before they travel overseas, their benefit payments (including Employment Transition Assistance) must stop.
To get Employment Transition Assistance while they are absent from New Zealand the client must be returning to their employment immediately on their return to New Zealand.
## Clients receiving non-beneficiary Extra Help
Clients who are getting Employment Transition Assistance and not getting a main benefit:
- must advise of their departure from New Zealand and
- can be absent and paid their Employment Transition Assistance for up to 28 days per absence, where it does not affect the client's eligibility for Employment Transition Assistance
Note when assessing the period of absence, do not include:
- the date of departure from New Zealand and
- the date of return to New Zealand

chunks.title: Action on return to New Zealand — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Action on return to New Zealand
You will need to look at the circumstances of the client's absence from and subsequent return to New Zealand to decide whether to stop or continue the Employment Transition payment.
You will need to consider the following:
- eligibility for this assistance
- the length of time that they have been absent
- the reason for the absence
- if the client will immediately continue to work more than 15 hours per week on their return
- if their circumstances have changed significantly during their absence
## Payment to stop
The Employment Transition payment must stop if:
- the client is absent from New Zealand for less than 28 days and does not immediately continue to work more than 15 hours on their return
- the client is absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days
## Payment to continue
When a client returns to New Zealand on or before the 29th day you can continue their Employment Transition payment without any break in payment.
For more information see:
- Client does not return

chunks.title: Advises more than 14 days after the event — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Advises more than 14 days after the event
As clients have an obligation to advise Work and Income of any changes that may affect their entitlement to Employment Transition Assistance it is expected that they will do so within a reasonable period. As a guideline, a reasonable period is considered to be within 14 days.
When a client advises of a change in circumstances more than 14 days after the event you should generally reduce, suspend or cancel Employment Transition payment from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.
## Good and sufficient reason
Where there is a good and sufficient reason (for example, bereavement or illness) for the client not advising Work and Income of a change in circumstances within 14 days you may reduce, suspend or cancel the Employment Transition Assistance from the first available date.
## False or misleading information
If a client gives false or misleading information you must review the Employment Transition Assistance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.

chunks.title: Advises more than 14 days after the event — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Advises more than 14 days after the event
As clients have an obligation to advise Work and Income of any changes that may affect their entitlement to Employment Transition Assistance it is expected that they will do so within a reasonable period. As a guideline, a reasonable period is considered to be within 14 days.
When a client advises of a change in circumstances more than 14 days after the event you should generally reduce, suspend or cancel Employment Transition Assistance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.
## Good and sufficient reason
Where there is a good and sufficient reason (for example, bereavement or a health condition) for the client not advising Work and Income of a change in circumstances within 14 days you may reduce, suspend or cancel Employment Transition Assistance from the first available date.
## False or misleading information
If a client gives false or misleading information you must review Employment Transition Assistance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.
For more information see:
- Change in income

chunks.title: Avoiding a debt — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Avoiding a debt
When a client dies, Employment Transition payment generally stops from the day after the date of death. You must take all possible steps to stop payments from this date.
When payment cannot be stopped from the day after the date of death there is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days after the date of death. You can use this discretion to stop payment from the first available date, that is, the earliest date that you can stop payments from so that no overpayment is established.
If the period between the date of death and the first available date to cancel payment from (to avoid creating a debt) is more than 28 days, you will have to establish an overpayment from the 29th day after death.
However, when there has been a deliberate intent to delay advising Work and Income of the client's death you should stop payment from the day after the date of death and establish an overpayment.
Note under no circumstances can payment continue for more than 28 days after the date of death.
For more information see:
- Terminal benefit

chunks.title: Calculating the period of absence — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Calculating the period of absence
The period of an absence from New Zealand for which payment of Employment Transition Assistance can continue (if approved or when approval is not needed) is up to 28 consecutive days, that is, Saturdays and Sundays are included.
In all cases, when assessing the period of absence do not include:
- the date of departure from New Zealand and
- the date of return to New Zealand
If a client is absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period the Employment Transition payment should be suspended from the 29th day (unless they are receiving a main benefit and meet the criteria to pay for longer than 28 days).
Note if a client is leaving New Zealand permanently, the Employment Transition payment must be cancelled from the day after departure.
## Calculating 52 week period
When a client who is receiving a main benefit is paid an Employment Transition payment while they are absent from New Zealand, a client can receive a payment for up to 28 days in total in a 52 week period. The 52 week period is counted in the following way:
- identify the day after the client is intending to leave New Zealand
- count back 52 weeks from this date
- identify any periods of paid absence they have used (counting from the day after they have left New Zealand to the day before they returned to New Zealand)
- subtract the number of days absent from New Zealand from 28 daysThe remainder is the client's entitlement to be paid a benefit while they are absent from New Zealand.
- pay the client the days they have available up to the period of absenceThis may not be the whole of the time they intend to be absent from New Zealand depending on how many days of their entitlement they have left.
For more information see:
- Return to New Zealand
- Permanent absence
