chunks.title: Change in family circumstances — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Change in family circumstances
You will need to review the Employment Transition Assistance to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment whenever there is a change in the client's:
- relationship status or
- the number of dependent children in the client's care
The date to review Employment Transition Assistance from will depend on the action involved. Generally, you should:
## Increase
- increase Employment Transition Assistance from the actual date of the change in circumstances
## Reduce, suspend or cancel
- reduce, suspend or cancel Employment Transition Assistance from the first available date except when the client advises of a change more than 14 days after the event
## False or misleading information
If a client gives false or misleading information you must review Employment Transition Assistance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.

chunks.title: Change in income — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Change in income
You will need to review the Employment Transition Assistance to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment whenever there is a change in the client's income.
All income received by the client must be taken into consideration when calculating the rate of payment for Employment Transition Assistance.
Note you will need to manually calculate the new rate for Employment Transition Assistance whenever there is a change in the client's income.
The date to review Employment Transition Assistance from will depend on the action involved. Generally, you should:

chunks.title: Change in relationship status — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text: The relationship status of a client is important to ensure that they meet the qualifications and are receiving the correct rate of Employment Transition Assistance. When a client has a change in relationship status, you should review the Employment Transition Assistance according to the change in relationship status of the client. You will need to re-calculate the following according to the change in relationship status of the client: - the average net specified income that the client received over the period of the Sustainable Employment Trial - the net specified income that the client now receives, according to the change in relationship status of the client

chunks.title: Re-calculating the average net specified income — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text: Use the average weekly gross amount (recorded in CMS), to calculate the average weekly net rate of abated Supported Living Payment payable according to the clients change in relationship status. You can use the Income Assessment tab in DREW for this calculation.

chunks.title: Step 1 — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text: Enter the client details in DREW and select the appropriate Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) category. Go to the Income Assessment screen and enter the average weekly gross amount (recorded in CMS notes), in the proposed gross field. Select secondary tax, calculate and continue. Enter the client personal earnings details and continue. The summary page in DREW under the proposed heading will provide the average weekly net income from earnings and the average weekly net rate of abated Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) payable.

chunks.title: Step 2 — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text: Add together the average weekly net income and the average weekly net rate of abated Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) shown on the summary page. This amount is the average net specified income amount over the period of the Sustainable Employment Trial.

chunks.title: Step 3 — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text: Record in CMS the: - average weekly gross income - average weekly net income - average weekly net rate of abated Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) - average net specified income

chunks.title: Rate of payment — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text: The payment amount is: - the average net specified income amount that the client received while on the Sustainable Employment Trial less - the net specified income amount a client is currently getting or - the maximum Employment Transition Assistance rate depending on the client's individual circumstances whichever is the lesser. Note if the net specified income amount that a client receives is greater than the average amount of net specified income calculated over the Sustainable Employment Trial, there is 'nil' payment.

chunks.title: Cancellation, suspension or adjustment to rate of payment — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text: When a client's relationship status changes, generally the Employment Transition Assistance should be suspended, cancelled or the rate of payment adjusted from the day after the event. However, there is discretion to cancel or suspend the Employment Transition Assistance from the first available date.

chunks.title: Change in the number of dependent children — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Change in the number of dependent children
The number of dependent children in the care of a client is important to ensure that they meet the qualifications and are getting the correct rate of Employment Transition Assistance.
When a client has a change in the number of dependent children, MSD should review the Employment Transition Assistance according to the change in the number of dependent children.
MSD will need to re-calculate the following according to the client's change in the number of dependent children, the:
- average net specified income that the client got over the period of the Sustainable Employment Trial
- net specified income that the client now gets, according to the change in relationship status of the client
## Re-calculating the average net specified income
Use the average weekly gross amount (recorded in CMS), to calculate the average weekly net rate of abated Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) payable according to the clients change in relationship status.
Use the Income Assessment tab in DREW for this calculation.
## Step 1
Enter the client details in DREW and select the appropriate Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) category. Go to the Income Assessment screen and enter the average weekly gross amount (recorded CMS notes), in the proposed gross field. Select secondary tax, calculate and continue. Enter the client personal earnings details and continue.
The summary page in DREW under the proposed heading will provide the average weekly net income from earnings and the average weekly net rate of abated Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) payable.
## Step 3
Record in CMS the average:
- weekly gross income
- weekly net income
- weekly net rate of abated Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability)
- net specified income
## Step 4
Send the client a manual letter from CMS.
## Rate of payment
The payment amount is the:
- average net specified income amount that the client got while on a Sustainable Employment Trial
less
- net specified income amount a client is currently getting
or
- maximum Employment Transition Assistance depending on the client's individual circumstances

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client is obliged to advise Work and Income of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Employment Transition payment.
You may also review Employment Transition payment at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.
Note whenever you review the Employment Transition payment you must send a manual letter from CMS to advise the client of any changes to their rate of payment.

chunks.title: Surviving partner or dependent child — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Surviving partner or dependent child
When a client dies (and there is a surviving partner or dependent child) before a decision is made on an application or review for Employment Transition payment you can continue the application or review process as if the client had not died.
## Single client
When there is no surviving partner or dependent children the application should generally be declined.
However, if there is a request for the application to be decided or the circumstances of the situation merit it, consult your manager client service delivery for a decision.

chunks.title: Client does not return — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Client does not return
If a client's Employment Transition payment is suspended because they are absent from New Zealand and they do not return their benefit record will automatically cancel in SWIFTT, 8 weeks after the date of suspension.
Note if the client had been approved continued payment of benefit for the first 28 days of the absence, this is not established as a debt.

chunks.title: Client receives main benefit income increased — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Client receives main benefit income increased
You will need to review the Employment Transition Assistance to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment whenever there is a change in the client's income.
## Reassessing the rate of payment
When a client receives an increase in income you must re-calculate the rate of payment to ensure the client is receiving the correct rate of Employment Transition Assistance.
## Main benefit suspended
If the client receives income above the income cut-out point for their benefit type, the main benefit will be suspended.
## Client receiving less than Supported Living Payment cut-out point
Clients receiving a main benefit and are receiving income less than the Supported Living Payment income cut-out point but their main benefit is suspended because of income, the client may still be eligible for an Employment Transition Assistance.
If the client is still eligible for this payment, calculate the new rate of Employment Transition Assistance as if the client was a non-beneficiary. This payment can be paid by completing a backdated review action.
## Income increase continues
If the increase in income is likely to continue you should test the client's eligibility to non-beneficiary assistance and reassess the rate of the Employment Transition Assistance for the client as a non-beneficiary.
If a client receives income above the Supported Living Payment income cut-out point, the rate of payment is nil and the assistance must be suspended.
If the client continues to receive income above Supported Living Payment income cut-out point for 8 consecutive weeks, the payment should be cancelled as the client does not qualify for the payment.
For more information see:
- Change in income
- Examples income increased
- Payment

chunks.title: Client receives main benefit income reduced — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Client receives main benefit income reduced
You will need to review the Employment Transition Assistance to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment whenever there is a change in the client's income.
## Reassessing the rate of payment
When a client receives a reduced level of income you must re-calculate the rate of payment to ensure the client is receiving the correct rate of Employment Transition Assistance.
## Income reduced to nil
If the client's income reduces to 'nil' you must determine if the client is still in employment.
If the client is still in employment but is not receiving any income from employment, the Employment Transition Assistance can be paid for a maximum of four consecutive weeks only. If the client receives this payment for four consecutive weeks the payment must then be cancelled from the 5th week as the client does not qualify for the payment.
## Cancel payment
If the client is not in employment the Employment Transition Assistance must be cancelled as the client does not qualify for the payment.
The Employment Transition Assistance cannot be re-granted after cancellation unless the client qualifies for Supported Living Payment and completes another Sustainable Employment Trial and meets the eligibility criteria for this payment.
Note when the clients Employment Transition Assistance has been cancelled or the client is no longer in employment you should check the client's eligibility to other benefits or assistance.
For more information see:
- Examples income reduced

chunks.title: Death of a client — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Death of a client
The Employment Transition payment generally stops from the day following the date of death. However, there is some discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days after the date of death:
- to avoid creating a debt or
- as terminal benefit when there are other circumstances that justify payment
Note when a client has a Community Services or SuperGold Card, the card must be manually cancelled and death details added to Person Details screen in CMS.
Contact the Card Centre on 0800 999 999 or email to request cancellation of the card.
## Cost of funeral
The person responsible for the cost of the funeral may be able to receive a Funeral Grant.
For more information see:
- Client dies before grant or review
- Death of a dependent child
- Debt recovery
- Terminal benefit
- Verification

chunks.title: Death of a dependent child — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Death of a dependent child
When a dependent child dies you will need to review the Employment Transition payment to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.

chunks.title: Arrears — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Arrears
When a client has arrears owing to them at the time of their death and they have an outstanding debt balance, you should attempt to recover the debt, in full, from the final payment.
## Terminal benefit
When a client has an outstanding debt balance and terminal benefit is payable, you should not recover the debt in full from the terminal benefit payment.

chunks.text: Example 1 - Rate a single non-beneficiary client aged 25 years earning $572.00 gross per week would get if they did not want to apply for a main benefit. Average net specified income (recorded in CMS) $627.19 Less net specified income for a non-beneficiary earning $572.00 gross per week (DREW primary tax rate) $481.60 Equals $145.59 The maximum Employment Transition payment for single client aged 25+ years (as at 1 April 2026) $424.60 Pay lesser amount $145.59 The new rate of payment for the client in this situation, earning $572.00 gross per week is $145.59. Example 2 - Rate of Employment Transition Assistance that a single client aged 25+ years earning $572.00 gross per week would get if they applied for Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability). Average net specified income (recorded in CMS) $627.19 Less net specified income for Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) client, earning $572.00 gross per week (net income $462.75 plus net rate of reduced Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) $72.92 as at 1 April 2026) $535.67 Equals Employment Transition Assistance payment $91.52 The maximum Employment Transition Assistance payment for single client aged 25+ years (as at 1 April 2026) $424.60 Pay lesser amount $91.52 The new rate of payment for the client in this situation earning $572.00 Gross per week is $91.52.

chunks.title: Imprisonment — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Imprisonment
Employment Transition assistance is generally not paid when a client is in prison.
The Employment Transition payment should stop from the day following the date of imprisonment as the client will not qualify for this assistance.

chunks.title: Non-beneficiary income increased — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Non-beneficiary income increased
You will need to review the Employment Transition Assistance to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment whenever there is a change in the client's income.
## Income above Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) income cut-out point
If a client receives income above the Supported Living Payment income cut-out point, the rate of payment is 'nil' therefore the Employment Transition Assistance must be suspended.
If the client continues to receive income above Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) income cut-out point for 8 consecutive weeks, the payment should be cancelled from the 9th week as the client does not qualify for the payment.

chunks.title: Non-beneficiary income reduced — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Non-beneficiary income reduced
You will need to review the Employment Transition Assistance to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is getting the correct rate of payment whenever there is a change in the client's income.
Note clients not getting a main benefit will be paying primary tax.
## Reassessing the rate of payment
When a client receives a reduced level of income you must re-calculate the rate of payment to ensure the client is getting the correct rate of Employment Transition Assistance.
## Income reduced
If a client's has a reduction in income that would make them eligible for a benefit, the client must be advised that they may be entitled to a benefit.
If this is a temporary situation the client may choose to continue to receive the Employment Transition Assistance as a non-beneficiary. All other non-beneficiary assistance should be reassessed to ensure that the client is receiving their full entitlement.
If the income reduction is likely to continue you will need to determine if the client qualifies for a main benefit. If the client chooses to receive a main benefit the Employment Transition Assistance must be calculated according to the client's income and main benefit.
The client must make the final decision on the assistance that they would like to receive after being given all relevant information.
## Income reduced to nil
If the client's income reduces to 'nil' you must determine if the client is still in employment.
If the client is still in employment but is not receiving any income from employment, the Employment Transition Assistance can be paid for a maximum of 4 consecutive weeks only.
If the client receives this payment for 4 consecutive weeks the payment must then be cancelled as the client does not qualify for the payment.
## Cancel payment
If the client is not in employment the Employment Transition Assistance must be cancelled from the first available date as the client does not qualify for the payment.
Note when the clients Employment Transition Assistance has been cancelled or the client is no longer in employment you should check the client's eligibility to other benefits or assistance.
The Employment Transition payment cannot be re-granted after cancellation unless the client qualifies for Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability), completes another Sustainable Employment Trial, and meets the eligibility criteria for this payment.

chunks.title: Obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand (main beneficiaries only) — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand (main beneficiaries only)
All clients getting a main benefit must tell the Ministry of Social Development before they leave New Zealand. If the client or partner does not tell the Ministry before they travel overseas, their benefit payments will stop from the day after they leave New Zealand.
Clients who do not continue getting a main benefit while overseas may be still be able to keep getting Employment Transition Assistance, if their absence does not affect the client's eligibility for this assistance and they told the Ministry of their absence before travelling overseas.
They must be returning to employment immediately after their absence from New Zealand and is limited to the first 28 days in any 52 week period.
For more information about absence from New Zealand see:
- Approved travel reasons in relevant main benefit
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period in relevant main benefit
## Approved Information Sharing Agreement with New Zealand Customs Service
The Ministry of Social Development has an Approved Information Sharing Agreement with New Zealand Customs Service that identifies clients who have left New Zealand if they are getting a main benefit.
Once identified, the client's eligibility to keep getting their benefit payments while they are absent from New Zealand is automatically determined by Ministry systems.
## Does not advise of departure
If the client has not told the Ministry they are leaving New Zealand their main benefit will be suspended immediately from the day after they leave New Zealand. As a result, their Employment Transition Assistance will also stop.
The Integrity Intervention Centre will determine if any overpayment has occurred and will establish the debt and advise the client.
If a client challenges the information match this process is managed by the Integrity Intervention Centre.
## Client contacts us from overseas
Clients may contact us from overseas to advise of their travel. When they do this their main benefit may be:
- resumed from the date they told the Ministry of their absence if their travel is allowed or
- backdated to the departure date (in limited circumstances)
For more information see:
- Paying benefit when client failed to advise of absence in relevant main benefit
- Approved travel reasons in relevant main benefit
- Action on return to New Zealand
- Calculating the period of absence

chunks.title: Client getting a main benefit — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Client getting a main benefit
Where a client is paid their main benefit while they are absent from New Zealand (either because they meet the criteria for approved travel or the requirement to approved travel does not apply to them) they can continue to receive their main benefit and their Employment Transition payment for up to 28 days in any 52 week period, unless they meet the criteria to be paid their main benefit for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
They must be going to return to their employment immediately after their absence from New Zealand.
Clients who do not continue to receive a main benefit while overseas because their travel is not allowed may still continue to receive Employment Transition Assistance, if their absence does not affect the client's eligibility for this assistance and they have advised Work and Income of their absence prior to their international travel.
They must be returning to their employment immediately after returning to New Zealand and this assistance is limited to the first 28 days in any 52 week period.
For more information about Absence from New Zealand see:
- Approved travel reasons in relevant main benefit
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period in relevant main benefit
## Information required from client when advising they intend to travel
When a client contacts you to advise that they intend travelling overseas you need to obtain the following information:
- date of departure
- date of return
## Non-beneficiary Extra Help payment to continue
In all cases where you have agreed to the continued payment of benefit for up to the first 28 days of absence, you will need to create a bring-up in BRUPA screen to check that the client has returned.
If the client has not returned on the 29th day you can suspend their benefit.
When you have agreed to the continued payment of benefit for the first 28 days of absence, and the client intends to be absent for more than 28 days, you will need to create a future suspension in their SWIFTT record for the 29th day of absence.
## Non-beneficiary Extra Help payment will not continue
Where payment of Employment Transition payment will not continue because they do not meet the eligibility criteria due to their absence you will need to suspend the benefit from:
- the day after departure

chunks.title: Permanent absence — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Permanent absence
If the client is leaving New Zealand permanently the Employment Transition payment must be cancelled from the day after departure.

chunks.title: Return to New Zealand — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Return to New Zealand
When the client returns to New Zealand you will need to confirm the following:
- date of return to New Zealand
- date of departure (if client did not advise before leaving New Zealand)
- reason for absence (if not already known)
- did the client apply for or receive any benefit or pension in the country that they travelled to or
an increase in the benefit or pension that they already receive from that country during their stay there?
For more information see:
- Action on return to New Zealand
- Client does not return
- Obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand (main beneficiaries only)

chunks.title: Six monthly Review — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Six monthly Review
The Employment Transition assistance must be reviewed every 6 months from the date the payment is granted.
The purpose of a 6 monthly review is to:
- ensure that the client stills meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment
- check for any changes to their circumstances
- verify any income received over the last 6 months
- check that the client still needs this assistance to continue to work more than 15 hours per week.
Note you will need to create a bring up in the BRUPA screen to review the payment 6 months after the Employment Transition assistance has been granted.
The Employment Transition payment must be reviewed whenever a client advises of a change in their circumstances.
You may also review Employment Transition payment at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.
Note whenever you review the Employment Transition payment you must send a manual letter from CMS to advise the client of any changes to their rate of payment.

chunks.title: Terminal benefit — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Terminal benefit
When a non-beneficiary client dies, Employment Transition payment generally stops from the day after the date of death. However, there is some discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days.
When payment is continued after the date of death, it is referred to as terminal benefit.
Circumstances where you might consider continued payment beyond a client's date of death include:
- when the deceased client's domestic situation results in a transition cost for a family member, causing hardshipExample: accommodation and other household costs when client has been sharing accommodation
or
- when there are exceptional and justified costs associated with the death of the clientExample: multiple deaths within one family
You should not continue payment for 28 days following the death of a client to meet funeral expenses. A Funeral Grant is available for this purpose.

chunks.title: Terminal benefit rate — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Terminal benefit rate
The provision to continue the payment for up to 28 days following the date of death is referred to as terminal benefit.
Employment Transition payment is continued at the rate which was payable to the client at the date of death.
## SWIFTT
If you are paying terminal benefit you will need to manually calculate entitlement and make an adhoc payment in the SAHPA screen.
There is no automatic provision for the payment of terminal benefit for Employment Transition payment in SWIFTT.

chunks.title: Verification — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Verification
You must be satisfied that you can accurately identify the deceased client's record.
Generally we will accept verbal notification of a client's death. This advice can be acted on when you determine the relationship of the caller to the deceased client and obtaining sufficient information to provide confirmation of the deceased's identity.
Follow-up verification should generally be requested. A copy of the death certificate or a copy of the death notice is acceptable support documentation.

chunks.title: Verification of changes — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Verification of changes
At the time of the review you should also check that the client has not had any other changes to their personal circumstances. It is the client's responsibility to provide appropriate verification of any changes in their circumstances for example:
- relationship status - the client may have commenced living in a relationship
proof: personal statement from the client
- children left care
proof: personal statement from client
- children came into care
Proof required, for example, letter from previous caregiver or birth certificate (if another child born to client).
Where you determine that the client has had a change in circumstances that affects their entitlement or rate of payment for the Employment Transition Assistance you must recalculate the payment and complete the following actions:
- amend the rate of payment
- note CMS
- send the client a manual letter from CMS

chunks.title: Verification of income — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance > changes and reviews employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Verification of income
At the time of the review the client is to provide verification of any income they have received during the review period of 6 months.
If the client cannot provide verification (for example payslips) then you can contact the employer to verify income details in the last 6 months if the client consents.

chunks.title: Commencement date — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
The Employment Transition Assistance is granted from:
- the date of application or
- 1 July 2005
whichever is the later.

chunks.title: Determining the reduced level of income — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Determining the reduced level of income
To qualify for Employment Transition Assistance the client must have a reduced level of income after completing a Sustainable Employment Trial.
To find the reduced level of income, the net specified income the client gets after the Supported Living Payment has been cancelled, must be less than the average net specified income the client earned while on the employment trial.
The average net specified income is calculated over the period the client participated in the employment trial.
## Example
A single client aged 26 years got an average net specified income over the Sustainable Employment Trial of $344.12 per week.
The client's Supported Living Payment has been cancelled after completing the Sustainable Employment Trial as the client keeps working more than 15 hours per week.
The client now qualifies for Jobseeker Support: health condition, injury or disability, and at the time of application for this payment their net specified income is $247.99.
The client has a reduced level of income as their net specified income after completing the trial and cancellation of their Supported Living Payment is less than their average net specified income over the Sustainable Employment Trial.

chunks.title: Ending the payment — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Ending the payment
The Employment Transition payment is paid until the client:
- ceases employment
- has earned income over the Supported Living Payment income cut-out point for eight consecutive weeks
- does not receive any income from employment for four consecutive weeks
- does not need this assistance to continue to work 15 hours or more per week in open employment
- qualifies for Supported Living Payment or
- is not in employment
whichever occurs first.
Note when the Employment Transition payment has been cancelled it cannot be re-granted unless the client qualifies for Supported Living Payment, completes another Sustainable Employment Trial, and then meets the qualifications for the Employment Transition payment.
For more information see:
- Payment
- Commencement date

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The Employment Transition Assistance is a non-taxable payment that is available for clients who have a reduced level of income after completing a Supported Living Payment Sustainable Employment Trial and need assistance to continue in employment.

chunks.title: Net specified income — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Net specified income
To calculate the net specified income, add the amount of net income (gross income less income tax and ACC earner levy) to the net rate of main benefit payable after income has been charged against that benefit.
If a client’s income is above the cut-out point for their main benefit, but less than the appropriate Supported Living Payment cut-out point, their net specified income is their net income only.
## Example
A married couple with no children earns $300 gross earnings per week and also receives a Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability.
## Step 1
Calculate the net income.
Gross wages
$300.00
Less secondary income tax and ACC levy (use "S" tax rate)
$57.75
Net income
$242.25
## Step 2
Calculate how the net income will affect the benefit payment
Gross weekly wages
$300.00
Less income allowed before benefit is affected
$160.00
Equals income that will reduce benefit payment
$140.00
Reduction in benefit rate $0.70 per $1.00 ($140 x 0.7)
$98.00
## Step 3
Calculate the net rate of Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) payable after charging income.
Maximum net rate of Jobseeker Support - married, civil union or de facto couple - without children (as at 1 April 2026)
$633.94
Less reduction due to income (from step 2)
$98.00
Net rate of Jobseeker Support payable
$535.94
## Step 4
Add the net income to the net rate of reduced Jobseeker Support.
Net income (from step 1)
$242.25
Plus net rate of Jobseeker Support payable (from step 3)
$535.94
Net specified income
$778.19

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Payment
The Employment Transition Payment can be paid to an eligible client who has a reduced level of income and needs assistance to continue to work 15 hours or more per week after completing the Sustainable Employment Trial.
## Rate of payment
The payment amount is:
- the average net specified income the client received while participating in the Sustainable Employment Trial
less
- the net specified income amount a client is currently getting
or
- the maximum Employment Transition Payment depending on the client's individual circumstances
whichever is the lesser.
Note if the net specified income amount that a client receives is greater than the average amount of net specified income calculated over the Sustainable Employment Trial, there is 'nil' payment.
## Payment code
It is important that all applications are coded correctly.
Payment should be made using the miscellaneous subsidy screen in SWIFTT using the following codes.
Miscellaneous subsidy code
835
Reason for payment code - Employment Transition Payment
519

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > employment transition assistance
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
A client may qualify for Employment Transition Assistance if they:
- have completed a Sustainable Employment Trial and are no longer eligible for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
- will have a reduced level of income after completing the Sustainable Employment Trial
- are still working in open employment (not sheltered employment) for 15 hours or more per week on a regular basis
- need the assistance to continue to work 15 hours or more per week in open employment
- are earning income below the Supported Living Payment gross income cut out point
- are eligible for a main benefit or non-beneficiary assistance
For more information see:
- Supported Living Payment Sheltered employment
- Supported Living Payment Sustainable Employment Trial
- Determining the reduced level of income
- Payment

chunks.title: Band 1 — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: To get a Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 1 a client must: - not meet the entry-level requirements of the job (as decided by the employer) and - be disadvantaged in the labour market and - meet all other eligibility criteria A client does not need to be at risk of long-term benefit receipt to qualify. Clients getting Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 1 are generally: - recently unemployed and affected by economic disruption to their occupation, industry or region e.g. pandemic - unemployed but not qualified to get a main benefit because they have a working partner with a low income - on a main benefit and disadvantaged in the labour market, but not at risk of long-term benefit receipt e.g. a client who needs support to get into or stay in unsubsidised employment, but they would not be expected to be on benefit for 6 months or more - underemployed or facing low job security in their employment Clients aged 65 years or over getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension may qualify under payment band 1.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Marama and Zeke are a low-income family with 3 children. Zeke works as a labourer and earns $940 gross per week. They get Accommodation Supplement and Working for Families but struggle most weeks with their living costs. Marama has been out of the workforce for several years raising their children, so she lacks recent work experience and has limited skills and education. This makes Marama disadvantaged in the labour market. MSD knows of a barista position available that would suit Marama, but she does not meet the entry level requirements and needs support to get the job. As Marama is disadvantaged in the labour market but not at risk of long-term benefit receipt, MSD approves a payment band 1 Flexi-wage Subsidy as this is the best fit for Marama's situation.

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Sefina is qualified in Human Resources and has been working in the industry for 5 years. Sefina has a partner earning $42,000 a year. After taking some time off, Sefina decided she wants to make a career change and likes the idea of project management. She has a project management qualification but has no work experience in the field, so she has not been able to find a job. Sefina wants to know if she can get Flexi-wage Subsidy so an employer would be more likely to give her a job. Sefina is not disadvantaged in the labour market because she has qualifications, considerable experience and transferrable skills, and is voluntarily making a career change so she does not qualify for a Flexi-wage Subsidy.

chunks.title: Band 2 — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Band 2
To get a Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 2, a client must
- not meet the entry-level requirements of the job (as decided by the employer) and
- be at risk of long-term benefit receipt and
- meet all other eligibility criteria
The client does not have to be disadvantaged in the labour market. However most clients who are at risk of long-term benefit receipt and getting a main benefit are disadvantaged.
Most clients getting Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 2 will have been on a main benefit for a long period of time.
However, there may be some who are not on a main benefit or have recently moved to a main benefit and who are at risk of long-term benefit receipt.
This could include those who would qualify under payment band 1 but they have recently been getting a main benefit and need more support to get into and stay in employment.
## Example
Toni was a full-time carer over the last 10 years for her mum until she passed away a year ago, she has been getting Jobseeker Support since that time.
Toni has learnt many caring skills while looking after her mother and she would like to work as a full-time caregiver in a rest home.
She is considered at risk of long-term benefit receipt due to the length of time she has been away from the workforce.
A local rest home has advertised a permanent vacancy for a full-time caregiver.
Toni wants the job but does not meet some of the entry level requirements. She needs a first aid certificate and a Level 1 caregiving certificate, with a component of hours working in the rest home under supervision and competency in managing electronic records.
The employer negotiates a Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 2 with MSD for a period of 36 weeks (the set period).
For the first 18 weeks the subsidy rate payable is a higher rate at $300 per week to cover the additional supervision needed when Toni first starts in the role. She will also be sitting her first aid certificate and Level 1 caregiving certificate in this time.
Over the remaining 18 weeks the subsidy is payable is lower at $200 per week as Toni will now be able to complete a number of her duties independently.
Extra assistance of $2,000 is granted for employment-related training, the First Aid course and the Caregiver Training course. The total amount payable over 36 weeks is $11,000.

chunks.title: Band 3 - Disadvantaged and at risk of long-term benefit receipt — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Band 3 - Disadvantaged and at risk of long-term benefit receipt
Clients who are assessed as disadvantaged in the labour market and at risk of long-term benefit receipt may qualify for Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 3.
This group are likely to have the most complex circumstances and are the hardest to place into unsubsidised employment. They are:
- likely to have significant barriers to employment and
- face serious disadvantage in the labour market and
- have a high level of risk of long-term benefit receipt
Clients in this group need more support than other groups to meet the entry level requirements of a job, including a higher rate of Flexi-wage Subsidy that may be paid over a longer period.
They are also more likely to need extra assistance for employment-related training and in-work support.
## Example
Marcus is 20 and has Downs Syndrome. He has been getting Supported Living Payment since he was 16 and has never worked but is really keen to find a job. Marcus is disadvantaged in the labour market and at risk of long-term benefit receipt.
There is a suitable opportunity for Marcus at a not-for-profit organisation providing work opportunities for people with disabilities.
Marcus will be working at his local mall in the food court; cleaning and clearing tables as well as general cleaning of the food court area. He will work 30 hours a week at the adult minimum wage.
MSD talks to the employer, and they decide Marcus will need mentoring, on-the-job experience and training over approximately 9 to 10 months to support him to reach the entry level requirements of the job.
Based on this, MSD approves a Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 3 at $350 per week over 40 weeks to reflect the level and duration of on the job training.
Extra assistance is also approved to cover the employment-related training costs for a Food and Hygiene certificate that Marcus needs as well as in-work support for mentoring and pastoral care to ensure Marcus has the support he needs to stay in work.

chunks.title: Band 3 - Disadvantaged, at risk and has specific needs — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Band 3 - Disadvantaged, at risk and has specific needs
Clients who are assessed as disadvantaged in the labour market and at risk of long-term benefit receipt may also have specific employment needs that mean they need tailored support to get into and stay in unsubsidised employment.
This group are not likely to have as high a level of disadvantage in the labour market or be at risk of long-term benefit receipt as other payment band 3 Flexi-wage Subsidy clients.
They may be clients who:
- have little or no previous work experience and are having difficulty gaining permanent employment even with a Flexi-wage Subsidy
- would benefit from subsidised temporary work to help them gain employment skills and experience that will support them towards unsubsidised employment
- are in a role at risk of redundancy and can move into a temporary job until their substantive role becomes more stable, however they do not meet the entry level requirements of the temporary job
- are in a temporary role and are having difficulty getting permanent, unsubsidised employment as they do not meet entry level requirements. These clients would benefit from support to help them into permanent, unsubsidised employment
## Example
Meika is 19 years old and left school with no NCEA qualifications. She has been getting Jobseeker Support since she turned 18 and lives at home with her parents in Woodville.
Meika has chronic kidney disease that impacts her ability to work more than 15 hours per week.
Her condition is long-term, and her work capacity is not expected to improve. She is both disadvantaged in the labour market and at risk of long-term benefit receipt.
She also has specific employment needs because she lives in a rural area with very few employment opportunities.

chunks.title: Band 3 - Setting the subsidy duration — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Flexi-wage Subsidy supports clients who need additional assistance to gain the skills and experience needed to meet the entry level requirements of a job. This supports the client to get into and stay in unsubsidised employment. The duration of a Flexi-wage Subsidy paid under payment band 3 is decided based on the: - expected length of time it will take a client to meet the entry level requirements of a job (as decided by the employer) and - duration of any extra assistance needed e.g. in-work Support or employment related training Note Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment bands 1 and 2 has a set duration.

chunks.title: Example — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Vanushi has been on a benefit for the last 7 years and is keen to get into work but needs some training and work experience. MSD finds an opportunity with an employer, and negotiates a Flexi-wage Subsidy for 6 months. This is how long the employer thinks it will take for Vanushi to complete her agreed training and gain on-the-job experience to meet the entry level requirements of the role.

chunks.title: Subsidy extensions — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: An extension of Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 3 can be negotiated if: - the client has not met the entry level requirements for the job within the originally agreed duration and - it is appropriate and necessary and - the employer has not reached the 52-week limit of $22,000 for the client Note only a Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 3 can be extended.

chunks.title: Appropriate and necessary — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Before extending a subsidy, MSD must consider: - the reason the employer believes the client has not reached the skill level required - if all previously agreed training has been delivered and the outcomes - if any other assistance is required e.g. in-work support that was not identified originally A Flexi-wage Subsidy must not be extended because the employer cannot afford to keep the client on without the subsidy.

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: After an initial subsidy period of 26 weeks, Lou hasn't met the entry level requirements of the role. Lou is determined and motivated and the employer would like to keep her on but she has struggled to keep up with the training she needs. Lou had been out of the workforce for an extended period of time. It has been years since Lou was in a learning environment, and she hasn't skilled up as fast as expected. The employer has delivered on the agreed training Lou needs and thinks another 8 weeks of on-the-job training would get Lou at the level that she needs to be. MSD agrees to extend Flexi-wage Subsidy for an additional 8 weeks at the same rate.

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Sara has not quite met the entry level requirements of the role as she is still having trouble using the coffee machine and making café standard coffees. The employer would like to extend the subsidy for a further 8 weeks, but the total amount paid to them for Sara over the last 52 weeks is $22,000, the maximum limit. MSD declines the employer’s request for the extension.

chunks.title: Example 3 — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Jonah has not quite met the entry level requirements of the role due to him not attending training the employer provided. He missed the training on a few occasions because he overslept when a friend was staying over, and they were catching up with other friends. The employer would still like to extend the subsidy for a further 2 months to enable Jonah to finish the training. MSD declines the application for an extension because Jonah should have attended the training when it was initially available, and he does not have a good reason for not attending.

chunks.title: Band 3 - Setting the subsidy rate — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Band 3 - Setting the subsidy rate
Flexi-wage Subsidy supports clients who need additional assistance to gain the skills and experience needed to meet the entry level requirements of a job.
The rate of Flexi-wage Subsidy paid under payment band 3 should reflect the:
- level of support required for the client to meet the entry level requirements of the job and
- time it will take for that to happen
The rate of subsidy should take account of:
- the client's specific barriers to employment
- the client's skills, qualifications and employment experience
- the rate of pay and the number of hours per week the employer is offering
- any extra assistance required e.g. in-work support, employment-related training
- the cost of any training and/or in-work support that will be needed
Note where Flexi-wage Subsidy is granted for a client working less than 30 hours per week, a pro rata subsidy rate is paid.
## Maximum weekly rate
The weekly rate of Flexi-wage Subsidy cannot be more than what a person earning the adult minimum wage for 30 hours work per week would get (gross).
## Example
Rino is 21 and on Jobseeker Support. He has a mild form of autism, so he struggles with social situations and being around a lot of people. Because of this, finding suitable work has been difficult.
A permanent full-time vacancy has become available in a packhouse that would allow Rino to work in his own space and at his own pace once trained.
The job description shows the entry level requirements as grading, packing, and storing produce as well as training in food, health and safety regulations.
Rino does not meet any of the requirements which means the employer will need to provide more support over a longer period than they would for someone who meets at least some of the requirements.
The employer tells MSD they expect it will take Rino around 4-5 months to meet the entry level requirements of the job.
The duration of the subsidy is agreed for a period of 20 weeks, the longest period of time the employer thinks it will take for Rino to meet the entry level requirements.

chunks.title: Band 3 — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Band 3
To get a Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 3, a client must:
- not meet the entry-level requirements of the job (as decided by the employer), and either: be disadvantaged in the labour market and at risk of long-term benefit receipt orbe disadvantaged in the labour market and at risk of long-term benefit receipt and have specific employment needs and
- be disadvantaged in the labour market and at risk of long-term benefit receipt or
- be disadvantaged in the labour market and at risk of long-term benefit receipt and have specific employment needs and
- meet all other eligibility criteria

chunks.title: Bands 1 and 2 - Setting the subsidy rate — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Bands 1 and 2 - Setting the subsidy rate
Flexi-wage Subsidy supports clients who need additional assistance to gain the skills and experience needed to meet the entry level requirements of a job.
This supports the client to get into and stay in unsubsidised employment.
The rate of Flexi-wage Subsidy paid under payment bands 1 and 2 should take account of:
- the client's specific barriers to employment
- the client's skills, qualifications, and employment experience
- the level of support required for the person to meet entry level requirements
- the rate of pay and the number of hours per week the employer is offering
- any extra assistance required e.g. in-work support, employment-related training
- the cost of any training and/or in-work support that will be needed
Note when Flexi-wage Subsidy is granted for a client working less than 30 hours per week, a pro rata subsidy rate is paid.

chunks.title: Client eligibility criteria — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Client eligibility criteria
To get Flexi-wage the client must:
- not meet the entry-level requirements of the job (as decided by the employer) and either: be disadvantaged in the labour market orbe at risk of long-term benefit receipt orhave specific employment needs and
- be disadvantaged in the labour market or
- be at risk of long-term benefit receipt or
- have specific employment needs and
- meet all other eligibility criteria
## At risk of long-term benefit receipt and disadvantaged in the labour market
Generally, a client does not have to be at risk of long-term benefit receipt and disadvantaged in the labour market to get a Flexi-wage Subsidy.
Although clients may be in both situations this is not a requirement.
There will be some situations when a client is disadvantaged in the labour market but not at risk of long-term benefit receipt, for example a client with a partner who is working and earning a low income, but not low enough to mean the couple qualify for a main benefit.
To qualify for Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 3, clients with specific employment needs must be both disadvantaged in the labour market and at risk of long term benefit receipt.
If they do not meet both of these criteria, they may qualify for Flexi-wage Subsidy but only under payment bands 1 or 2.
## Income test
All clients not getting a main benefit when they apply must meet an income test to qualify for Flexi-wage Subsidy.

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
Clients aged 65 or over getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension generally only qualify for Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 1. To qualify under payment band 1, MSD must consider the client to be disadvantaged in the labour market.
Clients in this situation generally do not qualify for Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 2 or 3 because they are not considered at risk of long-term benefit receipt.
Note clients who are aged 65 and over who are not getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension may qualify for Flexi-wage Subsidy under any payment band, if they meet all the qualifications.
## Clients who turn 65 when getting Flexi-wage Subsidy
An employer can keep getting Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 2 or 3 for a client who turns 65 years and qualifies for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension, if MSD is satisfied, they should continue to get it.
Some considerations to determine being satisfied are:
- whether the client is benefiting from Flexi-wage Subsidy and
- if the individual intends to continue working, rather than retiring

chunks.title: Core eligibility criteria — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Core eligibility criteria
To qualify for a Flexi-wage Subsidy, the client must:
- be aged 16 or older and
- meet the residence requirements and
- meet the income test if they are not getting a main benefit and
- not be getting other assistance paid for the same or a similar purpose
For clients aged over 65 years, see:
- Clients 65 years and over
Note if the client does not meet one of the qualifications above, they cannot get Flexi-wage Subsidy.
## Other eligibility criteria
If the client meets the qualifications above, MSD must also consider if they:
- meet the client eligibility criteria and
- have a job offer that meets the job eligibility criteria and
- have an employer that meets the employer eligibility criteria

chunks.title: Deciding if a client has specific employment needs — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Deciding if a client has specific employment needs
A client who has specific employment needs is likely to be disadvantaged in the labour market and may qualify for Flexi-wage if they meet all other eligibility criteria.
Specific employment needs means:
- the client has no or limited employment skills and experience and would benefit from temporary work to help them develop the skills and experience they need to staircase towards unsubsidised employment
- the client's job is at risk of redundancy, and they would benefit from temporary work until their substantive job is no longer at risk, but they need to develop employment skills to meet the entry level requirements of the temporary job
## Example
Sam has an extensive criminal history and has recently been released from prison after serving a 6 year sentence.
He is getting Jobseeker Support and is keen to get into work and turn things around but has gone to several interviews with no success.
Due to his criminal record and6 years away from the labour market, he is disadvantaged, as well as at risk of long-term benefit receipt.
He is unlikely to be employed in a position that involves handling money because of his previous convictions, which is a significant barrier to gaining employment.
However, an employer is looking for a temporary full-time welder, 40 hours a week at $25 per hour for the next 9 months.
Sam has his MIG welding certificate but hasn't worked in the industry for a long time.
The employer is willing to take Sam on with some support to help him meet the entry level requirements for the job.
This will include Sam working alongside an engineer so he can get his Arc welding certificate and learn to read engineering plans.
This will assist Sam with his specific employment needs, to help him get the skills for permanent employment.

chunks.title: Deciding if a client is at risk of long-term benefit receipt — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: A client who is at risk of long-term benefit receipt may qualify for Flexi-wage if they meet all other eligibility criteria. At risk of long-term benefit receipt means there is a risk the client will get or continue getting a main benefit for an indefinite period. To decide whether a client is at risk of getting a benefit long-term, you need to consider a number of factors. These include: - demographic information e.g. age, gender, ethnicity and location - level of skills, employment experience and education - specific barriers to employment e.g. medical conditions, caring responsibilities - benefit status and history e.g. current period they have been getting a main benefit, time spent on and off benefit, age when they first started getting a benefit - previous times they got, or participated in, MSD employment programmes and services

chunks.title: Example 1 — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Ben lives in Auckland and has been getting Jobseeker Support for a year and a half. He left school in Year 12 with NCEA Level 1. He does not have any other qualifications. Ben suffers from generalised anxiety disorder which wasn't diagnosed until just before he started getting Jobseeker Support. Because of this, Ben has a patchy work history as his anxiety made it hard for him to hold down a job. These factors mean Ben is at risk of long-term benefit receipt and an employer may be able to get a Flexi-wage Subsidy for him if all the eligibility criteria are met.

chunks.title: Getting or qualify to get a main benefit — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Generally, a client at risk of long-term benefit receipt is either: - getting or qualifies for a main benefit or - has a partner who is getting or qualifies for a main benefit

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Kris is 46 and has been on Jobseeker Support for several years. A back injury meant he could not keep working as a storeman due to the heavy lifting requirements. Kris has found an employer willing to take him on as a dispatcher. Kris hasn't worked in dispatching for over 15 years and technology has advanced, which means he does not meet the entry level requirements set out in the job description. As Kris has been getting a main benefit for some time and needs help to return to work, he is considered at risk of long-term benefit receipt. An employer may be able to get Flexi-wage Subsidy for him if all the eligibility criteria are met.

chunks.title: On benefit and not at risk — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Not everyone getting a main benefit is at risk of long-term benefit receipt, for example a person who is work ready, is considered capable of getting into and staying in work without our help, and only needs a benefit for a short time while they find work. These clients would not meet the criteria to get a Flexi-wage Subsidy as they are not at risk of long-term benefit receipt.

chunks.title: Example 3 — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Sergei is a qualified engineer of 8 years and recently lost his job as the firm he worked for was put into receivership and he applied for Jobseeker Support. Sergei has never been on a benefit before as he came straight out of university into employment. He has been on Jobseeker Support for 2 months and has been actively searching for work. An employer wants to hire him as a project lead due to his transferrable skills, qualifications and experience, so Sergei's employer applies for a Flexi-wage Subsidy as Sergei is changing industries to take on a new role and does not meet all the entry level criteria. MSD declines the application because Sergei's lack of benefit history means he is not considered at risk of long-term benefit receipt.

chunks.title: Not on a main benefit but at risk of long-term benefit receipt — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Sometimes people who are not on a main benefit and are in employment are at-risk of long-term benefit receipt. For example, a person who is underemployed or in a role at risk of redundancy, and who would qualify for a main benefit if they were not working. This could also include people who were recently getting a main benefit. Note clients who are not getting a main benefit must meet an income test to qualify for Flexi-wage Subsidy.

chunks.title: Example 4 — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Edwina works in a hotel for 35 hours a week. She has two children aged 8 and 11 and she gets Accommodation Supplement and Working for Families Tax Credits. Before she started working at the hotel, Edwina was getting Sole Parent Support. A new main road has been built which takes traffic away from the town Edwina works in and the hotel is closing. Over the last 3 months her hours have dropped to an average of about 20 hours each week. Edwina expects to lose her job altogether. Edwina is now considered under-employed as in her current job full time hours are no longer available. Edwina has worked in hospitality for her whole working career but there are no other job opportunities available, and she does not have the skills or experience to find work in another industry. Although Edwina is not getting a main benefit, she is at risk of long-term benefit receipt. An employer may be able to get a Flexi-wage Subsidy for her if all the eligibility criteria are met.

chunks.title: Partners of students — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Individuals who are in a recognised relationship with a student getting Student Allowance, whether studying themselves or not, cannot be considered at risk of long-term benefit receipt. This is as they cannot qualify for a main benefit and have no immediate need for a main benefit. When a couple is not in a recognised relationship for Student Allowance purposes, the studying partner is paid as a single person. In this case, the non-studying partner may be considered at risk of long-term benefit receipt if they are getting or qualify for a main benefit (or meet the other criteria).

chunks.title: Deciding if a client is disadvantaged in the labour market — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Deciding if a client is disadvantaged in the labour market
A client who is disadvantaged in the labour market may qualify for Flexi-wage If they meet all other eligibility criteria.
Disadvantaged in the labour market means someone who has, or is expected to have, difficulty getting into or staying in unsubsidised employment.
This includes a client who:
- has significant barriers to employment or
- is underemployed or is in a job with low job security or
- is in a job, or recently lost a job, and their occupation, industry or region is expected to be, affected by an economic downturn
## Example
Sione is getting Jobseeker Support, he is recently unemployed after the fishing boat he worked on ceased operating. He has only ever worked as a fisherman and is disadvantaged in the labour market.
Sione enjoys baking and is interested in a full-time job at a local bakery. However, this requires learning a whole new set of skills to produce bakery items on a commercial scale.
The employer can offer Sione 30 hours a week at the adult minimum wage and thinks it will take him around 6 months to meet the entry level requirements.
MSD and the employer negotiate a subsidy under payment band 1 over 24 weeks of $5,638.68, payable every 4 weeks in advance.
The full amount of subsidy is required as Sione needs to be trained in all aspects of the role to become a commercial baker.

chunks.title: Deciding if a client meets the entry level requirements of a job — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Deciding if a client meets the entry level requirements of a job
Every job has a set of minimum or entry level requirements a client must meet to be considered for the job.
This usually means specific skills, experience, qualifications, or a combination. These entry level requirements are decided by the employer.
To qualify for a Flexi-wage Subsidy for a particular job, the client must not meet one or more of the entry-level requirements of that job.
## Example
Jack has been getting Jobseeker Support for the last 3 years and is at risk of long-term benefit receipt.
Initially he had a health condition that meant he could not work for 15 hours or more a week, but his condition improved about 6 months ago, and he can now work full-time.
MSD knows of an employer looking for someone to sell motorbike parts at his dealership. Jack is interested in the role but doesn’t have any sales or customer service experience, which are entry requirements for the role.
The employer is willing to provide training and support to Jack, so he can gain the skills to meet the entry level requirements for the role. These factors mean the employer may be able to get Flexi-wage Subsidy for him if all the eligibility criteria are met.

chunks.title: Displacement due to economic downturn — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Displacement due to economic downturn
A client who has been, or is expected to be, displaced due to an economic downturn is likely to be disadvantaged in the labour market and may qualify for Flexi-wage if they meet all other eligibility criteria.
This is a person in employment, or who has lost employment, and their occupation, industry or region has been, or is expected to be, affected by an economic downturn. This could include clients in:
- industries that have been negatively affected by an economic downturn, (e.g. extreme weather events resulting in the business closing, particularly in industries with a high concentration of people with low-medium education levels)
- regions reliant on a large number of industries affected by an economic downturn, or a small number of large employers who have been affected
- occupations that are no longer in high demand by employers, or when the client has skills which are mismatched to the jobs available
## Economic downturn
An economic downturn is a general slowdown in economic activity over an extended period, sometimes known as a recession.
This may be at a regional, national or global level e.g. a global financial crisis.
The key features of economic downturn include rising unemployment, falling share prices, and less retail spending.
## Example 1
Bailey is 21 years old and is getting Jobseeker Support.
Bailey worked as a store manager for a boutique clothing store in the CBD but lost their job as more people are working from home and a large drop in sales meant the store owners closed their business.
Bailey is unable to find a similar job as other retail stores were facing same issues.
These factors mean Bailey has been disadvantaged in the labour market due to an economic downturn

chunks.title: Employer eligibility criteria — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Employer eligibility criteria
To qualify for a Flexi-wage, an employer must:
- be based and operating in New Zealand and
- pay at least the adult minimum wage and
- guarantee employment that lasts longer than the subsidy period and
- be solvent and
- not be an inappropriate business and
- comply with any other terms and conditions set out in the contract between MSD and the employer

chunks.title: Employment-related training assistance — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Employment-related training assistance
Extra assistance for employment related training is available if the client has specific skills deficits and training is needed to help them meet the entry level requirements of the job. This can include pre-employment training, on-the-job-training, or a specific course or programme.
## Short-term training
This means short-term training courses, on-the-job training or other short-term training approved by MSD, for example:
- Licence endorsements e.g. Wheels, Tracks and Rollers, or Dangerous Goods
- Food Safety and Hygiene course
- Real Estate Continuing Education course
- Vehicle Inspectors Preparatory course
- Working at Heights course
## New Zealand Qualifications Framework training
Flexi-wage extra assistance can be paid for the costs of New Zealand Qualifications Framework employment-related training for courses at Level 3 or below, for example:
- National Certificate in Hospitality
- Certificate in Forestry Driving
- Certificate in Driver Education
- Certificate in General Horticulture
- Certificate in Business Administration and Technology
Note Flexi-wage extra assistance cannot be used for the cost of an apprenticeship or industry training qualification. Mana in Mahi or Apprenticeship Boost should be considered for these clients.
## Training and development employers are expected to provide
Extra assistance cannot be used to pay for training and development the employer is expected to provide for any new employee. It can only be used to pay for training and development that helps the client develop skills the employer would expect a new employee to already have.
## Training needs identified after employment starts
If the need for employment-related training isn't identified until after the client starts work, extra assistance can be considered if it is appropriate and essential to the client's development and ability to meet the entry level requirements of the job.
Example
Anahila is working in a storehouse and her employer is getting a Flexi-wage Subsidy for her. No formal training needs were identified before Anahila started work, she just needed on the job-training and experience.
Anahila is progressing well, and her employer thinks she can work unsupervised. To do this, she needs a forklift license as deliveries may come in when no one else is around.
MSD approves $700 for the cost of the forklift course.

chunks.title: Extra assistance — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Extra assistance
Extra assistance is available to support Flexi-wage Subsidy clients with some extra costs they may have to help them meet the entry level requirements of the job. This is limited to employment-related training and in-work support services.
Note extra assistance can only be paid alongside a Flexi-wage Subsidy, it cannot be paid by itself.
Types of assistance
Payment amount
Employment-related training - short-term
Up to $2,000 every 52 weeks
Employment-related training - NZQF
Up to $5,000 every 52 weeks
In-work support
Actual and reasonable costs (no maximum)
Extra assistance is available for clients under any payment band of Flexi-wage Subsidy.
Note the total combined amount of any Flexi-wage Subsidy and extra assistance cannot be more than $22,000 in a 52-week period.
## Payment
Extra assistance is paid in a lump sum to the:
- employer - if training or in-work support is provided in-house or
- provider - if training or in-work support is provided externally
## Assistance with other employment-related costs
Flexi-wage extra assistance can only be paid for the costs of employment-related training and in-work support services.
If a client needs help with other employment-related costs e.g. work gear, equipment, or transport, check if they qualify for other assistance like Transition to Work Grant.
## Example
Philly works at a service station for 8 hours per week and gets Jobseeker Support.
His employer is unable to provide more hours because of its rural location.
A local work broker knows of a full-time window cleaner position that would suit Philly, but he does not meet the entry-level requirements and would need some support to do the job. Philly requires a Working at Heights certificate before he can start.
As Philly is underemployed and is currently disadvantaged in the labour market, the work broker approves the Flexi-wage Subsidy under payment band 1 as well as the extra assistance cost for the Working at Heights course.

chunks.title: In-work support assistance — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## In-work support assistance
Extra assistance is available to pay for the actual and reasonable costs of in-work support services needed to help the client stay in employment. These services may be provided by a contracted provider (approved by MSD) in some cases. This includes:
- coaching
- mentoring
- pastoral care
