Note in-work support is not intended to be used for employment-related training or other employment-related costs e.g. work gear, equipment, or transport. If an individual needs these items when they are starting work, they may qualify for other assistance.
## In-work support employers are expected to provide
Extra assistance cannot be used to pay for in-work support the employer is expected to provide for any new employee. It can only be used to pay for in-work support needed to help the client stay in employment that an employer would not normally provide.
## Needs identified after employment starts
If the need for in-work support isn't identified until after the client starts work, extra assistance can be considered if it is appropriate and essential to the client's ability to stay in work.
Example
Poto has 2 children aged 7 and 10. She came off Sole Parent Support to start work at her local bakery. Flexi-wage Subsidy was granted to help her do this.
She starts work at 7am meaning she has to drop the kids off at a before school programme and picks them up from school at 3.30pm. After several years out of the workforce Poto is struggling to find work/life balance. She is feeling overwhelmed and mentions this to MSD when we call to see how she's going.
MSD talks to Poto and the employer about in-work support and what they can do to support her to stay in work. They identify that pastoral care is the right kind of support service for Poto and MSD approves extra assistance to help with the cost of this.
The pastoral care will involve counselling and working with a life coach to identify what she is looking to achieve in her life and how she can set goals to get there.
The life coach costs $150 a session and there are 6 sessions over 6 months (within the period the subsidy is payable). Counselling costs $75 each session and Poto is booked in for 3 sessions at a cost of $225.
The total cost of extra assistance is $1,125.

chunks.title: Inappropriate businesses — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Inappropriate businesses
Before entering into a contract with an employer, MSD should consider whether it is appropriate for Flexi-wage Subsidy to be paid for employment with a business that is unlikely to be safe for the employee, not appropriate or acceptable to the wider community and may bring MSD into disrepute.
Some examples of businesses that may be inappropriate include (but are not limited to):
- massage parlours
- strip clubs
- premises for sex workers to operate in
- gambling
- money lending
- paramilitary services
- multi-level marketing enterprises e.g. pyramid schemes
- speculative services
If you are unsure whether a business is inappropriate please contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Income test — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Income test
Client's not getting a main benefit must meet an income test to qualify for Flexi-wage.
The combined income of the client and their partner (if they have one) must be less than the Accommodation Supplement income cut-out point for a single non-beneficiary and 16 years or older, living in Area 1.
Note this income test applies to all family circumstances and areas, not just single clients living in Area 1.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Flexi-wage provides a wage subsidy and extra assistance to support employers to take on people who do not meet the entry level requirements of the job.
This helps people get the employment skills and experience they need to get into and stay in unsubsidised employment.
To get a Flexi-wage Subsidy a client must:
- not meet the entry-level requirements of the job (as decided by the employer) and is either: disadvantaged in the labour market orat risk of long-term benefit receipt orhave specific employment needs and
- disadvantaged in the labour market or
- at risk of long-term benefit receipt or
- have specific employment needs and
- meet all other eligibility criteria
The amount paid and the duration is based on a client's needs and their barriers to employment and reflects the level of support they need to reach the entry-level requirements of the job.
Employers must retain employees after the Flexi-wage Subsidy has ended.
## Extra assistance
The client may also qualify for extra assistance for training and in-work support if they need this to help them meet the entry-level requirements of the job.
## Starting up a business
Flexi-wage Subsidy cannot be paid for a client entering self-employment.
If a client needs support to start their own business, they may be able to get Flexi-wage Self-Employment.

chunks.title: Job eligibility criteria — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Job eligibility criteria
To qualify for a Flexi-wage, the client must have a job offer for:
- at least 30 hours per week for clients with full-time work obligations o
- at least 15 hours per week for clients with part-time work obligations, no work obligations or an exemption from work obligations (unless there are specific circumstances) and
- longer than the subsidised period
Note the hours requirement also applies to clients not getting a main benefit. The work obligations they would have if they were getting a main benefit are used to work out whether the job needs to be for at least 15 or 30 hours per week.
## Specific circumstances
In specific circumstances a Flexi-wage Subsidy can be paid for a client who cannot work 15 hours per week. Circumstances include (but are not limited to):
- a client getting Supported Living Payment on medical grounds
- a client getting another benefit who has a health condition, injury or disability, with medical advice stating they can only work less than 15 hours per week, but have some capacity to work
- a client with caring responsibilities which impacts on the number of hours they are able to work
- a client recently bereaved which impacts on the number of hours they are able to work
- where it would be appropriate to staircase the client towards a higher level of part-time work, for example: a client with a health condition, injury or disability who cannot work 15 hours per week now, but could staircase towards working 15 hours or more over timea client who has been out of the work force for an extended period and cannot work 15 hours now but could staircase towards working 15 hours or more over time
- a client with a health condition, injury or disability who cannot work 15 hours per week now, but could staircase towards working 15 hours or more over time
- a client who has been out of the work force for an extended period and cannot work 15 hours now but could staircase towards working 15 hours or more over time

chunks.title: Low job security or underemployed — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Low job security or underemployed
A client who has low job security or is underemployed is likely to be disadvantaged in the labour market and may qualify for Flexi-wage if they meet all other eligibility criteria.
## Client has low job security
Low job security means there is a high chance the client will lose their job, or they have no guarantee of ongoing employment.
Generally, this means clients who are in:
- a role at risk of redundancy or
- casual employment or
- fixed term employment
## Example 1
Claire works as a tour guide for an eel farm in the Marlborough Sounds.
The business has not recovered after access to it was blocked twice due to significant weather events.
Claire's hours are continuing to reduce, and low tourist numbers mean the business is not viable in the long term.
Her employers decide to reduce costs, by laying off staff.
Claire is experiencing low job security and her role will end altogether in 4 weeks time.
## Client is under-employed
A client is considered to be under-employed when they are able and willing to work full-time but are working part-time as there are no full-time employment opportunities available to them.
## Example 2
Ana has worked full-time in a packing house in the Hawkes Bay for several years.
The market garden providing food for packing was hit by a cyclone recently and Ana's employer can only offer her 20 hours work per week for the foreseeable future. This means Ana is underemployed.
Equally Ana is facing low job security as the market garden still needs to regenerate after the cyclone damage and it is uncertain whether the business will be able to keep her on in the long term.
## Example 3
Ann works part-time at the local dairy.
She would like to work full-time but there are no full-time opportunities available as many businesses closed in the area after a new motorway bypassing the town significantly reduced passing traffic. Ann is underemployed.

chunks.title: Maximum payable in a 52-week period — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Maximum payable in a 52-week period
An employer cannot be paid Flexi-wage of more than $22,000 in a 52-week period for each employee. This includes the value of any:
- Flexi-wage Subsidy and
- Flexi-wage extra assistance and
- wage subsidy paid under clause 2 of the schedule of the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme, including Mana in Mahi
## 52-week period
The 52-week period starts on the date the assistance is approved, which is usually the date the contract is signed.
Each instalment of Flexi-wage Subsidy does not start its own 52-week period.
Note when extra assistance is approved after employment starts a new 52-week period begins for the amount of extra assistance granted at that time.
## Client applies for Flexi-wage more than once in a 52-week period
Flexi-wage Subsidy can be paid for a client more than once for different employers, but they must meet the qualifications. This includes being disadvantaged in the labour market and/or at risk of long-term benefit receipt.
You must consider the skills and experience they have gained since Flexi-wage was last approved and how this relates to the qualifications. You should also consider whether Flexi-wage is the most appropriate employment support product for the client's needs and circumstances.
Note more than $22,000 of Flexi-wage cannot be paid to the same employer for a client. However, another Flexi-wage of up to $22,000 can be paid to a different employer for the same client in the same 52-week period.

chunks.title: Other assistance for the same or a similar purpose — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Other assistance for the same or a similar purpose
A client cannot get any part of the Flexi-wage Subsidy that is the same or similar to any other assistance they are getting or recently got.
For example, if a client is getting Mana in Mahi they cannot get a Flexi-wage Subsidy.
## Wage Subsidy assistance
There are specific types of assistance under the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme paid for a same or similar purpose as Flexi-wage.
When a client or an employer is getting this specific assistance, they cannot get any Flexi-wage Subsidy and extra assistance.
The specific types of assistance paid under the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme and are limited to the following:
- Wage subsidies (includes Mana in Mahi)
- Education and employment-related training
- additional assistance associated with Mana in Mahi
- Wage subsidy for clients with a health condition, injury or disability
## Education and training assistance
A client cannot get Flexi-wage for employment-related training if they have had education or training assistance from MSD for the same or a similar reason.
When a one-off payment was made for employment-related training, any Flexi-wage component for the same or a similar reason cannot be paid during the period the payment was intended to cover i.e. the enrolment period of the course.
This includes the following education and training assistance:
- Additional assistance associated with Mana in Mahi
- Course Participation Assistance [no link find out why]
- any other education or employment-related training assistance paid under the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme

chunks.title: Payment bands — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Flexi-wage Subsidy is made up of 3 different payment bands based on the eligibility criteria the client meets. There are set durations for 2 of the payment bands.

chunks.title: Payment bands, eligibility and payment amount — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Payment band Payment amount (gross) Band 1 Up to a maximum of $5,638.68 over 24 consecutive weeks. Band 2 Up to a maximum of $11,277.36 over 36 consecutive weeks. Band 3 A maximum payable of $22,000 in a 52-week period. Note all rates include GST. This means the GST the employer is required to pay is included in the subsidy rate. Employers are responsible for paying the GST themselves, but MSD compensates them for the cost.

chunks.title: Pro-rata subsidy working less than 30 hours per week — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: A pro-rata Flexi-Wage Subsidy is paid for clients working less than 30 hours per week.

chunks.title: Payment frequency — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Flexi-wage Subsidy payments can be made at a frequency that suits the employer. For most employers this will be fortnightly or 4-weekly payments.

chunks.title: Variable payment rates — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Generally, Flexi-wage Subsidy is paid at the same weekly rate over the set or agreed period. The subsidy can also be paid at a variable weekly rate when appropriate. This allows for more subsidy to be paid at the start of a client's employment when an employer needs to provide more support to them.

chunks.title: Example — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Sascha needs to learn how to operate a complex piece of machinery vital to their role and so they can learn to use the machinery safely. In the first 4 weeks they need training and constant supervision. In the second 4-week period the need is reduced by half as they only need supervision not training. In the third 4-week period they are confident operating the machine and only need occasional supervision. In this situation the total subsidy payable is agreed at $2,400 for a 12-week period at a rate of $300 a week for the first 4 weeks, $200 a week for the second 4 weeks and $100 a week for the final 4 weeks.

chunks.title: Maximum weekly rate — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: The weekly rate of Flexi-wage Subsidy cannot be more than what a person earning the adult minimum wage for 30 hours work per week would get (gross). This applies even if Flexi-wage Subsidy is not paid weekly or is paid at a variable rate.

chunks.title: Extra assistance — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: An employer must be getting Flexi-wage Subsidy for a client to get extra assistance. Extra assistance is available in any payment band.

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Payment
Flexi-wage is made up of 2 components to help clients meet the entry level requirements of a job.
## Flexi-wage Subsidy
Flexi-wage Subsidy is paid to employers to subsidise the wages of the client they are employing.
Flexi-wage Subsidy is paid under 3 payment bands.
The amount payable is based on a client's needs and their barriers to employment and reflects the level of support they need to meet the entry-level requirements of the job.
## Flexi-wage Subsidy - extra assistance
Flexi-wage extra assistance helps with the costs of employment-related training and in-work support. The amount payable depends on the type and duration of employment -related training that a client is enrolled in or the in-work support required.
This is paid in a lump sum either to the employer or the provider, depending on who provides the training or in-work support.
## Maximum payable in 52-week period
The total amount of Flexi-wage Subsidy and extra assistance paid to an employer for each individual client cannot exceed more than $22,000 in a 52-week period.

chunks.title: Pro-rata subsidy — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: A pro-rata Flexi-wage Subsidy is only available to clients with: - part-time work obligations who are working 15 hours or more per week or - no work obligations who are working 15 hours or more per week In specific circumstances, it may be appropriate to pay a Flexi-wage Subsidy for a client who is working less than 15 hours per week. For more information see: - Job eligibility criteria Note a pro-rata rate of subsidy is available for all Flexi-wage Subsidy payment bands.

chunks.title: Calculating a pro-rata subsidy — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Step Process 1 Determine the full-time subsidy rate the client would qualify for if they were working full-time. 2 Divide the number of part-time hours by 30 to find the percentage of hours offered for the part-time position. 3 Multiply the percentage with the amount of subsidy calculated for the full-time position. (% of part-time hours x full-time subsidy rate) 4 Add 10% of the full-time subsidy rate to the part-time subsidy rate.

chunks.title: Example — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text: Yvonne is getting Sole Parent Support and has 2 dependent children. Her youngest child has just turned 3 and she is now looking for part-time work. Yvonne is disadvantaged in the labour market and at risk of long-term benefit receipt because she has no previous employment history and has been getting a benefit for 5 years. A jewellers shop in her local area is looking for a sales assistant for 15 hours a week paying minimum wage. The job description states the employer wants someone with sales experience, with good communication and basic computer skills. The employer is willing to train the right person and wants to employ Yvonne even though she doesn't meet the entry level requirements. They expect Yvonne to be fully trained in 12 weeks. If Yvonne was working 30 hours a week the rate of subsidy would be $300 weekly. This reflects the level of support Yvonne needs to learn the role. Yvonne will be trained in all aspects of the role, including learning how to operate the computer system used by the company. A pro rata subsidy is calculated based on the amount of subsidy payable to an employer for a full-time employee as follows: Step Formula Calculation 1 Determine the subsidy rate the client would qualify for if they were working full-time. $300.00 a week 2 Divide the number of part-time hours by 30 to find the percentage of hours offered for the part-time position. (part-time hours / 30 x 100 = % of part-time hours) 0.50 (50%) 3 Multiply the percentage with the amount of subsidy calculated for the full-time position. (% of part-time hours x full-time subsidy rate) 300 x 0.50 (A) = $150.00 4 Add 10% of the full-time subsidy rate to the part-time subsidy rate. 300 x 0.10 (B) = $30.00 Add the amounts payable from steps 3 (A) and 4 (B) to confirm the total amount payable. The weekly subsidy rate payable is $180. The total amount of Flexi-wage Subsidy payable over 12 weeks is $2,160.00.

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for Flexi-wage, the client must:
- meet the core eligibility criteria and
- have a job offer that meets the job criteria and
- meet the client eligibility criteria and
- have an employer that meets the employer criteria

chunks.title: Residence — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Residence
To qualify for Flexi-wage, the client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or hold (or be deemed to hold) a residence class visa that permits the holder to work in New Zealand or
- be a refugee or protected person or
- hold a temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 that permits the person to work in New Zealand and who is: awaiting the outcome of their claim for recognition as a refugee or a protected person orapplying for a residence class visa and is compelled to remain in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances and
- awaiting the outcome of their claim for recognition as a refugee or a protected person or
- applying for a residence class visa and is compelled to remain in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand at the time of their application

chunks.title: Significant barriers to employment — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Significant barriers to employment
A client who has significant barriers to employment is likely to be disadvantaged in the labour market and may qualify for a Flexi-wage Subsidy if they meet all other eligibility criteria.
Having significant barriers to employment means a client has one or more barriers that makes it hard for them to get into and stay in employment without help to address those barriers. This could include clients who have:
- low or no educational qualifications
- limited or no work experience
- limited employment skills, or their skills are mismatched with the labour market
- a health condition, injury or disability, including learning difficulties, and alcohol and drug dependency
- caring responsibilities e.g. children, a person with health needs
- transportation issues or live somewhere with limited employment opportunities
- frequent contact with the justice system, including those with previous criminal convictions
- family violence issues
An individual may have more than one barrier to employment, or one barrier that is very impactful and affects them getting into or staying in work.
## Example
Jayde left school at 16 before she finished NCEA Level 1 and has never had a job.
She is now 19 and has been getting Jobseeker Support for a year.
Jayde has been applying for jobs but has not been successful.
She wants to work but has no skills, or experience as well as a limited education.
These factors mean she has significant barriers to employment as she has no work experience in relation to most of her peers.
An employer may be able to get a Flexi-wage Subsidy for her, if all the eligibility criteria are met.

chunks.title: Solvency — specific employment related assistance > flexi wage subsidy
chunks.text:
## Solvency
To qualify for Flexi-wage, an employer must be solvent.
This means the employer can pay their debts and meet any other financial obligations, including being able to pay the client's wages or salary without a subsidy.
Solvency is a measure of an employer's financial health and shows they are able to keep operating for the foreseeable future.
Employers are not required to provide any proof of their solvency; however, for Flexi-wage to be granted they must agree in the contract with MSD that they are solvent.

chunks.title: Assistance for employers in Mana in Mahi — specific employment related assistance > mana in mahi
chunks.text:
## Assistance for employers in Mana in Mahi
The following assistance is available to an employer in the Mana in Mahi programme.
## Assistance towards pre-employment or on-the-job training
Employers can get up to $2,000 (plus GST) for pre-employment training or on-the-job training at the start of the Mana in Mahi contract between the Ministry and employer.
This training can be provided before employment or after the participant's employment start date. If provided prior to employment and the participant is receiving beneficiary assistance they can remain on benefit while the pre-employment training is carried out.
## Course fees for education or training
A placement for a Mana in Mahi participant can be purchased for an educational course or an employment-related training course. Employers can get up to $8,000 (plus GST) over 1 year towards the course fees charged by the provider.
The placement must be for an education or training programme that is:
- at level 7 or below on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (or an equivalent international qualification) and
- not already covered by other publicly funded assistance
Note employers cannot get Mana in Mahi for course fees if the participant can use their remaining first-year Fees Free entitlement in 2025.
The total payment to the employer for course fees does not need to be reduced by any payment made towards the participant's additional educational support costs for Mana in Mahi.
## Wage Subsidy
Employers can get a wage subsidy of up to $16,000 (plus GST) over 1 year for the participant under Mana in Mahi.
If the participant works for the employer part-time, the wage subsidy amount may be pro-rata (paid proportionally) based on their hours of work.

chunks.title: Assistance for participants in Mana in Mahi — specific employment related assistance > mana in mahi
chunks.text:
## Assistance for participants in Mana in Mahi
The following assistance is available to a participant in the Mana in Mahi programme.
## Incentive payments
Incentive payments can be made to a Mana in Mahi participant to encourage them to continue in the Mana in Mahi programme. These are paid in 3 instalments of $1,000 over 1 year if the participant achieves attendance or training milestones (up to a maximum of $3,000 in total over one year).
## Additional educational support costs
Additional financial assistance is available to help participants with the costs of any additional educational support needed to complete their studies.
These costs include (but are not limited to):
- literacy and numeracy training eg tutoring costs
- equipment relevant to their work or course that would allow them to work from home eg modem, desk chair, desk, school books, stationery etc
The actual and reasonable costs of the additional educational support costs can be paid, but not more than $2,000 in total over 1 year.
## Pastoral care
Pastoral care is available to support the participant through any issues they may encounter while training
There are a variety of mentoring, counselling, goals-based coaching, and in-work support options available to the participant.

chunks.title: Deciding if a person is at risk of long-term benefit receipt — specific employment related assistance > mana in mahi
chunks.text:
## Deciding if a person is at risk of long-term benefit receipt
At risk of long-term benefit receipt, means there is a risk the client will get or continue getting a main benefit for an indefinite period.
To decide whether a person is at risk of getting a benefit long-term, you need to consider a number of factors. These include:
- demographic information eg age, gender, ethnicity and location
- level of skills, employment experience and education
- specific barriers to employment that may apply eg health conditions or disabilities, caring responsibilities (eg sole parent, young parent), criminal convictions
- benefit status and history eg current period the person and/or their partner have been getting a main benefit (if applicable), time spent on and off benefit, age when they or their partner first started getting a main benefit
- previous times they got, or participated in, Ministry of Social Development employment programmes and services
## Getting or qualifying to get a main benefit
Generally, a person at risk of long-term benefit receipt is either:
- getting or qualifies to get a main benefit or
- has a partner who is getting or qualifies to get a main benefit
## On a main benefit and not at risk of long-term benefit receipt
Not everyone getting a main benefit is at risk of long-term benefit receipt. For example a person who is work ready is considered capable of getting into and staying in work without our help and only needs a benefit for a short time while they find work.
These clients would not meet the criteria for Mana in Mahi because they are not at risk of long-term benefit receipt.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > mana in mahi
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Mana in Mahi (Strength in Work) is a one-year programme that supports people who are at risk of long-term benefit receipt to get an apprenticeship, or other formal industry qualification, to gain sustainable employment.
The Mana in Mahi programme is administered by the Ministry of Social Development under the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme. The Ministry determines whether a participant and their employer are eligible for, and will be accepted in, Mana in Mahi. The employer also needs to meet the requirements set out in the Mana in Mahi contract between the Ministry and the employer.
Mana in Mahi participants may qualify for incentive payments, financial assistance to support their education or training, pastoral care and mentoring.
Mana in Mahi employers are paid a wage subsidy for the participant and may also get financial assistance towards the cost of the participant’s course fees, education and training.
Mana in Mahi, like all assistance provided for under the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme, is discretionary assistance. There are matters the Ministry needs to consider before granting assistance to a participant under the Mana in Mahi programme.

chunks.title: Participant accepted in Mana in Mahi before 5 August 2022 — specific employment related assistance > mana in mahi
chunks.text:
## Participant accepted in Mana in Mahi before 5 August 2022
Before 5 August 2022, the Mana in Mahi programme provided assistance to participants and employers over a 2-year period (rather than the current 1-year period).
If a participant was accepted in Mana in Mahi before 5 August 2022, the participant (and their employer) remain eligible for the Mana in Mahi assistance rates that applied to them before 5 August 2022. They can continue to be paid at these payment rates until the end of their participation in the programme (including a second year contract, if they are eligible).
We can consider a participant to be 'accepted in Mana in Mahi' and eligible for the 2-year programme and previous payment rates when the following has been confirmed and/or completed before 5 August 2022:
- the participant meets the Mana in Mahi qualifications, including being in the target cohort and
- the Ministry is satisfied the employer is suitable to take on a Mana in Mahi participant and
- an employment start date has been agreed and
- the Mana in Mahi contract/application has been approved by the Ministry (this generally becomes the 'accepted' in Mana in Mahi date)
## Agreed employment start date is on or after 5 August 2022
An agreed employment start date is required before a participant can be accepted in the Mana in Mahi programme. This is the start date in the employment agreement.
The Ministry may still consider a participant to be accepted in Mana in Mahi before 5 August 2022 when their employment start date is on or after 5 August 2022, if the Ministry considers the reason for the later employment start date is acceptable and consistent with the purpose of Mana in Mahi.

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > mana in mahi
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for Mana in Mahi, a participant must:
- meet the eligibility criteria for assistance under the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme and
- be within the target group for Mana in Mahi, which is that the participant is a person who is at risk of long-term benefit receipt

chunks.title: Target group for Mana in Mahi — specific employment related assistance > mana in mahi
chunks.text:
## Target group for Mana in Mahi
The Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme provides that the Ministry of Social Development may target assistance towards specified cohorts of eligible people (target groups) who the Ministry considers most at risk of long-term benefit receipt.
## Participants
Mana in Mahi is a one-year targeted programme for participants who:
- are at risk of long-term benefit receipt and
- want to gain an apprenticeship or industry training qualification (at New Zealand Qualifications Framework Level 7 or below) that will lead to long-term, sustainable employment and
- need support to meet and maintain the study or training commitment

chunks.title: Breakdown in childcare — specific employment related assistance > new employment transition grant
chunks.text:
## Breakdown in childcare
A client can receive a New Employment Transition Grant when they are unable to work because there has been a break down in childcare arrangements and where:
- no paid leave is available for this purpose or
- the client has exhausted their entitlement to paid leave
Note in these situations the client is required to access any paid annual leave that is available and any sick leave that the employer makes available for this purpose. However, the client is not required to anticipate such leave.
The 'childcare arrangements' are not limited to cases where the child attends a childcare centre. It can be for a breakdown in private childcare arrangements also.

chunks.title: Cash Asset test — specific employment related assistance > new employment transition grant
chunks.text:
## Cash Asset test
A client cannot receive a New Employment Transition Grant unless their cash assets and the cash assets of their partner (if any) are below the appropriate asset limit.
There is no income test for the New Employment Transition Grant.

chunks.title: Cash assets — specific employment related assistance > new employment transition grant
chunks.text:
## Cash assets
Cash assets mean assets of the client and partner (if any) that can be easily converted into cash.
## Cash assets include
- bills of exchange or promissory notes
- building society shares
- money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society
- money invested with or lent to any bank, other financial institution or person
- mortgage investments and other long term loans
- shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds, and other bonds
- the client's share in any partnership
- the net equity held in any property or land not used as the person's home and
## Cash assets do not include
- the home property and land on which it is situated
- personal effects
- a motor vehicle principally used by the client for private use
- a caravan, boat, or other vehicle with a net equity of less than $2000, or which is used by the person or a member of their family for day to day accommodation
- Christchurch mosques attack support payments
- Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments
- funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts
- Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income
- Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to a system processing error from 1993 to 2014
- Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination
- Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- specified Ex gratia and Compensation payments
- FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received
A bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.
Payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client received the payment.

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — specific employment related assistance > new employment transition grant
chunks.text:
## Deciding ordinarily resident
Generally a client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand to receive a benefit.
Ordinarily resident means someone who is normally and lawfully in New Zealand and intends to stay here, that is they consider New Zealand to be their home.
Whether a person is ordinarily resident is a question of fact and degree and their intentions during any period of absence is the most important factor.
Where it is not clear if a client is ordinarily resident, consider the following:
(a) the clients intentions toward New Zealand (that is, the reasons for their absence from New Zealand and the reasons for their return). Are they going overseas for a holiday or are they intending to live overseas permanently (sighting return air tickets is a good indication)?
(b) the length of time they spend in New Zealand on a continual basis
(c) property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans)
(d) where are their cash assets held?
(e) is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and do they pay New Zealand taxes?
(f) do they still vote (or are they eligible to vote) in the New Zealand election?
(g) their commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in the community, community events, clubs and other groups)?
Note a person cannot be ordinarily resident in two places at the same time.
## How to decide
You must consider all the factors of each individual case.
You may need to ask more questions (or for clarification of information you have) to get all the relevant information and then you must weigh up all the facts and make a decision.
The client should be given the benefit of the doubt in situations where their ordinarily residence isn't clear.
## Clients not ordinarily resident
If you decide that a client is not ordinarily resident in New Zealand that does not mean that they cannot be granted a New Employment Transition grant as section 205 contains discretion. You have discretion to refuse to grant a New Employment Transition Grant or to grant at a reduced rate.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > new employment transition grant
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The New Employment Transition Grant provides a payment to clients with a dependent child or children during the first six months that their benefit is stopped due to employment.
A payment can be made when the client is unable to work because they, their partner (if any) or their dependent child becomes sick or because of a break down in childcare arrangements.
The grant is non-recoverable and non-taxable.
For more detailed information see:
- Qualifications
- Payment
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals

chunks.title: Method of Payment — specific employment related assistance > new employment transition grant
chunks.text:
## Method of Payment
The payment is processed in CMS Hardship Assistance using the need type NET Payment.
The client needs to specify the details of the unpaid leave and that they still have a dependent child or children. The client also needs to provide proof to support their application.
Generally the New Employment Transition Grant is to be paid retrospectively. Employees are paid retrospectively so they will not have to face any loss of income until the payday after the unpaid leave was taken.
Note manager client service delivery approval is not required for New Employment Transition Grant payments.
Payment is always made direct to the client's bank account. As the client's benefit is cancelled or suspended you must check that the client's bank account number is still current.
The New Employment Transition Grant is paid the same way as other assistance for people not getting a main benefit. The client may already have a non-beneficiary record, if they don't, you will need to register a non-beneficiary record to pay the New Employment Transition Grant.

chunks.title: No paid sick leave available — specific employment related assistance > new employment transition grant
chunks.text:
## No paid sick leave available
A client can receive a New Employment Transition Grant when they are unable to work because they are sick, their partner (if any) or dependent child is sick and:
- no paid sick leave is available or
- the client has exhausted their entitlement to paid sick leave
The client is not expected to use paid annual leave or to anticipate annual leave for this purpose.

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > new employment transition grant
chunks.text:
## Payment
The maximum daily rate payable is limited to:
- $96.00 gross per day (as at 1 April 2026) or
- the actual loss of gross income
whichever is the lesser amount.
The maximum amount payable is $960.00 (as at 1 April 2026) in any qualifying 6-month period. This amount cannot be exceeded.
Where the actual loss of gross income is greater than the $96.00 daily maximum (as at 1 April 2026), other Special Needs Grants or payments under the Recoverable Assistance Programme cannot be used to top up the New Employment Transition Grant.
While the amounts used to calculate the payment are gross, and would normally be subject to tax payable by the recipient (client), Inland Revenue does not collect tax on these payments.

chunks.title: Proof — specific employment related assistance > new employment transition grant
chunks.text:
## Proof
The client must provide the following proof from their employer:
- the number of days of any unpaid leave
- the purpose of the unpaid leave
- that no paid leave was available for the purpose for which the client is applying and
- the total loss of gross income
You need a clear statement from the employer that paid leave was not available, otherwise there is a risk that some employers may use the New Employment Transition Grant as an alternative to paid leave.
If the employer refuses to provide the required information, a request for the information can be made under schedule 6 Social Security Act 2018. Any requests for information must comply with the code of conduct under schedule 6 of the Social Security Act 2018.
Clients must provide the following verification of their own circumstances:
- cash assets, for example, bank statements
- parental status (when they have a dependent child in their care), for example, by stating this in a written personal statement
- if necessary, medical evidence in relation to their, their partner's (if any) or child's illness or evidence concerning the breakdown in childcare arrangements

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > new employment transition grant
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To be able to get a New Employment Transition Grant, a client must:
- have a dependent child or children
- have had their benefit cancelled or suspended (within the last 6 months) because they have moved into employment
- still have a dependent child or children at the time they apply for the grant
- meet a cash asset test (however there is no income test)
- be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (ie not be in New Zealand unlawfully or here on a temporary permit) and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
For more information see: Deciding ordinarily resident
In addition to this, clients must be unable to work because:
- they are sick
- their partner (if any) or dependent child is sick or
- there has been a breakdown in childcare arrangements

chunks.title: Qualifying Period — specific employment related assistance > new employment transition grant
chunks.text:
## Qualifying Period
A client can only receive a New Employment Transition Grant if their illness, the illness of their partner (if any) or a dependent child, or a breakdown in childcare arrangements happened within 6 months of their benefit stopping.
The 6-month period commences on:
- the effective date the benefit was cancelled or
- the effective date the benefit was suspended
whichever is the later.
Each time a client cancels / suspends their benefit to move into employment, a new 6-month period begins that is, when a client applies, count back to the most recent cancellation / suspension.

chunks.title: Self-Employment — specific employment related assistance > new employment transition grant
chunks.text:
## Self-Employment
A client who meets all the relevant qualifications but who is self-employed may apply for a New Employment Transition Grant, however, there will be some difficulties because the employer and the employee are the same person.
In many cases, self-employed people do not accumulate or have access to paid leave in similar circumstances to wage and salary earners.
You will need to look closely at applications from self-employed people.
You will need to seek medical or other evidence as to why the person was unable to work. It would need to be clear that they were unable to have any involvement in the business over the period because of their illness, illness of their partner (if any) or child, or breakdown in childcare arrangements.
The client must declare that there actually was a loss of income and the extent of the loss (it may be that work is simply re-scheduled for another day, so there is no loss of income), and that provision was not available from the business to cover this loss.
The New Employment Transition Grant is not to be used to subsidise the income of self-employed people during a period where no work was available or to cover fluctuations in income.
To assess the income of a self-employed client see:
- Income

chunks.title: Adequate accommodation — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: To qualify for Relocate for Work Support the client must have obtained accommodation in their new location that is adequate for themselves and any immediate family moving with them. What is adequate depends on the circumstances of the client and their immediate family (if any) and must be considered on a case-by-case basis.

chunks.title: Factors to consider — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: To decide whether the client has obtained adequate accommodation for themselves and their immediate family (if any), MSD should consider the following factors: - health and disability needs e.g. wheelchair access, accessible toilets, or showers - distance to essential services e.g. travel to a hospital for dialysis - safety of environment e.g. there are no drugs, violence, or other unsafe behaviours, property is safe for children - proximity to a perpetrator of violence against the client or their immediate family - impact on court, bail, or release conditions e.g. the accommodation is not in an area they are not permitted to be - distance from education providers the client or their immediate family are or will be enrolled with - distance from where the client works or will be working - whether it is intended for human habitation and is in accordance with relevant local government bylaws e.g. the following are not adequate: a barn, shack, or shelter which lack walls or some or all the usual household amenities such as electric lighting, piped water, bathroom, toilet, and kitchen facilitiesa caravan or other removable structure on a residential site which is located against relevant local government bylaws - a barn, shack, or shelter which lack walls or some or all the usual household amenities such as electric lighting, piped water, bathroom, toilet, and kitchen facilities - a caravan or other removable structure on a residential site which is located against relevant local government bylaws - for commercial accommodation, whether the provider meets the relevant building and safety requirements e.g. fire-safety regulations, building code requirements or local authority rules MSD do not need to check the accommodation complies with applicable regulations. However, if MSD are told it does not comply this may be considered when deciding whether the client has obtained adequate accommodation - MSD do not need to check the accommodation complies with applicable regulations. However, if MSD are told it does not comply this may be considered when deciding whether the client has obtained adequate accommodation

chunks.title: Short-term accommodation — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: Some clients may obtain short-term accommodation initially with the intention of finding longer-term accommodation when they move to their new location. Short-term accommodation can be considered adequate accommodation for the purposes of Relocate for Work Support. Examples of short-term accommodation that is adequate include, but are not limited to: - a single client who has been offered a friend's couch to sleep on while finding alternative arrangements (when the client has no other needs that would make this inadequate e.g. health, disability, or social needs) - accommodation with family or friends who have a spare bedroom/s (appropriate to their family size) - a single client or couple without children staying in a tourist cabin - a single client or couple living at a caravan park with shared kitchen and shower facilities with no other reasons that this arrangement is unsuitable - caravan park or camping ground if the facilities meet the client's and their immediate family's (if any) needs. Examples of short-term accommodation that is not adequate include, but are not limited to: - a family with children staying at a friend's house if the accommodation is not adequate for the family's needs, even in the short-term e.g. children must sleep on the floor - situations where the only place to stay is a vehicle, sleeping on the street, or in a tent - has a place to stay but they are the perpetrator of family violence and cannot remain at the property - has left a place due to family violence and cannot return while the perpetrator is still there - the only place available to stay is an unsafe environment e.g. drugs, violence, and other crime - an elderly person is staying in a caravan park in winter, sharing a kitchen, and they must walk to the shower and toilet block (this would impact on their health due to the cold and not having easy access to facilities) - the place to stay will impact on the client's health needs e.g. too far away from a hospital where they are having treatment for cancer or dialysis - a family with young children in a caravan park and the facilities do not meet their needs e.g. distance to amenities, risk to children's safety by other users, risk to health due to the cold Example 1 Jean is a single client who lives in Dannevirke and has recently been made redundant. She is currently getting Jobseeker Support and is looking for a job.

chunks.title: Short-term accommodation — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: Jean has been unable to get a job locally and has been offered a job in Auckland. She applies for Relocate for Work Support. Jean will be staying with her friend in Auckland while she searches for an apartment of her own. The room Jean will be staying in is fully furnished and she will have access to all the usual household amenities. Jean has no individual circumstances that would make the accommodation unsuitable for her. MSD is satisfied that her accommodation is adequate and approves Jean's Relocate for Work Support application. Example 2 Jo is a sole parent who lives in Invercargill. She is currently getting Jobseeker Support and is looking for a full-time job. Jo has been unable to get a job locally and has been offered a full-time job in Christchurch. She applies for Relocate for Work Support. Jo and her child will be staying with her friend in Christchurch while she searches for an apartment. When asked about the arrangement, Jo says that her child will be sleeping on the floor as her friend's single bedroom apartment is small. MSD determines the accommodation is not adequate and declines her Relocate for Work Support application.

chunks.title: Evidence — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: The client must provide evidence confirming they have obtained accommodation in their new location that is adequate for themselves and their immediate family (if any).

chunks.title: At risk of long-term benefit receipt — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: To qualify for Relocate for Work Support the client must be at risk of long-term benefit receipt. At risk of long-term benefit receipt means there is a risk the client will get or continue getting a main benefit for an indefinite period. To decide whether a client is at risk of getting a benefit long-term, MSD must consider a number of factors. These include: - demographic information, for example: agegenderethnicitylocation - age - gender - ethnicity - location - level of skills, employment experience and education - if there are any specific barriers to employment, for example: health conditions or disabilitiescaring responsibilities (e.g. sole parent, young parent)criminal convictions - health conditions or disabilities - caring responsibilities (e.g. sole parent, young parent) - criminal convictions - benefit status and history, for example: how long the client has been getting a main benefittime spent on and off benefitage when the client first started getting a main benefit - how long the client has been getting a main benefit - time spent on and off benefit - age when the client first started getting a main benefit - previous times the client got, or participated in, MSD employment programmes and services Generally, a combination of factors will determine whether a client is at risk of long-term benefit receipt, for example a client who is: - 60 years old, has only ever had 2 jobs and has no further work experience or education or - 19 years old, has caring responsibilities, has not finished school, and has been on a main benefit for a year However, a single factor can also determine whether a client is at risk of long-term benefit receipt, for example a client who has a: - criminal conviction(s) or - serious illness or disability

chunks.title: On a main benefit and not at risk of long-term benefit receipt — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: Not everyone getting a main benefit is at risk of long-term benefit receipt, for example a client who: - is work ready and - is considered capable of getting into and staying in work without help from MSD and - only needs a main benefit for a short time while they find work These clients are not at risk of long-term benefit receipt and do not qualify for Relocate for Work Support. Example 1 Jane is 24. She lives in Waikanae and has been on and off Jobseeker Support since she was 20. Jane has not been in further education and has been in and out of work since leaving high school. Jane has been unable to get a job locally and has been offered a job in Upper Hutt. She applies for Relocate for Work Support. MSD determines that she is at risk of long-term benefit receipt because of her benefit history, education level and because she has struggled staying in work since leaving high school. This means Jane may qualify for Relocate for Work Support if she meets all the other qualifications. Example 2 Mary is 45. She lives in Hamilton and has been in and out of prison. She has struggled to stay in employment and is currently on Jobseeker Support. Mary has been unable to get a job locally and has been offered a job in Christchurch. She applies for Relocate for Work Support. MSD determines that she is at risk of long-term benefit receipt because of her criminal conviction history. This means Mary may qualify for Relocate for Work Support if she meets all other qualifications. Example 3 Matai is a public servant who lives in Wellington and has been made redundant. He has not been to university or had further education but has years of professional experience. He is currently getting Jobseeker Support while looking for work. Matai has been unable to get a job locally and has been offered a job in Auckland. He applies for Relocate for Work Support. Matai is not considered to be at risk of long-term benefit receipt. This is because he is work ready and considered capable of getting into and staying in employment without further assistance from MSD.

chunks.title: Chosen method of travel — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text:
## Chosen method of travel
Before paying Relocate for Work Support for travel, MSD must decide if a client's chosen method of travel is appropriate based on their individual circumstances.
To decide if a method of travel is appropriate, MSD should consider:
- the distance they will be travelling
- the route the client is taking (e.g. whether the travel method is possible)
- if any dependent children are traveling with them, and how old they are
- if the client or any immediate family traveling with them have a health condition or disability
- any other factors that are relevant to the client and their immediate family (if any)
Note MSD may decline a clients Relocate for Work Support application or pay from a travel category with a lower payment rate if it determines the method of travel is not appropriate.
Example 1
Sanjay applies for Relocate for Work Support to move from Dunedin to Christchurch for a job. He meets all other qualifications.
Sanjay is planning to fly to Christchurch as he doesn't have a car and is moving at short notice. There is no affordable alternative transport that would allow him to move himself and his possessions.
MSD is satisfied that he will be using an appropriate method of travel and approves Sanjay's Relocate for Work Support application under the "air or sea travel" category.
Example 2
Bella applies for Relocate for Work Support to move from Motueka to Christchurch for a job.
Bella is planning to fly from Nelson to Christchurch. She also needs a moving van to move her bed, couch, and dresser.
Bella plans to leave her car in Motueka and return later to drive it back to Christchurch as she wants to get settled in first.
MSD determines that Bella doesn't have a good reason to fly, and that driving would be a more appropriate method of travel for her. This is because Bella needs to move her car to Christchurch anyway.
MSD approves Bella's Relocate for Work Support application under the "land travel" category.

chunks.title: Conditions of grant — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text:
## Conditions of grant
Relocate for Work Support is subject to conditions of grant. If a client fails to meet one or more conditions of grant without a good and sufficient reason, the whole amount of Relocate for Work Support paid to them is recoverable. MSD must recover this amount from the client in full.
The conditions of grant for Relocate for Work Support mean the client must:
- use the payment to relocate for their new job and
- relocate by air or sea if they get a payment for this method of travel and
- move their possessions if they get a payment for this need and
- relocate for their new job within 28 calendar days of getting the payment and
- cancel their main benefit from the date they start their new job and
- not get a main benefit or Student Allowance within 182 days of the date their job starts
Note if a client fails to meet the condition to cancel their main benefit, there is no discretion to decide if they had a good and sufficient reason. A grant of Relocate for Work Support is always recoverable if this condition is not met.

chunks.title: Doesn't move within 28 calendar days — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: It is a condition of grant of Relocate for Work Support that the client must move within 28 calendar days of the payment being made. If the client fails to meet this condition without a good and sufficient reason, the whole amount of Relocate for Work Support paid to them is recoverable. MSD must recover this amount from the client.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: If a client has a good and sufficient reason for not moving within 28 calendar days, Relocate for Work Support is not recoverable. MSD must consider each client's individual circumstances and be satisfied that a good and sufficient reason exists before deciding not to make Relocate for Work Support recoverable. Examples of good and sufficient reason include, but are not limited to, when a client: - was temporarily unwell or injured and they have a medical certificate to prove this - delayed their relocation because their job start date was delayed by their employer - had a death or serious illness in their immediate family - could not realistically transport themselves on the day they intended due to unforeseen circumstances (e.g. their car broke down or flight was cancelled) - was dependent on their Relocate for Work Support payment to move and the payment was delayed because of MSD - has new information that indicates the job they are relocating for is no longer suitable for them - cannot start employment or work at reduced hours because of a health condition, illness, or disability and has a medical certificate to show this Example 1 Luke is granted Relocate for Work Support on 7 April and knows he needs to move by 4 May. However, on the day he was planning to travel (30 April) his car broke down and he couldn't use it. Instead, Luke tries to use his Relocate for Work Support payment to book a flight to Christchurch but there are none available. Due to flight availability, he was unable to fly till 5 May. MSD is satisfied Luke has a good and sufficient reason for being unable to move within 28 calendar days of the Relocate for Work Support being granted and does not make the payment recoverable. Example 2 Mark is granted Relocate for Work Support for himself and his partner Wendy on 1 May and knows he needs to move by 28 May. However, Mark finds out it's his friends 21st birthday on 30 May. Mark and Wendy decide to stay and celebrate the birthday before moving. They end up moving on 1 June. MSD is made aware of this and makes his Relocate for Work Support grant recoverable as Mark did not have a good and sufficient reason for not moving within 28 days.

chunks.title: Gets a main benefit or Student Allowance — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: It is a condition of grant of Relocate for Work Support that the client must not get a main benefit or Student Allowance for at least 182 days from the date they start their new job. If the client fails to meet this condition without a good and sufficient reason, the whole amount of Relocate for Work Support paid to them is recoverable. MSD must recover this amount from the client.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: If a client has a good and sufficient reason for getting a main benefit or Student Allowance within 182 days of their job start date, Relocate for Work Support is not recoverable. MSD must consider each client's individual circumstances and be satisfied that a good and sufficient reason exists before deciding not to make Relocate for Work Support recoverable. Examples of good and sufficient reason include, but are not limited to, when a client: - could no longer transport themselves to their employment for reasons beyond their control (e.g. the client's place of employment moved or they sustained a long-term illness or injury that impacted their ability to get to work) - had a long-term change in childcare arrangements that meant they could no longer work their agreed hours, and their hours of employment could not be changed - had an unexpected event occur (e.g. they had to return to the family home in another location to care for a sick relative for an extended period) - had a significant change in their employment conditions which meant the employment was no longer suitable (e.g. the employer changed their hours) - was not able to continue working, or is working reduced hours due to a health condition, injury, or disability and has a medical certificate to verify this - lost their job during the 90-day trial period (except when it was due to misconduct) Trial period Some employment agreements include a trial period of up to 90 days. This means the employer can dismiss the employee for any reason at any time before the end of the trial period without giving a reason. However, this does not mean a reason will not be given. If a client is dismissed during a trial period, MSD must try to determine the reason for the dismissal. This may include asking the employer to complete the Employment and earnings information for applications form. If a reason cannot be established, Relocate for Work Support must not be made recoverable. Note this does not apply when the client has been dismissed due to misconduct during the trial period. Example 1 Jason has been granted Relocate for Work Support and has moved from New Plymouth to Auckland for a full-time job as a builder. Jason sustained a serious back injury playing rugby and ended up in hospital. Since then, he has been permanently and severely restricted in his capacity to work. Due to the nature of his job Jason is unable to keep working and agrees with his manager to leave the job.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: Jason applies for Supported Living Payment. Even though he is reapplying for a main benefit within 182 days of starting his job, MSD does not make his Relocate for Work Support payment recoverable as he has a good and sufficient reason for getting a main benefit. Example 2 Sally has been granted Relocate for Work Support and has been employed as a customer service agent in Wellington CBD. However, after 5 months her employer relocates the office to the Hutt Valley due to a cheaper lease. Sally now needs to travel further to get to work in the Hutt Valley. Her hours of employment mean she can get a bus or train to commute to work and it would take her less than an hour. Sally leaves her job as she doesn't want to commute to the Hutt Valley. She reapplies for Jobseeker Support as she no longer has a job. MSD does not consider Sally to have a good and sufficient reason for returning to a main benefit. MSD makes the full amount of her Relocate for Work Support recoverable.

chunks.title: Getting a main benefit — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text:
## Getting a main benefit
To qualify for Relocate for Work Support the client must be getting one of the following main benefits:
- Emergency Benefit
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance
- Jobseeker Support
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Youth Payment
- Young Parent Payment
Note this includes partners getting an apportioned amount of one of the above main benefits.
## Under 18-year-olds
Clients under 18 years old who get a main benefit do not qualify for Relocate for Work Support because they are not of working age. For example, a 17-year-old getting Youth Payment will not qualify. However, if that client continues to get Youth Payment when they turn 18 years old, they can get Relocate for Work Support if they meet all other qualifications.
## Effect of an initial stand-down or non-entitlement period
Clients do not qualify for Relocate for Work Support while subject to an initial stand-down or non-entitlement period because they are not getting a main benefit. However, a client who is subject to a 13-week non-entitlement period (e.g. voluntary unemployment) can qualify if they are:
- getting a provisional benefit, and
- participating satisfactorily in an approved recompliance activity
## Residency
There are no specific residency criteria for Relocate for Work Support as clients must meet residency criteria to qualify for a main benefit.

chunks.title: Hours of employment — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text:
## Hours of employment
To qualify for Relocate for Work Support, the client must have accepted a job offer that meets the hours of employment criteria. This means the employment must be:
- at least 30 hours per week or
- less than 30 hours per week if the income earned is equal to 30 hours at minimum wage or
- at least 20 hours per week for sole parents with part-time work obligations
## Income equal to 30 hours at minimum wage
This means the salary or wages the client will earn from their new job are equal to or more than what a person would earn working 30 hours per week at the relevant minimum wage.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Relocate for Work Support provides financial assistance to help clients relocate to another area to start a new job if they haven't been able to get a suitable and sustainable job in their local area.
To get Relocate for Work Support, a client must be:
- on a main benefit and
- of working age and
- at risk of long-term benefit receipt and
- meet all other qualifications
The amount paid depends on the client's needs, how far they are moving, the type of transport they will be using, and if they are moving alone or with their immediate family.
Note young persons aged 16-17 cannot get Relocate for Work Support.

chunks.title: Job offer criteria — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text:
## Job offer criteria
To qualify for Relocate for Work Support the client must have accepted a job offer for employment that:
- is in New Zealand and
- meets the hours of employment requirement and
- is suitable and sustainable and
- pays at least the relevant minimum wage and
- is in a location where it is not viable for the client to commute
## Evidence
The client must provide written evidence confirming they have accepted a qualifying job offer.

chunks.title: Main benefit not cancelled — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text:
## Main benefit not cancelled
It is a condition of grant of Relocate for Work Support that the client must cancel their main benefit from the date they start their new job. If the client continues to get their main benefit when they start work, the whole amount of Relocate for Work Support paid to them is recoverable. MSD must recover this amount from the client.
Note unlike other conditions of grant, there is no discretion for MSD to determine whether the client had a good and sufficient reason for not cancelling their main benefit.

chunks.title: Moving possessions — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: Clients who get a payment under the travel category may also qualify for support to move their possessions to their new location if they have a genuine need. The amount the client can get is based on the number of people moving with them and the distance between their principal place of residence and new accommodation. It is not affected by their chosen method of travel or how they move their possessions e.g. hiring a moving truck or paying a company to do it for them.

chunks.title: Distance between locations — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: This is the number of kilometres between the client's principal place of residence and their new accommodation. The number of kilometres between locations is the number produced by the Google Maps directions function when selecting the recommended driving route between the client's principal place of residence and their new accommodation. It does not include any variations from the recommended route e.g. to pick up or drop off possessions along the way.

chunks.title: Client must have a genuine need — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: This means the client needs financial assistance to move their possessions that: - are essential for their employment e.g. tools or equipment needed for their job or - are essential for a reasonable living situation e.g. a bed and - they are unable to move themselves e.g. they will not fit in their car When deciding if a client has a genuine need to move their possessions, MSD must consider the individual circumstances of the client and their immediate family (if any). Note if a client needs to move their possessions but their employer covers the cost of this, they do not have a genuine need. Example 1 Tino is a sole parent and has applied for Relocate for Work Support to move from Mount Maunganui to Auckland with their 6-year-old child Riley. Tino will be driving themself and Riley to Auckland. They have household possessions that also need to be moved, including their beds and living room furniture. Tino cannot fit all of this in their car and needs to hire a moving van. MSD is satisfied that Tino has a genuine need for financial assistance to move their possessions from Mount Maunganui to Auckland. MSD approves Tino's Relocate for Work Support application and is granted a sole parent amount to travel by land and an amount to move their possessions. Example 2 Lucy is a single Jobseeker Support client moving to Wellington from Te Awamutu. Lucy will be driving to Wellington, and she doesn't need to move any large household possessions as her accommodation in Wellington is fully furnished. Lucy contacts MSD to see if any help is available for moving her possessions. However, MSD determines she does not have a genuine need for financial assistance to move her possessions as she can fit them all in her car. As Lucy meets all other qualifications, MSD approves her Relocate for Work Support application at a single client amount to move herself by land to Wellington.

chunks.title: Must cancel main benefit — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: To qualify for Relocate for Work Support, the client must agree to cancel their main benefit from the date their job starts. Some clients will have their main benefit cancelled when they start work because they no longer qualify due to their income or the number of hours they work. However, some clients such as sole parents with part-time work obligations will continue to qualify for their main benefit. If these clients do not agree to cancel their main benefit, they will not qualify for Relocate for Work Support. Example 1 Mark is a single parent living in New Plymouth with his 12-year-old daughter. Mark gets Sole Parent Support and has part-time work obligations. He has been looking for a job locally but has been unable to find one that works around his daughter's school hours. He has been offered a job in Wellington for 22.5 hours a week at living wage. His hours of work will vary each week, but they fit in with school hours. Mark applies for Relocate for Work Support to move himself and his daughter to Wellington. Because Mark would still qualify for Sole Parent Support while working, he must agree to cancel his benefit to get Relocate for Work Support. Mark agrees to cancel his main benefit and meets all other qualifications, so MSD approves his Relocate for Work Support application. Example 2 Ann is a single parent to 2 children living in Taihape. Ann gets Sole Parent Support and has part-time work obligations. She has been looking for a job locally but has been unable to find one that works around her children's school hours. Ann can only work between 9.00am-2.30pm because she needs to be available before and after school. She has been offered a job in Taupō for 25 hours a week at minimum wage. She would be working 9.00am-2.00pm Monday to Friday which fits in with school hours. Ann applies for Relocate for Work Support to move herself and her family to Taupō. Because Ann would still qualify for Sole Parent Support while working, she must agree to cancel her benefit to get Relocate for Work Support. Ann decides she wants to continue getting her main benefit and doesn't agree to cancel her main benefit. MSD declines her Relocate for Work Support application. Example 3 Liam lives in Ōamaru and gets Supported Living Payment because of an ongoing health condition.

chunks.title: Must cancel main benefit — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: Liam has been looking for jobs, but his health condition means he can only work up to 15 hours a week. There are jobs available in his local area but none of them fit in with the limited hours he can work. Liam has been offered a permanent job in Christchurch for 15 hours a week with a salary of $36,650 a year. He applies for Relocate for Work Support to move to Christchurch. Because Liam would still qualify for Supported Living Payment while working, he must agree to cancel his main benefit to get Relocate for Work Support. Liam agrees to cancel his main benefit and meets all other qualifications, so MSD approves his Relocate for Work Support application.

chunks.title: Not viable to commute — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: To qualify for Relocate for Work Support the client must have accepted a job in a location that is not within viable commuting distance of their principal place of residence. This means it is not practical for the client to travel between their principal place of residence and their job location. Note principal place of residence is the address where the client lives most of the time. To decide whether a job is within viable commuting distance, MSD must consider the client's individual circumstances rather than whether it would be a viable commute for the average person.
