The factors that should be considered include, but are not limited to: - health conditions or disabilities: if they impact or prevent the client using public transport or drivingif the employer offer can be more flexible to meet the client's needs - if they impact or prevent the client using public transport or driving - if the employer offer can be more flexible to meet the client's needs - family circumstances: if the client has care arrangements (e.g. childcare) that impact the hours they can workif the client's commute would fit with their care arrangements - if the client has care arrangements (e.g. childcare) that impact the hours they can work - if the client's commute would fit with their care arrangements - distance from their principal place of residence: how far away the client's job istime it would take the client to commute each day - how far away the client's job is - time it would take the client to commute each day - financial impacts of commuting: if transport would cost more than the client could affordif the client would be financially disadvantaged by the cost of commuting - if transport would cost more than the client could afford - if the client would be financially disadvantaged by the cost of commuting - availability of transport: if the client has their own transportavailability of public transport services between the client's principal place of residence and their jobif the client's hours of work fall within the hours public transport services operate - if the client has their own transport - availability of public transport services between the client's principal place of residence and their job - if the client's hours of work fall within the hours public transport services operate Note any location 150km or more from the client's principal place of residence is not considered to be within viable commuting distance. Example 1

chunks.title: Not viable to commute — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: Geoff is single and lives in Bluff. He is currently getting Jobseeker Support and Disability Allowance for the extra costs he has from his epilepsy. Geoff has been looking for a full-time job in Bluff but has been unable to find anything that meets the flexibility he needs to manage his disability. Due to his epilepsy Geoff cannot drive and gets Disability Allowance for transport and other costs related to his epilepsy. Geoff is offered a permanent job of 35 hours per week at minimum wage in Invercargill. This job has the flexibility he needs with his disability and means he will be able to stop his Jobseeker Support. Invercargill is only a 25-minute drive from Bluff, however public transport is infrequent and expensive. Geoff applies for Relocate for Work Support to help with his move to Invercargill. MSD determines Geoff meets all the qualifications, including that it is not viable for him to commute between Bluff and Invercargill due to his disability. MSD approves Geoff's Relocate for Work Support application. Example 2 Tina lives in Marton and is getting Sole Parent Support with part-time work obligations. She has sole custody of her 7-year-old child, and the father is not involved in their lives. Tina's child is in school from 9.00am-3.00pm Monday to Friday. Tina has been searching for jobs locally that work around the hours her child is home but has been unable to find anything. She has been offered a 2-year fixed-term job as a librarian in Palmerston North which is a 40-minute drive from Marton. Her hours are contracted from 9.00am till 2.00pm 5 days a week. However, because of the distance she wouldn't be able to drop her child off at school and make it to work on time. Driving to work every day would also be financially difficult. Tina applies for Relocate for Work Support to help her move to Palmerston North. MSD determines it is not viable for her to commute to Palmerston North and that she meets the other qualifications. Tina's Relocate for Work Support application is approved. Example 3 Bella and her partner Dan currently live in Orewa. Neither Bella nor Dan work and they get a couple's rate of Jobseeker Support. Bella has been looking for a job but has been unable to get a job locally that would support both her and Dan.

chunks.title: Not viable to commute — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: Bella is offered a permanent job in Manukau as a cleaner for 37 hours per week at minimum wage. Bella and Dan have a car and Bella can drive herself to this new job as it is only one hour away. However, commuting from Orewa to Manukau and back every day would be expensive. Using public transport would take around 2.5 hours each way. If Bella and Dan stay in Orewa and Bella commutes to work every day, after tax, rent and utilities, they will be left with less than $100 per week for food and any other expenses. This is not financially viable for Bella. Bella and Dan have found accommodation in Manukau and moving there would mean they would be left with around $450 a week after tax, rent and utilities. Bella applies for Relocate for Work Support to help with their moving costs. MSD approves Bella's Relocate for Work Support application as it is not viable for her to commute to her new job, and she meets all other qualifications. Example 4 Peter lives in Island Bay, Wellington. He is currently getting Jobseeker Support and has been unable to get a job close to where he lives. He has been offered a 1-year fixed term full-time job in the suburb of Thorndon of 40 hours a week at slightly higher than the minimum wage. Thorndon is a 40-minute bus ride away from his home. Peter does not have a car or driver licence so is not able to drive to work. His job's rostered hours are from 6.30am-2.30pm 5 days a week. This means that Peter will need to leave home at 5.45am to get to work on time. Peter applies for Relocate for Work Support to help move closer to his new job. Although Peter meets the other qualifications, MSD determines that a 40-minute bus ride is a viable commute for Peter. He doesn't meet this qualification and his Relocate for Work Support application is declined. Example 5 Karan and his partner Anahera have one child and live in Rakaia. They get Jobseeker Support. Their child, Jai, is 12 years old and goes to school from 8.30am-3.30pm 5 days a week.

chunks.title: Not viable to commute — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: Karan has full-time work obligations and Anahera has part-time work obligations. Anahera works part-time at the local school from 9.00am-2.00pm for a total of 25 hours per week. Karan has been looking for a job locally that works around being home with Jai when he is home from school but has been unable to find anything. Karan has been offered a permanent full-time job of 40 hours per week in Christchurch. Christchurch is a 45-minute drive from Rakaia. His proposed work hours are 8.30am to 4.30pm. This means that Karan won't be home till around 5.30pm (accounting for rush hour). As he is keen to spend more time with his son after school, he is looking for ways to move his family closer to his new job. Karan applies for Relocate for Work Support to help with his family's moving costs. MSD determines that the distance Karan needs to commute for his job is viable. As Anahera can be home with Jai after school, Karan's desire to be home doesn't make this commute non-viable as his childcare arrangements are not affected. MSD declines his Relocate for Work Support application.

chunks.title: Number of people relocating — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text:
## Number of people relocating
If a client has immediate family, the rate of Relocate for Work Support they can get for travel is based on who is actually moving with them. This does not mean the whole family has to move at the same time. If some family members are moving at a later date, the amount paid must include them.
Note clients are required to move within 28 calendar days of getting Relocate for Work Support, but this requirement does not apply to their immediate family.
Example 1
Joy is applying for Relocate for Work Support and meets all the qualifications. She is moving from Carterton to New Plymouth.
However, Joy's husband and son will not be moving with her, as they want to stay in Carterton to be closer to extended family who can help support their son.
As Joy's immediate family are not moving with her, MSD approves her Relocate for Work Support application at the rate for a single client.
Example 2
Kahu has a partner and one daughter. He is applying for Relocate for Work Support and meets all the qualifications. He has been offered a full-time job in Christchurch and will be moving from Picton.
Kahu's daughter is in primary school. Since it is mid-term, Kahu's partner and daughter will stay in Picton till the end of the school term and then move down to Christchurch to be with Kahu.
As Kahu's immediate family will be moving with him (even though they are not moving at the same time) MSD approves his Relocate for Work Support application at the rate for a couple with a dependent child.

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text:
## Payment
Relocate for Work Support is a non-taxable one-off payment that helps clients relocate to start a new job. It is paid directly to the client in one lump sum.
## Payment structure
Relocate for Work Support is paid at a flat rate based on the client's needs, family circumstances, their method of travel, and how far they are moving. It is not based on the client's actual and reasonable costs. This means some clients will get more or less than they need.
Relocate for Work Support has two need categories:
- Travel
- Moving possessions
Every eligible client will get a payment from the travel category, but only clients with a genuine need to move their possessions can get a payment from the moving possessions category.
## Maximum payable in a 52-week period
A client can only get Relocate for Work Support once in a 52-week period. If the client or their current partner (if any) received Relocate for Work Support in the last 52 weeks, they will not qualify.

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for Relocate for Work Support the client must:
- be getting a main benefit and
- be of working age and
- be ordinarily resident and present in New Zealand when applying and
- meet a cash assets test and
- be at risk of long-term benefit receipt and
- have accepted a job offer that meets the job offer criteria and
- have been unable to get a suitable and sustainable job locally and
- have obtained adequate accommodation in the location they are moving to and
- not have moved for the job offer before applying and
- agree to cancel their main benefit from their job start date and
- not have received other assistance for a same or similar purpose for the same job offer and
- not have received $5k to Work in the last 52 weeks
Note clients must provide evidence they meet some of the above qualifications.
## Cash assets test
The client and their partner (if any) must have cash assets below or equal to the relevant cash asset limit. Relocate for Work Support uses the same definition of cash assets as Temporary Additional Support.
## Other assistance for a same or similar purpose
Transition to Work
If the client has received Transition to Work - Job Placement for relocation costs for the same job offer, they do not qualify for Relocate for Work Support. However, if the client has received Transition to Work for other work-related costs (e.g. equipment or clothing), they can still get Relocate for Work Support.
New Zealand Seasonal Work Scheme
If the client has received a New Zealand Seasonal Work Scheme incentive payment for the same job offer, they do not qualify for Relocate for Work Support.
Housing Support Products
A client who gets for Relocate for Work Support can also get Housing Support Products if they qualify. However, this would only cover the costs over and above the amount they got through Relocate for Work Support.
## $5k to Work
If the client or their current partner (if any) have received $5k to Work in the 52 weeks before applying for Relocate for Work Support, they do not qualify.

chunks.title: Students and recent graduates — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: To qualify for Relocate for Work Support the client must be at risk of long-term benefit receipt. Generally, students and recent graduates are not considered at risk of long-term benefit receipt because they are working towards or have recently completed a qualification that will help them get and stay in work. However, some students and recent graduates are considered at risk of long-term benefit receipt because of their individual circumstances. To decide whether a student or recent graduate is at risk of long-term benefit receipt, MSD must consider: - how long ago they finished study and - what subject they studied and the availability of jobs in that field and - where they are moving to and if they have connections there, for example if they: are returning to their hometown orwill be living with family and - are returning to their hometown or - will be living with family and - the usual factors when deciding whether someone is at risk of long-term benefit receipt, for example specific barriers to employment Note both full-time and part-time students may be able to get Relocate for Work Support if they are at risk of long-term benefit receipt. However, part-time study may affect a client's ability to meet the job offer criteria.

chunks.title: Recent graduates — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: Recent graduates are clients who have completed study in the last 3 months. The 3-month period starts from the date the client completed study. This will generally be the: - day they complete their last exam or - last day of required attendance if they have no exams to sit Note the day a student graduates is not considered the date they completed study. Example 1 Ben is 21. He lives in Dunedin and completes a business management degree in November. He also completed a business marketing internship while studying but has since been unable to get a job locally. He started getting Jobseeker Support in December last year. In February he is offered a job in New Plymouth and applies for Relocate for Work Support. Ben does not qualify for Relocate for Work Support because his education, age, level of skill and work experience means he is not at risk of long-term benefit receipt. Example 2 Tui is 19 and has been getting Young Parent Payment since she was 16. She is a sole parent and is undertaking a 1-year certificate in Cookery at Whitireia in Petone, where she lives. Tui's study is coming to an end, and she has been unable to get a cooking job locally or a job that works around her childcare commitments. She has extended her search and has been offered a job in Napier that meet her needs, right after she completes her studies. Even though Tui is a current student and will be a recent graduate when she starts her job, MSD considers her to be at risk of long-term benefit receipt. This is due to her age, childcare responsibilities, lack of work experience, amount of time spent on a main benefit, and how old she was when she started getting a main benefit. She may qualify for Relocate for Work Support if she meets all other qualifications. Example 3 Jennifer studied in Hamilton. When she finished her tourism degree in January, she moved home to support her family. Her hometown has a high unemployment rate and Jennifer has been unable to find a job relating to her degree, despite applying for many jobs (including jobs not in the tourism industry) within a viable commuting distance. Jennifer starts getting Jobseeker Support. In March, Jennifer starts applying for jobs in other areas as she wants to help support her family and has been unable to get a job locally. Jennifer is offered a job in Wellington as a travel agent. She applies for Relocate for Work Support in April to help with the costs of moving.

chunks.title: Recent graduates — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: Even though Jennifer is a recent graduate. MSD considers her be at risk of long-term benefit receipt because of the high unemployment rate and limited job opportunities in her area. She may qualify for Relocate for Work Support if she meets all the other qualifications.

chunks.title: Support not used for the reason it was paid — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: It is a condition of grant of Relocate for Work Support that the client must: - use the payment to relocate for their new job and - relocate by air or sea if they get a payment for this method of travel and - move their possessions if they get a payment for this need If the client fails to meet one or more of these conditions without a good and sufficient reason, the whole amount of Relocate for Work Support paid to them is recoverable. MSD must recover this amount from the client.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: If a client has a good and sufficient reason for not using the support for the reason it was paid, Relocate for Work Support is not recoverable. MSD must consider each client's individual circumstances and be satisfied that a good and sufficient reason exists before deciding not to make Relocate for Work Support recoverable. Examples of good and sufficient reason include, but are not limited to, when a client: - did not relocate because: they sustained a long-term illness or injury (and have a medical certificate to prove this) that impacted their ability to start worktheir new employer went out of business before their job start datethey had a long-term change in childcare arrangements that meant they could no longer work their agreed hours, and their hours of employment could not be changedthey had an unexpected event occur (e.g. they had to stay where they were to care for a sick relative for an extended period) - they sustained a long-term illness or injury (and have a medical certificate to prove this) that impacted their ability to start work - their new employer went out of business before their job start date - they had a long-term change in childcare arrangements that meant they could no longer work their agreed hours, and their hours of employment could not be changed - they had an unexpected event occur (e.g. they had to stay where they were to care for a sick relative for an extended period) - was paid to travel by air but travels by bus because their flight was cancelled, and this was the only alternative to ensure they relocated in time to start their new job - was paid to move their possessions but some or all their possessions were stolen or damaged in a fire or other disaster before they were due to relocate Example 1 - did not relocate Jasmine was granted Relocate for Work Support to move herself from Kerikeri to Rotorua. Jasmine's job starts on 1 July, and she is planning to move on 20 June to allow herself time to set up. However, Jasmine does not relocate to Rotorua or start her new job as she fell down the stairs in her apartment building and has sustained a serious leg injury. Her recovery time is long, and she is unable to work even at reduced hours. She has a medical certificate to prove this. MSD is satisfied Jasmine has a good and sufficient reason for not relocating or starting work and does not make Relocate for Work Support recoverable. Example 2 - moved by bus

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: Leon was granted Relocate for Work Support to fly from Invercargill to Christchurch. He plans to move on 14 May. However, on 14 May his flight is cancelled due to bad weather, and he is rescheduled onto a flight on 16 May. His job starts on 16 May. Instead, Leon buys an overnight bus ticket to get from Invercargill to Christchurch. This was the only alternative route that would get him to Christchurch in time to start his new job. MSD is satisfied Leon has a good and sufficient reason for relocating by bus when he was paid to relocate by air and does not make Relocate for Work Support recoverable. Example 3 - possessions were stolen Christian was granted Relocate for Work Support to move himself and his possessions from Napier to Hamilton. He has hired a moving van to move his possessions. His job starts on 7 April, and he plans to move a few days before to settle into his new area. A few nights before Christian is planning to move there is a fire in his apartment building and although no one was injured his possessions were significantly damaged and are now unusable. Christian moves to Hamilton as planned and starts his job, however, he didn't need the moving van as he could fit his remaining possessions in his car. MSD is satisfied Christian has a good and sufficient reason for not moving his possessions when he was paid for this need and does not make Relocate for Work Support recoverable.

chunks.title: Travel — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text:
## Travel
Every client who qualifies for Relocate for Work Support will get a payment from the travel category to relocate themselves and their immediate family (if any) to their new location.
The amount the client can get is based on who is relocating with them and their method of travel. It is not affected by how far they are travelling.
Clients can get a payment for:
- land travel (such as bus, train, or private vehicle) or
- air or sea travel (such as flights or ferry)
Note clients cannot get a payment from both travel categories, even if they have mixed methods of travel.
## Mixed methods of travel
If a client is using mixed methods of travel, they must be paid for the method of travel with the higher payment rate. For example, a client who is driving and travelling by ferry will get the "air or sea travel" rate instead of the "land travel" rate.
This includes when a client relocates using a different method of travel than members of their immediate family. For example, a client decides to fly, and their partner and children will drive. The client will get the "air or sea travel" rate instead of the "land travel" rate.

chunks.title: Unable to get a suitable and sustainable job locally — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: To qualify for Relocate for Work Support the client must have been unable to get a suitable and sustainable job in their local area. This means there are: - no suitable and sustainable job opportunities locally or - suitable and sustainable job opportunities locally, but the client has been unsuccessful getting one Note local area means anywhere that is a viable commute from the client's principal place of residence.

chunks.title: Suitable and sustainable jobs available locally — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: If there are suitable and sustainable jobs available in the client's local area, they must demonstrate they have applied for those jobs and been unsuccessful getting one. Clients are expected to apply for jobs in all fields relevant to their skills and experience. For example, if a client has experience in both hospitality and retail, they must have been unable to get a suitable and sustainable job in both fields.

chunks.title: Evidence — specific employment related assistance > relocate for work support
chunks.text: The client must provide evidence to show they have been unable to get a suitable and sustainable job locally unless MSD already holds this information. Example 1 Ross is getting Jobseeker Support and has full-time work obligations. He has been applying for suitable and sustainable jobs locally for the last few months but has been unsuccessful. MSD has been supporting Ross with his job search and work readiness. He has been offered a job in Auckland and needs assistance to move there from Gisborne. He applies for Relocate for Work Support. MSD is satisfied Ross has been unable to get a suitable and sustainable job locally and grants him Relocate for Work Support. Example 2 Simon applies for Relocate for Work Support so they can move from Nelson to Wellington for a job offer. There are a few suitable jobs available in Simon's local area, but they are all fixed-term contracts of less than 12 months, meaning they are not sustainable. MSD is satisfied Simon has been unable to get a suitable and sustainable job locally and grants them Relocate for Work Support. Example 3 Sydney applies for Relocate for Work Support as she has a job offer in Christchurch and needs assistance to move from Taupō. At her appointment, Sydney shows MSD 2 rejection letters and says she hasn't applied for any other jobs. MSD can see there are a range of jobs available in Taupō that are suitable and sustainable for Sydney. MSD is not satisfied that Sydney has been unable to find a job locally and declines her application for Relocate for Work Support. Example 4 Edward lives in New Plymouth and has been applying for plenty of local jobs over the last few months but hasn't been successful. There are still jobs available locally, but Edward is not confident they will get one and decides to look for jobs outside New Plymouth. Edward is offered a job in Auckland and applies for Relocate for Work Support to help with the cost of moving. Even though there are jobs in New Plymouth, MSD is satisfied Edward has been unable to get a suitable and sustainable job locally. This is because of the number of jobs they have applied for and been unsuccessful getting. MSD grants Relocate for Work Support to help Edward with their move.

chunks.title: Application process — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## Application process
A Seasonal Work Assistance application form must be completed by the client for the period the payment is being made. See:
- Seasonal Work Assistance application form
The client's employer must confirm:
- number of hours lost
- net wages lost and
- reason the client could not work
## For the minimum requirements see:
- Processing standards Request for financial assistance [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Cash assets — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text: Cash assets mean the assets of the client and their partner (if any) that can be easily converted into cash.

chunks.title: Cash assets include — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text: - bills of exchange or promissory notes - building society shares - money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society - money invested with or lent to any bank, other financial institution or person - money withdrawn from a KiwiSaver scheme - mortgage investments and long term loans - pre-paid funeral expenses (in some circumstances) - shares, stocks, debentures, Bonus Bonds and bonds - the client's share in any partnership - the net equity held in any investment property or land not used as the client's home Note if you are unsure contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Cash assets do not include — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text: - a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2000, or which is used by the person or a member of their family for day to day accommodation - the home property and land on which it is situated - a motor vehicle principally used by the client for private use - Christchurch Mosques attack support payments - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts - Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income - Māori land when the title is in tribal trust and individual ownership cannot be identified, the client cannot realise or readily convert the land into a cash assetNote consult Legal Services if you are unsure about the ownership of Maori land. - MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments from the Crown for the purchase of property in the Canterbury red zone - Payments from Earthquake Commission and insurance companies (Canterbury earthquake 2010 and 2011 aftershock) - Payments from Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) - personal effects - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made - specified Ex gratia and Compensation payments - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received A bank overdraft is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client. Canterbury earthquake related payments Payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client received the payment.

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## Deciding ordinarily resident
Generally a client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand to receive a benefit.
Ordinarily resident means someone who is normally and lawfully in New Zealand and intends to stay here, that is they consider New Zealand to be their home.
Whether a person is ordinarily resident is a question of fact and degree and their intentions during any period of absence is the most important factor.
Where it is not clear if a client is ordinarily resident, consider the following:
(a) The client's intentions toward New Zealand (that is, the reasons for their absence from New Zealand and the reasons for their return). Are they going overseas for a holiday or are they intending to live overseas permanently (sighting return air tickets is a good indication)?
(b) The length of time they spend in New Zealand on a continual basis
(c) Property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans)
(d) Where are their cash assets held?
(e) Is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and do they pay New Zealand taxes?
(f) Do they still vote (or are they eligible to vote) in the New Zealand election?
(g) Their commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in the community, community events, clubs and other groups)?
Note a person cannot be ordinarily resident in two places at the same time.
## Clients not ordinarily resident
If you decide that a client is not ordinarily resident in New Zealand that does not mean that they cannot be granted a Seasonal Work Assistance Payment as section 204 contains discretion. You have discretion to refuse to grant a Seasonal Work Assistance Payment or to grant at a reduced rate.

chunks.title: Effect on Extra Help — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## Effect on Extra Help
Seasonal Work Assistance Payments are to be treated as income in the assessment of other Extra Help assistance such as:
- Recoverable Assistance Payments
- Special Benefit
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Needs Grants
Seasonal Work Assistance payments will not be treated as income by Inland Revenue when assessing qualification for Working for Families Tax Credits

chunks.title: Calculating the amount to pay — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## Calculating the amount to pay
You will need to use the following information (which must be supplied by the employer):
- the number of hours lost during the week and
- the net earnings lost during the week
## Example 1
Step 1
You must determine the maximum payment that is allowed based on the number of hours lost.
For example:
- if a client lost 13 hours of work, the maximum payment is $324.00 (as at 1 April 2026)
Step 2
You must compare the maximum payment allowable (calculated in Step 1) with the actual net earnings lost and pay whichever is the lesser amount.
For example:
- if the client's lost earnings were $330.00 for 13 hours work, you would pay $324.00 (as at 1 April 2026) as this is the lesser amount
## Example 2
Step 1
You must determine the maximum payment that is allowed based on the number of hours lost.
For example:
- if a client lost 17 hours of work, the maximum payment allowed is $486.00 (as at 1 April 2026)
Step 2
You must compare the maximum payment allowable (calculated in Step 1) with the actual net earnings lost and pay whichever is the lesser amount.
For example:
- if the client's lost earnings were $393.55 for 17 hours work, you would only pay $393.55 as this is the lesser amount

chunks.title: Income limit — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## Income limit
A client cannot get a Seasonal Work Assistance Payment, unless their income and the income of their partner (if any) is below the appropriate income limit.
## Asset limit
A client's and partner's (if any) combined cash assets must not be greater than the appropriate asset limit to receive a Seasonal Work Assistance Payment.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Seasonal Work Assistance provides a non-taxable payment to help a client who is a seasonal worker.
It encourages clients to take up jobs in seasonal work, without worrying about any loss of income, by providing financial assistance when they are unable to work (and lose income), due to poor weather conditions.
The amount paid depends on how many hours the client loses due to poor weather and the actual net income lost for the week.

chunks.title: Jobs in the horticultural and viticultural industries — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## Jobs in the horticultural and viticultural industries
Jobs for seasonal workers in the horticultural and viticultural industries may include but are not limited to:
- Cool Store stackers
- General Labourer
- Harvesting
- Hydra ladder operator
- Pack house grading
- Pack house stacking
- Pack house tray filling
- Picking
- Planting
- Process workers
- Pruning
- Quality Control
- Tractor/truck/forklift driving
- Training
- Weeding or thinning

chunks.title: Lost income — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## Lost income
Before you grant a Seasonal Work Assistance payment you must also consider the following factors:
- the number of hours lost by the client for the period they have been unable to work because of the weather conditions
- whether the client's future work may be affected by the weather conditions
- the number and amount of Seasonal Work Assistance payments already received and
- whether granting an Emergency Benefit would be more appropriate given the period the client is unable to work

chunks.title: Method of payment — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## Method of payment
The payment is processed in CMS Hardship Assistance.
Note the client's benefit must have been stopped using the suspension/cancellation reason code 700 (in seasonal work) to make a Seasonal Work Assistance payment.
The reason code 700 should only be used for clients moving into seasonal work in the horticultural industry. Code 038 (return to work) must be used for all other types of seasonal work.
Payment is always made directly to the client's bank account. As the client's benefit is cancelled or suspended you must check that the client's bank account number is their current bank account number.
If the client has changed their bank account number since their benefit was stopped, you will need to register a non-beneficiary record and add the correct bank account number.

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## Payment
You pay either the:
- maximum payment or
- actual net income lost for the week
whichever is the lesser amount.
The maximum amount that can be paid in any qualifying 26-week period is $2,754 (as at 1 April 2026) for each applicant. The maximum amount cannot be exceeded.
If the client is unable to work for more than 1 week you should consider if the client qualifies for Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To get a Seasonal Work Assistance Payment, a client must:
- have had their working age benefit cancelled or suspended (within the last 26 weeks) because they are a seasonal worker
- have lost income because they could not work because of adverse weather conditions
- meet an income and asset test
- be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (ie not be in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand

chunks.title: Qualifying period — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## Qualifying period
A client can get a Seasonal Work Assistance Payment if they have lost income due to poor weather conditions within 26 weeks of their benefit stopping because they had started seasonal horticultural work.
The 26 week period commences on:
- the effective date the benefit was either suspended or cancelled because the client had started seasonal horticultural work
Each time a client cancels or suspends their benefit to move into seasonal horticultural work, a new 26 week period begins, that is, when a client applies, count back to the most recent cancellation or suspension.

chunks.title: The horticultural and viticultural industries — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## The horticultural and viticultural industries
They include but are not limited to:
- Berry (including kiwifruit) growing
- Fruit (including stone, pip and citrus) growing
- Grape growing
- Growing cut flowers and flower seeds
- Growing hops, tobacco and hemp
- Olive farming
- Plant nurseries
- Vegetable growing

chunks.title: Working age benefit — specific employment related assistance > seasonal work assistance
chunks.text:
## Working age benefit
For the purposes of the Seasonal Work Assistance payment a working age benefit is:
- Emergency Benefit (other than an emergency benefit payable under section 17(2)(c) of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001)
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Jobseeker Support
- Young Parent Payment
- Youth Payment

chunks.title: 52-week maximum payment — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## 52-week maximum payment
The maximum Training Incentive Allowance that can be paid in a 52-week period is $5,723.20 as at 1 April 2026.
A 52-week period means a period of 52 weeks commencing from the date assistance commences.
This means that clients applying for the Training Incentive Allowance who have been granted Training Incentive Allowance within the past 52 weeks will have the amount they have already received included as part of their overall entitlement.
Note there is no limit on how many times a client may be granted Training Incentive Allowance within a 52 week period for multiple courses of study. The maximum payable must not exceed the total 52-week limit and the qualifications must be met for each Training Incentive Allowance grant.

chunks.title: Capital items — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Capital items
Capital items (e.g. computers, cameras, gym clothing, shoes) may be included in Training Incentive Allowance, if the Ministry is satisfied that:
- the costs are directly related to their training and
- they could not complete the training/course without the item, or equipment
Consider the following:
- Is the client more interested in completing the course because it gives them an opportunity to own a particular piece of equipment or item?
- Would Training Incentive Allowance be primarily subsidising this item rather than providing training that will lead to a realistic paid work opportunity?

chunks.title: Childcare — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Childcare
To include childcare as an allowable cost in Training Incentive Allowance, the care can be provided informally (for example, through family or friends) or through a registered provider.
If the care is provided informally, the costs must be considered reasonable. If the childcare costs are higher than those generally charged at a registered childcare centre, you would generally include the lower amount as an allowable cost for Training Incentive Allowance.
If childcare is provided through a registered provider, the client should firstly test their eligibility for Childcare Subsidy, Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment, or an OSCAR Subsidy.
If the client is receiving a Childcare Subsidy, Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment or OSCAR Subsidy, the total amount of the subsidy must be deducted from the cost of the childcare before including the cost in the Training Incentive Allowance assessment.
## Other care costs
Other care costs include care for disabled people, people with health conditions or older people and associated costs eg transport to the care provider (less any other government assistance available).
Clients may make their own private arrangements or utilise the Ministry of Health's carer support. However, the number of hours or days that Carer Support is funded for depends on the client's needs and those of the person being cared for.
If the care is provided informally, the costs must be considered reasonable.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance > changes and reviews training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
Training Incentive Allowance can be paid as an ongoing payment for the necessary and reasonable costs of attending a course such as childcare, other care, transport or disability related costs.
If the client is overseas and continues to get benefit payments, Training Incentive Allowance can continue for up to 28 days.
However, if the client does not qualify for continued payment under the absence from New Zealand rules then the client is not entitled to their benefit or Training Incentive Allowance.
## Permanent Absence
If the client is leaving New Zealand permanently Training Incentive Allowance will stop from the day after departure.
If a lump-sum payment has been made for costs the client must request from the Course Provider a refund of the course fees paid.
If the Course Provider provides a refund, or a partial refund, this must be repaid to the Ministry of Social Development to offset the amount paid as a lump sum through the Training Incentive Allowance.

chunks.title: Cancellation of qualifying benefit — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance > changes and reviews training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Cancellation of qualifying benefit
If the client's main qualifying benefit is cancelled, they no longer meet the qualification for Training Incentive Allowance. Training Incentive Allowance must stop from the same date as the client's main qualifying benefit stops.
You will not need to establish an overpayment for any Training Incentive Allowance already paid as lump sum or weekly amount while the client was getting a qualifying benefit (unless the client did not qualify to get the payment during this period).
## Exception
If the client transfers to another qualifying benefit Training Incentive Allowance may continue. You will need to:
- Review the client's course costs
## Repayments
Repayment will generally not be required if the client continues the course, however if the client stops the course a refund of any lump sums paid for course fees should be requested.
## Refunds
Clients who fail or fail to complete a course are not required to repay the Training Incentive Allowance. This is because Training Incentive Allowance is based on actual and reasonable costs that the client incurs.
The client is not required to repay the Training Incentive Allowance. However, they may not be able to access the Training Incentive Allowance for 5 years if they do not have a good and sufficient reason for not completing or failing the course.
If a lump-sum payment has been made for course fees or any additional course-related costs the client must request a refund from the Course Provider (or equivalent supplier).
If the Course Provider (or equivalent supplier) provides a refund, or a partial refund, this must be repaid to the Ministry of Social Development to offset the amount paid as a lump sum through the Training Incentive Allowance.
Note if a client has died a refund is not required.

chunks.title: Change in costs — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance > changes and reviews training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Change in costs
You will need to review Training Incentive Allowance to make sure the client is getting the correct rate of payment whenever there is a change to weekly ongoing costs such as (but not limited to):
- care including childcare or older person care
- transport or
- disability related costs
Note although you can include all of the client's allowable costs in the calculation of Training Incentive Allowance, the maximum Training Incentive Allowance payable may not be sufficient to cover all of their actual costs.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance > changes and reviews training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client is obliged to advise the Ministry of Social Development of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Training Incentive Allowance.
You may also review Training Incentive Allowance at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is getting the correct rate of payment.

chunks.title: Client starts a new course — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance > changes and reviews training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Client starts a new course
If a client wants to start another approved course, they will have to reapply for Training Incentive Allowance.
Consideration would be given to whether the new course of study would improve the client’s skills for employment.

chunks.title: Client withdraws or stops attending a course — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance > changes and reviews training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Client withdraws or stops attending a course
Training Incentive Allowance must stop from the day after the client:
- withdraws from a course before the course ends or
- stops attending the course permanently.
whichever is earlier.
## Refunds
Clients who fail a course or fail to complete a course are not required to repay the Training Incentive Allowance. This is because Training Incentive Allowance is based on actual and reasonable costs that the client incurs.
While the client is not required to repay the Training Incentive Allowance, they may not be able to access the Training Incentive Allowance for 5 years if they do not have a good and sufficient reason for not completing or failing the course.
## Lump sum payments
If a lump-sum payment has been made for course fees the client must request a refund from the Course Provider (or equivalent supplier).
If the Course Provider (or equivalent supplier) provides a refund, or a partial refund, this must be repaid to the Ministry of Social Development to offset the amount paid as a lump sum through the Training Incentive Allowance.
Note if the client has died no refund is required.

chunks.title: Review date — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance > changes and reviews training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Review date
The date to review Training Incentive Allowance from will depend on the action involved. Generally, you should:
- increase Training Incentive Allowance from the actual date of the change in costs
- reduce, suspend or cancel Training Incentive Allowance from the first available date (FAD) except when the client advises of a permanent change more than 14 days after the event (ie withdrew from the course)
- if a client has a good and sufficient reason for not advising within 14 days, you can review from the first available date
- suspend Training Incentive Allowance from the 29th day when a client has a temporary change (ie absence from New Zealand)
## Client advises more than 14 days after the event
Clients have an obligation to tell the Ministry of Social Development when there are any changes that may affect their entitlement to Training Incentive Allowance. It is also expected that they will do so within a reasonable period. As a guideline, a reasonable period is considered to be within 14 days.
Therefore, when a client advises of a change in circumstances more than 14 days after the event you should generally reduce, suspend or cancel Training Incentive Allowance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.
Where there is a good and sufficient reason (for example, bereavement or illness) for the client not advising the Ministry of a change in circumstances within 14 days you may reduce, suspend or cancel Training Incentive Allowance from the first available date.
Note if the client gives false or misleading information you must review Training Incentive Allowance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.

chunks.title: Reviews and Appeals — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance > changes and reviews training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Reviews and Appeals
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have received formal notification of (and do not agree with) a decision which has been made under:
- any provisions of (or of any regulations made for the purposes of any provisions of) Parts 1 to 6 and Schedules 1 to 5 or
- a special assistance programme approved by the Minister under section 100 or 101 or
- any regulations in force under section 437 (regulations: issue and use of entitlement cards)
- any provisions of, or of regulations made under, the Residential Care and Disability Support Services Act 2018 or
- Part 6 of the Veterans' Support Act 2014, subject to section 175(2) of that Act or
- Part 1 of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001 or
- the Family Benefits (Home Ownership) Act 1964
A client can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority where they do not agree with a decision, which was:
- upheld or upheld in part by the Benefits Review Committee under an application for Review of Decision or
- made by the Chief Executive (and not delegated for an employee to decide)

chunks.title: Temporary absence from course — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance > changes and reviews training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Temporary absence from course
Training Incentive Allowance can be paid as an ongoing payment for the necessary and reasonable costs when attending a course eg childcare, transport or disability related costs. Reasons for not attending a course could include:
- bereavement
- childcare responsibilities
- hospitalisation or
- illness
Training Incentive Allowance can continue during these periods up to 4 weeks, as long as the main benefit is still being paid, and the client intends to continue with the course.

chunks.title: Client got a level 7 qualification within the past 5 years — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Client got a level 7 qualification within the past 5 years
Clients who completed any level 7 NZQF qualification within the last 5 years cannot get Training Incentive Allowance unless it will significantly improve the client's employment outcomes.
A further qualification at the same or lower level is unlikely to increase their skills for employment. However, every application must be decided based on individual circumstances.
Clients who have completed a level 7 qualification more than 5 years ago can get a Training Incentive Allowance if the course significantly improves the client's employment outcomes.
Example 1
Chyna has recently completed a degree in tourism. Because of COVID-19 the travel agent role she was employed in has been disestablished and the business closed due to COVID 19.
While Chyna was at university, she worked for student IT as she had great IT skills. Chyna would like to further her skills in this area so she can get a higher paid IT job.
Chyna applies for Training Incentive Allowance to study for a Bachelor of Applied Information Technology.
Training Incentive Allowance can be granted in this situation.
Example 2
Turama finished studying fine arts 2 years ago, however, she is now on benefit and struggling to find her preferred job as an Art Gallery curator.
Turama would like to study Te Reo Māori through Te Wānanga o Aotearoa as galleries and museums list knowledge of Te Ao Māori as a desired skill when hiring new staff.
Turama may be granted Training Incentive Allowance to study Te Reo Māori.
Example 3
Chris completed a degree in sociology last year and is now applying for Training Incentive Allowance to complete a further degree in philosophy.
The philosophy degree is unlikely to increase their employability, as the skills it provides them are similar to what they have previously gained from their sociology degree (e.g. writing and research skills).
Chris is unable to provide a compelling case for how a philosophy degree on top of their existing sociology degree would improve their employment skills.
Chris will not be granted Training Incentive Allowance to complete a further degree.

chunks.title: Client received Training Incentive Allowance for previous course of study — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Client received Training Incentive Allowance for previous course of study
A person who received a Training Incentive Allowance in the past 5 years for a previous course may be eligible to receive the Training Incentive Allowance for a new course. However, each situation must be assessed on a case-by-case basis to determine the outcome of the previous course of study for which Training Incentive Allowance was paid.
In specific circumstances an application might be declined on a case-by-case. These circumstances are when a client:
- does not tell us or refuses to answer questions about the outcome of a previous course when the Training Incentive Allowance was paid or
- has failed to complete a course when Training Incentive Allowance was paid, without a good and sufficient reason
Note that if a client received Training Incentive Allowance more than five years ago the outcome of the previous course of study does not need to be considered.
For more information see:
## Examples of good and sufficient reasons
Example 1
Sue has an accident in June, her rehabilitation includes surgery and physiotherapy. Sue does not complete her course the year of the accident.
This is a good and sufficient reason for not completing her course therefore Sue may still qualify for Training Incentive Allowance in future years.
Example 2
Daniel is in his first year of health sciences in Dunedin and is receiving Training Incentive Allowance to pay for his additional costs.
In the first semester Daniel's kuia (grandmother) gets very ill, and Daniel cancels his study to moves back to Rotorua to care for her.
A year later Daniel applies for Training Incentive Allowance to complete a nursing degree at the Rotorua Toi Ohomai (Institute of Technology).
Daniel may be granted Training Incentive Allowance to complete this study.
Example 3
Erin is enrolled in her first year of a Bachelor of Arts in Communication at the University of Otago.
Erin keeps missing her assignments and lectures. Erin misses half her exams and Erin fails the course.
She cannot provide a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete her course, therefore, Erin would not be granted Training Incentive Allowance the next year.
Erin may qualify for Student Allowance or Student Loan living costs.

chunks.title: Commencement date — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
Training Incentive Allowance cannot commence earlier than 28 days before the client's course starts. This is because any earlier than 28 days before the course start date gives no guarantee that the client will be receiving a qualifying benefit at the time the course starts.
## Lump-sum payments
Lump sum payments can be made at any point during a client's course of study but no earlier than 28 days prior to the course start date.
If a client receives a Training Incentive Allowance lump-sum payment for a cost part-way through their course of study, their ongoing weekly payments may need to be reassessed (eg if client's costs exceed the maximum).
## Ongoing costs
If the application is received within 28 days of the course start date the commencement date of Training Incentive Allowance is the later of:
- the date the course starts or
- the date client's qualifying benefit commences
If the application is received after 28 days from the course start date, the commencement date of Training Incentive Allowance is the later of:
- the date the application is received or
- the date client's qualifying benefit commences

chunks.title: Considerations when granting Training Incentive Allowance — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Considerations when granting Training Incentive Allowance
Training Incentive Allowance aims to help clients increase their skills for employment and extend the number of roles for which they may qualify.
When deciding whether to grant Training Incentive Allowance you need to consider:
- whether the course is likely to increase the client's skills and lead to obtaining employment in a field relevant to the course and
- whether employment opportunities are likely to be available in the labour market at the end of the course and
- whether the course enhances the client's skill set

chunks.title: Costs exceed maximum — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Costs exceed maximum
When the client's combined one-off course costs and ongoing costs exceed the maximum Training Incentive Allowance payable the client is given the choice on how they would like to split the payments, either:
- the client can choose to have all their one-off course costs paid first with the balance of Training Incentive Allowance being paid towards their ongoing costs or
- the client can choose to have their ongoing costs paid first, with the balance of Training Incentive Allowance being paid towards their one-off course costs
Clients may also apply for a Student Loan to cover their course fees and/or course related costs.

chunks.title: Course costs — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Course costs
Course costs mean the client's necessary and reasonable costs of attending the course and can include (but are not limited to):
- Capital items
- Course equipment and materials
- Course fees
- Care costs including childcare costs (less any Childcare Assistance) and care costs associated with older or disabled people, eg transport costs to the care provider
- Babysitting or other child-minding costs
- Books and stationery
- Laptops
- Internet costs
- Installation of internet
- Accommodation (for those extra mural courses that may have a compulsory residential study component)
- Transport to and from the course, including car running costs and parking
- Travel
- Essential field trip costs
Course costs can be either one-off or ongoing costs.
Although you can include all the client's course costs in the calculation of Training Incentive Allowance, the maximum Training Incentive Allowance payable may not cover all the costs. You should tell the client of all the options available to them.

chunks.title: Course fees — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Course fees
Only fees that are compulsory for every student when they enrol can be included in Training Incentive Allowance. These include:
- tuition costs
- compulsory student service fees
Optional fees cannot be included in Training Incentive Allowance. These include:
- penalties for late enrolment
- administration charges for paying by instalment
- optional service fees

chunks.title: Courses not allowed — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Courses not allowed
Training Incentive Allowance cannot be paid for:
- any course of study provided by the Ministry of Social Development
- New Zealand Qualifications Framework level 8 and above
- any course that is less than 12 weeks long
Note level 8 and above includes Postgraduate Diplomas and Certificates, Masters and Doctorates.

chunks.title: Courses that include work experience — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Courses that include work experience
Some courses require the student to undertake work experience as a part of their programme of study.
The part of the course that is work experience still needs to meet the definition of a recognised course of study for the Training Incentive Allowance to be paid.
If the work experience is provided through a business or community organisation that is not associated with the training provider, it may not meet the qualifications for Training Incentive Allowance.
When you are assessing payment of Training Incentive Allowance, do not include the cost or the period required to undertake work experience through an outside organisation. The component of the course that meets the eligibility (e.g. is a recognised course of study) can still be paid for by Training Incentive Allowance.
However, if a client claims the work experience is a compulsory component of the course or if the work experience is not completed this will result in a failure, then we should consider accepting the fee as part of the recognised part of study.

chunks.title: Disability related costs — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Disability related costs
If a client has a disability or a health condition, they may have additional costs associated with their disability that arise due to participating in training (eg taxi costs for transport or cost of a note-taker for lectures). A client may include these costs in their Training Incentive Allowance.
If the cost is large, the client may test their eligibility to Support Funds to cover the costs rather than using their Training Incentive Allowance.
Support Funds assist disabled people or people with a health condition to take up employment or undertake employment-related training. This is a payment of up to a maximum of $15,600 per person over their lifetime.
Note a client is not required to exhaust Support Funds prior to accessing the Training Incentive Allowance.
Support Funds can cover items like:
- support person ie interpreters, reader/writers
- teacher aide assistance.
If a client has a disability cost included in their Training Incentive Allowance, they cannot include the same cost in their Disability Allowance, Temporary Additional Support or Support Funds.

chunks.title: Emergency Benefit including Emergency Maintenance Allowance (sole parents) — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Emergency Benefit including Emergency Maintenance Allowance (sole parents)
Clients getting an Emergency Benefit, or an Emergency Maintenance Allowance are paid an equivalent benefit that best fits the client's reason(s) that prevents them from earning a sufficient income.
The benefit they are paid depends on the client's individual circumstances and the reason they are not working.
Training Incentive Allowance is usually paid to clients aged 16-64 years. It can also be paid to clients aged 65 years or over who are getting their Emergency Benefit if they are a sole parent.
To qualify for Training Incentive Allowance, the Emergency Benefit they are granted will be equivalent to:

chunks.title: Example of payment calculation — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text: A client meets all the Training Incentive Allowance qualifications and has total course costs of $5,620.00. The course costs are made up of course fees of $2500 and books and stationery costs of $650, transport costs of $15 per week, and childcare costs of $50 per week. The course of study is 38 weeks long. This includes 3 short breaks over the academic year totalling 6 weeks. Remember breaks are included when calculating entitlement.

chunks.title: Calculation — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text: One-off course costs Total cost Ongoing costs Total cost Course fees $2,500 Travel (38 weeks x $15.00) $570 Books and stationery $650 plus childcare (38 weeks x $50.00) $1,900 Total one-off costs $3,150 Total ongoing costs $2,470 Total combined course costs $5,620 Maximum Training Incentive Allowance for this example (weekly rate $143.08 as at 1 April 2026 multiplied by 38 weeks = $5,437.04) The total costs associated with the course are $5,620. While the maximum Training Incentive Allowance available is $5,437.04 (38 weeks x $143.08 as at 1 April 2026), the client's costs of $5,620 exceed this maximum payable.

chunks.title: Costs can be paid in different ways — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text: All the one-off course costs paid If all the one-off course costs are paid by Training Incentive Allowance ($3,150) the balance remaining $2,287.04 ($5,437.04 - $3,150) can be paid weekly over the course duration (38 weeks) for the client's ongoing costs. The client would get $60.18 a week ($2,287.04 divided by 38 weeks) towards their ongoing costs. All of the ongoing costs paid Instead of paying all the course costs, the client can get their Training Incentive Allowance on a weekly basis to cover their ongoing costs of $2,470. The calculation of childcare and transport should be calculated based on the number of weeks these costs are incurred including holidays. This means the client gets $65 a week ($2,470 divided by 38 weeks = $65). The remainder of $2,967.04 (maximum Training Incentive Allowance for the client less ongoing costs) is paid to the course provider towards the client's fees and costs. The client may test their eligibility to Student Loan to cover the remainder of their course fees.

chunks.text:

chunks.title: Full-time study definition — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Full-time study definition
Tertiary programmes have an Equivalent Full-Time Student (EFTS) value assigned to them. For the course to be approved as full-time, the length of that course must meet a certain EFTS value.
Full-time study is calculated depending on the length of the course and assigned value of EFTS (equivalent full-time student).
Any study less than full-time is considered part-time.
