chunks.title: Guidelines for determining if the course will improve the client's skills for employment — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Guidelines for determining if the course will improve the client's skills for employment
Each case must be considered on its own merits:
- Is the proposed training directly related to the client's employment goals?
- Is the training going to help the client secure and sustain paid employment in the labour market?
- Will the course of study build on the client's skillset?
## Example 1
Mariah is on Sole Parent Support client with 4 dependent children. Mariah has spent the past 10 years raising her children and would now like to use the skills she has learnt to become an Early Childcare teacher.
Mariah is applying Training Incentive Allowance to undertake a Bachelor of Education (Teaching) Early Childhood at Victoria University.
Mariah will be granted Training Incentive Allowance to complete this course of study as this will improve her skills for employment.
## Example 2
Elena is getting Supported Living Payment and has been on benefit for the past 3 years. Elena speaks fluent Te Reo Māori and has expressed interest in working as a Te Reo Māori teacher.
Elena would like to study Te Reo Māori through Te Wānanga o Aotearoa to formalise the skills she has already, helping her reach her employment goals.
Elena will be granted Training Incentive Allowance to study Te Reo Māori.
## Example - not for recreational purposes
Kevin is a sole parent who would like to undertake a Level 5 Diploma in Golf Coaching, however, all of Kevin's work experience and work goals have been around graphic design.
Kevin enjoys golf in his free time while his mother cares for his children; however, he does not plan to work in the golf industry.
Kevin will not be granted Training Incentive Allowance to complete a golf coaching course.

chunks.title: Increasing skills for employment — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Increasing skills for employment
A course of study will increase a client’s skills for employment when it will:
- provide or increase specific work skills which will enhance the client's employment skills and opportunities and
- is not for recreational or interest purposes

chunks.title: Internet — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Internet
Generally the internet is necessary for all clients to participate in study.
When the client has costs related to study, they can be included as an allowable cost in Training Incentive Allowance.
## Client has internet connected before studying
The internet can be considered one of a client's necessary and reasonable costs of participating in study.
## Options for accessing the internet
The client may choose to:
- have the internet connected at home and include the monthly charge in their assessment of allowable costs or
- have the ongoing internet cost already in place included or
- purchase internet time from the training facility, library or other venue and include this amount in their assessment of allowable costs

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Training Incentive Allowance is a non-taxable payment for clients who meet the qualifications and are getting specific types of benefits.
This assistance is to help clients take up education or training to:
- increase their employment skills and
- improve future employment outcomes

chunks.title: Jobseeker Support sole parents and full-time study — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Jobseeker Support sole parents and full-time study
Clients studying full-time do not qualify for Jobseeker Support.
Clients who want to study full-time can check whether they qualify for Student Allowance, Student Loan and other tertiary student supports. This also applies for clients getting Emergency Benefit equivalent benefit to Jobseeker Support depending on the conditions of grant.
A full-time tertiary student is a person enrolled in a full-time course or study programme within the meaning of the Student Allowances Regulations 1998.

chunks.title: Jobseeker Support sole parents and part-time study — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Jobseeker Support sole parents and part-time study
Clients studying full-time do not qualify for Jobseeker Support.
To qualify for Training Incentive Allowance clients may study, but must enrol part-time only, this enables them to meet their work obligations.
Sole parent clients can get Jobseeker Support, and be studying or in training part-time as long as they:
- can meet their work or work preparation obligations at the same time or
- qualify for an exemption from their work obligations
Each application for Training Incentive Allowance must be considered on its own merits.

chunks.title: Method of payment — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Method of payment
Training Incentive Allowance can be paid as a lump sum or as ongoing payments or as a combination of both depending on what type of course costs the client has.
## Lump sum payments
Lump sum payments can only be made for one-off costs (not ongoing costs) and can be paid directly to the provider or to the client if appropriate.
## Ongoing costs
The calculation of care, transport and course costs should be calculated based on the number of weeks these costs are incurred. The actual ongoing payment can be spread out over the academic year including short breaks.

chunks.title: Money Management and youth money management — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Money Management and youth money management
Clients can still get Training Incentive Allowance if they are:
- getting Young Parent Payment and are youth money managed or
- getting a main benefit and have Money Management imposed as a non-financial sanction
Training Incentive Allowance payments will not be money managed.
Training Incentive Allowance payments can be paid directly to the client or young person, although course fees can be paid directly to the provider.

chunks.title: Payment calculation — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Payment calculation
Training Incentive Allowance is assessed by the Annual General Adjustment at 1 April each year.
The rate as at 1 April 2026 is $143.08 per week or $5,723.20 per year.
The following can be used to calculate the rate of payment for Training Incentive Allowance:
Course costs
Ongoing costs
Course fees
$_____
Travel
$_____
Plus other costs
$_____
Plus childcare
$_____
$_____
Plus other costs
$_____
Total course costs
$_____
Total ongoing costs
$_____
The maximum Training Incentive Allowance payable can be no more than $143.08 per week up to $5,723.20 a year (as at 1 April 2026).

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Payment
Training Incentive Allowance is paid for the actual costs the client will have when they are attending a course, up to a maximum of $143.08 (as at 1 April 2026) for each week of the course (maximum of $5,723.20 in a 52-week period as at 1 April 2026).
- for example, if a client's course is 30 weeks, the maximum Training Incentive Allowance payable is $4,292.40 ($143.08 x 30 weeks).
Note the maximum payable in a 52-week period is 40 weeks equivalent of the weekly payment.
The ongoing childcare, transport and course costs should be calculated using the number of weeks these costs are incurred including holidays. The actual ongoing payment can be spread out over the academic year.
## Clients who will lose eligibility to Training Incentive Allowance part way through their course
For clients who will no longer qualify for Training Incentive Allowance part way through their course, the maximum payable amount must be calculated based on the number of weeks the client is qualified for Training Incentive Allowance.

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To get a Training Incentive Allowance, a client must be getting:
- Emergency Benefit and be a sole parent
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment - caring for a person
- Supported Living Payment health condition, injury or disability
- Young Parent Payment and be a sole parent
- Jobseeker Support and be a sole parent (part-time study only):
and
- be aged between 16 and 64 or
- be 65 years or over, and not be qualified to get New Zealand Superannuation
and
- meet the residence requirements
and
- be enrolled in a recognised course of study that increases the client's skills for employment and is: Level 1 to 7 on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF) and12 weeks or longer
- Level 1 to 7 on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF) and
- 12 weeks or longer
and
- if the client has completed a level 7 NZQF qualification in the past 5 years, the Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that further assistance will significantly improve the client's employment outcomes in the future
Note the partner of a client getting Supported Living Payment cannot get a Training Incentive Allowance unless they qualify for Supported Living Payment in their own right.

chunks.title: Recognised course of study — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Recognised course of study
A Training Incentive Allowance can only be paid to a client who is enrolled in a recognised course of study, as defined in Regulation 2(1)(a) of the Student Allowances Regulations 1998, ie:
- the programme of study is funded by Tertiary Education Commission (TEC) or
- funded by Ministry of Education (if secondary school).
The course of study must also increase the client’s skills for employment, and be:
- Level 1 to 7 on NZQF and
- 12 weeks or more in duration

chunks.title: Reimbursing costs — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Reimbursing costs
Clients may be reimbursed through the Training Incentive Allowance for actual and reasonable one-off course-related costs needed for undertaking study.
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, the client cannot be reimbursed for costs paid more than 28 days before the:
- course start date or
- date they applied for Training Incentive Allowance (if client applied more than 28 days after the course start date)
Note one-off course-related costs (not including compulsory course fees) that have been covered by other government funded financial assistance (both recoverable and non-recoverable) will not be reimbursed. For more information on compulsory course fees see:
Ongoing costs can only be paid from the date the client's Training Incentive Allowance commences.
## Example of exceptional circumstances
Ruth enrolled in study and paid for a laptop and the books needed for her course. However, just before Ruth's course started her youngest child developed a serious health condition and Ruth cancelled her enrolment.
Ruth re-enrolled in the same course the following semester. Ruth is granted Training Incentive Allowance for the following semester and is reimbursed for the course costs paid for initially, because the Ministry considers Ruth's child's health condition to be an exceptional circumstance.
## Examples of non-exceptional circumstances
Example 1
Lucy gets Supported Living Payment. Lucy enrolled and purchased a laptop for her Level 4 computer science course commencing on 9 March 2026. On 5 April 2026 Lucy applies for the Training Incentive Allowance to cover the costs of her course, and requests to have the cost of her laptop reimbursed.
As the Ministry does not consider Lucy's circumstances exceptional, she will not be reimbursed for the cost of purchasing a laptop.
Example 2
Mana and his 4-year-old child moved into an apartment and purchased a new set of knives, a slow cooker, an air fryer and a cast iron pan.
Six months later, Mana enrolled in a culinary arts course and asked to be reimbursed for the cooking utensils as he would now use them for the course.
Mana cannot be reimbursed for the supplies because these were not paid for in order to undertake his course of study.

chunks.title: Residency requirements — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Residency requirements
To qualify for Training Incentive Allowance, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or be a deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 that allows the client or partner to work in New Zealand
or
- be recognised as a refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009
or
- hold a temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 that permits the person to work in New Zealand and who is: awaiting the outcome of their claim for recognition as a refugee or a protected person ora person applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 who is compelled to remain in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances
- awaiting the outcome of their claim for recognition as a refugee or a protected person or
- a person applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 who is compelled to remain in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances
and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit

chunks.title: Scholarships — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Scholarships
In some cases a client applying for Training Incentive Allowance may also get a scholarship.
Scholarship payments may affect a client's entitlement to Training Incentive Allowance and may also impact on other forms of assistance.
When a scholarship is paid for course fees and other related course costs, these costs or the part of these costs paid by the scholarship cannot be included as a cost for Training Incentive Allowance.
A scholarship which includes a payment for living costs and is paid as a one-off payment or by regular instalments is income for benefit purposes and will be charged over the period the payment represents.
Any scholarship paid directly to the client may also be considered an asset for the purposes of assessing entitlement to supplementary assistance.

chunks.title: Secondary school — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Secondary school
Clients undertaking secondary school courses to gain an educational qualification can get a Training Incentive Allowance.
The course must be longer than 12 weeks.

chunks.title: Sole Parent Support — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Sole Parent Support
Before approving Training Incentive Allowance, consider whether the course or study will:
- increase the client's skills for employment and
- improve employment outcomes in the future
Sole Parent Support clients have part-time work obligations or work preparation obligations depending on the age of their youngest child.
Clients can get Sole Parent Support and undertake study or training as long as either they:
- can meet their work or work preparation obligations at the same time or
- are eligible for an exemption from their work obligations to complete study or training
Note study for which Training Incentive Allowance is payable can be considered a work preparation activity.
Each application for Training Incentive Allowance must be considered on its own merits.

chunks.title: Sole Parent Support clients who no longer qualify for benefit while studying full-time — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Sole Parent Support clients who no longer qualify for benefit while studying full-time
Sole parent clients do not qualify for Sole Parent Support when their youngest dependent child turns 14.
If a client studying full-time no longer qualifies for Sole Parent Support part way through the year as their youngest dependent child turns 14, there are 2 options the client may consider:
- continue full-time study and check whether they qualify for Student Allowance or Student Loan (including Student Loan living costs) - they will no longer qualify for Training Incentive Allowance under this option
- change to part-time study, keep getting Training Incentive Allowance, and transfer to Jobseeker Support. They must also be available for full-time work.
If a client tells the Ministry of Social Development of a change in circumstances, which means they will qualify for Jobseeker Support, from the date they no longer qualify for Sole Parent Support (e.g. they changed to part-time study), their rate of Training Incentive Allowance will be reassessed

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment - caring for a person — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Supported Living Payment - caring for a person
Clients getting Supported Living Payment caring for a person can get a Training Incentive Allowance.
Before granting a Training Incentive Allowance, you should consider whether the course the applicant intends to undertake is likely to help them increase their skills for employment and improve their employment outcomes in the future.

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
Clients getting Supported Living Payment with a health condition, injury or disability, can get a Training Incentive Allowance.
Before deciding to grant a Training Incentive Allowance, you should consider whether the course the applicant intends to undertake is likely to help them increase their skills for employment and improve their employment outcomes in the future.
For clients who have work preparation obligations study for which Training Incentive Allowance is payable can be considered a work preparation activity.
## Partner of a client getting Supported Living Payment
The partner of a client getting Supported Living Payment cannot get a Training Incentive Allowance unless they qualify for Supported Living Payment in their own right.
Each application for Training Incentive Allowance must be considered on its own merits.

chunks.title: Tertiary education — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Tertiary education
Training Incentive Allowance can be paid for tertiary courses up to level 7 on the New Zealand Qualifications and Certifications Framework. Courses for Level 8 and above do not qualify.
The client may need to seek a Student Loan to cover course fees if the fees exceed the maximum available through Training Incentive Allowance.

chunks.title: Training Incentive Allowance and Fees Free — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Training Incentive Allowance and Fees Free
The first-year Fees Free programme applied to first time students starting study on or after 1 January 2018. This scheme ended on 31 December 2024 and was replaced by final-year Fees Free from 1 January 2025.
## Final-year Fees Free
The final-year Fees Free programme was introduced from 1 January 2025. Eligible learners starting their final year of study from 2025 can claim their fees for their final year once they complete their study.
Note if a client uses Training Incentive Allowance for course fees in their final calendar year of study, they cannot get final-year Fees Free for fees in that calendar year.
Clients who are in their final year of study must decide whether to use Training Incentive Allowance towards their course fees, or fund their course fees another way (e.g. Student Loan) to claim final-year Fees Free if they complete their qualification. MSD will support clients in making this decision.
For more information, see:
- Tertiary Education Commission Entitlement - final-year Fees Free
## Clients with remaining entitlement to first-year Fees Free in 2025
Some clients who used first-year Fees Free in 2024 may be able to use their remaining entitlement in 2025. This is determined by the Tertiary Education Commission.
Clients who can use their remaining first-year Fees Free entitlement in 2025, cannot get Training Incentive Allowance for the same course fees. However, if the client’s remaining first-year Fees Free entitlement does not fully cover their course fees, they may use Training Incentive Allowance for the fees not already covered.
## Example – client has remaining first-year Fees Free entitlement
Josie started study in July 2024 and had her full course fees of $8,000 paid through the first-year Fees Free programme.
As her course fees were fully covered by first-year Fees Free, Josie could not use Training Incentive Allowance towards her course fees.
Josie continues the same qualification in 2025 with course fees of $7,000.
She is eligible to use her remaining $4,000 first-year Fees Free entitlement towards her total course fees.
Josie can use Training Incentive Allowance of $3,000 to cover her remaining course fees that are not covered by first-year Fees Free.

chunks.title: Training Incentive Allowance and Student Loan — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text: Clients studying while getting a main benefit cannot get a Student Allowance, or Student Loan living costs. However, some clients who get a Student Loan for course fees and course related costs, may also qualify for Training Incentive Allowance.

chunks.title: Student Loans for course fees — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text: Clients do not have to apply for a Student Loan to cover their course fees, before applying for the Training Incentive Allowance. It is up to the client to decide how to use their Training Incentive Allowance. Note if a client has already been granted a Student Loan before they apply for Training Incentive Allowance, they can still use the Training Incentive Allowance to pay for course fees by using it to reduce their Student Loan balance.

chunks.title: Student Loans and course related costs — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text: Students may get a Student Loan lump sum payment for course related costs. Clients getting a Training Incentive Allowance may get a Student Loan for course related costs (up to $1,000), less any Training Incentive Allowance they got for one-off course related costs. Note this deduction does not include Training Incentive Allowance payments for childcare, transport and disability related costs. This means that the order in which the client is granted each assistance can affect the maximum amount they can borrow for course related costs through a Student Loan, as in the following situations: Training Incentive Allowance paid before Student Loan for course related costs If a client's Student Loan has not been granted when their Training Incentive Allowance is paid, then their Student Loan course related cost payment of $1,000 will be reduced by any Training Incentive Allowance one-off payments for course related costs. Student Loan course related costs paid before Training Incentive Allowance If a client's Student Loan is approved and their course related costs of $1,000 is paid before the Training Incentive Allowance is granted, then their Student Loan course related cost entitlement of $1,000 is not reduced by the Training Incentive Allowance they get. However, Training Incentive Allowance cannot be used to pay for costs that have already been covered. Part-payment of Student Loan course related costs before Training Incentive Allowance When only part of a client's Student Loan course related cost entitlement of $1,000 has been paid, before their Training Incentive Allowance is granted, then their remaining Student Loan course related cost entitlement will be reduced by any Training Incentive Allowance one-off payments.

chunks.title: Student Loan eligibility — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text: Student Loan eligibility is limited to a maximum amount of study (generally around 7 or 8 years of full-time study per student). It is important we explain this to clients to help them understand this, and other parts of the Student Loan Scheme to allow them to make decisions that best suit their circumstances

chunks.title: Transport — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Transport
If the client is travelling to and from the course by public transport, you should include the client's actual and reasonable public transport cost as an allowable cost in the Training Incentive Allowance assessment.
Clients who have a Community Services Card can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect and should apply for this if it is the most cost-effective way to meet their transport costs.
When a client has not used their Community Services Card to apply for the 50% discount, you must discuss their reasons if their actual public transport costs are higher than they would be if the 50% discount was applied.
The client may have a good reason for not applying for the 50% discount (e.g. they lost their Community Services Card and have applied for a replacement, meaning their transport costs will be higher for a short period of time or the client has a disability and there are accessibility issues with the public transport provider's application process).
When there is a good reason, the client's actual public transport costs should be included as an allowable cost. If there is no good reason, their allowable costs for travel should not be more than the cost of the subsidised public transport fare.
If the client is not using public transport, the allowable cost must be:
- reasonable and
- based on the distance that the client has to travel and
- can include parking and vehicle running costs and
- take into account any special needs (for example, clients with certain disabilities may only be able to travel by taxi)
If the client has a transport cost included in their Training Incentive Allowance, they cannot include the same cost in their Temporary Additional Support, Disability Allowance or Support Funds.
Clients using a private car to get to and from study would be paid the same rates as Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: University preparation programmes — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## University preparation programmes
Clients undertaking university preparation programmes to gain an educational qualification can get a Training Incentive Allowance.
University preparation programmes are programmes that assist people to prepare for university study.
These courses are usually undertaken by people who wish to participate in university study but do not meet the entry requirements for their chosen field of study or are returning to study after an extended absence.
Most major New Zealand universities offer preparation programmes. The course must be run for longer than 12 weeks for the client to get Training Incentive Allowance.

chunks.title: Young Parent Payment (sole parents) — specific employment related assistance > training incentive allowance
chunks.text:
## Young Parent Payment (sole parents)
Youth Providers work closely with young clients to support them into education, training or work-based learning.
Providers support young parents to identify their educational goals, education options and anything else a young person needs to improve and shape their future.
The providers assist with applications for Training Incentive Allowance and review all circumstances when recommending payment.

chunks.title: Benefit cancelled moving into paid employment — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text:
## Benefit cancelled moving into paid employment
To receive Work Bonus, a client or partner must have cancelled their benefit because they are moving into paid employment.
This can occur when the client:
- gains new full-time employment
- Increases their hours of employment
The client will need to provide employer details and confirmation of the date they will be starting employment.
Note Work Bonus is paid automatically when a client or partner cancels their benefit to enter paid employment. You must ensure that you used the correct code when cancelling the benefit.
For more information see:
- Clients who may have their income exempted
- Specific benefits for Work Bonus
- Debt recovery at cancellation
- Payment

chunks.title: Client elects to cancel Work Bonus — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text:
## Client elects to cancel Work Bonus
If a client asks to cancel their Work Bonus payment, you should check that they understand that:
- Work Bonus is non-recoverable
- Work Bonus is non-taxable and is not included as income for Working For Families, Child Support or Accommodation Supplement
Discuss with the client why they wish to cancel their Work Bonus payments.
If the client confirms that they still wish to cancel their Work Bonus, you should use backdated review to cancel the payment.
## Client has already received some Work Bonus
If a client has already received some of a Work Bonus payment, the client can choose to keep what they have received.
It is the client's choice as to whether they keep any Work Bonus already paid out or not.
If the client elects to return what they have received, you need to establish a debt in order for them to be able to return the payment to Work and Income. You can then talk with the client to establish how they would prefer to repay the Work Bonus payment.
For more information see:
- Effect of Work Bonus on other assistance
- Work Bonus [no link find out why]
- Repayment options [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Client reapplies for benefit while receiving Work Bonus — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text:
## Client reapplies for benefit while receiving Work Bonus
If a client re-applies for benefit while they are receiving Work Bonus, and they qualify for a benefit, Work Bonus payments will continue to be paid during any stand-down period. This should be taken into consideration if the client makes a hardship application.
Work Bonus payments will automatically stop from the commencement date of the new benefit.
## Non-entitlement period applies
If a client who is receiving Work Bonus reapplies for a benefit and has a 13 week non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment, the client cannot receive Work Bonus payments from the date the non-entitlement period starts.
If a client recomplies and is granted a provisional benefit, their Work Bonus payment cannot be restarted.
## Client separates
If a couple separate and only one partner of the relationship applies for a benefit, the person not returning to a benefit will continue to receive their portion of the Work Bonus at the same rate.
The payments of Work Bonus to the client granted the new benefit will automatically stop from the commencement date of the new benefit.

chunks.title: Clients who cannot receive Work Bonus — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text:
## Clients who cannot receive Work Bonus
A client or partner cannot receive Work Bonus in the following situations:
- when they have part-time or full-time work obligations
- when a client or partner advises Work and Income outside 14 days of their employment start date unless there is a good and sufficient reason for not advising of employment within 14 days, Work Bonus may be granted
- when their benefit is suspended or not being paid for a reason other than a grade 3 sanction (eg because the client has an outstanding warrant to arrest or a voluntary unemployment non-entitlement period)
Work Bonus can be paid when the client is moving into qualifying employment. Employment that is not qualifying employment for Work Bonus is:
- employment that started before 15 July 2013
- employment in an unsuitable business
- client or partner has received a Work Bonus within the last 12 months
- self-employment
- employment outside of New Zealand
Note clients and partners who do not qualify for Work Bonus may be able to receive assistance to transition into employment.
For more information see:
- Transition to Work [no link find out why]
- Client reapplies for benefit while receiving Work Bonus
- Good and sufficient reason
- Qualifications
- Specific benefits for Work Bonus

chunks.title: Clients who may have their income exempted — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text:
## Clients who may have their income exempted
Clients receiving Supported Living Payment can have some or all of their income from employment exempted under:
- personal earnings exemption for a totally blind person
- exemption for severe disablement
These clients or their partners may be financially disadvantaged if their benefit is cancelled to move into employment, even if they would be granted Work Bonus.
Before cancelling a client or partner's Supported Living Payment, you should discuss the options available with them.
For more information see:
- Supported Living Payment Exemption for severe disablement
- Supported Living Payment Personal earnings exemptions
- Payment

chunks.title: Debt recovery at cancellation — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text:
## Debt recovery at cancellation
If the client has a debt with Work and Income you will need to make arrangements with them for repayment of the debt.
Work Bonus should not be used to recover any outstanding debt balances for clients when their benefit is cancelled.
## Debt recovery suspension
If a client is cancelling their benefit to start or to continue in paid employment, the debt recovery can be suspended for a three-month period provided the client remains in employment.
As there is no application for Work Bonus, clients who want to apply for Debt Recovery Suspension will need to complete an application for Assistance to transition into employment.
Note we can still accept repayments if the client wishes to start paying the outstanding debt straight away.
For more information see:
- Transition to Work (TTW) - Debt Recovery Suspension - Overview [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Effect of Work Bonus on other assistance — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text:
## Effect of Work Bonus on other assistance
Work Bonus is non-taxable and is not included as income for Working for Families assistance (WFF) including Working for families tax credits, Child Support, Childcare Assistance or Accommodation Supplement. It is included as income for Temporary Additional Support, Special Needs Grant and Special Benefit.
This means that the payment of Work Bonus will not prevent a client from receiving work related tax credits when they start work.

As the Work Bonus is in excess of the Assistance to Transition into Employment - bridging finance maximum, the client cannot get Assistance to Transition into Employment - bridging finance. The client is also entitled to $155.87 Work Bonus in the third week after starting work.

chunks.title: Example 2 — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text: A client with a partner is getting Supported Living Payment. They have cancelled their benefit as they have moved into employment. They have applied for Assistance to Transition into Employment for bridging finance only.

chunks.title: Work Bonus — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text: Last benefit payment $721.44 (as at 1 April 2026) Week 1 $721.44 Week 2 $621.44 Week 3 $521.44 Week 4 $421.44 Week 5 $321.44 Week 6 $221.44 Week 7 $121.44 Week 8 $21.44 Interface with Assistance to Transition into Employment - bridging finance Assistance type Week 1 and Week 2 Week 3 Week 4 Week 5 Week 6 Week 7 Week 8 Assistance to Transition into Employment - bridging finance over 2 week period $500 maximum Nil Nil Nil Nil Nil Work Bonus for first 2 weeks $1,342.88 ($721.44 + $621.44) $521.44 $421.44 $321.44 $221.44 $121.44 Assistance to Transition into Employment - bridging finance payable Nil Nil Nil Nil Nil Nil The client is entitled to $1,342.88 Work Bonus for weeks 1 and 2. chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason
A good and sufficient reason may include, (but is not limited to) the client:
- was temporarily medically unfit
- had a death or illness in their immediate family
Consider when the client would have reasonably been able to advise Work and Income of their change of circumstance.
In these cases, Work Bonus may be able to be granted.

chunks.title: Introduction — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Work Bonus is a non-taxable, non-recoverable payment that can be made to clients (or partners) on specific benefits who do not have either part-time or full-time work obligations and who cancel their benefits to move into employment.
Work Bonus is paid as an incentive to and in recognition of clients' (or partners') efforts to gain and commence paid employment and exit the benefit system when they do not have work obligations.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Payment
- Debt recovery at cancellation
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals

chunks.title: Payment — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text:
## Payment
The amount of Work Bonus payable is:
- equivalent to the client's full unabated net benefit rate (before any reductions or deductions) including partner's benefit rate (if any)
- including partner's benefit rate (if any)
Note Work Bonus does not include any Extra help paid with their benefit prior to the benefit cancellation
- decreased in increments of $100 ($50 each for couples) each week
- stopped when remaining amount is less than $10 ($5 each for couples)
Only one payment of Work Bonus can be made in a 52 week period, regardless:
- of the duration the original Work Bonus was paid for or
- if the client and partner both start employment (even at different times)
Work Bonus is not income and asset tested.
Work Bonus is paid automatically when a client or partner cancels their benefit to enter paid employment. You must ensure that you use the correct code when cancelling the benefit. For more information see:
- Examples of paying Work Bonus
- Client elects to cancel Work Bonus
## Correcting Work Bonus payments
Work Bonus payments are made automatically when a specific benefit is cancelled and a Work Bonus applicable code is used.
In some situations a client may be eligible to get Work Bonus, but it is paid incorrectly or it is not paid at all. Generally, you should use a backdated review to correct the payment.
For more information see:
- Work Bonus [no link find out why]
## Emergency Benefit clients
SWIFTT will not pay Work Bonus automatically for Emergency Benefit (equivalent to Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury, disability or total blindness) clients or partners cancelling their benefit to enter paid employment. For the process to make Work Bonus payments to these clients contact Helpline.
## Client starts work mid-way through a pay period
If a client starts work mid-way through a pay period, their last benefit payment received may be a partial payment. However the rate payable for the Work Bonus is still based on their full unabated net benefit rate.

chunks.title: Qualifications — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To receive Work Bonus a client or partner must:
- have been receiving a specific benefit
- have their benefit cancelled as they are moving into qualifying paid employment in New Zealand (eg not employment in Australia)
- have advised Work and Income that they are starting paid employment within 14 days of doing so, unless there is a good and sufficient reason they could not advise Work and Income of their change within 14 days
Generally, a client does not have to apply for Work Bonus, and it is paid automatically to clients who meet the qualifications. However, there are some exceptions. For more information about when and how to pay Work Bonus manually, see:
- Work Bonus [no link find out why]
- Work Bonus not paid automatically [no link find out why]
Note Work Bonus is not income or asset tested.
For more information see:
- Clients who cannot receive Work Bonus
- Client reapplies for benefit while receiving Work Bonus
- Good and sufficient reason
- Specific benefits for Work Bonus

chunks.title: Specific benefits for Work Bonus — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text:
## Specific benefits for Work Bonus
To qualify for Work Bonus, clients must be getting a specific benefit, this can be one of the following:
## Supported Living Payment
- granted on the grounds that the client is permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work, because of a health condition, injury, disability or total blindness
## Supported Living Payment (partners)
- partner would qualify for Supported Living Payment in their own right, as they are permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work, because of a health condition, injury or disability or
- partner is caring for a dependent child under 3 years of age, which may include a child for whom the client is getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit
## Emergency Benefit equivalent to Supported Living Payment
- granted on the grounds that the client is permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work, because of a health condition, injury, disability or total blindness
## Emergency Benefit equivalent to Supported Living Payment (partners)
- partner would qualify for Emergency Benefit equivalent to Supported Living Payment in their own right, as they are permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work because of a health condition, injury or disability or
- partner is caring for a dependent child under 3 years of age, which may include a child for whom the client is getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit
## Sole Parent Support
- client is caring for a dependent child under 3 years of age, which may include a child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid
## Emergency Maintenance Allowance
- client is caring for a dependent child under 3 years of age, which may include a child for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid

chunks.title: Work Bonus and Assistance to Transition into Employment — specific employment related assistance > work bonus
chunks.text:
## Work Bonus and Assistance to Transition into Employment
Clients receiving Work Bonus can also receive Assistance to Transition into Employment.
However, Work Bonus will reduce the amount of Assistance to Transition into Employment - bridging finance dollar-for-dollar. Both payments provide non-recoverable assistance for a transitional period when the client leaves the benefit to move into employment.
Assistance to Transition into Employment - bridging finance cannot be paid if the total Work Bonus payable for the first 2 weeks following the benefit cancellation date is equal to or more than $500.
If the Work Bonus payments are less than $500 over the fortnight, the amount of bridging finance payable is the difference between the Assistance to Transition into Employment - bridging finance and Work Bonus.
## Calculation
Assess total amount of bridging finance required to cover 2 weeks
Assess total amount of the first 2 weeks of Work Bonus
Subtract total amount of bridging finance from the total amount of Work Bonus
If Work Bonus is less than bridging finance
Pay the difference between Work Bonus and Assistance to Transition into Employment (bridging finance) as bridging finance
If Work Bonus is more than bridging finance
There is no entitlement to bridging finance
Where a client has other job placement costs, job placement assistance can be granted following the existing process.
Clients receiving Work Bonus may also apply for Debt Recovery Suspension through Transition to Work - Debt recovery suspension [no link find out why]
For more information see:
- Examples of Work Bonus and Assistance to transition into employment

chunks.text:

chunks.title: Accessing a client's file to obtain personal information — core policy > agents
chunks.text:
## Accessing a client's file to obtain personal information
A client may authorise their agent to have access to information held by the Ministry of Social Development about the client. Generally, this involves making enquiries into the client's file. This could be used in situations such as (but not limited to):
- a client is unable to physically visit an office
- an agent is acting on behalf of the client in cases of complaints and reviews
- an agent being appointed as a result of a trespass notice
## One-off requests for information
If the request to obtain personal information is a one-off request, there is no need for the 'Appointment of an Agent' form to be completed. Unless the client and agent are present together, the client's written permission is still required.
Any documentation provided, such as a signed note from the client, should be retained on the client's file, and the request noted in the client's CMS record.

chunks.title: Agent appointed by a Court Order — core policy > agents
chunks.text: In certain circumstances, the Courts may appoint an individual to act on behalf of someone who is incapacitated. These Court Orders are made under the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988, and are described below. The Order will list the rights and powers granted to the person named, or any restrictions to these rights and powers.

chunks.title: Order in relation to personal care and welfare — core policy > agents
chunks.text: The Court may make an order appointing someone to make and implement decisions on behalf of a person in relation to aspects of their personal care and welfare. The order could appoint a Welfare Guardian. A Welfare Guardian is only appointed if the person wholly lacks the capacity to make or communicate decisions relating to their personal care and welfare. The powers of a Welfare Guardian are granted for a set period, which can be no longer than three years. To amend or extend these powers, an application for review must be made to the Court prior to the expiry of the order.

chunks.title: Order in relation to property — core policy > agents
chunks.text: A Court Order may appoint someone to make and implement decisions on behalf of a person in relation to their property. 'Property' in this context may include a client's financial affairs, including the ability to act on the client's behalf with Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment. The powers of Orders to administer property are granted for a set period, which can be no longer than three years. To amend or extend these powers, an application for review must be made to the Court prior to the expiry of the order. The Court may also issue a temporary Property Order; this can be valid for a period of no more than three months. Note once a Property Order is invoked, the client loses the legal ability to exercise the rights given to the person named in the Order.

chunks.title: Court Orders and the Ministry of Social Development — core policy > agents
chunks.text: An individual may present Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment with such a Court Order covering the client's affairs, requesting to be appointed as the client's agent. While this can be acted upon, what they can do on behalf of the client is determined by what is granted by the Court Order. In some cases, the powers of agency being requested by the person named in the Court Order may fall outside the powers granted by the Order. In some cases the client may be able and willing to consent to the individual being appointed an agent for their dealings with Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment. If this is inappropriate, or does not occur, it may be appropriate to request that the individual has the Court determine whether they should have the power to represent the client with Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment. Consult your Service Delivery solicitor if you are unsure about a Court Order.

chunks.title: Process — core policy > agents
chunks.text: For information on how to deal with Court Orders, see: - Process for dealing with Court Orders

chunks.title: Agents — core policy > agents
chunks.text: An agent is a person or organisation who acts in the interests of another. A person can be made an agent by the consent of both the client and the prospective agent, by way of a Court Order or, in exceptional circumstances, without a client's consent. 'Agency' refers to the relationship that arises where one person is appointed to act as the representative of another. The granting of agency is not controlled by the Social Security Act 2018; it is contract-based, and is governed by common law. Clients When a client appoints an agent, the client still has the right to discuss their circumstances with Work and Income, Senior Services and Housing Assessment. A client can appoint more than one agent to act for them for different purposes, such as, one person to provide information about changes in circumstances, and another person to act for them in respect of a review of decision or appeal. A client can authorise the Ministry of Social Development to pass on their agent's details to social housing providers who may have properties available to offer them. The agent also has to agree for their details to be given to the provider, and the provider will decide whether they will deal with the agent directly or the client.

chunks.title: What can an agent do? — core policy > agents
chunks.text: The rights and responsibilities an agent has over a client's affairs are determined by the client, and are dependent on what role the client wishes to give the agent. In general, anything a person can do for themselves, they may authorise an agent to do. For more information on this see: - What an agent can do - What an agent cannot do

chunks.title: Length of agency — core policy > agents
chunks.text: The length of agency is determined by the client. For ongoing representation it is necessary that a letter or form granting agency is completed; this will preferably be the Ministry of Social Development 'Appointment of an Agent' form. In some situations a client may wish to grant temporary agency for one-off, short-term roles.

chunks.title: Agent is the client's responsibility — core policy > agents
chunks.text: When a client requests an agent to be appointed, they are responsible for both the choice of agent, and for any actions that the agent carries out on their behalf; the client needs to be made fully aware of this at the time the agent is appointed. Exceptions to this are when the agent has been appointed by a Court Order, or at any time where the agent is appointed without the client's consent. However, in these situations the actions of an agent may still be binding on the client.

chunks.title: Ending agency — core policy > agents
chunks.text: Agency can be revoked at any time by either the client or the agent. The exceptions to this are when the agent: - has been appointed by a Court Order, made under the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1998 or - holds an Enduring Power of Attorney In some cases, it may also be appropriate for the Ministry of Social Development to not deal with a client's chosen agent, if it is for a fully justifiable reason, as we do have the discretion not to deal with an agent.

chunks.title: Limits to appointing an agent — core policy > agents
chunks.text: While it may be beneficial for the client to appoint an agent to act as their representative for Work and Income, Senior Services, or Housing Assessment purposes, you cannot insist that a client appoints one. This includes where a trespass notice has been issued against a client who has been prohibited from entering specific Ministry of Social Development sites.

chunks.title: Appointing an agent without the client's informed consent — core policy > agents
chunks.text:
## Appointing an agent without the client's informed consent
In some situations, an agent may be appointed without the client's consent.
This may be relevant, for example, if the client is mentally incapacitated, or physically incapacitated in a way that prevents them from conveying their consent.
If an agent holds an Enduring Power of Attorney over the client's affairs, the agent is not being appointed without the client's consent as the client has given prior approval.
## Agent appointed by a Court Order
In certain circumstances, the Courts may appoint an individual to act on behalf of someone who is incapacitated.
These orders are made under the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988.
## Agent not appointed by a Court Order
While a court order to formalise a person's legal right to act on behalf of a permanently incapacitated person is preferable, you cannot insist that one is obtained.
However, you must be satisfied that the client's representative is acting in the client's best interest.
## Temporary incapacity
In exceptional circumstances an agent may be required to act on the client's behalf due to the client being temporarily but totally incapacitated, for example if the client is in a coma and requires support from Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment.
For more information see:
- Agent appointed by a Court Order
- Permanently incapacitated
- Temporary incapacity

chunks.title: Client representatives — core policy > agents
chunks.text:
## Client representatives
A client may ask that a client representative be appointed as a client's agent. This may be an individual person such as a benefit advocate. They do not have to be part of an organisation.
## Process
The client's informed consent is required before we can deal with a client representative as an agent. You need to ensure that the client approves of the agent, and is aware of what rights and responsibilities they are agreeing to give the client representative as their agent.
Whenever a client representative acting as the client's agent makes contact with Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment you must always:
- request identification to confirm the representative's identity
- confirm the client representatives authority to act on the clients behalf and
- ensure they exercise only the rights and responsibilities granted by the client (establish this by checking the agent latch in the client's CMS record)
For more information see:
- Process for appointing an agent
- Examples of where agency may be relevant
- Processing standards Agents [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Discretion not to deal with an agent — core policy > agents
chunks.text:
## Discretion not to deal with an agent
While a client has the right to appoint any individual or organisation as their agent, in certain circumstances it may be appropriate for the Ministry of Social Development not to deal with their chosen agent.
The discretion not to deal with a client's chosen agent must be exercised in a reasonable and fair manner, and be for a fully justifiable reason. Examples of where it may be relevant include:
- the agent chosen by the client is their 12 year old child (if the child is acting as interpreter you should suggest they contact the translation line)
- the agent has had a trespass notice issued against them, prohibiting them from being present in Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment offices
If you decide not to deal with a client's chosen agent, you must inform the client of this. This would preferably occur at the start of the agency, however if you become aware of valid reasons why Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment should not deal with the agent after they have already been appointed, it would still be appropriate to inform the client of this. You will also need to make notes in the client's CMS record, including:
- the name of the agent and
- the reasons why you have determined Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment should not deal with the agent
## Letter
You also need to inform the client of your decision in writing.

chunks.title: Enduring Power of Attorney — core policy > agents
chunks.text:
## Enduring Power of Attorney
An Enduring Power of Attorney, unlike an ordinary Power of Attorney, comes into effect after the person becomes mentally incapacitated. Enduring Powers of Attorney can be made in 2 ways.
## In relation to personal care and welfare
Such Enduring Powers of Attorney comes into effect only if and when the individual named becomes mentally incapacitated.
## In relation to personal property
'Property' in this context may include a client's financial affairs, including the ability to act on the client's behalf with Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment.
Under this form, the person granting the Power of Attorney can decide when the power may be used: namely, as soon as the Power of Attorney is signed and continuing in the event of mental incapacity, or deferring it until the client becomes mentally incapacitated.
Note once such a Power of Attorney is invoked, the client loses the legal ability to exercise the rights given to the 'attorney'.
## Process
For information on how to deal with Enduring Powers of Attorney, see:
- Process for dealing with Enduring Powers of Attorney
## Ending an Enduring Power of Attorney
Once commenced, an Enduring Power of Attorney will continue to operate unless it is revoked by the client. This can be done at any time provided they have full capacity, or where this is not the case, by the Court if it is satisfied that termination is in the best interests of the client.
Consult your service delivery solicitor if you are unsure of the nature of an Enduring Power of Attorney document.

chunks.title: Examples of what an agent can do — core policy > agents
chunks.text: The following rights and responsibilities are those listed on the Ministry of Social Development "Appointment of an Agent" form - other forms or letters granting agency may be worded differently, or may have different rights and responsibilities. Whatever form or letter is used, it is important to ensure that all parties (the client, the agent and Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment) have a clear and common understanding of what is being agreed to. A client can give (or not give) an agent any of the following agency powers, and place limitations on the scope of the powers: - Accessing a client's file to obtain personal information Where the client has given the agent this power, the agent can have access to information held by the Ministry of Social Development about the client, under the Privacy Act 2020 - Provide information such as income details, housing needs, change in circumstancesWhere the client has given the agent this power, the agent can provide information on their behalf, for example changes of address or income details - Change details that appear in the client's personal fileWhere the client has given the agent this power, the agent can update or correct information held on the client's record - Receive the client's mail from the Ministry of Social DevelopmentWhere the client has given the agent this power, the agent can receive correspondence from Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment. For more information see: Adding an agent [no link find out why] - Complete and sign Ministry of Social Development forms on behalf of the clientWhere the client has given the agent this power, the agent can fill out and sign forms on behalf of the client. Ensure that the client is fully aware of the serious nature of this power, and that responsibility for the agent's actions remains with the client - Receive part or all of the client's benefit paymentsWhere the client and the Ministry of Social Development approve the arrangement, an agent can be authorised to receive part or all of the client's benefit payments as a redirection of benefit or pension payment. This is at the discretion of the Ministry of Social Development, and is dependent on there being good cause to do so, therefore it must be treated separately from the agency. The client and agent are required to complete a Redirection of Benefit Payment form - Deal with money the client owes to the Ministry of Social Development, which may include arranging repayment

chunks.title: Examples of what an agent can do — core policy > agents
chunks.text: - Speak or make enquiries on behalf of the client - Have authority over the client's affairs, as granted by a current Power of Attorney or Enduring Power of AttorneyRelevant if the client has previously signed a Power of Attorney with the agent, and the document is still current - Provide information about housing need to the Ministry of Social Development - Speak to social housing provider when there is a potential property match or offer, and the agent has agreed for their details to be given to the provider For more information see:

chunks.title: Examples of where agency may be relevant — core policy > agents
chunks.text:
## Examples of where agency may be relevant
The following are some common situations where it may be relevant for the client to consider appointing an agent.
## Specific issues
A client may wish to appoint an agent to deal with a specific issue, for example to act on their behalf in relation to a Review of Decision.
In such cases, the agent's rights and responsibilities will normally be limited to only those required to deal with the issue.
## Clients with language or mobility issues
Clients with difficulties communicating, or clients who have physical difficulty visiting Ministry of Social Development offices may find it beneficial to appoint an agent to act on their behalf.
## Clients who are ill
The appointment of an agent may be appropriate in situations where a client is ill.
If the client is receiving financial assistance they may also wish to redirect their benefit payment to the agent (as long as there is good cause to do so).
For more information see:
## Clients in homes or institutions
If a client is being maintained as a resident of a home or institution, the client may wish for the home or institution to be appointed as their agent.
## Clients served with trespass notices
Clients who have had trespass notices served, prohibiting them from entering specific Ministry of Social Development sites, are advised by letter to appoint an agent to act as their representative.

chunks.title: Guidelines for clients who are incapacitated — core policy > agents
chunks.text: When a client is temporarily or permanently incapacitated, an agent may be appointed to undertake various tasks on behalf of the client, for example completing an application for a benefit, or a Confirmation of Circumstances form. As the client is unable to immediately verify any information provided by the agent it is important that these guidelines are followed. The agent's role should be limited to the minimum rights and responsibilities that they require to assist meeting the client's immediate needs with Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment.

chunks.title: Medical evidence required — core policy > agents
chunks.text: The Ministry of Social Development must be supplied with written advice from a registered medical practitioner or other health professional, verifying why the client is unable to sign the application form and stating the likely period of incapacity.

chunks.title: Information required from agent — core policy > agents
chunks.text: The person applying to be appointed the client's agent needs to: - state what their relationship with the client is - prove that they have a close personal relationship to the client such that the Ministry of Social Development can be satisfied that they are able to 'act on behalf of' the client in these circumstances and - provide two forms of identification for themselves

chunks.title: Adding agent details — core policy > agents
chunks.text: You must add the details of the agency to the client's CMS record, select the rights and responsibilities the agent is being granted and add notes in the comment field of the Agent to include details of: - the client's incapacity, including the period of time they are expected to be incapacitated and the name of the authority who provided the medical evidence - the nature of the relationship between the client and the agent, and the evidence to support this and - for what purpose they need these rights and responsibilities

chunks.title: Client regains capacity — core policy > agents
chunks.text: When the client is no longer incapacitated, the agency relationship should be stopped. If the client wishes for the agent to continue in this role, then they will need to apply.

chunks.title: Verification of information — core policy > agents
chunks.text: If the information that was provided by the agent is incorrect, you will need to review the client's entitlement to a benefit, if appropriate.

chunks.title: On-going incapacity — core policy > agents
chunks.text: If the incapacity is ongoing or if the client's affairs are particularly complex, you could ask the family to consider that an agent appointed by a Court Order is established. However, you cannot insist that this is done. Consult your service delivery solicitor if you are unsure about this. For more information see: - Agent appointed by a Court Order - Processing standards Accepting forms [no link find out why] - Processing standards Agents [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Organisation or company as agent — core policy > agents
chunks.text:
## Organisation or company as agent
A client may ask that an organisation or company be appointed as their agent. This may be used, for example, to appoint a voluntary organisation, beneficiary advocacy group or rest home as a client's agent.
Any individual member of the organisation can act as the client's agent as long as they continue to work for and on behalf of that organisation.
## Process
Ensure that the agency is in the name of the company or firm and not in the name or position of any employee in the organisation.
You may also accept any agency privacy waiver or similar document which describes what information can be shared and under what circumstances. For example, when a client appoints a beneficiary advocacy group to act on their behalf.
Whenever a representative from the organisation or company acting as the client's agent makes contact with Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment you must always request the representative provides a business card or letter on official letterhead that:
- confirms the representative's link to the organisation or company and
- ensure they exercise only the rights and responsibilities granted by the client (establish this by checking notes in the client's CMS record)
For more information see:
- Process for appointing an agent
- Examples of where agency may be relevant
- Processing standards Agents [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Permanently incapacitated — core policy > agents
chunks.text:
## Permanently incapacitated
When a client is permanently incapacitated, that is, they are not mentally or physically able to manage their own affairs, a person may undertake various tasks on behalf of the client if Ministry of Social Development is satisfied that the person is acting in the client's best interests.
## Court Orders
An application can be made to the Family Court to appoint a person to act on their behalf. These orders are made under the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988.
The Court Order will provide verification that the person has been appointed to act on the client's behalf and the duties they may perform. While a court order is the preferred option it cannot be insisted upon.
For more information see:
- Agent appointed by a Court Order
## No Court Order
In exceptional circumstances, a person can still act on behalf of a client when there is no court order in place.
The Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1998 does not require a court order to be in place, however, you must ensure that the person acting of the client will act in the client's best interests and in good faith.
In these circumstances, the agent may:
- complete application forms on behalf of the client and
- supply relevant personal information about the client to enable assessment of their entitlement to benefits, for example details of income and assets
The use of such an agency should be made carefully, and should be in place to ensure the client's needs are met. Generally, for long-term or complex cases, you should recommend that the client's agent apply to have their role confirmed by the Court. Consult your service delivery solicitor if you are unsure about this.
For the guidelines to follow when appointing an agent due to the client being permanently incapacitated, see:
- Guidelines for client's who are incapacitated

chunks.title: Power of Attorney — core policy > agents
chunks.text: A Power of Attorney is a formal legal document, authorising one person to act on behalf of another person. It can be general, for example, allowing the agent to look after all financial matters, or specific, such as managing a bank account while the client is overseas. An individual granted a Power of Attorney over the affairs of a client may have the right to act as the client's agent when dealing with Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment. In such cases it is important to: - get the 'attorney' to complete a Certificate of Non-Revocation that certifies that: they have been appointed the client's attorney andto the best of their knowledge the Power of Attorney has not been revoked - they have been appointed the client's attorney and - to the best of their knowledge the Power of Attorney has not been revoked - check what powers are granted by the document - confirm what these powers will enable the agent to do on the client's behalf, in terms of dealing with Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment and - select the rights and responsibilities in the client's record in CMS Note you must add the date the Power of Attorney was signed to the comments field for the Agent. If a client wishes to grant an agent the full legal right to make all decisions on their behalf, you should recommend that they arrange for a Power of Attorney between themselves and the agent. Consult your Service Delivery solicitor if you are unsure of the nature of a Power of Attorney document.

chunks.title: Complete 'Appointment of an Agent' form — core policy > agents
chunks.text: Even if a Power of Attorney is provided by the client or the agent, you should also request that the 'Appointment of an Agent' be completed as this provides us with information which may be used to identify the agent when they contact Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment. While it is preferable that this occurs, it cannot be insisted upon. For more information see:

chunks.title: Client not present or has not signed 'Appointment of an Agent' form — core policy > agents
chunks.text: If a person wishing to act on behalf of a client provides a Power of Attorney form when the client is not present, they should be requested to complete the 'Appointment of an Agent' form, however the client's declaration will be left unsigned. If possible, it is also advisable you contact the client by phone to ensure they are aware of their attorney's actions.

chunks.title: Enduring Power of Attorney — core policy > agents
chunks.text: An Enduring Power of Attorney, unlike an ordinary Power of Attorney, comes into effect when a person is determined to be mentally incapacitated. For more information see: - Enduring Power of Attorney - Office for Seniors, Te Tari Kaumātua Promoting enduring power of attorney (EPA) - Adding an agent [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Process for appointing an agent — core policy > agents
chunks.text: When considering a request for an agent to be appointed, you need to take the following action:

chunks.title: Step 1. Determine that the agent is appropriate — core policy > agents
chunks.text: A client has the right to appoint any individual or organisation as their agent, however in rare cases the chosen agent may be inappropriate. In such cases Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment have the discretion not to deal with an agent. For more information see: - Discretion not to deal with an agent - Who can be an agent?

chunks.title: Step 2. Client's consent and understanding — core policy > agents
chunks.text: Generally, the client's informed consent is required before we can deal with an agent. You need to ensure that the client approves of the agent, and is aware of what rights and responsibilities they are agreeing to give the client.

chunks.title: Exceptions — core policy > agents
chunks.text: The cases where the client's informed consent is not always required are: - where the agent has been appointed by a Court Order made under the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988 - where the client is temporarily incapacitated, and in certain circumstances it may be appropriate for you to appoint an agent without their informed consent If the agent holds an Enduring Power of Attorney, the client has given prior consent.

chunks.title: Step 3. Obtain the agency in writing — core policy > agents
chunks.text: The Ministry of Social Development requires the agency authority in writing. You should encourage the client and the agent to complete the Ministry of Social Development "Appointment of an Agent" form. You may also accept any agency privacy waiver or similar document which describes what information can be shared and under what circumstances. For example, when a client appoints a beneficiary advocacy group or beneficiary advocate to act on their behalf. It must also: - name both the client and the person (or organisation) being appointed agent and - be signed by both the client and the agent and - confirm exactly what rights and responsibilities the agent is being granted You also need to ensure that the agent provides 2 forms of identification for themselves. In certain situations the client may be unable to complete the form, due to either the appointment being made without their informed consent (such as a Court Order being made), or the agent holding an Enduring Power of Attorney). Also, in certain situations of temporary agency it may not be relevant or possible to have the agency in writing, for example telephone conversations. Add the details of the agent to the client's CMS record. For more information see: - Agent appointed by a Court Order - Enduring Power of Attorney - Temporary agency - Organisation or company as agent - Appointment of an agent form

chunks.title: Step 4. Record the agency in CMS — core policy > agents
chunks.text: You will need to add the details of the agency to the client's CMS record. In cases of temporary agency, a standard note in CMS should be completed. If the client has appointed more than one agent, you will need to create a separate "agent record" for each agent. For more information on what needs to be recorded in this note see: - Creating an Agent [no link find out why] See also: - Appointing an agent without the client's informed consent - Temporary agency - Agent appointed by a Court Order - Processing standards Agents [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Process for dealing with Court Orders — core policy > agents
chunks.text:
## Process for dealing with Court Orders
When you receive a Court Order made under the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988, you must:
- confirm whether the court order is still current now
- check what powers are granted by the Court Order
- confirm what these powers will enable the agent to do on the client's behalf, in terms of dealing with Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment and
- you must add the details of the agency to the client's CMS record, select the rights and responsibilities the agent is being granted and add notes in the comment field of the 'agent' to include details of: the type of orderthe expiry date
- the type of order
- the expiry date
Consult your Service Delivery solicitor if you are unsure about a Court Order.
## Complete "Appointment of an Agent" form
Even when a Court Order is provided, you should also request that the 'Appointment of an agent' form be completed as this provides us with information which may be used to identify the agent when they contact Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment.
While it is preferable that this occurs, it cannot be insisted upon. In these cases, the agent (the person named in the Order) should complete the form, and the client's declaration will be left blank. The 'agent' also needs to provide two forms of identification for themselves.
For more information see:
- Appointment of an agent form

chunks.title: Process for dealing with Enduring Powers of Attorney — core policy > agents
chunks.text: If you are presented with an Enduring Power of Attorney, ensure that you follow the following process. - get the attorney to complete a 'Certificate of Non-Revocation' that certifies: they have been appointed the client's attorney andto the best of their knowledge the Power of Attorney has not been revoked - they have been appointed the client's attorney and - to the best of their knowledge the Power of Attorney has not been revoked - for all Enduring Powers of Attorney in relation to personal care and welfare and those in relation to personal property that are valid, only, once the client becomes mentally incapacitated: ensure that evidence of the client's incapacity is supplied. This could be either a medical certificate or evidence supplied by the Court. - ensure that evidence of the client's incapacity is supplied. This could be either a medical certificate or evidence supplied by the Court. - for Enduring Powers of Attorney in relation to personal property that are valid immediately upon the document being signed: where the client is not present, it would be advisable to contact the client to ensure they are aware of their attorney's actions. - where the client is not present, it would be advisable to contact the client to ensure they are aware of their attorney's actions. - check what powers are granted by the document - confirm what these powers will enable the agent to do on the client's behalf, in terms of dealing with Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment and - select the agent's rights and responsibilities in the client's CMS record Note you must add the date the Enduring Power of Attorney was signed, and the type of Enduring Power of Attorney (property, or personal care and welfare) in the comments field of the agent.

chunks.title: Complete 'Appointment of an Agent' form — core policy > agents
