chunks.text: Even when an Enduring Power of Attorney is provided, you should also request that the 'Appointment of an agent' form be completed as this provides us with information which may be used to identify the agent when they contact Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment. While it is preferable that this occurs, it cannot be insisted upon. In these cases, the agent (the 'attorney') should complete the form, and the client's declaration will be left blank. The 'agent' also needs to provide two forms of identification for themselves. Consult your Service Delivery solicitor if you are unsure of the nature of an Enduring Power of Attorney document.

chunks.title: Public Trust Certificate of Administration — core policy > agents
chunks.text:
## Public Trust Certificate of Administration
The Public Trust manages the finances of many clients and issues a Certificate of Administration as proof of their authority to act on behalf of a client.
This certificate should be accepted as sufficient evidence that the Public Trust has the right to act either alone or jointly with another person on behalf of a client.
There are two types of Public Trust Certificate of Administration forms:
- Enduring Power of Attorney - this confirms that the client has signed an Enduring Power of Attorney and appointed the Public Trust to act on their behalf
- Family Court Order - this confirms that the Family Court has appointed the Public Trust as the manager of the clients affairs under the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1998
These certificates must be dated and signed by an authorised signatory of the Public Trust.
## Letter of instruction
The Public Trust will also issue a letter of instruction with the Certificate of Administration requesting actions to be completed, for example, redirection of correspondence or redirection of benefit payments.
Note the Public Trust is not required to complete an agent form, redirection of benefit form or change of address form. A Certificate of Administration is to be accepted as proof of evidence that the Public Trust can act on behalf of the client.
## Adding agency details
Details of the agency must be added to the client's CMS record, the rights and responsibilities selected to include the powers given to the Public Trust (outlined on the Certificate of Administration), and notes added in the comment field of the agent to advise that a Public Trust Certificate of Administration has been received.
This note must include the date that the Public Trust has been appointed, and any additional instructions, for example, redirection of benefit.
For more information see:
- Public Trust Certificate of Administration [no link find out why]
- Creating a 'Must View' notes for agents [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Temporary agency — core policy > agents
chunks.text:
## Temporary agency
A client may consent to another person or organisation temporarily acting on their behalf or for one-off situations, for example:
- the client provides a signed letter or note, giving permission for the named person to carry out specific instructions on their behalf
- the client and their temporary agent are present in the office together
- the client grants permission during a telephone conversation for another person to talk about specific issues concerning the client, for example their Disability Allowance
- the client gives a Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment staff member permission to act on their behalf, for example they may give you their consent to ring their landlord for personal information
Note in situations of temporary agency the Appointment of an Agent form does not need to be completed. However, unless the client and agent are present together, the written permission of the client is still required.
## Length of temporary agency
Temporary agency powers exist only as long as the client and/or agent are present in the office, or as long as the conversation or meeting lasts, or until the specific situation as covered in the letter or note is concluded.
You must get the authorised consent of the client again before any further dealings with the temporary agent.
## Client permission
- ensure the temporary agent carries out only what the client has given them permission to do and
- if you have any doubts, discuss the situation with the client
## Recording temporary agency
In cases of temporary agency, a full note must be made in the client's CMS record stating:
- the names of the parties involved
- that the client's consent has been given
- the topic or situation discussed and
- the reason for the client needing a temporary agent (if given)
For more information see:
- Process for appointing an agent
- Accessing a client's files to obtain personal information
- Guidelines to the Privacy Act 2020
- Enforcing agency [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Temporary incapacity — core policy > agents
chunks.text:
## Temporary incapacity
In exceptional circumstances an agent may be required to act on the client's behalf due to the client being temporarily but totally incapacitated, for example if the client is in a coma.
To be appointed as an agent in such a situation, the person must be able to demonstrate that they have a close personal relationship to the client, such as being a family member.
In these circumstances, the agent may:
- complete application forms on behalf of the client and
- supply relevant personal information about the client to enable assessment of their entitlement to benefits, for example details of income and assets
The use of such an agency should be made carefully, and should only be in place for the period of time it takes to ensure the client's immediate needs are met.
Generally, for long-term or complex cases, you should recommend that the client's agent apply to have their role confirmed by the Court. Consult your Service Delivery solicitor if you are unsure about this.
For the guidelines to follow when appointing an agent due to the client being temporarily incapacitated, see:
- Guidelines for clients who are incapacitated

chunks.title: What an agent can do — core policy > agents
chunks.text: What an agent can do depends on what role the client wishes them to have. The client must decide exactly what rights and responsibilities they wish to grant their agent; the client may also specifically exclude the agent from doing certain things. The agent's powers may be wide, or limited to cover a specific issue, for example to assist with a Review of Decision. Note appointing an agent does not limit a client's right to act for themselves.

chunks.title: Social housing clients — core policy > agents
chunks.text: A client who is on the social housing register or applying for social housing can authorise MSD to pass on their agent's details to social housing providers who may have properties available to offer them. The agent must agree that their details can be given to the provider, and the provider has discretion to decide whether they will deal with the agent directly or the client. Note the agency relates only to the placement process and the authority does not extend to the on-going relationship between the housing provider and the client. If the client wants the agent to represent them in all future matters with the housing provider, they will have to arrange this directly with the housing provider.

chunks.title: Completing the 26 week reapplication process for Jobseeker Support — core policy > agents
chunks.text: An agent may complete the eligibility, obligations and intent to reapply parts of the 26 week reapplication on behalf of the client or partner (if any included in their Jobseeker Support) if they have been given the appropriate rights to act on their behalf. Note agents can only complete the employment engagement on a client’s behalf if MSD decides there is a reason that means this is unavoidable. For more information see: - Completing the 26 week reapplication process - Specific engagements - Specific eligibility engagement

chunks.title: Agency in writing — core policy > agents
chunks.text: The role of the agent (and any exclusions) must be confirmed on the form granting agency; this will preferably be MSD's 'Appointment of an Agent' form. Whatever form is used, MSD must ensure that the agent only ever carries out the rights and responsibilities they have been granted.

chunks.title: Power of Attorney — core policy > agents
chunks.text: If the client wishes to grant another person the full legal right to make all decisions on their behalf, MSD can suggest to the client that they investigate having a Power of Attorney drawn up between themselves and their agent. They then need to supply a copy of this to MSD. Note in most cases, this will cover more than the client's dealings with MSD. For more information see: - Power of Attorney

chunks.title: Court Order or Enduring Power of Attorney — core policy > agents
chunks.text: If an individual is an agent appointed by a Court Order, or has authority over the client's affairs via an Enduring Power of Attorney, what they can do on behalf of the client is determined by what is granted by the appropriate document (either the Enduring Power of Attorney form or Court Order or Public Trust Certificate of Administration). This must be confirmed at the time of application to make ensure the agent acts within the boundaries they have been given. - Agent appointed by a Court Order - Enduring Power of Attorney - Public Trust Certificate of Administration

chunks.title: Temporary incapacity — core policy > agents
chunks.text: If an agent is appointed when the client is temporarily incapacitated (for example, in a coma), the agent's role should be limited to the minimum rights and responsibilities that they require to assist meeting the client's immediate needs with MSD. For more information see: - Temporary incapacity

chunks.title: Adding agent details — core policy > agents
chunks.text: Details of the agent must be added to the client's record to show that an agent has been appointed. This must include the date the agent is appointed, the powers given to the agent and any specific instructions regarding a client's affairs.

chunks.title: Examples — core policy > agents
chunks.text: For more information about the rights and responsibilities that agents may be granted, as provided for on the Ministry of Social Development 'Appointment of an Agent' form, see: - Examples of what an agent can do - Appointment of an agent form - What an agent cannot do For more information see: - Process for appointing an agent - Appointing an agent without the client's informed consent - Temporary agency - Examples of where agency may be relevant

chunks.title: What an agent cannot do — core policy > agents
chunks.text:
## What an agent cannot do
There are some actions that an agent is unable to carry out on behalf of the client.
## Job search obligations
The client must meet their job search obligations themselves and cannot appoint their agent to undertake these activities on their behalf.
## Employment engagement for 26 week reapplication process
When completing the 26 week reapplication for Jobseeker Support the client or partner (if any included in their Jobseeker Support) must complete the employment engagement themselves.
An agent cannot complete the employment engagement on the client's behalf unless MSD decides there is a reason that means this is unavoidable.
For more information see:
- Completing the 26 week reapplication process
- Specific engagements
- Specific eligibility engagement
## Social housing assessment
The client must attend the first appointment (either in person, or over the phone) when their housing need is being assessed, even if they have appointed an agent.
The agent or support person can attend the social housing assessment interview with the client.
The agent can only complete the assessment on behalf of the client when there is a very good reason why the client cannot attend the interview.
For example, the client is temporarily in hospital, or the assessment is being done over the phone and the client is unable to be present with the agent.
The agent can only deal with the social housing provider when there is a potential property offer if the client has requested that we give the agent's details to the social housing provider and the agent has agreed.
The housing provider decides whether they will deal with the agent or the client.
For more information see:
- What an agent can do
- Agents

chunks.title: Who can be an agent? — core policy > agents
chunks.text: A client has the right to appoint any individual or organisation as their agent; however, in certain circumstances Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment have the discretion not to deal with an agent of the client's choice. Generally an agent: - should be a person of credible reputation and - will generally be over 18 years of age (an exception to this could be a partner) and - will be a person the client knows well and can depend on for their support, such as a family member, spouse, partner or close friend For more information see: - Discretion not to deal with an agent

chunks.title: Organisation or company as agent — core policy > agents
chunks.text: An organisation or company may be appointed as a client's agent. This may be used, for example, to appoint a volunteer organisation, beneficiary advocacy group or rest home as a client's agent. For more information see: - Organisation or company as agent

chunks.title: Client representative as agent — core policy > agents
chunks.text: A client may ask for a client representative to be their agent. This may be an individual person. For more information see: - Client representatives

chunks.title: Ministry of Social Development employee as agent — core policy > agents
chunks.text: If a client wishes to appoint an employee of the Ministry of Social Development (including Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment) as their agent, this should be discussed with the employee's manager. The manager should decide whether it is appropriate for this to occur; they should consider whether there are any conflict of interest or internal security issues. Note while it may be acceptable in most circumstances for an employee to act as a client's temporary agent for one-off events, such arrangements should still be discussed with the employee's manager. For more information see: - Temporary agency

chunks.title: Power of Attorney or Court Order — core policy > agents
chunks.text: An individual granted a Power of Attorney or an agent appointed by a Court Order under the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988, may be appointed as an agent. Their role will be limited to the powers that are granted in the Power of Attorney or Court Order document. For more information see: - Power of Attorney - Agent appointed by a Court Order

chunks.title: Lawyer as agent — core policy > agents
chunks.text: A lawyer may act on behalf of a client to deal with MSD. The lawyer should provide a written statement on their law firm letterhead or email address that they are acting on behalf of the client. The lawyer should be registered in New Zealand. If you are satisfied that the client has given permission for a lawyer to act for them, the lawyer does not need to complete an appointment of agent form or be added as an agent in CMS. For more information see: - Procedures [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Public Trust — core policy > agents
chunks.text: The Public Trust can issue a Certificate of Administration as proof of their authority to act on behalf of a client. They will also issue a letter of instruction requesting actions to be completed, for example, redirection of correspondence or redirection of benefit payments. - Public Trust Certificate of Administration [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Limits to appointing an agent — core policy > agents
chunks.text: While it may be beneficial for the client to appoint an agent to act as their representative for Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment purposes, you cannot insist that the client do so. This includes situations where a trespass notice has been issued against a client who has been prohibited from entering specific Work and Income, Senior Services or Housing Assessment offices. These clients can contact us using the 0800 number or in some circumstances be assisted by the Remote Client Unit. For more information see: - Process for appointing an agent - Appointing an agent without the client's informed consent - Temporary incapacity

chunks.title: Care and protection concerns for a child or young person — core policy > care and protection
chunks.text: If MSD believes any child has been, or is likely to be harmed (physically, emotionally or sexually), ill-treated, abused, neglected, deprived or MSD has concerns about the wellbeing of the child, the case must be referred to Oranga Tamariki. Sole caregiver goes to prison or is on remand Where a sole caregiver is remanded in custody and/or sentenced to a term of imprisonment, the case must be referred to Oranga Tamariki. In other situations, the following is a guide to some of the things that may indicate a care and protection concern: - Age of the childThe younger the child (including a foetus), the more dependent they will be on the parent or caregiver and therefore more at risk. As the child gets older it is more likely they can run away or ask for help. Children with health conditions or disabilities are more at risk with a change in caregiver. - Baby not bornMSD should consider the wellbeing of unborn children. An unborn baby may also be at risk of harm from adult behaviour such as violence, alcohol and drug use, poor diet, and adult health concerns. - Stability and continuity of careFrequent changes of caregiver can prevent a child forming lasting relationships. There may be a history of changes of caregiver. The effect may be lessened if the change is from one relative to another who is known to the child. Whether the child will be able to maintain links with the first caregiver makes a difference to their care. Children with health conditions or disabilities are more at risk with a change in caregiver. - ConflictIf the parties (caregivers and/or parents) do not get on together, or there is disagreement about the child's care, the arrangement is not likely to work. Conflict could be within the household (e.g. between the adults in the home or between an adult and the child etc). Conflicts need to be resolved first. This is not the case manager's responsibility so a referral should be made in this situation. - Concern of abuseHints of abuse by parents, caregivers or their close circle of friends. - Child is reluctantThe child does not want to go to the parent or caregiver (this is observed, or the child says so).

chunks.title: Care and protection concerns for a child or young person — core policy > care and protection
chunks.text: - Specific needs of childChildren and young people who are being moved because of behavioural problems (e.g. glue-sniffing, missing school, violence or offending) are likely to need special help and the parents or caregivers may need extra support. - Caregiver overburdenedThe parent or caregiver has many children, and/or children who need extra support and care (for example, preschoolers, children with health conditions or disabilities) and another child might be too much. - Arrangements unsureTake seriously any instinct or feeling that suggests the situation does not seem right, is idealistic, or unlikely in some way.

chunks.title: Carers getting Child Support income — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Carers getting Child Support income
Child Support payments carer's get may be chargeable as income.
This depends on the type of benefit the carer is getting, the type of child support arrangement in place, and the type of payment.

chunks.title: Carers who do not need to apply for Child Support — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Carers who do not need to apply for Child Support
Some carers applying for Unsupported Child's Benefit may not be required to apply for Child Support.
MSD will assess when carers must apply for Child Support depending on their personal circumstances.
## The carer does not need to apply in any of the following situations
Clients applying for Unsupported Child's Benefit will not be asked to apply when MSD has decided that a carer does not need to apply for Child Support. However, the carer can choose to apply if they want to.
Carers who are not applying for Unsupported Child's Benefit do not need to apply for Child Support.

chunks.title: Carers who need to apply for Child Support — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Carers who need to apply for Child Support
Depending on their circumstances carers getting Unsupported Child's Benefit may need to apply for a formula assessment of Child Support for children in their care.
Carers getting an Unsupported Child's Benefit may need to apply for Child Support if all the following criteria are met:
- there is sufficient legal evidence available to establish who one or both of the liable parent(s) is and
- there is no risk of violence to the carer, the carer's immediate family, the Unsupported Child's Benefit child, or their immediate family, if the carer applied and
- one or both of the liable parents is not deceased and
- the child was not conceived as a result of incest or sexual violation and
- there are no other compelling circumstances
No other carers are required to apply for Child Support.

chunks.title: Change in receiving carer's circumstances — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Change in receiving carer's circumstances
Changes to a receiving carer's circumstances can affect the Child Support they get, or their Child Support obligations when they are getting Unsupported Child's Benefit.
Receiving carers getting Child Support through a formula assessment should contact Inland Revenue about changes to their situation, as changes may affect the amount of their assessed Child Support.
## Change of benefit type
Carers applying for or transferring to an Unsupported Child's Benefit for a child may need to apply for a formula assessment of Child Support. If they are getting Child Support for that child, they may no longer get these payments directly.
There may be situations when a carer continues looking after a child but is no longer getting Unsupported Child's Benefit for them, e.g. they qualify for a main benefit and decide to include the child in their main benefit instead of getting Unsupported Child's Benefit. These carers may be able to get Child Support payments directly.
These carers should be advised to contact Inland Revenue about changes to their personal circumstances, which may affect their Child Support payments
## Carer has another child
When a receiving carer has another child come into their care, they may need to apply for Child Support if they are applying for Unsupported Child's Benefit for that child.

chunks.title: Changes to liable parent's situation — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Changes to liable parent's situation
Changes to a liable parent's situation can affect the Child Support they pay, or their Child Support deductions when they are getting a benefit.
Liable parents should be informed that when there is a change in their situation, they should contact Inland Revenue to tell them about the change in their circumstances.
## Liable parent goes into hospital
A liable parent can apply for an exemption from their Child Support deduction if they are in hospital or a rehabilitation centre for 13 weeks or more.
The liable parent must apply for the exemption in writing to Inland Revenue.
To qualify for this exemption the liable parent's income must:
- be only at the hospital rate of benefit or
- be no more than $23.00 per week (as at 1 April 2026) if they have other income and Child Support is payable under a formula assessment or
- be no more than $10.00 per week if they have other income and a voluntary agreement for Child Support or
- be nil
When the liable parent is a long-term hospital patient but is getting a higher rate of benefit than the hospital rate, they cannot apply for an exemption
## Liable parent is imprisoned
A liable parent can apply for an exemption from their Child Support deduction when they are in prison for 13 weeks or more.
The liable parent must apply to Inland Revenue for the exemption in writing while they are an inmate. Applications for exemptions received by Inland Revenue after the date of their release will not be accepted.
To be eligible for this exemption the liable parent's income must:
- be nil or
- be no more than $23.00 per week (as at 1 April 2026) if they have other income and Child Support is payable under a formula assessment or
- be no more than $10.00 per week if they have other income and voluntary agreement for Child Support
## Liable parent's benefit is cancelled
When a liable parent's benefit is cancelled, their Child Support deduction will stop. When the benefit is cancelled part way through a week, the deduction will not be made from the final payment.
The liable parent should be advised that future Child Support payments are their responsibility, and they should contact Inland Revenue as soon as possible to tell them of their change in circumstances and arrange payments.

chunks.title: Child conceived as a result of incest or sexual violation — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Child conceived as a result of incest or sexual violation
An Unsupported Child’s Benefit carer does not need to apply for Child Support for a child, if that child was conceived as a result of incest or sexual violation.
MSD does not require details of events that led to the child being conceived.
When a carer is uncomfortable or reluctant to discuss the issue, we should not push the matter. The information from the client should be accepted.
Police reports, or written proof is not required.

chunks.title: Child Support deducted from benefit — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Child Support deducted from benefit
When a liable parent is getting a benefit, any Child Support they need to pay is automatically deducted from their benefit.
Inland Revenue decides the amount of Child Support, based on a formula assessment, and sends deduction notices to MSD. The deductions from the liable parent’s benefit are compulsory.
MSD is considered the liable parent's employer for Child Support payments.
## Protected earnings
Child Support deductions cannot be more than 40% of the liable parent's total net income.
When a liable parent’s only source of income is their benefit, this means 40% of their benefit amount is the most that can be deducted. If a liable parent has more than one source of income, more than 40% of their benefit can be deducted at the liable parent's request.
Child Support deductions take precedence over all other deductions.

chunks.title: Client is a carer — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Client is a carer
A carer may get Child Support payments from a liable parent or paying parent to help with the cost of raising a child.
When Child Support is arranged through a formula assessment or a voluntary agreement, Inland Revenue collects Child Support from the liable parent and passes this on. In these situations the person getting the Child Support payments is called a receiving carer.
When there is a private arrangement, the paying parent pays Child Support directly to the carer.
Carers getting Unsupported Child's Benefit for a child may have to apply for a formula assessment.
Carers getting other assistance can decide if they want to apply and what arrangement they have, if any.

chunks.title: Client is a liable parent — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Client is a liable parent
A liable parent pays Child Support to help with the cost of raising children when they are not providing the ongoing daily care.
When Child Support is arranged through a formula assessment or a voluntary agreement, the liable parent pays Child Support to Inland Revenue and this is passed on to the receiving carer. However, if the receiving carer is getting Unsupported Child's Benefit for the child, the Child Support is used to help pay for the carer's benefit.
Clients that are a liable parent, and have Child Support arranged through Inland Revenue, have their Child Support payments deducted from their benefit. Liable parents may be able to include their Child Support payments as an allowable cost in Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit if they qualify for these payments, and the Child Support is a formula-assessed amount.
When there is a private arrangement in place, Child Support payments are paid directly from the paying parent to the carer.

chunks.title: Compelling circumstance or reason — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Compelling circumstance or reason
When there is a compelling circumstance or reason that means an Unsupported Child's Benefit carer cannot apply for Child Support, MSD must consider if the carer needs to apply.
Compelling circumstances need to be considered depending on the client's personal circumstances.
If it is considered that a carer does not need to apply, Helpline should be contacted to discuss individual client circumstances.

chunks.title: Formula assessment of Child Support — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Formula assessment of Child Support
A formula assessment of Child Support is when Inland Revenue calculates the amount of Child Support the liable parent must pay and arranges payments to the receiving carer.
All carers can apply to Inland Revenue for a formula assessment of Child Support, regardless of the type of benefit they are getting.
For carers getting an Unsupported Child's Benefit, applying for a formula assessment is generally required.
When Unsupported Child's Benefit carers need to apply for a formula assessment of Child Support, the amount paid by the liable parent is used to help pay for that benefit.
When the Child Support paid is more than the Unsupported Child's Benefit rate, any excess is paid to the carer.

chunks.title: Insufficient evidence available to identify liable parent — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Insufficient evidence available to identify liable parent
There must be enough (sufficient) legal evidence available to establish who one or both of the liable parents are, for an Unsupported Child's Benefit carer to need to apply for Child Support.
## Enough evidence available
Enough legal evidence to establish who the liable parent is means any of the following:
- parenthood acknowledged by liable parent - any situation a person has accepted they are a parent of the child or
- liable parent named on child's Birth Certificate - parent(s) of the child is or are recorded by the Register of Births or overseas jurisdiction or
- liable parent named in legal declaration - a person has acknowledged or declared, in writing or before a court, they are a parent of the child or
- liable parent named on Marriage Certificate - one parent was married to the other recognised parent when the child was conceived or
- liable parent named on court decision documents - a New Zealand court or overseas authority has appointed, declared, or found a person to be a parent of the child, made a paternity order against that person, declared that person a step-parent, or found that person to be the father of the child
As long as one or both parents can be legally identified, the carer is generally required to apply for Child Support. Inland Revenue will assess the identified parent(s) and decide how much Child Support they need to pay.
However, if only one parent is legally identified but another specified reason applies, the carer is not required to apply for a formula assessment from Inland Revenue. For example, there would be a risk of violence if the carer was to apply for Child Support from that parent.

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > child support
chunks.text: Child Support is money paid by parents who do not live with their children, or who share care with someone else. These payments help with the cost of raising a child. There are 2 main ways that Child Support is arranged and paid in New Zealand. This can be: - through Inland Revenue or - by other arrangements Inland Revenue arranges and pays 2 different types of Child Support: - formula assessment - Inland Revenue works out who should pay Child Support and how much. The liable parent can set up payments or arrange direct deductions from their wages through Inland Revenue, who collects and passes the money from the liable parent to the receiving carer - voluntary agreement - Parents agree who will pay Child Support and how much. They register this agreement with Inland Revenue, who collects and passes the money from the liable parent to the receiving carer. People may also choose to make their own payment arrangements that are like Child Support without involving Inland Revenue. These include: - private arrangement - Parents agree who will pay Child Support and how much. The paying parent pays directly to the carer and there is no involvement from Inland Revenue. This may be a cash payment or specific goods and services. - foreign Child Support payment - This is a payment similar to Child Support, it is required to be paid under the laws of another country or territory outside New Zealand, and subject to an agreement made between the government of the country or territory, and the Government of New Zealand.

chunks.title: Carers applying for Unsupported Child's Benefit — core policy > child support
chunks.text: Carers applying for Unsupported Child's Benefit may need to apply for Child Support through Inland Revenue. Formula assessment Child Support is the only option for carers applying for Unsupported Child's Benefit, when MSD has decided they are required to apply for Child Support. The assessed amount of Child Support paid by liable parents is used to help pay for the Unsupported Child's Benefit the child's carer gets. When the amount of Child Support paid is more than the rate of Unsupported Child's Benefit, any excess is paid to the receiving carer and is not charged as income. All other carers can choose whether they want to apply for Child Support.

chunks.title: MSD's role — core policy > child support
chunks.text: MSD's role is: - advising clients applying for Unsupported Child's Benefit they may have an obligation to apply for Child Support - deciding whether an Unsupported Child's Benefit carer meets any of the reasons they are not required to apply for Child Support whenever information is provided to MSD - advising Unsupported Child's Benefit carers they do not need to apply if they meet any of the reasons for a carer not being required to apply - providing Child Support application forms to Unsupported Child's Benefit carers who are required to apply - collecting and sending completed Child Support application forms to Inland Revenue (including any supporting documents provided to MSD by the client) - managing queries from Inland Revenue about carers and parents who are required to pay Child Support - deducting Child Support payments from liable parents' benefits

chunks.title: Liable parent is deceased — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Liable parent is deceased
To establish a family breakdown, which is required to qualify for Unsupported Child's Benefit, at least one parent must be legally identified.
Carers who have provided proof that one liable parent of the child is deceased only need to apply for Child Support from the remaining liable parent.
Proof can be any of the following:
- a copy of the liable parent's death certificate
- a copy of the liable parent's death notice
- a written declaration completed by the carer that affirms the liable parent is deceased and including the date of death
However, if another specified reason applies to the remaining liable parent e.g. there would be a risk of violence if the carer applied for Child Support from that parent, the carer is not required to apply for a formula assessment from Inland Revenue

chunks.title: Private arrangements for Child Support — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Private arrangements for Child Support
A 'private arrangement' of Child Support is when carers and paying parents agree between themselves who will pay Child Support and how much will be paid. This is arranged without any involvement from Inland Revenue.
Under a private arrangement, the paying parent pays Child Support directly to the carer.
A carer may get:
- regular cash payments
- payment for specific goods and services
- one-off payments
Carers who get Unsupported Child's Benefit and are required to apply for Child Support cannot have a private arrangement and may need to apply to Inland Revenue for a formula assessment of Child Support.

chunks.title: Risk of violence to the carer or their children — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Risk of violence to the carer or their children
An Unsupported Child's Benefit carer does not need to apply for Child Support if, by applying or taking steps to apply for Child Support from the liable parent, there would be a risk of violence to the carer, any of their immediate family, the Unsupported Child's Benefit child or the child's immediate family.
## All risks of violence to the carer, children in their care, or other people in their household must be taken seriously
Violence means any of the following:
- physical abuse
- sexual abuse
- psychological abuse including intimidation
- harassment
- damage to property
- financial or economic abuse or
- threats of abuse
A carer does not need to give details of events that have led to concerns about violence. The information from the carer should be accepted at face value. Written proof such as police reports, or third-party verification are not required.
Some examples of situations when there is a risk of violence and a carer does not need to apply for Child Support include when:
- MSD is aware of concerns about violence e.g. we have existing information that the carer or a member of their family has been or could be at risk of violence from the liable parent, a family member, or a close associate of the liable parent or
- the carer has informed us about concerns of violence they have e.g. the carer states they believe, or are concerned, that applying for Child Support may place themselves, the children in their care, or someone in their immediate family at risk of violence from the liable parent or close associate of that liable parent
Even if the risk of violence only applies to one of the child's two parents, the carer is not required to apply for Child Support.

chunks.title: Voluntary agreements for Child Support — core policy > child support
chunks.text:
## Voluntary agreements for Child Support
A voluntary agreement for Child Support is when a carer and liable parent agree who pays Child Support and how much will be paid. They register this agreement with Inland Revenue, who collects and passes the money from the liable parent to the receiving carer.
Carers getting an Unsupported Child's Benefit, can only keep a voluntary agreement of Child Support if they have applied for formula-assessed Child Support and the voluntary agreement amount is more than the formula assessment amount.
The formula-assessed amount is used to help pay the carer's Unsupported Child's Benefit and any amount over the benefit rate is paid to the carer

chunks.title: Assistance that is not a benefit when a child turns 18 — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: Some assistance that is not a benefit or Community Costs is affected when a child turns 18. Assistance that is not a benefit for these purposes is limited to: - Assessment of eligibility for social housing (including tenancy reviews) - Emergency Housing Grants - Flexible Funding Assistance - Recoverable Assistance Payments - Employment and Work Readiness Assistance - Seasonal Work Assistance - Special Needs Grants - Student Allowance Transfer Grant

chunks.title: Getting a benefit or Community Costs — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: When a parent or caregiver gets a benefit or Community Costs as well as other assistance, the 18-year-old child is excluded from all their payments from the start of the pay period following the date of event (i.e. the child's 18th birthday, or the date they no longer meet the criteria to be included). They must not be included any later than the start of the pay period following 31 December of the year they turn 18. Example Liza is getting Jobseeker Support and her daughter Grace turns 18 on 11 November 2026. Grace is not continuing in education, and she will be excluded from Liza's Jobseeker Support from 16 November 2026 (the start of the pay period following her 18th birthday). On 13 November 2026, Liza contacts MSD to apply for a Special Needs Grant for food. When MSD assesses her entitlement for a Special Needs Grant for food, Grace is still included as a dependent child. If Liza applies for a Special Needs Grant on or after 16 November 2026, Grace will not be included in that application.

chunks.title: Client is not getting a benefit or Community Costs — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: When the parent or caregiver is not getting a benefit or Community Costs, the 18-year-old child must generally be excluded from all their parent or caregiver's other assistance from the date of event. They must not be included any later than the start of the week following 31 December of the year they turn 18. Start of the week Some assistance may be paid to cover a specific period, such as an Emergency Housing Grant that is paid for 7 nights, or on an ongoing basis, such as Social Housing. The 18-year-old generally should not be included in the assistance, or in any future grants of that assistance, from the start of the week following the date of event. Note some grants that cover a specific period are not always paid from Monday to Sunday. In these cases, the child can no longer be included from the client's next application. For payments that can be made for multiple weeks at a time, MSD should consider when the child should be excluded before making the grant. For example, if an Emergency Housing Grant can be made for 21 days, but the child will turn 18 in the first 7 nights of the grant, MSD should only grant the payment for 7 nights. MSD may then grant any additional payments with the 18-year-old excluded. Example - grant not paid from Monday to Sunday Rob gets an Emergency Housing Grant paid for 7 nights to cover the period Friday 18 September 2026 to Thursday 24 September 2026 for himself and his son Marcus. Marcus turns 18 on 20 September 2026. As he is not continuing in education, he can no longer be included in any new Emergency Housing Grants Rob applies for on or after Friday 25 September 2026.

chunks.title: Child turns 18 and may continue to be included — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: When a dependent child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and will be excluded from their parent or caregiver's assistance, or the assistance paid for them must stop, from the start of the pay period following the child's 18th birthday. However, an 18-year-old child may continue to be considered a dependent child and be included in their parent or caregiver's assistance, or have assistance paid for them, for a limited period if they are: - continuing in education and - not financially independent In this situation, the 18-year-old must be excluded from their parent or caregiver's assistance, or the assistance paid for them must stop, from the start of the pay period following: - the date the child is no longer enrolled in school or tertiary education - the date the child is no longer attending school or tertiary education as required - the date the child is financially independent - the date the child leaves the parent or caregiver's care or - 31 December of the year they turned 18 whichever is earlier. If an 18-year-old child is enrolled in education for the following year (e.g. they are finishing high school and are enrolled in tertiary education for next year), the child may continue to be considered a dependent child and be included or have assistance paid for them until the start of the pay period following 31 December of the year in which they turn 18. Note children who are born on 29 February and turn 18 in a non-leap year are considered to have their birthday on 1 March. If a parent or caregiver is getting assistance that is not a benefit when the child turns 18 (for example, Social Housing or a Special Needs Grant), the child may be excluded from a different date.

chunks.title: Continuing in education — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: To be considered continuing in education, an 18-year-old child must be enrolled in school or tertiary education and attending as required. For a child to be considered attending school or tertiary education as required, they should be meeting the attendance expectations of their school or tertiary education provider. A child is considered to be attending as required during school holidays when they are on a break between terms, between school years, or between semesters. For example, Zoe turns 18 on 3 February. She finished high school last year, and isn't attending university in semester one, but has enrolled in classes for semester two which starts on 20 July. Because she is enrolled in tertiary education, and attending as required (she doesn't need to attend until semester two starts), she can continue to be considered a dependent child and be included in her caregiver's benefit for a limited period after her 18th birthday. An 18-year-old is not considered to be continuing in education when they are: - homeschooled but not enrolled in correspondence school, distance learning, or another tertiary training establishment - intending to enrol in further education, but have not yet enrolled An 18-year-old cannot be considered a dependent child and be included in their parent or caregiver's benefit if they are not continuing in education. They may qualify for a benefit in their own right. Child under 18 leaves school or education When a child under the age of 18 leaves school or tertiary education, they can continue to be included in their parent or caregiver's financial assistance, or have assistance paid for them, as long as the child is considered to be a dependent child.

chunks.title: Financially independent — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: An 18-year-old child is considered financially independent when they: - are in full-time employment - get a Student Allowance or an Independent Circumstances Allowance under the Student Allowances Regulations 1998 or - get a main benefit in their own right There may be other situations where an 18-year-old is considered financially independent because all their financial needs (including the provision of accommodation and material needs) are being met by someone other than the parent or caregiver or from some other source. For example: - a family trust or - the parent who is not the day-to-day caregiver An 18-year-old cannot be considered a dependent child and be included in their parent or caregiver's benefit, or their parent or caregiver cannot get other assistance for them, if they are financially independent.

chunks.title: Applies for assistance in their own right — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: When a child has applied for a Student Allowance or main benefit in their own right and they are continuing in education, they may continue to be considered a dependent child and be included in their parent or caregiver's benefit until the start of the pay period following the commencement date of that assistance. If the commencement date is in the middle of a pay period, there may be a short overlap in payment between the parent or caregiver's assistance, and the assistance paid to the child in their own right. If the child has applied for assistance in their own right and they are not continuing in education, they will no longer be considered a dependent child and will be excluded from their parent or caregiver's benefit from the start of the pay period following their 18th birthday.

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: A dependent child must generally be under the age of 18 to be included in their parent or caregiver's assistance. When a child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and will be excluded from their parent or caregiver's assistance from the start of the pay period following the child's 18th birthday. This also applies when their parent or caregiver is getting assistance on their behalf, such as Orphan's Benefit, Unsupported Child's Benefit or Child Disability Allowance. However, if the 18-year-old child is continuing in education and is not financially independent, they may continue to be considered a dependent child and be included in their parent or caregiver's assistance for a limited period. In these situations, the child must be excluded from the start of the pay period following: - the date they no longer meet these criteria or - 31 December of the year they turn 18 whichever is earlier. If a parent or caregiver is getting assistance that is not a benefit when the child turns 18 (for example, Social Housing or a Special Needs Grant), the child may be excluded from a different date. Note if a parent or caregiver gets a discretionary benefit, they must complete a review of circumstances when a dependent child turns 18, or when the child no longer qualifies to be included in their benefit. If they do not complete the review, their benefit will be suspended.

chunks.title: Notice period — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: Parents and caregivers are notified at least 20 working days before their child's 18th birthday that the child will be excluded from their assistance if they do not advise MSD that the child is continuing in education and not financially independent. The notice period allows sufficient time for parents and caregivers to respond to the notice. Note there may be some situations where MSD cannot give 20 working days' notice. In this case, MSD will notify the parent or caregiver as soon as possible.

chunks.title: Responding to the notice — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: To respond to the notice, the parent or caregiver must: - confirm their child is continuing in education and is not financially independent and - if they are getting a discretionary benefit, complete a review of circumstances Parents or caregivers must respond to the notice before the child's 18th birthday. An extension cannot be given when a parent or caregiver needs more time to respond. Generally, the parent or caregiver does not need to respond to the notice if the child is not continuing in education or is financially independent. However, parents or caregivers who are getting a discretionary benefit in this situation must still respond to the notice to complete a review of circumstances.

chunks.title: Does not respond to the notice — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: When a parent or caregiver does not respond to the notice before the child's 18th birthday, the child will no longer be considered a dependent child and will be excluded from their assistance. The assistance will be reassessed without the child included and will continue at the same rate, a different rate, suspend, or cancel. If the assistance is suspended, it will cancel after 8 weeks if the parent or caregiver still hasn't responded to the notice.

chunks.title: Outcomes when child turns 18 — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: Parents and caregivers must contact MSD to respond to the notice before their child's 18th birthday. If they do not, the child will be no longer be considered a dependent child and will be excluded from their assistance, assistance paid for the child will stop, or the parent or caregiver's discretionary benefit will suspend. An extension cannot be given when a parent or caregiver needs more time to respond.

chunks.title: Child excluded on or before 18th birthday — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: When a parent or caregiver advises MSD that the child is not continuing in education after their 18th birthday, or if the parent or caregiver does not respond to the notice, the child is no longer considered a dependent child and will be excluded from the start of the pay period following their 18th birthday. When a parent or caregiver advises MSD that the child is not financially dependent on them from a date on or before their 18th birthday, the child is excluded from the start of the pay period following that date. For example, the start of the pay period following the date the child started full-time work, or the date they left the parent or caregiver's care.

chunks.title: Child excluded after 18th birthday — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: When a parent or caregiver has responded to the notice and MSD is satisfied that the child is continuing in education and not financially independent, their payments may continue with the 18-year old included as a dependent child for a limited period. The child must be excluded from the start of the pay period following: - the date the child is no longer enrolled in school or tertiary education - the date the child is no longer attending school or tertiary education as required - the date the child is financially independent - the date the child leaves the parent or caregiver's care or - 31 December of the year they turned 18 whichever is earlier If the parent or caregiver responds to the notice and the 18-year-old can continue to be included in the discretionary benefit for a limited period, they must complete another review of circumstances when the child is excluded.

chunks.title: Assistance suspends — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: If a parent or caregiver's main benefit suspends when the 18-year-old child is excluded, all of the parent or caregiver's extra help will also suspend, except for the following payments: - Child Disability Allowance - Childcare Subsidy - Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment - Orphan's Benefit - Out of School Care and Recreation Subsidy - Unsupported Child's Benefit However, if the above assistance is paid on behalf of the 18-year-old child, they may also suspend when the child is excluded. For example, if a parent or caregiver's main benefit suspends when their child is excluded and they get Child Disability Allowance for the excluded child, their Child Disability Allowance will also suspend. If a parent or caregiver's extra help suspends when the child is excluded, generally any other assistance the parent or caregiver gets may continue (unless that assistance is also paid on behalf of the child). Temporary Additional Support suspends A parent or caregiver's Temporary Additional Support will suspend (even if the parent or caregiver has a deficiency of income) if the following assistance suspends or cancels when an 18-year-old child is excluded: - Accommodation Supplement - Disability Allowance - Child Disability Allowance MSD must reassess Temporary Additional Support to determine if the parent or caregiver still qualifies. Disability Allowance may cancel Disability Allowance will cancel when a parent or caregiver is: - only getting Disability Allowance for the 18-year-old child that gets excluded and no other Disability Allowance payments and - not getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for that child If the parent or caregiver contacts MSD within 8 weeks after the cancellation, and MSD is satisfied that Disability Allowance can continue to be paid for the 18-year-old child for a limited period, MSD may regrant it if there is sufficient evidence, including a current Disability Allowance medical certificate.

chunks.title: Family tax credits — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: Family tax credits cannot be paid for a child who is no longer dependent. These payments should be stopped from the start of the pay period following the date the child is no longer dependent to avoid an overpayment with Inland Revenue for the parent or caregiver.

chunks.title: Responds to notice after child is excluded — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: If a child is excluded from their parent or caregiver's benefit or assistance paid for them stops at the start of the pay period after their 18th birthday, they may be included again, or have payments made for them again, in certain circumstances. This may happen when the parent or caregiver responds to the notice after the child's 18th birthday. It may also happen when the child enrols in education after their 18th birthday. In these situations, the 18-year-old child may be considered a dependent child and be included from the date MSD is satisfied that they are continuing in education and not financially independent. For children who enrol in education after their 18th birthday, they may be included from the date they enrol. The child can continue to be considered a dependent child and be included in their parent or caregiver's assistance or have assistance paid for them for a limited period. The child must be excluded no later than the start of the pay period after 31 December in the year they turn 18. Example Kasumi gets Supported Living Payment at a sole parent rate, Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support with one dependent child included. Her child Aika is turning 18 on 16 May 2027. MSD notifies Kasumi 20 working days before Aika's 18th birthday that Aika will be excluded from her Supported Living Payment, Accommodation Supplement, and Temporary Additional Support, unless she responds to the notice and confirms that Aika is still continuing in education and is not financially independent. Kasumi does not respond to the notice, and Aika is excluded from 17 May 2027 (the start of the pay period following Aika's 18th birthday). Her Supported Living Payment and Accommodation Supplement rates change from sole parent rates to single rates and Temporary Additional Support is reassessed based on the new rates from 17 May 2027. On 20 May 2027 Kasumi contacts MSD as her benefit payment had changed and advises that she forgot to complete the form. She advises that Aika is financially dependent on her, still in school and attending as required, and will finish on 8 December 2027.

chunks.title: Responds to notice after child is excluded — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: MSD reviews Kasumi's payments based on the information provided and determines that Aika should be included in her assistance until 13 December 2027 (the start of the pay period following the date Aika is no longer enrolled in school). Because Aika was in her care for the whole period, MSD reincludes Aika from 17 May 2027, and reassesses her Supported Living Payment, Accommodation Supplement, and Temporary Additional Support from this date. Kasumi's payments will be reassessed on 13 December 2027 to exclude Aika.

chunks.title: Review of discretionary benefit when child turns 18 — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: When a parent or caregiver gets a discretionary benefit and their dependent child turns 18, they must complete a review of circumstances. The purpose of this review is to: - confirm if the child will be continuing in education and if they are not financially independent and - determine if the parent or caregiver still meets the qualifications for the discretionary benefit and - review the rate of discretionary benefit payable The parent or caregiver must complete the review of circumstances before the child's 18th birthday, or the benefit will suspend from the start of the pay period following the child's 18th birthday.

chunks.title: Second review required — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: If the parent or caregiver responds to the notice and the 18-year-old can continue to be included in the discretionary benefit for a limited period, they must complete another review of circumstances when the child is excluded. This is to check if the parent or caregiver still qualifies for the discretionary benefit and review the rate of payment. If the parent or caregiver does not complete their review, their benefit will suspend from the start of the pay period following the date the child is excluded.

chunks.title: Recently completed another review — core policy > child turns 18
chunks.text: If a parent or caregiver has recently confirmed their circumstances, such as a Mandatory Review or 26-week reapplication for Jobseeker Support, MSD may use this information if it is satisfied that there is enough information to complete the review of circumstances for their discretionary benefit. To be considered recent, the parent or caregiver must generally have confirmed their circumstances within 13 weeks before the child's 18th birthday or the date the child is excluded from the benefit. Note the parent or caregiver must always respond to the notice to confirm the child's details before the child's 18th birthday or the discretionary benefit will suspend. Example Jonny is getting Emergency Benefit paid at the Supported Living Payment sole parent rate. He is permanently and severely restricted in his capacity to work due to his health condition, but he does not meet the residency criteria for Supported Living Payment and is unable to earn a sufficient livelihood. Jonny's oldest child Luke is turning 18 on 4 August 2027. Jonny responds to the notice and advises that Luke is still financially dependent on him and will finish school on 3 December 2027. Jonny must also complete a review of his Emergency Benefit to check he continues to qualify and the rate payable. MSD reviews Jonny's information and sees that he completed his Mandatory Review for Emergency Benefit on 17 June 2027. Because the Mandatory Review was completed recently, MSD uses the information from the Mandatory Review to determine Jonny qualifies for Emergency Benefit and the rate payable. MSD continues Emergency Benefit until 6 December 2027 (the start of the pay period following the date Luke is no longer enrolled in school). Jonny must complete another review of circumstances before 6 December to check if he continues to qualify and the rate payable for his Emergency Benefit, otherwise his Emergency Benefit will suspend.

chunks.title: Accident compensation payments — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Accident compensation payments
A client can be granted a specified benefit while waiting for an accident compensation claim to be approved.
If the claim is successful, their entitlement to benefit is reassessed taking into account the amount of weekly compensation paid. A debt is established for the net specified benefit amount.
Case managers make a refund request from the accident insurer using the "Claim refund from accident insurer form".
The Central Processing Unit is responsible for the processing of all accident compensation reimbursements.
For more information see:
- Claim refund from accident insurer [no link find out why] form
- Types of income Accident Compensation

chunks.title: Adding a debt to the tax year — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Adding a debt to the tax year
When you create a taxable debt in SWIFTT on a cancelled record or for a previous tax year, SWIFTT will generate a memo via LSUM. The memo has the details of the debt that needs to be added to the appropriate tax year. The following outlines the SWIFTT process to follow.
SBDR
action to create the debt
LSUM
print the memo produced as a result of the backdated review with details of the debt amount to be added to the appropriate tax year
SDBTI
debt inquiry for the client - select F4 to go to STAXI screen
STAXI
select the appropriate year and DBT which takes you into SDBTA screen
SDBTA
add the following details:- benefit/pension code- the net debt amount- the period that the debt represents- debt recoverable regulation 208 indicator- debt status and breach type- comments as appropriate
## New debt established on or after 26 September 2002
New debt established on or after 26/09/2002 must be checked against the debt write-off criteria to decide if the debt or part of the debt is recoverable.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Adding a payee in SWIFTT — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Adding a payee in SWIFTT
When a non-beneficiary client wishes to make repayments of their debt from Extra Help they are receiving, this is done as a payee in SWIFTT to MSD Collections.
SSTAI
Type in the client number and press ENTER
PYECI
Choose PYEES and press HOME
PYEES
Select the payee name MSD Collections and press ENTER
Select record to action number and LNK to link it to your client
Tab down to the amount field and add the weekly amount that you want to deduct
Enter the client number in the format D123456789 and press ENTER
LSUM
Check the letter before releasing it to the client
Remember to record details in the SDPAA screen and the client event note. This is helpful to anyone else looking at the client's record.

chunks.title: Arranging repayments at cancellation — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Arranging repayments at cancellation
When a client has a debt at cancellation, case managers are responsible for arranging repayments with the client. The arrangement must be:
- negotiated with the client
- noted correctly on the SDPAA screen including the SWIFTT cancellation letter LSUM reference and
- the employer's details entered in the SBFTZ screen
Note clients advising to stop their payment through MyMSD will provide debt repayment information as part of their submitted form.
The client must be advised by letter of the cancellation giving details of their debt, including how it was established, and review rights.
## Methods of repayment
There are a number of ways a client can choose from to make debt repayments. The preferred method is by wage deduction. There is no cost to the client and repayments are assured.
Note if you are unable to make an arrangement with the client, make notes to this effect on SDPAA screen - this will be helpful to anyone else viewing the clients record, for example Debt Units.
For help at any time you can contact Client Support - Debt Management or for more information see:
- Non-current client debt Repayment methods [no link find out why]
- Non-beneficiary client debt
- Debt on suspended record
- Debt Repayment Protection
- Debt recovery suspension

chunks.title: Automatic transfer from TRACE — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Automatic transfer from TRACE
When a client with an existing Work and Income debt returns to a main benefit, and this is authenticated by the system or manually by a user, the debt will transfer automatically from TRACE to SWIFTT. These automatic transfers happen from 7.30am to 9.30pm daily, generally within 5 minutes of the grant action occurring.
A daily SWIFTT report is generated at Service Centres that shows the clients details, and the amount of debt transferred. This is the "Debts Transferred from TRACE" report (LOADTRDEBT).
When you receive this report you will need to add offsets to commence repayment of the debt. The amount of the offset should be negotiated with the client.
For more information see:
- Negotiating repayment of debt
- Debt recovery maximum
- Changing and reviewing debts
- Transfer between benefits
Some debts are not transferred to SWIFTT. See:
- Debt types retained in TRACE
- Changes and reviews, Deductions in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Changed their position — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Changed their position
Has the client changed their position in the belief that they were entitled to the money and would not have to repay it?
It needs to be established that the client has made a different decision to that which they would otherwise have made based on the genuine belief that they were entitled to the payment they received.
The change in position may be subtle and therefore not immediately obvious.
When determining whether a change in position has occurred, the focus needs to be on actions and decisions beyond simply using the payment for daily living expenses.
Where the money from the payment is still in the client's bank account it generally cannot be said they have changed their position, unless for example, the client has entered into commitments on the basis of having that money.
Where the client has spent the money knowing that they were not entitled to it, we should take recovery action.
For information about the other criteria that must be met, see:
- Received the money in good faith
- Inequitable in all circumstances
- Did not intentionally contribute

chunks.title: Changing and reviewing debts — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Changing and reviewing debts
There are a number of situations when MSD may need to review or adjust a client's debt or repayments.

chunks.title: Client fails to advise of absence overseas — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Client fails to advise of absence overseas
When a client getting a main benefit does not tell the Ministry of Social Development they are intending to travel overseas, they will be identified under the Approved Information Sharing Agreement with New Zealand Customs. The Integrity Intervention Centre processes these cases, but the client may contact their case manager.
For more information see:
- Absence from New Zealand in relevant Main benefit
- Establishing debt

chunks.title: Client not receiving full and correct entitlement — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Client not receiving full and correct entitlement
When data match detects cases where a client is not receiving their full and correct entitlement, they will refer these cases to case managers to follow-up.

chunks.title: Client self-employed, paid on commission or a contractor — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Client self-employed, paid on commission or a contractor
All clients who are identified through Inland Revenue data match and have been assessed as having personal income from commission, contract or self-employment will be referred to the Service Centre where the client is registered for further investigation.
The following is an outline of the agreed process between Data Match and Work and Income:
1. National Data Match Centre will contact the client to seek a response to the information obtained from the data match to ensure the data is for the client detected.
2. When a client indicates to the Integrity Intervention Centre they are paid on commission, contract or self-employed, the data match information will be sent to the Service Centre responsible for the client's benefit.
3. A cover sheet will be attached with details of:
- the data match information
- the client's response
- an outline of the actions required
4. The case manager will need to:
- determine the client's income and eligibility for benefit
- decide if a review of the client's benefit is required based on their income
- decide whether any further action is required
To support this process the following information is available:
- memo dated 02/04/2003 which includes a template letter to send to clients advising them of the data match and the effect on their benefit
- Integrity Intervention Centre and Service Delivery Interface document for commission sales, self-employed and contractors. See: National Data Match Centre and Service Delivery Interface agreement [no link find out why]
Also see:
- Establishing debt

chunks.title: Current client debt — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Current client debt
Current client debt is debt that is being repaid by clients who are currently receiving a main benefit. The debt is usually where the client has received:
- an Advance Payment of Benefit
- a recoverable Special Needs Grant
- Housing Support Products or
- an overpayment of benefit entitlement
Current client debts are held in the client's SWIFTT record on SDBTI screen.
When a client's benefit is cancelled their debt is transferred to TRACE system and is administered by Client Support - Debt Management. Debt on TRACE is termed non-current debt (NCD).
Clients with MyMSD are able to view their current debt balances and repayments online.
Debt transfers between SWIFTT and TRACE, depending on the status of a client's benefit, until the debt is repaid in full or it is decided the debt is non-recoverable.
## Income Related Rent debt
Income Related Rent debt is created when a client in social housing receives a calculated rate of Income Related Rent lower than they were entitled to. For more detailed information see:
- Social Housing Income Related Rent debt

chunks.title: Debt at cancellation — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Debt at cancellation
When a client's benefit is cancelled the balance of any debt they have been repaying is transferred to the TRACE system and becomes non-current debt administered by the Client Support - Debt Management.
Case managers are responsible for arranging repayments at cancellation
Note clients advising to stop their payment through MyMSD will provide debt repayment information as part of their submitted form.
## New debt established at cancellation
The cancellation of a benefit may create a new debt for the client. For example the benefit is cancelled from a date in the past. You may receive a SWIFTT warning that a backdated review SBDR is required - this must be done to ensure the debt is created for the correct amount.
## New debt established on or after 26 September 2002
New debt established on or after 26/09/2002 must be checked against the debt write-off criteria to decide if the debt or part of the debt is recoverable.
For more information see:
- Process for debt on cancelled record
- Arranging repayments at cancellation
- Debt created on cancelled record
- Debt Repayment Protection
- Debt recovery suspension

chunks.title: Debt created on cancelled record — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Debt created on cancelled record
Debts can be created or adjusted on a cancelled benefit record. For example where you need to change the date the benefit was cancelled.
A backdated review is required in these cases to ensure details of the debt are recorded correctly in SWIFTT.
## Debt established on or after 26 September 2002
Debt established on or after 26/09/2002 must be checked against the debt write-off criteria to decide if the debt or part of the debt is recoverable.
For information on how to process these debts see:
- Process for debt on cancelled record
Also see:
- Establishing debt

chunks.title: Debt is repaid — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Debt is repaid
When a client's debt is about to be repaid, SWIFTT automatically:
- calculates the amount of the final deduction (if different from regular offset)
- stops the deduction from benefit and
- issues a letter to the client advising of this action
## Client has other debts
Where a client is repaying more than one debt, a weekly report called Debts Being Cleared Potential Adjustment is available for you in CM Reports. The report identifies when a debt is about to be repaid. You can access the Debts Being Cleared Potential Adjustment report weekly through CM Reports in Briefcase.
You can increase the recovery rate of the client's other debts by the amount of the deduction for the debt that is about to be repaid. There is no requirement to contact the client about this change. To avoid confusion for the client you will also need to suppress the SWIFTT generated letter.
Example
The client has a $30 per week offset which is being split to repay two debts at $15 per week each. One of the debts is about to be repaid and has a balance of $2.50, the other debt still has a balance of $350. To retain the offset at $30 per week over the next two pay periods, adjustments will need to be made to the offset rates of the debts as follows:
Week 1 Adjustments:
increase offset of the $350 debt to $27.50
decrease offset of the $2.50 debt to $2.50
Week 2 Adjustments:
increase offset of the $350 debt to $30
the other debt has been fully repaid
The client's debt recovery is maintained at the same rate without affecting the client's weekly benefit rate.
Note all clients with offsets greater than $40 per week have been excluded from this report.
For more information see:
- SWIFTT process maximum debt recovery

chunks.title: Debt is the result of an error - provisional write-off — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Debt is the result of an error - provisional write-off
The definition of 'error' in regard to the provisional write-off of debts (established before 26 September 2002) is very broad. A debt is considered to be the result of an error when a:
- benefit is paid and there is no entitlement
- benefit is paid at a higher rate than there is entitlement to or
- incorrect advice from Work and Income about a debt has contributed to a client's indebtedness
## Example of incorrect advice from Work and Income
Work and Income advises a client that they owe a certain amount. Work and Income then realises that the debt had been calculated incorrectly and that the person actually owes more money than they were advised.
The portion of the debt that was omitted by Work and Income can be considered for provisional write-off because its omission was the result of an error.
## Exceptions - not an error
A debt is not considered the result of an error when:
- a compensation payment is subsequently received, benefit entitlement is reviewed retrospectively and an overpayment established
- a benefit is paid provisionally under section 228 the grievance action is unsuccessful and misconduct is later proved. Provisional benefit then becomes a debt.
- legislation provides for entitlement to a benefit, but a subsequent function of the legislation creates a debt.For example, a client on New Zealand Superannuation travels overseas intending to stay less than 30 weeks. They are entitled to receive their pension for up to 26 weeks. They later decide to extend their overseas holiday to 40 weeks. Benefit paid during the initial 26 weeks of absence subsequently becomes a debt. The resulting debt is not as a result of an error.
For information about the other criteria that must be met, see:
- Changed their position
- Did not intentionally contribute
- Inequitable in all circumstances
- Received the money in good faith
Note these criteria are the same as for debts established on or after 26 September 2002.
Also see:
- Legislation before 26 September 2002

chunks.title: Debt on suspended record — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Debt on suspended record
Where a client's benefit is suspended for some time and they have a debt owing you should investigate these cases with a view to cancelling the benefit record and negotiating debt repayment with the client. Details of these cases are reported as follows:
## Debts on suspended records (SBFDBTSUSW)
This report is generated each Wednesday by SWIFTT.
## 6 weeks suspended
This Case Manager's report lists clients who have an existing debt on SWIFTT and whose benefit has been suspended for 6 weeks or more.
For more information see:
- Arranging repayments at cancellation

chunks.title: Debt recovery maximum — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
