## Debt recovery maximum
The recommended maximum recovery rate for clients currently receiving income support is set at no more than $40.00 a week unless the client volunteers to pay more.
Debt types included in this maximum recovery rate are:
- Advance Payment of Benefit
- recoverable Special Needs Grant and
- overpayment of benefit
There are some types of debt retained in TRACE that are not included in the debt recovery maximum.
For more information see:
- Debt types retained in TRACE
- SWIFTT process maximum debt recovery

chunks.title: Debt recovery suspension — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text: When a client is cancelling their benefit (ie they have taken reasonable steps to ensure it has been cancelled) to start or to continue in paid employment, and has an outstanding debt, the client can request their debt recovery be suspended for 3 months. When a client incurs new debt during the suspension period, the recovery should also be suspended until the suspension period ends. We can still accept repayments if the client wishes to start paying the outstanding debt straight away. Debt recovery suspension is processed through the SBFTZ screen in SWIFTT. The SDPAA screen will automatically update by entering 'Y' in the Debt Recovery Suspension field in the SBFTZ screen. A client does not have to access any other components of assistance to transition into employment such as bridging finance to be eligible for debt recovery suspension. Note debt recovery suspension is not available for temporary employment and students moving into holiday employment.

chunks.title: Clients not being paid a main benefit — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text: A client does not need to be cancelling a main benefit to be eligible for debt recovery suspension. If a non-beneficiary is moving into or between permanent, full-time employment and has an outstanding Work and Income debt or Student Allowance debt, they may be eligible for the 3 month debt recovery suspension period. However, we can still accept repayments if the client wishes to start paying the outstanding debt straight away. Debt recovery suspension for non-beneficiaries is processed through the SSNAR screen in SWIFTT or by notifying the Debt Unit if the client is not accessing any other components of assistance to transition into employment.

chunks.title: Application process — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text: Assistance to transition into employment application form must be completed if a client wants their debt recovery suspended for 3 months. The client does not need to be accessing other components of the assistance to transition into employment to apply for debt recovery suspension. When a client applies for debt recovery suspension without accessing other components of assistance to transition into employment, you must complete CMS notes with full employer details and the reason why the client qualifies for the debt recovery suspension.

chunks.title: SWIFTT process — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text: If the client wishes to make voluntary debt repayments the following screens need to be completed: - enter 'Y' in the paying arrangement field in SBZC if transferring to Working for Families Assistance or - enter 'Y' in the paying arrangement field in SBFTZ - add arrangement type, value of regular payments and frequency of payment in the SDPAA screen Note the first payment date must always remain as the date that was pre-filled by SWIFTT.

chunks.title: Debt Repayment Protection — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Debt Repayment Protection
Where a client was receiving a sole parent rate of benefit and their benefit is cancelled because they have moved into employment, the existing debt recovery rate as they had on benefit is maintained for 91 days.
However, you can accept repayments at a higher level if the client requests this.
Case managers must record a comment in the SDPAA screen - sole parent, 91 day non-review period from [date].
Remember to include full details of employment on SBFTZ screen.
For more information see:
- Arranging repayments at cancellation

chunks.title: Debt the result of an error — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Debt the result of an error
It can be considered that an error has been made when a debt has been caused wholly or partly because MSD:
- gave the client the wrong information and/or
- didn't do something that should have been done or did something wrong
## Other criteria
When it has been determined that the debt has been caused wholly or partly by an error, you will need to consider all the other debt write-off criteria before deciding whether or not the debt is recoverable.
You will need to consider the following:
- Was there a deliberate mistake made by the client?
- Did the client have good reason to believe they were entitled to receive the overpaid amounts at the time those payments were made?
- Have they spent the money?
- Would it be fair, now, to require the client to repay the debt?
- Is the client in a better financial position now than they were when the overpayment occurred?
- Could they afford to repay the debt in small regular payments?

chunks.title: Debt types retained in TRACE — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Debt types retained in TRACE
The following types of debt do not transfer from TRACE to SWIFTT when a client is granted a benefit and are not included in the debt recovery maximum of $40.00 per week:
- Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC)
- Child Disability Allowance (HCA) previously known as Handicapped Child Allowance
- Family Benefit Capitalisation (FBC)
- Fraudulent Student Loan (FSL)
- Housing debt (HSG)
- Liable Parent Contribution (LPC)
- Maintenance debt
- Major Repairs Advances (MRA)
- Reparation debt (REP)
- Residential Support Services debt
- Student Allowance Debt (SAD)
- Suspensory Loans
- Work Services debt
These debts are 'specialised debts' and are administered by Client Support - Debt Management. When a client is receiving a benefit, repayments are usually by way of deduction from their benefit using the payee process.
For more information see:
- Debt recovery maximum

chunks.title: Debt write-off criteria — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Debt write-off criteria
Every debt established on or after 26 September 2002 must be checked against the debt write-off criteria to decide if the debt or part of the debt is recoverable.
You must first consider if the debt or any part of the debt was caused by error. You can use the information held on SWIFTT and CMS client event notes to help you decide, such as:
- check client event notes for details about information that client has provided - e.g. dates, amounts, change in circumstances
- check SWIFTT to see if all necessary actions taken
If the debt was not caused by error, or there is no indication of error on the client's record, then you can continue with debt recovery action.
Record your decision in SWIFTT (Debt recoverable indicator).
For more information see:
- Debt the result of an error
- Did not intentionally contribute
- Received the money in good faith
- Changed their position
- Inequitable in all circumstances
Note there should be no action to start recovering the debt while you are considering the debt write-off criteria. You may need to contact the client for information to help you decide the case.

chunks.title: Delegation levels — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Delegation levels
These are the benefit administration and financial delegations for decisions relating to:
- non recoverable debt
- provisional debt write-off
- write-off of non-recoverable debt and
- write-off of provisionally written-off debt
where the debt is not required to be repaid under regulation 208 of the Social Security Regulations 2018.
Debt less than $2,500
Service Delivery Service Managers or equivalent
Debt more than $2,500 less than $10,000
Regional Directors and Central Processing Unit Managers
National Manager Debt
Debt more than $10,000 less than $25,000
General Manager Integrity and Debt
Service Delivery General Managers
Regional Commissioners for Social Development
Debt more than $25,000 less than $50,000
Service Delivery Group General Managers
Debt more than $50,000 less than and $200,000
Deputy Chief Executive Service Delivery jointly with the Chief Financial Officer (in that order).
Debt over $200,000
Chief Executive

chunks.title: Did not intentionally contribute — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Did not intentionally contribute
You must consider if the client intentionally contributed to the error. Intent can be difficult to decide. You need to determine whether the client deliberately or intentionally took some action, failed to take some action or delayed a course of action which resulted in an overpayment. For example:
- the client entered into a marriage or civil union type relationship and did not inform Work and Income knowing that they had an obligation to do so
- the client started work and didn't advise Work and Income for 2 weeks knowing that their earnings may affect their entitlement to benefit
Note the benefit of the doubt must always be given to the client.
## Refer to Fraud Investigation
Where the client did intentionally contribute to the overpayment, you should consider referring the case to Fraud Investigation for further investigation.
For information about the other criteria that must be met, see:
- Received the money in good faith
- Changed their position
- Inequitable in all circumstances

chunks.title: Establishing debt — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Establishing debt
Debts must be established in SWIFTT. This creates a record in SWIFTT of the action taken to establish the debt - i.e. dates, rates of payment, benefit type and reason.
Debts are established for the current and previous tax years at the net amount not the gross amount of taxable benefits.
## Debts established on or after 26 September 2002
All debts established on or after 26/09/2002 must be checked against the criteria of regulation 208 to determine if the debt is recoverable.
All debts, regardless of the status of the benefit i.e. current, at cancellation or post cancellation, must be assessed against regulation 208 before recovery action commences.
For more information see:
- Debt write-off criteria
- Process for debt write-off decision
- Recommendation for Current Debt Write-Off [no link find out why] form
## Debts established before 26 September 2002
Any debt established before 26/09/02 that is the result of "office error" can only be provisionally written off.
Debts established before 26/09/02 can only be considered for provisional write-off irrespective of when you are reviewing the debt.
## Accidental debt
Debt created by a processing mistake is termed 'accidental debt' to distinguish it from situations of genuine overpayment where the client received benefit payments they were not entitled to.
There is an administrative process that must be followed to correct accidental debt.

chunks.title: Inequitable in all circumstances — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Inequitable in all circumstances
Before a debt can be regarded as non-recoverable under regulation 208 you must be satisfied that it is inequitable to require repayment.
You will need to consider the client's full circumstances, in particular:
- their financial position
- whether they have the resources to repay the debt
- the degree of any error made by Work and Income
For information about the other criteria that must be met, see:
- Received the money in good faith
- Changed their position
- Did not intentionally contribute

chunks.title: Integrity Intervention Centre — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Integrity Intervention Centre
The Integrity Intervention Centre is a centralised processing unit responsible for receiving, processing and, where appropriate, destruction of data produced from authorised information matching programmes.
The information matching programmes undertaken are:
- Corrections/Work and Income - Penal Institutions Match
- Customs/Work and Income - Arrivals/Departures Match
- Inland Revenue/Work and Income - Commencement/Cessation Match
The purpose of the matching is to:
- detect clients who are getting or have been getting income support which they were not entitled to and
- assess the amount of any payments to which they are not entitled
Some cases are referred to case managers to resolve, this can include establishing debt.
For help with these cases you can contact Data Match.

chunks.title: Legislation before 26 September 2002 — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Legislation before 26 September 2002
Section 86(9A) of the legislation as it applied to the provisional write-off of debt before 26 September 2002 is as follows.
"(9A) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this section, the chief executive may, in the chief executive's discretion, authorise the provisional writing-off of a debt which arose as a result of an error, made by an officer or employee of the Department, not intentionally contributed to by the debtor if the chief executive is satisfied that the person receiving the amount so paid in error did so in good faith and has so altered his position in reliance on the validity of the payment that it would be inequitable in all the circumstances, including his financial circumstances, to require repayment."

chunks.title: Negotiating repayment of debt — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Negotiating repayment of debt
Current debt can be repaid by regular deductions from a client's benefit. You will need to negotiate the repayment rate with the client.
The rate of repayment needs to be realistic, taking into account the client's circumstances.
When setting the rate of repayment, you need to consider the following factors (where relevant):
- the circumstances of the client and their dependents
- the ability of the client to meet their needs and the needs of their dependents
- the amount of the debt - we want clients to pay off their debts as fast as they can, but need to always bear in mind the circumstances of the client and their ability to repay without placing them in undue hardship. If the debt is large you should consider a higher repayment rate if the client can afford it
- the effect the rate of recovery will have on the client's ability to support themselves
- whether the rate of recovery would cause undue hardship to the client or their dependents
- the effect the rate of recovery would have on the client's ability to fulfil their work and social obligations - eg ensuring their child is enrolled with a General Practitioner or enrolled with a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation if required to do so
If the client does not agree with the rate of repayment you must record why you decided to set it at that rate.
## Rate of repayment for Advance Payment of Benefit and Recoverable Assistance
When setting repayment rates make sure you give priority to recovery of advances and recoverable assistance to maximise the client's access to further Advance Payment of Benefits and recoverable assistance.
All requests must be approved by a manager client service delivery.

chunks.title: Existing non-current debt — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Existing non-current debt
When a client is granted non-beneficiary assistance and they have a non-current debt the debt is not transferred to SWIFTT. If the client is already repaying the debt (for example by automatic payments) when Extra Help is granted then this arrangement can continue.
However, if the client is granted non-beneficiary accommodation supplement and they have a non-current debt in TRACE that is not being recovered, then the debt should be added to SWIFTT from TRACE and offset in the normal way. You must inform Client Support - Debt Management for the TRACE record to be updated.
## New debt created on non-beneficiary record
When a client is getting non-beneficiary assistance and a debt is created as a result of a review of that assistance, the debt remains on SWIFTT.
## Recoverable Assistance Payments
Repayment of Recoverable Assistance Payments is negotiated with the client at the time of granting the assistance. The repayment arrangement and the client's employment details should be recorded on the SDPAA screen.
## Deductions from extra help
If the client does not have an arrangement to repay the debt, for example Accommodation Supplement is granted when their main benefit is cancelled, then you can consider deductions from extra help as an option when negotiating a debt repayment arrangement with the client.
When a client would like to have debt repayments deducted from their extra help they should request this in writing. Deductions from extra help are made using the payee system.
## Exceptions
Deductions cannot be made from Child Disability Allowance.
As a general rule, only make deductions from Disability Allowance, Special Benefit or Temporary Additional Support if the client requests this.

chunks.title: Process for debt on cancelled record — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Process for debt on cancelled record
When you establish a debt on a cancelled record or create a debt at cancellation of benefit the regulation 208 indicator will not display. Instead you will receive a message stating:
- "Debt created, is the debt recoverable in terms of regulation 208?"
You will need to decide whether or not the debt is recoverable.
If the debt is recoverable:
- add notes in the client event to record your decision
If you need to investigate further:
- advise Client Support – Debt Management immediately to stop debt recovery action by phone and confirm by email
If the debt is non-recoverable:
- add notes in the client event to record your decision
- email Client Support – Debt Management who can view the Recommendation for regulation 208 from the client event and who will update the debt details in TRACE
- advise the client that the debt is non-recoverable
## SWIFTT process
If the debt created is non-taxable (for example Accommodation Supplement), the debt automatically transfers to TRACE.
If the debt created is taxable (for example Jobseeker Support) SWIFTT will generate a memo via LSUM. The memo has the details that you need to add the debt correctly in the appropriate tax year. For information about how to do this, see:
- Adding a debt to the tax year

chunks.title: Process for debt write-off decision — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text: The following process is to be followed when considering debt write-off. For an overview of the process, see: - Process for debt write-off flowchart

chunks.title: Step 1 — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text: Was the debt or part of the debt the result of an error? For more information see: - Debt the result of an error It may not be necessary to contact the client to help you decide this. You may be able to make your decision based on the information held by the Ministry of Social Development. If the answer is no, record your decision in SWIFTT (Debt recoverable indicator) and continue debt recovery action. If the answer is yes, the "Recommendation for Current Debt Write-Off" form must be completed: - if the benefit is current, the debt status shows as "recovery undecided" while the debt write-off is being considered or - if the benefit is cancelled, advise Client Support - Debt Management immediately that enforcement of debt recovery is to be suspended until a decision is made on debt write-off You do not need to advise the client of the debt until a decision is made.

chunks.title: Step 2 — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text: Consider all other debt write-off criteria: - Changed their position - Did not intentionally contribute - Inequitable in all circumstances - Received the money in good faith You may need to contact the client for more information to determine if these criteria are met.

chunks.title: Step 3 — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text: Submit the completed "Recommendation for Current Debt Write-Off" form to the appropriate delegated authority who decides: - whether the debt is recoverable or not and - approves or declines the debt write-off If the decision is that the debt is recoverable you will need to advise the client of the decision by letter and negotiate debt recovery. You will need to change the debt status to 'recoverable' in SWIFTT.

chunks.title: Step 4 — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text: Decision is that debt is non-recoverable and can be written off. If the benefit is current: - in SWIFTT:- change the Debt recoverable indicator to [N]- the debt status code to [13] Written off - non recoverable, debt established on/after 26/09/02 - give all documentation to a debt write off approving officer to check and action in SWIFTT - advise the client by letter that the debt is non-recoverable If the benefit is cancelled: - advise Client Support - Debt Management that this debt is non-recoverable and debt write off has been approved - send a copy of the completed and approved recommendation form and any other relevant documentation to Client Support - Debt Management who will complete the write-off action on TRACE - advise the client by letter that the debt is non-recoverable All documentation relating to the process is "critical data" and should be scanned saved and linked to the client's record. For more information see: - Delegation levels - Recommendation for Current Debt Write-Off [no link find out why] form

chunks.title: Process for debt write-off flowchart — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Process for debt write-off flowchart
The process in the following flowchart should be used when considering debt write-off.

chunks.title: Process for provisional write-off — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Process for provisional write-off
Generally the investigation of a debt for provisional write-off will involve an interview with the client, however the client should not be informed of any decision until the review is completed.
## Step 1
Complete the 'Recommendation for Provisional Debt Write off' form and forward it to your manager client service delivery for approval or referral to appropriate delegation. Scanned and saved in CMS and linked to a client event and complete.
## Step 2
Once approval is obtained, update SWIFTT. If the benefit is record is cancelled advise Client Support - Debt Management.
## Step 3
Advise the client in writing. Place the record in Bring-up for 3 months to consider full debt write off.
A debt that has been provisionally written off can, after 3 months, be considered for full financial write off.

chunks.title: Provisional write-off — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Provisional write-off
Any debt established before 26 September 2002 can only be considered for provisional write-off, irrespective of when you are reviewing the debt.
The debt can only be provisionally written off when all of the criteria are met. You must first consider whether the:
- Debt is the result of an error - provisional write-off
The following criteria that must be met for provisional write-off, are the same as those for debts established on or after 26 September 2002:
- Changed their position
- Did not intentionally contribute
- Inequitable in all circumstances
- Received the money in good faith
## Full financial write-off after 3 months
A debt which has been provisionally written off can, after 3 months, be considered for full financial write off.

chunks.title: Rate of benefit changes — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text: When a client's rate of benefit changes, it may mean that they are now receiving insufficient benefit to meet the deductions from their benefit. For example, where an increase in the client's income reduces their rate of benefit. Where the rate of benefit changes and the changes and the change is not temporary, you will need to negotiate a new rate and possibly method of debt repayment with the client. For example, the client may need to consider making automatic payments from bank account, rather than having repayments deducted from their benefit. The rate of repayment needs to be realistic, taking into account the client's circumstances. When setting the rate of repayment, you need to consider the following factors (where relevant): - the circumstances of the client and their dependents - the ability of the client to meet their needs and the needs of their dependents - the amount of the debt - we want clients to pay off their debts as fast as they can, but need to always bear in mind the circumstances of the client and their ability to repay without placing them in undue hardship. If the debt is large you should consider a higher repayment rate if the client can afford it - the effect the rate of recovery will have on the client's ability to support themselves - whether the rate of recovery would cause undue hardship to the client or their dependents - the effect the rate of recovery would have on the client's ability to fulfil their work and social obligations - eg ensuring their child is enrolled with a General Practitioner or enrolled with a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation if required to do so If the client does not agree with the rate of repayment you must record why you decided to set it at that rate.

chunks.title: Rate of repayment for Advance Payment of Benefits and recoverable assistance — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text: When setting repayment rates make sure you give priority to recovery of Advance Payment of Benefits and recoverable assistance to maximise the client's access to further Advance Payment of Benefits and recoverable assistance. Note you will need to record details of the arrangement in SDPAA screen and client event note - this is important for anyone else looking at the client's record. Create a bring-up in the BRUPA screen to check that repayments have commenced. For more information see: - Using benefit arrears to recover debt - Debt treatment Repayment options available to clients [no link find out why] - Jobseeker Support Priority for deductions

chunks.title: Received money in good faith — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Received money in good faith
In order to have received the money in good faith the client will have had to receive the money without any knowledge of their lack of entitlement to it.
For example, if a client asks for their benefit to be cancelled, then it is unlikely that any money received afterwards will have been received in good faith.
For more information about other criteria that must be met see:
- Changed their position
- Inequitable in all circumstances
- Did not intentionally contribute

chunks.title: Review of Decision of debt — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Review of Decision of debt
Where an application for Review of Decision involves a debt currently being recovered from a benefit, in most cases it will be appropriate to suspend repayments until the review and appeal process is completed.
You need to consider what aspect of the debt is under review before you suspend recovery:
- where establishment of the whole debt or the decision to recover is under review, ceasing recovery for the duration of the Review of Decision is appropriate
- where there is more than one debt, continue to recover the other debts not being reviewed
- where a client is reviewing a part of the debt (not the complete debt) you should continue to recover the portion of the debt not under dispute
Note you do not refund any repayments already deducted until the outcome of the review or appeal is known.
## SWIFTT action
In the SDBTC screen:
- change the debt status to [2] 'Recovery undecided'
- add a note in the comments field [Debt under review]
For more information see:
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals

chunks.title: Review of repayments due to hardship — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Review of repayments due to hardship
If a client advises that they are experiencing hardship, you can consider reducing their current debt repayments.
Each case must be considered on its own merits.
1. Find out what is causing the hardship and consider ways that this could be addressed.
2. Check that the client is receiving their full and correct entitlement to benefits (including any extra help and family tax credit) and rate of benefit. For more information see:
- Family tax credit
3. In deciding whether to reduce the client's debt repayments, you should consider the following factors (where relevant):
- the circumstances of the client and their dependents
- the ability of the client to meet their needs and the needs of their dependents
- the amount of the debt - we want clients to pay off their debts as fast as they can, but need to always bear in mind the circumstances of the client and their ability to repay without placing them in undue hardship. If the debt is large you should consider a higher repayment rate if the client can afford it
- the effect the rate of recovery will have on the client's ability to support themselves
- whether the rate of recovery would cause undue hardship to the client or their dependents
- the effect the rate of recovery would have on the client's ability to fulfil their work and social obligations - eg ensuring their child is enrolled with a General Practitioner or enrolled with a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation if required to do so
If the client does not agree with the rate of repayment you must record why you decided to set it at that rate.
## Rate of repayment for Advance Payment of Benefits and recoverable assistance
When setting repayment rates make sure you give priority to recovery of Advance Payment of Benefits and recoverable assistance to maximise the client's access to further Advance Payment of Benefits and recoverable assistance.
## Change in circumstances
You can review this arrangement at any time when the client's circumstances change.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support Priority for deductions

chunks.title: Maximum debt recovery exceeded — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Maximum debt recovery exceeded
When you add or review a debt in SWIFTT and the total debt recovery rate on the client's record is $40.00 or more a week, you will receive the following warning message:
[Maximum Debt Recovery Rate Exceeded]
If the client does not wish to exceed this maximum recovery rate you will need to adjust the new offset rate or reduce the other debt recovery rates so that the total debt recovery rate is no more than $40.00 a week.
## Client volunteers to pay more
If the client wishes to pay an amount that will exceed the maximum $40.00 a week they must put this in writing. You must enter a comment on the reason for this decision in the comments field on SOFSA or SOFSC screen. For example:
[Client volunteered to pay more than $40.00 a week]
Note this is a mandatory SWIFTT action required whenever an offset amount is entered that results in the client's total offset rate of more than $40 a week. The decision to accept repayments of $40 per week or more must be recorded in a client event note under the note subject - Debt Details - Other.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support, Deductions Priority for deductions

chunks.title: Third party debt — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Third party debt
In certain situations benefit payments can be made to a third party on behalf of a client. Where overpayments of benefit occur a debt is created which is repayable by the third party.
Examples of this can include:
- benefit paid to a residential care service on behalf of a client
- Childcare subsidy or OSCAR subsidy paid to a centre on behalf of a child
- wage subsidy paid to an employer
For more detailed information on specific third party debts, see:
- Childcare Subsidy Debts
- OSCAR Subsidy Debts
- Residential Support Subsidy Debts
- Non-current client debt Employment assistance debt [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Transfer between benefits — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Transfer between benefits
When a client transfers between benefits any debt will need to be transferred to the new benefit record.
## Transfer using STRFB screen
When you transfer the client between benefits using the STRFB screen any debt automatically transfers to the new benefit record. You will need to manually recommence deductions for repayment.
If you print the SOFSI screen before cancelling the previous benefit you have all the information needed to re-load the offsets.
## Cancel previous benefit
When you transfer a client between benefits by cancelling the previous benefit and granting another, any debt on the previous benefit will automatically transfer to the new service, generally within 5 minutes of the new grant being authenticated.
You will be able to offset the debt from the arrears, when a benefit is cancelled and a new grant has occurred on the same day.
You must use the most relevant code to the client's circumstances.
## Debt created by transfer action
Transferring a client between benefits from a date in the past creates a debt of the previous benefit and arrears of the new benefit.
Remember, these arrears will need to be put on hold by mid-day so any debt can be recovered from the arrears.
If this is not done, the arrears will get paid into the client's bank account.
There is no need to consult with the client in this situation.
## Partner inclusion
When including a partner into a primary client's service and the partner has a debt in TRACE, or the partners service has been cancelled, and the inclusion action has occurred on the same day.
Any debt will automatically transfer to the partner's new service within 5 minutes of the spouse inclusion occurring in SWIFTT.

chunks.title: Using benefit arrears to recover debt — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Using benefit arrears to recover debt
Where a client is due benefit arrears; these arrears can be used to repay current debt. The client must agree to this, unless the deduction from the arrears is for a regular offset, or the debt and arrears are for the same period, for example a backdated review for a period in the past.
Consider the client's full circumstances to avoid creating hardship.
## Exceptions
Transferring between benefits
Transferring a client between benefits from a date in the past creates a debt of the previous benefit and arrears of the new benefit. In this situation the arrears must be used to offset the new debt created. There is no need to consult with the client in this situation.
Arrears and debt for the same period
When you are reviewing a client's benefit for a period in the past, and both arrears and debts are established for the same period, the debt can be recovered in full from the arrears. In this situation there is no requirement to contact the client as the debt is considered to be administrative action.

chunks.title: Youth service providers considered officers of MSD — core policy > current client debt
chunks.text:
## Youth service providers considered officers of MSD
A youth service provider is considered to be an officer of the Ministry of Social Development.
This means that it can be considered that an error has been made when a debt has been caused wholly or partly because a youth service provider:
- gave the client the wrong information and/or
- didn't do something that should have been done or did something wrong
For more information see:
- Debt write-off criteria
- Debt the result of an error

chunks.title: FamilyBoost Tax Credit — core policy > familyboost tax credit
chunks.text: FamilyBoost tax credit is available from Inland Revenue to help eligible parents or caregivers pay for the cost of early childhood education from licensed providers. Eligible parents or caregivers can claim up to 40 per cent of their remaining childcare costs, after 20 hours ECE and the deduction of assistance for childcare costs from MSD for licenced early childhood education. Examples of assistance for parents and caregivers with childcare costs from MSD for licenced early childhood education are: - Childcare Subsidy - Early Learning Payment - Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment - Training Incentive Allowance

chunks.title: FamilyBoost Tax Credit lump sum payments — core policy > familyboost tax credit
chunks.text: Parents or caregivers can submit invoices for the previous three months of remaining ECE costs to Inland Revenue. Inland Revenue will pay a lump sum of up to $120 per week per eligible household for the FamilyBoost Tax Credit for the three-month period.

chunks.title: Income and Asset exemption — core policy > familyboost tax credit
chunks.text: Any FamilyBoost Tax Credit made to an individual by Inland Revenue is not chargeable income or a cash asset for 12 months from the date that parent or caregiver gets each payment for the following types of assistance: - main benefits - New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension - Accommodation Supplement - Advance Payment of Benefit - Childcare Assistance - Community Costs - Disability Allowance - Employment and Work Readiness Assistance - Flexible Funding Assistance - Funeral Grant - Home Help - Housing Support Products - Income Related Rent - New Employment Transition Grant - Recoverable Assistance Payment - Residential Care Subsidy and Loan - Seasonal Work Assistance - Social Rehabilitation Assistance - Special Benefit - Special Needs Grant - Student Allowance Transfer Grant - Student Allowance - Temporary Additional Support

chunks.title: Applications for hardship assistance payments — core policy > familyboost tax credit
chunks.text: When a client applies for hardship assistance, their income and assets need to be assessed for eligibility. If a client got a FamilyBoost payment within the last 12 months of this application, that payment is exempt from being considered income or a cash asset for qualification purposes. However, clients must use their own resources before seeking hardship assistance. If the client has enough money to meet their need using a FamilyBoost payment, they generally won't qualify for a payment. If the client only has enough money available to meet part of the cost, hardship assistance can be considered for the remaining amount. In each case MSD must consider the individual circumstances of the client against the eligibility criteria.

chunks.title: Example — core policy > familyboost tax credit
chunks.text: George visited the dentist for a sore tooth and required three fillings. The cost of the dentist visit, including the fillings, was $212.50. This was an unforeseen cost and as a result George has applied for a Special Needs Grant for food because he cannot cover the cost of his groceries this week. George and his family's weekly groceries usually cost $200. George has received a FamilyBoost Tax Credit payment of $350 for the past 3 months of childcare costs and used part of it to pay for his dental treatment. After paying the dentist George has $137.50 left. This is not considered to be a cash asset for hardship assistance; however, it is still considered a resource available, and George can partially meet his own need for food. George is granted $62.50, the difference between his available resources ($137.50) and the usual cost of his weekly groceries ($200).

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > income
chunks.text:
## Introduction
This manual will help you determine what income is for benefit and pensions from MSD, and how that income should be treated.
Deciding what is and what is not income is important, as clients need to get the correct rate of payment.
Clients need to know what is income so they can declare their income correctly and reduce the likelihood of overpayments and debt being created.
The provisions for the effect of a client's income on their benefit entitlement are in the Social Security Act 2018.

chunks.title: Capital payments — core policy > income > definition of income
chunks.text:
## Capital payments
A capital payment is usually a lump sum asset payment which may be received periodically or as a one-off payment.
Examples of capital payments could include:
- getting a house
- a property
- a gift
- donations made through crowdfunding website e.g. Givealittle and PledgeMe
- a lottery win
- an inheritance or
- proceeds from the sale of a house
- money to pay for braces for a child instead of paying Child Support
Generally the definition of income does not include capital payments.
If the capital payment received is paid as a one-off lump sum payment, it is not considered as income. However, where capital payments are received periodically and are made for and used for an income-related purpose they will be treated as income.
If the payment received is a capital payment then you need to consider what the client may do with this payment. If they choose to invest the payment then the interest received from the investment would be treated as income. For more information see: Income from assets
Each case should be considered on its own merits, where you are having difficulty determining whether a payment received is a capital payment then you should contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Guidelines for determining whether a payment is income — core policy > income > definition of income
chunks.text:
## Guidelines for determining whether a payment is income
In most cases deciding whether a payment is income will be straightforward, that is the payment is money received that is not a capital payment. You must also check whether the payments are specifically included or excluded as income.
Guidelines for specific types of income can be found in:
- Types of income
In other cases where you are unsure whether a payment is income or not, consider the following guidelines:
- why was the payment made? is the payment received for an income-related purpose?is the payment to be used for an income-related purpose?
- is the payment received for an income-related purpose?
- is the payment to be used for an income-related purpose?
- is the payment received periodically?
- what is the source of the payment?
- has the client received free goods, services, transport or accommodation on a regular basis?
You need to assess the nature and circumstances of the payment and having considered all of these points, determine whether or not the payment, credit or service is income.
## Expenses
In some cases income can be reduced if the client has had expenses. For example:
- where the client has had expenses related to producing a product for sale
- non-taxable allowances such as: attendance fees for jury servicea clothing allowance for Orphans Benefit, Unsupported Childs Benefit, or Residential Care Subsidy clientsa travel allowance
- attendance fees for jury service
- a clothing allowance for Orphans Benefit, Unsupported Childs Benefit, or Residential Care Subsidy clients
- a travel allowance

chunks.title: Income from assets — core policy > income > definition of income
chunks.text:
## Income from assets
Although main benefits do not generally have an asset test, the income from any asset may affect the client's rate of payment and entitlement to a benefit.
An asset is cash or property owned by a person which has a realisable value, which could include but is not limited to:
- money saved or invested
- money invested in securities, bonds or debentures
- money invested in shares
- money loaned to another person or advanced as a mortgage
- real estate
- copyright
When assets owned by a client are not producing income, consider whether the client is depriving themselves of income. For more information see:
- Types of income
- Verification of income and assets
- Deprivation of income and assets [no link find out why]
## For more information on Main benefits and Extra help that have a specific asset test see:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Advance Payment of Benefit
- Emergency Benefit
- Funeral Grants
- Residential Care Subsidy
- Special Benefit
- Special Needs Grant
- Temporary Additional Support
- Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: Income-related purpose — core policy > income > definition of income
chunks.text:
## Income-related purpose
Payments, capital payments or the value of credits or services received periodically that are made and used for an income-related purpose, are considered to be income.
A payment would be deemed as being used for an income-related purpose if it is:
- replacing lost or diminished incomeFor example, a client receives payments from an income-related insurance policy to cover loss of employment or a client receives payment from a family member because the client has no income.
or
- maintaining a client or a member of their familyFor example, the payment is for the provision of essential living costs such as rent, food, power and clothing.
or
- purchasing goods or services (commonly paid for from income) for the client or a member of their family or
- enabling the client to make payments that they are liable to make and that are commonly made from income
Examples of the last 2 points are payments made to pay hire purchase accounts, insurance payments, payment of fines or Child Support payments.

chunks.title: Income that must be excluded — core policy > income > definition of income
chunks.text: Legislation defines some types of payments that must be excluded as income, these are: - any benefits, pensions, grants, allowances or concessions payable under the: Social Security Act 2018New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001 orVeterans' Support Act 2014 - Social Security Act 2018 - New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001 or - Veterans' Support Act 2014 - any amount of output tax charged in respect of a supply of goods and services made by that person If a business is registered it must charge GST on all goods and services. This section reinforces that if a person collects GST as an agent for the Inland Revenue Department, then the amount collected is not treated as income. - any formula-assessed Child Support for liability periods before 1 July 2023 paid in excess of a benefit rate - any formula-assessed Child Support paid in excess of the Unsupported Child's Benefit rate (including mixed Child Support payments) - any information share Child Support payments received between the commencement and grant dates of a benefit - any information share Child Support payments received shortly after transferring between benefits on different pay cycles - any amount of offset Child Support - a debt, health, or disability related insurance payment - any lump sum payments from life insurance or super schemes - any money received by a caregiver, a young person (including a young adult), or other person under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 including: board paymentsfoster care allowancesTransition Support Service payments - board payments - foster care allowances - Transition Support Service payments - any amount of goods and services tax payable by Inland Revenue to that personIf the Inland Revenue makes a refund to a client because the client has paid too much GST, then the amount of the refund is not income. - a Participation Allowance - rent and 62% of board payments a client gets that are less than or equal to their accommodation costs (after the deduction of the cost of any part of the property not being lived in by the client) - 38% of board payments a client gets (not received as part of a business venture) - 62 % of additional occupant contributions a client gets that are less than or equal to their market rent - 38% of additional occupant contributions a client gets - funeral benefits from any friendly society - Independence Allowance from ACC - income included in the Residential Care Subsidy financial means assessment

chunks.title: Income that must be excluded — core policy > income > definition of income
chunks.text: - Income Related Rent, which is not a payment or a benefit but a calculated rate of subsidised rent - Kāinga Ora energy subsidy - money paid for any military decoration. For example, a decorations allowance - the value of any assistance provided to a person with a sickness, injury, or disability to obtain or remain in employment. For example, an employer pays for transport to and from work due to the client's disability. - War pensions or other war allowances paid periodically by the government of any other Commonwealth country - Working for Families Tax Credits - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received

chunks.title: Income that must be included — core policy > income > definition of income
chunks.text:
## Income that must be included
Legislation defines some types of payments that must be included as income, these are:
- any income-related insurance payment
- any payment relating to a situation involving a seasonal layoff
- any payment dependent on the completion of either a fixed-term engagement or a contract. For example, a bonus payment for completing work on time.
- any payment in lieu of notice terminating employment. For example, 4 weeks pay in lieu of notice
- any payment (including holiday pay) which, if it had not been made in relation to termination of employment, would have been paid so as to constitute monetary remuneration. For example, accumulated sick leave
- any payment in relation to termination of employment made by a company to any of its directors
- the value of any goods, services, transport or accommodation supplied on a regular basis, before the deduction of income tax
- any COVID-19 Income Relief Payment, which is non-taxable and cannot be paid with a main benefit
- any information share Child Support payments
- any non-information share Child Support payments made for an income-related purpose (except where a specific exclusion applies)
Note any income not used in the financial means assessment for Residential Care Subsidy and that is otherwise not excluded, must be included in the benefit and/or extra help assessment the client in the community is entitled to.

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > income > definition of income
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Income is defined as:
- any money received (before income tax) which is not a one-off capital payment
For example: wages, salary, commission, parental leave payments, net profit before tax from self-employment
- the value of any interest (before income tax) acquired which is not a one-off capital payment
Interest is much broader than just the interest received from savings and investments. Interest can refer to the value in money's worth rather than money itself
For example where a client has their rent being paid for by their parents or their ex-partner, they don't get the rent money as this is paid directly to the landlord. They get the value in money's worth of an acquired interest which would be considered as free rent
- payments, capital payments or the value of credits or services received periodically that are made and used for an income-related purpose
- the value of goods, services, transport or accommodation supplied on a regular basis. For example, free board, free rent, an income-related insurance payment
Information share Child Support payments have a specific income definition. This definition is narrower than the description above.
For more information see:
## Taxable income
Although some forms of income are not taxed they are still considered to be income.
Whether income is taxed or not, it can still be considered as income e.g. a tax-exempt pension from a superannuation fund paid as a 'tax free' payment is considered chargeable income.

chunks.title: Partner of client in long-term residential care — core policy > income > definition of income
chunks.text:
## Partner of client in long-term residential care
When the partner of the client in long-term residential care is residing in the community and receiving an income tested benefit or Extra help, some of their income may be excluded from the income assessment.
The client in residential care may be in a:
- hospital or
- rest home
The income of the partner in the community that was included in the means assessment of their partner in residential care, cannot be included as chargeable income.
This is because the client and partner are each required to contribute toward the cost of residential care.
Note if the client in residential care has been financially means assessed for Residential Care Subsidy but is not eligible, the income used in the assessment is still disregarded when assessing all the partner in the community's benefit and Extra help entitlements.

chunks.title: Verification of income and assets — core policy > income > definition of income
chunks.text:
## Verification of income and assets
All income and assets must be verified, this can be through the use of MSD verification forms or clients providing documentation.

chunks.title: ACC child weekly compensation — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## ACC child weekly compensation
ACC child weekly compensation payments are made to caregivers (for the child). This is regarded as the child's income and is to compensate any income that would have been provided by a deceased parent before their death, due to personal injury covered by ACC.
It is payable until the end of the year that the child turns 18 years of age unless they are in full-time study. In this case, ACC child weekly compensation payments can continue until the earliest of the following dates:
- completes full-time study or
- reaches 21 years of age
## Effect on specified benefit
Although the ACC child weekly compensation payment is not considered as income, payments of ACC child weekly compensation are a direct deduction from a client's specified benefit. For every $1.00 of the net ACC child weekly compensation payment received, $1.00 is deducted from the net specified benefit rate.
## Extra help, hardship assistance and non-beneficiary clients
Payments of ACC child weekly compensation are not considered as income, a direct deduction or a cash asset when assessing Extra help, hardship assistance or non-beneficiary clients receiving Extra help.

chunks.title: ACC childcare payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## ACC childcare payments
The ACC child care payment is a non-taxable payment and made to caregivers in recognition of loss of supervisory or personal care (or financial support to provide this care) provided by a deceased parent before their death, due to personal injury covered by ACC.
The ACC child care payment is the income of the child and not the income of the child’s caregiver.
ACC child care payments are not:
- treated as income when assessing entitlement of a main benefit, supplementary assistance (including Childcare Assistance) or hardship assistance
- deducted from the rate of or eligible hours when assessing Childcare Assistance
ACC child care payments may continue until the earliest of the following dates:
- 5 years after the date of entitlement to child care started or
- the date on which the child reaches 14 years of age
## Child with a disability, physical or mental condition
If a child has a disability, physical or mental condition, ACC can reassess the case when the child turns 14 years old to determine if payments should continue. Payments can continue for up to a maximum of 5 years.
## Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit
ACC child care payments should be considered as ‘other income’ if the child’s caregiver is receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Accident Compensation — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Accident Compensation
The Accident Compensation Scheme provides personal injury cover for all New Zealand citizens, residents and temporary visitors to New Zealand. The Accident Compensation Scheme is administered by Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC).
This section has information on how to treat payments from ACC for benefit purposes. Assistance available from ACC may include weekly compensation, lump sum payments for impairment, a survivor's grant, an independence allowance and payments for attendant care, home help and childcare.
When a client is receiving payments from ACC, it is important to establish what the payments are paid for, so that the payment is treated in the correct manner for benefit purposes.

chunks.title: Additional occupant contributions — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: From 2 March 2026, when a social housing tenant gets contributions from additional occupants living in the same premises, the accommodation income must be assessed to determine whether there is chargeable income. Additional occupant contributions for periods prior to 2 March 2026 are charged as income based on previous settings. When accommodation income is more than the market rent for the social housing property, the excess amount is income and must be charged against any income tested assistance that uses the definition of income in the Social Security Act 2018. This includes but is not limited to main benefits and supplementary assistance. Income from additional occupant contributions is charged over the period it represents. When a property is tenanted by more than one person, the client who gets the payment will have it assessed as income. When the payment is split between multiple tenants (e.g., gets paid into a joint account), the payment will be split when assessing it as income. For social housing tenants or those on the housing register, contributions from additional occupants are not treated as assessable income when calculating Income Related Rent and eligibility for social housing. For more information see: - Income Related Rent Assessable income

chunks.title: Accommodation income — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When a client gets contributions from additional occupants living in the same premises, 62% of the contribution is accommodation income. Note 38% of the contribution is excluded as income.

chunks.title: Market rent — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: For social housing tenants getting Income Related Rent, the market rent of the property is the market rent as at the most recent change in circumstances or annual rent review. Example - social housing tenant with additional occupant contributions Carlos is a social housing tenant in a 3-bedroom house with market rent of $500 a week. He gets Jobseeker Support and he works part time earning $250 a week. His two sons live with him, and they each pay contributions of $412.50 a week. The total accommodation income is $511.50 (62% of all contributions). The accommodation income he gets is more than the market rent for the property and is chargeable income for his Jobseeker Support. His income is calculated as $511.50 - $500 = $11.50 a week. $11.50 a week is combined with his earnings from part time work ($250 a week) and is charged against his Jobseeker Support. Accommodation income Board payments $825.00pw Accommodation income (62% of the board payment) $511.50pw Chargeable income Accommodation income $511.50pw Less accommodation costs (market rent) $500.00pw Equals chargeable income $11.50pw

chunks.title: Annuities and pension payments from superannuation schemes — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Annuities and pension payments from superannuation schemes
Annuity payments and pension payments from private and employer superannuation schemes are chargeable income for benefit purposes.
## Income exemption
Some people who receive a pension under a retirement scheme or payments under an annuity paid in respect of a life insurance policy may have 50% of their income disregarded for benefit purposes.
This income exemption applies to:
- the income of any client who meets the qualifying criteria and
- any benefit or extra help assistance
This income exemption does not apply to the income and asset test for Residential Care Subsidy, where 50% of income from a superannuation scheme or annuity is to be disregarded as income at all times.
For more information see:
- Residential Care Subsidy Income excluded
## Qualifying criteria for income exemption
For the superannuation scheme or annuity payments to meet the income exemption criteria, the scheme must:
- be offered or entered into in New Zealand or
- be offered or entered into by a life insurer that is resident in New Zealand
For 50% of a superannuation scheme payment to be excluded from income assessments, the client must meet all of the following conditions:
- the residential qualification for New Zealand superannuation and
- be aged 60 years or older and
- their pension or annuity meets the criteria for exclusion and
- they started getting payments from the scheme before 1 April 1992 and
- they were not less than 55 years and not more than 59 years when they started getting payments from the scheme
## Clients with a partner
If the client has a partner, the partner must:
- be aged 60 years or older and
- have been aged 55 years or older when payments commenced and
- be younger than the client

chunks.title: Applications for hardship assistance payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Applications for hardship assistance payments
When a client with an exemption applies for a hardship assistance payment, the exempt amount must be disregarded from the cash asset test.
However, generally a client won't qualify if they have enough money available to meet their need. This is because clients must use their own resources before seeking hardship assistance.
If the client only has enough money available to meet part of the cost, hardship assistance can be considered for the shortfall.
In each case you must consider the individual circumstances of the client against the qualifications.
## Example
Isaac lives rurally and relies on a water tank for his water supply. He has needed a refill for several weeks.
Isaac has been quoted $450 for his water tank to be refilled and delivered.
Earlier in the year Isaac got an insurance payment of $16,150 which is exempt from income and cash asset testing.
Isaac applies for a Special Needs Grant to cover the cost of the water tank refill. At the time of his application Isaac had $12,600 left of his insurance payment.
In this case Isaac's application for a Special Needs Grant is declined because he can cover the cost of the water tank refill from his own resources.

chunks.title: Armed service personnel — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Armed service personnel
If an Armed Service employee still has a period of leave in reserve at the time of death, the government approves the continuation of pay and allowances to cover the leave that is outstanding.
This forms part of the deceased's estate. If the widow or widower applies for a main benefit, the outstanding leave payment is not charged as income and does not impact on the commencement date of benefit.
## NZ Defence Force Termination Package
The New Zealand Defence Force has an arrangement with their personnel, whereby at the end of their agreed term of duty they can sign on for an additional period, or leave the Service.
For those who choose to leave the Service the usual termination type payments are received (eg long service leave or holiday pay), as well as what is called a 'Terminal Benefit'. This payment is a standard component of a serving member's contract, payable at the time of finishing their agreed term of duty. This can be taken as an ongoing payment, or as a lump sum.
Whether taken as a lump sum or as an ongoing payment, is taken into account when assessing the date of cessation of employment. In many cases this will result in an extended period of 'continued employment'. Treat the payment as a continuation of wages or salary.
## Territorial soldiers
Part-time soldiers can earn a gratuity, which is an annual monetary bonus. Charge this gratuity payment as income in the pay period it is received for weekly benefits.
Please refer to the appropriate main benefit type for more information on charging income see:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Backdated ACC weekly compensation payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Backdated ACC weekly compensation payments
Sometimes clients will wait a long period of time for ACC to decide their claim and will rely on MSD assistance during this period.
When the claim is later approved, ACC will backdate the weekly compensation to the original entitlement date and make a backdated ACC payment for that period.
When this happens MSD must review any specified benefit paid to a client for the same period. The backdated ACC payment is a dollar-for-dollar reduction against the specified benefit.
ACC will reimburse MSD for the amount of overpaid specified benefit out of the client's backdated ACC payment before it is paid to the client.
## Effect on specified supplementary assistance
If the backdated ACC payment reduces the client's specified benefit to zero MSD must treat the client as a non-beneficiary and review their entitlement to specified supplementary assistance.
Any debt established as a result of this review is recovered directly from the client.
## Example
Torben is granted backdated weekly compensation of $19,800 for the period 6 October 2025 to 8 March 2026.
For this period, Torben also received:
- Jobseeker Support of $361.32 per week (totalling $7,949.04)
- Accommodation Supplement of $60 per week (totalling $1,320)
Torben's Jobseeker Support is reduced to zero for the period 6 October 2025 to 8 March 2026. ACC reimburse MSD the full amount of overpaid Jobseeker Support out of Torben's backdated ACC payment.
Because Torben's Jobseeker Support is reduced to zero, MSD must review his Accommodation Supplement as a non-beneficiary.
Toben's Accommodation Supplement entitlement reduced to $4.00 per week for the period 6 October 2025 to 8 March 2026 and an overpayment of $1,232 is established. This is a debt that Torben is required to repay to MSD.

chunks.title: Backdating benefit when weekly compensation is overpaid — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Backdating benefit when weekly compensation is overpaid
These requests are managed by the Central Processing Unit.
In some cases, ACC may review a client's entitlement to weekly compensation after they have been receiving it for a period of time. This may result in an overpayment of the weekly compensation.
A client who was not previously receiving a benefit may be able to receive a benefit for the period that the weekly compensation has been overpaid.
Where ACC believe a client may have had entitlement to a benefit, they will send MSD a letter detailing the situation and asking us to consider a back-dated grant of benefit for the client.
Any benefit that is paid for a period that the weekly compensation was overpaid, will be redirected to ACC to reduce the client's debt with them.
For more information see:
- ACC weekly compensation
- Effect on Extra help
- Reimbursement requests from ACC reviews

chunks.title: Bonus payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Bonus payments
A bonus payment is included in determining the average weekly income. For treatment of bonus payments when a client stops work and applies for benefit see initial stand down
Clients receiving a benefit and who are currently working, may receive a bonus payment from their job which can be a performance bonus or paid as part of their contract. Bonus payments are treated as income and charged over the pay period in which the payment is received for weekly benefits.
Please refer to the appropriate benefit type for more information on charging income, see:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Capital payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Capital payments
A one off capital payment from a will or an estate is not income for benefit purposes.
If a client receives a series of capital payments these may be income for benefit purposes. For more information see:
- Interim payments
- Core policy Capital payments
- Core policy Income related purpose
When a client receives money from a will or an estate, any income from investment of the money is chargeable income for benefit purposes.
For example a client puts their inheritance into a savings account earning 5% interest, the interest earned would be changed as income against the benefit.
Money or other assets received from a will or an estate may be considered as a cash asset and therefore could affect entitlement to Extra help such as Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support. Extra help should be reviewed when the payment is received.

chunks.title: Carer's Allowance — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Carer's Allowance
Carer's Allowance is paid to people carrying out alternative care or carer support. It is charged as income when assessing entitlement to a benefit.
When a client can show that they have actual costs associated with the care function, these are deducted from the income figure.
If travel allowance is paid as a general allowance to all carers at the same rate, and forms part of an employment package, then this is also charged as income with the Carer's Allowance.
If a payment is made to the individual carer as a specific reimbursement of actual identified travel costs, then this is not treated as income.
## Idea Services board payments and foster care payments
Idea Services board payments, less expenses directly related to the care function are charged as income. Expenses must be verified and you should ask for confirmation from Idea Services that they must be paid by the caregiver.
Whenever a client can show they have incurred actual costs associated with the care function, these should be deducted from the income figure.
## Funded Family Care
Funded Family Care payments are made to family members caring for the disabled person with high or very high needs and are considered income for the carer. See Whaikaha Disability services
Payments may affect the assistance the carer can get from MSD (including non-beneficiary assistance).
## For more information on charging income see:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Changes and reviews for payments before 1 July 1999 — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews for payments before 1 July 1999
There will be clients who have their ACC weekly compensation treated as income when they were granted the weekly compensation prior to 1 July 1999 and the benefit is being paid for a different reason to the weekly compensation. These clients may have a change in circumstance which requires a review.
Below are guidelines on how to treat these clients when their benefit is suspended, they transfer between benefits, and when they have changes to the amount of weekly compensation they receive.
## Benefit stops
When ACC weekly compensation has been charged as income and a benefit has been suspended for less than eight weeks and then resumed, the weekly compensation continues to be charged as income.
If the benefit is suspended for eight weeks or more, the weekly compensation is no longer charged as income and is treated as a direct deduction. This also applies to any subsequent reapplication for benefit.
## Transfer between benefits
When a client transfers to another benefit, and that benefit is paid for a different reason than the weekly compensation, the weekly compensation continues to be charged as income.
When the client transfers to another benefit and that benefit is paid for the same reason as the weekly compensation, the weekly compensation is a direct deduction.
## Changes to weekly compensation payments
You can review a benefit when there is a change in the rate of weekly compensation or when payments cease.
There may be cases where weekly compensation payments from ACC have stopped and the client reviews the ACC decision. If the client's review is successful and payments are reinstated then the previous income charge or direct deduction continues as if the payments of weekly compensation never stopped.
Where weekly compensation payments have stopped and the client begins receiving payments after 1 July 1999 for a different injury then the new payments of weekly compensation are a direct deduction.
For more information see:
- Backdating benefit when weekly compensation is overpaid
- Weekly compensation payments started before 1 July 1999
- Quick reference guide for the treatment of ACC payments

chunks.title: Changes in the client's cash asset levels — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Changes in the client's cash asset levels
An exemption for a severe weather event payment must be equal to the payment the client got, or the amount they have left when they declare the payment to us.
Clients are not expected to keep track of any changes to the value of an exempt payment.
The exemption amount will stay the same for the 12-month period unless the client's total cash assets reduce below the exempt amount.
When this happens, the exemption must be updated to match the client's new level of cash assets. The exemption must be removed if we identify the client has zero cash assets.
The exemption will only increase or be applied again if the client gets another exempt payment.
## Example
Zara receives an insurance payment of $32,000 on 6 December 2023 to repair damage to her home caused by Cyclone Gabrielle.
Seven months later at her annual review, Zara tells MSD she has spent some of the payment on repairs and has $17,200 left. Her exemption is updated to $17,200.

chunks.title: Assistance not included in automated income charging — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Assistance not included in automated income charging
Some types of assistance have an income test, but do not have an automated income charge for Child Support.
All income is calculated manually for these payments.
## Student Allowance
Student Allowance is an income-tested payment. However, the automated income charging rules for Child Support do not apply.
Students must declare any Child Support payments they get and Child Support income is calculated manually, like other income.
This applies even if the client is also getting extra help and information share Child Support payments are automatically charged as income for their other payments. This information cannot be used when calculating income for Student Allowance.
## Clients living overseas
Some types of benefits paid under a Reciprocal Agreement have an income test. However, the automated income charging rules for Child Support do not apply.
Clients who get this type of assistance must declare any Child Support payments they get and Child Support income is charged under the rules that apply to the relevant Agreement, like other income.
## Social Housing assistance
A client’s income is used to assess their rate of Income Related Rent and eligibility for Social Housing. However, the automated income charging rules for Child Support do not apply.
Social Housing clients do not need to declare their information share Child Support payments if they are also getting a benefit or extra help. This information can be used when calculating their assessable income for social housing assistance.
If a social housing client is not getting any other assistance, they must declare any Child Support payments they get.
All Child Support income is calculated manually for social housing clients, like other assessable income.
## Hardship
All hardship payments are income-tested.
If a client applying for hardship is not getting a benefit or extra help, they must declare any Child Support payments they get when applying for hardship. This includes Flexible Funding Assistance, Recoverable Assistance Payment, and Special Needs Grants. Child Support income is calculated manually using the general income charging rules for these clients, like other income.
If a client applying for hardship is also getting an income-tested benefit or extra help, the automated income charging rules do apply to hardship payments. This includes Advance Payment of Benefit.
## All other payments
All other types of income-tested benefits and extra help are included in the information share with Inland Revenue and have the automated income rules applied.

chunks.title: Automated income charging rules — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Automated income charging rules
Income charging for information share Child Support payments is automated. This means MSD charges the income automatically, generally with no involvement from staff.
As income charging is automated, these types of payments are always charged in the same way, using defined rules.
There are only a few situations when MSD can change how the system charged income for these payments. For more information see:
## Charging income forward
Information share Child Support payments are always charged forward as income. This avoids creating debt for clients because the income can be used to work out the correct rate before the client is paid their assistance from MSD.
Other types of income are charged against the period that the income was earned in or represents. Other income, such as wages, can usually be declared in the same week the income was earned. If information share Child Support payments were charged in this way, it could create debt for clients. This is because Child Support is paid in arrears and would be charged as income after the client's assistance was paid to them.
For example, if Inland Revenue paid a client in-cycle Child Support in September, it would represent their entitlement for August. If the income was charged for the same period that the payment represents, the client may have a debt. This would happen if the new income charge meant they were overpaid their benefit in August.
Automatically charging information share Child Support payments forward minimises the risk of overpayments.
## Charging income for a defined period
The charging period for an information share Child Support payment is always 4 or 5 weeks. This is because most Child Support payments are for a month of Child Support liability.
The period of the income charge is determined by the:
- type of Child Support payment and
- type of financial assistance the client is getting and
- the deemed receipt of the payment
To make the income charging rules clear for staff and clients, the charging period is always 4 or 5 weeks. This applies even if the Child Support is an out-of-cycle payment and may represent a longer period.
## Removing discretion
As these payments are automated, there is no discretion when charging income. MSD cannot charge information share Child Support payments in a different way.
For other types of income, MSD can determine what period income relates to, based on a client's individual circumstances, and charge it accordingly.

chunks.title: Cash asset exemption for information share Child Support payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
