chunks.text: Information share Child Support payments are not treated as cash assets for the person who received the payment (or their partner, if any) until the day after the income charge for the payment ends.

chunks.title: Cash asset exemption period — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Information share Child Support payments are charged forward as income for 4 or 5 weeks. The full amount of the payment is not treated as a cash asset for this period.

chunks.title: End of exemption period — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: At the end of the exemption period, any remaining amount of the information share Child Support payment is treated as a cash asset. Any income earned from investment of the remaining amount is treated as income.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances for extending the exemption period — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Sometimes a client may not spend the information share Child Support payment during the income charging period due to exceptional circumstances. In these situations, an additional period may be allowed for the client to make a decision about how they will use the money (i.e. as income on income-related purposes or save it as a cash asset). Exceptional circumstances for extending the cash asset exemption period are limited to: - bereavement in the client's immediate family (including their partner, child, sibling, parent or grandparent) - serious illness or injury of the client or a member of their immediate family - hospitalisation of the client or a member of their immediate family - the client, or a child the client is a legal guardian of, is a victim of crime and MSD is satisfied the client's experience as a victim of crime is a good and sufficient reason for not spending the information share Child Support payment before the end of the exemption period - living in or visiting (and cannot reasonably leave) an area that is or may be affected by an emergency or exceptional adverse event e.g. Civil Defence emergency, or outbreak of quarantinable disease If the client meets the exceptional circumstances criteria, MSD can extend the exemption period for another 28 days from the end of the original exemption period.

chunks.title: Applications for hardship assistance payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Generally, a client won't qualify for hardship assistance if they have enough money available to meet the need, even if that money is exempt from the cash asset test. This includes information share Child Support payments. Clients must use their own resources before seeking hardship assistance. If the client only has money available to meet some of the cost, hardship assistance can be considered for the remaining cost. In each case you must consider the individual circumstances of the client against the eligibility criteria.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews - information share Child Support — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews information share child support
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews - information share Child Support
Income charging for information share Child Support payments is generally automated.
However, in some situations, MSD may need to change an income charge to fix an error with the information share or the way the information share has been used.
MSD is only able to change an automated information share Child Support payments in specific situations.
## Treatment of debt
Any debt created because of an incorrect amount of income being charged is not recoverable in this situation.
## Mandatory Reviews for clients with information share Child Support
When clients have information share Child Support charged as income it is not reviewed as part of their Mandatory Review.

chunks.title: Child Support not received by deemed receipt — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews information share child support
chunks.text:
## Child Support not received by deemed receipt
In some situations, a client may get an information share Child Support payment later than the deemed receipt. This could happen if the payment takes more than 1 business day to arrive in their bank account.
If MSD determines that a client's payment arrived at a later date than the deemed receipt, the income charge may be changed to reflect the actual date of receipt.
Note if it was an in-cycle payment, changing the deemed receipt may result in stacking when their next in-cycle payment is made. If the client decides they would prefer to avoid this happening, the original deemed date can still be used with the client's agreement.
## Example
Yigal is getting a sole parent rate of Jobseeker Support while caring for his 16-year-old daughter. He gets $150 Child Support a month from his ex-partner.
On Thursday 23 November, Inland Revenue pays Yigal his regular information share Child Support payment. MSD calculates the deemed receipt as Friday 24 November. The income charge starts on Monday 20 November and is charged forward for 5 weeks.
On Wednesday 29 November, Yigal tells MSD there was a delay at his bank and he only got the Child Support payment in his account that morning.
MSD changes the deemed receipt to 29 November, as this is the date that Yigal got the money in his bank account.
This means the income charge is changed to start a week later, on Monday 27 November and is charged forward for 4 weeks.
Yigal's benefit entitlement for the week of 20 November is reassessed, and any arrears are paid to him.

chunks.title: Client unable to access payment — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews information share child support
chunks.text: Sometimes an information share Child Support payment may be paid to a client's bank account, but the client is unable to access it. In this situation, MSD must determine if the client got any of the money and if it should be charged as income. The client must have a good and sufficient reason as to why they cannot access the payment. A good and sufficient reason may include (but is not limited to): - the Child Support was paid to an agent's bank account and the agent has unfairly withheld the payment or - the client has separated from their partner and the Child Support was paid to a bank account they no longer have access to The client may be able to access some of a payment. For example, if their agent has passed on a portion of the total amount. In this case, only the amount the client actually got can be charged as income. MSD must consider if the client has previously advised they are unable to access a payment. MSD must also consider if it is reasonable that the client had not updated their details with Inland Revenue before the payment was made. If the client cannot provide a good and sufficient reason, the information share Child Support payment is considered income and the charge is not changed or removed. Note if the payment has been used to repay a debt belonging to the client (such as an overdraft on a client's account or a genuine debt owed to a client's agent), the whole payment is charged as income.

chunks.title: Example 1 — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews information share child support
chunks.text: On Thursday 16 May, Inland Revenue pays Isobel an out-of-cycle payment of $1,500. This information share Child Support payment is automatically charged as income against Isobel's benefit. Isobel cannot access the payment due to separating from a partner who is currently in sole charge of their shared bank account. The ex-partner is stopping Isobel from accessing the money. She forgot to update her account with Inland Revenue as she was not getting regular Child Support payments at the time they separated. After getting a letter about her reduced benefit payments, Isobel contacts MSD and explains her situation. Isobel has a good and sufficient reason for being unable to access the payment. MSD removes the income charge effective from 16 May and reassesses Isobel's benefit. Any benefit arrears are paid to her.

chunks.title: Example 2 — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews information share child support
chunks.text: Lucretia gets $200 Child Support paid by Inland Revenue on Tuesday 23 April. MSD is notified through the information share and the payment is charged as income against Lucretia's Accommodation Supplement. The Child Support payment goes into Lucretia's bank account, but her account is overdrawn by $200. After paying the overdraft fee, she only has access to $50 of the payment. Lucretia contacts MSD to ask if the charge can be removed as she doesn't have enough money to cover her costs this week. MSD determines that Lucretia does not have a good and sufficient reason for being unable to access the information share Child Support payment. As the payment was used to pay off a debt she owed, MSD considers that the income was received and used. MSD does not remove the income charge but discusses other financial assistance that may be available to help Lucretia meet her costs this week.

chunks.title: Death of a client before deemed receipt — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews information share child support
chunks.text:
## Death of a client before deemed receipt
If a client dies during an income charge for an information share Child Support payment, any Terminal Benefit is fixed at the rate they were getting on the date they died.
Sometimes there may be a delay in MSD being told about a client's death. At this time, the deceased client may have already been charged for a new information share Child Support payment. This may reduce their payments to a different rate than they were getting on the date they passed away.
A client cannot be charged for a Child Support payment that they did not get. If a client has been charged for income after the date of death, the income is not chargeable. If any Terminal Benefit is payable, the rate is changed as appropriate.
This may result in arrears to be paid to the client's estate.

chunks.title: Errors with the information share — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews information share child support
chunks.text: If a client tells MSD an income charge from an information share Child Support payment is wrong, staff must check the information with Inland Revenue. The information from Inland Revenue is used to verify if the income charge needs to be changed. MSD can only change an income charge in this situation when: - the information share is correct but: the MSD system has used the information incorrectly orthe information was used incorrectly by a staff member or - the MSD system has used the information incorrectly or - the information was used incorrectly by a staff member or - the information share was incorrect due to an error by Inland Revenue MSD cannot change an automated income charge if Inland Revenue reassesses the amount of Child Support a client was entitled to get. Note any debt created because of an error is not recoverable in the situations below.

chunks.title: Incorrect client charged income — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews information share child support
chunks.text: There is a small risk an information share Child Support payment may be charged to the wrong client. This may happen because of human error or an issue with the information share. Information share Child Support payments can only be charged as income for the client who gets the payment. If a client has been charged income for a payment they did not get, the income charge should be removed.

chunks.title: Incorrect amount of income charged — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews information share child support
chunks.text: Although unlikely, it is possible that a client could be charged an incorrect amount of income from an information share Child Support payment. This may happen because of human error or an issue with the information share. Information share Child Support payments can only be charged as income for the amount the client has received. Inland Revenue must verify the correct amount of income before an income charge can be changed or removed in this situation.

chunks.title: Child Support paid but income not charged — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews information share child support
chunks.text: MSD may be notified about an information share Child Support payment but may discard the information in error. This would result in no Child Support income being charged for a client. If a client advises MSD this has happened, Inland Revenue must verify the payment information. The payment should then be charged as income using the same rules as payments notified through the information share.

chunks.title: Information share delayed — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews information share child support
chunks.text: A system failure or sudden unplanned event may affect either Inland Revenue or MSD's systems (or both). This may cause a delay to the information share. For example, if MSD's systems aren't working because of a significant natural disaster, there could be days or weeks between when Inland Revenue paid someone Child Support and when MSD is notified of the payment. In this situation, when the information share is received from Inland Revenue, the income is charged as if MSD got the information on time (using the original deemed receipt). For example, if a client on a weekly benefit got an information share Child Support payment on 5 October, but MSD did not get the information until 15 October there would be no income added until MSD got the information. The income charge would be backdated to start on (or before) 5 October.

chunks.title: Reviews of information share Child Support payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews information share child support
chunks.text:
## Reviews of information share Child Support payments
Clients have standard review and appeal rights if they want to review a decision on the treatment of information share Child Support payments. They can also ask the Ombudsman to undertake their own review.
If a client requests a review:
MSD can only change the treatment of information share Child Support payments when there has been an error.
Clients can request a review of the information MSD has used if they think there has been an error.
An error is when a client has been charged income for an information share Child Support payment but they:
- did not get the payment or
- got a different amount of Child Support than was charged as income or
- got the payment later than the deemed receipt
MSD cannot change the treatment of information share Child Support payments if there is no error identified.
This includes when a client disagrees with:
- how the income charge for a payment has been calculated (e.g. if the client believes that the income should have been charged over a different period - 12 weeks instead of 4) or
- the amount of income that has been charged for a payment (e.g. if the Child Support payment was used to repay the client's overdraft on their bank account)

chunks.title: Unposted credits — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews information share child support
chunks.text:
## Unposted credits
An unposted credit is when a payment cannot be made to a client's bank account and is returned by the bank.
An information share Child Support payment may be an unposted credit if a client's bank account has closed. The bank generally returns unposted credits to Inland Revenue within 2 to 5 business days after the payment was made.
If a client has not got a Child Support payment in their bank account, it cannot be charged as income.
When Inland Revenue tells MSD a payment has been returned unposted, the income charge is automatically removed. The client's entitlement to assistance is also reassessed. This may result in arrears for the client.
Once the client gets the Child Support payment, Inland Revenue will tell MSD another payment has been made. The new information share Child Support payment will be charged as income, as appropriate.
## Example
On Friday 22 March, Inland Revenue pay Jane $100 Child Support. This information share Child Support payment is automatically charged as income against Jane's benefit.
The income charge is $25 per week for 4 weeks, starting on Monday 18 March.
On Wednesday 27 March, the payment is returned to Inland Revenue as an unposted credit because Jane's bank account is closed. Jane gets a letter from Inland Revenue telling her to update her bank account details.
MSD is notified through the information share that Jane's $100 Child Support has been returned as an unposted credit.
The $100 income charge is automatically removed effective from Monday 18 March. Jane's benefit entitlement is reassessed, and any arrears are paid to her.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews - non-information share Child Support payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews non information share child support
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews - non-information share Child Support payments
For non-information share Child Support payments, the income charge is not automated.
This means clients must declare these payments as income for benefit purposes. The Child Support is then charged as income using the general charging rules.
This means the Child Support payment must be charged over the period it is earned or relates to.
If the payment does not represent a specific period or if MSD cannot determine the actual period it represents, MSD must determine the most appropriate period to charge the income. This may be the week in which it is received, provided or supplied.
A client can apply for a review of decision when they are notified of a decision that they do not agree with. MSD may also decide to review assistance at any time to ensure the client still meets the qualifications and is getting the correct rate of payment.
This may result in benefit debt or payments owing if there is a change in an income charge from a non-information share Child Support payment.
Note this is different to information share Child Support payments, which can only be reviewed in specific situations.

chunks.title: Child Support paid for a period before client was getting a benefit — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews non information share child support
chunks.text:
## Child Support paid for a period before client was getting a benefit
Any income that represents a period when a client was not getting income-tested assistance from MSD is generally not charged as income.
MSD must charge income for the period it is earned or relates to.
If the payment does not represent a specific period or if MSD cannot determine the actual period it represents, MSD must determine the most appropriate period it relates to. This may be the period in which it is received, provided or supplied.
If MSD determines the income relates to a period when the client was not getting income-tested assistance, it is not chargeable income.
Example a receiving carer has been getting private Child Support payments before applying for a benefit. The client gets their next Child Support payment after their benefit is granted. This payment represents Child Support for the month before the grant of the benefit and so is not charged as income.
Note this does not apply to information share Child Support payments. These payments are charged as income regardless of what period the payment relates to.
## Example
Ora has a Child Support arrangement through Inland Revenue with her ex-partner, Taika.
Taika gets behind in his payments to Inland Revenue and owes Ora $500 for May and June 2023.
In July 2023, Ora applies for Accommodation Supplement, which is income-tested.
When Taika eventually pays the Child Support he owes her in August 2023, this is not charged as income against her Accommodation Supplement. This is because it represents a period when she was not getting any income-tested assistance.

chunks.title: Offsetting Child Support — core policy > income > types of income > child support income > changes and reviews non information share child support
chunks.text:
## Offsetting Child Support
Offsetting is where two parents are each liable to pay the other a regular amount of Child Support.
For example, in a split care situation, where each parent is a receiving carer for one of their children and a liable parent for another child, Inland Revenue may offset one liability against the other.
The parent with the higher liability pays the difference to Inland Revenue and this is passed on to the receiving carer. Only the amount the receiving carer gets is chargeable income.
If these clients have a formula assessment, they may be able to have these costs included as an allowable cost in their Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit.
## Example
If Sam owes Alex $120 in Child Support and Alex owes Sam $100 in Child Support, this amount can be offset by Inland Revenue and Sam only has to pay $20 to Alex. When this is paid, Inland Revenue notifies MSD through the information share.
Alex has an income charge of $20. Sam has no Child Support income charged, as they don't receive any cash payment.
Alex and Sam would each be able to include their formula-assessed Child Support as an allowable cost if they get Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit.

chunks.title: Charging from grant date or commencement date — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Information share Child Support payments are not charged as income before the commencement date of a benefit. This includes when a client's assistance commences earlier than the application date, i.e. when the 28 day rule applies. This means some information share Child Support payments are not charged as income. Whether they are charged as income depends on when a client's assistance is granted and when MSD is notified of their information share Child Support payments. Only information share Child Support payments with a deemed receipt on or after the grant date or the commencement date (whichever is later) are charged as income.

chunks.title: Future commencement date — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Sometimes a client's assistance may start from a date in the future. When the commencement date is after the grant date, only information share Child Support payments with a deemed receipt on or after the commencement date are charged as income. This means only payments a client gets after their benefit starts being paid are charged as income. Information share Child Support payments a client gets before this date are only considered when calculating income for an initial stand-down. Example Martha resigns from her job on Friday 21 July and applies for Supported Living Payment. Her only income will now be monthly payments of Child Support from her ex-partner. This is a voluntary agreement paid through Inland Revenue. Martha got 2 weeks of holiday pay on Friday 21 July. She also gets a Child Support payment on Monday 24 July and is expecting the next payment on 23 August. The commencement date for Martha's benefit is the day after her holiday pay ends on Monday 7 August. Only information share Child Support payments she gets on or after 7 August will be charged as income against her benefit. The payment Martha gets on 24 July is not charged as income as she got it before her benefit commenced.

chunks.title: Past commencement date — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: In some situations, a client's assistance can start from a date in the past. This is called a backdated commencement. When the commencement date is before the grant date, only information share Child Support payments with a deemed receipt after the grant date are charged as income. This means only payments a client gets on or after their benefit is granted are charged as income in this situation. Information share Child Support payments a client gets before this date are not chargeable income. Example Damon is the primary caregiver for his son Benji and gets formula-assessed Child Support through Inland Revenue. He's in a new relationship with Lucia, who is supporting him financially. On Sunday 27 August, Damon and Lucia separate. Damon decides to apply for a benefit, but it takes him a while to make the application. He applies on Monday 18 September and the next day is granted Sole Parent Support. The commencement date of his benefit is Monday 11 September because he has a 2 week initial income stand-down. Only information share Child Support payments that Damon gets on or after 19 September will be charged as income against his benefit. This is because his benefit was granted on 19 September and only payments he gets after the grant date are chargeable income.

chunks.title: Child Support income when applying for extra help — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Child Support income when applying for extra help
When applying for new forms of ongoing extra help, information share Child Support payments are only charged as income after a client's assistance is granted.
Non-information Child Support payments are declared and charged as income under the general income charging rules.
For more information see: Charging from grant date or commencement date
When applying for one-off forms of extra help e.g. a Special Needs Grant, Child Support payments must be used in the income assessment as appropriate.
## Weekly income test and other income-tested assistance
The same amount of weekly income charged against their other income-tested assistance is used when determining their total income for that week.
This includes any information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income.
## Annual income test for hardship assistance
Any Child Support payments related to the relevant period are used to work out a client's total annual income.
This includes information share Child Support payments that were or are currently being charged as income.
If a client's information share Child Support payments are not disclosed to MSD and not charged as income, the client must self-declare all Child Support payments they received during the relevant income assessment period.
These payments are considered income under the general income charging rules.

chunks.title: Child Support paid for periods before 1 July 2023 — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Child Support paid for periods before 1 July 2023
Any Child Support paid for a liability period before 1 July 2023 is considered a non-information share Child Support payment. These payments are not included in the information share with Inland Revenue.
Child Support for periods before 1 July 2023 is treated under the policy and legislation that applied at the time the payment relates to. This also applies when these payments are made after 1 July 2023.
These Child Support payments are charged as income using the general charging rules.
This means the Child Support payment must be charged over the period it is earned or relates to.
If the payment does not represent a specific period or if MSD cannot determine the actual period it represents, MSD must determine the most appropriate period to charge the income. This may be the week in which it is received, provided or supplied.
## Types of Child Support relating to periods before 1 July 2023
There are 4 types of Child Support payments that Inland Revenue can make to clients relating to a liability period before 1 July 2023:
Child Support payments not paid through Inland Revenue, are treated the same before and after 1 July 2023.

chunks.title: Clients getting Child Support while living overseas — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Clients getting Child Support while living overseas
Clients getting a New Zealand benefit paid under a reciprocal agreement when living overseas may also get Child Support payments through Inland Revenue.
These payments are considered a non-information share Child Support payment, as they are not included in the information share with Inland Revenue.
These clients need to declare all Child Support payments they get.
These Child Support payments are charged according to the specific rules of the reciprocal agreement they are subject to.

chunks.title: Clients transferring between benefits — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Clients transferring between benefits
A client getting income-tested assistance may transfer between benefits or start getting extra help.
This applies to clients getting:
- income-tested extra help, for example Accommodation Supplement, who start getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation, or Veteran’s Pension
- a main benefit, who start getting income-tested extra help
- a main benefit, who transfer to another type of benefit
- a main benefit, who transfer to New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension with income-tested extra help
- New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension as a non-qualified partner, who transfer to their own main benefit or income-tested extra help
A transfer to another type of assistance may happen on any day of the week. The transfer date is based on the date of entitlement to the new benefit.
Clients may have an information share Child Support payment being charged as income at the time they transfer.
The income charge is calculated based on the benefit type (weekly or fortnightly) the client is getting at the time they get the payment. The end of the charge may need to be recalculated if the client is transferring to assistance on a different pay period.

chunks.title: Couples with different pay periods — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Couples with different pay periods
If a New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client paid fortnightly has a partner getting a weekly benefit, they will get their payments from MSD at different times.
New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension are generally not income tested.
However, the couple's combined income is assessed for the partner paid a weekly main benefit and any extra help.
When clients in this situation get information share Child Support payments, the income is charged using the rules that apply to the receiving carer.
If the receiving carer has a fortnightly pay period, the income charge follows the fortnightly charging rules. If the receiving carer has a weekly pay period, the income charge follows the weekly charging rules.
The couple's joint income is still charged against any income-tested assistance either client is getting.
Example 1
Derek gets New Zealand Superannuation payments fortnightly. His partner Meredith gets Supported Living Payment paid to her weekly.
Derek is the receiving carer for his granddaughter and gets formula-assessed Child Support of $100 a month from the child's mother. MSD is notified of the Child Support income through the information share with Inland Revenue.
The information share Child Support payments Derek gets are calculated over a 4-week period. This follows the fortnightly charging rules because Derek gets his New Zealand Superannuation payment fortnightly.
The income is charged against Meredith's weekly Supported Living Payment. This means that the income charge is $25 per week for 4 weeks.
Example 2
Daphne gets New Zealand Superannuation and Disability Allowance payments fortnightly. Her partner Fred gets Jobseeker Support payments weekly.
Fred is the receiving carer for his son and gets monthly Child Support of $100 from his son's mother. This Child Support is a voluntary agreement through Inland Revenue.
The information share Child Support payments Fred gets are calculated over a 4- or 5-week period, as Fred's Jobseeker Support is on a weekly pay cycle.
Because both Fred and Daphne are getting income-tested assistance, the weekly amount that is charged against Fred's Jobseeker Support is also counted towards the couple's total fortnightly income for Daphne's Disability Allowance payments.
The income charge is $25 per week in 4-week months, and $20 per week in 5-week months.

chunks.title: Court ordered lump sum payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Court ordered lump sum payments
In some situations, a liable parent may be ordered by the Family Court to pay an amount of Child Support to a receiving carer.
These payments are collected by Inland Revenue and paid to receiving carers in one lump sum. They may also be paid in instalments.
Payments may represent any liability period of formula-assessed Child Support (i.e. in the past or future). They may also be a one-off payment for a specific expense.
Court ordered lump sum payments of Child Support are considered a non-information share Child Support payment, as they are not included in the information share with Inland Revenue.
These Child Support payments are charged as income using the general charging rules.
Court ordered lump sum payments may sometimes be intended for an income-related purpose.
Other payments may be a capital payment.
It is important to determine if a payment is a capital payment or income before charging it as income.

chunks.title: Deemed Receipt — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Deemed Receipt
MSD must determine when a Child Support payment is available to a client to use as income (i.e. when it arrives in their bank account). This is called the deemed receipt.
The deemed receipt is used to work out the start of an income charge for an information share Child Support payment. The deemed receipt is generally automated. This means it is worked out automatically, generally with no involvement from staff.
## Calculating the deemed receipt
The date when Inland Revenue sends Child Support payments to the bank is called the transaction date.
The transaction date is generally:
- 2 business days after the 19th of the month for in-cycle payments or
- any business day for out-of-cycle payments
After Inland Revenue sends the payment to the bank, the money may take a day or so to arrive in the client’s bank account. The deemed receipt is 1 business day after the transaction date. This is the latest date a client is expected to get an information share Child Support payment in their bank account.
The deemed date is calculated automatically based on the transaction date.
Note in some situations, clients may get an information share Child Support payment later than the deemed receipt. When a client tells MSD this has happened, the deemed receipt can be changed to a later date.
Example
Megan gets Child Support from her ex-partner through Inland Revenue. She is also getting Jobseeker Support.
On Tuesday 22 August, Inland Revenue sends the Child Support payment to the bank. Inland Revenue tells MSD that Megan was paid Child Support on 22 August (the transaction date).
MSD uses the transaction date to work out when Megan will get the payment in her bank account (the deemed receipt). The deemed receipt for Megan’s Child Support payment is Wednesday 23 August. This is 1 business day after the transaction date.

chunks.title: Deprivation and Child Support — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Deprivation and Child Support
From 1 July 2023, a client’s decision not to apply for Child Support or to revoke an existing Child Support arrangement is not considered deprivation of income when they are accessing financial assistance from MSD.
This applies to all types of Child Support arrangements, but does not apply for Unsupported Child’s Benefit carers.
When a client applies for one-off financial assistance, MSD can still consider the resources available to a client to meet the particular need. For example, a client may still be expected to ask the other parent of a child to help with a cost for the child where this is reasonable.
## Unsupported Child's Benefit carers
Unsupported Child's Benefit carers generally have an obligation to apply for Child Support in respect of the qualifying child.
MSD may still consider an Unsupported Child's Benefit carer has deprived themselves of income if they may be entitled to an excess payment of Child Support and are required to apply but choose not to.

chunks.title: Foreign Child Support payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Foreign Child Support payments
Foreign Child Support payments are similar to Child Support paid through Inland Revenue but are arranged through the government of another country. These payments are made directly to clients.
Foreign Child Support payments are considered a non-information share Child Support payment, as they are not included in the information share with Inland Revenue.
These Child Support payments are charged as income using the general charging rules.
Carers needs to declare these payments as income for benefit purposes.

chunks.title: Formula assessment excess (liability periods before 1 July 2023) — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Formula assessment excess (liability periods before 1 July 2023)
Before 1 July 2023, most sole parent carers and people applying for an Unsupported Child's Benefit were required to apply for a formula assessment of Child Support through Inland Revenue.
For these carers, Inland Revenue kept Child Support paid by the liable parent. This was used as a contribution to the cost of the receiving carer's benefit.
When the assessed amount of Child Support was more than the carer's benefit rate, Inland Revenue paid the difference to the receiving carer. This is called a formula assessment excess payment.
The excess was not charged as income against the receiving carer's main benefit.
The excess was only chargeable income for:
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit
- Childcare Assistance
## Formula assessments excess paid from 1 July 2023 (for periods before 1 July 2023)
From 1 July 2023 a client may get a formula assessment excess payment for a liability period before 1 July 2023.
Inland Revenue will continue to keep the amount of Child Support up to the carer's benefit rate for the period the payment covers.
These payments are charged as income using the general charging rules that were in place before 1 July 2023.
Any excess paid to the receiving carer is only chargeable income for Temporary Additional Support, Special Benefit and Childcare Assistance.
## Examples
Before 1 July 2023
Enzo is getting Sole Parent Support. He has a formula assessment of Child Support with the mother of his child Sofia. Sofia pays Inland Revenue $2500 a month of formula-assessed Child Support.
Inland Revenue keeps most of the Child Support payment Sofia pays to help cover the cost of Enzo's benefit. Enzo only gets $300 formula assessment Child Support excess each month.
This excess payment is not charged as income against his Sole Parent Support.
After 1 July 2023
From 1 July 2023, Enzo's Child Support payments are passed on to him by Inland Revenue. However, overdue Child Support paid for a period before 1 July 2023 is still kept.
Sofia was late in paying her May and June 2023 Child Support to Inland Revenue and makes a payment of $5000 in August 2023.
As this relates to a period before 1 July 2023, Inland Revenue keeps most of the payment. Enzo only gets $600 formula assessment Child Support. This excess payment is not charged as income against his main benefit.

chunks.title: Sole parent and Unsupported Child's Benefit carers before 1 July 2023 — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Before 1 July 2023, most sole parent carers and people applying for an Unsupported Child's Benefit were required to apply for a formula assessment of Child Support through Inland Revenue. For these carers, Inland Revenue kept the formula-assessed Child Support payments up to the amount of their benefit rate. Any payment over the benefit rate (excess) was paid directly to the client.

chunks.title: Other carers before 1 July 2023 — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Carers getting a couple's or single rate of benefit, or non-beneficiary clients, could also have a formula assessment of Child Support before 1 July 2023. For these receiving carers, Inland Revenue paid the entire amount of Child Support to them. These payments were chargeable income for all income-tested assistance.

chunks.title: Formula assessments paid from 1 July (for periods before 1 July 2023) — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: From 1 July 2023, a client may get or continue to get a formula assessment payment for a Child Support liability period before 1 July 2023. These payments are charged as income using the general charging rules in place before 1 July 2023. This means formula assessment payments are chargeable income for all income-tested assistance. Note Inland Revenue will still keep Child Support paid for a period before 1 July 2023, for carers who were required to apply before 1 July 2023.

chunks.title: Example — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Before 1 July Tiana gets Accommodation Supplement as a non-beneficiary. She has a formula assessment for Child Support with her ex-partner Naveen. Naveen pays $850 a month of Child Support to Inland Revenue, who pays this to Tiana. Tiana declares her Child Support payments as income. This is charged as income against her Accommodation Supplement. After 1 July 2023 Naveen was late in paying Child Support to Inland Revenue for June 2023. Naveen pays this amount, as well as the July amount, in August. Tiana gets the $1700 payment on 22 August. As $850 of this payment relates to a period before 1 July 2023, Tiana needs to declare this. This amount is charged as income for the period it relates to. This means Tiana may have a debt if she was overpaid in June. The other $850 amount relates to a period after 1 July 2023, so it comes through the information share. This is charged as an information share Child Support payment.

chunks.title: Income charging for fortnightly pay periods — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Income charging for fortnightly pay periods
Information share Child Support payments are always charged as income for 4 weeks for clients with fortnightly pay periods e.g. New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension clients.
Income charges for these payments are generally automated. This means income is charged automatically, generally with no involvement from staff.
## Fortnightly pay periods
Clients getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension are paid fortnightly.
If a New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client is also getting extra help, such as Accommodation Supplement, this is paid at the same time as their benefit.
Clients with a fortnightly pay period are paid 2 weeks in arrears. Income is charged from a Wednesday to the Tuesday 2 weeks later.
## Starting income charges for fortnightly pay periods
The first day of the income charge for an information share Child Support payment is the first available date which will not create a debt for the client. For clients on a fortnightly pay period this depends on when a payment is received in their bank account.
For these types of payments the first available date is:
- the Wednesday on or before the deemed receipt, if this is in the first week of the pay cycle or
- the Wednesday immediately after the deemed receipt if this is in the second week of the pay cycle
## Ending income charges for fortnightly pay periods
For clients with a fortnightly pay period, all income charges for information share Child Support payments end on the Tuesday 4 weeks after the start of the charge. This applies to both in-cycle and out-of-cycle payments. This means all income charges end after 4 weeks, or 2 benefit pay periods.
Example 1
Dolores gets New Zealand Superannuation and Temporary Additional Support. These are paid to her every fortnight.
She gets her next benefit payment on Tuesday 21 November.
On Friday 24 November, Dolores gets an information share Child Support payment. As this is the first week of her fortnightly pay period, the income charge starts on Wednesday 22 November.
The income charge lasts for 4 weeks in total, and her Temporary Additional Support is reduced from Wednesday 22 November until Tuesday 19 December.
Dolores gets her next in-cycle payment of Child Support on Friday 22 December. The income charge starts from Wednesday 20 December. The income charge lasts 4 weeks and ends on Tuesday 16 January.

chunks.title: Income charging for weekly pay periods — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Information share Child Support payments are charged as income for 4 or 5 weeks for clients with weekly pay periods, depending on the calendar month. Income for these payments is generally charged automatically, with no involvement from staff.

chunks.title: Weekly pay periods — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Main benefits are paid weekly. If a client getting a main benefit is also getting extra help, such as Accommodation Supplement, this is paid at the same time as their benefit. Clients who only get extra help are paid weekly. Clients with a weekly pay period are paid 1 week in arrears. Income is charged from a Monday to the following Sunday.

chunks.title: Starting income charges for weekly pay periods — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: The first day of the income charge for an information share Child Support payment is the start of the pay period the deemed receipt falls in. For clients on a weekly pay period, this is the Monday of the week the client got the payment in their bank account. Example Ramesh gets Sole Parent Support paid to him weekly on a Tuesday. His ex-partner Amelia pays him $800 of Child Support each month through Inland Revenue. On Wednesday, Ramesh gets an information share Child Support payment. The deemed receipt is the next business day (Thursday). The income charge starts on the Monday of that week. However, as Ramesh's Sole Parent Support is paid a week in arrears, income from this week affects his benefit payment next week.

chunks.title: Ending income charges for weekly pay periods — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: The last day of the income charge for an information share Child Support payment depends on whether the payment is in-cycle or out-of-cycle. For in-cycle payments, the last day of the income charge is the Sunday before the expected date of the next in-cycle payment. For out-of-cycle payments, the last day of the income charge is the Sunday before the same date as the deemed receipt in the next month. When the same date as the deemed receipt does not exist in the next month, the corresponding date is the 1st of the following month. For example, when the deemed receipt is 31 January there is no 31 February, so the corresponding date is 1 March. In this situation, the income charge would end on the Sunday before 1 March. This means an income charge may be 4 or 5 weeks depending on how many weeks there are between the start date and end date of the income charge. Example 1 Miri gets an in-cycle information share Child Support payment on 22 September. The income charge starts on the Monday of that week (Monday 18 September). The last day of the income charge is Sunday 22 October, which is the Sunday immediately before 24 October. 24 October is the expected date of the next in-cycle payment. Miri is deemed to have received another in-cycle information share Child Support payment on 24 October, and the next income charge starts on the Monday of that week (23 October). The income charge lasted for 5 weeks, as there are 5 weeks between 18 September and 22 October. Example 2 Solomon gets an out-of-cycle payment on 9 February. The income charge for the out-of-cycle payment starts on the Monday of that week (5 February). The last day of the income charge is the Sunday before 9 March (3 March). However, Solomon also gets an in-cycle payment on 22 February. The income charge for the in-cycle payment starts on the Monday of that week (19 February). The last day of the income charge is the Sunday before the expected date of the next in-cycle payment. The next payment is expected on 22 March, so the charge ends on Sunday 17 March. Both income charges last for 4 weeks, as there are 4 weeks between the deemed receipt dates in February and the end of the charges in March.

chunks.title: Income exemption when transferring between benefits — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Income exemption when transferring between benefits
When a client transfers between benefits, any remaining income charge from an information share Child Support payment is added from the commencement date of the new benefit.
Sometimes these payments cannot be charged as income correctly i.e. from the beginning of the pay period. This happens when a client gets an information share Child Support payment shortly after transferring between benefits on different pay periods and the beginning of the income charge is meant to start before the commencement date of their new benefit.
In this situation, the whole information share Child Support payment is exempt as income because it is unable to be charged correctly following the defined rules.
For an information share Child Support payment to be exempt as income in this situation it must meet all of the following:
- the client transfers from a weekly benefit to a fortnightly benefit or vice versa and
- the deemed receipt for the information share Child Support payment is on or after the commencement date of the new benefit and
- the income charge is calculated to start before the commencement of the new benefit
Example 1
Francois is getting Accommodation Supplement and is the receiving carer for his granddaughter, Irina. Francois has a voluntary agreement of Child Support through Inland Revenue and Irina's parents pay Francois $200 Child Support a month.
On Monday 30 October, Francois applies for New Zealand Superannuation as he is turning 65 the following week. His New Zealand Superannuation starts on Friday 10 November, which is part way through week 1 of the new fortnightly pay period. His Accommodation Supplement is now paid with his New Zealand Superannuation fortnightly.
On Monday 13 November, Francois gets an out-of-cycle payment of $400 Child Support from Irina's parents.
If Francois was on a fortnightly pay cycle for the whole period, the income charge would have started on Wednesday 8 November. However, this is before his new benefit commenced on the Friday.
The whole $400 payment is exempt as income, which means that none of this payment is charged as income against his Accommodation Supplement.
If Francois had transferred on or before Wednesday 8 November, or if the information share Child Support payment was received in or after week 2 of the new pay period, the payment would be considered income as the normal information share Child Support charging rules could be applied.

chunks.title: Information share Child Support payment received before transfer date — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Information share Child Support payment received before transfer date
When a client transfers to a new benefit type, the income charge is calculated based on the benefit type the client was entitled to when they got the information share Child Support payment.
When the start of the income charge is later than the date the client transfers to the new benefit type, the charge is calculated based on the new benefit type.
If a client's new benefit is backdated and the client transfers from a date before the start of the income charge, the income charge is recalculated against the new benefit.
Example 1
Quinn is included in their partner's New Zealand Superannuation as a non-qualified partner. Quinn gets an information share Child Support payment on 2 June. This is charged as income for 4 weeks against their payments starting on Wednesday 7 June.
Quinn separates from their partner on 15 June and transfers to Supported Living Payment from the next day (16 June).
The remaining Child Support income charge needs to be carried across and completed against Quinn's Supported Living Payment.
As the income charge started before Quinn transferred to the Supported Living Payment benefit, the original 4-week calculation still applies. The remaining income charge follows the transfer rules that apply to information share Child Support payments when moving from a fortnightly to weekly pay period.
Example 2
Rosie gets Accommodation Supplement as a non-beneficiary and gets an information share Child Support payment on Friday 22 September. This is charged against her weekly Accommodation Supplement payments for 5 weeks, starting on Monday 18 September to Sunday 22 October.
Rosie turns 65 on 19 September and qualifies for New Zealand Superannuation. The processing of her application was delayed, and Rosie is transferred to New Zealand Superannuation on 27 September. She continues to get Accommodation Supplement and is paid retrospectively for New Zealand Superannuation, from 19 September.
Rosie qualified for New Zealand Superannuation before getting the information share Child Support payment on 22 September. The income charge is removed from her previous non-beneficiary assistance and re-calculated against her New Zealand Superannuation for 4 weeks from 26 September which is the beginning of the nearest pay period.

chunks.title: Information share Child Support payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Information share Child Support payments
MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about most types of Child Support.
Inland Revenue tells MSD when they pay this Child Support to receiving carer's and MSD matches this information to clients.
MSD uses the information from Inland Revenue to automatically charge these Child Support payments as income in most situations. These are called information share Child Support payments.
An information share Child Support payment is money that:
- a person gets in their bank account and
- is a formula assessment or voluntary agreement of Child Support collected and paid via Inland Revenue and
- relates to a Child Support liability period on or after 1 July 2023 and
- is notified to MSD through the information share with Inland Revenue
## Charging information share Child Support payments as income
Information share Child Support payments are charged forward as income, using defined rules. The income charging is generally automated.
The income charge for an information share Child Support payment is for 4 or 5 weeks for clients on a weekly pay period. Whether the charge is 4 or 5 weeks depends on the calendar month.
The income charge for an information share Child Support payment is always 4 weeks for clients paid fortnightly.
The automated rules for information share Child Support payments do not apply to non-information share Child Support payments or any social housing-related product.

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Child Support is money paid by parents who do not live with their children, or who share care with someone else. These payments are to help with the cost of raising a child.
There are 2 main ways that Child Support is arranged and paid in New Zealand. This can be:
- via Inland Revenue or
- through a private arrangement
## Child Support Income
MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about Child Support payments.
MSD uses the information to automatically treat these payments as income in most situations. These payments are called information share Child Support payments.
The information share with Inland Revenue does not include all Child Support payments made.
Clients still need to declare other types of Child Support payments they get, such as private arrangements. These are called non-information share Child Support payments. MSD must charge these payments as income for the period it is earned or relates to.
Note if the payment does not represent a specific period or if MSD cannot determine the actual period it represents, MSD must determine the most appropriate period to charge the income. This may be the week in which it is received, provided or supplied.
Generally, all Child Support payments a client gets are considered income for the receiving carer. The Child Support income is treated differently depending on whether the payment is an information share Child Support payment or a non-information share Child Support payment.

chunks.title: Manual income charging rules — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Manual income charging rules
When a client declares their Child Support payments to MSD, staff must determine if non-information share Child Support payments are income or a capital payment.
Generally, non-information share Child Support payments are charged as income using the general charging rules on the basis the payment is for an income-related purpose.
If the payment is income, MSD must charge the income for the period it was earned or relates to.
This is different to information share Child Support payments. Those payments are automatically charged forward as income using defined rules.
## Charging income for the period it relates to
A client's income must be charged over the period it is earned or relates to. This could be a period in the past or may be for a future date.
For example, a client may get a late payment of Child Support that relates to a period 6 months ago. In this situation, the payment would be charged as income for the same period in the past.
A client could also get a payment intended to support their child for the next month. This would be charged as income over the next month.
For clients who have an annual review of income, income should generally be charged forward for the appropriate length of time. This avoids creating debt for clients where possible.
If the Child Support income does not represent a specific period or if MSD cannot determine the actual period it represents, MSD must determine the most appropriate period to charge the income. This may be the week in which it is received, provided or supplied.

chunks.title: Mixed Child Support payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: A receiving carer may get Child Support for a child who they are getting Unsupported Child's Benefit for. They may also get Child Support for another child in their care who they are not getting Unsupported Child's Benefit for. In some situations, both types of Child Support may be paid by the same liable parent. If the amount of Child Support for the Unsupported Child's Benefit child is more than the benefit rate, the carer is entitled to the excess amount of Child Support for that child. This is in addition to the full amount of Child Support payable for the other child. In this case, Inland Revenue pay any Child Support to the receiving carer as one payment. This is called a mixed Child Support payment. Mixed Child Support payments are considered a non-information share Child Support payment. These payments are not included in the information share with Inland Revenue. These Child Support payments are charged as income using the general charging rules. Carers may need to declare these payments as income for benefit purposes. This means mixed Child Support payments must be charged over the period it is earned or relates to. If the payment does not represent a specific period or if MSD cannot determine the actual period it represents, MSD must determine the most appropriate period to charge the income. This may be the week in which it is received, provided or supplied.

chunks.title: Income charging for mixed Child Support payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: These payments are treated the same as formula agreement excess payments. This means mixed Child Support payments are only charged as income for: - Temporary Additional Support - Special Benefit - Childcare Assistance

chunks.title: Example — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Lionel and Prudence were in a relationship and had a child together, Stanley. Lionel also had a child from a previous relationship, Grace, who does not live with them. Lionel and Prudence separate in January, and Prudence has full-time care of Stanley. In June, Prudence also starts caring for Lionel's other child, Grace. Grace had been living with Lionel's sister following a relationship breakdown with Grace's parents. Prudence gets Sole Parent Support, Accommodation Supplement, and Temporary Additional Support and has Stanley included in her benefit. From June, Prudence also gets Unsupported Child's Benefit for Grace. Lionel and Prudence have a formula assessment of Child Support through Inland Revenue for both children. Lionel is liable to pay Child Support for both children. Prudence gets the full amount of Child Support for Stanley. She is also entitled to excess payments for Grace. The Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payment, and the Child Support paid in relation to Stanley are passed on to Prudence from Inland Revenue. Prudence gets this as one payment in her bank account. Prudence declares this Child Support income. The whole payment is treated as an Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payment. This is only considered income for her Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Non-information share Child Support payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Non-information share Child Support payments
Any Child Support payments not included in the information share between MSD and Inland Revenue are non-information share Child Support payments.
These include:
- a Child Support payment relating to a liability period before 1 July 2023 or
- a private arrangement of Child Support or
- a foreign Child Support payment or
- a court ordered lump sum payment or
- an excess payment of Child Support, including mixed Child Support payments made to an Unsupported Child's Benefit carer or
- a Child Support payment made to a client living overseas and getting a benefit under a Reciprocal Agreement
Clients must declare all non-information share Child Support payments they get. These payments are chargeable income for most types of income-tested assistance.
## Charging non-information share Child Support payments as income
Non-information share Child Support payments are charged as income using the general charging rules. These income charges are not automated.

chunks.title: Payment cycle — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Inland Revenue assess Child Support as an annual amount. The total amount for the year is then divided by 12 to work out how much the liable parent has to pay each calendar month. Payments are due from the liable parent on the 20th of each month. Each payment represents the amount owed for the previous month. For example, the payment due in August is the Child Support for July.

chunks.title: Regular or in-cycle Child Support payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Regular or in-cycle payments are Child Support that is paid on time. This is the amount the liable parent owed for the calendar month immediately before the due date. When the liable parent pays Child Support on time, Inland Revenue pays the money to the receiving carer on the first business day after the due date. This means Inland Revenue pay all in-cycle payments to the receiving carer 2 business days after the 19th of each month. This allows for weekends and public holidays. For example, if the 20th of the month is not on a weekday (e.g. a Sunday), then payments will be made to banks on the Tuesday to allow time for the liable parent's payments to be processed. Tuesday (the 22nd of the month in this example) is 2 business days after the 19th of the month. If the 20th of the month is a weekday, e.g., a Wednesday, payments will be due on that day. Inland Revenue send payments to banks on the business day after the due date, which is Thursday. In this example, Thursday is the 21st of the month and is 2 business days after the 19th.

chunks.title: Late or out-of-cycle Child Support payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Late or out-of-cycle payments are Child Support that is paid late. This happens when the liable parent pays Child Support after the due date. In this situation, Inland Revenue pays the receiving carer as soon as the payment is made to Inland Revenue. Out-of-cycle payments can be paid on any business day of the month and can represent any length of time. They are sometimes called arrears payments of Child Support. Example Mariana is entitled to $80 of Child Support each month from the liable parent, Garth. Garth pays when he can, but Mariana hasn't got any Child Support since January. On 10 June, Garth pays $320 to Inland Revenue. This is the Child Support he owes for the previous 4 months. Inland Revenue pays the $320 to Mariana on 10 June. This is an out-of-cycle payment as it is Child Support that was due on 20 February, 20 March, 20 April, and 20 May.

chunks.title: Payment stacking — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Payment stacking
Inland Revenue pay in-cycle payments at the same time each month. Out-of-cycle payments can be made at any time.
If a client gets an out-of-cycle payment soon after an in-cycle payment, or vice versa, a client may have multiple Child Support payments stacked on top of each other. This means the income charges may overlap.
Example
Reiko gets Sole Parent Support and has primary care of his son Elijah. Reiko also gets Child Support from Elijah's mother Shannon. Shannon pays last month's Child Support late, and Reiko gets this out-of-cycle payment on 9 February.
The income charge starts on the Monday of that week (5 February). The last day of the income charge is the Sunday before the 9th of the following month (3 March).
Shannon pays the Child Support payment due in February on time. Reiko gets this as an in-cycle payment on 22 February.
The income charge for the in-cycle payment starts on the Monday of that week (19 February). The last day of the income charge is the Sunday before the 22nd of the following month (17 March).
As Reiko gets 2 Child Support payments within the same month, the Child Support income charges are stacked on top of each other between 19 February and 3 March. This means that Reiko has a higher Child Support income charge in those weeks.

chunks.title: Private arrangements — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Private arrangements
When a client is getting payments from the paying parent as an informal arrangement, this is known as a private arrangement of Child Support.
A private arrangement is considered a non-information share Child Support payment. These payments are not included in the information share with Inland Revenue.
These Child Support payments are charged as income using the general charging rules.
This means the Child Support payment must be charged over the period it is earned or relates to.
If the payment does not represent a specific period or if MSD cannot determine the actual period it represents, MSD must determine the most appropriate period to charge the income. This may be the week in which it is received, provided or supplied.
## Types of private arrangement
Most private arrangements will be cash payments.
Clients may also get other types of private Child Support such as:
- payment for specific goods and services
- in-kind payments (goods or services provided as payment instead of cash)
- one-off payments
Examples of a private arrangement that is not a cash payment include (but are not limited to) the paying parent:
- buying groceries for the carer and their household
- covering the cost of the carer's monthly phone bill
- paying the child's school fees instead of transferring money to the carer's bank account to pay for them
When a client gets regular Child Support through a private arrangement that is intended for an income-related purpose this is chargeable income.
Carers need to declare these payments as income for benefit purposes.
## One-off payments
When a client gets a payment for a one-off item that they do not get on a regular basis, these payments are treated as a capital payment and are not chargeable income.
This includes payments that are no more than once a year, such as annual school fees.
## Loan or hire purchase payments
Any personal loan or hire purchase payments the paying parent makes on behalf of the carer are not charged as income provided the agreements started before the marriage breakdown or separation.
If the agreement started after the separation, any payments made by the paying parent are charged as income.

chunks.title: Transferring between weekly benefits — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: For weekly benefits, an information share Child Support payment is charged as income for 4 or 5 weeks. When a client on a weekly pay period transfers to, or starts getting, a new weekly benefit type, the balance of any income charges continues against the new benefit from the date of transfer. Example Mary is getting Jobseeker Support. They get an $800 information share Child Support payment on 5 August. The income is charged for 4 weeks. The charge starts from Monday 2 August. The income is charged as $200 per week for 4 weeks until 29 August. Mary gives birth to another child on 18 August. Mary now qualifies for Sole Parent Support from 18 August. Mary is transferred to Sole Parent Support and the income charge continues at $200 per week against their Sole Parent Support entitlement until 29 August (the end of the 4-week charging period).

chunks.title: Relationship changes while getting Child Support — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: A client who has an information share Child Support payment charged as income, and who has a change in relationship status, is treated the same as a client transferring between weekly benefit types. Any Child Support income charge follows the receiving carer and the combined income charge ends for the other client. The Child Support income only impacts the assistance of the partner when the couple is on joint income-tested assistance. Example 1 Hemi gets Sole Parent Support and is paid $500 Child Support monthly from his ex-partner. This is through a formula assessment with Inland Revenue. Hemi gets an information share Child Support payment on 5 July and the income is charged as $100 per week for 5 weeks, starting on Monday 1 July. The income charge will end on Sunday 4 August. On 15 July, Hemi advises he is now in a relationship with Sally, who currently gets Jobseeker Support as a single person. Hemi and Sally are transferred to a joint Jobseeker Support benefit from 15 July. The remaining Child Support income charge continues at $100 per week on their newly joint entitlement. Example 2 Priyanka and Raj get a joint Jobseeker Support benefit with Priyanka's child included. Priyanka gets $400 Child Support each month from her ex-partner. This is through a formula assessment with Inland Revenue. Priyanka gets an information share Child Support payment on 9 October. This income charge is calculated as $100 per week over a 4-week period, starting on Monday 7 October. On 15 October, Priyanka and Raj decide to separate and apply for their own benefits. Priyanka is granted Sole Parent Support from Wednesday 16 October. The remainder of her Child Support income charge continues at $100 per week until Sunday 3 November. Raj is granted Jobseeker Support as a single person from 16 October. The income charge does not apply to him from this date as he is no longer in a relationship with Priyanka

chunks.title: Transferring from a fortnightly to weekly benefit — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Transferring from a fortnightly to weekly benefit
Clients getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension payments before 9 November 2020 could include their non-qualified partner in their payments. In these cases, their joint entitlement is income-tested.
Grandparented non-qualified partners are the only clients that may transfer from a fortnightly benefit to a weekly benefit while getting information share Child Support payments.
Weekly and fortnightly pay periods start and end on different days.
When a client getting a fortnightly benefit is transferring to a weekly benefit, it is not possible to continue charging the information share Child Support income using the fortnightly income charging rules. The income charged fortnightly needs to be recalculated as a weekly amount.
The full amount of an information share Child Support payment must be charged as income when a client transfers between benefits. To charge the full amount, the income charge continues at the original rate until the Monday before it was due to end.
Any remaining income charge is then calculated as a weekly amount and charged against the new weekly benefit for one week only.
Example
Hilary is included in her partner's New Zealand Superannuation as a grandparented non-qualified partner. She gets an information share Child Support payment of $280. The charge is calculated as $70 per week for 4 weeks. At some point during those 4 weeks, Hilary's partner decides to exclude her from their New Zealand Superannuation. Hilary transfers to a weekly benefit and the existing charge is carried across at the already-calculated rate of $70 per week.
If Hilary was still a grandparented non-qualified partner, the income charge would finish on a Tuesday.
However, Hilary is now on a weekly benefit, and the income charging period ends on a Sunday. This means the income charge has only been applied for 3 weeks and 5 days, and there are 2 days of income left to charge.
The remaining amount of the income charge is calculated at a pro-rata rate of $20 for Monday and Tuesday. The remaining $20 amount is charged as a final weekly amount from the beginning of the next pay period, which is the Monday.

chunks.title: Transferring from a weekly to fortnightly benefit — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Clients getting a weekly benefit may have an information share Child Support payment charged as income against their benefit. If they transfer to a fortnightly benefit, the income charge needs to be completed against their new benefit. Weekly and fortnightly pay periods start and end on different days. This means the income charge must be shortened or extended to fit with the new fortnightly pay period. This is a discretionary decision. The full amount of an information share Child Support payment must be charged as income when a client transfers between benefits. The end of the income charge should also stay as close as possible to the original end date of the charge on the client's weekly benefit. When deciding whether to shorten or extend an income charge, you should consider what is in the best interests of the client. For example: - if the client is likely to get another information share Child Support payment soon (i.e. taking into account payment stacking) - if the client has other income (i.e. taking into account other income being charged over the same period) - the abatement impacts of either extending or shortening the balance of the income charge. Example 1 Jameson is getting Jobseeker Support and Accommodation Supplement, and gets a $400 information share Child Support payment on Wednesday 22 May. This is calculated over 4 weeks and is charged as income from Monday 20 May. On Tuesday 28 May (week 2 of the income charge), Jameson qualifies for New Zealand Superannuation and Accommodation Supplement. The income charge was meant to end on Sunday 16 June. This falls partway through his new fortnightly pay period, which means the balance of the charge needs to be shortened or extended to end on a Tuesday. The balance of the charge needs to be either: - shortened to finish on Tuesday 4 June (in the same New Zealand Superannuation pay period as the effective date of the transfer) or - extended to finish on Tuesday 18 June (in the next pay period). As the Tuesday 18 June is only 2 days after the original end date, extending the charge is the best option for Jameson. The income charge lasts for 4 weeks and 2 days in total. Example 2 Cora is getting Sole Parent Support and Accommodation Supplement, and gets a $500 information share Child Support payment. This is charged as income over a 5-week period from Monday 11 September to Sunday 15 October.

chunks.title: Transferring from a weekly to fortnightly benefit — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: On Tuesday 3 October (week 4 of the income charge) Cora qualifies for New Zealand Superannuation and Accommodation Supplement. The balance of the charge needs to be either: - shortened to finish on Tuesday 10 October (in the same New Zealand Superannuation pay period as the effective date of the transfer) or - extended to finish on Tuesday 24 October (in the next pay period) If the income charge were to be extended, it would last for 6 weeks and 2 days. This is much longer than the original 5-week period. With this option, it is likely there would be payment stacking of Child Support if Cora gets another information share Child Support payment while the income from the previous payment is still being charged. The best option for Cora is to shorten the income charge and end it on Tuesday 10 October. The income charge lasts for 4 weeks and 2 days in total.

chunks.title: Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: Unsupported Child's Benefit carers must apply for a formula assessment of Child Support. This rule applies unless they have a voluntary agreement in place before applying for Unsupported Child's Benefit. For these carers, Inland Revenue keeps Child Support paid by liable parents to help pay for the Unsupported Child's Benefit received by the child's carer. When the amount of Child Support paid is more than the rate of Unsupported Child's Benefit, Inland Revenue pay the difference to the receiving carer.
