This is called an Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payment. Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payments are considered a non-information share Child Support payment. These payments are not included in the information share with Inland Revenue. Carers may need to declare these payments as income for benefit purposes. These Child Support payments are charged as income using the general charging rules. This means the Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payment must be charged over the period it is earned or relates to. If the payment does not represent a specific period or if MSD cannot determine the actual period it represents, MSD must determine the most appropriate period to charge the income. This may be the week in which it is received, provided or supplied.

chunks.title: Income charging for Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payments — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: There are 2 types of Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payments: - formula assessment excess (the most common type) - voluntary agreement excess If the formula assessment is higher than the benefit rate, Inland Revenue pays the difference to the receiving carer. This is called a formula assessment excess payment and is only charged as income for Temporary Additional Support, Special Benefit and Childcare Assistance. It is not chargeable income for main benefits. If the formula assessment is lower than the voluntary agreement amount, Inland Revenue can only keep the amount of the formula assessment. The rest is paid to the receiving carer. This is called a voluntary agreement excess payment and is chargeable income for all income-tested assistance. Note in rare cases a receiving carer may get an excess payment and another type of Inland Revenue Child Support payment from the same liable parent. This is called a mixed Child Support payment, which is treated the same way as a formula assessment excess payment.

chunks.title: Assessing Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payments for the initial income stand-down — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text: All types of Child Support are considered income for the purposes of an initial income stand-down. This includes all Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payments.

chunks.title: Voluntary agreement excess (liability periods before 1 July 2023) — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Voluntary agreement excess (liability periods before 1 July 2023)
Before 1 July 2023, most sole parent carers and people getting an Unsupported Child's Benefit, who were able to have a voluntary agreement, would have the Child Support paid by the liable parent kept by Inland Revenue up to the formula-assessed amount.
When the voluntary agreement amount of Child Support was more than formula assessment, Inland Revenue paid the difference to the carer. This is called a voluntary agreement excess payment.
These excess payments were chargeable income for all income-tested assistance, including main benefits.
## Voluntary agreement excess paid from 1 July (for periods before 1 July 2023)
From 1 July 2023, a client may get a voluntary agreement excess payment for a liability period before 1 July 2023.
Inland Revenue will continue to keep the amount of Child Support up to the carer's benefit rate for the period the payment covers.
These payments are charged as income using the general charging rules that were in place before 1 July 2023.
Any excess paid to the receiving carer is chargeable income for all income-tested assistance.
## Example
Before 1 July 2023
Reema gets Sole Parent Support and Child Support for her child, paid by her ex-partner Josiah. They have a voluntary agreement through Inland Revenue of $200 per month.
Under a formula assessment, Josiah would only have to pay $100 per month. Because they have a voluntary agreement to pay $200 per month, Inland Revenue keeps $100 of Reema's Child Support payments.
This means Reema gets $100 per month as a voluntary agreement excess Child Support payment.
From 1 July 2023
Josiah is behind on paying Child Support, and in August 2023 Reema gets a $100 payment for the liability period in June 2023.
The same income charging rules apply to Reema's voluntary agreement excess payments before 1 July 2023 as they do after 1 July 2023.
This means the payment is still charged as income against her Sole Parent Support.

chunks.title: Sole parent and Unsupported Child's Benefit carers before 1 July 2023 — core policy > income > types of income > child support income
chunks.text:
## Sole parent and Unsupported Child's Benefit carers before 1 July 2023
Before 1 July 2023, most sole parent carers and people applying for an Unsupported Child's Benefit could only have a voluntary agreement of Child Support through Inland Revenue in certain situations.
This happened when:
- they already had a voluntary agreement in place before applying for their benefit and
- the amount of the voluntary agreement was equal to or more than the formula assessment amount
For these carers, Inland Revenue kept voluntary agreement Child Support payments up to the amount of their formula assessment.
## Other carers before 1 July 2023
Carers getting a couple's or single rate of benefit, or non-beneficiary clients, could also have a voluntary agreement before 1 July 2023.
For these receiving carers, Inland Revenue paid the entire amount of Child Support to them. These payments were chargeable income for all income-tested assistance.
## Voluntary agreements paid from 1 July (for periods before 1 July 2023)
From 1 July 2023, a client may get a voluntary agreement payment for a Child Support liability period before 1 July 2023.
These payments are charged as income using the general charging rules that were in place before 1 July 2023.
This means voluntary agreement payments are chargeable income for all income-tested assistance.
Note Inland Revenue will still keep voluntary agreement Child Support paid for a period before 1 July 2023 for sole parent carers and people getting Unsupported Child's Benefit.
## Example
Before 1 July
Nadine and their partner are getting Jobseeker Support. Nadine has a voluntary agreement for Child Support with their ex-partner Taylor. Taylor pays $3000 a month of voluntary agreement Child Support to Nadine.
Nadine gets $3000 Child Support each month. This payment is charged as income against Nadine and their partner's benefit and their benefit payments are reduced.
After 1 July 2023
Taylor was late in paying Child Support to Inland Revenue for May and June 2023. Taylor makes a $6000 payment in September 2023.
As this relates to a period before 1 July 2023, the payment is charged as income for the period it relates to. This means Nadine and their partner may have a debt if they were overpaid in May and June.

chunks.title: Childs income from estates — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Childs income from estates
A will may state that the income of a child's share of the estate should be used for the child's maintenance. The trustee of the estate trust will organise this.
Any income paid each year for a child's maintenance, education or advancement must be taken into account when assessing the rate of Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit.
Note any income paid for a child is not taken into account for any benefit or extra help assistance, other than Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit.
For more information see:
- Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit Childs income
- Estate income and wills

chunks.title: Christchurch mosques attack support payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: People affected by the mosque attacks in Christchurch on 15 March 2019, may receive financial donations. These payments are not treated as income or cash assets.

chunks.title: Identifying Christchurch mosques attack support payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Donations may come from a range of sources and through a range of fundraising methods including (but not limited to): - organisations such as Victim Support, New Zealand Islamic Information Centre, Canterbury Muslim Community Trust, Our People, Our City: The Christchurch Foundation - donations made through crowdfunding websites such as www.givealittle.co.nz which may be collected for groups or individuals - businesses - employers - individuals - overseas governments Payments may come to an affected person through an organised fundraising source, or may be paid directly to the affected person by the donor. Generally a person can identify if they have received one of these payments and will have information to support this.

chunks.title: Income and cash asset exemption — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Christchurch mosques attack support payments are not considered as chargeable income or cash assets for the person who received the payment. This includes any income earned from investment of the payment. There is no time limit on this exemption. Note employment related income payments from an employer are not covered by this exemption. For more information see: - Employment related income If you are unsure whether a donation payment can be exempt please contact Helpline before taking any action.

chunks.title: Changes in the client's cash asset levels — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: An exemption for a Christchurch mosques attack support payment must be equal to the payment the client received, or the amount they have left when they declare the payment to us. Clients are not expected to keep track of any changes to the value of the payment. The exemption amount will stay the same indefinitely, unless the client's total cash reduces below the exemption amount. When this happens, the exemption must be updated to match the client's new level of cash. The exemption must be removed if we identify the client has no cash. The exemption will only increase or be applied again if the client gets another exempt payment. Note for this exemption, cash means physical cash and money in the bank (including savings and term deposit accounts). It does not include anything purchased with the payment, such as shares. Example Fatima receives a Christchurch mosques attack support payment of $20,000 which is exempt from income and cash asset testing. 6 months later at her annual review, Fatima lets us know that her total cash has reduced to $10,000. Her exemption is updated to $10,000. A few months later Fatima applies for Accommodation Supplement and shows us her cash has increased by $5,000 because she got an ACC Survivor's Grant. This payment is not exempt from income and cash asset testing, and Fatima's exemption remains at $10,000.

chunks.title: Client receives additional exempt payment — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: A client may get more than one Christchurch mosques attack support payment. In this case the exemption will be equal to the amount of the new payment (or the amount they have left when they tell us) plus the remaining amount of the previous payment. To identify how much the client has left of the previous payment, check the amount of cash the client had when they received the new payment. Example Khaled received a $5,000 Christchurch mosques attack support payment which is exempt from income and cash asset testing. He already has an exemption of $12,000 for a payment he got last year. We check Khaled's cash at the time he received the new payment and he had $9,500. Khaled will now have a combined exemption of $14,500.

chunks.title: Client earns income from exempt and non-exempt assets — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When a client is earning income on both exempt and non-exempt assets, the earnings from the exempt assets must be excluded from the client's income. To do this, subtract the exempt amount from the total assets that are generating income. You can then multiply the remaining amount by the interest rate being earned. If the interest rate is unknown, use the Reserve Bank 6-month Term Deposit rate. Example Imran has $20,000 invested in a term deposit which earns interest of 3.29% per annum. $15,000 of this is from a Christchurch mosques attack support payment he received last year and is exempt from income and cash asset testing. The remainder is from savings and isn't exempt. Imran's income from assets will be calculated using the 3.29% interest rate as follows: Income-earning assets less exempt assets$20,000 - $15,000 = $5,000 Annual chargeable income$5,000 x 0.0329 = $164.50 Weekly chargeable income$164.50 / 52 = $3.16 Imran also earns $123.90 per week from wages, so he will have a total of $127.06 charged against his benefit as income each week.

chunks.title: Applications for hardship assistance payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When a client with an exemption applies for a hardship assistance payment, the exempt amount must be disregarded from the cash asset test. However, generally a client won't qualify if they have enough money available to meet their need. This is because clients must use their own resources before seeking hardship assistance. If the client only has enough money available to meet part of the cost, hardship assistance can be considered for the shortfall. In each case you must consider the individual circumstances of the client against the eligibility criteria. Example Karam has been suffering tooth pain and went to the dentist to get it checked. The dentist advised she will need emergency dental treatment that will cost $500. A few months ago, Karam got a Christchurch mosques attack support payment of $15,000 which is exempt from income and cash asset testing. After paying some bills, Karam still has $9,000 left. Karam remembers the Ministry helped with her dental bill a couple of years ago, so she applies for a Special Needs Grant to cover the cost of the emergency dental treatment. In this case, Karam won't qualify for a Special Needs Grant because she has enough money available to cover the cost of emergency dental treatment herself.

chunks.title: Client earns interest from exempt and non-exempt assets — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Client earns interest from exempt and non-exempt assets
When a client is earning interest on both exempt and non-exempt assets, the earnings from the exempt assets must be excluded from the client's income.
To do this, subtract the exempt amount from the total assets that are earning interest.
Then multiply the remainder by the interest rate being earned.
If the interest rate is unknown, use the Reserve Bank 6-month term deposit rate.

chunks.title: Client gets additional exempt payment — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Client gets additional exempt payment
A client may get more than one severe weather event payment. Each payment is exempt for 12 months from the date the client got it. This means some exemption periods will overlap.
When a client gets an additional severe weather event payment, check the value of their cash assets.
If their cash assets are the same or higher than the current exemption, the total exempt amount will be the value of the new payment plus the value of the current exemption.
If their cash assets are less than the current exemption, the total exempt amount will be the value of the new payment plus the value of their cash assets.
## Example
On 2 December 2023 Yaz got a donation of $6,000 from a Give a Little fundraiser which is exempt from income and cash asset testing.
They already had an exemption of $8,500 for an insurance payment they got on 10 November 2023. We check Yaz's cash assets at the time they got the new payment and they had $7,900.
From 2 December 2023, $13,900 is exempt ($7,900 plus $6,000). This reduces to $6,000 from 10 November 2024.

chunks.title: Clients waiting for compensation — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Clients waiting for compensation
A client may be able to get a specified benefit and/or Extra help while they are waiting for a decision on their ACC claim.
The specified benefit is granted on the condition that the specified benefit paid will be refunded out of the weekly compensation subsequently paid for the same period.
Where a client is receiving a specified benefit but not receiving Extra help, you should advise the client of the Extra help that is available to them.
In some situations a client may already be receiving a specified benefit at the time they make their ACC claim. The client should be advised that their benefit will be reassessed and the specified benefit will be reduced or stopped, in the event they receive weekly compensation that is paid for the same period as the specified benefit.
For information see:
- Backdated ACC weekly compensation payments
- Reimbursement requests from ACC reviews
- Effect on Extra help
- Weekly compensation payments started before 1 July 1999
- Weekly compensation backdated prior to 1 July 1999
- ACC weekly compensation
- Quick reference guide for the treatment of ACC payments

chunks.title: Clients who have not met their obligations with ACC — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Clients who have not met their obligations with ACC
When a client has not met their obligations with ACC, their weekly compensation may be stopped or not granted. The most common reason for this is where a client has unreasonably refused to comply with a rehabilitation programme.
You should discuss with the client why they have not met their obligations with ACC and why they are not receiving weekly compensation. This is to make sure they are able to comply and if there is anything we can do to help them for example with Extra help. They will need to discuss this with ACC to resolve any issues they have.
When a client is not receiving weekly compensation because they have not met their obligations with ACC, the weekly compensation a client would have been entitled to, is still treated as a direct deduction against the benefit.
For more information see:
- ACC weekly compensation
- Backdating benefit when weekly compensation is overpaid

chunks.title: Commission work — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Commission work
Clients with commission earnings are treated in a similar way to self-employed clients with business income. That is you need to look at their business accounts to determine the net income to be charged.
Some commission salespeople such as real estate agents may receive income from commission only, or, from commission and a retainer (like an ongoing wage). Some forms of commission work generate income on a regular cycle and others, like real estate agents, are irregular. Other types of commission work may be from part time self-employment such as selling Tupperware or Avon products.
If a client has just started commission work you need to discuss with the client what income/expenses that they may have, and whether or not there is a pattern of income already established.
Where possible clients should be encouraged to estimate their income and expenses for the particular commission work that they are involved in, this will enable estimated income to be charged and upon completion of the work the actual income verified and any adjustment on benefit made. This may need to be reviewed on a regular basis.
The client should provide financial statements prepared by an accountant. If the client has only been a commission worker for a short time the client may not have any business accounts. The client should have their own records from which financial statements would be prepared. It will then be necessary to decide the income using the information available.
For more information on charging income, see:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Compassionate grants — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Compassionate grants
A lump sum compassionate grant made by the government or any other person or organisation on the death of a spouse or partner is a capital payment and is not chargeable income for benefit purposes.
Any income received from the investment of the funds received from a compassionate grant is chargeable income.
Funds retained from a compassionate grant are considered as a cash asset and may affect entitlement to extra help such as Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, Special Needs Grants or Advances.
Where a client is not receiving income from a compassionate grant following the death of a spouse then these cases should be dealt with sensitively. It may take some time for a person to make adjustments and deprivation of income provisions will need to be explained to the client.
A client should be given time to invest any remaining funds depending on their circumstances.

chunks.title: Compensation or damages — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Compensation or damages
There may be two types of payments made where a person receives compensation or damages from any other person for wrongful or unjustified dismissal or due to a disability (caused by an accident or disease). These are:
## In lieu of wages
The payment of compensation or damages is paid in lieu of wages for a number of weeks. No benefit or a benefit at a reduced rate may be paid for the period the payment of compensation or damages represents.
For example a client receives compensation of $1600 for unjustified dismissal, their weekly wage was $400 per week. This compensation payment represents 4 weeks wages and must be taken into account when determining the benefit commencement date.
Note where a client receives the payment of compensation or damages in lieu of wages after the benefit has commenced, then the initial stand down and commencement date must be reassessed.
## Personal payment
A client may receive a one off personal payment for humiliation, loss of face, injury to feelings. Personal payment is not paid in lieu of wages.
Personal payment for humiliation, loss of face, injury to feelings, must be treated as a capital payment only and not income. It does not form part of the income received in the 26 or 52 weeks prior to commencement of benefit.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer
- Accident Compensation payments
For more information on charging income, see:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Continuing income from an estate — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Continuing income from an estate
When a client is entitled to continuing income from an estate, for example rent from a rental property, annuity, or income from a life interest or lease for life, the amount the client receives from this is chargeable income for benefit purposes.
Note if the client is entitled to income and chooses not to receive it deprivation should be considered.
If the client receives rental income from an estate or will, costs such as rates, insurance and other outgoings on that property are allowed as a deduction against the gross estate rental income received. The allowable costs on the rental property can be deducted if the client is liable for the costs. For more information on calculating rental income see: Rental property income
Note no income is charged when a client is living rent free as a result of a life interest in a property.
For more information see:
- Estate income and wills
- Capital payments
- Interim payments
- Childs income from estates
- Core policy Income related purpose
- Employment related income Goods, services, accommodation in lieu of money

chunks.title: Debt insurance — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Debt insurance
A client may have insurance to cover repaying existing debts such as mortgages, personal loans, hire purchase commitments and credit card debts.
Debt Insurance payments are not income for benefit purposes. These payments may reduce the allowable costs for Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit.
For more information see:
- Accommodation Supplement Home ownership
- Special Benefit Allowable costs
- Temporary Additional Support Allowable costs
- Insurance
- Mortgage protection insurance
- Loan protection insurance

chunks.title: Delayed redundancy payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Delayed redundancy payments
If the client has been granted a benefit and then receives a redundancy payment within 52 weeks after the date the client's employment ceased, the benefit stand-down and date employment ceased must be reassessed.
To review the initial stand-down:
- divide the redundancy payment by 26 weeks (and 52 weeks if the client's entitlement date to benefit is on or after 1 May 2005). Add the appropriate weekly redundancy amount to the client's average weekly income received before employment ceased.
- re-assess the length of the initial stand-down period to determine a new commencement date. (Remember to use the calculation that provides the client with the lesser stand-down period).
and
- establish an overpayment for any monies paid to the client prior to the reassessed commencement date
## Payments received more than 52 weeks after retirement
If the client receives a redundancy payment more than 52 weeks after the date the client's employment ceased, the payment is treated as a capital payment. The client's entitlement to any Extra Help must also be reassessed.

chunks.title: Disability Support payments paid directly by or on behalf of the Crown — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Disability Support payments paid directly by or on behalf of the Crown
Disability Support payments are paid directly:
- by or on behalf of the crown
- to a person or: their dependent childa dependent who is not their dependent child but has an illness, sickness, injury or disabilityand the person has the responsibility for their care
- their dependent child
- a dependent who is not their dependent child but has an illness, sickness, injury or disability
- and the person has the responsibility for their care
- for the purpose of purchasing or obtaining disability support services
These payments are made as part of:
- the Waikato Enabling Good Lives demonstration
- the Mid Central Health prototype and
- Flexible Respite budgets
## Effective date of the income and cash asset exemption
The income and cash asset exemption applies to payments made on or after 1 October 2018.
## Example
Toni (aged 21) lives in Palmerston North (Mid Central region). Toni has a physical disability and lives at home with her elderly mother. Her mother’s health is getting worse and Toni is restricted in where she can live as she needs significant assistance with day to day tasks.
The prototype being trialled by Mid Central Health gives Toni the opportunity to choose the services she needs.
Before these changes Toni would have been told that, to receive the same level of care that her mother provided, she would need to live in a residential facility. As there are very few residential services for young people with Toni’s disability this would probably be a rest home.
With Disability Support payments Toni has been introduced to a ‘connector’ in her community. This person helps Toni identify her options, listening to what Toni wants rather than telling Toni what she must do. Toni is considering living in a flat with other disabled people. Toni will then have the option of receiving the funding directly and can pay for the support she needs.
These payments are not counted as income or as cash assets for the Supported Living Payment and all types of extra help (e.g. Disability Allowance, Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support).

chunks.title: Education payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Education payments
For information on education payments see:
- Income from scholarships
- Student Loans
- Supervision allowances

chunks.title: Effect on Accommodation Supplement — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Effect on Accommodation Supplement
Accommodation Supplement paid to clients receiving a main benefit is not affected by weekly compensation payments. This is because Accommodation Supplement is not income tested for main beneficiaries.
Note New Zealand Superannuation clients must meet the appropriate income limit.
Weekly compensation is treated as income to assess the rate of Accommodation Supplement payable to clients receiving it as a non-beneficiary.
For more information see:
- Accommodation Supplement Chargeable income - non- beneficiaries
- Accommodation Supplement New Zealand Superannuation and Veterans Pension

chunks.title: Effect on Child Disability Allowance — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Effect on Child Disability Allowance
Child Disability Allowance cannot be paid where weekly compensation is received by or for the child.
- Child Disability Allowance Child Disability Allowance not payable

chunks.title: Effect on Disability Allowance — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Effect on Disability Allowance
Certain clients must come under the appropriate income limit to receive Disability Allowance.
ACC weekly compensation is treated as income for all New Zealand Superannuation clients (including non-qualifying partners) and for all non-beneficiary clients.
ACC weekly compensation does not affect Disability Allowance paid to clients or their partners who are getting:
- Supported Living Payment
- Sole Parent Support
- Jobseeker Support
- Youth Payment
- Young Parent Payment or
- a related Emergency Benefit
For more information see:
- Disability Allowance Income test

chunks.title: Effect on Disability Allowance — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Effect on Disability Allowance
Any costs that are reimbursed by a Health and Disability insurance payment are not allowable costs for Disability Allowance.
Where the cost is not completely covered by the policy, the portion that is not covered can be included as an additional cost for Disability Allowance.
## Example
A client has a health insurance policy that meets the full cost of doctor's visits and prescription charges. These costs are not qualifying costs for Disability Allowance.
If the health insurance covers only 80% of the costs, the 20% not covered by the policy is an allowable cost for Disability Allowance.
For more information see:
- Disability Allowance Medical insurance premiums
- Insurance

chunks.title: Effect on Extra help — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Effect on Extra help
When a person is receiving weekly compensation, this needs to be taken into account when reviewing entitlement to Extra help.
Weekly compensation payments are included as income when determining if a client is below the appropriate income limit for Special Needs Grants, Advance Payment of Benefit and Recoverable Assistance Payments.
In some situations, weekly compensation will affect entitlement to Extra help, see:
- Effect on Accommodation Supplement
- Effect on Child Disability Allowance
- Effect on Temporary Additional Support and Special Benefit
- Effect on Disability Allowance
- Backdated ACC weekly compensation payments
For more information see:
- Extra help
- Special Needs Grant Income limit
- Advance Payment of Benefit Income limits
- Recoverable Assistance Payment Income limits

chunks.title: Effect on Temporary Additional Support and Special Benefit — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Effect on Temporary Additional Support and Special Benefit
The full net ACC weekly compensation is chargeable income for Temporary Additional Support and Special Benefit for both main beneficiaries and non-beneficiaries. This includes when the ACC weekly compensation is direct deducted against the main benefit.
For more information see:
- Temporary Additional Support Chargeable income
- Special Benefit Chargeable income
- ACC weekly compensation

chunks.title: Employment related income — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Employment related income
It is important to know employment related income may be treated differently for the commencement of a client's benefit, to when a client is getting an ongoing benefit.
The treatment of payments from employment related income provided here relate to clients already getting a benefit unless specifically referred to under 'commencement date'.
For information on how to treat income at commencement, under the appropriate benefit type, see: Commencement date
## For information about employment related payments for client's currently getting a benefit, see:
- Wages and salary
- Parental leave payments
- Self-employment
- Commission work
- Goods, services, accommodation in lieu of money
- Compensation or damages
- Payments from home-based education and care services
- Honoraria, payments to board of trustee members or local body members
- Carers Allowances and other payments
- Fees for jury service
- Sponsorship
- Payments from friendly and like societies
- Green dollar trading
- Voluntary work Expenses reimbursed by employers [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Energy Trust Dividends — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Energy Trust Dividends
Energy trust dividend payments are made to people by an energy trust or lines company
- as a discount on their power bill or
- as a payment made directly to them
The income exemption also applies to any income earned from an energy trust dividend payment.
Note there is no exemption for payments made to clients from any shares they own in a company or trust.
## Effective date of the income exemption
This income exemption applies to a dividend payment and any income received from it on or after 18 August 2017.
## Income exemption period
Energy Trust dividend payments and any income earned from them are not included as income for 12 months after the payment is made.
## End of income exemption period
At the end of the first 12 months after the payment is made, any income earned from investment of the remaining amount is treated as income.
## Example
A lines company pays an annual dividend to its customers as a discount off the customers power bill. This discount is not considered income for the first 12 months after it is made.

chunks.title: Estate income and wills — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Estate income and wills
The policy guidelines about the effect on benefits of money received from an estate or will.
Money from an estate, such as, money left to a client in a will can be received as:
- Capital payments
- Continuing income from an estate (for example as an annuity or rent from property)
- Interim payments
or
- a combination of the above
If you or the client feels that the client has been unfairly treated in a will or by an estate, they may be able to make a claim against the deceased's estate. If you have a client who may have been treated unfairly refer the case to your regional solicitor.
For more information see:
- Childs income from estates
- Residential Care Subsidy Income from life interest or lease for life
- Residential Care Subsidy Life interest or lease for life

chunks.title: EVSA (Neville Wallace Memorial) Children's and Grandchildren's Trust payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## EVSA (Neville Wallace Memorial) Children's and Grandchildren's Trust payments
Some clients or their families may receive a payment, (similar to an ex gratia payment), from the EVSA (Neville Wallace Memorial) Children's and Grandchildren's Trust. The trust was established in 1993.
## Cash assets and income exemption
Payments made from the EVSA (Neville Wallace Memorial) Children's and Grandchildren's Trust are not treated as income or cash assets for financial assistance provided by Work and Income - for a 12 month period from the date of payment (including any income earned from the payment).
At the end of the 12 month period any remaining amount that a client has will be treated as a cash asset. Also any income derived from the cash asset will be treated as chargeable income for benefit purposes.
## Retrospective reviews
If a client or their family member received a payment from the EVSA (Neville Wallace Memorial) Children's and Grandchildren's Trust payments between 17 August 2007 and 31 December 2009, and their payment was not exempt from the cash asset test, you may need to retrospectively review their financial assistance.
Note payments cannot be retrospectively exempt from the income and asset test for Temporary Additional Support or Residential Care Subsidy. Payments can only be exempt from Temporary Additional Support and Residential Care Subsidy from 1 January 2010 onwards.
## Process
When a client receives a payment you need to create a 'must view' note in CMS. The note should state:
- the client has received a payment from the EVSA (Neville Wallace Memorial) Children's and Grandchildren's Trust
- the date the client received the payment
- the amount of the payment and
- the expiry date of the 12 month exemption
If a client is currently receiving financial assistance, a bring-up needs to be added via BRUPI in SWIFTT to reassess entitlement at the end of the 12 month exemption period.
A letter must be sent to the client when you add the 12 month exemption (a letter template is available in CMS) or complete a retrospective review.
For more information see:
- Ex gratia and compensation payments
Also see:
- Ex gratia payments from Veterans' Affairs New Zealand

chunks.title: Ex gratia and compensation payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: An ex gratia payment is paid in recognition of harm experienced by a person. The payee does not have any legal obligation to pay it, and does not have to accept any liability. A compensation payment is made in recognition that a person has experienced harm, or to settle a claim of harm. Compensation payments can be made: - as the result of a Court order (otherwise known as damages) or award by a tribunal such as the Human Rights Tribunal - to settle a claim of harm that has been formally filed, or - to settle a claim of harm where a claim has not been filed in the Court Generally, ex gratia and compensation payments for harm, or for a claim of harm, are not treated as income or cash assets.

chunks.title: Specific income and cash asset exemptions — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: The following types of payments have specific exemptions from income and cash asset testing: - Ex gratia payments from Veterans' Affairs New Zealand - EVSA (Neville Wallace Memorial) Children and Grandchildren's Trust payments - Viet Nam Veterans and Their Families Trust payments - Hepatitis C ex gratia payments - Lake Alice ex gratia and compensation payments

chunks.title: Generic ex gratia and compensation payment exemption — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Ex gratia and compensation payments not covered by 1 of the specific exemptions may be covered by the generic ex gratia and compensation payment exemption. The payment must be in recognition of harm experienced by the client, or to settle a claim of harm, and must be made by 1 of the following: - the Crown - a faith-based institution - a charity or charitable trust - an incorporated society Payments may also be made by a person or agency who was licensed, registered, engaged or funded by the Crown or a Crown entity to provide services at the time the harm occurred or was alleged to have occurred. This could include payments from: - early childhood education centres - residential care facilities - schools (including private) - school boarding hostels Payments that meet the generic ex gratia and compensation payment exemption criteria will not be treated as income or cash assets for the person who received the payment. This includes any income earned from investment of the payment. There is no time limit on this exemption.

chunks.title: Payments that cannot be exempt — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Ex gratia or compensation payments cannot be exempt from the income and cash asset tests when the payment is being made: - to recognise economic loss, a reduction in value of property or financial assets (sometimes referred to as pecuniary damages) - because of an employment relationship. For more information see compensation or damages for employment - in respect of a contract to provide goods and services or - to parents or adoptive parents on return to work from a period of parental or extended leave (including maternity and partner's/paternity leave) Note these guidelines do not cover ACC lump sum compensation payments. Also note a natural mother may be any gender but must have been pregnant with the child.

chunks.title: Evidence required — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Clients must provide evidence of the payment. Generally, they will have a letter from the organisation making the payment. Some clients may not have a letter, or they may be subject to a non-disclosure agreement that prevents them from sharing information. In this case, a bank statement showing the amount of the payment, the date it was received and who it was made by is acceptable. The exemption only applies to payments made by organisations that are registered and operating in New Zealand. You must be satisfied of this before adding the exemption.

chunks.title: Changes in the client's cash asset levels — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When an ex gratia or compensation payment exemption is applied, it must be equal to the payment the client received, or the amount they have left when they declare the payment to us. The exemption amount will stay the same indefinitely, unless the client's total cash reduces below the exemption amount. Clients are not expected to keep track of any changes to the value of the payment. When this happens, the exemption must be updated to match the client's new level of cash. Where we identify that the client has no cash, the exemption must be removed. This exemption will only increase or be applied again if the client gets another payment which is exempt from income and asset testing. Note for this exemption, cash means physical cash and money in the bank (including savings and term deposit accounts). It does not include anything purchased with the payment, such as shares. Example Sophie receives an ex gratia payment of $50,000 and qualifies to have this exempt. 6 months later at her annual review, Sophie lets us know that her total cash has reduced to $30,000. Her exemption is updated to $30,000. A few months later Sophie applies for Accommodation Supplement and shows us that her cash has increased by $5,000 due to a lotto win. Lotto winnings cannot be exempt from income and cash asset testing, so Sophie's exemption remains at $30,000.

chunks.title: Client receives subsequent exempt payment — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: A client may be paid a subsequent ex gratia or compensation payment that qualifies to be exempt. In this case the exemption will be equal to the amount of the new payment (or the amount they have left when they tell us) plus the remaining amount of the previous payment. To identify how much the client has left of the previous payment, check the amount of cash the client had when they received the new payment. Example Nikau received a $20,000 compensation payment which qualifies to be exempt from income and asset testing. He already has an exemption of $60,000 in place for an ex gratia payment he received 2 years ago. We check Nikau's cash at the time he received the new payment and he had $55,000. Nikau will now have a combined exemption of $75,000.

chunks.title: Client earns income from exempt and non-exempt assets — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When a client is earning income on both exempt and non-exempt assets, the earnings from the exempt assets must be excluded from the client's income. To do this, subtract the exempt amount from the total assets that are generating income. You can then multiply the remaining amount by the interest rate being earned. If the interest rate is unknown, use the Reserve Bank 6-month Term Deposit rate. Example Sam has $70,000 invested in a term deposit which earns interest of 3.29% per annum. $60,000 of this is from an ex gratia payment he received last year which is exempt from income and asset testing. The remainder is from a lotto win and isn't exempt. Sam's income from assets will be calculated using the 3.29% interest rate as follows: Income-earning assets minus exempt assets$70,000 - $60,000 = $10,000 Annual chargeable income$10,000 x 0.0329 = $329.00 Weekly chargeable income$329.00 / 52 = $6.32 Sam also earns $123.90 per week from wages, so he will have a total of $130.22 charged against his benefit as income each week.

chunks.title: Applications for hardship assistance payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Generally a client will not qualify for hardship assistance if they have enough money available to meet their need, even if that money is exempt from the cash asset test. This is because clients must use their own resources before seeking hardship assistance. If the client only has money available to meet part of the cost, hardship assistance can be considered for the shortfall. In each case you must weigh the individual circumstances of the client against the eligibility criteria. Example Hemi has been suffering tooth pain and went to the dentist to get it checked out. The dentist advised he'll need emergency dental treatment that will cost $500. A few months ago, Hemi got a compensation payment of $60,000 which is exempt from income and cash asset testing. After paying some bills, Hemi still has $35,000 left. Hemi remembers the Ministry helped with his dental bill last year, so he applies for a Special Needs Grant again to cover the cost of the emergency dental treatment. In this case, Hemi will not qualify for a Special Needs Grant because he has enough money available to cover the cost of emergency dental treatment himself.

chunks.title: Ex gratia payments from Veterans' Affairs New Zealand — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Ex gratia payments from Veterans' Affairs New Zealand
Some clients or their families may receive an ex gratia payment from Veterans' Affairs New Zealand (VANZ) on behalf of the Crown.
Veterans' Affairs New Zealand determines eligibility and provides letters to all clients receiving this payment explaining the reasons for the payment and the income and asset test exemptions that apply.
## Cash assets and income exemption
These ex gratia payments are not treated as income or a cash asset for any financial assistance provided by Work and Income.
Where the ex gratia payments are earning income, the additional income must be exempt permanently from the date of payment.
## Process
When a client receives a payment you need to create a 'must view' note in CMS. The note should state:
- the client has received an ex gratia payment from Veterans' Affairs New Zealand
- the date the client received the payment
- the amount of the ex gratia payment
- that the payment is permanently exempt from the cash asset test and
- any income derived from the ex gratia payment will be not be treated as chargeable income for benefit purposes
A letter should be sent to the client to advise them that their payment is exempt (a letter template is available in CMS).
For more information see:
- Ex gratia and compensation payments
Also see:
- Viet Nam Veterans and Their Families Trust payments
- EVSA (Neville Wallace Memorial) Children's and Grandchildren's Trust payments

chunks.title: Example of an aggregated payment — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Example of an aggregated payment
A single client who is 25 years old and getting Jobseeker Support currently gets $100.00 per week net weekly compensation from ACC.
The $100.00 is a direct deduction against the Jobseeker Support as follows:
Jobseeker Support rate
$372.55 (as at 1 April 2026)
Less weekly compensation
$100.00
Benefit entitlement
$272.55
The client then chooses to get their weekly compensation converted to an aggregated payment for the period 1 July 2026 to 31 December 2026 from ACC.
The client provides verification that this amount is equivalent to $125.00 per week until 31 December 2026. This is a direct deduction from the client's benefit until 31 December 2026 as follows:
Jobseeker Support rate
$372.55 (as at 1 April 2026)
Less weekly compensation
$125.00
Benefit entitlement
$247.55

chunks.title: Expenses deducted from home-based education and care services — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Expenses deducted from home-based education and care services
Actual expenses directly related to the provision of home-based care services can be deducted from any payments received. All allowable expenses must be verified.
Expenses can include, but are not limited to:
- Electricity
- Food
- Travel (including outings)
- Laundry and cleaning
- Educational resources
- Modifications
- Equipment
- First Aid supplies
Payment in excess of these allowable expenses is regarded as income.

chunks.title: Fees for jury service — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Fees for jury service
The daily fee paid for jury service attendance is charged as income.
Any amount paid for reimbursement of actual expenses such as travel is to be deducted from the jury service fee.
The client must provide verification of any money paid for expenses.
Please refer to the appropriate benefit type for more information on charging income see:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Fire and general insurance policies — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Fire and general insurance policies
Money received from an insurance policy for loss of or destruction or damage to buildings or other property by fire, earthquake, flood or other cause is not charged as income.
However if the payment from an insurance policy is invested for a period of time, for example while awaiting rebuilding, then the interest received is charged as income for main benefit and extra help.
For more information see:
- Insurance

chunks.title: Funds withdrawn from KiwiSaver — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Funds withdrawn from KiwiSaver
Funds withdrawn from KiwiSaver or any other superannuation scheme are treated as a cash asset if they are held as cash or in a form that can be readily converted into cash.
Income earned from the funds is treated as income for income tested assistance.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Funds withdrawn from superannuation scheme accounts — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Funds withdrawn from superannuation scheme accounts
Funds withdrawn from superannuation scheme accounts are treated as a cash asset if they are held as cash or in a form that can be readily converted into cash.

chunks.title: Gifts — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Gifts
A once only gift of cash is a capital payment and is not chargeable income for benefit purposes. This includes a once only gift of real estate or personal property.
When a client gets goods or services, or gifts of cash periodically the value of these should be charged as income.
MSD must charge the value of the gift as income for the period it relates to.
If the gift does not relate to a specific period or if MSD cannot determine the actual period it relates to, MSD must determine the most appropriate period to charge the income. This may be the week in which it is received, provided or supplied.
Example - gift relates to a period
Sarah's mother pays her $250 per week towards general living expenses in respect of that week.
In this situation MSD charge the $250 as income against the week the payment relates to.
Example - gift is intended to be used for specific purpose in period
Cas' friend periodically sends them money to assist with various living expenses. On 1 June Cas is given $90, which is intended to be used towards their groceries in that week.
In this situation MSD charge the $90 as income for the week it is received.
Example - gift does not relate to a period and is intended to be used as and when needed
Jase's uncle sporadically sends him money of varying amounts, intended to be used however and whenever Jase chooses.
In this situation MSD charges the payments as income for the week it is received as it does not relate to any period.
Note any income received from the investment of a cash gift is chargeable income.
Funds retained from a cash gift may affect entitlement to extra help such as Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit.

chunks.title: Goods, services, accommodation in lieu of money — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Goods, services, accommodation in lieu of money
Some clients may get goods, services or accommodation instead of money for work completed. In these situations, charge the value of the goods, services or accommodation as income. If in doubt the client can ask the employer who should be able to provide verification of the value of goods, services or accommodation.
When a client gets accommodation instead of paying money, the value of the accommodation must be considered when assessing a clients accommodation costs.
When a client provides accommodation instead of getting money, the value and nature of the accommodation provided needs to be considered to determine if there is an income charge and/or effect on their weekly qualifying accommodation costs. This is because the client would otherwise be paying money for a service (which would be income for the person getting the money) and the person doing the service would then be paying them money for accommodation.
## Example
A client receives 'free rent' to live together with their landlord for working in the landlord's shop one day a week. The amount the landlord would have charged for the room in their house is $190 per week. The $190 per week is treated as the client's income.
The client’s accommodation cost is treated as $190 rent per week when assessing their weekly qualifying accommodation costs.
If the landlord is a client, the $190 per week will reduce their weekly qualifying accommodation costs and will be charged as income if it is more than the costs of the part of the property they live in.
For more information on charging income, see:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit
- Rent and board payments
- Rental property income

chunks.title: Green Dollar Trading — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Green Dollar Trading
Green Dollar trading is a system of barter and exchange in which goods, services, and credits can be given without the need for cash. Trading with 'green dollars' falls within the definition of income. Green dollars are treated as income when you assess the rate of benefit payment.
A Management Board administers each scheme. The Management Board keeps a record, similar to a banking system and each member is, from time to time, issued a statement showing their debit and credit situation.
The value of any goods, services, or credits is to be charged as income at the time the service or credit is given. Confirmation of regular trading should be obtained through these statements.
Note it is stressed that a liberal interpretation of what constitutes regular trading and income is to be adopted. Periodic payments for what is little more than a good deed for another person will not be considered as regular income in the assessment of the respective benefit.
As a guide to help you decide cases, you should consider whether the person has clearly established themselves as a regular trader within the scheme then income received will be chargeable.
## Example
Joe receives Sole Parent Support and also cuts firewood and is a member of the local Green Dollar scheme. Verna is a welder and wants firewood but has no money. As Joe is a member of their local Green Dollar scheme, Verna can get Joe to deliver the firewood and Joe can use his credit to trade with other members in the system. Verna telephones the 'Green Dollar answer-phone Bank' and asks that Joe's account be credited $50 for firewood with Verna's account being debited by $50. Charge $50 as income on Joe's benefit.
Please refer to the appropriate benefit type for more information on charging income, see:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Health and Disability insurance — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Health and Disability insurance
Health and Disability insurance usually reimburses medical expenses and may include the cost of operations, hospital care and specialist fees. Payments that reimburse medical expenses are not treated as income for benefit purposes however they may affect a client's entitlement to Disability Allowance.
Some policies may also provide:
- tax free cash payments on a nightly basis, to help meet expenses a person may have had to meet while being in hospital (excluding the cost of health care)
- a regular payment to reimburse income lost due to ill health or disability
Payments that are made to help meet expenses a person or their family may have had to meet while in hospital (excluding the costs of health care), or reimbursement of lost income, are charged as income for benefit purposes.
These payments may also affect a client's entitlement to Disability Allowance.
For more information see:
- Income replacement insurance
- Effect on Disability Allowance
- Insurance

chunks.title: Health and Disability payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Health and Disability payments
There are 2 income and cash asset exemptions available for payments from the Crown for health and disability support services.
They are:
- Health and Disability support services funded or provided by the Crown effective on (or after) 18 August 2017 for: Funded Family care (exemption for person requiring care)Individualised Funding payments
- Funded Family care (exemption for person requiring care)
- Individualised Funding payments
and
- Direct Disability Support payments made directly to people on (or after) 1 October 2018 as part of: the Waikato Enabling Good Lives demonstrationthe Mid Central Health prototype andFlexible Respite budgets
- the Waikato Enabling Good Lives demonstration
- the Mid Central Health prototype and
- Flexible Respite budgets
For more information see:

chunks.title: Health and Disability Support services funded or provided by the Crown — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Health and Disability Support services funded or provided by the Crown
Funding and items provided to a client for health and disability support services are not income or cash assets (except for assessing income and cash assets for Temporary Additional Support).
The income exemption also applies to any interest earned from any funding or payments received.
This income and cash asset exemption applies to payments and items provided:
- to the client or
- their dependent child or
- for a person where they are their primary carer
Crown funding or services for health and disability support services cover Ministry of Health payments, such as:
- Funded Family Care and
- Individualised Funding payments
The funding is paid directly to a disabled person who may directly employ a carer or support worker with these funds.
## Person getting paid for providing services
A person being paid money as wages is an employee and these payments are counted as income for any benefits or allowances they are getting.
## Effective date of the income and cash asset exemption
Carol (aged 47) has a disability that has been getting progressively worse, she needs extra help to stay in her home. Carol was assessed by Needs Assessment and Service Co-ordination (NASC) and she is entitled to help every day to shower, dress, and 3 additional hours per week for someone to clean her flat (attached to the main house).
Carol will be paid directly for this assistance and Carol then pays her sister (using this funding), who is providing the agreed support and assistance.
These payments are not counted as income or as cash assets for the Supported Living Payment and most types of extra help (e.g. Disability Allowance, Accommodation Supplement). However, it is for assessing income or cash assets for Temporary Additional Support.
If her sister receives any income tested assistance, the payment she gets from Carol is income and could affect entitlement to the benefit payments or any extra help payments.

chunks.title: Hepatitis C ex gratia payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Hepatitis C ex gratia payments
People who were infected with Hepatitis C through the New Zealand blood supply collected before 27 July 1992 may be eligible for a one off ex gratia payment.
ACC will take the initial application for assistance and provide these to the Ministry of Health. The Ministry of Health will investigate all applications before determining if a person is eligible and then determine how much a person will receive.
## Income exemption
These ex gratia payments are paid as a one-off lump sum and are not treated as chargeable income for benefit purposes or extra help assistance. This includes any income earned from any investment of the payment for the first 12 months following the date the payment was received by the client.
## Cash asset exemption
Do not include this payment or any income as a cash asset when determining entitlement to extra help such as Temporary Additional Support, Home Help, Special Needs Grants and Special Benefit. This applies for the first 12 months following the date the payment was received by the client.
Example if a client is currently receiving an Accommodation Supplement the lump sum payment is not taken into consideration until 12 months following the date the payment was received by the client.
## Process
When a client receives a payment you need to create a 'must view' note in CMS.
The note should state:
- the client has received a Hepatitis C payment that must not be considered as income or as a cash asset for 12 months
- the date the client received the payment
- the date in 12 months that we will need to reassess any Extra help assistance the client may be receiving or makes an application for
If a client is currently receiving extra help assistance, a bring-up needs to be added via BRUPI in SWIFTT to reassess entitlement.
At the end of the 12 month period any remaining amount that a client has will be treated as a cash asset.

chunks.title: History of ACC — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## History of ACC
The Accident Compensation Scheme came into operation on 1 April 1974.
Up until 1 July 1999 the treatment of weekly compensation depended on the reason the client was receiving a benefit.
From 1 July 1999 weekly compensation became a direct deduction from income tested benefits. However weekly compensation is still charged as income for some clients whose payment of weekly compensation started before 1 July 1999.
For the period 1 July 1999 to 30 June 2000 private insurers were able to provide work-related accident insurance cover.
From 1 July 2000, ACC became the sole provider of accident insurance for all work and non-work injuries and has taken over all clients from the private providers.
There were changes to the Accident Compensation Scheme from 1 April 2002 which included:
- lump sum payments for impairment were reintroduced. These were previously removed in 1992
- recipients of Independence Allowance are able to convert their entitlement to a lump sum payment
- the lump sum payments for impairment and Independence Allowance are exempt from the asset test for Accommodation Supplement and Residential Care Subsidy for a period of 12 months from the date of receipt
- surviving spouses are able to convert their entitlement to weekly earnings related compensation to a lump sum payment
For more information see:
- Weekly compensation payments started before 1 July 1999
- Private accident insurers
- ACC weekly compensation
- Lump sum payments
- Other payments from ACC
- Accident Compensation

chunks.title: Sick leave, family violence leave and long service leave — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Sick leave, family violence leave and long service leave
For treatment of sick leave, family violence leave and long service leave when a client stops work and applies for a benefit, see Employment ceased.
For clients currently getting a benefit, income from sick leave, family violence leave and long service leave is regarded as a continuation of wages.
Long service leave is additional leave paid on top of the statutory leave entitlements in recognition of a person's length of employment.
Sick leave, family violence leave and long service leave is charged for the number of days that the payment represents.
To do this MSD must determine:
- the amount before tax (the gross amount) of sick leave, family violence leave or long service leave
- the number of days the sick leave, family violence leave or long service leave represents
Note family violence leave is also known as domestic violence leave.
## Example
A current client is paid $200 for long service leave. Their daily rate of pay is $50.
To calculate the period to charge the income, the total long service leave payment is divided by the daily rate ($200 ÷ $50 = 4 days).
Charge the $200 against the client's benefit for the 4 days it represents.
Please refer to the appropriate benefit type for more information on charging income:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Holiday pay — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: For treatment of holiday pay when a client stops work and applies for a benefit, see Employment ceased. MSD charges income from holiday pay in a specified manner for clients getting a benefit.

chunks.title: Holiday pay for leave taken — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When a client takes a period of annual leave and is paid holiday pay, MSD must charge the holiday pay for the period the leave relates to. Example 1 Chan is getting Jobseeker Support and is working part time. Her weekly income of $250 reduces her Jobseeker Support to $298.32 per week. Chan lets MSD know that she is taking 5 days annual leave for Monday 16 February to Friday 20 February and will be paid $250 holiday pay for that period. MSD charge Chan's holiday pay of $250 against her Jobseeker Support for the period 16 February to 22 February. Chan's Jobseeker Support rate is not affected and continues to be paid at the reduced rate of $298.32.

chunks.title: Holiday pay when employment ends — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: This treatment applies when: - a client is paid their remaining holiday pay entitlement when their employment ends or - a client was approved cashed up holiday pay while employed, but it was paid on or after the first week day after their employment ended In these cases, MSD will charge the holiday pay from the first week day after their employment ended, for the number of week days the payment represents. Note for the purpose of charging holiday pay in this scenario, week day: - means a day of the week that is not a Saturday or Sunday and - includes public holidays Example 2 Blake is getting Jobseeker Support of $193.32 per week and is working part time. Blake lets MSD know he is ceasing employment and his last day of work is Friday 13 February. The first week day after his employment ends is Monday 16 February. Blake is paid out holiday pay of $800, representing 10 days. To calculate the daily rate, the holiday pay is divided by the number of days it represents, i.e. $800 ÷ 10 days = $80 per day. MSD charge Blake's holiday pay as follows: - Monday 16 February to Sunday 22 February: $400 (5 week days in period) - Monday 23 February to Sunday 1 March: $400 (5 week days in period) Blake's Jobseeker Support continues at $193.32 for Monday 16 February to Sunday 1 March. From Monday 2 March, Blake's Jobseeker Support increases to $361.32 because he has no holiday pay remaining from this date.

chunks.title: Holiday pay that is cashed up while in employment — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When a client is paid any amount of cashed up holiday pay while still employed, MSD must charge the cashed up holiday pay for the period that it is received. Example 3 Mele is getting Accommodation Supplement of $95 per week and is working full time. Each week she is paid $960.00 wages in for her previous week of work. In the week beginning 12 January Mele is paid $960 in cashed up holiday pay in addition to her normal weekly pay of $960 (in respect of her previous week of work). This equals a total of $1,920. MSD charges the cashed up holiday pay against the week it was received, and charges her normal weekly pay for the period it was earned. This means that her income is charged against her as follows: - Monday 5 January to Sunday 11 January: $960 standard week of earnings - Monday 12 January to Sunday 18 January: $1,920 income from earnings and cashed up holiday pay Mele's Accommodation Supplement is reduced to zero for the week that the cashed-up holiday pay is received because her income is over the cut-out point for that week.

chunks.title: Home equity conversion schemes — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Home equity conversion schemes
A home equity conversion scheme is a type of loan and not considered income for benefit purposes.
A home equity conversion scheme allows a person to borrow against the equity in their home. When they die, or if the home is sold, the loan (including any interest) is repaid from the sale of the home.
This is also known as a reverse mortgage or home equity release scheme.
A home equity conversion scheme is not considered income for benefit purposes. This is regardless of whether it’s a:
- regular payment (periodic), eg when the client gets two or three (or more) payments within a 52 week period or
- one-off lump sum payment
## When the scheme is considered a cash asset
The home equity conversion scheme is considered a cash asset when it's paid as a:
- one-off lump sum, or
- periodic payment and held as a cash asset in the client's bank account.
If the lump sum or periodic payments are held in a bank account and isn't used to pay for a major expense, it may affect other payments, such as Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support.
Examples of major expenses include but are not limited to:
- a new car
- house repairs or maintenance
- a holiday
- a medical operation
Note it is not appropriate for clients to be referred to equity conversion schemes if they are in hardship.

chunks.title: Homestays — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Homestays
Homestay accommodation is similar to bed and breakfast accommodation and offers people an opportunity to experience Kiwi culture and language with a New Zealand homestay family.
People who run a homestay, which is similar to a 'Bed & Breakfast' (B&B), are generally running a business and are doing this to make a profit.
## Overseas students
Accommodation for overseas students is also referred to as 'homestay', this is usually more like an 'extended family' type relationship and is not usually taken on as a profit making venture.
When a family take on an international student(s), this is usually more of a boarding situation, and generally includes taking additional responsibilities for the international student, and the board fee reflects this.
A family providing board for an international student in most cases are not doing this as a business, it is a boarding arrangement and should be treated as such for benefit purposes.
When the amount an overseas student pays for their accommodation includes other costs (e.g. food or service costs) and these costs can be separated out from the amount they pay for accommodation, they are considered renting.

chunks.title: Honoraria — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Honoraria
An honorarium is a payment, although nominal, for services rendered. A client receives an honorarium for acting as secretary or treasurer of a club. Charge this payment as income over the period it represents (not the week in which it is received).
## Payments to Local Body members
Payments to Local Body members are charged as income in the same way as salary or wages for benefit purposes.
## Payments to Board of Trustee members
Payments to Board of Trustee members are charged as income in the same way as salary or wages for benefit purposes.
Expenses allowed should be those that the client would not ordinarily be expected to meet. This would include cost of transport to extra-ordinary meetings, stationery and other items not provided by the school. The client must provide verification of the expenses.
Transport to ordinary meetings is not allowed as an expense to be deducted from wages or salary.
For more information on charging income, see:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Income from scholarships — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Income from scholarships
Clients or their partner may receive an educational scholarship payment to help assist with their study and associated costs. Depending on the scholarship agreement some or all of the scholarship payment may be assessed as income.
Some scholarships have a portion that is set aside for fees, where the client must use the portion outlined in the scholarship agreement to pay for their fees. The fee portion generally would not be considered income because the client or their partner cannot use that portion to support themselves and their family.
If any of the scholarship is paid to the recipient to use as they wish, this portion would generally be included as income for the period that it represents.
Similarly, some scholarships may not have a portion set aside for fees and the scholarship can be used as the recipient wishes. In this case the entire scholarship payment would generally be charged as income for the period that it represents.
## Period that the scholarship represents
Scholarships are awarded for study in a particular year, and therefore the income from the scholarship payment is to be attributed to that year or study period (if the study period is less than a year).
To be sure what part of the scholarship payment is chargeable as income, you will need to view the scholarship agreement.

chunks.title: Income replacement insurance — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Income replacement insurance
Income Replacement Insurance provides payments when a client is unable to work due to:
- health condition
- accident or
- redundancy
Income Replacement Insurance is intended to help with ongoing living expenses such as accommodation, food, power and telephone. It generally pays a percentage of the income that the client was receiving prior to finishing work.
The client may receive Income Replacement Insurance as an ongoing weekly payment or as a lump sum.
## Weekly payment
Charge any ongoing weekly payments received from Income Replacement Insurance as income for the period that the payment represents.
## Lump sum payment
There will be occasions when a client may receive a lump sum payment that represents a weekly payment for a specified period. This would usually be where a claim is settled some time after the person has ceased work.
Charge lump sum Income Replacement Insurance payments as income for the period the payment represents. If the client wasn't on benefit for this period, the lump sum payment will have no effect on the clients benefit payment.
Where the client invests the lump sum you will need to take into account (and charge as income) any interest received.
For more information see:
- Mortgage protection insurance
- Insurance

chunks.title: Independence Allowance — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Independence Allowance
A person who is permanently impaired as a result of an injury that occurred before 1 April 2002 may be eligible for an Independence Allowance. The Independence Allowance is paid to recognise ongoing disability. ACC assess the Independence Allowance as a weekly amount, but it is paid quarterly and in advance.
Independence Allowance is not weekly compensation and is not charged as income for main benefit or Extra help.
The Independence Allowance (introduced in 1992) has been replaced by Lump Sum Impairment payments. Independence Allowance will not be granted for injuries that have occurred after 1 April 2002. However clients may claim this allowance for injuries sustained before this date.
Clients receiving Independence Allowance can elect to have the allowance paid in a lump sum (for up to 5 years' worth of entitlement, and then after 5 years they get to choose again). Independence Allowance received this way is treated the same as lump sum payments for impairment.
Any Independence Allowance lump sum payments are not treated as cash assets, when assessing a client for Accommodation Supplement or Residential Care Subsidy for a period of 12 months, following the date the lump sum payment was received by the client.
Any income generated from the Independence Allowance lump sum, for example, interest earned from the investment of a lump sum, is to be treated as income for benefit purposes.
At the end of the 12 month period, the Independence Allowance lump sum (or any remaining amount) must be treated as a cash asset, and included in the asset test for Accommodation Supplement and Residential Care Subsidy.
Note this exemption does not apply to any other asset tested assistance. Independence Allowance lump sum payments must be treated as cash assets in the assessment of any other asset-tested assistance, for example: Temporary Additional Support, Special Needs Grants, Advance Payment of Benefits.
For more information see:
- Sensitive claims
- Lump sum payments for impairment
- Lump sum payments

chunks.title: Insurance — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Insurance
There are a number of different insurance policies that a client may have to cover them for events such as illness or redundancy. The payments received from these policies can be to cover loss of income or to cover costs such as mortgage payments, hire purchase payments or disability related costs.
The effect of insurance payment on the client's benefit depends on the type of insurance policy and the reasons that the payment is made.
For more information see:
- Debt insurance
- Fire and general insurance policies
- Health and disability insurance
- Income replacement insurance
- Life insurance
- Loan protection insurance
- Mortgage protection insurance

chunks.title: Interim payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Interim payments
The administrator of an estate may make interim payments from an estate before the final distribution is made. These interim payments may be income or capital payments.
