If they are capital payments they are generally not considered as income for benefit purposes, but may be treated as chargeable income if they are paid periodically and are being used for an income related purpose. See:
- Core policy Income related purpose
Any income tested assistance must be reviewed when interim payments are received.
For more information see:
- Estate income and wills
- Continuing income from an estate
- Capital payments
- Childs income from estates

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Introduction
For information on specific types of income see:
- Accident Compensation
- Additional occupant contributions
- Child Support income
- Christchurch mosques attack support payments
- Compassionate grants
- Education payments
- Employment related income
- Energy Trust Dividends
- Estate income and wills
- Ex gratia and compensation payments
- Gifts
- Health and Disability payments
- Home equity conversion schemes
- Insurance
- Loans
- Lottery prizes and gambling wins
- MSD lump sum payments
- Payments from Earthquake Commission and insurance companies (Canterbury earthquake 2010 and 2011 aftershock)
- Payments from the Crown for the purchase of property in the Canterbury red zone
- Payments from the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross)
- Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014
- Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support
- Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination
- Payments to victims of crime and their families
- Profit from boarders
- Relationship Property Settlements
- Rent and board payments
- Rental property income
- Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds
- Sale of assets
- Superannuation scheme accounts
- Voluntary portion of overseas pension
Also see:
- Income that must be excluded
- Income that must be included

chunks.title: KiwiSaver — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## KiwiSaver
Money in a KiwiSaver account which is 'locked-in' will have no impact on benefit entitlement. It is not treated as a cash asset and income earned from the KiwiSaver fund is not income for income tested assistance.
Generally, all KiwiSaver funds have a lock-in period until age 65 years.
## KiwiSaver funds not locked-in are cash assets
From 1 July 2019, people can join KiwiSaver at any age. Generally, the funds of members who join when they are 65 or over are not locked-in. This means they are cash assets.
Income received from the invested funds is treated as income.
## A lock-in period may exist for some client's aged 65 years and over depending on when they joined KiwiSaver
Before 1 July 2019, clients who were age 60 to 64 when they joined KiwiSaver were subject to a 5 year 'locked-in' period before they could access their funds.
When these client's turn 65 on or after 1 April 2020 they will have a choice of:
- accessing their KiwiSaver funds or
- continuing for the remainder of the locked-in period
For more information on when a lock-in period exists for those aged 65 years and over and how it may affect their payments, see: Lock-in period exists for some clients over age 65 years
## Client joined KiwiSaver before aged 60
Clients who joined KiwiSaver before aged 60 will be able to access their funds when they reach the age of 65.
At age 65 these funds are a cash asset and any income from the funds is treated as income.

chunks.title: Lake Alice ex gratia and compensation payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Some former patients of the Lake Alice Hospital may get an ex gratia or compensation payment from the Crown. These payments started being made in 2001, and some former patients may get more than 1.

chunks.title: Cash assets and income exemption — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Ex gratia or compensation payments made to former patients of the Lake Alice Hospital are not treated as income or cash assets for the person who got the payment. This includes any income earned from investment of the payment. There is no time limit on this exemption.

chunks.title: Evidence — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Clients must provide evidence of the payment. Generally, they will have a letter from the agency making the payment. If a client does not have a letter, a bank statement showing the amount of the payment, the date it was paid, and who it was made by can be accepted.

chunks.title: Changes in the client's cash asset levels — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Clients are not expected to keep track of changes to the value of a Lake Alice payment. When the exemption is applied, it must be equal to the amount the client got, or the amount they have left when they tell MSD. The exempt amount stays the same unless the client's total cash reduces below the exempt amount. When this happens, the exempt amount is the client's new level of cash. If the client has no cash, the exemption must be removed. The exemption will only increase or be applied again if the client gets another Lake Alice payment. Note for this exemption, cash means physical cash and money in the bank (including savings and term deposit accounts). It does not include anything purchased with the payment, such as shares. Example Sophie gets a $50,000 Lake Alice payment which is exempt. Six months later at her annual review, Sophie lets MSD know her total cash has reduced to $30,000. Her exemption is updated to $30,000. A few months later Sophie applies for Accommodation Supplement and shows MSD her cash has increased by $5,000 from a lotto win. Lotto winnings are not exempt from income and cash asset testing, so Sophie's exemption stays at $30,000.

chunks.title: Client gets additional exempt payment — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: A client may get more than 1 Lake Alice payment. When this happens, the exempt amount is equal to the value of the new payment (or the amount they have left when they tell MSD) plus the remaining amount of the previous payment. To work out how much of the previous payment the client has left, check the amount of cash they had when they got the new payment. Example Nikau gets a $20,000 Lake Alice payment. He already has an exemption of $60,000 for a Lake Alice payment he got 2 years ago. We check Nikau's cash at the time he got the new payment and he had $55,000. Nikau will have a combined exemption of $75,000.

chunks.title: Client earns income from exempt and non-exempt assets — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When a client earns income on exempt and non-exempt assets, the earnings from the exempt assets must be excluded from the client's income. To do this, subtract the exempt amount from the total assets that are earning income. Then multiply the remaining amount by the interest rate being earned. If the interest rate is not known, use the Reserve Bank six-month term deposit rate. Example Sam has $70,000 invested in a term deposit earning interest of 3.29% per annum. Of this, $60,000 is from a Lake Alice payment they got last year which is exempt. The rest is from a lotto win and is not exempt. Sam's income from assets will be calculated using the 3.29% interest rate as follows: Income-earning assets minus exempt assets$70,000 - $60,000 = $10,000 Annual chargeable income$10,000 x 0.0329 = $329.00 Weekly chargeable income$329.00 / 52 = $6.32 Sam also earns $123.90 per week from wages. They will have a total of $130.22 charged against their benefit as income each week.

chunks.title: Applications for hardship assistance payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Generally, a client will not qualify for hardship assistance if they have enough money available to meet their need, even if that money is exempt from income and cash asset testing. This is because clients must use their own resources before seeking hardship assistance. If the client only has money available to meet part of the cost, hardship assistance can be considered for the shortfall. In each case you must weigh the individual circumstances of the client against the eligibility criteria. Example Hemi has been suffering tooth pain and went to the dentist to get it checked out. The dentist advised he will need essential dental treatment that will cost $500. A few months ago, Hemi got a Lake Alice payment of $60,000 which is exempt. After paying some bills, Hemi still has $35,000 left. Hemi remembers MSD helped with his dental costs last year, so he applies for a Special Needs Grant again to cover the cost of the essential dental treatment. In this case, Hemi will not qualify for a Special Needs Grant because he has enough money available to cover the cost of the dental treatment himself.

chunks.title: Licensed home-based education and care services — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Licensed home-based education and care services
Some clients are employed as caregivers through licensed home-based education and care services.
For a list of licensed home-based education and care service providers see:
- Education Counts Early Learning Services
For licensed home-based education caregivers regulated under the Education (Early Childhood Services) Regulations 2008, a portion of the payment received by the caregiver may be disregarded as income.
The amount of any payment received to be disregarded as income, for each child, is the greater of:
- $4.60 per hour (as at 1 April 2026) or
- the caregiver's actual expenses (verified by receipts)
The remainder of the payment is treated as income.

chunks.title: Life insurance — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Life insurance
There are two types of life insurance policies:
- whole of life - which only pays on the death of the person and
- endowment - which pays a specified amount of money when the insured person reaches a certain age
These payments are treated as once only capital payments and are not treated as income for benefit purposes.
Any bonuses paid on a policy or lump sum received from surrendering the policy are also treated as a once only capital payment.
If the payment from a policy, bonus or lump sum from surrendering a policy is invested, the interest received is charged as income.
For more information see:
- Capital payments
- Insurance

chunks.title: Loan protection insurance — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Loan protection insurance
In the event of redundancy or illness, Loan Protection Insurance policies will generally cover:
- various loan agreements
- credit card payments and
- hire purchases
Loan Protection Insurance payments cover the loan repayment or hire purchase payments for a specified period.
Where a client has no choice as to how payments under a Loan Protection Insurance policy can be used, and the payments are made direct to the supplier/company to cover the payments due, the payments are not charged as income for benefit purposes. Where the client receives the Loan Protection Insurance payments this is charged as income for benefit purposes.
These payments may reduce the allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit.
For more information see:
- Insurance
## Effect on Accommodation Supplement, Special Benefit or Temporary Additional Support
Deduct the amount of the Loan Protection Insurance payable from the client's actual loan or hire purchase repayment to give you the allowable cost for Accommodation Supplement, Special Benefit or Temporary Additional Support.
For more information see:
- Accommodation Supplement Home ownership
- Special Benefit Allowable costs
- Temporary Additional Support Allowable costs

chunks.title: Loans — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Loans
If a client gets a ‘true’ loan, it’s not considered income for benefit eligibility. A ‘true’ loan is a loan that:
- transfers a sum of money from one person to another and
- there is an obligation to repay that money
This could be a loan from:
- a registered bank, eg: a personal loan ormortgage top-up for a specific purpose
- a personal loan or
- mortgage top-up for a specific purpose
- another lending institution, eg. finance companycredit unionbuilding societies
- finance company
- credit union
- building societies
- a family trust they must pay back
- family and/or friends they must pay back
If a client is given money with no obligation to pay it back, it's considered as either income or a cash asset, depending on how often it’s paid. This could be gifts from:
- a family trust they don’t have to pay back
- family and/or friends they don’t have to pay back
If a client is given money as a one-off, then it is a cash asset. If they are regularly given money (eg. more than once a year), then it is considered income.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Lock in period exists for some clients over age 65 years — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Lock in period exists for some clients over age 65 years
Before 1 July 2019, clients who were age 60 to 64 when they joined KiwiSaver were subject to a 5 year locked in period before they could access their funds.
When these client’s turn 65 on or after 1 April 2020 they will have a choice of:
- accessing their KiwiSaver funds or
- continuing for the remainder of the locked in period
## Client chooses to access KiwiSaver funds
If a client chooses to access their KiwiSaver before the locked in period ends their funds are treated as a cash asset.
## Client chooses to remain in Kiwisaver until their locked in period ends
When clients choose to continue contributing to their KiwiSaver until their locked in period ends, their funds will not be included in a means assessment of assets. The funds will only be a cash asset when the locked in period expires.
## Examples of clients choosing to access their KiwiSaver funds or continuing to keep their funds locked in
Example 1
Client turned 61 on 1 June 2017 and joined KiwiSaver the same day:
- 5 year locked in period ends on 1 June 2022
- client turns 65 on 1 June 2021
Client turns 65 on 1 June 2021 and can then choose to:
- access their KiwiSaver funds or
- continue making contributions until the locked in period ends on 1 June 2022
Example 2
Client age 63 joined KiwiSaver on 1 March 2018:
- 5 year locked in period ends on 1 March 2023
- client turns 65 on 10 March 2020
Client must wait until 1 April 2020 when they can choose to:
- access their KiwiSaver funds or
- continue making contributions for the locked in period ending 1 March 2023

chunks.title: Lottery prizes and gambling wins — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Lottery prizes and gambling wins
Lottery, Bonus Bonds, and Lotto prizes, race and totalisator (TAB) winnings, or other gambling winnings are not chargeable income for benefit purposes, unless the client is running some sort of betting scheme.
However, any income, such as interest, received from the investment of winnings or prizes is chargeable income.
Funds retained from prize money or proceeds from the sale or disposal of prizes received are considered as a cash asset and may affect entitlement to extra help such as Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, Special Needs Grants or Advances.
If the winnings or part of the winnings are given away, for example to relatives, or invested in Bonus Bonds, consider deprivation of property.
When winnings are paid periodically, please contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Lump sum payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Lump sum payments
Some assistance paid by ACC is made by a lump sum payment. The effect on benefit entitlement will depend on the reason for the lump sum payment.
For more information see:
- Lump sum payments for impairment
- Payments for surviving spouses
- Survivors grant
- Quick reference guide for the treatment of ACC payments
- Accident Compensation

chunks.title: Lump sum payments for impairment — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: A person, who is permanently impaired as a result of an injury that occurred after 1 April 2002, may be eligible for a lump sum payment for impairment. These payments are to compensate for the permanent loss of function caused by an injury.

chunks.title: Treatment of lump sum payments for impairment — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Lump sum payments for impairment are not charged as income and are not a direct deduction for benefit purposes. Any lump sum payments for impairment are not treated as cash assets, when assessing a client for Accommodation Supplement or Residential Care Subsidy for a period of 12 months following the date the lump sum payment was received by the client. Any income generated from the lump sum payment for impairment, for example, interest earned from the investment of a lump sum, is to be treated as income for benefit purposes. At the end of the 12 month period, the lump sum payment for impairment (or any remaining amount) must be treated as a cash asset, and included in the asset test for Accommodation Supplement and Residential Care Subsidy. Note this exemption does not apply to any other asset tested assistance. Lump sum payments for impairment must be treated as cash assets in the assessment of any other asset-tested assistance, for example: Temporary Additional Support, Special Needs Grants, and Advance Payment of Benefits.

chunks.title: Cash asset test for all Hardship Benefits — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Lump sum payments for impairment are made to compensate for the permanent loss of function caused by an injury. These payments are made for non-economic loss. You should consider whether good cause exists to disregard lump sum payments for impairment from the cash asset test for an Emergency Benefit, or Jobseeker Support on the grounds of hardship. When considering if good cause exists to disregard the lump sum payment for impairment think through the following: - If the client is declined will it have a serious adverse effect on their health or welfare? If yes this would indicate good cause exists to disregard the lump sum for payments for impairment. - Is the need for assistance temporary? If yes this may indicate good cause does not exist. - Are the clients other assets (besides the lump sum payment for impairment) cash assets? If yes then good cause does not exist, if the other assets are non cash assets or cash assets that are not easily realisable then good cause may exist. Other circumstances may be considered, each case will need to be considered on its own merits. If you are unsure if good cause exists consult your regional solicitor. Note lump sum payments for impairment are not the same as Lump sum payments for surviving spouses. For more information see: - Independence Allowance - Effect on Extra help - Income Support Emergency Benefit - Quick reference guide for the treatment of ACC payments - Lump sum payments - Other payments from ACC

chunks.title: Mortgage protection insurance — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Mortgage protection insurance
Mortgage Protection Insurance pays all or part of a client's mortgage payment in the event that they are made redundant or are unable to work because of illness.
Mortgage Protection Insurance payments are not charged as income against the client's benefit but are taken into account when assessing Accommodation Supplement. The Mortgage Protection Insurance payment is deducted from the client's weekly accommodation costs to determine the allowable accommodation cost for assessing entitlement to Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, or Special Benefit.
## Example
A client's mortgage payment, rates, and insurance costs come to $150.00 per week and they receive Mortgage Protection Insurance payments of $100.00 per week.
The accommodation cost to assess entitlement to Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, or Special Benefit is $50 per week ($150 - $100).
For more information see:
- Accommodation Supplement Home ownership
- Temporary Additional Support Formula for Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit Accommodation costs
- Insurance

chunks.title: MSD lump sum payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## MSD lump sum payments
MSD lump sum payments are any lump sum payment of benefit that is not a client’s regular weekly or fortnightly benefit payment.
This includes, but is not limited to, lump sum payments because of:
- the grant of a benefit
- the correction of a Ministry error
- a change in a client’s circumstances
- a review of a client’s benefit eg an Annual Review
## MSD lump sum payments include all benefits
MSD lump sum payments include any benefit paid under the Social Security Act 2018. It also includes special assistance paid under a Welfare Programme eg Away from Home Allowance.
MSD lump sum payments do not include:
- Funeral Grants
- Income Related Rent refunds
- tax credits paid under the Income Tax Act 2007 eg Family tax credit
- ex gratia and compensation payments from the Ministry, which may be covered by the generic ex gratia and compensation payments income and cash asset exemption
## Income and cash asset exemption
MSD lump sum payments are not treated as income or cash assets for the person who received the payment, for the first 12 months after the payment is made. This includes any income earned from investment of the payment.
## End of exemption period
At the end of the first 12 months after the payment is made, any remaining amount a client has is treated as a cash asset. Any income earned from investment of the remaining amount is treated as income.
## Client earns income from exempt and non-exempt assets
When a client is earning income on both exempt and non-exempt assets, the earnings from the exempt assets must be excluded from the client’s income.
To do this, subtract the exempt amount from the total assets that are earning income. Then multiply the remainder by the interest rate being earned.
If the interest rate is unknown, use the Reserve Bank six-month term deposit rate.
## Applications for hardship assistance payments
Generally a client won’t qualify for hardship assistance if they have enough money available to meet the need, even if that money is exempt from the cash asset test.
Clients must use their own resources before seeking hardship assistance. If the client only has money available to meet some of the cost, hardship assistance can be considered for the remaining cost.
In each case you must consider the individual circumstances of the client against the eligibility criteria.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Non taxable allowances — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Non taxable allowances
Non-taxable allowances are allowances that are exempt from income tax. Many employers pay their employees non-taxable allowances to compensate for costs which are directly related to their jobs such as clothing, meals, mileage, tools, footwear or laundry allowances. The employer may pay the allowances as part of the weekly wage, or periodically in a lump sum to reimburse for actual expenses incurred.
Where the allowances are paid to reimburse the employee for actual costs that are directly related to their employment these are not charged as income.
Any allowance that is not used by the employee to pay for employment related costs is treated as income and should be added onto the gross amount of wages paid.
Example
A person has part-time work and receives
$123.62 gross
Plus an additional overnight allowance payment of
$42.50
Deduct actual expenses associated with the overnight stay
$23.88
Leaving
$18.62
Add gross income
$123.62 gross
Total income to charge is
$142.24
Please refer to the appropriate benefit type for more information on charging income, see:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Other payments from ACC — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Other payments from ACC
There is assistance from ACC to help manage at home following an injury. This includes housework, personal care and childcare.
For more information on how to treat these payments for benefit purposes see:
- ACC childcare payments
- ACC child weekly compensation
- Sensitive claims
- Payments for attendant care, home help and rehabilitation services
Other assistance such as Disability Allowance, Special Needs Grants and Funeral Grants have specific provisions in respect of payments from ACC.
For more information see:
- Quick reference guide for the treatment of ACC payments
- Disability Allowance Services provided through another agency
- Funeral Grant Qualifications
- Special Needs Grant Other sources of assistance
- Accident Compensation

chunks.title: Outgoings paid by former partner — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Outgoings paid by former partner
The amount of outgoings paid by the person's former partner to be charged as income, depends on whether or not there has been a relationship property settlement (matrimonial property settlement) under a Property Agreement or Property Order.
## Before the Property settlement
Before the property settlement, charge as income against the client's benefit any outgoings the former partner is paying in excess of 50% of the total outgoings.
## After the Property settlement
After the property settlement there should be an agreement stating the amount of accommodation costs to be paid by each partner. Any amount, over the agreed amount, paid by the former partner towards the property is charged as income.
When the former partner is meeting the client's rental costs, charge the amount paid as income.

chunks.title: Outgoings paid by someone else — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Outgoings paid by someone else
In some circumstances a client may have their accommodation costs paid for by another person (for example a client's parent).
Where accommodation costs are paid for by someone else then the amount paid by the 'other' person is charged as income for benefit purposes.

chunks.title: Paid parental leave payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Paid parental leave payments
If they are eligible, parents can get Paid Parental Leave from Inland Revenue for the first 26 weeks of parental leave.
For treatment of Paid Parental Leave when a client stops work and applies for a benefit, see:
- Jobseeker Support Average weekly income
For all other clients currently getting a benefit, Paid Parental Leave payments must be treated as income in the same way as any other wage or salary, for main benefits and extra help.
## Parental tax credit
This Paid Parental Leave should not to be confused with parental tax credit which was also paid by Inland Revenue for children born before 1 July 2018.

chunks.title: Partner made redundant — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Partner made redundant
If the partner of a client currently receiving a benefit is made redundant, any redundancy payment received is not treated as income and there is no need to review the initial stand-down.
However, it will be regarded as a cash asset and may affect any extra help the client is receiving.
## Interest received
Any interest (before tax) paid on any lump sum received is treated as income and charged against the benefit.
To decide whether or not the client is in a de facto relationship see:
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit

chunks.title: Payment made by instalment — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Payment made by instalment
In some instances an asset, such as a property or business, can be sold under an agreement for sale and purchase, or on a table mortgage where regular or periodical instalments of the principal sum and interest are paid to the client.
You should check the sale and purchase agreement to determine the amount and frequency of the payments and any interest payable.
When determining whether the payments of capital are income, you will need to consider whether:
- the payments are made for an income related purpose and
- the payments are used for an income related purpose
Both of these criteria must be satisfied for a periodic payment of capital to be treated as income.
Any interest received is charged as income for benefit purposes. You will also need to consider whether deprivation of income has occurred if only a small amount or no interest is being paid.
If you are unsure whether payments made by instalment are income, contact your Service Delivery Solicitor.
## Example
A client has sold a boat they own for $30,000 and the sale and purchase agreement provides for the purchaser to pay $10,000 in three instalments, plus interest of $500 over an 18 month period.
In this case this arrangement has been made so the purchaser can buy the boat and to satisfy the sale price of the boat which is a capital related transaction. The three $10,000 payments are not income as they have not been made for an income related purpose. The interest payments are chargeable income for benefit purposes.
For more information see:
- Definition of income Income related purpose
- Accommodation Supplement Rent to buy

chunks.title: Payments for attendant care, home help and rehabilitation services — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Payments for attendant care, home help and rehabilitation services
Payments made by ACC for attendant care, home help and rehabilitation services are payments made to the client to purchase a service or to meet the cost of travel and accommodation for accessing rehabilitation services.
Note the Service Provider may be paid directly by ACC.
The ACC payment amount used to purchase the services is disregarded as income for benefit purposes. If the ACC payment is not used to purchase services and is used for income related purposes then this is treated as income.
## Example
A client receives $70.00 per week from ACC for Home Help. The client pays $60.00 per week for the Home Help service.
$70.00 payment received by client from ACC
less $60.00 rate charged by Home Help service provider
equals $10.00 per week charged as income
Note the client should be asked to provide proof of the services purchased.
For more information see:
- Sensitive claims
- Quick reference guide for the treatment of ACC payments
- ACC Childcare payments
- Definition of income Income-related purpose
- Accident Compensation

chunks.title: Payments for surviving spouses — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Payments for surviving spouses
A client may get ACC weekly compensation if their partner died as a result of an injury.
The client can choose to get this as a weekly payment or convert their full entitlement to an aggregated payment. An aggregated payment is the future value of weekly compensation payments paid as a lump sum.
If the client gets the weekly compensation weekly it is treated in the same way as other ACC weekly compensation payments.
For more information see:
- ACC weekly compensation
## Aggregated payments of weekly compensation
Clients need to apply to ACC to have their weekly compensation converted to an aggregated payment.
Note aggregated payments are different to lump sum payments for impairment and independence allowance lump sum payments, and are included in the assessment of any asset tested assistance.
A client can get an aggregated payment as:
- a single payment or
- a series of two or more payments. The payments must be at least 6 months apart.
The lump sum calculation by ACC takes things like inflation and interest into account, so the equivalent weekly rate of the aggregated payment may be higher than what the client is currently getting.
## Effect on client's benefit entitlement
The amount paid to a client as a lump sum represents weekly compensation over a specific period and must be direct deducted against any specified benefit paid for the same period.
The client will get a decision letter from ACC with details of the payment including the weekly rate and the period the payment represents. Clients will need to provide this letter as verification when advising MSD of the aggregated payment.
In some cases, a client will not be entitled to a benefit until the end of the period the aggregated payment represents. MSD must explain this to the client before completing a review or an assessment of their entitlement to Extra help such as Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Payments from Earthquake Commission and insurance companies (Canterbury earthquake 2010 and aftershock 2011) — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Clients who were affected by the Canterbury earthquake and who were insured may receive payments from the Earthquake Commission and insurance companies for: - the costs of renting temporary accommodation because they can no longer live in their home due to damage from the Canterbury earthquake 2010 (including aftershocks) - rebuilding or repairing the damage to their homes caused by the Canterbury earthquake 2010 (including aftershocks)

chunks.title: Income exemptions for payments by insurance companies for rental accommodation when the homes cannot be lived in — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Payments made by insurance companies for the costs of rental accommodation (for situations where people affected by the Canterbury earthquakes are unable to inhabit their home due to damage) are not considered income for benefit purposes.

chunks.title: Income and cash asset exemption — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Payments from the Earthquake Commission and insurance companies for rebuilding, repairing or purchasing a new home as a result of the Canterbury earthquake are not to be treated as chargeable income or a cash asset for the period set out below when determining entitlement to a main benefit and other assistance paid under the Social Security Act 2018. Examples include: - Accommodation Supplement - Away from Home Allowance - Community Cost Programme - Course Participation Costs - Funeral Grant - Home Help - Seasonal Work Assistance - Special Benefit - Special Needs Grants - Special Transfer Allowance - Student Allowance Transfer Grant - Temporary Additional Support This includes any income earned from investment of the payment.

chunks.title: Period of exemption — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: The exemption period is 48 months where the client intends to use the payments to: - repair or rebuild their home or - purchase a replacement home In all other cases the income and cash asset exemption applies up until the later of: - 31 March 2012 or - 12 months from the date the client receives full settlement for their home and land

chunks.title: Full settlement for home and land — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Clients who were affected by the Canterbury earthquake and who were insured may negotiate settlements for the damage to their home and land from one or more of the following: - the Crown - Earthquake Commission - their insurance company Clients may receive one or more payments from any of the above. Full settlement is the date of the final payment that is due to complete the purchase/damage to their home and land. Example a client accepts the Government offer for purchase of their land and agrees to an offer of settlement from their insurance company. The client receives payments as follows: Date Received from Reason 2 February 2019 Crown Deposit for land 25 March 2019 Insurance Company Full settlement for house 1 April 2019 Crown Final payment for land The date of full settlement for the home and land is 1 April 2023. The client intends to rebuild, therefore these payments would not be included as a cash asset until 1 April 2023.

chunks.title: Retrospective exemption — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: This exemption applies retrospectively from 24 December 2010. Clients who had already received payments from the Earthquake Commission and/or private insurers, and have had their financial assistance reduced by interest earned on these payments can have their assistance reviewed.

chunks.title: Process — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When a client receives a payment you need to create a 'must view' note in CMS. The note should state: - the client has received a payment from the Earthquake Commission or another insurance company to repair damage caused by the Canterbury earthquake 2010 that must not be considered as income (including any interest earned off the payment) or as a cash asset - the date the client received the payment - whether the client intends to use the payment to repair or rebuild the home or purchase a further home - whether this is the final payment of the settlement and if so, the date the exemption will end - any assistance a client may be receiving or makes an application for will need to be reviewed at the end of the exemption period A bring-up needs to be added via BRUPI in SWIFTT to reassess entitlement.

chunks.title: End of the exemption period — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: At the end of the exemption period any remaining amount that a client has will be treated as a cash asset and income earned from investment of the remaining amount will be treated as chargeable income. Note where the exemption period allowed was less than 48 months and the client now intends to: - repair or rebuild their home or - purchase a replacement home you must extend the income and cash asset exemption to 48 months.

chunks.title: Payments from friendly and like societies — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Payments from friendly and like societies
Payments received from friendly and like societies are charged as income, however an additional income exemption of $2.00 per week is allowed for the following benefits:
- Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability $2.00 per week
- New Zealand Superannuation (Income tested), Jobseeker Support grandparented, Sole Parent Support, Supported Living Payment $104 per year
Deduct $2.00 from the payment before adding the income in SWIFTT. Add details in notes to the client event.
## Exception
Registered friendly societies normally pay a sick benefit on receiving medical evidence of incapacity. Some societies also make continuing payments to each member who has reached a certain age. Regard these extra payments as sick benefits for the purposes of section 422.
The above concession applies only while the client is receiving a sick benefit from a society registered as a Friendly Society or like society under the Friendly Societies and Credit Unions Act 1982. You will need to check with your regional solicitor whether a friendly or like society is approved for this exemption.
Please refer to the appropriate benefit type for more information on charging income, see:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Payments from home-based education and care services — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Payments from home-based education and care services
Home-based education and care services place children in private homes during the day while the parent(s) is in employment.
When clients provide care through home-based education and care services in their own homes, payments received are treated as income.
## Expenses are deducted from payments
If a client has expenses directly related to providing childcare these can be deducted from any payment received and are disregarded as income.
For more information see:
- Expenses deducted from home-based education and care payments
## Licensed home-based education and care services
For licensed home-based education caregivers regulated under the Education (Early Childhood Services) Regulations 2008, a portion of the payment received by the caregiver may be disregarded as income.

chunks.title: Payments from the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Payments from the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross)
The Canterbury Earthquake Commission was established in September 2010 to provide assistance to people affected by the Canterbury earthquake on 4 September 2010 and all its aftershocks (including the 22 February 2011 aftershock). This is a body set-up by the Mayors of affected areas to administer the fund created by donations made to the Red Cross Canterbury Earthquake appeal.
Note the Canterbury Earthquake Commission should not be confused with the Earthquake Commission (EQC) which is a different organisation.
## Income and cash asset exemption
Payments made by the Canterbury Earthquake Commission are not treated as chargeable income or as a cash asset for any financial assistance provided by Work and Income. This includes any income earned from any investment of the payment.
In cases where the client intends to use the payment to repair or rebuild the home or purchase a further home the exemption period is 48 months from the day after payment. In all other cases the exemption period is 12 months from the date of payment.
## Retrospective
This regulation applies from 13 September 2010. Clients who had already received payments from the Canterbury Earthquake Commission and have had their financial assistance reduced by interest earned on these payments can have their assistance reviewed.
## End exemption period
At the end of the exemption period any remaining amount that a client has will be treated as a cash asset.
## Process
When a client receives a payment you need to create a 'must view' note in CMS.
The note should state:
- the client has received a payment made by the Canterbury Earthquake Commission that must not be considered as income (including interest earned from the payment) and as a cash asset for 12 months
- the date the client received the payment
- the amount of the payment
- whether the client intends to use the payment to repair or rebuild the home or to purchase a new home and
- the expiry date of the 12 month exemption
A bring-up needs to be added via BRUPI in SWIFTT to reassess entitlement.
For more information see:
- Payments from Earthquake Commission and insurance companies (Canterbury Earthquake 2010 and 2011 aftershock)
- Payments from the Crown for the purchase of property in the Canterbury red zone

chunks.title: Payments from the Crown for the purchase of property in the Canterbury red zone — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: A client affected by the Canterbury Earthquake whose property has been designated in the red zone may accept a Government offer to purchase their home and/or land. When the offer is accepted, the Crown pays for the purchase price of their home and/or land in the red zone. The Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority (CERA) administers these payments on behalf of the Crown.

chunks.title: Income and cash asset exemption — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Payments made by the Crown for the purchase of red zone properties are not to be treated as income or a cash asset for the period set out below when determining entitlement to a main benefit and other assistance paid under the Social Security Act 2018. Examples include: - Accommodation Supplement - Away from Home Allowance - Community Cost Programme - Course Participation Costs - Funeral Grant - Home Help - Residential Care Subsidy - Seasonal Work Assistance - Special Benefit - Special Needs Grants - Special Transfer Allowance - Student Transfer Allowance Grant - Temporary Additional Support This includes any income earned from the investment of the payment.

chunks.title: Period of exemption — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: The exemption period is 48 months from the date of full settlement for their home and land (see below) where the client intends to use the payment to: - repair or rebuild their home or - purchase a replacement home In all other cases, except for clients applying for or receiving Residential Care Subsidy or Temporary Additional Support, the exemption period is 12 months from the date of full settlement for their home and land (see below). For clients who are applying for or receiving Residential Care Subsidy and Temporary Additional Support, where there is no intent to use the payment to repair or rebuild their home, or purchase a replacement home the payment is not exempt.

chunks.title: Full settlement for home and land — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Clients whose property has been designated in the red zone may opt to settle with the Government for the purchase of their home and land, or their land only. In cases where the client settles with the Government for the purchase of their home and land one or more payments may be received from the Crown. The date of full settlement is the date of the final payment from the Crown. Where the client settles with the Government for the purchase of the land only, the client will claim the damages to the home through the Earthquake Commission and insurance company. In these cases the client may receive one or more payments from the Crown and one or more payments from: - their insurance company and/or - the Earthquake Commission Full settlement is the date the client receives the final payment that is due to complete the purchase/settlement of damages to their home and land. Example a client accepts the Government offer for the purchase of their land and agrees to an offer of settlement from their insurance company. The client receives payments as follows: Date Received Reason 2 February 2014 Crown Deposit for land 25 March 2014 Insurance Company Full settlement for house 4 April 2014 Crown Final payment for land The date of settlement for the home and land is 4 April 2014. The client intends to rebuild, therefore these payments would not be included as a cash asset until 4 April 2018.

chunks.title: Process — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When a client receives a payment you need to create a 'must view' note in CMS. The note should state: - the client has received a payment from the Crown for the purchase of the home and/or land which is in the red zone in Canterbury that must not be considered as income (including any interest earned off the payment) or as a cash asset - the date the client received the payment - whether the client intends to use the payment to repair or rebuild the home or purchase a further home - whether this is the final payment of the settlement and if so, the date the exemption ends - any assistance a client may be receiving or makes an application for will need to be reviewed after 12 or 48 months of receiving the payment

chunks.title: End of exemption period — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: At the end of the exemption period any remaining amount that a client has will be treated as a cash asset, and income earned from investment of the remaining amount will be treated as chargeable income. Note where the exemption period allowed was 12 months, and the client now intends to: - repair or rebuild their home or - purchase a replacement home you must extend the income and cash asset exemption for a further 48 months. For more information see: - Payments from the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) - Payments from Earthquake Commission and insurance companies (Canterbury Earthquake 2010 and 2011 aftershock) - Residential Care Subsidy Exempt assets - Temporary Additional Support Cash assets

chunks.title: Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014
As a result of the Accommodation Supplement arrears due to the system processing error from 1993 to 2014, some clients will be issued a back payment to correct their entitlement. When this payment occurs the following applies:
## Lump sum payment exemption
Lump-sum payments made to clients to correct their entitlement to Accommodation Supplement, where they were affected by the system processing error, should be excluded from the cash asset test for the first 12 months following the date the client received the payment.
## Interest exemption
Any interest derived from a payment, which was made to a client to correct their entitlement to Accommodation Supplement, where they were affected by the system processing error, is exempt as income for the first 12 months after payment is made.

chunks.title: Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: After 1 April 2006, when Temporary Additional Support was introduced, some clients who were receiving Special Benefit would have been better off receiving Temporary Additional Support, but were not given an opportunity to apply for this assistance. This was an error by the Ministry of Social Development. Because of the error, a client may receive a back payment of Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Qualifications — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: A client may receive Temporary Additional Support arrears due to the Ministry’s error if the client: - was receiving Special Benefit on 1 April 2006 - would have received more assistance from Temporary Additional Support on or after 1 April 2006 - was advised by the Ministry on or after 18 August 2017 that they would have been better off receiving Temporary Additional Support at any point on or after 1 April 2006 - cancels Special Benefit from an earlier date - retrospectively applies for Temporary Additional Support for the period Special Benefit was cancelled Note clients who cancelled their Special Benefit after 1 April 2006 and before 18 August 2017 may still receive Temporary Additional Support arrears if they were advised by the Ministry on or after 18 August 2017 that they would have would have received more assistance from Temporary Additional Support. The Temporary Additional Support arrears is the net amount of the Temporary Additional Support payment a client would have received, less the Special Benefit paid for the same period.

chunks.title: Identifying affected clients — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Affected clients were identified and notified by the Ministry through the Alignment implementation - Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support. Some clients assessed as better off on Temporary Additional Support after 18 August 2017 but outside of the implementation may be eligible for arrears. For more information see:

chunks.title: Arrears payment is not income — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Arrears paid on or after 18 August 2017 to Special Benefit clients who would have been better off receiving Temporary Additional Support are a lump sum payment. Generally, the arrears should not be treated as income for the period the payment represents.

chunks.title: Cash asset exemption — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When determining entitlement to main benefits and other assistance paid under the Social Security Act 2018, Temporary Additional Support arrears paid to Special Benefit clients who would have been better off receiving Temporary Additional Support are not a cash asset for the first 12 months after the arrears payment is made. Examples include: - Accommodation Supplement - Advance Payment of Benefit - Away from Home Allowance - Community Cost Programme - Course Participation Costs - Funeral Grant - Home Help - Seasonal Work Assistance - Special Benefit - Special Needs Grants - Special Transfer Allowance - Student Allowance Transfer Grant - Temporary Additional Support This exemption only applies to Temporary Additional Support arrears paid on or after 18 August 2017 to Special Benefit clients who would have been better off receiving Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Income exemption — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Any income earned from the arrears is exempt as income for the first 12 months after the payment of the arrears is made.

chunks.title: End of exemption period — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: At the end of the first 12 months after the arrears are paid, any remaining amount that a client has is treated as a cash asset, and any income earned from investment of the remaining amount is treated as chargeable income.

chunks.title: Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination
Between 1 July 2013 and 1 June 2018, some Kāinga Ora tenants had their tenancies terminated because of methamphetamine contamination of a property.
Kāinga Ora has reviewed their zero tolerance methamphetamine contamination policies. As a result, some former tenants may get a lump sum payment.
From 30 November 2018 some clients may get a lump sum payment from Kāinga Ora for costs following the termination of their tenancy. When this payment is made, the following applies:
## Lump sum payment is not income
Generally, the lump sum payments are not treated as income for the period the payment represents.
## Cash asset exemption
These lump sum payments are not a cash asset for the first 12 months after the payments are made on or after 30 November 2018.
This exemption only applies to lump sum payments made on or after 30 November 2018.
Examples include:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Advance Payment of Benefit
- Away from Home Allowance
- Community Cost Programme
- Course Participation Costs
- Funeral Grant
- Home Help
- Seasonal Work Assistance
- Special Benefit
- Special Needs Grants
- Special Transfer Allowance
- Student Allowance Transfer Grant
- Temporary Additional Support
## Income exemption
Any income earned from the lump sum payment is exempt as income for the first 12 months after payment is made.
## End of exemption period
At the end of the first 12 months after the lump sum payment is made, any remaining amount that a client has is treated as a cash asset, and any income earned from investment of the remaining amount is treated as chargeable income.

chunks.title: Payments to victims of crime and their families — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Payments to victims of crime and their families
Victim Support offers a range of financial assistance to victims of crime and their families through the Victim Assistance Scheme.
Victim Support determines eligibility and administers the payments.
## Victim Assistance Scheme
Victim Support provides the following financial assistance through the Victim Assistance Scheme:
- Court attendance allowance - to support family members of a homicide victim to attend court proceedings if they lose income
- Travel and accommodation payments - to cover costs of attending trials, sentencing, hearings, and other justice proceedings
- Discretionary grant - to support family members of a homicide victim with immediate costs e.g. funeral expenses, travel to the scene
- Crime scene grant - to support a victim who has been displaced from their home because a police cordon has been put in place
## Income and cash asset exemption
Victim Assistance Scheme payments are not chargeable income or a cash asset for any MSD financial assistance for the first 12 months, after the date the client gets the payment.
This includes any income earned from investment of the payment.
## End of 12 month period
At the end of the 12 month period any remaining amount a client has will be treated as a cash asset.
Any income earned from the cash asset will be treated as chargeable income for any MSD financial assistance.

chunks.title: Private accident insurers — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Private accident insurers
For the period 1 July 1999 to 30 June 2000 private insurers were able to provide work related accident insurance cover.
From 1 July 2000, the Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) became the sole provider of accident insurance for all work and non-work injuries and has taken over all old clients from the private providers.
Some clients may still be receiving payments from these private insurers (if they had a work related accident between 1 July 1999 to 30 June 2000) but it will be now be paid by ACC. Any accident related payments that are still being received from private insurers are treated the same way as those from ACC. Any enquiries in regard to private providers should be directed to ACC.
For more information see:
- History of ACC
- Accident Compensation

chunks.title: Quick reference guide for the treatment of ACC payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: ACC Payment Description of ACC payment Effect on benefit A payment made to compensate for the loss of earnings as a result of injury. It is based on 80% of the weekly income before the injury occurred. It may also be paid for sensitive claims. Direct deduction from specified benefits. Note special provisions apply for New Zealand Superannuation. Weekly compensation payments started before 1 July 1999 A payment made to compensate for the loss of earnings as a result of injury. It is based on 80% of the weekly income before the injury occurred. If paid for a different reason to the benefit, it is charged as income. If the benefit is paid for the same reason as the weekly compensation it is a direct deduction. Weekly compensation for surviving spouses (can be received as a lump sum payment) Weekly compensation as a result of the death of their partner. May be paid as a converted lump sum or as weekly payments. Direct deduction from specified benefits. Lump sum payment for impairment For an injury that occurred after 1 April 2002, these payments compensate for the permanent loss of function caused by an injury. Not income and not a direct deduction. Excluded as a cash asset for Accommodation Supplement or Residential Care Subsidy for the first 12 months. Independence Allowance Assessed weekly but paid quarterly in advance, it is a tax-free allowance paid to recognise ongoing disability for an injury that occurred before 1 April 2002. Not income and not a direct deduction. Excluded as a cash asset for Accommodation Supplement or Residential Care Subsidy for the first 12 months. Survivor's grant A one-off payment to the partner, children and other dependents of someone whose death was the result of an injury. Capital payment and not income. Payments for attendant care, home help and rehabilitation services Payments made to purchase a service or to meet the cost of travel and accommodation for accessing rehabilitation services. Disregard the amount used to purchase services or pay costs. The balance (if any) is charged as income. ACC childcare payments ACC childcare payments are made to caregivers in recognition of loss of supervisory or personal care (or financial support to provide this care) provided by a deceased parent before their death due to personal injury covered by ACC. ACC childcare payments are not: - treated as income for benefit purposes or - deducted from the rate of or eligible hours when assessing Childcare Assistance For Orphans and Unsupported Childs Benefit, ACC childcare payments should be considered as "other income". ACC child weekly compensation

chunks.title: Quick reference guide for the treatment of ACC payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: ACC child weekly compensation payments are to compensate for income that would have been provided by a deceased parent. ACC child weekly compensation payments are: - a direct deduction from the caregiver's specified benefits - not income or a cash asset for Extra help assistance and hardship assistance New Zealand Superannuation payments depend on when weekly compensation and New Zealand Superannuation are granted, see: - New Zealand Superannuation and ACC weekly earnings-related compensation

chunks.title: Redundancy payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: A redundancy payment is a lump sum payment to compensate a person when their employer terminates their employment as their position is surplus to the employer's needs.

chunks.title: Cessation leave — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Cessation leave is a component of a redundancy payment that recognises the employees length of service to the employer. The amount paid is based on the number of years' continuous service the employee completed. Cessation leave has nothing to do with "leave" entitlements and does not affect the date employment ceased.

chunks.title: Being made redundant — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Redundancy can happen voluntarily, where an employee accepts redundancy willingly, or as an enforced decision. In both cases employees can get payments to compensate for loss of: - employment - tangible benefits or rights - prospects and promotions - status and security - income Redundancy must not be confused with other reasons for an employee losing their job, e.g. an employee who is unable to perform duties, or has been laid off due to misconduct.

chunks.title: What a redundancy payment is not — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: It is important to differentiate between the types of payments a person gets when their employment ends to know how they affect benefit entitlement. Redundancy payments do not include: - payments made solely due to a seasonal lay-off - payments to a company director to compensate for loss of office - payments for the completion of work specified in a contract or a fixed term engagement - payment in lieu of notice - severance payments - retirement payments or - payments that would have been paid as salary or wages if the person is not made redundant, e.g. holiday pay, performance payments, time in lieu Note some of these payments may affect the date employment ceased and may be included as income when calculating the length of the initial stand-down for a main benefit (where relevant).

chunks.title: How redundancy payments affect benefit payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Payment received before a benefit is granted Redundancy payments are included in the assessment of a person’s last 26 or 52 weeks' income to determine the length of their initial stand-down (where relevant). Redundancy payments do not affect the date employment ceased. Payment received after a benefit is granted When a client receiving a benefit has been working and having their earnings charged then receives a redundancy payment, this payment is not regarded as income for benefit purposes. However, it will be regarded as a cash asset and may affect any Extra Help the client is receiving. If the redundancy payment is received within 52 weeks of the client's employment ceasing, review the client's initial stand-down and commencement date.

chunks.title: Reimbursement requests from ACC reviews — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Reimbursement requests from ACC reviews
In some cases, ACC may review a client's entitlement to weekly compensation after they have been receiving it for a period of time.
When ACC review a client's weekly compensation payments, their benefit must be reassessed and arrears/debts established for the same period if the review changes their entitlement to benefit.
If ACC retrospectively reduce or cancel the client's weekly compensation, they will request a reimbursement from Work and Income for any period that the client was receiving or would otherwise have been entitled to a main benefit.
Note in most cases this is managed by the Central Processing Unit
For more information see:
- Clients waiting for compensation
- Backdating benefit when weekly compensation overpaid
- Effect on Extra help
- ACC weekly compensation
- Accident Compensation - Income [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Relationship Property Settlements — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Relationship Property Settlements
Relationship Property Settlements are not chargeable income for benefit purposes whether they are paid as a lump sum or periodic payment.
Generally Relationship Property Settlements are paid as a lump sum, however in some cases these may be paid as a periodic payment. Any income from the investment of the proceeds of a Relationship Property Settlements is chargeable income for benefit purposes.
Money received from a Relationship Property Settlements may also affect entitlement to extra help such as Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit.

chunks.title: Rent and board payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: From 2 March 2026, when a client gets rent or board payments from someone living in the same premises, the accommodation income must be assessed to determine whether there is chargeable income. Rent and board payments for periods prior to 2 March 2026 are charged as income based on previous settings. When accommodation income is more than the client's accommodation costs for the part of the property they live in, the excess amount is income and must be charged against any income tested assistance that uses the definition of income in the Social Security Act 2018. This includes but is not limited to main benefits and supplementary assistance. Income from rent and board is charged over the period it represents. When a property is tenanted or owned by more than one person, the client who gets the payment will have it assessed as income. When the payment is split between multiple tenants or owners (e.g., gets paid into a joint account), the payment will be split when assessing it as income. Note for board payments received as part of a business venture, such as a boarding house, bed and breakfast or home stay, then the income from the business should be charged and the payments will not be part of the accommodation income. For more information see: - Homestays

chunks.title: Accommodation income — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When a client gets rent or board payments from someone living in the same premises, they will have accommodation income. Clients are considered to be living in the same premises when they live in the same part of the property (e.g. not self-contained). Accommodation income includes: - rent a client gets from another person (not being additional occupants or boarders) residing in the same premises, except where the person paying the rent is in a self-contained part of the premises or the rent payment is part of the income of a business on the premises - 62% of payments for board a client gets from another person residing in the same premises, except where the board payment is part of the income of a business on the premises Note 38% of payments for board are excluded as income.

chunks.title: Accommodation costs for part of the property lived in — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When a client doesn't live in part of their property, that part of the property is deducted from their accommodation costs. The client's accommodation cost is the amount they pay for rent, board or home ownership. To get the cost of the part of the property lived in by the client, reduce their accommodation costs by the parts of the property that are: - primarily used for business purposes, - self-contained and rented to another person/s, or - rented to another person/s who does not reside there Note when a client rents out part of their property, rental income is calculated separately. For more information see: Rental income when part of property is rented out. Example - self-employed homeowner with a boarder Nusrat gets Jobseeker Support and owns a two-bedroom house. His home ownership costs are $500 every four weeks ($125 a week) and he uses 20% of his home to operate a business. The business is not generating income yet. The cost for the part of the property used for the business is $25 a week. He has taken in a boarder to get some extra income. His boarder pays $450 a week. The accommodation income is $279 per week (62% of the board payment). Nusrat's accommodation income is more than his accommodation costs for the part of the property being lived in by him and the excess amount is chargeable income. Therefore, $179 a week is charged against his Jobseeker Support. Note he doesn't qualify for Accommodation Supplement as he has no weekly qualifying accommodation costs. Cost of part of property lived in Total homeownership costs for property Total A $125.00pw Total square metres Total B 300m2 Square metres of property that is used for business purposes Total C 60m2 Proportion of property used for business purposes Total C ÷ Total B = Total D 0.2 Cost of part of property not lived in Total A x Total D = Total E $25.00pw Cost of part of property lived in Total A - Total E $100.00pw Accommodation income Board payment $450.00pw Accommodation income (62% of the board payment) $279.00pw Chargeable income Accommodation income $279.00pw Less cost of part of property the client lives in $100.00pw Equals chargeable income $179.00pw

chunks.title: Rental income when part of property is rented out — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Rental income when part of property is rented out
When a client rents out a portion of their home property use the following guidelines. Their property may have separate facilities for the tenant but the facilities are still an integral part of the home and the property will only be on one Certificate of Title.
When a client rents out part of their property, only expenses attributable to the rented portion of the home can be deducted. To determine the expenses for the portion of the home rented out, calculate the area of the rental portion as a percentage of the total home. The rental area is the area of the home that is used only by the tenant and does not include any common areas that are used by the client and tenant.
To determine the proportion of expenses use the following formula:

For an example see:
- Accommodation Supplement Homeowner renting out part of their property

chunks.title: Rental property income — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Rental property income
Generally, the assessable income from a rental property is the difference between the actual rent the client receives and the allowable expenses.
## Allowable expenses
When someone has a rental property and you are determining income the following expenses are considered allowable and can be deducted from the rental income:
- interest payments on money borrowed for the purchase of the rental property but not capital instalments for the reduction of mortgage
- rates
- house insurance
- agent fees and commission if a property manager or agent is used
- repairs and maintenance
- other fees for example bank administration fees for the mortgage, tenancy agreement costs, any valuation required for mortgage purposes, accounting fee's, etc
These are the only expenses that are taken into account for rental property income.
Verification of expenses is required, and should be kept by anyone renting a property for Inland Revenue.
## Calculating assessable income from a rental property
To assess the income a client receives from the rental property, use the following chart:
Rental income assessment
Amount
Total rent received per annum
$
Allowable expenses for property (per annum):
Mortgage interest only
$

$

$
Only record the assessable rental property income where there is a profit.
When a client rents out part of property, only a portion of the expenses can be deducted from the total rent. For more information see:
- Rental income when part of the property is rented out
If the rental property is set up as a business, assess the business income. For more information see:
## Multiple rental properties
To assess the rental income when a client has more than one rental property, add all the rents together and subtract the total allowable expenses from all the properties. This will enable any loss on one property to be offset against the profit on another property.
## Review of annual income or Income Related Rent
When assessing the rental property income at the clients' review of annual income, not all allowable expenses need to be confirmed if the recurring expenses (eg rates and insurance) have been confirmed at application and the client indicates they haven't changed. Expenses which may need to be checked are:
- those recurring expenses where the amount being claimed has changed considerably
- where the expense is for repairs and maintenance

chunks.title: Repairs and maintenance — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When making decisions about whether a cost can be included as a repair or maintenance allowable expense in a rental income assessment, you need to consider: - were the repairs or maintenance essential in order to maintain the house and property to a habitable standard - were the repairs and maintenance required to meet the client and/or their tenants current housing needs - have the costs claimed been verified with receipts which, if necessary, are detailed enough to verify the work undertaken was essential or needed for maintenance Expenses incurred in developing a rental property which may increase the value of the property, or enable a higher rent to be charged, are not an allowable expense. For example, additions to the property (including painting costs directly associated with the additions) would not be an allowable expense.

chunks.title: Essential repairs — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Repairs to existing essential services that may be considered allowable expenses include: - water - gas - power - sewerage services (including showers, toilets, sinks and the drains attached to them) Other repairs can be considered if they are essential to: - the structural stability of the house or property (repairs to buildings or sheds on the property that are not used for accommodation purposes are not to be considered) - wiring and light fittings - septic tanks (provided repairs have not been paid as a non recoverable Special Needs Grant) - any repairs required to meet building regulations

chunks.title: Major appliance repairs — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Repairs to any major appliance that helps maintain the house in a habitable state can be included, such as: - gas or electric stove and - hot water cylinder The cost of repairs or replacement of household contents is not considered an allowable expense, for example: - microwaves - furnishings - fridges and - washing machines Note if the washing machine or fridge is included in the tenancy agreement then repairs or replacement may be included. Repairs that are allowable expenses can only be included in the rental income assessment if the bills are incurred while the benefit is being received.

chunks.title: Maintenance expenses — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Maintenance expenses that may be considered an allowable expense include any reasonable maintenance carried out on the house or grounds, which is necessary to prevent damage or substantial deterioration to the house. This may include but is not limited to: - clearing chimneys - replacing broken windows - removing tress (when necessary) - painting (internal and external) if required Painting expenses can be considered an allowable expense only if the costs are incurred while receiving a benefit. Maintenance costs do not include: - mowing lawns - work carried out for cosmetic purposes For help deciding whether repairs and maintenance expenses are considered an allowable expense for calculating rental income, contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds
Some clients will have a historic review of their financial means assessment for Residential Care Subsidy and may get a lump sum refund.
These refunds are exempt from means testing for a period of 12 months from the date the payment is made.
## Retrospective reviews
A decision clarifying how the Ministry of Social Development can exercise discretion for including deprivation in financial means assessments for Residential Care Subsidy was made by the Court of Appeal on 31 May 2019.
Clients (or their estates) can request a historic review of their financial means assessment to make sure the Ministry applied discretion in relation to deprivation correctly.
The historic review may find that a client's previous financial means assessment was incorrect, and they were assessed to pay too much towards the cost of their residential care.
These clients may get a lump sum refund of Residential Care Subsidy and/or other payments they, or their partner, were entitled to.
Residential Care Subsidy refunds due to historic reviews may include any or all of the following:
- Residential Care Subsidy
- a benefit, eg Emergency Benefit
- extra help, eg Special Disability Allowance, Disability Allowance and Clothing Allowance
## Cash assets and income exemption
Residential Care Subsidy refunds due to historic reviews are not treated as income or cash assets for the first 12 months after the payment is made, on or after 11 June 2021.
This exemption only applies to the client whose financial means assessment is being reviewed, and their partner (if any).
If both the client and their partner have died, and a refund of Residential Care Subsidy due to a historic review is made to their estate or another family member, then this exemption does not apply.
Note Residential Care Subsidy refunds not made as part of a historic review are not exempt from means testing.
## End of exemption period
At the end of the first 12 months after the refund is made, any remaining amount a client has is treated as a cash asset for the client and their partner (if any).
Any income earned from the cash asset is also treated as income after the first 12 months, and a review of income may be initiated.

chunks.title: Royalties — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Royalties
When clients declare income from royalties, there is generally a contract negotiated which should state the details of how much and over what period any royalties will be paid. The income from royalties should be charged against the benefit for the period the contract represents.
Royalty payments may be received infrequently and may comprise returns from various sources for differing periods such as music, advertising or literary works. It is reasonable for you to estimate the royalty income over a set period depending on the individual circumstances of the client and review the income charge as appropriate.
A client may receive royalties from the sale of things such as:
- Advertisements
- Recordings
- Books
- Manuscripts
- Film
## Self employed
For those clients who are operating as a sole trader, company or small business, any earnings generated from royalties are to be assessed as business income. That is you need to look at their business accounts to determine the income to be charged.
Please refer to the appropriate benefit type for more information on charging income, see:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit
