chunks.title: Sale of assets — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Sale of assets
A once only capital payment received from the sale or exchange of assets is not chargeable income.
Assets include:
- a property
- a business
- a car
- a boat or
- other chattels
Any income from the investment of the proceeds from the sale of assets is chargeable income for benefit purposes.
Money received from the sale of an asset may also affect entitlement to Extra help such as Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit.
For more information see:
- Payment made by instalment
- TradeMe or similar trading sites
- Accommodation Supplement Cash assets
- Temporary Additional Support Cash assets test
- Special Benefit Cash assets test

chunks.title: Allowable expenses — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text: Allowable expenses are the necessary costs that a sole trader pays in the day-to-day running of their business. A sole trader's gross income is reduced by their allowable expenses to determine the net profit before tax used to assess their entitlement to benefits and other assistance, and the rate payable. Generally, we will accept a sole trader's net profit before tax when supported by evidence. We may make some adjustments to their net profit before tax if a sole trader's business accounts show expenses that have been included that are not allowable business expenses, or are mixed use, i.e. personal and business use.

chunks.title: Losses — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text: When reviewing income for a client who is a sole trader and they made a loss during the previous 52 weeks when they were getting a benefit, we need to determine when that loss was made and adjust their income charge for the same period. Their rate of benefit was based on their estimated future income. When their accounts are available their rate of payment needs to be checked as they may have been underpaid because their income was estimated. If we cannot identify the actual period when the loss happened, the amount should be averaged across 52 weeks. Example Brian's lawnmowing business made a loss last year as Brian did not earn enough to pay all his business expenses. Because this loss was in the past, it should not be included in assessing Brian's estimated income for the next 52 weeks. However, it may affect any entitlements Brian received in the previous 52 weeks. When completing a review of Brian's income, we ask for more information about the loss. Brian tells us he did not have any lawnmowing jobs for four months due to a combination of bad weather and his worsening health. Brian has letters from his doctor and records of cancelled bookings that confirm this. Brian was getting a benefit during that time based on his accounts from the year before when he made a small profit. Brian's payments must be reviewed to ensure he was getting the correct rate of payment when he had no income. Brian will get arrears for the period he was underpaid.

chunks.title: Bad debts — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text: A bad debt is a debt that cannot be collected, for example if a customer orders a customised item and does not pay for it. Historic bad debt expenses (including debt recovery costs) are not an allowable expense for determining a client's current or estimated future income for benefits or other assistance. Bad debts should be treated in the same way as losses. Note this level of assessment should only be needed if a sole trader does not have business accounts.

chunks.title: Losses from separate income sources — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text: Sole traders may have more than one source of income. When a sole trader makes a net loss from one source of income and makes a net profit on another income source, the net loss amount must not be deducted from the other income source. It is treated as nil. A review of the client's income is needed to make sure the amount being charged reflects the net loss The profit from any other business also needs to be checked against historical benefit payments in case it reduces the rate payable. Example Kevin gets New Zealand Superannuation and a Disability Allowance. Kevin is a sole trader operating as a fishing charter operator between December and April each year. The business is weather dependent. Last summer Kevin's fishing charter business made a loss due to bad weather. Although he didn't have many charters booked, he still had to maintain his certification and compliance costs. Kevin and his sister own a rental property and Kevin gets a share of the net rental income after the expenses are paid. Kevin has 3 income sources and wants to deduct the fishing charter loss from his other income. The fishing charter loss cannot be deducted from Kevin's other income. Kevin's gross weekly income is calculated as follows. Type of income Gross weekly amount New Zealand superannuation (single living alone at 1 April 2026) $647.37 Rental income (gross rental income less allowed business costs divided by 2) $196.79 Fishing charter business income -$115.38 Total income $844.16 Kevin's income is still under the threshold for Disability Allowance. His entitlement remains the same.

chunks.title: Business assets and depreciation — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text: Capital assets are assets useful to a business over a long period and cost more than the usual day to day running costs of the business. Capital assets may be property, infrastructure or equipment. Capital assets lose value over time as they get older. This loss of value is called depreciation. Sole traders can claim depreciation as a deduction expense each tax year. There are 2 different approaches to depreciation, immediate deduction or depreciation. When a capital asset is purchased by a sole trader they can claim the full cost as an immediate deduction and spread the depreciation of the new asset over several years. The future replacement of that asset can't be claimed as an immediate replacement because it has deducted through the depreciation approach. A sole trader can claim immediate replacement costs and depreciation for different capital assets in their business accounts. To determine a sole trader's net profit before tax we must choose the correct approach for each client's situation and apply it as follows.

chunks.title: Immediate deduction approach — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text: An immediate deduction is when the full cost of the asset is claimed as an expense at the time the asset is purchased. Immediate deductions are allowable expenses and should not be added back to a sole trader's net profit before tax. Example Lagi is a widow with 3 children under 14 years old and is getting Sole Parent Support. She makes traditional dresses and hats on commission for local celebrations and community events. Lagi's sewing machine breaks down and needs to be replaced. Lagi purchases a new sewing machine for $650.00. This is recorded as an immediate deduction in Lagi's business accounts and is an allowable business expense. It is not added back to Lagi's net profit before tax when calculating her income for benefit purposes.

chunks.title: Depreciation approach — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text: Depreciation is when a sole trader is making deductions in their business accounts over time to reflect the asset's loss of value (i.e. spreading the cost of the asset over its lifespan). Depreciation is an allowable business expense. The partial cost to replace an asset set aside for the future by a sole trader (depreciation approach) is an allowable business expense. When a client has used depreciation for a specific asset, they cannot claim immediate deduction when the asset is replaced in the future. Example Brian's accounts for his lawn mowing business show he replaced his industrial ride-on mower worth $8,500 last year. This was an immediate deduction. Brian has also started deducting depreciation using a depreciation rate of 16% of the value of his new ride-on mower. Both the replacement cost and the depreciation amount are allowable expenses and are not income for benefit purposes. When Brian's mower needs to be replaced in the future, he has already had the benefit of depreciation and the immediate deduction option won't be available to him next time he needs to replace it.

chunks.title: No evidence of depreciation costs — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text: If a sole trader has deducted money for depreciation which is not replacing a capital asset necessary for the business, and is available to the person to support themselves the amount deducted should be added back to the sole trader's net profit before tax. Deducting money for depreciation that is not intended to replace a capital asset may be considered as an act of deprivation. Whether deprivation has occurred should be determined after the sole trader's income assessment is completed.

chunks.title: Business related training — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Business related training
Some training expenses are allowable for income assessment purposes.
Formal training for the sole trader or employees that is directly related to an existing business operation is an allowable business expense if the business is already trading.
Training costs in preparation for starting a business are not allowable expenses.
When a sole trader has identified training expenses in their business accounts, MSD may need to ask the client to explain what the training was for and how it relates to their current business.
## Example 1
Brian has a lawnmowing business, he uses his business account to pay $150 for a short training course on repairing and servicing lawnmowers so he can perform these tasks himself.
The cost of the course is an allowable expense because it relates directly to his existing business.
## Example 2
Brian uses his lawnmowing business account to pay $200 for a beginners beekeeping course because he'd like to have some beehives as another income stream.
This is not an allowable business expense because he has not set up a beekeeping business, so it must be added back to his net profit before tax.

chunks.title: Clothing — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Clothing
Buying and looking after clothing items that are necessary for the operation of the business for example overalls for a painter or yard boots for a gardener, are allowable expenses that can be deducted from a sole trader's gross income. This includes the cost of cleaning or repairing these items.
Personal clothing items that are not necessary for the business and have been paid for by the business and claimed as an expense are added back to the net profit (or loss) before tax when assessing income for benefit purposes.
## Example 1
Brian buys a pair of steel-capped work boots and a Hi-Viz vest to wear when he is mowing lawns.
These are necessary for work and are an allowable expense.
## Example 2
Lagi buys a coat and hat she wears for some business meetings as well as for church and other social occasions.
These are personal clothing items and are not an allowable business expense.

chunks.title: Deprivation of income — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Deprivation of income
Deprivation is when a person or their partner directly or indirectly gives away their assets or income for less value than they get in exchange.
They have put themselves at a financial disadvantage that means they may qualify for a benefit, or a higher rate of benefit.
The deprivation does not have to be deliberate. We don't need to decide whether a business expense was necessary when calculating income.
Example Brian is a sole trader with a lawnmowing business that has made a loss. Brian decides to get new branding for his work clothing and work vehicle. This is money that Brian could have used for his personal living expenses.
The expenses or decisions may need to be discussed with the client to determine whether deprivation has happened, and whether it is appropriate to grant, cancel or reduce the rate of benefit they get.
When we have confirmed a person (or their partner) has deprived themselves of income or property, the deprivation may affect their (or their partner's) qualification for a benefit, or their rate of benefit. We need to consider the following:
- Does our assessment correctly identify the client's income?
- If we use discretion to include deprived income and reduce the rate of benefit or decline the grant of benefit, does the client have resources to support themselves?
- Does our assessment help the client to find or stay in paid employment?
We need to look at each act of deprivation and decide whether to use discretion to include the deprived assets or income back into the assessment as though the deprivation had not occurred.
This requires consideration of the consequences of using discretion. We need to use discretion to decide whether to:
- refuse to grant a benefit or
- cancel or reduce a benefit already granted or
- grant a benefit at a reduced rate
If including deprived income in an assessment would result in the client not getting a benefit and there is evidence the client has no income or resources to support themselves, including the deprived income charge would not be appropriate.
If deprivation is identified, you may need to ask for advice before making a decision.

chunks.title: Donations — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Donations
A donation made in a fair value exchange for goods or services received (for example advertising in exchange for plumbing work) is not a true donation, and is considered as goods or services received in lieu of money, and treated as an allowable expense.
Donations for personal reasons are not an allowable expense.
## Example
Brian donates $200 to his local RSA each year because his father is a veteran, he pays the donation out of his business account.
This is not a business related expense because the donation is for a personal reason, and the donated amount is added back to Brian's net profit (or loss) before tax

chunks.title: Drawings — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Drawings
Any money that a sole trader withdraws from their business is called drawings. Generally, MSD uses a sole trader's net profit (or loss) before tax as their income for benefit purposes not drawings.
Drawings may need to be added back to a sole trader's net profit (or loss) if they have been recorded as a business expense in their accounts.
This will depend on the source of the drawings. The source needs to be confirmed by the client if this is not clear in their business accounts.
## Treating drawings as income
Drawings are only income if they add to the resources of the sole trader. They do not add to the resources of the sole trader if the drawings are a loan or have paid for a capital asset, for example new equipment for the business.
Drawings from a sole trader's net profit withdrawn for personal use may add to the resources of the client and should be added back to their net profit before tax if they do.
## Example 1 - including drawings in the assessment of net profit
Ngaire had a successful month of sales in December and made a higher than usual net profit. She withdrew $500 from her business bank account and recorded this in her accounts as business expenses.
When calculating Ngaire's income, MSD asks her about the drawings, she confirms that she withdrew the money to pay for Christmas presents for her family.
MSD adds the $500 back to Ngaire's net profit because the drawings were not a loan or net profit used for a business expense, they were for personal use.
## Example 2 - drawings not income
Lagi has 3 children and gets Sole Parent Support. She works as a sole trader making traditional dresses and hats for local celebrations and community events.
Lagi business accounts show she withdrew $50 a week from her business account over a period of 20 weeks ($1,000).
MSD ask Lagi to confirm and verify the source of this money. Lagi provides a loan contract to MSD confirming the amount loaned, the amount to be repaid, the date the loan was made to Lagi and the date the loan term ends.
MSD does not add the $1,000 back to Lagi's net profit before tax because a loan that must be repaid is not income.

chunks.title: Entertainment — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Entertainment
Entertainment expenses directly related to the running of the business are allowable expenses and can be deducted from a sole trader's gross income.
Personal entertainment costs paid by the business are not allowable expenses and should be added back to the net profit before tax.
## Example 1
Lagi has a sewing business making traditional dresses and hats and hosts a monthly social meal in her home for her neighbours and church friends.
Sometimes these occasions result in sewing commissions for Lagi.
These meals are a social, not business activity and the cost of providing the meals is not an allowable expense.
## Example 2
Lagi serves refreshments (tea, coffee, fruit juice, biscuits and cake) for clients who book an appointment to get a new dress or hat made.
The expense of providing these refreshments is allowable.

chunks.title: General unspecified expenses — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## General unspecified expenses
We can accept business expenses directly related to the income earned from a sole trader's business.
Sometimes business accounts will show general unspecified expenses or miscellaneous expenses which can cover all sorts of costs that may be business related or personal.
We need to ask the sole trader to identify which expenses are related to the business and which are personal. Any expenses that are not identified or are identified as personal are not allowable expenses and should be added back to the sole trader's net profit (or loss) before tax.
## Example
Brian's business accounts show other expenses of $540. MSD asks Brian about the expenses, and he explains that he often buys his lunch in-between jobs.
This is not an allowable business expense and MSD adds the $540 back to his net profit before tax.

chunks.title: Gifts and koha — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Gifts and koha
Gifts or koha can be money, or goods, or services.
When a sole trader receives a one-off gift or a koha without giving something in return, it is not income.
The value of gifts or koha given to a sole trader in exchange for goods or services should be treated as income in the same way as goods and services instead of money.
If a sole trader gives a gift or a koha and does not get something in return we should consider if deprivation has occurred.
Periodic gifts of money received by a sole trader with no obligation to be repaid should be treated as income.

chunks.title: Goods and services instead of money — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Goods and services instead of money
Goods and services received by a sole trader instead of money are treated as business income.
MSD calculates the value in money of the goods or services received and adds this back into the business net profit (or loss) before tax.
## Example
Brian's neighbour Mike is a plumber. Brian has a lawn mowing business and has been mowing Mike's lawn in exchange for repairing his leaky shower.
This would have cost Brian $300 if he had paid for the work.
The cost of the plumbing work Mike has done for Brian is added back to Brian's net profit before tax.

chunks.title: Holiday home or boat expenses — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Holiday home or boat expenses
If a sole trader uses a holiday home or boat for business purposes, for example if they hold an event for potential clients using fuel for the boat or generator for the holiday home, these expenses should be treated as business entertainment expenses.
If a sole trader uses their business to pay for repairs and maintenance of a holiday home or boat these are not allowable expenses.
The client needs to tell us whether the business paid any non-business costs relating to the holiday home or boat.
All personal use that has been claimed or recorded in their business accounts as a business expense is added back to the net profit (or loss) before tax as income.
Example Andrew is a sole trader who operates a small golfing tourism business and holds an annual function at his family’s holiday home to showcase his business to tourism companies. Expenses directly related to hosting the function are allowable business expenses and are deducted from his gross income.
More information may be requested from the sole trader to check if the holiday home or boat is owned solely by them and if it should be considered as a realisable asset. Assets not owned in full by the client may not be realisable.
Note while there is no cash asset test for main benefit purposes, holiday homes, boats and other non-business property a person owns may be “realisable assets” for other financial assistance, such as Accommodation Supplement.
## Exceptional circumstances
There is an exception to the cash asset test on grounds of hardship for Jobseeker Support, Youth Payment, Young Parent Payment, Emergency Benefit and Emergency Maintenance Allowances.

chunks.title: Home office — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Home office
Home office expenses include running an office from a sole trader's home, based on the floor area of the house. They can claim a portion of their home office costs as a business expense for tax purposes.
Sole traders who are renting can claim a proportion of their rent as a mixed-use business cost for tax purposes. If they have a mortgage on their home they can claim some of their rates, insurance and mortgage interest as business expenses.
When a sole trader can show they have business expenses, they can either:
- calculate the % of home space used as office and apportion their allowable expenses, or
- use the square metre rate option provided by Inland Revenue
When a sole trader is claiming business related expenses for their home office, the portion of the home used for the business may affect their entitlement to or the rate payable of some types of extra help the client is entitled to get, e.g. Accommodation Supplement.
For more information see:
- Using your home for your business - Inland Revenue
## Example
Lagi rents her home and pays $600 per week. Lagi uses the ‘percentage’ of home space used for business to calculate her home office expenses.
Lagi uses 8% of the house as a sewing room/home office and claims home office expenses of $2,496 per year ($48 per week) in her accounts. The amount claimed as an expense should be considered when determining the business income.
Lagi gets Accommodation Supplement and the amount that Lagi claims as a home office expense is deducted from her rent when calculating her weekly qualifying accommodation costs as $552 per week ($600 - $48).
The $48 that Lagi claims as a home office expense cannot be included as part of her weekly qualifying accommodation cost for Accommodation Supplement. This is also the same for Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit.

chunks.title: Identifying income from self-employment — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Identifying income from self-employment
All self-employed people need to provide business accounts of some kind to Inland Revenue for tax purposes. Inland Revenue advises self-employed people to keep their business records for at least 7 years, as they may be audited during this period.
These accounts should be used as a starting point for assessing a client's business income.
The records of a client's business accounts need to be available to confirm their income when assessing entitlement to income tested assistance and ensure the correct rate is paid.
## Multiple income sources
When a self-employed person gets income from more than one business, for example if they are a sole trader working as an electrician and have a partnership, trust or company that rents property, they may have more than one set of accounts.
Or there might be one set of accounts that includes their income from all sources, which makes it difficult to identify the income from the sole trader business.
Income from partnerships, trusts and companies have different accounting rules.
In these cases you may need to seek advice before making a decision.

chunks.title: Income equalisation deposits — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Income equalisation deposits
When a business has been running for more than 12 months, and the client has accounts showing income equalisation scheme deposits are being made, the self-employed client should be requesting a refund of these deposits from Inland Revenue before they apply for a benefit.
The client will need to provide some form of evidence to show they have income below the income threshold, such as an accounts statement, or bank statements.
They must also meet all the other qualifications for support.
## Exception
Sole parents and grandparented Jobseeker Support clients can work full-time in self-employment for a temporary period provided their income when assessed over a 52 week period does not fully reduce the benefit.

chunks.title: Internet and phone — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Internet and phone
A sole trader may use their home internet and phone for business purposes. They are allowed to claim a percentage of this usage under home office costs.
When a sole trader client gets other financial assistance from MSD to help pay for home internet and phone charges they use for their business activity, the portion of costs that are allowable business expenses must be deducted from the total costs they are asking for support to help cover.
## Example
Lagi rents her home and pays $590 per week. Lagi uses the ‘percentage’ of home space used for business to calculate her home office expenses. Lagi uses 8% of the house as a sewing room/home office and claims home office expenses of $2,496 per year ($48 per week) in her accounts.
If Lagi applies for Disability Allowance or Temporary Additional Support to cover her internet and phone costs, we have to deduct the portion of her internet costs that are paid by the business.
The monthly internet and phone bill is $75. We have to deduct the 8% that is paid by the business ($6) and assess Lagi's internet and phone costs using the lower amount of $69 ($79 minus $6).

chunks.title: Legal expenses — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Legal expenses
If a client's business accounts include legal expenses, it is reasonable for us to check whether the expenses are business related.
Some legal expenses incurred by a self-employed person in the operation of their business may be allowable expenses.
Personal legal costs not related to the running of the business should be treated as income and added to the net profit (or loss) before tax if they have been claimed as an expense.
Each case must be considered on the facts. We may need to ask the client for more information about their expenses if we cannot clearly identify if there are business related or personal legal costs.
## Example 1
Brian pays a lawyer to draft a standard contract for his customers to sign when they decide to use him as their regular lawn mower service.
As the costs are directly related to the operation of his business, this is an allowable expense.
## Example 2
Brian gets a speeding ticket while driving his work vehicle and hires a lawyer to challenge it.
The legal fees Brian pays to challenge the ticket are not an allowable business expense.

chunks.title: Net profit — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Net profit
Income from self-employment for sole traders for benefits and other financial assistance is generally their net profit before tax.
- Gross income less allowable business expenses = net profit before tax
Gross income means the total income of a business before any expenses or tax is deducted.
Net profit before tax means the difference between a sole trader's gross business income and what is left after their allowable business expenses have been deducted, and before tax is deducted.
If the difference is negative, it is called a net loss.
Net profit before tax or net loss is what we use as the starting point for assessing a sole trader's income.
Some businesses may refer to net income before tax in their accounts, which has the same meaning.
Net profit before tax should be used as the starting point for assessing business income for benefit purposes.
For example, a sole trader hairdresser’s business earns $60,000 gross income per year. If the hairdresser paid $35,000 in business expenses each year, their net profit before tax is $25,000 or $480.76 per week ($25,000 divided by 52).
## Adjusted net profit
Adjusted net profit is when we add expenses that are not allowed back to the net profit before tax. For example:
- donations made for personal reasons
- losses from other business activities
- clothing items that are not needed for business purposes (e.g. school uniforms), or
- the value of goods and services received instead of money

chunks.title: Personal and business mixed-use expenses — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Personal and business mixed-use expenses
Sole traders can deduct business related expenses from their business income.
Personal (non-business) expenses paid by the business are income for benefit purposes and must be added back to the net profit (or loss) before tax if they have been deducted as an expense.
When an asset is used for both personal and business activities, for example a vehicle, the expenses that relate to these items need to be apportioned. That is they need to be identified as either business or personal expenses.
Personal items paid for by the business and deducted as business expenses are income and must be added back to the net profit (or loss) before tax.
When a sole trader is claiming business related expenses for their home office, car, or internet and telephone charges, these deductions may affect their entitlement to or the rate payable of some types of extra help the client is entitled to get, e.g. Accommodation Supplement.
Clients must be advised their income includes any amounts identified for personal use, that have been deducted as a business expense.
The most common types of mixed-use expenses include:
- Home office
- Vehicle
- Internet and phone
- Holiday homes and boats
- Training
- Legal expenses
- Clothing
- Entertainment

chunks.title: Sale of assets or capital assets — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text: When a sole trader sells a business asset after it has been either immediately deducted or depreciated MSD will need to check whether an adjustment to their benefit is needed.

chunks.title: Immediate deduction — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text: When an immediately deducted asset is sold, the lesser of the following amounts must be included as income in that income (business) year: - The amount that the sole trader sold the asset for, or - The amount immediately deducted by the sole trader when the asset was purchased (the asset's original cost) Example Tammy has purchased a new generator for her spray-painting business for $5,000. At the time of purchase, the cost of the generator was immediately deducted as an expense, offsetting some of the gross income received by the business. Six months later, Tammy decided to sell the Generator for $4,500. The proceeds from this sale should now be assessed as income as the business had already claimed the cost of the generator as an expense. If Tammy decided to use the proceeds of this sale to purchase another generator, the cost of that generator may be deducted from the gross income of the business as a separate capital asset.

chunks.title: Depreciation approach — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text: Depreciation is an estimate of the value that an asset loses over time. This means that when a depreciated asset is sold, an adjustment is needed to correct the difference between the assets book value (the original cost minus the accumulated depreciation and the amount the asset was sold for. When a depreciated asset is sold for more than its book value, an adjustment is needed to show that the sole trader depreciated the asset at a higher rate than the asset lost value. This adjustment will increase the sole trader's gross profit. When a depreciated asset is sold for more than its original price, the sole trader only needs to account for the accumulated depreciation on that asset as income. That is because the amount received by the sole trader that is in excess of the original purchase price is a capital gain and not treated as income. This means that when an asset is sold for more than its book value the lesser of the following amounts must be added to the gross profit in that income year: - The amount the sole trader sold then asset for, minus its book value, or - The total amount of depreciation claimed against the asset over its lifetime (accumulated depreciation) Example Tammy purchased a new generator for her spray-painting business for $5,000. At the time of this purchase, the cost of the generator was not immediately deducted and was instead deducted over time using the depreciation approach. Tammy's business is already generating enough income to support her, so the depreciation approach was most appropriate for her circumstances. Tammy believes that the generator will only last her five years and will not be worth anything after that time; she therefore applies depreciation at a rate of 20% per year. Two years later, Tammy sells the generator. Tammy has depreciated 40% of the value of the generator ($2,000), meaning that the generator's book value is $3,000. The amount of money that Tammy received tells us what approach to take. If Tammy receives $2,500.00 for the sale of the generator, there is a $500 shortfall between the amount that has been claimed as an expense, and what the actual expense to the business was. As such, an additional $500 should be included as a business expense when calculating the net profit of the business to ensure that the entire $2,500 expense to the business is recorded.

chunks.title: Depreciation approach — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text: If Tammy receives $4,500 for the sale of the generator, then $2,000 of depreciation expense has been claimed when the business has only lost $500 over the generator's life. In these circumstances, a review must be conducted and $1,500 must be added to the sole trader's gross income for that income year (being the difference between the sale price of the generator and its book value). If Tammy receives $6,000 for the sale of the generator, she makes a capital gain on the sale of the asset. Tammy needs to record as income the total amount of depreciation claimed against the asset over its lifetime. This is because the generator gained value, meaning that it was incorrect to claim $2,000 for the loss in value of the generator. The $1,000 that Tammy received more than the generator's original purchase price is a capital gain and is not considered income in accordance with the general definition of income in Schedule 3 of the Social Security Act 2018.

chunks.title: Assets sold at a loss — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text: If a sole trader makes a loss when they sell business assets or capital assets for less than their book value in the sole trader's accounts, for example, machinery vehicles or other equipment or property, the money they get from the sale is not included in current or estimated income assessments. It is recorded as an expense and reduces the sole trader's gross profit. A review into the previous year's business income may be needed to adjust any benefit payments made during that period. If the period of the loss can't be identified, the loss amount needs to be averaged over the previous 52 weeks. Note This level of assessment should only be needed if a sole trader does not have business accounts.

chunks.title: Self-employment — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Self-employment
Self-employment (mahi ā-kiri) is when a person carries out business activities on their own, or in a partnership.
Self-employment can include contracting, working as a sole trader, or a small business owner in a partnership or a shareholder in a company.
## Sole traders
A sole trader is a person who starts a business or is professionally contracting on their own, without registering as a company.
Although a sole trader may have employees working for them, they must be the only person controlling the business and get all profits from their business to be identified as a sole trader.
Examples of sole traders include:
- tradespeople, e.g. plumbers, house painters, electricians
- small business owners, e.g. hairdressers, landscape gardeners, house cleaners
- people who turn a hobby into a business, e.g. artists, furniture makers, jewellery makers
A sole trader uses their individual Inland Revenue number to pay tax on their business income. They are responsible for paying their own tax and ACC levies.
## Contractors
Contractors are self-employed and earn income by invoicing the person or business that hires their services. Contractors can be sole traders, in partnerships or registered as a company. You will need to ask the contractor how they operate their business (are they a sole trader, in a partnership or registered as a company or trust?).
## Partnerships
Partnerships are businesses that share ownership between 2 or more people who manage the business, and share its resources, profits and liabilities.
A partnership has an IRD number of its own, and the profit (or loss) is shared between the partners, who each pay tax on their share.
Each partner pays tax on their share of the profits.
## Companies
Companies are a type of business structure that are legally separate from the people who own them. Company owners are called shareholders.
## Trading trusts
A trading trust is a trust formed to carry on a business.
Companies and trusts have different rules and tax requirements from sole traders, contractors and partnerships.

chunks.title: Shareholder salary — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Shareholder salary
A shareholder salary is generally a paper entry completed at year-end and applies to self-employed people operating as a company. This is often paid via drawings during the year out of the company bank account.
If a sole trader is declaring a shareholder salary as an expense or drawings in their business accounts, we need to ask them for more information. Drawings may need to be added to the net profit before tax when calculating their income.
If the drawings are from the sole trader's business, we need to know if the money was a loan or the proceeds from the sale of capital assets, e.g. equipment belonging to the business.
Clients who are self-employed as a company should have the assessment of their income checked by the Financial Determination team.

chunks.title: Vehicle — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Vehicle
Business related vehicle costs are an allowable expense and can be calculated by a sole trader using one of the following methods:
- using the actual business related running costs as recorded by the sole trader in a vehicle logbook or
- if no records are kept in a logbook, 25% of business related running costs claimed by the sole trader
Actual business related running costs recorded in a logbook is the preferred method and should be the default option for calculating expenses.
The 25% method should only be used as a last resort if there is no logbook.
Personal use expenses should be included as income if these have been paid by the business.
## Example 1
Brian keeps a logbook for the running costs of the small truck he uses for his lawnmowing business.
The recorded costs are an allowable expense and any personal use costs paid by the business are added back to the net profit (or loss) before tax as income.
## Example 2
Lagi sometimes uses the family car for business purposes and does not keep a logbook. Lagi's schedule of business income (IR3B) shows vehicle costs of $600 for the year.
As there is no logbook, only 25% ($150) of the claimed vehicle costs are an allowable expense.

chunks.title: Verification of income — core policy > income > types of income > self employment
chunks.text:
## Verification of income
Sole traders applying for benefits should provide documentation showing their gross business income, expenses and net profit (or loss). Generally, this means they should provide:
- profit and loss statement or statement of financial performance or
- their completed individual income tax return (IR3)
and
- schedule of business income (IR3B) or
- a financial statements summary (IR10)
## Lack of accounts
When a self-employed person applying for or getting a benefit does not have their complete business accounts, we must assess their income from business as accurately as possible.
We need to ask clients to gather their business bank statements, receipts, invoices, claimed expenses and any other information that can be used to identify their business income.
They must use this information to prepare a statement or declaration that sets out their gross business income and expenses.

chunks.title: Sensitive claims — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Sensitive claims
Clients may get a range of possible payments for a sensitive claim from ACC which may include:
- treatment (for example counselling, medical treatment, surgery)
- additional help during recovery (for example personal care, home help, childcare, equipment, prescriptions, travel costs, changes to the home)
- ACC weekly compensation
- lump sum or independence allowance for long term impairment
If a client has a sensitive claim you will need to be clear about what payments they are getting.
Payments for additional help and treatment are not income and will only need to be considered if the client is applying for Extra help, to make sure any costs are not already covered by ACC payments.
Lump sum or independence allowance payments are not counted as income.
If the client receives a lump sum payment this should be treated as a cash asset, any income derived from the lump sum, for example interest earned on investment, is to be treated as income for benefit purposes.
## Lump sum cash asset exception
Any lump sum payments made to a client are not to be counted as cash assets when assessing a client for Accommodation Supplement or Residential Care Subsidy, for a period of 12 months following the date the lump sum was received by the client.
At the end of the 12 month period, the lump sum (or any remaining amount, if the client has spent some or all of the payment) must be treated as a cash asset, and included in the asset test.
Note this exception does not apply to any other asset tested assistance.

chunks.title: Severance payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Severance payments may be made by an employer as part of a severance agreement to help resolve an unsatisfactory employment situation by ending the employment relationship. They are over and above what a person is entitled to under their employment agreement. The term severance is often used in place of redundancy, however redundancy payments and severance payments are different. A severance agreement is usually made when there is no suitable solution to a problem, such as when there are no valid grounds for the employer to end the person's employment or doing so would mean a lengthy formal process. A severance agreement may also be made when the employer faces risky and costly adverse action from the employee, such as a personal grievance claim or legal action. Common situations that lead to a severance agreement include: - the employer is not satisfied with the employee's performance - the employee is facing a disciplinary process - the employee makes a personal grievance or constructive dismissal claim - a dispute over renegotiation of position description, remuneration, or terms of employment - claims of bullying, harassment or stress - a dispute about the process or outcome of a restructure - a personality clash between an employee and their manager, or between managers

chunks.title: Make-up of a severance agreement — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Depending on the circumstances, a severance agreement can include payments for more than one reason. Payments may include: - an extension of the required period of notice in the employment agreement - contractual entitlements that have not yet accrued such as long service leave - compensation for loss of future earnings for a specified period - compensation for hurt and humiliation - a contribution towards legal fees - reimbursement for other costs incurred such as medical costs, relocation, career services, retraining The make-up of a severance agreement is usually specified in the terms of settlement or other formal severance agreement documentation. However, some agreements are subject to a confidentiality or non-disclosure clause which means the client will not be able to tell us about the details of their severance package.

chunks.title: What a severance payment is not — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: It is important to differentiate between the types of payments a person gets when their employment ends to know how they affect benefit entitlement. Any payment the person is entitled to under their employment agreement is not a severance payment. These include: - holiday pay - pay in lieu of notice - pay in lieu of accumulated leave e.g. sick leave - pay in lieu of completing a fixed-term contract (if it ends early) - redundancy payments - retirement payments - benefits the person became entitled to before they left e.g. bonus payments, incentive payments Note some of these other payments may affect the date employment ceased. They may also be included in the income assessment when calculating the length of the initial stand-down (where relevant).

chunks.title: How severance payments affect benefit payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Payment received before a benefit is granted Severance payments are included in the assessment of a person's last 26 or 52 weeks' income to determine the length of their initial stand-down (where relevant). Severance payments do not affect the date employment ceased. Payment received after a benefit is granted Severance payments are charged as income except for the following payments: - compensation for hurt and humiliation - contribution towards legal fees - reimbursement for other costs incurred e.g. medical costs, relocation, career services, retraining These payments must not be treated as income. For treatment of severance payments when a person stops work and applies for benefit, see 'Severance payments' in the relevant main benefit.

chunks.title: Severe weather event payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Severe weather event payments
People affected by a severe weather event may get one or more severe weather event payments.
These payments are not treated as income or cash assets.
## Severe weather event payments
Severe weather event payments are limited to the following:
- severe weather event insurance payments
- severe weather event donations
- severe weather event buyout payments
- Kaupapa Māori pathway grants
## Income and cash asset exemption
Severe weather event payments are not treated as income or a cash asset for the first 12-months from when the client got the payment. This includes any interest earned on the payment.
If you are unsure whether a payment can be exempt, please contact Helpline before taking any action.
## End of exemption period
At the end of the first 12 months after the client gets the payment, any amount they have left is treated as a cash asset. Any interest earned on the remaining amount is treated as income.
## Retrospection
The exemption applies to any income or cash asset test or assessment MSD does from 6 November 2023. It does not apply to any income or cash asset test or assessment done before this date.
If a client got a severe weather event payment before 6 November 2023, any amount they have left on 6 November 2023 is exempt. This includes any interest earned on the payment. The exemption will end 12 months after they got the payment.
## Example 1
Jeremy got a donation of $5,000 on 6 May 2023 because his home was damaged in the Nelson flooding. He plans to use this to repair his home but won't be able to get the work done until 2024.
From 6 May 2023 to 5 November 2023 the payment is treated as a cash asset.
On 6 November 2023 Jeremy's donation of $5,000 becomes exempt from being treated as a cash asset. The payment will be exempt until 6 May 2024, which is 12 months from the date he got the payment.
## Example 2
Tara gets a Kaupapa Māori pathway grant of $250,000 on 11 December 2023.
From 11 December 2023 to 11 December 2024 this payment is exempt from being treated as a cash asset. Any interest Tara earns on the payment is exempt from being treated as income.

chunks.title: Significant lump sums deposited in a KiwiSaver account — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Significant lump sums deposited in a KiwiSaver account
Depositing significant lump sum funds into KiwiSaver or other superannuation schemes may be considered deprivation of assets and/or income. This depends on the size and frequency of those deposits and the individual circumstances of the client.
Deprivation affects entitlement to financial assistance that has income or asset tests if we decide these sums were deposited into a superannuation scheme in order to qualify for a benefit or a higher rate of benefit. Each case needs to be considered on its merits and you should talk to Helpline.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Significant lump sums deposited in a superannuation scheme account — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Significant lump sums deposited in a superannuation scheme account
Depositing significant lump sum funds into a superannuation scheme may be considered deprivation of income or cash assets. This depends on factors such as the size and frequency of those deposits and the individual circumstances of the client.
Deprivation will affect entitlement to financial assistance that has income or asset tests if we consider that these sums were deposited into a superannuation scheme in order to qualify for a benefit or a higher rate of benefit. Each case needs to be considered on its merits and you should talk to Helpline

chunks.title: Sponsorship — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Sponsorship
When a client receives sponsorship payments from a company or organisation you may need to determine whether the payments are made and used for an income-related purpose
Generally, there is a written agreement between both parties. This agreement will detail the amounts involved, the frequency of payment and obligations the person has to the sponsor.
Obtain a copy of the agreement or contract and check with your regional solicitor to determine whether the sponsorship payments come within the definition of income
Please refer to the appropriate benefit type for more information on charging income see:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Student Loans — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Student Loans
Student Loans, including the Living Costs component, are not chargeable income for benefit purposes.
## Exception
The Living Costs component of Student Loans is chargeable income for Special Benefit and Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Superannuation scheme accounts — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Superannuation scheme accounts
Funds in superannuation scheme accounts which are registered under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 with a qualifying lock-in clause will generally have no impact on benefit entitlement.
## Qualifying lock-in clause
A qualifying lock-in clause prevents a member of the scheme from making or receiving a withdrawal from the scheme until the member:
- reaches the stated time of retirement or
- leaves the employment which established the scheme
## Scheme with a qualifying lock-in clause not a cash asset
Funds held in a superannuation scheme account including KiwiSaver schemes with a qualifying lock-in clause are not considered a cash asset for benefits or Extra help. Income generated from funds in a scheme with a lock-in clause in a not considered chargeable income. This applies to all means tested benefits and Extra help.
## Lock-in clause no longer applies
When a person reaches the age when the lock-in clause no longer applies or when they leave the employment which established the scheme, they are able to withdraw their funds from their superannuation scheme account. At this point any funds should be included in an income and asset test.
Note a person leaving employment cannot withdraw their KiwiSaver funds because they resigned. KiwiSaver funds are locked in until the locked in provisions do not apply.

chunks.title: Supervision allowances — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Supervision allowances
Parents whose children are enrolled with the Correspondence School or a home education programme with the Ministry of Education may receive the following supervision allowances:
- a "student support payment" paid by the Correspondence School (previously known as a "Payment for Supervision")
- a "home education supervision allowance" paid by the Ministry of Education (previously known as a "Homeschooling Supervision Allowance")
These allowances are paid to recognise the provision of study facilities, text books and other educational material within the home.
The student support payment and the home education supervision allowance are not charged as income for benefit purposes because they are a reimbursement of expenses, rather than income.

chunks.title: Survivor's grant — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Survivor's grant
A survivor's grant is a one-off payment to the partner, children and other dependents of someone whose death was the result of an injury.
A survivor's grant is a capital payment and is not treated as income.
Note any interest earned from an investment of the capital payment is charged as income, e.g. the interest earned on the bank account or other investment.
For more information see:
- Lump sum payments
- Payments for surviving spouses
- Accident compensation

chunks.title: TradeMe or similar trading sites — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## TradeMe or similar trading sites
Proceeds from the sale of surplus personal and household items on internet websites such as TradeMe are not to be treated as income.
If a client is regularly buying and selling items on TradeMe or similar trading sites, it is possible they may be trading for profit. You will need to investigate these cases to determine if they are actively engaged in trading for profit. The chargeable income assessment is the same as for self-employed clients.

chunks.title: Viet Nam Veterans and Their Families Trust payments — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Viet Nam Veterans and Their Families Trust payments
Some clients or their families may receive a payment, (similar to an ex gratia payment), from the Viet Nam Veterans and Their Families Trust (VNVFT). The trust was established on 16 August 2007.
## Cash assets and income exemption
Payments made from the Viet Nam Veterans and Their Families Trust are not treated as income or cash assets for financial assistance provided by Work and Income - for a 12 month period from the date of payment (including any income earned from the payment).
At the end of the 12 month period any remaining amount that a client has will be treated as a cash asset. Also any income derived from the cash asset will be treated as chargeable income for benefit purposes.
## Retrospective reviews
If a client or their family member received a payment from the Viet Nam Veterans and Their Families Trust between 16 August 2007 and 3 November 2008, and their payment was not exempt from the cash asset test, you may need to retrospectively review their financial assistance.
Note payments cannot be retrospectively exempt from the income and asset test for Temporary Additional Support or Residential Care Subsidy. Payments can only be exempt from Temporary Additional Support and Residential Care Subsidy from 3 November 2008 onwards.
## Process
When a client receives a payment you need to create a 'must view' note in CMS. The note should state:
- the client has received a payment from the Viet Nam Veterans and Their Families Trust
- the date the client received the payment
- the amount of the payment and
- the expiry date of the 12 month exemption
If a client is currently receiving financial assistance, a bring-up needs to be added via BRUPI in SWIFTT to reassess entitlement at the end of the 12 month exemption period.
A letter must be sent to the client when you add the 12 month exemption (a letter template is available in CMS) or complete a retrospective review.
For more information see:
- Ex gratia and compensation payments
Also see:
- Ex gratia payments from Veterans' Affairs New Zealand

chunks.title: Wages or salary — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Wages or salary
For treatment of wages or salary when a client stops work and applies for a benefit see Jobseeker Support Employment ceased.
For other clients currently getting a benefit, income from wages or salary is charged over the period it represents.
How you treat income from wages or salary may vary depending on the type of employment, including part-time, full-time, casual or weekend work. Wages or salary can also include other payments such as:
- sick leave, family violence leave and long service leave
- holiday pay
- bonus payments
- redundancy payments
- severance payments
- non-taxable employment allowances
- Armed service personnel
The client needs to provide the following information in respect of their income from wages or salary:
- the amount earned before tax (the gross amount)
- the period the wages or salary represents and
- the employer's details
## Employment agency fees
When a client is placed in employment by an employment agency, the client may be required to pay a percentage of their gross weekly income as a fee to the employment agency. The agency fee is not treated as income for benefit purposes and should be deducted from the wages.
Please refer to the appropriate benefit type for more information on charging income:
- Changes and reviews, Charging income in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: ACC weekly compensation — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## ACC weekly compensation
Weekly compensation is paid to compensate for the loss of earnings or loss of potential earning capacity as a result of injury. It is based on 80% of the lost weekly income before the injury occurred and is paid to the ACC client.
Weekly compensation may also be paid to:
- a person with a sensitive claim in relation to mental injury
- a surviving spouse or partner or
- to the caregiver of a child whose parent has passed away
## Specified benefits
Payments of weekly compensation are a direct deduction from a client's specified benefit. For every $1.00 of the net weekly compensation payment received, $1.00 is deducted from the net specified benefit rate. This includes weekly compensation payable to a client, their partner or in respect of dependent children in their care.
The weekly compensation is deducted even if the money payable is not paid directly to them.
Note there are different rules for clients who were getting a benefit and weekly compensation before 1 July 1999.
## New Zealand Superannuation
There are some limitations on clients getting both ACC weekly compensation and New Zealand Superannuation.
For more information see:
- New Zealand Superannuation and ACC weekly earnings-related compensation
## Other financial assistance
ACC weekly compensation payments are treated as income when assessing other income tested financial assistance.

chunks.title: Weekly compensation backdated prior to 1 July 1999 — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text:
## Weekly compensation backdated prior to 1 July 1999
There are some situations where the weekly compensation has been granted after 1 July 1999 but the commencement date is prior to 1 July 1999.
When weekly compensation is granted after 1 July 1999 but starts before 1 July 1999, the reason the client is receiving a main benefit must be considered. If the main benefit is being paid for the same reason the weekly compensation is paid, the weekly compensation is a direct deduction. When the weekly compensation is paid for a different reason to the benefit, weekly compensation is charged as income.
For more information see:
- Weekly compensation payments started before 1 July 1999
## Example
Sarah is getting Sole Parent Support to care for her children and is working part time. Sarah had an accident at work on 1 May 1999 and was granted weekly compensation from ACC from 1 May 1999.
Weekly compensation payments did not start until 1 September 1999. The reason Sarah is getting Sole Parent Support is because she has children and the reason she is getting weekly compensation is because of an injury which has prevented her working.
In this case weekly compensation is charged as income against the client's benefit as the payment started prior to 1 July 1999 and weekly compensation is paid for a different reason than what the benefit is paid for.
## For more information on what to do when the benefit stops or there are changes to the weekly compensation rate see:
- Changes and reviews for payments before 1 July 1999
- Effect on Extra help
- Weekly compensation payments started before 1 July 1999
- Clients who have not met their obligations with ACC
- Backdating when weekly compensation is overpaid
For more information see:
- History of ACC
- ACC weekly compensation

chunks.title: Weekly compensation payments started before 1 July 1999 — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Weekly compensation payable before 1 July 1999 may be a direct deduction or charged as income for benefit purposes. The reason the client is receiving the benefit and weekly compensation will determine this. Note if the weekly compensation is payable from or after 1 July 1999 it is a direct deduction from all benefits except New Zealand Superannuation. Is the client applying for a benefit because of the injury they are receiving ACC weekly compensation for?

chunks.title: Yes - direct deduction — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: Prior to 1 July 1999 when a client receives a main benefit and weekly compensation for the same reason (i.e. because of the injury preventing them from working), the weekly compensation is a direct deduction. In most cases the benefit type is likely to be Sickness Benefit or Invalids Benefit. For example: Sam is a chef and had a car accident in 1996 which left him with a spinal injury. Prior to 1 July 1999, Sam was receiving weekly compensation for his loss of earnings due to his injury. In 1997 Sam decided to apply for an Invalid's Benefit after ACC reviewed his case and decided his injury was long term, ACC reduced his weekly compensation so that it was below the benefit cut out point. Sam is receiving the Invalids Benefit because of his injury, which is for the same reason as the weekly compensation payments. The weekly compensation is a direct deduction, as the benefit is paid for the same reason as the weekly compensation.

chunks.title: No - charge as income — core policy > income > types of income
chunks.text: When weekly compensation starts before 1 July 1999 and is paid for a different reason to the benefit, then weekly compensation is charged as income. While a client continues to get weekly compensation and a main benefit for a different reason, the weekly compensation continues to be charged as income. For example: John is a painter who fell off the scaffolding while at work and injured his back. John made a claim to ACC for his work place accident. Prior to 1 July 1999, John was receiving weekly compensation. John has two children and is receiving Sole Parent Support, following separation from his partner in November 1998. The weekly compensation is being paid because of John's injury and Sole Parent Support is being paid because he is a sole parent, therefore they are being paid for different reasons. The weekly compensation is charged as income, as the benefit is paid for a different reason to the weekly compensation. Note if you find it difficult to determine whether you should charge the compensation as income or as a direct deduction, you should discuss this with your regional solicitor.

chunks.title: Advising a client about job interview or job offer requirement — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Advising a client about job interview or job offer requirement
When requiring a client to attend and participate in a pre-benefit job interview or job offer requirement MSD must remind them of:
- their obligation to attend an interview or accept an offer of employment and
- the consequences of failing to comply with this requirement
For more information see:
- Pre-benefit interviews for and offers of employment
- Client fails job interview or job offer requirement
- Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements

chunks.title: Advising a client about a pre-benefit activity — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Advising a client about a pre-benefit activity
When a client is assigned a pre-benefit activity, they must be advised of:
- their obligations relating to the pre-benefit activity
- the timeframe for completing the assigned pre-benefit activity
- the consequences of failing to complete the assigned pre-benefit activity
When MSD assigns a pre-benefit activity as part of the application, confirmation must be provided of:
- a client's date of first contact
- the date a client must complete the application by, including any assigned pre-benefit activity and the consequences of not doing so and
- review rights for the pre-benefit activity

chunks.title: Advising a partner about job interview or job offer requirement — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Advising a partner about job interview or job offer requirement
When requiring a partner to attend and participate in a pre-benefit job interview or job offer requirement MSD must remind them of:
- their obligation to attend an interview or accept an offer of employment and
- the consequences of failing to comply with this requirement
For more information see:
- Pre-benefit interviews for and offers of employment
- Partner fails job interview or job offer requirement
- Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements

chunks.title: Advising a partner about a pre-benefit activity — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Advising a partner about a pre-benefit activity
When a partner is assigned a pre-benefit activity, they must be advised of:
- their obligations relating to the pre-benefit activity
- the timeframe for completing the assigned pre-benefit activity
- the consequences of failing to complete the assigned pre-benefit activity
MSD cannot advise a client about the pre-benefit activity that their partner should complete - the partner must be advised.
When MSD assigns a pre-benefit activity as part of the application, confirmation must be provided of:
- a client's date of first contact
- the date a client must complete the application by, including any assigned pre-benefit activity and the consequences of not doing so and
- review rights for the pre-benefit activity

chunks.title: Client does not complete assigned pre-benefit activity — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Client does not complete assigned pre-benefit activity
If a client does not complete an assigned pre-benefit activity within 20 working days of their date of first contact, the client's application lapses. When this occurs the client will need to re-establish their eligibility for benefit. The date the client makes contact to do this will become their new date of first contact.
If there are no good and sufficient reasons for not completing an assigned pre-benefit activity, the 20 working day period cannot be extended to allow the client more time to complete it. However, there may be situations where it is no longer reasonable for the client to complete the assigned activity.
If the client has a partner, the partner can apply for benefit in their own right (existing guidelines apply).
## Client completes activity before their partner
When a primary client completes their pre-benefit activity before their partner does, MSD should continue processing the application for benefit for the client. The client can be paid the half-married rate of benefit. See:
- Examples primary client paid half couple rate
## Change of circumstances before grant
A client may have a change of circumstances before their benefit is granted and they may qualify for a benefit that is not subject to pre-benefit requirements.
For more information see:
- Pre-benefit activity no longer reasonable
- Client has a change of circumstances before grant
- Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements
- Core policy Application for benefit

chunks.title: Client fails job interview or job offer requirement — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Client fails job interview or job offer requirement
When MSD gets notification that a client has failed to comply with the pre-benefit requirement of attending and participating in an interview for suitable employment or accepting an offer of suitable employment, MSD should first check if the client has a good and sufficient reason.
## Client has a good and sufficient reason
If the client has a good and sufficient reason MSD can continue with the application process including pre-benefit activity requirements.
## Client has no good and sufficient reason
Where the client has no good and sufficient reason then the action taken depends on the status of their application for benefit at the time. For more information see:
- Process when client fails job interview or job offer requirement
## Application form not completed prior to failure
A client may fail to comply with the pre-benefit requirement of attending and participating in an interview for suitable employment, or accepting an offer of suitable employment before they have completed an application form for benefit.
When this occurs the client will have to re-establish their eligibility for benefit. The date the client makes contact to do this, will become their new date of first contact.
For more information see:
- Good and sufficient reason
- Process when client fails job interview or job offer requirement
- Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements
- Core policy Application for benefit

chunks.title: Client has a change of circumstances before grant — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Client has a change of circumstances before grant
If a client has a change of circumstances before their benefit is granted and the benefit applied for is no longer the most appropriate one for them, they do not have to complete any pre-benefit activity they may have been assigned.
For example:
- the client becomes permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, an injury or a disability and they would qualify for Supported Living Payment
MSD should grant the original application for benefit in the first instance, even though the pre-benefit activity hasn't been undertaken, and then decide if it is appropriate to transfer the client to another benefit from the date they became entitled to get it.
Important the client will need to provide any supporting evidence or additional information relating to the new benefit such as a medical certificate for Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Completing a Jobseeker Profile not reasonable for partners — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Completing a Jobseeker Profile not reasonable for partners
If it is not reasonable for a partner to complete their Jobseeker Profile before their benefit can be granted, MSD can use its discretion to revoke the requirement.
Circumstances that may mean the requirement is not reasonable could include (but are not limited to) where a partner:
- is applying for a benefit following a death or serious illness in the family
- has learning difficulties or disabilities that would make it very difficult to complete the Jobseeker Profile, even with support from MSD
- has had an accident and is in hospital, but has provided all other required information
When the requirement to complete a Jobseeker Profile has been revoked, MSD may assign it after their benefit has been granted as an obligation-related activity that the partner must complete.

chunks.title: Completing a Jobseeker Profile not reasonable — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Completing a Jobseeker Profile not reasonable
If it is not reasonable for a client to complete their Jobseeker Profile before their benefit can be granted, MSD can use its discretion to revoke the requirement.
Circumstances that may mean it's not reasonable could include (but is not limited to) where a client:
- is applying for a benefit following a death or serious illness in the immediate family
- has learning difficulties or disabilities that would make it very difficult to complete the Jobseeker Profile, even with support from MSD
- has had an accident and is in hospital, but has provided all other required information
When the requirement to complete a Jobseeker Profile has been revoked, MSD may assign it after the benefit has been granted as an obligation-related activity that a client must complete.

chunks.title: Completing a Jobseeker Profile — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Completing a Jobseeker Profile
A Jobseeker Profile is a form provided by MSD where clients provide information about their work skills, qualifications, and preferences. This information helps MSD to match clients to job vacancies or identify skill gaps that MSD may be able to help clients bridge through referrals to courses or training.
Clients applying for specified benefits must complete a Jobseeker Profile to MSD's satisfaction before their benefit can be granted. These benefits are:
- Jobseeker Support, including Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
- Sole Parent Support, or
- Emergency Benefit, including Emergency Maintenance Allowance (with work-related conditions of grant only)
Note this does not apply to reapplications for Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support.
## Conditions of grant for Emergency Benefit
Clients who are applying for Emergency Benefit only have to complete a Jobseeker Profile if they will have conditions of grant that are similar to work obligations.
Clients who are applying for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship have to register for Student Job Search as part of their application. This registration includes all the same information as a Jobseeker Profile, which means this is enough to satisfy the Jobseeker Profile requirement for students.
## Student Job Search
Clients who are applying for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship have to register for Student Job Search as part of their application. This registration includes all the same information as a Jobseeker Profile, which means this is enough to satisfy the Jobseeker Profile requirement for students.
## Completed to MSD’s satisfaction
The Jobseeker Profile must be completed to MSD’s satisfaction in order to meet the Jobseeker Profile requirement.
This means that a client must provide up to date and relevant information. If a client has had a Jobseeker Profile previously, MSD must make sure that this has been updated to include current information.

chunks.title: Completing a Jobseeker Profile for partners — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text: A Jobseeker Profile is a form provided by MSD where clients provide information about their work skills, qualifications, and preferences. This information helps MSD to match clients to job vacancies or identify skill gaps that MSD may be able to help clients bridge through referrals to courses or training. Partners of clients applying for specified benefits are required to complete a Jobseeker Profile to MSD's satisfaction before their benefit can be granted. These benefits are: - Jobseeker Support, including Jobseeker Support Student Hardship - Emergency Benefit (with work-related conditions of grant only) Note this does not apply to reapplications for Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: Conditions of grant for Emergency Benefit — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text: When a primary client is being granted an Emergency Benefit, their partner is only required to complete a Jobseeker Profile if the primary client will have conditions of grant that are similar to work obligations. For example, if a primary client is being granted Emergency Benefit with conditions of grant that are similar to work obligations for Jobseeker Support, the partner will be required to complete a Jobseeker Profile. If the primary client does not have work-related conditions of grant, the partner is not required to complete a Jobseeker Profile. However, as the partner will have work or work-preparation obligations, MSD may still assign a Jobseeker Profile as a pre-benefit activity. For more information see: - Emergency Benefit - Pre-benefit activity for partners

chunks.title: Student Job Search — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text: Partners of students who are applying for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship have to register for Student Job Search as part of their application, if they are also a student. This registration includes all the same information as a Jobseeker Profile, which means this is enough to satisfy the Jobseeker Profile requirement for students.

chunks.title: Partners with youth activity obligations — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text: Some clients applying for Jobseeker Support or Emergency Benefit may have a partner who is subject to youth activity obligations.
