Youth activity obligations are focused on education and training rather than employment. Partners who are subject to youth activity obligations are not required to complete a Jobseeker Profile. For more information see: - Youth activity obligations

chunks.title: Completed to MSD’s satisfaction — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text: The Jobseeker Profile must be completed to MSD’s satisfaction before the partner’s requirement to complete a Jobseeker Profile can be met. This means that a partner must provide up to date and relevant information. If a partner has had a Jobseeker Profile previously, MSD must make sure that this has been updated to include relevant information.

chunks.title: Examples primary client paid half couple rate — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Examples primary client paid half couple rate
The following examples show when to pay a half couple rate of benefit to the primary client, when granting the benefit and the partner has not completed their assigned pre-benefit activity.
## Couple with dependent child
A married client with one child (aged 10 years) has applied for Jobseeker Support. The client has completed their pre-benefit activity.
The couple live in Auckland and pay rent of $450.00 a week. The partner has not completed their pre-benefit activity.
Jobseeker Support (couple rate)

Accommodation Supplement
$185.00
Temporary Additional Support
$169.80
Benefit payable

## Couple no children
A married client with no children has applied for Jobseeker Support.
The client has completed their pre-benefit activity. The partner has not completed their pre-benefit activity.
The partner has income of $180.00 gross a week.
Jobseeker Support (couple rate)

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason
MSD should make contact with the client to obtain their reason for not attending and participating in an interview for suitable employment or accepting an offer of suitable employment. If the client has a good and sufficient reason they will not have failed to comply with this pre-benefit requirement.
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'. Having considered the circumstances, would it have been 'reasonable' for the client to have attended and participated in the interview or accepted the offer of employment?
Decide in favour of the client if any doubt remains.
A good and sufficient reason may include, (but is not limited to):
- the client was temporarily medically unfit - ie they have a medical certificate
- death or illness in the family
- due to unforeseen circumstances, the client could not realistically transport themselves on the day
- new information indicates that the job was not suitable for the client
- due to unforeseen circumstances, the client's childcare arrangements fell through on the day
- client has one or more dependent children and participation in the employment involves hours when it would be unreasonable to expect any child to be without that client's supervision

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason
It is important to make contact with the partner to obtain their reason for not attending and participating in an interview for suitable employment or accepting an offer of suitable employment. If the partner has a good and sufficient reason they will not have failed to comply with this pre-benefit requirement.
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'. Having considered the circumstances, would it have been 'reasonable' for the partner to have attended and participated in the interview or accepted the offer of employment?
Decide in favour of the partner if any doubt remains.
A good and sufficient reason may include, (but is not limited to):
- the partner was temporarily medically unfit - ie they have a medical certificate
- death or illness in the family
- due to unforeseen circumstances, the partner could not realistically transport themselves on the day
- new information indicates that the job was not suitable for the partner
- due to unforeseen circumstances, the partner's childcare arrangements fell through on the day
- partner has one or more dependent children and participation in the employment involves hours when it would be unreasonable to expect any child to be without that partner's supervision

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for not completing Jobseeker Profile within timeframe for partners — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason for not completing Jobseeker Profile within timeframe for partners
A partner may have a good and sufficient reason for being unable to complete their Jobseeker Profile within 20 working days. If MSD determines that they have a good and sufficient reason, a partner can be given more time to complete their Jobseeker Profile.
A good and sufficient reason may include, but is not limited to:
- the partner suddenly had to go to hospital
- there was a death or illness in the partner’s family
- MSD required additional time to determine that the partner can only be granted Emergency Benefit with conditions of grant similar to work obligations
- the partner had to leave the country for an emergency reason
A partner should advise MSD of their circumstances as soon as reasonably possible.
MSD must use its discretion to determine how much extra time would be reasonable for the partner to complete their Jobseeker Profile. This can happen before or after the 20 working day timeframe lapses, depending on when the reason occurs and when the partner notifies MSD.
## Example
Wilson and Jackie apply for a benefit on 5 August 2025. They have 20 working days to complete their application, and their lapse date is 1 September.
Jackie meets the criteria for Jobseeker Support and is assigned the pre-benefit requirement to complete her Jobseeker Profile on 5 August.
Wilson does not have a residence class visa but is applying for residency and is compelled to remain in New Zealand. MSD can't assign any pre-benefit requirement until it's clear what Wilson might qualify for.
On 18 August, 10 working days after Wilson’s date of first contact, MSD assesses his application and determines that he would be eligible for Emergency Benefit with conditions of grant that are similar to the full-time work obligations for Jobseeker Support.
Because MSD required additional time to assess his application, they provide Wilson more time to complete his Jobseeker Profile before his benefit application lapses. He is given 10 extra working days, and his application will now lapse on 15 September.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for not completing Jobseeker Profile within timeframe — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason for not completing Jobseeker Profile within timeframe
A client may have a good and sufficient reason for being unable to complete their Jobseeker Profile within 20 working days. If MSD determines that they have a good and sufficient reason, a client can be given more time to complete their Jobseeker Profile.
A good and sufficient reason may include, but is not limited to:
- the client suddenly had to go to hospital
- there was a death or illness in the client’s family
- MSD required additional time to determine that the client can only be granted Emergency Benefit with conditions of grant similar to work obligations
- client had to leave the country for an emergency reason
A client should advise MSD of their circumstances as soon as reasonably possible.
MSD must use its discretion to determine how much extra time would be reasonable for the client to complete their Jobseeker Profile. This can happen before or after the 20 working day timeframe lapses, depending on when the reason occurs and when the client notifies MSD.
## Example
Bill is a sole parent and applied for a benefit on 5 August 2025. He has 20 working days to complete his application and his lapse date is 1 September. He only got his permanent residency a year ago so he doesn’t meet the normal residency criteria. MSD can’t assign any pre-benefit requirement until it’s clear what Bill might qualify for.
On 18 August, 10 working days after Bill’s date of first contact, MSD assesses his application and determines that he would be eligible for Emergency Maintenance Allowance with conditions of grant that are similar to the part-time work obligations for Sole Parent Support.
Because MSD required additional time to assess his application, they provide Bill more time to complete his Jobseeker Profile before his benefit application lapses. He is given 10 extra working days, and his application will now lapse on 15 September.

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Clients applying for the following benefits may be required to undertake pre-benefit requirements:
- Emergency Benefit
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance
- Jobseeker Support
- Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
- Sole Parent Support
Partners of clients applying for the following benefits may be required to undertake pre-benefit requirements:
- Emergency Benefit
- Jobseeker Support
- Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
- Supported Living Payment (granted on ground of a health condition, injury, disability, or total blindness)
## Pre-benefit requirements do not apply to all benefits
Pre-benefit requirements do not apply to applicants for:
- Supported Living Payment (caring for a person)
- New Zealand Superannuation
- Veterans Pension
When it is identified during the application process that the client or their partner qualifies for a benefit with no pre-benefit requirements, then pre-benefit requirements do not apply.

chunks.title: Partner does not complete assigned pre-benefit activity — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Partner does not complete assigned pre-benefit activity
If there are no good and sufficient reasons for not completing an assigned pre-benefit activity, the 20 working day period cannot be extended to allow the partner more time to complete it. However, there may be situations where it is no longer reasonable for the client to complete the assigned activity.
MSD should encourage the partner to complete their assigned pre-benefit activity as soon as possible and remind them of the consequences of not completing the pre-benefit activity.
If a partner has not completed their assigned pre-benefit activity, MSD should continue processing the application for benefit for the client.
For more information see:
## Partner completes pre-benefit activity after grant
If the partner completes the pre-benefit activity within 20 working days of the primary client's date of first contact, and they meet the qualifications for the benefit, they can be included in the benefit from the date of grant. This can be back-dated.
## Partner can be included after 20 working days from date of first contact
After 20 working days from the primary client's date of first contact, the partner does not have to complete their pre-benefit activity because the period for completing a pre-benefit activity has ended.
After the 20 working days have passed, the partner can be included in the benefit (if they meet the qualifications) from the date they made contact to be included. The inclusion of the partner cannot be back-dated to the start date of the benefit.
A client may have a change of circumstances before their benefit is granted, and they may qualify for a benefit that does not have pre-benefit requirements.
For more information see:
- Pre-benefit activity no longer reasonable for partner
- Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements for partners
- Core policy Application for benefit

chunks.title: Partner fails job interview or job offer requirement — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Partner fails job interview or job offer requirement
When MSD gets notification that a partner has failed to comply with the pre-benefit requirement of attending and participating in an interview for suitable employment or accepting an offer of suitable employment, it should be determined whether the partner has a good and sufficient reason.
## Partner has a good and sufficient reason
If the partner has a good and sufficient reason MSD can continue with the application process including pre-benefit requirements.
## Partner has no good and sufficient reason
Where the partner has no good and sufficient reason then the action taken depends on the status of their application for benefit at the time. For more information see:
- Process when partner fails job interview or job offer requirement
## Application form not completed prior to failure
A partner may fail to comply with the pre-benefit requirement of attending and participating in an interview for suitable employment, or accepting an offer of suitable employment before they have completed an application form for benefit.
When this occurs the partner will have to re-establish their eligibility for benefit.
The date the partner makes contact to do this will become their new date of first contact.
For more information see:
- Good and sufficient reason
- Process when partner fails job interview or job offer requirement
- Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements
- Core policy Application for benefit

chunks.title: Partner has a change of circumstances before grant — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Partner has a change of circumstances before grant
If a partner has a change of circumstances before the benefit is granted and the benefit applied for is no longer the most appropriate one for them to get, they do not have to complete any pre-benefit activity they may have been assigned.
For example:
- the partner becomes permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, an injury or a disability, and they would qualify for Supported Living Payment
The original application for benefit should be granted in the first instance, even though the pre-benefit activity hasn't been undertaken, and MSD will determine if it is appropriate to transfer the partner to another benefit from the date they became entitled to get it.
Important the partner will need to provide any supporting evidence or additional information relating to the new benefit such as a medical certificate for Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Pre-benefit activity — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Pre-benefit activity
A pre-benefit activity is an employment-related activity a client may be required to complete as part of their application for benefit. This is to help a client find and retain paid employment.
A client applying for benefit is obliged to complete this activity once it has been assigned to them for their application for benefit to progress (otherwise the application will lapse after 20 working days). However, there may be situations where it is no longer reasonable for the client to complete the assigned activity.
## Client's individual circumstances
A pre-benefit activity may be assigned based on the client's individual circumstances.
For example, contact through the client's agent may be appropriate for clients if they are a:
- child sex offender
- home detainee
- trespass client or
- person with difficulties with language, literacy or numeracy
## Activity must not be assigned
A pre-benefit activity must not be assigned where it is determined that a client does not have the capacity to seek, undertake and be available for part-time work of at least 15 hours per week.
For more information see:
- Pre-benefit activity should not be assigned
- Advising a client about a pre-benefit activity
- Pre-benefit activity no longer reasonable
- Client does not complete assigned pre-benefit activity
- Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements
- Timeframes for assigning and completing an activity

chunks.title: Pre-benefit activity for partners — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Pre-benefit activity for partners
A pre-benefit activity is an employment-related activity that a partner may be required to complete as part of their application for benefit. This is to help the partner find and retain paid employment.
The partner is obliged to complete this activity once it has been assigned to them for their application for benefit to progress (otherwise the application will lapse after 20 working days). However, there may be situations where it is no longer reasonable for the partner to complete the assigned activity.
## Client's individual circumstances
A pre-benefit activity may be assigned based on the partner's individual circumstances.
For example, contact through the partner's agent may be appropriate for partners, if they are a:
- child sex offender
- home detainee
- trespass client or
- person with difficulties with language, literacy or numeracy
## Activity must not be assigned
A pre-benefit activity must not be assigned when it is determined that a partner does not have the capacity to seek, undertake and be available for part-time work.
For more information see:
- Pre-benefit activity should not be assigned to a partner
- Advising a partner about a pre-benefit activity
- Pre-benefit activity no longer reasonable for partner
- Partner does not complete assigned pre-benefit activity
- Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements for partners
- Timeframes for assigning and completing an activity for partners

chunks.title: Pre-benefit activity no longer reasonable — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Pre-benefit activity no longer reasonable
If, once assigned, a client is unable to complete a pre-benefit activity MSD may revoke the requirement if completing the activity is no longer reasonable.
Circumstances that may result in the activity no longer being reasonable could include (but is not limited to) where:
- there has been a deterioration in the client's health condition, injury or disability
- there has been a death or illness in the family
- the client has a literacy or numeracy issue which was not evident when the activity was assigned
If MSD decides to revoke a pre-benefit activity because it is no longer reasonable, MSD must advise the client that the pre-benefit activity is no longer required to be completed.
## Example
A client has applied for Jobseeker Support and has a pre-benefit activity assigned to attend an employment-related seminar provided by MSD. The client had an accident and is in hospital. In this situation attending an employment-related seminar is no longer reasonable.
MSD must let the client know that they do not have to attend the seminar, and the requirement to do so has been removed.

chunks.title: Pre-benefit activity no longer reasonable for a partner — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Pre-benefit activity no longer reasonable for a partner
If, once assigned, a partner is unable to complete a pre-benefit activity MSD can revoke the requirement if completing the activity is no longer reasonable.
Circumstances that may result in the activity no longer being reasonable could include (but is not limited to) where:
- there has been a deterioration in the client's or partner's health condition, injury or disability
- there has been a death or illness in the family
- the partner has a literacy or numeracy issue which was not evident when the activity was assigned
If MSD decides to revoke a pre-benefit activity because it is no longer reasonable, MSD must advise the partner that the pre-benefit activity is no longer required.
## Example
A partner has applied for Jobseeker Support and has a pre-benefit activity assigned to attend an employment-related seminar provided by MSD. The partner had an accident and is in hospital. In this situation attending an employment-related seminar is no longer reasonable.
MSD must let the partner know that they do not have to attend the seminar, and the requirement to do so has been removed.

chunks.title: Pre-benefit interviews for and offers of employment — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Pre-benefit interviews for and offers of employment
As part of their application for benefit, and at any time before their benefit commences, the client may be required to:
- attend and participate in any interview for suitable employment to which they are referred and
- accept any offer of suitable employment
Note after the benefit has commenced the client is subject to work obligations.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support Suitable employment
- Advising a client about job interview or job offer requirement
- Client fails job interview or job offer requirement

chunks.title: Pre-benefit interviews for and offers of employment for partners — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Pre-benefit interviews for and offers of employment for partners
As part of their pre-benefit requirements, and at any time before their benefit commences, the partner may be required to:
- attend and participate in any interview for suitable employment to which they are referred and
- accept any offer of suitable employment
Note after the benefit has commenced the partner is subject to work obligations.
For more information see:
- Advising a partner about job interview or job offer requirement
- Partner fails job interview or job offer requirement
- Suitable employment

chunks.title: Pre-benefit requirements for clients — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Pre-benefit requirements for clients
As part of the application process for benefit, clients may be required to:
- undertake an assigned pre-benefit activity
- at any time before their benefit commences, attend and participate in any interview for suitable employment to which they are referred
- at any time before their benefit commences, accept any offer of suitable employment
- complete a Jobseeker Profile
When it is identified during the application process that the client or their partner qualifies for a benefit with no pre-benefit requirements, then pre-benefit requirements do not apply.
## Pre-benefit requirements do not apply to all benefits
Pre-benefit requirements do not apply to applicants for:
- Supported Living Payment (caring for a person)
- New Zealand Superannuation
- Veterans Pension

chunks.title: Pre-benefit requirements for partners — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Pre-benefit requirements for partners
Partners of clients applying for the following benefits may have pre-benefit requirements:
- Emergency Benefit
- Jobseeker Support
- Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
- Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury, disability or total blindness)
A partner may be required to:
- undertake an assigned pre-benefit activity
- at any time before their benefit commences, attend and participate in any interview for suitable employment to which they are referred
- at any time before their benefit commences, accept any offer of suitable employment
- create a Jobseeker Profile
When it is identified during the application process that the client or partner qualifies for a benefit with no pre-benefit requirements, then pre-benefit requirements do not apply.

chunks.title: Process when client fails job interview or job offer requirements — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Process when client fails job interview or job offer requirements
Where a client fails to comply with the pre-benefit requirement of attending and participating in an interview for suitable employment or accepting an offer of suitable employment, MSD should check if they had a good and sufficient reason.
If the client does not have a good and sufficient reason then the action MSD should take depends on the status of their application for benefit at the time MSD decides:
Failure is prior to the benefit being granted
- the benefit lapses from the date MSD makes the decision that the client has failed
Benefit has been granted
- cancel the benefit from the commencement date (if the benefit has already commenced this may establish a debt)
## Client still requires financial assistance
In all cases, if the client still requires financial assistance they will have to re-establish their eligibility for benefit. The date the client makes contact to do this, will become their new date of first contact.
For more information see:
- Good and sufficient reason
- Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements

chunks.title: Process when partner fails job interview or job offer requirements — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Process when partner fails job interview or job offer requirements
Where a partner fails to comply with the pre-benefit requirement of attending and participating in an interview for suitable employment or accepting an offer of suitable employment, it should be determined whether they had a good and sufficient reason.
If the partner does not have a good and sufficient reason then the action taken depends on the status of their application for benefit.
Failure is prior to the benefit being granted
- lapse the partner's portion of the benefit from the date MSD made the decision that the partner has failed
Benefit has been granted
- suspend the partner's portion of the benefit from the commencement date (if the benefit has already commenced this may establish a debt)
## Partner still requires financial assistance
In all cases, if the partner still requires financial assistance they will have to re-establish their eligibility for benefit. The date the partner makes contact to do this, will become their new date of first contact.
For more information see:
- Good and sufficient reason
- Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements

chunks.title: Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text: Whether a client can request a review of decision about their pre-benefit requirements depends on which aspect of the pre-benefit requirements they wish to review.

chunks.title: Assigned pre-benefit activity — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text: A client can request a review of the decision to assign a pre-benefit activity. In these cases, while the review of decision is being decided, MSD would proceed with the application process. If the client does not complete the assigned pre-benefit activity within 20 working days of their date of first contact, the application for benefit would lapse on the 21st working day. If the client still wishes to apply for a benefit, they will need to re-start the application process and re-establish their eligibility. A Benefit Review Committee cannot change the 20 working day rule of the application process. The client should be advised that the review may not be completed within 20 working days of the date of first contact, and the application for benefit will still lapse on the 21st working day.

chunks.title: Mandatory Jobseeker Profile — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text: If a client is applying for a benefit that requires a Jobseeker Profile to be completed before benefit can be granted, a client can apply for a review if they consider it is not reasonable for them to complete it and MSD has decided not to revoke the requirement. In these cases, while the review of decision is being decided, MSD would proceed with the application process. If the client does not complete the Jobseeker Profile within 20 working days of their date of first contact, the application for benefit would lapse on the 21st working day. If the client still wishes to apply for a benefit, they will need to re-start the application process and re-establish their eligibility. A Benefit Review Committee cannot change the 20 working day rule of the application process. The client should be advised that the review may not be completed within 20 working days of the date of first contact, and the application for benefit will still lapse on the 21st working day.

chunks.title: Client does not complete a pre-benefit activity or mandatory Jobseeker Profile — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text: A client cannot request a review of decision where their application for benefit has lapsed because they have not completed their pre-benefit activity or mandatory Jobseeker Profile within 20 working days from their date of first contact. There are no good and sufficient reasons for failure to complete an assigned pre-benefit activity or mandatory Jobseeker Profile and the 20 working day period cannot be extended to allow the client more time to complete it.

chunks.title: Interview or offer of suitable employment — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text: A client can request a review of the decision to decline their application for benefit or to cancel a benefit already granted for a failure to comply with a request to attend an interview for or accept an offer of suitable employment. For more information see: - Pre-benefit activity requirements for clients - Core policy Reviews and Appeals - Request for financial assistance [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Timeframe to assign and complete the Jobseeker Profile for partners — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Timeframe to assign and complete the Jobseeker Profile for partners
A partner has 20 working days from their date of first contact to complete their Jobseeker Profile before their benefit can be granted.
Partners who do not complete their Jobseeker Profile within 20 working days will have their application lapse.
## Client completed Jobseeker Profile but partner has not
If a client has completed their Jobseeker Profile within 20 working days but their partner has not completed theirs, MSD can only grant a benefit to the primary client. This includes any relevant supplementary assistance.
The client is entitled to half of the joint rate of entitlement to Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support. They are also entitled to the full rate of Disability Allowance for their own medical costs, as well as the full couple’s rate of Winter Energy Payment (during the period this is payable).
The partner can only be granted their half of the payments from the date they have completed their Jobseeker Profile to MSD’s satisfaction, or the date MSD decides it isn’t reasonable for them to complete it.
## Extensions
Partners who have a good and sufficient reason for being unable to complete their Jobseeker Profile within 20 working days may be given more time.
This can happen before or after the 20 working day timeframe lapses, depending on when the reason occurs and when the client notifies MSD.
## Example
Suki and her partner James apply for a benefit on 24 June 2025 and have until 21 July to complete their applications. Suki and James both need to complete a Jobseeker Profile before their benefit can be granted.
Suki attends her appointment on 3 July with all of her information and her completed Jobseeker Profile. She advises that James is currently in hospital and may need additional time to complete his Jobseeker Profile.
Suki’s benefit is granted from her date of first contact, 24 June.
James contacts MSD on 17 July to arrange an appointment as he is now out of the hospital. The next appointment is 23 July, which is more than 20 working days after he made his application.
When he attends his appointment, he provides all his documents, including his completed Jobseeker Profile. MSD is satisfied that there is a good reason why he was not able to complete this within the 20-working day window and grants an extension so his application is not lapsed. His benefit is granted from 24 June.

chunks.title: Timeframe to assign and complete the Jobseeker Profile — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Timeframe to assign and complete the Jobseeker Profile
A client has 20 working days from their date of first contact to complete their Jobseeker Profile. This must happen before their benefit can be granted.
Clients who do not complete their Jobseeker Profile within 20 working days will have their application lapse.
## Extensions
Clients who have a good and sufficient reason for being unable to complete their Jobseeker Profile within 20 working days may be given more time.
This can happen before or after the 20 working day timeframe lapses, depending on when the reason occurs and when the client notifies MSD.
Example
Nicole applied for a benefit on 24 June 2025 and had until 21 July to complete her application. She was told that she needed to complete a Jobseeker Profile before her benefit can be granted. She was scheduled to attend an appointment on 3 July but she didn't make it.
Nicole contacts MSD on 17 July to advise that she has been in hospital for the past three weeks and has not been able to provide everything she needs for her application, including completing her Jobseeker Profile. The next available appointment is 23 July, which is more than 20 working days after she made her application.
When she attends her appointment, she provides all her documents, including her completed Jobseeker Profile. MSD is satisfied there was a good reason why Nicole was not able to complete this within the 20-working day window and grants an extension so her application is not lapsed. Her application date remains 24 June.
## Not reasonable to complete their Jobseeker Profile
In some situations, it may not be reasonable for a client to complete their Jobseeker Profile.

chunks.title: Timeframes for assigning and completing an activity — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Timeframes for assigning and completing an activity
A pre-benefit activity must be available for and assigned to a client to undertake no later than 10 working days after their date of first contact.
However the client may choose to undertake the activity later than the first date it is available, as long as the activity is completed within 20 working days of their date of first contact.
For more information see:
- Advising a client about a pre-benefit activity
- Client does not complete assigned pre-benefit activity

chunks.title: Timeframes for assigning and completing an activity for partners — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Timeframes for assigning and completing an activity for partners
A pre-benefit activity must be available for and assigned to the partner to undertake no later than 10 working days after their date of first contact.
However the partner may choose to undertake the activity later than the first date it is available, as long as the activity is completed within 20 working days of the date of first contact.
For more information see:
- Advising a partner about a pre-benefit activity
- Partner does not complete assigned pre-benefit activity

chunks.title: Transfer between benefits for partners — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Transfer between benefits for partners
Partners who are transferring between benefits may have the requirement to complete a Jobseeker Profile, depending on the type of assistance they are transferring to.
This is because transferring to a new benefit is considered to be a new application.
## Transferring to a specified benefit
Partners who are transferring with a primary client to Jobseeker Support or Emergency Benefit (where a client has work-related conditions of grant) are required to complete a Jobseeker Profile, unless their circumstances mean the requirement is not reasonable. This includes transferring from Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment to one of these benefits, unless they continue to have youth activity obligations.
The Jobseeker Profile must be completed before a partner can be transferred onto their new benefit.
Partners will have 20 working days to complete their Jobseeker Profile from their date of first contact about transferring their benefit. If the Jobseeker Profile is not completed within this timeframe, a new application will need to be made.

chunks.title: Transfer between benefits — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Transfer between benefits
Clients who are transferring between benefits may have the requirement to complete a Jobseeker Profile, depending on the type of benefit they are transferring to.
This is because transferring to a new benefit is considered a new application for a benefit.
## Transferring to a specified benefit
Clients who are transferring to:
- Jobseeker Support
- Sole Parent Support, or
- Emergency Benefit with work-related conditions of grant (including Emergency Maintenance Allowance)
are required to complete a Jobseeker Profile, unless their circumstances mean the requirement is not reasonable. This includes clients transferring from Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment to one of these benefits.
The Jobseeker Profile must be completed before a client can be transferred to the new benefit.
Clients will have 20 working days to complete the Jobseeker Profile from their date of first contact. If the Jobseeker Profile is not completed within this timeframe, a new application will need to be made.
## Sole Parent Support transfer to Jobseeker Support when youngest child turns 14
Clients who are getting Sole Parent Support will automatically transfer to Jobseeker Support when their youngest child turns 14.
In this situation, a client doesn't need to complete a Jobseeker Profile as they're not considered to be making a new application for a benefit.
MSD may assign an obligation-related activity for a client to complete the Jobseeker Profile at a later date.

chunks.title: Pre-benefit activity should not be assigned — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Pre-benefit activity should not be assigned
There are some situations when a pre-benefit activity should not be assigned.
These include when:
- a pre-benefit activity is unable to be assigned within 10 working days of the client's date of first contact
- the pre-benefit activity is not available for the client to undertake within 10 working days of their date of first contact
- a pre-benefit activity can only be assigned if there is reasonable opportunity for the client to undertake it at any time during the 20 working day period
- initial contact is from a third party, eg an agent or partner. MSD must have direct contact with the primary client before a pre-benefit activity can be assigned. The date the third party makes contact can be used as the client's date of first contact.
- the client has a job to go to or is starting a job within 13 weeks

chunks.title: Pre-benefit activity should not be assigned to a partner — core policy > pre benefit requirements
chunks.text:
## Pre-benefit activity should not be assigned to a partner
There are some situations when a pre-benefit activity should not be assigned.
These include when:
- the date MSD assigns a pre-benefit activity is not within 10 working days of the partner's date of first contact
- the pre-benefit activity is not available for the partner to undertake within 10 working days of the date of first contact
- a pre-benefit activity can only be assigned if there is reasonable opportunity for the partner to undertake it at any time during the 20 working day period.
- initial contact is from a third party, eg an agent or the primary client. MSDmust have direct contact with the partner before a pre-benefit activity can be assigned. The date the third party makes contact can be used as the partner's date of first contact.
- the partner has a job to go to or is starting a job within 13 weeks

chunks.title: Changing and ending Income Related Rent redirections — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Changing and ending Income Related Rent redirections
Once we have established good cause to redirect a client's Income Related Rent or Income Related Rent arrears we will not change, suspend or stop the redirection before the tenancy ends or the arrears are paid unless there is strong evidence to support it.
## Client requests redirection to be stopped
Redirections of benefit may be cancelled at the client's request if they can show strong evidence that there is no longer good cause to redirect rent for social housing.
You must carefully consider the evidence that is received to support that there is no good cause. Examples of strong evidence include:
- client showing that they have a good history of rent payments prior to the redirection (for example, a superannuitant can show they have consistently paid their rent on time for several years before entering social housing)
- the client having no history of hardship requests
- the client showing a history of meeting their weekly financial commitments
- a recommendation from a budget advisory service, mental health service, or other welfare or support agency
Note this is not an exhaustive list.
## Changes in the benefit level prevents redirection
If the amount of benefit the client receives is reduced (eg due to income, Child Support payments, Ministry debt repayments), there may be insufficient money for a redirection of benefit to be paid.
Where a change in the benefit level results in there being insufficient benefit funds available to redirect the Income Related Rent or Income Related Rent arrears, the client will need to be advised that they will have to make the payment arrangements themselves.

chunks.title: Redirections cannot be transferred — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Redirections cannot be transferred
Redirection of benefit payments cannot be transferred from one party to another. The client must make a new application, and you will need to consider it as a new request. You will need to confirm that the client has tried any viable alternatives to redirection and, that good cause, exists.
For more information see:
## Ending redirection
Redirections of benefit made with the consent of the client can be cancelled by the client at any time.
Where the redirection of benefit has been made without the client's consent, the client cannot cancel the redirection. However, whenever there is a change in the client's circumstances, it is appropriate to review whether the redirection continues to be justified.
## The Ministry makes a decision to end redirection
A redirection can end if you receive evidence that it should not continue. This would be relevant if it became apparent that good cause no longer existed. For example, a client may have had a redirection approved because they were in a coma, therefore unable to manage to own finances. Once they regain consciousness, good cause may no longer exist, therefore the redirection should be reviewed.
If you make a decision to cancel the redirection, you need to:
- attempt to contact the client by phone to discuss the matter
- send them the 'redirection cancelled' template letter and
- give them a minimum of 10 working days to set up an alternative arrangement before the redirection is cancelled
## Recipient requests end to redirection
The recipient of the benefit redirection payments may request for the redirection to end. In these cases, you should not cancel the redirection before first having contacted the client to discuss the matter. If you make a decision to cancel the redirection, you need to:
- send them the 'redirection cancelled' template letter and
- give them a minimum of 10 working days to set up a different arrangement before the redirection is cancelled, if appropriate
Once we have established good cause to redirect a client's Income Related Rent or emergency housing contribution without their consent we will not change, suspend or stop the redirection unless there is strong evidence to support a change.

chunks.title: Changing and ending redirections for emergency housing contribution — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Changing and ending redirections for emergency housing contribution
Once good cause has been established to redirect a client's emergency housing contribution, MSD will not change, suspend or stop the redirection before the client moves out of emergency housing unless there is strong evidence to support.
## Client requests redirection to be stopped
Redirections of benefit may be cancelled at the client's request if they can show strong evidence that there is no longer good cause to redirect their emergency housing contribution.
MSD must carefully consider the evidence they have been given to support that there is no good cause. Examples of strong evidence include:
- the client showing they have a good history of rent payments before the redirection (e.g. a superannuitant can show they have consistently paid their rent on time for several years before entering emergency housing)
- the client has consistently paid their emergency housing contribution by the next available date or dates (e.g. existing redirections have been successful)
- the client has no history of hardship requests (excluding an Emergency Housing Grant)
- the client showing a history of meeting their weekly financial commitments
- a recommendation from a budget advisory service, mental health service, or other welfare or support agency
Note this is not an exhaustive list.
## Changes in the benefit level prevents redirection
If the amount of benefit the client receives is reduced (due to income, Child Support payments, MSD debt repayments, etc.), there may be insufficient money for a redirection of benefit to be paid.
Where a change in the benefit level results in there being insufficient benefit funds available to redirect the emergency housing contribution, the client will need to be advised that they will have to make the payment arrangements themselves, e.g. bank transfer or wage deduction.

chunks.title: Decision guidelines for redirection — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: When a client applies for part or all of their benefit to be paid to another party as a redirection of benefit payment, MSD should follow the steps below.

chunks.title: Step 1 - Client to look at other options — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: Are there other options (alternatives) to redirection available to clients to avoid having to redirect part or all of their benefit payments? The client needs to explain what other options to redirection they have looked at - if MSD feels the client has not explored any good alternatives, MSD can request they do this before considering their application for redirection. Exceptions Social Housing clients and clients in accommodation funded by an Emergency Housing Grant will generally have a redirection from their main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension to pay their Income Related Rent or emergency housing contribution. These clients do not need to look at other options.

chunks.title: Step 2 - Is it practical? — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: Is it practical to redirect the benefit payment? For example, a client's benefit payment may fluctuate too frequently to enable a regular redirection to occur.

chunks.title: Step 3 - Good cause — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: There must be good cause to approve a redirection of benefit. This means the individual circumstances of the client must be able to justify the payment of benefit to the other party. Each case must be judged on its own merits. Generally, there is no routine approval of redirection of benefit, for example the approval of all benefit redirections to a particular organisation. There are some specific situations where MSD can consider there is good cause, and MSD can redirect a person's benefit. For more information see: - Specific situations where there is good cause for redirection of benefit Before making a decision, MSD can discuss the application with the capability developer or manager Client Service Delivery. Good cause is considered to have been met in most cases when redirecting a client's benefit for: - Income Related Rent paid to a social housing provider or - emergency housing contributions paid to MSD’s designated account For more information on redirection of benefit payment for Income Related Rent or for emergency housing contribution see:

chunks.title: Step 4 - Client's consent — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: In most cases the client must agree to the redirection of their benefit, however in certain circumstances it may occur without the client's consent.

chunks.title: Step 5 - Use discretion — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: Even where good cause exists, MSD can use discretion to decline a request for a redirection of benefit.

chunks.title: Decision guidelines - without the client's consent — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Decision guidelines - without the client's consent
When considering a redirection of benefit without the clients consent (including for clients who were in social housing prior to 9 February 2015) you need to work through the decision guidelines below.
Exception
There are different decision guidelines for new social housing clients from 9 February 2015.
For more information see:
## 1. Contact client
Contact the client and attempt to gain their approval for the redirection of benefit. This may not be appropriate in all circumstances.
## 2. Good cause
Ensure that good cause exists to approve the redirection of benefit.
For more information see:
## 3. Supporting evidence
Check that there is verification of the need to redirect payment without the client's consent, such as:
- written advice from a registered health practitioner or other health professional
- a Court Order, made under the Protection of Property Rights Act (1988)
- an Enduring Power of Attorney
- other information that supports the need to redirect the benefit for the benefit of the client's partner or dependent children or to pay for the client's lawful debts or liabilities (eg outlining the repercussions for the client or partner and/or children if the benefit payment is not redirected)
## 4. Redirection application form
Check that the relevant sections of the application form have been completed by a person who has a close personal relationship with the client, such as their agent, their partner, or a relative, and that the person has signed the appropriate declaration.
Note from 9 February 2015 a 'Redirection of Benefit Payment' application form is not required where Income Related Rent will be redirected from a client's main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension to be paid to their social housing provider.
## 5. CMS client event note
For more information see:
- Processing standards Redirection of benefit payment [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Discretion to decline redirection — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Discretion to decline redirection
Generally, benefit payments should be made directly to the client. You must be satisfied that good cause exists before recommending the approval of a redirection of benefit.
Even when good cause exists, MSD is not always required to approve the redirection payment. MSD has discretion to approve a redirection of benefit, and this should only be used in appropriate circumstances.
You need to look at all the impacts of approving a redirection of benefit.
## Impractical to redirect
You can decline to redirect a client's benefit payment even if they meet the criteria for good cause where it would be impractical to redirect the payment due to the level of payment. This might be due to the benefit level being reduced because of:
- income
- any required deductions from the client's benefit through a deduction notice or attachment order
- overseas pension payable
- direct deduction due to weekly accident compensation
Redirection of benefit must not occur:
- for reasons of convenience or simply to reduce the client's bank fees
- to provide security of payment to outside organisations or companies (other than where 'good cause' is established)
- in response to a request from an outside party, such as landlord or power company (other than where 'good cause' is established)
All requests for redirection of benefit must be:
- generally made as a last resort
- the best option for, and in the best interests of, the client

chunks.title: Effect of changes in benefit level — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Effect of changes in benefit level
If the amount of benefit the client receives is reduced (due to income, Child Support payments, Ministry debt repayments etc), there may be insufficient money for a redirection of benefit to be paid.
It is important that the client is aware that the Ministry is not responsible for the failure of redirection of benefit payments due to insufficient benefit levels.
## New applications for redirection
If it is expected that a client's benefit level will fluctuate, it is likely that redirection of a large proportion of a client's benefit will not be appropriate. In such cases it may be appropriate to decline the client's redirection application, or suggest that they consider redirecting a lesser amount.
If a client's benefit level fluctuates and they need to pay an emergency housing contribution, a redirection of the contribution from their benefit may not be appropriate. We should not set up a redirection of benefit if the client's main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension is insufficient to cover the full amount of emergency housing contribution they need to pay.
In these cases, you must advise the client to pay their emergency housing contribution by bank transfer or wage deduction to the Ministry's designated account.
## Existing redirections
The client should be advised when an existing redirection is not made due to insufficient benefit funds being available they will have to make the payment themselves.
If the reduction in benefit level is on-going and will affect future redirection of benefit payments you should discuss with the client:
- the appropriateness of continuing the redirection
- reducing the amount that is redirected and
- whether good cause still exists
Where the benefit has been resumed, you can manually pay the redirection from any arrears. However, check with the client first - they may have already made the payment themselves.

chunks.title: Good cause — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Good cause
You cannot pay part or all of a client's benefit to another party unless you are satisfied that there is good cause to do so. Good cause means that the merits of the individual case justify the payment of benefit to the other party.
However, there are some specific situations where you can consider there is good cause to redirect a person's benefit. In these circumstances, you may decide to redirect the client's benefit.
Note even where good cause exists, the Ministry is not always required to approve the redirection payment.
For assistance on deciding whether good cause exists, see:

chunks.title: Good cause decision guidelines — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: There are some specific situations where MSD considers there is good cause to redirect a person's benefit. In these circumstances, MSD may decide to redirect the client's benefit. Note even when good cause exists, MSD is not always required to approve the redirection payment. For more information see:

chunks.title: Deciding if good cause exists — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: Some clients circumstances won't be covered by the specific situations where it has been identified there is good cause to redirect. For these clients, MSD should consider if there is good cause to redirect part or all of a client's benefit payment to another party. MSD should consider the following factors: - the reasons for paying part or all of the benefit to the other party - if the reasons involve a serious risk to the client's and/or their family's wellbeing - the severity of the client's situation, and their ability to sort out and manage their own affairs - if the redirection is in relation to an essential service, such as housing and power (a hire purchase agreement may not be considered essential, and a redirection of benefit would not normally be used for this purpose) - if refusing the redirection of benefit places the client in a worse position, for example, refusing would result in the client being evicted from their accommodation - the clients payment history, for example, substantial history of frequently missed payments to MSD, eviction from their accommodation, or disconnection from essential services such as power - if there a supporting recommendation from a budget advisory service, mental health service, or other welfare or support agency - if the client has exhausted other viable alternatives - the client’s history of frequent requests for extra assistance from MSD for the same purpose, for example, power disconnection or rent bond Note this is not an exhaustive list.

chunks.title: Establishing good cause — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: Good cause is not necessarily established through meeting a single factor or scenario listed above - when a client is having difficulty managing their affairs it does not automatically follow that good cause exists. MSD must weigh up all relevant circumstances before making a decision on whether good cause exists. For example, if a client requests redirection and has a documented problem, such as gambling addiction or mental illness that is resulting in financial mismanagement, good cause may be established.

chunks.title: Redirection without client consent — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: A redirection of benefit can be made without the client's consent as a last resort for payment of a client's lawful debts and liabilities, or when it is considered totally necessary for the support of their partner and/or dependent children.

chunks.title: Social Housing clients — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: Generally social housing clients will have a redirection from their main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension for their Income Related Rent to be paid to their social housing provider. For more information see: - Redirection for social housing

chunks.title: Clients in accommodation funded by an Emergency Housing Grant — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: Generally clients will have a redirection from their main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension for their emergency housing contribution to be paid to MSD’s designated account.

chunks.title: Identifying clients with history of poor financial management — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Identifying clients with history of poor financial management
You may redirect a client's benefit where the person has a history of poor financial management and the redirection is necessary to ensure the priority needs of the client and their dependants are met.
To identify a client with a history of poor financial management consider the following:
- Has the client advised they have trouble managing their income and payments?
- Has the client been to a budget advisory service?
- Does the budget advisory service recommend the client discuss the redirection of part or all of the client's benefit?
- Does the client apply for additional hardship assistance on a regular basis?
- Does the client have an income deficit ie more outgoings than income?
- Is the client eligible for and receiving ongoing assistance such as Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit?
- Does the client have other costs that cannot be included in the assessment of Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit that has been granted?
- Does the client still have a deficit after Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit has been granted?
- Has the client been in arrears in the past for any essential items such as rent or power?
Remember this is not an exhaustive list.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Insufficient capacity — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Insufficient capacity
Where the client has insufficient capacity to consent to a redirection, as long as good cause exists, redirection of benefit payment can occur without the client's consent.
For more information see:
Generally, a client is regarded as having insufficient capacity when they are unable to understand the consequences of their decisions. This means that they do things that are not in the best interests of their personal care and welfare, but have no way of understanding the effect of these decisions.
If a person is able to understand the consequences of their decisions but has no way of communicating these desired decisions they can also be considered to have insufficient capacity.
## Proof of insufficient capacity
Acceptable proof that a person lacks sufficient capacity in law can be:
- a Court Order made under the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act (1988)
- written advice from a registered medical practitioner or specialist that the client cannot understand the nature of their decisions or communicate decisions affecting their care and welfare
- an Enduring Power of Attorney
If acceptable proof is provided, part or all of a client's benefit may be redirected to another party, as long as you are satisfied that good cause exists.
## Temporary insufficient capacity
Redirection of benefit may be possible where the client is temporarily incapacitated, however it should only be in place for as long as the client is incapacitated. When the client regains the capacity to make their own decisions, (for example, coming out of a coma), the redirection should be discussed with the client and, if appropriate, stopped.
## Examples
Some possible situations where a client may lack sufficient capacity in law include:
- a client in a coma
- a client who is mentally capable but physically paralysed, and therefore unable to communicate
- a client who is mentally incapacitated
Note any redirection of benefit made where the client lacks sufficient capacity does not mean the recipient of the payments is considered the client's agent, or give them any powers of agency, unless those powers are already held by the recipient.
For more information see:
See also:

chunks.title: Other options available to clients — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: Redirection of benefit will generally be considered as a last resort. MSD is committed to actively encouraging all clients to become more independent. Clients should be encouraged to take responsibility for managing their own financial affairs. However there are certain situations where MSD can consider if there is good cause to redirect a person's benefit. In these circumstances, MSD may decide to redirect the client's benefit. Note even where good cause exists, MSD is not always required to approve the redirection payment. For more information see:

chunks.title: Social Housing clients — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: Generally clients will have a redirection from their main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation, or Veteran's Pension for Income Related Rent to be paid to their social housing provider. The client does not need to look for other options in this situation. For more information see:

chunks.title: Clients in accommodation funded by an Emergency Housing Grant — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: Generally clients will have a redirection from their main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension for their emergency housing contribution to be paid to MSD's designated account. The client does not need to look at other options in this situation. Non-beneficiary clients (including students getting Student Allowance, Student Loan, or people getting only extra help), will need to pay their emergency housing contribution, by bank transfer or wage deduction, to MSD’s designated account. For more information see:

chunks.title: Other options for redirection must be considered — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: A client applying for a redirection of benefit (other than for Income Related Rent to be paid to a social housing provider or an emergency housing contribution to be paid to MSD's designated account) must have first investigated viable alternatives. MSD should discuss with the client other ways to arrange payments such as: - referring the client to a budget advisory service - direct debit allows for bills to be paid automatically and regularly from the client's bank account. Direct debit costs are paid for by the organisation receiving the payment - not the client. This is suitable for bills that vary, such as telephone or electricity bills. - automatic payment differs from direct debit in that each regular payment is for a fixed amount, therefore ideal for unvarying bills such as rent. Established and paid for by the client. Can also be used for telephone and electricity bills, if regular set payments have been negotiated with the company. - telephone banking, internet banking clients can arrange for most bill payments, including those to private landlords, to be set up as 'bill payees', enabling bills to be paid over the telephone or the internet. - choosing more appropriate banking services the client may want to 'shop around' for the best banking deal available to them; this may mean opening a different bank account with a better fee structure (e.g. a student account), or even changing banks.

chunks.title: Redirection for accommodation cost for vulnerable tenants — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection for accommodation cost for vulnerable tenants
There is good cause to redirect a client's benefit where the person is a vulnerable tenant and the redirection is required to reassure the person's landlord or prospective landlord, that the person will meet their rental commitments.
## Vulnerable tenant
A client is considered to be a vulnerable tenant if:
- they are a tenant or a prospective tenant of accommodation that is not social housing who are considered at risk of eviction or homelessness
- they are on the housing register but have not been allocated social housing by a social housing provider
- they are in social housing but are waiting for a transfer to other social housing
## At risk of eviction or homelessness
A client would be considered at risk of eviction or homelessness if they:
- are homeless as they only have accommodation in a caravan, garage or mobile home provided by family or friends for a temporary period
- have a notice to vacate current accommodation
- have no permanent accommodation and staying in temporary accommodation where the situation is not sustainable (this is their friends or family have asked them to leave)
- are staying in emergency accommodation
- are ready to leave institutional accommodation
- are squatting in a property
- are living in a property that has been illegally sublet to the client
- are living in a mobile home or caravan with minimal access to facilities and amenities (for example a caravan park)
- have rent arrears that are putting their tenancy at risk
## Discretion not to redirect
Even when good cause exists, MSD is not always required to approve the redirection payment.

chunks.title: Redirection for client required to contribute to care costs — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection for client required to contribute to care costs
There is good cause to redirect a client's benefit if the client is:
- a resident assessed as requiring care or
- a person receiving residential care services and
- required to contribute from their benefit to the cost of contracting services provided to the person or the cost of residential care services provided to the person
Note all requests associated with Residential Care Subsidy (RCS) and Residential Support Subsidy (RSS) must be forwarded to the Residential Subsidy Unit in Whangarei.
## Redirection of Personal Allowance to the Residential Care Provider
Sometimes a client will need to have their Personal Allowance redirected to the home or institution. This might be because the client does not have any family to assist in purchasing personal items the client may need or the family are not using the personal allowance to provide the items needed by the client. In these situations, the Personal Allowance is being redirected not to fund the client's care but for use by the client. You need to ensure that:
- the bank account is not the business account of the home or institution
- the home or institution is acting in the best possible interests of the client
## Discretion not to redirect
Even where good cause exists, the Ministry is not always required to approve the redirection payment.
For more information see:
- Residential Care Subsidy Benefit or pension contribution
- Residential Care Subsidy Personal allowance
- Specific situations where there is good cause
- Residential Support Subsidy Client authorisation for benefit redirection
- Residential Support Subsidy Personal Allowance
- Residential Support Subsidy Payment

chunks.title: Redirection for emergency housing contribution — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection for emergency housing contribution
Most clients staying in accommodation funded by an Emergency Housing Grant to pay an emergency housing contribution towards their accommodation costs.
The emergency housing contribution will generally be paid directly to MSD by redirection from a client's main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension. As long as good cause exists, the client's benefit can be redirected for the payment of their emergency housing contribution.
Good cause is generally considered to be met for clients getting a Emergency Housing Grant because:
- the client has an immediate housing need that they cannot address through their own resources and
- redirection of benefit to pay their emergency housing contribution will help the client meet their emergency housing responsibilities, which gives them a place to stay while they find suitable and sustainable long-term housing
Note a 'Redirection of Benefit Payment' application form is not needed for redirection of benefit payment for emergency housing contribution.
## No good cause
In some circumstances the client may be able to show strong evidence that there is no good cause to redirect their emergency housing contribution.
MSD must carefully consider the evidence the client has provided in support that there is no good cause. Examples of strong evidence include:
- the client showing they have a good history of rent payments (e.g. a superannuitant who can show they have consistently paid for their rent on time for several years)
- the client having no history of hardship requests (excluding an Emergency Housing Grant)
- the client showing a history of meeting weekly financial commitments
- a recommendation from a budget advisory service, mental health service, or other welfare or support agency
If, after considering the client's evidence, MSD considers there is no good cause to redirect the client's emergency housing contribution, MSD should advise the client about their payment options, e.g. bank transfer or wage deduction.
MSD must still advise the client that a redirection may be put in place for subsequent emergency housing grants if the client's emergency housing contribution(s) has not been paid by the next available date.

chunks.title: Redirection for essential services — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection for essential services
There is good cause to redirect a client's benefit where, because of non-payment, they are at risk of (or have a history of):
- being disconnected from essential services (electricity, gas or water) or telecommunication services (land-line telephone, mobile or Internet)
- incurring late payment penalties and/or recognition charges and
- redirection is required to help prevent this risk
Note there can be no routine approval of redirection of benefit, for example, the approval of all benefit redirections to a particular organisation. All redirections must be approved on a case-by-case basis.
## Discretion not to redirect
Even where good cause exists, the Ministry is not always required to approve the redirection payment.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Redirection for money due after a New Zealand court or tribunal judgement — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection for money due after a New Zealand court or tribunal judgement
There is good cause to redirect a client's benefit where the client has money due under any judgement or order of any Court or tribunal of New Zealand and the redirection is required to make payments towards the amount due.
For example, clients may have to make payments as a result of an outcome from a decision from the:
- Tenancy Tribunal - a specialist tribunal that resolves disputes between landlords and tenants
- Disputes Tribunal - a tribunal that helps resolve a wide range of civil disputes up to $15,000 or if both parties agree, up to $20,000
Note a client may also have attachment orders from the Court. These provide for mandatory deductions directly from the client's benefit and are undertaken by the Central Processing Unit. They cannot be stopped without authorisation from the Ministry of Justice.
## Discretion not to redirect
Even where good cause exists, the Ministry is not always required to approve the redirection payment.

chunks.title: Redirection for priority needs — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection for priority needs
You may redirect a client's benefit where the person has a history of poor financial management and the redirection is necessary to ensure the priority needs of the client and their dependants are met.
Priority needs include (but are not limited to) the following:
- essential services - electricity, gas and water
- telecommunication services - land-line telephone services, mobile telephone services and internet services
- accommodation costs - rent and rent arrears, mortgage, damages
- medical costs - health practitioner visits, prescription costs
- education costs - school fees, stationery costs
## Definition of dependants
For a redirection to pay for priority needs purposes, a client's dependants may include:
- their partner
- their dependent child or children
- any other person who ordinarily lives with the client, and who is wholly or primarily dependent on the client for financial support
- a person who is in the clients care, due to their inability to live independently due to health condition, injury, disability or advanced age
## Identifying clients with history of poor financial management
To redirect to ensure priority needs are met, the client must have a history of poor financial management and the redirection must be necessary to ensure their or their dependants' priority needs are met.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Redirection for social housing — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: For social housing tenancies, Income Related Rent will generally be paid directly to the social housing provider by redirection from a client's main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension. As long as good cause exists, the client's benefit can be redirected for the payment of Income Related Rent without their consent. Good cause is generally considered to be met by social housing clients because: - the client has been assessed as having a high need for social housing and - redirection of benefit to pay Income Related Rent will help towards providing security of tenure and tenancy sustainability Note a 'Redirection of Benefit Payment' application form is not required for redirection of benefit payment for Income Related Rent.

chunks.title: No good cause — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: In some circumstances the client may be able to show strong evidence that there is no good cause to redirect rent for social housing. You must carefully consider the evidence that is received to support that there is no good cause. Examples of strong evidence include: - the client showing that they have a good history of rent payments (for example, a superannuitant who can show they have consistently paid for their rent on time for several years) - the client having no history of hardship requests - the client showing a history of meeting weekly financial commitments - a recommendation from a budget advisory service, mental health service, or other welfare or support agency If, after considering the client's circumstances, you consider there is no good cause to redirect the client's Income Related Rent you must advise the client that a redirection may be put in place if: - the social housing provider informs MSD they have fallen behind in their rent or - they apply for hardship assistance with rent arrears

chunks.title: Multiple signatories — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: Each signatory to the tenancy agreement is jointly and severally liable for the payment of any Income Related Rent required under the tenancy. If there are multiple signatories to the tenancy agreement, the Income Related Rent should be split evenly between each of the signatories unless it is requested that a different split is used. When a different split is requested, all signatories must agree to their share of the Income Related Rent. For example, where there are two signatories to the tenancy agreement, each would be assigned 50% of the assessed Income Related Rent. For information on liability for Income Related Rent debt where there are multiple signatories, see:

chunks.title: Redirection for Income Related Rent arrears — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: Where a client owes money to their current social housing provider for unpaid Income Related Rent, a redirection for the arrears can be made from their main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension without the client's consent. The client's inability to meet their rental commitments demonstrates that there is good cause for the redirection to be established. A 'Redirection of Benefit Payment' application form is not required when MSD has been notified of the Income Related Rent arrears by the client's current social housing provider.

chunks.title: Redirection for the costs of damages to a social housing property — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: Generally, the client's consent is required before a redirection can be made from their main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension for money owed to a social housing provider for damages to a property. A 'Redirection of Benefit Payment' application form is not required when MSD has been notified of the amount owing for damages by the client's current social housing provider. Note consent is not required to redirect a client's benefit where the client has money due for damages under a judgement or order of any Court or tribunal of New Zealand. For more information see: - Redirection for money due after a New Zealand Court or tribunal judgement
