chunks.title: Redirection for the costs of water consumption — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text: A client may request a redirection for their water consumption charges. For information of whether or not to establish a redirection see: The social housing landlord is responsible for the payment of all water charges to the respective council or organisation responsible for water. The social housing landlord will then charge the client for their water consumption. The client should only be charged for actual water usage and should not be charged for estimated amounts, base costs or line charges. Generally, the client's consent is required before a redirection for water consumption can be made from their main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension unless there is good cause. For more information see: Before the redirection is established, the social housing landlord should provide verification that the client will have to pay for water usage and an estimated cost for redirection purposes.

chunks.title: Redirection for the benefit of partner or children — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection for the benefit of partner or children
Where there is good cause, part or all of a client's benefit may be redirected to the client's partner or another party for the benefit of the partner and/or children.
For more information see:
- Good cause
- Specific situations where there is good cause
For example, this may be appropriate where a client is misusing the benefit and the redirection is necessary to ensure that their dependents continue to have their basic needs met (such as housing, food and power).
These redirections can be made:
- preferably, directly to the client's partner or
- to a third party
Generally, the partner will already be receiving half of the client's benefit payments. In such cases, you can consider redirecting the full payment to the partner.
## Redirection without the client's consent
As long as good cause exists, a redirection of benefit may occur for the benefit of the partner and/or children without the client's consent as a last resort.
If a redirection is made to the partner, in most cases they will already be receiving half of the client's benefit payments. In such cases, you may consider redirecting the full payment to the partner.
If a redirection is made to a third party, you need to ensure that the third party is:
- appropriate, considering the relationship to the family
- receiving the redirection solely for the benefit of the client's partner and/or any dependent children and
- responsive to the partner and/or children
For more information see:

chunks.title: Redirection of benefit payment — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection of benefit payment
Redirection of benefit payment is when part or all a client's benefit payment is paid directly to another person or organisation, instead of to the client.
Redirection of benefit can only be done when there is good cause.
In specific situations you can redirect a person's benefit if you consider there is 'good cause'.
For more information see:
- Good cause
- Specific situations when there is good cause to redirect
Generally, you cannot pay any part of a client's benefit to another party.
The exceptions to this rule are:
- when MSD is legally required to pay the benefit or a portion of the benefit to another party, for example Court deduction notices or attachment ordersFor more information see: Deductions
- when the benefit is being paid at a couple rate and the benefit is split between the client and their partner (apportionment of benefit) or
- a redirection of benefit payment for good cause
Note even when good cause exists, MSD is not always required to approve the redirection payment.
For more information see:
## Redirecting a benefit payment
In certain circumstances, part or all a client's benefit can be paid to another person or organisation as a redirection of benefit. This:
- can only be done if there is good cause and
- will generally only be a last resort - the client should have explored alternatives and
- is discretionary
Note the granting of a redirection of benefit does not give the recipient of the payments any other decision-making powers over the client's affairs, or grant them access to personal information about the client. They are not considered an agent.

chunks.title: Redirection to pay essential lawful debt or other liability — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection to pay essential lawful debt or other liability
There is good cause to redirect a person's benefit if the client is required to pay any debt or other liability for goods or services that the Ministry of Social Development considers essential for the person or any of their dependants and the redirection is necessary to make payments towards the amount due.
Lawful debts or other liabilities can cover any cost a person is legally or contractually required to pay in return for the goods or service. However, for there to be good cause, the cost needs to be essential for the person or any of the person's dependants.
## Examples of goods or services that may be essential
The following are examples of goods or services that may be considered essential for the client or any of their dependants:
- essential services - electricity, gas and water
- telecommunications services - land-line telephone services, mobile telephone services and Internet services
- accommodation costs - rent and rent arrears, mortgage
- medical costs - health practitioner visits, prescription costs
- education costs - school fees, stationery costs, childcare costs
- vehicle repayments where vehicle is needed for needs of daily life or for employment
- hire purchase repayments for essential household items such as: bed (including mattress) or mattressdining suitecombined fridge/freezer, or a fridge and freezer, or a fridge, or freezerlounge suiteportable heaterstovetelevisionwashing machine
- bed (including mattress) or mattress
- dining suite
- combined fridge/freezer, or a fridge and freezer, or a fridge, or freezer
- lounge suite
- portable heater
- stove
- television
- washing machine
- any other cost that is essential for the client or any of their dependants
## Definition of dependants
For a redirection to pay lawful debts or other liability purposes, a client's dependents may include:
- their partner
- their dependent child or children
- any other person who ordinarily lives with the client and who is wholly or primarily dependent on the client for financial support
- a person who is in the clients care due to the inability to live independently due to health condition, injury, disability or advanced age

chunks.title: Redirection to pay for fines — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection to pay for fines
There is good cause to redirect a client's benefit where the client has been ordered to pay or is in default of payment of a fine and the redirection is required to make payments towards that fine.
A fine includes:
- any amount of money that a person is required to pay under a sentence or order imposed by a court. This payment might be described as a fine, costs, levies, expenses, fees or reparation
- any offender level and any prescribed costs, expenses or fees required to be paid to enforce an obligation to pay the fine imposed by the court
A fine does not include any amount of money ordered to be paid in a civil proceeding.
Note a client may also have attachment orders from the court. These provide for mandatory deductions directly from the client's benefit and are undertaken by the Central Processing Unit. They cannot be stopped without authorisation from the Ministry of Justice.
## Discretion not to redirect
Even where good cause exists, MSD is not always required to approve the redirection payment.

chunks.title: Redirection to pay the client's debts or liabilities — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection to pay the client's debts or liabilities
Where there is good cause, a client's benefit payment may be redirected to pay their lawful debts or liabilities. This type of redirection involves paying part or all of a client's benefit to a person or organisation to pay for a specific cost.
Lawful debts or other liabilities can cover any costs a person is legally or contractually required to pay in return for the goods or service.
For example, where good cause exists, a redirection could be made for the person's specific debts or liabilities. These might include (but not limited to) payments for:
- electricity, gas and water
- telecommunications services - land-line telephone services, mobile telephone services and Internet services
- accommodation costs - rent and rent arrears, mortgage
- medical costs - health practitioner visits, prescription costs
- education costs - school fees, stationery costs, childcare costs
- vehicle repayments
- hire purchase repayments
- personal loan repayments
For more information see:
## Redirection without the client's consent
In certain circumstances, and as long as good cause exists, a redirection of benefit may occur without the client's consent to pay the client's debts or liabilities.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Redirection without the client's consent — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection without the client's consent
Generally, the client's consent is required before a redirection of benefit is approved. However, there are some exceptions to this, as outlined below. Redirection of benefit without the client's consent should only occur as a last resort.
## Client unable to give informed consent
Some clients may be unable to give their informed consent to a redirection of benefit, for example, a client in a coma, or a client who is mentally incapacitated. As long as good cause exists, a redirection of benefit may occur where the client can be shown to have insufficient capacity.
For more information see:
## Client refuses to give consent
There may be a situation where others (such as the client's family) believe that part or all of the client's benefit should be redirected to another party, but the client disagrees with this. For example, a client may have a gambling addiction that is resulting in such financial mismanagement that their partner's wellbeing is placed at risk.
As long as good cause exists, it may be appropriate to approve a redirection of benefit payment, even when the client does not consent to it. This could occur in one of the following situations:
- Redirection for social housing
- Redirection for emergency housing contribution
- Redirection to pay the client's debts or liabilities
- Redirection for the benefit of partner or children
- where the client has insufficient capacity
## Guidelines
To help you decide whether to redirect a benefit without the client's consent, see:

chunks.title: Reviews and Appeals — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Reviews and Appeals
A client may apply for a Review of Decision where they have received formal notification of (and does not agree with) a decision associated with redirection of benefit payment, for example the Ministry declining a redirection application.

chunks.title: Social housing clients before 9 February 2015 — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Social housing clients before 9 February 2015
Clients living in social housing before 9 February 2015 who do not already have a redirection in place will not have their Income Related Rent redirected from their benefit and paid to their social housing provider unless:
- the client requests that their Income Related Rent be redirected from their benefit or
- it is determined that good cause exists to redirect the client's Income Related Rent without their consent
For more information see:

chunks.title: Specific situations where there is good cause — core policy > redirection of benefit payment
chunks.text:
## Specific situations where there is good cause
There are some specific situations where you can consider there is good cause to redirect a person's benefit. These include the following:
If a client is in one of these situations, you can consider there is good cause and may decide to redirect their benefit:
- to another person, on behalf of the client or
- to pay for the client's debts or liabilities (anything that the client is required to pay) or
- for the benefit of the client's partner and/or dependent children
Note even where good cause exists, the Ministry is not always required to approve the redirection payment.
In most cases the client must agree to the redirection of part or all of their benefit, however, in certain circumstances it may be required without the client's consent.

chunks.title: Jointly and severally liable — core policy > relationship debt sharing
chunks.text:
## Jointly and severally liable
This is where 2 or more people are each liable for 100% of a debt. Each is responsible for the full amount of the debt until it is repaid. Payment may be sought from any one of the parties, or from any and all of the parties, in various amounts until the debt is paid in full.
If any of the parties do not have enough money to pay, the other parties must make up the difference.
## Ought to have known
This is a common expression of the legal concept called constructive or objective knowledge. It is knowledge that a person would have had if they had made inquiries that any reasonable person would have made in the same circumstances.
A person 'ought to have known' they were benefiting from welfare payments if they had made inquiries that any reasonable person would have. For example:
- they made no attempt to question where the money coming into the household was from
- they did not question how their partner or spouse was paying for living expenses
For more information see:
- Prosecuting partners

chunks.title: Prosecuting partners — core policy > relationship debt sharing
chunks.text:
## Prosecuting partners
The Ministry is able to prosecute a partner of a beneficiary where they:
- knowingly benefited or
- were reckless as to whether they are benefiting from their partner's welfare fraud
## Knowingly benefited
Knowingly benefited involves the partner having a degree of knowledge of the beneficiaries fraud and benefiting in some way from any overpayments. The partner does not need to know the precise nature of the fraud or the actual amount of overpayment.
Where the partner knows or is reckless as to whether their beneficiary partner is receiving benefit payments in excess of their entitlement by way of fraud and the partner benefits in some way, directly or indirectly, from the overpayment, the partner can be prosecuted.
Benefiting from a fraudulent overpayment can occur either directly or indirectly, for example as part of a common household.
Other examples may include, but are not limited to:
- the client and their partner's intentions were to commit fraud
- they made false or misleading statements knowing they were receiving benefit entitlements they would otherwise not be entitled to
- the partner was aware the client was receiving a benefit they were not entitled to (or at a higher rate than they were entitled to) and failed to declare this

chunks.title: Recklessness — core policy > relationship debt sharing
chunks.text:
## Recklessness
Reckless knowledge involves a subjective and objective component. These are what the individual themselves thought (subjective) and what an ordinary person in the same circumstances would have considered reasonable (objective). For example:
- the partner perceived that there was a risk, or that a set of circumstances existed, and decided to proceed or run the risk regardless (subjective) and
- the partner's decision to run the risk was unreasonable based on what an ordinary person, in the same circumstances, would have considered reasonable (objective)
Examples include, but are not limited to:
- if a partner inquires and forms a belief that fraud is being committed, but stays silent and benefits from their beneficiary partner's fraud, that person could be said to have reckless knowledge
- if a partner does not make any inquiries, or turn their mind to whether the beneficiary partner is committing fraud, because they fear the answer or want to be able to deny it later then they could also be said to have reckless knowledge
- if a partner inquires and forms a belief that fraud is not being committed, they may be held liable for the fraudulent debt if a reasonable and honest person, in the same circumstances, would have appreciated the risk. This is because an appreciation of risk can be inferred. These cases often turn on the evidence.
If a partner does not make any inquiries, or turn their mind to whether their beneficiary partner is committing fraud, because they truly believe their partner is not committing fraud, then they are unlikely to be found to have reckless knowledge and cannot be prosecuted. This is because they genuinely and honestly believe it to be true (subjective knowledge).

chunks.title: Relationship debt sharing — core policy > relationship debt sharing
chunks.text:
## Relationship debt sharing
From 7 July 2014, partners as well as beneficiaries are accountable for welfare fraud or dishonest behaviour in certain circumstances.
## Fraud
When a person receives money they are not entitled to as a result of a false or misleading statement or omission this is regarded as fraudulent.
In the context of relationship debt, fraud is not limited to someone who has been prosecuted or the individual concerned. There must however, be some degree of fraud on the part of the person in receipt of the benefit. In the case of partners, if they 'knowingly benefited' or 'ought to have known' that fraud was occurring, then this will constitute relationship debt.
When the Ministry establishes an overpayment by mistake the payments made to the client are not considered to be as a result of fraud.
## Shared debts
From 7 July 2014, an undeclared partner is 'jointly and severally' liable for a debt where the Ministry proves that they:
- knowingly benefited, or ought to have known they were benefiting from welfare payments being received fraudulently by their beneficiary partner in excess of entitlements or
- made a false statement or mislead the Ministry and, as a result, their beneficiary partner is paid in excess of their actual entitlement

chunks.title: Review of decision for relationship debt sharing — core policy > relationship debt sharing
chunks.text:
## Review of decision for relationship debt sharing
From 7 July 2014, partners have the right to review and appeal the Ministry's decision that they are liable for a debt and/or establishment of a debt.
A partner cannot review or appeal against a decision that relates to the temporary deferral of debt or the rate, or method of debt recovery from their beneficiary partner.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — core policy > relationship status for benefit > changes and reviews relationship status for benefit
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client is obliged to advise the Ministry of Social Development of any changes in their circumstances that affects their entitlement to a benefit.
You may also review a benefit at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is getting the correct rate of payment.
A change in a client's circumstances may also mean that the client qualifies for another benefit.

chunks.title: Reconciles, marries or separates — core policy > relationship status for benefit > changes and reviews relationship status for benefit
chunks.text:
## Reconciles, marries or separates
Review the client's benefit from the date after the event where they:
- reconcile with former partner
- marry or
- separate
## New or formative relationship
When a client is entering into a new relationship there is discretion to cancel or suspend the benefit from the first available date.
## Overpayments
You should only establish an overpayment if:
- the client has failed to advise of a change in circumstances or
- they have deliberately misled the Ministry of Social Development
If you are unable to make a decision regarding the client's relationship you can discuss the case with your Regional Solicitor or local National Fraud Investigation Unit Investigator.

chunks.title: Facilitation — core policy > relationship status for benefit > changes and reviews relationship status for benefit
chunks.text:
## Facilitation
The facilitation process helps clients to determine what effect their de facto relationship will have on their benefit. A loss of benefit is not easy and commitment to a long-standing relationship does not happen overnight.
You should give the client as much information as possible about their benefit entitlement and how moving into a de facto relationship would affect their benefit. This allows the client to make an informed decision.
A time frame can be negotiated with the client to allow them to decide whether they will enter into a de facto relationship and therefore surrender entitlement to a single or sole parent rate of benefit. This can be a period of up to 6 weeks. This period will give them time to consider the consequences for them and to discuss the matter with their partner.
They should be advised that if they enter into a de facto relationship before that time, they should cancel their benefit.
If a client decides to move into a stable relationship then the Ministry of Social Development must support this decision.
If you are unable to make a decision regarding the client's relationship you can discuss the case with your Regional Solicitor or local National Fraud Investigation Unit Investigator.

chunks.title: New or formative relationships — core policy > relationship status for benefit > changes and reviews relationship status for benefit
chunks.text:
## New or formative relationships
As soon as a client gets married; or enters into a civil union or de facto relationship they no longer have entitlement to a single or sole parent rate of benefit.
For de facto relationships it can be difficult to determine when a relationship has developed to the stage where it could be considered to be in the nature of marriage or civil union.
When a client enters a new or formative de facto relationship the case manager should help the client identify whether they are moving towards a more permanent relationship.
If you are unable to make a decision regarding the client's relationship you can discuss the case with your Regional Solicitor or local National Fraud Investigation Unit Investigator.

chunks.title: Clients living in a de facto relationship — core policy > relationship status for benefit
chunks.text:
## Clients living in a de facto relationship
Clients in a de facto relationship are assessed as a couple.
Note it is important to establish whether a de facto relationship exists or not before benefit entitlement is determined or reviewed.
A client who was in a de facto relationship may be assessed as single or a sole parent if they can show a genuine breakdown in the relationship. As with married or civil union couples, people sometimes live separately for reasons other than a breakdown in their relationship or rearrange their circumstances to qualify for a benefit.
## Living in separate homes
Some couples may live in separate homes because of (but are not limited to):
- financial reasons
- health reasons
- one party lives overseas or
- business/employment reasons (eg truck driver, shearer etc)
This does not mean they are no longer in a de facto relationship. You can only pay a single or sole parent rate of benefit if the relationship has genuinely ended.
## Features of a de facto relationship
For a de facto relationship to exist the client and the other adult must have a relationship that has similar characteristics to a marriage or civil union. When considering whether a client is in a de facto relationship these characteristics can be used to help determine relationship status. These are:
- Emotional commitment
- Financial interdependence
Note the absence of either of these characteristics means that the client is not in a de facto relationship for benefit purposes.
If you are unable to make a decision regarding the client's relationship with the other adult you can discuss the case with your regional solicitor or local fraud investigator.

chunks.title: Clients who are married or in a civil union — core policy > relationship status for benefit
chunks.text:
## Clients who are married or in a civil union
Clients who are married or in a civil union and are living together are considered a couple unless it is clear the relationship has ended.
A client who is married or in a civil union may be assessed as single or a sole parent if they can show they are living apart from their partner.
Note the term 'living apart' does not refer solely to living in separate homes.
When a client considers their marriage or civil union has ended but is unable to leave the relationship because of family violence, discuss the client's circumstances with your regional solicitor or local fraud investigator.

chunks.title: De facto relationship (definition) — core policy > relationship status for benefit
chunks.text:
## De facto relationship (definition)
A de facto relationship is when 2 people:
- are both aged 16 years or older and
- live together as a couple in a relationship in the nature of marriage or civil union
## Client or their partner is 16 or 17 years old
If a client or their partner are 16 or 17 years old, they can only be treated as a couple if they have an order from a Family Court Judge giving consent for the de facto relationship.
Consent from a Family Court Judge for the relationship is required whether or not the couple has a dependent child.
If consent is not given, MSD should consider if each client qualifies for a benefit in their own right.

chunks.title: Emotional commitment — core policy > relationship status for benefit
chunks.text:
## Emotional commitment
When considering if a client is in a de facto relationship you need to determine whether they have an emotional commitment to each other. The relationship must demonstrate a degree of companionship and a level of emotional commitment that is ongoing.
Every relationship is different and to assist you determine if a client and another adult are emotionally committed to each other a list of possible indicators is provided. Not all relationships will have all these indicators, but this list is provided to help you discuss the relationship with the client:
- client perception - the client and the other adult see their relationship as a relationship in the nature of marriage or civil union; they consider the relationship is likely to continue
- public perception - they are viewed as a couple by their community (this may include their family, local church, sports clubs etc)
- history - the length of time the client and the other adult have known each other and/or have resided at the same address; shared children
- extent to which their lives are merged - socialising together and how often this occurs; going out as a family; belonging to and attending the same clubs/sports teams or interest groups together; having meals together as a couple/family; their sleeping and sexual relationships
- shared responsibilities - arrangements for domestic duties such as gardening, cleaning, cooking; the caring arrangements for any children including when children are sick; joint decision making and plans together
- support - the emotional support that the client and the other person provide to each other; the nature of any companionship and support that the client and the other person provide to each other
Note that when considering if a client is in a relationship and the client indicates they are a victim of family violence, extra care must be taken when determining if the required level of emotional commitment is present.
If you are unable to make a decision regarding the client's relationship you can discuss the case with your regional solicitor or local fraud investigator.

chunks.title: Family violence — core policy > relationship status for benefit
chunks.text:
## Family violence
When a client has advised they are a victim of family violence, extra care must be taken when considering if a relationship with another adult exists and the impact the violence has on the relationship. If the client only stays with the other adult because they are fearful or powerless, then they are not in a de facto relationship for benefit purposes.
Note that if you believe a client has been, or is likely to be harmed (physically, emotionally or sexually), ill treated, abused, neglected or deprived, discuss the situation with your local Family Violence Response Co-ordinator.
When determining if a client is in a relationship you will need to consider if the required level of emotional commitment is present.
Before making a decision, you should encourage your client to provide proof of the family violence. This may include:
- the client's health practitioner
- statements from family and friends
- Police reports
- Community Family Violence prevention agency (eg Women's Refuge)
- Court papers
- a social worker
- the client's church
- any other reputable person or organisation that is in a position to support a client's statement
When the client provides proof of the family violence you must then consider whether a relationship with another adult exists.
## Client unable to provide written proof
Where the client is unable to provide written proof of the family violence, you should consult with your regional family violence response co-ordinator for advice.
From this discussion you should make a recommendation whether the client is in a relationship with another adult or not, to your manager client service delivery for sign off.

chunks.title: Financial interdependence — core policy > relationship status for benefit
chunks.text:
## Financial interdependence
When considering if a client is in a de facto relationship, you need to determine if the client and the other person are financially interdependent. This includes the sense of at least a willingness to support the other person if that person cannot support themselves. This does not mean that the financial support already exists, but that it would if needed.
Note financial interdependence also exists if the client and the other person have a mutual understanding as to how the family unit will be supported.
You can only pay a single or sole parent rate of benefit if there is a genuine absence of financial interdependence. This means that a couple cannot rearrange their circumstances just to qualify for a benefit for which they would otherwise not qualify.
## Determining financial interdependence
Every relationship is different and to assist you to determine if a client and another adult are financially interdependent a list of possible indicators is provided. Not all relationships will have all these indicators. To help you discuss the relationship the client may have with the other adult, you may consider:
- joint bank accounts, assets or joint loans/credit
- joint ownership of real estate or other major assets and any joint liabilities e.g. both the client and the other adult own a rental property
- significant pooling of financial resources especially in relation to major financial commitments eg saving for a house, car or holiday
- legal obligation owed by one person in respect of the other person eg the other adult is the guarantor for a TV hire purchase
- joint ownership of a car. Do they both use it?
- items the other adult pays for, if any? eg SKY television rental, internet broadband
- arrangements for paying bills or for groceries
- the sharing of day to day household expenses
If you are unable to make a decision regarding the client's relationship you can discuss the case with your regional solicitor or local fraud investigator.

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > relationship status for benefit
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Knowing a client's relationship status is important to ensure they are receiving the correct benefit at the correct rate.
Clients are considered to be part of a couple when they are in a relationship with another adult, regardless of the sex or gender of either partner. This includes a couple who are married or in a civil union and they are not 'living apart', or a couple who are living in a de facto relationship.
The client's marital status helps you decide whether or not they are in a relationship where there is uncertainty.
There are 3 types of relationship that are defined as:
- Marriage - is a legally recognised union between 2 people, for the purpose of: the formation of a family unit; social stability; education and development of offspring; economic stability; security; companionship or various combinations of these purposes.
- Civil Union - is a legally recognised union equivalent to marriage that provides couples with rights, benefits and responsibilities equal to those enjoyed by married couples.
- De facto relationship - a de facto relationship exists where 2 people live together as if they were married but they have not been legally married or entered a civil union.
Note if 1 of the people is under 18 years, special requirements must be met before a de facto relationship exists. See: Partners under 18 years

chunks.title: Living apart — core policy > relationship status for benefit
chunks.text:
## Living apart
Generally, if a client is married or in a civil union you can accept that a couple is living apart when it is clear the relationship has ended and they live in different homes.
Note the term 'living apart' does not refer solely to living in separate homes.
## Living in separate homes
When a client advises the relationship with their spouse or civil union partner has ended and they are living in separate homes, you need to look at the reasons why they are not living together. Sometimes couples live apart for reasons other than a breakdown in their relationship or rearrange their circumstances to qualify for a benefit.
Some couples may live in separate homes because of (but are not limited to):
- financial reasons
- health reasons
- one party lives overseas or
- business/employment reasons (eg truck driver, shearer etc)
You can only pay a single or sole parent rate of benefit if the relationship has ended.
## Living in the same home
Generally, when a married or civil union couple are sharing the same accommodation they will be considered a couple. When a client advises the relationship with their spouse or civil union partner has ended, but they still share the same accommodation you need to look at the reasons why they are still cohabitating.
If the arrangement is transitional (eg the spouse or partner is looking for separate accommodation and will move out) and the client considers that they have separated, you can accept this for a short period.
If the arrangement is not transitional, you need to assess whether they are living together or whether they are living apart in the same home.
Note unless the relationship has ended you cannot assess the client as a single or sole parent.
If you are unable to make a decision regarding the client's relationship you can discuss the case with your regional solicitor or local fraud investigator.

chunks.title: Partners under 18 years — core policy > relationship status for benefit
chunks.text:
## Partners under 18 years
If a client aged 18 years or older qualifies for a benefit and has a 16 or 17 year old partner, the partner can be included in the benefit when they are:
- legally married or
- in a civil union
## De facto relationship
If a client is in a de facto relationship with a person aged 16 or 17 years old, the partner can be included in the benefit if they have an order from a Family Court Judge giving consent for the de facto relationship.
Consent from a Family Court Judge for the relationship is required whether or not the couple has a dependent child.
If consent is not given, MSD should treat both clients as single and consider whether the partner qualifies for a benefit in their own right.

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > requests for financial assistance
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The Ministry has a duty to investigate and decide all applications made where it has the relevant information to do so.
The client is required to make an application and provide the information necessary for the Ministry to investigate and determine entitlement.
When a client contacts the Ministry and makes a request for financial assistance the way you deal with their request (or application for financial assistance) depends on whether the assistance is included in the definition of a benefit.
## Application for benefit
These guidelines apply to applications:
- that are included in the definition of a benefit or
- where it is unknown whether the application will be for a benefit
For more information see:
- Application for benefit
## Applications for assistance
These guidelines apply to:
- any applications for assistance that are not included in the definition of a benefit
For more information see:
- Application for assistance
## Re-assessing previous applications
Where a client approaches Work and Income and states that they made an application months or years ago, you will need to determine whether an application was made.
We have the ability to pay a benefit that should have been paid from an earlier date. This is known as correction power and can be used when:
- a client did not make or did not complete an application for a benefit at an earlier date and
- the reason the client did not make or did not complete an earlier application for a benefit was due to an error or omission on the part of the Ministry
For more information see:
- Re-assessing previous applications

chunks.title: Applications in review forms — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for assistance
chunks.text:
## Applications in review forms
The Ministry of Social Development issue review forms to gather information to review a client's current entitlement.
The information that is submitted by the client in the review form may contain information that is essentially a request for assistance other than a benefit for a particular need or purpose (ie an application). Where this is the case, this must be regarded as an application and investigated by the Ministry.
For more information see:
- Guidelines - Application for assistance
- What may be considered to be a written application

chunks.title: Applications that must be in writing — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for assistance
chunks.text:
## Applications that must be in writing
Applications for some forms of assistance must be in writing.
These forms of assistance include:
- Recoverable Assistance Payments
- Social Rehabilitation Assistance
- Employment and Work Readiness Assistance
For more information see:
- Guidelines - Application for assistance
- What may be considered a written application

chunks.title: Expired applications — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for assistance
chunks.text:
## Expired applications
Where a client makes a verbal application for assistance other than a benefit, but does not take the relevant steps to continue their application, their application will be considered expired.
The information regarding their application will, however, remain in CMS. Where a client later requests consideration of an expired application you must investigate and decide the application at that time.
Each application will be determined on the individual circumstances of the case so it will be necessary to obtain information from the client regarding their eligibility.
For more information see:
- Verbal requests for assistance
- Timeframes for providing information
- Core policy Re-assessing previous applications

chunks.title: Guidelines - Application for assistance — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for assistance
chunks.text:
## Guidelines - Application for assistance
These guidelines apply to any applications for assistance that are not included in the definition of a benefit.
An application is any request for assistance for a particular need or purpose.
An application does not:
- need to be made in writing and can be made verbally
- have to be on a specific form or
- have to name a particular type of assistance
Note there are some forms of assistance that must be in writing. For a list of these, see: Applications that must be in writing.
## An application for assistance can be regarded as an application for all assistance for that purpose
A person does not have to request a particular type of assistance when they make an application and their application can be for more than one type of assistance.
When a client makes an application (ie makes a request for assistance for a particular need or purpose) they are making an application for all forms of assistance for that particular need or purpose. You must make sure that you gather all information necessary to assess a client's full and correct entitlement.
Note a simple request for information is not an application but you should ask the client whether they want to make an application.
For more information see:
- Verbal requests for assistance
- Timeframes for providing information
- What may be considered to be a written application
- Expired applications

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for assistance
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The Ministry of Social Development has a duty to investigate and decide all applications made where it has the relevant information to do so.
The client is required to make an application and provide the information necessary for the Ministry to investigate and determine entitlement.
These guidelines apply to:
- any applications for assistance that are not included in the definition of a benefit
For more information see:
- Guidelines - Application for assistance

chunks.title: Timeframe for providing information — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for assistance
chunks.text:
## Timeframe for providing information
Once it has been established that a client has made an application, they should be asked to provide all required information necessary to investigate their application.
You must advise the client that they have 20 working days to continue their application (ie supply all the relevant required information) or their application will expire.
Note this is an administrative process only and should not be confused with the 20 working day rule for the applications for assistance that are included in the definition of a benefit.
If the client chooses to continue with their application, they will be asked to complete a written application form for all assistance to which they may be entitled.
If a client is unable to take action or supply the relevant required information within this timeframe and has legitimate reasons for their delay, you should agree to an appropriate period within which they can supply the required information and record this agreement in CMS.
For more information see:
- Expired applications
- Guidelines - Application for assistance
- Verbal requests for assistance
- What may be considered to be a written application

chunks.title: Verbal requests for assistance — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for assistance
chunks.text:
## Verbal requests for assistance
When a client contacts the Ministry and makes enquiries about financial assistance, that enquiry may be a request for information only or it may be a request for financial assistance.
If they are just requesting information, you should ask them whether they want to make an application now.
If they do, you must determine whether or not the client needs to make an application for a benefit or for assistance other than a benefit.
If they are applying for assistance other than a benefit then you must acknowledge their verbal request for assistance and record the relevant details in CMS.
If the client is applying for a benefit see: Application for benefit
For more information see:
- Timeframe for providing information

chunks.title: What may be considered to be a written application — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for assistance
chunks.text:
## What may be considered to be a written application
A written application does not need to be on a specific form.
There are a number of documents that are used for variety of purposes during the administration of financial assistance and these documents may also be regarded as applications for assistance.
Where any document indicates that a client requires assistance for another need or purpose (ie one that they are not already receiving assistance for), this document should be regarded as an application.
Examples of these documents include:
- applications for other forms of financial assistance
- applications in review forms
- letters or other correspondence where the client makes a request for assistance for a particular need or purpose
Note any document within which the client, in addition to providing the review information required, makes a request for assistance for a particular need or purpose should be regarded as an application for assistance other than a benefit. Correspondence from a client may also be an application where that correspondence indicates that the client has a particular need or purpose for which they require assistance.
For more information see:
- Applications that must be in writing
- Applications in review forms

chunks.title: Application form can be used for more than one type of assistance — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## Application form can be used for more than one type of assistance
When a completed application form is received that relates to one specific type of financial assistance, this is sufficient to be able to investigate and if entitled, grant financial assistance of another kind.
The application form and any supporting evidence reasonably required must be received within 20 working days of the client's date of first contact or the application will lapse unless the client has a good and sufficient reason.
When their application lapses, if the client still wishes to apply for a benefit they will need to re-start the application process and re-establish their eligibility. The date the client makes contact to do this will become their new date of first contact.
If the client immediately re-starts the application process and they had fully completed a written application form, this completed form can be used to re-investigate benefit entitlement.

chunks.title: Application form may not be required — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## Application form may not be required
The requirement to provide an application form may be waived if the Ministry of Social Development already holds a form relating to an application that has recently lapsed, provided the client immediately re-starts the application process.
To help decide what timeframe is acceptable to re-start the application process immediately after an application has lapsed you may consider the following:
- did the client make contact immediately (eg within 10 working days) after being notified of the application being lapsed
- if not, was there a good reason why the client did not make contact immediatelyFor example was there a delay from when the letter was delivered to when the client received it.
Using a previous application form is discretionary and will depend on a case by case basis. Discuss with your manager client service delivery if you are uncertain about waiving the requirement for a client to provide a new application form.
If you are waiving the requirement for a client to provide a new application form you will need to obtain details from the client if they have had any change of circumstances since the lapsed application form was received. The client must make a written statement (eg by completing a Personal Details form), confirming whether or not they have had any change in circumstances and what these are.
If you decide the client's changes in circumstances are substantial you may require a new application form to be completed.
When a client makes contact with us to reapply after a previous application has lapsed, a new date of first contact must be noted in a new request note in CMS as the application process starts again. When the requirement to provide an application form is waived you need to date stamp the form again, on the date you interview the client when they reapply.

chunks.title: Application lapses — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## Application lapses
The application process is only considered to be completed when a client has:
- completed a written or online application form and
- provided supporting evidence and
- completed any assigned pre-benefit activities where required
The applicant has 20 working days to complete the application process. If the applicant does not complete the application process by the end of the 20th working day after the date of first contact, their request for financial assistance is lapsed on the 21st working day.
The lapse date is automatically calculated by the system from the client's date of first contact.
The 20 working days exclude public holidays and the period commencing 25 December and ending 15 January in the following year.
If the client has a good and sufficient reason for not completing an application form or providing supporting evidence, you can extend the 20 working day period.
There are no review or appeal rights when a client's application lapses. This is because no decision has been made, the application is incomplete.
When their application lapses, if the client still wishes to apply for a benefit, they will need to re-start the application process and re-establish their eligibility. The date the client makes contact to do this will become their new date of first contact.
If the client immediately re-starts the application process and they had fully completed a written application form, this completed form can be used to re-investigate benefit entitlement.

chunks.title: Applications from clients living overseas — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## Applications from clients living overseas
When a client living overseas applies for a benefit under a Reciprocal Agreement with another country they do not have to meet the 20 working day period for the application process.
Note clients applying for a benefit under a Reciprocal Agreement while living in New Zealand are subject to the 20 working day period.
## Process
When processing applications from clients living overseas International Services staff should tick the Overseas Application box in the CMS Request screen.

chunks.title: Date of first contact — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text: The date a client first contacts us to request financial assistance is their date of first contact. A client may contact the Ministry of Social Development at any time, through various methods, eg at reception in a service centre, via telephone through one of the contact centres, or in writing. Clients may also apply for financial assistance online. The client has 20 working days from their date of first contact to complete the application process. The client does not need to specify, at the date of first contact the type of assistance they may require. Therefore, the date of first contact may apply to more than one type of assistance. You should send the client a letter (available in CMS) to confirm their date of first contact.

chunks.title: Exception — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text: For young people aged 16 or 17 (without dependent children) or 16 to 19 years (with a dependent child) who are potentially eligible for Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment the letter to confirm their date of first contact does not need to be sent. This is because they will be advised of what they need to do to complete their application process when they apply online.

chunks.title: Application date for benefit — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text: For the purpose of calculating the commencement date of the benefit, the application date is date of first contact.

chunks.title: Application form lodged without prior contact — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text: If a client lodges an application form without any prior contact with the Ministry, the date this application is received is their date of first contact. If a client submits an online application form without any prior contact, the date that the client starts completing the online application form is their date of first contact. For more information on the 20 working day period (and possible exceptions) see: - Guidelines - Application for benefit

chunks.title: Client contacts the Ministry more than once — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text: If the client contacts the Ministry more than once within the 20 working day period, the date of first contact does not change unless a change of circumstances has occurred. If the change of circumstances means that the client requires additional assistance, a new (additional) date of first contact is established for the additional assistance. Example a client applies for Jobseeker Support while living at home and does not have any accommodation costs. During the application process they move into a flat (sharing expenses). The date the client advises us of their new circumstances becomes their date of first contact for testing their eligibility for, and any subsequent grant of, Accommodation Supplement. The original date of first contact that applies to the application for Jobseeker Support does not change.

chunks.title: Client makes contact after application has lapsed — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text: When a client's application lapses and they still wish to apply for a benefit, they will need to re-start the application process and re-establish their eligibility. The date the client makes contact to do this will become their new date of first contact.

chunks.title: Extending the 20 working day period — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## Extending the 20 working day period
The 20 working day period can be extended if the client has a good and sufficient reason for not being able to provide a written application form, or any supporting evidence reasonably required within 20 working days from their date of first contact.
If this occurs you should agree to an appropriate period within which they can provide the required information and record this agreement in CMS.
If the client fails to provide the required information within the extended period, their application will lapse.
There is no discretion to extend the period allowed to complete an assigned pre-benefit activity. An assigned pre-benefit activity must be undertaken within 20 working days of the date of first contact.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason
The guiding principle in determining "good and sufficient" reason is one of "reasonableness".
Having considered the circumstances, would it have been "reasonable" for the client to have met the 20 working day period for:
- completing a written or online application form or
- providing supporting evidence
MSD should decide in favour of the client if any doubt remains.
A good and sufficient reason may include, but is not limited to:
- the client having an injury, physical or intellectual disability or medical condition that makes accessing services difficult, i.e. they have a medical certificate
- the client having a family emergency, such as a death or illness, that caused a delay.
## IRD number information
A good and sufficient reason for extending the 20 working day period when MSD requests an IRD number or evidence of an IRD number may include, but is not limited to:
- the reasons set out above
- when MSD requests IRD number evidence less than 10 working days before the 20 working day period ends as MSD must give the client at least 10 working days to provide IRD number evidence
- processing delays with an external agency (e.g., Inland Revenue, Department of Internal Affairs, Immigration New Zealand)
- the client does not speak English as a first language, and they have difficulty understanding what is needed from MSD or Inland Revenue
- the client having difficulty accessing the internet, a device, or their local MSD Service Centre.
Example
Jackson is 18 years old and is applying for Jobseeker Support. He has an IRD number but has not worked before.
The Inland Revenue information share result is a No Match on day one of the application. Jackson misses his first 2 appointments with MSD and only attends an appointment on day 18 of this application period. As he has not previously provided evidence of his IRD number, MSD requests this during his appointment.
Jackson must be given at least 10 working days to provide IRD number evidence. MSD considers this delay as a good and sufficient reason and extends Jackson's application timeframe by an additional 8 working days.

chunks.title: Guidelines - Application for benefit — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## Guidelines - Application for benefit
These guidelines apply to applications:
- that are included in the definition of a benefit or
- where it is unknown whether the application will be for a benefit
The application process for benefit can be considered to be complete when:
- a written or online application form is completed and received by the Ministry of Social Development and
- any supporting evidence reasonably required for that benefit is received by the Ministry and
- any assigned pre-benefit activities have been completed, if applicable
The application form and any supporting evidence required must be received within 20 working days after the client's date of first contact or the application for benefit lapses.
The 20 working day period can be extended if the client has a good and sufficient reason for not being able to provide a written application form, or any supporting evidence reasonably required within 20 working days from date of first contact.
If this occurs MSD should agree to an appropriate period within which they can supply the information and record this agreement in CMS.
There is no discretion to extend the period allowed to complete an assigned pre-benefit activity. An assigned pre-benefit activity must be undertaken within 20 working days of the date of first contact.

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The Ministry of Social Development has a duty to investigate and decide all applications made where it has the relevant information to do so.
The client is required to make an application and provide the information necessary for the Ministry to investigate and determine entitlement.
These guidelines apply to applications:
- that are included in the definition of a benefit or
- where it is unknown whether the application will be for a benefit

chunks.title: Investigating applications — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## Investigating applications
On receipt of a completed application form and on completion of any pre-benefit activities, the Ministry of Social Development has an obligation to investigate the application including the client's eligibility for any other benefit.
The application form and any supporting evidence required must be received within 20 working days after the client's date of first contact or the application for benefit will lapse unless the client has a good and sufficient reason.
The application process for benefit can be considered to be complete, and therefore cannot lapse, when:
- a written or online application form is completed and received and
- any supporting evidence reasonably required for that benefit is received and
- any assigned pre-benefit activities have been completed, if applicable
Investigation of the application continues until a decision is made to either:
- grant the application or
- decline the application
An application cannot be granted until all additional information is received.
## Example
A client completes an application form for Jobseeker Support. During the course of the interview the case manager establishes that the client has accommodation costs.
The client's eligibility for Accommodation Supplement can be investigated as part of their application for Jobseeker Support.
The client will need to provide verification of their costs and provide any other additional information required to grant Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: IRD number not required in certain circumstances — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## IRD number not required in certain circumstances
MSD may not require an IRD number to complete an application in certain circumstances, including, but not limited to, when:
- a client or their partner (if any) have significant difficulties with getting an IRD number that are out of the client's control and the client must urgently need the assistance before the IRD number can be given to client. Significant difficulties include, but are not limited to: a national emergency that affects Inland Revenue timeframes to give the client an IRD numberclients moving from the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre before Inland Revenue can give the client an IRD number
- a national emergency that affects Inland Revenue timeframes to give the client an IRD number
- clients moving from the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre before Inland Revenue can give the client an IRD number
- a partner's (if any) income is not included in MSD's assessment of the client's level of income and the partner will not be apportioned a payment from MSD
- a partner is not a New Zealand tax resident.
This does not include situations when:
- the client can address difficulties themselves, e.g. the client cannot apply for an IRD number themselves but can have an agent do this for them
- assistance is not urgently needed before Inland Revenue can give the client an IRD number.
Example - Partner's income not included in the income test and not apportioned benefit
Milah is applying for New Zealand Superannuation (NZS). Milah's partner, Casey, is working and has an IRD number, but MSD does not need this because Casey's income won't affect Milah's NZS rate and he is not receiving any apportionment of Milah's NZS payments.

chunks.title: Non-tax resident partner's IRD number not required — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## Non-tax resident partner's IRD number not required
MSD does not need an IRD number or evidence of a partner's IRD number if the partner is not a New Zealand tax resident, including when they:
- are a new migrant to New Zealand but have not been in New Zealand for more than 183 days in any 12 month period, or they do not have a permanent place of abode in New Zealand, or
- they were a tax resident in New Zealand and no longer have a permanent place of abode in New Zealand and have been away from New Zealand for more than 325 days in a 12 month period.
Generally, MSD can determine a later point to request the evidence of the partner's IRD number.
Example - partner is not a tax resident and IRD number is not required
Wirema is receiving Disability Allowance. Wirema's partner Lani has been living and working in Samoa for more than 325 days continuously. Lani currently has no intention to move to New Zealand. Lani is not a tax resident in New Zealand and Wirema does not need to provide an IRD number for Lani. Wirema is still required to declare Lani's income to MSD.
Example - partner is a tax resident and IRD number is required
Willow is receiving Jobseeker Support. Willow's partner Theo moved to New Zealand, on a resident's visa, from the United Kingdom (UK) 50 days ago. Theo continues to work for their UK employer. Even though Theo has only been in New Zealand for 50 days their permanent place of abode is New Zealand and will be apportioned Willow's Jobseeker Support payments. Theo is considered a tax resident by Inland Revenue and can get an IRD number. MSD requests Willow to provide Theo's IRD number.

chunks.title: Notice to provide IRD number evidence — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## Notice to provide IRD number evidence
MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a client or their partner's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there is an error, MSD should ask the client (in writing) to provide evidence of their or their partner's IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this.
When an IRD number cannot be successfully matched MSD must send the client, or their partner (if any) a written notice (adverse action notice) requesting evidence of the IRD number. This must give the client a minimum of 10 working days to send their IRD number evidence before lapsing their application.
MSD can:
- give the client until the end of the 20-day application period when there are more than 10 days until the application lapses or
- extend the 20-day application period to give the client at least 10 working days to provide their IRD number evidence.
Example
Ropata applies for a benefit on 1 July and has 20 working days, until 29 July, to complete his application or his benefit application will lapse. He has an IRD number and so it is reasonable to expect that he can provide evidence of this.
IRD number information held by Inland Revenue does not match that held by MSD. Ropata attends an appointment with MSD, and MSD requests IRD number evidence on the fifth day of his application, 8 July.
MSD is obliged to provide Ropata with at least 10 working days to provide IRD number evidence. The minimum period will end on day 15 of his benefit application, 22 July, and this falls within his benefit application period. He would still have until 29 July to provide his evidence.

chunks.title: Supporting evidence — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## Supporting evidence
The supporting evidence that must be received by MSD within 20 working days of the client's date of first contact is:
- appropriate identification for the primary client and each family member within the application, if applicable
- evidence of any name change for the primary client and partner, if applicable
- a completed medical certificate for applications for: Jobseeker Support Client has a health condition, injury or disabilitySupported Living Payment Caring for a person
- Jobseeker Support Client has a health condition, injury or disability
- Supported Living Payment Caring for a person
The client is required to provide proof of their identity before the benefit can be granted. Proof of identity may be provided up to 20 working days from the client's date of first contact. This timeframe can be extended if the client has a good and sufficient reason.
For more information see:
- Extending the 20 working day period
## IRD number evidence
For benefits that are taxable and/or income-tested an IRD number is required. It's reasonable to request evidence of an IRD number when the IRD number information MSD holds does not match the information that Inland Revenue holds.
MSD may not need IRD number evidence for applications when:
- there are significant factors, that are outside the client's or partner's (if any) control, that delay providing evidence of their IRD number and
- the client needs assistance urgently, before the evidence can be provided
or
- the partner is not a New Zealand tax resident.
Significant factors outside the client's or partner's (if any) control includes, but is not limited to, a national emergency that affects Inland Revenue's ability to provide the evidence.
For more information see:
- Non-tax resident partner's IRD number not required
- Guidelines - Application for benefit
- Notice to provide IRD number evidence
## Additional information
Any additional information, for example the Employment and earnings information for applications form (V06) required to complete the processing of an application, is not restricted to 20 working days from the date of first contact, but should be requested at the earliest opportunity.
However the benefit cannot be granted until all the necessary supporting evidence and additional information is received.
In some cases, the need for supporting evidence can be waived.

chunks.title: Supporting evidence can be waived — core policy > requests for financial assistance > application for benefit
chunks.text:
## Supporting evidence can be waived
The requirement for a client to provide supporting evidence to enable the Ministry of Social Development to investigate their application can be waived when the Ministry already holds the supporting evidence required, or sufficient additional information that will enable a benefit to be granted.
The client must still provide any additional information needed to complete the application before the benefit can be granted.
This may be provided after 20 working days from the client's date of first contact but should be requested at the earliest opportunity.

chunks.title: Approval letters — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Approval letters
There are 2 correction power approval letters. These letters can be found in CMS.
## Letter 1 - Correction Power Approved No Review of Decision
This letter is used when the reason for considering correction power did not come from a Review of Decision.
## Letter 2 - Correction Power Approved Review of Decision received
This letter is used when the reason for considering correction power came from a Review of Decision, for example, about commencement date.

chunks.title: Backdating of commencement date — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Backdating of commencement date
Where you have determined that the client completed an application you should consider backdating the commencement date.
If it is clear an application was made, all the necessary information was, or has now been provided and the client continued to be eligible, the commencement date should be calculated using the date the original application was made.
Note if the application was made and declined, the normal Review of Decision process applies.

chunks.text:

chunks.title: Correction power decision approved — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Correction power decision approved
When correction power is approved the following process will occur:
## Step 1
The delegated authority will:
- complete the CMS correction power decision template
- email the manager client service delivery to advise them of the decision
- print off the CMS correction power decision template and sign it
- mail the signed template to the manager client service delivery
## Step 2
- the email is provided to the case manager by the manager client service delivery
- the case manager forwards the email to Data Integrity Unit
- the manager client service delivery gives the signed template to the case manager to place on the client's file
## Step 3
- Data Integrity Unit access the payment details from the CMS correction power assessment note template and the correction power decision template
## Step 4
Data Integrity Unit issues the payment completing the SAHPA and/or AHPAY SWIFTT screens and:
- in the SAHPA and/or AHPAY screen, enter code 004 Correction Power in the Proj Payment Reason code
- authenticate the payment
- note CMS using the "DIU correction power" note template that a correction power payment has been made and
- email the case manager and manager client service delivery to confirm
Note Data Integrity will also keep a record of all correction power payments made.
## Step 5
When the case manager receives the confirmation email from Data Integrity Unit, they will:
- send a Correction Power letter of approval advice to the client
- file all original paperwork as critical data on the clients file and
- update CMS including recording that an approval letter has been sent to the client

chunks.title: Correction power decision declined — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Correction power decision declined
When the delegated authority has made the decision not to use the correction power, the following steps will be completed:
## Step 1
- the delegated authority emails the manager client service delivery to advise them of the decision
- the delegated authority completes the CMS correction power decision template, giving the reasons for the decline
- the delegated authority prints off that CMS template, signs it, and mails it to the manager client service delivery
## Step 2
- the email is provided to the case manager by the manager client service delivery
- the service centre manager gives the signed template to the case manager to place on the client's file
## Step 3
The case manager will:
- send a letter of advice to the client, that must be reviewed by the manager client service delivery and the regional solicitor
- file all original paperwork as critical data on the clients file and
- update CMS including recording that a decline letter has been sent to the client

chunks.title: Decline letters — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text: When a correction power decision is declined every situation is different and each letter should be written on a case by case basis. There will be no CMS letter for a declined correction power decision, so you will need to write the letter, and below are some suggested paragraphs to help you. Before it is sent to the client the decline letter must be reviewed by the manager client service delivery and then the regional solicitor. There are 2 possible situations where a decline letter could be sent, including where:

chunks.title: Consideration of correction power did not arise from a related Review of Decision — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text: When something other than a Review of Decision led you to consider correction power, you will need to send a letter to the client advising them of the decision. Consideration of correction power may have come from Ministry staff so the client may not be aware of the situation. Depending on whether the client was contacted during the correction power assessment or not, here are some possible paragraph options for a decline letter: - We are now able to backdate the payment of a benefit when, because of a mistake we have made, you did not make or complete an application for a benefit at an earlier time. - In your case we found that we did not make a mistake that stopped you from making or completing an application for a benefit at an earlier time. This means we cannot backdate the payment of a benefit or grant you a benefit from an earlier date Note include the following review rights paragraph: - You can ask for this decision to be reviewed if you do not agree with it. We have forms available for you to use, or you can write to us. You must do this within 3 months of the date on this letter. When there is a good reason for a delay, a review may still be possible after this time. If you want to contact us, we can explain more about our decision and the review process.

chunks.title: Consideration of correction power arose from a related Review of Decision — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text: Where a Review of Decision in relation to a commencement date led you to consider correction power you will need to send a letter to the client advising them of the decision. The client needs to be aware that if they choose to review the decision to decline the use of correction power, they have the opportunity to combine this review with their existing review about their commencement date. Depending on the client's situation here are some possible paragraph options for a decline letter: - We are now able to backdate the payment of a benefit when, because of a mistake we have made, you did not make or complete an application for a benefit at an earlier time - On [date] we received your application for a review of our decision to start your [benefit] from [date]. As part of this review we have found that we did not make a mistake that stopped you from making or completing an application for benefit at an earlier time Note include the following review rights paragraph: - You can ask for this decision to be reviewed if you do not agree with it. We have forms available for you to use, or you can write to us. You must do this within three months of the date on this letter. When there is a good reason for a delay, a review may still be possible after this time. If you want to contact us, we can explain more about our decision and the review process. Plus - You can combine this with your existing Review of Decision. Please let us know if you want to do this and we will arrange for both reviews to take place at the same time.

chunks.title: Use of correction power — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Use of correction power
Every decision to approve or decline the use of correction power must be made by the Deputy Chief Executive Service Delivery.
## Payment under correction power
When the Ministry of Social Development has made a decision to approve the use of correction power, the final amount of payment must be decided and approved by the Deputy Chief Executive Service Delivery.

chunks.title: Error or omission on the part of the Ministry — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Error or omission on the part of the Ministry
These guidelines apply to assistance included in the definition of a benefit.
We have the ability to pay a benefit that should have been paid from an earlier date. This is known as correction power and can be used when:
- a client did not make or did not complete an application for a benefit at an earlier date and
- the reason the client did not make or did not complete an earlier application for a benefit was due to an error or omission on the part of the Ministry of Social Development
