Note in all cases the error or omission must have contributed to the client not making or completing an application for a benefit at an earlier time.
## For more information on correction power see:
- What is an error or omission on the part of the Ministry?
- When to consider correction power
- Types of correction power cases
- Youth service provider considered officer of the Ministry

chunks.title: Guidelines for deciding if an application has been made — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Guidelines for deciding if an application has been made
All applications for assistance should be investigated. If you are unsure if an application has been made, and the client has returned after a period of months or years, you can seek advice from your capability developer, your regional solicitor or Helpline.
Your capability developer, your regional solicitor or Helpline can help you to make a decision. Therefore you should document and summarise all information that would help them to help you. This information may include:
- copies of forms completed by the client
- correspondence from the client
- notes recorded on CMS or earlier notes recorded on SWIFTT (often held on the BTCHI screen) and
- any submission made by the client or any agent of the client in relation to an earlier application for assistance
You should also speak with any staff member the client has indicated they spoke with, to confirm they had contact with the client. You should document their recollection of events.
From 24 September 2007 applications for assistance included in the definition of a benefit that are not completed within 20 working days of the client's date of first contact will lapse. A benefit cannot be granted if the application has lapsed.
For more information see:
- Core policy Application for benefit
## Legal rules to consider
As part of your decision making process you should also consider the following legal rules:
Scoble
An application for assistance for a particular purpose means the Ministry must consider all available types of financial assistance that relates to a particular purpose.
Taylor
An application for assistance for a particular purpose does not need to be in writing and can be made verbally to any staff member, during work hours, regardless of their role.
Section 311 Commencement of benefits
A benefit shall commence on the later of the date of application, or the date of entitlement, subject to stand down provisions. Limited backdating applies to some benefits, for example, the 28 day rule.
For more information see:
- Commencement date of main benefits
There are number of situations that can arise as a result of your investigations.

chunks.title: Guidelines for re-assessing expired applications — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Guidelines for re-assessing expired applications
Use these guidelines if your investigation determines that the client started an application but did not complete it and the application expired.
The key point to consider is:
Did the client continue to meet the eligibility criteria for the relevant assistance?
To help you make your decision you should collate all relevant information. This may include:
- copies of forms completed by the client or other information provided by the client
- correspondence from the client
- notes recorded on CMS or earlier notes recorded on SWIFTT (often held on the BTCHI screen) and
- any submission made by the client or any agent of the client in relation to an earlier application for assistance
If you establish that an application was made and the client continued to be eligible, and now you have all the information required, you can:
- re-activate the application
- calculate the commencement date taking into account the date the original application was made
- grant the assistance

chunks.title: Requests for financial assistance — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Requests for financial assistance
When a client approaches the Ministry of Social Development and states that they made an application months or years ago, you will need to determine whether an application was made.
Your manager client service delivery, legal services or Helpline can provide advice on whether an application was made.

chunks.title: Outcome of investigation — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Outcome of investigation
The outcome of your investigation should determine which of the following situations applies:
- application was not completed due to an error or omission on the part of the Ministry of Social Development For more information see: Error or omission on the part of the Ministry
- application was started by the client but was not completed and the application expired For more information see: Guidelines for re-assessing expired applications
- application was completed and assistance granted, but the client was entitled to additional assistance For more information see: Backdating of commencement date
- application was completed and was declined at that time For more information see: Review of Decision [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Procedure for class cases of correction power — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Procedure for class cases of correction power
A class case is a situation that affects 2 or more clients.
For example, a class case could arise where a brochure provides incorrect information to a number of clients that causes them to not make or complete an application for a benefit.
When a potential correction power case is identified that may affect a group of clients the following procedure should be used:
## Step 1
- advise the manager client service delivery of the potential class case scenario
- work out how many clients are affected, including their client numbers if possible
## Step 2
- the manager client service delivery should be the first person who investigates the potential class case situation, not a case manager and
- the manager client service delivery must consult with legal services
## Step 3
If legal services advice confirms there is a potential class case, the manager client service delivery must email the operations manager.
## Step 4
If the operations manager agrees, they will contact the relevant general manager.
## Step 5
That general manager will discuss the case with relevant business units at National Office, (for example Policy and Legal Services).
Once the class case has been confirmed, appropriate National Office managers will make decisions about the next step in the process, that is, who completes the assessment and how payment is made.

chunks.title: Procedure for individual cases of correction power — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Procedure for individual cases of correction power
Once it is established that correction power should be considered in a particular situation, and that situation is for an individual case, you will need to use the following steps:
## Step 1
The client must complete the relevant application form and provide the relevant verification for that benefit before you consider correction power.
Note if the client is making a current application for a benefit, the client should fill out an application form and complete the application process to ensure the current application is not delayed.
## Step 2
If it is not clear that an earlier application was made you will need to complete an assessment using the correction power assessment note template and answer the following information:
- are section 311 (commencement of benefits), Scoble or Taylor legal rules applicable?
- what is the possible error or omission?
- has the client been contacted and what evidence exists?
- the benefit types and periods that are affected and
- using the income deduction assessment form to calculate the amount of potential payment
Support for completing the assessment is available from your service centre trainer, your manager client service delivery and Helpline.
The regional solicitor must be consulted by the manager client service delivery before the CMS correction power recommendation template is completed.
For more information see:
- Guidelines for deciding if an application has been made
## Step 3
The service centre trainer checks the income deduction assessment form for the correct dates and rates of benefit.
## Step 4
Your service centre manager will complete the necessary fields in the CMS correction power recommendation template.
Note the should also consider if the individual case could lead to a class case.
## Step 5
The manager client service delivery sends all the information to the delegated authority via email asking them to make a decision on this individual case.
The email from the manager client service delivery should explain that the recommendation is that correction power be used to pay the client and should briefly cover the following:
- the client's details, including client number so the delegated authority can check CMS
- the total amount payable
- the name of the benefit(s) concerned and
- the period(s) the payment covers
For more information see:
- Delegated authority
## Step 6
The delegated authority will:
- refer to the CMS template assessment and recommendation notes
- consider if the benefit can be backdated using correction power
- consult with Legal Services to assist them in either approving or declining the use of correction power

chunks.title: Review Rights where correction power approved — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Review Rights where correction power approved
The decision by the delegated authority to approve correction power has its own review rights.
If the client has already lodged a Review of Decision about an earlier commencement date, the advice letter about correction power advises the client they can combine both reviews.

chunks.title: Review Rights where correction power declined — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Review Rights where correction power declined
The decision by the delegated authority to decline correction power has its own review rights.
Note if the client has already lodged a Review of Decision about an earlier commencement date, the advice letter about correction power advises the client they can combine both reviews.
Where correction power is declined, the client has already lodged a Review of Decision about the commencement date the case manager will:
- update the Review of Decision process in HIYA
- send the appropriate Review of Decision letter in HIYA to the client, which advises the decision to uphold the commencement date has automatically been escalated to the Benefit Review Committee

chunks.title: Types of correction power cases — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Types of correction power cases
There can be 2 types of correction power cases, one that affects an individual client and another that can affect a group of 2 or more clients with the same situation, known as a class case.
To help you decide if an individual client may be affected see:
- When to consider correction power
To help you process an individual case of correction power, see:
- Procedure for individual cases of correction power
If you think that you may have identified a class case you need to discuss this with your manager client service delivery.
Note the manager client service delivery should discuss the class case with their regional solicitor.

chunks.title: What is an error or omission on the part of the Ministry? — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## What is an error or omission on the part of the Ministry?
An error or omission on the part of the Ministry of Social Development generally results from:
- applying an incorrect interpretation of the legislation or
- administrative failure
## Incorrect interpretation of the legislation
The application of an incorrect interpretation of the legislation includes:
- staff providing information based on an incorrect interpretation of the legislation or
- policy or instructions to staff differ from what is written in the legislation
## Administrative failure
An administrative failure on the part of the Ministry includes:
- giving incorrect advice either verbally or in writing or
- failing to provide information about how and when to apply for financial assistance, such as not making pamphlets available at a service centre
Note in all cases the error or omission must have contributed to the client not making or not completing an application for a benefit at an earlier time.

chunks.title: When to consider correction power — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## When to consider correction power
Important, before considering the use of the correction power, staff should follow the usual process and must consider whether the matter can be resolved either using section 317 of the Social Security Act 2018 or by using another legal rule such as Scoble or Taylor. Most cases are likely to be resolved using one of these methods.
If after considering the above, the matter is still not resolved, staff should consider whether the correction power is appropriate for the particular case.
Correction power can be used when:
- a client did not make or did not complete an application for a benefit at an earlier date and
- the reason the client did not make or did not complete an earlier application for a benefit was due to an error or omission on the part of the Ministry
Note in all cases the error or omission must have contributed to the client not making or completing an application for a benefit at an earlier time.
You should consider correction power when no other legal rule applies and the case meets the above criteria. This could be in the following situations:
- where the Ministry had been incorrectly interpreting legislation and becomes aware of this through (for example) client notification or through a review or appeal or
- a client (or their agent) requests a review of their commencement date or asks for the commencement date to be reassessed (note this is for situations that cannot be resolved using Scoble and Taylor) or
- Ministry staff identify a client's commencement date could be from an earlier date due to a potential error or omission by the Ministry (note this is for situations that cannot be resolved using Scoble and Taylor)
Clients will not have to complete a specific correction power form for correction power to be considered.
## If the client is making a current application
If the client is making a current application for a benefit, the client should fill out an application form and complete the application process to ensure the current application is not delayed. The benefit is granted and the commencement date is the date of application or the day after the initial stand down ends, whichever is the later.
You must now consider how to resolve the claim that the client did not make or did not complete an earlier application because of an error or omission on the part of the Ministry.

chunks.title: Youth service provider considered officer of the Ministry — core policy > requests for financial assistance > re assessing previous applications
chunks.text:
## Youth service provider considered officer of the Ministry
For the purposes of deciding error or omission on the part of the Ministry, a youth service provider is considered to be an officer of the Ministry.
This means that any action or inaction of a youth service provider must be treated as an action or inaction of an officer of the Ministry.

chunks.title: Australian citizens and permanent residents — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## Australian citizens and permanent residents
Australian citizens and Australian permanent residents complete an application for a residence class visa when arriving at the New Zealand border.
If Immigration New Zealand allows them to enter New Zealand, Australian citizens and Australian permanent residents are generally granted a resident visa and can stay in New Zealand indefinitely.
For the purpose of deciding if a person meets the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD, Australian citizens and Australian permanent residents hold a residence class visa.
Note people from Australia must generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand to qualify for financial assistance from MSD.

chunks.title: British citizens who arrived before 1 January 1962 — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## British citizens who arrived before 1 January 1962
Before 1 January 1962, people with British birth and parentage were allowed in New Zealand without a visa or permit.
British citizens who arrived in New Zealand before 1 January 1962 are deemed to hold a residence class visa, provided they:
- arrived in New Zealand lawfully for the purpose of permanent residence or
- were granted a permit for the purpose of permanent residence and
- lived in New Zealand continuously from 2 April 1974 (or the date their permit was granted) and up to 1 November 1987 without absence (except for time spent in Australia, the Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau) and
- were lawfully in New Zealand immediately before 1 November 1987 and
- have not had the permit, visa, or any other corresponding visa (where applicable) expire or be cancelled
Some people in this situation may have got their residence status officially endorsed by an immigration officer and have a paper record of their residence. However, others may not have taken these steps.
For the purpose of deciding if a person meets the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD, people in this situation are deemed to hold a residence class visa.
## British citizens from 1 January 1962
From 1 January 1962, all British citizens arriving in New Zealand must apply for a visa or citizenship if they intend to stay in New Zealand for more than six months. If they intend to work or study in New Zealand, they must apply for a relevant visa.
British citizens who arrived in New Zealand on or after 1 January 1962 must be a New Zealand citizen or have been granted a residence class visa (or temporary entry class visa, where relevant) to meet the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD.
Note there may be additional residence requirements that a person must meet to qualify for some types of financial assistance.

chunks.title: Calculating the period of residence — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## Calculating the period of residence
A period of residence in New Zealand starts from the date the person was lawfully resident in New Zealand as a:
- New Zealand citizen or
- residence class visa holder
A person may have had temporary absences during a period of residence (for example, when going overseas temporarily on a holiday). However, they must have been lawfully resident in New Zealand for the whole period.
Note time spent lawfully in New Zealand on a temporary entry class visa is generally not included when calculating the period of residence. The only exception is when calculating periods of residence and presence for the purposes of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension.

chunks.title: Compelled to remain in New Zealand — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## Compelled to remain in New Zealand
Temporary entry class visa holders generally do not meet the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD.
However, a person in this situation may meet the residence requirements for specific assistance if they are:
- applying for a residence class visa and
- compelled to stay in New Zealand due to unforeseen circumstances
Note people applying for a residence class visa who are compelled to remain in New Zealand do not need a valid temporary entry class visa to meet the residence requirements for specific assistance. However, they must meet all other qualifications to get financial assistance from MSD.
## Strong and compelling reasons
These circumstances must relate to a serious and unforeseen reason that prevents them from leaving New Zealand, for example life-maintaining medical treatment.
Note it is not possible to detail every circumstance under which this may occur as this will depend on the person's individual situation. However, there must be very strong and compelling reasons why the person is unable to leave New Zealand.
Lack of funds is generally not regarded as a reason for not being able to leave. When the person originally arrived in New Zealand, a condition of their entry would have been an air ticket to another country (that is, the ability to leave New Zealand).
Note temporary entry class visa holders may also meet the residence requirements for specific assistance if they are awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protected person status.

chunks.title: Evidence of residence — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## Evidence of residence
People are required to provide evidence of their residence status so that MSD can determine if they qualify for financial assistance.
The type of documents a person provides to verify their residence status depends on when they were issued.
From 29 November 2010, people with an existing visa or permit are deemed to hold the corresponding type of visa under the Immigration Act 2009.
Note people who had an existing permit or visa without an expiry date (such as a residence permit) had this replaced by the corresponding visa. They may never have had their visa updated if they did not intend to leave New Zealand.
## Documents not available
If a person cannot provide evidence or evidence is unclear, they must obtain confirmation of their residence status from Immigration New Zealand (for a residence class visa or temporary entry class visa) or the Department of Internal Affairs (for New Zealand citizens).
If MSD needs to contact Immigration New Zealand or the Department of Internal Affairs about a person's residence status, the person must give their consent. MSD cannot collect or disclose information regarding a person's application for financial assistance without the person's consent.
Note Immigration New Zealand may be unable to verify the residence status for some people who are deemed to hold a residence class visa. This includes people of British birth and parentage who arrived in New Zealand before 1 January 1962 and who do not have a passport.
Where necessary, other supporting evidence can be used to support a person's claim about when they arrived in New Zealand and the length of time they have lived here.
This includes (but is not limited to) New Zealand:
- school records (such as proof of enrolment or a Record of Achievement)
- work records (such as employment contracts or pay slips)
- tax records
- tenancy agreements
- bank statements
- old utility bills

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## Introduction
There are standard residence criteria that a person must meet to get a benefit or extra help from MSD. Generally, a person must be lawfully present and ordinarily resident in New Zealand.
Some types of assistance have additional rules about residence. For example, some types of benefits require a person to have lived in New Zealand for a specific length of time before they will qualify. Other types of benefits have rules for payment when a person is living overseas.
This manual outlines the standard residence criteria that apply to most types of main benefits and extra help. Specific qualifications for different payments can be found in the individual manuals.

chunks.title: Lawfully resident and present in New Zealand — core policy > residence
chunks.text: Generally, a person must be both lawfully resident and present in New Zealand to meet the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD. Note lawfully resident is about legal residence status and is different to ordinarily resident. To be lawfully resident and present in New Zealand means a person: - is either a New Zealand citizen or - holds or is deemed to hold a valid residence class visa or - holds a valid temporary entry class visa that allows them to live in New Zealand and - has been granted permission by Immigration New Zealand to enter New Zealand (unless their visa was granted in New Zealand) and - is physically in New Zealand People with recognised refugee or protected person status under the Immigration Act 2009 must have a valid visa or have been granted entry permission to be considered lawfully resident and present in New Zealand. Note in some situations a person can keep getting financial assistance from MSD when they are absent from New Zealand for a temporary period. Some people who are living overseas may also qualify for assistance under a reciprocal agreement or portability provisions.

chunks.title: New Zealand citizenship — core policy > residence
chunks.text: A New Zealand citizen can enter and live in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Tokelau, or Niue indefinitely. There is no limitation on the length of stay. People who do not qualify for New Zealand citizenship by birth may still be able to get citizenship by grant or descent.

chunks.title: Residence class visa holder — core policy > residence
chunks.text: A residence class visa holder can generally enter and live in New Zealand indefinitely. There is no limitation on the length of stay, but they may have conditions attached to their visa. For example, conditions about how often and for how long the holder can travel outside of New Zealand over a stated period of time. A residence class visa is valid if it has not expired or been cancelled. A person can verify the details of their visa with Immigration New Zealand.

chunks.title: Temporary entry class visa holder — core policy > residence
chunks.text: A temporary entry class visa holder can enter New Zealand but can only stay temporarily. They are only permitted to stay for the duration and purposes indicated on their visa. A temporary entry class visa is valid if it has not expired or been cancelled. A person can verify the details of their visa with Immigration New Zealand. Temporary entry class visa holders are considered lawfully resident in New Zealand. However, they generally do not qualify for assistance from MSD unless they have specific circumstances. Note to qualify for some types of employment assistance, temporary entry class visa holders must have a visa that allows them to work in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Ordinarily resident in New Zealand — core policy > residence
chunks.text: To meet the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD, a person must generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date they apply for assistance. To be included in the person's financial assistance, their partner must also be ordinarily resident in New Zealand. They must generally remain ordinarily resident in New Zealand on an on-going basis to keep getting financial assistance.

chunks.title: Being ordinarily resident — core policy > residence
chunks.text: To be ordinarily resident in New Zealand a person must have a close and clear connection to New Zealand on the date they apply for financial assistance. Other factors that indicate a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand include: - the person making their home in New Zealand, that is, they have been living in New Zealand on a permanent basis - their physical presence in New Zealand is not casual or as a traveller - they intend to stay in New Zealand for the foreseeable future (e.g. they intend to live, work or study here) - even if they temporarily leave New Zealand, they usually live here - they prefer residence in New Zealand to any other country (i.e. are not ordinarily resident in any other country, as a person cannot be ordinarily resident in 2 places at one time) When it is not clear if a person is ordinarily resident, they may need to provide more information. For example: - if the person is going overseas, whether or not they plan on coming back to New Zealand (sighting return air tickets is a good indication that they plan on returning) - the length of time they spend in New Zealand compared to their time away and the reasons for their absences - property ownership (this generally shows permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (e.g. boats, cars, or caravans) - where cash assets are principally held (New Zealand banks or investment entities or overseas based holdings) - do they earn their income in New Zealand or overseas, and are they tax resident in New Zealand - see Inland Revenue Deciding whether you are a resident or non-resident - for people who are 18 years or older, whether or not they are on the electoral role and if they can vote in central and local body elections - personal commitments in New Zealand (e.g. their involvement in their immediate and extended family community, community events and activities, clubs, and other groups) Whether a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand is a question of fact and degree. To make this determination, MSD must consider all the factors on a case-by-case basis. If there is reason to believe the person may no longer be ordinarily resident in New Zealand after assistance is granted, the key attributes of being ordinarily resident can also be considered at that point.

chunks.title: Exceptions — core policy > residence
chunks.text: In limited situations, some people who are not ordinarily resident in New Zealand may still meet the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD. For example, in some situations people may qualify for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension under Special Portability when they are ordinarily resident in the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau.

chunks.title: Partner's residence status — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## Partner's residence status
When a person with a partner applies for financial assistance from MSD, their partner can generally only be included in their payments (where applicable) if they are ordinarily resident in New Zealand and are a New Zealand citizen or residence class visa holder.
This means a partner cannot be included in a person's financial assistance when the partner:
- is a temporary entry class visa holder or
- is resident or present in New Zealand unlawfully or
- is ordinarily resident overseas (including when they intend to live in New Zealand but have not arrived yet) or
- does not meet any other residence requirements specific to that assistance
In some situations, a partner may separately qualify for specific assistance. For example:
- Refugee or protected person status
- Compelled to remain in New Zealand
## Rate of benefit if partner does not qualify
The partner's residence status and reasons for the partner not meeting the residence criteria must be considered when deciding the rate of payment.
The person who meets the residence criteria in this situation can generally be paid a single or sole parent rate (depending on their family circumstances). This includes when the partner is:
- in New Zealand but does not meet the residence requirements or
- overseas and cannot get to New Zealand due to circumstances beyond their control (e.g. they are detained in another country or overseas refugee camp, or have applied for a visa that has not been granted) or
- missing or their whereabouts are unknown
In all other situations, if the person still considers themselves in a relationship, the rate payable is the applicable half couple's rate. This includes when the partner is living overseas and has no definite plans to move to New Zealand.
People who were getting a couple's rate of benefit before 8 August 2001, and had a partner who does not meet the residence requirements included in their benefit, will continue to be paid at the full couple rate until their benefit is cancelled.
Note even when a partner does not meet the residence requirements, all of the couple's income and assets are taken into consideration when assessing the rate payable.

chunks.title: People from the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## People from the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau
For New Zealand citizenship, New Zealand includes the self-governing states of:
- the Cook Islands
- Niue
- Tokelau
A person born in the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau is a New Zealand citizen by birth (if they meet the criteria for New Zealand citizenship by birth).
Note people from the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau must generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand to meet the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD.

chunks.title: People in specific circumstances - residence criteria — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## People in specific circumstances - residence criteria
In some situations, temporary entry class visa holders and people who are deemed to hold a residence class visa may meet the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD.

chunks.title: Refugee or protected person status — core policy > residence
chunks.text: A person can be recognised as either a refugee or a protected person, but must still have a valid visa issued by Immigration New Zealand to be lawfully resident and present in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Mandate or quota refugees — core policy > residence
chunks.text: Some people come to New Zealand under the New Zealand Refugee Quota Programme. The refugee quota is the number of refugees the New Zealand Government has committed to accepting under an international agreement with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. People accepted under the refugee quota are generally selected before arrival and granted entry into New Zealand for humanitarian reasons. They are known as mandate or quota refugees. A person in this situation is recognised as a refugee under the Immigration Act 2009. They are normally granted a residence class visa before their arrival in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Convention or asylum refugees — core policy > residence
chunks.text: Other people may apply for refugee or protected person status under the Immigration Act 2009 after they have arrived in New Zealand. Some people may do this when they arrive at the New Zealand border (usually international air and seaports). Other people may enter New Zealand on a temporary entry class visa and apply for refugee or protected person status after being in New Zealand for some time. Most people in this situation arrive with identification or official documents and live in the community while their application is processed. A lack of official papers does not prevent someone from making a claim for refugee or protection status. However, Immigration New Zealand may detain the person if they do not have any identification or official documents. A person in this situation is generally known as a spontaneous refugee, convention refugee, or asylum seeker. If they do not already hold one, they are generally issued a temporary entry class visa while waiting for the outcome of their claim for refugee or protected person status.

chunks.title: Waiting for outcome of refugee or protected person claim — core policy > residence
chunks.text: Temporary entry class visa holders generally do not meet the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD. However, a person in this situation may meet the residence requirements for specific assistance such as Emergency Benefit or Temporary Additional Support if they: - are lawfully present in New Zealand (i.e. they have a valid temporary class entry visa) and - have made an application for refugee or protected person status and - are waiting for a decision on their application from Immigration New Zealand or are appealing a decline decision to the Immigration and Protection Tribunal Successful claim If a person's claim is successful, they will be granted refugee or protected person status. They must apply for a residence class visa or citizenship to stay in New Zealand indefinitely. However, they generally cannot be deported from New Zealand, even if their temporary entry class visa expires. Note a person with recognised refugee or protected person status does not need a valid visa to meet the residence requirements for specific assistance. However, they must also meet all the other qualifications. This includes any conditions of grant about making efforts to improve their financial situation, such as applying for a visa that enables the person to work in New Zealand. Unsuccessful claim If a person's claim for refugee or a protected person status is unsuccessful, they may appeal the decision. If their temporary entry class visa is valid while waiting for the outcome of the appeal, they may meet the residence requirements for specific assistance such as Emergency Benefit or Temporary Additional Support. If their visa expires or is cancelled while they appeal the decision (or after the application has been declined), they are generally considered to be unlawfully resident in New Zealand and will not meet the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD. Note temporary entry class visa holders may also meet the residence requirements for specific assistance if they are applying for a residence class visa and are compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances.

chunks.title: Specific visas and sponsorship — core policy > residence
chunks.text: All the visa types listed on this page fall into the categories of temporary entry class visa or residence class visa. The type of assistance the visa holder may qualify for will depend on what category of visa they have and their individual circumstances. Immigration New Zealand has a range of visas that allow people to join family in New Zealand. These include partner, children, parent, or grandparent visas. Immigration New Zealand also has visas that allow people to work in New Zealand. This includes (but is not limited to): - working holiday visas for specific countries - skilled migrant visas - visas for people with job offers from accredited employers in areas with skills shortages - visas that allow people to start a business or invest in New Zealand Other types of visas fulfil New Zealand's obligations as a good international citizen, for example: - the Refugee Quota category - Refugee Family Support visas - Pacific Access visas, and - Samoan Quota visas

chunks.title: Visa based on offer of employment — core policy > residence
chunks.text: If a person was granted a visa based on a definite offer of employment (supplied in writing), MSD may need to determine what happened to the job offer before deciding what assistance they qualify for. This may include contacting the employer. Immigration New Zealand will decide on any action to be taken with regard to the person's visa if the offer was withdrawn or the employment was terminated.

chunks.title: Visa based on cash assets — core policy > residence
chunks.text: In some situations a person may be granted a visa based on their personal cash assets. If they apply for assistance from MSD that has a cash asset test, MSD may need to determine what happened to the assets before deciding what assistance they qualify for. If there is a significant drop in the person's cash assets declared, MSD should determine: - what cash assets the person included in their visa application and - what has happened to these cash assets It is not acceptable for these cash assets to be used to purchase capital items such as a house, furniture or motor vehicle. Settlement funds can be used to purchase capital items, as these are not the same as cash assets declared as personal resources.

chunks.title: Sponsorship — core policy > residence
chunks.text: For some people, their visa is granted on the condition that they will be supported by a New Zealand sponsor for a specific period or until the person can sustain themselves. If a person with a sponsored visa applies for financial assistance, MSD may consider any assistance the sponsor has given to the person or their family when determining what resources are available to the person. However, the sponsor's own finances are not considered available. MSD has an approved information sharing agreement with Immigration New Zealand to provide Immigration New Zealand with information about people who have been granted financial assistance from MSD within their sponsorship period. If the sponsor is no longer supporting the person, MSD must verify the reasons why. If the person has chosen not to get support from the sponsor, this may result in MSD declining financial assistance or granting assistance at a reduced rate. This may happen if MSD considers that a person has (directly or indirectly) deprived themselves of income or property and this results in them qualifying for a benefit or an increased rate of benefit.

chunks.title: Two years continuous residence — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## Two years continuous residence
Generally, to meet the residence requirements for a main benefit, a person must have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 or more years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or residence class visa holder.
Only the person applying for the assistance must meet the continuous residence requirement - this does not apply to the person's partner.
Note the 2-year period of residence must be 2 years continuous residence without absence from New Zealand. However, there are some circumstances when a person can be absent from New Zealand during this time. For example, when they have an approved travel reason.
People born in the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau must have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years at any one time before they can meet the 2-year continuous residence criteria.
## Determining continuous residence
To be resident in New Zealand means that the person either:
- makes New Zealand their home, that is, they have been living in New Zealand on a permanent basis or
- has an intention to make New Zealand their home for the foreseeable future
Relevant factors to consider include whether the person:
- has a fixed abode in New Zealand
- owns property in New Zealand
- has frequent absences from New Zealand (and what the duration of and reason for those absences are)
- is involved with New Zealand society (e.g. community activities, employment, membership of clubs or local faith-based organisations)
Note residence in a place is not the same as being ordinarily resident or lawfully resident.
## Exceptions to the two years continuous residence
People with refugee or protected person status who have a residence class visa do not need to meet the 2-year continuous residence requirement to meet the residence requirements for a main benefit.
If a person meets the residence requirements for a main benefit, except the 2-year continuous residence requirement, they may qualify for a main benefit on the grounds of hardship:
- Jobseeker Support Granting on grounds of hardship
- Young Parent Payment Granting on grounds of hardship
- Youth Payment Granting on grounds of hardship
Note unless it is imposed as a condition of grant, the 2-year continuous residence requirement does not apply to Emergency Benefit or Emergency Maintenance Allowance.

chunks.title: Unlawful residence or presence — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## Unlawful residence or presence
To reside in New Zealand lawfully a person must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- hold or be deemed to hold a valid residence class visa or
- hold a valid temporary entry class visa and
- be granted permission by Immigration New Zealand to enter New Zealand (unless their visa was granted in New Zealand)
People with recognised refugee or protected person status under the Immigration Act 2009 generally cannot be deported from New Zealand. However, they must have a valid visa or have been granted entry permission to be considered lawfully resident and present in New Zealand.
If a person in New Zealand does not fulfil one of the above, the person is deemed to be in New Zealand unlawfully.
Any periods of unlawful residence are excluded when calculating the person's period of residence when deciding if a person meets the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD (where relevant).

chunks.title: Victims of family violence — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## Victims of family violence
Some people who have moved to New Zealand may be in a relationship with a New Zealand citizen or residence class visa holder, or hold a partnership-based visa with a temporary entry class visa holder.
If their relationship with that partner ends due to family violence, the person may qualify for a temporary entry class visa on the grounds they are a victim of family violence.
Victims of family violence who have been granted a temporary entry class visa on these grounds may meet the residence requirements for a Special Needs Grant.

chunks.title: Victims of people trafficking — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## Victims of people trafficking
The New Zealand Police make a formal certification for any person who is identified as a suspected victim of people trafficking.
If the person is in New Zealand unlawfully but is required to remain here, Immigration New Zealand may grant them a temporary entry class visa (for example, if they are required to assist with the investigation of their traffickers or attend to their immediate health and welfare needs).
Police-certified victims of people trafficking can also apply for special visas that allow them to stay in New Zealand and work, study or live here permanently in some cases.
In some cases, these people may be granted a residence class visa which allows the holder to reside indefinitely in New Zealand.
Victims of people trafficking with a temporary entry class visa may meet the residence requirements for specific assistance such as a Special Needs Grant.
Financial assistance for people in these situations is decided by Helpline.

chunks.title: Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings — core policy > residence
chunks.text:
## Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
A person can be considered lawfully resident and present in New Zealand during periods of overseas employment when their employer (or another relevant person):
- deducted PAYE (pay as you earn income tax) or source deductions from their wages or salary and
- paid them to Inland Revenue New Zealand
The period that a person was considered resident and present while working overseas can be used to meet the continuous residence requirement for some main benefits.
A partner or any dependent child who was with the person while they were working overseas can also be treated as resident and present in New Zealand for the same periods.
For the purpose of deciding if a person meets the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD, if the person has a child born outside of New Zealand during the period they were working overseas, the child is deemed to have been born in New Zealand.
The person can still be regarded as resident and present in New Zealand during the period of overseas employment if the:
- employer (or other relevant person) has deducted the tax but failed to pay it to Inland Revenue New Zealand and
- person did not contribute to the employer (or other relevant person)'s failure to pay the tax
Note a person cannot be considered lawfully resident and present in New Zealand if they are self-employed and working overseas.
Example
Sam works for a New Zealand tech company. She originally came to New Zealand on a temporary entry class visa, but has recently applied for a residence class visa.
6 months after Sam is granted a residence class visa, her employer sends her to Australia to help set up a new branch for the company. Sam continues to be paid as a New Zealand employee while in Australia, and is overseas for 12 months before returning to New Zealand.
Shortly after returning, Sam applies for financial assistance from MSD. Although Sam only held a residence class visa for 6 months before going to Australia, her time spent working for the New Zealand company in Australia can be used as continuous residence in New Zealand when deciding if she meets the residence criteria for financial assistance from MSD.

chunks.title: Additional medical examinations — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: If the Medical Appeals Board is unable to make a decision on the evidence available at the hearing, the Board may ask the client if they will agree to an additional medical examination. The purpose of the medical examination is to assist the Board in making its decision. If the client agrees, the hearing should be adjourned. In this case, the Board should refer the client to a specialist or other medical practitioner. The medical examination must not be completed by any member of the Board. The requirement of the Board to make a final decision must not be dependent on whether the client agrees to undergo an additional medical examination. If the client does not agree to be referred for further medical opinion, then the Board decides appeal based on the written evidence provided and evidence presented during hearing. The Ministry will arrange the appointment for the client to see a specialist or other medical practitioner and arrange a new hearing date.

chunks.title: Reciprocal Agreements — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: For clients applying for the Supported Living Payment under a Reciprocal Agreement a referral could be made to an overseas agency or a contracted medical assessor in New Zealand (where appropriate), to carry out the additional medical examination. For more information see: - Countries with Reciprocal Agreements

chunks.title: Medical reports — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: The specialist or medical practitioner sends the medical report directly to the Ministry. A copy of the medical report is sent to the client and the Medical Appeals Board. The co-ordinator will look at the report and determine if the original decision made was correct. If the original decision is correct, the Medical Appeals Board hearing will reconvene. If the original decision is incorrect, the Ministry will make submissions to the Board explaining why the original decision was not correct, and recommend it be overturned. The Medical Appeals Board will consider the resubmission and will write to the Ministry and the client with their decision. You should send the medical invoice to the National Accounting Centre who will arrange payment.

chunks.title: Payment for health related travel for medical examination — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: Travel costs can be paid if the client is referred by the Medical Appeals Board for an additional medical to establish whether the right decision was made to: - decline or cancel: Child Disability AllowanceSupported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability)− this includes countries where New Zealand has a Reciprocal Agreement under which clients can receive the Supported Living PaymentJobseeker Support orVeteran's Pension (under 65 years of age and with a health condition, injury or disability that is not related to their service) - Child Disability Allowance - Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability)− this includes countries where New Zealand has a Reciprocal Agreement under which clients can receive the Supported Living Payment - Jobseeker Support or - Veteran's Pension (under 65 years of age and with a health condition, injury or disability that is not related to their service) This includes decisions made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner. - apply or enforce work obligations or work preparation obligations for Jobseeker Support, Supported Living Payment, Sole Parent Support, or are a partner of a main beneficiary (including decisions made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner) This includes where an application for an exception is declined using information provided in a Work Capacity Medical Certificate. - apply an obligations failure on the grounds that the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for not complying with a drug test obligation and/or failing to apply for suitable work that requires drug tests, on the basis that they are addicted to or dependent on drugs The payment is intended to ensure that the client is reimbursed for any costs as a result of being referred.

chunks.title: Appeal Authority process — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## Appeal Authority process
Step 1. Client's application for appeal is sent direct to the Social Security Appeal Authority.
Step 2. The Social Security Appeal Authority advises the appropriate Ministry of Social Development appeals officer.
Step 3. Appeals officer advises service centre and obtains relevant information from case manager.
Step 4. Appeals officer completes report in accordance with regulation 249 of the Social Security Regulations 2018.
Step 5. The Social Security Appeal Authority sets a hearing date. The hearing can be heard in person or on papers only. The Ministry of Social Development appeals officer or solicitor will represent the Ministry at the hearing. The case manager may be required to give evidence.
Step 6. The Social Security Appeal Authority will advise the Ministry of Social Development and the client of the outcome.
Step 7. The appeals officer will advise the client's case manager of any benefit action to be taken.

chunks.title: Appeals to the Social Security Appeal Authority — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## Appeals to the Social Security Appeal Authority
A client can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority hearing when the Benefits Review Committee has upheld or upheld in part an original decision under:
- any provisions of (or of any regulations made for the purposes of any provisions of) Parts 1 to 6 and Schedules 1 to 5 or
- a special assistance programme approved by the Minister under section 100 or 101 or
- any regulations in force under section 437 (regulations: issue and use of entitlement cards)
- any provisions of, or of regulations made under, the Residential Care and Disability Support Services Act 2018 or
- Part 6 of the Veterans’ Support Act 2014, subject to section 175(2) of that Act or
- Part 1 of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001 or
- the Family Benefits (Home Ownership) Act 1964
A client's application for appeal should be sent directly to the Social Security Appeal Authority.
Note when the Benefits Review Committee has declined to hear an out of time review of decision and the client applies for the matter to be heard by the Social Security Appeal Authority, forward the case to the Appeal Authority.
For more information see:
## Expenses
The client's actual and reasonable expenses for travel and accommodation, to attend the Social Security Appeal Authority hearing, must be paid.
## Outcome
The Social Security Appeal Authority will advise both parties to the appeal (the client and the Ministry of Social Development) of the outcome.
## High Court action
Where either party to the appeal disagrees with the outcome, there is one further course of action and that is an appeal to the High Court. Appeals of this nature are restricted to questions of law.

chunks.title: Client wishes to withdraw application for review — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## Client wishes to withdraw application for review
If a client wishes to withdraw their application for Review of Decision at any stage, they must put this in writing and that will be the end of the review process.
## Acknowledge the client's request to withdraw
You need to acknowledge the client's request to withdraw their application for Review of Decision in writing. There is a template letter available for you to do this on HIYA ROD.

chunks.title: Countries with Reciprocal Agreements — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## Countries with Reciprocal Agreements
Countries with a Reciprocal Agreement where the Supported Living Payment can be paid are:
- Australia
- Canada
- Denmark
- Greece
- Ireland
- Jersey and Guernsey
- Netherlands
- United Kingdom (inside New Zealand)
For more information see:
- Reciprocal Agreements
## Medical Appeals
When the Medical Appeals Board considers an appeal from a client covered by a Reciprocal Agreement, the Board will assess the client based on the qualifications for Supported Living Payment in the Social Security Act 2018. This excludes clients covered under the Reciprocal Agreement with Australia.
## Work obligations when living overseas
When a client is paid Supported Living Payment under a Reciprocal Agreement and they are living in a country other than New Zealand, they are exempt from work test obligations.

chunks.title: Decisions not reviewable by the Benefit Review Committee — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## Decisions not reviewable by the Benefit Review Committee
Decisions about programmes and services that are not made under the Social Security Act 2018 cannot be reviewed by the Benefit Review Committee.
If a client, or a member of the public, wishes to review a decision regarding a programme or service that is not provided for under the Social Security Act 2018 such as Flexi-wage self-employment, the original decision should be reconsidered.
A review should be based on whether an 'informed' decision was made and should consider the following:
- was all relevant information obtained
- were the appropriate options and implications considered
- was the decision made at the appropriate level of delegation
Having regard to the delegation level of the original decision, the review should be carried out by the:
- manager client service delivery
- Regional Director or
- Regional Commissioner

chunks.title: Medical Appeals Board — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: The Medical Appeals Board is an independent body established to ensure that correct decisions are made based on medical grounds or on grounds relating to a person's capacity for work. The Medical Appeals Board takes a fresh look at all the information about a client's medical circumstances and work capacity.

chunks.title: Which decisions can be appealed to a Medical Appeals Board? — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: A client can appeal to the Medical Appeals Board if they: - do not agree with a decision made on medical grounds to decline or cancel: Child Disability AllowanceSupported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability)This includes countries where New Zealand has a Reciprocal Agreement under which clients can receive the Supported Living PaymentJobseeker SupportVeterans Pension (under 65 years of age and with a health condition, injury or disability that is not related to their service) - Child Disability Allowance - Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability)This includes countries where New Zealand has a Reciprocal Agreement under which clients can receive the Supported Living Payment - Jobseeker Support - Veterans Pension (under 65 years of age and with a health condition, injury or disability that is not related to their service) Note this includes decisions made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner. - are on Jobseeker Support, Supported Living Payment, Sole Parent Support, or are a partner of a main beneficiary and disagree with a decision made on medical grounds regarding their full-time work obligations, part-time work obligations or work preparation obligations (including decisions made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner) Note this includes where an application for an exemption is declined using information provided in a Work Capacity Medical Certificate. - have work obligations and the Ministry determines that they do not have a good and sufficient reason for not complying with a drug test obligation and/or failing to apply for suitable work that requires drug tests, on the basis that they are addicted to or dependent on drugs For more information see: - Which decisions can be appealed to a Medical Appeals Board - Who can make an appeal - Who is on the Medical Appeals Board

chunks.title: When the appeal relates to a decision on eligibility — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: If the appeal relates to a decision on eligibility the Medical Appeals Board must decide whether the client meets the medical criteria or work capacity criteria for the relevant benefit and consider whether the right decision was made to decline or cancel the benefit.

chunks.title: When the appeal relates to a decision on work obligations or work preparation obligations — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: If the appeal relates to a decision about work obligations or work preparation obligations, the Medical Appeals Board must decide whether the client has capacity to meet those obligations and whether the correct decision was made to enforce or apply the obligations on medical grounds. Note when determining the client's capacity for work, capacity to meet work obligations or capacity to meet work preparation obligations, only the client's capacity on medical grounds relating to their health condition, injury or disability can be considered by the Board.

chunks.title: When the appeal relates to a decision on drug test obligations — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: Where the decision is in relation to drug test obligations, the Board must decide whether the client has a good and sufficient reason, on the basis that they are addicted to or dependent on controlled drugs, for: - not complying with a drug test obligation or - failing to apply for suitable work that requires drug tests Note other decisions about drug test obligations may be reviewed by the Benefits Review Committee.

chunks.title: Additional medical examinations required by the Medical Appeals Board — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: If the Medical Appeals Board is unable to make a decision on the evidence available at the hearing, the Board may ask the client if they will agree to an additional medical examination. For more information see: - Additional medical examinations

chunks.title: Outcome of appeal — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: The decision of the Board is final and will direct what Work and Income are required to do. Both Work and Income and the client are bound by the decision and there is no right of future appeal.

chunks.title: Re-application for benefit after decline from Medical Appeals Board — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## Re-application for benefit after decline from Medical Appeals Board
If the Medical Appeals Board:
- upholds the decision to decline or cancel the client's application for Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability)*, Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability), Veteran's Pension or Child Disability Allowance
and
- the client re-applies for the same benefit with the same health condition
then the application should be declined.
If the client:
- provides a medical opinion that their condition has deteriorated since the appeal decision
or
- re-applies for the same benefit with a new health condition
then the application for Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability)*, Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability), Veteran's Pension or Child Disability Allowance should be considered.
If the client then appeals, it must go the Medical Appeals Board.
*This includes countries where New Zealand has a Reciprocal Agreement under which clients can receive the Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Rehabilitation professional — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## Rehabilitation professional
To be appointed to the Medical Appeals Board, a rehabilitation professional is:
- a person who is professionally engaged in the rehabilitation of people
- an Occupational therapist
- a Physiotherapist
- a Nurse or
- a Psychologist
Rehabilitation professionals must be registered with their appropriate authority under the Health Practitioners Competence and Assurance Act 2003, for their scope of practice.

chunks.title: Review of decision for debts — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## Review of decision for debts
When an application for Review of Decision involves a debt currently being recovered from a benefit, it is appropriate to suspend recovery until the review and appeal process is completed.
Note you do not refund any offsets already deducted until the outcome of the review or appeal is known.

chunks.title: Review of decision for Mandatory Reviews — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## Review of decision for Mandatory Reviews
A client cannot review the requirement to complete a Mandatory Review of their benefit as it is a statutory requirement rather than a reviewable decision made by MSD.
However, a client can apply for a Review of Decision of the Mandatory Review process when they:
- do not agree with a decision about a change to the rate or, a decision to suspend or cancel their benefit
- do not agree with a decision to not undertake the Mandatory Review
- have provided a reason to be exempt from doing their Mandatory Review, which was not deemed by MSD to be unforeseen or beyond their control
- have provided a reason for an extension of time to respond to their Mandatory Review, which was not deemed by MSD to be good and sufficient reason
- have been granted an extension of less than 20 working days and disagree with the length of time provided
## Automated Decision-Making
Where Automated Decision-Making is used to determine that a client continues to qualify for their benefit as the result of a Mandatory Review, it is automatically continued.
If MSD or the client does not agree with the decision to automatically continue the benefit, MSD can review the decision.
A client can then apply for a Review of Decision if they do not agree with the outcome of MSD's review of the decision made through Automated Decision-Making.
Note Automated Decision-Making is not used when the Mandatory Review is for Emergency Benefit or Emergency Maintenance Allowance.

chunks.title: Review of decision when child turns 18 — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## Review of decision when child turns 18
A parent or caregiver can apply for a Review of Decision when they do not agree with a decision about whether, or for how long, their child is considered to be a dependent child and is included in their payments on or after their child's 18th birthday.
This includes (but is not limited to):
- a decision to exclude their child on their 18th birthday - for example, when the parent or caregiver has information that would mean the child can still be considered a dependent child for a limited period
- the date that MSD has excluded their child from their payment if they were still considered a dependent child after their 18th birthday
- a decision about whether, or for how long, to continue paying the benefit (or rate of benefit, where relevant) after the 18-year-old child would otherwise have been excluded - for example after the death of a client getting a benefit
## Automated decision-making
When a parent or caregiver has not responded to the notice that their child will be excluded, automated decision-making is used to automatically exclude the child when they turn 18. This exclusion may result in the parent or caregiver's payments continuing at the same rate, continuing at a different rate, suspending, or cancelling.
Note discretionary benefits will always suspend when a parent or caregiver does not respond to the notice.
The parent or caregiver can apply for a Review of Decision if they do not agree with the decision to exclude their child from their payments made through automated decision-making.

chunks.title: Exceptions — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: A client has no right of appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority (and therefore no right to apply for a Review of Decision): - for a decision made on medical grounds for Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability), Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability), Child Disability Allowance or Veterans Pension - for a decision made (on medical grounds or on grounds relating to capacity to work) to require a Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) client to be subject to or continue to be subject to part-time work obligations - for a decision to decline or revoke a deferral of work obligations on medical grounds of Jobseeker Support - for a decision under that the client did not have a good and sufficient reason for failing their drug test obligations, as they are not addicted to or dependent on controlled drugs - for a decision to decline entitlement to a Veteran's Pension on the basis that the service is not qualifying operational service - though Veterans' Affairs can be asked to review that decision - if an application for benefit has lapsed under section 297 of the Social Security Act 2018 If a client disagrees with any of the decisions listed above on medical grounds the client may appeal the decision to the Medical Appeals Board. The client has the right to apply for a Review of Decision at any time within 3 months of the original decision being advised. When a client has applied for a hearing outside the three month time limit the Benefits Review Committee must decide whether or not to accept the application before it considers the decision under review. A client has the right to have their decision reviewed once. If they wish to have the same decision reviewed again refer the case to MSD Legal Services.

chunks.title: Three stage process — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: There are 3 stages to the review and appeal process: Stage 1 - Internal review This is an administrative process only. When a client applies for a Review of Decision, it is appropriate for the Ministry of Social Development to take another look at the decision, review any new information, as well as that which was available at the time of the decision, and check the decision was in accordance with legislation. Stage 2 - Benefits Review Committee An application for a Review of Decision is an application for the decision to be heard by the Benefits Review Committee. Note when the internal review outcome is not favourable or only favourable in part for the client, the decision must go before the Benefits Review Committee without any further request from the client. Stage 3 - Social Security Appeal Authority hearing When the original decision is upheld (or partially upheld) by the Benefit Review Committee, the client can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority. See:

chunks.title: Reviews of information share Child Support payments — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## Reviews of information share Child Support payments
Clients have standard review and appeal rights if they want to review a decision on the treatment of information share Child Support payments. They can also ask the Ombudsman to undertake their own review.
If a client requests a review:
MSD can only change the treatment of information share Child Support payments when there has been an 'error'.
Clients can request a review of the information MSD has used if they think there has been an error.
An 'error' is when a client has been charged income for an information share Child Support payment but they:
- did not get the payment or
- got a different amount of Child Support than was charged as income or
- got the payment later than the deemed receipt
MSD cannot change the treatment of information share Child Support payments if there is no error identified.
This includes when a client disagrees with:
- how the income charge for a payment has been calculated (e.g. if the client believes that the income should have been charged over a different period - 12 weeks instead of 4) or
- the amount of income that has been charged for a payment (e.g. if the Child Support payment was used to repay the client's overdraft on their bank account)

chunks.title: When to advise a client of their right to review — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## When to advise a client of their right to review
Explain a client's right of review when you provide formal notification about a decision to:
- grant or decline a benefit (all benefits including extra help, Community Services Card etc)
- review their benefit affecting the rate of payment
- establish, amend or recover a debt or
- when initiating a work preparation or work obligations failure
## Notify decision in full
When you advise a client of a decision, in particular an unfavourable decision, you should explain your decision in full and explain the relevant legislation.
Note it is not appropriate to just quote a section of the Act verbatim, you should explain the relevant legislation to the client and how it applies to their situation.

chunks.title: Which decisions can be appealed to a Medical Appeals Board — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: The following table summarises the decisions that clients or their partners (when the decision is in relation to the partner) can appeal to the Medical Appeals Board. For more information see: - Child Disability Allowance Qualifications Jobseeker Support The decision to decline or cancel Jobseeker Support on medical grounds or grounds relating to the client's capacity for work (including decisions made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner). For more information see: - Jobseeker Support Qualifications The decision to apply part-time work obligations (at application or review) based on the determination that the client has the capacity to seek, undertake, and be available for part-time work (including decisions made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner).
