(This includes countries where New Zealand has a Reciprocal Agreement under which clients can receive the Supported Living Payment.) For more information: - Supported Living Payment Qualifications The decision that the client has the capacity to undertake work preparation activities and plan for employment (including decisions made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner) Note this includes where a decision is made using information provided in a Work Capacity Medical Certificate. For more information see: - Supported Living Payment Obligations Supported Living Payment on the grounds of caring for a person who requires full-time care and attention The decision that the client has the capacity to undertake work preparation activities and plan for employment (including decisions made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner) Note this includes where a decision is made using information provided in a Work Capacity Medical Certificate. For more information see: - Supported Living Payment Obligations Sole Parent Support The determination that a client subject to work preparation obligations has the capacity to undertake work preparation activities and plan for employment, where the decision is made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner Note this includes where an application for an exemption is declined using information provided in a Work Capacity Medical Certificate. For more information see: - Sole Parent Support Obligations - Sole Parent Support Exemptions The determination that a client subject to work obligations has the capacity to meet those obligations, where the decision is made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner Note this includes where an application for an exemption is declined using information provided in a Work Capacity Medical Certificate For more information see: - Sole Parent Support Obligations - Sole Parent Support Exemptions The decision that a client with work obligations does not have a good and sufficient reason, on the basis that they are not addicted to or dependant on controlled drugs, for: - not complying with a drug test obligation or - failing to apply for suitable employment that requires candidates to undertake drug tests For more information see: - Sole Parent Support Drug test obligations Partners of main beneficiaries The determination that a partner subject to work preparation obligations has the capacity to undertake work preparation activities and plan for employment, where the decision is made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner. Note this includes where an application for an exemption is declined using information provided in a Work Capacity Medical Certificate.

chunks.title: Which decisions can be appealed to a Medical Appeals Board — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: For more information see: - Jobseeker Support Work or work preparation obligations - Jobseeker Support Exemptions The determination that a partner subject to work obligations has the capacity to meet those obligations, where the decision is made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner. Note this includes where an application for an exemption is declined using information provided in a Work Capacity Medical Certificate. For more information see: - Jobseeker Support Work or work preparation obligations - Jobseeker Support Exemptions The decision that a partner with work obligations does not have a good and sufficient reason, on the basis that they are not addicted to or dependant on controlled drugs, for: - not complying with a drug test obligation or - failing to apply for suitable employment that requires candidates to undertake drug tests For more information see: - Jobseeker Support Drug test obligations Veteran's Pension The decision to decline or cancel on medical grounds the Veteran's Pension for clients under 65 years of age and with a health condition, injury or disability that is not related to their service. For more information see: - Veteran's Pension Note when determining the client's capacity for work, capacity to meet work obligations or capacity to meet work preparation obligations, only the client's capacity on medical grounds relating to their health condition, injury or disability can be considered.

chunks.title: Who can apply for a review or appeal — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## Who can apply for a review or appeal
The following people can apply for a Review of Decision:
- the client
- the client's spouse or partner - when the decision is in relation to the spouse or partner or
- an agent with appropriate authorisation from the client
## Persons not able to apply for a review or appeal
A third party, without authorisation, is not able to apply for a Review of Decision.
Example
- the parent or family member of a young person receiving Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment
- a health practitioneror
- a childcare centre
Note if a client disagrees with a decision on medical grounds the client may appeal the decision to the Medical Appeals Board. For more information see:
- Medical Appeals Board

chunks.title: Who can make an appeal? — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: The following people can appeal to the Medical Appeals Board: - the client - the client's partner - when the decision is in relation to the partner or - an agent with appropriate authorisation from the client

chunks.title: Persons not able to apply for a review or appeal — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: A third party, without authorisation, is not able to appeal to the Medical Appeals Board.

chunks.title: Lodging an appeal — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: An appeal can be made to the Medical Appeals Board if it: - is lodged within 3 months of the client receiving notification of the original decision and - has not been heard by a Medical Appeals Board previously and - is an appeal within the jurisdiction of the Board When a client applies for a decision to be heard by the Medical Appeals Board, the client should get a copy of the factsheet 'A Guide to Medical Appeals Board Hearings'.

chunks.title: Out of time — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: When an appeal is received more than 3 months after the client has been notified of the decision a hearing must still be arranged. The first thing the board must do is decide whether there was good reason for the delay in lodging the appeal. If the board is satisfied that there is good reason for the delay they will consider whether the right decision was made, to: - decline or cancel: Child Disability AllowanceSupported Living PaymentJobseeker SupportVeteran's Pension (under 65 years of age and with a health condition, injury or disability that is not related to their service) - Child Disability Allowance - Supported Living Payment - Jobseeker Support - Veteran's Pension (under 65 years of age and with a health condition, injury or disability that is not related to their service) Note this includes decisions made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner. - apply or enforce work obligations or work preparation obligations for Jobseeker Support, Supported Living Payment, Sole Parent Support, or are a partner of a main beneficiary (including decisions made based on any work ability assessment undertaken by a health practitioner) Note this includes when an application for an exemption is declined using information provided in a Work Capacity Medical Certificate - apply an obligations failure on the grounds that the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for not complying with a drug test obligation and/or failing to apply for suitable work that requires drug tests, on the basis that they are addicted to or dependent on drugs

chunks.title: Withdrawals — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: The client may withdraw their appeal at any time before an appeal is heard and a decision made. If the client advises that they wish to withdraw their appeal, the Ministry of Social Development will notify the board immediately and confirm this in writing.

chunks.title: Appeal heard previously — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text: A client has the right to have their decision reviewed once. If the decision has already been heard by the Medical Appeals Board, it cannot be heard again. However, what seems like a request for an appeal on the same decision, may relate to a different decision. For example, a client's first appeal may be the decision to cancel the Supported Living Payment on medical grounds. The client may then reapply for the Supported Living Payment due to their condition deteriorating and if that application is declined, the client can then seek a further appeal to the Medical Appeals Board. If the client applies again for the same decision to be heard by the Medical Appeals Board, they should be advised that this decision is outside of the jurisdiction of the Medical Appeals Board and given the opportunity to withdraw their request for an appeal. If the client does not withdraw their request for an appeal, and the Ministry considers that it is not appealable, the case should be referred to the Medical Appeals Board to hold a jurisdiction hearing.

chunks.title: Who is on the Medical Appeals Board? — core policy > reviews and appeals
chunks.text:
## Who is on the Medical Appeals Board?
The Board is made up of 3 of the following:
- medical practitioners (preferably not more than one designated health practitioner)
- rehabilitation professionals
- other persons having appropriate expertise in the fields of vocational training or vocational support for persons with a health condition, injury or disability
Practitioners included on the Medical Appeals Board for a client's hearing must be impartial. They must not have a prejudice for or against any person involved in the appeal, and therefore must not have had any involved any assessment used to make the original decision.
## Rehabilitation professional
The rehabilitation professional give a rehabilitation point of view to the Board, which will help in determining the client's capacity to undertake work.
Health and Disability teams should make contact with rehabilitation professionals in their region to check on their availability for the Medical Appeals Board for when the need arises.
For more information on rehabilitation professionals who can be appointed as members of the Medical Appeals Board, see:
- Rehabilitation professional
## Specific individuals approved for the Medical Appeals Board
There is a list of approved medical practitioners, rehabilitation professionals, and others with appropriate expertise who are available for Medical Appeals Board hearings.
## Fees for board members
The fee to pay Board members needs to be negotiated. The current arrangement used for designated health practitioners can be used as a guide.
For more information about medical appeals see:

chunks.title: Benefit or student information that can be used for housing purposes — core policy > use of social housing benefit and student information
chunks.text:
## Benefit or student information that can be used for housing purposes
The following information is collected for benefit or student assistance purposes and may be used for social housing purposes without any further agreement from the client:
- income
- child details
- partner details
- absence from New Zealand
- death of a client, partner or child
- change in relationships status
- change of address
- hospitalisation
- imprisonment
Note this list is not exhaustive. There may be other information collected for benefit and student assistance purposes that may be used for housing purposes without any further agreement from the client. If you are unsure whether the information can be used without any further agreement from the client, please contact Helpline.
For more information see:
- Benefits included for benefit purposes
- Housing information that can be used for benefit and student purposes
- Examples of how information can be collected and used
- Dealing with conflicting information

chunks.title: Benefits included for benefit purposes — core policy > use of social housing benefit and student information
chunks.text:
## Benefits included for benefit purposes
Benefits included for benefit purposes are:
- Emergency Benefit
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance
- Jobseeker Support
- Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
- Living alone payment
- New Zealand Superannuation/Veteran's Pension
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Young Parent Payment (including incentive payments)
- Youth Payment (including incentive payments)
and
- Accommodation Supplement
- Child Care Assistance payments
- Child Disability Allowance
- Disability Allowance
- Temporary Additional Support
For more information see:
- Benefit or student information that can be used for housing purposes
- Housing information that can be used for benefit and student purposes
- Dealing with conflicting information

chunks.title: Verify conflicting information with the client first — core policy > use of social housing benefit and student information
chunks.text: Where you receive information that conflicts with information already held for social housing and/or benefit or student assistance purposes you must attempt to verify the situation with the client first. This can be undertaken by phone or in writing. Once you have had this discussion with the client you need to make a decision on the next steps based on the information that you have. For example: - you find the income declared in the benefit or student assistance space does not change the client's eligibility for social housing or Income Related Rent - you may make the change in the social housing system to correct the information but no other action would be taken - a partner is declared in the social housing space but client is receiving Sole Parent Support - an interview would need to be booked to include the partner in the benefit

chunks.title: Benefit or Student Assistance information cannot be verified with the client — core policy > use of social housing benefit and student information
chunks.text: If more information is required to confirm student assistance or benefit eligibility or entitlement you can contact the client in writing and ask for this information to review their eligibility for this assistance. If they don't respond, their benefit or student assistance may be suspended.

chunks.title: Social housing information cannot be verified with the client — core policy > use of social housing benefit and student information
chunks.text: If the information is required to confirm housing you can contact the client in writing and require them to provide information to confirm (but not limited to) their circumstances in relation to their: - eligibility to be allocated social housing or to be referred to any particular social housing provider - housing needs (property requirements) - Income Related Rent If the client fails or refuses to answer (or answer satisfactorily) or you believe on reasonable grounds that the client has deliberately given false or misleading information in response to the information required, you may take the following actions. For a prospective tenant: - who is being assessed for eligibility to be allocated social housing: suspend their application to determine whether the client is eligible to be allocated social housing ordecline the client's application to become a tenant of social housing - suspend their application to determine whether the client is eligible to be allocated social housing or - decline the client's application to become a tenant of social housing - who has been assessed as eligible for social housing but is on the register: suspend the process to refer the client to Housing New Zealand or a community housing provider to be allocated a suitable housedecline the client's application to become a tenant of social housing and remove from the registercalculate an Income Related Rent for the client on the basis of the Ministry of Social Development's own understanding of the circumstances of the client (this information may be from other sources)set the client's rate of Income Related Rent at the market rent - suspend the process to refer the client to Housing New Zealand or a community housing provider to be allocated a suitable house - decline the client's application to become a tenant of social housing and remove from the register - calculate an Income Related Rent for the client on the basis of the Ministry of Social Development's own understanding of the circumstances of the client (this information may be from other sources) - set the client's rate of Income Related Rent at the market rent For an existing tenant (someone who is already eligible to be living in social housing): - treat the client as having had a change in circumstances (and the date in change in circumstances) on the basis of the information you do have - calculate an Income Related Rent for the client on the basis of the Ministry of Social Development's own understanding of the circumstances of the client (this information may be from other sources) - set the client's rate of Income Related Rent at the market rent For more information see:

chunks.title: Social housing information cannot be verified with the client — core policy > use of social housing benefit and student information
chunks.text: - Social housing Income Related Rent - Income Related Rent Increasing the rate of Income Related Rent to the market rent rate

chunks.title: Examples of how information can be collected and used — core policy > use of social housing benefit and student information
chunks.text:
## Examples of how information can be collected and used
The following are examples of how information that is collected for one purpose could be used for another.

Information collected:
Can be used to:

For more information see:
- Benefits included for benefit purposes

- Housing information that can be used for benefit or student purposes

chunks.title: Housing information that can be used for benefit or student purposes — core policy > use of social housing benefit and student information
chunks.text:
## Housing information that can be used for benefit or student purposes
The following information is collected for social housing purposes and may be used for benefit or student assistance purposes without any further agreement from the client:
- change in household composition such as children joining or leaving the household, change in relationship status, other additional occupants, death of a joint tenant or other household member
- income for initial assessment of eligibility and Income Related Rent
- client allocated social housing eg change of address, reassessing entitlement to other types of financial assistance, checking Accommodation Supplement being paid for board
Note this list is not exhaustive. There may be other information collected for social housing purposes that may be used for benefit or student assistance purposes without any further agreement from the client. If you are unsure whether the information can be used without any further agreement from the client, please contact Helpline.
For more information see:
- Benefits included for benefit purposes
- Benefit or student information that can be used for housing purposes
- Examples of how information can be collected and used
- Dealing with conflicting information

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > use of social housing benefit and student information
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Work and Income, Senior Services and StudyLink collect information from various sources for different purposes.
Generally, information can only be used for the purpose for which it was gathered.
## Information gathered for social housing and benefit purposes
Information gathered for social housing purposes and for benefit purposes can be used to perform the functions, duties and powers in each of these areas.
For example:
- information obtained for housing purposes can be used for assessing benefits and entitlement to benefits
- information obtained for benefit purposes can be used for assessing housing entitlement and Income Related Rent
## Use of Student Allowance (including Accommodation Benefit) and Student Loan information for social housing assistance (and vice versa)
Information gathered for student assistance purposes and information gathered for social housing purposes can also be used to perform the functions, duties and powers in each of these areas.
For example:
- information obtained for social housing purposes can be used for assessing eligibility and entitlement to student assistance
- information obtained for student assistance purposes can be used for assessing social housing entitlement and Income Related Rent

chunks.title: Advising client once benefit has been suspended — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Advising client once benefit has been suspended
Once the benefit has been suspended, because the warrant to arrest states that the client is a risk to public safety, Central Services will send a letter to the client advising them:
- that their benefit has been suspended
- that it has been suspended because of the warrant for their arrest
- the specific actions that they need to take if they dispute they are the person to whom the warrant applies
- the specific actions they need to take to resolve the warrant
A special caution will be displayed in CMS when the client's record is opened. It will also show in the SSTAI screen as Warrant to Arrest.
For more information see:
- Risk to public safety
- Challenging a warrant to arrest
- Overview of steps to resolve a warrant
- Guidelines for Warrants to Arrest [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Age of the warrant — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Age of the warrant
The warrant to arrest policy applies to a client who has an unresolved warrant to arrest regardless of the date that the warrant was issued.
For example, a client may appear in the data match for an outstanding warrant that was issued against them 3years ago.

chunks.title: Challenge to warrant is unsuccessful — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Challenge to warrant is unsuccessful
If a challenge to a warrant to arrest is unsuccessful, a debt is not established. The client is given another 10 working day notice period to clear their warrant before their benefit is suspended.
For more information see:
- Effect on benefit
- Client requires financial assistance to resolve warrant
- Overview of steps to resolve a warrant

chunks.title: Challenging a warrant to arrest — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Challenging a warrant to arrest
If the client thinks that the warrant to arrest has been issued to the wrong person, they can challenge the warrant to arrest.
This can be either a challenge to the Ministry of Social Development's data match, or to the identity information held by the Ministry of Justice.
Where a client challenges a warrant to arrest, Work and Income will not take any action to suspend their benefit until the challenge has been resolved.
Note a client can challenge a warrant at any point. This process is managed by the Integrity Intervention Centre (IIC). Depending on the challenge reason, the Integrity Intervention Centre will give the client the appropriate amount of time to resolve the challenge.
As soon as a client advises Work and Income that they are challenging the warrant, the benefit will not suspend. If the benefit has already been suspended, then it must be resumed from the suspension date.
Evidence may need to be provided from the Ministry of Justice or the police.
For more information see:
- Challenge to warrant is unsuccessful
- Client requires financial assistance to resolve warrant
- Overview of steps to resolve a warrant

chunks.title: Client has not taken all reasonable steps — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Client has not taken all reasonable steps
If a client or partner has not taken all reasonable steps to resolve the warrant to arrest and the reason that they have been unable to do so is not due to reasons beyond their control, do not resume their benefit until they provide evidence they have resolved their warrant.
Once a client has cleared their warrant, their benefit can be resumed but it cannot be backdated. You can only resume it from the date they clear their warrant.
## Example
A client contacts Work and Income because their benefit is suspended as they chose not to make an attempt to clear their warrant to arrest within the 10 working day notice period. They now say that the court won't be open until the end of the week.
Do not resume their benefit until they provide evidence they have cleared their warrant to arrest. This is because they did not take reasonable steps in the notice period to clear their warrant. The benefit will be resumed from the date they clear their warrant to arrest.

chunks.title: Client requires financial assistance to resolve a warrant — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Client requires financial assistance to resolve a warrant
Generally it is expected that a client uses their weekly benefit payment to pay any costs required to resolve their warrant.
Costs can be incurred when the nearest court is some distance from the client's home and they will need to travel there to resolve their warrant.
The client will not generally qualify for a Special Needs Grant or an Advance Payment of Benefit for any transport costs required.

chunks.title: Client was absent from New Zealand — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Client was absent from New Zealand
Taking all reasonable steps applies to clients and partners receiving a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's pension who continue to be paid their benefit or pension while they are temporarily absent from New Zealand.
For example, if the client was overseas during the notice period, the reason they haven't cleared their warrant to arrest is beyond their control. If their benefit has been suspended, it should be resumed from the date it was suspended. In the case of a client receiving New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension, this could be up to 26 weeks.
For more information see:
- Other circumstances beyond a client's control
- Client has not taken all reasonable steps

chunks.title: Clients with a partner and no dependent children — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Clients with a partner and no dependent children
Where a client or partner has a warrant to arrest and they have not resolved the warrant to arrest within 10 working days, their portion of the main benefit and Extra help will be stopped.
## Client has warrant to arrest
Where a client has not resolved the warrant to arrest within the 10 working day notice period, for the partner to receive their portion of main benefit and any Extra help, the client's portion will be reduced to zero using the SWTAR screen in SWIFTT.
The partner can continue to receive their portion of the main benefit and any Extra help (this includes being paid the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment) for 28 days after the benefit has been suspended. Prior to the benefit suspending at 28 days, the primary client will automatically be sent a letter which advises that the entire benefit will stop in two weeks if the warrant has not been resolved.
Where the client's portion of benefit has been stopped for more than 28 days, the partner will need to contact Work and Income to determine if they qualify for a benefit in their own right.
## Partner has warrant to arrest
Where a partner has not resolved the warrant to arrest within the 10 working day notice period, their portion of the main benefit and Extra help will be stopped.
The client will continue to receive their portion of the main benefit and Extra help (including the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment).
## Both have a warrant to arrest
Where both the client and their partner are identified as having a warrant to arrest and they both have not resolved the warrant to arrest within 10 working days, their main benefit and any Extra help (including Winter Energy Payment) will stop.
For more information see:
- Couple with one or more dependent children
- Effect on benefit if already sanctioned
- Taking all reasonable steps to resolve a warrant
- Restarting the benefit

chunks.title: Couple with one or more dependent children — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Couple with one or more dependent children
When a client or partner (with one or more dependent children) does not resolve the warrant to arrest within 10 workings days, 50% of the main benefit and any Extra help will be stopped.
## Client has warrant to arrest
Where a client has not resolved the warrant to arrest within the 10 working day notice period, for the partner to receive their portion of main benefit and any Extra help, the client's portion will need to be reduced to zero using the SWTAR screen in SWIFTT. The partner must be paid the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment.
If the client has not resolved their warrant after two weeks, you will need to contact them to discuss financial assistance and resolving their warrant. If the client has still not cleared the warrant at four weeks you will need to send the client a letter advising they need to attend an appointment to discuss on-going entitlement to benefit.
## Partner has warrant to arrest
Where a partner has not resolved the warrant to arrest within the 10 working day notice period, their portion of the main benefit and Extra help will be stopped.
The client will continue to receive their portion of the main benefit and Extra help. The full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment will be paid to the client.
## Both have a warrant to arrest
Where both the client and their partner are identified as having a warrant to arrest and they both have not resolved the warrant to arrest within 10 working days, they will continue to receive half of their portion of their main benefit and any Extra help.
Each partner can receive 25% of the main benefit and any Extra help. Both the client and partner must have their rate of payment of main benefit and Extra help adjusted using the SWTAR screen in SWIFTT. However, the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment will be paid to the couple as they are still receiving a portion of their main benefit.
Note where the benefit has been reduced for more than 28 days, you will need to contact the couple to discuss financial assistance and resolving their warrant. If the couple have still not cleared the warrant at four weeks you will need to send the client a letter advising they need to attend an appointment to discuss on-going entitlement to benefit.
For more information see:
- Effect on benefit if already sanctioned
- Taking all reasonable steps to resolve a warrant
- Restarting the benefit

chunks.title: Effect of last child leaving care — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Effect of last child leaving care
Sole parents and single clients receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit who have a warrant to arrest issued and have not resolved this warrant have 50% if their main benefit suspended.
## Supported Living Payment and Jobseeker Support
For clients receiving Supported Living Payment or Jobseeker Support, when the last child leaves their care (including a child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid) all their benefit will be suspended, including any Extra help.
Winter Energy Payment will no longer be paid as they are not receiving a qualifying benefit.
## Sole Parent Support
For Sole Parent Support clients the benefit will suspend due to not caring for a child under 14 years, not because of the warrant to arrest. If the Sole Parent Support client is transferring to another benefit you can transfer them to the new benefit type but the warrant to arrest will need to be resolved before the new benefit payments can start.
Note the benefit will need to be suspended manually in the system.
Winter Energy Payment will no longer be paid while the sole parent is not receiving a qualifying benefit.

chunks.title: Effect on benefit — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Effect on benefit
Clients and partners have 10 working days to contact Work and Income and provide evidence of resolving the warrant to arrest.
## Contact made within 10 day notice period
There will be no effect on the client's benefit and Extra help if they contact Work and Income within the 10 working day notice period and provide evidence that they:
- have resolved the warrant
- they have taken reasonable steps to resolve the warrant but have been unable to do so because of reasons outside of their control
- are not the person to whom the warrant applies
Payment of benefit is not affected if someone is challenging the warrant because they are:
- not the person to whom the warrant applies or
- they disagree with the Ministry of Justice information that they have a warrant for their arrest
Note if a challenge is unsuccessful, a debt is not established. The client is given another 10 day notice period to clear their warrant before their benefit is suspended or reduced.
## Contact made outside of the 10 day notice period
The effect on a client's or partner's benefit will be determined by their family circumstances if they contact Work and Income outside of the 10 working day notice period.
## Winter Energy Payment
If a client has their benefit suspended due to a warrant to arrest, they are generally not eligible to receive Winter Energy Payment as they are not receiving a qualifying benefit. However, for clients with dependent children, 50% of their main benefit is protected therefore, the Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid.
For more information see:
- Extra help Winter Energy Payment
- Single clients
- Single clients receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit
- Sole parents
- Clients with a partner and no dependent children
- Couple with one or more dependent children
- Effect on benefit if already sanctioned
- Taking all reasonable steps to resolve a warrant
- Restarting the benefit

chunks.title: Introduction — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Introduction
A warrant to arrest is a document issued by the courts that authorises the arrest and detention of a person. They are initiated and resolved by the Ministry of Justice and actioned by the police when possible.
A warrant to arrest is issued in a range of circumstances, usually for not attending a scheduled court appearance.
While the police do not actively pursue every individual who has a warrant to arrest, it does mean that a person with a warrant to arrest could be arrested at any time.
This policy applies to warrants to arrest for defendants issued in criminal proceedings. It does not apply to warrants to arrest for a witness.
A data matching agreement allows the Ministry of Justice to supply MSD with information about people with unresolved warrants.

chunks.title: No access to court services — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## No access to court services
Where a client or partner is unable to clear their warrant because of issues with access to court services, the benefit can continue to be paid until they can reasonably be expected to clear their warrant. This must be because of reasons beyond their control. Having no access to court services might include (but is not limited to) the following reasons:
- no access to a District Court due to adverse event or natural disasters
- inability to get a court staff member to clear the warrant due to resourcing issues at the Court
- the hearing centre is not set to be in the area until a later date
- the client must go before a judge and there is no opportunity until a later date
A client or partner may not always be able to provide written evidence. You need to be satisfied with the reason why the client has not been able to clear the warrant and the date they would reasonably be able to do so in order for the benefit to continue.
In these situations, the benefit may continue to be paid until:
- the new court sitting date (this will be verified by a Notice of Hearing from the Court) or
- the date the hearing centre is next in the area (check the court hearing schedules)
Clients should first be directed to clear their warrant at their local District Court or hearing centre. If a client has exhausted all their options and still has difficulty accessing court services, they can go to a police station.
For more information see:
- Other circumstances beyond a client's control
- Client has not taken all reasonable steps
- Client requires financial assistance to resolve a warrant

chunks.title: Notice period — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Notice period
Work and Income can only take action if it has been 28 days (including Saturdays and Sundays) from when the warrant to arrest was issued. At this point, Integrity Intervention Centre (IIC) will need to send the client a letter advising them:
- they have a warrant for their arrest
- they have a period of 10 working days to dispute that they are the person to whom the warrant applies or to take steps to resolve the warrant
- the specific actions that they need to take if they dispute they are the person to whom the warrant applies
- the specific actions they need to take to resolve the warrant
- the specific consequences for their benefit payment if they do not resolve the warrant within 10 working days
Note once the letter has been sent by IIC, the client is given four calendar days before the 10 working-day notice period allowing the client to receive the notice. This process is automated.
For more information see:
- Challenging a warrant to arrest
- Effect on benefit
- Taking all reasonable steps to resolve a warrant

chunks.title: Other circumstances beyond a client's control — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Other circumstances beyond a client's control
There may be other reasons a client or partner is unable to clear their warrant that are beyond their control.
In these circumstances, where a client or partner has taken all reasonable steps but has still been unable to resolve their warrant, we would resume their benefit from the date that it suspended and give them another 10 working days to resolve their warrant.
Circumstances may include (but are not limited to):
- client or partner is in hospital
- client or partner has limited funds for transport and has no other way to get to the court but has made a priority for the next pay day
- the court is outside of the client's town and the public transport or alternative form of transport is not available until a later date
- client or partner is challenging that the Warrant to Arrest applies to them (Integrity Intervention Centre will resume in this case)
- a client or partner receives the letter during the 10 working day notice period and then advises that they have been in hospital for 10 days andthere was no time for them to address this before they entered hospital andthey advised us as soon as they left hospital
- there was no time for them to address this before they entered hospital and
- they advised us as soon as they left hospital
- a client or partner receives the letter during the 10 working day notice period and hasn't been able to address this because a close family member dies
- client or partner was overseas during the notice period and did not receive the letter until they returned
Generally, we would not give the client more than 10 working days to clear their warrant to arrest from when they notify us of the reason why they have not already been able to do so.
However, in some circumstances, a client may need longer than 10 working days to clear their warrant. In these cases, the benefit may be able to be extended for a further 10 working days.
For more information see:
- Client requires financial assistance to resolve a warrant

chunks.title: Overview of steps to resolve a warrant — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Overview of steps to resolve a warrant
Step 1Go to a court, or as a last resort, a police stationTo resolve a warrant to arrest, the person must either: go to a criminal counter at the court any day it is open and make a voluntary appearance or present to a police stationStep 2Court staffSome arrest warrants can be cancelled straight away - for others the decision must be made by a judge. Once the arrest warrant is cancelled, the client will be given a new court dateStep 3Provide evidence that arrest warrant is resolvedMost clients will not need to provide evidence that their warrant has been resolved - the information will be picked up in the data match with the Ministry of JusticeIf the clients benefit is already suspended, the client will need to provide evidence that: their warrant to arrest has been resolved or their warrant to arrest is still in place but they are taking reasonable steps to resolve it but haven't done so yet due to reasons beyond their control
Step 1
Go to a court, or as a last resort, a police station
To resolve a warrant to arrest, the person must either:
- go to a criminal counter at the court any day it is open and make a voluntary appearance or
- present to a police station
Step 2
Court staff
Some arrest warrants can be cancelled straight away - for others the decision must be made by a judge. Once the arrest warrant is cancelled, the client will be given a new court date
Step 3
Provide evidence that arrest warrant is resolved
Most clients will not need to provide evidence that their warrant has been resolved - the information will be picked up in the data match with the Ministry of Justice
If the clients benefit is already suspended, the client will need to provide evidence that:
- their warrant to arrest has been resolved or
- their warrant to arrest is still in place but they are taking reasonable steps to resolve it but haven't done so yet due to reasons beyond their control
For more information see:
- Clients requires financial assistance to resolve their warrant
- Taking all reasonable steps to resolve a warrant

chunks.title: Restarting the benefit — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Restarting the benefit
When a client's or partner's benefit has been suspended or reduced by 50%, the benefit can only be re-started if you are satisfied that:
- the client is not the person to whom the warrant applies
- the client has taken reasonable steps to resolve the warrant but have been unable to do so because of reasons outside of their control
- the warrant has been resolved
Note the warrant to arrest will show in SWIFTT in the SSTAI screen as "Warrant To Arrest".
## Date to re-start the benefit
Generally the benefit can't be backdated to the date it was suspended or reduced, unless the client or partner has taken reasonable steps to resolve the warrant.
For more information see:
- Client has not taken all reasonable steps
- Taking all reasonable steps to resolve a warrant

chunks.title: Risk to public safety — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Risk to public safety
Generally, to allow the client time to resolve their warrant to arrest, Work and Income cannot begin the process to stop a client's benefit until 28 days after the warrant was issued (and then after the client has been given a further 10 day notice period).
However in some circumstances, the benefit and any Extra help, including non-beneficiary assistance, can be suspended immediately when:
- the police provide a written request to suspend the client's benefit and
- the Commissioner of Police has reasonable grounds to consider the client to be a risk to public safety and
- the request is signed by the Commissioner of Police or a constable who is of, or above, the level of inspector
People who have a warrant to arrest and who have been assessed as a risk to public safety are being actively pursued by the police. The police will take all reasonable steps to locate the person; however, if they are unable to locate them, they will use the warrant to arrest policy to aid this process.
Note the 50% protection for clients with dependent children does not apply to non-beneficiary assistance in public risk situations. When a non-beneficiary client with dependent children is identified as being a public risk, all of their assistance is suspended immediately.
This process is managed by Centralised Services.
For more information see:
- Advising client once benefit has been suspended

chunks.title: Single clients — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Single clients
A single client's benefit and any Extra help (including Winter Energy Payment) will be suspended the day after the 10 day notice period ends if the client has not:
- resolved the warrant
- provided evidence they have taken reasonable steps to resolve the warrant but have been unable to do so because of reasons beyond their control
- provided evidence to dispute they are the person to whom this warrant applies
For more information see:
- Effect on benefit if already sanctioned
- Taking all reasonable steps to resolve a warrant
- Restarting the benefit

chunks.title: Single clients receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Single clients receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit
A 50% protection is applied to the benefit rate of single clients receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit. The child being cared for is considered a dependent child for warrant to arrest provisions.
For these clients, 50% of their main benefit only is suspended when they have been issued a notice advising they have a warrant to arrest outstanding and within 10 working days of the notice the client has not:
- resolved the warrant
- provided evidence they have taken reasonable steps to resolve the warrant but have been unable to do so because of reasons outside of their control
- provide evidence to dispute they are the person to whom this warrant applies
Note any Extra help (including Winter Energy Payment) and Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit are not affected by the warrant to arrest and will continue to be paid.
If the client has not resolved their warrant after 2 weeks, you will need to contact them to discuss financial assistance and resolving their warrant. If the client has still not cleared the warrant at four weeks you will need to send the client a letter advising they need to attend an appointment to discuss on-going entitlement to benefit.
For more information see:
- Effect on benefit if already sanctioned
- Taking all reasonable steps to resolve a warrant
- Restarting the benefit

chunks.title: Sole parents — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Sole parents
A 50% protection is applied to the benefit rate of sole parents.
For these clients, 50% of their main benefit only is suspended when they have been issued a notice advising they have a warrant to arrest outstanding and within 10 working days of the notice the client has not:
- resolved the warrant
- provided evidence they have taken reasonable steps to resolve the warrant but have been unable to do so because of reasons outside of their control
- provide evidence to dispute they are the person to whom this warrant applies
To pay the sole parent's reduced benefit, the SWTAR screen in SWIFTT will be used.
Note any Extra help and Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit aren't affected by the warrant to arrest and will continue to be paid.
If the client has not resolved their warrant after two weeks, you will need to contact them to discuss financial assistance and resolving their warrant. If the client has still not cleared the warrant at four weeks you will need to send the client a letter advising they need to attend an appointment to discuss on-going entitlement to benefit.
For more information see:
- Effect of last child leaving care
- Effect on benefit if already sanctioned
- Taking all reasonable steps to resolve a warrant
- Restarting the benefit

chunks.title: Specific benefits for warrant to arrest — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Specific benefits for warrant to arrest
The warrant to arrest policy can be applied to clients and partners receiving the following main benefits:
- Emergency Benefit
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance
- Jobseeker Support
- Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
- New Zealand Superannuation
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Veterans Pension
- Young Parent Payment
- Youth Payment
Note the warrant to arrest policy only applies to clients and partners aged 17 years or over.
For more information see:
- Warrant to arrest criteria
- Warrant to arrest does not apply

chunks.title: Taking all reasonable steps to resolve a warrant — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Taking all reasonable steps to resolve a warrant
A client's and partner's benefit and any Extra help will be suspended the day after the 10 day notice period ends if the client has not resolved the warrant.
However, you shouldn't suspend the benefit if the client or partner provides evidence that they are taking all reasonable steps to resolve their warrant but due to circumstances beyond their control, they have not been able to resolve it.
Circumstances beyond a client's control may include (but is not limited to):
- access to a District Court due to adverse event or natural disasters
- inability to get a Court Staff member to clear the warrant due to resourcing issues at the Court
- client is challenging that the Warrant to Arrest applies to them
- client is in hospital
- the court is outside of the client's town and the public transport or alternative form of transport is not available until a later date
- the client has limited funds for transport and has no other way to get to the court but has made a priority for the next pay day
## Benefit already suspended - 10 day period lapsed
If the benefit is already suspended because the 10 day notice period has lapsed, the client's benefit can be resumed from the date it was suspended if the client:
- has taken all reasonable steps to resolve the warrant
- has been unable to resolve the warrant because of reasons beyond their control and
- they can provide evidence of the reasons beyond their control
## Time period for clients to complete reasonable steps
The reason the client has not been able to resolve the warrant will determine the extension that is given to the client to clear their warrant. You should not give the client any more time than is necessary in the circumstances.
For more information see:
- Client was absent from New Zealand
- No access to court services
- Other circumstances beyond a client's control
- Client has not taken all reasonable steps
- Client requires financial assistance to resolve a warrant

chunks.title: Warrant to arrest criteria — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Warrant to arrest criteria
A client's or partner's benefit is no longer payable if you are satisfied (based on information from Ministry of Justice data match) that:
- the client or partner is receiving a specific benefit and
- the client or partner is aged 17 years or over and
- criminal proceedings have been started against the client or partner and a warrant for the client's or partner's arrest has been issued by a New Zealand court because of, or in connection to these criminal proceedings and
- the warrant does not apply to a witness and
- at least 28 days have passed since the date the warrant to arrest was issued and
- the client or partner has been given 10 working day notice period and within this period they have not: resolved the warrant to arrestprovided evidence they have taken reasonable steps to resolve the warrant but have been unable to do so because of reasons outside of their controldisputed they are the person to whom this warrant applies
- resolved the warrant to arrest
- provided evidence they have taken reasonable steps to resolve the warrant but have been unable to do so because of reasons outside of their control
- disputed they are the person to whom this warrant applies
Note in special circumstances, the benefit (including the total amount of non-beneficiary assistance) can be suspended immediately from when the police notify Work and Income that the client is a public risk. This is only on request from the police and where they believe on reasonable grounds there is a risk to public safety.
For more information see:
- Age of the warrant
- Challenging a warrant to arrest
- Specific benefits for warrant to arrest
- Risk to public safety
- Warrant to arrest does not apply
- Notice period
- Effect on benefit
- Overview of steps to resolve a warrant

chunks.title: Warrant to arrest does not apply — core policy > warrant to arrest
chunks.text:
## Warrant to arrest does not apply
The warrant to arrest policy does not apply to:
- a person aged 16 years of age or under
- a caregiver receiving only Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit and no other main benefit
- a person not on a main benefit who is receiving non-beneficiary assistance (except for when they have met the criteria for being assessed by the Police Commissioner as a risk to public safety)
- people living overseas receiving New Zealand benefits under reciprocal agreements and other specified portable payments
- people who apply from overseas for a New Zealand benefit under a reciprocal agreement
- a person who is receiving the hospital rate of benefit
- a person who is receiving Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy
Note people who are overseas and are not receiving New Zealand benefits under reciprocal agreements or other portable payments are subject to this policy.
For more information see:
- Warrant to arrest criteria
- Specific benefits for warrant to arrest

chunks.title: Accommodation costs — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Accommodation costs
An Accommodation Supplement is paid to a client to help with the payment of their accommodation costs.
There are 3 types of accommodation cost:
- Rent
- Board or
- Home ownership costs
Note clients can only claim one type of accommodation cost at a time.
Accommodation costs do not always need to be verified:
- rent and board costs should be verified where costs claimed are unusually high or where there are doubts about the authenticity of a claim
- all costs claimed by homeowners need to be verified
Additional information is required for clients who:
- live in a Relocatable cabins, caravans, and motor homes
- were once Idea Services residents
- live in a Retirement village
- are Retirement village residents with 'Licence to Occupy'
- are in a Rent to buy situation
- become Prisoners
- have outgoings paid by former partner see: beneficiaries or non-beneficiaries
- are social housing tenants

chunks.title: Accommodation costs for two premises due to moving — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Accommodation costs for two premises due to moving
When moving, a client will sometimes need to take up the costs of the new accommodation before they can stop paying for their current accommodation. This will generally be when the tenant enters into a new rental agreement or a boarding arrangement.
During the period the tenant needs to pay accommodation costs for 2 tenancies they will generally not be eligible for the costs of the place they do not occupy as a home.
Clients will need to notify MSD when the accommodation they are occupying as a home changes.
Note an applicable person who is living in a property owned or managed by a social housing provider cannot get Accommodation Supplement.
## Example
Astrid has signed the tenancy agreement for a slightly more expensive apartment closer to work and takes possession in a week. She immediately gives the required 28-day notice to her current landlord and as a result, will have to pay rent on 2 tenancies for 3 weeks. Astrid moves into the new apartment a week after she takes possession and is still required to pay rent on her old place until the notice period ends.
Over this period, Astrid can keep getting Accommodation Supplement for the accommodation costs of her old place for the 2 weeks she continues living there. Once she moves to the new accommodation, she can start getting Accommodation Supplement for her new higher costs, but not for her old place as she no longer lives there.
Astrid cannot get Accommodation Supplement for both accommodation costs at the same time.
## Payments for the former home when staying in emergency housing or transitional housing due to violence
In certain circumstances a client may continue getting Accommodation Supplement for their former home (except when a partner remains at the home) if they are staying in emergency housing or transitional housing due to violence.

chunks.title: Armed forces — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Armed forces
Armed forces personnel may receive:
- housing allowances
- mortgage interest subsidies
Note if a client in the Armed Forces boards in barracks, add the separate standard meal charge to their board costs when assessing Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Assets - beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Assets - beneficiaries
Clients must meet a cash asset test before they can receive an Accommodation Supplement. To perform this test we need to know the cash value of their assets.
A client may be able to receive Accommodation Supplement if they (and any partner) have cash assets that don't exceed:
- $8,100 for a single person
- $16,200 for a sole parent, or a married, civil union or de facto couple
If cash assets are greater than the above amounts, the client cannot get Accommodation Supplement. There are two exceptions. For more information see:
- Lump sum paid for impairment
- Lump sum payment of an Independence Allowance

chunks.title: Assets - non-beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Assets - non-beneficiaries
A non-beneficiary must meet a cash asset test before an Accommodation Supplement can be granted. To perform this test we need to know the cash value of their assets.
A non-beneficiary may be able to get the full rate of Accommodation Supplement if their assets are less than:
- $2,700 for a single person
- $5,400 for a sole parent, or a married, civil union or de facto couple
For every $100 that a non-beneficiary has over these limits, add $1.00 to their income amount for Accommodation Supplement purposes.
See example for detailed look at this process.
A non-beneficiary may be able to receive Accommodation Supplement if they (and any partner) have cash assets that don't exceed:
- $8,100 for a single person
- $16,200 for a sole parent or a married, civil union or de facto couple
If a non-beneficiary (and any partner) has cash assets greater than the limit shown above, they cannot get Accommodation Supplement. There are two exceptions, for more information see:
- Lump sum paid for impairment
- Lump sum payment of an Independence Allowance
## SWIFTT process
Add the value of the cash assets to the INCMA screen.
Enter the net equity of non-cash assets on the SADTA screen.
In the case of a non-beneficiary, SWIFTT will automatically assess $1.00 income for every $100 of assets when Accommodation Supplement is granted or reassessed.

chunks.title: Beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Beneficiaries
A client getting an income-tested benefit may get Accommodation Supplement.
Accommodation Supplement can be paid for a client who has ongoing accommodation costs and who meets the other qualifications.
Note there is no income test for clients getting a main benefit, however, New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran Pension clients must meet the appropriate income limit.

chunks.title: Board — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Board is an arrangement where a person pays a set amount that includes the cost of residing at the premises along with food and may include other costs such as power, water, and internet. When a person pays board, 62% of their total payment is considered to be their accommodation cost. A person is considered to be a boarder when they are: - making payments for their accommodation and food for residing at the premises and - the accommodation cost can't be separately identified as part of the amount they pay or - living in a commercial boarding house and the amount they pay for residing at the premises includes accommodation and food costs.

chunks.title: Accommodation costs include food — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: A person is considered to be a boarder when the amount paid for their accommodation also includes food, and potentially other costs, and the accommodation cost cannot be separately identified as part of the amount they pay.

chunks.title: Joint tenants with shared food costs — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Sometimes joint tenants, for example flatmates, will contribute money to cover shared costs. This could include cleaning suppliers, groceries, and service costs (e.g. power and internet). When these costs are shared among all tenants, this is not board. Note a client does not have to have their name on a tenancy agreement to be considered renting. For more information see: - Rent - Rent includes service costs - Examples of when a person is paying rent or board

chunks.title: Accommodation costs include service costs and water rates — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Accommodation costs can sometimes include service costs and water rates. For boarders, these costs are not separated out from the amount they pay for their accommodation and 62% of their total payment will be their accommodation costs.

chunks.title: Additional occupant living in a social housing property — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Additional occupants may pay a contribution towards accommodation costs while living in the social housing property. The contribution amount may include food and sometimes other costs. Whether it includes food (and/or other costs) or not, the contribution is always considered board for the purpose of calculating Accommodation Supplement. This means that only 62% of the additional occupant's contribution can be considered as their allowable accommodation cost even if it does not include food (and/or other costs). Note an applicable person who is living in a property owned or managed by a social housing provider cannot receive Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Living in a commercial boarding house — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: If a person lives in a boarding house, and the amount they pay for their accommodation includes food, MSD will consider them a boarder. However, if the amount they pay does not include food, MSD will consider them a renter. For more information see: - Contributions from additional occupants - Extra Help application form for new clients (which include Accommodation Supplement assistance) - Accommodation Supplement application form for current clients

chunks.title: Boarders - beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Boarders - beneficiaries
When assessing the rate of Accommodation Supplement, 62% of money received from boarders (when it is not received through a business venture) is deducted from a client's accommodation costs to determine their weekly qualifying accommodation costs.
When money received from boarders is more than the client's accommodation costs (after the deduction of the cost of any part of the property not being lived in by the client), the excess amount is income and must be charged against the main benefit. In this case, the client will have no weekly qualifying accommodation costs and will not qualify for Accommodation Supplement.
Note if a client doesn't live in part of their property, the cost of that part of the property is deducted from their accommodation costs before deducting money received from boarders when calculating the weekly qualifying accommodation costs.
For more information see:
- Weekly qualifying accommodation costs
- Tenant or homeowner has a boarder
- Rent and board payments
If it is clear that the arrangement is a business venture, such as a boarding house, bed and breakfast or home stay, then the amount received will need to be assessed as part of the business income.
For more information see:
- Income
- Homestays

chunks.title: Boarders - non-beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Boarders - non-beneficiaries
When assessing the rate of Accommodation Supplement, 62% of money received from boarders (when it is not received through a business venture) is deducted from a client's accommodation costs to determine their weekly qualifying accommodation costs.
When money received from boarders is more than the client's accommodation costs (after the deduction of the cost of any part of the property not being lived in by the client), the excess amount is income and must be charged against the non-beneficiary assistance. In this case, the client will have no weekly qualifying accommodation costs and will not qualify for Accommodation Supplement.
Note if a client doesn't live in part of their property, the cost of that part of the property is deducted from their accommodation costs before deducting money received from boarders when calculating the weekly qualifying accommodation costs.
For more information see:
- Weekly qualifying accommodation costs
- Tenant or homeowner has a boarder
- Rent and board payments
If the arrangement is a business venture, such as a boarding house, bed and breakfast or home stay, then the amount received from any boarder will need to be assessed as part of the business income.
For more information see:
- Income
- Homestays

chunks.title: Body corporate fees — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Body corporate fees
Body corporate is a term generally used when referring to cross-leased or shared properties where one or more properties are sited on the same land.
The body corporate comprises the owners of a unit-titled property under the Unit Title Act 1972.
This can include accommodation such as townhouse complexes, apartment blocks and flats. Each unit has a separate legal title and is individually owned.
These homeowners are usually required to pay a regular fee or levy to cover joint expenses for the whole property.
These body corporate fees are to be included in the assessment of Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Calculating rate - general formula — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Calculating rate - general formula
An Accommodation Supplement is assessed using a client's weekly qualifying accommodation costs. This is calculated by reducing the accommodation costs (rent, board or home ownership) by the cost of any part of the property not lived in by the client and any accommodation income they get.
An Accommodation Supplement is paid when a client's weekly qualifying accommodation costs are more than the entry threshold. The entry threshold varies depending on the family situation.
For every dollar over the entry threshold that a client pays in weekly qualifying accommodation costs they receive a 70% subsidy.
This subsidy has a limit which differs from region to region.
Boarders are eligible for the 70% subsidy on their weekly qualifying accommodation costs which is assessed on the portion of their board that is considered accommodation costs (62%) but not their total board costs.
The amount that a person is entitled to may be reduced depending on the level of their income or assets.

chunks.title: Relocatable cabins, caravans, and motor homes — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: If a client lives in a relocatable cabin, caravan, or motor home, they may have more than one type of accommodation cost. Accommodation Supplement can only be paid for one cost type at a time. In these cases, Accommodation Supplement is generally assessed on the cost of the cabin, caravan, or motor home as this is the place the client occupies as a home.

chunks.title: More than one accommodation cost type — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: If a client has more than one type of accommodation cost, assess them as a: - homeowner if they are repaying a loan for the purchase of the cabin, caravan, or motor home - renter if they are renting the cabin, caravan, or motor home For example, Enzo pays $180 a week to rent the cabin he lives in. He owns the land the cabin is situated on and pays $4412 a year for local authority rates. Enzo is considered renting, and his Accommodation Supplement is assessed on rent of $180 a week. Note when the cost of the cabin, caravan, or motor home is below the entry threshold, assess Accommodation Supplement on the costs for the land the cabin, caravan, or motor home is situated on.

chunks.title: Same accommodation cost type — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: The cost of a cabin, caravan, or motor home and the land it is situated on can be included as the same type of accommodation cost if the client: - owns the land and is repaying a loan for the purchase of the cabin, caravan, or motor home, or - rents the land (e.g. site fees at a park) and rents the cabin, caravan, or motor home For example, Liz pays $100 to hire a caravan and $80 rent for the land it is situated on. Because the caravan and land are being rented, Liz is considered renting and her total weekly rent costs are $180.

chunks.title: Landlord provides cabin, caravan, or motor home — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: If the client lives in a cabin, caravan, or motor home provided by their landlord, they are assessed as renting or boarding depending on the arrangement they have with the landlord.

chunks.title: No cost for cabin, caravan, or motor home — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Sometimes a client will not have a cost for the cabin, caravan, or motor home they are living in (e.g. because they own it outright), but they must pay for the land it is situated on. The accommodation cost type will depend on whether they own or rent the land.

chunks.title: Cash assets include — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: - bills of exchange or promissory notes - building society shares - money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society - money invested with or lent to any bank, or other financial institution - money withdrawn from a KiwiSaver scheme - mortgage investments and other long-term loans - pre-paid funeral expenses (in some circumstances) - proceeds from the sale of the family home - shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds and bonds and - the client's share in any partnership Note if you are unsure of a case please contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Cash assets do not include — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: - a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2000, or which is used by the person or a member of their family for day-to-day accommodation - a home property and land on which it is situated - a motor vehicle principally used by the client for private use - information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income - Christchurch mosques attack support payments - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts - Māori land where the title is in tribal trust and individual ownership cannot be identified, the client cannot realise or readily convert the land into a cash assetNote you should consult your Legal Services if you are unsure about the ownership of Māori land. - MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to a system processing error from 1993 to 2014 (and any interest earned on the payment), for the first 12 months from when the payment was received - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after payment is made - personal effects - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment) - specified Ex gratia and compensation payments - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received A bank overdraft is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client. Canterbury earthquake related payments Payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12, or 24 months following the date the client received the payment. For more information see, Types of income - KiwiSaver - Superannuation scheme accounts - Health and Disability payments - Payments from the Crown for the purchase of property in the Canterbury red zone - Payments from the Earthquake Commission and insurance companies (Canterbury earthquake 2010 and aftershock 2011) - Payments from the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) - Types of income

chunks.title: Other property — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: If a client owns other property (including boats and caravans) that is capable of being realised as a cash asset for their personal use, this may affect whether they qualify for financial assistance. To help you decide whether a property is a realisable asset see: - Property not used as home

chunks.title: Cash assets gifted — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Cash assets gifted
A client is not able to directly or indirectly deprive themselves of any income or assets so that they can qualify for Accommodation Supplement.
If a client has gifted small amounts of money to others, it may be disregarded as a cash asset. However, large sums of money gifted by a client should be treated as a cash asset for Accommodation Supplement purposes.
There may be circumstances where any amount gifted (large or small) can be considered as a cash asset.
## Guidelines
When a client applies for Accommodation Supplement or has a Mandatory Review, any money they have gifted in the last year may be treated as a cash asset if the client has gifted an amount over:
- $2,700 for a single client or
- $5,400 for a married, civil union or de facto couple or sole parent
The amount is treated as a cash asset for 52 weeks after the client applied Accommodation Supplement, or from when the client responded to their Mandatory Review.
The value of the cash asset should be reduced at each subsequent Mandatory Review.
For a review over a 26 week period:
- reduce the value of the cash asset by $500 for a single client
- reduce the value of the cash asset by $1,000 for a client who is a sole parent, or who is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship
For a review over a 52 week period:
- reduce the value of the cash asset by $1,000 for a single client
- reduce the value of the cash asset by $2,000 for a client who is a sole parent, or who is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship
## Example
A gift of $4,000 was gifted by a single client. At the first Mandatory Review this becomes $3,000.
At the next Mandatory Review, 52 weeks later, the value of the gift becomes $2,000.
As long as the client has no other cash assets then this should be disregarded because the cash asset is now below the exemption level.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
Clients can be absent from New Zealand and keep getting Accommodation Supplement for the first 28 days of any absence if it does not affect the client's qualification for Accommodation Supplement.
MSD will need to check if the client's accommodation costs are continuing.
Generally, a client can keep getting their Accommodation Supplement while the client is absent from New Zealand if the client is still getting a main benefit.
## Clients getting a main benefit
All clients getting a main benefit must tell MSD before they leave New Zealand. If the client or partner does not tell MSD before they travel overseas, their main benefit payments (including Accommodation Supplement) must stop.
To get Accommodation Supplement while they are absent from New Zealand the client must have ongoing accommodation costs.
## Clients getting non-beneficiary Extra Help
Clients who are getting Accommodation Supplement and are not getting a main benefit:
- are required to advise MSD when they are leaving New Zealand and
- can be absent from New Zealand and paid their Accommodation Supplement for up to 28 days per absence when it does not affect the client's eligibility for Accommodation Supplement
Note when assessing the period of absence, do not include:
- the date of departure from New Zealand and
- the date of return to New Zealand
## Mandatory Review while overseas
Clients getting Accommodation Supplement who have temporarily left New Zealand must still respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date.
Temporary absence from New Zealand (e.g. personal travel) does not pause or defer the Mandatory Review.
Clients must contact MSD before their review date to talk about their situation if they are unable to respond to the review or if they need more time to do it.

chunks.title: Accommodation Supplement suspended before Mandatory Review date — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Accommodation Supplement suspended before Mandatory Review date
Clients getting Accommodation Supplement are always notified about their Mandatory Review, even if their Accommodation Supplement is suspended, unless it is suspended due to the client being temporarily overseas or in prison.
MSD must not undertake the Mandatory Review unless the client contacts MSD to resume their Accommodation Supplement.
If the client contacts MSD before their review date to resume their Accommodation Supplement, they may be able to get an extension if they need more time to do their Mandatory Review. MSD can resume the benefit before the Mandatory Review has been responded to.
However, if the client contacts MSD on or after the Mandatory Review date, the review must be completed before MSD can resume the benefit.
Example
James' Mandatory Review is due on 2 September 2027. However, on 25 August MSD was notified by New Zealand Police that James has a warrant for his arrest and is a risk to public safety. MSD suspends James' Accommodation Supplement the same day.
For MSD to resume James' Accommodation Supplement, James must resolve or take steps to resolve the warrant to arrest and provide evidence of this.
On 6 September 2027 James tells MSD that he resolved his warrant to arrest and provides a notice of hearing as evidence.
