When you need to reduce deductions you adjust from the lowest priority up to those with a higher priority taking into account the protected earnings rules for each.
## Example
A client has both Child Support and Ministry of Social Development debt deductions to be made from their benefit. When the level of Ministry of Social Development debt would reduce the client's benefit payments below the Child Support protected earnings rate, the Ministry of Social Development debt deduction must be reduced not any Child Support payments.
This is because Child Support deductions take priority over Ministry of Social Development debt repayments.

chunks.title: Protected earnings rate — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Protected earnings rate
Both the District Court Act and the Summary Proceedings Act provide that every attachment order must specify a 'protected earnings rate'.
The protected earnings rate is usually 60% of the client's net earnings after PAYE tax has been deducted or withheld.
If the attachment order will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate, then the order will not operate and you must cancel or return the attachment order to the Ministry of Justice.
Calculating the client's income differs between attachment orders made under the Summary Proceedings Act and the District Court Act, as different benefits are taken into account.
Therefore it is important to determine what type of attachment order has been issued.
Summary Proceedings Act 1957
For orders made under this Act, the calculation of the client's income does not include Special Benefit, Temporary Additional Support, Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance, Winter Energy Payment, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit
District Court Act 2016
For orders made under the District Court Act, the client's income includes Special Benefit, Temporary Additional Support and Disability Allowance but does not include Child Disability Allowance, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit
## Example
An attachment order is received from the Ministry of Justice for $60.00 per week.
The attachment order shows that the client's protected earnings rate is $286.53 per week.
We need to calculate whether adding the deduction of $60.00 will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate.
Calculate protected earnings rate
Jobseeker Support - single person 25+ net rate (as at 1 April 2026)
$372.55
Plus Accommodation Supplement (Area 2)
$105.00
Total net earnings
$477.55
60% of total net earnings (= protected earnings)
$286.53
Calculate if Attachment Order will exceed protected earnings
Total net earnings
$477.55
Less Child Support deduction
$95.00
Less Ministry of Social Development debts
$40.00
Sub-total
$342.55
Less Attachment Order
$60.00
Total net income remaining for the client per week
$282.55
The attachment order amount of $60.00 takes the client's total net income to $282.55, which is below the protected earnings rate of $286.53 per week.
The attachment order will not operate therefore you must return it to the Ministry of Justice for the order to be amended.

chunks.title: Mandatory Review for Accommodation Supplement — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: MSD must review a client's Accommodation Supplement within 52-weeks of when it commenced, or within 52 weeks of the date the client's last Mandatory Review was completed. Clients must respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date, or their payments will suspend. The purpose of a Mandatory Review for Accommodation Supplement is to: - check for any changes to a client's circumstances - determine if the client stills meets the qualifications for Accommodation Supplement - check for any changes in a client's accommodation costs and - review the rate of Accommodation Supplement payable Generally, all clients getting Accommodation Supplement will have a Mandatory Review for this assistance (except clients getting Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment). Note New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients and non-beneficiaries getting Accommodation Supplement must meet the income test.

chunks.title: Mandatory Review of only Accommodation Supplement and Disability Allowance — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When a client is getting Accommodation Supplement and Disability Allowance, the Mandatory Review date is determined by which assistance commenced first. This will only apply to clients who are getting: - non-beneficiary assistance - Veteran's Pension - New Zealand Superannuation (unless they have a grandparented non-qualified partner included in their benefit) Example Emi has been getting Accommodation Supplement since 11 March 2026. Emi applied for Disability Allowance, which commenced on 2 April 2026. Because the initial Mandatory Review date is determined by which assistance commenced first, the review for both Accommodation Supplement and Disability Allowance is set for 52 weeks from 11 March 2026.

chunks.title: Clients getting a benefit subject to a Mandatory Review — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Clients who are getting some benefits that are subject to a Mandatory Review will have their Accommodation Supplement reviewed at the same time as that benefit. These benefits are: - Supported Living Payment - Emergency Benefit (when the expiry date for the benefit is more than 52 weeks or there is no expiry date) - Emergency Maintenance Allowance (when the expiry date for the benefit is more than 52 weeks or there is no expiry date) - New Zealand Superannuation with a grandparented non-qualified partner included Example Justin was granted Accommodation Supplement on 11 March 2026. He was diagnosed with a serious illness that will last and restrict his capacity for work for longer than 2 years and was granted Supported Living Payment on 5 May 2026. Because the review date is based on the commencement date of Justin's main benefit, the Mandatory Review for Justin's Accommodation Supplement and Supported Living Payment is reset to 52 weeks from 5 May 2026.

chunks.title: Clients getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When a client is getting Accommodation Supplement and Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit, they will have a Mandatory Review for their Accommodation Supplement at least once in a 52-week period, but it will be separate to the Mandatory Review for Orphan's Benefit and Unsupported Child's Benefit.

chunks.title: Clients getting Sole Parent Support or Jobseeker Support — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Clients who are getting a main benefit with a 26-week or 52-week reapplication will have their Accommodation Supplement reviewed as part of their reapplication.

chunks.title: Clients getting a benefit that does not have a Mandatory Review, 26-week, or 52-week reapplication — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When a client is getting Accommodation Supplement and a benefit that does not have a Mandatory review, 26-week or 52-week reapplication, they will still have a Mandatory Review for their Accommodation Supplement at least once in a 52-week period. Clients getting Youth Parent Payment or Youth Payment do not have a Mandatory Review of their Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Notice period for a Mandatory Review — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Clients are notified at least 20 working days before their Mandatory Review date, unless their Accommodation Supplement is suspended due to the client being temporarily overseas or in prison. The notice period allows sufficient time for clients to respond to the Mandatory Review. Note if a client's Accommodation Supplement is suspended when the Mandatory Review notice is sent, they are not required to respond to their Mandatory Review until their Accommodation Supplement is to be resumed.

chunks.title: Responding to the Mandatory Review — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: To respond to the Mandatory Review, the client must: - confirm or provide current information about their circumstances and - provide further information to MSD if requested Clients must confirm the information MSD holds is correct or provide any new information before their review date. When a client has responded to the Mandatory Review and MSD has determined they continue to qualify for Accommodation Supplement, their next review date is 52 weeks from the date their Mandatory Review was completed.

chunks.title: Client does not respond to the Mandatory Review — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When a client does not respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date, the Accommodation Supplement will suspend. If the client does not respond to the Mandatory Review to confirm their circumstances within 8 weeks after their payments have suspended, the Accommodation Supplement will be cancelled. A client can still do their Mandatory Review during those 8 weeks. However, once the Accommodation Supplement has cancelled, the client will need to reapply for Accommodation Supplement if they still need this assistance. A client's Accommodation Supplement cannot be resumed before they have responded to their Mandatory Review during the 8-week suspension period.

chunks.title: Accommodation Supplement suspends — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: If a client's Accommodation Supplement suspends as a result of the client not responding to their Mandatory Review, all of their assistance will also suspend, except for the following payments: - Child Disability Allowance - Orphan's Benefit - Unsupported Child's Benefit - Childcare Subsidy - OSCAR (Out of School Care and Recreational Subsidy) - New Zealand Superannuation (unless they have a grandparented non-qualified partner included) - Veteran's Pension - Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment

chunks.title: When the Mandatory Review is completed — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: The Mandatory Review is complete when MSD makes a decision about the client's eligibility for Accommodation Supplement and the rate of benefit payable. MSD will either: - continue paying the benefit at the existing rate - adjust the rate of benefit so the client is getting the correct rate - suspend the benefit if there is no rate payable for a period (e.g. client has variable income) - cancel the benefit if the client no longer qualifies

chunks.title: Mandatory Reviews for clients with partners — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When a client has a partner, both the client and the partner's circumstances are included in the review. Changes to the partner's circumstances (e.g. income, employment, living arrangements and other factors) must be included in the Mandatory Review.

chunks.title: Specific engagements — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Specific engagements
Specific engagements are interactions that can meet the same purpose as the Mandatory Review. These interactions can capture information that confirms if a client still qualifies for Accommodation Supplement.
Specific engagements are when a client has an interaction with MSD, and this results in a full review of the client's circumstances.
For example, specific engagements may include when a client contacts MSD to:
- discuss a change in circumstances or
- apply for assistance.
If the specific engagement meets the same purpose as a Mandatory Review, and the client still qualifies, their Mandatory Review date is set 52-weeks from when the specific engagement was completed.

chunks.title: Student Loans — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Student Loans
Clients with a Student Loan must make repayments to Inland Revenue when the income they receive exceeds a pre-determined level. This level is called the 'income threshold'.
A person must make repayments to Inland Revenue when their income exceeds $464.00 gross per week ($24,128 gross per year) as at 1 April 2026. Note non-taxable Extra help such as family tax credit and Accommodation Supplement do not count as income in this instance.
If the client's income is over this income threshold, the Ministry of Social Development can make the required deduction. However, this is only done if the client requests it.
If the client's portion of benefit is below the income threshold, there is no provision to make voluntary repayments through SWIFTT. The client can make voluntary payments direct to Inland Revenue at any time.
Note the following:
- Student Loan deductions can only be made from taxable benefits
- Student Loan deductions cannot be made if the client's benefit is below the income threshold
- when a client receives a married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit only the client's portion is taken into consideration when assessing Student Loan repayments
- when a client is receiving a reduced rate of payment due to other income, the Student Loan deduction is assessed on the net payment after income deduction
## For more information on Student Loans see:
- Students Student Loan

chunks.title: Terminal benefit — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Terminal benefit
When a non-beneficiary client dies, Accommodation Supplement generally stops from the day after the date of death. However, there is some discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days.
When payment is continued after the date of death, it is referred to as terminal benefit.
Circumstances to consider when continuing payment beyond a client's date of death include:
- when the deceased client's domestic situation results in a transition cost for a family member, causing hardship
Example: accommodation and other household costs when client has been sharing accommodation
or
- when there are exceptional and justified costs associated with the death of the client
Example: multiple deaths within one family
Payment should not continue for 28 days following the death of a client to meet funeral expenses. A Funeral Grant may be available for this purpose.
## Child turns 18
A child will not be excluded from the parent or caregiver's Accommodation Supplement when the child turns 18 during the continuation of payment period.

chunks.title: Terminal benefit rate — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Terminal benefit rate
The provision to continue the payment for up to 28 days following the date of death is referred to as terminal benefit.
Accommodation Supplement is continued at the rate which was payable to the client at the date of death.
## SWIFTT
If you are paying terminal benefit you will need to manually calculate entitlement and make an adhoc payment in the SAHPA screen. There is no automatic provision for the payment of terminal benefit for Accommodation Supplement in this case on SWIFTT.

chunks.title: Transfer — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Transfer
MSD must review a client’s Accommodation Supplement to ensure they still meet the qualifications and are getting the correct rate of payment when the client moves between the following categories:
- main benefit
- New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension or
- non-beneficiary

chunks.title: When an extension or exemption can be given — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When a client needs more time to respond to the Mandatory Review, they may be able to get an extension. If a client is unable to respond to the review, they may be able to get an exemption. Clients must contact MSD before their review date to discuss their situation if they need an extension or exemption. A client cannot get an extension or exemption on or after the Mandatory Review date. Note even if a client gets an extension or exemption, they must still advise MSD of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their eligibility for Accommodation Supplement or the rate payable.

chunks.title: Extension - client needs more time to respond to review — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Clients may be able to get an extension if there is a good and sufficient reason why they cannot respond to their Mandatory Review before the review date. When a client needs more time to respond to the review, they must let MSD know before their Mandatory Review date. The extension can only be granted before the review date. Good and sufficient reasons may include (but are not limited to): - the client is unexpectedly hospitalised - death or illness in the client's immediate family - the client experiencing or escaping a family violence situation If MSD determines the client has a good and sufficient reason, the client can get an extension of up to 20 working days. Note a client can get multiple short extensions, however the maximum amount of time that can be given for an extension is a total of 20 working days from the client's original review date.

chunks.title: Exemption - client is unable to respond to review — extra help > accommodation supplement > changes and reviews accommodation supplement
chunks.text: A client may be able to get an exemption when they are experiencing an unforeseen event or situation that is beyond their control, and this means they are unable to respond to their Mandatory Review (even if they had more time). The client must let MSD know before their review date to discuss their circumstances. Exemption reasons may include (but are not limited to): - localised natural disaster that affects the client but not the whole region (e.g. the client's property is affected by a landslip) - unexpected serious illness or an accident affecting the client or their immediate family member - the client's benefit is ending because a child has left their care suddenly and the Mandatory Review is due during the 28-day continuation of payment If MSD determines an exemption applies, the client won't be required to respond to the Mandatory Review, and the review date is reset to 52 weeks from their current review date. Example Danny is getting Accommodation Supplement and has a Mandatory Review due on 15 October 2026. However, Danny's child becomes sick with a serious illness and is admitted to hospital for an extended period. Danny has to travel to the hospital often while also caring for his other children at home. Due to Danny's circumstances, MSD determines it is not reasonable for Danny to respond to his Mandatory Review by his review date. In this case, MSD grants an exemption. Danny's next Mandatory Review is set for 52 weeks from the original review date.

chunks.title: Counted as income — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: - ACC weekly compensation - actual income from cash assets - Flexi-Wage Self Employment weekly subsidy (excluding the GST component of 15%) and any income generated from the business - Information share Child Support payments - net profit before tax from self-employment - Non-information share Child Support payments made for an income-related purpose (excluding any that are specifically listed below) - wages or salary

chunks.title: Not counted as income — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: - ACC Independence Allowance - Assistance to transition into employment - rent and 62% of board payments a non-beneficiary gets that are less than or equal to their accommodation costs (after the deduction of the cost of any part of the property not being lived in by the client) - 38% of board payments a client gets (not received as part of a business venture) - Child Disability Allowance - children's income - formula-assessed Child Support for liability periods before 1 July 2023 paid in excess of the benefit rate - formula-assessed Child Support paid in excess of the Unsupported Child's Benefit rate (including mixed Child Support payments) - information share Child Support payments received between commencement and grant dates of Accommodation Supplement - information share Child Support payments received shortly after transferring between benefits on different pay cycles - Offset Child Support - Christchurch mosques attack support payments and income earned on the payment - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - Disability Allowance - Energy Trust Dividends and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after payment is made - gallantry awards - Kāinga Ora energy subsidy - MSD lump sum payments and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after payment is made - Orphans Benefit - overseas pensions similar to Social Security benefits if there has already been a direct deduction from the basic benefit - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after payment is made - Severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment) - specified Ex gratia and compensation payments and income earned on those payments - Student Loans - Participation Allowance - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 (and any interest earned on the payment), for the first 12 months from when the payment was received - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after payment is made - Temporary Accommodation Assistance weekly payments - Unsupported Child's Benefit - war disablement, war widows and other similar overseas war pensions - Working for Families Tax Credits from Inland Revenue

chunks.title: Not counted as income — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received A bank overdraft is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.

chunks.title: Child should be included — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Child should be included
We are required to pay a certain rate of payment to clients depending on the number of dependent children in their care. If a child is considered to be dependent, that child should be included in the caregiver's benefit.
In cases where the client has genuine concerns about including the child in their benefit (such as concerns about violence from the other parent) advise the client that all information contained in their benefit record is confidential.
If you have any concerns regarding the welfare of the child, the case should be referred to Oranga Tamariki.
A dependent child is a child who is financially dependent. Where the client states that they do not want a child included in their benefit because the other parent is providing financial support, you must:
- decide whether or not the client is providing financial support and
- for Non-beneficiaries advise the client that any income received from the other parent (in all situations) will be charged against their benefit
For more information see:
- Chargeable income - non-beneficiaries

chunks.title: Clients with non-qualified partners — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Clients with non-qualified partners
There are situations where a client's partner does not qualify for a benefit because they:
- do not meet the residence requirements, or
- are Overseas or
- are On a stand down or
- are On strike
The rate of Accommodation Supplement is calculated differently in these situations

chunks.title: Commencement date — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: The commencement date for Accommodation Supplement depends on whether a client is applying for Accommodation Supplement: - as a non-beneficiary or - at the same time as applying for a main benefit or - after a main benefit has been granted

chunks.title: Non-beneficiary application — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: If the client is applying for Accommodation Supplement as a non-beneficiary and does not have a current main benefit then the commencement date is the later of either: - the date of application or - the date accommodation costs begin Example - non beneficiary Sarah is single and rents in Wellington. She worked 32 hours weekly as a receptionist for a small family business for 7 years. She recently applied for and now receives non-beneficiary Accommodation Supplement. Sarah hours of work are reduced to 15 hours per week and she is concerned about paying her rent and living expenses. Sarah applies for Jobseeker Support and has a 1-week stand-down. Sarah's Accommodation Supplement continues at the same rate during the stand-down and is reviewed when Jobseeker Support commences as it is no longer income tested for beneficiaries.

chunks.title: Applying for a main benefit and Accommodation Supplement at the same time — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When a client applies for a main benefit and Accommodation Supplement at the same time, the commencement date for Accommodation Supplement depends on whether the client has a stand-down or non-entitlement period for their main benefit. If the Accommodation Supplement is applied for on the same day as a main benefit with a stand-down or non-entitlement period imposed, MSD must grant the Accommodation Supplement from the day after the stand-down or non-entitlement period ends. If no stand-down or non-entitlement period applies to the main benefit, Accommodation Supplement commences from the later of: - the date of application or - the date accommodation costs begin. The 28-day rule for main benefits does not apply to Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Example 1 – applies for Sole Parent Support and Accommodation Supplement, initial stand-down applies to main benefit — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: June has 2 children who are both under the age of 5. She separated from her husband on 13 September. Her husband is no longer in the family home and does not provide support. June had to stop working to take care of her children because she can't afford childcare on her part time wage. She currently remains in their Auckland family home but needs help. June applies for Sole Parent Support and Accommodation Supplement on 13 November. The 28-day rule does not apply because June's application for Sole Parent Support was not lodged within 28 days of her entitlement date (13 September). June has a 1 week stand-down and her Accommodation Supplement and Sole Parent Support commence the day after the stand-down ends.

chunks.title: Example 2 – applies for Supported Living Payment and Accommodation Supplement, stand-down and 28-day rule applies to main benefit — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Salesi is 20 years old and rents a flat in Dunedin. After completing his study, Salesi became unwell and was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder. Salesi is unable to work and has no income or savings now his studies have ended. Salesi is admitted to hospital on 14 November for a week for observation and treatment. He then returns to his flat, where he needs help to pay rent. Salesi visits his GP on 23 November and the GP helps him apply for a Supported Living Payment and Accommodation Supplement and provides a medical certificate confirming that Salesi's condition is permanent and severe. The application for both benefits is made on 24 November. Salesi has a 1 week stand-down applied. As Salesi applied within 28 days of his entitlement date to Supported Living Payment, the 28-day rule applies to his Supported Living Payment. The 28-day rule does not apply to Accommodation Supplement. Salesi's Accommodation Supplement commences on the day after his stand-down ends.

chunks.title: Receiving a main benefit – later application for Accommodation Supplement — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When a person has been getting a main benefit and then applies for an Accommodation Supplement, the commencement date is the later of either: - the date of application or - the date accommodation costs begin

chunks.title: Dependent child — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
A dependent child for Accommodation Supplement is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Accommodation Supplement does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- child for whom Orphan's or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
In some situations, a child may not be living at home but is still considered to be a dependent child.
Dependent children should be included in the assessment of Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Determining accommodation costs — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Determining accommodation costs
In most cases determining the accommodation costs will be straight forward but there are certain circumstances where you will have to consider what costs to include.

chunks.title: Emergency housing and transitional housing — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Generally, a client cannot get Accommodation Supplement for the cost of premises they do not occupy as a home.

chunks.title: Accommodation funded by an Emergency Housing Grant — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When a client's emergency accommodation is funded through an Emergency Housing Grant, it is not intended that the accommodation will be the client's home. The stay in temporary accommodation used as emergency housing is a last resort and is generally intended to be for a maximum grant period of 7 nights at a time. Some clients may need more than one 7-night grant and may also qualify for a longer period. Emergency accommodation is not the client's permanent home, regardless of the grant period or number of grants. During the grant period of the Emergency Housing Grant the client is required to make reasonable efforts to find an alternative place to stay. Clients staying in emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant do not qualify for Accommodation Supplement, even when they pay an emergency housing contribution towards their accommodation costs. The only exception is when the client is staying in emergency housing due to violence and has accommodation costs for their former home. For more information see:

chunks.title: Other emergency housing or transitional housing — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Emergency housing that is not funded by an Emergency Housing Grant (including contracted emergency housing and transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development), provides short-term, temporary accommodation while the client is unable to access sustainable housing. Clients in contracted emergency housing and transitional housing generally also get tailored social support while they are assisted into sustainable housing. Generally, a client staying in emergency housing that is not funded by an Emergency Housing Grant, or in transitional housing (including contracted emergency housing and transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development), does not qualify for Accommodation Supplement. The only exception to this is when the client is staying in emergency housing or transitional housing due to violence and has accommodation costs for their former home. When determining if the other emergency housing or transitional housing is occupied as the client's home, and they qualify for Accommodation Supplement, consider the specific circumstances and arrangements for the accommodation, including: - the amount of time the client has already been in the accommodation and how long they are likely to stay there - whether the client can stay in the accommodation until they have found permanent accommodation or if they must leave after a set amount of time - the level of autonomy the client has while in the accommodation, such as: are they allowed guestscan they come and go as they chooseare they expected to clean the area of the accommodation they occupy - are they allowed guests - can they come and go as they choose - are they expected to clean the area of the accommodation they occupy Note clients in transitional housing who are getting Social Rehabilitation Assistance for that transitional housing are not eligible for Accommodation Supplement. For more information see:

chunks.title: Long-term lease of a motel room — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: A client who arranges a long-term lease of a motel room may be considered to be occupying the premises as their home. However, this is not considered emergency housing and a client would not get an Emergency Housing Grant for emergency housing to pay for this. The client may qualify for Accommodation Supplement for these accommodation costs.

chunks.title: Accommodation Supplement for the former home when client staying in emergency housing or transitional housing due to violence — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: In certain circumstances a client may continue getting Accommodation Supplement for their former home (except when a partner remains at the home) if they are staying in emergency housing, contracted emergency housing, or transitional housing due to violence.

chunks.title: Entry threshold — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Entry threshold
There is an amount of money that a client is expected to contribute towards their housing costs before they will receive an Accommodation Supplement. This amount is called the entry threshold.
For the entry thresholds for clients see:
- Entry thresholds and maximum rates
Clients who are receiving a Special Transfer Allowance will have their accommodation costs worked out, by finding out the rent they have to pay and taking away the amount they get from the Special Transfer Allowance.

chunks.title: Essential repairs and maintenance — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Essential repairs and maintenance
Homeowners can claim the cost of essential repairs and maintenance to the house they occupy as accommodation costs. There are some general guidelines to consider when deciding if something is an accommodation cost:
- repairs or maintenance must be essential to maintain the house and property to a habitable standard
- any repairs and maintenance should be made to meet the homeowner and families current housing needs
- all costs claimed must be verified with receipts which, if necessary, are detailed enough to verify the work undertaken was essential or needed for maintenance
Note essential repairs and maintenance can be included as an accommodation cost when recoverable assistance has also been paid for the cost. This does not apply when non-recoverable assistance has been paid e.g. a Special Needs Grant for effluent treatment system maintenance or repair.
For more information see:
- Repairs
- Maintenance
- Essential repairs and maintenance [no link find out why]

Nadiya is living in Wellington (Area 2), is married with 2 children, and pays rent of $375.00 a week. First we need to know the entry threshold for a couple with 2 children, see: Entry thresholds and maximum rates The entry threshold for Supported Living Payment for a health condition, injury or disability is $227.00 as at 1 April 2026. chunks.text: A client may be able to get Accommodation Supplement if they are not a student but their partner is a student. The non-student partner can apply for Accommodation Supplement as a non-beneficiary. To work out how much Accommodation Supplement to pay the non-student partner MSD will need to: 1. Determine the couple's gross income. 2. Determine the amount of any Student Accommodation Benefit the student partner is receiving. 3. Calculate the rate to pay Accommodation Supplement as a non-beneficiary. 4. Deduct the amount of the Student Accommodation Benefit. For details on how to process on SWIFTT see: - Steps to follow in SWIFTT [no link find out why] When the student does not receive an Accommodation Benefit their partner's application should be processed as a non-beneficiary application.

chunks.title: Example - Property settlement - beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Example - Property settlement - beneficiaries
Where a client has separated from their partner and there has not yet been a Property agreement made, you need to work out what accommodation costs to use to calculate Accommodation Supplement.
A client lives in a house where the rent is $200.00 per week. They have just separated from their partner. Their partner is paying $150.00 to the client a week to help with rent while they sort out their accommodation situation.
50% of $200.00 is $100.00. The partner of the client is paying $150.00 dollars towards accommodation costs.
$150.00 - $100.00 = $50.00. The partner is paying $50.00, more than half the accommodation costs. This extra $50.00 is treated as income for the client.
Note in the case of a beneficiary the $50.00 is treated as income against the main benefit only.
The client is paying $200.00 - $150.00 = $50.00. The client's accommodation costs are $50.00.
Accommodation Supplement is now calculated using the appropriate single rate entry threshold. The Accommodation Supplement is based on $50.00 accommodation costs.

chunks.title: Example - Property settlement - non-beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Example - Property settlement - non-beneficiaries
Where a client has separated from their partner and there has not yet been a Property agreement made, we need to work out what accommodation costs to use to calculate Accommodation Supplement.
A client lives in a house where the rent is $200.00 per week. They have just separated from their partner. Their partner is paying $150.00 to the client a week to help with rent while they sort out their accommodation situation.
50% of $200.00 is $100.00. The partner of the client is paying $150.00 dollars towards accommodation costs.
$150.00 - $100.00 = $50.00. The partner is paying $50.00; this is more than half the accommodation costs. This extra $50.00 is treated as income for the client. Note that in the case of a non-beneficiary the $50.00 is treated as income against the Accommodation Supplement.
The client is paying $200.00 - $150.00 = $50.00. The client's accommodation costs are $50.00.
Accommodation Supplement is now calculated using the appropriate single rate entry threshold. The Accommodation Supplement is based on $50.00 accommodation costs and will be reduced due to the $50.00 income.

chunks.title: Example 1 — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: A New Zealand Superannuation client is single, living alone and pays rent of $150.00 per week (Area 1). The client is working part-time and earning $200.00 gross per week. The rate of New Zealand Superannuation is $647.37 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026). As the earnings from employment work are below the Accommodation Supplement income limit for a single adult ($740.81 gross per week, as at 1 April 2026), the client can get Accommodation Supplement. chunks.title: Example 2 — extra help > accommodation supplement

As the earnings from employment are above the Accommodation Supplement income limit for a couple ($1,076.04 gross per week, as at 1 April 2026), the client cannot get Accommodation Supplement. The client works part-time and earns $75.00 per week. As the earnings from employment are below the income limit for a couple ($1,076.04 gross per week, as at 1 April 2026), the client can get Accommodation Supplement. For more information see: - Accommodation Supplement Income limit The calculation for Accommodation Supplement is as follows: Accommodation costs (Rent) $220.00 Less cost of part of property not lived in $0 Less accommodation income $0 Equals weekly qualifying accommodation costs $220.00 Less entry threshold (as at 1 April 2026) $203.00 Equals $17.00 Client is eligible for up to 70% of $17.00 Multiply $17.00 x 0.70 $11.90 Accommodation Supplement payable (Round up to the nearest whole dollar) $12.00

chunks.title: Example 1 — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: A couple lives in Area 1 with no children and pays $400.00 per week in rent. The client gets New Zealand Superannuation and is applying for Accommodation Supplement, while their partner currently gets Jobseeker Support. Determine the entry threshold for a couple with no children, see: Entry thresholds and maximum rates The entry threshold for a married couple with no children on these different benefits, paying rent is $186.00 (as at 1 April 2026). The client is getting Veteran's Pension and their partner is working, earning $500.00 gross per week. As the earnings from employment are below the income limit for a couple ($1,076.04 gross per week, as at 1 April 2026), the client can get Accommodation Supplement. chunks.title: Examples of Accommodation Supplement for emergency and transitional housing — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Client situation Description of the housing Eligibility for Accommodation Supplement Client who has decided on a long-term lease in a motel or boarding facility. This is not emergency housing. Client should test their eligibility for Accommodation Supplement. Client is getting an Emergency Housing Grant. This is emergency housing. A client with this type of emergency housing arrangement will not qualify for Accommodation Supplement. When a client's emergency accommodation is funded through an Emergency Housing Grant, there is no expectation that this accommodation will be the client's home. The stay in temporary accommodation, used as emergency housing, is intended to be for 7 nights at a time (or up to 21 nights in some cases). During the grant period, the client is required to make reasonable efforts to find alternative accommodation. Client who is staying in transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development. This is transitional housing (but in some circumstances the client may be eligible for Accommodation Supplement). A client staying in this type of accommodation will generally not qualify for Accommodation Supplement. Transitional housing is usually provided as short-term accommodation for people with an immediate housing need while support is put in place to transition them into sustainable housing (e.g. for 12 weeks). There is no expectation that this temporary accommodation will be the client's home. However in some circumstances, the features of the accommodation (e.g. length of the stay, some level of access to the property for as long as they do not have other permanent housing and autonomy while they are staying in the premises) might support a view that the person is occupying the premises as their home. Client can test their eligibility for Accommodation Supplement. Note clients in transitional housing who are receiving Social Rehabilitation Assistance for that transitional housing are not eligible for Accommodation Supplement. See: Social Rehabilitation Assistance Client who is staying in emergency housing not funded by an Emergency Housing Grant. This is emergency housing (but in some circumstances the client may qualify for Accommodation Supplement). A client staying in this type of accommodation will generally not qualify for Accommodation Supplement. Emergency housing is short-term accommodation for people with an immediate housing need. There is no expectation that the emergency accommodation will be the client's home.

chunks.title: Examples of Accommodation Supplement for emergency and transitional housing — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: However in some limited circumstances, the features of the accommodation (e.g. length of the stay, some level of access to the property for as long as they do not have other permanent housing and autonomy while they are staying in the premises) might support a view that the person is occupying the premises as their home. Client can test their eligibility for Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Examples of when a client is paying rent or board — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Scenario Is this rent or board? Reason Janine and Robert own their own house, it is a 3-bedroom home. They decide to advertise for a boarder to help reduce some of their costs. They advertise $150 for the room, food, power, and internet. Imogen agrees to move in as a boarder. Board This is a boarding arrangement. The amount Imogen pays for her accommodation includes food and other costs. The different costs can't be separated out from what she pays in total. Isabelle is an international student who moved from Russia to Wellington for study. Isabelle lives with her host family in Wellington while she is studying. Isabelle pays a board fee of $250 a week, this covers internet, electricity and 3 meals every day. Board This is a boarding arrangement. The amount Isabelle pays for her accommodation includes food and other costs. The different costs can't be separated out from what she pays in total. The boarding arrangement also includes taking on additional responsibilities for the international student. Randall is living in a social housing property with his brother. His brother is the signatory of the property, and Randall is an additional occupant. Randall pays his brother a contribution of $300 a week towards accommodation costs. The contribution amount includes payment for accommodation, food, power, and internet. Board This is a boarding arrangement. The contribution amount includes food and other costs. The different costs can't be separated out from what Randall pays in total to stay in Social Housing. Randall is also an additional occupant in Social Housing. Regardless of what the contribution amount covers, only 62% of the contribution can be considered the accommodation cost. Dani is living in a social housing property with her parents. Her parents are the signatories of the property, and Dani is an additional occupant. Dani pays her parents a contribution of $270 a week towards accommodation costs. The contribution amount is for accommodation only. Board This is a boarding arrangement. Dani is an additional occupant in Social Housing. Regardless of what the contribution amount covers, only 62% of the contribution can be considered the accommodation cost. Dorian, George, and Vincent live in a flat together. They are each responsible for paying $200 a week.

chunks.title: Examples of when a client is paying rent or board — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Separate to their rent, they pay power and internet which is roughly $325 per month ($25 per week each) and food costs them about $80 per week each. They all decide to put the money for their bills and rent in a shared account. Each flatmate pays $305 ($200+$25+$80) into the shared account. Sometimes in winter the bills get more expensive so they each top up this account. Their rent is always paid out from the shared account each week to their landlord. Rent This is a flatting situation where the tenants are paying rent and not board. The only cost being paid to the landlord is their weekly rent. The tenants have organised their own power, food and internet. When these costs are shared among all tenants, this is not board.

chunks.title: Example 1 - Married client and their partner is getting a benefit as well — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: A married client is living in Area 1 with no children and pays $450.00 per week in rent. The partner is on Jobseeker Support on the ground of having a health condition, injury or disability and the client is receiving Supported Living Payment - caring for a person while caring for her mother. We need to know the entry threshold for a couple with no children, see: Entry thresholds and maximum rates The entry threshold for a married couple with no children on different benefits, paying rent is $169.00 (as at 1 April 2026). Using the following calculation the couple's rate of Accommodation Supplement can be assessed. Accommodation costs (Rent) $450.00 Less cost of part of property not lived in $0 Less accommodation income $0 Equals weekly qualifying accommodation costs $450.00 Less entry threshold (as at 1 April 2026) $169.00 Equals $281.00 The couple is eligible for up to 70% of $281.00 Multiply $281.00 x 0.70 $196.70 Round up to the nearest whole dollar $197.00 Now check the regional maximum Accommodation Supplement payable to this couple. For Auckland (Area 1) this is $235.00 per week (as at 1 April 2026). The couple will receive $197.00 per week. This is less than the maximum payment. Manually calculate the Accommodation Supplement payable to the couple, halve the amount and add to each SWIFTT record.

chunks.title: Example 2 - A civil union client with a partner working full-time — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: The civil union client lives in Area 2 with 2 children and pays $475.00 per week for their mortgage. The partner is working and earns $500.00 gross per week and the client is receiving Supported Living Payment - caring for a person while caring for his father. First we need to know the entry threshold for a couple with 2 children, see: - Entry thresholds and maximum rates Use the entry threshold for a couple with children on different benefits paying a mortgage. For a client receiving Supported Living Payment - caring for a person with a non-beneficiary partner, this is $260.00 per week (as at 1 April 2026). Using the following calculation to assess the couple's rate of Accommodation Supplement. Accommodation costs (Mortgage) $475.00 Less cost of part of property not lived in $0 Less accommodation income $0 Equals weekly qualifying accommodation costs $475.00 Less entry threshold (as at 1 April 2026) $260.00 Equals $215.00 The couple is eligible for up to 70% of $215.00 Multiply $215.00 x 0.70 $150.50 Round up to nearest whole dollar $151.00 Check the regional maximum Accommodation Supplement payable to this couple. For Porirua (Area 2) this is $220.00 per week (as at 1 April 2026). Manually calculate the Accommodation Supplement payable and pay $151.00 to the client.

chunks.title: Habilitation centres — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Habilitation centres
A client who is on parole and is living at a Habilitation Centre can receive Accommodation Supplement.
Although Habilitation Centres are fully funded by the Department of Corrections the client is required to pay to stay there.

chunks.title: Home ownership — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Home ownership
Homeowners can claim several things as accommodation costs for Accommodation Supplement. Generally, these are:
- mortgage repayments (interest and principal repayments on mortgages to purchase a house)
- payment towards a deposit if included in a rent to buy contract
- retirement village residents with 'Licence to occupy'
- body corporate fees
- local authority rates (if they get a rebate, this must be deducted)
- water rates
- house insurance premiums (must not include contents insurance)
- mortgage protection insurance or life insurance (only if this is compulsory for the mortgage)
- cost of essential repairs and maintenance to the home
Other costs that can be claimed are:
- leasehold rental for leasehold land and for Māori rent
- principal and interest repayments made under the Loans for Major Repairs Advances to Homes scheme
- costs of a farm residence (but only if these costs are not claimed as an expense in the farm business account)
- costs of a home that is also being used as a business (but only if these costs are not claimed as an expense for the business)
## Costs that cannot be included
Service costs, mortgage arrears, rates arrears, and insurance arrears cannot be included as accommodation costs.

chunks.title: Homeowner renting out a room — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Homeowner renting out a room
Where a client who owns their own home is renting out a room to another person (sublets), the rent payment they get is accommodation income and deducted from their accommodation costs (including mortgage interest and principal payments) to determine the clients weekly qualifying accommodation costs when assessing the rate of Accommodation Supplement.
When money received from renters is more than the client's accommodation costs (after the deduction of the cost of any part of the property not being lived in by the client), the excess amount is income. In this case, the client will have no weekly qualifying accommodation costs and will not be eligible for Accommodation Supplement.
Note if a client doesn't live in part of their property, the cost of that part of the property is deducted from their accommodation costs before deducting money received from renters when calculating the weekly qualifying accommodation costs.
For more information about how to calculate income from rent see:
- Rent and board payments
## Examples
Jennifer is a sole parent who owns her own home and is paying off her mortgage. Her total accommodation costs are $376 a week. She sublets a room in her house for $150 a week. Her weekly qualifying accommodation costs are $376 less $150 (rent received) so $226 a week. There is no income charge.
Accommodation costs (Mortgage)
$376pw
Less cost of part of property not lived in
$0
Less accommodation income
$150
Equals weekly qualifying accommodation costs
$226pw
Jane owns a mortgage-free 2-bedroom house. Her total accommodation costs are $70 a week. She rents out the spare room for $180 a week. Jane will not qualify for accommodation supplement as she receives more in rent than she pays for her accommodation costs. There will be a $110 income charge ($180 less $70).
Accommodation costs (Rates and Insurance)
$70pw
Less cost of part of property not lived in
$0
Less accommodation income
$180
Equals weekly qualifying accommodation costs
$0 (-$110)
Chargeable income
$110pw
For more information see:
- Home ownership
- Tenant or homeowner has a boarder
- Tenant renting out a room
- Homeowner renting out part of their property
- Weekly qualifying accommodation costs

chunks.title: Homeowner renting out part of their property — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Homeowner renting out part of their property
Where a client who owns their own home is renting out part of a property (for example another house on the same section, a self-contained flat that is a part of the home or part of the property to a person not living there) the client's Accommodation Supplement is assessed on the proportion of the property they live in.
## Calculating the cost of part of the property not lived in
Use the following calculation to determine the cost of part of the property not lived in:
- Determine the total costs for the property.
- Calculate the proportion of the floor area that the client lives in.
- Multiply the total costs by the proportion that the client does not live in.
This calculates the cost to deduct from the client's accommodation costs to determine the weekly qualifying accommodation costs.
Note if a client uses part of their property primarily for business purposes or has accommodation income, this also needs to be deducted from the accommodation costs to determine the weekly qualifying accommodation costs.
## Example

$5,000 per month (pm)
Rates
$140pm
Insurance (excluding contents)
$60pm
Repairs and maintenance
$100pm
Total costs for property

$5,300pm

Total B
300m2
Square metres of the property that the client does not live in
Total C
90m2
Proportion that the client does not live in
Total C ÷ Total B = Total D
0.3
Cost of part of property not lived in
Total A x Total D
$1,590pm
Weekly qualifying accommodation cost
Accommodation costs (Mortgage)
$5,300pm
Less cost of part of property not lived in
$1,590
Less accommodation income
$0
Equals weekly qualifying accommodation costs
$3,710pm = $856.15pw
The income, if any, is the rent received from the room less the total accommodation costs for the property.
For more information see:
- Weekly qualifying accommodation costs
- Home ownership
- Tenant renting out a room
- Homeowner renting out a room

chunks.title: Housing allowances — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Housing allowances
There may be clients who have their accommodation costs subsidised (such as Armed Forces personnel).
For the purpose of Accommodation Supplement consider their accommodation costs as:
- the weekly rent the landlord charges less the weekly housing allowance received
Clients with housing allowances are eligible for Accommodation Supplement if their costs are still high enough.

chunks.title: Idea Services residents and drug and alcohol abuse facilities — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Idea Services residents and drug and alcohol abuse facilities
Most Idea Services residents and those staying at a drug and alcohol abuse facility will get a Residential Support Subsidy. In this case they cannot get Accommodation Supplement.
If residents at an Idea Services, or drug and alcohol abuse facility are not getting Residential Support Subsidy, they may be able to get Accommodation Supplement.
When the amount a resident pays for their accommodation includes other costs (e.g. food or service costs) and these costs can be separated out from the amount they pay for accommodation, they are considered renting.
When the resident pays for their accommodation and food, and the food costs can't be separated out from the amount they pay, they are considered boarding.
Former residents of Idea Services facilities may get extra support from Idea Services.
Extra support could include:
- someone taking the client grocery shopping
The costs of this support cannot be included as an accommodation cost.
People in approved Social Rehabilitation Programmes can receive Accommodation Supplement but are then not eligible to receive Social Rehabilitation Assistance.

chunks.title: Income calculations - non-beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Income calculations - non-beneficiaries
If a non-beneficiary has income or assets the amount of Accommodation Supplement payable to them may be reduced.
For more information see:
- Income non-beneficiaries
- Chargeable income non-beneficiaries
- Assets - non-beneficiaries
- Non-beneficiaries
- Nil income

chunks.title: Income - non-beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Income - non-beneficiaries
A non-beneficiary may be able to receive Accommodation Supplement. There is a formula to work out how a non-beneficiary's income changes their entitlement to Accommodation Supplement.
Note employment and work readiness assistance is disregarded as income in the assessment of Accommodation Supplement.
How much Accommodation Supplement the person is eligible for will depend on their level of income. Use the following chart to help work out the amount payable.
