chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Introduction
An Accommodation Supplement is a non-taxable benefit that provides assistance towards a client's accommodation costs.
A person does not have to be getting a benefit to qualify for Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: IRD number for client or partner who is apportioned assistance — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: MSD may make a written request for evidence of an IRD number for a primary client who is being paid Accommodation Supplement. MSD can also request evidence of an IRD number for a partner when they are apportioned a part of the primary client's assistance payment.

chunks.title: Setting or extending the timeframe for providing evidence — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: MSD must provide the client or partner with a minimum of 10 working days to provide IRD number evidence that has been requested in writing. MSD can extend the 10 working day period (in writing) if the client or partner has a reasonable explanation for requiring more than 10 days to provide evidence of their IRD number. This includes considering factors outside of the client's control that cause delays, including, but not limited to: - client or partner has a family emergency that caused a delay - processing delays with an external agency (e.g. Inland Revenue, Department of Internal Affairs, etc) - client or partner does not speak English as a first language and has difficulty navigating evidence requirements - client or partner has limited access to the internet, a device, or their local service centre - client or partner has a physical or intellectual disability that makes accessing services difficult - client or partner is injured, disabled, or has a medical condition that makes accessing services difficult.

chunks.title: Notice following an unsuccessful match — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a client or partner's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the client or partner (in writing) to provide evidence of their IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the client or partner a minimum of 10 working days to provide their IRD number evidence or the client or partner's assistance must be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Accommodation Supplement and MSD holds an IRD number on record. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Isla's IRD number. MSD provides a notice in writing, giving 10 working days in writing for Isla to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Isla already having an IRD number - Isla not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD must suspend assistance if evidence of IRD number is not received — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: MSD must suspend all taxable and/or income tested assistance the client is getting, including their Accommodation Supplement, if evidence of their IRD number is not provided within 10 working days from the written request, or extended period if this has been applied. If the partner has not provided evidence of their IRD number, the partner's taxable and/or income tested assistance must be suspended. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance. Example Koa is receiving Accommodation Supplement and MSD does not have an IRD number on file on record. MSD sends a written request giving 10 working days for Koa to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD receives no response to this request. MSD suspends all Koa's taxable and/or incomed tested assistance because Koa has not supplied MSD with evidence of their IRD number within the timeframe provided.

chunks.title: IRD evidence may not be requested in some circumstances — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - significant factors, that are outside the client or partner's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number (e.g., a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence), and - the client needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided or - there are significant factors related to a health, injury or disability that are outside the client or partner's control that prevents them from providing evidence of an IRD number, and - an agent cannot be appointed to act on the client or partner's behalf. MSD can determine at a later point to request evidence of the IRD number. Example Sienna is 23 and receiving Accommodation Supplement. Sienna's mother (Sara) is Sienna's agent and acts on Sienna's behalf with MSD. Sienna does not have an IRD number and Sara is not a recognised agent for Sienna for Inland Revenue. Sienna has a serious head injury, is unconscious and expected to be in hospital for at least 8 weeks. Sienna is not able to give consent to appoint Sara as an agent for Inland Revenue to apply for an IRD number due to their injury. MSD can request this information later when Sienna's situation has changed. Note there is different guidance for requesting evidence of an IRD number for partners who are not apportioned assistance but their income is relevant to the Accommodation Supplement, or when a client is applying for Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Kāinga Ora (previously Housing NZ) mortgage — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Kāinga Ora (previously Housing NZ) mortgage
If a client with a mortgage from Kāinga Ora (previously Housing NZ) receives a subsidised rate of interest, they are not entitled to an Accommodation Supplement.
A subsidised rate is any percentage of interest, which is less than the prime interest rate.
If the client does not receive a subsidised rate of interest they can apply for an Accommodation Supplement.
Current prime interest rates are available at Mortgage rates (use the Kāinga Ora floating rate).

chunks.title: Lump sum paid for impairment — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Lump sum paid for impairment
If the client (partner or dependent child) has received a lump sum paid under the Accident Compensation Act 2001, the cash asset limit is increased by the amount of the lump sum payment for 12 months from the date the payment is received.
After 12 months, the client's Accommodation Supplement must be reviewed to test their ongoing entitlement.
For more information see:
- Assets - beneficiaries
- Assets - non-beneficiaries
- Cash assets

chunks.title: Lump sum payment of an Independence Allowance — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Lump sum payment of an Independence Allowance
If a client (partner or dependent child) has received a lump sum payment of an Independence Allowance under the Accident Insurance Act 1998 the cash asset limit is increased by the amount of the lump sum payment for 12 months from the date the payment is received.
After 12 months the client's Accommodation Supplement must be reviewed to test their ongoing entitlement.
For more information see:
- Assets - beneficiaries
- Assets - non-beneficiaries
- Cash assets
- Types of income Independence Allowance

chunks.title: Maintenance — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Maintenance
Maintenance costs that may be considered include any reasonable maintenance carried out on the house or grounds, which is necessary to prevent damage or substantial deterioration to the house. This may include but is not limited to:
- clearing chimneys and gutters
- replacing broken windows
- removing trees (when necessary)
- painting (internal and external) if required
Maintenance costs will not include:
- mowing lawns or
- work carried out for cosmetic purposes
For help in deciding whether a repair or maintenance is essential contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Manual calculation — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Manual calculation
In some situations, a manual rate of Accommodation Supplement should be calculated. For example, where the partner of a client is overseas, or does not meet the residence requirements.
Note when the Accommodation Supplement is reviewed due to a change in the client's circumstances, the manual rate must be reassessed.
## Example partner is overseas
A client is getting half the married, civil union or de facto rate of Jobseeker Support while their partner is overseas:
Accommodation costs (Rent)
$300.00
Less cost of part of property not lived in
$0
Less accommodation income
$0
Equals weekly qualifying accommodation costs
$300.00
Less entry threshold (as at 1 April 2026)
$158.00
Equals
$142.00
The client qualifies for up to 70% of $142.00
$142.00 x 0.70
$99.40
Round up to the nearest whole dollar
$100.00

chunks.title: Married, civil union or de facto couples in a joint tenancy — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Married, civil union or de facto couples in a joint tenancy
When the premises are occupied by joint tenants and there are one or more couples, each couple is treated as one joint tenant.
The accommodation costs of the couple, as one joint tenant, are the total of the accommodation costs for both partners.
Note the cash assets and income of the one joint tenant, is the total of the cash asset and income of each of the partners.
For more information see:
- Assets - beneficiaries
- Assets - non-beneficiaries
- Cash assets

chunks.title: Mortgage interest subsidies — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Mortgage interest subsidies
There may be some clients who have their mortgage interest subsidised through employment (such as Armed Forces personnel).
For the purposes of Accommodation Supplement consider the client's accommodation costs:
- the weekly mortgage payment less the weekly mortgage subsidy received
Clients with mortgage interest subsidies are eligible for Accommodation Supplement if their costs are still high enough.

chunks.title: Mortgage repayments — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: A mortgage is a type of loan to buy property e.g. a home. It is a contract between a borrower and lender where the lender provides funds, and the borrower agrees to repay the lender over time. The property is used as security for the loan, and the lender can sell the property if the borrower defaults on their repayments. Homeowners can claim mortgage repayments for the home they occupy as an accommodation cost. This is limited to mortgage repayments towards: - the mortgage principal (amount they borrowed) for the purchase of the home - any mortgage principal for essential repairs and maintenance - interest (amount the lender charges for providing the loan)

chunks.title: Minimum repayment amount — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: The minimum repayment is the least amount a homeowner must pay towards their mortgage principal and interest. This amount can change as interest rates change. Homeowners can only claim minimum mortgage repayments as an accommodation cost. Note if a homeowner has a revolving credit mortgage, only repayments towards the principal and interest for the purchase of the home and any essential repairs and maintenance can be included.

chunks.title: Increasing a mortgage — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: A homeowner may increase their mortgage to do things like buy a car, take a holiday, or make improvements to their home. This increases the minimum repayment the homeowner must pay. The increased amount cannot be included in their accommodation costs unless it is for essential repairs and maintenance. If the mortgage was increased for more than one reason, only the increased amount for essential repairs and maintenance can be included.

chunks.title: Refinancing a mortgage — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Refinancing means transferring a mortgage to a new lender e.g. from one bank to another. When a homeowner refinances, they pay off their existing mortgage and take out a new one. A homeowner may borrow more than they need to pay off their mortgage to do things like consolidate debt, buy a car, or make improvements to their home. Only repayments towards the mortgage principal for the original purchase of the home, any essential repairs and maintenance, and any related interest can be included. The homeowner must provide verification from their lender showing how much of their repayments relate to accommodation costs that can be included in Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Joint ownership — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: If a homeowner has joint ownership with one or more other people but they are the only owner living in the home, the actual costs they are paying can be included as an accommodation cost. Note some homeowners have a mortgage through the Shared Equity Scheme administered by Kāinga Ora. Repayments on these mortgages are voluntary and cannot be included as an accommodation cost.

chunks.title: Net equity — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: The net equity of a house or boat or vehicle is the amount of money that the owner can get from the sale of the item. For example, where a client does not have a loan to help pay for a boat their net equity is the total amount of cash they could receive for the boat. Where a person has a loan to help pay for an item then their net equity is the total value of the item minus the money they still owe on the item.

chunks.title: House and land — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When assessing net equity on a house and/or land, use the rateable valuation or the amount insured. Use whichever value is the greater. Example House valued at $100,000 Land valued at $100,000 Total combined value $200,000 Less outstanding Mortgage principal $150,000 Net equity $50,000 There will be some cases where District Councils only use the Capital value of a property which will be noted on the rate notice. In these instances the Capital value is the value of both the house and land value combined. Example Capital value $200,000 Less outstanding Mortgage principal $150,000 Net equity $50,000

chunks.title: Boat or caravan — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: The value of leisure boats or caravans will be the insured value. Where the leisure boat or caravan is not insured, the client will be required to provide, and pay for, written verification of: - the leisure boat's value from a boat dealer and/or - the caravan's value from a caravan dealer Example Boat valued at $10,000 Less outstanding loan on boat $3,000 Net equity $7,000

chunks.title: Vehicle — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When assessing the net equity of a vehicle use the estimated value of the vehicle. Example Vehicle valued at $15,000 Less outstanding loan on vehicle $7,000 Net equity $8,000 Exemption The client can have the value of a motor vehicle excluded from their net equity if the motor vehicle is used for private use. For instance, if the need for the vehicle is to get to work, disability reasons or to take children to school, then the vehicle is not treated as an asset.

chunks.title: Client has more than one vehicle — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When a client has more than one vehicle, you will need to assess whether the vehicles are used for private use. Example A family with 3 adults own 5 vehicles and all are claimed to be used for personal use. One is a vintage car used for Sunday outings and another a 4 wheel drive used on weekends only. The 4 wheel drive and vintage car are additional to the needs of the family. Therefore, for Accommodation Supplement purposes, the net equity of these vehicles will need to be assessed. For more information see: - Property not used as home - Cash assets

chunks.title: Net equity in former family home - beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Net equity in former family home - beneficiaries
When a client has separated, they may own, or jointly own the family home.
In this case do not assess the client's net equity in the home as an asset until:
- a decision on the sale of the home is made or
- there is a Relationship Property Settlement (previously a matrimonial property settlement) - under a Property Agreement or Property Order
whichever is earlier.
Note that rent received from the property by the beneficiary is charged as income against the main benefit only.

chunks.title: Net equity in former family home - non-beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Net equity in former family home - non-beneficiaries
When a person has separated they may own, or jointly own the family home.
In this case do not assess the person's net equity in the home as an asset until:
- a decision on the sale of the home is made or
- there is a Relationship Property Settlement (previously matrimonial property settlement) - under a Property Agreement or Property Order
whichever is earlier.
Note that rent received from the property by a non-beneficiary needs to be counted as income against the Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension
New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients with no other income are entitled to the maximum rate of Accommodation Supplement for their ongoing accommodation costs if they meet the qualifying criteria.
New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients with other income are eligible for Accommodation Supplement if their combined income is less than the income limit.
If a New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension client has other income that is more than the appropriate income limit, they cannot receive Accommodation Supplement.
Note do not include New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension payments as income.

chunks.title: Nil income — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Nil income
There is nothing to stop a client who has no income from getting an Accommodation Supplement.
However, as Accommodation Supplement only contributes to the total cost of accommodation, ensure the client is aware that:
- they are required to pay the balance of costs and
- they may need to review their living arrangements and
- there is other Extra help they may be able to receive and
- there is other benefit assistance

chunks.title: Non-beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Non-beneficiaries
Accommodation Supplement can be paid to any person who has ongoing accommodation costs and who meets the other qualifications.
A person may still be able to get Accommodation Supplement if they have income. Income will reduce the rate payable in most cases.
For exceptions see:
- Boarders - non-beneficiaries
Information on the effect of income on the rate of Accommodation Supplement payable can be found in:
- Income calculations - non-beneficiaries
## Community Services Card
If a client is getting any financial assistance from MSD, they may qualify for a Community Services Card.
Community Services Cards are not automatically issued to clients who get non-beneficiary assistance. They must make a separate application.

chunks.title: Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid
When a client is receiving an Orphans Benefit or an Unsupported Childs Benefit, the child is not treated as a dependent child and is not included in the assessment of Accommodation Supplement.
The client's Accommodation Supplement is assessed on their family circumstances excluding the child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid.

chunks.title: Outgoings paid by former partner - beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Outgoings paid by former partner - beneficiaries
The amount of outgoings paid by the client's former partner to be charged as income against the main benefit depends on whether or not there has been a relationship Property settlement (previously a Matrimonial Settlement) - whether by Property agreement or Property Order.
## Before property settlement
Before the property settlement, in the case of a beneficiary, charge as income against the client's benefit any outgoings the former partner is paying in excess of 50% of the total outgoings.
## After the property settlement
After a Property settlement there should be an agreement stating the amount of accommodation costs to be paid by each partner.
Any amount, over the agreed amount, paid by the former partner towards the property is to be charged as income against the client's benefit in the case of a beneficiary.
## Client's accommodation costs
The client's accommodation costs are considered to be the amount they actually pay for their accommodation, not the total accommodation cost of the home.

chunks.title: Outgoings paid by former partner - non-beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Outgoings paid by former partner - non-beneficiaries
The amount of outgoings paid by the person's former partner to be charged as income depends on whether or not there has been a Relationship Property Settlement (previously Matrimonial settlement) - whether by Property Agreement or Property Order.
## Before the property settlement
In the case of a non-beneficiary, before the property settlement, charge as income against the Accommodation Supplement any outgoings the former partner is paying in excess of 50% of the total outgoings.
## After the property settlement
After property settlement there should be an agreement stating the amount of accommodation costs to be paid by each partner. Any amount, over the agreed amount, paid by the former partner towards the property is charged as income against the Accommodation Supplement in the case of a non-beneficiary.
## Accommodation costs
Accommodation costs are considered to be the amount a person actually pay's for their accommodation, not the total accommodation cost of the home.

chunks.title: Outgoings paid by someone else - beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Outgoings paid by someone else - beneficiaries
In some circumstances a client may have their accommodation costs paid for by another person (for example a client's parent).
Where accommodation costs are paid for by someone else, you can still pay the client, Accommodation Supplement. In the case of a beneficiary you must:
- charge the amount of money that is contributed by the 'other' person against their main benefit as income
- regard the total rent or outgoings as the client's accommodation costs
## Exception
Where a couple have separated and the client's former partner is contributing to the outgoings of the joint family home, outgoings paid for by the partner (in some circumstances) may be disregarded as income.
For more information see:
- Outgoings paid by former partner - beneficiaries
Also see:
- Outgoings paid by someone else - non-beneficiaries

chunks.title: Outgoings paid by someone else - non-beneficiaries — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Outgoings paid by someone else - non-beneficiaries
In some circumstances a person may have their accommodation costs paid for by another person (for example a client's parent).
Where accommodation costs are paid for by someone else, you can still pay the non-beneficiary Accommodation Supplement. In the case of a non-beneficiary you must:
- charge as income, the amount of money that is contributed by the 'other' person against the Accommodation Supplement
- regard the total rent or outgoings as their accommodation costs
## Exception
Where a couple have separated and the former partner is contributing to the outgoings of the joint family home, outgoings paid for by the former partner (in some circumstances) may be disregarded as income.
For more information see:
- Outgoings paid by former partner - non-beneficiaries
Also see:
- Outgoings paid by someone else - beneficiaries

chunks.title: Overseas benefit or pension — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Overseas benefit or pension
When a client is applying for Accommodation Supplement, how their overseas pension affects it depends on other assistance the client is getting.
The overseas pension is treated differently depending on whether the client applying for Accommodation Supplement is:
- getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension, or a main benefit
or
- not getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension, or a main benefit
## Clients getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension or a main benefit
When a client is getting an overseas pension that is more than the New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension, or main benefit rate, the overseas pension amount above the rate is directly deducted from any:
- Accommodation Supplement and
- other benefits they are getting
MSD will calculate the amount of New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension, or main benefit the client is entitled to get and the rate of Accommodation Supplement payable with their benefit or pension.
When deducting an overseas pension, MSD must first calculate the total New Zealand benefit amount the client is entitled to (including Accommodation Supplement). For example, New Zealand Superannuation plus Accommodation Supplement.
The overseas pension is then deducted from the total amount of Accommodation Supplement plus New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension, or main benefit.
The balance left is the actual rate of Accommodation Supplement payable.
## Clients not getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension or a main benefit
When a client is getting an overseas pension and they are not getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension, or a main benefit their overseas pension is directly deducted from any Accommodation Supplement they may get.
MSD will calculate the rate of Accommodation Supplement payable alongside the client’s overseas pension.
The overseas pension is deducted from the Accommodation Supplement, and the balance left is the actual rate of Accommodation Supplement payable.

chunks.title: Partner of a student — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Partner of a student
The partner of a student may be able to receive Accommodation Supplement if:
- they are not a full-time student and
- they meet all relevant qualifying criteria for Accommodation Supplement
Where the student is receiving a Student Allowance, all Accommodation Supplement payable is paid to the partner of the student, as the student does not qualify for Accommodation Supplement.
## Where the student does not receive an Accommodation Benefit
Where the student does not receive an Accommodation Benefit their partner's application should be treated as a non-beneficiary application.
## Where the student receives an Accommodation Benefit
Where the student receives an Accommodation Benefit this must be taken into account when considering the amount of the Accommodation Supplement to pay to the partner. To determine this you need to:
- assess the rate of Accommodation Supplement payable to the couple as if they were non-beneficiaries and
- reduce the rate by the amount of Accommodation Benefit the student is receiving
For a detailed example of how to perform this calculation where the student partner receives an Accommodation Benefit see:
For details on how to process on SWIFTT see:

chunks.title: Partner on strike — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Partner on strike
If a client applies for Accommodation Supplement while their partner is on strike, the full rate payable is paid to the client.
In these cases Accommodation Supplement is assessed manually as if both the client and the partner qualify for Accommodation Supplement.
If the client gets a main benefit in their own right, the full Accommodation Supplement is paid with the client's benefit payment.

chunks.title: Partner overseas — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Partner overseas
Where one partner of a married, civil union or de facto couple is overseas and the partner remaining in New Zealand is getting half the married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit, Accommodation Supplement is assessed using the married, civil union or de facto rate of entry threshold.
The full rate of Accommodation Supplement calculated is paid to the client.
Note in some situations, the partner overseas may qualify for or be getting a benefit. For more information refer to the appropriate main benefit.

chunks.title: Partner subject to a non-entitlement period — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Partner subject to a non-entitlement period
There may be cases where a client is applying for Accommodation Supplement but their partner does not qualify due to being on a 13 week non-entitlement period.
In these cases Accommodation Supplement is assessed manually as if both the client and the partner qualify for Accommodation Supplement.
Note where neither the client nor their partner qualifies for a main benefit (due to a non-entitlement period or an obligations failure), no Accommodation Supplement can be paid.

chunks.title: Payment during stand downs — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Payment during stand downs
A person may already be receiving Accommodation Supplement as a non-beneficiary when they apply for a main benefit.
In this case they may continue to receive their original rate of Accommodation Supplement during their stand-down. This is the case whether the client is having an ordinary stand down or a voluntarily unemployment stand down.
A person who previously would have qualified on grounds of income, but, did not apply prior to application of benefit will not become eligible during the stand-down prior to grant of benefit.
A client who would not previously have qualified for an Accommodation Supplement and was not receiving an Accommodation Supplement prior to application cannot be paid an Accommodation Supplement during a stand-down.
## Delayed application for main benefit
A person who would be subject to a non-entitlement period or a stand down and is not receiving Accommodation Supplement as a non-beneficiary cannot choose to delay their application for a main benefit and apply for Accommodation Supplement first.
For more information see:
- Partner subject to a non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Payment
The amount of Accommodation Supplement payable is assessed taking into account a client's:
- accommodation costs
- income
- assets
- family status and
- residential region
For more information see:
- Determining accommodation costs
- Calculating rate - general formula
- Income calculations - non-beneficiaries
- Social housing tenants
- New Zealand Superannuation and Veterans Pension
- Supported Living Payment caring for a person
- Overseas benefit or pension
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit
- IRD number for client or partner who is apportioned assistance
There are maximum amounts of Accommodation Supplement that can be paid, these depend on family size and the area in New Zealand the client lives in.
For more information see:
- Deskfile Entry thresholds and maximum rates
All payments of Accommodation Supplement are rounded up to the nearest whole dollar.

chunks.title: Payments for the former home when in emergency housing or transitional housing due to violence — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Payments for the former home when in emergency housing or transitional housing due to violence
Generally, a client cannot get an Accommodation Supplement if they do not occupy the place they are paying accommodation costs for as a home.
However, a client may keep getting Accommodation Supplement for their former home (except when a partner remains at the home) if due to violence:
- they are staying in: emergency housing, including emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant or contracted emergency housing ortransitional housing, including transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development
- emergency housing, including emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant or contracted emergency housing or
- transitional housing, including transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development
and
- Accommodation Supplement is not being paid for their current accommodation
When a partner remains in the home, the partner becomes responsible for the costs of the home.
## Client chooses to use costs of former home
If the client chooses to get Accommodation Supplement for the costs of their former home:
- continue the Accommodation Supplement for their former home while they are in emergency housing, contracted emergency housing, or transitional housing and
- review the circumstances in 6 weeks

chunks.title: Client in long term care — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Client in long term care
If a client is in long term care and they get a Residential Care Subsidy, they are not eligible for Accommodation Supplement.
## Client does not qualify for Residential Care Subsidy
If a client is in long term care and they do not qualify for Residential Care Subsidy, they may be able to get Accommodation Supplement. Their accommodation costs must be verified by their residential care provider.
## Client has a partner
If a client enters long term care and their partner stays in the community, they may be able to get Accommodation Supplement individually. To assess Accommodation Supplement in these situations, MSD must:
- halve the couple's gross income and assets for the assessment
- use the appropriate single entry threshold and maximum rate
- use the cost of residence as a board cost for the partner in care (if they qualify)
Note any income of the partner in the community that was included in the means assessment of the partner in care must not be included as chargeable income for Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Pre-paid funeral expenses — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Pre-paid funeral expenses
A pre-paid funeral trust fund or account is money put aside (usually in a trust) exclusively for the payment of funeral expenses. If the money can be accessed by the client and so used for other purposes, it is not considered exclusively for funeral expenses then this money is a cash asset for Accommodation Supplement.
It is usually clear whether or not the trust fund or account has been genuinely set aside for funeral expenses. Evidence that it has been set aside exclusively for funeral expenses include:
- the trust fund/account is only paid out on production of a death certificate
- the client cannot usually access the funds
- if a client can access the fund, there are limited conditions on withdrawal, such as re-locating overseas
- the trust fund/account is only payable to the funeral director or administrator of the client's estate
- the client cannot generally access the interest earned from the trust fund or account
Where the trust fund or account has been set aside for funeral expenses and cannot be accessed or converted into cash then this money is not a cash asset for Accommodation Supplement.
For more information see:
- Cash assets

chunks.title: Principal place of residence — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Principal place of residence
Accommodation Supplement is assessed on the costs of the place where the client is actually living at the time of application.
## Married, civil union or de facto clients
If a client and partner decide to live apart in different accommodation, only the costs where the client and partner determine as their principal place of residence are used in the assessment of Accommodation Supplement.
Where both the client and partner are living in the same accommodation, but have separate accommodation costs, the total costs are used in the assessment of Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Prisoners — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Prisoners
Prisoners and clients on remand cannot generally receive Accommodation Supplement while detained.
However, clients on home detention may qualify.
In exceptional circumstances Accommodation Supplement can continue when the client is imprisoned. For assistance contact Helpline.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support Court imposed conditions

chunks.title: Property not used as home — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Property not used as home
A client may have a property (including boats and caravans) they do not use as a home for themselves or their family. Consider whether that property is a realisable asset. There is an expectation that clients will utilise their own resources to support themselves, including any property that they may own or have an interest in that is not their home property or land on which their home is situated.
Points to consider when determining whether the property should be considered as a realisable asset include:
- What was the property originally bought for?
- What is the client's intention with the property?
- Is the property on the market?
- Is the asking price realistic?
- Is the property listed with a real estate agent?
- Location of property
If the property is a realisable asset you must then decide what effect this has on entitlement to Accommodation Supplement. When assessing the value of any realisable asset (for example a piece of land or a rental property) you will need to calculate the net equity that the client holds in the asset.
In general you should treat any realisable asset the way you would 'cash assets'. If the client's combined cash assets and realisable assets exceed the asset threshold then Accommodation Supplement cannot be granted.
## Exception
A client's net equity in the former family home may be disregarded for a period of time.
For more information see:
- Assets - beneficiaries
- Assets -non beneficiaries
- Net equity
- Net equity in former family home - beneficiaries
- Net equity in former family home - non-beneficiaries

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for Accommodation Supplement, a client must:
- meet a cash asset testFor more information about how to apply a cash asset test see: Beneficiaries or Non-beneficiaries
- meet an income test
- have weekly qualifying accommodation costs
- be a New Zealand citizen or residence class visa holder (i.e. not in New Zealand unlawfully, or here on a temporary entry class visa) and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
A client cannot get an Accommodation Supplement if:
- they do not occupy, as a home, the house where they are paying accommodation costs
- they are aged 16 or 17 years old unless they are financially independent
- they get (or would get if they were to apply) a Student Allowance under the Student Allowances Regulations 1998
- they would be entitled to get a basic Student Allowance (were they to apply) but for the level of their income or their partner's/combined income, or their parents' income (if aged under 24 years)
- are getting a Residential Care Subsidy or
- are making payments under mortgage security to Kāinga Ora at a rate less than the prime interest rate
- they are an applicable person who is living in a property owned or managed by a social housing providerA client who pays board to someone to live in a social housing property may be able to get an Accommodation Supplement based on their board costs.
Note a client who is paying rent to a registered community housing provider for a property that is not contracted for Income Related Rent purposes may get Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Refuge board costs — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Refuge board costs
Sometimes clients who are staying in accommodation provided by a refuge will apply for an Accommodation Supplement to help pay their costs. These clients may currently be getting an Accommodation Supplement or it may be a new application.
Clients can choose:
- to apply for an Accommodation Supplement for refuge board costs or
- continue to have Accommodation Supplement paid for their home (except when a partner remains at home - the partner becomes responsible for the costs of the house)
They cannot get Accommodation Supplement for both.
In this context a refuge is emergency accommodation provided by an agency or organisation. This includes (but is not restricted to) agencies such as Women's Refuge, Home and Family Society, Emergency Housing Trusts, Iwi and cultural organisations, and church organisations.
Accommodation Supplement cannot be paid for both home and refuge accommodation costs.
If the client chooses to have the costs of their home used for Accommodation Supplement purposes:
- continue the Accommodation Supplement for their home while they are at a refuge and
- review the situation after 6 weeks
## Payments for the former home when in other emergency housing or transitional housing due to violence
In certain circumstances a client may continue getting Accommodation Supplement for their former home (except when a partner remains at the home) if they are staying in emergency housing or transitional housing due to violence.

chunks.title: Rent — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: For people who are renting their actual rent costs are their accommodation costs. When the amount a client pays for their accommodation includes other costs (e.g. service costs) and the accommodation cost can be separately identified as part of the amount they pay, they will be considered renting. Note rent arrears cannot be included as an accommodation cost.

chunks.title: Rent includes service costs — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Sometimes a client's rent includes service costs such as electricity or a telephone. When this occurs, service costs must be deducted from their accommodation costs. For more information: - Rent includes service costs

chunks.title: Water rates — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Water rates can be included as a rental cost for Accommodation Supplement when the rental property has a separate water meter, and the tenancy agreement states the tenant is responsible for this cost. If a client is renting with other people and their name is not on the tenancy agreement, they can still have their portion of water rates included as a rental cost.

chunks.title: Joint tenants — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Where there are joint tenants, for example flatmates, each tenant may apply for the portion of the rent that they pay in separate applications. A client does not need to have their name on a tenancy agreement to be considered renting. There is one exception: - Married, civil union or de facto couples in a joint tenancy

chunks.title: Clients with renters or boarders — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When a client gets rent or board payments from someone living in the same premises, it is accommodation income and is deducted from their accommodation costs when calculating the weekly qualifying accommodation costs. Accommodation income includes: - Rent a client gets from another person (not being additional occupants or boarders) residing in the same premises, except where the person paying the rent is in a self-contained part of the premises or the rent payment is part of the income of a business on the premises - 62% of payments for board a client gets from another person residing in the same premises, except where the board payment is part of the income of a business on the premises Note when accommodation income is more than the client's accommodation costs (after the deduction of the cost of any part of the property not being lived in by the client), the excess amount is income and must be charged against any financial assistance the client gets. In this case, the client will have no weekly qualifying accommodation costs and will not qualify for Accommodation Supplement. For more information see: - Boarders - beneficiaries - Boarders - non-beneficiaries - Tenant or homeowner has a boarder - Tenant renting out a room - Homeowner renting out a room - Weekly qualifying accommodation costs - Rent and board payments

chunks.title: Temporary Accommodation Service — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's Temporary Accommodation Service helps households affected by a natural disaster to find temporary accommodation while their home is being repaired, rebuilt or until they find alternative accommodation. Households staying in Temporary Accommodation Services are generally required to pay a rent contribution. Clients may need to contribute to the cost of their temporary accommodation. MSD may consider the rent contribution for the assessment of Accommodation Supplement when they occupy the premises as a home. If MSD considers the client does not occupy the premises as a home, Accommodation Supplement cannot be paid for the Temporary Accommodation Service rental costs. Note Accommodation Supplement can only be paid for one home. For more information about how to determine if someone occupies a premises as a home see: Temporarily absent from a premises

chunks.title: Rent includes service costs — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Rent includes service costs
Sometimes a client's rent includes service costs. If the client is renting, any service costs must be deducted from their accommodation costs.
Generally, the service costs and cost of accommodation will be itemised separately on the tenancy or rental agreement. Use the accommodation cost only to calculate Accommodation Supplement.
## Costs not clear
Where the service costs are not itemised separately MSD will need to assess the cost of the service(s) and deduct it from the total rent, to determine the cost of accommodation.
The first part of the assessment is to have the client ask the landlord to provide an estimate of the accommodation and service costs. Use the accommodation cost only.
Where this is not possible or if there is a disagreement between the landlord and client about the cost split between accommodation and service costs, MSD can use a variety of sources to estimate the service cost depending on what that cost is.
For example, if the total rent includes electricity, the Powerswitch website can be used to calculate the cost of the electricity to be deducted from the total rent.
## Example
John pays $250 total rent a week for a room and electricity. As there is only one meter box for the boarding house the landlord is unable to provide an estimate of the service cost.
Powerswitch estimates his weekly electricity costs to be $32 a week. To calculate John's accommodation cost, deduct $32 (electricity) from $250 (total rent). John's accommodation costs are $218 rent a week.

chunks.title: Rent to buy — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Rent to buy
A person may enter into a rent to buy contract (also called a deferred payment disposition). In such a case the client is considered as a home owner.
The client must supply a copy of the contract. All payments stated in the rental contract as mortgage repayments and payments made towards a deposit can be included as accommodation costs.
The contract will also state whether the client has responsibility for costs such as rates, insurance and maintenance.
If the client has responsibility for things like rates, insurance and maintenance these may be included as accommodation costs. If the client does not have responsibility for these things they cannot claim them as accommodation costs.

chunks.title: Repairs — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Repairs
Repairs that may be considered, as accommodation costs would include, those needed for the continuation of existing:
- water
- gas
- power and
- sewerage services (including showers, toilets, sinks and the drains attached to them)
Other repairs can be considered if they are essential to:
- the structural stability of the house or property (repairs to buildings or sheds on the property that are not used for accommodation purposes are not to be considered)
- wiring and light fittings
- septic tanks (provided repairs have not been paid as a non-recoverable Special Needs Grant)
- any repairs required to meet building regulations
Repairs to any major appliance that helps maintain the house in a habitable state may be included, such as:
- gas or electric stove and
- hot water cylinder
Home contents costs should not be considered, for example:
- microwaves
- furnishings
- fridges and
- washing machines
For help in deciding whether a repair or maintenance is essential contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get Accommodation Supplement, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- have a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
Note for Accommodation Supplement no period of residence is required.
People who are in New Zealand unlawfully or here on a temporary entry class visa generally do not qualify for a benefit.
## Clients without citizenship or a residence class visa
If a client does not have New Zealand citizenship or a residence class visa, they cannot get Accommodation Supplement.
However, if a client in this situation has accommodation costs, they may be able to get Temporary Additional Support if they are:
- a person who has refugee or protected person status in New Zealand or
- awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protected person status and are lawfully in New Zealand (i.e. they have a valid temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009) or
- applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 and are compelled to remain in New Zealand due to some unforeseen circumstances
Once the client has been granted citizenship or a residence class visa and they meet all the other qualifications, Accommodation Supplement can be granted.
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other criteria to qualify for Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Retirement village — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Retirement village
There are a number of different situations that a person can be in when living in a retirement village.
When the amount a resident of a retirement village serviced apartment pays for their accommodation includes other costs (e.g. food or service costs) and these costs can be separated out from the amount they pay for accommodation, they are considered renting.
When the client pays for their accommodation and food, and the food costs can't be separated out from the amount they pay, they are considered boarding.
If a client owns the apartment, they are considered a homeowner.
For more information see:
- Rent
- Board
- Home ownership
- Retirement village residents with 'Licence to Occupy'

chunks.title: Retirement village residents with 'Licence to Occupy' — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Retirement village residents with 'Licence to Occupy'
Some retirement village residents have a 'Licence to Occupy' or 'Occupational Rights Agreement'. These clients are considered homeowners for Accommodation Supplement and must provide:
- verification of their 'Licence to Occupy' title or 'Occupational Rights Agreement' and
- verification or breakdown of expenses
Note residents may pay for a variety of costs, and not all will be qualifying costs for Accommodation Supplement. MSD must assess each case on its own merits and only include costs related to the client's accommodation.
## Examples of costs to include
- repayments on a loan or mortgage taken out to obtain the client's licence to occupy their villa or unit
- local authority rates (if the client gets a rebate, this must be deducted)
- water rates
- insurance premiums relating to their villa or unit (must not include contents insurance)
- cost of essential repairs and maintenance relating to their villa or unit
## Examples of costs not to include
- village outgoings for construction or further development of the village
- service charges e.g. home care services, the provision of meals
- utility charges that include the supply of electricity, gas, telephone, internet, television and other services and utilities
- health service charges, including provision of medical and pharmaceutical services
- village outgoings connected with common facilities within the centre e.g. recreation centre and sport facilities
## Payment of rates
Some residents may pay their rates with a service fee directly to the retirement village. In these cases, the cost for rates can be included in the Accommodation Supplement assessment. The client must provide verification of the rates they pay for the villa or unit they occupy.

chunks.title: Self-employed claiming home office expenses — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Self-employed claiming home office expenses
Home office expenses are the costs for running a business from a sole trader's home, based on the floor area of the house.
Home office expenses may include power, water, internet, mortgages and rates, or rent.
For example it could be a room set up as an office, a workshop, art studio or for hairdressing, massage or therapy services.
A self-employed person who is renting and uses part of their home for business purposes can claim a proportion of their rent as a mixed-use business expense. A self-employed person who has a mortgage can claim some of their rates, insurance and mortgage interest as business expenses.
When a self-employed person is applying for or getting Accommodation Supplement any home office expenses for the portion of the property used by the business need to be deducted from the accommodation costs being claimed by the client.
This is part of the calculation to determine what a client's weekly qualifying accommodation cost is.
For more information see:
- Weekly qualifying accommodation costs
## Example
Lagi rents her home and pays $600 per week. Lagi uses the percentage of home space used for business to calculate her home office expenses.
Lagi uses 8% of the house as a sewing room/home office and claims home office expenses of $2,496 per year ($48 per week) in her accounts.
Lagi applies for Accommodation Supplement. The amount that Lagi claims as a home office expense is deducted from her rent and her weekly qualifying accommodation costs are calculated as $552 per week ($600 - $48).

chunks.title: Shared equity schemes — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Shared equity schemes
The Shared Equity Scheme provides loans to first home buyers receiving a modest income. This was a 2 year pilot administered by the Kāinga Ora (previously Housing NZ) and ran from 1 July 2008 until 30 June 2010. While there will be no new loans given there are still existing clients who may apply Accommodation Supplement.
To be eligible for a Shared Equity Scheme loan, clients must have had a Kiwibank approved mortgage.
Clients who receive a loan through the Shared Equity Scheme may elect to repay the loan but this is not required unless:
- the client defaults on Kiwibank repayments, rates, insurance etc
- the client defaults on the Shared Equity Scheme loan conditions
- the client sells the property
- all borrowers on the Shared Equity Scheme loan are deceased
- the client refinances with another bank or building society
- the clients voluntary repays the total Shared Equity Scheme loan before it matures (ten years)
Where mortgage repayments are not required they cannot be included as accommodation costs.
## Client sells house
When a client sells the house on which a Shared Equity Scheme loan has been taken, the Shared Equity Scheme loan must be repaid reducing the net asset the client may receive.

chunks.title: Social housing tenants — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Social housing tenants
An applicable person who is living in a property owned or managed by a social housing provider cannot receive Accommodation Supplement.
## Property not contracted for Income Related Rent purposes
A client who is paying rent to a registered community housing provider for a property that is not contracted for Income Related Rent purposes can receive Accommodation Supplement.
In this situation if another client was paying rent to the tenant living in a property registered with the community housing provider, they can get Accommodation Supplement for the rent they pay.
## Additional occupants living in a social housing property
Additional occupants may pay a contribution towards accommodation costs while living in the social housing property.
The contribution amount may include food and sometimes other costs. Whether it includes food (and/or other costs) or not, the contribution is considered board for the purpose of calculating Accommodation Supplement.
This means that only 62% of the additional occupant's contribution can be considered as their allowable accommodation cost even if it does not include food (and/or other costs).
For more information see about what a contribution is, see:
- Contributions from additional occupants
## Subletting in social housing
A social housing tenant cannot get Accommodation Supplement. If a social housing tenant sublets to another person, this person also cannot get Accommodation Supplement for the full rent cost they pay the social housing tenant. This is because rent paid by any person in respect of a social housing property is not an allowable cost for Accommodation Supplement.
A social housing tenant can, after seeking agreement from their provider, take on an additional occupant. An additional occupant may be able to get Accommodation Supplement where they pay a contribution towards accommodation costs while living in the social housing property and their contributions will be treated like a board payment.
The contribution amount may include food and sometimes other costs. Whether it includes food (and/or other costs) or not, the contribution is considered board for the purpose of calculating Accommodation Supplement.
This means that only 62% of the additional occupant's contribution can be considered as their allowable accommodation cost even if it does not include food (and/or other costs).
Social housing tenants are not generally allowed to sub-let their property. Information indicating that sub-letting is occurring is relevant to their eligibility for social housing and an Income Related Rent.
Information on sub-letting in social housing should be referred to Client Service Integrity for follow up if the tenant has not advised of the change in their circumstances.

chunks.title: Specific circumstances — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Specific circumstances
There are a number of specific circumstances that will affect a client's entitlement to Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Striking workers — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Striking workers
Where a single client is not employed because of a strike, they can receive an Accommodation Supplement. However, you can consider that they have deprived themselves of income and assess entitlement to Accommodation Supplement by taking into account pre-strike earnings.
This approach will ensure that:
- clients already receiving Accommodation Supplement do not qualify for a higher rate as a result of going on strike
- clients who previously did not qualify for Accommodation Supplement on the grounds of income, will not become eligible as a result of going on strike and
- clients who previously would have qualified on the grounds of income but did not apply prior to striking are eligible
For information about Accommodation Supplement for married, civil union or de facto clients where one partner is on strike see:
- Partner on strike

chunks.title: Situations where a student is eligible to get an Accommodation Supplement — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Situations where a student is eligible to get an Accommodation Supplement
Students can get an Accommodation Supplement when:
- they are getting a benefit and not a Student Allowance, for example they are getting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship during the vacation period
- they have been declined a Student Allowance for a reason other than their income or their partner's/combined income, or their parents income (if aged under 24)
- they have used their maximum weeks of Student Allowance entitlement
- they are enrolled in a course that is not an approved course of study under the Student Allowance Regulations 1998 or
- they are a part-time student and not eligible to get Student Allowance
## Situations where a student is not eligible to get Accommodation Supplement
A student is not eligible for an Accommodation Supplement if:
- the student would be eligible to get a Student Allowance, were the student to apply or
- the student has been declined a Student Allowance because of: the student's incometheir partner's or combined incometheir parents' income (if aged under 24 years)
- the student's income
- their partner's or combined income
- their parents' income (if aged under 24 years)
Note students cannot opt out of Student Allowance support and apply for an Accommodation Supplement.
A student may not need to apply for Student Allowance to assess Accommodation Supplement entitlement, where we can determine, based on the information we have that they will not be eligible or entitled for a Student Allowance.
## Accommodation location
Accommodation Supplement is assessed on the costs of the place where the client is actually living at the time of application.
If a student moves home during the vacation period and decides to keep their accommodation in their place of study, these costs cannot be included in the assessment of Accommodation Supplement.
In some situations, the partner of a student can get an Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment - caring for a person — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Supported Living Payment - caring for a person
The income calculation for a Supported Living Payment - caring for a person is the same as for any other beneficiary.
For more information see:
- Examples - Supported Living Payment - caring for a person

chunks.title: Temporarily absent from a premises — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: A client may be temporarily absent from their home because they are unable to live in it due to a natural disaster or fire, they are in hospital or are travelling overseas. When a client is temporarily absent from their home but are required to pay accommodation costs for their home, those costs may be included in Accommodation Supplement if the client still lives in the premises as a home.

chunks.title: Occupy the premises as a home — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: To decide if someone continues to occupy the premises as a home when they are temporarily absent, the following questions all need to be answered 'yes': - Is the client away from their home for a temporary reason? - Did they occupy the premises as a home before they left? - Did they intend to continue living in their home before leaving? - Does the client intend to return to live in their home? If the client is absent from their home for some time, they could be considered to no longer occupy it as a home. MSD must consider: - the reason for leaving and not yet returning, and - whether they intend to return to their home once they can. If a client will not or cannot return to live at the home they are absent from, the accommodation costs for that home cannot be included in Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Home unable to be lived in — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: If a client's home has been severely damaged or there is no longer a house on the property e.g. the house has been washed away by flooding, or had to be demolished, the client may still be considered to occupy it as a home. MSD needs to consider whether they still occupy the premises as a home.

chunks.title: Hospitalisation or travelling overseas — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Clients may be absent from their home while they are in hospital or travelling overseas. A clients accommodation costs for the home they are temporarily absent from can generally be included in Accommodation Supplement if we consider they occupy the premises as a home and continue to meet the qualifications. For specific guidance about when Accommodation Supplement can be paid for a home when the client is temporarily absent see:

chunks.title: Accommodation Supplement — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Clients who qualify, can get Accommodation Supplement for their affected home. Note a client cannot get Accommodation Supplement for both their affected home and their temporary accommodation costs. If a client chooses to get Accommodation Supplement for their temporary accommodation costs, they cannot get Temporary Accommodation Assistance payments.

chunks.title: Costs can only be included for 1 premises — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Accommodation costs can only be included for 1 home. If the client continues to have costs for the home they temporarily can't return to and the place they are currently staying, the client will need to tell MSD which home they want to get Accommodation Supplement for. MSD will need to assess if the client is occupying that premises as a home.

chunks.title: Examples — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: Example 1 The client's home was severely damaged in a house fire, and they had to move out. The client is staying with a friend until the repairs are completed. The client has no accommodation costs at the friend's house, but they are contributing towards the household expenses such as power and food. The client doesn't have mortgage insurance cover, and still needs to pay the mortgage costs for the house they can't return to. The client contacts MSD to see if they can continue to get Accommodation Supplement for their mortgage costs. The client tells MSD they were living in their home and intended to continue living there before being forced to move out. The client also tells us it will take roughly 4 months for the repairs to be completed and they are intending to return to live at the property once the repairs are done. The client may be able to continue getting Accommodation Supplement for their mortgage costs as it could be considered the client continues to occupy the premises as a home. It is considered they were occupying the premises as a home before being forced to leave and are intending to return. Example 2 The client's house was damaged beyond repair in a severe weather event, and they have moved into the MBIE Temporary Accommodation Service. The client doesn't have mortgage insurance cover, and still needs to pay mortgage costs for the home they can't return to. The client is also required to pay a weekly contribution towards their MBIE temporary accommodation. The client has house insurance, however this doesn't include temporary accommodation cover. The cost of the mortgage repayments is higher than the MBIE Temporary Accommodation Service contribution. The client asks MSD to include the mortgage repayment accommodation costs instead of the MBIE accommodation contribution when assessing their Accommodation Supplement. MSD needs to assess whether the client is still occupying their original premises as a home. The client tells MSD they were living at and intended to continue living there before being forced to move out. The client also tells MSD they are investigating options to rebuild or get a house moved there, but they don't know how long this will take before they can move back. The client is considered to continue to occupy the premises as a home, as the client was living there before being forced to leave, and they are intending to return. Note If the clients' temporary absence from their home extends for a long period of time, MSD may consider whether the client continues to occupy the premises as a home. Example 3

chunks.title: Examples — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: The client was renting, and the house was flooded and is no longer fit to live in. The client's rental property had been modified based on their disability needs. The landlord has discussed the situation with the client and advised them that repairs will take 3 months. The client wants to wait for the repairs to be done then move back in as it is difficult to find a suitable place. The landlord has advised that no rent will be charged over that 3-month period. The client is currently in the MBIE Temporary Accommodation Service and is required to pay a weekly contribution toward their MBIE accommodation. The client calls MSD to see what help is available. The client was getting the Accommodation Supplement for the rental property which will stop being paid, as the client no longer pays rent for their rental property. MSD needs to assess whether the client is considered to occupy the MBIE Temporary Accommodation Service premises as a home. If they are occupying this premises as a home, the Accommodation Supplement can be reviewed to include the MBIE Temporary Accommodation Service costs

chunks.title: Tenant or homeowner has a boarder — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Tenant or homeowner has a boarder
If a tenant or homeowner has one or more boarders, 62% of money received from the boarders is accommodation income and deducted from a client's accommodation costs (rent or mortgage interest and principal repayments) to determine the clients weekly qualifying accommodation costs when assessing the rate of Accommodation Supplement.
When money received from boarders is more than the client's accommodation costs (after the deduction of the cost of any part of the property not being lived in by the client), the excess amount is income. In this case, the client will have no weekly qualifying accommodation costs and will not be eligible for Accommodation Supplement.
Note if a client doesn't live in part of their property, the cost of that part of the property is deducted from their accommodation costs before deducting money received from boarders when calculating the weekly qualifying accommodation costs.
For more information about how to calculate income from rent see:
- Rent and board payments
## Examples
Al is single and renting a 2-bedroom house for $550 a week. He takes on a boarder who pays him $350 a week. His weekly qualifying accommodation costs are $333 ($550 less $217 (62% of $350)). There is no income charge.
Accommodation costs (Rent)
$550pw
Less cost of part of property not lived in
$0
Less accommodation income
$217
Equals weekly qualifying accommodation costs
$333pw
Jinwoo owns a 2-bedroom house and is paying off his mortgage. His accommodation costs are $300 a week. He has a boarder who pays $500 a week. Jinwoo will not qualify for Accommodation Supplement as 62% of the board payment, $310, is more than he pays for his accommodation costs. There will be a $10 income charge ($310 less $300).
Accommodation costs (Mortgage)
$300pw
Less cost of part of property not lived in
$0
Less accommodation income
$310
Equals weekly qualifying accommodation costs
$0 (-$10)
Chargeable income
$10pw
For more information see:
- Tenant renting out a room
- Homeowner renting out a room
- Homeowner renting out part of their property
- Weekly qualifying accommodation costs

chunks.title: Tenant renting out a room — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text:
## Tenant renting out a room
If a client is renting and rents out a room to another person, the rent payment they get is accommodation income and deducted from their accommodation costs to determine the clients weekly qualifying accommodation costs when assessing the rate of Accommodation Supplement.
When money received from renters is more than the client's accommodation costs (after the deduction of the cost of any part of the property not being lived in by the client), the excess amount is income. In this case, the client will have no weekly qualifying accommodation costs and will not be eligible for Accommodation Supplement.
Note if a client doesn't live in part of their property, the cost of that part of the property is deducted from their accommodation costs before deducting money received from renters when calculating the weekly qualifying accommodation costs.
For more information about how to calculate income from rent see:
- Rent and board payments
## Examples
Jennifer is a sole parent renting a 3-bedroom house for $700 a week. She rents 1 room out for $250 a week. Her weekly qualifying accommodation cost is $450 ($700 less $250) a week. There is no income charge.
Accommodation costs (Rent)
$700pw
Less cost of part of property not lived in
$0
Less accommodation income
$250
Equals weekly qualifying accommodation costs
$450pw
Jane is renting a 2-bedroom flat for $320 a week. She rents out the spare room for $330 a week. Jane will not qualify for Accommodation Supplement as she gets more in rent than she pays. The $10.00 is charged as income.
Accommodation costs (Rent)
$320pw
Less cost of part of property not lived in
$0
Less accommodation income
$330
Equals weekly qualifying accommodation costs
$0 (-$10)
Chargeable income
$10pw
For more information see:
- Weekly qualifying accommodation costs
- Rent
- Tenant or homeowner has a boarder
- Homeowner renting out a room
- Homeowner renting out part of the property
- Social housing tenants

chunks.title: Weekly qualifying accommodation costs — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: From 2 March 2026, a client's weekly qualifying accommodation costs must be determined to assess the rate of Accommodation Supplement a client can get. Accommodation Supplement paid prior to 2 March 2026 will be based on previous settings. The weekly qualifying accommodation cost is calculated based on the client's accommodation costs, the part of the property they live in and any accommodation income they get. Accommodation costs The client's accommodation cost is the amount they pay for rent, board or home ownership. Not part of property they live in When a client doesn't live in part of their property, that part of the property is deducted from their accommodation costs when calculating the weekly qualifying accommodation costs. This includes when part of the property is: - primarily used for business purposes, - self-contained and rented to another person/s, or - rented to another person/s who does not reside there For information on how to calculate part of a property see: - Self-employed claiming home office expenses - Homeowner renting out part of their property Accommodation income When a client gets rent or board payments from someone living in the same premises, it is accommodation income and is deducted from their accommodation costs when calculating the weekly qualifying accommodation costs. Accommodation income includes: - rent a client gets from another person (not being additional occupants or boarders) residing in the same premises, except where the person paying the rent is in a self-contained part of the premises or the rent payment is part of the income of a business on the premises - 62% of payments for board a client gets from another person residing in the same premises, except where the board payment is part of the income of a business on the premises Note when accommodation income is more than the client's accommodation costs (after the deduction of the cost of any part of the property not being lived in by the client), the excess amount is income and must be charged against any financial assistance the client gets. In this case, the client will have no weekly qualifying accommodation costs and will not qualify for Accommodation Supplement.

chunks.title: Calculation — extra help > accommodation supplement
chunks.text: When calculating the weekly qualifying accommodation costs to assess Accommodation Supplement, the cost of part of the property not lived in must be deducted from the client's accommodation costs before any accommodation income. For example: Franky rents a 3-bedroom house for $850 per week. He uses his home to run a bespoke boat building business with a workshop in the double garage and a bedroom as an office. He calculates the percentage of home space used for his business to determine the business-related costs from using his home. Franky uses 45 percent of the property where he lives (135sqm/300sqm) for his bespoke boat building business and claims the portion of business home expenses of $19,890 per year ($382.50 per week) in his business accounts. Franky's friend, Chopper, also boards with him and pays $400 per week (62% of the board payment is $248 accommodation income). Franky's weekly qualifying accommodation costs for Accommodation Supplement exclude the portion of his home that he uses to run his business and are then reduced by 62% of the board payments he gets. His weekly qualifying accommodation costs are calculated as $219.50 per week. Cost of part of property not lived in Total rent costs for property Total A $850.00pw Total square metres Total B 300m2 Square metres of property that is used for business purposes Total C 135m2 Proportion of property used for business purposes Total C ÷ Total B = Total D 0.45 Cost of part of property not lived in Total A x Total D $382.50pw Accommodation income Board payment $400.00 Accommodation income (62% of the board payment) $248.00 Weekly qualifying accommodation costs Accommodation costs (rent) $850.00 Less cost of part of property not lived in $382.50 Less accommodation income $248.00 Equals weekly qualifying accommodation costs $219.50

chunks.title: Ambulance subscription fees — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Ambulance subscription fees
Instead of paying one-off ambulance fees, clients can pay a one year subscription to St Johns Ambulance. The subscription gives the client and their family's unlimited access to emergency services for one year.
If the client meets all qualifications, they may be able to receive an Advance Payment of Benefit for subscription fees.
