As an Advance Payment of Benefit is for items of particular immediate need, you should consider the following:
- whether the client and/or their family is likely to require ambulance services
- how regular an ambulance would be required by the client and/or their family
- whether there is a history of expectation of the requirement to use an ambulance
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for Ambulance Subscription fees should not be more than $200.

chunks.title: Appliances and furniture — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Appliances and furniture
If a client meets all qualifications, they can get an Advance Payment of Benefit for essential appliances and furniture. The items should be the most economical option to meet the client’s immediate and essential need.
Note fridges, fridge-freezers, freezers and washing machines (whiteware) are not included in the appliance category.
Quotes must be provided from new or second-hand retailers and must include details of the warrantee/guarantee for essential appliances.
An Advance Payment of Benefit cannot be approved to buy appliances or furniture through private sales.
As a guideline only, an Advance Payment of Benefit for appliances and furniture should not be more than $200.
## Whiteware
Fridges, fridge-freezers, freezers and washing machines (whiteware) must be purchased from a preferred supplier at the rates set in the preferred supplier arrangement.

chunks.title: Applying hardship obligations to partners — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Applying hardship obligations to partners
Hardship obligations can apply to a client and/or their partner.
It may be appropriate to apply hardship obligations to a partner when:
- previous assistance has been provided to meet the need of both the client and partner (eg food grants have been provided because both the client and partner need food)
- the partner has contributed to the need for assistance (eg where assistance with a power bill is required because both the client and partner have not paid a previous bill)
- the partner's actions are adversely affecting the client's ongoing financial position
Generally, when a partner has not taken reasonable steps or not completed a budgeting activity, an application from the client for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment will be declined unless exceptional circumstances exist.
For more information see:
- Hardship obligations
- Reasonable steps obligation
- Budgeting activity obligation
- Failure to meet hardship obligations
- Partners with youth activity obligations

chunks.title: Assessing a client's debt balance — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Assessing a client's debt balance
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, an advance would not be paid where Work and Income debt equals or exceeds the advance limits. Consideration must be given to the client's circumstances and the impact of yet another loan on the net benefit before allowing the client to go further into debt.
For example:
Advance limit$1300.00Less Advance debt balance$800.00Advance balance$500.00Less other departmental debts$700.00Total debts less Advance balance-$200.00
Advance limit
$1300.00
Less Advance debt balance
$800.00
Advance balance
$500.00
Less other departmental debts
$700.00
Total debts less Advance balance
-$200.00
Though the client has a $500 Advance balance of their 6-week advance limit left, total Work and Income debts are greater than the client's total 6-week Advance limit.
Note the clients Advance debt balance and advance balance available, are shown on the SADVI screen in SWIFTT.
You will need to check the SOFSI screen in SWIFTT to check the client's current debt level. The SOFSI screen will contain all the client's current debt balances with the exception of Liable Parent Contribution and Major Repairs Advance which you will need to check on the TRACE system.
For more information see:
- Income Related Rent and Advance Payment of Benefit

chunks.title: Assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early
If a client qualifies for an Advance Payment of Benefit it may be paid to meet the actual and reasonable costs a tenant is charged by the landlord for assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early.
An Advance Payment of Benefit cannot be more than 6 weeks of benefit entitlement unless exceptional circumstances exist. As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for costs due to assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early should not be more than $200.
Verification of the amount required for each cost, and the landlord's full name and address, must be seen.
## Types of costs
If a landlord incurs actual and reasonable costs due to assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early, they can recover the costs from the tenant.
A landlord can only charge for their actual and reasonable costs once they have provided a breakdown of the expenses to the tenant.
Not all costs a tenant may have to pay can be included in assistance paid to meet the costs of assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early.
For more information see:
## Social housing tenants
Generally, social housing tenants will not need to pay the social housing provider for costs related to assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early.
Any applications for assistance with the costs of assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early for social housing tenancies should be discussed with Helpline or your manager.

chunks.title: Attendance at funerals and tangihanga — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Attendance at funerals and tangihanga
If a client meets all qualifications, an Advance Payment of Benefit of up to $200 (as a guideline) can be made for bereaved relatives towards the expenses of attending Funerals/Tangihanga and are limited to the deceased's:
- parents (including step-parents and foster parents)
- partner (providing they were living with the deceased at the time of death)
- grandparents
- children (including grandchildren, stepchildren, foster children, mokopuna - grandchildren who have been raised by the grandparents as the principal caregivers, and whāngai - children who have been raised, normally by a relation or other person within the wider whānau to which the child belongs) and
- siblings (including half siblings and step siblings, but excluding members of organisations/gangs referring to themselves as 'blood brothers and sisters')
Assistance is not available to the deceased's:
- parents' siblings (including aunts and uncles)
- siblings' children (including nieces and nephews)
- cousins
- in-laws or
- friends
Advance Payment of Benefit's approved for funerals and tangihanga are not to include:
- assistance toward costs arising as a result of a funeral/tangihanga
- costs associated with unveiling ceremonies or
- the cost of contributing toward a koha (for example, food)
For assistance toward the cost of a funeral/tangihanga itself, see:
- Funeral Grants

chunks.title: Attending a budgeting advice service — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Attending a budgeting advice service
A client or their partner may need to attend a budgeting advice service if they have a budgeting activity obligation.
Budget advice services involve a client working with a budgeting advisor on an individual basis.
A client can self-refer to budgeting advice services at any time.
Attending a budgeting advice service may help clients who:
- have difficulty with numeracy and literacy
- speak English as a second language
- have previously completed a budgeting worksheet and attended a budgeting seminar or course
- have an ongoing deficiency in their weekly income
## Acceptable budgeting advice service
Clients should be referred to the budgeting advice services that are the most likely to help given their individual circumstances and needs.
Budgeting advice should be provided by a reputable and independent budgeting service.
## Budgeting advice requirements
Clients will often attend budgeting advice services on an ongoing basis.
Clients can be considered to be completing their budgeting activity if they can show that they have seen their budgeting advisor at least once since their last grant date, or that they are following a current budgeting advice programme or individual plan.
For more information see:
- Attending a budgeting course or seminar
- Completing a budgeting worksheet
- Budgeting activity obligation
- Reasonable steps obligation
- Failure to meet hardship obligations
- Adding plan items and resulting activities in CMS [no link find out why] procedures
- Building Financial Capability services [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Attending a budgeting course or seminar — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Attending a budgeting course or seminar
A client or partner may need to attend a budgeting course or seminar if they have a budgeting activity obligation.
Attending a budgeting course or seminar may help clients:
- who have never developed a budget before or
- who have basic budgeting skills but want to learn some tips and tricks
## Acceptable budgeting course or seminar
A budgeting course or seminar does not have to be provided by a budgeting service (eg it may be provided by another community organisation or a bank).
To be considered a budgeting activity the course or seminar must include information on:
- learning how to budget or
- developing a budget or
- improving budgeting skills
For more information see:
- Attending a budgeting advice service
- Completing a budgeting worksheet
- Budgeting activity obligation
- Reasonable steps obligation
- Failure to meet hardship obligations
- Building Financial Capability services [no link find out why] procedures
- Adding plan items and resulting activities in CMS [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Bedding — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Bedding
If a client cannot receive a Special Needs Grant for bedding, and they meet all advance qualifications, they may be able to receive an Advance Payment of Benefit.
The need for bedding must be immediate and essential.
Quotes are to be produced for new or second-hand dealers or retailers. Payment should not be approved for purchases of bedding through private sales.
If the client has been granted a Special Needs Grant for bedding, an Advance Payment of Benefit can be granted to 'top up' the payment if the client does not have exceptional circumstances to increase the maximum Special Needs Grant payable.
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for bedding should not be more than $200.

chunks.title: Beds, chairs and tables — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Beds, chairs and tables
If a client meets all qualifications, an Advance Payment of Benefit may be made for the purchase of the most economical items of essential beds, chairs and tables.
Note that beds include cots, bassinets and pepi-pods.
Quotes are to be produced from new or second-hand dealers or retailers. Payment should not be approved for purchases of furniture through private sales.
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for beds, chairs and tables should not be more than $200.

chunks.title: Budgeting activity obligation — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Clients who frequently access Advance Payments of Benefit, Special Needs Grants and Recoverable Assistance Payments may need to meet a budgeting activity obligation. This obligation requires clients to take part in activities that will help them improve their ability to budget and make the most of the resources available to them. Clients may be required to: - complete or review a budgeting worksheet - attend a budgeting course or seminar or - attend a budgeting advice service The specific activity the client is required to complete should be the activity that is most likely to meet their needs and be helpful given their personal situation. Note you must make sure the client is getting their correct entitlement at every interaction with them.

chunks.title: Applying budgeting activity obligation — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Generally clients are not required to complete a budgeting activity until after they have received Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit and/or Recoverable Assistance Payment on at least 3 grant dates during the past 12 months. Before applying a budgeting activity obligation, you need to ensure that you understand the client's circumstances and how applying the obligation could help them. A budgeting activity obligation should only be applied if you have been in contact with the client and determined: - the client is likely to benefit from completing a budgeting activity the client is likely to benefit from completing a budgeting activity - the client's financial situation could improve as a result and the client's financial situation could improve as a result and - the client has previously:been offered services to help them build their financial capability, understood how they could benefit from participating, and chose to not take up the services orused a building financial capability or similar service and their circumstances have substantially changed from when they used the service the client has previously: - been offered services to help them build their financial capability, understood how they could benefit from participating, and chose to not take up the services or - used a building financial capability or similar service and their circumstances have substantially changed from when they used the service Before applying a budgeting activity obligation, also consider: - the number of previous applications for hardship assistance and why the assistance was needed eg is there a pattern of not being able to meet regular, ongoing costs or were there a number of separate unforeseeable events? - eg is there a pattern of not being able to meet regular, ongoing costs or were there a number of separate unforeseeable events? - if the current need is related to unforeseeable events, or circumstances out of the client's control eg a recent bereavement or separation, emergency or other adverse event, etc - eg a recent bereavement or separation, emergency or other adverse event, etc - why the client has not taken up services to help them build their financial capability if previously offered If you have decided that the client should have a budgeting activity obligation, discuss which budgeting activity will be most helpful for them, make sure they know the activity they choose is an obligation and explain the consequence if they do not complete the activity. Note in some circumstances partners must also complete a budgeting activity.

chunks.title: Applying budgeting activity obligation — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: For information on when it would not be appropriate to require a client to complete a budgeting activity see: - Budgeting activity obligation not applied

chunks.title: Applying the budgeting activity obligation before the third grant date — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Generally clients are only required to complete a budgeting activity after they have received Special Needs Grants, Advance Payment of Benefit and/or Recoverable Assistance Payment on at least 3 grant dates during the past 12 months. However, you can apply the budgeting activity obligation before 3 grant dates. When deciding whether to apply the budgeting activity obligation before their third grant date you must also consider if the client has: - received repeated grants for the same costs - a history of receiving multiple hardship payments - a significant debt with the Ministry of Social Development

chunks.title: Budgeting activity obligation not applied — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Budgeting activity obligation not applied
You should not apply a budgeting activity obligation if it is unlikely to help the client and their financial situation would not improve as a result.
Clients applying for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payments who should not be required to complete a budgeting activity for a period of time, or until their circumstances change, include those who:
- have high unavoidable costs and are unlikely to benefit from the budgeting activity
- previously completed the same budgeting activity and their circumstances have not substantially changed since completing that activity
- had a recent sudden change in circumstances - eg a recent bereavement or separation
- had a temporary change in their situation - eg an unforeseen drop in income or a change in needs due to family violence

chunks.title: Car repairs — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Car repairs
If a client meets all qualifications, an Advance Payment of Benefit may be made for repairs to a vehicle when the use of a car is essential for the client, or their dependent partner and children.
The car should be considered essential due to illness, disability, employment, or lack of access to public transport.
The car should be owned by the client or their partner, and not another family member or a friend.
Assistance should not be given to approve foreseen costs (for example, fuel, warrant of fitness, car insurance, car registration), or for regular servicing costs.
## Car insurance excess
Car insurance excess is the cost a person has to pay towards their insurance claim, with the insurance company meeting the remaining cost.
If the client meets all qualifications, an Advance Payment of Benefit may be made for the cost of car insurance excess.
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for car repairs should not be more than $400.

chunks.title: Cash asset limits — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Cash asset limits
Except where exceptional circumstances exist, a client and partner (if any) cannot get an Advance Payment of Benefit if their cash assets exceed the appropriate asset limit.
Single person
Asset limit for a single person without dependent children
Married, civil union or de facto couple (with or without dependent children) or
Sole parents
Asset limit for a married, civil union or de facto couple (with or without dependent children)

chunks.title: Cash assets include — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: - bills of exchange or promissory notes - building society shares - money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society - money invested with or lent to any bank, other financial institution or person - money withdrawn from a KiwiSaver scheme - mortgage investments and other long term loans - shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds and bonds - the client's share in any partnership and - the net equity held in any property or land not used as the person's home

chunks.title: Cash assets do not include — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: - the home property and land on which it is situated - a motor vehicle principally used by the client for their personal use - a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2000, or which is used by the person or a member of their family for day to day accommodation - personal effects of the person or their partner - Christchurch mosques attack support payments - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts - Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income - Māori land where the title is in a tribal trust and individual ownership cannot be identified, the client cannot realise or readily convert the land into a cash assetNote you should consult Legal Services if you are unsure about the ownership of Māori land. - MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment) - specified Ex gratia and Compensation payments - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received A bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client. Canterbury earthquake related payments Payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12, or 24 months following the date the client received the payment.

chunks.title: Child restraints for motor vehicles, and safety helmets — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Child restraints for motor vehicles, and safety helmets
If a client meets all qualifications, Advance Payments of Benefit can be made to:
- purchase a new approved child restraint for a motor vehicle, for each child under 7 years of age who is a dependent child of the client
- hire an approved child restraint for a motor vehicle from reputable agencies, for each child under 7 years of age who is a dependent child of the client or
- purchase a new cycle safety helmet for each school aged dependent child of the client
Where the motor vehicle needs an attachment to fit the child restraint, this cost can be included in the purchase.
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for child restraints or safety helmets should not be more than $200 for each dependent child.

chunks.title: Clients getting a reduced benefit — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Clients getting a reduced benefit
If a client is receiving a reduced rate of benefit because of extra income, advance payments can be approved to an amount equivalent to 6 weeks of the full benefit rate.
If the client is receiving a non-standard rate of benefit, for example their partner is under 24 and getting Student Allowance, Advance Payments of Benefit can be approved to an amount equivalent to the full benefit rate for 6 weeks. However, consider whether the amount can be recovered in 2 years from the non-standard rate.

chunks.title: Clothing — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Clothing
If a client meets all qualifications, Advance Payments of Benefit may be made to purchase essential clothing (excluding school uniforms).
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for clothing should not be more than:
Single people$150Married, civil union or de facto couples without dependent children$300Married, civil union or de facto couples with dependent children$400Sole parents with one or more dependent children$400
Single people
$150
Married, civil union or de facto couples without dependent children
$300
Married, civil union or de facto couples with dependent children
$400
Sole parents with one or more dependent children
$400
Assistance for clothing can only be authorised to meet essential needs and this need should be met through the most economic item(s) available.

chunks.title: Completing a budgeting worksheet — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Completing a budgeting worksheet
A client or their partner may need to complete a budgeting worksheet if they have a budgeting activity obligation.
A budgeting worksheet is a written budget showing the income a person has and what bills and expenses they spend their money on.
Completing a budgeting worksheet may help clients who have difficulty managing their budget.
A budgeting worksheet may also be useful for clients who are unable to attend a budgeting course or seminar.
## Acceptable budgeting worksheet
Clients can complete any budgeting worksheet as long as it records and compares information on income and expenses.
To complete this budgeting activity a client's budget must include:
- all of their costs (and their partner's costs), including weekly, fortnightly, monthly and annual costs and
- their income from all sources
All clients will have costs related to accommodation, power, food and transport but you should also check they have included everything they spend money on throughout the year, eg school uniforms, clothing, medical bills, birthday presents, etc.
For more information see:
- Budgeting activity obligation
- Attending a budgeting advice service
- Attending a budgeting course or seminar
- Reasonable steps obligation
- Failure to meet hardship obligations
- Building Financial Capability services [no link find out why] procedures
- Adding plan items and resulting activities in CMS [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Debt types not included — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Debt types not included
Debt types not included in the maximum recovery rate of debt of $40.00 per week are:
- Child Disability Allowance debt
- Family Benefit Capitalisation debt
- Fraudulent Student Loans
- Liable Parent Contributions (LPC)
- Maintenance debt
- Major Repairs Advance (MRA)
- Residential Support Services debt
- Student Allowance debt
- Suspensory Loans
- Work Services debt

chunks.title: Dental treatment — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Dental treatment
If a client cannot get a Special Needs Grant for essential dental treatment, and they meet all qualifications, they may be able to get an Advance Payment of Benefit.
The need for dental treatment must be immediate and essential.
A client may not be able to get a Special Needs Grant because the treatment they need is not covered e.g. a crown, or they have already used the maximum in a 52-week period.
If the client has been granted a Special Needs Grant for essential dental treatment, an Advance Payment of Benefit can be granted to 'top up' the payment if the client does not have exceptional circumstances to increase the maximum Special Needs Grant payable.
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for dental treatment should not be more than $200.

chunks.title: Dentures and hearing aids — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Dentures and hearing aids
If a client meets all qualifications, an Advance Payment of Benefit can be made for dentures and hearing aids.
Subsidies may be available from District Health Boards towards the cost of dentures and hearing aids. Before considering an Advance Payment of Benefit reduce the amount required to reflect any subsidy provided by the hospital or health agency.
Advance Payments of Benefit should not be approved for any services or item where ACC or a private insurer has paid part of the fees or charges unless there is an immediate need.
The cost of the consultation can be included in the cost, but as a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for dentures or hearing aids should not be more than $1,000.

chunks.title: Duration of benefit — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Duration of benefit
In determining whether an Advance Payment of Benefit would best meet the immediate need of a client you must consider:
- whether the client is likely to continue to be in receipt of the benefit for the period over which the advance would be repayable
Consider whether the benefit is likely to continue for the period during which the advance would be recovered. Special consideration should be given to clients receiving short-term benefits such as Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.

chunks.title: Effect of not using services to build financial capability — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Effect of not using services to build financial capability
When a client applying for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment chooses to not use services to help them build their financial capability, the effect depends on whether the client:
- was offered information on the services or
- must use the service as a budgeting activity obligation
Information offered
Budgeting activity obligation required
Process
Information about services to build financial capability is offered to all clients as part of the general hardship application process.
A client or partner must use a specific service to build financial capability to meet their budgeting activity obligation.
Effect of not using services to build financial capability
There is no adverse impact if the client does not access the services offered.
The staff member will determine if the client has met their obligations through any activities completed and if not, may decline the application for hardship assistance.
For more information see:
- Offering services to build financial capability at application
- Budgeting activity obligation
- Failure to meet hardship obligations

chunks.title: Electricity, gas and water — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Electricity, gas and water
If a client meets all the qualifications, an Advance Payment of Benefit may be made to assist with:
- outstanding electricity, gas and water bills or
- the cost of reconnecting electricity, gas and water supplies
Before approving applications, other ways of meeting the costs should be investigated.
If a client is having difficulty meeting their payments their electricity or gas company should be asked by the client to check whether they are on the correct tariff.
The retailer should assist the consumer to move to their desired tariff.
The client should also have discussed with the retailer any alternative payment options available to them such as:
- payment arrangements to recover debt within a reasonable timeframe
- prepayment meters
- smoothed payments
- regular direct credits
- redirection of income
Clients do not need to be at the stage of being disconnected to be granted an Advance Payment of Benefit for electricity or gas.
Client's should be encouraged to request assistance before their electricity and gas is threatened with disconnection and reconnection costs.
## Disability Allowance or other Health Subsidy
You will need to determine if it is appropriate to make an Advance Payment of Benefit. when the costs for electricity or gas have already been included in existing Disability Allowance payments or other Health Subsidy.
Disability Allowance is only paid for the additional electricity, gas or heating costs a person has because of their disability (not the total cost).
An Advance Payment of Benefit can be considered if there is an immediate and essential need for electricity, gas or heating costs not covered by Disability Allowance or another Health Subsidy.
Where a portion of the costs was covered by Disability Allowance or another Health Subsidy, consider whether the client could reasonably have been expected to have paid that portion of the costs. If they could have, you may in your discretion decline to include those costs.
## Payment
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for electricity, gas and water should not be more than $200.
## Utility disputes
If the client has a complaint about their energy or water company they can contact Utilities Disputes. See:
- Utilities Disputes Complaint form
## Winter Energy Payment
If a client was paid Winter Energy Payment during the period that the client is seeking an Advance Payment of Benefit to assist with power or heating costs, this does not automatically stop clients from receiving assistance.
When the client has an immediate and essential need, Advance Payment of Benefit may be considered.

chunks.title: Essential home repairs — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Essential home repairs
If a client meets all qualifications, they may be able to receive an Advance Payment of Benefit:
- to carry out essential repairs and maintenance to the client's home, or to the paths, fences and retaining walls of the property on which that home is located or
- to provide essential services to the client's home such as sewerage, water or electricity connection.
In addition to the Advance Payment of Benefit qualifications, a grant for Essential Home Repairs, may not be made unless:
- the client must provide proof of ownership (or joint ownership) and occupation of the property to which the advance is to be applied,
- that the work to be done is essential in order to maintain the property in a reasonable living standard; and
- the client must show proof they unsuccessfully applied for financial assistance from any other agency that provides assistance to beneficiaries for such purposes.
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for Essential Home Repairs should not be more than $1000.

chunks.title: Example - applying hardship obligations — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Kerry has significant debt and since being granted a main benefit, she has received hardship grants to pay for both ongoing regular costs like food and power, and help with annual and unexpected costs like car repairs. Hardship application Event 1. January While attending a work focused appointment, Kerry says that she needs help to pay for food. The case manager: - finds out more about Kerry’s current financial situation, and - assesses what assistance is available and whether she is currently getting the correct payments for her circumstances - grants a Special Needs Grant for food - offers Kerry information on the building financial capability services available 2. January Kerry applies online via MyMSD for assistance with food 3 weeks after her last grant. The reasonable steps obligation is covered in MyMSD and Kerry indicates what steps she will take. Assistance is granted and she is provided with a link to information on building financial capability services via MyMSD. 3. March Kerry applies online for assistance with food again. Assistance is granted and she is provided with a link to information on building financial capability services via MyMSD. 4. April Kerry is in the service centre and asks for help with her power bill. The case manager: - talks to Kerry about her financial situation - assesses what assistance is available and whether she is currently getting the correct payments for her circumstances - discusses what Kerry has done to meet the reasonable steps obligation and what else may be possible including: setting up a direct deduction to pay for power weeklylooking for a smaller house to rent - setting up a direct deduction to pay for power weekly - looking for a smaller house to rent - grants hardship assistance for power - checks if Kerry has attended any building financial capability services - but Kerry has not - explains how the services could help and provides the information on how to access services again 5. May Kerry’s car needs repair work so she can get to work and she comes in to the service centre to get help. Kerry works rurally so the car is essential as there is no public transport in her area. The case manager discusses what Kerry did between grants to improve her financial situation. Kerry reviewed listings for several cheaper rental houses but did not set up a direct deduction. They discuss what other options may be available to help Kerry manage her money. Kerry has not taken up the offer of services to build her financial capability so information is offered again. After assessing if Kerry’s payments are correct, an Advance is approved for the car repairs.

chunks.title: Example - applying hardship obligations — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: They agree that as reasonable steps Kerry will set up the redirection, keep looking for less costly housing, and look for cheaper phone and internet options before she applies for another grant. 6. May Kerry applies online for assistance with food. She is under the limit and signals that she has done what was agreed to take reasonable steps. Assistance is granted and she is provided with a link to information on building financial capability services via MyMSD. 7. July In July Kerry comes in to the service centre as she can’t make a payment on her car loan. After assessing whether she is getting the correct payments for her circumstances, they discuss what Kerry did between grants, including: - continuing to look for cheaper housing - changing her internet plan to a cheaper one Payment is made for the car costs as Kerry has taken reasonable steps but they agree that before she applies for another grant Kerry will: - set up the direct deduction for power - look at ways to reduce her food bill via planning - look at ways to reduce power usage. Kerry has not taken up the offer of services to build her financial capability so information is offered again – the case manager strongly suggests Kerry take up the budgeting advice as it appears there are still some things she can do to improve her financial situation. 8. September Kerry comes in to the service centre to get help with her power payments as she has fallen behind and is at risk of disconnection. Kerry has not set up the direct deduction for power as discussed at previous appointments and has been struggling to reduce her food and power bills. Kerry has not accessed any of the services offered but has started looking for a job that pays more or can offer more hours. The case manager checks that Kerry is getting everything she is entitled to. Payment is made to Kerry for this month’s power bill as Kerry has taken reasonable steps. However, the case manager decides that Kerry should have a budgeting activity obligation applied as there are a number of ways for her to improve her ability to manage her money. They agree that seeing a budget advisor would be the most helpful activity and Kerry is told that she may be declined future hardship assistance if she does not complete this activity. An appointment is made for a week later to see how the activity goes. Kerry does not attend and this is noted for follow up the next time Kerry applies for hardship assistance. 9. September

chunks.title: Example - applying hardship obligations — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Two weeks later Kerry comes in for a food grant. She has not done the budgeting activity or taken reasonable steps but after discussion with the case manager about her situation, it is clear there were exceptional circumstances as Kerry has been unwell and off work for most of the last 2 weeks. A Special Needs Grant is paid and Kerry is aware she will need to attend the budgeting service. 10. October While attending another appointment, Kerry asks for help to pay for food. She has not attended the budgeting service and does not have a good reason. She is still looking for a job with more hours and cheaper housing. She is not over the limit but has met the reasonable steps obligation but not the budgeting activity obligation. She is given enough money for food until she attends the budgeting service later that week. For more information see: - Hardship obligations - Reasonable steps obligation - Budgeting activity obligation

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances
A client must have exceptional circumstances for an Advance Payment of Benefit of an amount more than 6 weeks of the full benefit entitlement.
Exceptional circumstances are those which set the client apart from others in a similar situation. The client must state what these circumstances are on the Advance Payment of Benefit application form.
In determining whether exceptional circumstances exist you must consider:
- the client's ability to repay the Advance Payment of Benefit
- whether the client could reasonably have been expected to have made provision for the particular immediate need
- whether the client is the principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver of a child of or under the age of 12 months
You should also consider the extent to which not making an Advance, or an Advance over the limit, or requiring recovery of the Advance within 24 months would:
- worsen the client's position
- increase or create any risk to the life or welfare of the client, or the client's partner or dependent children or
- cause serious hardship to the client, or the client's partner or dependent children and
- any other matters you consider relevant in the circumstances of the particular case. Example when the least amount required under a preferred supplier arrangement means they will exceed their 6 week limit
## Payment
If exceptional circumstances exist, you can:
- make an Advance when the client and partner (if any) have cash assets or income over the cash asset and income limits
- make an Advance of more than the 6-week limit or the maximum limits for Essential Home Repairs and
- recover an Advance at a lower rate than needed to repay the Advance within 24 months

chunks.title: Existing debt level — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Existing debt level
In determining whether an Advance Payment of Benefit would best meet the immediate need of a client you must consider:
- the client's existing level of debt, and whether the rate of repayment of the proposed Advance of Benefit would be manageable considering
- whether the reduction of the amount of benefit payable will leave enough for the client's living expenses and any other debt repayments and
- the likelihood it would cause the client to seek further advances or other Extra Help
If a client (and their partner, if any) has Work and Income debt equal to, or greater than the Advance limits, they would not generally qualify for payment.
Assess the existing debt balance by combining Work and Income debt totals for both the client and partner (if any).
For the purpose of determining entitlement to an advance, Work and Income debt includes the following: Special Needs Grants, Advances, Liable Parent Contribution, Major Repairs Advance and Overpayments of benefit.
Reduce the client's advance limit by their existing Work and Income debt level. For more information see:
- Assessing a client's debt balance
The client's total debt level needs to also be considered, and this includes amounts owed outside Work and Income as well (eg hire purchases, personal loans, court fines etc).
Consideration must be given to the client's circumstances and the impact of yet another loan on the net benefit. Bear in mind the client's current income/expenses and ability to live within the reduced income and the likelihood they may need further assistance if the payment is approved.

chunks.title: Failure to meet hardship obligations — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Failure to meet hardship obligations
Generally, clients who fail to meet their hardship obligations should have their application for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment declined.
This may be where they did not take reasonable steps or failed to complete a budgeting activity.
## Exception
You may approve an application for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment for a client who failed their hardship obligations if there are exceptional circumstances. This includes circumstances that prevented a client from completing their obligations.
Acceptable exceptional circumstances include:
- unforeseen hospitalisation
- seriously sick or injured
- bereavement of immediate family
- emergency or adverse event
- victim of violent crime or family violence
If a client does not have any of the above reasons you can consider whether the reason provided:
- is an unforeseen out-of-the ordinary event that could not be planned for
- is beyond the client's control or
- sets the client apart from others in a similar situation

chunks.title: Fire loss or burglary — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Fire loss or burglary
If a client meets all qualifications, an Advance Payment of Benefit can be made to assist with the cost of replacing essential items lost through fire or burglary, particularly where the person is not insured.
The burglary incident must be verified by a police report. If in doubt, a fire report may be requested to confirm loss of property because of fire.
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for fire loss or burglary should not be more than $1000.
## Preferred supplier arrangement
When a preferred supplier arrangement is in place the client must purchase the specified goods and services from a preferred supplier.
The following specified goods and services have a preferred supplier arrangement:
- fridges, freezers, fridge-freezers and washing machines (whiteware)
- glasses (optical goods and services)

chunks.title: Fridges, freezers and washing machines — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Fridges, freezers and washing machines
If a client meets all qualifications, they can get an Advance Payment of Benefit for fridges, fridge-freezers, freezers and washing machines (collectively known as whiteware).
There is a preferred supplier arrangement in place for whiteware. This means clients must purchase their whiteware from a preferred supplier.
If a client refuses to purchase from a preferred supplier the application for an Advance Payment of Benefit must be declined.
A client may purchase more than one type of goods if they meet the qualifications for both. For example, a client may purchase both a washing machine and fridge-freezer.
Assistance for repairs to whiteware should be considered under the Appliances category.
## Subsequent applications for whiteware
If a client purchases whiteware from a preferred supplier and subsequently applies for further assistance for the same item, MSD must consider what has happened to cause their need.
If the whiteware has broken down within 5 years of the date of purchase, consider whether the client has checked if help is available from the preferred supplier in accordance with:
- the warranty period or
- consumer protections in the Consumer Guarantees Act 1993
## Approval for subsequent applications
There will be some circumstances that lead to the client no longer having the original goods. For example, they have left a violent relationship and had to leave their possessions behind.

chunks.title: Glasses — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: If a client meets all qualifications, an Advance Payment of Benefit for optical goods and services (collectively known as glasses) may be made. There is a preferred supplier arrangement in place for glasses. If a client resides in an urban area covered by a preferred supplier agreement for glasses then the client must use a preferred supplier. If a client resides in an urban area with a preferred supplier for glasses and refuses to purchase from a preferred supplier, their application for an Advance Payment of Benefit must be declined. If a client resides in a non-coverage area they have the option to use a non-preferred supplier or they can travel to a preferred supplier at their own cost.

chunks.title: Clients with high clinical needs — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Some clients have high clinical needs which means the glasses they require cannot be provided at the standard contract price. Hardship assistance for a higher amount than the standard package amount can be provided for clients with high clinical needs. Some types of high clinical needs are: - vision which is outside of 'normal' ranges (+ or - 6 or higher) - severe astigmatism that requires a special lens grind - growths on eyes due to severe UV exposure - some forms of medication make eyes very sensitive to light and glasses require a special coating - prescription for glasses that are heavy and a higher grade of progressive lenses that are required to avoid frames buckling or the weight tearing the clients skin Lens coatings or glasses specifically for Irlen Syndrome are not covered by MSD or the Ministry of Health.

chunks.title: Assistance for children's glasses — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Whaikaha provide a Spectacle Subsidy for children 15 years and younger with vision problems. The subsidy is paid for each qualifying child up to $287.50 (including GST) and can be accessed annually. To qualify either the child or parent/guardian must have a Community Services Card or the child must have a High Use Health Card. The subsidy covers the eye exam, frames, lenses, eye patches and repairs. There is also an additional amount of $51.11 (including GST) available for children who need adult sized frames if the child's vision is changing quickly or if they have an amblyopia (lazy eye) or strabismus (squint). There is no discretion to top-up the Ministry of Health subsidy unless the full subsidy has been claimed within the 1-year period and the child has a high clinical need. Then a client can apply for hardship assistance for their child through MSD. These are processed using the preferred supplier arrangement.

chunks.title: Top-up payments — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: There is no discretion to pay any shortfall where the cost of the glasses has been subsidised by another agency (government or private) or is subject to an insurance claim.

chunks.title: Hardship obligations — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Hardship obligations
All clients and their partners who apply for Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit, and Recoverable Assistance Payments, may have the following hardship obligations:
- a reasonable steps obligation and/or
- a budgeting activity obligation
Generally, clients must meet any hardship obligations that have been applied to them before they can get additional hardship assistance.
These obligations do not apply to:
- payments to people in specific circumstances
- young people getting youth support payments (Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment) or
- payments to obtain or renew a driver licence
Note you must make sure the client is getting their correct entitlement at every interaction with them.
## Newborns
When a client is the principal caregiver of a child 12 months of age or younger, you must consider the presence of the newborn when deciding whether or not to apply hardship obligations. This includes a principal temporary caregiver of a child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid.
## Multiple obligations
Depending on the client’s circumstances at the time, they may have none, one or both of the hardship obligations applied to them.

chunks.title: Identifying reasonable steps — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Generally, clients who have received an Advance Payment of Benefit, Special Needs Grants and/or Recoverable Assistance Payments on 3 or more grant dates during the past 12 months must take reasonable steps before they can get any additional payments. Reasonable steps clients can take are those that will: - reduce their costs - increase their income or - improve their financial management When identifying possible reasonable steps you must consider each client's individual circumstances. When with the client, it may be useful to review any budget or budgeting worksheet that the client has previously completed to see what costs the client has and check whether they are essential. You should discuss with the client what they can do to meet the reasonable steps obligation. Note clients are only required to take specific actions for their reasonable steps when you have discussed the actions with them, e.g. setting an automatic payment to pay for power.

chunks.title: Examples of reasonable steps — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Reasonable steps could include (but are not limited) to: - seeking part-time or full-time paid employment, or increasing hours to increase income - having their Child Support payments reviewed (especially if they have a reduction in income) - cancelling non-essential services e.g. Pay TV services - quitting smoking - Quitline can provide support, information, and low cost nicotine patches, gum, and lozenges - 0800 778 778 - reducing regular costs by moving to cheaper alternatives eg moving to cheaper accommodation or taking up a less expensive phone or internet plan, or using public transport when those costs are cheaper than the cost of using a private vehicle - renegotiating debt repayments to a lesser repayment amount e.g. court fines - refinancing or consolidating debt to reduce interest and repayment amounts - suspending contributions to KiwiSaver and/or other voluntary retirement schemes - setting up a separate account and/or automatic payments for bills - agreeing to MSD setting up a redirection of benefit where there is good cause Note if the client has completed reasonable steps for Temporary Additional Support, the client should generally be considered to have met the reasonable steps obligation at the next application for a Special Needs Grant, Recoverable Assistance Payment, or Advance Payment of Benefit. You need to check the CMS notes to confirm what steps have been taken.

chunks.title: Some budgeting activities may be considered reasonable steps — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: A client can voluntarily complete a budgeting activity such as doing a budgeting worksheet or seeing a budgeting advisor as a reasonable step. Clients can also be considered to have met their reasonable steps obligation for a Special Needs Grant if they recently completed a budgeting activity obligation for an Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment.

chunks.title: Meeting reasonable steps obligation — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Clients have met their obligation if they have taken reasonable steps to reduce their costs, increase their income or improve their financial management since their previous grant date.

chunks.title: Immediate and essential needs — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Immediate and essential needs
In order for a client to be considered for an Advance Payment of Benefit they must be able to identify a particular immediate need for an essential item or service.
In determining if a particular immediate need exists, consider:
- the effect on the client and partner or dependent children (if any) if the need is not met
- when that effect might be expected to impact on that or those persons
- the client's ability to meet the need from their own resources
- the assistance that is or might be available to the client from other sources or other Extra Help from Work and Income that may be available to the client to meet the particular immediate need
- the client's existing level of debt, and whether the rate of repayment of the proposed Advance of Benefit would be manageable considering:
- whether the reduction of the amount of benefit payable will leave enough for the client's living expenses and any other debt repayments and
- the likelihood it would cause the client to seek further advances or other Extra Help
- whether the client is likely to continue to be in receipt of the benefit for the period over which the Advance would be repayable and
- any other matters put forward by the client to justify the advance
Consideration must be given to all the circumstances and other sources of assistance available to the client.

chunks.title: Income limit — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Income limit
Except where exceptional circumstances exist a client and partner (if any) cannot get an Advance Payment of Benefit if their income exceeds the appropriate income limits.
If a client is getting an income-tested benefit, they would generally meet the income test for an Advance Payment of Benefit.
For New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients you should check their income does not exceed the appropriate income limit. New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension must be included as income when assessing eligibility for these clients.
Winter Energy Payment is not considered income when assessing eligibility for an Advance Payment of Benefit.

chunks.title: Income Related Rent debt and Advance Payment of Benefit — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Income Related Rent debt and Advance Payment of Benefit
Income Related Rent debt is not used when determining the amount of Advance Payment of Benefit available.
Income Related Rent debt is considered when deciding if an Advance Payment of Benefit is the best option and the client's ability to repay it.
For more information see:
- Existing debt level
- Assessing a client's debt balance

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Introduction
All clients getting a main benefit, Orphans Benefit, Unsupported Childs Benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension who need assistance to meet a particular immediate need for an essential item or service, may get an Advance of up to 6 weeks of their benefit.
Consideration must be given to whether an Advance would best meet their immediate need. You must investigate other sources of assistance to meet the immediate need, and consider the client's ability to repay the Advance. This includes when an essential need is provided under the Advance Payment of Benefit categories.

chunks.title: Item or service not in client's name — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Item or service not in client's name
Generally, immediate and essential needs are considered for an Advance Payment of Benefit only if the item or service is in the client's or their family's (if any) name. Essential items or services not in the client's or partner's name are not considered for an advance as the client or partner is not liable for the payments.
## Exception
There may be situations where a client or their partner (if any) has entered into an informal arrangement with another person to pay for an essential item or service using the other person's name and/or credit rating for the contract.
You need to be satisfied that the client or their partner is the person with the immediate and essential need and is required to make the payment for the item or service. You must also be satisfied that it is or was the intention of the parties to the informal arrangement, that the client or their partner would have responsibility for the payments and the use and control of the essential item or service.
A full statement from the client or partner and the other person named in the contract is required along with a copy of the agreement to determine if the cost can be considered for an advance.
Note in these situations the client is not able to meet the cost of the item or service from their own resources and the need must be immediate and essential.

chunks.title: Laser therapy for the removal of birthmarks — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Laser therapy for the removal of birthmarks
If a client cannot receive a Special Needs Grant for laser therapy for the removal of birthmarks, and they meet all qualifications, they may be able to receive an Advance Payment of Benefit.
The need for removal of birthmarks must be immediate and essential.
If the client has been granted a Special Needs Grant for laser therapy for the removal of birthmarks, an Advance Payment of Benefit can be granted to 'top up' the payment if the client does not have exceptional circumstances to increase the maximum Special Needs Grant payable.
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for laser therapy for removal of birthmarks should not be more than $200.

chunks.title: Maximum debt recovery rate — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Maximum debt recovery rate
The recommended maximum recovery rate for clients currently getting income support is no more than $40 a week, unless the client volunteers to pay more.
Debt types included in this maximum recovery rate are:
- Advance Payment of Benefit
- Recoverable Assistance for Study Costs
- Housing Support Products
- Special Needs Grant and
- overpayments of benefit
If the client does not wish to exceed this maximum recovery rate you will need to adjust the repayment rate or reduce the other debt recovery rates so that the total is no more than $40.00.
## Client volunteers to pay more
If the client wishes to pay more than $40.00 a week they need to put this in writing, which then needs to be scanned and linked to the client event note.
## Other debt information
The SOFSI screen in SWIFTT will automatically display:
- all debts being repaid from the client's current benefits (excluding Child Disability Allowance)
- the total amount owing on all debts and
- the total weekly amount of repayments
You can view the debts for a particular benefit/pension type by entering the benefit/pension code.
For more information see:
- Debt types not included

chunks.title: Offering services to build financial capability at application — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Offering services to build financial capability at application
When clients apply for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment they will be offered information on services to help them build their financial capability, eg help them manage their money.
For more information see:
- Building Financial Capability services [no link find out why] procedures
- Hardship Assistance [no link find out why] procedures
## Clients who do not use the services offered
When clients apply for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment and are offered information on services to help them build their financial capability, the client can choose not to use them as they are optional.
If a client chooses not to use the services offered this is not a reason to fail a client's reasonable steps or budgeting activity obligation.
A client can be required to complete budgeting activities, including those provided by building financial capability services only if they have:
- had a budgeting activity obligation applied and
- been told about the obligation and what they must do to meet it

chunks.title: Other sources of assistance — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Other sources of assistance
Before making an Advance Payment of Benefit, MSD should discuss other options with the client that they may not have considered.
Some examples may include (but are not limited to):
- meeting the need from the next income payment due
- assistance from other government agencies
- arranging automatic payments
- negotiating payment of accounts by instalments
- hire purchase
- other income assistance
Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.
## Other income assistance
MSD must also check to see if the client qualifies for any other assistance before granting an Advance Payment of Benefit (including when the essential need is specified in the Advance categories).
For example:
- when there is an emergency need, or when the client or their family would suffer serious hardship without the item or service, it may be more appropriate to grant Special Needs Grant- other emergency grants if the item is not specified as an essential or emergency need, and there are special circumstances. This could be recoverable or non-recoverable.
- when a client needs help to get accommodation or is at risk of losing their existing accommodation, MSD should consider Housing Support Products
- when a client has an emergency housing need, MSD should consider granting an Emergency Housing Grant
Consider:
- Special Needs Grants when urgent assistance is needed to relieve immediate hardship
- Emergency Housing Grant when a client cannot access other accommodation adequate for their needs
- Accommodation Supplement
- Disability Allowance
- Temporary Additional Support
- Assistance to transition into employment
- Housing Support Products
If you need help deciding whether the client qualifies for other assistance contact Helpline.
## Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora assistance
An Advance Payment of Benefit can be approved to assist with items partially subsidised by Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora where the client still has to pay a shortfall. For example, spectacles, dentures, hearing aids. Payment is for the unsubsidised portion only.
## Student assistance
Consider the balance of any Student Loan available. Consideration should be given to declining the application if this option has not been exhausted.
Note under no circumstances are students to be told to apply for institution hardship funds.
Students may qualify for a Special Needs Grant.

chunks.title: Partners with youth activity obligations — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Partners with youth activity obligations
A young partner of a main beneficiary who has youth activity obligations may also have hardship obligations when they are applying for a Special Needs Grants or Advance Payment of Benefit.
However, where a young partner is engaged with a service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service they will already be meeting the reasonable steps and budgeting activity obligations because as part of their youth activity obligations they must:
- participate in ongoing discussions with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service about their budget (which would include talking about ways they can stay within their budget and potentially reduce their costs)
- undertake a budgeting programme
Note a service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service may provide support for the young person's circumstances but they may not know the full circumstances of the family and therefore this support should only be used as one piece of the information.
For more information about the youth activity obligations that apply to young partners see:
- Youth activity obligations in the relevant main benefit

chunks.title: Payment categories — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: The amount of an Advance Payment of Benefit should be the least amount required to meet the client's particular immediate need. Advances should be used to buy the most economical item available, not expensive items of furniture or appliances. Advances can be paid for new or used appliances. Appliances do not include fridges, fridge-freezers, freezers and washing machines (collectively known as whiteware). These items must be considered under the fridges, freezers and washing machines category. Advances should generally not be approved if the amount available is insufficient to cover the full cost of the essential item or service. Advances should not be approved to pay a deposit on an item.

chunks.title: Advance category guideline limits — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: The following list is a guideline only for the amount of an Advance Payment of Benefit. If an essential item or service is not on the list, use a payment of $200 as a guideline. Further details are listed under each category: Category Guideline Ambulance subscription fees $200 Appliances and furniture (excluding whiteware) $200 Assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early $200 Attendance at funerals and tangihanga $200 Bedding* $200 Beds, chairs and tables $200 Car repairs $400 Child restraints for motor vehicles, and safety helmets $200 Clothing single client without children $150 couple without children $300 sole parent or couple with children $400 Dental treatment* $200 Dentures and hearing aids $1,000 Electricity, gas and water $200 Essential home repairs $1,000 Fire loss or burglary $1,000 Fridges, freezers and washing machines (whiteware) at rates set in the preferred supplier arrangement Glasses if a client lives in an urban area with a preferred supplier $280 if a client lives in a non-coverage area and chooses to use a non-preferred supplier $1,000 Laser therapy for the removal of birthmarks* $200 Safety footwear $130 School costs $200 School stationery $200 School uniforms (for each dependent child) $300 Telephone installation $200 Tenancy tribunal fees $28 Travel for stranded clients $200 *Consider first a non-recoverable Special Needs Grant when the client qualifies for a Special Needs Grant for the cost.

chunks.title: Housing assistance — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: The "Bond and rent" category was removed on 13 March 2023. If a client needs help to get or retain rental housing, they may qualify for assistance under the Housing Support Programme. Clients who do not qualify for Housing Support Products due to the type of housing they need assistance for (e.g. non-rental housing), MSD can consider whether the client qualifies for assistance under "Other".

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Payment
The amount of an Advance Payment of Benefit should be the least amount required to meet the client's particular immediate need.
Advances can be paid for new or used appliances excluding fridges, fridge-freezers, freezers and washing machines (collectively known as whiteware).
When there is a preferred supplier arrangement in place MSD should consider the least amount required within the range of specified goods and services.
Every Advance Payment of Benefit paid for goods or services must be paid to the seller of those goods or services.
The seller must be a reputable supplier, for example a GST registered supplier or an established trustworthy business.
Payments cannot be made for private sales.
## Preferred supplier arrangement
When a preferred supplier arrangement is in place the payment must be made directly to the preferred supplier by direct credit or payment card.
MSD currently has preferred supplier arrangements in place for whiteware and optical goods and services.
## Dependent children
In exceptional circumstances only, Advance Payment of Benefit for goods and services can be paid to the client or to a parent or caregiver who applies for assistance on behalf of a dependent child.
## Maximum limit
Except where exceptional circumstances exist, a payment must not exceed:
- 6 weeks of the client's full benefit rate
A client can get more than one advance at any time, as long as the outstanding balance does not exceed the 6-week limit at any one time.
The maximum limit is not restricted to a 52-week period. The 6 week limit is assessed at each advance application. Consider the client's current debt balances and expected duration of benefit as at the advance application date.

chunks.title: Preferred supplier arrangement - fridges, freezers and washing machines — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Preferred supplier arrangement - fridges, freezers and washing machines
The following specified goods have a preferred supplier arrangement:
- fridges
- fridge-freezers
- freezers
- washing machines
The preferred supplier arrangement includes the following services in the purchase price:
- delivery
- installation
- removal of old goods if required
- repairs or replacement of goods while under warranty
- loan goods if needed while goods are being repaired, or assessed for repair
- disposal of any packaging

chunks.title: Preferred supplier arrangement - glasses — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Preferred supplier arrangement - glasses
The Ministry of Social Development has a preferred supplier arrangement with selected optometrists and opticians to supply glasses to people in some urban areas.
If a client who resides in an urban area covered by a preferred supplier arrangement for glasses (optical goods and services) refuses to purchase from a preferred supplier, the application for an Advance Payment of Benefit must be declined.
The preferred supplier arrangement includes the following goods and services in the purchase price:
Goods
- spectacle frames
- spectacle lenses
- ready to wear spectacles
- spectacle protection cases
- spectacle care products
Services
- eye examinations
- fitting of spectacle frames, spectacle lenses and ready to wear spectacles
- fitting of spectacle lenses to frames supplied by the purchaser
- adjustment of spectacle frames, spectacle lenses and ready to wear spectacles

chunks.title: Preferred supplier arrangements — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Preferred supplier arrangements
When a preferred supplier arrangement is in place the client must purchase the specified goods and services from a preferred supplier.
The following specified goods and services have a preferred supplier arrangement:
- fridges, fridge-freezers, freezers and washing machines (whiteware)
- glasses (optical goods and services)
When a client applies for an Advance Payment of Benefit for one of the specified goods or services they must be told about the preferred supplier arrangement. MSD must also provide this information in writing to the client.
## Whiteware
If a client refuses to purchase from a preferred supplier the application for Advance Payment of Benefit must be declined.
## Glasses
If a client who resides in an urban area that is covered by a preferred supplier arrangement for glasses (optical goods and services) refuses to purchase from a preferred supplier the application for an Advance Payment of Benefit must be declined.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To get an Advance Payment of Benefit a client must:
- be getting a main benefit, Orphans Benefit, Unsupported Childs Benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension
- have an immediate and essential need
- have met any hardship obligations that have been applied to them
- meet an income and asset test and
- purchase goods and services from a preferred supplier when there is an arrangement in place

chunks.title: Reasonable steps obligation — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Reasonable steps obligation
Clients who frequently access Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit, and Recoverable Assistance Payments may have to meet a reasonable steps obligation. This obligation means clients need to take personal responsibility for managing their money and take steps to:
- reduce their costs
- increase their income or
- improve their financial management
Note you must make sure the client is getting their correct entitlement at every interaction with them.
## Applying reasonable steps obligation
Generally, clients who have received Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit, and/or Recoverable Assistance Payments on 3 or more grant dates during the past 12 months must take reasonable steps before they get any additional payments.
Reasonable steps are actions that increase their income, reduce their costs, or improve their financial management.
You should let clients know at their third grant date and each subsequent grant date that they must take reasonable steps before they can get further assistance.
Note in some circumstances partners must also take reasonable steps.
## Applying reasonable steps obligation before third grant date
Generally clients are only required to take reasonable steps after they have received Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit and/or Recoverable Assistance Payments on at least 3 grant dates during the past 12 months. However, you can apply the reasonable steps obligation before 3 grant dates.
When deciding whether to apply the reasonable steps obligation before their third grant date you must also consider if the client has:
- received repeated grants for the same costs
- a history of receiving multiple hardship payments
- a significant debt with the Ministry of Social Development
For more information see:
- Identifying reasonable steps
- Failure to meet hardship obligations
- Hardship obligations
- Budgeting activity obligation
- Example - applying hardship obligations
- Applying hardship obligations to partners

chunks.title: Recovery of payment — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Recovery of payment
Every Advance Payment of Benefit is to be recovered from the client at a rate that will ensure the Advance Payment of Benefit is repaid within 24 months, unless exceptional circumstances exist.
The exception to this is Advance Payment of Benefit for safety footwear.
An Advance Payment of Benefit for safety footwear when the client gets a Participation Allowance for attending a Job Seeker Development Activity should be recovered at $5.00 or more a week, unless exceptional circumstances exist.
When a client has other debts, priority should be given to recovery of the Advance Payment of Benefit and recoverable assistance.
When a client is suffering hardship, you can consider reducing their current debt repayments.
## Recovery rate
The rate of recovery must be negotiated with the client, considering all their circumstances.
When setting the rate of recovery, you need to consider the following factors (where relevant):
- the circumstances of the client and their dependents
- the ability of the client to meet their needs and the needs of their dependents
- the amount of the debt - we want clients to pay off their debts as fast as they can, but always bear in mind the circumstances of the client and their ability to repay without placing them in undue hardship. If the debt is large you should consider a higher repayment rate if the client can afford to pay
- the effect the rate of recovery will have on the client's ability to support themselves
- whether the rate of recovery would cause undue hardship to the client or their dependents
- the effect the rate of recovery would have on the client's ability to fulfil their work and social obligations e.g. ensuring their child is enrolled with a Health Practitioner or enrolled with a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation if required to do so
- the ability of the client to get a further Advance Payment of Benefit or recoverable assistance if needed
If the client does not agree with the rate of repayment you must record why you decided to set it at that rate.
It is important that the client knows what amount will be deducted from their benefit, and when the deductions will end.
## Reducing an existing recovery rate
When possible, Advance Payment of Benefit needs to be recovered within 24 months to maximise clients' access to further Advance Payment of Benefits.
Clients, who request a reduction of their recovery rate that will extend beyond 24 months, must be considered against and meet the exceptional circumstances criteria.

chunks.title: Safety footwear — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Safety footwear
If a client meets all qualifications, an Advance Payment of Benefit may be made to a client who:
- is a client with work obligations who is required to participate in an activity that involves undertaking work
- is a client who participates in an Activity in the Community [no link find out why] project that involves undertaking work and has agreed to do so
