- is required for the client's safety while participating in that activity, by the provider of the work to wear safety footwear not supplied by that provider
- does not already own suitable safety footwear and
- could not participate in the activity without purchasing safety footwear
A client may not be refused an Advance Payment of Benefit under this category because of their existing debt level or the expected duration of their benefit.
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for Safety Footwear should not be more than $130.
Where the client receives a Participation Allowance for participating in an Activity in the Community, an Advance Payment of Benefit under this category should be recovered at a rate of $5.00 or more a week, unless exceptional circumstances exist.

chunks.title: School costs — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Schools may request payment for costs such as: - school donations - computing equipment - school camps and trips - attendance dues - other core education goods and services

chunks.title: Applicants — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Applicants for this type of assistance can include: - clients (for their dependent children) - a young person getting Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment or - the partner of a specified beneficiary who has youth activity obligations and is attending secondary school Note a sole parent getting Young Parent Payment may be able to get education and employment-related training assistance to meet their additional training costs. For more information see: - Education and employment-related training [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Clients getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: If a client getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit applies for school costs, check if they've applied for the School and Year Start-up Payment. If they have not applied, and the application window is still open, help them make an application. See: - School and Year Start-up Payments If the client did get the School and Year Start-up Payment for the child, establish if the need for school costs have been meet. If not, you can consider the Advance Payment of Benefit if they meet the qualifications. Note generally receipts are not needed to show how the School and Year Start-up Payment was used.

chunks.title: School donations — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Advance Payment of Benefit is not available for school donations that are part of the core learning programme (curriculum). This is because donations are voluntary (parents/caregivers have a choice to pay) so they don't meet the immediate and essential needs criteria. If a client applies for assistance to pay school donations, we should make sure the client understands this cost is voluntary (they have a choice to pay), and let them know the school cannot stop their child being included in all aspects of the curriculum. For more information see:

chunks.title: School camps, school trips and health camps — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Advance Payment of Benefit is not available for school camps, school trips or health camps that are part of the core learning programme (curriculum). These payments are voluntary (parents/caregivers have a choice to pay) so are not immediate and essential needs.

chunks.title: Core goods and services costs that are not donations — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Costs that are not part of donations (that is, are not voluntary) can still be considered for assistance where the client has an immediate and essential need. These can include (but not limited to) costs for some core goods and services: - stationery eg exercise books and pads, pens, pencils, computing equipment etc - subject workbooks eg, Maths, English, Physics - school/kura uniform (purchased from the uniform shop or second-hand) - some competitions eg Otago Maths - attendance dues - only for state-integrated schools or kura - after-hours/lunchtime/weekend cultural or sports activities - attending non-curriculum performances eg visiting drama or music groups - course materials that parents have agreed to purchase eg, a take-home component like a letterbox, item of clothing

chunks.title: Computing equipment (devices) — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Access to devices is a key part of digital learning and is becoming common in schools. Digital technology skills, knowledge and capabilities are necessary for our increasing digital society and economy. Schools or kura may ask students to bring their own (BYOD) computing equipment, eg an iPad, laptop or tablet. If the school makes this a requirement, in the first instance they should be supporting those families and students who may not be able to afford them, eg having a school set available for students to use. Advance assistance for devices can be considered where a parent/caregiver has identified an immediate and essential need for the child to have their own device. This could include (but not limited to): - a child has a specific learning needs and having their own device supports their learning both at school and at home - they need specialist software installed eg, voice technology - the child is taking a specialist subject eg graphics and needs a device with certain specifications - a child is expected to do extra work after school hours, and this is easiest done on a device For clients getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit see:

chunks.title: Attendance dues — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: State-integrated schools have the same core learning programme (curriculum) as state schools but have their own special character (usually a philosophical or religious belief). Attendance dues cover the property related costs of the school and are compulsory for students attending a state-integrated school or kura. Advance Payment of Benefit can be considered if the client meets the qualifications.

chunks.title: School or Kura Donations Scheme — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: The School Donations Scheme allows decile 1-7 state and state-integrated schools to opt-in to get $150 per domestic student (aged 5-19) per year if the school agrees not to ask parents/caregivers for donations (excluding school camps). As donations are voluntary (parents/caregivers have a choice if they pay), no hardship assistance is available for clients whether their school has opted in or not (including decile 8–10 schools). If the parent/caregiver chooses not to pay the donation, the child cannot be stopped from attending an activity if it is part of the core learning programme (curriculum). If any schools insist the donation must be paid (all schools), please tell the client to talk to the Ministry of Education so they can follow up with the school directly: - school.donations@education.govt.nz For more information see: - Ministry of Education Fees and charges at school

chunks.title: School camps — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Schools/Kura can continue to ask for donations for overnight school camps if they are part of the core learning programme (curriculum), but they cannot insist on payment. This applies whether the school has opted-in to the donations scheme or not. In these instances, no hardship assistance is available to clients regardless of whether their school has opted in or not (including decile 8 - 10 schools). If the parent/caregiver chooses not to pay the donation, the child cannot be stopped from attending an activity if it's part of the core learning programme (curriculum). Parents/caregivers may still need assistance to cover specific items for school camp eg a raincoat or an additional pair of shoes. Hardship assistance can be considered in these circumstances if they qualify. For more information see: - Advance Payment of Benefit

chunks.title: What parents can and cannot be asked to pay — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: The below table shows what parents/caregivers can and can't be asked to pay (note, this is not an exhaustive list).

chunks.title: Core goods/services — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: - Stationery e.g. exercise books and pads, pens, pencils etc (there is no obligation to purchase this from the school) - School or Kura uniform - Exam fees (excluding NCEA) - Attendance dues - only for state-integrated schools or kura

chunks.title: Optional materials/resources — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: - Optional workbooks - Purchase of non-compulsory hardware or software e.g. tablet, laptop - Purchase of school or kura magazine - School photos

chunks.title: Optional activities — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: - Charge/fee for optional event e.g. weekend ski trip, school or kura ball - After-hours/lunchtime/weekend culture or sports activity e.g. music tuition and instrument hire, school sports team (including uniform fees).

chunks.title: Camps, Trips and Outside Education — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: - Overnight camp or field trip as part of a specific course e.g. Year 12 Outdoor Education or Year 13 Geography trip - Overnight camp as part of the core learning programme (curriculum) e.g. Year 9 orientation camp or primary school year 7-8 camp.

chunks.title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: - Access to school network - Use of school hardware - Contributions towards devices such as tablets, smartphones, netbooks, laptops, Chrome Books - Software or software licenses - Calculators

chunks.title: Programmes and Courses — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: - English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) - Reading Recovery and Learning Support - High school 'subject fees' - Specialist units e.g. Montessori, Te Reo etc - Supplementary programmes e.g. Mathletics

chunks.title: Resources — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: - Textbooks - Workbooks (compulsory) - Photocopying/printing as part of the Core Learning Programme (curriculum)

chunks.title: Swimming — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: - Swimming classes as part of the core learning programme (curriculum - either onsite or offsite)

chunks.title: Checking if schools have opted in — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text: Schools or Kura will decide each year whether to opt-in to the donations scheme or not. Staff can check if a school has opted-in by: - checking Education Counts Find your nearest school and - searching the school's name Whether a school has opted-in or not will show in the 'Donations' information: - Opted-in: 'Donations should not be requested, unless for a school camp' - not opted-in (doesn't qualify): 'Donations may be requested'

chunks.title: School stationery — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## School stationery
When all the qualifications are met, an Advance Payment of Benefit to assist with the cost of essential school or training stationery/materials can be made to:
- client's for their dependent children
- a young person receiving Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment or
- the partner of a specified beneficiary who has youth activity obligations and attending secondary school
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for school or training stationery/materials should not be more than $200 for each dependent child, young person or partner.
## Clients receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit
Check if a client has applied for a School and Year Start-up Payment if a client receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit applies for an Advance for school costs between the first Monday after the 10th January and the last day of February. If the client has not applied for a School and Year Start-up Payment, assist the client to make an application for the School and Year Start-up Payment.
When a client has received a School and Year Start-up Payment for a child, discuss with the client if the need for assistance with school stationery has been met. If the need for school stationery has not been met, consider the advance using the usual process.
Note generally no receipts are required to show how the School and Year Start-up Payment was used.
## Sole parent receiving Young Parent Payment
A sole parent receiving Young Parent Payment may be able to receive education and employment-related training to meet their additional training costs. For more information see:
- Education and employment-related training
For more information see:
- Immediate and essential needs
- Existing debt level
- School uniforms
- School costs
- Exceptional circumstances
- School and Year Start-up Payment

chunks.title: School uniforms — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## School uniforms
When all the qualifications are met, an Advance Payment of Benefit to purchase school uniforms can be made to:
- clients for their dependent children
- a young person receiving Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment or
- the partner of a specified beneficiary who is subject to youth activity obligations and attending secondary school
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for school uniforms should not be more than $300 for each dependent child, young person or partner.
## Clients receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit
Check if a client has applied for a School and Year Start-up Payment. Clients getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit can apply for a School and Year Start-Up Payment for a school uniform between the first Monday after the 10th January and the last day of February. If the client has not applied for a School and Year Start-up Payment, assist the client to make an application for the School and Year Start-up Payment.
When a client has received a School and Year Start-up Payment for a child, discuss with the client if the need for assistance with a school uniform has been met. If the need for a school uniform has not been met, consider the advance using the usual process.
Note generally no receipts are required to show how the School and Year Start-up Payment was used.
## Sole parent receiving Young Parent Payment
A sole parent receiving Young Parent Payment may be able to receive Education and employment-related training to meet their additional training costs. See:
- Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme Education and employment-related training [no link find out why] process
For more information see:
- Immediate and essential needs
- Existing debt level
- School stationery
- School costs
- Exceptional circumstances
- School and Year Start-up Payment

chunks.title: Telephone installation — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Telephone installation
If a client meets all qualifications, an Advance Payment of Benefit may be made to assist with the cost of telephone installations, providing a telephone is essential for:
- the maintenance of the client's or their partner's, or their dependent child's health
- to access emergency assistance or
- because of geographical isolation, age or psychological condition of the client, client's partner or dependent child
As a guideline, an Advance Payment of Benefit for telephone installation should not be more than $200.
Note usually clients can make arrangements with the respective Telephone Company to pay the connection fee by instalments.

chunks.title: Tenancy Tribunal fees — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Tenancy Tribunal fees
Tenancy Services charges a flat fee of $28 (including GST) for all applications. Where a tenant wishes to take action against their landlord, they will have to pay this fee before any proceedings can be taken.
It is expected that most clients will be able to fund this application fee. However, a client may be able to receive an Advance Payment of Benefit if they meet the qualifications.
Applications for Tenancy Tribunal fees must be supported by a Tenancy Tribunal application form that has been validated by Tenancy Services (either by a stamp or a confirmation slip or letter).
The tear off portion of the Tenancy Tribunal application form should be retained and attached to the Advance Payment of Benefit application form.
## Process for recording payments
You should add the client's Tenancy Tribunal reference number in the invoice field.
The correct supplier is: Tenancy Tribunal Fee, supplier no. 312916, bank account 03 0539 0207670 00.

chunks.title: Travel for stranded clients — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Travel for stranded clients
If a client meets all qualifications, an Advance Payment of Benefit of not more than $200 can be made for the client to return to their usual place of residence where they are:
- stranded away from their usual place of residence; and
- unable to pay for travel due to circumstances which could not reasonably have been foreseen
If the client's spouse or partner and/or dependent child/ren are together with the client in the above circumstances, an advance payment of not more than $200.00 for each such dependent can be made.
If the partner of a client is stranded by themselves they can apply for an advance payment of benefit in their own right.
If the client is using public transport and has a Community Services Card, they can get a 50% discount on public transport fares for themselves through Community Connect.
## Payment
Except where exceptional circumstances exist:
- payment cannot exceed $200 for each person
- payment is restricted to one for the same or similar purpose in any 52 week period
These payments are to cover the most economical mode of transport.

chunks.title: Types of costs that can be included — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Types of costs that can be included
Landlords can require tenants to pay the actual and reasonable costs incurred due to agreeing to assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early. Depending on the specific situation, this may include costs such as:
- advertising for new tenants
- completing credit checks for new tenants
- labour costs - e.g. the landlord's time to check references, complete the required paperwork or undertake the final inspection, or the property manager's fees for their time for these activities
- the rent lost until a new tenant is found
## Types of costs not included
The following costs cannot be included by landlords as costs due to assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early, and cannot be included in assistance paid to meet the costs of assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early:
- blanket fees for assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early (i.e. set fees that do not correspond to actual and reasonable costs incurred by the landlord)
- costs that are not directly related to assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early, such as cleaning costs, rent arrears, costs to repair damages to the property
Other assistance may be available for costs at the end of a tenancy that cannot be included as costs due to assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early. For example, if the client qualifies and the costs relate to the bond for a new tenancy, it may be paid as a Housing Support Product, Bond Grant.
## Costs are not reasonable
If a tenant thinks the costs they are being asked to meet are not reasonable, they may choose to discuss this with their landlord and/or dispute the amount through the Tenancy Tribunal under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986.
Note if a client disputes the amount the landlord is charging, they may qualify for assistance to meet the costs of lodging the dispute with the Tenancy Tribunal.
If you are unsure if a cost can be included, contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances and the specific cost before deciding whether to grant the assistance.

chunks.title: Youth support payments and hardship obligations — extra help > advance payment of benefit
chunks.text:
## Youth support payments and hardship obligations
A young person receiving Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment will not have hardship obligations when they are applying for a Special Needs Grant or an Advance Payment of Benefit.
These young people already have budgeting obligations and youth money management as part of their youth activity obligations.

chunks.title: Calculating rate — extra help > away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Calculating rate
An Away From Home Allowance is assessed using a child's weekly qualifying accommodation costs. This is calculated by reducing the accommodation costs (rent or board) by the cost of any part of the property not lived in and any accommodation income they get.
An Away From Home Allowance is paid when the child's weekly qualifying accommodation costs are more than the entry threshold.
For every dollar paid over the entry threshold the client can receive a 70% subsidy.
This subsidy has a limit which differs from region to region.
The amount that a client can receive for their child's costs may be reduced depending on the level of the client's income or assets.
For more information see:
- Weekly qualifying accommodation costs
- Example
For information about board and rent see:
- Accommodation Supplement Board
- Accommodation Supplement Rent

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text: Clients (and children that Away from Home Allowance is paid for) can be absent from New Zealand and continue to get payment for the first 28 days of any absence if it does not affect the client's qualification for Away from Home Allowance. The client and child do not have to travel overseas together to continue Away from Home Allowance. Where one or the other travels overseas ensure that the child continues to meet the definition of dependent child and the caregiver continues to be the principal caregiver. When the child is overseas you will need to check that the child's accommodation costs are continuing and the course has not finished. To pay Away from Home Allowance while the client is absent from New Zealand depends on whether the client is also getting a main benefit.

chunks.title: Clients getting a main benefit — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text: All clients getting a main benefit must advise MSD before they leave New Zealand. If the client or partner does not advise MSD before their international travel, their benefit payments (including Away from Home Allowance) must stop. When a client is paid their main benefit while they are absent from New Zealand (either because they meet the criteria for approved travel or the requirement to approved travel does not apply to them) they can continue to receive their main benefit and their Away from Home Allowance for up to 28 days in any 52 week period, unless they meet the criteria to be paid their main benefit for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. Clients who do not continue to receive main benefit while overseas (because they do not meet the criteria for approved travel) may still be able to continue to receive Away from Home Allowance, if their absence does not affect the client's eligibility for this assistance and they advised MSD of their absence prior to their international travel. This is limited to 28 days in a 52 week period. For more information about Absence from New Zealand see: - Approved travel reasons in relevant main benefit - Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period in relevant main benefit

chunks.title: Clients getting non-beneficiary Extra Help — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text: Clients who are getting Away from Home Allowance and who are not also getting a main benefit: - are required to advise of their departure from New Zealand and - can be absent and paid their Away from Home Allowance for up to 28 days per absence where it does not affect the client's eligibility for Away from Home Allowance, that is where they have continuing accommodation costs

chunks.title: Information required from client when advising they intend to travel — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text: When a client getting a main benefit contacts you to advise that they intend travelling overseas you need to obtain the following information: - date of departure and - date of return and - whether the child or young person is remaining in New Zealand

chunks.title: Non-beneficiary Extra Help payment will not continue — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text: Where payment of Away from Home Allowance will not continue because they do not meet the eligibility criteria due to their absence you will need to suspend the benefit from: - the day after departure

chunks.title: Calculating period of absence — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text: When assessing the period of absence, do not include: - the date of departure from New Zealand and - the date of return to New Zealand For more information about Absence from New Zealand see: - Calculating period of absence in relevant main benefit

chunks.title: Permanent absence — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text: If the client (or the children that Away from Home Allowance is paid for) is leaving New Zealand permanently Away from Home Allowance should be cancelled from the day after departure.

chunks.title: Advises more than 14 days after the event — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Advises more than 14 days after the event
As clients have an obligation to advise Work and Income of any changes that may affect their entitlement to Away from Home Allowance it is expected that they will do so within a reasonable period. As a guideline, a reasonable period is considered to be within 14 days.
Therefore, when a client advises of a change in circumstances more than 14 days after the event you should generally reduce, suspend or cancel Away from Home Allowance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.
Where there is a good and sufficient reason (for example, bereavement or illness) for the client not advising Work and Income of a change in circumstances within 14 days you may reduce, suspend or cancel Away from Home Allowance from the first available date.
Note if the client gives false or misleading information you must review Away from Home Allowance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.

chunks.title: Advises more than 14 days after the event — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Advises more than 14 days after the event
As clients have an obligation to advise Work and Income of any changes that may affect their entitlement to Away from Home Allowance it is expected that they will do so within a reasonable period. As a guideline, a reasonable period is considered to be within 14 days.
Therefore, when a client advises of a change in circumstances more than 14 days after the event you should generally stop Away from Home Allowance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.
Where there is a good and sufficient reason (for example, bereavement or illness) for the client not advising Work and Income of a change in circumstances within 14 days you may stop Away from Home Allowance from the first available date.
Note if the client gives false or misleading information you must review Away from Home Allowance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.

chunks.title: Advises more than 14 days after the event — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Advises more than 14 days after the event
As clients have an obligation to advise MSD of any changes that may affect their entitlement to Away from Home Allowance it is expected that they will do so within a reasonable period. As a guideline, a reasonable period is considered to be within 14 days.
Therefore, when a client advises of a change in circumstances more than 14 days after the event MSD should generally reduce, suspend or cancel Away from Home Allowance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.
Where there is a good and sufficient reason (for example, bereavement or illness) for the client not advising MSD of a change in circumstances within 14 days MSD may reduce, suspend or cancel Away from Home Allowance from the first available date.
Note if the client gives false or misleading information MSD must review Away from Home Allowance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.

chunks.title: Age changes — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Age changes
To be able to receive an Away from Home Allowance the client must be the principal caregiver of a 16 or 17 year old dependent child.
When the child turns 18 years old, Away from Home Allowance must stop from that day.
The child may be able to receive a:
- Student Allowance or
- Jobseeker Support Training

chunks.title: Change in accommodation — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Change in accommodation
You will need to review the Away from Home Allowance to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment whenever there is a change in the child's:
- accommodation costs
- type of accommodation rent, board or home ownership or
- residential area (region) or
- part of the property they live in
MSD will need to update and reassess the clients weekly qualifying accommodation costs.
If the child stops living away from home (excluding living at home during holiday periods) payment must stop.
The date to review Away from Home Allowance from will depend on the action involved. Generally, you should:
- increase Away from Home Allowance from the actual date of the change in circumstances or
- reduce, suspend or cancel Away from Home Allowance from the first available date except when the client advises of a change more than 14 days after the event
Note if the client gives false or misleading information you must review Away from Home Allowance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.

chunks.title: Change in accommodation income — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Change in accommodation income
Clients must tell MSD when the child starts getting accommodation income or there is a change in accommodation income the child gets from renters or boarders so the correct rate of Away From Home Allowance can be paid.
When there is a change in accommodation income that a child gets, review the Away From Home Allowance to make sure they still meet the qualifications and are getting the correct rate of payment. The date to review Away from Home Allowance from will depend on the action involved. Generally, MSD should:
- increase Away from Home Allowance from the actual date of the change in circumstances or
- reduce, suspend or cancel Away from Home Allowance from the first available date except when the client advises of a change more than 14 days after the event
Note if the client gives false or misleading information MSD must review Away from Home Allowance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.

chunks.title: Change of caregiver — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Change of caregiver
When a client is no longer the principal caregiver payment must stop.
MSD should stop Away from Home Allowance from the first available date except when the client advises of the change more than 14 days after the event
Note if the client gives false or misleading information MSD must review Away from Home Allowance from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.

chunks.title: Change of course — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Change of course
Away from Home Allowance stops from:
- the date the course ends
- the date the academic year ends (for a course that extends beyond one academic year) or
- the date the child permanently stops attending the course
whichever is earliest.
When the child will be starting a new course the client will need to make a new application.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client is obliged to advise MSD of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Away From Home Allowance.
MSD may also review Away From Home Allowance at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.
For more information see:
- Absence from New Zealand
- Age changes
- Core policy Agents
- Change in accommodation
- Change in accommodation income
- Change of caregiver
- Change of course
- Death of a client or child
- Deductions
- Family tax credit stops
- Hospitalisation
- Core policy Redirection of benefit payment
- Renewals
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals

chunks.title: Court attachment orders — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Court attachment orders
All court attachment requests are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit for processing. Court attachments are administered via the CORBI screen.
The Ministry of Justice has the authority to make attachment orders on benefits to meet outstanding court fines. The attachment order may include:
- court finesthese are fines payable to the District Court
- civil attachmentsthese are generally paid to a private individual or organisation that is owed money. Occasionally a District Court will act as a collection agent for civil debts.
Attachment Orders issued by the Ministry of Justice can be made under either the Summary Proceedings Act 1957 or the District Court Act 2016.
## Protected earnings rate
No attachment order can, whether on its own or when combined with any other attachment order, Child Support deduction, or Ministry of Social Development debt repayment, take a client's total income below the protected earnings rate.
For more information see:
- Protected earnings rate
## Priority for deductions
Court attachment orders do not take priority over any Child Support deductions, Ministry of Social Development deductions, Inland Revenue deductions or any attachment order made under the Family Proceedings Act.
For more information see:
- Priority for deductions
## Information provided by the Ministry of Justice
The information that will be received from the Ministry of Justice will have:
- the client's name
- the amount to be deducted from the benefit
- the fine's reference number
If a client is suffering undue hardship because of the amount of the attachment order then they should be directed to a Registrar of the District Court for a reassessment of the rate.
For more information see:
- Court request for information

chunks.title: Court request for information — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Court request for information
The Ministry of Justice can request the following information when they are considering either making an attachment order or assessing the client's protected earnings rate under section 87AA of the Summary Proceedings Act 1957:
- the amount of any benefit paid to the client
- the amount of any attachment orders or deduction notices issued under the following Acts: Social Security Act 2018Family Proceedings Act 1980Child Support Act 1991Tax Administration Act 1994
- Social Security Act 2018
- Family Proceedings Act 1980
- Child Support Act 1991
- Tax Administration Act 1994
- any Ministry of Social Development debt that is being recovered from the client
- the composition of the client's family, including the number of family members who are dependent on the client, as known by Work and Income
This information is used to determine how much the client can reasonably be expected to pay each week on any outstanding fines.
## Information that can be provided
Work and Income can provide the Ministry of Justice with the last known address and telephone number of a client under Schedule 6, clause 13 of the Social Security Act 2018.
This only applies where the Ministry of Justice is unable to locate a client who is in default of a court fine.
## Information that cannot be provided
The following information cannot be provided to the Ministry of Justice:
- the client's benefit number
- the benefit type and
- employer details
For more information see:
- Protected earnings rate

chunks.title: Death of a client or child — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Death of a client or child
When the caregiver or child (that Away from Home Allowance is paid for) dies, payments stop from the day after death.
Note when a client has a Community Services or SuperGold Card, the card must be manually cancelled and death details added to Person Details latch in CMS.
Contact the Card Centre on 0800 999 999 or email to request cancellation of the card.
## Cost of funeral
The person responsible for the cost of the funeral may be able to receive a Funeral Grant.
## Verification
You must be satisfied that you can accurately identify the client's record.
Generally, we will accept verbal notification of death. This advice can be acted on when you determine the relationship of the caller to the deceased and obtaining sufficient information to provide confirmation of the deceased's identity.
Follow-up verification should generally be requested. A copy of the death certificate or a copy of the death notice is acceptable support documentation.

chunks.title: Debt Repayment Orders — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Debt Repayment Orders
All Debt Repayment Orders are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit for processing.
Debt Repayment Orders are issued by the Ministry of Justice under the Insolvency Act 2006 and can be issued where the client is an un-discharged bankrupt.
Unlike other court attachment orders, Debt Repayment Orders are not subject to any protected earnings rate. Payment is generally made to the supervisor of the debt but occasionally the District Court will act as an agent for collection of the debt.
Payment continues for 3 years or until further notice is received from either the supervisor or the District Court.
Debt Repayment Orders are administered via the PYECI screen, not through CORBI.

chunks.title: Deductions — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Deductions
In certain circumstances Work and Income can be required to pay part of the client's benefit to another party.
Work and Income is legally required to make deductions when served with a properly issued Deduction Notice or Attachment Order. In these cases, the consent of the client is not required.
Certain forms of deductions take priority over others.

chunks.title: Family tax credit stops — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Family tax credit stops
When the client no longer qualifies for family tax credit, Away From Home Allowance must stop.
Generally, you should cancel Away from Home Allowance from the first available date except when the client advises of the change more than 14 days after the event.
## Exception
There will be instances where clients have received family tax credit and Away From Home Allowance, only to learn when they file their tax return that they were not entitled to the family tax credit they received.
In this case, the client has been overpaid Away From Home Allowance. Do not count the money paid as an overpayment except in cases where client has:
- clearly given false or misleading information or
- where they have failed to give notification of a change in circumstances
For more information see:
- Family tax credit

chunks.title: Hospitalisation — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Hospitalisation
When a client (or a child that Away From Home Allowance is paid for) is admitted to any hospital payment can continue if it does not affect the client's qualification for Away From Home Allowance.
You will need to check factors such as:
- if the child continues to meet the definition of dependent child and the caregiver continues to be the principal caregiver
- is the client still able to receive family tax credit
- are accommodation costs continuing and
- whether the child has permanently stopped attending the course

chunks.title: Inland Revenue deduction notices — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Inland Revenue deduction notices
Inland Revenue may request for a client's unpaid taxes to be directly deducted from their benefit payments.
Note all Inland Revenue deduction notices are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit for processing.
The instructions of the deduction notice will be to deduct the lowest of either:
- 10% of the total debt which Inland Revenue specify in the notice, on a weekly basis, or
- 20% of the client's gross earnings on a weekly basis
Where there are insufficient funds to cover the deduction, Work and Income must advise Inland Revenue immediately that the deduction will not start or will start at a reduced rate.
Inland Revenue deductions have a lower priority than Child Support deductions.
For more information see:
- Priority for deductions

chunks.title: Ministry of Social Development debt repayments — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Ministry of Social Development debt repayments
When a client has a Ministry of Social Development debt, this can be recovered by regular deductions from their current benefit.
Note Income Related Rent historical Housing New Zealand debt should be given equal priority to Ministry of Social Development debt.
For more information see:
- Current client debt Negotiating repayment of debt

chunks.title: Priority for deductions — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Priority for deductions
Certain forms of deductions take priority over others; the following list gives the order of priority, highest to lowest:
Highest priority
- Child Support deductions made under the Child Support Act 1991
- Inland Revenue tax deductions
- Ministry of Social Development debt repayments including Liable Parent Contributions (LPC), child maintenance debts and Major Repairs Advances (MRA), Student Allowance debt, Student Loan debt converted to Ministry of Social Development debt, Income Related Rent historical Housing New Zealand debt, Income Related Rent Ministry of Social Development debt
- attachment orders made under the Family Proceedings Act 1980
- court attachment orders issued under the Summary Proceedings Act 1957
- court attachment orders issued under the District Court Act 2016
- Student Loan repayments
Lowest priority
Determining the priority of deductions is necessary where a client has more than one order issued in respect of their benefit. Also each order and deduction notice is subject to its own protected earnings rule.
When you need to reduce deductions you adjust from the lowest priority up to those with a higher priority taking into account the protected earnings rules for each.

chunks.title: Protected earnings rate — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Protected earnings rate
Both the District Court Act and the Summary Proceedings Act provide that every court attachment order must specify a 'protected earnings rate'.
The protected earnings rate is usually 60% of the client's net earnings after PAYE tax has been deducted or withheld.
If the attachment order will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate, then the order will not operate and you must cancel or return the attachment order to the Court, Ministry of Justice.
Calculating the client's income differs between attachment orders made under the Summary Proceedings Act and the District Court Act, in that different benefits are taken into account. Therefore it is important to determine what type of attachment order has been issued.
Summary Proceedings Act 1957
For orders made under the Summary Proceedings Act, the calculation of the client's income does not include Special Benefit, Temporary Additional Support, Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance, Winter Energy Payment, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit
District Court Act 2016
For orders made under the District Court Act, the client's income includes Special Benefit, Temporary Additional Support and Disability Allowance but does not include Child Disability Allowance, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit
## Example
An attachment order is received from the Ministry of Justice for $80.00 per week.
The order lists the client's protected earnings rate as $286.53 per week.
We need to calculate whether adding the deduction of $80.00 will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate:
Calculate protected earnings rate
Jobseeker Support - single person 25+ net rate (as at 1 April 2026)
$372.55
Plus Accommodation Supplement (Area 2)
$105.00
Total net earnings
$477.55
60% of total net earnings (= protected earnings)
$286.53
Calculate if Attachment Order will exceed protected earnings
Total net earnings
$477.55
Less Child Support deduction
$50.00
Less Ministry of Social Development debt
$70.00
Sub total
$357.55
Less Attachment Order
$80.00
Total net income remaining for the client per week
$277.55
The attachment order amount of $80.00 takes the client's total net income to $277.55, which is below the protected earnings rate of $286.53 per week.
The attachment order will not operate therefore you must return it to the Ministry of Justice for the order to be amended.

chunks.title: Renewals — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Renewals
Away from Home Allowance is renewed every 26 weeks.
The purpose is to:
- ensure that the client stills meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment and
- check for any change to the child's accommodation costs or course
## Process
SWIFTT does not automatically issue the renewal forms.
A 26-week expiry must be added to the client's record.
You must manually issue a renewal form 4 weeks before the expiry date to enable the client to complete and return the form. See:
- Away from Home Allowance Review form [no link find out why]
## Verification of changes
The client does not need to provide verification of any costs previously included if the costs have not changed.
However, they do still need to provide verification of:
- all new accommodation costs or
- any accommodation costs that have changed (that is increased or decreased)
For example, the client should provide proof such as a tenancy agreement or a letter from the child's landlord.

chunks.title: Student Loans — extra help > away from home allowance > changes and reviews away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Student Loans
Clients with a Student Loan must make repayments to Inland Revenue when the income they receive exceeds a pre-determined level. This level is called the 'income threshold'.
A person must make repayments to Inland Revenue when their income exceeds $464.00 gross per week ($24,128 gross per year) as at 1 April 2026. Note non-taxable Extra help such as family tax credit and Accommodation Supplement do not count as income in this instance.
If the client's income is over this income threshold, the Ministry of Social Development can make the required deduction. However, this is only done if the client requests it.
If the client's portion of benefit is below the income threshold, there is no provision to make voluntary repayments through SWIFTT. The client can make voluntary payments direct to Inland Revenue at any time.
Note the following:
- Student Loan deductions can only be made from taxable benefits
- Student Loan deductions cannot be made if the client's benefit is below the income threshold
- where a client receives a married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit only the client's portion is taken into consideration when assessing Student Loan repayments
- where a client is receiving a reduced rate of payment due to other income, the Student Loan deduction is assessed on the net payment after income deduction
## For more information on Student Loans see:
- Students Student Loan

chunks.title: Child's income and assets — extra help > away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Child's income and assets
When calculating the amount of Away From Home Allowance, ignore any income or assets of the young person who is living away from home.

chunks.title: Commencement date — extra help > away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
The Away From Home Allowance begins on:
- the date the dependent child started to live away from home to attend the course
- the date of application for the allowance or
- the date the course commences
whichever is the later.
Payment continues throughout term breaks and would cease on the earliest of the following:
- the date the course ends
- for a course that extends beyond one academic year, the date the academic year ends
- the date the dependent child permanently ceases to attend the course
- the date the dependent child ceases to live away from home (not counting any living at home during holiday periods throughout the academic year)
- the date that is six months after the allowance began or was last renewed
- the date the client is no longer eligible to receive family tax credit for the dependent child
- the date the dependent child ceases to be dependent or
- the date the dependent child turns 18 years old
For more information see:
- Overpayments
- Core policy Application for assistance

chunks.title: Dependent child — extra help > away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
Away From Home Allowance can only be paid to a client on behalf of a dependent child.
A dependent child for Away from Home, is a dependent of the client when:
- their care is primarily the responsibility of the client
- they are being maintained as a member of that family
- they are financially dependent on the client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Away from Home does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 and
- child getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
- child who is 18
A child is deemed independent if they:
- are in full-time employment
- get any parent benefit including Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment
- get a Student Allowance or
- are getting any other payment through a Government assisted scheme which is considered the same as, or similar to, a benefit

chunks.title: Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples — extra help > away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples
To help you identify when there is a "dependent child", please see the examples below:
Household
Payments
Outcome
Parent and young person, aged between 16-18 years old.
Parent receiving Sole Parent Support (SPS), Young person receiving no assistance.
Young person is a dependent child.
Parent and young person aged between 16-18 years old and young person’s baby.
Parent receiving Sole Parent Support, young person receiving Young Parent Payment (YPP).
Young person is no longer dependent on their parent however the baby is a dependent child of the young person.
Parent and young person aged between 16-18 years old and young person’s baby.
Parent receiving Sole Parent Support, young person receiving no assistance.
Both the young person and the young person’s baby are dependent children of the parent.
Couple (parents) and young person aged between 16-18 years old and young person’s baby.
Parents receiving Jobseeker Support half married rate, young person receiving no assistance.
Both the young person and the young person’s baby are dependent children of the parents.
Couple (parents) and young person aged between 16-18 years old and young person’s baby.
Parents receiving Jobseeker Support half married rate, young person receiving Young Parent Payment.
Young person is no longer dependent on their parents however the baby is a dependent child of the young person.

chunks.title: Evidence of entitlement to family tax credit — extra help > away from home allowance
chunks.text: To qualify for Away From Home Allowance a client must be getting, or entitled to get family tax credit for the dependent child. However, they are still able to get Away from Home Allowance if a client cannot receive a family tax credit due to them getting: - Christchurch mosques attack support payments - payments from the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) for the first 12 months following the date of payment - payments from the Earthquake Commission and insurance companies for: rebuilding or repairing the damage to homes caused by the Canterbury Earthquake 2010 (including aftershocks) orthe costs of renting temporary accommodation because people can no longer live in their home due to damage from the Canterbury Earthquake 2010 (including aftershocks) - rebuilding or repairing the damage to homes caused by the Canterbury Earthquake 2010 (including aftershocks) or - the costs of renting temporary accommodation because people can no longer live in their home due to damage from the Canterbury Earthquake 2010 (including aftershocks) - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts - MSD lump sum payments and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after payment is made - Energy Trust Dividends and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after payment is made - payments made on or after 20 June 2011 by the Crown as a payment or part payment for the purchase price for any property or land in the red zone under a Government offer that has been accepted by the homeowner - payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 - payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after payment is made - payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support and income earned on the arrears for the first 12 months after payment is made - specified Ex gratia and Compensation payments and income earned on those payments - an ex-gratia payment after becoming infected with Hepatitis C through the New Zealand Blood Supply for the first 12 months following the date the client received the payment - payments to clients whose Housing New Zealand tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after payment is made - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after the payment is made

chunks.title: Evidence of entitlement to family tax credit — extra help > away from home allowance
chunks.text: If the client is getting a main benefit with the young person included as a dependent child then they do not have to provide evidence. If the client does not receive a main benefit then they must provide evidence from Inland Revenue that they receive, or are entitled to receive, family tax credit. If the caregiver receives any of the following benefits in respect of the dependent child they are not eligible for family tax credit, and do not qualify for Away From Home Allowance: - Unsupported Child's Benefit - Orphans Benefit - Child's War Pension or - War Orphan's Benefit For more information about war pensions and allowances, please contact Veterans' Affairs New Zealand

chunks.title: Example - Away from Home Allowance — extra help > away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Example - Away from Home Allowance
The 17 year old dependent child of a MSD client is attending a motor mechanics course in Area 4.
He is living away from home and pays board costs of $160.00 per week.
## Accommodation costs
62% of the cost of board is considered to be an accommodation cost.
Cost of board
$160.00
$160.00 x 0.62
$99.20
Accommodation costs
$99.20
The Away From Home Allowance pays a 70% subsidy for the weekly qualifying accommodation cost that is paid over the threshold (up to a maximum limit):
Accommodation costs (board)
$99.20
Less cost of part of property not lived in
$0
Less accommodation income
$0
Equals weekly qualifying accommodation costs
$99.20
Less entry threshold for a single Jobseeker Support client (as at 1 April 2026)
$93.00
Equals
$6.20
$6.20 x 0.70
$4.34
Round up to nearest dollar
$5.00
$5.00 is less than the maximum payable in Area 4 of $70.00 (as at 1 April 2026), so the full $5.00 per week is paid to the child's caregiver.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The Away from Home Allowance provides assistance with accommodation costs for the caregivers of dependent 16 and 17 year olds who move away from home to undertake tertiary study or employment related training.
The Away from Home Allowance is non-taxable and although an income test must be met, it is not asset tested.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Payment
- Commencement date
- Changes and Reviews
For a copy of the application form, see:
- Away from Home Allowance Application

chunks.title: Overpayments — extra help > away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Overpayments
There will be instances where clients have received family tax credit and Away From Home Allowance, only to learn when they file their tax return that they were not entitled to the family tax credit they received.
In this case, the client has been overpaid Away From Home Allowance. Do not count the money paid as an overpayment except in cases where client has:
- clearly given false or misleading information or
- where they have failed to give notification of a change in circumstances

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Payment
The rate of payment of Away From Home Allowance is calculated using the same formula as for Accommodation Supplement
Away From Home Allowance is only paid for dependent children with board or rent costs. Children who are homeowners are deemed independent from their caregivers.
All the rules about what counts as accommodation costs, weekly qualifying accommodation costs and the maximum amounts payable for different regions are the same as for Accommodation Supplement. All costs must be verified.
The entry threshold for Away From Home Allowance is that which would be used for a single 18 year old on Jobseeker Support.
The only major difference between working out the rate of Accommodation Supplement and Away From Home Allowance is that there are no income reduction calculations. Both the client and the dependent may earn money and this will not affect the level of Away From Home Allowance payable as long as:
- the client remains entitled to family tax credit for the dependent and
- the dependent is not in full time employment
For more information see:
- Calculating rate
- Example
- Overpayments

chunks.title: Principal caregiver — extra help > away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Principal caregiver
Away From Home Allowance can only be paid to the "caregiver" of a dependent child.
A "caregiver" may be a:
- parent
- step-parent
- guardian or
- person who otherwise has the care of the young person
If the caregiver receives any of the following benefits in respect of the dependent child they are not eligible for family tax credit and so do not qualify for Away From Home Allowance:
- Unsupported Child's Benefit
- Orphans Benefit

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > away from home allowance
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To be able to receive an Away From Home Allowance for their child's accommodation costs, the child must be living away from home and the client must:
- be the principal caregiver of the 16 or 17 year old dependent child and
- be entitled to receive family tax credit for the child
In addition to this, the course the child takes must be:
- a tertiary course that would qualify the child for Student Allowance if they were old enough or
- a course that would qualify as approved training on Jobseeker Support if they were old enough
Verification is required to confirm the child's course details and the client must sign the application stating they will apply the allowance towards the cost of the care of their child while on the course.
Note the Away From Home Allowance is not asset tested.
For more information see:
- Principal caregiver
- Dependent child
- Child's income and assets
- Evidence of entitlement to family tax credit
For a copy of the application form, see:
- Away From Home Allowance Application

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — extra help > best start tax credit > changes and reviews best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
When a main benefit is suspended or cancelled because the client is absent from New Zealand, the client information will be transferred to Inland Revenue.
Inland Revenue will assess any ongoing entitlement to Best Start tax credit and Working for Families Tax Credits.
The client information will be transferred to Inland Revenue at the:
- grant of benefit
- suspension of benefit
- resumption of benefit
- cancellation of benefit
- transfer to non-beneficiary assistance

chunks.title: Best Start tax credit impact on other assistance — extra help > best start tax credit > changes and reviews best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Best Start tax credit impact on other assistance
Best Start tax credit is treated as income for:
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit
- Community Services Card
Best Start tax credit is not treated as income for some programmes. For example:
- main benefit
- Accommodation Supplement for non-beneficiaries
- Disability Allowance (income test for New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension)
- Childcare Assistance
- Income Related Rent eligibility assessments and assessments of affordability
- Special Needs Grant
- Student Allowance
- Recoverable assistance payments for non-beneficiary clients

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — extra help > best start tax credit > changes and reviews best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client is obliged to advise the Ministry of Social Development of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Best Start tax credit.
You may also review Best Start tax credit at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Child dies — extra help > best start tax credit > changes and reviews best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Child dies
When a child for whom Best Start tax credit is being paid dies, payment continues until the earlier of:
- 28 days following the date of death or
- the day before the child's 3rd birthday
This differs from the family tax credit which ends from the beginning of the next pay period or first available pay period after notice of the child's death.

chunks.title: Child leaves care — extra help > best start tax credit > changes and reviews best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Child leaves care
When a child leaves the care of a person getting a main benefit, Best Start tax credit and family tax credit payments paid for that child should be stopped from the beginning of the next pay period. This includes if the child left care suddenly.
The primary client's main benefit rate, obligations and any extra help may need to be reviewed following the child leaving their care.

chunks.title: Child turns 3 — extra help > best start tax credit > changes and reviews best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Child turns 3
Best Start tax credit will end on the 3rd birthday for qualifying children. The Best Start tax credit is paid up to the day before the child's 3rd birthday, payments will then automatically stop.
The family tax credit will continue for the child.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Main benefit clients dies - Terminal benefit — extra help > best start tax credit > changes and reviews best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Main benefit clients dies - Terminal benefit
When a main benefit client dies who was paid Best Start tax credit for their dependent child the assessment of terminal benefit following the date of death does not include the Best Start tax credit or the family tax credit.
Any surviving partner’s on-going rate of payment (or appropriate benefit) should be reviewed for any change in obligations including paying Best Start tax credit and family tax credit to the surviving partner if they meet the qualifications.

chunks.title: Overpayments of Best Start tax credit — extra help > best start tax credit > changes and reviews best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Overpayments of Best Start tax credit
Debts are not established by the Ministry of Social Development for Best Start tax credit or family tax credit payments which may have been paid incorrectly with a main benefit eg main benefit payments obtained fraudulently.
When a main benefit is stopped, Best Start tax credit and family tax credits will be notified to Inland Revenue through the information exchange.

chunks.title: Review and Appeal rights — extra help > best start tax credit > changes and reviews best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Review and Appeal rights
Best Start tax credit and family tax credit payments are provided under the Income Tax Act 2007 and the Tax Administration Act 1994.
The review and appeal provisions in the Social Security Act 2018 cannot be used for decisions made only for Best Start tax credit and family tax credits.
Youth clients cannot appeal the payment of their Best Start tax credit and family tax credits only paid by the Ministry of Social Development.
In some cases, Best Start tax credit may be stopped for an indefinite period because the main benefit is suspended. Stopping the Best Start tax credit payments with the main benefit is not covered by the Ministry’s review and appeal process.
The client should be advised to contact Inland Revenue for continued payment of Best Start tax credit and family tax credit.
The review rights for the main benefit still apply.

chunks.title: Children born before 1 July 2018 — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Children born before 1 July 2018
A child born before 1 July 2018 was not eligible for Best Start tax credit unless the expected date of the child's delivery was on or after 1 July 2018.
A transitional provision enabled the principal caregiver to qualify for Best Start tax credit when a child was born before 1 July 2018, but the expected date of delivery was on or after 1 July 2018.
When this was confirmed Best Start tax credit could be paid for the child born before 1 July 2018.

chunks.title: Children in the care of the Chief Executive Oranga Tamariki — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Children in the care of the Chief Executive Oranga Tamariki
Caregivers getting Foster Care Allowance for children in the care of Oranga Tamariki have their Best Start tax credit entitlements assessed and paid by Inland Revenue.
## Agency responsible for paying Best Start tax credit for Foster Care Allowance, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit children
Inland Revenue pay Best Start tax credit and family tax credit for:
- main benefit clients with foster children and their own children
- non-main benefit clients who receive Orphan's Benefit and Unsupported Child's Benefit for a child eligible for Best Start tax credit
- non-main benefit clients with foster children who are eligible for Best Start tax credit and the client's natural children
The Ministry of Social Development pay family tax credit and Best Start tax credit for:
- main benefit clients with dependent children
- main benefit clients who also get Orphans Benefit and Unsupported Childs Benefit for a child eligible for Best Start tax credit.

chunks.title: Clients not entitled to Best Start tax credit — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Clients not entitled to Best Start tax credit
A principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver is not eligible for Best Start tax credit for a child if they are getting at the same time:
- paid parental leave or
- parent's allowance or a children's pension

chunks.title: Commencement date for clients previously paid by Inland Revenue — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Commencement date for clients previously paid by Inland Revenue
Best Start tax credit can start from the date the main benefit is granted if the client was not getting their Best Start tax credit payments from Inland Revenue previously.
If the client is still having their Best Start tax credit paid by Inland Revenue but want to get it from the Ministry of Social Development instead, it will start from the beginning of the next full pay period after the benefit has been granted.

chunks.title: Commencement date — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
Best Start tax credit is paid with a main benefit for children born on or after 1 July 2018 from the later of:
- 1 July 2018 or
- the commencement date of the main benefit or
- the commencement date of the Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit if the client also receives a main benefit or
- the day after the end of payment of paid parental leave or
- the date the child came into care

chunks.title: Dependent child — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
A dependent child for Best Start tax credit and family tax credit differs slightly depending on whether payments are made by Oranga Tamariki, or if an Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid for a child.
For Best Start tax credit a dependent child, means a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of that person and
- maintained as a member of that person's family and
- financially dependent on that person
A dependent child includes when payments are made under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 for a foster child, or if an Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid for the child.
Foster care payments paid by Oranga Tamariki, and Orphan's Benefit and Unsupported Child's Benefit rates have an amount equal to the family tax credit rates included in the payment, which means these caregivers cannot get family tax credit payments.
Best Start tax credit is not included in foster care payments, or Unsupported Child's Benefit and Orphan's Benefit so caregivers of these children are able to apply to Inland Revenue for Best Start tax credit payments.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Best Start tax credit is a payment to help families with costs in a child's early years.
Best Start tax credit payments can be paid to main benefit clients by the Ministry of Social Development on behalf of Inland Revenue.
When a person is working, Inland Revenue pays the Best Start tax credit.
From 1 April 2026 the Best Start tax credit is income tested for all three years of the payment except when the Best Start tax credit is paid to a caregiver who is getting a main benefit.

chunks.title: Paid parental leave — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Paid parental leave
Paid parental leave must be charged as income in the assessment of the main benefit. A client who receives paid parental leave for a newborn child cannot receive Best Start tax credit for that child until the paid parental leave ends.
Once Best Start tax credit starts the time for which the Best Start tax credit can be paid is limited to 3 years from the child's date of birth. The 3 year period includes any period during which paid parental leave is paid.
A client can receive paid parental leave for a newborn child and continue to receive Best Start tax credit payments for an older eligible child.

chunks.title: Parent's Allowance and children's pension — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Parent's Allowance and children's pension
If a client receives a parent's allowance or children's pension payable under the Veteran's Support Act 2014, they are not entitled to Best Start tax credit for the same child the allowance or pension is paid for.

chunks.title: Payment from Ministry of Social Development or Inland Revenue — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Payment from Ministry of Social Development or Inland Revenue
Main benefit clients can choose to have their Best Start tax credit and family tax credit paid by the Ministry of Social Development or Inland Revenue.
This would be more practical for clients who are expecting to receive a main benefit for only a short period of time. Best Start tax credit and family tax credit must be paid together by either the Ministry or Inland Revenue.
Foster care parents that receive a main benefit and have children of their own have their Best Start tax credit and family tax credit paid by Inland Revenue.
Note clients getting Young Parent Payment cannot choose to have their Best Start tax credit and family tax credits paid by Inland Revenue.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Payment
Best Start tax credit as at 1 April 2026 is $77.50 a week until the child turns 3 years old.
The Ministry of Social Development pays the maximum rate of Best Start tax credit until the child turns 3 years old if the client is getting a main benefit.
From 1 April 2026 all three years of the payment are income tested.

chunks.title: Principal caregiver — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Principal caregiver
Best Start tax credit is paid to the principal caregiver of the dependent child.
The definition of a principal caregiver for Best Start tax credit is defined under the Income Tax Act 2007. This is different to the definition of principal caregiver used for other payments made by the Ministry of Social Development.
For Best Start tax credit, a principal caregiver is the person who:
- has the primary responsibility for the day-to-day care of the child, not on a temporary basis
The principal caregiver cannot be:
- a group of people (whether incorporated or unincorporated) or
- the partner of a transitional resident under the Income Tax Act 2007 or
- any person who is the owner or employed in: a residence established under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 ora residential disability care institution under the Health and Disability Services (Safety) Act 2001 orany other institution where a child is being cared for
- a residence established under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 or
- a residential disability care institution under the Health and Disability Services (Safety) Act 2001 or
- any other institution where a child is being cared for
Best Start tax credit is automatically paid to the primary client. When the partner of the primary client is the principal caregiver, the Best Start tax credit payments should be paid to the partner.
In a sole parent family, Best Start tax credit is paid in full to the parent who has the most day-to-day care of the child or children.
Note some clients getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit as principal temporary caregivers may still meet the qualifications for Best Start tax credit. These clients will need to contact Inland Revenue to check they qualify before Best Start tax credit can be paid.

chunks.title: Protected Best Start tax credit while getting a main benefit — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Protected Best Start tax credit while getting a main benefit
Best Start tax credit is part of an annual tax system and paid in for children under the age of 3 years.
From 1 April 2026 all three years of the payment are income tested for clients not getting a main benefit.
Payment is assessed using the family's income from the whole of the tax year.
## Clients getting a main benefit
Best Start tax credit payments are protected for any month clients are getting a main benefit.
Regardless of the income earned in other parts of the financial year when clients were not getting a main benefit, they will get the maximum Best Start tax credit for each calendar month they were getting a main benefit.
A client who gets a main benefit for a week will have their Best Start tax credit protected for the entire month. Inland Revenue manages the reconciliation of Best Start tax credit and family tax credits while taking into account the protected periods.
Example
A married client with one child born on 1 July 2026.
The client worked for 7 months from April 2027 until the job ended at the end of November 2027 earning $80,000 annually.
The client was granted Jobseeker Support and Best Start tax credit in December 2027 but started another job in February 2022 and earned another $17,500 before 31 March 2028.
The employment income for the financial year was more than the $93,858 abatement level for Best Start tax credit.
At the end of the tax year Inland Revenue will not include the protected Best Start tax credit paid for the whole months the client was getting a main benefit and the Best Start tax credit payments.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
The Ministry of Social Development pays Best Start tax credit to principal caregivers for dependent children born (or due) on or after 1 July 2018.
The principal caregiver must be getting one of the following benefits:
- Emergency Benefit
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance
- Jobseeker Support
- Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Young Parent Payment or
- Youth Payment
New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients who have a qualifying child apply to Inland Revenue to get Best Start tax credit payments.
