Note clients getting a main benefit and Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit can choose to get Best Start tax credit from the Ministry of Social Development if they meet the qualifications. Caregivers getting an Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit but not getting a main benefit need to apply to Inland Revenue for Best Start tax credit payments.

chunks.title: Shared care — extra help > best start tax credit
chunks.text:
## Shared care
With shared care arrangements there can be more than one principal caregiver.
Both parents of a dependent child can qualify as a principal caregiver in shared care cases expected to be for more than 4 months in duration, and be entitled to a proportional Best Start tax credit if:
- they are living apart and
- they are both qualifying persons and
- they care for the dependent child on average for at least one third of the time. Over a year this is at least 122 days or 5 days a fortnight.
If a child is under the care of each parent for more than one third of the parental entitlement period then Inland Revenue recognises the shared care arrangement, and each parent can be paid the appropriate portion of the Best Start tax credit payment.
For the Ministry of Social Development to pay Best Start tax credit payment in shared care cases, the client must have a formal agreement and supply a copy of either:
- the signed care agreement or
- the court order stating the arrangement
When one parent has care of the child for 2 days or less a week then they cannot get a proportional Best Start tax credit payment. In this situation the Best Start tax credit payment is to be paid to the caregiver with the majority of the care.
Note clients with an informal care agreement should be referred to Inland Revenue for Best Start tax credit payments.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
Clients and/or their children can be absent from New Zealand and keep getting their payment for the first 28 days if it does not affect the client's eligibility for Child Disability Allowance. To pay Child Disability Allowance while the client is absent from New Zealand depends on whether the client is also getting a main benefit.
The client and child do not have to travel overseas together to keep getting Child Disability Allowance.
When one or the other travels overseas ensure that the child continues to meet the definition of dependent child and the caregiver continues as the principal caregiver. This includes a principal temporary caregiver of a child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid.
## Clients getting a main benefit
All clients getting a main benefit must tell the Ministry of Social Development before they leave New Zealand.
If the client or partner does not tell the Ministry before they travel overseas, their benefit payments (including Child Disability Allowance) must stop.
## Clients getting non-beneficiary Extra Help
Clients who are getting Child Disability Allowance, and who are not getting a main benefit:
- must tell the Ministry when they are leaving New Zealand and
- can be absent and paid their Child Disability Allowance for up to 28 days per absence, when it does not affect the client's eligibility for Child Disability Allowance
## Information required from client when they tell us they intend to travel
When a client contacts you to advise they intend travelling overseas you need to obtain the following information:
- date of departure
- date of return
- whether the child or young person is remaining in New ZealandThe person who has the care and control for the child while the client is overseas may be able to get Child Disability Allowance during the client's absence. See: Temporarily out of care
For more information see:
- Obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand
- Payment
- Permanent absence
- Client does not return
- Action on return to New Zealand

chunks.title: Action on return to New Zealand — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Action on return to New Zealand
MSD must look at the circumstances of the client's absence from and subsequent return to New Zealand to decide when to recommence Child Disability Allowance and when to treat it as a new application.
Consider the following:
- the client's intention at the time of their departure, for example, did they cancel their Child Disability Allowance before leaving New Zealand because they did not intend to return?
- did the client remain ordinarily resident during the period of absence?
- the length of time that they have been absent
- the reason for the absence
- if their circumstances changed significantly during their absence?
## Payment can recommence
If a client returns to New Zealand on or before the 29th day (where continued payment of benefit was allowed) Child Disability Allowance can recommence without any break in payment.
Generally, for other short periods of absence (where continue payment was not approved) Child Disability Allowance can recommence from:
- the date the client returned to New Zealand as long as they contact MSD within 14 days of their return or
- the date they contacted MSD to advise they have returned if more than 14 days after date of return
## New application
In all other circumstances, the client may need to reapply using a new application after reviewing the circumstances above.

chunks.title: Change in age — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Change in age
A change in the age of the child (that Child Disability Allowance is paid for) can affect whether or not they still meet the definition of a dependent child and if the client will still meet the qualifications for Child Disability Allowance.
## Child turns 16
When a child turns 16 they may be able to get Supported Living Payment. Child Disability Allowance must stop if Supported Living Payment is granted.
A child who turns 16 can still be considered a dependent child unless the child is:
- in full-time employment
Note generally a child is still a dependent child when they start part-time employment
- getting a basic Student Allowance or an Independent Circumstances Allowance
Note getting a Student Loan does not always mean a child is financially independent
- getting a main benefit in their own right or
- financially independent
Note a child does not have to be attending school to remain a dependent child up until the age of 18.
## Child turns 18
When a child turns 18, Child Disability Allowance must stop from the start of the pay period following their 18th birthday except where a child is continuing in education and is not financially independent.

chunks.title: Death of a caregiver — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Death of a caregiver
When the caregiver dies, Child Disability Allowance payments generally stop from the start of the pay period following the date of death.
MSD will need to find out what care arrangements have been made for the child.
The new caregiver may meet the qualifications for Child Disability Allowance, and the child may be able to be included as a dependent child if the new caregiver is getting a main benefit.

chunks.title: Change in living arrangements — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Change in living arrangements
MSD must review if a client qualifies for Child Disability Allowance whenever a child (that Child Disability Allowance is paid for) moves into:
- the care of Oranga Tamariki
- a state institution
- a residential hostel
- a residential home or
- a specialist school or daycare centre
Where the client no longer qualifies for Child Disability Allowance, payment must stop from the beginning of the pay period following the date living arrangements changed.
Child Disability Allowance is paid 2 weeks in arrears and is paid fortnightly on a Tuesday. The first day of the pay period would be the Wednesday after the Child Disability Allowance payday.

chunks.title: Change of caregiver — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Change of caregiver
Where a child (that Child Disability Allowance is paid for) has a change in their principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver Child Disability Allowance must stop from the beginning of the pay period following the date the event took place.
MSD should invite the new caregiver to apply for Child Disability Allowance.
Where the child has left the previous caregiver suddenly and Child Disability Allowance is continued for 28 days, the new caregiver can get Child Disability Allowance for the same child at the same time from the date the event happened.
Note Child Disability Allowance is paid 2 weeks in arrears and is paid fortnightly on a Tuesday. The first day of the pay period would be the Wednesday after the Child Disability Allowance payday.
## Care and protection concerns
When a child has come into a client’s care, MSD should consider if there are any care and protection concerns.
If MSD believes any child has been, or is likely to be harmed (physically, emotionally or sexually), ill-treated, abused, neglected, deprived or MSD has concerns about the wellbeing of the child, the case must be referred to Oranga Tamariki.
MSD staff must notify Oranga Tamariki if they are aware that the child’s sole caregiver has been remanded in custody and/or sentenced to a term of imprisonment.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
Clients have an obligation to advise MSD of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Child Disability Allowance.
MSD may also review Child Disability Allowance at any time to check if the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.

chunks.title: Child leaves sole parents care suddenly — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Child leaves sole parents care suddenly
When a child stops being a dependent child for a sole parent because of a sudden change of circumstances beyond the control of the client, payment of Child Disability Allowance should continue for 28 days following the date the child stopped being dependent.
## Child turns 18
Generally, clients getting Child Disability Allowance must respond to their notice before the child's 18th birthday or Child Disability Allowance for the child will stop.
If Child Disability Allowance is continuing at the existing rate for 28 days because a child has left a sole parent's care suddenly, and that child turns 18 during that period, the client is not required to respond to the notice and Child Disability Allowance will not stop during that period.
However, if Child Disability Allowance is continuing at the existing rate for 28 days because a child has left a sole parent's care suddenly, and a different child in their care (that Child Disability Allowance is paid for) turns 18, the client must respond to the notice, or Child Disability Allowance for the 18-year-old will stop.

chunks.title: Child stops attending specialist school or daycare centre — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Child stops attending specialist school or daycare centre
Child Disability Allowance can be granted without a medical certificate where the child is attending a specialist school or daycare centre.
When the child stops attending, you will need to decide:
- if the child continues to be a dependent child for Child Disability Allowance purposes and
- whether a medical certificate or review of the child's medical condition is required
For more information see the following changes and reviews:
- Change in living arrangements
- Medical Examination review
- Age changes

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Child turns 18
A dependent child must generally be under the age of 18 for a parent or caregiver to get Child Disability Allowance for them.
When a child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and Child Disability Allowance must stop from the start of the pay period following the child's 18th birthday.
However, if the 18-year-old child is continuing in education and is not financially independent, the child may continue to be considered a dependent child and to have Child Disability Allowance paid for them for a limited period.
In these situations, Child Disability Allowance must stop from the start of the pay period following:
- the date they no longer meet these criteria or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18
whichever is earlier.
Note if the parent or caregiver also gets Child Disability Allowance for other children, the payments for the other children will not be affected by another child turning 18.

chunks.title: Client or child dies before grant or review — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Client or child dies before grant or review
When a client or child dies before a decision is made on an application or review for Child Disability Allowance you can continue the application or review process as if the client or child had not died.

chunks.title: Date of Review — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Date of Review
Where there is no longer qualification for Child Disability Allowance, payments must stop from the beginning of the pay period following the date the child no longer qualifies.
Note Child Disability Allowance is paid 2 weeks in arrears and is paid fortnightly on a Tuesday. The first day of the pay period would be the Wednesday, after the Child Disability Allowance payday.

chunks.title: Death of a child — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Death of a child
When the child dies, Child Disability Allowance payments generally stop from the start of the pay period following the date of death.
## Sole parent caregivers
When the client is a sole parent and a dependent child dies, payment of Child Disability Allowance should continue at the existing rate for 28 days following the date the child died.
This provides a transition for the client to adjust to their change in circumstances.
## Child turns 18
Generally, clients getting Child Disability Allowance must respond to their notice before the child's 18th birthday or Child Disability Allowance for the child will stop.
If Child Disability Allowance is continuing at the existing rate for up to 28 days because a sole parent's child (that Child Disability Allowance is paid for) has died, and the child that died was due to turn 18 during that period, the caregiver is not required to respond to the notice and Child Disability Allowance will not stop during the continuation of payment period.
However, if Child Disability Allowance is continuing for up to 28 days because a sole parent's child has died, and a different child in their care (that Child Disability Allowance is also paid for) turns 18, the caregiver must respond to the notice or Child Disability Allowance for the 18-year-old will stop.

chunks.title: Arrears — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Arrears
When a client has arrears owing to them at the time of their death (or the childs) and they have an outstanding debt balance, you should attempt to recover the debt, in full, from the final payment.
## Terminal benefit
When a client has an outstanding debt balance and terminal benefit is payable, you should not attempt to recover the debt in full from the terminal benefit payment.

chunks.title: Hospitalisation — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Hospitalisation
Child Disability Allowance can continue to be paid when the child needs to be admitted to hospital, as long as the stay in hospital is temporary. Use the following checklist to decide whether or not to continue payment:
- is the child normally cared for in the home or in a voluntarily run home or hostel where the parents/caregiver are contributing?
- is there a reasonable expectation that the child will be returning to the home?
- is there an expected discharge date from the hospital in the foreseeable future?
You would generally continue to pay Child Disability Allowance if the answers to the above checklist are yes.
If the child is expected to be in hospital long-term, only suspend Child Disability Allowance from:
- the first day of the pay period following the date of admission or
- where respite care is provided while the child is in hospital, the expiry of this assistance
whichever is the later
Note Child Disability Allowance is paid 2 weeks in arrears. Payday is fortnightly on Tuesdays. The first day of the pay period would be Wednesday after the Child Disability Allowance payday.

chunks.title: Medical Examination review — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Medical Examination review
In some cases, the child will also be required to have their medical condition reviewed to determine whether they still meet the medical qualifications for Child Disability Allowance.
The medical practitioner or nurse practitioner completing the initial application will indicate whether or not the child's condition needs to be reviewed at a later date.
The Medical Examination review form will be issued by SWIFTT 8 weeks before the medical review date. This allows time for the client to visit their medical practitioner or nurse practitioner for a medical examination.
## Medical Examination form indication
If the Medical Examination form indicates:
- that the child's medical condition has been reassessed with a future date, then extend the medical expiry until the date indicated by the health practitioner
- that the child's medical condition has not been reassessed with a future date, then cancel the Child Disability Allowance with the expiry date on the current Medical Examination form
For more information see:
- Medical Grounds
- Guidelines when determining a serious disability
- Constant care and attention
- Child Disability Allowance - Medical Certificate (this certificate replaced the Medical Examination form)

chunks.title: Obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand (main beneficiaries only) — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand (main beneficiaries only)
All clients getting a main benefit must tell the Ministry of Social Development before they leave New Zealand.
If the client does not tell the Ministry of Social Development before they go overseas, their main benefit payments will stop from the day after they leave New Zealand.
If a client tells us they will be absent from New Zealand, and they have an approved travel reason, they may be able to keep getting payments for up to 28 days.
Clients who do not keep getting a main benefit while overseas may still be able to get Child Disability Allowance, if their absence does not affect the client's eligibility for this assistance and they told the Ministry of their absence before they travelled overseas.
This assistance is limited to 28 days in any 52 week period.
## Does not advise of departure
If the client did not tell the Ministry they were leaving New Zealand their benefit will be suspended immediately from the day after they left New Zealand. As a result their Child Disability Allowance must also stop.
The Integrity Intervention Centre will determine if there has been an overpayment, establish any debt and advise the client.
If a client challenges the information match refer them to the Integrity Intervention Centre.
## Client contacts us from overseas
Clients may contact us from overseas to advise of their travel. When they do this their benefit may be:
- resumed from the date they notified the Ministry of their absence, if their travel is allowed or
- backdated to the departure date (in limited circumstances)
For more information about absence from New Zealand see:
- Paying benefit when client failed to advise of absence, in relevant main benefit
- Approved travel reasons, in relevant main benefit
- Calculating period of absence, in relevant main benefit
- Action on return to New Zealand

chunks.title: Client receiving a main benefit — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Client receiving a main benefit
Where the client is paid their main benefit while they are absent from New Zealand (either because they meet the criteria for approved travel or the requirement to approved travel does not apply to them) they can continue to receive their main benefit and their Child Disability Allowance for up to 28 days in any 52 week period, unless they meet the criteria to be paid their main benefit for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
Clients who do not continue to receive a main benefit while overseas (because they do not meet the criteria for approved travel) may still be able to continue to receive Child Disability Allowance, if their absence:
- does not affect the client's eligibility for this assistance and
- they advised the Ministry of Social Development of their absence before their international travel
This is limited to 28 days in any 52 week period.
For more information about Absence from New Zealand see:
- Approved travel reasons, in relevant main benefit
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period, in relevant main benefit
## Non-beneficiary Extra Help payment will not continue
Where payment of Child Disability Allowance will not continue because they do not meet the eligibility criteria due to their absence, you will need to suspend the benefit from:
- the day after departure
For more information see:
- Permanent absence
- Client does not return
- Return to New Zealand

chunks.title: Permanent absence — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Permanent absence
If the client or child is leaving New Zealand permanently, Child Disability Allowance must be cancelled from the day after departure.
Child Disability Allowance may be payable to the new caregiver if the child is remaining in New Zealand and the new caregiver meets the qualifications for Child Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Temporary change in care — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Temporary change in care
The Health Funding Authority provides for alternative care for disabled children. This care may be by another person or hospital/institution. Child Disability Allowance can continue to be paid to the principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver when the child is in alternative care.
If the child goes into the care of another person temporarily and the client no longer meets the definition of principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver, Child Disability Allowance can be paid to the person who has the care of the child for the time being.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Verification — extra help > child disability allowance > changes and reviews child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Verification
You must be satisfied that you can accurately identify the deceased client's (or child's) record.
Generally, we will accept verbal notification of a client's death. This advice can be acted on when you determine the relationship of the caller to the deceased client and obtaining sufficient information to provide confirmation of the deceased's identity.
Follow-up verification should generally be requested. A copy of the death certificate or a copy of the death notice is acceptable support documentation.

chunks.title: Child Disability Allowance not payable — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Child Disability Allowance not payable
A Child Disability Allowance cannot be paid where:
- the child is granted: a benefit in their own right (other than Orphans Benefit, Unsupported Childs Benefit or Disability Allowance)a pension under the Veterans' Support Act 2014 (other than Children's Pension) orweekly compensation, as defined in section 6 of the Accident Compensation Act 2001, and which is paid to the child
- a benefit in their own right (other than Orphans Benefit, Unsupported Childs Benefit or Disability Allowance)
- a pension under the Veterans' Support Act 2014 (other than Children's Pension) or
- weekly compensation, as defined in section 6 of the Accident Compensation Act 2001, and which is paid to the child
- the child is in the care of Oranga Tamariki or
- the child is in a state institution
For more information see:
- Child in care of Oranga Tamariki
- State institutions

chunks.title: Child in care of Oranga Tamariki — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Child in care of Oranga Tamariki
Child Disability Allowance cannot be granted for a child or young person in the care of Oranga Tamariki.
The caregivers of these children may be able to receive foster care and other allowances under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989. These allowances can be adjusted to meet the needs of seriously disabled children and young people where necessary.

chunks.title: Commencement date — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
Child Disability Allowance can be granted from:
- the date of application or
- the date of eligibility
whichever is the later.
For more information see:
- Core policy Application for benefit

chunks.title: Constant care and attention — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Constant care and attention
To determine whether the child needs constant care and attention, the child must meet 1 of the following requirements:
- needs frequent attention from another person for their bodily functions
due to the child's disability they need recurrent or regular attention to perform bodily functions such as bathing, toileting, dressing or eating.
or
- needs substantially more attention and supervision than is normally required by a child
as the child has a physical, sensory, psychiatric or intellectual disability, they require care and supervision over and above that normally required by a child of the same age and gender.
or
- needs regular supervision from another person so they do not harm themselves or others
due to the child's disability, they need supervision of their day to day activities to avoid significant danger to themselves or others.
This extra care must be permanent or be needed for more than 12 months.

chunks.title: Dependent child — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
To get a Child Disability Allowance, the client must be the principal caregiver of a dependent child. This includes a principal temporary caregiver of a child for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid.
A dependent child for Child Disability Allowance is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- not a child for whom Orphan's Benefit or an Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Child Disability Allowance does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
If the child is living in a home or hostel they can be considered as dependent on the client if the:
- client is required to contribute to the cost of maintaining the child and
- child is cared for by the client during school holidays or weekends

chunks.title: Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples
To help you identify when there is a "dependent child", please see the examples below:
Household
Payments
Outcome
Parent and young person, aged between 16-18 years old.
Parent receiving Sole Parent Support, Young person receiving no assistance.
Young person is a dependent child.
Parent and young person aged between 16-18 years old and young person’s baby.
Parent receiving Sole Parent Support, young person receiving Young Parent Payment.
Young person is no longer dependent on their parent however the baby is a dependent child of the young person.
Parent and young person aged between 16-18 years old and young person's baby.
Parent receiving Sole Parent Support, young person receiving no assistance.
Both the young person and the young person's baby are dependent children of the parent.
Couple (parents) and young person aged between 16-18 years old and young person's baby.
Parents receiving Jobseeker Support half married rate, young person receiving no assistance.
Both the young person and the young person’s baby are dependent children of the parents.
Couple (parents) and young person aged between 16-18 years old and young person's baby.
Parents receiving Jobseeker Support half married rate, young person receiving Young Parent Payment.
Young person is no longer dependent on their parents however the baby is a dependent child of the young person.

chunks.title: Criteria for eligibility — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Criteria for eligibility
MSD should consider if the child or young person meets 1 or more of the 3 criteria for constant care and attention below:
- requires frequent assistance to manage their self-care
- needs more attention and supervision than normally required by a person of the same age and gender
- is likely to cause substantial danger to themselves or others without regular supervision
MSD can grant or decline Child Disability Allowance if it is satisfied the medical information provided is relevant, accurate and sufficient to assess eligibility.
However there are times when it is difficult to decide whether to grant or decline because it is not clear if the disability is serious enough to require constant care and attention for more than 12 months.
In these cases, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor. They may suggest:
- getting additional information from the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner who completed the medical certificate or
- an assessment by a designated health practitioner for a second opinion
Note when requesting additional information MSD doesn’t need the caregiver's consent when the matter relates directly to the medical information given by the medical or nurse practitioner.

chunks.title: Information on specific conditions and disabilities — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text: To qualify for a Child Disability Allowance, the child must: - have a physical, sensory, psychiatric or intellectual disability and - need constant care and attention because of that disability and - be likely to need that care for more than 12 months Eligibility is not based on the presence of a specific condition or disability, but on the effect that it has on the child's need for constant care and attention. The extent of impairment or impact of the condition or disability should be indicated on the medical certificate signed by their registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and should be used to assess the level of constant care and attention required.

chunks.title: Seek advice when eligibility is unclear — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text: When it is unclear from the information provided whether Child Disability Allowance should be granted or declined, MSD should seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor.

chunks.title: Specific conditions and disabilities — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text: The information below includes several conditions and disabilities that may require extra consideration, depending on the: - severity of the condition or disability and - age/stage of the child. It also includes some additional factors that should be considered when determining eligibility for Child Disability Allowance. Note the list of conditions below is not a complete list. Each case should be considered on its own circumstances. If it is unclear, MSD should seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor. Amputees or loss of limb(s) The loss of a single limb does not necessarily qualify a child for Child Disability Allowance, particularly where rehabilitation services and prostheses are available, and the child is managing their disability independently. Children who are severely impacted and need constant care and attention due to amputation or loss of limb(s) would likely qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Clients may qualify for Civilian Amputee Assistance to help with some of the costs when they are required to attend a limb centre to a have an artificial limb fitted, adjusted, or repaired. For more information see: - Civilian Amputee Assistance Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that affects many children. It impacts the part of the brain that helps people to plan, control impulses and execute tasks. ADHD is a spectrum, which means that some children can be severely impacted, whilst others can be less impacted. Children who are less impacted by their ADHD may not qualify for Child Disability Allowance. However, children who are more impacted, or have co-existing conditions such as anxiety disorder, and therefore need constant care and attention, are more likely to qualify. Example 1 Meg is a 7-year-old child with severe ADHD who also suffers from an anxiety disorder. Meg's parents have provided a medical certificate that confirms this and states that Meg is likely to need constant care and attention at home and school for at least the next 2 years due to their impulsivity and behavioural issues. This means that Meg will qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Example 2 Jack is a 15-year-old child with ADHD. Jack's ADHD is well managed, and they are less impacted by the symptoms of their ADHD. Jack can be left unsupervised at home or school and does not struggle to inform an adult when they are struggling with their symptoms.

chunks.title: Specific conditions and disabilities — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text: This means that Jack does not qualify for Child Disability Allowance because they do not need constant care and attention. Asthma Many children with asthma can manage their symptoms independently with regular medication and would not qualify for Child Disability Allowance. However, for some children, asthma is an ongoing disability which may not be fully controlled by medication and they need constant care and attention. This means the child would generally qualify for Child Disability Allowance in these circumstances. Autism Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect an individual in the areas of social interaction, communication, and development. It is a spectrum disorder that affects each person differently. Children with autism may also have an intellectual disability. Autism frequently co-exists with other psychological disorders including anxiety and depression. To qualify for Child Disability Allowance, MSD must consider whether the severity of the condition means the child needs constant care and attention. Behavioural and psychiatric conditions Behavioural and psychiatric conditions are common in childhood and the impact of these can vary and change as a child gets older. For example, the impact of behavioural conditions may reduce as a child gets older, but the impact of psychiatric conditions may worsen. Examples of behavioural conditions include Oppositional Defiant Disorder and Conduct Disorder. Examples of psychiatric conditions include Anxiety Disorder, Obsessive Compulsive Disorder, Anorexia (and other eating disorders), Depression and Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. If a medical practitioner or nurse practitioner consider that the impact of a child's behavioural condition means they need constant care and attention, they may qualify for Child Disability Allowance. A specialist or psychological report (if available) from a health practitioner may support their application. If a child's behavioural or psychiatric condition improves over time and they no longer need constant care and attention, they would no longer qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Cerebral Palsy Cerebral Palsy is a physical disability that can affect: - body movement - muscle control - muscle coordination - muscle tone - reflex - posture - balance It is a permanent condition that can improve or worsen over time. Children with Cerebral Palsy may also have visual, learning, hearing, speech and intellectual impairments, epilepsy or incontinence. The physical effects of Cerebral Palsy range from very mild to severe. Children with Cerebral Palsy who have minimal physical disabilities, and no intellectual or other disability would generally not qualify for Child Disability Allowance. However, children who are severely impacted and require constant care and attention would likely qualify for Child Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Specific conditions and disabilities — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text: Coeliac disease Coeliac disease is a chronic autoimmune disorder that occurs when the body's immune system attacks the small intestine after consuming gluten. This creates inflammation and prevents the body from absorbing some nutrients. Children with coeliac disease may suffer from symptoms including but not limited to: - abdominal pain - digestive issues - vomiting - weight loss - rashes - iron deficiency - stunted growth The physical effects of coeliac disease range from mild to severe. Children who are unable to manage their coeliac disease by avoiding foods containing gluten, will need constant care and attention and would likely qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Often as a child gets older, they become more independent and may be able to manage their coeliac disease. If a child no longer needs constant care and attention, they will no longer qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Deafness Deafness is long term or permanent hearing loss in one or both ears and includes Auditory Neuropathy Spectrum Disorder. Children who have a severe and profound hearing loss or are very impacted by their hearing loss and need constant care and attention would likely qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Many older children with profound hearing loss may have gained more independence from their parents. As these children adapt to their deafness, they may no longer need constant care and attention. If a child no longer needs constant care and attention, they will no longer qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Diabetes mellitus Diabetes mellitus is a condition that can be managed with oral medication or injected insulin, depending on the type and severity. Although all cases must be assessed on the particular circumstances, many children with insulin dependent diabetes (type 1) would generally qualify for Child Disability Allowance if their diabetes means they need constant care and attention. Older children or those whose diabetes is managed with oral medication and dietary changes (for example, type 2) may not qualify for Child Disability Allowance if they do not need constant care and attention. MSD must consider any complications from the disease, other medical disabilities, and a child's level of familiarity with and ability to manage their condition when assessing if they qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Example Melinda is a 6-year-old child who has recently been diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. Melinda is not yet able to manage their diet or insulin requirements on their own. This means that Melinda needs constant care and attention, and they qualify for Child Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Specific conditions and disabilities — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text: However, Melinda may no longer qualify for Child Disability Allowance when they become able to manage their diet and insulin requirements on their own. Dyslexia Dyslexia is a condition where someone has difficulty in interpreting written or printed language and may struggle to read properly as a result. Children and adults with dyslexia of all ages can learn effectively but often need a different approach and can benefit from support with their education. Dyslexia can vary in severity from person to person. Children with dyslexia may not qualify for Child Disability Allowance unless they have another condition or disability (for example, anxiety or a behavioural disorder), as they would not need constant care and attention. Example Tane is a 10-year-old child with dyslexia. Tane does not have another condition or disability. This means that Tane does not qualify for Child Disability Allowance because they do not need constant care and attention. Epilepsy Epilepsy is an umbrella term for a group of conditions that cause seizures. Children who have epilepsy can often be assisted by anticonvulsant medication. If a child has an ongoing risk of seizures and needs constant care and attention, they are likely to qualify for Child Disability Allowance. The severity of epilepsy can vary, and the age of a child may be a factor that a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner may consider. If the severity of a child's epilepsy means they need constant care and attention, they would likely qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Intellectual disability There are different types of intellectual disabilities, which can be classified as mild, moderate, severe, or profound. In all cases an intellectual disability is lifelong. A child with an intellectual disability could have difficulty with memory, speech, understanding, concentrating, and learning. Intellectual disabilities may be linked to a genetic or chromosomal abnormality, such as Down Syndrome, or an injury. Children with intellectual disability may have developmental delays and intellectual functioning that ranges from just below to significantly below average. They may also have limitations with behaviour, self-care, day to day tasks, and social skills. To qualify for Child Disability Allowance, MSD must consider that the severity of the child's condition means the child needs constant care and attention. The child would also qualify if they attended a specialist school, or a special day-care centre. Leukaemia

chunks.title: Specific conditions and disabilities — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text: Leukaemia is a cancer of the blood or bone marrow. During treatment, children with leukaemia will need constant care and attention. After treatment, children affected by leukaemia can be cured or go into remission. They may need periodic screening over the course of several years. Children in remission from leukaemia would generally not qualify for Child Disability Allowance unless they still require constant care and attention. Loss of sight Loss of sight can occur as a result of a variety of diseases and may develop gradually or suddenly. Loss of sight can affect one or both eyes partially or completely. The condition may be temporary or long term. When a child's loss of sight cannot be corrected by glasses, contact lenses or other methods, it may mean that it is serious enough for them to need constant care and attention. If the child's loss of sight means that they need constant care and attention, they would likely qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Example 1 Manu is a 12-year-old child who is completely blind and requires constant care and attention. This means that Manu would qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Example 2 Kyle is a 9-year-old child who has partial loss of sight in one eye. Kyle wears glasses to help correct this and does not need constant care and attention. This means that Kyle would not qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Meningomyelocele and spina bifida Spina bifida is a birth defect that occurs when a baby's spine and spinal cord doesn't form properly. Meningomyelocele is a severe type of spina bifida. The severity of spina bifida can range from mild to severe and is a permanent condition. Many children with spina bifida will have a serious disability due to leg weakness or paralysis, increased pressure on their brain, seizures, incontinence and/or intellectual disability. These children are likely to need constant care and attention and would generally qualify for Child Disability Allowance. However, there are some children with milder spina bifida that may not need constant care and attention. This means they would not qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Muscular dystrophy Muscular dystrophy refers to a group of conditions that cause progressive weakness and degeneration of skeletal muscles. The symptoms of muscular dystrophy can develop at different ages and can affect different muscles. The severity worsens over time.

chunks.title: Specific conditions and disabilities — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text: Almost all children with muscular dystrophy need constant care and attention and would qualify for Child Disability Allowance. Other long-term severe illness To qualify for Child Disability Allowance, MSD should consider each case on its own circumstances and review eligibility at regular intervals. A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner should clearly indicate if the child needs constant care and attention on the medical certificate.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Child Disability Allowance is a non-taxable allowance that is available to the principal caregiver of a dependent child who has a serious disability.
It is paid because of the extra care that may be needed by a child who has a physical, sensory, psychiatric or intellectual disability.
The client may also be able to receive a Disability Allowance to meet any additional costs the child has because of their disability.
There is no income and asset test for Child Disability Allowance.
Once a child turns 16 years of age they may be able to get Supported Living Payment on the ground of having a health condition, injury or disability.

chunks.title: Living arrangements — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Living arrangements
Child Disability Allowance is paid to assist people who prefer to provide care at home for their seriously disabled child. However it can also be paid for children living in residential homes or hostels as it is recognised that caregivers in this position are often faced with additional costs.
Child Disability Allowance can be paid for children who are in:
- the caregiver's home or
- a home or hostel run by a voluntary organisation where the child returns home for weekends or school holidays and where the client has to pay towards the child's care

chunks.title: Medical certificate not required — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Medical certificate not required
There are some cases where the application form does not need to be completed by the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner:
MSD can accept that the client meets the medical qualifications for Child Disability Allowance in the following situations.
- the child is attending on a daily basis: a specialist school ora school group, special unit or special class for children with intellectual disabilities in a mainstream school operated by a Board of Trustees (Note a medical certificate is required if the child is attending a special class that is not specifically for children with intellectual disabilities at an ordinary school) or
- a specialist school or
- a school group, special unit or special class for children with intellectual disabilities in a mainstream school operated by a Board of Trustees (Note a medical certificate is required if the child is attending a special class that is not specifically for children with intellectual disabilities at an ordinary school) or
- when a child aged 5 years or over has been exempted from attending a mainstream school and is attending a special day-care centre operated by IDEA Services
Where a decision is clear on medical grounds, a medical certificate does not need to be completed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner.

chunks.title: Medical grounds — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Medical grounds
To qualify for a Child Disability Allowance, the child must:
- have a physical, sensory, psychiatric or intellectual disability and
- need constant care and attention because of that disability and
- be likely to need that care for more than 12 months
Generally a medical certificate must be completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner.
However, there are some cases where a medical certificate is not required.

chunks.title: Other assistance — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Other assistance
Child Disability Allowance can be paid if the client is receiving:
- Unsupported Childs Benefit
- Orphans Benefit
- Childs War Pension or
- War Orphans Pension
Note if the child or client's circumstances change and they are no longer able to receive one of the above benefits, you should review the client's eligibility for a Child Disability Allowance.
A Child Disability Allowance cannot be paid if the child receives:
- a benefit in their own right (other than those listed above) or
- a War Pension
## Disability Allowance
A Disability Allowance can also be paid to a client who is receiving a Child Disability Allowance. Disability Allowance is subject to:
- an income test and
- the extent of the additional costs that are a result of the disability

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Payment
Child Disability Allowance is a non-taxable allowance which is usually paid to the principal caregiver of the child.
If there is no principal caregiver, you can pay the Child Disability Allowance to the person who is responsible for the care and control of the child for the time being.
For more information see:
- Shared care - principal caregiver
Also see:
- Deskfile Child Disability Allowance rates
- Commencement date

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for Child Disability Allowance, a client must:
- generally be 16 years or over
- be the principal caregiver of a dependent child with a disability (or if there is no principal caregiver, have the care and control of the child for the time being)
- be a New Zealand citizen or residence class visa holder (i.e. not be in New Zealand unlawfully, or here on a temporary entry class visa) and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
In addition to this the child must:
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
- be a dependent child
- have a physical, sensory, psychiatric or intellectual disability
- need constant care and attention because of the disability
- be likely to need care permanently, or need care for more than 12 months and
- meet the required living arrangements

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get Child Disability Allowance, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- have a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
Note for Child Disability Allowance no period of residence is required.
People who are in New Zealand unlawfully or here on a temporary entry class visa generally do not qualify for a benefit.
## Clients without citizenship or a residence class visa
If a client does not have New Zealand citizenship or a residence class visa, they cannot get Child Disability Allowance.
However, if a client in this situation has disability costs for their child, they may be able to get Temporary Additional Support if they are:
- a person who has refugee or protected person status in New Zealand or
- awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protected person status and are lawfully in New Zealand (i.e. they have a valid temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009) or
- applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 and are compelled to remain in New Zealand due to some unforeseen circumstances
Once the client has been granted citizenship or a residence class visa and they meet all the other qualifications, Child Disability Allowance may be granted.
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other criteria to qualify for Child Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Residential home — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Residential home
To receive Child Disability Allowance for children in residential homes the following criteria must be met:
- the principal caregiver is required to pay a board charge and
- the child is in the care of the principal caregiver during weekends and school holidays
This includes a principal temporary caregiver of a child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid.
Note a liberal interpretation can be applied when assessing the last criteria if there is a board charge. If a child returns home for some weekends or school holidays over a 6 month period and a board charge is paid, accept that the criteria is fulfilled.
The Child Disability Allowance can be paid to the principal caregivers of children in the following residential homes:
- IDEA Services homes
- CCS homes
- Hohepa homes or
- other religious hostels run by religious or welfare organisations

chunks.title: Residential hostels — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Residential hostels
If a child is in a home or hostel, Child Disability Allowance can only be paid where:
- the home or hostel is run by a voluntary organisation
- the caregiver is required to contribute to the cost of maintaining the child and
- the child is cared for by the caregiver during school holidays or weekends
If a child is in a hostel, check with the hostel at regular intervals to ensure that:
- the child still returns home for some weekends or school holidays
- the parents or guardians are taking an interest in the child and
- board is being paid

chunks.title: Shared care - principal caregiver — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Shared care - principal caregiver
To get Child Disability Allowance, the client must be the principal caregiver of the child. The client must have the primary responsibility for the day-to-day care of the child, not on a temporary basis.
If it is difficult to assess who is the principal caregiver, review the decision guidelines for:
- Child Disability Allowance shared care [no link find out why]
The principal caregiver cannot be:
- a group of people (whether incorporated or unincorporated) or
- any person who is the owner, or employed in: a residence provided under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 orany other institution where a child is being cared for
- a residence provided under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 or
- any other institution where a child is being cared for
## Exception
A principal temporary caregiver getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is considered to have primary responsibility for the child and may get Child Disability Allowance while the child is in their care.
However, they cannot be considered a principal caregiver for the purposes of decisions on shared care.
## Shared care - deciding principal caregiver
Shared care only applies when the parents or caregivers of a child are living apart, the child lives for at least 40% of the time with each parent and both parents apply for a Child Disability Allowance for the child.
Only one parent/caregiver (the principal caregiver) can get the Child Disability Allowance. The parent or caregiver must meet all the qualifications.

chunks.title: Specialist school or daycare centre — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Specialist school or daycare centre
Child Disability Allowance can be paid for children who attend the following facilities on a daily basis:
- day specialist school
- daycare centre
- training centre or
- sheltered workshop

chunks.title: State institutions — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## State institutions
Child Disability Allowance cannot be paid when a seriously disabled child is in one of the following institutions:
- a psychiatric hospital or
- a Ministry of Education residential specialist school
## Residential specialist schools in New Zealand
Residential specialist school for deaf and hearing-impaired students
- Ko Taku Reo Deaf Education New Zealand (a merger of the Kelston Deaf Education Centre in Auckland and the van Asch Deaf Education Centre in Christchurch)
Residential specialist school for blind and vision-impaired students
- Blind and Low Vision Education Network NZ or BLENNZ (previously known as Homai National School for the Blind and Vision Impaired)
Residential specialist schools specialising in working with students with educational, social and emotional needs, together with an underlying intellectual impairment
- Halswell Residential College co-educational, Christchurch
- Salisbury School girls, Nelson
- Westbridge Residential School co-educational, Auckland
These schools determine who meets the entry criteria for their services including any specific rules relating to sex or gender.
## Periods of leave from state institutions
Child Disability Allowance cannot be paid for children who reside in a state institution for more than 3 nights in 1 week.
However, Child Disability Allowance can be paid to the principal caregiver if a child leaves a state institution for a continuous period of 7 nights or more (including school holidays). This includes a principal temporary caregiver of a child for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid. Payments can be made for the full period at home.

chunks.title: Temporarily out of care — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Temporarily out of care
The Health Funding Authority provides for alternative care for disabled children by another person or hospital/institution. Child Disability Allowance can continue to be paid to the principal caregiver when the child is in alternative care. This includes a principal temporary caregiver of a child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid.
If the child goes into the care of another person temporarily and the client no longer meets the definition of principal caregiver (or principal temporary caregiver), Child Disability Allowance can be paid to the person who has the care of the child for the time being.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Shared care - principal caregiver

chunks.title: Terminal illness — extra help > child disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Terminal illness
If a child has a terminal illness they are considered to meet the medical qualifications for Child Disability Allowance.
The medical certificate still needs to be completed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner.

chunks.title: 20 Hours Early Childhood Education compulsory payments — extra help > childcare assistance programme
chunks.text:
## 20 Hours Early Childhood Education compulsory payments
There are 2 types of compulsory payments that providers may charge.
## Fees
Fees are compulsory payments that a caregiver must pay as a condition of their child's enrolment. A provider may enforce fees by withholding or withdrawing enrolment or part of their service if a caregiver does not pay.
Providers cannot charge fees for the same hours as 20 Hours Early Childhood Education (ECE). Providers can only request fees for hours of enrolment not covered by 20 Hours ECE.
## Home-based educator top up payments
A home-based educator may charge a home-based educator top up payment for the same hours as 20 Hours ECE.
A provider may also charge home-based educator top up payments on their behalf.
These payments may be enforced in the same way as fees.

chunks.title: Absences — extra help > childcare assistance programme
chunks.text:
## Absences
Most providers charge a fee when a child is temporarily away. The fee is charged to hold the child's place open at the service or centre.
MSD can pay the Childcare Subsidy for up to 3 weeks at any one time when a child is away from the service or centre and the period of absence coincides with the time the programme is available.
This can occur more than one time in the client's review year. However, if a child is consistently absent their hours of attendance should be reviewed to ensure that the subsidy paid reflects this.
## Medical exceptions
Payment can continue for up to 6 weeks if the child is absent due to their medical condition and the period of absence coincides with the time the programme is available.
For example, if the child has a medical certificate from a registered medical practitioner, or nurse practitioner stating they need to be away from the centre for longer than 3 weeks.
A medical certificate is not required if the child gets:
- Child Disability Allowance or
- Group Special Education funding
This can occur more than once in the client's review year. However, if a child is consistently absent, their hours of attendance should be reviewed to ensure that the subsidy paid reflects this.

chunks.title: Absences — extra help > childcare assistance programme
chunks.text:
## Absences
Most providers charge a fee when a child is temporarily away. This fee is charged to hold the child's place open at the service or the centre.
MSD can pay the OSCAR Subsidy for up to 3 weeks at any one time when a child is away from the service or centre and the period of absence coincides with the time the programme is available.
This can occur more than once in the client's review year. However, if a child is consistently absent their hours of attendance should be reviewed to ensure that the subsidy paid reflects this.
## Medical exceptions
Payment can continue for up to 6 weeks if the child is absent due to their medical condition and the period of absence coincides with the time the programme is available. For example if the child:
- has a medical certificate from a Health Practitioner stating that they will be away from the centre for longer than 3 weeks
For example if the child has a medical certificate from a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner stating they need to be away from the centre for longer than 3 weeks
A medical certificate is not required if the child gets:
- Child Disability Allowance or
- Group Special Education funding
This can occur more than once in the client's review year. However, if a child is consistently absent, their hours of attendance should be reviewed to ensure that the subsidy paid reflects this.

chunks.title: Absences due to COVID-19 requirements — extra help > childcare assistance programme
chunks.text:
## Absences due to COVID-19 requirements
When a child is absent due to COVID-19 requirements, Childcare Subsidy can continue being paid if the client still qualifies. A fee does not need to be charged to hold the child's place open for payment to continue.
A child may be absent due to COVID-19 requirements because they are:
- unwell and cannot attend childcare while unwell
- at high risk of severe illness if they contract COVID-19
- in self-isolation or quarantine due to COVID-19 public health requirements
- connected to a confirmed or probable case of COVID-19
- being kept home during Alert Level 3
This is not an exhaustive list. If a child is absent and you are unsure if it is due to COVID-19 requirements, please check the COVID-19 Alert System website for the most up to date COVID-19 guidelines.
## Number of weeks payment can continue
There is no limit on how long Childcare Subsidy can be paid when a child is absent due to COVID-19 requirements.
However, the subsidy can only be paid for a period that relates to COVID-19 requirements. If a child is absent for other reasons, you will need to check the general absence guidelines to see how long they can be paid.
## Example
Amina's son Gabriel suffers from a respiratory condition which means he is at high risk of severe illness if he contracts COVID-19. Due to this, Amina withdrew him from childcare for 7 weeks while New Zealand was at Alert Level 3.
Because the COVID-19 Alert Level 3 guidelines state that high risk people should stay home if they can, Childcare Subsidy can continue for the full period of Gabriel’s absence.

chunks.title: Absences when the Centre closes — extra help > childcare assistance programme
chunks.text:
## Absences when the Centre closes
Centres usually close for a set period of time each year, this is usually at the Christmas period. The set closure periods are not included in the calculation of a 3 week or 6 week absence.
## Example
A child is absent for 2 weeks leading up to the Friday prior to Christmas. The centre that the child attends is closing for 2 weeks from Christmas Eve.
The absence calculation only counts the 2 weeks leading up to Christmas Eve. If the child is away when the centre reopens the count continues for 1 more week, then the subsidy stops.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > childcare assistance programme
chunks.text:
## Example
A child is absent for 2 weeks leading up to the Friday prior to Christmas. The centre that the child attends is closing for 2 weeks from Christmas Eve.
The absence calculation only counts the 2 weeks leading up to Christmas Eve. If the child is away when the centre reopens the count continues for one more week, then the subsidy stops.

chunks.title: Additional contributions towards the cost of childcare fees — extra help > childcare assistance programme
chunks.text:
## Additional contributions towards the cost of childcare fees
Some employers make contributions towards the cost of their employees' childcare fees.
These payments should be a direct deduction off the total cost of the fee, when paid to the employee or to the employees' childcare provider. The payment must be identified as a contribution towards the cost of childcare fees.
## Employer contributions to the cost of childcare - example
Nicky's payslip shows that her employer contributes $15.00 per week.
Fee for child's care
$215.00 per week
Employer contribution
$15.00 per week
Weekly fee assessed for entitlement to subsidy
$200.00
Child attends 40 hours per week
Hourly fee equals
$5.00
The manual rate to pay (Nicky's income is within the income limits) is $5.00 per hour. This is manually added on CCSRG (when granting) and CCSC when reviewing.
## Employer includes the subsidy with the client's income - example
If the employer includes the subsidy with the client's income, the calculation is as follows:
Shelley's payslip shows she receives $46,300 per annum, and her payslip clearly shows that $1,000 per year is a contribution towards her childcare fees.
Shelley's annual income
$46,300 per year
Contribution to childcare fees
$1,000 per year
Income to take into account when calculating the income for childcare
$45,300 per year
Gross weekly income
$871.15 per week
Hourly rate of subsidy - 1 child (1 April 2026)
$6.72 per hour
The manual rate to pay is $6.72 per hour. This is manually added on CCSRG (when granting) and CCSC when reviewing.

chunks.title: Additional contributions towards the cost of OSCAR fees — extra help > childcare assistance programme
chunks.text:
## Additional contributions towards the cost of OSCAR fees

These payments should be a direct deduction off the total cost of the fee, when paid to the employee or to the employee's OSCAR provider.
The payment must be identified as a contribution towards the cost of OSCAR fees.

If the employer includes the OSCAR subsidy with the client's income, the calculation is as follows:
