Limb centres are open daily from 8.00am to 4.30pm.
A client may need to attend one of the 5 limb centres or a regional clinic. The limb centre will decide where the client needs to attend.

chunks.title: Loss of earnings — extra help > civilian amputee assistance
chunks.text:
## Loss of earnings
Assistance for loss of earnings may only be paid where the client does not have any sick leave available.
The client must provide a letter from their employer confirming the client has no sick leave available and stating the wages (net) lost.
The loss of earnings of an attendant cannot be met by Civilian Amputee Assistance.
## Maximum amount payable
The maximum amount paid to the client for loss of weekly earnings must not be more than the current rate paid for ordinary time weekly wage.
Overtime or penal rates for the client cannot be considered.

chunks.title: Meals — extra help > civilian amputee assistance
chunks.text:
## Meals
A client (and attendant) can receive assistance for the cost of each meal (up to three meals per day) required during travel times and overnight stays when attending a limb centre.
The maximum payment a client can receive is:
- the actual cost of the meal or
- $13.05 per meal
whichever is less.
Meal costs should not be paid for more than 10 days per assessment.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > civilian amputee assistance
chunks.text:
## Payment
Generally, Civilian Amputee Assistance is paid before the client attends the appointment at the limb centre. Clients must provide a quote or estimate of their costs to attend the appointment.
Payments should be made to the supplier where this is possible.
## Reimbursement
The full cost of some items may not be known prior to attendance at the limb centre or regional clinic. Your client can apply for reimbursement of any additional costs if the amount paid in advance did not meet the full cost.
When a client elects to meet the costs themselves, they can apply for a reimbursement after they have attended their appointment.
Clients who receive Civilian Amputee Assistance before they attend the limb centre will need to complete a second application for a reimbursement of any further costs. All applications for reimbursement should be made within 6 months of attending the appointment.
Payment for reimbursement of costs can be made direct to the client.
## Attendants' costs
Payments can also be made for an attendant in some situations.
The attendant can claim, travel, accommodation and meals.
No assistance is provided to the attendant for loss of earnings.
For more information see:
- Attendant
## Costs allowed
For information about the types of costs a client can get assistance for see:
- Types of costs

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > civilian amputee assistance
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To receive Civilian Amputee Assistance to help with the costs of attending a limb centre, a client must provide proof of their appointment at a limb centre.
This assistance is not subject to an income or asset test.
Assistance is also available for the costs of an attendant in some situations.
For more information see:
- Attendant
## No assistance available
If a client has lost a limb due to an accident, they can get Accident Compensation. You should refer the client to their nearest ACC office.
If the client has incurred costs for a dependent child who is in the care of Oranga Tamariki, refer the client to their social worker.

chunks.title: Travel expenses — extra help > civilian amputee assistance
chunks.text:
## Travel expenses
A client (and attendant) can receive financial assistance for travel costs to a limb centre. The amount paid will depend on the method of travel, but should generally be based on the most economical means of transport having regard to the particular needs of the client.
Your client will need to provide details of the method of travel that will be used. If payment is required before they attend the limb centre an estimate of the likely cost is required. Where the client is eligible for subsidised travel you should only meet the actual cost remaining following any reduction to the full fare.
The types of travel cost allowed include:
- public transport
- taxi fares
- private car
- air travel
## Private car
A client (and attendant) can receive assistance for travel by private car based on:
- mileage or
- petrol costs if receipts are produced (but should not be more than the mileage)
The amount paid per kilometre travelled depends on the cc rating of the vehicle as follows:
cc rating
Rate payable per km
up to 1000
29 cents per km
1001 - 1350
30 cents per km
1351 - 2000
35 cents per km
2000+
40 cents per km
If the client and attendant travel by taxi or private vehicle then only one set of travel costs should be incurred and paid.
## Air travel
A client (and attendant) can receive assistance for the cost of air travel where there is written evidence that this is the most appropriate form of travel, (such as a letter from an orthopaedic surgeon or manager of the limb centre).

chunks.title: Types of costs — extra help > civilian amputee assistance
chunks.text:
## Types of costs
Financial assistance for Civilian Amputees is available for the following costs:
- Travel expenses
- Accommodation costs
- Meals
- Attendant
- Loss of earnings
Also see:
- How to apply

chunks.title: Agreed period payments — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Agreed period payments
An agreed period payment is a written agreement of credit under a consumer credit contract or by other regular payments which must be in writing and have regular payments over an agreed period.
The client must provide satisfactory verification that they have purchased the essential item and that they are making regular repayments towards the item.
## Not included
Agreed period payments do not include:
- revolving credit payments
- Advance Payments of Benefits
- Recoverable Assistance Payments
For more information see:
- Allowable costs
- Consumer credit contract (hire purchase)

chunks.title: Allowable costs — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Allowable costs
Allowable costs that can be considered for Community Costs are the client's ongoing costs in the community that are essential to help them to reintegrate into the community at the end of their treatment.
For the assessment of Community Costs, all costs are calculated on a weekly basis.
Allowable costs include (but are not limited to):
- accommodation costs(including mortgage, rates and insurance)
- storage costs
- childcare costs for any dependent child
- agreed period payments(for example hire purchase for essential household furniture or appliances)
- employment and employment-related training costs(for example an apprentice paying off their work tools)
There could be costs other than those listed, that because of the client's individual circumstances should be included as an allowable cost.
Note you can only consider costs that the client had prior to or as a result of entering the programme.
## SWIFTT process
Community Costs is paid as a Miscellaneous Subsidy using reason code 513 RSS In community costs.
For more information see:
- Allowable costs not in client's name
- Costs not allowed
- Factors to consider when deciding costs
- Deciding what rate to pay

chunks.title: Allowable costs not in client's name — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Allowable costs not in client's name
Generally, costs not in the client's or partner's name are not included in the assessment of Community Costs as the client or partner is not liable for the repayments.
There may be situations where a client or their partner has entered an informal arrangement with another person to purchase an essential item using the other person's name and/or credit rating for the hire purchase agreement.
You need to be satisfied that the client or their partner is the person making the payments and that it was the intention of the parties to the informal arrangement that the client or their partner would have responsibility for the payments and would benefit from the use and control of the item.
Note you must also be satisfied that the client is responsible for the cost and has the use of the goods or service is required. The onus is on the client in the first instance to provide any further information required. Ask for further information if you are not satisfied.
A full statement from the client or partner and the other party is required along with a copy of the purchase agreement to determine if the cost can be included in the Community Costs assessment.
To assist in making a decision as to whether the client is responsible for the cost the following should be considered:
- Why are the goods or service in another person's name? You will need to establish why the goods or service is not in the client's name. For example, but not limited to, is the client bankrupt and cannot obtain this essential goods or service item with their current credit rating?
- Is it possible to transfer the goods or service into the client's name?
- Has any other person contributed to the goods or service payments in any way?
Contact Helpline if you need assistance deciding whether or not the cost can be included.
For more information see:
- Costs not allowed

chunks.title: Calculating rate when partner in the community — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Calculating rate when partner in the community
You will need to complete the following steps to calculate the amount of Community Costs to pay when the client has a partner in the community.
## Step 1
Calculate in weekly amounts:
- (A) the client's essential ongoing costs to return to the community and
- (B) any new costs incurred as a result of the entry into the programme
## Step 2
Calculate the couple's combined net income before the client's entry into the programme.
## Step 3
Calculate the couple's income now.
You will need to exclude:
- any amount the client is required to pay towards the cost of their care and
- an amount equivalent to the personal allowance
Remember to check that the partner in the community is getting all their entitlements to income support and Working for Families Tax Credits (if applicable).
## Step 4
Calculate the difference between the couple's combined net income before the client's entry into the programme (Step 2) and their net income now (Step 3).
## Step 5
Calculate the difference between the client's essential ongoing costs (Step 1A) and any assistance being received for those costs (Step 3).
## Step 6
Calculate the rate of Community Costs to pay.
You can pay the essential ongoing costs not being met by any assistance (Step 5) up to the difference in income calculated at Step 4, unless the client has new costs as a result of their entry into the programme (Step 1B), in which case you can pay an additional amount to meet the new costs.
Remember if the amount you decide to pay is more than the $300 maximum, you will need manager client service delivery approval.

chunks.title: Cash assets — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Cash assets
Cash assets mean the assets of the client or their partner (if any) that can be easily converted into cash.
## Cash assets include
- bills of exchange or promissory notes
- building society shares
- money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society
- money invested with or lent to any bank, financial institution or other person whether on mortgage, other security or unsecured
- shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds, and bonds
- the net equity held in any property or land not used as the person's home
- the share in any partnership
## Cash assets do not include
- a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2000 or which is used by the client or a member of their family for day to day accommodation
- a motor vehicle or other vehicle required by the client for their personal use (this is limited to one vehicle for a single person or two vehicles for a married, civil union or de facto couple)
- the home property and land on which it is situated
- personal effects
- Christchurch mosques attack support payments
- Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments
- funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts
- Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income
- MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014
- Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after payment is made
- Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after payment is made
- Severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment)
- specified Ex gratia and Compensation payments
- Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received
A bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.
Canterbury earthquake related payments
Payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client received the payment.

chunks.title: Cash assets test — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Cash assets test
A client will not be able to receive Community Costs if they (and their partner if any) have cash assets equal to or more than:
Single person
Asset limit for a single person without dependent children
Married, civil union or de facto couple, orsole parent
Asset limit for a married, civil union or de facto couple with or without dependent children, or sole parent with children
Note the sole parent asset limit is the same as the married, civil union or de facto couple limit.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text: Clients can be absent from New Zealand and continue to receive payment for the first 28 days of any absence if it does not affect the client's qualification for Community Costs (that is the client remains enrolled as a resident in the treatment programme). To pay Community Costs while the client is absent from New Zealand depends on whether the client is also getting a main benefit.

chunks.title: Clients getting a main benefit — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text: All clients receiving a main benefit must advise Work and Income before they leave New Zealand. If the client or partner does not advise Work and Income prior to their international travel, their benefit payments (including Community Costs) must stop. Where a client is paid their main benefit while they are absent from New Zealand (either because they meet the criteria for approved travel or the requirement to approved travel does not apply to them) they can continue to receive their main benefit and their Community Costs payment for up to 28 days in any 52 week period, unless they meet the criteria to be paid their main benefit for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. Clients who do not continue to receive main benefit while overseas (because they do not meet the criteria for approved travel) may still be able to continue to receive Community Costs payment, if their absence does not affect the client's eligibility for this assistance and they have advised Work and Income of their absence prior to their international travel. This is limited to 28 days in a 52 week period. For more information about Absence from New Zealand see: - Approved travel reasons in relevant main benefit - Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period in relevant main benefit

chunks.title: Clients getting non-beneficiary Extra Help — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text: Clients who are receiving Community Costs and who are not also getting a main benefit: - are required to advise of their departure from New Zealand and - can be absent and paid their Community Costs for up to 28 days per absence where it does not affect the client's eligibility for Community Costs, that is, where they are still enrolled as a resident in the treatment programme

chunks.title: Information required from client when advising they intend to travel — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text: When a client receiving a main benefit contacts you to advise that they intend travelling overseas you need to obtain the following information: - date of departure - date of return

chunks.title: Non-beneficiary Extra Help payment will not continue — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text: Where payment of Community Costs will not continue because they do not meet the eligibility criteria due to their absence you will need to suspend the benefit from: - the day after departure

chunks.title: Permanent absence — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text: If the client is leaving New Zealand permanently Community Cost should be cancelled from the day after departure.

chunks.title: Advises more than 14 days after the event — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Advises more than 14 days after the event
Clients have an obligation to advise Work and Income of any changes that may affect their entitlement to Community Costs and it is expected that they will do so as soon as possible.
When a client advises of a change in circumstances more than 14 days after the event you should generally reduce, suspend or cancel Community Costs from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.
## Good and sufficient reason
Where there is a good and sufficient reason (for example, bereavement or illness) for the client not advising Work and Income of a change in circumstances within 14 days you may reduce, suspend or cancel Community Costs from the first available date.
## False or misleading information
If a client gives false or misleading information you must review Community Costs from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.

chunks.title: Change in costs — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Change in costs
You will need to review Community Costs to ensure that the client is receiving the correct rate of payment whenever there is a change in the client's costs such as when the amount of a cost increases or reduces.
Any increase in the client's costs in the community must be verified. You will need to be satisfied that the increase in costs is for an ongoing essential item that is currently included in the client's Community Costs payment. For example the client is receiving Community Costs for storing their furniture and they have received notice that the storage fees have increased.
For more information see:
- Allowable costs
## Date to review
The date to review Community Costs from will depend on the action involved. Generally, you should:
Increase
- increase Community Costs from the actual date of the change in circumstances
Reduce, suspend or cancel
- reduce, suspend or cancel Community Costs from the first available date except when the client advises of a change more than 14 days after the event

chunks.title: Change in family circumstances — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Change in family circumstances
MSD should review Community Costs to check that the client still meets the qualifications and is getting the correct rate of payment whenever there is a change in the client's:
- relationship status or
- the number of dependent child/ren in the client's care(for example the client may be getting Community Costs for childcare and the child leaves their care permanently)
The date to review Community Costs from will depend on the action involved. Generally, MSD should:
## Increase
- increase Temporary Additional Support from the actual date of the change in circumstances
## Reduce, suspend or cancel
- reduce, suspend or cancel Community Costs from the first available date except when the client advises of a change more than 14 days after the event
## False or misleading information
If a client gives false or misleading information MSD must review Community Costs from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.
## Child turns 18
A child must generally be under the age of 18 to be considered a dependent child and be included in their parent or caregiver's Community Costs.
The parent or caregiver must also complete a review of circumstances to determine if they continue to qualify for their discretionary benefit such as Community Costs, and the rate payable.

chunks.title: Change in income or assets — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Change in income or assets
You will need to review Community Costs to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment whenever there is a change in the client's:
- income or
- cash assets
The date to review Community Costs from will depend on the action involved. Generally, you should:
## Increase
- increase Community Costs from the actual date of the change in circumstances

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client must advise the Ministry of Social Developmnet of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement or rate of assistance payable.
You may also review a benefit at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.
For more information see:
- Absence from New Zealand
- Core policy Agents
- Change in costs
- Change in family circumstances
- Change in income or assets
- Client transfers to a new service provider
- Client leaves the programme
- Death of a client
- Deductions
- Core policy Redirection of benefit payment
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Review at 26 weeks

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Child turns 18
A dependent child must generally be under the age of 18 to be included in their parent or caregiver's Community Costs.
When a child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and must be excluded from their parent or caregiver's Community Costs from the start of the pay period following the child's 18th birthday. The parent or caregiver must also complete a review of circumstances to determine if they continue to qualify for their discretionary benefit such as Community Costs, and the rate payable.
However, if the 18-year-old child is continuing in education and is not financially independent, the child may continue to be considered a dependent child and be included in their parent or caregiver's Community Costs for a limited period.
In these situations, the child must be excluded from the start of the pay period following:
- the date they no longer meet these criteria or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18
whichever is earlier
Note a parent or caregiver getting Community Costs must complete a review of circumstances when a dependent child turns 18, and when the child is excluded (if they continued to be included in the parent or caregiver's Community Costs after the child turned 18). If the parent or caregiver does not complete the review, their Community Costs will be suspended.

chunks.title: Client leaves the programme — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Client leaves the programme
Community Costs payment ends on:
- the date the client's eligibility ends
- the date the client's residential treatment programme ends or
- the date the client leaves the programme
whichever is earliest.
When a client is receiving a main benefit and returns to live in the community, the case manager will need to reassess the client's eligibility for benefit assistance, and invite applications for Extra Help where applicable.
If the client has been resident in a treatment programme for six months or more, they may be eligible for a re-establishment grant.
For more information see:
- Special Needs Grant Re-establishment grants
- Extra Help
- Main Benefits

chunks.title: Client transfers to a new service provider — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Client transfers to a new service provider
If a client transfers from one service provider to another, their Community Costs can be paid provided that:
- they complete a new Community Costs Payment application form
- the client meets the qualifications for Community Costs
- they have costs in the community and
- the treatment programme is not intended to be more than 39 weeks
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Allowable costs
- Period of payment of Community Costs

chunks.title: Court attachment orders — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Court attachment orders
All court attachment requests are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit for processing. Court attachments are administered via the CORBI screen in SWIFTT.
The Ministry of Justice has the authority to make attachment orders on benefits to meet outstanding court fines. The attachment order may include:
- court finesthese are fines payable to the District Court
- civil attachmentsthese are generally paid to a private individual or organisation that is owed money. Occasionally the District Court will act as a collection agent for civil debts.
Attachment Orders issued by the Ministry of Justice can be made under either the Summary Proceedings Act 1957 or the District Court Act 2016.
## Protected earnings rate
No attachment order can, whether on its own or when combined with any other attachment order, Child Support deduction, or Ministry of Social Development repayment, take a client's total income below the protected earnings rate. For more information see:
- Protected earnings rate
## Information provided the Court
The information that will be received from the Ministry of Justice will have:
- the client's name
- the amount to be deducted from the benefit
- the fine's reference number
If a client is suffering undue hardship because of the amount of the attachment order then they should be directed to a Registrar of the District Court for a reassessment of the rate.
For more information see:
- Court request for information

chunks.title: Death of a client — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Death of a client
When a client who is receiving Community Costs dies, payments stop from the day after death.
Note when a client has a Community Services or SuperGold Card, the card must be manually cancelled and death details added to Person Details latch in CMS.
Contact the Card Centre on 0800 999 999 or email to request cancellation of the card.

chunks.title: Debt Repayment Orders — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Debt Repayment Orders
All Debt Repayment Orders are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit for processing.
Debt Repayment Orders are issued by the Ministry of Justice under the Insolvency Act 2006 and can be issued where the client is an un-discharged bankrupt.
Unlike other Ministry of Justice attachment orders, Debt Repayment Orders are not subject to any protected earnings rate. Payment is generally made to the supervisor of the debt but occasionally the District Court will act as an agent for collection of the debt.
Payment continues for 3 years or until further notice is received from either the supervisor or the District Court.
Unlike Ministry of Justice attachment orders, Debt Repayment Orders are administered via the PYECI screen in SWIFTT, not through CORBI.

chunks.title: Deductions — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Deductions
In certain circumstances Work and Income can be required to pay part of the client's benefit to another party.
Work and Income is legally required to make such deductions when served with a properly issued Deduction Notice or Attachment Order. In these cases, the consent of the client is not required.
Certain forms of deductions take priority over others.

chunks.title: Inland Revenue deduction notices — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Inland Revenue deduction notices
Inland Revenue may request for a client's unpaid taxes to be directly deducted from their benefit payments.
Note all Inland Revenue deduction notices are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit to process.
The instructions of the deduction notice will be to deduct the lowest of either:
- 10% of the total debt which Inland Revenue specify in the notice, on a weekly basis or
- 20% of the client's gross earnings on a weekly basis
When there are insufficient funds to cover the deduction, the Ministry of Social Development must advise Inland Revenue immediately that the deduction will not start or will start at a reduced rate.
Inland Revenue deductions have a lower priority than Child Support deductions.
For more information see:
- Priority for deductions

chunks.title: Priority for deductions — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Priority for deductions
Certain forms of deductions take priority over others; the following list gives the order of priority, highest to lowest:
Highest priority
- Child Support deductions made under the Child Support Act 1991
- Inland Revenue tax deductions
- Ministry of Social Development debt repayments including Liable Parent Contributions (LPC), child maintenance debts and Major Repairs Advances (MRA), Student Allowance debt, Student Loan debt converted to Ministry of Social Development debt, Income Related Rent historical Housing New Zealand debt, Income Related Rent Ministry of Social Development debt
- Attachment orders made under the Family Proceedings Act 1980
- Court attachment orders issued under the Summary Proceedings Act 1957
- Court attachment orders issued under the District Court Act 2016
- Student Loan repayments
Lowest priority
Determining the priority of deductions is necessary when a client has more than one order issued in respect of their benefit. Also each order and deduction notice is subject to its own protected earnings rule.
When you need to reduce deductions you adjust from the lowest priority up to those with a higher priority taking into account the protected earnings rules for each.

chunks.title: Protected earnings rate — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Protected earnings rate
Both the District Court Act and the Summary Proceedings Act provide that every attachment order must specify a 'protected earnings rate'.
The protected earnings rate is usually 60% of the client’s net earnings after PAYE tax has been deducted or withheld.
If the attachment order will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate, then the order will not operate and you must cancel or return the attachment order to the Ministry of Justice.
Calculating the client's income differs between attachment orders made under the Summary Proceedings Act and the District Court Act, as different benefits are taken into account. Therefore it is important to determine what type of attachment order has been issued.
Summary Proceedings Act 1957
For orders made under the Summary Proceedings Act, the calculation of the client's income does not include Special Benefit, Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance, Winter Energy Payment, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit
District Court Act 2016
For orders made under the District Court Act, the client's income includes Special Benefit and Disability Allowance but does not include Child Disability Allowance, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit
## Example
An attachment order is received from the Ministry of Justice for $80.00 per week. The attachment order shows that the client's protected earnings rate is $286.53 per week:
We need to calculate whether adding the deduction of $80.00 will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate.
Calculate protected earnings rate
Jobseeker Support - single person rate (as at 1 April 2026)
$372.55
Plus Accommodation Supplement (area 2)
$105.00
Total net earnings
$477.55
60% of total net earnings (= protected earnings)
$286.53
Calculate if Attachment Order will exceed protected earnings
Total net earnings
$477.55
Less Child Support deduction
$55.00
Less Ministry of Social Development debt
$65.00
Sub total
$357.55
Less Attachment order
$80.00
Total net income remaining for the client per week
$277.55
The attachment order amount of $80.00 takes the client's total net income remaining to $277.55, which is below the protected earnings rate of $286.53 per week. The attachment order will not operate, therefore you must return it to the Ministry of Justice for the order to be amended.

chunks.title: Review at 26 weeks — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Review at 26 weeks
Community Costs is reviewed when the client:
- has completed a period (or total period) of 26 weeks residence in a treatment programme within a 52 week period and
- it has been clinically determined that the client needs and would benefit from further treatment in the programme
The client will need to:
- complete a Community Costs Payment application form
- ensure that the Service Provider states on the application form that it has been clinically determined that they need, and would benefit from, further treatment
- provide verification of any increases in existing costs or advise of any reductions in costs
## Approval
Only Service Managers can approve payment of Community Costs for any period more than 26 weeks up to the maximum period of 39 weeks within a 52 week period.
## Client in care for more than 39 weeks
Where it has been clinically determined that a client needs further treatment beyond the initial 26 weeks and that the further treatment period would exceed the maximum payment period allowed of 39 weeks, you will need to advise them that there is no authority to extend payment beyond the 39 weeks.
If the client intends to stay in the programme beyond the 39 weeks maximum, you will need to advise them that they should start to make other arrangements for their costs in the community before the 39 weeks ends as these costs will not be met by Community Costs after this time.
When the client is ready to reintegrate into the community on completion of their treatment programme, they may be able to receive other assistance such as:
- Advance Payment of Benefit
- Special Needs Grant (including a re-establishment grant)
- other Extra Help
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Payment

chunks.title: Student Loans — extra help > community costs > changes and reviews community costs
chunks.text:
## Student Loans
Clients with a Student Loan must make repayments to Inland Revenue when the income they receive exceeds a pre-determined level. This level is called the 'income threshold'.
A person must make repayments to Inland Revenue when their income exceeds $464.00 gross per week ($24,128 gross per year) as at 1 April 2026. Note non-taxable Extra help such as family tax credit, Best Start tax credit and Accommodation Supplement do not count as income in this instance.
If the client's income is over this income threshold, the Ministry of Social Development can make the required deduction. However, this is only done if the client requests it.
If the client's portion of benefit is below the income threshold, there is no provision to make voluntary repayments through SWIFTT. The client can make voluntary payments direct to Inland Revenue at any time.
Note the following:
- Student Loan deductions can only be made from taxable benefits
- Student Loan deductions cannot be made if the client's benefit is below the income threshold
- when a client receives a married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit only the client's portion is taken into consideration when assessing Student Loan repayments
- when a client is receiving a reduced rate of payment due to other income, the Student Loan deduction is assessed on the net payment after income deduction
## For more information on Student Loans see:
- Students Student Loan

chunks.title: Childcare costs — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Childcare costs
MSD can include childcare costs in the assessment of Community Costs. For example where a dependent child is:
- placed in the care of a temporary caregiver or
- resides with the parent in the treatment programme and there is a charge for childcare assistance
However, MSD must include any payments gotten on behalf of the child, for example family tax credit, Best Start tax credit and Childcare Assistance as income, in the assessment of Community Costs.
As a guide to what is a reasonable cost for childcare where the child is being cared for in the community by a temporary caregiver, use the appropriate rate of Unsupported Child's Benefit.

chunks.title: Clients who cannot receive Community Costs — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Clients who cannot receive Community Costs
A client cannot receive Community Costs if:
- they (or their partner if any) are receiving Special Benefit
- they are a dependent child (which includes a child for whom an Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid)
- they are a child for whom payments are being made under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- they have been assessed as needing to live in a residential care facility on a long-term basis (such as clients with mental health, physical or intellectual disabilities)
- they have been needs assessed as requiring long term residential care in a hospital or rest home indefinitely (such as clients in age-related care)
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Partner in the community

chunks.title: Commencement date — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
The commencement date of Community Costs is:
- the date of application or
- the date the client enters the residential treatment programme if that application is made within 28 days of entering the residential treatment programme
Note if the application is not received within 28 days you cannot backdate the commencement date.
- Core policy Application for assistance

chunks.title: Consumer credit contract (hire purchase) — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Consumer credit contract (hire purchase)
A consumer credit contract (hire purchase) is where a client enters into a contract to purchase personal, domestic or household items, including any agreement where:
- interest charges may be payable under the contract or
- credit fees may be payable under the contract or
- security may be required under the contract and
- the creditor is in the business of providing credit
A client who has used a consumer credit contract to purchase an essential item that is an allowable cost can have this item included in their assessment for Community Costs.
The client must purchase the item from a supplier and establish a credit contract through that supplier. The credit contract does not have to be with the supplier but the supplier must introduce the client to the creditor.
For example, a client would like to establish a consumer credit contract with a supplier to purchase a washing machine. The supplier then asks the client to complete a credit application form for a finance company.
For more information see:
- Allowable costs
- Agreed period payments

chunks.title: Costs not allowed — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Costs not allowed
The following costs are not considered as essential and ongoing costs in the community:
- payments of child support or maintenance
- debt repayments, fine repaymentsThese include payments to collection agencies, Inland Revenue, personal loans, visa and bankcard repayments, MSD debts, Debt Repayment Orders, attachment orders, court fines, Student Loan repayments.
- fees charged by banks or other financial institutions
Note some costs, particularly fines and debt repayments can be renegotiated and the repayment level decreased. Work and Income debt repayments should be suspended while the client is receiving Community Costs.
## Costs not essential or reasonable
Costs considered non-essential or not reasonable for the item or service are not allowed in the assessment of Community Costs.

chunks.title: Deciding what rate to pay — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Deciding what rate to pay
The amount that can be paid under Community Costs, after considering all of the factors for deciding costs and client's individual circumstances, is the difference between:
- the client's income (excluding an amount equivalent to the personal allowance and any amount they are required to contribute to the cost of the treatment programme from their income) and
- the total of their ongoing essential costs in the community
Community Costs can be paid on a dollar for dollar basis up to the maximum weekly amount.
Important note the client (and their partner if any) should not receive any more in total financially (excluding an amount equivalent to the personal allowance) than they did prior to the client entering the treatment programme.
Remember to fully document your decision, including the factors you have taken into consideration in reaching your decision.
For more information see:
- Maximum weekly amount payable
- Period of payment of Community Costs
- Factors to consider when deciding costs
- Documenting your decision
- Calculating rate when partner in the community

chunks.title: Documenting your decision — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Documenting your decision
Community Costs involves the use of discretion, therefore it is important to show the process used to arrive at that decision.
In particular you must give reasons for your decision, including the factors you have taken into consideration in reaching your decision. You should also document what costs you have or have not considered at each point in the decision process and why.
## Reviews
Any review of Community Costs is treated as a reassessment of the application and you should go through all the steps that were done for the initial application and document your decision as above.
## Recording notes in CMS
You should record the following information in CMS:
- provider/institution client is attending
- costs included in the calculation
- reasons why a particular cost was included
- date of grant
- intended length of programme
- amount of weekly payment
All other information should be retained with the Community Costs Payment Application form on the client's file.
For more information see:
- Factors to consider when assessing Community Costs
- Allowable costs
- Changes and reviews
- Processing standards Applications [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances
When considering whether the client has exceptional circumstances, consider the following factors:
- Is the maximum amount of Community Costs insufficient to meet the client's essential ongoing costs in the community?
- What would be the effect of not meeting all of the client's costs?
- What are the minimum costs the client has to meet? For example, is the mortgage being paid at the minimum amount required?
- Can the client reduce the cost? For example, are cheaper childcare options available?
- Are there any other circumstances of the client's situation you consider relevant?
In addition to the above, remember to consider the assistance that might be available from other sources to meet the client's need.
Interviewing the client by phone may be appropriate to help you decide whether the client has exceptional circumstances.
For more information see:
- Clients who cannot receive Community Costs
- Deciding what rate to pay
- Documenting your decision
- Factors to consider when deciding costs
- Other sources of assistance

chunks.title: Factors to consider when deciding costs — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Factors to consider when deciding costs
When a client meets the qualifications for Community Costs, you should then consider the following factors when deciding to allow a community cost:
- Is the amount of the community cost a reasonable cost for that item or service?
- If the client is receiving a benefit, how much are they required to contribute to the cost of the treatment programme from their benefit? or
If the client is not receiving a benefit, how much are they required to contribute to the cost of the treatment programme from their income?
- Does the client have a spouse or partner residing in the community who may be entitled to receive income support such as Extra help?
- Has the client or their partner (if any) explored all other sources of assistance that may be available to help them meet their costs?
- Would paying Community Costs result in the applicant and their partner (if any) receiving more in total financially (excluding an amount equivalent to the personal allowance) than they did prior to the client entering the programme?
- Are there any other circumstances of the client's particular situation you consider relevant?
You should consider the nature of the cost and the reason behind it. Individual factors may not be out of the ordinary on their own but taken together they may warrant payment of Community Costs.
In addition to the above remember that Community Costs should only be considered in respect of ongoing costs that are essential to help the client reintegrate into the community.
For more information see:
- Other sources of assistance
- Allowable costs
- Payment
- Documenting your decision

chunks.title: Income test — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Income test
A client cannot receive Community Costs if their income is more than the appropriate income limit.
Note income includes the income of the client's partner (if any).
If a client is receiving a main benefit or pension, they would usually qualify under the income test.
For more information about what income includes and does not include see:
- Core Policy Definition of income
Also see:
- Cash asset test

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Community Costs is a non-taxable payment that can be paid to clients receiving treatment in short-term residential treatment programmes to help them to reintegrate into the community at the end of their treatment.
The payment of Community Costs is discretionary and is assessed on a case by case basis taking into account the client's individual circumstances.
It provides financial assistance to clients to help meet their essential ongoing costs in the community that cannot be met from an amount equivalent to the personal allowance or other resources.
Community Costs for the whole of New Zealand is administered by the Residential Subsidy Unit in Whangarei.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Payment
- Commencement date
- Changes and reviews

chunks.title: Maximum weekly amount payable — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Maximum weekly amount payable
Generally the maximum amount of Community Costs payable is $300 a week.
If the client has exceptional circumstances, Service Managers only may approve an increase in the amount payable above $300 a week.
You must fully document your decision and the reasons why the amount being paid exceeds $300 a week.
For more information see:
- Exceptional circumstances
- Deciding what rate to pay
- Factors to consider when deciding costs
- Period of payment of Community Costs
- Payment

chunks.title: Other sources of assistance — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Other sources of assistance
Rather than paying Community Costs, the client (or their partner if any) may have other options that they have not considered. These may include (but are not limited to):
- eligibility to income support (main benefit or extra help)
- assistance from other government agencies(such as Working for Families Tax Credits from Inland Revenue)
- negotiating payment of accounts by instalments at a reduced rate
- refinancing
Consider each option and decide if there is something that could better meet the needs of the client.
Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a resource available to a client.
## Partner in community
Check to see if the partner in the community qualifies for income support. This will need to be done before the Residential Subsidy Unit can consider paying Community Costs to the client.
Consider:
- Main Benefits
- Accommodation Supplement
- Advance Payment of Benefit
- Disability Allowance
- Temporary Additional Support
Note if the client or partner (if any) is already receiving or continues to be eligible to receive Special Benefit, you can review this to include the ongoing essential costs in the community, see:
- Receiving Special Benefit
- Documenting your decision

chunks.title: Partner in the community — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Partner in the community
Where a client has a partner in the community, the partner in the community cannot receive Community Costs.
For any application received from the client, the Community Costs is assessed for joint income, assets and costs of both the client and their partner in the community.
## Client is receiving a benefit
When a client who is receiving a main benefit and has a partner in the community applies for Community Costs, the Residential Subsidy Unit will contact the partner's case manager.
The case manager will need to:
- ensure that the partner in the community is receiving their full and correct entitlement to any Extra Help and
- check that the partner has explored all other financial resources available
The Residential Subsidy Unit can only consider paying Community Costs when all of the above have been done.
## SWIFTT process
The Residential Subsidy Unit will reassess the main benefit for the client and the partner in the community.
## Client is not receiving a benefit
When a client who is not receiving a benefit and has a partner, applies for Community Costs, they and their partner should be invited to apply for income support (if appropriate).
For more information see:
- Other sources of assistance
- Receiving Special Benefit
- Payment
- Calculating rate when partner in the community
- Main Benefits
- Extra Help
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Payment
Community Costs is a non-taxable payment that can be paid to clients in short-term residential treatment programmes to help them to reintegrate into the community at the end of their treatment.
Community Costs is paid directly to the client.
If the intended duration of a treatment programme is more than 39 weeks then Community Costs is not payable.
Note the client and their partner (if any) should not receive any more in total financially (excluding an amount equivalent to the personal allowance) than they did prior to the client entering the treatment programme.
## SWIFTT process
Community Costs is paid as a Miscellaneous Subsidy using reason code 513 RSS In community costs.
For more information see:
- Deciding what rate to pay
- Factors to consider when deciding costs
- Maximum weekly amount payable
- Period of payment of Community Costs
- Calculating rate when partner in the community
Also see:
- Changes and reviews

chunks.title: Period of payment of Community Costs — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Period of payment of Community Costs
Community Costs can be paid initially for up to 26 weeks within any 52 week period, starting from the client's entry into the programme, or their first treatment programme (if they change programmes).
The 26 weeks do not need to be continuous or in the same programme.
## Payment beyond 26 weeks
Community Costs can be paid for up to a further 13 weeks where it has been clinically determined that:
- the client needs and would benefit from further treatment in the programme and
- the client continues to be a resident in the treatment programme
Any extension beyond 26 weeks is treated as a re-application for Community Costs and the client's circumstances and costs in the community should be confirmed.
Manager client service delivery approval is required for all extensions beyond 26 weeks.
Note Community Costs cannot be paid for more than 39 weeks in total within the 52 week period.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for Community Costs, a client must:
- be aged 16 years or more
- meet an income test
- meet a cash assets test
- be resident in a short-term residential treatment programme
- complete a Community Costs Payment Application form
- have ongoing costs in the community that are essential
- have no other means of financial assistance or resources to meet their ongoing costs
- be a New Zealand citizen or residence class visa holder (i.e. not be in New Zealand unlawfully, or here on a temporary entry class visa) and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand

chunks.title: Receiving Special Benefit — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Receiving Special Benefit
A client or their partner (if any) who are receiving current, suspended or expired Special Benefit or continue to be eligible for a Special Benefit cannot get Community Costs.
The Residential Subsidy Unit will treat an application for Community Costs from these clients as a review of their Special Benefit. The client's essential ongoing community costs may be considered in the reassessment of Special Benefit.
Note Special Benefit should be reviewed if it is current, suspended, or expired at the time of application for Community Costs.
For more information see:
- Partner in the community
- Extra help Special Benefit
- Payment

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get Community Costs, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- have a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
Note for Community Costs no period of residence is required.
People who are in New Zealand unlawfully or here on a temporary entry class visa generally do not qualify for assistance from MSD.
## Clients without citizenship or a residence class visa
If a client does not have New Zealand citizenship or a residence class visa, they cannot get Community Costs.
However, if a client in this situation has ongoing costs in the community, they may be able to get Temporary Additional Support if they are:
- a person who has refugee or protected person status in New Zealand or
- awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protected person status and are lawfully in New Zealand (i.e. they have a valid temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009) or
- applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 and are compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other criteria to qualify for Community Costs.

chunks.title: Short-term residential treatment programme — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Short-term residential treatment programme
For the purposes of Community Costs Programme, a short-term residential treatment programme means a programme that provides alcohol or other drug treatment or treatment of any other medical or psychological disorders (including eating disorders), and is:
- of an intended duration of not more than 39 weeks and
- funded by the Ministry of Health under the New Zealand Public Health and Disability Act 2000 or certified under the Health and Disability Services (Safety) Act 2001
If the intended duration of a treatment programme is for more than 39 weeks then Community Costs is not payable as the programme does not meet this definition.
Note Community Costs Programme is not payable to clients in long-term residential disability care with an intellectual, physical, psychiatric, or sensory disability (or a combination of 2 or more such disabilities) to help them function independently.
For more information see:
- Period of payment of Community Costs

chunks.title: Storage costs — extra help > community costs
chunks.text:
## Storage costs
When the client is not retaining their accommodation while resident in their treatment programme, they may need to store their belongings.
You can consider paying storage costs for items such as:
- a motor vehicle
- household furniture and
- effects

chunks.title: Additional costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Additional costs
Disability Allowance can be paid if a client is assessed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner who confirms the client's disability and need for treatment on the Disability Allowance medical certificate.
The certificate must also confirm the disability requires ongoing support, supervision or treatment, that treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are:
- additional and
- ongoing and
- directly related to the client's disability
The following points must be considered when deciding if a cost is additional:
- the relationship between the client's disability and the need for the cost and
- the need for, and therapeutic value of, the goods or services - and how long that need is expected to last and
- if the client had that type of cost before their disability arose, and the reasons they had that type of expense and
- if the client would have the cost if they did not have the disability and
- the extent to which the client's life or health would be put at risk, or their disability aggravated if they could not receive the goods or services and
- if the type and amount of cost is over and above that of people in a similar general position who don't have a disability and
- if there are less costly goods or services that might meet the client's need and
- any other relevant matters
Note when a medical practitioner or nurse practitioner indicates on the client's Disability Allowance medical certificate that treatment by another registered health practitioner is necessary, that practitioner must verify the costs of their services.
## For more information on costs paid for under Disability Allowance see:
- Proof of costs
- Types of costs
- Costs not included
- Definition of disability

chunks.title: Additional counselling sessions — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Additional counselling sessions
Disability Allowance can be paid for the cost of additional counselling sessions if the client has attended 10 counselling sessions and:
- their medical practitioner or nurse practitioner has indicated that further counselling is still necessary, beneficial and of therapeutic value to the client because of the stated disability or
- the counsellor has recommended further visits
Assistance for up to 20 additional sessions can be considered on the recommendation of the client's medical practitioner or nurse practitioner.
## More than 30 sessions
If a client is assessed as needing further sessions after they have reached the limit of 30 counselling sessions, they will need to provide supporting evidence from their medical practitioner or nurse practitioner that the counselling is directly related to their disability and is still necessary and beneficial to their disability.
Further sessions beyond 30 can only be paid if there are exceptional circumstances.
When a client reaches the limit of 30 counselling sessions, MSD should seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor before approving assistance for further counselling sessions.
The Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor will consider if exceptional circumstances exist, and if the client is getting the most appropriate type of counselling.
The Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor may consider that the client is receiving psychological therapy rather than counselling. In these cases, the client may not qualify for more counselling sessions as they are not getting counselling but may still qualify for Disability Allowance as they are seeing a psychologist.
The Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor may also be aware of other Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora provided services available.

chunks.title: Alternative treatment — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Alternative treatment
Disability Allowance can be paid for fees for alternative treatment needed by a client because of their disability.
A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, need for treatment and that alternative treatment is necessary. The alternative treatment must be provided or supervised by a health practitioner.
The certificate must confirm the client has a:
- disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or
- life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness
The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are:
- additional and
- ongoing and
- directly related to the client's disability
Note as the alternative treatment must be provided or supervised by a health practitioner that practitioner must verify the costs of their services.
Disability Allowance cannot be paid for:
- alternative treatment that is not provided by or supervised by a registered health practitioner or
- treatment that is not additional or directly related to the client's disability
## Proof of alternative treatment costs
The client must provide:
- a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and
- proof of fees and the frequency of treatment (receipts or invoices or quotes from provider of the alternative treatment) and
- evidence that the alternative treatment is being supervised by or provided by a registered health practitioner (this can be confirmed by the client’s medical or nurse practitioner)
Note it is not appropriate for MSD to approach the registered health practitioner directly. The client should provide the receipts or invoices or quotes.

chunks.title: Ambulance fees and subscriptions — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Ambulance fees and subscriptions
If a client is regularly required to pay ambulance fees or subscription fees, these costs can be included in Disability Allowance when:
- the fee is directly related to their disability and
- the cost is on an on-going basis
When considering whether to include ambulance fees and subscription fees in Disability Allowance consider the following:
- whether the client and/or their family is likely to require ambulance services
- how regular an ambulance would be required by the client and/or their family and
- whether there is a history of expectation of the requirement to use an ambulance
The client should provide proof of fees and the frequency of the service.
For more information see:
- Definition of disability

chunks.title: Application process - counselling — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Application process - counselling
When a client is applying for assistance towards the on-going costs of counselling, they will need to complete a Disability Certificate - Counselling form and have the relevant sections of the form completed by their registered:
- medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and
- counsellor
The client will also need to complete an application for Disability Allowance if they are not already receiving this allowance.
If the client requires assistance with additional counselling sessions, after the initial 10 sessions they will need to provide a further Disability Certificate - Counselling form.
## Record of Counselling card
A Disability Allowance - Record of Counselling card is also available and should be given to clients when they are granted Disability Allowance for counselling costs.
The Record of Counselling card will help clients to keep a record of the number of counselling sessions they have completed. This will provide a reminder of the need to reapply if they need further counselling sessions.

chunks.title: Appropriate use of Powerswitch — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Appropriate use of Powerswitch
The Powerswitch website tool (PSW) is owned and operated by Consumer NZ.
This tool is to be used as a guide only to establish the base level power usage for assessment of additional power costs.
This is because:
- the tool was not built for the purpose of assessing additional power needs
- consumption values are based on averages
- refining the results for a specific household (e.g. adjusting a 1-2 household estimate for a 1-person household) is technically not justifiable based on the data
The Powerswitch tool breaks down the estimates on 3 household sizes. These sizes are 1-2 people, 3-4 people or 5+ people.
Example
If the average for a 1-2 person household is $110 a month then we could expect a 1 person household to be slightly lower ($90), and a 2 person household to be slightly higher ($130).
If a 1 person household is using $150 a month then we could assume they require additional power costs of $50-$60 a month. Likewise if we have a 2 person household using $80 a month then they may not require additional power costs.
For more information see:
- Appliance running costs list [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Assessing additional food costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Assessing additional food costs
Additional food expenditure must be verified by comparing the cost of the special diet with the cost of a regular diet.
Use the following table to assess the cost of additional foods.
Product

Regular alternative
Price difference per unit

Additional expenses per week
The dietitian recommending the diet should be able to supply details of the expected or average consumption of each item.
## Example
For example, if a client cannot drink standard milk because of their disability, but instead requires soya milk.
Product

Regular alternative

Additional expenses per week
Standard milk
1.5 litres per week

chunks.title: Assessment of additional power — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: To assess additional power for Disability Allowance, consider a client's individual circumstances. The additional power is the amount of power that is a direct result of a client's disability or health condition. Generally, the amount of additional power to be included in a client's Disability Allowance is the difference between the power usage for a client with a disability or health condition and a person's usage without a disability or health condition. A discussion may be required with the client, either face to face or via telephone, to obtain the information needed to accurately assess the additional cost of power, gas and heating for Disability Allowance. The client may have other means of heating such as firewood and gas (including bottled gas). These costs would also need to be considered. Discuss the assessment with the client and complete all steps: Step 1 Ask the client what additional power costs they are incurring due to their disability. - Does the client have any specific additional power costs that should be considered - for example - but not limited to: re-charging a mobility scooter, clothes dryer? - Does the client purposely not use appliances or undertake activities authorised by their health practitioner (such as a heater or extra baths) to save their money for other essential costs? Step 2 Are the clients only extra power costs due to running specific appliances, such as a dehumidifier or heater? If no go to step 3. If yes obtain the following for each appliance: - wattage of the appliance - additional running time per annum - access the Appliance running costs [no link find out why] Note not all appliance running costs are listed. Where an appliance is not listed talk with the client to identify a similar appliance. Complete the following assessment for each appliance to determine additional power costs: - multiply running cost per hour/day by, additional running time per annum = additional running costs per annum - add total annual additional running costs to Disability Allowance Step 3 Obtain from the client: - number of persons in their household - power company they are registered with - type of plan they have with the power company - obtain the clients last 52 weeks power costs Note if the client is unable to provide 52 weeks power costs, calculate an amount from the power costs provided to estimate an annual amount. _____________ _____________

chunks.title: Assessment of additional power — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: _____________ $____________ per annum Step 4 To help you assess an estimate of 'normal' power usage based on a similar sized household access the Powerswitch website.Appropriate use of Powerswitch (please view before obtaining an estimate) $_____________ per annum Step 5 Subtract the estimate from the client's actual usage. Divide this by 52 to get a weekly figure. Note if the estimate is higher than the client's usage, this figure is NIL. $_____________ per annum $_____________ per week Step 6 Consider the amount calculated in step 5. Discuss with the client the weekly/annual figure from step 5. If this seems a reasonable figure based on discussion with the client about their individual circumstances, then use this amount as the additional power usage to be included in the client's Disability Allowance. If the client disagrees or you think the figure is unrealistic, go to step 7. $___________ per week Step 7 If the client has disagreed or you think the figure is unrealistic discuss these points with the client. - Why does the client or you think this figure is not realistic? - Has the client advised of all their circumstances for the calculation for additional power? For example: How long has the client been living at these premises? - Does the client have any other circumstances that should be considered? - Are these circumstances related to the client's disability? Taking into account the discussions above and the costs calculated in steps 5 and 7, discuss with the client what a realistic figure for additional power would be on a weekly basis (if applicable). Add this amount to the client's Disability Allowance as additional power costs $_____________ Actual cost per week $_____________ per week If you are having difficulty in determining the average power cost for your client please contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Authorised consumables — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance can be paid to cover the ongoing cost of consumable items needed by a client because of a disability. A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, need for treatment and that consumables are necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a: - disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or - life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability Some examples of consumable items commonly paid for are: - batteries for hearing aids - sensors for diabetic monitors - printer ribbons and paper for computers (if the computer is necessary for the client's communications e.g. a deaf client who doesn't communicate orally) - food or vet's fees for disability assistance guide dogs (e.g. guide dogs, hearing dogs and mobility dogs) - incontinence pads if they are not provided through Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora Disability Allowance cannot be paid for: - items not directly related to the client's disability (e.g. art supplies, even if their registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner recommends them as beneficial for the client) or - one-off costs, such as buying a computer, nebuliser or blood glucose monitor (the client may qualify for assistance through Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora) or - items fully funded, subsidised, or provided through other agencies (e.g. items such as blood glucose monitoring strips, syringes, needles or pen devices used by diabetics; these items will usually be fully funded through Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora) If a client applies for Disability Allowance for an item that should be paid for by Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora or ACC, MSD should refer them to the correct organisation. If the organisation won't cover the full cost (or there is excess), and the client has a letter confirming this and stating why, the remainder of the cost may be included in Disability Allowance. An example might be a physiotherapy appointment that is partially funded under ACC.

chunks.title: Proof of authorised consumable costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The client must provide: - a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and - receipts as proof of actual costs

chunks.title: Beneficiaries — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Beneficiaries
Disability Allowance can be paid for a client, partner or dependent child(ren) who has an ongoing disability and who is getting:
- Jobseeker Support, Supported Living Payment, Sole Parent Support, or related Emergency Benefits, Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment or
- New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran's Pension, Disablement Pension, and meets the appropriate income limit or
- Child Disability Allowance, Orphans Benefit, or Unsupported Child Benefit and meets the appropriate income limit
Note if the person with a disability is a dependent child, the income test is applied to their parent(s) or guardian(s).

chunks.title: Calculating rate and expiry date - counselling — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Calculating rate and expiry date - counselling
When a client meets the criteria to have Disability Allowance paid for the on-going cost of counselling, the rate of payment and the expiry date for the assistance will need to be determined from the information provided by the counsellor on the Disability Certificate - Counselling.
The cost can only be included for the period that the client is attending the counselling sessions.
The details from the Counsellor's statement section of the Disability Certificate - Counselling can be used to help determine the date to include the counselling cost in the Disability Allowance as well as to calculate the rate to pay and the expiry date.
The cost per visit multiplied by the recommended number of visits will give the total cost of the counselling. The frequency of the counselling sessions indicates the period over which it is expected that the client will attend, and this is then counted from the start date to determine the expiry date.
## Payment period
In order to ensure the client receives the correct amount of assistance you will need to include the cost from the beginning of the pay period during which the first session is due, as the expiry date must be the beginning of the next pay period following the last counselling session.
Example if a client has been approved assistance for 10 counselling sessions and the first counselling session is on Thursday 19 November, the cost of counselling should be included in Disability Allowance from Monday 16 November, and the expiry date will be Monday 25 January.
## Less than 10 sessions recommended
If the counsellor recommends less than 10 sessions on the first application, a further Disability Certificate - Counselling will be required before any further assistance can be considered.
This second application can be approved for the balance of the 10 sessions, plus up to an additional 20 sessions.
## More than 30 counselling sessions
A further application will be required if the client is assessed as needing further counselling sessions after they have reached the limit of 30 sessions.
They can only be paid in exceptional circumstances.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
Clients (including non-beneficiaries) can leave New Zealand and keep getting Disability Allowance for the first 28 days of any absence, if it does not affect the client's qualification for Disability Allowance.
To keep getting Disability Allowance while they are absent from New Zealand the client must have ongoing costs.
Paying Disability Allowance while the client is absent from New Zealand depends on whether the client is also getting a main benefit.
## Clients getting a main benefit
All clients getting a main benefit must tell MSD before they leave New Zealand. If the client or partner does not tell MSD before they go overseas, their benefit payments (including Disability Allowance) must stop.
If a client tells us they will be absent from New Zealand, and they have an approved travel reason, they may be able to keep getting payments for up to 28 days.
## Clients getting non-beneficiary Extra Help
Clients who are getting Disability Allowance, but are not getting a main benefit:
- must tell us they are leaving New Zealand and
- can be absent and paid their Disability Allowance for up to 28 days per absence, when it does not affect the client's eligibility for Disability Allowance
Note when assessing the period of absence, do not include:
- the date of departure from New Zealand and
- the date of return to New Zealand
## Mandatory Review while overseas
Clients getting Disability Allowance who have temporarily left New Zealand must still respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date.
Temporary absence from New Zealand (e.g. personal travel) does not pause or defer the Mandatory Review.
Clients must contact MSD before their review date to talk about their situation if they are unable to respond to the review or if they need more time to do it.
