The purpose of a Mandatory Review for Disability Allowance is to: - check for any changes to a client's circumstances - determine if the client stills meets the qualifications (except for the medical qualifications, they are reviewed separately) - check for any changes to a client's ongoing costs for Disability Allowance (e.g. including or removing a cost, an increase in cost, or a decrease in cost) and - review the rate payable Note the Mandatory Review will check a client’s circumstances but will not be a reassessment of their disability, known as a medical review. Medical reviews will take place separately.

chunks.title: Clients getting Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text: Clients getting Sole Parent Support or Jobseeker Support have a reapplication process they must complete to continue getting their benefit. These clients will have a Mandatory Review for Disability Allowance when: - they are completing the reapplication process for the benefit and - their disability costs have not been reviewed in the last 44 weeks If a client’s disability costs have been reviewed in the last 44 weeks, there will be no Mandatory Review for Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Specific engagements — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Specific engagements
Specific engagements are interactions that can meet the same purpose as the Mandatory Review. These interactions can capture information that confirms if a client still qualifies for Disability Allowance.
Specific engagements are when a client has an interaction with MSD, and this results in a full review of the client's circumstances.
For example, specific engagements may include when a client contacts MSD to:
- discuss a change in circumstances or
- apply for assistance.
If the specific engagement meets the same purpose as a Mandatory Review, and the client still qualifies, their Mandatory Review date will be set 52 weeks from when the specific engagement was completed.

chunks.title: Student Loans — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Student Loans
Clients with a Student Loan must make repayments to Inland Revenue when the income they receive exceeds a pre-determined level. This level is called the 'income threshold'.
A person must make repayments to Inland Revenue when their income exceeds $464.00 gross per week ($24,128 gross per year) as at 1 April 2026. Note non-taxable Extra help such as family tax credit and Accommodation Supplement do not count as income in this instance.
If the client's income is over this income threshold, the Ministry of Social Development can make the required deduction. However, this is only done if the client requests it.
If the client's portion of benefit is below the income threshold, there is no provision to make voluntary repayments through SWIFTT. The client can make voluntary payments direct to the Inland Revenue at any time.
Note the following:
- Student Loan deductions can only be made from taxable benefits
- Student Loan deductions cannot be made if the client's benefit is below the income threshold
- when a client receives a married or civil union rate of benefit, only the client's portion is taken into consideration when assessing Student Loan repayments
- when a client is receiving a reduced rate of payment due to other income, the Student Loan deduction is assessed on the net payment after income deduction
## For more information on Student Loans see:
- Students Student Loan

chunks.title: Study — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Study
If a client receiving Disability Allowance starts full-time or part-time study it does not affect their qualification for Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Debt Repayment Orders — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Debt Repayment Orders
All Debt Repayment Orders are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit for processing.
Debt Repayment Orders are issued by the Ministry of Justice under the Insolvency Act 2006 and can be issued where the client is an un-discharged bankrupt.
Unlike other Ministry of Justice attachment orders, Debt Repayment Orders are not subject to any protected earnings rate. Payment is generally made to the supervisor of the debt but occasionally a District Court will act as an agent for collection of the debt.
Payment continues for three years or until further notice is received from either the supervisor or the District Court.
Unlike Ministry of Justice attachment orders, Debt Repayment Orders are administered via the PYECI screen in SWIFTT, not through CORBI.

chunks.title: Terminal benefit — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Terminal benefit
When a non-beneficiary client dies, Disability Allowance generally stops from the day after the date of death. However, there is some discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days.
When payment is continued after the date of death, it is referred to as terminal benefit.
Circumstances where MSD might consider continued payment beyond a client's date of death include:
- when the deceased client's domestic situation results in a transition cost for a family member, causing hardship
Example: accommodation and other household costs when client has been sharing accommodation
or
- when there are exceptional and justified costs associated with the death of the client
Example: multiple deaths within one family
Payment should not be continued for 28 days following the death of a client to meet funeral expenses. A Funeral Grant may be available for this purpose.
## Mandatory Reviews
There are no Mandatory Reviews of Disability Allowance when the client has died.

chunks.title: Terminal benefit rate — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Terminal benefit rate
The provision to continue the payment for up to 28 days following the date of death is referred to as terminal benefit.
Disability Allowance is continued at the rate which was payable to the client at the date of death.
## SWIFTT
If you are paying terminal benefit you will need to manually calculate entitlement and make an adhoc payment in the SAHPA screen. There is no automatic provision for the payment of terminal benefit for Disability Allowance in this case on SWIFTT.

chunks.title: Transfer — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Transfer
MSD must review a client's Disability Allowance to ensure they still meet the qualifications and are getting the correct rate of payment when the client moves between the following categories:
- main benefit
- New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension or
- non-beneficiary

chunks.title: Verification of costs — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Verification of costs
At the time of the review of Disability Allowance, clients do not generally need to provide verification of any costs previously included in their allowance if the costs have not changed or have reduced.
However, they do still need to provide verification of:
- all new additional costs and
- costs that were previously included on the basis of a quote and
- any costs previously included in their allowance that have increased
## New costs
If a client has a new cost to be included in their Disability Allowance, the client must provide a new medical certificate completed by their registered medical practitioner or specialist that confirms the new cost is on-going, how the need relates to the client's disability and that it is of therapeutic value.
The client must also provide receipts or invoices or quotes that verify the amount and frequency of the new cost.
If a fee has been charged by a health practitioner or chemist for the cost of a report or print out to verify medical fees or pharmaceutical charges, this fee or other administration related cost can be included as a cost for Disability Allowance.
## Dependent children - Zero fees scheme
When a client declares a new cost or a change in costs, and they are getting Disability Allowance for a dependent child with costs relating to medical fees or prescription charges, these costs should be reviewed as they may be covered by a zero-fees scheme.
Most general practices offer zero-fee general practitioner or nurse visits for children under 14 years old.

chunks.title: Verification of income — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text: To be eligible for Disability Allowance, New Zealand Superannuation clients', Veteran's Pension clients' and non-beneficiaries' income must be below the appropriate income threshold, depending on their family circumstances. Note this also applies to clients who get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit when they get Disability Allowance for those children, and they aren't getting a main benefit. Clients getting a main benefit automatically meet the income test.

chunks.title: Exception — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text: New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran’s Pension clients Clients getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension who also get Disability Allowance are not required to provide verification of their income if it is below the relevant income limit by at least $20.00 per week ($1040.00 per annum). Note if a client has a grandparented non-qualified partner included in their New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension, they are not required to provide verification of their income if it is below the grandparented non-qualified partner income exemption by at least $20.00 per week ($1040.00 per annum). Example 1 A single New Zealand Superannuation client, who is getting the single living alone rate and has other income, has been getting Disability Allowance for the previous year. The client is now due for a Mandatory Review of their Disability Allowance, and has stated their other income as $7,020.00 per annum. The assessment would be as follows: New Zealand Superannuation gross (as at 1 April 2026) $33,663.24 per annum plus other gross income $7,020.00 per annum Total gross income - Total A $40,683.24 per annum Disability Allowance single person income threshold (as at 1 April 2026) Total B $45,240.00 per annum Difference is threshold (Total B) less total gross income (Total A) $4,556.76 per annum Difference (per week) $87.63 per week As the client's total gross income is more than $20.00 per week below the single person income threshold, no verification of the client's income is required. Example 2 A single New Zealand Superannuation client who is getting the single sharing accommodation rate has other income, has been getting Disability Allowance for the previous year. The client is now due for a Mandatory Review of their Disability Allowance, and has stated their other income as $9,400.00 per annum. The assessment would be as follows: New Zealand Superannuation gross (as at 1 April 2026) $30,969.64 per annum Other gross income $9,400.00 per annum Total gross income - Total A $40,369.64 per annum Disability Allowance single person income threshold (as at 1 April 2026) Total B $45,240.00 per annum

chunks.title: Exception — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text: Difference is threshold (Total B) less total gross income (Total A) $4,870.36 per annum Difference (per week) $93.66 per week As the client's total gross income is more than $20.00 per week below the single person income threshold, no verification of the client's income is required.

chunks.title: When an extension or exemption can be given — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text: When a client needs more time to respond to the Mandatory Review, they may be able to get an extension. If a client is unable to respond to the review, they may be able to get an exemption. Clients must contact MSD before their review date to discuss their situation if they need an extension or exemption. A client cannot get an extension or exemption on or after the Mandatory Review date. Note even if a client gets an extension or exemption, they must still advise MSD of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their eligibility for Disability Allowance or the rate payable.

chunks.title: Extension - client needs more time to respond to review — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text: Clients may be able to get an extension if there is a good and sufficient reason why they cannot complete their Mandatory Review before the review date. When a client needs more time to complete their review, they must let MSD know before their review date. The extension can only be granted before the review date. If MSD determines the client has a good and sufficient reason, the client can get an extension of up to 20 working days. Good and sufficient reasons may include (but are not limited to): - the client is unexpectedly hospitalised - death or illness in the client's immediate family - the client experiencing or escaping a family violence situation Note a client can get multiple short extensions, however the maximum amount of time that can be given for an extension is a total of 20 working days from the client's original review date.

chunks.title: Exemption - client is unable to complete review — extra help > disability allowance > changes and reviews disability allowance
chunks.text: A client may be able to get an exemption when they are experiencing an unforeseen event or situation that is beyond their control, and this means they are unable to respond to the Mandatory Review (even if they had more time). The client must let MSD know before their review date to discuss their circumstances. Exemption reasons may include (but are not limited to): - localised natural disaster that affects the client but not the whole region (e.g. the client's property is affected by a landslip) - unexpected serious illness or an accident affecting the client or their immediate family member - the client's benefit is ending because a child has left their care suddenly and the Mandatory Review is due during the 28-day continuation of payment If MSD determines an exemption applies, the client won't be required to complete the Mandatory Review, and the review date will be reset to 52 weeks from their current review date. Example Sina is getting Supported Living Payment and has a Mandatory Review due on 15 October 2026. However, Sina's home is badly damaged by a landslip. Because Sina has lost all of their possessions and is focused on finding accommodation, MSD determines it is not reasonable for Sina to respond to his Mandatory Review by his review date. In this case, MSD grants an exemption. Sina's next Mandatory Review is set for 52 weeks from the original review date.

chunks.title: Chargeable income — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Chargeable income
There are income limits for non-beneficiaries and clients getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension to qualify for Disability Allowance.
## Chargeable income for Disability Allowance includes, but is not limited to
- any earnings from wages or salary
- actual income from cash assets
- ACC weekly compensation
- Accommodation Benefit paid to students
- Flexi-Wage Self Employment weekly subsidy (excluding the GST component of 15%) and any income generated from the business
- New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
- Paid parental leave
- Profit from boarders or renters
- Student Allowance
- Information share Child Support payments
- Non-information share Child Support payments made for an income-related purpose
- any portion of an overseas pension (excluding overseas war pensions) that has not been directly deducted from the basic benefit

chunks.title: Child Disability Allowance clients — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Child Disability Allowance clients
A client can receive both Child Disability Allowance and Disability Allowance for a dependent child as the two allowances are paid for different reasons.
If you get a Disability Allowance application for a child who is not already getting Child Disability Allowance, consider inviting an application for Child Disability Allowance as well.

chunks.title: Client's IRD number — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: MSD may make a written request for evidence of an IRD number for a client who is being paid Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Setting or extending the timeframe for providing evidence — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: MSD must provide the client with a minimum of 10 working days to provide IRD number evidence that has been requested in writing. MSD can extend the 10 working day period (in writing) if the client has a reasonable explanation for requiring more than 10 days to provide evidence of their IRD number. This includes considering factors outside of the client's control that cause delays, including, but not limited to: - client has a family emergency that caused a delay - processing delays with an external agency (e.g. Inland Revenue, Department of Internal Affairs, etc) - client does not speak English as a first language and has difficulty navigating evidence requirements - client has limited access to the internet, a device, or their local service centre - client has a physical or intellectual disability that makes accessing services difficult - client is injured, disabled, or has a medical condition that makes accessing services difficult.

chunks.title: Notice following an unsuccessful match — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a client's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the client (in writing) to provide evidence of the IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the client a minimum of 10 working days to provide the IRD number evidence or the client's assistance must be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Disability Allowance and MSD holds an IRD number on record. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Isla's IRD number. MSD provides a notice in writing giving 10 working days for Isla to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Isla already having an IRD number - Isla not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD must suspend assistance if evidence of IRD number is not received — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: MSD must suspend all taxable and/or income tested assistance, including Disability Allowance, the client is getting, if evidence of an IRD number is not provided within 10 working days from the written request, or extended period if this has been applied. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance. Example Koa is receiving Disability Allowance and MSD does not have an IRD number on record. MSD sends a written request giving 10 working days for Koa to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD receives no response to this request. MSD suspends all Koa's taxable and/or income tested assistance because Koa has not supplied MSD with evidence of their IRD number within the timeframe provided.

chunks.title: IRD evidence may not be requested in some circumstances — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - significant factors, that are outside the client's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number (e.g. a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence), and - the client needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided or - there are significant factors related to a health, injury or disability that are outside the client's control that prevents them from providing evidence of an IRD number, and - an agent cannot be appointed to act on the client's behalf. MSD can determine at a later point to request evidence of the IRD number. Example Sienna is 23 and receiving Disability Allowance. Sienna's mother (Sara) is Sienna's agent and acts on Sienna's behalf with MSD. Sienna does not have an IRD number and Sara is not a recognised agent for Sienna for Inland Revenue. Sienna has a serious head injury, is unconscious and expected to be in hospital for at least 8 weeks. Sienna is not able to give consent to appoint Sara as an agent for Inland Revenue to apply for an IRD number due to their injury. MSD can request this information later when Sienna's situation has changed. Note there is different guidance for requesting evidence of an IRD number for partners whose income is relevant to a client's Disability Allowance, or when a client is applying for Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Accreditation is revoked — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Clients who are with a medical alarm supplier who has their MSD-accreditation revoked can continue getting Disability Allowance for medical alarm services with that supplier under a grandparenting arrangement. When there is a change in circumstance, it may be reasonable for MSD to have a conversation with the client about changing to an MSD-accredited supplier.

chunks.title: Changing to an MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: In some cases grandparenting may no longer be relevant. It would be appropriate for clients who have medical alarm services with a non MSD-accredited supplier to change to an MSD-accredited supplier. Types of changes include, but are not limited to: - Price increase - if a grandparented non MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier increases their prices, the client needs to contact MSD and inform us of this change. It would be appropriate for the client to change to an MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier. - Additional alarm - if another occupant in the same home as the client now needs a medical alarm service, it would be appropriate for the client to change to an MSD-accredited alarm supplier. - Change in need - MSD can cover medical alarm costs for in-home and anywhere services. If a client’s disability improves or deteriorates, this may mean that they need to change from one of these services to the other. It is appropriate to discuss with the client changing to an accredited supplier.

chunks.title: Example 1 — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Anna has an in-home medical alarm and has been with a non-accredited supplier for several years. Anna is getting Disability Allowance to cover the cost of this alarm and the costs are grandparented as the supplier used to be an accredited supplier. Anna's partner Mateo has been to see their medical practitioner who recommends that Mateo also get a medical alarm due to his disability. Mateo and Anna complete all the necessary paperwork and have a conversation with their case manager, Lani. Lani explains there are a range of accredited suppliers that could provide for both Anna and Mateo on a new contract. As they are making changes anyway, Anna and Mateo agree to change to an accredited provider after they see out the 30-day notice period with Anna's current supplier.

chunks.title: Example 2 — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Alia has had an in-home medical alarm with a medical alarm supplier for the last 2 years due to chronic arthritis in her hips and knees. At the most recent re-accreditation process, their supplier became non MSD-accredited. Over the last 6 months Alia has received 2 hip replacements and a knee replacement that means Alia is now more mobile and can leave the house. Alia's doctor agrees the medical alarm service should be modified to make sure Alia is covered when out and about. Alia completes the necessary application forms and is required to select from the list of accredited medical alarm suppliers.

chunks.title: Clothing — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Clothing
Disability Allowance can be paid for additional clothing costs that a person has because of their disability. For example additional costs may arise because of:
- greater frequency of washing or
- wear and tear resulting from use of a prosthetic aid (e.g. artificial limb or splints) or wheelchair or
- the need to have clothes or shoes made-to-measure
A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that clothing is necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a:
- disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or
- life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness
The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are:
- additional and
- ongoing and
- directly related to the client's disability
Disability Allowance pays the difference between having an item made-to-measure and buying normal clothing items through a shop.
Disability Allowance does not pay for the normal clothing costs a client has.
## Proof of clothing costs
The client must provide:
- a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and
- receipts or invoices or quotes showing the extra costs of the clothing
If the clothing is made-to-measure, the client must provide evidence of how much more it costs than buying a normal item through a shop.
The issue of clothing is not always straightforward and needs to be treated with sensitivity. It can be difficult to quantify their additional costs. MSD should assess on a case-by-case basis.

chunks.title: Commencement date — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
Disability Allowance is generally granted from:
- the date of application or
- the date the qualifying cost arose
whichever is the later.
## Disability Allowance and main benefits
If the client is applying for a Disability Allowance at the same time as they apply for one of the following benefits:
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
then Disability Allowance is granted from the date that benefit commences.
If a non-beneficiary receiving Disability Allowance is later granted a benefit, the allowance is then paid in conjunction with the main benefit.
## Disability Allowance for counselling costs
In order to ensure the client receives the correct amount of assistance you will need to include the cost from the beginning of the pay period during which the first session is due, as the expiry date must be the beginning of the next pay period following the last counselling session.
## Disability Allowance declined
If a client is declined a Disability Allowance because their disability is not expected to continue for 6 months or more and they:
- later provide information that the disability has lasted, or will last, 6 months or more and
- would have met the other qualifications for Disability Allowance during that time
then Disability Allowance is granted from the date of the original application.
For more information see:
- Core policy Application for benefit

chunks.title: Costs not included — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Costs not included
Disability Allowance is not paid for the following types of costs.
- Costs provided by residential care services
- Purchase of equipment and one-off items
- Services provided through another agency
- Koha
- Medical insurance premiums
- Medical emergencies
- Rest home fees
- Retirement villages
- Vocational services

chunks.title: Costs paid for — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Costs paid for
Disability Allowance can be paid to help people (or their partner or dependent children) with disabilities to meet costs that are:
- regular and ongoing and
- a direct result of a disability which is expected to continue for at least 6 months and
- additional to, or over and above those costs that a person without a disability would have and
- not fully funded by another agency (for example, Health New Zealand – Te Whatu Ora, ACC or other accident insurers, Ministry of Education, or regional councils) and
- not a residential care service

chunks.title: Costs provided by residential care services — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Costs provided by residential care services
Disability Allowance cannot be paid to cover costs relating to a client's disability, which are covered by their contract with the residential care services provider, when a person is getting:
- Residential Care Subsidy or
- Residential Support Subsidy
Most people getting Residential Care Subsidy will have all their costs covered in their contract.

chunks.title: Counselling — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance can be paid for counselling fees or transport to counselling if the: - client's registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner has confirmed the need for counselling is directly related to the client's disability and - cost of counselling is not fully funded by another agency, (e.g. Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora, ACC, Group Special Education, or Oranga Tamariki) and - counselling is provided by: a psychologist who holds a current practising certificate, and is registered with the Psychologists Board ora bona fide counsellor who is a member (or an applicant or provisional member) of one of the following organisations: Australian, New Zealand and Asian Creative Arts Therapy Association (ANZACATA) - previously known as the Australian and New Zealand Arts Therapy Association (ANZATA)Drug and Alcohol Practitioners Association of Aotearoa New Zealand (DAPAANZ) - this only includes Registered Competent Practitioners and Associate Practitioners (it doesn't include support workers)NZ Association of Counsellors (NZAC)NZ Christian Counsellors AssociationPsychotherapists Board of Aotearoa New ZealandSocial Workers Registration Board (SWRB) - a psychologist who holds a current practising certificate, and is registered with the Psychologists Board or - a bona fide counsellor who is a member (or an applicant or provisional member) of one of the following organisations: Australian, New Zealand and Asian Creative Arts Therapy Association (ANZACATA) - previously known as the Australian and New Zealand Arts Therapy Association (ANZATA)Drug and Alcohol Practitioners Association of Aotearoa New Zealand (DAPAANZ) - this only includes Registered Competent Practitioners and Associate Practitioners (it doesn't include support workers)NZ Association of Counsellors (NZAC)NZ Christian Counsellors AssociationPsychotherapists Board of Aotearoa New ZealandSocial Workers Registration Board (SWRB) - Australian, New Zealand and Asian Creative Arts Therapy Association (ANZACATA) - previously known as the Australian and New Zealand Arts Therapy Association (ANZATA) - Drug and Alcohol Practitioners Association of Aotearoa New Zealand (DAPAANZ) - this only includes Registered Competent Practitioners and Associate Practitioners (it doesn't include support workers) - NZ Association of Counsellors (NZAC) - NZ Christian Counsellors Association - Psychotherapists Board of Aotearoa New Zealand

chunks.title: Number of sessions — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Generally, counselling assistance will be limited to a maximum of 10 sessions on the first application. Assistance for up to 20 additional counselling sessions can be considered on the recommendation of the client's medical practitioner or nurse practitioner. If the client has exceptional circumstances, assistance for more than 30 sessions can be considered. Note if a client has exceptional circumstances MSD should refer the client to the Regional Health Advisor and Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] for consideration.

chunks.title: Disability Allowance cannot be paid — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance cannot be paid: - for counselling not directly related to the client's disability (for example relationship counselling) - for counselling provided through hospitals or community mental health services as no charge is made for these services (the cost of transport to these sessions may be paid) - for the costs of childcare while the client is attending counselling - if appropriate services provided through Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora are available

chunks.title: ACC — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance can be paid for the portion of counselling costs that is not met by ACC.

chunks.title: Dependent children — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance is usually not paid for counselling for dependent children, except if the child cannot get counselling through another agency.

chunks.title: Special Benefit — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Generally, counselling costs not met by Disability Allowance (because they are unrelated to the client's disability) are not an allowable cost for Special Benefit. However, there may be some instances where counselling costs meet the definition of an allowable cost for Special Benefit.

chunks.title: Temporary Additional Support — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Counselling costs (including transport to attend counselling sessions) not met by Disability Allowance cannot be included as an allowable cost for Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Counselling for children — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Counselling for children
The child's registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner should consider referring the child to a suitable agency for counselling. Counselling may be available for children free of charge through a range of agencies depending on their criteria, for example:
- Oranga Tamariki who may support children experiencing serious problems such as abuse or youth offending
- Regional Child and Adolescent mental health services, who may support children or adolescents experiencing very serious or life-threatening mental health problems
- ACC who may support children experiencing problems arising from an accident, or a sexual abuse claim
If a client submits an application for a dependent child and they do not yet have a counsellor, MSD should refer the client to the:
- duty social worker at Oranga Tamariki as they may be able to refer them to an appropriate counsellor or
- Regional Health Advisor and Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] for advice
If the child cannot get free counselling, Disability Allowance may be paid for the counselling.
If the cost of counselling is only partly funded by another agency such as ACC or another accident insurer, the portion of counselling costs not paid by the agency can be considered for Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Day care for older disabled people — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Day care for older disabled people
Disability Allowance can be paid to help meet the costs of:
- an elderly disabled client (usually aged 65 or over) attending a day care centre and/or
- the cost of transport to the centre.
This is intended to enable the client to remain in or return to their own home, or family/whānau care.
Disability Allowance cannot be paid:
- for the costs of people in residential care services
- if the client is entitled to carer relief through Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora funding (MSD should refer the person to the local Hospital and Health Services to check their entitlement for carer relief as this may be more appropriate than using Disability Allowance for day care)
A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that day care is necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a:
- disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or
- life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness
The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are:
- additional and
- ongoing and
- directly related to the client's disability
## Proof of cost of day care for the elderly disabled
The client must provide:
- a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and
- receipts to verify the costs of day-care (one receipt is enough proof if it shows the regular cost of each visit)
Note the requirement to get a medical practitioner or nurse practitioner signature at the annual review is waived if the costs are for attendance at an IHC day programme (regardless of whether the costs have changed).

chunks.title: Definition of disability — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Definition of disability
We use section 21(1)(h) of the Human Rights Act 1993 to define disability for Disability Allowance.
Disability means:
- physical disability or impairment
- physical illness
- psychiatric illness
- intellectual disability, psychological disability or impairment
- any other loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological, or anatomical structure or function
- reliance on a guide dog, wheelchair, or other remedial means
- the presence in the body of organisms capable of causing illness

chunks.title: Definition of discharged from care — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Definition of discharged from care
A child/young person is considered discharged from care when they are discharged from:
- the sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency
- the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency under a custody order made under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 or
- the care of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency under an agreement made under section 140 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989

chunks.title: Dependent child — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
A dependent child for Disability Allowance is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- not a child for whom Orphan's Benefit or an Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Disability Allowance does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
In some situations, a child may not be living at home but is still considered to be a dependent child.
The child may be involved, or have been previously involved, with Oranga Tamariki.

chunks.title: Disablement Pension clients — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Disablement Pension clients
Disability Allowance can be paid to a person getting a service-related Disablement Pension from Veterans Affairs who meets all the qualifications.
Disability Allowance cannot be paid for the same disability-related costs as those met by the Veterans' Support programme.
When assessing eligibility for Disability Allowance:
- a disablement pension paid by Veterans' Affairs is not included as income in the assessment
- the gross rate of any New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension that the client or the client's partner is getting is included as income when assessing eligibility for Disability Allowance
- the Winter Energy Payment is not included as income when assessing eligibility for Disability Allowance
A person getting weekly income compensation from Veterans' Affairs is not entitled to a Disability Allowance.
If you need information about the Veterans' Support programme, contact Veterans' Affairs by:
email veterans@nzdf.mil.nz
free phone 0800 483 8372 (0800 4 VETERAN)

chunks.title: Discharged from care — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Discharged from care
When Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency has care, custody or sole guardianship of the child, and returns the child to the care of the immediate previous caregiver, they do not make payments for the child.
The child is then a dependent child and Disability Allowance can be paid to the caregiver.
Once a child has been discharged from care the child can be considered a dependent child even when Oranga Tamariki or any other authorised agency involvement continues, for example:
- Additional Guardianship Order
- Support Order or
- Services Order
When there is a Service or Support Order in place, you will need to make sure that the Court's intent allows you to consider the child as a dependent child.
For further details on what discharged from care means see:
- Definition of discharged from care

chunks.title: Example of additional power costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Example of additional power costs
A client is aged 61 years and getting Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury, or disability. They have additional costs (including power) due to their health condition. The client uses a mobility scooter and needs to keep warm to assist their joint movements. The client cannot reach the clothesline due to limited arm movements and uses the clothes dryer on a regular basis.
The client's registered medical practitioner verified the client needed additional power on the Disability Allowance medical certificate and the client's registered health practitioner indicated on the Disability Allowance application that they required extra power for heating, recharging their mobility scooter and clothes dryer usage.
The client is getting a Disability Allowance for the additional costs arising from their health condition. At present, additional power is not one of those costs. To help make ends meet, the client has decided to reduce their power requirements to spread their limited income over essential items such as food, rent and the other disability costs they are incurring.
Discussions between the case manager and the client determined that the actual costs of extra heating, running the clothes dryer and recharging the mobility scooter worked out to be $31.76 per week ($1.62 dryer, $24.36 heating and $5.76 battery charging).
The discussions above and accessing some of the actual costs of running appliances listed enabled the case manager and client to decide on a more realistic figure of $31.76 per week to help cover the additional power usage costs of the client.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances - non MSD-accredited suppliers — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: A client should get their medical alarm services from an MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier unless there are exceptional circumstances that mean the client needs to get their medical alarm services from a non MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier. When considering whether the client has exceptional circumstances, consider the following factors: - the client has special needs, such as non-English speaking, deaf or hearing impaired, that cannot be met by an MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier - the client currently gets medical alarm services from a non MSD-accredited supplier, and has current contract limitations which prevent them from changing suppliers immediately - medical alarm services are not provided by an MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier in the area where the client lives - any other circumstances the client has that you consider relevant Contact Helpline if you need any assistance in making your decision. Note the client will need to provide a copy of the contract they have with their non MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier.

chunks.title: Cost can be included — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The cost can only be included in their Disability Allowance if: - the client has exceptional circumstances and - the service being supplied is a monitored medical alarm and - the type of medical alarm is the same as one of the types of medical alarms provided by an MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier and - the supplier of the medical alarm is a registered company

chunks.title: New applications for clients with non MSD-accredited supplier — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Some clients applying for Disability Allowance may already have a medical alarm from a non MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier. You should discuss with the client reasons we have accreditation (e.g. meet standards, client's protection, clear complaints process) and the option of changing to an MSD-accredited supplier. You will need to discuss the client's reasons for having a medical alarm from this supplier, and check if they have any exceptional circumstances. If the client does not have exceptional circumstances, you will need to discuss changing to an MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier if they want to include their medical alarm service cost in their Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances exist — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The client should be advised of the decision in writing, including: - the reasons why it has been agreed to include the cost of their medical alarm service from a non MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier in their Disability Allowance and - the expiry date of their assistance (if it has been agreed to include the cost until their existing contract expires) and - their obligation to advise immediately if there is any change in their circumstances

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances do not exist — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: You can decline assistance for a client with a medical alarm from a non MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier if: - you determine the service being provided is not a monitored medical alarm (e.g. a security alarm) or - the client does not have exceptional circumstances for services not available through an MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier

chunks.title: Gardening, lawns and outside window cleaning — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance can be paid to cover the costs of gardening, lawn-mowing, and outside window cleaning for the client's own home or private residence. A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that gardening, lawn-mowing or outside window cleaning is necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a: - disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or - life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability Disability Allowance can only be paid if the client is unable to do these tasks themselves because of their disability. This cost cannot be included in Disability Allowance solely based on the client's age. Disability Allowance cannot be paid for: - house repairs or house painting as these are part of normal living costs, and are not due to the clients disability (clients may be able to get Essential Home Repairs advance) - indoor household maintenance (e.g. carpet cleaning) as funding for home help is available through Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora MSD should refer the client to the local Hospital and Health Services home support services - gardening, lawn-mowing or window cleaning costs that are included in a standard service fee charged for all residents of a retirement village or complex. However there are exceptions, for more information see: Retirement Villages. While Disability Allowance should not generally be paid for gardening, lawn-mowing or window cleaning carried out by family members, MSD should use its discretion to consider the individual circumstances of each case. The cost can be included if it seems appropriate. For example, when the family member does not live with the client and incurs a cost to travel to the client's home to provide the service. When a client has high gardening costs (e.g. due to the extra work involved in maintaining a large property, or high maintenance gardens) the client should look at other options for meeting or alleviating the cost.

chunks.title: Proof of gardening, lawns and outside window cleaning costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The client must provide: - a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and - receipts or invoices or quotes for the cost of the gardening work - a receipt showing actual costs is preferred Note sometimes gardening costs are covered as part of the client's tenancy agreement. MSD should check if this applies to the client before accepting these as allowable costs. The costs must be reasonable in the client's circumstances and for the season of the year. Generally, lawns will not require mowing every week throughout the colder months. If the client has difficulty getting a receipt, the client's statement of the hourly rate paid, plus a quote from the gardener stating the time taken per week is acceptable.

chunks.title: Gym and swimming pool fees — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Gym and swimming pool fees
Disability Allowance is generally not paid for exercise activities, such as at a gym or swimming pool.
However, Disability Allowance can be paid for gym or swimming pool fees when the exercise activities are:
- are directly related to a person's disability and will have a therapeutic value and
- is an additional cost due to the person's disability and
- supported by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and
- either provided or supervised by a registered health practitioner
A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that the gym or swimming is necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a:
- disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or
- life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness
The certificate must also confirm the exercise is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are:
- additional and
- ongoing and
- directly related to the client's disability

chunks.title: In the care of Oranga Tamariki — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## In the care of Oranga Tamariki
Where a child or young person is in the care, custody or sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, the cost of the child's care is the responsibility of Oranga Tamariki and it is responsible for making payments under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989. The child is not considered a dependent child and Disability Allowance cannot be paid.
This applies even if the payment is being made at a "nil" rate i.e. an order or agreement about care under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 is in place, even though no actual payments are being made by Oranga Tamariki.
However, where there is a sole guardianship order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but the child or young person is in the custody of the caregiver, the caregiver may be entitled to Unsupported Childs Benefit if all other criteria are met.
Where Oranga Tamariki is involved, but there are no orders or agreements about care, the child can be considered a dependent child (for example when Oranga Tamariki provides services to family groups under a Family Group Conference plan only).
For information on different orders and whether they mean the child can be considered a dependent child while the order is still in place, see:
- Oranga Tamariki order in place
## Parents as caregivers
When Oranga Tamariki places a child with a parent who was not the immediate previous caregiver, this is an Oranga Tamariki "placement" and the caregiver will receive Board Payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989. Board payments in this situation are made at a "nil" rate. The child is not considered a dependent child and cannot be included in the parent's benefit.
When a child is returned to the care of a parent who was the immediate previous caregiver, the child can be accepted as a dependent child and included in any benefit payable to the parent. In these situations, returning the child to the parent is not considered a "placement". This is an agreed protocol between Oranga Tamariki and Work and Income.
- Discharged from care
- Definition of discharged from care
- Oranga Tamariki order in place

chunks.title: Income test — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Income test
A client must meet the appropriate income limit or be getting an income-tested benefit to qualify for Disability Allowance.
The client's dependent partner or dependent child may also qualify for Disability Allowance if the client is receiving an income-tested benefit or meets the appropriate income limit.
## New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
There are special income limits for clients getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension.
The gross rate of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension the client or their partner is getting is included as income when assessing income limits for Disability Allowance
## Blind clients
Blind clients getting Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability, who have their personal earnings exempt, qualify for a Disability Allowance as they are getting an income-tested benefit.

chunks.title: Chargeable income for Disability Allowance does not include — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: - ACC Independence Allowance - Accommodation Supplement - Assistance to transition into employment - the amount of any main benefit - Childcare assistance (e.g. Childcare Subsidy, Early Learning Payment, Flexible Childcare Assistance, Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment) - Child Disability Allowance - children's income - any regular periodical payments made under a Welfare Programme paid to replace lost income - formula assessed Child Support for liability periods before 1 July 2023 paid in excess of the benefit rate - formula-assessed Child Support paid in excess of the Unsupported Child's Benefit rate (including mixed Child Support payments) - information share Child Support payments received between commencement and grant dates of Disability Allowance - information share Child Support payments received shortly after transferring between benefits on different pay cycles - Offset Child Support - Christchurch mosques attack support payments and income earned on the payments - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - Energy Trust Dividends and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after payment is made - gallantry awards - Incentive payments (for Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment) - Kāinga Ora energy subsidy - MSD lump sum payments and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after payment is made - Orphan's Benefit - Overseas pensions similar to Social Security benefits if there has already been a direct deduction from the basic benefit - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds& and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Redundancy payments and retirement payments - Severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment) - specified Ex gratia and compensation payments and income earned on those payments - Student Loans - Participation Allowance - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Temporary Accommodation Assistance weekly payments (ended 30 June 2025) - Unsupported Child's Benefit - Working for Families Tax Credits from Inland Revenue - Temporary Additional Support - War Pension or allowances - Winter Energy Payment

chunks.title: Chargeable income for Disability Allowance does not include — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received A bank overdraft is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Disability Allowance provides non-taxable assistance to people who have ongoing, additional costs because of a disability.
## Special Disability Allowance
Clients who have a partner in hospital or long-term residential care may be able to get a Special Disability Allowance.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Koha — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Koha
Disability Allowance is not paid to cover the costs of koha as this cost is not an extra expense due to having a disability.

chunks.title: Medical alarms — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: A medical alarm is a device worn by a person so they can call for emergency medical help at any time. There are 2 types of medical alarms that can be included in Disability Allowance: - In-home medical alarms - which provide support to clients while at home - Anywhere medical alarms - which provide support to clients while at home and out in the community The disability and need for a medical alarm must be verified by the client's registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner on the Disability Allowance - Medical Alarm Assessment form. The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability Note when a medical practitioner or nurse practitioner indicates on the client's Disability Allowance medical certificate that treatment by another registered health practitioner is necessary, that practitioner must verify the costs of their services. Disability Allowance can be paid to cover the costs of medical alarm rental and monitoring if the: - client meets the qualifications for Disability Allowance and - medical alarm is necessary for normal daily living, and without it the client's life or health would be put at risk, or their disability would get worse and - need for the medical alarm is an ongoing, additional cost directly related to the client's disability or personal health need and - medical alarm is supplied by an MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier, unless exceptional circumstances exist where the medical alarm services the client requires are not available through an MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier Disability Allowance cannot be paid to cover the costs of: - buying medical alarms or smoke alarms (which are often marketed with medical alarms) because this is a one-off cost, not an ongoing cost or - alarms installed for security reasons as this is not a cost directly related to the client's disability or - a medical alarm cost that is included in the standard service fee for a client living in a retirement village or complex

chunks.title: Medical Alarms - additional pendant — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: When there is more than 1 occupant in the home needing a medical alarm service, MSD may fund an additional pendant if: - the second person qualifies for Disability Allowance in their own right and - a separate Medical Alarm Assessment form has been completed for the second person by their registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner If 1 client needs an in-home alarm and 1 client needs an anywhere alarm, pricing for these combinations will differ across MSD-accredited suppliers because their products differ. Clients need to consider this when selecting a supplier.

chunks.title: Medical Alarms for Retirement Village residents — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance generally cannot be paid for the medical alarm costs of a client living in a retirement village or complex, however there are some exceptions.

chunks.title: Medical alarms for Retirement Village residents — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Medical alarms for Retirement Village residents
Clients who live in retirement villages generally pay a standard service fee to cover services provided. This service fee may include the cost of medical alarm services, and these may vary between retirement villages.
These costs cannot be included in Disability Allowance as they are not directly related to a clients’ particular disability.
Clients living in a retirement village may have the cost of a medical alarm included in their Disability Allowance if they meet all Disability Allowance and medical alarm criteria and:
- the medical alarm is additional to anything supplied by the village and
- the cost is not included in the standard fee paid by all residents of the retirement village
or
- the cost of the medical alarm is included in the standard service fee and
- the client was getting Disability Allowance for the cost of a medical alarm before moving and the same cost still exists in the retirement village
Note Disability Allowance cannot be paid for the cost of a medical alarm if the client is getting Residential Care Subsidy.
## Example
Hugh lives in a retirement village and part of the service fee they pay covers an in-home medical alarm. Hugh is active in the community and will often go out alone.
Hugh wants to apply for an anywhere medical alarm and meets all eligibility criteria. Hugh's doctor has verified the need for the anywhere medical alarm service.
As this service is additional to the service that is covered by the retirement village and the cost of this additional service is not included in the standard fee, Hugh can have the anywhere medical alarm service cost included in his Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Medical emergencies — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Medical emergencies
Disability Allowance cannot be paid to meet the costs of a medical emergency, as this is not an ongoing cost. Consider whether the person could qualify for a Special Needs Grant.

chunks.title: Medical fees — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, and that the need for treatment is necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a: - disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or - life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability Treatment that is beneficial and of therapeutic value means the treatment may improve the client's condition, maintain the client's condition or prevent it from getting worse.

chunks.title: Medical fees included — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: If the fees, or a portion of the fees, claimed are not covered by the Community Services Card or the High Use Health Card, ACC or other accident insurers, or medical insurance they can be included in Disability Allowance. Note unless there are exceptional circumstances (e.g. when a public medical specialist doesn't exist in the client's region) Disability Allowance cannot usually be paid for private medical specialist fees. Public specialist fees are free. Medical fees can also include the fee charged by the medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or their teams) to complete a repeat prescription for ongoing conditions without the client attending a consultation (including faxing or electronically sending the prescription to the chemist). This category can also include fees for the following services if a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner verifies the disability and need for the services on the client's Disability Allowance medical certificate: - occupational therapy - physiotherapy - speech-language therapy (for adults) - audiological - orthotic - podiatry - dental services

chunks.title: Dependent children - Zero fees scheme — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Most general practices offer zero-fee general practitioner or nurse visits for children under 14 years old. The zero-fees scheme applies to: - a standard daytime visit to a general practitioner or nurse at the usual practice where the child is enrolled or - an after-hours visit to a participating clinic or - injury-related visits covered by ACC Zero fees does not cover fees charged by medical specialists, dentists or other medical services. Some centres or clinics that offer zero fees for under 6-year-olds have the option of remaining on their current scheme or opting into the new scheme for under 14s.

chunks.title: Proof of medical fees costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The client must provide: - a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and - receipts as proof of their medical/therapy fees (one receipt is enough proof if it shows the regular cost of each visit, and the registered medical or nurse practitioner who signed the certificate indicates how often the client gets treatment) Note if a fee has been charged by a health practitioner or chemist for the cost of a report or print out to verify medical fees or pharmaceutical charges, this fee or other administration related costs can be included as a cost for Disability Allowance. It is not appropriate for MSD to approach the health practitioner directly for proof. The client should provide the receipts. When a client has an overdue account with their health practitioner, any late payment fee is not an allowable cost for Disability Allowance. Example 1 A client is charged $20 for their doctor's visit. This includes an administration fee of $5. This fee is deducted from the total if the account is paid within 7 days, and the account is reduced to $15. If this is not paid within 7 days, the total charge of $20 can be included as a cost for Disability Allowance. Example 2 A client has an overdue account with their doctor and has been charged a $10 late fee. The late fee is not an allowable cost for Disability Allowance as this fee is not a direct result of their health condition or disability but due to the client not paying the overdue account. Example 3 A client goes to see a private rheumatologist specialist and applies for the cost to be covered by Disability Allowance. This is not an allowable cost for Disability Allowance as there is a publicly funded rheumatologist specialist in their region.

chunks.title: Medical insurance premiums — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Medical insurance premiums
Disability Allowance cannot be paid to cover the cost of medical insurance premiums as this is not an additional cost arising from a disability.
Disability Allowance can be paid to people with medical insurance. However, it can only be paid for the costs over and above what the insurance covers.
## Example
The client’s registered medical practitioner has verified their disability and need for treatment on their Disability Allowance medical certificate.
The client has to visit their registered health practitioner more often than is covered by their medical insurance, Disability Allowance can be paid to meet the difference.

chunks.title: MedicAlert costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The MedicAlert bracelet or pendant is personalised with the client's key diagnoses and a unique MedicAlert ID number which gives access to vital medical information. Clients sign up to MedicAlert, pay a one-time enrolment fee to join (which includes the basic MedicAlert bracelet or pendant) and then a membership fee. A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that a MedicAlert bracelet is necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a: - disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or - life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness The ongoing MedicAlert membership fee can be included as a cost for Disability Allowance if a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner confirms that it is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the cost is: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability Examples of when clients may need a MedicAlert bracelet include: - severe allergies or - anaphylaxis or - diabetes or - epilepsy The cost of the one-time initial enrolment fee is excluded and is not an allowable cost for Disability Allowance. Note when a medical practitioner or nurse practitioner indicates on the client's Disability Allowance medical certificate that treatment by another registered health practitioner is necessary, that practitioner must verify the costs of their services. For more information see: - MedicAlert Foundation

chunks.title: Proof of MedicAlert costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: To verify the MedicAlert costs MSD needs to see evidence to: - confirm the client is paying for the MedicAlert cost the registered medical or nurse practitioner has advised they need and - determine the total amount of the membership fee incurred

chunks.title: Costs not included — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: MSD must ensure the following costs are not included: - ongoing membership fees for MedicAlert services if the need for the service is not directly related to the client's disability or the client has chosen to have a MedicAlert for other reasons or - one-time costs such as the initial enrolment fee or - one-off costs such as a bracelet, pendant or card that sets out medical information or - MedicAlert member donations

chunks.title: One-time enrolment fee — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: When the one-time enrolment cost cannot be met by the client and it is considered to be an essential and immediate need, the cost may be met through an Advance or Recoverable Assistance Payment. The client would need to meet the qualifications required for this type of payment.

chunks.title: Mobility Parking Permits — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Mobility Parking Permits
Disability Allowance can be paid to cover the ongoing cost of a Mobility Parking Permit that a person requires because of their disability.
There are 2 types of permits that can be included as an allowable cost for Disability Allowance:
- Short-term (from 3 months to 12 months)
- Long-term (5 years)
## Payments for annual costs, paid in advance for a number of years
A client may choose to pay a lump sum that covers the cost of purchasing a long-term Mobility Parking Permit.
These costs can be included in Disability Allowance for the 12 month period from when it was purchased, if the cost involved is a modest amount, or spread over the number of years the payment covers, if the person pays a substantial amount.

chunks.title: Nature of disability — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Nature of disability
A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client has a:
- disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or
- life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness
## Disability
The client's disability must mean they have a reduction in independent functioning to the extent that they need ongoing:
- supervision or treatment from a health practitioner or
- help with normal living tasks
The client must also be assessed as having ongoing, additional costs arising directly from that disability, and that other assistance available to meet those costs is insufficient to cover them.
Note Disability Allowance should not be granted to a client just because of their age. However, an older client may have an age-related disability.

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients
When assessing eligibility for Disability Allowance:
- the gross rate of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension the client or the client's partner is receiving is included as income when assessing eligibility for Disability Allowance
- but a war pension is not included as income in the assessment
Note the Winter Energy Payment is not included as income.
## Client was receiving Disability Allowance before transferring
If a client was receiving Disability Allowance while receiving an income tested benefit before transferring to New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension, you can continue to pay the Disability Allowance at the same rate until the next Review of Circumstances, if all their other circumstances have remained the same.
However, if the clients' circumstances or income have significantly changed you will need to review their Disability Allowance at the time they, transfer to New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension.
For more information see:
- Rates and income limits
- Winter Energy Payment

chunks.title: Nicotine replacement products — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Nicotine replacement products
Generally, nicotine replacement products such as patches and gum are not allowable costs for Disability Allowance for clients who want to give up smoking.
However, a client's registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner may recommend that a client gives up smoking as part of the treatment/management of a health condition or disability such as a client with cardiovascular disease.
In a situation such as this, when the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner verifies the disability, the need for nicotine replacement products and prescribes a nicotine replacement product on the client's Disability Allowance medical certificate this can be included as an allowable cost in Disability Allowance. Many nicotine replacement products are fully subsidised.
The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are:
- additional and
- ongoing and
- directly related to the client's disability

chunks.title: Non beneficiaries — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Non beneficiaries
Disability Allowance can be paid to any person whose income, including their partner's income, is below the appropriate income limit.
If the person with a disability is a dependent child, the non-beneficiary income test is applied to their parents or guardians.
Note New Zealand Superannuation and Veterans Pension clients must also meet the appropriate income limit
## Community Services Card
If your client is getting any financial assistance from MSD you should check their entitlement to a Community Services Card.
Community Services Cards are not automatically issued to clients who get non-beneficiary assistance. They must make a separate application.

chunks.title: Non-subsidised pharmaceuticals — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: To determine if the cost of a non-subsidised pharmaceutical can be included in Disability Allowance, MSD needs to consider: - the availability of another suitable subsidised or partly subsidised pharmaceutical item and - if funding from PHARMAC under their Named Patient Pharmaceutical Assessment Policy has been applied for and if so, whether the application has been accepted or declined, and the reasons for it being declined (this was previously known as the Exceptional Circumstances Panel Policy) The cost of the non-subsidised pharmaceutical can be included as an additional expense for Disability Allowance if the client's medical practitioner or nurse practitioner verifies the clients disability and their need for the pharmaceutical item on the Disability Allowance medical certificate. They must verify that the item is essential and there are no suitable subsidised or partly subsidised alternatives. The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability The client will need to provide a letter from their registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner confirming the following information: - the reasons for prescribing the non-subsidised pharmaceutical and - that there is not a suitable subsidised or partly subsidised alternative and - that the medication is essential and directly related to the client's disability and - if PHARMAC funding has been applied for and declined, the reasons for this decision and - if there is no suitable subsidised or partly subsidised alternative, and if PHARMAC funding has not been applied for, the reasons why funding has not been requested Note MSD should refer applications for non-subsidised pharmaceuticals to the Regional Health Advisor and Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] .

chunks.title: Application to PHARMAC not always necessary — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: It's not necessary for an application to PHARMAC for funding to be lodged in every case. If the client's registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner confirms funding has not been applied for, because they are aware that PHARMAC's criteria will not be met, the cost of the non-subsidised pharmaceutical can be included in Disability Allowance. The registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must still verify that there is not a suitable subsidised or partly-subsidised alternative, and that the pharmaceutical item is essential and directly related to the client's disability.

chunks.title: Obtaining proof on behalf of clients — extra help > disability allowance
