chunks.text: There are 3 options for obtaining proof on behalf of the client: - if appropriate MSD can use the Privacy Statement - asking the client to provide further information or seeking the client's consent using the 'consent to release of health or disability information' form - if the client is unable to obtain the information and all other options have been pursued, a Schedule 6 request for information can be used in limited cases

chunks.title: Clarifying or verifying information use the Privacy Statement — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The privacy statement on application forms permits case managers to contact the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner who completed the client's Disability Allowance medical certificate to verify information they have provided. The form does not allow MSD to collect additional information about the client from their original practitioner or any other health practitioner. The part of the Privacy Statement that is relevant is MSD may share information with health practitioners if it needs medical information to assess the client's eligibility. This gives MSD the authorisation to contact the appropriate health practitioner(s) to confirm or clarify the information they have already provided as part of the application process. This includes information that is unclear or hard to read.

chunks.title: Additional information - use client consent form — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: MSD must give the client every opportunity to provide the information before the client consent form is used. If further information is required, the 'consent to release of health or disability information' form may be used. Generally, the consent form is valid for a particular purpose.

chunks.title: Additional information in limited circumstances use a Schedule 6 request — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Before making a Schedule 6 request MSD must take the following steps: 1. MSD must request the information from the client before seeking it from the appropriate health practitioners. 2. The client must be allowed sufficient time to respond. MSD must ensure they are fully aware of the time restriction. 3. MSD must consider all other avenues for obtaining information from the client before a Schedule 6 request is used. A determination will need to be made on a case-by-case basis as to whether there is a legitimate inability to provide proof of information that is requested. If a client is not able to complete the 'consent to release of health or disability information form' due to their disability (for example they are unable to physically sign the form), then a schedule 6 request for verification can be used to obtain the information. Only the Manager Client Service Delivery can contact health practitioners. When requesting information from a client's health practitioners using a schedule 6 request, the Manager Client Service Delivery must do the following: - make the request in writing and - specify that the request is made under schedule 6 of the Social Security Act 2018 and - specify the information and/or documents sought and - specify how long they have to provide that information

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki order in place — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The following table identifies when a child can be considered a dependent child and when it can't, depending on the type of order that is in place and section of Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 that applies. When to include as a dependent child When not to include as a dependent child section 139: Agreements for temporary care of child or young person by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 140: Agreements for extended care of child or young person by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 78: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, pending determination of court proceedings. If Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki has returned the child or young person into the care of the immediate previous caregiver. section 78: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, pending determination of court proceedings. section 101: Custody order in favour of principal caregiver. Guardianship order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki under section 110. section 101: Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 102: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 110(2)a: Sole Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. Section 101 Custody Order in favour of principal caregiver and other dependent child criteria are met. Please refer case to your local solicitor for consideration. section 110(2)a: Sole Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 110(2)b: Additional Guardianship Order, to any other guardian in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 112: Guardianship Order in favour of Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki for a specific purpose. Please refer case to your local solicitor for consideration. section 86: Services Orders that provide for particular services and assistance required by the child or young person (e.g. counselling fees, special education costs). section 86: Services Orders that provide for general financial support to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 91: Support Orders. The child may be considered a dependent child where the documentation states that specific financial support is to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki.

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki order in place — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: section 91: Support Orders. The child cannot be considered a dependent child where the documentation states that general financial support is to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. Contact your local solicitor if you receive a case in this category. When a child or young person is discharged from the care, custody or sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, the child can be considered as a dependent child and Disability Allowance can be paid to the caregiver - The legislation referenced above is the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Payment
Disability Allowance covers additional costs directly related to the client's disability.
The amount paid is estimated in relation to the actual costs that have been or will be incurred on a regular basis.
For more information see:
- Rates and income cut-out points
If the costs are less than the maximum payable, round up the grant to the next 5 cents.
Round up any payments of less than 50 cents per week, up to 50 cents per week.
## Payments for annual costs, paid in advance for a number of years
A client may choose to pay for an item or service as a lump sum that covers the cost for a number of years, such as purchasing a long-term Mobility Parking Permit.
These costs can be included in Disability Allowance for the 12 month period from when it was purchased, if the cost involved is a modest amount, or spread over the number of years the payment covers, if the person pays a substantial amount.
Note from 20 November 2017, except for the Counselling (45) and Transport Counselling (53) cost codes (which must have an expiry date), all other Disability Allowance cost codes will have an optional expiry date.

chunks.title: Payments for dependent children — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Payments for dependent children
If the Disability Allowance application is made on behalf of a dependent child:
- establish the Disability Allowance in the parent's name and
- show the allowance as being paid for the child

chunks.title: Pharmaceutical charges — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance can be used to cover the costs of regular, ongoing pharmaceutical charges a client has because of their disability. A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client’s disability, the need for treatment and that pharmaceuticals are necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a: - disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or - life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability Disability Allowance can only be paid for the portion of costs not covered by the Community Services Card, High Use Health Card, Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card, medical insurance, ACC or other accident insurer. Disability Allowance is generally only paid to assist with the cost of pharmaceutical products that are fully or partially subsidised under Healthy Futures (Pae Ora) Act 2022 (formerly the New Zealand Public Health and Disability Act 2000). When a client applies for assistance with the cost of a non-subsidised pharmaceutical there are additional factors that must be considered before the cost can be included in Disability Allowance. The amount paid for a pharmaceutical item will depend on what prescription item is needed, whether it was prescribed by a publicly funded health provider or a privately funded health provider, and if the client holds a Community Services Card, Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card and/or High Use Health Card. From 1 February 2026, prescribers can issue prescriptions for up to 12 months in some cases. Any co-payment charged is per prescription, rather than each time it is dispensed. This means clients may only have to pay for one $5.00 co-payment within a 12-month period.

chunks.title: Publicly funded prescriptions for subsidised groups — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Fully subsidised prescription items from health providers working in the public health system (including general practitioners and public specialists) are free for people: - under 14 or - holding a Community Services Card (and their dependents aged 14-17 years old) or - 65 years or older (from 1 July 2024) If someone in one of the above groups is prescribed a partially subsidised or non-subsidised item from a publicly funded health provider, they may still have to pay a fee. This includes clients who hold a Community Services Card, Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card and/or High Use Health Card. Example 1 - client is not in a subsidised group George has asthma that has been stable for 10 years. He visits a general practitioner to get a prescription for his inhaler. He requests to change from one of the partially subsidised inhalers to a fully subsidised inhaler. His doctor notes that both inhalers do the same thing, so prescribes George the fully subsidised inhaler. At the pharmacy George pays a $5.00 co-payment for his initial inhaler as he does not fall into one of the subsidised groups. He does not pay any other charge as his medication is fully subsidised, and any extra inhalers needed in that 12-month period will not have another co-payment. Example 2 - client is in a subsidised group Tina visits her general practitioner. They prescribe her several medications that she needs for her ongoing disability. The medications prescribed are all fully subsidised. At the pharmacy Tina does not have to pay anything for her medications as they are fully subsidised. She also does not need to pay a co-payment, as she has a Community Services Card.

chunks.title: Privately funded providers — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: When prescriptions are prescribed by privately funded health providers (private specialists) there is a cost. This includes fully subsidised, partially subsidised and non-subsidised prescription items. Prescriptions from privately funded health providers have a: - $10.00 co-payment for people aged 14-17 years old, or - $15.00 co-payment for people aged 18 years and older Example Sarah has an ongoing skin condition and visits her private specialist. She is prescribed a fully subsidised cream. As Sarah is over 18 years old, she is charged a $15.00 co-payment for her medicine at the pharmacy.

chunks.title: Extra costs in relation to pharmaceutical charges — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: In addition to the charges for medication, clients may have additional charges which can be included as allowable costs in Disability Allowance. These can include: - printed reports that list what pharmaceutical charges were paid over a period of time - blister packs (this refers to the way a client's medication may be packaged) - assistance to pick up medication from the pharmacy that incurs a cost (e.g. courier costs) - the cost to print, fax or electronically send prescriptions

chunks.title: Costs not included — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance cannot be paid for: - pharmaceutical items not related to the client's disability (e.g. a cough suppressant for the flu, as the flu is not an ongoing disability) or - illegal drugs used for medical purposes (e.g. recreational cannabis that has not been prescribed by a doctor that may be used for pain relief)

chunks.title: Proof of pharmaceutical costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The client must provide: - a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and - receipts as proof of their ongoing pharmaceutical costs Note if a fee has been charged by a registered health practitioner or pharmacist for the cost of a report or print out to verify medical fees or pharmaceutical charges, this fee or other administration related cost can be included as a cost for Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Pharmaceutical subsidies — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The amount pharmaceuticals are subsidised by will depend on: - what prescription item is needed - if it was prescribed by a publicly funded health provider or a privately funded health provider and - if the person holds a Community Services Card, Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card and/or High Use Health Card From 1 February 2026, prescribers can issue prescriptions for up to 12 months in some cases. Any co-payment charged is per prescription, rather than each time it is dispensed. This means clients may only have to pay for one $5.00 co-payment within a 12-month period. Anyone getting a prescription may have to pay other pharmacy fees that are not subsidised (e.g. packaging, printing and faxing). This includes clients with a Community Services Card or a Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card, and families with children under 14 years old. Disability Allowance cannot be paid for the portion of costs covered by the Community Services Card, High Use Health Card, Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card, ACC or other accident insurer, or medical insurance.

chunks.title: Publicly funded providers — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Fully subsidised prescription items from publicly funded health providers (including public specialists) are free for people: - under 14 or - holding a Community Services Card (and their dependents aged 14-17 years old) or - 65 years or older (from 1 July 2024) If someone in one of the above groups is prescribed items from a publicly funded health provider, they may still have to pay a fee. For example, if they are prescribed partially subsidised and non-subsidised prescription items. This includes clients who hold a Community Services Card, Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card and/or High Use Health Card. Example 1 - client is not in a subsidised group George has asthma that has been stable for 10 years. He visits a publicly funded specialist for his inhaler. He requests to change from one of the partially subsidised inhalers to a fully subsidised inhaler. His doctor notes that both inhalers do the same thing. At the pharmacy George pays a $5.00 co-payment for his initial inhaler as he does not fall into one of the subsidised groups, and any extra inhalers needed in that 12-month period will not have another co-payment. Example 2 - client is in a subsidised group Tina visits her general practitioner (GP). They prescribe her medication she needs for her ongoing disability. The medication prescribed is fully subsidised. At the pharmacy Tina does not have to pay anything for her medication as she has a Community Services Card.

chunks.title: Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: An individual or family unit pays the co-payment for the first 20 prescription items that are prescribed in any "pharmaceutical year" (defined as 1 February to 31 January). Note this applies to every new prescription and does not apply to repeat supplies on the same prescription. After 20 pharmaceutical items have been purchased by an individual or family from the same pharmacy, the pharmacist issues a Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card. Once a Pharmaceutical Subsidy Card is issued that individual or family unit will not have to pay the co-payment for the rest of the pharmaceutical year.

chunks.title: Non-subsidised pharmaceuticals — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: When a client has non-subsidised pharmaceutical costs, additional factors must be considered before the cost can be included in Disability Allowance. For example, if there is a subsidised or partially subsidised alternative that could be used. The part-charge and pharmacy fees for non-subsidised services such as packaging and faxing are allowable costs for Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Power, gas, and heating — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Power, gas, and heating
Disability Allowance can be paid for the additional electricity, gas, or heating costs a client has because of their disability.
A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that help towards additional power, gas or heating costs are necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a:
- disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or
- life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness
The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are:
- additional and
- ongoing and
- directly related to the client's disability
Payment is for the costs over and above the normal power consumption of similar-sized households in the area at the same time of the year.
Costs for additional power cannot be included in Disability Allowance based solely on the client's age.
Disability Allowance:
- only covers the portion of the client's power costs over and above normal usage and
- should not be paid automatically because the client has a disability and lives in a colder part of the country (the additional expense must be due to the client's disability not the area of New Zealand they live in)
- can be paid for the cost of firewood over and above normal usage if the client uses this method of heating
## Extra help
A client may be able to apply for an Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment for assistance with:
- outstanding electricity and gas bills and
- the cost of reconnecting electricity and gas.
## Proof of power, gas and heating costs
The client must provide:
- a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and
- copies of power accounts or receipts for gas, coal, or firewood

chunks.title: Private paying patients — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Private paying patients
When a person is in a rest home as a private paying patient (and not receiving a Residential Care Subsidy), Disability Allowance can be paid for any costs they pay that are:
- in addition to the rest home fee for service and
- directly related to their disability
Note that Disability Allowance cannot be paid for any of the rest home fee, as this fee covers their day to day living costs, and for general care, this is the same for everyone in the rest home.
For more information see:
- Rest home fees
- Definition of disability

chunks.title: Proof of costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Proof of costs
Before Disability Allowance can be granted, a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must verify on the Disability Allowance medical certificate that the client:
- has a disability that is likely to continue for more than 6 months
- requires on-going support
- requires on-going supervision or treatment by a registered health practitioner
The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are:
- additional and
- ongoing and
- directly related to the client's disability
The client must provide receipts or invoices as evidence of their extra costs. If a receipt is not available, a quote or estimate of the costs must be provided. The quote or estimate must be completed by an appropriate provider of such goods or services.
The registered health practitioner administering the treatment must verify that the:
- additional costs of their treatment are the direct result of the client's disability and
- costs are on-going and
- goods or services are beneficial and are of therapeutic value to the client

chunks.title: Proof of counselling costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Proof of counselling costs
A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must verify:
- the disability and
- the need for counselling and
- that the counselling costs are additional and ongoing and
- that the counselling is beneficial and of therapeutic value and directly related to the client's disability
Note treatment that is beneficial and of therapeutic value means the treatment may improve the client's condition, maintain the client's condition, or prevent it from getting worse.
The client must provide:
- a Disability Certificate - Counselling completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and counsellor and
- receipts or invoices or quotes showing the weekly cost of counselling and
- evidence that the counsellor has an appropriate qualification (for example proof that they are: a counsellor or a registered member of the Social Workers Registration Board (SWRB), this evidence may be printed on the receipt or letterhead)
When Disability Allowance is granted for counselling an expiry date is created and the cost is automatically excluded when the expiry date is reached.
If the client applies for additional sessions they will need to supply receipts or invoices, as proof that they are attending the counselling. MSD should tell the client about this requirement at their initial interview.
For their Disability Allowance review, the client must also:
- keep a receipt for every counselling session as proof of attendance and
- record every visit on the 'Record of Counselling card'

chunks.title: Proof of medical alarm costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Proof of medical alarm costs
A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance - Medical Alarm Assessment form that verifies:
- the need for a medical alarm is ongoing, directly related to the client's disability or personal health need and beneficial and of therapeutic value and
- the medical alarm is required to maintain independent living and
- if the client needs an in-home or anywhere medical alarm
The client must provide a copy of the contract or receipt for the installation/rental of the medical alarm.
MSD must check the costs claimed are:
- for the rental and monitoring of the medical alarm, and do not include: the cost of installing the medical alarm orany costs related to smoke alarms
- the cost of installing the medical alarm or
- any costs related to smoke alarms
and
- for a service provided by an MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier
## Clients with a non MSD-accredited medical alarm supplier
The client will need to provide a copy of their contract from their supplier, when it has been agreed that a client can have the cost of a medical alarm from a non MSD-accredited supplier included in their Disability Allowance due to their exceptional circumstances.
The contract must clearly show the service being provided is a monitored medical alarm service.

chunks.title: Proof of transport costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Proof of transport costs
The costs of travelling to receive treatment, support services or counselling, or to visit their registered health practitioner may be considered as additional expenses arising from the client's disability.
The client must provide:
- a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner verifying that the travel is an additional and ongoing expense arising from the client's disability and
- proof of their ongoing travel costs
## Travel not specifically stated on the Medical Certificate
Where 'travel' is not specifically written on the Disability Allowance disability certificate it can be included as an allowable cost without further verification if the medical practitioner or nurse practitioner has verified the:
- client will be attending a specific treatment, counselling or support service as a result of their disability and
- frequency of the treatments, counselling or support service
## Public transport and taxis
If the client is using public transport or taxis, they must provide receipts as proof of their costs.
When a client has a Total Mobility card or vouchers, the cost of their travel fares is subsidised.
Clients with a Community Services Card can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect.
## Private vehicle
If the client is using their own car, the rates listed in the table below are used to calculate the costs.
The following rates have been set and reflect the reasonable running costs (excluding fixed costs) of a vehicle dependent on engine size.
Running costs include consumables such, as petrol and oil. Fixed costs (not included in the calculation) include costs such as, relicensing, insurance and Warrants of Fitness.
Fixed costs are not included as all clients will incur these costs when they own a vehicle. For example, people without a disability would still incur fixed costs.
Use these rates to calculate the allowable vehicle running costs.
cc rating
paid per kilometre
Up to 1000
29 cents per km
1000-1350
30 cents per km
1351-2000
35 cents per km
Over 2000
40 cents per km

chunks.title: Purchase of equipment and one-off items — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Purchase of equipment and one-off items
The cost of buying equipment or other one-off items cannot be included in Disability Allowance. This is because the costs are not regular or ongoing.
The person should be referred to Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora who may be able to assist, or assistance under the Special Needs Grant programme can be considered.
If you are unsure whether a particular cost is a one-off or ongoing you should contact Helpline for advice.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for Disability Allowance, a client must:
- meet an income test and
- have a disability which is likely to last at least 6 months and
- have ongoing, additional costs arising from that disability and
- be a New Zealand citizen or residence class visa holder (i.e. not be in New Zealand unlawfully, or here on a temporary entry class visa) and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand

chunks.title: Receives a Student Allowance — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Receives a Student Allowance
When a child receives Student Allowance or an Independent Circumstances Allowance under the Student Allowances Regulations 1998, they are no longer a dependent child.
Student Allowance is treated as income when you are determining a student's entitlement to Disability Allowance as a non-beneficiary.

chunks.title: Gets a Student Loan — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Gets a Student Loan
Getting a Student Loan (including the living cost component) does not mean the child is financially independent.
If the child continues to be the client's primary responsibility, is maintained as a member of their family and continues to be financially dependent (that is the parent is meeting some of the costs for the child) Disability Allowance for the child can be paid to the client as the principal caregiver (or principal temporary caregiver getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the child) until the start of the pay period following:
- the date they turn 18 or
- where the child is 18 and continuing in education, the earlier of: the date they are no longer enrolled in school or tertiary education orthe date they are no longer attending school or tertiary education as required orthe date they are financially independent orthe date they leave the parent or caregiver's care or31 December of the year they turn 18
- the date they are no longer enrolled in school or tertiary education or
- the date they are no longer attending school or tertiary education as required or
- the date they are financially independent or
- the date they leave the parent or caregiver's care or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18

chunks.title: Rental equipment — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance can be paid for necessary rental equipment when the client: - has a need for the item or service but cannot get funding through Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora or another state funded agency and - their life or health would be put at risk, or their disability aggravated if they could not hire the equipment because the expense was not included in their Disability Allowance Examples of rental equipment that may be paid for are a closed-circuit television, or a computer, for vision impaired person, or a nebuliser for a severe asthmatic. A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment, and that rental equipment is necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a: - disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or - life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability Note treatment that is beneficial and of therapeutic value means that the treatment may improve the client's condition, maintain the client's condition or prevent it from getting worse.

chunks.title: Equipment cannot be funded from another agency — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: MSD should refer the client back to their medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or someone from their team) who will be able to refer them to the local hospital, health services or publicly funded equipment services to see if they can get the equipment provided. If the hospital, health service or publicly funded equipment service won't provide the equipment, the client should get a letter stating why.

chunks.title: Exception — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: A vision impaired person may rent equipment from the Pacific Vision International, Lighthouse Trust, and Blind Low Vision NZ through the Sir Arthur Pearson Memorial Fund (Pearson Fund) that enables them to read or hear written material. In this situation they are not required to seek verification from the local hospital, health service or publicly funded equipment service that funding is not available for the equipment. This type of equipment is generally not provided by the local hospital or health services and people will only qualify for the equipment through the Pearson Fund if public funding cannot be found elsewhere. For more information see: - Verification of costs for equipment rented by blind people

chunks.title: Disability Allowance not paid — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance cannot be paid for prostheses (e.g. artificial limbs) or hearing aids as they are not a regular and on-going cost. Note Disability Allowance can be used for hearing aid batteries, see Authorised Consumables.

chunks.title: Proof of rental equipment costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The client must provide: - a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and - receipts as proof of the equipment rental costs and - a letter from Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora stating that funding is not available for the item or service and why it is not available and - a letter from a registered medical or nurse practitioner stating what the consequences would be if the client, or their dependent child did not receive the item/service

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get Disability Allowance, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- have a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
Note for Disability Allowance no period of residence is required.
People who are in New Zealand unlawfully or here on a temporary entry class visa generally do not qualify for a benefit.
## Clients who do not meet the residence requirements
If a client does not meet the residence requirements, they cannot get Disability Allowance.
However, if a client in this situation has disability costs, they may be able to get Temporary Additional Support if they are:
- a person who has refugee or protected person status in New Zealand or
- awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protected person status and are lawfully in New Zealand (i.e. they have a valid temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009) or
- applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 and are compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances
Once the client has been granted citizenship or a residence class visa and they meet all the other qualifications, Disability Allowance can be granted.
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand as they hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other criteria qualify for Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Residential care services — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Residential care services
Clients receiving Residential Support Subsidy who have ongoing disability related costs may qualify for Disability Allowance.
Disability Allowance can be paid to cover costs relating to a client's disability, which are not covered by their contract with the residential care services provider, when a person is receiving Residential Support Subsidy.
Due to the complexity of assessing Disability Allowance for Residential Support Subsidy clients, all Disability Allowance applications, reviews and inquiries from clients receiving Residential Support Subsidy are managed by Senior Services - residential care
For more information see:
- Costs not included
- Definition of disability
- Extra help Residential Support Subsidy

chunks.title: Rest home fees — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Rest home fees
Disability Allowance is not paid to cover the costs of rest home fees as this is not an additional cost because of a disability but is an accommodation cost.
The person could consider applying for a Residential Care Subsidy through Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora.

chunks.title: Restrictions on the information requested — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Restrictions on the information requested
Requests for information made directly to the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner who completed the client’s Disability Allowance medical certificate must not include a request for:
- an opinion, or information about whether the client has a partner or
- any additional information regarding the client's other physical and mental health conditions, or any information that is considered to be of a highly confidential nature

chunks.title: Retirement villages — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Retirement villages
Residents of a retirement village or complex generally pay a standard service fee. This covers services such as gardening, window cleaning, and an alarm.
These costs cannot be included in Disability Allowance as these are the same for all residents and are not directly related to their disability.
## Exceptions
In some circumstances a person living in a retirement village or complex may be able to have the cost of a medical alarm included in their Disability Allowance.
There is also an ability to include certain costs that are included in the standard service fee when:
- a disability is one of the reasons the client moved from their own accommodation into a retirement village complex and
- the client was getting Disability Allowance for the cost before moving and that same cost still exists in the retirement village
When a client's move to a retirement village is partly caused by their inability to carry out tasks they are getting Disability Allowance for, and there is an ongoing cost for the same tasks in their new accommodation, the client may get Disability Allowance for these ongoing costs.
## Costs
Only the costs associated with maintaining the clients own immediate area can be considered. Do not consider costs associated with maintaining communal areas.
You can use discretion for the amount of Disability Allowance that can be paid. It would generally be expected that a client's maintenance costs in a retirement village should be less than their costs were in their previous accommodation. Generally, the space to be maintained will be smaller.
## Example
The client may have had a large property with an expansive lawn area, and/or high maintenance gardens, and the costs for this would be high due to the level of work required.
The client's costs for a much smaller lawn and garden area in the retirement village complex would be expected to be lower as the work involved will be less.

chunks.title: Services provided through another agency — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Services provided through another agency
Disability Allowance is not paid for items or services fully funded or provided through another state agency such as:
- learning costs of children with disabilities, as the educational costs for children and students with disabilities are funded through the Ministry of Education
- speech-therapy for school-age children funded through the Ministry of Education
- items/services fully funded, subsidised, or provided through Health New Zealand – Te Whatu Ora. This includes costs that Health New Zealand started funding then stopped because they were no longer considered necessary
Disability Allowance can be paid to cover the portion of the client’s costs that are not met by ACC or another accident insurer. In some cases a client may have other costs that are not covered by ACC, or costs due to another disability not caused by an accident. These costs can be considered for Disability Allowance.
Note in circumstances where costs are incurred over the amount that is funded or provided through another agency, Disability Allowance can be considered for the portion of costs that is not funded.
## ACC Independence Allowance
Disability Allowance is not affected by a client receiving an Independence Allowance from ACC as this is not paid to meet specific disability-related costs.

chunks.title: Shared care — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Shared care
Shared care is when the parents of a child are living apart and the child lives (for at least 40% of the time) with each parent.
In shared care situations Disability Allowance for the child should be paid to the parent that has the greater responsibility for meeting the child's disability related costs.

chunks.title: Special Disability Allowance — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Special Disability Allowance
A Special Disability Allowance can be paid to a client who is not in hospital or residential care when:
- they are getting a main benefit or pension and
- their partner is a patient in hospital or residential care and
- their partner is getting a reduced rate of benefit or pension due to hospitalisation.
It is paid to the partner in the community to help with extra costs because of their partner's hospitalisation.
Special Disability Allowance should be granted from the date the partner starts getting a hospital rate of benefit, or becomes financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy.
Note if a Veteran's Pension client is in hospital for more than 13 weeks their payments are not reduced to the hospital rate and their partner cannot get Special Disability Allowance. This is because Veteran's Pension is not affected by hospitalisation.
## Partner is admitted to hospital
Special Disability Allowance should be stopped from the first available date if the person receiving it is also admitted to hospital or residential care.
## Client in hospital dies
Following the death of the client in hospital or residential care Special Disability Allowance should be stopped from:
- the day after the death of the client (if in the current pay-period) or
- the first available date if advice of the death is received within 14 days or
- the day after the date of death of the client if the advice is received more than 14 days after the date of death
## Partner in the community dies
Following the death of the partner in the community, Special Disability Allowance is part of the terminal benefit and can continue for 4 weeks.
This applies to the partner in the community getting New Zealand Superannuation in their own right, Emergency Benefit paid at the Supported Living Payment rate, or as a partner getting a joint (apportioned) benefit.

chunks.title: Special Education Transport — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Special Education Transport
The Ministry of Education Special Education School Transport Assistance Policy provides transport to and from school, for students identified through Special Education 2000 as having special education needs.
The following outlines the 2 main criteria:
## Category 1 - Safety
Special needs transport assistance is available for students who require it for safety reasons, to enable them to attend their nearest school, or the nearest school that is able to meet their special need. For example when:
- the student has an intellectual disability that impedes their ability to go to and from school safely
- the student has a health condition that impedes their ability to go to and from school safely or
- there are significant safety risks for the student or for others during the passage to and from school
Some specific examples under the safety category are:
- transport to and from a women's refuge
- transport to a centre for extra support and
- transport to and from school when this was the recommendation within a multi-element support plan within the Behaviour Education Support Team framework
## Category 2 - Mobility
Special needs transport assistance is available for students who require it for mobility reasons, to enable them to attend their nearest school, or the nearest school that is able to meet their special need. For example when:
- wheelchairs or other specialist equipment, must accompany the student
- the student is unable (for mobility reasons) to independently make their way to school
There are no other criteria aside from these two. For example transport to and from school cannot be provided from this funding, for psycho-social or social reasons. Assistance is not available from this fund to transport students to meet parenting order or access requirements.
The provision of transport assistance is not dependent on any factors other than the criteria. For example, the financial circumstances of the family are not a determining factor in regard to the eligibility for transport assistance.

chunks.title: Special foods — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance may be paid to cover the additional costs of special foods that a client needs because of their disability. A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability the need for treatment and that special foods are necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a: - disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or - life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability When a medical practitioner or nurse practitioner indicates on the client's Disability Allowance medical certificate that treatment by another registered health practitioner is necessary (e.g. a dietician), that practitioner must verify the costs of their services. Note treatment that is beneficial and of therapeutic value means the treatment may improve the client's condition, maintain the client's condition, or prevent the client's condition from getting worse. The cost of special foods may be included if they are: - for additional food or food supplements beyond most people's everyday needs and - above usual food costs (e.g. soya milk costs more than cow's milk) and - part of a diet that has been supervised by a registered dietitian, if relevant Note MSD only pays the difference between a special food item and its non-special equivalent i.e. normal milk vs lactose free milk, gluten free bread vs gluten containing bread. Some examples of special food costs included for Disability Allowance are: - gluten free food for people who are diagnosed with Coeliac disease or gluten intolerance (e.g. gluten free flours, bread or pasta) - low or no dairy foods for people who are diagnosed with a dairy allergy or intolerance (e.g. soy or coconut milk alternatives) - high protein and high calorie foods for people who are diagnosed with 'Failure to Thrive' (e.g. chickpeas or yoghurt) - greater quantities of foods than is normally expected i.e. the product is not necessarily special, but the amount is (e.g. people who are diagnosed with 'iron-deficient anaemia' and require additional silver beet or meat in their diet)

chunks.title: Special foods — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: - low or no sugar food for people with diabetes or sugar intolerances (e.g. whole grains like barley or quinoa or sugar alternatives) The issue of special foods is not always straightforward and needs to be treated with sensitivity and discretion. When it is unclear refer to the Regional Health Advisor and Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] for more information and advice. For example, clients with diabetes may need to follow a specific diet, but it can be difficult to quantify their additional costs. Assess each case on its merits. Disability Allowance cannot be paid for: - specialist foods that are fully funded, subsidised or provided through another agency such as Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora or - extra costs of a self-imposed diet or lifestyle choice or - the normal costs of healthy eating (e.g. fresh vegetables and fruit) The diet or special food must be confirmed as not being fully funded, subsidised or provided by another agency such as Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora. For further information about specific food items that may be fully-funded or subsidised through PHARMAC see: PHARMACs online schedule Special foods.

chunks.title: Proof of special food costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The client must provide: - a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and - proof of their extra food costs and - evidence that the treatment is being supervised by or provided by a registered dietician, if relevant

chunks.title: Telephone — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Telephone rental and line rental costs are not usually accepted as allowable costs for Disability Allowance because these are ordinary living costs for most people. Each new application should be checked carefully to determine if the costs are additional and directly related to the client's disability. Disability Allowance can be paid for telephone costs to a client with a disability only when the ongoing cost of the telephone is directly related to their disability. A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that a telephone is necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a: - disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or - life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability The telephone cost can be accepted as being directly related to the client's disability if MSD knows they did not previously have a telephone connected and has had to have one connected due to their disability. Telephone rental costs means the regular and ongoing costs of renting a basic telephone and/or telephone line rental and can include wiring maintenance charges. Disability Allowance cannot be paid for: - the costs of buying a phone or having it installed as these are not ongoing costs (Consider the possibilities of an Advance or the Recoverable Assistance Programme for installation costs) or - extra costs such as toll calls, call minder, or call waiting (unless it can be shown that it is, necessary and directly related to the client's disability, and an additional expense)

chunks.title: Including charges for getting a telephone account statement in the mail — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: Costs associated with getting a telephone account statement in the mail can be included as part of the telephone costs for Disability Allowance if the client is unable to access their account online due to their disability. MSD needs to have a conversation with the client to determine this. If MSD is satisfied the client needs to get their telephone account statement in the mail due to their disability, the costs associated with this can be included in the Disability Allowance. If the need for a telephone has been indicated on the medical certificate and included in the Disability Allowance, the cost of getting their telephone account statement in the mail does not need to be stated on the medical certificate. If the need for a telephone has not been stated on the medical certificate, the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner will need to verify the need for getting the telephone account statement in the mail. MSD can get verification over the phone.

chunks.title: Mobile phone — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The ongoing cost of a mobile phone (e.g. pre-pay call time or plan charges) should only be allowed in exceptional circumstances when it is the most cost-effective solution. This may be when the client does not have a landline at their residence or there are no telephone lines available. The maximum cost paid, should be no more than the cost of the standard monthly landline rental in the area. Note mobile phones would not be considered an additional expense if the medical alarm needs a landline to operate.

chunks.title: Proof of telephone costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: MSD must ensure the client is not getting a Special Benefit or Temporary Additional Support for telephone costs. If the client qualifies to have telephone costs included in Disability Allowance the cost must be removed from their Special Benefit or Temporary Additional Support and included in their Disability Allowance. The client must provide a: - Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and - copy of their telephone account showing their telephone and line rental costs or - copy of their mobile plan account showing plan charges When a client's mobile is pre-paid, MSD can include the reasonable costs of the pre-paid call time without receipts. Note the maximum cost paid for should be no more than the cost of a standard monthly landline rental for the area.

chunks.title: Telephone Costs Payment — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Telephone Costs Payment
The Telephone Costs Payment (TCP) is paid to people with disabilities who:
- were receiving Disability Allowance for telephone costs before 1 April 1999
- don't meet the criteria relating to additional costs introduced on 1 April 1999 but
- still meet the other qualifying criteria for Disability Allowance
On 1 April 1999 a Ministerial Direction was introduced to clarify the criteria for Disability Allowance. Some people receiving Disability Allowance no longer qualified for assistance with telephone costs under the new criteria. To ensure these people did not experience hardship, a welfare programme was introduced to allow their payments to continue.
People in this group had their existing telephone costs payments under Disability Allowance capped and transferred to Telephone Costs Payment (their Telephone Costs Payment cannot be increased from their previous level of payment).
From 20 November 2017 TCP costs can no longer be selected. For any telephone costs that are included in Disability Allowance as a Telephone Costs Payment you should use the cost code 95 (Telephone Costs) in the SDAWA screen.

chunks.title: Temporary care — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Temporary care
Generally, a client will not be considered as the person primarily responsible for the child when the period of care is temporary.
Examples of temporary care are:
- school holidays
- Christmas or other public holidays
- during the temporary incapacity of the primary caregiver or
- primary caregiver is in prison
A principal temporary caregiver receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is considered to be primarily responsible for the child and may receive Disability Allowance while the child is in their care.
## Extra assistance during temporary care
Any assistance for additional costs due to temporary care situations should be met, in the first instance, by the principal caregiver. When this is not available, you can consider Special Needs Grants assistance for the client.
For more information see:
- Special Needs Grants

chunks.title: Total Mobility Scheme — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Total Mobility Scheme
The Total Mobility Scheme provides a subsidised taxi service to people with serious mobility constraints by way of taxi vouchers or cards that provide a discount on the normal taxi fare.
When a client has a Total Mobility card or vouchers their taxi fares are subsidised. The cost of the fare that is not covered by the subsidy can be included in Disability Allowance as an additional travel cost.
For more information see:
- Transport - disability
- Total Mobility Scheme

chunks.title: Transport - counselling — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Transport - counselling
Disability Allowance may be paid for the cost of transport to counselling if the need for counselling is directly related to a person's disability.
If a client with a disability applies for assistance with the cost of transport to counselling, as well as the cost of counselling, this can only be included for transport to the number of sessions that Disability Allowance is being paid for.
If a client is applying for the cost of transport to counselling only, this will not be limited to a specific number of sessions. Provided the client is attending counselling that is directly related to their disability, the cost of transport can be included for the full period that the client is attending the counselling.
Travel costs to attend alcohol or drug related counselling can be paid.
Note the fees for these counselling sessions do not qualify for Disability Allowance if they are provided free of charge through a public hospital.
Public transport should be used in preference to taxis if it is available, and if the client's disability does not prevent them from using it.
## Community Services Card
If a client is using public transport and has a Community Services Card, they can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect and should apply for this if it is the most cost-effective way to meet their additional transport needs.
If a client has not used their Community Services Card to apply for the 50% discount, MSD must discuss their reasons if their actual public transport costs are higher than they would be if the 50% discount was applied.
The client may have a good reason for not applying for the 50% discount (e.g. there are accessibility issues with applying for the Community Connect discount through a public transport provider's website, and it is the only way to apply).
## Allowable transport costs
If there is good reason, the client’s allowable costs for additional travel should be their actual costs. If there is no good reason, their allowable costs for travel should not be more than the cost of the subsidised public transport fare.
Disability Allowance cannot be paid for travel costs for:
- attending treatment at a hospital when the costs are fully funded by Health New Zealand – Te Whatu Ora or a Special Needs Grant Health Travel Costs
Note the costs of transport to counselling, and counselling combined cannot exceed the maximum rate for Disability Allowance.
Counselling costs cannot be carried over to the Special Benefit or Temporary Additional Support assessment formula.

chunks.title: Transport - disability — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Transport - disability
Disability Allowance may be paid for ongoing and additional travel costs that a client has because of their disability. These additional travel costs can be incurred when a client with a disability is carrying out everyday activities.
Examples of everyday activities may include but is not limited to:
- shopping
- vocational services
- work
When Disability Allowance is payable for the additional travel costs a client has because of their disability, the amount payable is the difference between the costs incurred by the disabled client and the costs a person in a similar position without the disability would have.
Note this may include travel to support services such as Alcoholics Anonymous, where the qualifications for Disability Allowance are met.
The cost of a Mobility Parking Permit and costs associated with a Total Mobility card/vouchers are examples of costs that can be included as additional travel costs.
Public transport should be used in preference to taxis if it is available and if the client's disability does not prevent them from using it.
## Community Services Card
If a client is using public transport and has a Community Services Card, they can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect and should apply for this if it is the most cost-effective way to meet their additional transport needs.
If a client has not used their Community Services Card to apply for the 50% discount, MSD must discuss their reasons if their actual public transport costs are higher than they would be if the 50% discount was applied.
The client may have a good reason for not applying for the 50% discount (e.g. there are accessibility issues with applying for Community Connect through a public transport provider's website, and it is the only way to apply).
## Allowable transport costs
If there is good reason, the client's allowable costs for additional travel should be their actual costs. If there is no good reason, their allowable costs for travel should not be more than the cost of the subsidised public transport fare.
Disability Allowance cannot be paid for travel costs for:
- attending treatment at a hospital if the costs are fully funded by Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora or other agency, or Special Needs Grant Health Travel Costs
- children/students with disabilities who qualify for assistance through the Ministry of Education. These clients should be referred to Group Special Education. If the child is not eligible for Special Education Transport, the client should get a letter stating why.

chunks.title: Transport - personal health — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that transport costs are necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a: - disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or - life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness The certificate must also confirm the transport is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability When a medical practitioner or nurse practitioner indicates on the client's Disability Allowance medical certificate that treatment by a registered health practitioner is necessary, Disability Allowance may be paid to cover the costs of regular travel to that practitioner for treatment of the client's disability. Note if the travel is for a particular course of treatment (e.g. chemotherapy) payment of costs may be met by Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora. Public transport should be used in preference to taxis if it is available and if the client's disability does not prevent them from using it. Disability Allowance cannot be paid for travel costs for attending treatment at a hospital when the costs are fully funded by Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora or a Special Needs Grant - Health Travel Costs.

chunks.title: Community Services Card — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: If a client is using public transport and has a Community Services Card, they can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect and should apply for this if it is the most cost-effective way to meet their additional transport needs. When a client has not used their Community Services Card to apply for the discount, MSD must discuss their reasons for this, if their actual public transport costs are higher than they would be if the 50% discount was applied.

chunks.title: Allowable transport costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: The client may have a good reason for not applying for the 50% discount (e.g. there are accessibility issues with applying for the Community Connect discount through a public transport provider's website, and it is the only way to apply). When there is a good reason, the client's allowable costs for additional travel should be their actual costs. If there is no good reason, their allowable costs for travel should not be more than the cost of the subsidised public transport fare.

chunks.title: Travel when there is a closer suitable health practitioner — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text: When a client chooses to travel some distance to see a registered health practitioner, Disability Allowance should only be paid for the costs of travel to a suitable local registered health practitioner. For example, a client moves to a new location and chooses to visit their registered health practitioner in their previous location rather than transfer to a suitable local health practitioner, only the costs of travelling to the local health practitioner should generally be included. Note when there is closer suitable registered health practitioner, any additional travel costs not met by Disability Allowance cannot be included as a cost for Special Benefit or Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Types of costs — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Types of costs
Disability Allowance only covers certain types of costs.
If a client has an additional cost that is not one of the types of costs listed below, they usually cannot be paid Disability Allowance. Call Helpline for advice.

chunks.title: Verification of costs for equipment rented by blind people — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Verification of costs for equipment rented by blind people
Pacific Vision International, Lighthouse Trust, and Blind Low Vision NZ provide a rental programme through the Sir Arthur Pearson Memorial Fund (Pearson Fund) for closed circuit televisions (CCTV) and other adaptive technology (including computers and specialised software) that enables a person to read or hear written material.
The Pearson Fund will not provide assistance where this is seen as the normal responsibility of another agency and before an application is submitted applicants are required to investigate funding from other agencies such as publicly funded equipment providers, ACC and Workbridge.
CCTV and other adaptive technology (including computers and specialised software) allow vision impaired clients to read or hear important text such as directions on medication and labels on food or other household products and poisons. The technology also provides vision impaired clients the independence to complete tasks such as managing finances and other day-to-day duties. Undertaking these activities without the technology could put the client's life or health at risk.
A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that equipment costs are necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a:
- disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or
- life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness
The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are:
- additional and
- ongoing and
- directly related to the client's disability
The client must provide:
- a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and
- confirmation from the Pearson Fund that advises the monthly cost of renting the equipment, this would generally be a copy of the rental agreement and
- a copy of the functional assessment report from Blind Low Vision NZ which outlines the tasks the client needs to achieve with the assistance of the CCTV or other adaptive technology. This provides evidence that the client's life or health would be put at risk or disability aggravated if the client could not read the information required to live safely in their home.

chunks.title: Vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals
A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies or minerals are necessary. The certificate must confirm the client has a:
- disability that is likely to last at least 6 months or
- life expectancy of less than 6 months because of a terminal illness
The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are:
- additional and
- ongoing and
- directly related to the client's disability
Treatment that is beneficial and of therapeutic value means that the treatment may improve the client's condition, maintain the client's condition or prevent it from getting worse.
Note when a medical practitioner or nurse practitioner indicates on the client's Disability Allowance medical certificate that treatment by another registered health practitioner is necessary, that practitioner must verify the costs of their services.
The cost of vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals can be included in Disability Allowance if:
- there are no alternative fully subsidised or partly subsidised pharmaceutical items
- funding from PHARMAC under their Named Patient Pharmaceutical Assessment Policy has been applied for where applicable and
- the client's registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner has verified that there are no suitable alternatives, and that the non-subsidised vitamin, supplement, herbal remedy or mineral product is essential
## Proof of vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and mineral costs
The vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals must be confirmed as not being fully funded, subsidised or provided by health authorities.
The client must provide:
- a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and
- proof of their vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals costs

chunks.title: Vocational services — extra help > disability allowance
chunks.text:
## Vocational services
Disability Allowance cannot be used to pay for fees to attend a vocational service. Funding for clients attending recognised vocational services is provided through Ministry of Health or MSD.
Clients may be able to get Disability Allowance for transport cost to attend a vocational service under Transport - disability

chunks.title: Approved early childhood education programme or service — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Approved early childhood education programme or service
An approved early childhood education programme means, early childhood education, provided by any of the following:
- a licensed early childhood service which includes: early childhood education and care centre (e.g. daycare centre, kōhanga reo, playcentre, kindergarten)home-based education and care servicehospital-based education and care service
- early childhood education and care centre (e.g. daycare centre, kōhanga reo, playcentre, kindergarten)
- home-based education and care service
- hospital-based education and care service
- a playgroup certificated by the Ministry of Education (this means a playgroup funded by the Ministry of Education and will meet certain standards)
and
- for which a fee is charged for the children to participate in the programme
Under no circumstances can we pay Early Learning Payment to a service that is not an approved early childhood education programme.

chunks.title: Centre charges a fee based on the attendance of a child — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Centre charges a fee based on the attendance of a child
When a centre or service charges a fee based on the hours attended by the child, we need to calculate the hourly fee.
To get an hourly fee, the weekly fee must be divided by the number of hours the child attends.
Example 1
Fee for attending
$50.00
Divided by hours attending each week
25 hours
Hourly fee equals
$2.00
The amount payable in this example is $2.00 per hour.
Example 2
Fee for attending
$315.00
Divided by hours attending each week
30 hours
Hourly fee equals
$10.50
The amount payable in example 2 is the maximum hourly subsidy rate of $10.02 per hour (as at 1 April 2026).
As the calculated hourly fee is higher than the maximum rate we can pay, this client would only be entitled to receive the maximum hourly rate of the subsidy.
We cannot pay more than the maximum rate.

chunks.title: Centre charges a flat fee — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Centre charges a flat fee
If the early childhood education centre or service charges a flat fee, calculate the amount of Early Learning Payment payable by dividing the service's weekly fee by the number of hours the child is enrolled for.
Enrolled hours means, the number of hours the child is booked to attend the centre or service, whether or not the child attends.
## Example 1
Weekly childcare centre fee
$140.00
Divided by enrolled hours
35 hours
Hourly fee equals
$4.00
The amount payable in this example is $4.00 per hour.
## Example 2
Weekly childcare centre fee
$315.00
Divided by enrolled hours
30 hours
Hourly fee equals
$10.50
The maximum amount payable is $10.02 per hour (as at 1 April 2026).
As the calculated hourly fee is higher than the maximum rate we can pay, this client would only be entitled to get the maximum hourly rate of the subsidy.
We cannot pay more than the maximum rate.

chunks.title: Absences allowed — extra help > early learning payment > changes and reviews early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Absences allowed
Some early childhood education programmes or services charge a fee when a child is temporarily away.
This can be to hold the child's place open and is normally a portion of the full fee charged.
When this kind of fee is payable, the Early Learning Payment can still be made to the early childhood education programme or service when a child getting the Early Learning Payment is absent.
Payment can continue for 15 working days, but this can extend to 30 working days if there is a good and sufficient reason.
Good and sufficient reasons deemed reasonable are determined in consultation with the child's family/whanau worker.
A good and sufficient reason is classed as an:
- injury
- illness
- family bereavement
- holiday or
- other reasonable circumstances
Note when the client has gone overseas or on holiday for a temporary period and the child continues to attend the early childhood education programme or service, the Early Learning Payment can still be paid. A temporary period where a child is away from the day to day care of a parent or caregiver does not mean the child is no longer a dependent of the parent or caregiver.

chunks.title: Absences due to COVID-19 requirements — extra help > early learning payment > changes and reviews early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Absences due to COVID-19 requirements
When a child is absent due to COVID-19 requirements, Early Learning Payment can continue being paid if the client still qualifies. A fee does not need to be charged to hold the child's place open for payment to continue.
A child may be absent due to COVID-19 requirements because they are:
- unwell and cannot attend childcare while unwell
- at high risk of severe illness if they contract COVID-19
- in self-isolation or quarantine due to COVID-19 public health requirements
- connected to a confirmed or probable case of COVID-19
- being kept home during Alert Level 3
This is not an exhaustive list. If a child is absent and you are unsure if it is due to COVID-19 requirements, please check the COVID-19 Alert System website for the most up to date COVID-19 guidelines.
## Number of weeks payment can continue
COVID-19 requirements means New Zealand's COVID-19 Alert System. The alert system is designed to manage and minimise the risk of COVID-19.
There is no limit on how long Early Learning Payment can be paid when a child is absent due to COVID-19 requirements.
However, the payment can only be paid for a period that relates to COVID-19 requirements. If a child is absent for other reasons, you will need to check the general absences allowed to see how long they can be paid.
## Example
Amina's son Gabriel suffers from a respiratory condition which means he is at high risk of severe illness if he contracts COVID-19. Due to this, Amina withdrew him from childcare for 7 weeks while New Zealand was at Alert Level 3.
Because the COVID-19 Alert Level 3 guidelines state that high risk people should stay home if they can, Early Learning Payment can continue for the full period of Gabriel's absence.

chunks.title: Amount payable during COVID-19 absence or closure — extra help > early learning payment > changes and reviews early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Amount payable during COVID-19 absence or closure
When a child is absent or a childcare centre is closed due to COVID-19 requirements, the amount the centre is paid depends on whether a fee is charged to hold open the child's place at the centre.
## Fee is charged
If a fee is charged, Early Learning Payment will be paid based on the child's enrolled hours and the fee charged by the centre.
Multiply the hourly fee (up to a maximum of $10.02 as at 1 April 2026) by the enrolled hours (up to a maximum of 20 hours per week).
## No fee is charged
If no fee is charged, Early Learning Payment will continue at the usual weekly amount before the absence or closure.
Note if during an absence or closure, the client decides their child will not return, payment must be stopped.
If a change in circumstance happens during an absence or closure, the Early Learning Payment must be reviewed, and the rate of payment may change.

chunks.title: Change in early childhood education programme or service — extra help > early learning payment > changes and reviews early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Change in early childhood education programme or service
A change in an early childhood education programme or service a child attends is considered a change in circumstances.
The early childhood education programme or service will need to verify their details.
## Families moving to another area
Clients must inform Centralised Services Whangarei if they relocate.
If the client remains with the same Family Start or Early Start and the child attends the same early childhood education programme or service, there should be no change to the Early Learning Payment.
If the family has moved and transferred or enrolled with a different Family Start or Early Start but the child is still at the same early childhood education programme or service, the new Family Start or Early Start will need to verify their details.
The client must still meet the qualifying criteria for the Early Learning Payment to continue getting the payment.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — extra help > early learning payment > changes and reviews early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client is obliged to advise MSD of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to the Early Learning Payment.
There are situations where Family Start or Early Start will also advise MSD of a change in a family's circumstances that could impact their entitlement to the Early Learning Payment.
You may also review the Early Learning Payment at any time to ensure the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.

chunks.title: Child leaves care or change of caregiver — extra help > early learning payment > changes and reviews early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Child leaves care or change of caregiver
The Early Learning Payment must be stopped from the day after the date the child leaves the client's care.
The Family Start or Early Start worker should encourage the client to advise MSD when the child has left their care.
