chunks.title: Closures due to COVID-19 requirements — extra help > early learning payment > changes and reviews early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Closures due to COVID-19 requirements
When a childcare centre is closed due to COVID-19 requirements, Early Learning Payment can continue being paid if the client still qualifies. A fee does not need to be charged to hold the child's place open for payment to continue.
A centre may close due to COVID-19 requirements because they:
- must close due to COVID-19 Alert Level 4
- are connected to a confirmed or probable case of COVID-19 and have been instructed to close
- are not able to operate safely and within public health guidelines
- temporarily do not have any children needing childcare because of COVID-19Note Early Learning Payment cannot continue being paid to a centre that is closed because it is not financially viable for them to stay open, or for any other reason that is not related to COVID-19 requirements.
This is not an exhaustive list. If a centre has closed and you are unsure if it is due to COVID-19 requirements, please check the COVID-19 Alert System website for the most up to date COVID-19 guidelines.
Note Early Learning Payment cannot continue being paid to a centre that is closed because it is not financially viable for them to stay open, or for any other reason that is not related to COVID-19 requirements.
## Number of weeks payment can continue
There is no limit on how long Early Learning Payment can be paid when a child is absent due to COVID-19 requirements.
However, the payment can only be paid for a period that relates to COVID-19 requirements.
If a centre is closed for longer than what is needed due to COVID-19 requirements, Early Learning Payment can only be paid for the period that relates to COVID-19 requirements.
## Example
Liam's daughter usually goes to a small, family run childcare centre. They had to close for 4 weeks when New Zealand was at COVID-19 Alert Level 4. They then stayed closed for an extra 2 weeks due to a family bereavement.
Liam's Early Learning Payment continued for the first 4 weeks the centre was closed because this was due to COVID-19 requirements. Early Learning Payment was stopped for the extra 2 weeks because the centre was closed for a reason not related to COVID-19 requirements.

chunks.title: Continuing payments when a family leaves Family Start or Early Start — extra help > early learning payment > changes and reviews early learning payment
chunks.text: From 1 October 2017, clients can continue to receive the Early Learning Payment if: - their family have left Family Start or Early Start and - the client received the Early Learning Payment at the time the family left Family Start or Early Start and - the child attends the same or any approved early childhood education programme or service Also, the dependent child(ren) who the Early Learning Payment was being paid for must still be dependent on the client and aged between 18 months and 3 years. Clients can access the Early Learning Payment for the dependant child(ren) who the Early Learning Payment was being paid for, at any time after leaving Family Start or Early Start until their child(ren) turns 3 years. For example, if a family was accessing the Early Learning Payment when they left Family Start or Early Start, then subsequently left the early childhood education programme or service and later enrolled in another early childhood education programme or service (before the child turned 3 years), they are eligible to re-apply for the Early Learning Payment. A re-application for the Early Learning Payment will only involve the client, Work and Income and the approved early childhood education programme or service. Client's don't need to reapply through Family Start or Early Start.

chunks.title: Client's not eligible for the continued Early Learning Payment — extra help > early learning payment > changes and reviews early learning payment
chunks.text: There are situations where a client will not qualify for the continuation of the Early Learning Payment. For example (but not limited to): - families that were enrolled in a Family Start or Early Start programme, but did not receive the Early Learning Payment before 1 October 2017 - clients who are granted the Early Learning Payment after 1 October 2017, family leaves Family Start or Early Start, dependent child(ren) is not yet 3 years of age and is not in an approved early childhood education programme or service - child is no longer a dependent child of the client or there has been a change in the caregiver for the child

chunks.title: Families that leave Family Start or Early Start before 1 October 2017 — extra help > early learning payment > changes and reviews early learning payment
chunks.text: Families who had left a Family Start or Early Start programme before 1 October 2017, regardless of whether they received the Early Learning Payment or not, cannot reapply for the Early Learning Payment as part of the continuation process above. However, clients in these cases can only apply or reapply for the Early Learning Payment, if their family is enrolled in a Family Start or Early Start programme, and meets all other qualifications for the Early Learning Payment.

chunks.title: COVID-19 absences and closures — extra help > early learning payment > changes and reviews early learning payment
chunks.text:
## COVID-19 absences and closures
When a child is absent from childcare or the childcare centre is closed due to COVID-19 requirements, Early Learning Payment can continue being paid if the client still qualifies.
A fee does not have to be charged to hold the child's place open for payment to continue.
## Client must continue to qualify
The client must continue to qualify for Early Learning Payment for it to be paid during an absence or closure due to COVID-19 requirements.
If the client has a change in circumstances that affects their eligibility, their Early Learning Payment must be reviewed. If they no longer qualify, Early Learning Payment must be stopped.
## Example
Kerry has been getting Early Learning Payment of 20 hours per week because she is enrolled in the Early Start Programme.
Her son has stayed home from childcare during Alert Level 3 and Early Learning Payment has continued. From next week Kerry's son will be going to live with his father and he will no longer be dependent on Kerry.
Her Early Learning Payment will stop from the beginning of next week because Kerry no longer qualifies.

chunks.title: Death of a client — extra help > early learning payment > changes and reviews early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Death of a client
When a client who is receiving an Early Learning Payment dies, the payment generally stops from the day after death.
There is discretion to continue paying until the next pay date following the date of death, if the child is still enrolled in Family Start or Early Start and/or attending the early childhood education programme or service. After this date the Early Learning Payment must be cancelled.
## Death of a child
When the dependent child who the Early Learning Payment is being paid for dies, the payment generally stops from the day after death.

chunks.title: Family leaves Family Start or Early Start — extra help > early learning payment > changes and reviews early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Family leaves Family Start or Early Start
Generally when a family leaves Family Start or Early Start, the Early Learning Payment will stop from the day after the family left the programme.
The Early Learning Payment can continue if the child that the Early Learning Payment was being paid for, still attends the same or an approved Early Childhood Education programme or service.

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Deciding ordinarily resident
Generally a client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand to receive a benefit.
Ordinarily resident means someone who is normally and lawfully in New Zealand and intends to stay here, that is, they consider New Zealand to be their home.
Whether a person is ordinarily resident is a question of fact and degree and their intentions during any period of absence is the most important factor.
Where it is not clear if a client is ordinarily resident, consider the following:
(a) the client's intentions toward New Zealand (that is, the reasons for their absence from New Zealand and the reasons for their return). Are they going overseas for a holiday or are they intending to live overseas permanently (sighting return air tickets is a good indication)?
(b) the length of time they spend in New Zealand on a continual basis
(c) property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans)
(d) where are their cash assets held?
(e) is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and do they pay New Zealand taxes?
(f) do they still vote (or are they eligible to vote) in the New Zealand election?
(g) their commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in the community, community events, clubs and other groups)?
Note a person cannot be ordinarily resident in two places at the same time.

chunks.title: Dependent child — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
For a client to get Early Learning Payment the child must be a dependent child.
A dependent child for Early Learning Payment is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- not a child not a child for whom Orphan's Benefit or an Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Early Learning Payment does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)

chunks.title: Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples
To help you identify when there is a 'dependent child', please see the examples below:
Household
Payments
Outcome
Parent and young person, aged between 16-18 years old.
Parent receiving Sole Parent Support (SPS), Young person getting no assistance.
Young person is a dependent child.
Parent and young person aged between 16-18 years old and young person's baby.
Parent getting Sole Parent Support, young person getting Young Parent Payment (YPP).
Young person is no longer dependent on their parent however the baby is a dependent child of the young person.
Parent and young person aged between 16-18 years old and young person's baby.
Parent getting Sole Parent Support, young person getting no assistance.
Both the young person and the young person's baby are dependent children of the parent.
Couple (parents) and young person aged between 16-18 years old and young person's baby.
Parents getting Jobseeker Support half married rate, young person getting no assistance.
Both the young person and the young person's baby are dependent children of the parents.
Couple (parents) and young person aged between 16-18 years old and young person's baby.
Parents getting Jobseeker Support half married rate, young person getting Young Parent Payment (YPP).
Young person is no longer dependent on their parents however the baby is a dependent child of the young person.

chunks.title: Early Learning Payment and Childcare Subsidy — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Early Learning Payment and Childcare Subsidy
Childcare Subsidy can also be paid for a child who is receiving Early Learning Payment, but only for the hours that we are not paying Early Learning Payment for.
## Clients eligible for up to 9 hours Childcare Subsidy
Clients who are receiving the maximum of 20 hours Early Learning Payment cannot also receive 9 hours Childcare Subsidy.
## Clients in work or training
If the parents are in work or training they may be eligible for Childcare Subsidy to pay for the hours not being covered by the Early Learning Payment.
For example, a child is attending a centre for 20 hours under the Early Learning Payment but the child actually attends for 30 hours. Because the parents are in work or training, they may be eligible for Childcare Subsidy to pay for the remaining 10 hours.
Note the maximum combined hours (Early Learning Payment and Childcare Subsidy) that can be considered for a client is 50 hours.

chunks.title: Fees — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Fees
The rate of payment is up to a maximum of $10.02 per hour (as at 1 April 2026) up to a maximum of 20 hours per week.
This should cover the full cost of attendance at most early childhood education programmes or services. Payment is made directly to the early childhood education programme or service. All payments are processed by Centralised Services Whangarei.
Some early childhood education centres or services charge a flat fee per session or per day, and other services or centres charge a fee based on the hours of attendance of a child.
The Early Learning Payment can only be paid for the maximum of 20 hours per week.
We cannot pay for more hours for the child when an early childhood education centre or service charges less than the maximum hourly rate.

chunks.title: Hours of attendance — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Hours of attendance
The Early Learning Payment can be paid up to a maximum of 20 hours per week. If a child attends for 30 hours per week, the most we can pay is for 20 hours a week.
If the hours a child attends their Early Childhood Education centre or service changes, the Early Learning Payment must be reviewed. The Early Childhood Education centre or service and/or client must advise us of the change in hours for their child.
Depending on a client’s circumstances, they may be able to receive Childcare Subsidy to pay for the hours that are not covered by the Early Learning Payment.
## Clients receiving the maximum hours of Early Learning Payment before 1 October 2017
Clients will not have their hours automatically increased to the new maximum of 20 hours if they were already being paid the Early Learning Payment for the maximum of 15 hours per week before 1 October 2017.
The child must be physically attending the Early Childhood Education centre or service up to 20 hours or more per week, in order to receive the maximum hours for Early Learning Payment.
If clients request to review their hours from 1 October 2017, this should be treated as a normal change of circumstances and the Early Learning Payment will need to be reviewed as per existing process.
The increased hours will only take effect from 1 October 2017 or the date the enrolment increased at the Early Childhood Education centre or service, whichever is the later.

chunks.title: Immigration status and supporting documents — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Immigration status and supporting documents
Generally, when people born overseas travel to New Zealand they are granted a visa by Immigration New Zealand. The visa shows the conditions under which they are allowed to be in New Zealand, for example temporarily (student, work, visitor) or as a resident.
The type of documents a client may provide to verify their immigration status depends on when they were issued.
From 29 November 2010 clients with an existing permit are 'deemed' to hold the corresponding type of visa under the Immigration Act 2009. This means that:
- permits continue to be valid until their expiry date. A person does not need to replace a permit in their passport with a new visa until the permit expires
- residents with an existing residence permit may never have this updated with a new type of visa
## Documents issued from 29 November 2010
Documents issued from 29 November 2010 include:
- New Zealand Citizenship certificate (issued by Internal Affairs)
- New Zealand citizen endorsement (in a foreign passport)
- Permanent resident visa
- Resident visa
- Visitor visa
- Work visa
- Student visa
- Limited visa
Only the permanent resident visa and resident visa show a person is a resident.
A visa is a sticker in the client's passport.
## Documents issued before 29 November 2010
Documents issued before 29 November 2010 that allow a person to stay in New Zealand include:
- New Zealand Citizenship certificate (issued by Internal Affairs)
- Residence permit (with or without returning resident's visa)
- Visitor permit
- Work permit
- Student permit
- Limited purposes permit
Only the residence permit (with or without returning resident's visa) was granted to residents.
Note that a visa issued before 29 November 2010 does not allow a person to stay in New Zealand.
A permit is a sticker in the client's passport.
## Unable to provide visa or permit
When a client is unable to provide an immigration visa or permit they may provide other Immigration New Zealand documents to verify their immigration status. Work and Income can also undertake an immigration status check directly with Immigration New Zealand.
Note Immigration New Zealand may be unable to verify immigration status for clients of British nationality who arrived in New Zealand before 2 April 1974 and do not have a passport.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The Early Learning Payment is a non-taxable payment to provide earlier access to early childhood education for families with specific needs.
The Early Learning Payment is delivered through a programme that pays the costs of early childhood education for children aged 18 months to 3 years, who are from families enrolled in Family Start or Early Start programmes.
Family Start and Early Start programmes have a number of components. The Early Learning Payment is the only part of Family Start and Early Start that is paid through MSD.
Families who are enrolled in Family Start or Early Start are assigned a family/whanau worker who will usually act as a liaison between the family and MSD.
Note the Early Learning Payment and/or the continuation of the Early Learning Payment when a child leaves Family Start or Early Start must be stopped from the day the child turns 3 years old.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Payment
The Early Learning Payment is for children aged 18 months to 3 years who are enrolled in a Family Start or Early Start programme.
The maximum amount payable is $10.02 per hour (as at 1 April 2026), up to a maximum of 20 hours per week until the child is 3 years old.
The number of hours of early childhood education that the Early Learning Payment can be paid for must be manually adjusted in SWIFTT. From 3 years old the child will no longer be eligible for the Early Learning Payment and the payment must be manually cancelled.
All Early Learning Payment is processed by Centralised Services, Whangarei.

chunks.title: Permanent residence — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Permanent residence
Generally migrants need to have permanent residence or New Zealand citizenship to receive an Early Learning Payment. Permanent residence is granted by Immigration New Zealand. Citizenship is granted by the Department of Internal Affairs.
In order to receive Early Learning Payment, a client must normally:
- have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 (which can either be a resident visa or a permanent resident visa) or
- have a residence permit under Immigration Act 1987 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) or
- be a British national who arrived in New Zealand before 2 April 1974 or
- be a New Zealand citizen
Note if you require further information about a client's application for permanent residence you must get consent from the client to contact Immigration New Zealand or the client should obtain the information themselves. Otherwise the application should be declined. You must not collect or disclose information regarding a client's application without the client's consent.

chunks.title: Proof of residence — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text: All documents should be originals. Photocopies and/or documents that have been changed in any way cannot be accepted. Where the client (or partner) cannot provide proof or proof is unclear, you should ask the client (or partner) to obtain confirmation of their residence status from Immigration New Zealand (for permanent residence) or Internal Affairs (for citizenship). Proof of citizenship and/or permanent residence in New Zealand can be a: - New Zealand birth certificate Generally a person born in New Zealand is a New Zealand citizen by birth. - New Zealand passport To hold a New Zealand passport you must be a citizen of New Zealand. - Certificate of Registration A child born outside New Zealand (to a parent who is a New Zealand citizen) may be a New Zealand citizen from birth. However, the child must apply for a Certificate of Registration to confirm their New Zealand citizenship. - Grant of Citizenship People who have permanent residence, may (normally after 5 years residence in New Zealand) apply for a Grant of Citizenship. They must meet the conditions of the Grant. - Certificate of Confirmation This is a certificate issued to confirm that the holder is a New Zealand citizen by birth, descent or Grant of Citizenship. British subjects, who immigrated to New Zealand prior to 1948 (and who resided in New Zealand for all of 1948) were made New Zealand citizens in 1949. These people are likely to have a Certificate of Confirmation or a Certificate of Naturalisation. - Certificate of Naturalisation Previously immigrants were naturalised as British Subjects and Citizens of New Zealand. Today they are given a Grant of Citizenship. - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence class visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009 - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987 Note that a visa issued before 29 November 2010 does not allow a person to stay in New Zealand - Letter of confirmation of permanent residence from Immigration New Zealand - Australian citizens Australian citizens are lawfully allowed in New Zealand without a residence class visa or residence permit and their date of entry is generally not recorded. Where possible supporting evidence should be sought, such as, tenancy agreements, bank statements or old utility bills to show that the client has been ordinarily resident for two continuous years. - British nationals

chunks.title: Proof of residence — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text: Clients of British nationality who came to New Zealand before 2 April 1974 were automatically allowed to enter New Zealand for residence, and will be unable to provide verification of their residence if they do not have a passport. Immigration New Zealand will have no record of these clients unless the client has contacted them after 2 April 1974. The client should be able to provide New Zealand school, work or tax records to support their claim about when they arrived in New Zealand and the length of time they have lived here.

chunks.title: Client qualifications — extra help > early learning payment
chunks.text:
## Client qualifications
To qualify for the Early Learning Payment a person must:
- be the caregiver of a dependent child
- be enrolled in Family Start or Early Start
For a list of providers see:
- Deskfile Early Learning Payment providers
## Child qualifications
The child on whose behalf the Early Learning Payment will be paid must:
- be aged between 18 months and 3 years
- attend an approved early learning education programme or service
## Residency
The client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (ie not be in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
Note refugees or protected persons who do not have permanent residence cannot get Early Learning Payment. Once the client has been granted permanent residence and they meet all the other qualifications, Early Learning Payment can be granted.
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they are deemed to hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other criteria to be eligible for Early Learning Payment.

chunks.title: 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A non-entitlement period of 13 weeks for emergency housing will be issued when a client is unable to receive an Emergency Housing Grant because they have: - received 2 formal warnings for the same emergency housing event and - not met their emergency housing responsibilities for the third time and - did not have good and sufficient reason for not meeting the emergency housing responsibilities agreed to at each grant The 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing begins from the day after the end of the client’s current (or most recent) Emergency Housing Grant. The 13 week non-entitlement period resets the client’s previous warnings to zero. If the client applies for an Emergency Housing Grant after their non entitlement period has ended, and it is the same emergency housing event, the client will be required to meet the responsibilities from their first night back in emergency housing. Note during the 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing, the client will only be able to get an Emergency Housing Grant under limited circumstances.

chunks.title: Partners and 13 week non-entitlement period — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If a client gets a 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing, this does not affect their partner qualifying for an Emergency Housing Grant. However if a client is on a 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing: - their income and cash assets must still be included when assessing if their partner (as the applicant) qualifies for an Emergency Housing Grant, and when calculating the emergency housing contribution and - they cannot be included in their partner’s accommodation paid for by an Emergency Housing Grant

chunks.title: Example - Partner 1 applies for Emergency Housing Grant while Partner 2 is on a 13 week non-entitlement period — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Terry (partner 1) and Hardin (partner 2) enter emergency housing together as a couple. Hardin applies for the grant and Terry is included as a partner staying in emergency housing on Hardin’s application. During their stay in emergency housing, Hardin received 2 warnings for not meeting his emergency housing responsibilities and failed to meet them again. Hardin again did not have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting his responsibilities and is now on a 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing. MSD advises Terry that Hardin cannot be included in Terry’s emergency housing accommodation as he is on a 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing. Terry will be able to access emergency housing as long as Hardin is not included in, or using the accommodation during his non-entitlement period for emergency housing. Note Hardin’s income and cash assets must still be included when assessing if Terry’s qualifies for an Emergency Housing Grant and calculating the emergency housing contribution.

chunks.title: New emergency housing events while on a non-entitlement period — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The client will not qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant until their 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing is completed even if a new emergency housing event arises.

chunks.title: Exception to non-entitlement period for emergency housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client may qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant during their non-entitlement period for emergency housing under limited circumstances. The client must still meet all the emergency housing qualifications as well as the limited circumstances criteria to get an Emergency Housing Grant during their non-entitlement period.

chunks.title: Access to other adequate accommodation — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When determining if the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) have access to other accommodation adequate for their needs, MSD will consider whether the place available is adequate for the short-term. This includes accommodation they can access from their own resources or other sources of assistance. Other accommodation that may be adequate in the short-term includes: - staying with friends or family who have spare bedrooms, or a couch (when this is adequate for the needs of the client, their partner, and dependent children) - paying for temporary accommodation (e.g., campground or hostel when this will not cause the client serious hardship) - other emergency housing (e.g. Women's Refuge) - transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - contracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development Accommodation that may be adequate for the client long-term includes: - social housing or - renting, flatting, or boarding Note there are factors that need to be considered when deciding if accommodation is adequate.

chunks.title: Deciding if the client has access — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The circumstances of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) must be considered when deciding if the client has access to other adequate accommodation. Factors to consider include (but are not limited to): - Can the client reasonably access the other option before they will have nowhere to stay? For example, does the client have a way to get to the accommodation?For example, are there essential arrangements the client needs to make before they can access the accommodation? - For example, does the client have a way to get to the accommodation? - For example, are there essential arrangements the client needs to make before they can access the accommodation? - Are there exceptional circumstances that make it unreasonable to expect the client to immediately access the other accommodation option? For example, it may be unreasonable to require a client who left their accommodation because they were experiencing family violence to access other accommodation options as this could cause increased stress, and negatively impact the wellbeing of the client, their partner, and dependent children (if any) - For example, it may be unreasonable to require a client who left their accommodation because they were experiencing family violence to access other accommodation options as this could cause increased stress, and negatively impact the wellbeing of the client, their partner, and dependent children (if any) Note when a client is not able to access other accommodation available immediately, or during some or all of the next 7 days, an Emergency Housing Grant must only be granted for the period they are unable to access other accommodation.

chunks.title: Actual and reasonable costs covered for emergency housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client can get an Emergency Housing Grant for the actual and reasonable costs for adequate emergency housing that meets their needs. This covers the nightly rate of the emergency accommodation. An Emergency Housing Grant is considered last resort funding. Generally MSD should pay for the lower cost option that is adequate for the needs of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any). Note if the client can meet the cost of emergency housing from their own resources, they are considered to have access to adequate accommodation. This means they do not have an immediate emergency housing need. In this situation, the Emergency Housing Grant will be declined.

chunks.title: Deciding actual and reasonable cost — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: An Emergency Housing Grant is considered last resort funding and can only be granted for an adequate emergency housing option that is a reasonable cost. Reasonable cost is either: - the lower cost option adequate to meet the needs of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) or - where MSD needs to use emergency housing to support managing availability, safety, and suitability in the region If there is more than 1 emergency housing option that is adequate and a reasonable cost, MSD may encourage a client to use a particular supplier but cannot require the client to use it.

chunks.title: Availability and suitability — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: MSD may need to use emergency housing options to support managing availability and suitability of emergency housing in the area. Availability means: - using suppliers with facilities more suited to a particular housing need when there is low availability Suitability means: - using particular suppliers to provide emergency housing more suitable for different households e.g. a particular supplier may be used for families MSD staff will be advised when emergency housing availability and suitability needs to be managed.

chunks.title: Hostel accommodation would generally be considered first — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A single client or a couple without children will generally be assisted to stay in a hostel or night shelter in the first instance. However, there may be good reasons why a hostel is not adequate for their needs in the short term. Good reasons may include: - health and disability reasons for not being able to be in shared accommodation or shared flatting - unreasonable distance from the hostel to work, or other essential services (e.g. medical services) - there is no hostel available Hostels will generally not be appropriate for households with children.

chunks.title: Night shelter may not be appropriate in some circumstances — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A night shelter may not be appropriate for a client if it does not provide a stable environment they can use to find alternative longer-term housing. For example, the night shelter might not allow access to the building during the day. Therefore the client cannot use the night shelter to search for other adequate accommodation.

chunks.title: Deciding if the accommodation is being provided by an appropriate supplier — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: An accommodation provider would generally be considered appropriate to provide accommodation if they: - are a commercial provider or a not-for-profit accommodation provider (including a marae) and - are approved by the relevant authority to provide accommodation services (e.g. meets the fire safety requirements, building code requirements, local authority bylaws etc) and - meet the requirements to become an MSD supplier

chunks.title: Adequacy of other accommodation and emergency housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: What is adequate in the short-term to meet an emergency housing need will depend on the circumstances of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any), and needs to be considered on a case-by-case basis. Short-term means a temporary arrangement that meets an immediate emergency housing need. The factors listed below can be considered when determining if the: - other accommodation options available to the client (their partner and dependent children, if any) are adequate - emergency housing accommodation is adequate

chunks.title: Factors to consider — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The following factors should be considered when deciding if the client, their family and dependent children (if any) have access to adequate accommodation: - any disability needs (e.g., wheelchair access, accessible toilets, or showers) - the distance to essential services for treatment (e.g., travel to a hospital treatment for dialysis) - whether the place to stay is safe (e.g. there are no drugs, violence, or other unsafe behaviour) - the living conditions foster a safe environment (e.g., safe for children, access to amenities such as a toilet, cleaning facilities and food preparation areas) - the location of the place to stay is suitable as it is not close to a perpetrator of violence - it does not prevent the client (or the people included in the clients application) from meeting their court, bail, or release conditions if they stay at the alternative accommodation option. For example:the location of the place available is in an area they are permitted to stay (e.g. a reasonable distance from a victim or school) - the location of the place available is in an area they are permitted to stay (e.g. a reasonable distance from a victim or school) - whether the accommodation is a reasonable distance from education providers the client or their family are enrolled in - whether the accommodation is a reasonable distance from where the client or their family work - is intended for human habitation and is located in accordance with relevant local government bylaws (e.g. the following are not adequate: barns, shacks or shelters which lack walls or some or all of the usual household amenities such as electric lighting, piped water, bathroom, toilet, and kitchen/cooking facilities, a caravan or other removable structure on a residential site which is located against relevant local government bylaws) - a commercial provider who meets the relevant building and safety requirements (e.g., meets fire-safety regulations, building code requirements or local authority rules) Note MSD do not need to actively check the accommodation complies with applicable regulations. However if MSD are told it does not comply (by the client or other third party) this may be taken into account when determining whether the client has access to adequate accommodation for the short-term

chunks.title: Factors to consider — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: - Note MSD do not need to actively check the accommodation complies with applicable regulations. However if MSD are told it does not comply (by the client or other third party) this may be taken into account when determining whether the client has access to adequate accommodation for the short-term

chunks.title: Paying for adequate emergency housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: MSD should only pay an Emergency Housing Grant for emergency housing that is adequate. However, there may be rare situations where there is no adequate emergency housing available. In these situations, MSD can pay for emergency housing that is not adequate when: - no adequate emergency housing options are available, and - not paying would impact the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) as they would not have access to any accommodation This should only be a short-term arrangement until adequate emergency housing becomes available.

chunks.title: Appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support
The appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support is the minimum amount MSD can use to calculate a client's emergency housing contribution.
This means if the client's actual net weekly income is lower than this (including cases where the client has no income), MSD will use the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support to calculate their emergency housing contribution.
The appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support is the rate that would apply to the client and their partner (if any):
- based on their circumstances at the time they apply for an Emergency Housing Grant and
- whether or not they would actually qualify for that rate
## Example
A client is single, 23 years old and only getting Student Loan living costs of $333.48 (as at 1 April 2026) a week as their main form of financial support. Student Loan living costs are not included as income for emergency housing, so their net weekly emergency housing income is assessed at zero.
They are unable to get Jobseeker Support as they are a full-time student.
The appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support to use for calculating the client's contribution will be the 'single 20 to 24 years' net rate of $324.50 a week (as at 1 April 2026).

chunks.title: Calculating the emergency housing contribution for overlapping grants — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: There may be situations when a client needs to leave their emergency housing accommodation before the end of their grant period. This may be outside of the client's control, or it may have been caused by the client. If the client still needs emergency housing accommodation after they move out, there may be an overlapping period of nights covered by 2 separate grants. In this situation, the client does not pay another contribution for the overlapping nights. Only 1 contribution is to be paid per night. This applies regardless of the reason for the overlapping grants.

chunks.title: Example 1 - Client moves accommodation due to flooding — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client is granted an Emergency Housing Grant of $2,000 for 14 nights (from 1 to 14 April) at Blue Motel. They will pay a contribution of $70 a week, or $140 total. However, on 8 April, the client needs to move out unexpectedly, due to flooding after a plumbing fault (outside of their control). The client is approved a further Emergency Housing Grant of $1,100 for 7 nights at Orange Motel from 8 April to 14 April. The client now has two grants covering an overlapping period from 8 April to 14 April. In this situation, the client already has a contribution applied for the period 8 to 14 April from their grant for the Blue Motel. The client does not have to pay another contribution for the same nights covered by their grant for Orange Motel.

chunks.title: Example 2 - Client moves accommodation due to safety reasons — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client is granted an Emergency Housing Grant for 13 nights from 15 to 28 June. On 26 June the client needs to move motels for safety reasons. MSD grants a further emergency housing grant for 7 nights, with a check out date of 3 July. The client already has a contribution in place for 26 and 27 June for their previous Emergency Housing Grant. For the new grant, MSD only needs to add a contribution for 5 nights from 28 June until 3 July.

chunks.title: Example 3 - Client moves accommodation due to intentional damage - overlapping grant is recoverable — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client is granted an Emergency Housing Grant for 7 nights from 15 to 22 June. However, on 18 June the motelier asks them to leave after causing intentional damage to their motel room. The client has a substance addiction, which appears to have contributed to the situation in which the damage occurred. The client applies for a further Emergency Housing Grant on the day they move out. MSD may consider whether the client has caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need, and whether their application should be declined. If MSD decides to grant a further Emergency Housing Grant, the client only needs to pay a contribution for nights covered by the new grant from 22 June.

chunks.title: Calculating the emergency housing contribution using the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Calculating the emergency housing contribution using the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support
When a client has to pay an emergency housing contribution, MSD needs to work out how much this is. To work it out, MSD needs to calculate the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support.
The emergency housing contribution is worked out using the higher of the:
- net weekly income calculation or
- the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support calculation
The contribution must be worked out using both methods and the higher amount is selected.
To work out the client's emergency housing contribution using the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support, MSD needs to calculate:
- 25% of the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support, based on the circumstances of the client and their partner (if any) and
- 25% of the client's and their partner's family tax credit entitlement (if applicable)
## Working out the contribution using the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support
Step 1
Add 25% of the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support and 25% of the family tax credit entitlement together
= $ 25% of nominal weekly income
Step 2
Divide 25% of nominal weekly income by 7
= $ net daily income
Step 3
Round net daily income to the nearest cent
= $ rounded daily income
Step 4
Multiply the rounded daily income by the number of nights of accommodation to which a contribution applies
= $ the client's emergency housing contribution using the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support for the grant

chunks.title: Calculating the emergency housing contribution using net weekly income — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Calculating the emergency housing contribution using net weekly income
When a client has to pay an emergency housing contribution, MSD needs to work out how much this is. To work it out, MSD needs to calculate the client's net weekly income.
The emergency housing contribution is worked out using the higher of the:
- net weekly income calculation or
- the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support calculation
The contribution must be worked out using both methods and the higher amount is selected.
To work out the client's emergency housing contribution using the net weekly income calculation MSD needs to determine:
- 25% of the net weekly 'emergency housing income' of the client and their partner and
- 25% of the client's and their partner's family tax credit entitlement (if they have children)
These 2 amounts added together are referred to as the client's combined weekly income.
## How to calculate net weekly income
The net weekly income calculation is the amount estimated by MSD for:
- a 7-night period, starting on the first night of the Emergency Housing Grant and
- divided by 7 and rounded to the nearest cent and
- multiplied by the number of nights of accommodation to which the contribution applies
## Steps to work out the contribution using net weekly income
Step 1
Add 25% of the net weekly emergency housing income and 25% of the weekly family tax credit entitlement together.
= $ 25% of combined weekly income
Step2
Divide 25% of combined weekly income by 7.
= $ net daily income
Step 3
Round net daily income to the nearest cent.
= $ rounded daily income
Step 4
Multiply the rounded daily income by the number of nights' accommodation the contribution applies for.
= $ the client's emergency housing contribution using the net weekly income for the grant.

chunks.title: Calculating 25% of family tax credit entitlement for emergency housing contribution — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Calculating 25% of family tax credit entitlement for emergency housing contribution
If the client or their partner qualify to get family tax credits a portion will go towards their emergency housing contribution.
The amount of their family tax credit entitlement included in the contribution calculation is:
- 25% of the total family tax credit they qualify for or
- 25% of the maximum rate of family tax credit payable for an eldest dependent child
whichever is lower.
The client or their partner may qualify for a family tax credit but have not applied for it. In this case, the family tax credit they would have been paid or is payable is still used in the contribution calculation.
For more information see:
- Examples of calculating 25% of family tax credit entitlement
When calculating the contribution, use the weekly amount of family tax credit entitlement, even if it is paid annually.
Note the Best Start tax credit, in-work tax credit, parental tax credit, child tax credit and minimum family tax credit are not included in the contribution calculation.
## Shared care
There may be a shared care arrangement where both caregivers are entitled to a portion of the family tax credit.
In this case, use only the portion of the family tax credit paid or payable to the client or their partner (if any) in the contribution calculation.

chunks.title: Calculating the emergency housing contribution — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Calculating the emergency housing contribution
Clients who qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant must pay an emergency housing contribution. This is an amount they pay, based on their income, towards their emergency housing costs.
The emergency housing contribution will be calculated using the higher of:
- 25% of the net weekly income of the client and their partner (if any) or
- 25% of the net rate of Jobseeker Support that would be appropriate, if the client or their partner (if any) were getting this assistance. This is referred to as the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support.
The contribution must be worked out using both methods, and the higher amount must be selected. Clients with no income will pay an emergency housing contribution based on the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support.
The emergency housing contribution also includes 25% of the clients (and their partner's, if any) weekly family tax credit entitlement.
The contribution cannot be more than the actual cost of emergency housing.
## No discretion for client to contribute less than 25% of income under either calculation
MSD has no discretion to change, suspend, or reduce the amount of emergency housing contribution calculated for the client. This is because everyone must contribute to their emergency housing costs.
If a client says they cannot afford to pay their contribution, MSD can:
- make sure the client and their partner (if any) are getting all the assistance they qualify for and
- refer them to a budget advisor or other social service where appropriate
- review any existing deductions being taken from their benefit to see if some may be reduced (if they are lower priority than the emergency housing contribution)
- discuss and set agreed activities to help the client pay the emergency housing contribution
If a client believes MSD has incorrectly calculated their emergency housing contribution, they can ask for a review of decision.
## When emergency housing contribution may become a debt
If a client does not pay their contribution in full by the date or dates determined by MSD, MSD will need to find out why.
There may be an issue with the client's benefit redirection that can be sorted out in the system. Alternatively, MSD may need to contact the client to discuss the reasons for non-payment and set up a new payment date.
If any part of the contribution remains unpaid, it will generally become an emergency housing debt. The emergency housing debt amount will be recovered from the client using existing debt recovery processes.

chunks.title: Cash asset limits — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Cash asset limits
To qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant, the cash assets of the client and the partner (if any) must not exceed the appropriate asset limit.
## Exceptional circumstances
If a client’s cash assets exceed the appropriate asset limit, check if there are exceptional circumstances. If there are, MSD can use discretion to grant an Emergency Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Changes in income - effect on emergency housing contribution rate — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Changes in income - effect on emergency housing contribution rate
The income of the client (and their partner, if any) is assessed at every application for an Emergency Housing Grant. If their income changes, it could affect the emergency housing contribution.
There may be times during the grant period when a client or their partner's income changes after MSD has calculated their contribution.
In these cases, MSD can only reassess the contribution based on the new income amount if it would make result in a material difference to their contribution.
A material difference is when, based on the new income amount, the new calculated contribution rate is:
- a net increase of $5 or more per week to their contribution rate or
- a net decrease of more than $1 per week to their contribution rate
Any difference to a client’s contribution would result from their net weekly income increasing by $20 or more or decreasing by $4 or more.
When considering whether to reassess the contribution, all relevant circumstances need to be considered.
## Decrease in client's contribution
If the change in income means there is a decrease to the client's contribution, MSD will generally reassess the contribution rate from the date of the change in income.
## Increase in client's contribution
If the change in income means there is an increase to the client's contribution, MSD generally does not reassess the client's contribution.
However, there may be some situations when we would reassess the client's contribution for an increase in income. For example, MSD may reassess the contribution for an increase when the client has a history of declaring their income late or incorrectly.
In all cases, the contribution amount cannot be more than the actual cost of the emergency housing.
Note if the client or their partner's income has increased, MSD also needs to ensure the client still qualifies for an Emergency Housing Grant.
## Annual General Adjustment occurs during a grant period
If there is a change in income due to the annual general adjustment, MSD does not generally reassess the contribution rate from the date of the change in income (1 April).
A client’s contribution will be reviewed by MSD when requested by the client if the annual general adjustment would result in a material difference to their emergency housing contribution.

chunks.title: Client can meet their immediate need in another way — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Client can meet their immediate need in another way
If a client can meet their immediate emergency housing need from their own resources or other sources of assistance, MSD cannot pay an Emergency Housing Grant as they do not have an immediate emergency housing need.
A client may be able to meet their immediate emergency housing need from their own resources or other sources when the client (and their partner, if any):
- has sufficient income to meet the need after paying essential expenses from their next income, benefit, or pension payment without causing serious hardship
- has cash assets that can be used to meet the need (that are not needed for essential expenses)
- can make a payment arrangement (e.g. for overdue rent with their landlord)
- qualifies for other assistance that can be used to meet the need, including (but not limited to): Temporary Additional SupportAccommodation Costs Arrears Grantother Housing Support ProductsRecoverable Assistance PaymentAdvance Payment of Benefit
- Temporary Additional Support
- Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant
- other Housing Support Products
- Recoverable Assistance Payment
- Advance Payment of Benefit
- can access assistance from other government agencies to meet the need (e.g. transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development)

chunks.title: Client has caused or contributed to their immediate need before applying for their first Emergency Housing Grant — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When a client applies for an Emergency Housing Grant, MSD may consider whether a client has caused or contributed to their immediate housing need. MSD can decline to pay an Emergency Housing Grant if the client caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need (or the situation that has led to the immediate need). A client has caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need if: - their situation is a result of their own actions (or actions of people they are responsible for) and - they were reasonably able to predict and prevent the situation For example, the client may be considered to have caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need if they: - cannot remain in their place of residence due to damaging the property or other anti-social behaviour (e.g. threats, intimidation, drug or alcohol abuse) - cannot remain in their place of residence because they have not paid their rent or board for reasons other than affordability - left their place of residence and moved to another area without a good reason and before securing accommodation for themselves, their partner and dependent children (if any) - cannot remain in the emergency housing provided due to instances of damage, theft, or other anti-social behaviour MSD will also take care when considering whether a client was reasonably able to predict and prevent a situation, as this depends on the client’s individual situation and capacity. Note people who left their housing due to experiencing family violence will not be considered to have caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need.

chunks.title: Not paying rent or board at previous accommodation — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: MSD may consider the following when assessing a client’s non-payment at previous accommodation: - if the client attempted to make payments (e.g. has the client made any part payments towards their rent or board arrears, or no payments) - the amount of rent or board arrears - any previous conversations MSD has had with the client about the need to pay their rent or board and any financial assistance granted to the client to assist (e.g. Housing Support Products) - any previous history of not paying rent or board MSD is aware of Examples of reasons for not paying rent or board include: - intentional non-payment or - insufficient income to pay their rent or board or - an unforeseen event that led to the client not being able to pay

chunks.title: Example - client has intentionally not paid their board — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Joy is getting Jobseeker Support and has recently received budgeting advice. As part of her budget, Joy has agreed with MSD the portion of her income that can be used to cover her board. Over the last three months Joy continued to use the portion of her income she’d allocated to her board costs for other, non-essential activities. As a result, she is now in arrears with her head tenant. Joy made no attempt to pay the board arrears and did not contact MSD to check if she would qualify for assistance that could help her pay the arrears. 3 weeks ago, the head tenant asked her to leave, and she has been sleeping on her friend’s couch since then. Staying with her friend is no longer an option, and Joy applies for an emergency housing grant. MSD decides Joy has caused (or contributed) to her immediate emergency housing need, as she knowingly used the income she allocated for board on other, non-essential activities. MSD can decline Joy’s application for an Emergency Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Client has caused or contributed to their immediate need while in emergency housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When a client applies for an Emergency Housing Grant, MSD may consider whether the client has caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need. This includes whether the client has caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need while staying in emergency housing. MSD can decline to pay an Emergency Housing Grant if the client has caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need (or the situation that has led to the immediate need). If they have, MSD may not be able to pay an Emergency Housing Grant. A client has contributed to their immediate emergency housing need if: - their situation is a result of their own actions (or actions of people they are responsible for) and - they were reasonably able to predict and prevent the situation

chunks.title: Client cannot remain in the emergency housing accommodation due to their actions (or people they are responsible for) — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client who applies for a subsequent Emergency Housing Grant may tell MSD they cannot stay at their existing emergency housing supplier because of their actions or the actions of people they are responsible for. MSD may consider the client has caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need if they had to leave their emergency housing because they: - broke the supplier's rules of stay or - intentionally damaged the property or - caused theft or loss or - showed anti-social behaviour (for example, threats or intimidation) Before making any decisions about further assistance, MSD needs to: - verify the client's reason for leaving the existing emergency accommodation and - confirm the client's view of the issues It is important accommodation providers report damage, losses, theft, or anti-social behaviour to police when it is warranted. If the security deposit was approved at the time of the client's stay, accommodation providers can use it to recoup damages for lower-level losses (for example, cutlery and plates and other cooking utensils) or damage.

chunks.title: Example - client cannot remain in their emergency housing accommodation because they have broken the suppliers rules of stay — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A single client (no children) getting Jobseeker Support has been staying in emergency housing for over a month. At each grant stage, the client has been advised of the expectations and conditions of payment for emergency housing (including the suppliers rules of stay). The client confirms they understood and agreed to meet the expectations and conditions of payment while getting an Emergency Housing Grant. The client applies again for another grant as they continue to meet the qualifications for emergency housing. At the follow-up appointment the client advises they need to change their emergency housing supplier. The client advises their brother intentionally damaged the motel room during a visit, and the supplier has asked the client to leave the emergency housing accommodation. The client will not provide further information about how or why the damage occurred. MSD decides the client has contributed to their immediate emergency housing need because they were unable to stay in the accommodation because of damage to the emergency housing property. The Emergency Housing Grant can be declined because the client has contributed to their emergency housing need.

chunks.title: Client needs to pay security deposit debt — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Client needs to pay security deposit debt
When a security deposit becomes recoverable from the client (i.e. some or all of it is paid to the supplier or provider), the MSD existing debt recovery process applies.
The security deposit amount paid to the supplier or provider is recoverable from the client from the date MSD pays it to the supplier or provider.
## Client is paying security deposit debt and emergency housing contribution
If the client is still getting an Emergency Housing Grant and a contribution applies to that grant, or is paying a contribution towards their current stay in transitional or contracted emergency housing, the Security Deposit Grant will be recovered from the client at a reasonable rate based on what the client can afford.
If the client is paying both a contribution and making debt repayments for emergency housing, MSD needs to consider whether the client can still afford to pay an amount towards the recoverable Security Deposit Grant at the same time.
If the client cannot afford to pay all these amounts at the same time, MSD may temporarily defer recovery of the Security Deposit Grant, until the client can afford to start repaying it. MSD cannot temporarily defer recovery of any debt relating to an unpaid emergency housing contribution.

chunks.title: Client does not pay emergency housing contribution on time — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: There may be situations when the client has not paid their emergency housing contribution by the date or dates determined by MSD. In these cases, when deciding if the client has failed to meet their responsibility or not, MSD needs to consider if the client has a good and sufficient reason for not paying their emergency housing contribution.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for not paying contribution — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: MSD will need to find out why a client has not paid their contribution in full by the agreed date or dates before giving the client a warning. Factors could include (but are not limited to): - the amount that is unpaid and if this amount relates to only one emergency housing contribution or more than one (e.g., is there a pattern of non-payment) - whether the client has attempted to make payments (e.g., has the client made any part payments towards the emergency housing contribution, or no payments) - any previous conversations MSD has had with the client about needing to pay the emergency housing contribution - any information MSD has given to the client about needing to pay the emergency housing contribution Examples of the reasons for non-payment include: - intentional non-payment or - their benefit redirection failed due to insufficient income or - an unforeseen event that led the client being unable to pay or - MSD error when setting up the redirection Note there may be other good and sufficient reasons a client was not able to pay their emergency housing contribution in time and this should be assessed on a case by case basis. For more information see: - Good and sufficient reason for not meeting responsibilities

chunks.title: Requiring supporting evidence — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: MSD may require a client to provide supporting evidence to determine they have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting the emergency housing responsibilities. If supporting evidence is required and the client refuses to provide it, MSD may determine whether or not the client has a good and sufficient reason on the information available. If MSD determines there is no good and sufficient reason, the client will receive a warning.

chunks.title: Client failed to meet their responsibility — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The client must meet the emergency housing responsibilities during their stay in emergency housing. This includes completing any agreed activities set for an Emergency Housing Grant, by the date determined by MSD. If the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for not paying the emergency housing contribution by the date determined by MSD, this will result in a warning.

chunks.title: Debt recovery for unpaid contribution — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If any part of the contribution remains unpaid after the due date, it will generally become an emergency housing debt (MSD debt). The emergency housing debt amount will be recovered from the client using existing debt recovery processes.

chunks.title: Types of costs covered by a security deposit — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The types of costs that may be covered by a Security Deposit Grant for emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing include, but are not limited to, the actual and reasonable costs of: - damage to the property, intentional or accidental, caused by the client and anyone staying with the client, including guests and - loss relating to the client's failure to meet the supplier’s or provider’s rules of stay and - unpaid client contributions (for transitional or contracted emergency housing only)

chunks.title: Damage — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Damage covers any breakages or damages caused by the client, or anyone staying with the client, to the property, whether intentional or accidental, such as damage to walls, doors, curtains, or furnishings. This may include damage to the room/unit the client is staying in, or other spaces and facilities such as a laundry room, hallways, etc. Note damage does not include general wear and tear costs as this is included in the nightly rate for the room. Any damage that the provider includes in a claim must be identified during the client's stay, or at the time the client completes their stay.

chunks.title: Loss — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Loss covers the costs of losses relating to the failure of the client, or anyone staying with the client, to meet their obligations to the provider under the agreement for stay with the provider. These costs for losses can include: - cost of replacement items (e.g. furnishings or fittings) that the client, or anyone staying with the client, have removed from the room - any excessive cleaning charges due to the room being left in an unacceptable state (this must be over and above the normal level of cleaning required) - cost of replacement room key(s) Sometimes a client may leave some of their belongings behind at their emergency accommodation (funded by an Emergency Housing Grant) after moving out. This can result in a loss to the provider as they cannot sell the room or unit until the belongings are removed. This loss is generally also covered by the security deposit. Methamphetamine testing A security deposit cannot be used to cover the cost of methamphetamine testing. However, if a positive test is returned and it can be directly linked to the client’s stay, the cost of cleaning and/or repairs required from that positive test may be covered.

chunks.title: Unpaid client contribution costs — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A transitional or contracted emergency housing provider can make a claim under a Security Deposit Grant for any unpaid amount of a transitional housing contribution or contracted emergency housing contribution. No claim can be made under a Security Deposit Grant for any unpaid emergency housing contribution, as this contribution is not paid to a supplier. MSD may recover an unpaid emergency housing contribution under its existing debt recovery process.

chunks.title: Types of costs not covered by a security deposit — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The security deposit cannot be used to cover costs that do not relate to the provision of the emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing to the client, such as (but not limited to): - telephone, internet, or pay-television charges - mini bar - laundry charges - meal charges - storage of excessive goods - carparking - utilities such as power or water charges - methamphetamine testing - general wear and tear The security deposit also cannot be used to cover unpaid accommodation costs for emergency accommodation. For any costs not covered by the security deposit, the supplier or provider needs to ask for reimbursement of the costs directly from the client (this may involve taking the client to the Disputes Tribunal) or seek compensation from their insurance company.

chunks.title: Counting the first 7 nights of a new emergency housing event — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Once MSD has established the client has a new emergency housing event, the client does not have to meet the emergency housing responsibilities for the first 7 nights. Generally, when a client has a new emergency housing event, their first Emergency Housing Grant is granted for 7 nights. However, sometimes these first grants can be for: - fewer than 7 nights (e.g. if granted after hours by the Contact Centre) or - longer than 7 nights (e.g. where there is low availability of emergency housing in the region) Note MSD cannot set agreed activities for those 7 nights because emergency housing responsibilities do not apply. However, MSD can still discuss opportunities, information, or services might help the client find other housing options during the first 7 nights.

chunks.title: Example 1 - First grant is longer than 7 nights due to low availability of emergency housing in the region — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client's first Emergency Housing Grant, for an emergency housing event, is paid for 10 nights due to low availability of emergency housing in the region. The client will not be required to meet the emergency housing responsibilities, including paying the emergency housing contribution for the first 7 nights. However, the responsibilities that will apply from night 8 are discussed and agreed to. They will need to pay the emergency housing contribution for the last 3 nights. At night 8, activities are set. The client must meet all the emergency housing responsibilities for the rest of the grant period. MSD must make sure the agreed activities set are reasonable for the client to complete in the period until their next emergency housing grant date. The Emergency Housing Grant is paid for 10 nights due to low availability: Nights in accommodation funded by an Emergency Housing Grant for the same event 1 to 7 nights 8 to 10 nights Contribution Responsibility does not apply Responsibilities must be met and MSD sets agreed activities for this period Make a reasonable effort in their circumstances to obtain other housing Responsibility does not apply Responsibilities must be met and MSD sets agreed activities for this period Engage with support services Responsibility does not apply Responsibilities must be met and MSD sets agreed activities for this period

chunks.title: Example 2 - Initial grant is shorter than 7 nights as granted after hours — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A clients first Emergency Housing Grant for an emergency housing event is paid for 3 nights. This is because they applied at the end of the week and cannot have their needs fully assessed by a case manager until Monday. On Monday they are granted a further 4 nights. They will not be required to meet the emergency housing responsibilities for either of these grants. However, if the client gets a further emergency housing grant for the same event after the first 7 nights, they must meet the responsibilities and activities agreed to. MSD must make sure the responsibilities set are reasonable for the client to complete in the period until their next emergency housing grant date. Initial Emergency Housing Grant is a shorter grant: Nights in accommodation funded by emergency housing grant for the same event 1 to 3 nights (initial grant paid for 3 nights) 4 to 7 nights (grant 2 is paid for 4 nights) 8 to 14 nights (grant 3 is paid for 7 nights) Contribution Responsibility does not apply Responsibility does not apply Responsibilities must be met and MSD sets agreed activities for this period Make a reasonable effort in their circumstances to obtain other housing Responsibility does not apply Responsibility does not apply Responsibilities must be met and MSD sets agreed activities for this period Engage with support services Responsibility does not apply Responsibility does not apply Responsibilities must be met and MSD sets agreed activities for this period Note the expectations and conditions of payment apply from night 1 in emergency housing.

chunks.title: Determining if a longer grant is appropriate in the client's circumstances — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Determining if a longer grant is appropriate in the client's circumstances
Even if the qualifications for a longer grant are met, MSD still needs to determine whether a longer grant is appropriate in the client's circumstances.
Examples of when MSD may determine a longer grant is appropriate in the client's circumstances include where:
- it is unreasonable for the client to reapply every 7 nights. For example: the client or client's dependant has significant health or mobility issuesthe client has a newborn and it's before their first immunisationfamily violence issues
- the client or client's dependant has significant health or mobility issues
- the client has a newborn and it's before their first immunisation
- family violence issues
- the client has signed a tenancy agreement for a new property, but their occupancy does not start until a future date and they do not have accommodation in the meantime
- the client has accepted a place with a social housing provider (Kāinga Ora or registered community housing provider) but their occupancy does not start until a future date and they do not have accommodation in the meantime

chunks.title: Determining maximum per night rates — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Determining maximum per night rates
Only actual and reasonable costs for emergency housing accommodation can be paid.
As a guideline, in most areas, the following maximum limits should be applied.
## Maximum payment rates
Accommodation type
Hostel (e.g. backpackers/night shelter
Motel
Single/couple without children
Up to $40 each per night
Up to $140 per night
Sole parent with 1 child
Not applicable - would not house children in a hostel
Up to $140 per night
Couple with 1 child
Sole parent with 2 children
Not applicable - would not house children in a hostel
Up to $175 per night
Couple with 2 or more children
Sole parent with 3 or more children
Not applicable - would not house children in a hostel
Up $260 per night
## Paying a rate higher than the maximum rates
There are some circumstances when MSD can pay above these rates.
For example:
- when there is no adequate accommodation to meet the needs of the client and their immediate family within the rate. This could be due to the actual accommodation rates in the area (e.g. night rates in major cities may be higher than the guideline)
- there are no available places at motels in the area within the per night guideline amount (this may be due to an event on in the area, that has increased the per night rate)
- where essential features required by the client and their partner and dependent children (if any) have increased the per night price above the maximum. For example: requirement for cooking facilitieswheelchair accessibilitythe location of the cheapest accommodation means it is an unreasonable distance to travel for schooling, work, or medical needs
- requirement for cooking facilities
- wheelchair accessibility
- the location of the cheapest accommodation means it is an unreasonable distance to travel for schooling, work, or medical needs

chunks.title: Determining when limited circumstances no longer apply — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Determining when limited circumstances no longer apply
If the client meets the criteria for limited circumstances and qualifies for an Emergency Housing Grant, their non-entitlement period will be paused.
A client must be assessed at each subsequent Emergency Housing Grant application against the limited circumstances criteria to determine eligibility.
When the client or their dependent child is no longer in a crisis situation, the clients application for an Emergency Housing grant must be declined and the 13 week non-entitlement period will resume.
## Limited circumstances no longer apply
