The client will no longer meet the criteria for limited circumstances to get an Emergency Housing Grant during the non-entitlement period when:
- they or their dependent children (if any) are no longer experiencing a crisis situation
The client can inform MSD, or MSD can determine, when the client or their dependent children (if any) are no longer in a crisis.
MSD must be satisfied the crisis situation has been appropriately dealt with before declining the limited circumstances grant and resuming the non-entitlement period.
## Example - Limited circumstances no longer apply, 13 week non-entitlement period resumes
Kori applies for an Emergency Housing Grant two weeks into their non-entitlement period. Kori and their dependent child experienced a family violence incident while on a 13-week non-entitlement period. The incident escalated to a serious incident.
Kori is experiencing a crisis situation, is at near-term risk of harm and has multiple risk factors (a dependent child under the age of 12 months, and in a violent situation).
Kori meets the criteria for limited circumstances and the Emergency Housing Grant is approved. Their non-entitlement period is paused.
Kori applies for a subsequent Emergency Housing Grant during their non-entitlement period.
MSD assesses if Kori continues to meet the limited circumstances criteria, and it is determined Kori is no longer experiencing a crisis situation, the perpetrator is being held in custody and an urgent protection order is in place.
Kori’s subsequent application is declined and the non-entitlement period resumes (after being paused) because limited circumstances no longer apply.
There are 11 weeks remaining of Kori’s non-entitlement period.

chunks.title: Effect of security deposit being paid out on future Emergency Housing Grants — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Effect of security deposit being paid out on future Emergency Housing Grants
If a Security Deposit Grant is paid out to an emergency housing supplier, and the client needs to apply for a further Emergency Housing Grant, MSD may consider whether the new Emergency Housing Grant should be declined.
For example MSD may consider whether, given the damage to the previous accommodation, the client has contributed to their immediate emergency housing need.
This needs careful consideration as sometimes the damage may have been unintentional or a one-off, e.g. damage caused by the client's young children, and it may not be reasonable to decline the Emergency Housing Grant.
It is also relevant to consider the period of time that has lapsed between the new application and the client's stay when the security deposit was paid out.

chunks.title: Emergency housing contribution cannot be more than cost of emergency housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Emergency housing contribution cannot be more than cost of emergency housing
In rare cases, a client's emergency housing contribution, based on their income, may work out to be higher than the actual cost of their emergency housing accommodation.
In this situation, it may be more appropriate for the client to pay for the accommodation themselves. For example, if they can afford to pay for their accommodation themselves without causing serious hardship.
However, the client may still need an Emergency Housing Grant. In this case, their calculated contribution must be reduced so that it is the same amount as the actual cost of the accommodation.
## Example
A single client's emergency housing in a camping ground costs $105 for 7 nights.
Their emergency housing contribution, based on 25% of their net weekly income, is $110.
The client's emergency housing contribution must be reduced to $105 for the 7 nights.

chunks.title: Emergency housing contribution payment date — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Emergency housing contribution payment date
Clients must pay their emergency housing contribution by the date or dates MSD determines for every Emergency Housing Grant where a contribution is payable.
Clients are required to pay a contribution from their 8th night in emergency housing.
## Payment dates
A client may need to pay their contribution over more than one payment date. It depends on:
- the date and length of grant and
- the date of the clients next pay day and
- the date of SWIFTT's payment extraction
For example, for a 7-night grant when the client is paid weekly, a client may pay 4 nights of their contribution on one pay day and then the rest of the contribution for 3 nights on their next pay day.
If a client gets a longer grant of up to 21 nights, they will usually have more than one date to pay the contribution. For example, if the client is paid weekly, they will pay their contribution for the 21-night grant across at least 3 pay days.
## Clients who do not have a regular pay day or source of income
There are some clients who may have irregular pay days or income sources. MSD will discuss their situation with the client, and determine the date(s) for payment of the contribution that is appropriate for the clients situation. In most cases, this will be a weekly payment date.

chunks.title: Emergency housing events — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Emergency housing events
There are a range of different circumstances that can lead to a client, their partner, and dependent children (if any) needing emergency housing.
An emergency housing event means the period starting when a client’s immediate emergency housing need first began and continues until MSD is satisfied the need has been resolved.
Typical examples of an emergency housing event include:
- client was staying with family but was asked to leave due to overcrowding
- client's landlord selling their rental property and the client cannot find another place to live
- client cannot get another rental due to tenancy history or affordability
- client needing to leave home suddenly due to experiencing family violence
It can also include a situation that has been ongoing but there has not been an Emergency Housing Grant paid for it yet (e.g. a client who has been living on the streets or sleeping in their car for months).
A client may get one or more Emergency Housing Grants for the same emergency housing event.
MSD needs to determine whether an application for an Emergency Housing Grant relates to either a new or existing emergency housing event. This is because for new emergency housing events, the emergency housing responsibilities do not apply for the first 7 nights.

chunks.title: Emergency housing responsibilities — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The emergency housing responsibilities are to support clients while they are staying in emergency housing accommodation to find alternative, and sustainable housing. This includes short-term and long-term housing options. The client must agree to meet the following emergency housing responsibilities to qualify for emergency housing: - pay the emergency housing contribution by the date or dates determined by MSD and - make reasonable efforts to get other housing and access other sources of housing assistance and - engage with support services (if MSD has referred the client to a support service) The emergency housing responsibilities apply from the client’s 8th night in emergency housing.

chunks.title: Responsibilities will be met through agreed activities — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Agreed activities are steps or actions a client must take to meet their emergency housing responsibilities. When the client is applying for an Emergency Housing Grant, MSD must: - set and agree with the client the agreed activities that must be completed before their next Emergency Housing Grant and - ensure the client understands the activities and what is expected of them and - provide the client with a written copy of the agreed activities and - advise the client of the consequences if they do not meet their emergency housing responsibilities Agreed activities must be reasonable for the client to do by their next appointment date to apply for a further Emergency Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Activities must be met on or before a date set by MSD — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The client must complete the activities on or before the date set by MSD. Any time between the date set by MSD, and the beginning of their next grant cannot be used as extra time to meet their responsibilities.

chunks.title: Example - Client understands and agrees to meet the activities discussed — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: After 7 nights in emergency housing, Jake applies for a further Emergency Housing Grant for another 7 nights. Jake is advised he must meet the emergency housing responsibilities for this grant. Activities are discussed to help Jake meet the responsibilities. Jake understands and agrees to the set activities. Jake’s Emergency Housing Grant is granted on 17 September. MSD advises Jake he must complete the activities set on or before 23 September (his next appointment date with MSD for a further grant).

chunks.title: Agreed activities must be reasonable — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: There is no maximum number of activities that need to be set for an Emergency Housing Grant. When a client has access to other accommodation that is adequate in the near future, but they currently have an immediate emergency housing need a minimum of 1 activity must be set. This could be an activity to help them prepare for the transition out of emergency housing.

chunks.title: Example - Reasonable activity set and agreed to — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: After 2 weeks in emergency housing, Wanda finds a flatting arrangement that is adequate to meet her immediate emergency housing need. The flat is available for Wanda to move into in 2 weeks. Wanda has no place to stay until she can move into the flat. She applies for a further Emergency Housing Grant for 7 nights. Activities are discussed to help Wanda meet the emergency housing responsibilities. Wanda tells MSD a good activity for her would be attending a budgeting appointment. MSD and Wanda agree this will help prepare her for the costs she will have while flatting. Wanda’s Emergency Housing Grant is granted on 21 January. MSD advises Wanda she must complete the activities set on or before 28 January (her next appointment date with MSD for a further grant).

chunks.title: Deciding whether the client has met their responsibilities — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: To determine if the client has met their emergency housing responsibilities, MSD must consider whether the client: - completed their activities by the date set by MSD, and if not: - was there a good and sufficient reason the client was unable to meet their emergency housing responsibilities. Note MSD must be satisfied the client has met their responsibilities. This means the client may be required to provide supporting evidence.

chunks.title: Client does not have good and sufficient reason for failing to meet responsibilities — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their emergency housing responsibilities, they will receive a warning.

chunks.title: Responsibilities and partners — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If a client and their partner are in emergency housing, and the client’s partner behaves in a way that means the client does not meet their responsibilities, only the client will receive a warning. The client is responsible for anyone staying with them in emergency housing.

chunks.title: Emergency housing supplier standards — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Emergency housing supplier standards
The emergency housing supplier standards set out expectations emergency housing suppliers need to meet to provide safe and suitable accommodation, and fair service.
Emergency housing suppliers can request to opt-in to the emergency housing supplier standards.
MSD will assign the supplier of the emergency housing a status of either:
- opted-in or
- not opted-in
The emergency housing supplier will be assigned the opted-in status, when they make a request to opt-in to the standards, and MSD has determined they meet the standards.
The emergency housing supplier will be assigned the not opted-in status if they decide not to opt-in to the standards, or MSD has determined the supplier does not meet the standards.
An Emergency Housing Grant can only be paid to a supplier that is opted-in to the standards unless an exception applies. An exception is a reason MSD can pay an Emergency Housing Grant to a supplier who has not opted-in.
## When MSD can grant to a supplier that is not opted-in to the standards
MSD needs to consider the supplier status before paying an Emergency Housing Grant.
MSD can only grant an Emergency Housing Grant to a not opted-in supplier when one of the following reasons apply:
- there are no opted-in suppliers available that are adequate for the needs of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) or
- the not opted-in supplier is the most appropriate option or
- there are exceptional circumstances
Exceptional circumstances should only be considered when the other 2 reasons do not apply.
If none of these exceptions apply, the Emergency Housing Grant must be declined.
Note MSD still needs to consider if the emergency housing is adequate and a reasonable cost before paying an Emergency Housing Grant.
## Declining a not opted-in supplier when no exception applies
When no exception applies, MSD must make sure the client has access to an available opted-in supplier before declining to grant to a not opted-in supplier.
## Dependent children included in the application
When there are children in the household, MSD can only decline a grant for a not opted-in supplier if:
- MSD has identified an available opted-in supplier that is a reasonable cost and is adequate for their needs and
- the client refuses to access this
This is to reduce the risk to the welfare of children in the household by ensuring there is emergency housing they can access.

chunks.title: Engage with support services — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: To qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant, clients must agree to, and meet the emergency housing responsibilities. This includes engaging with support services (if MSD has referred the client to a support service, or MSD is satisfied with a self- or third-party referral). To meet this responsibility, clients must engage with support service they have been referred to. A support service is any government-funded or community-based service intended to support the client’s underlying needs. The emergency housing responsibilities apply from client's 8th night in emergency housing.

chunks.title: Agreed activities to meet responsibility — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Agreed activities are steps or actions a client must take to meet their emergency housing responsibilities. Clients must understand and agree to meet the responsibilities including any activities set by MSD. MSD can discuss and set agreed activities to help the client meet engaging with support services responsibility.

chunks.title: Engaging with the support service generally means — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: - MSD has referred or assigned the client to a support service (or MSD is satisfied with a client's self-referral, or the referral of another agency e.g. a community organisation referral), and - MSD is satisfied the client has had sufficient contact with that support service, and - MSD is satisfied the client has a plan in place with the support service (e.g. reasonable steps), and - the client has taken at least one of the steps on their action plan (or a sufficient number of steps given the client's individual circumstances)

chunks.title: Client not required to engage with support services — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: In some cases, MSD may not need to refer a client to a support service. For example: A client in emergency housing may have signed a tenancy agreement for a new property but has nowhere to stay until the tenancy begins. MSD may determine they do not need to be referred to a support service during this time.

chunks.title: Requiring supporting evidence — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: MSD may require a client to provide supporting evidence to determine if they have met their emergency housing responsibilities. If supporting evidence is required and the client refuses to provide it, MSD may determine whether or not the client has met their responsibilities on the information available. If MSD determines the responsibilities have not been met and there is no good and sufficient reason, the client will receive a warning.

chunks.title: Client failed to engage with support services — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Clients must meet the emergency housing responsibilities during their stay in emergency housing. This includes completing any agreed activities set by MSD for an Emergency Housing Grant, by the date determined by MSD. This date will be no later than the client’s next scheduled appointment to apply for a further Emergency Housing Grant. The client will be considered not to be engaging with a support service when they: - are referred or assigned to a support service but the service cannot make contact with the client (despite at least three attempts), or - have met with the support service but have not agreed to the steps/plan they have put in place, or - have not taken reasonable action on the plan If the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for not engaging with a support service when a referral has been made, this will result in a warning.

chunks.title: Examples of other adequate accommodation — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When considering if the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) have access to other adequate accommodation, consider whether the place they have to stay is adequate for the short-term. What is adequate depends on the circumstances of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) and needs to be considered on a case-by-case basis.

chunks.title: Examples of accommodation adequate in the short-term — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Examples of when a client is considered to have access to adequate accommodation include, but are not limited to: - a single person who has been offered a friend's couch to sleep on while finding alternative arrangements (when the client has no other needs that would make this inadequate this e.g. health, disability, or social needs) - they could stay with family or friends who have a spare bedroom/s (appropriate to their family size) - a single person or couple without children can stay in a tourist cabin - a single person or couple living at a caravan park with shared kitchen and shower facilities with no other reasons that this arrangement is unsuitable - caravan park or camping ground when the facilities meet the client, their partner or dependent children (if any) needs

chunks.title: Examples of accommodation not adequate in the short-term — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Examples of when a client is not considered to have access to adequate accommodation include, but are not limited to: - family with children staying at a friend's house where the option is not adequate for the family needs, even in the short-term (e.g. children must sleep on the floor) - only place to stay is a vehicle, sleeping on the street, or in a tent - has a place to stay but they are the perpetrator of family violence and cannot remain at the property - has left a place due to family violence and cannot return while the perpetrator is still there - the only place available to stay is an unsafe environment (e.g. drugs, violence, and other crime) - an elderly person is staying in a caravan park in winter and shares a kitchen and they have to walk to the shower and toilet block. This would impact on their health due to the cold and not having easy access to facilities - the place to stay will impact on the client's health needs (e.g. too far away from a hospital where they are having treatment for cancer or dialysis) - a family with young children in a caravan park and the facilities do not meet their needs (e.g. distance to amenities, risk to children's safety by other users, risk to health due to the cold) It is important to record the factors considered when making a decision. Note transitional housing is an example of accommodation that may be adequate in the short-term, however it should only be considered once it has been determined the client has an immediate emergency housing need.

chunks.title: Example 1 - Sole parent, 2 children — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Example 1 - Sole parent, 2 children
Client has two children and gets a total family tax credit of $275.69 a week (1 April 2026). The maximum rate of family tax credit payable for the eldest child is $151.91 a week (1 April 2026).
Use 25% of $151.91 as this is the lesser amount (less than 25% of $275.69).
The client's portion of family tax credit entitlement for the contribution calculation is:
- 25% of $151.91 = $37.97 (based on the maximum rate of family tax credit payable for the eldest child, which is lower than the client's total family tax credit entitlement)
## Example 2 - Single parent, child in shared care
Client has one child aged 10, who lives with them 4 nights a week under a shared care arrangement with their former partner.
The maximum rate of family tax credit payable for the eldest child is $151.91 a week (1 April 2026).
Under the shared care arrangement, the client's family tax credit is apportioned, based on the 4 nights the child lives with them as follows:
4 divided by 7 multiplied by $151.91 = $86.80. The client's total family tax credit is $86.80.
Use 25% of $86.80 as this is the lesser amount (lesser than 25% of $151.91).
The client's portion of family tax credit entitlement for the contribution calculation is:
- 25% of $86.80 = $21.70
## Example 3 - Non-beneficiary parent, qualifies for family tax credit but does not get it paid
Client has one child aged 12. The client does not get a main benefit and qualifies for (but does not get paid) a total family tax credit of $41.00 (excluding in-work tax credit).
$41.00 is less than the maximum rate of family tax credit payable for the eldest child of $151.91 (1 April 2026).
Use 25% of $41.00, as this is the lesser amount (less than 25% of $151.91).
The client's portion of family tax credit entitlement for the contribution calculation is:
- 25% of $41.00 = $10.25

chunks.title: Examples of calculating the emergency housing contribution — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The emergency housing contribution will be calculated using the higher of the: - net weekly income calculation of the client and their partner (if any) or - the net rate of Jobseeker Support that would be appropriate, if the client and their partner were getting this assistance (referred to as the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support) The contribution must be worked out using both methods and the higher amount is selected.

chunks.title: Example 1 - Client on New Zealand Superannuation - single living alone rate — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The client meets the criteria for a longer grant of 21 nights' accommodation. This is because the client has secured a new tenancy at a council-owned flat. The client will move into the flat on 29 July. The Emergency Housing Grant is granted from 8 July to 28 July. This works out at 21 nights' accommodation for the grant. Note a contribution applies to the entire 21-night period. This is because the client has already been in emergency housing for at least 7 nights for the emergency housing event to qualify for a 21-night grant. The client's net weekly income is $555.15 (New Zealand Superannuation only, as at 1 April 2026). The appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support based on the client's circumstances is Jobseeker Support single rate, 25 years and over, of $372.55 (as at 1 April 2026). The client's contribution is calculated as follows: Step 1 Work out emergency housing contribution using both the net weekly income calculation and the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support calculation $555.15 x 25% = $138.78 $372.55 x 25% = $93.13 Weekly client contribution is $138.78 because it is the higher figure Step 2 Work out the daily rate of client contribution $138.78 weekly contribution divided by 7 = $19.82 (rounded to nearest cent) to get rounded daily contribution Step 3 Work out the pay period fortnights (in this example it is aligned with pay period for New Zealand Superannuation) Fortnight 1: 08/07 to 12/07 which is 5 nights Fortnight 2: 13/07 to 26/07 which is 14 nights Step 4 Work out the contribution for each fortnight by multiplying the number of nights' accommodation in each fortnight by the rounded daily income. Fortnight 1: 08/07 to 12/07 which is 5 nights Fortnight 2: 13/07 to 26/07 which is 14 nights 5 x $19.82 = $99.10 14 x $19.82 = $277.48 2 x $19.82 = $39.64

chunks.title: Example 2 - Client is on sole parent rate of Supported Living Payment with one child (no shared care) — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The client meets the criteria for a longer grant of 18 nights' accommodation. This is because the client has health needs and has been funded to go overseas for medical treatment. The Emergency Housing Grant is paid from 7 July to 24 July. Note a contribution applies to the entire 18-night period. This is because the client has already been in emergency housing for at least 7 nights for the emergency housing event to qualify for an 18-night grant. The client's net weekly income is $581.96 (Supported Living Payment only, as at 1 April 2026). The appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support based on the client's circumstances is Jobseeker Support sole parent of $521.52 (as at 1 April 2026). The client's contribution is calculated as follows: Step 1 Work out emergency housing contribution based on income using both the net weekly income calculation and the appropriate net rate of Jobseeker Support calculation $581.96 x 25% = $145.49 $521.52 x 25% = $130.38 Weekly client contribution is $145.49 because it is the higher figure. Step 2 Then add 25% of client's family tax entitlement (as at 1 April 2026) to use for total weekly emergency housing contribution $151.91 x 25% = $37.97 family tax entitlement for eldest child Step 3 Work out the daily rate of client contribution $183.46 combined weekly income divided by 7 = $26.20 (rounded to nearest cent) to get rounded daily income Step 4 Work out the pay period weeks (in this example it is aligned with pay period for main benefits) Week 1: 07/07 to 10/07 which is 4 nights Week 2: 11/07 to 17/07 which is 7 nights Step 5 Work out the contribution for each week by multiplying the number of nights' accommodation in each week by the rounded daily income: Week 1: 07/07 to 10/07 which is 4 nights Week 2: 11/07 to 17/07 which is 7 nights 4 x $26.20= $104.80 7 x $26.20 = $183.40 7 x $26.20 = $183.40 Total contribution over 18 nights = $471.60

chunks.title: Examples of deciding new vs same emergency housing event — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When a client applies for an Emergency Housing Grant, it may be because of a new emergency housing event or the same event. It depends on their situation. Generally, an emergency housing event will be resolved when: - a client moves out of emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant and - moves into medium or long-term accommodation that is expected to lead to or be sustainable housing (e.g. transitional housing, a private rental, or social housing) Below are some examples to help MSD decide when it would be a new emergency housing event or the same event.

chunks.title: Housing event scenarios — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Scenario Is it a new or same event? Reason Is the client required to meet emergency housing responsibilities Client gets an Emergency Housing Grant for 4 weeks. Then they are placed in a private rental. 6 months later, the clients landlord sells the property and terminates the clients tenancy agreement. The client cannot find other accommodation and applies for emergency housing assistance again. New event The clients previous emergency housing event was resolved when they moved into medium or long-term accommodation that was expected to be sustainable housing (a private rental). They have not contributed to their latest emergency housing need. No emergency housing responsibilities for first 7 nights Client gets an Emergency Housing Grant for 2 weeks. During their third week, they leave the emergency accommodation to attend a tangi in a different town for 8 nights. The next day after the tangi finishes, they apply again for emergency housing assistance. Same event The clients emergency housing need was not resolved by them moving to medium or long-term accommodation. Emergency housing responsibilities apply from night 1 of their emergency housing grant (the first grant applied for after the tangi). Client gets an Emergency Housing Grant for 7 nights for themselves and their partner. On day 8, the clients partner applies for a further emergency housing grant (for the partner and the client). New event (for the partner only) The partner has not received an Emergency Housing Grant before. Their first application for an Emergency Housing Grant is treated as a new emergency housing event (even though it arises from the same circumstances as their partner's emergency housing event). No emergency housing responsibilities for first 7 nights A client gets emergency housing assistance for several weeks as they were asked to leave their parents' house and have nowhere to go. The client decides they cannot afford the contribution anymore. They leave the emergency accommodation funded to live in their car and on their friend's couch. 6 months later, the client applies for emergency housing assistance again. Same event The clients previous emergency housing need (after they left their parents' house) was not resolved by moving into medium or long-term accommodation that was expected to lead to or be sustainable housing. It has also been fewer than 52 weeks since their last emergency housing assistance. This means MSD would consider their latest application for emergency housing assistance to be for the same emergency housing event. Emergency housing responsibilities apply from night 1 of their emergency housing grant (the first grant applied for after they return to emergency housing).

chunks.title: Housing event scenarios — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Same situation as above but the client applies for emergency housing assistance after 12 months of living in their car and on their friend's couch. New event It has been more than 52 weeks since the end of their last Emergency Housing Grant. No emergency housing responsibilities for first 7 nights. Client gets emergency housing assistance for several weeks as a single person. At the end of their 10th emergency housing grant, their relationship status changes to a couple. The clients new partner has been living with relatives in a garage. The relatives can no longer accommodate them, and the partner cannot find alternative housing. The partner has not been in emergency housing before. The partner applies for an emergency housing grant (including the client in the accommodation). New event (for the partner only) The partner's emergency housing event is new (although the client does not have a new emergency housing event). No emergency housing responsibilities for first 7 nights. A client gets emergency housing assistance as they had to leave their home because of family violence. After 2 weeks, they return to their home. 5 months later, the client applies again for emergency housing assistance as they have left their home due to family violence. New event The clients last emergency housing event (5 months ago) was resolved by them moving back to their home. The client is unable to stay at their home again due to family violence and their new need for emergency housing is a new event. No emergency housing responsibilities for first 7 nights. Client is on a 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing. During the 13 weeks the client has been sleeping on a friends couch. At the end of the 13 weeks, the client returns to MSD to apply for an Emergency Housing Grant. Same event During the client's 13 week non-entitlement period, their emergency housing event was not resolved by moving into medium or long-term accommodation. Emergency housing responsibilities apply from night 1 of their emergency housing grant (the first grant applied for after they return to emergency housing).

chunks.title: Example 1 - Client and dependent children are being assessed for an Emergency Housing Grant under limited circumstances — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Ron and their 2 dependent children experience a family violence incident while on a 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing. The incident escalates to a serious incident, and Ron and the dependent children are at risk of current harm. Ron’s dependent children are 7 years old, and 9 months old. Ron is receiving Child Disability Allowance for their eldest dependent child. Ron approaches MSD for an Emergency Housing Grant. Ron is experiencing a crisis situation, is at current risk of harm and has multiple risk factors and meets the limited circumstances criteria to get a 7-night Emergency Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Three step assessment to determine if limited circumstances apply for Ron and his dependent children: — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Crisis situation: - Ron and their dependent children experience a family violence incident while on a 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing. The incident escalates to a serious incident At risk of current or near-term harm: - Ron and their dependent children are at risk of experiencing physical or mental injury Multiple risk factors: - Ron’s eldest dependent child qualifies for Child Disability Allowance, and - Ron is the principal caregiver of a dependent child aged 12 months or younger

chunks.title: Example 2 - Client meets the criteria for limited circumstances (client has a partner and dependent children) — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Cynthia, her partner, and their dependent child entered emergency housing together. Cynthia is now on a 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing. While on the 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing, Cynthia, and her family return to MSD to apply for emergency housing. Cynthia and the dependent child are assessed for an Emergency Housing Grant under limited circumstances and meet the criteria. She is granted an Emergency Housing Grant for 7 nights. Cynthia’s partner is not part of the assessment for limited circumstances (as only the circumstances of the client on the 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing and any dependent children are considered). However, the partner can be included in the emergency housing accommodation under the Emergency Housing Grant granted to Cynthia.

chunks.title: Example 3 - Client does not meet the criteria for limited circumstances and partner applies in their own right for an Emergency Housing Grant — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Zayn, his partner (Tom), and their dependent child entered emergency housing together. Zayn is now on a 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing. While on the 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing, Zayn, and his family return to MSD to apply for emergency housing. Zayn and their dependent child are assessed for an Emergency Housing Grant under limited circumstances, but do not meet the criteria and are declined an Emergency Housing Grant. Zayn’s partner applies for an Emergency Housing Grant in his own right, and includes their dependent child in the application. Tom qualifies for Emergency Housing in his own right, and enters emergency housing with their dependent child. Zayn continues on his 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing, and he cannot be included in Tom’s Emergency Housing Grant. If Tom included Zayn in the application, Tom would not qualify for emergency housing.

chunks.title: Example 4 - Single client meets the criteria for limited circumstances — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Callie is on a 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing. She has been living in her car. Callie gets into a serious car accident, suffers a brain injury, and her car is written off. Callie’s injury meets the definition for restricted work capacity. Due to her situation, Callie starts experiencing mental health issues. Callie is released from hospital and must attend rehab for the brain injury. She was unable to find other accommodation before she had to leave hospital and approaches MSD for an Emergency Housing Grant. Callie is experiencing a crisis situation, is at current risk of harm and has multiple risk factors and meets the limited circumstances criteria to get a 7-night Emergency Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Three step assessment to determine if limited circumstances apply for Callie: — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Crisis situation: - client suffered a serious medical injury (e.g. car accident) At risk of current or near-term harm: - the client is experiencing physical injury (e.g. brain injury that impairs decision making and meets the definition for restricted work capacity or total blindness) - unable to sleep in car (car written off) Multiple risk factors: - brain injury that impairs her decision making and - due to the accident, the client is experiencing mental health issues

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances for income and cash asset limits — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances for income and cash asset limits
If MSD determines the client has exceptional circumstances, the client may still qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant if their income or cash assets exceed the relevant limit.
In determining whether the client has exceptional circumstances, consider the following factors:
- if the client has any special or unusual costs compared to others in a similar position
- if the client has any special or unusual reasons for any costs that have caused or contributed to the need
- the age and health of the client and any dependants
- if the client the principal caregiver of a child 12 months or younger
- the client's ability to improve their financial situation
- the causes of the client's financial difficulty, particularly if the client caused or contributed to their financial difficulty because they have used their money unwisely
- the extent to which the client's basic necessities of life would be at risk if an Emergency Housing Grant is not granted
- if the client is escaping from an unsafe environment
- any other circumstances about the client's situation MSD considers relevant

chunks.title: Expectations and conditions of payment for emergency housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Expectations and conditions of payment for emergency housing
When an Emergency Housing Grant is granted, clients must be advised of the expectations and conditions of payment for emergency housing.
The expectations and conditions of payment apply from the client’s first night in emergency housing and continue to apply until the end of their emergency housing event.
These include that the client:
- is aware of the emergency housing supplier’s rules of stay while staying in the accommodation, for example:keeping their room cleanobeying noise and other usage policies (e.g. maximum occupancy rates)not removing any of the motel propertyfollowing the supplier's check-out procedures
- keeping their room clean
- obeying noise and other usage policies (e.g. maximum occupancy rates)
- not removing any of the motel property
- following the supplier's check-out procedures
- understands the consequences of not following the rules (e.g. the client is responsible for the costs arising from damage caused by them or anyone staying with them)
- understands the consequences of contributing to their immediate emergency housing need
- knows if there are costs that aren't covered by the Security Deposit Grant, the emergency housing supplier will follow these up with them directly
- understands that if they leave their emergency accommodation early, they should notify MSD as soon as they can
- knows that if any of the payment needs to be refunded, the emergency housing supplier will pay this refund to MSD. If they are paid a refund directly by the emergency housing supplier, they will need to repay this to MSD
- knows that if they are responsible for any damage or loss and agree with the amount of costs incurred when they check out, or if the client fails to check out, MSD will pay the provider up to the security deposit amount. This amount will be recovered from the client
If the client does not meet the expectations and conditions of grant for emergency housing their Emergency Housing Grant may be declined.
Note there are also security deposit requirements.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for not meeting responsibilities — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client may have a good and sufficient reason why there were unable to meet their responsibilities or complete the agreed activities set. If there is a good and sufficient reason why a client could not meet a responsibility or activity, MSD can decide not to give the client a warning. Good and sufficient reasons may include the client: - experiencing or escaping a violent or family violence situation - having to comply with court-imposed conditions - having to meet study requirements - having to attend a job interview or job training or could not get time off work - temporarily being medically unfit: this could include (but not limited to): experiencing severe symptoms or episodes from a medical condition, mental disorder, mental health condition, or disability - this could include (but not limited to): experiencing severe symptoms or episodes from a medical condition, mental disorder, mental health condition, or disability - experiencing a death or serious illness in their family - being unable to realistically transport themselves on the day, due to unforeseen circumstances - having childcare arrangements that fell through on the day of an activity, due to unforeseen circumstances - being dependent on the provision of assistance by MSD or other agencies to complete the activity (e.g. Housing Support Products to access private accommodation), and that assistance was not supplied - having an unexpected event occur on that day of an activity, such as providing care for a sick relative - completing another activity (not set by MSD) during the relevant period that MSD is satisfied achieves a similar or same outcome (in terms of meeting the particular responsibility) as the agreed activity that the client did not complete

chunks.title: Client only completes some of the agreed activities — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When the client does not complete all their agreed activities for a responsibility, MSD should consider whether they have made enough progress. The client will have still met their responsibilities if MSD determines the client: - has completed a different activity or activities and - this achieves a similar outcome to the agreed activity (set by MSD) they did not complete In this case, the client is considered to have a good and sufficient reason for not completing the agreed activity or activities.

chunks.title: Example - client must engage with support services when a referral is made — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: MSD sets the Shonda two agreed activities to meet the responsibility: - attend scheduled appointment with a Budgeting Service - attend weekly counselling session at Family Mental Health Services Shonda only does one agreed activity (attended their counselling session). She did not attend their appointment with the Budgeting Service. This is because Shonda went to a Budgeting clinic run by another agency. Although Shonda did not complete one of the agreed activities, MSD determines that she had a good and sufficient reason for this. The good and sufficient reason is that Shonda did another activity that MSD determines is equivalent to the agreed activity that was originally set but not completed. MSD determines Shonda has met the responsibility.

chunks.title: Client does not have a good and sufficient reason — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting one or more of the agreed activities, they have not met their responsibilities for emergency housing. When MSD determines the client has not met their emergency housing responsibilities, the client must be issued a written warning by MSD.

chunks.title: Immediate emergency housing need — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Immediate emergency housing need
A client has an immediate emergency housing need if, on the date of application for an Emergency Housing Grant, or during some or all of the next 7 nights, they:
- cannot remain in their usual place of residence (if any) and
- will not have access to other accommodation adequate for the needs of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any)
## Remain in their usual place of residence
MSD must consider if the client can remain in their usual place of residence.
It may not be appropriate for the client to remain in their usual place of residence when remaining there would create or increase any risk to the wellbeing of the client, their partner, or dependent children (if any).
For example, a client needs to leave their usual place of residence as they are experiencing family violence.
## Access to other adequate accommodation
MSD needs to consider if the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) have access to other accommodation adequate for their needs, even if it is only in the short-term.
This includes accommodation they can access from their own resources or other sources of assistance.
When the client does not have access to other accommodation adequate for their needs, MSD will need to check the availability of transitional housing providers before the client can get an Emergency Housing Grant.
Note the circumstances of the client, their partner, and dependent children (if any) must be considered when deciding if the client has access to other adequate accommodation.
## When there is no immediate emergency housing need
If a client has access to other accommodation adequate for the short-term, but they are declining to stay there without a good reason, they do not have an immediate emergency housing need.
MSD cannot pay an Emergency Housing Grant if the client is not considered to have an immediate emergency housing need.

chunks.title: Income limit - New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Income limit - New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients
When assessing whether a client who gets New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension qualifies for an Emergency Housing Grant, the appropriate income limit must be applied.
If a client (and/or their partner, if any) gets New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension, this must be included as income when assessing if the client meets the income limit for emergency housing. If a client (and/or their partner, if any) gets any other income, this must also be included.
Note Winter Energy Payment is not considered income.
## Examples
The below examples show how income is assessed for New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients.
In the examples, the gross New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension rates are as at 1 April 2026.
The income limits below apply from 1 April 2026.

chunks.title: Income limit — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Income limit
A client cannot get an Emergency Housing Grant if their income and their partner's (if any) income exceeds the appropriate income limit.
The income limit depends on:
- the client's age and
- their relationship status and
- if they have any dependent children
If the client is applying on behalf of their dependent child, the income limit applies to the parent or caregiver's income.
Income for an Emergency Housing Grant includes:
- New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension the client or their partner (if any) are getting and
- the amount of any payments made to the client or their partner (if any) under the following programmes: New Employment Transition Grant Programme orSeasonal Work Assistance Programme orWork Bonus Programme
- New Employment Transition Grant Programme or
- Seasonal Work Assistance Programme or
- Work Bonus Programme
Note Winter Energy Payment is not considered income.
If the client is getting a main benefit, they would generally meet the income test for an Emergency Housing Grant.
Note for New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients, the appropriate income limit applies.
## Exceptional circumstances
If a client's income exceeds the appropriate income limit, check if there are exceptional circumstances. If there are, MSD can use discretion to grant an Emergency Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Insufficient income to cover emergency housing contribution — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Insufficient income to cover emergency housing contribution
The client may not have enough income to cover their contribution when it is due to be redirected from their benefit or paid from their bank account.
If payment doesn't go through on the due date, MSD should contact the client and put an arrangement in place.
## Insufficient funds for benefit redirection
There are times when a client is not required to pay their contribution with a benefit redirection.
This is when the client has insufficient funds for the benefit redirection due to:
- reduction of their benefit because of declared income or
- required deductions from their benefit under a deduction notice or
- required reduction of their benefit under the Social Security Act 2018 (e.g. a reduction as they are getting an overseas pension)
In these circumstances, the client can pay their contribution by a different method (e.g. direct credit into MSD's account).
## Benefit reduced or suspended
A client may have insufficient income as they are waiting for their application for a main benefit to be granted or their benefit has been suspended. In this case, MSD may recover the contribution from the client's benefit arrears.
MSD also needs to check the reason the benefit is suspended. Clients will not qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant if their benefit is reduced or suspended for a failure to meet their main benefit obligations.
MSD must explain to the client what they need to do to get their full benefit rate again. This includes explaining how the client can recomply if they have a 13 week non-entitlement period, so they can get a provisional benefit.
## No income when applying for an Emergency Housing Grant
Sometimes a client tells MSD they won't agree to pay their contribution as they have no income and they:
- refuse to apply for a benefit or
- refuse to take the required steps to meet their benefit obligations (so that a sanction can be removed)
Depending on the client’s situation, MSD may consider the client has caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need.
This is because by choosing not to have an income, they are unlikely to be housed or able to pay for their housing costs.
## Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit
Clients may be able to include their emergency housing contribution as an allowable cost for Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: An Emergency Housing Grant is a last resort payment for clients with an immediate emergency housing need. It can be used to pay for emergency accommodation when a client cannot remain where they are and don't have access to other accommodation adequate for their needs in the short-term. A client does not have to be getting a benefit to qualify for this assistance, but they must meet all qualifications including an income and asset test.

chunks.title: Emergency housing definition — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Emergency housing is short-term accommodation. It is for individuals, their partner and dependent children (if any) who have an urgent need for housing. This may be because: - they cannot stay in their usual place of residence (for example, they have been asked to leave or there are safety concerns) and - they do not have access to other accommodation adequate for their needs Emergency housing provides a stable place for people to stay while their needs can be understood and addressed, and other suitable accommodation is being found. Other accommodation may include short-term, or longer-term options.

chunks.title: What the Emergency Housing Grant pays for — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The Emergency Housing Grant pays for emergency accommodation provided by an emergency housing supplier. An emergency housing supplier may be a: - commercial provider (e.g. motels, hostels, camping grounds), or - community based provider (e.g. housing providers, night shelters, marae)

chunks.title: Security Deposit Grant — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If a client qualifies for an Emergency Housing Grant, MSD will need to approve a Security Deposit Grant for the client, before their stay in emergency housing. The types of costs that are covered by a Security Deposit Grant include, but are not limited to, the actual and reasonable costs of: - damage to the property (intentional or unintentional) caused by the client and anyone staying with the client (including guests) - loss relating to the client's failure to meet the emergency housing supplier’s rules of stay Note Security Deposit Grants can also be approved for clients moving into transitional housing or contracted emergency housing. Transitional or contracted emergency housing are funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development.

chunks.title: Payment of the security deposit — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Payment of the security deposit to the emergency housing supplier, transitional or contracted emergency housing provider can only be paid when: - the supplier or provider makes a claim that it is needed to cover the actual and reasonable cost incurred for loss and damage and - the client agrees with the amount claimed by the supplier or provider, or the client has failed to check out Security Deposit Grants are always recoverable from the client.

chunks.title: Limited circumstances during non-entitlement for emergency housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When a client is on a 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing, they cannot get an emergency housing grant unless they (or their dependent child) meet the limited circumstances criteria. To get an Emergency Housing Grant during the 13 week non-entitlement period, the client must: - meet the qualifications for an emergency housing grant andmeet the criteria for limited circumstances orhave a dependent child staying with them in emergency housing that meets the criteria for limited circumstances - meet the criteria for limited circumstances or - have a dependent child staying with them in emergency housing that meets the criteria for limited circumstances If the client or their dependent child meets the criteria for limited circumstances, the clients non-entitlement period for emergency housing will be paused.

chunks.title: Criteria for limited circumstances — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Only the client and their dependent child can be assessed for limited circumstances. To qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant during a non-entitlement period, the client, or their dependent children (if any) must meet all three of the following criteria: - be experiencing an unforeseen crisis situation that is beyond the client’s control and - be at risk of harm or likely to be at risk of harm within the next 7 days (current or near-term harm) and - have 2 or more risk factors The client or their dependent child must meet all 3 criteria for limited circumstances to apply. Note the client must also meet the emergency housing qualifications. If the Emergency Housing Grant is granted under limited circumstances, the emergency housing responsibilities do not apply. However, the client must still pay their Emergency Housing Contribution.

chunks.title: Determining if the client or their dependent child is experiencing a crisis situation — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A crisis situation is a period of time where a client or their dependent child (if any), is experiencing a higher level of need than usual due to an unforeseen event outside of the client’s control. Examples of when the client or their dependent child could be considered to be experiencing a crisis situation include if: - they are escaping an unsafe environment, or a serious crime or incident has occurred or - the client is in a financial crisis where and an event has worsened the clients situation or - the client or their dependent child suffers a serious medical event or injury

chunks.title: Determining if the client or their dependent child is at risk of current or near-term harm — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The client or their dependent child/ren is considered to be at risk of current or near-term harm when: - a negative outcome is occurring or - there is a possibility of a negative outcome occurring within the next 7 nights

chunks.title: Client or their dependent child has multiple risk factors — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Generally, the client or their dependent child must have two risk factors. However, depending on the seriousness of a risk factor, MSD can determine the client meets the criteria for limited circumstances if there are at least two risk factors shared between the client and their dependent children (if any).

chunks.title: Risk factors could include where the client or their dependent child: — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: - is at risk of causing harm to themselves or others - has a terminal illness (e.g., kidney failure) - has a serious health condition, injury or disability that meets the definition of restricted work capacity or total blindness, or similar medical certificate (whether or not they receive assistance on this basis) - is receiving Supported Living Payment because they are caring for a dependent child, who requires full-time care and attention at home - the client qualifies for Child Disability Allowance for their child - the client is the principal caregiver of a child 12 months or younger - the child has been, or is in, the care or custody of Oranga Tamariki - the client or their dependent child has become unwell during their non-entitlement period for emergency housing due to being homeless - the client or the dependent child are escaping an unsafe environment

chunks.title: How to assess limited circumstances for client with a partner — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When a client is on a 13 week non-entitlement period and applies for an Emergency Housing Grant, only the client, or their dependent child (if any), may be assessed for limited circumstances. If the clients partner (if any) is experiencing a situation similar to the limited circumstances criteria, their circumstances cannot be considered when assessing the client for limited circumstances. However, if the limited circumstances criteria is met and the client qualifies for an Emergency Housing Grant, their partner may still be included in their Emergency Housing Grant. If the client (or their dependent child) does not meet the criteria for limited circumstances, the Emergency Housing Grant must be declined and the client will remain on their non-entitlement period. In this case, the partner can still apply for an Emergency Housing Grant in their own right (with the dependent child). However, the client cannot enter Emergency Housing under the partner’s application.

chunks.title: Longer grants during a pandemic, natural disaster or other emergency event — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Longer grants during a pandemic, natural disaster or other emergency event
The usual criteria for grants of up to 21 nights still apply to applications for an Emergency Housing Grant during a pandemic, natural disaster, or other emergency event.
However, the client may not be required to meet the emergency housing responsibilities during a pandemic, natural disaster, or other emergency event if there is a good and sufficient reason they would be unable to meet them.
For example:
- there is no support service available for the client to be referred to due to the pandemic, natural disaster, or other emergency event or
- it would be unreasonable or impractical for the client to engage with the support service or
- if there is a pandemic or severe flood, and it would not be reasonable for MSD to require the client to obtain other housing e.g., by attending a rental viewing (as the area the client was meant to attend the viewing has been flooded)
MSD needs to consider the clients individual circumstances and the circumstances of the event.
Note generally, the client must still pay the emergency housing contribution.
If the client does not meet the criteria for a longer grant, they can only be granted an Emergency Housing Grant for:
- up to 7 nights at a time or
- up to 14 nights at a time if there is low availability of emergency housing in their region

chunks.title: Longer grant periods — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Longer grant periods
Generally, an Emergency Housing Grant will be paid for up to 7 nights at a time. However, MSD has discretion to pay for periods longer than 7 nights in several situations:
- for up to 14 nights at a time, when there is low availability of emergency housing in the region or
- for up to 21 nights at a time, when: the client has been granted an emergency housing grant (or grants) for at least 7 nights in total, for the same emergency housing event andthe client has not received a warning for the Emergency Housing Grant that was immediately granted before their current grant andan emergency housing grant of up to 21 nights is appropriate in the client’s circumstances
- the client has been granted an emergency housing grant (or grants) for at least 7 nights in total, for the same emergency housing event and
- the client has not received a warning for the Emergency Housing Grant that was immediately granted before their current grant and
- an emergency housing grant of up to 21 nights is appropriate in the client’s circumstances
- for up to 21 nights at a time, during a pandemic, natural disaster, or other emergency event
Even if the qualifications for a longer grant are met, MSD still needs to determine if a longer grant is appropriate in the client's circumstances.

chunks.title: Longer grants when there is low availability of emergency housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Longer grants when there is low availability of emergency housing
An Emergency Housing Grant may be paid for up to 14 nights when there is low availability of emergency housing in the region.
The region generally refers to the city or town in which the client is needing emergency housing. This can also include neighbouring towns and cities when appropriate.
If there is a period of low availability of emergency housing, MSD may pay the Emergency Housing Grant for up to 14 nights. This is regardless of whether it is the client's first or subsequent grant for the emergency housing event.
## Regions will advise of periods of low availability
MSD regional offices will advise their staff when and where there is a period of low availability of emergency housing.
Low availability means:
- there are regional issues in the supply of emergency accommodation and
- room/unit bookings are limited and need to be secured for longer periods
Reasons for low availability of emergency accommodation generally include:
- longer public holiday periods (e.g. Christmas and Easter)
- big, one-off special events in the region (e.g. sporting, cultural, or international conferences)
- natural disasters such as floods or earthquakes
## Shortage of public or private housing not a reason for longer grants
Low availability of emergency housing does not include a shortage of public or private housing in the region. MSD cannot approve a longer grant for this reason.

chunks.title: Main benefit rate used to calculate the emergency housing contribution using net weekly income — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Main benefit rate used to calculate the emergency housing contribution using net weekly income
When a client gets a main benefit, their emergency housing contribution is worked out using the net main benefit rate, before any other sanctions, redirections, or deductions (e.g. child support, Ministry debt or court fines).
However, the client or their partner's net main benefit rate may have been reduced due to income. In this case, MSD needs to use the reduced rate in the contribution calculation. This includes when the client's main benefit rate has been reduced because the client gets weekly compensation for loss of earnings or potential earning capacity (from either ACC or an insurer under the Accident Compensation Act 2001).
## Example - Main benefit rate has been reduced
A client applying for an Emergency Hosing Grant is getting Sole Parent Support. This is paid at the net rate of $521.52 a week (as at 1 April 2026).
They also earn income of $250.00 net a week.
The client's income has reduced their Sole Parent Support rate by $27.00 to $494.52 net a week.
MSD needs to use $494.52 (rate of benefit reduced by income) when calculating the contribution:
Client's net weekly income is: $494.52 + $250 = $744.52
- 25% of $744.52 = $186.13 (don't round until the daily rate is worked out)
Note this example does not include 25% of the client's family tax credit entitlement. This still needs to be included when calculating the total contribution.
## Student Allowance rate reduced due to income
When a client gets a Student Allowance and the net rate of Student Allowance is reduced due to their income, MSD needs to use the reduced rate of Student Allowance, together with the client’s other income, in the contribution calculation.

chunks.title: Making a reasonable effort to get other housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: To qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant, clients must agree to, and meet the emergency housing responsibilities. This includes making a reasonable effort in their circumstances to get other housing, including accessing other assistance. To meet the responsibility, clients must look for other adequate housing options to meet their emergency housing need. This includes accessing other assistance available to them to find other housing. The emergency housing responsibilities apply from clients 8th night in emergency housing.

chunks.title: Agreed activities to meet the emergency housing responsibilities — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Agreed activities are steps or actions the client must take to meet the emergency housing responsibilities. The client must understand and agree to meet the responsibilities including any activities set by MSD. MSD can discuss and set agreed activities to help the client get other housing.

chunks.title: Examples of agreed activities: — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: - searching and applying for long term accommodation (e.g., using Trade Me property, property management companies, flatmates wanted advertisements) - working with MSD to explore if they may qualify for: other accommodation assistance such as Housing Support Products or Accommodation Supplementother assistance to help improve the clients ability to afford other housing, such as employment, training and work readiness assistance (e.g. Training Incentive Allowance, or extra help such as Temporary Additional Support) - other accommodation assistance such as Housing Support Products or Accommodation Supplement - other assistance to help improve the clients ability to afford other housing, such as employment, training and work readiness assistance (e.g. Training Incentive Allowance, or extra help such as Temporary Additional Support) - checking whether the client could stay with family and friends locally or in another town (note the client must choose to stay in another town, MSD cannot require them to do this) - making an attempt to repair the relationship with the person that asked the client to leave where it is safe to do so (e.g. if they have been asked to leave a boarding or flatting situation) - undertaking screening and assessment for social housing (if applicable) and provide any information needed to complete the assessment - engaging with and attending any courses or seminars as required (e.g. budget services, addiction services, or tenancy courses) that will assist the client to find alternative housing - engaging and working with community providers as required Note MSD must be satisfied the client has met their responsibilities. This means the client may be required to provide supporting evidence.

chunks.title: Requiring supporting evidence — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: MSD may require a client to provide supporting evidence to determine if they have met their emergency housing responsibilities. If supporting evidence is required and the client refuses to provide it, MSD must determine whether or not the client has met their responsibilities on the information available. If MSD determines the responsibilities have not been met and there is no good and sufficient reason, the client will receive a warning.

chunks.title: Client failed to meet their responsibility — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Clients must meet the emergency housing responsibilities during their stay in emergency housing. This includes completing any agreed activities set by MSD for an Emergency Housing Grant, by the date determined by MSD. This date will be no later than the client’s next scheduled appointment to apply for a further Emergency Housing Grant. If the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for not making a reasonable effort to get other housing, including accessing other assistance, they will get a warning.

chunks.title: Medium or long-term accommodation expected to lead to or be sustainable housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Client's housing needs are resolved if they move into medium or long-term accommodation that is expected to lead to or be sustainable housing. Medium or long-term accommodation that is expected to lead to or be sustainable housing includes: - a transitional housing place funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - contracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - social housing - private rental - boarding arrangement

chunks.title: Client does not move into medium or long-term accommodation - same event — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A clients emergency housing need is resolved if they move into medium or long-term accommodation that's expected to lead to or be sustainable housing. An emergency housing event will be the same emergency housing event when the client: - has already received at least 7 nights of an Emergency Housing Grant and - has not moved to medium or long-term accommodation that is expected to be or lead to sustainable housing and - applies for a further Emergency Housing Grant within 52 weeks

chunks.title: Example 1 — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client gets emergency housing assistance for more than 7 nights. They had to move out of their emergency accommodation to stay with a friend for a week because there were no available emergency housing accommodation options. They then apply for further emergency housing assistance as they do not have access to other accommodation and can longer stay with their friend. This is still the same emergency housing event. The client did not move into medium or long-term accommodation and still requires assistance.

chunks.title: Example 2 — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client gets emergency housing assistance for more than 7 nights. They move out of the emergency accommodation to work on an orchard for 3 months. The orchard supplies temporary accommodation for its seasonal workers, including the client. After the work is completed, the client applies again for an Emergency Housing Grant. This is still the same emergency housing event. The client did not move into medium or long-term accommodation that was expected to be or lead to sustainable housing and still requires assistance.

chunks.title: Example 3 — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client gets emergency housing assistance for more than 7 nights. The motelier asks them to leave before the end of their grant because they damaged the motel room. The client needs a further Emergency Housing Grant to cover their stay in another motel. However, the subsequent Emergency Housing Grant will cover some of the same period of nights as the previous grant. This is still the same emergency housing event. The client did not move into medium or long-term accommodation and still requires assistance.

chunks.title: Example 4 — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Rose and their partner, Erin, get an Emergency Housing Grant for more than 7 nights. Rose has been applying for the couples Emergency Housing Grants. While in emergency housing, the Rose and Erin’s relationship deteriorates and they separate. Both Rose and Erin apply for a subsequent Emergency Housing Grant each as single individuals. Neither person has moved from emergency housing into medium or long-term accommodation and each still requires assistance. The new application for Rose is for the same emergency housing event. This means Rose’s emergency housing responsibilities continue to apply.

chunks.title: Method of payment for emergency housing contribution — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Method of payment for emergency housing contribution
Clients who qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant must pay the emergency housing contribution by the date or dates determined by MSD.
How it is paid depends on whether or not the client is getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation, or Veterans Pension.
## Client is getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension
A client getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension will generally pay their emergency housing contribution with a redirection of benefit payment from their main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation, or Veteran's Pension.
Clients who are required to pay an emergency housing contribution generally have good cause for a redirection, but the client may be able to show strong evidence there is no good cause. Each case must be considered on its own facts.
## Client is not getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension
Clients who do not get a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation, or Veteran's Pension are required to pay their contribution to MSD by bank transfer or wage deduction.
## Salary or wage deduction
Clients may choose to have their emergency housing contribution paid using a salary or wage deduction. In these cases, MSD can issue an employer deduction notice to the client's employer, for the amount of their contribution.
However, the employer must not make the deduction if it would reduce the amount of salary or wages below the protected earnings rate.
If it does, the client will need to arrange to pay the contribution themselves by bank transfer to MSD's designated account.

chunks.title: Net weekly emergency housing income — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Net weekly emergency housing income
MSD uses a clients net weekly emergency housing income to work out their emergency housing contribution.
The net weekly 'emergency housing income' is the total of the client and their partner's (if any) weekly income, after the deduction of any income tax and any ACC premiums or levies (whether paid or payable).
## What is included in net weekly emergency housing income
Net weekly emergency housing income includes any of the following income received by the client and their partner (if any):
- any income included for benefit income assessments (including information share Child Support payments) and
- the following main benefits: Jobseeker SupportSole Parent SupportSupported Living PaymentYouth Payment or Young Parent PaymentEmergency Benefit - including Emergency Maintenance AllowanceJobseeker Support Student HardshipNew Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension (excluding Military decoration payments, Surviving Spouse or Partner Pension, War Pensions) and
- Jobseeker Support
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment
- Emergency Benefit - including Emergency Maintenance Allowance
- Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
- New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension (excluding Military decoration payments, Surviving Spouse or Partner Pension, War Pensions) and
- any amounts received from ACC or an insurer under the Accident Compensation Act 2001, as well as weekly compensation for loss of earnings or potential earning capacity and
- Student Allowances and Accommodation Benefit
## What is not included in net weekly emergency housing income
The following income is not included in the calculation of net weekly emergency housing income:
- any income excluded from benefit income assessments (except most main benefits, New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension are still included as income.)
- Orphan's Benefit and Unsupported Child's Benefit (including Clothing Allowance)
- Extra help, including, but not limited to: Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, Special Benefit, Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance and Winter Energy Payment
- Military decoration payments, Surviving Spouse or Partner Pension, war pensions
- Student Loans
- tax credits including Best Start tax credit, in-work tax credit, parental tax credit, child tax credit, minimum family tax credit and family tax credit
Note a portion of the family tax credit is included in the contribution calculation but is not a part of net weekly emergency housing income.

chunks.title: New emergency housing events — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: There are a number of situations when we would consider that the client has a new emergency housing event.
