A client will be considered to have a new emergency housing event when: - the client has not been paid an Emergency Housing Grant before or - the client's last Emergency Housing Grant was paid at least 52 weeks ago or - the clients last Emergency Housing Grant was less than 52 weeks ago andMSD determined that emergency housing event was resolved by the client moving into medium or long-term accommodation that was expected to lead to or be sustainable housing - MSD determined that emergency housing event was resolved by the client moving into medium or long-term accommodation that was expected to lead to or be sustainable housing

chunks.title: Client has never been paid an Emergency Housing Grant — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When a client applies for an Emergency Housing Grant and has not received one before, their emergency housing event is new. The client will not be required to meet the emergency housing responsibilities for their first 7 nights in emergency housing.

chunks.title: Last Emergency Housing Grant was at least 52 weeks ago — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If the current emergency housing event takes place 52 weeks or more since the last night of the clients Emergency Housing Grant, it is a new emergency housing event.

chunks.title: Last Emergency Housing Grant was less than 52-weeks — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client may still have a new emergency housing event within the same 52 week period as their previous emergency housing event. When deciding whether or not the client has a new emergency housing event within a 52-week period, MSD needs to consider: - whether the client's earlier emergency housing event was 'resolved' by the client moving into medium to long-term accommodation that was expected to lead to or be sustainable housing and - the reason for the client's current emergency housing event

chunks.title: Example - Applying for a further Emergency Housing Grant after a period away from emergency housing, within 52 week period — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Client qualifies for and gets Emergency Housing Grants for 4 weeks in total. Then they are placed in a private rental. 6 months later, the clients landlord sells the property and terminates the clients tenancy agreement. The client cannot find other accommodation and applies for an Emergency Housing Grant. This is a new event. The clients previous emergency housing event was resolved when they moved into medium or long-term accommodation that was expected to be sustainable housing (a private rental). No emergency housing responsibilities are required to be met for the first 7 nights.

chunks.title: Client in emergency housing for family violence — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client's immediate need for emergency housing may have arisen because they had to leave their home due to family violence. The client may not be able to stay in their home because they are: - escaping from family violence or - the perpetrator of family violence and cannot return home for safety or legal reasons (e.g. there is a protection order that prevents their return) Clients who get an Emergency Housing Grant due to family violence may subsequently return to their home. If the client applies again for emergency housing within 52 weeks of their previous grant because they had to leave their home again due to family violence, MSD will treat this as a new event.

chunks.title: Assistance for the client — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Discuss the situation with your local Family Violence Response Coordinator if a client has been, or is likely to be: - harmed (physically, emotionally, or sexually) - ill-treated - abused - neglected or - deprived Further information about the help that can be offered to victims of family violence is provided here:

chunks.title: No opted-in suppliers available — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## No opted-in suppliers available
An Emergency Housing Grant may be granted to not opted-in suppliers if MSD determines there are no opted-in suppliers available that are adequate for the needs of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any).
Before paying an Emergency Housing Grant for a not opted-in supplier, we must consider if it is:
- adequate for the needs of the client and their immediate family (if any) and
- a reasonable cost
Generally, when there are no opted-in suppliers available, if the client needs a further emergency housing grant, there must be a reasonable attempt made to find an available opted-in supplier.
## No adequate opted-in emergency housing available
What is adequate for needs depends on the circumstances of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) and needs to be considered on a case-by-case basis.
For example:
- Daniel needs wheelchair access but the opted-in suppliers in the area he can stay does not have wheelchair access, however a not opted-in supplier does. In this situation MSD can pay for the not opted-in supplier as it will meet Daniel's needs.
## No opted-in suppliers with vacancies
If there are adequate opted-in suppliers, but they do not have vacancies from the date the client has nowhere to stay, a not opted-in supplier can be considered.
This includes when an opted-in supplier has vacancies, but not for 7 consecutive nights, and requiring the client to apply again within 7 nights would be unreasonable in their circumstances. For example:
- having to apply again so soon would cause additional stress that would impact on the client, their partner and dependent children (if any)'s wellbeing
## Not enough time to find an available opted-in option
If there is not enough time to find an available opted-in supplier before the client has nowhere to stay, MSD can consider paying for a not opted-in supplier.
A reasonable effort must still be made in the time available to find an opted-in supplier before paying for the not opted-in supplier.

chunks.title: Not opted-in supplier is the most appropriate option — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: An Emergency Housing Grant can be paid for a not opted-in supplier if it is the most appropriate option (even if the client has access to an opted-in supplier adequate for their needs). A not opted-in supplier may be considered the most appropriate option when: - it will lead to improved overall outcomes for the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) or - it will support MSD to manage availability, safety, and suitability Note MSD will still need to consider if the emergency housing accommodation is adequate and a reasonable cost.

chunks.title: Not opted-in supplier is the most appropriate option for the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When there are both opted-in suppliers and not-opted in suppliers adequate for the needs of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any), a not opted-in supplier can be considered when it is the most appropriate option. When deciding if a not opted-in supplier is the most appropriate option we need to consider whether paying for the not opted-in supplier will: - lead to improved overall outcomes for the client, their partner and dependent children (if any)

chunks.title: Improved overall outcomes for the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Factors to consider when deciding if the not opted-in supplier is the most appropriate option include: - if the not opted-in supplier is more suitable for the needs of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) - if the financial circumstances of the household would be improved if they accessed the not opted-in supplier - requiring the client to access an opted-in supplier would cause unreasonable disruption for the household (where a client is already staying with a not opted-in supplier) when deciding if it is an unreasonable disruption, consider if being moved would have adverse impacts or create instability for the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) - when deciding if it is an unreasonable disruption, consider if being moved would have adverse impacts or create instability for the client, their partner and dependent children (if any)

chunks.title: Example 1: Facilities and amenities are more suitable for the needs of the client or their immediate family — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Harry has a young child who has Autism Spectrum Disorder. There is an opted-in supplier available that is adequate. However, there is also a not opted-in supplier that is adequate, fully fenced and has an outdoor play area that would better enable Harry to support their child with Autism Spectrum Disorder. MSD determines the not opted-in supplier is more appropriate than the opted-in supplier for Harry, their partner and dependent children (if any). The safer fencing and outdoor playground at the not opted-in supplier will lead to improved outcomes as Harry will be able to better support their child's needs. The exception applies and an Emergency Housing Grant can be granted for the not opted-in supplier.

chunks.title: Example 2: Improved financial circumstances for the household — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Lilly's release conditions require her to report to her probation officer daily. There is an opted-in supplier available that is adequate to meet Lilly's needs, including that it is a reasonable distance from the probation service as Lilly can use public transport to get there. Lilly is struggling financially and is getting support from budgeting services. Lilly has reduced her non-essential costs (as much as she is able to), and the budget service has suggested Lilly reduces her transport costs. There is a not opted-in supplier available that is a reasonable cost and located much closer to the probation service. MSD determines that paying for the not opted-in supplier would reduce Lilly's ongoing transport costs, and will mean she has more income to meet her other essential costs. This will improve the Lilly's financial circumstances. The exception applies and an Emergency Housing Grant can be granted for the not opted-in emergency housing supplier.

chunks.title: Example 3: Unreasonable disruption — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Robert has 2 young children, the family has been staying at an opted-in supplier. When Robert applied for a further Emergency Housing Grant, the opted-in supplier was no longer available due to upcoming bookings. There were no other opted-in suppliers available and an Emergency Housing Grant was paid for a not opted-in supplier. Robert had to make arrangements at short notice for someone to look after the children while a friend helped him move all their belongings to the new emergency housing accommodation. After staying at the not opted-in supplier for 7 nights an opted-in supplier is now available. MSD determines that not requiring Robert to access the opted-in supplier would lead to improved overall outcomes because it is unreasonable in Robert’s circumstances for him and his immediate family to move again so soon. The exception applies and the Emergency Housing Grant can be granted for the not opted-in emergency housing supplier.

chunks.title: Example 4: Adverse impact — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Connie is staying at a not opted-in supplier as there were no vacancies at an opted-in supplier. She has recently lost a close family member and is affected by the bereavement. Connie is already experiencing mental health distress. When she applies for a further Emergency Housing Grant, there are now vacancies at an opted-in supplier. MSD determines that not requiring Connie to access the opted-in supplier would lead to improved overall outcomes because she is currently dealing with a bereavement and moving at this time would adversely impact her. The exception applies and the Emergency Housing Grant can be granted for the not opted-in emergency housing supplier.

chunks.title: Availability and suitability — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Availability means: - using suppliers with facilities more suited to a particular housing need when there is low availability Suitability means: - using particular suppliers to provide emergency housing more suitable for different households e.g. a particular supplier may be used for families Staff will be advised when emergency housing availability and suitability needs to be managed.

chunks.title: Example: — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Making accommodation with wheelchair access available for households who have this accessibility requirement. This could include placing those who do not have wheelchair accessibility needs with a different supplier.

chunks.title: Paying an Emergency Housing Grant when limited circumstances apply — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: During a 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing, a client can only get an Emergency Housing Grant when limited circumstances apply. If the client meets the criteria for limited circumstances and qualifies for an Emergency Housing Grant, the Emergency Housing Grant should generally be paid for no more than 7 nights at a time.

chunks.title: Longer grant period when limited circumstances apply — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If there is low availability of emergency housing in the clients region at the time of application for an Emergency Housing Grant, the grant can be paid for up to 14 nights. A client who is approved an Emergency Housing Grant when limited circumstances apply cannot get a grant for up to 21 nights. This is because grants of up to 21 nights may only be granted for clients who have met their responsibilities for their previous grant.

chunks.title: Responsibilities for Emergency Housing Grant when limited circumstances apply — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When a client is granted an Emergency Housing Grant under limited circumstances, they are not required to meet the emergency housing responsibilities. Instead, at each application, the client, or their dependent child (if any) must be assessed against the limited circumstances criteria.

chunks.title: Emergency housing contribution when limited circumstances apply — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Clients must still pay their Emergency Housing Contribution by the date or dates MSD determines during the limited circumstances period. If the client does not pay the emergency housing contribution by the date or dates determined by MSD, the unpaid amount will be recovered from the client as an emergency housing debt.

chunks.title: Example: — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Alden is getting Supported Living Payment and is on a 13-week non-entitlement period for emergency housing. Alden is granted an Emergency Housing Grant for 7 nights under limited circumstances and his non-entitlement period is paused. Alden is not required to meet the emergency housing responsibilities; however, he is advised he must still pay the emergency housing contribution. A redirection of benefit is set up for his emergency housing contribution from his Supported Living Payment. Alden applies for a further Emergency Housing Grant under limited circumstances. He has not paid the emergency housing contribution for the previous grant by the due date, as he had insufficient income to cover the redirection from his benefit. This does not affect Alden being able to get a further Emergency Housing Grant (as limited circumstances continues to apply) and another 7 nights is approved. MSD advises Alden that the un-paid amount will be a debt he needs to pay back to MSD from his Supported Living Payment and a debt recovery process is set up.

chunks.title: Paying emergency housing contribution by date or dates determined by MSD — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Paying emergency housing contribution by date or dates determined by MSD
Clients who qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant must pay an emergency housing contribution. This is an amount they pay, based on their income, towards their emergency housing costs.
Clients must pay 25% of their net income or 25% of the appropriate Jobseeker Support rate (whichever is higher).
Clients must pay the contribution for each Emergency Housing Grant by the date or dates determined by MSD. This is one of their emergency housing responsibilities.
## When clients must pay an emergency housing contribution
When a client applies for an Emergency Housing Grant for a new emergency housing event, they:
- will not have to pay the contribution for the first 7 nights and
- will have to pay the contribution from the 8th night onwards
MSD needs to decide if the client has a new emergency housing event to know when to start the client’s contribution.
## Agreed activities to meet responsibility
Agreed activities are steps or actions the client must take to meet their emergency housing responsibilities.
The client must:
- understand and agree to meet the responsibilities including any activities set by MSD and
- understand the activities and what is expected of them
MSD can discuss and set agreed activities to help the client pay the emergency housing contribution.
Agreed activities must be reasonable for the client to do given their circumstances and by their next Emergency Housing Grant date.
## Examples of agreed activities
In most cases, where a client is getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension, the client will need to agree to have their contribution paid using a redirection of benefit. From this point, there are unlikely to be any other activities for this responsibility and as long as the redirection of benefit is paid, MSD can consider the responsibility met.
If a client is not getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension, or a redirection of benefit is not possible, MSD can discuss and set agreed activities to help the client meet the emergency housing contribution responsibility.
For example:
- client agrees to make weekly payments by bank transfer or wage deduction
Note if a client does not pay their contribution in full by the date or dates determined by MSD, MSD will need to find out the reason for this.
For more information see:
- Emergency housing contribution payment date
- Client does not pay emergency housing contribution on time

chunks.title: Payment of the security deposit to a supplier or provider — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: MSD will only pay a Security Deposit Grant approved for emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing to a supplier or provider, if the supplier or provider has incurred damage or loss covered by the security deposit. If there is no damage or loss, the security deposit will not be needed, and no payment can be made to the supplier or provider. A Security Deposit Grant must be granted to a client before their supplier or provider makes a claim. If there is no Security Deposit Grant in place at the time the supplier or provider incurred loss or damage, MSD cannot approve or pay the claim. The supplier or provider will need to claim the amount directly from the client, under their insurance or another avenue such as the Disputes Tribunal.

chunks.title: Claim period of up to 3 months — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Emergency housing suppliers and transitional housing or contracted emergency housing providers have up to 3 months to make a claim under a Security Deposit Grant. The 3 months start from the date after the client ends their stay in the accommodation.

chunks.title: Damage or loss incurred by the supplier or provider — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When there is damage or loss, the supplier or provider must identify this during the client's stay or by the time the client completes their stay. The decision about whether the client must pay for damage or loss is between the supplier or provider and the client. If there is agreement between the supplier or provider and the client that the client is responsible for the costs due to the damage or loss, MSD can pay the provider up to the security deposit amount originally approved. Security Deposit payments are recoverable from the client as an MSD debt. Note before payment can be made, the provider must confirm the client is responsible for damage or loss arising from their stay, and there was no known dispute of that responsibility by the client when they completed the check-out process. Any dispute between the client and emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing provider as to the client's responsibility for the costs potentially covered by a security deposit is to be resolved between the client and the provider (not MSD). This may involve the matter being taken to the Disputes Tribunal.

chunks.title: Client does not complete check-out process — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If the client fails to check out, and the supplier or provider says the client is responsible for damage or loss during their stay, MSD can pay the provider for these costs up to the security deposit amount originally approved. The security deposit amount paid will be recovered from the client as an MSD debt. The supplier or provider must confirm: - there is damage or loss that is the client's responsibility - the client did not complete the check-out process to enable the issue to be discussed directly with the client - the client has not disputed the damage or loss Sometimes a client may leave some of their belongings behind at the accommodation after moving out. This can result in a loss to the provider if they cannot sell the accommodation until the client's belongings are removed. This loss is generally covered by the security deposit.

chunks.title: If security deposit is paid to a provider, that amount becomes recoverable from the client — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If a Security Deposit Grant is paid to the supplier or provider, the amount becomes recoverable from the client from the date it was paid. The amount paid will be recovered from the client using MSD's existing debt recovery process. Clients are encouraged to talk to MSD when they do not understand or disagree with a decision about payment of a security deposit. Clients have the right to have decisions formally reviewed. The client can apply for a review of decision when: - they dispute the recovery rate or - a payment has been made for more than the approved amount or - they consider payment has been made for costs that are not covered by the security deposit However, any dispute between the client and the supplier or provider for the responsibility of costs covered by a security deposit must be resolved between the client and the supplier or provider, not MSD. For more information see:

chunks.title: Damage or loss incurred is above the amount originally approved for the security deposit — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When the value of the damage or loss is above the amount originally approved for the security deposit, the emergency housing supplier, transitional or contracted emergency housing provider may seek: - reimbursement of the remaining amount directly from the client (this may involve taking the client to the Disputes Tribunal) or - compensation from their insurance company

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If a client qualifies for an Emergency Housing Grant, MSD can pay for the actual and reasonable costs of adequate emergency housing. MSD must also consider the supplier status of the emergency housing accommodation before deciding to pay. It is important to only grant the Emergency Housing Grant for the number of nights of accommodation the client needs. Generally 7 days would allow them to stabilise their situation and take active steps to find other accommodation. MSD does not need to routinely grant 7 nights per application. If the client still has an immediate emergency housing need at the end of the grant period, MSD can assess their eligibility for another payment. Some clients who have been paid for more than 7 nights of emergency accommodation may be able to get a longer grant of up to 21 nights, where appropriate. Note Emergency Housing Grants should be paid directly to the emergency housing supplier.

chunks.title: Client applies late for an Emergency Housing Grant — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Clients who are not already in emergency housing must apply for an Emergency Housing Grant before they incur any cost for emergency housing. A client’s immediate emergency housing need is based on the 7-day period is assessed from the date of their application for emergency housing. If a client applies late for an Emergency Housing Grant, MSD can only grant it from the date of their application.

chunks.title: Example - client applies late for an Emergency Housing Grant — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Mason applies for an Emergency Housing Grant 30/11/2024, he advises MSD he checked into the emergency housing accommodation 28/11/2024. Mason meets the qualifications for an Emergency Housing Grant. MSD approves the grant for 7 nights from 30/11/2024 (the date of application). Note if a client does not attend their appointment to apply for an Emergency Housing Grant, MSD is unable to grant it until they attend their next appointment.

chunks.title: Security deposits — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client accessing emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing can be approved a Security Deposit Grant before they move into the accommodation. However, payment of the security deposit to the supplier can only be made if: - the supplier makes a claim that it is needed to cover the actual costs incurred for loss or damage and - the client agrees to the amount claimed or has failed to check out Note security deposits are always recoverable from the client.

chunks.title: Client leaves accommodation before end of grant period — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If a client leaves their emergency accommodation early, they should notify MSD as soon as they can. The unused portion of their Emergency Housing Grant may be refunded to MSD by the supplier. This depends on the supplier's refund policy. If a client leaves early and does not notify the supplier or MSD (and/or leaves their belongings in their room and is uncontactable), the supplier may not be able to re-sell the room or refund us (regardless of any refund policy). The supplier may be able to accommodate a new client for the remaining period of the previous client's Emergency Housing Grant. In these circumstances, MSD will need to make a separate grant and payment to the accommodation supplier for the new client. MSD will also need to seek a refund of the previous payment if the supplier agrees to refund the payment.

chunks.title: Priority of deductions — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Priority of deductions
Some clients have existing deductions being paid from their benefit (e.g. Child Support or Ministry debt repayments). The emergency housing contribution and any emergency housing debts are included as deductions under 'Ministry debt repayments'.
Some types of deductions take priority over others. If the client has more than one order issued on their benefit, you will need to determine the priority of deductions.
## Order of priority
The following list gives the order of priority, from highest to lowest:
- Child Support deductions made under the Child Support Act 1991
- Inland Revenue tax deductions
- MSD debt repayments including the emergency housing contribution and emergency housing contribution debt
- Attachment orders made under the Family Proceedings Act 1980
- Court attachment orders issued under the Summary Proceedings Act 1957
- Court attachment orders issued under the District Court Act 2016
- Student Loan repayments
## Reducing deductions
When MSD needs to reduce deductions, they are adjusted from the lowest priority up to those with a higher priority.
MSD needs to consider the protected earnings rules for each order or deduction notice.
## Emergency housing contribution as a deduction
Some clients may have deductions from their benefit that are a higher priority than the emergency housing contribution. These clients will still pay the full amount of the emergency housing contribution.
However, MSD may need to recover the contribution in instalments over a longer number of paydays. This is so the contribution does not reduce a client's protected earnings.
Example
A client has a child support deducation and an emergency housing contribution to be paid from their benefit. Because of the order of priority, the child support deductions takes priority over the emergency housing contribution.
When the amount of emergency housing contribution would reduce the client's benefit payment below the protected earnings rate, the emergency housing contribution must be recovered in instalments over a longer number of pay days.

chunks.title: Qualifications for emergency housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Qualifications for emergency housing
A client may be able to get an Emergency Housing Grant if they meet the qualifications.
To qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant, the client must:
- have an immediate emergency housing need and
- meet an income and cash asset test (unless there are exceptional circumstances) and
- meet the residence criteria and
- understand and agree to meet the emergency housing responsibilities and
- not be otherwise ineligible for an Emergency Housing Grant
The client must also agree to the expectations and conditions of payment for emergency housing.
## For emergency housing there are additional criteria that need to be considered
When the client meets the qualifications for an Emergency Housing Grant, there are other criteria that needs to be considered before paying.
MSD must consider:
- the client's ability to meet their immediate emergency housing need in another way
- whether the emergency housing supplier is opted-in to the supplier standards
- if the emergency housing accommodation is adequate and an actual and reasonable cost
MSD may also consider if the client has caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need.
## Emergency housing responsibilities
Clients must agree to, and meet, the following responsibilities while staying in emergency housing:
- pay the emergency housing contribution by the date (or dates) MSD determines and
- make reasonable efforts to obtain other housing, including accessing other sources of housing assistance and
- be engaged with support services (if MSD has referred the client to these services)
Clients must meet the emergency housing responsibilities from their 8th night in emergency housing until the end of their emergency housing event.

chunks.title: Refunding the emergency housing contribution — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Refunding the emergency housing contribution
There may be situations when MSD needs to refund part or all of a client's emergency housing contribution.
Refunds can be given when:
- MSD has made an error in the calculation of the contribution, and the client has already paid it or
- the client has overpaid the contribution, for example, their redirection of benefit or wage deduction was not cancelled or updated in time and they have paid more than is required for their grant or
- the client has paid their contribution for the grant but left their emergency accommodation early (before the end of their grant period) because they moved into medium to long-term accommodation that is expected to lead to or be sustainable housing. For example, transitional housing funded by the transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, contracted emergency housing, social housing or a private rental or boarding arrangement
## Example
A client is paid an Emergency Housing Grant for 12 nights. They pay their emergency contribution upfront by bank transfer. On day 3 they notify MSD that they have found a rental property and the tenancy will begin on day 10 of their grant.
In this situation, MSD can refund the client's contribution for their 3 unused nights (nights 10-12 of the grant). This is because they will have moved to sustainable long-term accommodation.
If the client has not yet paid their contribution, instead of a refund, MSD will need to update the contribution amount to remove the nights of accommodation no longer needed and update any redirections accordingly.
## When no refunds may be given
MSD may not refund a client's emergency housing contribution when the client has (not a complete list):
- left, or been asked to leave, their emergency accommodation part way through their grant period (for whatever reason) and
- not moved into medium or long-term accommodation that is expected to lead to or be sustainable housing. This includes when the client has left the emergency accommodation: to move into different emergency accommodation (e.g. a different motel) and both places are funded by an Emergency Housing Grant orto serve a sentence in prison orto have a short-term stay in hospital
- to move into different emergency accommodation (e.g. a different motel) and both places are funded by an Emergency Housing Grant or
- to serve a sentence in prison or
- to have a short-term stay in hospital

chunks.title: Requiring supporting evidence — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Requiring supporting evidence
MSD may require a client to provide supporting evidence to determine whether they:
- have an immediate emergency housing need
- meet the income limit and cash asset limit
- meet the residence criteria
- can meet their immediate emergency housing need from their own or other resources
- have caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need
- have met their emergency housing responsibilities
- have a good and sufficient reason if they were unable to meet the emergency housing responsibilities
- meet the criteria for an Emergency Housing Grant under limited circumstances
Supporting evidence can only be requested from the client if MSD is not already satisfied the client has met any of the above criteria.
When MSD requires the client to provide supporting evidence, the information MSD asks for must be both necessary and reasonable for the client to provide and related to the purpose of the request.
Note if the client cannot provide supporting evidence, and they have given their consent, MSD can get this evidence from a third party. This information and how it impacts the client can be shared with the client.

chunks.title: Residence criteria — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Residence criteria
To qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant, a client must meet the following residence criteria:
- qualify for and be getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension or
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand at time of application and be a New Zealand citizen orhold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 orbe recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 orqualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy, but the relationship has ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- hold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- qualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy, but the relationship has ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
## Australia clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they are considered to hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other qualifications for an Emergency Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Review of Decision — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Review of Decision
If a client has received formal notification of a decision made under the Emergency Housing Grantds Programme that they disagree with, they can apply for a Review of Decision.
## Decisions that may be reviewed under Emergency Housing Grants
- declining to pay an Emergency Housing Grant because the client does not meet the qualifications for emergency housing
- determining the client has failed to meet their emergency housing responsibilities without good and sufficient reason (e.g. where a warning or 13-week non-entitlement period has been issued)
- the amount of emergency housing contribution the client has to pay
- declining to pay an Emergency Housing Grant after deciding a client or their dependent child does not have limited circumstances
- declining to pay a subsequent Emergency Housing Grant (and resuming a 13-week non-entitlement period) after deciding the client or their dependent child no longer has limited circumstances
## Decisions that may be reviewed under Security Deposit Grants
- declining to grant a Security Deposit Grant because the client does not meet the qualifications
- declining to pay out some or all of a security deposit amount
- the amount of security deposit paid out to an emergency housing supplier or to a transitional housing or contracted emergency housing provider
- the recovery rate for the client to repay a security deposit amount that has been paid out to an emergency housing supplier, or to a transitional housing or contracted emergency housing provider
A client can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority when they do not agree with a decision which was upheld by the Benefits Review Committee under an application for Review of Decision.

chunks.title: Security deposit approved for a household — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The security deposit is approved for the client who applies for housing assistance for their household. This is the client who was granted an Emergency Housing Grant, or accepted into transitional or contracted emergency housing. A household includes the client, their partner and dependent children (if any). The client who is approved a Security Deposit Grant is responsible for repaying it to MSD, if the security deposit is paid to a supplier or provider for loss or damage caused either by the client, a member of their household or a guest.

chunks.title: Multiple adults in a household — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Emergency Housing Grant If a household of more than one adult (who are not in a relationship, e.g. sisters), are applying for an Emergency Housing Grant, they must be treated as separate households, and each client must apply for an Emergency Housing Grant and a Security Deposit Grant in their own right. They can choose to stay in individual units or share one unit between them. If one unit is shared, each client must apply for an Emergency Housing Grant for their portion of the accommodation costs and security deposit. How the accommodation costs are split must be agreed to by each client. The amount covered by each security deposit will be based on how their portion of the accommodation costs is split. Example A mother and her adult daughter apply for an Emergency Housing Grant to stay in the same motel unit. Both apply for an Emergency Housing Grant in their own right. The accommodation cost is $800 for 7 nights. The mother and daughter agree to split the cost 50/50, so an Emergency Housing Grant is approved to each of them for $400. The security deposit amount required by the motel provider is $800 (equivalent of 7 nights’ accommodation) and will be split the same way as the Emergency Housing Grant (50/50). A security deposit for $400 is approved for each client. Transitional and contracted emergency housing For transitional and contracted emergency housing, the treatment of more than one adult (who are not in a relationship) for payment and the security deposit is at the discretion of the provider (with the household's agreement). The provider will determine whether the adults are treated as one household, and only one client needs to apply for the Security Deposit Grant, or if each adult needs to apply as separate households. The number of units required for the household may also be taken into consideration. How the household is made up and the amount of security deposit required will be indicated by the provider when the security deposit is applied for.

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When there is a change in circumstances and the client who was approved a Security Deposit Grant moves out, it is up to the provider to check for damages at that time and make a claim if necessary. The provider should also ensure anyone remaining in the emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing has applied for, and been approved a Security Deposit Grant, to ensure the relevant cover is in place. If a new security deposit is not agreed and applied for, by the remaining client straight away, the period in between will generally not be covered by a security deposit, and the provider can only make a claim from the date the new security deposit is approved. If a security deposit amount was split (e.g. 50/50) between 2 clients and 1 client moves out, the provider will need to ensure the client who remains in the accommodation applies to increase the security deposit to cover their continued stay. If there is a period where the security deposit has not been increased, the provider will only be able to make a claim up to the original split amount of security deposit.

chunks.title: Security Deposit Grant must be a reasonable amount — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: MSD must be satisfied that the amount of a Security Deposit Grant a supplier or provider requires is reasonable. When considering what amount a client’s Security Deposit Grant should be, MSD uses the following general guidelines:

chunks.title: General guidelines on what is a reasonable security deposit — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Supplier/Provider Reasonable security deposit Emergency housing supplier e.g. hostels or motels, when an Emergency Housing Grant has been granted to the client for emergency accommodation. 7 times the nightly rate of the accommodation that has been granted. Transitional and contracted emergency housing providers. Up to $1,000. For emergency housing, the security deposit is generally based on 7 times the nightly rate of the accommodation for which an Emergency Housing Grant has been granted, even for longer grants of more than 7 nights. For example an Emergency Housing Grant granted for 21 nights should still have a security deposit of no more than 7 times the nightly rate of the accommodation.

chunks.title: When general guidelines for amount of security deposit grant can be exceeded — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The amount of a security deposit grant for emergency housing, which is generally based on 7 times the nightly rate of the accommodation for which the Emergency Housing Grant has been granted, can be exceeded in some circumstances. Example MSD may be unable to find an emergency housing supplier that will take the client without a higher security deposit amount. In these circumstances, MSD may grant a security deposit of more than 7 times the nightly rate. Note the amount of a security deposit cannot be increased after the original date it was approved, unless the cost of the client’s emergency housing accommodation has increased during the clients stay in emergency housing. The client must be advised of and agree to the new security deposit grant amount.

chunks.title: Claim paid during a client's stay — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If part of a security deposit is paid during a client's stay, for example, to fix a broken window, the security deposit will be reduced by that amount, and the remaining amount will be available for the rest of the client's stay. The amount of a security deposit would generally not be increased back to the original amount approved at the beginning of the client's stay, unless the provider will not allow the client to remain in the accommodation with the reduced security deposit, and there are no other suitable options available for the client. If the amount of security deposit is increased, the client must agree to the new amount.

chunks.title: Damage or loss is above the amount approved for the security deposit — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: When the value of the damage or loss is above the amount approved for the security deposit, the provider may seek: - reimbursement of the remainder directly from the client (this may involve taking the client to the Disputes Tribunal) or - compensation from their insurance company If you are unsure about the level of security deposit that is reasonable for a certain situation, talk to a manager.

chunks.title: Example 1 — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client has been granted an Emergency Housing Grant to cover 7 nights in a motel at $140 per night. The case manager advises the motel that a security deposit of $980 could be paid. The motel agrees and a Security Deposit Grant is approved for this amount.

chunks.title: Example 2 — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client has been granted an Emergency Housing Grant to cover 15 nights in a motel at $140 per night. The case manager advises the motel that a security deposit of $980 could be paid (based on 7 times the nightly rate, even though the client's grant is for 15 nights). The motel agrees and a Security Deposit Grant is approved for this amount.

chunks.title: Example 3 — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client with 1 child has been granted an Emergency Housing Grant to cover 7 nights in a motel at $980. This is the client's second placement in a motel, as they were evicted for recklessly damaging the property at their previous emergency housing accommodation. The new supplier is prepared to let the client stay but is aware $1,500 worth of damage occurred at the last motel. The client has no other accommodation options and a Security Deposit Grant is approved for $1,500.

chunks.title: Example 4 — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client and their partner have been accepted into transitional housing. The provider requests a security deposit for the couple before they can stay. The case manager advises the provider a security deposit of $1,000 can be approved. The provider agrees and a Security Deposit Grant is approved for this amount.

chunks.title: Example 5 — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client's children caused significant damage to the motel room they were staying in. The Security Deposit Grant of $880 that was approved at the start of the client's stay was paid in full to the supplier for the cost of the damage. Now, the supplier will only accept the client and their children for a further stay with a higher security deposit. When granting the next Emergency Housing Grant for 7 nights' accommodation, the case manager advises the provider that a new security deposit of $1,500 can be approved. The provider agrees and accepts to extend the stay for the client and their children.

chunks.title: Example 6 — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client was accepted into transitional housing on 1 November and a Security Deposit Grant was approved for $1,000. On 5 November, the provider made a claim against the security deposit for $200 to fix a broken window, which was granted and paid on the client's behalf. This means that when the client checks out on 10 November, the amount of security deposit available to be claimed by the provider is $800. When the client was checking out, the provider identified damages of $1,000, which the client agreed to. A security deposit payment can only be granted for $800, which is the amount remaining from the original amount approved at the beginning of the client's stay, and the provider will need to follow up the remaining $200 directly with the client or through their insurance company.

chunks.title: Security deposit qualifications — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Security deposit qualifications
A Security Deposit Grant can be approved for all emergency housing, transitional or contracted emergency housing.
To qualify for a Security Deposit Grant the client must:
- qualify for emergency housing accommodation or
- be accepted into transitional housing or contracted emergency housing and
- meet an income and cash asset test (unless there are exceptional circumstances and
- meet the residence criteria and
- understand and agree to the security deposit requirements and
- require payment for actual and reasonable costs for a security deposit
A client getting an Emergency Housing Grant when limited circumstances apply will also qualify for a Security Deposit Grant.
Note when a Security Deposit Grant has been approved, the security deposit qualifications a client must meet do not need to be reviewed if the supplier or provider makes a claim for payment of the security deposit.
## Security deposit requirements
Before a Security Deposit Grant is approved, MSD must ensure the client understands:
- what the security deposit is for
- what the security deposit covers
- how much the Security Deposit Grant is when a supplier or provider requires one for the client to stay in the accommodation
- their rights when the supplier or provider has made a claim
- they are responsible for repaying any amount of security deposit paid out to the supplier or provider for any loss or damage
The client must agree to the security deposit requirements before MSD can approve a Security Deposit Grant.
## Security deposit is approved for a client and their household
The security deposit is approved for the client who is granted an Emergency Housing Grant or accepted into transitional or contracted emergency housing.
The client is responsible for repaying the security deposit if it is paid to a supplier or provider for loss or damage caused either by the client or a member of their household.
## Exception to the income and asset limit for clients in exceptional circumstances
When a client and partner (if any) have income or assets above the appropriate limit, but there are exceptional circumstances, MSD may grant the client a Security Deposit Grant.

chunks.title: Security deposit required for emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Security deposit required for emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing
Emergency housing suppliers, transitional or contracted emergency housing providers usually require a security deposit as security against loss or damage to their property before they will allow clients to move into their accommodation.
MSD may approve a Security Deposit Grant for all emergency accommodation funded by either:
- an Emergency Housing Grant or
- the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development (transitional or contracted emergency housing providers)
As part of the expectations and conditions of stay in the above accommodation, clients must be advised what a Security Deposit Grant is for, the grant amount approved by MSD, what is does and does not cover and what happens if a claim for loss or damage is made.
## Security deposits, if paid out, are always recoverable from client
In all cases, when a Security Deposit Grant is paid to an emergency housing supplier, transitional or contracted emergency housing provider for loss or damage, the amount paid out is recoverable from the client as an MSD debt.
## Amount of security deposit must be approved before start of stay
An initial Security Deposit Grant must be approved by MSD before the start of the client's stay.
However, a new Security Deposit Grant can be approved by MSD after the client has entered the accommodation if:
- MSD is satisfied a new Security Deposit Grant is required and
- it would be appropriate for MSD to approve a new Security Deposit Grant
## Claim for loss or damage under a security deposit
If MSD accepts a claim for payment under a security deposit, MSD can only pay the supplier or provider the amount needed to cover the actual and reasonable costs incurred for loss or damage (up to the security deposit amount originally approved).
The emergency housing supplier, transitional or contracted housing provider must contact MSD to claim this payment.

chunks.title: Supplier standards exceptional circumstances — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Supplier standards exceptional circumstances
If there are exceptional circumstances, MSD can grant an Emergency Housing Grant to a supplier that is not opted-in to the standards.
## Deciding if a client has exceptional circumstances
Before deciding if there are exceptional circumstances for the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) to stay with a not opted-in supplier, you must consider whether the following reasons apply first:
- there are no opted-in suppliers available that are adequate to meet the needs of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) or
- a not opted-in supplier is the most appropriate option
If these reasons do not apply, the exceptional circumstances reason can be considered.
## Client has exceptional circumstances
Criteria to consider when deciding if the clients situation is an exceptional circumstance:
- it is an unforeseen out-of-the ordinary event that cannot be planned for and
- it is beyond the client's control and
- it sets the client apart from others in a similar situation
## Exceptional circumstances impacting MSD's ability to apply supplier standards
Exceptional circumstances also include situations where MSD's ability to administer the emergency housing supplier standards policy is temporarily impacted (e.g. a business disruption such as an IT system outage disabling MSD's ability to identify opted-in suppliers).
Generally staff will be advised when there are exceptional circumstances that impact the ability to apply the supplier standards.

chunks.title: Transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The Ministry of Housing and Urban Development funds transitional housing providers. They provide temporary accommodation and support for clients and their immediate family. Transitional housing is available to clients who: - cannot stay in their usual place of residence and - have no access to other adequate accommodation Transitional housing providers provide temporary accommodation while they support clients to access longer-term housing such as renting, flatting, boarding or social housing. Transitional housing is intended to provide accommodation for up to 12 weeks but can be for longer. Transitional housing providers may cater for specific groups of people (for example, single adults or sole parent families). Clients in transitional housing must pay a contribution towards their transitional housing costs. The contribution is calculated by the transitional housing provider and is generally 25% of the client’s income and their partner’s (if any) income.

chunks.title: Referrals — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client may approach a transitional housing provider directly. They can also be referred to a provider by: - MSD or - another social services agency Before referring a client to a transitional housing provider MSD needs to confirm they meet the following qualifications, based on the relevant Emergency Housing Grant qualifications. - have an immediate emergency housing need (including that they do not have access to other accommodation adequate for their needs in the short-term) and - meet an income and cash asset test (unless there are exceptional circumstances) and - meet the residence criteria Note MSD cannot refer a client to transitional housing when the client is on a 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing. The provider will complete an assessment with the client to check if the provider’s service is suitable for the client and their immediate family. If the client has access to a transitional housing place adequate for their needs and unreasonably refuses to access it, they will not qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant as they do not have an immediate emergency housing need.

chunks.title: Referral outcomes — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The transitional housing provider will tell MSD whether the client: - has accepted or declined an offer or - has not been made an offer after being referred

chunks.title: No suitable provider or vacancies — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The client may qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant if: - there are no suitable transitional housing providers available or - there are no suitable vacancies in transitional housing

chunks.title: Security deposit required by transitional housing provider — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Transitional housing providers usually require a security deposit before clients can move in. If a security deposit is required, MSD must: - approve the initial Security Deposit Grant before the client moves in and - ensure the client agrees to the amount approved and understands what the security deposit is for A new Security Deposit Grant can be made after the client has moved into the accommodation when: - MSD is satisfied a new grant is required and - it is appropriate to approve a new Security Deposit Grant

chunks.title: Payment of a security deposit — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A security deposit is paid as security against loss or damage (such as intentional or unintentional damage to the provider’s property). A Security Deposit Grant will only be paid to the transitional housing provider if they make a claim for loss or damage covered by the security deposit and the client agrees to the claim or has failed to follow the provider’s check out process. The amount of security deposit paid must only be for the actual amount required to cover the costs. It cannot be more than the security deposit amount originally approved. The transitional housing provider must contact MSD to get this payment. The amount paid to the provider is always recoverable from the client. Note the emergency housing supplier and transitional housing provider has up to 3 months to make a claim under a Security Deposit Grant. The 3 months start from the day after the client ends their stay in emergency or transitional housing.

chunks.title: Types of cash assets — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Cash assets mean assets that can be easily converted into cash. These include assets of the client and their partner.

chunks.title: Cash assets include — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: - bills of exchange or promissory notes and - building society shares and - money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society and - money invested with or lent to any bank, other financial institution, or other person and - mortgage investments and other long-term loans and - shares, stocks, debentures, bonds and - the client's share in any partnership and - the net equity held in any property or land not used as the person's home

chunks.title: Cash assets do not include — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: - any grant made under the Emergency Housing Grants Programme - a motor vehicle or other vehicle required by the client or the clients partner for their personal use - a caravan, boat, or other vehicle that: has a net equity of less than $2000 oris used by the client, their partner, or dependent child for day to day accommodation - has a net equity of less than $2000 or - is used by the client, their partner, or dependent child for day to day accommodation - the personal effects of the client and their partner - the net equity of the clients home property and land on which it is situated - Christchurch mosques attack support payments - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts - Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income - MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after payment is made - personal effects - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment) - specified Ex gratia and Compensation payments - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received Canterbury earthquake related payments Payments made relating to the Canterbury earthquake by the: - Crown - Earthquake Commission - insurance companies or - the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) These payments are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client got the payment.

chunks.title: Warnings for failing to meet responsibilities — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Warnings for failing to meet responsibilities
When a client has failed to meet their emergency housing responsibilities, and they do not have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting them, they will receive a warning.
Warnings are applied to each Emergency Housing Grant. The client can only receive 1 warning per grant for not meeting their responsibilities.
A 13 week non-entitlement period for emergency housing will be imposed when the client:
- has received 2 formal warnings for the same emergency housing event and
- does not meet their emergency housing responsibilities for the third time and
- does not have good and sufficient reason for not meeting the emergency housing responsibilities
Note MSD must make sure the client has understood and agreed to the emergency housing responsibilities when granting an Emergency Housing Grant.
## Warnings only apply to the same emergency housing event
When a client has a new emergency housing event, any warnings they received for a previous emergency housing event do not apply.
However, if a client has caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need, MSD may determine it is the same emergency housing event. In this case, the warnings from the previous event would still apply.
## Partners and warnings
Responsibilities, agreed activities, and warnings only apply to the client who is granted an Emergency Housing Grant, not the partner (if any).
Where a client and their partner are in emergency housing, and the partner behaves in a way that means the client does not meet their responsibilities, only the client will receive a warning. The client is responsible for anyone staying with them in emergency housing.
Any warnings the client has received, does not affect the partner qualifications to get an Emergency Housing Grant if they decided to apply in their own right.

chunks.title: When a longer grant will not be paid — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## When a longer grant will not be paid
There are situations where MSD will generally not grant an emergency housing grant for more than 7 nights at a time.
MSD will not grant an emergency housing grant for more than 7 nights at a time when:
- the client has a warning for their most recent previous Emergency Housing Grant
- emergency accommodation is not available to be booked for longer than 7 nights
MSD will generally not grant an emergency housing grant for more than 7 nights at a time when:
- the client or their partner has not meet the expectations and conditions of payment for their previous stay(s) in emergency housing. For example the client of their partner has: a history of leaving emergency accommodation without notifying MSD and/or motela history of damaging their emergency or transitional accommodation (whether or not it was the client who did the damage)had more than half of their security deposit(s) paid out for their emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing within the last 6 months
- a history of leaving emergency accommodation without notifying MSD and/or motel
- a history of damaging their emergency or transitional accommodation (whether or not it was the client who did the damage)
- had more than half of their security deposit(s) paid out for their emergency, transitional or contracted emergency housing within the last 6 months
- the client is currently trespassed from MSD or other agencies
- the client is a low trust client
- the costs of the accommodation are high or tend to vary
- MSD needs to move the client to more suitable accommodation once it becomes available e.g. a larger room
- the emergency accommodation provider has a non-refundable policy if the client leaves accommodation early
- the client is staying with a supplier that is not opted-in to the standards, but an opted-in supplier may be available at the next grant

chunks.title: When MSD can decline an Emergency Housing Grant — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## When MSD can decline an Emergency Housing Grant
An Emergency Housing Grant is a discretionary hardship grant. There are circumstances when MSD can decline to pay one.
These circumstances include when the client:
- can meet their emergency housing need in another way or
- has caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need or
- has failed to meet the expectations and conditions of grant for emergency housing
## Emergency housing assistance cannot be used to part-fund accommodation
An Emergency Housing Grant is only available for emergency housing that is considered adequate for the client, their partner, and dependent children (if any).
When a client refuses to be assisted to stay in adequate accommodation, an Emergency Housing Grant will not be used to part-fund accommodation at another place.
In these cases, the client may be considered to be able to meet their immediate emergency housing need from their resources. If MSD determines this, the Emergency Housing Grant can be declined as they don't have an immediate emergency housing need.
## Before deciding to decline
Before declining an Emergency Housing Grant, MSD needs to consider if:
- the client has failed to meet the expectations and conditions of payment (e.g. the client contributed to their emergency housing need) despite being told and understanding what was required of them, and the consequences of not doing this
- the client has had access to appropriate services to support them to meet their needs
- there are children in the household and the impact
## Declining the Emergency Housing Grant
The client must be advised in writing and provided with their right to review the decision.
If a decision is made to decline when there are children, all reasonable efforts need to be made to manage any risk to their wellbeing.
If a child has been, or is likely to be harmed (physically, emotionally, or sexually), ill-treated, abused, neglected, or deprived, the case must be referred to Oranga Tamariki.

chunks.title: When MSD cannot pay an Emergency Housing Grant — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: There are situations when MSD cannot pay an Emergency Housing Grant and the grant must be declined. An Emergency Housing Grant will not be granted if the client: - does not meet the qualifications for a grant or - has refused to provide supporting evidence required to MSD to determine whether they qualify for a grant or - has a non-entitlement period of 13 weeks for emergency housing and limited circumstances do not apply or - is applying for an Emergency Housing Grant, and has included their partner who is on a non-entitlement period for emergency housing in the emergency housing accommodation or - has their main benefit sanctioned for failing to meet their benefit obligations or - is applying for assistance when they have moved out of social housing at short notice due to housing provider business reasons or - the client is applying for an emergency housing option MSD can’t pay for because it is: a not opted-in supplier and an exception does not apply ornot adequate for the needs of the client, their partner, and dependent children (if any) ornot a reasonable cost - a not opted-in supplier and an exception does not apply or - not adequate for the needs of the client, their partner, and dependent children (if any) or - not a reasonable cost The Emergency Housing Grant will not be granted (unless limited circumstances apply) when the client is: - on an initial stand-down or - on a benefit non-entitlement period or - in the process of their benefit application or - completing pre-benefit activities as part of their application for a benefit and - they qualify for, and have not yet received their maximum entitlement to, one of the following Special Needs Grants: Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application processAssistance during non-entitlement periodsAssistance when client is on strike - Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process - Assistance during non-entitlement periods - Assistance when client is on strike

chunks.title: Does not meet the qualifications for a grant — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: This includes when the client does not have an 'immediate emergency housing need' if they have access to other accommodation adequate for the needs of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) in the short-term, including transitional housing.

chunks.title: Client's main benefit is reduced or suspended for a failure to meet an obligation — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: A client does not qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant if their main benefit is suspended or reduced under a sanction for failing to meet their obligations. They will need to get their full benefit rate reinstated before MSD can grant an Emergency Housing Grant. MSD must explain to the client what they need to do to get their full benefit rate reinstated. This includes explaining recompliance if they have a 13 week non-entitlement period, so they can get a provisional benefit.

chunks.title: Client has a non-financial sanction imposed for a failure to meet an obligation — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: Clients who have a non-financial sanction imposed will need to complete their non-financial sanction period and recomply with their obligations before MSD can grant an Emergency Housing Grant. MSD must explain to the client what they need to do to recomply. The recompliance requirements for each non-financial sanction are different. For more information see: - Non-financial sanctions

chunks.title: Cannot be used to fund social housing tenants for a business-initiated transfer — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: If a social housing tenant must move out at short notice due to housing provider business reasons, MSD cannot pay an Emergency Housing Grant. The social housing provider is responsible for helping the client find other accommodation.

chunks.title: Client is on an initial stand-down, benefit non-entitlement period, in the process of their benefit application or completing pre-benefit activities — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text: The client may qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant, if they have received their maximum entitlement to: - Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process - Assistance during non-entitlement periods - Assistance when client is on strike In these cases, clients must also meet the following criteria to qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant. The client or their dependent child/ren must: - be experiencing an unforeseen crisis situation that is beyond the applicant’s control and - be at risk of harm or likely to be at risk of harm within the next 7 days (current or near-term harm) and - have 2 or more risk factors Note although these are the same criteria for assessing limited circumstances, this doesn’t mean the client is on a non-entitlement period for emergency housing. However in these cases, the emergency housing responsibilities will apply from the client’s 8th night in emergency housing.

chunks.title: When the emergency housing responsibilities apply — extra help > emergency housing
chunks.text:
## When the emergency housing responsibilities apply
The client must agree to, and meet the emergency housing responsibilities while staying in emergency housing.
Clients are required to meet the responsibilities from their 8th night in emergency housing for the duration of their emergency housing event.
The client who applies for the Emergency Housing Grant is responsible for meeting the emergency housing responsibilities.
Note the emergency housing responsibilities, agreed activities, and warnings only apply to the client, not the partner.
## No responsibilities apply for the first 7 nights
A client is not required to meet the emergency housing responsibilities during their first 7 nights in emergency housing.
However, when the client is applying for an Emergency Housing Grant and it is their first 7 nights, MSD must:
- explain the emergency housing responsibilities to the client in a way they understand
- advise the client of what they will need to do from their 8th night, and the consequences of not meeting their responsibilities
If it is appropriate in the clients situation, MSD can still discuss what opportunities, information, or services might help them find other housing options during the first 7 nights.
The client will not receive a warning if they do not to complete an activity during their first 7 nights in emergency housing. This is because their first 7 nights can be considered a settling-in period while they adjust.
## First grant is more than 7 nights
Generally, when a client has a new emergency housing event, their first grant will be paid for up to 7 nights. However, MSD can pay for up to 14 nights when there is low availability of emergency housing in the region.
If a client is granted an emergency housing grant for up to 14 nights, the emergency housing responsibilities will still only apply from night 8.
MSD must set agreed activities with the client before their 8th night in emergency housing. The client is only required to complete the activities on or after night 8 of their emergency housing grant.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — extra help > family tax credit > changes and reviews family tax credit
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
When a main benefit is suspended or cancelled because the client is absent from New Zealand, the client information will be transferred to Inland Revenue so that they can assess any ongoing family tax credit and Best Start tax credits.
The client information will be transferred to Inland Revenue at the:
- grant of benefit
- suspension of benefit
- resumption of benefit
- cancellation of benefit
- transfer to non-beneficiary assistance

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — extra help > family tax credit > changes and reviews family tax credit
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client is obliged to advise the Ministry of Social Development of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to family tax credit.
We may also review family tax credit at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.
For more information see:
- Absence from New Zealand
- Child dies
- Child leaves care
- Main benefit client dies - terminal benefit
- Overpayments of family tax credit
- Review and Appeal rights

chunks.title: Child dies — extra help > family tax credit > changes and reviews family tax credit
chunks.text:
## Child dies
Family tax credit must be cancelled from the beginning of the next pay period or first available pay period after notice of the child’s death.
This differs from Best Start tax credit which has a special provision to continue the Best Start tax credit for a period of 4 weeks following the child’s date of death.

chunks.title: Child leaves care — extra help > family tax credit > changes and reviews family tax credit
chunks.text:
## Child leaves care
Family tax credit payment is excluded from the main benefit at the beginning of the next pay period. This includes if the child left the principal caregiver's care suddenly.
The primary client's main benefit rate, obligations and any extra help may need to be reviewed after the child leaves their care.

chunks.title: Main benefit client dies - terminal benefit — extra help > family tax credit > changes and reviews family tax credit
chunks.text:
## Main benefit client dies - terminal benefit
When a main benefit client dies who was paid family tax credit and Best Start tax credit for their dependent child the assessment of terminal benefit following the date of death does not include the family tax credit and Best Start tax credit payments.
For a surviving partner, the on-going rate of payment (or appropriate benefit) should be reviewed for any change in obligations including paying family tax credit and Best Start tax credit to the surviving partner if they are the principal caregiver.

chunks.title: Overpayments of family tax credit — extra help > family tax credit > changes and reviews family tax credit
chunks.text:
## Overpayments of family tax credit
Debts are not established for family tax credit or Best Start tax credit payments which may have been paid incorrectly with a main benefit eg main benefit payments obtained fraudulently.
When a main benefit, family tax credits and Best Start tax credit are cancelled, the Ministry of Social Development advises Inland Revenue through the information exchange.

chunks.title: Review and Appeal rights — extra help > family tax credit > changes and reviews family tax credit
chunks.text:
## Review and Appeal rights
Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit payments are provided under the Income Tax Act 2007 and the Tax Administration Act 1994.
The review and appeal provisions in the Social Security Act 2018 cannot be used for decisions made only for family tax credit and Best Start tax credit.
Youth clients cannot appeal the payment of their family tax credits and Best Start tax credit only paid by the Ministry of Social Development.
