chunks.text: The client or their immediate family must have additional or increased needs that have happened because they are staying in accommodation funded by an Emergency Housing Grant. These needs must be related to education, early childhood or wellbeing. Existing, additional or increased needs that are not because of staying in emergency housing cannot be included in Flexible Funding Assistance. For example, when a client's travel costs to and from their childcare provider have not increased, no assistance for these costs can be paid through Flexible Funding Assistance.

chunks.title: Deciding if immediate need has occurred because of stay in emergency housing — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text: Whether the client or their immediate family have additional or increased needs because they are staying in emergency housing, and what these needs are, will depend on the individual circumstances of the client, their partner (if any) and their dependent children staying in the same emergency housing. MSD should consider both the: - location and type of facilities at the client's particular emergency housing and - the immediate family's particular needs in emergency housing while they stabilise their housing situation and find social or alternative housing Because a client and their immediate family are staying in emergency housing, they may have additional needs, or their existing needs may increase because of the following (but not limited to): - facilities at the accommodation are not suited to families with dependent children staying on a longer-term basis e.g. there is limited study and activity space available that is appropriate for the age of the children, lack of storage or lack of cooking facilities - location of the accommodation e.g. the emergency housing is further away from the client's or partner's or dependent child's school, childcare centre, medical practice or place of work, resulting in additional travel costs - additional costs for finding social or alternative housing e.g. the client needs additional childcare while they attend property viewings, or additional transport to get to rental agencies and viewings, due to the location of the emergency accommodation

chunks.title: Increased needs — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text: When a client or their immediate family's existing needs have increased due to staying in emergency housing, only the additional needs can be included for Flexible Funding Assistance. Example A family that is ineligible for the OSCAR subsidy have been paying for after school care for their 7-year-old child for 1 day a week. After their move to emergency housing, the child needs to go to after school care for 5 days a week as the emergency housing only has a limited age appropriate space. Only the additional 4 days in after school care can be included in Flexible Funding Assistance where the qualifications are met.

chunks.title: No longer staying in emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text: If the client was previously staying in accommodation funded by an Emergency Housing Grant, but their current accommodation is no longer funded this way, they will not qualify for Flexible Funding Assistance unless another Emergency Housing Grant is paid.

chunks.title: Client is staying in same accommodation but not funded by an Emergency Housing Grant — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text: This includes when the client is still in the same accommodation but: - the accommodation is no longer funded by an Emergency Housing Grant or - a subsequent application for an Emergency Housing Grant been declined or - the client has not re-applied for another Emergency Housing Grant In these cases, clients will generally be paying for the accommodation themselves from their own resources or using assistance other than an Emergency Housing Grant or they may not have yet paid for their own accommodation.

chunks.title: Flexible Funding has already been paid and client move elsewhere before end of grant period — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text: Clients who have been paid an Emergency Housing Grant and Flexible Funding Assistance for the current period but move elsewhere before the end of the grant period, generally cannot continue to get Flexible Funding Assistance for the remainder of the grant period. However, where the Flexible Funding Assistance has been paid upfront, the client can continue to receive this assistance but will not be able to be granted any further Flexible Funding Assistance. Where reasonable and practicable, MSD may request the contracted provider to get a refund from the supplier of the unused portion of assistance paid to meet on-going needs, such as transport costs.

chunks.title: Examples — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text: Scenario: Reason: Client moves to rental property, school lunches already paid for by Flexible Funding Assistance We have paid Flexible Funding Assistance for a dependent child's school lunches for the week while they are staying in a motel funded by an Emergency Housing Grant. Although there are 4 nights remaining for their grant, the family has moved into a rental property As the Flexible Funding Assistance has already been paid to cover this period, the client can continue to receive this assistance to pay for the school lunches until the end of the week that has already been paid Client moves to rental property, transport to after school activities already paid for by Flexible Funding Assistance We have paid Flexible Funding Assistance for a dependent child's after school sporting activities for the week while they are staying in a motel funded by an Emergency Housing Grant. Although there are 4 nights remaining for their grant, the family has moved into a rental property. As the Flexible Funding Assistance has already been paid to cover this period, the client can continue to receive this assistance to pay for the after school sports activity until the end of the week that has already been paid

chunks.title: Paying Flexible Funding Assistance when over income and cash asset limits — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text:
## Paying Flexible Funding Assistance when over income and cash asset limits
When a client and partner (if any) have income or cash assets over the appropriate limits but have been paid, or would have been paid, an Emergency Housing Grant due to exceptional circumstances, Flexible Funding Assistance can be paid for the same period if they meet the other qualifications.
## Example 1
A non-beneficiary couple and their 4 dependent children need help with emergency housing as their property has been found to have asbestos, so they need to leave. They have $3000 in savings, so their combined cash assets are over the limit. However, they cannot access this money as it is needed to pay for a root canal at the dentist the following week.
They are unable to move in with family or friends and have no alternative accommodation. The case manager decides the family has exceptional circumstances and pays an Emergency Housing Grant.
They are also paid Flexible Funding Assistance to buy school lunches for the children as the emergency housing only has a small fridge.
## Example 2
A non-beneficiary client earns $1000 gross per week. They have had to leave their home due to family violence.
They have 2 children aged 7 and 4 years old and no other family support or place to go.
Even though they earn over the income limit ($947.09 gross as at 1 April 2026) they are unable to pay for emergency accommodation because they need to use their own resources to pay lawyer fees for a protection order and custody arrangements.
The case manager pays an Emergency Housing Grant as the client has exceptional circumstances.
As the emergency housing does not have laundry facilities, the client is paid Flexible Funding Assistance so they can use the laundromat next to their workplace.

chunks.title: Payment consistent with Flexible Funding Programme — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text:
## Payment consistent with Flexible Funding Programme
You must be satisfied the payment of Flexible Funding Assistance for the client's immediate need is consistent with the purpose of the Programme.
The purpose of the Programme is to help with meeting the educational, early childhood and wellbeing needs of families with children, where those families have additional costs because they are staying in emergency housing.

chunks.title: Payment not used as intended — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text:
## Payment not used as intended
When Flexible Funding Assistance is not used by the client for the purpose for which it was paid, it may become a recoverable debt under the Ministry's existing integrity and debt recovery processes.
This includes where the client seeks a refund from the supplier after the Contracted Provider has paid the supplier for the goods or services.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text:
## Payment
Flexible Funding Assistance provides one-off, non-taxable financial assistance for clients with dependent children staying in accommodation funded by an Emergency Housing Grant.
Actual and reasonable costs that may be covered by Flexible Funding Assistance include additional or increased costs relating to:
- participation in education, including early childhood education
- accessing childcare
- meeting wellbeing needs resulting from the families accommodation in emergency housing including: accessing health servicesfinding suitable social or alternative housing
- accessing health services
- finding suitable social or alternative housing
Note Flexible Funding Assistance is a discretionary payment (there is no maximum amount payable) and should only be considered after other sources of assistance to meet the need (including help from MSD), and the client's own available resources have been exhausted.
## Contracted providers
MSD has contracted with providers throughout regions to administer and make payments of Flexible Funding Assistance on MSD’s behalf.
Once MSD has decided to grant Flexible Funding Assistance for a client's need, MSD will need to identify (where possible) a supplier to provide the item or service. This is done by requesting the contracted provider in the client's region to make the payment to the supplier.
For more information on this process see:
- Flexible Funding Assistance [no link find out why]
Note Flexible Funding Assistance cannot be paid directly to suppliers.
## Other options to meet the need
If there are other less expensive suitable options to meet the client’s need, generally MSD should help with this option. However, if there is a good reason for the more expensive one, MSD may grant Flexible Funding Assistance.

chunks.title: Payments to people in specific circumstances — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text:
## Payments to people in specific circumstances
Some specific circumstances can affect whether a person can qualify or continue to be paid Flexible Funding Assistance.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
Flexible Funding Assistance is a last resort and non-recoverable assistance that helps meet the immediate needs of families with dependent children staying in emergency housing. The needs must relate to education, early childhood or the family's wellbeing and have happened because the client and their immediate family are staying in emergency housing.
To get Flexible Funding Assistance, a client must:
- qualify for and be staying in accommodation funded by an Emergency Housing Grant and
- have at least one dependent child in their care, staying with them in the same accommodation covered by an Emergency Housing Grant and
- meet an income limit and cash asset test (unless the client qualifies for an Emergency Housing Grant with excess income or assets due to exceptional circumstances) and
- meet the residence requirements for an Emergency Housing Grant
Note a person does not have to be getting a main benefit to qualify for Flexible Funding Assistance.
Hardship obligations do not apply to Flexible Funding Assistance.
## Client or their immediate family must also have an immediate need for assistance
In addition to the qualifications above, you must also be satisfied that the client or their immediate family has an immediate need for flexible funding assistance.

chunks.title: Qualifies for, and staying in emergency housing — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text:
## Qualifies for, and staying in emergency housing
To get Flexible Funding Assistance the client needs to:
- qualify for and be paid an Emergency Housing Grant and
- be staying with at least 1 of their dependent children in the same emergency housing paid for that Emergency Housing Grant
## Qualify for emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant
When considering Flexible Funding Assistance, MSD must be satisfied the client continues to meet the qualifications for an Emergency Housing Grant.
For example, a client is paid an Emergency Housing Grant and part way through the grant period, they accept and move into a social housing place. They no longer qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant, so they would not qualify for Flexible Funding Assistance if they applied for it during the remaining grant period.
## Staying in emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant
A client is staying in emergency housing if they or their partner (if any) and at least 1 dependent child in the client's care have been paid an Emergency Housing Grant and are either:
- staying in the emergency housing under a current Emergency Housing Grant or
- moving into the emergency housing today or within the next 7 nights
## Staying in emergency housing not funded by an Emergency Housing Grant
Some clients stay in emergency or temporary accommodation that is not funded by an Emergency Housing Grant. These clients are not eligible for Flexible Funding Assistance.
For more information see:
## No longer staying in emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant
A client who is no longer staying in emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant no longer qualifies to get Flexible Funding Assistance.

chunks.title: Residence requirements — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text:
## Residence requirements
To get Flexible Funding Assistance, a client must:
- qualify for and be getting a main benefit, New Zealand superannuation or veteran’s pension or
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand at the time of their application, and be a New Zealand citizen, orhold, or be deemed to hold, a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009, or
- be a New Zealand citizen, or
- hold, or be deemed to hold, a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009, or
- be recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009, or
- qualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary entry class visa with intention of applying for a residence class visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy but the relationship has ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)

chunks.title: Reviews and appeals — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text:
## Reviews and appeals
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have received formal notification of (and do not agree with) a decision made under the Flexible Funding Programme.

chunks.title: Staying in other emergency accommodation — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text:
## Staying in other emergency accommodation
Clients who are in emergency accommodation that is not funded by an Emergency Housing Grant do not qualify for Flexible Funding Assistance. This includes where the client is staying in:
- transitional housing (including transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development)
- contracted emergency housing
- short term boarding arrangements

chunks.title: Using discretion to pay Flexible Funding Assistance — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text: Flexible Funding Assistance is discretionary assistance. This discretion is used to make sure the assistance is available to those with the greatest need. MSD needs to consider the client's circumstances including if the assistance will directly meet the needs of the target group for this assistance.

chunks.title: Matters MSD must consider when using discretion — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text: When deciding whether to grant Flexible Funding Assistance, MSD must consider: - the purpose of the Flexible Funding Assistance programme: whether the need is directly related to education, early childhood or wellbeing, particularly any dependent children in the accommodation and - whether the need is directly related to education, early childhood or wellbeing, particularly any dependent children in the accommodation and - if declining the assistance would cause serious hardship to the client or their immediate family and - the impact of granting or not granting assistance on the client or their immediate family's ability to secure suitable social or other alternative housing and - if the client and their partner (if any) could reasonably be expected to have made provision for the need and - the availability of the funding

chunks.title: Serious hardship — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text: A decision not to grant Flexible Funding Assistance would be considered to cause serious hardship if: - the client would be unable to meet the other immediate needs of their family (eg, food or health costs) from their remaining resources (including other assistance from MSD) or - will have a serious effect on the client or their immediate family's health or welfare particularly any dependent children in the accommodation

chunks.title: Examples of immediate needs for Flexible Funding Assistance — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text: Families in emergency housing often have complex needs and their ability to secure suitable alternative housing may require the client to commit to a regular accommodation search and other wellbeing activities such as budgeting, counselling, health and meetings with other providers. These activities may result in additional costs for the client, e.g. travel or childcare, that, if not met, could impact their ability to secure suitable alternative housing. Where the needs, if not met, could impact on the client's ability to get suitable alternative housing you should consider using Flexible Funding Assistance to meet these needs.

chunks.title: Target group — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text: Flexible Funding Assistance is discretionary assistance and targeting is used to make sure this help is given to client's in situations where the: - impact of staying in accommodation funded by an Emergency Housing Grant is significant, and - need for assistance is greatest - in particular meeting the education, early childhood and wellbeing needs of any dependent children staying in accommodation funded by the Emergency Housing Grant. When the eligibility criteria have been met, there may be good reasons to approve this assistance outside of the target group. This is particularly important if it means there will be a positive impact on the family as a whole. For example, a client needs help to go to a property viewing as this will have benefits for the entire family.

chunks.title: Client or partner should have made provision for the need — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text: If it was reasonable to expect a client or their partner (if any) to have made provision for that need then MSD could decide not to provide Flexible Funding Assistance to meet that need. However, what is reasonable to expect a client or their partner (if any) to have made provision for will depend on the client's individual circumstances. What is reasonable for the client to have made provision for the need is dependent on their individual situation and every case must be addressed on their own merits. For example MSD may expect: - people who have been unexpectedly evicted or asked to leave their living environment and are staying in emergency housing to not have provision in their budget for getting their children from the new location to a school across town because they had not needed transport for this before as they had been able to walk the children to school been prepared to have an extra transport cost to get their children to school - people living in emergency housing to have extra food costs due to not being able to store food in bulk like they once did, however, it would have been reasonable to expect them to have their usual family food budget to use - a family who had their child change schools to be closer to the place they are staying, to not have made provisions for a new school uniform part-way through the term, however, if the child was intended to start the school anyway, you might consider that Flexible Fund Assistance is not appropriate

chunks.title: Warrant for the client's arrest — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text:
## Warrant for the client's arrest
Generally, clients with a warrant for their arrest may be considered to have caused or contributed to their immediate emergency housing need by not resolving their warrant (and leaving themselves unable to pay for accommodation costs).
They also may not have an emergency housing need if they would otherwise be in a correctional facility or other accommodation when their warrant is resolved.
## Applying for an Emergency Housing Grant
Clients who have their main benefit payments reduced, suspended or stopped because of an unresolved warrant for their arrest, will generally not be granted an Emergency Housing Grant until the:
- warrant has been resolved and
- benefit has been reinstated
Clients cannot get Flexible Funding Assistance if they have a warrant for their arrest because they do not qualify for an Emergency Housing Grant.
This applies even if they were getting Flexible Funding Assistance before an Emergency Housing Grant had been made.
## Currently getting an Emergency Housing Grant
If the client meets all the qualifying criteria (including continued eligibility for an Emergency Housing Grant), Flexible Funding Assistance may be granted to a client with an unresolved warrant for the remaining period of their Emergency Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Wellbeing needs created due to staying in emergency housing — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text:
## Wellbeing needs created due to staying in emergency housing
To determine if a client or their immediate family have immediate wellbeing needs because they are staying in emergency housing, we need to compare the circumstances of the client and their immediate family and their needs, from both before and during their stay in emergency accommodation.
## Assistance to continue to participate in regular activities they were already doing
In some circumstances Flexible Funding Assistance may be needed to allow clients to continue to participate in regular activities they were involved in before staying in emergency housing. Regular activities might be related to education, early childhood, employment, health and wellbeing, or social, religious or cultural pursuits.
## Assistance to do additional activities to support wellbeing while in emergency housing
Flexible Funding Assistance can also be used to decrease the impact on a person’s wellbeing of staying in emergency housing by helping them to participate in additional activities to support their wellbeing while in emergency housing. Example this may include enrolling children in additional out of school activities due to limited space in the emergency accommodation.

chunks.title: Who can get payments — extra help > flexible funding assistance
chunks.text:
## Who can get payments
MSD has contracted providers in each region who administer and make payments of Flexible Funding Assistance on MSD's behalf.
Once MSD has confirmed a client qualifies for Flexible Funding Assistance, the contracted provider will pay the assistance to the appropriate supplier.
Payments cannot be made directly to the client.
## Payments to contracted provider, to administer and make payments to supplier
MSD will not pay suppliers of the needed item or service directly.
Contracted providers will pay the supplier once they get the Flexible Funding Assistance request form.
## Preferred suppliers
MSD may have a contract with preferred suppliers. MSD currently has 2 preferred supplier arrangements in place for whiteware and glasses.
If a client needs help with getting whiteware or glasses, assistance should first be considered under an Advance Payment of Benefit, Recoverable Assistance Payment or Special Needs Grant.
When a preferred supplier arrangement is in place that covers an item or service the client needs e.g. whiteware/glasses but the client does not qualify for other assistance then Flexible Funding Assistance can be granted (if the criteria is met).
Where practical, MSD should generally use a preferred supplier to purchase this from when using Flexible Funding Assistance to pay for whiteware or glasses.
However, if there is a good reason not to, e.g. the client as an immediate need that the preferred supplier could not supply in time, MSD can use another supplier.
Example
A client wears glasses and cannot do their everyday living tasks without them eg, reading, driving, cooking etc. Their glasses break so need to get a new pair.
The preferred supplier in their area is fully booked up for the coming month but the client cannot wait that long. An optometrist who is not a preferred supplier can see the client the next day.
In this instance, we could look at paying the optometrist who is not a preferred supplier as the client needs their glasses as soon as possible.

chunks.title: Conditional payment of Funeral Grant — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Conditional payment of Funeral Grant
MSD may consider making a conditional payment of Funeral Grant where there is a request made on the grounds that the cash in the estate or the parental assets are not immediately available, or the income details of surviving partner or parents has not been finally determined and hardship will result if a payment is not made.
When a conditional payment is approved, MSD will obtain an authority from the person the payment is paid to, that they agree to repay all or part of it if it is later confirmed there was no eligibility for all or part of the payment.
The authority must be scanned and saved into the deceased person's record. A copy of the authority will be sent to the administrator of the estate or to the parents of a deceased child, advising that the estate is not to be distributed until MSD has been contacted.
Regular contact must be made with the administrator of the estate or the parents to determine the progress of the estate administration.
If on finalisation of the estate it is found that there was no eligibility for all or part of the conditional Funeral Grant payment, MSD will establish a debt and start recovery action.

chunks.title: Assessable estate of the deceased person — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Assessable estate of the deceased person
Assessable Estate means the estate of a deceased person. An estate is not limited to cash assets, it includes all of the assets and property owned solely by the deceased including land, cash assets, vehicles and household items.
For Funeral Grant, the assessable estate does not include:
- any asset that MSD considers to be impracticable to realise and
- any administration expenses (the actual costs incurred in the administration of the deceased's estate)
Note there are specific assets that must be excluded if the deceased person has a surviving partner or surviving children, or if the deceased was a child. These are called non-assessable assets.
For more information see:
- Non-assessable assets
## Joint tenancy and tenancy in common
Joint tenancy is the joint ownership of a property where all owners have an equal share.
If one owner dies, their share passes to the surviving owner(s). Joint tenancy does not become part of the deceased's estate and is not included in the assessable estate.
Tenancy in common is where each owner has a defined share in the property. If one owner dies, their share becomes part of their estate, and is included in the assessable estate.

chunks.title: Asset test - deceased child — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Asset test - deceased child
A Funeral Grant can be paid for the reasonable funeral expenses of a child's funeral if those expenses cannot be met by the total assessable assets.
Total assessable assets are the total of:
- the deceased child's assessable estate before the payment of any debts and
- the combined assets of the parent's, that are in excess of the asset exemption
Note the parents must also meet an income test.
A Funeral Grant cannot be paid if the reasonable funeral expenses can be met by the total assessable assets.
There are specific assets that must be excluded if the deceased person was a child. These are called non-assessable assets.
## Asset exemption for parent's assets
An asset exemption applies to the parent's assets. Any parental assets that are less than the asset exemption must not be included in the Funeral Grant assessment.
The asset exemption does not apply to the deceased person's assessable estate.
Note if the parents are separated, asset and income details are not required for the estranged other parent or any other person who is liable in law to maintain the child.

chunks.title: Asset test - deceased person with surviving partner — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Asset test - deceased person with surviving partner
A Funeral Grant can be paid towards the reasonable funeral expenses of a person's funeral if there is a surviving partner and the reasonable funeral expenses cannot be met by the total assessable assets.
Total assessable assets are the total of:
- the deceased person's assessable estate before the payment of any debts and
- the assets of the surviving partner that are in excess of the asset exemption
Note the surviving partner must also meet an income test.
A Funeral Grant cannot be paid if the reasonable funeral expenses can be met by the total assessable assets.
The deceased person's assessable estate and the surviving partner's assets do not include non-assessable assets.
## Asset exemption for surviving partner's assets
An asset exemption applies to the surviving partner's assets. Any assets of the surviving partner that are less than the asset exemption must not be included in the Funeral Grant assessment.
The asset exemption does not apply to the deceased person's assessable estate.
Note if the deceased person was getting a benefit, and terminal benefit was paid, the continued payment may form part of the deceased person's assessable estate.

chunks.title: Calculation of Funeral Grant payment — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Calculation of Funeral Grant payment
To calculate the Funeral Grant payable, complete the following steps:
## Step 1 - calculate the total assessable assets
Deceased person's assessable estate
$ _____
Add surviving partner or parents total assetsif applicable)
$ _____
Less asset exemption for surviving partner or parents
$ _____
Equals total assessable assets
$ _____
## Step 2 - calculate balance of reasonable funeral expenses
Note Funeral Grant is not payable if the reasonable funeral expenses are less than the total assessable assets.
Reasonable funeral expenses
$ _____
Less total assessable assets
$ _____
Equals balance of reasonable funeral expenses
$ _____
## Step 3 - calculate Funeral Grant payable
Compare the balance of reasonable funeral expenses to the maximum Funeral Grant. The Funeral Grant payable is the lesser amount.

chunks.title: Death referred to coroner — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Death referred to coroner
There are times when a person's death is referred to the coroner to investigate the cause of death.
The coroner's inquiry to determine the cause of death can be a lengthy process. A Funeral Grant application should not be delayed while awaiting the outcome of a coroner's inquiry if there is enough information to determine entitlement to assistance.
For example, it is enough to know the death is not the result of an accident without needing to know the exact cause of death.

chunks.title: Costs that are not related to a funeral — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Costs that are not related to a funeral
Sometimes an applicant may claim for costs that are not related to the funeral.
If it is found that a cost has not arisen directly from the funeral, it must not be included in the Funeral Grant assessment.
Costs that are not related to a funeral include:
- transport for attendees e.g. petrol, vehicle hire, or flights
- items purchased for anyone other than the deceased person e.g. formal funeral wear for a surviving partner
- accommodation costs for people attending the funeral e.g. a hotel
- costs associated with unveiling ceremonies
- cost of an urn
There is no discretion to include costs that are not directly related to a funeral in the Funeral Grant assessment.
## Example - cost is not related to a funeral
Hana has applied for a Funeral Grant for her father Ahman's funeral costs. She has provided evidence of the following costs:
- a formal dress for Hana to wear to the funeral
- a pine casket
- transport of the deceased to the crematorium
- cremation fees
The cost of the dress Hana purchased cannot be included in the Funeral Grant assessment as it is not a funeral cost. The other costs may be included in the Funeral Grant assessment as they are directly related to the funeral.
## Administration expenses
Administration expenses are costs incurred by the administrator in managing and carrying out the terms of a deceased person's estate. These expenses are deducted from the estate prior to the asset test rather than being treated as funeral costs.

chunks.title: Deceased child — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Deceased child
A Funeral Grant can be paid for the reasonable funeral expenses of a child's funeral if:
- the deceased child was ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date of death and
- the reasonable funeral expenses cannot be met by the total assessable assets, meaning: the deceased child's assessable estate before the payment of any debts andthe combined assets of the parents, that are in excess of the asset exemption and
- the deceased child's assessable estate before the payment of any debts and
- the combined assets of the parents, that are in excess of the asset exemption and
- the parent's income is below the appropriate income limit
If the parents are separated, asset and income details are not required for the estranged other parent or any other person who is liable in law to maintain the child.
A Funeral Grant can be paid for the reasonable funeral expenses of a stillborn child.
A baby is stillborn if the baby was not alive when born, and:
- weighed 400g or more at birth or
- was born after the 20th week of pregnancy
A Funeral Grant can be paid if the child was born alive and then died, whether or not the pregnancy was longer than 20 weeks.
## Effect on parent's financial assistance
If the child was included in their parent's main benefit or ongoing Extra help assistance, that assistance should be reviewed to determine if they are no longer eligible or if there is any change in the rate payable.
For more information see:
- Child changes in the relevant Main benefit
- Changes and reviews in the relevant Extra help

chunks.title: Deceased person died in New Zealand but their funeral is overseas — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Deceased person died in New Zealand but their funeral is overseas
A Funeral Grant may be paid in respect of a deceased person who died in New Zealand and is repatriated overseas, if they were ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they died.
## Costs associated with repatriation to another country
Repatriation is when the deceased person's body is moved from one country to another following their death. Repatriation may occur for many reasons including:
- fulfilling the deceased person's wishes
- to honour religious, cultural or spiritual beliefs
- allow for mourning and commemoration in the deceased person's home country
Costs that are associated with moving the deceased person's body from New Zealand to another country can be included in the assessment of Funeral Grant if they are determined to be reasonable by MSD.
Example
Mukai moved permanently to New Zealand from Zimbabwe in 2010 and is ordinarily resident. In June Mukai passed away while in New Zealand.
Mukai is to be repatriated to Zimbabwe to be buried in line with her wishes. As she was ordinarily resident in New Zealand when she died a Funeral Grant may be paid in respect of her reasonable funeral expenses. This may include the expenses related to moving her body to from New Zealand to another country.
## Funeral held overseas
If the funeral is held overseas MSD may consider a Funeral Grant for any funeral costs that are determined to be reasonable.
Example
Sabina moved permanently to New Zealand from Nepal in 2014 and is ordinarily resident. In August Sabina passed away while still living in New Zealand.
Sabina's family have organised for her to be repatriated to Nepal, where a funeral service will be held. This will allow her family to mourn and commemorate Sabina in her home country.
As Sabina was ordinarily resident in New Zealand when she died a Funeral Grant may be paid in respect of her reasonable funeral expenses.

chunks.title: Deceased person died overseas — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text: A Funeral Grant may be paid in respect of a deceased person who died overseas if they were ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they died.

chunks.title: Costs associated with repatriation to New Zealand — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text: Repatriation is when a deceased person's body is moved from one country to another following their death. Repatriation may occur for many reasons including: - fulfilling a deceased person's wishes - to honour religious, cultural or spiritual beliefs - allow for mourning and commemoration in the deceased person's home country Costs that are associated with moving a deceased person's body back to New Zealand can be included in the assessment of Funeral Grant if they are determined to be reasonable by MSD. Example - deceased person is ordinarily resident Javi has lived in New Zealand since childhood and is ordinarily resident in New Zealand. On 25 May he left New Zealand to visit friends in Spain. On 3 June Javi passed away while still in Spain. Javi will be repatriated to New Zealand for his funeral. As he was ordinarily resident in New Zealand when he died a Funeral Grant may be paid in respect of his reasonable funeral expenses, including the cost of moving his body back to New Zealand. Example - deceased person is not ordinarily resident Hoani is a New Zealand citizen and lived here since birth. In June Hoani sold his property and left New Zealand to move permanently to Canada. Hoani passed away in November while still living in Canada. Hoani will be repatriated to New Zealand for a tangihanga. As Hoani left New Zealand to move permanently to another country, he was not ordinarily resident in New Zealand when he died. A Funeral Grant cannot be paid towards Hoani's reasonable funeral expenses as he was not ordinarily resident in New Zealand when he died.

chunks.title: Funeral held overseas — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text: If the funeral of a deceased person who was ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they died is held overseas, MSD may consider a Funeral Grant for any funeral costs that are determined to be reasonable. Example Linh moved to New Zealand permanently in 2010 and is ordinarily resident in New Zealand. On 20 November she left New Zealand to visit her family in Viet Nam. Linh passed away on 11 December while she was in Viet Nam. Linh's family organised a funeral service to be held in Viet Nam which honours Linh's wishes. This means she will not be repatriated to New Zealand. As Linh was ordinarily resident in New Zealand when she died a Funeral Grant may be paid in respect of her reasonable funeral expenses.

chunks.title: Deceased person with a surviving partner — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Deceased person with a surviving partner
A Funeral Grant can be paid towards the reasonable funeral expenses of a deceased person with a surviving partner if:
- the deceased person was ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date of death and
- the surviving partner has income below the appropriate income limit and
- the reasonable funeral expenses cannot be met by the total assessable assets, meaning: the deceased person's assessable estate before the payment of any debts andthe assets of the surviving partner in excess of the asset exemption
- the deceased person's assessable estate before the payment of any debts and
- the assets of the surviving partner in excess of the asset exemption
A Funeral Grant cannot be paid if the reasonable funeral expenses can be met by the total of the deceased person's assessable estate and the partners assets.
## Deceased person with a surviving child or children
If the deceased person does not have a surviving partner, but they have a surviving child or children, a Funeral Grant can be paid towards their reasonable funeral expenses if:
- the deceased person was ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date of death and
- the reasonable funeral expenses cannot be met by the deceased person's assessable estate before the payment of any debts
A Funeral Grant cannot be paid if the reasonable funeral expenses can be met by the deceased person's assessable estate.
## Terminal benefit payments
If the deceased person was getting a benefit, and terminal benefit was paid, the continued payment may form part of the deceased person's assessable estate.

chunks.title: Deceased single person with no children — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Deceased single person with no children
A Funeral Grant can be paid towards the reasonable funeral expenses of a single person with no surviving children if:
- the deceased person was ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date of death and
- the reasonable funeral expenses cannot be met by the deceased person's assessable estate before the payment of any debts
A Funeral Grant cannot be paid if the reasonable funeral expenses can be met by the deceased's assessable estate.
Note a deceased person under 18 years of age is considered to be a child, unless they were 16 or 17 years old and financially independent.
## Terminal benefit payments
If the deceased person was getting a benefit, and payment continued after the date of death as terminal benefit or to avoid establishing debt, the continued payment may form part of the deceased person's assessable estate.

chunks.title: Cash assets include — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Cash assets include
Any assets of the deceased person, the surviving partner (if any), or the parent (if a deceased child) should be considered when assessing entitlement to a Funeral Grant. This includes the following:
- shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds, and other bonds
- bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society
- money invested with or lent to any bank or other financial institution
- for a deceased person who was single and had no dependent children: the net equity held in any property that was owned by the deceased person
- for other deceased persons: the net equity held in any property or land not used as the family home
- building society shares
- Information share Child Support payments no longer being charged as income (i.e. the payment was being charged when the client died but Terminal Benefit is not payable)
- mortgage investments and other long term loans
- bills of exchange or promissory notes
- the parents' share in any partnership
- proceeds from life insurance policies or retirement funds
- prepaid funeral account (the total amount in the account before it is used towards the funeral expenses)
## Cash assets do not include
When the deceased is a child, or the deceased person is survived by a partner or children there are certain assets that are defined as non-assessable assets that must not be included when considering entitlement a Funeral Grant. These are:
- the family home
- the family car, caravan or boat
- Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income
- furniture in the family home
- personal possessions and ornaments
- Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014
- Severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment)
- FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received

chunks.title: Determining if a funeral cost is reasonable — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Determining if a funeral cost is reasonable
MSD must always determine if a funeral cost is a reasonable funeral expense before it can be included in the Funeral Grant assessment.
MSD may determine any cost to be reasonable if it is:
- related to the proper disposal of the body
- associated with tikanga practices related to tangihanga
- related to any service or ceremony including but not limited to: cultural, spiritual, or religious practicesother customs in respect or commemoration of the person who has died
- cultural, spiritual, or religious practices
- other customs in respect or commemoration of the person who has died
If a cost does not fit into one of the above categories, MSD must still determine if it is reasonable.
Note this includes giving consideration to secular or personalised funerals.
If MSD needs more information to determine if a cost is reasonable, this must be requested with sensitivity and in a way that upholds the dignity of both the deceased person and the person being asked.
## Example
Tiana has applied for a Funeral Grant for her brother Tama's tangihanga costs.
Included in the tangihanga costs is $1,050 for kai (food), which was verified with receipts.
The cost of kai (food) is a reasonable funeral expense and can be included in the assessment of Funeral Grant.
## Funeral costs may not be reasonable
In most cases, costs that arise directly from a funeral should not be scrutinised.
Note if it cannot be determined that a funeral cost is reasonable, MSD may exercise discretion to consider it to be reasonable and include it in the Funeral Grant assessment.
If MSD staff are unsure if a funeral cost is reasonable, they can contact Helpline for advice.

chunks.title: Reasonable funeral expenses — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Reasonable funeral expenses
MSD must determine whether a funeral cost is a reasonable funeral expense before it can be included in the Funeral Grant assessment.
MSD may determine any cost to be reasonable if it is:
- related to the proper disposal of the body
- associated with tikanga practices related to tangihanga
- related to any service or ceremony including but not limited to: cultural, spiritual, or religious practicesother customs in respect or commemoration of the person who has died
- cultural, spiritual, or religious practices
- other customs in respect or commemoration of the person who has died
If a cost does not fit into one of the above categories, MSD must still determine if it is reasonable. This is done on a case-by-case basis, by taking into account whether the cost was appropriate for the ceremony that was held in respect of the deceased person.
## Types of reasonable funeral expenses
Common types of reasonable funeral expenses may include:
- any professional services fees charged by a funeral director
- cost of a casket, coffin or burial shroud
- hearse fees
- burial fees (including plot and interment)
- cremation fees (including water cremation)
- food including kai (food) for a tangihanga
- ministers, celebrant or clergy fees
- flowers
- a pictorial tribute or slideshow
Costs such as alcohol are generally not considered reasonable, though may be determined to be reasonable on a case-by-case basis when considering individual circumstances.
If MSD staff are unsure if a funeral cost is reasonable, they can contact Helpline for advice.
Note if it cannot be determined that a funeral cost is reasonable, MSD may exercise discretion to consider it to be reasonable and include it in the Funeral Grant assessment.
## Costs related to moving the body from one country to another
Costs associated with moving the deceased person's body to or from New Zealand may be included in the Funeral Grant assessment if the cost is determined to be reasonable.
Note the deceased person must have been ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they died.

chunks.title: Estate not finalised — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Estate not finalised
In some cases, the deceased person's estate will not be finalised when the applicant applies for a Funeral Grant.
In this situation, MSD may make a payment of Funeral Grant, on the condition that all or part of it must be repaid if it is later found that there was no eligibility.

chunks.title: Example - married couple — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text: Virantha has made an application for Funeral Grant for his partner Maia's reasonable funeral expenses. They were getting Jobseeker Support at the time of Maia's death, without any other income. Terminal benefit was not paid. Virantha provided evidence of the funeral costs and MSD determined the following to be reasonable funeral expenses: Flowers $150 Food for reception $250 Cremation fee (and related expenses) $1,030 Pine casket $1,200 Transport to crematorium $150 Musician hire $240 Venue hire $640 Professional services $2,920 Celebrant fee $200 Total reasonable funeral expenses $6,780 Step 1 - calculate the total assessable assets Deceased person's assessable estate $1,890.00 Add surviving partners total assets $2,530.00 Less asset exemption for surviving partner $2,280.58 Equals total assessable assets $2,139.42 Step 2 - calculate balance of reasonable funeral expenses Note Funeral Grant is not payable if the reasonable funeral expenses are less than the total assessable assets. Reasonable funeral expenses $6,780.00 Less total assessable assets $2,139.42 Equals balance of reasonable funeral expenses $4,640.58 Step 3 - calculate Funeral Grant payable The balance of Maia's reasonable funeral expenses is more than the maximum Funeral Grant of $2,697.43 (as at 1 April 2026). The maximum Funeral Grant of $2,697.43 can be paid towards Maia's reasonable funeral expenses.

chunks.title: Example - single client — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text: Mikaere has applied for a Funeral Grant for his sister Kara's tangihanga costs. Kara was single with no children. Kara was getting Supported Living Payment when she passed away and terminal benefit was not paid. Mikaere provided evidence of the tangihanga costs and MSD determined the following to be reasonable funeral expenses: Kai (food) $1,120.00 Cooling mats (to keep Kara's body cool) $154.00 Casket $1,615.00 Petrol to transport Kara's body to the urupā (burial ground) $145.00 Total reasonable funeral expenses $3,034.00 Step 1 - calculate the total assessable assets As Kara is not a child and does not have a surviving partner her total assessable assets are equal to her assessable estate of $980. Step 2 - calculate balance of reasonable funeral expenses Note Funeral Grant is not payable if the reasonable funeral expenses are less than the total assessable assets. Reasonable funeral expenses $3,034.00 Less total assessable assets $980.00 Equals balance of reasonable funeral expenses $2,054.00 Step 3 - calculate Funeral Grant payable The balance of Kara's reasonable funeral expenses is less than the maximum Funeral Grant of $2,697.43 (as at 1 April 2026). A Funeral Grant of $2,054.00 can be paid towards Kara's reasonable funeral expenses.

chunks.title: Funeral costs — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Funeral costs
Funeral costs are any costs that arise directly from a funeral and would usually be paid for from the deceased person's estate. Funeral costs will vary depending on the kind of funeral that is held.
Although funerals may share similar traits, each funeral is unique and will depend on a range of factors such as:
- tangihanga practices in accordance with tikanga or
- cultural, religious or spiritual practices or
- modern and personalised funeral services
## Reasonable funeral expenses
Only reasonable funeral expenses can be included in the Funeral Grant assessment.
If it is confirmed that a cost is directly related to a funeral, MSD must then determine if it is a reasonable funeral expense.

chunks.title: Income test for parents — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Income test for parents
A Funeral Grant can be paid towards a deceased child's reasonable funeral expenses if the parents have annual income below the appropriate income limit.
Note parents who are getting a main benefit must also meet the income test. The parent's annual income is their estimated income for the 52 weeks from the day following the child's death.
Main benefit payments must not be included as income.
A Funeral Grant cannot be paid if the parents income exceeds the income limit.
The income limit will depend on the parent's circumstances following the date of the child's death.
Note if the parents are separated, asset and income details are not required for the estranged other parent or any other person who is liable in law to maintain the child.
## Example
Pia has applied for a Funeral Grant for her child Tiana's reasonable funeral expenses.
Pia is a sole parent with 1 other child. She is getting Sole Parent Support and is working part-time. Her total estimated annual income from her part-time job is $46,898.
The Funeral Grant income limit for a single parent with 1 other child is $46,745.92 as at 1 April 2026.
A Funeral Grant cannot be paid as Pia's estimated annual income from her part-time job exceeds the Funeral Grant income limit.

chunks.title: Income test for surviving partner — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Income test for surviving partner
A Funeral Grant can be paid if the surviving partner has annual income below the appropriate income limit.
Note surviving partners who are getting a main benefit must also meet the income test. Main benefit payments must not be included as income.
The surviving partner's annual income is their estimated income for the 52 weeks from the day following the deceased person's death.
The income limit will depend on the surviving partner's circumstances following the date of their partner's death.
A Funeral Grant cannot be paid if the surviving partner's income exceeds the income limit.
## Example
Samir has applied for a Funeral Grant for his partner Nina's reasonable funeral expenses.
Following Nina's death, Samir is a sole parent with 1 child. He is totally blind and gets Supported Living Payment. His total estimated annual income from his job is $47,450.
The Funeral Grant income limit for a surviving partner with 1 child is $46,745.92 as at 1 April 2026.
A Funeral Grant cannot be paid as Samir's estimated annual income exceeds the income limit.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The Funeral Grant is a non-taxable lump sum payment that provides assistance towards a deceased person's reasonable funeral expenses.
The Funeral Grant is intended to help with the actual and reasonable funeral expenses that cannot be met by other means (up to a maximum amount).
The deceased person did not need to be getting a benefit to be eligible for a Funeral Grant.

chunks.title: Key words within trusts — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Key words within trusts
Trust
A trust is a legal obligation accepted by the trustees to hold property for the benefit of beneficiaries of the trust.
The trust property is commonly gifted or sold by the 'settlor'.
Settlor
The person(s) who sets up the trust. Normally this is the person(s) intending to sell or gift assets to the trust but sometimes it is another person (such as a lawyer) who is merely setting up the mechanism of a trust to be used by someone else (such as the client).
Trustees
The people appointed to hold legal ownership of the trust's assets under an obligation to manage these in a way that will benefit the beneficiaries.
Their prime duty is to carry out the terms of the trust deed and preserve trust property.
Beneficiaries
Individual(s) or group(s) for whose benefit the trust was established. Beneficiaries have a legal right to seek disbursements from the trust.
It is at the Trusts discretion to make distributions (for example, regular payments) to discretionary beneficiaries. It is a legal obligation to distribute Trust contents to the final beneficiaries when it is wound up.
Trust deed
This is the document that establishes the trust. It will be signed by the settlor and the trustee(s) and outline who the trustees and beneficiaries are.
The deed usually states the purpose of the trust which may include how the property should be invested, when distributions can be made, as well as what powers are given to the Trustees.

chunks.title: Method of payment and reimbursements — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Method of payment and reimbursements
A Funeral Grant can be paid to any of the following:
- a funeral director
- the surviving partner or child of the deceased
- the deceased person's estate
- the parent of a deceased child
- any person who has paid the deceased's funeral expenses
## Reimbursements
If the reasonable funeral expenses have already been paid, MSD may pay a Funeral Grant directly to the person who paid for those costs. The person must provide proof of payment.
Note the payment must be made directly to the person who paid the reasonable funeral expenses even if someone else made the application.

chunks.title: Net equity — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Net equity
Net equity in a property is considered in the asset test when a deceased person who is single with no surviving children owned their own house or when a deceased person (with or without a surviving partner or children) owned more than 1 house.
The net equity of a house is the amount of money the owner would get from the sale of the property.
For example, where a person owned their home and had a mortgage, the net equity is the total value of the home minus the mortgage owing.
If a person did not have a mortgage the net equity is the total amount of money they could get for the property.
## House and land
When assessing the net equity of a house and/or land, use the rateable valuation or the amount insured, whichever value is greater.
Note If the property is jointly owned with another person and is being passed to the surviving owner it will not form part of the deceased person's estate.
Example
House valued at
$300,000
Land valued at
$400,000
Total combined value
$700,000
Less outstanding Mortgage principal
$150,000
Net equity
$550,000
In some cases Councils use the Capital value of a property which will be noted on the rate notice. Capital value is the value of both the house and land value combined.
Example
Capital value
$700,000
Less outstanding Mortgage principal
$150,000
Net equity
$550,000
## Secondary property
If a deceased person with a surviving partner or surviving children, had 2 properties that they resided in equally, MSD will determine which house was the primary place of residence in order to assess the deceased's assessable estate.
To determine which property is the primary place of residence, consider what their primary residential address was for electoral rolls, vehicle registration, dentist, health practitioner, lawyer, council rates etc.

chunks.title: Non-assessable assets — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Non-assessable assets
Non-assessable assets are specific assets that must be excluded from:
- the assessable estate of: a deceased person who has a surviving partner ora deceased child
- a deceased person who has a surviving partner or
- a deceased child
- the assets of a surviving partner
- the assets of the parents of a deceased child
Non-assessable assets of a deceased person, a surviving partner, or the parents of a deceased child are:
- that person's interest (on the date of death) in their own principal place of residence, including the land on which it is built and any other buildings or improvements on that land that are used mainly for the purposes of that person's household, and
- any undivided beneficial interest in common Māori land and
- any of the following items that the person owned or possessed through hire purchase, a conditional sales agreement, or an agreement for lease or hire: furniture, appliances, tools, ornaments, or other items used mainly for the purposes of the deceased's household ormotor vehicles, caravans, trailers, or boats used mainly for family purposes
- furniture, appliances, tools, ornaments, or other items used mainly for the purposes of the deceased's household or
- motor vehicles, caravans, trailers, or boats used mainly for family purposes
Note non-assessable assets do not apply to the assessable estate of a deceased person who is single and is aged 18 years or over.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Payment
Once eligibility has been established, MSD must assess the amount of Funeral Grant that can be paid.
The amount of Funeral Grant payable is the lesser of the:
- reasonable funeral expenses that cannot be met by the total assessable assets or
- the maximum Funeral Grant
The maximum Funeral Grant that can be paid to meet reasonable funeral expenses is $2,697.43 (as at 1 April 2026).
Note there is no time limit on when a Funeral Grant application must be made following a person's death.
## Circumstances at date of death
Funeral Grant must be assessed using the following regardless of when the application was submitted:
- the deceased person's family circumstances on the date of death
- the deceased person's assessable estate, before the distribution of assets.
The income limits and asset exemptions that were current on the date of death must be used when completing the Funeral Grant assessment.

chunks.title: Proof — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Proof
A Funeral Grant cannot be assessed until evidence of the following has been received:
- proof of death, such as a death certificate or a newspaper notice. If the person applying for the Funeral Grant is unable to provide proof of death, a death verification form should be sent to Births, Deaths and Marriages.
- proof of reasonable funeral expenses
MSD may also require the applicant to provide evidence of:
- the deceased person's assessable estate
- the income and assets of a surviving partner or parents of a deceased child
- whether the funeral is funded elsewhere
- any involvement in a trust by the deceased person, a surviving partner, or the parents of a deceased child
Note if an applicant declares that a deceased child has no estate, this should be accepted unless there is reason to doubt the information provided.
## Stillborn
Stillbirths require a birth registration, but not a death registration. This means a death certificate will not be available for a stillborn child.
The applicant will need to provide information to confirm the child was stillborn. This could be:
- proof of birth registration (as a stillbirth)
- a medical certificate confirming the baby was stillborn at birth
- a hospital discharge summary
- a letter from the midwife or obstetrician confirming the child was stillborn

chunks.title: Funeral is funded elsewhere — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Funeral is funded elsewhere
A Funeral Grant must not be paid if any of the following are payable in respect of the deceased person:
- an ACC Funeral Grant -(paid when the death was caused by an accident or injury covered by ACC) or
- a Veterans Pension Lump Sum payment on death -(paid upon the death of a veteran or their partner) or
- a War Funeral Grant (paid when a qualifying veteran dies, or the surviving partner and/or dependent children are eligible for Surviving Spouse Pension or Child Pension or other similar grant)
Note a Funeral Grant cannot be used towards any remaining funeral costs that cannot be covered by the above assistance.
## Determining if other funding is available
In most cases it will be clear whether or not the funeral can be funded elsewhere e.g. if a person has died as the result of an accident, they may qualify for an ACC Funeral Grant.
In cases where it is not clear whether the funeral may be funded elsewhere, MSD must request proof before a Funeral Grant can be approved.
## Example 1
An application is received for a Funeral Grant. The death is not the result of an accident, and the deceased person was not a veteran.
Proof that assistance for funeral expenses is not available elsewhere is not required in this case.
## Example 2
An application is received for a Funeral Grant. The applicant advises that the deceased person died as the result of an accident.
Based on this, a funeral grant under the Accident Compensation Act 2001 may be payable.
The applicant should be referred to ACC to test their eligibility.
A Funeral Grant may still be payable if the applicant provides proof that there is no eligibility to an ACC Funeral Grant.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
For a Funeral Grant to be paid:
- the deceased person must have been ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they died and
- their reasonable funeral expenses are unable to be met by the: deceased person's estateassets of a surviving partner in excess of the asset exemptioncombined assets of the parents of a deceased child, in excess of the asset exemption
- deceased person's estate
- assets of a surviving partner in excess of the asset exemption
- combined assets of the parents of a deceased child, in excess of the asset exemption
An income test must also be met by any surviving partner or the parents' of a deceased child.
Note a Funeral Grant must not be paid if other specified funding is available.
For more information see:
- Funeral is funded elsewhere

chunks.title: Terminal benefit — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Terminal benefit
If the deceased person was getting a benefit when they died and terminal benefit was paid, the continued payment may form part of the deceased person's assessable estate.
## Surviving partner
If the benefit is paid to a couple, both the deceased person's and the surviving partner's portion of the benefit is paid as terminal benefit.
The deceased person's portion of terminal benefit is generally paid to their own bank account. However, a surviving partner can apply to have the deceased person's portion of terminal benefit paid to them.
## Surviving child
If the deceased person has no surviving partner, but has a surviving child, the payment of terminal benefit can be made to the person caring for the deceased person's child.
## When terminal benefit is included in the deceased person's estate
Terminal benefit payments become part of the deceased person's assessable estate when it is paid to the deceased person's nominated bank account.
## When terminal benefit is not included in the deceased person's estate
Terminal benefit payments do not become part of the deceased person's estate when it is paid to the surviving partner or to an account that is shared with the surviving partner.
In this case the payment may become a cash asset of the surviving partner.
Note terminal benefit payments do not become part of the deceased person's estate if is paid to a person caring for their surviving child.

chunks.title: Total assessable assets — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Total assessable assets
If a deceased person was single without children, their total assessable assets are equal to their assessable estate.
In all other situations the total assessable assets for Funeral Grant are the total of:
- the deceased person's assessable estate before the payment of any debts and
- if the deceased person is a child, the combined assets of the parents that are in excess of the asset exemption or
- if the deceased person has a surviving partner, the assets of the surviving partner that are in excess of the asset exemption
A Funeral Grant cannot be paid if the reasonable funeral expenses can be met by the total assessable assets.
## Calculating total assessable assets
The total assessable assets are calculated as follows:
Surviving partner or parents total assets(if applicable)
$ _____
Less asset exemption for surviving partner or parents
$ _____
Equals surviving partner or parents assessable assets
$ _____
Add deceased person's assessable estate
$ _____
Equals total assessable assets
$ _____

chunks.title: Trusts — extra help > funeral grant
chunks.text:
## Trusts
A trust is a legal arrangement that is created when a settlor sells or gifts assets such as real estate, life insurance and investments into a trust for the benefit of others.
Involvement by any of the following people in a trust may affect the entitlement to a Funeral Grant:
- the deceased person (including a deceased child) and
- a surviving partner and
- the parents of a deceased child
MSD must determine if there is any asset balance owed by the trust to any of these people, or any continuing income from the trust to a surviving partner or to the parents of a deceased child.
If the deceased person, the surviving partner, or the parents of a deceased child was getting a main benefit or Extra help, MSD may already hold details of the trust.
If details of the trust are not already held, the following information will be required.
## Assets
Any balances owed by a trust to the deceased person, a surviving partner or the parents of a deceased child are assets for that person.
Asset balances will show in the trust's financial statements, or in the last Deed of Forgiveness of Debt (a legal document used to record when a person gives away their own assets).
Note assets that have been fully gifted (given away with no balance still owed) in the past cannot be included in the asset test.
## Income
Any continuing income that a surviving partner or the parents of a deceased child gets from a trust must be included in the income assessment for that person.
If there is only a home in the trust, there is no continuing income. If there are investments of any kind in the trust MSD must determine what income, if any, will continue to be paid from that investment.

chunks.title: 20 Hours Early Childhood Education and Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment — extra help > guaranteed childcare assistance payment
chunks.text:
## 20 Hours Early Childhood Education and Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment
Children aged 3, 4 and 5 years old attending early childhood education services (kindergartens, centre based, home-based, kōhanga reo and playcentres) offering 20 Hours Early Childhood Education (ECE) may be able to get up to 6 hours per day, 20 hours per week of subsidised early childhood education.
Generally, young parents eligible for Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment will be better off getting 20 Hours ECE where their provider offers it.
This is because 20 Hours ECE fully funds early childhood education for up to 20 hours a week.
Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment subsidises childcare up to a maximum amount per hour, meaning young parents may still have costs to pay after the subsidy is paid.
However, young parents can choose to take up either:
- 20 Hours ECE only or
- Guaranteed Childcare Assistance payment when they qualify or
- a combination of both, but generally not for the same hours. For example, Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment can be used to pay for any extra hours not covered by 20 Hours ECE
## When a young parent takes up 20 Hours ECE
- They can get Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment for any other hours not covered by 20 Hours ECE up to a maximum of 30 hours per week.
- Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment cannot be paid for the same hours 20 Hours ECE is paid except when home-based educator top up payments are charged for those hours.
## Young parent does not take up 20 Hours ECE
If a young parent is enrolled in an early childhood education programme or service that does not offer the 20 Hours ECE or the young parent chooses not to take up 20 Hours ECE, they can apply for Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment under the current qualifications.

chunks.title: Fees — extra help > guaranteed childcare assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Fees
Fees are compulsory payments a caregiver must pay as a condition of their child's enrolment.
A provider may enforce fees by withholding or withdrawing enrolment or part of their service if a caregiver does not pay.
Providers cannot charge fees for the same hours as 20 Hours Early Childhood Education (ECE). Providers can only request fees for other hours of enrolment that are not covered by the 20 Hours ECE.

chunks.title: 20 Hours Early Childhood Education optional payments — extra help > guaranteed childcare assistance payment
chunks.text:
## 20 Hours Early Childhood Education optional payments
Optional payments may be charged by providers for costs not covered in the hourly fee for childcare funded by Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment and 20 Hours Early Childhood Education (ECE).
There are 2 types of optional payments that providers may charge.
## Donations
Donations are voluntary payments. There is no obligation for a caregiver to pay these charges and the childcare provider cannot enforce payment.
Examples of donations include requests for extra funds to help pay for a school mural or a gift for a teacher leaving.
## Optional charges
Optional charges are costs for a specific purpose that a caregiver can choose whether to pay or not.
They can be one-off or ongoing costs.
Providers formally agree optional charges with caregivers and may enforce charges if a caregiver does not pay.
Optional charges must reflect the real and actual cost of the item or activity.
Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment cannot be used to pay for optional payments.

chunks.title: Activity requirements — extra help > guaranteed childcare assistance payment
chunks.text: To get Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment, the child must be enrolled in an approved early childhood education programme while the young parent is: - complying with a youth activity obligation, or - in full-time education, approved training, or work-based learning if their youngest child is less than 12 months old, or - working part-time If a young parent is exempt from their youth activity obligations they will generally not qualify for Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment.

chunks.title: Youth activity obligations — extra help > guaranteed childcare assistance payment
chunks.text: Youth activity obligations include being enrolled in and undertaking, or being available for: - full-time secondary or tertiary education, or - approved training, or - work-based learning Young parents may also have other obligations related to budgeting and parenting education. For more information on youth activity obligations for people getting Young Parent Payment see: - Young Parent Payment Youth activity obligations For more information on youth activity obligations for partners of specified beneficiaries see: - Emergency Benefit Youth activity obligations - Jobseeker Support Youth activity obligations - Supported Living Payment Youth activity obligations - New Zealand Superannuation Obligations - Veteran's Pension Obligations Young parents must attend (or be about to attend) secondary school full-time if they are not getting an income-tested main benefit and are either: - single, or - in a relationship and have a partner who is also not getting an income-tested main benefit

chunks.title: Youngest dependent child is under 12 months — extra help > guaranteed childcare assistance payment
chunks.text: Some Young Parent Payment clients, and some partners of specified beneficiaries do not have to be in full-time education, training or work-based learning because their youngest child is less than 12 months old. In these cases, the obligation to be in or available for full-time education, training or work-based learning applies on the earlier of: - the day the child turns 6 months old if there is a suitable place available for the young person in a teen parent unit andMSD is satisfied that there are no special circumstances justifying the obligation starting at a later date - if there is a suitable place available for the young person in a teen parent unit and - MSD is satisfied that there are no special circumstances justifying the obligation starting at a later date or - the day the child becomes 12 months old If a young parent is not required to be in full-time education, training or work-based learning because of the age of their youngest child but is taking actions that would be considered to meet this youth activity obligation, they may also qualify for Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment.

chunks.title: Young parent is working — extra help > guaranteed childcare assistance payment
chunks.text: Young parents may also be able to get Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment to help with childcare costs while they are in paid employment. However, Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment can only be paid for these hours if the young parent is not required to participate in activity requirements at the same time. For example, a young parent attending high school cannot get Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment to pay for childcare costs while they are working if their work hours are at times when they should be at school. Part-time work Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment can only be paid for childcare hours for a maximum of 15 hours each week while the young parent is at work. This is in addition to childcare they may need while they are in education, training or work-based learning. If the young parent is working more than 15 hours a week, Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment cannot be paid for any additional hours of childcare required while they are at work. Full-time work Young parents working full-time generally do not qualify for Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment. This is because they cannot meet the activity requirements. For example, they can't attend secondary school full-time or comply with their youth obligations while working full-time.

chunks.title: Approved early childhood education programme or service — extra help > guaranteed childcare assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Approved early childhood education programme or service
An approved early childhood education programme means early childhood education provided by any of the following:
