chunks.title: Young parent has a sanction imposed — extra help > guaranteed childcare assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Young parent has a sanction imposed
Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment can continue when a young parent is sanctioned as long as they still meet the qualifications to receive it.
## Example 1 - Payment should stop
If a young parent is receiving Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment for childcare when they are in school and then they are sanctioned for not attending school, Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment should stop if the young parent has not recomplied within 30 days.
## Example 2 - Payment should continue
If a young parent is receiving Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment for childcare when they are in school and then they are sanctioned for not attending a parenting programme but they are continuing to attend school, Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment should continue to be paid.
Service providers will advise the YSSU by updating the activity participation status when a young parent fails to comply with their obligations and also when they recomply via the ART tool.
## Young Parent Payment is cancelled
When a young parent is no longer entitled to Young Parent Payment or they are not meeting their obligations to be in education, training or work-based learning, they will either have to qualify as a non-beneficiary for Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment or apply for other Childcare Assistance.

chunks.title: Young parent is a dependent child of a parent or guardian — extra help > guaranteed childcare assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Young parent is a dependent child of a parent or guardian
Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment can be paid when the young parent is a dependent child of their parent or guardian. A young parent is still considered to be dependent child of their parent or guardian when they are:
- the primary responsibility of the parent or guardian
- maintained as members of that family
- financially dependent on the parent or guardian
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 and
- not a child for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid
In some situations, a child (for example the young parent and their child) may not be living at home but are still considered to be dependent children of the parent or guardian.
## Parent or guardian getting a main benefit
If the parent or guardian is getting a main benefit for their dependent child (for example the young parent and their child) they can continue getting their main benefit.
However, they cannot get assistance for the same childcare costs when the young parent is getting the Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment for the eligible child.
They can get childcare costs for another child.
## Parent should accompany young person
When a young person aged 16 or 17 years is single and getting this payment because they are considered a dependent child of their parent, the parent or guardian should accompany the young parent to appointments with MSD regarding this payment.

chunks.title: Young parent is not participating in youth activity obligations — extra help > guaranteed childcare assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Young parent is not participating in youth activity obligations
When a young parent is not participating in education, training or work-based learning, Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment will stop unless there are exceptional circumstances.
Exceptional circumstances include (but are not limited to):
- the young parent cannot attend education, training or work-based learning because they are or their child is injured or ill
- because of a family bereavement
- any other exceptional circumstances
When there are exceptional circumstances, Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment can continue to be paid for 30 days.
Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment will also stop if the client no longer has youth activity obligations. This includes when a young parent qualifies for an exemption from the youth activity obligations.

chunks.title: Young parent's circumstances — extra help > guaranteed childcare assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Young parent's circumstances
Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment can be paid when the young parent is in the following circumstances:
- Young parent is a dependent child of a parent or guardian
- Young parent with a partner
- Partner getting a main benefit
- Young parent is not participating in youth activity obligations
- Young parent has a sanction imposed

chunks.title: Young parent with a partner — extra help > guaranteed childcare assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Young parent with a partner
Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment can be paid when the young parent is married, in a civil union or in a de facto relationship.
Where the young parent has a partner, the partner does not need to meet the qualifications for the Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment.
However, the YSSU needs to be satisfied that, based on information provided by the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service, the partner has a good and sufficient reason for not providing childcare while the young parent is undertaking activities or attending full-time secondary school.

chunks.title: Cash asset test — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Cash asset test
MSD may consider an application for Home Help Domestic Support or Domestic Emergency if the client has cash assets that are less than:
- $4,300 if the client is single or
- $7,464 if the client is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, or is a sole parent
## Clients partner in care
When the client's partner is in a private or public hospital, rest home or residential care, MSD should combine the couple's assets then use 50% of the total in the cash asset assessment.
## Age of dependent child in sole parent's care
To be considered a sole parent, the client will need to have at least one dependent child who is under the age of 18.

chunks.title: Cash assets include — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Cash assets include
- bills of exchange or promissory notes
- building society shares
- money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society
- money invested with or lent to any bank or other financial institution or person
- money withdrawn from a KiwiSaver scheme
- mortgage investments and other long term loans
- the net equity held in any property or land not used as the person's home
- shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds and bonds and
- the client's share or interest in any partnership
## Cash assets do not include
- a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity of less than $2000, or which is used by the client or a member of their family for day to day accommodation
- a motor vehicle principally used by the client for private use
- the home property and land on which it is situated
- Christchurch mosques attack support payments
- Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments
- funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts
- Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income
- MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after payment is made
- Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 for the first 12 months after payment is made
- Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after payment is made
- Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after payment is made
- personal effects
- Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- Severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment)
- specified Ex gratia and Compensation payments
- FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received
A bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.
Canterbury earthquake related payments
Payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client received the payment:

chunks.title: Absences — extra help > home help > changes and reviews home help
chunks.text:
## Absences
Home Help provides financial assistance to clients who require temporary part-time home help to complete tasks normally performed in the home.
Home Help cannot be paid if the client is absent from the home unless the support is essential for other family members, such as an elderly partner or children.
Absences include any temporary or permanent absence for reasons such as holidays or hospitalisation.

chunks.title: Change in income or assets — extra help > home help > changes and reviews home help
chunks.text:
## Change in income or assets
You will need to complete a new financial assessment to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications for Home Help whenever there is a change in the client's:
- Cash assets
Note that Home Help for multiple births is not income or asset tested.
If the new financial assessment means that the client is:
- able to receive partial payment (when previously receiving full payments)
- able to receive full payment (when previously receiving partial payments) or
- is no longer qualified for Home Help
The client must be advised in writing of the change.
## Effective date
Generally, the effective date for any change will be 5 working days from the date the client is notified of the change.
This allows time for the client to receive the letter and make changes (if required) with the home-helper.
This means you can confirm payments to the home-helper for work completed up until this date.
Note if the client gives false or misleading information you must review the Home Help from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment to the client where appropriate.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — extra help > home help > changes and reviews home help
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client is obliged to advise MSD of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Home Help.
You may also review Home Help at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.

chunks.title: Review of Home Help — extra help > home help > changes and reviews home help
chunks.text:
## Review of Home Help
Home Help for Domestic Emergency or Domestic Support is granted for a maximum period of 3 months at any one time.
A client must make a new application if they still require assistance after the 3 month period.
Note that there is no further entitlement to Home Help for multiple births once the hours have been used or at the end of the maximum period.

chunks.title: Client lives with relatives — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Client lives with relatives
If the client lives with a relative, the issue is not whether we charge the relatives income but whether we should approve domestic emergency or families needing domestic support Home Help in the first place.
Do not charge the income of other people living with the client.
If you are unsure whether Home Help should be approved contact Helpline to discuss.

chunks.title: Clients who do not have a Community Services Card — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Clients who do not have a Community Services Card
A Community Services Card is available to low or middle income earners to enable them and their family to access subsidised health services. Community Services Card holders can also get a 50% discount on public transport fares for themselves. If a client (or their partner) does not have a current Community Services Card they should be invited to apply for one.
You will need to hold their Home Help application until such time as we know whether or not they have qualified for a Community Services Card. If they do not have a Community Services Card they will not qualify for Home Help Domestic Support or Domestic Emergency regardless of whether or not they meet the cash asset test.
However, if a client cannot receive a Community Services Card due to them receiving an ex-gratia payment after becoming infected with Hepatitis C through the New Zealand Blood Supply they are still able to receive Home Help Domestic Support or Domestic Emergency (for the first 12 months following the date the client received the payment).

chunks.title: Multiple births — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Multiple births
Home Help is granted from the date of birth if the children were born at home, or from the date of hospital discharge if the children were born in hospital.
## Other categories
Home Help will commence from the date the application is received.

chunks.title: Current Community Services Card — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Current Community Services Card
A client (and any partner) cannot get Home Help for Domestic Support or Domestic Emergency unless:
- they or their partner have a current Community Services Card and
- meet an asset test
## No Community Services Card
If a client (or any partner) does not have a current Community Services Card they need to apply and be granted a Community Services Card before you process their application for Home Help.

chunks.title: Domestic Emergency — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Domestic Emergency
Home Help may be granted for a limited time to families with young children or other dependants when:
- a sudden change of circumstances creates a crisis situation and
- there are no close relatives or friends able to assist and
- they (or their partner) have a current Community Services Card and
- they meet a cash asset test
Examples include a parent in full-time employment who suddenly loses a partner and there is no one to care for the family or a sole parent becomes ill.
Note a child is no longer considered a dependent child for Home Help when they turn 18. However, they may be considered an "other dependant" if they still require support.

chunks.title: Families needing Domestic Support — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Families needing Domestic Support
Sometimes families with young children or other dependants need short term Domestic Support. This may include training young parents in parenting skills or assistance with household tasks where family pressures are causing undue stress.
In the first instance clients should explore all other options of home support through community organisations providing services under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989.
If assistance is not available under any other provision, the client may be able to get Home Help for domestic support if:
- they (or their partner) have a current Community Services Card and
- meet a cash asset test and
- obtain written confirmation of the need for Home Help from a health practitioner, other health professional or a social worker
Note a child is no longer considered a dependent child for Home Help when they turn 18. However, they may be considered an "other dependant" if they still require support.

chunks.title: Family Group conferences — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Family Group conferences
Sometimes Home Help may be recommended as a result of a family group conference or a family whanau agreement under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989.
MSD is obliged to comply with decisions made at a family group conference unless it is clearly impractical to do so.
The client must still meet the qualifications to be able to get Home Help.

chunks.title: Financial Assessment - Home Support — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Financial Assessment - Home Support
This financial assessment only applies to Home Support.
To decide whether a client can receive Home Support, both the client and the partner's income is taken into consideration you must compare the client's (and partner if any) income to their financial commitments. The client must provide proof of all income, assets and commitments.
To decide whether a client can receive Home Support and at what rate, you need to look at the difference between the client's income and commitments as follows:
Income is less than the clients financial commitments
The client can receive the full cost of Home Help
Income is greater than the clients financial commitments by:
$1.00 a week or less
The client can receive the full cost of Home Help
More than $1.00 but less than the actual cost of Home Help
The client can receive partial payment of Home Help
Equal to or greater than the actual cost of Home Help
The client cannot receive Home Help
Travel costs are not included in this assessment. If a client can receive Home Help, you can pay the home helper's travel costs in certain circumstances. For more information see:
- Travel costs
You should use the Certificate of Disposal Home Help form (ISS465) to help you decide whether a client meets the financial assessment.

chunks.title: Guidelines — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Guidelines
Use the following guidelines to decide whether to grant Home Help for domestic emergencies.
Ask yourself these questions:
- Is there anyone else who can provide assistance for example, family, church or voluntary organisations?
- Who is the Home Help for?
- If the help is specifically for a person suffering from age, ill health, a disability or a post-operative condition, they should be referred to their health practitioner or their local District Health Board to access Home Support.
- Is the Home Help for childcare?
MSD is often asked to provide Home Help under this category for childcare as the client is too sick to take care of their children.
When deciding these applications check whether:
- The client may be eligible for Childcare Assistance
- Be sure that the Home Help is for the care of the children and not to take care of the sick person, as they may be able to access Home Support
- Is there anyone else that can care for the children? for example, a friend or relative
- Does the client have a partner?
Home Help is generally not payable where the client has a partner, even if the partner is in employment. However, consider the length the Home Help would be required and whether the partner has paid leave available from their employment. If the partner has work obligations but is no longer able to meet their obligations because they are required to take care of the client, consider granting an Emergency Benefit
- The Home Help rates are designed to pay for domestic chores, it does not recognise the higher level of expertise and responsibility needed to care for children
- Has wherever possible, a social worker from Oranga Tamariki, Manatū Hauora/Ministry of Health, or other recognised agency been involved to assess the situation?

chunks.title: Home Support — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Home Support
Home Support means home help funded under the New Zealand Public Health and Disability Act 2000 for people needing it because of age, ill health, or infirmity.
The client must be needs assessed by the Manatū Hauora / Ministry of Health and if they have a Community Services Card they will automatically meet the income and asset limits.
If the client does not have a Community Services Card these clients must complete an 'Application for Home Support Services Subsidy' (S05) form.
MSD only involvement is determining if the client meets the financial assessment. There is a specific financial assessment applied to Home Support applicants.
Clients with enquiries about assistance with caring for themselves or family in their own home should be referred to their health practitioner or Manatū Hauora / Ministry of Health for information about Home Support.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Home Help is a non-taxable payment that provides financial assistance to clients who require temporary part-time home help to complete tasks normally performed in the home such as laundry, housework and food preparation.
This could be because of a multiple birth, a domestic emergency or because the client requires domestic support.
Clients (or any partner) applying for Home Help Domestic Support or Domestic Emergency must have a current Community Services Card and meet an asset test.
If a client (or any partner) does not have a current Community Services Card they need to apply and be granted a Community Services Card before you process their application for Home Help.
A client does not have to be getting a benefit to get Home Help assistance.
Home Help is not paid for needs relating to age, ill health and infirmity. Clients in these categories may be able to get Home Support from Manatū Hauora, Ministry of Health NZ.

chunks.title: Multiple births — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Multiple births
A client may be able to get Home Help for multiple births or adoption of 2 or more surviving babies born from a single pregnancy.
If a client has given birth or adopted twins, they can only get Home Help for multiple births if they also have another child who is under the age of 5 years old. Assistance is not available if the twins are born first and then the further child.
Clients who have given birth or adopted triplets, quads, and quins do not have to have another child in their care to qualify for Home Help.
The client must provide proof of the birth. This could be birth certificates, newspaper notices or hospital discharge papers.
Home Help is granted from the date of birth if the children were born at home or from the date of hospital discharge if the children were born in hospital. If the client does not meet this criteria but they are having trouble coping in the home, they may be able to get Home Help under Domestic Support or Domestic Emergency.
Payments of Home Help for multiple births are available if the client's partner, immediate family member or an occupant of the home is the home helper. The payment of Home Help is paid to the home helper.
Note clients applying for Home Help because of a multiple birth do not have to have a current Community Services Card or meet an asset test.

chunks.title: Number of hours - Domestic Emergency — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Number of hours - Domestic Emergency
A maximum of 45 hours Home Help per week for up to 3 months may be approved to clients requiring Home Help due to a Domestic Emergency. This is to allow the family to adapt to the new situation.
Each application must be examined carefully to determine a suitable number of hours and reviewed after 3 months.
A maximum of 2 further applications for Home Help per family may be approved (9 months in total).

chunks.title: Number of hours - Domestic Support — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Number of hours - Domestic Support
Generally, a maximum of 15 hours per week for up to 3 months can be approved. A social worker from Oranga Tamariki, Manatū Hauora / Ministry of Health, or other recognised agency should be consulted if:
- assistance is requested for longer than 3 months
- there are repeated referrals and/or
- there is serious concern for the safety of children
A maximum of 3 applications for Home Help per family may be granted for Domestic Support in any 2 year period (9 months in total).

chunks.title: Number of hours - multiple births — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Number of hours - multiple births
The following hours of Home Help are available to clients who have had a multiple birth:
Twins
240 hours for 12 months
Triplets, quads, quins or more
1,560 hours for 24 months
Hours of Home Help must be used from the date of the babies' birth if the babies were born at home, or from the date of return home from hospital.
The parent(s) may use the Home Help hours at any time over the maximum period. The parent(s) may wish to use all of the hours in the first few months if this is what will suit them best.
There is no further entitlement when the hours have been used or at the end of the maximum period.

chunks.title: Partner in hospital or residential care — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Partner in hospital or residential care
When the client's partner is in a private or public hospital, rest home or residential care, combine the couples assets then use 50% of the total in the cash asset assessment.
You are no longer required to assess a client's income against their commitments, unless you are completing a financial assessment for Home Support.

chunks.title: Paying accounts — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Paying accounts
Once Home Help has been completed MSD will usually get an invoice, schedule or timesheet.
Pay the agency or individual:
- the maximum hourly rate (plus GST if applicable) or
- the claimed amount, whichever is the lesser
Payment is made through the client's record and payment is made to the home helper or agency.
If the client is not getting a benefit or non-beneficiary assistance, you will need to create a non-beneficiary record.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Payment
Payment can be made directly to either:
- the home helper
- the organisation providing the Home Help or
- in exceptional circumstances to the client
The maximum hourly rate of Home Help payable for Multiple Births, Domestic Emergency and Domestic Support is $25.21 per hour plus holiday pay (which equals $27.23 per hour) as at 1 April 2026.
When Home Help is provided by an agency registered for Goods and Services Tax (GST), pay GST on the total amount, that is:
- hourly rate plus holiday pay
- plus travel allowance (if applicable)
- plus GST
If you think there is a good reason why payment should be made directly to the client, contact Helpline to discuss.
Home-helpers may also be able to receive assistance for their travel costs in addition to the hourly rate.
## Absence
Home Help cannot be paid if the client is absent unless the support is essential for other family members e.g. an elderly partner or children.
Absence includes temporary or a permanent absence for example on holiday or in hospital.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for Home Help assistance, a client must:
- have had a multiple birth or adopted 2 or more children from the same pregnancy or
- have a domestic emergency or
- need domestic support and
- be a New Zealand citizen or residence class visa holder (i.e. not be in New Zealand unlawfully, or here on a temporary entry class visa) or
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and
- hold a current Community Services Card or their partner holds a current Community Services Card (except for multiple birth cases) and
- meet a cash asset test (except for multiple birth cases)
## Age, ill health or infirmity related care
Home Help is not paid for needs relating to age, ill health or infirmity.
Clients with these needs may be able to get home support from Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora. See:
- Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora Home support services for older people and others
## Multiple births
Clients applying for Home Help because of a multiple birth do not need to have a current Community Services Card or meet an asset test.

chunks.title: Re-applications for Domestic Emergency — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Re-applications for Domestic Emergency
There may be occasions where a client reapplies for assistance after a short break in payment of Home Help.
For example a client may have received Home Help for Domestic Emergency for 6 months, manages by themselves for 6 months and then reapplies.
While it may be appropriate in rare cases to approve additional assistance, it is important to remember that the Domestic Emergency category of Home Help is not designed as an ongoing solution to a crisis.
It is intended to support the client and their family during the crisis situation while more long-term measures are explored.

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get Home Help, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- have a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
Note for Home Help no period of residence is required. People who are in New Zealand unlawfully or here on a temporary entry class visa generally do not qualify for assistance from MSD.
## Clients who don't meet the residence requirements
If a client does not meet the residence requirements, they cannot get Home Help.
However, a client in this situation may be able to get Temporary Additional Support if they are:
- a person who has refugee or protected person status in New Zealand or
- awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protected person status and are lawfully in New Zealand (i.e. they have a valid temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009) or
- applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 and are compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances
Once the client has been granted citizenship or a residence class visa and they meet all the other qualifications, Home Help can be granted.
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other criteria to qualify for Home Help.

chunks.title: The home helper — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## The home helper
The person carrying out the home help can be:
- self-employed
- employed by the client
- employed by a home help agency or
- employed by Manatū Hauora / Ministry of Health
Home helpers not employed by a home help agency or Manatū Hauora / Ministry of Health are paid directly by MSD at a gross rate. The home-helper is responsible for paying their own taxes and ACC levies to Inland Revenue.
Note the employment of the home-helper is the responsibility of the client. The employment contract is between the home-helper and the client, not MSD. MSD pay the home-helper on behalf of the client.
Home Help wages must be declared as income if the home-helper is receiving an income tested benefit.
## Proof
The home helper must provide identification of who they are and a confirmed bank account number, this is to ensure they are a genuine helper (but do not have to meet the residence test), before Home Help can be paid to them.
## Holiday Pay
The maximum hourly rate includes holiday pay.
Do not add holiday pay to the hourly amount.

chunks.title: Travel costs — extra help > home help
chunks.text:
## Travel costs
Home-helpers may be reimbursed for their actual and reasonable travel expenses from their home to the clients' home.
Note this includes between the homes of clients where they are providing home help for more than one client.
Home-helpers paid directly by MSD may get:
- up to 40 cents per kilometre to a maximum of 12 kilometres or
- their actual public transport cost
You cannot pay travel costs where the Home-helper has taken the client out or on errands.
Note a home-helper may be reimbursed for travel expenses for more than 12 kilometres in certain circumstances, such as a great distance to travel in rural areas or cases of cultural or linguistic need. This must be agreed in advance with MSD.
Calculate GST on the travelling allowance when paying to an agency.
If a home-helper uses public transport, you must reimburse their actual public transport costs. This applies even if they have paid full price fares and can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect as they are a Community Services Card holder.
MSD cannot reimburse a home helper a lower amount than they have paid.

chunks.title: Actual income — extra help > house modification funding
chunks.text:
## Actual income
When assessing a client's income to see if they qualify for House Modification Funding include the income of:
- the person with the disability
- any partner of the person with the disability
- the house owners when they share the same property - if they live with the person with the disability and
- where the person with a disability is a child, the income of the parents should be taken into account

chunks.title: Assessed income — extra help > house modification funding
chunks.text:
## Assessed income
To determine a client's assessed income, you must take into consideration their cash assets.
For each $1,000 of assets, or portion thereof, the sum of $10.00 per week is charged as assessable income.
Assessed income is then compared with the actual income received from the assets. The amount charged as income when assessing the loan will be:
- the assessed income or
- the actual income
whichever is the greater.

chunks.title: Cash assets include — extra help > house modification funding
chunks.text:
## Cash assets include
- bills of exchange or promissory notes
- building society shares
- money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society
- money invested with or lent to any bank, other financial institution or person
- mortgage investments and other long term loans
- money withdrawn from a KiwiSaver scheme
- shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds, and other bonds (including shares in energy organisations)
- the client's share in any partnership and
- the net equity held in any property or land not used as the person's home
## Cash assets do not include
- a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2000 or which is used by the client or a member of their family for day to day accommodation
- a home property and land on which it is situated
- a motor vehicle principally used by the client or their partner for private use
- funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts
- Christchurch mosques attack support payments
- Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments
- MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to a system processing error from 1993 to 2014
- Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- payments made by the Crown that are exempt as cash assets, including: payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client received the payment
- payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client received the payment
- personal effects
- Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- Severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment)
- specified Ex gratia and compensation payments
Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.

chunks.title: Commitments — extra help > house modification funding
chunks.text:
## Commitments
When income and assets are being determined, the following costs are allowed as deductions:
- living costs
an amount equal to the appropriate rate of Supported Living Payment, plus family tax credit is made. This is to cover normal household costs such as food, clothing, travel, car running expenses, contents insurance, savings, hire purchase, entertainment and personal expenses
- Accommodation costs
an amount is allowed equal to that allowed as accommodation costs for Accommodation Supplement
- employment-related expenses
union fees, superannuation scheme contributions, welfare fund contributions can be deducted
- life insurance premiums can be deducted
- tax
- telephone rental
note that rental only is deducted. Costs associated with special phones, tolls or accounts in arrears are not allowable deductions
- extra medical expenses
the amount paid for regular medical expenses, other than normal visits to the health practitioner or dentist, can be deducted

chunks.title: Income and asset test — extra help > house modification funding
chunks.text:
## Income and asset test
All applications are subject to some form of income and asset testing. There are different tests for different funding levels:
Amount requestedTestUp to $200No income test is applied but cash assets must not be more than 4 times the appropriate Supported Living Payment rate.$201 - $8,076No income or asset test is applied.Over $8,076An income and asset test is applied only with regard to the amount over the $8,076 level.
Amount requested
Test
Up to $200
No income test is applied but cash assets must not be more than 4 times the appropriate Supported Living Payment rate.
$201 - $8,076
No income or asset test is applied.
Over $8,076
An income and asset test is applied only with regard to the amount over the $8,076 level.
For more information see:
- Income and asset test for amounts over $8,076
- Supported Living Payment rates

chunks.title: Income and asset test for amounts over $8,076 — extra help > house modification funding
chunks.text:
## Income and asset test for amounts over $8,076
If a client is applying for a loan of more than $8,076 we look at their chargeable income and their assessed income to determine what to charge. This is then compared to the client's commitments.
## Assessment of amounts in excess of $8,076
The level of assistance is determined by comparing income and commitments and the following shall apply:
Amount approved
if commitments exceed income
the amount applied for
if income exceeds commitments by $20 or less
the amount applied for
for every complete $10 in excess of $20
the grant offer shall be $1,000 less than the amount applied for in excess of $8,076
Note the guideline being used is that for each $10 of income the client can afford to repay a loan of $1,000.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > house modification funding
chunks.text:
## Introduction
House Modification Funding is paid by a Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora contracted provider and provides funding for people with serious disabilities to enable them to have essential alterations made to their home to meet their specific needs.
Work and Income administer the income and asset test.
A client does not have to be getting a main benefit to qualify for House Modification Funding.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > house modification funding
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To be able to receive a House Modification Funding, the client must have been needs assessed as requiring the alterations by a Ministry of Health contracted provider.
Assessments for house modifications are carried out by an Occupational Therapist.
The contracted provider decides whether the client meets the qualifications for funding. Work and Income administers the income and asset test.

chunks.title: Review of decision — extra help > house modification funding
chunks.text:
## Review of decision
When a client disagrees with a decision regarding the income and asset assessment for House Modification Funding there is no right of review to a Benefit Review Committee or the Social Security Appeal Authority.
However, if a client wishes to review a decision the original decision should be reconsidered.
A Review should be based on whether an 'informed' decision was made and should have regard to the following:
- relevant policy
- the information presented at the time
- any new information to hand
- reasons for the original decision and
- the reason the client is not happy with the decision
A senior Ministry of Social Development staff member (eg manager client service delivery) who was not involved in the original decision should carry out the Review.
Note if the client does not agree with the Review decision there are no further appeal rights.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > housing support products
chunks.text: Housing Support Products are individual products that provide financial assistance for clients needing help to obtain and retain accommodation. Housing Support Products, with the exception of Transition to Alternative Housing Grant, are recoverable discretionary grants and can be considered for any client who meets the qualifications. Assistance can be declined if it is not appropriate after discussing the circumstances of the client and their partner (if any) and dependent children (if any). The type of Housing Support Product that a client can receive also depends on whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to their accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: The Housing Support Products are — extra help > housing support products
chunks.text: - Moving Costs GrantAlso known as Accommodation Moving Costs GrantProvides recoverable assistance to help a client with costs to move their furniture, appliances, personal effects, and personal belongings into accommodation. - Bond GrantProvides recoverable assistance to help with the cost of a rental bond charged by a landlord to the client as a tenant. This payment is limited to accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. - Accommodation Costs in Advance GrantAlso known as Rent in Advance GrantProvides recoverable assistance to help with the cost of accommodation costs in advance charged by an accommodation supplier to the client - Accommodation Costs Arrears GrantAlso known as Rent Arrears GrantProvides recoverable assistance to help clients retain their accommodation if they are at risk of losing their accommodation due to being behind on their accommodation costs. - Tenancy Costs CoverA conditional grant for clients who are having difficulty getting rental housing due to their personal circumstances. It provides landlords with assurance the client will be able to meet any tenancy related costs over and above the rental bond (up to a limit) if owed at the end of the tenancy. Tenancy Costs Cover is payable to the landlord, but recoverable from the client. This payment is limited accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. - Transition to Alternative Housing GrantA one-off, non-recoverable incentive payment for clients who are ready and able to move out of social housing and into alternative housing. This payment is limited to clients moving into accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. - Accommodation Security Cover GrantA conditional, recoverable grant that provides assurance to accommodation suppliers that the client will be able to pay any outstanding costs, up to a limit, at the end of their accommodation agreement. This payment is limited to accommodation agreements that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. Clients can receive multiple Housing Support Products if they meet the qualifications for each individual grant. Note The Statement of Satisfactory Tenancy and Conditional Grant for Housing Assistance are no longer available from 13 March 2023.

chunks.title: Able to retain the current accommodation — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Able to retain the current accommodation
To qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, MSD must consider whether the client is likely able to keep their current accommodation if the assistance is granted.
MSD will need to discuss with the client whether they can keep the current accommodation, including whether the accommodation supplier is likely to continue the client’s accommodation agreement if the arrears are paid. The client must not have already received:
- an order terminating the tenancy that is not a conditional or interim order; or
- a notice under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 terminating the tenancy which has not been revoked
The client’s ability to afford (with any financial assistance, income and other resources available to them) the ongoing costs of the accommodation is a key factor in this assessment.
A client may be considered as being likely to retain their current accommodation when:
- the proposed accommodation cost will generally not be over 60 per cent of their net income (and their partner’s, if any) taking into account the client’s individual circumstances and
- MSD has discussed the client’s budget, or have other evidence showing they can manage their future outgoings
If the Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant available to the client does not cover the full amount of arrears, the client can still be considered able to keep the accommodation if the accommodation supplier is likely to continue the accommodation agreement with the remaining arrears.
In this instance, the client would generally be encouraged to agree to a repayment plan with the accommodation supplier for the remaining arrears.

chunks.title: Accommodation agreement ends after an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant is paid — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation agreement ends after an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant is paid
In some cases, a client may have had an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant for accommodation that is later ended by either the client or the accommodation supplier. This may be because of new arrears or another reason.
MSD must be satisfied the accommodation will continue in the immediate term if the arrears are paid and the client is likely to be able to keep the accommodation before granting an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. Providing this assistance does not impose an obligation on the client to stay in the property or on the accommodation supplier to continue the accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: Tenant under a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to any tenancy with a written tenancy agreement from Tenancy Services. Some examples are a: - tenancy agreement for rental housing, including with: a private landlordlocal governmenta non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) - a private landlord - local government - a non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) or - tenancy agreement for social housing, including with a community housing provider Clients in this accommodation may be eligible for a Rent Arrears Grant.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Ahere owns a house that they let to Stevie, Aio and Alex. Ahere provides a written tenancy agreement from Tenancy Services. The tenancy agreement is signed by all parties. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to the tenancy agreement.

chunks.title: Flatmate or subletting without a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Clients may be living in a rental property as a flatmate or subletter without a tenancy agreement. The tenant on the tenancy agreement that the client pays their accommodation costs to takes responsibility for these clients and acts as their accommodation supplier. Flatmates generally pay any accommodation costs to the tenant instead of the landlord. This includes clients who are an additional occupant in a social housing property, as they are not on the tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these clients and they may be eligible for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Hunu rents a home from a private landlord. Hunu’s accommodation supplier is their landlord. The tenancy agreement is between the landlord and Hunu and it allows Hunu to sublet 1 room. Hunu is responsible for any accommodation cost payments to the landlord, including bond and accommodation costs in advance. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to Hunu’s accommodation. Hunu sublets 1 room in the property to Kahu. Kahu pays her accommodation costs to Hunu. Hunu is Kahu’s accommodation supplier. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to Kahu’s accommodation.

chunks.title: Service tenancies — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: A client may be provided accommodation as part of their employment where their landlord is their employer. This is known as a service tenancy. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to service tenancies. Clients in a service tenancy will generally be provided with a written tenancy agreement. These clients may be eligible for a Rent Arrears Grant.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Morgan is a supervisor for Apple Orchard Ltd. Apple Orchard Ltd provide accommodation for Morgan under a tenancy agreement and removes the cost of the accommodation from Morgan’s pay each week. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to Morgan’s accommodation.

chunks.title: Tenancy orders — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: A tenant of a property through a tenancy order made under the Family Violence Act 2018 or Property (Relationships) Act 1976 does not need to have signed a written tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to clients in a tenancy order. These clients may be eligible for a Rent Arrears Grant.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Reese’s ex-partner Dylan is on the accommodation agreement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. Reese separates from Dylan because of family violence. Reese applies for a tenancy order to stay in the accommodation under the Family Violence Act 2018. The Court issues a tenancy order for Reese to stay in the property even though their name is not on the tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to Reese’s accommodation.

chunks.title: Boarding arrangements — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Clients who are boarding have an agreement for one room in the property, rather than the whole house. Boarders have access to shared facilities such as a kitchen and bathroom. When the accommodation has 6 or more occupants, this is known as a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to boarding houses when the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more. The client may be eligible for a Rent Arrears Grant if they meet these qualifications. When there are 5 or fewer occupants this is not considered a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these boarding arrangements, including private boarding where the client lives with the owner of the property. Clients in these arrangements may be eligible for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. The accommodation costs a client pays under a boarding accommodation agreement generally includes service and facility costs such as power, grounds maintenance, rubbish disposal, etc. MSD generally should not include any service costs in an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. For more information about what costs can be included in an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, see: - Service costs and water rates

chunks.title: Example 1 - Boarding arrangement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Ngaio has an accommodation agreement to rent a room in a boarding house with 5 other people. She has her own room in the house and shares a bathroom and kitchen with other boarders. She intends to stay there for at least 6 months. Ngaio plays board which includes accommodation costs and service costs (including power, water, cleaning and rubbish disposal costs). The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to this accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: Example 2 - Boarding arrangement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Malosi is boarding with their aunt Vaima. Vaima owns the house and Malosi pays her board that includes accommodation, food, and service costs, including internet and power costs. Malosi and Vaima have an accommodation agreement which sets out these costs. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to this accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: Rent to buy — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: A client may enter into a rent to buy contract (also called a deferred payment disposition). In these situations, the client is considered to be a homeowner and is not eligible for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Elisapeta has entered a rent to own programme to buy their home. They have a 5-year accommodation agreement and at the end of the 5-year arrangement they will have the option to purchase the home. They pay 30% of their gross income as accommodation costs. This is rent to buy accommodation arrangement that is not eligible for a Housing Support Product.

chunks.title: Relocatable accommodation — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: A client may enter a hire agreement or a rental contract for relocatable accommodation, such as a cabin, mobile home, or caravan. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 only applies to relocatable accommodation if it is: - hired from and located on a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner Clients in this accommodation may be eligible for a Rent Arrears Grant. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply if the relocatable accommodation is: - on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days or - placed on any other premises where the land and the accommodation are not owned by the same person or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner Clients in this accommodation may be eligible for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant.

chunks.title: Example 1 - campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Rarahu has been staying in a cabin in a commercial campsite and intends to stay for a year. She requires assistance with accommodation costs arrears of 2 weeks or her accommodation is at risk. As Rarahu intends to stay in the cabin for 51 days or more, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to their accommodation arrangement. MSD can approve a Rent Arrears Grant for Rarahu to keep the cabin.

chunks.title: Example 2 - campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Arama is staying in a cabin in a commercial campsite for 30 days while she waits for her new job to start, which will provide her with long-term accommodation while she's employed. She requires assistance with accommodation costs arrears of 1 week or her accommodation is at risk. As Arama is intending to stay in the cabin for under 51 days, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to her accommodation arrangement. MSD can approve an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant for Arama to keep the cabin.

chunks.title: Example 3 - relocatable accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Jericho has a hire agreement directly with a caravan provider for a caravan that is placed on his mother’s property. He moved in after his previous tenancy ended. They have agreed that he will stay on her property for six months while he looks for work and different accommodation. Because he has hired the caravan from a different person than the land he is staying on, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to Jericho’s accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: Multiple accommodation agreements — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: If a client is an occupant under multiple accommodation agreements (i.e. required to pay accommodation costs for more than one accommodation agreement), the Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant is only payable for the client's principal place of residence. MSD must assess their principal place of residence to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies, and whether the client is eligible for a Rent Arrears Grant or Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant at this accommodation. If the client and their partner have separate accommodation, they may each have a different principal place of residence. Generally, the client will determine what is their principal place of residence. If there is evidence the client is not using the property as their principal place of residence, MSD should generally decline an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. For example, if the client is using the property to store excess personal goods or sub-letting the property while living elsewhere, MSD should not pay an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. Note a grant can be paid for multiple accommodation agreements if they are for the same accommodation. For example, where a client has a rental contract for a cabin hire and a separate rental contract for the land that the cabin sits on.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Jiang lives in accommodation in Auckland. His ex-partner lives in Hamilton and has custody of their children. Jiang visits Hamilton for four days each month to visit his children and has an accommodation agreement with a friend where he pays $150 each month to stay at their place when he visits. Jiang has not been able to pay his friend for the last three months, and his friend has said he will end the accommodation agreement if Jiang does not pay the arrears of $450. Jiang applies for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant for the accommodation agreement in Hamilton. As this is not his primary place of residence, MSD declines the grant.

chunks.title: Accommodation is suitable to live in — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation is suitable to live in
MSD may consider whether the accommodation will be suitable for the client to live in if the grant is made.
Factors MSD may consider include (but are not limited to) if the:
- accommodation has been modified to suit the accessibility needs for the client, their partner (if any) or their dependent children (if any)
- client has access to facilities such as clean drinking water, cooking facilities, electricity, heating, beds and mattresses, toilet and bathing facilities and a food refrigerator that the client can access
- accommodation has enough bedrooms
- accommodation is fit for human habitation, including being structurally safe to live in.
MSD does not need to assess if a client’s accommodation is suitable at every Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant assessment. However, if it is clear through the conversation with the client that the accommodation is not suitable for the client, their partner (if any) or their dependent children (if any), MSD may decline the application.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to
The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 provides rights and protections for tenants and landlords in rental agreements.
MSD can pay a Rent Arrears Grant for people who are living in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. This includes, but is not limited to:
- rental tenancies
- boarding houses with at least 6 tenants or boarders where the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more
- service tenancies where an employer provides accommodation to an employee
- multi-unit residential housing developments to provide long-term (minimum of 10 years) rental accommodation to tenants (also known as build to rent tenancies)
- social housing (including Kainga Ora and private social housing) if the client is a tenant or a signatory
- hire agreements for relocatable homes including cabins, mobile homes and caravans where they are: hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more oron a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner
- hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or
- on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner
If you are unsure if the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to an accommodation agreement, contact Helpline or your Capability Developer.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: An Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant can be granted for clients who live in specific accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. These accommodation agreements may include, but are not limited to: - a flat or house share agreement where the client has not signed a tenancy agreement (e.g. a flatmate that sub-lets from a head tenant) - hire agreement for a relocatable home including a cabin, mobile home or caravan where: it is on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days, oron any other premises for any amount of time where the land and accommodation are not owned by the same person oron a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner - it is on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days, or - on any other premises for any amount of time where the land and accommodation are not owned by the same person or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner - a lodging arrangement - a boarding agreement where the client is either: in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to and does stay for less than 28 daysin accommodation that is not a boarding house - in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to and does stay for less than 28 days - in accommodation that is not a boarding house - commercial accommodation such as hotels, motels, and homestays that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. This excludes the following accommodation as they are not eligible to get a Rent Arrears Grant: emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Granttransitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development andcontracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant - transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development and - contracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - an additional occupant in a social housing property that is not a tenant or a signatory to the tenancy agreement MSD will need to assess a client’s accommodation agreement to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Clients may be living in accommodation that is not included in the above list. They may still be eligible for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant if the accommodation they are living in is not specifically excluded.

chunks.title: Agreement with accommodation supplier to pay arrears — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Agreement with accommodation supplier to pay arrears
To qualify for a Rent Arrears Grant the client must be at risk of losing their current accommodation if their arrears are not paid.
When a client has not paid their accommodation costs, they may be able to make an agreement with the accommodation supplier to pay the arrears, either informally or through a dispute resolution process such as mediation through Tenancy Services, or through the Disputes Tribunal or Tenancy Tribunal.
When an agreement has been made to pay the accommodation cost arrears, but the client is unable to pay the arrears, including when the agreement was made verbally, the client can be considered at risk of losing their accommodation due to accommodation cost arrears.
Note generally only clients and accommodation suppliers in accommodation agreements that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to can resolve disputes through Tenancy Services. Clients that are not protected by the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 can go to the Disputes Tribunal or court.

chunks.title: Assessing an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Assessing an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant
When a client needs help with accommodation costs arrears, an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant should be considered if they meet the qualifications.
An Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant is available for people who are likely to be able to keep their accommodation.
An Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant is a discretionary grant. MSD needs to consider the client's individual circumstances to determine whether the Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant should be granted.
In order to make a decision to grant, MSD must consider:
- the purpose of the Housing Support Programme, including whether granting an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant would be the correct use of the payment
- any other financial assistance available to the client that could be used to meet their need
- whether the client and their partner (if any) could meet the need from their own resources, including accessing cash assets or receiving support from other Government agencies
- any impact on the client, their partner (if any), and their dependent children (if any) if their need is not met and
- whether the client intends to stay in the accommodation for fewer than 28 days
Depending on the client’s circumstances, MSD may also consider the following factors:
- whether the client or their partner (if any) has caused or contributed to the need for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant
- whether the client or their partner (if any) will be able to meet their essential living expenses if an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant is paid
- the existing debt of the client and their partner (if any)
- whether their accommodation is suitable to live in
- any other matters MSD think are relevant
An Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant can be declined if a grant would not be appropriate after considering the circumstances of the client and their partner (if any) and their dependent children (if any).

chunks.title: Assessing weekly income — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Income limits for Housing Support Products are determined based on a client’s weekly income. MSD has discretion to determine the period that weekly income relates to. When working out which period of income to use, MSD may consider: - how much income was earned during the period - how much income the client expects to receive for that period, (e.g. investment interest was accrued but has not yet paid) - the period for which income was received by the client Generally, MSD will base the client and their partner’s (if any) weekly income on the average income over the previous four weeks, unless MSD considers a different timeframe is appropriate (for example the client has been earning for a shorter or longer time). This means the last four weeks of income is totalled and then divided by four. In some cases, MSD can use a different period to calculate the weekly income period, to consider the client’s circumstances, including whether the client or their spouse or partner’s income: - has been inconsistent over the previous four weeks - is variable week by week - has either increased or decreased recently - will increase or decrease in the immediate future (in the next four weeks) - future income is uncertain, including where there is a history of the employer not paying wages or paying late - has been earned but not paid (e.g. the client earned income but not been paid on time)

chunks.title: Example 1 - variable income — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Piper works in a casual role in a supermarket. Their employment started 3 weeks ago, they have no set weekly hours and their income will change from week to week, depending on the number of hours they will work. Their employer has indicated they should receive a minimum of 20 hours work per week at $24 per hour ($480 per week) but this is not set out in Piper’s employment agreement. Piper’s 3-week income so far has been: Week 1 = $400Week 2 = $200Week 3 = $300 In this case, Piper’s income will be estimated using the average wage over the previous three weeks as they do not have four weeks of income to assess. The calculation is: $400 + $200 + $300 = $900$900/3 (weeks) = $300

chunks.title: Example 2 - recent income change — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Moana has been earning $900 per week over the previous 12 months. However, Moana has changed from a full-time role to a part-time role due to starting study. Moana started earning $300 a week starting last week. When calculating Moana’s weekly income for a Housing Support Product, MSD bases this on $300 per week as this will be her income going forward.

chunks.title: At risk of losing accommodation due to arrears — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: To qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant the client must be at risk of losing their current accommodation if their arrears are not paid. A client may be at risk of losing their accommodation due to accommodation costs arrears if they meet any of the following qualifications: - the client has made an agreement with the accommodation supplier for the payment of the arrears and is unable to meet the costs - the accommodation supplier has given the client a notice to remedy for accommodation cost arrears, regardless of the number of previous notices for arrears For clients who are in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to, it could also include the following situations: - the landlord has applied to the Tenancy Tribunal seeking: the payment of accommodation costs arrears orto have the tenancy ended due to rent arrears or - the payment of accommodation costs arrears or - to have the tenancy ended due to rent arrears or - the tenant has received an order, including an interim or conditional order, from the Tenancy Tribunal for payment of accommodation costs arrears - the landlord has applied to Tenancy Services for dispute resolution or mediation due to accommodation costs arrears Note accommodation cost arrears must be specified on the Tenancy Tribunal or Tenancy Services application or order/resolution but does not need to be the only issue being disputed. Often this is recorded as unpaid rent. If there are other issues being disputed through the Tenancy Tribunal or Tenancy Services, this will be considered when assessing the client's ability to keep the accommodation. A client may also be at risk of losing their current accommodation due to accommodation cost arrears when: - the client has not paid or only partially paid at least 1 week of accommodation costs for their current tenancy and - the landlord confirms they intend to give a notice to remedy once the accommodation costs have been in arrears for at least 5 working days, or apply to the Tenancy Tribunal or Tenancy Services (for dispute resolution or mediation) for accommodation costs arrears, if the client gets more arrears The client will not qualify for a Rent Arrears Grant if they or their accommodation supplier indicates they are not 'at risk' as their accommodation agreement will not be ended due to the arrears.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Clients and accommodation suppliers who are in accommodation agreements that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to are generally not able to resolve disputes through the Tenancy Tribunal. They are able to access the Disputes Tribunal or court to resolve issues. Clients who are in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to can be evicted from their accommodation without notice. This can be taken into consideration when a client advises their accommodation is at risk.

chunks.title: Kāinga Ora tenancies — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Kāinga Ora does not generally end tenancies when accommodation cost arrears are owing and they will work with their tenants to recover any accommodation cost arrears. However, when assessing whether a client qualifies for an Accommodation Cost Arrears Grant, it is important to confirm Kāinga Ora have indicated they will end the tenancy due to their tenant’s accommodation costs arrears.

chunks.title: Cash asset limit — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Cash asset limit
A client and their partner (if any) cannot get an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant if their cash assets are more than the cash asset limit.
We need to know the cash value of their cash assets.
There is no discretion to grant an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant to a client whose cash assets (including the cash assets of their partner, if any) are above the asset limit.

chunks.title: Cash assets include — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Cash assets mean the assets of the client and their partner (if any) that can be easily converted into cash and include: - cash - bills of exchange or promissory notes - building society shares - money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society - money invested with or lent to any bank, financial institution or other person whether on mortgage or other security, or unsecured - money withdrawn from a KiwiSaver scheme - mortgage investments and other long-term loans - the net equity held in any property or land not used as the person's home - pre-paid funeral expenses (in some circumstances) - shares, stocks, debentures bonus bonds and other bonds (including shares in energy organisations) and - the client's share in any partnership Note if you are unsure of a case contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Cash assets do not include — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: - the home property and land on which it is situated - a motor vehicle or other vehicle principally used by the client or their partner for their personal use (this is limited to 1 vehicle for a single person or 2 vehicles for a couple) - a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2000, or which is used by the client or a member of their family for day-to-day accommodation - any payments received under Housing Support Products assistance (Moving Costs Grant, Bond Grant, Rent in Advance Grant, Rent Arrears Grant, Transition to Alternative Housing Grant, Accommodation Security Cover Grant, Tenancy Costs Cover) - Personal effects - Christchurch mosques attack support payments for the first 12 months after the payment is received - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - funds held in KiwiSaver and other retirement schemes accounts (unless the person is able to withdraw them as the person is over 65) - Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income - Māori land - MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is received - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after the payment is made - personal effects - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made - specified ex gratia and compensation payments - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received A bank overdraft is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.

chunks.title: Christchurch earthquake related payments — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client received the payment. See: - Payments from the Crown for the purchase of property in the Canterbury red zone - Payments from the Earthquake Commission and insurance companies (Canterbury earthquake 2010 and aftershock 2011) - Payments from the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross)

chunks.title: Client caused or contributed to the need — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Client caused or contributed to the need
