When deciding whether to grant an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, MSD may consider the extent the client has caused or contributed to their need for assistance with accommodation cost arrears.
Examples of when a client may be considered to have caused or contributed to the need for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant include when they have not paid their rent because:
- they decided to pay less than required for several weeks and made no effort to catch up
- they donated or gifted a substantial portion of their income or assets to another person or group
- they used money that they could have used to pay their accommodation costs for expensive concert tickets
A client is not considered to have contributed to the need if the only reason for the accommodation cost arrears was caused by the client paying for an essential expense (e.g. food, medical costs, power, car repairs) that had to be met and left insufficient money for the accommodation cost payment. This includes when the client had a decrease in their income (e.g. due to a reduction in hours worked) and when their regular earnings have not changed.
The discretion to decline a grant is generally only used when the client has made an intentional decision to prioritise getting non-essential items or services over the accommodation cost payments.
Each client's situation must be assessed on their individual circumstances.

chunks.title: Clients who cannot get an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Clients who cannot get an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant
Clients living in one of the following accommodation agreements are not eligible for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant:
- accommodation owned by the client or their spouse or partner
- tents, including those joined to a vehicle
- homeless shelters
- prisons and correctional facilities
- accommodation for which they are receiving an Emergency Housing Grant or Transitional or Contracted Emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development
There is no discretion to approve a payment for a client living in one of these accommodation agreements.
A client must not be granted an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant if the arrears were incurred:
- for accommodation that is ending because: an order has been made by the Tenancy Tribunal terminating the tenancy (excluding interim or conditional orders)notice has been given by the accommodation supplier or client terminating the accommodation agreement (excluding notices that have been revoked)
- an order has been made by the Tenancy Tribunal terminating the tenancy (excluding interim or conditional orders)
- notice has been given by the accommodation supplier or client terminating the accommodation agreement (excluding notices that have been revoked)

chunks.title: Clients with existing debt — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Clients with existing debt
When deciding whether to approve an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, MSD may consider the existing debt of the client and their partner (if any). Existing debt includes both MSD debt and non-MSD debt.
A client's existing debt repayments may impact their ability to repay an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant.
When a client has existing MSD debt, MSD may consider whether it is appropriate to reduce those repayments to allow for the repayment of the Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant.
When a client is getting all the financial assistance they qualify for, but are not likely to be able to repay an amount paid under an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, the grant may be declined.

chunks.title: Determining whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Determining whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies
A client must have accommodation with a tenancy agreement for the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 to apply.
Generally, this will be a tenancy agreement from Tenancies Services. However, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 may still apply if the client does not have a tenancy agreement from Tenancies Services.
Other evidence of a tenancy agreement could be written communication between the accommodation supplier and the client if they are in an accommodation agreement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to.
If there is a verbal agreement, the accommodation supplier should write this down when the client is applying for a Housing Support Product so that MSD can determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies.
## Information on a tenancy agreement
If it is unclear whether a document is a tenancy agreement under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 or not, below is a list of information that is usually part of this type of agreement:
- the full name and contact address of the landlord
- the landlord’s contact mobile telephone number (if any)
- the landlord’s contact email address (if any)
- the full name and contact address (when different from the address of the premises to which the agreement relates) of the tenant
- the tenant’s contact mobile telephone number (if any)
- the tenant’s contact email address (if any)
- the address of the premises
- the date of the tenancy agreement
- the date of commencement of the tenancy (when different from the date of the tenancy agreement)
- the landlord’s address for service
- the tenant’s address for service
- whether the tenant is under the age of 18
- the amount of any bond
- the rent payable
- the frequency of the rent payments
- the place or bank account number where the rent is to be paid
- a list of any chattels provided by the landlord
- if the tenancy is a fixed-term tenancy, the date on which the term will expire
- Healthy Homes compliance statement
- insulation statement
- insurance statement
The agreement should be signed by both parties but if it's not signed, it may still be a valid agreement. In these cases, MSD can use other evidence to determine that there is an agreement in place. For example, bank account statement showing rent payments.

chunks.title: Dispute resolution or mediation through Tenancy Services — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Dispute resolution or mediation through Tenancy Services
To qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant the client must be at risk of losing their current accommodation if their accommodation costs arrears are not paid.
For clients in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to, Tenancy Services can help resolve tenancy related disputes through their dispute resolution or mediation processes, including where a client has accommodation costs arrears.
Where the landlord has applied to Tenancy Services for dispute resolution or mediation due to accommodation cost arrears, the client can be considered at risk of losing their accommodation due to accommodation cost arrears.
Clients not covered by the Residential Tenancies Act will generally need to resolve disputes through a Disputes Tribunal or court.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances
A client cannot be paid more than two Accommodation Costs Arrears Grants in a 52-week period, unless there are exceptional circumstances. This includes any Rent Arrears Grants.
Exceptional circumstances are where the circumstance:
- sets the client apart from others in a similar situation and
- are beyond the client's control
The following situations are generally considered as exceptional circumstances (but not limited to):
- unforeseen or emergency hospitalisation meant the client was unable to pay their accommodation costs, e.g.: when a client has been unable to work or earn their usual income due to hospitalisation following a medical emergency
- when a client has been unable to work or earn their usual income due to hospitalisation following a medical emergency
- serious sickness or injury that has meant the client was unable to pay their accommodation costs, e.g.: when a client has been unable to work and/or earn their usual income due to treatment for cancer, or due to mandatory quarantine or isolation for a serious contagious disease
- when a client has been unable to work and/or earn their usual income due to treatment for cancer, or due to mandatory quarantine or isolation for a serious contagious disease
- the client was a victim of a violent crime or family violence and has had a change in their housing circumstances, e.g.: no longer living with their partner after seeking a protection order (including if the client stays in the same property without their partner)
- no longer living with their partner after seeking a protection order (including if the client stays in the same property without their partner)
There may be other reasons for exceptional circumstances.
There is still a requirement that the client must be able to keep and will not be evicted from the accommodation if accommodation cost arrears are paid when there are exceptional circumstances.

chunks.title: Fixed-term tenancy due to expire — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Fixed-term tenancy due to expire
To qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, a client must be likely to retain their current accommodation if the assistance is granted.
A fixed-term tenancy under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 of more than 90 days will become a periodic tenancy if no action is taken before it expires. When this happens, the client can be considered to have kept the accommodation despite the type of accommodation agreement changing.
When a fixed-term tenancy does not continue as a periodic tenancy after the expiry, the impact on an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant will depend on the action taken:
- when the landlord and client have agreed to renew or extend the fixed-term tenancy at the expiry provided the rent arrears are paid, the client can be considered to retain the accommodation
- when the landlord and client have agreed to end the tenancy at expiry even if the accommodation cost arrears were to be paid, depending on the time until expiry, the client may not meet the requirement to be able to keep the accommodation and not qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant
- when the landlord or tenant gives written notice to terminate the tenancy under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986, an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant cannot be granted

chunks.title: Impact on the client and their family — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Impact on the client and their family
When considering whether to make an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, MSD must consider the likely impacts on the client, their partner (if any), and their dependent children (if any) if the client's accommodation need is not met.
MSD should consider what other accommodation or options are available to the client if they do not get the grant.
Factors that MSD may consider include (but are not limited to) if:
- the client is likely to require emergency housing if assistance is not granted
- the client will need to stay in accommodation that is close to a perpetrator of violence if assistance is not granted
- the client will need to stay in accommodation that is near drug use or gang related activity if assistance is not granted
- the client can afford any of their other options
- there are enough bedrooms in the other accommodation
- they will be staying in suitable accommodation if they do not get the grant
- they will be a reasonable distance from work, school or essential services if assistance is not granted
- their other options meet the accessibility needs the client, their partner (if any), or their children (if any) may have
MSD must assess each client's circumstances on a case-by-case basis and determine how significant any impacts on the client's family will be.
## Example
Sam lives with their partner and two children in a cabin in a campground. It is suitably sized and appropriate for their family.
Sam is three weeks behind on their cabin payments and has been told by the cabin company to pay these immediately or they will be at risk of losing the accommodation. Sam has applied for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant to keep their cabin.
Sam and their family have an option to stay with their brother that would have a lower weekly accommodation cost for Sam, however it would take over an hour and a half for Sam to get to work and to their children's school during peak traffic times.
MSD and Sam agree that the impacts on their family to travel and pay for travel costs will be significant, and MSD grants Accommodation Costs Arrears for the cabin.

chunks.title: Income limit — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Income limit
A client and their partner (if any) cannot get an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant if their income is more than the income limit.
There is one set of income limits for all clients including those getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension, and non-beneficiaries
For New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients you should check their income is not over the income limit. New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension must be included as income when assessing if the client qualifies.
There is no discretion to grant an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant to a client whose income (including the income of their partner, if any) is above the income limit.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Introduction
An Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant is a Housing Support Product for clients who need help to retain their accommodation. It provides recoverable assistance to help clients with overdue accommodation costs, who are at risk of losing their accommodation due to their arrears and who will be able to keep the accommodation if the arrears are paid.
An Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant is a discretionary grant and can be considered for any client who meets the qualifications.
## Rent Arrears Grant
Clients can be paid a Rent Arrears Grant if they are in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to.
MSD will need to assess the client’s accommodation agreement to determine whether the client is in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to.
Clients will need to meet all other eligibility criteria to receive the grant.

chunks.title: Net equity — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: The net equity of a house, boat or vehicle is the amount of money the owner can get from the sale of the item once they've paid any debt owed on it. For example, when a client does not have a loan to help pay for a boat their net equity is the total amount of cash they could get for selling the boat. When a client got a loan to pay for an item, their net equity is the total value of the item minus the money they still owe on the item.

chunks.title: House and land — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Only assess the net equity of house and land not used as the client’s principal place of residence. When assessing net equity on a house and/or land, use the rateable valuation or the amount insured. Use whichever value is the greater. Example House valued at $100,000 Land valued at $100,000 Total combined value $200,000 Less outstanding mortgage principal $150,000 Net equity $50,000 Some District Councils only use the capital value of a property. This is recorded on the rate notice. In these cases, the capital value is the value of both the house and land value combined. Example Capital value $200,000 Less outstanding mortgage principal $150,000 Net equity $50,000

chunks.title: Boat or caravan — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Boats or caravans used by the client or a member of their family for day-to-day accommodation are not considered a cash asset. The value of leisure boats or caravans will be the insured value. When the leisure boat or caravan is not insured, the client will be required to provide, and pay for, written verification of: - the leisure boat's value from a boat dealer and/or - the caravan's value from a caravan dealer Example Boat valued at $10,000 Less outstanding loan on boat $3,000 Net equity $7,000

chunks.title: Vehicle — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: When assessing the net equity of a vehicle use the estimated value of the vehicle. Do not assess the net equity of any vehicle used by the client or their partner for their personal use (this is limited to 1 vehicle for a single person or 2 vehicles for a couple). Example Vehicle valued at $15,000 Less outstanding loan on vehicle $7,000 Net equity $8,000

chunks.title: Client has more than one vehicle — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: When a client has more than one vehicle, MSD will need to assess whether the vehicles are used for private use. Example A family of 3 adults owns 5 vehicles, and all are claimed to be used for personal use. One is a vintage car used for Sunday outings and another a 4-wheel drive used on weekends only. The 4-wheel drive and vintage car are additional to the needs of the family. Therefore, for a Rent Arrears Grant, the net equity of these vehicles will need to be assessed.

chunks.title: Notice to remedy for rent arrears — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Notice to remedy for rent arrears
To qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant the client must be at risk of losing their current accommodation if their arrears are not paid.
For clients who are in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to, an accommodation supplier may give the client a notice to remedy due to rent arrears.
The client has the following amounts of time to pay the arrears:
- at least 14 calendar days, if they are on a periodic or fixed-term tenancy agreement or
- at least 10 calendar days, if they are on a boarding house tenancy agreement
When the accommodation supplier has issued the client with a notice to remedy due to rent arrears, the client can be considered at risk of losing their accommodation due to accommodation cost arrears.
If the client does not pay the accommodation cost arrears within the provided timeframes, the landlord can:
- apply to the Tenancy Tribunal for an order to end the tenancy, if the client is on a periodic or fixed-term tenancy agreement
- end the tenancy with 48-hours written notice, if the client is on a boarding house tenancy agreement
Note Accommodation suppliers cannot give a client a notice to remedy due to accommodation cost arrears if the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to the accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: Other financial assistance available to the client — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Other financial assistance available to the client
MSD must assess whether the client can receive other financial assistance before granting an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant.
This assistance could include any one-off or ongoing payments from MSD. When a client is granted other financial assistance for accommodation cost arrears, but it doesn't cover the full amount needed, MSD can consider an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant for the remaining amount.
An Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant should not be paid for costs already paid for by any other financial assistance.
Some clients may have access to other forms of assistance. They may still be eligible for Housing Support Products but only once they have exhausted all other forms of support first. For example:
- tertiary students staying in university accommodation (e.g. Halls of Residence)
- clients in rest homes and retirement villages
- clients in institutions for the care of sick and disabled people
## Assessing additional assistance
Make sure the client is aware of all the additional financial assistance available from MSD. This includes Extra Help such as Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support and other Housing Support Products such as Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant or Moving Costs Grant.
Additional assistance may help reduce hardship and prevent the client from needing further assistance for housing related costs.
## Example
Saane is a tenant in a property and applies for an Accommodation Costs in Arrears Grant of $400 for two weeks of accommodation costs. They are receiving a reduced rate of Student Allowance of $150 per week due to their parent's income and received a scholarship payment of $750 earlier in the year. They have not accessed their Student Loan Living Costs.
MSD does not grant the payment as the student could speak to their parents for support, or access their scholarship payment to cover their accommodation cost arrears. MSD also advises the student to access their Student Loan Living Costs entitlement so that they can cover their accommodation costs going forward.

chunks.title: Paying someone other than the accommodation supplier — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Paying someone other than the accommodation supplier
Generally, an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant should only be paid directly to the accommodation supplier or property manager.
However, in some situations, MSD may pay an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant to the client's payment card or directly to the client.
The Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant:
- can be paid to the client's payment card when the accommodation supplier or property manager indicates this is their preferred payment method
- can only be paid directly to the client (eg bank account) when the accommodation supplier or property manager or their agent is not in MSD’s system and the client needs an immediate grant paid to keep the accommodation

chunks.title: Maximum amount for a grant — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: The maximum Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant payable is limited to the lesser of the following: - the amount of accommodation cost arrears the client and their partner (if any) combined must pay the accommodation supplier or - the equivalent of 4 weeks accommodation costs or the accommodation or - if the client is in a shared accommodation the client and their partner's (if any) portion of 4 weeks rent

chunks.title: Social housing — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: When a client is applying for rent arrears assistance for social housing, the maximum amount they can apply for is based on 4 times: - the weekly rate of Income Related Rent charged by their social housing provider for the arrears period or - if they do not pay Income Related Rent, the weekly market rent for the social housing during the arrears period Note to pay an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant to a social housing provider, the client must be at risk of losing their social housing tenancy if the accommodation cost arrears are not paid. Kāinga Ora generally does not end tenancies when accommodation cost arrears are owing and they will work with their tenants to recover any accommodation cost arrears. When all options have been exhausted, they may then end the tenancy.

chunks.title: Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant can be paid twice in a 52-week period — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: An Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant cannot be paid more than twice in a 52-week period to a client unless there are exceptional circumstances. This includes any payments made as a Rent Arrears Grant. The period of 52 weeks starts on the date a grant is paid. When a client applies for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, MSD must check how many Accommodation Costs Arrears Grants or Rent Arrears Grants the client has had in the last 52 weeks. Any Accommodation Costs Arrears Grants or Rent Arrears Grants paid in the 52-week period before the latest application are counted, including any grants paid due to exceptional circumstances. If a client gets more than one payment of an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant in a 52-week period, they can get up to the maximum amount for each grant. For more information see: - Exceptional Circumstances

chunks.title: Payments made under other forms of assistance — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: The Housing Support Programme, introduced on 13 March 2023, was only available to clients in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. A client who was in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to could have been assisted with accommodation support through an Advance Payment of Benefit, Recoverable Assistance Payment, or Special Needs Grant. From 1 July 2024, the Housing Support Programme was expanded to include clients who are in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. Any payments a client got for accommodation cost arrears before 1 July 2024 either as an Advance Payment of Benefit, Recoverable Assistance Payment, or Special Needs Grant are not included in the grant count.

chunks.title: Paying someone other than the landlord or property manager — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Generally, an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant is paid directly to the accommodation supplier or property manager. However, in some situations, MSD may pay an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant to the client's payment card or directly to the client.

chunks.title: Pre-paid funeral expenses — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Pre-paid funeral expenses
A pre-paid funeral trust fund or account is money put aside (usually in a trust) exclusively for the payment of funeral expenses.
If the money can be accessed by the client and used for other purposes, it is not considered exclusively for funeral expenses and can be treated as a cash asset.
It is usually clear whether a trust fund or account has been genuinely set aside for funeral expenses. Evidence it has been set aside exclusively for funeral expenses include:
- the trust fund/account is only paid out when there is a death certificate
- the client cannot usually access the funds
- if a client can access the fund, there are limited conditions on withdrawal, such as re-locating overseas
- the trust fund/account is only payable to the funeral director or administrator of the client's estate
- the client cannot generally access the interest earned from the trust fund or account
When the trust fund or account has been set aside for funeral expenses and cannot be accessed or converted into cash this money is not a realisable asset.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant a client must:
- meet the residency qualifications
- meet the income and assets limits
- be required to pay accommodation cost arrears to their accommodation supplier
- be at risk of losing their current accommodation due to their arrears
- be likely to retain their current accommodation if given an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant
While a client may qualify, the approval of an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant is discretionary and should be considered according to each client's specific situation and need.

chunks.title: Recovery of payment — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Recovery of payment
Before approving an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, MSD must discuss a repayment plan with the client.
The client has a number of repayment options available as listed below:
- deductions from a main benefit, Student Allowance, or Working for Families assistance paid to the client by MSD
- employer deduction notice (Client Support - Debt Management will arrange this - case managers cannot issue a wage deduction notice)
- automatic payment from the client's bank account
- internet/telebanking payment
- payment through New Zealand Post Shop
## Recovery rate
An Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant must have a recovery rate that means the client will pay back the debt owed within 24 months of the grant unless they have exceptional circumstances.
The rate and method of recovery must be discussed with the client, and be based on their individual circumstances and ability to live within the reduced income.
It is important the client knows the length of time the Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant will be repaid over.
Clients who have already been granted an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant may have their recovery rate adjusted at a later date if their circumstances change.
When determining the rate of repayment by instalments MSD must consider:
- whether the instalment reductions will leave enough for the client's living expenses and any other debt repayments
- the impact on the individual (and/or their immediate family) when establishing further recoverable debt and
- the likelihood it would cause the client to seek further Housing Support Product payments or other extra help assistance
## Maximum recovery rate for beneficiaries
The recommended maximum recovery rate for clients currently getting income support cannot be more than $40 a week unless the client volunteers to pay more.

chunks.title: Accommodation cost arrears for tenants of Kāinga Ora — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation cost arrears for tenants of Kāinga Ora
To qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant the client must be at risk of losing their current accommodation if their accommodation cost arrears are not paid and will be likely to keep their accommodation if an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant is paid.
Kāinga Ora as the Government's Public Housing provider operates differently to how a private landlord may act.
Kāinga Ora is less likely to end a tenancy for overdue accommodation costs and will work with their tenants to recover any arrears. They may consider ending the tenancy only after all options have been exhausted.
When a Kāinga Ora social housing tenant is in arrears, generally, Kāinga Ora will arrange for any accommodation cost arrears owing to be repaid to them directly.
A redirection of benefit for accommodation costs arrears can be made to Kāinga Ora when tenants are getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran Pension.
For more information see:
Kāinga Ora tenants may qualify for a Rent Arrears Grant, if you are satisfied Kāinga Ora has:
- exhausted all reasonable efforts to recover the rent arrears and
- confirmed they are taking, or about to take, active steps to end the tenancy due to the arrears

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant a client must:
- qualify for and be getting a main benefit or
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand at the time of their application, andbe a New Zealand citizen orhold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 orbe recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009qualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with the intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy, but the relationship ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- hold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009
- qualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with the intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy, but the relationship ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they are considered to hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other qualifications for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant.

chunks.title: Resources available to the client — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Resources available to the client
When deciding whether to grant an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, MSD may consider the ability the client and their partner (if any) have to meet the cost of the accommodation cost arrears from their own resources.
If the client and their partner (if any) have resources available to them, these should generally be used to pay for their accommodation cost arrears, unless this would mean they're unable to meet their essential living expenses.
Examples of a client using the resources they have available to them may include:
- using any cash assets to pay the accommodation cost arrears
- accessing assistance available from other government agencies
- paying the accommodation cost arrears from their next income payment due to them
- paying the rent arrears to the landlord through an ongoing redirection of benefit or automatic payment
Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.

chunks.title: Reviews and Appeals — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Reviews and Appeals
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have received formal notification of and disagree with a decision on their application for assistance under the Housing Support Programme.
A client can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority when they do not agree with a decision, which was upheld or upheld in part by the Benefits Review Committee under an application for Review of Decision.
The client has the right to apply for a Review of Decision at any time within 3 months of the original decision being advised. When a client has applied for a hearing outside the 3-month time limit the Benefits Review Committee must decide whether or not to accept the application before it considers the decision under review.
A client has the right to have their decision reviewed once. If they wish to have the same decision reviewed again refer the case to Legal Services.

chunks.title: Service costs and water rates — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Sometimes a client’s accommodation costs include service costs such as electricity or an internet connection. Service costs do not include water rates.

chunks.title: Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: When a client is living in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to, service costs cannot be included. Only the portion of the costs that relates to their accommodation can be included in a Rent Arrears Grant. Generally the service costs and cost of accommodation will be itemised separately on the tenancy agreement. Use the accommodation cost only to calculate a Rent Arrears Grant.

chunks.title: Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Clients living in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to may have service costs included in their Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant if these are unable to be separated from their accommodation costs. MSD should try to identify and separate service costs wherever possible.

chunks.title: Service costs not clear — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: When the service costs are not itemised separately, assess the cost of the service(s) and deduct it from the total accommodation costs to determine the cost of accommodation. The accommodation supplier should provide an estimate of the accommodation and service cost components of the client's accommodation cost payment. If the client is unable to get an estimate from the accommodation supplier or if there is a disagreement between the accommodation supplier and client about the cost split between accommodation and service costs, estimate the service costs based on information already available about those costs. The information sources used will depend on the specific service cost. For example, if the total rent includes electricity costs, you can use the Powerswitch website to calculate the cost of the electricity to be deducted from the total rent.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: John pays $250 total rent a week for a room and electricity in a boarding house. As there is only one meter box for the boarding house the landlord is unable to provide an estimate of the service cost. Powerswitch estimates the weekly electricity costs of the household to be $120 a week. There are 6 people in the household, so John’s share of the electricity costs would be $120 divided by 6 (the total number of the people in the household) which is $20. To calculate John's accommodation costs, deduct $20 (electricity) from $250 (total rent). John's accommodation costs are $230 a week.

chunks.title: Water rates — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: When a client's rent includes water rates (also referred to as water charges), the portion of costs that relates to the water rates can be included for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant if: - the accommodation has a separate water meter and - the accommodation agreement states the client is responsible for this cost Note Water rates do not include the cost of filling water tanks.

chunks.title: Shared accommodation — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Shared accommodation
To qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, a client must be likely to keep their current accommodation if the assistance is granted.
When there is more than one occupant that is not the client’s partner or dependent child (if any) under the accommodation agreement this is referred to as shared accommodation.
## Accommodation costs arrears
In shared accommodation, all occupants may be responsible for a share of the accommodation costs but this does not mean that the amount of accommodation costs arrears must be shared equally.
For example, one occupant may be the only person to have not paid their share of the accommodation costs and can apply for the full amount of their outstanding accommodation costs.
When accommodation is shared, the client must indicate the portion of the total accommodation cost arrears they need to pay when applying for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant.
Each occupant under the accommodation agreement can apply for the portion of the accommodation arrears they are responsible for paying in separate applications if they are eligible.
## Example
Pedro lives in a flat with 3 other occupants. The rent for the flat is $600 a week, and Pedro’s share is $150.
Pedro has not paid his share of the rent for the past 3 weeks. The landlord has contacted the tenants to tell them that the flat is $450 in arrears and these will need to be paid immediately or their accommodation will be at risk.
As Pedro is the only one responsible for the arrears, he can apply for the full amount of $450.
## Likely to keep the accommodation
When one occupant in shared accommodation plans to leave the accommodation or is unlikely to be able to keep their accommodation (for example they are unable to pay their share of the accommodation costs on an ongoing basis), this may impact on the other occupants.
If the client applying for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant has a reasonable plan to be able to stay in the accommodation, MSD should consider that they will be able to keep their current accommodation.
What is reasonable will depend on the specific circumstances but may include options such as:
- advertising for a new flatmate
- negotiating a reduced accommodation cost for a period of time or
- paying a higher share of the total accommodation cost, if affordable

chunks.title: Staying in accommodation for more than 28 days — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: To qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant a client should intend to be staying in accommodation for at least 28 days. This is because the client should be able to keep their accommodation when an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant is made. MSD can consider granting an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant when the client is staying for less than 28 days on a discretionary basis. When a client requests an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant for accommodation that they will stay in for less than 28 days, MSD should consider if: - the client will require emergency housing if an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant is not granted - there will be an impact to the client, their partner, and/or their children if the assistance is not granted - a short-term grant will make it more likely for the client to stay in accommodation long-term. For example, a boarding house owner will only accept the client for a week to see how things go before they commit to the client staying long-term - the client has long-term accommodation arranged, but requires a short-term grant somewhere else before the accommodation is available. For example, they need to stay with their friend for 2 weeks before their rental tenancy begins

chunks.title: Example 1 — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Tegan has been staying in a lodging house and she is in two weeks of accommodation costs arrears due to issues with her employment. She is moving out of the lodging house in three weeks’ time to move into a rental property and can afford the ongoing accommodation costs, but cannot pay the arrears. The owner of the lodging house tells her that she has to pay the arrears immediately or she will be evicted. Tegan applies for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. There is no other accommodation available (including staying with family or friends temporarily until the rental property is available), and her only alternative would be to apply for emergency housing if she is evicted from the motel. MSD decides to grant the Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant even though she will be staying there for less than 28 days so that Tegan can keep her accommodation until she moves into the new rental property.

chunks.title: Example 2 — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Dylan is moving out of a flat in Wellington where they are a tenant in three weeks' time because they are moving to Auckland to look for work. They are two weeks behind on their accommodation costs and apply for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant to pay the arrears before their accommodation ends. Dylan has other accommodation options available as he can stay with his friend. MSD declines the Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant because Dylan has other options available and will be staying at this accommodation for less than 28 days.

chunks.title: Tenancy reviews for social housing — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Tenancy reviews for social housing
To qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, a client must be likely to keep their current accommodation if the assistance is granted.
When a client applying for a grant is in social housing and subject to a tenancy review, this doesn't affect MSD’s consideration of the client's ability to keep the accommodation. Except when a 90-day notice has been issued as a result of the tenancy review as this may impact on whether the client can keep the tenancy.
Note granting an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant to a client in social housing does not mean the tenancy or Income Related Rent has to continue. The client may still have a tenancy review, provider-initiated transfer or eviction, as appropriate.
## 90-day notice has been issued as a result of the tenancy review
When the client no longer qualifies for social housing and has been issued a 90-day notice by the social housing provider at the end of the tenancy review process, the client will not qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant.

chunks.title: Tenancy Tribunal orders — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: The Tenancy Tribunal can make a range of orders including to: - end a tenancy and require the tenant to leave the property - require a landlord or tenant to pay money to the other person - require a landlord or tenant to do maintenance work or repair damage Tenancy Tribunal orders may have specific conditions or no conditions. These orders generally only apply to accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. Example conditional orders can be used when the Tenancy Tribunal requires a tenant to pay rent arrears within a specified period or the tenancy will be ended. If the tenant does not pay the rent arrears on time, the order becomes final and the tenancy ends without the landlord having to go back to the Tenancy Tribunal.

chunks.title: Impact of Tenancy Tribunal applications and orders on Accommodation Costs Arrears Grants — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Issue before the Tenancy Tribunal How the application or order applies to Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant Payment of rent arrears A landlord may apply for a Tenancy Tribunal order requiring the client to pay accommodation costs arrears as soon as their accommodation costs are overdue. This is sometimes known as a monetary order. If the landlord is applying to the Tenancy Tribunal to have the arrears paid before the client owes at least 21 days of rent (and is not ending the tenancy), they do not have to give a notice to remedy and give the client 14 days to pay the rent arrears before applying to the Tenancy Tribunal.

chunks.title: Application to the Tenancy Tribunal — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: When the landlord has applied for a Tenancy Tribunal order for the payment of rent arrears, the client can be considered at risk of losing their tenancy due to accommodation costs arrears.

chunks.title: Order of the Tenancy Tribunal — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Ending the tenancy The Tenancy Tribunal may make an order to end the tenancy and for the landlord to take possession of the property due to accommodation costs arrears if the landlord has applied for the order and: - the landlord gave notice that a tenant was at least 5 working days late with their rent payment on 3 separate occasions within a 90-day period (for a periodic tenancy) or - the client owes at least 21 days' rent. Regardless of whether a notice to remedy was given (for a periodic or fixed-term tenancy) Tenancy Tribunal orders will indicate the grounds on which the tenancy is ended

chunks.title: Application to the Tenancy Tribunal — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: If the landlord has applied for a Tenancy Tribunal order to have the tenancy ended due to accommodation costs arrears, the client can be considered at risk of losing their tenancy due to accommodation costs arrears.

chunks.title: Order of the Tenancy Tribunal — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: When the Tenancy Tribunal has made an order ending the tenancy that is not an interim or conditional order, the tenant is not eligible for Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. Interim or conditional orders may impact on whether the client is likely to be able to keep the tenancy and will be considered with the client's circumstances

chunks.title: Tenancy Tribunal — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Tenancy Tribunal
To qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant the client must be at risk of losing their current accommodation if their accommodation costs arrears are not paid.
Generally only clients and accommodation suppliers who are in accommodation agreements that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to are able to resolve disputes through the Tenancy Tribunal.
A client is considered to be at risk of losing their accommodation due to accommodation cost arrears when:
- the accommodation supplier has made an application to the Tenancy Tribunal to have the accommodation cost arrears paid
- the accommodation supplier has made an application to the Tenancy Tribunal to have the tenancy ended due to accommodation cost arrears or
- the Tenancy Tribunal has made an order for the client to pay the accommodation cost arrears

chunks.title: Tenants — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: A client who signs the tenancy agreement at a property is known as a tenant. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to them, and they are responsible to the landlord for any rent and damages due at the accommodation. When a client is a tenant, their accommodation supplier is the landlord and any Rent Arrears Grants are made to the landlord directly.

chunks.title: Flatmates — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: A client who is living at the accommodation and has not signed the tenancy agreement is usually known as a flatmate. They Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to them. When a client is a flatmate, their accommodation supplier is the tenant who the flatmate is responsible for paying their accommodation costs to. The tenant that the client pays accommodation costs to at the property takes responsibility for the client instead of the client dealing directly with the landlord. This is also sometimes called subletting. Any Accommodation Cost Arrears Grants are made to the tenant that the flatmate pays their accommodation costs to, who will then pay the landlord.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Jene is a flatmate in a property and pays their accommodation costs to Hannah, the head tenant in the household. Jene gets into three weeks of accommodation costs arrears and owes Hannah $900. As Hannah is responsible for paying the rent to the landlord, she has advised Jene that she will need to pay immediately or she cannot live with her any more. Jene applies for and is granted an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. This is paid to Hannah as she is Jene’s accommodation supplier. Hannah then pays this money to their landlord.

chunks.title: Rent and accommodation costs arrears — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Tenants who get into arrears are eligible for a Rent Arrears Grant if they meet the criteria and they are at risk of losing their tenancy. Rent Arrears Grants will be paid to the landlord unless exceptional circumstances exist. When a flatmate gets into arrears, they are responsible to the tenant that they pay their accommodation costs to. A flatmate can receive an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant if they meet the criteria and are at risk of losing the accommodation. An Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant will be paid to the tenant who is responsible for the client unless exceptional circumstances exist.

chunks.title: Tenant at risk due to flatmate not paying arrears — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: When a tenant is in arrears due to the flatmate not paying their accommodation costs, they can contact the flatmate to arrange repayments. If the flatmate is unable to pay the arrears and the tenant is at risk of losing their tenancy, a Rent Arrears Grant can be made for the tenant as they are responsible under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 to pay any rent due to the landlord. The tenant will still need to meet all other eligibility criteria, and discretion will need to be applied to determine if they are likely to keep the accommodation and that they have made reasonable efforts to organise repayments with the flatmate.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text: Peta is a tenant at her accommodation and has asked her friend James to be a flatmate. James has fallen behind on his accommodation costs payments to Peta for 6 weeks. Peta’s landlord has advised her that if this is not paid in full in a week, she will lose her tenancy. Peta talks to James about paying the arrears, however he cannot afford to pay the arrears and he is not eligible for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant as he does not meet the residential criteria. As Peta is responsible to her landlord for the total accommodation costs, she contacts MSD and is granted a Rent Arrears Grant in her own right to cover the arrears.

chunks.title: Unable to meet essential living expenses — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs arrears grant
chunks.text:
## Unable to meet essential living expenses
When assessing an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, MSD may assess whether the client will be unable to meet their other essential living expenses if the assistance is paid. This includes when the client is unable to meet the essential living expenses for their partner and/or dependent children (if any).
Essential living expenses for the purposes of Housing Support Products may include, but are not limited to:
- accommodation
- food
- fuel (including petrol, diesel and oil)
- telephone costs, this may include: internet connection and mobile service charges
- internet connection and mobile service charges
- motor vehicles costs - repayment and running costs
- essential travel, this may include: employment related traveltravel when accessing essential services and supplies (including children's education and groceries)
- employment related travel
- travel when accessing essential services and supplies (including children's education and groceries)
- power
- childcare costs
- hire purchase expenses for essential household items only, it may also include employment related items. It does not include luxury items such as fishing/jet boats or small planes
- transport cost due to disability
- disability and personal health costs
- counselling
- education costs for dependent children
- clothing
Essential living expenses may vary between clients and should be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

chunks.title: Able to obtain and retain accommodation — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Able to obtain and retain accommodation
To qualify for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant, MSD must consider the client is likely to be able to obtain and retain accommodation.
MSD will need to discuss with the client whether they can likely afford (with any financial assistance, income and other resources available to them) to obtain and retain accommodation, including the ongoing costs of the accommodation.
A client may be considered as being likely to get and keep accommodation when:
- the proposed accommodation costs will generally not be over 60 per cent of their net income (and their partner's, if any) taking into account the client's individual circumstances and
- MSD has discussed the client's budget, or have other evidence showing they can manage their future outgoings

chunks.title: Tenant under a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to any tenancy with a written tenancy agreement from Tenancy Services. Some examples are a: - tenancy agreement for rental housing, including with: a private landlordlocal governmenta non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) - a private landlord - local government - a non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) or - tenancy agreement for social housing, including with a community housing provider Clients in this accommodation may be eligible for a Rent in Advance Grant.

chunks.title: Flatmate or subletting without a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Clients may be living in a rental property as a flatmate or subletter without a tenancy agreement. The tenant on the tenancy agreement that the client pays their accommodation costs to takes responsibility for these clients and acts as their accommodation supplier. Flatmates generally pay any accommodation costs to the tenant instead of the landlord. This includes clients who are an additional occupant in a social housing property, as they are not on the tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these clients and they may be eligible for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant.

chunks.title: Service tenancies — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: A client may be provided accommodation as part of their employment where their landlord is their employer. This is known as a service tenancy. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to service tenancies. Clients in a service tenancy will generally be provided with a written tenancy agreement. These clients may be eligible for a Rent in Advance Grant.

chunks.title: Tenancy orders — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: A tenant of a property through a tenancy order made under the Family Violence Act 2018 or Property (Relationships) Act 1976 does not need to have signed a written tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to clients in a tenancy order. These clients may be eligible for a Rent in Advance Grant.

chunks.title: Boarding arrangements — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Clients who are boarding have an agreement for one room in the property, rather than the whole house. Boarders have access to shared facilities such as a kitchen and bathroom. When the accommodation has 6 or more occupants, this is known as a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to boarding houses when the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more. The client may be eligible for a Rent in Advance Grant if they meet these qualifications. When there are 5 or fewer occupants this is not considered a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these boarding arrangements, including private boarding where the client lives with the owner of the property. Clients in these arrangements may be eligible for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant. The accommodation costs a client pays under a boarding accommodation agreement generally includes service and facility costs such as power, grounds maintenance, rubbish disposal, etc. MSD generally should not include any service costs in an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. For more information about what costs can be included in an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, see: - Service costs and water rates

chunks.title: Example 2 - Boarding arrangement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Malosi is boarding with their aunt Vaima. Vaima owns the house and Malosi pays board that includes accommodation, food, and service costs, including internet and power costs. Malosi and Vaima have an accommodation agreement which sets out these costs. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to this accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: Rent to buy — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: A person may enter into a rent to buy contract (also called a deferred payment disposition). In these situations, the person is considered to be a homeowner and is not eligible for a Housing Support Product.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Elisapeta has entered a rent to own programme to buy their home. They have a 5-year accommodation agreement and at the end of the 5-year arrangement they will have the option to purchase the home. They pay 30% of their gross income as accommodation costs. This is a rent to buy accommodation arrangement that is not eligible for a Housing Support Product.

chunks.title: Relocatable accommodation — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: A person may enter a hire agreement or a rental contract for relocatable accommodation, such as a cabin, mobile home, or caravan. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 only applies to relocatable accommodation if it is: - hired from and located on a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner Clients in this accommodation may be eligible for a Rent in Advance Grant. The Residential Tenancies Act 1896 does not apply if the relocatable accommodation is: - on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days or - placed on any other premises where the land and the accommodation are not owned by the same person or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner Clients in this accommodation may be eligible for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant.

chunks.title: Example 1 - campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Rarahu intends to stay in a cabin in a commercial campsite for a minimum of 90 days. She requires assistance with accommodation costs in advance to get the cabin. As Rarahu intends to stay in the cabin for 51 days or more, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to their accommodation arrangement. MSD can approve a Rent in Advance Grant for Rarahu to get the cabin.

chunks.title: Example 2 - campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Arama intends to stay in a cabin in a commercial campsite for 30 days while she waits for her new job to start, which will provide her with long-term accommodation while she's employed. She requires assistance with accommodation costs in advance to get the cabin. As Arama intends to stay in the cabin for under 51 days, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to her accommodation arrangement. MSD can approve an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant for Arama to get the cabin.

chunks.title: Multiple accommodation agreements — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: If a client is an occupant under multiple accommodation agreements (i.e. required to pay accommodation costs for more than one accommodation agreement), the Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant is only payable for the client's principal place of residence. MSD must assess their principal place of residence to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies, and whether the client is eligible for a Rent in Advance or Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant at this accommodation. If the client and their partner have separate accommodation, they may each have a different principal place of residence. Generally, the client will determine what is their principal place of residence. If there is evidence the client is not using the property as their principal place of residence, MSD should generally decline an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant. For example, if the client is using the property to store excess personal goods or sub-letting the property while living elsewhere, MSD should not pay an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant. Note a grant can be paid for multiple accommodation agreements if they are for the same accommodation. For example, where a client has a rental contract for a cabin hire and a separate rental contract for the land that the cabin sits on.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Jiang lives in accommodation in Auckland. His ex-partner lives in Hamilton and has custody of their children. Jiang is planning to visit Hamilton for four days each month to visit his children and has an accommodation agreement with a friend where he will pay $150 each month to stay at their place when he visits. His friend has requested one month of accommodation costs in advance before Jiang moves into his accommodation. Jiang applies for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant for the accommodation agreement in Hamilton. As this is not his primary place of residence, MSD declines the grant.

chunks.title: Accommodation is suitable to live in — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation is suitable to live in
MSD may consider whether the accommodation will be suitable for the client to live in if the grant is made.
Factors MSD may consider include (but are not limited to) if the:
- accommodation has been modified to suit the accessibility needs for the client, their partner (if any) or their dependent children (if any)
- client will have access to facilities such as clean drinking water, cooking facilities, electricity, heating, beds and mattresses, toilet and bathing facilities and a food refrigerator that the client can access
- accommodation has enough bedrooms
- accommodation is fit for human habitation, including being structurally safe to live in
MSD does not need to assess if a client’s accommodation is suitable at every Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant assessment. However, if it is clear through the conversation with the client that the accommodation is not suitable for the client, their partner (if any) or their dependent children (if any), MSD may decline the application.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Accommodation Costs in Advance can be granted for clients who are moving into specific accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. These accommodation agreements may include, but are not limited to: - a flat or house share agreement where the client has not signed a tenancy agreement (e.g. a flatmate that sub-lets from a head tenant) - hire agreement for a relocatable home including a cabin, mobile home or caravan where: it is on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days, oron any other premises for any amount of time where the land and accommodation are not owned by the same person oron a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner - it is on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days, or - on any other premises for any amount of time where the land and accommodation are not owned by the same person or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner - a lodging arrangement - a boarding agreement where the client is either: in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to and does stay for less than 28 daysin accommodation that is not a boarding house - in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to and does stay for less than 28 days - in accommodation that is not a boarding house - commercial accommodation such as hotels, motels, and homestays that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. This excludes the following accommodation as they are not eligible to receive an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant: emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Granttransitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development andcontracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant - transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development and - contracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - an additional occupant in a social housing property that is not a tenant or a signatory to the tenancy agreement MSD will need to assess a client’s accommodation agreement to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Clients may be living in accommodation that is not included in the above list. They may still be eligible for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant if the accommodation they are living in is not specifically excluded.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to
The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 provides rights and protections for tenants and landlords in rental agreements.
MSD can pay a Rent in Advance Grant for clients who are moving into accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. This includes, but is not limited to:
- rental tenancies
- boarding houses with at least 6 tenants or boarders where the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more
- service tenancies where an employer provides accommodation to an employee
- multi-unit residential housing developments to provide long-term (minimum of 10 years) rental accommodation to tenants (also known as build to rent tenancies)
- social housing (including Kainga Ora and private social housing) if the client is a tenant or a signatory
- hire agreements for relocatable homes including cabins, mobile homes and caravans where they are: hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more oron a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner
- hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or
- on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner
If you are unsure if the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to an accommodation agreement, contact Helpline or your Capability Developer.

chunks.title: Assessing an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Assessing an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant
When a client needs help with accommodation costs in advance, an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant should be considered if they meet the qualifications.
An Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant is available for clients who are likely to be able to keep accommodation but require some assistance to get it.
An Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant is a discretionary grant. MSD needs to consider the client's individual circumstances to determine whether the Accommodation Costs in Advance should be granted.
In order to make a decision to grant, MSD must consider:
- the purpose of the Housing Support Programme, including whether granting Accommodation Costs in Advance would be the correct use of the payment
- any other financial assistance available to the client that could be used to meet their need
- whether the client and their partner (if any) could meet the need from their own resources, including accessing cash assets or receiving support from other Government agencies
- any impact on the client, their partner (if any), and their dependent children (if any) if their need is not met and
- whether the client intends to stay in the accommodation for fewer than 28 days
Depending on the client’s circumstances, MSD may also consider the following factors:
- whether the client or their partner (if any) has caused or contributed to the need for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant
- whether the client or their partner (if any) will be able to meet their essential living expenses if Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant is paid
- the existing debt of the client and their partner (if any)
- whether their accommodation is suitable to live in
- any other matters MSD think are relevant
A Rent in Advance Grant can be declined if a grant would not be appropriate after considering the circumstances of the client and their partner (if any) and their dependent children (if any).

chunks.title: Example 1 - variable income — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Example 1 - variable income
Piper works in a casual role in a supermarket. Their employment started 3 weeks ago, they have no set weekly hours and their income will change from week to week, depending on the number of hours they will work. Their employer has indicated they should receive a minimum of 20 hours work per week at $24 per hour ($480 per week) but this is not set out in Piper’s employment agreement. Piper’s 3-week income so far has been:
Week 1 = $400Week 2 = $200Week 3 = $300
In this case, Piper’s income will be estimated using the average wage[CA6] [JO7] [CA8] over the previous three weeks as they do not have four weeks of income to assess. The calculation is:
$400 + $200 + $300 = $900$900/3 (weeks) = $300.

chunks.title: Cash asset limit — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Cash asset limit
A client and their partner (if any) cannot get an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant if their assets are more than the cash asset limit.
We need to know the cash value of their assets.
There is no discretion to grant an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant to a client whose cash assets (including the cash assets of their partner, if any) are above the asset limit.
For more information about what cash assets include and do not include see:
- Cash assets

chunks.title: Cash assets include — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: - cash - bills of exchange or promissory notes - building society shares - money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society - money invested with or lent to any bank, financial institution or other person whether as a mortgage, other security, or unsecured - money withdrawn from a KiwiSaver scheme - mortgage investments and other long-term loans - the net equity held in any property or land not used as the client's home - pre-paid funeral expenses (in some circumstances) - shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds and bonds (including shares in energy organisations) and - the client's share in any partnership Note if you are unsure of a case please contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Cash assets do not include — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: - the home property and land on which it is situated - a motor vehicle or other vehicle principally used by the client or their partner for their personal use (this is limited to 1 vehicle for a single person or 2 vehicles for a couple) - a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2000, or which is used by the client or a member of their family for day to day accommodation - any payments clients get under Housing Support Products assistance (Moving Costs Grant, Bond Grant, Rent in Advance Grant, Rent Arrears Grant, Transition to Alternative Housing Grant, Tenancy Costs Cover, Accommodation Security Cover) - Personal effects - Christchurch mosques attack support payments - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts - Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income - Māori land - MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after payment is made - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made - specified Ex gratia and compensation payments - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received A bank overdraft is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.

chunks.title: Christchurch earthquake related payments — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies, or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client got the payment. See: - Payments from the Crown for the purchase of property in the Canterbury red zone - Payments from the Earthquake Commission and insurance companies (Canterbury earthquake 2010 and aftershock 2011) - Payments from the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross)

chunks.title: Client caused or contributed to the need — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Client caused or contributed to the need
When deciding whether to grant an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant, MSD may consider the extent the client has caused or contributed to their need for accommodation costs in advance.
