Examples of when a client may be considered to have caused or contributed to the need for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant include when:
- they have caused or contributed to intentional or reckless damage to their previous accommodation resulting in termination of their tenancy or accommodation agreement.
- they have not met their obligations for the previous accommodation, eg non-payment of rent, leaving without notice, additional occupants not approved by landlord etc resulting in termination of their accommodation agreement
Each client’s situation must be assessed on their individual circumstances.

chunks.title: Clients who cannot get an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Clients who cannot get an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant
Clients living in one of the following accommodation agreements are not eligible for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant:
- accommodation owned by the client or their partner
- tents, including those joined to a vehicle
- homeless shelters
- prisons and correctional facilities
- accommodation for which they are receiving an Emergency Housing Grant or Transitional or Contracted Emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development
There is no discretion to approve a payment for a client living in one of these accommodation agreements.

chunks.title: Clients with existing debt — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Clients with existing debt
When deciding whether to approve an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant, MSD may consider the existing debt of the client and their partner (if any). Existing debt includes both MSD debt and non-MSD debt.
A client's existing debt repayments may impact their ability to repay an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant.
When a client has existing MSD debt, MSD may consider whether it is appropriate to reduce those repayments to allow for the repayment of the Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant.
When a client is getting all the financial assistance they qualify for, but are not likely to be able to repay an amount paid under an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant, the grant may be declined.

chunks.title: Information on a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Information on a tenancy agreement
If it is unclear whether a document is a tenancy agreement under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 or not, below is a list of information that is usually part of this type of agreement:
- the full name and contact address of the landlord
- the landlord’s contact mobile telephone number (if any)
- the landlord’s contact email address (if any)
- the full name and contact address (when different from the address of the premises to which the agreement relates) of the tenant
- the tenant’s contact mobile telephone number (if any)
- the tenant’s contact email address (if any)
- the address of the premises
- the date of the tenancy agreement
- the date of commencement of the tenancy (when different from the date of the tenancy agreement)
- the landlord’s address for service
- the tenant’s address for service
- whether the tenant is under the age of 18
- the amount of any bond
- the rent payable
- the frequency of the rent payments
- the place or bank account number where the rent is to be paid
- a list of any chattels provided by the landlord
- if the tenancy is a fixed-term tenancy, the date on which the term will expire.
- Healthy Homes compliance statement
- insulation statement
- insurance statement
The agreement should be signed by both parties but if it's not signed, it may still be a valid agreement. In these cases, MSD can use other evidence to determine that there is an agreement in place. For example, bank account statement showing rent payments.

chunks.title: Unable to meet essential living expenses — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Unable to meet essential living expenses
When assessing an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant, MSD may assess whether the client will be unable to meet their other essential living expenses if the assistance is paid. This includes when the client is unable to meet the essential living expenses for their partner and/or dependent children (if any).
Essential living expenses for the purposes of Housing Support Products may include, but are not limited to:
- accommodation
- food
- fuel (including petrol, diesel and oil)
- telephone costs, this may include: internet connection and mobile service charges
- internet connection and mobile service charges
- motor vehicles costs - repayment and running costs
- essential travel, this may include: employment related traveltravel when accessing essential services and supplies (including children's education and groceries)
- employment related travel
- travel when accessing essential services and supplies (including children's education and groceries)
- power
- childcare costs
- hire purchase expenses for essential household items only, it may also include employment related items. It does not include luxury items such as fishing/jet boats or small planes
- transport cost due to disability
- disability and personal health costs
- counselling
- education costs for dependent children
- clothing
Essential living expenses may vary between clients and should be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances
A client cannot be paid more than two Accommodation Costs in Advance Grants in a 52-week period, unless there are exceptional circumstances. This includes any payments made as a Rent in Advance Grant.
Exceptional circumstances are where the circumstance:
- sets the client apart from others in a similar situation and
- are beyond the client's control
The following situations are generally considered as exceptional circumstances (but not limited to):
- the client needs to move through no fault of their own, e.g: the client has been notified the owner will move back into the accommodationthe property is deemed uninhabitable due to damage (such as a burst waterpipe) and major repairs are needed.
- the client has been notified the owner will move back into the accommodation
- the property is deemed uninhabitable due to damage (such as a burst waterpipe) and major repairs are needed.
- the client was a victim of a violent crime or family violence and has had a change in their housing circumstances, e.g: needing to move to a different property following a violent crime orno longer living with their partner after seeking a protection order (including if the client remains in the same property without their partner)
- needing to move to a different property following a violent crime or
- no longer living with their partner after seeking a protection order (including if the client remains in the same property without their partner)
There may be other reasons for exceptional circumstances.

chunks.title: Impact on the client and their family — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Impact on the client and their family
When considering whether to make an Accommodation Costs in Advance grant, MSD must consider the likely impacts on the client, their partner (if any), and their dependent children (if any) if the client's accommodation need is not met.
MSD should consider what other accommodation or options are available to the client if they do not get the grant.
Factors that MSD may consider include (but are not limited to) if:
- the client is likely to require emergency housing if assistance is not granted
- the client will need to stay in accommodation that is close to a perpetrator of violence if assistance is not granted
- the client will need to stay in accommodation that is near drug use or gang related activity if assistance is not granted
- the client can afford any of their other options
- there are enough bedrooms in the other accommodation
- they will be staying in suitable accommodation if they do not get the grant
- they will be a reasonable distance from work, school or essential services if assistance is not granted
- their other options meet the accessibility needs the client, their partner (if any), or their children (if any) may have
MSD must assess each client's circumstances on a case-by-case basis and determine how significant any impacts on the client's family will be.
## Example
Sam lives with their partner and two children. Their current tenancy is ending due to the landlord selling the property. Sam has applied for Accommodation Costs in Advance and a Moving Costs Grant to move into a cabin in a campground near her old tenancy. The cabin is suitably sized and appropriate for her family.
Sam and their family have an option to stay with their brother that would have a lower weekly accommodation cost for Sam, however it would take over an hour and a half for Sam to get to work and to their children's school during peak traffic times.
MSD and Sam agree that the impacts on her family to travel and pay for travel costs will be significant, and MSD grants Housing Support Product assistance for the cabin.

chunks.title: Income limit — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Income limit
A client and their partner (if any) cannot get an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant if their income is more than the income limit.
There is one set of income limits for all clients including those getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension, and non-beneficiaries.
For New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients MSD should check their income is not over the income limit. New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension must be included as income when assessing if the client qualifies.
There is no discretion to grant an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant to a client whose income (including the income of their partner, if any) is above the income limit.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Introduction
An Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant is a Housing Support Product for clients needing help to get accommodation. It provides recoverable assistance to help with accommodation costs in advance charged by an accommodation supplier to the client in order to move into the accommodation.
An Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant is a discretionary grant and can be considered for any client who meets the qualifications.
## Rent in Advance Grant
Clients can be paid a Rent in Advance Grant if they're in a tenancy that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to.
Staff will need to assess the client’s accommodation agreement to determine whether they are in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to.
Clients will need to meet all other eligibility criteria to receive the grant.

chunks.title: Net equity — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Net equity
The net equity of a house or boat or vehicle is the amount of money that the owner can get from the sale of the item once they've paid any debt owed on the item.
For example, where a client does not have a loan to help pay for a boat, their net equity is the total amount of cash they could get for selling the boat.
When a client got a loan to pay for an item, their net equity is the total value of the item minus the money they still owe on the item.
## House and land
Only assess the net equity of house and land not used as the client’s principal place of residence.
When assessing net equity on a house and/or land, use the rateable valuation or the amount insured. Use the higher value.
Example
House valued at
$100,000
Land valued at
$100,000
Total combined value
$200,000
Less outstanding Mortgage principal
$150,000
Net equity
$50,000
Some District Councils only use the Capital value of a property, this will be noted on the rate notice. In these cases the Capital value is the value of both the house and land value combined.
Example
Capital value
$200,000
Less outstanding Mortgage principal
$150,000
Net equity
$50,000
## Boat or caravan
Boats or caravans used by the client or a member of their family for day-to-day accommodation are not considered a cash asset.
The value of leisure boats or caravans will be the insured value. Where the leisure boat or caravan is not insured, the client will be required to provide, and pay for, written verification of:
- the leisure boat's value from a boat dealer and/or
- the caravan's value from a caravan dealer
Example
Boat valued at
$10,000
Less outstanding loan on boat
$3,000
Net equity
$7,000
## Client has more than one vehicle
When a client has more than one vehicle, MSD will need to assess whether the vehicles are used for private use.
Example
A family with 3 adults own 5 vehicles and all are claimed to be used for personal use. One is a vintage car used for Sunday outings and another a 4 wheel drive used on weekends only.
The 4 wheel drive and vintage car are additional to the needs of the family. Therefore, for Moving Assistance purposes, the net equity of these vehicles will need to be assessed.

chunks.title: Other financial assistance available to the client — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Other financial assistance available to the client
MSD must assess whether the client can receive other financial assistance before granting an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant.
This assistance could include any one-off or ongoing payments from MSD. When a client is granted other financial assistance for accommodation costs in advance, but it doesn't cover the full amount needed, MSD can consider an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant for the remaining amount.
An Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant should not be paid for costs already paid for by any other financial assistance.
Some clients may have access to other forms of assistance. They may still be eligible for Housing Support Products but only once they have exhausted all other forms of support first. For example:
- tertiary students staying in university accommodation (e.g. Halls of Residence)
- clients in rest homes and retirement villages
- clients in institutions for the care of sick and disabled people
## Assessing additional assistance
Make sure the client is aware of all the additional financial assistance available from MSD. This could include Extra Help such as Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support and other Housing Support Products.
Additional assistance may help reduce hardship and prevent the client from needing further assistance for housing related costs.
## Example
Saane is going to be a tenant in a property and applies for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant of $400 for two weeks of accommodation costs. They are receiving a reduced rate of Student Allowance of $150 per week due to their parent’s income and received a scholarship payment of $750 earlier in the year. They have not accessed their Student Loan Living Costs.
MSD does not grant the payment as the student could speak to their parents for support, or access their scholarship payment to cover their accommodation costs in advance. MSD also advises the student to access their Student Loan Living Costs entitlement so that they can cover their accommodation costs going forward.

chunks.title: Paying someone other than the accommodation supplier — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Paying someone other than the accommodation supplier
Generally, an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant should only be paid directly to the prospective accommodation supplier or property manager.
However, in some situations, MSD may pay an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant to the client's payment card or directly to the client. The Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant:
- can be paid to the client's payment card when the accommodation supplier or property manager indicates this is their preferred payment method
- can only be paid directly to the client (eg bank account) when the accommodation supplier or property manager is not in MSD's system and the client needs an immediate grant paid to obtain the accommodation

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Accommodation Costs in Advance Grants are recoverable and must be paid back to MSD. If a client qualifies for a non-recoverable re-establishment Special Needs Grant for accommodation costs in advance, this assistance should be considered first. MSD can consider any remaining amount still needed for accommodation costs in advance under an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant.

chunks.title: Maximum amount for a grant — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: The maximum Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant payable is limited to the lesser amount of the following: - the amount of accommodation costs in advance the client and their partner (if any) combined must pay for the accommodation or - the equivalent of 2 weeks accommodation costs for the accommodation or - if the client is in a shared accommodation, the client and their partner's (if any) portion of 2 weeks' rent

chunks.title: Social housing — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: When a client is applying for a Rent in Advance Grant for social housing, the amount they can apply for is based on: - the weekly rate of Income Related Rent charged by their social housing provider or - if they do not pay Income Related Rent, the weekly market rent for the social housing

chunks.title: Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant can be paid twice in a 52-week period — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: An Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant cannot be paid more than twice to a client in a 52-week period unless there are exceptional circumstances. This includes any payments made as a Rent in Advance Grant. When a client applies for a Rent in Advance Grant, MSD must check how many Accommodation Costs in Advance Grants or Rent in Advance Grants the client has had in the last 52 weeks. Any Accommodation Costs in Advance Grants or Rent in Advance Grants in the 52-week period before the latest application are counted, including any grants paid due to exceptional circumstances. If a client gets more than one payment of an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant or Rent in Advance Grant in a 52-week period, they can get up to the maximum amount for each grant. For more information see: - Exceptional Circumstances

chunks.title: Payments made under other forms of assistance — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: The Housing Support Programme, introduced on 13 March 2023, was only available to clients in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. A client who was in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to could have been assisted with accommodation support through an Advance Payment of Benefit, Recoverable Assistance Payment, or Special Needs Grant. From 1 July 2024, the Housing Support Programme was expanded to include clients who are in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. Any payments a client got for accommodation costs in advance before 1 July 2024 either as an Advance Payment of Benefit, Recoverable Assistance Payment or Special Needs Grant are not included in the grant count.

chunks.title: Paying someone other than the accommodation supplier or property manager — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Generally, an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant should only be paid directly to the accommodation supplier or property manager. However, in some situations, MSD may pay an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant to the client's payment card or directly to the client.

chunks.title: Pre-paid funeral expenses — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Pre-paid funeral expenses
A pre-paid funeral trust fund or account is money put aside (usually in a trust) exclusively for the payment of funeral expenses.
If the money can be accessed by the client and used for other purposes, it is not considered exclusively for funeral expenses and can be treated as a cash asset.
It is usually clear whether a trust fund or account has been genuinely set aside for funeral expenses. Evidence it has been set aside exclusively for funeral expenses include:
- the trust fund/account is only paid out on production of a death certificate
- the client cannot usually access the funds
- if a client can access the fund, there are limited conditions on withdrawal, such as re-locating overseas
- the trust fund/account is only payable to the funeral director or administrator of the client's estate
- the client cannot generally access the interest earned from the trust fund or account
When the trust fund or account has been set aside for funeral expenses and cannot be accessed or converted into cash, this money is not a realisable asset.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant the client must:
- meet the residency qualifications
- meet the income and asset limits
- be considered to be likely to retain the accommodation, but requires assistance to obtain it
- be required to pay accommodation costs in advance as part of their accommodation agreement
While a client may qualify, the approval of an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant is discretionary and should be considered according to each client's specific situation and need.

chunks.title: Recovery of payment — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Recovery of payment
Before granting Rent in Advance Grant, MSD must discuss a repayment plan the client.
The client has a number of repayment options available as listed below:
- deductions from a main benefit, Student Allowance or Working for Families assistance paid by MSD
- employer deduction notice (Client Support - Debt Management will arrange this - case managers cannot issue a wage deduction notice)
- automatic payment from the client's bank account
- internet/telebanking payment
- payment through New Zealand Post Shop
## Recovery rate
Accommodation Costs in Advance Grants must have a recovery rate that means the client will pay back the debt owed within 24 months of the grant unless they have exceptional circumstances.
The rate and method of recovery must be discussed with the client, and be based on their individual circumstances and ability to live within the reduced income.
It is important the client knows the length of time the Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant will be repaid over.
Clients who have already been granted an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant may have their recovery rate adjusted at a later date if their circumstances change.
When determining the rate of repayment by instalments MSD must consider:
- whether the instalment reductions will leave enough for the client's living expenses and any other debt repayments
- the impact on the individual (and/or their immediate family) when establishing further recoverable debt and
- the likelihood it would cause the client to seek further Housing Support Product payments or other extra help assistance
## Maximum recovery rate for beneficiaries
The recommended maximum recovery rate for clients currently getting income support is no more than $40 a week, unless the client volunteers to pay more.

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant a client must:
- qualify for and be getting a main benefit or
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand at the time of their application andbe a New Zealand citizen orhold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 orqualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy, but the relationship has ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- hold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- qualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy, but the relationship has ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they are considered to hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other qualifications for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant.

chunks.title: Resources available to the client — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Resources available to the client
When deciding whether to grant an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant, MSD may consider the ability of the client and their partner (if any) to meet the cost of accommodation costs in advance from their own resources.
If the client and their partner (if any) have resources available to them, these should generally be used to pay for their accommodation costs in advance, unless this would mean they're unable to meet their essential living expenses.
Examples of a client using the resources they have available to them may include:
- using any cash assets to pay the accommodation costs in advance
- accessing assistance available from other government agencies
- paying the accommodation costs in advance from their next income payment due to them
Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.

chunks.title: Reviews and Appeals — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Reviews and Appeals
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have had formal notification of and disagree with a decision on their application for assistance under the Housing Support Programme.
A client can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority when they do not agree with a decision, which was upheld or upheld in part by the Benefits Review Committee under an application for Review of Decision.
The client has the right to apply for a Review of Decision at any time within 3-months of the original decision being advised. When a client has applied for a hearing outside the 3-month time limit the Benefits Review Committee must decide whether or not to accept the application before it considers the decision under review.
A client has the right to have their decision reviewed once. If they wish to have the same decision reviewed again refer the case to Legal Services.

chunks.title: Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies
When a client is living in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to, service costs cannot be included. Only the portion of the costs that relates to their accommodation can be included in a Rent in Advance Grant.
Generally the service costs and cost of accommodation will be itemised separately on the tenancy agreement. Use the accommodation cost only to calculate Rent in Advance.
## Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply
Clients living in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to may have service costs included in their Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant if these are unable to be separated from their accommodation costs.
MSD should try to identify and separate service costs wherever possible.
## Service costs not clear
When the service costs are not itemised separately, assess the cost of the service(s) and deduct it from the total accommodation costs to determine the cost of accommodation.
The accommodation supplier should provide an estimate of the accommodation and service cost components of the client's accommodation cost payment.
If the client is unable to get an estimate from the accommodation supplier or if there is a disagreement between the accommodation supplier and client about the cost split between accommodation and service costs, estimate the service costs based on information already available about those costs. The information sources used will depend on the specific service cost.
For example, if the total rent includes electricity costs, the Powerswitch website can be used to calculate the cost of the electricity to be deducted from the total rent.
## Water rates
When a client's rent includes water rates (also referred to as water charges), the portion of costs that relates to the water rates can be included for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant if:
- the accommodation has a separate water meter and
- the accommodation agreement states the client is responsible for this cost
Note Water rates do not include the cost of filling water tanks.

chunks.title: Staying in accommodation for more than 28 days — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: To qualify for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant, a client should intend to be staying in accommodation for at least 28 days. This is because the client should be able to keep their accommodation when an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant is made. MSD can consider granting Accommodation Costs in Advance when the client is staying for less than 28 days on a discretionary basis. When a client requests an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant for accommodation that they will stay in for less than 28 days, MSD should consider whether: - the client will require emergency housing if the Accommodation Costs in Advance is not granted. - there will be an impact to the client, their partner, and/or their children if the Accommodation Costs in Advance grant is not granted - a short-term grant will make it more likely for the client to stay in accommodation long-term. For example, a boarding house owner will only accept the client for a week to see how things go before they commit to the client staying long-term - the client has long-term accommodation arranged, but requires a short-term grant somewhere else before the accommodation is available. For example, they need to stay with their friend for 2 weeks before their rental tenancy begins

chunks.title: Example 1 — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Ripeka has applied for an Accommodation Costs in Advance grant to move into a lodging house for 2 and a half weeks. Her previous accommodation ended as the head tenant and other flatmates are moving out and Ripeka cannot afford to rent the property on her own. The lodging house is booked out after 2 and a half weeks so Ripeka cannot stay any longer. They require 1 week of accommodation costs in advance, which Ripeka cannot afford. She can afford the ongoing costs of the accommodation once this is paid. Ripeka has already received 1 Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant in the last 52 weeks. There is no other accommodation available (including staying with family or friends temporarily), and her only alternative would be to apply for emergency housing. MSD decides to grant the Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant due to Ripeka’s circumstances, and advises her to continue looking for accommodation that she can retain.

chunks.title: Example 2 — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text: Dylan is moving out of a flat in Wellington where they are a tenant because they want to move to Auckland to look for work. They apply for an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant to move into their friend’s place in Auckland for three weeks while the friend’s flatmate is on holiday. MSD declines the Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant because Dylan is moving out of long-term accommodation into short term accommodation and they have contributed to the need for a grant.

chunks.title: Tenants — extra help > housing support products > accommodation costs in advance grant
chunks.text:
## Tenants
A client who signs the tenancy agreement at a property is known as a tenant. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to them, and they are responsible to the landlord for any rent and damages due at the accommodation.
When a client is a tenant, their accommodation supplier is the landlord and any Rent in Advance Grants are made to the landlord directly.
## Flatmates
A client who is living at the accommodation and has not signed the tenancy agreement is usually known as a flatmate. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to them.
When a client is a flatmate, their accommodation supplier is the tenant who the flatmate is responsible for paying their accommodation costs to. The tenant that the client pays accommodation costs to at the property takes responsibility for the client instead of the client dealing directly with the landlord. This is also sometimes called subletting.
Any Accommodation Costs in Advance Grants are made to the tenant that the flatmate pays their accommodation costs to, who will then pay the landlord.
## Example
Jene is planning to be a flatmate in a property and will pay their accommodation costs to Hannah, the head tenant in the household.
Hannah requests that Jene pay 2 weeks of accommodation costs in advance as the old flatmate is moving out two weeks before Jene can move in.
Jene applies for and is granted an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant. This is paid to Hannah as she is Jene’s accommodation supplier.
Hannah then pays this money to their landlord.

chunks.title: Able to obtain and retain accommodation — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Able to obtain and retain accommodation
To qualify for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant, MSD must consider whether the client is likely to be able to obtain and retain the accommodation the Accommodation Security Cover Grant is for.
MSD needs to discuss with the client whether they can likely afford (with any financial assistance, income and other resources available to them) to get and keep the accommodation, including the ongoing costs of the accommodation.
A client may be considered as being likely to get and keep the accommodation when:
- the proposed accommodation cost is generally under 60 per cent of their net income (and their partner’s, if any) taking into account the client’s individual circumstances, and
- MSD has discussed the client's budget, or have other evidence showing they can manage their future outgoings

chunks.title: Tenant under a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to any tenancy with a written tenancy agreement from Tenancy Services. Some examples are a: - tenancy agreement for rental housing, including with: a private landlordlocal governmenta non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) - a private landlord - local government - a non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) or - tenancy agreement for social housing, including with a community housing provider Clients in this accommodation are not eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant. Example Ahere owns a house that they let to Stevie, Aio and Alex. Ahere provides a written tenancy agreement from Tenancy Services. The tenancy agreement is signed by all parties. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to the tenancy agreement.

chunks.title: Flatmate or subletting without a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Clients may be living in a rental property as a flatmate or subletter without a tenancy agreement. The tenant on the tenancy agreement that the client pays their accommodation costs to takes responsibility for these clients and acts as their accommodation supplier. Flatmates generally pay any accommodation costs to the tenant instead of the landlord. This includes clients who are an additional occupant in a social housing property, as they are not on the tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these clients and they may be eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Service tenancies — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: A client may be provided accommodation as part of their employment where their landlord is their employer. This is known as a service tenancy. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to service tenancies. Clients in a service tenancy will generally be provided with a written tenancy agreement. These clients are not eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Tenancy orders — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: A tenant of a property through a tenancy order made under the Family Violence Act 2018 or Property (Relationships) Act 1976 does not need to have signed a written tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to clients in a tenancy order. These clients are not eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Boarding arrangements — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Clients who are boarding have an agreement for one room in the property, rather than the whole house. Boarders have access to shared facilities such as a kitchen and bathroom. When the accommodation has 6 or more occupants, this is known as a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to boarding houses when the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more. the client is not eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant if they meet these qualifications. When there are 5 or fewer occupants this is not considered a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these boarding arrangements, including private boarding where the client lives with the owner of the property. Clients in these arrangements may be eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant. The accommodation costs a client pays under a boarding accommodation agreement generally includes service and facility costs such as power, grounds maintenance, rubbish disposal, etc. MSD generally should not include any service costs in an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. For more information about what costs can be included in an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, see: - Service costs and water rates

chunks.title: Example 1 - Boarding arrangement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Ngaio has an accommodation agreement to rent a room in a boarding house with 5 other people. She has her own room in the house and shares a bathroom and kitchen with other boarders. She intends to stay there for at least 6 months. Ngaio pays board which includes accommodation costs and service costs (including power, water, cleaning and rubbish disposal costs). The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to this boarding arrangement.

chunks.title: Example 2 - Boarding arrangement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Malosi is boarding with their aunt Vaima. Vaima owns the house and Malosi pays board that includes accommodation, food and service costs, including internet and power costs. Malosi and Vaima have an accommodation agreement which sets out these costs. This boarding arrangement does not have the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 apply to it.

chunks.title: Rent to buy — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: A client may enter into a rent to buy contract (also called a deferred payment disposition). In these situations, the client is considered to be a homeowner and is not eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Relocatable accommodation — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: A client may enter a hire agreement or a rental contract for relocatable accommodation, such as a cabin, mobile home, or caravan. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 only applies to relocatable accommodation if it is: - hired from and located on a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner Clients in this accommodation are not eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply if the relocatable accommodation is: - on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days or - placed on any other premises where the land and the accommodation are not owned by the same person or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner Clients in this accommodation may be eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Example 1 - campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Rarahu intends to stay in a cabin in a commercial campsite for a minimum of 90 days. She requires assistance to secure the cabin. As Rarahu intends to stay in the cabin for 51 days or more, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to their accommodation arrangement. MSD can approve a Bond Grant for Rarahu to secure the cabin.

chunks.title: Example 2 - campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Arama intends to stay in a cabin in a commercial campsite for 30 days while she waits for her new job to start, which will provide her with long-term accommodation while she's employed. She requires assistance to get the cabin. As Arama intends to stay in the cabin for under 51 days, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to her accommodation arrangement. MSD can conditionally approve an Accommodation Security Cover Grant for Arama to secure the cabin.

chunks.title: Multiple accommodation agreements — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: If a client is an occupant under multiple accommodation agreements (i.e. required to pay accommodation costs for more than one accommodation agreement), the Accommodation Security Cover Grant is only payable for the client's principal place of residence. MSD must assess their principal place of residence to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies, and if the client is eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant at this accommodation. If the client and their partner have separate accommodation, they may each have a different principal place of residence. Generally, the client will determine what is their principal place of residence. If there is evidence the client is not using the property as their principal place of residence, MSD should generally decline an Accommodation Security Cover Grant. For example, if the client is using the property to store excess personal goods or sub-letting the property while living elsewhere, MSD should not pay an Accommodation Security Cover Grant. Note a grant can be paid for multiple accommodation agreements if they are for the same accommodation. For example, where a client has a rental contract for a cabin hire and a separate rental contract for the land that the cabin sits on.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Jiang lives in accommodation in Auckland. His ex-partner lives in Hamilton and has custody of their children. Jiang is planning to visit Hamilton for four days each month to visit his children and has organised an accommodation agreement with a friend where he will pay $150 each month to stay at their place when he visits. His friend has requested that he has been conditionally granted an Accommodation Security Cover Grant to move into the property. As this is not his primary place of residence, MSD declines the grant.

chunks.title: Outstanding accommodation costs and expenses not covered — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Outstanding accommodation costs and expenses not covered
Accommodation Security Cover Grant does not cover any outstanding accommodation costs and expenses that:
- the client doesn't agree with (unless there is a Disputes Tribunal, Tenancy Tribunal or court order confirming the client must pay the costs), and/or
- the client is not liable to pay under the terms of the accommodation agreement or a Disputes Tribunal, Tenancy Tribunal or court order and/or
- relate to an accommodation agreement that has not ended

chunks.title: Accommodation is suitable to live in — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation is suitable to live in
MSD may consider whether the accommodation will be suitable for the client to live in if the grant is made.
Factors MSD may consider include (but are not limited to) if the:
- accommodation has been modified to suit the accessibility needs for the client, their partner (if any) or their dependent children (if any)
- client has access to facilities such as clean drinking water, cooking facilities, electricity, heating, beds and mattresses, toilet and bathing facilities and a food refrigerator that the client can access
- accommodation has enough bedrooms
- accommodation is fit for human habitation, including being structurally safe to live in
MSD does not need to assess if a client’s accommodation is suitable at every Accommodation Security Cover Grant assessment.
However, if it is clear through the conversation with the client that the accommodation is not suitable for the client, their partner (if any) or their dependent children (if any), MSD may decline the application.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to
The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 provides rights and protections for tenants and landlords in rental agreements.
MSD cannot pay an Accommodation Security Cover Grant for people who are living in or moving into accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. This includes, but is not limited to:
- rental tenancies
- boarding houses with at least 6 tenants or boarders where the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more
- service tenancies where an employer provides accommodation to an employee
- multi-unit residential housing developments to provide long-term (minimum of 10 years) rental accommodation to tenants (also known as build to rent tenancies)
- social housing (including Kainga Ora and private social housing) if the client is a tenant or a signatory
- hire agreements for relocatable homes including cabins, mobile homes and caravans where they are: hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more oron a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner
- hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or
- on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner
Clients living in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to may be eligible for a Bond Grant or a Tenancy Costs Cover.
If you are unsure if the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to an accommodation agreement, contact Helpline or your Capability Developer.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Accommodation Security Cover Grant is only available to clients who are entering accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. These accommodation agreements may include, but are not limited to: - flat or house share agreements where the client has not signed a tenancy agreement (e.g. a flatmate that sub-lets from a head tenant) - hire agreement for a relocatable home including a cabin, mobile home or caravan where: it is on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days, oron any other premises for any amount of time where the land and accommodation are not owned by the same person oron a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner - it is on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days, or - on any other premises for any amount of time where the land and accommodation are not owned by the same person or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner - a lodging arrangement - a boarding agreement where the client is either: in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to and does stay for less than 28 daysin accommodation that is not a boarding house - in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to and does stay for less than 28 days - in accommodation that is not a boarding house - commercial accommodation such as hotels, motels, and homestays that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. This excludes the following accommodation as they are not eligible to get an Accommodation Security Cover Grant: emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Granttransitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development andcontracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant - transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development and - contracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - an additional occupant in a social housing property that is not a tenant or a signatory on the tenancy agreement MSD will need to assess a client’s accommodation agreement to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Clients may be living in accommodation that is not included in the above list. They may still be eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant if the accommodation they are living in is not specifically excluded.

chunks.title: Accommodation Security Cover Grant letter — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: When a client gets a conditional grant of Accommodation Security Cover Grant, MSD will give them and their accommodation supplier an Accommodation Security Cover Grant letter of assurance. The letter explains what Accommodation Security Cover Grant is and shows the client has been approved for financial assistance from MSD to help pay any outstanding accommodation costs and expenses at the end of their accommodation agreement. It also explains what both the accommodation supplier and client need to do to meet the conditions of the Accommodation Security Cover Grant. Accommodation Security Cover Grant cannot be paid to the accommodation supplier (or their agent) unless all the conditions of the grant are met.

chunks.title: Conditions of Accommodation Security Cover Grant — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: The conditions of Accommodation Security Cover Grant are as follows. At the start of the accommodation agreement: - the client meets the eligibility criteria, and - the accommodation supplier has only entered the accommodation agreement on the condition that Accommodation Security Cover Grant is granted - the client has given MSD a copy of the accommodation agreement At the end of the accommodation agreement: - the accommodation agreement has ended within 12 months of the Accommodation Security Cover Grant being made (including any subsequent grants) - the client owes the accommodation supplier outstanding accommodation costs and expenses, and - the client or accommodation supplier has claimed payment of the outstanding accommodation costs and expenses within 3 months of the end of the accommodation agreement (unless they qualify to extend the claim period), and - MSD has the supporting evidence it needs to decide whether to pay the claim

chunks.title: Client must agree to the costs claimed, or there is an order for costs — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Even if all of the conditions are met, MSD can only pay a claim for payment under Accommodation Security Cover Grant when: - the client agrees with the amount of costs claimed or - there is a Disputes Tribunal, Tenancy Tribunal or court order confirming that the client must pay the outstanding accommodation costs and expenses Clients who have been granted an Accommodation Security Cover Grant can only resolve disputes with their accommodation supplier through the Tenancy Tribunal when the parties to the accommodation agreement have contracted into the jurisdiction and powers of the Tenancy Tribunal under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986.

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: The conditions of Accommodation Security Cover Grant are not affected by a change in the client’s circumstances after the accommodation agreement has started.

chunks.title: Number of times a client can be conditionally granted Accommodation Security Cover Grant — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: There is no limit on how many times a client can be conditionally granted Accommodation Security Cover Grant in a 52-week period unless: - the client has already received 2 payments under Accommodation Security Cover Grant or Bond Grant within a 52-week period and - there are no exceptional circumstances to justify another conditional grant of Accommodation Security Cover Grant during that same 52-week period

chunks.title: Assessing Accommodation Security Cover Grant — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Assessing Accommodation Security Cover Grant
An Accommodation Security Cover Grant is available for people who are likely to be able to keep accommodation but require some assistance to get it.
Accommodation Security Cover Grant is a discretionary grant. MSD needs to consider the client's individual circumstances and determine whether the Accommodation Security Cover Grant should be granted.
In order to make a decision to grant, MSD must consider:
- the purpose of the Housing Support Programme, including whether making a conditional grant for Accommodation Security Cover Grant would be the correct use of the payment
- any other financial assistance available to the client that could be used to meet their need
- whether the client and their partner (if any) could meet the need from their own resources, including accessing cash assets or receiving support from other Government agencies
- any impacts on the client, their partner (if any), and their dependent children (if any) if the Accommodation Security Cover Grant is not granted and
- whether the client intends to stay in the accommodation for fewer than 28 days
There are also factors MSD may consider, such as:
- whether the client or their partner (if any) has caused or contributed to the need for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant and
- the ability of the client and their partner (if any) to meet their essential living expenses if assistance is granted
- the existing debt of the client and their partner (if any)
- whether the accommodation is suitable to live in
- any other matters MSD think are relevant
An Accommodation Security Cover Grant can be declined if a grant would not be appropriate after having considered the circumstances of the client and their partner (if any) and dependent children (if any).

chunks.title: Assessing weekly income — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Assessing weekly income
Income limits for Housing Support Products are determined based on a client’s weekly income. MSD has discretion to determine the period that weekly income relates to. When working out which period of income to use, MSD may consider:
- how much income was earned during the period, and/or
- how much income the client expects to receive for that period, (e.g. investment interest was accrued but has not yet paid) and/or
- the period for which income was received by the client
Generally, MSD will base the client and partner’s (if any) weekly income on the average income over the previous four weeks, unless MSD considers a different timeframe is appropriate (for example the client has been earning for a shorter or longer time). This means the last four weeks of income is totalled and then divided by four.
In some cases, MSD can use a different period to calculate the weekly income period, to consider the client’s circumstances, including if the client or their partner’s income:
- has been inconsistent over the previous four weeks
- is variable week by week
- has either increased or decreased recently
- will increase or decrease in the immediate future (in the next four weeks)
- future income is uncertain, including where there is a history of the employer not paying wages or paying late
- has been earned but not paid (e.g. the client earned income but has not been paid on time)

chunks.title: Cash asset limit — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Cash asset limit
A client and their partner (if any) cannot get an Accommodation Security Cover Grant if their assets are more than the cash asset limit.
MSD needs to know the cash value of their assets.
There is no discretion to grant an Accommodation Security Cover Grant to a client whose cash assets (including the cash assets of their partner, if any) are above the asset limit.
## For more information about what assets include and do not include see:
- Cash assets

chunks.title: Cash assets — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Cash assets mean the assets of the client and their partner (if any) that can be easily converted into cash

chunks.title: Cash assets include — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: - cash - bills of exchange or promissory notes - building society shares - money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society - money invested with or lent to any bank, financial institution or other person whether in mortgage or other security, or unsecured - money withdrawn from a KiwiSaver scheme - mortgage investments and other long-term loans - the net equity held in any property or land not used as a person’s home - pre-paid funeral expenses (in some circumstances) - shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds and other bonds (including shares in energy organisations) and - the client’s share in any partnership Note if you are unsure of a case contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Cash assets do not include — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: - the home property and land on which it is situated - a motor vehicle or other vehicle principally used by the client or their partner for their personal use (this is limited to 1 vehicle for a single person or 2 vehicles for a couple) - a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2000, or which is used by the client or a member of their family for day-to-day accommodation - payments people get under Housing Support Products (Bond Grant, Moving Costs Grant, Rent in Advance, Rent Arrears Grant, Transition to Alternative Housing Grant, Accommodation Security Cover, Tenancy Costs Cover) - personal effects - Christchurch mosques attack support payments - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts - Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income - Māori land - MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is received - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after the payment is received - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made - specified Ex gratia and compensation payments A bank overdraft is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client. Christchurch earthquake related payments Payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client got the payment. See: - Payments from the Crown for the purchase of property in the Canterbury red zone - Payments from the Earthquake Commission and insurance companies (Canterbury earthquake 2010 and aftershock 2011) - Payments from the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross)

chunks.title: Client caused or contributed to need — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Client caused or contributed to need
Before deciding whether or not to grant an Accommodation Security Cover Grant, MSD may consider the extent the client or their partner (if any) has caused or contributed to their need for assistance.
Examples of when a client may be considered to have caused or contributed to the need for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant include when:
- they have recently caused or contributed to intentional or reckless damage to their previous accommodation, including damage that may have resulted in the end of their accommodation agreement
- they have a pattern of not meeting their obligations for previous accommodation, e.g. non-payment of rent, leaving without notice, additional occupants not approved by accommodation supplier
Each client's situation must be assessed on their individual circumstances.

chunks.title: Clients who cannot get Accommodation Security Cover Grant — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Clients who cannot get Accommodation Security Cover Grant
Clients living in one of the following accommodation agreements are not eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant:
- accommodation owned by the client or their spouse or partner
- tents, including those joined to a vehicle
- homeless shelters
- prisons and correctional facilities
- accommodation for which they are receiving an Emergency Housing Grant or Transitional or Contracted Emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development
- accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to
There is no discretion to approve a payment for a client living in one of these accommodation agreements.

chunks.title: Clients with existing debt — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Clients with existing debt
When deciding whether to approve an Accommodation Security Cover Grant, MSD may consider the existing debt of the client and their partner (if any). Existing debt includes both MSD debt and non-MSD debt.
A client's existing debt repayments may impact their ability to repay an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.
When a client has existing MSD debt, MSD may consider whether it is appropriate to reduce those repayments to allow for the repayment of the Accommodation Security Cover Grant.
When a client is getting all the financial assistance they qualify for, but are not likely to be able to repay an amount paid for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant, the grant may be declined.

chunks.title: Determining whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: A client must have accommodation with a tenancy agreement for the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 to apply. Generally, this will be a tenancy agreement from Tenancies Services. However, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 may still apply if the client does not have a tenancy agreement from Tenancies Services. Other evidence of a tenancy agreement could be written communication between the accommodation supplier and the client if they are in an accommodation agreement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. If there is a verbal agreement, the accommodation supplier should write this down when the client is applying for a Housing Support Product so that MSD can determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies. Note Parties to an accommodation agreement can choose to contract into some or all of the provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act 1986. This may include things like lodging a bond with tenancy services or agreeing to use the Tenancy Tribunal for dispute resolution. However, contracting into the provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 in this way does not mean that the accommodation agreement is an RTA agreement for the purposes of the Housing Support Programme.

chunks.title: Information on a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: If it is unclear whether a document is a tenancy agreement under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 or not, below is a list of information that is usually part of this type of agreement: - the full name and contact address of the landlord - the landlord’s contact mobile telephone number (if any) - the landlord’s contact email address (if any) - the full name and contact address (when different from the address of the premises to which the agreement relates) of the tenant - the tenant’s contact mobile telephone number (if any) - the tenant’s contact email address (if any) - the address of the premises - the date of the tenancy agreement - the date of commencement of the tenancy (when different from the date of the tenancy agreement) - the landlord’s address for service - the tenant’s address for service - if the tenant is under the age of 18 - the amount of any bond - the rent payable - the frequency of the rent payments - the place or bank account number where the rent is to be paid - a list of any chattels provided by the landlord - if the tenancy is a fixed-term tenancy, the date on which the term will expire - Healthy Homes compliance statement - insulation statement - insurance statement The agreement should be signed by both parties but if it's not signed, it may still be a valid agreement. In these cases, MSD can use other evidence to determine that there is an agreement in place. For example, a bank account statement showing rent payments.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances
A client cannot get more than two payments for Accommodation Security Cover Grant or Bond Grants in a 52-week period, unless MSD is satisfied there are exceptional circumstances.
When a client has Accommodation Security Cover Grant paid twice in the last 52 weeks, MSD should consider if there is a need for the assistance and if there are exceptional circumstances.
Exceptional circumstances are where the circumstance:
- sets the client apart from others in a similar situation and
- is beyond the client’s control.
Factors to consider include:
- whether the client has any special or unusual circumstances that separates them from other clients which contributed to their need
- the age and health of the client and any dependents
- whether the client caused or contributed to their need
- whether the client needs to move through no fault of their own
- the client was a victim of a violent crime or family violence and has had a change in their housing circumstances, e.g.: needing to move to a different property following a violent crime orno longer living with their partner after seeking a protection order (including if the client remains in the same property without their partner)
- needing to move to a different property following a violent crime or
- no longer living with their partner after seeking a protection order (including if the client remains in the same property without their partner)
- any other circumstances about the client's situation MSD consider relevant

chunks.title: Impact on the client and their family — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Impact on the client and their family
When considering whether to make an Accommodation Security Cover Grant, MSD must consider the likely impacts on the client, their partner (if any), and their dependent children (if any) if the client's accommodation need is not met.
MSD should consider what other accommodation options are available to the client if they do not get the grant.
Factors that MSD may consider include, but are not limited to are:
- the client is likely to require emergency housing if assistance is not granted
- the client will need to stay in accommodation that is close to a perpetrator of violence if assistance is not granted
- the client will need to stay in accommodation that is near drug use or gang related activity if assistance is not granted
- the client can afford any of their other options
- there are enough bedrooms in the other accommodation
- they will be staying in suitable accommodation if they do not get the grant
- they will be a reasonable distance from work, school or essential services if assistance is not granted
- their other options meet the accessibility needs the client, their partner (if any), or their children (if any) may have
MSD must assess each client's circumstances on a case-by-case basis and determine how significant any impacts on the client's family will be.
## Example
Sam lives with their partner and two children. Their current tenancy is ending due to the landlord selling the property. Sam has applied for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant to move into a cabin on a friend's property near her old tenancy. The cabin is suitably sized and appropriate for her family.
Sam and their family have an option to stay with their brother that would have a lower weekly accommodation cost for Sam, however it would take over an hour and a half for Sam to get to work and to their children's school during peak traffic times.
MSD and Sam agree that the impacts on her family to travel and pay for travel costs will be significant, and MSD grants Housing Support Product assistance for the cabin.

chunks.title: Income limit — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Income limit
A client and their partner (if any) cannot get an Accommodation Security Cover Grant if their income is more than the appropriate income limit.
There is one set of income limits for all clients including those getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension, and non-beneficiaries. New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension must be included as income when assessing if the client qualifies.
There is no discretion to grant an Accommodation Security Cover Grant to a client whose income (including the income of their partner, if any) is above the income limit.
For more information about what is included as income and what is not included see:
- Core Policy Income

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Accommodation Security Cover Grant provides support for clients needing help to get or keep accommodation.
Accommodation Security Cover Grant is a conditional grant providing an accommodation supplier with an assurance that the client will be able to meet any outstanding accommodation costs and expenses (up to a maximum amount) if owed at the end of the accommodation agreement.
Accommodation Security Cover Grant is paid to the accommodation supplier or their agent at the end of the accommodation agreement to ensure the payment is used in a similar way to a bond payment. The client must pay the amount of any Accommodation Security Cover Grant that has been paid back to MSD.
Accommodation Security Cover Grant cannot be paid to the accommodation supplier or their agent until all the conditions of the grant are met.
## Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply
Accommodation Security Cover Grant is only available to clients who are moving into accommodation where the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply.
Where the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does apply to the client’s accommodation, MSD can consider paying a Bond Grant and/or Tenancy Cost Cover grant instead.

chunks.title: Net equity — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: The net equity of a house, boat or vehicle is the amount of money the owner can get from the sale of the item once they’ve paid any debt owed on it. For example, when a client does not have a loan to help pay for a boat their net equity is the total amount of cash they could get for selling the boat. When a client got a loan to pay for an item, their net equity is the total value of the item minus the money they still owe on the item.

chunks.title: House and land — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Only assess the net equity of house and land not used as the client’s principal place of residence. When assessing net equity on a house and/or land, use the rateable valuation or the amount insured. Use the higher value.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: House valued at $100,000 Land valued at $100,000 Total combined value $200,000 Less outstanding Mortgage principal $150,000 Net equity $50,000 Some District Councils only use the Capital value of a property, this will be noted on the rate notice. In these cases the Capital value is the value of both the house and land value combined.

chunks.title: Boat or caravan — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Boats or caravans used by the client or a member of their family for day-to-day accommodation are not considered a cash asset. The value of leisure boats or caravans will be the insured value. When the leisure boat or caravan is not insured, the client will be required to provide, and pay for, written verification of: - the leisure boat’s value from a boat dealer and/or - the caravan’s value from a caravan dealer

chunks.title: Vehicle — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: When assessing the net equity of a vehicle use the estimated value of the vehicle. Do not assess the net equity of any vehicle used by the client or their partner for their personal use (this is limited to 1 vehicle for a single person or 2 vehicles for a couple).

chunks.title: Client has more than one vehicle — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: When a client has more than one vehicle, you will need to assess whether the vehicles are used for private use.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: A family of 3 adults own 5 vehicles and all are claimed to be used for personal use. One is a vintage car used for Sunday outings and another a 4-wheel drive used on weekends only. The 4-wheel drive and vintage car are additional to the needs of the family. Therefore, for Bond Grant purposes, the net equity of these vehicles will need to be assessed.

chunks.title: Other financial assistance available to the client — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Other financial assistance available to the client
MSD must assess whether the client can receive other financial assistance before granting an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.
This assistance could include any one-off or ongoing payments from MSD.
An Accommodation Security Cover Grant should not be granted for costs already paid for by any other financial assistance.
Some clients may have access to other forms of assistance. They may still be eligible for Housing Support Products but only once they have exhausted all other forms of support first. For example:
- tertiary students staying in university accommodation (e.g. Halls of Residence)
- clients in rest homes and retirement villages
- clients in institutions for the care of sick and disabled people
## Assessing additional assistance
Make sure the client is aware of all the additional financial assistance available from MSD. This could include Extra Help such as Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support or other Housing Support Products such as Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant or Moving Costs Grant.
Additional assistance may help reduce hardship and prevent the client from needing further assistance for housing related costs.
## Example
