Saane is a tenant in a property and applies for Rent in Arrears Grant of $400 for two weeks of accommodation costs. They are receiving a reduced rate of Student Allowance of $150 per week due to their parent’s income and received a scholarship payment of $750 earlier in the year. They have not accessed their Student Loan Living Costs.
MSD does not grant the payment as the student could speak to their parents for support, or access their scholarship payment to cover their arrears. MSD also advises the student to access their entitlement to Student Loan Living Costs so that they can cover their accommodation costs going forward.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Accommodation Security Cover Grant can be claimed if the client owes their former accommodation supplier outstanding accommodation costs and expenses at the end of their accommodation agreement. Clients who have entered into an accommodation agreement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to are generally not able to lodge a tenancy bond with Tenancy Services and are not protected by the Residential Tenancies Act 1986. Note Clients can contract into the provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 to lodge a bond with tenancy services. However, contracting into the provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 in this way does not mean that the accommodation agreement is an RTA agreement for the purposes of the Housing Support Programme. Accommodation Security Cover Grant is paid to cover costs at the end of the accommodation agreement to ensure that the payment is used in a similar way to a bond payment. Accommodation Security Cover Grants are recoverable. The client must pay back any costs paid under an Accommodation Security Cover Grant to MSD.

chunks.title: Maximum amount of costs payable — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: The maximum amount of outstanding accommodation costs and expenses payable is equal to 4 weeks accommodation costs based on the accommodation costs agreed to at the start of the accommodation agreement. Payment is calculated as total costs up to 4 weeks accommodation costs.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: The maximum amount payable based on accommodation costs of $350 per week is $1,400. Total costs claimed by accommodation supplier $3,000 Balance of costs owing by client $3,000 Accommodation Security Cover Grant payable (equivalent to 4 weeks accommodation costs) $1,400 Remaining costs not covered (accommodation supplier needs to claim these directly from client) $1,600

chunks.title: Bond Grant and Accommodation Security Cover Grant — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Any Bond Grants that the client has been granted are included in the grant count amount for Accommodation Security Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Accommodation Security Cover Grant and Bond Grant can be paid twice in a 52-week period — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Accommodation Security Cover Grant cannot be paid more than twice in a 52-week period unless exceptional circumstances exist. The count for Accommodation Security Cover Grant includes any Bond Grant payments. When a client applies for Accommodation Security Cover Grant, MSD must check how many Accommodation Security Cover Grants or Bond Grants have been paid in the last 52 weeks. Any Accommodation Security Cover Grants paid in the 52-week period before the latest application are counted, including any Accommodation Security Cover Grant claims paid due to exceptional circumstances. If a client was conditionally granted Accommodation Security Cover Grant but it was not paid, this is not included in their grant count. If a client gets more than one payment under a conditional grant of Accommodation Security Cover Grant or Bond Grant in a 52-week period, they can get up to the maximum amount for each grant.

chunks.title: Paying the client in exceptional circumstances — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: A payment under Accommodation Security Cover Grant can only be paid to the client's former accommodation supplier or their agent (e.g. a property manager) unless MSD is satisfied exceptional circumstances exist. If exceptional circumstances exist, MSD may pay Accommodation Security Cover Grant to the client's payment card or directly to the client.

chunks.title: Client agrees to part of the outstanding accommodation costs and expenses — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Sometimes a client may agree with the accommodation supplier that they owe a part, but not all, of the outstanding accommodation costs and expenses that the accommodation supplier wants to charge the client. In these cases, MSD can approve the costs that are agreed by the client. Any additional outstanding cost will need to either be agreed by the client and accommodation supplier or a Disputes Tribunal, Tenancy Tribunal or court order would need to be provided by the client or accommodation supplier.

chunks.title: Who can lodge a claim — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Generally, a client or their agent will need to be the person to contact MSD to request that their Accommodation Security Cover Grant be paid out. Their accommodation supplier cannot request that MSD pay the claim unless there is an order from the Disputes Tribunal, Tenancy Tribunal or court confirming that the client is responsible for the costs.

chunks.title: Period of Accommodation Security Cover Grant — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Period of Accommodation Security Cover Grant
A conditional grant can only be made when a client is entering into an accommodation agreement.
Accommodation Security Cover Grant is active for 12 months from the beginning of the accommodation agreement. A claim for costs can be made if the accommodation period ends within 12 months.
If a client is still in the accommodation at the end of the 12-month period, then the Accommodation Security Cover Grant will end (lapse) and claims for costs can no longer be made.
## Subsequent Accommodation Security Cover Grant
In some cases, a client may stay in accommodation longer than the 12-month grant period. If the accommodation supplier will only continue the accommodation agreement if the client has an Accommodation Security Cover Grant, another conditional grant can be made.
The client must still meet the eligibility criteria for Accommodation Security Cover Grant to be granted a subsequent Accommodation Security Cover Grant.
Note an accommodation supplier cannot claim for any outstanding accommodation costs and expenses if they are requesting a subsequent grant. This is because the accommodation agreement has not ended.
## Example - subsequent grant
Kanav is conditionally granted an Accommodation Security Cover Grant to enter an accommodation agreement as a flatmate. The Accommodation Security Cover Grant period is for 12 months.
He stays in the accommodation for 12 months, and then requests that his accommodation supplier let him continue to stay in the accommodation.
His accommodation supplier is a head tenant in the property and they are worried about the risk of being responsible for any damages Kanav might cause to the property. They agree to let him stay as a flatmate but only if he continues to have an active Accommodation Security Cover Grant.
MSD makes a subsequent Accommodation Security Cover Grant for a 12-month period so that Kanav can keep his accommodation.

chunks.title: Period to claim payment under Accommodation Security Cover Grant — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: A payment under Accommodation Security Cover Grant can be claimed if the client owes their former accommodation supplier (or the accommodation supplier’s agent) outstanding accommodation costs and expenses at the end of their accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: 3-month period to claim costs — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: The client or the accommodation supplier generally has up to 3 months from the end of the accommodation agreement to make a claim to MSD for outstanding accommodation costs and expenses. However, the claim period may be extended in certain circumstances. Claims for payment under Accommodation Security Cover Grant can only be made for accommodation agreements that end within 12 months. If MSD approves a claim for payment, it is paid to the client's accommodation supplier (or the accommodation supplier's agent, e.g. a property manager). However, if exceptional circumstances exist, the claim may be paid directly to the client.

chunks.title: Extending claim period if a decision has not been made — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: An accommodation supplier or the client can dispute whether the client is responsible for the outstanding accommodation costs and expenses through the Disputes Tribunal, Tenancy Tribunal or court. If a claim has been lodged with a Disputes Tribunal, Tenancy Tribunal or court but a decision has not been made, the 3-month claim period may be extended. An extension of the claim period cannot be made for any other reason. A client or their accommodation supplier must contact MSD before the 3-month period ends to request an extension. If no contact is made, the grant ends (lapses) and there is no discretion to extend the 3-month period. When a claim has been lodged with the Tenancy Tribunal, a request to extend the claim period can only be considered when it is made on or after 2 March 2026, and within the 3-month claim period.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: On 20 February 2026, Liam contacts MSD to make a claim against Susan's Accommodation Security Cover Grant with a Tenancy Tribunal order confirming that Susan must pay the outstanding accommodation costs and expenses of $750. The accommodation agreement ended after 4 months on 10 January 2026. As the 3-month claim period ends after 2 March 2026, MSD advises Liam to submit the claim on or after 2 March 2026, but before the claim period ends. On 4 March 2026, Liam submits his claim, and MSD grants a payment of $750 to him from Susan's Accommodation Security Cover Grant. Each case and extension must be looked at on its own circumstances.

chunks.title: Maximum limit on claim period extensions — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: When a client or their accommodation supplier request an extension on their claim period, this may only be extended for a maximum of 3 months. An extension should generally be applied for 3 months unless there is good reason to extend for less time. A claim period may only be extended twice. There is no discretion to extend the claim period more than twice.

chunks.title: Example - 3-month extension — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Logan was conditionally granted an Accommodation Security Cover Grant. He stays in the accommodation for 10 months before moving to new accommodation. His accommodation supplier wants to make a claim for damages but Logan does not agree that he is responsible for them. The accommodation supplier lodges a claim with the Disputes Tribunal that Logan should be responsible for these costs. After 2 and a half months, the accommodation supplier contacts MSD to request an extension to the three-month claim period as the Disputes Tribunal has not resolved this. MSD grants a three-month extension. After 3 months, there is still not progress on the Disputes Tribunal claim as Logan hasn’t been contactable. The accommodation supplier contacts MSD for another extension. MSD grants the second and final three-month extension. The Disputes Tribunal makes the verdict that Logan is responsible for the damages 8 months after Logan left the property. The accommodation supplier contacts MSD with the Disputes Tribunal claim, and MSD grants the Accommodation Security Cover Grant to pay for the damages.

chunks.title: Client applied for new grant during three-month claim period — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: When a client has been granted an Accommodation Security Cover Grant and their accommodation agreement ends within 12 months, they have three months to make a claim for their costs. Most clients will move straight from one property to another. This means a client may apply for another Accommodation Security Cover Grant during the three-month period to claim costs from their previous accommodation. If a client has already received a Bond Grant or claimed an Accommodation Security Cover Grant in the last 52 weeks, MSD must discuss with the client if it’s likely there will be a claim for costs on their current Accommodation Security Cover Grant before making a new grant for their next accommodation. If the client advises that they will not make a claim for the costs, or if it is not clear whether they will make a claim, MSD can grant an Accommodation Security Cover Grant for their next accommodation. If they advise that they will make a claim for the costs and will have been paid two grants in the last 52 weeks, MSD may decline the Accommodation Security Cover Grant for their next accommodation if they do not have exceptional circumstances.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Rushika received a Bond Grant to move into accommodation and lived there for 6 months. There was some damage to the property and the Bond Grant was used to pay for this. She applied for a Security Cover Grant to move into her second accommodation and was granted. She moved out after 4 months. The Security Cover Grant remains active for 3 months from the date she moved out of the accommodation. Rushika has now contacted MSD to apply for a Security Cover Grant to move into her next property two weeks after she moved out of her last accommodation. She has already received 1 Bond Grant in the last 52 weeks, and currently has an active Security Cover Grant as it has not expired or been claimed yet. If the Security Cover Grant is claimed, Rushika will have received 2 Bond/Security Cover Grants in the last 52 weeks and will have reached her grant limit. In order to ensure Rushika does not receive 3 grants in 52 weeks, MSD contacts Rushika to determine if her second Security Cover Grant will be claimed. Rushika advises that there were damages to the property that will likely require the Security Cover Grant to be paid. MSD declines her third request for a Security Cover Grant as the second grant is likely to be paid. If Rushika and her accommodation supplier advised that they were not intending to claim the payment, MSD could assist with her third Security Cover Grant application.

chunks.title: Pre-paid funeral expenses — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Pre-paid funeral expenses
A pre-paid funeral trust fund or account is money put aside (usually in a trust) exclusively for the payment of funeral expenses.
If the money can be accessed by the client and used for other purposes, it is not considered exclusively for funeral expenses and can be treated as a cash asset.
It is usually clear a trust fund or account has been genuinely set aside for funeral expenses. Evidence it has been set aside exclusively for funeral expenses include:
- the trust fund/account is only paid out on production of a death certificate
- the client cannot usually access the funds
- if a client can access the fund, there are limited conditions on withdrawal, such as re-locating overseas
- the trust fund/account is only payable to the funeral director or administrator of the client’s estate
- the client cannot generally access the interest earned from the trust fund or account
When the trust fund or account has been set aside for funeral expenses and cannot be accessed or converted into cash this money is not a realisable asset.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant a client must:
- meet the residency qualifications and
- meet the income and assets limits and
- be likely to retain the accommodation but requires assistance to obtain it and
- be entering accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to and
- be required by the accommodation supplier to have an Accommodation Security Cover Grant to enter the accommodation agreement or
- be continuing in accommodation which an Accommodation Security Cover Grant was previously granted and the accommodation supplier will only continue the agreement if the Accommodation Security Cover Grant is renewed
While a client may qualify, the approval of an Accommodation Security Cover Grant is discretionary and should be considered according to each client's specific situation and need.

chunks.title: Recovery of payment — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Recovery of payment
Before paying an Accommodation Security Cover Grant, MSD must discuss a repayment plan with the client.
There are a variety of repayment options available to a client as listed below:
- deductions from a main benefit, Student Allowance or Working for Families assistance paid by MSD
- employer deduction notice (Client Support - Debt Management will arrange this - case managers do not have the delegation to issue a wage deduction notice)
- automatic payment from client's bank account
- internet/telebanking payment
- payment through New Zealand Post Shop
## Recovery rate
Accommodation Security Cover must have a recovery rate that means the client will pay back the debt owed within 24 months of the grant unless they have exceptional circumstances.
The rate and method of recovery must be discussed with the client, and be based on their individual circumstances and ability to live within the reduced income.
It is important the client knows the length of time the Accommodation Security Cover Grant will be repaid over.
Clients who have already been paid an Accommodation Security Cover Grant may have their recovery rate adjusted at a later date if their circumstances change.
When determining the rate of repayment by instalments MSD must consider:
- whether the instalment reductions will leave enough for the client's living expenses and any other debt repayments
- the impact on the individual (and/or their immediate family) when establishing further recoverable debt and
- the likelihood it would cause the client to seek further Housing Support Product payments or other extra help assistance

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get an Accommodation Security Cover Grant a client must:
- qualify for and be getting a main benefit or
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand at the time of their application and
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- hold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- qualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy but the relationship has ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they are considered to hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other qualifications for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Resources available to the client — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Resources available to the client
When deciding whether to grant an Accommodation Security Cover Grant, MSD may consider the ability of the client and their partner (if any) to meet the costs from their own resources.
If the client and their partner (if any) have resources available to them, these should generally be used to pay for any outstanding accommodation costs or expenses, unless this would mean they’re unable to meet their essential living expenses.
Examples of a client using the resources they have available to them may include:
- using any cash assets to pay the outstanding accommodation costs and expenses
- accessing assistance available from other government agencies
- paying the costs from their next income payment due to them
Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.

chunks.title: Service costs and water rates — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Service costs and water rates
Sometimes a client’s accommodation costs include service costs such as electricity or an internet connection.
Service costs do not include water rates.
Clients may have service costs included in their Accommodation Security Cover Grant only if these are unable to be separated from their accommodation costs.
MSD should try to identify and separate service costs wherever possible.
## Water rates
When a client's rent includes water rates (also referred to as water charges), the portion of costs that relates to the water rates can be included for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant if:
- the accommodation has a separate water meter and
- the accommodation agreement states the client is responsible for this cost
Note Water rates do not include the cost of filling water tanks.

chunks.title: Staying in accommodation for more than 28 days — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: To qualify for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant a client should intend to be staying in accommodation for at least 28 days. This is because the client should be able to keep their accommodation when an Accommodation Security Cover Grant is made. MSD can consider granting an Accommodation Security Cover Grant when the client is staying for less than 28 days on a discretionary basis. When a client requests an Accommodation Security Cover Grant for accommodation that they will stay in for less than 28 days, MSD should consider if: - the client is likely to require emergency housing if an Accommodation Security Cover Grant is not granted. - there will be an impact to the client, their spouse or partner, and/or their children if the Accommodation Security Cover Grant is not granted - a short-term grant will make it more likely for the client to stay in accommodation long-term. For example, a boarding house owner will only accept the client for a week to see how things go before they commit to the client staying long-term - the client has long-term accommodation arranged, but requires a short-term grant somewhere else before the accommodation is available. For example, they need to stay with their friend for 2 weeks before their rental tenancy begins

chunks.title: Example 1 — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Ripeka has applied for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant to move into a her friend’s house for 2 and a half weeks. Her previous accommodation ended as the head tenant and other flatmates are moving out and Ripeka cannot afford to rent the property on her own. The friend’s flatmate is moving back in after 2 and a half weeks so Ripeka cannot stay any longer. They have requested that Ripeka provide an assurance that she can pay for any damages as they are worried that their landlord might have an issue with a new person staying and risk their tenancy. Ripeka can afford the ongoing costs of the accommodation but would not be able to afford any unexpected damages. Ripeka has already been paid 1 Accommodation Security Cover Grant in the last 52 weeks. There is no other accommodation available and her only alternative would be to apply for emergency housing. MSD decides to conditionally grant the Accommodation Security Cover Grant due to Ripeka’s circumstances, and advises her to continue looking for accommodation that she can keep.

chunks.title: Example 2 — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text: Dylan is moving out of a flat in Wellington where they’re a tenant because they want to move to Auckland to look for work. They apply for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant to move into their friend’s place in Auckland for two weeks while the friend’s flatmate is on holiday. MSD declines the Accommodation Security Cover Grant because Dylan is moving out of long-term accommodation into short term accommodation and they have contributed to the need for a grant.

chunks.title: Tenants — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Tenants
A client who signs the tenancy agreement at a property is known as a tenant. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to them, and they are responsible to the landlord for any rent and damages due at the accommodation.
When a client is a tenant, they are not eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant. They may be eligible for a Bond Grant or a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant.
## Flatmates
A client who is living at the accommodation and has not signed the tenancy agreement is usually known as a flatmate. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to them.
When a client is a flatmate, their accommodation supplier is the tenant who the flatmate is responsible for paying their accommodation costs to. The tenant that the client pays accommodation costs to at the property takes responsibility for the client instead of the client dealing directly with the landlord. This is also sometimes called subletting.
Any Accommodation Security Cover Grants would generally be made to the tenant that the flatmate pays their accommodation costs to, who will then pay the landlord.
## Example
Jene is applying to be a flatmate in a property. Hannah is the head tenant and wants reassurance that Jene would be able to pay for any outstanding costs if she leaves the accommodation.
Jene applies for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant as Hannah will only allow her to get the accommodation if this is granted.
During her accommodation period, Jene damages a door which will cost $300 to repair. When the accommodation agreement ends, Hannah’s landlord requests that the repairs be paid for.
Jene and Hannah agree that Jene is responsible for the costs and MSD pays Jene’s Accommodation Security Cover of $300. MSD pays this to Hannah as she is Jene’s accommodation supplier. Hannah will then pay for the repairs or pay her landlord.

chunks.title: Types of outstanding accommodation costs and expenses covered — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Types of outstanding accommodation costs and expenses covered
The Accommodation Security Cover Grant is paid for outstanding accommodation costs or expenses at the end of the accommodation agreement. Accommodation costs can be regular payments or paid as a lump sum.
The client must be liable to pay these costs under the terms of their accommodation agreement, or by a Disputes Tribunal, Tenancy Tribunal or court order.
These could include the cost of:
- accommodation costs arrears
- any damages to the property that the client is responsible for (including any damages made by a person the client is responsible for)
- rubbish removal or cleaning costs incurred by the accommodation supplier after the tenant has vacated
- missing chattels
- change of locks or replacement keys, when lost by the client (does not include routine changing of locks at the end of an accommodation agreement)
- storage or disposal of the client’s abandoned personal effects and belongings
- any claims relating to the accommodation agreement
- an insurance excess if it is less than the cost of any damages

chunks.title: Unable to meet essential living expenses — extra help > housing support products > accommodation security cover grant
chunks.text:
## Unable to meet essential living expenses
When assessing an Accommodation Security Cover Grant, MSD may assess whether the client will be unable to meet their other essential living expenses if the assistance is granted. This includes when the client is unable to meet the essential living expenses for their partner and/or dependent children (if any).
Essential living expenses for the purposes of Housing Support Products may include, but are not limited to:
- accommodation
- food
- fuel (including petrol, diesel and oil)
- telephone costs, this may include: internet connection and mobile service charges
- internet connection and mobile service charges
- motor vehicles costs - repayment and running costs
- essential travel, this may include: employment related traveltravel when accessing essential services and supplies (including children's education and groceries)
- employment related travel
- travel when accessing essential services and supplies (including children's education and groceries)
- power
- childcare costs
- hire purchase expenses for essential household items only, it may also include employment related items. It does not include luxury items such as fishing/jet boats or small planes
- transport cost due to disability
- disability and personal health costs
- counselling
- education costs for dependent children
- clothing
Essential living expenses may vary between clients and should be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

chunks.title: Ability of client to meet need from own resources — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Ability of client to meet need from own resources
When deciding whether to grant a Bond Grant, MSD may consider the ability of the client and their partner (if any) to meet the cost of bond from their own resources.
If the client and their partner (if any) have resources available to them, these should generally be used to pay for their bond (including any increase in bond), unless this would mean they’re unable to meet their essential living expenses.
Examples of a client using the resources they have available to them may include:
- using any cash assets to pay the bond
- accessing assistance available from other government agencies
- paying the bond from their next income payment due to them
Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.
Assistance paid or available to the client and their partner from MSD (eg main benefit, extra help) is not included as a resource available to the client.

chunks.title: Able to obtain and retain accommodation — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Able to obtain and retain accommodation
To qualify for a Bond Grant, MSD must consider whether the client is likely to be able to get and keep the accommodation the bond is for.
MSD will need to discuss with the client whether they can likely afford (with any financial assistance, income and other resources available to them) to get and keep the accommodation, including the ongoing costs of the accommodation.
A client may be considered as being likely to get and keep accommodation when:
- the proposed rent will generally not be over 60 per cent of their net income (and their partner's, if any) taking into account the client's individual circumstances and
- MSD has discussed the client's budget, or have other evidence showing they can manage their future outgoings

chunks.title: Tenant under a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to any tenancy with a written tenancy agreement from Tenancy Services. Some examples are a: - tenancy agreement for rental housing, including with: a private landlordlocal governmenta non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) - a private landlord - local government - a non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) or - tenancy agreement for social housing, including with a community housing provider Clients in this accommodation may be eligible for a Bond Grant.

chunks.title: Flatmate or subletting without a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Clients may be living in a rental property as a flatmate or subletter without a tenancy agreement. The tenant on the tenancy agreement that the client pays their accommodation costs to takes responsibility for these clients and acts as their accommodation supplier. Flatmates generally pay any accommodation costs to the tenant instead of the landlord. This includes clients who are an additional occupant in a social housing property, as they are not on the tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these clients and they are not eligible for a Bond Grant.

chunks.title: Service tenancies — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: A client may be provided accommodation as part of their employment where their landlord is their employer. This is known as a service tenancy. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to service tenancies. Clients in a service tenancy will generally be provided with a written tenancy agreement. These clients may be eligible for a Bond Grant.

chunks.title: Tenancy orders — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: A tenant of a property through a tenancy order made under the Family Violence Act 2018 or Property (Relationships) Act 1976 does not need to have signed a written tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to clients in a tenancy order. These clients may be eligible for a Bond Grant.

chunks.title: Boarding arrangements — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Clients who are boarding have an agreement for one room in the property, rather than the whole house. Boarders have access to shared facilities such as a kitchen and bathroom. When the accommodation has 6 or more occupants, this is known as a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to boarding houses when the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more. The client may be eligible for a Bond Grant if they meet these qualifications. When there are 5 or fewer occupants this is not considered a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these boarding arrangements, including private boarding where the client lives with the owner of the property. Clients in these arrangements are not eligible for a Bond Grant. The accommodation costs a client pays under a boarding accommodation agreement generally includes service and facility costs such as power, grounds maintenance, rubbish disposal, etc. MSD generally should not include any service costs in an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. For more information about what costs can be included in an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, see: - Service costs and water rates

chunks.title: Example 1 – Boarding arrangement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Ngaio has an accommodation agreement to rent a room in a boarding house with 5 other people. She has her own room in the house and shares a bathroom and kitchen with other boarders. She intends to stay there for at least 6 months. Ngaio plays board which includes accommodation costs and service costs (including power, water, cleaning and rubbish disposal costs). The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to this accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: Example 2 – Boarding arrangement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Malosi is boarding with their aunt Vaima. Vaima owns the house and Malosi pays board that includes accommodation, food and service costs, including internet and power costs. Malosi and Vaima have an accommodation agreement which sets out these costs. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to this accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: Rent to buy — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: A client may enter into a rent to buy contract (also called a deferred payment disposition). In these situations, the client is considered to be a homeowner and is not eligible for a Bond Grant.

chunks.title: Relocatable accommodation — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: A client may enter a hire agreement or a rental contract for relocatable accommodation, such as a cabin, mobile home, or caravan. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 only applies to relocatable accommodation if it is: - hired from and located on a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner Clients in this accommodation may be eligible for a Bond Grant. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply if the relocatable accommodation is: - on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days or - placed on any other premises where the land and the accommodation are not owned by the same person or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner Clients in this accommodation are not eligible for a Bond Grant.

chunks.title: Example 1 – campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Rarahu intends to stay in a cabin in a commercial campsite for a minimum of 90 days. She requires assistance to secure the cabin. As Rarahu intends to stay in the cabin for 51 days or more, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to their accommodation arrangement. MSD can approve a Bond Grant for Rarahu to secure the cabin.

chunks.title: Example 2 – campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Arama intends to stay in a cabin in a commercial campsite for 30 days while she waits for her new job to start, which will provide her with long-term accommodation while she's employed. She requires assistance to get the cabin. As Arama intends to stay in the cabin for under 51 days, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to her accommodation arrangement. MSD can conditionally approve an Accommodation Security Cover Grant for Arama to secure the cabin.

chunks.title: Multiple accommodation agreements — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: If a client is an occupant under multiple accommodation agreements (i.e. required to pay accommodation costs for more than one accommodation agreement), the Bond Grant is only payable for the client's principal place of residence. MSD must assess their principal place of residence to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies, and whether the client is eligible for a Bond Grant at this accommodation. If the client and their partner have separate accommodation, they may each have a different principal place of residence. Generally, the client will determine what is their principal place of residence. If there is evidence the client is not using the property as their principal place of residence, MSD should generally decline a Bond Grant. For example, if the client is using the property to store excess personal goods or sub-letting the property while living elsewhere, do not pay a Bond Grant. Note a grant can be paid for multiple accommodation agreements if they are for the same accommodation i.e. a rental contract for a cabin hire and a separate rental contract for the land that the cabin sits on.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Jiang lives with his parents in Auckland. His ex-partner lives in Hamilton and has custody of their children. Jiang is planning to visit Hamilton every weekend to visit his children and has organised to rent a small flat under a tenancy agreement so that he can stay there on the weekends. The landlord has requested that he pay a bond to move into the property. Jiang applies for a Bond Grant to move into the accommodation agreement in Hamilton. As this is not his primary place of residence, MSD declines the grant.

chunks.title: Accommodation is suitable to live in — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation is suitable to live in
MSD may consider whether the accommodation will be suitable for the client to live in if the grant is made.
Factors MSD may consider include but are not limited to whether the:
- accommodation has been modified to suit the accessibility needs for the client, their partner (if any) or their dependent children (if any)
- client has access to facilities such as clean drinking water, cooking facilities, electricity, heating, beds and mattresses, toilet and bathing facilities and a food refrigerator that the client can access
- accommodation has enough bedrooms
- accommodation is fit for human habitation, including being structurally safe to live in
MSD does not need to assess if a client's accommodation is suitable at every Bond Grant assessment. However, if it is clear through the conversation with the client that the accommodation is not suitable for the client, their partner (if any) or their dependent children (if any), MSD may decline the application.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to
The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 provides rights and protections for tenants and landlords in rental agreements.
MSD can pay a Bond Grant for people who are living in or moving into accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. This includes, but is not limited to:
- rental tenancies
- boarding houses with at least 6 tenants or boarders where the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more
- service tenancies where an employer provides accommodation to an employee
- multi-unit residential housing developments to provide long-term (minimum of 10 years) rental accommodation to tenants (also known as build to rent tenancies)
- social housing (including Kainga Ora and private social housing) if the client is a tenant or a signatory
- hire agreements for relocatable homes including cabins, mobile homes and caravans where they are: hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more oron a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person, and facilities are not shared with the owner
- hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or
- on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person, and facilities are not shared with the owner
If you are unsure if the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to an accommodation agreement, contact Helpline or your Capability Developer.

chunks.title: Assessing a Bond Grant — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: When a client needs help with a rental bond, a Bond Grant should be considered if they meet the qualifications. A Bond Grant is available for people who are likely to be able to retain rental housing but require some assistance to get or keep it. A client may need help with a General Bond, a Pet Bond or both. For the purposes of a Bond Grant, these two types of bond are considered to be the same. A Bond Grant is a discretionary grant. MSD needs to consider the client's individual circumstances and determine whether the Bond Grant should be granted. In order to make a decision to grant, MSD must consider: - the purpose of the Housing Support Programme, including whether granting a Bond Grant would be the correct use of the payment - any other financial assistance available to the client that could be used to meet their need - whether the client and their partner (if any) could meet the need from their own resources, including accessing cash assets or receiving support from other Government agencies - any impact on the client, their partner (if any), and their dependent children (if any) if their need is not met and - whether the client intends to stay in the accommodation for fewer than 28 days Depending on the client's circumstances, MSD may also consider the following factors: - whether the client or their partner (if any) has caused or contributed to the need for a Bond Grant - whether the client or their partner (if any) will be able to meet their essential living expenses if a Bond Grant is paid - the existing debt of the client and their partner (if any) - whether their accommodation is suitable to live in - any other matters MSD think are relevant A Bond Grant can be declined if a grant would not be appropriate after having considered the circumstances of the client and their partner (if any) and their dependent children (if any). When assessing a Bond Grant for the cost of a Pet Bond, MSD must consider the same eligibility and discretionary criteria as for any other Bond Grant application.

chunks.title: Pet Bond — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: From 1 December 2025, a Pet Bond of up to two weeks rent may be included in a tenancy agreement or by written request from the landlord. A Pet Bond can be considered as part of the Bond Grant. A Pet Bond cannot be requested for a pet that was already kept at the property, by mutual agreement between the landlord and tenant, before 1 December 2025. Assistance with a Pet Bond can only be considered at the start of the tenancy if the total Bond Grant (including any Pet Bond) is at or under the relevant payment limit. For example, if a landlord requires two weeks of General Bond and two weeks of Pet Bond. A Bond Grant can only be considered for an increase to a Pet Bond when the client needs an extra bond payment due to an increase in rent and the total Bond Grant is at or under the relevant payment limit. Below are different scenarios and examples related to Pet Bonds. These are provided to help you understand how Pet Bond requirements may apply in various situations. Tenancy Renewals and Variations A tenancy renewal or variation is not considered a new tenancy for Bond Grant purposes if the client remains in the same property with the same landlord. If a Bond Grant has already been issued for the tenancy, MSD cannot approve a second Bond Grant, regardless of the type of renewal or variation. This includes where a tenancy is renewed or varied to allow a pet and the landlord is requesting a Pet Bond. Example - Tenancy renewal with a Right of Renewal Clause Jordan entered a tenancy in June 2025 and received a Bond Grant from MSD at that time. His tenancy agreement includes a right of renewal clause, allowing him to continue the tenancy on the same terms and conditions. - Existing pet: Jordan already has a dog. At renewal on 1 December 2025, the landlord requests a Pet Bond. Under the Residential Tenancies Act, the landlord cannot request a Pet Bond for a pet that was already lawfully kept before 1 December 2025.

chunks.title: Pet Bond — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: - New pet: Jordan adopts a dog at renewal. The landlord consents and adds a Pet Bond clause to the renewed agreement. He requests MSD for a Bond Grant to cover the Pet Bond cost. MSD will consider this on a case-by-case basis: If Jordan asks MSD for a Bond Grant before adopting the dog, MSD will decline because the cost is avoidable. This aligns with MSD's HSP intent to help clients obtain and retain accommodation, not to fund discretionary choices.If Jordan adopts the dog and then requests a Bond Grant for the Pet Bond cost, MSD will assess whether Jordan caused or contributed to the situation. If MSD determines that Jordan caused or contributed to the cost (for example, by choosing to adopt the pet without budgeting for it), the Bond Grant will be declined. - If Jordan asks MSD for a Bond Grant before adopting the dog, MSD will decline because the cost is avoidable. This aligns with MSD's HSP intent to help clients obtain and retain accommodation, not to fund discretionary choices. - If Jordan adopts the dog and then requests a Bond Grant for the Pet Bond cost, MSD will assess whether Jordan caused or contributed to the situation. If MSD determines that Jordan caused or contributed to the cost (for example, by choosing to adopt the pet without budgeting for it), the Bond Grant will be declined. Example - Tenancy renewal without a Right of Renewal Clause Sophie entered a tenancy in July 2025 with her cat and received a Bond Grant from MSD at that time. Her fixed term tenancy ends in December 2025, and she signs a new agreement with the same landlord to continue living in the same property. The new agreement includes a Pet Bond clause. The agreement is legally treated as a new tenancy under tenancy law. MSD can consider approving a Bond Grant for the Pet Bond cost because this is an additional cost associated with the new tenancy, and the client did not cause or contribute to this change. Example – Bond increase due to an increase in rent

chunks.title: Pet Bond — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Gabrielle has received a notice that her rent will be increasing by $40 a week, to a total rent of $465 a week from 3 August 2026. She will need to pay an additional $80 to her landlord to top up her existing general bond of 2 weeks rent and $80 to top up her existing Pet Bond which is also 2 weeks rent. MSD can consider approving a Bond Grant for the general and Pet Bond increase of $160 as it is not more than the relevant payment limit (4 weeks of the amount of the increase in rent).

chunks.title: Assessing weekly income — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Income limits for Housing Support Products are determined based on a client's weekly income. MSD has discretion to determine the period that weekly income relates to. When working out which period of income to use, MSD may consider: - how much income was earned during the period - how income the client expects to receive for that period, (e.g. investment interest was accrued but has not yet paid) - the period for which income was received by the client Generally, MSD will base the client and their partner's (if any) weekly income on the average income over the previous four weeks, unless MSD considers a different timeframe is appropriate (for example the client has been earning for a shorter or longer time). This means the last four weeks of income is totalled and then divided by four. In some cases, MSD can use a different period to calculate the weekly income period, to consider the client's circumstances, including whether the client or their partner's income: - has been inconsistent over the previous four weeks - is variable week by week - has either increased or decreased recently - will increase or decrease in the immediate future (in the next four weeks) - future income is uncertain, including where there is a history of the employer not paying wages or paying late - has been earned but not paid (e.g. the client earned income but not been paid on time)

chunks.title: Example 1 - variable income — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Piper works in a casual role in a supermarket. Their employment started 3 weeks ago, they have no set weekly hours and their income will change from week to week, depending on the number of hours they will work. Their employer has indicated they should receive a minimum of 20 hours work per week at $24 per hour ($480 per week) but this is not set out in Piper's employment agreement. Piper's 3-week income so far has been: Week 1 = $400Week 2 = $200Week 3 = $300 In this case, Piper's income will be estimated using the average wage over the previous three weeks as they do not have four weeks of income to assess. The calculation is: $400 + $200 + $300 = $900$900/3 (weeks) = $300.

chunks.title: Example 2 - recent income change — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Moana has been earning $900 per week over the previous 12 months. However, Moana has changed from a full-time role to a part-time role due to starting study. Moana started earning $300 a week starting last week. When calculating Moana's weekly income for a Housing Support Product, MSD bases this on $300 per week as this will be her income going forward.

chunks.title: Cash asset limit — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Cash asset limit
A client and their partner (if any) cannot get a Bond Grant if their assets are more than the cash asset limit.
We need to know the cash value of their assets.
There is no discretion to grant a Bond Grant to a client whose cash assets (including the cash assets of their partner, if any) are above the asset limit.

chunks.title: Cash assets include — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: - cash - bills of exchange or promissory notes - building society shares - money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society - money invested with or lent to any bank, financial institution or other person whether in mortgage or other security, or unsecured - money withdrawn from a KiwiSaver scheme - mortgage investments and other long-term loans - the net equity held in any property or land not used as a person's home - pre-paid funeral expenses (in some circumstances) - shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds and other bonds (including shares in energy organisations) and - the client's share in any partnership Note if you are unsure of a case contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Cash assets do not include — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: - the home property and land on which it is situated - a motor vehicle or other vehicle principally used by the client or their partner for their personal use (this is limited to 1 vehicle for a single person or 2 vehicles for a couple) - a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2000, or which is used by the client or a member of their family for day-to-day accommodation - payments people get under Housing Support Products (Bond Grant, Moving Costs Grant, Rent in Advance, Rent Arrears Grant, Transition to Alternative Housing Grant, Accommodation Security Cover, Tenancy Costs Cover) - personal effects - Christchurch mosques attack support payments - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts - Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income - Māori land - MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is received - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after the payment is received - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made - specified Ex gratia and compensation payments - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received A bank overdraft is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client. Christchurch earthquake related payments Payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client got the payment. See:

chunks.title: Client caused or contributed to the need — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Client caused or contributed to the need
Before deciding whether or not to grant a Bond Grant, MSD may consider the extent the client has caused or contributed to their need for bond.
Examples of when a client may be considered to have caused or contributed to the need for a Bond Grant include when:
- they have recently caused or contributed to intentional or reckless damage to their previous accommodation, including damage that may have resulted in termination of their tenancy(s)
- they have a pattern of not meeting their obligations for previous accommodation, e.g. non-payment of rent, leaving without notice, additional occupants not approved by landlord etc
Each client's situation must be assessed on their individual circumstances.
Note if the client has already received a Bond Grant for the tenancy, MSD cannot issue a second Bond Grant for a Pet Bond.
If the client has chosen to get a pet and now needs a Pet Bond, this may be considered an avoidable cost rather than one necessary to obtain or retain housing. When assessing the Bond Grant, MSD will need to consider whether the client has caused or contributed to the need for an additional bond.

chunks.title: Clients who cannot get a Bond Grant — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Clients living in one of the following accommodation agreements are not eligible for a Bond Grant: - accommodation owned by the client or their partner - tents, including those joined to a vehicle - homeless shelters - prisons and correctional facilities - accommodation for which they are receiving an Emergency Housing Grant or Transitional or Contracted Emergency Housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development There is no discretion to approve a payment for a client living in one of these accommodation agreements.

chunks.title: Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Clients living in, or moving into, an accommodation agreement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to cannot receive a Bond Grant for General Bond or Pet Bond costs. These include, but are not limited to: - a flat or house share agreement where the client has not signed a tenancy agreement (e.g. a flatmate that sub-lets from a head tenant) - hire agreement for a relocatable home including a cabin, mobile home or caravan where: it is on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days, oron any other premises for any amount of time where the land and accommodation are not owned by the same person oron a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person, and facilities are shared with the owner - it is on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days, or - on any other premises for any amount of time where the land and accommodation are not owned by the same person or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person, and facilities are shared with the owner - a lodging arrangement - a boarding agreement where the client is either: in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to and does stay for less than 28 daysin accommodation where there are less than 6 boarders - in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to and does stay for less than 28 days - in accommodation where there are less than 6 boarders - commercial accommodation such as hotels, motels, and homestays that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. This excludes the following accommodation as they are not eligible to get Housing Support Product Assistance: emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Granttransitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development andcontracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant - transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development and - contracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - an additional occupant in a social housing property that is not a tenant or a signatory on the tenancy agreement Clients living in one of the above accommodation agreements may be eligible to receive an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Pet Bond — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: If a Bond Grant has already been issued for a tenancy, then: - the Bond Grant cannot be revised or topped up to include the cost of a Pet Bond - a second Bond Grant cannot be granted for a Pet Bond Note if a Bond Grant is paid due to an increase in rent, any increase to the Pet Bond can be included as long as the total Bond Grant is at or under the relevant limit. Example - Pet added after Bond Grant already paid Lisa received a Bond Grant of 3 weeks rent for her current tenancy 3 months ago. She now wants to get a pet, and her landlord has requested a Pet Bond. Lisa applies for another Bond Grant. MSD cannot approve a second Bond Grant for the same tenancy to cover the Pet Bond. Example - New 52-week period, same tenancy Jed received a Bond Grant for his current tenancy 15 months ago. He is now in a new 52-week period and has adopted a cat. His landlord requests a Pet Bond and Jed applies for another Bond Grant. MSD cannot approve a second Bond Grant for the same tenancy to cover the Pet Bond, even if the 52-week period has reset. The tenancy is not new, and Jed does not risk losing it.

chunks.title: Clients with existing debt — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Clients with existing debt
When deciding whether to approve a Bond Grant, MSD may consider the existing debt of the client and their partner (if any). Existing debt includes both MSD debt and non-MSD debt.
A client's existing debt repayments may impact their ability to repay a Bond Grant.
When a client has existing MSD debt, MSD may consider whether it is appropriate to reduce those repayments to allow for the repayment of the Bond Grant.
When a client is getting all the financial assistance they qualify for, but are not likely to be able to repay an amount paid under a Bond Grant, the grant may be declined.

chunks.title: Information on a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Information on a tenancy agreement
If it is unclear whether a document is a tenancy agreement under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 or not, below is a list of information that is usually part of this type of agreement:
- the full name and contact address of the landlord
- the landlord's contact mobile telephone number (if any)
- the landlord's contact email address (if any)
- the full name and contact address (when different from the address of the premises to which the agreement relates) of the tenant
- the tenant's contact mobile telephone number (if any)
- the tenant's contact email address (if any)
- the address of the premises
- the date of the tenancy agreement
- the date of commencement of the tenancy (when different from the date of the tenancy agreement)
- the landlord's address for service
- the tenant's address for service
- whether the tenant is under the age of 18
- the amount of any bond
- the rent payable
- the frequency of the rent payments
- the place or bank account number where the rent is to be paid
- a list of any chattels provided by the landlord
- if the tenancy is a fixed-term tenancy, the date on which the term will expire
- Healthy Homes compliance statement
- insulation statement
- insurance statement
The agreement should be signed by both parties but if it's not signed, it may still be a valid agreement. In these cases, MSD can use other evidence to determine that there is an agreement in place. For example, bank account statement showing rent payments.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances
A client cannot be paid more than two Bond Grants or Accommodation Security Cover Grants (combined) in a 52-week period, unless MSD is satisfied there are exceptional circumstances.
Exceptional circumstances are where the circumstance:
- sets the client apart from others in a similar situation and
- is beyond the client's control
The following situations are generally considered as exceptional circumstances (but not limited to):
- the client needs to move through no fault of their own, e.g.: the client has been notified the owner will move back into the rental propertythe property is deemed uninhabitable due to damage (such as a burst waterpipe) and major repairs are needed
- the client has been notified the owner will move back into the rental property
- the property is deemed uninhabitable due to damage (such as a burst waterpipe) and major repairs are needed
- the client was a victim of a violent crime or family violence and has had a change in their housing circumstances, e.g.: needing to move to a different property following a violent crime orno longer living with their partner after seeking a protection order (including if the client remains in the same property without their partner)
- needing to move to a different property following a violent crime or
- no longer living with their partner after seeking a protection order (including if the client remains in the same property without their partner)
There may be other reasons for exceptional circumstances.

chunks.title: Impact on the client and their family — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: When considering whether to make a Bond Grant, MSD must consider the likely impacts on the client, their partner (if any), and their dependent children (if any) if the client's accommodation need is not met. MSD should consider what other accommodation or options are available to the client if they do not get the grant. Factors that MSD may consider include (but are not limited to) if: - the client is likely to require emergency housing if assistance is not granted - the client will need to stay in accommodation that is close to a perpetrator of violence if assistance is not granted - the client will need to stay in accommodation that is near drug use or gang related activity if assistance is not granted - the client can afford any of their other options - there are enough bedrooms in the other accommodation option/s - the client is likely to stay in suitable accommodation if they do not get the grant - the client is a reasonable distance from work, school or essential services if assistance is not granted - their other options meet the accessibility needs the client, partner (if any), or their children (if any) may have MSD must assess each client's circumstances on a case-by-case basis and determine how significant any impacts on the client's family will be.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Sam lives with their partner and two children. Their current tenancy is ending due to the landlord selling the property. Sam has applied for a Bond Grant to move into a cabin in a campground near her old tenancy. The cabin is suitably sized and appropriate for her family. Sam and their family have an option to stay with their brother that would have a lower weekly accommodation cost for Sam, however it would take over an hour and a half for Sam to get to work and to their children's school during peak traffic times. MSD and Sam agree that the impacts on her family to travel and pay for travel costs will be significant, and MSD grants Housing Support Product assistance for the cabin.

chunks.title: Pet Bond costs — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: MSD can consider the impacts that having a pet would have on the client and their family. This could also include the impact if the family were unable to keep a pet. However, this also needs to be considered alongside the client's decision to adopt a pet and appropriate planning and budgeting for this decision. Note the definition of pet in the legislation excludes a disability assist dog and a person does not need consent for these animals. A disability assist dog is a dog certified by an authorised organisation as being a dog that has been trained (or is being trained) to assist a person with a disability.

chunks.title: Income limit — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Income limit
A client and their partner (if any) cannot get a Bond Grant if their income is more than the appropriate income limit.
There is one set of income limits for all clients including those getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension, and non-beneficiaries.
For New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients you should check their income is not over the income limit. New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension must be included as income when assessing if the client qualifies.
There is no discretion to grant a Bond Grant to a client whose income (including the income of their partner, if any) is above the income limit.
For more information about what is included as income and what is not included see:
- Core Policy Income

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Introduction
A Bond Grant is a Housing Support Product for clients needing help to get or keep accommodation. It provides recoverable assistance to help with the cost of a rental bond (General Bond and/or Pet Bond) charged by a landlord to the client as a tenant.
A Bond Grant is a discretionary grant and can be considered for any client who meets the qualifications.
## Residential Tenancies Act 1986
Bond Grants are only available to clients who are in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to.
Clients in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to may be eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.

chunks.title: House and land — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## House and land
Only assess the net equity of house and land not used as the client's principal place of residence.
When assessing net equity on a house and/or land, use the rateable valuation or the amount insured. Use the higher value.
Example
House valued at
$100,000
Land valued at
$100,000
Total combined value
$200,000
Less outstanding Mortgage principal
$150,000
Net equity
$50,000
Some District Councils only use the Capital value of a property, this will be noted on the rate notice. In these cases the Capital value is the value of both the house and land value combined.
Example
Capital value
$200,000
Less outstanding Mortgage principal
$150,000
Net equity
$50,000
## Client has more than one vehicle
When a client has more than one vehicle, you will need to assess whether the vehicles are used for private use.
Example
A family of 3 adults own 5 vehicles and all are claimed to be used for personal use. One is a vintage car used for Sunday outings and another a 4-wheel drive used on weekends only.
The 4-wheel drive and vintage car are additional to the needs of the family. Therefore, for Bond Grant purposes, the net equity of these vehicles will need to be assessed.

chunks.title: Other financial assistance available to the client — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Other financial assistance available to the client
MSD must assess whether the client can receive other financial assistance before granting a Bond Grant.
This assistance could include any one-off or ongoing payments from MSD. When a client is granted other financial assistance for bond, but it doesn't cover the full amount needed, MSD can consider a Bond Grant for the remaining amount.
A Bond Grant should not be paid for costs already paid for by any other financial assistance.
Some clients may have access to other forms of assistance. They may still be eligible for Housing Support Products but only once they have exhausted all other forms of support first. For example:
- tertiary students staying in university accommodation (e.g. Halls of Residence)
- clients in rest homes and retirement villages
- clients in institutions for the care of sick and disabled people
## Example
Saane is a tenant in a property and applies for Rent in Arrears Grant of $400 for two weeks of accommodation costs. They are receiving a reduced rate of Student Allowance of $150 per week due to their parent's income and received a scholarship payment of $750 earlier in the year. They have not accessed their Student Loan Living Costs.
MSD does not grant the payment as the student could speak to their parents for support, or access their scholarship payment to cover their arrears. MSD also advises the student to access their Student Loan Living Costs entitlement so that they can cover their accommodation costs going forward.

chunks.title: Paying someone other than the landlord — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Paying someone other than the landlord
Generally, a Bond Grant should only be paid directly to the prospective landlord or property manager.
However, in some situations, MSD may pay a Bond Grant to the client's payment card or directly to the client.
The Bond Grant:
- can be paid to the client's payment card when the landlord or property manager indicates this is their preferred payment method
- can only be paid directly to the client (e.g. bank account) when the landlord or property manager is not in MSD's system and the client needs an immediate grant paid to get or keep the tenancy
When the Bond Grant is paid, advise the client:
- the landlord is legally required to send the bond to Tenancy Services
- Tenancy Services must send the client notice they got the bond and
- if the client does not get a notice they should check with the landlord and Tenancy Services
Note a Bond Grant cannot be paid directly to Tenancy Services.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Bond Grants are recoverable and must be paid back to MSD. If a client qualifies for a non-recoverable re-establishment Special Needs Grant for a bond (General Bond and/or Pet Bond), this assistance must be considered first. MSD can consider any remaining amount still needed for bond under a Bond Grant.

chunks.title: Maximum amount for a grant — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: The maximum Bond Grant payable is limited to: - When entering or renewing a tenancy agreement: the amount of the bond the client and their partner (if any) combined must pay for the accommodation orthe equivalent of 4 weeks rent for the accommodation orif the client is in shared accommodation, the client and their partner's (if any) portion of 4 weeks rentwhichever is the lesser amount. - the amount of the bond the client and their partner (if any) combined must pay for the accommodation or - the equivalent of 4 weeks rent for the accommodation or - if the client is in shared accommodation, the client and their partner's (if any) portion of 4 weeks rentwhichever is the lesser amount. - When due to an increase in rent: the extra amount required to top up the bond orthe equivalent of 4 weeks of the increased rent amountwhichever is the lesser amount. - the extra amount required to top up the bond or - the equivalent of 4 weeks of the increased rent amountwhichever is the lesser amount. MSD cannot pay more than the limits set out above. In general, four weeks rent is the bond amount asked for. This means if General Bond and Pet Bond costs exceed four weeks rent in total, MSD can only pay a maximum of 4 weeks and the client will need to cover the remainder. Example Sarah is entering into a new tenancy agreement. Her landlord has requested payment of: - 4 weeks General Bond and - 2 weeks Pet Bond (because Sarah will be keeping a pet) Sarah has not received any Bond Grant from MSD in the past 52 weeks. MSD assesses her eligibility and approves a Bond Grant for up to four weeks rent. MSD cannot pay more than four weeks total, so Sarah must pay the remaining two weeks herself.

chunks.title: Social housing — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: When a client is applying for bond assistance for social housing, the amount they can apply for is based on: - the weekly rate of Income Related Rent charged by their social housing provider or - if they do not pay Income Related Rent, the weekly market rent for the social housing

chunks.title: Refund of bond for previous tenancy — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: When deciding whether to grant a Bond Grant, and the grant amount, consider whether the client has, or will have, a refund of their previous bond by the date their new bond must be paid. For example, a client applies for a Bond Grant of $1,500. They will get a refund for the previous bond of $900 before their new bond is due. MSD must discuss this with the client, who says they will use the $900 toward the new bond. MSD can approve a Bond Grant for $600, as this is the amount still needed by the client.

chunks.title: Accommodation Security Cover Grant — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Any Accommodation Security Cover Grant that the client has been paid is included in their Bond Grant count. When an Accommodation Security Cover Grant has been conditionally granted, it is not included in the grant count until it has been paid out.

chunks.title: Bond Grant and Accommodation Security Cover Grant can be paid twice in a 52-week period — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Bond Grants and Accommodation Security Cover Grants (combined) cannot be paid more than twice in a 52-week period to a client, unless the Bond Grant is paid due to a rent increase in certain situations or there are exceptional circumstances. When a Bond Grant is paid due to a rent increase and the client did not get a Bond Grant for entering or renewing the same tenancy, it is included in the grant count. However, a Bond Grant paid due to a rent increase for the same accommodation a Bond Grant has already been made for is excluded from the grant count.
