There is no limit on the number of Bond Grants that can be paid due to a rent increase but rent increases are limited to once every 12 months under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986. When a client applies for a Bond Grant, MSD must check how many Bond Grants and Accommodation Security Cover Grants, that are included in the grant count, the client has had paid in the last 52 weeks. Bond Grants and Accommodation Security Cover Grants in the 52-week period before the latest application are counted, including any Bond Grants and Accommodation Security Cover Grants paid due to exceptional circumstances. If a client gets more than one payment of a Bond Grant or Accommodation Security Cover Grant in a 52-week period, they can get up to the maximum amount for each grant. For more information see: - Exceptional circumstances

chunks.title: Paying someone other than the landlord or property manager — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Generally, a Bond Grant should only be paid directly to the landlord or property manager. However, in some situations, MSD may pay a Bond Grant to the client's payment card or directly to the client.

chunks.title: Pre-paid funeral expenses — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Pre-paid funeral expenses
A pre-paid funeral trust fund or account is money put aside (usually in a trust) exclusively for the payment of funeral expenses.
If the money can be accessed by the client and used for other purposes, it is not considered exclusively for funeral expenses and can be treated as a cash asset.
It is usually clear a trust fund or account has been genuinely set aside for funeral expenses. Evidence it has been set aside exclusively for funeral expenses include:
- the trust fund/account is only paid out on production of a death certificate
- the client cannot usually access the funds
- if a client can access the fund, there are limited conditions on withdrawal, such as re-locating overseas
- the trust fund/account is only payable to the funeral director or administrator of the client's estate
- the client cannot generally access the interest earned from the trust fund or account
When the trust fund or account has been set aside for funeral expenses and cannot be accessed or converted into cash this money is not a realisable asset.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for a Bond Grant a client must:
- meet the residency qualifications
- meet the income and assets limits
- be considered to be likely get and keep the accommodation if assistance is granted
- be entering a tenancy that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to, that requires a bond payment or
- be an existing tenant who is required to pay an extra bond payment when they: are renewing their tenancy agreement orhave an increase in rent
- are renewing their tenancy agreement or
- have an increase in rent
While a client may qualify, the approval of a Bond Grant is discretionary and should be considered according to each client's specific situation and need.

chunks.title: Recovery of payment — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Recovery of payment
Before granting a Bond Grant, MSD must discuss a repayment plan with the client.
There are a variety of repayment options available to a client as listed below:
- deductions from a main benefit, Student Allowance or Working for Families assistance paid by MSD
- employer deduction notice (Client Support - Debt Management will arrange this - case managers do not have the delegation to issue a wage deduction notice)
- automatic payment from client's bank account
- internet/telebanking payment
- payment through New Zealand Post Shop
## Recovery rate
A Bond Grant must have a recovery rate that means the client will pay back the debt owed within 24 months of the grant unless they have exceptional circumstances.
The rate and method of recovery must be discussed with the client, and be based on their individual circumstances and ability to live within the reduced income.
It is important the client knows the length of time the Bond Grant will be repaid over.
Clients who have already been granted a Bond Grant may have their recovery rate adjusted at a later date if their circumstances change.
When determining the rate of repayment by instalments MSD must consider:
- whether the instalment reductions will leave enough for the client's living expenses and any other debt repayments
- the impact on the individual (and/or their immediate family) when establishing further recoverable debt and
- the likelihood it would cause the client to seek further Housing Support Product payments or other extra help assistance

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get a Bond Grant a client must:
- qualify for and be getting a main benefit or
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand at the time of their application andbe a New Zealand citizen orhold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 orbe recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 orqualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy but the relationship has ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- hold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- qualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy but the relationship has ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they are considered to hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other qualifications for a Bond Grant.

chunks.title: Service costs and water rates — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Service costs and water rates
Sometimes a client's accommodation costs include service costs such as electricity or an internet connection.
When a client is moving into accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to, service costs cannot be included. Only the portion of the costs that relates to their accommodation can be included in a Bond Grant.
Generally the service costs and cost of accommodation will be itemised separately on the tenancy agreement. Use the accommodation cost only to calculate the Bond Grant.
## Example
John pays $250 total rent a week for a room and electricity in a boarding house. As there is only one meter box for the boarding house the landlord is unable to provide an estimate of the service cost.
Powerswitch estimates the weekly electricity costs of the household to be $120 a week. There are 6 people in the household, so John's share of the electricity costs would be $120 divided by 6 (the total number of the people in the household) which is $20. To calculate John's accommodation costs, deduct $20 (electricity) from $250 (total rent). John's accommodation costs are $230 a week.

chunks.title: Staying in accommodation for more than 28 days — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: To qualify for a Bond Grant, a client should intend to be staying in accommodation for at least 28 days. This is because the client should be able to keep the accommodation when a Bond Grant is made. MSD can consider granting a Bond Grant when the client is staying for less than 28 days on a discretionary basis. When a client requests a Bond Grant for accommodation that they will stay in for less than 28 days, MSD should consider whether: - the client will require emergency housing if a Bond Grant is not granted - there will be an impact to the client, their spouse or partner, and/or their children if the Bond Grant is not granted - a short-term grant will make it more likely for the client to stay in accommodation long-term. For example, a boarding house owner will only accept the client for a week to see how things go before they commit to the client staying long-term - the client has long-term accommodation arranged, but requires a short-term grant somewhere else before the accommodation is available. For example, they need to stay with their friend for 2 weeks before their rental tenancy begins

chunks.title: Example 1 — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Ripeka has applied for a Bond Grant to move into a boarding house for 2 and a half weeks. Her previous accommodation ended as the head tenant and other flatmates are moving out and Ripeka cannot afford to rent the property on her own. The boarding house is booked out after 2 and a half weeks so Ripeka cannot stay any longer. They require 1 week of accommodation costs as bond, which Ripeka cannot afford. She can afford the ongoing costs of the accommodation once this is paid. Ripeka has already received 1 Bond Grant in the last 52 weeks. There is no other accommodation available (including staying with family or friends temporarily), and her only alternative would be to apply for emergency housing. MSD grants the Bond Grant due to Ripeka's circumstances, and advises her to continue looking for accommodation that she can keep.

chunks.title: Example 2 — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text: Dylan[JO1] wants to move out of a flat in Wellington where they are a tenant because they want to move to Auckland to look for work. They apply for a Bond Grant to move into a boarding house in Auckland for two weeks to look for work without securing long-term accommodation. MSD declines the Bond Grant because Dylan is moving out of long-term accommodation into short term accommodation, they have not moved out of their long-term accommodation yet, and they have contributed to the need for a grant.

chunks.title: Tenants — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Tenants
A client who signs the tenancy agreement at a property is known as a tenant. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to them, and they are responsible to the landlord for any rent and damages due at the accommodation.
A Bond Grant can only be paid to accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to as this must be lodged with Tenancy Services.
Note only tenants (those who have signed the tenancy agreement) may be asked to pay a Pet Bond.
Where a Pet Bond is required, all tenants named on the tenancy agreement are jointly responsible for any pet-related damage, regardless of who owns the pet.
## Flatmates
A client who is living at the accommodation and has not signed the tenancy agreement is usually known as a flatmate. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to them and they cannot receive a Bond Grant.
A flatmate may be eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Unable to meet essential living expenses — extra help > housing support products > bond grant
chunks.text:
## Unable to meet essential living expenses
When assessing a Bond Grant, MSD may assess whether the client will be unable to meet their other essential living expenses if the assistance is paid. This includes when the client is unable to meet the essential living expenses for their partner and/or dependent children (if any).
Essential living expenses for the purposes of Housing Support Products may include, but are not limited to:
- accommodation
- food
- fuel (including petrol, diesel and oil)
- telephone costs, this may include: internet connection and mobile service charges
- internet connection and mobile service charges
- motor vehicles costs - repayment and running costs
- essential travel, this may include: employment related traveltravel when accessing essential services and supplies (including children's education and groceries)
- employment related travel
- travel when accessing essential services and supplies (including children's education and groceries)
- power
- childcare costs
- hire purchase expenses for essential household items only, it may also include employment related items. It does not include luxury items such as fishing/jet boats or small planes
- transport cost due to disability
- disability and personal health costs
- counselling
- education costs for dependent children
- clothing
Essential living expenses may vary between clients and should be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

chunks.title: Able to obtain and retain accommodation — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Able to obtain and retain accommodation
To qualify for a Moving Costs Grant, MSD must consider whether the client is likely to be able to get and keep the accommodation.
MSD will need to discuss with the client whether they can likely afford (with any financial assistance, income and other resources available to them) to get and keep the accommodation, including the ongoing costs of the accommodation.
A client may be considered as being likely to get and keep accommodation when:
- the proposed accommodation costs will generally not be over 60 per cent of their net income (and their partner's, if any) taking into account the client's individual circumstances) and
- MSD has discussed the client's budget, or have other evidence which shows they can manage their future outgoings

chunks.title: Tenant under a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to any tenancy with a written tenancy agreement from Tenancy Services. Some examples are a: - tenancy agreement for rental housing, including with: a private landlordlocal governmenta non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) - a private landlord - local government - a non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) or - tenancy agreement for social housing, including with a community housing provider Clients in this accommodation may be eligible for a Moving Costs Grant.

chunks.title: Flatmate or subletting without a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: Clients may be living in a rental property as a flatmate or subletter without a tenancy agreement. The tenant on the tenancy agreement that the client pays their accommodation costs to takes responsibility for these clients and acts as their accommodation supplier. Flatmates generally pay any accommodation costs to the tenant instead of the landlord. This includes clients who are an additional occupant in a social housing property, as they are not on the tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these clients and they may be eligible for an Accommodation Moving Costs Grant.

chunks.title: Service tenancies — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: A client may be provided accommodation as part of their employment where their landlord is their employer. This is known as a service tenancy. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to service tenancies. Clients in a service tenancy will generally be provided with a written tenancy agreement. These clients may be eligible for a Moving Costs Grant.

chunks.title: Tenancy orders — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: A tenant of a property through a tenancy order made under the Family Violence Act 2018 or Property (Relationships) Act 1976 does not need to have signed a written tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to clients in a tenancy order. These clients may be eligible for a Moving Costs Grant.

chunks.title: Boarding arrangements — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: Clients who are boarding have an agreement for one room in the property, rather than the whole house. Boarders have access to shared facilities such as a kitchen and bathroom. When the accommodation has 6 or more occupants, this is known as a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to boarding houses where the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more. The client may be eligible for a Moving Costs Grant if they meet these qualifications. When there are 5 or fewer occupants this is not considered a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these boarding arrangements, including private boarding where the client lives with the owner of the property. Clients in these arrangements may be eligible for an Accommodation Moving Costs Grant. The accommodation costs a client pays under a boarding accommodation agreement generally includes service and facility costs such as power, water, grounds maintenance, rubbish disposal, etc.

chunks.title: Example 1 - Boarding arrangement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: Ngaio has an accommodation agreement to rent a room in a boarding house with 5 other people. She has her own room in the house and shares a bathroom and kitchen with other boarders. She intends to stay there for at least 6 months. Ngaio pays board which includes accommodation costs and service costs (including power, water, cleaning and rubbish disposal costs). The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to this accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: Example 2 - Boarding arrangement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: Malosi is boarding with their aunt Vaima. Vaima owns the house and Malosi pays board that includes accommodation, food, and service costs, including internet and power costs. Malosi and Vaima have an accommodation agreement which sets out these costs. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to this boarding arrangement.

chunks.title: Rent to buy — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: A client may enter into a rent to buy contract (also called a deferred payment disposition). In these situations, the client is considered to be a homeowner and is not eligible for a Moving Costs Grant.

chunks.title: Relocatable accommodation — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: A client may enter a hire agreement or a rental contract for relocatable accommodation, such as a cabin, mobile home, or caravan. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 only applies to relocatable accommodation if it is: - hired from and located on a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner Clients in this accommodation may be eligible for a Moving Costs Grant. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply if the relocatable accommodation is: - on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days or - placed on any other premises where the land and the accommodation are not owned by the same person or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner Clients in this accommodation may be eligible for an Accommodation Moving Costs Grant.

chunks.title: Example 1 - campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: Rarahu intends to stay in a cabin in a commercial campsite for a minimum of 90 days. She requires assistance with moving costs to move into the cabin. As Rarahu intends to stay for 51 days or more, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to their accommodation arrangement. MSD can approve a Moving Costs Grant for Rarahu to secure the cabin.

chunks.title: Example 2 - campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: Arama intends to stay in a cabin in a commercial campsite for 30 days while she waits for her new job to start, which will provide her with long-term accommodation while she's employed. She requires assistance with moving costs to move into the cabin. As Arama intends to stay in the cabin for under 51 days, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to her accommodation arrangement. MSD can approve an Accommodation Moving Costs Grant for Arama to move into the cabin.

chunks.title: Multiple accommodation agreements — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: If a client is an occupant under multiple accommodation agreements (i.e. required to pay accommodation costs for more than one accommodation agreement), the Moving Costs Grant is only payable for the client's principal place of residence. MSD must assess their principal place of residence to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies, and whether the client is eligible for a Moving Costs Grant or Accommodation Moving Costs Grant at this accommodation. If the client and their partner have separate accommodation, they may each have a different principal place of residence. Generally, the client will determine what is their principal place of residence. If there is evidence the client is not using the property as their principal place of residence, MSD should generally decline a Moving Costs Grant. For example, if the client is using the property to store excess personal goods or sub-letting the property while living elsewhere, MSD will not pay a Moving Costs Grant. Note a grant can be paid for multiple accommodation agreements if they are for the same accommodation. For example, where a client has a rental contract for a cabin hire and a separate rental contract for the land that the cabin sits on.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: Jiang lives in accommodation in Auckland. His ex-partner lives in Hamilton and has custody of their children. Jiang visits Hamilton for four days each month to visit his children and has an accommodation agreement with a friend where he pays $150 each month to stay at their place when he visits. Jiang has not been able to pay his friend for the last three months, and his friend has said he will end the accommodation agreement if Jiang does not pay the arrears of $450. Jiang applies for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant for the accommodation agreement in Hamilton. As this is not his primary place of residence, MSD must decline the grant.

chunks.title: Accommodation is suitable to live in — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation is suitable to live in
MSD may consider whether the accommodation will be suitable for the client to live in if the grant is made.
Factors MSD may consider include (but are not limited to) if the:
- accommodation has been modified to suit the accessibility needs for the client, their partner (if any) or their dependent children (if any)
- client has access to facilities such as clean drinking water, cooking facilities, electricity, heating, beds and mattresses, toilet and bathing facilities and a food refrigerator that the client can access
- accommodation has enough bedrooms
- accommodation is fit for human habitation, including being structurally safe to live in
MSD does not need to assess if a client’s accommodation is suitable at every Moving Costs Grant assessment. However, if it is clear through the conversation with the client that the accommodation is not suitable for the client, their partner (if any) or their dependent children (if any), MSD may decline the application.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to
The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 provides rights and protections for tenants and landlords in rental agreements.
MSD can pay a Moving Costs Grant for people who are moving into accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. This includes, but is not limited to:
- rental tenancies
- boarding houses with at least 6 tenants or boarders where the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more
- service tenancies where an employer provides accommodation to an employee
- multi-unit residential housing developments to provide long-term (minimum of 10 years) rental accommodation to tenants (also known as build to rent tenancies)
- social housing (including Kainga Ora and private social housing) if the client is a tenant or a signatory
- hire agreements for relocatable homes including cabins, mobile homes and caravans where they are: hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more oron a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner
- hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or
- on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner
If you are unsure if the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to an accommodation agreement, contact Helpline or your Capability Developer.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to
An Accommodation Moving Costs Grant can be granted for clients who are moving into specific accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to.
These accommodation agreements may include, but are not limited to:
- a flat or house share agreement where the client has not signed a tenancy agreement (e.g. a flatmate that sub-lets from a head tenant)
- hire agreement for a relocatable home including a cabin, mobile home or caravan, that is on a campground for less than 51 days or on any other premises for any amount of time
- a lodging arrangement
- a boarding agreement where the client is either: in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to stay for less than 28 daysin accommodation that is not a boarding house
- in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to stay for less than 28 days
- in accommodation that is not a boarding house
- commercial accommodation such as hotels, motels, and homestays that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. This excludes the following accommodation as they are not eligible to get a Moving Costs Grant: emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Granttransitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development andcontracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development
- emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant
- transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development and
- contracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development
- an additional occupant in a social housing property that is not a tenant or a signatory on the tenancy agreement
MSD will need to assess a client’s accommodation agreement to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies.
Clients may be living in accommodation that is not included in the above list. They may still be eligible for an Accommodation Moving Costs Grant if the accommodation they are living in is not specifically excluded.

chunks.title: Assessing a Moving Costs Grant — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Assessing a Moving Costs Grant
When a client needs help with moving costs, a Moving Costs Grant should be considered if they meet the qualifications.
A Moving Costs Grant is available for people who are likely to be able to get and keep accommodation.
A Moving Costs Grant is a discretionary grant. MSD needs to consider the client's individual circumstances to determine whether the Moving Costs Grant should be granted.
In order to make a decision to grant, MSD must consider:
- the purpose of the Housing Support Programme, including whether granting a Moving Costs Grant would be the correct use of the payment
- any other financial assistance available to the client that could be used to meet their need
- whether the client and their partner (if any) could meet the need from their own resources, including accessing cash assets or receiving support from other Government agencies
- any impact on the client, their partner (if any), and their dependent children (if any) if their need is not met and
- whether the client intends to stay in the accommodation for fewer than 28 days
Depending on the client’s circumstances, MSD may also consider the following factors:
- whether the client or their partner (if any) has caused or contributed to the need for a Moving Costs Grant
- whether the client or their partner (if any) will be able to meet their essential living expenses if a Moving Costs Grant is paid
- the existing debt of the client and their partner (if any)
- whether their accommodation is suitable to live in
- any other matters MSD think are relevant
A Moving Costs Grant can be declined if a grant would not be appropriate after considering the circumstances of the client and their partner (if any) and their dependent children (if any).

chunks.title: Assessing weekly income — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Assessing weekly income
Income limits for Housing Support Products are determined based on a client’s weekly income. MSD has discretion to determine the period that weekly income relates to. When working out which period of income to use, MSD may consider:
- how much income was earned during the period
- how income the client expects to receive for that period, (e.g. investment interest was accrued but has not yet paid)
- the period for which income was received by the client
Generally, MSD will base the client and their partner’s (if any) weekly income on the average income over the previous four weeks, unless MSD considers a different timeframe is appropriate (for example the client has been earning for a shorter or longer time). This means the last four weeks of income is totalled and then divided by four.
In some cases, MSD can use a different period to calculate the weekly income period, to consider the client’s circumstances, including if the client or their spouse or partner’s income:
- has been inconsistent over the previous four weeks
- is variable week by week
- has either increased or decreased recently
- will increase or decrease in the immediate future (in the next four weeks)
- future income is uncertain, including where there is a history of the employer not paying wages or paying late
- has been earned but not paid (e.g. the client earned income but has not been paid on time).
## Example 1 - variable income
Piper works in a casual role in a supermarket. Their employment started 3 weeks ago, they have no set weekly hours and their income will change from week to week, depending on the number of hours they will work. Their employer has indicated they should receive a minimum of 20 hours work per week at $24 per hour ($480 per week) but this is not set out in Piper’s employment agreement. Piper’s 3-week income so far has been:
Week 1 = $400Week 2 = $200Week 3 = $300
In this case, Piper’s income will be estimated using the average wage over the previous three weeks as they do not have four weeks of income to assess. The calculation is:
$400 + $200 + $300 = $900$900/3 (weeks) = $300.

chunks.title: Cash asset limit — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Cash asset limit
A client and their partner (if any) cannot get a Moving Costs Grant if their assets are more than the cash asset limit.
We need to know the cash value of their assets.
There is no discretion to grant a Moving Costs Grant to a client whose cash assets (including the cash assets of their partner, if any) are above the asset limit.
For more information about what cash assets include and do not include see:
- Cash assets

chunks.title: Assets included as cash assets — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: Cash assets mean the assets of the client and their partner (if any) that can be easily converted into cash and include: - cash - bills of exchange or promissory notes - building society shares - money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society - money invested with or lent to any bank, financial institution or other person whether as a mortgage, other security, or unsecured - money withdrawn from a KiwiSaver scheme - mortgage investments and other long-term loans - the net equity held in any property or land not used as the person's home - pre-paid funeral expenses (in some circumstances) - shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds and bonds (including shares in energy organisations) and - the client's share in any partnership Note if you are unsure of a case please contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Assets not included as cash assets — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: Cash assets do not include: - the home property and land on which it is situated - a motor vehicle or other vehicle principally used by the client or their partner for their personal use (this is limited to 1 vehicle for a single person or 2 vehicles for a couple) - a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2000, or which is used by the client or a member of their family for day to day accommodation - any payments people get under Housing Support Products assistance (Moving Costs Grant, Bond Grant, Rent in Advance Grant, Rent Arrears Grant, Transition to Alternative Housing Grant, Tenancy Costs Cover, Accommodation Security Cover Grant) - Personal effects - Christchurch mosques attack support payments - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts - Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income - Māori land - MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after payment is made - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made - specified Ex gratia and compensation payments' - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received A bank overdraft is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.

chunks.title: Client caused or contributed to the need — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Client caused or contributed to the need
Before deciding whether or not to grant a Moving Costs Grant, MSD may consider the extent the client has caused or contributed to their need for moving costs.
Examples of when a client may be considered to have caused or contributed to the need for a Moving Costs Grant include when:
- they have caused or contributed to intentional or reckless damage to their previous accommodation resulting in termination of their tenancy or accommodation agreement
- they have not met their obligations for the previous accommodation, e.g. non-payment of accommodation costs, leaving without notice, additional occupants not approved by the accommodation supplier etc resulting in termination of their tenancy or accommodation agreement
Each client's situation must be assessed on their individual circumstances.

chunks.title: Clients who cannot get a Moving Costs Grant — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Clients who cannot get a Moving Costs Grant
Clients moving into one of the following accommodation agreements are not eligible for a Moving Costs grant:
- accommodation owned by the client or their spouse or partner
- tents, including those joined to a vehicle
- homeless shelters
- prisons and correctional facilities
- accommodation for which they are receiving a Emergency Housing Grant or Transitional or Contracted Emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development
There is no discretion to approve a payment for a client living in one of these accommodation agreements.

chunks.title: Clients with existing debt — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Clients with existing debt
Before deciding whether to approve a Moving Costs Grant, MSD may consider the existing debt of the client and their partner (if any).
Existing debt includes both MSD debt and non-MSD debt (if any).
A client's existing debt may impact their ability to repay a Moving Costs Grant.
When a client has existing MSD debt, MSD may consider whether it is appropriate to reduce those repayments to allow for the repayment of the Moving Costs Grant.
When a client is getting all the financial assistance they qualify for, but are not likely to be able to repay an amount paid under a Moving Costs Grant, the grant may be declined.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances
A client cannot be paid more than two Moving Costs Grants or more than $1,500 total in a 52-week period, unless MSD is satisfied there are exceptional circumstances. This includes any payments made as an Accommodation Moving Costs Grant.
Exceptional circumstances are where the circumstance:
- sets the client apart from others in a similar situation and
- is beyond the client’s control
The following situations are generally considered as exceptional circumstances:
- the client needs to move through no fault of their own, e.g: the client has been notified the owner will move back into the accommodationthe property is deemed uninhabitable due to damage (such as a burst waterpipe) and major repairs are needed.
- the client has been notified the owner will move back into the accommodation
- the property is deemed uninhabitable due to damage (such as a burst waterpipe) and major repairs are needed.
- the client was a victim of a violent crime or family violence and has had a change in their housing circumstances, e.g: needing to move to a different property following a violent crime orno longer living with their partner after seeking a protection order (including if the client remains in the same property without their partner)
- needing to move to a different property following a violent crime or
- no longer living with their partner after seeking a protection order (including if the client remains in the same property without their partner)
There may be other reasons for exceptional circumstances.

chunks.title: Impact on the client and their family — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Impact on the client and their family
When considering whether to make a Moving Costs Grant, MSD must consider the likely impacts on the client, their partner (if any), and their dependent children (if any) if the client’s accommodation need is not met.
MSD should consider what other accommodation options are available to the client if they do not get the grant.
Factors that MSD may consider include (but are not limited to) if:
- the client is likely to require emergency housing if assistance is not granted
- the client will need to stay in accommodation that is close to a perpetrator of violence if assistance is not granted
- the client will need to stay in accommodation that is near drug use or gang related activity if assistance is not granted
- the client can afford any of their other options
- there are enough bedrooms in the other accommodation
- they will be staying in suitable accommodation if they do not get the grant
- they will be a reasonable distance from work, school or essential services if assistance is not granted
- their other options meet the accessibility needs the client, their partner (if any), or their children (if any) may have
MSD must assess each client's circumstances on a case-by-case basis and determine how significant any impacts on the client's family will be.

chunks.title: Income limit — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Income limit
A client and their partner (if any) cannot get a Moving Costs Grant if their income is more than the income limit.
There is one set of income limits for all clients including those getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension, and non-beneficiaries.
For New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients MSD should check their income is not over the income limit. New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension must be included as income when assessing if the client qualifies.
There is no discretion to grant a Moving Costs Grant to a client whose income (including the income of their partner, if any) is above the income limit.
For more information about what is included as income and what is not included see:
- Core Policy Income

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Introduction
A Moving Costs Grant is a Housing Support Product for clients who need help to get accommodation. It provides recoverable assistance to help with the physical cost of moving into accommodation.
A Moving Costs Grant is a discretionary grant and can be considered for any client who meets the qualifications.
It can be used to move the furniture, appliances, personal effects and belongings of a client into accommodation.
Costs are not paid for moving items into storage, or with the cost of moving people between locations.
## Accommodation Moving Costs Grant
Clients who are not in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to will be paid an Accommodation Moving Costs Grant.
MSD will need to assess the client’s accommodation agreement to determine whether the client is in accommodation the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to.
Clients will need to meet all other eligibility criteria to receive the grant.

chunks.title: Client has more than one vehicle — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Client has more than one vehicle
When a client has more than one vehicle, you will need to assess whether the vehicles are used for private use.
Example
A family with 3 adults own 5 vehicles and all are claimed to be used for personal use. One is a vintage car used for Sunday outings and another a 4 wheel drive used on weekends only.
The 4 wheel drive and vintage car are additional to the needs of the family. Therefore, for Moving Assistance purposes, the net equity of these vehicles will need to be assessed.

chunks.title: Other financial assistance available to the client — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Other financial assistance available to the client
MSD must assess whether the client can receive other financial assistance before granting a Moving Costs Grant.
This assistance could include any one-off or ongoing payments from MSD. When a client is granted other financial assistance for moving costs, but it doesn't cover the full amount needed, MSD can consider a Moving Costs Grant for the remaining amount.
A Moving Costs Grant should not be paid for costs already paid for by any other financial assistance.
Some clients may have access to other forms of assistance. They may still be eligible for Housing Support Products but only once they have exhausted all other forms of support first. For example:
- tertiary students staying in university accommodation (e.g. Halls of Residence)
- clients in rest homes and retirement villages
- clients in institutions for the care of sick and disabled people
## Assessing additional assistance
Make sure the client is aware of all the additional financial assistance available from MSD. This could include Extra Help such as Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support and other Housing Support Products such as Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant.
Additional assistance may help reduce hardship and prevent the client from needing further assistance for housing related costs.
## Example
Saane is moving into a property and applies for a Moving Costs Grant of $400 and Rent in Advance Grant of $500. They are receiving a reduced rate of Student Allowance of $150 per week due to their parent’s income and received a scholarship payment of $750 earlier in the year. They have not accessed their Student Loan Living Costs.
MSD does not grant the payment as the student could speak to their parents for support, or access their scholarship payment to cover their moving in costs. MSD also advises the student to access their Student Loan Living Costs entitlement so that they can cover their accommodation costs going forward.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: A Moving Costs Grant is recoverable and the client must pay it back to MSD.

chunks.title: Maximum amount for a grant — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: The maximum amount payable to a client for a Moving Costs Grant is the actual costs up to $1,500 in a 52-week period, unless exceptional circumstances exist. This includes any payments made as an Accommodation Moving Costs Grant. Other economical options for moving should be considered first, such as using a friend's trailer or moving assistance from a social housing provider (for a business initiated transfer). MSD should also consider whether employment and work readiness assistance has been granted for the same move they are asking for the Moving Costs Grant.

chunks.title: Moving costs for a household — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: A Moving Costs Grant should generally be paid to one client for the moving costs of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any). A Moving Cost Grant cannot include the moving costs for other people in the client’s household. When any members of the household, including a partner and dependent children (if any), are moving to different properties, this can be regarded as separate for the purposes of a Moving Costs Grant.

chunks.title: Moving Costs Grant can be paid twice in a 52-week period — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: A Moving Costs Grant cannot be paid to a client more than twice in a 52-week period, regardless of whether the maximum amount of $1500 is granted, unless there are exceptional circumstances. This includes any payments made as an Accommodation Moving Costs Grant. When a client applies for a Moving Costs Grant, MSD must check how many Moving Costs Grants or Accommodation Moving Costs Grants the client has had in the last 52 weeks. Any Moving Costs Grants or Accommodation Moving Costs Grants in the 52-week period before the latest application are counted, including any grants paid due to exceptional circumstances. For more information see: - Exceptional circumstances

chunks.title: Transitional arrangements — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text: The Housing Support Programme, introduced on 13 March 2023, was only available to clients in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applied to. A client who was in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 did not apply to could have been assisted with accommodation support through an Advance Payment of Benefit, Recoverable Assistance Payment or Special Needs Grant. From 1 July 2024, the Housing Support Programme was expanded to include clients who are in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. Any payments a client got for moving costs before 1 July 2024, either as an Advance Payment of Benefit,, Recoverable Assistance Payment, or Special Needs Grant are not included in the grant count.

chunks.title: Pre-paid funeral expenses — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Pre-paid funeral expenses
A pre-paid funeral trust fund or account is money put aside (usually in a trust) exclusively for the payment of funeral expenses.
If the money can be accessed by the client and so used for other purposes, it is not considered exclusively for funeral expenses and can be treated as a cash asset.
It is usually clear whether a trust fund or account has been genuinely set aside for funeral expenses. Evidence it has been set aside exclusively for funeral expenses include:
- the trust fund/account is only paid out on production of a death certificate
- the client cannot usually access the funds
- if a client can access the fund, there are limited conditions on withdrawal, such as re-locating overseas
- the trust fund/account is only payable to the funeral director or administrator of the client's estate
- the client cannot generally access the interest earned from the trust fund or account
Where the trust fund or account has been set aside for funeral expenses and cannot be accessed or converted into cash, this money is not a realisable asset.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for a Moving Costs Grant a client must:
- meet the residency qualifications
- meet the income and asset limits
- be considered to be likely to obtain and retain accommodation
- be entering accommodation that is not excluded from receiving a Moving Costs Grant and
- have moving costs
While a client may qualify, the approval of a Moving Costs Grant is discretionary and should be considered according to each client's specific situation and need.

chunks.title: Recovery of payment — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Recovery of payment
Before granting a Moving Costs Grant, MSD must discuss a repayment plan with the client.
There are a variety of repayment options available to a client as listed below:
- deductions from a main benefit, Student Allowance or Working for Families assistance paid by MSD
- employer deduction notice (Client Support - Debt Management will arrange this - case managers do not have the delegation to issue a wage deduction notice)
- automatic payment from client's bank account
- internet/telebanking payment
- payment through New Zealand Post Shop
## Recovery rate
A Moving Costs Grant must have a recovery rate that means the client will pay back the debt owed within 24 months of the grant unless they have exceptional circumstances.
The rate and method of recovery must be discussed with the client, and be based on their individual circumstances and ability to live within the reduced income.
It is important the client knows the length of time the Moving Costs Grant will be repaid over.
Clients who have already been granted a Moving Costs Grant may have their recovery rate adjusted at a later date if their circumstances change.
When determining the rate of repayment by instalments MSD must consider:
- whether the instalment reductions will leave enough for the client's living expenses and any other debt repayments
- the impact on the individual (and/or their immediate family) when establishing further recoverable debt and
- the likelihood it would cause the client to seek further Housing Support Product payments or other extra help assistance

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get a Moving Costs Grant a client must:
- qualify for and be getting a main benefit or
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand at the time of their application andbe a New Zealand citizen orhold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 be recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 orqualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy, but the relationship has ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- hold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009
- be recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- qualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy, but the relationship has ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they are considered to hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other qualifications for a Moving Costs Grant.

chunks.title: Resources available to the client — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Resources available to the client
Before deciding whether or not to grant a Moving Costs Grant, MSD must consider the ability the client and their partner (if any) have to meet the cost of moving from their own resources.
If the client and their partner (if any) have resources available to them, these should generally be used to pay for their moving costs, unless this would mean they're unable to meet their essential living expenses.
Examples of a client using the resources they have available to them may include:
- using any cash assets to pay the moving costs
- accessing assistance available from other government agencies
- paying the moving costs from their next income payment due to them
Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.

chunks.title: Reviews and Appeals — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Reviews and Appeals
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have had formal notification of and disagree with a decision on their application for special assistance under the Housing Support Programme.
A client can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority when they do not agree with a decision, which was upheld or upheld in part by the Benefits Review Committee under an application for Review of Decision.
The client has the right to apply for a Review of Decision at any time within 3-months of the original decision being advised. When a client has applied for a hearing outside the 3-month time limit the Benefits Review Committee must decide whether or not to accept the application before it considers the decision under review.
A client has the right to have their decision reviewed once. If they wish to have the same decision reviewed again refer the case to Legal Services.

chunks.title: Shared moving costs — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Shared moving costs
A Moving Costs Grant generally covers the moving costs for the client and their partner and dependent children (if any) who are moving to the same property.
In situations where a client and their partner are moving into separate properties or are moving from separate properties, the client and their partner can apply for a Moving Cost Grant in their own right if required.
## Shared belongings
Shared belongings are when a client has belongings they share with another person that is not their partner or their dependent child. A Moving Costs Grant can be paid for the client’s portion of any shared belongings where this is possible to determine.
MSD can pay the full cost of moving the shared belonging if it is unclear how the item’s ownership is shared or if the items are being moved in bulk (e.g. a payment for a moving truck).
The costs of moving a shared belonging can only be paid once.
## Example
Arama and her 2 flatmates are moving into new accommodation together. They need to move a dining table that they bought together and split the costs equally.
The cost to move the dining table is $600. As Arama and her flatmates each own one third of the table, Arama is eligible for $200 of the moving cost in her Moving Cost Grant.

chunks.title: Staying in accommodation for more than 28 days — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Staying in accommodation for more than 28 days
To qualify for a Moving Costs Grant a client should intend to be staying in accommodation for at least 28 days. This is because the client should be able to keep their accommodation when a Moving Costs Grant is made.
MSD can consider granting a Moving Costs Grant when the client is staying for less than 28 days on a discretionary basis.
When a client requests a Moving Costs Grant for accommodation that they will stay in for less than 28 days, MSD should consider if:
- the client will require emergency housing if a Moving Costs Grant is not granted
- there will be an impact to the client, their partner, and/or their children if the Moving Costs Grant is not granted
- a short-term grant will make it more likely for the client to stay in accommodation long-term. For example, a boarding house owner will only accept the client for a week to see how things go before they commit to the client staying long-term
- the client has long-term accommodation arranged, but requires a short-term grant somewhere else before the accommodation is available. For example, they need to stay with their friend for 2 weeks before their rental tenancy begins
## Example 1
Ripeka has applied for an Accommodation Moving Costs Grant to move into a lodging house for 2 and a half weeks. Her previous accommodation ended as the head tenant and other flatmates are moving out and Ripeka cannot afford to rent the property on her own.
The lodging house is booked out after 2 and a half weeks so Ripeka cannot stay any longer.
Ripeka has already received 1 Moving Costs Grant in the last 52 weeks. There is no other accommodation available (including staying with family or friends temporarily), and her only alternative would be to apply for emergency housing.
MSD decides to grant the Accommodation Moving Costs Grant due to Ripeka’s circumstances, and advises her to continue looking for accommodation that she can keep.
## Example 2
Dylan is moving out of a flat in Wellington where they are a tenant because they want to move to Auckland to look for work. They apply for an Accommodation Moving Costs Grant to move into their friend’s place in Auckland for two weeks while the friend’s flatmate is on holiday.
MSD declines the Moving Costs Grant because Dylan is moving out of long-term accommodation into short term accommodation and they have contributed to the need for a grant.

chunks.title: Types of moving costs — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Types of moving costs
A Moving Costs Grant can be used to move the furniture, appliances, personal effects and personal belongings of a client into accommodation.
A Moving Costs Grant covers moving a client and their belongings from their previous accommodation and/or storage, to their new accommodation.
## Costs that can be included
The following actual and reasonable costs can be included in a Moving Costs Grant:
- trailer, van or truck hire
- petrol vouchers
- moving companies (for clients unable to assist in the move. For example, clients who are sick, injured, disabled, or elderly)
- costs related to moving a pet
Costs that are not listed above can be paid for if they are considered actual and reasonable for the client to move into the accommodation.
## Costs that cannot be included
The following costs cannot be included in a Moving Costs Grant:
- the client's personal cost of moving (for example, airfares to a new location)
- overseas relocation
- the cost of moving items into storage or between different storage units
- payment for a storage unit
- moving relocatable homes such as cabins, mobile homes, and caravans (including delivery fees)
Clients should be assessed to see if they can receive other forms of assistance for their costs that cannot be included in a Moving Costs Grant.
For example, if a client needs help with moving their relocatable home or to have it delivered, MSD can assess an Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment for the cost. The client must meet all the eligibility criteria for these payments before they can be granted.

chunks.title: Unable to meet essential living expenses — extra help > housing support products > moving costs grant
chunks.text:
## Unable to meet essential living expenses
When assessing a Moving Costs Grant, MSD may assess whether the client will be unable to meet their other essential living expenses if the assistance is paid. This includes when the client is unable to meet the essential living expenses for their partner and/or dependent children (if any).
Essential living expenses for the purposes of Housing Support Products may include, but are not limited to:
- accommodation
- food
- fuel (including petrol, diesel and oil)
- telephone costs, this may include: internet connection and mobile service charges
- internet connection and mobile service charges
- motor vehicles costs - repayment and running costs
- essential travel, this may include: employment related traveltravel when accessing essential services and supplies (including children's education and groceries)
- employment related travel
- travel when accessing essential services and supplies (including children's education and groceries)
- power
- childcare costs
- hire purchase expenses for essential household items only, it may also include employment related items. It does not include luxury items such as fishing/jet boats or small planes
- transport cost due to disability
- disability and personal health costs
- counselling
- education costs for dependent children
- clothing
Essential living expenses may vary between clients and should be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

chunks.title: Able to obtain and retain alternative housing — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Able to obtain and retain alternative housing
To qualify for Tenancy Costs Cover, MSD must consider the client is likely to be able to obtain and retain alternative housing.
MSD will need to discuss with the client whether they can afford (with any financial assistance, income and other resources available to them) to get and keep alternative housing, including the ongoing costs of the housing.
A client may be considered as being likely to get and keep alternative housing when:
- the proposed rent will generally not be over 60 per cent of their net income (and their partner's, if any), taking into account the client's individual circumstances and
- MSD has discussed the client's budget, or have other evidence showing they can manage their future outgoings

chunks.title: Tenant under a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to any tenancy with a written tenancy agreement from Tenancy Services. Some examples are a: - tenancy agreement for rental housing, including with: a private landlordlocal governmenta non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) - a private landlord - local government - a non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) or - tenancy agreement for social housing, including with a community housing provider Clients moving into this accommodation may be paid a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Flatmate or subletting without a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Clients may be living in a rental property as a flatmate or subletter without a tenancy agreement. The tenant on the tenancy agreement that the client pays their accommodation costs to takes responsibility for these clients and acts as their accommodation supplier. Flatmates generally pay any accommodation costs to the tenant instead of the landlord. This includes clients who are an additional occupant in a social housing property, as they are not on the tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these clients and clients moving into this accommodation cannot be paid a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant. These clients may be eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Service tenancies — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: A client may be provided accommodation as part of their employment where their landlord is their employer. This is known as a service tenancy. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to service tenancies. Clients in a service tenancy will generally be provided with a written tenancy agreement. Clients moving into this accommodation may be paid a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Tenancy orders — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: A tenant of a property through a tenancy order made under the Family Violence Act 2018 or Property (Relationships) Act 1976 does not need to have signed a written tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to clients in a tenancy order. These clients may be paid a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Boarding arrangements — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Clients who are boarding have an agreement for one room in the property, rather than the whole house. Boarders have access to shared facilities such as a kitchen and bathroom. When the accommodation has 6 or more occupants, this is known as a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to boarding houses when the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more. The client may be paid Tenancy Costs Cover if they have moved into this accommodation. When there are 5 or fewer occupants this is not considered a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these boarding arrangements, including private boarding where the client lives with the owner of the property. Clients in these arrangements cannot be paid Tenancy Costs Cover, even if they have been conditionally granted Tenancy Costs Cover. They may be eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant. The accommodation costs a client pays under a boarding accommodation agreement generally includes service and facility costs such as power, grounds maintenance, rubbish disposal, etc. MSD generally should not include any service costs in an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. For more information about what costs can be included in an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant, see: - Service costs and water rates

chunks.title: Example 1 – Boarding arrangement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Ngaio has an accommodation agreement to rent a room in a boarding house with 5 other people. She has her own room in the house and shares a bathroom and kitchen with other boarders. She intends to stay there for at least 6 months. Ngaio pays board which includes accommodation costs and service costs (including power, water, cleaning and rubbish disposal costs). The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to this accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: Example 2 – Boarding arrangement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Malosi is boarding with their aunt Vaima. Vaima owns the house and Malosi pays board that includes accommodation, food and service costs, including internet and power costs. Malosi and Vaima have an accommodation agreement which sets out these costs. This Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to this boarding arrangement.

chunks.title: Rent to buy — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: A client may enter into a rent to buy contract (also called a deferred payment disposition). In these situations, the client is considered to be a homeowner and cannot be paid a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Relocatable accommodation — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: A client may enter a hire agreement or a rental contract for relocatable accommodation, such as a cabin, mobile home, or caravan. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 only applies to relocatable accommodation if it is: - hired from and located on a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner Clients in this accommodation may be paid a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply if the relocatable accommodation is: - on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days or - placed on any other premises where the land and the accommodation are not owned by the same person or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner Clients in this accommodation cannot be paid Tenancy Costs Cover, even if they have been conditionally granted Tenancy Costs Cover. They may be eligible to be conditionally granted an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Example 1 – campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Rarahu intends to stay in a cabin in a commercial campsite for a minimum of 90 days. She has been conditionally granted a Tenancy Costs Cover to assist her in finding alternative housing. As Rarahu intends to stay in the cabin for 51 days or more, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to their accommodation arrangement. The Tenancy Costs Cover Grant may be paid at the end of this accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: Example 2 – campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Arama intends stay in a cabin in a commercial campsite for 30 days while she waits for her new job to start, which will provide her with long-term accommodation while she's employed. She has been conditionally granted a Tenancy Costs Cover to assist her in finding alternative housing. As Arama intends to stay in the cabin for under 51 days, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to her accommodation arrangement. MSD cannot pay a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant for this accommodation.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to
The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 provides rights and protections for tenants and landlords in rental agreements.
MSD can pay a Tenancy Costs Cover for people who are moving into accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. This includes, but is not limited to:
- rental tenancies
- boarding houses with at least 6 tenants or boarders where the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more
- service tenancies where an employer provides accommodation to an employee
- multi-unit residential housing developments to provide long-term (minimum of 10 years) rental accommodation to tenants (also known as build to rent tenancies)
- social housing (including Kainga Ora and private social housing) if the client is a tenant or a signatory
- hire agreements for relocatable homes including cabins, mobile homes and caravans where they are: hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more oron a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner
- hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or
- on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner
If you are unsure if the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to an accommodation agreement, contact Helpline or your Capability Developer.

chunks.title: Assessing Tenancy Costs Cover — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Assessing Tenancy Costs Cover
When a client needs help getting alternative housing, Tenancy Costs Cover should be considered if they meet the qualifications.
Tenancy Costs Cover is available for people who are likely to be able to keep alternative housing but require some assistance to get it.
Tenancy Costs Cover is a discretionary grant. MSD need to consider the client's individual circumstances to determine whether Tenancy Costs Cover should be granted.
In order to make a decision to grant, MSD must consider:
- the purpose of the Housing Support Programme, including whether granting Tenancy Costs Cover would be the correct use of the payment
- any other financial assistance available to the client that could be used to meet their need
- whether the client and their partner (if any) could meet the need from their own resources, including accessing cash assets or receiving support from other Government agencies
- any impact on the client, their partner (if any), and their dependent children (if any) if their need is not met and
- whether the client intends to stay in the accommodation for fewer than 28 days
Depending on the client’s circumstances, MSD may also consider the following factors:
- whether the client or their partner (if any) has caused or contributed to the need for a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant
- whether the client or their partner (if any) will be able to meet their essential living expenses if a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant is granted
- the existing debt of the client and their partner (if any)
- whether their accommodation is suitable to live in
- any other matters MSD think are relevant
Tenancy Costs Cover can be declined if a grant would not be appropriate after having considered the circumstances of the client and their partner (if any) and their dependent children (if any).

chunks.title: Client caused or contributed to their need — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Client caused or contributed to their need
Before deciding whether to grant Tenancy Costs Cover, MSD may consider the extent the client caused or contributed to their need for Tenancy Costs Cover.
Examples of when a client may be considered to have caused or contributed to the need for Tenancy Costs Cover include when the client is having difficulty obtaining alternative housing because:
- they have recently caused or contributed to intentional or reckless damage to their previous accommodation, including damage that may have resulted in termination of their tenancy(s) or accommodation agreement
- they have a pattern of not meeting their obligations for previous tenancies or accommodation agreements, e.g. not paying rent, leaving without notice, having additional occupants not approved by landlord etc
Each client's situation must be assessed on their individual circumstances.

chunks.title: Clients who cannot get Tenancy Costs Cover — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Clients who cannot get Tenancy Costs Cover
Clients moving into one of the following accommodation agreements are not eligible for Tenancy Costs Cover:
- accommodation owned by the client or their spouse or partner
- tents, including those joined to a vehicle
- homeless shelters
- prisons and correctional facilities
- accommodation for which they are receiving an Emergency Housing Grant or Transitional or Contracted Emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development
There is no discretion to approve a payment for a client living in one of these accommodation agreements.
## Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply
Clients moving into an accommodation agreement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to cannot be paid a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant.
These include, but are not limited to:
- a flat or house share agreement where the client has not signed a tenancy agreement (e.g. a flatmate that sub-lets from a head tenant)
- hire agreement for a relocatable home including a cabin, mobile home or caravan where: it is on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days oron any other premises for any amount of time where the land and accommodation are not owned by the same person oron a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner
- it is on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days or
- on any other premises for any amount of time where the land and accommodation are not owned by the same person or
- on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner
- a lodging arrangement
- a boarding agreement where the client is either: in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to and does stay for less than 28 daysin accommodation where there are less than 6 boarders
- in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to and does stay for less than 28 days
- in accommodation where there are less than 6 boarders
- commercial accommodation such as hotels, motels, and homestays that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to
- an additional occupant in a social housing property that is not a tenant or a signatory to the tenancy agreement

chunks.title: Difficulty obtaining alternative housing — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Difficulty obtaining alternative housing
