To qualify for Tenancy Costs Cover, a client must be having difficulty trying to obtain alternative housing because of their personal circumstances.
When discussing the client's situation, ask the client what is making it difficult for them to get alternative housing.
The client may identify one or more of the following personal circumstances they consider to be a barrier to them getting alternative housing (clients may have other examples):
- credit history: a client says they have a poor or limited credit history (this may include unpaid rent in the past)
- tenancy history: a client says they have a lack of references, limited tenancy history or have been through the Tenancy Tribunal or Court
- family size: e.g. number of children or 2 households looking to live together
- criminal record: of the client or their partner
- language barriers: e.g. English is not the client's first language, they speak limited English, or have other communication difficulties
- employment or social factors: e.g. the nature or hours of their employment may be seen as 'anti-social' or the number of vehicles the household owns may deter a property owner
- religion, culture, race, ethnicity, or sexual orientation
- young age: a client says their age is the reason they are unable to get a rental and thinks owners or landlords may consider young people to not be responsible tenants
- physical or mental health and/or a disability: a client is having difficulty getting suitable accommodation due to a physical or mental disability, e.g. they need modifications to a property or there is a perception of risk associated with mental health issues
- personal appearance: e.g. facial tattoos
## Options and Advice
When considering whether Tenancy Costs Cover will best meet the client's need, MSD should consider whether any of the barriers can be addressed or reduced.
Examples of this may include (but are not limited to):
- if the client is able to get a character reference from an employer or other suitable member of the community
- budget advice to remedy or demonstrate their ability to pay rent
- rent re-direction from their benefit payment
Some of the barriers faced by clients may be addressed or reduced by providing support or more information. MSD should discuss with the client the relevant housing options.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances
A client cannot get more than two payments for Tenancy Costs Cover in a 52-week period, unless MSD is satisfied there are exceptional circumstances.
When a client has Tenancy Costs Cover paid twice in the last 52 weeks, MSD should consider whether there are exceptional circumstances for another conditional grant of Tenancy Costs Cover and there is a need for the assistance.
Exceptional circumstances are where the circumstance:
- sets the client apart from others in a similar situation and
- is beyond the client's control.
The following situations are generally considered as exceptional circumstances (but not limited to):
- Tenancy Costs Cover is paid for costs that are outside of the clients control, e.g.: when damages are done by someone other than the client's household, such as a visiting friendwhen serious sickness or injury has meant the client was unable to work and/or earn their usual income and had fallen behind on their rent
- when damages are done by someone other than the client's household, such as a visiting friend
- when serious sickness or injury has meant the client was unable to work and/or earn their usual income and had fallen behind on their rent
There may be other reasons for exceptional circumstances.

chunks.title: Impact on the client and their family — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Impact on the client and their family
When considering whether to make a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant, MSD must consider the likely impacts on the client, their partner (if any), and their dependent children (if any) if the client's accommodation need is not met.
MSD should consider what other accommodation or options are available to the client if they do not get the grant.
Factors that MSD may consider include (but are not limited to) if:
- the client is likely to require emergency housing if assistance is not granted
- the client will need to stay in accommodation that is close to a perpetrator of violence if assistance is not granted
- the client will need to stay in accommodation that is near drug use or gang related activity if assistance is not granted
- the client can afford any of their other options
- there are enough bedrooms in the other accommodation
- they will be staying in suitable accommodation if they do not get the grant
- they will be a reasonable distance from work, school or essential services if assistance is not granted
- their other options meet the accessibility needs the client, their partner (if any), or their children (if any) may have
MSD must assess each client's circumstances on a case-by-case basis and determine how significant any impacts on the client's family will be.
## Example
Jacob is currently staying on a friend's couch due to recently being released from prison. His friend lives in an area with gang activity.
Jacob is looking for alternative housing where he is away from the gang activity and where he can have his children stay with him on the weekends to meet his custody arrangements. He is facing difficulty getting accommodation due to his previous imprisonment.
Jacob applies for a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant to assist him in getting alternative housing.
MSD determines that there will be an impact on the client and his family if he is not able to get alternative housing. MSD conditionally grants a Tenancy Costs Cover.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Tenancy Costs Cover provides support for clients who are having difficulty getting housing due to their personal circumstances.
Tenancy Costs Cover is a conditional grant providing landlords with an assurance that the client will be able to meet any tenancy related costs over and above the bond (up to a maximum amount), if owed at the end of the tenancy.
Tenancy Costs Cover cannot be paid to the landlord or their agent until all the conditions of the grant are met.
Tenancy Costs Cover is paid to the landlord or their agent. However, the client must pay the amount of any Tenancy Costs Cover back to MSD.
## Residential Tenancies Act 1986
Tenancy Costs Cover is only available to clients who are in an accommodation agreement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to.
Clients entering accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to may be eligible for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant.

chunks.title: Other financial assistance available to the client — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Other financial assistance available to the client
MSD must assess whether the client can receive other financial assistance before granting a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant.
This assistance could include any one-off or ongoing payments from MSD.
Some clients may have access to other forms of assistance. They may still be eligible for Housing Support Products but only once they have exhausted all other forms of support first.
For example:
- tertiary students staying in university accommodation (e.g. Halls of Residence)
- clients in rest homes and retirement villages
- clients in institutions for the care of sick and disabled people

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Tenancy Costs Cover can be claimed if, at the end of the tenancy, the client owes their former landlord (or the landlord's agent) tenancy costs not covered by their bond amount. The client must pay back any costs paid under Tenancy Costs Cover to MSD.

chunks.title: Maximum amount of costs payable — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: The maximum amount of tenancy costs payable is equal to 4 weeks rent based on the rent agreed at the start of the tenancy. Payment is calculated as total costs, less 4 weeks bond, up to 4 weeks rent. Example The maximum amount payable based on rent of $350 per week is $1,400. Total costs claimed by landlord $4,000 Less four 4 weeks bond (already paid by client) $1,400 Balance of costs owing by client $2,600 Tenancy Costs Cover payable (equivalent to 4 weeks rent) $1,400 Remaining costs not covered (landlord needs to claim these directly from client) $1,200

chunks.title: Tenancy Costs Cover can be paid twice in a 52-week period — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Tenancy Costs Cover cannot be paid more than twice in a 52-week period to a client, unless exceptional circumstances exist. When a client applies for Tenancy Costs Cover, MSD must check how many Tenancy Costs Cover grants have been paid in the last 52 weeks. Any Tenancy Costs Cover grants paid in the 52-week period before the latest application are counted, including any Tenancy Costs Cover claims paid due to exceptional circumstances. If a client gets more than one payment under a conditional grant of Tenancy Costs Cover in a 52-week period, they can get up to the maximum amount for each grant.

chunks.title: Payments made on or after 13 March 2023 for Tenancy Costs Cover conditionally granted before 13 March 2023 — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: When a client has been conditionally granted Tenancy Costs Cover before 13 March 2023 (under the former Housing Support Assistance Programme) and that grant is paid on or after 13 March 2023, the payment is not included in the grant count of the client under the Housing Support Programme. Tenancy Costs Cover that was conditionally granted under the former Housing Support Assistance Programme must be paid under the conditions of that former programme.

chunks.title: Payments made under other forms of assistance — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: The Housing Support Programme, introduced on 13 March 2023, was only available to clients in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to. A client who was in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to could have been assisted with accommodation support through an Advance Payment of Benefit, Recoverable Assistance Payment, or Special Needs Grant. From 1 July 2024, the Housing Support Programme was expanded to include clients who are in accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. Any payments a client got for outstanding accommodation costs and expenses before 1 July 2024 either as an Advance Payment of Benefit, Recoverable Assistance Payment or Special Needs Grant are not included in the grant count.

chunks.title: Paying the client in exceptional circumstances — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: A payment under Tenancy Costs Cover can only be paid to the client's former landlord or their agent (e.g. a property manager) unless the Ministry is satisfied exceptional circumstances exist. If exceptional circumstances exist, MSD may pay Tenancy Costs Cover to the client's payment card or directly to the client.

chunks.title: Initial 6 month period - to enter into a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Tenancy Costs Cover is a conditional grant. MSD will provide the client a Tenancy Costs Cover letter of assurance to show to potential landlords, which is valid for 6 months from the date it is issued. As one of the grant’s conditions, the client must enter into a tenancy agreement for housing within the 6 month period. If the client has been unable to get a tenancy within 6 months, the conditional grant of Tenancy Costs Cover will end (lapse). The client will need to reapply if they need Tenancy Costs Cover again. There is no limit on how many times a client can be conditionally granted Tenancy Costs Cover in a 52-week period. However, if the client has already received 2 payments under Tenancy Costs Cover within a 52-week period, they cannot get another conditional grant of Tenancy Costs Cover within that period, unless there are exceptional circumstances.

chunks.title: Cover period for tenancy up to 24 months — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Tenancy Costs Cover covers the first 24 months of the tenancy, and expires at the end of the 24-month period. If the tenancy goes beyond the 24-month period of cover, no costs can be claimed under Tenancy Costs Cover. There is no discretion to extend this cover period. Tenancy Costs Cover remains conditionally granted throughout the cover period. If a fixed-term tenancy is for fewer than 24 months but gets extended, the Tenancy Costs Cover can continue up to 24 months in total from the start of the first fixed-term tenancy. The extension must be a continuation of the same tenancy the Tenancy Costs Cover was conditionally granted for, however any rent or bond increase will not increase the amount of Tenancy Costs Cover that can be claimed. If a fixed-term tenancy ends within 24 months, and the client moves to another rental property with a fixed-term tenancy, the Tenancy Costs Cover ends. For Tenancy Costs Cover to apply to the new fixed-term tenancy, the client would need to meet the qualifications and be conditionally granted Tenancy Costs Cover prior to entering the tenancy.

chunks.title: End of Tenancy Costs Cover after 24 months — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: If the tenancy continues past the 24 month period of cover, then the Tenancy Costs Cover will end (lapse), and claims for costs can no longer be made. There is no discretion to extend this cover period.

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Any change in the client's circumstances after a tenancy starts will not affect the terms of the Tenancy Costs Cover conditionally granted for that tenancy.

chunks.title: Period to claim payment under Tenancy Costs Cover — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: A payment under Tenancy Costs Cover can be claimed if, at the end of the tenancy, the client owes their former landlord (or the landlord's agent) tenancy costs that are not covered by their bond.

chunks.title: 3-month period to claim costs — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: The client or the landlord generally has up to 3 months from the end of the tenancy to make a claim to MSD for tenancy costs. However, the claim period may be extended in certain circumstances. Claims for payment under Tenancy Costs Cover can only be made for tenancies that end within 24 months. If MSD approves a claim for payment, it is paid to the client's landlord (or the landlord's agent, e.g. a property manager). However, if MSD is satisfied exceptional circumstances exist, the claim can be paid directly to the client.

chunks.title: Extending claim period if a decision has not been made — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: An accommodation supplier or the client can dispute whether the client is responsible for the outstanding accommodation costs and expenses through the Tenancy Tribunal or court. If a claim has been lodged but a decision has not been made, the 3-month claim period may be extended. An extension of the claim period cannot be made for any other reason. A client or their accommodation supplier must contact MSD before the 3-month period ends to request an extension. If no contact is made, the grant ends (lapses) and there is no discretion to extend the 3-month period. Each case and extension must be looked at on its own circumstances.

chunks.title: Example – 3-month extension — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Logan was conditionally granted a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant. He enters a rental tenancy due to having a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant. He stays in the accommodation for 10 months before moving to new accommodation. His accommodation supplier wants to make a claim for damages but Logan does not agree that he is responsible for them. The accommodation supplier lodges a claim with the Tenancy Tribunal that Logan should be responsible for these costs. After 2 and a half months, the accommodation supplier contacts MSD to request an extension to the three-month claim period as the Tenancy Tribunal has not resolved this. MSD grants a three-month extension. After 3 months, there is still not progress on the Tenancy Tribunal claim as Logan hasn’t been contactable. The accommodation supplier contacts MSD for another extension. MSD grants the second and final three-month extension. The Tenancy Tribunal makes the verdict that Logan is responsible for the damages 8 months after Logan left the property. The accommodation supplier contacts MSD with the Tenancy Tribunal claim, and MSD grants the Tenancy Costs Cover Grant to pay for the damages.

chunks.title: Client agrees to part of the outstanding accommodation costs — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Sometimes a client may agree with the accommodation supplier that they owe a part, but not all, of the outstanding tenancy costs that the accommodation supplier wants to charge the client. In these cases, MSD can approve the costs that are agreed by the client. Any additional outstanding costs will need to either be agreed by the client and accommodation supplier or a sealed Tenancy Mediator's Order, or Tenancy Tribunal Order or court order would need to be provided by the client or accommodation supplier.

chunks.title: Who can lodge a claim — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Generally, a client or their agent will need to be the person to contact MSD to request that their Tenancy Costs Cover be paid out. Their accommodation supplier cannot request that MSD pay the claim unless there is a sealed Tenancy Mediator's Order, Tenancy Tribunal Order or court order confirming that the client is responsible for the costs.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for Tenancy Costs Cover a client must:
- meet the residence qualifications
- be considered likely to retain alternative housing but requires some assistance to get it
- have taken reasonable steps to find alternative housing
- have difficulty obtaining housing because of their personal circumstances
- intend to be a tenant with a tenancy agreement covered by the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 and requires a bond payment
## Income and asset limits
There are no income or cash asset limits for Tenancy Costs Cover.
While a client may qualify, the approval of Tenancy Costs Cover is discretionary and should be considered according to each client's specific situation and need.

chunks.title: Reasonable steps to find alternative housing — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Reasonable steps to find alternative housing
Tenancy Costs Cover provides support for clients who have difficulty getting alternative housing due to their personal circumstances.
To qualify for Tenancy Costs Cover a client must have taken reasonable steps to find alternative housing before applying for this assistance.
## Examples of reasonable steps
Reasonable steps to find alternative housing, may include (but are not limited to), the client:
- applying for rental properties
- going to rental property viewings
- registering with a rental agency and/or housing broker
- taking steps to address any barriers they have, such as a character reference from an employer or other suitable member of the community
MSD must decline a Tenancy Costs Cover when the client has not taken reasonable steps to find alternative housing before applying for the assistance.
MSD should discuss with the client the relevant housing options and support services available to them, e.g. referral to a housing broker or community provider.

chunks.title: Recovery of payment — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Recovery of payment
Once a Tenancy Costs Cover payment is made to the landlord, you must discuss a repayment plan with the client.
The client has a variety of repayment options available as listed below:
- deductions from a main benefit, Student Allowance or Working for Families assistance paid by MSD
- employer deduction notice (Client Support – Debt Management will arrange this - case managers cannot issue a wage deduction notice)
- automatic payment from the client's bank account
- internet/telebanking payment
- payment through New Zealand Post Shop
## Recovery rate
Tenancy Costs Cover must have a recovery rate that means the client will pay back the debt owed within 24 months of the grant unless they have exceptional circumstances.
The rate and method of recovery must be discussed with the client, and be based on their individual circumstances and ability to live within the reduced income.
It is important the client knows the length of time the Tenancy Costs Cover will be repaid over.
Clients who have already been granted Tenancy Costs Cover may have their recovery rate adjusted at a later date if their circumstances change.
When determining the rate of repayment by instalments MSD must consider:
- whether the instalment reductions will leave enough for the client's living expenses and any other debt repayments
- the impact on the individual (and/or their immediate family) when establishing further recoverable debt and
- the likelihood it would cause the client to seek further Housing Support Product payments or other extra help assistance

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get Tenancy Costs Cover assistance a client must:
- qualify for and be getting a main benefit or
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand at the time of application and: be a New Zealand citizen orhold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 orbe recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 orqualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy but the relationship has ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- hold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- qualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy but the relationship has ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they are considered to hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand at the time of their application for Tenancy Costs Cover and meet all other qualifications.

chunks.title: Reviews and Appeals — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Reviews and Appeals
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have received formal notification of and disagree with a decision on their application for special assistance under the Housing Support Programme.
A client can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority where they do not agree with a decision, which was upheld or upheld in part by the Benefits Review Committee under an application for Review of Decision.
The client has the right to apply for a Review of Decision at any time within three months of the original decision being advised. When a client has applied for a hearing outside the three month time limit the Benefits Review Committee must decide whether or not to accept the application before it considers the decision under review.
A client has the right to have their decision reviewed once. If they wish to have the same decision reviewed again refer the case to Legal Services.

chunks.title: Service costs and water rates — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Service costs and water rates
Sometimes a client’s accommodation costs include service costs such as electricity or an internet connection.
Service costs do not include water rates.
Service costs cannot be included in the accommodation costs for a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant. Only the portion of the costs that relates to their accommodation can be included in a Tenancy Costs Cover Grant.
Generally the service costs and cost of accommodation will be itemised separately on the tenancy agreement. Use the accommodation cost only to calculate Tenancy Costs Cover.
## Water rates
When a client's rent includes water rates (also referred to as water charges), the portion of costs that relates to the water rates can be included for Tenancy Costs Cover if:
- the accommodation has a separate water meter and
- the accommodation agreement states the client is responsible for this cost
Note: Water rates do not include the cost of filling water tanks.

chunks.title: Tenancy Costs Cover letter — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: When a client gets a conditional grant of Tenancy Costs Cover, MSD will give them a Tenancy Costs Cover letter of assurance. Clients can show the letter to potential landlords to assist them in getting a tenancy. The letter explains what Tenancy Costs Cover is and shows the client has been approved for financial assistance from MSD to help pay outstanding costs above their bond amount at the end of the tenancy. It also explains what both the landlord and client need to do to meet the conditions of the Tenancy Costs Cover grant. Tenancy Costs Cover cannot be paid to the landlord (or their agent) unless all the conditions of the grant are met. An approved Tenancy Costs Cover Grant only applies to a tenancy that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to.

chunks.title: Conditions of Tenancy Costs Cover — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: The conditions of Tenancy Costs Cover are: At the start of the tenancy - the client, either alone or with other people, has entered into a tenancy agreement for housing that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to within 6 months from the date of the Tenancy Costs Cover letter and - the landlord (or their agent) has entered into the tenancy agreement because the client has Tenancy Costs Cover and - the client, either alone or with other people, has paid a bond that is the same amount as 4 weeks' rent for the housing (using the rent amount agreed to at the start of the tenancy) and - the client or landlord (or their agent) has given MSD a copy of the tenancy agreement and a receipt for the bond At the end of the tenancy - the tenancy has ended within 24 months after it started and - the client owes the landlord for tenancy costs over and above the bond paid at the start of the tenancy and - the client or landlord has claimed payment of the tenancy costs within 3 months of the end of the tenancy (unless they qualify to extend the claim period) and - MSD has the supporting evidence it needs to decide whether to pay the claim

chunks.title: Client must agree to the costs claimed, or there is an order for costs — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: Even if all of the conditions are met, MSD can only pay a claim for payment under Tenancy Costs Cover when: - the client agrees with the amount of costs claimed or - there is a sealed Tenancy Mediator's Order, Tenancy Tribunal Order or Court order confirming the client must pay the costs

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: The conditions of Tenancy Costs Cover are not affected by a change in the client’s circumstances after the tenancy has started.

chunks.title: Number of times a client can be conditionally granted Tenancy Costs Cover — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text: There is no limit on how many times a client can be conditionally granted Tenancy Costs Cover in a 52-week period unless: - the client has already received 2 payments under Tenancy Costs Cover within a 52-week period and - there are no exceptional circumstances to justify another conditional grant of Tenancy Costs Cover during that same 52-week period

chunks.title: Tenancy costs not covered — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Tenancy costs not covered
Tenancy Costs Cover does not cover any tenancy costs that:
- the client doesn't agree with (unless there is a sealed Tenancy Mediator's Order, Tenancy Tribunal Order or Court order confirming the client must pay the costs), and/or
- can be fully covered by the client's bond, and/or
- relate to a tenancy that has not ended
Costs that cannot be claimed under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 are not covered by the Tenancy Costs Cover.
If a client is unsure about the costs a landlord is claiming they should be referred to Tenancy Services for advice.

chunks.title: Types of tenancy costs covered — extra help > housing support products > tenancy costs cover
chunks.text:
## Types of tenancy costs covered
Tenancy Costs Cover covers tenancy costs the client must pay their landlord at the end of their tenancy, if there are costs not covered (or only partially covered) by the client's bond.
Tenancy costs are any costs the landlord can claim under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 and include:
- any costs in a sealed Tenancy Mediator's Order, or Tenancy Tribunal Order or court order
- rent arrears
- damages to the property or chattels
- rubbish removal or cleaning costs incurred by the landlord after the client has moved out of the property
- missing chattels
- change of locks or replacement keys, when lost by the client
- an insurance excess if it is less than the tenancy costs

chunks.title: Able to obtain and retain alternative housing — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text:
## Able to obtain and retain alternative housing
To qualify for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant, MSD must consider whether the client is likely to be able to obtain and retain alternative housing.
MSD will need to discuss with the client whether they are likely to afford (with any financial assistance, income and other resources available to them) to get and keep the alternative housing, including the ongoing costs of the alternative housing.
A client may be considered as being likely to get and keep alternative housing when:
- the proposed rent will generally not be over 60 per cent of their (and their partner's, if any) net income (taking into account the client's individual circumstances) and
- MSD has discussed the client's budget, or has other evidence showing they can manage their future outgoings

chunks.title: Tenant under a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text: The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to any tenancy with a written tenancy agreement from Tenancy Services. Some examples are a: - tenancy agreement for rental housing, including with: a private landlordlocal governmenta non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) - a private landlord - local government - a non-government organisation (this may include housing offered by a registered community housing provider that is not contracted for social housing purposes) or - tenancy agreement for social housing, including with a community housing provider Clients moving into this accommodation may be eligible for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Flatmate or subletting without a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text: Clients may be living in a rental property as a flatmate or subletter without a tenancy agreement. The tenant on the tenancy agreement that the client pays their accommodation costs to takes responsibility for these clients and acts as their accommodation supplier. Flatmates generally pay any accommodation costs to the tenant instead of the landlord. This includes clients who are an additional occupant in a social housing property, as they are not on the tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these clients and a client moving out of social housing to sublet or be a flatmate is not eligible to receive a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Service tenancies — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text: A client may be provided accommodation as part of their employment where their landlord is their employer. This is known as a service tenancy. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to service tenancies. Clients in a service tenancy will generally be provided with a written tenancy agreement. Clients moving into a service tenancy may be eligible for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Tenancy orders — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text: A tenant of a property through a tenancy order made under the Family Violence Act 2018 or Property (Relationships) Act 1976 does not need to have signed a written tenancy agreement. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to clients in a tenancy order. These clients may be eligible for a Transitional to Alternative Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Boarding arrangements — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text: Clients who are boarding have an agreement for one room in the property, rather than the whole house. Boarders have access to shared facilities such as a kitchen and bathroom. When the accommodation has 6 or more occupants, this is known as a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to boarding houses when the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more. A client moving into a boarding house may be eligible for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant if they intend to stay for 28 days or more When there are 5 or fewer occupants this is not considered a boarding house. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to these boarding arrangements, including private boarding where the client lives with the owner of the property. Clients moving into these arrangements are not eligible for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant. The accommodation costs a client pays under a boarding accommodation agreement generally includes service and facility costs such as power, grounds maintenance, rubbish disposal, etc.

chunks.title: Example 2 – Boarding arrangement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text: Malosi is boarding with their aunt Vaima. Vaima owns the house and Malosi pays board that includes accommodation, food and service costs, including internet and power costs. Malosi and Vaima have an accommodation agreement which sets out these costs. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to this boarding agreement.

chunks.title: Rent to buy — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text: A client may enter into a rent to buy contract (also called a deferred payment disposition). In these situations, the client is considered to be a homeowner and is not eligible for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Relocatable accommodation — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text: A client may enter a hire agreement or a rental contract for relocatable accommodation, such as a cabin, mobile home, or caravan. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 only applies to relocatable accommodation if it is: - hired from and located on a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner Clients moving into this accommodation may be eligible for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant. The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply if the relocatable accommodation is: - on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days or - placed on any other premises where the land and the accommodation are not owned by the same person or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner Clients moving into this accommodation are not eligible for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Example 1 – campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text: Rarahu intends to stay in a cabin in a commercial campsite for a minimum of 90 days. She has applied for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant. As Rarahu intends to stay in the cabin for 51 days or more, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to their accommodation arrangement. MSD can approve a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Example 2 – campsite accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 doesn’t apply to — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text: Arama intends to stay in a cabin in a commercial campsite for 30 days while she waits for her new job to start, which will provide her with long-term accommodation while she's employed. She applied for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant. As Arama intends to stay in the cabin for under 51 days, the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to her accommodation arrangement. MSD cannot grant a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text:
## Accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to
The Residential Tenancies Act 1986 provides rights and protections for tenants and landlords in rental agreements.
MSD can pay a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant for people who are moving into accommodation that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to.
This includes, but is not limited to:
- rental tenancies
- boarding houses with at least 6 tenants or boarders where the client intends to or does stay for 28 days or more
- service tenancies where an employer provides accommodation to an employee
- multi-unit residential housing developments to provide long-term (minimum of 10 years) rental accommodation to tenants (also known as build to rent tenancies)
- social housing (including Kainga Ora and private social housing) if the client is a tenant or a signatory
- hire agreements for relocatable homes including cabins, mobile homes and caravans where they are: hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more oron a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner
- hired from and located in a campground and the client intends to stay for 51 days or more or
- on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are not shared with the owner
If you are unsure if the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to an accommodation agreement, contact Helpline or your Capability Developer.

chunks.title: Clients who cannot get a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text: Clients do not qualify for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant if they have: - previously been paid a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant or - been found to be no longer eligible for social housing following a tenancy review or - been given notice to terminate their social housing tenancy (on or before the date MSD got their application for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant) A client living in the same household as someone who had previously been paid a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant, may qualify for this grant if it hasn't been paid to them before. The whole household must still move out of the social housing.

chunks.title: Excluded accommodation agreements — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text: Clients living in one of the following accommodation agreements are not eligible for Transition to Alternative Housing: - accommodation owned by the client or their spouse or partner - tents, including those joined to a vehicle - homeless shelters - prisons and correctional facilities - accommodation for which they are receiving an Emergency Housing Grant or Transitional or Contracted Emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development. There is no discretion to approve a payment for a client living in one of these accommodation agreements.

chunks.title: Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text: Clients moving into an accommodation agreement that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to cannot receive a Transitional to Alternative Housing Grant. These include, but are not limited to: - a flat or house share agreement where the client has not signed a tenancy agreement (e.g. a flatmate that sub-lets from a head tenant) - hire agreement for a relocatable home including a cabin, mobile home or caravan where: it is on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days, oron any other premises for any amount of time where the land and accommodation are not owned by the same person oron a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner - it is on a campground and the client intends to stay for less than 51 days, or - on any other premises for any amount of time where the land and accommodation are not owned by the same person or - on a property where both the land and accommodation are owned by the same person and facilities are shared with the owner - a lodging arrangement - a boarding agreement where the client is either: in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to and does stay for less than 28 daysin accommodation where there are less than 6 boarders - in a boarding house with 6 or more boarders but the client intends to and does stay for less than 28 days - in accommodation where there are less than 6 boarders - commercial accommodation such as hotels, motels, and homestays that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 does not apply to. This includes the following accommodation: emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Granttransitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development andcontracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - emergency housing funded by an Emergency Housing Grant - transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development and - contracted emergency housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - an additional occupant in a social housing property that is not a tenant or a signatory to the tenancy agreement

chunks.title: Conditional grant — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text:
## Conditional grant
A Transition to Alternative Housing Grant is a conditional grant, and cannot be paid to applicant(s) until:
- the applicant, and any other tenants of the social housing, have voluntarily agreed with MSD and their social housing provider to end their social housing tenancy and
- the tenancy has ended and
- all occupants have moved out of the social housing and
- the applicant(s) who have been granted the conditional grant have moved to alternative housing within 6 months after the date MSD got their application for the Transition to Alternative Housing Grant

chunks.title: Information on a tenancy agreement — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text:
## Information on a tenancy agreement
When it is unclear whether a document is a tenancy agreement under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 or not, below is a list of information that is usually part of this type of agreement:
- the full name and contact address of the landlord
- the landlord’s contact mobile telephone number (if any)
- the landlord’s contact email address (if any)
- the full name and contact address (when different from the address of the premises to which the agreement relates) of the tenant
- the tenant’s contact mobile telephone number (if any)
- the tenant’s contact email address (if any)
- the address of the premises
- the date of the tenancy agreement
- the date of commencement of the tenancy (when different from the date of the tenancy agreement)
- the landlord’s address for service
- the tenant’s address for service
- whether the tenant is under the age of 18
- the amount of any bond
- the rent payable
- the frequency of the rent payments
- the place or bank account number where the rent is to be paid
- a list of any chattels provided by the landlord
- if the tenancy is a fixed-term tenancy, the date on which the term will expire
- Healthy Homes compliance statement
- insulation statement
- insurance statement
The agreement should be signed by both parties but if it's not signed, it may still be a valid agreement. In these cases, MSD can use other evidence to determine there is an agreement in place. For example, bank account statement showing rent payments.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text:
## Introduction
A Transition to Alternative Housing Grant is a one off, non-recoverable payment to encourage social housing tenants, who are ready and able to rent in the private housing market, to move out of social housing and into alternative housing.
A Transition to Alternative Housing Grant is a conditional grant, which means it cannot be paid until all of the conditions of the grant have been met.
The Transition to Alternative Housing Grant is an incentive payment. It is not intended to meet the costs of moving out of social housing or into alternative housing, e.g. relocation costs or bond.
Clients may qualify for other financial assistance for these costs, such as a Moving Costs Grant, Bond Grant, or Rent in Advance Grant.
## Residential Tenancies Act 1986
A Transition to Alternative Housing Grant is only available to clients who are entering accommodation agreements that the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 applies to.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text:
## Payment
A Transition to Alternative Housing Grant is a one-off, non-recoverable grant of $3,000.
This grant is paid to the named client on the tenancy agreement who meet the qualifications.
A maximum time limit of 6 months will apply to the conditional grant of a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant.
The payment will only be processed after the client(s) and their household/occupants (if any) have moved out of the social housing property and into alternative housing within 6 months.
The property must be available for other people on the social housing register.
## More than one tenant (signatory) on the tenancy agreement
Transition to Alternative Housing Grant can only be paid to the qualifying signatory on the tenancy agreement.
If there is more than one signatory on the tenancy agreement, the Transition to Alternative Housing Grant should only be shared equally between the qualifying signatories.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant the applicant(s) must:
- meet the residential qualifications
- be a current tenant (signatory) on a tenancy agreement with a social housing provider
- be considered likely to be able to obtain and retain alternative housing
- be moving out of social housing voluntarily (as agreed with the social housing provider and MSD)
Note there are clients who cannot get a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant. For more information see: Clients who cannot get a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant
There are no income or cash asset limits for Transition to Alternative Housing Grant.
A Transition to Alternative Housing Grant is a conditional grant, and all the conditions of the grant must be met before it can be paid.
MSD must grant Transition to Alternative Housing if a client applies for it and is eligible to be paid. There is no discretion required when deciding to make a grant.

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant a client must:
- qualify for and be getting a main benefit or
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand at the time of their application and be a New Zealand citizen orhold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 orbe recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 orqualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with the intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy, but the relationship ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- hold or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- qualify for and be getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary visa with the intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy, but the relationship ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support)
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they are considered to hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they apply for a Transition to Alternative Housing Grant and meet all other qualifications.

chunks.title: Reviews and Appeals — extra help > housing support products > transition to alternative housing grant
chunks.text:
## Reviews and Appeals
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have had formal notification of and disagree with a decision on their application for assistance under the Housing Support Programme.
A client can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority when they do not agree with a decision, which was upheld or upheld in part by the Benefits Review Committee under an application for Review of Decision.
The client has the right to apply for a Review of Decision at any time within 3 months of the original decision being advised. When a client has applied for a hearing outside the 3-month time limit the Benefits Review Committee must decide whether or not to accept the application before it considers the decision under review.
A client has the right to have their decision reviewed once. If they wish to have the same decision reviewed again refer the case to Legal Services.

chunks.title: Clients who cannot get in-work tax credit — extra help > in work tax credit
chunks.text:
## Clients who cannot get in-work tax credit
A client (and their partner, if they have one) cannot get the in-work tax credit if the client or their partner get any of the ‘specified payments’ below:
Income-tested benefits
Student support
Certain veterans' assistance paid under Veterans' Support Act 2014
- Jobseeker Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Sole Parent Support
- Youth Payment
- Young Parent Payment
- Emergency Benefit
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance
- Payments granted under clauses 9 or 11 of the COVID-19 New Zealanders Stranded Overseas Support Programme
- Student Allowance
- Independent Circumstances Allowance
- Parent's Allowance
- Children's pension
Note clients getting Orphan’s Benefit, Unsupported Child’s Benefit, Foster Care Allowance, New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran's Pension or weekly compensation from Veterans’ Affairs New Zealand can get the in-work tax credit, as long as the client or their partner does not also get one of the payments in the table above.

chunks.title: Grace period for in-work tax credit — extra help > in work tax credit
chunks.text: From 1 April 2021, people getting the in-work tax credit can continue to get it for a grace period of up to 2 weeks when their employment ends or they are taking an unpaid break from work. Situations covered by the grace period include: - people whose employment has ended (for whatever reason) - people taking unpaid leave (ie not earning income) but who remain employed - teacher aides and other support staff in schools or universities who are unpaid during school holidays (as they are employed only during the school term) It does not include people who have stopped work because they are on paid parental leave, or getting ACC weekly compensation (including survivor payments), as they can still get the in-work tax credit. Note there is no limit on the number of grace periods a person can get in a year, as long as they meet the qualifications each time.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > in work tax credit
chunks.text: During the grace period, the person can continue getting their in-work tax credit paid by Inland Revenue at the same rate as their most recent in-work tax credit payment. If there has been a change of circumstances during the grace period, eg new partner or child, Inland Revenue will reassess the in-work tax credit amount. Any in-work tax credit payments paid during a grace period are chargeable income for Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Client is granted a specified payment — extra help > in work tax credit
chunks.text: If a client is granted a specified payment and the commencement date is within the: - first week of the grace period, they will not qualify for any in-work tax credit payments during the grace period - second week of the grace period, they only qualify for an in-work tax credit payment during the first week of the grace period. If the specified payment is backdated to a date that falls within the grace period, Inland Revenue may create a debt for any in-work tax credit payments the client got (but no longer qualifies for) during the grace period. If the client was getting Temporary Additional Support during this period, it must be reviewed to remove the in-work tax credit as chargeable income for any period the client didn’t qualify for in-work tax credit.

chunks.title: Paying in-work tax credit during an initial stand-down — extra help > in work tax credit
chunks.text: If a client is getting a main benefit, they do not qualify for in-work tax credit. However, a client may qualify for in-work tax credit during an initial stand-down if they qualify for an in-work tax credit grace period. This only applies when the grace period and the initial stand-down period cross over. Note in-work tax credit cannot be paid after the benefit commencement date.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > in work tax credit
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The in-work tax credit is paid by Inland Revenue to low-income working families with dependent children.
There are no minimum hours of work required to get this payment (from 1 July 2020).
Working families can get up to $97.50 a week for the first 3 children (total) and up to $15.00 extra per week for each additional child.
In-work tax credit is chargeable income for Temporary Additional Support.
Note the in-work tax credit was known as the in-work payment before 1 April 2007.

chunks.title: Orphans Benefit and Unsupported Childs Benefit products — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products
chunks.text:
## Orphans Benefit and Unsupported Childs Benefit products
The following additional assistance is available to caregivers who meet specific qualifications, and are getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit:
- Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported childrenThe Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children provides weekly financial assistance to caregivers, to help meet the costs of clothing, a travel bag, and school uniforms for the child, or children, in the caregiver’s care. These non-taxable payments are made automatically.
- Establishment GrantThe Establishment Grant is a one-off, non-recoverable payment to caregivers who meet the qualifications for Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit. The non-taxable payment helps towards the upfront cost of items such as bed or bedding. It is paid automatically when Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is approved.
- Extraordinary Care FundThe Extraordinary Care Fund provides non-recoverable financial assistance to caregivers who are caring for a child who is experiencing difficulties that have a sufficient impact on their development or a child who is showing promise. Clients must apply for this non-taxable assistance.
- Holiday Allowance and Birthday AllowanceHoliday Allowance and Birthday Allowance are annual payments to help with the costs of preparing a celebration, purchasing gifts, or planning an event or experience for the child, or children, in the caregiver's care.The non-taxable payment is generally made automatically.
- School and Year Start-up PaymentThe School and Year Start-up Payment provides non-recoverable financial assistance to assist with school related costs or other costs relating to the care of the child at the start of each year. Clients must apply for this non-taxable assistance.

chunks.title: Advance Payment of Benefits and Special Needs Grants — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Advance Payment of Benefits and Special Needs Grants
Caregivers are able to receive other payments from time to time (Advance Payment of Benefits and Special Needs Grants) where reasonable, to pay for additional clothing requirements when they meet the qualifications.
Example a teenager loses their school shoes, and the caregiver provides them with a new pair out of the Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children. Three weeks later the teenager leaves that second pair at rugby practice. In this situation it is reasonable for a caregiver, with limited financial options, to apply for an Advance Payment of Benefit to cover the cost of another new pair of shoes, if they don’t have the available resources.
Note the time of the year must also be taken into consideration. If the application is between January – February, advise the carer to apply for the School and Year Start-Up Payment instead as they don’t have to pay that back.
See:
- Extra help School and Year Start-Up

chunks.title: Bank account — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Bank account
Unless there are special circumstances, it is a condition of every benefit that the caregiver provides or opens a bank account or membership to a credit union to receive their benefit payment.
## Bank and bank account
An appropriate bank is:
- a private savings bank, a trustee savings bank, or The Co-operative Bank
- a registered bank which on the 31st March 1987 was a trading bank or
- any other registered bank or a building society approved by the Minister after consultation with the Minister of Finance
All payments of Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children are direct credited into the caregiver’s bank account.

chunks.title: Caregivers income — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Caregivers income
The income and assets of the caregiver do not affect payment of Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
A caregiver may still be paid Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children if the child or children:
- meet all the qualifications and
- the absence from New Zealand is temporary and
- the child/children is returning to New Zealand
For more information see:
- Permanent absence
- Reciprocal Agreements
- Payment
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Orphans Benefit and Unsupported Childs Benefit Absence from New Zealand

chunks.title: Caregiver dies — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Caregiver dies
When a caregiver who was receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children dies you can continue to pay Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children for up to 4 weeks after the date of death.
Staff must identify what care arrangements have been made for the child.
The new caregiver may meet the qualifications for Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children, or the child may be able to be included as a dependent child if the new caregiver is receiving a main benefit.
## Caregiver or child dies before benefit granted or reviewed
Where a caregiver or child dies before a decision is made on an application or review for Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children you can continue the application or review process as if the caregiver or child had not died.

chunks.title: Caregiver reapplies for Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Caregiver reapplies for Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit
If a caregiver has previously been receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit and reapplies, when they are granted Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit again, they will also be granted Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children.
For more information see:
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Change in age — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Change in age
A child's age may affect:
- the rate of Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit payable to the caregiver and
- the rate of Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children payable and
- whether the child is still a dependent child
Note a change in a child's age may affect a caregiver's obligations (and those of their partner if they have one). This depends on what other financial assistance they are getting and the obligations that apply.
## Child is not dependent
A child is not a dependent child if they are:
- in full-time employment
Note generally a child is still a dependent child when they start part-time employment
- getting a basic Student Allowance or an Independent Circumstances Allowance
Note getting a Student Loan does not always mean a child is financially independent
- getting a main benefit in their own right or
- financially independent
## Child turns 18
When a dependent child turns 18, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit can no longer be paid for them unless they are continuing in education and are not financially independent.

chunks.title: Change of address — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Change of address
When a caregiver advises that they have changed their address it is important to check that the move does not affect their entitlement to Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children.
If the caregiver is receiving extra help or any other benefit this may also need to be reviewed to take into account their new circumstances.
The change of address may also indicate a change in the caregiver's circumstances.
Examples of changes that may affect entitlement are:
- the child or children may have returned to live with their parents
- children have come into or left the caregiver's care
For more information see:
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Change of caregiver — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Change of caregiver
To get Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children, the caregiver must be an eligible caregiver of the child.
For more information see:
- Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit Change of caregiver
## Temporary change of caregiver
If the change in the caregiver is temporary, for example, school holidays or a short stay in hospital, the Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children can continue being paid to the caregiver, provided contact and support of the child is maintained and the caregiver continues to be the principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver.
## Long-term change of caregiver
If the change of caregiver is long term, and the caregiver is no longer the principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver, the benefit should stop.
The new caregiver should be invited to apply for Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit in their own right.
## Date of review
When a dependent child leaves the caregiver's care, the Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children should stop from the beginning of the next pay period.
However, there is discretion to continue payments for up to 28 days following the event.
This discretion is generally used to avoid financial hardship for the family when the change has been unexpected, or when processing deadlines have passed.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
Caregivers have an obligation to advise MSD of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Orphan's Benefit and Unsupported Child's Benefit. Any such change may affect the caregivers' ability to get Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported Children.
A benefit can also be reviewed at any time to check that the caregiver still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.
## Mandatory Review for Orphan's Benefit and Unsupported Child's Benefit
MSD must review a caregivers Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit within 52-weeks of when their benefit commenced, or within 52-weeks from when the caregivers last Mandatory Review was completed.
While there are no Mandatory Reviews for Clothing Allowance, if a caregiver doesn't respond to their Mandatory Review for their Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit and the benefit suspends, the Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported Children will also suspend.

chunks.title: Child applies for a benefit in their own right — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Child applies for a benefit in their own right
A dependent child cannot apply for a benefit (in their own right) until they have attained the qualifying age for that benefit. When the child's benefit is granted they will have an initial stand-down period.
When a child applies for a benefit in their own right, the Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children must stop from:
- the beginning of the next pay period in which the event took place or
- the date the child's benefit is granted
whichever is earlier.
Wherever possible (and in appropriate circumstances) the date the Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children stops and the commencement date of the child's benefit should coincide.
There is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days following the event. This discretion is generally used to avoid financial hardship for the family when the change has been unexpected or when processing deadlines have passed.
For more information see:
- Youth Payment [no link find out why]
- Young Parent Payment [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Child changes — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Child changes
Change to a dependent child's circumstances is generally going to affect the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children.

chunks.title: Child dies — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Child dies
When a child (that Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid for) dies you can continue to pay Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children for 4 weeks following the date of death.

chunks.title: Child leaves care — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text: When a dependent child leaves the caregiver's care Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported Children should stop from the start of the pay period following the date of event. However, there is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days following the event to allow for a period of financial adjustment, generally to avoid hardship for the client.

chunks.title: Temporary return to parents — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text: In Unsupported Child's Benefit cases where the child leaves the care of the principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver and returns to their parents for a short period, MSD needs to establish: - the reason for the change - the intended length of stay - whether the child will return to the caregiver - who made arrangements for the change - whether it is likely to happen again and - who will be providing the support, care and control of the child (that is, will the caregiver still be responsible for the child) "Short period" is not defined. A decision whether to continue paying Unsupported Child's Benefit and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported Children is to be made on the facts available. It is necessary to determine in these cases if the principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver remains the primary carer for the child. While Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid, the parents continue to be liable to pay their assessed Child Support.

chunks.title: Return to parents for a trial period — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text: When a child returns to their parents care for a trial period, Unsupported Child's Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported Children continues to be paid to the principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver only.

chunks.title: Permanent return to parents care — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text: When the child returns to live with their parents permanently, and the parents resume primary responsibility for the child other than on a temporary basis, then the caregiver getting Unsupported Child's Benefit and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported Children no longer meets the definition of principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver. Unsupported Child's Benefit and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported Children should stop from the start of the payday following the date of event. However, there is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days following the event to allow for a period of financial adjustment, generally to avoid hardship for the client.

chunks.title: Child under the age of 18 years — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Child under the age of 18 years
When a child under 18 leaves school or tertiary education, MSD can continue to pay Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for that child, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children until the start of the pay period following their 18th birthday as long as the child remains a dependent child.
## Child aged 18
When a child aged 18 years leaves school or tertiary education, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the child, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children should stop from the start of the pay period following the date the child left school or tertiary education.
There is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days following the date the child left school or tertiary education to allow for a period of financial adjustment, generally to avoid hardship for the caregiver. MSD needs to consider the activity the child is going to when considering the use of this discretion.

chunks.title: Child starts part-time employment — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Child starts part-time employment
Part-time employment does not make a child financially independent. Do not take the child's earnings into account when assessing the rate of Clothing Allowance for Orphans or Unsupported children payments.
For more information on children's income see:
- Child's income
## Exception
There may be situations where a child starts (or is in) part-time employment and can no longer be considered a dependent child for some other reason such as:
- no longer maintained as a member of the family or
- the caregiver is no longer primarily responsible for them
## Child starts full time employment
A child in full-time employment and financially independent is not treated as a dependent child for Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported Children.
Note a child is still considered a dependent child if they are working full-time during the school holidays and they will be returning to school after the holidays.
For more information see:
- Full-time employment
- Child remains dependent
- Core policy Income [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Child turns 18
A dependent child must generally be under the age of 18 for a caregiver to get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for them, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children.
When a child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and are no longer eligible for Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children should stop from the start of the pay period following the child's 18th birthday.
However, if the 18-year-old child is continuing in education and is not financially independent, the child may continue to be considered a dependent child and to have Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit paid for them. In this situation, Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children can continue for a limited period.
In these situations, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children must stop from the start of the pay period following:
- the date they no longer meet these criteria or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18
whichever is earlier
However, there is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days following the date the child turns 18 to allow for a period of financial adjustment, generally to avoid hardship for the caregiver.
Note if the caregiver also gets Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit and Clothing Allowance for other children, these payments will continue for the other children when the 18-year-old child is excluded.

chunks.title: Financially independent — extra help > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit products > clothing allowance > changes and reviews clothing allowance
chunks.text:
## Financially independent
A child is considered to be financially independent when the child:
- is in full-time employment or
- gets a Student Allowance or
- receives a benefit in their own right
## Other situations where a child is considered to be financially independent
There may be other situations where all a child's financial needs (including the provision of accommodation and material needs) are being met by someone else or from some other source. For example:
- a family trust or
- the parent who is not the principal caregiver
## Date of review
When a child becomes financially independent Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children should stop from the beginning of the next pay period in which the child became financially independent.
However, there is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days following the event. This discretion should generally be used when cancelling payment due to the child becoming independent.
## Not financially independent
