chunks.title: Clothing — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Clothing
If a client meets all qualifications, a Recoverable Assistance Payment may be made to purchase essential clothing (excluding school uniforms).
Assistance for clothing can only be authorised to meet essential needs and this need should be met through the most economic item(s) available.
## Payment
Except where exceptional circumstances exist, payment cannot exceed:
- 6 weeks of the appropriate rate of Supported Living Payment that the client would be entitled to receive or
- the amount indicated below
whichever is the least amount.
Single people without dependent children
$150
Married, civil union or de facto couples without dependent children
$300
Married, civil union or de facto couples with dependent children
$400
Sole parents with one or more dependent children
$400

chunks.title: Acceptable budgeting worksheet — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Acceptable budgeting worksheet
Clients can complete any budgeting worksheet as long as it records and compares information on income and expenses.
To complete this budgeting activity a client's budget must include:
- all of their costs (and their partner's costs), including weekly, fortnightly, monthly and annual costs and
- their income from all sources
All clients will have costs related to accommodation, power, food and transport but you should also check they have included everything they spend money on throughout the year, eg school uniforms, clothing, doctor's bills, Christmas presents, etc.
A client must also complete reasonable steps. From their sixth grant date they will be required to attend a budgeting advice service as their budgeting activity.

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Deciding ordinarily resident
Generally a client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand to receive a Recoverable Assistance Payment.
Ordinarily resident means someone who is normally and lawfully in New Zealand and intends to stay here, that is they consider New Zealand to be their home.
Whether a person is ordinarily resident is a question of fact and degree and their intentions during any period of absence is the most important factor.
Where it is not clear if a client is ordinarily resident, consider the following:
(a) the client's intentions toward New Zealand (that is, the reasons for their absence from New Zealand and the reasons for their return). Are they going overseas for a holiday or are they intending to live overseas permanently (sighting return air tickets is a good indication)?
(b) the length of time they spend in New Zealand on a continual basis
(c) property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans)
(d) where are their cash assets held?
(e) is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and do they pay New Zealand taxes?
(f) do they still vote (or are they eligible to vote) in the New Zealand election?
(g) their commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in the community, community events, clubs and other groups)?
Note a person cannot be ordinarily resident in two places at the same time.
## Clients not ordinarily resident
If you decide that a client is not ordinarily resident in New Zealand that does not mean that they cannot be granted a Recoverable Assistance Payment as section 74(1)(a) contains discretion. You have discretion to refuse to grant a Recoverable Assistance Payment or to grant it at a reduced rate.

chunks.title: Dentures and hearing aids — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Dentures and hearing aids
If a client meets all qualifications, a Recoverable Assistance Payment can be made for dentures and hearing aids.
Subsidies may be available from a Health Agency toward the cost of dentures and hearing aids.
Before considering a Recoverable Assistance Payment, reduce the amount required by:
- any subsidy provided by the hospital or health agency
- any subsidy available to Community Services Card holders
- any health or disability insurance payment
- any disability allowance paid for the disability that led to the need for the item
Recoverable Assistance Payments should only be paid for the user-part charge the client is required to meet. The cost of the consultation can be included in the cost.
## Payment
Except where exceptional circumstances exist, total payment cannot exceed:
- 6 weeks of the appropriate rate of Supported Living Payment that the client would be entitled to receive or
- $1000
whichever is the least amount.

chunks.title: Driver licences — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Driver licences
A Recoverable Assistance Payment may be made for a client to:
- get a new driver licence
- renew their driver licence
- reinstate their driver licence
- re-sit their driver licence test (after paying the initial test fee)
- reschedule their driver licence test
Note the re-sit fee only applies for Class 1 (car) drivers who have failed to pass their driver licence test twice.
A Recoverable Assistance Payment is available for all classes of driver licence.
Recoverable Assistance Payments for driver licence costs must not be more than the actual fees payable.
This assistance is not available to pay for endorsements on driver licences.
## Rescheduling drivers licence tests
If a client reschedules their drivers licence test within 2 working days of their test, they may be charged a rescheduling fee.
Clients are not charged a fee if they reschedule their drivers licence test more than 2 working days (a full 48 hours) before the day of their test, or they reschedule their test online.
Where possible, clients should reschedule their test online. If clients are unable to do this online, MSD may be able to cover the rescheduling fee under a Recoverable Assistance Payment.
MSD cannot cover the costs associated with cancelling a driver’s licence tests.
## Assistance cannot be paid
A client will not qualify for a Recoverable Assistance Payment for driver licence costs if they:
- are disqualified from holding or getting a driver licence or
- have not renewed their driver licence before the expiry date without a good and sufficient reason

chunks.title: Effect of not using services to build financial capability — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Effect of not using services to build financial capability
When a client applying for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment chooses not to use services to help them build their financial capability, the effect depends on whether the client:
- was offered information on the services or
- must use the service as a budgeting activity obligation
Information offered
Budgeting activity obligation required
Process
Information about services to build financial capability is offered to all clients as part of the general hardship application process.
A client or partner must use a specific service to build financial capability to meet their budgeting activity obligation.
Effect of not using services to build financial capability
There is no adverse impact if the client does not access the services offered.
The staff member will determine if the client has met their obligations through any activities completed and if not, may decline the application for hardship assistance.

chunks.title: Electricity, gas, or water — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Electricity, gas, or water
If a client meets all the qualifications, a Recoverable Assistance Payment may be made to assist with:
- outstanding electricity, gas and water bills and
- the cost of reconnecting electricity, gas and water supplies
Before approving applications, other ways of meeting the costs should be investigated. For example, can arrangements be made with their electricity or gas company, for the client to pay off outstanding bills or reconnection charges.
If a client is having difficulty meeting their payments their electricity or gas company should be asked by the client to check whether they are on the correct tariff.
The client should also have discussed with their retailer any alternative payment options available to them such as:
- payment arrangements to recover debt within a reasonable timeframe
- prepayment meters
- smoothed payments
- regular direct credits
- redirection of income
Clients do not need to be at the stage of being disconnected to be granted a Recoverable Assistance Payment for electricity or gas.
Clients should be encouraged to request assistance before their electricity or gas is threatened with disconnection or is disconnected, to avoid disconnection and reconnection costs.
## Payment
Except when there are exceptional circumstances, the total payment cannot exceed:
- 6 weeks of the appropriate rate of Supported Living Payment the client would be entitled to get or
- $200
whichever is the least amount.
## Disability Allowance or other Health Subsidy
You will need to determine if it is appropriate to make a Recoverable Assistance Payment when the costs for electricity, gas or heating have already been included in existing Disability Allowance payments or another Health Subsidy.
Disability Allowance is only paid for the additional electricity, gas or heating costs that a person has because of their disability (not the total cost).
A Recoverable Assistance Payment can be considered if there is an immediate and essential need for electricity, gas or heating costs not covered by Disability Allowance or another Health Subsidy.
When a portion of the costs was covered by Disability Allowance or another Health Subsidy, consider whether the client could reasonably have been expected to have paid that portion of the costs. If they could have, you may in your discretion decline to include those costs.
## Utility Disputes
If the client has a complaint about their energy or water company, they can contact Utilities Disputes. See:
- Utilities Disputes Complaint form

chunks.title: Example - applying hardship obligations — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Kerry has significant debt and since being granted a main benefit she has received hardship grants to pay for both ongoing regular costs like food and power, and help with annual and unexpected costs like car repairs. Hardship application Event 1. January While attending a work focused appointment, Kerry says that she needs help to pay for food. The case manager: - finds out more about Kerry's current financial situation - assesses what assistance is available and, whether she is currently getting the correct payments for her circumstances - grants a Special Needs Grant for food - offers Kerry information on the building financial capability services available 2. January Kerry applies online via MyMSD for assistance with food 3 weeks after her last grant. The reasonable steps obligation is covered in MyMSD and Kerry indicates what steps she will take. Assistance is granted and she is provided with a link to information on building financial capability services via MyMSD. 3. March Kerry applies online for assistance with food again. Assistance is granted and she is provided with a link to information on building financial capability services via MyMSD. 4. April Kerry is in the service centre and asks for help with her power bill. The case manager: - talks to Kerry about her financial situation - assesses what assistance is available and whether she is currently getting the correct payments for her circumstances - discusses what Kerry has done to meet the reasonable steps obligation and what else may be possible including: setting up a direct deduction to pay for power weeklylooking for a smaller house to rent - setting up a direct deduction to pay for power weekly - looking for a smaller house to rent - grants hardship assistance for power - checks if Kerry has attended any building financial capability services - but Kerry has not - explains how the services could help and provides the information on how to access services again 5. May Kerry's car needs repair work so she can get to work and she comes in to the service centre to get help. Kerry works rurally so the car is essential as there is no public transport in her area. The case manager discusses what Kerry did between grants to improve her financial situation. Kerry reviewed listings for several cheaper rental houses but did not set up a direct deduction. They discuss what other options may be available to help Kerry manage her money. Kerry has not taken up the offer of services to build her financial capability, so information is offered again. After assessing if Kerry's payments are correct, an Advance is approved for the car repairs.

chunks.title: Example - applying hardship obligations — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: They agree that as reasonable steps Kerry will set up the redirection, keep looking for less costly housing, and look for cheaper phone and internet options before she applies for another grant. 6. May Kerry applies online for assistance with food. She is under the limit and signals that she has done what was agreed to take reasonable steps. Assistance is granted and she is provided with a link to information on building financial capability services via MyMSD. 7. July In July Kerry comes into the service centre as she can't make a payment on her car loan. After assessing whether she is getting the correct payments for her circumstances, they discuss what Kerry did between grants, including: - continuing to look for cheaper housing - changing her internet plan to a cheaper one Payment is made for the car costs as Kerry has taken reasonable steps but they agree that before she applies for another grant Kerry will: - set up the direct deduction for power - look at ways to reduce her food bill via planning - look at ways to reduce power usage Kerry has not taken up the offer of services to build her financial capability so information is offered again – the case manager strongly suggests Kerry take up the budgeting advice as it appears there are still some things she can do to improve her financial situation. 8. September Kerry comes into the service centre to get help with her power payments as she has fallen behind and is at risk of disconnection. Kerry has not set up the direct deduction for power as discussed at previous appointments and has been struggling to reduce her food and power bills. Kerry has not accessed any of the services offered but has started looking for a job that pays more or can offer more hours. The case manager checks that Kerry is getting everything she is entitled to. Payment is made to Kerry for this month's power bill as Kerry has taken reasonable steps. However, the case manager decides that Kerry should have a budgeting activity obligation applied as there are a number of ways for her to improve her ability to manage her money. They agree that seeing a budget advisor would be the most helpful activity and Kerry is told that she may be declined future hardship assistance if she does not complete this activity. An appointment is made for a week later to see how the activity goes. Kerry does not attend, and this is noted for follow up the next time Kerry applies for hardship assistance. 9. September

chunks.title: Example - applying hardship obligations — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Two weeks later Kerry comes in for a food grant. She has not done the budgeting activity or taken reasonable steps but after discussion with the case manager about her situation, it is clear there were exceptional circumstances as Kerry has been unwell and off work for most of the last 2 weeks. A Special Needs Grant is paid and Kerry is aware she will need to attend the budgeting service. 10. October While attending another appointment, Kerry asks for help to pay for food. She has not attended the budgeting service and does not have a good reason. She is still looking for a job with more hours and cheaper housing. She is not over the limit but has met the reasonable steps obligation but not the budgeting activity obligation. She is given enough money for food until she attends the budgeting service later that week.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances
Exceptional circumstances are those which set the client apart from others in a similar situation.
In determining whether exceptional circumstances exist you must have regard to:
- the client's ability to repay the Recoverable Assistance Payment
- whether the client could reasonably have been expected to have made provision for the particular immediate need
- whether the client is the principal caregiver of a child of or under the age of 12 months
- the extent to which not making a Recoverable Assistance Payment would: worsen the client's positionincrease or create any risk to the life or welfare of the client or the client's partner or dependent children orcause serious hardship to the client, or the client's partner or dependent children and
- worsen the client's position
- increase or create any risk to the life or welfare of the client or the client's partner or dependent children or
- cause serious hardship to the client, or the client's partner or dependent children and
- any other matters relevant to the circumstances of the particular case. Example is when the least amount required under a preferred supplier arrangement means that they will exceed their 6-week limit
## Payment
If you have determined that exceptional circumstances exist, you can exceed the:
- maximum amount payable and
- minimum 24-month payment recovery period
There is no discretion to disregard the residency criteria, or exceed the income and asset limits.

chunks.title: Exception — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Exception
You may approve an application for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment for a client who failed their Hardship obligations if there are exceptional circumstances. This includes circumstances that prevented a client from completing their obligations.
Acceptable exceptional circumstance include:
- unforeseen hospitalisation
- seriously sick or injured
- bereavement of immediate family
- emergency or adverse event
- victim of violent crime or family violence
If a client does not have any of the above reasons staff can consider whether the reason provided:
- is an unforeseen out-of-the ordinary event that could not be planned for
- is beyond the client's control or
- sets the client apart from others in a similar situation

chunks.title: Fire loss or burglary — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Fire loss or burglary
If a client meets all qualifications, a Recoverable Assistance Payment can be made to assist with the cost of replacing essential items lost through fire or burglary, where the person is not insured or where relatives are unable to assist with the replacement of essential items.
The burglary incident must be verified by a police report. If in doubt, a fire report may be requested to confirm loss of property because of fire.
## Preferred supplier arrangement
When a preferred supplier arrangement is in place the client must purchase any specified goods and services from a preferred supplier.
The following specified goods and services have a preferred supplier arrangement:
- fridges, freezers, fridge-freezers and washing machines (whiteware)
- glasses (optical goods and services)
## Payment
Except where exceptional circumstances exist, payment cannot exceed:
- 6 weeks of the appropriate rate of Supported Living Payment the client would be entitled to get or
- $1000
whichever is the least amount.

chunks.title: Fridges, freezers and washing machines — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Fridges, freezers and washing machines
If a client meets all qualifications, they can get a Recoverable Assistance Payment for fridges, fridge-freezers, freezers and washing machines (collectively known as whiteware).
There is a preferred supplier arrangement in place for whiteware. This means clients must purchase their whiteware from a preferred supplier.
If a client refuses to purchase from a preferred supplier, the application for a Recoverable Assistance Payment must be declined.
A client may purchase more than one type of goods if they meet the qualifications for both. For example, a client may purchase both a washing machine and fridge-freezer.
## Amount of payment
Except where exceptional circumstances exist, the total payment cannot exceed:
- 6 weeks of the appropriate rate of Supported Living Payment the client would be entitled to get or
- rates set in the preferred supplier arrangement
whichever is lower.
## Subsequent applications for whiteware
If a client purchases whiteware from a preferred supplier and subsequently applies for further assistance for the same item, MSD must consider what has happened to cause their need.
If the whiteware has broken down within 5 years of the date of purchase, consider whether the client has checked if help is available from the preferred supplier in accordance with:
- the warranty period or
- consumer protections in the Consumer Guarantees Act 1993.

chunks.title: Glasses — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Glasses
If a client meets all qualifications, a Recoverable Assistance Payment for optical goods and services (collectively known as glasses) may be made.
There is a preferred supplier arrangement in place for glasses.
If a client resides in an urban area covered by a preferred supplier agreement for glasses, then the client must use a preferred supplier.
If a client resides in an urban area with a preferred supplier for glasses and refuses to purchase from a preferred supplier, their application for a Recoverable Assistance Payment must be declined.
If a client resides in a non-coverage area, they have the option to use a non-preferred supplier or they can travel to a preferred supplier at their own cost.
## Clients with high clinical needs
Some clients have high clinical needs which means the glasses they require cannot be provided at the standard contract price.
Hardship assistance for a higher amount than the standard package amount can be provided for clients with high clinical needs.
Some types of high clinical needs are:
- vision which is outside of 'normal' ranges (+ or - 6 or higher)
- severe astigmatism that requires a special lens grind
- growths on eyes due to severe UV exposure
- some forms of medication make eyes very sensitive to light and glasses require a special coating
- prescription for glasses that are heavy and a higher grade of progressive lenses that are required to avoid frames buckling or the weight tearing the client's skin
Lens coatings or glasses specifically for Irlen Syndrome are not covered by MSD or the Ministry of Health.

chunks.title: Hardship obligations — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Hardship obligations
Clients and their partners who apply for Recoverable Assistance Payments may have the following hardship obligations:
- a reasonable steps obligation and/or
- a budgeting activity obligation
Generally, clients must meet any hardship obligations that have been applied to them before they can get additional hardship assistance.
These obligations do not apply to:
- payments to people in specific circumstances or
- payments to get a new, renew, or reinstate a driver licence.
Note you must make sure the client is getting their correct entitlement at every interaction with them.
## Newborn
When a client is the principal caregiver of a child 12 months of age or younger, you must consider the presence of the newborn when deciding whether to apply hardship obligations.
This includes the principal temporary caregiver of a child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid.
## Multiple obligations
Depending on the client's circumstances at the time, they may have none, one or both hardship obligations applied to them.

chunks.title: Identifying reasonable steps — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Generally, clients who have received Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit and/or Recoverable Assistance Payments on 3 or more grant dates during the past 12 months must take reasonable steps before they can get any additional payments. Reasonable steps clients can take are those that will: - reduce their costs - increase their income or - improve their financial management When identifying possible reasonable steps you must consider each client's individual circumstances. When with the client, it may be useful to review any budget or budgeting worksheet that the client has previously completed to see what costs the client has and check whether they are essential. You should discuss with the client what they can do to meet the reasonable steps obligation. Note clients are only required to take specific actions for their reasonable steps when you have discussed the actions with them, e.g. setting an automatic payment to pay for power.

chunks.title: Examples of reasonable steps — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Reasonable steps could include (but are not limited to): - seeking part-time or full-time paid employment, or increasing hours to increase income - having their Child Support payments reviewed (especially if they have a reduction in income) - cancelling non-essential services eg pay TV services - quitting smoking - Quitline can provide support, information and low-cost nicotine patches, gum, and lozenges - 0800 778 778 - reducing regular costs by moving to cheaper alternatives e.g. moving to cheaper accommodation, taking up a less expensive phone or internet plan, or using public transport when those costs are cheaper than the cost of using a private vehicle - renegotiating debt repayments to a lesser repayment amount (eg court fines) - refinancing or consolidating debt to reduce interest and repayment amounts - suspending contributions to KiwiSaver and/or other voluntary retirement schemes - setting up a separate account and/or automatic payments for bills - agreeing to the MSD setting up a redirection of benefit where there is good cause Note if the client has completed reasonable steps for Temporary Additional Support, the client should generally be considered to have met the reasonable steps obligation at the next application for a Special Needs Grant, Recoverable Assistance Payment, or Advance Payment of Benefit. You need to check the CMS notes to confirm what steps have been taken.

chunks.title: Some budgeting activities may be considered reasonable steps — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: A client can voluntarily complete a budgeting activity such as doing a budgeting worksheet or seeing a budgeting advisor as a reasonable step. Clients can also be considered to have met their reasonable steps obligation for a Special Needs Grant if they recently completed a budgeting activity obligation for an Advance Payment of Benefit or a Recoverable Assistance Payment.

chunks.title: Immediate and essential needs — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Immediate and essential needs
In order for a client to be considered for a Recoverable Assistance Payment they must be able to identify a particular immediate need for an essential item or service.
In considering any application for payment consider:
- whether a payment would best meet the particular immediate need of the client
- the client's ability to meet the need from their own resources
- the assistance that is or might be available to the client from other sources to meet the need
- the existing debt level of the client from all sources
- the effect on the client or their immediate family (if any) if the need is not met and when that effect might be expected to impact on that or those persons and
- the extent to which the client has caused or contributed to the immediate need or to the situation that has given rise to the particular immediate need.
Consideration must be given to all the circumstances and other sources of assistance available to the client.
It must be established that the client has an immediate need for an essential item or service before a Recoverable Assistance Payment can be made.

chunks.title: Documents issued from 29 November 2010 — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Documents issued from 29 November 2010
Documents issued from 29 November 2010 include:
- New Zealand Citizenship certificate (issued by Internal Affairs)
- New Zealand citizen endorsement (in a foreign passport)
- Permanent resident visa
- Resident visa
- Visitor visa
- Work visa
- Student visa
- Limited visa
Only the permanent resident visa and resident visa show a person is a resident.
A visa shows as a sticker in the client's passport.
## Unable to provide visa or permit
When a client is unable to provide an immigration visa or permit they may provide other Immigration New Zealand documents to verify their immigration status. Work and Income can also undertake an immigration status check directly with Immigration New Zealand.
Note that Immigration New Zealand may be unable to verify immigration status for clients of British nationality who arrived in New Zealand before 2 April 1974 and do not have a passport.

chunks.title: Income limit — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Income limit
A client cannot get a Recoverable Assistance Payment, if their income and the income of their partner (if any) exceeds the appropriate annual income limits.
This income includes the amount of any payment made under the New Employment Transition Grant Programme or the Seasonal Work Assistance Programme to the client or partner (if any).
Note if the client is applying for a Recoverable Assistance Payment on behalf of their dependent child, the income limit applies to the parent/caregivers income.
The client's relationship status, age and whether they have dependent children must be taken into account to assess the appropriate annual income limits.
To assess a client's income if they're self-employed see:
- Types of income
Note do not assume that clients getting non-beneficiary assistance will automatically meet the income test for a Recoverable Assistance Payment.
An income assessment must be completed for all clients, as it is possible that a client getting Extra help (for example Accommodation Supplement) may have income over the income limit.
For more information see:
- Deskfile rates Income limits
## Estimating income
The estimated income of a client is any income they got in the previous 52 weeks from the date of application for a Recoverable Assistance Payment.
The Ministry can modify the estimate of the person's income and get a more accurate assessment of what the person's actual income is likely to be, by adding or removing income.
Example
A client was working full-time in a high paying position for the previous 52 weeks. However, the client has been diagnosed with a serious illness and will be working reduced hours for the next 52 weeks.
Their current income is restricted to part-time earnings, and their partner's income.
The income now taken into account is the part-time earnings and the partner's estimated income, not their income for the previous 52 weeks.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The Recoverable Assistance Programme provides non-taxable, interest free, recoverable financial assistance to non-beneficiaries to meet essential immediate needs for specific items or services.
Clients who meet the income and cash asset tests may have access to Recoverable Assistance Payments up to a maximum amount of six weeks of the rate of Supported Living Payment.
The client must be able to identify a particular immediate need for an essential item or service.
Consideration must be given to whether a Recoverable Assistance Payment would best meet the immediate need, including investigating other sources of assistance.
You must negotiate a repayment arrangement with the client before you grant an application for Recoverable Assistance Payment. If you are unable to do so the application may be considered to have lapsed.

chunks.title: Item or service not in client's name — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Item or service not in client's name
Generally, immediate and essential needs are considered for a Recoverable Assistance Payment only if the item or service is in the client's or their family's (if any) name.
Essential items or services not in the client's or partner's name are not considered for a Recoverable Assistance Payment as the client or partner is not liable for the payments.
## Exception
There may be situations where a client or their partner (if any) has entered into an informal arrangement with another person to pay for an essential item or service using the other person's name and/or credit rating for the contract.
You need to be satisfied that the client or their partner is the person with the immediate and essential need, and is required to make the payment for the item or service. You must also be satisfied it is/was the intention of the parties to the informal arrangement that the client or their partner would have responsibility for the payments, and the use and control of the essential item or service.
A full statement from the client or partner and the other person named in the contract is required along with a copy of the agreement to determine if the cost can be considered for a Recoverable Assistance Payment.
Note in these situations the client is not able to meet the cost of the item or service from their own resources and the need must be immediate and essential.

chunks.title: Maximum amount payable — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Maximum amount payable

chunks.title: Method of payment — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Method of payment
Every Recoverable Assistance Payment for goods or services must be paid to the seller of those goods or services on verification that the client has received the goods or service.
The seller must be a reputable supplier, for example a GST registered supplier or an established trustworthy business.
Note payments cannot be made for private sales.
In exceptional circumstances only, Recoverable Assistance Payments for goods and services can be paid to the client or to a parent or caregiver, when the parent or caregiver applies for assistance on behalf of a dependent child.
## Preferred supplier arrangement
When a preferred supplier arrangement is in place the payment must be made directly to the preferred supplier.

chunks.title: New Driver Licences — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## New Driver Licences
A Recoverable Assistance Payment may be made to a client to get a new driver licence when they have:
- not previously had a full driver licence and
- an immediate and essential need to get a driver licence
A payment can be made for the actual fees for applying and taking a test for a learner licence, a restricted licence, or a full licence of any class.
A Recoverable Assistance Payment is available for a client and their partner to each get a learner licence, restricted licence, and full licence.
Clients can apply for a Recoverable Assistance Payment to cover the costs of the:
- initial test fee covering 2 tests (the initial test and 1 re-sit), and
- re-sit test fee for any additional tests
Note the re-sit fee only applies for Class 1 (car) drivers who have failed to pass their driver licence test twice.
Generally, only 1 payment each can be made to a client and their partner per licence category in a 52-week period. MSD can use discretion to grant more than 1 Recoverable Assistance Payment in a 52-week period if the client has exceptional circumstances.
For more information see:
- Exceptional circumstances
## Essential need
An essential need exists if MSD is satisfied it is necessary for the client to get a driver licence:
- to participate in a required activity to improve their work-readiness at least once every fortnight or
- to apply for employment when a driver licence is an essential requirement or
- to undertake an available employment opportunity or
- when they, or any member of their immediate family have a disability and needs help with transport to undertake their daily living activities (including getting treatment for their disability, or undertaking education or employment) or
- for any other special reason
When considering if a driver licence is necessary, MSD must consider the:
- availability and suitability of public transport, and any other transport options and
- circumstances of the client and their immediate family
## Actual fees
Recoverable Assistance Payments for a new driver licence must not be more than the actual fee payable.
## Dependent children
A parent can apply on behalf of their dependent child for a Recoverable Assistance Payment to get a learner, restricted or full driver licence.

chunks.title: Clients who do not use the services offered — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Clients who do not use the services offered
When a client applies for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment and is offered information on services to help them build their financial capability, the client can choose not to use them as they are optional.
If a client chooses not to use the services offered this is not a reason to fail a client's reasonable steps or budgeting activity obligation.
A client can be required to complete budgeting activities, including those provided by building financial capability services only if they have:
- had a budgeting activity obligation applied and
- been told about the obligation and what they must do to meet it

chunks.title: Other emergency payments — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Other emergency payments
When a client applies for a Recoverable Assistance Payment for an item or service that does not fit an existing category, and they meet all qualifications, the 'other emergency payment' category may be considered if:
- special circumstances exist and
- the client and their partner (if any) or dependent children (if any) would suffer serious hardship without that item or service
If you consider a client's situation means a Recoverable Assistance Payment should be made under the 'other emergency payment' category discuss this with Helpline and/or your manager.
When the 'other emergency payment' category is used, clearly identify and record the reasons and decisions made.
Reasons such as 'account fees', 'approved by manager', and 'hire purchase', are not satisfactory as they could relate to a range of items.
## Payment
Except when there are exceptional circumstances payment cannot be more than:
- 6 weeks of the appropriate rate of Supported Living Payment that the client would be entitled to get or
- $200
whichever is the least amount.

chunks.title: Other sources of assistance — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Other sources of assistance
Rather than payment of a Recoverable Assistance Payment, discuss with the client other options that they may not have considered. Some examples may include (but are not limited):
- meeting the need from the next income payment due
- assistance from other government agencies
- arranging automatic payments
- negotiating payment of accounts by instalments
- hire purchase
Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.
## Other income assistance
You must check to see if the client qualifies for other assistance before granting a Recoverable Assistance Payment.
Consider:
- Special Needs Grants when urgent assistance is needed to relieve immediate hardship
- Housing Support Products for help to get and retain rental housing
- Accommodation Supplement
- Disability Allowance
- Temporary Additional Support
## District Health Boards assistance
Recoverable Assistance Payments can be approved to assist with items partially subsidised by District Health Boards where the client still has to pay a shortfall. For example, dentures and hearing aids. Payment is for the unsubsidised portion only. This does not apply to glasses (optical goods and services).
## Student assistance
Consider the balance of any student loan available. Consideration should be given to declining the application if this option has not been exhausted. Note under no circumstances are students to be referred to institution hardship funds. Students may be eligible for Special Needs Grant assistance.

chunks.title: Payment categories — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: The following is a list of the various payment categories and maximum limits of Recoverable Assistance Payments. If MSD wants to make a payment for an item not on the list, contact Helpline. Except where exceptional circumstances exist, payment must not be more than 6 weeks of the appropriate rate of Supported Living Payment or the maximum amount stated below. Further details are listed under each category: Category Maximum limit Ambulance subscription fees $200 Assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early $200 Attendance at funerals and tangihanga $200 Beds, chairs and tables $200 Car repairs $400 Child restraints for motor vehicles, and safety helmets $200 Clothing single client without children $150 couple without children $300 sole parent or couple with children $400 Dentures and hearing aids $1,000 Driver licence renewal client 65 years or under $32.40 client 66 or 67 years $22.60 client 68 or 69 years $19.00 client 70 or 71 years $14.80 client 72 or 73 years $10.80 client 74 years $9.00 client 75 years or over $21.50 new learner licence class 1 $96.10 class 2, 3 or 5 $77.50 class 4 $27.10 class 6 $90.60 restricted licence class 1 $167.50 class 6 $54.20 full licence class 1 $98.90 class 2, 3, 4 or 5 $39.80 class 6 $47.40 re-sit fee learner licence class 1 $54.60 restricted licence $102.80 full licence $71.90 driver licence test reschedule fee $16.40 reinstatement of driver licence $48.00 Electricity, gas or water $200 Fire loss or burglary $1,000 Fridges, freezers and washing machines (whiteware) at rates set in preferred supplier arrangement Glasses if a client lives in an urban area with a preferred supplier $280 if a client lives in a non-coverage area and chooses to use a non-preferred supplier $1,000 Other emergency payments $200 School costs $200 School stationery $200 School uniforms (for each dependent child) $300 Telephone installation $200 Tenancy tribunal fees $28 Travel for stranded persons $200

chunks.title: Housing assistance — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: The 'Bond and rent' category was removed on 13 March 2023. If a client needs help to get or retain rental housing, they may qualify for a Housing Support Product. if a client does not qualify for Housing Support Products due to the type of housing they need assistance for (e.g. non-rental housing), MSD can consider whether the client qualifies for assistance under: Other emergency payments

chunks.title: Payments — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Payments
The amount of a Recoverable Assistance Payment should be the least amount required to meet the client's particular immediate need.
Note the maximum payment must be reduced by the client's MSD debt balance unless exceptional circumstances exist.
Recoverable Assistance Payments should not generally be approved if the amount available is insufficient to cover the full cost of the item or service. Recoverable Assistance Payments should not be approved to pay a deposit on an item.
Any payment made must be recovered. MSD cannot make a Recoverable Assistance Payment non-recoverable. If MSD thinks a payment should be non-recoverable, a Special Needs Grant may be considered instead.
## Maximum limits
Except where exceptional circumstances exist, a payment must not exceed:
- 6 weeks of the appropriate rate of Supported Living Payment the client would be entitled to get or
- the maximum amount stated in the payment categories
whichever is the least amount.
A client can get more than one Recoverable Assistance Payment as long as the outstanding balance does not exceed the maximum limits.
The maximum limit is not restricted to a 52-week period. The maximum limit is assessed at each Recoverable Assistance Payment application.

chunks.title: Permanent residence — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Permanent residence
Generally migrants need to have permanent residence or New Zealand citizenship to receive a Recoverable Assistance Payment.
Permanent residence is granted by Immigration New Zealand.
Citizenship is granted by the Department of Internal Affairs.
In order to receive a Recoverable Assistance Payment, a client must normally:
- have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 (which can either be a resident visa or a permanent resident visa) or
- have a residence permit under Immigration Act 1987 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) or
- be a British national who arrived in New Zealand prior to 2 April 1974 or
- be a New Zealand citizen
Note if you require further information about a client's application for permanent residence you must get consent from the client to contact Immigration New Zealand or the client should obtain the information themselves. Otherwise the application should be declined. You must not collect or disclose information regarding a client's application without the client's consent.

chunks.title: Preferred supplier arrangement - glasses — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Preferred supplier arrangement - glasses
The Ministry of Social Development has a preferred supplier arrangement with selected optometrists and opticians to supply glasses to people in some urban areas.
If a client who resides in an urban area covered by a preferred supplier arrangement for glasses (optical goods and services) refuses to purchase from a preferred supplier, the application for a Recoverable Assistance Payment must be declined.
The preferred supplier arrangement includes the following goods and services in the purchase price:
Goods
- spectacle frames
- spectacle lenses
- ready to wear spectacles
- spectacle protection cases
- spectacle care products
Services
- eye examinations
- fitting of spectacle frames, spectacle lenses and ready to wear spectacles
- fitting of spectacle lenses to frames supplied by the purchaser
- adjustment of spectacle frames, spectacle lenses and ready to wear spectacles

chunks.title: Preferred supplier arrangements — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Preferred supplier arrangements
When a preferred supplier arrangement is in place the client must purchase the specified goods and services from a preferred supplier.
The following specified goods and services have a preferred supplier arrangement:
- fridges, freezers, fridge-freezers and washing machines (whiteware)
- glasses (optical goods and services)
When a client applies for a Recoverable Assistance Payment for one of the specified goods or services they must be told about the preferred supplier arrangement. MSD must also provide this information in writing to the client.
## Whiteware
If a client refuses to purchase whiteware from a preferred supplier the application for a Recoverable Assistance Payment must be declined.
## Glasses
If a client who resides in an urban area that is covered by a preferred supplier arrangement for glasses (optical goods and services) refuses to purchase from a preferred supplier the application for a Recoverable Assistance Payment must be declined.

chunks.title: Proof of residence — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: All documents should be originals. Photocopies and/or documents that have been changed in any way cannot be accepted. Where the client (or partner) cannot provide proof or proof is unclear, you should ask the client (or partner) to obtain confirmation of their residence status from Immigration New Zealand (for permanent residence) or Internal Affairs (for citizenship). Proof of citizenship and/or permanent residence in New Zealand can be a: - New Zealand birth certificate Generally a person born in New Zealand is a New Zealand citizen by birth. - New Zealand passport To hold a New Zealand passport you must be a citizen of New Zealand. - Certificate of Registration A child born outside New Zealand (to a parent who is a New Zealand citizen) may be a New Zealand citizen from birth. However, the child must apply for a Certificate of Registration to confirm their New Zealand citizenship. - Grant of Citizenship People who have permanent residence, may (normally after 5 years residence in New Zealand) apply for a Grant of Citizenship. They must meet the conditions of the Grant. - Certificate of Confirmation This is a certificate issued to confirm that the holder is a New Zealand citizen by birth, descent or Grant of Citizenship. British subjects, who immigrated to New Zealand prior to 1948 (and who resided in New Zealand for all of 1948) were made New Zealand citizens in 1949. These people are likely to have a Certificate of Confirmation or a Certificate of Naturalisation. - Certificate of Naturalisation Previously immigrants were naturalised as British Subjects and Citizens of New Zealand. Today they are given a Grant of Citizenship. - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence class visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009 - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987 Note that a visa issued before 29 November 2010 does not allow a person to stay in New Zealand - Letter of confirmation of permanent residence from Immigration New Zealand - Australian citizens Australian citizens are lawfully allowed in New Zealand without a residence class visa or residence permit and their date of entry into New Zealand is generally not recorded. Where possible supporting evidence should be sought, such as, tenancy agreements, bank statements or old utility bills to show that the client has been ordinarily resident for two continuous years. - British nationals

chunks.title: Proof of residence — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Clients of British nationality who came to New Zealand before 2 April 1974 were automatically allowed to enter New Zealand for residence, and will be unable to provide verification of their residence if they do not have a passport. Immigration New Zealand will have no record of these clients unless the client has contacted them after 2 April 1974. The client should be able to provide New Zealand school, work or tax records to support their claim about when they arrived in New Zealand and the length of time they have lived here.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To get a Recoverable Assistance Payment a client must:
- meet an income and asset test
- have an immediate and essential need
- have met any hardship obligations that have been applied to them
- be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (i.e. not be in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or temporary permit)
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and
- purchase goods and services from a preferred supplier when there is an arrangement in place
Clients must provide proof of their income and assets (for example current payslips and bank statements).
For more information see:
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Preferred supplier arrangements
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they are considered to hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other eligibility criteria for a Recoverable Assistance Payment.
If a client is receiving a benefit, they may be able to receive an Advance Payment of Benefit.
## Rental housing
If a client needs help to get or retain rental housing, they may qualify for assistance under the Housing Support Products.

chunks.title: Reasonable steps obligation — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Reasonable steps obligation
Clients who frequently access Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit and Recoverable Assistance Payments may have to meet a reasonable steps obligation. This obligation means clients need to take personal responsibility for managing their money and take steps to:
- reduce their costs
- increase their income or
- improve their financial management
Note you must make sure the client is getting their correct entitlement at every interaction with them.
## Applying reasonable steps obligation
Generally, clients who have received Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit and/or Recoverable Assistance Payments on 3 or more grant dates during the past 12 months, must take reasonable steps before they get any additional payments.
Reasonable steps are actions that increase their income, reduce their costs, or improve their financial management.
You should let clients know at their third grant date, and each subsequent grant date that they must take reasonable steps before they can get further assistance.
Note in some circumstances partners must also take reasonable steps.
## Applying reasonable steps obligation before third grant date
Generally clients are only required to take reasonable steps after they have received Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit and/or Recoverable Assistance Payments on at least 3 grant dates during the past 12 months. However, you can apply the reasonable steps obligation before 3 grant dates.
When deciding whether to apply the reasonable steps obligation before their third grant date you must also consider if the client has:
- received repeated grants for the same costs
- a history of receiving multiple hardship payments
- a significant debt with the Ministry of Social Development

chunks.title: Recovery of payment — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Before granting a Recoverable Assistance Payment a repayment plan must be negotiated with the client. There are a variety of repayment options available to clients (and/or their partners), as listed below: - payee deductions from Working for Families assistance paid by MSD - deductions from Student Allowance - employer deduction notice (a debt management officer at Client Support - Debt Management will arrange this - case managers do not have the delegation to issue a wage deduction notice) - automatic payment from client's bank account - internet/telebanking payment - payment through New Zealand Post Shop The necessary forms for repayment must be completed and signed by the client before the Recoverable Assistance Payment is issued. The person whose wage/salary will be repaying the debt must agree to an employer deduction notice. If a client has a Recoverable Assistance debt balance when applying for a benefit or pension, deductions from the benefit or pension can be made to continue recovery of the Recoverable Assistance Payments. For more information see: - Current client debt Non-beneficiary client debt - Current client debt Negotiating repayment of debt - Repayment options available to clients Recoverable Assistance Payment [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Recovery rate — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Recoverable Assistance Payments must have a recovery rate that ensures the amount of the payment is repaid within 24 months after the payment is granted, unless exceptional circumstances exist. The rate of recovery must be negotiated with the client taking into account their circumstances. It is important the client knows the length of time the Recoverable Assistance Payment will be repaid over. When setting the rate of recovery, you need to consider the following factors (where relevant): - the circumstances of the client and any dependents - the ability of the client to meet their needs and the needs of any dependents - the amount of the debt - we want clients to pay off their debt as fast as they can, but always consider the circumstances of the client, and their ability to repay without placing them in undue hardship. If the debt is large, you should consider a higher repayment rate if the client can afford to pay - the effect the rate of recovery will have on the client's ability to support themselves - whether the rate of recovery would cause undue hardship to the client and any dependents - the effect the rate of recovery would have on the client's ability to fulfil their work and social obligations, e.g. ensuring their child is enrolled with a Health Practitioner or enrolled with a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation if required to do so - the ability of the client to gain access to further advances and recoverable assistance If the client does not agree with the rate of repayment you must record why you decided to set it at that rate.

chunks.title: Reducing an existing recovery rate — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: In most cases a Recoverable Assistance Payment needs to be recovered within 24 months. Clients, who request a reduction of recovery rate that will extend beyond 24 months, will need to be considered against and must meet the exceptional circumstances criteria.

chunks.title: Reinstating driver licences — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Reinstating driver licences
A Recoverable Assistance Payment may be made for a client to reinstate a driver licence of any class if they:
- had their driver licence disqualified and/or
- surrendered their driver licence because they were required to give it up or decided not to drive anymore and handed it in and
- qualify for their driver licence to be reinstated
Note payments can only be made to clients who have completed their suspension/disqualification period and who are eligible to reinstate their licence. This does not include a person who has been disqualified for more than 12 months as they would need to apply for a new licence.
Generally, 1 payment each may be made to the client and their partner during a 52-week period. MSD can use discretion to grant more than 1 Recoverable Assistance Payment in a 52-week period if the client has exceptional circumstances.
For more information see:
- Exceptional circumstances
## Actual fees
Any payment made for the costs to reinstate a driver licence must not be more than the actual fee payable.
## Disqualified for longer than 12 months
Clients who have had their driver licence disqualified for longer than 12 months need to complete and pass a test to get their driver licence back. They need to pay a requalification fee, which includes the cost of the test.
A Recoverable Assistance Payment for the requalification fee cannot be made under the driver licence category, MSD should consider if the client would qualify under the 'other emergency payment' category.
## Dependent children
A parent can apply on behalf of their dependent child for a Recoverable Assistance Payment to reinstate their driver licence under the driver licence category.

chunks.title: Renewals of existing driver licences — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Renewals of existing driver licences
A Recoverable Assistance Payment may be made for a client to renew their driver licence if they:
- hold an unexpired driver licence or
- hold an expired driver licence and had a good or sufficient reason why they could not renew it before the expiry date and
- are applying for a renewal of a driver licence of the same or equivalent class or classes
Generally, a client and their partner can get 1 payment each, during a 52-week period. MSD can use discretion to grant more than 1 Recoverable Assistance Payment in a 52-week period if the client has exceptional circumstances.
For more information see:
- Exceptional circumstances
## Actual fees
Recoverable Assistance Payments to renew a driver licence must not be more than the actual fee payable.
For more information see:
## Renewals for a client 75 or over
A client aged 75 or over may also be required to take an on-road safety test as a condition to renew their driver licence.
The cost for this test is included in the renewal fee.
## Assistance cannot be paid
A client will not qualify for a Recoverable Assistance Payment for driver licence costs if they:
- are disqualified from holding or getting a driver licence

chunks.title: School costs — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Recoverable Assistance Payments may be available for some school costs. Schools may request payment for costs such as: - school uniforms - school stationery - Other school costs including: school donationscomputing equipmentschool camps and trips - school donations - computing equipment - school camps and trips

chunks.title: Clients getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: If a client getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit applies for school costs, check if they've applied for the School and Year Start-up Payment. If they have not applied and the application window is still open, help them make an application. See: - School and Year Start-up Payments qualifications If the client did get the School and Year Start-up Payment for the child, establish if the need for school costs have been met. If not, you can consider the advance if they meet the qualifications. Note generally, receipts are not needed to show how the School and Year Start-up Payment was used.

chunks.title: School donations — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Recoverable Assistance Payments are not available for school donations that are part of the core learning programme (curriculum), This is because donations are voluntary (parents/caregivers have a choice to pay) so they do not meet the immediate and essential needs criteria. If a client applies for assistance to pay school donations, we should make sure the client understands this cost is voluntary (they have a choice to pay) and let them know the school cannot stop their child being included in all aspects of the curriculum.

chunks.title: School camps, school trips and health camps — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Recoverable Assistance Payments are not available for school camps, school trips or health camps that are part of the core learning programme (curriculum). These payments are voluntary (parents/caregivers have a choice to pay) so are not an immediate and essential need.

chunks.title: Core goods and services costs that are not donations — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Costs that are not part of donations (that is, are not voluntary) can still be considered for assistance where the client has an immediate and essential need. These can include (but not limited to) costs for some core goods and services: - stationery, eg exercise books and pads, pens, pencils, computing equipment etc - school workbooks, eg Maths, English, Physics - school/kura uniform (purchased from the uniform shop or second-hand) - some competitions eg Otago Maths - attendance dues - only for state-integrated schools or kura - after-hours/lunchtime/weekend cultural or sports activities - attending non-curriculum performances eg visiting drama or music groups - course materials that parents have agreed to purchase eg, a take-home component like a letterbox, item of clothing For more information see:

chunks.title: Computing equipment (devices) — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Access to devices is a key part of digital learning and is becoming common in schools. Digital technology skills, knowledge and capabilities are necessary for our increasingly digital society and economy. Schools or Kura may ask students to bring their own (BYOD) computing equipment eg an iPad, laptop or tablet. If the school makes this a requirement, in the first instance they should be supporting those families and students who may not be able to afford them eg having a school set available for students to use. A Recoverable Assistance Payment for devices can be considered where a parent or caregiver has identified an immediate and essential need for the child to have their own device. This could include (but not limited to): - a child has specific learning needs and having their own device supports their learning both at school and at home - they need specialist software installed eg, voice technology - the child is taking a specialist subject eg, graphics and needs a device with certain specifications - a child is expected to do extra work after school hours, and this is easiest done on a device

chunks.title: Attendance dues — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: State-integrated schools have the same core learning Programme (curriculum) as state schools but have their own special character (eg philosophical or religious belief). Attendance dues cover the property related costs of the school and are compulsory for students attending state-integrated school/kura. Recoverable Assistance Payments can be considered if the client qualifies for this.

chunks.title: Other school costs — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: A client may be able to make a payment arrangement with their school for the cost of school and educational expenses that are not part of the core learning programme (curriculum) such as: - attendance dues - school camps - school trips or - health camps Where a payment arrangement cannot be made, and special circumstances exist, and the client would suffer serious hardship, then discretion can be used to consider a Recoverable Assistance Payment under 'Other Emergency Payment' for these costs.

chunks.title: Example — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: A client's child is part of the school orchestra which meets together after school each week for an hour to practice. There is a nationwide competition coming up, so the school has organised a 2-day music camp in preparation for it. The child is required to attend so they can take part in the competition. This music camp is outside of the core learning programme (because it's an extra-curricular activity) so the client is required to pay. However, they have been unable to put aside sufficient money to meet the cost. The client has discussed payment options with the school but has been unable to come to a satisfactory arrangement. A Recoverable Assistance Payment under Other emergency payments may be considered to meet the cost of the school camp when special circumstances exist, and the client's child would suffer serious hardship without this assistance.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Except where exceptional circumstances exist, payment for each dependent child cannot be more than: - 6 weeks of the appropriate rate of Supported Living Payment that the client would be entitled to get or - $200 whichever is the least amount.

chunks.title: School or Kura donations scheme — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: The School Donations Scheme allows decile 1-7 state and state-integrated schools to opt-in to get $150 per domestic student (aged 5-19) per year if the school agrees not to ask parents/caregivers for donations (excluding school camps). As donations are voluntary (parents/caregivers have a choice if they pay), no hardship assistance is available for clients whether their school has opted in or not (including decile 8 - 10 schools). If the parent/caregiver chooses not to pay the donation, the child cannot be stopped from attending an activity if it is part of the core learning programme (curriculum). If any schools insist the donation must be paid (all schools), please tell the client to talk to the Ministry of Education so they can follow up with the school directly: - school.donations@education.govt.nz For more information see: - Ministry of Education Fees and charges at school

chunks.title: School camps — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Schools or Kura can continue to ask for donations for overnight school camps if they are part of the core learning programme (curriculum), but they cannot insist on payment. This applies whether the school has opted-in to the donations scheme or not. In these instances, no hardship assistance is available to clients regardless of whether their school has opted in or not (including decile 8 - 10 schools). If the parent/caregiver chooses not to pay the donation, the child cannot be stopped from attending an activity if it's part of the core learning programme (curriculum). Parents/caregivers may still need assistance to cover specific items for school camp eg a raincoat or an additional pair of shoes. Hardship assistance can be considered in these circumstances if they qualify. For more information see:

chunks.title: What parents can and cannot be asked to pay — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: The below table shows what parents/caregivers can and cannot be asked to pay (note, this is not an exhaustive list).

chunks.title: Core goods/services — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: - Stationery e.g. exercise books and pads, pens, pencils etc (there is no obligation to purchase this from the school) - School/Kura uniform - Exam fees (excluding NCEA) - Attendance dues - only for state-integrated schools/kura

chunks.title: Optional materials/resources — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: - Optional workbooks - Purchase of non-compulsory hardware or software eg tablet, laptop - Purchase of school/kura magazine - School photos

chunks.title: Optional activities — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: - Charge/fee for optional event eg weekend ski trip, school/kura ball - After-hours/lunchtime/weekend culture or sports activity eg music tuition and instrument hire, school sports team (including uniform fees)

chunks.title: Camps, Trips and Outside Education — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: - Overnight camp or field trip as part of a specific course e.g. Year 12 Outdoor Education or Year 13 Geography trip - Overnight camp as part of the core learning programme (curriculum) e.g. Year 9 orientation camp or primary school year 7-8 camp

chunks.title: Programmes and Courses — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: - English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) - Reading Recovery and Learning Support - High school 'subject fees' Specialist units eg Montessori, Te Reo etc - Supplementary programmes e.g. Mathletics Resources - Textbooks - Workbooks (compulsory) - Photocopying/printing as part of the Corer Learning Programme (curriculum) Swimming - Swimming classes as part of the core learning programme (curriculum - either onsite or off-site) For more information see: - Ministry of Education The school donations scheme

chunks.title: Checking if schools have opted in — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text: Schools/Kura will decide each year whether to opt-in to the donations scheme or not. Staff can check if a school has opted-in by: - checking Education Counts Find your nearest school and - searching the school's name Whether a school has opted-in or not will show in the 'Donations' information: - Opted-in: 'Donations should not be requested, unless for a school camp' - Not opted-in (does not qualify): 'Donations may be requested'

chunks.title: School stationery — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## School stationery
If a client meets all qualifications, a Recoverable Assistance Payment can be made to assist with the cost of essential school stationery required by the client's dependent children.

chunks.title: School uniforms — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## School uniforms
If a client meets all qualifications, a Recoverable Assistance Payment can be made to purchase school uniforms for dependent children where there is an immediate need.
## Payment
Except where exceptional circumstances exist, payment for each dependent child cannot exceed:
- 6 weeks of the appropriate rate of Supported Living Payment that the client would be entitled to receive or
- $300
whichever is the least amount.

chunks.title: Telephone installation — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Telephone installation
If the client meets all qualifications, a Recoverable Assistance Payment may be made to assist with the cost of telephone installations, providing a telephone is essential for:
- the maintenance of the client's or their partner's, or their dependent child's health
- to access emergency assistance or
- because of geographical isolation, age or psychological condition of the client, client's partner or dependent child.
Note usually clients can make arrangements with the respective telephone company, to pay the connection fee by instalments.
## Payment
Except where exceptional circumstances exist, payment cannot exceed:
- six weeks of the appropriate rate of Supported Living Payment that the client would be entitled to get or
- $200
whichever is the least amount.

chunks.title: Tenancy Tribunal fees — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Tenancy Tribunal fees
Tenancy Services charges a flat fee of $28 (including GST) for all applications. Where a tenant wishes to take action against their landlord, they will have to pay this fee before any proceedings can be taken.
It is expected that most clients will be able to fund this application fee. However, a client may be able to receive a Recoverable Assistance Payment if they meet the qualifications.
Applications for Tenancy Tribunal fees must be supported by a Tenancy Tribunal application form that has been validated by Tenancy Services (either by a stamp or a confirmation slip or letter).
The tear off portion of the Tenancy Tribunal application form should be retained and attached to the Recoverable Assistance Payment application form.

chunks.title: Travel for stranded persons — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Travel for stranded persons
If a person meets all qualifications, a Recoverable Assistance Payment can be made for that person to return to their usual place of residence where they are:
- stranded away from their usual place of residence and
- unable to pay for travel due to circumstances which could not reasonably have been foreseen
If the person's dependent children are together with the client in the above circumstances, a Recoverable Assistance Payment of not more than $200 for each dependent can be made.
## Payment
Except where exceptional circumstances exist, payment cannot exceed $200 for each person.
These payments are to cover the most economical mode of transport. If the person is using public transport and has a Community Services Card, they can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect.
For more information see:
- Community Services Card - Public transport (Community Connect)

chunks.title: Types of costs not included — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Types of costs not included
The following costs cannot be included by landlords as costs due to assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early, and cannot be included in assistance paid to meet the costs of assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early:
- blanket fees for assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early (ie set fees that do not correspond to actual and reasonable costs incurred by the landlord)
- costs that are not directly related to assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early, such as cleaning costs, rent arrears, costs to repair damages to the property
Note other assistance may be available for costs at the end of a tenancy that cannot be included as costs due to assignment, subletting or ending a tenancy early. For example, if the client qualifies and the costs relate to the bond for a new tenancy a Bond Grant may be paid under Housing Support Products.

chunks.title: Types of licence endorsement — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Types of licence endorsement
The Recoverable Assistance Payments for driver licences is not available to pay for the following endorsements on driver licences:
Identifying letter
Endorsement
D
Dangerous goods endorsement
I
Driving instructor endorsement
O
Testing officer endorsement
P
Passenger endorsement
F
Forklift endorsement for use with special-type vehicles that are forklifts
R
Roller endorsement for use with special-type vehicles that run on rollers
T
Tracks endorsement for use with special-type vehicles that run on self-laying tracks
W
Wheels endorsement for use with special-type vehicles that run on wheels and are not forklifts
V
Vehicle recovery endorsement

chunks.title: Work and Income debt balance — extra help > recoverable assistance payment
chunks.text:
## Work and Income debt balance
The maximum Recoverable Assistance Payments available are reduced by the client's Work and Income debt balance unless exceptional circumstances exist.
If a client (and their partner, if any) has Work and Income debt equal to, or greater than their maximum Recoverable Assistance Payments limit, they would not generally qualify for payment unless exceptional circumstances exist.
Assess the existing debt balance by combining Work and Income debt totals for both the client and partner (if any). Reduce the client's Recoverable Assistance Payment limit by their existing Work and Income debt level.
Consider the client's current income/expenses and ability to live within the reduced income and the likelihood they may need further assistance if the payment is approved.
When determining entitlement to a Recoverable Assistance Payment, include the following Work and Income debt(s): Special Needs Grants, Recoverable Assistance Payments, Housing Support Products, Liable Parent Contribution, Major Repairs Advance and Benefit overpayments.
For example:
Recoverable Assistance Payment maximum payment limit
$1300.00
Less outstanding Recoverable Assistance Payment debt balance
$800.00
Recoverable Assistance Payment balance
$500.00
Less other Work and Income debts
$700.00
Total debts less Recoverable Assistance Payment maximum limit
-$200.00
Although the client has a $500.00 Recoverable Assistance balance, total Work and Income debts are greater than the maximum Recoverable Assistance payable.

chunks.title: Amount of deferred loan — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Amount of deferred loan
An assessment must be completed to ensure that the loan balance to be deferred does not exceed the value of the client's equity at the date the loan would have become due for repayment (under the original agreement).
