The loan balance to be deferred will be based on the capital value of the property less the following:
- the client's protected equity
- actual funeral costs (if a prepaid funeral was not held) and
- any prior changes recorded in the agreement
The loan balance to be deferred will be capped at this amount. The Ministry of Health will confirm the balance.
For more information see:
- Duration of loan deferment approved in exceptional circumstances
- Review of loan deferment

chunks.title: Application process — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Application process
The person who wants the Residential Care Loan repayment to be deferred must complete a Deferred Loan Application form.
The applicant must provide details of the circumstances that they wish to be taken into account to support their application with verification of their assets and income.
The applicant (and their spouse or partner) will be subject to an asset and income test to ensure that the applicant meets the eligibility criteria.
The application will be referred to a legal executive who will assess the person's entitlement to a loan deferral.
For more information see:
- Roles and responsibilities of legal executives
- Deferred loan approved
- Deferred Loan Application form

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances
Clients are obliged to advise Work and Income of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their eligibility for Residential Care Loan.
Repayment of a Residential Care Loan will be sought:
- upon the sale of the home or
- 6 months after the client dies
whichever is earlier.
Legal Executives are responsible for advising Ministry of Health to stop loan payments and for arranging repayment.
In some situations, the loan repayment can be deferred if a non-core family member remains in the home.
For more information see:
- Repayment of Residential Care Loan
- Deferment of loan repayment
- Property sold
- Review client with a partner
- Loan terms and conditions

chunks.title: Changes to Residential Care Loan policy — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Changes to Residential Care Loan policy
This policy will be reviewed and updated periodically. Any changes to the policy will be gazetted.
For more information see:
- Roles and responsibilities of legal executives
- What is a Residential Care Loan
- Eligibility criteria
- Exceptional circumstances
- Loan terms and conditions
- Repayment of a loan
- Deferment of loan repayment
- Write-off of a loan
- Residential Care Subsidy Qualifications

chunks.title: Default interest — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Default interest
Default interest will be charged at the rate stated in the deferred loan agreement (currently 10%), and added to the balance repayable, for any breach of the deferred loan agreement (including the term of the loan deferment).
Interest may be charged under the original loan agreement if a deferred loan application or agreement has not been executed by the time the loan is due to be repaid (ie 12 months after death).

chunks.title: Deferment of loan in exceptional circumstances — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Deferment of loan in exceptional circumstances
If any of the loan deferral criteria is not met, a loan deferral may be considered only in exceptional circumstances.
The applicant will need to complete the exceptional circumstances section of the application and provide details of the circumstances that they wish to be taken into account to support their application.
For all exceptional circumstances applications, the Ministry of Health must be asked to make the final decision regarding whether a deferred loan is offered or not.
For more information see:
- Deferment of loan repayment
- Repayment criteria
- Application process
- Duration of loan deferment approved in exceptional circumstances

chunks.title: Deferment of loan repayment — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Deferment of loan repayment
The offer of deferred loan is discretionary. Neither the Ministry of Social Development nor the Ministry of Health is under any obligation to offer a deferred loan.
A deferred loan may be offered to a person living in the borrower's former home (as described in the schedule of the residential care loan agreement between the Crown and the borrower) if the person meets all of the following eligibility criteria:
- they were living in the former home immediately before the borrower entered long-term residential care, and had lived there on a continuous full-time basis for at least 5 year immediately before the borrower entered long term residential care
- they continued to live in the former home while the borrower was in long term residential care and remained living there after the borrower's death
- they inherited the former home or taken it by survivorship, or inherited an estate or interest in the former home jointly or in common with some other person or has been left a life interest by the borrower and has a legal right to live there
- the applicant does not have the ability to repay or refinance the residential care loan
and one of these criteria:
- the applicant is mentally or physically impaired or
- the applicant has given up employment or the opportunity for employment to care for the parent, delaying the borrowers entry into residential care or
- the applicant has bought the property together with another family member (being the borrower)
Deferment of the loan repayment is only available in respect of the first person who meets the above criteria, and only applies while that person remains living in the borrower's former home.
If the former home is sold or otherwise disposed of or the person moves out (other than temporarily), the loan balance becomes immediately repayable.
The deferred loan will be interest-free for the period of the deferred loan.
The person must complete an application form to assess whether they meet the criteria.
If the applicant does not meet all of these criteria, a deferred loan may be offered in exceptional circumstances.
For more information see:
- Application process
- Deferred loan approved
- Default interest
- Repayment criteria
- Deferment of loan in exceptional circumstances

chunks.title: Deferred loan approved — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Deferred loan approved
When a deferred loan is approved, the deferral will be strictly applied to the original home only and cannot be transferred to another home, unless there are exceptional circumstances in which case a new application will be required. The Ministry of Health will be required to make the final decision in these situations.
A loan deferral agreement will be drawn up setting out details of the loan, including the amount of the loan, the term of loan and when the loan deferral will be due for review. The agreement must be signed by the relevant parties and a legal executive from the Ministry of Social Development.
For more information see:
- Amount of deferred loan
- Duration of loan deferment approved in exceptional circumstances
- Default interest
- Deferment of loan in exceptional circumstances

chunks.title: Duration of loan deferment approved in exceptional circumstances — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Duration of loan deferment approved in exceptional circumstances
When a loan deferment is offered in exceptional circumstances, the loan will generally be offered for no more than two years or as approved by the Ministry of Health.
Two years is a reasonable period to allow the applicant to assess their situation and make arrangements to repay the loan.
Six months prior to the deferred loan becoming repayable, the applicant will be given notice that the loan is due to be repaid.
The applicant can make a further application for deferral prior to the expiry date. This will again be considered by the Ministry of Health who will make the decision to either approve or decline an extension.
For more information see:
- Deferred loan approved
- Application process
- Review of loan deferment

chunks.title: Eligibility criteria — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Eligibility criteria
The Ministry of Social Development considers each application for a loan on a case-by-case basis. There is no obligation on the Ministry of Social Development, or the Ministry of Health to offer a loan.
A loan may be offered if the Ministry of Social Development is satisfied that the loan offer fits within the purpose of the loan scheme and that the applicant meets all of the following key eligibility criteria:
(a) The applicant is a resident assessed as requiring care.
(b) The applicant's assets are above the applicable asset threshold and the applicant is liable to pay for the cost of contracted care services.
(c) The applicant has assets above the applicable asset threshold only because the applicant owns the former home.
There are three factors that need to be met here:
(i) The applicant must have legal ownership of the former home; and
(ii) the applicant does not qualify for a subsidy because the value of their former home means that the applicant has assets above the applicable asset threshold; and
(iii) the applicant's assets other than the former home must amount to no more than $15,000.00 for a single person and $30,000.00 for a married, civil union or de facto couple or such other amounts as may be gazetted in accordance with paragraph 30.
(d) The Crown can obtain sufficient security.
A loan will only be offered if the Ministry of Social Development is satisfied that the loan can be adequately secured over the applicant's former home.
(e) The loan can be recovered.
The Ministry of Social Development must be satisfied that there are no significant risks that would affect its ability to enforce repayment of the loan.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances
If the applicant does not meet the key eligibility criteria, but has raised individual circumstances that the Ministry of Social Development considers to be exceptional, the Ministry of Social Development (sometimes in consultation with the Ministry of Health) may offer a loan based on those circumstances.
Any loan offer will be on such terms and conditions as the Ministry of Social Development considers appropriate in those circumstances. There is no obligation on the Ministry of Social Development or the Ministry of Health to offer a loan.
For more information see:
- Loan terms and conditions

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Introduction
You must not discuss the details of individual client applications or give any indication of whether a loan is likely to be offered. The client or their representative must be referred to a legal executive if they wish to discuss any aspect of the Residential Care Loan scheme.
If a client's assets are assessed as being above the applicable asset threshold because they own the family home, and the client has limited cash assets, they may be eligible for a Residential Care Loan.
Note that loan applicants are not means assessed for income as their assets have been assessed as being above the relevant asset threshold.
For more information see:
- Roles and responsibilities of legal executives
- What is a Residential Care Loan?
- Eligibility criteria
- Exceptional circumstances
- Loan terms and conditions
- Repayment of a loan
- Write-off of a loan
- Deferment of loan repayment
- Changes to Residential Care Loan policy
- Change in circumstances
- Residential Care Subsidy Qualifications
- Residential Care Loan Application form [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Loan terms and conditions — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text: The loan will be issued on the terms and conditions deemed appropriate by the Ministry of Social Development. If the key eligibility criteria are met, these will generally be as set out below. The client will be required to enter into a loan agreement recording the terms and conditions of the loan. If the former home is co-owned with another party or parties, each of the other co-owners will also be required to enter into the loan agreement for the purpose of obtaining adequate security for the loan. Generally, a caveat will be lodged against the title to the former home as notice of the loan agreement. The client is required to maintain the former home and pay all rates (which may be by way of a deferred rates scheme), insurance and other outgoings until the loan is repaid. The cash assets referred to in paragraph 10(c)(iii) ($15,000.00 for a single person and $30,000.00 for a married, civil union or de facto couple) are intended to be for living expenses and for these purposes. The client is required to contribute directly to the provider the New Zealand Superannuation, or any other benefit, the client receives, less the personal allowance. The amount to be advanced to the provider on the client's behalf under the loan agreement will be reduced accordingly. The Ministry of Health will send a statement of the loan balance to the client on a quarterly basis. The loan will continue until the earliest of the following events: (a) the client dies or (b) the former home is sold or otherwise disposed of or (c) a new means assessment determines that the client's assets are equal to or below the applicable asset threshold If a new means assessment has determined that the client's assets are equal to or below the applicable asset threshold, the client will transfer from the loan scheme to a subsidy. Payments drawn against the loan will cease from the date of means assessment, the client will be informed of the loan balance, and the repayment provisions under the loan agreement will apply. However, if a client does not apply to the Ministry of Social Development for a new means assessment, or does not provide sufficient information to enable the Ministry of Social Development to determine the means assessment, the client will not be able to have a subsidy (to which the client might otherwise have been entitled) paid on their behalf.

chunks.title: Loan terms and conditions — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text: In such a situation, loan advances will continue to be paid to the provider on behalf of the client.

chunks.title: Repayment criteria — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Repayment criteria
A loan deferral will only be offered if the estate and the applicant/ co-owner do not have the ability to repay or refinance the Residential Care Loan.
For example, if there have been other assets provided to the estate resulting from the borrower's death (such as an insurance payout) these must be applied to repayment of the loan in the first instance. The balance of the loan may then be deferred.
Loans of less than $10,000 will not be deferred unless it can be shown that repayment of the loan will create hardship for the applicant.
The applicant will also need to meet the eligibility criteria.
## Multiple owners
If there will be multiple owners and one is likely to meet the criteria for deferral, a deferred loan will not be offered until the other owner(s) have either:
- repaid a share of the loan equal to (or greater than) their share of the property or
- provided verification of the circumstances that prevent them from doing so
If any of the other co-owners are able to repay their share of the loan, their repayment amount will be deducted from the outstanding loan, and the remaining balance will be offered to the applicant as a deferred loan (unless under $10,000).
The new deferred loan agreement will be between the Crown, the applicant and the co-owner(s).
Where the applicant has been left a Life Interest, the deferred loan agreement will be between the Crown, the trustees of the estate and the applicant. The residual owners will not be asked to repay any share of the loan when the application is made.
## Verification of payment of rates and insurance
Every applicant must verify that the rates and insurance are up-to-date or that other arrangements have been made such as a rates deferral.
A deferred loan should not be offered if the outstanding rates that are deferred are likely to exceed the equity in the home before the loan can be settled.
For more information see:
- Deferment of loan repayment
- Deferment of loan in exceptional circumstances
- Application process

chunks.title: Repayment of a loan — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Repayment of a loan
The loan must be repaid within 12 months after the client dies or when the former home is sold or otherwise disposed of, whichever date is earlier. If repayment is more than three months' late, penalty interest may be charged.
The loan must be repaid before the security or obligation under the loan agreement will be released.
The client is entitled to receive their protected equity after all of the amounts set out in paragraph 25 (that are owing at the date of loan repayment) have been paid. The client's protected equity is calculated by deducting the following amounts from the relevant asset threshold:
(a) any rates that have been postponed during the term of the loan; and
(b) the total amount of assets (other than the former home) that the client was assessed as having in:
(i) the means assessment at the time of the loan application, if the client has never transferred to a subsidy; or
(ii) the means assessment that determined that the client was eligible for a subsidy.
The relevant asset threshold for the purposes of paragraph 22 is the asset threshold that was applicable on:
(a) the day before the client became (or would have become) eligible for a subsidy; or
(b) the day before payments drawn against the loan ceased, if the client has not yet become eligible for a subsidy
For more information see:

chunks.title: Repayment of Residential Care Loan — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Repayment of Residential Care Loan
Clients are obliged to advise Work and Income of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their eligibility for Residential Care Loan.
Repayment of a Residential Care Loan will be sought:
- upon the sale of the home or
- 6 months after the client dies
whichever is earlier.
Legal Executives are responsible for advising Ministry of Health to stop loan payments and for arranging repayment.
In some situations, the loan repayment can be deferred if a non-core family member remains in the home.
For more information see:
- Deferment of loan repayment
- Property sold
- Review client with a partner
- Loan terms and conditions

chunks.title: Review of loan deferment — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Review of loan deferment
Once a deferred loan has been approved (does not include loans approved under exceptional circumstances), the deferral will remain in place until the applicant has a change in their circumstances that means they can repay the loan or it is found that a breach of the agreement has occurred.
These deferred loans will be reviewed every 2 years to confirm that:
- there have been no changes in the applicant's circumstances that would allow the loan to be repaid
- the applicant is still residing in the property and
- that the rates have been paid up to date and a comprehensive insurance policy is in place
## Deferred loans already in place
Deferred loans already in place prior to 1 July 2011 are to be reviewed every two years to determine that no breach of the agreement has occurred. This will include checks with regards to:
- the applicant is still residing in the former home and
- that rates are current and a comprehensive insurance policy is in place
The applicant will also be invited to repay the loan if applicable.
For more information see:
- Default interest
- Duration of loan deferment approved in exceptional circumstances

chunks.title: Roles and responsibilities of legal executives — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Roles and responsibilities of legal executives
You must not discuss the details of individual client applications or give any indication of whether a loan is likely to be offered.
The client or their representative must be referred to a legal executive if they wish to discuss any aspect of the Residential Care Loan Scheme.
## Loan agreements
Legal executives manage the entire loan process from application to repayment after the Residential Subsidy Unit completes the financial means assessment.
Legal executives liaise directly with the loan applicants and/or their solicitor. They determine whether the Crown will offer a loan. If so, they prepare loan contract documents, and if necessary, register caveats against the applicant's property. When a loan is due to be repaid, legal executives organise withdrawal of caveats and repayment of loans.
Legal executives may arrange further documentation when the loan repayment meets the deferment criteria.
Legal executives are acting as agents of the Ministry of Health in this process and sometimes need to discuss a case directly with the Ministry of Health.
## Financial means assessment
Residential Subsidy Unit staff sometimes need legal advice to determine a financial means assessment. The Service Centre Trainer will contact the legal executive for the client's region.
When appropriate, legal executives will discuss the financial means assessment with a solicitor.
For more information see:
- Introduction

chunks.title: What is a Residential Care Loan — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## What is a Residential Care Loan
It is an agreement between the Crown and a borrower ("client") under which the Crown advances funds to a provider, on the client's behalf, for any contracted care services received by the client.
Generally, a residential care loan ("loan") is secured over the client's former home, with the Crown's interest being protected by a caveat lodged against the title to the former home.
The loan is generally due to be repaid when the client dies or the former home is sold or otherwise disposed of, whichever happens earlier.
## Purpose of the loan scheme
The purpose of the loan scheme is to assist older people who, because they own their former home, have assets above the applicable asset threshold and are obliged to pay for the cost of contracted care services. The loan scheme recognises that for many older people their home is their principal asset, and that they may wish to retain it when they enter residential care.
Any private agreement between the client and the provider for any services that are not contracted care services is not varied by the loan agreement and remains a personal liability of the client.
## Roles and responsibilities
The Ministry of Health is responsible for the loan scheme policy, funding residential care under the loan scheme, and issuing loan statements to clients.
The Ministry of Social Development administers the loan scheme as an agent of the Ministry of Health through a Power of Attorney, and provides certain legal and administrative services in relation to the loan scheme.
All references to the Ministry of Social Development in this policy are as agent for the Ministry of Health.

chunks.title: Write-off of a loan — extra help > residential care loan
chunks.text:
## Write-off of a loan
The Ministry of Social Development may remit all or any part of the loan if the loan balance exceeds the value of the client's estate or interest in the former home less the client's protected equity or if, in the opinion of the Director-General of Health, the circumstances raised by the client or any person resident in the former home are exceptional.
The Ministry of Social Development may allow any of the following amounts to be deducted from the sale proceeds before the loan is repaid:
(a) Reasonable and necessary legal fees and disbursements on the sale of the former home (other than the cost of registration of the withdrawal of caveat).
(b) Real estate agent fees payable on the sale of the former home, up to a maximum of 5% of the value of the sale proceeds.
(c) Funeral expenses up to a maximum of $10,000.00 or such other amount as may be gazetted in accordance with paragraph 30 (provided the client had not previously purchased a pre-paid funeral).
(d) If the client has not died and has not previously purchased a pre-paid funeral, funds for this purpose up to a value of $10,000.00 (or such other amount as may be prescribed by Regulations made under section 155 of the Act).
(e) Gifts in recognition of high-level care provided to the client (up to the maximum value prescribed by Regulations made under section 155 of the Act), and any other prior mortgages or charges accepted in the means assessment at the time of the loan application as having priority over the loan.
(f) Any rates that have been postponed during the term of the loan.
After any allowable amounts have been deducted from the sale proceeds, the Ministry of Social Development may accept the remainder of the sale proceeds in full and final settlement of the loan.

chunks.title: Additional assistance — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Additional assistance
Clients getting Residential Care Subsidy may be able to get a Special Needs Grant or Advance Payment of Benefit for essentials items, for example glasses, dentures, hearing aids or additional clothing.
Before considering an Advance Payment of Benefit, check the item the client is applying for is not paid by, or the responsibility of, the Service Provider.
Clients getting Residential Care Subsidy cannot get Disability Allowance, Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit.
## Partner living in the community
If the client has a partner living in the community, the partner may be able to get extra help with their additional costs, eg accommodation or regular on-going health related costs.
Any income that has been included in the Residential Care Subsidy financial means assessment that is the income of the partner living in the community, is not included as income for extra help.
## Clients getting a Residential Care Loan
Clients getting a Residential Care Loan may qualify for Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Advance payment of benefit — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Advance payment of benefit
A client who is financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy may be able to get an Advance Payment of Benefit if they meet all of the qualifications.
Note before considering an Advance Payment of Benefit, check that the item that they are applying for is not paid by, or the responsibility of, the service provider.
## Repayment
The Advance Payment of Benefit must not be recovered from the client's Personal Allowance unless the client gives their permission.
Do not start recovery of an Advance Payment of Benefit when the client is getting Residential Care Subsidy.
In the event of death seek recovery from the client's estate.

chunks.title: Assessing the amount of deprived assets — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Assessing the amount of deprived assets
The amount of deprivation is the actual value of the asset the person deprived themselves of.
Generally, the amount of deprivation counted back in, will have regard to the level of resources available to the client.
## Example 1
A client sells their former family home to their child for less than market value.
The difference between the amount received and the actual value at the time, would be the amount of the deprived asset.
## Example 2
A single client applies for a Residential Care Subsidy on 13/11/2020. The client is assessed to have $150,000 current assets and $500,000 worth of deprivation.
If the deprivation is included the client's assets would be assessed as $650,000. The client would be over the asset threshold by $420,000 and not qualify for Residential Care Subsidy.
The client is a beneficiary of a family trust. The trust agrees to pay the client a capital disbursement of $200,000 on 2/12/2020. This is regarded as reasonable for the size of the trust.
Deprivation of $200,000 would be included in the Financial Means Assessment based on the knowledge that $200,000 worth of resources will be made available to the client.
No other resources are available to the client so deprivation of $300,000 is not included. The client is informed that they can re-apply for a Residential Care Subsidy when their assets fall below the threshold.
## Example 3
A single client has deprived themselves of $500,000 that will result in total assets of $650,000 if counted into the financial means assessment. The client is a beneficiary of a modest family trust that has not been providing disbursements to the client.
The trust agrees to pay the client $450 a week. This is the total income generated from the trust's assets. The amount is regarded as reasonable.
The deprived asset of $500,000 is replaced with the actual income figure of $450 per week in an income review.
Note excess gifting in the 5 year gifting period is considered deprivation and must be included in the financial means assessment.

chunks.title: Assessing the amount of deprived income — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Assessing the amount of deprived income
If deprivation of income has occurred and discretion is being used to include it in the financial means assessment, we need to determine the level of financial resources available to the client.
For example, if the client has significant levels of cash in a non-interest earning account, firstly invite the client to change this arrangement so that they do earn interest. If the client does not agree to change this arrangement, use the Reserve Bank 6-month term deposit rate to calculate the amount of deprived income.
For more information see:
- Example of using Reserve Bank interest rate
In general, the amount of deprived income counted into the financial means assessment will be replaced by the level of resources available to the client.
Sometimes it is reasonable to assume other resources are available to the client. For example, a family trust has resources available, but the client refuses to seek assistance from the trust. In these cases, it might be reasonable to count in a deprived income amount based on the actual level of deprivation.
## Gifts include the future earning potential of an asset
No notional income charge is assessed against gifts made under the allowable gift limits.
Generally, no notional income charge is assessed against gifts made in excess of the allowable gift limits.
This is because the gifted amount includes the future income earning potential of that asset.

chunks.title: Asset thresholds — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Asset thresholds
To be financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy, clients aged 65 years or over must have assets equal to or below the applicable asset threshold.
The asset threshold used depends on the client's circumstances:
Client circumstance
Asset limit (as at 1 July 2026)
Single client
$300,811
Couple - both in care
$300,811
Couple - one partner is living in the community
$164,731* (excluding family home and car)
or
$300,811 (including family home and car)
*This asset threshold automatically applies to couples when one partner is living in the community (not assessed as requiring care). A client in this situation can choose to have the higher $300,811 (as at 1 July 2026) asset threshold (including family home and car) applied to their financial means assessment.
For previous asset thresholds see: Deskfile Asset thresholds.
## Residential Care Loan
Clients who are not financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy due to excess assets, and who have been needs assessed as requiring long-term residential care in a hospital or rest home indefinitely, may be offered a Residential Care Loan.

chunks.title: Assets — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Assets
When completing a means assessment of assets, you must include the realisable assets of the client and their partner (if they have one).
## Value of the assets
The value of the assets is determined by:
- excluding exempt assets
- deducting genuine liabilities
- deducting outstanding debt
## Date of value assessment
In all cases the value of the assets is as at the date of application for financial means assessment. If the client or their partner has money set aside for a specific purpose, but it is still held by the client or their partner then it is included in the means assessment of assets.
Assets may include but are not limited to:
- cash
- bank account balances (credit balances only)
- bonus bonds
- car(s)
- net equity in property
- licence to occupy
- shares
- pre-paid funerals (any amount over $10,000 per person)
- life insurance policies
- KiwiSaver accounts (entitled to withdraw/outside the locked-in period)
- Māori land
- personal loans
- pre-paid estate administration fees
- life interest or lease for life
- excess gifting
- deprived assets
- assets covered by a relationship property agreement
## Rest home fees paid in advance
Most rest homes charge clients a month in advance.
If the client has paid hospital, or rest home fees more than a month in advance, the amount the client has paid in advance is considered realisable and is included in the means assessment of assets.

chunks.title: Assets sold or gifted — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Assets sold or gifted
If a client gifted or sold for fair value any assets these are not included in the client's means assessment of assets. This is because the client no longer owns the assets. The client might have sold or gifted assets to any other entity including (but not limited to) a trust, family member, charity, or other organisation.
When a client or their partner (if any) sells an asset in exchange for a loan, any outstanding debt must be included as an asset in the financial means assessment.

chunks.title: Available resources — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: When considering using discretion to include deprivation in the financial means assessment, consider if the client has access to other resources to meet the personal contribution they would have to make as a result. In general, we would not use discretion to count deprivation back into the financial means assessment if the client has no resources to meet their cost of care other than their exempt income or assets, or assets below the applicable threshold.

chunks.title: Available resources - trusts — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: When deprivation is identified and the client or their partner (if any) is a beneficiary, they are required to ask the trust for assistance to pay for their care. In a family trust, it is assumed resources are available to the client. If a trust refuses to support the client or agrees to provide what looks like an unreasonable amount of support, it is important to find out why and consider whether this is reasonable or not. Factors to consider include: - position of trust (wealth, income etc) - the number and needs of other beneficiaries - terms of the trust deed - historic patterns of support to client and other beneficiaries - scale of deprivation - reasons for trust or client's decision Note when a client is a beneficiary of a trust they are expected to request support from the trust regardless of deprivation having occurred. For more information see: Client is a trust beneficiary

chunks.title: Resources from a trust - not a beneficiary — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: If the client or their partner (if any) is not a beneficiary, they have minimal (if any) rights to seek support from the trust. In these cases, we cannot assume the client has access to other resources. However, there may be some cases where the client has received support from a trust in the past and it might be reasonable for the client to approach this trust for support.

chunks.title: Not appropriate to approach trust — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: In some situations, we would not expect the client to ask the trust for support. For example, if the client has a negative relationship with a trustee. For more information see: - Trusts - Client is a trust beneficiary

chunks.title: Available resources - family — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: If a client or their partner (if any) deprived themselves in a way that directly benefitted one or more of their family members it might be reasonable for the client to ask their family for assistance to pay for their care. This will depend on the facts of each case including the circumstances of the client’s family and the facts of the deprivation. Family is not obligated to support the client so if the client refuses to ask for support, or the family refuses to provide support, this is not deprivation and no resources are considered available to the client.

chunks.title: Benefit or pension contribution — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Benefit or pension contribution
Clients eligible for Residential Care Subsidy must contribute any New Zealand benefit or pension they are getting (less a personal allowance) towards the cost of their contracted care. This is usually done by a redirection of benefit. They may also have to make a further contribution if they get other income.
It is the client's responsibility to pay their benefit or pension contribution to the service provider and keep their personal allowances.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
A client is obliged to advise Work and Income of any change in their circumstances that may affect the payment of their main benefit, for example, if they (or their partner) are going to be absent from New Zealand.
When a client or their partner contacts you to advise that they intend travelling overseas you need to obtain the following information:
- date of departure (flight numbers if possible)
- date of return (flight numbers if possible)
Please refer to existing main benefit, changes and reviews for current policy instruction.
For those clients who are receiving a Residential Care Loan advise Legal Services.
For more information see:
- Leaving rest home
- Temporary absence
- New Zealand Superannuation Absence from New Zealand
- Supported Living Payment Absence from New Zealand

chunks.title: Advance payment of benefit — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Advance payment of benefit
A client financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy may be able to receive an Advance Payment of Benefit if they meet all of the qualifications.
Before considering an Advance Payment of Benefit, check that the item that they are applying for is not paid by, or the responsibility of, the service provider.
When processing a recoverable Advance Payment of Benefit in SWIFTT, the Residential Care Subsidy must be stopped first to view the client's correct entitlement and to recommend/approve/decline the Advance Payment of Benefit. You must contact the Residential Subsidy Unit in Whangarei who will do this for you. They will be responsible for re-starting the Residential Care Subsidy and re-directing the benefit contribution.
## SWIFTT
When recommending an Advance Payment of Benefit, an offset amount is required to be entered in SWIFTT. This offset amount is then removed by the Residential Subsidy Unit when re-starting the Residential Care Subsidy.
## Repayment
The Advance Payment of Benefit must not be recovered from the client's Personal Allowance unless the client gives their permission.
If the client gives their permission to recover the Advance Payment of Benefit from their Personal Allowance the appropriate MSD Collections is added as a payee on the client's record.
Do not commence recovery of an Advance Payment of Benefit until the client is released from care, or in the event of death, seek recovery from the client's estate.

chunks.title: Advises more than 14 days after the event — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Advises more than 14 days after the event
As clients have an obligation to advise Work and Income of any changes that may affect their entitlement to Extra help, it is expected that they will do so within a reasonable period. As a guideline, a reasonable period is considered to be within 14 days.
When a client advises of a change in circumstances more than 14 days after the event you should generally reduce or stop Extra help from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.
## Good and sufficient reason
Where there is a good and sufficient reason for the client not advising Work and Income of a change in circumstances within 14 days you may reduce, or stop Extra help from the first available date.
## Individual circumstances
You will need to consider the individual circumstances of the client to find out why they did not advise Work and Income of a change in their circumstances within 14 days. As a guideline, good and sufficient reason may include, but is not limited to, bereavement or onset of illness.
## False or misleading information
If the client gives false or misleading information you must review Extra help from the actual date of the change in circumstances and establish an overpayment where appropriate.

chunks.title: Annual review of income — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Annual review of income
A client can choose whether they wish to complete an 'Income Only' review form on an annual basis.
All clients with a private contribution towards the cost of their care are sent an 'Income Only' review form when Residential Care Subsidy is granted. The information sheet advises the client that they can request a review of their contribution at any time and that they can contact Senior Services - residential care to obtain an 'Income Only' review form.
For more information see:
- Means assessment of income
- Financial means assessment quick reference table
- Examples - Income reviews
- Review of financial means assessment
- Income only reviews

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client is obliged to advise the Ministry of Social Development of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their financial eligibility for Residential Care Subsidy.
For more information see:
- Absence from New Zealand
- Advance payment of benefit
- Advises more than 14 days after the event
- Death of a client
- Emergency assistance
- Entering rest home
- Existing client debt or payees
- Hospitalisation
- Income changes
- Leaving rest home
- Palliative care
- Property sold
- Repayment of loan
- Temporary absence
- Transfer between rest homes
## Reviews
- Review of Financial Means Assessment
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Review actions [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Death of a client — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Death of a client
When a client dies the service provider has no further entitlement to the client's benefit contribution from the day after death.
If the client was receiving a Residential Care Loan, Legal services must be informed and are responsible for seeking repayment from the estate.
For more information about when to cancel the main benefit see:
- Death of a client, changes and reviews New Zealand Superannuation
- New Zealand Superannuation Terminal Benefit rate
For information about loan repayment see:
- Repayment of loan
## Client with a partner
When the client had a partner, the rate of the partner's main benefit can be reassessed to the single rate from the day after the death of the client.
The only exception to this is if the new rate is less than the existing rate being paid to the surviving partner, such as when they are receiving Emergency Benefit paid at the single Supported Living Payment rate. This can continue to be paid for 28 days after death.
The partner is to be advised that any Extra help they received has been stopped and provided with details of their future payments. If the partner is receiving the single living alone rate this may continue unless the client has had a change in circumstances that means they are no longer living alone.
For more information see:
- Change in circumstances
- Advises more than 14 days after the event
- Special Disability Allowance

chunks.title: Emergency assistance — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Emergency assistance
A client receiving Residential Care Subsidy may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant if they meet all of the qualifications.
Before considering a Special Needs Grant, check that the item that they are applying for is not paid by, or the responsibility of, the service provider.
When processing a recoverable Special Needs Grant in SWIFTT, the Residential Care Subsidy must be stopped first to access the appropriate screen in SWIFTT and recommend/approve/decline the Special Needs Grant. You must contact the Residential Subsidy Unit in Whangarei who will do this for you. They will be responsible for re-starting the Residential Care Subsidy and re-directing the benefit contribution.
## SWIFTT
When recommending a recoverable Special Needs Grant an offset amount is required to be entered in SWIFTT. This offset amount is then removed by the Residential Subsidy Unit when re-starting the Residential Care Subsidy.
## Personal allowances
The recoverable Special Needs Grant must not be recovered from the client's Personal Allowance unless the client gives their permission. Do not commence recovery of any recoverable Special Needs Grant until the client is released from care, or in the event of death, seek recovery from the client's estate.
If the client gives their permission to recover the Special Needs Grant from their Personal Allowance the appropriate MSD Collections is added as a payee on the client's record.

chunks.title: Entering rest home — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Entering rest home
When notification is received that a client has entered residential care, stop all Extra help until it is determined whether or not the client is financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy.
Stop Extra help from the:
- date the client entered the rest home (current processing) or
- first available processing date if the client has advised of a change within 14 days of the event or
- date the client entered the rest home if the advice is received more than 14 days after the event
For more information see:
- Advises more than 14 days after the event

chunks.title: Example 1 - Mistaken Financial Means Assessment — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Financial means assessment (FMA) completed on 2 May 2010 and private contribution assessed based on 2009 financial accounts as these were the only financial accounts supplied and/or available at the time. On 10 October 2010 the client requests an income review as the 2010 financial accounts are now available and show less income. The FMA completed 2 May 2010 is mistaken as we did not have the most up to date accounts at the time. The client should have been asked whether the accountant is able to supply an estimate of income for the coming year. This would ensure our estimate is based on current information. The review date is 2 May 2010, the date of the mistaken FMA.

chunks.title: Example 2 - Income review — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Financial Means Assessment (FMA) is completed on 15 March 2010 and the client's private contribution is assessed from their term deposit interest. On 1 December 2010 the client phones to advise that the term deposit has been reinvested at a lesser rate. The client requests an income review form and this is sent the same day. On 11 December 2010 the income review form is received and shows that the term deposit changed on 20 November 2010. The review date is 1 December 2010, the date the client advised us of the change. An income review can be completed from the date the client advised us of the change, or the date the form is received whichever is to the client's advantage. In this case it is to the client's advantage to review from the date the client advised of the change. The income review cannot be completed from 20 November 2010, the date the term deposit was reinvested at a lower rate, as we cannot go back any earlier that the date the client advises us, or the date we become aware their circumstances have changed. The only exception to this is when a review is being completed due to: - partner enters care - partner dies - change in relationship status

chunks.title: Example 3 - Income review — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Financial means assessment (FMA) is completed on 14 January 2011 and private contribution is assessed from interest. On 4 March 2011 the client rings to advise term deposit will mature in a couple of weeks and requests income review form which is sent that day. On 4 April 2011 the form is received showing interest rate was reduced from 21 March 2011. The review can be completed from the date the client advised us of the change, or the date the form is received whichever if to the client's advantage. In this case the client advised us before the change happened so the review would be completed from 21 March 2011. Note if the interest rate had increased from the 21 March then the review would be completed from 4 April 2011 - the date the form was received.

chunks.title: Example 4 - Income review — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Financial means assessment completed on 10 April 2010 and the client is financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy based on a house and minimal cash. On 10 May 2011 the client phones to advise that the house has been sold. An income review should be initiated by MSD as it is reasonable to assume that their income is likely to have changed. An income review form should be sent to the client together with a letter requesting that they complete and return the form to enable an income review to be completed. If the income review form is not received within a reasonable time, the client will need to be contacted and requested to provide the information required for the income review to be completed. The review date is 10 May 2011, the date the client advised us of the change.

chunks.title: Existing client debt or payees — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Existing client debt or payees
When a client is granted Residential Care Subsidy any existing client debt recovery and payee links will need to be reviewed.
## Payees
The following payee deductions are required by legislation or court order and should not be stopped:
- Child Support
- Court deductions
- Court fines
- Debt Repayment Orders
- Liable Parent Contribution
- Maintenance
If a client entering residential care has any of these payments to a payee, encourage the client (or their agent) to approach the relevant agency to review the amount they need to pay.
All other payee deductions should be stopped from the day the client enters long-term residential care or the first available date if the client entered care in the past pay period.
## Kāinga Ora or community housing provider, and partner in the community
The Housing Processing Hub will be advised when a tenant goes into residential care. The Housing Processing Hub will delete the payee and reassess the Income Related Rent rate for the person remaining in the community.
## Client benefit debts
When a client is granted Residential Care Subsidy all client debt repayments are stopped from the date Residential Care Subsidy is granted or the first available date.
Clients who have been granted Residential Care Subsidy can continue to have their benefit debts recovered from their personal allowance if they have given permission. In this case the appropriate MSD Collections is then added as a payee on the client's record.
Note clients not eligible for Residential Care Subsidy, continue to have their benefit debt recovered.
Benefit debt includes overpayments, recoverable Special Needs Grants, Recoverable Assistance Payments and Advance Payment of Benefit, and Major Repairs Advances.
In the event of death, seek recovery of the benefit debt, Advance Payment of Benefit or Special Needs Grant debt from the client's estate.
