chunks.title: Hospitalisation — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Hospitalisation
If advice is received that the client has entered public hospital and is intending to return to the rest home, you must find out from the service provider how long the client is expected to remain in hospital.
The service provider must advise Work and Income in the event that the client:
- does not return to the rest home or
- transfers to another rest home or
- the client is in hospital for more than 13 weeks
## Client in hospital less than 13 weeks
If a client is to be in hospital less then 13 weeks, and the service provider is holding the client's bed and they will be returning to the rest home, continue paying the client's benefit contribution to the service provider unless the client elects to stop their benefit contribution. Add notes in CMS.
## Client in hospital for more than 13 weeks
From the beginning of the 14th week, you should stop the benefit redirection for Residential Care Subsidy. The client reduces to the hospital rate of payment. You must follow up the circumstances to determine whether the benefit re-direction for Residential Care Subsidy is to be re-started or whether the client leaves hospital and re-enters residential care. Add notes in CMS and update the client's address details.
## Residential Care Subsidy paid for 3 weeks only
Ministry of Health will only continue paying the client's Residential Care Subsidy for a maximum of 3 weeks.

chunks.title: Income changes — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Income changes
From 22 November 2006 when a client applies for a review of income contribution on the 'Residential Care Subsidy Application to Review form' a means assessment of income only, may be completed. Clients are not required to have a means assessment of assets completed.
## Overseas pensions
When a client is receiving an overseas pension that is similar in purpose to a New Zealand benefit or pension it will be directly deducted from the New Zealand benefit or pension.
Note before 22 November 2006, the entire overseas private pension was included in the means assessment of income.
## Reciprocal agreements
A client may be receiving a pension from a country that has a reciprocal agreement with New Zealand and therefore special provisions apply.
Any queries relating to the overseas pension should be directed to International Services.
For more information see
- Financial means assessment quick reference guide
- Income
- Income excluded
- Review of financial means assessment

chunks.title: Income only reviews — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Income only reviews
A client can request an income only review at any time if they know their income has changed or is about to change. The means assessment of income is to be completed from the date the review is initiated.
Generally the date of review is the date the client requested the review or the date the form is returned. See: Financial means assessment quick reference table
Clients are not required to have a means assessment of assets.
If the form is not returned by the client within a reasonable period of time, there is discretion around which date to use for the financial means assessment, depending on the circumstances. You need to consider the client's reason for the delay in returning the form to determine the date of the means assessment of income.
An income review can also be initiated if Senior Services - residential care become aware that the client's income has changed, or is about to change.
Examples include (but are not limited to):
- an inheritance
- proceeds from the sale of a property
- a win in a lottery
An income review form should be issued to the client.
If the client does not provide the necessary details to complete a review of income, or chooses not to generate income from the proceeds, the case should be referred to the manager client service delivery for direction.

chunks.title: Leaving rest home — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Leaving rest home
Where possible, stop any re-direction of benefit to the service provider from the date of discharge (current processing) or from the first available date.
If the client returns to live in the community, update the client's address details and invite applications for Extra help if appropriate. Add notes to CMS.
## Establishing debt
Do not establish a debt to the service provider if you are unable to stop the payments of the client's benefit from the date of discharge due to internal processing deadlines.
You must advise the client to discuss any payment owed to them with the rest home.
## Clients with a partner
You will need to review the rate of New Zealand Superannuation and stop the Special Disability Allowance paid to the partner from:
- the date the client left care (current processing) or
- the first available date if the advice of the change was received within 14 days of the client leaving care or
- the date the client left care if advice of the change was received more than 14 days after the event.
For more information see:
- Advises more than 14 days after the event

chunks.title: Palliative care — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Palliative care
Clients receiving palliative care are generally not required to complete a financial means assessment.
Note if an application for Residential Care Subsidy Financial Means Assessment form is received, Work and Income are obliged to complete a financial means assessment in all cases.

chunks.title: Sale after financially eligible for subsidy — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Sale after financially eligible for subsidy
When a single client in care or a client with a partner (or dependent child) who is not in care, owns a family home at the time a financial means assessment is completed and they qualify financially for a subsidy, their financial eligibility to the subsidy will not be affected if they subsequently sell the family home.
While a client is obliged to advise us of any change in their circumstances that might affect their financial means assessment, a review of the financial means assessment can generally only be completed if the client applies for a review.
For more information see:
- Review of financial means assessment
- Means assessment of assets
- Election process
- Sale of family home to re-purchase

chunks.title: Repayment of loan — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Repayment of loan
Repayment of a Residential Care Loan will be sought:
- upon the sale of the home or
- 6 months after the client dies
whichever is earlier.
Legal Executives are responsible for advising Ministry of Health to stop loan payments and for arranging repayment.
In some situations, the loan repayment can be deferred if a non-core family member remains in the home.
For more information see:
- Deferment of loan repayment
- Property sold
- Review client with a partner

chunks.title: Review client with a partner — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Review client with a partner
A review of the client's financial means assessment must be completed when a client's circumstances have changed as a result of:
- their partner in the community becoming a resident assessed as requiring care
- the death of their partner or
- a change in their relationship status
A review of the financial means assessment must assess the assets and if necessary, the income of the client whose circumstances have changed.
For more information see:
- Review of financial means assessment
- Financial means assessment quick reference table
- Review partner enters care
- Review partner dies

chunks.title: Review if there is a mistake — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Review if there is a mistake
A mistake can arise when (but is not limited to) a client or Senior Services - residential care identifies:
- assets or income not included in the financial means assessment
- assets or income have been included at an incorrect amount in the financial means assessment or
- assets or income have been included in the financial means assessment but should not have been included
It is not considered to be a mistake where income actually received is different from an estimated amount.
When it is considered a mistake has been made Senior Services - residential care can review the earlier financial means assessment.
## Example 1
A term deposit account was forgotten by the client and not entered on the financial means assessment form. The earlier mistake means assessment should be reviewed.
## Example 2
The case manager assessed the income contribution and Government Superannuation was included twice. The earlier mistaken means assessment should be reviewed.
If you are unsure what is a mistake you must discuss the circumstances with your Service Centre Trainer.
For more information see:
- Review of financial means assessment
- Financial means assessment quick reference table
- Examples - Income reviews

chunks.title: Review - not financially eligible — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Review - not financially eligible
If after a review of a client's means assessment of assets, it is found that the client is no longer financially eligible to receive Residential Care Subsidy, this may result in an overpayment of subsidy paid by Ministry of Health.
You need to advise the Ministry of Health of the outcome of the review of financial means assessment.
The recovery of any overpaid subsidy is between Ministry of Health and the service provider. Senior Services has no authority to deduct any Ministry of Health subsidy overpayment from the client's benefit unless an attachment order is received from the Ministry of Justice.

chunks.title: Review of financial means assessment — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Review of financial means assessment
A client who was previously means assessed and was not financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy can reapply for a further financial means assessment at any time.
The reapplication for financial means assessment is called a 'review' because it is a review of the client's initial financial means assessment. The client will need to fill in an Application to Review Financial Means Assessment form and provide updated information.
Clients receiving a Residential Care Loan who want to apply for a Residential Care Subsidy must fill in an Application to Review Financial Means Assessment form.
Note use the Needs Assessment Certificate from the initial application form.
Some reviews will need to consider whether eligibility should be backdated up to 90 days. For more information see: Financial Means Assessment quick reference table
A client's financial means assessment must be reviewed in each of the following circumstances:
- the client applies for review on the Application to Review Financial Means Assessment form or
- there is a reason to believe that there was a mistake in the earlier assessment or
when there is a partner and
- the partner becomes a resident assessed as requiring care or
- the partner dies or
- the partner's marital/relationship status has changed
Note unless one of the above situations apply, we are not obliged to review the financial means assessment.
Any client paying a private contribution can have an 'income only review' done when their income changes and Senior Services - residential care can initiate an income review by sending the appropriate form.
A client is obliged to inform us of any change in their circumstances. However, a review of their financial means assessment can only be completed if the client applies for a review on the Residential Care Subsidy Application to Review Financial Means Assessment form.
For more information see:
- Annual review of income
- Income only reviews
- Review if there is a mistake
- Review client with a partner
- Means assessment of assets
- Means assessment of income
- Residential Care Subsidy financial means assessment [no link find out why]
- Residential Care Subsidy procedures Review actions [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Review - partner dies — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Review - partner dies
When the partner of a person who has been financially means assessed dies, you must complete a review of the person's financial means assessment. A review must be done if the client is receiving a Residential Care Subsidy.
The effective date of the review is the day after the date of death of the partner.
If the previous financial means assessment confirms that the client would still be eligible for Residential Care Subsidy with no private contribution, then the information can be used to complete the review. A review form is not required in this situation.
Note if both partners were in receipt of the Residential Care Subsidy, the deceased partner's gifting is not included in the review of the surviving client's gifting assessment. This practice is applicable in this situation only.
For more information see:
- Review of financial means assessment

chunks.title: Review - partner enters care — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Review - partner enters care
When the partner of a person who has been means assessed becomes a resident assessed as requiring care, you must complete a review of the person's financial means assessment as at the date the partner entered care.
Note that a review of financial means assessment must be done regardless of whether the client is receiving a subsidy or a loan or is a private payer.
A form is not required unless used for gathering information.
If the previous financial means assessment is sufficient to confirm the client would continue to be eligible for Residential Care Subsidy with no private contribution, the information on the previous financial means assessment can be used to complete the review.
For more information see:
- Review of financial means assessment
- Review client with a partner

chunks.title: Temporary absence — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Temporary absence
If advice is received that the client will be absent from residential care for a temporary period, and the service provider is holding the client's bed, continue paying the client's benefit contribution to the service provider.
## Client's authorisation withdrawn
If the client withdraws their authorisation for benefit re-direction Work and Income is obliged to stop the re-direction. However where appropriate every effort should be made to discuss this with the service provider.
For more information see:
- Absence from New Zealand

chunks.title: Re-direction of benefit — extra help > residential care subsidy > changes and reviews residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Re-direction of benefit
If a client transfers from one rest home to another, stop the re-direction of benefit from the date the client leaves the previous rest home and re-direct to the new service provider from date of transfer (if within the current pay period) or from the first available date if the current processing deadline has passed.
## No re-direction of benefit
If a client transfers from one rest home to another, add the new service provider from the first available date.
## Do not establish a debt
Do not establish a debt to the previous service provider. The service providers are responsible for payment of benefit contribution between themselves until such time as the re-direction is made to the new rest home.

chunks.title: Client is a trust beneficiary — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Client is a trust beneficiary
Any income received from a trust is included in the means assessment of income.
When a client is assessed as needing residential care, they need to use resources available to them to meet the cost of their care. If the client is a beneficiary of a trust they are entitled and expected to request support from the trust.
If the client refuses to ask the trust for support this could be considered deprivation.
## When deprivation has been identified
When a client has deprived themselves of assets or income we can look to the trust as a source of other resources.
If the client or their partner (if any) is a beneficiary of a trust or is not a beneficiary but has a history of receiving support from the trust, we would expect them to ask for support to meet the cost of their care.
For more information see:
## Good cause not to ask the trust for support
In some cases, we would consider it reasonable for the client or their partner (if any) not to seek support from the trust.
Cases where it is reasonable for the client not to ask the trust for support include (but are not limited to):
- the trust has no resources so would not be able to support the client anyway
- the client has recently asked the trust for support
- there has been a relationship breakdown between the client and the trustee

chunks.title: Client not financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Client not financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy
If a client is not financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy, they must make their own arrangements to pay for their care from their own means.
The client will keep getting their New Zealand Superannuation, or any other benefit or pension, and it is up to the client how they pay for their care. It is up to the client to make payment arrangements to meet the cost of their care.
## Residential Care Loan
Clients not eligible for Residential Care Subsidy may apply for a Residential Care Loan.

chunks.title: Client with a partner — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Client with a partner
When a client aged 65 years or over has a partner, the financial means assessment includes the assets and income of both the client and their partner.
A partner, in relation to the client, means a person who is either:
- legally married to, or in a civil union with the client or
- in a de facto relationship with the client
A client is not considered single for the Financial Means Assessment if they are living apart only because one partner is in residential care, or is unable to reaffirm their marriage or civil union.
## Means assessment of assets
Clients who are over 65 must have assets equal to or below the applicable threshold to be financially eligible for a Residential Care Subsidy.
Assets that can be realised by the client and/or the client's partner are included in the financial means assessment. This may include the value of assets that the client and/or their partner have deprived themselves of or gifted in excess of allowable limits.
Even if the partner regards their assets as their own separate property, they are still included in the means assessment. If they are subject to a Property (Relationships) Act 1976 agreement, then the separate property assets will still be counted unless the couple have separated.
For more information see:
- Assets
- Asset thresholds
- Exempt assets
- Means assessment of assets
## Means assessment of income
The client and their partner's income are included in the means assessment of income when we are determining the client's contribution towards the cost of their care.

chunks.title: Client with a partner in the community — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Client with a partner in the community
If a client is in long-term residential care in a hospital or rest home and has a partner living in the community, the partner living in the community may get:
- New Zealand Superannuation paid at the single sharing accommodation rate or the single living alone rate
- Veterans Pension paid at the single sharing accommodation rate or the single living alone rate or
- Emergency Benefit paid at the Supported Living Payment single or sole parent rate (if they have a dependent child)
The benefit or pension type and rate the partner living in the community gets, is determined by the benefit or pension type they are getting when their partner enters long-term residential care in a hospital or rest home.
For New Zealand Superannuation it also depends on whether the partner living in the community is getting New Zealand Superannuation in their own right, or if they are getting a main benefit or ACC-Earnings Related Compensation.
For more information see:
- Summary rates of payment
- New Zealand Superannuation Grandparented non-qualified partner with a partner in long-term residential care
- New Zealand Superannuation Qualified client with a partner in long-term residential care
- Partner in community not receiving a benefit
## Special Disability Allowance
If the client in long-term residential care is receiving Residential Care Subsidy, the partner living in the community qualifies for a Special Disability Allowance if they are receiving a New Zealand benefit or pension.
For more information see:
- Special Disability Allowance
- Residential Care Subsidy Special Needs Grant and Advance Payments [no link find out why]
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit
- Advance payment of benefit

chunks.title: Clothing Allowance — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Clothing Allowance
The Clothing Allowance for Residential Care Subsidy is paid annually to all clients who are getting a Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Care Loan.
The annual payment is made automatically around the 1 April each year to the bank account that the client's Personal Allowance is paid to.
Clients qualify for a Clothing Allowance for Residential Care Subsidy if they:
- have applied for Residential Care Subsidy before 1 April in any year
and
- are financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy or if a Residential Care Loan is approved

chunks.title: Date of financial eligibility — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Date of financial eligibility
The Ministry of Health's liability to pay the cost of contracted care for a person starts from the date of financial eligibility.
The date of financial eligibility for a client aged 65 years or over is:
- the date the client entered long term residential care (if within 90 days of date application was received)
- the date the client's assets are equal to or below the relevant asset threshold (if within 90 days of date application was received) or
- the date 90 days prior to the date of application
whichever is the later.
Clients aged between 50 and 64 years, single with no dependent children, are considered to have assets equal to or below the threshold therefore the date of financial eligibility is:
- 1 July 2005
- the date of entry into care or
- the date they were needs assessed as requiring long-term residential care in a hospital or rest home i.e. date of entry to service
whichever is the later.
Note a client is liable for paying the full cost of their contracted care until the date of financial eligibility for Residential Care Subsidy.

chunks.title: Deprivation of assets and income — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Deprivation is a deliberate act or inaction resulting in assets or income not being available to the client. It may be direct or indirect. Deprivation is generally when a client or their partner (living or deceased) gives away more than the allowable limits or sells financial resources (assets) for less than fair value. Deprivation can only be of a client's own assets, income or entitlements. Once an asset has been gifted (for example, to a trust or family member), what is done with the asset and any income it generates cannot be attributed to the client. The act or inaction does not need to have been done for the purpose of getting Residential Care Subsidy. Each act of deprivation factually established might be counted back into the financial means assessment. A client and/or their partner (living or deceased) can deprive themselves of assets or income individually or as a couple. For more information see: - Examples of deprivation - Gifting

chunks.title: Bad investment decisions are not deprivation — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Deprivation is a factual determination and includes transactions where one person benefits at the expense of the other (for example an interest free loan). This is different to a bad investment decision where a transaction took place for fair value or in good faith, but the client had a loss or did not get a return. Poor investment decisions are not considered to be deprivation. For example, if the client invested in a family members company by purchasing shares at a fair value there has been no deprivation even if the company fails. However, if the client purchased shares in a family members company for significantly more than market value this could be considered deprivation because the intent of the transaction was to benefit family at the expense of the client.

chunks.title: Deprivation of income after entering care — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: When a client enters care, they are expected to generate income from their investments (where possible) to pay for their care. This means past investments that would not be considered deprivation might be assessed as deprivation going forward if the client does not make any changes to start earning income. For example, historic investments in bonus bonds would not be considered deprivation of income because the client had a chance of increasing their capital. However, once the client enters care they are expected to rearrange this so that the funds can earn an income. Failure to do so would be deprivation of income. The deprivation could be calculated based on the interest that would be received if the funds were in an interest earning account.

chunks.title: 3 step test — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Discretion is available to include deprived assets or income in the financial means assessment as if the deprivation had not occurred. When deprivation has occurred, this does not necessarily mean we should use discretion to include the deprived property and/or income in the assessment. A 3-step test is used to determine if deprivation has occurred and how much, if any, deprived amounts will be included.

chunks.title: Deprivation test — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Deprivation test
Discretion is available to include deprived assets or income in the financial means assessment as if the deprivation had not occurred. When deprivation has occurred, this does not necessarily mean we should use discretion to include the deprived property and/or income in the assessment.
A 3-step test is used to determine if deprivation has occurred and how much, if any, deprived amounts will be included.
1. Has deprivation occurred?
This is a factual consideration. Specific acts of deprivation need to be identified and assessed individually.
Please see:
- Deprivation of assets and income
- Examples of deprivation
2. Should discretion be used to include the deprivation?
Would including the deprivation make a difference to the financial means assessment outcome? For example, will it push the client’s assets over the threshold, or result in a lesser subsidy?
Are there other resources available to the client to meet the cost of care if a deprived amount is counted back? Generally, we do not use discretion to count the deprived amount in the financial means assessment if the client has no other resources except their exempt assets or assets below the threshold to meet the personal contribution they would have to pay towards their care as a result.
In some instances, resources may be assumed to be available to the client. For example, if the client and/or their partner is a beneficiary of a family trust, it might be reasonable to expect the trust to support the clients.
For more information see:
- Using discretion
- Available resources
3. How should the deprivation be applied?
Calculate the amount that was deprived (e.g. asset value, actual or notional income).
Determine a reasonable amount to include in the financial means assessment. The client must have resources available (other than assets under the threshold) to meet any extra contribution this amount will result in.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Election process — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Election process
Clients who have a partner who is not being assessed for residential care can choose the asset threshold used for their means assessment of assets. This decision is known as "election".
Clients in the above situation automatically have the lower "house and car exempt" asset threshold of $164,731 (as at 1 July 2026) applied to their means assessment of assets.
They can choose to have the higher "house and car not exempt" asset threshold of $300,811 (as at 1 July 2026) applied to their means assessment of assets instead.
If the lower "house and car exempt" asset threshold of $164,731 (as at 1 July 2026) is applied, the client's family home and/or one car (if they have one) are exempt from the means assessment of assets providing:
- the family home is the principal place of residence of the client's partner or dependent child
- the car is for the personal use of the client's partner
If the client chooses the higher "house and car not exempt" asset threshold of $300,811 (as at 1 July 2026), the current value of the family home and car must be included in the means assessment of assets.

chunks.title: Example 1 — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: A couple own their home which is worth $250,000 and a car worth $15,000. They also have $60,000 worth of investments. One partner enters residential care, and the other partner continues to live in the family home. The lower "house and car exempt" asset threshold of $164,731 (as at 1 July 2026) applies automatically. This allows the family home and car to be exempt from the means assessment of assets. The client's remaining assets will be included in their means assessment of assets. These assets of $60,000 (investments) are below the lower asset threshold of $164,731. It is unlikely that the client will choose the higher "house and car not exempt" asset threshold of $300,811 (as at 1 July 2026), because their total assets of $325,000 (including their family home and car) would exceed this threshold.

chunks.title: Example 2 — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: A couple own their home worth $120,000 and have investments worth $170,000. They do not own a car. One partner enters residential care, and the other partner continues to live in the family home. The lower "house and car exempt" asset threshold of $164,731 (as at 1 July 2026) applies automatically. The client's assets of $170,000 (excluding their family home) exceed the lower asset threshold. It is likely that the client will choose the higher "house and car not exempt" asset threshold of $300,811 (as at 1 July 2026), and have the family home included in the means assessment. Their total assets, including the family home of $290,000, are below the higher asset threshold of $300,811.

chunks.title: Example 3 — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: A couple do not own a home (as they are living with their adult daughter) but have a car valued at $6,000 and investments totalling $160,000. One partner goes into care and the other partner continues to live with their daughter. The lower "house and car exempt" asset threshold of $164,731(as at 1 July 2026) applies automatically. It is likely that the client will choose the higher "house and car not exempt" asset threshold of $300,811 (as at 1 July 2026), as they do not own a family home and their assets are above $164,731 This means the client will have their car included in the means assessment of assets. Their total assets of $166,000 are below the higher "house and car not exempt" threshold of $300,811.

chunks.title: Eligible before date of financial means assessment — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Eligible before date of financial means assessment
Generally, the means assessment of assets is determined as at the date the client has applied for Residential Care Subsidy.
However, a client's assets may be equal to or less than the asset threshold before the date the Residential Care Subsidy application was received.
If the assets are over the asset limit on the date the client entered the rest home the case manager will need to identify the date the assets went under the asset limit.
In these situations, the financial means assessment can be determined anytime within 90 days before the application date for a financial means assessment. The date from which the client's assets are equal to or below the threshold within the 90 days is the date they are financially eligible and the date the Ministry of Health's liability to pay Residential Care Subsidy begins.

chunks.title: Examples of deprivation — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Examples of deprivation
These are examples of deprivation. They are illustrative only and not intended to be a complete list. Deprivation must be assessed on a case by case basis.
Deprivation may have occurred in a number of circumstances including when the client or their partner (living or deceased):
- re-arranges their financial circumstances (including any gifting) which reduces their income or assets after having received written advice of the income contribution they are required to make
- does not generate past and/or current reasonable income from loans made to others,
- lends significant amounts of cash interest free (e.g. parents loaning deposit for house to children and not charging interest)
- makes a property transaction for less than the fair value, for example selling a property for less than current value; or renting a house for less than market rent.
- gifts over $27,000 per year outside the 5-year gifting period
- changes the ownership of land or the home registered as a joint tenancy, or where there is insufficient reason for the change (for which evidence may be required)
- makes a significant contribution to purchasing or improving property they have no ownership in
- sells or gifts a property to a trust or family member for inadequate financial return (e.g. does not get a life interest or deed of debt in exchange, or does not charge interest on loan)
- has cash assets which do not generate a reasonable income
- fails to request distributions from a trust or estate of which they are a beneficiary
- does not claim an inheritance
- fails to demand a payment or waives a right to income
- does not charge interest, or charges less than 2/3 of the Reserve Bank 6-month term deposit rate
- client instructs a trust or estate to cease distributions
- client consents to an estate ceasing distributions
- after entering care, keeps investments in a capital growth fund that does not earn a reasonable income, or exchanges income for capital
- has significant investments or financial arrangements that are structured and managed in a way that does not generate a reasonable income
The facts in each case must be considered individually.

chunks.title: Examples of life interest given in a will — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Examples of life interest given in a will
Examples of life interest given in a will
Full or broad life interest
- client is beneficiary of a will that says they have the full use, occupation and enjoyment of the estate's property for life
- the word 'use' generally includes any income generated from the property, unless there are other clauses in the will that limit or restrict the life interest
- there may also be provision in the will for the beneficiary to relocate if the residence no longer meets their needs and to purchase a replacement property
- there are no 'extinguishing events' set out in the will which limit the life interest. This means the life interest will remain in place until either the client chooses to transfer or dispose of it, or until the client dies
Limited life interest
- client or their partner has a right to ask the estate administrators for financial support and the estate administrators have 'absolute discretion' to make disbursements of income (payments) to them. (However if the discretion allows the estate administrators to gift estate assets to a beneficiary absolutely, then this may allow for an absolute gift rather than a life interest)
- client or their partner has the right to reside in estate property, but any income generated by the estate goes to another beneficiary of the will (eg a surviving sibling or an adult child of the deceased person) or
- the will sets out the 'extinguishing events' in which the life interest is to end eg when the surviving partner remarries, or leaves the property
Life interest has ended
- the life interest was only a right to occupy the estate's share of the family home. The client has left the property, which has now been sold
- the life interest was limited and the conditions for ending the life interest (an extinguishing event, eg leaving the property) have been met
## Read the will carefully
Wills need to be read carefully and in full to understand the terms of a life interest. The wording of life interest clauses can differ from case to case.
If the type of life interest given in a will is unclear, contact Legal Services for advice.

chunks.title: Excess gifting outside the 5 year gifting period — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Outside the 5-year gifting period, gifting over $27,000 in any one year is considered deprivation. MSD has discretion to include excess gifts made by a client or their partner (living or deceased) in the financial means assessment. For more information see: - Deprivation of assets and income When using discretion to include excess gifting outside of the gifting period, MSD must consider the impact this would have on the client, and if they have access to alternative resources to pay for their care.

chunks.title: Example - excess gifting inside and outside the 5-year gifting period - couple with one person in residential care — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: The clients own a family home in 2016 valued at $350,000 in 2015. The clients sell the home to a trust on 1 August 2020 for $350,000, complete an Acknowledgement of Debt and begin a gifting programme. The clients each make gifts (using forgiveness of debt) at $27,000 per year, from 1 August 2020. The final gifts are made on 1 August 2026. The gifting period for the 5 years before application is from 12 September 2021 to 11 September 2026. The excess of gifting of $54,000 outside of the 5-year period is considered deprivation and may (at MSD's discretion) be included in the financial means assessment.

chunks.title: Excess gifting within the 5-year gifting period — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Excess gifting within the 5-year gifting period
The 5-year period immediately before the Residential Care Subsidy application is called the 'gifting period'
A client and their partner (living or deceased) may gift up to a certain amount of assets or income per year, per application, without it affecting their financial means assessment.
When a client or their partner gifts more than the allowable gifting amount in any year within the 5-year gifting period, the excess gifting is offset in the following years of the gifting period providing they gift less than the allowable gifting amount in any of those years.
## Current allowable gifting amount
The allowable gifting amount within the 5 year gifting period is $8,500 per year from 1 July 2026.
For more information on the allowable gifting amounts that applied before 1 July 2026, see:
- Allowable gifting amounts (current)

chunks.title: Excluding life interest from the means assessment — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Clients applying for a Residential Care Subsidy need to tell the Ministry of Social Development if they have a life interest (also known as a lease for life) in their application. A life interest is only included in the financial means assessment of assets if the Ministry considers the life interest can be realised as a cash asset.

chunks.title: Client gets income from life interest — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: If the client gets an income from the life interest, or there is an intention by the estate to pay a reasonable income to the client, the Ministry may consider the life interest is not realisable. If the Ministry considers the life interest is not realisable, the life interest is excluded from the means assessment of assets and is included as income instead. The client cannot use the income-from-assets exemption for the income, as the life interest is not a realisable asset. In some cases a life interest may give an income and also be a realisable asset. The Ministry will consider these on a case by case basis.

chunks.title: Time to prepare a property for sale or rent — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: If an estate needs time to prepare a property for sale or renting in order to generate income or realise a life interest, and intends to honour the will provisions, the Ministry may not consider the life interest to be a realisable asset. Instead, the Ministry may undertake a review of income once the property has sold or been rented out, as there has been a change in the circumstances of the client. The Ministry may allow up to 6 months for the estate or trust to prepare a property for sale or rent. This may be necessary when a client has lived in the property for many years, and the property requires considerable maintenance before it can be sold or tenanted.

chunks.title: Life interest has ended but client not paid out — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: If a client or estate advise the life interest has ended, and the client has not been paid out by the estate, the Ministry may consider deprivation of an asset may have occurred. The Ministry must consider the client's role in any decision to transfer or dispose of their life interest without being paid out, the specific circumstances of the client and the structure of the life interest. Any decision to include a deprived asset or income stream from a life interest outside the 5 year gifting period in the financial means assessment depends on whether there are any other resources available to the client that can be used to pay for their residential care.

chunks.title: Life interest in will, not honoured by the estate — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: When the terms of a life interest given in a will are not honoured by an estate, the Ministry may calculate the fair value of the life interest and consider whether it should be included as deprivation in the financial means assessment. This will depend on the client's full circumstances, including the nature of the life interest, the terms of the will, the reason the terms are not being honoured and the relationship between the client and the administrators of the estate. If this is unclear please contact Legal Services who will be able to assist.

chunks.title: Calculating the fair value of a life interest — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: The fair value of a life interest is calculated by the Ministry using tables in Schedule 2 of the Estate and Gift Duties Act 1968. The life interest is calculated using the asset values, and client's age on the date they applied for a Residential Care Subsidy.

chunks.title: Exempt assets — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Assets exempt from the means assessment of assets are as follows: - any interest in a residential dwelling that is the principal place of residence of the client's partner or dependent child (unless the client has elected the higher asset threshold through the election process). - any interest in one car or similar vehicle that is for the use of the client's partner or dependent child (unless the client has elected the higher asset threshold through the election process). - any compensatory or ex gratia payments from any country to a client or their partner (if any) because they were a prisoner of war, civilian internee or a victim of persecution of any country during the Second World War or were a dependent child of someone that was - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Christchurch mosques attack support payments - specified Ex gratia and Compensation payments - pre-paid funeral trust funds or accounts for the client and their partner up to the value of $10,000 each - payments to victims of crime and their families administered by Victim Support - payments made by the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) are: exempt as an asset for a period of 48 months from the day after the payment is made, if the client intends to use the payment to repair or rebuild the home, or purchase a further home orexempt as an asset for a period of 12 months from the day after the payment is made in all other cases - exempt as an asset for a period of 48 months from the day after the payment is made, if the client intends to use the payment to repair or rebuild the home, or purchase a further home or - exempt as an asset for a period of 12 months from the day after the payment is made in all other cases

chunks.title: Exempt assets — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: - payments from the Earthquake Commission and insurance companies for rebuilding or repairing the damage to homes caused by the Canterbury Earthquake 2010 (including aftershocks) or the costs of renting temporary accommodation because people can no longer live in their home due to damage from the Canterbury Earthquake 2010 (including aftershocks) are: exempt as an asset for a period of 48 months from the day after the payment is made, if the client intends to use the payment to repair or rebuild the home, or purchase a further home orexempt as an asset for a period of 12 months from the day after the payment is made in all other cases - exempt as an asset for a period of 48 months from the day after the payment is made, if the client intends to use the payment to repair or rebuild the home, or purchase a further home or - exempt as an asset for a period of 12 months from the day after the payment is made in all other cases - payments or part payments from the Crown for the purchase of property in the Canterbury red zone that are made on or after 23 June 2011 are: exempt for a period of 48 months from the day after the last payment is made for their home and land, where the client intends to use the payment to repair or rebuild the home, or purchase another home - exempt for a period of 48 months from the day after the last payment is made for their home and land, where the client intends to use the payment to repair or rebuild the home, or purchase another home - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after the payment is made - funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts - an ACC lump sum payment or a lump sum payment of an Independence Allowance made to a client. This exemption applies only in the first 12 months after the payment is made. - personal belongings such as clothing and jewellery, personal collectibles, or family treasure/taonga such as art, books, stamps, antiques - household appliances and furniture and effects - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 - Payments to clients whose Housing New Zealand tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made

chunks.title: Exempt assets — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: - severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment) - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received

chunks.title: Farms — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Farms
If the client owns a house on a farm, and the house is the principal residence of the client's partner or dependent child, the farm is not included as an asset in the financial means assessment.
If the client has chosen to have the $300,811 (as at 1 July 2026) threshold applied, the house and farm are not exempt (they must be included as an asset in the financial means assessment).
If the client applies for a review of their financial means assessment and the house is no longer the principal residence of their partner or dependent child, or they choose the $300,811 (as at 1 July 2026) threshold, the house and farm must be included as an asset in the financial means assessment.

chunks.title: Financial means assessment — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Financial means assessment
The financial means assessment determines if a client is financially eligible to get Residential Care Subsidy and the contribution a client is required to make towards the cost of their contracted care services.
The Residential Care Subsidy Financial Means Assessment application form must be accompanied by the completed Needs Assessment Certificate.
Note Needs Assessment Service Co-ordination Agencies are responsible for distributing the Residential Care Subsidy Financial Means Assessment application forms to clients. The Residential Care Subsidy Financial Means Assessment application form is only given to an eligible person.
There are 2 parts to the financial means assessment:
- means assessment of assets
determines if a client is financially eligible by assessing if a client's assets are at or below the applicable threshold
- means assessment of income
determines the contribution a client is required to make towards the cost of their contracted care services
Note the means assessment of income is only completed when the means assessment of assets has determined a client is financially eligible.

chunks.title: Gifting — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Gifting describes gifts of real or personal property including assets, income and cash that the client or their partner (living or deceased) gives away. This can be by: - an established gifting programme with an Acknowledgement of Debt and/or Inland Revenue Gifting Statements (which were required to be filed until October 2011) or - assets, income or cash being given to another person or entity Gifting is assessed on the facts and on what the client or their partner (living or deceased) have done, not what they intended to do or intend to do in the future. Intended gifts or gifts not completed cannot be assessed.

chunks.title: Gifting within the gifting period — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: The 5-year period immediately before the Residential Care Subsidy application is called the 'gifting period'. During the gifting period, a client and their partner (living or deceased) can gift up to a certain amount of assets or income per year, per application without it affecting their financial means assessment. This allowable gifting amount can only be applied from the date of the first gift, within the 5-year gifting period. Gifts over the allowable gifting amount (excess gifts) must be included in the means assessment of assets. There is no discretion not to include excess gifts made during the gifting period.

chunks.title: Current allowable gifting amount — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: The allowable gifting amount within the 5-year gifting period is $8,500 per year from 1 July 2026. For previous allowable gifting amounts, see: - Allowable gifting amounts

chunks.title: Couples gifting — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: The allowable gifting amount is up to $8,500 per year, per application, within the 5 year gifting period. This limit applies regardless of whether a client is single, or has a spouse or partner. If only one application is received for a client with a partner, the allowable gifting amount is not $8,500 per year each but is a total of $8,500 for both. If both clients apply for a Residential Care Subsidy, then each client can have gifted $8,500 per year.

chunks.title: Before the 5-year gifting period — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Before the 5-year gifting period, gifting up to $27,000 in any one year is allowed. For couples this is not $27,000 per year each but is a total of $27,000 for both. Any gifting over this amount each year is considered deprivation. At MSD's discretion, it may be included in the means assessment of assets.

chunks.title: Gifts by deceased partner — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Gifts made by a deceased partner are included in the assessment of gifting in both the gifting period (ie the last 5-years) and in the assessment of gifting before the 5-year gifting period.

chunks.title: Gifts in recognition of care — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Gifts in recognition of care can be allowable gifts provided they meet set criteria. These gifts are included in the allowed maximum gifting of $42,500 in the 5 year gifting period (as at 1 July 2026), along with any other gifts the client or their partner have made. There is no extra allowance for gifts made in recognition of care.

chunks.title: Gifting in recognition of care — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: If allowable gifting during the gifting period is less than $42,500 as of 1 July 2026 a gift in recognition of care may be considered as an allowable gift. Gifts may be made by the client or partner (living or deceased) to another person who has provided a high level of care to the client. A gift in recognition of care may be regarded as an allowable gift if it meets all the following criteria: - the gift was made within the 12-month period immediately before the client's date of application for Residential Care Subsidy - the client received care for a continuous period of at least 12 months during the gifting period - the client lived in the same household as the person providing the care - the gift was made to the person who provided the care - the client had the care provided to them by a person, who is not their partner or dependent child - the client received a high level of care in the form of necessary assistance around the home, for example, personal care such as assistance with bathing and toileting, domestic assistance - the client did not receive any Ministry of Health funded home-based disability support services, while living in the home including Home Support (this includes household management, domestic assistance or personal assistance), meals on wheels or other Ministry of Health home-based assistance and - the client remained in their home, as crucial care was provided which delayed the need to access Ministry of Health funded residential care Note clients getting Carer Support (formerly Aid to Families, Respite Care, Alternative Care or 90-days relief) can still qualify for the gifting in recognition of care.

chunks.title: Amount of gift in recognition of care — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: A gift in recognition of care must be made within the 12 months before the clients application for Residential Care Subsidy. Gifts in recognition of care can be up to $8,500 (as at 1 July 2026) for each 12-month period of care received. For previous gifting amounts see: - Allowable gifting amounts Gifts in recognition of care, when combined with other allowable gifting in the gifting period, cannot exceed $42,500. The allowable gifting limit in recognition of care applies to a couple regardless of whether both have applied. The limits do not double if both partners gift in recognition of care and each apply for Residential Care Subsidy.

chunks.title: Example - gifting in recognition of care — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: A client who meets all the criteria for gifting in recognition of care has applied for a Residential Care Subsidy on 2 September 2026. The client received care for the past 3 years from their child and made a gift of $18,000 to them in recognition of this care on the 2 August 2026 (within the 12 months immediately before the client's application for Residential Care Subsidy). The client also gifted $12,000, 2 years ago on 22 September 2024 to their sibling. During the 5-year gifting period, a client can gift up to $8,500 per year. The client can also make additional gifts in recognition of care up to a maximum of $42,500 during the gifting period (if total gifting does not exceed $42,500). Allowable gifting in recognition of care is 3 years x $8,500 = $25,500. Because total gifting ($18,000 + $12,000) within the gifting period does not exceed $42,500, all gifting is allowable.

chunks.title: Granny flats — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Granny flats
Granny flats are usually co-sited on one property with a main residential dwelling. Granny flats range from 'outside rooms' to fully self-contained units.
Assets that are capable of being realised must be included in the means assessment of assets. If a client is able to sell the granny flat then it should be included as an asset in the financial means assessment.
Sometimes the client can't sell the granny flat but has a right to occupy it, either by contract or by an arrangement (example, a licence to occupy). In this case, the right to be paid money when that contract or arrangement ends is a realisable asset. Take into account any conditions or restrictions on the right to be paid money.
For more information see:
## Deprivation
If the client has spent significant amounts on building, purchasing or maintaining a granny flat, but has no share in the ownership of it, you may need to consider if deprivation has occurred. This will be case dependent.

chunks.title: Historic deprivation — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Historic deprivation
Deprivation is factually determined based on specific acts. Where deprivation of income took place in a historical period it can still be assessed.
## Adjusting investments
Bad investment decisions or chance investments that took place in the past are generally not considered deprivation. When a client applies for Residential Care Subsidy they are required to adjust investments to generate a reasonable income from the resources available to them.
For example, historic investments in bonus bonds would not be considered deprivation of income because the client had a chance of increasing their capital. However, once the client enters care they are expected to rearrange this so that the funds can earn an income. Failure to do so would be deprivation of income. The deprivation could be calculated based on the interest that would be received if the funds were in an interest earning account.
For more information see:
- Deprivation of assets and income
## Including historic deprivation
If a client made a transaction that was intended to benefit the other party, it is reasonable to assess deprivation of income for a historical period. For example, the sale of an asset in exchange for an interest free debt.
If the sales transaction also involved benefits for the client, you can offset these benefits from the interest forgone for the historic period.
When we have identified deprivation of income for a historic period, the amount of deprivation can be calculated by crystallising the income forgone. There is discretion to include the crystallised amount as a deprived asset in the financial means assessment.
For more information see:
- Using discretion
## Calculating interest forgone
When possible, calculate the amount of deprived income from interest forgone by using the interest rate specified in the loan for its duration.
After the loan repayment period, calculate any compounded amounts using the Reserve Bank 6 month term deposit rate. If there was no interest rate specified in the loan, use the Reserve Bank 6-month term deposit interest rate for the entire calculation.
Example:
A single client sells their house to a trust in exchange for an interest-free debt. The debt is progressively forgiven over the years, within the allowable threshold.
The client lived in the house rent free until entering care. The value of free rent the client received can be used to offset the interest forgone on the debt owed to the client.

chunks.title: Income — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Income
The estimated net annual income is assessed as at the date of financial means assessment. The annual income is used to determine the weekly contribution, up to the maximum contribution, that the client must pay towards the cost of their contracted care.
Always use net income. If the income is non-taxable use the amount the client gets, do not deduct an amount for tax.
Note although some forms of income are not taxed they are still considered income. Whether income is taxed or not, is irrelevant. An example is Government Superannuation, which is paid as a 'free of tax' payment but is still considered income.
The means assessment of income includes (but is not limited to):
- any income from assets of the client and partner (less the income from assets exemption)
- any benefit received by the client but not their partner (if any)
- 50% of any private pension received by the client or their partner (if any) under a superannuation scheme constituted in New Zealand or overseas
- 50% of any payments received by the client or their partner (if any) under a life insurance policy issued either in New Zealand or overseas
- any income distributed to the client or their partner (if any) from a trust or estate
- any interest or other income derived from a KiwiSaver account outside the locked-in period for the client or their partner
Note information share Child Support payments must not be included in the means assessment of income. Any Child Support a person gets must be self-declared for the purposes of Residential Care Subsidy (including any payments that may have been notified to MSD through the information share with Inland Revenue).
All Child Support payments are generally treated as non-information share Child Support payments and considered income under the general income charging rules.
For more information see:
- Client with a partner
- Private pensions
- Income from assets
- Income from life interest or lease for life
- Income from a trust
- Income from an estate
- Income from rent
- Income from royalties
- Income excluded
- Maximum contribution
- Means assessment of income
- Income verification [no link find out why]
## Advances or loans
If a client is advanced or loaned amounts by a third party (e.g. a trust or family member) it is important to check if there is a genuine expectation for the client to repay these amounts.
If the debt is not genuine the amounts are considered income and should be included in the financial means assessment.

chunks.title: Income excluded — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Do not include the following income when completing the means assessment of income: - any income that is earned by the client's partner (if any) from personal effort - any benefit paid to the client's partner (if any) - any pension or allowance paid under the Veterans' Support Act 2014 for the person’s own disablement (except for weekly income compensation and weekly compensation payments, which must be included as income) - any overseas war pension paid by the government of any Commonwealth country provided they are the equivalent of the New Zealand disablement pensions, surviving spouse or dependent pensions - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - Energy Trust Dividends and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after payment is made - MSD lump sum payments and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after payment is made - Christchurch mosques attack support payments and income earned on the payment - 50% of any pension received by a client or their partner (if any) under a superannuation scheme constituted in New Zealand or overseas - 50% of any payments received by a client or their partner (if any) under a life insurance policy either issued in New Zealand or overseas - any compensatory or ex gratia payments from any country to a client or their partner (if any) because they were a prisoner of war, civilian internee or a victim of persecution of any country during the Second World War or were a dependent child of someone that was - ex gratia payments paid to people who have suffered a personal injury that is or was caused by a Hepatitis C infection contracted through the New Zealand blood supply. This exemption applies only in the first 12 months after the payment is made - ex gratia payments made by the New Zealand Government to Viet Nam Veterans, their partner (including former partners) or their natural children and their children's immediate family - specified Ex gratia and Compensation payments and income earned on those payments - any interest generated from the compensatory or ex-gratia payments referred to above - any interest derived from any pre-paid funeral of the client or their partner (if any) - any interest derived from any KiwiSaver account or superannuation scheme account within the locked-in period of the client or their partner (if any) - any ACC Independence Allowance paid as a continuing payment - any Temporary GST Assistance paid to the client or their partner
