chunks.text: - payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after the payment is made - severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment) - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received Note while information share Child Support payments must not be included in the means assessment of income, any Child Support a person gets must be self-declared for the purposes of Residential Care Subsidy. All Child Support payments are generally treated as non-information share Child Support payments and considered income under the general income charging rules.

chunks.title: Income from a trust — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Income from a trust
Any income a client or their partner (if any) receives from a trust is included in the means assessment of income.
## Client is a beneficiary of a trust
Clients are expected to use the resources available to them before seeking financial support through a Residential Care Subsidy.
If a client is a beneficiary of a trust and not receiving disbursements or receiving lower disbursements than they were immediately before entering care, we would generally expect them to approach the trust for assistance. If the client does not want to approach the trust, the trust declines disbursements, or the trust refuses to increase the current level of distributions, ask for an explanation why.
If a client has instructed the trust to stop or reduce disbursements, this would be considered deprivation of income.
## Initiate an income review
If the trust agrees to provide disbursements or increase support from a date later than their application date for Residential Care Subsidy, you will need to complete an income review from that date.

chunks.title: Income from an estate — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Income from an estate
If a client is entitled to income from an estate (eg dividends from shares), failure to claim this could be deprivation.
If the executor of an estate fails to distribute to the client what they are entitled to under the terms of the Will, the client has not deprived themselves unless they instructed or gave prior consent to the executor to do so.
A client cannot be held accountable to decisions of the estate. However, when a client (or their partner or agent) has refused or failed to request an entitlement under the terms of the estate, deprivation could be considered.

chunks.title: Income from assets — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Income from assets
Income from assets may include (but is not limited to) income from:
- a business
- Maori land
- rental properties
- investments
- shares
- personal loans
- royalties
- company or partnership
- a life interest (eg rental income from family home)
## Charging deprived income
A deprived income charge may apply if a reasonable income is not earned from assets or investments, and there are resources available to the client to pay for their residential care.
Example
A client chooses to keep savings in a capital growth fund that does not earn reasonable interest. A reasonable interest amount is at least 2/3 of the Reserve Bank 6-month term deposit rate.
## Loss of income from assets gifted or sold
When a person sells or gives away an asset, the future income earning potential is included in the transaction.
This means the Ministry of Social Development cannot assess deprivation of income on a gifted or sold asset.
If an asset is gifted in excess of allowable amounts or sold for less than fair value, the deprived asset amount is inclusive of the future income potential of that asset, and so no deprivation of income is assessed.
Any decision to include a deprived asset or income stream in the financial means assessment outside the 5 year gifting period, depends on whether there are any other resources available to the client that can be used to pay for their residential care.

chunks.title: Income from assets exemption — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Income from assets exemption
Some income generated from assets is exempt from the means assessment of income.
This income exemption applies to any income the client and their partner (if any) get from their assets. The amount of the income exemption depends on the client's circumstances.
The income from assets exemption (as at 1 July 2026) is:
Category
Net income exemption (per year)
Single person
$1,306
Client with a partner - both in care
$2,612
Client with a partner in the community
$3,918
This exemption does not apply to income that is not from the client's and partner's (if any) assets.

chunks.title: Income from life interest or lease for life — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Income from life interest or lease for life
A life interest gives the holder (known as the life tenant) specified or full rights of occupation and enjoyment of the asset. The life tenant can surrender the interest at any time however they cannot gift it by will, as it ends at the time of their death.
When a client (or their partner) is receiving income from a life interest or lease for life the income must be included in the means assessment of income, unless the income from assets exemption applies.
If the life interest or lease for life is not a realisable asset it is not included in the means assessment of assets, and the income from assets exemption cannot be applied.

chunks.title: Income from rent — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Income from rent
Rental income is assessed at the net rate by:
- deducting all allowable outgoings from the rental income
Outgoings can include:
- local authority rates (including water rates charged by a local authority, regardless of how the rates are calculated). If the applicant receives a rebate on any of these items, this must always be deducted.
- building insurance
- contents insurance (only if rental property is furnished)
- mortgage interest
- agents' fees
- essential repairs and maintenance
- body corporate levies

chunks.title: Income from royalties — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Income from royalties
Royalties are generally paid for the use of intellectual property or physical assets.
Assessment of income from royalties is based on the amounts received in the last 52 weeks, and the amount received (less tax) is to be included in the means assessment of income.
## Personal earnings exemption does not apply
The personal earnings exemption does not apply as the 'effort' was made previously, and there is no further 'effort' being made.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Residential Care Subsidy is a subsidy paid through Health New Zealand – Te Whatu Ora.
The subsidy assists with the cost of contracted care for a client in long-term residential care in a hospital or rest home indefinitely.
The amount of subsidy is the difference between the cost of contracted care and the amount a client is required to contribute for that care.
Eligibility for most people is determined through an asset and income test known as the Financial Means Assessment.
A Financial Means Assessment is required under the Residential Care and Disability Support Service Act 2018 when clients are applying for Residential Care Subsidy. Clients applying for this assistance need to use the resources available to them before seeking assistance under this Act.
Senior Services - residential care assess a client's financial eligibility to Residential Care Subsidy and the income contribution they are required to make.
The Ministry of Health is responsible for the payment of Residential Care Subsidy to the hospital or rest home where the client resides.
Note people aged between 50 and 64 with a partner and/or a dependent child are fully funded by the Ministry of Health and are not means assessed.

chunks.title: Trust — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Trust
A trust is a legal obligation accepted by the trustees to hold property for the benefit of beneficiaries of the trust.
The trust property is commonly gifted or sold by the 'settlor'.
## Settlor
The person(s) who sets up the trust. Normally this is the person(s) intending to sell or gift assets to the trust but sometimes it is another person (such as a lawyer) who is merely setting up the mechanism of a trust to be used by someone else (such as the client).
## Trustees
The people appointed to hold legal ownership of the trust's assets under an obligation to manage these in a way that will benefit the beneficiaries.
Their prime duty is to carry out the terms of the trust deed and preserve trust property.
## Beneficiaries
Individual(s) or group(s) for whose benefit the trust was established. Beneficiaries have a legal right to seek disbursements from the trust.
It is at the Trusts discretion to make distributions (for example, regular payments) to discretionary beneficiaries. It is a legal obligation to distribute Trust contents to the final beneficiaries when it is wound up.
## Trust deed
This is the document that establishes the trust. It will be signed by the settlor and the trustee(s) and outline who the trustees and beneficiaries are.
The deed usually states the purpose of the trust which may include how the property should be invested, when distributions can be made, as well as what powers are given to the Trustees.

chunks.title: KiwiSaver — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## KiwiSaver
Money held in a KiwiSaver account is included in the means assessment of assets if the funds are no longer locked in.
Generally, all KiwiSaver funds have a lock in period until age 65 years.
## KiwiSaver funds not 'locked in' are cash assets
From 1 July 2019, people can join KiwiSaver at any age.
Generally, the funds of members who join when they are 65 or over are not 'locked in'. This means they are cash assets.
Income received from the invested funds is treated as income.
## A lock in period may exist for some client's aged 65 years and over depending on when they joined KiwiSaver
Before 1 July 2019, clients who were age 60 to 64 when they joined KiwiSaver were subject to a 5-year locked in period before they could access their funds.
When these client's turn 65 on or after 1 April 2020 they will have a choice of:
- accessing their KiwiSaver funds or
- continuing for the remainder of the locked in period
For more information on when a lock-in period exists for those aged 65 years and over and how it may affect their payments see: Lock-in period exists for some clients over age 65 years
## KiwiSaver funds withdrawn
When the client is entitled to withdraw their KiwiSaver balance, they may choose to reinvest it with the same provider or another investment provider, buy an annuity or receive cash. When this applies the funds are cash assets.
Any interest or other income received by the client or their partner from KiwiSaver funds outside the locked-in period is included in the means assessment of income.

chunks.title: Licence to occupy — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Licence to occupy
Clients who live in flats or houses on hospital or rest home grounds, and clients living in retirement villages usually purchase a licence to occupy rather than purchase the premises.
When a client purchases the licence to occupy, the surrender value will normally be refundable, and should be included as an asset in the means assessment of assets.
## Client with a partner living in the community
If the client has a partner in the community living in the licence to occupy flat or house, this may be exempt unless the client has chosen the higher $300,811 (as at 1 July 2026) asset threshold on the application form.
## Licence to occupy purchased by another person or entity
If the licence to occupy is in the client's name, but the licence was purchased by another person or entity (for example, a family member or trust), then any money due upon surrender would be paid to the other party. The license would not be included as an asset in the financial means assessment if the client can prove this is the arrangement.

chunks.title: Life insurance — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Life insurance
A life insurance policy can be included in the means assessment of assets if the policy has a cash value (also known as surrender value) that is realisable.
If the life insurance policy is payable only on the client's death, do not include it as an asset because it is not a realisable asset.

chunks.title: Life interest as an asset or income stream — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Life interest as an asset or income stream
A client's life interest may include a right to get income from a deceased persons estate for their lifetime.
If the estate's administrators honour the client's right to income from the estate, instead of purchasing the life interest from the client, then the income is included in the client's financial means assessment.
In this situation an income stream from a life interest is confirmed and the estate administrators are not going to purchase the life interest. The income from the life interest is included in the client's financial means assessment. The life interest is not considered to be realisable and is not included as an asset in the financial means assessment.
In some cases a life interest may give an income and also be a realisable asset. The Ministry will consider these on a case by case basis.
If the estate purchases the client's life interest and pays the client a lump sum in exchange, the lump sum payment is an asset and is included in the financial means assessment of assets. The payment needs to be of fair value otherwise deprivation may need to be considered.
If the type of life interest is unclear, contact Legal Services for advice.

chunks.title: Life interest given in a will — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: There are different kinds of life interests (also known as a lease for life) that may be given to a person in a will, including but not limited to a: - right to use, occupy and enjoyment of a property, or part of the estate from a will (a lease for life) - right to income from an estate, including from investments or other assets - right to rental income from a property A person who is given a life interest is sometimes called a 'life tenant'. When a person is given a life interest, legal ownership of the property or other assets is not included in the life interest. The property or other assets remain held by the estate or trust. In determining the nature and extent of the interest the specific wording used is important. Life interest clauses will need to be reviewed on a case by case basis, as the extent of the interest may change depending on the specific wording of the will.

chunks.title: Extinguishing events — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: The person will generally have the right to benefit from the life interest for their lifetime, or until an earlier 'extinguishing' event written in the will. Examples of extinguishing events may include the person remarrying, or being unable to maintain or live in the property they have a life interest in.

chunks.title: Disposing of a life interest — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: A person may be able to transfer or dispose of their life interest as they choose during their lifetime, but the life interest will not continue past the death of the original life tenant.

chunks.title: Life interest in share of property as a tenant in common — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: A life interest may be created when a couple owned a family home in individual half shares as tenants in common. In the will the deceased partner may leave the surviving partner a life interest over the deceased partner's share of the property. This is different to when a couple own a family home as joint tenants. A joint tenancy is when there is no distinct share of the property owned by each partner, they own the property together. In this case, when one partner dies, the legal ownership of the whole property automatically transfers to the surviving partner by survivorship (regardless of what the will says). There is no life interest in this case. This is why it is important to confirm ownership of the property. You can generally confirm this by obtaining a copy of the certificate of title for the property. If the type of life interest is unclear, contact Legal Services for advice.

chunks.title: Life interest from matching wills — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: A couple may have matching wills that each provide for a life interest to the other. The partner given the life interest will generally keep ownership of their own share in the property or other assets, as well as get a life interest in the deceased partner's share.

chunks.title: Example of life interest given in a will — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Bernard is a widower and owns half of the family home he and his wife June owned, and June's estate holds the other half. June's Will says that until Bernard dies, he has a life interest in her share of the property. It also says that when Bernard dies the estates of both June and Bernard will be distributed to their children. When Bernard applies for a Residential Care Subsidy, the Ministry needs to consider whether his life interest in June's share of the house is realisable. Factors to consider are: - whether the house is going to be sold and will the estate administrator pay Bernard for his life interest as a lump sum asset or - will the estate administrator rent the house out and pay Bernard a regular income stream instead or - is the house already rented out or sold, and is the estate administrator already paying Bernard income from the estate or - is there no intention by the estate administrator to pay anything to Bernard? If the type of life interest is unclear, contact Legal Services for advice.

chunks.title: Life interest must be realisable to be included in means assessment — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Clients applying for a Residential Care Subsidy need to tell the Ministry of Social Development if they have a life interest (also known as a lease for life) in their application. A life interest must be included in the client's financial means assessment of assets if the life interest can be realised as a cash asset. A life interest is realisable as a cash asset if it can be converted into cash for the client to use towards the cost of their residential care. If a life interest cannot be realised as a cash asset it is not included in the financial means assessment of assets. You will need to factually determine whether or not the life interest is capable of being realised as a cash asset. If it is realisable, the life interest is valued as at the date of the client's application for a Residential Care Subsidy.

chunks.title: Factors that may indicate life interest is realisable — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Factors that may indicate life interest is realisable: - a value was attached to the life interest when it was given to the client (eg a value set out in the will or property agreement). - it can generate an income - there are minimum, if any, restrictions on the life interest - a market of potential buyers for the interest exists A life interest that gives the client broad rights with few or no limits to income from a property, or allows them to retain effective control of the property, is likely to have a market of potential buyers.

chunks.title: Factors that may indicate life interest is not realisable — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Factors that may prevent a life interest from being realised include: Advanced age of the client The life interest's value is linked to the client's age. The older a client is, the lower the value of their life interest, and it is less likely the interest is going to be valuable or profitable to buy. This may support a decision that the life interest would not be a realisable asset. However, if a property has increased in value it may still be realisable, regardless of the client's age. Lack of willing buyers If there is a very limited market of buyers for the life interest it may not be a realisable asset as the client cannot use it to meet the cost of their residential care. - Example:Carol is widowed and has a broad life interest in the family home she owned with her husband Dennis. Carol allows their adult child, Donald, who is getting Supported Living Payment, and his dependent children, to live in the family home instead of renting it out or selling it. Donald will inherit the property when Carol dies and has no means to buy the life interest. In this example we advise Carol that she needs to get an income from renting the property to Donald, if there is no intention or ability for him to buy her life interest. Carol asks Donald to start paying rent or outgoings on the property, which are treated as income for the means assessment of income. Limited life interest The fewer rights given to the client under the life interest, the more likely it is that it cannot be realised. - Example:Edith holds a limited life interest after her family home was sold to her Family Trust. The life interest only gives Edith a right to occupy the property which ends when she enters residential care. She has no right to generate an income from the property. The property is not likely to be purchased or leased. The Ministry would not consider this as a realisable asset, and does not include it in Edith's financial means assessment. Estate asset is a debt owed by the client If the only asset held in the estate is a debt owed by the client for the purchase of a property the client lived in, the life interest cannot be realised by the client until the property is sold.

chunks.title: Factors that may indicate life interest is not realisable — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: - Example:Marlene holds a life interest in her late partner Greta's estate. When their family home was sold, Greta's estate loaned all its cash to Marlene to buy a unit in a retirement village.Any residual interest that Marlene is due once the house is sold and the loan is repaid, would be a realisable cash asset at that point.

chunks.title: Life interest or lease for life — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Life interest or lease for life
A life interest (also known as a lease for life) gives a person the right to use or have the benefit of a property or other assets for their lifetime or an earlier specified event.
If the Ministry of Social Development considers a client's life interest is a realisable asset, the fair value of the life interest should be included in the client's financial means assessment of assets.
A client will usually get a life interest either:
- from a will (estate) or
- as a condition of gifting or selling an asset (eg to a family member, or a trust)
A life interest gift can generally be identified when:
- the interest is defined
- it is specified when the interest will terminate, eg on death or an earlier extinguishing event and
- it is specified what will happen following termination of the life interest
If the type of life interest is unclear, contact Legal Services for advice.
## Calculating the fair value of a life interest
The fair value of a life interest is calculated by the Ministry using the tables in Schedule 2 of the Estate and Gift Duties Act 1968.
The life interest is calculated using the asset values and the client's age on the date they apply for a Residential Care Subsidy.

chunks.title: Life interest retained from the sale of a property — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Life interest retained from the sale of a property
Sometimes a life interest is still retained (held) by a client after the property the client had a self-interest in, is sold by the estate. The client's life interest may be carried over to a new property or investments made with the proceeds of the sale. The terms of the will should specify what may happen in this case, and the arrangement between the estate and the client.
If the type if life interest is unclear, contact Legal Services for advice.
The Ministry of Social Development should find out if the estate is going to pay the client a regular income from the new property or investments, or buy out the life interest and pay the client a lump sum.
If the life interest has been paid as a lump sum to the client, it is no longer a life interest and is treated as a cash asset in the financial means assessment.
If the client invests the lump sum payment and is getting an income stream from their new investment, some or all of the income may be exempt from the income assessment under the income-from-assets exemption. The new investment itself is included as an asset in the client's financial means assessment.
When a client still holds a life interest after property has been sold, and the estate has not paid them a lump sum or other income from the sale, the Ministry may calculate the fair value of the life interest and consider whether it should be included as a realisable asset in the financial means assessment.

chunks.title: Lock in period exists for some clients over age 65 years — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Lock in period exists for some clients over age 65 years
Before 1 July 2019, clients who were age 60 to 64 when they joined KiwiSaver were subject to a 5 year locked in period before they could access their funds.
When these clients turn 65 on or after 1 April 2020 they will have a choice of:
- accessing their KiwiSaver funds or
- continuing for the remainder of the locked in period
## Examples of clients choosing to access their KiwiSaver funds or continuing to keep their funds locked in
Example 1
Client turned 61 on 1 June 2018 and joined KiwiSaver the same day:
- 5 year locked in period ends on 1 June 2023
- client turns 65 on 1 June 2022
Client turns 65 on 1 June 2022 and can choose to:
- access their KiwiSaver funds or
- continue making contributions until the locked in period ends on 1 June 2023
Example 2
Client age 63 joined KiwiSaver on 1 March 2020:
- 5 year locked in period ends on 1 March 2025
- client turns 65 on 10 March 2022
Client can choose to:
- access their KiwiSaver funds or
- continue making contributions for the locked in period ending 1 March 2025

chunks.title: Māori land — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Māori land
There are situations when a client may have an individual financial interest in Māori freehold land. When individual ownership of Māori land can be identified and realised the value of this should be included in the means assessment of assets.
When the title is in tribal trust and individual ownership cannot be identified, the client's interest is not able to be realised by the client, therefore do not include its value in the means assessment of assets.
Note if the client receives income from their Māori land this may need to be included in the means assessment of income.

chunks.title: Maximum contribution — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Maximum contribution
The maximum contribution limits the weekly amount that individuals must pay towards their contracted care. This applies to all clients who have been needs assessed as requiring long-term residential care.
The maximum contribution applies to a person regardless of whether they are financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy or not.
The maximum contribution will vary depending on which Territorial Local Authority the hospital or rest home is located in.
Note a client is not required to make a private contribution if the means assessment of income determines their contribution is less than $5.00 per week.

chunks.title: Means assessment of assets — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Means assessment of assets
The means assessment of assets determines if a client's assets are equal to or below the applicable threshold and only applies to clients aged 65 years or over.
Note clients aged between 50 and 64 years who are single with no dependent children are automatically determined as having assets equal to or below the threshold.
Assets are included in the means assessment if they are able to be realised by the client or their partner (if any).
Clients, who have assets equal to or below the threshold, are considered financially eligible and must have an income assessment to determine the amount they are required to contribute to the cost of their care.
If their assets are above the threshold they are not eligible for Residential Care Subsidy and must pay for the cost of their contracted care, up to the maximum contribution set for their region by the Ministry of Health. The client can apply for a review of their means assessment or reapply if any circumstances have changed.

chunks.title: Means assessment of income — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Means assessment of income
The means assessment of income determines the contribution a client must make towards the cost of their contracted care. A client's estimated annual net income at the date of the financial means assessment is used and includes the income of their partner (if any).
Clients aged 65 years or over should only have the means assessment of income completed after the means assessment of assets has been completed and their assets are equal to or below the asset threshold.
Clients who are aged 50 to 64 years, single with no dependent children, are required to have a means assessment of income to assess the contribution they are required to pay towards the cost of their contracted care.
Note a means assessment of income is not completed for clients who are aged 65 years or over and have assets over the threshold.
If the means assessment of income determines the private contribution is less than $5.00 per week the client is not required to make a private contribution.

chunks.title: Needs assessment — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Needs assessment
Needs Assessment Service Co-ordination Agencies are contracted by Health New Zealand – Te Whatu Ora to needs assess clients.
The Needs Assessment Service Co-ordination Agency determines if a client requires long-term residential care in a hospital or rest home indefinitely.
## Needs Assessment Certificate
The Needs Assessment Certificate confirms that the client qualifies for a financial means assessment to be completed, including that:
- the client is eligible for publicly funded health and disability services and
- the client has been needs assessed as requiring long term residential care in a hospital or rest home indefinitely
Note a full copy of the needs assessment is not required to process a financial means assessment for Residential Care Subsidy, only the Needs Assessment Certificate is required.

chunks.title: Outstanding debt — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: When completing the means assessment of assets, you need to determine the balance of any current outstanding genuine debts the client and their partner (if any) have, and deduct these from the total of their assets, if the client's assets are above the asset threshold. Outstanding debts include genuine liabilities owed by the client or the client's partner (if any). The debt may be secured or unsecured. Outstanding debts may include (but are not limited to): - rates - insurances - household expenses such as phone, power, Sky TV, newspaper - credit card balances, hire purchases, personal loans - outstanding rest home fees - debt owed to the Ministry of Social Development If a debt is incurred to purchase an exempt asset, eg a pre-paid funeral plan or residential dwelling (whether secured or unsecured), it can only be deducted from the value of that exempt asset. The debt is not deducted from the total value of all assets.

chunks.title: Debts to purchase exempt assets — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: If a debt is incurred to purchase an exempt asset, eg a pre-paid funeral plan or residential dwelling (whether secured or unsecured), it can only be deducted from the value of that exempt asset. The debt is not deducted from the total value of all assets.

chunks.title: Genuine debt — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: Genuine debts include the following features: - incurred by and for the benefit of the client or their partner (if they have one) and in their name(s) - there is evidence that the debt occurred, when it occurred and what it was incurred for - documents support the existence of the debt and its terms - for example, bank statements showing the transfer of money and a deed of acknowledgement of debt made at the time the debt was incurred setting out repayment terms - a clear understanding by all parties that the transaction was not a gift but created a debt to be repaid - for example, when a client's child has looked after their affairs the client is not genuinely indebted to them, as this is part of normal family commitments - the debt is legally actionable and can be recovered - steps have been (or can be) taken to recover the debt if it is not paid - for example evidence of the basis for debt recovery could be that the creditor has invoiced the client for the debt or has begun legal action to recover it - the principal debt remains stable and is not continually increased over time, particularly if it is not being repaid - the debt balance appears in relevant accounts

chunks.title: Mortgage debt — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: A mortgage against a property is accepted as a genuine debt for the purposes of establishing equity. However, if the client raises the mortgage to benefit a third party (for example, to provide a loan to a family member), and the amount was over the allowable gifting limits or is owed back to the client, it could be included in the means assessment of assets.

chunks.title: Debt balance as at date of Financial Means Assessment — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text: In all cases the value of the outstanding debt is the debt balance at the date of the financial means assessment.

chunks.title: Partner in community not getting a benefit — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Partner in community not getting a benefit
If the partner in the community is not receiving a benefit, they may qualify for an Emergency Benefit payable at the Supported Living Payment single, or sole parent rate if they have a dependent child.
Note the commencement date of the Emergency Benefit is generally subject to the usual stand-down. In some cases the individual circumstances may justify waiving the stand-down.
If the partner in care has applied for a Residential Care Subsidy, the income of the partner in the community, that was included in the means assessment of their partner in residential care, cannot be included as chargeable income for Emergency Benefit.
The Emergency Benefit is not asset tested.

chunks.title: Personal allowance — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Personal allowance
Clients who are eligible for Residential Care Subsidy retain a portion of their New Zealand Superannuation or other benefit/pension (referred to as the personal allowance) for their personal needs before the balance is paid to the service provider.
The personal allowance enables the client to purchase items such as shampoo, magazines and postage stamps. It is not intended to be used to cover services which are included in the fee paid to the service provider.
## Personal allowance and overseas superannuation or social security payments
A personal allowance amount cannot be excluded from any payment that is not a New Zealand benefit or pension, e.g. private superannuation scheme or foreign social security payments.
## Payment of personal allowance
The personal allowance should be paid to a personal bank account nominated by the client, or a close relative or agent appointed by the client (not to the service provider).
When the client is unable to nominate an agent, they should be offered assistance from an organisation such as Age Concern NZ, the Accredited Visitors Service, the Retired Persons' Association or other church or service group.
## Exception
If it is the express wish of the client, payment of the personal allowance may be made to the service provider, but it must be made to a separate trust account, not the business operating account.

chunks.title: Personal loans to others — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Personal loans to others
When a client or their partner (if any) has made a loan to another party (for example person, business or trust) the principal amount outstanding to the client is an asset and must be included in the means assessment of assets.
## Interest received is income
Any interest being received must be included in the financial means assessment of income. If the loan is being repaid, repayment of principal is not considered income in the financial means assessment of income.
If no interest is being received wherever possible the client should request interest payments. Failure to do so could be deprivation of income.
Note if interest was not charged on debts owed to the client in the past this could be historic deprivation of income which may crystallise into a deprived asset.

chunks.title: Pre-paid estate administration fees — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Pre-paid estate administration fees
Pre-paid estate administration fees is money put aside exclusively to cover any fees associated with the administration of an estate. These fees are not exempt from the financial means assessment of assets and income.

chunks.title: Pre-paid funerals — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Pre-paid funerals
The value of a pre-paid funeral trust fund or account in excess of:
- $10,000 for a single client
- $10,000 each for couples where they both have a pre-paid funeral trust fund or account is included in the means assessment of assets
Note for couples this is $10,000 each, not a total of $20,000 between them.
There may be situations where a client's pre-paid funeral trust fund or account has gained interest. If the client or their partner cannot access the interest, only include the original value of the pre-paid funeral trust fund or account in the means assessment of assets.
It is usually clear whether or not the trust fund or account has been genuinely set aside for funeral expenses.

chunks.title: Private pensions — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Private pensions
For the purpose of a client's means assessment of income:
- include 50% of any amount received by the client or their partner (if any) by way of a private pension
## Overseas pensions
When a client is getting an overseas pension that is similar in purpose to a New Zealand benefit or pension it will be directly deducted from the New Zealand benefit or pension.
The client will be required to contribute the rate of New Zealand benefit or pension and the overseas pension, less the personal allowance amount, towards the cost of their care. This rate will be equivalent to the standard benefit or pension contribution.
If the client gets an overseas pension that reduces their New Zealand benefit or pension to nil, there is no personal allowance.
If the client is getting an overseas pension that is a private pension not directly deducted from the New Zealand benefit or pension, it will be included in the means assessment of income.

chunks.title: Property ownership — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Property ownership
When the client or their partner (if any) has an interest in a property (house and/or land), their net equity is included as an asset in the means assessment of assets.
## House and car exemption
Clients in rest homes who have a partner living in the community, automatically have the "house and car exempt" threshold $164,731 (as at 1 July 2026) applied to their means assessment. This threshold allows the net equity in the family home, in which their partner lives, to be exempt.
For previous asset thresholds see: Deskfile Asset thresholds.
For more information see:
- Election process
## Joint tenancy
Joint tenancy is the joint ownership of a property where all owners have an equal share.
To calculate joint tenancy you should assess equal shares in the property for all of the owners (that is 50% each for 2 people, 33.3% each for 3 people), and include the client and their partner's share as an asset in the means assessment of assets.
If the property has been registered as a joint family home under the Joint Family Homes Act 1964, the property is treated the same way as a joint tenancy for the purposes of valuation and the means assessment of assets.
## Tenancy in common
Both the client and their partner's share of a tenancy in common (as set out in the title) are included as an asset in the means assessment of assets.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for Residential Care Subsidy, a client must be eligible for publicly funded health and disability services and be aged:
- 65 years or over or
- between 50 and 64, single with no dependent children
and they must:
- have been needs assessed as requiring long-term residential care in a hospital or rest home indefinitely and
- be financially eligible as determined by a financial means assessment
Note eligibility to publicly funded health and disability services is determined by the Needs Assessor on behalf of Health New Zealand – Te Whatu Ora.

chunks.title: Client intends to purchase a new house — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Client intends to purchase a new house
When a client has sold their house and intends to purchase a new home that will be the principal place of residence of the client's partner or dependent child, the proceeds from the sale are included as an asset in the means assessment of assets.
If the client is not financially eligible for a Residential Care Subsidy, the client may apply for a review of their financial means assessment once a new home has been purchased.
## Sale after financial means assessment
If the client's house is sold after the financial means assessment is completed, there is no automatic review of the means assessment of assets. However, the means assessment of assets may be reviewed if:
- the client applies for a review or
- the partner's circumstances have changed, for example the partner has died, or becomes a resident assessed as requiring care, or their marital/relationship status has changed

chunks.title: Shares — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Shares
The current value of any shares held by the client or their partner (if any) must be included in the means assessment of assets.
To assess the value of shares you will need to calculate:
- total number of shares
multiplied by
- share value (buy price) as at the date of financial means assessment

chunks.title: Single living alone rate — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Single living alone rate
The partner of a client that has entered a hospital or rest home indefinitely may be eligible for the single living alone rate if they are living alone in their principal place of residence and:
- qualify for New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension in their own right
or
- were included in their partner's New Zealand Superannuation as a non-qualifying partner before 1 October 1991
The following partners cannot receive the single living alone rate:
- partners living in institutions
- partners paying private board
The single living alone rate can be paid from:
- the date the partner commenced living alone or
- 2 September 2013
whichever is the later.

chunks.title: Sold or gifted assets to a trust — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Sold or gifted assets to a trust
If the client and/or their partner (if any) sold assets to a trust make sure this was for fair value. If the sale was not for fair value, deprivation might have occurred.
Verification of the value of the property at the time of the transaction should be provided.
## Deed of acknowledgement of debt
If an asset was sold to the trust it should be recorded as either, a deed of acknowledgement of debt, or deed of sale.
The deed of acknowledgement of debt should show the terms of interest payable and repayment details. If there is no interest on the loan establish the reasons for this.
If there is an outstanding debt owed to the client from the trust, this is included in the means assessment of assets. The latest deed of forgiveness of debt should show the value of any outstanding debt.
For more information see:
- Income from a trust
- Gifting
- Deprivation of assets and income
## Life interest
If the client retained a life interest that was from a sale of assets to a trust and it is capable of being realised, include it in the means assessment of assets.
The sale and purchase agreement or a separate deed will generally show you if there was a life interest retained when the client sold the property to the trust.

chunks.title: Special Disability Allowance — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Special Disability Allowance
A Special Disability Allowance is paid to partners living in the community to help with extra costs associated with their partner living in residential care when:
- the partner is getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veterans Pension, Supported Living Payment, Jobseeker Support or a related Emergency Benefit and
- the client is getting Residential Care Subsidy and
- the client is required to pay a benefit contribution towards their own care
Special Disability Allowance should be started from:
- the date the client in care became financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy
When the client leaves the rest home or the person receiving the Special Disability Allowance is also admitted to hospital or long-term residential care the Special Disability Allowance should be stopped from:
- the date of the event (if in the current pay-period) or
- the first available date if the advice of the change in circumstances is received within 14 days of the event or
- the date of event if the advice of change in circumstances is received more than 14 days after the event
Following the death of the client in care Special Disability Allowance should be stopped from the 29th day.
Following the death of the partner in the community, Special Disability Allowance forms part of the Terminal Benefit and can continue for 4 weeks. This applies to the partner in the community receiving New Zealand Superannuation in their own right, Emergency Benefit paid at the Supported Living Payment rate, or as a partner receiving a joint (apportioned) benefit.

chunks.title: Summary rates of payment — extra help > residential care subsidy
chunks.text:
## Summary rates of payment
The following rates and benefit types are paid to the partner living in the community when a client enters long-term residential care in a hospital or rest home:
Partner living in the community currently gets
Benefit or Pension type and rate paid when their partner enters care
May qualify for the single living alone rate?
May qualify for a Special Disability Allowance?
New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension in their own right
Single sharing accommodation rate of New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension
Yes
Yes (if partner in care is eligible for Residential Care Subsidy)
New Zealand Superannuation as a grandparented non-qualified partner who was included before 1 October 1991
Single sharing accommodation rate of New Zealand Superannuation
Yes
Yes (if partner in care is eligible for Residential Care Subsidy)
New Zealand Superannuation as a grandparented non-qualified partner included in New Zealand Superannuation on or after 1 October 1991
