If the client applies on or after 30 September, formula-assessed Child Support costs can be included in their Special Benefit assessment from the later of: - the date the client is liable for the cost or - the date the client applies to have the cost included

chunks.title: Maximum Child Support costs — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text: There is no maximum amount of formula-assessed Child Support liability that can be included as an allowable cost. The allowable cost is the amount of Child Support Inland Revenue determines the client is liable to pay.

chunks.title: Changes to formula-assessed Child Support costs — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text: Inland Revenue may reassess how much Child Support a client is liable to pay, based on changes in the liable parent or receiving carer's circumstances. This may mean a client's formula-assessed Child Support costs change. The change may take effect from a date in the past or a date in the future. For changes to formula-assessed Child Support costs, clients generally must notify MSD of a change in their costs within 14 days of the date that Inland Revenue notifies the client of the outcome of their reassessment. This is different to the 14-day rule for changes in other allowable costs, where clients must tell MSD of a change in circumstances within 14 days of the date of the change (i.e. the date of the event).

chunks.title: Guidelines — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text: You should take all the following steps when assessing whether a client can be granted a Special Benefit. In particular note that the formula assessment (steps 2 and 3) is subject to the consideration of the client's individual circumstances (step 4). The Ministerial Direction requires that you give consideration to the following points in making your assessment of whether a client can be granted a Special Benefit.

chunks.title: Step 1 Is there any other more appropriate assistance available to alleviate the client's need? — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text: Have other appropriate alternatives been explored? For example: - Is the client receiving the correct rate of benefit? - Can the client receive other Extra Help such as Accommodation Supplement, Disability Allowance or Child Disability Allowance or Winter Energy Payment (during the winter period)? - Would an Advance Payment of Benefit or Special Needs Grant be more appropriate? You may be able to eliminate or reduce a client's hardship by paying a one-off Special Needs Grant for a specific need. Although this does not mean that the client's circumstances no longer warrant payment of a Special Benefit also. Note as advance payments and some Special Needs Grants are recoverable, the effect on the client's circumstances needs to be taken into account when considering if this is more appropriate. - Would the client receive more assistance from Temporary Additional Support? If a client is entitled to more assistance from Temporary Additional Support, discuss the implications of any potential change in assistance. The client must be given the opportunity to choose to receive Temporary Additional Support or retain Special Benefit. The payment that is most appropriate will depend on the client’s individual circumstances and may vary as the client’s circumstances change. For more information see: Special Benefit process [no link find out why] Choosing to receive Special Benefit instead of Temporary Additional Support does not mean that the client is refusing to access alternative sources of assistance. - Is the client receiving all their entitlements from other government agencies? The client may not be aware of assistance they can receive through other agencies such as Working for Families Tax Credits from Inland Revenue. Although some payments are not included as chargeable income for Special Benefit purposes, accessing other payments may eliminate or reduce the client's hardship. - Is the client entitled to Student Allowance or has unused Student Loan entitlement for living costs? - Can the client obtain relief or reduction in their expenditure, for example by negotiating or applying for reduced payments of court fines, Child Support payments, and hire purchases? Consideration should be given to reducing the rate or declining Special Benefit where the client refuses to access alternative sources of appropriate assistance, depending on the extent of other assistance available and the particular circumstances of the client.

chunks.title: Step 2 Assess the client's income deficiency — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text: You firstly need to determine if and by how much the client's expenses exceed their income. Even if there is no deficiency of income a person may still be eligible to receive a Special Benefit and an assessment must still be made of the client's individual circumstances. The formula rate of Special Benefit is generally the lesser of the deficiency or: - 25% for clients with dependent children or - 30% for clients without dependent children of the client's allowable costs. However, you must take the client's individual circumstances into consideration (step 4) to decide whether to depart from this rate, including not paying a Special Benefit. For more information see: - Assessment of income deficiency - Allowable costs - Chargeable income - Assessing whether a client's individual circumstances justify payment

chunks.title: Step 3 Assess the client's cash assets — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text: You need to decide whether it is reasonable to expect the client to meet the costs they face from their own resources. You need to check whether the client meets the cash assets test and take this into consideration when deciding eligibility for Special Benefit. For more information see: - Cash assets test

chunks.title: Step 4 Assess whether the client's individual circumstances justify payment — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text: Regardless of the client's deficiency or lack of one under the formula, you must consider all of the client's individual circumstances to decide whether granting a Special Benefit is justified or not and if so what rate is justified. For more information see: - Assessing whether a client's individual circumstances justify payment

chunks.title: Step 5 Assess what rate to pay — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text: Special Benefit is generally paid at the deficiency of income over expenses but may be paid at a higher or lower rate or not at all, if the client's individual circumstances justify it. For more information see: - Assessing whether a client's individual circumstances justify payment You may depart from the formula assessed rate where you consider the client's circumstances justify it. The departure from the rate may be by granting the Special Benefit at a higher or lower rate or by declining the application.

chunks.title: Hire purchase agreements — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text: Allowable costs are any regular essential expenses, calculated on a weekly basis arising out of the special circumstances of the client. They are costs that cannot be readily avoided or varied. Hire purchases and other types of regular payments for items where the acquisition was essential can be included in the assessment of Special Benefit. Such items include: - washing machines - fridges - television sets - household furniture (for example beds, dining suites, lounge suites and stoves) There may be some instances where a cost does not fit the description detailed above but it may still be considered if the cost meets the definition of an allowable cost. If the hire purchase agreements have provisions to defer repayment where earnings are reduced because of a health condition or an accident, this option should be explored. Advice should also be given to the client to explore the possibility of deferring or re-negotiating the terms of repayment, eliminating or reducing the need for Special Benefit. You may consider including the hire purchase cost and give the client time to explore their options before their next review. Any other payments made in relation to any debt, fine or other liability of the applicant or their partner other than those listed in the Special Benefit Ministerial Direction may not be included as an allowable cost. Hire purchase repayments should not be included as an allowable cost unless the acquisition was essential and unavoidable. However, you may consider whether the hire purchase was realistic (i.e. adequate to meet their need and at a reasonable price given the clients circumstances) at the time the client entered into it and use your discretion to determine whether the obligation to make hire purchase repayments justify a higher rate of Special Benefit. If the client has entered into unrealistic hire purchase commitments, you can, in the exercise of your discretion, consider decreasing the rate of Special Benefit paid or consider the rate of Special Benefit paid based on other allowable costs or declining the application. Consider payment of Special Benefit as a lump sum if it eliminates the need for an ongoing Special Benefit. For more information see: - Lump sum payments When a hire purchase agreement has been included in the assessment of Special Benefit, record the costs and end date of the agreement in the SSPWA screen. If you feel that the client's individual circumstances warrant consideration even though the above criteria is not met, you may take into consideration when deciding, through the use of your discretion, whether or not to grant Special Benefit and/or at what rate to pay.

chunks.title: Income that is not chargeable — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Income that is not chargeable
Chargeable income for Special Benefit does not include:
- assistance to access childcare or care for people with a health condition, injury or disabilities or elderly people
- Away from Home Allowance
- Best Start tax credit lump sum payment of arrears
- Rent and 62% of board payments a client gets that are less than or equal to their accommodation costs (after the deduction of the cost of any part of the property not being lived in by the client)
- 38% of board payments a client gets (not received as part of a business venture)
- 62% of additional occupant contributions a client gets that are less than or equal to their market rent
- 38% of additional occupant contributions a client gets
- Childcare Subsidy and OSCAR Subsidy
- child tax credit
- Christchurch mosques attack support payments and income earned on the payment
- Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments
- Education and employment-related training
- Energy Trust Dividends and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- income earned on Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- in-work tax credit
- Kāinga Ora energy subsidy
- minimum family tax credit
- MSD lump sum payments and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- Orphans Benefit and Unsupported Childs Benefit
- Participation Allowance
- Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014
- Payments to clients whose Housing New Zealand tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- Severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment)
- specified Ex gratia and Compensation payments and income earned on those payments
- Temporary Accommodation Assistance weekly payments (ended 30 June 2025)
- Travel Allowance paid for training courses
- FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Special Benefit is a discretionary non-taxable benefit. Its intent is to provide assistance to clients whose particular circumstances are causing them hardship.
A client does not need to be getting a benefit to qualify for Special Benefit. However, payments of Special Benefit cannot be made to people who were not getting it or had not applied for it immediately before 1 April 2006. Special Benefit was replaced by Temporary Additional Support on this date.
Special Benefit continues to be payable to clients who were getting it, or had applied for it, immediately before 1 April 2006. Payments can continue until they:
- no longer qualify to get Special Benefit or
- choose to cancel Special Benefit
There is no time limit on Special Benefit if payment continues to be justified. However, Special Benefit is not intended as a long-term solution to a client's financial shortfall unless the client's individual circumstances justify this. It is paid to help clients meet their essential living costs while they make efforts to reduce their commitments and live within their usual income.
The rate of Special Benefit should be regularly reviewed and adjusted as required to reflect the client's needs.

chunks.title: KiwiSaver and superannuation scheme account contributions — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## KiwiSaver and superannuation scheme account contributions
To be eligible for Special Benefit a client must take all reasonable steps to reduce their costs or increase their income.
Reducing costs can include suspending KiwiSaver and superannuation scheme account contributions.
If a client has questions about how to suspend their contributions to KiwiSaver or superannuation scheme accounts, they should contact their scheme provider.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Lump sum payments — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Lump sum payments
It may be appropriate, if the client's circumstances warrant it, to pay the full Special Benefit or a portion of the Special Benefit as a lump sum where it will reduce the need for a continuing grant by eliminating an essential cost.
A lump sum payment should not usually exceed the value of Special Benefit the client would receive in a 3 month period (13 weeks).
As a guideline, when deciding whether a client's circumstances warrant a lump sum payment versus an ongoing payment, consider:
- how much the grant would be and what the grant is for and
- the ability of the client to improve their finances through their own immediate or future means
There may be some instances where a client has arrears owing for an item as well as ongoing costs and that item is considered an allowable cost. A lump sum can be considered to alleviate the hardship caused by the arrears owing and Special Benefit may still be considered for the ongoing cost of that item.
Only 'regular essential expenses reckoned on a weekly basis' should be included in the formula assessment, therefore any ongoing allowable costs should be included in the formula assessment. Any costs that are not ongoing amounts (e.g. debts as a result of arrears due) should be taken into account after the formula assessment, see example 3.
When you have paid a lump sum payment, you should recheck whether the client still meets the qualifications for Special Benefit. It may be that by paying the lump sum, the item that gave rise to the special or unusual circumstances faced by the client no longer exists.
Note ensure you discuss and document your decision fully.
For Lump sum payment examples see:
- Examples - Lump sum payments

chunks.title: Motor vehicles — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text: Allowable costs are any regular essential expenses, calculated on a weekly basis arising out of the special circumstances of the client. They are costs that cannot be readily avoided or varied.

chunks.title: Non-beneficiaries — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text: Motor vehicle repayments and reasonable running costs can be included in the assessment of Special Benefit for non-beneficiaries providing: - the client or their partner needs the vehicle to travel to and from work or - the client or any member of their family needs the vehicle because they suffer a chronic illness or have a disability and the vehicle is required for that person's transport and there is no suitable public transport available.

chunks.title: Beneficiaries — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text: Motor vehicle repayments and reasonable running costs can be included in the assessment of Special Benefit for beneficiaries, providing: - the client or their partner needs the vehicle to travel to and from work or - the client or any member of their family needs the vehicle because they suffer a chronic illness or have a disability and the vehicle is required for that person's transport and there is no suitable public transport available. If beneficiaries do not meet the above criteria, motor vehicle repayments, but not reasonable running costs, can be included in the assessment of special benefit, providing: - the client entered into the arrangement to purchase the vehicle before applying for benefit and there is no public transport available. There may be some instances where the cost does not fit the description detailed above but it may still be considered if the cost meets the definition of an allowable cost. If a client is receiving a Disability Allowance, disability costs contained in SWIFTT will automatically be included as allowable costs for Special Benefit. You do not need to add them manually in the SSPWA screens. If your client's individual circumstances fall outside of these provisions or warrant consideration of disability and personal health expenses that are not accepted for Disability Allowance, even though the criteria is not met, motor vehicle repayments and running costs may still be considered, when deciding through the use of your discretion, whether or not to grant a Special Benefit and/or at what rate to pay.

chunks.title: Reasonable running costs — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text: The following rates have been set and reflect the reasonable 'running costs' (excluding fixed costs) of a vehicle dependent on engine size. Running costs include consumables such as, petrol and oil. Fixed costs (not included in the calculation) include costs such as, relicensing, insurance and Warrants of Fitness. Fixed costs are not included as all clients incur these costs when they own a vehicle. The rates recognise the reasonable 'running costs' of a vehicle as opposed to 'fixed costs' and are consistent with the intent of the legislation, where the Special Benefit Ministerial Directive refers to allowable costs including any motor vehicle 'running costs'. Use these rates to calculate the allowable vehicle running costs cc rating payable per kilometre up to 1000 29 cents 1001 to 1350 30 cents 1351 to 2000 35 cents over 2000 40 cents However, there is discretion to apply a different rate if the client has evidence of running costs. Add the appropriate costs of the motor vehicle in the SSPWA screen.

chunks.title: Non beneficiaries — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Non beneficiaries
Non beneficiaries can apply for Special Benefit and should be assessed in the normal way. For more information see:
- Guidelines
You should make sure that the client is aware of other forms of assistance that may reduce or eliminate their hardship, for example:
- Working for Families Tax Credits from Inland RevenueWorking for Families Tax Credits including family tax credit, in-work tax credit, and minimum family tax credit
- Non beneficiary assistance, Accommodation Supplement, Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance and Childcare subsidies
When assessing a client, who is not getting a benefit, use the appropriate Jobseeker Support standard cost (current).

chunks.title: Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid
When a client is receiving an Orphans and /or an Unsupported Childs Benefit and applies for Special Benefit, the child:
- is not treated as a dependent child and
- is not included in the assessment of the income deficiency of Special Benefit
The client's Special Benefit is assessed on their family circumstances excluding the child for which Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid.
Note any regular essential expenses, calculated on a weekly basis arising out of the orphan's or unsupported child's circumstances are not to be included in the assessment of income deficiency of Special Benefit.

chunks.title: Partners overseas — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Partners overseas
Where one partner of a married, civil union de facto couple is overseas and the partner remaining in New Zealand is receiving half of the married, civil union or de facto rate, the full rate of that benefit is generally included as chargeable income.
Note in some situations, the partner overseas can continue to receive a benefit or may qualify when they are overseas. For more information refer to the appropriate benefit.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Payment
Special Benefit is a non-taxable allowance that is generally paid together with a client's benefit payment or weekly for clients not receiving a benefit. There is no maximum amount payable for Special Benefit if the client's circumstances warrant it.
You must ensure that where it is practical, the client is receiving appropriate advice with the objective that wherever possible, the need for Special Benefit is reduced or eliminated within 6 months. You should particularly do so where the client's rate of payment is over $50 per week.
Note SWIFTT rounds up Special Benefit payments to the nearest 50 cents.
If you need advice on the rate of payment of Special Benefit contact Helpline.
If the client's individual circumstances warrant it, Special Benefit can be paid as a lump sum and/or as an ongoing payment. For more information see:
- Lump sum payments
As Special Benefit is generally intended to be short-term assistance, any payments made are reviewed 3 months after grant and then at 6 month intervals to assess ongoing need for Special Benefit and steps that may be taken to reduce the need for Special Benefit.
For more information see:
- Changes and Reviews

chunks.title: People not able to receive Special Benefit — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## People not able to receive Special Benefit
There are a number of instances where an applicant is ineligible for Special Benefit. These are:
- clients (and their partners) who have an initial stand-down imposed
- clients who have a non-entitlement period Note a client can receive a Special Benefit when their partner has a non-entitlement period. To assess eligibility for Special Benefit clients whose partners have a non-entitlement period, use the appropriate Jobseeker Support standard costs.
- applicants who have 100% of their benefit suspended due to:
(a) the first failure to accept an offer of suitable employment; or
(b) first or second failure to participate in or complete any organised activity.
The client or partner may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant depending on their circumstances.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support standard cost

chunks.title: Pre-paid funeral expenses — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Pre-paid funeral expenses
A pre-paid funeral trust fund or account is money put aside (usually in a trust) exclusively for the payment of funeral expenses. If the money can be accessed by the client and so used for other purposes, it is not considered exclusively for funeral expenses then this money is a cash asset for Special Benefit.
It is usually clear whether or not the trust fund or account has been genuinely set aside for funeral expenses. Evidence that it has been set aside exclusively for funeral expenses include:
- the trust fund/account is only paid out on production of a death certificate
- the client cannot usually access the funds
- if a client can access the fund, there are limited conditions on withdrawal, such as re-locating overseas
- the trust fund/account is only payable to the funeral director or administrator of the client's estate
- the client cannot generally access the interest earned from the trust fund or account
Where the trust fund or account has been set aside for funeral expenses and cannot be accessed or converted into cash then this money is not a cash asset for Special Benefit.
For more information see:
- Cash assets

chunks.title: Public transport to work — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Public transport to work
Allowable costs are any regular essential expenses, calculated on a weekly basis arising out of the special circumstances of the client. They are costs that cannot be readily avoided or varied.
If a client is in paid employment you can include the costs of public transport to and from their place of work in the assessment of Special Benefit.
If a client chooses not to use public transport but elects an alternative, the allowable cost will be:
- the public transport cost or
- the alternative cost
whichever is the lesser amount.
If the client has a Community Services Card, they can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect and should apply for this if it is the most cost-effective way to meet their transport needs.
If the client has not used their Community Services Card but is eligible and does not apply for the discount, you must discuss reasons if their actual public transport costs are higher than they would be if the 50% discount was applied.
The client may have good reason for not applying for the 50% discount (e.g. the client has a disability and there are accessibility issues with applying for the Community Connect discount through a public transport provider's website, and this is the only way to apply).
When there is a good reason, the client's allowable costs for public transport to work should be their actual costs. If there is no good reason, their allowable costs for travel should generally not be more than the cost of the subsidised public transport fare.
There may be some instances when a cost does not fit the description detailed above but it may still be considered if the cost meets the definition of an allowable cost.
If there is no public transport available, you can include car running costs as an allowable cost. For more information see:
- Motor vehicles
- Community Services Card - Public transport (Community Connect)
If you feel the clients individual circumstances warrant consideration of public transport costs to and from work even though the above criteria is not met, you may take this into consideration when deciding, through the use of your discretion, whether or not to grant Special Benefit and/or at what rate to pay.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
Special Benefit is only available for people, or their spouses or partners, who were getting, or applied for, Special Benefit immediately before 1 April 2006.
The grant of Special Benefit is discretionary and only made where justified. To properly exercise discretion, MSD must take into account all factors that are relevant and disregard factors that are irrelevant.
For a client's circumstances to warrant payment, they generally must:
- meet a cash assets test
- have an ongoing reasonably substantial deficiency of income over expenditure and commitments
- have expenses which are essential and not reasonably avoidable
- have no other means of financial assistance or resources to reduce their deficiency
- generally be a New Zealand citizen or residence class visa holder (i.e. not be in New Zealand unlawfully, or here on a temporary entry class visa) and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
A client cannot get Special Benefit and Temporary Additional Support at the same time.
Applications need to be considered on a case-by-case basis taking all of the client's circumstances into account.
Clients must provide proof of their income, assets (for example current payslips and bank statements) and expenses.

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get Special Benefit, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- have a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
People who are in New Zealand unlawfully or here on a temporary entry class visa generally do not qualify for a benefit.
## Clients who don’t meet the residence requirements
If a client does not meet the residence requirements, they cannot get Special Benefit. However, they may be able to get Temporary Additional Support.
## Partner non-residentially qualified
Special Benefit can only be paid in respect of the person who meets the residence criteria. However, MSD must take into consideration the income and assets of both the client and their partner when assessing entitlement to Special Benefit.
When calculating the formula assessment, the standard costs are those that would apply to the client if they were single or a sole parent.
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other criteria to qualify for Special Benefit.

chunks.title: Residential Support Services — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Residential Support Services
Special Benefit cannot be paid to a person who has a psychiatric, intellectual, physical or sensory disability for costs of their residential care services including residential support services:
- if they are receiving funding from a purchaser towards their own accommodation or
- when a purchaser is funding their own care (other than in their own home) by any person or organisation
Residential care services are disability services supplied to a person with a disability in an appropriately licensed or registered home including:
- supervision and support services
- hotel-type services (including the provision of sleeping facilities, meals, laundry, cleaning services and supplies, household furniture and furnishings, lighting, heating, hot water and other household utilities)
- services that support daily living (including financial management and gardening)
- personal care services (including toileting, bathing, hair washing, teeth cleaning, nail care, feeding and mobility)
- services within that home intended to provide satisfying activity to the person (including the provision of educational, social, recreational and other activities) and
- clinical support services, including health services (within the meaning of the Health and Disability Services Act 1993) consultations with medical practitioners, pharmaceuticals, incontinence aids and other treatment costs

chunks.title: Seasonal workers — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Seasonal workers
If a client has been in seasonal work and is receiving a benefit during the off-season, sometimes they are able to make suitable financial provisions for their commitments during the period of their employment.
Always investigate the client's pre-benefit earnings. If these earnings are high, the client should normally be able to absorb any hardship, at least for an initial period but still consider the individual circumstances of the applicant.

chunks.title: Self-employed clients — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Self-employed clients
Special Benefit can be considered for self-employed clients as well as other non-beneficiaries depending on the client's individual circumstances.
Special Benefit should not generally be used to financially assist a business. However, the reasons and likely length of the financial difficulty should be taken into account.
In some cases it may be possible for the client to meet their income deficiency by rearranging their business expenses to increase their net profit from the business, for example, if they can arrange with their bank to temporarily reduce their loan repayments.
It is important to remember that the applicant is the client not the business.
Each case must be considered individually and the financial accounts of the client's business as well as the client's personal expenses should be carefully examined.

chunks.title: Shared care - family tax credit and Best Start tax credit — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Shared care - family tax credit and Best Start tax credit
Shared care is when the family tax credit is apportioned between caregivers.
In a shared care arrangement the amount of family tax credit and Best Start tax credit received by the applicant will be treated as chargeable income when assessing Special Benefit.
## Example
A child aged 10 lives with his mother for 4 days per week and with his father for the remaining 3 days per week. Family tax credit for that child is $151.91 (as at 1 April 2026) per week.
The mother is getting Special Benefit and the amount of family tax credit that will be included as chargeable income is:
Family tax credit amount for chargeable income purposes
Family tax credit amount for standard costs purposes
$86.80 (4/7 of $151.91)
$151.91
($151.91 divided by 7 = $21.70 x 4)
Example
A child born on 10 April 2025 lives with one parent for 4 days per week, and the other parent for the remaining 3 days per week. This is a constant care arrangement.
Best Start tax credit is $77.50 per week (rate at 1 April 2026). The parent with care for 4 days gets Special Benefit and the Best Start tax credit included as chargeable income is:
Best start tax credit amount for chargeable income
Best Start tax credit amount
$44.28 (4/7 of $77.50)
$77.50
($77.50 divided by 7 = $11.07 x 4)
Note Best Start tax credit is not included in the standard costs for Special Benefit.

chunks.title: Social Rehabilitation programmes — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Social Rehabilitation programmes
When a client enters an approved Social Rehabilitation programme they can receive Social Rehabilitation Assistance which is paid as a miscellaneous subsidy directly to the social rehabilitation service provider.
Clients cannot receive both Special Benefit and Social Rehabilitation Assistance.
If a client receiving Special Benefit enters an approved Social Rehabilitation programme, Special Benefit should be reassessed in the normal manner having regard to the client's income and expenses.
If the rate of Special Benefit is less than the appropriate rate of Social Rehabilitation Assistance, discuss with the client if they would like to cancel Special Benefit and apply for Social Rehabilitation Assistance.
Note you will need to ensure that the client is aware that if they choose to cancel their Special Benefit, they cannot be granted Special Benefit at a later date.
If Special Benefit will continue to be paid and the social rehabilitation provider is not the client’s agent, discuss with the client the possibility of redirecting an amount equal to the relevant rate of Social Rehabilitation Assistance to the provider.
For more information see:
- Extra Help Social Rehabilitation Assistance

chunks.title: Standard costs — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Standard costs
Standard costs are the proportion of the everyday living costs of the client (including any partner and dependants) that they can be expected to meet from:
- their benefit or
- in the case of a non-beneficiary, from the appropriate rate of Jobseeker Support that would be payable to the client, if they were entitled to that benefit
For clients with dependent children, the standard cost is 70% of the full main benefit and 70% of full family tax credit.
For clients without dependent children, their standard cost is as per the Ministerial Direction schedule.
For the current standard costs see:
- Deskfile Standard cost rates
## Shared care
For shared care arrangements, when there is a dependent child, the family tax credit included in the standard costs is 70% of the total amount of family tax credit payable in respect of that child regardless of whether the caregiver receives partial payment of family tax credit.
For example, if a child is in the care of a person for 3/7 days then the full family tax credit is 7 days, even if the person is only caring for the child 3 days of the period.
## Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit
When a client is paid a main benefit and is also being paid an Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, you would use the standard cost that relates to the main benefit only.
For example, a client is receiving Sole Parent Support with 1 child and also gets Unsupported Childs Benefit for another child you would use the standard cost for a Sole Parent Support with 1 child.
## Everyday living costs
These may include (but are not limited to):
- gas, electricity and water
- food and grocery items
- house contents insurance
- clothing
For the current standard costs see:
- Deskfile Standard cost rates

chunks.title: Student Allowance declined due to parental income — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Student Allowance declined due to parental income
For full-time tertiary students who are under 24 years and single or living in a de facto relationship without children, the Student Allowance is parental income tested.
In general, if the Student Allowance has been declined due to the parental income test, the client will not be entitled to Special Benefit unless they have extraordinary expenses that their parents cannot provide assistance for.
For more information see:
- Expenses
- Extraordinary expenses
- Students chargeable income

chunks.title: Students — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Students
Full-time tertiary students (and their dependent spouse or partner) applying for Special Benefit have additional criteria to meet.
Note that clients receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship are also full-time students.
The availability of financial support during the academic year under the Student Allowance and Student Loan schemes must be assessed.
In deciding whether a cost may be included as an allowable cost you need to consider whether the cost is the type of expense that the Student Allowance and Student Loan schemes are intended to cover.
Any expense that those schemes are intended to cover should not be included unless:
- it is an extraordinary expense and
- the student has exhausted all their entitlements under those schemes
For more information see:
- Expenses
- Extraordinary expenses
- Student Allowance declined due to parental income

chunks.title: Students chargeable income — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Students chargeable income
Student Loans for course fees or course-related costs are not to be included as chargeable income. However, the living cost component of any Student Allowance or Student Loan is included as chargeable income for Special Benefit purposes. This is because the living component of a Student Loan is a means of financial assistance available to students to assist with their living costs.
Clients should first use the balance of any Student Loan and hardship grants available at the time before you would grant them Special Benefit. You should consider declining Special Benefit if these sources have not been utilised.
Parental income does not affect eligibility for Special Benefit and questions about parent's income should not be asked. However, any contribution from parents for living costs, excluding lump sum gifts, should be included as chargeable income.
For more information see:
- Student Allowance declined due to parental income

chunks.title: Telephone rental — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Telephone rental
Allowable costs are any regular essential expenses, calculated on a weekly basis arising out of the special circumstances of the client. They are costs that cannot be readily avoided or varied. Allowable costs are not restricted to the examples listed.
Basic telephone rental (excluding toll charges) can be included in the assessment of Special Benefit if the telephone is necessary because of:
- health or disability
- family circumstances
- personal safety or securityfor example, an elderly person living on their own or a separated person with a protection order against a partner
- employmentfor example an electrical worker on call or a client with work obligations seeking employment
There may be some instances where a cost does not fit the description detailed above but it may still be considered if the cost meets the definition of an allowable cost.
If the client's circumstances fall outside these provisions, telephone costs may still be considered, in the exercise of your discretion, whether or not to grant a Special Benefit and/or at what rate to pay.
Note you would generally not include extra telephone costs in addition to the basic telephone rental such as cell phones, pagers, message services. However, sometimes cell phones can be an option for clients instead of telephone rental. In this situation, cell phone charges can be included as an allowable cost up to the cost of a basic telephone rental.
If telephone rental is already included as a cost in any Disability Allowance payable, do not manually add the cost in the SSPWA screen. SWIFTT will automatically transfer telephone rental as an allowable cost.
If you feel that the client's individual circumstances warrant consideration even though the above criteria is not met, you may take into consideration when deciding, through the use of your discretion, whether to grant Special Benefit and/or what rate to pay.

chunks.title: Transport costs due to a disability — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Transport costs due to a disability
Allowable costs are any regular essential expenses, calculated on a weekly basis due to the special circumstances of the client. They are costs that cannot be readily avoided or varied.
The disability and personal health transport expenses accepted for Disability Allowance can be included as an allowable cost in Special Benefit.
For more information see:
- Disability Allowance Types of costs
If the client has a Community Services Card, they can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect and should apply for this if it is the most cost-effective way to meet their transport needs.
If the client has not used their Community Services Card but is eligible and does not apply for the discount, you must discuss reasons if their actual public transport costs are higher than they would be if the 50% discount was applied.
The client may have good reason for not applying for the 50% discount (e.g. there are accessibility issues with applying for the Community Connect discount through a public transport provider's website, and this is the only way to apply).
When there is a good reason, the client's allowable costs for public transport to work should be their actual costs. If there is no good reason, their allowable costs for travel should generally not be more than the cost of the subsidised public transport fare.
There may be some instances when a cost does not fit the description detailed above but it may still be considered if the cost meets the definition of an allowable cost.
If you feel the client's individual circumstances warrant consideration of disability and personal health expenses that are not accepted for Disability Allowance, even though the above criteria is not met, you may take this into consideration when deciding, through the use of your discretion, whether or not to grant Special Benefit and/or at what rate.

chunks.title: Welfare programmes that are chargeable income — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Welfare programmes that are chargeable income
The following welfare programmes are chargeable income for Special Benefit purposes:
- Assistance to Live Organ Donors Programme for lost income
- Assistance to transition into employment for bridging finance
- Civil Defence Payments for loss of livelihood
- Employment Transition Programme
- New Employment Transition Grant Programme
- Seasonal Work Assistance Programme
- Sole Parent Study Assistance Programme
- Special Needs Grants rural assistance
- Telephone Costs Payment Programme
- Temporary Accommodation Assistance (Canterbury Earthquake) Programme (ended 30 June 2025)
- Work Bonus Programme for bridging finance
For more information see:
- Chargeable income
- Income that is not chargeable

chunks.title: Year end family tax credit — extra help > special benefit
chunks.text:
## Year end family tax credit
People can receive their family tax credit as a weekly, fortnightly or end of year lump sum.
If a client has chosen not to receive family tax credit, they will need to take steps to obtain this assistance, and in most cases, you should encourage them to receive it as a weekly payment. There may however be circumstances where it would be more beneficial for the client to receive an end of year payment, such as for those who receive fluctuating income, especially those who expect more income at the end of the tax year than the beginning.
If it is more beneficial for the client to receive family tax credit as a lump sum at the end of the tax year, you will need to estimate the amount they would receive if paid on a weekly basis. You will need to include this estimated weekly amount of family tax credit as chargeable income and note CMS stating that the client will receive a year end payment and that you have estimated family tax credit for the client.
For more information about how to do this see:
- Estimating weekly family tax credit
Where a non-beneficiary client decides to change to weekly or fortnightly payments of family tax credit they must contact Inland Revenue. It may take Inland Revenue time to reassess the client's entitlement. Where there will be a delay in Inland Revenue providing verification of family tax credit, you must enter the estimated amount of family tax credit payable to the client.
Estimated family tax credit should be updated with actual family tax credit when the client receives verification from Inland Revenue.
Where the estimated amount of family tax credit is different to the amount verified by Inland Revenue, you will need to reassess the client's Special Benefit from the beginning of the current pay period.
For more information see:
- Verification of family tax credit [no link find out why] process
- Clients receiving a main benefit

chunks.title: Accompanying medical treatment overseas — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Accompanying medical treatment overseas
A Special Needs Grant for reasonable costs may be made to clients who are accompanying their child or partner overseas for medical treatment.
To be able to receive a Special Needs Grant:
- the patient's treatment overseas must have been approved and subsidised by the District Health Board
- the client must have cash assets less than $5000 and
- the funding provided by the Ministry of Health and other sources such as public appeal is insufficient to cover the client's cost
## Payment
Payment can be made for reasonable costs for the client's airfares, accommodation and/or living expenses less:
- any amount received from the District Health Board or other source and
- the amount of the client's cash assets
Special Needs Grants for this purpose are non-recoverable.
The Ministry of Health is responsible for payment of the patient's expenses and should provide verification for the client.
For more information see:
- Cash assets

chunks.title: Ambulance fees — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Ambulance fees
For emergency services accessed through 111, there is sometimes a charge per call out for an Ambulance. If the client meets all qualifications, they may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant for Ambulance fees if:
- special circumstances exist and
- the client and/or their family would suffer serious hardship without the item or service
To consider whether special circumstances exist, consider the following:
- the consequences to the client if they did not have the service (that is, was the service a preference or a must?) and
- whether there were other medical alternatives that could have met the need
Sometimes the client also pays for a private ambulance to return them to their home. You can consider a Special Needs Grant in this situation if there was no alternative transport available.
Note it is reasonable to expect that the client would be applying for assistance after the event. You should consider payment of a Special Needs Grant if the client has no other way of paying (for example through instalments) or their current budget does not leave room to meet this unexpected cost.
## Subscription schemes
St Johns also offer a subscription scheme. This is a prepaid service of a yearly amount that gives the client unlimited access to emergency services for 1 year.
It may be an alternative for families who use the services frequently, for example, families with severe asthma sufferers. A Special Needs Grant would not normally be paid for the subscription fee, however, the client may be able to receive an Advance or a Recoverable Assistance Payment (for non-beneficiaries).
## Payment
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, the maximum amount payable towards emergency medical treatment is $500.
Although Special Needs Grants under this category may be recoverable or non-recoverable, generally grants for Ambulance fees are recoverable. However, if you consider it equitable in the circumstances for the client not to pay the grant back, you may decide the Special Needs Grant should be non-recoverable.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Exceptional circumstances
- Advance Payment of Benefit Ambulance subscription fees
- Recoverable Assistance Payment Ambulance subscription fees
- Recovery of payment

chunks.title: Application procedure — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Application procedure
Generally, when family violence has occurred, clients are referred to Work and Income by a refuge organisation or New Zealand Police.
When a client contacts, or is referred to, Work and Income or contacts Work and Income direct, Work and Income staff should take an application and refer the client to Immigration New Zealand
## Work and Income - National Office to co-ordinate
Entry onto this programme will be co-coordinated through National Office, with service centres responsible for administration of weekly Special Needs Grant payments.
Note clients can complete an application for a Special Needs Grant when they make first contact, however, the application cannot be decided until National Office have advised that the application for a Special Needs Grant has been approved.
## Work and Income - National Office role
National Office is responsible for:
- co-ordinating entry onto this programme
- maintaining a central register for all clients and
- providing the service centre with confirmation of eligibility under the Welfare Programme
When a client applies for a Special Needs Grant you must contact National Office to confirm the client's eligibility under the Welfare Programme. The initial Special Needs Grant payment is not to be made without approval from Helpline.
## Service Centre for weekly payments
Clients must make an application for a Special Needs Grant on a weekly basis.

chunks.title: Application procedure - International Custody Dispute Payment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Application procedure - International Custody Dispute Payment
All clients need to complete a Special Needs Grant - International Custody Dispute Payment form.
Clients must have a court order in relation to care and custody arrangements before applying.
A client must meet all qualifications and verification of this supplied.
Clients can access the application form from the Work and Income website and applications need to be sent to:
International Custody Dispute PaymentHelplineMinistry of Social DevelopmentPO Box 1556Wellington 6140New Zealand
For a copy of the form see:
- Special Needs Grant - International Custody Dispute Payment form
If the client is overseas and was previously getting Sole Parent Support or Supported Living Payment, this payment should continue to be paid for 28 days after they leave the country. If an application for a Special Needs Grant - International Custody Dispute Payment is completed the transition from benefit to the Special Needs Grant International Custody Dispute Payment, should commence from the 29th day.
Overseas clients should send certified copies of their identification, and not their original identification.
Certified copies must be stamped or endorsed as being true copies of the originals by a person authorised by law to take statutory declarations in the applicant's country or in New Zealand. Examples of these include but are not limited to:
- a lawyer
- notary public
- Justice of the Peace or
- court official
If a client is overseas and needs to get certified copies of originals sighted they can be advised to use their lawyer or should be directed to the New Zealand Embassies (there is a cost involved).
Accept faxed copies of certified documents only if the originals, or certified copies, are then submitted at the earliest opportunity.
## Court dates
International custody disputes may take numerous court hearings to reach a final decision. The client may not know all the court dates in advance and may not be able to provide verification of the next court date immediately.
After a decision has been made a client has 28 days in which to lodge an appeal.
Use BRUPA for the day after the court date to contact the client and check the status of the court proceedings. If a new court date is set, we must receive the verification within 28 days of the previous court date.
Verification of the court date can be a letter from the court or clients lawyer confirming the court date.

chunks.title: Application - Civil Defence Payment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Application - Civil Defence Payment
When a Civil Defence emergency or other adverse event arises, asking people for proof of their details may be difficult. They may have little, if any, documentation with them.
In order to provide Civil Defence payments the following proof is required:
- confirmation from the Ministry of Civil Defence and Emergency Management that a Civil Defence Emergency has been declared (this will usually come from the Work and Income regional office) or
- direction from your Regional Commissioner that an emergency situation meets qualifications to make Civil Defence Payments and
- confirmation that the person has been affected by the civil defence emergency or adverse event and
- confirmation by the affected person that costs will not be met by insurance, or if insured any excess on insurance cover
## Confirmation a person has been affected by the Civil Defence Emergency or Adverse event
To confirm that a person has been affected by the Civil Defence emergency or adverse event you can look at what is happening in their region to establish whether they have been affected or not. This may be done through Local Council, media, or contacting Regional Office.
Note a person does not need a civil defence registration number to qualify for Civil Defence Payments.
## Affected person is unsure if their costs will be covered by insurance
If a person is unsure if the costs for their immediate needs will be covered by insurance, an initial payment to meet the immediate need can be made.
If the person's insurance later covers any costs paid for with a Civil Defence Payment, the person will need to refund the amount paid.
## Civil Defence Payments application forms
- Civil Defence Payments to Evacuees - Application form
- Civil Defence Adverse Event - Payments to hosts for accommodation form

chunks.title: Applying hardship obligations to partners — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Applying hardship obligations to partners
Hardship obligations can apply to a client and/or their partner.
It may be appropriate to apply hardship obligations to a partner when:
- previous assistance has been provided to meet the need of both the client and partner (eg food grants have been provided because both the client and partner need food)
- the partner has contributed to the need for assistance (eg where assistance with a power bill is required because both the client and partner have not paid a previous bill)
- the partner's actions are adversely affecting the client's ongoing financial position
Generally, when a partner has not taken reasonable steps or not completed a budgeting activity, an application from the client for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment will be declined unless exceptional circumstances exist.
For more information see:
- Partners with youth activity obligations
- Hardship obligations
- Reasonable steps obligation
- Budgeting activity obligation
- Failure to meet hardship obligations

chunks.title: Assistance available when Civil Defence Payments are not activated — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Assistance available when Civil Defence Payments are not activated
Clients who are affected by an adverse event but the situation does not meet the requirements to activate the Civil Defence Payment programme may be able to get other types of financial assistance.
If, because of an adverse event, a client needs to replace some items including, food, clothing, bedding, beds, tables, chairs, drawers, fridges, freezers, etc, they can get financial assistance if they are facing hardship.
The following assistance is available:
- Housing Support Products(assistance with re-establishment costs to obtain rental housing such as bond and rent in advance)
- Advance Payment of Benefit(assistance with re-establishment costs such as connection of utilities, furniture etc)
- Recoverable Assistance Payment(assistance with re-establishment costs such as connection of utilities, furniture etc)
- Special Needs Grants
- Emergency Benefit(interruption in employment and income due to an emergency or other event)
Applicants must meet all the qualifications (income and assets etc.) for these forms of assistance.
When people have been affected by adverse events you can accept this is an exceptional circumstance, and consider to exceeding the guidelines for the maximum amount of assistance payable.
Note if the person has insurance they need to apply for this first and will not be eligible for assistance. If there is any delay in their insurance claim assistance can be provided on the basis that repayment will be made when they get their insurance payment.

chunks.title: Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process
A client or partner may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant during the application process for a benefit and/or during their initial stand-down if they meet all the qualifications.
This type of Special Needs Grant can be paid from the date of first contact up until either:
- the date of decline of the benefit or
- the date of grant of the benefit or
- the commencement date of the benefit or
- the date the application for benefit lapses
whichever is the later.
Special Needs Grants for this purpose are recoverable.
## Restriction on payments
Only when a client or partner has received their maximum entitlement to recoverable assistance during the initial stand-down can you consider providing other assistance, either recoverable or non-recoverable (eg food grants). To get other emergency grants they or a member of their immediate family must be:
- experiencing an emergency situation or
- in extreme hardship
A client or partner is still required to meet all the qualifications for any other Special Needs Grant assistance they apply for, including non-recoverable assistance.
The exception to the restriction, are grants relating to re-establishment situations (eg Steps to Freedom).
## Assistance available
The hardship assistance a client or partner is able to get will depend on their relationship status and whether or not they have children.
## Temporary removal of initial stand-downs between 23 March 2020 and 24 July 2021
Due to the impacts of COVID-19, initial stand-downs were temporarily removed for all clients applying for a main benefit when:
- their entitlement date and benefit grant date were on or after 23 March 2020 and
- their application date and entitlement date were not later than 24 July 2021

chunks.title: Assistance during non-entitlement periods — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Assistance during non-entitlement periods
Special Needs Grant assistance is not available to a client or their partner if they or their partner have a non-entitlement period.
## Exception
A client may receive a non-recoverable payment during a non-entitlement period, if the client:
- is sick or injured during a non-entitlement period and
- is unable to participate: in employment orin an activity to improve work readiness
- in employment or
- in an activity to improve work readiness
## Payment
More than one payment may be made, but the maximum amount payable in any one week cannot be more than the combined total of the:
- maximum weekly rate of Jobseeker Support the client would have received if they were entitled to that benefit and
- Accommodation Supplement at the rate the client would have received if they were entitled to that assistance (this payment cannot be made if the client was receiving payment as a non-beneficiary and this is continuing)
Special Needs Grants for this purpose are non-recoverable.

chunks.title: Assistance when a client is sanctioned — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Assistance when a client is sanctioned
Clients who have failed their obligations and are subject to a grade one or two sanction are not eligible for a Special Needs Grant.
This includes financial and non-financial sanctions.
Clients who are on a grade three sanction are subject to a 13-week non-entitlement period.

chunks.title: Assistance when client is on strike — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Assistance when client is on strike
When a married, civil union or de facto client with dependent children is on strike, their partner may be able to receive a recoverable Special Needs Grant.
## Married, civil union or de facto couples without dependent children, single or sole parent clients
There is no specific circumstances Special Needs Grant assistance available to couples (married, civil union or de facto) without dependent children, single or sole parent clients when on strike.
When a client, partner or their dependent children are in extreme hardship or an emergency situation exists they may be able to receive other Special Needs Grant assistance.
A client is still required to meet all the qualifications for any other Special Needs Grant assistance they apply for, including non-recoverable assistance.
## Assistance for married, civil union or de facto couples with dependent children
The partner must have 1 or more dependent children and:
- meet all the qualifications
- must not be eligible for a benefit in their own rightFor example you cannot pay a Special Needs Grant when the partner can receive part payment of a Jobseeker Support
- the immediate family has no cash assets and cannot obtain credit facilities
- the immediate family has taken all reasonable steps to reduce their fixed commitments and
- the immediate family is not receiving assistance to meet their basic needs from another source
## Payment
More than one payment can be made to a client, but in any 1 week, this cannot be more than:
- the maximum single under 25 years rate of Jobseeker Support
Special Needs Grants for this purpose are recoverable.
## Restriction on payments
Only when the partner has received their maximum entitlement to recoverable assistance during the period that their partner is on strike, can you consider providing other assistance, either recoverable or non-recoverable.
The exception to this restriction are grants for re-establishment situations (eg Steps to Freedom).
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Recovery of payments
- Essential Needs
- Emergency needs
- Deskfile Jobseeker Support rates

chunks.title: Attendants costs — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Attendants costs
A Special Needs Grant for health travel costs may be extended up to a maximum of $400 for the cost of 1 attendant if:
- the person needing treatment is a child
- whanau support is required or
- the medical practitioner or nurse practitioner recommends an attendant.
## Public transport costs
People with a Community Services Card can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect.
If an attendant is a parent or guardian applying on behalf of a child in their care and the attendant is a Community Services Card holder, the attendant's health travel costs should be no more than the cost of the discounted fare if they are using public transport, unless they cannot get the discount for good reason.
Note in other situations, you cannot require an attendant to confirm if they are eligible for or use the 50% discount through Community Connect.
Example: Good reason
The attendant has a disability and there are accessibility issues with applying for the Community Connect discount through a public transport provider's website, and this is the only way to apply.

chunks.title: Acceptable budgeting advice service — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Acceptable budgeting advice service
Clients should be referred to the budgeting advice services that are most likely to help given their individual circumstances and needs.
Budgeting advice should be provided by a reputable and independent budgeting service.

chunks.title: Bedding — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Bedding
If the client meets all qualifications, they may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant for the cost of bedding if:
- there is a long-term health condition or disability in the client's immediate family causing extraordinary wear and tear on bed linen or
- an additional child has been incorporated into the immediate family by way of birth or adoption
Special Needs Grants for bedding should not be granted when a Special Needs Grant for re-establishment costs has already been granted or when bedding is included as a consumable item in the payment of a Disability Allowance.
## Payment
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, the maximum amount payable towards the cost of bedding is $200.
Special Needs Grant for this purpose are:
- non-recoverable and
- restricted to one payment for the same or similar purpose in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Billeting — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Billeting
Accommodation providers who billet an evacuee can include private homes where the host is the evacuee's parent, relative, friend or partner (providing they were not living together at the time of the civil defence emergency).
If billet costs include the provision of food, ensure that any further payments for food are for additional food requirements not supplied by the accommodation provider.
At a local level, the Ministry of Civil Defence and Emergency Management is likely to be involved in organising billets for evacuees.
Payments are only available until the evacuees are able to return to their home.

chunks.title: Budgeting activity obligation — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Clients who frequently access Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit and Recoverable Assistance Payment may need to meet a budgeting activity obligation. This obligation requires clients to take part in activities that will help them improve their ability to budget and make the most of the resources available to them. Clients may be required to: - complete or review a budgeting worksheet - attend a budgeting course or seminar or - attend a budgeting advice service The specific activity the client is required to complete should be the activity that is most likely to meet their needs and be helpful given their personal situation. Note you must make sure the client is getting their correct entitlement at every interaction with them.

chunks.title: Applying budgeting activity obligation — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Generally clients are not required to complete a budgeting activity until after they have received Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit and/or Recoverable Assistance Payments on at least 3 grant dates during the past 12 months. Before applying a budgeting activity obligation, you need to ensure that you understand the client’s circumstances and how applying the obligation could help them. A budgeting activity obligation should only be applied if you have been in contact with the client and determined: - the client is likely to benefit from completing a budgeting activity - the client’s financial situation could improve as a result and - the client has previously: been offered services to help them build their financial capability, understood how they could benefit from participating, and chose to not take up the services orused a building financial capability or similar service and their circumstances have substantially changed from when they used the service - been offered services to help them build their financial capability, understood how they could benefit from participating, and chose to not take up the services or - used a building financial capability or similar service and their circumstances have substantially changed from when they used the service Before applying a budgeting activity obligation, also consider: - the number of previous applications for hardship assistance and why the assistance was needed eg is there a pattern of not being able to meet regular, ongoing costs or were there a number of separate unforeseeable events? - eg is there a pattern of not being able to meet regular, ongoing costs or were there a number of separate unforeseeable events? - if the current need is related to unforeseeable events, or circumstances out of the client’s control eg a recent bereavement or separation, emergency or other adverse event, etc - eg a recent bereavement or separation, emergency or other adverse event, etc - why the client has not taken up services to help them build their financial capability if previously offered If you have decided that the client should have a budgeting activity obligation, discuss which budgeting activity will be most helpful for them, make sure they know the activity they choose is an obligation and explain the consequence if they do not complete the activity. Note in some circumstances partners must also complete a budgeting activity. For information on when it would not be appropriate to require a client to complete a budgeting activity see:

chunks.title: Applying budgeting activity obligation before third grant date — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Generally clients are only required to complete a budgeting activity after they have received Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit and/or Recoverable Assistance Payments on at least 3 grant dates during the past 12 months. However, you can apply the budgeting activity obligation before 3 grant dates. When deciding whether to apply the budgeting activity obligation before their third grant date you must also consider if the client has: - received repeated grants for the same costs - a history of receiving multiple hardship payments - a significant debt with the Ministry of Social Development For more information see: - Completing a budgeting worksheet - Attending a budgeting course or seminar - Offering services to build financial capability at application - Attending a budgeting advice service - Hardship obligations - Reasonable steps obligation - Example - applying hardship obligations - Applying hardship obligations to partners - Partners with youth activity obligations - Failure to meet hardship obligations

chunks.title: Budgeting activity obligation not applied — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Budgeting activity obligation not applied
You should not apply a budgeting activity obligation if it is unlikely to help the client, and their financial situation would not improve as a result.
Clients applying for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payments of Benefit and Recoverable Assistance Payment who should not be required to complete a budgeting activity for a period of time, or until their circumstances change, include those who:
- have high unavoidable costs and are unlikely to benefit from the budgeting activity
- previously completed the same budgeting activity and their circumstances have not substantially changed since completing that activity
- had a recent sudden change in circumstances, eg a recent bereavement or separation
- had a temporary change in their situation, eg an unforeseen drop in income or a change in needs due to family violence

chunks.title: Calculation of maximum amounts payable — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Step 1 Has the client applied for the re-establishment grant within 1 year (or 2 years for English language courses) of them entering New Zealand? Yes - go to step 2. No - client is not eligible to receive a payment for a re-establishment grant. Step 2 Maximum amounts Examples Did the client get a re-establishment grant before 9 November 2020? No - total maximum is $5000 and within that amount, the maximum for accommodation costs is $3500. Yes - go to step 3 to work out new maximum amount payable. Client can be granted up to $3500 for accommodation costs. The balance of up to the maximum of $5000 can be used for other costs. Step 3 Client got a re-establishment grant for accommodation costs and other costs before 9 November 2020. Total maximum payable is $5000 less the amount of any grants received before 9 November 2020. New maximum for accommodation costs of $3500 less the amount previously paid for accommodation costs = the new maximum amount available for accommodation costs. Previous grants $1200 (other costs) + 800 (accommodation) = $2000. $5000 - 2000 = $3000 - the new maximum payable for all costs. Note the client must continue to pay back the $800 previously received for accommodation costs. $3500 - $800 = $2700 the new maximum for accommodation costs. Client got a re-establishment for accommodation cost only. Total maximum payable is $5000 less the amount of any grants received before 9 November 2020. New maximum for accommodation costs is $3500 less the amount previously paid for accommodation costs = new maximum for accommodation cost. Previous grant for accommodation costs of $750 (recoverable) Client has new maximum of: $5000 - $750 = $4250 for all costs. Note the client must continue to pay back the $750 previously received for accommodation. $3500 - $750 = $2750 maximum for accommodation costs. Client got a re-establishment grant for other costs only before 9 November 2020. Total new maximum is $5000 less the amount of any grants received before 9 November 2020. New maximum for accommodation costs is $3500. Previous grant of $750 for other costs (recoverable) Client has a maximum of: $5000 - $1500 = $3500 for all costs A maximum of $3500 for accommodation costs as the client did not previously receive a grant for accommodation costs Note the full amount can be used for accommodation costs, if needed

chunks.title: Cash asset limits — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Cash asset limits
For most categories of Special Needs Grant, the cash assets of the client and their partner (if any) applying for a Special Needs Grant must not exceed the appropriate asset limit:
Single person
Asset limit for a single person without dependent children
Married, civil union or de facto couple (with or without dependent children) orSole parents
Asset limit for a married, civil union or de facto couple with or without dependent children
## Special Needs Grant for food
Clients must have no cash assets when they apply for a Special Needs Grant for food.
Clients will not be eligible if they or their partner (if any) have any cash assets.
## Bank overdraft
In most circumstances, a bank overdraft or credit facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.
However, a bank overdraft or credit facility is considered a cash asset or resource for a sole parent or couple with one or more dependent children who is applying for assistance during the initial stand-down and/or application process. These clients must have no cash assets and cannot obtain credit facilities.

chunks.title: Cash assets — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Cash assets mean assets of the client and their partner (if any) and if the client is a dependent child, their parents, that can be easily converted into cash.

chunks.title: Cash assets include — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Cash assets mean assets of the client and their partner (if any) and if the client is a dependent child, their parents, that can be easily converted into cash and include: - bills of exchange or promissory notes - building society shares - money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society - money invested with or lent to any bank, other financial institution or other person - mortgage investments and other long term loans - shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds, and other bonds - the client's share in any partnership and - the net equity held in any property or land not used as the person's home

chunks.title: Cash assets do not include — extra help > special needs grant
