chunks.text: - a caravan, boat, or other vehicle with a net equity of less than $2000, or which is used by the person or a member of their immediate family for day to day accommodation - a motor vehicle principally used by the client for private use - the home property and land on which it is situated - Christchurch mosques attack support payments - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts - Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income - MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to system processing error from 1993 to 2014 for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after payment is made - personal effects - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment) - specified Ex gratia and Compensation payments - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received A bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client, except for couples or sole parents applying for assistance during the initial stand-down and/or application process. Canterbury earthquake related payments Payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client received the payment.

chunks.title: Cash assets - rural assistance — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Cash assets mean assets of that person and partner (if any) that can be easily converted into cash.

chunks.title: Cash assets include — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Cash assets mean assets of that person and partner (if any) that can be easily converted into cash and include: - building society shares - bills of exchange or promissory notes - money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society - money invested with or lent to any bank or other financial institution - mortgage investments and other long term loans - share, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds, and other bonds - the client's share in any partnership and - the net equity held in any property or land not used as the person's home (except the net equity in the Primary Industry is not included in the clients cash assets)

chunks.title: Cash assets do not include — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: - a caravan, boat, or other vehicle with a net equity of less than $2,000 and which is used by the person or a member of their family for day to day accommodation - Christchurch mosques attack support payments - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - ex gratia payments made to clients that the Ministry of Social Development does not include in calculation of income or cash assets - funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts - Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income - motor vehicle principally used by the client for private use - MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after the payment is made - personal effects - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made - shares that are required to access farming services eg, Ravensdown, Fonterra, Farmlands or Silver Fern FarmsIf you need help to decide a farming service please contact Helpline. - the proceeds from the sale of capital pastoral stock (whether held or not held in any of the assets above) - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client. The normal cash assets exemption applies to rural assistance.

chunks.title: Civil Defence Payment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Civil Defence Payments are available to meet the immediate needs of people affected by a civil defence emergency or adverse event. A Civil Defence Payment is available to people resident in an area when: - a civil defence emergency has been declared under the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act 2002 or - a Regional Commissioner in consultation with the Group General Manager Client Service Delivery and a Local Authority and/or other relevant emergency service has directed that an event meets the established guidelines for a civil defence emergency or adverse event and - the person has left their home as a result of the civil defence emergency or adverse event, or was away from their home at the time of the emergency and is unable to return to their home due to the emergency or - the person must stay confined in their home as a result of the civil defence emergency or adverse event or - the person is unable to work as a result of the civil defence emergency or adverse event and - the person does not have insurance to cover the cost of their immediate needs

chunks.title: No income and asset test — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: There is no income or asset test. Civil Defence Payments are non-taxable and do not affect a person's eligibility for most other forms of social assistance. This is due to the exceptional circumstances of those affected by a civil defence emergency or an adverse event. Exception is Temporary Additional Support when Civil Defence Payments for 'loss of livelihood' are counted as chargeable income. Payments for accommodation costs can't be made in a situation where an offer of alternative and free accommodation is available, or when a person is able to return to their home but chooses not to.

chunks.title: Lawfully present in New Zealand — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: A Civil Defence Payment is only available to people who are lawfully present in New Zealand. This means the person must: - be a New Zealand citizen or - hold, or be deemed to hold, a current visa under the Immigration Act 2009 This includes temporary visa holders and international tourists. In the first instance, international tourists must contact their travel agent or consulate for assistance. If assistance is not available or cannot be provided quickly enough, a Civil Defence Payment can be considered. Note a Civil Defence Payment is not available to a person who is unlawfully in New Zealand e.g. an overstayer.

chunks.title: Insurance claim — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: If a person has made an application to their insurance company to cover the cost of their immediate needs, but there is a delay in their insurance claim, assistance can be provided on the basis that repayment will be made when the insurance payment is received.

chunks.title: Client qualifies for and is getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Client qualifies for and is getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme
The Family Violence Programme is part of the Special Needs Grants Welfare Programme and may be paid to clients on the grounds of hardship.
The payment enables a client, who is an ex-partner of a New Zealand citizen or resident, to get assistance from the Ministry of Social Development when the client intended to seek residence on the basis of their relationship. The relationship then ended because of domestic violence to themselves and/or their dependent children by their partner or another person that lives at the same address.
A client getting payment under this programme will qualify for social housing on residency grounds if they are ordinarily resident in New Zealand.
## Residency status reconfirmed regularly while client on Social Housing Register
The residency status must be reconfirmed regularly while the client is on the Social Housing Register. This ensures that if a formal offer of housing is made by a social housing provider the client meets the residency criteria.
If it is identified the client is on the Social Housing Register and no longer qualifies for this Special Needs Grant, the client no longer qualifies for social housing. They will be removed from the register, unless they now meet another of the residency qualifications.

chunks.title: Clients transferring from a main benefit to New Zealand Superannuation — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Clients transferring from a main benefit to New Zealand Superannuation
If a client meets all qualifications, they may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant if they:
- are currently receiving a main benefit
- are transferring to New Zealand Superannuation and
- require assistance to make the transfer
In some situations clients who transfer to New Zealand Superannuation from a weekly benefit will not experience a reduction in income as they are paid in arrears. If the client is suffering hardship and meets all the qualifications then you may consider a Special Needs Grant.
## Payment
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, the amount of the grant can be no more than:
- the equivalent of 1 week's main benefit the client was entitled to receive immediately before transferring to New Zealand Superannuation and
- one week's Accommodation Supplement and any other supplementary assistance the client was entitled to receive before the transfer
Special Needs Grants for this purpose are:
- non-recoverable
Where exceptional circumstances exist you can exceed the maximum amount payable.

chunks.title: Acceptable budgeting worksheet — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Acceptable budgeting worksheet
Clients can complete any budgeting worksheet as long as it records and compares information on income and expenses.
To complete this budgeting activity a client's budget must include:
- all of their costs (and their partner's costs), including weekly, fortnightly, monthly and annual costs and
- their income from all sources
All clients will have costs related to accommodation, power, food and transport but you should also check they have included everything they spend money on throughout the year, eg school uniforms, clothing, doctor's bills, birthday presents, etc.
For more information see:
- Budgeting activity obligation
- Attending a budgeting advice service
- Attending a budgeting course or seminar
- Reasonable steps obligation
- Failure to meet hardship obligations
- Building Financial Capability services [no link find out why] procedures
- Adding plan items and resulting activities in CMS [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Costs covered — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Costs covered
Civil Defence Payments can cover the following costs (up to the maximum allowed):
- payments to hosts for billeting evacuees in private homes
- accommodation costs for evacuees in temporary accommodation e.g. in motels, hotels, camping grounds or home-stays
- loss of livelihood when a person can't work and loses income due to the emergency - e.g. they can't get to work, the workplace is closed, or they need to stay with their family or whanau
- food, clothing and bedding for immediate needs
Note payments for food, clothing, bedding, and loss of livelihood are not limited to evacuees.
## Other assistance
Assistance for other one-off items such as tables, chairs, drawers, beds, fridges, freezers etc, can be considered under normal Special Needs Grant/Advance Payment of Benefit/Recoverable Assistance Payment provisions.
This means a person's income and assets will be taken into account as part of the assessment.
## Pet-related costs
A Civil Defence Payment is not available for any pet-related costs as a result of a civil defence emergency or adverse event.
This includes food, veterinary costs, and temporary accommodation costs e.g. kennels and catteries.

chunks.title: Cover under Accident Rehabilitation and Insurance — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Cover under Accident Rehabilitation and Insurance
You may decide a Special Needs Grant for health travel costs is to be recoverable if:
- the client has or it is considered likely that the client has cover under the Accident Rehabilitation Compensation and Insurance Act 1992 or the Accident Insurance Act 1998 in respect of the treatment, assessment or services and
- the client cannot show that they have no entitlement to travel costs under the applicable Acts, as stated above
ACC have specific criteria that must be met before they make a contribution for travelling to treatment and this cannot be assessed by ACC until the client provides evidence of actual costs after the treatment.
When the client provides evidence at a later date that ACC have declined their application, the Special Needs Grant decision can be reviewed and made non-recoverable.
For more information see:
- Recovering payments

chunks.title: Debt types not included — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Debt types not included
Debt types not included in the maximum recovery rate of debt of $40.00 per week are:
- Child Disability Allowance debt
- Family Benefit Capitalisation debt
- Fraudulent Student Loans
- Liable Parent Contributions (LPC)
- Maintenance debt
- Major Repairs Advances (MRA)
- Residential Support Services debt
- Student Allowance debt
- Suspensory Loans
- Work Services debt

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Deciding ordinarily resident
Generally a client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand to receive a Special Needs Grant.
Ordinarily resident means someone who is normally and lawfully in New Zealand and intends to stay here, that is, they consider New Zealand to be their home.
Whether a person is ordinarily resident is a question of fact and degree and their intentions during any period of absence is the most important factor.
Where it is not clear if a client is ordinarily resident, consider the following:
(a) the clients' intentions toward New Zealand (that is, the reasons for their absence from New Zealand and the reasons for their return). Are they going overseas for a holiday or are they intending to live overseas permanently (sighting return air tickets is a good indication)?
(b) the length of time they spend in New Zealand on a continual basis
(c) property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans)
(d) where are their cash assets held?
(e) is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and do they pay New Zealand taxes?
(f) do they still vote (or are they eligible to vote) in the New Zealand election?
(g) their commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in the community, community events, clubs and other groups)?
Note a person cannot be ordinarily resident in two places at the same time.

chunks.title: Dental treatment costs not covered — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Dental treatment costs not covered
The following dental treatments and services are not considered essential for the purposes of Special Needs Grants for essential dental treatment and are specifically excluded, except for molar root canal treatment and clean, scale and polish in specific circumstances.
Treatment
Explanation
Regular dental check-ups
Regular dental check-ups are periodic dental care for the purposes of maintaining oral health and preventing oral health issues and may include teeth cleaning and x-rays.
The cost of regular dental check-ups cannot be covered by the Special Needs Grant even when an immediate need for essential dental treatment is identified during the check-up.
Cosmetic treatments
Dental treatment that improves the appearance of teeth, gums, and/or bite. This includes crowns, veneers, implants, and teeth whitening.
Clean, scale and polish
Periodic teeth cleaning that removes plaque and tartar build up.
The cost of teeth cleaning cannot be included in a Special Needs Grant for essential dental treatment unless the treatment is required because of a gum infection.
Cast Restorations
Tooth restoration constructed outside of the mouth, then cemented back into the cavity of the tooth.
This includes crowns, inlays, onlays, and overlays.
Orthodontic treatment
Correction of crooked teeth, wide gaps in teeth, and/or an improper bite through the placement of braces or a retainer
Molar root canal treatment
Treatment to eliminate bacteria from an infected root canal, prevent reinfection, and attempt to save the tooth.
The cost of molar root canal treatment cannot be covered by a Special Needs Grant for essential dental treatment unless exceptional circumstances exist.
Dentures
An artificial replacement for one or several teeth (partial dentures), or all teeth (full dentures).
## Exceptions
The following treatments can be included in specific circumstances:
- molar root canal treatment in exceptional circumstances
- clean, scale and polish that is required to treat a gum infection
## Molar root canal treatment in exceptional circumstances
It may be appropriate to cover the cost of this treatment if the client has exceptional circumstances that mean a molar root canal is the only treatment option for them. This is usually when extraction of a tooth is not recommended for medical reasons. For example:
- the client has had previous radiation therapy in the area or
- they must take medication that may lead to medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw if teeth are extracted

chunks.title: Designated health practitioner assessment travel — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Designated health practitioner assessment travel
If the client meets all qualifications, they may be able to get a Special Needs Grant for travel costs if they are being referred to a designated health practitioner to establish medical entitlement, or when you are reviewing their medical entitlement to Jobseeker Support or Supported Living Payment.
The payment is intended to ensure that the client is not out of pocket as a result of being referred.
## Payment
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, a maximum of up to $200 can be paid for:
- actual or reasonable travel expenses for a return journey of at least 8 km to the place of examination
- travel costs when the client cannot use public transport because of their disability
- travel costs if there is no public transport available when the travel is less than 8kms
Special Needs Grants for this purpose are non-recoverable.
This amount can be extended to $400 if the client requires an attendant to assist them.
This amount can be extended to $400 if the client requires an attendant to assist them.
Note If a person has a Community Services card, they can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect.

chunks.title: Driver Licence — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Driver Licence
A recoverable Special Needs Grant may be made for a client to:
- get a new driver licence
- renew their driver licence
- reinstate their driver licence
- re-sit their driver licence test (after paying the initial test fee)
- reschedule their driver licence test
Note the re-sit fee only applies for Class 1 (car) drivers who have failed to pass their driver licence test twice.
A Special Needs Grant is available for all classes of driver licence.
Special Needs Grants for driver licence costs must not be more than the actual fees payable.
This assistance is not available to pay for endorsements on driver licences.
## Rescheduling drivers licence tests
If a client reschedules their drivers licence test within 2 working days of their test, they may be charged a rescheduling fee.
Clients are not charged a fee if they reschedule their drivers licence test more than 2 working days (a full 48 hours) before the day of their test, or they reschedule their test online.
Where possible, clients should reschedule their test online. If clients are unable to do this online, MSD may be able to cover the rescheduling fee under a Special Needs Grant.
MSD cannot cover the costs associated with cancelling a driver's licence tests.
## Assistance cannot be paid
A client will not qualify for a Special Needs Grant for driver licence costs if they:
- are disqualified from holding or getting a driver licence or
- have not renewed their driver licence before the expiry date without a good and sufficient reason

chunks.title: Effluent Treatment System maintenance and repair — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Effluent Treatment System maintenance and repair
If the client meets all qualifications, they may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant for the cost of the repair and maintenance of an on-site effluent treatment system (such as a septic tank) if:
- the need for the repair or maintenance is immediate and essential and
- the client is a homeowner who resides in the house
or
- the client: is residing in a dwelling on Māori land held in multiple ownership with the permission of the landowners andis responsible for the maintenance of the on-site effluent treatment system which services that dwelling andmakes no or minimal payments for either the right to occupy the land or for the right to occupy the dwelling
- is residing in a dwelling on Māori land held in multiple ownership with the permission of the landowners and
- is responsible for the maintenance of the on-site effluent treatment system which services that dwelling and
- makes no or minimal payments for either the right to occupy the land or for the right to occupy the dwelling
An on-site effluent treatment system is any system for treating human effluent located on land on which an applicant's dwelling is erected and which services that dwelling. It includes, but is not limited to, septic tanks, long drop toilets and compost based toilets.
Note maintenance includes the cleaning and/or emptying of a septic tank.
## Payment
The maximum amount payable towards the repair or maintenance of an on-site effluent treatment system is $300.
Special Needs Grants for this purpose:
- are non-recoverable
- are not restricted to one payment for the same or similar purpose in any 104 week period and
- must not exceed in total $300 in any 104 week period

chunks.title: Eligibility to the Family Violence Programme — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Eligibility to the Family Violence Programme
To qualify for payment under the Family Violence Programme, the client must:
- be in New Zealand
- have a written referral from Immigration New Zealand supporting the client's application for assistance, which confirms the client: has lodged or intends to lodge an application with Immigration New Zealand for a residence class visa under the Partnership Category (on the ground of marriage or civil union, in a de facto relationship, or living in a stable relationship) andbe living apart from and have lost the financial support of their partner andhave a work visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009 (or a work permit, if granted before 29 November 2010) on the grounds the person is a victim of family violence
- has lodged or intends to lodge an application with Immigration New Zealand for a residence class visa under the Partnership Category (on the ground of marriage or civil union, in a de facto relationship, or living in a stable relationship) and
- be living apart from and have lost the financial support of their partner and
- have a work visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009 (or a work permit, if granted before 29 November 2010) on the grounds the person is a victim of family violence
- meet a cash asset test
and
- be in need of financial support, including financial support for their dependent children (if any)
## Partner a temporary migrant and not a New Zealand citizen or resident
The client will not qualify for assistance if their partner was a temporary migrant and not a New Zealand citizen or resident.

chunks.title: Emergency and essential needs not in client's name — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Emergency and essential needs not in client's name
Emergency and/or essential items may be considered for a Special Needs Grant but generally these are only considered if the cost is in the client's or their family's (if any) name.
Where an emergency and/or essential item is not in their name they are not liable for the payment and a Special Needs Grant generally is not considered.
## Exception
There may be situations where a client or their partner (if any) have entered an informal arrangement with another person to pay for an emergency and/or essential item using the other person's name and/or credit rating for the contract.
You need to be satisfied that the client or their partner is the person making the payment(s) and that it was the intention of the parties to the informal arrangement that they would have responsibility for the payment(s) and the use and control of the emergency and/or essential item.
A full statement from the client or partner and the other person named in the contract is required along with a copy of the agreement to determine if the cost can be considered for a Special Needs Grant.
Note in these situations the client is not able to meet the cost of the item from their own resources and the need must be an emergency and/or essential.

chunks.title: Emergency medical equipment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Emergency medical equipment
If the client meets all qualifications, they may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant for medical equipment if:
- they have a need for the item or service but cannot receive funding through the District Health Board
- special circumstances exist and
- the client and/or their family would suffer serious hardship without the item or service
To consider whether special circumstances exist, consider the following:
- whether an emergency exists
- the consequences to the client if they do not have the item or service (that is, is the item or service a preference or a must?) and
- whether there are other medical alternatives that can meet the need
A Special Needs Grant for medical equipment should not be paid when the client has been declined assistance from the District Health Board because they do not have an essential need or they do not meet their medical criteria.
## Proof
The following proof is required for Special Needs Grants for medical equipment:
- a letter from the District Health Board stating that funding is not available for the item or service and why it is not available and
- a letter from a health official stating what the consequences would be if the client, their partner or dependent child did not receive the item or service
## Payment
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, the maximum amount payable towards emergency medical equipment is $500.
Although Special Needs Grants under this category may be recoverable or non-recoverable, generally grants for emergency medical equipment are non-recoverable. However, if you consider it equitable in the circumstances for the client to pay the grant back, you may decide the Special Needs Grant should be recoverable.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Exceptional circumstances
- Recovering payment

chunks.title: Emergency medical treatment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: If the client meets all qualifications, they may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant towards the cost of emergency medical treatment including doctor's fees, prescription charges or hospital care. Special Needs Grants cannot be used to 'top up' any shortfall when the medical treatment is as a result of an accident that has been accepted by ACC. However, when travel is required, see Health travel costs. Where the client is liable for the part user-charges of any medical expenses, grants are limited to the amounts after the deduction of subsidy from the Community Services Card or any amount paid by Disability Allowance. Special Needs Grants should not generally be approved for emergency treatment in a private hospital, unless there is a good reason why they cannot be transferred to a public hospital, such as being in critical condition.

chunks.title: Outstanding accounts — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Where the client needed emergency medical treatment and was unable to seek prior Work and Income approval for the service. You can consider paying the account if the client has no other way of paying (for example through instalments) or their current budget does not leave room to meet this unexpected cost. You can make a grant for this purpose to each family member of an immediate family.

chunks.title: Reimbursements — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: There may be situations where a client needs emergency medical treatment and is unable to make arrangements for repayment of the cost of the treatment, as they are required to pay for this immediately. You can consider a non-recoverable Special Needs Grant as a reimbursement for the actual costs incurred where the client is required to make immediate payment for the visit. Note the emergency medical treatment must be a situation that could not have been foreseen or predicted.

chunks.title: Example 1 — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: A client has an appointment with their health practitioner at 4.30pm on a Friday as they require immediate treatment. The client is unable to seek Work and Income approval for payment prior to the treatment. The client pays for the account, as the health practitioner/surgery requires immediate payment but they have no money left for their normal daily expenses. The client contacts the service centre on Monday for financial assistance. A Special Needs Grant can be considered in this case as a reimbursement.

chunks.title: Example 2 — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: A client with a serious illness goes to their health practitioner on Monday, however, by Friday their condition has got worse and the client needs to make an emergency appointment to see their health practitioner again. The client pays for the account, as the health practitioner/surgery requires immediate payment but they have no money left for their normal daily expenses. The client contacts the service centre on the following Monday for financial assistance. A Special Needs Grant can be considered in this case as the client did not know their condition would deteriorate and that they would require an additional appointment. A reimbursement for the Friday appointment with their health practitioner can be considered as an emergency medical treatment Special Needs Grant.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Unless exceptional circumstances exist, the maximum amount payable towards emergency medical treatment is $300. Special Needs Grants for this purpose are: - non-recoverable and - not restricted to 1 payment for the same or similar purpose in any 52 week period Deduct any health-related subsidy and/or insurance payments from the total amount required. For more information see: - Qualifications - Health travel costs - Exceptional circumstances

chunks.title: Emergency needs — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Emergency needs
Emergency Special Needs Grants may be made only when an emergency situation exists, which has given rise to an immediate need.
In determining whether an emergency situation exists, consider:
- whether the situation was unforeseen
- if the situation could have been foreseen or predicted, whether the client could reasonably have expected to make provision in advance in order to meet the need
- the extent to which not making a grant would worsen the client's positionincrease or create any risk to the life or welfare of the client or the client's partner or dependent children orcause serious hardship to the client, or the client's partner or dependent children
- worsen the client's position
- increase or create any risk to the life or welfare of the client or the client's partner or dependent children or
- cause serious hardship to the client, or the client's partner or dependent children
Where the client needed emergency medical treatment and was unable to seek prior Ministry of Social Development approval for the service you can consider paying the account if the client has no other way of paying (e.g. through instalments) or their current budget does not leave room to meet this unexpected cost.
Special Needs Grants for Emergency Needs are non-recoverable unless otherwise stated. The following table lists the various Emergency Needs categories. Further details are listed under each category.
## Emergency needs categories
Category

Emergency medical equipment

chunks.title: Entering residential facility — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Entering residential facility
A prisoner may also get a Steps to Freedom grant when they have been released from prison to a residential facility.
Steps to Freedom payments should only be made for valid and reasonable costs associated with re-establishment that are not paid for or the responsibility of the residential support provider. For example clothing or toiletry items are unlikely to be provided, but accommodation costs are likely to be covered by the residential home.
## Leaving residential facility
An ex-prisoner who is moving into independent accommodation from a residential facility may also apply for a Steps to Freedom grant.
The client must have valid re-establishment costs and the amount paid must not exceed the maximum amount payable of $350 (less any amount paid when the client entered the residential facility).

chunks.title: Essential dental treatment costs covered — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Essential dental treatment costs covered
Special Needs Grants for essential dental treatments and services include (but are not limited to):
Treatment
Explanation
Consultations
Ad-hoc consultations (and associated x-rays) to investigate a particular oral health need or concern e.g. toothache or sensitivity.
Note
Extractions
Removal of a tooth beyond repair or restoration.
Fillings (tooth restoration)
Treatment to restore a tooth to full function, often by removing damaged tooth tissue and filling the space with a filling material.
Note
Root canal treatment (excluding molars)
Treatment to eliminate bacteria from an infected root canal, prevent reinfection, and save the tooth. Root canals are generally only performed on incisors, canines, and pre-molars. This treatment is not generally suitable for molars.
Note
Treatment of infection
Treatment of a tooth abscess or gum infection. Treatment may be done in stages, with the infection being treated first and the repair or restoration completed once the infection has healed.
Some dental treatments and services are not essential and cannot be included in a Special Needs Grant for essential dental treatment.
However, the following treatments can be included in specific circumstances:
- molar root canal treatment in exceptional circumstances
- clean, scale and polish required to treat a gum infection

chunks.title: Essential dental treatment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Essential dental treatment
A Special Needs Grant for dental treatment is available for a client or their immediate family if they have an immediate need for essential dental treatment.
The dental treatment needs to be essential, and must be required immediately for an oral health issue that:
- has deteriorated or would begin to deteriorate if left untreated and
- is having, or is likely to have, a detrimental effect on the client's oral health and/or their physical health
The essential dental treatment must be provided:
- by a dentist or
- by a health agency for a fee

chunks.title: Essential living expenses — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Essential living expenses
Essential living expenses for rural assistance payments may include but are not limited to:
- food
- fuel (including petrol, diesel and oil)
- telephone rental, this may include: internet connection
- internet connection
- motor vehicles costs - repayment and running costs
- essential travel, this may include: employment related traveltravel when accessing essential services and supplies (including children's education and groceries)
- employment related travel
- travel when accessing essential services and supplies (including children's education and groceries)
- power
- accommodation
- childcare costs
- hire purchase expenses for essential household items only, it may also include employment related items. It does not include luxury items such as fishing/jet boats or small planes
- transport cost due to disability
- disability and personal health costs
- counselling
- education costs for dependent children

chunks.title: Essential Needs — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Special Needs Grants are available for clients with a qualifying immediate and essential need. In general, these situations may be expected and do not come under the emergency criteria. An immediate need must be established in all cases before a Special Needs Grant is approved. Special Needs Grants for Essential Needs are generally non-recoverable.

chunks.text: Category Maximum amount in a 26-week period unless exceptional circumstances exist Status Food Single person $200 non-recoverable Married, civil union or de facto person $300 non-recoverable Married, civil union or de facto couple or sole parent with 1 or 2 dependent children $450 non-recoverable Married, civil union or de facto couple or sole parent with 3 or more dependent children $550 non-recoverable

chunks.title: Evacuees in temporary accommodation — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Evacuees in temporary accommodation
At a local level, Civil Defence and Emergency Management is likely to be involved in organising alternative accommodation for evacuees and is responsible for housing evacuees in the emergency phase of an event.
In the recovery phase, payment can be made where evacuees are accommodated in temporary accommodation (in motels, hotels, camping grounds or home-stays, for example).
The amount paid to accommodation providers can cover the actual costs provided this does not exceed the set maximum amount payable.
If accommodation costs include provision of food ensure that any further payments for food are for additional food requirements not supplied by the accommodation provider.
Payments are only available until the evacuees are able to return to their home.
For more information see:
- Application process - Civil Defence payment
- Deskfile Civil Defence payment rates
- Payment process - Civil Defence payment
- Review of ongoing payments

chunks.title: Example - applying hardship obligations — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Kerry has significant debt and since being granted a main benefit she has received hardship grants to pay for both ongoing regular costs like food and power, and help with annual and unexpected costs like car repairs. Hardship application Event 1. January While attending a work focused appointment, Kerry says that she needs help to pay for food. The case manager: - finds out more about Kerry's current financial situation - assesses what assistance is available and whether she is currently getting the correct payments for her circumstances - grants a Special Needs Grant for food and - offers Kerry information on the building financial capability services available 2. January Kerry applies online via MyMSD for assistance with food 3 weeks after her last grant. The reasonable steps obligation is covered in MyMSD and Kerry indicates what steps she will take. Assistance is granted and she is provided with a link to information on building financial capability services via MyMSD. 3. March Kerry applies online for assistance with food again. Assistance is granted and she is provided with a link to information on building financial capability services via MyMSD. 4. April Kerry is in the service centre and asks for help with her power bill. The case manager: - talks to Kerry about her financial situation - assesses what assistance is available and whether she is currently getting the correct payments for her circumstances - discusses what Kerry has done to meet the reasonable steps obligation and what else may be possible including: setting up a direct deduction to pay for power weeklylooking for a smaller house to rent - setting up a direct deduction to pay for power weekly - looking for a smaller house to rent - grants hardship assistance for power - checks if Kerry has attended any building financial capability services - but Kerry has not - explains how the services could help and provides the information on how to access services again 5. May Kerry's car needs repair work so she can get to work and she comes into the service centre to get help. Kerry works rurally so the car is essential as there is no public transport in her area. The case manager discusses what Kerry did between grants to improve her financial situation. Kerry reviewed listings for several cheaper rental houses but did not set up a direct deduction. They discuss what other options may be available to help Kerry manage her money. Kerry has not taken up the offer of services to build her financial capability so information is offered again. After assessing if Kerry's payments are correct, an Advance is approved for the car repairs.

chunks.title: Example - applying hardship obligations — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: They agree that as reasonable steps Kerry will set up the redirection, keep looking for less costly housing, and look for cheaper phone and internet options before she applies for another grant. 6. May Kerry applies online for assistance with food. She is under the limit and signals that she has done what was agreed to take reasonable steps. Assistance is granted and she is provided with a link to information on building financial capability services via MyMSD. 7. July In July Kerry comes into the service centre as she can't make a payment on her car loan. After assessing whether she is getting the correct payments for her circumstances, they discuss what Kerry did between grants, including: - continuing to look for cheaper housing - changing her internet plan to a cheaper one Payment is made for the car costs as Kerry has taken reasonable steps but they agree that before she applies for another grant Kerry will: - set up the direct deduction for power - look at ways to reduce her food bill via planning - look at ways to reduce power usage. Kerry has not taken up the offer of services to build her financial capability so information is offered again – the case manager strongly suggests Kerry take up the budgeting advice as it appears there are still some things, she can do to improve her financial situation. 8. September Kerry comes into the service centre to get help with her power payments as she has fallen behind and is at risk of disconnection. Kerry has not set up the direct deduction for power as discussed at previous appointments and has been struggling to reduce her food and power bills. Kerry has not accessed any of the services offered but has started looking for a job that pays more or can offer more hours. The case manager checks that Kerry is getting everything she is entitled to. Payment is made to Kerry for this month's power bill as Kerry has taken reasonable steps. However, the case manager decides that Kerry should have a budgeting activity obligation applied as there are a number of ways for her to improve her ability to manage her money. They agree that seeing a budget advisor would be the most helpful activity and Kerry is told that she may be declined future hardship assistance if she does not complete this activity. An appointment is made for a week later to see how the activity goes. Kerry does not attend and this is noted for follow up the next time Kerry applies for hardship assistance. 9. September

chunks.title: Example - applying hardship obligations — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Two weeks later Kerry comes in for a food grant. She has not done the budgeting activity or taken reasonable steps but after discussion with the case manager about her situation, it is clear there were exceptional circumstances as Kerry has been unwell and off work for most of the last 2 weeks. A Special Needs Grant is paid and Kerry is aware she will need to attend the budgeting service. 10. October While attending another appointment, Kerry asks for help to pay for food. She has not attended the budgeting service and does not have a good reason. She is still looking for a job with more hours and cheaper housing. She is not over the limit but has met the reasonable steps obligation but not the budgeting activity obligation. She is given enough money for food until she attends the budgeting service later that week.

chunks.title: Exceeding the maximum payment in a 52-week period for essential dental treatment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Exceeding the maximum payment in a 52-week period for essential dental treatment
In some situations, a client will need essential dental treatment that costs more than $1,000. This could be for:
- a single need or
- more than once in a 52-week period.
In either situation, the client must have exceptional circumstances to get a Special Needs Grant for essential dental treatment over the maximum of $1,000.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances
When deciding whether the client has exceptional circumstances, consider the following factors:
- does the client have any special or unusual costs compared to others in a similar position
- does the client have any special or unusual reasons for any costs that has caused or contributed to the need
- the age and health of the client and any dependants
- is the client the principal caregiver of a child 12 months or younger
- the client's ability to improve their financial situation
- the causes of the client's financial difficulty. In particular has the client caused or contributed to their financial difficulty because they have used their money unwisely
- the extent to which the client's basic necessities of life would be at risk if a Special Needs Grant was not granted
- is the client escaping from an unsafe environment
- any other circumstances about the client's situation you consider relevant
## Payment
If exceptional circumstances exist, MSD can:
- exceed the maximum amount payable
- make more than one payment for the same or similar purpose in any 52 week period and/or
- recover the Special Needs Grant at less than $4.00 per week

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances - additional considerations for essential dental treatment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: The maximum limit of $1,000 in a 52-week period for a Special Needs Grant for essential dental treatment can be exceeded in exceptional circumstances. Exceptional circumstances are those which set a client apart from others in a similar situation.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances - additional considerations — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: To help you decide if a client has exceptional circumstances to exceed the maximum limit you should also consider whether any of the following situations apply: - whether the client could have reasonably afforded or been able to access regular dental check-ups - whether the cause of the oral health issue is special or unusual when compared with others with the same or a similar issue e.g. they have an underlying health condition or take a medication that increases risk of tooth decay - whether the oral health issue was reasonably foreseeable

chunks.title: Client not able to afford or access regular dental check-ups — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: When considering whether a client could afford or access regular dental check-ups you should determine if they have high essential outgoings, e.g. accommodation, employment, or health costs. Example Ariki has been suffering from significant tooth pain when she eats and drinks for the last few days. She's just been to the dentist who advised she'll need a root canal on one of her incisors and a filling in one of her pre-molars. The cost of the consultation, x-ray and treatment is $1,379. Ariki has been getting Sole Parent Support for the last 3 years. Her accommodation costs are high, she gets Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support to help her with the rent. Ariki has not been able to reduce her essential costs and has not been able to increase her income because of her parental responsibilities. Ariki has not been able to put aside any money for regular dental check-ups. She also didn't start experiencing symptoms until recently, so she didn't have a specific reason to see a dentist any earlier. This means Ariki's oral health issues weren't identified and treated early, and the cost of treatment is now much higher than it would have been. In this case exceptional circumstances exist because Ariki was not in a financial position to be proactive about her oral health by having regular dental check-ups and had no indication that she had any oral health issues. Ariki is now facing essential dental treatment costs over the maximum payment limit for reasons beyond her control.

chunks.title: Cause of oral health issue is special or unusual compared to others — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: You should consider any information provided by a client or their dentist that explains why the client may have special or unusual circumstances relating to their dental needs, e.g. the client has a health condition or takes medication that affects their oral health. Example Nick has been experiencing tooth sensitivity lately and went to the dentist to get it checked out. It turns out that Nick has widespread early tooth decay and requires fillings in 4 teeth to address his tooth sensitivity and to prevent his oral health deteriorating. The cost of the consultation, x-rays and treatment is $1,168. When talking to Nick about what might have caused his tooth decay, the dentist identified that Nick has good oral hygiene, but he takes regular medication for blood pressure issues which is highly likely to have caused his tooth decay. Nick was not aware that this is a side effect for some people. In this case exceptional circumstances exist because Nick's oral health issues were probably caused by a regular medication he must take. This sets him apart from other people in similar circumstances.

chunks.title: Oral health issue was reasonably foreseeable — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: You'll need to establish if a client could reasonably foresee that they would develop the oral health issue that means they now need essential dental treatment. The client dentist may have provided advice on what they can do to improve their oral health to prevent issues in the future, and they may not have followed the advice. Example Emeni has been suffering from bad breath and swelling around some of his teeth. He went to see his dentist who advised Emeni that he needs two teeth extracted and a filling in one other tooth, totalling $670. Emeni received a Special Needs Grant for essential dental treatment of $515 earlier in the year. At the time, the dentist discussed with that Emeni that he had not been taking basic care of his oral health and advised he needed to brush his teeth twice a day and floss once a day. This is advice Emeni had been given by his dentist several times before. Unfortunately Emeni has continued not to take care of his oral health, and it has deteriorated as a result. Exceptional circumstances do not exist because Emeni could have reasonably foreseen and prevented this issue by improving his oral health. He can get a Special Needs Grant for essential dental treatment of up to $475, but the shortfall will need to be considered under recoverable assistance.

chunks.title: Exception — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Exception
You may approve an application for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment for a client who failed their hardship obligations if there are exceptional circumstances. This includes circumstances that prevented a client from completing their obligations.
Acceptable exceptional circumstances include:
- unforeseen hospitalisation
- seriously sick or injured
- bereavement of immediate family
- emergency or adverse event
- victim of violent crime or family violence
If a client does not have any of the above reasons staff can consider whether the reason provided:
- is an unforeseen out-of-the ordinary event that could not be planned for or
- is beyond the client's control or
- sets the client apart from others in a similar situation

chunks.title: Family violence - sole parents — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Family violence - sole parents
If the client meets all the qualifications, a Special Needs Grant may be paid to sole parents to re-establish themselves in the community immediately following separation if they:
- are the victim of family violence and
- are being assisted by a social service agency to relocate after initial separation and
- have no other resources
For re-establishment grants initial separation means at the time, or immediately after the client's situation resulted in them having to re-establish themselves and their dependent children.
When there has been a delay in making an application, MSD needs to consider whether a good and sufficient reason existed for the delay. If there was a delay, MSD must also consider whether the need is immediate and essential.
Note re-establishment grants for sole parents who are the victims of family violence are not limited to one separation from the same or different partners.
In most cases, representatives from an appropriate agency will accompany the client and be able to verify their situation. When a client is unaccompanied, MSD must confirm their request for assistance through an appropriate agency. If necessary, a regional Family Violence Response co-ordinator will be able to provide an assessment of the appropriateness of an agency.
Further information about help that can be offered to victims of family violence is provided here:
- Family Violence Intervention Programme [no link find out why]
## Other family violence situations
A sole parent who is a victim of family violence from another family member such as a parent or sibling may also get a re-establishment grant if they meet all the qualifications and the criteria above.
## Payment
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, the maximum amount payable is:
- a recoverable grant for accommodation up to $800 and/or
- a non-recoverable grant for beds, bedding and essential appliances, costs for connecting a telephone, electricity and gas of up to $600
When a client needs help with bond or rent in advance, consider whether the client qualifies for Housing Support Products.
## Fridges, freezers and washing machines
There is a preferred supplier arrangement for fridges, fridge-freezers, freezers and washing machines (collectively known as whiteware). This means clients must purchase their whiteware from a preferred supplier.
If a client refuses to purchase from a preferred supplier, they cannot get a Special Needs Grant for these items.

chunks.title: Food — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Food
If the client meets all qualifications, they may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant for food, if:
- the client or the client's immediate family (if any) has an immediate need to purchase food
- the client and the client's partner (if any) have no resources to meet that need, and would otherwise have to rely on a food bank and
- the need for food or lack of resources to meet it, was caused by an essential expense that had to be met and which left insufficient money to buy food
The purchase of grocery items must exclude the purchase of:
- alcohol
- appliances
- electronics
- gift cards or vouchers
- lotto products
- tobacco and
- vaping products

chunks.title: Food, clothing and bedding — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Food, clothing and bedding
Additional payments can be made to affected people for food, clothing and bedding to meet immediate and essential needs during the recovery from the civil defence emergency or adverse event.
Civil Defence Payments for food, clothing and bedding up to the allowable maximum, are not counted when calculating the amount of Special Needs Grant assistance available during a 52 week period and no income or asset test applies.
Note payments for evacuees are generally only available until they can return to their home.
However payments can be made at the point they return to their home if they need to replace household food and bedding, subject to the maximum limits.

chunks.title: Fridges, freezers and washing machines — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Fridges, freezers and washing machines
There is a preferred supplier arrangement in place for fridges, fridge-freezers, freezers or washing machines (collectively known as whiteware). This means clients must purchase their whiteware from a preferred supplier.

chunks.title: Hardship obligations — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Hardship obligations
Clients and their partners who apply for a Special Needs Grants may have the following hardship obligations:
- a reasonable steps obligation and/or
- a budgeting activity obligation
Generally, clients must meet any hardship obligations that have been applied to them before they can get additional hardship assistance.
These obligations do not apply to:
- payments to people in specific circumstances
- young people getting youth support payments (Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment) or
- payments to get a new, renew or reinstate a driver licence
Note you must make sure the client is getting their correct entitlement at every interaction with them.
## Newborn
When the client is the principal caregiver of a child 12 months of age or younger, you must consider the presence of the newborn when deciding whether to apply hardship obligations.
This includes the principal temporary caregiver of a child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid.

chunks.title: Health travel costs — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Health travel costs
If the client meets all qualifications, they may be able to receive a non-recoverable Special Needs Grant to assist with Health-related travel costs if they:
- are referred by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner to a secondary health service for medical treatment, assessment or services
- are not receiving assistance for travel or accommodation for that treatment, assessment or services from any Health Agency (other than the Accident Rehabilitation Compensation and Insurance Corporation or an insurer within the meaning of the Accident Insurance Act 1998 see: Cover under Accident Rehabilitation and Insurance)
- are not receiving assistance under the National Travel Assistance Scheme and
- cannot receive a Disability Allowance for that travel or accommodation
For information about Special Needs Grants for other travel costs see:
- Designated health practitioner assessment travel
- Pregnancy terminations
## Reimbursements
Except where specifically provided for in the Special Needs Grants programme (that is, for terminations, vasectomies, overseas medical treatment and secondary health travel costs), travel costs are the responsibility of the patient's local District Health Board.
Some District Health Board's provide assistance with travel costs on a reimbursement system (that is, the patient pays the costs and seeks reimbursement from the District Health Board). Because the District Health Board is funded to meet these travel costs it is not appropriate to use a Special Needs Grant to meet the travel costs. In these situations, you may consider granting a recoverable Other emergency grants
## Payment
Travel costs can be paid when these costs are the result of a one-off appointment, for example, day surgery, or consultations such as grommets or tonsillitis etc.
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, the maximum amount payable is $300. This can be made for:
- the actual and reasonable travel expenses for a return journey of least 8 kilometres to the place of treatment, assessment or services and
- the actual and reasonable cost of accommodation and meals if overnight stay away from home is necessary to attend the treatment, assessment or services
Note If a person has a Community Services Card, they can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect
Special Needs Grants for this purpose are:
- non-recoverable
- not restricted to one payment for the same or similar purpose in any 52-week period

chunks.title: How to pay - International Custody Dispute Payment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## How to pay - International Custody Dispute Payment
First set up a non-beneficiary record on SWIFTT.
The Special Needs Grants International Custody Dispute Payment will commence from the date of application.
Payment must be made into a New Zealand bank account.
Use the assessment sheet for SNG International Custody Dispute Payment to work out the amount of the Miscellaneous Subsidy payable to the client. See:
- SNG International Custody Dispute Payment [no link find out why] assessment sheet
When granting the Special Needs Grants - International Custody Dispute Payment, use Miscellaneous Subsidy with the code 518.
If income or accommodation costs change the client will need to contact us to advise us of the change in circumstances and allow for the payment to be recalculated.
Payment will continue until the:
- client gains employment or
- client is able to support themselves some other way (e.g. overseas government, or work) or
- client leaves the country or is unable to stay in the country or
- custody dispute is resolved, this includes any rights of appeal or
- child reaches an age where they no longer require an order relating to possession and care
For more information see:
- Payment rate - International Custody Dispute Payment
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals

chunks.title: Identification — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Identification
The client will need to produce:
- passport with a visa that allows the person to work in New Zealand (or a valid work permit, if granted before 29 November 2010).Note when the client has no supporting means of identification, you can accept their passport as a single source of proof and, if appropriate, follow-up on further identification at a later date.
- current bank balance to show cash assets
- income details
- verification of accommodation costs
- a written referral by Immigration New Zealand supporting the client's application for assistance, which confirms that the client: has lodged or intended to lodge an application with Immigration New Zealand for a residence class visa, under the Partnership Category (on the ground of marriage or civil union or in a de facto relationship, or in a stable de facto relationship)is living apart from, and have lost the financial support of their partneris the holder of a work visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009 (or a work permit, if granted before 29 November 2010) on the ground that the person is a victim of family violence
- has lodged or intended to lodge an application with Immigration New Zealand for a residence class visa, under the Partnership Category (on the ground of marriage or civil union or in a de facto relationship, or in a stable de facto relationship)
- is living apart from, and have lost the financial support of their partner
- is the holder of a work visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009 (or a work permit, if granted before 29 November 2010) on the ground that the person is a victim of family violence

chunks.title: Identification document fees — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Identification document fees
A client who meets all qualifications, they may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant for the cost of an identification document where the document is reasonably required as supporting evidence for an application for benefit. The type of document assisted with depends on whether the client was born in New Zealand.
The grant can cover:
- the application fee for a New Zealand birth certificate or
- the application fee, or any other fee, for a document of identification if the client's birth certificate is not registered in New Zealand
This assistance is available to clients applying for a benefit, including those who are imprisoned or detained in prison under a sentence of imprisonment, preventative detention or corrective training, or who are remanded in custody by a Court pending a further appearance before a Court.
A grant can be made for members of the client's immediate family where each family member is included in the benefit application and is required to provide the identification document to support the application.
Note if the client already has a document that shows the legal identity exists, a Special Needs Grant will generally not be required for further identification documents to support an application for benefit.
## Payment
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, the maximum amount payable towards identification document fees is $500 in any 52 week period.
A Special Needs Grant for identification document fees may be recoverable or non-recoverable. To help you decide whether the Special Needs Grant should be repaid, consider:
- the purpose of the grant
- the nature of the needs
- whether it would be fair in regard to other clients, to require repayment and
- the effect on the client if they were required to repay the Special Needs Grant

chunks.title: Identifying reasonable steps — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Generally, clients who have received Special Needs Grants, Advance Payments of Benefit and/or Recoverable Assistance Payments on 3 or more grant dates during the past 12 months must take reasonable steps before they can get any additional payments. Reasonable steps clients can take are those that will: - reduce their costs - increase their income or - improve their financial management When identifying possible reasonable steps you must consider each client's individual circumstances. When with the client, it may be useful to review any budget or budgeting worksheet that the client has previously completed to see what costs the client has and check whether they are essential. You should discuss with the client what they can do to meet the reasonable steps obligation. Note clients are only required to take specific actions for their reasonable steps when you’ve discussed the actions with them, eg setting an automatic payment to pay for power.

chunks.title: Examples of reasonable steps — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Reasonable steps could include (but are not limited to): - seeking part-time or full-time paid employment, or increasing hours to increase income - having their Child Support payments reviewed (especially if they have a reduction in income) - cancelling non-essential services eg pay TV services - quitting smoking - Quitline can provide support, information and low cost nicotine patches, gum, and lozenges - 0800 778 778 - reducing regular costs by moving to cheaper alternatives e.g., moving to cheaper accommodation, taking up a less expensive phone or internet plan, using public transport when those costs are cheaper than the cost of using a private vehicle - renegotiating debt repayments to a lesser repayment amount e.g., court fines - refinancing or consolidating debt to reduce interest and repayment amounts - suspending contributions to KiwiSaver and/or other voluntary retirement schemes - setting up a separate account and/or automatic payments for bills - agreeing to MSD setting up a redirection of benefit where there is good cause. Note if the client has completed reasonable steps for Temporary Additional Support, the client should generally be considered to have met the reasonable steps obligation at the next application for a Special Needs Grant, Recoverable Assistance Payment, or Advance Payment of Benefit. You need to check the CMS notes to confirm what steps have been taken.

chunks.title: Meeting reasonable steps obligation — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Clients have met their obligation if they have taken reasonable steps to reduce their costs, increase their income or improve their financial management since their previous grant date. For more information see: - Reasonable steps obligation - Example - applying hardship obligations - Failure to meet hardship obligations - Community Services Card - Public transport (Community Connect)

chunks.title: Income assessment - rural assistance — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Income assessment - rural assistance
When assessing income the first $160.00 gross of the client's income (includes income of a partner) does not affect the rate of the rural assistance payment.
The gross income over $160.00 reduces the rural assistance payment by $1.00 for each complete $1.00 received. Do not include family tax credit payments.
## Example
gross weekly income
$250.00
less income allowed before payment is affected
$160.00
Equals income (to be deducted from rural assistance payment)
$90.00
Rural assistance payment (couple, without children as at 1 April 2026)
$633.94
less income
$90.00
Weekly rural assistance payment payable
$543.94
Note the rate of New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension a client (including their partner) gets, must also be included as income when assessing rural assistance payments for these clients.

chunks.title: Income limit — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Income limit
A client cannot get a Special Needs Grant if their income and their partner's (if any) income exceeds the appropriate income limit.
The income limit depends on:
- the client's age
- their relationship status and
- if they have any dependent children.
Income for Special Needs Grants includes:
- New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension the client or their partner (if any) are getting
- the amount of any payments made to the client or their partner (if any) under the following programmes: New Employment Transition Grant ProgrammeSeasonal Work Assistance Programme orWork Bonus Programme
- New Employment Transition Grant Programme
- Seasonal Work Assistance Programme or
- Work Bonus Programme
If the client is applying for a Special Needs Grant on behalf of their dependent child, the income limit applies to the parent or caregiver's income.
If a client is getting a main benefit, they would generally meet the income test for a Special Needs Grant.
The Winter Energy Payment is not considered income when making a Special Needs Grant assessment.
Note for New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients, the appropriate income limit applies.
For more information see:
- Income limit - New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients

chunks.title: Income limit - New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Income limit - New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients
When assessing Special Needs Grant eligibility for New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients, the appropriate income limit must be applied.
The rate of New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension a client (including their partner) gets, must be included as income when assessing Special Needs Grant eligibility.
If a client and/or their partner gets other income, in addition to their New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension, both sources of income must be included when assessing Special Needs Grant eligibility for these clients.
## Winter Energy Payment is not considered income
Winter Energy Payment is not considered income when assessing eligibility for a Special Needs Grant.
## Examples
The below examples show how income is assessed for New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients when applying for a Special Needs Grant.
In the examples, the gross New Zealand Superannuation and Veterans Pension rates are as at 1 April 2026.
The income limits are the income limits that apply from 1 April 2026.
Married, civil union or de facto couple, both get New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension with no other income.
