chunks.title: Interface with advances — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Interface with advances
Sometimes the amount available under a non-recoverable Special Needs Grant will not be enough to cover all the costs eg, when a client does not have exceptional circumstances to increase the maximum payable.
The client may qualify for an Advance Payment of Benefit to cover the difference between the non-recoverable Special Needs Grant assistance the client qualifies for the amount needed.

chunks.title: International Custody Dispute Payment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: The Special Needs Grant International Custody Dispute Payment is a weekly, non-recoverable payment, paid to a parent who is awaiting the outcome of an international custody dispute who has no other means of support (such as work, support from their government or family, or other support from New Zealand) and is facing financial hardship. The maximum weekly rate of payment is equivalent to the Sole Parent Support rate, plus an accommodation component equivalent to the Accommodation Supplement. You will need to check the client's entitlement to other benefits before considering this payment. To get a Special Needs Grant International Custody Dispute Payment a client must: - be the principal caregiver of a dependent child - be in the country the child would normally live - not be able to meet their needs from their own resources or through other sources and - meet the hardship criteria which is an asset limit. Any income not reduced will need to be considered in relation to costs to determine hardship Note the client does not need to be ordinarily resident. And either be: - in New Zealand on a temporary entry class visa (or a temporary or limited purpose permit, if granted before 29 November 2010) with the child to resolve custody and access proceedings or - a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident and in another country under the Hague convention to resolve the international custody dispute Note Australian citizens cannot access this payment, as they may qualify for Emergency Benefit. And one of the following situations must apply: - the child has been returned to New Zealand due to a Hague Convention order and the applicant accompanied the child - the child has been returned to New Zealand voluntarily to resolve custody and access proceedings and the applicant accompanied the child - the applicant has remained in New Zealand following the breakdown of their relationship in order to resolve custody and access proceedings and is the principal caregiver of that child - the child has been required to return to another country (other than New Zealand) due to a Hague Convention order and the applicant has accompanied the child or - a Hague Convention application has been made and the applicant has returned the child to another country (other than New Zealand) voluntarily and has accompanied the child We must be satisfied the applicant has exhausted all financial resources reasonably available to them, and is in the process of pursuing any other avenue of financial support available in respect of the child (for example, domestic maintenance, employment or child support).

chunks.title: International Custody Dispute Payment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: If the applicant is legally able to work but unable to obtain employment case manager discretion should be used to determine if this is reasonable. It may be unreasonable to expect them to gain employment if for example they have to provide full-time care for their child. The applicant should be taking all reasonable steps to have the custody and access proceedings heard as soon as reasonably practicable. If the client qualifies for the Special Needs Grant International Custody Dispute Payment, the rate of payment includes an accommodation component similar to Accommodation Supplement. If a client is eligible for a Special Needs Grant International Custody Dispute Payment no other extra help or supplementary payments are available.

chunks.title: International Custody Dispute Payment and income — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## International Custody Dispute Payment and income
The Special Needs Grants International Custody Dispute Payment is reduced dollar for dollar by any gross weekly income the client gets.
Other money that is not considered income may impact on the client's ability to meet the hardship criteria, for example cash assets like savings in a bank account.
## Financial resources
To determine if a client is in hardship you will need to assess their financial resources minus costs.
Example
A sole parent with 2 children is staying in a refuge in Australia paying $60 per week accommodation plus other costs of $60 (food and power) per week. They also receive $200 per week in Child Support payments.
Income
$200.00
Less costs
$120.00
Equals
$80.00
If the client has enough money to cover their costs, the client is not in hardship.
If a client is not able to meet their costs with the income they get, the client is considered to be in hardship.

chunks.title: International Custody Dispute proof — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## International Custody Dispute proof
Assistance will only be available in cases where all other available resources have been exhausted and there is hardship. Cash asset limits for Special Needs Grants and any income will determine if there is hardship.
The client will need to supply one of the following:
- a letter from the courts advising of the court application and hearing date or
- a letter from their lawyer advising of the court date(s)
When a client has left New Zealand to resolve the international custody dispute you will need to ask if there is any assistance available in that country and for proof that the court proceedings are under the Hague convention.
Any documents that require translation can be directed to the Department of Internal Affairs at the client's expense.
If the client is an overseas resident and they have completed the overseas residents section of the application form, the details will need to be entered on to the CMS client record.
If Specialised Processing Services advise you there is entitlement to an overseas pension a debt will need to be established.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Special Needs Grants provide non-taxable, one-off recoverable or non-recoverable financial assistance to clients to meet immediate needs.
A client does not have to be getting a benefit to qualify for Special Needs Grants.

chunks.title: Laser therapy for the removal of birthmarks — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Laser therapy for the removal of birthmarks
If the client meets all qualifications, they may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant to assist with the costs related to removing birthmarks by laser therapy if:
- a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner certifies that a client has a birth mark that is disfiguring and visible in normal clothing
If financial assistance has been provided by the District Health Board, this assistance must be deducted from the total payment required. Also deduct any health-related subsidy and/or insurance payments.
## Payment
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, the maximum amount payable for the costs, including travel costs, associated with laser treatment for the removal of the birthmark is $300.
Special Needs Grant for removal of birthmarks are:
- non-recoverable and
- restricted to one payment for the same or similar purpose in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Late representation for weekly payment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Late representation for weekly payment
When a client fails to apply for a payment in a particular week they can apply at a later date.
Payment for any week missed would depend on the client proving they were eligible for the payment in the week they had missed and that there was a 'need' for the payment missed.

chunks.title: Long-term patients — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Long-term patients
If a client meets all qualifications, they may be able to get a Special Needs Grant if they have lived in a hospital unit or residential home for 6 months or more and are re-establishing themselves in independent accommodation in the community.
Re-establishing themselves in the community does not include former patients moving from one form of established care to another, for example, from a hospital or residential home back to their family or accommodation under supervision of the IHC. The person must be establishing themselves in their own independent accommodation.
Before payment is approved, the client's case worker or hospital social worker must provide an itemised list of the patient's requirements.
Note clients leaving social rehabilitation programmes do not qualify for a re-establishment grant when leaving this type of programme, regardless of the period they were resident with the provider. Re-establishment grants are provided for patients who have been getting medical treatment. Social Rehabilitation does not provide medical treatment.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Social Rehabilitation Assistance
## Payment
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, the maximum amount payable is:
- a recoverable grant for accommodation up to $800 and/or
- a non-recoverable grant for beds, bedding, essential appliances, costs of connecting a telephone, electricity or gas, substantial clothing requirements (several sets of clothes) and toiletry items of up to $1,200
More than one grant may be made in a 52-week period, but the maximum cannot exceed $2,000.
For more information see:
- Exceptional circumstances
Note when a client needs help with bond or rent in advance, consider whether the client qualifies for Housing Support Products.

chunks.title: Loss of livelihood — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Loss of livelihood
During a civil defence emergency or adverse event, situations may arise that will prevent a person from being able to work.
Payment can be considered when a person cannot work and loses income due to the civil defence emergency or adverse event as:
- their workplace is closed
- they cannot travel to work due to the emergency or
- they need to stay with their family or whanau
Note a Civil Defence Payment for loss of livelihood can only be made to a person who is legally allowed to work in New Zealand. This means they need to be a New Zealand citizen or have a visa that allows them to work in New Zealand
The person needs to provide confirmation they are unable to work and their employer is not continuing to pay salary or wages.
For self-employed people, confirmation is needed that they are unable to run their business and income from the business has stopped.
## Part-time employment (beneficiaries)
People getting a benefit who work part-time and unable to work due to the civil defence emergency or adverse event are not eligible for payments for loss of livelihood.
As they would have been declaring their income from part-time employment their benefit will be restored to the full rate for the period they are unable to work.
## Part-time employment (non-beneficiaries)
People not a getting benefit who work part-time and are unable to work due to the civil defence emergency or adverse event may get payments for loss of livelihood.
Payment is the lesser of the loss of net earnings or the maximum amount.
## Maximum payment
The maximum weekly payment cannot exceed the set limits or the actual loss of net earnings:
- for people in billeted or temporary accommodation (e.g. in motels, hotels, camping grounds or home-stays), payments are based on 75% of the net weekly rate of Jobseeker Support
- for people not billeted, payments are based on the equivalent net weekly rate of Jobseeker Support
For more information see:
- Deskfile Civil Defence Payment rates
Payments are only available until the person is able to return to work, or the activation of Civil Defence Payments for the event ends.
If Civil Defence Payments are no longer available and the person is unable to return to work, an Emergency Benefit can be considered.
When work has stopped or is unlikely to be available for a substantial period, consider Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: Married, civil union or de facto couple with no children — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Married, civil union or de facto couple with no children
Married, civil union or de facto couples with no dependent children are not eligible for any specific circumstances Special Needs Grant assistance during their initial stand-down.
When a client or partner is in extreme hardship or an emergency situation exists they may be able to receive other Special Needs Grant assistance.
A client is still required to meet all the qualifications for any other Special Needs Grant assistance they apply for, including non-recoverable assistance.

chunks.title: Married, de facto or civil union couple (with children) — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Married, de facto or civil union couple (with children)
While a married, civil union or de facto client with dependent children is completing an application for benefit and/or is on their initial stand-down their partner may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant if they meet all the qualifications.
This type of Special Needs Grant can be paid from the date of first contact up until either:
- the date of decline of the benefit or
- the date of grant of the benefit or
- the commencement date of the benefit or
- the date the application for benefit lapses
whichever is the later.
The partner must have one or more dependent children and:
- meet all the qualifications
- must not be eligible for a benefit in their own rightFor example, you cannot pay a Special Needs Grants when the partner can receive part payment of Jobseeker Support
- the immediate family has no cash assets and cannot obtain credit facilities
- the immediate family has taken all reasonable steps to reduce their fixed commitments and
- if the client received a redundancy payment, the payment was used to meet ongoing costs and not to reduce capital debts
## Payment
More than one payment can be made, but the maximum amount payable in any 1 week cannot be more than:
- the maximum single under 25 years rate of Jobseeker Support
Special Needs Grants for this purpose are recoverable.
## Restriction on payments
Only when a client has received their maximum entitlement to recoverable assistance during their initial stand-down can you consider providing other assistance, either recoverable or non-recoverable. To receive other emergency grants they or a member of their immediate family must be:
- experiencing an emergency situation or
- in extreme hardship
A client is still required to meet all the qualifications for any other Special Needs Grant assistance they apply for, including non-recoverable assistance.
The exception to the restriction are grants relating to re-establishment situations (eg Steps to Freedom).

chunks.title: Maximum amounts payable — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Maximum amounts payable
For applications received on or after 9 November 2020, a total maximum of $5000 is payable.
Within the total maximum of $5000, a maximum of $3500 can be paid for accommodation costs.
All payments are non-recoverable.
When the applicant has more than 2 children, the total maximum payable is increased by $100 for each additional child only.
Examples:
- single client, the total maximum amount is $5000 ($3500 can be used for accommodation costs)
- single client or couple with 2 children, the total maximum is $5000 ($3500 can be used for accommodation costs)
- single client or couple with 3 children, total maximum amount payable is $5100 ($3500 can be used for accommodation costs)
## Clients who got a re-establishment grant before 9 November 2020
For applications received before 9 November 2020, the maximum grant payable for:
- accommodation costs was $800, this is a recoverable grant or
- other costs was $1200, this is a non-recoverable grant
If a client got a re-establishment grant before 9 November 2020, and they are still within their 1 year (or 2 years for English language costs) since they came into New Zealand, the maximum amount they can get is reduced by the amount of the previous grant for accommodation or other costs.
For example, a client that got a re-establishment grant for accommodation costs before 9 November 2020, and is applying for further accommodation costs, because they are now moving into permanent accommodation, the maximum amount payable for the new accommodation need is $3500, less the amount of the earlier grant for accommodation costs.
Note a re-establishment grant paid before 9 November 2020 for accommodation costs is still recoverable.

chunks.title: Maximum debt recovery rate — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Maximum debt recovery rate
The recommended maximum recovery rate for clients currently getting income support is no more than $40 a week, unless the client volunteers to pay more.
Debt types included in this maximum recovery rate are:
- Advance Payment of Benefit
- Recoverable Assistance for Study Costs
- Housing Support Products
- Security Deposit Grants for emergency housing and transitional housing
- Special Needs Grants and
- overpayments of benefit
## Client volunteers to pay more
If the client would like to pay more than $40.00 a week, they must put this in writing

chunks.title: Maximum payment for essential dental treatment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Maximum payment for essential dental treatment
Special Needs Grants for essential dental treatment are non-recoverable and unless exceptional circumstances exist the maximum amount payable is $1,000 in a 52-week period.
Note when a client qualifies for assistance through a health agency, a non-recoverable payment may be made after deducting any health-related subsidy and/or insurance payments from the total cost of treatment.
However, a non-recoverable payment cannot be made to pay the balance of dental treatment where part of the cost of the treatment has been paid by ACC.
## No exceptional circumstances
If a client does not have exceptional circumstances to exceed the maximum Special Needs Grant payable for essential dental treatment, they may be eligible for recoverable assistance.
An Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment can be considered for the balance of the essential dental treatment costs.

chunks.title: Maximum payment for food — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Maximum payment for food
More than one food grant may be made in a 26-week period but unless exceptional circumstances exist, grants during a 26 week period must not exceed in total:
single person with no dependent children
$200.00
married, civil union or de facto couple with no dependent children
$300.00
married, civil union or de facto couple, or sole parent with 1 or 2 dependent children
$450.00
married, civil union or de facto couple, or sole parent with 3 or more dependent children
$550.00

chunks.title: Multiple applications for the same need — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Multiple applications for the same need
Some people may need help with the same need more than once during an event, e.g., when there is an ongoing weather event causing multiple impacts over the affected period.
In these situations, one or more additional Civil Defence Payments can be considered for the same need.
Before making Civil Defence Payments in this situation, you must be satisfied:
- there is a genuine additional immediate need e.g. the original item purchased was damaged or is no longer available as a direct result of the emergency or adverse event and
- the person has explored all other options to meet their need but has been unable to
## Example
During the Auckland Floods Event, Maraea’s home became inaccessible due to flooding, and she was moved to emergency accommodation.
Because her home was inaccessible, she couldn’t take any bedding or clothing with her. MSD assisted with a Civil Defence Payment for food, clothing, and bedding.
Over the next few days significant rain continued to fall, and on Monday Maraea’s emergency accommodation was flooded.
Maraea was moved to the local welfare centre but was unable to take any of her bedding as it was saturated with contaminated flood water.
The welfare centre didn’t provide bedding and Maraea couldn’t source any elsewhere. MSD assisted with another Civil Defence Payment to enable Maraea to purchase replacement bedding.

chunks.title: National Travel Assistance scheme — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## National Travel Assistance scheme
Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora provides assistance for travel and accommodation costs for people who have been referred by their health or disability specialist (not a health practitioner) to a specialist, specialist health or a specialist disability service.
Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora has certain criteria that must be met to qualify. In some cases, Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora may be able to prepay for travel costs when a client must travel and they do not have the means to pay for their costs.
Clients should contact:
- a hospital social worker
- a hospital travel coordinator or
- Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora - National Travel Assistance
to enquire whether they qualify for National Travel Assistance.

chunks.title: New driver licences — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## New driver licences
A recoverable Special Needs Grant may be made to a client to get a new driver licence when they have:
- not previously had a full licence and
- an immediate and essential need to get a driver licence
A payment can be made for the actual fees for applying and taking a test for a learner licence, a restricted licence, or a full licence of any class.
A Special Needs Grant is available for a client and their partner to each get a learner licence, restricted licence, and a full licence.
Clients can apply for a Special Needs Grant to cover the costs of the:
- initial test fee covering 2 tests (the initial test and 1 re-sit), and
- re-sit test fee for any additional tests
Note the re-sit fee only applies for Class 1 (car) drivers who have failed to pass their driver licence test twice.
Generally, only 1 payment each can be made to a client and their partner per licence category in a 52-week period. MSD can use discretion to grant more than 1 Special Needs Grant in a 52-week period if the client has exceptional circumstances.
## Essential need
An essential need exists if MSD is satisfied it is necessary for the client to get a driver licence:
- to participate in a required activity to improve their work readiness at least once every fortnight
- to apply for employment when a driver licence is an essential requirement
- to undertake an available employment opportunity
- when they, or any member of their immediate family have a disability, and needs help with transport to undertake their daily living activities (including receiving treatment for the disability, or undertaking education or employment) or
- for any other special reason
When considering if a driver licence is necessary, MSD must consider the:
- availability and suitability of public transport and any other transport options and
- circumstances of the client and their immediate family
## Actual fees
Special Need Grants for a new driver licence must not be more than the actual fee payable.
## Dependent children
A parent can apply on behalf of their dependent child for a Special Needs Grant to get a learner, restricted or full driver licence.
## Assistance cannot be paid
A client will not qualify for a Special Needs Grant for driver licence costs if they:
- are disqualified from holding or getting a driver licence or
- have not renewed their driver licence before the expiry date without a good and sufficient reason.

chunks.title: No longer entitled to payment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## No longer entitled to payment
A client may receive a weekly payment until the date they:
- receive a residence class visa
- marry, enter into a civil union or a de facto relationship
- reconcile with their previous partner or
- leave New Zealand
whichever is earliest.

chunks.title: North and South Island drought 2025 — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:

chunks.title: Clients who do not use the services offered — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Clients who do not use the services offered
When a client applies for a Special Needs Grant, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment and is offered information on services to help them build their financial capability, the client can choose not to use them as they are optional.
If a client chooses not to use the services offered this is not a reason to fail a client’s reasonable steps or budgeting activity obligation.
A client can be required to complete budgeting activities, including those provided by building financial capability services only if they have:
- had a budgeting activity obligation applied and
- been told about the obligation and what they must do to meet it
For more information see:
- Budgeting activity obligation
- Failure to meet hardship obligations
- Effect of not using services to build financial capability

chunks.title: Other emergency grants — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Other emergency grants
If the client meets all qualifications, they may be able to get a Special Needs Grant for an item or service not specified as an essential need or an emergency need if:
- special circumstances exist and
- they and/or their family would suffer serious hardship without the item or service
If you need help deciding whether to pay an emergency Special Needs Grant in these cases contact Helpline.
For more information on essential needs and emergency needs see:
## Payment
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, the maximum amount payable towards an 'other emergency grant' is $500.
To help you decide whether the Special Needs Grant should be recoverable or non-recoverable, consider:
- the reason for the grant
- the clients particular need
- whether it would be fair to other clients to require or not require payment and
- the effect on the client if they had to repay the Special Needs Grant
## Housing assistance
If a client needs help to get or retain accommodation, they may qualify for a Housing Support Product.
When a client does not qualify for Housing Support Products, consider whether the client qualifies for assistance under 'other emergency grants'.
## Emergency housing
MSD must not grant a Special Needs Grant to help clients with any costs associated with emergency housing. This includes security deposits for emergency housing or transitional housing.
If a client needs help with emergency housing, including a security deposit for emergency housing or transitional housing, the client needs to apply for an Emergency Housing Grant or a Security Deposit Grant.
Note If the client is not eligible for an Emergency Housing Grant or Security Deposit Grant, they cannot get a Special Needs Grant for these costs.

chunks.title: Other help available — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Other help available
If a client does not qualify for a Special Needs Grant for essential dental treatment, they may be able to get an Advance Payment of Benefit or a Recoverable Assistance Payment.
## Dentures
If a client needs help with dentures, e.g. they need new dentures or their dentures are broken or damaged and need to be repaired, they may be able to get an Advance Payment of Benefit or a Recoverable Assistance Payment.
## Additional disability related costs
When a client has regular and ongoing additional costs for dental care relating directly to a disability (e.g. gum disease or an ongoing dental condition), they may qualify for a Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Other sources of assistance — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Other sources of assistance
Before approving a Special Needs Grant, discuss with the client other options that they may not have considered. Some examples may include (but are not limited to):
- meeting the need from the next income payment due
- assistance from other government agencies
- arranging automatic payments
- negotiating payment of accounts by instalments
- hire purchase
A bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client, except for couples or sole parents applying for assistance during the initial stand-down and/or application process.
For more information see:
- Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or application process
## Other income assistance
You must check to see if the client qualifies for other assistance before granting a Special Needs Grant.
Consider:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Disability Allowance
- Temporary Additional Support
For more information see:
- Advance Payment of Benefit
- Interface with advances
## Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora assistance
A Special Needs Grant can be approved to assist with items partially subsidised by Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora when the client still has to pay a shortfall. For example, spectacles, dentures, hearing aids.
Payment is only for the portion not subsidised.
## Student assistance
Consider the balance of any Student Loan available. Consideration should be given to declining the application if this option has not been exhausted.
Note under no circumstances are students to be referred to institution hardship funds.

chunks.title: Partners with youth activity obligations — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Partners with youth activity obligations
A young partner of a main beneficiary who has youth activity obligations may also have hardship obligations when they are applying for a Special Needs Grant or Advance Payment of Benefit.
However, when a young partner is engaged with a service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service they will already be meeting the reasonable steps and budgeting activity obligations because as part of their youth activity obligations they must:
- participate in ongoing discussions with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service about their budget (which would include talking about ways they can stay within their budget and potentially reduce their costs)
- undertake a budgeting programme
Note a service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service may provide support for the young person's circumstances but they may not know the full circumstances of the family and therefore this support should only be used as one piece of the information.
For more information about the youth activity obligations that apply to young partners see:
- Youth activity obligations in relevant Main benefit

chunks.title: Payment after treatment and reimbursements — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Payment after treatment and reimbursements
Generally, clients apply for a Special Needs Grant for essential dental treatment before having the treatment
However, there may be times when a client needs essential dental treatment in an emergency, and they are unable to apply for a Special Needs Grant first. When this happens, a client may have:
- an outstanding account (a debt) to pay immediately after the treatment has been provided or
- to pay for the treatment before it is provided
## Outstanding accounts
A Special Needs Grant can be considered to pay an account if the client had essential dental treatment in an emergency and was unable to apply before they had the treatment.
The client must meet the qualifications, including that they have no other way of paying the account (e.g. through instalments), or their current budget does not allow them to pay for this unexpected cost.
## Reimbursements
A Special Needs Grant can be considered to reimburse a client if they had essential dental treatment in an emergency, were unable to apply before they had the treatment, and they had to pay for the treatment immediately using resources that were set aside for another essential purpose e.g. accommodation or groceries.
## Example
A client develops a toothache at the weekend. They are in extreme pain and go to an emergency dentist who confirms they have an abscessed tooth that needs to be treated immediately.
The dentist advises the treatment will cost $200 and must be paid for in advance. The only money the client has is their rent money for next week. They pay the $200 from their rent money to get the treatment they need.
The client contacts MSD on Monday to apply for financial assistance. The client meets the qualifications for a Special Needs Grant for essential dental treatment and they are reimbursed the $200.

chunks.title: Payment of Family Violence Programme — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Payment of Family Violence Programme
The client can apply for a weekly non-recoverable Special Needs Grant.
## The basic amount of the grant
The basic amount of the grant a client is entitled to, is dependent on the client's family circumstances and is the appropriate Jobseeker Support rate.
For more information see:
- Deskfile Jobseeker Support rates
## Income
As the client has been granted a work visa under the Immigration Act 2009 (or a work permit under the Immigration Act 1987) they are able to earn income.
Income is charged weekly at the following rate:
- 70 cents is taken from the payment for each $1.00 of income over $160.00 (before tax) a week (as at 1 April 2026)
## Accommodation costs
The client can receive an additional amount no more than the weekly amount of an Accommodation Supplement that would be payable if the client was receiving a main benefit.
This means you would assess the amount of the Accommodation Supplement the client would be entitled to (depending on their accommodation costs, their family circumstances and the area in which they live) as if they were receiving Jobseeker Support.
The assessed amount of Accommodation Supplement is paid with the basic grant.
## DREW assessment
For all grants of Family Violence Programme that include the assessment amount for income or accommodation costs, a DREW assessment can be completed with an assessment calculation sheet attached to the application form.
## Other assistance
As these clients are not a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident, generally they will not be eligible for any other assistance.

chunks.title: Payment of refugee, protected person, Afghan interpreter or Afghan evacuee re-establishment grants — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Payment of refugee, protected person, Afghan interpreter or Afghan evacuee re-establishment grants
A refugee, protected person, Afghan interpreter or Afghan evacuee who do not qualify for other forms of government assistance that are not provided by MSD, may be paid a Special Needs Grant to re-establish themselves in the community.
## Applications
An application must be made within 1 year of their first arrival in New Zealand, or within 2 years of their first arrival in New Zealand if the assistance is for the cost of attending English language classes.
A client can apply for more than 1 grant, however the total assistance paid cannot exceed the maximum amount.
## Re-establishment costs
Accommodation costs - including payments for a tenancy bond and rent in advance.
Other costs, include:
- beds, bedding and essential appliances
- connecting a telephone, electricity and gas
- clothing requirements
- the cost of attending English language classes (including transport costs)
- translation costs for work-related documents
There is a preferred supplier arrangement for whiteware.
For more information see:
Note a re-establishment grant cannot be paid for emergency housing costs.
## Maximum amounts
A total maximum of $5000 is payable. Within the total maximum of $5000, a maximum of $3500 can be paid for accommodation costs. The whole grant is non-recoverable.
When the applicant has more than 2 dependent children, the total maximum payable is increased by $100 for each additional dependent child only.
Please see:
When the re-establishment grant does not cover the full amount needed for bond or rent in advance, consider whether the client qualifies for any Housing Support Products for the remaining amount.

chunks.title: Payment of Steps to Freedom grants — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Payment of Steps to Freedom grants
A Steps to Freedom grant can be paid to help with the actual costs the client will have to re-establish themselves in the community.
The maximum amount of a Steps to Freedom grant is $350 (less any cash on release).
The Steps to Freedom grant can be paid:
- directly to the supplier
- to a Westpac Steps to Freedom card or
- by direct credit to the clients (or their agents) bank account
Note Steps to Freedom grants are non-recoverable.
## More than one payment
You can make more than one payment of a Steps to Freedom grant for the same or similar purpose to a client provided the total amount paid does not exceed $350 (less any cash on release).
Steps to Freedom grants are not restricted to one grant for the same or similar purpose in any 52 week period.
## Cash on release
The amount of the Steps to Freedom grant payable must be reduced by the total of the prisoner's available cash on release as recorded on the Steps to Freedom form. This includes any amount held in the prisoner's trust account, canteen account and earnings account.
For example if a prisoner is (or is about to be) released with $26.50 cash, this needs to be deducted from the amount of the grant that would otherwise be payable.
## Examples of calculating payment
The maximum payment of a Steps to Freedom grant is $350, and reduced by any cash on release.
Example 1
A client has $26.50 on release and needs assistance for re-establishment costs of $250.
The total amount payable for the grant is $223.50 with the client contributing $26.50 toward the remaining costs.
This will leave $100 of the Steps to Freedom grant available for further re-establishment costs if required.
Example 2
A client has $30.50 on release and needs help to pay re-establishment costs of $150 to assist with clothing.
The amount payable for the grant is $119.50 with the client contributing $30.50 toward the remaining costs.
This will leave $200 of the Steps to Freedom grant available for further re-establishment costs if required.
## The Prisoner Reintegration team
The Prisoner Reintegration team can pay a Steps to Freedom grant up to 5 days before a prisoner is released.

chunks.title: Payment of Transition from Care to Independence — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Payment of Transition from Care to Independence
Payment is based on individual needs.
The maximum amount payable is a:
- recoverable grant for accommodation up to $800.00 and
- non-recoverable grant, up to but not more than $1,200 for the following: bedbeddingessential appliances andthe cost of connecting telephone, electricity and gas
- bed
- bedding
- essential appliances and
- the cost of connecting telephone, electricity and gas
Payments must not be made for clothing or toiletries.
More than one payment can be made within a 52-week period, and for the period the initiative applies to the client, however, the total assistance received must not exceed $2,000.
When a client needs help with bond or rent in advance, consider whether the client qualifies for Housing Support Products.
## Income limit
A client cannot get a Transition from Care to Independence payment if their income is more than $1,010.41 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026).
This income limit applies to all Transition from Care to Independence clients regardless of their age.
For more information see:
## Fridges, freezers and washing machines
There is a preferred supplier arrangement in place for fridges, fridge-freezers, freezers and washing machines (collectively known as whiteware).
This means clients must purchase their whiteware from a preferred supplier.
If a client refuses to purchase from a preferred supplier, they cannot get a Special Needs Grant for these items.
For more information see:
- Preferred supplier arrangements
- Preferred supplier arrangement - fridges, freezers and washing machines
## Discretion
There is no discretion to exceed the appropriate maximum limit for each grant ($800.00 recoverable and $1200 non-recoverable) or the $2000 total limit for grants.
When considering payments for qualifying items within the $1200 non-recoverable grant, the maximum amount payable for a particular item is considered on a case-by-case basis. The guideline limits for Advance Payment of Benefit or Special Needs Grants to specific items do not apply.
Decisions should consider the transition plan that has been prepared by the personal adviser as part of the Transition from Care to Independence initiative.

chunks.title: Payment process - Civil Defence Payment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Payment process - Civil Defence Payment
The following payment arrangements apply:
- payments for people billeting evacuees and for evacuees in other temporary accommodation (in motels, hotels, camping grounds or home-stays, for example) are to be made directly to the accommodation provider
- payments for loss of livelihood are to be made to the applicant
- payments for food, clothing and bedding should generally be made to the supplier, however, as this is an exceptional circumstance payment can be made directly to the client
All applications should be granted from the date of the event.
Payments for food, clothing and bedding, up to the allowable maximum, made under the Civil Defence payment are not counted when calculating the amount of Special Needs Grant assistance available during a 52 week period.
No stand-down period applies to payments for loss of livelihood. Payment can commence from the day following the date payment of wages or salary ceased. Where a person is available for alternative employment, all available opportunities should be considered.
For a dependent child payment should be made through the parent's, guardian's or primary caregiver's SWIFTT record. If the whereabouts of the parent, guardian or primary caregiver is unknown then you will need to create a non-beneficiary record for the caregiver so that payments can be made for the child.

chunks.title: Payment rate - International Custody Dispute Payment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: The maximum weekly rate of payment must not exceed the equivalent of the Sole Parent Support payable to a sole parent plus an accommodation component equivalent to the Accommodation Supplement. Any income is reduced dollar for dollar. For more information see: - International Custody Dispute Payment and income - SNG International Custody Dispute Payment [no link find out why] assessment sheet

chunks.title: Assessment of accommodation costs — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: If the client is in New Zealand for the custody dispute, the maximum accommodation costs payable is equivalent to the amount of Accommodation Supplement that person would receive, if eligible and getting a main benefit (considering their location, accommodation costs and family composition, etc). Example A sole parent with 2 children living in Area 3 paying $225.00 per week rent would be able to get $160.00 as that is the maximum rate for Area 3 (as at 1 April 2026). per week Client pays rent of $225.00 Less entry threshold (as at 1 April 2026) $160.00 Equals $65.00 The client is eligible for up to 70% of $65.00 $73.00 x 0.70 $45.50 Round up to the nearest whole dollar $46.00 Check against maximum for Accommodation Supplement - Area 3 $160.00 (as at 1 April 2026) Total payment for accommodation costs $46.00 Sole Parent Support net rate (as at 1 April 2026) $521.52 Less any income received $0.00 Total amount of SNG International Custody Dispute Payment $567.52

chunks.title: Clients who are overseas — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: If the client is overseas for the custody dispute the maximum additional amount payable for accommodation costs is equivalent to the amount of Accommodation Supplement that the person would receive, if eligible and a non-beneficiary residing in Accommodation Supplement Area 1. The client's accommodation costs are those resulting from the accommodation in which they are currently residing (not in respect of any ongoing accommodation costs in New Zealand). You will need to transfer the accommodation costs to New Zealand dollars. You can do this using SELXT. Use the New Zealand dollar amount in the general formula for calculating the amount of accommodation supplement and treat the client as a non-beneficiary. For determining the maximum, assume the client is living in Accommodation Supplement Area 1. Example A sole parent with one child living in Sydney paying A$180.00 per week rent. A$180.00 = NZ$194.32. This person also receives $50.00 per week in income from an investment. per week Client pays rent of $194.32 Less entry threshold (as at 1 April 2026) $160.00 Equals $34.32 The client is eligible for up to 70% of $34.32 $34.32 x 0.70 $24.02 Round up to the nearest whole dollar $25.00 Check against maximum for Accommodation Supplement - Area 1 $235.00 (as at 1 April 2026) Total payment for accommodation costs $25.00 Sole Parent Support rate (as at 1 April 2026) $521.52 Less any income received $50.00 Total amount of Special Needs Grants - International Custody Dispute Payment $496.52 The assessment of accommodation costs (for the exchange rate calculation) will need to be recalculated when the payment is extended due to new court dates or if requested by the client.

chunks.title: Payment - rural assistance — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Payment - rural assistance
The following non-recoverable Special Needs Grants can be paid:
- 100% of the applicable weekly Jobseeker Support rate
Note an income exemption of $160.00 gross per week applies. Income in excess of $160.00 gross reduces the weekly amount payable by $1.00 for each $1.00 of income. For more information see: Income assessment - rural assistance
## Period client can get payment
Payments are not restricted to one payment for the same or similar purpose, but payments cannot be made for longer than:
- one year in total or
- the period approved by the Minister
whichever is the lesser.
## Making payments
Payments can only be made for the period approved by the Minister.
Applications should generally be granted from the Monday of the week of application. If the period approved by the Minister begins on a day other than Monday, applications in that week should be granted from the start of the period approved.
Payments should generally be made in a lump sum representing a 4-week period commencing from the Monday of the week of application.
The client will need to reapply every 4 weeks if they need ongoing assistance by completing a Continuation of the Rural Assistance Payment Application form, (and an up-to-date financial statement once every 3 months).
Note that payments may need to be made on a weekly basis if the client indicates their off farm income is likely to vary. In these cases the client can phone in their income each week to enable the rate of payment to be assessed and paid into their bank account. The client will still need to reapply every 4 weeks, and provide an up-to-date Recovery Facilitator authorisation every 3 months.
A debt should be established if the client does not notify a change in income and the payment has been made in advance.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Payment
Every Special Needs Grant paid for goods or services must be paid to the seller of those goods or services.
The seller must be a reputable supplier, for example a GST registered supplier or an established trustworthy business.
When a preferred supplier arrangement is in place the payment must be made directly to the preferred supplier by direct credit or payment card.
Note payments cannot be made for private sales.
## Preferred supplier arrangement
The Ministry currently has preferred supplier arrangements in place for whiteware and optical goods and services.
## Dependent children
In exceptional circumstances only, Special Needs Grants for goods and services can be paid to the client or to the parent or caregiver when the parent or caregiver applies for assistance on behalf of a dependent child.

chunks.title: Payments to people in specific circumstances — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Payments to people in specific circumstances
A client may be able to get a Special Needs Grant in specific circumstances.

chunks.title: Permanent residence — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Permanent residence
Generally migrants need to have permanent residence or New Zealand citizenship to receive Special Needs Grant assistance. Permanent residence is granted by Immigration New Zealand. Citizenship is granted by the Department of Internal Affairs.
To get a Special Needs Grant, a client must normally:
- have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 (which can either be a resident visa or a permanent resident visa) or
- have a residence permit under Immigration Act 1987 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) or
- be a British national who arrived in New Zealand prior to 2 April 1974 or
- be a New Zealand citizen
Note if you require further information about a client's application for permanent residence you must get consent from the client to contact Immigration New Zealand, or the client should obtain the information themselves. Otherwise the application should be declined. You must not collect or disclose information regarding a client's application without the client's consent.

chunks.title: Preferred supplier arrangement - fridges, freezers and washing machines — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Preferred supplier arrangement - fridges, freezers and washing machines
The following goods have a preferred supplier arrangement:
- fridges
- fridge-freezers
- freezers
- washing machines
The preferred supplier arrangement includes the following services in the purchase price:
- delivery
- installation
- removal of old goods if required
- repairs or replacement of goods while under warranty
- loan goods if needed while goods are being repaired, or assessed for repair
- disposal of any packaging

chunks.title: Preferred supplier arrangement - glasses — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: The Ministry of Social Development has a preferred supplier arrangement with selected optometrists and opticians to supply glasses to people in some urban areas. If a client who resides in an urban area covered by a preferred supplier arrangement for glasses (optical goods and services) refuses to purchase from a preferred supplier, the application for a Special Needs Grant must be declined. The preferred supplier arrangement includes the following goods and services in the purchase price: Goods - spectacle frames - spectacle lenses - ready to wear spectacles - spectacle protection cases - spectacle care products Services - eye examinations - fitting of spectacle frames, spectacle lenses and ready to wear spectacles - fitting of spectacle lenses to frames supplied by the purchaser - adjustment of spectacle frames, spectacle lenses and ready to wear spectacles

chunks.title: Subsequent applications — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Only one grant may be made to an applicant or any other person for the same item, or for the same or a similar purpose within a 52-week period, except where exceptional circumstances exist.

chunks.title: Clients with high clinical needs — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Some clients have high clinical needs which means the glasses they require cannot be provided at the standard contract price. Hardship assistance for a higher amount than the standard package amount can be provided for clients with high clinical needs. Some types of high clinical needs are: - vision which is outside of 'normal' ranges (+ or - 6 or higher) - severe astigmatism that requires a special lens grind - growths on eyes due to severe UV exposure - some forms of medication make eyes very sensitive to light and glasses require a special coating - prescription for glasses that are heavy and a higher grade of progressive lenses that are required to avoid frames buckling or the weight tearing the clients skin Lens coatings or glasses specifically for Irlen Syndrome are not covered by the Ministry of Social Development or the Ministry of Health.

chunks.title: Assistance for children's glasses — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text: Whaikaha provide a Spectacles Subsidy for children 15 years and younger with vision problems. The subsidy is paid for each qualifying child up to $287.50 (including GST) and can be accessed annually. To qualify either the child or parent/guardian must have a Community Services Card or the child must have a High Use Health Card. The subsidy covers the eye exam, frames, lenses, eye patches and repairs. There is also an additional amount of $51.11 (including GST) available for children who need adult sized frames if the child's vision is changing quickly or if they have an amblyopia (lazy eye) or strabismus (squint). There is no discretion to top-up the Ministry of Health subsidy unless the full subsidy has been claimed within the 1-year period and the child has a high clinical need. Then a client can apply for hardship assistance for their child through the Ministry of Social Development. This would be processed using the preferred supplier arrangement.

chunks.title: Preferred supplier arrangements — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Preferred supplier arrangements
When a preferred supplier arrangement is in place the client must purchase the specified goods and services from a preferred supplier.
The following specified goods and services have a preferred supplier arrangement:
- fridges, fridge-freezers, freezers and washing machines (whiteware)
- glasses (optical goods and services)
When a client applies for a Special Needs Grant for one of the specified goods or services, they must be told about the preferred supplier arrangement. MSD must also provide this information in writing to the client.
## Whiteware
If a client refuses to purchase whiteware from a preferred supplier the application for a Special Needs Grant must be declined.
For more information see:
- Preferred supplier arrangement - fridges, freezers and washing machines
- Whiteware hardship assistance [no link find out why] procedures
## Glasses
If a client who resides in an urban area that is covered by a preferred supplier arrangement for glasses (optical goods and services) refuses to purchase from a preferred supplier the application for a Special Needs Grant must be declined.

chunks.title: Pregnancy terminations — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Pregnancy terminations
In most cases the District Health Board pays the full cost of the operation and this avenue of funds must be exhausted first. Special Needs Grants may be approved for termination operation fees when the client has to pay a user part-charge.
A Special Needs Grant for termination travel and accommodation may be paid when:
- a health practitioner refuses to exercise their powers to refer clients for terminations on moral grounds. Payment may be made to clients who wish to travel to another area for referral or
- the client must travel away from home to access surgery and will not receive financial assistance from the District Health Board
On some occasions the District Health Board pays the client's cost of travel and accommodation. That avenue of funds should be exhausted before any Grant is made.
## Payment
Unless exceptional circumstances exist, the maximum amount payable for the total of both the part-user charge surgery fee, and travel/ accommodation is $300.
Special Needs Grants for this purpose are:
- non-recoverable
- restricted to one payment in any one 52 week period
## Proof
On application for a Special Needs Grant for termination of pregnancy, the following proof is required:
for operation fees:
for travel and accommodation:
confirmation of user part-charges
Confirmation that the District Health Board will not fund and
proof of the cost of travel and accommodation

chunks.title: Private hospital fees — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Private hospital fees
A Special Needs Grant is not payable for termination of pregnancy private hospital fees including:
- applications when accessing operations privately is out of choice, not necessity and
- applications resulting from the District Health Board declining an operation because the client does not meet the medical criteria
Some public hospitals, contract private hospitals to carry out operations on their behalf. However, they fund the operation and the client should only be required to pay the user part-charge.
A client may be able to get a Special Needs Grant for the user part-charge.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To get a Special Needs Grant a client must:
- meet an income and cash asset testFor more information see: Verification
- have an essential need, emergency need or need a payment for specific circumstances
- not be able to meet the need from their own resources or through other sources
- have met any hardship obligations that have been applied to them
- be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (ie not be in New Zealand unlawfully, here or on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) - except for Afghan evacuees who can get a re-establishment grant if they hold a temporary entry visa and have applied for a Afghan Emergency Resettlement Visa)
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and
- purchase goods and services from a preferred supplier when there is an arrangement in place
For more information see:
- Income limit
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Preferred supplier arrangements
You may also consider the extent to which the client has caused or contributed to the immediate need or to the situation that has led to the immediate need.
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they are considered to hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other eligibility criteria for a Special Needs Grant.

chunks.title: Re-establishment grants — extra help > special needs grant
chunks.text:
## Re-establishment grants
A re-establishment grant can be paid to people in specific situations who are re-establishing themselves in the community.
Each application is considered on a case by case basis.
A re-establishment grant cannot be used for emergency housing costs.
## Maximum amounts payable for re-establishment grants
Category

A total maximum of $5000 can be paid for the qualifying person and their immediate family.
Within that total maximum of $5000, a maximum of $3500 can be paid for accommodation costs.
When the applicant has more than 2 dependent children, the maximum of $5000 is increased by $100 for each additional dependent child.
For more information see: Payment of refugee, protected person, Afghan interpreter or Afghan evacuee re-establishment grants
Note for fridges, freezers and washing machines, the amounts payable, up to the maximum, are under the preferred supplier arrangement
