chunks.title: Accessing and sustaining tenancies in areas of limited housing — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: In some areas there are limited housing options and accommodation costs are less affordable, for example in Auckland. In these areas it is unreasonable to expect clients, who have secured a tenancy and have limited housing options, to be looking for less expensive housing solutions where the housing option is the most reasonable option for their situation. In this situation, you can consider that trying to find other more affordable housing is not a reasonable step that the client needs to take before they may be granted Temporary Additional Support, to help meet the regular and essential costs of the accommodation they have already found. You can consider paying at the start of the tenancy to help a client access a tenancy or during the tenancy to help them sustain the tenancy. Examples A sole parent with 2 children has been offered a tenancy for a house that meets their needs but the amount of rent means that the client would struggle to meet other costs once the rent is paid. It is a suitable area for the client to live in, and the area has limited housing options. It would be reasonable to grant Temporary Additional Support and not expect the client to find other accommodation to reduce their costs. A couple with 2 children own their own home. The main income earner recently lost their job and now receives Jobseeker Support. If they sold their house, they would have difficulty in finding a rental that they could afford as the area they live has limited housing options. Their mortgage payments are less than the current market rents for the area. It would be reasonable to grant Temporary Additional Support and not expect the client to reduce their costs by finding other accommodation. For more information see:

chunks.title: Refugees, protected persons or residence applicants — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Refugees, protected persons or residence applicants
Temporary Additional Support is calculated differently for certain refugee and protected person applicants, and people applying for a residence class visa (residence applicants).
If a client does not have New Zealand citizenship or a residence class visa, they can only get Temporary Additional Support if they:
- have been recognised as a refugee or protected person in New Zealand or
- are applying for refugee or protected person status and
- are waiting for a decision from Immigration New Zealand on their application or are appealing a decline decision to the Immigration and Protection Tribunal and
- are lawfully present in New Zealand (i.e. they have a valid temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009) or
- are applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 and are compelled to remain in New Zealand due to some unforeseen circumstances
## Different upper limit
There is a different upper limit for certain refugees, or protected persons or residence applicants.
This is:
- the appropriate rate payable of Accommodation Supplement maximum or
- 30% of the applicant's unabated main benefit
whichever is the greater.

chunks.title: Rent — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: MSD must check whether the client qualifies for Accommodation Supplement in respect of their accommodation costs. If the client qualifies for Accommodation Supplement it must be granted before Temporary Additional Support can be paid for those costs. If the client has a deficiency of income based on other allowable costs, they can get Temporary Additional Support. However, the accommodation costs must not be included until the Accommodation Supplement has been granted. Rent (including Kāinga Ora and community housing rental properties) may still be included in Temporary Additional Support if the client does not qualify for Accommodation Supplement. If the amount a client pays for their accommodation includes other costs (e.g. service costs) and the accommodation costs can be separately identified as part of the amount they pay, they will be considered renting.

chunks.title: Rent includes service costs — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: Sometimes a client's rent includes service costs such as electricity or a telephone network connection. When this occurs, service costs must be deducted from their accommodation costs. For more information see: - Rent includes service costs

chunks.title: Joint tenants — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: When there are joint tenants e.g. flatmates, each tenant may apply for the portion of the rent they pay in separate applications. A client does not need to have their name on a tenancy agreement to be considered renting. There is one exception: - Married, civil union or de facto couples in a joint tenancy

chunks.title: Client with renters, boarders or additional occupants — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: When a client gets rent, board or additional occupant contribution payments from someone living in the same premises, it is accommodation income and is deducted from their accommodation costs when calculating the weekly qualifying accommodation costs. Accommodation income includes: - Rent a client gets from another person (not being additional occupants or boarders) residing in the same premises, except where the person paying the rent is in a self-contained part of the premises or the rent payment is part of the income of a business on the premises - 62% of payments for board a client gets from another person residing in the same premises, except where the board payment is part of the income of a business on the premises - 62% of contributions a client gets from an additional occupant residing in the same premises Note when accommodation income is more than the client’s accommodation costs (after the deduction of the cost of any part of the property not being lived in by the client), the excess amount is income and must be charged against any financial assistance the client gets. In this case, the client will have no weekly qualifying accommodation costs. For more information see: - Weekly qualifying accommodation costs - Rent and board payments - Additional occupant contributions

chunks.title: Rent to buy — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: People may be in a rent to buy property. These clients are considered homeowners. For more information see: - Rent to buy

chunks.title: Temporary Accommodation Service — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's Temporary Accommodation Service helps households affected by a natural disaster to find temporary accommodation while their home is being repaired, rebuilt or until they find alternative accommodation. Households staying in Temporary Accommodation Services are generally required to pay a rent contribution. Clients may need to contribute to the cost of their temporary accommodation. MSD may consider the rent contribution for the assessment of Accommodation Supplement when the client occupies their premises as a home. If MSD considers the client does not occupy the premises as a home, Accommodation Supplement cannot be paid for the Temporary Accommodation Service rental costs. Note Accommodation Supplement can only be paid for 1 home. For more information about how to determine if someone occupies a premises as a home see: - Temporarily absent from a premises

chunks.title: Rent arrears not allowed — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: Arrears that were incurred while the client was getting an Accommodation Supplement, Accommodation Benefit (Students), Rent Rebate Allowance, Tenure Protection Allowance or Income Related Rent, are not allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Rent includes service costs — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Rent includes service costs
Sometimes a client's rent includes service costs. If the client is renting, any service costs must be deducted from their rent to determine their accommodation costs.
Generally, the service costs and accommodation costs will be itemised separately on the tenancy or rental agreement. MSD can only use the accommodation cost to calculate the allowable weekly qualifying accommodation costs for Temporary Additional Support.
## Service costs not clear
Where the service costs are not itemised separately MSD will need to assess the cost of the service(s) and deduct it from the total rent, to determine the cost of accommodation.
The first part of the assessment is to have the client ask the landlord to provide an estimate of the accommodation and service costs. Use the accommodation cost only.
Where this is not possible or if there is a disagreement between the landlord and client about the cost split between accommodation and service costs, MSD can use a variety of sources to estimate the service cost depending on what that cost is.
For example, if the total rent includes electricity, the Powerswitch website can be used to calculate the cost of the electricity to be deducted from the total rent.

chunks.title: Rent to buy — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Rent to buy
MSD must check whether the client qualifies for Accommodation Supplement. If the client is entitled to an Accommodation Supplement this must be granted before assessing whether the client qualifies for Temporary Additional Support.
Rent to buy costs may still be included in Temporary Additional Support if the client does not qualify for Accommodation Supplement.
A person may enter into a rent to buy contract (also called a deferred payment disposition). In such a case the client is considered as a home owner.
The client must supply a copy of the contract. All payments stated in the rental contract as mortgage repayments and payments made towards a deposit can be included as accommodation costs.
The contract will also state whether the client has responsibility for costs such as rates, insurance and maintenance.
If the client has responsibility for things like rates, insurance and maintenance these may be included as accommodation costs. If the client does not have responsibility for these things they cannot claim them as accommodation costs.
## Verification
The client must provide verification of their accommodation costs.

chunks.title: Rental equipment — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: MSD must check whether the client qualifies for Disability Allowance for the cost of rental equipment needed for their disability. If the client qualifies for Disability Allowance, this must be granted before MSD assess whether the client qualifies for Temporary Additional Support. The client may have allowable health and disability costs for Temporary Additional Support if they do not qualify for Disability Allowance when: - they do not meet the Disability Allowance income limit or - their disability will last less than 6 months or - they are certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants. A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that rental equipment is necessary. The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability Allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support can include necessary rental equipment when the client: - has a need for the item or service but cannot funding through Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora and - their life or health would be put at risk, or their disability aggravated if they could not hire the equipment because the expense was not included in their Disability Allowance. MSD should refer the client back to their medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or someone from their team) who will be able to refer them to the local Hospital and Health Services to see if they can get the equipment provided. If the Hospital and Health Service won't provide the equipment, the client should get a letter stating why. Examples of rental equipment that may be paid for are a closed-circuit television, or a computer, for a client with a visual impairment, or a nebuliser for a severe asthmatic. Allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support do not include: - the cost of buying equipment (e.g. hearing aids) as this is not a regular ongoing cost. (It can be used for hearing aid batteries - see Authorised consumables) or - prostheses (e.g. artificial limbs)

chunks.title: Proof of rental equipment costs — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: The client must provide: - a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and - receipts as proof of the equipment rental costs and - a letter from the Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora stating funding is not available for the item or service and why it is not available and - a letter from a registered medical or nurse practitioner stating what the consequences would be if the client, or their dependent child did not get the item/service

chunks.title: Repairs — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Repairs
MSD must check whether the client qualifies for Accommodation Supplement. If the client is entitled to an Accommodation Supplement this must be granted before assessing whether the client qualifies for Temporary Additional Support.
Essential repairs may still be included in Temporary Additional Support if the client does not qualify for Accommodation Supplement.
Repairs that may be considered as accommodation costs would include those which are needed for the continuation of existing:
- water
- gas
- power and
- sewerage services (including showers, toilets, sinks and the drains attached to them)
Other repairs can be considered if they are essential to:
- the structural stability of the house or property (repairs to buildings or sheds on the property that are not used for accommodation purposes are not to be considered)
- wiring and light fittings
- septic tanks (provided repairs have not been paid as a non-recoverable Special Needs Grant)
- any repairs required to meet building regulations
Repairs to any major appliance that helps maintain the house in a habitable state may be included, such as:
- gas or electric stove and
- hot water cylinder
Costs that should not be considered include:
- microwaves
- furnishings
- fridges and
- washing machines
## Verification
The client must provide verification of their accommodation repair costs.
For help on deciding whether a repair or maintenance is essential contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Residence — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get Temporary Additional Support, a client generally must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- have a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
People who are in New Zealand unlawfully or here on a temporary entry class visa generally do not qualify for a benefit.
## Clients without citizenship or a residence class visa
If a client does not have New Zealand citizenship or a residence class visa, they can only get Temporary Additional Support if they are:
- a person who has refugee or protected person status in New Zealand
- awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protected person status and are lawfully in New Zealand (i.e. they have a valid temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009) or
- applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 and are compelled to remain in New Zealand due to some unforeseen circumstances
Important note Temporary Additional Support is calculated differently for these clients. For information about how to do this see:
- Refugees, protected persons or residence applicants
MSD must look at each case on an individual basis.
## Partner non-residentially qualified
Temporary Additional Support can only be paid in respect of the person who meets the residence criteria. However, MSD must take into consideration the income and assets of both the client and their partner when assessing entitlement to Temporary Additional Support.
In calculating the formula assessment when a partner is unlawfully in New Zealand, the standard costs are those that would otherwise apply if the client were single or a sole parent.
## Australian clients
Australian citizens or residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand as they hold a residence class visa.
However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other criteria to qualify for Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Restrictions on the information requested — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Restrictions on the information requested
Requests for information made directly to the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner who completed the client's Disability Allowance medical certificate must not include a request for:
- an opinion, or information about whether the client has a partner or
- any additional information regarding the client's other physical and mental health conditions, or any information that is considered to be of a highly confidential nature

chunks.title: Retirement village — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Retirement village
MSD must check whether the client qualifies for Accommodation Supplement. If the client is entitled to an Accommodation Supplement this must be granted before assessing whether the client qualifies for Temporary Additional Support.
Accommodation costs for a retirement village may still be included in Temporary Additional Support if the client does not qualify for Accommodation Supplement.
There are a number of different situations that a person can be in when living in a retirement village.
When the amount a resident of a retirement village serviced apartment pays for their accommodation includes other costs (e.g. food or service costs) and these costs can be separated out from the amount they pay for accommodation, they are considered renting.
When the client pays for their accommodation and food, and the food costs can't be separated out from the amount they pay, they are considered boarding.
If a client owns the apartment, they are considered a homeowner.
## Verification
The client must provide verification of their accommodation costs.

chunks.title: Retirement village residents with 'Licence to Occupy' — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Retirement village residents with 'Licence to Occupy'
MSD must determine whether the client qualifies for Accommodation Supplement. If the client is entitled to an Accommodation Supplement this must be granted before assessing whether the client qualifies for Temporary Additional Support.
Accommodation costs for retirement village residents with 'Licence to Occupy' or an 'Occupational Rights Agreement' may still be included in Temporary Additional Support if the client does not qualify for Accommodation Supplement.
Some retirement village residents have a 'Licence to Occupy' or 'Occupational Rights Agreement'. These clients are considered homeowners and must provide:
- verification of their 'Licence to Occupy' title or 'Occupational Rights Agreement' and
- verification or breakdown of expenses
Note residents may pay for a variety of costs, and not all will be considered accommodation costs for Temporary Additional Support. MSD must assess each case on its own merits and only include costs related to the client's accommodation.
## Examples of costs to include
- repayments on a loan or mortgage taken out to obtain the client's licence to occupy their villa or unit
- local authority rates (if they get a rebate, this must be deducted)
- water rates
- insurance premiums relating to their villa or unit (must not include contents insurance)
- cost of essential repairs and maintenance relating to their villa or unit
## Payment of rates
Some residents may pay their rates with a service fee directly to the retirement village. In these cases, the cost for rates can be included in the Temporary Additional Support assessment. The client must provide verification of the rates they pay for the villa or unit they occupy.
## Verification
The client must provide verification of their accommodation costs.

chunks.title: Revolving credit payment calculation — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Revolving credit payment calculation
To calculate the amount of revolving credit payments to include in the assessment of Temporary Additional Support use the formula below.
You will need the following information:
- purchase price
- purchase dateNote if the purchase date is 29 February, use 28 February.
- revolving credit balance at time of application for Temporary Additional Support
- application date for Temporary Additional Support
## Step 1
Divide the purchase price by 20 to get the monthly payment.
## Step 2
Add 20 months to the purchase date to get expiry date 1. Start counting the months from the first month after the purchase date. For example if 01/04/19 is the purchase date then 01/05/19 is month 1, and 01/06/19 is month 2 etc.
Note if the end date falls on a non-existent date eg 30 February, use the first day of the following month.
## Step 3
Divide the revolving credit balance by the monthly payment to get a number of months (round up to the nearest whole number of months).
Important note if the number of months is more than 20, use expiry date 1 as the expiry date. See SWIFTT process below - you do not need to complete this step or step 4.
If the number of months is less than 20, then add the number of months to the application date to get expiry date 2.
Start counting the months from the first month after the purchase date. For example if 10/04/19 is the purchase date then 10/05/19 is month 1, and 10/06/19 is month 2 etc.
Note if the end date falls on a non-existent date eg 30 February, use the first day of the following month.
## Step 4
Use the earlier of expiry date 1 and expiry date 2 as the expiry date.
## SWIFTT process
Add the following information to the applicable allowable cost in the STAWA screen in SWIFTT:
- the expiry date from step 3 or 4 (as applicable)
- the monthly payment from step 1
For help with calculating the months see:
- Revolving credit payment calculation table
Also see:
- Examples of revolving credit payment calculations

chunks.title: Revolving credit payment calculation table — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Revolving credit payment calculation table
The months listed down the left hand side of the table represent the starting point to find the expiry dates 1 and 2.
The numbers along the top of the table are numbers of months.
## To find expiry date 1 (20 months from purchase date)
Find the month of the purchase date in the left hand column. Then go to the column 20. The point where these two columns meet is the month of the expiry date. Add the years indicated at the bottom of that shaded section to the year of the purchase date. This is expiry date 1.
Example
Purchase date is 15 January 2022. Select January in the left hand column and column 20 - the month is September. Add 1 year to 2022 to get the year of expiry. Expiry date 1, is 15 September 2023.
## To find expiry date 2 (number of months from application date)
Find the month of the application date in the left hand column. Then go to the appropriate number of month's column (this is the number of months from step 3 of the formula). The point where these 2 columns meet is the month of the expiry date. Add the years indicated at the bottom of that shaded section to the year of the application date. This is expiry date 2.
Example
Application date is 24 March 2022 and the number of months from step 3 is 15. Select March in the left hand column and column 15 - the month is June. Add 1 year to get the year of expiry. Expiry date 2 is 24 June 2023.
## Expiry date calculation monthly table
Use this table to help you determine the expiry dates when calculating credit card payments to use in the assessment of Temporary Additional Support. (This is also available in a format that provides a better print quality .)

chunks.title: Revolving credit payments — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Revolving credit payments
A revolving credit payment is a credit contract that may or may not have a credit limit. This will allow multiple purchases to be made and does not restrict what the client purchases.
Types of revolving credit can include:
- credit card purchases
- store card purchases (eg Farmers card)
Clients may include the following revolving credit payments in their assessment for Temporary Additional Support:
- essential household items
- a vehicle or
- a dryer
For more information see:
- Dryer
- Essential household items
- Vehicle repayments - essential household items
- Vehicle repayments - employment related costs
- Vehicle repayments - health and disability
## Payment amount
When a client has purchased an allowable item using a revolving credit payment the calculation for the assessment of Temporary Additional Support will:
- be a monthly payment of 5% of the purchase price of the item and
- be paid for a period which is the lesser of: 20 months from date of purchase orthe term required to pay the amount owing under the contract at the time of application for Temporary Additional Support
- 20 months from date of purchase or
- the term required to pay the amount owing under the contract at the time of application for Temporary Additional Support
For information about how to calculate this see:
- Revolving credit payment calculation
## Verification
The client must provide proof of the:
- item purchased to ensure it is an allowable cost
- purchase price
- purchase date and
- revolving credit balance at the time of the application
For more information see:
- Allowable costs
- Agreed period payments
- Hire or rental essential household items

chunks.title: Self-employed clients — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Self-employed clients
A client does not have to be getting a main benefit to qualify for Temporary Additional Support but they must meet the qualifications for Temporary Additional Support.
This includes the client taking all necessary steps to obtain all other sources of assistance that may be available. They also need to be taking reasonable steps to reduce their costs or increase their chargeable income.
Temporary Additional Support should not be used to financially assist a business. However, the reasons and likely length of the financial difficulty should be taken into account.
In some cases it may be possible for the client to meet their income deficiency by rearranging their business expenses to increase their net profit from the business, for example, if they can arrange with their bank to temporarily reduce their loan repayments.
It is important to remember though that the applicant is the client, not the business.
Each case must be considered on its own merits and the financial accounts of the client's business as well as the client's personal expenses should be examined carefully.

chunks.title: Shared care family tax credit and Best Start tax credit — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Shared care family tax credit and Best Start tax credit
For family tax credit purposes, shared care is when family tax credit is apportioned between caregivers.
In a shared care arrangement the apportioned amount of family tax credit payable to the applicant will be treated as chargeable income when assessing Temporary Additional Support.
For calculating standard costs, the full amount of family tax credit is taken into account, even where the client is only entitled to a portion of it.
## Example 1
A child aged 10 lives with his mother for 4 days per week and with his father for the remaining 3 days per week. Family tax credit for that child is $151.91 per week (as at 1 April 2026).
The mother applies for Temporary Additional Support and the amount of family tax credit that will be included as chargeable income is:
Family tax credit amount for chargeable income purposes
Family tax credit amount for standard costs purposes
$86.80 (4/7 of $151.91)
$151.91
## Example 2
A child born on 10 April 2025 lives with his mother for 4 days per week and his father the remaining 3 days per week. Best Start tax credit is $77.50 per week (as at 1 April 2026).
The mother gets Temporary Additional Support, and the Best Start tax credit included as chargeable income is:
Best Start tax credit amount for chargeable income
Best Start tax credit amount
$44.28 (4/7 of $77.50)
$77.50
Note Best Start tax credit is not included in the standard costs for Temporary Additional Support.
## For more information about shared care, see:
- Shared care standard costs
Also see:
- Verification of Working for Families Tax Credits [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Shared care - standard costs — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Shared care - standard costs
When family tax credit is paid for any shared custody arrangements of any child, the family tax credit included in the standard costs is 70% of the total amount of family tax credit payable in respect of that child regardless of whether the caregiver gets a full or partial payment of family tax credit.
For example, if family tax credit is payable for a child who is in the care of a person for 3/7 days, then the full unabated family tax credit for 7 days is used to calculate standard costs even if the person is only caring for the child 3 days of the period.
Standard costs
Benefit
Standard costs
family tax credit
Non-beneficiary married, civil union or de facto couple with 1 dependent child (aged 5) and a child (aged 7) who is in the client's care for 3 days per week under a shared custody arrangement (The couple get a full rate of family tax credit for one child and an apportioned rate of family tax credit for the other).
70% of the net rate of unabated Jobseeker Support for a married, civil union or de facto couple (with children)
70% of full unabated rate of family tax credit for 2 children aged 5 and 7 years
A client getting Sole Parent Support for a dependent child (aged 9) who is in the client's care for 5 days per week under a shared custody arrangement. The client gets an apportioned rate of family tax credit.
70% of the net rate of unabated Sole Parent Support
70% of full unabated rate of family tax credit for 1 child aged 9.
A single client getting Jobseeker Support who has a child aged 10 in their care for 3 days per week under a shared custody arrangement. The client gets an apportioned rate of family tax credit.
70% of the net rate of unabated Jobseeker Support for a single person.
70% of full unabated rate of family tax credit for 1 child aged 10
A single client getting Jobseeker Support who has a child aged 7 in their care for 1 day per week under a shared custody arrangement. The client does not get family tax credit.
70% of the net rate of unabated Jobseeker Support for a single person.
Nil (no family tax credit is payable)

chunks.title: Single client in residential care — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Single client in residential care
A single client in residential care can get Temporary Additional Support.
## Rate of payment
If the client meets the qualifications for Temporary Additional Support when they are in residential care, the rate payable for Temporary Additional Support should be calculated as follows:
Chargeable income
- Net rate of single main benefit paid (before any sanction or other deduction)
- Any other net income received or earned by the client
Assets
Use the assets owned by the client
Allowable costs
Include the allowable costs for the client (excludes any accommodation costs for the client's residential care or any costs towards their residential services)
Standard costs
Calculate the standard costs for a single person
Upper limit
Calculate the upper limit for a single person
Disability exception amount
A single client in residential care can qualify for the disability exception amount
Rate of payment
Assess the client as a single person

chunks.title: Special Education Transport — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Special Education Transport
You must check whether the client qualifies for Disability Allowance. If the client is entitled to a Disability Allowance it must be granted before you assess whether the client qualifies for Temporary Additional Support.
The client may have allowable health and disability costs for Temporary Additional Support where they do not qualify for Disability Allowance because:
- they do not meet the Disability Allowance income limit or
- their health or disability condition will last less than 6 months or
- they are certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants
Allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support can include additional travel costs that a person has because of their special education needs. These additional travel costs can be incurred in two main areas.
The Ministry of Education Special Education School Transport Assistance Policy aims to provide transport to and from school for students identified through Special Education 2000 as having special education needs. The following outlines the two main criteria:
## Category 2 - Mobility
Special needs transport assistance is available for students who require it for mobility reasons, to enable them to attend their nearest school, or the nearest school that is able to meet their special need. For example when:
- wheel chairs or other specialist equipment, must accompany the student
- the student is unable (for mobility reasons) to independently make their way to school
There are no other criteria aside from these two. For example transport to and from school cannot be provided from this funding, for psycho-social or social reasons. Assistance is not available from this fund to transport students to meet parenting order or access requirements.
The provision of transport assistance is not dependent on any factors other than the criteria. For example, the financial circumstances of the family are not a determining factor in regard to the eligibility for transport assistance.

chunks.title: Special foods — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: MSD must check if the client qualifies for Disability Allowance for special foods. If the client qualifies for a Disability Allowance, it must be granted before MSD assess if the client qualifies for Temporary Additional Support. The client may have allowable health and disability costs for Temporary Additional Support where they do not qualify for Disability Allowance because: - they do not meet the Disability Allowance income limit or - their disability will last less than 6 months or - they are certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that special foods are necessary. The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability Note when a medical practitioner or nurse practitioner indicates on the client's Disability Allowance medical certificate that treatment by another registered health practitioner is necessary, that practitioner must verify the costs of their services. Allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support can include additional costs of special foods that a client needs because of their disability. The cost of special foods can be included if they are: - for additional food or food supplements beyond most people's everyday needs and - above usual food costs (e.g. soya milk costs more than cow's milk) and - part of a diet that has been supervised by a registered dietician, if relevant Note MSD only pays the difference between a special food item and its non-special equivalent (e.g. lactose-free milk vs normal milk, and gluten-free bread vs gluten-containing bread). Some examples of special food costs included as allowable costs are: - gluten free food for people who are diagnosed with Coeliac disease or gluten intolerance (such as gluten free flours, bread or pasta) - low or no dairy foods for people who are diagnosed with a dairy allergy or intolerance (such as soy or coconut milk alternatives) - high protein and high calorie foods for people who are diagnosed with 'Failure to Thrive' (such as chickpeas or yoghurt)

chunks.title: Special foods — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: - greater quantities of foods than is normally expected i.e. the product is not necessarily special, but the amount is (such as people who are diagnosed with 'iron-deficient anaemia' and require additional silver beet or meat in their diet) - low or no sugar food for people with diabetes or sugar intolerances (such as whole grains like barley or quinoa or sugar alternatives) - food and vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals when these are recommended as necessary by a client's registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or dietician, such as for people with terminal illnesses Note the issue of special foods is not always straightforward and needs to be treated with sensitivity and discretion. When it is unclear refer to the Regional Health Advisor and Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] for more information and advice. Allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support do not include: - specialist foods fully funded, subsidised or provided through the Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora or - extra costs of a self-imposed diet or lifestyle choice or - the normal costs of healthy eating (e.g. fresh vegetables and fruit) The diet or special food must be confirmed as not being fully funded, subsidised or provided by another agency such as Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora. For further information about specific food items that may be subsidised through PHARMAC see: PHARMACs online schedule Special foods.

chunks.title: Proof of special foods costs — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: The client must provide: - a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and - proof of their extra food costs and - evidence that the treatment is being supervised by or provided by a registered dietician, if relevant

chunks.title: Partner does not qualify — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Partner does not qualify
A partner does not qualify for Temporary Additional Support if they are:
- subject to a non-entitlement period or
- subject to a stand-down or
- subject to a 100% suspension of their benefit because of a sanction or
- a full-time student (with no dependent children or no disability costs for any family member that exceed the maximum rate of Disability Allowance paid)
If the partner does not qualify, MSD assesses the client's Temporary Additional Support application as if they were a couple, but only pays 50% of the calculated Temporary Additional Support rate to the qualifying client.
## Rate of payment
If the client meets the qualifications for Temporary Additional Support, the rate payable for Temporary Additional Support should be calculated as follows:
Chargeable income
- Net rate of main benefit (before any sanction or deduction) as a couple.
- Any Disability Allowance paid to the client for any qualifying family member (including any child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid)
- Any Accommodation Supplement paid to the client
- Any other net income received or earned by the client and their non-qualified partner
- Any Working for Families Tax Credits payments payable to the client and their non-qualified partner
Assets
Use the assets owned by both the client and their non-qualified partner
Standard costs
Calculate 70% of the net rate of benefit paid at the couple's rate
Calculate 70% of the net rate of family tax credit payable
Upper limit
Calculate the upper limit for a couple
Rate of payment
Assess the client as a couple and pay only 50% of this rate to the qualifying client
Note Best Start tax credit is not included in the calculation of standard costs.

chunks.title: Partner in residential care — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Partner in residential care
When a partner is in residential care they may qualify for Temporary Additional Support.
Either they or their partner in the community can apply for Temporary Additional Support but they are assessed as a couple with all their combined chargeable income, allowable costs and assets included in their calculation.
In these cases, it is likely that the partner in residential care may get a different benefit type from the client in the community. You would combine the net rate of each benefit type for both the chargeable income and the standard costs.
## Manual calculation required to determine rate of payment
If both the client in the community and their partner in residential care meet the qualifications for Temporary Additional Support, the rate payable for Temporary Additional Support should be calculated manually as follows:
Chargeable income
- Combined net rate of main benefits (before any sanction or deduction including Residential Support Subsidy or Residential Care Subsidy) as a married, civil union or de facto couple
- Any Disability Allowance paid to the client in the community (or any other family member including a child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid)
- Special Disability Allowance paid to the client in the community
- Accommodation Supplement paid to the client in the community for their accommodation costs
- Any other net income received or earned by the client, and partner (apart from income of the partner in the community, included in the means assessment of their partner in residential care)
- Any Working for Families Tax Credits payments payable
Assets
Use the assets owned by both the client and partner
Allowable costs
Include the allowable costs for the client in the community and the partner in care (excludes any accommodation costs for the client's residential care or any costs towards their residential services)
Standard costs
Calculate 70% of the combined unabated main benefit rates and unabated family tax credit payments
Upper limit
Calculate 30% of the combined unabated main benefits
Rate of payment
Assess the client as a married, civil union or de facto couple and pay the full married, civil union or de facto rate
Note in these cases, the client in the community should be encouraged to make the application for the couple. It may be appropriate to pay the full calculated rate of Temporary Additional Support to the client in the community as they would usually manage the finances for the family.

chunks.title: Partner is overseas — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Partner is overseas
If a client's partner is overseas and they still consider themselves to be in a relationship, MSD must take into consideration the partner's residency status and reason for the partner being overseas before deciding the rate of payment.

chunks.title: Partner overseas long-term — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Partner overseas long-term
If a partner was resident in New Zealand but has left the country and has no definite plans to return (for example, they are working overseas) they are not considered ordinarily resident in New Zealand and cannot be included in the benefit.
If they still consider themselves to be in a relationship, then they are assessed as a couple as below.
## Rate of payment
If the client meets the qualifications for Temporary Additional Support when their partner is overseas long-term, the rate payable for Temporary Additional Support should be calculated as follows:
Chargeable income
- Half of the couple's main benefit net rate (before any sanction or deduction)
- Any Disability Allowance paid to the client for any qualifying family member
- Any Accommodation Supplement paid to the client
- Any other net income received or earned by the client and their non-qualified partner
- Any Working for Families Tax Credits payments payable to the client and their non-qualified partner
Assets
Use the assets owned by both the client and their non-qualified partner
Allowable costs
Include the allowable costs for the client
Standard costs
Calculate 70% of the net rate of benefit paid at the unabated half couple rate
Calculate 70% of the net rate of family tax credit payable
Upper limit
Calculate the upper limit for a couple
Rate of payment
Assess the client as receiving the half couple rate and pay the calculated rate to the qualifying client
Note the single/sole parent rate can only be paid when the relationship no longer exists. Best Start tax credit is not included in the calculation of standard costs.

chunks.title: Partner gets a different main benefit — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Partner gets a different main benefit
If a partner is getting a different main benefit from the client, and both the partner and the client meet the qualifications for Temporary Additional Support, you may grant Temporary Additional Support on the applicant's record.
Combine the net rate of each benefit type for both the chargeable income and the standard costs.
## Rate of payment
If both the client and their partner meet the qualifications for Temporary Additional Support, the rate payable for Temporary Additional Support should be calculated as follows:
Chargeable income
- combined net rate of main benefits (before any sanction or deduction) as a married, civil union or de facto couple
- Disability Allowance paid to the client and partner (or any other family member including a child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid)
- Accommodation Supplement paid to the client and partner
- Special Disability Allowance paid to the client in the community
- any other net income received or earned by the client and partner (apart from income of the partner in the community, included in the means assessment of their partner in residential care)
- Working for Families Tax Credits payments payable to the client and partner
Assets
Use the assets owned by both the client and partner
Allowable costs
Include the allowable costs for the client and partner
Standard costs
Calculate 70% of the combined unabated main benefit rates and unabated family tax credit payments
Upper limit
Calculate 30% of the combined unabated main benefits
Rate of payment
Assess the client as a married, civil union or de facto couple and pay the full couple rate
For more information see:
- Example - partner gets a different main benefit
## SWIFTT process
SWIFTT automatically assesses these clients, as it does for other couples who get the same benefit.
SWIFTT automatically combines the net rate of each main benefit type for the chargeable income and will apply the 70% standard costs calculation to this combined amount.
SWIFTT automatically combines the chargeable income and allowable costs held in both records, for example, Accommodation Supplement and Disability Allowance
Manual adjustments may need to be made to the income charge to exclude income of the partner in the community when that income is included in the means assessment of their partner in residential care.
You would enter all the family's allowable costs in the applicant's record in STAWA.

chunks.title: Partner temporarily overseas — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Partner temporarily overseas
If the partner was resident in New Zealand but has left the country temporarily, MSD must take into consideration the individual circumstances of the person who has left the country when deciding whether or not to continue Temporary Additional Support.
The partner overseas may continue to get Temporary Additional Support at the existing rate for up to 28 days provided none of their other circumstances have changed. The partner's Temporary Additional Support should be stopped from the 29th day if they have not returned.
In no circumstances should payment continue when the partner is overseas for longer than 28 days.
## Rate of payment
If the client meets the qualifications for Temporary Additional Support and their partner is temporarily overseas, the rate payable for Temporary Additional Support should be calculated as follows:
Chargeable income
- net rate of main benefit (before any income reduction or deduction) as a couple
- any income earned by client and partner
- any Working for Families Tax Credits payments
Assets
Use the assets owned by both the client and partner
Allowable costs
Include the allowable costs for the client and partner
Standard costs
Calculate the standard costs for a couple
Upper limit
Calculate the upper limit for a couple
Rate of payment
Assess the client as a couple and pay the full calculated couple's rate
For information how to calculate Temporary Additional Support after the 28 day period see:
- Partner overseas long-term

chunks.title: Partner unlawfully resident in New Zealand or here temporarily — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Partner unlawfully resident in New Zealand or here temporarily
If the client meets the qualifications for Temporary Additional Support but their partner is unlawfully resident in New Zealand, or has a temporary entry class visa (such as visitor, work or student) the qualifying client should be assessed as a single person or sole parent.
Note a partner who meets the criteria for certain refugee and protected person applicants, or a partner who is applying for a residence class visa (residence applicants) may be included in Temporary Additional Support.
## Rate of payment
If the client meets the qualifications for Temporary Additional Support and their partner does not qualify, the rate payable for Temporary Additional Support should be calculated as follows:
Chargeable income
Net rate of main benefit (before any sanction or other deduction) as a single person or sole parent.
Any other net income received or earned by client and partner.
Any Working for Families Tax Credits payments payable to the client and partner.
Allowable costs
Include the allowable costs of the qualifying client.
Assets
Use the assets owned by both the client and partner
Standard costs
Calculate the standard costs for a single person or a sole parent
Upper limit
Calculate the upper limit for a single person or a sole parent
Rate of payment
Assess the client as if they are single or a sole parent and pay the calculated rate to the qualifying client.

chunks.title: Standard costs — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Standard costs
Standard costs are the proportion of living costs that the client (and their partner, if any) are expected to meet from their benefit or income.
The following table is used to calculate standard costs for Temporary Additional Support:
Standard costs for a client getting a main benefit
70%
Net rate of main benefit (before any income reduction or other deduction) payable to the client and their partner (if any) and
70%
family tax credit (before any income reduction or other deduction) payable for "any children" to the client or their partner according to the client's family circumstances
Standard costs of client not getting a main benefit
70%
Net rate of Jobseeker Support (before any income reduction or other deduction) that would be payable to the client and their partner (if any) as if they qualified for Jobseeker Support and
70%
family tax credit (before any income reduction or other deduction) payable for 'any children' to the client or their partner according to the client's family circumstances
Note 'any children' includes dependent children and shared care children who qualify for family tax credit. Best Start tax credit is not included in the calculation of the standard costs.
For more information about calculating standard costs see:
- Non-beneficiaries
- Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit
- Shared care - standard costs

chunks.title: Striking workers — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Striking workers
Where a single client is not employed because of a strike, they can get Temporary Additional Support.
However, you should consider whether they have deprived themselves of income and, if so, assess entitlement to Temporary Additional Support by taking into account pre-strike earnings.
This approach will ensure that clients already getting Temporary Additional Support do not qualify for a higher rate as a result of going on strike.
## Partner on strike
If the client meets the qualifications for Temporary Additional Support and their partner is on strike, the client can still get Temporary Additional Support. They are assessed as married, civil union or de facto couple with all their combined income, allowable costs and assets included in their calculation. The full rate payable should be paid to the client.
In these cases you can:
- assess Temporary Additional Support for the couple as both the client and the partner qualify for Temporary Additional Support and
- you should consider whether the partner has deprived themselves of income and, if so, assess entitlement to Temporary Additional Support by taking into account pre-strike earnings

chunks.title: Surplus — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Surplus
When the client has a surplus there is no entitlement to Temporary Additional Support. A surplus occurs when the client's disposable income is greater than their standard costs.
Note to get Temporary Additional Support the client must have a deficiency and the deficiency must not be less than $1.00.
## Example
A non-beneficiary married, civil union or de facto client with no dependent children has the following:
Weekly Chargeable income
Weekly Allowable costs
Net weekly wages (after Tax and ACC levy)
$747.75
Weekly qualifying accommodation costs (Rent $390.00) less $34.13 accommodation deduction as at 1 April 2026
$355.87
Accommodation Supplement (rent $390.00 per week, Area 1 as at 1 April 2026 - rounded up) based on wages $800.00 per week before tax
$168.00 (income of $900.00 is below the income threshold of $1,066.00 (as at 1 April 2026) so no income reduction to the Accommodation Supplement rate payable)
Allowable consumer credit contracts
$66.71
Total
$915.75
Total
$422.58
## Step 1
Calculate the amount of disposable income.
To do this, determine the client's weekly amount of chargeable income and weekly amount of allowable costs.
Chargeable income
$915.75
Less Allowable costs
$422.58
Equals Disposable income
$493.17
## Step 2
Calculate the income deficiency or surplus for the client.
Standard costs
70% of net rate of married, civil union or de facto rate Jobseeker Support (no children) $633.94 x 70% (as at 1 April 2026)
$443.75
Less disposable income
$493.17
Equals income surplus
$49.42 (surplus)
The client does not qualify for Temporary Additional Support because their disposable income is more than their standard costs which means they have a surplus of income.

chunks.title: Telephone rental costs - disability — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: MSD must check whether the client qualifies for Disability Allowance for telephone rental costs or mobile phone plans directly related to their disability. If the client qualifies for Disability Allowance, it must be granted before MSD assess if the client qualifies for Temporary Additional Support. The client may have allowable health and disability costs for Temporary Additional Support where they do not qualify for Disability Allowance because: - they do not meet the Disability Allowance income limit or - their disability will last less than 6 months or - they are certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants Allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support can include rental of a basic telephone and telephone line rental costs (including wiring maintenance charges) or a basic mobile phone plan (prepay or monthly) for a client with a disability only when the ongoing cost of the telephone or mobile plan is directly related to the client's disability. A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that a telephone or mobile phone is necessary. The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability The telephone rental and line costs can be accepted as being directly related to the client's disability if MSD is satisfied that they did not previously have a telephone connected, and has had to have one connected due to their disability. Mobile phone plans The ongoing cost of a mobile phone (e.g. pre-pay call time or monthly plan charges) should only be allowed in exceptional circumstances when this is the most cost-effective solution. This may be when the client does not have a landline at their residence or there are no telephone lines available. The maximum cost paid, should be no more than the cost of the standard monthly landline rental in the area. Note mobile phones would not be considered an additional expense if the medical alarm needs a telephone line to operate. Allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support do not include: - the costs of buying a phone or having it installed as these are not ongoing costs (consider the possibilities of an Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment for installation costs) or - extra costs such as toll calls, call minder, or call waiting (unless it can be shown that it is an additional expense, necessary and directly related to the client's disability)

chunks.title: Telephone rental costs - disability — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: - the cost of purchasing a mobile phone through a plan, e.g. paying for the phone in instalments under a monthly plan.

chunks.title: Proof of telephone or mobile costs — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: The client must provide a: - Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and - copy of their telephone account proving they have a telephone and showing their telephone and line rental costs (including wiring maintenance charges) or - copy of their mobile plan account showing plan charges (charges should be no more than a landline in the area)

chunks.title: Telephone rental costs - essential household items — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: Allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support can include rental of a basic telephone and telephone line rental costs (including wiring maintenance charges and mobile phone plans) for a client when the ongoing cost of the telephone is: - directly related to the client's personal safety or security or - directly related to the client's special family circumstances In addition, these costs must be regular and essential to meet the family's daily living needs and could not be readily avoided or varied when the expense was incurred. Note the cost of buying a phone (including a mobile phone) or having it installed is not an allowable cost for Temporary Additional Support as this is not an ongoing cost. This includes fixed term mobile phone plans through which the mobile phone itself is purchased.

chunks.title: Personal safety or security — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: The cost of telephone rental for a basic telephone and telephone line rental costs (including wiring maintenance charges and mobile phone plans but excluding toll charges) can be included as an allowable cost for Temporary Additional Support where a telephone is essential for the client's personal safety or security. For example, a frail client living on their own, or a separated client with a protection order against a partner. A client must provide verification of their circumstances to have the cost of a telephone included such as documentation from: - police - court order - women's refuge - previous history held by MSD - Oranga Tamariki or - any other relevant organisation

chunks.title: Special family circumstances — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: The cost of a telephone rental for a basic telephone and telephone line rental costs (including wiring maintenance charges and mobile phone plans but excluding toll charges) can be included as an allowable cost for Temporary Additional Support where a telephone is an essential item for a family. For example, a telephone may be essential to enable a client to be contacted by the school their children attend. Note a client must provide verification of their special family circumstances to have the cost of a telephone included.

chunks.title: Mobile phone plans — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: The cost of a mobile phone plan can be considered an allowable cost for Temporary Additional Support. This includes prepaid plans and account-based plans with regular instalments e.g. pay monthly plans. The cost of purchasing a mobile phone through a plan is not included as an allowable cost for Temporary Additional Support. For example, paying for the phone in instalments. If a client has a landline, then a mobile phone plan cannot be considered as an allowable cost. However, if the client does not have a landline, then a mobile phone plan may be considered as an allowable cost. The maximum cost that can be included is the lowest amount to meet the client's needs. This should be no more than the cost of: - a standard monthly landline rental in the client's local area or - the cheapest mobile phone plan whichever is cheaper.

chunks.title: Telephone rental costs for employment — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Telephone rental costs for employment
Allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support can include rental of a basic telephone and telephone line rental costs (including wiring maintenance charges and mobile phone plans) for a client when the ongoing cost of the telephone is a condition of the client's paid employment. For example an electrical worker who is on-call 24 hours per day.
In addition, these costs must be regular and essential to meet the family's daily living needs and could not be readily avoided or varied when the expense was incurred.
Note the cost of buying a phone (including a mobile phone) or having it installed is not an allowable cost for Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Transitional housing contribution — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Transitional housing contribution
Clients who are staying in transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development pay a transitional housing contribution of up to 25 percent of their income towards their accommodation costs.
Clients who are staying in transitional housing and who pay a transitional housing contribution towards their accommodation costs generally do not qualify for Accommodation Supplement. See: Examples of Accommodation Supplement for emergency and transitional housing
The transitional housing contribution may still be included in Temporary Additional Support if the client does not qualify for Accommodation Supplement. Some providers may charge a service fee, in addition to the transitional housing contribution. This fee, which generally covers utilities such as internet and power, is not considered an accommodation cost and cannot be included in the client's Temporary Additional Support.
## Arrears
Arrears for transitional housing contribution can be included as an accommodation cost.
## Verification
The client needs to provide us with verification of their transitional housing contribution (unless it's already set up in SWIFTT as a benefit redirection).
This verification should generally be a letter or agreement between the client and the transitional housing provider, showing the amount of transitional housing contribution the client must pay.

chunks.title: Transport - disability — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: MSD must check if the client qualifies for Disability Allowance for the costs of regular additional travel a client has because of their disability. If the client qualifies for Disability Allowance, this must be granted before MSD assess if the client qualifies for Temporary Additional Support. The client may have allowable health and disability costs for Temporary Additional Support if they do not qualify for Disability Allowance when: - they do not meet the Disability Allowance income limit or - their disability will last less than 6 months or - they are certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants. A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that transport costs are necessary. The certificate must also confirm the transport is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability Allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support can include additional travel costs that a person has because of their disability. These additional travel costs can be incurred when a person with a disability is carrying out everyday activities. Examples of everyday activities may include but are not limited to: - shopping - work. The amount of the allowable cost is the difference between the costs incurred by the disabled person and the costs that a person in a similar situation without a disability would have.

chunks.title: Public transport and Community connect — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: Public transport should be used in preference to taxis if it is available and if the client's disability does not prevent them from using it. Note when the client has a Total Mobility card/vouchers and their taxi fares are subsidised, you should only use the unsubsidised amount in the assessment. If a client is using public transport and has a Community Services Card, they can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect and should take reasonable steps to reduce their costs by applying for the discount. When a client has not used their Community Services Card to apply for the discount, MSD must discuss their reasons for this, if their actual public transport costs are higher than they would be if the 50% discount was applied. The client may have a good reason for applying for the 50% discount (e.g. there are accessibility issues with applying for the Community Connect discount through a public transport provider's website, and this is the only way to apply). Note MSD may already hold this information if the client is getting a Disability Allowance with public transport costs included. MSD should consider this information when making a decision about the client's allowable costs. When there is a good reason, the client's allowable costs for travel should be the client's actual costs. If there is no good reason, their allowable costs for travel should not be more than the cost of the subsidised public transport fare. Allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support do not include: - attending treatment at a hospital when the costs are fully funded by Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora or other agency or Special Needs Grant Health travel costs - children or students with disabilities who qualify for assistance through the Ministry of Education. Refer clients in these cases to the Group Special Education. If the child is not eligible for Special Education Transport, the client should get a letter stating why. Contact Helpline for advice - the cost of travel to attend counselling sessions - this can only be included in a Disability Allowance

chunks.title: Transport - personal health — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: MSD must check if the client qualifies for Disability Allowance for the costs of regular travel to a health practitioner for treatment of their disability. If the client qualifies for Disability Allowance, this must be granted before MSD assess if the client qualifies for Temporary Additional Support. The client may have allowable health and disability costs for Temporary Additional Support if they do not qualify for Disability Allowance when: - they do not meet the Disability Allowance income limit or - their disability will last less than 6 months or - they are certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants. A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that transport costs are necessary. The certificate must also confirm the transport is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are: - additional and - ongoing and - directly related to the client's disability This includes costs for ambulance fees, subscriptions and getting to medical appointments. Note if the travel is for a particular course of treatment (e.g. chemotherapy) payment of costs may be met by Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora. - Allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support do not include attending treatment at a hospital when the costs are fully funded by Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora or Special Needs Grant Health travel costs - the cost of travel to attend counselling sessions - this can only be included in a Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Public transport and Community Connect — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: Public transport should be used in preference to a taxi if it is available and if the client's disability does not prevent them from using it. If a client is using public transport and has a Community Services Card, they can get a 50% discount on public transport fares through Community Connect and should take reasonable steps to reduce their costs by applying for the discount. When a client has not used their Community Services Card to apply for the discount, MSD must discuss their reasons for this, if their actual public transport costs are higher than they would be if the 50% discount was applied. The client may have good reason for not applying for the 50% discount (e.g. there are accessibility issues with applying for the Community Connect discount through a public transport provider's website, and this is the only way to apply). Note MSD may already hold this information if the client is getting a Disability Allowance with public transport costs included. MSD should consider this information when making a decision about the client's allowable costs. When there is a good reason, the client's allowable costs for travel should be the client's actual costs. If there is no good reason, their allowable costs for travel should not be more than the cost of the subsidised public transport fare.

chunks.title: Travel when there is a closer suitable health practitioner — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text: When a client chooses to travel some distance to see a registered health practitioner, this should generally not be included as an allowable cost for Temporary Additional Support. For example a client moves to a new location and chooses to visit their registered health practitioner in their previous location rather than transfer to a suitable local health practitioner, only the costs of travelling to the local health practitioner should generally be included. Note when there is closer suitable registered health practitioner, any additional travel costs not met by Disability Allowance cannot be considered an allowable cost for Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Types of health and disability costs — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Types of health and disability costs
Health and disability costs for the client and any member of their family that are allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support but are not allowable costs for Disability Allowance are:
- Childcare if the caregiver is incapacitated
- Dryer
- Vehicle repayments - health and disability
Health and disability costs that are allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support and Disability Allowance should only be manually included when the client (or any member of their family) does not qualify for Disability Allowance.
These are:
- Ambulance fees and subscriptions
- Alternative treatment
- Authorised consumables
- Clothing
- Day care for the older disabled people
- Gardening, lawns and outside window cleaning
- Gym and swimming pool fees
- Medical alarms
- Medical fees
- Power, gas and heating
- Pharmaceutical charges
- Rental equipment
- Special foods
- Telephone rental costs - health and disability
- Transport - disability
- Transport - personal health
- Vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals
Note Counselling costs and transport to attend counselling sessions can only be included in Disability Allowance. They cannot be included in Temporary Additional Support.
## Verification
A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client’s disability and need for treatment. The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are:
- additional and
- ongoing and
- directly related to the client's disability
Note when a medical practitioner or nurse practitioner indicates on the client's Disability Allowance medical certificate that treatment by another registered health practitioner is necessary, that practitioner must verify the costs of their services.

chunks.title: Upper limit — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Upper limit
The upper limit is the maximum amount that can be paid for Temporary Additional Support unless the client qualifies for a disability exception amount or is a certain refugee, protected person or residence applicant.
If the client qualifies for a disability exception amount, the upper limit is added to this amount to calculate the disability exception rate of payment for Temporary Additional Support.
The following tables are used to calculate the upper limit for Temporary Additional Support:
Upper limit for a client getting a main benefit
30%
Net rate of main benefit (before any income reduction or other deduction) payable to the client and their partner (if any)
Upper limit for a client not getting a main benefit
30%
Net rate of Jobseeker Support (before any income reduction or other deduction) that would be payable to the client and their partner (if any) if they qualified for Jobseeker Support
Important note there is a different 'upper limit for certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants'.

chunks.title: Upper limit for certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Upper limit for certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants
When assessing the upper limit for certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants, you would use either:
- the appropriate Accommodation Supplement maximum rate payable or
- 30% of the net rate of the applicant's unabated main benefit
whichever is the greater.
Deficiency
Calculate the deficiency by deducting the disposable income from the standard costs
Upper limit for certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants
Manually calculate the appropriate upper limit for refugees, protected persons or residence applicants which is the greater of:
- the appropriate maximum rate of Accommodation Supplement or
- 30% of the net rate of the applicant's unabated main benefit
Compare
Compare the calculated deficiency to the 'upper limit for certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants'
Rate of payment
The rate for Temporary Additional Support is the lesser of the deficiency or the 'upper limit for certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants'

chunks.title: Vehicle repayments - essential household items — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Vehicle repayments - essential household items
For a motor vehicle or other vehicle repayments (for example mobility scooter) to be included in the assessment of Temporary Additional Support the vehicle must be considered as an essential household cost.
For more information about vehicle repayments for disability and employment reasons see:
- Vehicle repayments - disability
- Vehicle repayments - for employment
The maximum weekly allowable cost for vehicle repayments per family is $85.96 (as at 1 April 2026).
Note there is no limit to the number of vehicles that can be included in Temporary Additional Support.
## Vehicle purchased before the client became a beneficiary
If the vehicle was purchased before the client became a beneficiary Temporary Additional Support can only be paid if:
- there is no public transport reasonably available
Note this includes clients who at the time of their application for Temporary Additional Support, are or have been a beneficiary at some point since purchasing the vehicle.
## Vehicle purchased while the client was a beneficiary
If a vehicle was purchased while a client was a beneficiary Temporary Additional Support can only be paid if:
- there is no public transport reasonably available
- the cost is essential to meet the family's daily living needs and
- the cost could not be easily avoided or reduced when the expense was incurred (for example there was no public transport available at the time of purchase)
## Verification
The client must provide verification of their vehicle repayment costs.
## SWIFTT process
If the client or any family members have allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support, you will need to manually add them into the STAWA screen.

chunks.title: Vehicle repayments - for employment — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Vehicle repayments - for employment
A motor vehicle or other vehicle repayments can be included in the assessment of Temporary Additional Support where the client or their partner require the vehicle to travel to and from paid employment and no alternative transport is available (e.g. public transport).
The maximum weekly allowable cost for vehicle repayments per family is $85.96 (as at 1 April 2026).
Note there is no limit to the number of vehicles that can be included in Temporary Additional Support.
## Vehicle purchased while the client was a beneficiary
If the vehicle was purchased while the client was a beneficiary Temporary Additional Support can only be paid if:
- there is no public transport reasonably available
