- the cost is essential to meet the family's daily living needs
- the cost could not be easily avoided or reduced when the expense was incurred (for example there was no public transport available at the time of purchase)

chunks.title: Vehicle repayments - health and disability — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Vehicle repayments - health and disability
A motor vehicle or other vehicle repayments can be included as an allowable cost where the client or any member of their family, need the vehicle because they suffer a chronic illness or have a disability that requires the use of a motor vehicle for transport.
The maximum weekly allowable cost for vehicle repayments per family is $85.96 (from 1 April 2026).
Note there is no limit to the number of vehicles that can be included in Temporary Additional Support.
## Verification
The client must provide verification of their vehicle repayments.
## SWIFTT process
If a client or any family members are getting Disability Allowance, the total of their Disability Allowance costs contained in SWIFTT will automatically be included as allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support.
If the client or any family members do not qualify for Disability Allowance but have allowable health and disability costs for Temporary Additional Support, you will need to manually add them into the STAWA screen.

chunks.title: Vehicle running costs - for employment — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Vehicle running costs - for employment
Allowable motor vehicle running costs for employment can be included in the assessment of Temporary Additional Support.
In addition, these costs must be essential to meet the client's daily living needs and could not be readily avoided or varied when the expense was incurred.
Motor vehicle running costs can be included in the assessment of Temporary Additional Support where:
- there is no suitable public transport available and
- the client or their partner needs the vehicle to travel to and from their place of paid employment
The following rates have been set and reflect the reasonable 'running costs' (excluding fixed costs) of a vehicle dependent on engine size.
Running costs include consumables such, as petrol and oil. Fixed costs (not included in the calculation) include costs such as, relicensing, insurance and Warrants of Fitness.
Fixed costs are not included as all clients will incur these costs when they own a vehicle.
The rates recognise the reasonable 'running costs' of a vehicle as opposed to 'fixed costs' and are consistent with the intent of the legislation, where it is stated that, 'running costs' are at a per kilometre rate as set by MSD, where no suitable public transport is available.
Use these rates to calculate the allowable motor vehicle running costs:
cc rating
payable per kilometre
up to 1000
29 cents
1001 to 1350
30 cents
1351 to 2000
35 cents
over 2000
40 cents
## Verification
The client must provide verification of their vehicle running costs, which must include the cc rating of their vehicle and the distance travelled to and from their employment.

chunks.title: Vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals
MSD must check if the client qualifies for Disability Allowance for these costs first.
If the client qualifies for a Disability Allowance it must be granted before MSD assess if the client qualifies for Temporary Additional Support.
The client may have allowable health and disability costs for Temporary Additional Support where they do not qualify for Disability Allowance because:
- they do not meet the Disability Allowance income limit or
- their disability will last less than 6 months or
- they are certain refugees, protected persons or residence applicants
A registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner must complete a Disability Allowance medical certificate confirming the client's disability, the need for treatment and that vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies or minerals are necessary. The certificate must also confirm the treatment is beneficial and of therapeutic value and that the costs are:
- additional and
- ongoing and
- directly related to the client's disability
Note treatment that is beneficial and of therapeutic value means that the treatment may improve the client's condition, maintain the client's condition or prevent it from getting worse.
When a medical practitioner or nurse practitioner indicates on the client's Disability Allowance medical certificate that treatment by another registered health practitioner is necessary, that practitioner must verify the costs of their services.
Allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support can include the cost of vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals if:
- there are no alternative fully subsidised or partly subsidised pharmaceutical items
- funding from PHARMAC under their Named Patient Pharmaceutical Assessment Policy has been applied for where applicable and
- the client's registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner has verified that there are no suitable alternatives, and that the non-subsidised vitamin, supplement, herbal remedy or mineral product is essential
Note vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals can also be included as special foods when they are recommended as necessary by the client's registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner.
## Proof of vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and mineral costs
The vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals must be confirmed as not being fully funded, subsidised or provided by health authorities.
The client must provide:
- a Disability Allowance medical certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner, or nurse practitioner and
- proof of their vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals costs

chunks.title: Working for Families Tax Credits — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Working for Families Tax Credits
All Working for Families Tax Credits are chargeable income for the assessment of Temporary Additional Support.
Working for Families Tax Credits, include:
- family tax credit
- Best Start tax credit
- in-work tax credit (formerly in-work payment)
- minimum family tax credit (formerly Family Tax Credit)
When assessing Working for Families Tax Credits as chargeable income, the following should be considered:
- Clients getting a main benefit

chunks.title: Year end Working for Families Tax Credits — extra help > temporary additional support
chunks.text:
## Year end Working for Families Tax Credits
People can get their Working for Families Tax Credits as a weekly, fortnightly or end of year lump sum.
If a client has chosen not to get Working for Families Tax Credits, they will need to take steps to obtain this assistance, and in most cases you should encourage them to get it as a weekly payment. There may however be circumstances where it would be more beneficial for the client to get an end of year payment, such as for those who have fluctuating income, especially those who expect more income at the end of the tax year than the beginning.
If it is more beneficial for the client to get Working for Families Tax Credits as a lump sum at the end of the tax year, you will need to estimate the amount they would get if paid on a weekly basis. You will need to include this estimated weekly amount of Working for Families Tax Credits as chargeable income and record that the client will get a year end payment and that you have estimated Working for Families Tax Credits for the client.
For more information about how to do this see:
- Estimating weekly Working for Families Tax Credits
When a non-beneficiary client decides to change to weekly or fortnightly payments of Working for Families Tax Credits they must contact Inland Revenue. It may take Inland Revenue time to reassess the client's entitlement. When there will be a delay in Inland Revenue providing verification of Working for Families Tax Credits, you must enter the estimated weekly amount of Working for Families Tax Credits payable to the client.
Estimated Working for Families Tax Credits should be updated with actual Working for Families Tax Credits when the client receives verification from Inland Revenue.
Where the estimated amount of Working for Families Tax Credits is different to the amount verified by Inland Revenue, you will need to reassess the client's Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Cash assets include — extra help > vehicle modification funding
chunks.text: - bills of exchange or promissory notes - building society shares - money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society - money invested with or lent to any bank or other financial institution - mortgage investments and long term loans - pre-paid funeral expenses - shares, stocks, debentures, bonus bonds and bonds (including shares in energy organisations) - the client's share in any partnership - the net equity held in any property or land, not used as the person's home

Severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment) - specified Ex gratia and compensation payments

chunks.title: Cash assets limit — extra help > vehicle modification funding
chunks.text:
## Cash assets limit
You must take into consideration their cash assets.
The cash asset exemption limit is $4,500.

chunks.title: Examples — extra help > vehicle modification funding
chunks.text: The following examples show how the contracted provider works out the amount payable. The examples are for case manager's reference only.

chunks.title: Example 1 — extra help > vehicle modification funding
chunks.text: A client has $2,500 in the bank, has earned interest on money invested with a bank, owns a vehicle and earns $439.80 gross a week. They have never applied for Vehicle Modification Funding before. They will need hand controls fitted to their vehicle. Income $ Wages = $439.80 per week x 52 weeks $22,869.60 Plus interest $25.00 Total income $22,894.60 Less exemption $40,000.00 Equals income Nil Assets Cash assets $2,500.00 Value of existing vehicle $5,000.00 Total assets $7,500.00 Less exemption $4,500.00 Equals assets in round dollars $3,000.00 Cost of new vehicle $19,000.00 Less assets $3,000.00 Purchase shortfall $16,000.00 Maximum amount available or purchase shortfall, whichever is less $12,165.00 Less income Nil Less unabated loan Nil Amount approved $12,165.00 Plus adaptations up to $12,165.00 Total amount available $24,330.00

chunks.title: Example 2 — extra help > vehicle modification funding
chunks.text: A client earns $810 per week. They have $2,500 in the bank and have received $20 interest. They received a loan of $5,000, 3 years ago that still has $2,000 still to pay off. They also have a person willing to pay $3,000 for their present vehicle. Income $ Wages = $810.00 per week x 52 $42,120.00 Interest $20.00 Total income $42,140.00 Less exemption $40,000.00 Equals income in complete $1000.00s $2,000.00 Assets Cash assets $2,500.00 Value of existing vehicle $3,000.00 Total assets $5,500.00 Less exemption $4,500.00 Equals assets (complete $1,000s) $1,000.00 Cost of new vehicle $20,000.00 Less assets $1,000.00 Purchase shortfall $19,000.00 Maximum amount available or purchase shortfall, whichever is less $12,165.00 Less income $2,000.00 Less loan $2,000.00 Amount approved $8,165.00

chunks.title: Income and asset test — extra help > vehicle modification funding
chunks.text:
## Income and asset test
All applications are subject to some form of income and asset testing.

chunks.title: Income limit — extra help > vehicle modification funding
chunks.text:
## Income limit
When assessing a client's income to see if they qualify for Vehicle Modification Funding, include the income of:
- the person with the disability and
- the partner of the person with the disability
There is an exemption amount of $40,000.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > vehicle modification funding
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Vehicle Modification Funding is paid by a Ministry of Health contracted provider and provides funding for people with serious disabilities to enable them to purchase or modify a vehicle. This is to allow them to retain or obtain full-time employment, look after dependent children, or attend study/training.
Work and Income administer the income and asset test. It is important that the client's consent is given for collecting the information, as the powers of investigating and obtaining information under the Social Security Act 2018 do not apply.
A client does not have to be getting a benefit to qualify for Vehicle Modification Funding.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > vehicle modification funding
chunks.text:
## Payment
The maximum amount payable to purchase a vehicle is $12,165 (GST inclusive).
The maximum amount payable for Vehicle Modification Funding is $12,165 (GST inclusive).

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > vehicle modification funding
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To be able to get Vehicle Modification Funding, the client must have been needs assessed as requiring the vehicle by a Ministry of Health contracted provider.
The contracted provider decides whether the client meets the qualifications for assistance. Assessments for vehicle modifications are carried out by an Occupational Therapist.

chunks.title: Review of decisions — extra help > vehicle modification funding
chunks.text:
## Review of decisions
When a client disagrees with a decision regarding the income and asset assessment for Vehicle Modification Funding there is no right of review to a Benefit Review Committee or the Social Security Appeal Authority.
However, if a client would like to review a decision the original decision should be reconsidered.
A review should be based on whether an 'informed' decision was made and should have regard to the following:
- relevant policy
- the information presented at the time
- any new information to hand
- reasons for the original decision and
- the reason the client is not happy with the decision
A Ministry of Social Development senior staff member (ie a manager client service delivery) who was not involved in the original decision should carry out the review.
Note if the client does not agree with the review decision there are no further appeal rights.

chunks.title: Accommodation type for Winter Energy Payment — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Accommodation type for Winter Energy Payment
The type of accommodation or energy source the client uses to heat their home (e.g. power, gas or woodfire) has no effect on Winter Energy Payments.
Clients in the following situations (but not limited to) can get Winter Energy Payments if they are getting a qualifying benefit:
- sharing accommodation, paying rent in the private market or living at home with their parents
- may or may not have the energy account in their name. Clients do not have to prove they are paying for energy costs
- living in social housing - the client does not have to be named on the tenancy agreement or paying Income Related Rent for the property
- staying in transitional housing, including transitional housing funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development
- staying in emergency housing, including if they are getting an Emergency Housing Grant
Clients generally contribute in some way to their living costs which includes the increased energy costs over winter, so if they meet the qualifications, they can get the payment, no matter what their living situation.
Note clients who get Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy cannot get Winter Energy Payment (but their partner in the community can continue receiving the couple rate of Winter Energy Payment).

chunks.title: Application for the Winter Energy Payment — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Application for the Winter Energy Payment
A client does not have to apply for the Winter Energy Payment, it is granted and paid automatically to clients who are getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension and meet all other eligibility criteria.
The Winter Energy Payment will be automatically included with all qualifying benefit payments when the winter payment period starts, unless the client has chosen not to get the Winter Energy Payment.

chunks.title: Calculating the rate of Winter Energy Payment — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Calculating the rate of Winter Energy Payment
The weekly rate of Winter Energy Payment is found by dividing the appropriate rate for the entire winter payment period.
The rates are $450 for single clients, and $700 for a couple or a single client with dependent children divided by:
- 22 weekly payments if the qualifying benefit is a main benefit or
- 11 fortnightly payments if the qualifying benefit is New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
Clients can be absent from New Zealand and keep getting payments for the first 28 days of any absence if it does not affect the client's qualification for Winter Energy Payment.
Generally, a client can keep getting Winter Energy Payment for the first 28 days if the client is still getting a qualifying benefit.
## Main beneficiaries have an obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand
All clients being paid a main benefit must tell the Ministry of Social Development before they leave New Zealand. If the client or partner does not tell the Ministry before their international travel, their main benefit payments will stop from the day after they leave New Zealand.
This means the client will no longer be getting a qualifying benefit for a Winter Energy Payment and their Winter Energy Payment will also stop from the same day.
If a client tells the Ministry before they leave New Zealand and they are paid their qualifying benefit while they are absent from New Zealand, they can keep getting their Winter Energy Payment for the first 28 days.
When the client has been absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days their Winter Energy Payments will stop on day 29.
If the client returns to New Zealand during the winter payment period their Winter Energy Payments can be reinstated from the day they return to New Zealand.
Unlike other Extra Help, payment of Winter Energy Payment is not limited to 28 days within a 52 week period.
## New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran’s Pension clients getting Winter Energy Payments
Clients getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension, and Winter Energy Payment do not have to tell the Ministry of Social Development when they leave New Zealand.
However, payments of the Winter Energy Payment will only continue for 28 days. On day 29 the Winter Energy Payment will stop being paid.
If a client has not told us they are leaving New Zealand an information match with customs will identify when they left the country. Their Winter Energy Payments will stop 28 days after they left New Zealand.
## Encourage New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran’s Pension clients with a partner to tell us if they are leaving New Zealand for more than 28 days
When a New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension client with a partner is absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days, we can pay Winter Energy Payment to their partner if the partner is still in New Zealand.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Action on return to New Zealand — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Action on return to New Zealand
A client who was receiving Winter Energy Payment and who has been absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days during the winter period, will need to advise the Ministry of Social Development when they return in order to receive Winter Energy Payment again.
## Clients receiving a main benefit
The Winter Energy Payment for a client who receives a main benefit who has been outside of New Zealand for more than 28 days qualifies to have Winter Energy Payment paid when they return to New Zealand (if it is within the winter period).
A single client, who has had their benefit stopped while they were outside of New Zealand, will qualify to receive the Winter Energy Payment again once they receive a main benefit again (and it is still the winter period).
A partner of a married, civil union or de facto client who has been absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days during the winter period, can continue to receive the Winter Energy Payment at the full couple rate (if they remain in New Zealand).
## New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension clients
The Winter Energy Payment for a client who receives New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension and has been outside of New Zealand for more than 28 days during the winter period qualifies to have Winter Energy Payment paid when they return to New Zealand (and it is still within the winter period). They will need to contact the Ministry to advise that they have returned and to get their payments re-started.
There is no need to change the person who is determined as eligible to receive the Winter Energy Payment when the client returns, unless the couple agree to change who this is.

chunks.title: Benefit extension periods of up to 28 days — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Benefit extension periods of up to 28 days
In some specific situations there is the ability to extend a main benefit beyond the period of entitlement. If a client is getting a Winter Energy Payment and they qualify for an extension to their benefit payments in one of the following situations then the Winter Energy Payment can continue until the benefit expiry date (when it is still within the Winter Energy Payment period):
- a client dies leaving a partner or dependent child
- the last or only dependent child of a sole parent leaves care suddenly or dies
- a person being provided with fulltime care and attention goes into residential care permanently or dies
- a client no longer meets the medical eligibility criteria for a Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability)
For more information see:
- terminal benefit in main benefits

chunks.title: Calculating the period of absence — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Calculating the period of absence
The period of an absence from New Zealand for which payment of Winter Energy Payment can continue (if approved or when approval is not needed) is up to 28 consecutive days during the winter period, that is, Saturdays and Sundays are included.
In all cases, when assessing the period of an absence, do not include:
- the date of departure from New Zealand and
- the date of return to New Zealand
If a client is absent for more than 28 days during the winter period, the Winter Energy Payment should be suspended from the 29th day.
Note Winter Energy Payment can be paid to a partner who remains in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Change in family circumstances affects rate of Winter Energy Payment — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Change in family circumstances affects rate of Winter Energy Payment
The rate of Winter Energy Payment paid may need to be increased or decreased when:
- there is a change in the client’s relationship status or
- the first dependent child comes into the client’s care, or the last dependent child leaves the client’s care
The date to apply the change in rate will depend on the action involved. Generally, MSD should:
## Increase
- increase Winter Energy Payment rate from the actual date of the change in circumstances. For example, the client adds a partner, or a single person includes a dependent child in their benefit.
## Reduce, suspend or cancel
- reduce, suspend or cancel Winter Energy Payment from the first available date except where the client advises of a change more than 14 days after the event. For example, the last dependent child is excluded from a single client’s benefit, or a couple separates.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client must tell the Ministry of Social Development of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their eligibility to a Winter Energy Payment.
You may also review Winter Energy Payment at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.
For more information see:
- Core policy Redirection of benefit payment
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit
- Core policy Reviews and appeals

chunks.title: Client does not return — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Client does not return
If a client’s benefit is suspended because they are absent from New Zealand and they do not return, their benefit record will automatically cancel in SWIFTT 8 weeks after the date of suspension. Winter Energy Payment would already have stopped after 28 days.

chunks.title: Protected earnings rate — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Protected earnings rate
No attachment order can, whether on its own or when combined with any other attachment order, Child Support deduction, or Ministry of Social Development debt repayment, take a client's total income below the protected earnings rate.
## Information provided by the Court
The information that will be received from the Ministry of Justice will have:
- the client's name
- the amount to be deducted from the benefit
- the fine's reference number
If a client is suffering undue hardship because of the amount of the attachment order then they should be directed to a Registrar of the District Court for a reassessment of the rate.

chunks.title: Death of a client — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Death of a client
When a client’s main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension stops during the winter period, the Winter Energy Payment will also stop from the same date.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Deductions — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Deductions
In certain circumstances the Ministry of Social Development can be required to pay part of the client's benefit to another party.
The Ministry is legally required to make these deductions when served with a properly issued Deduction Notice or Attachment Order. The consent of the client is not required.
Certain forms of deductions take priority over others.

chunks.title: Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital
When a person who has been remanded in custody or is imprisoned, is detained in or transferred to a psychiatric hospital, the client can receive either:
- New Zealand Superannuation (paid at full rate for the first 13 weeks after admission to psychiatric hospital and then reduced to the hospital rate)
- Veterans Pension (paid at full rate unless the qualifications for it to be reduced to hospital rate are met)
- Emergency Benefit (paid at hospital rate from date of grant)
## Winter Energy Payment can be paid until hospital rate begins
Until the New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension is reduced to the hospital rate, Winter Energy Payment can still be paid.
Note in some cases, Veteran’s Pension won’t ever be reduced to the hospital rate.
## Winter Energy Payment can be paid after the hospital rate begins even if the client has no heating costs
When the New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension or Emergency Benefit reduces to the hospital rate, Winter Energy Payment can still be paid.
Clients in these situations can be paid Winter Energy Payment even if they do not pay for any heating costs. For more information see:
- New Zealand Superannuation Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital
- Veteran’s Pension Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital
- Emergency Benefit Person serving their sentence of imprisonment in a psychiatric hospital
- Paying Winter Energy Payment to clients with a public protection order

chunks.title: Effect on Winter Energy Payment when a single client is absent from New Zealand — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Effect on Winter Energy Payment when a single client is absent from New Zealand
The table below shows the effect on payment of Winter Energy Payment when a single client is absent from New Zealand.
Effect on Winter Energy Payment
They are not eligible for Winter Energy Payment as they are not getting a qualifying benefit.
Winter Energy Payment can be paid while their qualifying benefit continues being paid.
Winter Energy Payment can be paid while their qualifying benefit continues being paid.
After the first 5 days their qualifying benefit stops, and they cannot keep getting the Winter Energy Payment as they are not being paid a qualifying benefit.
They will keep getting Winter Energy Payment at the full single rate for the first 28 days.

chunks.title: Effect on Winter Energy Payment when couples absent from New Zealand — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text: Effect on Winter Energy Payments when one or both partners are absent from New Zealand. Client leaves country Effect on the other person Client and their partner get a qualifying benefit The primary client is eligible for Winter Energy Payment and leaves New Zealand. They are eligible for Winter Energy Payment for up to 28 days and get their portion over this time. The partner gets their portion for 28 days as they are in New Zealand. The partner who is not the primary client leaves New Zealand. They can get their portion of Winter Energy Payment for up to 28 days as long as their portion of their qualifying benefit continues. The primary client continues getting their portion of Winter Energy Payment for 28 days. The partner who is not the primary client leaves New Zealand for more than 28 days. They will continue getting 50% of the Winter Energy Payment for the first 28 days they are absent from New Zealand. From day 29, the partner is no longer eligible to get their portion of the Winter Energy Payment The primary client gets 50% of the Winter Energy Payment for 28 days as they are in New Zealand. The primary client continues being paid the full couple rate of the Winter Energy Payment from day 29. The system will automatically apportion the Winter Energy Payment. The full couple rate must be paid to the primary client as a manual action from the 29th day. The primary client is eligible to get Winter Energy Payment and leaves New Zealand for more than 28 days. The primary client will keep getting 50% of the Winter Energy Payment for the first 28 days they are absent from New Zealand. From day 29 they no longer qualify for Winter Energy Payment. The partner is paid 50% of the Winter Energy Payment for 28 days as they are in New Zealand. From day 29, the partner becomes the person eligible to get Winter Energy Payment and the whole amount is paid to the partner. Note when the client's qualifying benefit also stops, the partner may need to apply for a qualifying benefit in their own right to be eligible to get Winter Energy Payment. The primary client is eligible to get Winter Energy Payment and leaves New Zealand for more than 28 days. The primary client will keep getting 50% of the Winter Energy Payment for the first 28 days they are absent from New Zealand. The partner also leaves New Zealand within the first 28 days. They keep getting 50% of the Winter Energy Payment for the first 28 days. From day 29, the primary client no longer eligible to get a Winter Energy Payment.

chunks.title: Effect on Winter Energy Payment when couples absent from New Zealand — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text: From day 29 when the primary client is outside of New Zealand, the Ministry can decide if the partner is eligible to get Winter Energy Payment, and the whole couple rate is paid to them. However, the period of absence for the partner must be counted from the day after the partner left New Zealand. New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client is eligible to get Winter Energy Payment leaves New Zealand for 15 days. The partner remains in New Zealand. The client eligible to get Winter Energy Payment will continue being paid the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment for the 15 days they are outside New Zealand. The partner is not eligible to get Winter Energy Payment as the full couple rate is being paid to the other person. New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client who is eligible to get Winter Energy Payment leaves New Zealand. They will continue being paid Winter Energy Payment at the full couple rate for up to 28 days. On day 29, the client who left New Zealand will no longer be eligible to get the Winter Energy Payment. New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension partner will not get the Winter Energy Payment for the first 28 days as the full couple rate is being paid to the other person. From day 29, the partner is eligible to get the Winter Energy Payment. Note this will need to be manually granted to the partner. New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client eligible to get Winter Energy Payment leaves New Zealand. Grandparented non-qualified partner remains in New Zealand. On day 29, they will no longer be eligible to get Winter Energy Payment. The grandparented non-qualified partner is not eligible for the Winter Energy Payment as the full couple rate is being paid to the other person. From day 29, the grandparented non-qualified partner becomes eligible to get Winter Energy Payment. Note this will need to be manually granted to the partner. New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client and partner (either qualified in their own right or grandparented non-qualified partner) leave New Zealand on the same day. They advised the Ministry that they will be travelling outside of New Zealand. The Winter Energy Payment will continue being paid to the client eligible to get Winter Energy Payment for up to 28 days. On day 29, the couple will no longer be eligible to get Winter Energy Payment. This will stop being paid to the client eligible to get Winter Energy Payment on day 29.

chunks.title: Effect on Winter Energy Payment when couples absent from New Zealand — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text: New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client getting the Winter Energy Payment leaves New Zealand. The partner remains in New Zealand. The partner also leaves New Zealand within the first 28 days. The partner does not get the Winter Energy Payment for first 28 days as it is paid to the other client. When the partner not eligible to get Winter Energy Payment also leaves, they will not be eligible for Winter Energy Payment until the end of the 28 day period for the client who left first. When the client has been away from New Zealand for 28 days their Winter Energy Payment will stop from day 29. The partner who left second will be eligible to get Winter Energy Payment for 28 days from the day they left New Zealand.

chunks.title: Hospitalisation — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Hospitalisation
When a client receiving a main benefit (or their partner) is admitted to hospital, their main benefit or New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension can continue at the full rate for the first 13 weeks.
The rate of payment is reduced to the hospital rate after the client has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks (not after receiving a benefit for 13 weeks).
Exception couples with dependent children do not have their benefit payment reduced regardless of how long they are in hospital.
## Single clients qualifying benefit is reduced to a hospital rate
A client who is getting the Winter Energy Payment and who has had their main benefit reduced to the hospital rate, (even if this is paid at a higher rate because the client cannot meet their continuing costs in the community from the hospital rate), can only get the Winter Energy Payment if they still require assistance with their winter energy costs.
When considering if the client still requires assistance with their winter energy costs, consider the:
- expected time of the clients stay in hospital, for example, has the client been given a discharge date within 2 weeks and is expecting to return to their accommodation?
- clients continuing contribution to their household winter energy costs while in hospital, and their expected discharge date
## Partner with no dependent children is hospitalised
When the partner is in hospital, the client living in the community can receive the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment.
This may have to be paid manually to the client living in the community as the system will automatically divide Winter Energy Payment for clients receiving a main benefit.

chunks.title: Imprisonment — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Imprisonment
Clients who are in prison generally do not qualify for a main benefit and therefore cannot get Winter Energy Payment.
When a client with a partner is imprisoned and they are the primary client, the partner who is still in the community will need to see if they qualify for assistance in their own right.
In cases where a main benefit can continue, e.g. for clients remanded in custody, Winter Energy Payment will continue to be paid.
Where the client's main benefit is continuing to be paid to a caregiver while the client is in prison, Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid.
## Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital
Sometimes a person who has been remanded in custody or is serving a term of imprisonment, is detained in or transferred to a psychiatric hospital.
In these circumstances, when the client’s payment reduces to the hospital rate of benefit, the Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid.
## Clients with a Public Protection Order
A person who has a Public Protection Order can get a main benefit at the hospital rate from the date the main benefit is granted. In these circumstances Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid.

chunks.title: Income changes — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Income changes
If a client’s income reduces their benefit rate to zero they do not qualify for Winter Energy Payment.
The Winter Energy Payment is paid from the date their benefit payments start again.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Information required when clients advise they intend to travel — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Information required when clients advise they intend to travel
When a client contacts you to advise that they intend travelling overseas you need to obtain the following information:
- date of departure
- date of return
- for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension, if they have a partner, whether they are also intending to leave New Zealand

chunks.title: Inland Revenue deduction notices — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Inland Revenue deduction notices
Inland Revenue may request for a client's unpaid taxes to be directly deducted from their benefit payments.
Note all Inland Revenue deduction notices are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit for processing.
The instructions of the deduction notice will be to deduct the lowest of either:
- 10% of the total debt which Inland Revenue specify in the notice, on a weekly basis or
- 20% of the client's gross earnings on a weekly basis
Where there are insufficient funds to cover the deduction, the Ministry of Social Development must advise Inland Revenue immediately that the deduction will not start or will start at a reduced rate.
Inland Revenue deductions have a lower priority than Child Support deductions.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Married, civil union or de facto clients — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Married, civil union or de facto clients
Only one person in the couple can be eligible to receive Winter Energy Payment at any one time.
This means that when one person in the couple becomes ineligible to be paid Winter Energy Payment because they have been absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days, the other person in the couple can become eligible.
## Couples receiving a main benefit
When couples are receiving a main benefit, one person is considered eligible to receive the Winter Energy Payment but this payment is paid equally, 50% to the primary client, and 50% to the partner.
If the person who is eligible to receive it, is absent from New Zealand, they may continue to receive it for up to 28 days (it will continue to be divided equally between the primary client and their partner).
When the client eligible to receive the Winter Energy Payment is absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days, the partner can be considered eligible and receive the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment.
If the partner also leaves New Zealand within the first 28 days, at the point that they begin to be eligible to receive Winter Energy Payment, they can only receive Winter Energy Payment for 28 days from the time that they left New Zealand.
## Couples receiving New Zealand or Veteran’s Pension
For New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension clients, the Winter Energy Payment is not paid equally and can only be paid to one person eligible for the payment. Note the person determined as eligible, can be changed if the couple asks for this to happen.
When a person who left New Zealand is no longer eligible to receive Winter Energy Payment, the partner who remains in New Zealand is the person eligible to receive Winter Energy Payment. The person who is eligible to receive the Winter Energy Payment is paid the full couple rate.
Note there is a manual process to ensure the partner who remains in New Zealand receives the correct rate of Winter Energy Payment.
If the partner also leaves New Zealand within the first 28 days, at the point that they begin to be eligible to receive Winter Energy Payment, they can only receive Winter Energy Payment for 28 days from the time that they left New Zealand.

chunks.title: Ministry of Social Development debt repayments — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Ministry of Social Development debt repayments
When a client has a Ministry of Social Development debt, this can be recovered by regular deductions from their current benefit.
Note Income Related Rent and historical Housing New Zealand debt should be given equal priority to the Ministry debt.
For more information see:
- Core policy Negotiating repayment of debt [no link find out why]

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension client outside New Zealand for more than 26 weeks — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension client outside New Zealand for more than 26 weeks
Clients (and partners) receiving New Zealand Superannuation can be absent from New Zealand and continue to receive payment for up to 26 weeks.
Where a client (and partners) receiving New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension are absent from New Zealand between 26 and 30 weeks, the client is entitled to receive their New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension for the first 26 weeks. They can also receive any Winter Energy Payment they were entitled to while they were overseas for the first 28 days. Payments for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension should not continue beyond 26 weeks.
If the client is overseas for 30 weeks or more there is no qualification from when the client left New Zealand, unless the client's return to New Zealand is delayed due to circumstances beyond the client's control, that could not have been foreseen before departure. This includes any Winter Energy Payment that had been paid as a client will not be entitled to any Winter Energy Payment if a qualifying benefit is not paid.

chunks.title: Paying Winter Energy Payment to clients with a Public Protection Order — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Paying Winter Energy Payment to clients with a Public Protection Order
A client with a Public Protection Order is paid the hospital rate of benefit from date of grant. A Public Protection Order is when a person has finished their sentence in prison but then for public safety they must remain in a secure residence. This is to protect members of the public from the almost certain harm from serious sexual or violent offences.
Winter Energy Payment can continue being paid to a client who is getting a hospital rate of benefit because they have a Public Protection Order, even if they do not pay for any heating costs.
For more information see:
- Emergency Benefit Person detained under a Public Protection Order
- New Zealand Superannuation Person detained under a Public Protection Order
- Veteran’s Pension Person detained under a Public Protection Order

chunks.title: Permanent absence — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Permanent absence
If the client is leaving New Zealand permanently, the Winter Energy Payment will be stopped from the day after their departure.
This includes where a client’s main benefit is continuing because they are moving to a country that has a reciprocal agreement.

chunks.title: Priority for deductions — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Priority for deductions
Certain forms of deductions take priority over others; the following list gives the order of priority, highest to lowest:
Highest priority
- Child Support deductions made under the Child Support Act 1991
- Inland Revenue tax deductions
- Ministry of Social Development debt repayments including Liable Parent Contributions (LPC), child maintenance debts and Major Repairs Advances (MRA), Student Allowance debt, Student Loan debt converted to Ministry debt, Income Related Rent (historical Housing New Zealand debt), Income Related Rent (Ministry of Social Development debt)
- Attachment orders made under the Family Proceedings Act 1980
- Court attachment orders issued under the Summary Proceedings Act 1957
- Court attachment orders issued under the District Court Act 2016
- Student Loan repayments
Lowest priority
Determining the priority of deductions is necessary when a client has more than one order issued from their benefit. Also each order and deduction notice is subject to its own protected earnings rule.
When you need to reduce deductions you adjust from the lowest priority up to those with a higher priority taking into account the protected earnings rules for each.
Example
A client has both Child Support and Ministry debt deductions to be made from their benefit. When the level of Ministry debt reduces the client's benefit payments below the Child Support protected earnings rate, the Ministry debt deduction must be reduced not the Child Support payments.
This is because Child Support deductions take priority over Ministry of Social Development debt repayments.

chunks.title: Qualifying benefit stops — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Qualifying benefit stops
As clients have an obligation to tell the Ministry of Social Development of any changes that may affect their entitlement to assistance and they are expected to do so within a reasonable period. Winter Energy Payment can only be paid if a qualifying benefit can be paid.
When a client advises of a change in circumstances after the event that would affect their entitlement to their qualifying benefit, Winter Energy Payment must be cancelled from the actual date of the change in circumstances and overpayment established when appropriate.
If a client gives false or misleading information, Winter Energy Payment must be reviewed from the actual date of the change in circumstances and an overpayment established when appropriate.

chunks.title: Return to New Zealand — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Return to New Zealand
When the client returns to New Zealand they will need to contact the Ministry of Social Development to confirm the following:
- date of return to New Zealand
- date of departure (if client did not advise before leaving New Zealand)
- reason for absence (if not already known)
- did the client apply for or receive any benefit or pension in the country that they travelled to or an increase in the benefit or pension they already receive from that country during their stay there?

chunks.title: Student Loans — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Student Loans
Clients with a Student Loan must make repayments to Inland Revenue when the income they receive exceeds a pre-determined level. This level is called the 'income threshold'.
A person must make repayments to Inland Revenue when their income exceeds $464.00 gross per week ($24,128 gross per year) as at 1 April 2026. Note non-taxable Extra help such as family tax credit, Best Start tax credit, Accommodation Supplement and Winter Energy Payment do not count as income. If the client's income is over this income threshold, the Ministry of Social Development can make the required deduction. However, this is only done if the client requests it.
If the client's portion of benefit is below the income threshold, there is no provision to make voluntary repayments through SWIFTT. The client can make voluntary payments direct to Inland Revenue at any time.
Note the following:
- Student Loan deductions can only be made from taxable benefits
- Student Loan deductions cannot be made if the client's benefit is below the income threshold
- when a client receives a married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit only the client's portion is taken into consideration when assessing Student Loan repayments
- when a client is receiving a reduced rate of payment due to other income, the Student Loan deduction is assessed on the net payment after income deduction
For more information on Student Loans see:
- Students Student loan [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Debt Repayment Orders — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Debt Repayment Orders
All Debt Repayment Orders are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit for processing.
Debt Repayment Orders are issued by the Ministry of Justice under the Insolvency Act 2006 and can be issued when the client is an un-discharged bankrupt.
Unlike other Ministry of Justice attachment orders, Debt Repayment Orders are not subject to any protected earnings rate. Payment is generally made to the supervisor of the debt but occasionally a District Court will act as an agent for collection of the debt.
Payment continues for 3 years, or until further notice is received from either the supervisor or the District Court.
Unlike Ministry of Justice attachment orders, Debt Repayment Orders are administered via the PYECI screen in SWIFTT, not through CORBI.

chunks.title: Transfer — extra help > winter energy payment > changes and reviews winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Transfer
When a client moves between the following categories of payments during the winter period, the Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid:
- Main benefit or
- New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran’s Pension
For more information see:
- Request for financial assistance procedures [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Client is receiving Social Rehabilitation Assistance — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Client is receiving Social Rehabilitation Assistance
Clients who are receiving Social Rehabilitation Assistance are eligible to receive Winter Energy Payment if they are receiving a qualifying benefit.

chunks.title: Client living in a country that provides portable benefits — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Client living in a country that provides portable benefits
A client must be living in New Zealand and receiving a qualifying benefit to be eligible for the Winter Energy Payment. Clients receiving a New Zealand benefit paid in another country (called a portable benefit) are not eligible for the Winter Energy Payment.

chunks.title: Client receives an overseas state pension — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Client receives an overseas state pension
Clients must be eligible for and getting some amount of New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran's Pension, or main benefit to qualify for a Winter Energy Payment.
Some clients eligible to get New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension (and sometimes main benefit clients), do not get any New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension payments due to excess overseas deduction. These clients will not get Winter Energy Payment as they are not receiving a qualifying benefit.
## Overseas pensions received by partners
For a client who gets an overseas pension and also gets New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran's Pension, or a main benefit, their overseas pension does not affect their partners New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran's Pension, or Winter Energy Payment.
Any overseas pension received by a partner is not deducted from the client's Winter Energy Payment.

chunks.title: Client getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, or Foster Care Allowance — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Client getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, or Foster Care Allowance
Clients must receive a qualifying benefit to get Winter Energy Payment.
Orphans Benefit, Unsupported Childs Benefit or Foster Care Allowance are not qualifying benefits.
## Client getting a main benefit and, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit
A client who is getting a qualifying benefit and who is also getting an Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit for a child in their care can get Winter Energy Payment, and at the higher rate.
A client who is only getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit for a child in their care, cannot get Winter Energy Payment, as they are not getting a qualifying benefit.
## Client receiving a Foster Care Allowance
A client who is getting a qualifying benefit and also getting a Foster Care Allowance from Oranga Tamariki can get the Winter Energy Payment, and at the higher rate.
Note when a foster child is the only child in a single client's care, they will need to tell the Ministry of Social Development to get paid the higher rate of Winter Energy Payment.
Where a client is only receiving a Foster Care Allowance and not receiving a qualifying benefit, they cannot get the Winter Energy Payment.

chunks.title: Client with 100% tax rate — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Client with 100% tax rate
When a New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client chooses to have a 100% tax rate, all of their New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension is paid to Inland Revenue. In these circumstances, the client is considered to be receiving New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension and can be paid Winter Energy Payment.
These clients will show as current in SWIFTT.

chunks.title: Clients can choose not to get the Winter Energy Payment — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Clients can choose not to get the Winter Energy Payment
Clients may choose not to get the Winter Energy Payment by advising the Ministry of Social Development:
- at the time they first apply for a qualifying benefit
- before Winter Energy Payments start or
- at any time during the winter period
## New client chooses not to get payment when applying for a qualifying benefit
Clients who have chosen not to receive the Winter Energy Payment before the winter period starts will not receive the Winter Energy Payment for that winter period, or any future winter periods.
If at a later date they decide they would like to receive Winter Energy Payments they must advise the Ministry.
## Client decides not to get payment after, or during winter period
Clients who have chosen not to receive the Winter Energy Payment after the winter period has started will have the payment stopped from the first available date, and will not receive the Winter Energy Payment for the remaining winter period, or any future winter periods.
## Couple decides not to get the Winter Energy Payment
When a married, civil union or de facto client chooses not to receive a Winter Energy Payment the Ministry must be satisfied the partner has also chosen not to receive the Winter Energy Payment. Couples are eligible for the Winter Energy Payment as a unit therefore one partner cannot choose to not get the payment if the other partner wants to keep getting it.
This also applies for New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension when a grandparented non-qualified partner is included in their New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension.
## Client chooses to get Winter Energy Payment again
When a client has decided not to get the Winter Energy Payment, they will not receive any payments. They can choose to get the payment again during that or any winter period, by advising the Ministry they would like to start getting Winter Energy Payments again. It will start from the first available date.
Winter Energy Payments will not be back paid for any winter period the client chose not to receive the Winter Energy Payment.

chunks.title: Clients not eligible for Winter Energy Payment — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Clients not eligible for Winter Energy Payment
There are situations when a person is not eligible for the Winter Energy Payment.
These are when:
- they or their partner do not receive a qualifying benefit
- they are residing overseas and receiving a portable payment of a qualifying benefit under the General or Special Portability provisions or paid under a social security agreement with another country
- they are in a residential care facility and receive Residential Care Subsidy (but any partner in the community will continue to be eligible for the couple rate)
- they are in a Residential Support Subsidy facility (but any partner in the community will continue to be eligible for the couple rate)
- they are in hospital and receive the hospital rate of payment and a decision has been made to not continue to pay Winter Energy Payment
- they receive an Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit but do not receive any other qualifying benefit
- they receive a Student Allowance
- the clients partner is already receiving the Winter Energy Payment for the couple
- they have chosen not to receive a Winter Energy Payment
Note if a single caregiver gets an Unsupported Child’s Benefit or Orphan's Benefit and also gets a qualifying benefit the child is regarded as a dependent child for the Winter Energy Payment rate of payment. This means the caregiver can receive the higher dependent child rate.

chunks.title: Commencement date — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
A client may start getting the Winter Energy Payment:
- on the commencement date of their qualifying benefit (initial application) or
- 1 May
whichever is later.
It is paid for a 22 week period from 1 May each year.
## Clients can choose not to get the Winter Energy Payment
Clients may choose not to get the Winter Energy Payment by advising the Ministry of Social Development at:
- the time they first apply for a qualifying benefit or
- any later date

chunks.title: Couple and child rate of Winter Energy Payment — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Couple and child rate of Winter Energy Payment
To receive the higher rate of the Winter Energy Payment, the client must be:
- a couple that is, married, in a civil union or de facto relationship or
- have a dependent child

chunks.title: Dependent child for Winter Energy Payment — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Dependent child for Winter Energy Payment
A dependent child for assessing Winter Energy Payment is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
A dependent child can also include a child:
- who payments are being made for under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- for whom Orphan's Benefit or an Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid or
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki who have been returned to the care of a parent
A young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child cannot be included in another main benefit as a dependent child.

chunks.title: Effect of Winter Energy Payment on other assistance — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Effect of Winter Energy Payment on other assistance
The Winter Energy Payment is non-taxable and is not treated as income, or chargeable income for other types of financial assistance.
Winter Energy Payment is not considered income or chargeable income when assessing eligibility for:
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit
- Disability Allowance
- Childcare Assistance
## Effect of Winter Energy Payment on Income Related Rent
The Winter Energy Payment is not considered assessable income for assessing eligibility for social housing (including assessing affordability), or for Income Related Rent.
## Effect on accessing Advance Payment of Benefit or Special Needs Grant for power or heating costs
Winter Energy Payment does not stop clients from applying for hardship assistance for power or heating costs. However, the Winter Energy Payment still needs to be considered when assessing the client's situation for Advance Payment of Benefit or Special Needs Grant.
Clients may have received the Winter Energy Payment but still meet the criteria for assistance due to their individual circumstances. For example, if a client only received the payment for part of the winter period, or if they had paid all of their Winter Energy Payment on their power account and their power costs were still in excess of this.
## Effect on clients receiving Disability Allowance for power and heating costs
'Power and Heating' as part of the Disability Allowance pays for additional energy costs required due to a disability over and above the standard energy costs of individuals without a disability.
As the Winter Energy Payment recognises the increased costs incurred for energy over the winter months for all eligible clients we do not expect the Winter Energy Payment to be used to cover additional costs related to a disability.
Disability Allowance costs for additional power are not reviewed due to the Winter Energy Payment.

chunks.title: Emergency housing and transitional housing — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Emergency housing and transitional housing
Clients who are staying in emergency housing or transitional housing, qualify to get Winter Energy Payment if they are getting a qualifying benefit.
This includes when clients are getting a qualifying benefit and staying in emergency housing funded through an Emergency Housing Grant.

chunks.title: Impact on Temporary Additional Support if choosing not to get Winter Energy Payment — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Impact on Temporary Additional Support if choosing not to get Winter Energy Payment
If a client decides not to get the Winter Energy Payment this may impact on their continued eligibility to receive Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit. The client is not taking necessary steps to get all financial assistance available to them.

chunks.title: Income and Asset test — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Income and Asset test
There are no income or asset limits for the Winter Energy Payment because eligibility for payment is based on whether the client is receiving a qualifying benefit.

chunks.title: Introduction — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The Winter Energy Payment is a non-taxable benefit paid with the client's main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension to support eligible clients to meet their household heating costs during the winter payment period.

chunks.title: Payment — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Payment
The Winter Energy Payment is a non-taxable payment paid with a client's qualifying benefit.
The rate paid depends on whether clients are single, married, or in a civil union or de facto relationship, or have children.
It is paid either weekly or fortnightly, depending on whether the clients are paid a benefit weekly or a pension fortnightly.
The rates of Winter Energy Payment are not changed annually.
## Winter Energy Payment divided equally for couples getting a main benefit
For client's getting a married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit, the Winter Energy Payment is paid equally to each person, 50% to the client and 50% to the partner.
For clients who are getting a main benefit the Winter Energy Payment is paid from Monday to Sunday and payment is made 1 week in arrears.
## When Winter Energy Payment not paid equally to couples
There are some situations when a couple will receive different benefits as they are receiving it in their own right.
In these cases, the Winter Energy Payment can only be paid to 1 person in the couple at the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment.
## Winter Energy Payment not paid equally to New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension couples
For couples receiving New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension, Winter Energy Payments are only paid at the full couple rate to 1 person.
Clients receiving New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension are paid the Winter Energy Payment fortnightly from Wednesday to Tuesday, in arrears.

chunks.title: Clients who get Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Clients who get Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy
When clients are in long-term care and they receive Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy they are not entitled to the Winter Energy Payment.
However, for married, civil union or de facto couples, where the partner is still living in the community and they meet all other criteria, they can receive the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment.
## Clients in care - no Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy
Single clients
If a client does not qualify for Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy but is living in long term residential care, they can get Winter Energy Payment. A single client will get the single rate of Winter Energy Payment.
Couples
For married, civil union or de facto couples, if the partner is in residential care but not getting Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy, they are eligible to get (or continue to get) the Winter Energy Payment. When the Winter Energy Payment is not paid equally to both people (eg clients receiving New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension), it is likely that the full couple rate will be paid to the person living in the community.
## Residential Care Loan
If a client is living in residential care and getting a Residential Care Loan to pay their contribution for their care, they are eligible to get Winter Energy Payment.

chunks.title: Qualifications — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To get a Winter Energy Payment the client must:
- be getting a qualifying benefit (or portion of it) during the winter period
- be either the person granted a qualifying benefit or their partner, and the qualifying benefit (or portion of it) is paid to the client
- not be disqualified from getting Winter Energy Payment
- not have chosen to opt out of getting the Winter Energy Payment
- be living in New Zealand (not be outside of New Zealand during the period that the Winter Energy Payment can be paid for more than 28 days during any one or more absences)
## Clients do not have to apply for Winter Energy Payments
Clients do not have to apply for Winter Energy Payments, it is automatically paid to clients who are getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension and meet all other eligibility criteria.
Winter Energy Payments are paid automatically in all following winter periods unless the client has chosen not to get it.

chunks.title: Qualifying benefit must be payable — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Qualifying benefit must be payable
Clients and their partners must be getting payments of a qualifying benefit each week (for main benefits) or fortnightly (for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension clients) to get paid Winter Energy Payment.
In any situation when a benefit is not being paid, the Winter Energy Payment will not be paid.
The types of situations where the Winter Energy Payment will not be paid include (but not limited to):
- benefit fully reduced due to income
- New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran's Pension or other main benefit reduced to nil because of an overseas pension
- imprisonment
- warrant to arrest
- benefit is suspended for any other reason
Note New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients who have 100% tailored tax code are entitled to get the Winter Energy Payment.

chunks.title: Receiving a qualifying benefit — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Receiving a qualifying benefit
Clients and their partners are eligible to receive Winter Energy Payments if they are receiving one of the following qualifying benefits:
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury and disability)
- Supported Living Payment (caring)
- Jobseeker Support
- Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
- Emergency Benefit
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance
- Youth Payment
- Young Parent Payment
- New Zealand Superannuation
- Veteran's Pension
Note clients not receiving a qualifying benefit are not eligible for a Winter Energy Payment.

chunks.title: Single client shares care of dependent child — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Single client shares care of dependent child
The higher rate of the Winter Energy Payment can only be paid to the principal caregiver when single clients share the care of a child.
To be considered the principal caregiver of the child the client must have the primary responsibility for the day to day care of the child, not on a temporary basis.
The client is considered the principal caregiver (and receives the higher rate of the Winter Energy Payment) when:
- they have the child included in their benefit (this suggests a decision has already been made that they are a principal caregiver for the purposes of benefit eligibility) or
- they are receiving Childcare Assistance payments for the child, even if they look after the child an equal number of days, (a decision has already been made that they are the principal caregiver for them to receive Childcare Assistance)

chunks.title: Social Housing tenants — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Social Housing tenants
Clients who are living in social housing are eligible to receive Winter Energy Payment as long as they are receiving a qualifying benefit.
The client do not have to be named on the tenancy agreement or paying Income Related Rent for the property.

chunks.title: Specific circumstances — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Specific circumstances
There are some specific circumstances that may or may not affect a client's entitlement to Winter Energy Payment.

chunks.title: Stopping the Winter Energy Payment — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Stopping the Winter Energy Payment
The Winter Energy Payment will stop when the:
- Winter Energy Payment period ends on 1 October each year (apart from 2018 when it is 29 September)
- client stops receiving a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension (except for terminal benefit, they can continue to get Winter Energy Payment for the length of time terminal benefit is paid within the winter period)
- client advises they no longer wish to get Winter Energy Payments
- client's qualifying benefit stops being paid (eg suspension, abatement, imprisonment, warrant to arrest, or the effect of a direct deduction from New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension due to an overseas pension)
- client starts receiving Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy
- client's qualifying benefit is reduced to the hospital rate of benefit and a decision is made not to continue to pay Winter Energy Payment
- client is absent from New Zealand for 28 days
- client moves overseas permanently
whichever occurs first.

chunks.title: Winter Energy Payment for couples — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Winter Energy Payment for couples
Only one person in the couple can be determined to be eligible to get Winter Energy Payment. But as with other extra help paid at a married, civil union or de facto rate, 50% of the couple rate is paid to the client and 50% to the partner. Note this can only occur when systems allow.
There is no ‘half-married’ rate of Winter Energy Payment. The effect of this is that where one person in the couple is no longer eligible to receive Winter Energy Payment, the other person can receive the full couple rate of payment. This may occur when one of the couple is (but not limited to):
- on a grade 2 or grade 3 sanction
- are receiving Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy or
- is overseas for longer than 28 days

chunks.title: Winter period — extra help > winter energy payment
chunks.text:
## Winter period
The winter period is the 22 week period starting from 1 May and finishes on 1 October (inclusive).

chunks.title: Ability of person requiring care to contribute to the cost of care — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Ability of person requiring care to contribute to the cost of care
Emergency Benefit is paid when a client is in hardship and the individual circumstances justify the payment.
You must consider the ability of the person requiring care to contribute towards the cost of this care, when a client is unable to earn a sufficient livelihood as:
- they are providing care for a person (not their partner) and
- by providing this care the person remains at home
Note this does not apply when a person is caring for their New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension partner.

chunks.title: Activity failures for young partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Activity failures for young partners
If a young partner fails to meet their youth activity obligations, the sanctions imposed depend on whether they have a dependent child and are youth money managed.
## Youth money managed
When a young partner is youth money managed and has an obligations failure and has not recomplied within the 5 working day notice period, the effect of the sanction on their assistance is the same as for Youth Payment.
For more information see:
## Not youth money managed
When a young partner is not youth money managed and has an obligations failure and has not recomplied within the 5 working day notice period, the effect of the sanction is the same as for their main benefit except with the inclusion of the removal of any incentive payments that might be being paid.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Activity Summary — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Activity Summary
After you have discussed with the partner the work obligations and activities they are required to complete, you may want to provide the partner with an Activity Summary as confirmation of these.
Partners do not sign the Activity Summary and it is not mandatory to provide the Activity Summary to them. You may think it is appropriate to provide the print out or the partner may request this.
For more information see:
- Setting appropriate activities for partners

chunks.title: Age — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Age
Generally, age alone will not be the reason a client is unable to earn a sufficient livelihood. Age is likely to be associated with other reasons such as disability or employment barriers. When considering Emergency Benefit for this reason, all the client's circumstances must be determined to establish the equivalent benefit.
When they are unable to work for a period, they may be eligible for a benefit such as (but not limited to) Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support.
To determine if age is the reason a client is unable to earn a sufficient livelihood consider the following:
- How did the client expect to support themselves (and any dependent family)?
- Specifically what has prevented them from supporting themselves (and any dependent family)?
- What options have they pursued?
- Are there things other than age preventing them finding work?
Where a client has made a choice that has restricted their ability to earn a sufficient livelihood, you will need to take this into account when determining entitlement to an Emergency Benefit
For more information see:
- Clients aged 65 years or over
- Clients aged 16 or 17 years
- Determining the reason for insufficient livelihood
- Conditions of grant
- Work or work preparation obligations - partners
- Qualifications Partners 65 years and over

chunks.title: Aged 16 or 17 years and in exceptional circumstances — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Aged 16 or 17 years and in exceptional circumstances
A person aged 16 or 17 years must be in exceptional circumstances to receive Emergency Benefit.
When considering whether a young person is in exceptional circumstances you should consider:
- the reasons why the young person would not qualify for a Youth Payment
- whether the young person is, or is not, in education, training or employment
- the length of time the Emergency Benefit is like to be payable
- the impact that granting the benefit would have on the young person's education or training and therefore prospects for employment
- the most likely effect on the young person's health or welfare, or the health and welfare of anyone who is dependent on them, if Emergency Benefit was not granted
- any other matters you consider relevant to the granting of Emergency Benefit

chunks.title: All reasonable steps to meet social obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
