There may be some situations where a client or their partner (if any) can't comply with their social obligations for reasons beyond their control. You can accept that a client has taken all reasonable steps to comply if they:
- have made a commitment to meet their social obligations at a more appropriate time and
- are working towards addressing any barriers they are facing
Every client's situation is different and what may be a barrier to meeting social obligations for one family may not be for another.
The decision about whether a client is taking all reasonable steps to comply lies with Work and Income.
Below are some of the situations you should take into account when considering that the client is taking all reasonable steps:
- Shared carer issues in the family or family court proceedings occurring
The parent who is not the principal caregiver does not support their child having to attend recognised early childhood education programmes. It would not be reasonable for the client to be held responsible for the actions of someone else.
- Family violence or safety concerns in the family
A client discloses family violence or they have safety concerns for the child.
- Supply or availability issues
A child is on a waiting list for:
- an early childhood education programme or
- a medical centre and the client has a plan or commitment to ensure their child can access primary health care if it is required
- Additional costs of participation or engagement may put the client in hardship
The travel costs or additional early childhood education programme costs associated with attendance would cause hardship to the family.
- The child has a health condition, injury or disability
A child has an injury or behavioural problems meaning that it would not be reasonable to expect them to participate in an approved programme either temporarily or permanently.
- Family has recently moved to a new area
The family has recently moved and is in the process of establishing networks.
For more information see:
- Social obligations
- Monitoring compliance with social obligations
- Enrolment and attendance at a recognised early childhood education programme

chunks.title: Amount of income exemption — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Amount of income exemption
When you have determined that a client is severely disabled you must then consider if they should have all or part of their income from employment disregarded for benefit purposes.
The amount of the income exemption depends on the client's individual circumstances after considering the guidelines - for severe disablement and should be:
- a reasonable amount as an incentive to recognise the personal effort that a severely disabled person has made to participate or continue in employment
- any additional costs that a severely disabled person has incurred to participate or continue in employment
- a reasonable amount to ensure that a severely disabled person is not disadvantaged by participating or continuing in employment
Note the client may be entitled to receive other types of assistance, for example Disability Allowance for transport costs to work or employment assistance.
Fully document your decision by recording the reasons and the amount of the exemption in the CMS note template, Income exemption S422
Contact Helpline if you need help with the assessment.
For more information see:
- Extra Help

chunks.title: Any other appropriate conditions — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Any other appropriate conditions
Depending on the client's reasons for not being able to earn a sufficient livelihood and be in hardship will determine the conditions that are applied to the Emergency Benefit.
Note any conditions of grant placed on the payment of an Emergency Benefit must be reasonable and appropriate for the individual client.
There may be a situation specific to a client that requires a condition that is not covered by other conditions of benefit. This condition may involve a one off activity, requirement or an ongoing obligation.
Note the client must be advised of any condition (both verbally and in writing) and CMS must be noted.
If the client fails to meet any condition of grant, the Emergency Benefit may be stopped.
Note where a client has advised a change of circumstances review their eligibility and if necessary the conditions of grant.
For more information see:
- Benefit paid for a specific period
- Conditions of grant

chunks.title: Any other reason — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Any other reason
There may be a number of different reasons where, due to the client's individual circumstances, a client is in hardship due to being unable to earn a sufficient livelihood for themselves (and any dependent family).
It is reasonable to consider an Emergency Benefit when you are satisfied that the client:
- cannot get another benefit
- cannot earn a sufficient livelihood
- is in hardship
You must also consider whether:
- they have contributed to their hardship
- they can change their circumstances to alleviate their hardship and
- their circumstances justify payment
Note 'Any other reason' is very wide and is the last resort where a client cannot earn a sufficient livelihood and is not eligible for another benefit or Emergency Benefit due to their health condition, injury or disability, domestic circumstances or age.
## Clients from Tokelau, Niue, Cook Islands or Australia
Clients from Tokelau, Niue and Cook Islands are not required to have permanent residence or a temporary entry class visa to be lawfully in New Zealand.
Australian citizens are lawfully allowed in New Zealand as they are deemed to hold a residence class visa.
For more information see:
- Australian clients
- Tokelau, Niue and Cook Island clients
- Person serving their sentence of imprisonment in a psychiatric hospital
- Person detained under a Public Protection Order
- Partner receiving New Zealand Superannuation in residential care
- Seasonal assistance during short breaks
- Lockouts
- Clients with permanent residence or citizenship
- Clients without permanent residence or citizenship
- Unlawful residents and clients in New Zealand temporarily
- Determining the reason for insufficient livelihood
- Conditions of grant
- Contributed to hardship

chunks.title: Approved budgeting programme activity — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Approved budgeting programme activity
Young partners may be required to participate in and complete an approved budgeting programme
An approved budgeting programme aims to provide young people with skills in financial management. Young people must be referred to a provider from the list of authorised courses and providers already contracted the Ministry of Social Development.
The providers of the budgeting programme will provide a programme that is in line with the Youth Services Guidelines for the content of the approved programme.
Where there are no budgeting providers contracted in a particular area, the service provider will have to deliver the budgeting programme themselves.
For more information see:
- Report to service provider or Work and Income on progress
- Money management activity
- Youth activity obligations

chunks.title: Approved early childhood education programmes or services — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Approved early childhood education programmes or services
An approved early childhood education programme or service includes:
- a licensed early childhood education service which includes:
- early childhood education and care centre (eg daycare centre, kōhanga reo, playcentre, kindergarten)
- home-based education and care service
- hospital-based education and care service
- a playgroup that has been certificated by the Ministry of Education (this means a playgroup is funded by the Ministry of Education and will meet certain standards)
- if before 1 December 2014, a licence-exempt early childhood education and care centre funded by the Ministry of Education (this means a playgroup is funded by the Ministry of Education and so meets certain standards)
and
- a fee is charged for children to participate in the early childhood education programme or service
Most early childhood education services offer 20 Hours Early Childhood Education. This means that children aged 3, 4 and 5 years old may be able to receive up to 6 hours per day, 20 hours per week of free early childhood education.
To help clients meet this social obligation you should discuss childcare assistance that may be available to the client.

chunks.title: Approved parenting programme — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Approved parenting programme
An approved parenting programme is:
- a programme the young partner has been referred to by a service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service or
- a programme that is provided by the service provider themselves or
- a programme that generally follows the guidelines for parenting programmes

chunks.title: Approved recompliance activities for young partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Approved recompliance activities for young partners
Approved recompliance activities for young partners include:
- education, training or work-based learning
- part-time work or work experience (where the young person is not already in part-time work)
- community activities
- any other activity approved by MSD that will enhance skills or motivation
Note the benefit will be resumed or increased from the date the young partner starts the recompliance activity.
For more information see:
- Recompliance for young partners

chunks.title: Approved training — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Approved training
For training to be approved, first you need to decide if training is the appropriate activity for the partner and then consider whether the course is the right course.
## Is training the appropriate activity
Consider whether a training course is the most suitable activity for the partner. Consider with the partner whether other activities (for example programmes, seminars, or work experience) might be more suitable for moving the partner towards full-time employment.
Discuss and take into account the partner's career or job preferences, consider:
- their educational qualifications
- their employment history
- their skills and
- whether training will help them find work at the earliest opportunity
## Is this the right course?
The course must:
- focus on teaching practical, employment-related skills
- support the partner to find work and
- be less than 12 weeks (other than approved Government sponsored courses)
Some additional things to note are:
- partners applying for courses longer than 12 weeks should be seeking assistance through StudyLink if the course has been approved by the Ministry of Education for Student Loans or Student Allowances and
- if a partner is undergoing pre-employment training under Flexi-Wage Basic [no link find out why] they cannot receive their portion of the benefit as they should be receiving a wage from the employer
For more information see:
- Examples of approved courses
## Extra Help for partners in approved training
The following assistance is available for partners in approved training:
- Course Participation Assistance [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Approved training (young partners) — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Approved training (young partners)
In a situation where a young partner cannot return to secondary education, the next appropriate activity to consider is approved training.
Generally they will be working towards a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification.
For youth activity obligations purposes approved training is defined as employment-related training.
Approved employment-related training must:
- be reputable and likely to teach the young partner skills that will help them find work
- have an emphasis on training rather than study
- offer full-time training (at least 30 hours per week) and
- offer NCEA or New Zealand Qualification Framework (NZQF) credits
When advising a young partner of approved training you need to consider their future goals and aspirations. You should try and match types of training that would be suitable for the young partner and their career path.
A young partner in full-time approved training must:
- regularly attend the programme
- complete assignments and
- complete other course requirements
## Employment-related training
Employment-training includes (but is not limited to):
- Workplace/industry training
- Youth Guarantee courses
## Extra Help for young people in approved training
The following assistance is available for Young people in approved training:
- Course Participation Assistance [no link find out why]
You should also keep in contact with the young partner during their course to ensure that they are regularly attending the training.
For more information see:
- Definition of 'full-time'
- NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification
- Youth activity obligations
- Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months

chunks.title: Assessed as financially competent — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Assessed as financially competent
A young partner is generally considered to be financially competent where they have:
- earned their budgeting incentive and
- shown consistent, sound financial judgement which may include the young person is spending their in-hand allowance on items that are appropriate for their situationany hardship assistance is justifiedthe young person has lowered their coststhe young person has found a part-time job and is managing the money they receive from that in a way that is appropriate for their situation
- the young person is spending their in-hand allowance on items that are appropriate for their situation
- any hardship assistance is justified
- the young person has lowered their costs
- the young person has found a part-time job and is managing the money they receive from that in a way that is appropriate for their situation
For more information see:

chunks.title: Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or application process — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or application process
Clients who have an initial stand-down cannot get an Emergency Benefit, Temporary Additional Support or Accommodation Supplement during the stand-down.
## Exception
If a client was getting Accommodation Supplement paid as a non-beneficiary they can continue to get this during the initial stand-down.
## In-work tax credit
Clients getting a main benefit do not qualify for in-work tax credit. However they may be able to get in-work tax credit during an initial stand-down if they qualify for an in-work tax credit grace period.
## Special Needs Grants
If a client is suffering hardship they may be able to get a Special Needs Grant.

chunks.title: Australian clients — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Australian clients
Australian citizens are lawfully allowed in New Zealand as they are deemed to hold a residence class visa. However, they must still be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet all other criteria to be eligible.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Average weekly income — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Average weekly income
Clients can choose an income assessment period of either 26 or 52 weeks to calculate their average weekly income for the initial stand-down. Therefore you will need to calculate the average weekly income for both 26 weeks and 52 weeks.Income (before tax) can include, but is not limited to:
- normal salary/wages
- bonus payments paid at the time of termination
- Child Support received
- earnings-related accident insurance payments
- gross income from investments
- holiday pay
- interest from savings or investments
- other benefit payments
- Paid Parental Leave payments
- pay in lieu of notice
- pay in lieu of accumulated leave
- payments dependent on the completion of a fixed term contract
- redundancy payments
- rent
- retirement payments
- Student Allowance and student Accommodation Benefit and
- any other income (for example family trust income)
To calculate the average weekly income over a 26 week period, divide by 26, the total amount of income received by the client in the 26 week period immediately before their entitlement date. If this is the one week minimum, then the stand-down period is one week, otherwise calculate the average weekly income over a 52 week period.
To calculate the average weekly income over a 52 week period, divide by 52, the total amount of income received by the client in the 52 week period immediately before their entitlement date.
You should use the calculation that gives the client a lesser stand-down period.
Note any overseas earnings received by the client before their entitlement date must be included in the calculation of the client's average weekly income.
## Partners
When the client has a partner who has been working or is still working, use the higher of their two incomes over the previous 26 or 52 weeks to calculate the stand-down.
Do not combine their incomes.
However, if the other partner's wages or holiday pay continues beyond the commencement date, charge this income against the benefit in the usual way.

chunks.title: Bank account — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Bank account
Unless there are special circumstances, it is a condition of every benefit that the client provides or opens a bank account or membership to a credit union to receive their benefit payment.
## Bank
An appropriate bank is:
- a private savings bank, a trustee savings bank, or The Co-operative Bank Limited (formerly PSIS)
- a registered bank which on the 31st March 1987 was a trading bank or
- any other registered bank or a building society approved by the Minister after consultation with the Minister of Finance
For more information see:
- Processing standards Bank account [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Benefit paid for a specific period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Emergency Benefit is temporary assistance for a client who: - is in hardship - is unable to earn enough income for themselves (and any dependent family) and - cannot receive another benefit When Emergency Benefit is granted, the reason the client is unable to earn a sufficient livelihood may be due to a particular situation for a certain period. Each application must be assessed on its own merits and Emergency Benefit should only be granted for the period it is needed. Note depending on the client's circumstances, the period the Emergency Benefit is paid for may vary.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Emine is an asylum seeker from Turkey. She has applied for refugee status and a decision on her application is due in 3 months. Emine is granted Emergency Benefit with a condition of grant that it will only be paid for a specific period. An expiry is added to her Emergency Benefit for 3 months' time. This is when she expects to have an outcome from her refugee status application.

chunks.title: Example 2 — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Max is a sixteen-year-old student who is getting Student Allowance. He needs benefit assistance during the Christmas break and doesn't qualify for Jobseeker Support. Max is granted Emergency Benefit and one of his conditions of grant is that it will only be paid for a specific period. An expiry is added for 8 weeks' time as this is when the Christmas break ends, and Max will start getting Student Allowance again.

chunks.title: Example 3 — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Kahurangi is married with a 12-year-old son. Her husband gets New Zealand Superannuation but Kahurangi doesn't qualify because she is under 65. She also doesn't qualify for Jobseeker Support because she is the principal caregiver of their son and can't meet the work obligations. Kahurangi is granted Emergency Benefit and one of her conditions of grant is that it will only be paid for a specific period. An expiry is added for her son's 14th birthday as this is when she should qualify for Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a client advises of a change in their circumstances, you must review their eligibility to Emergency Benefit. You should also review their conditions of grant to make sure they are relevant to their circumstances.

chunks.title: End of specific period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When Emergency Benefit expires because it was granted for a specific period, you must assess the client's circumstances to see what assistance they are eligible for. The client may be eligible for another benefit or continue to be eligible for Emergency Benefit for the same or a different reason. If the client is eligible for another benefit, they must be transferred unless it is in the client's best interests to continue getting Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Best interests of the client — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Best interests of the client
There may be situations where a client has applied for or is receiving a benefit and it has been identified by the client or the case manager, in the best interests of the client (and any dependent family) the client should undertake one of the following activities or tasks:
- undergo a course of training in any occupation
- submit themselves for examination at any medical or psychological clinic
- receive any medical or other treatment
- undergo any course of training for the improvement of their physical or mental capacities or
- take more adequate steps to secure suitable employment
Where the current benefit does not require the client to undertake one of these activities and it is in the best interests of the client to do so, after discussions with the client and Helpline you may transfer the client to Emergency Benefit and have this activity as a condition of continuing payment.
Note generally, this provision should only be considered after the legislative provisions of other main benefits have been considered and is not to be used to avoid the obligations failures sanction process. Before granting an Emergency Benefit for this reason, you must contact Helpline to discuss.
If an Emergency Benefit is to be granted in substitution for another benefit, for the client to undertake a certain activity or task, full notes must be placed on CMS justifying the reason for the grant of Emergency Benefit and the conditions applied.
For more information see:
- Conditions of grant

chunks.title: Step 1 — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Step 1
Find out the number of days represented by the payment received. If this is not clearly shown on the 'verification of payments received' provided by the client, use either of the following formula.
Note extra payments paid to the client for example holiday pay, should not be included in the gross salary figure used to calculate the daily rate of pay. However these payments will be included in the client's last 26 and 52 weeks gross earnings.
Formula 1
Determine gross salary over last 52 weeks of employment
Divide by 52 weeks = weekly rate of pay
Divide by 5 days = daily rate of pay
Confirm total amount of holiday pay etc
Divide this amount by daily rate of pay = number of days pay
Formula 2
Determine gross salary over last 4 weeks of employment
Divide by 20 (number of working days in 4 weeks) = daily rate of pay
Confirm total amount of holiday pay etc
Divide by daily rate of pay = number of days pay
Note only calculate the period covered by holiday pay using the applicants' last four weeks income if it does not disadvantage the client. If the income earned in the last four weeks does not reflect what the client normally earned, you may need to request extra weeks or calculate the daily rate of pay using the last 26 weeks gross salary.
## Step 2
Add the number of days pay to the last day the client worked.
This is the date that employment ceased.
Remember, do not count Saturdays and Sundays - use Monday to Friday weekdays only. For example, if a client stopped work on a Friday, add the days from the following Monday.
## Step 3
The entitlement date is the day after this date. The stand-down commences from the entitlement date.

chunks.title: Capacity issues prevent a young partner meeting their parenting obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Capacity issues prevent a young partner meeting their parenting obligations
A young partner may be granted a parenting incentive without meeting the criteria if:
- there are capacity issues preventing a young person from: undertaking a parenting programmeenrolling their dependent child/ren with a primary health organisationkeeping their dependent child/ren aged five years or under up-to-date with their Wellchild checkshaving their children under five years attends an approved early childhood education programme or being placed in other suitable child care which the young person is in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work
- undertaking a parenting programme
- enrolling their dependent child/ren with a primary health organisation
- keeping their dependent child/ren aged five years or under up-to-date with their Wellchild checks
- having their children under five years attends an approved early childhood education programme or being placed in other suitable child care which the young person is in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work
and
- the young person has agreed with their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service on steps they must take to fulfil these obligations (for example being on a waiting list) and
- the young person has taken the agreed steps to the satisfaction of their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service

chunks.title: Caring for a child or foster child with special needs — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Caring for a child or foster child with special needs
This exemption may apply to partners with work or work preparation obligations.
A partner can be exempt from some or all of their work or work preparation obligations if they are the:
- principal caregiver of a dependent child or
- foster parent of a foster child
who has special needs and whose welfare would be unduly harmed if the client attended employment or training, and for whom alternative care arrangements are not available, or are unable to be made.
This means the child must have 1 or more of the following:
- a physical or intellectual disability
- a medical condition
- a chronic or recurring illness
- a learning or behavioural difficulty and
- be unable to attend school on a regular basis
or
- be a foster child aged 3 years or older who is adjusting to a placement with a new carer
Note this can be a full or partial exemption.
## Foster child is under 3 years
A partner may also be exempt from some of their work obligations if they are caring for a foster child under the age of 3 years.
## Evidence
The partner must provide written evidence of the child's special needs from a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, psychologist or social worker stating:
- what the child's illness is and its likely duration or
- an assessment of the child's behavioural difficulty and
- the need for full-time care
- the risk to the child if the client is sent to training or an activity and
- that the child is unable to attend school
Note MSD should also consider eligibility to Child Disability Allowance. However, a child getting Child Disability Allowance does not guarantee the partner will meet the criteria for this exemption.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months.
This exemption should then be reviewed.
At the review MSD should consider the client's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption. MSD can ask the client to provide evidence that the exemption should be extended.

chunks.title: Caring for a child under 3 years who is not their dependent child — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Caring for a child under 3 years who is not their dependent child
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
In some cases a client may be caring for a foster child or children under the age of 3 years who is in Oranga Tamariki care. Foster children are not considered to be dependent children.
These clients may be exempt from meeting some of their work obligations.
This is a partial exemption only.
## Proof
The client must provide:
- confirmation of their situation - for example, a letter from Oranga Tamariki
- confirmation of the age of the child
## Duration
This exemption can be granted in SWIFTT for 12 months or to when the child turns 3 years old - whichever is earlier.
This exemption can be renewed after 12 months provided the child is still under 3 years and the parent still qualifies for benefit.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason "Caring for a foster child".
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions

chunks.title: Caring for a child with special needs (young partners) — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Caring for a child with special needs (young partners)
A young partner with a dependent child can be exempt from some or all of their activity obligations if they are the:
- principal caregiver of a dependent child or
- foster parent of a foster child
who has special needs and whose welfare would be unduly harmed if the young partner attended education, training or work-based learning and for whom alternative care arrangements are not available, or are unable to be made.
This means the child must have 1 or more of the following:
- physical disability or intellectual disability
- health condition
- chronic or recurring illness
- learning or behavioural difficulty
- be unable to attend school on a regular basis or
- be a foster child, aged 1 years or older, who is adjusting to a placement with a new foster carer
This can be a full or partial exemption.
## Foster child is under 1 year
A young partner may also be exempt from some of their activity obligations if they are caring for a foster child under the age of 1 years.
## Evidence
The young partner must provide written evidence from a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, psychologist, or social worker stating:
- what the child's illness is and its likely duration or
- an assessment of the child's behavioural difficulty and
- the need for full-time care
- the risk to the child if the young partner is required to meet their activity obligations and
- that the child is unable to attend school
Note MSD should also consider eligibility to Child Disability Allowance. However, a child getting Child Disability Allowance does not guarantee the partner will meet the criteria for this exemption.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months.
This exemption should then be reviewed. At the review MSD should consider the young partner's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption. MSD can ask the young partner to provide evidence that their exemption should be extended.

chunks.title: Caring for a person requiring care — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Caring for a person requiring care
When it is determined a client is prevented from working and unable to earn a sufficient livelihood due to caring for a person who requires care (other than their partner), the client's eligibility to the Supported Living Payment - caring for a person must be tested.
If the client is not able to get any other benefit, you will need to consider all the reasons a client cannot earn a sufficient livelihood, and if alternative arrangements can be made to allow the client to be in paid work.
Note you need to look at each application for Emergency Benefit on its own merits and the payment of Emergency Benefit must be justified.
## Caring for a New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension partner
Generally, Emergency Benefit cannot be paid to a person who is caring for their partner.
There is an exception when a person is caring for their New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension partner. This can only be considered when the person providing care is not eligible for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension in their own right.

chunks.title: Caring for foster child under 12 months old (young partners) — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Caring for foster child under 12 months old (young partners)
In some cases a young partner may be caring for a foster child under the age of 12 months who is in Oranga Tamariki care. Foster children are not considered to be dependent children.
This is a partial exemption only. The young partner can be exempt from meeting their obligation to be in full-time education, training and work-based learning.
The budgeting and parenting obligations, along with the obligation to meet with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service still apply.
## Proof
The young partner must provide:
- confirmation of the care arrangement - for example, a letter from Oranga Tamariki
- confirmation of the age of the child
## Duration
This exemption can be granted until the foster child turns 12 months of age or until the foster child is six months old and there is a suitable place available at a Teen Parent Unit.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason "UCB/OB Foster Child under 12 months".
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemption
For an overview of the exemptions see:
- Table of exemptions for young partners

chunks.title: Caring full-time for a spouse or partner with a health condition, injury or disability (young partners) — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Caring full-time for a spouse or partner with a health condition, injury or disability (young partners)
A young partner may be caring for a spouse or partner who has a health condition, injury or disability and needs to be cared for on a full-time basis.
This can be a full or partial exemption.
## Evidence
The young partner must provide a medical certificate from a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner:
- that their spouse or partner needs the young partner's full-time care and
- without that care their spouse or partner would need hospital care or care of an equivalent kind and
- the length of time their spouse or partner will need that care

chunks.title: Caring full-time for person with health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Caring full-time for person with health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to partners with work or work preparation obligations.
A partner may be caring for a person who has a health condition, injury or a disability and who needs to be cared for on a full-time basis.
This can be a full exemption.
## Evidence
The partner must provide a medical certificate from a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner:
- that the person needs the client's full-time care and
- without that care the person would need hospital care or care of an equivalent kind and
- the length of time the person will need that care

chunks.title: Caring responsibilities — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Caring responsibilities
From time to time a client's caring responsibilities will restrict their ability to earn a sufficient livelihood to support themselves (and any dependent family). Caring responsibilities means the client is caring for another person.
They could be:
- a dependent child or
- caring for a person requiring care
Before an Emergency Benefit is considered, determine:
- Who is the client caring for?
- How long is the care required?
- Are there any other reasonable caring arrangements, options or financial assistance available?
- Is the care full-time or part-time?
- How did they expect to support themselves (and any dependent family) while caring?
Can the client get another benefit?
Test the client's eligibility to:
- Supported Living Payment - caring for a person
Provides assistance to clients caring full-time for a person (other than their partner) who would otherwise receive hospital care.
- Sole Parent Support
Provides assistance to single clients caring for a dependent child.
- Unsupported Childs Benefit
Provides support to a client caring for a child that is not their own because of a breakdown in the dynamics of the child's family.
- Orphans Benefit
Provides support to a client caring for a child that is not their own because the child's parents are dead, missing or unable to care for the child as they are severely disabled.
In addition, you need to determine if there are other reason(s) the client is unable to earn a sufficient livelihood as all the client's circumstances must be considered before a decision is made and the payment can be justified.
For more information see:
- Single and caring for a child
- Caring for a person requiring care
- Determining the reason for insufficient livelihood

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances
Clients must tell us straight away of any changes in their circumstances or their family's situation that may affect entitlement to Emergency Benefit. Clients agree to this by signing the Emergency Benefit application form.
A change of circumstance may also affect the client's social obligations.
Examples of changes and how to deal with these can be found in Changes and Reviews
For more information see:
- Child changes and social obligations
- Changes and reviews Child changes

chunks.title: Change in circumstances during Money Management — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances during Money Management
Clients or partners may have a change in circumstances during Money Management, such as a change in income, which may change their rate of benefit.
If a client or partner declares a change in circumstances after their payment has been issued onto the payment card, it may mean this payment is incorrect resulting in a debt being established or arrears due to the client.
Any debt will generally be repaid from their future benefit payments.
If a client is owed arrears, it will be paid directly to their bank account. This is different when their benefit stops during Money Management. For more information see:
- Period of Money Management.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
All clients getting an Emergency Benefit must tell MSD before they leave New Zealand.
If the client or partner does not tell MSD before they go overseas, their benefit payments will stop from the day after they leave New Zealand.
If a client tells MSD they will be absent from New Zealand for an approved travel reason, they may be able to keep getting payments for up to 28 days.
## Approved Information Sharing Agreement with New Zealand Custom Service
MSD has an Approved Information Sharing Agreement with New Zealand Customs Service that identifies clients getting a benefit who have left New Zealand.
Once identified, the clients eligibility to keep getting their benefit payments while they are absent from New Zealand is automatically determined by MSD's systems.
## Does not advise of departure
If the client did not tell MSD they were leaving New Zealand their benefit will be suspended immediately from the day after they left New Zealand.
The Integrity Intervention Centre will determine if there has been an overpayment, establish any debt and advise the client.
If a client questions the information match refer them to the Integrity Intervention Centre.
## Approved travel reasons
Generally, a client or their partner is not entitled to get Emergency Benefit while they are absent from New Zealand.
However, in limited circumstances, Emergency Benefit can be paid for up to 28 days in a 52 week period when a client (or their partner) is absent from New Zealand.
## Payment of benefit while absent for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period while the client is absent from New Zealand. However, there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
## Mandatory Review while Overseas
Clients getting Emergency Benefit who have temporarily left New Zealand must still respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date.
Temporary absence from New Zealand (e.g. personal travel) does not pause or defer the Mandatory Review.
Clients must contact MSD before their review date to talk about their situation if they are unable to respond to the review or if they need more time to do it.

chunks.title: Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period while the client is absent from New Zealand. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
These circumstances are:
- travel is required for an approved reason, and either: it is the client's first absence within 52 weeks and the permitted reason the client needs to be absent from New Zealand necessitates a period longer than 28 days orthe client has had other prior approved absences within the 52 week period and they require further approved absences which will require them to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- it is the client's first absence within 52 weeks and the permitted reason the client needs to be absent from New Zealand necessitates a period longer than 28 days or
- the client has had other prior approved absences within the 52 week period and they require further approved absences which will require them to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- the client is absent from New Zealand for an approved travel reason and their return is prevented by a new circumstance that requires them to be absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period
- the client is a young partner of a main beneficiary with youth activity obligations and they are travelling to receive support from a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family) who is residing overseas
For more information see:
- Paying more than 28 days for an approved reason
- Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
- Paying for more than 28 days - receive support from family overseas (young partner)

chunks.title: Action on return to New Zealand — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Action on return to New Zealand
You will need to look at the circumstances of the client's absence from and subsequent return to New Zealand to decide when to recommence their benefit and when to treat it as a new application.
You will need to consider the following:
- the client's intention at the time of their departure for example, did they cancel their benefit before leaving New Zealand because they did not intend to return
- did the client remain ordinarily resident during the period of absence?
- the length of time that they have been absent
- the reason for the absence
- have their circumstances changed significantly during their absence?
- is the client eligible to have their benefit backdated to the day after their departure date or date of return?
For more information see:
- Backdating benefit to the day after departure date
## Payment can recommence
When a client returns to New Zealand on or before the 29th day (where continued payment of benefit was allowed) you can recommence their benefit without any break in payment.
Generally, for other short periods of absence (where continued payment was not approved and the benefit was not paid while the client was absent) you can recommence the benefit payments, if they are eligible, from:
- the date the client returned to New Zealand as long as they contact you within 14 days of their return or
- the date they contacted you to advise they have returned if more than 14 days after date of return
## New application
In all other circumstances you may need to consider a new application from the client after reviewing the circumstances above.

chunks.title: Approved travel reasons — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Approved travel reasons
A client and partner receiving Emergency Benefit are generally not able to continue to receive their main benefit payments while they are absent from New Zealand unless they meet the criteria for approved travel. Approved travel includes:
- travel for a permitted reason
Note partners with work obligations are not required to meet their job search obligations while absent from New Zealand on approved travel.
For more information see:
- Permitted travel reasons
- Length of travel for an approved travel reason

chunks.title: Avoiding a debt — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Avoiding a debt
When a single client (with no children) dies, payment generally stops from the day after the date of death. You must take all possible steps to stop payments from this date.
When payment cannot be stopped from the day after the date of death there is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days after the date of death. You can use this discretion to stop payment from the first available date, that is, the earliest date that you can stop payments from so that no overpayment is established.
If the period between the date of death and the first available date to cancel payment from (to avoid creating a debt) is more than 28 days, you will have to establish an overpayment from the 29th day after death.
However, when there has been a deliberate intent to delay advising Work and Income of the client's death you should stop payment from the day after the date of death and establish an overpayment.
Note under no circumstances can payment continue for more than 28 days after the date of death.
## SWIFTT
You will need to cancel payments from the earliest possible date (but not more than 28 days after the date of death) in SBFTZ. However, the date of death entered in CMS must be the client's actual date of death. You must make full notes in CMS of your actions.
Wherever possible you should enter the next of kin or the executor of the deceased's estate on SWIFTT.
For more information see:
- Terminal benefit for a single client

chunks.title: Backdating benefit to the day after departure date — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Backdating benefit to the day after departure date
A client who leaves New Zealand without advising Work and Income of their travel, can only have their benefit backdated to the day after their departure date if they:
- have a humanitarian reason that justifies their reason for travel and their failure to tell Work and Income before they left
- contacted Work and Income as soon as they could reasonably have been expected to, given their circumstances after they departed and
- meet the criteria to continue to be paid their benefit while overseas (either because they meet the criteria for approved travel, or the requirement that travel be approved does not apply to them)
For more information see:
- Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure
- Contacting Work and Income as soon as the client reasonably can
- Approved travel reasons
- Paying a benefit when a client has not advised before departure
- Action on return to New Zealand

chunks.title: Birth of a child — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Birth of a child
When a client applies to have their newborn child included in their benefit, the following information is required:
- full birth certificate of the child, or confirmation from Internal Affairs that the childs birth was registered online, and permission was given to share the birth registration with MSD
- written statement from the client requesting inclusion of the child
If a child's birth certificate is not available immediately, you can include the child in the benefit (without delay) when the client can provide:
- Plunket records
- birth notices
- confirmation from the client's midwife or doctor of the date of birth of the new child or
- hospital papers
Note you must follow-up to make sure the client produces a copy of the birth certificate.
## Extra help
If a child is born with a mental or physical disability, needs constant care and attention because of a disability or is likely to require care for at least 12 months, the client should test their eligibility for Child Disability Allowance.
When a child has ongoing additional costs because of a disability they may be able to receive a Disability Allowance.
For more information see:
- Core policy Child Support
- Date of review (including backdating)
- Dependent child
- Effect on benefit
- Family tax credit
- Best Start tax credit
- Verification from Internal Affairs

chunks.title: Calculating the period of absence — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Calculating the period of absence
The period of an absence from New Zealand for which payment of Emergency Benefit can continue (if approved) is up to 28 consecutive days, that is, Saturdays and Sundays are included.
In all cases, when assessing the period of absence do not include:
- the date of departure from New Zealand and
- the date of return to New Zealand
If a client is absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period the benefit should be suspended from the 29th day (unless they meet the criteria to pay for longer than 28 days).
Note if a client is leaving New Zealand permanently, the benefit must be cancelled from the day after departure.
## Calculating 52 week period
When a client is paid a benefit while they are absent from New Zealand, a client can receive a payment for up to 28 days in total in a 52 week period. The 52 week period is counted in the following way:
- identify the day after the client is intending to leave New Zealand
- count back 52 weeks from this date
- identify any periods of paid absence they have used (counting from the day after they have left New Zealand to the day before they returned to New Zealand)
- subtract the number of days absent from New Zealand from 28 days. The remainder is the client's entitlement to be paid a benefit while they are absent from New Zealand
- pay the client the days they have available up to the period of absence. This may not be the whole of the time they intend to be absent from New Zealand depending on how many days of their entitlement they have left.
For more information see:
- Examples of calculating absence from New Zealand
- Permanent absence
- Reciprocal Agreements

chunks.title: Carer arrangements — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Carer arrangements
Where parents of a child live apart and the child comes into the care of the other parent it is important to establish that the arrangements made have been agreed to by both parents before you include the child in the other parents benefit.
In some cases the arrangement between both parents may not be a legal arrangement but the child has been placed with the other parent by mutual agreement.
## Verification
You must obtain written proof of the new care arrangement. Written proof could be (but is not limited to):
- statement from the other parent
- parenting order or
- documentation from Oranga Tamariki
For more information see:
- Child comes into care
## Permanent or long term
To include a child as a dependent child, the change in care arrangements should be with the intent of permanency or at least capable of being a long-term arrangement.
For more information see:
- Temporary care
- Shared care
- Split care

chunks.title: Change in age — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Change in age
A child's age may affect:
- the family tax credit payable
- the Best Start tax credit payable
- the conditions of grant
- the partner's obligations and
- whether the child is still a dependent child
## Conditions of grant
Payment of Emergency Benefit can be paid with certain conditions.
Generally, the conditions reflect the obligations or conditions that apply to the equivalent benefit such as job search, work planning and medical assessments.
It can also include paying Emergency Benefit for a specific period.
A change in a dependent child's age can affect conditions relating to job search, planning requirements and paying Emergency Benefit for a specific period.
These conditions should be reassessed when a dependent child turns 3, 14 and 18 to ensure they are still relevant to the client's circumstances.
## Example
Kerry is the sole parent of 1 child and getting Emergency Benefit as they don't meet the qualifications for Sole Parent Support.
Because Kerry's daughter was under 3 when Emergency Benefit was granted, a condition of granting the benefit was to take steps to prepare for work.
When Kerry's daughter turns 3 the conditions of granting the benefit will be reassessed, and they may have a part-time job search condition assigned.
## Partner's obligations
Depending on the age of the youngest dependent child a partner may have:
- work preparation obligations when their youngest dependent child is under 3 years
- work obligations and required to look for part-time work of 20 hours or more a week, when their youngest dependent child is aged between 3 and 13 years or
- work obligations and required to look for full-time work of 30 hours or more a week, when the youngest dependent child is aged 14 years or over.
## Child is not dependent
A child is not dependent if they are:
- in full-time employment
Note generally a child can still be a dependent child when they start part-time employment.
- getting a basic Student Allowance or an Independent Circumstances Allowance
Note getting a Student Loan does not always mean a child is financially independent.
- getting a benefit in their own right or
- financially independent

chunks.title: Change of address — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Change of address
When a client advises that they have changed their address it is important to check that the move does not affect their entitlement to Emergency benefit.
Note you will need to update the address in CMS.
If the client is receiving Extra Help this will also need to be reviewed to take into account their new costs.
If the client has a portion of their benefit paid to Housing New Zealand or Te Puni Kokiri this may need to be changed or cancelled.
The change of address may also indicate a change in the client's circumstances. You will need to find out the reason for the grant of Emergency Benefit and whether the reasons for the grant of Emergency Benefit still exist.
## Example
A client who has been receiving an Emergency Benefit while caring for a child who is not their own, gets married or enters a civil union. This change in circumstance means that the customer's entitlement to Emergency Benefit must be reassessed.
Other changes that may affect entitlement are:
- the client and or their partner has commenced employment, study or training
- the client is no longer providing care for their partner or a person who is sick
- the client has left a residential programme
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Obligations

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
Clients have an obligation to advise MSD of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Emergency Benefit or the rate payable.
A change in a client's circumstances may mean that the client qualifies for another benefit.
MSD may also review a benefit at any time to check that the client still meets the qualifications and is getting the correct rate of payment (if applicable).
## Mandatory Review for Emergency Benefit
Mandatory Reviews for Emergency Benefit will only apply to clients whose benefit has an expiry date of more than 52-weeks, or whose Emergency Benefit has no expiry date.
MSD must review a client’s Emergency Benefit within 52-weeks of when the benefit commenced, or within 52-weeks from when the client’s last Mandatory Review was completed.
Clients must respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date, or their payments will suspend.

chunks.title: Child absent — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Child absent
A dependent child who travels overseas can continue to be included in a benefit as long as they continue to meet the definition of dependent child.
Examples of when a dependent child can be absent from New Zealand are:
- child is overseas on an American Field Scholarship or other student exchange programme
- child is overseas visiting a parent who does not act as caregiver
For more information about the effect of absence from New Zealand for a client receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit see:
- Orphans and Unsupported Childs Benefit Absence from New Zealand

chunks.title: Child admitted to hospital — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Child admitted to hospital
Where a client's dependent child is admitted to hospital, there is no change to the rate of payment, irrespective of how long the child remains in hospital. Family tax credit payments continue to be paid for a child who is admitted to hospital.
Depending on the nature of the child's injury, illness or disability the client may be able to receive Child Disability Allowance. Child Disability Allowance is a non-taxable allowance paid to the principal caregiver of a child with a serious disability, who is need of constant care and attention for a period longer than 12 months.
For more information see:
- Child Disability Allowance

chunks.title: Child applies for a benefit in their own right — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Child applies for a benefit in their own right
Where a child applies for a benefit in their own right, exclude the child from the client's Emergency Benefit from:
- the start of the pay period following the date of event
Note there is discretion to continue payment for one more payday following the event.
or
- the date the child's benefit is granted
whichever is earlier.
Wherever possible (and in appropriate circumstances) the date of exclusion of the child from the client's benefit and the commencement date of the child's benefit, should coincide to avoid financial hardship for the family.
Note there are specific rules for deciding whether a child is considered a dependent child when the child turns 18.

chunks.title: Child changes — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Child changes
The number of dependent children in an Emergency Benefit client's care and any change to the circumstances of a child can affect:
- the basic rate of benefit payable
- the rate of family tax credit payable
- payment of Best Start tax credit
- the rate of extra help payable and
- the client's obligations
## Including a child in Emergency Benefit
For a child to be included in a client's Emergency Benefit the child must be a dependent child and generally ordinarily resident in New Zealand.
When the child is not the client's natural or adoptive child, the client may be able to get Unsupported Child's Benefit (instead of having the child included in their Emergency Benefit). This will mainly depend on the care arrangements.
## Changes to a child's circumstances
Change to a dependent child's circumstances is generally going to affect the client's Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Child comes into care — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Child comes into care
When a client has made an application to have another child included in their benefit and that child was in the care of another person the following information is required:
- full birth certificate of the childSee: Verification from Internal Affairs
- written statement from the applicant stating they are the principal caregiver and requesting inclusion in the Emergency Benefit
- (where appropriate) letter from previous caregiver confirming that child has left their careIf the client cannot get written confirmation from the previous caregiver, the new caring arrangement can be confirmed by a referee such as a teacher, Plunket nurse, minister or Justice of the Peace.
Any benefit payments the previous caregiver was getting for the child must stop.
## Single client has child come into care
When a single client has a child come into their care the client may be able to get another benefit such as Sole Parent Support.
For more information see:
- Qualifies for another benefit.
## Date of review
Include the child in the benefit from:
- the date the child came into the client's care or
- the date the Emergency Benefit was granted,
whichever is the later.
## Backdating
When a client requests the backdated inclusion of a child and the previous caregiver was getting a benefit for the child, you will need to review the date the child was excluded from the previous caregivers benefit.
Generally, a child cannot be included in multiple benefits for the same period. In some situations, the previous caregiver may continue to get a benefit in respect of that child for up to 28 days.
Consider all the circumstances and decide whether a debt should be established for the previous caregiver.
If the date you are including the child from is a date in the previous tax year, MSD can only pay arrears of family tax credit and Best Start tax credit from the beginning of the current tax year, that is, 1 April. The client will need to apply for any arrears of tax credits before this date from Inland Revenue.
A review of entitlement needs to be completed to determine the amount of any benefit arrears owed to the client for the backdated period.
For more information see:
- Effect on the benefit
- Discharged from Oranga Tamariki care
- Carer arrangements
- Shared care
- Split care
- Temporary care
- Child's income
- Parent in prison
- Processing standards Child changes [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Personal earnings — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Personal earnings
A dependent child's personal earnings are not charged as income against the Emergency Benefit.
However, a child in full-time employment and is financially independent cannot be included as a dependent child in the benefit.
## Other income
A child may receive other income that is not personal earnings. For more information about how to treat other forms of child's income see:
- Core policy Income

chunks.title: Child leaves care — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Child leaves care
When a dependent child leaves the client's care, the child should be excluded from the start of the pay period following the date the child leaves care and any extra help the client gets should be reassessed to the appropriate rate where applicable.
Note different rules apply when a child stops being a dependent child of a sole parent client because of a sudden change of circumstances beyond the control of the client.
## Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit
Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit should be stopped from the start of the pay period following the date the event took place, to avoid an overpayment with Inland Revenue for the client.

chunks.title: Child under the age of 18 years — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Child under the age of 18 years
When a child under the age of 18 years leaves school or tertiary education, they can continue to be included in the parent or caregiver's Emergency Benefit until the start of the pay period following their 18th birthday as long as the child remains a dependent child.
## Child aged 18 years old
When a child aged 18 years old leaves school or tertiary education, they should be excluded from their parent or caregiver's payment from the start of the pay period following the date the child left school or tertiary education. The parent or caregiver must complete a review of circumstances to determine if they continue to qualify for their discretionary benefit such as Emergency Benefit, and the rate payable.
## Family tax credit
When a child leaves school or tertiary education, family tax credits should be stopped from the day the child is excluded from the parent or caregiver's Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Child leaves sole parents care suddenly — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a child stops being a dependent child of a sole parent client because of a sudden change of circumstances beyond the control of the client, payment of the benefit may continue at the existing rate for 28 days following the date the child stopped being dependent. This is to allow a period of transition for the client to adjust to their change in circumstances. For example when a child suddenly goes into the care of Oranga Tamariki, payment may continue for 28 days from the date the child is no longer dependent on the client. Extra help payments that can be continued for 28 days are: - Accommodation Supplement - Child Disability Allowance - Disability Allowance - Temporary Additional Support - Winter Energy Payment The exception is Childcare Assistance which must be stopped on the day after the client stopped caring for the dependent child. During the 28 days continuation of payment, if the client has other changes of circumstances such as a change in income, the rate of main benefit and extra help will need to be reassessed using sole parent threshold rates.

chunks.title: Mandatory Reviews — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Generally, clients getting Emergency Benefit must respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date or their payments will suspend. If a child leaves a sole parent's care suddenly and the client qualifies for Emergency Benefit after the 28-day continuation period, they may be able to get an extension if they need more time to respond to the Mandatory Review. If the client is unable to respond to the review (even if they had more time) based on their individual circumstances, they may qualify for an exemption. Generally, when the Mandatory Review is only for Emergency Benefit and the benefit will stop at the end of the continuation period e.g. if they are over the income limit, and the review is due, an exemption will apply. The client must contact MSD before their review date to discuss their situation if they need an extension or exemption.

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Generally, clients getting a discretionary benefit such as Emergency Benefit must respond to their notice before the child's 18th birthday or the child will be excluded from their payments. The client must also complete a review of circumstances to determine if they continue to qualify for Emergency Benefit and the rate payable, or their payments will suspend. If Emergency Benefit and any extra help is continuing at the existing rate for up to 28 days because a child has left a sole parent's care suddenly, and that child turns 18 during that period, the client is not required to complete a review of circumstances. However, if Emergency Benefit and any extra help is continuing at the existing rate for up to 28 days because a child has left a sole parent's care suddenly, and a different child in their care turns 18, the client must still complete the review of circumstances or their payments will suspend.

chunks.title: Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit should be stopped from the start of the pay period following the date the child left care (whether planned or suddenly) to avoid an overpayment with Inland Revenue for the client.

chunks.title: Child should be included — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Child should be included
A client is obliged to tell us of all their circumstances including the number of children in their care.
If a child is considered to be dependent that child is to be included in the caregiver's benefit and the appropriate rate of benefit paid.
## Client doesn't want to include a child
In cases where the client has genuine concerns about including the child in their benefit (such as concerns about violence from the other parent) advise the client all information contained in their benefit record is confidential.
If you have any concerns regarding the welfare of a child, the case should be referred to Oranga Tamariki.
## Deciding if a child is financially dependent
When a client states that they are receiving payments to pay for a child's expenses you must decide whether the child is a dependent child of the client.
A child does not have to be solely financially dependent on a client to be considered a dependent child. All that is required is that the child is financially dependent on the person to some degree.
However, being financially dependent on a client is only part of the qualifications of a dependent child. The child must still meet all the qualifications to be considered dependent.
If another person or body is paying for the child's expenses, including payments for the care provided, the child is not financially dependent on the client.
If a client is receiving payments toward the expenses of a dependent child this is regarded as income for benefit purposes.
For more information see:
- Charging income at commencement
- Dependent child

chunks.title: Child starts work — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Child starts work
When a child starts work you need to know if the employment is:
- Full-time employment or
- Part-time employment
Note if the dependent child is temporarily working more than 30 hours per week during the school holidays and they are returning to school after the holidays, they are not considered in full-time employment.

chunks.title: Child turns 14 — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Child turns 14
When a dependent child turns 14 years old it can affect the client's eligibility to Emergency Benefit, their conditions of grant and the partner's obligations (if they have a partner).
## Eligible for Jobseeker Support
When a client is granted Emergency Benefit equivalent to Jobseeker Support as they can't meet the work obligations due to caring for a dependent child, their eligibility should be reviewed when their youngest child turns 14 years old. The client may be eligible for Jobseeker Support.
## Conditions of grant
Generally a client whose youngest child is aged between 3 and 13 years old will have a condition of grant to search for part-time work. When the child turns 14 years old, this should be reviewed to determine whether the client should be searching for full-time work.
## Partner's obligations
The partner of an Emergency Benefit client may have:
- work preparation obligations when their youngest dependent child is under 3 years
- work obligations and required to look for part-time work of 20 hours or more a week, when their youngest dependent child is aged between 3 and 13 years or
- work obligations and required to look for full-time work of 30 hours or more a week when the youngest dependent child is aged 14 years or over
When a client's youngest child turns 14 years old, a partner with existing part-time work obligations will be assigned full time work obligations. A letter will be automatically generated to advise the partner of the changes to their obligations.

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Child turns 18
A dependent child must generally be under the age of 18 to be included in their parent or caregiver's Emergency Benefit.
When a child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and must be excluded from their parent or caregiver's Emergency Benefit from the start of the pay period following the child's 18th birthday. The parent or caregiver must also complete a review of circumstances to determine if they continue to qualify for their discretionary benefit such as Emergency Benefit, and the rate payable.
However, if the 18-year-old child is continuing in education and is not financially independent, the child may continue to be considered a dependent child and included in their parent or caregiver's Emergency Benefit for a limited period.
In these situations, the child must be excluded from the start of the pay period following:
- the date they no longer meet these criteria or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18
whichever is earlier
Note a parent or caregiver getting Emergency Benefit must complete a review of circumstances when a dependent child turns 18, and when the child is excluded (if they continued to be included in the parent or caregiver's benefit after the child turned 18).
If the parent or caregiver does not complete the review, their Emergency Benefit will be suspended.

chunks.title: Client becomes sick — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Client becomes sick
A client who becomes sick, injured or disabled may no longer meet the qualification for which they were granted an Emergency Benefit. You will need to consider if the client qualifies under a different category for Emergency Benefit or qualifies for another benefit.
If a partner with work obligations has a health condition, injury or disability they may be exempt from meeting their work obligations until they are well again. In all cases, consider the partner's eligibility to Jobseeker Support (for a health condition, injury or disability).
Where a client (or partner's) health condition permanently and severely restricts their ability to work, they may be able to receive Supported Living Payment.
If the client (or partner) is admitted to hospital it may affect their rate of payment.
For more information see:
- Exemptions - partners
- Jobseeker Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Hospitalisation

chunks.title: Surviving partner or dependent child — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Surviving partner or dependent child
When a client dies (and there is a surviving partner or dependent child) before a decision is made on an application or review for Emergency Benefit, you can continue the application or review process as if the client had not died.
## Single client
When there is no surviving partner or dependent children the benefit application should generally be declined.
However, if there is a request for the application to be decided or the circumstances of the situation merit it, consult your manager client service delivery for a decision.
## Funeral Grant
In situations where the decision to grant or review Emergency Benefit is made after the date of death of the client, you decide any Funeral Grant as if the deceased client were getting Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Partner with child under 14 years old — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner with child under 14 years old
When a temporary visa holder dies and the surviving partner has a dependent child aged under 14 years, the partner may be able to get Emergency Benefit.
## Partner with a child over 14 years old
If the partner has a dependent child 14 years old or over, they may be able to receive Emergency Benefit with conditions of grant applicable to Jobseeker Support.
You can set the conditions of grant to ensure the partner is given time to adjust to their new circumstances.
## Partner with no dependent children
When there are no dependent children, the surviving partner must apply for a benefit, in their own right. The surviving partner may be granted a new benefit (instead of terminal benefit) from the day after their partner's death if they will get more money.
## Delay in granting ACC payments
When the death was the result of an accident, the surviving partner may be able to receive weekly compensation payments from ACC.
If there will be a delay in deciding their claim, the partner can apply for a benefit while waiting. The temporary visa holder must acknowledge, in writing, that benefit payments made will be refunded once weekly compensation payments are granted from ACC.

chunks.title: Client does not return — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Client does not return
If a client's benefit is suspended because they are absent from New Zealand and they do not return their benefit record will automatically cancel in SWIFTT, eight weeks after the date of suspension.
Note if the client had been approved continued payment of benefit for the first 28 days of the absence, this is not established as a debt.
For more information see:
- Action on return to New Zealand

chunks.title: Client engaged in study — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Client engaged in study
When an Emergency Benefit client intends to or has commenced study as a full-time student they should apply for a Student Allowance. If the client qualifies for Student Allowance, Emergency Benefit should have a future suspension from the Monday of the week the Student Allowance starts using the reason code '032 - Full-time student'.
If the client does not qualify for a Student Allowance you will need to determine whether the study affects the qualification for which the client was granted Emergency Benefit. This will include meeting any additional obligations similar to those of the benefit that the client doesn't qualify for. You will need to determine each case on its own merits.
If you are unsure whether a student is full-time or not, ask the student to provide verification from the institution where they are studying.
The Emergency Benefit should be stopped from the:
- day the client commences full-time study if they are not going to receive Student Allowance or Student Loan living costs
- Monday of the week the client commences full-time study if they are going to receive Student Allowance or Student Loan living costs (these payments are paid for the full week)
## Part-time study
