Whether a client can be a part-time student and still receive Emergency Benefit will depend on whether or not the study affects the qualification for which the client was granted Emergency Benefit. This will include meeting any conditions of grant imposed so that the Emergency Benefit mirrors the equivalent benefit.
You will need to determine each case on its own merits.

chunks.title: Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum) — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Where a client makes contact from overseas and advises their reason for travel has changed they may be able to continue to receive their payments or begin to receive payments while overseas.

chunks.title: Being paid a benefit for an approved travel period — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Where the client had already left New Zealand for an approved travel period, they may receive their payment for longer (where they have sufficient days left from their 28 days within a 52 week period).

chunks.title: Absent from New Zealand but benefit not being paid — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Where a client had left New Zealand and their benefit wasn't paid as they didn't qualify for an approved travel reason, and they now qualify for an approved travel reason, their benefit may be started from the date the client became eligible to receive the benefit overseas (where they have sufficient days left from their 28 days within a 52 week period). Examples (but not limited to: Client situation Outcome A primary client on Emergency Benefit was out of New Zealand visiting his father in Australia. His Emergency Benefit was suspended the day after he left New Zealand as it wasn't an approved travel reason. The client contacts Work and Income three days later to say that his father is in hospital as he has had a heart attack. The client has been paid for five days in the previous 52 weeks while he was absent from New Zealand leaving a balance of 23 days. The reason for travel now meets the criteria for approved travel. The benefit is resumed from the date the client became eligible to receive the benefit overseas. The client must contact Work and Income from overseas. The benefit cannot be back-dated if the client advises Work and Income when they return to New Zealand. A partner receiving Emergency Benefit left New Zealand to visit her sick mother. Two days before she was due to return, her mother's house burnt down. The client has been paid for 20 days in the previous 52 weeks while she was absent from New Zealand leaving a balance of eight days. The reason for travel has changed and the client has not been absent from New Zealand for up to 28 days in any 52 week period. The benefit expiry is extended for an additional five days. If the client hadn't informed Work and Income their benefit would have stopped from the day they were meant to return. Note that where the client has already been absent for 28 days in a 52 week period, consider whether the client meets the criteria for receiving a payment for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. For more information see: - Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return - Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event (within 28 day maximum) — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event (within 28 day maximum)
Generally, a client must advise Work and Income if there is a change in their return date. A client may need to change their return date when:
- they cannot return to New Zealand due to an event or new circumstances
- they couldn't have reasonably foreseen the event or circumstance when they left New Zealand and
- the event or circumstance is outside of their control
## Examples include (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A person receiving Emergency Benefit left New Zealand to see a sick family member. While she was in Australia there was severe flooding which meant she could not return to New Zealand on the day she was meant to return. She contacts Work and Income. The client has been paid for 20 days in the previous 52 weeks while she was absent from New Zealand, leaving a balance of eight days.
The client cannot return due to circumstances that were not reasonably foreseeable and they were outside the client's control. Work and Income would extend the client's benefit for a reasonable period for her to be able to return.
If the client hadn't informed Work and Income, their benefit would have stopped from the day they were meant to return.
A client receiving Emergency Benefit has been overseas for five days to attend his father's funeral. He is delayed in Sydney due to fog. He must remain a further three days.
The client cannot return due to circumstances that were not reasonably foreseeable and they were outside the client's control. Work and Income would extend the client's benefit for a reasonable period for him to be able to return. Also consider whether there is any grounds to pay for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Client obtains employment overseas — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Client obtains employment overseas
Where the client:
- is successful in their job prospect or job search overseas and
- they are not returning to New Zealand
the Emergency Benefit should be cancelled from the day after the notice of job appointment.
If the client returns to New Zealand for the period between getting the job and actually starting employment, the Emergency Benefit can be continued until they leave the country. The benefit must be cancelled from the day after they leave New Zealand to commence the job.

chunks.title: Client or partner remains in New Zealand — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Client or partner remains in New Zealand
Qualification for Emergency Benefit may be affected for a married, civil union or de facto couple when one of them remains in New Zealand.
This will depend on whether:
- it is the primary client or their partner who remains in New Zealand and
- payment has been approved to continue if it is the primary client overseas
## Client remains in New Zealand
If the primary client remains in New Zealand, they will continue to receive the half married, civil union or de facto rate of Jobseeker Support. If the partner is receiving any income while overseas this must be charged against the benefit.
Note you must continue to treat the couple as married or in a civil union unless they are living apart with the intention of ending their marriage or civil union.
## Partner remains in New Zealand
If the partner remains in New Zealand, they can continue to receive the half married, civil union or de facto rate of Emergency Benefit as long as payment to the primary client has been approved and is continuing to be paid while they are overseas for up to 28 days.
If payment will not continue to the client, or has been stopped, the partner will no longer qualify to receive any payment. You will need to determine if the partner qualifies for another benefit in their own right, or they may be able to receive an Emergency Benefit.
For more information see:
- Emergency Benefit Qualifications
Note the partner can only receive the half married, civil union or de facto rate of Emergency Benefit while the client is overseas, unless the couple are living apart with the intention of ending their marriage or civil union. If the primary client is receiving any income while overseas this must be charged against the benefit.
## Exception
However, there are some situations that allow Emergency Benefit client to be absent from New Zealand and continue to receive payment for a period of absence.
For details of these situations see:
- Approved travel reasons
- Overseas medical treatment

chunks.title: Clients with a partner — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Clients with a partner
When a married, civil union or de facto client is imprisoned the Emergency Benefit will generally need to be cancelled to enable the partner to be granted a benefit in their own right.
Note the Emergency Benefit should be cancelled from the day following imprisonment.
## Primary client imprisoned
If the primary client is imprisoned, the partner should be invited to apply for an alternative benefit in their own right, for example Sole Parent Support or Jobseeker Support.
## Partner of client imprisoned
If the partner of a client is imprisoned the Emergency Benefit can continue provided the primary client is not eligible for another benefit and in hardship as they are unable to earn a sufficient livelihood due to their:
- health condition, an injury or a disability
- domestic circumstances
- age or
- any other reason
Depending on their family circumstances, the Emergency Benefit will be paid at the single or sole parent rate.
When the client has dependent children, they may now be able to receive another benefit, for example Sole Parent Support. Before the Emergency Benefit is continued, the client must test their eligibility to other benefits. Only where the client is not eligible for another benefit can Emergency Benefit be considered.
## Exception
There is discretion to pay all or part of the Emergency Benefit to the partner of the person who has been imprisoned. This will depend on the length of time imprisoned.
There is also discretion to continue payment if the client is remanded in custody pending a further court appearance.
However, Emergency Benefit may be considered when a client is in hardship. Before all or part of the Emergency Benefit is paid to the partner of the person who has been imprisoned, the partner must test their eligibility to other benefit assistance.
For more information to help you decide, see:
- Decision guidelines -clients with a partner
- Remanded in custody
- SWIFTT process to pay a partner

chunks.title: Contacting Work and Income as soon as the client reasonably can — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Contacting Work and Income as soon as the client reasonably can
A client who leaves New Zealand without advising Work and Income of their travel can only have their benefit backdated to the day after departure date if they contact Work and Income as soon as they could reasonably have been expected to, given the circumstances.
This may be while the client is still absent from New Zealand, or once they have returned.
For more information see:
- Backdating benefit to the day after departure date
## Determining reasonable contact time
In order to determine whether a client contacted Work and Income as soon as they could reasonably have been expected to, you need to take into account the circumstances of the client.
The reason why the client did not contact Work and Income until after returning to New Zealand may be the same reason why they left New Zealand without advising Work and Income of their absence, or a different humanitarian reason.
Reasons for not contacting Work and Income sooner may include (but are not limited to) that the client:
- did not contact Work and Income due to the stress of the event that led to them leaving New Zealand without informing Work and Income
- left with a humanitarian reason, and then could not access the technology to communicate with Work and Income while absent from New Zealand
- left for a humanitarian reason, and then was temporarily medically unfit while overseas and they have a medical certificate that shows this
- left for humanitarian reason, and then had a death or illness in the immediate family while overseas or on return to New Zealand and/or
- left for a humanitarian reason, and then experienced an adverse event or natural disaster while overseas or on return to New Zealand that meant they were unable to contact Work and Income
## Contacting Work and Income on return to New Zealand
Generally, it would be reasonable to expect a client to contact Work and Income within 10 working days of returning to New Zealand. However, you should consider whether the client's circumstances meant they were unable to inform Work and Income in this period.
For more information see:
- Approved travel reasons
- Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure
- Partner with work or work preparation obligations or an exemption
- Partners of a main beneficiary who have youth activity obligations
- Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy

chunks.title: Court attachment orders — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Court attachment orders
All court attachment requests are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit for processing. Court attachments are administered via the CORBI screen.
The Ministry of Justice has the authority to make attachment orders on benefits to meet outstanding court fines. The attachment order may include:
- court finesthese are fines payable to the District Court
- civil attachmentsthese are generally paid to a private individual or organisation that is owed money. Occasionally the District Court will act as a collection agent for civil debts.
Attachment Orders issued by the Ministry of Justice can be made under either the Summary Proceedings Act 1957 or the District Court Act 2016.

chunks.title: Court request for information — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Court request for information
The Ministry of Justice can request the following information when they are considering either making an attachment order or assessing the client's protected earnings rate under section 87AA of the Summary Proceedings Act 1957.
- the amount of any benefit paid to the client
- the amount of any attachment orders or deduction notices issued under the following Acts: Social Security Act 2018Family Proceedings Act 1980Child Support Act 1991Tax Administration Act 1994
- Social Security Act 2018
- Family Proceedings Act 1980
- Child Support Act 1991
- Tax Administration Act 1994
- any Ministry of Social Development debt that is being recovered from the client
- the composition of the client's family, including the number of family members who are dependent on the client, as known by Work and Income
This information is used to determine how much the client can reasonably be expected to pay each week on any outstanding fines.
For more information see:
- Protected earnings rate
## Information that can be provided
Work and Income can provide the Ministry of Justice with the last known address and telephone number of a client under schedule 6, cl 13 Social Security Act 2018. This only applies when the Ministry of Justice is unable to locate a client who is in default of a court fine.

chunks.title: Date of review (including backdating) — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Date of review (including backdating)
Include the new born child in the benefit and pay family tax credit from the:
- date of birth or
- date the client's benefit was granted
whichever is the later.
## Backdating
When a client requests the backdated inclusion of a child and the previous caregiver was getting a benefit for the child, you will need to review when the child was excluded from the previous caregivers benefit.
Note a child cannot be included in two benefits for the same period.
Consider all the circumstances and decide whether a debt should be established for the previous caregiver.
If the date you are including the child from is a date in the previous tax year, SWIFTT will only pay arrears of family tax credit from the beginning of the current tax year, that is, 1 April. You will need to advise the client that any arrears of family tax credit before this date will need to be claimed from Inland Revenue.
You will need to do a backdated review in the SBDR screen to pay any benefit arrears to the client for the previous tax year. A backdated review may be required for the current year if other rate changes have occurred - check the SRAUI screen for details.
For more information see:
- Processing standards Child changes [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Date payment should be reduced — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Date payment should be reduced
The hospital rate is paid when the client has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks, not after receiving a benefit for 13 weeks. Reduce the client's benefit to the hospital rate or appropriate higher rate from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation.
## Client in hospital when benefit commences
If the client has been in hospital for 13 weeks or more at the commencement date of the benefit, the rate of payment is the hospital rate or a higher rate (if applicable).
If the client has been in hospital for less than 13 weeks at the commencement date of the benefit, the full rate of payment is paid until the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation.
The date of admission and the date of discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital and are not included in the 13-week calculation.
## SWIFTT
Add the client's admission date on the SHODA screen. SWIFTT will automatically reduce the rate of payment to the hospital rate from the beginning of the 14th week after the admission date.
## Transfer between hospitals
Transfer from one hospital to another does not interrupt the period of hospitalisation, which will be taken as continuous from the original admission date. Ensure that SHODA is updated to show the new hospital details.
## Consider any short-term leave
Any periods of leave from hospital of 28 days or less are to be ignored when deciding the date from which the benefit is to be reduced. Calculate the period in hospital from the original admission date. If the client has been allowed out of hospital for more than 28 days, the calculation of the period in hospital begins again after the client has been re-admitted.
## Client formally discharged
If the client has been formally discharged from the hospital and then re-admitted, the 13 week calculation starts again from the day after they are re-admitted (even if the client has been re-admitted within 28 days of being discharged).
For more information see:
- Paying a higher rate

chunks.title: Death of a child — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a dependent child dies, the child should be excluded from a couple's benefit from the start of the pay period following the date of the child's death. When a dependent child dies they should be excluded from a sole parent's benefit 28 days following the date of death. Payment of the benefit may continue at the existing rate for 28 days following the date the child died. This provides a transition period for the client to adjust to their change in circumstances. Note during the 28-day continuation of payment, if the client has other changes of circumstances e.g. a change in income, the rate of any benefit will need to be reassessed using the sole parent threshold rates.

chunks.title: Mandatory Reviews — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Clients must still respond to a Mandatory Review for Emergency Benefit during the 28-day continuation of payment. They may be able to get an extension or an exemption.

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Generally, clients getting a discretionary benefit such as Emergency Benefit must respond to their notice before the child's 18th birthday or the child will be excluded from their payments. The client must also complete a review of circumstances to determine if they continue to qualify for Emergency Benefit and the rate payable, or their payments will suspend. If Emergency Benefit and any extra help is continuing at the existing rate for up to 28 days because a sole parent's child has died, and the child that died was due to turn 18 during that period, the client is not required to complete a review of circumstances. However, if Emergency Benefit and any extra help is continuing at the existing rate for up to 28 days because a sole parent's child has died and a different child in their care turns 18, the client must still complete the review of circumstances or their payments will suspend.

chunks.title: Childcare assistance — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Childcare assistance paid for the child must be stopped on the day after the child died.

chunks.title: Family tax credit — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Family tax credits should be stopped from the start of the pay period following the date the child died, to avoid an overpayment with Inland Revenue for the client.

chunks.title: Best Start tax credit — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Best Start tax credit is continued for 28 days following the child's date of death. If the child's third birthday occurs in the 28-day period the Best Start tax credit stops from the date of the child's third birthday.

chunks.title: Cost of funeral — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: The person responsible for the cost of the child's funeral may be able to get a Funeral Grant.

chunks.title: Death of a client — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Death of a client
The date benefit payment stops following the death of a client depends on whether the client has:
- a partner
- a dependent child
## Mandatory Reviews
There are no Mandatory Reviews of Emergency Benefit when the client has died.
## Child turns 18
A child will not be excluded from the parent or caregiver's Emergency Benefit when the child turns 18 during the terminal benefit period.
The review of circumstances for a discretionary benefit such as Emergency Benefit when their child turns 18 is not required when the client has died.

chunks.title: Death of a client with a partner or child — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Emergency Benefit can continue to be paid for 28 days after the death of a client when there is a surviving partner or child, and the surviving partner is not entitled to a survivor's grant from ACC. Emergency Benefit can also continue to be paid for 28 days after the death of a single client who is a: - liable person and paying Child Support payments or - caregiver getting Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit Continuing payments after the date of death is known as a terminal benefit. When terminal benefit is being paid to a couple, both the deceased person and the surviving person's portion of the benefit continues to be paid. The total benefit, including the surviving person's portion, plus any extra help continues for 28 days.

chunks.title: Surviving partner will get more money on other assistance — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Sometimes the surviving partner or the caregiver of the child would get more money (based on their new circumstances) on: - a new main benefit or - their existing benefit at a higher rate instead of getting their portion of their current assistance for 28 days.

chunks.title: New benefit paid at a higher rate — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: If the surviving person's benefit is reviewed and they qualify for a new benefit at a higher rate, they may be granted a new benefit instead of terminal benefit from the day after a client's death. If the deceased person qualified for a terminal benefit their portion will continue to be paid.

chunks.title: Current benefit paid at a higher rate — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: If the surviving person's current benefit is reviewed and they qualify for a higher rate, their benefit rate increases from the day after their partner's death. MSD pays this instead of their portion of the terminal benefit as they will get more money. If the deceased person qualified for a terminal benefit their portion will continue to be paid.

chunks.title: Changing benefits or the benefit rate — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: What the surviving person needs to do depends on whether the benefit they were getting before their partner's death was as the primary client or the dependent partner.

chunks.title: Surviving person is entitled to a survivor's grant from ACC — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: When the death of the person was the result of an accident, entitlement to a survivor's grant from ACC needs to be decided before terminal benefit can be paid. If the surviving person or child is entitled to a survivor's grant from ACC there is no entitlement to terminal benefit. If Emergency Benefit payments have continued after the date of death, an overpayment is established and the debt should be recovered from the estate.

chunks.title: Funeral costs — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: The person responsible for the cost of the funeral may also be able to get a Funeral Grant.

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: A child will not be excluded from the parent or caregiver's Emergency Benefit when the child turns 18 during the 28-day continuation of payment period. The review of circumstances for a discretionary benefit such as Emergency Benefit when their child turns 18 is not required when the client has died.

chunks.title: Death of a single client — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Death of a single client
When a single client (with no children) dies, payment generally stops from the day after the date of death, but there is some discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days.
Payment should stop from the first available date if we have been notified within 28 days of the date of death. This will avoid creating a debt.
When there are other circumstances that justify payment of terminal benefit, payment should continue for the full 28 days after death.
Note a single client who is a liable person and paying Child Support payments, or a caregiver getting Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit is regarded as having children.

chunks.title: Debt Repayment Orders — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Debt Repayment Orders
All Debt Repayment Orders are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit for processing.
Debt Repayment Orders are issued by the Ministry of Justice under the Insolvency Act 2006 and can be issued when the client is an un-discharged bankrupt.
Unlike other Ministry of Justice attachment orders, Debt Repayment Orders are not subject to any protected earnings rate. Payment is generally made to the supervisor of the debt but occasionally the District Court will act as an agent for collection of the debt.
Payment continues for three years or until further notice is received from either the supervisor or the District Court.
Unlike Ministry of Justice attachment orders, Debt Repayment Orders are administered via the PYECI screen in SWIFTT, not through CORBI.

chunks.title: Deciding if surviving person would be better off getting terminal benefit or another benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Deciding if surviving person would be better off getting terminal benefit or another benefit
Terminal benefit is paid for 28 days when a client dies and has a surviving partner and/or children.
When terminal benefit is being paid to a couple, both the deceased person and the surviving person’s portion of the benefit is paid. Payment is the total benefit including any ongoing Extra help. It does not include family tax credit and Best Start tax credit.
Sometimes the surviving person or the caregiver of the children would get more money (based on their new circumstances) on a new benefit or their existing benefit at a higher rate, instead of getting their portion of their current assistance for 28 days.
Compare the surviving person’s potential new benefit and ongoing Extra help (from the date after death) against the surviving person’s portion of benefit and ongoing Extra help they were getting before their partner’s death.
Generally, the surviving person will get more money if they change to a single rate of benefit.
If the deceased person qualified for terminal benefit, their portion will continue to be paid to their bank account.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Decision guidelines - clients with a partner — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Decision guidelines - clients with a partner
While Emergency Benefit should generally be stopped when the primary client is imprisoned, there is discretion for payment to be continued and paid to the partner not in prison. This discretion allows payment of all or part of the Emergency Benefit to the partner.
Note if the partner is eligible for another benefit, the other benefit should be granted and Emergency Benefit cancelled.
If you feel that payment should be continued, and paid to the partner, this should generally be at the single or sole parent rate. However you can pay the full married, civil union or de facto rate if you feel this is warranted after having regard to the particular circumstances of the client and their partner.
To help you decide whether it is reasonable to pay the Emergency Benefit to the partner while the client is in prison, and the rate to pay, consider the following:
- has the period in prison already passed?
- is the client due to be released from prison shortly?
- is the likely period in prison less than six months?
- does the partner qualify for a statutory benefit in their own right?
- do they intend to live together when the partner is released?
- has the partner in prison applied for Home Detention?
- are there exceptional circumstances that justify paying the full married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit to the partner who is not in prison?
For further help you can contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances before you make your decision.
For more information see:
- SWIFTT process to pay a partner

chunks.title: Decision guidelines for shared care — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Decision guidelines for shared care
The parent with greater responsibility is usually the parent who has the child for most of the time. If a parent has the child for at least 60% of the time they have the primary responsibility.
Where parents have equal time, to help you decide which parent has greater responsibility, consider the following:
- who pays for the child's material support (furniture, clothes etc)
- who decides about the child's daily activities
- who takes them to and from school and supervises leisure activities
- who makes decisions about their education and health
- who pays for which expenses
If it is not clear who has greater responsibility or the parents share the responsibility equally, the parent who was mainly responsible for the day to day care of the child before the separation is the person who can have the child included.
If you can't decide who is entitled to have the child included, the parents must make the decision. Don't include the child in any income support until they have decided.

chunks.title: Decision guidelines - sole parents — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Decision guidelines - sole parents
When a sole parent Emergency Benefit client is imprisoned it is important that financial assistance is available to support any dependent children.
While Emergency Benefit should generally be stopped when the client is imprisoned, there is discretion for payment to be continued and paid to the person who is caring for the client's dependent children.
To help you decide whether it is reasonable to pay the Emergency Benefit to a temporary caregiver while the client is in prison consider the following:
- has the period in prison already passed
- is the client due to be released from prison shortly
- is the likely period in prison less than 12 months
- will the children return to the client's care on their release from prison
- has the caregiver ceased work to care for the children
- has the caregiver lost entitlement to their own benefit due to having children in their care
For further help you can contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances before you make your decision.
For more information see:
- Temporary caregiver
- Rate of payment - sole parents
- Examples - sole parents
- Remanded in custody

chunks.title: Definition of discharged from Oranga Tamariki care — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Definition of discharged from Oranga Tamariki care
A child/young person is considered discharged from care when they are discharged from:
- the sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency
- the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency under a custody order made under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 or
- the care of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency under an agreement made under section 140 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
For more information see:
- Oranga Tamariki order in place

chunks.title: Definition of family member — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Definition of family member
A family member includes a client's:
- partner
- sibling (includes half-sibling and step-sibling but excludes members of organisations/gangs referring to themselves as 'blood brothers and sisters')
- children (includes, stepchildren, foster children, and whāngai - children who have been raised, normally by a relation or other person within the wider whānau to which the child belongs)
- grandchildren or mokopuna (includes grandchildren raised by the client as the principal caregivers)
- grandparents
- parent (includes step-parents and foster parents)
- partner's parent
- parent’s sibling (includes aunt, uncle, step-aunt, step-uncle)
- cousin
A family member can also be another person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family.

chunks.title: Definition of imprisonment — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Definition of imprisonment
A person is regarded as serving a sentence of imprisonment if they are detained in any of the following:
- a prison
- a police jail
- remand prison
Note a prisoner who has escaped from custody is considered to be serving a sentence of imprisonment.
They may be serving a term of:
- imprisonment
- preventive detention or
- corrective training
Note people remanded in custody or serving a term of imprisonment who are temporarily hospitalised for treatment of an injury or illness are still considered to be in prison. However, where a prisoner serving a sentence of imprisonment is detained in or transferred to, a psychiatric hospital they may qualify for financial assistance from Work and Income.
For more information see:
- Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital

chunks.title: Definition of 'support' from a family member residing overseas — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Definition of 'support' from a family member residing overseas
'Support' means assistance that the young person could not reasonably obtain from a family member in New Zealand, and includes (but is not limited to):
- emotional support
- educational support
- mentoring/guidance
- any other assistance that is beneficial to the welfare of the young person.
Note in assessing whether the young person could not reasonably obtain the support from a family member in New Zealand, you should consider:
- the type and nature of the relationship with the family member residing overseas
- whether there are features of the young person's relationship with that family member that are absent from their relationships with other family members residing in New Zealand (such as shared experiences and the nature of the relationship)

chunks.title: Dependent child — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
A dependent child for Emergency Benefit is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Emergency Benefit does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- child for whom Orphan's or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
- not a child for whom a Young Parent Payment is being paid (except in relation to that child's parent or step-parent). That is, a young person getting Young Parent Payment (and their child) cannot also be included in another main benefit as neither of them are considered a dependent child. For more information see:Examples of dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent
## Primary responsibility
The client must be responsible for the day-to-day care of the child and be the person who makes the major decisions concerning the child's life (for example schooling and health care).
There are some situations where the person who has primary responsibility of a child is not clear.
## Maintained as a member of the family
The child should be an integral part of the family, participating in the usual family activities (for example outings and annual holidays).
In some situations, a child may not be living at home but is still considered to be a dependent child.
Dependent children should be included in the assessment of Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Continuing dependent partner's portion of benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Continuing dependent partner's portion of benefit
When the partner of an Emergency Benefit client dies, the partner’s portion of benefit is continued for 28 days at the same rate that was being paid at their date of death. Benefit payments that continue after the day a client has died are called ‘terminal benefit’.
## Dependent children
When there are dependent children included in the benefit, family tax credit payments should be transferred to the primary client. Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit payments are not part of the terminal benefit.
## Client's benefit options
A surviving client, with dependent children, can remain on Emergency Benefit if they meet the qualifications for an Emergency Benefit and are not entitled to receive a statutory benefit such as a Sole Parent Support from the date after the death.
It is important that the client's entitlement to a statutory benefit is checked before continuing an Emergency Benefit.
## No dependent children
A client would stay on Emergency Benefit if they have no dependent children.
## Date of review
When the surviving client remains on Emergency Benefit review the client's benefit from the date after the death of their partner. You need to:
- increase their benefit to the single or sole parent rate and
- adjust any Extra help to the single or sole parent rate
When the client applies for (and is granted) Sole Parent Support, cancel their Emergency Benefit from the date after the death of their partner.
Note when the surviving client decides to receive a new benefit or their existing benefit at the increased rate, the deceased partner’s portion of the benefit is continued for 28 days at the rate being paid at the date of death (if the deceased person qualifies for terminal benefit).
## Funeral costs
The person responsible for the cost of the funeral may be able to receive a Funeral Grant.
For more information see:
- Sole Parent Support

chunks.title: Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital
When person who has been remanded in custody or serving a term of imprisonment, is detained in or transferred to a psychiatric hospital you may be able to pay an Emergency Benefit at the hospital rate.
People who are remanded in custody or serving a term of imprisonment who are temporarily hospitalised for treatment of an injury or illness are still considered to be in prison and the Department of Corrections will meet their costs. Therefore an Emergency Benefit or any other financial assistance cannot be paid.
For more information see:
- Emergency Benefit Person serving their sentence of imprisonment in a psychiatric hospital
- Release from prison

chunks.title: Discharge from hospital — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Discharge from hospital
Where a client is receiving the hospital rate and they are discharged from hospital:
- increase their benefit to the appropriate full rate from the date of discharge
- for married, civil union or de facto clients reduce the partner's benefit to the half married, civil union or de facto rate and cancel Special Disability Allowance and
- review any Extra Help from the same date
Note the dates of admission and discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital.
## Re-admitted to hospital
Where a client (who has been formally discharged from hospital) is re-admitted, the 13 week period starts again from the day after they are re-admitted (even if the client has been re-admitted within 28 days of being discharged).
Note this only refers to clients who are formally discharged from hospital not clients on leave. For more information about clients on leave from hospital see:
- On leave from hospital

chunks.title: Discharged from Oranga Tamariki care — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Discharged from Oranga Tamariki care
Where Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency has care, custody or sole guardianship of the child, and returns the child to the care of the immediate previous caregiver, they do not make payments for the child.
The child is then a dependent child and can be included in the Emergency Benefit.
Where the relationship is not one of care, but more of a boarding arrangement, the young person may be able to receive Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment.
Once a child has been discharged from care the child can be considered a dependent child even when Oranga Tamariki or any other authorised agency involvement continues, for example:
- Additional Guardianship Order
- Support Order or
- Services Order
When there is a Service or Support Order in place, you will need to make sure that the Court's intent allows you to consider the child as a dependent child.
For further details on what discharged from care means see:
- Definition of discharged from Oranga Tamariki care

chunks.title: Effect on benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Effect on benefit
Any inclusion or exclusion of a dependent child from a client's benefit will result in a general review of the client's Emergency Benefit and any extra help they are getting.
You may need to review the following:
- Emergency BenefitPartner's work obligations may change.
When a single client has a child come into their care they may no longer be able to meet their work obligations. They may be able to receive Sole Parent Support - Work or work preparation obligations or an Emergency Benefit - Single and caring for a child.
- Accommodation SupplementChanges to the family composition may result in a change to the Accommodation Supplement entry thresholds.
- Non-standard benefit rateWhen a child is added or removed you may need to manually adjust the non-standard rate of payment.
- Special BenefitAny change to family circumstances will result in a review of Special Benefit. A child included or excluded from the Emergency Benefit may result in a change to the allowable costs for Special Benefit.
- Temporary Additional SupportAny change to family circumstances will result in a review of Temporary Additional Support. A child included or excluded from the Emergency Benefit may result in a change to the allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support.
- Disability Allowance

chunks.title: Effect on Extra Help — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Extra help can continue to be paid to the temporary visa holder for the first 13 weeks that they are in hospital. When the temporary visa holder's benefit is reduced to the hospital rate, any Extra help they receive will need to be reviewed. Note temporary visa holders stranded in New Zealand cannot receive any additional assistance except for Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit,

chunks.title: Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: As long as the child continues to be a dependent child, family tax credit payments and Best Start tax credits continue to be paid regardless of how long the temporary visa holder is in hospital.

chunks.title: Special Benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: For a single client stop the Special Benefit from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation. Check whether the client still has to meet their continuing costs. If so, increase the benefit rate above the hospital rate to meet the costs. For a married, civil union or de facto couple Special Benefit must be stopped from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation for the client who is in hospital. From the same date you will need to review Special Benefit and pay the full amount to the partner not in hospital. Generally no additional costs associated with the hospitalisation should be added to Special Benefit for a married, civil union or de facto client. However you will need to have regard to their individual circumstances taking into consideration that the partner not in hospital is increased to the single rate of payment and can receive Special Disability Allowance to cover any extra costs.

chunks.title: Temporary Additional Support — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: For a single client stop Temporary Additional Support from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation. Check whether the client still has to meet their continuing costs. If so, increase the benefit rate above the hospital rate to meet the costs. For a married, civil union or de facto couple Temporary Additional Support must be stopped from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation for the client who is in hospital. From the same date you will need to review Temporary Additional Support and pay the full amount to the partner not in hospital. No additional costs associated with the hospitalisation should be added to Temporary Additional Support for married civil union or de facto client. However you will need to have regard to their individual circumstances taking into consideration that the partner not in hospital is increased to the single rate of payment and can receive Special Disability Allowance to cover any extra costs.

chunks.title: Disability Allowance — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Cancel the client's Disability Allowance from the date the benefit is reduced to the hospital rate. All costs associated with the client's disability are the responsibility of the hospital.

chunks.title: Family tax credit — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: As long as the child continues to be a dependent child, family tax credit payments continue to be paid regardless of how long the client is in hospital.

chunks.title: Winter Energy Payment — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: For a single client who is getting the Winter Energy Payment and who has had their main benefit reduced to the hospital rate, they can only get the Winter Energy Payment if they still require assistance with their energy costs. Where a partner is in hospital (no dependent children) the client who is still living in the community can receive the full couple rate of the Winter Energy Payment. For more information see: - Winter Energy Payment - Hospitalisation

chunks.title: Emergency Benefit suspended before Mandatory Review date — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Emergency Benefit suspended before Mandatory Review date
Clients getting Emergency Benefit are always notified about their Mandatory Review, even if their Emergency Benefit is suspended, unless it is suspended due to the client being temporarily overseas or in prison.
MSD must not undertake the Mandatory Review unless the client contacts MSD to resume their Emergency Benefit.
If the client contacts MSD before their review date to resume their benefit, they may be able to get an extension if they need more time to do their Mandatory Review. MSD can resume the benefit before the Mandatory Review has been responded to.
However, if the client contacts MSD on or after the Mandatory Review date, the review must be completed before MSD can resume the benefit (if they still qualify).
## Example
Sean is single, has no dependent children, and does not meet the residency or job search requirements to qualify for Jobseeker Support. Sean is getting Emergency Benefit, which expires in 2 years. A Mandatory Review of his circumstances is scheduled for 2 August 2027, prior to the benefit's expiry.
Sean left New Zealand to go on holiday on 29 July 2027 and did not tell MSD that he was leaving. His Emergency Benefit suspended on 30 July 2027.
On 14 August 2027 Sean contacts MSD and advises that he arrived back in New Zealand on 7 August 2027.
MSD advises Sean that he will need to respond to the Mandatory Review and confirm his circumstances before MSD can resume his Emergency Benefit.
On 17 August Sean responds to his Mandatory Review and confirms that he has had no change in circumstances.
MSD determines that Sean continues to qualify for Emergency Benefit at the same rate and resumes his benefit from 7 August 2027.
MSD completes Sean's Mandatory Review on 17 August 2027 and sets the next review date for 52 weeks from the date the review was completed.
Sean's next Mandatory Review date is 15 August 2028.

chunks.title: Ending payment for client who needs an approved reason to travel (within 28 day maximum) — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Ending payment for client who needs an approved reason to travel (within 28 day maximum)
When a client or their partner is receiving their payments while they are absent from New Zealand for an approved reason their payments will suspend automatically on their agreed return date.
For example, a client has been approved travel to attend a job interview in Sydney. They are approved 3 days. The benefit will suspend automatically on the day they were meant to return.
Where the client or partner is receiving their payments while they are absent from New Zealand because they have an approved travel reason and their return date changes, they must advise the Ministry of Social Development from overseas, otherwise their payment will be stopped from the day they originally advised they would return to New Zealand.
## Benefit can be backdated once back in New Zealand in very limited circumstances
A client who is continuing to be paid while they are absent from New Zealand for an approved reason may be able to have their benefit backdated if there is an unforeseen reason they cannot notify the Ministry while they are overseas.
For example, a client boards a plane to return home on schedule and the plane is held up due to fog. There is no way the client could notify the Ministry due to an event outside of their control. When the client contacts the Ministry once they are back in New Zealand, their benefit would be resumed from the original date the client was due to return (this will be on the itinerary or e-ticket).
For more information see:
- Approved travel reasons
- Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Ending payment for partner who can travel for any reason (within 28 day maximum) — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Ending payment for partner who can travel for any reason (within 28 day maximum)
Where a partner can travel for any reason their payments will suspend automatically on the 29th day in a 52 week period they have been absent from New Zealand and continued to receive a payment.
## Partner may need to be absent for more than 28 days
A partner may be required to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days.
For more information see:
- Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
- Ending payments for client who needs an approved reason to travel
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Essential travel — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Essential travel
A client not otherwise entitled to be paid their Emergency Benefit while they are absent from New Zealand may have their payments continue for up to 28 days in any 52 week period if they have to travel outside of New Zealand to attend a significant event relating to a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family).
These events are ones which the client or partner would reasonably be expected to attend. That is, the travel is essential to them and where not attending the event would cause the person emotional distress. This may include, but is not limited to, travel that allows the client to:
- be with a seriously ill or dying person who is a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family)
- attend a funeral or an unveiling in relation to a family member
- pay respect to a family member of the deceased in the event of the client missing the funeral
- attend to legal matters in relation to the affairs of the deceased family member
- attend a birth of a family member or be with a family member around the time of their giving birth
- provide support to a party or witness to a court case
- attend a wedding of a family member - the client does not need to be a member of the bridal party or play a significant part in the wedding in order for the payment of benefit to continue while they are absent from New Zealand
- travel for a court ordered custody arrangement
For more information see:
- Definition of family member
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect
- Permitted travel reasons
- Paying a benefit when client failed to advise of absence
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within a 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: The following examples show situations where a benefit may be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period (but not limited to): Client's reason for travelling for 28 days within 52 week period Client's current reason for travel within 52 week period Outcome Essential travel reasons Essential travel reason eg a seriously ill family member Generally consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if reasonable in the circumstances Job interview or job prospect Essential travel reason eg a funeral Generally would consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if reasonable in the circumstances Young partners of a person receiving Emergency Benefit who has youth activity obligations to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with these obligations. The client wishes to be absent from New Zealand for another general holiday This is not an approved reason for paying for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. The client would not be able to receive a benefit while absent from New Zealand for this reason even if the travel will not prevent them meeting their obligations (eg even if the travel is at a time when they are not required to be in education, training or work-based learning) Young partners of a person receiving Emergency Benefit who has youth activity obligations to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with these obligations. To provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster or similar adverse event. Generally would allow further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. This is an unforeseen event and it is reasonable for them to help their family member. Young partners of a person receiving Emergency Benefit who has youth activity obligations to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with these obligations. Essential travel reason Generally would consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if the essential travel reason was unforeseen. Young partners of a person receiving Emergency Benefit who has youth activity obligations to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with these obligations. Needs to attend a wedding of a family member. Generally would not consider allowing a further period of payment for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.

chunks.title: Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Weddings are usually known about in advance and this should have been planned for when they used the 28 days to go on holiday. However, where the wedding is genuinely unforeseen, consideration could be given to allowing travel for a period of more than 28 days in a 52 week period. Young partners of a person receiving Emergency Benefit who has youth activity obligations had to spend four days at a funeral overseas. The young partner had booked a holiday prior to the attendance at the funeral overseas. This holiday was booked for 28 days because they are able to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with their obligations. The client does not have the full 28 days left Travelling for a general holiday is not an approved reason for paying a benefit for more than 28 days in a 52 week period The benefit will only be paid for the number of days the client has available (that is, 24 days).

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Carlos contacts MSD on 19 November to advise that he has returned from travelling to Malaysia to be with his dying mother. He left in a hurry and didn't contact MSD before his departure. His Emergency Benefit stopped on 4 November, the day after he left the country. He returned to New Zealand on 14 November, but then had to organise a New Zealand-based funeral for his mother, as a large number of people are based in New Zealand. Carlos didn't advise MSD of his travel before leaving New Zealand, but he has a humanitarian reason that justifies his travel and the reason he didn't contact MSD before he left. Given Carlos' circumstances, he contacted MSD as soon as it would have been reasonable to expect him to and he meets the criteria for an approved travel reason. Carlos' Emergency Benefit can be backdated to 4 November.

chunks.title: Example 2 — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Sanjay left New Zealand for India on 7 December because his father had become suddenly seriously ill and been hospitalised. While in India, Sanjay's father passed away and Sanjay stayed in India for the funeral. Sanjay returned on 16 December, after staying for 2 weeks for the Hindu funeral and mourning period. On 19 December, Sanjay contacts MSD to explain that he has been overseas after learning of his father's illness, and that he stayed for the funeral. On return, Sanjay spent time mourning with his own family and has been distraught. He explains that he only realised last night that he had not informed MSD of his absence. Sanjay's reason for leaving New Zealand is a humanitarian reason and he meets the criteria for backdating his payment to the day after departure. Given Sanjay's circumstances, he informed MSD as soon as he reasonably could. Sanjay's Emergency Benefit can be backdated to 8 December, the date it was suspended.

chunks.title: Example 3 — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Tusila calls MSD on 5 October to tell them she will leave New Zealand on 7 October to help her sister, who just lost her house in a flood. When asked how long she will be gone for, Tusila says that she hasn't bought a return ticket yet and was considering staying on to catch up with family and see how her sister is going. MSD informs Tusila that she can only keep getting her Emergency Benefit if she is absent for essential travel. Helping her sister after a flood is considered essential travel, however if she is going to stay longer for a holiday, she won't be able to get Emergency Benefit during the time she is on holiday. Tusila returns to MSD the next day with an airline quote showing that the cheapest return flight is on 14 October. She thinks it will take her a week to ensure her sister has sorted out insurance, medium-term accommodation, and access to basic goods like clothing and food. She has decided not to stay on for the holiday. MSD agrees this is reasonable and tells Tusila she can keep getting Emergency Benefit from 7 to 14 October, while she is overseas helping her sister.

chunks.title: Example 4 — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Christy is getting Emergency Benefit and contacts MSD to advise that her sister is getting married in Australia on 8 September. Christy is going to Australia to her sister's wedding but intends to stay on for a further 2 weeks to visit other family. Christy is leaving New Zealand on 4 September as she has to help her sister prepare. She will stay until10 September to help clean up. Christy then begins the holiday leg of her trip, returning to New Zealand on 25 September. Christy's travel is divided as follows: - 5 September to 10 September period meets the essential travel criteria - 11 September to 24 September period is considered other travel (holiday) and does not meet the essential travel criteria. Christy's Emergency Benefit can only be paid until 10 September, for the period that meets the essential travel criteria.

chunks.title: Example 5 — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Graeme left New Zealand on 16 August to help his sister in Australia after she lost her house in a fire. He returns to New Zealand on 23 August. A week later, on 30 August he attends an appointment and asks why he hasn't been getting his Emergency Benefit. His case manager informs him that his payments stopped when he left the country and asks why he didn't contact MSD sooner. Graeme explains that he left to help his sister after a house fire, and he meant to contact MSD once he had helped his sister sort out accommodation and insurance, but he forgot. The case manager explains that because he didn't contact MSD as soon as he reasonably could have been expected to (i.e. once he had helped his sister), his Emergency Benefit can only be backdated to 23 August, the date he returned to New Zealand.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Example 1
A client applies for benefit to be paid for 10 days when they are going to be absent from New Zealand. In the past 52 weeks the client has had 10 days absence from New Zealand and continued being paid their benefit
Step
Calculation
Identify the day after the client is intending to leave New Zealand.
14 September 2019
Count back 52 weeks from this date.
15 September 2018
Count the number of days the client continued getting their benefit while they were overseas in this 52 week period.
Days client has continued to get their benefit while absent from New Zealand between 14 September 2018 and 15 September 2019 = 10 days
Subtract the number of days the client has been paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand from 28 days.
28 - 10 days = 18 days available
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay the client for the days they have available.
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay them for the 10 days they are out of the country.
## Example 2
A client applies for benefit to be paid for 10 days when they are going to be absent from New Zealand. In the past 52 weeks the client has had 20 days absent from New Zealand and continued to be paid their benefit
Step
Calculation
Identify the day after the client is intending to leave New Zealand.
14 September 2014
Count back 52 weeks from this date.
15 September 2013
Count the number of days the client has continued to getting their benefit while they were overseas in this 52 week period.
Days client has continued to get their benefit while absent from NZ between 14 September 2013 and 15 September 2014 = 20 days
Subtract the number of days the client got their benefit while absent from New Zealand from 28 days.
28 - 20 days = 8 days available
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay the client for the days they have available.
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay them for the 8 days they are out of the country. For 2 of the days they are absent from New Zealand they will not get their payments.
Check if the client meets the criteria to receive their benefit for more than 28 days in a 52 week period - they meet these criteria, they may be able to continue getting their payment for the additional 2 days of absence.

chunks.title: Examples of job interviews and prospects overseas — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: - Some examples of job interviews and prospects overseas are: Client situationOutcomeClient on Emergency Benefit has a job interview for a maintenance position with a mining company in Kalgoorlie, Western Australia. He has a definite job interview for an advertised position and has an email confirming this.This client can continue to be paid his Emergency Benefit for the five days he is absent from New Zealand to attend the job interview.An employer in Sydney has asked a client to come over and meet him to discuss a job prospect in his factory. It is not a formal interview, but a discussion about what the role would involve. If the client meets the employer and they agree, there may be a job offer.The client can continue to be paid their Emergency Benefit for three days while he is absent from New Zealand.A client has made appointments with specific recruitment companies in Melbourne, Australia.There are interview times booked with specific consultants.This client can continue to be paid their Emergency Benefit for the three days while they are absent from New Zealand.A client advises they are heading to the Gold Coast to 'look for work' and undertake job search. They do not have a job interview or a specific job prospect. Their aim is to undertake general job search and go and see a few employers which they will find when they get there.This provision cannot be used to allow general job search overseas and the client will not be able to continue to receive payment if they are absent from New Zealand for this reason. Client situation Outcome Client on Emergency Benefit has a job interview for a maintenance position with a mining company in Kalgoorlie, Western Australia. He has a definite job interview for an advertised position and has an email confirming this. This client can continue to be paid his Emergency Benefit for the five days he is absent from New Zealand to attend the job interview. An employer in Sydney has asked a client to come over and meet him to discuss a job prospect in his factory. It is not a formal interview, but a discussion about what the role would involve. If the client meets the employer and they agree, there may be a job offer. The client can continue to be paid their Emergency Benefit for three days while he is absent from New Zealand. A client has made appointments with specific recruitment companies in Melbourne, Australia. There are interview times booked with specific consultants. This client can continue to be paid their Emergency Benefit for the three days while they are absent from New Zealand.

chunks.title: Examples of job interviews and prospects overseas — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: A client advises they are heading to the Gold Coast to 'look for work' and undertake job search. They do not have a job interview or a specific job prospect. Their aim is to undertake general job search and go and see a few employers which they will find when they get there. This provision cannot be used to allow general job search overseas and the client will not be able to continue to receive payment if they are absent from New Zealand for this reason.

chunks.title: Examples of Mandatory Review outcomes — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD must review a client's Emergency Benefit within 52-weeks of the commencement date of their benefit, or 52-weeks from when the client's last Mandatory Review was completed. The Mandatory Review is completed when MSD has determined if the client continues to qualify for Emergency Benefit and the rate payable (if applicable). When a client responds to the review, there are a number of outcomes that can occur. Once MSD has determined if the client qualifies, MSD will either: - continue paying the benefit at the existing rate - adjust the rate of benefit so the client is getting the correct rate - suspend the benefit if there is no rate payable for a period (e.g. client has variable income) - cancel the benefit if the client no longer qualifies

chunks.title: Examples of outcomes that can occur — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Outcomes of a Mandatory Review Examples Client declares no change (exception doesn't apply) Ashley is a single person and does not meet the 2-year continuous residency criteria for Supported Living Payment. Ashley is getting Emergency Benefit at the Supported Living Payment single 18+ rate. It will expire 18 months after it commenced, when Ashley will meet the residency criteria for Supported Living Payment. Her first Mandatory Review is due on 15 July 2026. Ashley responds to her Mandatory Review on 14 July 2026 and confirms she has had no change to her circumstances. Because Ashley has declared no change in circumstances, MSD continues her Emergency Benefit at the same rate. MSD completes Ashley's Mandatory Review on 14 July 2026. No future Mandatory Review is set for Ashley because her Emergency Benefit will expire in 6 months. Client declares no change (exception applies) Mae is getting Emergency Benefit, Accommodation Supplement and Disability Allowance and pays rent of $350.00 per week in Area 1. Her Mandatory Review is due on 9 June 2027, and she responds on 7 June 2027 to confirm she has had no change in her circumstances. While her Disability Allowance costs were updated last year, she hasn't declared a change in rent since January 2024. Because Mae has been getting Accommodation Supplement and declared no change in her accommodation costs for three consecutive years, MSD must consider whether further information is required before completing the Mandatory Review. MSD considers Mae's circumstances and sees that she hasn't provided verification of her accommodation costs since moving to her current apartment in 2024. Given Mae lives in an area where rental accommodation is very limited and rents have increased significantly, MSD determines that it is reasonable to request verification of her accommodation costs to confirm that the information is correct before making a decision about her entitlement. Mae is asked to provide this information before 7 July 2027 (her new deadline for the review) or her Emergency Benefit, Accommodation Supplement and Disability Allowance will stop. Mae contacts MSD on 1 July 2027 with the evidence requested. MSD determines that Mae's circumstances have changed as her rent increased in January 2027. MSD adjusts the rate of payment for Accommodation Supplement and exercises discretion to backdate the payment to the date of the increase in costs, and continues Emergency Benefit and Disability Allowance at the same rate.

chunks.title: Examples of outcomes that can occur — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD completes Mae's Mandatory Review on 1 July 2027, and her next Mandatory Review date is set for 52 weeks in the future on 29 June 2028. Client declares a change in circumstances Kerryn is a single person with no dependent child and meets the qualifications for Supported Living Payment except for the 2 years continuous residency qualification. They are caring for their mother full-time. Kerryn is getting Emergency Benefit at the Supported Living Payment single 18+ rate that will expire in 2 years (in 2028). Kerryn's Mandatory Review is due on 10 February 2027. Kerryn responds to their Mandatory Review on 5 February 2027 and tells MSD that on 1 February 2027 they started part time work at 6 hours a week earning $170.00 (before tax). Because Kerryn is still caring for their mother full-time and they are not earning enough to sustain themselves, MSD determines that Kerryn can continue getting Emergency Benefit paid at the Supported Living Payment rate. MSD reassesses Kerryn's rate of Emergency Benefit and charges their income from 1 February 2027. MSD completes the Mandatory Review on 5 February 2027. There is no future Mandatory Review date as the expiry date of Kerryn's Emergency Benefit is in less than 52 weeks. If Kerryn meets the residency qualifications when their Emergency Benefit expires, they may qualify for Supported Living Payment. Mandatory Review was not completed, and benefit has suspended Frank is 65 and does not meet the residency qualifications for New Zealand Superannuation and does not qualify for any other benefit. He lived in Thailand for 20 years and has not been resident and present in New Zealand for 5 years since the age of 50. Frank is getting Emergency Benefit at the Jobseeker Support single 25+ rate that will expire in 3 years when he will qualify for New Zealand Superannuation. Frank's Mandatory Review is due on 16 May 2027. However, Frank does not respond to the Mandatory Review before his review date and his Emergency Benefit suspends on 16 May 2027. Frank does not contact MSD or respond to the Mandatory Review for 8 weeks after his Emergency Benefit suspended. Because Frank didn't respond during the 8 weeks after his benefit suspended, his Emergency Benefit is cancelled from 16 May 2027 (the date his benefit originally suspended). Not enough information to complete Mandatory Review

chunks.title: Examples of outcomes that can occur — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Jack is a sole parent with 1 dependent child in their care. He has a temporary visa but is applying for residency and is compelled to remain in New Zealand because they are getting life sustaining medical treatment in New Zealand that they cannot get in their country of birth. Jack is getting Emergency Benefit at the Supported Living Payment sole parent rate. There is no expiry date. Jack's Mandatory Review is due on 18 May 2027. Jack responds to the Mandatory Review on 14 May 2027 and tells MSD their son is no longer in their care and that he is now living with his grandparents. Jack has declared a change in circumstances that affects their rate of Emergency Benefit. However, MSD does not have enough information to determine when the rate of Emergency Benefit should be reviewed from as they have not confirmed the date or the reason their son left their care. MSD cannot complete the Mandatory Review without requesting more information from Jack. MSD sets a new reasonable deadline of 21 May 2027 for Jack to provide further information. Jack's Emergency Benefit will continue to be paid at the same rate during this time. If Jack does not provide information before 21 May 2027, their Emergency Benefit will suspend on this date. Jack contacts MSD on 20 May 2027 and confirms their son left their care on 10 May 2027 because their health condition makes it difficult to provide day to day care for their son. MSD updates Jack's rate of Emergency Benefit to a Supported Living Payment single 18+ rate from the start of the next pay period, 22 May 2027. MSD completes the review on 20 May 2027 and sets Jack's next review for 52 weeks from the date MSD completed the review. Jack's next Mandatory Review date is 18 May 2028. Note when there is a change in circumstances that means they no longer qualify for Emergency Benefit, MSD should consider if the client is eligible for other types of assistance.

chunks.title: Examples of paying for more than 28 days for obtaining family support for young partners — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Examples of paying for more than 28 days for obtaining family support for young partners
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period while a client is absent from New Zealand.
