However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period where the client is travelling to receive support from a family member (including any other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family) who is residing overseas.
## Young partner of a main beneficiary generally won't meet requirements of obtaining support
A partner of a main beneficiary who has youth activity obligations would generally not meet the requirements to be paid a benefit in this circumstance, because usually they would be receiving the support of their partner. If they are receiving the support of their partner it could not be justified for them to travel overseas to receive the support of a different family member.
## Young partner of main beneficiary may meet the requirements in some circumstances
However, they may be able to be paid their payment for more than 28 days for the purpose of obtaining support from a family member overseas:
- the support they require can't be given by their partner because the main beneficiary themselves is absent from New Zealand or
- it is support the young partner cannot receive from their partner (for example, it is support from a parent or grandparent or the partner and the young person are having relationship difficulties).

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Example 1
The temporary caregiver is to be paid Supported Living Payment at the equivalent Unsupported Childs Benefit rate while caring for 1 child, aged 14 years during the client's imprisonment.
Unsupported Child's Benefit (as at 1 April 2026)
$350.58
Less family tax credit (as at 1 April 2026)
$151.91
Equals amount to add as a non-standard rate
$198.67
## Example 2
The temporary caregiver is to be paid Supported Living Payment at the equivalent Unsupported Childs Benefit rate while caring for 2 children aged 14 and 10 years during the client's imprisonment.
Unsupported Childs Benefit (as at 1 April 2026):
- $350.58 for 14-year old and
- $327.16 for 10-year old
$677.74
Less family tax credit (as at 1 April 2026):
- $151.91 for first child and
- $123.78 for second child
$275.69
Equals amount to add as a non-standard rate
$402.05
## Example 3
The temporary caregiver is to be paid Supported Living Payment while caring for 2 children aged 14 and 10 years during the client's imprisonment. It has been agreed to include the rent of the client's home of $180.00.
Unsupported Childs Benefit (as at 1 April 2026):
- $350.58 for 14-year old and
- $327.16 for 10-year old
$677.74
Plus rent on client's home
$180.00
Sub total
$857.74
Less family tax credit (as at 1 April 2026):
- $151.91 for first child and
- $123.78 for second child
$275.69
Equals calculated amount required to assist the temporary caregiver to care for the client's children (rent included)
$600.05
Maximum Supported Living Payment - Sole parent rate (net as at 1 April 2026)
$581.96
In this case the amount payable is the maximum Supported Living Payment - Sole parent rate of $581.96. You don't need to add a non-standard rate.

chunks.title: Exceptions when a client declares no change in circumstances for Mandatory Review — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a client responds to their Mandatory Review and confirms they have no change in circumstances, MSD must generally continue their Emergency Benefit at the same rate. However, there are some exceptions when MSD can request further information from the client to determine if they continue to qualify for Emergency Benefit or that the rate of payment is correct. Exceptions include when, at the time the client responds to their Mandatory Review, they: - have been getting Disability Allowance and have had no change in their disability related costs for three consecutive years or - have been getting Accommodation Supplement and have had no change in their accommodation costs for three consecutive years or - have had no change to their confirmed income amount for three consecutive years If a client has one or more of these exceptions, MSD must consider if further information is required from the client before deciding the outcome of the Mandatory Review.

chunks.title: Requesting further information — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: The decision to request further information from the client should be assessed on a case-by-case basis. Consider additional factors such as: - the type of costs the client has (e.g. food, transport, power, and accommodation costs vary with economic conditions and would be unlikely to have no change over an extended period) - when the client last provided verification of their costs (if it was required e.g. new or increased disability related costs or home ownership costs) - other resources available to meet their costs (e.g. when the client's income has not changed over an extended period)

chunks.title: Further information is needed to complete the Mandatory Review — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: If further information is needed to determine if the client continues to qualify for Emergency Benefit or that the rate of payment is correct, MSD must give a reasonable timeframe for the client to provide it. The date the client is given to provide the information by becomes the client's new deadline to respond to the Mandatory Review. If the client does not provide the information that was asked for, MSD must suspend the Emergency Benefit from the new deadline date. If the client provides the information that was asked for and MSD determines the client continues to qualify for Emergency Benefit (including the rate payable), the future Mandatory Review date is set 52 weeks from the date MSD completed the review.

chunks.title: Further information not needed to complete the Mandatory Review — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: In some situations, there may be good reason for the client having no change in their costs or income, and further information may not be needed for MSD to determine whether they continue to qualify for Emergency Benefit. For example, the client may have provided recent evidence of their costs or income, or they may have recently discussed their circumstances with MSD. If no further information is needed for MSD to determine the client continues to qualify for Emergency Benefit (including the rate payable), the future Mandatory Review date is set 52 weeks from the date MSD completed the review. Example Jack is getting Emergency Benefit and he works 10 hours a week as a carpenter with a local employer. Jack is paid more than the minimum wage in this role in recognition of his skills and experience. Jack's Mandatory Review for Emergency Benefit is due on 12 February 2027 and he responds on 10 February 2027 to confirm he has had no change in his circumstances. This includes no change in his income (which has remained unchanged since he moved into his current role in 2024). As Jack has been getting Emergency Benefit and declared no change in his income for three consecutive years at the time the mandatory review is returned, MSD must consider whether further information is required before completing the Mandatory Review. MSD considers Jack's circumstances and notes that Jack recently contacted MSD to discuss another employment opportunity. However, Jack didn't get the job. As part of that conversation, MSD confirmed Jack's income hadn't changed (as he is paid more than the minimum wage, annual changes to the minimum wage have not impacted his income). MSD determines that no further information is required to determine that Jack continues to qualify for Emergency Benefit. His Emergency Benefit continues at the same rate, and his next review date is set for 52 weeks in the future (9 February 2028).

chunks.title: Financially independent — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Financially independent
A child is considered to be financially independent when the child:
- is in full-time employment
- gets a Student Allowance or
- receives a benefit in their own right
## Other situations where a child is considered to be financially independent
There may be other situations where all a child's financial needs (including the provision of accommodation and material needs) are being met by someone else or from some other source. For example:
- a family trust or
- the parent who is not the day-to-day caregiver
## Date of review
Where a child becomes financially independent it should be excluded from the benefit payment from the start of the next pay period in which the child became financially independent.
There is discretion to continue payment for one payday following the event.
This discretion only applies when the exclusion of the child affects the rate of payment of Emergency Benefit and is generally used when processing deadlines have passed.
## Family tax credit
Stop family tax credit payments from the start of the next payday in which the child became financially independent, to avoid an overpayment (with Inland Revenue) for the client.
## Not financially independent
Generally, getting a Student Loan (including the living cost component) does not mean a child is financially independent.

chunks.title: Full-time employment — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Full-time employment
When a child starts full-time employment the child is no longer a dependent child.
Note if the dependent child is temporarily working more than 30 hours per week during the school holidays and they are returning to school after the holidays, they are not considered in full-time employment.
## Date of review
Exclude the child from the Emergency Benefit from the beginning of the next pay period in which the child started work.
## Family tax credit
Family tax credit payments should be stopped from the start of the next pay period in which the child starts full-time employment to avoid an overpayment (with Inland Revenue) for the client.
For more information see:
- Effect on benefit

chunks.title: Guidelines for paying a higher rate — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Guidelines for paying a higher rate
Payment can be increased above the hospital rate to a rate that (together with the client's other income) will be sufficient to meet the client's continuing commitments.
Use the following guidelines to assess whether the client's rate should be higher.
1. Have the client complete an Increased payment while you are in hospital form.
2. Accept stated expenses where they appear reasonable, but ask for proof if there is doubt.
3. If the client is a sole parent and has childcare costs:
- include the childcare costs when assessing whether a higher rate should be paid
- include family tax credit payments as income (as these payments will continue)
4. If a client is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, do not include home outgoings or accommodation expenses. These are the responsibility of the partner not in hospital. (The partner may qualify for Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support.)
5. Check that all possible action has been taken to reduce expenses. For example, giving up the lease on a flat where the hospital stay is indefinite.
6. If the increase in payment request is for one-off items such as clothing, you can pay the increase by:
- a backdated review of the benefit rate to create a lump sum payment or
- increasing the benefit rate for a limited time
## Example
Continuing commitments per week
$55.00
less other weekly income (bank interest)
$5.00
rate of increase
$50.00
plus hospital rate (net, as at 1 April 2026)
$58.34
rate of benefit payable
$108.34
Add the rate payable as a non-standard rate on the SNSRA screen.
A parent benefit reassessment SPBR may also be required.

chunks.title: Home detention — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Home detention
A client may be in prison for a short time before being released on home detention.
## Period in prison is less than 31 days
If the period in prison is less than 31 days an initial stand-down is not imposed if they apply for a benefit immediately after their release.
## Period in prison is more than 31 days
If the period in prison is 31 days or more, an initial stand-down will be imposed.
## Partner
Where the partner of a person in prison has been receiving a benefit, this will need to be reviewed from the date of release.
For more information see:
- Transfer between benefits

chunks.title: Hospitalisation — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Hospitalisation
When an Emergency Benefit client is admitted to hospital you will need to check that the hospitalisation does not affect the qualification for which the client was granted Emergency Benefit. This will include meeting any additional obligations similar to those of the benefit that the client doesn't qualify for.
## Client no longer qualifies
If the client no longer meets the qualification for which they were granted Emergency Benefit you will need to consider whether the client qualifies under a different category for Emergency Benefit or qualifies for another benefit.
For more information when a client still qualifies or their partner is in hospital see:
- In hospital

chunks.title: Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure
Where a client does not advise of their departure from New Zealand before they go, they may be able to have their benefit paid from the day after their departure date if the client has a humanitarian reason that justifies their reason for travel and their failure to tell Work and Income before they left.
Humanitarian reasons are:
- to provide aid or assistance to a family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member) immediately following a natural disaster (for example, flood, earthquake, bush fires) or similar adverse event (eg house fire)
- to be with a suddenly seriously ill, or dying family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member)
- to attend the sudden funeral of a family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member)
For more information see:
- Client not returned due to unforeseeable event (within 28 day maximum)
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Imprisonment — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Imprisonment
Generally, when an Emergency Benefit client is imprisoned or detained in custody, they are no longer entitled to get the Emergency Benefit.
In some circumstances Emergency Benefit can continue when the client is imprisoned.
To get an Emergency Benefit the client must not qualify for another main benefit and must be in hardship as they are unable to earn a sufficient livelihood due to their:
- health condition, injury or a disability
- domestic circumstances
- age or
- any other reason
The Emergency Benefit should stop from the day following the date of imprisonment.
MSD must decide whether to suspend or cancel the Emergency Benefit after considering the likely period in prison and whether the client has a partner and or dependent children.

chunks.title: In hospital — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## In hospital
When an Emergency Benefit client (or their partner) is admitted to hospital their benefit can continue at the existing rate for the first 13 weeks. The rate of payment will need to be reduced to the hospital rate after the client (or their partner) has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks (not after getting a benefit for 13 weeks).
## Exception
Couples with dependent children do not have their benefit payment reduced regardless of how long they are in hospital.
Note if a client (or partner) is getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for a child in their care, this child is regarded as a dependent child.
## Hospital rate
The hospital rate allows for the cost of personal items, which patients are expected to provide for themselves. The net weekly hospital rate is $58.34 (as at 1 April 2026).
An amount above the hospital rate can be paid where there are financial circumstances to warrant paying a higher rate.
Note MSD cannot pay an amount less than the hospital rate.
## Client in hospital during Mandatory Review
Clients getting Emergency benefit must respond to their Mandatory Review before their review date or their payments will suspend.
However, when a client is in hospital (for 13 weeks or less) and needs more time to respond to the review, they may be able to get an extension. If a client is unable to respond to the Mandatory Review, they may be able to get an exemption.
A client must contact MSD before their review date to discuss their situation if they need an extension or exemption.
Note clients who are in hospital for more than 13 weeks do not have a Mandatory Review.

chunks.title: In the care of Oranga Tamariki — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## In the care of Oranga Tamariki
Where a child or young person is in the care, custody or sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, the cost of the child's care is the responsibility of Oranga Tamariki and it is responsible for making payments under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989. The child is not considered a dependent child and Unsupported Childs Benefit cannot be paid.
However, where there is a sole guardianship order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but the child or young person is in the custody of the caregiver, the caregiver may be entitled to Unsupported Childs Benefit if all other criteria are met.
Where Oranga Tamariki is involved, but there are no orders or agreements about care, the child can be considered a dependent child (for example when Oranga Tamariki provides services to family groups under a Family Group Conference plan only).
For information on different orders and whether they mean the child can be considered a dependent child while the order is still in place, see:
- Oranga Tamariki order in place
## Parents as caregivers
When a child is returned to the care of a parent by Oranga Tamariki the child can be considered as a dependent child and included in a main benefit that the parent is receiving.
This is regardless of whether or not the parent was the immediate previous caregiver of the child.
For more information see:
- Discharged from Oranga Tamariki care
- Definition of discharged from Oranga Tamariki care

chunks.title: Income — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Income
When a client has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks and has income, the rate payable is:
- the hospital rate or
- the full benefit rate less the deduction due to income
whichever is the lower rate.
For more information see:
- Paying a higher rate
## Example 1
A client receiving an Emergency Benefit has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks.
This client has other income which reduces the main benefit rate to $20.00 per week.
In this case we pay the rate $20.00 per week which is lower than the hospital rate of $58.34 (as at 1 April 2026).
## Example 2
A client receiving an Emergency Benefit has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks.
This client has other income which reduces the main benefit rate to $70.00 per week.
In this case we pay the hospital rate of $58.34 per week (as at 1 April 2026) which is the lower rate.

chunks.title: Inland Revenue deduction notices — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Inland Revenue deduction notices
Inland Revenue may request for a client's unpaid taxes to be directly deducted from their benefit payments.
Note all Inland Revenue deduction notices are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit for processing.
The instructions of the deduction notice will be to deduct the lowest of either:
- 10% of the total debt which Inland Revenue specify in the notice, on a weekly basis or
- 20% of the client's gross earnings on a weekly basis
When there are insufficient funds to cover the deduction, Work and Income must advise Inland Revenue immediately that the deduction will not start or will start at a reduced rate.
Inland Revenue deductions have a lower priority than Child Support deductions.
For more information see:
- Priority for deductions

chunks.title: IRD number for partner who is not apportioned assistance — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: As part of a review of benefit, MSD may make a written request to the client for evidence of their partner's IRD number when the: - partner is not apportioned the primary client's Emergency Benefit, and - partner's income is relevant to a client's Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Setting or extending the period for providing evidence — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD can request a client to provide evidence of their partner's IRD number within a reasonable time period (usually 10 working days). MSD can set a different period or extend the period to provide evidence of an IRD number when it is expected to take longer to get the evidence. This includes considering factors outside of the client or partner's control that may cause delays, including, but not limited to: - the partner or client has a family emergency that caused a delay - processing delays with an external agency (e.g. Inland Revenue, Department of Internal Affairs, etc) - the client or partner does not speak English as a first language and has difficulty navigating evidence requirements - the client or partner has limited access to the internet, a device, or their local service centre - the client or partner has a physical or intellectual disability that makes accessing services difficult.

chunks.title: Notice following an unsuccessful match — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a partner's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the client (in writing) to provide evidence of their partner's IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the client a minimum of 10 working days to provide their partner's IRD number evidence or the client's assistance may be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Emergency Benefit. Isla's partner, Ariki, has income that is included in MSD's income test to determine eligibility for Emergency Benefit and MSD holds an IRD number for Ariki. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Ariki's IRD number. As part of a review of Isla's benefit, MSD provides a notice in writing, giving 10 working days for Isla to provide evidence of Ariki's IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Ariki already having an IRD number - Ariki not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD may suspend assistance if evidence is not received — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD may suspend all taxable and/or income tested assistance (including Emergency Benefit) the client is getting if evidence of a partner's IRD number evidence is not provided within a reasonable timeframe (usually 10 working days) or within the extended period if this has been applied. In rare cases, depending in the client's circumstances, MSD may consider cancelling or varying the client's assistance. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance.

chunks.title: IRD number not requested in some circumstances — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - significant factors, that are outside the client's or partner's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number, e.g. a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence, and - the client needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided. A partner's IRD number and evidence of their IRD number does not need to be provided when they are not a New Zealand tax resident. MSD can determine at a later point to request evidence of the IRD number. For more information see: - Non-tax resident partner's IRD number not required Note there is different guidance for requesting evidence of an IRD number for clients and partners apportioned a part of the primary clients Emergency Benefit, or when a client is applying for Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect
A client or partner can continue to receive payment of their benefit for an absence from New Zealand if it can be confirmed that the travel is to:
- attend a job interview
- follow up a definite job prospect
Benefit payments cannot continue if the client is leaving New Zealand to carry out general job search, that is, to 'have a look' for a job.
You will need to treat each case on its merits and take the following into account:
- does the client have proof of the interview or specific job prospect?
They will need to provide the employer's name and phone number and the date of the interview or meeting with the employer
- is it a realistic job opportunity for the client? That is, does it match the skills and qualifications of the client
- how long are they going for?
Consider what would be a reasonable time period for the client to complete the trip, for example, x number of days to get there, 1 day for the interview, x number of days to return home and frequency of flights to and from the destination
- what arrangements have they made for the continuing care of their children, partner and accommodation while they are absent?
## Client chooses to be absent for longer than reasonably necessary
Where a client or partner chooses to be absent for longer than is reasonably necessary to attend the job interview or investigate a potential job prospect, their benefit will not continue to be paid for those extra days.
For more information see:
- Examples of job interview or job prospects overseas
- Client obtains employment overseas
- Approved travel reasons

chunks.title: Length of travel for an approved travel reason — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Length of travel for an approved travel reason
Clients can travel for up to 28 days on Emergency Benefit for an approved travel reason. Discuss with the client the amount of time that they need to be absent from New Zealand as a result of the approved reason. The client should explain the length of their intended absence.
Consider:
- the length of time the event or reason for travel will take
- the duties the client will have as part of their reason (eg if they are travelling for a funeral, do they have responsibilities beyond attending the funeral itself such as estate duties or sorting out the possessions of the deceased?)
- flight availability and travel time
Remember to advise clients that generally they are only able to continue to be paid their benefit for up to 28 days in a 52 week period. This should be taken into account when deciding the approved travel period.
## Client travelling for multiple reasons
Some clients may travel overseas for an approved travel reason but elect to stay longer for another reason that is not an approved travel reason. In this case, the client can generally only receive their main benefit payments for the period of time that the approved travel reason applies to.
For more information see
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy
- Retrospective travel notifications [no link find out why] procedures
- Change of return date - Client makes contact upon return [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Mandatory Review dates for Emergency Benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Mandatory Review dates for Emergency Benefit
MSD must review a client's Emergency Benefit within 52-weeks of the commencement date of the benefit, or within 52-weeks from when the client's last Mandatory Review was completed.
A future Mandatory Review date will only be set if the expiry date for the Emergency Benefit is more than 52 weeks or there is no expiry date.
The clients next review date is set 52 weeks from the date MSD determined the client continues to qualify for Emergency Benefit and the rate of benefit payable (i.e. when MSD completes the review).
Note when MSD has an interaction with a client that confirms all of the same circumstances as a Mandatory Review, this can push out the client’s Mandatory Review date by 52 weeks. This is known as a specific engagement.
## Initial Mandatory Review dates
Benefit commencement date
Mandatory Review dates
Benefit commenced before 2 March 2026
Clients whose Emergency Benefit commenced before 2 March 2026 will have their initial Mandatory Review either:
- 52 weeks from the commencement date of the benefit
or
- 52 weeks from when their last periodic review was completed
or
- 52 weeks from when MSD last contacted the client to confirm if the information MSD holds about their circumstances is correct (annual circumstances letter).
Whichever date is later.
Benefit commenced on or after 2 March 2026
If a client's Emergency Benefit commenced on or after 2 March 2026, their initial Mandatory Review date is either:
- 52 weeks from the commencement date of the Accommodation Supplement
or
- 52 weeks from the completion of a specific engagement
## Clients who have been notified to complete 26 week review before 2 March 2026
Clients who have an "in-flight" 26 week periodic review
On 2 March 2026, some clients will have an "in-flight" 26 week periodic review and will still need to complete this.
This only applies to clients who have already been notified about the 26 week review before 2 March 2026.
Their initial Mandatory Review is set for 52 weeks from when their 26 week periodic review was completed.

chunks.title: Mandatory Review not required — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Mandatory Review not required
There is no Mandatory Review for Emergency Benefit for clients with an expiry date of more than 52 weeks or no expiry date in the following circumstances:
- the client is hospitalised for more than 13 weeks
- the client is in residential disability care or rest home
- the client has died
- the living in or visiting a region affected by an emergency or adverse event and they are unable to reasonably leave the area
- living in or visiting a region affected by an outbreak of a quarantinable disease and an epidemic notice has been given and is in force
or when:
- there is a major system outage that prevents MSD from carrying out mandatory reviews of specified benefits.
MSD will also stop the review for any clients who are in these circumstances after they have been notified about their Mandatory Review.
MSD will notify the client when they are not required to complete the review. The Mandatory Review date is reset to 52 weeks in the future from the client's original review date.
Note a notification will not be sent when the client has died.

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension partner being cared for dies — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension partner being cared for dies
When a client is getting Emergency Benefit because they are caring for their New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension partner and their partner dies, they no longer qualify for Emergency Benefit. However, Emergency Benefit can continue at the existing rate for 28 days to allow the client time to adjust to changes in their circumstances.
Note during the 28-day continuation of payment, if the client has other changes of circumstances, such as a change in income, the rate of main benefit and Extra help will need to be reviewed.
## Client would qualify for higher rate of payment during 28-day period
Sometimes the client would qualify for a higher rate of payment if they were transferred to another benefit. In this case you can increase the rate of Emergency Benefit to match the rate of payment the client would get if they were transferred to that benefit.
This is to make sure the client is not financially disadvantaged and doesn't have to go through a benefit transfer process immediately after the death of their partner.
## Example
Marita is getting Emergency Benefit while caring for her partner getting New Zealand Superannuation. Marita's partner passed away last week, making Marita a sole parent to their son. If Marita transferred to Sole Parent Support, this would be a higher rate of payment than if she stayed on Emergency Benefit.
To make sure Marita isn't disadvantaged and doesn't have to go through the benefit transfer process straight away, we increase her Emergency Benefit to the Sole Parent Support rate.
## End of the 28-day period
At the end of the 28-day period you will need to determine if the client qualifies for another benefit.

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension partner enters long-term residential care — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension partner enters long-term residential care
When a client is getting Emergency Benefit because they are caring for their New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension partner, and their partner enters long-term residential care in a rest home or hospital, the Emergency Benefit client's entitlement depends on whether the partner is getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension.
## Partner being cared for gets New Zealand Superannuation
The client can continue getting Emergency Benefit and their rate of payment must be increased to the single or sole parent rate of Supported Living Payment (on the ground of restricted work capacity), depending on their circumstances.
## Partner being cared for gets Veteran's Pension
The Emergency Benefit client must be transferred to Veterans Pension from the date their partner enters residential care. They will be paid at the single or single living alone rate depending on their circumstances.

chunks.title: Obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand
All clients getting a main benefit must tell the Ministry of Social Development before they leave New Zealand.
If the client does not tell the Ministry before they go overseas, their benefit payments will stop from the day after they leave New Zealand.
If a client tells us they will be absent from New Zealand, and they have an approved travel reason, they may be able to keep getting payments for up to 28 days.
## Does not advise of departure
If the client did not tell the Ministry they were leaving New Zealand their benefit will be suspended immediately from the day after they left New Zealand.
The Integrity Intervention Centre will determine if there has been an overpayment, establish any debt and advise the client.
If a client questions the information match refer them to the Integrity Intervention Centre.
For more information see:
- Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure
- Backdating benefit to the day after departure date
- Approved travel reasons
- Action on return to New Zealand
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy

chunks.title: On leave for 28 days or less — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## On leave for 28 days or less
Where a client who is getting the hospital rate is on leave from hospital for 28 days or less:
- increase their benefit to the appropriate full rate from the date of discharge on leave
- for married, civil union or de facto clients reduce the partner's benefit to the half married, civil union or de facto rate and suspend Special Disability Allowance and
- review any Extra help from the same date
On re-admission to hospital:
- reduce the benefit to the rate payable prior to the period of leave
- for married, civil union or de facto clients increase the partner's benefit and resume Special Disability Allowance and
- review any Extra help from the same date
Note the dates of admission and discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital.

chunks.title: On leave for more than 28 days — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## On leave for more than 28 days
Where a client who is getting the hospital rate is on leave from hospital for more than 28 days:
- increase their benefit to the appropriate full rate from the date of discharge on leave
- for married, civil union or de facto clients reduce the partner's benefit to the half married, civil union or de facto rate and suspend Special Disability Allowance and
- review any Extra Help
On re-admission to hospital continue to pay the full rate of benefit and any Extra help for a further 13 weeks of hospitalisation.
Note calculation of the 13 week period in hospital begins again after the client has been re-admitted when on leave for more than 28 days.
The dates of admission and discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital.

chunks.title: On leave from hospital — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## On leave from hospital
Emergency Benefit is paid at the full rate for any period of leave from hospital. Where the client has been getting the hospital rate increase their benefit for any period they are on leave.
The benefit action to take, on the client's re-admission to hospital, will depend on how long they were on leave.
## Effect of leave on 13 week count
Any periods of leave from hospital of 28 days or less are to be ignored when deciding the date from which the benefit is to be reduced to the hospital rate. Calculate the period in hospital from the original admission date.
If the client has been allowed out of hospital for more than 28 days, the calculation of the 13 week period in hospital begins again after the client has been re-admitted.
For more information see:
- On leave for 28 days or less
- On leave for more than 28 days
- Weekend leave
- Discharge from hospital

chunks.title: Ongoing assistance for dependent children — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Ongoing assistance for dependent children
When a surviving dependent child is to be cared for by a person other than a parent, the caregiver may be able to receive an Orphan's Benefit or an Unsupported Child's Benefit.

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki order in place — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: The following table identifies when a child can be considered a dependent child and when it can't, depending on the type of order that is in place and section of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 that applies. When to include as a dependent child When not to include as a dependent child section 139: Agreements for temporary care of child or young person by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 140: Agreements for extended care of child or young person by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 78: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, pending determination of court proceedings. If Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki has returned the child or young person in to the care of the immediate previous care giver. section 78: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, pending determination of court proceedings section 101: Custody order in favour of principal caregiver. Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki under section 110. section 101: Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 102: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 110(2)a: Sole Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. Section 101 Custody Order in favour of principal caregiver and other dependent child criteria are met. Please refer case to your local solicitor for consideration. section 110(2)a: Sole Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 110(2) b: Additional guardianship Order, to any other guardian in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 112: Guardianship Order in favour of Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki for a specific purpose. Please refer case to your local solicitor for consideration. section 86: Services Orders that provide for particular services and assistance required by the child or young person (e.g. counselling fees, special education costs) section 86: Services Orders that provide for general financial support to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 91: Support Orders. The child may be considered a dependent child where the documentation states that specific financial support is to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki.

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki order in place — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: section 91: Support Orders. The child cannot be considered a dependent child where the documentation states that general financial support is to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. See your local solicitor if you receive a case in this category. When a child or young person is discharged from the care, custody or sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, always consider including the child in the clients Emergency Benefit or granting Unsupported Childs Benefit. - The legislation referenced above is the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989

chunks.title: Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit child turns 14 years of age — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit child turns 14 years of age
Where a client has been granted Emergency Benefit equivalent to Jobseeker Support and is caring for a child for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid, and that child reaches the age of 14 years, the client's eligibility to Emergency Benefit should be reviewed, as they may now be eligible for a main benefit.

chunks.title: Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid
When a client is receiving an Orphans Benefit or an Unsupported Childs Benefit, the child is not treated as a dependent child and is not included in the assessment of Emergency Benefit.
The client's Emergency Benefit is assessed on their family circumstances excluding the child for which Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid.

chunks.title: Outcomes of a Mandatory Review — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Clients must respond to their Mandatory Review before their Mandatory Review date, or their payments will suspend. When a client responds to the review, there are a number of outcomes that can occur. Once MSD has determined if the client qualifies, MSD will either: - continue paying the benefit at the existing rate - adjust the rate of benefit so the client is getting the correct rate - suspend the benefit if there is no rate payable for a period (e.g. client has variable income) - cancel the benefit if the client no longer qualifies The Mandatory Review is complete when MSD makes a decision about the client's eligibility for Emergency Benefit and the rate of benefit payable (if applicable). MSD may also carry out a separate review of Emergency Benefit at any time, where there is good reason.

chunks.title: Client declares no change — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a client responds to their Mandatory Review and confirms they have had no change in circumstances, MSD must review the client's eligibility and rate of Emergency Benefit. If the client remains eligible following the Mandatory Review a future date for the next review will be set if the expiry date for the Emergency Benefit is more than 52 weeks from the commencement of the benefit or last Mandatory Review, or there is no expiry date. The next Mandatory Review date is 52 weeks from the date MSD completed the review (if the expiry date for the Emergency Benefit is more than 52 weeks or there is no expiry date). Exceptions when a client declares no change When a client responds to their Mandatory Review and confirms they have no change in circumstances, there are some situations when MSD can request further information from the client before deciding whether to continue Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Client declares a change in circumstances — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a client responds to the Mandatory Review with a change in circumstances, MSD must use the information provided to determine if the client continues to qualify for Emergency Benefit, or any other benefits they get that are subject to a Mandatory Review (excluding Orphan's Benefit and Unsupported Child's Benefit) and the rate payable. MSD may request further information from the client if it is unclear if the client continues to qualify for Emergency Benefit. Date of change When a client declares a change in circumstances, MSD will need to assess if the client still qualifies for Emergency Benefit and the rate payable and from what date, depending on when the change in circumstances happened or will happen. Client is also getting other assistance When the client has provided information as part of the Mandatory Review that could affect their entitlement to or the rate payable of any other assistance (e.g. Temporary Additional Support or Flexible Childcare Assistance), MSD may use this information to review that assistance. When the other assistance is affected by the outcome of the Mandatory Review, MSD must change the rate, suspend or cancel that assistance where appropriate. For example, if the outcome of the Mandatory Review is that the client is no longer entitled to Emergency Benefit, their Temporary Additional Support must be reviewed, and the rate may change or stop if they no longer qualify.

chunks.title: Further information is needed to complete the Mandatory Review — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: If further information is needed to determine if the client continues to qualify for Emergency Benefit or that the rate of payment is correct, MSD must give a reasonable timeframe for the client to provide it. The date the client is given to provide the information by becomes the client's new deadline to respond to the Mandatory Review. If the client doesn't provide the information that was asked for before the deadline, MSD must suspend the Emergency Benefit from the new deadline date. If the client provides the information that was asked for and MSD determines the client continues to qualify for Emergency Benefit (including the rate payable), a future Mandatory Review date is set 52-weeks from the date MSD completed the review (if the expiry date for the Emergency Benefit is more than 52 weeks or there is no expiry date).

chunks.title: Completing the Mandatory Review when there are new costs — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: In some circumstances MSD can still complete the Mandatory Review when a client has declared a change in circumstances that doesn't affect the client's eligibility for Emergency Benefit, e.g. the client has declared a new cost. Example 1 Marya is getting Emergency Benefit and has a Mandatory Review for her benefit. Marya responds to her Mandatory Review to confirm her circumstances. Marya tells MSD she now has accommodation costs but nothing else has changed. MSD completes the Mandatory Review and continues the Emergency Benefit at the existing rate as the change declared by Marya doesn't affect his eligibility for Emergency Benefit. Marya can apply for Accommodation Supplement based on her new accommodation costs. This application is separate to the Mandatory Review. Example 2 Anne is getting Emergency Benefit and Disability Allowance and has a Mandatory Review for both. Anne responds to the Mandatory Review to confirm their circumstances. Anne tells MSD they have a new disability cost but nothing else has changed. MSD completes the Mandatory Review and continues the Emergency Benefit and Disability Allowance at the existing rate. MSD advises Anne that they need to provide a medical certificate from their medical or nurse practitioner to confirm the additional cost, and they must provide proof of cost to have the new cost included in their Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Overseas medical treatment — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Overseas medical treatment
When a client is receiving assistance for overseas medical treatment from the Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora - High Cost Treatment Pool, the client can continue to receive benefit payments for up to 2 years while absent from New Zealand.
Payment can also continue if the partner, dependent child, or sibling of a client is the person who is being assisted under the High Cost Treatment Pool. Payment may also continue for partners and siblings when they are required to accompany the client overseas.
## Proof
The client needs to provide proof that Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora is assisting with their treatment through the High Cost Treatment Pool.
For the Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora criteria see:
- Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora High Cost Treatment Pool

chunks.title: Part-time employment — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Part-time employment
Part-time employment does not make a child financially independent. Nor do you take the child's earnings into account when assessing the rate of Emergency Benefit payments. For more information on children's income see:
- Child's income
## Exception
There may be situations where a child starts (or is in) part-time employment and can no longer be considered a dependent child for some other reason such as:
- no longer maintained as a member of the family or
- the client is no longer primarily responsible for them

chunks.title: Partner donates a kidney or liver tissue — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner donates a kidney or liver tissue
When a partner is donating a kidney or liver tissue, they can keep getting an Emergency Benefit. Exempt the partner from any work obligations during the recovery period.
The partner cannot choose to have their benefit cancelled to receive live organ donor income assistance.
Add the appropriate exemption to the SWTDA screen in SWIFTT.
The exemption starts from the date of their operation and can continue while the partner:
- is recovering from their operation and
- they cannot meet their part-time or full-time work obligations
This exemption must not be for more than 12 weeks.
Do not apply any obligations failures:
- for the maximum period of 12 weeks or
- until the client has recovered from the operation
whichever is earlier.
## Partner has an obligation failure
if the partner currently has an obligation failure, donating a kidney or liver tissue is a 'good and sufficient reason'. The work obligations failure must be overturned.
This will remove the failure from the partner's 12 month obligation failure count, and there is no sanction.
## Childcare Assistance
Clients may be eligible for Childcare Assistance payments while they are recovering.
For more information and additional qualifications see:
- Childcare Subsidy Temporary illness
- OSCAR Temporary illness
- Donating a kidney or liver tissue

chunks.title: Partners with children under 3 years — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partners with children under 3 years
A partner with their youngest child aged under 3 years old is not required to meet work obligations and can be a part or full-time student without it affecting their Emergency Benefit.
## Partners with work obligations
Partners with no children or with their youngest child aged 3 years or over, may be a part-time or full-time student without it affecting their Emergency Benefit if they have been granted an exemption from their work obligations because they:
- were part way through a course of study at the time at the time they became subject to work obligations or
- were part way through a course of study when their youngest child reached the age of 3 years
A partner can be considered to be meeting their work obligations if their study timetable allows enough time for job search activity, for example, if the hours of the part-time study are outside of normal working hours.
If a partner starts part-time study and they no longer meet their work obligations and they do not have an exemption from meeting their work obligations you may need to initiate an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Work obligations - partners
## Partner engaged in full time study
If a partner is engaged in full time study and does not meet the criteria for an exemption they can apply for a Student Allowance.
If they qualify for a Student Allowance, the client can be included in the Student Allowance when:
- they are legally married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and
- both are aged 24 years or more or
- they have a dependent child
Where the client cannot be included, the partner will be regarded as single and may be able to receive the single rate of Student Allowance.
For Emergency Benefit purposes they are still regarded as a married, civil union or de facto couple. You will need to charge the Student Allowance against the rate of benefit they are receiving and pay the client half the reduced benefit.
Because the Emergency Benefit and Student Allowance rules are different in this situation there are particular procedures to follow. There is a flowchart to help you, see:
- Couple under 24 years - partner not granted an exemption in non approved study flowchart
For more information see:
- Work obligations - partners
- Exemptions for partners
- Student Allowance
- Student Allowance Student with a partner

chunks.title: Partner obtains employment overseas — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner obtains employment overseas
Where the partner:
- is successful in their job prospect or job search overseas and
- they are not returning to New Zealand
their portion of the Emergency Benefit should be cancelled from the day after the notice of job appointment.
If the partner returns to New Zealand for the period between getting the job and actually starting employment, the Emergency Benefit can be continued until they leave the country. Their portion of the Emergency Benefit must be cancelled from the day after they leave New Zealand to commence the job.

chunks.title: Partner with work or work preparation obligations or an exemption — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner with work or work preparation obligations or an exemption
The partner of a person receiving Emergency Benefit can continue to receive a benefit for up to 28 days in any 52 week period if they meet the criteria for approved travel.
This applies whether a partner has work or work preparation obligations or an exemption from these obligations.
For more information see:
- Approved travel reasons

chunks.title: Partners of a main beneficiary who have youth activity obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Young partners receiving a main benefit cannot generally be absent from New Zealand and continue to receive payment of their portion of their benefit. The Government's obligation to pay income support usually stops when the client leaves New Zealand. A young partner can continue to be paid their portion of their benefit for up to 28 days in a 52 week period while they are absent from New Zealand: - if they have an approved travel reason or - for any reason if the travel will not prevent them from continuing to meet their youth activity obligations (eg because they are attending school and the travel is during the school holidays or they are attending a training course and the travel is during a term or semester break, and they do not need to be in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations during the travel period) or - overseas for medical treatment For more information see: - Permitted travel reasons

chunks.title: Examples (but not limited to) — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Client situation Outcome A young partner is meeting their education obligation by attending secondary school and they wish to travel to Australia during the school holidays. The client is not required by their Service Provider to undertake a budgeting course or attend any meetings with them during the period they wish to travel. The travel will not prevent the young partner from meeting any of their youth activity obligations so it will be approved. Therefore, the young partner can be absent from New Zealand for this reason and continue to receive their payment for up to 28 days in any 52 week period. A young partner is meeting their education obligation by participating in a full time training course and decides to take time off from the course in the middle of the term so that they can holiday in Australia. The travel will not be approved as it will prevent the young partner from meeting their obligation to be in full-time education or training. A young partner is enrolled in a full-time training course, however, the course has not yet started, and the young person wishes to travel to the United States for a holiday before the course commencement date. The young partner does not have to be in New Zealand to meet any other obligations during the travel period (eg they do not have to attend a budgeting course during the time of the travel). The travel will not prevent the client from meeting any of their youth activity obligations so it will be approved. The young person can continue to receive their payment for up to 28 days in any 52 week period while they are absent from New Zealand. For more information see: - Young partner not yet subject to obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning - Young partner who is exempt from their youth activity obligations - Absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days for an approved reason

chunks.title: Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure
Generally, clients receiving a main benefit must advise Work and Income of their intention to leave New Zealand prior to their departure to be eligible to continue to receive their payments.
Only in specific circumstances can a client receiving a benefit who leaves New Zealand without telling us be able to have their benefit either:
- resumed from the date they notified Work and Income of their absence if their travel is allowed or
- backdated to the day after their departure date
Note this can occur either while the client is still overseas or once they have returned.
## Resuming benefit when client failed to advise of absence
If a client contacts Work and Income after they have left New Zealand, and is not eligible to have their payment backdated, their benefit can only be resumed from:
- the date that they notified us of their absence and
- only if the travel is allowed (ie they meet the criteria to continue to be paid their benefit while overseas either because they meet the criteria for approved travel, or the requirement that travel be approved does not apply to them)
Otherwise, the client cannot have their benefit resumed until they return to New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Backdating benefit to the day after departure date
- Action on return to New Zealand
- Approved travel reasons
- Payment when client or partner absent from New Zealand
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy

chunks.title: Paying a higher rate — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Paying a higher rate
You can make payment at a rate higher than the hospital rate where the client cannot meet their continuing costs from the hospital rate of payment and any other income they receive.
You will need to take into consideration:
- the client's financial commitments and
- access to other income
Note when you are considering payment of benefit at a rate higher than the hospital rate, generally you do not take cash assets into account as rates of benefit payment are not subject to an assets test.
If a temporary visa holder is required to make Child Support payments and does not qualify for an exemption from Inland Revenue Child Support, you can increase the hospital rate to include any Child Support payments that are required to be apportioned from the benefit.
For more information about paying at a higher rate see:
- Guidelines for paying a higher rate
## Maximum amount payable
You can pay a rate higher than the hospital rate up to the maximum rate of Emergency Benefit that would otherwise be payable.
## When not to pay a higher rate
A client cannot be paid a higher rate of benefit (because of hospitalisation) than they would otherwise receive. Where their usual benefit payment is less than the hospital rate, you don't increase their benefit to the hospital rate (or any other higher rate).
A benefit may be paid at less than the hospital rate because of:
- the client's income (if it continues while in hospital)
- maintenance deductions or
- overseas pension deductions

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period when the client is absent from New Zealand. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. To pay a benefit more than 28 days during any 52 week period: - the client must be continuing to receive their benefit while absent from New Zealand because: they have an approved travel reason, orthey are not required to have an approved travel reason in order to be paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand - they have an approved travel reason, or - they are not required to have an approved travel reason in order to be paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand - the client could not return to New Zealand because of new circumstances that: they could not reasonably foresee at the time when they left New Zealand, andthat are outside of the client's control - they could not reasonably foresee at the time when they left New Zealand, and - that are outside of the client's control and - Work and Income is satisfied that the extension of the absence is no longer than is necessary to address the new circumstances

chunks.title: Examples — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: A client who is absent from New Zealand for an approved reason may be prevented from returning by new unforeseen circumstances which could include (but are not limited to): - travel delays due to unforeseen weather events eg fog, volcano, flooding, earthquakes, terrorism - travel delays due to transport options being cancelled - health condition or injury or hospitalisation preventing return

chunks.title: Benefit can be backdated once back in New Zealand in very limited circumstances — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: A client who is continuing to be paid while they are absent from New Zealand for an approved reason may be able to have their benefit backdated if there is an unforeseen reason they cannot notify Work and Income while they are overseas. For example, a client boards a plane to return home on schedule and the plane is held up due to fog. There is no way the client could notify Work and Income due to an event outside of their control. When the client contacts Work and Income once they are back in New Zealand, their benefit would be resumed from the original date client was due to return (this will be on the boarding pass and/or in the custom tab in WASP). For more information see: - Overseas for medical treatment - Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period - Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days for an approved reason — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period when the client is absent from New Zealand. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. To pay a benefit more than 28 days during any 52 week period of absence from New Zealand, the client must be travelling for one of the following reasons: - essential travel - to attend a significant event relating to a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family), that the client would reasonably be expected to attend (eg visit a person who is seriously ill, seriously injured or whose death is imminent, attend a funeral, provide support to a party or witness to a court case, travel required for a court ordered custody arrangement) - to attend a court case which the person is required to attend as a party or a witness - to attend a job interview or follow up on a job prospect - for clients with a disability, to receive vocational training or disability assistance-dog training not available in New Zealand during the period or periods of absence - for clients with a disability, to travel overseas for the sole or predominant purpose of competing in any overseas multinational or international Special Olympic or Paralympic Games competition - to provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster (flood, earthquake, fire) or similar adverse event (eg house fire) and - Work and Income must be satisfied, when considering the client's reason for travel, that the length of the absence is no longer than necessary for the reason for travel. In addition, where the client has already been paid a benefit while absent from New Zealand in the 52 week period Work and Income must be satisfied that either: - the client could not have reasonably foreseen them needing to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in a 52 week period or - the client could not have rearranged their affairs to avoid being absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in a 52 week period and - it would be unreasonable for the benefit not to be paid Note generally we would not pay more than 28 days extra travel per absence. For more information see: - Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason - Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event (within 28 days maximum) - Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days - receive support from family overseas (young partner) — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period where the client is absent from New Zealand. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period where the young partner is travelling to receive support from a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family) who is residing overseas. For more information see: - Definition of 'support' from a family member residing overseas This applies (and is limited to a further 28 days in any 52 week period) when: - the young partner has already been paid a benefit while absent from New Zealand for one or more approved reasons for all or most of 28 days in a 52 week period and - the young partner will be absent from New Zealand for the purpose of obtaining support from a family member residing overseas and - the support that the young partner needs cannot reasonably be provided to the client by one of their family members in New Zealand and - the absence does not prevent the young partner from meeting their youth activity obligations because the absence is at a time when: they are not required to attend education, training or work-based learning (for example, they are exempt from meeting their obligationsthey are not yet required to be undertaking education, training or work-based learning because of the age of their youngest child orthey are undertaking education or training but it is semester or term break or they are between academic years) or the course has not yet started andthey are not required to be in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations during the time of the absence (eg they do not need to attend a parenting or budgeting course during the time they will be overseas) - they are not required to attend education, training or work-based learning (for example, they are exempt from meeting their obligations - they are not yet required to be undertaking education, training or work-based learning because of the age of their youngest child or - they are undertaking education or training but it is semester or term break or they are between academic years) or the course has not yet started and - they are not required to be in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations during the time of the absence (eg they do not need to attend a parenting or budgeting course during the time they will be overseas)

chunks.title: Cannot be paid for more than 28 days for purposes of obtaining support — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: The maximum amount of time that a young partner can continue to receive their payment while overseas on the grounds the absence does not prevent them meeting their obligations is 28 days in any 52 week period. Therefore, if a client subject to youth activity obligations has already received their payment for 28 days while they were overseas on a holiday on the grounds that the travel did not prevent them meeting their obligations, they will not be able to travel and continue to receive their payment under the 'obtaining support from a family member' circumstance. For more information see: - Examples of paying for more than 28 days for obtaining family support for young partners

chunks.title: Payment to partners — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Payment to partners
When a client with a partner (with no dependent children) has their Emergency Benefit reduced to the hospital rate, their partner in the community from the same date can:
- have their portion of benefit or pension increased by the difference between the maximum half married, civil union or de facto rate and single rate of that benefit or pension and
- get a Special Disability Allowance
Note couples with dependent children do not have their rate reduced to the hospital rate.
Check to see that the partner is not in hospital. If they are in hospital then the same rules apply as when a client is in hospital. You will need to make sure that they have been in hospital for less than 13 weeks or else their Emergency Benefit will need to be reduced to the hospital rate as well.
## Partner is also in hospital
If the partner is also in hospital, the same rules apply as when the client is in hospital. If they have been in hospital for more than 13 weeks their benefit or pension is also reduced to the hospital rate.
Note if the partner is getting Veteran's Pension and is in hospital for more than 13 weeks, their payment must not be reduced to the hospital rate. This is because Veteran's Pension is not affected by hospitalisation. The partner of the Veteran's Pension client cannot have their payments increased or get Special Disability Allowance.
## Charging income
You need to charge any income the couple receives against the married, civil union or de facto couple rate before you can determine the amount to pay.
The partner in the community will get the half married, civil union or de facto rate (after charging income) plus the difference between the maximum married, civil union or de facto rate and the single rate.
The client in hospital will get the lesser of the:
- half married, civil union or de facto rate (after charging income) or
- hospital rate of payment

chunks.title: Payment when client or partner absent from New Zealand — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Payment when client or partner absent from New Zealand
There are some situations where the benefit payments will be affected when the client is absent from New Zealand. The action required by the Ministry of Social Development will depend on the reason the client is absent from New Zealand and whether they are continuing to be paid a benefit.
Whether a partner of an Emergency Benefit client can be absent from New Zealand and continue getting their benefit payments depends on their work or work preparation obligations.
For more information see:
- Partner with work or work preparation obligations
Also see:
- Approved travel reasons
- Client or partner remains in New Zealand
- Ending payment for partner who can travel for any reason
- Ending payment for client who needs an approved reason for travel
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum)
- Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event (within 28 day maximum)
- Child absent

chunks.title: Permanent absence — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Permanent absence
If a client is leaving New Zealand permanently, Emergency Benefit must be cancelled from the day after departure.
## Moving to the United Kingdom
If the client is moving to the United Kingdom they may qualify for a benefit or pension in that country.
## Moving to Australia
If the client is moving to Australia it is important that they are aware that they may not be able to receive a benefit until they have resided in Australia for two years after being granted permanent residence status.
For more information see:
- United Kingdom Reciprocal Agreement Jobseekers Allowance
- Australia Reciprocal Agreement New Zealand benefits and pensions in Australia
- Payments from overseas Reciprocal Agreements

chunks.title: Permitted travel reasons — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Permitted travel reasons
A client or partner not otherwise entitled to be paid their Emergency Benefit while absent from New Zealand may have their payments continue for up to 28 days in any 52 week period, if their travel is for one (or a combination) of, the following permitted travel reasons:
- essential travel - to attend a significant event relating to a family member or a person who fulfils a role in relation to the client that is similar to that of a family member, that the client would reasonably be expected to attend
- to attend a court case which the person is required to attend as a party or a witness - this is to allow clients who are required by law to attend court and supports the maintenance of the law. A client would generally be expected to provide evidence that they are required to attend a court overseas. This would include documents from the court.
- to attend a job interview or follow up on a job prospect
- for clients with a disability, to receive vocational training or disability assistance-dog training not available in New Zealand during the time the client is absent
- for clients with a disability, to travel overseas for the sole or predominant purpose of competing in any overseas multinational or international Special Olympic or Paralympic Games competition
- to provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster (eg flood, earthquake, fire) or similar adverse event (eg house fire)
## Evidence of the client's situation
Although it may not be possible for the client to get proof of their situation, they should make a reasonable effort to do so.
For more information see:
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Definition of family member
- Essential travel
- Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect

chunks.title: Person temporarily leaves care — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: To get Emergency Benefit while caring for a person the client must be providing full time care and attention at home. However, payments can continue for up to 28 days while the person being cared for is in someone else's care. This allows the client to have a break. For example the person may enter respite care for up to 28 days to give the client a short break from caring responsibilities.

chunks.title: Person permanently leaves care — main benefits > emergency benefit > changes and reviews emergency benefit
chunks.text: When the person leaves the care of the client permanently, the client no longer qualifies for Emergency Benefit on the ground of caring for a person.
