chunks.title: Criteria for Community Work Experience — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Criteria for Community Work Experience
Partners must meet certain criteria to have Community Work Experience imposed.
A partner can only be placed in Community Work Experience if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they have current work obligations, and
- they meet with MSD within the 5-working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure is not disputed and overturned, and
- Community Work Experience is the most appropriate sanction to impose based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or have dependent children.
## Partner failed a drug test obligation
Community Work Experience cannot be imposed if a partner fails a drug test obligation.
Partners who have failed a drug test obligation may be considered for Money Management if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.
## Partner does not have work obligations
Community Work Experience cannot be imposed on a partner who only has work-preparation or social obligations.
These partners may be considered for Money Management as an alternative to a financial sanction if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.
## Partner fails more than one obligation at the same time
A partner may fail more than one obligation on the same day and have multiple failures they need to recomply with.
Community Work Experience cannot be imposed if a partner has failed multiple obligations at the same time.
Partners may be considered for Money Management if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.

chunks.title: Criteria for Money Management — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Criteria for Money Management
Clients must meet certain criteria in order for Money Management to be imposed.
A client can have Money Management imposed if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they contact MSD within the 5 working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure decision is not disputed and overturned, and
- Money Management would be the most appropriate sanction to impose based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or they have dependent children.
## Client or partner failed a drug test or a social obligation
Money Management may be imposed on clients who have failed a social obligation, or partners who have failed either a drug test or a social obligation if they meet the above criteria.
Depending on the activity a client fails, they may be able to recomply within 5 working days of the failure instead of imposing Money Management.
## Client failed more than one obligation at the same time
A client may fail more than one obligation on the same day and have multiple failures they need to recomply with.
A client may have Money Management imposed instead of receiving a financial sanction for these failures. Clients will need to complete a recompliance activity for each of their failures before Money Management ends in order to recomply with their obligations.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Criteria for Report Job Search — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Criteria for Report Job Search
Partner's must meet certain criteria to have Report Job Search imposed.
A partner can only have Report Job Search imposed if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure) and
- they have current work obligations and
- they meet with MSD within the 5-working day notice period and
- the obligation failure is not disputed and overturned and
- Report Job Search is the most appropriate sanction to impose based on their circumstances and
- they are in active case management or have dependent children
## Partner failed a drug test obligation
Report Job Search cannot be imposed if a partner fails a drug test obligation.
Partners who have failed a drug test obligation may be considered for Money Management if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.
## Partner does not have work obligations
Report Job Search cannot be imposed on a partner who only has work-preparation or social obligations.
These partners may be considered for Upskilling or Money Management as an alternative to a financial sanction if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.
## Partner fails more than one obligation at the same time
A partner may fail more than one obligation on the same day and have multiple failures they need to recomply with.
Report Job Search cannot be imposed if a partner has failed multiple obligations at the same time.
Partners may be considered for Money Management if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.

chunks.title: Criteria for Upskilling — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Criteria for Upskilling
Clients must meet certain criteria to have Upskilling imposed.
A client can only have Upskilling imposed if:
- they are in active case management or have dependent children and
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure) and
- they have current work, work preparation or social obligations and
- they meet with MSD within the 5-working day notice period and
- the obligation failure is not disputed and overturned and
- Upskilling is the most appropriate sanction to impose based on their circumstances
## Partner failed a drug test obligation
Upskilling cannot be imposed if a partner fails a drug test obligation.
Partners who have failed a drug test obligation may be considered for Money Management if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.
## Client fails more than one obligation at the same time
A client may fail more than one obligation on the same day and have multiple failures they need to recomply with.
Upskilling cannot be imposed if a client has failed multiple obligations at the same time.
Clients may be considered for Money Management if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.

chunks.title: Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities
After a discussion with the young partner, you will need to determine the most appropriate education, training or work-based learning activity for them to undertake. To decide what activities are most appropriate, you should consider:
- the young partner's individual circumstances
- whether the activity is suitable for the young partner
- other information you already have about the young partner (for example a plan may have been established by Oranga Tamariki)
- the young partner's overall future goals and needs
A young person must undertake education, training or work-based learning to receive their benefit, unless they qualify for an exemption, or the obligation to be in education or training doesn't apply because their youngest dependent child is under six months.
Where the youngest dependent child reaches the age of six months, the young person may be required to attend a Teen Parent Unit if a suitable place is available. For more information see:
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months
You do not need the young partner's agreement to the activities you set for them.
## When education or training will be most appropriate
The first approved activity to consider for young partners is secondary education.
You will need to assess whether the young partner should continue to attend, or return to secondary education.
There may be reasons why secondary education will not be appropriate for the young partner. These include (but are not limited to) where the young partner:
- has been expelled and not able to attend another school
- has experienced severe bullying
- leaves school in October and turns 18 or 19 in November
In situations where a young partner cannot return to secondary education, the next option to consider is employment-related training or work-based learning.
For more information see:
- Secondary education
- Tertiary education
- Approved training (young partners)
- Work-based learning
## When developmental activities will be appropriate
A young partner may require other support and services to successfully participate in or achieve their activity obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning as well as gain and retain sustainable employment in the future.
For more information see:
- Developmental activities

chunks.title: Deciding if suitable place at Teen Parent Unit available — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Deciding if suitable place at Teen Parent Unit available
Where there is a Teen Parent Unit in the area, generally the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service will investigate this education option first for a young partner.
A place in the Teen Parent Unit is considered suitable if:
- the Teen Parent Unit and approved Early Childhood Education or other suitable childcare is a reasonable travel distance for the young partner taking into account their transport options
- there is a suitable approved Early Childhood Education place available or other suitable childcare that meets the child's needs
- the Teen Parent Unit is considered the best learning option for the young partner and
- there is a place available for the young partner
## Suitable place available but young partner does not want to attend
If there is a suitable place available, and the young partner has reasons for not wanting to attend the Teen Parent Unit, you must consider whether special circumstances exist that justify the young partner not being subject to the obligation to be education, training or work-based learning until a later date.
Where there are no special circumstances that justify the delay in the obligation for the young partner to return to education at a Teen Parent Unit, the young partner will be required to attend.
## No suitable place available
If there is no suitable place available in the Teen Parent Unit, the obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning applies from when:
- a suitable place becomes available
- the young partner's youngest dependent child reaches the age of 12 months
whichever is earlier.
For more information see:
- Special circumstances justifying delay in activity obligation
- Teen Parent Unit

chunks.title: Deciding non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or misconduct — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Deciding non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or misconduct
Before applying a 13 week non-entitlement period, you should consider the client's individual circumstances to determine whether or not it is appropriate to impose a 13 week non-entitlement period. You should:
- have a conversation with the client about why they left their employment and consider: if there was a good and sufficient reason for the client voluntarily stopping workif their employment ceased due to misconduct, what was the misconduct by the employee, and whether there is any evidence of the misconductwhether the misconduct was relatively minor, or whether there are circumstances surrounding their conduct which go a way towards excusing itwhether the client is challenging their dismissal or loss of employment
- if there was a good and sufficient reason for the client voluntarily stopping work
- if their employment ceased due to misconduct, what was the misconduct by the employee, and whether there is any evidence of the misconduct
- whether the misconduct was relatively minor, or whether there are circumstances surrounding their conduct which go a way towards excusing it
- whether the client is challenging their dismissal or loss of employment
- contact the employer to confirm the reason the client left their employment and ask the employer to complete the Employment and earnings information for applications (V06) form
if the employer refuses to return the form or provide a reason for the client's employment having ended, no further contact with the employer should be made - instead ask the client for a statement of events regarding why they left or were dismissed from employment
- consider whether there is conflicting evidence between what the client has advised and what the employer has advised
the client must be advised of the reasons given by the employer if those reasons are the basis of a decision to impose a non-entitlement period
if there is conflicting evidence or the reason for leaving employment is not agreed between the client and the employer, you should give the client the benefit of the doubt
- consider whether there are specific circumstances where a non-entitlement period should not be imposed
If you are uncertain whether a voluntary unemployment stand-down should be imposed, discuss the client's circumstances, in the first instance, with a service centre trainer and then with Helpline (if still required).
For more information see:
- Misconduct
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Generally a client must continue to remain ordinarily resident in New Zealand to get an Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Attributes associated with being ordinarily resident — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Ordinarily resident incorporates a number of factors. The key attributes to being ordinarily resident in New Zealand is a person must have a close and clear connection to New Zealand. Some of the key attributes that indicate that a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand include: - their physical presence in New Zealand is other than casually or as a traveller - they are in New Zealand because they want to be - they are here voluntarily - there is some intention to remain in New Zealand for a settled purpose - despite temporary absences from New Zealand they regularly or customarily live in New Zealand - they prefer residence in New Zealand to any other country (a person cannot be ordinarily resident in two countries at the same time) Whether a person is ordinarily resident is a question of fact and degree. You may need to ask the client for further information. Some of the following questions may help get more information: - if the client is going overseas, what are their intentions towards New Zealand (sighting return air tickets is a good indication) - the length of time they spend in New Zealand compared to their periods absence and the reasons for the absences - property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans) - where are their cash assets principally held (New Zealand banks or investment entities or overseas based holdings) - is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and are they tax resident in New Zealand - see Inland Revenue New Zealand tax residence guide IR292 - are they still on an electoral role and vote in central and local body elections - do they have a personal commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in their immediate and extended family, community, community events, clubs and other groups)

chunks.title: How to decide — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Whether a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand is a question of fact and degree. You must consider all the factors of each individual case and decide whether they show a clear and close connection to New Zealand. You may need to ask more questions (or seek clarification of information you have) to get all the relevant information and then you must weigh up all the facts and make a decision having regard to the attributes associated with a person being ordinarily resident in New Zealand (see above). If on the balance of facts you are not sure if the client is ordinarily resident in New Zealand contact the Helpline or see your manager client service delivery for advice.

chunks.title: Clients not ordinarily resident — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If you decide that a client is not ordinarily resident in New Zealand, this does not mean that they cannot be granted an Emergency Benefit as section 204 of the Social Security Act 2018 contains discretion. You have discretion to refuse to grant an Emergency Benefit or to grant it at a reduced rate. For example, a client may be in New Zealand temporarily to care for a relative but their home is overseas. They may have travelled to New Zealand suddenly and could not re-arrange their finances at short notice. Jobseeker Support may be appropriate if the client meets all of the qualifications. You should first consider eligibility to Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Definition of 'full-time' — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Definition of 'full-time'
Young partners must be in or available for full-time:
- secondary or tertiary education
- employment-related training or
- work-based learning
## Secondary school
For secondary school, a full-time course is defined as:
- 20 class hours a week
## Correspondence school
For young people studying at correspondence school full-time is:
- four subjects at NCEA level 1 or
- three subjects at NCEA levels 2 and 3
## Tertiary education
Tertiary programmes have an equivalent full-time student (EFTS) value assigned to them. The EFTS value determines if the course of study is full-time or not. To be full-time, a young partner must be studying the minimum EFTS in regards to weeks, as used for assessing full-time for Student Allowance purposes.
For more information see:
- Table of weeks for EFTS
## Work-based learning and other approved training
For work-based learning and all other types of training, full-time means the young partner must be engaged for 30-40 hours.
For more information see:
- NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification

chunks.title: Delayed retirement payments — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Delayed retirement payments
If the client has been granted a benefit and then receives a retirement payment within 52 weeks after the date the client's employment ceased, the benefit stand-down and date employment ceased must be reassessed.
To review the initial stand-down:
- divide the redundancy payment by 26 weeks (and 52 weeks if the client's entitlement date to benefit is on or after 1 May 2005). Add the appropriate weekly redundancy amount to the client's average weekly income received before employment ceased.
- re-assess the length of the initial stand-down period to determine a new commencement date. (Remember to use the calculation that provides the client with the lesser stand-down period).
and
- establish an overpayment for any monies paid to the client prior to the reassessed commencement date
## Payments received more than 52 weeks after retirement
If the client receives a retirement payment more than 52 weeks after the date the client's employment ceased, the payment is treated as a capital payment. The client's entitlement to any Extra help must also be reassessed.
Any interest received from the investment of any lump sum must be charged as income.
## Not retiring
In some situations, a person may cease their employment for a reason other than retirement and get a retirement payment as part of their final pay. For example, when a person resigns from their role voluntarily because they want to change careers or have a holiday.
When a person gets a retirement payment as part of their final pay but is not retiring, the retirement payment forms part of their earnings received in the 26 weeks prior to the commencement of benefit.
Retirement pay received when a person is not retiring is not used to determine the date employment ceased.

chunks.title: Dependent child — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
A dependent child for Emergency Benefit is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Emergency Benefit does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- child for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
In some situations, a child may not be living at home but is still considered to be a dependent child.
In some situations a client may not be the natural or adoptive parent of the child but MSD can still regard the child as their own when the child's parents are unable, or in exceptional circumstances unwilling, to look after the child.
## Long term care
The care situation should be permanent or long term.
MSD should not grant an Emergency Benefit to a client to care for a child who comes to stay with them for a short period such as the school holidays.
All dependent children should be included in the benefit.

chunks.title: Determining the reason for insufficient livelihood — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Determining the reason for insufficient livelihood
The reason a client is in hardship must be considered to determine whether the grant of Emergency Benefit is justified. The following guidelines have been created to assist you (but are not limited to):
- What barriers specifically are preventing the client from working to earn a sufficient livelihood for themselves (and any dependent family)?
- If they did not have these barriers how would they be supporting themselves (and any dependent family)?
- How did the client expect to support themselves (and any dependent family)?
- What other options has the client pursued and what was the outcome of those options?
- Is there any other assistance that the client can access to alleviate their hardship?
Note the client may be in hardship because of a combination of reasons. You will need to get the client's full circumstances before you make a decision.
## Decision
Take into account all the client's responses to establish:
- the circumstances preventing the client from earning an income
- the circumstances that placed the client in hardship
- options available to the client to alleviate their hardship
- whether the client contributed to their hardship and the extent to which they have contributed and
- on balance, consider whether payment of Emergency Benefit is justified
## No hardship
If hardship cannot be shown and/or the client has the ability to earn a sufficient livelihood, discuss the situation with the client. Consider other benefit assistance the client may be eligible for and decline the application for Emergency Benefit.
For more information see:
- Contributed to hardship
- Health condition, injury or disability
- Domestic circumstances
- Age
- Any other reason
- Example of equivalent benefit

chunks.title: Determining when a client became non-compliant — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a client fails to complete Upskilling without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must determine from which point the client was non-compliant. The client's benefit will be suspended or reduced from the first day of the week that MSD determines a client was non-compliant. The start of each week is based on when Upskilling was imposed. This means the week may not begin on a Monday. For example, if a client's Upskilling is imposed on a Wednesday, the beginning of the week for the sanction will be Wednesday.

chunks.title: Client engaged initially and then stopped — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A client may engage with Upskilling for a period of time, and then fail to meet the requirements before their Upskilling has ended. In this case, MSD will consider that a client was non-compliant from first day of the week in which a client stopped meeting the requirements.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Nami failed a work obligation and MSD imposed Upskilling as a non-financial sanction. In the third week of her sanction period, she does not participate in or report on at least 5 hours of her employment-related training or course. Her benefit is automatically stopped. She contacts MSD says she did not participate as she forgot to attend the course and report the hours. MSD is satisfied that Nami was complying with the requirements of Upskilling in weeks 1 and 2, but she was no longer compliant in week 3. MSD determines non-compliance from day one of week 3. Nami's payments are stopped from this date, and a debt is established. She is given a different recompliance activity to complete.

chunks.title: Client does not provide evidence — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a client attends their recompliance appointment and has been reporting on their employment-related training or courses in MyMSD but cannot provide MSD with evidence of this (without a good and sufficient reason) non-compliance should be backdated to the beginning of the week they stopped meeting their sanction requirements.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Robin had Upskilling imposed and successfully participated in 5 hours of employment-related training a week over a 4-week period. At the end of the 4-week period, Robin attends her recompliance meeting but does not provide verification of the employment-related training she did. She informs MSD she doesn't have sufficient evidence of her participation because she thought reporting in MyMSD would be enough. MSD determines this is not a good and sufficient reason and that she has not meet the requirements of Upskilling. MSD determines Robin was non-compliant from week one of her sanction as she was unable to provide any supporting evidence of the employment-related training or courses she did. Her payments are stopped from the beginning of week one and a debt is established.

chunks.title: Client does not make contact — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a client does not make contact with MSD at the end of their 4-week period, they will be considered non-compliant from the first day after the 4-week period ended. If a client later makes contact with MSD and has no good and sufficient reason for not meeting their requirements (including not providing sufficient evidence), non-compliance should be backdated to the beginning of the week in which they were no longer complying with the sanction.

chunks.title: MSD cannot determine when non-compliance occurred — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a client makes contact with MSD, MSD must use the information provided to determine when their non-compliance occurred. If the client does not provide enough information for MSD to determine this, non-compliance must be backdated to the beginning of the sanction period.

chunks.title: Determining when a partner became non-compliant — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a partner fails to complete Report Job Search without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must determine from which point the partner was non-compliant. The partner's benefit will be suspended or reduced from the first day of the week that MSD determines a partner was non-compliant. The start of each week is based on when Report Job Search was imposed. This means the week may not begin on a Monday. For example, if a partner's Report Job Search is imposed on a Wednesday, the beginning of the week for the sanction will be Wednesday.

chunks.title: Partner engaged initially and then stopped — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A partner may engage with Report Job Search for a period of time and then fail to meet the requirements before their Report Job Search has ended. In this case, MSD will consider that a partner was non-compliant from first day of the week in which a partner stopped meeting the requirements.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Tien failed a work obligation and MSD imposed Report Job Search as a non-financial sanction. He contacts MSD in his third week of Report Job Search and says he did not complete or report on his 3 job-search activities. When MSD asks about why he could not complete his job-search activities he says after week 2 he could not think of another activity to complete. MSD is satisfied that Tien was complying with the requirements of Report Job Search in week one and 2, but he was no longer compliant in week 3. MSD determines non-compliance from day one of week 3. Tien's payments are stopped from this date, and he is given a different recompliance activity to complete.

chunks.title: Partner does not provide evidence — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a partner attends their recompliance appointment and has been reporting on their job-search activities in MyMSD but cannot provide MSD with evidence of this (without a good and sufficient reason), non-compliance should be backdated to the beginning of the week they stopped meeting their sanction requirements.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Dende failed a work obligation and his case manager imposed Report Job Search as a non-financial sanction. Throughout the 4-week sanction period, Dende reports on 4 job-search activities each week. At the end of the four-week sanction period, when Dende meets with his case manager, he's unable to provide sufficient supporting evidence of his job-search activities because he forgot this was part of his sanction requirements and so didn't collect evidence throughout. As he doesn't have a good and sufficient reason for this, MSD determines that he hasn't met the requirements of the sanction. MSD determines Dende became non-compliant at the beginning of week one of his sanction, as he was unable to provide any supporting evidence of his job-search activities. His payments are stopped from the beginning of week one and a debt is established.

chunks.title: Partner does not make contact — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a partner does not make contact with MSD at the end of their 4-week period, they will be considered non-compliant from the first day after the 4-week period ended. If a partner later makes contact with MSD and has no good and sufficient reason for not meeting their requirements (including not providing sufficient evidence), non-compliance should be backdated to the beginning of the week in which they were no longer complying with the sanction.

chunks.title: MSD cannot determine when non-compliance occurred — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a partner makes contact with MSD, MSD must use the information provided to determine when their non-compliance occurred. If the partner does not provide enough information for MSD to determine this, non-compliance must be backdated to the beginning of the sanction period.

chunks.title: Determining when a partner became non-compliant — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Determining when a partner became non-compliant
When a partner fails to find or complete Community Work Experience without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must determine from which point the partner was non-compliant.
MSD may consider information shared by an organisation when determining if a partner has a good and sufficient reason for failing to find or complete Community Work Experience, however MSD must also consider information provided by the partner.
The partner's benefit will be suspended or reduced from the first day of the week that MSD determines a partner was non-compliant.
The start of each week is based on when the Community Work Experience was imposed. This means the week may not begin on a Monday.
For example, if a partner's Community Work Experience is imposed on a Wednesday, the beginning of the week for the sanction will be Wednesday.
## Partner engaged initially and then stopped
A partner may engage with Community Work Experience for a period of time, and then fail to meet the requirements before their Community Work Experience has ended.
In this case, MSD will consider that the partner was non-compliant from first day of the week that the partner stopped meeting the requirements.
## Partner does not make contact
When a partner does not provide verification or make contact with MSD at the end of their search period or the end of their position period, they will be considered non-compliant from the first day after the respective period ended.
If a partner later makes contact with MSD and has no good and sufficient reason for not meeting their requirements, non-compliance should be backdated to the beginning of the week in which they were no longer complying with the sanction.
## MSD cannot determine when non-compliance occurred
When a partner makes contact with MSD, MSD must use the information provided to determine when their non-compliance occurred. If the partner does not provide enough information for MSD to determine this, non-compliance must be back-dated to the beginning of the search or position period, depending on which period the partner was in when non-compliance occurred.

chunks.title: Determining whether Community Work Experience is appropriate — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Determining whether Community Work Experience is appropriate
MSD must assess whether Community Work Experience is suitable for a partner and their circumstances before it may be imposed as a non-financial sanction.
Partners will keep getting their full benefit while in Community Work Experience, instead of a 50% financial sanction.
MSD must consider any relevant factors before choosing to impose Community Work Experience. Examples of some factors to consider are listed below.
## Partner's obligations
Partners with work obligations who fail a social obligation may have Community Work Experience imposed. However, it may be more appropriate for a partner to recomply with their failure by meeting their social obligations, rather than completing Community Work Experience.
## Skills and experience
Community Work Experience may be best if the partner has limited work experience or levels of work readiness.
For example, if a partner has significant work history, or tertiary-level qualifications, Community Work Experience may not help them to become more employable.
However, if a partner has a large gap in their work history, or no connections in their local community, Community Work Experience may still be suitable, depending on their circumstances.
## Levels of confidence
Community Work Experience is intended to help a partner build work-related skills and confidence. However, they may find it overwhelming to approach organisations to find and complete a position for the purpose of a sanction.
Community Work Experience will only be suitable if MSD is reasonably satisfied that a partner can find and complete a position.
## Previous experience with community or voluntary work
If a partner has previous experience participating in community or voluntary work, it may be more likely that they would commit to carrying out Community Work Experience. This could also help them find a position.
## Local availability
In larger towns or cities, there may be more options for a partner to find a suitable position for Community Work Experience. In smaller areas, a partner may not be likely to find a position, or MSD may already know there is less availability there.
It would not be reasonable to impose Community Work Experience if it is unlikely that a partner would be able to successfully find a position in their area.
## Known risk factors
It would not be appropriate to impose Community Work Experience as a sanction if MSD is aware of something that could be a risk to the partner, organisation or other people involved. This can include things like known sex offenders or partners with a history of violence.

chunks.title: Determining whether Money Management is appropriate — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD must assess whether Money Management is suitable for a client and their circumstances before it may be imposed as a non-financial sanction. Clients will continue to get their full benefit payment while on Money Management with 50% of their main benefit going to a payment card and 50% paid to their bank account. This is instead of a 50% financial sanction. MSD may consider any relevant factors before choosing to impose Money Management. Some examples of factors that should be considered are outlined below.

chunks.title: Ability to recomply with their obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Clients who get a 50% financial sanction will have their full benefit rate restored as soon as they recomply with their obligations. This is different from Money Management, which always lasts for 4 weeks, no matter when a client completes their recompliance activity. It may be more suitable for a client to get a financial sanction than be subject to Money Management if they are able to complete their recompliance activity quickly. For example, if there is an activity available on the first day the sanction would be applied, it may be better to impose a financial sanction for one day instead of imposing Money Management for 4 weeks. If an activity isn’t available for 2 weeks, it may be better to impose Money Management instead of reducing their benefit for 2 weeks.

chunks.title: Housing stability — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Clients will have to pay their accommodation costs using the payments they receive into their bank account (including any Working for Families tax credits and supplementary assistance) as the Money Management supplier group doesn’t include housing providers. If a client is unable to pay their housing costs from the benefit payments that go into their bank account while on Money Management, this will seriously impact their living situation. It would not be suitable to impose Money Management if it would worsen their housing situation compared to a different sanction.

chunks.title: Redirections and offsets — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Any redirections, offsets, or debt repayments will be deducted from the benefit payments going into a client’s bank account. It may not be possible for a client to make some of these payments while they are under Money Management. MSD should discuss this with the client before deciding whether to impose Money Management.

chunks.title: Hardship applications — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Clients or partners who make frequent hardship applications may benefit from Money Management as the payment card can only be used to buy essential items. If a client or partner is already working with a budgeting service to manage their finances, Money Management may not be appropriate.

chunks.title: Changes in income — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Money Management may not be suitable for clients who frequently have changes in income. If a client or partner declares a change in their income after their payment has been issued to their payment card, it may result in an overpayment. If they are overpaid, a debt will be established as the payment cannot be adjusted. If a client is underpaid, they will be issued arrears directly into their bank account. This may reduce the effectiveness of the sanction.

chunks.title: Access to suppliers — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Payments on a client’s payment card can only be used at particular suppliers. Depending on where a client lives, they may not have access to many suppliers in their area. Money Management would not be suitable if a client cannot reasonably spend the money on their payment card.

chunks.title: Client circumstances — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a client or partner has particular circumstances that would be worsened by being money managed, Money Management is not appropriate. For example, if a client or partner is experiencing family violence or a domestic emergency, Money Management may cause additional stress. MSD should consider a different sanction where possible.

chunks.title: Determining whether Report Job Search is appropriate — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD must assess whether Report Job Search is suitable for a partner and their circumstances before it may be imposed as a non-financial sanction. Partners will keep getting their full benefit while completing Report Job Search, instead of a 50% financial sanction. MSD must consider any relevant factors before choosing to impose Report Job Search. Examples of some factors to consider are listed below. If Report Job Search is not suitable, a different non-financial sanction may be appropriate.

chunks.title: Partner's obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Partners with work obligations who fail a social obligation may have Report Job Search imposed. However, it may be more appropriate for a partner to recomply with their failure by meeting their social obligations, rather than completing Report Job Search. Note if a partner doesn't have work obligations they cannot have Report Job Search imposed on them.

chunks.title: What work activities the partner has assigned to them — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a partner is already reporting their job-search activities, as part of an obligation or work-testable activity, it may not be appropriate to impose Report Job Search on them.

chunks.title: Local employment availability — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a partner lives in a limited employment location, there may be fewer job-search activities available for partners to complete. MSD should consider a partner's local labour market when determining if Report Job Search is appropriate. Note partners who live in areas with limited job opportunities must be able to meet their obligations to look for and find suitable work. This can include being willing and realistically able to commute to nearby towns or centres to find employment.

chunks.title: Work readiness — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Partners with limited skills or work experience (e.g. recent school leavers) need to be looking for any suitable work available in their area. A lack of work history shouldn't prevent a partner from being able to complete Report Job Search. However, a partner's barriers to employment and personal circumstances should also be considered when deciding if Report Job Search is appropriate.

chunks.title: Accessibility — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Partners must be able to report their job-search activities on MyMSD. MSD should consider a partner's ability to access and report on MyMSD before imposing Report Job Search. For example: - the partner must have access to a device they can access the internet on (this can include the kiosks at a service centre) - if the partner doesn't have access to a device they can access the internet on, consider their ability to get to a service centre, - the partner must have adequate digital literacy skills to report their job-search activities

chunks.title: Determining whether Upskilling is appropriate — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD must assess whether Upskilling is suitable for a client and their circumstances before it may be imposed as a non-financial sanction. Clients will keep getting their full benefit while completing Upskilling, instead of a 50% financial sanction. MSD must consider any relevant factors before choosing to impose Upskilling. Examples of some factors to consider are listed below. If Upskilling is not suitable a different non-financial sanction may be more appropriate.

chunks.title: Client's obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Clients with work or work preparation obligations who fail a social obligation may have Upskilling imposed. However, it may be more appropriate for a client to recomply with their failure by meeting their social obligations, rather than completing Upskilling.

chunks.title: Skills and experience — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Upskilling is intended for clients with limited work experience, levels of work readiness, or clients who want to upskill in a new field of work. If a client has a significant work history, or has completed tertiary-level qualifications, Upskilling may not help the client get closer to finding work in their current field. If a client has a gap in their work history, lacks certain skills, or is interested in changing their field of work, Upskilling may still be considered based on the client's circumstances.

chunks.title: Local availability — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Most employment-related training and courses for Upskilling will be completed online. If there are no suitable online options, MSD should consider local availability of in-person courses. In larger towns or cities, there may be suitable courses for a client to attend. In smaller areas, it may be harder to find a suitable training or course, or MSD may already know there is less availability there. It would be unreasonable to impose Upskilling if local knowledge/expertise indicates a low likelihood of a client successfully being enrolled in an Upskilling course.

chunks.title: Levels of confidence — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: For some clients, a chance to upskill and develop their capability will provide an opportunity to build their confidence. For others, completing an Upskilling course for skills they already have may be inappropriate.

chunks.title: Previous engagement with Upskilling courses — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a client has already participated in and completed Upskilling courses, this may mean they are likely to commit to completing another Upskilling course. However, if a client has participated in and completed several Upskilling courses already, a different type of sanction should be considered. This should be assessed based on the client's individual circumstances.

chunks.title: Accessibility — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Clients must be able to report their participation in employment-related training or courses on MyMSD. MSD should consider a client's ability to access and report on MyMSD before imposing Upskilling. For example: - the client must have access to a device they can access the internet on (this can include the kiosks at a service centre) - if the client doesn't have access to a device they can access the internet on, consider their ability to get to a service centre - the client must have adequate digital literacy skills to access and report on their employment-related training or course

chunks.title: Developmental activities — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Developmental activities
To provide additional support to the young person, developmental activities may also be included alongside other activities that a young person is undertaking. A young person can undertake other developmental activities and still be considered to be meeting their youth activity obligations as long as:
- they are continuing to participate, or are available to undertake, full-time education, training or work-based learning
- you have assessed that the person needs to address other needs while they undertake full-time education, training or work-based learning and
- the young person agrees to participate
Note a young person can be asked to participate in developmental activities but they cannot be required to. The young person cannot be sanctioned for not agreeing to undertake a developmental activity.
Other developmental activities include (but are not limited to):
- Interpersonal skills - increasing a young person's people or communication skills
- Self motivation (for example confidence or motivation courses)
- Writing and language - young people who have learned English as their second language may require extra tuition to complement their main education or training activity
- Counselling/family violence related programmes
- Drug and alcohol counselling
- Social rehabilitation programmes
Note the Limited Service Volunteer programme will generally not be appropriate for partners of main beneficiaries unless they are transitioning out of the service and have job seeking as their destination.

chunks.title: Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes where when a partner is diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence.
Drug addiction or dependence, for the purposes of the drug test requirements, means a person who has been diagnosed with
- severe substance abuse or
- dependency or drug addiction issues
The partner can be asked to provide verification from a registered health practitioner or by a registered AOD practitioner who will have completed a formal assessment and given the diagnosis of drug dependency. The verification should also state the duration or time that the partner will need to address their drug issue dependency. There is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that MSD can provide to the partner.

chunks.title: Disputes and reviews of an obligations failure — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Disputes and reviews of an obligations failure
A client or partner has the right to dispute or review if they disagree with any decision relating to:
- an obligations failure or
- a sanction being imposed or
- the type of sanction being imposed
A client or partner can do this by:
- disputing the decision or
- lodging a formal Review of Decision
- lodging an appeal to the Medical Appeals Board (drug test failure only)
A Review of Decision or appeal to the Medical Appeals Board can be lodged at any stage, within three months of the obligations failure being initiated, or within three months of the sanction being imposed.
If a client or partner disputes their obligations failure or sanction more than 20 working days after it is initiated or imposed, MSD must advise the client or partner to lodge a formal Review of Decision or an appeal to the Medical Appeals Board (drug test failure only) in writing.
For more information see:
- Disputing more than one obligations failure
- The disputes process
- Recording decisions on a dispute
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Core policy Medical Appeal Board

chunks.title: Disputing more than one obligations failure — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Disputing more than one obligations failure
If a client or partner has failed more than one obligation at the same time, they can dispute any of the failed activities by providing a good and sufficient reason for each failure.
## Example
A partner has failed their social obligations and two of their work obligations, and the failures have been initiated on the same day. The partner disputes some of these failures as they have good and sufficient reasons. The partner also recomplies to one. The partner is not sanctioned but the failure is counted because they recomplied with one of the failures.
Obligation
Recompliance
Action
Social obligation - failed to enrol child in ECE
Partner must comply with all social obligations
Partner disputes failure - has good and sufficient reason
Work obligations - failed to attend interview
Must attend another job interview - or similar activity
Partner disputes failure - has good and sufficient reason
Work obligations - refused to take drug test
Must agree to being drug free
Partner has no good and sufficient reason for the failure - agrees to recomply
## Example
A partner has failed their obligations and the failures have been initiated on the same day. The partner recomplies for one failure but not for the other failure. The sanction remains imposed until the client recomplies.
Obligation
Recompliance
Action
Work obligation - failed to attend a job interview
Partner must participate in another job interview
Partner has no good and sufficient reason for not attending the job interview - the sanction remains imposed until the partner recomplies with this activity
Work obligations - failed to attend job seminar
Must attend another job seminar - or similar activity
Partner recomplies by attending another job seminar

chunks.title: District Health Board assistance — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: For a District Health Board to provide assistance a Needs Assessment and Service Co-ordination Agency (NASC) assessment has to be completed to determine the needs of the client. The assessment outcome ranges from very low to very high and can assist you to determine if an Emergency Benefit is justified. Just because a person has been assessed as very low or low, does not mean the client is not eligible for Emergency Benefit. The client's full circumstances must be taken into account. The ranges are: ScaleDescriptionVery lowDisabled person, family/whanau needs are minimal and the safety and wellbeing of both is not compromisedLowAlthough well supported the needs of the disabled person are increasingSignificant changes in need mean the level of support required must be consideredThe disabled person is not achieving age appropriate milestonesMediumOpportunities and potential for development are limited or developed for example physical, cognitive, communication, behaviourFamily/ whanau are stressed and are not being effectively supportedThe disabled person's disability is becoming more significant and the impact on the family/ whanau is constantThe disabled person's behaviour means that there is a risk of isolation from their communityHighDisabled person's developmental milestones are severely delayedFamily/ whanau are unable to manage the disabled person's needs. chunks.title: Domestic circumstances — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Domestic circumstances
A client's domestic circumstances may prevent them from earning a sufficient livelihood to support themselves (and any dependent family). Generally, this is due to caring responsibilities.
There may be other reasons and these will need to be determined before a decision can be made on the equivalent benefit.
For more information see:
- Caring responsibilities
Note when a client has made a choice that has restricted their ability to earn a sufficient livelihood, you will need to consider the client's ability to change their circumstances to alleviate their hardship and whether payment of Emergency Benefit is justified.

chunks.title: Donating a kidney or liver tissue — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Donating a kidney or liver tissue
Generally, clients receiving a main benefit, who are donating a kidney or liver tissue, will still meet the qualifications for benefit and can continue to receive it.
However, if the client has a change of circumstances that prevents continued entitlement to their current benefit, they may still require income and childcare assistance during their recovery time. Consider transferring the client to Emergency Benefit.
Clients receiving Jobseeker Support, Sole Parent Support or Supported Living Payment due to a health condition, injury or disability may continue to receive their current benefit.
## Client no longer entitled to benefit
A client receiving Supported Living Payment - caring for a person, cannot receive the Supported Living Payment while recovering from surgery. The client should be transferred to Emergency Benefit following the donation of a kidney or liver tissue.
## No hardship test
No hardship test applies if a client donates a kidney or liver tissue, while they are receiving Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Drug test job referral not suitable — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Drug test job referral not suitable
There are certain situations where it is not appropriate to refer a partner to drug tested jobs as the job is not considered to be suitable. These situations include where a partner is:
- taking prescribed medication
- diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- in or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence or
- has a drug issue identified by a provider and is engaging and participating in services and support offered by that provider
These situations are also to be taken into account when deciding whether a partner has a good and sufficient reason for failing their drug test requirements. For more information see:
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons
The first time a partner presents with one of these situations, you should:
- accept that it is not appropriate to refer the partner to drug tested jobs
- add a deferral from drug test obligations for an initial 30 working day period and
- advise the client that if they think they require a deferral from drug test obligations for more than 30 working days, then verification will be required
- there is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to the partner
For more information see:
- Drug test - Referral delay [no link find out why]
Depending on the clients circumstances and the verification provided you can extend the deferral from drug test obligations up to six months.
For more information see:
- Taking controlled prescription medication
- Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence
- Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence
- Employers requiring pre-employment drug tests
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: Drug test obligation failures - Good and sufficient reasons — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Drug test obligation failures - Good and sufficient reasons
Before you initiate an obligations failure you need to be satisfied that the partner does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their drug test work obligations.
There are certain situations that must be considered to be good and sufficient reasons for drug test obligations failures, these situations include where a partner:
- is taking controlled prescribed medication
- is diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- is in or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence or
- has a drug issue identified by the Alcohol Drug Helpline - Work and Income Support Service and is engaging and participating in services and support offered by the 0800 AOD Helpline
## Drug tested job referral not suitable
These situations are also to be taken into account when deciding whether it is appropriate to refer a partner to drug tested jobs. If you decide that, due to one of these situations, it is not appropriate to refer a partner to further drug tested jobs you must add a Drug test obligations deferral.
For more information see:
- Drug Test - Referral Delay [no link find out why] procedure
## Client provides a good and sufficient reason
The first time a partner fails the drug test obligation and provides a good and sufficient reason, you should:
- accept that the partner has a good and sufficient reason
- add a deferral from drug test obligations for an initial 30 working day period and
- advise the client that if they think they require a deferral from drug test obligations for more than 30 working days, then verification will be required
- there is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to your client
For more information see:
- Drug test job referral not suitable
- Taking controlled prescription medication
- Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence
- Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence
- Reviewing or disputing the drug test failure
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures

chunks.title: Drug test obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Partners of clients receiving Emergency Benefit who have work obligations are subject to drug test obligations. Partners must undertake and pass drug tests when Work and Income have identified: - a suitable job and pre-employment drug tests are required by a prospective employer or - a suitable course and a pre-course drug test is required as part of the admission process by a training provider A partner will fail their drug test work obligations if they have no good and sufficient reason and: - a suitable job is available and they advise they will not apply for the job as they will not pass the pre-employment drug test - they have been referred to or have applied for a suitable job or course and they refuse to take the pre-employment drug test or - they have been referred to a suitable job or course and they fail or refuse a drug test If a partner fails their drug test work obligations the same 5 day notice period and sanctions apply as for any other obligations failure.

chunks.title: Partner will not apply as they will not pass the drug test — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: An immediate obligations failure should be initiated if a partner, without a good and sufficient reason, has: - been matched to a job opportunity and refuses to apply for it as they advise they will fail the pre-employment drug test or - attended a seminar to discuss a job opportunity and advises they will fail the pre-employment drug test

chunks.title: Partner refuses to take the drug test — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: An obligations failure should be initiated if a partner without a good and sufficient reason, has been referred to a suitable job and refuses to take the pre-employment drug test.

chunks.title: Partner fails the drug test — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: An obligations failure should be initiated, if a partner, without good and sufficient reason, has: - been referred to a suitable job and the employer advises that they have failed the pre-employment drug test or - been referred to a suitable course and the training provider advises that they have failed the pre-course drug test Note the employer or training provider must confirm that a partner has failed the drug test before you initiate the obligations failure.

chunks.title: Partner fails pre-employment alcohol test — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Job applicants may be required to be tested for alcohol use prior to being hired. However, the drug test obligation requirements do not include alcohol. If a partner failed a test for alcohol use, without a good and sufficient reason, then a work test failure could be initiated because the partner has failed to participate in the job interview process. For more information see: - Informing clients of their obligations - Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements - Employers requiring pre-employment drug tests - Training providers requiring a drug test - Types of drug tests and standards - Partner has failed a screening drug test

chunks.title: Drug test recompliance count — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Drug test recompliance count
The obligation failure that is initiated or the sanction that is imposed depends on how often the partner has failed to comply with their obligations in the previous 24 months while getting a benefit. This is called the 24- month failure count.
The recompliance activity that the partner has to complete depends on whether the partner has failed their drug test obligation before within the last 24 months.
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation the partner must complete a six-week approved activity.
## Example 1
Obligation / activity failed
Recompliance
24 month failure count
Work obligations - failed pre-employment drug test requirement
Drugs test recompliance 1
eg must verbally agree to stop using drugs
Obligations failure 1 or Grade 1 sanction
Work obligations - refused to apply for a job due to pre-employment drug test requirement
Drugs test recompliance 2
eg - agree to take and pass a drug test within 25 working days (of the agreement)
Obligations failure 2 or Grade 2 sanction
## Example 2
Obligation / activity failed
Recompliance
24 month failure count
Work obligations - did not attend job interview
Must recomply by completing the same or similar activity eg must attend another job interview
Obligations failure 1 or Grade 1 sanction
Work obligations - refused to apply for a job due to pre-employment drug test requirement
Drugs test recompliance 1
eg must verbally agree to stop using controlled drugs
Obligations failure 2 or Grade 2 sanction
Work obligations - failed pre-employment drug test requirement
Six week approved activity or programme of activities
Obligations failure 3 or Grade 3 sanction
For more information see:
- Counting previous obligations failures

chunks.title: Duration of Emergency Benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Duration of Emergency Benefit
Emergency Benefit should only be paid for as long as it is needed. You can grant Emergency Benefit for a specified period, depending on the client's circumstances.
For example, a partner is overseas doing job search and hasn't provided any financial support for their family. Emergency Benefit may be granted but only until the partner can be expected to return to New Zealand or arrange financial support for their family.
## Eligible for another benefit
If the client will be eligible for another benefit in the future, only grant Emergency Benefit until the date they are expected to be eligible for another benefit.
Example a client is getting Emergency Benefit as they are the partner of a New Zealand Superannuation client and the principal caregiver of a dependent child. They do no not qualify for Jobseeker Support because they can't meet the work obligations due to their caring responsibilities. Emergency Benefit can only be paid until the client's child turns 14. They should then qualify for Jobseeker Support.
## SWIFTT expiry date
When adding an expiry date into SWIFTT, you need to consider:
- when the client or partner will qualify for another benefit and
- when their eligibility to Emergency Benefit will be affected
whichever is the later should be added as the expiry date.
## Undertaking specific activity or task
If Emergency Benefit has been granted and the client must undertake a specific activity or task, the duration of Emergency Benefit should be until the client has completed that activity or task.

chunks.title: Earning incentive payments — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Earning incentive payments
Young partners getting Emergency Benefit can earn the following incentive payments:
- education incentive of $10 a week
- budgeting incentive of $10 a week
- parenting education incentive of $10 a week
## Education incentive
A young partner on Emergency Benefit can earn the education incentive if:
- their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service has confirmed to YSSU that since they started receiving their benefit, they have continuously attended and participated in either education, training or work-based learning for at least 6 calendar months
## Budgeting incentive
A young partner on Emergency Benefit can earn the budgeting incentive if:
- their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service has confirmed to YSSU that since they started receiving their benefit they have: attended and participated in discussions on budgeting with the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service provider for at least 3 calendar months andattended and completed a budgeting programme
- attended and participated in discussions on budgeting with the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service provider for at least 3 calendar months and
- attended and completed a budgeting programme
## Parenting incentive
A young partner with a child on Emergency Benefit can earn the parenting education incentive if:
- the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service has confirmed that, since they started to receive the benefit, they have regularly engaged with their service provider or Work and Income "in-house service" for at least 3 calendar months and
- they have participated in and completed a parenting education programme
- each of their dependent children is enrolled with a primary health organisation
- each of their dependent children aged 5 years or under are up-to-date with their Wellchild checks
- each of their dependent children aged 5 years or under attends an approved early childhood education programme or is placed in other suitable childcare during any time the young person is in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work
Note the earliest date the 3 month period can be calculated from is the date the young partner was granted their Emergency Benefit.
For more information see:
- Removing incentive payments
- Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose
- Incentive payments can continue
- Restoring incentive payments
- Obligations
## Capacity issues prevent a young partner meeting their parenting obligations
Sometimes a young partner may be able to get a parenting education incentive payment without meeting the criteria.

chunks.title: Earning the right to receive payment directly — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Earning the right to receive payment directly
Young partners who are subject to youth money management can earn the right to have their portion of main benefit, family tax credit and any extra help paid directly to them.
The young partner can gain control of their payment if:
- they have demonstrated continued compliance with their obligations and
- their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service considers that they are financially competent
A young partner who has earned control over their payment has the choice to have their benefit paid directly to them and they will be responsible for paying their costs.
Note when young partners are sanctioned and they are not subject to youth money management because they have earned the right to manage their own money, they won't be put back on youth money management like those clients on Youth Payment and Young Parent Payment. This ensures the sanctions for clients who aren't subject to youth money management remain graduated through any obligation failures.

chunks.title: Effect of 13-week non-entitlement - couple wishes to change primary status — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Effect of 13-week non-entitlement - couple wishes to change primary status
In some cases, a primary client with a partner who has no work obligations may have a 13 week non-entitlement period as a result of:
- voluntary unemployment
- dismissal as a result of misconduct
- grade 3 sanction
- refusing an offer of suitable employment (job refusal)
and may request to have their partner become the primary client.
Before the partner and primary status can be changed, it must be confirmed that the client to be the primary would be eligible for Emergency Benefit. They need to be actively seeking and available for full-time work.
You need to confirm that the client who will be the primary about whether they can meet the job search requirements.
To help decide if a client is able to meet the job search requirements, you will need to consider the following:
1. If the client had the opportunity, would they:
- be available for work for 30 hours or more a week (full-time work obligations)
- accept any suitable job offers within their abilitiesNote that this can include weekend work depending on the client or partner's individual circumstances
- not restrict their job search to vacancies within their own trade
- not restrict their job search to vacancies in their chosen occupation
- not move frequently from one area to another with no intention of getting a job
2. Has the client begun to take steps to find work? For example by:
- searching newspapers and other media for vacancies
- making applications for suitable jobs
- contacting employers about vacancies
Have a conversation with the client about what this will mean for their and their partner's obligations, and confirm the reasons for the change.
If the client subject to a 13-week non-entitlement period becomes the partner and is no longer subject to the type of obligation that they failed, then it may be unreasonable for them to complete a recompliance activity. The client's benefit can then be resumed.
Note if the client in this scenario was subject to an obligations failure, while they may not have to complete a recompliance activity, their failure count will still include the obligations failure that caused their non-entitlement period.
For more information see:
- Processing standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Effect of a non-entitlement period on financial assistance — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Effect of a non-entitlement period on financial assistance
When a client is subject to a non-entitlement period, their benefit is cancelled and they have no entitlement to a benefit for 13 weeks unless they recomply. Clients with dependent children have 50% protection applied during a non-entitlement period.
## 50% protection for sole parents and couples with dependent children
Sole parents or couples with one or more dependent children, who are subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period do not have their whole benefit affected.
Instead, a maximum sanction of 50% of the main benefit may be imposed. The balance payable is known as 50% protection.
## Example
A sole parent with 50% protection has only 50% of their rate of benefit cancelled before any income reduction. During the cancellation, they are entitled to receive a 50% rate of that benefit with the income test applied, but at half the rate of the income test.
## Grade 3 sanction for couples without dependent children
If one partner of a couple with no dependent children is subject to a grade 3 sanction, this is only applied to half the couple's benefit. The non-sanctioned partner is entitled to half the couple rate of benefit, with any income reduced at half the rate of the income test that applies.
If both partners of a couple with no dependent children are subject to a grade 3 sanction, the benefit is stopped (as 50% is stopped for each partner who failed).
For more information see:
- Effect on supplementary assistance - voluntary unemployment
- Effect on supplementary assistance - grade 3 sanction or job refusal
- Financial assistance during a non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Effect of certain drugs — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Effect of certain drugs
To fail a drug test a partner must have drugs present in their system that reach a certain threshold or cut out level. Passing a drug test does not require a 100% drug free sample.
## Effect of certain drugs
How long certain drugs stay in a person's systems depends on a variety of factors, including (but not limited to) the:
- amount and frequency of use
- persons body mass, age, overall health and
- persons drug tolerance
Below are some examples of drugs and the average 'duration' that they are present in a person's system. This information has been sourced from several publications by experts in this area, however, this must not be considered to be 'absolute' because how drugs affect a person does depend on the factors above.
Drug
Average duration
Amphetamines (including methamphetamine)
1 to 7 days
Ecstasy, Cocaine
2 to 4 days
Benzodiazepines
2 to 10 days
Marijuana / cannabis (including medicinal cannabis)
3 to 30 days
LSD
1 to 3 days
Opioids
Note this covers drugs such as codeine, fentanyl, heroin, oxycodone, morphine and tramadol
1 to 3 days
Cannabis can stay in a person's body for several weeks, particularly if the person is a heavy or regular user. The recompliance period accounts for the general length of time it takes for cannabis to be metabolised out of the body.
Partners have 25 working days to take and pass a drug test and MSD allows an additional 5 working days to receive and process the results from the partner.
Partners can consult with their registered health practitioner or the Alcohol Drug Helpline - Work and Income Support Service [no link find out why] for further guidance on how drugs may affect them.
