chunks.title: Young partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a young partner has had an obligations failure, the assistance available to them depends on the failure number and whether the young partner is money managed or not. For more information see:

chunks.title: Effect on supplementary assistance - voluntary unemployment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Effect on supplementary assistance - voluntary unemployment
Clients who have a 13 week non-entitlement period because they became voluntarily unemployed cannot receive the following during their non-entitlement period:
- Emergency Benefit
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit
Note a client who was receiving an Accommodation Supplement as a non-beneficiary prior to applying and being subject to a non-entitlement period upon application can continue to receive an Accommodation Supplement during their non-entitlement period.
If eligible, clients can still receive:
- Assistance to transition into employment
- Disability Allowance
For more information see:
- Financial assistance during a non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Effective date of transfer — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Effective date of transfer
A client getting Supported Living Payment caring for someone can be transferred to Emergency Benefit following the donation of a kidney or liver tissue.
Clients receiving other benefit types or who are a partner included in a benefit, can continue to be eligible for their benefit and are not eligible to be transferred to Emergency Benefit.
Note young people getting Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment can remain on their payment and be granted an exemption from their activity obligations (for up to 12 weeks).
## Effective date
When a client has made an application to transfer from their current benefit to the Emergency Benefit because they are donating a kidney or liver tissue, you can transfer them to an Emergency Benefit from the:
- surgery date (if they have applied within 28 days of their surgery) or
- application date for Emergency Benefit
Application within 28 days of surgery
When a client applies for Emergency Benefit before or within 28 days of the date of surgery, transfer the client from the date of surgery.
If the client applies for Emergency Benefit more than 28 days following the date of surgery, transfer the client to Emergency Benefit from the date the application is received.
Note if the client applies for Emergency Benefit more than 12 weeks following the date of surgery, Emergency Benefit cannot be considered for convalescence.
For more information see:
- Medical certificates for live organ donors

chunks.title: Employers requiring pre-employment drug tests — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Employers requiring pre-employment drug tests
Some industries require potential employees to pass a pre-employment drug test as a condition of employment.
Employers usually only drug test where there are health and safety reasons and where there are industry requirements to test. If an employee works in a safety sensitive area the employer has an obligation to provide all employees a safe working environment. For these jobs, drug testing is justified where an employee's ability to perform their job has the potential to affect the safety of others or themselves.
Pre-employment drug tests are typically required in industries such as fishing, horticultural factory work and forestry.
Note that Work and Income will have checked with the employer why the job is being drug tested and whether the testing is to the required drug test standards.
Employers that require pre-employment drug testing may also require regular or random testing of employees to ensure those working in safety sensitive areas are not impaired while at work.
## Who administers the test?
Drug testing is generally provided to individual employers and recruitment agencies by contracted drug test providers. Some large organisations have their own specialised in-house staff, such as nurses, who are accredited in workplace drug testing.
Employment-related drug testing is:
- conducted at a workplace, established testing site or a laboratory and
- through observed collection

chunks.title: Employment ceased — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Employment ceased
When a person applies for benefit as they have finished work, their entitlement date is usually the day after their employment ceased. The date employment ceased is not always the person's last working day.
Some payments a person gets when they finish work affect the date their employment ceased.
Below are the payments that affect the date employment ceased:
- holiday pay
- pay in lieu of notice
- pay in lieu of accumulated leave
- payments dependent on the completion of a fixed term contract
- retirement payments
If a person has received one or more of these payments, you need to calculate the date their employment ceased. See:
- Calculation of employment ceased
Note redundancy payments and severance payments do not affect the date employment ceased.

chunks.title: Employment during stand-down — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Employment during stand-down
If a client gains temporary full-time employment during the initial stand-down period, this may change the date the benefit can start from.
The new entitlement date is the date the temporary employment stops. Reassess the client's initial stand-down period using the income for the 26 and 52 weeks earned immediately before the new entitlement date.
- Example of employment during the stand-down

chunks.title: Employment trial period of up to 90 days — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Employment trial period of up to 90 days
A partner may continue to meet their work obligations if their employment agreement includes an employment trial period. This is assessed the same as any other employment.
Employment agreements, signed by the employer and employee, can include an employment trial period of up to 90 days.
Features of an employment trial:
- an employment trial may be offered by an employer regardless of the number of employees a business has and
- an employer may terminate the employment agreement during a trial at any time before the end of the employment trial period even if the last day of work occurs after the expiry of the employment trial period and
- an employer is not required to provide a reason for ending the employment trial if the notice of termination was given before the employment trial period ended and
- an employee cannot generally bring a personal grievance against the employer in respect of the ending of their employment during the employment trial period
The partner can still challenge the ending of their employment agreement including on the grounds of:
- discrimination or
- sexual harassment or
- racial harassment or
- duress imposed by the employer in relation to a client's union affiliations or not as the case may be
For more information about when a client's employment ceases before the end of the employment trial see:

chunks.title: Enrolled in and attending school — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Enrolled in and attending school
A client and their partner (if any) getting Emergency Benefit must take all reasonable steps to ensure their children, are enrolled in and attending school from the age of 5 or 6 years old (depending on when they start school).
## Age of child
Clients with a dependent child aged 5 or 6 years (depending on when they start school) to 15 years of age will be required to take all reasonable steps to ensure the child is enrolled in and regularly attending school.
If a child is aged between 5 or 6 years it is the parent or caregivers choice as to whether they have their child in early childhood education or school.
A child does not legally have to attend school until they are 6 years old, but most children start school at 5 years.
A client must meet the early childhood education social obligation if they choose not to enrol their 5 year old in school.
A child can legally leave school when they are 16 years or at 15 years, if they have an early leaving exemption from the Ministry of Education.
A parent or caregiver cannot be asked to comply with the attendance at school social obligation if the child has legally left school or has an early leaving exemption, and is no longer legally required to attend school.
## Verification of child enrolled and attending school
All children aged from 6 to 15 years old are legally required to attend school. In most cases you should take your client's word that they are meeting their social obligations.
However, if you have information that indicates the child may not be attending school you may ask the client to get verification, for example, a letter from the child's school that says the child is enrolled and attending.
There are some situations where a client may be taking all reasonable steps but their child is not attending school.
For more information see:
- Taking all reasonable steps for enrolling in and attending school
## Home schooling
A client can home school their children and meet their social obligations.
If the child is aged 6 years or over they will need to have a Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School issued by the Ministry of Education.
However, if they have work obligations, they are likely to need an exemption from those obligations.

chunks.title: Enrolment and attendance at a recognised early childhood education programme — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Enrolment and attendance at a recognised early childhood education programme
A client and their partner (if any) receiving Emergency Benefit must take all reasonable steps to ensure that their child is enrolled in and attending a recognised early childhood education programme from the age of three until they start school.
Generally, clients should have their children participating in a recognised early childhood education programme for 15 hours a week. This is a target number of hours; if a child is attending less hours this will be acceptable.
Recognised early childhood programmes for the purposes of social obligations include programmes that are:
- approved (licensed and certificated under the Education Act 1989) early childhood education (ECE) programmes
- Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School or
- another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme
Generally, a place in approved early childhood education (ECE) service should be considered first. Where a place in early childhood education is not available or is not suitable (for example due to hours of operation, distance or family circumstances) then other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes should be considered.
## Hours of attendance
Generally you should encourage your clients to take reasonable steps to have their children participating in early childhood programmes for 15 hours a week. This is a target number of hours. It is acceptable for a child to be attending for less than this.
## Age of child
This obligation only applies to parents of children aged between 3 and 6 years (except where the child has started school at 5 years old).
If a child is aged between 5 and 6 years, the parent or caregiver can choose whether to have their child in a recognised early childhood education programme or school.
A child does not legally have to attend school until they are 6 years (but most children start school at 5 years).
## Verification
In most cases, you should take the client's word that they are meeting this social obligation.
However, where you have information that the client may not be taking all reasonable steps towards this social obligation you can check if a Childcare Subsidy is being paid for the child or you may ask the client to provide verification.
For example, if you receive information that a child is not attending you can ask the client to get a letter from their childcare provider that confirms the child's attendance. You can also check the client's current Childcare Subsidy information.

chunks.title: Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits
A young partner must:
- register their child or children with a Well Child or Tamariki Ora provider and
- keep up-to-date with the child's checks
Note a young partner is only required to meet this obligation from the time they begin to get an Emergency Benefit. They will be meeting this obligation if they meet the relevant checks for the child's age from the time they are required to do so.
## Proof of visits
The Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book issued to parents when their child is born is sufficient evidence of the child's attendance at visits.
The Health Book has helpful advice and information about what is happening at different stages in the child's development, and has places to record all the Well Child appointments and other special and important things that happen to the child in their first 5 years.

chunks.title: Enrolment with a primary health care provider - young partner — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Enrolment with a primary health care provider - young partner
A young partner must enrol their dependent child or children with a primary health provider. This means being enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation.
## Exception
If a young partner is unable to enrol their child at a practice or with a practitioner, they can be considered to be meeting this obligation if they have a plan in place to:
- be enrolled with a practice or practitioner when a place becomes available and
- get health care for their child if the child becomes unwell

chunks.title: Enrolment with a primary health care provider — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Enrolment with a primary health care provider
A client and their partner (if any) getting an Emergency Benefit must take all reasonable steps to enrol their child or children in a primary healthcare service. This means being enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation.
Taking all reasonable steps to enrol
If a client is unable to enrol their child at a practice or with a practitioner due to shortages, they can be considered to be meeting this obligation if they have a plan in place to:
- be enrolled with a practice or practitioner when a place becomes available and
- get health care for their child if the child becomes sick
## Age of child
The primary health care obligation applies in relation to all dependent children in the care of a client and their partner getting a main benefit. Dependent children include:
- children included in the client or their partner’s main benefit and
- children the client or partner is getting Orphan’s Benefit or Unsupported Child’s Benefit for
## Verification
Most children will already be enrolled with a primary healthcare provider and in most cases MSD should take the client's word that they are meeting this social obligation.
However, if MSD has information that the client may not be taking all reasonable steps to meet this social obligation, MSD may ask them to get verification.
For example, verification could be a letter from their medical practice or registered practitioner that says they are enrolled (most medical practices will send this when a client is enrolled).

chunks.title: Ensuring child attends suitable childcare — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Ensuring child attends suitable childcare
A young partner is required to ensure their child's attendance at an approved early childhood education programme or other suitable childcare while they are in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work.
## Approved early childhood education programme
An approved (licensed or chartered) early childcare education centre or service includes:
- an early childhood centre licensed under the Education (Early Childhood Services) Regulations 2008
- a care programme approved by the Minister of Education (this includes care in the child's own home)
- a Kōhanga Reo chartered by the Te Kōhanga Reo National Trust
- a fee charging kindergarten licensed by the Ministry of Education and affiliated to either the New Zealand Free Kindergarten Association Inc or the Kindergarten Federation or
- a fee charging playcentre licensed by the Ministry of Education and affiliated to the New Zealand Playcentre Federation
Generally a place in approved Early Childhood Education should be looked at first. Where a place in Early Childhood Education is not available or is not suitable (due to hours of operation or distance from their place of study) then other suitable childcare must be used.
## Other suitable childcare
Suitable informal care may include family and friends.
The service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service must be satisfied that the childcare is safe and appropriate for the needs of the child.
For more information see:
- Parenting obligations
- Extra Help Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Programme

chunks.title: Entering a refuge — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Entering a refuge
When a client is applying for Emergency Benefit after entering a refuge following the break-up of a relationship, the initial stand-down period can be waived.
Generally the client must enter the refuge immediately following the break-up of their relationship. This means entering the refuge within a period similar in duration to the stand-down (that is, within seven to 14 days). Where there is a delay between the separation and the client entering the refuge, general commencement date rules apply.
In this context a refuge is emergency accommodation provided by an agency or organisation. This includes (but is not restricted to) agencies such as Women's Refuge, Home and Family Society, Emergency Housing Trusts, Iwi and cultural organisations, and church organisations.
Note that accommodation provided by family or friends of the client is not considered to be refuge accommodation.
For more information see:
- Commencement date

chunks.title: Entitlement date — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Entitlement date
The entitlement date for Emergency Benefit is usually:
- the day after employment ceased (that is, after any holiday pay, sick pay, etc. has expired)
- the day after separation or financial assistance from partner ceased
- the day after weekly work-related insurance payments ceased
- the day after full-time study or student allowances ceased
- the day after last exam
- the day after school finished (if client has just left school)
- the day after the date the living costs component of student loan was paid to
- the date of arrival in New Zealand (if client has returned to New Zealand)
- the date of release from prison or
- the date job search commenced
Note where the client has more than one event, you use the later event for their entitlement date.

chunks.title: Equivalent benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Equivalent benefit
The equivalent benefit is the benefit that best fits the client's reason(s) that prevents them from earning a sufficient livelihood. To determine the equivalent benefit, consideration of the reason(s) why they cannot earn a sufficient livelihood and is in hardship must be made.
Note the equivalent benefit cannot be New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension.
## Maximum rate of payment and conditions for Emergency Benefit
Generally, the equivalent benefit establishes the maximum rate of benefit.
The maximum rate of the equivalent benefit cannot be equal to New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension.
The equivalent benefit provides guidelines for the conditions attached to a grant of Emergency Benefit. The conditions will generally align to the obligations that apply to the equivalent benefit.
Note identifying an equivalent benefit does not mean a person is automatically eligible for an Emergency Benefit. The client's circumstances must still be considered to justify payment.

chunks.title: Equivalent to Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Equivalent to Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability)
Where a client is limited in their capacity to find work because they have a health condition, an injury or a disability and the client does not meet the 2 year residence requirement for Jobseeker Support, consider Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship in the first instance.
You may consider Emergency Benefit when the client is not eligible for any other benefit and they are in one of the following situations:
- Patients from Tokelau, Niue and Cook Islands
- Donating a kidney or liver tissue
- Not eligible for another benefit

chunks.title: Equivalent to Supported Living Payment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Equivalent to Supported Living Payment
Where a client is permanently restricted and severely restricted in their capacity to work because of a health condition, an injury or a disability or totally blind but does not meet the residential requirements for Supported Living Payment (on ground of health condition, injury or disability), an Emergency Benefit equivalent to Supported Living Payment may be considered.
Note if the client's health condition, injury or disability does not permanently and severely restrict them from working more than 15 hours a week in open employment, consider in the first instance Jobseeker Support, Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship then Emergency Benefit equivalent to Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Keriana is getting Emergency Benefit at the Jobseeker Support rate of $372.55 a week (as at 1 April 2026). She fails an obligation without a good and sufficient reason and her case manager decides to impose Money Management. Her first day of Money Management is Thursday 10 July. Because Keriana’s Money Management begins in the middle of the week, only part of her benefit payment for the following week will be under Money Management. This means she will get more than 50% of her benefit into her bank account. Note: the benefit might not divide evenly by 2. When this happens, the higher amount (1 cent more) will be paid to the client’s bank account.

chunks.text: Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday Money Management imposed Client's weekly benefit amount = $372.55 50% put onto payment card Remainder paid into client’s bank account (weekly benefit amount minus amount paid to payment card) = $372.55 - $186.28 = $186.28 Total payment into client’s bank account for the week: $186.28

chunks.title: Example of equivalent benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Example of equivalent benefit
A client aged 66 years and came to New Zealand to seek employment. They do not meet the residence requirements for New Zealand Superannuation. The client has had difficulty finding employment and has applied for an Emergency Benefit.
The reason why the client is unable to earn a sufficient livelihood is that they were unable to get a job. The equivalent benefit would be Jobseeker Support.
The client then suffered a stroke that prevented him from earning a sufficient income.
The equivalent benefit needs to reflect the client's circumstances and the appropriate benefit is now either:
- Equivalent to Jobseeker Support health condition, injury or disability or
- Equivalent to Supported Living Payment health condition, injury or disability
In this situation, the age of the client was not the reason the client could not earn a sufficient livelihood - it was because they were not able to find work and had a health condition.

chunks.title: Example 1 – approved position starts during search period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Example 1 – approved position starts during search period
Greer has Community Work Experience imposed on Monday as her non-financial sanction after failing a work obligation. She already volunteers at her local city mission and arranges with them to complete her Community Work Experience position.
She provides verification of the organisation and the position on Friday, and advises she can start the next day and complete her required hours for the week.
MSD approves the organisation and position, and Greer's position period begins on Saturday.
## Sunday
First day of search period
Greer provides verification.
MSD approves organisation and position.
Search period ends.
Greer's position starts - First day of position period.
## Example 2 – approved position starts after search period ends
Anaru has had Community Work Experience imposed as his non-financial sanction after failing a work obligation. On day 10 of his search period, Wednesday 10 June, he finds out his marae is starting a working bee next week.
They are happy to offer Anaru the required hours and weeks for a Community Work Experience position, but the first day they need him is 3 days after the search period ends, Wednesday 17 June. They can give him 3 hours on the first day and 3 hours the day after. He contacts MSD to let them know about his position.
As Anaru found the position within the search period, he's able to do 5 hours within the first week, and the organisation and position are approved. His position period starts on Monday 15 June, and he starts doing the required hours on day 3 of the position period, Wednesday 17 June.
## Sunday 7 June
First day of search period
## Sunday 14 June
Anaru confirms position with marae and provides verification.
MSD approves organisation and position.
Last day of search period.
## Sunday 21 June
First day of position period.
Anaru's position begins.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Example 1
Adrian failed a work obligation and MSD imposed Community Work Experience as a non-financial sanction. He contacts MSD at the end of the search period and says he didn't find a position. When MSD asks about what steps he took to find one, Adrian says he contacted a few places in the first week but had no luck, so he gave up trying.
MSD is satisfied that Adrian was complying with the requirements of the search period in week one, but he was no longer compliant in week 2. MSD determines non-compliance from day one of week 2, Thursday 19 June 2025. Adrian's payments are stopped from this date, and he is given a different recompliance activity to complete.
## Sunday 15 June
Search period imposed
## Sunday 22 June
2nd week of search period began.
MSD determines Adrian was non-compliant from this date.
Payments stopped from this date.
## Sunday 29 June
Search period ended.
Adrian made contact with MSD to advise that he did not find a position.
## Example 2
Rick had Community Work Experience imposed and found a suitable position working with an environmental organisation cleaning up local rivers.
At the end of his position period, Rick does not provide verification or make contact with MSD. MSD suspends his benefit from the end of his position period.
Rick contacts MSD and asks why his benefit stopped. He is unable to provide any verification of completing his Community Work Experience. MSD also received an email from the organisation advising that Rick had stopped attending.
Because they are unable to confirm exactly when Rick became non-compliant, MSD considers him non-compliant from the beginning of the position period. Because he was not entitled to receive his benefit payments from the beginning of the position period, this results in a debt being established.
MSD then assigns a recompliance activity for Rick to complete to get his payments resumed.

chunks.title: Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose
Incentive payments can be removed where the young partner has acted on purpose in a way that is inconsistent with the reason the incentive is being paid.
Acting in a way that is inconsistent with an incentive includes (but is not limited to):
Education incentive
Budgeting incentive
Have conditions imposed by the court which impact on them attending activities
Continuous unexplained absences from the school or training programme
Didn't pay core costs (rent, power etc) without a good reason
Suspended from school
Purchased an unnecessary item on credit and this has put them in hardship
Being disruptive or not completing assignments
Not appropriate choices for their situation when spending their payment card or their in-hand allowance
For more information see:

chunks.title: Examples of approved courses — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Examples of approved courses
Examples of approved courses include (but are not limited to):
- Be Your Own Boss training programme
- Drug, alcohol rehabilitation and anger management courses arranged by the Department of Corrections for offenders
- Regional training courses
- Limited Service Volunteer (LSV) [no link find out why]
- Outward Bound [no link find out why]
- Modularised Seminars [no link find out why]
- Skills for Industry [no link find out why]
- Targeted Training [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Examples of couples with other income — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The rates of benefit payable in the following two examples are the rates as at 1 April 2026.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Married couple (no children), one partner is working full-time the other partner is providing full-time care for an aged or sick person. The couple's income is $750.00 gross per week. Income deduction 35 cents for every $1.00 earned over $13,000 per year $750.00 gross per week less $250.00 ($13,000 ÷ 52 weeks) $500.00 x 35 cents = $175.00 income deduction Income deduction 15 cents for every $1.00 earned over $8,320 per year but less than $13,000 per year $250.00 gross per week less $160.00 ($8,320 ÷ 52 weeks) $90.00 x 15 cents = $13.50 income deduction plus $175.00 (from above) Total income deduction $188.50 client partner maximum benefit payable (as at 1 April 2026) $360.72 $360.72 less income deduction $188.50 $188.50 Benefit payable $172.22 plus $172.22 equals = $344.44 As $344.44 is less than the maximum rate of Emergency Benefit generally paid to care for an aged or sick person, you pay the client $344.44.

chunks.title: Example 2 — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Civil union couple (no children), one partner is working full-time, the other partner is providing full-time care for an aged or sick person. The couple's income is $370.00 gross per week. Income deduction 35 cents for every $1.00 earned over $13,000 per year $370.00 gross per week Less $250.00 (13,000 ÷ 52 weeks) $120.00 x 35 cents = $42.00 deduction Income deduction 15 cents for every $1.00 earned over $8,320 per year but less than $13,000 per year $250.00 gross per week Less $160.00 ($8,320 ÷ 52 weeks) $90.00 x 15 cents = $13.50 deduction Plus $42.00 (deduction from above table) Total income deduction $55.50 client partner maximum benefit payable (as at 1 April 2026) $360.72 $360.72 less income deduction $55.50 $55.50 Benefit payable $305.22 plus $305.22 equals $610.44 As $610.44 is greater than the maximum rate of Emergency Benefit generally paid to care for an aged or sick person as at 1 April 2026, you pay the client $360.72 (the maximum rate payable under the schedule).

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances for cash assets — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances for cash assets
You can disregard some or all of a client's cash assets when you are looking at granting an Emergency Benefit on the grounds of hardship. You can only do this if you think there are exceptional circumstances.
Things you need to consider:
- if you refuse to grant an Emergency Benefit on the grounds of hardship: will it have a serious effect on the client's (and any family) health or welfare?would the likely alternatives cost the Government more?
- will it have a serious effect on the client's (and any family) health or welfare?
- would the likely alternatives cost the Government more?
- can the client realise (that is sell or get access to) their cash assets which would be over the appropriate cash asset limit?
- what is the total amount of the client's assets, including assets that are not cash assets?
- is the need for an Emergency Benefit temporary? and
- what are the other matters you consider relevant to determining whether hardship exists?
Every case has to be looked at on its own merits. If you have a case where you think you can disregard some or all of a client's cash assets, contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances before you make your decision.
Note if a person can't be included in their partners New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension, this isn't considered exceptional circumstances.

chunks.title: Exemption for severe disablement — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Exemption for severe disablement
As an incentive for the personal effort of a severely disabled person to participate or continue in employment, you can use your discretion to disregard all or part of any income earned from employment as chargeable income for benefit purposes.
Consideration for this special income exemption should be given to clients with a severe disability who are extremely limited in their ability to participate in employment, the community and take care of themselves.
You must first consider whether or not the client is severely disabled. The Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement will help you do this.
Each case should be assessed on an individual basis.
If the client is severely disabled you should consider whether or not to disregard all or part of any income earned by the client. To help you do this, see Amount of income exemption
Note clients who are not severely disabled cannot receive this exemption.
For more information see:
- Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement
- Amount of income exemption

chunks.title: Exemptions for young partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Exemptions for young partners
Exemptions from youth activity obligations recognise that there are a number of common reasons why it is unreasonable to expect a young partner to meet their activity obligations for a specified period.
The service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service can recommend that a young partner is granted an exemption.
## Young partners without dependent children
Young partners without dependent children can be granted a full or partial exemption from their youth activity obligations for the following reasons:
- Family violence young partners
- Young partner would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
- Caring for foster child under 12 months old
- Caring full-time for a spouse or partner with a health condition, injury or disability
- Young partner would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
- Court imposed conditions
## Young partners with dependent children
Young partners with dependent children can be granted a full or partial exemption from their youth activity obligations for the following reasons:
- Family violence young partners
- Young partner would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
- Caring for a child with special needs
- Caring for foster child under 12 months old
- Caring full-time for a spouse or partner with a health condition, injury or disability
- Young partner would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
- Court imposed conditions
The young partner can be granted a temporary exemption from some or all of their activity obligations. Proof may be required before an exemption is granted.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions (young partners)
## SWIFTT process
Exemptions for young partners are processed by Service Centres.
If the young partner is granted an exemption, add the exemption on the SWTDA screen using the appropriate reason code. You must also add an expiry date.
## Duration of the exemption
Each exemption has a specific duration for which it can be granted. In some cases these can be extended if appropriate.
For an overview of the exemptions see:
- Table of exemptions for young partners

chunks.title: Exemptions - partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Exemptions - partners
There are several reasons why it may be unreasonable to expect a partner to meet their work preparation or work obligations for a specified period.
If the partner qualifies, they may be granted an exemption from some or all of their work preparation or work obligations. Evidence may be required before an exemption is granted.
## Duration of the exemption
Each exemption has a specific period it can be granted for. In some cases these can be extended (if appropriate).

chunks.title: Extra help for clients without permanent residence — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Extra help for clients without permanent residence
Clients without permanent residence do not qualify for:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Disability Allowance or
- Childcare Assistance
Any extra help a client may qualify for is determined by the reason they are in New Zealand.
## Clients granted refugee or protected person status
Clients who have refugee or protected person status without permanent residence, may qualify for a Re-establishment Special Needs Grant and Temporary Additional Support.
## Person has applied for refugee or protected person status
A client granted an Emergency Benefit who has applied for refugee or protected person status, and has a visa or permit to be lawfully in New Zealand, does not qualify for a re-establishment Special Needs Grant. This client may be eligible for Temporary Additional Support.
## Clients compelled to remain in New Zealand
A client granted an Emergency Benefit who has applied for permanent residence, has a valid temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit and is compelled to remain in New Zealand due to some unforeseen circumstance may qualify for Temporary Additional Support.
## Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit
From 1 April 2020, Emergency Benefit clients (including those who do not have permanent residence) can get family tax credit and Best Start tax credit if they and their child/ren meet all the other eligibility criteria for these payments.
People on Emergency Benefit automatically qualify for the other requirements of family tax credit and Best Start tax credit if they have a dependent child in their care.
The family tax credit and Best Start tax credit will be paid with their Emergency Benefit payment if they choose to get this from the Ministry of Social Development (MSD).
Note clients who are no longer getting an Emergency Benefit will need to talk to Inland Revenue about their eligibility for Working for Families tax credits.

chunks.title: Payments that can be redirected — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Payments that can be redirected
Most ongoing extra help payments paid to a young person are included in the redirection of payment if the young person is under youth money management, for example:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- family tax credit
- Best Start tax credit
- Winter Energy Payment
Note because Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, family tax credit and Best Start tax credit can only be paid to one person, for couples, the person getting them is generally responsible for any debt created.
## Payments that are not redirected
The following payments are not included in youth money management and can be paid to the young person, their agent (if authorised) or a supplier (as appropriate):
- Disability Allowance
- Child Disability Allowance
- Flexible Childcare Assistance
- Training Incentive Allowance
- one-off payments of hardship assistance, for example Special Needs Grants for food
- any Advance Payment of Benefit
## Flexible Childcare Assistance
Flexible Childcare Assistance must be used to pay for costs associated with informal childcare. This means that any amount of Flexible Childcare Assistance a young person gets cannot be used to pay for other essential costs.
Note as Flexible Childcare Assistance is only a contribution towards informal childcare costs, the young person is required to pay any remaining costs from their in-hand allowance or other resources (e.g. if their Flexible Childcare Assistance does not cover their informal childcare cost in full).
For more information see:
## Hardship obligations do not apply to clients who have youth activity obligations
Young partners who are required to get Youth Services will not have hardship obligations if they are accessing Special Needs Grants or Advance Payment of Benefits.
These young people are already working with their service provider or MSD 'in-house' service, on activities that already meet the budgeting activity or reasonable steps hardship obligations.
Generally, all clients and their partners, who apply for Special Needs Grants, Advance Payment of Benefits and Recoverable Assistance Payments, have hardship obligations.
Hardship obligations include:
- a reasonable steps obligation and
- a budgeting activity obligation
Generally, clients must meet their hardship obligations before they get any additional payments.
These obligations do not apply to:
- payments to people in specific circumstance
- young people getting youth support payments (Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment) or have youth activity obligations and are required to get Youth Services
- payments to obtain or renew a driver licence

chunks.title: Factors to consider when recommending payment distribution between payment cards and in-hand allowance — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Factors to consider when recommending payment distribution between payment cards and in-hand allowance
When making a recommendation as to how a young partner's payment should be distributed between the in-hand allowance and the payment card, the Service provider will consider the young partner's circumstances, including (but not limited to) the following:
- what level of need does the client have for costs that can be met through the payment card, eg if they are boarding and their food is covered they may not need as much money on the payment card as most of their main meals will be covered
- what essential costs does the client need to meet from their in-hand allowance eg do they have clear essential needs such as travel costs on which they need to spend their in-hand allowance, or do they have access to a food supplier (eg fruit and vegetable market) where it would be more cost effective for them to shop, however that supplier does not accept the payment card
- does the client have sufficient budgeting skills to ensure their in-hand allowance is prioritised to meet essential costs, such as food and groceries, where necessary
- has the client demonstrated poor budgeting skills in relation to the way they have been using their current distribution of payment eg has the client failed to provide food or other essentials for their children out of their in-hand allowance, where this has been necessary due to them not having enough credit on their payment card
YSSU makes the decision as to how the young person's payment will be distributed between the payment card and in-hand allowance, taking into account the information supplied by the young partner's service provider.
When making this decision, YSSU must be satisfied that the distribution between the two payment methods is reasonable given the client's individual circumstances.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Failing a social obligation — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Failing a social obligation
If a client and their partner have received regular engagement and support, and they are still not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, they still need to attend a final appointment.
A social obligations failure can be initiated when you consider that a client has, without a good and sufficient reason, failed to meet their social obligations by:
- not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations following the process of regular engagement and support (that involves at least 3 stages) or
- not attending the final appointment during their regular engagement and support process
Before you initiate an obligations failure for social obligations you must get your manager client service delivery's approval.
An obligation failure should only be used when all other efforts to encourage engagement and support with the client have been exhausted.

chunks.title: Failing more than one obligation at the same time — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Failing more than one obligation at the same time
If a client fails more than one obligation or activity at the same time and does not have a good and sufficient reason for one or more of the failures, the failures are counted as one failure. However, the client will need to recomply with all the failures before the sanction can be lifted.
Note Money Management is the only non-financial sanction that can be imposed when a client has failed more than one obligation at the same time at grade 1. A client must resolve all of these failures during the 4-week Money Management period in order to recomply.
For grade 1 and 2 failures, if the client successfully disputes one of the failures, the sanction imposed will remain until they recomply with any remaining failures initiated at the same time.
This policy only applies to the first and second time a client or partner fails their obligations in a 24-month period.
For grade 3 failures, a client will need to complete one 6-week approved activity or programme of activities (if they wish to recomply).
Note Disability Allowance can continue to be paid during a non-entitlement period.
## Initiating the failures on the same day
The obligations or activities that a client or their partner has not complied with can be over a recent period (eg within the last five days) or they may not have been complied with all on the same day. However, the client or partner can only be required to recomply with failures that are initiated on the same day.
As soon as MSD is aware that a client or their partner has failed their obligations without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must initiate an obligations failure - it cannot be delayed.
For more information see:
- Work obligations - partner
- Work preparation obligations -partner
- Social obligations
- Drug test obligations - partner
- Recompliance
- Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations
A client and their partner (if any), when required, must:
- attend and participate in interviews with Work and Income to discuss compliance with their social obligations and
- report on compliance with specific social obligations
If during any of the three steps of engagement and support, the client does not attend or participate in interviews with Work and Income to discuss compliance with their social obligations or report on compliance with specific social obligations, you should move to the next steps of engagement and support.
For more information on the three steps process of engagement see:
- Social obligations - Actively engaging with clients [no link find out why]
- Failure to comply following engagement and support process
- Obligations failures - partners

chunks.title: Failure to comply following regular engagement and support — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Failure to comply following regular engagement and support
Clients will need to attend a final appointment if they are still not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations after the 3 step process of regular engagement and support.
A social obligations failure will only be initiated when you consider that a client has, without a good and sufficient reason, failed to meet their social obligations by:
- not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations following the three stage process of regular engagement and support and
- does not attend the final appointment, or attends and is still not meeting their social obligations, following the three stage process engagement and support
Before you initiate an obligations failure for social obligations you must get your manager client service delivery's approval. A social obligation failure should only be used when all other efforts to encourage engagement and support the client have been exhausted.

chunks.title: Failure within the position period – good and sufficient reason — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Failure within the position period – good and sufficient reason
A partner must be able to complete 5 hours of Community Work Experience each week during the 4-week period.
The position duties or conditions may change during this period and make it impossible or unreasonable for the partner to complete their Community Work Experience.
A partner must inform MSD as soon as possible that they are no longer able to complete their Community Work Experience so that MSD may place them onto an alternative recompliance pathway.
A Grade 1 financial sanction will be imposed from the date MSD has been informed and is satisfied that they are unable to complete their position and a recompliance activity must be arranged for the partner to complete as soon as possible.
## Example
Marco has had Community Work Experience imposed and is searching for a suitable position. Marco quickly found a suitable position doing odd jobs at his church.
This worked well for the first 2 weeks, but in week 3 there was very little for Marco to do and the church only needed him for 2 hours that week. He contacted MSD to let them know he would not have enough hours for this week.
As this is a change outside Marco’s control, MSD informs him that his period of Community Work Experience will be ended, and a financial sanction is imposed from that day. MSD also arranges the first available recompliance activity he can complete, so that Marco can recomply quickly and his payments can return to normal as soon as possible.
## Example
Marcia started a Community Work Experience position with her local sports club. One of the volunteers hears that Marcia is there because she’s on a benefit and this position is a sanction for her.
They tell other people who volunteer there and some people start picking on her, making unkind comments about why she’s there. Marcia feels very uncomfortable and contacts MSD to let them know what’s happening.
MSD decides that the position is no longer appropriate for Marcia to complete, because she’s being bullied and feels unsafe. MSD imposes a replacement sanction from that day and arranges for her to do a different recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Failure within the search period – good and sufficient reason — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Failure within the search period – good and sufficient reason
A partner may inform MSD at the end of their 2-week search period that they have made a reasonable effort to find a position and have been unsuccessful.
If MSD is satisfied that the partner made a reasonable effort to find a position, a grade 1 financial sanction will be imposed from the day after the search period ends and a recompliance activity must be arranged for the partner to complete as soon as possible.
## Partner contacts MSD in the middle of the search period
A partner may advise MSD before their search period ends that they will be unable to find a suitable position. For example, if a partner lives in a small community and has not been able to find a position at any local organisations in the first 10 days.
MSD can consider this a good and sufficient reason if it is satisfied that the partner made a reasonable effort and it is unrealistic that the partner will find a position by the end of the search period. A Grade 1 financial sanction will be imposed from the date MSD has been informed and determines the partner has a good and sufficient reason for failing to find a suitable position.
## Partner finds suitable position that does not begin within the first week of position period
If a partner finds a suitable position but it does not begin within the first week of the position period, it does not meet the requirements for Community Work Experience.
A partner may continue looking for a position during the 2-week search period if it is reasonable for them to do so.
MSD may consider the partner to have a good and sufficient reason for failing to find Community Work Experience from the:
- day the position is confirmed to be unsuitable, if it is not reasonable for the partner to find another position by the end of the search period or
- day after the 2-week search period ends, if the partner makes a reasonable effort to find another position but is unsuccessful.
A Grade 1 financial sanction will be imposed from the date MSD has been informed and determines the partner has a good and sufficient reason for failing to find a suitable position.

chunks.title: Family tax credit — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Family tax credit
Young partners getting Emergency Benefit will be paid family tax credit along with their benefit. They cannot get it from Inland Revenue.
Family tax credit can only be paid to one person in a couple. Generally it is paid to the primary caregiver.
Inland Revenue is responsible for establishing and recovering any debt created.
Note a young partner cannot review the decision on how their portion of Emergency Benefit is paid to them.

chunks.title: Family violence (young partners) — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Family violence (young partners)
A young partner who has left a situation of family violence may be exempt from meeting all their activity obligations until they have had time to adjust to their new living circumstances.
This is a full exemption.
## Definition of family violence
Family violence is a term used to describe violence within the family and close personal relationships.
Family violence covers a broad range of controlling behaviours which typically involve fear, intimidation, and emotional deprivation.
Family violence is defined as:
- physical abuse
- sexual abuse
- psychological abuse including but not limited to intimidation, harassment, damage to property or threats of physical, sexual or psychological abuse
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 3 months.
## Evidence
Young people who have recently left situations of family violence will not have to provide evidence.
If a young partner still needs an exemption after 3 months, MSD can ask for supporting evidence.
Evidence can include statements from:
- their registered health practitioner
- their church
- their lawyer
- the police
- Women's Refuge
- any other person or organisation that is able to support the young partner's application

chunks.title: Family violence — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Family violence
This exemption may apply to partners with work preparation obligations or work obligations.
A client who has left a situation of family violence may be exempt from meeting all their work preparation obligations or work obligations until they have had time to adjust to their new living circumstances. This is a full exemption.
You should talk to the regional Family Violence Response Co-ordinator before granting an exemption. You should also consider:
- Is the client living in temporary refuge accommodation while they seek a permanent home?
- Are they helping children adjust to a new family situation?
## Definition of family violence
Family violence is a term used to describe violence within the family and close personal relationships.
Family violence covers a broad range of controlling behaviours which typically involve fear, intimidation and emotional deprivation.
Family violence is defined as:
- physical abuse
- sexual abuse
- psychological abuse including but not limited to intimidation, harassment, damage to property or threats of physical, sexual or psychological abuse
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 3 months.
## Proof
Clients who have recently left situations of family violence will not have to provide proof.
If a client still needs an exemption after three months you can ask for proof. You should consult the regional Family Violence Response Co-ordinator for advice on the most appropriate way to proceed.
Proof can include statements from:
- their doctor
- their church
- their lawyer
- the police
- Women's Refuge
- any other person or organisation that is able to support the client's application
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Family Violence'.

chunks.title: Financial assistance during non-entitlement period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Financial assistance during non-entitlement period
If a client needs financial assistance during a non-entitlement period, they will need to recomply to be granted a provisional benefit.
## Special Needs Grants
Clients are not entitled to a Special Needs Grant if a sanction has been imposed, unless they become:
- sick or injured and
- incapable of participating in employment or an approved activity for at least six weeks
In this case, the client can get more than one Special Needs Grant, but the amount granted in any one week cannot be more than the combined total of:
- what the client would be entitled to that week if they were entitled to Emergency Benefit and
- the rate of Accommodation Supplement that the applicant would have gotten
For more information see:
- Effect of a non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Assistance when a client is sanctioned
## Recoverable Assistance Payments
Generally clients will not be entitled to Recoverable Assistance Payments when they are subject to a non-entitlement period. This is because they will be contributing to their hardship through not recomplying. The client's first option is to recomply.
A Recoverable Assistance Payment cannot be paid when the client has no means of repaying it.
For more information see:
## Advance Payments of Benefit
Generally, clients whose benefit continues to be paid (i.e. clients with dependent children) will not be entitled to an Advance Payment of Benefit when they have a 13 week non-entitlement period imposed. This is because they will be contributing to their hardship through not recomplying.
The client's first option to improve their financial situation is to recomply.
## Exemptions or transfers
In some instances it may be appropriate to consider an exemption or a transfer to another benefit that does not have work obligations.
For more information on transfers and exemptions see:
- Exemptions
- Changes and reviews Client qualifies for another benefit

chunks.title: Five-day verification window — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Five-day verification window
A partner must provide MSD with verification of their Community Work Experience before the end of the 2-week search period, and at the end of their position period. This is to verify that they have:
- found a position with an organisation during the 2-week search period, and
- completed all the requirements of their Community Work Experience during the 4-week period.
However, there may be times when MSD is not able to process the information within that same period.
To prevent a partner from being disadvantaged due to processing delays, there is a 5-day verification window at the end of the 2-week search period and at the end of the position period. This allows MSD to process information a partner has provided and ensures a partner’s payment will continue.
Note this is not extra time for a partner to secure a position or provide verification to MSD. Partners must still complete their search and provide verification before the end of the 2-week search period.
## No action from MSD
The partner will be considered non-compliant if, after 5 days:
- MSD has not confirmed if the position is suitable (or unsuitable) for their Community Work Experience, or
- MSD has not been able to confirm if the partner has completed their Community Work Experience, or
- the partner has not provided the required verification for either their search period or position period.
Their payments will suspend or reduce from the day after the search period or the position period ended, depending on which verification window was in place. This may result in a debt for a partner.

chunks.title: Full or partial exemptions — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Full or partial exemptions
A partner may be granted a temporary exemption from meeting some or all of their work preparation obligations or work obligations.
Before MSD grants an exemption, they must check if the exemption reason is full, partial or both.
The partner can be granted a partial exemption from their work obligations if they can still:
- plan for employment and
- undertake some work related activities
If the partner is not able to do either of the above they should be granted a full exemption.
A partner who has a full exemption from their work obligations may still be required to attend an interview with MSD to discuss their circumstances, and when it might be appropriate for them to start to plan towards a return to work.
## Partners with work preparation obligations
Partners with work preparation obligations can only be considered for a full exemption.
Work preparation obligations mean they are required to plan for employment and undertake work preparation activities.
## Duration of exemption
Each exemption has a maximum duration. The period an exemption is granted for depends on the partner's circumstances.
At the time of granting the exemption MSD should:
- advise the partner of the temporary nature of their exemption and
- a date to review the exemption if appropriate
At the review MSD should consider the partner's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption. MSD can ask the partner to provide evidence that their exemption should be extended.
Note the duration of an exemption for partners because of a health condition, injury or disability is based on the next reassessment date recorded on their medical evidence.

chunks.title: Full or partial exemptions (young partners) — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Full or partial exemptions (young partners)
A young partner may be granted a temporary exemption from meeting some or all of their youth activity obligations on recommendation from their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service.
The Service Centre will make the decision to decline or approve any exemption.
Before you grant an exemption, check if the exemption reason is full or partial (or both).
## Full exemptions
A full exemption means the young partner is exempt from all activities that are part of their obligations. They may be granted a full exemption if they are unable to meet any of their youth activity obligations.
A young partner who has a full exemption from their youth activity obligations may still be required to attend an interview to discuss their circumstances and when it might be appropriate for them to start to plan towards a return to education, training or work-based learning.
## Partial exemptions
The young partner can be granted a partial exemption from their activities when they can participate in some, but not all, of their youth activity obligations.
For example, a young partner granted a partial exemption from education, training or work-based learning, may still be required to:
- attend a budgeting programme and
- meet with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service
## Duration
Each exemption has a maximum duration. The period the exemption is granted for depends on the young partner's circumstances.
At the time of granting the exemption the young partner should be:
- advised of the temporary nature of the exemption and
- if appropriate, a date scheduled to review the exemption
At the review you should discuss the young partner's circumstances and consider whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption for a further period. You can ask the young partner to provide proof that their exemption should be extended.
For an overview of the exemptions see:
- Table of exemptions for young partners

chunks.title: Full-time care and attention — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Full-time care and attention
Full-time care and attention means the person will need 24-hour access to care and attention.
This does not mean the client is expected to give 24-hour care, but they must be available if needed. The level of care and attention must be over and above the ordinary care and attention needed by someone of the same age.
A client can be away from the home for short periods a day and still considered to be providing full-time care and attention if arrangements are made for the person's care and their safety is not compromised.
## At home
To get Emergency Benefit the client must provide full-time care and attention at home. The home can be the client's or the person's home. A client may live in the same house as the person being cared for.
If the client lives in different accommodation their ability to provide full-time care and attention may be compromised. Consider each case on its merits.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure
You need to be satisfied that the client or partner does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their obligations, based on the information you have, before you initiate an obligations failure.
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'. Having considered the circumstances, was it reasonable for the client or partner not to have met their obligations?
For social obligations you will need to assess whether the client and partner (if any) is taking all reasonable steps to meet all of their social obligations for each dependent child.
Good and sufficient reasons will depend on the obligation the client or partner has failed. For more information see:
- Social obligations All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Drug test obligation failures good and sufficient reasons - partners
- Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation
- Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting obligation to work with a contracted service provider
- Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation
Decide in favour of the client or partner if any doubt remains.
If you are aware that the client or partner has a good and sufficient reason, do not initiate an obligations failure.
If the client or partner does not have a good and sufficient reason, see:
- Effect of sanctions on assistance
- Failing more than one obligation at the same time
- Activity failures for young partners
## Disputing the obligations failure
A client or partner can dispute the decision to initiate the obligations failure or the sanction. For more information see:
- Disputes and Reviews of an obligations failure

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for failure to complete Report Job Search — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A partner may be unable to complete Report Job Search for a good and sufficient reason. These reasons may include, but are not limited to, the partner: - was unable to complete and/or report on the required number of job-search activities in any one of the four weeks due to reasons outside of their control, for example: there was a death or serious illness in the partner's familythey were sick or injured within the sanction period and this impacted their ability to complete the required number of job-search activitiesthey had an unexpected event occur (e.g. they were involved in an accident that affected their ability to complete the required number of job-search activities) - there was a death or serious illness in the partner's family - they were sick or injured within the sanction period and this impacted their ability to complete the required number of job-search activities - they had an unexpected event occur (e.g. they were involved in an accident that affected their ability to complete the required number of job-search activities) - faced an unsafe environment while completing their job-search activities - could no longer report and/or complete their job-search activities as the device they were using was unavailable (through loss, damage, or theft) and they were unable to access another device or get to their nearest service centre Note before deciding there was a good and sufficient reason for not completing a job-search activity (e.g. an unsafe environment or their device not being available), MSD should consider if the partner could have completed a different activity or used different methods to meet Report Job Search requirements.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Alois failed a work obligation and his case manager imposed Report Job Search as a non-financial sanction. He was one week into his 4-week sanction period when he had a minor accident and was in hospital for a few days. By the time he got home, he had not completed the required 3 job-search activities and missed self-reporting in MyMSD for week one. His benefit has stopped. He calls his case manager to let them know what happened. His case manager is satisfied there is a good and sufficient reason Alois was unable to complete the requirements of Report Job Search and that he contacted MSD as soon as he reasonably could. A replacement financial sanction is imposed from the date his payments stopped and Alois is given a different recompliance activity. Alois is paid arrears for the period his benefit was stopped for being non-compliant.

chunks.title: Notifying MSD within a reasonable period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a partner is delayed in notifying MSD of their good and sufficient reason, the delay must only be for a reasonable period. MSD will determine on a case-by-case basis whether the length of the delay is reasonable or not. If MSD determines that they are unable to complete Report Job Search for a good and sufficient reason, and a partner has notified MSD within a reasonable period, MSD must impose a Grade 1 financial sanction. The date the financial sanction is imposed depends on when MSD determines the partner has a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete their Report Job Search requirements. MSD must also assign a recompliance activity to the partner as soon as possible. Note if a partner informs MSD of a good and sufficient reason within a reasonable period, but after the Report Job Search sanction period has ended, a replacement sanction can no longer be imposed. They must be given a different recompliance activity to complete, after which their payments can be increased or resumed.

chunks.title: No good and sufficient reason — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a partner does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete Report Job Search, or they did not notify MSD within a reasonable period, they will be considered non-compliant.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for failure to complete Upskilling — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A client may be unable to complete Upskilling for a good and sufficient reason. These reasons may include, but are not limited to, the client was: - unable to complete the required hours in any one of the four weeks due to reasons outside of their control, for example: there was a death or serious illness in the client's familythey were sick or injured within the sanction period and this impacted their ability to participate in their employment-related training or coursethey had an unexpected event occur (e.g. they were involved in an accident that affected their ability to participate intheir employment-related training or course) - there was a death or serious illness in the client's family - they were sick or injured within the sanction period and this impacted their ability to participate in their employment-related training or course - they had an unexpected event occur (e.g. they were involved in an accident that affected their ability to participate in - their employment-related training or course) - faced with an unsafe environment while completing their employment-related training or course - could no longer complete their online courses as the device they were using was unavailable (through loss, damage, or theft) and they were unable to access another device or get to their nearest service centre

chunks.title: Notifying MSD within a reasonable period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a client is delayed in notifying MSD of their good and sufficient reason, the delay must only be for a reasonable period. MSD will determine on a case-by-case basis whether the length of the delay is reasonable or not. If MSD determines that they are unable to complete Upskilling for a good and sufficient reason, and a client has notified MSD within a reasonable period, MSD must impose a Grade 1 financial sanction. The date the financial sanction is imposed depends on when MSD determines the client has a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete their Upskilling requirements. MSD must also assign a recompliance activity to the client as soon as possible. Note if a client informs MSD of a good and sufficient reason within a reasonable period, but after the Upskilling sanction period has ended, a replacement sanction can no longer be imposed. They must be given a different recompliance activity to complete, after which their payments can be increased or resumed.

chunks.title: No good and sufficient reason — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a client does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete Upskilling, or they did not notify MSD within a reasonable period, they will be considered non-compliant.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Jacob failed a work-preparation obligation and his case manager imposed Upskilling as a non-financial sanction. He had just started a four-week IT skills course when his child became very sick and required full time care. By the time Jacob's child recovered, he had not done the required five hours of employment-related training or courses and missed self-reporting in MyMSD for week one. His benefit is reduced. He calls his case manager to let them know what happened. His case manager is satisfied there is a good and sufficient reason Jacob was unable to complete the requirements of his Upskilling non-financial sanction and that he contacted MSD as soon as he reasonably could. A replacement financial sanction is imposed from the date his payments reduced and Jacob is given a different recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Edward failed a work-preparation obligation and his case manager imposed Upskilling as a non-financial sanction. He is two weeks into his barista course when someone else on the course hears that Edward is there because he's on a benefit and this course is a sanction for him. They tell other people who are at the course and some people start harassing him and making unkind comments about why he's there. Edward feels very uncomfortable and contacts MSD to let them know what's happening. MSD decides the course is no longer appropriate for Edward to complete because he's being bullied and feels unsafe. MSD imposes a replacement sanction from that day and arranges for him to do a different recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for failure to find or complete Community Work Experience — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason for failure to find or complete Community Work Experience
A partner may be unable to find or complete Community Work Experience for a good and sufficient reason. These reasons may include, but are not limited to:
- a partner has made reasonable efforts to find a position but has not found one during the 2-week search period – for example, if a partner has contacted many volunteer organisations but they do not have any available positions
- they are unable to complete the required hours in any of the 4 weeks for reasons beyond their control
- the conditions of the organisation and/or requirements of the position make it unsafe for the partner to continue
If a client is delayed in notifying MSD of their good and sufficient reason, the delay must only be for a reasonable period. MSD will determine on a case-by-case basis whether the length of the delay is reasonable or not.
If MSD determines that they are unable to complete Community Work Experience for a good and sufficient reason, and a partner has notified MSD within a reasonable period, MSD must impose a Grade 1 financial sanction. The date the financial sanction is imposed depends on where the client is in their Community Work Experience period.
When a partner is in their search or position period, the Grade 1 financial sanction is imposed from the day a partner meets with MSD and MSD is satisfied there is a good and sufficient reason and they have notified MSD within a reasonable period.
When a partner’s search period has finished and they did not secure a position, the Grade 1 financial sanction is imposed from the day after the search period ended.
MSD must assign a recompliance activity to the partner as soon as possible.
If a partner does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to find or complete Community Work Experience, or they did not notify MSD within a reasonable period, they will be considered non-compliant.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation
Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting work ability assessment obligations include (but are not limited to) when a client is:
- in hospital
- experiencing an acute mental health episode
Note if a client refuses to complete a Self-Assessment or a Work Ability Assessment, and they do not have a good and sufficient reason, they will have an obligations failure.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
