You need to be satisfied that the partner does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their work or work preparation obligations, based on the information you have, before you initiate an obligations failure.
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'. Having considered the circumstances, was it reasonable for the client not to have met their obligations?
Good and sufficient reasons may include (but are not limited to), that the partner:
- was temporarily medically unfit and they have a medical certificate that shows this
- had a death or illness in the immediate family
- could not realistically transport themselves on the day, due to unforeseen circumstances
- had childcare arrangements that fell through on the day, due to unforeseen circumstances
- was dependent on the provision of assistance by Work and Income to complete the activity, and that assistance was not supplied
- had an unexpected event occur on that day, such as providing care for a sick relative
Decide in favour of the partner if any doubt remains.
If you are aware that the partner has a good and sufficient reason, do not initiate an obligations failure.
If the client does not have a good and sufficient reason, see:
- Effect of sanctions on assistance
## Disputing the obligations failure
A client can dispute the decision to initiate the obligations failure or the sanction. For more information see:
- Disputes and reviews of an obligations failure

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation
Once a client has been through the regular engagement and support process and is not taking all reasonable steps to meet one of their social obligations, you then need to be satisfied that they do not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their social obligation, based on the information you have, before you initiate an obligations failure.
You should also consider whether a client has a good and sufficient reason for failing to comply with their social obligations if they dispute an obligations failure after it has been initiated.
## Good and sufficient reasons
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'. Having considered the circumstances, was it reasonable for the client not to have met their obligations?
Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation may include (but are not limited to) when a client:
- is in hospital
- has a death or illness in the immediate family
- is experiencing family violence
- experiences an emergency or adverse event
- was dependent on the provision of assistance by Work and Income to complete the activity, and that assistance was not supplied
- is being prosecuted under the Education and Training Act 2020
Decide in favour of the client if any doubt remains.
If you are aware that the client has a good and sufficient reason, do not initiate an obligations failure.
Note where a client has a partner, social obligations apply to both. If a client has a good and sufficient reason for failing a social obligation, talk with them to find out whether their good and sufficient reason also applies to their partner. In most cases, it is likely that if the client has a good and sufficient reason this reason will also apply to their partner.
## Other factors to consider before determining a client has failed to comply
You should also consider whether a client has taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligation before deciding that they have failed to comply with their social obligation.
There are also some circumstances where social obligations do not apply. For example, when a child leaves school at 15 with a Ministry of Education Early Leaving Exemption, the obligation to ensure that child is enrolled in and attending school no longer applies.
Make sure you have provided the client with the appropriate engagement and support before considering that the client has failed their obligation and that this has been recorded in OBMAN.
If the client does not have a good and sufficient reason, see:
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting obligation to work with a contracted service provider — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting obligation to work with a contracted service provider
Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting the obligation to work with a contracted service provider include (but are not limited to) when a client:
- has a change in capacity to work
- experiences a deterioration to their existing health condition, injury, or disability
- is in hospital
- has a death or illness in the immediate family
- had their transport or childcare arrangements fall through
- is experiencing family violence
- experiences an emergency or adverse event
Note if a client refuses to meet their obligation to work with a contracted service provider, and they do not have a good and sufficient reason, they have an obligations failure.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment
You need to consider if there was a good and sufficient reason for the client to stop work.
Examples of good and sufficient reasons for ceasing employment include (but are not limited to) when the client:
- could no longer realistically transport themselves to their employment (e.g. where a client's place of employment has moved)
- had childcare arrangements that were not adequate or fell through
- had an unexpected event occur (e.g. they had to return to the family home in another location to care for a sick relative)
- left the job because the job was outside of their capabilities or the job was not suitable
- had a significant change in conditions of employment that meant the employment was no longer suitable
- needed to take leave without pay to protect their job in the future, e.g. due to an economic downturn, or an unexpected the temporary closure of the premises as a result of an event such as a fire or flood
- was not able to continue working full-time (and was unable to work reduced hours) as a result of a health condition, illness, or disability and has a medical certificate to show this
Remember you will need to consider the circumstances of each case.
For more information see:
- Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed

chunks.title: Failing 3 obligations in a 24 month period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Failing 3 obligations in a 24 month period
If a client does not meet their obligations without a good and sufficient reason, an obligations failure will be initiated and a graduated sanction may be imposed.
The graduated sanction regime applies to all obligations, including social obligations.
If a client fails 3 obligations without a good and sufficient reason in a 24-month period, they are subject to a Grade 3 sanction - 13-week non-entitlement period.
This means:
- for clients without dependent children, 3 obligations failures in a 24-month period may result in a benefit cancellation and a 13-week non-entitlement period
- for partnered clients with dependent children, only the partner with a Grade 3 failure is affected
- for sole parents with dependent children, 3 obligations failures in a 24-month period will result in a 50% cancellation of benefit for 13 weeks
Note for young partners with youth activity obligations, their obligation failures are only counted for 12 months.
## Job refusal
A client who refuses an offer of suitable employment is subject to a Grade 3 sanction, regardless of their failure count in the 24-month period.
Note when an applicant fails their pre-benefit activity to accept an offer of suitable employment, they are not subject to a 13-week non-entitlement period or job refusal failure, as these can only be imposed once a client is getting a main benefit.
For more information see:
- Core policy Pre-benefit requirements
- Effect of 13-week non-entitlement period - couple wishes to change primary status
- Effect of non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Financial assistance during non-entitlement period
- Recompliance - 13-week non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Granting Emergency Benefit on grounds of hardship (65 years or over) — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Granting Emergency Benefit on grounds of hardship (65 years or over)
When clients aged 65 years or over do not qualify for New Zealand Superannuation there are usually a range of reasons that they are unable to earn a sufficient livelihood, such as disability, language or skill barriers as well as their age.
## Determining the equivalent benefit
Before granting Emergency Benefit for a client 65 years or over who is not residentially qualified for New Zealand Superannuation MSD needs to determine the equivalent benefit by looking at the reason the client is unable to earn sufficient livelihood such as:
- disability
- language
- skill barriers
- age
Generally, if the client is unable to earn sufficient livelihood because they are unable to get a job, the equivalent benefit would be Jobseeker Support.
If a client is not available for or seeking full-time employment they do not qualify for Jobseeker Support, except when they have limited work capacity because of a health condition, injury or disability.
Note MSD cannot pay Emergency Benefit at the equivalent rate of New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension.
## Jobseeker Support
If a client 65 years or over is getting Jobseeker Support they can remain on it provided they meet all the qualifications, their obligations and the 26 week reapplication process.
Generally, the client will no longer qualify for Jobseeker Support if they inform MSD they are:
- unable to seek full time employment or
- it is unreasonable or unrealistic to expect them to seek full time employment
If the client does not qualify for another benefit such as Sole Parent Support or Supported Living Payment, consider their eligibility for Emergency Benefit. The client will need to meet all of the qualifications for Emergency Benefit including the hardship test.
For more information see:
- Equivalent benefit
- Example of equivalent benefit
- Determining the reason for insufficient livelihood
- Conditions of grant
- Work or work preparation obligations - partners
- Partners 65 years and over
- Not eligible for another benefit

chunks.title: Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement
A special income exemption for severe disablement may be given to a client as an incentive for their personal effort to participate or continue in employment.
To help you to decide if a person is severely disabled consider the following:
- Does the client have to put in more effort in order to participate in employment? (for example, they may take a considerably long time to get ready in the morning or a longer time to travel to their place of employment)?
- Is the client's capacity to earn the same wage as a person without a severe disability reduced because of their disability (for example, does the client work reduced hours or receive less money for the job they undertake because of their disability)?
- Does the client have additional expenses to undertake employment (for example additional transport or equipment costs)?
- Does the client have difficulties participating in employment or completing their tasks because of their disability (for example, they may experience difficulties with mobility around the work place, be limited in the tasks they undertake or on occasion may not complete their work duties)?
- Does the client require assistance from another person to carry out some of their daily tasks (for example, washing, dressing or cooking)?
- Does the client require the assistance from another person to travel to work or to ensure their physical safety while at work (for example, does the client have difficulty using public transport)?
- Any other relevant factors that should be considered.
- If the client answers 'yes' to one or more of these questions you will have to decide if the client is severely disabled or if you need further information to make this decision.
Contact Helpline if you need help with the assessment.
For more information see:
- Amount of income exemption
- Exemption for severe disablement

chunks.title: Health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Health condition, injury or disability
Where a client is not eligible for another benefit and is unable to earn a sufficient livelihood primarily due to a health condition, an injury or a disability, an Emergency Benefit may be considered.
Note before an Emergency Benefit is granted consider the client's eligibility to Jobseeker Support on ground of health condition, injury or disability.
If it is justified that an Emergency Benefit is paid, the nature of the health condition, injury or disability needs to be assessed. This will determine the equivalent benefit to which the Emergency Benefit will be granted.
For more information see:
- Equivalent to Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability)
- Equivalent to Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability)
- Donating a kidney or liver tissue
- Determining the reason for insufficient livelihood
- Conditions of grant

chunks.title: Help with paying for the recompliance drug test - partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Help with paying for the recompliance drug test - partners
When a partner has failed their drug test obligations the second time, they must agree that they will take and pass a drug test within 25 days of agreeing to do so.
Work and Income can help them meet the full costs of taking the drug test if they cannot meet the cost upfront.
In this case Work and Income will arrange to cover the cost of the drug test with the provider and then recover the cost from the partner by way of debt repayment.
In order for Work and Income to help meet the costs of taking the drug test, the partner must agree:
- to take and pass a drug test within 25 working days
- to contact drug test provider and arrange and then take the drug test; and
- to provide the results to Work and Income
Work and Income will provide the partner with names and contact details for drug test providers in the local area.
A partner can only apply once during the 25 working day period for upfront help with the costs of the recompliance drug test. The 25 working days start from the day after the partner agrees to recomply.
Note that Work and Income has an additional five working days to receive the results from the partner and to process the information.
## Partner pays for drug test themselves
A partner can pay for the recompliance test themselves, if they choose to do this, they must:
- take a drug test within 25 working days
- arrange with a drug test provider to take the drug test and
- ensure that they provide Work and Income with the drug test results
## Debt recovery and reimbursement to the drug test provider
Work and Income will arrange with the drug test provider to cover the cost of the drug test.
Once the cost of the drug test is reimbursed to the drug test provider it must be established as a debt to the partner. The amount of the debt is the same amount that has been repaid to the drug test provider.
The recovery rate should be at the appropriate level giving consideration to any other debts the partner may have. Debt repayment options must be discussed with the partner at the earliest opportunity.
This upfront assistance is only available for one recompliance drug test to be undertaken during the 25 working day period. The cost of further tests undertaken within that period will have to be met by the partner upfront.

chunks.title: Home schooling — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Home schooling
Clients with dependent children aged 5 or 6 years (depending on when they start school) to 16 years of age will be required to take all reasonable steps to ensure the child is enrolled in and attending school. Home schooling meets this obligation in some circumstances.
Clients can home school their children and meet their social obligation if they have a "Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School" issued by the Ministry of Education.
However, if a client and their partner (if any) have work obligations, generally they won't be able to home school their child as this could impact on their ability to actively seek or be available for work. They may qualify for an exemption from their work obligations to home school their children.
For more information see:
## Certificate of exemption from enrolment at a registered school
A child does not legally have to attend school until they are aged 6 years (but most children start school at 5 years). If a child is aged between 5 and 6 years it is the parent's or caregiver's choice whether to have their child in early childhood education or school. A "Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School" issued by the Ministry of Education is not needed while the child is aged 5.
Once a child is aged 6 years a "Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School" issued by the Ministry of Education is required by law to enable a parent to home school their child.
For more information see:
## Social obligations cannot be required if child has legally left school
A child can legally leave school when they are 16 years or at 15 years if they have an early leaving exemption. A parent or caregiver cannot be asked to comply with the attendance at school social obligation if the child has legally left school or has an early leaving exemption and is no longer legally required to attend school.
## Social obligations and work obligations
When a client has work obligations as well as social obligations they must meet both sets of obligations at the same time. If the client is unable to meet their work obligations because they are home schooling a dependent child, you can consider granting an exemption from their work obligations. The client must meet the additional criteria for the home schooling exemption.
For more information see:
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Home schooling a dependent child
- Work obligations - partners
- Exemptions - partners

chunks.title: Home schooling a dependent child — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Home schooling a dependent child
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
A client can, in very limited circumstances, be exempt from meeting some of their work obligations:
- if they are home schooling a dependent child or a foster child and
- they have restricted circumstances that make the child's attendance at school unreasonable
Before granting an exemption MSD should:
- gather all the proof required
- get the approval of the manager client service delivery to the exemption
This is a partial exemption only.
## Transitional arrangements for a person home schooling a child when they become a beneficiary with work obligations
If a client is home schooling a child prior to becoming a beneficiary with work obligations then an exemption can be granted until the end of that school year, if they have an exemption certificate from the Ministry of Education.
## Proof
The client must provide:
- proof of the restricted circumstances that makes their child's attendance at school unreasonable and
- their 'Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School', issued by the Ministry of Education (if it's not a recently issued certificate, the client needs to contact the Ministry of Education to get another certificate)
For an 'Application for exemption from enrolment at a registered school', see the 'Home education application form' link at the bottom of the Home education page (the application form is the same for primary and secondary schooling).
All exemptions for home schooling must be approved by a service centre manager.
## Child is aged 17 or 18 years
If the child being home schooled is aged 17 or 18 years:
- the restricted circumstances criteria still apply
- the client must complete a personal statement stating that they are home schooling the child and that the child is not attending a registered school
The Ministry of Education issues a 'Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School' only for the years of compulsory schooling.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months or the end of the current school year, whichever is earlier.

chunks.title: Hours range for suitable employment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Hours range for suitable employment
Partners with work obligations must make themselves available for suitable employment of:
- at least 30 hours a week (partner with full-time work obligations)
- at least 20 hours a week (partner with part-time work obligations)
Although the target to meet work obligations is 20 or 30 hours per week a job can be considered suitable if the hours of work per week are within a range of hours required to meet their work obligations.
## Hours range for partners with part-time work obligations
A person with part-time work obligations could be expected to undertake a job of between 15 and 25 hours per week if all other aspects of the job were suitable.
## Example
Anna is a partner with part-time work obligations. She is an experienced hair dresser. A hairdressing vacancy arises for 16 hours per week at the local salon. The details of the job suit Anna's circumstances in all ways, including her caring responsibilities. This job is considered 'suitable employment' and Anna must apply and accept the job (if it is offered to her) or fail to meet her obligations. If Anna is offered the job, she would still be expected to be available for other work, training or other activities as she is in employment less than 20 hours per week.
Note if another job with more hours is found for Anna in another salon but the hourly rate is less and overall she would be no better off financially, the job would not be considered suitable. A suitable job would be one that was for more hours that paid the same or greater than what she was earning in her current part-time job.
## Hours range for partners with full-time work obligations
A person with full-time work obligations could be expected to undertake a job of between 20 and 40 hours per week if all other aspects of the job were suitable.
## Example
James is a partner with full-time work obligations. A vacancy arises for a forecourt attendant at the petrol station for 25 hours per week. The details of the job suit James' circumstances. This job is considered 'suitable employment' and James must apply and accept the job (if it is offered to him) or fail to meet his obligations. If James is offered the job, he would still be expected to be available for other work, training or other activities as he is in employment less than 30 hours per week.
For more information see:
- Work obligations - partners
- Suitable employment
- Meeting job search requirements

chunks.title: Unable to provide visa or permit — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Unable to provide visa or permit
When a client is unable to provide an immigration visa or permit they may provide other Immigration New Zealand documents to verify their immigration status. Work and Income can also undertake an immigration status check directly with Immigration New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Permanent residence
- Immigration status [no link find out why]

chunks.title: In approved full-time training — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## In approved full-time training
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
A client can be partially exempt from meeting some of their work obligations if they are engaged in approved full-time training.
Note a client who has started approved training or is about to start an approved training course before they apply for a benefit must still meet all of the qualifications for Jobseeker Support before their benefit can be granted.
Consider whether the training course is the most suitable activity for the client. Also consider if other activities (for example programmes, seminars or work experience) might be a more appropriate option for moving the client towards paid work.
Discuss and take into account the client's career background, including:
- their educational qualifications
- their employment history
- their skills and
- whether training will help them find work at the earliest opportunity
Examples of approved training courses include but are not limited to:
- Limited Service Volunteer
- Skills for Industry
- Targeted Training
- training approved by the regional contracts manager
The approved training must:
- be full time (at least 20 hours a week)
- focus on teaching practical, employment-related skills
- support the client to gain the skills that will help them find work
Approved training does not include a course undertaken by a full-time student, as defined by the Student Allowance Regulations 1998.
## Proof
Generally if a partner has been referred to the training, they will not need to provide proof. However, if there is any doubt, you can ask the client to provide a training statement signed by the course provider.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'In approved training'.

chunks.title: In approved study — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## In approved study
Partners who are in study approved by MSD may qualify for an exemption from their work obligations.
When an exemption is approved, MSD may set conditions for the exemption. For example, the partner must be passing their course of study.
## Exemption from work obligations
A partner can be exempt from meeting some or all of their work obligations if they:
- are in full-time study approved by MSD or
- were in MSD approved study when their work obligations started, and they are still in that study
## Proof
The partner must provide proof they are in study, such as enrolment forms or a training statement from their training provider.
## Duration
When an exemption is approved, MSD sets a duration for the exemption.
Generally an exemption can be in place until the earlier of:
- the end of the client’s current course of study or
- the end of the current academic year or
- up to 12 months
## Continuing study
If the partner is continuing their study the following year, they must get a new exemption approved.
They must also provide confirmation they passed at least 50% of their course the previous year.

chunks.title: In approved training (no children or child 14+) — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## In approved training (no children or child 14+)
If a partner is in approved training they must continue to meet their work obligations, including being available for full-time employment unless they are granted an exemption for approved full-time training.
They are still expected to be available for work or any other activity up to a total of 30 hours each week.
The partner must understand that they have to accept suitable paid work if it becomes available.
For more information see:
- Approved training

chunks.title: In-hand allowance — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a young partner getting Emergency Benefit is subject to youth money management, they can get an amount of up to $50 a week paid directly to them as an in-hand allowance. After the young partner's accommodation, service costs and lawful debts are paid by redirection, the balance of payment, if any, is distributed between the young partner's payment card and the in-hand allowance. The maximum amount that can be paid direct to a young partner as an in-hand allowance is $50.

chunks.title: Distribution of payment after redirections — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Generally, where there is more than $50 available after all of a young partner's redirections have occurred, $50 would be paid direct to the young partner and the remainder would be placed on their payment card, unless YSSU is satisfied that another distribution would be more appropriate for the young partner. Youth Service providers are responsible for making recommendations to YSSU as to how their client's payments should be distributed between the payment card and in-hand allowance. When making these recommendations to YSSU, providers consider what would be the most appropriate distribution for the young partner, given their individual circumstances. YSSU then makes the decision as to how the young partner's payment will be distributed, taking into account the information supplied by the young partner's service provider.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A young partner with a toddler in a boarding situation has $80 left after her board costs (which include food) and any debts have been paid. The young partner has transport costs to get to and from school and must use public transport to drop her child off at day-care. The young person must pay for the child's nappies and formula from the supermarket herself. After discussions with the young partner, the provider recommends paying a $40 in-hand allowance to the young partner and placing $40 on the payment card to be used to purchase nappies, wipes and formula. YSSU decides to agree with the recommendation and decides to pay the client a $40 in-hand allowance and to put $40 on the payment card.

chunks.title: Altering the distribution of payment for existing clients already subject to youth money management — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If, at any time, a Youth Service provider considers that the current distribution of an existing client's payment between the payment card and in-hand allowance is inappropriate for the client's circumstances, they can make a recommendation to YSSU that this distribution be altered. When determining whether it is appropriate to make a recommendation that a client's payment distribution be altered, providers must take into account a range of factors. Note a young partner cannot review the decision on how the Emergency Benefit is paid to them.

chunks.title: In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes where a partner is in or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence.
Treatment for the purposes of the drug test requirements means any specialist treatment service provided for a person because of a diagnosed drug dependency.
The partner can either be participating in or on the waiting list for a specialist treatment service.
Specialist treatment services are services:
- that provide specific medical or psychological interventions with the goal of helping a person to overcome drug dependency
- that a partner has been referred to following a formal assessment by the Community Alcohol and Drug Service (CADS) or by a registered AOD practitioner
The partner can be asked to provide verification from the person recommending the treatment or from the treatment service. The verification must state the duration or time that the partner will need to address their drug dependency and whether they are participating or on the wait list for treatment. There is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to the partner.
For more information see:
- Drug test obligation failures - good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: Incentive payments can continue — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Incentive payments can continue
Generally, the incentive payment will continue if a young partner has earned them and then is exempt from their activity obligations.
Where a young partner is granted an exemption from their activity obligations, continued eligibility for the incentive payment needs to be assessed. Where a person has acted in a way that is inconsistent with the purpose of the incentive, all of or some of the incentives may be removed, for example, when an exemption is required due to court imposed conditions.
## School and tertiary holidays
Any incentive payments earned by the young person will continue to be paid during any school or tertiary holiday periods while they are receiving Emergency Benefit.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Incentive payments — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Incentive payments
If a young partner is under youth money management, any incentive payments earned are included in the redirection of their payment.
Young partners can earn incentive payments for demonstrating a commitment to their activity obligations.
A young partner getting Emergency Benefit can earn the following incentives:
- budgeting - $10 per week
- education - $10 per week
- parenting - $10 per week
## Young person not under youth money management
When a young person is not under youth money management, incentive payments are paid directly to them.
For more information see:
## Review of decision
A young partner cannot review the decision on how their portion of Emergency Benefit is paid to them.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Income from overseas — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Income from overseas
When a client has been working overseas within the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before their entitlement date you include this in their average weekly income.
If the client cannot provide verification of their earnings, accept the information provided on their application for benefit. For help to convert foreign currency to the equivalent New Zealand dollars see the instructions below.
There is no ability to take higher living costs into account. If the client is in financial hardship during an initial stand-down they can apply for a Special Needs Grant. For more information see: Assistance during an Initial stand down and/or benefit application process
## Receiving a benefit from overseas
When a client has been receiving an overseas benefit or pension within the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before their entitlement date you include this in their average weekly wage.
If the overseas benefit or pension payments have stopped and the client cannot provide verification of their payments, accept the information provided on their application for benefit. There is no requirement to obtain verification through International Services
Note when the overseas benefit or pension payments are continuing and the client cannot provide verification, you will need to verify details of these payments. For further assistance contact International Services.
## Converting foreign currency
To estimate the foreign currency to the equivalent New Zealand dollars use the exchange rate provided in SELXT. The client must be informed that this calculation is not based on the current rate.
To obtain a current exchange rate, contact Westpac bank to request the 'Westpac buys cash' foreign exchange rate. Use the exchange rate as at the date the client returned to New Zealand.
Consideration must be given to the calculation that is in the client's favour. The exchange rate accepted by the client, (the estimated rate from SELXT or current rate from bank) should be noted in CMS.

chunks.title: Income of person requiring care — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Income of person requiring care
You can consider that the person has the ability to pay for their care if:
- they receive New Zealand Superannuation and their total income is $2,600 (before tax) or more over the rate of New Zealand Superannuation (before tax) that is due to them and their partner or
- their total income is $2,600 (before tax) or more than the gross rate of Supported Living Payment that is or would be due to them and their partner
If the person is able to pay for their care then the client cannot receive an Emergency Benefit.
## Cash assets assessed as income
Cash assets are also included in the assessment of the patient's income. For more information see:
- Cash assets of person requiring care
You also need to look at whether the person has recently given any money away or sold any assets.
Example
For a detailed example of determining whether a patient can contribute to their care see:
- Example assessing cash assets

chunks.title: Income test applied to Emergency Benefits — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Income test applied to Emergency Benefits
The reason the client is unable to earn a sufficient livelihood for themselves (and any dependent family) will determine the equivalent benefit and the income test that should be applied.
For example, a client granted an Emergency Benefit analogous to Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability, will have the same income test that applies to Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability.
Similarly, a client granted an Emergency Benefit equivalent to the Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability, will have the same income test that applies to Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability.
## Applying the income test in SWIFTT
SWIFTT currently assesses the rate of payment based on Jobseeker Support income tests.
## Jobseeker Support
Where an Emergency Benefit has been granted replacing Jobseeker Support SWIFTT will assess any income charged correctly.
## Supported Living Payment and Sole Parent Support
Where a client has been granted an Emergency Benefit equivalent to Supported Living Payment or Sole Parent Support, the rate of payment has to be assessed manually.
This will include the income exemptions that may be applied to clients receiving these benefits.
A non-standard rate using the SNSRA screen must be used to ensure the correct rate of benefit is paid.
Note a Client Event Must View Note must be added to CMS when a non-standard rate is used.
For more information see:
- Equivalent benefit

chunks.title: Inform young partner of their activity obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Inform young partner of their activity obligations
Once the benefit has been granted, and the activity has been set for the young person, they must be advised of:
- the activity obligations they are required to meet and the specific activities that have been set for them (eg school, training or work-based learning, parenting and budgeting)
- the consequences of failing to comply with their activity obligations without a good and sufficient reason, in particular the sanctions that will be imposed and
- their right to review and dispute any decisions relating to a failure to comply with their activity obligations
The activity obligations cannot be enforced until the main benefit commencement date.
For more information see:
- Young partner without children
- Young partner with dependent child
- Youth activity obligation failures

chunks.title: Informing a partner of the drug test obligation failure — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Informing a partner of the drug test obligation failure
Once MSD has decided that the partner has failed a drug test work obligations, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. The partner will then be sent a letter stating that their benefit will be sanctioned and that their benefit will only be increased, restarted, regranted, or continued if they:
- complete a recompliance activity
- dispute the decision to impose the sanction and MSD accepts that they have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting their work obligations or
- lodge a Review of Decision and MSD reconsiders their position and agrees with the partner's review
For some partners, if it's their first obligation failure they may be eligible for a non-financial sanction instead of a financial sanction. For more information see: Non-financial sanctions.
## Recompliance for a drug test work obligation failure
Partners may have their benefit increased or restarted from the date they start a drug test failure recompliance activity.
For more information see:
- Obligations failures
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Drug test obligation failures - Good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: Informing clients of their obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Informing clients of their obligations
MSD must ensure that the client understands:
- their obligations
- the consequences of failing to meet those obligations, in particular the sanctions that may be imposed and
- their right to review and dispute any decisions relating to a failure to comply with their obligations
Clients and partners applying for Emergency Benefit must:
- sign their application form and
- be given a copy of their obligations from their application form
Note that work obligations cannot be enforced until the main benefit commencement date.
## Clients transferring between benefits
When a client is getting a benefit and they have a change in obligations, a letter will be sent advising them what their new obligations are. They do not need to re-sign an obligations form.
This includes where a partner is transferring between having work preparation obligations and part-time work obligations when their youngest dependent child turns 3 years of age within Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Informing partners of their obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Informing partners of their obligations
Before granting a benefit, you must ensure that the partner understands:
- their obligations (dependent on the age of their child or if they have no children)
- the consequences of failing to meet those obligations, in particular the sanctions that may be imposed and
- their right to review and dispute any decisions relating to a failure to comply with their work obligations
Partners of clients receiving Emergency Benefit must be notified in writing if they have work or work preparation obligations. To do this, you must:
- note on the partner's obligations section of the application form that you have decided they should have work or work preparation obligations and
- give the partner a copy of their obligations from the application form
Note that the work or work preparation obligations cannot be enforced until the main benefit commencement date.
For more information see:
- Obligations
- Work or work preparation obligations - partners
- Work preparation obligations - partners
- Work obligations - partners

chunks.title: Initial stand-down — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Initial stand-down
This is a period of up to a maximum of 2 weeks where the client cannot get any benefit payment. The length of the stand-down depends on:
- the client's average weekly income (before tax) in the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before the client's entitlement date and
- the number of dependent children in their care at any time during the same period
The initial stand-down starts on the client's entitlement date.
Note clients can choose an income assessment period of either 26 or 52 weeks to calculate their average weekly wage for the initial stand-down.
## For more information on the initial stand-down see:
- Average weekly income
- Number of dependent children
- Employment during stand-down
- Self-imposed stand-down
- Initial stand-down procedure
- Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process
- No stand-down applies
- Deskfile Initial stand-down

chunks.title: Initial stand-down procedure — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Initial stand-down procedure
Step 1. Find the client's entitlement date.
Step 2. Calculate the client's average weekly income for a 26 and 52 week period.
Step 3. Find out whether the client has or had any dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement date. When determining the correct stand down period, you must take into account any children that were in the clients care during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to the entitlement date
Step 4. Using the information from Steps 2 and 3, determine the initial stand-down for the client over a 26 and 52 week period by looking at the Initial stand-down period rates in Deskfile.
Step 5. Use the calculation of average weekly income that gives the client a lesser stand-down period.
Step 6. Apply the initial stand-down from the client's entitlement date to find the commencement date.
Remember; if you enter the correct information into SWIFTT it will automatically calculate the initial stand-down and commencement date for you.
Note if the client has had a dependent child (or children) in their care during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement date and the child (or children) is no longer in their care, you will have to use a work around. Contact Helpline for this information.

chunks.title: Introduction — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Emergency Benefit is an income and asset tested benefit payable to people who are in hardship and who:
- are unable to earn enough income for themselves (and any dependent family)
and
- cannot receive another benefit
Each application for Emergency Benefit should be assessed on its own merits.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Obligations
- Conditions of grant
- Commencement date
- Non-entitlement period for 13 weeks
- Payment
- Changes and reviews

chunks.title: Job search — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Job search
In some circumstances, you may consider that an Emergency Benefit should include job search requirements. Where the equivalent benefit is subject to work obligations, generally you will include job search obligations as part of your conditions of grant. These conditions can be similar to the work obligations and may include part-time job search.
You cannot apply the work obligations or the sanctions as such. You can grant the Emergency Benefit and require the client to meet certain conditions that look similar to the work obligations. Where a person fails to meet this condition of grant, the Emergency Benefit may be stopped.
The conditions that may be applied to the Emergency Benefit are the client to:
- be currently registered in CMS and
- provide proof of job search when requested
Note if the job search is part-time, you may specify a certain number of hours the client must undertake.
From time to time, a client's circumstances may change and the conditions of grant of Emergency Benefit may need to be reviewed.
Note where a client fails to meet this condition, review their entitlement for other benefit assistance before considering another equivalent Emergency Benefit for a different reason.
For more information see:
- Equivalent benefit
- Benefit paid for a specific period
- Conditions of grant

chunks.title: Job-search activities must be reasonable steps towards employment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: As part of completing Report Job Search, partners must do at least 3 job-search activities each week for 4 weeks. Partners also need to report to MSD on all of the job-search activities they complete each week (minimum of 3 per week). To meet the requirements of Report Job Search, MSD must consider that the partner's job-search activities are reasonable steps towards them finding suitable employment. Factors MSD should consider when determining whether a job-search activity is a reasonable step include (but are not limited to): - the partner's current skills, experience, and employment history - if the partner already has an appropriate CV and cover letter - if the partner has already completed skills-based courses (such as, first aid or barista courses) - the work-readiness of the partner (e.g. work-appropriate clothing, caring responsibilities, access to transport) Note partner's individual circumstances will determine what is considered a reasonable step for them. Each activity should be considered on a case-by-case basis. Examples of job-search activities that are considered reasonable steps could include (but are not limited to) a partner: - writing different cover letters that focus on the skills for specific job applications - updating their CV - attending a CV writing workshop to improve their chances of finding employment - checking MyMSD for suitable jobs in their area - calling Job Connect for more details about a specific role - checking an employment site for suitable roles (e.g. Trade Me, Seek, Indeed) - visiting local suitable businesses to submit CVs or check for any openings - attending a skills-based course to improve their chances of securing a suitable role - taking steps to get suitable clothing for a job interview - expanding the range of roles they are looking for beyond their employment history - applying for suitable roles (including if the application is unsuccessful or they don't hear anything back) - attending an interview (including where the interview is unsuccessful) - registering with a recruitment agency or career advice service Note partners are only expected to provide evidence of their job-search activity where it is reasonable for them to get it in their circumstances.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Lizzy has told their case manager that they have not updated their CV with their recent employment history. They also noted that they would like to gain employment in the hospitality industry, but they do not have the skills to support this. Lizzy then fails a work obligation and their case manager determines that Report Job Search would be the most appropriate non-financial sanction for them. Lizzy's 4-week sanction period comes to an end, and they have a meeting with their case manager to provide evidence and determine whether their job-search activities were reasonable steps towards them finding suitable employment. The case manager can see that for each of the 4 weeks Lizzy has been updating their CV, attending a barista course, applying for jobs, and had an interview. Lizzy has reported on more than 3 suitable job-search activities per week over the 4-week period. Their case manager determines that based on their individual circumstances, the job-search activities Lizzy has undertaken are reasonable steps as they align with their skills and experience, developing their capability and help them towards finding suitable employment. As Lizzy has completed the requirements of their sanction, they are considered to have recomplied.

chunks.title: Job-search activity is not considered a reasonable step — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If MSD determines a client's reported job-search activities are not reasonable steps to find suitable employment, they are considered non-compliant. MSD may backdate non-compliance to the start of the week that the client failed to meet the requirements of Report Job Search. This may result in a debt for the client. During the appointment, clients will have an opportunity to give a good and sufficient reason why they considered their job-search activity to be a reasonable step. Examples of job-search activities that are not considered reasonable steps to finding suitable employment could include (but are not limited to), where the client: - only looked online for jobs, even though they could have used a variety of methods to look for work - applied for jobs where it was unreasonable for them to be hired (e.g., applied to be a doctor with no medical training, or applied to be a bus driver with no licence) - recorded the same job-search activity multiple times where this would be considered unreasonable (e.g., updated their CV three times each week, or contacted the same employer multiple times each week)

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Tim has failed a work obligation and his case manager determines that Report Job Search would be the most appropriate sanction for him. Tim was previously working in an IT job and agrees he will focus on job-search activities that are steps towards being more employable in both IT and wider jobs. Tim's 4-week sanction period comes to an end, and he has a meeting with his case manager to determine whether his job search activities are considered reasonable steps towards finding suitable employment. The case manager can see that for each of the four-weeks Tim has updated his CV, attended an IT skills course, and has been applying for a wide range of jobs. Tim has reported three job-search activities per week, however his case manager determines one of the job-search activities he has undertaken is not a reasonable step to finding suitable employment. This is because he was attending IT courses he had already completed/has the skills to do. As Tim has not completed the requirements of his sanction, he is considered to be non-compliant.

chunks.title: Lockouts — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Lockouts
People that are officially "locked out" of their workplace by their employer may be able to access additional financial assistance from Work and Income if they are in hardship.
Generally, when a lockout occurs Work and Income have established relationships with union officials in affected area. This is to establish whether any issues require resolution and to understand the impacts for workers of continued industrial action.
Given that locked out workers are not unemployed and actively seeking work, their entitlement to benefit is considered under the Emergency Benefit provisions.
To be entitled to Emergency Benefit applicants affected by a lockout must meet the hardship criteria. This requires an income and cash asset test. Those with sufficient other income (eg a spouse working) or cash assets (eg savings) may not be eligible for Emergency Benefit under the hardship criteria.
For more information see:
- Client in hardship
The entitlement to Emergency Benefit starts from the day the client is locked out or the date the client can prove they are in hardship from, whichever date is the later.
Emergency Benefit granted for clients in Lockout situations are considered a benefit for a specific period and the initial stand down period is not imposed when the benefit is granted from the day the client is locked out. If the benefit is granted from a date after the lockout because they do not meet the Hardship criteria until that date, then the initial stand-down should be imposed.
Emergency Benefit entitlement ends when the lockout ends.
For more information see:
- Benefit paid for a specific period
- Lockouts [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Maximum rate of payment for clients donating an organ — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Maximum rate of payment for clients donating an organ
When a client is transferred from Supported Living Payment - care of a person to the Emergency Benefit, the client can get the maximum rate of benefit they would be entitled to Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support.
They are not entitled to the Supported Living - care of a person rate.
For more information see:
- Deskfile Supported Living Payment rates
- Deskfile Jobseeker Support rates
- Deskfile Sole Parent Support rates
- Clients donating an organ income test and asset test

chunks.title: Maximum rates - caring for a person — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Maximum rates - caring for a person
The rate of Emergency Benefit paid to clients caring for their New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension partner, is generally the same as the rate for Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).
Important note the rate of payment:
- does not include a dependent partner however
- the partner's income is taken into account when assessing the rate
If the client has a partner, you must see whether the partner can get another benefit. If they cannot get any other benefit, then you can see if the partner could get an Emergency Benefit at the half couple rate.
Depending on the circumstances of the client, the following rates (the same as for Supported Living Payment - caring for a person) are generally paid:
Client circumstances
The maximum net rate that can be paid is the:
Couple without dependent children
Half-married, civil union or de facto rate
$360.72 (as at 1 April 2026)
Couple with a dependent child - partner on benefit
Half-married, civil union or de facto couple rate
$378.47 (as at 1 April 2026)
Couple with a dependent child - partner not on benefit
Half-married, civil union or de facto couple rate
$392.94 (as at 1 April 2026)
For more information see: Partner not receiving a benefit
Single with dependent children
Note check to see if the client can receive Supported Living Payment (caring for a person)
Caring for a person, sole parent rate
$581.96 (as at 1 April 2026)
Single aged 18 years or older without dependent children
Single 18 years or older rate
$424.60 (as at 1 April 2026)
These benefit rates are as at 1 April 2026.

chunks.title: Maximum rates - caring for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension partner — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Maximum rates - caring for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension partner
The rate of Emergency Benefit paid to clients caring for their New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension partner is generally the same as the rate for Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).
Note the partner's income is taken into account when assessing the rate, see: Charging income - caring for New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension partner
The following rates are generally available depending on the client's circumstances:
Client circumstances
Maximum net rate that can be paid is:
Married, civil union or de facto couple without dependent children - partner on New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
$360.72 (as at 1 April 2026)
Married, civil union or de facto couple with dependent children - partner on New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
$392.94 (as at 1 April 2026)
These benefit rates are as at 1 April 2026.

chunks.title: Medical assessments — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Medical assessments
In some circumstances, you may want to consider if an Emergency Benefit should include providing medical evidence of continued restriction in their capacity for work and the degree of that restriction. Where the equivalent benefit is subject to continued medical assessments, generally you will include medical certificate conditions as part of your conditions of grant. These conditions can be similar to the medical assessments of Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability, or Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability.
Note you cannot apply the same requirements as Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability, or Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability. You can grant the Emergency Benefit and require the client to meet certain conditions that look similar to the medical certificate requirements. Where a person fails to meet this condition of grant, the Emergency Benefit may be stopped.
The conditions of grant may be:
- limited in their capacity or unable to work for a period of time because of a health condition
- because of a health condition, cannot work for an indefinite period of time or
- in employment but their earnings are reduced because of a health condition, an injury or a disability
and
- a medical certificate is required as proof of their limited capacity for work
From time-to-time, a client's circumstances may change and the conditions of grant of Emergency Benefit may need to be reviewed.
Note where a client has advised a change of circumstances review their eligibility and if necessary the conditions of grant.
For more information see:
- Equivalent benefit
- Benefit paid for a specific period
- Conditions of grant

chunks.title: Medical certificates for live organ donors — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Medical certificates for live organ donors
A client must provide a medical certificate as evidence they have been accepted as a live organ donor for the retrieval of a kidney or liver tissue.
The medical certificate must be signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner.
Note MSD can accept any medical certificate or letter from the client’s registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner. Evidence does not have to be a Work Capacity Medical Certificate.
## Twelve weeks maximum medical coverage
The maximum period an Emergency Benefit can be paid for recovery following the donation of a kidney or liver tissue is 12 weeks.
The first medical certificate coverage can be the lesser of either:
- the period specified by the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner or
- 12 weeks
If the first medical certificate is for less than 12 weeks and the client still requires financial assistance during their recovery time, the client must get another medical certificate for their Emergency Benefit to continue.
The medical certificate may be extended up to the maximum of 12 weeks from the date of surgery by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner.

chunks.title: Medical criteria for person who requires care — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Medical criteria for person who requires care
For a client to qualify for Emergency Benefit as they are caring for a person, the person must require full-time care and attention at home and without that care the person would need:
- hospital care
- rest home care
- residential disability care
- care of the kind referred to in section 141 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989, which is extended care services provided for severely disabled children and young persons or
- care of an equivalent kind
## At home
The home of the person requiring care may be the home of the client or the person. It is not expected that a caregiver live in the same house as the person who requires care.
## District Health Board assistance
The person who requires care may be able to receive assistance from the District Health Board that will allow the client caring for the person to earn a sufficient livelihood. Consider each case on its merits.
## Person requiring care contributing to the cost of care
When the client is caring for the person in the home of the person requiring care, the person's financial circumstances must be assessed to determine if they can contribute to their own care.
Note this does not apply when a person is caring for their New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension partner.

chunks.title: Medical evidence — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Medical evidence
If a client is caring for another person, they must provide medical evidence about the person being cared for that confirms:
- the person requires care at home and
- without that care the person would not be able to remain at home and
- indicate the duration that the care is required
The medical evidence must be signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and can be:
- a letter or
- the Supported Living Payment medical certificate

chunks.title: Medical evidence for patients from Tokelau, Niue and Cook Islands — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Medical evidence for patients from Tokelau, Niue and Cook Islands
If a client has arrived in New Zealand from these countries, they must provide a:
- referral form from their home country advising they are under a Patient Referral Scheme or
- letter from their medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or equivalent in their country of origin), from their home country referring them to a secondary or tertiary Ministry of Health (NZ) services provider and confirmation from the provider of their appointment and treatment

chunks.title: Meeting job search requirements — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Meeting job search requirements
Job search requirements apply to:
- partners with full-time and part-time work obligations
To help decide if a partner is meeting the job search requirements, you will need to consider the following:
1. If the partner had the opportunity, would they:
- be available for work of at least 20 hours per week (part-time work obligations)
- be available for work of at least 30 hours per week (full-time work obligations)
- accept any suitable job offers within their abilities
Note this can include weekend work depending on their individual circumstances
- not restrict their job search to vacancies within their own trade
- not restrict their job search to vacancies in their chosen occupation
- not move frequently from one area to another with no intention of getting a job
2. Has the partner begun to take steps to find work? For example by:
- searching newspapers and other media for vacancies
- making applications for suitable jobs
- contacting employers about vacancies

chunks.title: Method of payment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Method of payment
There are 2 ways that young partners aged 16 or 17 years with no children and 16 to 19 years with dependent children can have their portion of their benefit paid to them depending on whether the young partner is subject to youth money management or not.
## Young person is not subject to youth money management
Where a young person is not subject to youth money management they can get their Emergency Benefit, support, family tax credit and any extra help directly to their bank account.
## Young person is subject to youth money management
Where a young person is subject to youth money management the Emergency Benefit, family tax credit and any extra help (except Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance) is paid via:
- payment directly to supplier (eg a payees redirection for accommodation costs, utility costs and lawful debts)
- in-hand allowance which is paid directly to the young person's bank account
- payment card - the young person is able to purchase goods (such as food and groceries) from approved suppliers
Note Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance is paid directly to the young person's bank account.
## Review of decision
A young person cannot review the decision on how the Emergency Benefit is paid to them.

chunks.title: Misconduct — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Misconduct
An employer can only terminate a client's employment on the basis of misconduct if the client has seriously breached their contract of employment.
Note that if a client's employment has been terminated during a 90 day employment trial, generally this is not the result of misconduct. An employer is not obligated to give a reason for dismissal during a 90 day employment trial.
However, if the employer alleges misconduct by the employee and provides some evidence, misconduct should be investigated in the usual way.
## Situations where the voluntary unemployment 13 week non-entitlement period would apply
Situations where a client would be subject to a 13 week non-entitlement include (but are not limited to):
- a previously self-employed client applies for Emergency Benefit because they have closed or sold a viable business without a good and sufficient reason
- a client is applying for Emergency Benefit on the ground of health condition, injury, or disability and is able to work part-time, and left a part-time job without a good and sufficient reason
- a partner who is currently receiving Emergency Benefit has a dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years and therefore has part-time work obligations. The partner has left their part-time job without a good and sufficient reason.
- a client has left a part-time job without a good and sufficient reason, a voluntary unemployment stand-down would apply if the income from the job was sufficient to support the person, and the job was for 13 weeks or more
For more information see:
- Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period
Before applying a 13 week non-entitlement period for misconduct, you should contact both the client and their employer. When you contact the employer you should ask them to complete the Employment and earnings information for applications (V06) form.
If the employer does not return the form or the reason for termination is not given, no further contact with the employer should be made.
If there is conflicting evidence or the reason for leaving employment is not agreed between the client and the employer, you should give the client the benefit of the doubt.
Each client's circumstances need to be carefully investigated. If you are uncertain whether a voluntary unemployment stand-down should be imposed, discuss the client's circumstances, in the first instance, with a service centre trainer and then with Helpline (if still required).
If you decide to apply a voluntary unemployment stand-down, you will need to:
- advise the client of your decision
- send the client the 'Voluntary Unemployed' letter to confirm your decision. A copy of the letter is available in CMS
- for couples or sole parents, the client's commencement date letter will confirm your decision and outline their rate of payment
- add the date that a non-entitlement period will apply from and the appropriate VU reason code to the SSTDA screen
- conditionally grant the benefit using code 024 (VU imposed) on the SPGRT screen
- note for sole parents the 13 week non-entitlement period only applies to 50% of the benefit
- make notes in CMS outlining your decision
Ensure the benefit remains conditionally granted. Do not decline the benefit.
For more information see:
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed
- Misconduct
- Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer

chunks.title: Youth money management activity — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Youth money management activity
Young partners who have youth activity obligations are required to co-operate with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service in managing the spending of their benefit and provide information as required.
The young person must:
- attend and participate in regular one-on-one discussions on budgeting
and provide information on:
- their accommodation costs (for example rent, board) and service costs (for example power, phone)
- any other lawful debts and liabilities (for example court fines, Work and Income debts, Child Support payments, hire purchase)
- how they spend their in-hand allowance and
- how they spend any money allocated to their payment card
For more information see:
- Youth money management
## Exception
A young partner aged 16 or 17 years (with no children) or 16 to 19 years (with dependent children) will not be subject to youth money management and will have their full payment paid directly to them when they have:
- demonstrated continued compliance with their obligations and been assessed as being financially competent or
- opted out of youth money management because they have turned 18 years (for young partners without dependent children), or 20 years (for young partners with dependent children), and have chosen to stay in the Youth Service and complete their course of study, training or work-based learning
For more information see:
- Youth money management
- Assessed as financially competent

chunks.title: Money Management — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Money Management
Money Management is a non-financial sanction that can be imposed on a client or their partner as an alternative to a Grade 1 financial sanction.
A client on Money Management will have 50% of their main benefit put onto a payment card that can only be used for essential expenses. Any remaining benefit payments go into the client’s bank account. Money Management lasts for 4 weeks from the date it is imposed.

chunks.title: Monitoring compliance with social obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Monitoring compliance with social obligations
If you have reasons to be concerned that a client and their partner (if any) may not be meeting their social obligations you should, in the first instance, discuss and explain their social obligations and ensure they understand these obligations. For example when:
- you receive information that a client is not requiring their school age child to attend school
- you receive information that a client's child has not been receiving their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks
In these situations, you should start the three step process of regular engagement and support with the client.
For more information see:
- Regular engagement and support process
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Social obligations

chunks.title: NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification
In order to meet the obligation to be in full-time education, training, or work-based learning the young partner must be working towards NCEA level 2 or an equivalent or higher qualification.
An equivalent qualification to NCEA level 2 would be any qualification at level 2 on the New Zealand Qualification Framework.
## Meeting education obligations
A young partner is meeting their education obligations if they are in (or available for) full-time education, training or work-based learning, working towards a qualification registered at:
- level 2 on the New Zealand Qualification Framework (which includes NCEA Level 2)
- level 3 or higher on the New Zealand Qualification Framework (NZQF)
Note young people undertaking courses at level 1 on the New Zealand Qualification Framework are considered to be meeting their obligations as long as it is a qualification which will build towards a level 2 NZQF qualification.

chunks.title: Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes where a client has a drug issue identified by the Alcohol Drug Helpline - Work and Income Support Service and is engaging and participating in services and support offered by the Alcohol Drug Helpline - Work and Income Support Service.
The client can be asked to provide verification from the Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] for beneficiaries. The verification must state the duration or time that the client is receiving support. There is a Drug test obligations Helpline verification form that will be completed by Helpline staff and sent to the client. It is up to the client to provide this form as verification.
The Alcohol Drug Helpline - Work and Income Support Service will offer the following support and services:
1. brief interventions (series of telephone contacts)
2. brief assessment (brief clinical assessment) or
3. referral for a comprehensive face to face AOD assessment and treatment plan or
4. referral to other health or social service agencies or
5. confirmation of drug treatment details
For more information see:
- Drug test obligation failures - good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: No stand-down applies — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## No stand-down applies
An initial stand-down is not imposed in the following situations:
- Temporary employment
- Prisoners
- Entering a refuge
Where no stand-down applies, the commencement date of the benefit is the later of either:
- the entitlement date or
- the application date
Note when no stand-down applies, the 28-day rule does not apply.

chunks.title: Non-compliance for Community Work Experience — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Non-compliance for Community Work Experience
A partner could fail Community Work Experience without a good and sufficient reason at any point. This could occur when:
- a partner does not find a position due to making minimal or no effort to search for one, or
- a partner does not complete the required hours in any of the 4 weeks of the position period, or
- an organisation advises MSD that a partner failed to perform the duties of the position, for example, a partner attends the organisation for the hours required but spends most of their time on their phone instead of completing assigned tasks.
MSD may consider information shared by an organisation when determining if a partner has a good and sufficient reason for failing to find or complete Community Work Experience, however MSD must also consider information provided by the partner.
For example, if an organisation advises MSD that a partner did not show up to do their 5 hours that week, MSD must contact the partner to see if there was a good and sufficient reason for their absence.
If MSD determines that a partner does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to find or complete Community Work Experience, the partner is considered non-compliant.
## Partners without dependent children
A partner without dependent children will have their benefit suspended from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
Their payments will remain suspended for up to 13 weeks after Community Work Experience was first imposed, unless they recomply.
A partner may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be resumed from the date that the partner recomplies.
When a partner’s benefit has remained suspended because they have not recomplied, their benefit will cancel 13 weeks after Community Work Experience was first imposed.
## Partners with dependent children
Partners with dependent children have 50% payment protection.
A partner with dependent children will have their payments reduce by 50% from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
A partner may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be resumed from the date that the partner has recomplied.
These partners will also be contacted after 2 weeks of receiving only 50% of their benefit.

chunks.title: Non-compliance for Report Job Search — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Non-compliance for Report Job Search
A partner could fail Report Job Search without a good and sufficient reason at any point. This could occur when the partner does not:
- complete at least 3 job-search activities within a week or
- report their job-search activities or
- provide sufficient supporting evidence of their job-search activities
If MSD determines that a partner does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete Report Job Search, the partner is considered non-compliant.
## Partners without dependent children
A partner without dependent children will have their benefit suspended from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
