Their payments will remain suspended for up to 13 weeks after Report Job Search was first imposed, unless they recomply.
A partner may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be resumed from the date that the partner recomplies.
When a partner's benefit has remained suspended because they have not recomplied, their benefit will cancel 13 weeks after Report Job Search was first imposed.
## Partners with dependent children
Partners with dependent children have 50% payment protection.
A partner with dependent children will have their payments reduced by 50% from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
A partner may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be increased from the date that the partner has recomplied.
These partners will also be contacted after 2 weeks of receiving only 50% of their benefit. For more information see: Effect of financial sanctions on assistance.

chunks.title: Non-compliance for Upskilling — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Non-compliance for Upskilling
A client could fail Upskilling without a good and sufficient reason at any point. This could occur when, the client does not:
- attend, participate in, and report on at least 5 hours of employment-related training or courses within a week
- provide sufficient supporting evidence of attending and participating in employment-related training or courses
If MSD determines that a client does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete Upskilling, the client is considered non-compliant.
## Clients without dependent children
A client without dependent children will have their benefit suspended from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
Their payments will remain suspended for up to 13 weeks after Upskilling was first imposed, unless they recomply.
A client may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be resumed from the date that the client recomplies.
When a client's benefit has remained suspended because they have not recomplied, their benefit will cancel 13 weeks after Upskilling was first imposed.
## Clients with dependent children
Clients with dependent children have 50% payment protection.
A client with dependent children will have their payments reduce by 50% from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
A client may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be increased from the date that the client has recomplied.
These clients will also be contacted after 2 weeks of receiving only 50% of their benefit. For more information see: Effect of financial sanctions on assistance.

chunks.title: Non-entitlement period for 13 weeks — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Non-entitlement period for 13 weeks
A non-entitlement period of 13 weeks, is a period where clients are unable to get a benefit because they:
- have become voluntarily unemployed without a good and sufficient reason
- are applying for a benefit because they were dismissed by their employer for misconduct
- have failed their obligations for a third time in the last 24 months (or 12 months for young partners with youth activity obligations) of continuous benefit receipt (as a grade 3 sanction) or
- have refused an offer of suitable employment (if they have work obligations)
## Non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or dismissal
Before imposing a 13-week non-entitlement period, the reason why the client has left employment needs to be carefully investigated to determine whether it is appropriate to apply a 13-week non-entitlement period.
For voluntary unemployment, or dismissal for misconduct the 13-week non-entitlement period starts from the day after the date the client's employment ended.
For more information see:
- Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
## Non-entitlement period for obligations failures
Where a client fails their obligations and has a grade 3 sanction imposed, they will have a 13-week non-entitlement period.
For imposing a grade 3 sanction the 13-week non-entitlement period starts the day after the 5 working day notice period.
For more information see:
- Grade 3 sanction or job refusal failure non-entitlement period
Also see:
- Effect of 13-week non-entitlement period - couple wishes to change primary status
- Effect of non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Financial assistance during a non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Non-entitlement period should not be imposed — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: There are specific circumstances where a non-entitlement period is not considered, because they are accepted to be good and sufficient reasons for leaving employment, but the initial stand-down must still apply. These situations include where a client has: - lost their job during a 90 day employment trial (except where the employer alleges misconduct) - recently returned to New Zealand - taken voluntary redundancy because another employee would lose their job if they remained - left work that isn't suitable - worked for a temporary period

chunks.title: Clients who lose their job during a 90 day employment trial — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: An employer may terminate the employee's employment trial for any reason at any time before the end of the employment trial period. An employer is not obliged to give a reason for ceasing the client's employment during an employment trial. A non-entitlement period is not considered if an employer does not give a reason for ending an employee's employment trial. Note when an employer alleges misconduct by the employee and provides some evidence of the misconduct then a non-entitlement period can be considered and investigated in the usual way.

chunks.title: Clients returning to New Zealand from overseas — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A non-entitlement period is not considered when a client returns to New Zealand after working overseas. Clients returning to New Zealand after working overseas do not receive a voluntary unemployment stand-down.

chunks.title: Voluntary redundancy — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Where clients have taken voluntary redundancy, they do not receive a voluntary unemployment stand-down if they or another employee must lose their job if the client remains in that job.

chunks.title: Client has left temporary employment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A 13 week non-entitlement period does not apply when the person was in temporary part-time or full-time employment (employment of less than 26 weeks) and they have applied for a benefit after their employment came to an end. It may be applied if the client voluntarily left their temporary employment before it was due to end. Temporary employment can include employment during an employment trial period of up to 90 days if the client was receiving a benefit and is reapplying for Emergency Benefit as their employment has ceased. This also applies when a client has been working more than 30 hours a week on Emergency Benefit and receiving a salary or hourly wage that does not fully reduce the benefit, and they have reached the end of their 26 week temporary period in which this is allowable. Note the client's average weekly income is not required where the client has been in temporary employment for less than 26 weeks. However, the client's final pay details are required to determine the date of event and entitlement date. For more information see: - Temporary employment - Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment - Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer

chunks.title: Non-financial sanctions — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Non-financial sanctions
Non-financial sanctions are an alternative to a financial sanction that can be imposed on eligible clients in some cases.
Non-financial sanctions should only be imposed when it would be more appropriate based on a client's circumstances than a financial sanction.
## Criteria to receive a non-financial sanction
A client can only get a non-financial sanction if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they meet with MSD within the 5 working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure decision is not disputed and overturned, and
- a non-financial sanction would be appropriate for them based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or they have dependent children
MSD must assess a client's circumstances and determine which non-financial sanction, if any, is most appropriate for them. Each non-financial sanction has different factors to consider.
Note Primary Emergency Benefit clients do not have work or work preparation obligations.
This means it is unlikely they will have an obligation failure, so they would generally not have a sanction imposed.
Partners of an Emergency Benefit client who have work or work preparation obligations are able to have a non-financial sanction imposed if they meet the criteria.
## Client contacts MSD after 5 working days
A non-financial sanction can only be imposed if a client or their partner contacts MSD within the 5 working day notice period. This is because a financial sanction will be automatically applied after 5 working days unless MSD has decided to impose a non-financial sanction instead.
If a client or partner contacts MSD after 5 working days, they are not eligible for a non-financial sanction. MSD cannot change a financial sanction to a non-financial sanction after it has been applied.
## Change in circumstances while subject to a non-financial sanction
A client may have a change in circumstances that means they are no longer required to comply with an obligation they have failed.
The non-financial sanction no longer applies from the day that their circumstances change.
For more information see:
## Non-financial sanctions, Emergency Housing Grants and Special Needs Grants
Clients who have a non-financial sanction imposed cannot get an Emergency Housing Grant or a Special Needs Grant. MSD should take this into consideration before choosing to impose a non-financial sanction.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Non residentially qualified for Supported Living Payment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Non residentially qualified for Supported Living Payment
The rate of Emergency Benefit that is generally paid for clients who are non-residentially qualified for Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) is the same as the rates for Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability).
- Deskfile Supported Living Payment rates

chunks.title: Not eligible for another benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Not eligible for another benefit
Before considering whether to pay an Emergency Benefit:
1. Check whether the client or partner (if any) can get another benefit.
Consider first the client's eligibility to:
- Jobseeker Support (this includes on grounds of hardship)
- New Zealand Superannuation
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Veterans Pension
- Young Parent Payment
- Youth Payment
2. Consider the client's full circumstances
Emergency Benefit is a last resort and the reason(s) why a client or partner (if any) cannot receive another benefit needs to be identified. For example if a client is caring for someone but the level of care did not meet the Supported Living Payment - caring for a person criteria, they may be able to meet the work obligations and receive Jobseeker Support.
3. Other emergency or hardship benefits
Where a client does not have sufficient residence to meet the qualifications for another benefit, you should first consider the client's eligibility to:
- Jobseeker Support Granting on grounds of hardship
- Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship
- Youth Payment on grounds of hardship
Note clients who do not have permanent residence or citizenship are not eligible for another benefit but may be able to receive an Emergency Benefit.
For more information see:
- Clients without permanent residence or citizenship
## Exceptions
There may be some situations that a client is eligible for another benefit but in the best interests of the client an Emergency Benefit may be considered.
For more information see;
- Best interests of the client
- Permanent residence
- Qualifications
- Client in hardship
- Unable to earn a sufficient livelihood

chunks.title: Not lawfully present or resident for youth support payments — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Not lawfully present or resident for youth support payments
Generally, a single client who is aged 16 or 17 years may be eligible for Young Parent Payment or Youth Payment.
## Client does not have two years residence in New Zealand
Where a client is not dependent on another person and meets all the qualifications for Young Parent Payment or Youth Payment except the requirement to have lived in New Zealand continuously for 2 years or more, you may consider Young Parent Payment or Youth Payment on grounds of hardship.
For more information see:
- Young Parent Payment Granting on grounds of hardship
- Youth Payment Granting on grounds of hardship
## Client does not have permanent residence or citizenship
If a client does not have permanent residence or citizenship, they may be able to receive Emergency Benefit if they are in exceptional circumstances and are:
- claiming refugee or protection status (also known as asylum seeker) and have a valid visa or permit to be lawfully in New Zealand or
- applying for permanent residence and are compelled to remain in New Zealand due to some unforeseen reason
Note to consider Emergency Benefit for sole parent clients aged 16 or 19 years see: Emergency Maintenance Allowance Sole parents who are 16 to 19 years old
It is reasonable to consider an Emergency Benefit when you are satisfied that the client:
- cannot get another benefit
- cannot earn a sufficient livelihood and
- is in hardship
You must also consider whether:
- they have contributed to their hardship
- they can change their circumstances to alleviate their hardship and
- their circumstances justify payment

chunks.title: Not lawfully resident or present for youth support payments — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Not lawfully resident or present for youth support payments
The rate of Emergency Benefit that is generally paid for 16 and 17 year old clients who are not lawfully resident or present for youth support payments is the same as the rates for Young Parent Payment or Youth Payment.
- Young Parent Payment Rates
- Youth Payment Rates

chunks.title: Number of dependent children — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Number of dependent children
If a client had a dependent child (or children) in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application the child (or children) must be taken into account when determining the stand-down.
For example, if a single client with one dependent child applies for benefit the stand down period will be based on a single client with one child. However, if this client had two dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application, the stand down period will be based on a single client with two dependent children.
This is regardless of whether the child is still in the client's care at the time of application.
See also:
- Dependent child
- Orphans Benefit/Unsupported Childs Benefit

chunks.title: Obligations failures - partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a client or partner fails to comply with their obligations, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. MSD must be satisfied that the client or partner would have had no good and sufficient reason for their failure based on the information available. For social obligations, MSD must consider whether the client and their partner (if any) has taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations and must go through the regular engagement and support process before considering that the client has failed their obligation. Note primary clients getting Emergency Benefit may have work obligations or work preparation obligations assigned as conditions of grant. Only the partner may have an obligation failure applied for failing to meet their work obligations, work preparation obligations or drug test obligations. For more information see: - Failing more than one obligation at the same time - Work obligations - partners - Work preparation obligations - partners - Social obligations - Regular engagement and support process - All reasonable steps to meet social obligations - Drug test obligations - partners - Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure - Youth activity obligations failures Note for a partner who has full-time or part-time work obligations leaving part-time work averaging less than 20 hours per week, without good and sufficient reason or through misconduct, is also an obligations failure, but may not be specified in the partner's work obligations. Once MSD has decided that the client or partner has failed their obligations, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. The client or partner will then be sent a letter stating that their benefit will be sanctioned and that their benefit will only be increased or resumed if they: - complete a recompliance activity - dispute the decision to impose the sanction and you accept that they have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting their obligations - lodge a Review of Decision and you reconsider your position and agree with the client's review or - lodge an appeal to the Medical Appeal Board (drug test failure only) Once a client has completed their recompliance activity, their benefit can be increased or resumed from the date MSD is satisfied the client started the activity. For some clients, if it’s their first obligation failure they may be eligible for a non-financial sanction instead of a financial sanction. For more information, see: Non-financial sanctions.

chunks.title: Obligations failures - partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: All clients have a five working day notice period to dispute or recomply before the sanction is imposed. If a client or partner recomplies within the five working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the obligations failure is recorded. For more information see: - When the sanction is imposed - Counting previous obligations failures - Failing more than one obligation at the same time Clients have not failed their obligations if they do not complete or undertake Voluntary Work or Activity in the Community.

chunks.title: Effect on rates payable — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: For financial sanctions, the reduction, suspension and cancellation applies to the main benefit the client or partner is getting. For couples it applies to each person's portion of the married rate of benefit. For young partners, the effect of a sanction on the client's assistance depends on whether the client has children and is youth money managed or not. The effect on supplementary assistance depends on the level of sanction imposed, the type of supplementary assistance, and whether the client or partner has dependent children. Non-financial sanctions do not affect the rate payable for a client or partner.

chunks.title: Obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Obligations
Emergency Benefit clients and partners (if any) have the following obligations:
they must advise of any change in circumstances that affect their entitlement, or rate of benefit payable and
- if they have dependent children, take all reasonable steps to meet social obligations that apply for each dependent child in their care
- for partners, if required, undertake and pass a pre-employment or pre-course drug test
- for partners, if required, meet all of their work obligations
- for partners, if required, meet all of their work preparation obligations
- if required, participate in a Work Ability Assessment
- if required, work with a contracted service provider
- advise Work and Income if they are intending to travel overseas, before they depart
## Work or work preparation obligations for partners
If a client has a partner included in their Emergency Benefit, test the partner's eligibility to another benefit in the first instance. If the partner is not eligible for another benefit, they may be included.
Partners of clients getting the Emergency Benefit may have work or work preparation obligations (including the drug test obligation). See:
- Work or work preparation obligations - partners
- Drug test obligations
## Partners aged 16 to 19 years old
Young partners (aged 16 to 19 years old) of clients getting Emergency Benefit have youth activity obligations and not work or work preparation obligations if they are:
- aged 16 or 17 years old without dependent children or
- aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children and
- married, or in a civil union or de facto relationship with a person getting Emergency Benefit
See:
- Youth activity obligations
Note social obligations do not apply to young partners of Emergency Benefit clients as some of their youth activity obligations are similar to social obligations.
## Conditions of grant
Emergency Benefit clients can also have conditions similar to those of the equivalent benefit.
These additional obligations are set as a condition of granting the benefit and you must advise the client in writing at the time of grant of these conditions for getting the Emergency Benefit.
For more information see:
- Conditions of grant

chunks.title: Opting out of youth money management — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Opting out of youth money management
A young partner aged 16 or 17 years with no dependent children who is not subject to a sanction will be able to get their full payment directly, when they have:
- turned 18 years of age
- chosen to continue to have youth activity obligations so they can complete their course of study, training or work-based learning and
- provided written notice to their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service that they opt out of youth money management
A young partner aged 16 to 19 years old with no dependent children who are not subject to a sanction will be able to get their full payment direction, when they have:
- turned 20 years of age
- chosen to continue to have youth activity obligations so they can complete their course of study, training or work-based learning and
- provided written notice to their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service that they opt out of youth money management
This applies even if the young partner aged 16 or 17 years with no dependent children or 16 to 19 years with dependent children haven't had youth activity obligations long enough to have earned all the incentives available to them.

chunks.title: Orphans Benefit/Unsupported Childs Benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Orphans Benefit/Unsupported Childs Benefit
If a client is getting, or has been getting, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit for a child in their care, this child is included as a dependent child in the stand-down calculation.
However, the Orphans Benefit/Unsupported Childs Benefit payments are not included as income for determining the average weekly income.

chunks.title: Other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes
Other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes are programmes that involve parents educating their children at home with external support.
Programmes will need to meet the approval criteria set out in the Ministerial Direction which states the programme must:
- provide early childhood education to children under the age of six in their own homes and not to other children
- deliver positive educational outcomes for the children to whom it is provided
- be supervised and have specific early learning outcomes
- be aligned with Government priorities relating to Early Childhood Education (ECE) and vulnerable children
For a list of the approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes for social obligations see:
- Deskfile Social obligations approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes

chunks.title: Outcome of case — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Outcome of case
Outcomes from mediation are strictly confidential to the parties involved, so any information about the settlement will have to be obtained from the client (or partner).
Where a client (or partner) wins their personal grievance case, and receives a wage settlement for a period during which a benefit with work obligations was paid:
- review the client's (or partner's) entitlement date and non-entitlement period assessments and
- establish any overpayments
If it is determined that the employer was not at fault, then a 13 week non-entitlement period for misconduct can be applied.
If the settlement order states that the payment or part payment is to cover legal or other costs, do not recover benefit received from the payment amount. If it is unclear what the client's (or partner's) settlement is for, contact Helpline for assistance.
If the case is settled but no party is admitting fault, a decision must be made as to whether the voluntary unemployed provisions apply. Use all evidence available but give the benefit of the doubt to the client (or partner). Contact your local solicitor for advice.
For more information see:
- Proof client is challenging dismissal
- Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer

chunks.title: Overview of social obligations according to age of the child — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Overview of social obligations according to age of the child
The table below shows the specific social obligations that apply to the client and their partner (if any) according to the age of their dependent children.

Not applicable

chunks.title: Parent is being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020 — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Parent is being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020
All parents are legally obliged to ensure their children are enrolled in and attending school from the age of 6 to 16.
Parents can be prosecuted and fined under Education and Training Act 2020 if their children don't attend school. This can happen when:
- there has been, without explanation, ongoing and irregular attendance by the child at school after support has been offered to the family or
- the parent has made little or no attempt to do anything about ensuring the child attends school
If a parent is in the process of being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020, you must not ask them to comply with this social obligation or initiate an obligations failure for non-attendance.
Note you need to record this as an exception in OBMAN using 'Parent is in prosecution for truant child' as the obligation exception reason.

chunks.title: Parent — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Parent
Generally, to be eligible for Sole Parent Support a client must be the child's natural or adoptive parent. If the client is not the child's natural or adoptive parent, you can regard the child as their own when:
- the child is being maintained by the client and
- was at any time maintained by the client's partner or
- each of the child's natural or adoptive parents are deceased, cannot be found, or suffers a serious long-term disablement which renders them unable to care for the child or
- due to a breakdown in the child's family no natural, adoptive or step parent is able to care for the child or provide fully to the child's support or
- the child's natural, adoptive or step parents and/or guardians are unwilling to support the child
For more information see:
- Sole Parent Support Child not supported
- Sole Parent Support Family breakdown
The legislation doesn't tell you how long the child must be maintained by the couple but it should be a reasonable period of time, not just a few weeks.
## Example
A couple takes responsibility for a close relative's child and maintains the child for some years before they separate. This child would be considered as their own child.
## Child is not considered the client's own
When a client is not the child's natural or adoptive parent and the child cannot be regarded as the client's own child, the client can test their eligibility to:
- Jobseeker Support or
- Jobseeker Support client with a health condition, injury or disability
- they may be eligible for an Emergency Benefit (if they cannot get Jobseeker Support)

chunks.title: Parenting obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Parenting obligations
Young partners aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children are required to:
- participate in an approved parenting programme
- enrol their child with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation, where a local provider is available
- register their child (if aged under 5 years old) with a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and keep up-to-date with their visits and
- ensure the child's attendance at an approved Early Childhood Education programme or in other suitable childcare, while they are in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work

chunks.title: Partner accepts the results of a failed screening test — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner accepts the results of a failed screening test
A client will be asked by the employer, training provider or the drug test provider to confirm that they accept the result of the failed screening test. They can accept the result of the failed drug test by:
- signing the Pre-employment Drug Test Result Confirmation Form or
- verbally accepting the result
When a client has accepted the results, this means that they understand:
- there is no requirement to send the failed screening test sample to a laboratory for evidential testing
- this may result in a sanction being imposed and
- they may have to repay Work and Income for the cost of the failed drug test
Before you initiate an obligations failure for a partner because they have failed a drugs test, without having a good and sufficient reason, you must receive confirmation from the employer that the partner has failed the test.
Once you have received confirmation from the employer or training provider that a client has failed the screening test, and all testing has been completed, an obligations failure should be initiated.
Although the client can still dispute other parts of the decision, by providing a good and sufficient reason for the obligations failure, they cannot dispute the result of the screening drug test because they have already accepted the failed result.
For more information see:
- Obligations failures
- Informing a partner of the drug test obligation failure
- Reimbursement of failed screening and evidential tests
- Drug test obligation failures - Good and sufficient reasons
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures

chunks.title: Partner does not accept the results of a failed screening test — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner does not accept the results of a failed screening test
If the partner does not accept the results of failed screening test the employer, training provider or drug test provider may decide to send the failed sample to the laboratory for evidential testing.
If you have received information back from the employer, training provider or drug test provider that the partner has subsequently failed the evidential drug test you must initiate a drug test obligations failure. Centralised Services will organise the debt recovery of both the screening and evidential drug tests (if the test was being conducted for a suitable job).
## Sample sent for evidential test
Some employers, training providers, or drug test providers, will send all screening test samples for evidential testing, regardless of whether the partner accepted the result of the failed screening test or not.
If the partner passes the evidential drug test, then the partner is not required to repay Work and Income for the cost of either the failed screening drug test or the evidential drug test.
If the partner also fails the evidential drug test, the partner is required to repay Work and Income for the costs of both the failed tests (screening and evidential).
## Partner disputes the results of an evidential drug test
A partner can dispute the result of a failed evidential test.

chunks.title: Partner donating a kidney or liver tissue — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner donating a kidney or liver tissue
When the partner of a client has been accepted as a donor of a kidney or liver tissue, they must provide a medical certificate.
Generally, the partner will continue to receive their current benefit payments. The partner cannot choose to have their benefit cancelled to receive live organ donor income assistance.
Note the partner may continue getting childcare assistance during their recovery period.
The appropriate exemption should be entered in the SWTDA screen in SWIFTT.
## Partner with work obligations
If a client decides to donate a kidney or liver tissue, they generally will not be able to meet those obligations and they should not be actively enforced during their recovery time.
If the partner has a 'work obligations in progress' or 'fails their work obligations', the donation of a kidney or liver tissue is considered a 'good and sufficient reason'. The work obligations failure must be overturned in OBMAN. This will remove the failure from the client's 12 month obligation failure count and no sanction will be imposed.
No obligations failure should be enforced:
- for the maximum period of 12 weeks or
- until the partner has recovered from the operation
whichever is earlier.

chunks.title: Partner has failed a screening drug test — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner has failed a screening drug test
If a partner fails a screening drug test with an employer, training provider or drug test provider, they will be advised that they have failed and they will be asked if they:
- accept the results of the screening drug test or
- do not accept the result of the screening drug test
For more information see:
- Informing a partner of the drug test obligation failure
- Partner accepts the results of a failed screening test
- Partner does not accept the results of a failed screening test

chunks.title: Partner made redundant — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner made redundant
If the partner of a client currently receiving a benefit is made redundant, any redundancy payment received is not treated as income and there is no need to review the initial stand-down.
However, this redundancy payment may affect the Emergency Benefit and any supplementary benefit as it may increase the couple's cash assets.
## Interest received
Also, any interest (before tax) paid on any lump sum received is treated as income and charged against the benefit.
To decide whether or not the client is in a de facto relationship see:
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit

chunks.title: Partner not qualified — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner not qualified
You can pay a special rate equal to half the married, civil union or de facto rate to a client (with or without dependent children) if their partner is:
- subject to a 13-week voluntary unemployment stand-down or
- on strike or
- subject to a work obligations failure
You can pay a single or sole parent rate to a client whose partner is unlawfully resident in New Zealand but you have to take the joint income and assets into account.
A higher married rate is payable to a client with 1 or more dependent children and their partner is not receiving a benefit. See:
- Partner not receiving a benefit
For more information see:
- Absence from New Zealand Payment when client or partner absent from New Zealand

chunks.title: Partner not getting a benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner not getting a benefit
There is a higher married rate of payment for a client with 1 or more dependent children whose partner is not getting a benefit.
The following chart describes the situations where the higher rate is applicable and shows the rate of payment for each.
Primary client
Partner's circumstances
Rate of payment
Granted Emergency Benefit equivalent to Supported Living Payment because they are caring for a person full-time.
Partner:
- is working
- is getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension
- does not qualify for any other benefit
$392.94 at 1 April 2026
Granted Emergency Benefit equivalent to Supported Living Payment because of a health condition, injury, or disability.
Partner:
- is getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension
- does not meet the residency criteria to be included in the benefit and sole parent rate of payment is not applicable for the couple's circumstances
$392.94 at 1 April 2026
Granted Emergency Benefit equivalent to Jobseeker Support
Partner:
- is getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension
- doesn't meet the residency criteria to be included in the benefit and the sole parent rate of payment is not applicable for the couple's circumstances
$334.70 at 1 April 2026
Granted Emergency Benefit equivalent to Young Parent Payment
Partner:
- is not getting any benefit
$334.70 at 1 April 2026
A higher rate of payment is not applicable for a client with 1 or more dependent children when their partner is subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period.
In these circumstances the rate payable is the half married rate for a couple with children.

chunks.title: Partner of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client and caring for a child — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client and caring for a child
A client may be able to get Emergency Benefit if they are:
- the principal caregiver of a dependent child aged under 14 years and
- the partner of a New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client and
- not eligible for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension in their own right and
- not eligible for another benefit (eg because they can't meet Jobseeker Support work obligations)
Note an Emergency Benefit granted for this reason will usually have conditions of grant relating to job search or planning, depending on the age of the child. This is because Jobseeker Support is the equivalent benefit.
## Principal caregiver
A principal caregiver is the person who has the day to day responsibility of the child on a permanent basis.
It is up to the couple to decide who the primary caregiver is, and MSD cannot:
- influence this decision in any way or
- ask the couple to choose the New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client to be the principal caregiver so their partner can qualify for another benefit
## Not contributing to own hardship
A non-qualifying partner who is the principal caregiver of a dependent child aged under 14 is not considered to be contributing to their own hardship or preventing themselves from earning a sufficient livelihood.

chunks.title: Partner receiving New Zealand Superannuation in residential care — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner receiving New Zealand Superannuation in residential care
If a client is receiving Residential Care Subsidy for their residential care has a partner who:
- is still in the community
- is a grandparented non-qualified partner for New Zealand Superannuation and
- the partner was included as a grandparented non-qualified partner on or after 1 October 1991
or
- receives another benefit
the partner is eligible for Emergency Benefit payable at the Supported Living Payment single or sole parent rate (if they have dependent children) from the date their partner enters care.
Note income that has already been included in the asset and income means assessment for Residential Care Subsidy is not included as income when assessing the rate of Emergency Benefit for the partner in the community.
For more information see:
- Residential Care Subsidy Client with a partner in the community

chunks.title: Partner's job ceases during an employment trial period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partner's job ceases during an employment trial period
Any employment that has an employment trial period included in a partner's employment agreement is assessed the same as any other employment.
A partner's job can cease during the employment trial period for any number of reasons, such as:
- the employer not being able to afford the partner's wages
- the employer's belief that the partner lacks the necessary skills
- misconduct
- any other reason the employer decides to cease the partner's employment or
- the partner leaving of their own accord
When an employer gives the partner notice during the employment trial, they are not required to advise why they have decided to end the partner's employment. They are however, required to provide details of their last date of employment and the date they will be paid to.
If the employer gave notice to the partner of ending their employment after the employment trial, the employer must provide the partner with the reason for ending their employment (ie the employment trial rules do not apply).
To determine the commencement date of the benefit, the partner needs to provide evidence and reasons for ceasing their employment, their last day of duty and last date paid to.
If the partner cannot provide this evidence and a reason for their employment ceasing, their last day of duty or last date paid to, you can contact the partner's employer and ask them to complete the Employment and earnings information for applications (V06) form.
If the partner's employer does not provide the reason for the partner's employment ceasing during the employment trial, accept the partner's reasons for the termination and continue with the application process. However, the employer must complete the date ceased and last pay details.
For more information see:
- Employment trial period of up to 90 days

chunks.title: Partners 65 years and over — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partners 65 years and over
If you are granting Emergency Benefit and the client has a partner 65 years and over the partner does not have any work or work preparation obligations.
For more information see:
- Age
- Clients aged 65 years or over

chunks.title: Partners undertaking voluntary work — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partners undertaking voluntary work
Partners can undertake voluntary work provided they continue to meet their work or work preparation obligations.
Partners with work preparation or work obligations may have to give up some or all of their voluntary activities if a work preparation activity is required or if a suitable job becomes available.
For more information see:
- Work confidence and motivation assistance
- Suitable employment

chunks.title: Partners with no children or youngest child 14+ years — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partners with no children or youngest child 14+ years
Full-time work obligations apply to:
- partners with no children and
- partners with youngest child aged 14 years or over
Partners with full-time work obligations must make themselves available for suitable employment, training or other suitable activities of at least 30 hours or more each week.
If a partner is in employment for less than 30 hours each week, they are still expected to be available for other work, training or other activities up to a total of 30 hours each week. The partner must understand that they are still required to accept suitable full-time work if it becomes available.
For more information see:
- Work obligations - partners
- Hours range for suitable employment
Partners may participate in approved training as long as they continue to meet their work obligations.
For more information see:
- In approved training (no children or child 14+)
- Approved training
Partners may undertake volunteer work as long as they continue to meet their work obligations.
For more information see:
- Work confidence and motivation assistance
Partners may apply for an exemption from their work obligations.
For more information on exemptions see:
- Exemptions - partners
- Table of Exemptions
If a partner fails to comply with their work obligations, their portion of the benefit may be stopped.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Effect of sanctions on assistance
## Partners aged 16 to 19 years old
Young partners (aged 16 to 19 years old) of clients receiving Emergency Benefit have youth activity obligations, and not work or work preparation obligations if they are:
- aged 16 or 17 years old without dependent children or
- aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children and
- married, or in a civil union or a de facto relationship with a person receiving Emergency Benefit
See:

chunks.title: Partners with other income — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partners with other income
There is no 'married, civil union or de facto' rate of payment for an Emergency Benefit paid for clients caring for a person. The client's partner will either qualify for a benefit in their own right or have some other form of income.
However, when you assess the rate of payment for the client you must take the clients and their partner's income into account.
## How to apply the income test
Charging income (for a couple) against an Emergency Benefit paid to a client caring for a person, is generally the same way as for Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).
You use Income Test 2
Income is charged weekly at the following rates:
- 15 cents is taken from the benefit for each dollar of income the client (and their partner) earns over $160 per week, but not more than $250 per week (as at 1 April 2022)
- 35 cents for every dollar of income more than $250 per week (as at 1 April 2022)
To assess the rate payable you:
- charge the income as if both the client and their partner qualify for Emergency Benefit in their own right (ie against 2 benefits)
- add the 2 benefit payments together
- compare this total with the maximum rate of Emergency Benefit payable (this is based on the maximum rate payable to a client getting Supported Living Payment - caring for a person) and
- pay the lesser amount
Note a different way of charging income applies when a person is getting Emergency Benefit because they are caring for their New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension partner. See: Charging income - caring for New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension partner

chunks.title: Partners with youngest child between 3 and 13 years — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partners with youngest child between 3 and 13 years
Part-time work obligations apply to:
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years
The partner must make themselves available for suitable employment, training or other activities of at least 20 hours a week.
For more information see:
- Work obligations - partners
Partners may do voluntary work but must be available to meet their work obligations.
For more information see:
- Partners undertaking voluntary work
Partners may apply for an exemption from their work obligations.
For more information on exemptions see:
- Exemptions - partners
- Table of Exemptions
If a partner fails to comply with their work obligations, there portion of the benefit may be stopped.
For more information see:
- Obligations failures - partners
If a partner with part-time obligations is already in employment for 20 hours or more each week, they are meeting their work obligations.
If they are in employment for less than 20 hours each week, they are still expected to be available for other work, training or any other activities.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations

chunks.title: Partners with youngest dependent child aged under 3 years — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Partners with youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
Work preparation obligations apply to:
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
The partner must take all reasonable steps to prepare them for work in the future.
For more information see:
- Work preparation obligations - partners
Partners may apply for an exemption from their work preparation obligations. Generally, they can only be considered for a full exemption as work preparation obligations mean that they are required to plan for employment and undertake work preparation activities - the equivalent of a partial exemption.
For more information see:
- Exemptions - partners
- Table of Exemptions
If a partner fails to comply with their work preparation obligations, they have an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Informing partners of their obligations
- Obligations failures - partners
- Effect of sanctions on assistance
## Partners aged 16 to 19 years old
Young partners (aged 16 to 19 years old) of clients receiving Emergency Benefit have youth activity obligations, and not work or work preparation obligations if they are:
- aged 16 or 17 years old without dependent children or
- aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children and
- married, or in a civil union or a de facto relationship with a person receiving Emergency Benefit
For more information see:

chunks.title: Patients from Tokelau, Niue and Cook Islands — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Patients from Tokelau, Niue and Cook Islands
Generally, clients resident in Tokelau, Niue or the Cook Islands have New Zealand citizenship and are therefore lawfully resident in New Zealand.
However, to be eligible for benefit assistance such as Emergency Benefit the client should generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand.
There are 2 groups of clients coming from these countries to New Zealand who access secondary and tertiary health services. These are:
- patients referred to New Zealand medical treatment through a Patient Referral Scheme, together with the patient's attendant (if any)
and
- patients referred by their country of origin medical practitioner or nurse practitioner and accepted for medical treatment by a secondary or tertiary medical service provider in New Zealand, together with the patient's attendant (if any)
## Clients who need assistance
Some clients coming to New Zealand for treatment will require an attendant to assist them. MSD may also consider Emergency Benefit for the attendant. This Emergency Benefit will need to be considered equivalent to Supported Living Payment - caring for a person. These clients (and attendants, if any) may not be ordinarily resident in New Zealand.
However, MSD may consider exercising its discretion to approve Emergency Benefit because the client and attendant (if any):
- meet all the other Emergency Benefit eligibility criteria and
- is under the supervision of a medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (applies only to the client and not the attendant)
## Patients referred to New Zealand through a Patient Referral Scheme
Clients referred to New Zealand through a Patient Referral Scheme from Tokelau, Niue and the Cook Islands cannot access or receive the health service they need in their own country as these services are not available.
An Emergency Benefit equivalent to Jobseeker Support on ground of health condition, injury or disability may be considered if a client has arrived under a Patient Referral Scheme.
## Patients referred by their own medical or nurse practitioner
There will be some clients from Tokelau, Niue or Cook Islands referred to secondary or tertiary medical treatment in New Zealand by their medical or nurse practitioner (or equivalent in their country of origin), rather than through a Patient Referral Scheme.
For these clients MSD may consider Emergency Benefit equivalent to Jobseeker Support on ground of health condition, injury or disability. However, if the client could afford the travel, MSD should check if they may be able to support themselves while present in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Paying other assistance during a sanction — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Clients are not entitled to the following forms of assistance when they have had a 100% benefit suspension or cancellation imposed due to an obligations failure: - Accommodation Supplement - Temporary Additional Support - Special Benefit

chunks.title: Winter Energy Payment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The Winter Energy Payment is treated slightly different to other Extra help. Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid in situations where a portion of main benefit continues to be paid. In some cases it can continue to be paid at the full couple rate in cases where one client has been fully sanctioned. Clients who have a dependent child, and who are getting Winter Energy Payment who are subject to a 100% suspension or cancellation have a maximum sanction of 50% of the total benefit imposed (including other Extra help). However, the full rate of Winter Energy Payment should continue to be paid. Sole parents also have a maximum sanction of 50% of the total benefit imposed but like other Extra help, will continue to get the total amount of the Winter Energy Payment, regardless of the grade of the sanction.

chunks.title: Disability Allowance — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: There are no obligations attached to Disability Allowance, so it can continue to be paid.

chunks.title: Special Needs Grants — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Clients are not entitled to Special Needs Grants if a sanction has been imposed. This applies to both financial and non-financial sanctions. The only exception to this is if a client or partner has a health condition, injury or disability when a grade 3 sanction is imposed and they are incapable of participating in full-time employment or an approved activity for 6 weeks. For more information see: - Special Needs Grants Assistance during non-entitlement periods - Special Needs Grants Assistance when a client is sanctioned

chunks.title: Emergency Housing Grants — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Clients are not entitled to Emergency Housing Grants if a sanction has been imposed. This applies to both financial and non-financial sanctions. For more information see: - When MSD cannot pay an Emergency Housing Grant

chunks.title: Advances — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a client or partner has a 50% sanction imposed, and the client or partner is experiencing hardship they may apply for an Advance Payment of Benefit. A discussion must be held with the client or partner about recomplying as the reduced rate of benefit will be contributing to their hardship. Generally clients will not be entitled to an Advance Payment of Benefit when they have a 100% sanction imposed. This is because they will be contributing to their hardship through not recomplying. The client's first option to improve their financial situation is to recomply with their obligations and an advance cannot be paid when the client or partner has no means of repaying it. A client can apply for an Advance Payment of Benefit if they have a non-financial sanction imposed, and may be eligible if they meet all the criteria.

chunks.title: Assistance to transition into employment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Clients can get assistance to transition into employment if a sanction has been imposed and they meet the qualifications for it. For more information see: - Transition to Work [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Young partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Where a young partner has an obligations failure, the assistance that is available to them depends on the failure number and whether the young partner is youth money managed or not. For more information see:

chunks.title: Work Bonus — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Clients can get Work Bonus if a sanction has been imposed and they meet the qualifications for it. For more information see: - Specific employment-related assistance Work Bonus

chunks.title: Payment process for a young partner — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The couple's main benefit and any supplementary assistance will be apportioned between the couple. The young partner who is youth money managed, will have their portion of accommodation, service costs and lawful debts paid direct to a supplier from their portion of their main benefit and any on-going extra help. The balance of payment, if any, is distributed between the young partner's payment card and the in-hand allowance. The maximum amount that can be paid direct to a young partner as an in-hand allowance is $50. The following process shows how a young partner's portion of benefit assistance is paid when they are subject to youth money management.

chunks.title: Step 2 — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Any incentive payment earned is added. Note to ensure the incentive payment is only paid to the person who earned it, the portion of incentive payment that will automatically be apportioned to the primary client will need to be re-directed back to the young person.

chunks.title: Step 3 — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Young partner's portion of extra help, such as Accommodation Supplement, Winter Energy Payment and Temporary Additional Support is added.

chunks.title: Step 5 — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: In-hand allowance (if any) is paid directly to the young partner and the remainder is redirected to the payment card.

chunks.title: In-hand allowance — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a young partner is subject to youth money management, they can get an amount of up to $50 a week paid directly to them as an in-hand allowance. After the young partner's portion of accommodation, service costs and lawful debts are paid by redirection from their portion of their main benefit and any on-going extra help, the balance of payment, if any, is distributed between the young partner's payment card and the in-hand allowance. The maximum amount that can be paid direct to a young partner as an in-hand allowance is $50.

chunks.title: Distribution of payment after redirections — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Generally, where there is more than $50 available after all of a young partner's redirections have occurred, $50 would be paid direct to the young partner and the remainder would be placed on their payment card, unless YSSU is satisfied that another distribution would be more appropriate for the young partner. Youth service providers are responsible for making recommendations to YSSU as to how their client's payments should be distributed between the payment card and in-hand allowance. When making these recommendations to YSSU, providers consider what would be the most appropriate distribution for the young partner, given their individual circumstances. YSSU then makes the final decision as to how the young partner's payment will be distributed, taking into account the information supplied by the young partner's service provider. Example 1 A young partner with a dependent child is renting and has $110 left after their accommodation and service costs and any debts have been paid. A maximum of $50 could be paid direct to the client. However, the service provider wants to ensure the young person has enough money to purchase a sufficient amount of food for her and her child. The young partner lives close to the school she is attending and the childcare centre her child is attending is also within walking distance. The provider discusses with the young person in their budgeting sessions what their spending habits are and the young partner advises that she goes to the market to get her fruit and vegetables. The provider decides to recommend the young person gets a $50 in-hand allowance and will review to see that she is doing this and has enough food with $60 on her payment card. YSSU makes a decision to agree with the recommendation, and decides to pay the client a $50 in-hand allowance, and to put $60 on her payment card. Example 2 A young partner with no dependent children in a boarding situation has $80 left after her board costs (which include food) and any debts have been paid. The young partner has transport costs to get to school. The young partner must pay for their own lunch everyday as this is not included in the board payment.

chunks.title: Distribution of payment after redirections — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: After discussions with the young person, the provider recommends paying a $40 in-hand allowance to the young person and placing $40 on the payment card to be used to purchase food for lunches. YSSU decides to agree with the recommendation and decides to pay the client a $40 in-hand allowance and to put $40 on the payment card.

chunks.title: Changing the distribution of payment for existing clients already subject to youth money management — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If, at any time, a Youth Service provider considers that the current distribution of an existing client's payment between the payment card and in-hand allowance is inappropriate for the client's circumstances, they can make a recommendation to YSSU that this distribution be altered. When determining whether it is appropriate to make a recommendation that a client's payment distribution be altered, providers must take into account a range of factors.

chunks.title: Payment rate - Permanently and severely restricted for work — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Payment rate - Permanently and severely restricted for work
The rate of Emergency Benefit that is generally paid for clients who are permanently and severely restricted for work is the same as the rates for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability (because they do not meet the residence requirements).
- Deskfile Supported Living Payment rates
- Supported Living Payment Qualifications

chunks.title: Payment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Payment
Emergency Benefit is paid weekly on a Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. Payment is from Monday to Sunday and is made 1 week in arrears.
Generally, payment must be made directly to the client. However, where there is good cause, the client's or partner's benefit can be paid to another person, agent or institution.
For more information see:
- Core policy Redirection of benefit payment
## Exception for young partners
There are 2 ways that young partners aged 16 or 17 years (with no children) and 16 to 19 years (with dependent children) can have their portion of their benefit paid to them, depending on whether the young partner is subject to youth money management or not.
## Young partner is not subject to youth money management
When a young partner is not subject to youth money management they can get their portion of their main benefit payment, family tax credit and any extra help paid directly to their bank account.
## Young partner is subject to youth money management
If a young partner is subject to youth money management the young partner's portion of main benefit, family tax credit and any extra help (except Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance) is paid via:
- payment directly to supplier (e.g. a payee redirection for accommodation costs, utility costs and lawful debts)
- in-hand allowance which is paid directly to the young person's bank account
- payment card - the young person is able to purchase goods (such as food and groceries) from approved suppliers
Note Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance is paid directly to the young person's bank account.
For more information see:
## Rate of payment
The Emergency Benefit rate that is generally paid is the same as for Jobseeker Support except for the following:
- Maximum rates - caring for a person
- Maximum rates - caring for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension partner
- Non residentially qualified for Supported Living Payment
- Not lawfully resident or present for youth support payments
- Special rates residential parole
- Permanently and severely restricted for work

chunks.title: Payments to the non-sanctioned client — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Payments to the non-sanctioned client
When a client has their portion of the benefit sanctioned, the non-sanctioned client will continue to get:
- their portion of the benefit and
- for a grade 2 or 3 sanction, 50% of the supplementary assistance the couple was entitled to (the couple's supplementary assistance is not affected by a grade 1 sanction) and the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment
MSD should check if the non-sanctioned client has had any changes in their circumstances or their family's situation. The non-sanctioned client should be advised about applying for a benefit in their own right (in this situation the benefit would only be paid at the half-married rate).
For more information see:
- Effect of financial sanctions on assistance
- Assistance for partners when the primary client has a non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Payments while on Money Management — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Payments while on Money Management
Clients on Money Management will be paid the following to their nominated bank account:
- 50% of their main benefit rate payable
- 100% of any Working for Families tax credits or supplementary assistance.
Any redirections, debt repayments, or offsets will continue to be deducted from the amount that is paid into their bank account. This must be considered before applying Money Management as this amount may be higher than the amount of benefit they will get.
If a client’s main benefit cannot be divided evenly by 2, the higher amount will be paid to their bank account. This means a client may receive 1 cent more in their bank account than on their payment card.
## Where a payment card can be used
The payment card is limited to approved suppliers who sell essential items specifically for:
- food
- transport
- healthcare related items and/or
- education related items.
## Money left on payment card when Money Management ends
A client may have money left on their payment card when Money Management ends. Clients are expected to use this balance as it can continue to be used to buy essential items.
The balance can be transferred to a client's bank account if they ask.
## Example
Tayla has been on Money Management for 3 weeks. In her 4th week, she finds full-time employment and cancels her benefit.
She has $220 remaining on her payment card. Tayla requests that this money be transferred to her bank account so that she can use it on work-related expenses.
MSD transfers the payment directly to her bank account.

chunks.title: Period of Community Work Experience — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Period of Community Work Experience
Partners who have found a suitable organisation and position for Community Work Experience during their 2-week search period must complete at least 5 hours of work per week over the 4-week period.
## 4-week period
The 4-week period of Community Work Experience generally starts immediately after the 2-week search period ends, unless the partner finds and begins a suitable position before the end of the search period.
The 4 weeks must be consecutive. For example, if the position offered is 4 weeks in total, but there is a 1-week break because the organisation is closed that week, the position would not be suitable for Community Work Experience.
## 5 hours per week
A partner must complete at least 5 hours per week over 4-week period. A partner can choose to do more hours if they wish, however any extra hours must not stop them from meeting their obligations, such as being available for and seeking employment.
Any extra hours a partner completes will not count towards their Community Work Experience. The partner must complete at least 5 hours each week. Any hours they did the previous week cannot be counted towards their 5 hours for a different week.
## Public holidays
A partner does not need to do Community Work Experience on a weekend, public holiday or regional holiday. However, they can choose to do their hours on these days if they want to.
MSD should consider upcoming holidays before imposing Community Work Experience. Many community organisations will be closed on these dates, for example over the Christmas period. If a partner is unlikely to complete their required hours due to public holidays, it would not be suitable to impose Community Work Experience.
## Option to secure multiple positions
A partner could find more than one suitable organisation and position to help them meet the required number of hours and weeks. This could be:
- finding 2 or more organisations who offer enough hours per week between them, or
- working at 2 or more organisations, who offer back-to-back positions, for example doing the first 2 weeks with one organisation, and the next 2 weeks with a different organisation, or
- a combination of both.
The partner can secure more than one position for their Community Work Experience, as long as they are able to meet the requirements of the sanction.
The organisations and positions must all be approved by MSD before they start the community work and before the 5-day verification window has ended.

chunks.title: Period of Money Management — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a client fails their obligations, they have 5 working days to dispute the failure before a sanction is imposed. Money Management when imposed starts the day after the 5 working day notice period. Clients are money managed for 4 weeks (28 days). This period includes weekends and public holidays. Money Management will end after 4 weeks, and a client’s payments will be made in full to their bank account if they have recomplied with their obligation failure during this time.

chunks.title: Money Management begins in the middle of a pay period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Money Management will be applied on any weekday, including public holidays. This means that Money Management is likely to begin in the middle of a pay period and will result in partial payments. For more information see:

chunks.title: Benefit stops during Money Management — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A client and their partner’s benefit may stop while they are being money managed, e.g. one week their income was over the income limit. The length of Money Management is not impacted by any breaks in payment, and will always end four weeks after it was imposed.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Kale fails their obligation and Money Management starts on 14 August. Their last day of Money Management will be 10 September. Kale travels to Australia from 18 August to 25 August for a holiday. They do not inform MSD before their travel and their benefit is stopped from the day after they left New Zealand. Kale’s benefit is resumed from the date they return to New Zealand. Their Money Management continues from 25 August, and will still end on 10 September.

chunks.title: Money Management ends while benefit is stopped — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a client is entitled to arrears when their benefit is resumed, any money owed to them for the period Money Management was imposed will be money managed.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Rahool is the partner of a client getting Emergency Benefit and meets the qualifications for Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability. He fails a work-preparation obligation on 3 March and is placed onto Money Management on 10 March. His Money Management period will end on 6 April. Rahool’s medical certificate expires on 31 March. His benefit stops until he gets a new medical certificate. He gets a new medical certificate on 10 April, 4 days after his Money Management period has ended. His benefit resumes from 31 March when his medical certificate first expired, and MSD issues arrears of his Emergency Benefit from 31 March to 10 April. Rahool’s arrears for the period of 31 March to 6 April, are subject to Money Management. 50% of those arrears are paid onto his payment card and the remainder to his bank account. The arrears owed after his Money Management ended, from 7 April to 10 April, are paid directly into Rahool’s bank account.

chunks.title: Period of Report Job Search — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Period of Report Job Search
Partners who have Report Job Search imposed on them must complete at least 3 suitable job-search activities per week over the 4-week period. They must also report to MSD each week on the job-search activities they have completed in that week.
## 4-week period
The 4-week period of Report Job Search begins the day after the 5-working-day notice period ends. This means Report Job Search may begin on any day of the week.
## 3 job-search activities per week
A partner must complete and report on at least 3 suitable job-search activities per week over the 4-week period. A partner can choose to do and report on more job-search activities if they wish, however any extra job-search activities a partner completes can only be counted in the week they completed them. Any extra job-search activities they completed in the previous weeks cannot be counted towards their 3 job-search activities for the current week.
Note MSD must consider a partner's job-search activities are reasonable steps towards them finding suitable employment.

chunks.title: Period of Upskilling — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Once a client has been assigned an employment-related training or course from MSD's Digital Suite courses, or MSD approves another suitable training or course, they must attend and participate in it for at least 5 hours each week over a 4-week period. They must also report to MSD each week on their participation in employment-related training and courses in that week.

chunks.title: 4-week period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The 4-week period of Upskilling begins the day after the 5 working day notice period ends. This means Upskilling may begin on any day of the week. The 4 weeks must be consecutive. For example, if the training or course is 4 weeks in total, but there is a 1-week break because the organisation is closed that week, the employment-related training or course would not be suitable for Upskilling.

chunks.title: 5 hours per week — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A client must attend and participate in at least 5 hours of employment-related training or courses per week over the 4-week period. A client can choose to do more hours if they wish, however any extra hours must not stop them from meeting their obligations, such as being available for and seeking employment. Any extra hours a client does can only be counted in the week they did them. Any hours they did in previous weeks cannot be counted towards their 5 hours for the current week. Note in situations where a client may pass or fail a course, the outcome doesn't affect their recompliance with their obligation failure. MSD will consider a client's attendance and participation in a course as meeting the requirements of this sanction.

chunks.title: Public holidays — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD should consider the availability of employment-related training or courses during periods that include a large number of public holidays, for example during December and January. MSD should be aware of the dates the employment-related training or course is set to take place and should be able to determine suitability before the client starts their course. Note if it seems like a client would be unable to meet the weekly requirements of Upskilling due to public holidays, MSD must not impose this as the client's sanction.

chunks.title: Option to attend multiple training courses — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A client could attend and participate in more than one suitable employment-related training or course to help them meet the required number of hours and weeks. This could be: - finding 2 or more courses that offer enough hours per week between them or - completing 2 or more courses back-to-back or - a combination of both A client can attend and participate in more than one course for Upskilling, as long as they are able to meet the requirements of the sanction.

chunks.title: Permanent residence — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Permanent residence
Generally migrants need to have permanent residence or New Zealand citizenship to receive benefit assistance. Permanent residence is granted by Immigration New Zealand. Citizenship is granted by the Department of Internal Affairs.
In order to receive a benefit, a client must normally:
- have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 (which can either be a resident visa or a permanent resident visa) or
- have a residence permit under the Immigration Act 1987 or
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents)
## Clients without permanent residence or citizenship
Emergency Benefit may be paid to some categories of migrants who do not have permanent residence or citizenship, eg people waiting for their application for refugee or protection status to be approved.
Note clients lawfully in New Zealand by virtue of a temporary permit or temporary entry class visa only (ie they do not have permanent residence) are not entitled to any benefit assistance.
For more information see:
- Immigration status and supporting documents
- Immigration status [no link find out why]
- Clients with permanent residence or citizenship
- Clients without permanent residence or citizenship

chunks.title: Person detained under a Public Protection Order — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Person detained under a Public Protection Order
A person who has a Public Protection Order may be eligible for an Emergency Benefit.
A Public Protection Order is when a person has finished their sentence in prison but for public safety they must remain in a secure residence. This is to protect members of the public from the almost certain harm from serious sexual or violent offences. Corrections fund the costs of the person being detained in a residence within the prison compound.
