Clients with a Public Protection Order can get an Emergency Benefit if they meet the basic eligibility criteria.
For more information see:
## Rate of payment
The rate of Emergency Benefit is paid at the hospital rate from the date of grant.
## Entitlement date
The entitlement date for Emergency Benefit for a person held under a Public Protection Order is generally the date of release. The usual stand-down provisions for prisoners apply when determining the commencement date.
## New Zealand Superannuation
A person who has a Public Protection Order may get New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension if they meet the qualifications.
For more information see:
- New Zealand Superannuation Person detained under a Public Protection Order

chunks.title: Person serving their sentence of imprisonment in a psychiatric hospital — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Person serving their sentence of imprisonment in a psychiatric hospital
If a person who is remanded in custody or serving a term of imprisonment is detained in or transferred to a psychiatric hospital and they are not eligible for New Zealand Superannuation they may be eligible for an Emergency Benefit. The Department of Corrections are not responsible for funding the costs of these clients.
To get an Emergency Benefit the client must meet the basic eligibility criteria. For more information see:
- Qualifications
## Temporarily hospitalised
People remanded in custody or imprisoned who are temporarily hospitalised for treatment of an injury or health condition are still considered to be in prison and cannot get an Emergency Benefit or any other financial assistance. The Department of Corrections will meet their costs.
## Rate of payment
People serving a sentence of imprisonment who are held in or transferred to a psychiatric hospital who are eligible for an Emergency Benefit, are paid at the hospital rate from the date they are transferred to the psychiatric hospital (this rate might be paid from date of grant). You can consider paying a higher rate in some circumstances. For more information see:
- Hospitalisation Paying a higher rate
## Entitlement date
The entitlement date for Emergency Benefit for a person serving their sentence (or part of their sentence) in a psychiatric hospital is generally the date of transfer to hospital. The usual stand-down provisions for prisoners apply when determining the commencement date.
## New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients
A person who is serving their sentence of imprisonment in a psychiatric hospital may be eligible for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension instead if they meet the qualifications.

chunks.title: Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer
A benefit can be conditionally paid if the client (or partner with work obligations) challenges the dismissal or loss of employment.
Before the benefit can be paid you must obtain verification that the client is challenging the dismissal or loss of employment.
When a client's former employer confirms the client ceased their employment during their employment trial but does not disclose the reason for the termination, accept the client's reason for the termination and continue with the application process. Contact with the client's former employer is still required to confirm the date ceased and any holiday pay etc.
## Exception
A client can challenge their former employer's decision to end their employment and take legal proceedings if the client thinks their former employer has ceased their employment on grounds of:
- discrimination
- sexual harassment
- racial harassment or
- duress imposed by the employer in relation to client union affiliations or not as the case may be
Where a client has lost their job through misconduct, their actions must have seriously breached their contract of employment in order for their employer to be able to terminate their employment.
Clients may choose to follow up their grievance using the Employment Relations Act 2000 or the Human Rights Act 1993. They cannot use both Acts for the same grievance.
## Conditions for granting the benefit
The client (or partner) is only granted their benefit on the condition that:
- they will repay all of the benefit received during the 13 week non-entitlement period if misconduct is proven and
- they may need to repay part or all of the benefit received during the 13 week non-entitlement period if they win wages, damages or other compensation
They will need to sign a statement to this effect.
When you grant a benefit (or pay a full rate of benefit) under these conditions, on the SDT1A screen you must use the 'reason for grant' code (48).
For more information see:
- Proof client is challenging dismissal
- Outcome of case

chunks.title: Planning requirements — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Planning requirements
In some circumstances, you may want to consider whether an Emergency Benefit should include preparing for employment. Generally, where the equivalent benefit has work preparation obligations, as a condition of grant of an Emergency Benefit you should include requirements that are similar to those obligations.
You cannot apply the work preparation obligations or sanctions as such. You can grant the Emergency Benefit and require the client to meet certain conditions that look similar to work preparation obligations. Where a person fails to meet their conditions of grant, the Emergency Benefit may be stopped.
The conditions of grant may include (but are not limited to):
- when required to undertake planning for employment
- when required to report to Work and Income on progress in meeting their work preparation obligations as often as required
- when required to attend and participate in any interview with Work and Income or on behalf of Work and Income and
- when required by Work and Income undertake any activity to improve their work readiness and employment prospects, including: any work assessmentany programme or seminarany work experience or work exploration activityany employment related trainingrehabilitation (but not medical treatment)an education programme
- any work assessment
- any programme or seminar
- any work experience or work exploration activity
- any employment related training
- rehabilitation (but not medical treatment)
- an education programme
From time-to-time, a client's circumstances may change and the conditions of grant of Emergency Benefit may need to be reviewed.
Where a client has advised a change of circumstances review their eligibility and if necessary the conditions of grant.
For more information see:
- Equivalent benefit
- Benefit paid for a specific period
- Conditions of grant

chunks.title: Pregnant 27 weeks or earlier if complications — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Pregnant 27 weeks or earlier if complications
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
A client who is pregnant can be exempt from meeting some of their work obligations from:
- week 27 of the pregnancy or
- earlier if there are complications associated with the pregnancy
Note this is a partial exemption when it is reasonable to plan with the client.
## Evidence
The partner must provide evidence from a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or midwife confirming the expected date of birth or nature of complications if their pregnancy is under 27 weeks.
## Duration
This exemption applies until the earliest date of either:
- the birth of the child or
- 6 months from the date it was granted

chunks.title: In prison less than 31 days — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## In prison less than 31 days
Clients who have been in prison or on remand for less than 31 days do not have a stand-down imposed if they were receiving a benefit before going into prison and apply for a benefit immediately following their release.
If the client was not receiving a benefit before being imprisoned or placed on remand, a stand-down is imposed.
There is no access to a Steps to Freedom Special Needs Grant for these clients.
## In prison 31 days or more
Clients who have been in prison or on remand for 31 days or more have a stand-down imposed.
These clients have access to a Steps to Freedom Special Needs Grants to assist them during the stand-down. They may also have access to other forms of assistance to help them re-establish themselves in the community.
## Calculating number of days
When counting the number of days that a client has been in prison or held on remand, you should include the date the client:
- enters prison or is held on remand and
- leaves prison or is released from remand
For more information see:
- Imprisonment Release from prison
- Transfer between benefits

chunks.title: Process for deciding appropriate activities — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Process for deciding appropriate activities
When you and the partner are considering appropriate activities for the partner to undertake, you should consider the following:
- what needs or barriers to employment is the activity designed to address for the partner
- what activities are available to help the partner move towards employment
- the Work and Income products that are available to help the partner move towards employment
Examples of appropriate activities include (but are not limited to):
- participating in the Job Search Service
- education or training to improve partners work-readiness or prospects for employment
For more information see:
- Activity Summary
- Informing partners of their obligations

chunks.title: Proof client is challenging dismissal — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Proof client is challenging dismissal
Clients may provide information showing that they are challenging a dismissal. This might be:
- evidence that they have a representative (union, lawyer, community law centre, industrial relations advocate)
- a letter from Mediation Services or the Employment Relations Authority
For more information see:
- Outcome of case
- Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer

chunks.title: Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A provisional benefit can be paid to the client or partner when they are undertaking an approved activity or programme of activities during the 13 week non-entitlement period.

chunks.title: Provisional benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: You can grant or increase a provisional benefit from the date the client or partner starts the approved activity. The benefit continues to be provisionally paid while the client or partner is satisfactorily participating in the approved activity. Payment continues until: - the 6 week activity period ends or - the 13 week non-entitlement period ends whichever is earlier. Some examples of this: - a client participates in an approved activity from the beginning of week 3 of the non-entitlement period. The client participates for a continuous period of 6 weeks and the remaining period of the 13 week non-entitlement is cancelled. After the follow up appointment with the client the benefit ceases to be paid on a provisional basis - a client participates in an approved activity from the beginning of week 10 of the non-entitlement period. The client participates in the approved activity for the remainder of the 13 week non-entitlement period (for 3 weeks). At the end of the 13 week non-entitlement period, the client's benefit ceases to be paid on a provisional basis

chunks.title: End of approved activity or non-entitlement period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: At the end of the approved activity a follow up appointment is required (in approximately 6 weeks). You should discuss with the client or partner whether they: - have satisfactorily participated in the approved activity and - can still meet the qualifications and obligations of the benefit Note that if the client or partner does not recomply, they must reapply at the end of the 13 week non-entitlement period to receive a benefit.

chunks.title: Leaves or has not satisfactorily participated in an approved activity — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If the client or partner leaves early or does not satisfactorily participate in the approved activity or programme of suitable activities, without a good and sufficient reason, their provisional benefit must be reduced or stopped from the date it was increased or granted. The amount of benefit that was provisionally paid during the 13 week non-entitlement period must be established as a debt and recovered. You cannot recover the provisional benefit if the client or partner does not complete the approved activity because they: - transferred to a benefit with no work obligations or - meet the criteria for a full exemption from their work obligations For more information see: - Recompliance 13 week non-entitlement period - Unable to recomply

chunks.title: Qualifications — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
An Emergency Benefit may be considered for a client who is:
- not eligible for another benefit and
- in hardship as they are unable to earn a sufficient livelihood due to their: health condition, an injury or a disabilitydomestic circumstances (for example caring responsibilities)age (for example 16 and 17 year olds) orany other reason (for example residence status)
- health condition, an injury or a disability
- domestic circumstances (for example caring responsibilities)
- age (for example 16 and 17 year olds) or
- any other reason (for example residence status)
Generally, the client also has to be:
- 16 years or older and
- ordinarily resident in New Zealand
For more information see: Deciding ordinarily resident
Each client's circumstances must be established to determine why the client cannot earn a sufficient livelihood and is in hardship. The reason a client cannot support themselves (and dependent family) will determine the 'equivalent benefit'. It is important to identify the equivalent benefit, as this will set the maximum rate of the benefit payable and provides a guide for the conditions of the Emergency Benefit.
Note Australian citizens who are in New Zealand for the purpose of resolving an international custody dispute should be granted Emergency Benefit at the sole parent rate of benefit.
## Sponsored clients
Some clients have been granted permanent residence on condition that they will be supported by a New Zealand sponsor.
Before a decision can be made about the client's application for benefit, any reasons why their sponsor can no longer support the client must first be determined and verified.
This is done for the purpose of assessing whether the client is in hardship.

chunks.title: Recompliance — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Recompliance is the activity a client or partner must undertake after they have failed an obligation. They must complete the recompliance activity to have their benefit: - increased or resumed if they have been financially sanctioned or - continued if they have a non-financial sanction imposed Generally, the activities a client or partner need to complete are the same or substantially similar to the obligation that initiated the failure. Clients with an obligations failure initiated who recomply within 5 working days will not have a sanction imposed, but the obligations failure will be counted. When a client or partner indicates that they want to recomply MSD must make a recompliance activity available for them at the earliest opportunity. The obligations failure that has reduced or stopped their benefit will determine the type of recompliance activity the client or partner will need to undertake. MSD must discuss with the client what activities they need to undertake in order to recomply. For more information see: - Recompliance for work obligation failures - Recompliance for social obligation failures - Recompliance for drug test obligation failures - Recomplying more than one failure - Recompliance for young partners

chunks.title: Allocating a recompliance activity — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When allocating the recompliance activity, MSD must: - discuss with the client what they need to do to satisfactorily undertake the recompliance activity and the implications of not doing this and - make a note of your discussion in the appropriate system MSD must decide whether the client has satisfactorily undertaken their recompliance activity. This will be dependent on the client's circumstances and the nature of the recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Same as or substantially similar activity — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a client is unable to undertake the same activity that they failed to do, they must undertake to your satisfaction another activity that is the same as or substantially similar to the activity they failed to do. The 'same as or substantially similar to' means that MSD must allocate an activity that, as much as possible, requires the same amount of time, effort and commitment as the activity the client failed to complete.

chunks.title: When to resume or increase a benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A client must have successfully completed the recompliance activity before their benefit is resumed or increased if they have been financially sanctioned. Once completed, the benefit can be resumed or increased from the date MSD is satisfied the client started the recompliance activity. Some examples of this: - if the recompliance activity is a one-off, such as attending an interview the benefit would be resumed from the date the client attended and participated in the interview - if the recompliance activity is ongoing, such as a training programme, the client must undertake the training programme to MSD's satisfaction. Once this is complete, the benefit can be resumed from the date the client started the training programme - if the client has multiple recompliance activities to complete (due to more than one failure), the date when they have completed a recompliance activity for the latest failure For what to do if a client cannot recomply, see: - Unable to recomply - Recompliance and change of circumstances

chunks.title: Recompliance when a non-financial sanction is imposed — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Non-financial sanctions each have different recompliance requirements that must be met within the sanction period. If the non-financial sanction period ends before the client has recomplied, their benefit will be suspended until they recomply. For more information on non-financial sanctions, see: - Non-financial sanctions

chunks.title: Client does not recomply when a financial sanction is imposed — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a client has a grade 1 financial sanction imposed and does not complete their recompliance activity within 4 weeks, their benefit will be suspended. Clients with a grade 2 financial sanction have their benefit suspended immediately. If a client does not recomply with a grade 1 or grade 2 financial sanction within 13 weeks, their benefit will automatically cancel. Clients who have had their benefit cancelled will need to reapply for a benefit if they need further support.

chunks.title: Client with dependent children does not recomply — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a client has a dependent child, they will have 50% payment protection and continue to receive 50% of their benefit. Their benefit can only return to the full rate payable when a client has completed their recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Allocating an extra activity — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Once a client or partner has recomplied and their benefit has been resumed or increased, they may be allocated appropriate additional activities or support. When determining whether to allocate additional activities, the client’s individual circumstances must be considered, including: - the type of obligations they have, and - if there are any suitable activities currently available for them If additional activities are assigned to the client or partner, they must complete them. Failure to complete these activities without a good and sufficient reason should be treated as a new obligations failure.

chunks.title: Recompliance (13-week non-entitlement period) — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A client or partner can complete certain activities to get a provisional benefit if they have a 13 week non-entitlement period due to: - leaving a job voluntarily - losing a job through misconduct - having a grade 3 sanction imposed or - refusing an offer of suitable employment If a client or partner wants to recomply, you must make a 6 week approved activity or programme of activities available to them at the earliest opportunity. There is no waiting period before an approved activity can start, after a sanction has been imposed.

chunks.title: Recompliance activities — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The client or partner must undertake an approved activity for a continuous period of 6 weeks or until the 13 week non-entitlement period ends (whichever is the earlier). This can be through: - satisfactory participation in a 6 week approved activity or programme of activities - satisfactory participation in full-time employment or - part-time employment (in the case of clients with part-time work obligations) Note that for clients with full-time obligations the 6 week approved activity should be full-time, and for clients with part-time obligations it should be part-time.

chunks.title: Recompliance for social obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If a client or partner fails their obligations for a third time, and the third failure is a social obligation failure, then the 6 week recompliance activity you require the client or partner to complete will be different. In this situation it may not be appropriate to require the client or partner to complete a 6 week approved activity that is focused on work outcomes, so a programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate for the client or partner. For more information see: - Failing a social obligation

chunks.title: Approved activity examples — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Here are some examples that may be a suitable 6 week approved activity for the client or partner: - Employment and Work Readiness Assistance - Wage subsidy - Work confidence and motivation assistance Note this list is an example only, an approved activity (or programme of suitable activities) should be relevant to the obligations failure and be fair and reasonable.

chunks.title: Programme of suitable activities — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If there is not an appropriate 6 week approved activity available, consider establishing a programme of suitable activities. For more information see: - Recompliance programme example For when to grant or increase the benefit, see: - Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period For what to do if a client or partner cannot recomply see: - Unable to recomply For more information see: - Recompliance for work obligation failures - partners - Recompliance for social obligation failures - Recompliance for drug test obligation failures - partners - Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Recompliance and change of circumstances — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Recompliance and change of circumstances
A client or partner who has a failure in progress or a sanction imposed may be unable to recomply because they:
- had a change of circumstances that means they can no longer recomply with a social obligation, or the social obligation is no longer relevant to them or
- had a change in obligations which means they are no longer required to comply with any activity that is specific to their previous obligations, for example a client moves between work obligations and work preparation obligations
In these situations, you should not require the client to recomply. However, the failure will still be included in the 24 month count.
Note young partners who failed a youth activity obligation will have this counted for 12 months, even if they are no longer subject to youth activity obligations.
Once the client has new obligations, MSD may ask them to complete any activities in relation to their new obligations.
## Examples
Examples of where MSD cannot require your client to complete a recompliance activity:
- where a child leaves care or changes age and the social obligation they had is no longer relevant (for example the client has failed the early childhood education social obligation and the child has now turned 6 years old)
- where a partner who has work obligations has failed a drug test obligation and is transferred to work preparation obligations
- where partner client who has work preparation obligations has failed to undertake planning for employment and is transferred to work obligations
- where a partner who has work or work preparation obligations has failed an obligation and has been transferred to Supported Living Payment or Emergency Benefit with no obligations
For more information see:
- Recompliance for work obligation failures - partners
- Recompliance for social obligation failures
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures - partners
- Recomplying more than one failure
- Work and work preparation obligations [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Recompliance and Community Work Experience — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Recompliance and Community Work Experience
Community Work Experience is both a sanction for an obligation failure, and a recompliance activity for a partner to recomply with their obligations.
This means that a partner who is completing Community Work Experience is not required to complete the same or similar activity that they originally failed to do.
If a partner completes the requirements of their position and provides verification, they will be considered to have recomplied from the day they complete their Community Work Experience.
Partners who do not complete their Community Work Experience will be considered non-compliant. Their payments will be reduced or stopped, and MSD must assign an alternative recompliance activity as soon as possible.

chunks.title: Recompliance and Report Job Search — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Recompliance and Report Job Search
Report Job Search is both a non-financial sanction for an obligation failure, and a recompliance activity for a partner to recomply with their obligations.
This means that a partner who is completing Report Job Search is not required to complete the same or similar activity that they originally failed to do.
If a partner completes the requirements of Report Job Search and provides verification, they will be considered to have recomplied from the day they complete Report Job Search.
Partners who do not complete Report Job Search will be considered non-compliant. Their payments will be reduced or stopped, and MSD must assign an alternative recompliance activity as soon as possible.

chunks.title: Recompliance and Upskilling — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Recompliance and Upskilling
Upskilling is both a sanction for an obligation failure, and a recompliance activity for a client to recomply with their obligations.
This means that a client who is completing Upskilling is not required to complete the same or similar activity that they originally failed to do.
If a client completes the requirements of Upskilling and provides verification, they will be considered to have recomplied from the day they complete Upskilling.
Clients who do not complete Upskilling will be considered non-compliant. Their payments will be reduced or stopped, and MSD must assign an alternative recompliance activity as soon as possible.

chunks.title: Recompliance for drug test obligation failures - partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for drug test obligation failures - partners
Partners who have failed their drug test obligations will need to complete a recompliance activity to increase, resume or continue their benefit.
Once a partner indicates they want to recomply MSD should have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply. The grade of the drug test obligation failure will determine the recompliance activity required.
For more information see:
- Recomplying first drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying third drug test obligation failure

chunks.title: Recompliance for social obligation failures — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for social obligation failures
Clients and their partners who have failed their social obligations need to meet all their social obligations as part of an activity to increase their benefit.
Once a client or partner indicates they want to recomply MSD must have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply.
Note when a client has a partner, social obligations apply to both the client and the partner.

chunks.title: Recompliance for work obligation failures - partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for work obligation failures - partners
Partners who have failed their work obligations need to recomply to have their benefit:
- increased or resumed if they have been financially sanctioned or
- continued if they have a non-financial sanction imposed
Once a partner or partner indicates they want to recomply MSD must have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply. The grade of the work obligations failure will determine the recompliance activity required.
## Work obligations failure (Grade 1 and 2)
For partners to recomply with a work obligations failure (grade 1 and 2) and have their benefit increased or resumed, the partner will need to complete:
- the activity they failed or
- an activity that is the same as or substantially similar to the activity they failed
Note for grade 1 failures where a non-financial sanction has been imposed, the recompliance requirements may be different. For more information see:
- Non-financial sanctions
## Work obligations failure or failure to accept an offer of suitable employment (Grade 3)
For partners to recomply to a work obligations failure (grade 3) and be granted a provisional benefit, the partner will need to start and complete a 6-week recompliance activity or programme of activities (13-week non-entitlement period) or wait until the end of the 13-week non-entitlement period.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13-week non-entitlement period)
- Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Recompliance for young partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Young partners with a youth activity obligations failure initiated must recomply within 5 working days. If they do this no sanction will be imposed but the activity obligations failure will be counted. If the sanction has been imposed the young partner must recomply to have their benefit increased or resumed. When a young partner indicates that they want to recomply an appointment must be made for them to discuss recomplying and make a recompliance activity available for them at the earliest opportunity.

chunks.title: Service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service role in recompliance — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service will need to discuss with the young partner the activities they need to undertake in order to recomply. To recomply they must: - undertake the original activity if it is still available or - if the original activity is not available, undertake another activity, to the satisfaction of MSD, that is the same as or substantially similar to the activity the young partner failed to do When a recompliance activity is allocated, you must: - discuss with the young partner what they need to do to satisfactorily undertake the recompliance activity and the implications of not doing this and - make a note of the discussion on the Activity Reporting Tool (ART)

chunks.title: Same or substantially similar activity — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If the young partner is unable to undertake the same activity that they failed to do, they must undertake to the satisfaction of MSD another activity that is the same as or substantially similar to the activity they failed to do. The 'same or substantially similar to' means that any recompliance activity should, as much as possible, require the same amount of time, effort and commitment as that which the young partner failed to complete.

chunks.title: YSSU role in recompliance — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The YSSU must decide whether the young partner has satisfactorily undertaken their recompliance activity based on the recommendation from the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service. This will depend on the young partner's circumstances and the nature of the recompliance activity.

chunks.title: When to resume or increase the benefit — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The YSSU will resume or increase the payment from the date the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service are satisfied that the young partner has started the recompliance activity. Some examples of this: - if the recompliance activity is a one-off, such as attending an interview with the service provider, the payment would be resumed from the date the young partner attended and participated in the activity - if the recompliance activity is ongoing, such as attending school or a training programme, the young partner must satisfactorily attend school or the training programme and the payment will be resumed from the date the young partner started to attend For what to do if a young partner cannot recomply due to a health condition see: - Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption Also see: - Approved recompliance activities for young partners

chunks.title: Recompliance programme example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Recompliance programme example
If a partner is recomplying through participating in an approved activity, there may not be a single activity long enough to meet the required 6 week period of recompliance. A programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate for the partner.
Note a programme of suitable activities for a partner with part-time work obligations should be for 15 hours or more each week.
## Example of short term approved activities
Week 1
CV Seminar - 20 hours
Week 2
Employment skills programme - 20 hours
Week 3
Employment skills programme - 20 hours
Week 4
Employment skills programme - 20 hours
Week 5
Presentation seminar approved by Work and Income
Week 5
Work experience
Week 6
Work experience
Week 6
Business Plan preparation interview with accountant or local business enterprise centre - 3 hours
Note a programme of short-term suitable activities should be relevant to the obligations failure and be fair and reasonable.
For more information see:
- Recompliance through employment
- Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Recompliance social obligations failure (Grade 1 and 2) — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When the client or partner fails 1 individual social obligation they need to comply with all other social obligations relevant to the age of their dependent child. MSD should discuss with the client or partner what activities they need to undertake to recomply. MSD must be satisfied the client and their partner (if any) have both satisfactorily undertaken their recompliance activity. The benefit will be resumed or increased from the date MSD is satisfied the client or partner has started the recompliance activity. In some situations, MSD may ask the client or their partner (if any) to get verification, for example: - a letter from their practitioner or medical practice that says they are enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation or - a letter from the child's school that says the child is enrolled and attending or - a letter from their early childhood education provider that says the child is enrolled and attending or - asking to see their Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book

chunks.title: Examples of recompliance — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Example 1 A client has a 3-year-old child. They are required to have their child enrolled in primary health care and attending a recognised early childhood programme. The child has not been attending an early childhood programme and the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for this. MSD is unsure if the child is enrolled in primary health care. The client has failed 1 of their social obligations. To recomply with their social obligations, MSD must be satisfied the client has enrolled their child in primary health care and that they will ensure their child attends an early childhood programme. MSD asks the client to provide verification of this. The client provides a letter from their medical practice confirming the child is enrolled, and a letter from the early childhood education provider confirming the child is enrolled and attending. MSD is satisfied that the client has recomplied with their social obligations. Example 2 A client has 2 children. The 5-year-old child must be enrolled in primary health care and attending school or an early childhood education programme. The 2-year-old child also needs to be enrolled in primary health care and up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks. Both children are enrolled in primary health care and the 5-year-old child is attending school. However, the 2-year-old child is not up to date with their core Well Child checks and the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for this. The client has failed 1 of their social obligations. To recomply with their social obligations, MSD must be satisfied that the 2-year-old child has or will get their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks. MSD asks the client to provide verification of this. The client brings their 2-year-old’s Well child/Tamariki Ora book to MSD which confirms the 2-year-old has upcoming Well child/Tamariki Ora checks booked. MSD is satisfied that the client has recomplied with their social obligations.

chunks.title: Full-time employment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Full-time employment
A partner with full-time work obligations who has a 13 week non-entitlement period applied can recomply through participation in full-time employment. The employment must be for a continuous period of at least 6 weeks.
At the end of the 6 week period of employment the 13 week non-entitlement period ends. The partner needs to reapply if they wish to receive a benefit. The benefit is granted from the date the employment ceased.
Note provisional benefit is not paid during the 6 week period of employment.
## Part-time employment
A partner with part-time work obligations who has a 13 week non-entitlement period applied can recomply through participation in part-time employment for a period of at least 6 weeks.
The part-time employment needs to be for an average of 20 hours or more each week.
At the end of the 6 week period of employment the 13 week non-entitlement period ends. The partner needs to reapply if they wish to receive a benefit. The benefit is granted from the date the employment ceased.
If the partner leaves this employment before the end of the 6 week period without a good and sufficient reason or through misconduct, any provisional benefit paid must be established as a debt and the remainder of the non-entitlement period is imposed.
The partner may still recomply during the remainder of the 13 week non-entitlement period by participating in another approved activity.
Note the income received from the part-time employment is charged against the benefit rate.
For when to grant or increase the benefit, see:
- Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Recompliance when subjected to Money Management — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Recompliance when subjected to Money Management
When a client fails an obligation and has Money Management imposed, they still need to recomply with their obligation. They can do this at any point during the 4-week Money Management period, but need to complete their recompliance activity before their Money Management period ends.
## Client recomplies
When a client completes their recompliance activity during their Money Management period, they will be recomplied at the end of the 4 weeks. Any benefit payments they are entitled to from the day after Money Management ends will go into their bank account.
Money Management will last 4 weeks regardless of when a client completes their activity.
## Client does not recomply
Clients who do not complete their recompliance activity while on Money Management will have their benefit suspended at the end of the four-week period.
Their benefit can only be resumed or returned to the full rate when a client has completed their recompliance activity. If a client’s benefit has been suspended following Money Management, their benefit will be automatically cancelled after 9 weeks (13 weeks total). For more information on how non-compliance affects assistance, see:
Clients who have had their benefit cancelled will need to reapply for benefit if they need further support.
## Client with dependent children does not recomply
If a client has children, they will have 50% payment protection and continue to receive 50% of their benefit.
Their benefit can only return to the full rate payable when a client has completed their recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Recomplying first drug test obligation failure - partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Recomplying first drug test obligation failure - partners
To recomply to a first drug test obligation failure a partner must verbally agree to stop using controlled drugs.
The day the partner agrees to stop taking controlled drugs is the date they can be considered to have recomplied. You must advise the partner of the consequences if they fail the drug test obligation again.
For more information see:
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying third drug test obligation failure
- Drug test recompliance count

chunks.title: Recomplying more than one failure — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Recomplying more than one failure
When more than one obligation failure has been initiated for a client on the same day, to increase, resume, or continue their full benefit the client or partner needs to successfully dispute or recomply to all the failures.
If the client disputes or recomplies with one obligation, the sanction must still be imposed due the other obligation failures not being successfully disputed or recomplied (within the 5 working day notice period).
## Client already has a failure in-progress or a sanction imposed
Once failures have been initiated, and the notice letter has been sent, any further failures cannot be initiated until each failure:
- has been recomplied with
- has been successfully disputed because the client provided a good and sufficient reason or reasons or
- is overturned (following a dispute)
These further failures will not be included in the 24 month count (or 12-month count for young partners with youth activity obligations) and the client cannot be required to recomply.
For more information see:
- Recompliance for work obligation failures - partners
- Recompliance for social obligation failures
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures - partners
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Recomplying second drug test obligation failure - partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a partner has failed their drug test obligations the second time, they must agree that they will take and pass a drug test within 25 working days (of the agreement). The benefit can be reinstated from the day the partner recomplies, ie the day the client or partner agrees to take the test. The drug test can be either a screening test or an evidential test.

chunks.title: Period to take and provide a drug test — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A partner has 25 working days, from the day after they have agreed to recomply with their second drug test obligations failure, to take and pass a drug test. The partner must within 30 working days from the day after they have agreed to recomply, provide proof of undertaking and passing the drug test. A partner cannot dispute the 25 working day period to take and pass the drug test. They must take and pass the drug test within that time period or they will fail their obligations for the third time. Work and Income has an additional 5 working days to receive the results from the partner and to process the information. Generally, the results of the drug test should be provided to Work and Income within the 25 working days, but they can be accepted in the 5 working day period following. Day 0 A second drug test failure is in-progress and partner has agreed to recomply by taking and passing a drug test within 25 working days Recompliance 2 is recorded and automatic count in IT system occurs overnight Partner can provide the results of the drug test at any time Day 1 - 25 Letter is sent to the partner advising them they have 25 working days to take and pass a drug test Day 26 - 30 Five working days to allow time to receive and process the results of the test starts Day 31 If no "passed" drug test results are received a work test failure three is initiated and five working day notice period prior to Grade 3 sanction starts They will not be considered to have recomplied until a passed drug test result is received by Work and Income. A partner can only access upfront help with the costs of the recompliance drug test once during the 25 working day period. During the 25 working day period a "drug test referral delay" will be automatically added in CMS.

chunks.title: Test not taken — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The partner must take and pass the drug test within the 25 working day period. If they do not do this, they will be considered to have failed their work obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, for the third time and a Grade 3 sanction will be imposed.

chunks.title: Verification required — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: In order to make a decision that a partner has taken and passed a drug test you must have received written confirmation from the partner. The written information that must be provided to Work and Income includes: - the name of the partner and the drug test provider and - confirmation of a "passed" test result The Drug test obligations verification [no link find out why] form can be used for this. For more information see: - Help with paying for the recompliance drug test - Recomplying first drug test obligation failure - Recomplying third drug test obligation failure - Drug test recompliance count

chunks.title: Recomplying third drug test obligation failure - partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Recomplying third drug test obligation failure - partners
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation a partner must complete a 6 week approved activity. A 6 week approved activity must be completed regardless of the obligation failed or whether the partner had failed more than one obligation failure.
## Partner fails a third time for another reason during the 25 working day period
A partner could fail their other obligations (not drug test obligations) for a third time during the 25 working day period. If this happens the third failure would override the count of the 25 working day period and the partner would not have to take and pass a drug test.
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation the partner must complete a six week approved activity.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Recomplying more than one failure
- Recomplying first drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Drug test recompliance count

chunks.title: Recording decisions on a dispute — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Recording decisions on a dispute
You must record the outcome of the client or partner's dispute in OBMAN. One of the following outcomes must be recorded for each dispute:
- Upheld - if you believe that the decision relating to an obligations failure or sanction being imposed was correct you must record this as 'dispute upheld'. The obligations failure will be counted.
- Withdrawn - a client or partner may, after disputing the obligations failure, decide to recomply before the sanction is imposed, or may withdraw their dispute and not recomply. In these cases you must record that the dispute has been withdrawn. The obligations failure will be counted.
- Overturned - when you believe that the client or partner had a good and sufficient reason or that they did not fail their obligations you must record this as overturned. The obligations failure will not be counted.
In all cases you must advise the client or partner of the outcome of their dispute. A letter is automatically sent to the client or partner.
If the client or partner does not agree with your decision, they can still request a formal Review of Decision or Medical Appeal Board appeal (drug test failure only). They must do this in writing. The Review of Decision and Medical Appeal Board process should be followed.
Note if the obligations failure was initiated against the wrong client or partner the status can be changed to 'failed in error' on the same day you initiate the failure. No letter is sent when the status is changed to 'failed in error'.
## Reviews of Decisions and appeals to the Medical Appeals Board for obligations failures
Reviews of Decisions for obligations failures are recorded in HIYA; appeals to the Medical Appeals Board for obligations failures are recorded in the Medical Appeals Database.
However, the outcome of the review or appeal must be recorded in OBMAN. This will ensure that the benefit status can be resumed or regranted in SWIFTT depending on the outcome of the review or appeal.
Note that if the Review of Decision or Medical Appeals Board process finds that the originally recorded 'upheld' outcome should be changed to overturned, you will need to make this change in OBMAN.
For more information see:
- The disputes process
- Core policy Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Core policy Medical Appeal Board

chunks.title: Redirection for young partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Redirection for young partners
For young partners subject to youth money management the Emergency Benefit, family tax credit and any ongoing extra help must be redirected to pay for:
- the young person's accommodation and service costs, for example rent, board, power, phone
- the young person's lawful debts or other liabilities, for example Child Support payments, MSD debts
- food and groceries via a payment card
## Payments that are not redirected
Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance, Flexible Childcare Assistance are not included in youth money management and can be paid directly to the young partner, their agent (if authorised) or a supplier (as appropriate).
If the young person qualifies for any of these payments, MSD will decide who the payment goes to after talking with the young person's youth service provider.

chunks.title: Redundancy payments — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Redundancy payments
A redundancy payment is a lump sum payment to compensate a person when their employer terminates their employment as their position is surplus to the employer's needs.
Redundancy payments do not include:
- payments made solely due to a seasonal lay-off
- payments to a company director to compensate for loss of office
- payments for the completion of work specified in a contract or a fixed term engagement
- payment in lieu of notice
- retirement payments or
- payments that would have been paid as salary or wages if the person is not made redundant, e.g. holiday pay, performance payments, time in lieu
Note some of these payments may affect the date employment ceased and may be included in the income assessment when calculating the length of the initial stand-down.
## Being made redundant
Redundancy can happen voluntarily, where an employee accepts redundancy willingly or as an enforced decision.
In both cases employees can get payments to compensate for loss of:
- employment
- tangible benefits or rights
- prospects and promotions
- status and security
- income
Redundancy must not be confused with other reasons for an employee losing their job, e.g. an employee who is unable to perform duties, or has been laid off due to misconduct.
## Cessation leave
Cessation leave is a component of a redundancy payment that recognises the employees length of service to the employer. The amount paid is based on the number of years continuous service the employee completed.
Cessation leave has nothing to do with leave entitlements and does not affect the date employment ceased.
## Severance payments
The term severance is often used in place of redundancy; however redundancy payments and severance payments are different.
Severance payments may be made by an employer as part of a severance agreement to help resolve an unsatisfactory employment situation. They are over and above what a person is entitled to under their employment agreement.
Severance payments do not affect the date employment ceased.
## How redundancy payments affect commencement date
Redundancy payments are included in the assessment of a person's last 26 or 52 weeks income to determine the length of their initial stand-down.
They are not used to calculate the date employment ceased.

chunks.title: Delayed redundancy payments — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Delayed redundancy payments
If the client has been granted a benefit and then receives a redundancy payment within 52 weeks after the date the client's employment ceased, the benefit stand-down and date employment ceased must be reassessed.
To review the initial stand-down:
- divide the redundancy payment by 26 weeks (and 52 weeks if the client's entitlement date to benefit is on or after 1 May 2005). Add the appropriate weekly redundancy amount to the client's average weekly income received before employment ceased.
- re-assess the length of the initial stand-down period to determine a new commencement date. Remember to use the calculation that provides the client with the lesser stand-down period.
and
- establish an overpayment for any monies paid to the client prior to the reassessed commencement date
## Payments received more than 52 weeks after redundancy
If the client receives a redundancy payment more than 52 weeks after the date the client's employment ceased, the payment is treated as a capital payment. The client's entitlement to any Extra Help must also be reassessed.

chunks.title: Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements
When you are referring a partner to a drug tested job, you should:
- consider if the job is suitable for the partner, regardless of the drug test
- let the partner know that the employer may require them to pass a pre-employment drug test
- ask the partner if they would pass a pre-employment drug test and
- ensure the partner understands the potential consequences of failing a pre-employment drug test
There are certain situations where may not be appropriate to refer a partner to drug tested jobs. In these situations you should consider that, because of the drug test requirements, the job is not suitable.
For more information see:
- Drug test job referral not suitable
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Employers requiring pre-employment drug tests
- Types of drug tests and standards
- Informing a partner of the drug test obligation failure
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons
- Effect of certain drugs
- Suitable employment
- Drug test obligations

chunks.title: Refugee or protected person — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Refugee or protected person
A person can be recognised as either a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand, but must still have a valid visa issued by Immigration New Zealand to be lawfully present in New Zealand.
A refugee can be accepted into New Zealand in two ways:
- through the refugee quota or
- as a spontaneous refugee claimant
People can also claim protection status on arrival to New Zealand.
Generally, to be eligible for a benefit a client who has been granted refugee or protected person status must also have permanent residence. Until permanent residence is granted, the client may be eligible for an Emergency Benefit.
When considering Emergency Benefit, the reason the client is unable to earn a sufficient livelihood must be considered in order to determine the equivalent benefit and set a maximum rate of payment and identify the appropriate conditions of grant.
Clients with refugee or protected person status who do not have permanent residence may also receive Temporary Additional Support. They are not eligible for other forms of Extra help such as Accommodation Supplement, Disability Allowance or Childcare Assistance.

chunks.title: Refugee or protection claimant — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Some migrants claim refugee or protection status (also known as spontaneous refugees or asylum seekers). The majority generally arrive with identification or official papers; are issued with a temporary entry class visa and live in the community while their refugee and protection claim is processed. A lack of official papers does not prevent a claim for refugee or protection status. Where a person has made a claim for refugee or protection status, is waiting for a decision and is lawfully in New Zealand, they can apply for Emergency Benefit and Temporary Additional Support. A claim for refugee or protection status can be made at any time and can include an appeal to the Immigration and Protection Tribunal.

chunks.title: Process for refugee and protection claimant clients — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The following are the steps for clients claiming refugee or protection status: Step 1: Client lodges a claim for refugee or protection status. This can be lodged on arrival into New Zealand or any time after arrival. If lodged on arrival, Immigration New Zealand may detain the client if they do not have any identification or official documents. Step 2: The client may already be living in the community or if a claim is made on arrival at the border and there are no security or other risks, they may be released into the community with a valid temporary entry visa (or temporary permit, if granted before 29 November 2010) issued by Immigration New Zealand. The client may apply for financial assistance. If the client does not have a valid visa or permit refer the client to Immigration New Zealand. Remember a work ready client must have a visa or permit allowing them to work in New Zealand Note a client cannot be considered for Emergency Benefit or Temporary Additional Support if they are not lawfully in New Zealand Step 3: Client is granted Emergency Benefit. Note when granting Emergency Benefit - enter in SWIFTT as an expiry: - the expiry date of the client's temporary entry visa or temporary permit or - 3 months from the date of grant whichever is the earlier. Step 4: A decision is made on the client's claim (including an appeal to the Immigration and Protection Tribunal) for refugee or protection status. Claim granted The client may still be eligible for Emergency Benefit and must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand. Part of this is applying for permanent residence. The reason a client does not make an application for permanent residence must be considered when assessing continuing eligibility. Claim declined From the date the application is declined, (at the Refugee Status Branch and the client does not appeal to the Immigration and Protection Tribunal within the statutory time period) the client is not eligible for Emergency Benefit. Immigration New Zealand may issue a deportation liability notice. If the client's visa has expired, they are in New Zealand unlawfully. Deportation may be executed once all appeal rights (if any) have been exhausted. Step 5:

chunks.title: Process for refugee and protection claimant clients — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The client may appeal to the Immigration and Protection Tribunal to remain in New Zealand. Immigration New Zealand can issue a temporary entry visa or residence visa to the client to allow them to remain in New Zealand lawfully while their appeal is being heard. If this is the case you should continue to pay Emergency Benefit until the appeal period has expired or the appeal has been determined. You should contact Legal Services for advice if necessary. Note this may be treated as an application for permanent residence and the client may be considered for Emergency Benefit if they are compelled to remain in New Zealand for some unforeseen circumstance. For more information see: Clients compelled to remain in New Zealand Note if the client is granted permanent residence, they are assessed the same as any other person granted permanent residence. For more information see: - Clients without permanent residence or citizenship - Extra help for clients without permanent residence - Refugee or protected person

chunks.title: Refugee quota — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Refugee quota
The refugee quota is the number of refugees the New Zealand Government has committed to accepting under an international agreement with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). These are generally selected before arrival and accepted into New Zealand for humanitarian reasons.
Clients who come to New Zealand under the New Zealand Refugee Quota programme spend their first 4-6 weeks in New Zealand at the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre receiving settlement services.
When a refugee leaves the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre, generally they will already have permanent residence and will:
- be looking for work
- be training for work
- be unable to work due to a health condition, injury, disability or pregnancy or
- have caring responsibilities
Refugees will have a letter stating they have permanent residence and are assessed for benefits the same as any other client. If the client cannot confirm they have permanent residence contact the Immigration New Zealand Contact Centre for verification.
Refugees with permanent residence who meet all the eligibility requirements except the period of residence for Jobseeker Support must be considered for Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship on grounds of hardship in the first instance. Where a client cannot meet the requirements for any other benefit, Emergency Benefit may be considered.
Note quota refugee clients who have not been granted permanent residence may still be considered for Emergency Benefit.
For more information see:
- Refugee or protected person
- Clients without permanent residence or citizenship
- Extra help for clients without permanent residence
- Determining the reason for insufficient livelihood
- Not eligible for another benefit

chunks.title: Regular engagement and support process — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Regular engagement and support process
Clients must be contacted at least 4 times by Work and Income before initiating a failure to meet a social obligation.
You must complete the 3 Contact Steps of regular engagement and support and then make a final appointment. You can only determine that the client has failed to meet their social obligations at the final appointment.
The Contact Steps can be over the phone or face to face.
The aim of this process is to support clients to meet their social obligations or for clients to take all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations.
At the first Contact Step of engagement and support you should discuss with the client and their partner (if any) whether they are meeting their social obligations and, if not, encourage them to do so.
The next two Contact Steps of engagement and support should be focused on encouraging and supporting the client to meet their social obligations, and following up what happened at the previous Contact Steps.
At each of the 3 Contact Steps you must:
- check that the client is taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, and actively help and encourage the client to meet those obligations
- ensure that the client is connected with local community information
- advise the client of the next stage of engagement and support and contact
- remind the client of their social obligations and consequences of not meeting these
For more information on the engagement and support see:
- Social obligations - Actively engaging with clients [no link find out why]
Also see:
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Client is meeting their social obligations
- Client's situation changes during engagement and support process
- Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations
- Failure to comply following regular engagement and support

chunks.title: Rehabilitation - partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Rehabilitation - partners
Rehabilitation is a process aimed at enabling people with ill health and disabled people to reach and maintain their optimal level.
It generally has a focus on restoration or improvement of the abilities of the partner.
Rehabilitation could include services such as re-training a partner unable to return to their previous occupation.
As part of the expectation that a partner will prepare towards a return to employment, partners with work preparation or work obligations may need support to undertake activities, including rehabilitation.
To improve the partner's work-readiness they may be required to undertake activities, including rehabilitation, however this must not include medical treatment.
## Medical treatment
Medical treatment may be part of the rehabilitation process but a partner cannot be required to complete medical treatment as an activity as part of their obligations.
If you are uncertain whether an activity would be considered as medical treatment, rehabilitation or other activity you should seek advice from your Regional Health or Regional Disability Advisor before you require a partner to undertake the activity.
## Rehabilitation activities
Requiring partners to undertake rehabilitation activities must be done with care. Generally you would ensure that they are willing and able to undertake activities.
Important before you require the partner to undertake a rehabilitation activity you must discuss the situation with your manager client service delivery.
The partner must be advised that if they are required to complete a rehabilitation activity, and if they fail to do this without a good and sufficient reason a sanction may be imposed.

chunks.title: Reimbursement to employers and debt recovery — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The potential employer can be reimbursed for a failed drug test for a client only when Work and Income receives confirmation a drug test has been completed that was part of the pre-employment process and the potential employer has completed the Pre-employment drug test claim form for employers which includes details such as: - the name of the employer - the type of test - whether it was a screening or evidential test, or both - confirmation that the drug test was to the drug test standard - confirmation of a failed test result and - the cost of the failed test and the payment rate they are claiming At the same time that the employer is reimbursed, a debt for the cost of the drug test will be manually added to the partners SWIFTT record by NPCU/NAC. For more information see: - Reimbursement and claims for employers / Drug test agencies [no link find out why] A training provider cannot be reimbursed for the costs of a failed drug test. In most cases the contract with the provider will have already factored these costs into account. Although a drug test provider may conduct the testing the employer will be the one to be reimbursed for the costs relating to the failed drug test. The information provided related to the failed drug tests is not to be shared with other employers, and is only to be used for the purposes of establishing whether a partner has failed, without good and sufficient reason, to meet the drug test obligations. The reimbursement of failed drug tests only apply to jobs where - the partner with work obligations has been referred by Work and Income - the vacancy is listed with Work and Income and - the vacancy requires a pre-employment drug test

chunks.title: Recruitment agencies — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A recruitment agency can be reimbursed by Work and Income for the cost of any failed drug tests where they will act as the employer once the job is secured, eg when the person's wages will be paid by the recruitment agency.

chunks.title: Standard rates that can be reimbursed for failed drug tests — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: There are standard rates that can be reimbursed to the potential employer for a failed drug test. These amounts only cover the actual and reasonable costs of the tests. The standard rate of payment will be paid to the employer regardless of the amount that they charge (ie regardless of whether the amount is higher or lower). For recompliance drug testing the full cost can be paid. Standard rate of payment for screening tests In-house testing When an employer has staff on their premises that have been trained to the New Zealand Drug Testing Standard, and have attained the relevant NZQA unit standards $30 External agency testing Where employers contract a drug testing company to do pre-employment drug testing procedures on their behalf $70 Standard rate of payment for evidential tests Evidential testing When an employer sends samples to a laboratory for evidential testing, the cost associated with this type of testing is significantly higher than a screening test $120 Standard rate of payment for recompliance Screening or evidential tests Actual and reasonable costs - generally this should be the same as the standard rates of payment The costs for alcohol testing cannot be reimbursed as this type of test is not included as a drug test.

chunks.title: Debt recovery — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Once the cost of the failed drug test is reimbursed to the employer, it must be established as a debt to the partner. The amount of the debt is the amount that has been reimbursed to the employer. For more information see: - Reimbursement and claims for employers / Drug test agencies [no link find out why] Debt repayment options must be discussed with the partner giving consideration to any other debts the partner may have. Add notes to the partner's record about the negotiated debt repayment.

chunks.title: Removing incentive payments — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Removing incentive payments
Incentive payments should be removed when the young partner:
- is subject to a grade 1, 2 or 3 sanction
- is in hospital for longer than 13 weeks and they are receiving the hospital rate of payment
- no longer has a dependent child (Parent education incentive only)
- has intentionally acted in a way that is inconsistent with the purpose of the incentives
Note young people can continue to receive their incentive payments once they are earned if they are granted an exemption from their obligations, unless the reason the exemption is needed is because they have acted in a way that is inconsistent with the purpose of the incentive.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Report Job Search — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Report Job Search
Report Job Search is a non-financial sanction that can be imposed on a partner instead of a Grade 1 financial sanction. It is intended to help partners actively participate in finding suitable employment.
In a 4-week period, a partner must:
- do at least 3 job search activities a week and
- report to MSD on the job-search activities they have done each week and
- provide MSD with evidence of their job-search activities at the end of the 4-week period
MSD must be satisfied the evidence provided is sufficient.
Once a partner completes 4 weeks of Report Job Search, they are considered to have recomplied with their obligations and don't need to complete any other recompliance activities.

chunks.title: Report to service provider or Work and Income on progress — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Report to service provider or Work and Income on progress
A young partner is required to report to their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service on how they are satisfactorily meeting their obligation to be:
- in education, training or work-based learning
- participating in a budgeting programme and
- if they are a parent, participating in a parenting education programme and other parenting obligations
A service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service can ask a young partner to report to them by either phone, email or in person and will determine how often the young partner must report.
The frequency of reporting must be reasonable and take into account:
- the length of the activity
- how often the young partner is required to attend
- whether a young partner has failed to comply with their obligations in the past
Generally a young partner should not be required to report more than once a week.
Example
The service provider sets an activity for a young partner to attend a budgeting programme and asks that they report on their progress when they commence the programme and when they attend each week.
A young partner undertakes the budgeting programme. They phone their service provider when they commence the programme and report in each week of the programme to confirm their attendance.
For more information see:
- Money management activity
- Youth activity obligations

chunks.title: Reporting progress — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Reporting progress
You can require a partner to report on their progress in meeting their work or work preparation obligations.
You must advise the partner that if they fail to comply with this obligation, without a good and sufficient reason, they have an obligations failure.
## Partners with work preparation obligations
You can require a partner to report on their progress in meeting their work preparation obligations. This may include reporting on progress of any activities they have been required to undertake.
A partner can report by either phone, email or in person.
## Example
You have asked a partner with a three year old child to research child care options and training options available in their community and to call you in a month to update you on their progress.
If the client does not contact you, you should initiate an obligations failure.
## Partners with work obligations
You can require a partner with work obligations to report on their job search progress.
A partner can report by either phone, email or in person. Generally a partner should not be required to report more than once a week.
## Example
You have asked the partner to register with various recruitment agencies and call you weekly to update on their job search progress.
If the partner does not contact you, you should initiate an obligations failure.

chunks.title: Restoring incentive payments — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Restoring incentive payments
The service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service can recommend that an incentive payment be returned to the young partner, if they are satisfied that the young partner is now acting in a way that is consistent with the aims of the incentive payment.
When the incentives will be returned depends on:
- the reason that the incentive was removed
- whether the young partner has undertaken or completed steps to address their actions
- whether the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service is satisfied that the young partner is now acting in a way that is consistent with the aims of the incentive payment
For more information see:

chunks.title: Restricted circumstances guidelines — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Restricted circumstances guidelines
You must consider the following factors in relation to the restricted circumstances that make the child's attendance at school unreasonable.
It can be unreasonable for that child to attend school:
- if there is a no school bus or
- no suitable transport and
- there is a significant distance between their home and school
It may also be unreasonable for the child to attend the nearest school because the child has particular needs that prevent them from attending the nearest school, for example:
- special needs such as physical or intellectual disability, chronic or recurring illness
- learning or behavioural difficulties or
- exclusion from the school

chunks.title: Retirement payments — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A retirement payment is a payment made to an employee on retirement when employment is fully terminated. It may also be known as retiring leave, a retiring allowance or a retiring gratuity. Common situations that lead to employment terminating due to retirement include: - the employee's decision - the terms of a union contract - the length of service of the employee - the employer's policy

chunks.title: What a retirement payment is not — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: It is important to differentiate between the types of payments a person gets when their employment ends to know how they affect benefit entitlement. Retirement payments do not include: - a payment solely due to a seasonal lay-off - a payment that depends on the completion of: a fixed-term engagement oran engagement to complete work specified in a contract - a fixed-term engagement or - an engagement to complete work specified in a contract - a payment instead of notice terminating the employment - any payment (including holiday pay) if MSD considers that, but for the termination of the employment, it would have been paid as monetary remuneration of the person - any payment made by a company, to a director of a company or - any payment from a superannuation fund or other similar payment Note some of these other payments may affect the date employment ceased and may be included in the income assessment when calculating the length of the initial stand-down.

chunks.title: How retirement payments affect benefit payments — main benefits > emergency benefit
