chunks.text: Retirement payments can be paid in one or more lump sums or on a periodical basis. Payment received before a benefit is granted Retirement payments are included in the assessment of a person's last 26 or 52 weeks' income to determine the length of their initial stand-down). Retirement payments do affect the date employment ceased. Payment received after a benefit is granted When a client receiving a benefit has been working and having their earnings charged then receives a retirement payment, this payment is not regarded as income for benefit purposes. However, it will be regarded as a cash asset and may affect any Extra Help the client is receiving. Different rules apply for retirement payments received more than 52 weeks after the person's employment ceased. For more information see: - Delayed retirement payments

chunks.title: Not retiring — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: In some situations a person may cease their employment for a reason other than retirement and get a retirement payment as part of their final pay. For example, when a person resigns from their role voluntarily because they want to change careers or have a holiday. When a person gets a retirement payment as part of their final pay but is not retiring, the retirement payment forms part of their earnings received in the 26 weeks prior to the commencement of benefit. Retirement pay received when a person is not retiring does not affect the date employment ceased.

chunks.title: Returned to youth money management — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Returned to youth money management
A young partner can be returned to youth money management for the following reasons:
- they are subject to a grade 1, 2 or 3 sanction or
- they have demonstrated poor financial judgement
If a young partner is subject to youth money management, they will continue to be subject to youth money management once they have recomplied.
## Exception
When young partners are sanctioned and they are not subject to youth money management because they have earned the right to manage their own money, they won't be put back on youth money management like those clients on Youth Payment and Young Parent Payment. This ensures the sanctions for clients who aren't subject to youth money management remain graduated through any obligation failures.
## Sanction has been imposed
After a sanction has been imposed, the young partner will be returned to youth money management when they recomply. To earn the right to manage their money again, the service provided or Work and Income 'in-house' service will need to be satisfied that the young person has been demonstrating a continued compliance with their obligations.
## Poor financial judgement
Generally a young partner may be considered to have poor financial judgement if they have:
- sought or accessed hardship assistance without a good and sufficient reason, or where they could have avoided the application (eg, they did not pay their power account, but spent the money on clothes)
- purchased an unnecessary item on credit
- spent their in-hand allowance on items that are inappropriate for their situation (eg, alcohol and cigarettes and had no money to buy their weekly bus pass)
- increased their costs unnecessarily (eg, moved into more expensive accommodation)
- not used their part-time earnings in a way that is appropriate for their situation (eg bought very expensive clothing items when they should have saved for their car registration)
- entered a relationship with a coercive partner, who is starting to control their money or are being unduly influenced by peer pressure
## In-hand allowance and incentives
When a young partner is returned to youth money management because they have demonstrated poor financial judgement, they will retain their in-hand allowance and any incentives earned.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Removing incentive payment as a result of an activity obligations failure — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Removing incentive payment as a result of an activity obligations failure
If a young partner has a grade 1 or grade 2 sanction and they are receiving an incentive payment, these payments are also suspended until the young partner recomplies with the obligation they failed.
If a young partner has a grade 3 sanction imposed, any incentive payment they are receiving is cancelled.
## Returning incentive payment if young partner recomplies
Grade 1 and 2 sanctions
Incentive payments can be returned from the date the young person has started their recompliance activity.
Grade 3 - Failure to comply with education obligation
Where the failure that led to the cancellation of the young partner's portion of the benefit was due to failing to comply with their obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning, the education incentive cannot be regranted if the main benefit is regranted.
The young partner must earn this incentive again by completing another 6 months commitment to education, training or work-based learning.
Example
A young partner fails their activity obligations for a third time because they did not go to school. They are receiving incentive payments for education and budgeting. When they undertake a 6 week approved activity their portion of the main benefit is restarted and their budgeting incentive is returned at the same time. The education incentive is not returned and the young partner must re-earn this incentive by completing a further 6 months of education or training.
## Failure for other reason
For any other failure reason, the incentive payment for budgeting and education can be regranted when the young partner recomplies.
Example
A young partner has earned the budgeting and education incentives. They fail activity obligations for a third time for refusing to attend their budgeting discussions with their service provider. The young partner undertakes a 6 week approved activity and their Youth Payment is restarted and both the budgeting and education incentives are returned at the same time.

chunks.title: Reviewing or disputing the drug test failure and sanction — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Reviewing or disputing the drug test failure and sanction
A partner has the right to dispute or review any decision they disagree with relating to:
- an obligations failure or
- a sanction being imposed
A partner can do this by:
- disputing the decision or
- lodging a formal Review of Decision
A Review of Decision can be lodged at any stage within 3 months of the obligations failure being initiated, or within 3 months of the sanction being imposed.
If a partner disputes their obligations failure or sanction more than 20 working days after it is initiated or imposed, you need to advise the partner to lodge a formal Review of Decision in writing.
For more information see:
- The disputes process
- Recording decisions on a dispute
## Appealing to the Medical Appeal Board
A partner can only lodge an appeal to the Medical Appeal board for a decision relating to a drug test failure when a decision was made that they:
- did not have a good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation, and
- the reason given for the failure was that the client was either: addicted to controlled drugs ordependent on controlled drugs
- addicted to controlled drugs or
- dependent on controlled drugs
A partner is not required to dispute a decision before lodging a review of decision or appealing to the Medical Appeal Board (drug test failure only).
For more information see:
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Core policy Medical Appeal Board

chunks.title: Sanctions for a couple with dependent children - both fail their obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Couples with dependent children who both fail their obligations at the same time do not have their whole benefit sanctioned. Instead, a maximum financial sanction of 50% of the total benefit may be imposed. The balance of the benefit payable is known as 50% protection. Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only 1 sanction will be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.

chunks.title: Young partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The effect of the sanction for a young partner depends on whether the client is youth money managed or not. For more information see:

chunks.title: Grade 1 sanction — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If both clients fail their obligations for the first time, each person's portion of the benefit is reduced by 50% unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed. The couple will continue to get a maximum of 50% of their married rate of benefit. While their benefit is reduced, the couple can continue to get extra help. This includes the Winter Energy Payment. If the client or partner does not recomply within 4 weeks, they will have their portion of the benefit suspended. While part of the benefit is suspended, the couple can get 50% of any Extra help they are entitled to. However, they can get the full rate of the Winter Energy Payment as they are still getting a qualifying benefit. Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or their portion of the benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks. For more information see: - Recompliance - Non-financial sanctions

chunks.title: Grade 2 sanction — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If both clients fail their obligations a second time, 50% of the couple's benefit is suspended. The couple will continue to get a maximum of 50% of their married rate of benefit. While part of the benefit is suspended, the couple can get 50% of any extra help they are entitled to. However, they can get the full rate of the Winter Energy Payment as they are still getting a qualifying benefit. Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or their portion of the benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks. Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If both clients fail their obligations a third time, 50% of the couple's benefit is cancelled. The couple will continue to get a maximum of 50% of their married rate of benefit until they recomply. If both clients have a non-entitlement period for 13 weeks, both clients may get a provisional benefit if they start a 6 week approved activity or programme of activities. While part of the benefit is cancelled, the couple gets 50% of any extra help they are entitled to. However, they can get the full rate of the Winter Energy Payment as they are still getting a qualifying benefit. For more information see: - Recompliance

chunks.title: Processing 50% payments — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When both clients fail their obligations at the same time and a financial sanction is imposed for each person, the couple must continue to get a maximum of 50% of their married rate of benefit. This must be paid manually, and will depend on which client failed their obligations first. For more information on this process see: - Work and work preparation obligations [no link find out why]

chunks.title: One client recomplies first — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If the primary client recomplies first, their portion of benefit and extra help must be resumed or regranted. The primary client will get the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment. The partner's benefit must remain sanctioned until they recomply. If the partner recomplies first, their portion of benefit and extra help is not able to be resumed or regranted as the primary record is not current. For information on how to process this see: - Work and work preparation obligations [no link find out why]

chunks.title: 50% protection and abatement of income — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The 50% protection is applied to half the main benefit rate (eg the married rate) before any reduction of income. Any income will reduce benefit by 35 cents for every $1.00 of total income over $160 per week from the 50% protection payment. For more information see: - Charging income

chunks.title: Client does not recomply — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If either client has not recomplied after 2 weeks, MSD will need to contact them to discuss financial assistance and recompliance. If they still have not recomplied at 4 weeks MSD will need to send a letter advising they need to attend an appointment to discuss ongoing entitlement to benefit. For more information on this process see: - Sanction period - Two week intervention [no link find out why] - Sanction period - Four week intervention [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Grade 1 sanction — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If both partners fail their obligations for the first time, each person's portion of the benefit is reduced by 50%, unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed. For more information on non-financial sanctions see: - Non-financial sanctions The couple will continue to get a total of 50% of the married rate. While their benefit is reduced, the couple can continue to get supplementary assistance. Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid as the client is still getting a qualifying benefit. If either partner has not recomplied within 4 weeks, they will have their portion of the benefit and supplementary assistance suspended. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid to the client who has not recomplied as they are not getting a qualifying benefit. Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or their portion of the benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures initiated on the same day.

chunks.title: Grade 2 sanction — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If both partners fail their obligations for the second time, each person's portion of the benefit is suspended. While the benefit is suspended, the couple's supplementary assistance is also suspended. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid as they are not getting a qualifying benefit. Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or their portion of the benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks. Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures initiated on the same day.

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: If both partners fail their obligations for a third time, each person's portion of the benefit is cancelled. They have a non-entitlement period for a period of 13 weeks. The client may get a provisional benefit if they start a 6 week approved activity or programme of activities. If they have not started a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities, they may reapply at the end of the non-entitlement period to get a benefit. When the client's benefit is cancelled, supplementary assistance is also cancelled. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid as they are not getting a qualifying benefit.

chunks.title: Grade 1 sanction — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Grade 1 sanction
A first obligations failure means the client's benefit is reduced by 50%, unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed.
For more information on non-financial sanctions see:
- Non-financial sanctions
While their benefit is reduced, the client can continue to get supplementary assistance. Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid as the client is still getting a qualifying benefit.
If the client has not recomplied within 4 weeks, they will have their benefit suspended along with all supplementary assistance (including Winter Energy Payment).
Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or the payment is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.
Note if a client has more than 1 obligation failure initiated on the same day, only 1 sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures initiated on the same day.
## Grade 2 sanction
A second obligations failure means the client's benefit is suspended. When their benefit is suspended, any supplementary assistance the client was getting is also suspended. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid as the client is not getting a qualifying benefit.
Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or the payment is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.
Note if a client has more than 1 obligation failure initiated on the same day, only 1 sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures initiated on the same day.
## Grade 3 sanction
A third obligations failure means the client's benefit is cancelled and they have a non-entitlement period for 13 weeks. The client may get a provisional benefit if they start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities.
When the client's benefit is cancelled, supplementary assistance is also cancelled. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid as the client is not getting a qualifying benefit.
If they have not started a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities, they may reapply at the end of the non-entitlement period to get a benefit.
For more information see:
- Recompliance

chunks.title: Sanctions for young partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The effect of the sanction of the client's assistance for a young partner depends on whether the client is money managed or not.

chunks.title: Client is youth money managed — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a client is youth money managed, has an obligations failure and has not recomplied within the 5 working day notice period, the effect of the sanction on the client's assistance is the same as for Youth Payment and Young Parent Payment (where they have dependent children).

chunks.title: Grade 1 and 2 sanctions — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The client who is not required to get Youth Services and is not youth money managed will continue to get their portion of the assistance. They can continue to get their portion of the Winter Energy Payment. For a client who is required to get Youth Services and is youth money managed, a first or second failure means suspension of the in-hand allowance and any incentive payments, until the client recomplies with the obligation they have failed (or obligations if they have failed to comply with one or more of their obligations). The client can continue to get any Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support to which they are entitled. The young partner can continue to get their portion of the Winter Energy Payment. If the client has not recomplied within 4 weeks the whole of their benefit and any incentive payments are suspended along with any Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Winter Energy Payment being the client gets. Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or the payment is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The client who is not required to get Youth Services and is not youth money managed will continue to get their portion of the assistance. The client will get the full couple rate of the Winter Energy Payment. If the person who is required to get Youth Services and is youth money managed fails their obligations for a third time: - their portion of the benefit, and any incentive payments, is cancelled immediately - their portion of Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support and Winter Energy Payment is cancelled and - the young person is subject to a non-entitlement period for 13 weeks from the date of cancellation The client may get a provisional benefit if they start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities. If the client does not start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities, they must reapply at the end of their non-entitlement period to get a benefit. Note Disability Allowance can continue to be paid during a non-entitlement period. For more information see:

chunks.title: Client is not youth money managed — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: When a client is not youth money managed and has an obligations failure and has not recomplied within the 5 working day notice period, the effect of the sanction on the client's assistance is the same as for their main benefit except that any incentive payments being paid will also stop, and unlike Youth Payment clients who have earned the right to get their payment directly, a young partner will not be returned to youth money management after they have been sanctioned. For more information see:

chunks.title: Seasonal Assistance during short breaks — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Seasonal Assistance during short breaks
Generally, clients requiring assistance during short breaks in seasonal work of less than 4 weeks should be considered for Seasonal Work Assistance.
However, many seasonal workers face short periods of unemployment or hardship where they are not paid by their employer and are not eligible for the Seasonal Work Assistance. This is because:
- they have accessed their full entitlement to Seasonal Work Assistance
- it is a short transition time between jobs (another employer but they are not starting work for a week or two)
- there is a delay with the same employer (ie pruning to picking) or
- because of other reasons such as the weather or machinery breakdowns
If the break in employment is for 4 weeks or more, benefit assistance such as Jobseeker Support should be considered.
Note to be eligible for Emergency Benefit the client must meet the basic eligibility requirements.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Determining the reason for insufficient livelihood
- Not eligible for another benefit
- Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: Secondary education — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Secondary education
Participating in secondary education is the preferred way for a young partner to meet their activity obligation of being in or available for full-time secondary or tertiary education, employment-related training or work-based learning.
They must be working towards a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification.
A young partner enrolled in secondary education (including composite schools, correspondence schools, and secondary schools) must:
- regularly attend classes
- compete assignments and
- complete other course requirements
## School holidays
You may require a young partner to undertake other activities that work towards NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualifications during the summer holidays.
For more information see:
- Definition of 'full-time'
- NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification
- Youth activity obligations
- Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months

chunks.title: Self-imposed stand-down — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Self-imposed stand-down
Where a client knows that they will have a stand-down and delays their application, the commencement date will be:
- the day after initial stand-down ends or
- the application date
whichever is the later.

chunks.title: Setting appropriate activities for partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Setting appropriate activities for partners
After a discussion with a partner you will need to determine the most appropriate activities for them to undertake. To decide which activities are the most appropriate you should consider:
- the partner's individual circumstances
- whether the activity is suitable for the partner
- whether the partner has work preparation obligations or work obligations
Note you do not need to seek the client's agreement to the activities that you require them to complete.
Once you and the partner have discussed which activities will be appropriate include them in the partner's Service Plan.
## Types of activities
You should refer the partner to appropriate activities to improve their work-readiness or prospects for employment.
Appropriate activities may include (but are not limited to):
Work obligations
Work preparation obligations
A job interview
Contacting employers
Developing or updating a C.V.
Developing or updating a C.V.
Obtaining a driver's licence
Obtaining a driver's licence
Work assessment
Work assessment
Programme or seminar to increase particular skills or enhance motivation
Programme or seminar to increase particular skills or enhance motivation
Work experience or work exploration activity
Work experience or work exploration activity
Employment related training
Employment related training
Completing a high school qualification
Completing further study
Completing further study
Researching childcare options available in the community
Researching childcare options available in the community
You must take reasonable steps to arrange for the partner to undertake an activity.
Note a partner must not be required to undertake Activity in Community. If a partner would like to undertake an Activity in the Community you may include it in their Service Plan. However, if the partner fails to complete the activity you must not initiate an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Process for deciding appropriate activities
- Work preparation obligations - partners
- Work obligations - partners
- Rehabilitation - partners
- Activity Summary

chunks.title: Severance payments — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Severance payments may be made by an employer as part of a severance agreement to help resolve an unsatisfactory employment situation by ending the employment relationship. They are over and above what a person is entitled to under their employment agreement. The term severance is often used in place of redundancy, however redundancy payments and severance payments are different. A severance agreement is usually made when there is no suitable solution to a problem, such as when there are no valid grounds for the employer to end the person's employment or doing so would require a lengthy formal process. A severance agreement may also be made when the employer faces risky and costly adverse action from the employee, such as a personal grievance claim or legal action. Common situations that lead to a severance agreement include: - the employer isn't satisfied with the employee's performance - the employee is facing a disciplinary process - the employee makes a personal grievance or constructive dismissal claim - a dispute over renegotiation of position description, remuneration, or terms of employment - claims of bullying, harassment or stress - a dispute about the process or outcome of a restructure - a personality clash between an employee and their manager, or between managers

chunks.title: What a severance payment is not — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: It is important to distinguish between the different types of payments a person gets when their employment ends to know how they affect benefit entitlement. Any payment the person is entitled to under their employment agreement is not a severance payment. These include: - holiday pay - pay in lieu of notice - pay in lieu of accumulated leave e.g. sick leave - pay in lieu of completing a fixed-term contract (if it is ended early) - redundancy payments - retirement payments - benefits the person became entitled to before they left e.g. bonus or incentive payments Note some of these payments may affect the date employment ceased and may be included in the income assessment when calculating the length of the initial stand-down.

chunks.title: How severance payments affect commencement date — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Payment received before a benefit is granted Severance payments are included in the assessment of a person's last 26 or 52 weeks' income to determine the length of their initial stand-down. Severance payments do not affect the date employment ceased. Payment received after a benefit is granted Severance payments are charged as income except for the following payments: - compensation for hurt and humiliation - contribution towards legal fees - reimbursement for other costs incurred e.g. medical costs, relocation, career services, retraining These payments must not be treated as income.

chunks.title: Single and caring for a child — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Single and caring for a child
Generally, a single client caring for a dependent child will get the Sole Parent Support (where their partner is deceased).
Where the client cannot get Sole Parent Support, Jobseeker Support or any other benefit, Emergency Benefit may be considered.
Note where it is justified an Emergency Benefit is to be granted equivalent to Sole Parent Support for a client where their youngest dependent child is under the age of 14 years, Emergency Maintenance Allowance is the appropriate Emergency Benefit.
Situations include:
- split care - other parent getting Sole Parent Support
Note if the court has ordered a split care arrangement, both parents can get Sole Parent Support
In addition to this:
- the child must be dependent and
- the client cannot work or look for work because they are caring for the child
## Caring for child not their own
When a client is caring for a child that is not their own, consider the following:
- Can the client be considered as the parent of the child
- What are the reasons they are caring for the child?
- How long will they be caring for the child?
- If long term, are more formal arrangements being considered (for example adoption)?
- Have any other reasonable caring arrangements been considered?
- Do the parents of the child have the ability to contribute to the cost of care?
- Is the child a qualifying child for Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit?
Note this emergency assistance is only available in cases of genuine need where a person has accepted responsibility for a child. It is not an incentive for people to take children into their care.
## Child is qualifying child for Unsupported Child Benefit or Orphans Benefit
When a client is eligible for an Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit, this assistance must be granted before Emergency Benefit is considered.

chunks.title: Social obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Social obligations
A client and their partner (if any) receiving Emergency Benefit have social obligations that apply for each dependent child in their care. This includes any children for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid.
A client and their partner (if any) must take all reasonable steps to meet all of the social obligations that apply for each child. The social obligations that apply for each child depend on the age of the child.
Where the client is in a relationship the social obligations apply to both the client and their partner.
When required, clients and their partner (if any) need to take all reasonable steps to meet the following social obligations. The child must be:
- enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation and
- up-to-date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks (for children aged under 5 years old) and
- enrolled in and attending 1 of the following from 3 years of age until they start school: an approved early childhood education programme orTe Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - The Correspondence School oranother approved parenting and early childhood home education programme
- an approved early childhood education programme or
- Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - The Correspondence School or
- another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme
- enrolled in and attending school from the age of 5 or 6 years of age (depending on when they start school)
When required, a client and their partner (if any) must:
- attend and participate in interviews with MSD to discuss meeting their social obligations and
- advise on progress where they have not been able to meet their social obligations
A client is only required to meet social obligations from the time they begin to receive a benefit.
Clients in the process of applying for Emergency Benefit or who have a future commencement date of their Emergency Benefit are not required to meet their social obligations. Clients are also not required to meet social obligations that would have been relevant prior to them receiving a benefit.
For example, a client who starts receiving a benefit when their child is between 3 and 4 months old cannot be sanctioned for not having completed the core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks a child should have at ages 4 to 6 weeks.

chunks.title: Social obligations recompliance (13-week non-entitlement period) — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Social obligations recompliance (13-week non-entitlement period)
If a client or partner fails their obligations for a third time, their benefit is reduced or cancelled. For the client or partner to increase their benefit they must undertake a 6 week recompliance activity or programme of activities and reapply for a benefit.
If the third obligation failure is a social obligation failure, the standard 6 week recompliance activities may not be appropriate as some partners do not have work obligations and cannot work or be in training for a period of 6 weeks.
In this situation, a programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate for the client.
## Example 1
Short term approved activities to consider for an Emergency Benefit partner with part-time work obligations and social obligations, where the third failure was a social obligations failure.
Week 1
Take reasonable steps to talk to providers of appropriate recognised early childhood education programme
Week 2
Take reasonable steps to enrol their child in a recognised early childhood education programmes
Week 3
CV seminar
Week 4
Attend presentation seminar approved by Work and Income
Week 5
Attend a local parenting programme that provides support for families
Week 6
Meet with case manager to talk about what reasonable steps have been taken to enrol the child in a recognised early childhood education programme and discuss how the other activities went
Note a programme of suitable activities for a client with part-time work obligations should be:
- for no more than 20 hours each week
## Example 2
Example of short term approved activities to consider for an Emergency Benefit client with social obligations, where the third failure was a social obligations failure.
Week 1
Make contact with the local Family Start whanau worker and arrange a meeting with them
Week 2
Family Start whanau worker visit
Week 3
Contact a Well Child/Tamariki provider and arrange a visit
Week 4
Contact the local medical centre to ensure the children are enrolled in primary health care
Week 5
Talk to appropriate providers of recognised early childhood education programmes
Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider visit
Week 6
Meet with a case manager about what steps have been taken

chunks.title: Social rehabilitation programmes — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Social rehabilitation programmes
Examples of social rehabilitation programmes include (but are not limited to):
- social rehabilitation for drug, alcohol or mental health
- social rehabilitation for abuse victims
- social rehabilitation for repeat offenders
A social rehabilitation provider can include (but are not limited to):
- Salvation Army
- Anglican Social Services
- Arohanui Christian Trust
For more information see:
- Extra help Social Rehabilitation Assistance

chunks.title: Special circumstances justifying delay in activity obligation — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Special circumstances justifying delay in activity obligation
A young partner may have special circumstances that justify not having to attend a Teen Parent Unit when their youngest dependent child is 6 months old even if there is a suitable place available.
Special circumstances include, but are not limited to, the:
- young partner's child having an uncontrolled health condition, such as asthma, or the child having specific health and disability needs
- young partner’s ability to return to school because of an illness or post-natal mental health issues
- young partner struggling with the challenge of being a new parent (supported by information received from their Well Child/Tamariki Ora or a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner) and returning to education or training being detrimental to them and/or their child
- young partner having difficulty bonding with their child (supported by information received from their Well Child/Tamariki Ora registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner) and returning to education or training being detrimental to them and/or their child
- dynamics with the other participants of the Teen Parent Unit making the young partner's attendance at the Teen Parent Unit inappropriate
## Special circumstances exist
If the service provider or MSD are satisfied there are special circumstances that justify the delay in the obligation to return to education at the Teen Parent Unit, the obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning will apply from the earliest of either:
- a suitable place becoming available and there are no longer special circumstances that delay the obligation to return to education at the Teen Parent Unit or
- the young partner's youngest child reaching the age of 12 months

chunks.title: Special rates - residential parole — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Special rates - residential parole
Single clients generally receive the single rate of benefit that is the same rate as Jobseeker Support.
## Clients with partners
It is important that the partner in the community does not suffer a reduction in income support payments as a result of the client's release to residential parole. When assessing the rate of payment for the client, the benefit is not split in half.
If the client's partner is receiving Sole Parent Support, the partner will continue to receive it at the sole parent rate of benefit.
The rate payable to the client will be the difference between:
- the full married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit and
- the full rate of Sole Parent Support paid to the partner in the community
Where the partner in the community receives a benefit other than Sole Parent Support, the partner can be included in the Emergency Benefit. The partner will continue to receive the same rate of benefit, sole parent rate of benefit or single rate if they do not have dependent children.
The rate of payment to the client will be the difference between:
- the married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit and
- the single/sole parent rate that the partner is receiving
For more information about including a client in their partner's benefit see:
- SWIFTT process - residential parole
Before working out the rate that can be paid to each partner, Extra help will need to be reviewed to reflect the new relationship status.
When the partner in the community has dependent children, family tax credit payments will need to be made to the primary record.
For a brief overview of what amount of benefit that can be paid in these situations see:
- Summary of rates

chunks.title: Students aged 16 or 17 years — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Students aged 16 or 17 years
If a client is 16 or 17 years old and is a full time student they may be eligible for Jobseeker Support for students on grounds of hardship during the term break.
Eligibility for Jobseeker Support for students on grounds of hardship should be considered before looking at Emergency Benefit.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
An Emergency Benefit may be considered for clients who do not meet the criteria for Jobseeker Support for students on grounds of hardship (that is either they are not a full-time student, they are not married or in a civil union, they do not meet the exceptional circumstances criteria for Youth Payment or they are not available for work) when they:
- cannot get another benefit
- cannot earn a sufficient livelihood and
- are in hardship
Note to consider Emergency Benefit for these clients determine the reason why they are not eligible.
You will also need to consider the ability of the client's partner or parents to support them during this term break.
For more information see:
- Independent Circumstances Allowance
- Client in hardship
- Determining the reason for insufficient livelihood
- Conditions of grant
- Not eligible for another benefit

chunks.title: Suitability of employment-related training or course — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The employment-related training and courses a client must attend and participate in as part of their Upskilling sanction will generally be online. In some instances, an in-person employment-related training or course can be recommended or approved if MSD staff consider it suitable for the client's circumstances. Suitability is based on a client's level of expertise and skills. There are some general factors that should be considered when determining if a training or course is suitable for a client. For example: - where a client lives (e.g. the distance the client has to travel to get to the training or course) - a client's age and family situation (e.g. caretaking responsibilities at certain times) - any previous job experience and education - any specific barriers to employment that an employment-related training or course may address, (e.g. a health condition or disability, or caring responsibilities) - if a client has already participated in other employment-related training or courses, or any of MSD's other employment programmes or services Note a client's individual circumstances will determine what is considered suitable. Each activity should be considered on a case-by-case basis.

chunks.title: MSD Digital Suite courses — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD has a wide range of Digital Suite courses that staff can assign to clients. These courses should be considered for clients who have Upskilling imposed on them first before any other option. MSD should consider assigning a different suitable employment-related training or course, or assigning a different type of sanction if: - a client has already completed the MSD Digital Suite courses or - the Digital Suite courses are not relevant for the client

chunks.title: Any other suitable courses — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: In some situations, a client may participate in a different employment-related training or course that is not part of MSD's Digital Suite. This will only be appropriate and approved by MSD if it is considered suitable for the client and meets the Upskilling requirements. Alternative suitable employment-related training or courses could include (but are not limited to): - online or in-person education courses offered by external providers (e.g. courses run through local libraries, Coursera, edX or Skillshare) - MSD-contracted courses such as (e.g. CV services or Work Readiness courses) - any other suitable courses identified by staff or clients that meet the requirements of the sanction (e.g. a barista course) It may be difficult for MSD to identify the legitimacy of these employment-related training or courses as well as attendance and participation as they are not included in MSD's Digital Suite courses. This is why other suitable employment-related training, and courses must be approved at the discretion of staff. Note as this is a non-financial sanction, there is no funding for clients to pay for costs associated with training or courses, such as course fees, travel, internet, a computer, or device.

chunks.title: Commitment to completing the requirements of Upskilling — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Before imposing an employment-related training or course on a client, MSD must be confident that the training or course has sufficient training, coursework and activity(s) to fulfil the required hours and weeks needed to complete Upskilling. If MSD is unsure that an employment-related training or course would meet the Upskilling requirements, it should not be imposed on a client. Note a client may be able to complete Upskilling through more than one employment-related training or course.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Francesca failed a work obligation, and her case manager has imposed Upskilling as a non-financial sanction. Francesca has already completed most of MSD's Digital Suite courses while looking for work. Francesca's case manager determines that assigning her another course from MSD's Digital Suite would not be suitable. Francesca asks to do a UX design course through Coursera as she has seen roles available in this industry and is interested in this work. Coursera is a reputable agency and Francesca's case manager determines that this course meets the requirements of the Upskilling sanction. This course is assigned to Francesca as a suitable employment-related training or course.

chunks.title: Suitability of position and organisation — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A partner is only required to complete the 4-weeks of Community Work Experience if MSD is satisfied the organisation and the position are suitable. Suitability will be different for each partner based on their level of capability, however there are general considerations for each position that MSD must take into account.

chunks.title: Organisation — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Suitable organisations can be community or volunteer organisations. These organisations may have existing relationship with MSD, however this is not required. To be suitable, an organisation should: - not be for profit - not be public sector, e.g. central or local government or a Crown entity - have an internal organisation structure, e.g. has defined key functions, roles and responsibilities - be self-governing – the organisation primarily controls its own management and operations - not be something people are required to contribute time to by law, e.g. jury duty. Organisations are not suitable if: - they have previously breached employment law, or - their area of focus would likely be inappropriate or unacceptable to the wider community, or - a partner completing Community Work Experience at this organisation is likely to be a reputational risk to MSD. The organisation must be confident they can provide a partner with the required hours and 4 consecutive weeks needed to complete their Community Work Experience. If the organisation is unsure, the position would not be suitable for the partner. Note partners may secure multiple positions to complete their Community Work Experience. For more information see: Period of Community Work Experience.

chunks.title: Position — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: To be suitable, a position should: - be for a role that would otherwise be met by a volunteer, e.g. is not a role that would normally be paid employment - have activities that are reasonable and fair for the partner to complete – for example, a position that requires a lot of work on the computer would not be suitable for a partner with low computer literacy - not put the personal safety of the partner or others at risk - not include activities that could be considered inappropriate or may damage MSD's reputation, e.g. serving alcohol, being involved in gambling, or supporting particular political gain

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Donna has Community Work Experience imposed and is searching for a suitable organisation and position. Donna contacts her local rugby club to see if they have any volunteer positions available that would help her to meet the Community Work Experience requirements. The rugby club can offer Donna at least 5 hours of work for 4 weeks, but tells her they mostly need her help to run the bar. Donna gets in touch with MSD and tells MSD what the position will involve. Although the rugby club is a suitable organisation, it's not appropriate for Donna to be serving alcohol as part of her Community Work Experience, as this could damage MSD's reputation. Donna is advised that the work needed at the rugby club is not suitable for the purpose of the sanction, and to continue looking for a suitable position.

chunks.title: Suitable employment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Suitable employment
Suitable employment varies between clients depending on their individual circumstances.
To meet their work obligations partners need to be available for or take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of:
- at least 30 hours a week (partners with full-time work obligations)
- at least 20 hours a week (partners with part-time work obligations)
## Deciding if a job is suitable
When deciding on whether a job is suitable for a partner, you need to consider the following (but is not limited to):
- appropriate hours of employment, eg hours are not excessive
- access to childcare
- family commitments
- religious commitments
- jobs which offend strongly held views
- days of the week
- type of employment
- skills required
- experience
- location of the job
- wages
- number of hours per week is between 15 and 25 hours for partners with part-time work obligations
- number of hours per week is between 20 and 40 hours for partners with full-time work obligations
For more information see:
- Hours range for suitable employment
- Meeting job search requirements
- Employment trial period of up to 90 days
- Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements

chunks.text:

chunks.title: SWIFTT process - residential parole — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## SWIFTT process - residential parole
When you include the partner in the clients benefit SWIFTT will automatically pay half of the benefit to the client and half to their partner.
To pay the client an amount less than 50%:
Step 1 Include the partner in the client's benefit.
Step 2 Set the partner up as a payee on the client's benefit and pay them the difference between the sole parent rate and the married, civil union or de facto rate of the benefit.
## Example
A client has been released onto a residential parole programme. His partner was getting Jobseeker Support paid at the sole parent rate. The client is granted an Emergency Benefit and his partner is included.
The partner cannot suffer a reduction in income therefore she must continue to be paid at the sole parent rate with the client in the rehabilitation programme paid the difference between the sole parent rate and the married, civil union or de facto rate.
Based on the benefit rates as at 1 April 2026 this is calculated as follows:
Jobseeker Support - married, civil union or de facto (with children) rate that SWIFTT will pay
$669.40 ($334.70 each)
Less rate payable to the partner (sole parent rate)
$521.52
equals rate that can be paid to the client
$147.88
Because SWIFTT automatically pays the client $334.70, you need to add the partner as a payee on the client's record to apportion $186.82 ($334.70 - $147.88) to the partner.
This ensures the partner will get the correct sole parent rate of $521.52 ($334.70 + payee $186.82).
