chunks.title: Taking all reasonable steps for enrolling in and attending school — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Taking all reasonable steps for enrolling in and attending school
Reasons to consider a client is taking all reasonable steps to meet this obligation may include (but are not limited to) that:
- the child has a health condition, injury or disability that affects their ability to attend school
- the child is regularly missing classes for no good reason but the Attendance Service is working with the family and the school to get the child attending school again
- the client is actively trying to encourage their child to attend school but the child has behavioural problems and attendance at school is out of the client's control Note you need to record this as an exception reason in OBMAN using 'Child is not permitted to attend' as the obligation reason.
Note if the parent is in the process of being prosecuted under the Education and Training Act 2020, you must not ask them to comply with this social obligation. You need to record this as an exception reason in OBMAN using 'parent is in prosecution for truant child' as the obligation reason.

chunks.title: Taking all reasonable steps to enrol in a recognised early childhood education programme — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Taking all reasonable steps to enrol in a recognised early childhood education programme
A client could be considered to be taking all reasonable steps to enrol their child in a recognised early childhood education programme for reasons including, (but not limited to) that:
- there are shortages of places or availability issues, and the client has a plan in place or has made a commitment to enrol their child when a place becomes available
- there are additional costs of participation that may cause financial hardship to the family, including: travel costs oradditional costs associated with attending the early childhood education programme
- travel costs or
- additional costs associated with attending the early childhood education programme
- the child has behavioural problems meaning attendance at an Early Childhood Education service would be difficult or not possible, for example the child is not currently permitted to attend. (This should be recorded as an exception in OBMAN using "child is not permitted to attend" as the obligation exception reason)
To help clients meet this social obligation you should discuss childcare assistance that may be available to the client.

chunks.title: Taking controlled prescribed medications — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Taking controlled prescribed medications
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes when a partner is taking prescription medication correctly.
Not all prescribed medications affect the results of a drug tests. Generally, only controlled prescribed medications do, such as morphine, codeine or medicinal cannabis. Controlled prescription medications can only be prescribed by a health practitioner or dentist monthly. Controlled prescribed medications need to be used correctly toat the dose the health practitioner recommends and by the person for whom they are prescribed.
Some controlled prescribed medications can may cause a person to be impaired on the job which can cause health and safety issues for employers.
In some situations, screening drug tests can show failed results where controlled prescribed medications have been used. Normally evidential tests will pick up the prescribed medications that have been used.
The partner can be asked to provide verification from a registered health practitioner that they are taking a controlled prescribed medication.
There is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you MSD can provide to the partner.
Note when a partner is asked to take a drug test, they will be asked to declare any prescribed medications they are taking.

chunks.title: IRD number for client or partner who is apportioned assistance — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD may make a written request for evidence of an IRD number for a primary client who is being paid Emergency Benefit. MSD can also request evidence of an IRD number for a partner when they are apportioned a part of the primary client's assistance payment.

chunks.title: Setting or extending the timeframe for providing evidence — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD must provide the client or partner with a minimum of 10 working days to provide IRD number evidence that has been requested in writing. MSD can extend the 10 working day period (in writing) if the client or partner has a reasonable explanation for requiring more than 10 days to provide evidence of their IRD number. This includes considering factors outside the client or partner's control that cause delays, including, but not limited to: - client or partner has a family emergency that caused a delay - processing delays with an external agency (e.g. Inland Revenue, Department of Internal Affairs, etc) - client or partner does not speak English as a first language and has difficulty navigating evidence requirements - client or partner has limited access to the internet, a device, or their local service centre - client or partner has a physical or intellectual disability that makes accessing services difficult - client or partner is injured, disabled, or has a medical condition that makes accessing services difficult.

chunks.title: Notice following an unsuccessful match — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a client and their partner's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the client or partner (in writing) to provide evidence of their IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and 'the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the client a minimum of 10 working days to provide their IRD number evidence or the client's assistance must be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Emergency Benefit and MSD holds an IRD number on record. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Isla's IRD number. MSD provides a notice in writing, giving 10 working days for Isla to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Isla already having an IRD number - Isla not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD must suspend assistance if evidence of IRD number is not received — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD must suspend all taxable and/or income tested assistance the client is getting, including their Emergency Benefit, if evidence of an IRD number is not provided within 10 working days from the written request, or extended period if this has been applied. If the partner has not provided evidence of their IRD number, the partner's taxable and/or income tested assistance must be suspended. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance. Example Koa is receiving Emergency Benefit and MSD does not have an IRD number on record. MSD sends a written request giving 10 working days for Koa to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD receives no response to this request. MSD suspends all Koa's taxable and/or income tested assistance because Koa has not supplied MSD with evidence of their IRD number within the timeframe provided.

chunks.title: IRD evidence may not be requested in some circumstances — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - there are significant factors, that are outside the client's or partner's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number (e.g. a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence), and - the client needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided or - there are significant factors related to a health, injury or disability that are outside the client or partner's control that prevent them from providing evidence of an IRD number, and - an agent cannot be appointed to act on the client or partner's behalf. MSD can determine a later point to request the evidence of the IRD number. Note there is different guidance for requesting an IRD number or evidence of an IRD number for partners who are not apportioned assistance but their income is relevant to the client's assistance or when a client is applying for Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School
Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School provides an early childhood education programme.
This programme provides learning material and the support of a distance teacher, but is home based and taught by the parent.
Parents must meet certain eligibility criteria to enrol their child in the Te Kura Early Childhood Education programme.

chunks.title: Teen Parent Unit — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Teen Parent Unit
A Teen Parent Unit is an educational facility attached to an already established host state school. Most units are led by a teacher-in-charge under the supervision of the school principal and board of trustees.
The unit is always linked to an Early Childhood Education provider so that the child is supported while the young parent is learning.
## Eligibility for Teen Parent Unit
Teen Parent Units provide for the educational needs of student who face barriers to learning because of their pregnancy and child rearing responsibilities.
Students who are within the age range to receive free education (that is, up to age 19 years and ending on the first day of January after the student's 19th birthday) are eligible for enrolment.
Where space permits the Teen Parent Unit's school may also enrol students who are over the age of 19. These students are enrolled as adult students.
For more information see:
- Deciding if suitable place at Teen Parent Unit available
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months
- Parenting obligations

chunks.title: Temporary employment — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Temporary employment
No stand-down is imposed where a client:
- has been in part-time employment or full-time employment for less than 26 weeks
- was receiving a benefit immediately before they were employed
- the benefit was stopped because they returned to work and
- has applied for a benefit after their employment ceased
Note the client's average weekly income is not required where the client has been in temporary employment for less than 26 weeks. However, the client's final pay details are required to determine the date of event and entitlement date.

chunks.title: Tertiary education — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Tertiary education
A young partner can meet their youth activity obligations by studying full-time at a university or polytechnic.
They must be working towards a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification.
A young partner enrolled in full-time tertiary education must:
- be enrolled in a course considered to be 'full-time'
- regularly attend classes
- complete assignments and
- complete other course requirements
## Tertiary holidays
You may require a young partner to undertake other activities that work towards NCEA level 2 or an equivalent or higher qualifications during the summer holidays.
For more information see:
- Definition of 'full-time'
- NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification
- Youth activity obligations
- Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months

chunks.title: The disputes process — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The disputes process is a quick process where you must respond to a client's dispute immediately. You must take into account any new information provided by the client or partner, and let the client or partner know your decision straight away. A letter is sent automatically to the client or partner once a decision has been recorded on the dispute. A client or partner can dispute the decision if they believe: - they did not fail their obligations including when they believe they have taken all reasonable steps to meet a social obligation or - that they had a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete the obligation Note if a client or partner has disputed the obligations failure and you have upheld your decision, the client or partner can only dispute it by following the Review of Decision or Medical Appeal Board appeal (drug test failure only) processes. If a sanction has been imposed you can still use the disputes process. This allows the client or partner an opportunity for a quick resolution to their dispute before proceeding with the Review of Decision process. For more information see: - Recording decisions on a dispute - Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements

chunks.title: Reason for dispute — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The client or partner can dispute the decision if they believe they did not fail their obligations, for one of the following reasons: - an obligations failure was initiated, but the client or partner had undertaken the activity or - an obligations failure was initiated, but the client had a good and sufficient reason for the failure or - undertaking or completing the activity was dependent on the provision of assistance by Work and Income and that assistance was not supplied or - reasonable steps weren't taken by Work and Income to inform a client or partner of the activity that they were required to do Note some clients may fail more than one obligation at the same time. In this case, for the obligation failure not to apply, the client will need to successfully dispute or review all failures in order to not have a sanction imposed. If only one failure is disputed, a sanction may still be imposed for obligation failures that were not disputed, or were disputed and upheld.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for failing — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: You must consider the circumstances of the client or partner, and determine whether it would have been reasonable for the client or partner to have undertaken the activity. Good and sufficient reasons for failing to undertake an activity will depend on the obligation the client and partner have failed. For social obligations you must consider whether the client has taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations. Note that if you are unsure if a client or partner has a good and sufficient reason then you should seek guidance from your capability developer, manager client service operations or manager client service delivery.

chunks.title: Tokelau, Niue and Cook Island clients — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Tokelau, Niue and Cook Island clients
Clients born in Tokelau, Niue and Cook Islands are automatically New Zealand citizens (by birth). Generally, they will travel to New Zealand on a New Zealand passport.
Other residents of the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau who are not New Zealand passport holders will be required to produce a proof of residence document.
Note generally, clients from the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau are lawfully in New Zealand, but are still required to be ordinarily resident in New Zealand to be eligible for a benefit. Patients (and their attendants) from Tokelau, Niue and Cook Islands receiving secondary and tertiary health services are the exception.
For more information see:
- Patients from Tokelau, Niue and Cook Islands
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Not eligible for another benefit

chunks.title: Training and secondary school — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Training and secondary school
In some circumstances, you may want to consider if an Emergency Benefit should include the requirement of attending training or secondary school.
When the equivalent benefit is subject to continued attendance at the training establishment or secondary school, you may include confirmation of the client attending as part of your conditions of grant.
The conditions of grant may be:
- an attendance record from the training establishment or secondary school
and
- a training statement or a letter from the secondary school
Note the client's Emergency Benefit conditions may have to be reviewed during the periods the training establishment or secondary school is closed during holiday periods.
From time-to-time, a client's circumstances may change and the conditions of grant of Emergency Benefit may need to be reviewed.
Note where a client has advised a change of circumstances review their eligibility and if necessary the conditions of grant.
For more information see:
- Equivalent benefit
- Benefit paid for a specific period
- Conditions of grant

chunks.title: Training providers requiring a drug test — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Training providers requiring a drug test
Some training providers will require potential trainees to pass a drug test as a prerequisite to being accepted on the course.
Training providers will use drug tests where the training programmes have a focus on employment outcomes. This includes training programmes that are:
- non classroom based programmes or on-the-job programmes where the tests are required for health and safely purposes
- classroom based training where the industry would require the trainee to be drug free for health and safety purposes to gain employment
Note a partner can only fail the drug test obligations for drug tests that are being taken as prerequisites to being accepted onto a course - not for any other on-going drug tests that a training provider may ask for.
## Reimbursement
A training provider cannot be reimbursed for the costs of a failed drug test. In most cases the contract with the provider will have already factored these costs into account.
## Verification
In order to make a decision that a partner has failed a drug test, without good and sufficient reason, you must have received confirmation from the training provider.
For more information see:
- Types of drug tests and standards
- Partner has failed a screening drug test

chunks.title: Transfer between benefits — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Transfer between benefits
A transfer between benefits can occur when a client qualifies for Emergency Benefit while currently receiving another benefit.
There is no stand-down imposed for clients who:
- transfer to Emergency Benefit from another benefit type or
- are included as a partner in another benefit type and are now applying as the primary client
Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Childs Benefit and Orphans Benefit are also a benefit in this situation. Where Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit has been paid and the child now qualifies for Emergency Benefit, no stand-down is imposed.
## Partner to be included
An initial stand-down is imposed, if a client receiving a benefit is to be included as a partner in a new application for Emergency Benefit.
There are situations where a partner can continue to receive payment of Sole Parent Support during the initial stand-down period where they are included as a partner in a new application for Emergency Benefit.
## Examples
Generally in the 3 examples below the payment of Sole Parent Support can be continued up to the actual commencement date of the Emergency Benefit.
Example 1A client has been receiving Sole Parent Support and is now to be included in a new application for Emergency Benefit as a partner an initial stand-down is imposed on the Emergency Benefit.
Example 2A client has been in prison or on remand for 31 days or more and has applied for an Emergency Benefit. On release, the client moves in with their former partner who was receiving Sole Parent Support. An initial stand-down is imposed on the Emergency Benefit.
Example 3A couple with children separated and the mother received Sole Parent Support and the father was working. The father's job ceased and the couple are now living together again. The father applied for Emergency Benefit and an initial stand-down is imposed. If there has been a delay in applying for Emergency Benefit then payment of Sole Parent Support may be cancelled from the date after the client has reconciled.
## Non-beneficiary clients
When a non-beneficiary client receiving Extra Help such as Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance applies for Emergency Benefit, it is not regarded as a transfer between benefits. An initial stand-down is imposed.
For more information see:
- Processing standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why]
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit
- Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process

chunks.title: Client intending to return to the same employer — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Client intending to return to the same employer
If a client has received any sick leave payments they would not be eligible for Emergency Benefit until these payments had stopped. You then assess any initial stand-down.
Clients are not required to use any sick leave they may have if they are intending to return to the same employer.
## Annual leave entitlement
Clients are not required to use up their annual leave entitlement if they are intending to return to the same employer.

chunks.title: 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down
When clients apply for Emergency Benefit within 28 days of their entitlement date, the commencement date rules are different when the equivalent benefit is:
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Jobseeker Support on the grounds of health condition, injury, or disability
- Jobseeker Support granted to a sole parent
- Jobseeker Support granted to a client who has recently lost the financial support of their partner due to death, commenced living apart (including imprisonment), or ending of a de facto relationship
- Youth Payment
- Young Parent Payment
For these clients, the commencement date is the day after the initial stand-down ends.
This means, in some situations, MSD can commence a benefit from a date earlier than the application date.
If the application is not received within 28 days, MSD cannot backdate the commencement date.
Note the 28-day rule only applies to clients who have an initial stand down imposed.

chunks.title: Two-week search period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Two-week search period
The Community Work Experience sanction begins the day after the 5-working day notice period ends.
A partner has 2 weeks from this date to find a suitable organisation and position. MSD can advise a partner of local groups that may be willing to provide an opportunity, however this is intended as a starting point only.
If the groups that MSD is aware of are not available or suitable, a partner will be expected to make their own enquiries with organisations in their area.
## Verification
A partner must provide MSD verification of their position. They can do this anytime during the 2-week search period, but must provide it before the end of that period.
Once a partner provides MSD with verification of their position, MSD must confirm whether the organisation and position are suitable before the partner can start. MSD has a 5-day verification window to confirm this.
At the end of the 2 weeks, if the client has not provided verification, they will have failed to find or complete their Community Work Experience and be considered non-compliant.

chunks.title: Types of drug tests and standards — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: The drug tests a partner participates in must comply with the Australian/New Zealand standard - AS/NZS 4308:2008 (the drug test standard). Drug testing detects residues of certain drugs and their metabolites in the body. Each drug has a set threshold or cut-off level for screening and evidential drug tests. To fail a test a person must have drugs present in their system that reach these thresholds or cut out levels. There are 2 types of tests that measure the presence of drugs, these are: - a screening test which shows whether drugs are or are not present - an evidential test which is completed by an accredited laboratory, which can identify the actual drugs, the drug family and the amount of drugs present In order to test, a urine sample must be provided by the person. Urine testing is the most common and accepted form of drug testing, and meets the drug test standard. To meet the drug test standard drug tests are undertaken by a person who is NZQA accredited for urine specimen collection in the workplace. The standard requires the collection of a sample to follow a process that minimises the chances of a person being able to affect the result of the sample through substitution or adulteration.

chunks.title: Screening tests — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Most employers and training providers will use a screening test as this provides them with enough information to help make the decision to employ a person or not. Screening tests are usually done using on-site urine tests as they provide a simple and cheaper method of detecting a wide range of drugs and can be undertaken outside of a laboratory. Screening tests detect the presence or absence of specific drugs and drug test providers advise that they are up to 98 per cent accurate. Very occasionally they can produce false results, this is usually because: - they have detected some prescribed medicines or - the level of a drug in a person's system is near to the threshold or cut-off points for a particular drug

chunks.title: Evidential tests — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Some employers, particularly larger employers, may require an evidential test and will not conduct screening tests or they may conduct both tests. Generally, evidential tests are used when a screening test is failed. Evidential tests are a more comprehensive and expensive method of detecting drugs. They can detect a wider range of substances and identify the specific substance. This test is also referred to as a confirmation test. Evidential testing is conducted in an accredited laboratory by qualified staff. Samples are sent to the laboratory by drug test providers or specialised staff, or the laboratory will arrange to take the sample themselves. For more information see: - Partner has failed a screening drug test - Effect of certain drugs

chunks.title: Unable to earn a sufficient livelihood — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Unable to earn a sufficient livelihood
Generally, clients apply for financial assistance because they are unable to earn a sufficient livelihood to support themselves (and any dependent family).
This may be due to:
- a health condition, an injury or a disability
- their domestic circumstances (for example caring responsibilities)
- their age (for example 16 and 17 year olds) or
- any other reason (for example residence status)
Each client's circumstances must be established to determine:
- how the person had intended to support themselves (and any dependent family) or
- could reasonably be expected to support themselves (and any dependent family)
- and
- the reasons they are not able to do this
Guidelines have been developed to help you decide the reason a person is unable to earn a sufficient livelihood and the equivalent benefit.
For more information see:
- Determining the reason for insufficient livelihood
- Contributed to hardship
- Equivalent benefit

chunks.title: Unable to meet work preparation obligations due to health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Unable to meet work preparation obligations due to health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to partners with work preparation obligations. This includes partners who have work preparation obligations as a result of being deferred from work obligations.
A partner may be unable to meet their work preparation obligations where their health condition, injury or disability restricts them.
For example, when a partner is:
- in hospital or
- is unable to attend an interview with MSD due to their condition
MSD should consider the information on the partner's Work Capacity Medical Certificate to see if it notes any restrictions to a partner's capacity to plan.
This is a full exemption.
## Evidence
To support their exemption, the partner is required to provide a Work Capacity Medical Certificate.
The medical certificate must confirm:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to work or to plan for work and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for work or planning for work and
- any other information that is required
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 13 weeks.

chunks.title: Unable to recomply — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Unable to recomply
A client or partner, who has a sanction or a 13 week non-entitlement period, may not need to complete a recompliance activity if:
- they meet the criteria for a full exemption from their work obligations or
- they qualify for a benefit that does not have the obligations to which they must recomply
Note social obligations are applied when a client or partner has a dependent child and are applied to all main benefits. This includes all clients who do not have work obligations, work preparation obligations or an exemption.
If a client or partner has a 13 week non-entitlement period, and is unable to complete the six week activity or programme of suitable activities, you cannot recover the provisional benefit if they do not complete the activity because they meet the criteria for a full exemption from their work obligations.
## Example
A partner who has a sanction who develops a health condition or becomes, injured or disabled, and meets the criteria for the exemption 'would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability'. They are unable to complete a recompliance activity.
In this situation you should add the exemption reason in SWIFTT, and follow the disputes process (so that the benefit can be resumed). Also consider the person's eligibility for Emergency Benefit on the ground of health condition, injury or disability.
For details of the requirements for a client or partner who has a health condition, injury or disability see:
- Paying other assistance during a sanction
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Unlawful residents and clients in New Zealand temporarily — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Unlawful residents and clients in New Zealand temporarily
Generally, clients who are unlawfully in New Zealand or are in New Zealand by virtue of a temporary entry class visa or temporary permit only are not eligible for benefit assistance.
## Exceptions
There are two exceptions:
- refugee or protection claimants
Note clients with refugee status are lawfully in New Zealand. For more information see: Refugee or protected person
or
- clients who are applying for permanent residence and compelled to remain in New Zealand through some unforeseen circumstance
## Temporary Additional Support
These clients are not entitled to any other benefit or Extra help. Temporary Additional Support should be considered to assist with accommodation, disability and childcare costs (if any).
For more information see:
- Refugee or protection claimant
- Refugee or protected person
- Clients compelled to remain in New Zealand

chunks.title: Up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A client and their partner (if any) receiving Emergency Benefit must take all reasonable steps to: - register their child or children with a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and - keep up-to-date with the child's core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks Note a client is only required to ensure their child completes core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks to meet this obligation from the time they begin to receive a benefit. For example, a client who starts receiving a benefit when their child is between 3 and 4 months old cannot be failed for not having completed the core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks the child should have had at ages 4 to 6 weeks.

chunks.title: Age of child — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: There are 8 core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks that apply to children aged from 4 weeks to 5 years. There are also 3 checks that occur shortly after birth. The obligation only applies for the 8 core checks that occur from around 4 months through to 5 years of age. For more information see: - Well Child or Tamariki Ora services and checks

chunks.title: Taking all reasonable steps — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Parents and caregivers should be taking all reasonable steps to register their child with a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and keep their child up to date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks. For more information on considering whether a client is taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, see: - All reasonable steps to meet social obligations

chunks.title: Verification — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Most parents will already have their child or children registered and up to date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks and in most cases you should take the client's word that they are meeting this social obligation. However, if you have information that indicates the client is not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations you may ask for proof that the checks have been completed, for example by asking to see their Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book. The Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book is issued to parents when their child is born and is sufficient evidence of the child's attendance. The Health Book has helpful advice and information about what is happening at different stages in the child's development and has places to record all the Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks. For more information see: - Well Child or Tamariki Ora services and checks - Overview of social obligations according to age of the child - All reasonable steps to meet social obligations

chunks.title: Upskilling — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Upskilling
Upskilling is a non-financial sanction that can be imposed on a client or their partner instead of a Grade 1 financial sanction. It is intended to help clients build work-related skills and confidence.
Each week for 4 weeks, a client must:
- regularly attend and participate in at least one employment-related training or course for at least 5 hours and
- report to MSD on the employment-related training or courses they have participated in
At the end of the 4-week period, a client must provide MSD with evidence of their employment related training or courses. MSD must be satisfied the evidence provided is sufficient.
Once a client completes 4 weeks of Upskilling, they are considered to have recomplied with their obligations and do not need to complete any other recompliance activities.
Note Some employment-related training or courses may be longer than 4 weeks. Clients should be made aware that, if they satisfactorily attend and participate in the training or course, they will be considered to have recomplied after 4 weeks even if the course lasts longer than this.

chunks.title: Verification of evidence at end of 4-week period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Verification of evidence at end of 4-week period
A partner must provide MSD with evidence of their job-search activities at the end of the 4-week period. This is to prove that:
- they have completed the required 3 job-search activities per week over the 4-week period and
- their job-search activities are considered reasonable steps towards finding suitable employment
MSD must determine the evidence provided is sufficient and that it matches the reported job-search activity. For example, if a partner reports that they have applied for jobs online, they must be able to provide evidence of this.
In some situations, it may not be reasonable for a partner to provide evidence for the job-search activity they completed. Partners are not expected to provide evidence that is unreasonable for them to get in their circumstances. For example, if a partner reports they have applied for jobs in person, they may not be able to provide evidence of this.
## 5-day verification window
There may be times when MSD is not able to process the information before the end of the 4-week sanction period.
To prevent a partner from being disadvantaged due to processing delays, there is a 5-day verification window at the end of the sanction period. This allows MSD to process information a partner has provided and ensures a partner's payment will continue.
Note this is not extra time for a partner to complete their job search activities.
## No action from MSD
The partner will be considered non-compliant if, after 5 days:
- MSD has not been able to confirm if the partner has completed at least 3 suitable job-search activities per week or
- the partner has not provided sufficient evidence of their job-search activities
This may result in a debt for the partner.

chunks.title: Verification of evidence at end of 4-week period — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Verification of evidence at end of 4-week period
A client must provide MSD with evidence of their attendance and participation in their employment-related training or course at the end of the 4-week period.
This is to prove that they have attended and participated in the required 5 hours of employment-related training or course per week over the 4-week period.
MSD must determine the evidence provided is sufficient and shows that the client has completed the requirements of Upskilling each week. For example, clients could show a record of their attendance in their employment-related training or course.
In some situations, it may not be reasonable for a client to provide evidence for parts of the employment-related training or course they have attended and participated in. Clients are not expected to provide evidence that is unreasonable for them to get in their circumstances.
## 5-day verification window
There may be times when MSD is not able to process the information before the end of the 4-week sanction period.
To prevent a client from being disadvantaged due to processing delays, there is a 5-day verification window at the end of the position period. This allows MSD to process information a client has provided and ensures a client's payment will continue.
Note this is not extra time for a client to attend or participate in their employment-related training or course.
## No action from MSD
The client will be considered non-compliant if, after 5 days:
- MSD has not been able to confirm if the client has attended and participated in their employment-related training or course or
- the client has not provided sufficient evidence for MSD to determine they have met the requirements of Upskilling
This may result in a debt for the client.

chunks.title: Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
A client and their partner (if any) who are applying for Emergency Benefit and have work obligations, can have a 13 week non-entitlement period if they:
- have become voluntarily unemployed without a good and sufficient reason
- are applying for a benefit because they were dismissed by their employer for misconduct
'Becoming voluntarily unemployed' means the client has resigned from, or otherwise left employment without a good and sufficient reason.
'Dismissal as a result of misconduct' means that the client has lost employment as a result of misconduct without a good and sufficient reason.
There are some circumstances where a 13 week non-entitlement period would not be imposed. For more information see:
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed
Note the 50% protection for clients and partners with dependent children applies.
For more information see:
- Deciding non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or misconduct
- Effect of non-entitlement period - couple wishes to change primary status
- Effect of non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment

chunks.title: Well Child or Tamariki Ora services and checks — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Well Child or Tamariki Ora services and checks
Well Child/Tamariki Ora services are a screening, education and support service offered to all New Zealand children and their families or whānau from birth to 5 years.
The services assist and support families and whānau to improve and protect their children's health. They are provided free to all children under 5 years by registered nurses and community health workers with specific training in child health.
First time parents and families requiring extra support are offered additional visits. Some visits are carried out in the home and others in clinics or community facilities.
Different providers run the Well Child/Tamariki Ora services, including:
- Plunket
- Māori health providers
- Pacific Island health providers
- Public Health Services - for example, public health nurses, community nurses, community health workers, social workers
## When do the checks happen?
The Well Child/Tamariki Ora schedule includes 12 health checks (contacts) with 8 of these offered to children aged from, 4 - 6 weeks to 5 years.
Only the 8 core Well Child checks are required to meet this social obligation.
## Between birth and four weeks
4 checks are provided by a midwife, health practitioner or obstetrician:
- soon after birth
- 24 hours after birth
- during the first week of baby's life
- between 2 and 4 weeks
Note the birth to 4 weeks checks listed above do not apply for social obligations purposes.
## Between 4 weeks and 5 years
The 8 core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks (listed below) for children between the ages of 4 - 6 weeks to 5 years are required to meet social obligations.
These are provided by the Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider when the child is:
- 4 - 6 weeks
- 8 - 10 weeks
- 3 - 4 months
- 5 - 7 months
- 9 - 12 months
- 15 - 18 months
- 2 - 3 years
- 4 - 5 years (this is the before school check, and the final Well Child health check)

chunks.title: Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks
Well Child/Tamariki Ora services are a screening, education and support service offered to all New Zealand children and their families or whanau from birth to 5 years.
The services assist and support families and whanau to improve and protect their children's health.
First time parents and families requiring extra support are offered additional visits. Some visits are carried out in the home and others in clinics or community facilities.
## When do the checks happen?
Well Child/Tamariki Ora services are provided by registered nurses and community health workers/kaiāwhina with specific training in child health.
The current Well Child/Tamariki Ora schedule includes 12 health checks (visits/contacts) with 8 of these offered to children aged from 4 - 6 weeks to 5 years.
## Between birth and 4 weeks
4 checks are provided by a midwife, health practitioner or obstetrician:
- soon after birth
- 24 hours after birth
- during the first week of baby's life
- between 2 - 4 weeks
Note the birth to 4 weeks checks listed above do not apply for social obligations purposes.
## Between 4 weeks and 5 years
Eight more checks are provided by the Well Child provider, at:
- 4 - 6 weeks
- 8 - 10 weeks
- 3 - 4 months
- 5 - 7 months
- 9 - 12 months
- 15 - 18 months
- 2 - 3 years
- 4 - 5 years (this is the before school check, and the final Well Child health check)

chunks.title: When the sanction is imposed — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## When the sanction is imposed
Sanctions can only be imposed 5 working days after the client has been sent a letter about their obligations failure. This is called the 5 working day notice period.
If a client recomplies within the initial 5 working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the obligations failure is counted.
Note if a client has more than 1 obligation failure initiated on the same day, only 1 sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures initiated on the same day.
## How to count the 'five working day notice' period
The 5 working day notice period is counted from the date after the obligations failure letter has been sent to the client, to allow for posting and delivery of the letter.
The 5 working day notice period excludes weekends, public holidays, or the period 25 December to 15 January each year.
The table below provides an example of how to count the notice period.
Day 0
Tuesday

Day 0
Wednesday

Day 1Day 2

Five working day notice period begins
Weekend
Saturday-Sunday

Five working day notice period continues
Day 6

chunks.title: Work ability assessment obligation — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Work ability assessment obligation
A client and their partner (if any) getting Emergency Benefit have a work ability assessment obligation that requires them, when asked, to attend and participate in:
- Self-Assessments
- Structured Interview
- Work Ability Assessments
## Reason for work ability assessment
A work ability assessment will help show what work a person is capable of doing and what Work and Income can do to help a client with their return to work.
A work ability assessment will help determine:
- the client's work ability
- what suitable work or work preparation activities are appropriate for the client
- what assistance, services or support Work and Income and/or other agencies should be providing
As a result of a work ability assessment a client's work obligations or benefit entitlement may change.
## Clients required to participate in a work ability assessment
Generally only clients who have a health condition, injury or disability will be required to undertake or participate in a work ability assessment.
## Failing to comply
If a client does not meet these obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, an obligations failure will be initiated and a sanction may be imposed.

chunks.title: Work-based learning — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Work-based learning
A young partner can meet their education activity obligation by being in work-based learning.
Work-based learning includes courses that offer more practical, hands-on learning than the school environment.
For a young partner to be considered to be in work-based learning they must be:
- employed and undertaking on-the-job learning and
- undertaking a course or programme that is relevant to their employment
While the young partner is in paid work, all usual workplace conditions, including the applicable minimum wage, will apply to the work element of work-based learning in the same way that they apply to all other forms of employment.
Note any income earned by the young partner is charged against the benefit rate. See: Charging income
Programmes that contain elements of work-based learning include:
- Youth Guarantee programmes and
- part-time industry partnerships
For more information see:
- Definition of 'full-time'
- NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification
- Youth activity obligations
- Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months

chunks.title: Work obligations - partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Work obligations - partners
Full-time work obligations apply to:
- partners with no dependent children and
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged 14 years or over
Part-time work obligations apply to:
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years
Partners with work obligations must:
- be available for, and take reasonable steps to obtain, suitable employment
- accept any offer of suitable employment, including temporary employment or seasonal employment
Note suitable employment can include employment that contains a 90 day employment trial.
- attend and participate in an interview for any opportunity of suitable employment to which the partner is referred
- when required to attend and participate in any interview with MSD or on behalf of MSD
- when required to undertake planning for employment
- report to MSD on progress in meeting their work obligations as often as required and
- when required by MSD, undertake any activity to improve their work readiness and employment prospects, including: any work assessmentany programme or seminarany work experience or work exploration activityany employment related training andrehabilitation (but not medical treatment)
- any work assessment
- any programme or seminar
- any work experience or work exploration activity
- any employment related training and
- rehabilitation (but not medical treatment)
Partners with full-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find, suitable employment of at least 30 hours or more per week.
Partners with part-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find, suitable employment of at least 20 hours per week.
However if suitable employment is available for hours other than 20 or 30 hours per week (as applicable), the partner can be required to accept an offer of this job.
Work obligations can be applied on any day of the week provided it is suitable for the partner's circumstances.
If a partner does not meet their work obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, you should initiate an obligations failure.
You should consider the partner's individual circumstances before referring them to a job or an activity, to ensure that they can realistically meet their obligations.
To help you decide if the job is suitable for the partner see:
- Suitable employment
- Hours range for suitable employment

chunks.title: Work or work preparation obligations - partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Work or work preparation obligations - partners
Partners of clients receiving Emergency Benefit have full-time or part-time work obligations or work preparation obligations depending on the age of their youngest child.
Full-time work obligations apply to:
- partners with no children and
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged 14 years or over
Partners with full-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of at least 30 hours or more per week.
Part-time work obligations apply to:
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years
Partners with part-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of at least 20 hours per week.
Work preparation obligations apply to:
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
Note if the partner is getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, these children are not considered dependent children for rates purposes but they are treated as dependent children for setting work or work preparation obligations.
## Partners aged 16 to 19 years old
Young partners (aged 16 to 19 years old) of clients getting Emergency Benefit have youth activity obligations and not work or work preparation obligations if they are:
- aged 16 or 17 years old without dependent children or
- aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children and
- married, or in a civil union or a de facto relationship with a person getting Emergency Benefit

chunks.title: Work preparation obligations - partners — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Work preparation obligations - partners
A person with work preparation obligations must take all reasonable steps to prepare for employment. When considering what is reasonable you must consider what is practical for their individual circumstances.
In addition, partners with a youngest dependent child aged under 3 years must:
- when required to undertake planning for employment
- when required to report to Work and Income on progress in meeting their work preparation obligations as often as required
- when required to attend and participate in any interview with Work and Income or on behalf of Work and Income and
- when required by Work and Income undertake any activity to improve their work readiness and employment prospects, including: any work assessmentany programme or seminarany work experience or work exploration activityany employment related trainingrehabilitation (but not medical treatment)an education programme
- any work assessment
- any programme or seminar
- any work experience or work exploration activity
- any employment related training
- rehabilitation (but not medical treatment)
- an education programme
Work preparation obligations can be applied on any day of the week provided it is suitable for the partner's circumstances.
If a partner does not meet their work preparation obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, you should initiate an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Informing partners of their obligations
- Setting appropriate activities for partners
- Reporting progress
- Rehabilitation - partners
- Exemptions - partners
- Table of Exemptions
- Obligations failures - partners

chunks.title: Work with contracted service provider obligation — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Work with contracted service provider obligation
When required to, certain clients (including partners), may be case managed by a contracted service provider.
When asked, clients have an obligation to co-operate with a contracted service provider and to:
- attend and participate in interviews with them
- report to them on how they are meeting their obligations, this could include their social, work or work preparation obligations and
- when required, complete assessments with the service provider

chunks.title: Workplace/industry training — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Workplace/industry training
Workplace/industry training includes course such as:
- Skills for Industry
- Training for work
These courses are generally less than 13 weeks.
Young people will be meeting their obligations where they are undertaking programmes linked to the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF) credits.
For more information see:
- Employment and training Job search, employment and in-work support services (young partners)

chunks.title: Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
If a partner meets the qualifications for Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their work obligations until their capacity for work improves.
The partner must be limited in their capacity to work because of a health condition, injury or disability and, depending on whether they have part-time or full-time work obligations, be:
- unable to look for part-time work of at least 15 hours per week or
- losing earnings because they are unable to work for at least 15 or 30 hours a week
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support
This is a partial exemption and the partner is able to:
- plan for employment and
- undertake certain work related activities
If a partner qualifies for a full exemption this means they are unable to meet any of their work obligations, including work planning.
## Evidence
To support their exemption, the partner must provide a medical certificate signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant). This is generally a Work Capacity Medical Certificate.
The medical certificate must confirm:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to work and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for work planning, training and part-time work and
- any other information that is required
## Duration of exemption
The period of an exemption is based on the reassessment date recorded on the medical certificate by a client's health practitioner.
This exemption should then be reviewed. At the review you should discuss the client's circumstances and consider whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption for a further period.
You can ask the client to provide proof that the exemption should be extended.

chunks.title: Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability, or totally blind — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability, or totally blind
This exemption may apply to partners with work or work preparation obligations.
If a partner meets the qualifications for Supported Living Payment on ground of a health condition, an injury, a disability or total blindness, they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their work or work preparation obligations.
The partner must be:
- both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, or injury or disability, from an accident, or a condition they have had since birth or
- totally blind
Note totally blind and legally blind are not the same.
For more information see:
- Supported Living Payment
This can be a full or partial exemption depending on the whether the partner can plan for a return to work.
MSD should discuss with the partner whether they can still:
- plan for employment and
- undertake certain work related activities
If it is unclear whether a full or partial exemption should be granted, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor.
## Evidence
To support their exemption, the partner must provide a Work Capacity Medical Certificate or medical information signed by a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist.
The medical certificate or information must confirm:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to work and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for work planning, training and part-time work and
- any other information that is required
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months.
This exemption should then be reviewed.
At the review MSD should consider the partner's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption. MSD can ask the partner to provide evidence that the exemption should be extended.

chunks.title: Young partner with dependent child — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Young partners aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children have the following activity obligations. They must: - be enrolled in and undertaking, or be available for, a full-time course of secondary or tertiary education, or approved training or work-based learning leading to a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification - when required to, participate in and complete an approved budgeting programme - when required to, participate satisfactorily in an approved parenting education programme - report to their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service on progress in meeting their education, parenting and budgeting obligations (above) as often as required - when required to, attend and participate in regular budgeting discussions with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service - when required to, attend and participate in any interview with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service - when asked, proved within 20 working days, to their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service, details of the young person's accommodation costs, service costs and lawful debts or other liabilities - co-operate with their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service in managing the spending of their benefit or portion of benefit and - attend and participate in regular discussions on budgeting at any discussion, or when asked, provide details on: their accommodation costs and service costs such as power and phonetheir lawful debts and liabilitieshow they spent any in-hand allowance and any money credited to their payment card or any other device - their accommodation costs and service costs such as power and phone - their lawful debts and liabilities - how they spent any in-hand allowance and any money credited to their payment card or any other device A young partner with a dependent child or children also has the following obligations. They must: - enrol their child with a Primary Health Organisation, where a local provider is available - keep their child or children under the age of 5 years up-to-date with their Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks - ensure their child's attendance at an approved Early Childhood Education (ECE) programme or other suitable childcare, while they are participating in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work These obligations apply from the time the benefit is first paid except where the young partner is caring for a child aged under 12 months. For more information see:

chunks.title: Young partner (with dependent children) turns 20 years old — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Generally, when a young partner with a dependent child or children turns 20 years old the youth activity obligations no longer apply. However, there are two situations where the obligations will continue to apply after they turn 20 years old. These are where a young partner: - is aged under 20 years when they first have youth activity obligations applied and must undertake Youth Activity obligations for a minimum of 6 months, even if they turn 20 years during this period - chooses to continue to have youth activity obligations so they can remain in education, training or work-based learning When a young partner with a dependent child or children reaches the age of 20 and has already had youth activity obligations for 6 months and does not choose to continue to have these obligations because they are not in education, training or work-based learning, the youth activity obligations no longer apply. Instead they will have the work or work preparation obligations applicable for their main benefit.

chunks.title: Choose to have Youth Activity obligations past 20 years of age — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Generally, when a young partner turns 20 years old the obligations for them to comply with youth activity obligations will no longer apply. However, to give a young partner a chance to complete the qualification they have started while having Youth Activity obligations, a young partner can choose to continue to have youth activity obligations and continue to participate in the Youth Service after they turn 20 years old if they remain in education, training or work-based learning. Attending secondary school When a young partner reaches the age of 20 years and is attending secondary school they will continue to have Youth Activity obligations and continue to participate in the Youth Service until the following 31 March. For example, a young partner attending school who turns 20 years old in June will continue in the Youth Service until the following 31 March. Attending tertiary education, training or work-based learning When a young partner is attending tertiary education, training or work-based learning and they turn 20 years old, they may choose to continue to have youth activity obligations and participate in the Youth Service until the course finishes, unless their course ends in December. If their course ends in December, they will continue to have youth activity obligations and participate in the Youth Service until 31 March the following year. Examples: - a young partner is part-way through a training course when they turn 20 years old. The training course finishes on 20 November. The young partner will be exited from the Youth Service on 21 November - a young partner is part-way through a training course when they turn 20 years old. The training course finishes on 20 December. The young partner will continue to have Youth Activity obligations and remain in the Youth Service until the following 31 March

chunks.title: Must have Youth Activity obligations for 6 months — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A young partner who is aged under 20 years when they first have Youth Activity obligations applied must undertake these obligations for a minimum of 6 months, even if they turn 20 during this period. This ensures that the young partner is able to have a reasonable chance to move towards a qualification by participating in education, training or work-based learning and other youth activity obligations before they focus on obligations attached to other main benefits. For example, a young partner first has Youth Activity obligations applied at the age of 19 years and 8 months old. When they turn 20 years old they will need to continue to have these Youth Activity obligations and participate in the Youth Service for another 2 months to complete the 6 month minimum period. After this point, the Youth Activity obligations will no longer apply and instead they will have the work obligations applicable to main benefit (unless they choose to continue to have Youth Activity obligations because they are in education, training or work-based learning). For more information see: - Deciding education, training or work-based learning activities - Approved budgeting programme activity - Report to service provider or Work and Income on progress - Parenting obligations - Money management activity - Youth activity obligations failures - Work or work preparation obligations

chunks.title: Young partner without children — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Young partners aged 16 or 17 years old without dependent children have the following youth activity obligations. They must: - be enrolled in and undertaking, or be available for, a full-time course of secondary or tertiary education, or approved training or work-based learning leading to a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification - when required to, participate in and complete an approved budgeting programme - report to their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service on progress in meeting their education and budgeting obligations (above) as often as required - when required to, attend and participate in regular budgeting discussions with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service - when required to, attend and participate in any interview with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service - when asked, provide within 20 working days, to their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service, details of the young person's accommodation costs, service costs and lawful debts or other liabilities - co-operate with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service in managing the spending of their benefit or portion of benefit and - attend and participate in regular discussions on budgeting at any discussion, or when asked, provide details on: their accommodation costs and service costs such as power and phonetheir lawful debts and liabilitieshow they spent any in-hand allowance and any money credited to their payment card or any other device - their accommodation costs and service costs such as power and phone - their lawful debts and liabilities - how they spent any in-hand allowance and any money credited to their payment card or any other device The activity obligations cannot be enforced until the main benefit commencement date.

chunks.title: Young partner (no dependent children) turns 18 years old — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Generally, when a young partner with no dependent children turns 18 years old the youth activity obligations no longer apply. However, there are two situations where the obligations will continue to apply after they turn 18 years old. These are where a young partner: - is aged under 18 years when they first have youth activity obligations applied and must undertake Youth Activity obligations for a minimum of 6 months, even if they turn 18 years during this 6 month period - chooses to continue to have youth activity obligations so they can remain in education, training or work-based learning When a young partner reaches the age of 18 and has already had youth activity obligations for 6 months and does not choose to continue to have these obligations because they are not in education, training or work-based learning, the youth activity obligations no longer apply. Instead they will have the work obligations applicable to the main benefit.

chunks.title: Choose to have youth activity obligations past 18 years of age — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: Generally, when a young partner turns 18 years old the obligations for them to comply with Youth Activity obligations will no longer apply. However, to give a young partner a chance to complete the qualification they have started while having youth activity obligations, a young partner can choose to continue to have youth activity obligations and continue to participate in the Youth Service after they turn 18 years old if they remain in education, training or work-based learning. Attending secondary school When a young partner reaches the age of 18 years and is attending secondary school they will continue to have youth activity obligations and continue to participate in the Youth Service until the following 31 March. For example, a young partner attending school who turns 18 years old in June will continue in the Youth Service until the following 31 March. Attending tertiary education, training or work-based learning When a young partner is attending tertiary education, training or work-based learning and they turn 18 years old, they may continue to have youth activity obligations and continue to participate in the Youth Service until their course finishes, unless their course ends in December. If their course ends in December, they will continue to have youth activity obligations and participate in the Youth Service until 31 March the following year. Examples: - a young partner is part-way through a training course when they turn 20 years old. The training course finishes on 20 November. The young partner will be exited from the Youth Service on 21 November - a young partner is part-way through a training course when they turn 20 years old. The training course finishes on 20 December. The young partner will continue to have Youth Activity obligations and remain in the Youth Service until the following 31 March

chunks.title: Must have youth activity obligations for 6 months — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text: A young partner who is aged under 18 years when they first have Youth Activity obligations applied must undertake these obligations for a minimum of 6 months even if they turn 18 years old during this period. This ensures that the young partner is able to have a reasonable chance to move towards a qualification by participating in education, training or work-based learning and other youth activity obligations before they focus on obligations attached to other main benefits. For example, a young partner first has Youth Activity obligations applied at the age of 17 years and 8 months old. When they turn 18 years old they will need to continue to have these Youth Activity obligations and participate in the Youth Service for another 2 months to complete the 6 month minimum period. After this point, the youth activity obligations will no longer apply and instead they will have the work obligations applicable as the partner of an Emergency Benefit client (unless they choose to continue to have youth activity obligations because they are in education, training or work-based learning).

chunks.title: Young partner would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Young partner would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
If a young partner meets the qualifications for Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their activity obligations until their capacity for education, training and work-based learning improves.
The young partner must be limited in their capacity to undertake activities because of a health condition, injury or disability.
This is a full or partial exemption.
## Evidence
To support their exemption, the young partner is required to provide a Work Capacity Medical Certificate or another medical certificate signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist, or midwife where relevant).
The medical certificate must confirm:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to undertake activity obligations and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for education, training and work-based learning and
- any other information that is required
## Duration
This exemption is initially granted until the earliest of either:
- 13 weeks or
- the next reassessment date recorded on the Work Capacity Medical Certificate
This exemption should then be reviewed.
At the review MSD should consider the young partner's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption.
MSD can ask the young partner to provide evidence that their exemption should be extended.

chunks.title: Young partner would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Young partner would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
If a young partner meets the qualifications for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, an injury, a disability or total blindness, they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their activity obligations.
The young partner must be:
- both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for education, training and work-based learning because of a health condition, or injury or disability, from an accident, or a condition they have had since birth or
- totally blind
Note totally blind and legally blind are not the same thing.
For more information see:
- Supported Living Payment Qualifications
This can be a full or partial exemption depending on the whether the young partner can plan for a return to education, training or work-based learning.
MSD should discuss with the young partner whether they can still:
- plan for education, training or work-based learning and
- undertake other activities such as budgeting
If about it is unclear whether a full or partial exemption should be granted, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor.
Note when appropriate MSD should consider the young partner's eligibility for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability.
## Evidence
The young partner must provide either a medical certificate or medical information signed by a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or psychologist.
The medical certificate or information must confirm:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is)
- the impact of the condition on their ability to undertake activities
- the likely duration of the impact
- their capacity for planning and undertaking activities part-time and
- any other information that is required

chunks.title: Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months
Youth activity obligations apply from the time the benefit is first paid except where the young partner is caring for their youngest dependent child, and that child is aged under 12 months old.
In these cases, the obligation to be in or available for full-time education, training or work-based learning begins to apply on the earlier of:
- the day the child becomes 6 months old
- if there is a suitable place available for the young partner in a teen parent unit and
- MSD is satisfied that there are no special circumstances justifying the obligation starting at a later date
or
- the day on which the child becomes 12 months old
For more information see:
- Deciding if suitable place at Teen Parent Unit available
- Special circumstances justifying delay in activity obligation
- Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities
- Parenting obligations
- Exemptions for young partners

chunks.title: Youth activity obligations — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Youth activity obligations
A young partner is subject to youth activity obligations and not to work preparation or work obligations if they are:
- aged 16 or 17 years old without dependent children or
- aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children and
- is married to, or in a civil union or in a de facto relationship with a person receiving Emergency Benefit
Note young partners may be able to get an exemption from some or all of their obligations where it is unreasonable to expect them to meet their obligations for a specified period.
For more information see:
- Inform young partner of their activity obligations
- Young partner without children
- Young partner with dependent child
- Dependent child
- Earning incentive payments
- Exemptions for young partners
- Youth activity obligations failures

chunks.title: Youth activity obligations failures — main benefits > emergency benefit
chunks.text:
## Youth activity obligations failures
If a young partner fails to comply with their youth activity obligations, an activity obligations failure needs to be considered.
The service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service:
- must to be satisfied that the young partner would have had no good and sufficient reason for their failure and
- if the young partner has no good and sufficient reason, recommend an activity obligations failure be imposed
The Youth Service Support Unit (YSSU):
- makes the decision to apply a sanction, based on the recommendation of the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service and
- initiates the activity obligations failure in the system
