chunks.title: Essential travel — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Essential travel
A client not otherwise entitled to be paid their Emergency Maintenance Allowance while they are absent from New Zealand may have their payments continue for up to 28 days in any 52 week period if they have to travel outside of New Zealand to attend a significant event relating to a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family).
These events are ones which the client would reasonably be expected to attend. That is, the travel is essential to them and where not attending the event would cause the person emotional distress. This may include, but is not limited to, travel that allows the client to:
- be with a seriously ill or dying person who is a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family)
- attend a funeral or an unveiling in relation to a family member
- pay respect to a family member of the deceased in the event of the client missing the funeral
- attend to legal matters in relation to the affairs of the deceased family member
- attend a birth of a family member or be with a family member around the time of their giving birth
- provide support to a party or witness to a court case
- attend a wedding of a family member - the client does not need to be a member of the bridal party or play a significant part in the wedding in order for the payment of benefit to continue while they are absent from New Zealand
- travel for a court ordered custody arrangement
For more information see:
- Definition of family member
- Absent from NZ more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect
- Permitted travel reasons
- Paying benefit when client failed to advise of absence
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within a 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason
The following examples show situations where we may pay for more than 28 days in any 52 week period (but are not limited to):
Client's reason for travelling for 28 days within 52 week period
Client's current reason for travel within 52 week period
Outcome
Essential travel reasons
Essential travel reason eg a seriously ill family member
Generally consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if reasonable in the circumstances
Job interview or job prospect
Essential travel reason eg a funeral
Generally would consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if reasonable in the circumstances

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Carlos contacts MSD on 19 November to advise that he has returned from travelling to Malaysia to be with his dying mother. He left in a hurry and didn't contact MSD before his departure. His Emergency Maintenance Allowance stopped on 4 November, the day after he left the country. He returned to New Zealand on 14 November, but then had to organise a New Zealand-based funeral for his mother, as a large number of people are based in New Zealand. Carlos didn't advise MSD of his travel before leaving New Zealand, but he has a humanitarian reason that justifies his travel and the reason he didn't contact MSD before he left. Given Carlos' circumstances, he contacted MSD as soon as it would have been reasonable to expect him to and he meets the criteria for an approved travel reason. Carlos' Emergency Maintenance Allowance can be backdated to 4 November.

chunks.title: Example 2 — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Sanjay left New Zealand for India on 7 December because his father had become suddenly seriously ill and been hospitalised. While in India, Sanjay's father passed away and Sanjay stayed overseas for the funeral. Sanjay returned on 16 December, after staying for 2 weeks for the Hindu funeral and mourning period. On 19 December, Sanjay contacts MSD to explain that he has been overseas after learning of his father's illness, and that he stayed for the funeral. On return, Sanjay spent time mourning with his own family and has been distraught. He explains that he only realised last night that he had not informed MSD of his absence. Sanjay's reason for leaving New Zealand is a humanitarian reason and he meets the criteria for backdating his payment to the day after departure. Given Sanjay's circumstances, he informed MSD as soon as he reasonably could. Sanjay's Emergency Maintenance Allowance can be backdated to 8 December, the date it was suspended.

chunks.title: Example 3 — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Tusila calls MSD on 5 October to inform them she will leave New Zealand on 7 October to help her sister, who just lost her house in a flood. When asked how long she will be gone for, Tusila says she hasn't bought a return ticket yet and was considering staying longer catch up with family and see how her sister is going. MSD informs Tusila that she can only keep getting her Emergency Maintenance Allowance if she is absent for essential travel. Helping her sister after a flood is considered essential travel, however if she is going to stay longer for a holiday, she won't be able to get Emergency Maintenance Allowance during the time she is on holiday. Tusila returns the next day with an airline quote showing that the cheapest return flight is on 14 October. She thinks it will take her a week to ensure her sister has sorted out insurance, medium-term accommodation, and access to basic goods like clothing and food. She has decided not to stay on for the holiday. MSD agrees this is reasonable and tells Tusila she can keep getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance from 7 to 14 October, while she is overseas helping her sister.

chunks.title: Example 4 — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Christy is getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance and contacts MSD to advise that her sister is getting married in Australia on 8 September. Christy is going to Australia to her sister's wedding but intends to stay on for a further 2 weeks to visit other family. Christy is leaving New Zealand on 4 September as she has to help her sister prepare. She will stay until10 September to help clean up. Christy then begins the holiday leg of her trip, returning to New Zealand on 25 September. Christy's travel is divided as follows: - 5 September to 10 September period meets the essential travel criteria - 11 September to 24 September period is considered other travel (holiday) and does not meet the essential travel criteria Christy's Emergency Maintenance Allowance can only be paid until 10 September, for the period that meets the essential travel criteria.

chunks.title: Example 5 — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Graeme left New Zealand on 16 August to help his sister in Australia after she lost her house in a fire. He returns to New Zealand on 23 August. A week later, on 30 August he attends an appointment and asks why he hasn't been getting his Emergency Maintenance Allowance. His case manager informs him that his payments stopped when he left the country and asks why he didn't contact MSD sooner. Graeme explains that he left to help his sister after a house fire, and he meant to contact MSD once he had helped his sister sort out accommodation and insurance, but he forgot. The case manager explains that because he didn't contact MSD as soon as he reasonably could have been expected to (i.e. once he had helped his sister), his Emergency Maintenance Allowance can only be backdated to 23 August, the date he returned to New Zealand.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Example 1
A client applies for benefit to be paid for 10 days when they are going to be absent from New Zealand. In the past 52 weeks the client has had 10 days absence from New Zealand and continued to be paid their benefit.
Step
Calculation
Identify the day after the client is intending to leave New Zealand.
14 September 2019
Count back 52 weeks from this date.
15 September 2018
Count the number of days the client has continued getting their benefit while they were overseas in this 52 week period.
Days client has continued getting their benefit while absent from New Zealand between 14 September 2018 and 15 September 2019 = 10 days
Subtract the number of days the client was paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand from 28 days.
28 - 10 days = 18 days available
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay the client for the days they have available.
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay them for the 10 days they are out of the country.
## Example 2
A client applies for benefit to be paid for 10 days when they are going to be absent from New Zealand. In the past 52 weeks the client has had 20 days absence from New Zealand and continued being paid their benefit.
Step
Calculation
Identify the day after the client is intending to leave New Zealand.
14 September 2019
Count back 52 weeks from this date.
15 September 2018
Count the number of days the client has continued to get their benefit while they were overseas in this 52 week period.
Days client has continued getting their benefit while absent from New Zealand between 14 September 2018 and 15 September 2019 = 20 days
Subtract the number of days the client has been paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand from 28 days.
28 - 20 days = 8 days available
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay the client for the days they have available.
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay them for the 8 days they are out of the country. For 2 of the days they are absent from New Zealand they will not receive their payments.
Check if the client meets the criteria to get their benefit for more than 28 days in a 52 week period - if they meet these criteria, they may be able to continue getting their payment for the additional 2 days of absence.

chunks.title: Examples of Mandatory Review outcomes — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: MSD must review a client’s Emergency Maintenance Allowance within 52 weeks of the commencement date of their benefit, or 52 weeks from when the client’s last Mandatory Review was completed. The Mandatory Review is completed when MSD has determined if the client continues to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance and the rate payable (if applicable). When a client responds to the review, there are a number of outcomes that can occur. Once MSD has determined if the client qualifies, MSD will either: - continue paying the benefit at the existing rate - adjust the rate of benefit so the client is getting the correct rate - suspend the benefit if there is no rate payable for a period (e.g. client has variable income) - cancel the benefit if the client no longer qualifies

chunks.title: Examples of outcomes that can occur: — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Outcomes of a Mandatory Review Examples Client declares no change (exception doesn't apply) Hazel is a sole parent with 2 dependent children in their care. Hazel is getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance with an expiry in 3 years when their youngest child turns 14. Hazel's Mandatory Review is due on 16 October 2026. Hazel responds to their Mandatory Review on 13 October 2026 and confirms that they have had no change in their circumstances. Because Hazel has declared there has been no change to their circumstances and an exception doesn't apply, MSD must continue the payment at the same rate. MSD completes Hazel's Mandatory Review on 13 October and sets the next Mandatory Review date for 52 weeks from the date the Mandatory Review was completed. Hazel's next Mandatory Review is 12 October 2027. Client declares no change (exception applies) Elliot is getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance, Accommodation Supplement and Disability Allowance and pays rent of $350.00 per week in Area 1. His Mandatory Review is due on 9 June 2027, and he responds on 7 June 2027 to confirm he has had no change in his circumstances. While his Disability Allowance costs were updated last year, he hasn't declared a change in rent since January 2024. Because Elliot has been getting Accommodation Supplement and declared no change in his accommodation costs for three consecutive years, MSD must consider whether further information is required before completing the Mandatory Review. MSD considers Elliot's circumstances and sees that he hasn't provided verification of his accommodation costs since moving to his current apartment in 2024. Given Elliot lives in an area where rental accommodation is very limited and rents have increased significantly, MSD determines that it is reasonable to request verification of his accommodation costs to confirm that the information is correct before making a decision about his entitlement. Elliot is asked to provide this information before 7 July 2027 (his new deadline for the review) or his Emergency Maintenance Allowance, Accommodation Supplement and Disability Allowance will stop. Elliot contacts MSD on 1 July 2027 with the evidence requested. MSD determines that Elliot's circumstances have changed as his rent increased in January 2027. MSD adjusts the rate of payment for Accommodation Supplement and exercises discretion to backdate the payment to the date of the increase in costs, and continues Emergency Maintenance Allowance and Disability Allowance at the same rate.

chunks.title: Examples of outcomes that can occur: — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: MSD completes Elliot's Mandatory Review on 1 July 2027, and his next Mandatory Review date is set for 52 weeks in the future on 29 June 2028. Client declares a change in circumstances Ivan is a sole parent with 1 dependent child. Ivan is getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance with no expiry date. Ivan's Mandatory Review is due on 18 February 2027. Ivan responds to their Mandatory Review on 15 February 2027 and tells MSD that on 10 February 2027 their son left their care to live with their mother long term. This was a planned change in care arrangements. Ivan's Emergency Maintenance Allowance is cancelled from 10 February 2027 as Ivan no longer has a dependent child in their care. MSD completes the Mandatory Review on 15 February 2027 and does not need to set a future review date. Mandatory Review was not completed, and benefit has suspended Jerry is a sole parent with 1 dependent child. Jerry is getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance with an expiry in 5 years when their child turns 14. Jerry's Mandatory Review is due on 9 August 2027. Jerry does not respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date and his Emergency Maintenance Allowance suspends on 9 August 2027. Jerry does not contact MSD or respond to the Mandatory Review for 8 weeks after their Emergency Maintenance Allowance suspended. Because of this Jerry's Emergency Maintenance Allowance is cancelled from the date their Emergency Maintenance Allowance suspended. Not enough information to complete Mandatory Review Christian is a sole parent with 3 dependent children. Christian is getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance with an expiry in 18 months when he is likely to meet the 2-year residence requirement for Sole Parent Support. Christian's Mandatory Review is due on 10 July 2026. Christian responds to the Mandatory Review on 7 July 2026 and tells MSD they are now working part time at a café and are earning income of $190.00 a week (before tax). Because Christian's income is not sufficient to support them or their children, MSD determines that Christian is still eligible to continue getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance. However, MSD cannot complete the Mandatory Review as more information is needed about when Christian's income started. MSD sets a new reasonable deadline for Christian to provide the information by 14 July 2026. MSD tells Christian if he doesn't provide the information by 14 July 2026, his Emergency Maintenance Allowance will be suspended on this date.

chunks.title: Examples of outcomes that can occur: — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Christian contacts MSD on 10 July 2026 to confirm his employment started on 29 June 2026. MSD charges the income and reassesses Christian's Emergency Maintenance Allowance from 29 June 2026. MSD completes the Mandatory Review on 10 July 2026. There is no future Mandatory Review date as the expiry date of Christian's Emergency Maintenance Allowance is in less than 52 weeks. If Christian meets the residency qualifications when his Emergency Maintenance Allowance expires, he may qualify for Sole Parent Support. Note MSD should consider if clients may be eligible for other types of assistance when there is a change in circumstances that means they no longer qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Example 1
The temporary caregiver is to be paid Emergency Maintenance Allowance at the equivalent Unsupported Childs Benefit rate while caring for 1 child aged 14 years during the sole parent client's imprisonment.
Unsupported Child's Benefit (as at 1 April 2026)
$350.58
Less family tax credit (as at 1 April 2026)
$151.91
Equals amount to add as a non-standard rate
$198.67
## Example 2
The temporary caregiver is to be paid Emergency Maintenance Allowance at the equivalent Unsupported Childs Benefit rate while caring for 2 children aged 14 and 10 years during the sole parent client's imprisonment.
Unsupported Childs Benefit (as at 1 April 2026):
- $350.58 for 14-year old and
- $327.16 for 10-year old
$677.74
Less family tax credit (as at 1 April 2026):
- $151.91 for first child and
- $123.78 for second child
$275.69
Equals amount to add as a non-standard rate
$402.05
## Example 3
The temporary caregiver is to be paid Emergency Maintenance Allowance at the Sole Parent Support rate while caring for 2 children aged 14 and 10 years during the sole parent client's imprisonment. It has been agreed to include the rent of the client's home of $150.00.
Unsupported Childs Benefit (as at 1 April 2026):
- $350.58 for 14-year old, and
- $327.16 for 10-year old
$677.74
Plus rent on client's home
$150.00
Sub total
$827.74
Less family tax credit (as at 1 April 2026):
- $151.91 for first child and
- $123.78 for second child
$275.69
Equals calculated amount required to assist the temporary caregiver to care for the client's children (rent included)

In this case the amount payable is the maximum Emergency Maintenance Allowance at Sole Parent Support rate of $521.52. You don't need to add a non-standard rate.

chunks.title: Exceptions when a client declares no change in circumstances for Mandatory Review — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: When a client responds to their Mandatory Review and confirms they have no change in circumstances, MSD must generally continue their Emergency Maintenance Allowance at the same rate. However, there are some exceptions when MSD can request further information from the client to determine if they continue to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance or that the rate of payment is correct. Exceptions include when, at the time the client responds to their Mandatory Review, they: - have been getting Disability Allowance and have had no change in their disability related costs for three consecutive years or - have been getting Accommodation Supplement and have had no change in their accommodation costs for three consecutive years or - have had no change to their confirmed income amount for three consecutive years If a client has one or more of these exceptions, MSD must consider if further information is required from the client before deciding the outcome of the Mandatory Review.

chunks.title: Further information is needed to complete the Mandatory Review — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: If further information is needed to determine if the client continues to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance or that the rate of payment is correct, MSD must give a reasonable timeframe for the client to provide it. The date the client is given to provide the information by becomes the client's new deadline to respond to the Mandatory Review. If the client does not provide the information that was asked for, MSD must suspend the Emergency Maintenance Allowance from the new deadline date. If the client provides the information that was asked for and MSD determines the client continues to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance (including the rate payable), the future Mandatory Review date is set 52 weeks from the date MSD completed the review.

chunks.title: Further information not needed to complete the Mandatory Review — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: In some situations, there may be good reason for the client having no change in their costs or income, and further information may not be needed for MSD to determine whether they continue to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance. For example, the client may have provided recent evidence of their costs or income, or they may have recently discussed their circumstances with MSD. If no further information is needed for MSD to determine the client continues to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance (including the rate payable), the future Mandatory Review date is set 52 weeks from the date MSD completed the review. Example Dion is getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance and he works 10 hours a week as a carpenter with a local employer. Dion is paid more than the minimum wage in this role in recognition of his skills and experience. Dion's Mandatory Review for Emergency Maintenance Allowance is due on 12 February 2027 and he responds on 10 February 2027 to confirm he has had no change in his circumstances. This includes no change in his income (which has remained unchanged since he moved into his current role in 2024). As Dion has been getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance and declared no change in his income for three consecutive years at the time the mandatory review is returned, MSD must consider whether further information is required before completing the Mandatory Review. MSD considers Dion's circumstances and notes that Dion recently contacted MSD to discuss another employment opportunity. However, Dion didn't get the job. As part of that conversation, MSD confirmed Dion's income hadn't changed (as he is paid more than the minimum wage, annual changes to the minimum wage have not impacted his income). MSD determines that no further information is required to determine that Dion continues to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance. His Emergency Maintenance Allowance continues at the same rate, and his next review date is set for 52 weeks in the future (9 February 2028).

chunks.title: Other situations where a child is considered to be financially independent — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Other situations where a child is considered to be financially independent
There may be other situations where all a child's financial needs (including the provision of accommodation and material needs) are being met by someone else or from some other source. For example:
- a family trust or
- the parent who is not acting as the principal caregiver
## Date of review
Where a child becomes financially independent it should be excluded from the benefit payment from the start of the next pay period in which the child became financially independent.
There is discretion to continue payment for one payday following the event.
This discretion only applies when the exclusion of the child affects the rate of payment of Emergency Maintenance Allowance and is generally used when processing deadlines have passed.
## Not financially independent
Generally, receipt of a Student Loan (including the living cost component) does not mean a child is financially independent.
For more information see:
- Gets a Student Loan
- Effect on benefit
- Processing standards Child changes [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Date of review — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Date of review
Exclude the child from the Emergency Maintenance Allowance from the beginning of the next pay period in which the child started work.

chunks.title: Guidelines for paying a higher rate — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Guidelines for paying a higher rate
Payment can be increased above the hospital rate to a rate that (together with the client's other income) will be sufficient to meet the client's continuing commitments.
Use the following guidelines to assess whether the client's rate should be higher.
1. Have the client complete an Increased payment while you are in hospital form.
2. Accept stated expenses where they appear reasonable, but ask for proof if there is doubt.
3. If the client is a sole parent and has childcare costs:
- include the child care costs when assessing whether a higher rate should be paid
- include family tax credit payments as income (as these payments will continue)
4. Check that all possible action has been taken to reduce expenses. For example, giving up the lease on a flat where the hospital stay is indefinite.
5. If the increase in payment request is for one-off items such as clothing, you can pay the increase by:
- a backdated review of the benefit rate to create a lump sum payment or
- increasing the benefit rate for a limited time
## Example
Continuing commitments per week
$55.00
less other weekly income (bank interest)
$5.00
rate of increase
$50.00
plus hospital rate (net, at 1 April 2026)
$58.34
rate of benefit payable
$108.34
Add the rate payable as a non-standard rate on the SNSRA screen.
A parent benefit reassessment SPBR may also be required.

chunks.title: Period in prison less than 31 days — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Period in prison less than 31 days
If the period in prison is less than 31 days an initial stand-down is not imposed if they apply for a benefit immediately after their release.
## Period in prison more than 31 days
If the period in prison is 31 days or more, an initial stand-down will be imposed.
## Exception
A client's Emergency Maintenance Allowance may have continued as a temporary caregiver was caring for the client's children. No stand-down will be imposed. The client's benefit will need to be reassessed and the agent will need to be removed.
For more information see:
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance Prisoners - no stand-down applies
- Transfer between benefits

chunks.title: Hospitalisation — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Hospitalisation
When an Emergency Maintenance Allowance client is admitted to hospital, their benefit can continue at the existing rate for the first 13 weeks.
The rate of payment will need to be reduced to the hospital rate after the client has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks (not after receiving a benefit for 13 weeks).
## Care of the child
MSD will need to confirm who is caring for the client's child, and the length of time the client is likely to be in hospital.
If requested, MSD may pay part of the benefit to the child's caregiver to cover the cost of alternative care or accommodation.
When the child is not going to remain in the care of the client, MSD should confirm what the continuing care arrangements are for the child. If the child is no longer a dependent child the client's benefit will stop. MSD will need to confirm if the client qualifies for another benefit.
If there are no other continuing financial costs, and it is likely that the client will remain in hospital long term, other means of income support for the children may be considered.
For example, the new caregiver may meet the qualifications for Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, or the child may be able to be included as a dependent child if the new caregiver is getting a main benefit.
## Hospital rate
The hospital rate allows for the cost of personal items, which patients are expected to provide for themselves.
As at 1 April 2026 the net weekly hospital rate is $58.34.
MSD may pay an amount above the hospital rate where there are financial circumstances to warrant paying a higher rate.
MSD cannot pay an amount less than the hospital rate.
## Client in hospital during Mandatory Review
Generally, clients getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance must respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date, or their payments will suspend.
However, when a client is in hospital (for 13 weeks or less) and needs more time to respond to the review they may be able to get an extension. If a client is unable to respond to the Mandatory Review, they may be exempt from needing to do it.
The client must contact MSD before their review date to discuss their situation if they need an extension or exemption.
Note clients who are in hospital for more than 13 weeks do not have a Mandatory Review.

chunks.title: Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure
Where a client does not advise of their departure from New Zealand before they go, they may be able to have their benefit paid from the day after their departure date if the client has a humanitarian reason that justifies their reason for travel and their failure to tell Work and Income before they left.
Humanitarian reasons are:
- to provide aid or assistance to a family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member) immediately following a natural disaster (for example, flood, earthquake, bush fires) or similar adverse event (eg house fire)
- to be with a suddenly seriously ill, or dying family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member)
- to attend the sudden funeral of a family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member)
For more information see:
- Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event (within 28 day maximum)
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Imprisonment — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Imprisonment
When an Emergency Maintenance Allowance client is imprisoned or detained in custody, they are generally no longer entitled to get the Emergency Maintenance Allowance.
In some circumstances Emergency Maintenance Allowance can continue when the client is imprisoned.
Generally to receive an Emergency Maintenance Allowance the client must be the parent of one or more dependent children.
As the client is in prison or remanded in custody the client generally is no longer the caregiver of dependent children.
The Emergency Maintenance Allowance should stop from the day following the date of imprisonment.
MSD must decide whether to suspend or cancel the Emergency Maintenance Allowance after considering the likely period in prison and whether the client has dependent children.
## Exception
The client may be imprisoned for less than one year and a temporary caregiver will be caring for the client's dependent children. In this situation, all or part of the Emergency Maintenance Allowance may continue and be paid to the temporary caregiver caring for the client's dependent children.
There is also discretion to continue payment if the client is remanded in custody pending a further court appearance.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Example 1
A client getting an Emergency Maintenance Allowance has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks. This client has other income which reduces the main benefit rate to $20.00 per week.
In this case we pay the rate $20.00 per week which is lower than the hospital rate of $58.34 (as at 1 April 2026).
## Example 2
A client getting an Emergency Maintenance Allowance has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks. This client has other income which reduces the main benefit rate to $70.00 per week.
In this case we pay the hospital rate of $58.34 per week (as at 1 April 2026) which is the lower rate.

chunks.title: Inland Revenue deduction notices — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Inland Revenue deduction notices
Inland Revenue may request for a client's unpaid taxes to be directly deducted from their benefit payments.
Note all Inland Revenue deduction notices are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit for processing.
The instructions of the deduction notice will be to deduct the lowest of either:
- 10% of the total debt which Inland Revenue specify in the notice, on a weekly basis or
- 20% of the client's gross earnings on a weekly basis
When there are insufficient funds to cover the deduction, Work and Income must advise Inland Revenue immediately that the deduction will not start or will start at a reduced rate.
Inland Revenue deductions have a lower priority than Child Support deductions.
For more information, see:
- Priority for deductions

chunks.title: Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect
A client can continue to receive payment of their benefit for an absence from New Zealand if it can be confirmed that the travel is to:
- attend a job interview
- follow up a definite job prospect
Benefit payments cannot continue if the client is leaving New Zealand to carry out general job search, that is, to 'have a look' for a job.
You will need to treat each case on its merits and take the following into account:
- does the client have proof of the interview or specific job prospect?
They will need to provide the employer's name and phone number and the date of the interview or meeting with the employer
- is it a realistic job opportunity for the client? That is, does it match the skills and qualifications of the client
- how long are they going for?
Consider what would be a reasonable time period for the client to complete the trip, for example, x number of days to get there, 1 day for the interview, x number of days to return home and frequency of flights to and from the destination
- what arrangements have they made for the continuing care of their children and accommodation while they are absent?
## Client chooses to be absent for longer than reasonably necessary
Where a client chooses to be absent for longer than is reasonably necessary to attend the job interview or investigate a potential job prospect, their benefit will not continue to be paid for those extra days.
For more information see:
- Examples of job interview or job prospects overseas
- Client obtains employment overseas
- Approved travel reasons

chunks.title: Mandatory Review dates for Emergency Maintenance Allowance — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Mandatory Review dates for Emergency Maintenance Allowance
MSD must review a client's Emergency Maintenance Allowance within 52 weeks of the commencement date of the benefit, or within 52 weeks from when the client's last Mandatory Review was completed.
A future Mandatory Review date will only be set if the expiry date for the Emergency Maintenance Allowance is more than 52 weeks. The next Mandatory Review date will be set 52 weeks from the date MSD determined the client continues to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance and the rate of benefit payable (if applicable) i.e. when MSD completes the review.
Note when MSD has an interaction with a client that confirms all of the same circumstances as a Mandatory Review, this can push out the client’s Mandatory Review date by 52 weeks. This is known as a specific engagement.
## Initial Mandatory Review dates
Benefit commencement date
Mandatory Review dates
Benefit commenced before 2 March 2026
Clients whose Emergency Maintenance Allowance commenced before 2 March 2026 will have their initial Mandatory Review either:
- 52 weeks from the commencement date of the benefit
or
- 52 weeks from when their last periodic review was completed
or
- 52 weeks from when MSD last contacted the client to confirm if the information MSD holds about their circumstances is correct (annual circumstances letter).
Whichever date is later.
Benefit commenced on or after 2 March 2026
If a client's Emergency Maintenance Allowance commenced on or after 2 March 2026, their initial Mandatory Review date is either:
- 52 weeks from the commencement date of the Emergency Maintenance Allowance
or
- 52 weeks from the completion of a specific engagement.

chunks.title: Mandatory Review for Emergency Maintenance Allowance — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Mandatory Reviews for Emergency Maintenance Allowance only applies to clients whose benefit has an expiry date of more than 52 weeks, or whose Emergency Maintenance Allowance has no expiry date. MSD must review a client's Emergency Maintenance Allowance within 52-weeks of when their benefit commenced, or 52-weeks from when the client's last Mandatory Review was completed. Clients must respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date, or their payments will suspend. The purpose of a Mandatory Review for Emergency Maintenance Allowance is to: - check for any changes to a client's circumstances - determine if the client still meets the qualifications for Emergency Maintenance Allowance and - review the rate of Emergency Maintenance Allowance payable. If a client declares a change in circumstances that may affect their conditions of grant, MSD should check if the client continues to meet the conditions of grant for the Emergency Maintenance Allowance. Note the Review of Annual Income is a separate process to a Mandatory Review.

chunks.title: Clients getting Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Clients also getting Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance will have these reviewed at the same time as their Mandatory Review for Emergency Maintenance Allowance. Example: client is getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance and Accommodation Supplement Eru has been getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance since 24 May 2026. His Accommodation Supplement commenced on 2 April 2027. Because the initial Mandatory Review date is determined by the Emergency Maintenance Allowance commencement date, the review date for both Accommodation Supplement and Emergency Maintenance Allowance is reset to 52 weeks from 24 May 2026.

chunks.title: Clients getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: A client getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance and Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit will have a Mandatory Review for their Emergency Maintenance Allowance at least once in a 52-week period, but it will be separate to the Mandatory Review for Orphan's Benefit and Unsupported Child's Benefit.

chunks.title: Notice period for a Mandatory Review — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Clients are notified at least 20 working days before their Mandatory Review date, unless their Emergency Maintenance Allowance is suspended due to the client being temporarily overseas or in prison. The notice period allows sufficient time for clients to respond to the Mandatory Review. Note if a client's Emergency Maintenance Allowance is suspended when the Mandatory Review notice is sent, they are not required to respond to their Mandatory Review until their Emergency Maintenance Allowance is to be resumed.

chunks.title: Responding to the Mandatory Review — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: To respond to the Mandatory Review, the client must: - confirm or provide current information about their circumstances and - provide updated information to MSD if requested. Clients must confirm the information MSD holds is correct or provide any new information before their review date. When a client has responded to the Mandatory Review and MSD has determined that they continue to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance, their next review date is 52 weeks from the date their Mandatory Review was completed.

chunks.title: Client does not respond to Mandatory Review — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: When a client does not respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date, the Emergency Maintenance Allowance will suspend. If the client does not respond to the Mandatory Review to confirm their circumstances within 8 weeks after their payments have suspended, the Emergency Maintenance Allowance will be cancelled. A client can still do their Mandatory Review during those 8 weeks. However, once the Emergency Maintenance Allowance has cancelled, the client will need to make a new application for benefit if they still need financial assistance. A client's Emergency Maintenance Allowance cannot be resumed before they have responded to their Mandatory Review during the 8-week suspension period.

chunks.title: Emergency Maintenance Allowance suspends — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: If a client's Emergency Maintenance Allowance suspends as a result of the client not responding to their Mandatory Review, all of their assistance will also suspend, except for the following payments: - Child Disability Allowance - Orphan's Benefit - Unsupported Child's Benefit - Childcare Subsidy - OSCAR (Out of School Care and Recreational Subsidy) - Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment

chunks.title: When the Mandatory Review is completed — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: The Mandatory Review is completed when MSD makes a decision about whether the client continues to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance and the rate of benefit payable. MSD will either: - continue paying the benefit at the existing rate - adjust the rate of benefit so the client is getting the correct rate - suspend the benefit if there is no rate payable for a period (e.g. client has variable income) - cancel the benefit if the client no longer qualifies

chunks.title: Cash assets — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Clients getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance may have met the exceptional circumstance criteria for having all or part of their cash assets disregarded when they were granted their benefit on the grounds of hardship. If a client has a Mandatory Review for their Emergency Maintenance Allowance and there has been a change to their assets, MSD may consider if the exceptional circumstances criteria still applies and if the cash assets should still be disregarded.

chunks.title: Mandatory Review not required — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Mandatory Review not required
There is no Mandatory Review for Emergency Maintenance Allowance for clients with an expiry date more than 52 weeks or no expiry at all in the following circumstances:
- the client is hospitalised for more than 13 weeks
- the client is in residential disability care or rest home care
- the client has died
- the client is living in or visiting a region affected by an emergency or adverse event and they are unable to reasonably leave the area
- the client is living in or visiting a region affected by an outbreak of a quarantinable disease and an epidemic notice has been given and is in force
or when:
- there is a major system outage that prevents MSD from carrying out mandatory reviews of specified benefits.
MSD will also stop the review for any clients who are in these circumstances after they have been notified about their Mandatory Review.
MSD will notify the client when they are not required to complete the review. The Mandatory Review date will be reset to 52 weeks in the future from the client's original review date.
Note a notification will not be sent when the client has died.

chunks.title: Ministry of Social Development debt repayments — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Ministry of Social Development debt repayments
When a client has a Ministry of Social Development debt, this can be recovered by regular deductions from their current benefit.
Note Income Related Rent historical Kāinga Ora debt should be given equal priority to Ministry of Social Development debt.
For more information see:
- Core policy Negotiating repayment of debt

chunks.title: Does not advise of departure — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Does not advise of departure
If the client did not tell the Ministry they were leaving New Zealand their benefit will be suspended immediately from the day after they left New Zealand.
The Integrity Intervention Centre will determine if there has been an overpayment, establish any debt and advise the client.
If a client questions the information match refer them to the Integrity Intervention Centre.
For more information see:
- Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure
- Approved travel reasons
- Backdating benefit to the day after departure date
- Action on return to New Zealand
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy

chunks.title: Ongoing assistance for dependent children — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Ongoing assistance for dependent children
When a surviving dependent child is to be cared for by a person other than a parent, the principal caregiver may be able to receive an Orphans Benefit or an Unsupported Child's Benefit.

chunks.title: On leave for 28 days or less — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## On leave for 28 days or less
Where a client who is receiving the hospital rate is on leave from hospital for 28 days or less:
- increase their benefit to the appropriate full rate from the date of discharge on leave and
- review any Extra Help from the same date
On re-admission to hospital:
- reduce the benefit to the rate payable prior to the period of leave and
- review any Extra Help from the same date
Note the dates of admission and discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital.

chunks.title: On leave for more than 28 days — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## On leave for more than 28 days
Where a client who is receiving the hospital rate is on leave from hospital for more than 28 days:
- increase their benefit to the appropriate full rate from the date of discharge on leave and
- review any Extra Help
On re-admission to hospital continue to pay the full rate of benefit and any Extra Help for a further 13 weeks of hospitalisation.
Note calculation of the 13 week period in hospital begins again after the client has been re-admitted when on leave for more than 28 days.
The dates of admission and discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital.

chunks.title: On leave from hospital — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## On leave from hospital
Emergency Maintenance Allowance is paid at the full rate for any period of leave from hospital.
When the client has been receiving the hospital rate increase their benefit for any period they are on leave.
The benefit action to take, on the client's re-admission to hospital, will depend on how long they were on leave.
## Effect of leave on 13-week count
Any periods of leave from hospital of 28 days or less are to be ignored when deciding the date from which the benefit is to be reduced to the hospital rate.
Calculate the period in hospital from the original admission date.
If the client has been allowed out of hospital for more than 28 days, the calculation of the 13-week period in hospital begins again after the client has been re-admitted.

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki order in place — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: The following table identifies when a child can be considered a dependent child and when it can't, depending on the type of order that is in place and section of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 that applies. When to include as a dependent child When not to include as a dependent child section 139: Agreements for temporary care of child or young person by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 140: Agreements for extended care of child or young person by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 78: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, pending determination of court proceedings. If Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki has returned the child or young person in to the care of the immediate previous care giver. section 78: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, pending determination of court proceedings section 101: Custody order in favour of principal caregiver. Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki under section 110. section 101: Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 102: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 110(2)a: Sole Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. Section 101 Custody Order in favour of principal caregiver and other dependent child criteria are met. Please refer case to your local solicitor for consideration. section 110(2)a: Sole Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 110(2) b: Additional Guardianship Order, to any other guardian in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 112: Guardianship Order in favour of Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki for a specific purpose. Please refer case to your local solicitor for consideration. section 86: Services Orders that provide for particular services and assistance required by the child or young person (e.g. counselling fees, special education costs) section 86: Services Orders that provide for general financial support to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 91: Support Orders. The child may be considered a dependent child where the documentation states that specific financial support is to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki.

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki order in place — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: section 91: Support Orders. The child cannot be considered a dependent child where the documentation states that general financial support is to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. See your local solicitor if you receive a case in this category. When a child or young person is discharged from the care, custody or sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, always consider including the child in the clients Emergency Maintenance Allowance or granting Unsupported Childs Benefit - The legislation referenced above is the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989

chunks.title: Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid
When a client is receiving an Orphans Benefit or an Unsupported Childs Benefit, the child is not treated as a dependent child and is not included in the assessment of Emergency Maintenance Allowance.
The client's Emergency Maintenance Allowance is assessed on their family circumstances excluding the child which Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid for.

chunks.title: Outcomes of a Mandatory Review — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Clients must respond to their Mandatory Review before their Mandatory Review date, or their payments will suspend. When a client responds to the review, there are a number of outcomes that can occur. Once MSD has determined if the client qualifies, MSD will either: - continue paying the benefit at the existing rate - adjust the rate of benefit so the client is getting the correct rate - suspend the benefit if there is no rate payable for a period (e.g. client has variable income) - cancel the benefit if the client no longer qualifies The Mandatory Review is completed when MSD makes a decision about whether the client continues to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance and the rate of benefit payable (if applicable). MSD may also carry out a separate review of Emergency Maintenance Allowance at any time, where there is good reason.

chunks.title: Client declares no change — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: When a client responds to the Mandatory Review and confirms they have had no change in circumstances, MSD must review the client's eligibility and rate of Emergency Maintenance Allowance. If the client remains eligible following the Mandatory Review a future date for the next review will be set if the expiry date for the Emergency Maintenance Allowance is more than 52 weeks from the commencement of the benefit or last Mandatory Review, or there is no expiry date. Exceptions when a client declares no change When a client responds to their Mandatory Review and confirms they have no change in circumstances, there are some situations when MSD can request further information from the client before deciding whether to continue Emergency Maintenance Allowance.

chunks.title: Client declares a change in circumstances — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: When a client responds to the Mandatory Review with a change in circumstances, MSD must use the information provided to determine if the client continues to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance, or any other benefits they get that are subject to a Mandatory Review (excluding Orphan's Benefit and Unsupported Child's Benefit) and the rate payable. MSD may request further information from the client if it is not possible to determine that the client continues to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance. Date of change When a client declares a change in circumstances, MSD will need to assess if the client still qualifies for Emergency Maintenance Allowance and the rate payable and from what date, depending on when the change in circumstance happened or will happen. Client is also getting other assistance When the client has provided information as part of the Mandatory Review that could affect their entitlement to or the rate payable of any other assistance (e.g. Temporary Additional Support or Flexible Childcare Assistance), MSD may use this information to review that assistance. When the other assistance is affected by the outcome of the Mandatory Review, MSD must change the rate, suspend or cancel that assistance where appropriate. For example, if the outcome of the Mandatory Review is that the client is no longer entitled to Emergency Maintenance Allowance, their Temporary Additional Support must be reviewed, and the rate may change or stop if they no longer qualify.

chunks.title: Further information is needed to complete the Mandatory Review — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: If further information is needed to determine if the client continues to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance or that the rate of payment is correct, MSD must give a reasonable timeframe for the client to provide it. The date the client is given to provide the information by will become the client's new deadline to respond to the Mandatory Review. If the client doesn't provide the information that was asked for before the deadline, MSD must suspend the Emergency Maintenance Allowance from the new deadline date. If the client provides the information that was asked for and MSD determines the client continues to qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance (including the rate payable), the future Mandatory Review date will be set 52 weeks from the date MSD completed the review (if the expiry date for the Emergency Benefit is more than 52 weeks or there is no expiry date).

chunks.title: Completing the Mandatory Review when there are new costs — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: In some circumstances MSD can still complete the Mandatory Review when a client has a change in circumstances that doesn't affect the client's eligibility for Emergency Maintenance Allowance, e.g. the client has declared a new cost. Example 1 Winston is getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance and has a Mandatory Review for his benefit. Winston responds to his Mandatory Review to confirm his circumstances. Winston tells MSD he now has accommodation costs but nothing else has changed. MSD completes the Mandatory Review and continues the Emergency Maintenance Allowance at the existing rate as the change declared by Winston doesn't affect his eligibility for Emergency Maintenance Allowance. Winston can apply for Accommodation Supplement based on his new accommodation costs. This application is separate to the Mandatory Review. Example 2 Eiza is getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance and Disability Allowance and has a Mandatory Review for both. Eiza responds to the Mandatory Review to confirm their circumstances. Eiza tells MSD they have a new disability cost but nothing else has changed. MSD completes the Mandatory Review and continues the Emergency Maintenance Allowance and Disability Allowance at the existing rate. MSD advises Eiza that they need to provide a medical certificate from their medical or nurse practitioner to confirm the additional cost, and they must provide proof of cost to have the new cost included in their Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Part-time employment — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Part-time employment
Part-time employment does not make a child financially independent. Nor do you take the child's earnings into account when assessing the rate of Emergency Maintenance Allowance payments. For more information on children's income see:
- Income Children's income

chunks.title: Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure
Generally, clients receiving a main benefit must advise Work and Income of their intention to leave New Zealand prior to their departure to be eligible to continue to receive their payments.
Only in specific circumstances can a client receiving a benefit who leaves New Zealand without telling us be able to have their benefit either:
- resumed from the date that they notified Work and Income of their absence if their travel is allowed or
- backdated to the day after their departure date
Note this can occur either while the client is still overseas or once they have returned.
## Resuming benefit when client failed to advise of absence
If a client contacts Work and Income after they have left New Zealand, and is not eligible to have their payment backdated, their benefit can only be resumed from:
- the date that they notified us of their absence and
- only if the travel is allowed (ie they meet the criteria to continue to be paid their benefit while overseas either because they meet the criteria for approved travel, or the requirement that travel be approved does not apply to them)
Otherwise, the client cannot have their benefit resumed until they return to New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Action on return to New Zealand
- Approved travel reasons
- Payment when client absent from New Zealand
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy
- Client does not return

chunks.title: Paying a higher rate — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Paying a higher rate
You can make payment at a rate higher than the hospital rate where the client cannot meet their continuing costs from the hospital rate of payment and any other income they receive.
You will need to take into consideration:
- the client's financial commitments and
- access to other income
Note when you are considering payment of benefit at a rate higher than the hospital rate, generally you do not take cash assets into account as rates of benefit payment are not subject to an assets test.
If a client is required to make Child Support payments and does not qualify for an exemption from IR-CS (Inland Revenue), you can increase the hospital rate to include any Child Support payments that are required to be apportioned from the benefit.
For more information about paying at a higher rate see:
- Guidelines for paying a higher rate
- Carers who do not need to apply
## Maximum amount payable
You can pay a rate higher than the hospital rate up to the maximum rate of Emergency Maintenance Allowance that would otherwise be payable.
## When not to pay a higher rate
A client cannot be paid a higher rate of benefit (because of hospitalisation) than they would otherwise receive. When their usual benefit payment is less than the hospital rate, you don't increase their benefit to the hospital rate (or any other higher rate).
A benefit may be paid at less than the hospital rate because of:
- the client's income (if it continues while in hospital) or
- maintenance deductions or
- overseas pension deductions

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period when the client is absent from New Zealand. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
To pay a benefit more than 28 days during any 52 week period:
- the client must be continuing to receive their benefit while absent from New Zealand because: they have an approved travel reason orthey are not required to have an approved travel reason in order to be paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand
- they have an approved travel reason or
- they are not required to have an approved travel reason in order to be paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand
- the client could not return to New Zealand because of new circumstances that: they could not reasonably foresee at the time when they left New Zealand, andthat are outside of the client's control
- they could not reasonably foresee at the time when they left New Zealand, and
- that are outside of the client's control
and
- Work and Income is satisfied that the extension of the absence is no longer than is necessary to address the new circumstances
## Examples
A client who is absent from New Zealand for an approved reason may be prevented from returning by new unforeseen circumstances which could include (but are not limited to):
- travel delays due to unforeseen weather events eg fog, volcano, flooding, earthquakes, terrorism
- travel delays due to transport options being cancelled
- health condition or injury or hospitalisation preventing return
For more information see:
- Overseas for medical treatment
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days for an approved reason — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period when the client is absent from New Zealand. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. To pay a benefit more than 28 days during any 52 week period of absence from New Zealand, the client must be travelling for one of the following reasons: - essential travel - to attend a significant event relating to a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family), that the client would reasonably be expected to attend (eg visit a person who is seriously ill, seriously injured or whose death is imminent, attend a funeral, provide support to a party or witness to a court case, travel required for a court ordered custody arrangement) - to attend a court case which the person is required to attend as a party or a witness - to attend a job interview or follow up on a job prospect - for clients with a disability, to receive vocational training or disability assistance-dog training not available in New Zealand during the period or periods of absence - for clients with a disability, to travel overseas for the sole or predominant purpose of competing in any overseas multinational or international Special Olympic or Paralympic Games competition - to provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster (flood, earthquake, fire) or similar adverse event (eg house fire) and - Work and Income must be satisfied, when considering the client's reason for travel, that the length of the absence is no longer than necessary for the reason for travel In addition, where the client has already been paid a benefit while absent from New Zealand in the 52 week period Work and Income must be satisfied that either: - the client could not have reasonably foreseen them needing to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, or - the client could not have rearranged their affairs to avoid being absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, and - it would be unreasonable for the benefit not to be paid Note generally we would not pay more than 28 days extra travel per absence. For more information see: - Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason - Client does not return due to an unforeseeable event (within 28 days maximum) - Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Payment when client absent from New Zealand — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Payment when client absent from New Zealand
There are some situations where the benefit payments will be affected when the client is absent from New Zealand. The action required by Work and Income will depend on the reason the client is absent from New Zealand and whether they are continuing to be paid a benefit.
For more information see:
- Ending payment for client who needs an approved reason for travel
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum)
- Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event (within 28 day maximum)
- Child absent

chunks.title: Permanent absence — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Permanent absence
If a client is leaving New Zealand permanently, Jobseeker Support must be cancelled from the day after departure.
## Moving to Australia
If the client is moving to Australia it is important that they are aware that they may not be able to receive a benefit until they have resided in Australia for two years after being granted permanent residence status.
For more information see:
- United Kingdom Reciprocal Agreement Jobseekers Allowance
- Australia Reciprocal Agreement New Zealand benefits and pensions in Australia
- Payments from Overseas Reciprocal Agreements
- Client does not return

chunks.title: Permitted travel reasons — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Permitted travel reasons
A client not otherwise entitled to be paid their Emergency Maintenance Allowance while absent from New Zealand may have their payments continue for up to 28 days in any 52 week period, if their travel is for one (or a combination) of, the following permitted travel reasons:
- essential travel - to attend a significant event relating to a family member or a person who fulfils a role in relation to the client that is similar to that of a family member
- to attend a court case which the person is required to attend as a party or a witness - this is to allow clients who are required by law to attend court and supports the maintenance of the law. A client would generally be expected to provide evidence that they are required to attend a court overseas. This would include documents from the court.
- to attend a job interview or follow up on a job prospect
- for clients with a disability, to receive vocational training or disability assistance-dog training not available in New Zealand during the time the client is absent
- for clients with a disability, to travel overseas for the sole or predominant purpose of competing in any overseas multinational or international Special Olympic or Paralympic Games competition
- to provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster (eg flood, earthquake, fire) or similar adverse event (eg house fire)

chunks.title: Priority for deductions — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Priority for deductions
Certain forms of deductions take priority over others; the following list gives the order of priority, highest to lowest:
Highest priority
- Child Support deductions made under the Child Support Act 1991
- Inland Revenue tax deductions
- Ministry of Social Development debt repayments including Liable Parent Contributions (LPC), child maintenance debts and Major Repairs Advances (MRA), Student Allowance debt, Student Loan debt converted to Ministry of Social Development debt, Income Related Rent historical Kāinga Ora debt, Income Related Rent Ministry of Social Development debt
- attachment orders made under the Family Proceedings Act 1980
- court attachment orders issued under the Summary Proceedings Act 1957
- court attachment orders issued under the District Court Act 2016
- Student Loan repayments
Lowest priority
Determining the priority of deductions is necessary when a client has more than one order issued in respect of their benefit. Also each order and deduction notice is subject to its own protected earnings rule.
When you need to reduce deductions you adjust from the lowest priority up to those with a higher priority taking into account the protected earnings rules for each.

chunks.title: Private hospital and homes — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Private hospital and homes
Emergency Maintenance Allowance can be paid at the full rate regardless of the period of hospitalisation when a client is:
- admitted to a private hospital or
- admitted to a private home that provides residential care disability services
If the client receives Extra Help, this will need to be reviewed to see if their costs are continuing.
For more information see:
- Residential Care Subsidy
- Residential Support Subsidy

chunks.title: Protected earnings rate — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Protected earnings rate
Both the District Court Act and the Summary Proceedings Act provide that every Ministry of Justice attachment order must specify a 'protected earnings rate'. The protected earnings rate is usually 60% of the client’s net earnings after PAYE tax has been deducted or withheld.
If the attachment order will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate, then the order will not operate and you must cancel or return the attachment order to the Ministry of Justice.
Calculating the client's income differs between attachment orders made under the Summary Proceedings Act and the District Court Act, in that different benefits are taken into account.
Therefore it is important to determine what type of attachment order has been issued.
Summary Proceedings Act 1957
For orders made under the Summary Proceedings Act, the calculation of the client's income does not include Special Benefit, Temporary Additional Support, Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance, Winter Energy Payment, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit
District Court Act 2016
For orders made under the District Court Act, the client's income includes Special Benefit, Temporary Additional Support and Disability Allowance but does not include Child Disability Allowance, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit
## Example
An attachment order is received from the Ministry of Justice for $70.00 per week. The order lists the client's protected earnings rate as $405.91 per week:
We need to calculate whether adding the deduction of $70.00 will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate:
Calculate protected earnings rate
Emergency Maintenance Allowance - sole parent benefit rate (as at 1 April 2026)
$521.52
Plus Accommodation Supplement (Area 2)
$155.00
Total net earnings
$676.52
60% of total net earnings (=protected earnings)
$405.91
Calculate if Attachment Order will exceed protected earnings
Total net earnings
$676.52
Less Child Support deduction
$130.00
Less Ministry of Social Development debts
$75.00
Sub total
$471.52
Less Attachment Order
$70.00
Total net income remaining for the client per week
$401.52
The attachment order amount of $70.00 takes the client's total net income remaining to $401.52, this is below the protected earnings rate of $405.91.
The attachment order will not operate, you must return it to the Ministry of Justice for the order to be amended.

chunks.title: Qualifies for another benefit — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Qualifies for another benefit
A client may qualify for another benefit due to a change in their circumstances. It is also important to determine if the client still qualifies for Emergency Maintenance Allowance.
For example the client reaches the qualifying age for Sole Parent Support or a 16 to 18 year old client obtains permanent residence or citizenship.
If the client qualifies for more than one benefit they must be told which benefit is the most beneficial for their particular circumstances. You will need to advise them of:
- benefit rates
- the effect of any income they may receive (income reduction and any exemptions) and
- benefit obligations
The client must make the final decision on which benefit they receive after being given all relevant information.
For more information see:
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance qualifications
- Sole Parent Support qualifications
- Young Parent Payment qualifications
- Processing standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Rate of payment — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Rate of payment
If payment of Emergency Maintenance Allowance is to continue while a sole parent client is in prison, you will need to determine the rate to pay to the temporary caregiver.
The Emergency Maintenance Allowance should generally be paid at the equivalent rate of Unsupported Child's Benefit less the family tax credit that would be payable if the caregiver qualified for this (see Examples).
## Exception
However there is discretion to continue payment at the full sole parent rate.
You can consider including the following costs to calculate the rate to pay the temporary caregiver while the client is in prison:
- rent or outgoings if the children are being cared for in the client's home
- the client's other commitments if these costs are for essential items and they cannot be suspended, such as Child Support payments (where the client does not qualify for an exemption) or a hire purchase for an essential item
The total amount paid to the temporary caregiver must not exceed the maximum amount of Emergency Maintenance Allowance payable. An application for this assistance must be made by the temporary caregiver.
## SWIFTT
The Emergency Maintenance Allowance and family tax credit should continue in the client's name and be paid to the caregiver as an agent in SWIFTT
When the temporary caregiver is to be paid less than the maximum rate of Emergency Maintenance Allowance, you will need to add this as a non-standard rate using the SNSRA screen in SWIFTT
