For more information see:
- Decision guidelines - sole parents
- Examples - sole parents
- Remanded in custody
- Temporary caregiver

chunks.title: Date of review — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Date of review
The child should be excluded from the beginning start of the next pay period in whichfollowing the date Student Allowance (or Independent Circumstances Allowance) commences.
Note there are specific rules for deciding whether a child is considered a dependent child when they turn 18 and are continuing in education.
## Family tax credit
Family tax credits should stop from the start of the pay period following the date Student Allowance was granted, to avoid an overpayment with Inland Revenue for the client.

chunks.title: Gets a Student Loan — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Gets a Student Loan
Getting a Student Loan (including the living cost component) does not mean the child is financially independent.
If the child continues to be the client's primary responsibility and maintained as a member of their family and financially dependent (that is the parent is meeting some of the costs for the child) the child can continue to be included in the benefit until the start of the pay period following:
- the date they turn 18 or
- where the child is 18 years old and continuing in education, the earlier of: the date they are no longer enrolled in school or tertiary education orthe date the child is no longer attending school or tertiary education as required orthe date the child is financially independent orthe date the child leaves the parent or caregiver's care or31 December of the year they turn 18
- the date they are no longer enrolled in school or tertiary education or
- the date the child is no longer attending school or tertiary education as required or
- the date the child is financially independent or
- the date the child leaves the parent or caregiver's care or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18
Note a client getting a discretionary benefit such as Emergency Maintenance Allowance must complete a review of circumstances when a dependent child turns 18, and when the child is excluded (if they continued to be included in the client's benefit after the child turned 18).

chunks.title: Release from prison — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Release from prison
A client may be entitled to Emergency Maintenance Allowance when they are released from prison. The date to recommence payment depends on the length of time the client has been in prison.
For more information see:
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance Prisoners no stand-down applies

chunks.title: Release on bail — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Release on bail
When a client is released on bail, Emergency Maintenance Allowance can be paid from the date of release providing the client:
- still meets the qualifications for Emergency Maintenance Allowance and
- has been in custody for less than 31 days and
- reapplies for Emergency Maintenance Allowance immediately after their release
The client must also meet the definition of the parent of 1 or more dependent children.
Note if the client has been in custody for more than 31 days an initial stand-down will be imposed.
For more information see:
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance Prisoners - no stand-down applies
- Home detention

chunks.title: Remanded in custody — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Remanded in custody
Generally, when a client is remanded in custody awaiting a further court appearance their benefit should stop. However, there is discretion to continue payment of Emergency Maintenance Allowance after taking the client's financial circumstances and commitments into account.
When deciding whether to continue paying Emergency Maintenance Allowance for the period of remand for a particular client, consider the following:
- has the client been remanded pending a further hearing or for sentencing
- does the client have continuing costs that cannot be avoided, such as rent and hire purchase for essential items
- does the client have a partner or dependent children
Every situation should be considered on a case-by-case basis.
For help contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances of the client before making a decision.

chunks.title: Review of Annual Income — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: The Review of Annual Income ensures that clients getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance have received the correct rate of payment for the past 52 weeks. Clients do not have a Review of Annual Income if their benefit has not been reduced at any point during the period that income is assessed (the 52-week review period). Clients who did not get any income during this period will also not have a review. Note the Review of Annual Income is a separate process to Mandatory Reviews.

chunks.title: Income received during the review period — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Income received during the 52-week period following the client's commencement date, and each 52-week period after that, is assessed against the benefit that was paid to the client during this time. Most types of income are charged against Emergency Maintenance Allowance for the review year the income was earned in or the period it relates to. The relevant period may be a period in the past or a future date. Only income charged during the current review period is considered for the Review of Annual Income. If the client has transferred between benefits, but has been continuously receiving a benefit that can have income charged annually, the commencement date is the date they first received their annual benefit.

chunks.title: Child Support income for Reviews of Annual Income — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Non-information share Child Support Non-information share Child Support payments are charged as income using the general charging rules that are used for most other types of income. Any non-information share Child Support payments charged as income during the current review period are included in the Review of Annual Income. Information share Child Support Information share Child Support payments are charged forward as income, using defined rules. The income charge is always for 4 or 5 weeks from when the client gets the payment, regardless of what period the payment relates to. Any information share Child Support payments charged as income during the current review period are included in the Review of Annual Income. Note the amount of information share Child Support payment charged as income may not be the same amount of Child Support a client got in the review period. This could happen if a client gets an information share Child Support payment shortly before the end of the review period. Only the income charged during the review period can be included in the Review of Annual Income. Example Tybalt gets an Emergency Maintenance Allowance and gets information share Child Support payments from his child's other parent. Tybalt's review period for his Review of Annual Income is 6 September to 5 September the following year. Tybalt gets an information share Child Support payment on 21 August. This payment is charged forward for 4 weeks, from the week beginning 19 August. Only the income charged from 19 August to 5 September will be included in this years' Review of Annual Income. The remainder of the 4-week income charge related to that Child Support payment will be included in the following year's review.

chunks.title: Shared care — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Shared care
Shared care only applies when the parents of a child are living apart, the child lives (for at least 40% of the time) with each parent and both parents apply for a benefit in respect of that child.
In shared care situations you can only pay a sole parent rate of benefit to the parent that has the greater responsibility.
For more information see:
- Decision Guidelines for shared care
Emergency Benefit cannot be paid to the 'other' parent on the basis that they care for the child for part of the time. Parents are expected to arrange care of their children to allow at least one parent to work.
Never pay two sole parent rates of benefit in respect of the same child (that is one child can't be included in two benefits at the same time).
## Family tax credit
For information on the payment of family tax credit in shared care situations see:
- Family tax credit Shared care
## Child Disability Allowance
For more information on the payment of Child Disability Allowance in shared care see:
- Child Disability Allowance Shared care - principal caregiver

chunks.title: Specific engagements — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Specific engagements
Specific engagements are interactions that can meet the same purpose as the Mandatory Review. These interactions can capture information that confirms if a client still qualifies for Emergency Maintenance Allowance.
Specific engagements are when a client has an interaction with MSD, and this results in a full review of the client's circumstances.
For example, specific engagements may include when a client contacts MSD to:
- discuss a change in circumstances or
- apply for assistance.
If the specific engagement meets the same purpose as a Mandatory Review, a client's Mandatory Review date will be set 52 weeks from when the specific engagement was completed (if the expiry date for the Emergency Maintenance Allowance is more than 52 weeks or there is no expiry date).

chunks.title: Split care — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Split care
Split care is when parents with two or more children are living apart and each parent has the care of at least one of their children on a full-time basis.
The child that is living with the Emergency Maintenance Allowance client can be included as a dependent child.
Note that in split care situations generally only one parent can receive Sole Parent Support. The other parent must qualify, in their own right, for another benefit.
For more information see:
- Sole Parent Support Split care

chunks.title: Student Loans repayments — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Student Loans repayments
Clients with a Student Loan must make repayments to Inland Revenue when the income they get is over the repayment threshold. This level is called the 'income threshold'.
A person must make repayments to Inland Revenue when their income is over $464.00 gross per week ($24,128 gross per year) as at 1 April 2026.
Note non-taxable Extra help such as family tax credit, Accommodation Supplement and Winter Energy Payment do not count as income.
If the client's income is over this income threshold, the Ministry of Social Development can make the required deduction. However, this is only done if the client requests it.
If the client's portion of benefit is below the income threshold, there is no provision to make voluntary repayments through SWIFTT.
The client can make voluntary payments direct to Inland Revenue at any time.
Note the following:
- Student Loan deductions can only be made from taxable benefits
- Student Loan deductions cannot be made if the client's benefit is below the income threshold
- when a client receives a married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit only the client's portion is taken into consideration when assessing Student Loan repayments
- when a client is receiving a reduced rate of payment due to other income, the Student Loan deduction is assessed on the net payment after income deduction
For more information on Student Loans see:
- Students Student loan

chunks.title: Debt Repayment Orders — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Debt Repayment Orders
All Debt Repayment Orders are sent directly to the Central Processing Unit for processing.
Debt Repayment Orders are issued by the Ministry of Justice under the Insolvency Act 2006 and can be issued when the client is an un-discharged bankrupt.
Unlike other Ministry of Justice attachment orders, Debt Repayment Orders are not subject to any protected earnings rate. Payment is generally made to the supervisor of the debt but occasionally a District Court will act as an agent for collection of the debt.
Payment continues for three years or until further notice is received from either the supervisor or the District Court.
Unlike Ministry of Justice attachment orders, Debt Repayment Orders are administered via the PYECI screen in SWIFTT, not through CORBI.

chunks.title: Exception — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Exception
Tax details can be issued if a client:
- dies - you can provide details to the estate solicitor, administrator, executor etc. or
- is paid a New Zealand benefit overseas - details will be automatically sent to the client in April each year

chunks.title: Tax codes — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Tax codes
Emergency Maintenance Allowance is taxed at the 'M' rate.
Emergency Maintenance Allowance is always considered the client's primary source of income regardless of the amount paid. If the client has other income this is always considered the client's secondary income. Clients can apply to Inland Revenue for a tailored tax code for their other income.

chunks.title: Taxation — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Taxation
Emergency Maintenance Allowance is a taxable benefit. MSD makes payments to clients at the net rate after the deduction of tax. MSD passes the tax on to Inland Revenue.
Generally MSD will request clients to give MSD their IRD number or evidence of their IRD number.

chunks.title: Extra assistance during temporary care — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Extra assistance during temporary care
Any assistance for additional costs due to temporary care situations should be met, in the first instance, by the principal caregiver. Where this is not available, you can consider Special Needs Grants assistance for the client.
For more information see:
- Special Needs Grants

chunks.title: Temporary caregiver — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Temporary caregiver
When a client is imprisoned, you will need to find out who is caring for the client's children; and the length of time the client is likely to be in prison. This information can be obtained by contacting the prison liaison officer at the Department of Corrections.
If another person is caring for the client's dependent children, generally the temporary caregiver will need to apply for financial assistance in their own right.
They may be entitled to:
- have the children included as dependent children in their current benefit
- Unsupported Childs Benefit if the period in prison is likely to be 12 months or more
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance Single and caring for a child who is not their own or
- family tax credit through Inland Revenue
## Exception
There is discretion to pay all or part of the Emergency Maintenance Allowance to a temporary caregiver caring for the client's children.
There is also discretion to continue payment if the client is remanded in custody pending a further court appearance.
For more information to help you decide, see:
- Decision guidelines - sole parents
- Examples - sole parents
- Rate of payment
- Remanded in custody

chunks.title: Terminal benefit rate — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: The provision to continue the benefit payment for 28 days following the date of death is referred to as terminal benefit. Emergency Maintenance Allowance is continued at the rate which was payable to the client at the date of death. A terminal benefit includes extra help being paid (for up to 28 days following the date of death), but does not include family tax credit and Best Start tax credit payments.

chunks.title: Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit payments do not form part of terminal benefit.

chunks.title: Benefit paid at a reduced rate — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: When the client's benefit was paid at a reduced rate at the date of death, the terminal benefit is also paid at the reduced rate. Benefit payments may have been reduced due to: - hospitalisationThe deceased client's benefit was reduced as they were in hospital for more than 13 weeks. - income - debt repayment when benefit arrears are due at the date of death attempt to recover the debt payment in full from the final benefit paymentdo not recover debts, in full, from terminal benefit payments - when benefit arrears are due at the date of death attempt to recover the debt payment in full from the final benefit payment - do not recover debts, in full, from terminal benefit payments - Child Support if a client had an information share Child Support payment being charged as income at their date of death, they may have been getting a reduced rate of benefit. The effect of the income charge for the information share Child Support will continue for the duration of the terminal benefit, as the rate payable cannot be reviewed.Child Support liability ends when the liable person dies; however MSD cannot remove a Child Support deduction from a benefit record without the authorisation of Inland Revenuewhen a surviving partner or family member makes enquires, refer them to Inland Revenue - if a client had an information share Child Support payment being charged as income at their date of death, they may have been getting a reduced rate of benefit. The effect of the income charge for the information share Child Support will continue for the duration of the terminal benefit, as the rate payable cannot be reviewed. - Child Support liability ends when the liable person dies; however MSD cannot remove a Child Support deduction from a benefit record without the authorisation of Inland Revenue - when a surviving partner or family member makes enquires, refer them to Inland Revenue - court attachment orders - redirection of benefit payment to Kāinga Ora or a community housing provider When the accommodation is being retained by a surviving partner or family member, continue the redirection to Kāinga Ora or the community housing provider. For more information see: Social housing, Assessment of eligibility Death of a client Note all of the above deductions will continue to be made from the terminal benefit payments unless they are manually stopped before cancellation.

chunks.title: Changes to benefit rate payable — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Rates of main benefits being paid as part of Terminal benefit are adjusted to reflect changes in the rate payable arising from legislative amendments such as the Annual General Adjustment of benefit rates on 1 April each year.

chunks.title: Underpaid — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Underpaid
When a client has been underpaid Emergency Maintenance Allowance and is owed arrears, MSD will work out the amount of tax and pass this on to Inland Revenue.
From 1 April 2024, if an arrears payment relates to a previous tax year, the arrears will not be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment. This means the client will not have to pay any more tax on the payment.
Only arrears payments relating to the current tax year will be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment.
Example
A client is paid arrears on 12 June 2026. This payment represents arrears for 25 March 2026 to 8 June 2026.
The arrears for 25 March to 31 March 2026 represent a past tax year, so they will not be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment. The arrears for 1 April to 8 June 2026 represent the current tax year, so they will be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment.
## Overpaid
If a client has been overpaid, the overpayment is always established for the net amount. Inland Revenue will return the tax portion of the overpayment directly to MSD.
The overpayment will reduce the amount of benefit and tax paid in the tax year in which the overpayment was made. That is, the overpayment will directly relate to the tax year(s) in which it occurred.

chunks.title: Verification from Internal Affairs — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Verification from Internal Affairs
If a client can't produce a copy of a birth certificate, you can request one using the "Request for NZ birth Certificate" form (BDM93B).
Requests for verification of births can be made to:
Certificate TeamBirths, Deaths and Marriages PO Box 10-526 Wellington 6143

chunks.title: Verification of income — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Verification of income
The client will need to provide verification of any income earned over their 52 week period.
If the client cannot provide verification (for example payslips) then you can contact the employer and ask them to complete the:
- Employment and earnings information for reviews form (V26) form
For further details on how to charge income see:
- Core Policy Income

chunks.title: Weekend leave — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Weekend leave
Where the client is receiving the hospital rate and they are on leave for the weekend only, you should pay the appropriate full rate of benefit for the equivalent number of days the client is on leave.
Example
Client is on leave from Friday to Monday, pay the appropriate full rate of benefit for 4 days. Generally, you will do this by completing a back dated review.
Note the dates of admission and discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital.

chunks.title: When an extension or exemption can be given — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: When a client needs more time to respond to the Mandatory Review, they may be able to get an extension. If a client is unable to respond to the review, they may be able to get an exemption. Clients must contact MSD before their review date to discuss their situation if they need an extension or exemption. A client cannot get an extension or exemption on or after the Mandatory Review date. Note even if a client gets an extension or exemption, they must still advise MSD of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Emergency Maintenance Allowance or the rate payable.

chunks.title: Extension - client needs more time to respond to review — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Clients may be able to get an extension if there is a good and sufficient reason why they cannot complete their Mandatory Review in time. When a client needs more time to complete their review, they must let MSD know before their review date. The extension can only be granted before the review date. Good and sufficient reasons may include (but are not limited to): - the client is unexpectedly hospitalised - death or illness in immediate family - the client is experiencing or escaping a family violence situation If MSD determines the client has a good and sufficient reason, the client can get an extension of up to 20 working days. Note a client can get multiple short extensions, however the maximum amount of time that can be given for an extension is a total of 20 working days from the client's original review date.

chunks.title: Exemption - client is unable to respond to review — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: A client may be able to get an exemption when they are experiencing an unforeseen event or situation that is beyond their control, and this means they are unable to respond to their Mandatory Review (even if they had more time). The client must let MSD know before their review date to discuss their circumstances. Exemption reasons may include (but are not limited to): - localised natural disaster that affects the client but not the whole region (e.g. the client's property is affected by a landslip) - unexpected serious illness or an accident affecting the client or their immediate family member - the client's benefit is ending because a child has left their care suddenly and the Mandatory Review is due during the 28-day continuation of payment If MSD determines an exemption applies, the client will be not required to respond to their Mandatory Review, and the review date will be reset to 52 weeks from their current review date. Example Harper is getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance and has a Mandatory Review due on 12 July 2026. However, Harper's home is damaged by a landslip, and she cannot return home. Because she has lost all her possessions and is focused on finding accommodation, MSD determines it is not reasonable for Harper to respond to her Mandatory Review before by her review date. In this case, MSD grants an exemption. Harper's next Mandatory Review is set for 52 weeks from original review date.

chunks.title: Youngest dependent child turns 14 years — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance > changes and reviews emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Youngest dependent child turns 14 years
When a dependent child turns 14 years old the client is no longer eligible to receive Emergency Maintenance Allowance. This is because Emergency Maintenance Allowance is paid equivalent to Sole Parent Support. To qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance equivalent to Sole Parent Support the client must have a dependent child under the age of 14 years.
## Date of review
Review the benefit from the date the child turns 14 years old. You should assess the client's entitlement to another main benefit. Where the client does not meet the qualifications for a main benefit, Emergency Benefit may be considered.
For more information see:
- Effect on benefit
- Processing standards Child changes [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Charging income — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Charging income
SWIFTT will automatically calculate the rate of benefit payable when you add the client's income on the INCMH screen.
A client who has income charged weekly can receive up to $160 per week before their income will affect their benefit.
For clients who get over $160 per week:
- income between $160 and $250 per week their benefit is reduced by 30 cents for each $1.00 of income
- income over $250 per week their benefit is reduced by 70 cents for every $1.00 of income
A client who has income charged annually can get up to $8,320 per year before their income will affect their benefit.
For clients who get over $8,320:
- income between $8,320 and $13,000 per year their benefit is reduced by 30 cents for each $1.00 of income
- income over $13,000 per year their benefit is reduced by 70 cents for every $1.00 of income
For further details on what is income and how to charge it, see:
- Core policy Income
- Core policy Types of income
- Exemption for severe disablement
- Weekly income example
- Review of Annual Income
## Income from Overseas Pensions
Income from overseas pensions is generally treated as a direct deduction from the benefit rate and this requires a separate calculation to charging other types of income.
For more information see:
- To or from Overseas Payments from Overseas
## Childcare costs
If an Emergency Maintenance Allowance client has to pay childcare costs because they are working they can get an additional income exemption.
For more information see:
- Childcare income exemption

chunks.title: Child changes and social obligations — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Child changes and social obligations
There are some changes of circumstance that may mean the client is no longer required to comply with their social obligations including where:
- a dependent child changes age and the social obligation that applied for the dependent child in their care is no longer relevant or
- child leaves care (for example starts to live with another parent or caregiver or goes into the care of Oranga Tamariki)
For more information see:
- Changes and reviews Child changes
- Clients situation changes during regular engagement and support process

chunks.title: Child not supported — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Child not supported
For Emergency Maintenance Allowance, you can consider as a dependent child any child whose parents are unable, or in exceptional circumstances, unwilling to support that child.
When a client is caring for a child that is not their own, consider the following:
- can the client be considered as the parent of the child?
- what are the reasons they are caring for the child?
- what are the parents circumstances?
- how long does the client expect to care for the child? (the legislation doesn't tell you how long the child is expected to be in the care of the client but it should be expected to be a long term arrangement, not just a few weeks)
- if long term, are more formal arrangements being considered (for example adoption)?
- do the parents of the child have the ability to contribute to the cost of care?
- is the child a qualifying child for Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit?
For help to determine whether parents may be unable or unwilling to care for the child, see:
- Parent circumstances
- Family breakdown

chunks.title: Child to be included — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Child to be included
A client is obliged to tell MSD of all their circumstances including the number of children in their care.
If a child is considered to be dependent that child is to be included in the caregiver's benefit.
## Client doesn't want to include a child
In cases where the client has genuine concerns about including the child in their benefit (such as concerns about violence from the other parent) advise the client all information contained in their benefit record is confidential.
If MSD has any concerns regarding the welfare of the child, the case must be referred to Oranga Tamariki.
## Deciding if a child is financially dependent
When a client states they are receiving payments for a child's expenses MSD must decide if the child is a dependent child of the client.
A child does not have to be solely financially dependent on a client to be considered a dependent child. All that is required is that the child is financially dependent on the person to some degree.
However, being financially dependent on a client is only part of the qualifications of a dependent child. The child must still meet all the qualifications to be considered dependent.
If another person or body is paying for the child's expenses, including payments for the care provided, the child is not financially dependent on the client.
If a client is receiving payments toward the expenses of a dependent child this is regarded as income for benefit purposes.
## Parents unable or unwilling to care for child
For Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients, a child whose parents are unable, or in exceptional circumstances, unwilling to support that child may be considered a dependent child.

chunks.title: Childcare cost income exemption — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Childcare cost income exemption
There is an additional $20 per week income exemption for Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients when they have to pay childcare costs while they are working.
It is not necessary for the child to go into an approved childcare centre, private arrangements can be accepted.
Entitlement to Childcare Subsidy and OSCAR is assessed first. If the total cost of childcare is not covered by the subsidy the client can receive the additional income exemption.
The exemption would be the lesser of:
- $20 per week or
- the cost of childcare not covered by a subsidy
The exemption only applies for the weeks the sole parent pays for childcare while they are working.

chunks.title: Client in hospital — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Client in hospital
A client's Emergency Maintenance Allowance rate of payment can be different if they are in hospital.
Generally, the rate is reduced to the hospital rate when the client has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks (not after getting a benefit for 13 weeks).
The hospital rate allows for the cost of personal items, which patients are expected to provide for themselves.
## Client in hospital at commencement date
If the client has been in hospital for 13 weeks or more at the commencement date of the benefit, the rate of payment is the hospital rate.

chunks.title: Client is meeting their social obligations — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Client is meeting their social obligations
If, during any of the three Contact Steps of engagement and support, you consider that the client is meeting their social obligations you will need to let the client know that:
- as they are meeting their social obligations, you do not require any more information or contact from them and
- if they require any support regarding their social obligations they can contact Work and Income at any time
The appropriate outcome for the specific social obligations that apply to each of the client's dependent children needs to be recorded in OBMAN.
For more information on the three step process of engagement see:
- Social obligations - Actively engaging with clients [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Client leaves Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Client leaves Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre
No stand-down applies to the commencement of a benefit when a client has left the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre.

chunks.title: Client's circumstances — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Client's circumstances
A client applying for Emergency Maintenance Allowance must be the parent of one or more dependent children and be one of the following:
- living apart from their partner
- divorced
- single (never had a partner)
- has lost the regular support of their partner as their partner has been imprisoned or is subject to release or detention conditions that prevent employment or
- their spouse or partner has died
## Exception
In some situations the client may not be the natural or adoptive parent of the child but you can still regard the child as their own. For more information see:
- Parent
Also see:
- Qualifying date
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit

chunks.title: Living at home (or away from home by choice) — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Living at home (or away from home by choice)
If the client is living at home (or living away from home by their own choice) the rate of Emergency Maintenance Allowance for 16 and 17 year old clients paid, is equivalent to the following rate:
- the rate paid to an 18 or 19 year old client
- living at home and
- who was granted benefit on or after 1 July 1998
## Living away from home
If the client is living away from home because it is unreasonable for them to live at home, the rate of Emergency Maintenance Allowance for 16 and 17 year old clients paid, is equivalent to the rate of Young Parent Payment.

chunks.title: Clients situation changes during regular engagement and support process — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Clients situation changes during regular engagement and support process
A client may have a change of circumstance which means they are no longer subject to a social obligation. These changes may include (but are not limited to):
- a dependent child leaves their care or
- a dependent child changes age and the social obligations that apply for the dependent child in their care are no longer relevant
If this happens during regular engagement and support, the client cannot be failed and they are no longer subject to the social obligation.
For more information see:
- Social obligations - Actively engaging with clients [no link find out why] procedures
- Overview of social obligations according to the age of the child
- Changes and reviews Child changes

chunks.title: Clients with dependent children - 50% protection — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Clients with dependent children - 50% protection
Clients in these situations do not have their whole benefit sanctioned. Instead, a maximum sanction of 50% of the total benefit may be imposed. The balance payable is known as 50% protection.
For more information, including treatment of supplementary assistance, see:
- Sanctions for sole parents
The 50% protection also applies to these two groups if they are subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period for voluntarily leaving employment without a good and sufficient reason or dismissal due to misconduct, or refusing to accept any offer of suitable employment.
Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
For more information see:
- Recompliance

chunks.title: Commencement date — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
To decide when the Emergency Maintenance Allowance can start you must first find the entitlement date. This is usually the date that a person no longer has a means of support.
For a list of these dates see:
- Entitlement Date
The Emergency Maintenance Allowance is generally subject to an initial stand-down of up to a maximum of 2 weeks after the entitlement date.
Generally, the commencement date is:
- the day after the initial stand-down ends or
- the application date
whichever is the later.
However, if a client applies for Emergency Maintenance Allowance within 28 days of their entitlement date, the commencement date rules are different, see:
- Twenty-eight day rule
## No stand-down applies
There are some situations when an initial stand-down is not imposed. When no stand-down applies, the commencement date of the benefit is:
- the entitlement date or
- the application date
whichever is the later.
For more information see:
- Core policy Application for benefit
- Severence payments
- Redundancy payments
- Employment ceased
- Initial stand-down
- No stand-down applies

chunks.title: Consequences of failing to meet conditions — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Consequences of failing to meet conditions
You must ensure that the client is clear about the conditions of grant attached to their benefit and the consequences of failing to meet those conditions.
If a client has been assigned work obligations or youth activity obligations as a condition of grant, and the client fails to meet them without a good and sufficient reason, their benefit can be affected.
Generally for Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients this is an immediate reduction of the main benefit rate to 50%.
For more information see:
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Counting previous obligations failures — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Counting previous obligations failures
The sanction imposed depends on how often the client has failed to comply with their obligations in the previous 24 months while getting a benefit.
Previous failures are only counted if the failure occurred within the last 24 months while continuously getting a benefit.
Note this does not apply to clients receiving Emergency Maintenance Allowance where the equivalent benefit is Young Parent Payment. These clients have youth activity obligations, and these failures are counted for 12 months.
The 24-month count starts from the day the obligation failure is imposed. Each obligation failure has its own 24-month count.
Example
A client fails their first obligation on 1 June 2025. They fail another obligation on 1 October 2025, and have an obligation failure count of two. Their obligation failure count is reset to one on 1 June 2027, 24 months after they failed their first obligation.
Their obligation failure count is reset to zero on 1 October 2027, 24 months after the second obligation failure.
## Failure of different obligations add to failure count
The failure count includes all obligation failures.
## Youth clients
When a client transfers from Young Parent Payment or Youth Payment to a benefit without youth activity obligations the count will be reset to zero. This is because the sanction regime is different for young people getting these payments.
## Transitional arrangements
From 26 May 2025, the obligations failure count period increased from 12 months to 24 months.
Any obligation failures that were initiated before 26 May 2025 will only be counted for 12 months.
Obligation failures (except youth activity obligation failures) initiated from 26 May 2025 onwards will be counted for 24 months.

chunks.title: Criteria for Money Management — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Criteria for Money Management
Clients must meet certain criteria in order for Money Management to be imposed.
A client can only have Money Management imposed if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they meet with MSD within the 5 working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure decision is not disputed and overturned, and
- Money Management would be the most appropriate sanction to impose based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or they have dependent children.
## Client failed a social obligation
Money Management may be imposed on clients who have failed a social obligation if they meet the above criteria.
Depending on the activity a client fails, they may be able to recomply within 5 working days of the failure instead of imposing Money Management.

chunks.title: Client fails more than one obligation at the same time — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Client fails more than one obligation at the same time
A client may fail more than one obligation on the same day and have multiple failures they need to recomply with.
Upskilling cannot be imposed if a client has failed multiple obligations at the same time.
Clients may be considered for Money Management if they meet the criteria, and it is appropriate for their circumstances.

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Deciding ordinarily resident
Generally, a client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand to receive a benefit.
Ordinarily resident means someone who is normally and lawfully in New Zealand and intends to stay here, that is, they consider New Zealand to be their home.
Whether a person is ordinarily resident is a question of fact and degree and their intentions during any period of absence is the most important factor.
Where it is not clear if a client is ordinarily resident, consider the following:
(a) the client's intentions toward New Zealand (that is, the reasons for their absence from New Zealand and the reasons for their return). Are they going overseas for a holiday or are they intending to live overseas permanently (sighting return air tickets is a good indication)?
(b) the length of time they spend in New Zealand on a continual basis
(c) property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans)
(d) Where are their cash assets held?
(e) Is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and do they pay New Zealand taxes?
(f) Do they vote (or are they eligible to vote) in the New Zealand election?
(g) their commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in the community, community events, clubs and other groups)?
Note a person cannot be ordinarily resident in two places at the same time.
## How to decide
You must consider all the factors of each individual case.
You may need to ask more questions (or seek clarification of information you have) to get all the relevant information and then you must weigh up all the facts and make a decision.
The client should be given the benefit of the doubt in situations where their ordinarily residence is not clear.

chunks.title: Payments received more than 52 weeks after retirement — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Payments received more than 52 weeks after retirement
If the client receives a retirement payment more than 52 weeks after the date the date the client's employment ceased, the payment is treated as a capital payment. The client's entitlement to any Extra help must also be reassessed.
Any interest received from the investment of any lump sum must be charged as income.

chunks.title: Dependent child — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
A dependent child for Emergency Maintenance Allowance is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of that client
- maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Emergency Maintenance Allowance does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- child for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
Dependent children should be included in the benefit.
In some situations, a child may not be living at home but is still considered to be a dependent child.
In some situations the client may not be the natural or adoptive parent of the child but MSD can still regard the child as their own.

chunks.title: Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples
To help you identify when there is a "dependent child", please see the examples below:
Household

chunks.title: Determining when a client became non-compliant — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: When a client fails to complete Upskilling without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must determine from which point the client was non-compliant. The client's benefit will be reduced from the first day of the week that MSD determines a client was non-compliant. The start of each week is based on when Upskilling was imposed. This means the week may not begin on a Monday. For example, if a client's Upskilling is imposed on a Wednesday, the beginning of the week for the sanction will be Wednesday.

chunks.title: Client engaged initially and then stopped — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: A client may engage with Upskilling for a period of time and then fail to meet the requirements before their Upskilling has ended. In this case, MSD will consider that a client was non-compliant from first day of the week in which a client stopped meeting the requirements.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Nami failed a social obligation and MSD imposed Upskilling as a non-financial sanction. In the third week of her sanction period, she does not participate in or report on at least 5 hours of her employment-related training or course. Her benefit is automatically reduced. She contacts MSD says she did not participate as she forgot to attend the course and report the hours. MSD is satisfied that Nami was complying with the requirements of Upskilling in weeks 1 and 2, but she was no longer compliant in week 3. MSD determines non-compliance from day one of week 3. Nami's payments are reduced from this date, and a debt is established. She is given a different recompliance activity to complete.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Robin had Upskilling imposed and successfully participated in 5 hours of employment-related training a week over a 4-week period. At the end of the 4-week period, Robin attends her recompliance meeting but does not provide verification of the employment-related training she did. She informs MSD she doesn't have sufficient evidence of her participation because she thought reporting in MyMSD would be enough. MSD determines this is not a good and sufficient reason and that she has not meet the requirements of Upskilling. MSD determines Robin was non-compliant from week one of her sanction as she was unable to provide any supporting evidence of the employment-related training or courses she did. Her payments are reduced from the beginning of week one and a debt is established.

chunks.title: Housing stability — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Housing stability
Clients will have to pay their accommodation costs using the payments they receive into their bank account (including any Working for Families tax credits and supplementary assistance) as the Money Management supplier group doesn’t include housing providers.
If a client is unable to pay their housing costs from the benefit payments that go into their bank account while on Money Management, this will seriously impact their living situation. It would not be suitable to impose Money Management if it would worsen a client’s housing situation compared to a different sanction.
## Redirections and offsets
Any redirections, offsets, or debt repayments will be deducted from the benefit payment going into a client’s bank account. It may not be possible for a client to make some of these payments while they are on Money Management.
MSD should discuss this with the client before deciding whether to impose Money Management.
## Hardship applications
Clients who make frequent hardship applications may benefit from Money Management as the payment card can only be used to buy essential items.
If a client is already working with a budgeting service to manage their finances, Money Management may not be appropriate.
## Changes in income
Money Management may not be suitable for clients who have frequent changes in their income.
If a client declares a change in their income after their main benefit payment has been issued to their payment card, it may result in an overpayment. If a client is overpaid, a debt will be established as the payment cannot be adjusted.
If a client is underpaid, they will be issued arrears directly into their bank account. This may reduce the effectiveness of the sanction.
## Client circumstances
If a client has particular circumstances that would be worsened by being money managed, Money Management is not appropriate.
For example, if a client is experiencing family violence or a domestic emergency, Money Management may cause additional stress. MSD should consider a different sanction where possible.

chunks.title: Accessibility — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Accessibility
Clients must be able to report their participation in employment-related training or courses on MyMSD. MSD should consider a client's ability to access and report on MyMSD before imposing Upskilling. For example:
- the client must have access to a device they can access the internet on (this can include the kiosks at a service centre)
- if the client doesn't have access to a device, they can access the internet on, consider their ability to get to a service centre
- the client must have adequate digital literacy skills to access and report on their employment-related training or course

chunks.title: Disputes and reviews of an obligations failure — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Disputes and reviews of an obligations failure
A client has the right to dispute or review if they disagree with any decision relating to:
- an obligations failure or
- a sanction being imposed or
- the type of sanction being imposed
A client can do this by:
- disputing the decision or
- lodging a formal Review of Decision
A Review of Decision can be lodged at any stage, within three months of the obligations failure being initiated, or within three months of the sanction being imposed.
If a client disputes their obligations failure or sanction more than 20 working days after it is initiated or imposed, MSD must advise the client to lodge a formal Review of Decision in writing.
For more information see:
- Disputing more than one obligations failure
- The disputes process
- Recording decisions on a dispute
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals

chunks.title: Disputing more than one obligations failure — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Disputing more than one obligations failure
If a client has failed more than one obligation at the same time, they can dispute any of the failed activities by providing a good and sufficient reason for the failure.
## Example
A client has failed three of their social obligations and the failures have been initiated on the same day. The client successfully disputes all three of these failures as they have good and sufficient reasons. The client is not sanctioned and the failures are not counted.
Obligation
Recompliance

Client must comply with all social obligations

chunks.title: Documenting the meeting — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Documenting the meeting
Full notes from the family meeting, including questions asked, and answers supplied, must be documented and placed with the benefit application.

chunks.title: Employment during stand-down — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Employment during stand-down
If a client gains temporary full-time employment during the initial stand-down period, this may change the date the benefit can start from.
The new entitlement date is the date the temporary employment stops. Reassess the client's initial stand-down period using the income for the 26 and 52 weeks earned immediately before the new entitlement date.
For more information see:
- Example of employment during the stand-down
Also see:
- Income less than a disqualifying rate

chunks.title: Enrolled in and attending school — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Enrolled in and attending school
Clients receiving Sole Parent Support must take all reasonable steps to ensure their children are enrolled in and attending school from the age of 5 or 6 (depending on when they start school).
## Age of child
Clients with a dependent child aged 5 or 6 years (depending on when they start school) to 15 years of age will be required to take all reasonable steps to ensure the child is enrolled in and regularly attending school.
If a child is aged between 5 and 6 years it is the parent or caregivers choice as to whether they have their child in early childhood education or school. A child does not legally have to attend school until they are aged 6 years but most children start school at 5 years. A client must meet the early childhood education social obligation if they choose not to enrol their 5 year old in school.
A child can legally leave school when they are 16 years or at 15 years if they have an early leaving exemption from the Ministry of Education. A parent or caregiver cannot be asked to comply with the attendance at school social obligation if the child has legally left school or has an early leaving exemption and is no longer legally required to attend school.
## Verification of child enrolled and attending school
All children aged from 6 to 15 years old are legally required to attend school. In most cases you should take your clients word that they are meeting their social obligations.
However, if you have information that indicates the child may not be attending school you may ask the client to get verification, for example, a letter from the child's school that says the child is enrolled and attending.
There are some situations where a client may be taking all reasonable steps but their child is not attending school.
For more information see:
- Taking all reasonable steps for enrolling in and attending school
- Parent is being prosecuted under the Education Act
## Home schooling
A client can home school their children and meet their social obligations. If the child is aged six years or over they will need to have a Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School issued by the Ministry of Education. However, if they have work obligations, they are likely to need an exemption from those obligations.

chunks.title: Enrolment and attendance at a recognised early childhood programme — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Enrolment and attendance at a recognised early childhood programme
Clients receiving Emergency Maintenance Allowance must take all reasonable steps to ensure that their child is enrolled in and attending a recognised early childhood education programme from the age of three until they start school.
Generally clients should have their children participating in a recognised early childhood education programme for 15 hours a week. It is acceptable for a child to be attending less than this.
Recognised early childhood programmes include programmes that are:
- approved (licensed and certificated under the Education Act 1989) early childhood education programmes
- Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School or
- another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme
Generally, a place in approved early childhood education (ECE) service should be considered first. Where a place in early childhood education is not available or is not suitable (for example due to hours of operation, distance or family circumstances) then other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes should be considered.
## Hours of attendance
Generally you should encourage your clients to take reasonable steps to have their children participating in early childhood programmes for 15 hours a week. It is acceptable for a child to be attending less than this.
## Age of child
This obligation only applies to parents of children aged between 3 and 6 years (except where the child has started school at 5 years).
If a child is aged between 5 and 6 years, the parent or caregiver can choose whether to have their child in a recognised early childhood education programme or school.
A child does not legally have to attend school until they are 6 years (but most children start school at 5 years).

chunks.title: Enrolment with a primary health care provider — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Enrolment with a primary health care provider
A client getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance must take all reasonable steps to enrol their child or children with a primary health care provider. This means being enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation.
Taking reasonable steps to enrol
If a client is unable to enrol their child at a practice or with a practitioner due to shortages, they can be considered to be meeting this obligation if they have a plan in place to:
- be enrolled with a practice or practitioner when a place becomes available and
- get health care for their child if the child becomes sick
Note the client must provide evidence if the medical practice cannot enrol the child because of shortages.
## Age of child
The primary health care obligation applies in relation to all dependent children in the care of a client getting a main benefit. Dependent children include:
- children included in the client’s main benefit and
- children the client is getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit for
## Verification
Most children will already be enrolled with a primary health care provider and in most cases MSD should take the client's word that they are meeting this social obligation.
However, if MSD has information that the client may not be taking all reasonable steps to meet this social obligation, MSD may ask them to get verification.
For example, verification could be a letter from their medical practice or registered practitioner that says they are enrolled (most medical practices will send this when a client is enrolled).

chunks.title: Entering a refuge — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Entering a refuge
When a client is applying for Emergency Maintenance Allowance after entering a refuge following the break-up of a relationship, the initial stand-down period can be waived.
Generally the client must enter the refuge immediately following the break-up of their relationship. This means entering the refuge within a period similar in duration to the stand-down (that is, within seven to 14 days). Where there is a delay between the separation and the client entering the refuge, general commencement date rules apply, including the twenty-eight day rule.
In this context a refuge is emergency accommodation provided by an agency or organisation. This includes (but is not restricted to) agencies such as Women's Refuge, Home and Family Society, Emergency Housing Trusts, Iwi and cultural organisations, and church organisations.
Note that accommodation provided by family or friends of the client is not considered to be refuge accommodation.
For more information see:
- Commencement date
- Twenty-eight day rule

chunks.title: Entitlement Date — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Entitlement Date
The entitlement date for Emergency Maintenance Allowance is usually:
- the day after employment ceased (that is, after any holiday pay, sick pay, cessation leave, etc. has expired) where the client was earning at a disqualifying rate
- the day after the breakdown in the family relationship
- the day after separation
- the day after financial assistance from partner ceased
- the day after their partner was taken into custody
- the date of their child's date of birth
- the date of arrival in New Zealand (if client has returned to New Zealand)
- the date of release from prison
Note where the client has more than one event, you use the later event for their entitlement date.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Keriana is getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance at the Sole Parent Support rate of $521.52 a week (as at 1 April 2026). She fails an obligation without a good and sufficient reason and her case manager decides to impose Money Management. Her first day of Money Management is Thursday 10 July. Because Keriana's Money Management begins in the middle of the week, only part of her benefit payment for the following week will be under Money Management. This means she will get more than 50% of her benefit into her bank account. Note: the benefit might not divide evenly by 2. When this happens, the higher amount (1 cent more) will be paid to the client's bank account.

chunks.title: How the first week of Money Management is paid — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday Full payment to client's bank account Money Management imposed Client's weekly rate ($521.52) x (number of days that week that Money Management is imposed (4) ÷ 7) = $298.01 50% put onto payment card Total payment onto payment card = $149.01 Remainder paid into client’s bank account (weekly benefit amount minus amount paid to payment card) = $521.52 - $149.01 = $372.51 Total payment into client’s bank account for the week: $372.51

chunks.title: How the second and third week of Money Management is paid — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday Money Management imposed Client's weekly benefit amount = $521.52 50% put onto payment card $521.52 x 0.5 = $260.76 onto payment card Remainder paid into client’s bank account (weekly benefit amount minus amount paid to payment card) = $521.52 - $260.76 = $260.76 Total payment into client’s bank account for the week: $260.76

chunks.title: How the final week of Money Management is paid — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday Money Management imposed Client's weekly benefit rate ($521.52) x (number of days that week that Money Management is imposed (3) ÷ 7) = $223.50 50% put onto payment card $223.50 x 0.5 = $111.75 Full payment to client's bank account Total payment onto payment card = $111.75 Remainder paid into client’s bank account (weekly benefit amount minus amount paid to payment card) = $521.52 - $111.75 = $409.77 Total payment into client’s bank account for the week: $409.77

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances
You can disregard some or all of a client's cash assets when you are looking at granting an Emergency Maintenance Allowance, only if you think that there are exceptional circumstances.
Things you need to consider:
- if you refuse to grant an Emergency Maintenance Allowance will it have a serious effect on the client's health or welfare
- if you refuse to grant an Emergency Maintenance Allowance on the grounds of hardship, to a client would the likely alternatives cost the Government more
- can the client realise (that is, sell or get access to) their cash assets for more than the appropriate cash asset limit
- is the need for assistance temporary
- what is the total amount of the client's assets, including assets that are not cash assets and
- what are the other matters that you would consider relevant to determining whether hardship exists
Every case has to be looked at on its own merits.
If you have a case where you think you can disregard some or all of a client's cash assets, discuss the circumstances before you make your decision with Helpline.

chunks.title: Failing a social obligation — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Failing a social obligation
If a client has received regular engagement and support and they are still not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, they still need to attend a final appointment.
A social obligations failure can be initiated when you consider that a client has, without a good and sufficient reason, failed to meet their social obligations by:
- not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations following the process of regular engagement and support (that involves at least 3 contact steps) or
- not attending the final appointment during their regular engagement and support process
Before you initiate an obligations failure for social obligations you must get approval from your manager client service delivery. An obligation failure should only be used when all other efforts to encourage engagement and support with the client have been exhausted.

chunks.title: Failing more than one obligation at the same time — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Failing more than one obligation at the same time
If a client fails more than one obligation or activity at the same time and does not have a good and sufficient reason for one or more of the failures, the failures are counted as one failure.
However, the client will need to recomply with all the failures before the sanction can be lifted.
Note Money Management is the only non-financial sanction that can be imposed when a client has failed more than one obligation at the same time at grade 1. A client must resolve all of these failures during the 4-week Money Management period in order to recomply.
For grade 1 and 2 failures, if the client successfully disputes one of the failures, the sanction imposed will remain until they recomply with any remaining failures initiated at the same time.
This policy only applies to the first and second time a client fails their obligations in a 24 month period, or 12-month period if the client has youth activity obligations.
For grade 3 failures, a client will need to complete one six-week approved activity or programme of activities (if they wish to recomply).
## Initiating the failures on the same day
The obligations or activities that the client has not complied with can be over a recent period (eg within the last 5 days) or they may not have been complied with all on the same day. However, the client can only be required to recomply with failures that are initiated on the same day.
As soon as MSD is aware that a client has failed their obligations without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must initiate an obligations failure – it cannot be delayed.

chunks.title: Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations
A client, when required, must:
- attend and participate in interviews with the Ministry of Social Development to discuss compliance with their social obligations and
- report on compliance with specific social obligations
If during the 3 steps of engagement and support, the client does not attend and participate in interviews with the Ministry to discuss compliance with social obligations or report on compliance with specific social obligations you should move to the next steps of engagement and support.
## For more information on the 3 step engagement process see:
- Failure to comply following regular engagement and support process
- Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation
- Obligations failures
- Social obligations - Actively engaging with clients [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Failure to comply following regular engagement and support — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Failure to comply following regular engagement and support
Clients will need to attend a final appointment if they are still not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations after the 3 step process of regular engagement and support.
A social obligations failure will only be initiated when you consider that a client has, without a good and sufficient reason, failed to meet their social obligations by:
- not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations following the 3 step process of regular engagement and support and
- does not attend the final appointment, or attends and is still not meeting their social obligations, following the 3 stage process engagement and support
Before you initiate an obligations failure for social obligations you must get your manager client service delivery approval.
A social obligation failure should only be used when all other efforts to encourage engagement and support the client have been exhausted.

chunks.title: Family breakdown — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Family breakdown
When including a child as a dependent child whose parents are unable or unwilling to support them, MSD must be satisfied that a breakdown in the child's family has occurred and is of a medium to long-term nature.
The applicant must be likely to be the principal caregiver for at least one year. This would indicate that the breakdown and the placement away from the child's family is not simply a shot-term measure.
At the interview with the caregiver, find out whether there has been any involvement with Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency.
MSD can obtain proof of a breakdown from:
- a Family Group Conference conducted by Oranga Tamariki (or other authorised agency) or
- if there has been no involvement with Oranga Tamariki (or other authorised agency) a family meeting that has been conducted by MSD
## Documentation
Documentation of the Family Group Conference must be approved and signed as a full and correct account of the meeting by a social worker or an elder of the iwi or cultural service who attended the meeting.
The Family Group Conference may have been a hui or cultural service meeting that discussed other matters not relevant to this child and their family. In these situations, only an extract of the relevant minutes of the hui or meeting is required. The extract will still need to be approved and signed by a social worker or an elder of the iwi or cultural service who attended the meeting.
When MSD have proof of a Family Group Conference, a decision must be made based on the information provided. However, just because a Family Group Conference has been completed does not mean a breakdown has occurred.

chunks.title: Family Meeting — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Family Meeting
A Family Meeting must be held to confirm that the parent is unable to care for the child or provide fully for the child's support because of a family breakdown. It is held between:
- the child's caregiver
- the child's parents and
- an MSD representative
Sometimes, the child, the social worker and the extended family may attend.
A family meeting is not required where:
- a Family Group Conference conducted by Oranga Tamariki has decided to place the child with the caregiver
- the parents are overseas on a long-term basis or
- the parents are in prison
## Care and protection concerns
When considering the above bullet points and whether a family breakdown has occurred it is important to consider any possible care and protection concerns for a child or young person.
If MSD believes any child has been, or is likely to be harmed (physically, emotionally or sexually), ill-treated, abused, neglected, deprived or MSD has concerns about the wellbeing of the child, the case must be referred to Oranga Tamariki.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure
You need to be satisfied that the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their obligations, based on the information you have, before you initiate an obligations failure.
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'. Having considered the circumstances, was it reasonable for the client not to have met their obligations?
For social obligations you will need to assess whether the client is taking all reasonable steps to meet all of their social obligations for each dependent child.
Good and sufficient reasons will depend on the obligation the client has failed. For more information see:
- Social obligations All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Good and sufficient reason for not meeting obligation to work with a contracted service provider
Decide in favour of the client if any doubt remains.
If you are aware that the client has a good and sufficient reason, do not initiate an obligations failure.
If the client does not have a good and sufficient reason, see:
- Failing more than one obligation at the same time
## Disputing the obligations failure
A client can dispute the decision to initiate the obligations failure or the sanction.

chunks.title: Notifying MSD within a reasonable period — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: If a client is delayed in notifying MSD of their good and sufficient reason, the delay must only be for a reasonable period. MSD will determine on a case-by-case basis whether the length of the delay is reasonable or not. If MSD determines that they are unable to complete Upskilling for a good and sufficient reason, and a client has notified MSD within a reasonable period, MSD must impose a Grade 1 financial sanction. The date the financial sanction is imposed depends on when MSD determines the client has a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete their Upskilling requirements. MSD must also assign a recompliance activity to the client as soon as possible. Note if a client informs MSD of a good and sufficient reason within a reasonable period, but after the Upskilling sanction period has ended, a replacement sanction can no longer be imposed. They must be given a different recompliance activity to complete, after which their payments can be increased.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Jacob failed an obligation to work with a contracted services provider and his case manager imposed Upskilling as a non-financial sanction. He had just started a four-week IT skills course when his child became very sick and required full time care. By the time Jacob's child recovered, he had not done the required five hours of employment-related training or courses and missed self-reporting in MyMSD for week one. His benefit is reduced. He calls his case manager to let them know what happened. His case manager is satisfied there is a good and sufficient reason Jacob was unable to complete the requirements of his Upskilling non-financial sanction and that he contacted MSD as soon as he reasonably could. A replacement financial sanction is imposed from the date his payments reduced and Jacob is given a different recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Edward failed an obligation to attend an interview and his case manager imposed Upskilling as a non-financial sanction. He is two weeks into his barista course when someone else on the course hears that Edward is there because he's on a benefit and this course is a sanction for him. They tell other people who are at the course and some people start harassing him and making unkind comments about why he's there.
