Edward feels very uncomfortable and contacts MSD to let them know what's happening. MSD decides the course is no longer appropriate for Edward to complete because he's being bullied and feels unsafe. MSD imposes a replacement sanction from that day and arranges for him to do a different recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation
Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting work ability assessment obligations include (but are not limited to) when a client is:
- in hospital
- experiencing an acute mental health episode
Note if a client refuses to complete a Self-Assessment or a Work Ability Assessment, and they do not have a good and sufficient reason, they have an obligations failure.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reasons — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reasons
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'.
Having considered the circumstances, was it reasonable for the client not to have met their obligations?
Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation may include (but are not limited to) when a client:
- is in hospital
- has a death or illness in the immediate family
- is experiencing family violence
- experiences an emergency or adverse event
- was dependent on the provision of assistance by the Ministry of Social Development to complete the activity, and that assistance was not supplied
- is being prosecuted under the Education and Training Act 2020
Decide in favour of the client if any doubt remains.
If you are aware that the client has a good and sufficient reason, do not initiate an obligations failure.
Note where a client has a partner, social obligations apply to both. If a client has a good and sufficient reason for failing a social obligation, talk with them to find out whether their good and sufficient reason also applies to their partner. In most cases, it is likely that if the client has a good and sufficient reason this reason will also apply to their partner.

chunks.title: Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement
A special income exemption for severe disablement may be given to a client as an incentive for their personal effort to participate or continue in employment.
To help you to decide if a person is severely disabled consider the following:
- Does the client have to put in more effort in order to participate in employment? (for example, they may take a considerably long time to get ready in the morning or a longer time to travel to their place of employment)?
- Is the client's capacity to earn the same wage as a person without a severe disability reduced because of their disability (for example, does the client work reduced hours or get less money for the job they undertake because of their disability)?
- Does the client have additional expenses to undertake employment (for example additional transport or equipment costs)?
- Does the client have difficulties participating in employment or completing their tasks because of their disability (for example, they may experience difficulties with mobility around the work place, be limited in the tasks they undertake or on occasion may not complete their work duties)?
- Does the client require assistance from another person to carry out some of their daily tasks (for example, washing, dressing or cooking)?
- Does the client require the assistance from another person to travel to work or to ensure their physical safety while at work (for example, does the client have difficulty using public transport)?
- Any other relevant factors that should be considered.
- If the client answers 'yes' to one or more of these questions you will have to decide if the client is severely disabled or if you need further information to make this decision.
Contact Helpline if you need help with the assessment.

chunks.title: Hardship criteria — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Hardship criteria
In addition to meeting other qualifying criteria, to pay an Emergency Maintenance Allowance, the client must be suffering hardship.
You can consider that a client is in hardship if the client has:
- no other means of supporting themselves and any dependent family
and
- cash assets of or less than: $4,300.00 if the client is single or$7,464.00 if the client is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, or is a sole parent
- $4,300.00 if the client is single or
- $7,464.00 if the client is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, or is a sole parent
In exceptional circumstances you can disregard some of the client's cash assets.
You also need to look at whether the client has recently given any money away or sold any assets.

chunks.title: Home schooling — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Home schooling
Clients with dependent children aged five or six years (depending on when they start school) to 16 years of age will be required to take all reasonable steps to ensure the child is enrolled in and attending school. Home schooling meets this obligation in some circumstances.
Clients can home school their children and meet their social obligation if they have a "Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School" issued by the Ministry of Education.
However, if a client has work obligations, generally they won't be able to home school their child as this could impact on their ability to actively seek or be available for work. They may qualify for an exemption from their work obligations to home school their children.
## Certificate of exemption from enrolment at a registered school
A child does not legally have to attend school until they are aged six years (but most children start school at five years). If a child is aged between five and six years it is the parent's or caregiver's choice whether to have their child in early childhood education or school. A "Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School" issued by the Ministry of Education is not needed while the child is aged five.
Once a child is aged six years a "Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School" issued by the Ministry of Education is required by law to enable a parent to home school their child.
## Social obligations and work obligations
When a client has work obligations as well as social obligations they must meet both sets of obligations at the same time. If the client is unable to meet their work obligations because they are home schooling a dependent child, you can consider granting an exemption from their work obligations. The client must meet the additional criteria for the home schooling exemption.
For more information see:
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Ministry of Education Home education
- Enrolled in and attending school

chunks.title: Documents issued from 29 November 2010 — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Documents issued from 29 November 2010
Documents issued from 29 November 2010 include:
- New Zealand citizenship certificate (issued by Internal Affairs)
- New Zealand citizenship endorsement (in a foreign passport)
- Permanent resident visa
- Resident visa
- Visitor visa
- Work visa
- Student visa
- Limited visa
Only the permanent resident visa and resident visa show a person is a resident.
A visa is a sticker in the client's passport.
## Unable to provide visa or permit
When a client is unable to provide an immigration visa or permit they may provide other Immigration New Zealand documents to verify their immigration status. Work and Income can also undertake an immigration status check directly with Immigration New Zealand.
Note that Immigration New Zealand may be unable to verify immigration status for clients of British nationality who arrived in New Zealand before 2 April 1974 and do not have a passport.
For more information see:
- Residence
- Immigration status [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Income from overseas — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Income from overseas
When a client has been working overseas within the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before their entitlement date you include this in their average weekly income.
If the client cannot provide verification of their earnings, accept the information provided on their application for benefit. For help to convert foreign currency to the equivalent New Zealand dollars see the instructions below.
There is no ability to take higher living costs into account. If the client is in financial hardship during an initial stand-down they can apply for a Special Needs Grant, see: Assistance during an initial stand-down.
## Receiving a benefit from overseas
When a client has been receiving an overseas benefit or pension overseas within the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before their entitlement date you include this in their average weekly wage.
If the overseas benefit or pension payments have stopped and the client cannot provide verification of their payments, accept the information provided on their application for benefit. There is no requirement to obtain verification International Services.
Note when the overseas benefit or pension payments are continuing and the client cannot provide verification, you will need to verify details of these payments. For further assistance contact International Services.

chunks.title: Income less than a disqualifying rate — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Income less than a disqualifying rate
Where an Emergency Maintenance Allowance client starts work during the initial stand-down period, you do not re-assess the client's commencement date when:
- their level of income is less than a disqualifying rate and
- employment continues beyond the original commencement date
In this situation you charge the clients earnings (income) against their benefit from the original commencement date.

chunks.title: Inform client of conditions of grant — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Inform client of conditions of grant
You must ensure that the client is clear about the conditions of grant attached to their benefit and the consequences of failing to meet those conditions.
Clients applying for Emergency Maintenance Allowance must be given a copy of their conditions of grant from their application form.
The conditions of grant apply on any day of the week provided it is suitable for the client's circumstances.
You should consider the client's individual circumstances to ensure that they can realistically meet their conditions of grant such as:
- access to childcare and other family commitments
- religious observances on a specific day
- number of hours and time of day
- religious commitments or jobs that offend strongly held views
- employment with excessive hours
- types of employment and the skills and experience required
- location of employment
- wages
- suitability of the job
For more information see:
- Additional conditions of grant for 16 to 19 year olds

chunks.title: Informing clients of their obligations — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Informing clients of their obligations
You must ensure that the client understands:
- their obligations
- the consequences of failing to meet those obligations, in particular the sanctions that may be imposed and
- their right to review and dispute any decisions relating to a failure to comply with their obligations
Clients applying for Emergency Maintenance Allowance must:
- sign their application form and
- be given a copy of their obligations from their application form
Note that obligations cannot be enforced until the main benefit commencement date.
For more information see:
- Sole Parent Support Obligations
- Social obligations
- Work ability assessment obligation
- Working with a contracted service provider obligation

chunks.title: For more information on the initial stand-down see: — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## For more information on the initial stand-down see:
- Average weekly income
- Number of dependent children
- Employment during stand-down
- Self-imposed stand-down
- Initial stand-down procedure
- No stand-down applies
- Deskfile Initial stand-down

chunks.title: Initial stand-down procedure — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Initial stand-down procedure
Step 1. Find the client's entitlement date.
Step 2. Calculate the client's average weekly income for a 26 and 52 week period.
Step 3. Find out whether the client has or had any dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement date. When determining the correct stand-down period, you must take into account any children that were in the clients care during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to the entitlement date.
Step 4. Using the information from Steps 2 and 3, determine the initial stand-down for the client over a 26 and 52 week period by looking at the Initial stand-down period chart in Deskfile.
Step 5. Use the calculation of average weekly income that gives the client a lesser stand-down period.
Step 6. Apply the initial stand-down from the client's entitlement date to find the commencement date.
Remember if you enter the correct information into SWIFTT it will automatically calculate the initial stand-down and commencement date for you.
Note if the client has had a dependent child (or children) in their care during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement date and the child (or children) is no longer in their care, you will have to use a work around. Contact Helpline for this information.

chunks.title: Introduction — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Emergency Maintenance Allowance is an Emergency Benefit. It provides income support for sole parents with one or more dependent children if they do not meet specific criteria for:
- Sole Parent Support or
- Young Parent Payment
and
- cannot receive any other benefit
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Obligations
- Commencement date
- Payment
- Changes and Reviews

chunks.title: Living apart — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Living apart
Generally, if a client is married or in a civil union you can accept that a couple is living apart when it is clear the relationship has ended, and they are living in different homes.
However, 'living apart' does not mean they must be living in separate homes.
If a client is not married or in a civil union, it is important to establish there is no relationship in the nature of marriage or a civil union before assessing the client's entitlement to Emergency Maintenance Allowance.
A relationship in the nature of marriage or civil union is determined by showing that a couple:
- is committed to each other emotionally and
- are financially interdependent
## Living in separate homes
When a client advises the relationship with their spouse or civil union partner has ended and they are living in separate homes, you need to consider why they are not living together.
Sometimes couples live apart for reasons other than a breakdown in their relationship or rearrange their circumstances to qualify for a benefit.
This can include (but is not limited to) the following reasons:
- business/employment reasons (e.g. truck driver, shearer etc) or
- health reasons or
- 1 partner lives overseas or
- financial reasons
Emergency Maintenance Allowance can only be paid when the relationship has ended.
## Living in the same home
Generally, when a married or civil union couple live in the same home, they are considered a couple.
When a client advises the relationship has ended but they still live in the same home, you must consider why they are cohabitating.
If the arrangement is transitional (e.g. the spouse or partner is looking for separate accommodation and will move out) and the client considers they have separated, you can accept this for a short period.
If the arrangement is not transitional, you need to assess whether they are living together or whether they are living apart in the same home.
Note you cannot assess the client as a sole parent unless the relationship has ended.
If you are unable to decide the client's relationship status you can discuss the case with your regional lawyer or local fraud investigator.

chunks.title: Money Management — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Money Management
Money Management is a non-financial sanction that can be imposed on a client as an alternative to a Grade 1 financial sanction.
A client on Money Management will have 50% of their main benefit put onto a payment card that can only be used for essential expenses. Any remaining benefit payments go into the client’s bank account. Money Management lasts for 4 weeks from the date it is imposed.

chunks.title: Monitoring compliance with social obligations — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Monitoring compliance with social obligations
If you have reasons to be concerned that a client may not be meeting their social obligations you should, in the first instance, discuss and explain their social obligations with them and ensure they understand these obligations. For example when:
- you receive information that a client is not requiring their school age child to attend school
- you receive information that a client's child has not been receiving their Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks
In these situations, you should start the three step process of regular engagement and support with the client.
For more information see:
- Regular engagement and support process
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Social obligations

chunks.title: No stand-down applies — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## No stand-down applies
An initial stand-down is not imposed in the following situations:
- Transfer between benefits
- Temporary employment
- Prisoners
- School holiday clients
- Entering a refuge
- Client leaves Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre
Where no stand-down applies, the commencement date of the benefit is the later of either:
- the entitlement date or
- the application date
Note when no stand-down applies, the 28-day rule does not apply.

chunks.title: Non-financial sanctions — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Non-financial sanctions
Non-financial sanctions are an alternative to a financial sanction that can be imposed on eligible clients in some cases.
Non-financial sanctions should only be imposed when it would be more appropriate based on a client’s circumstances than a financial sanction.
## Criteria to receive a non-financial sanction
A client can only get a non-financial sanction if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they meet with MSD within the 5 working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure decision is not disputed and overturned, and
- a non-financial sanction would be appropriate for them based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or they have dependent children.
MSD must assess a client’s circumstances and determine which non-financial sanction, if any, is most appropriate for the client. Each non-financial sanction has different factors to consider.
Note Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients do not have work or work preparation obligations.
This means it is unlikely they will have an obligation failure, so they would generally not have a sanction imposed.
## Client meets with MSD after 5 working days
A non-financial sanction can only be imposed if a client meets with MSD within the 5 working day notice period. This is because a financial sanction will be automatically applied after 5 working days unless MSD has decided to impose a non-financial sanction instead.
If a client meets with MSD after 5 working days, they are not eligible for a non-financial sanction. MSD cannot change a financial sanction to a non-financial sanction after it has been applied.
## Change in circumstances while subject to a non-financial sanction
A client may have a change in circumstances that means they are no longer required to comply with an obligation they have failed.
In this case, the non-financial sanction no longer applies from the day that a client’s circumstances change.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Number of dependent children — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Number of dependent children
If a client had a dependent child (or children) in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application the child (or children) must be taken into account when determining the stand-down.
For example, if a single client with one dependent child applies for benefit the stand-down period will be based on a single client with one child. However, if this client had two dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application, the stand-down period will be based on a single client with two dependent children.
This is regardless of whether the child is still in the client's care at the time of application.
See also:
- Dependent child
- Orphans Benefit/Unsupported Child's Benefit

chunks.title: Obligations failures — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Obligations failures
If a client fails to comply with their obligations, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. MSD must be satisfied that the client would have had no good and sufficient reason for their failure based on the information MSD has.
For social obligations, MSD must consider whether the client has taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations and go through the regular engagement and support process before considering that the client has failed their obligation.
For more information see:
- Failing more than one obligation at the same time
- Social obligations
- Social obligations Regular engagement and support process
- Social obligations All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure
Note clients getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance may have conditions of grant assigned that are similar to work obligations or work preparation obligations.
Once MSD has decided that the client has failed their obligations, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. The client will then be sent a letter stating that their benefit will be sanctioned and that their benefit will only be increased or resumed if they:
- complete a recompliance activity
- dispute the decision to impose the sanction and MSD accepts that they have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting their obligations or
- lodge a Review of Decision and MSD reconsiders their position and agrees with the client's review
Once a client has completed their recompliance activity, their benefit can be increased or resumed from the date MSD is satisfied the client started the activity.
For some clients, if it’s their first obligation failure they may be eligible for a non-financial sanction instead of a financial sanction.
For more information, see:
- Non-financial sanctions
All clients have a 5 working day notice period to dispute or recomply before the sanction is imposed.
If a client recomplies within the 5 working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the obligations failure is recorded.
For more information see:
- When the sanction is imposed
- Counting previous obligations failures
- Failing more than one obligation at the same time
Clients have not failed their obligations if they do not complete or undertake Voluntary Work or Activity in the Community.
## Effect on rates payable
The reduction, suspension and cancellation applies to 50% of the main benefit the client is getting.
The effect on their extra help depends on the type of extra help they are getting.
Non-financial sanctions do not affect the rate payable for a client.

chunks.title: Obligations — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Obligations
Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients have the following obligations:
- they must advise of any change in circumstances that affects their entitlement or rate of benefit payable
- they may need to meet additional conditions of grant
- they must take all reasonable steps to meet social obligations that apply for each dependent child in their care
- if required, participate in a Work Ability Assessment
- if required, work with a contracted service provider
- advise Work and Income if they are intending to travel overseas, before they depart

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki documentation — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Oranga Tamariki documentation
Where there has been Oranga Tamariki involvement and a Family Group Conference held, you will need to obtain copies of the relevant Oranga Tamariki documents from the client.
If the client cannot show the required 'proof' of a breakdown from Oranga Tamariki you will need to hold a Family Meeting.
A supporting letter from Oranga Tamariki (or other authorised agency) alone is not proof of a breakdown but may provide supporting information relevant to a Family Meeting by confirming the continuation of placement with the alternative caregiver.
## Relevant documentation from Oranga Tamariki
Relevant documentation from Oranga Tamariki, obtained via the client, to prove a family breakdown has occurred, include:
- a copy of the Family Group Conference outcome
- copies of all current Court Orders in respect of the child
- a copy of the court-approved Plan
These documents confirm current care arrangements and also include future care arrangements, including the reason that the child has come into the client's care.
If the client cannot show Oranga Tamariki documentation, it will be necessary to conduct a Family Meeting.
For more information see:
- Family Meeting

chunks.title: Other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes
Other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes are programmes that involve parents educating their children at home with external support.
Programmes will need to meet the approval criteria set out in the Ministerial Direction which states the programme must:
- provide early childhood education to children under 6 years old in their own homes and not to other children
- deliver positive educational outcomes for the children to whom it is provided
- be supervised and have specific early learning outcomes
- be aligned with Government priorities relating to early childhood education (ECE) and vulnerable children
For a list of the approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes for social obligations see:
- Deskfile Social obligations approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes

chunks.title: Other clients — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Other clients
The rate of Emergency Maintenance Allowance that can be paid is equivalent to the Sole Parent Support rate and depends on the number of dependent children the client has in their care.

chunks.title: Overview of social obligations according to age of the child — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Overview of social obligations according to age of the child
The table below shows the specific social obligations that apply to the client according to the age of their dependent children.
Age of client's dependent children
4 weeks - 2 years
3 and 4 years
5 years
6 - 15 years
16 - 18 years
Core Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider visits
Applies for each dependent child
Not applicable
Enrolled in and attending recognised early childhood education programmes
Not applicable
Applies for each dependent child
Applies for each dependent child where they are not in school
Not applicable
Enrolled in and attending school
Not applicable
Applies for each dependent child (except where child is aged between 5 and 6 years and is enrolled in and attending a recognised early childhood programme)
Not applicable
Enrolled in primary health care
Applies for each dependent child

chunks.title: Parent is being prosecuted under the Education and Training Act — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Parent is being prosecuted under the Education and Training Act
All parents are legally obliged to ensure their children are enrolled in and attending school from the age of 6 to 16 years.
Parents can be prosecuted and fined under the Education and Training Act 2020 if their children don't attend school. This can happen when:
- there has been, without explanation, on-going and irregular attendance by the child at school after support has been offered to the family or
- the parent has made little or no attempt to do anything about ensuring the child attends school
If a parent is in the process of being prosecuted, you must not ask them to comply with the social obligation or initiate an obligations failure for non-attendance.
Note you need to record this as an exception in OBMAN using 'Parent is in prosecution for truant child' as the exception reason.

chunks.title: Parent — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Parent
A client for Emergency Maintenance Allowance must be the child's natural or adoptive parent.
If the client is not the child's natural or adoptive parent, you can regard the child as their own when:
- the child is being maintained by the client and
- was at any time maintained by the client's partner or
- each of the child's natural or adoptive parents are deceased, cannot be found, or suffers a serious long-term disablement which renders them unable to care for the child or
- due to a breakdown in the child's family no natural, adoptive or step parent is able to care for the child or provide fully to the child's support or
- the child's natural, adoptive or step parents and/or guardians are unwilling to support the child
For more information see:
- Child not supported
- Parents circumstances
The legislation doesn't tell you how long the child must be maintained by the couple but it should be a reasonable period of time, not just a few weeks.

chunks.title: Parents cannot be found — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Parents cannot be found
If the child's parents cannot be found, make sure the caregiver is not helping to keep the parents uninvolved.
Make a decision on all available information.
If the parents cannot be located, decide whether an application for Orphans Benefit is more appropriate.

chunks.title: Parents circumstances — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Parents circumstances
For Emergency Maintenance Allowance, you can consider as a dependent child any child whose parents are unable, or in exceptional circumstances, unwilling to support that child.
## Parents unable to care for child
To help you determine whether the parents may be unable to care for their child, consider whether the parents:
- are deceased or otherwise cannot be found
- are physically incapable of caring for the child (for example because of a disability, alcohol or other drug dependency etc)
- are emotionally or psychologically unable to care for the child
- are financially unable to care for the child or
- there has been a breakdown in the child's family and the child's parents are unable to care for, or provide fully for the child
For further information see:
- Family breakdown
## Parents unwilling to care for child
To help you determine whether the parents may have exceptional circumstances and may be unwilling to care for the child, consider whether the parents:
- feel that their child would be better cared for in another environment (for example, a child with special needs who requires full-time attention from their caregiver that they feel they cannot give)
- feel that their family is at risk while that child remains in their care (for example, their child has behavioural problems or other issues which could result in other family members being placed at risk should the child remain in their care)
Note these are examples only, and other situations may also fit the criteria of a parent being unable or, in exceptional circumstances, unwilling to care for the child.

chunks.title: Parents do not attend — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Parents do not attend
If parents are unwilling to attend the family meeting, they cannot be forced to. They must be encouraged to come as it is in the child's best interests that they do.
If parents remain unwilling to come, decide whether there are any issues that need to be looked at by Oranga Tamariki.
There may be a genuine reason why parents cannot come to the family meeting. They may be sick or disabled, or unable to get leave from work.
When parents do not attend the Family Meeting, you must try and contact them to confirm that they are unable to care for their child.
You can do this by:
- writing to them and asking for information
- arranging for them to be interviewed at another service centre (if they live in another location) or
- interviewing them at their home (if they request this)
If information cannot be gained from the parents, make every effort to ensure that the information given by the caregiver is correct.
If, after attempts to get full details from the parent and the caregiver, there is still not enough information to grant the benefit, the application can be declined.
For more information see:
- Parents cannot be found

chunks.title: Paying other assistance during a sanction — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Paying other assistance during a sanction
Clients are not entitled to the following forms of assistance when they have had a 50% benefit suspension or cancellation imposed due to an obligations failure:
- Emergency Benefit
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit
## Winter Energy Payment
Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid in situations where a portion of main benefit continues to be paid.
Sole parents have a maximum sanction of 50% of the total benefit imposed but like other Extra help, will continue to get the total amount of the Winter Energy Payment, regardless of the grade of the sanction.
## Special Needs Grants
Clients are not entitled to Special Needs Grants if a sanction has been imposed. This applies to both financial and non-financial sanctions.
The only exception to this is if a client has a health condition, injury or disability when a grade 3 sanction is imposed and they are incapable of participating in part-time employment or an approved activity for six weeks. For more information see:
- Assistance during non-entitlement period
- Assistance when a client is sanctioned
## Advance Payments of Benefits
If a client has a 50% sanction imposed, and the client is experiencing hardship they may apply for an advance payment of benefit. A discussion must be held with the client about recomplying as the reduced rate of benefit will be contributing to their hardship.
A client can apply for an advance if they have a non-financial sanction imposed, and may be eligible if they meet all the criteria.
## Assistance to transition into employment
Clients can get assistance to transition into employment if a sanction has been imposed and they meet the qualifications for it.
For more information see:
- Assistance to transition into employment

chunks.title: Payment — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Payment
Emergency Maintenance Allowance is paid weekly on a Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. Payment is from Monday to Sunday and is made one week in arrears.
Generally, payment must be made directly to the client. However, where there is good cause, the client's benefit can be paid to another person, agent or institution.
For more information see:
- Deductions
- Core policy Agents
- Core policy Redirection of benefit payment
It is a condition of receiving a benefit that the client provides a bank account number.
MSD can request the client to provide an IRD number or evidence of their IRD number.
For more information see:
- Client’s IRD number
## Rate of payment
There are different rates of payment for:
- 16 and 17 year old clients and
- Other clients

chunks.title: Payments while on Money Management — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Payments while on Money Management
Clients on Money Management will be paid the following to their nominated bank account:
- 50% of their main benefit rate payable
- 100% of any Working for Families tax credits or supplementary assistance
Any redirections, debt repayments, or offsets will continue to be deducted from the amount that is paid into their bank account. This must be considered before applying Money Management as this amount may be higher than the amount of benefit they will get.
If a client’s main benefit cannot be divided evenly by 2, the higher amount will be paid to their bank account. This means a client may receive 1 cent more in their bank account than on their payment card.
## Where a payment card can be used
The payment card is limited to approved suppliers who sell essential items, specifically for:
- food
- transport
- healthcare related items and/or
- education related items.

chunks.title: People aged 16 or 17 in exceptional circumstances — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## People aged 16 or 17 in exceptional circumstances
A person aged 16 or 17 years must be in exceptional circumstances to receive Emergency Maintenance Allowance.
When considering whether a young person is in exceptional circumstances you should consider:
- the reasons why the person would not qualify for Young Parent Payment
- whether the young person is, or is not, in education, training or employment
- the length of time the Emergency Maintenance Allowance is likely to be payable
- the impact that granting the benefit would have on the young person's education or training and therefore their prospects for employment
- the most likely effect on the young person's health or welfare, or the health and welfare of anyone who is dependent on them, if Emergency Maintenance Allowance was not granted
- any other matters you consider relevant to the granting of Emergency Maintenance Allowance

chunks.title: Period of Money Management — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: When a client fails their obligations, they have 5 working days to dispute the failure before a sanction is imposed. Money Management when imposed, starts the day after the 5 working day notice period. Clients are money managed for 4 weeks (28 days). This period includes weekends and public holidays. Money Management will end after 4 weeks, and a client’s payments will be made in full to their bank account if they have recomplied with their obligation failure during this time.

chunks.title: Money Management begins in the middle of a pay period — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Money Management will be applied on any weekday, including public holidays. This means that Money Management is likely to begin in the middle of a client's pay period and will result in partial payments. For more information see:

chunks.title: Benefit stops during Money Management — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: A client's benefit may stop while they are being money managed, e.g. one week their income was over the income limit. The length of Money Management is not impacted by any breaks in payment, and will always end 4 weeks after it was imposed.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Kale fails their obligation and Money Management starts on 14 August. Their last day of Money Management will be 10 September. Kale travels to Australia from 18 August to 25 August for a holiday. They do not inform MSD before their travel and their benefit is stopped from the day after they left New Zealand. Kale's benefit is resumed from the date they return to New Zealand. Their Money Management continues from 25 August, and will still end on 10 September.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Rahool is getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance and fails a social obligation on 3 March. He is placed onto Money Management on 10 March and his Money Management period will end on 6 April. He advises MSD that he is helping to set up an event for two weeks from 31 March to 13 April and will be paid over the income limit. MSD stops his benefit for this period due to his income. On 14 April Rahool contacts MSD to advise that the concert set up didn't go ahead and he forgot to inform MSD in time. He did not receive any income, so he is owed arrears, and MSD issues arrears of his Emergency Maintenance Allowance from 31 March to 13 April. Rahool's arrears for the period of 31 March to 6 April are subject to Money Management. 50% of those arrears are paid onto his payment card and the remainder to his bank account. The arrears owed after his Money Management ends, from 7 April to 13 April, are also paid directly into Rahool's bank account.

chunks.title: Permanent residence — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Permanent residence
Generally migrants need to have permanent residence or New Zealand citizenship to receive benefit assistance. Permanent residence is granted by Immigration New Zealand. Citizenship is granted by the Department of Internal Affairs.
In order to receive a benefit, a client must normally:
- have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 (which can either be a resident visa or a permanent resident visa) or
- have a residence permit under the Immigration Act 1987 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) or
- be a British national who arrived in New Zealand prior to 2 April 1974 or
- be a New Zealand citizen
## Clients without permanent residence or citizenship
Emergency Maintenance Allowance may be paid to some categories of migrants who do not have permanent residence or citizenship, eg people waiting for their application for refugee or protection status to be approved.
Note clients lawfully in New Zealand by virtue of a temporary permit or temporary entry class visa only (ie they do not have permanent residence) are not entitled to any benefit assistance.
For more information see:
- Immigration status and supporting documents
- Immigration status [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: In prison less than 31 days — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## In prison less than 31 days
Clients who have been in prison or on remand for less than 31 days do not have a stand-down imposed if they were receiving a benefit before going into prison and apply for a benefit immediately following their release.
If the client was not in receipt of benefit prior to being imprisoned or placed on remand, a stand-down is imposed.
There is no access to a Steps to Freedom Special Needs Grant for these clients.
## In prison more than 31 days
Clients who have been in prison or on remand for 31 days or more have a stand-down imposed.
These clients have access to a Steps to Freedom Special Needs Grant to assist them during the stand-down. They may also have access to other forms of assistance to help them re-establish themselves in the community.
## Calculating number of days
When counting the number of days that a client has been in prison or held on remand, you should include the date the client:
- enters prison or held on remand and
- leaves prison or is released from remand
For more information see:
- Imprisonment Release from prison

chunks.title: Proof of residence — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: All documents should be originals. Photocopies and/or documents that have been changed in any way cannot be accepted. Where the client cannot provide proof or the proof is unclear, you should ask the client to obtain confirmation of their residential status from Immigration New Zealand (for permanent residence) or Internal Affairs (for citizenship). Proof of citizenship and/or permanent residence in New Zealand can be a: - New Zealand birth certificate Generally, any person born in New Zealand is a New Zealand citizen by birth. - New Zealand passport To hold a New Zealand passport you must be a citizen of New Zealand. - Certificate of Registration A child born outside New Zealand (to a parent who is a New Zealand citizen) may be a New Zealand citizen from birth. However, the child must apply for a Certificate of Registration to confirm their New Zealand citizenship. - Grant of Citizenship People who have permanent residence may (normally after 5 years residence in New Zealand) apply for a Grant of Citizenship. They must meet the conditions of the Grant. - Certificate of Confirmation This is a certificate issued to confirm that the holder is a New Zealand citizen by birth, descent or Grant of Citizenship. British subjects, who immigrated to New Zealand prior to 1948 (and who resided in New Zealand for all of 1948) were made New Zealand citizens in 1949. These people are likely to have a Certificate of Confirmation or a Certificate of Naturalisation. - Certificate of Naturalisation Previously immigrants were naturalised as British Subjects and Citizens of New Zealand. Today they are given a Grant of Citizenship - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence class visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009 - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987 Note that a visa issued before 29 November 2010 does not allow a person to stay in New Zealand. - Letter of confirmation of permanent residence from Immigration New Zealand - Australian citizens Australian citizens are lawfully allowed in New Zealand without a residence class visa or residence permit and their date of entry into New Zealand is generally not recorded. Where possible, supporting evidence should be sought, such as tenancy agreements, bank statements or old utility bills to show that the client has been ordinarily resident for two continuous years - British nationals

chunks.title: Proof of residence — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Clients of British nationality who came to New Zealand before 2 April 1974 were automatically allowed to enter New Zealand for residence, and will be unable to provide verification of their residence if they do not have a passport. Immigration New Zealand will have no record of these clients unless the client has contacted them after 2 April 1974. The client should be able to provide New Zealand school, work or tax records to support their claim about when they arrived in New Zealand and the length of time they have lived here. For more information see: - Immigration status and supporting documents

chunks.title: Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period
A provisional benefit can be paid to the client when they are undertaking an approved activity or programme of activities during the 13 week non-entitlement period.
## Provisional benefit
You can grant or increase a provisional benefit from the date the client starts the approved activity or programme of suitable activities.
The benefit continues to be provisionally paid while the client is satisfactorily participating in the approved activity. Payment continues until:
- the 6 week activity period ends or
- the 13 week non-entitlement period ends
whichever is earlier.
Some examples of this:
- a client participates in an approved activity from the beginning of week three of the non-entitlement period. The client participates for a continuous period of 6 weeks and the remaining period of the 13 week non-entitlement is cancelled. After the follow up appointment with the client the benefit ceases to be paid on a provisional basis
- a client participates in an approved activity from the beginning of week 10 of the non-entitlement period. The client participates in the approved activity for the remainder of the 13 week non-entitlement period (for 3 weeks). At the end of the 13 week non-entitlement period, the client's benefit ceases to be paid on a provisional basis
## End of approved activity or non-entitlement period
At the end of the approved activity or programme of suitable activities a follow up appointment is required (in approximately 6 weeks time).
You should discuss with the client whether they:
- have satisfactorily participated in the approved activity and
- can still meet the qualifications and obligations of the benefit
Note that if the client does not recomply, they must reapply at the end of the 13 week non-entitlement period to receive a benefit.
## Leaves or has not satisfactorily participated in an approved activity
If a client leaves early or does not satisfactorily participate in the approved activity or programme of suitable activities, without a good and sufficient reason, their provisional benefit must be reduced or stopped from the date it was increased or granted.
The amount of benefit that was provisionally paid during the 13 week non-entitlement period must be established as a debt and recovered.
For more information see:
- Recompliance
- Unable to recomply

chunks.title: Purpose of the meeting — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Purpose of the meeting
The purpose of the family meeting is to find out:
- if a breakdown in the child's family has taken place. This can be found out by asking about the parents' financial and housing situation, or if they have any disabilities (the parents are not expected to provide proof of their financial circumstances)
- whether the parents are able but unwilling to provide full support for the child
- why (due to the breakdown) the child's natural, adoptive or step-parent is unable to provide fully for the child
- the period the parent(s) are unable to provide fully for the child
- how long the caregiver is likely to have the child in their care
- what the caregiver's responsibilities are
The meeting is not the time to discuss the best place for the child, resolve family problems or resolve care and protection concerns.
## Information MSD should give at the meeting:
- provide the parents and caregiver with the opportunity to consider the information that is given to them in the meeting and decide whether to continue with the application
- advise the parents that there is a financial responsibility to pay Child Support
- explain the alternative to including the child as a dependent child for benefit purposes
- explain that under family law, the parents keep the legal right to make decisions about their child and the caregiver has the day-to-day care of the child

chunks.title: Qualifications — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for Emergency Maintenance Allowance, sole parents must have 1 or more dependent children aged under 14 years, and be one of the following:
- getting reduced income due to annual closedown periods
- unpaid during a break in employment
- a 16-19 year old sole parent who is in exceptional circumstances and does not qualify for Young Parent Payment
- a client with split care arrangements who does not qualify for Sole Parent Support
- single and caring for a child not their own when the client cannot get Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit for the child
- does not meet the 2 year residence for Sole Parent Support
Note if the client qualifies for another benefit they cannot get Emergency Maintenance Allowance.
## Client can get another benefit
If the client qualifies for another benefit you cannot pay an Emergency Maintenance Allowance.
You should consider paying Jobseeker Support (including on the ground of hardship) if the client is available and actively seeking work.
In addition, the client must meet other criteria before you grant Emergency Maintenance Allowance:
- Additional conditions of grant
- Residence
- Age
- Client's circumstances
- Dependent child
- Hardship criteria
- Obligations
## Length of Emergency Benefit
Emergency Benefits can continue for a period that is determined at grant.

chunks.title: Qualifying date — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Qualifying date
The qualifying date is the date the client met the following criteria for Emergency Maintenance Allowance:
- date the client started living apart from their partner
- date of family breakdown
- date of birth of child (for single clients)
- date of imprisonment of partner or
- day after the death of their partner

chunks.title: Recompliance — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Recompliance is the activity a client must undertake after they have failed an obligation. They must complete the recompliance activity to have their benefit: - increased or resumed if they have been financially sanctioned or - continued if they have a non-financial sanction imposed Generally, the activities a client needs to complete are the same as or substantially similar to the obligation that initiated the failure. Clients with an obligations failure initiated who recomply within 5 working days will not have a sanction imposed, but the obligations failure will be counted. When a client indicates that they want to recomply MSD must make a recompliance activity available for them at the earliest opportunity. The obligations failure that has reduced or stopped their benefit will determine the type of recompliance activity the client will need to undertake. MSD must discuss with the client what activities they need to undertake in order to recomply. For more information see: - Recompliance for social obligation failures - Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Allocating a recompliance activity — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: When allocating the recompliance activity, MSD must: - discuss with the client what they need to do to satisfactorily undertake the recompliance activity and the implications of not doing this and - make a note of the discussion in the appropriate system MSD must decide whether the client has satisfactorily undertaken their recompliance activity. This will be dependent on the client's circumstances and the nature of the recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Same as or substantially similar activity — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: If a client is unable to undertake the same activity that they failed to do, they must undertake to MSD’s satisfaction another activity that is the same as or substantially similar to the activity they failed to do. The 'same as or substantially similar to' means that MSD must allocate an activity that, as much as possible, requires the same amount of time, effort and commitment as the activity the client failed to complete.

chunks.title: When to resume or increase a benefit — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: A client must have successfully completed the recompliance activity before their benefit is resumed or increased if they have been financially sanctioned. Once completed, the benefit can be resumed or increased from the date MSD is satisfied the client started the recompliance activity. Some examples of this: - if the recompliance activity is a one-off, such as attending an interview the benefit would be resumed from the date the client attended and participated in the interview - if the recompliance activity is ongoing, such as a training programme, the client must undertake the training programme to MSD’s satisfaction. Once this is complete, the benefit can be resumed from the date the client started the training programme - if the client has multiple recompliance activities to complete (due to more than one failure), the date when they have completed a recompliance activity for the latest failure Once MSD has made the decision to recomply a client through an on-going activity, and the client subsequently does not participate or complete the on-going activity (without a good and sufficient reason), then MSD may initiate another failure from the day they subsequently did not comply. When a client cannot recomply, see: - Unable to recomply - Recompliance and change of circumstances

chunks.title: Allocating an extra activity — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Once a client has recomplied and their benefit has been resumed or increased, they may be allocated appropriate additional activities or support. When determining whether to allocate additional activities, the client’s individual circumstances must be considered, including: - the type of obligations they have, and - if there are any suitable activities currently available for them If additional activities are assigned to the client, they must complete them. Failure to complete these activities without a good and sufficient reason should be treated as a new obligations failure.

chunks.title: Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period) — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
A client can complete certain activities to get a provisional benefit if they are subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period due to:
- leaving a job voluntarily
- losing a job through misconduct
- having a Grade 3 sanction imposed or
- refusing an offer of suitable employment
If a client wants to recomply, you must make a 6 week approved activity or programme of activities available to them at the earliest opportunity.
There is no waiting period before an approved activity can start after a sanction has been imposed.
## Recompliance activities
The client must undertake an approved activity for a continuous period of 6 weeks or until the 13 week non-entitlement period ends (whichever is the earlier). This can be through:
- satisfactory participation in a 6 week approved activity or programme of activities
## Recompliance for social obligations
If a client fails their obligations for a third time, and the third failure is a social obligation failure, then the 6 week recompliance activity you require the client to complete will be different.
In this situation it may not be appropriate to require the client to complete a 6 week approved activity that is focused on work outcomes, so a programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate for the client.
For more information see:
- Failing a social obligation
## Programme of suitable activities
If there is not an appropriate 6 week approved activity available, consider establishing a programme of suitable activities.
For when to grant or increase the benefit, see:
- Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period
For what to do if a client cannot recomply see:
- Unable to recomply
For more information see:
- Recompliance for social obligation failures
- Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Recompliance and change of circumstances — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Recompliance and change of circumstances
A client who has a failure in progress or a sanction imposed may be unable to recomply because they:
- had a change of circumstances that means they can no longer recomply with a social obligation or the social obligation is no longer relevant to them or
- had a change in obligations which means they are no longer required to comply with any activity that is specific to their previous obligations
In these situations, the client should not be required to recomply. However, the failure will still be included in the 24 month count, or 12 month count for clients with youth activity obligations.
Once the client has new obligations, MSD may ask them to complete any activities in relation to their new obligations.
## Examples
Examples of where MSD cannot require a client to complete a recompliance activity:
- where a child leaves care or changes age and the social obligation they had is no longer relevant (for example the client has failed the early childhood education social obligation and the child has now turned 6 years)
For more information see:
- Recompliance for social obligation failures
- Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Recompliance for social obligation failures — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for social obligation failures
Clients who have failed their social obligations need to meet all their social obligations as part of an activity to increase their benefit.
Once a client indicates they want to recomply you should have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply. The grade of the social obligations failure will determine the recompliance activity required.

chunks.title: Recompliance social obligations failure (Grade 1 and 2) — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: When the client fails 1 individual social obligation they need to comply with all other social obligations relevant to the age of their dependent child. MSD should discuss with the client what activities they need to do to recomply. MSD must be satisfied that the client has satisfactorily undertaken their recompliance activity. The benefit will be resumed or increased from the date MSD is satisfied the client has started the recompliance activity. In some situations, MSD may ask the client to get verification, for example: - a letter from their practitioner or medical practice, that says they are enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation or - a letter from the child's school that says the child is enrolled and attending or - a letter from their early childhood education provider that says the child is enrolled and attending or - asking to see their Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book

chunks.title: Examples of recompliance — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Example 1 client does not have a good and sufficient reason for this. MSD is unsure if the child is enrolled in primary health care. The client has failed 1 of their social obligations. To recomply with their social obligations, MSD must be satisfied the client has enrolled their child in primary health care and that they will ensure their child attends an early childhood education programme. MSD asks the client to provide verification of this. The client provides a letter from their medical practice confirming the child is enrolled, and a letter from the early childhood education provider confirming the child is enrolled and attending. MSD is satisfied that the client has recomplied with their social obligations. Example 2 A client has 2 children. The 5-year-old child must be enrolled in primary health care and attending school or an early childhood education programme. The 2-year-old child also needs to be enrolled in primary health care and up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks. Both children are enrolled in primary health care and the 5-year-old child is attending school. However, their 2-year-child is not up to date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks and the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for this. The client has failed 1 of their social obligations. To recomply with their social obligations, MSD must be satisfied that the 2-year-old child has or will get their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks. MSD asks the client to provide verification of this. The client brings their 2-year-old’s Well child/Tamariki Ora book to MSD which confirms the 2-year-old has upcoming Well child/Tamariki Ora checks booked. MSD is satisfied that the client has recomplied with their social obligations.

chunks.title: Recompliance when subjected to Money Management — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Recompliance when subjected to Money Management
When a client fails an obligation and has Money Management imposed, they still need to recomply with their obligation. They can do this at any point during the four-week Money Management period, but they need to complete their recompliance activity before their Money Management period ends.
## Client recomplies
When a client completes their recompliance activity during their Money Management period, they will be recomplied at the end of the 4 weeks. Any benefit payments they are entitled to from the day after Money Management ends will go into their bank account.
Money Management will last 4 weeks regardless of when a client completes their recompliance activity.
## Client does not recomply
Clients who do not complete their recompliance activity while on Money Management will have their benefit reduced by 50% at the end of the 4-week period. This is because clients with dependent children have 50% payment protection.
For more information on how non-compliance affects assistance, see:
Their benefit can only return to the full rate payable when a client has completed their recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Recomplying more than one failure — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Recomplying more than one failure
When more than one obligation failure has been initiated for a client on the same day, to get their full benefit the client needs to dispute or recomply to all the failures.
If the client disputes or recomplies with one obligation, the sanction may still be imposed due the other obligation failures not being disputed or recomplied.
## Client already has a failure in-progress or a sanction imposed
Once failures have been initiated, and the notice letter has been sent, any further failures cannot be initiated until each failure:
- has been recomplied with
- has been successfully disputed because the client provided a good and sufficient reason or reasons or
- is overturned (following a dispute)
These further failures will not be included in the 24 month count (or 12 month count for clients with youth activity obligations) and the client cannot be required to recomply.
For more information see:
- Recompliance for social obligation failures
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Recording decisions on a dispute — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Recording decisions on a dispute
You must record the outcome of the client's dispute in OBMAN. One of the following outcomes must be recorded for each dispute:
- Upheld - if you believe that the decision relating to an obligations failure or sanction being imposed was correct you must record this as 'dispute upheld'. The obligations failure will be counted.
- Withdrawn - a client may, after disputing the obligations failure, decide to recomply before the sanction is imposed, or may withdraw their dispute and not recomply. In these cases you must record that the dispute has been withdrawn. The obligations failure will be counted.
- Overturned - when you believe that the client had a good and sufficient reason or that they did not fail their obligations you must record this as obligations failure overturned. The obligations failure will not be counted.
In all cases you must advise the client of the outcome of their dispute. A letter is automatically sent to the client.
If the client does not agree with your decision, they can still request a formal Review of Decision or Medical Appeals Board appeal (drug test failure only). They must do this in writing. The Review of Decision and Medical Appeals Board process should be followed.
Note if the obligations failure was initiated against the wrong client the status can be changed to 'failed in error' on the same day you initiate the failure. No letter is sent when the status is changed to 'failed in error'.
## Reviews of Decisions and appeals to the Medical Appeals Board for obligations failures
Review of Decisions for obligations failures are recorded in HIYA; appeals to the Medical Appeals Board for obligations failures are recorded in the Medical Appeals Database. However, the outcome of the review or appeal must be recorded in OBMAN. This will ensure that the benefit status can be resumed or regranted in SWIFTT depending on the outcome of the review or appeal.
Note that if the Review of Decision or Medical Appeals Board process finds that the originally recorded 'upheld' outcome should be changed to overturned, you will need to make this change in OBMAN.
For more information see:
- The disputes process
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Core policy Medical Appeals Board

chunks.title: Regular engagement and support process — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Regular engagement and support process
Clients must be contacted at least four times by Work and Income before initiating a failure to meet a social obligation. You must complete the three Contact Steps of regular engagement and support and then make a final appointment. You can only determine that the client has failed to meet their social obligations at the final appointment.
The contact with the client can be over the phone or face to face.
The aim of this process is to support clients to meet their social obligations or for clients to take all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations.
At the first Contact Step of engagement and support you should discuss with the client whether they are meeting their social obligations and, if not, encourage them to do so.
The next two Contact Steps of engagement and support should be focused on encouraging and supporting the client to meet their social obligations and following up what happened at the previous Contact Steps.
At each of the three contacts you must:
- check that the client is taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, and actively help and encourage the client to meet those obligations
- ensure that the client is connected with local community information
- advise the client of the next stage of engagement and support and contact
- remind the client of their social obligations and consequences of not meeting them
For more information on the engagement and support process, see:
- Social obligations - Actively engaging with clients [no link find out why] process
Also see:
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Client is meeting their social obligations
- Client changes during regular engagement and support process
- Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations

chunks.title: Residence — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Residence
To receive an Emergency Maintenance Allowance a client should:
- be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (ie not be in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens and residents) and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
For more information see:
- Deciding ordinarily resident
## Sponsored clients
Some clients have been granted permanent residence on condition that they will be supported by a New Zealand sponsor.
Before a decision can be made about the client's application for benefit, any reasons why their sponsor can no longer support the client must first be determined and verified. This is done for the purpose of assessing whether the client is in hardship.
For more information see:
- Sponsored clients [no link find out why]
## Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau
Clients born in the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau are automatically New Zealand citizens (by birth). Generally, they will travel to New Zealand on a New Zealand passport.
Other residents of the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau will be required to produce a proof of residence document.
## Reciprocal Agreements
Emergency Maintenance Allowance is not included in any reciprocal agreements.
For more information see:
- Permanent residence
- Proof of residence

chunks.title: Sanctions for sole parents — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Sanctions for sole parents
When sole parents fail their obligations they do not have their whole benefit sanctioned. Instead, a maximum sanction of 50% of the total benefit may be imposed. The balance payable is known as 50% protection.
Sole parents who are sanctioned can continue to get full Extra help assistance, regardless of the grade of sanction. This includes the Winter Energy Payment.
For more information on what a client can continue to get when sanctioned, see:
- Paying other assistance during a sanction
If the client has not recomplied after 2 weeks, MSD will need to contact them to discuss financial assistance and recompliance. If the client has still not recomplied at 4 weeks MSD will need to send the client a letter advising they need to attend an appointment to discuss ongoing entitlement to benefit.
For more information on this process see:
- Sanction period - Two week intervention [no link find out why]
- Sanction period - Four week intervention [no link find out why]
Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
## Grade 1 and 2 sanctions
For a first and second obligations failure, a sole parent's benefit is reduced by 50% until they recomply, unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed (for a first failure only). They continue to get full Extra help assistance (including the full rate of Winter Energy Payment).
For more information on non-financial sanctions see:
- Non-financial sanctions
Note Non-financial sanctions are not available for clients getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance when their equivalent benefit is Young Parent Payment.
## Grade 3 sanction
For a third obligations failure a sole parent is subject to a non-entitlement period for a period of 13 weeks and will have 50% of their benefit cancelled. The sole parent may get a provisional benefit and have their benefit increased to 100% if they start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities.
They continue to get full Extra help assistance (including the full rate of Winter Energy Payment).
For more information see:
- Recompliance

chunks.title: School holiday clients — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## School holiday clients
There is no stand-down imposed for clients applying for Emergency Maintenance Allowance during school holidays.
For more information see:
- Unpaid during break in employment

chunks.title: Self-imposed stand-down — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Self-imposed stand-down
Where a client knows that they will have a stand-down and delays their application for Emergency Maintenance Allowance, the commencement date depends on whether the client has applied within 28 days of their entitlement date.
If the application is received within 28 days of the client's entitlement date, the commencement date will be:
- the day after the initial stand-down ends
If the application is received more than 28 days after the client's entitlement date, the commencement date will be:
- the day after initial stand-down ends or
- the application date
whichever is the later.

chunks.title: Single and caring for a child not their own — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Single and caring for a child not their own
There may be situations when a single client is unable to earn a sufficient livelihood, as they are caring for a child that is not their own and not be eligible for another benefit.
Note this emergency assistance is only available in cases of genuine need where a person has accepted responsibility for a child. It is not an incentive for people to take children into their care.
When a client is caring for a child that is not their own, consider the following:
- Can the client be considered as the parent of the child?
- What are the reasons they are caring for the child?
- How long will they be caring for the child?
- If long term, are more formal arrangements being considered (for example adoption)?
- Have any other reasonable caring arrangements been considered?
- Do the parents of the child have the ability to contribute to the cost of care?
- Is the child a qualifying child for Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit?
## Child is qualifying child for Unsupported Child Benefit or Orphans Benefit
When a client is eligible for an Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit, this assistance must be granted before Emergency Maintenance Allowance is considered.
For more information see:
- Client eligible for Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit
- Emergency Benefit Not eligible for another benefit

chunks.title: Social obligations — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Social obligations
Clients getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance have social obligations that apply for each dependent child in their care. This includes a child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid.
A client must take all reasonable steps to meet all of the social obligations that apply for each child. The social obligations that apply for each child depend on the age of the child.
When required, clients need to take all reasonable steps to meet the following social obligations. The child must be:
- enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or with a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation and
- up-to-date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks (for children aged under 5 years old) and
- enrolled in and attending 1 of the following from the age of 3 years until they start school: an approved early childhood education programme orTe Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - The Correspondence School oranother approved parenting and early childhood home education programme
- an approved early childhood education programme or
- Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - The Correspondence School or
- another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme
- enrolled in and attending school from the age of 5 or 6 years old (depending on when they start school)
When required a client must:
- attend and participate in interviews with MSD to discuss meeting their social obligations and
- advise on progress where they have not been able to meet their social obligations
A client is only required to meet social obligations from the time they begin to get a benefit.
Clients in the process of applying for Emergency Maintenance Allowance or who have a future commencement date of their Emergency Maintenance Allowance are not required to meet their social obligations.
