Clients are also not required to meet social obligations that would have been relevant to them before getting a benefit.
For example, a client who starts getting a benefit when their child is between 3 and 4 months old, cannot be sanctioned for not having completed the core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks, a child should have had at ages 4 to 6 weeks.

chunks.title: Social obligations recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period) — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Social obligations recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
If a client fails their obligations for a third time, their benefit is reduced or cancelled. For the client to increase their benefit they must undertake a 6 week recompliance activity or programme of activities and reapply for a benefit.
If the third obligation failure is a social obligation failure, the standard 6 week recompliance activities may not be appropriate as some clients do not have work obligations, and cannot work or be in training for a period of 6 weeks.
In this situation, a programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate for the client.
## Example
Example of short term approved activities to consider for an Emergency Maintenance Allowance client with social obligations, when the third failure was a social obligations failure.
Week 1
Make contact with the local Family Start whanau worker and arrange a meeting with them.
Week 2
Family Start whanau worker visit.
Week 3
Contact a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and arrange a visit.
Week 4
Contact the local medical centre to ensure the children are enrolled in primary health care.
Week 5
Talk to appropriate providers of recognised early childhood education programmes.
Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider visit.
Week 6
Meet with a case manager about what steps have been taken.

chunks.title: Sole parents who are 16 to 19 years old — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Sole parents who are 16 to 19 years old
There is specific assistance available to clients aged 16-19 years in some situations. These clients may be eligible for:
- Young Parent Payment or
- Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
Note young people aged 16 or 17 without children may also be entitled to Youth Payment.
Where a sole parent aged 16-19 years does not meet all the requirements for any other benefit, they may be eligible for an Emergency Maintenance Allowance. However, you will need to:
- consider why they are unable to earn a sufficient livelihood to support themselves (and any dependent family)
- confirm the client is in hardship and
- determine they are not eligible for any other benefit
When considering hardship for 16 or 17 year olds, you must consider other means of support available, which includes the client's parent's ability to support them.
## Does not meet residency requirements to receive Young Parent Payment
If a sole parent client aged 16 to 19 years old does not have permanent residence or New Zealand citizenship they cannot receive Young Parent Payment (even if they have lived in New Zealand continuously for 2 years). They may be able to receive Emergency Maintenance Allowance if they are:
- lawfully present in New Zealand and are waiting for the outcome of their application for refugee or protection status in New Zealand or
- applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act and are compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances
## Additional criteria for sole parents aged 16 or 17 years
Before you grant an Emergency Maintenance Allowance to a sole parent who is aged 16 or 17 years there are additional criteria to consider. For more information see:
- Additional criteria for sole parents aged 16 or 17 years
For more information see:
- Additional conditions of grant for 16 to 19 year olds
- Age
- Client's circumstances
- Dependent child
- Hardship criteria
- Residence

chunks.title: Split care arrangements — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Split care arrangements
In a split care situation you can only pay Sole Parent Support to one parent unless the care arrangement has the recognition, authority or approval of the Family Court.
When a sole parent client does not qualify for Sole Parent Support or any other benefit, and is unable to earn sufficient income to support themselves because of their current childcare commitments, you can pay an Emergency Maintenance Allowance.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Example
Francesca failed to complete a Work Ability Assessment, and her case manager has imposed Upskilling as a non-financial sanction. Francesca has already completed most of MSD's Digital Suite courses while looking for work. Francesca's case manager determines that assigning her another course from MSD's Digital Suite would not be suitable.
Francesca asks to do a UX design course through Coursera as she has seen roles available in this industry and is interested in this work. Coursera is a reputable agency and Francesca's case manager determines that this course meets the requirements of the Upskilling sanction. This course is assigned to Francesca as a suitable employment-related training or course.

chunks.title: Taking all reasonable steps for enrolling in and attending school — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Taking all reasonable steps for enrolling in and attending school
Reasons to consider a client is taking all reasonable steps to meet this obligation may include (but are not limited to) that:
- the child has a health condition, injury or disability that affects their ability to attend school
- the child is regularly missing classes for no good reason but the Attendance Service is working with the family and the school to get the child attending school again
- the client is actively trying to encourage their child to attend school but the child has behavioural problems and attendance at school is out of the client's control Note you need to record this as an exception from the obligation in OBMAN using 'Child is not permitted to attend' as the obligation reason.
Note if the parent is in the process of being prosecuted under the Education and Training Act 2020, you must not ask them to comply with this social obligation. You need to record this as an exception reason in OBMAN using 'parent is in prosecution for truant child' as the obligation reason.

chunks.title: Taking all reasonable steps to enrol in a recognised early childhood education programme — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Taking all reasonable steps to enrol in a recognised early childhood education programme
A client could be considered to be taking all reasonable steps to enrol their child in an early childhood education programme for reasons including (but not limited to) that:
- there are shortages of places or availability issues, and the client has a plan in place or has made a commitment to enrol their child when a place becomes available
- there are additional costs of participation that may cause financial hardship to the family, including:
travel costs or
additional costs associated with attending the early childhood education programme
- the child has behavioural problems meaning attendance at an ECE service would be difficult or not possible (for example the child is not currently permitted to attend) (This should be recorded as an exception in OBMAN using 'child is not permitted to attend' as the obligation exception reason)
Note to help clients meet this social obligation you should discuss childcare assistance that may be available to the client.

chunks.title: Client's IRD number — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: MSD may make a written request for evidence of an IRD number for a client who is being paid Emergency Maintenance Allowance.

chunks.title: Setting or extending the timeframe for providing evidence — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: MSD must provide the client with a minimum of 10 working days to provide IRD number evidence that has been requested in writing. MSD can extend the 10 working day period (in writing) if the client has a reasonable explanation for requiring more than 10 days to provide evidence of their IRD number. This includes considering factors outside the client's control that cause delays, including, but not limited to: - client has a family emergency that caused a delay - processing delays with an external agency (e.g. Inland Revenue, Department of Internal Affairs, etc) - client does not speak English as a first language and has difficulty navigating evidence requirements - client has limited access to the internet, a device, or their local service centre - client has a physical or intellectual disability that makes accessing services difficult - client is injured, disabled, or has a medical condition that makes accessing services difficult.

chunks.title: Notice following an unsuccessful match — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a client's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the client (in writing) to provide evidence of their IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the client a minimum of 10 working days to provide their IRD number evidence or the client's assistance must be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Emergency Maintenance Allowance and MSD holds an IRD number on record. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Isla's IRD number. MSD provides 10 working days in writing for Isla to provide evidence their IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Isla already having an IRD number - Isla not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD must suspend assistance if evidence of IRD number is not received — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: MSD must suspend all taxable and/or income tested assistance the client is getting, including their Emergency Maintenance Allowance, if evidence of an IRD number is not provided within 10 working days from the written request, or extended period if this has been applied. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance. Example Koa is receiving Emergency Maintenance Allowance and MSD does not have an IRD number on record. MSD sends a written request giving 10 working days for Koa to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD receives no response to this request. MSD suspends all Koa's taxable and/or income tested assistance because Koa has not supplied MSD with evidence of their IRD number within the timeframe provided.

chunks.title: IRD evidence may not be requested in some circumstances — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - there are significant factors, that are outside the client's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number (e.g. a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence), and - the client needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided or - there are significant factors related to a health, injury or disability that are outside the client's control that prevent them from providing evidence of an IRD number, and - an agent cannot be appointed to act on the client's behalf. MSD can determine a later point to request the evidence of the IRD number. Note there is different guidance for requesting an IRD number or evidence of an IRD number when a client is applying for Emergency Maintenance Allowance.

chunks.title: Temporary employment — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Temporary employment
No stand-down is imposed where a client:
- has been in part-time employment or full-time employment for less than 26 weeks
- was receiving a benefit immediately before they were employed
- the benefit was stopped because they returned to work and
- has applied for a benefit after their employment ceased
Note the client's average weekly income is not required when the client has been in temporary employment for less than 26 weeks. However, the client's final pay details are required to determine, the date of event and entitlement date.

chunks.title: The disputes process — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## The disputes process
The disputes process is a quick process where you must respond to a client's dispute immediately.
You must take into account any new information provided by the client and let the client know your decision straight away.
A letter is sent automatically to the client once a decision has been recorded on the dispute.
A client can dispute the decision if they believe:
- they did not fail their obligations including when they believe they have taken all reasonable steps to meet a social obligation or
- that they had a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete the obligation
- Note if a client has disputed the obligations failure and you have upheld your decision, the client can only dispute it again by following the Review of Decision or Medical Appeal Board appeal (drug test failure only) processes.
If a sanction has been imposed you can still use the disputes process. This allows the client an opportunity for a quick resolution to their dispute before proceeding with the Review of Decision process.
For more information see:
- Recording decisions on a dispute
## Reason for dispute
The client can dispute the decision if they believe they did not fail their obligations, for one of the following reasons:
- an obligations failure was initiated, but the client had undertaken the activity or
- an obligations failure was initiated, but the client had a good and sufficient reason for the failure or
- undertaking or completing the activity was dependent on the provision of assistance by Work and Income and that assistance was not supplied or
- reasonable steps weren't taken by Work and Income to inform a client of the activity that they were required to do
Note some clients may fail more than one obligation at the same time. In this case, for the obligation failure not to apply, the client will need to successfully dispute or review all failures in order to not have a sanction imposed. If only one failure is disputed, a sanction may still be imposed for obligation failures that were not disputed, or were disputed and upheld.
## Good and sufficient reason for failing
You must consider the circumstances of the client, and determine whether it would have been reasonable for the client to have undertaken the activity.
Good and sufficient reasons for failing to undertake an activity will depend on the obligation the client has failed. For social obligations you must consider whether the client has taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations.
Note that if you are unsure whether a client has a good and sufficient reason you should seek guidance from your capability developer, Helpline, manager client service operations, manager client service delivery.

chunks.title: Time limits on grant of Emergency Benefit — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Time limits on grant of Emergency Benefit
Emergency Benefits can continue for a period that is determined at grant of benefit. Generally Emergency Maintenance Allowance clients are granted for a one year period.
When deciding the length of grant you should take into consideration:
- when the client will qualify for a statutory benefit
- any additional conditions of grant and
- any perceived changes in circumstances
The length of grant should be advised to the client at grant. When the period has expired, you should review the client's eligibility to an Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Transfer between benefits — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Transfer between benefits
A transfer between benefits can occur when a client qualifies for Emergency Maintenance Allowance while currently receiving another benefit.
There is no stand-down imposed for clients who:
- transfer to Emergency Maintenance Allowance from another benefit type or
- are included as a partner in another benefit type
Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Childs Benefit and Orphan's Benefit are also a benefit in this situation. Where Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit has been paid and the child now qualifies for Emergency Maintenance Allowance, no stand-down is imposed.
## Non-beneficiary clients
When a non-beneficiary client receiving Extra Help such as Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance applies for Emergency Maintenance Allowance, it is not regarded as a transfer between benefits. An initial stand-down is imposed.
For more information see:
- Processing standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Client intending to return to the same employer — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Client intending to return to the same employer
If a client has received any sick leave payments they would not be eligible for Emergency Maintenance Allowance until these payments had stopped. You then assess any initial stand-down.
Clients are not required to use any sick leave they may have if they are intending to return to the same employer.

chunks.title: 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down
When a client applies for Emergency Maintenance Allowance within 28 days of the entitlement date, the commencement date is the day after the initial stand-down ends.
This means, in some situations, MSD can commence a benefit from a date earlier than the application date.
If the application is not received within 28 days, MSD cannot backdate the commencement date.
Note the 28-day rule only applies to clients who have an initial stand down imposed.

chunks.title: Unable to recomply — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Unable to recomply
A client, who is subject to a sanction or a 13 week non-entitlement period, may not need to complete a recompliance activity if:
- they qualify for a benefit that does not have the obligations to which they must recomply
## Example
A client who is subject to a sanction who develops a health condition or becomes, injured or disabled, and meets the criteria for the exemption 'would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability'. They are unable to complete a recompliance activity.
In this situation you should add the exemption reason in SWIFTT, and follow the disputes process (so that the benefit can be resumed).
For details of the requirements for a client or who has a health condition, injury or disability see:
- Paying other assistance during a sanction

chunks.title: Unpaid during break in employment — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Unpaid during break in employment
There are two different situations to be considered.
## Holidays not included in contract
Sole parents who had an employment contract that does not include employment over the holiday period may qualify for Sole Parent Support because they only expect to return (do not have a new contract) to that employment. At the most they have an expectation of returning to their employment. The initial stand-down rules will apply.
## Insufficient income to cover holiday period
Where the employer closes the business for a holiday period and the employee must take paid leave, but, do not have enough holiday pay to cover the holiday period (for example Teacher Aides with a contract to return to that employment). The employee may qualify for Sole Parent Support.
In these instances, most clients would generally qualify for the statutory benefit. However, in cases where the client's income precludes entitlement to the benefit, that is, their income is such that Sole Parent Support would be paid at a disqualifying rate or the rate of payment would be insufficient, you should consider paying Emergency Maintenance Allowance on the grounds of hardship.
If a client qualifies for more than one benefit they must be told which benefit is the most beneficial for their particular circumstances.
For more information see:
- Qualifies for another benefit

chunks.title: Up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: A client receiving Emergency Maintenance Allowance must take all reasonable steps to: - register their child or children with a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and - keep up-to-date with the child's core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks Note a client is only required to ensure their child completes core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks to meet this obligation from the time they begin to receive a benefit. For example, a client who starts receiving a benefit when their child is between 3 and 4 months old cannot be failed for not having completed the core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks the child should have had at ages 4 to 6 weeks.

chunks.title: Age of child — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: There are 8 core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks that apply to children aged from 4 weeks to 5 years. There are also 3 checks that occur shortly after birth. The obligation only applies for the 8 core checks that occur from around 4 months through to 5 years of age. For more information see: - Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks

chunks.title: Taking all reasonable steps — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Parents and caregivers should be taking all reasonable steps to register their child with a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and keep their child up to date with their core Well Child checks. For more information on considering whether a client is taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, see: - All reasonable steps to meet social obligations

chunks.title: Verification — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text: Most parents will already have their child or children registered and up to date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks and in most cases you should take the client's word that they are meeting this social obligation. However, if you have information that indicates the client is not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations you may ask for proof that the checks have been completed, for example by asking to see their Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book. The Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book is issued to parents when their child is born and is sufficient evidence of the child's attendance. The Health Book has helpful advice and information about what is happening at different stages in the child's development and has places to record all the Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks. For more information see: - All reasonable steps to meet social obligations - Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks - Overview of social obligations according to age of the child

chunks.title: Upskilling — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Upskilling
Upskilling is a non-financial sanction that can be imposed on a client instead of a Grade 1 financial sanction. It is intended to help clients build work-related skills and confidence.
Each week for 4 weeks, a client must:
- regularly attend and participate in at least one employment-related training or course for at least 5 hours and
- report to MSD on the employment-related training or courses they have participated in
At the end of the 4-week period, a client must provide MSD with evidence of their employment related training or courses. MSD must be satisfied the evidence provided is sufficient.
Once a client completes 4 weeks of Upskilling, they are considered to have recomplied with their obligations and do not need to complete any other recompliance activities.
Note Some employment-related training or courses may be longer than four weeks. Clients should be made aware that, if they satisfactorily attend and participate in the training or course, they will be considered to have recomplied after four weeks even if the course lasts longer than this.

chunks.title: Weekly income example — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Weekly income example
Below are examples of calculating the income reduction for weekly income for Emergency Maintenance Allowance.
## Example 1
Weekly gross income
$350.00
Less income allowed before benefit is affected
$160.00
Equals income that will affect benefit
$190.00
Reduction will be 30 cents per $1.00 of income over $160 but not more than $250 ($90 x 0.3 = $27)
$27.00
And 70 cents from every $1.00 of income over $250 ($100 x 0.7 = $70.00)
$70.00
$97.00 reduction
## Example 2
Weekly gross income
$400.00
Less income allowed before benefit is affected
$160.00
Equals income that will affect benefit
$240.00
Reduction will be 30 cents per $1.00 of income over $160 but not more than $250 ($90 x 0.3 = $27)
$27.00
And 70 cents from every $1.00 of income over $250 ($150 x 0.7 = $105.00)
$105.00
$132.00 reduction

chunks.title: Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks
Well Child /Tamariki Ora services are a screening, education and support service offered to all New Zealand children and their families or whānau from birth to 5 years.
The services assist and support families and whānau to improve and protect their children's health. They are provided free to all children under 5 years by registered nurses and community health workers with specific training in child health.
First time parents and families requiring extra support are offered additional visits. Some visits are carried out in the home and others in clinics or community facilities.
Different providers run the Well Child/Tamariki Ora services, including:
- Plunket
- Māori health providers
- Pacific Island health providers
- Public Health Services - for example, public health nurses, community nurses, community health workers, social workers
## When do the checks happen?
The Well Child/Tamariki Ora schedule includes 12 health checks (contacts) with 8 of these offered to children aged from 4 to 6 weeks, to 5 years.
Only the 8 core Well Child checks are required to meet this social obligation.
## Between birth and 4 weeks
4 checks are provided by a midwife, health practitioner or obstetrician:
- soon after birth
- 24 hours after birth
- during the first week of baby's life
- between 2 and 4 weeks
Note the birth to 4 weeks checks listed above do not apply for social obligations purposes.
## Between 4 weeks, and 5 years
The 8 core Well Child checks (listed below) for children between the ages of 4 to 6 weeks, to 5 years are required to meet social obligations.
These are provided by the Well Child provider when the child is:
- 4 - 6 weeks
- 8 - 10 weeks
- 3 - 4 months
- 5 - 7 months
- 9 - 12 months
- 15 - 18 months
- 2 - 3 years
- 4 - 5 years (this is the before school check, and the final Well Child health check)

chunks.title: What is a breakdown in the child's family — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## What is a breakdown in the child's family
The breakdown of a childs family involves a failure or collapse of the normal family dynamics that results in no natural, adoptive, or step-parent being able to fulfil their role as parents to their child or children.
Note not all traumatic events within a family will result in a breakdown of a child's family.
## Family able to support
In times of a crisis, a child may not be able to reside with their parents therefore close family members or friends may take care of the child. The new caregivers should look to the child's parents in the first instance for financial support.
The parents could still be able to support the child financially. A crisis does not necessarily mean a breakdown of the child's family. In addition, there is a possibility that the child may not be likely to be in that applicant's care for at least 1 year.
## Client would like to be the primary caregiver
Where a person (for example a grandparent) would like to be the child's primary caregiver but there is a natural, adoptive or step-parent able to provide care for the child, it would not be appropriate to consider the child as dependent for Emergency Maintenance Allowance.
For more information see:
- Breakdown in the child's family cannot be established

chunks.title: When the sanction is imposed — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## When the sanction is imposed
Sanctions can only be imposed 5 working days after the client has been sent a letter about their obligations failure. This is called the 5 working day notice period.
If a client recomplies within the initial 5 working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the obligations failure is counted.
Also note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only 1 sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
## How to count the '5 working day notice' period
The 5 working day notice period is counted from the date after the obligations failure letter has been sent to the client, to allow for posting and delivery of the letter.
The 5 working day notice period excludes weekends, public holidays, or the period 25 December to 15 January each year.
The table below provides an example of how to count the notice period.
Day 0
Tuesday
Automatic failure in CMS occurs overnight
Day 0
Wednesday
An obligations failure letter is sent
Day 1 Day 2
Thursday Friday
Five working day notice period begins
Weekend
Saturday-Sunday
Day 3 Day 4 Day 5
Monday Tuesday Wednesday
Five working day notice period continues
Day 6
Thursday
Benefit sanction occurs in SWIFTT

chunks.title: Work ability assessment obligation — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Work ability assessment obligation
Clients getting Emergency Maintenance Allowance has a work ability assessment obligation that requires them, when asked, to attend and participate in:
- Self-Assessments
- Structured Interview
- Work Ability Assessments
## Failing to comply
If a client does not meet these obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, an obligations failure will be initiated, and a sanction may be imposed.

chunks.title: Work with a contracted service provider obligation — main benefits > emergency maintenance allowance
chunks.text:
## Work with a contracted service provider obligation
When required to, certain clients may be case managed by a contracted service provider.
When asked, clients have an obligation to co-operate with a contracted service provider and to:
- attend and participate in interviews with them
- report to them on how they are meeting their obligations, this could include their social, work or work preparation obligations and
- when required, complete assessments with the service provider
For more information see:
- Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting obligation to work with a contracted service provider

chunks.title: 52 week reapplication process for clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Some clients who were getting Jobseeker Support before 1 July 2025 and are still getting their benefit on 1 July 2025 maintain their 52 weeks expiry date. These clients (and any partner included in their Jobseeker Support) must complete the 52 week reapplication process before their benefit expiry date. This applies to the following client only: - clients who have an 'in-flight' 52 week reapplication on 1 July 2025. When these clients complete the reapplication process before their final 52 week expiry date and their Jobseeker Support is regranted, they move to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. For more information see: - Expiry date for clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025

chunks.title: 52 week reapplication process — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: To continue getting Jobseeker Support these clients must attend a reapplication appointment and complete a Comprehensive Work Assessment. To complete the 52 week reapplication process a client must: - meet the qualifications for Jobseeker Support, and - attend a reapplication appointment, and - complete a re-application (within 52 weeks) form online, or with a case manager, and - provide any supporting evidence required, and - participate in and complete a Comprehensive Work Assessment for 52 week reapplication process. For more information see: - Overview of the 52-week reapplication process [no link find out why] Doogle - Processing standards [no link find out why] Doogle

chunks.title: Exceptions — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: There are situations where a client or partner do not need to complete the reapplication process. Note clients who maintain their 52 week expiry date and do not need to complete the reapplication process will have their expiry date cleared and will move to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. For more information see: - Client does not need to complete the reapplication process

chunks.title: Actions required at completion — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Once MSD is satisfied that the client has completed the reapplication process, MSD will: - advise the client that their Jobseeker Support will continue and - that they have moved to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle and - refer the client to suitable work or appropriate employment related activity in line with their obligations.

chunks.title: Clients getting Disability Allowance — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client is getting Disability Allowance this may need to be reviewed at the same time as their reapplication. Clients will be advised if their Disability Allowance needs to be reviewed in the 'initial notice to reapply' letter. Note this applies to the Review of Disability Allowance only, it does not apply when the disability is due for medical reassessment (unless that happens to align). For more information see: - Review of Disability Allowance

chunks.title: Clients aged 65 or older — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients aged 65 years or older who do not qualify for New Zealand Superannuation may get Jobseeker Support if they meet all of the qualifications. For more information see: - Reapplication process for clients aged 65 or older

chunks.title: Review of Decision – 52 week reapplication process — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: There are no review rights in the 'notice to reapply' letter because it is a requirement for clients to complete the 52 week reapplication process if they want to continue getting Jobseeker Support. For more information see: - Review of decision - 26 week reapplication process - Core policy Reviews and Appeals

chunks.title: Activity failures for young partners — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Activity failures for young partners
If a young partner fails to meet their youth activity obligations, the sanctions imposed depend on whether they have a dependent child and are youth money managed or not.
## Not youth money managed
When a young partner is not youth money managed and has an obligations failure and has not recomplied within the 5 working day notice period, the effect of the sanction is the same as for their main benefit except with the inclusion of the removal of any incentive payments that might be being paid.

chunks.title: Activity Summary — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Activity Summary
After you have discussed with the client their work obligations and activities they are required to complete, you may want to provide the client an Activity Summary as confirmation of these.
Clients do not sign the Activity Summary and it is not mandatory to provide the Activity Summary to them.
You may think it is appropriate to provide the printout, or a client may request this.

chunks.title: Age — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Age
To get Jobseeker Support, a client must be aged:
- 18 years or older if they do not have dependent children or
- 20 years or older if they have dependent children
## Partners under 18 years
If a client qualifies for Jobseeker Support and has a 16 or 17 year old partner, the partner can be included in the benefit when they are:
- legally married or
- in a civil union or
- in a de facto relationship with Family Court Judge consent

chunks.title: All reasonable steps to meet social obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
There may be some situations where a client or their partner (if any) can't comply with their social obligations for reasons beyond their control. You can accept that a client has taken all reasonable steps to comply if they:
- have made a commitment to meet their social obligations at a more appropriate time and
- are working towards addressing any barriers they are facing
Every client's situation is different and what may be a barrier to meeting social obligations for one family may not be for another.
The decision about whether a client is taking all reasonable steps to comply lies with Work and Income.
Below are some of the situations you should take into account when considering that the client is taking all reasonable steps:
- Shared care issues in the family or family court proceedings occurring
The parent who is not the principal caregiver does not support their child having to attend recognised early childhood education programmes. It would not be reasonable for the client to be held responsible for the actions of someone else.
- Family violence or safety concerns in the family
A client discloses family violence or they have safety concerns for the child.
- Supply or availability issues
A child is on a waiting list for
an early childhood education programme or
a medical centre and the client has a plan or commitment to ensure their child can access primary health care if it is required
- Additional costs of participation or engagement may put the client in hardship
The travel costs or additional early childhood education programme costs associated with attendance would cause hardship to the family.
- The child has a health condition, injury or disability
A child has an injury or behavioural problems meaning that it would not be reasonable to expect them to participate in an approved programme either temporarily or permanently.
- Family has recently moved to a new area
The family has recently moved and is in the process of establishing networks.

chunks.title: Annual closedown periods — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Annual closedown periods
Employers may close their operation or discontinue the work of one or more of their employees at a certain time every year. This is traditionally done over a holiday period, and is called a closedown period.
During a closedown period the employer requires their employees to take all or some of their annual holidays. If the employee is entitled to leave at the start of the closedown period, the Holidays Act 2003 requires that they take paid leave.
If an employee has no annual holiday entitlement for the period of the close down the employer must pay the employee 8% of their gross earnings since they began work or since they last became entitled to annual holidays. In addition an employer and employee can agree that the employee may take annual holidays in advance to cover some or all, of the annual closedown.
## Clients covered by holiday pay not entitled to Jobseeker Support
If a client is covered by holiday pay during the annual closedown period they are not unemployed and therefore they are not entitled to Jobseeker Support.
## Clients not covered by holiday pay
Clients not covered by holiday pay during any period of an annual closedown are unemployed for that period (that is, they are no longer in paid employment). They can be considered for Jobseeker Support.
However, due to the short-term duration of the closedown period, many clients in this situation may not meet the job search requirements to receive Jobseeker Support.
In these cases, if the client is suffering hardship they may apply for third tier assistance (a Special Needs Grant or Recoverable Assistance Payment etc) or an Emergency Benefit.
When you consider emergency assistance you need to look at the client's cash assets and the reason why insufficient paid leave is available.
You will need to consider the extent to which the client has caused or contributed to the hardship and the impact on the client and any dependent family.
For example, you may consider paying Emergency Benefit if a person used their annual leave entitlement to cover an extended period of illness.

chunks.title: Approved activity examples — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Approved activity examples
Here are some examples that may be a suitable 6 week approved activity for the client or partner:
- Training for work
- Unpaid work experience
- Voluntary Work
Note this list is an example only, an approved activity (or programme of suitable activities) should be relevant to the obligations failure and be fair and reasonable.
For more information see:
## Programme of suitable activities
If there is not an appropriate 6 week approved activity available, consider establishing a programme of suitable activities.
For more information see:
- Recompliance programme example
For when to grant or increase the benefit, see:
- Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period
For what to do if a client or partner cannot recomply see:
- Unable to recomply

chunks.title: Approved budgeting programme activity — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Approved budgeting programme activity
Young partners may be required to participate in and complete an approved budgeting programme
An approved budgeting programme aims to provide young people with skills in financial management. Young people must be referred to a provider from the list of authorised courses and providers already contracted with MSD.
The providers of the budgeting programme will provide a programme that is in line with the Youth Services Guidelines for the content of the approved programme.
When there are no budgeting providers contracted in a particular area, the service provider will have to deliver the budgeting programme themselves.

chunks.title: Approved recompliance activities for young partners — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Approved recompliance activities for young partners
Approved recompliance activities for young partners include:
- education, training or work-based learning
- part-time work or work experience (where the young person is not already in part-time work)
- community activities
- any other activity approved by MSD that will enhance skills or motivation
Note the benefit will be resumed or increased from the date the young partner starts the recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Approved training — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Approved training
For training to be approved, first you need to decide if training is the appropriate activity for the client and then consider whether the course is the right course.
## Is training the appropriate activity
Consider whether a training course is the most suitable activity for a client.
Consider with the client whether other activities (for example programmes, seminars, or work experience) might be more suitable for moving the client towards full-time employment.
Discuss and take into account the client's career or job preferences, and consider:
- their educational qualifications
- their employment history
- their skills and
- whether training will help them find work at the earliest opportunity
## Is this the right course?
The course must:
- focus on teaching practical, employment-related skills
- support the client to find work and
- be less than 12 weeks (other than approved Government sponsored courses)
Some additional things to note are:
- clients applying for courses longer than 12 weeks should be seeking assistance through StudyLink if the course has been approved by the Ministry of Education for Student Loans and/or Student Allowances and
- if a client is undergoing pre-employment training under Flexi-Wage they cannot receive the Jobseeker Support as they should be getting a wage from the employer
## Approval of local courses
A manager client service delivery can approve a local course (for the purpose of paying Jobseeker Support when it meets the above criteria.
Examples
- Examples of approved courses
## Extra Help for clients in approved training
The following assistance is available for clients in approved training:
- Course Participation Assistance [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Employment-related training — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Employment-related training
Employment-related training includes (but is not limited to):
- Regional training courses
- Workplace/industry training
- Youth Guarantee courses
## Extra Help for young partner in approved training
The following assistance is available for young partner in approved training:
- Course Participation Assistance [no link find out why]
You should also keep in contact with the young partner during their course to ensure that they are regularly attending the training.

chunks.title: Assessed as financially competent — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Assessed as financially competent
A young partner is generally considered to be financially competent where they have:
- earned their budgeting incentive and
- shown consistent, sound financial judgement which may include the young person is spending their in-hand allowance on items that are appropriate for their situationany hardship assistance is justifiedthe young person has lowered their coststhe young person has found a part-time job and is managing the money they receive from that in a way that is appropriate for their situation
- the young person is spending their in-hand allowance on items that are appropriate for their situation
- any hardship assistance is justified
- the young person has lowered their costs
- the young person has found a part-time job and is managing the money they receive from that in a way that is appropriate for their situation

chunks.title: Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process
Clients who have an initial stand-down cannot get an Emergency Benefit, Temporary Additional Support or Accommodation Supplement during the stand-down.
## Special Needs Grants
If a client is suffering hardship they may be able to get a Special Needs Grant.
For more information see:
- Special Needs Grants Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process

chunks.title: Assistance to move back to an area that is not a limited employment location — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Assistance to move back to an area that is not a limited employment location
This applies where a client has moved to a limited employment location and cannot meet the work obligations, and they have decided to move back to an area that is not a limited employment location.
In this situation, the client has put themselves into hardship by moving to a limited employment location where they cannot meet their work obligations. Therefore, we would generally not provide assistance to help them relocate.
However, when hardship is preventing the client from moving to an area that is not a limited employment location, you may look at an Advance Payment of Benefit using the 'other' category.
This payment is recoverable and requires your manager client service delivery's approval.

chunks.title: Bank — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Bank
An appropriate bank is:
- a private savings bank, a trustee savings bank or The Co-operative Bank
- a registered bank which on the 31st March 1987 was a trading bank or
- any other registered bank or a building society approved by the Minister after consultation with the Minister of Finance

chunks.title: Benefit eligibility and rate while partner is in prison — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Benefit eligibility and rate while partner is in prison
The rate of Jobseeker Support paid while a client's partner is in prison depends on whether there are dependent children included in the benefit.
## No dependent children
A client with no dependent children will receive the single rate of Jobseeker Support and be subject to a full-time income test.
## Dependent child or children
A client with dependent children will receive the sole parent rate of Jobseeker Support if the dependent child is over 14 years
Note a client who has children aged under 14 years may be eligible to receive Sole Parent Support (subject to part-time income test).
For more information see:
- Charging income
## Partner released from prison
When a client's partner is released from prison the couple's benefit eligibility and rate will need to be reviewed. The client will no longer be eligible for a sole parent or single rate of benefit unless they are no longer in a relationship with their partner.

chunks.title: Benefit eligibility and rate while the partner is in home detention — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Benefit eligibility and rate while the partner is in home detention
Where a client who has been in prison is released and is subject to a sentence of supervision, intensive supervision, or home detention and is subject to conditions (including post-detention conditions of a sentence of home detention) that prevent them from undertaking employment, there are two options for the client who is not in home detention.
This will depend on whether the client is living in the same house as their partner.
## Living in the same house
The client and partner may qualify for Jobseeker Support.
The client who is subject to home detention will qualify for Jobseeker Support because they would meet the eligibility criteria to be available for and seeking full-time work, except that they qualify for an exemption from these obligations.
The exemption reason is court imposed conditions.
## Living in separate premises
The client who is not in home detention would continue to meet the qualifications to receive Sole Parent Support or Jobseeker Support at the sole parent rate if the couple's youngest dependent child is aged 14 or over.
The client who is in home detention would meet the qualifications to receive Jobseeker Support as they would meet the eligibility criteria to be available for and seeking full-time work, except that they qualify for an exemption from these obligations.
The exemption reason is court imposed conditions.
The rate of Jobseeker Support payable to the client in home detention is the half married rate for a couple with a dependent child.

chunks.title: Bereavement of immediate family — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Bereavement of immediate family
It may be determined that a client has an exceptional circumstance for not completing their reapplication process before their expiry date if they have experienced a bereavement of an immediate family member during the notice period which affected their ability to reapply.
Immediate family, for the purposes of exceptional circumstances, are a:
- spouse or partner
- parents (including step-parents and foster parents)
- grandparents (including grandmother and grandfather)
- children (including grandchildren, stepchildren, foster children, mokopuna - those grandchildren who have been raised by the grandparents as the principal caregivers, and whāngai - children who have been raised, normally by a relation or other person within the wider whānau to which the child belongs)
- siblings (including half siblings and step siblings, but excluding members of organisations/gangs referring to themselves as 'blood brothers and sisters')
## Evidence
MSD may require the client to provide evidence of the bereavement. In most cases the client should just be asked to sign a personal statement.
In some cases clients may also be asked to provide further evidence, this could include:
- a death certificate
- a newspaper notice
- an online obituary which clearly shows the date of death
- a birth certificate showing relationship to deceased
- confirmation of the death from the lawyer administering the estate, or from the minister or funeral director.
For more information see:
- Exceptional circumstances for reapplication
- Client does not need to complete the reapplication process

chunks.title: Birth of a child — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Birth of a child
Eligibility for a Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) should be reviewed when the baby is born. If the client includes the child, payment can continue for up to 13 weeks after the birth of the child. However, you can test their eligibility for another benefit, such as Jobseeker Support (if client has a partner) or Sole Parent Support any time after the birth of the child.
Where the payment of Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) has been continued for four weeks after the birth of the child, the benefit can be extended for another nine weeks.
- Core policy Child Support
## Child not going to be included in benefit
If the client does not keep the child, or the child is stillborn or dies shortly after birth, payment may continue for up to 4 weeks after the birth.
No medical certificate is required - a statement will be sufficient.
This will allow the client to recover from the birth and make alternative arrangements. For Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) to continue after this 4 week period a medical certificate showing incapacity to work is required.

chunks.title: Calculating the period of residence — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Calculating the period of residence
A period of residence in New Zealand starts from the date the client was:
- lawfully resident in New Zealand or
- was granted New Zealand citizenship or permanent residence
To be resident at a particular time a client must be lawfully resident, that is, the client must be one of the following:
- a New Zealand citizen
- a permanent resident in New Zealand
- an Australian citizen or passport holder or
- a New Zealand passport holder
For more information see:
- Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
- Permanent residence
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Unlawful residence
- Granting on grounds of hardship

chunks.title: Step 1 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Step 1
Find out the number of days represented by the payment received. If this is not clearly shown on the 'verification of payments received' provided by the client, use either of the following formula.
Note extra payments paid to the client (for example holiday pay), should not be included in the gross salary figure used to calculate the daily rate of pay. However these payments will be included in the client's last 26 and 52 weeks gross earnings.
Formula 1
Determine gross salary over last 52 weeks of employment
Divide by 52 weeks = weekly rate of pay
Divide by 5 days = daily rate of pay
Confirm total amount of holiday pay etc
Divide this amount by daily rate of pay = number of days pay
Formula 2
Determine gross salary over last 4 weeks of employment
Divide by 20 (number of working days in 4 weeks) = daily rate of pay
Confirm total amount of holiday pay etc
Divide by daily rate of pay = number of days pay
Note only calculate the period covered by holiday pay using the applicants' last four weeks income if it does not disadvantage the client. If the income earned in the last four weeks does not reflect what the client normally earned, you may need to request extra weeks or calculate the daily rate of pay using the last 26 weeks gross salary.

chunks.title: Capacity issues prevent a young partner meeting their parenting obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Capacity issues prevent a young partner meeting their parenting obligations
A young partner may be granted a parenting incentive without meeting the criteria if:
- there are capacity issues preventing a young person from: undertaking a parenting programmeenrolling their dependent child/ren with a primary health organisationkeeping their dependent child/ren aged 5 years or under up-to-date with their Well Child checkshaving their children under five years attends an approved early childhood education programme or being placed in other suitable childcare which the young person is in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work
- undertaking a parenting programme
- enrolling their dependent child/ren with a primary health organisation
- keeping their dependent child/ren aged 5 years or under up-to-date with their Well Child checks
- having their children under five years attends an approved early childhood education programme or being placed in other suitable childcare which the young person is in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work
and
- the young person has agreed with their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service on steps they must take to fulfil these obligations (for example being on a waiting list) and
- the young person has taken the agreed steps to the satisfaction of their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service

chunks.title: Caring for a child or foster child with special needs — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Caring for a child or foster child with special needs
This exemption may apply to:
- partners and sole parent clients with work obligations
- all clients with work preparation obligations (including those who have a deferral from their work obligations)
A client can be exempt from some or all of their or work or work preparation obligations if they are:
- the principal caregiver of a dependent child or
- the foster parent of a foster child
who has special needs and whose welfare would be unduly harmed if the client attended employment or training, and for whom alternative care arrangements are not available, or are unable to be made.
This means the child must have 1 or more of the following:
- physical or intellectual disability
- a medical condition
- a chronic or recurring illness
- a learning or behavioural difficulty and
- be unable to attend school on a regular basis
or
- be a foster child, aged 3 years or older, who is adjusting to a placement with a new foster carer
This can be a full or partial exemption.
## Foster child is under 3 years
A client may also be exempt from some of their work obligations if they are caring for a foster child under the age of 3 years.
## Evidence
The client must provide written evidence from a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner, psychologist, or social worker stating:
- what the child's illness is and its likely duration or
- an assessment of the child's behavioural difficulty or
- the need for full-time care and
- the risk to the child if the client has work or work preparation obligations and
- that the child is unable to attend school
Note MSD should also consider eligibility to Child Disability Allowance. However, a child getting Child Disability Allowance does not guarantee the client or their partner will meet the criteria for this exemption.

chunks.title: Caring for a child under 3 years who is not their dependent child — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Caring for a child under 3 years who is not their dependent child
This exemption may apply to partners and sole parents with work obligations.
In some cases a client may be caring for a foster child or children under the age of 3 years who is in Oranga Tamariki care. Foster children are not considered to be dependent children.
These clients may be exempt from meeting some of their work obligations.
This is a partial exemption only.
## Proof
The client must provide:
- confirmation of their situation - for example, a letter from Oranga Tamariki and
- confirmation of the age of the child
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason "Caring for foster child".
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions

chunks.title: Caring for a child or foster child with special needs (young partners) — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Caring for a child or foster child with special needs (young partners)
A young partner with a dependent child can be exempt from some or all of their activity obligations if they are the:
- principal caregiver of a dependent child or
- the foster parent of a foster child
who has special needs and whose welfare would be unduly harmed if the young partner attended education, training or work-based learning and for whom alternative care arrangements are not available, or are unable to be made.
This means the child must have 1 or more of the following:
- a physical or intellectual disability
- a medical condition
- a chronic or recurring illness
- a learning or behavioural difficulty and
- be unable to attend school on a regular basis
or
- be a foster child, aged 1 year or older, who is adjusting to a placement with a new foster carer
This can be a full or partial exemption.
## Foster child is under 1 year
A young partner may also be exempt from some of their work obligations if they are caring for a foster child under the age of 1 years.
## Evidence
The young partner must provide written evidence from a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, psychologist or social worker stating:
- what the child's illness is and its likely duration or
- an assessment of the child's behavioural difficulty or
- the need for full-time care and
- the risk to the child if the young partner is required to meet their activity obligations and
- that the child is unable to attend school
Note MSD should also consider eligibility to Child Disability Allowance. However, a child getting Child Disability Allowance does not guarantee the partner will meet the criteria for this exemption.

chunks.title: Caring for foster child under 12 months old (young partners) — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Caring for foster child under 12 months old (young partners)
In some cases a young partner may be caring for a foster child under the age of 12 months who is in Oranga Tamariki care. Foster children are not considered to be dependent children.
This is a partial exemption only. The young partner can be exempt from meeting their obligation to be in full-time education, training and work-based learning.
The budgeting and parenting obligations, along with the obligation to meet with their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service still apply.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted until the foster child turns 12 months of age or until the foster child is 6 months old and there is a suitable place available at a Teen Parent Unit.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason "UCB/OB/Foster Child under 12 months".
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions (young partners)
For an overview of the exemptions see:
- Table of exemptions for young partners

chunks.title: Caring full-time for a partner with a health condition, injury or disability (young partners) — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Caring full-time for a partner with a health condition, injury or disability (young partners)
A young partner may be caring for a partner or spouse who has a health condition, injury or disability and who needs to be cared for on a full-time basis.
This can be a full or partial exemption.
## Evidence
The young partner must provide evidence from a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner:
- that their partner or spouse needs the young partner's full-time care and
- that without that care their partner or spouse would need hospital level care or care of an equivalent kind and
- the length of time their partner or spouse will need that care

chunks.title: Caring full-time for person with health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Caring full-time for person with health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to clients or partners with work preparation obligations, or partners with work obligations.
A client or partner may be caring for a person who has a health condition, injury or a disability and who needs to be cared for on a full-time basis.
This can be a full exemption.
Note MSD should consider whether the client or partner should transfer to Supported Living Payment on the ground of caring for a person.
## Evidence
The client or partner must provide evidence from a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner:
- that the person needs the client's full-time care and
- that without that care the person would need hospital level care or care of an equivalent kind and
- the length of time the person will need that care

chunks.title: Cash assets do not include — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Cash assets do not include
- the home property and the land on which it is situated
- a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2000, or is used by the client or a member of their family for day to day accommodation
- Christchurch mosques attack support payments
- Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income
- motor vehicle principally used by the client for private use
- MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- personal effects
- Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received
Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.
Generally, ex gratia payments and compensation payments made by the Crown are excluded for the first 12 months following the date the client received the payment. For more information see:
- Core Policy Ex gratia and Compensation payments
In exceptional circumstances you can disregard some of the client's cash assets see:
- Exceptional circumstances for cash assets

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances
Clients must tell us straight away of any change in their circumstances or their family's situation that may affect their entitlement to Jobseeker Support. Clients agree to this by signing the Jobseeker Support application form.
A change of circumstance may also affect the client's social obligations.
Examples of changes and how to deal with these can be found in Changes and Reviews.
For more information see:
- Child changes and social obligations
- Changes and reviews Child changes

chunks.title: Change in circumstances during Money Management — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances during Money Management
Clients may have a change in circumstances during Money Management, such as a change in income, which may change their rate of benefit.
If a client declares a change in circumstances after their payment has been issued onto the payment card, it may mean this payment is incorrect resulting in a debt being established or arrears due to the client.
Any debt will generally be repaid from their future benefit payments.
If a client is owed arrears, it will be paid directly to their bank account. This is different when a client's benefit stops during Money Management. For more information see:
- Period of Money Management.

chunks.title: Change in personal resources — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Change in personal resources
Immigration New Zealand requires applicants to sign a Declaration of Personal Resources when applying for permanent residence under the following categories:
- Skilled/Business Stream and
- Family Stream
Note people do not have to sign a declaration if they are granted permanent residence under the categories of International/Humanitarian Stream which includes the:
- Refugee Family Support Category
- Pacific Access Category
- Samoan Quota Scheme
- Victims of Family Violence and
- various other special policies for specific countries
By signing the Declaration of Personal Resources, the client declares they are able to support themselves and family (if any) for the first 2 years residence in New Zealand.
The requirement for an immigrant to maintain themselves for the first 2 years does not mean they cannot access benefit assistance as a non-beneficiary. However, the client may not have entitlement to non-beneficiary assistance due to those resources.
For the above categories a client's permanent residence has been assessed on the following resources:
- a definite offer of employment (supported in writing)
- financial support from family members in New Zealand (supported in writing)
- and/or
- personal cash assets
Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship is income and asset tested. To assess a client's entitlement to Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship confirmation of the client's income and assets declared on application for permanent residence is required from Immigration New Zealand.
Confirmation of the client's current income and assets is also required. If there is a change in financial circumstances further investigation will need to be done to establish the client's entitlement to benefit assistance.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
Clients receiving Jobseeker Support must be:
- available for and seeking full-time work or
- taking steps to become available for it if they are temporarily prevented from doing so by a health condition, injury or disability
## Jobseeker Support clients generally cannot be absent and continue to receive payment
Clients receiving Jobseeker Support cannot generally be absent from New Zealand and continue to receive payment of their benefit. The Government's obligation to pay income support usually stops when the client leaves New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Client with work obligations, an exemption or deferral
- Permanent absence
## All clients have an obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand
All clients receiving a main benefit must advise Work and Income before they leave New Zealand. If the client or partner does not advise Work and Income prior to their international travel, their benefit payments will stop from the day after they leave New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand
## Paying a benefit while a Jobseeker Support client is absent from New Zealand
A client or partner not otherwise entitled to be paid their Jobseeker Support may be able to continue to receive their payments for up to 28 days in a 52 week period, while they are absent from New Zealand for:
- Approved travel reasons
- Overseas for medical treatment
## Partner absent from New Zealand
Whether a partner of a Jobseeker Support client can be absent from New Zealand and continue to receive payment of their benefit depends on their work or work preparation obligations.
For more information see:
- Partner with work or work preparation obligations
## Payment of benefit while absent for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period while the client is absent from New Zealand. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Absent for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Calculating the period of absence
- Payment when client or partner absent from New Zealand

chunks.title: Absences that do not prevent partner from meeting obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Absences that do not prevent partner from meeting obligations
Generally, a partner receiving Jobseeker Support who has work obligations or work preparation activities assigned cannot be absent from New Zealand and continue to be paid a benefit unless:
- it is for one of the permitted travel reasons or
- they are already meeting their work obligations (by being in employment ) or work preparation activities (by participating in employment related training)
and
- the travel will not prevent them continuing to meet these obligations (eg because it is during a period of annual leave or a term or semester break)
Note that the ability to travel because the client is already meeting their work obligations, and the travel will not prevent them from continuing to meet these obligations, does not apply for primary clients receiving Jobseeker Support.
For more information see:
- Partner meeting their work preparation activities
- Partner meeting their work obligation requirements

chunks.title: Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
These circumstances are:
- travel is required for an approved reason, and either: it is the client's first absence within 52 weeks and the permitted reason the client needs to be absent from New Zealand necessitates a period longer than 28 days orthe client has had other prior approved absences within the 52 week period and they require further approved absences which will require them to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- it is the client's first absence within 52 weeks and the permitted reason the client needs to be absent from New Zealand necessitates a period longer than 28 days or
- the client has had other prior approved absences within the 52 week period and they require further approved absences which will require them to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- the client is absent from New Zealand for an approved travel reason and their return is prevented by a new circumstance that requires them to be absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period
- the client is a young partner of a main beneficiary with youth activity obligations and they are travelling to receive support from a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family) who is residing overseas
For more information see:
- Paying more than 28 days for an approved reason
- Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
- Paying for more than 28 days - receive support from family overseas (young partner)
- Calculating the period of absence

chunks.title: Amount of income exemption — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Amount of income exemption
When you have determined that a client is severely disabled you must then consider if they should have all or part of their income from employment disregarded for benefit purposes.
The amount of the income exemption depends on the client's individual circumstances after considering the guidelines - for severe disablement and should be:
- a reasonable amount as an incentive to recognise the personal effort that a severely disabled person has made to participate or continue in employment
- any additional costs that a severely disabled person has incurred to participate or continue in employment
- a reasonable amount to ensure that a severely disabled person is not disadvantaged by participating or continuing in employment
Note the client may be entitled to receive other types of assistance, for example Disability Allowance for transport costs to work or employment assistance.
Fully document your decision by recording the reasons and the amount of the exemption in the CMS note template, Income exemption amount
Contact Helpline if you need help with the assessment.
For more information see:
- Extra Help
- Effect of income on Extra help

chunks.title: Annual income for sole parent and grandparented clients before 30 June 2026 — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: Sole parent and grandparented Jobseeker Support clients whose benefit commenced (or last commenced) before 1 July 2025 can have their income charged annually until they reach their next 52 week expiry date. Clients who have their income charged annually can get up to $8,320 gross per year before their income will affect their benefit. Clients whose annual income is over $8,320 gross per year will have their benefit reduced by: - 30 cents for every $1.00 of income that is between $8,320 and $13,000 gross per year - 70 cents for every $1.00 of income that is more than $13,000 gross per year. Note from 30 June 2026 all sole parent and grandparented Jobseeker Support clients will have moved to weekly income charging and will have had their final Review of Annual Income.

chunks.title: Income change — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: Generally, any income a client receives should be charged against the benefit for the period in which the income was earned or represents. However, for sole parent and grandparented clients with annual income charging, MSD will estimate the prospective income the client is likely to receive over the next 52 weeks and update income from the first available date. If the client indicates their income is likely to vary week to week and prospective income cannot be estimated then income should be charged for the actual period it was earned or represents. This reduces the likelihood of debt when they complete their final Review of Annual Income.

chunks.title: Clients moving from annual to weekly income charging — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
