chunks.title: Ongoing assistance for dependent children — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Ongoing assistance for dependent children
When a surviving dependent child is to be cared for by a person other than a parent, the caregiver may be able to receive an Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki order in place — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: The following table identifies when a child can be considered a dependent child and when it can't, depending on the type of order that is in place and section of Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 that applies. When to include as a dependent child When not to include as a dependent child section 139: Agreements for temporary care of child or young person by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 140: Agreements for extended care of child or young person by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 78: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, pending determination of court proceedings. If Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki has returned the child or young person in to the care of the immediate previous care giver. section 78: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, pending determination of court proceedings section 101: Custody order in favour of principal caregiver. Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki under section 110. section 101: Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 102: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 110(2)a: Sole Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. Section 101 Custody Order in favour of principal caregiver and other dependent child criteria are met. Please refer case to your local solicitor for consideration. section 110(2)a: Sole Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki section 110(2) b: Additional Guardianship Order, to any other guardian in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 112: Guardianship Order in favour of Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki for a specific purpose. Please refer case to your local solicitor for consideration. section 86: Services Orders that provide for particular services and assistance required by the child or young person (e.g. counselling fees, special education costs) section 86: Services Orders that provide for general financial support to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 91: Support Orders. The child may be considered a dependent child where the documentation states that specific financial support is to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki.

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki order in place — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: section 91: Support Orders. The child cannot be considered a dependent child where the documentation states that general financial support is to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. See your local solicitor if you receive a case in this category. When a child or young person is discharged from the care, custody or sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, always consider including the child in the client's Jobseeker Support or granting Unsupported Childs Benefit - The legislation referenced above is the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989

chunks.title: Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid
When a client is receiving an Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, the child is not treated as a dependent child and is not included in the assessment of Jobseeker Support.
The client's Jobseeker Support is assessed on their family circumstances excluding the child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid.

chunks.title: Parents aged under 20 years old — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Parents aged under 20 years old
To receive Jobseeker Support with a dependent child included, a client must be aged 20 years or older.
When a client aged under 20 years applies to have a child included in their benefit, they no longer meet the age qualification for Jobseeker Support and must apply for Young Parent Payment.
## Couple, both aged under 20 years old
When clients who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and who are both aged under 20 years, apply to have a child included in their benefit they no longer meet the age qualification for Jobseeker Support. Both clients must apply for Young Parent Payment in their own right.

chunks.title: Part-time employment — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Part-time employment
Part-time employment does not make a child financially independent. Nor do you take the child's earnings into account when assessing the rate of Jobseeker Support payments. For more information on children's income see:
- Child income

chunks.title: Part-time employment — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Part-time employment
When Jobseeker Support client or their partner commences employment that is less than 30 hours a week payment of the Jobseeker Support can continue as the client will still be able to meet their job search requirements.
If the partner has commenced full time employment then the Jobseeker Support can continue with the partner's earnings being charged as income against the benefit. This is regardless of whether the partner is subject to work obligations.
You will need to check whether family tax credit should continue to be paid at the full rate, or refer the client to Inland Revenue to avoid an overpayment.
For more information see:
- Family tax credit
- Guidelines for suspension or cancellation
- Income from employment
- Income stops
- Charging income

chunks.title: Partner donates a kidney or liver tissue — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partner donates a kidney or liver tissue
When a partner is donating a kidney or liver tissue, they can keep getting Jobseeker Support.
Grant the partner the exemption 'Would qualify for Jobseeker Support–health condition, injury or disability'.
Manually record the exemption in the SWTDA screen in SWIFTT.
This exemption starts from the date of their operation, and can continue while the client:
- is recovering from their operation and
- they cannot meet their part-time or full-time work obligations
The exemption must not be more than 12 weeks.
Do not apply any obligations failures:
- for the maximum period of 12 weeks or
- until the client has recovered from the operation
whichever is earlier.
## Partner has an obligation failure
If the partner currently has an obligation failure, donating a kidney or liver tissue is considered a 'good and sufficient reason'.
The work obligations failure must be overturned. This will remove the failure from the client’s 12 month obligation failure count and there is no sanction.
## Childcare Assistance
Clients may be eligible for Childcare Assistance payments while they are they are recovering.
For more information see:
- Childcare Subsidy Temporary illness
- OSCAR Temporary illness
- Partner with an exemption from their work obligation

chunks.title: Partners with children under 3 years — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partners with children under 3 years
A partner with their youngest child aged under 3 years old has work preparation obligations, and can be a part or full-time student without it affecting their Jobseeker Support.
## Partners with work obligations
Partners with no children or with their youngest child aged 3 years or over, may be a part or full-time student without it affecting their Jobseeker Support if they have been granted an exemption from meeting their work obligations because they:
- were part way through a course of study at the time that the client applied for Jobseeker Support or
- were part way through a course of study when their youngest child reached the age of 3 years
A partner can be considered to be meeting their work obligations if their study timetable allows enough time for job search activity, for example, if the hours of the part-time study are outside of normal working hours.
If a partner starts study and they can no longer meet their work obligations and they do not have an exemption from meeting their work obligations you may need to initiate an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures
- In approved study before subject to work obligations
## Partner engaged in full-time study
If a partner is engaged in full time study and does not meet the criteria for an exemption they can apply for a Student Allowance. If they are qualified for a Student Allowance the client can be included in the Student Allowance when:
- they are legally married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and
- both are aged 24 years or more or
- they have a dependent child
Where the client cannot be included, the partner will be regarded as single and will receive the single rate of Student Allowance.
For Jobseeker Support purposes we still regard them as a married, civil union or de facto couple. You will need to charge the student allowance against the married, civil union or de facto rate of Jobseeker Support and pay the client half of the abated benefit.
Because the Jobseeker Support and Student Allowance rules are different in this situation there are particular procedures to follow. There is a flowchart to help you, see:
- Couple under 24 years - partner not granted an exemption in non-approved study
For more information see:
- Work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures
- Exemptions
- Student Allowance
- Student Allowance Student with a partner
- Client intends to study full-time

chunks.title: Partner meeting their work obligation requirements — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partner meeting their work obligation requirements
A client who is a partner of someone receiving Jobseeker Support can continue to be paid a benefit while they are absent from New Zealand for any reason:
- when they are meeting their work obligations by being in paid employment and
- the travel will not prevent them from continuing to meet these work obligations (eg during a period of annual leave from employment)
## Examples (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
Partner of a person receiving Jobseeker Support with part-time work obligations is employed for 22 hours per week. They have taken annual leave from their employment to travel to Australia.
The client is already meeting their part-time work obligations by being in suitable employment of over 20 hours per week. Their benefit will continue to be paid for up to 28 days in any 52 week period while they are absent from New Zealand.
A Jobseeker Support couple go overseas on holiday. The partner is meeting their obligations by working part-time for 24 hours per week. The holiday is taken while the partner is on annual leave.
The primary job seeker cannot continue to be paid while overseas on a holiday.
The partner is already meeting their part-time work obligations by being in suitable employment of over 20 hours per week. The partners share of the benefit will continue to be paid for up to 28 days in a 52 week period while they are absent from New Zealand.
The full rate of accommodation supplement can continue to be paid for up to 28 days in any 52 week period while they are absent from New Zealand.
## Partners obligations
From 1 April 2016, partners will need an approved reason to travel if:
- their youngest dependent child is 3 or 4 years old
- they are working between 15 and 20 hours per week
Discretion to continue payments while temporarily overseas is available for clients that:
- will change from work preparation to part-time work obligations on 1 April 2016 because their youngest dependent child is aged 3 or 4 years old or
- will no longer be meeting their part-time work obligations on 1 April 2016 because the definition of part-time work increased from 15 to 20 hours per week and
- book overseas travel before they are aware of the changes to their work obligations that come into effect on 1 April 2016 and
- would continue to receive their payment based on their obligations at the time they booked travel
Note all other Absence from New Zealand policy applies when applying this discretion.

chunks.title: Partner meeting their work preparation activities — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partner meeting their work preparation activities
A client who is a partner of someone receiving Jobseeker Support can continue to be paid a benefit while they are absent from New Zealand for any reason:
- when they are meeting their work preparation obligations by attending and participating in employment related training and
- the travel will not prevent them from continuing to meet these work obligations (eg during a semester or term break)
## Examples (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
Partner receiving Jobseeker Support with work preparation obligations who has been required to undertake an approved training course. During their term break from the course they are going to Australia to visit family.
The client is already meeting their work preparation obligations and therefore can be absent from New Zealand and continue to be paid their benefit for up to 28 days in any 52 week period.
Partner is receiving Jobseeker Support who is in part-time study who wishes to go on holiday during the term break to visit family in Australia.
The partner is already meeting their work preparation obligations and therefore can be absent from New Zealand and continue to be paid their benefit for up to 28 days in any 52 week period.

chunks.title: Partner obtains employment overseas — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partner obtains employment overseas
Where the partner:
- is successful in their job prospect or job search overseas and
- they are not returning to New Zealand
their portion of the Jobseeker Support should be cancelled from the day after the notice of job appointment.
If the partner returns to New Zealand for the period between getting the job and actually starting employment, the Jobseeker Support can be continued until they leave the country. Their portion of the Jobseeker Support must be cancelled from the day after they leave New Zealand to commence the job.

chunks.title: Partner with an exemption from their work obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partner with an exemption from their work obligations
Generally, a partner cannot continue to receive their payment when they temporarily leave New Zealand if they have work obligations, unless they meet the criteria for approved travel. A client may have a full or partial exemption from their work obligations.
## Partner with a full exemption from work obligations
A partner who has a full exemption from their work obligations can continue to be paid a benefit while they are absent from New Zealand for up to 28 days in a 52 week period.
## Partner with a partial exemption from work obligations
A partner with a partial exemption from their work obligations cannot continue to receive their payment when they temporarily leave New Zealand (unless they meet the criteria for approved travel). Where they meet the criteria for approved travel they can continue to receive their payment for up to 28 days in any 52 week period if:
- the benefit would continue to be paid except for them having left New Zealand
- the absences do not affect the client's eligibility for the benefit
- they have notified Work and Income of their intention to temporarily leave New Zealand
For more information see:
- Partner with work or work preparation obligations or an exemption
- Approved travel reasons
- Exemptions

chunks.title: Partner with work obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partner with work obligations
A partner cannot continue to receive their payment when they temporarily leave New Zealand if they have work obligations unless they meet the criteria for approved travel.
Where they meet the criteria for approved travel they can continue to receive their payment for up to 28 days in any 52 week period if:
- the benefit would continue to be paid except for them having left New Zealand
- they have notified Work and Income of their intention to temporarily leave New Zealand
For more information see:
- Partner with work or work preparation obligations or an exemption
- Partner meeting their work obligation requirements
- Partner with an exemption from their work obligations
- Approved travel reasons

chunks.title: Partner with work or work preparation obligations or an exemption — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partner with work or work preparation obligations or an exemption
Whether a partner of a Jobseeker Support client can be absent from New Zealand and continue to receive payment of their benefit depends on their work or work preparation obligations.
For more information see:
- Partner with work preparation obligations
- Partner with work obligations
- Partner with an exemption from their work obligations

chunks.title: Partner with work preparation obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partner with work preparation obligations
A partner with work preparation obligations may be able to continue to receive their benefit if absent from New Zealand. A decision about whether the benefit can be paid for up to 28 days in any 52 week period will depend on whether activities have been assigned.
## Partner has work preparation activities assigned
A partner of someone receiving Jobseeker Support cannot continue to receive their payment when they temporarily leave New Zealand if they have work preparation obligations and have activities assigned (unless they meet the criteria for approved travel). Where they meet the criteria for approved travel they can continue to receive their payment for a period of up to 28 days in any 52 week period if:
- the benefit would continue to be paid except for them having left New Zealand
- they have notified Work and Income of their intention to temporarily leave New Zealand
## Partner has no work preparation activities assigned
A partner of someone receiving Jobseeker Support who has work preparation obligations but has not had work preparation activities assigned can continue to receive their payment for up to 28 days in any 52 week period when they are absent from New Zealand if:
- the benefit would continue to be paid except for them having left New Zealand
- the absences do not affect the client's eligibility for the benefit
- they have notified Work and Income of their intention to temporarily leave New Zealand
For more information see:
- Approved travel reasons
- Partner with work obligations
- Partner with an exemption from their work obligations

chunks.title: Examples (but are not limited to) — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Examples (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A young partner is meeting their education obligation by attending secondary school and they wish to travel to Australia during the school holidays. The client is not required by their Service Provider to undertake a budgeting course or attend any meetings with them during the period they wish to travel.
The travel will not prevent the young partner from meeting any of their youth activity obligations so it will be approved.
Therefore, the young partner can be absent from New Zealand for this reason and continue to receive their payment for up to 28 days in any 52 week period.
A young partner is meeting their education obligation by participating in a full time training course and decides to take time off from the course in the middle of the term so that they can holiday in Australia.
The travel will not be approved as it will prevent the young partner from meeting their obligation to be in full-time education or training.
A young partner is enrolled in a full-time training course, however, the course has not yet started, and the young person wishes to travel to the United States for a holiday before the course commencement date.
The young partner does not have to be in New Zealand to meet any other obligations during the travel period (eg they do not have to attend a budgeting course during the time of the travel)
The travel will not prevent the client from meeting any of their youth activity obligations so it will be approved. The young person can continue to receive their payment for up to 28 days in any 52 week period while they are absent from New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Young partner not yet subject to obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning
- Young partner who is exempt from their Youth Activity Obligations
- Absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Activity failures for young partners

chunks.title: Resuming benefit when client failed to advise of absence — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Resuming benefit when client failed to advise of absence
If a client contacts Work and Income after they have left New Zealand, and is not eligible to have their payment backdated, their benefit can only be resumed from:
- the date they notified us of their absence and
- only if the travel is allowed (ie they meet the criteria to continue to be paid their benefit while overseas either because they meet the criteria for approved travel, or the requirement that travel be approved does not apply to them)
Otherwise the client cannot have their benefit resumed until they return to New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Backdating benefit to the day after departure
- Action on return to New Zealand
- Approved travel reasons
- Payment when client or partner absent from New Zealand
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy

chunks.title: Paying a higher rate — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Paying a higher rate
You can make payment at a rate higher than the hospital rate where the client cannot meet their continuing costs from the hospital rate of payment and any other income they receive.
You will need to take into consideration:
- the client's financial commitments and
- access to other income
Note when you are considering payment of benefit at a rate higher than the hospital rate, generally you do not take cash assets into account as rates of benefit payment are not subject to an assets test.
If a client is required to make Child Support payments and does not qualify for an exemption from Inland Revenue Child Support, you can increase the hospital rate to include any Child Support payments that are required to be apportioned from the benefit.
For more information about paying at a higher rate see:
- Guidelines for paying a higher rate
## Maximum amount payable
You can pay a rate higher than the hospital rate up to the maximum rate of Jobseeker Support that would otherwise be payable.

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period when the client is absent from New Zealand. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
To pay a benefit more than 28 days during any 52 week period:
- the client must be continuing to receive their benefit while absent from New Zealand because: they have an approved travel reason orthey are not required to have an approved travel reason in order to be paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand
- they have an approved travel reason or
- they are not required to have an approved travel reason in order to be paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand
- the client could not return to New Zealand because of new circumstances that: they could not reasonably foresee at the time when they left New Zealand andthat are outside of the client's control
- they could not reasonably foresee at the time when they left New Zealand and
- that are outside of the client's control
and
- Work and Income is satisfied that the extension of the absence is no longer than is necessary to address the new circumstances
## Benefit can be backdated once back in New Zealand in very limited circumstances
A client who is continuing to be paid while they are absent from New Zealand for an approved reason may be able to have their benefit backdated if there is an unforeseen reason they cannot notify Work and Income while they are overseas.
For example, a client boards a plane to return home on schedule and the plane is held up due to fog. There is no way the client could notify Work and Income due to an event outside of their control. When the client contacts Work and Income once they are back in New Zealand, their benefit would be resumed from the original date they were due to return (this will be on the boarding pass and/or in the custom tab in WASP).
For more information see:
- Overseas for medical treatment
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days for an approved reason — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period when the client is absent from New Zealand. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. To pay a benefit more than 28 days during any 52 week period of absence from New Zealand, the client must be travelling for one of the following reasons: - essential travel - to attend a significant event relating to a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family), that the client would reasonably be expected to attend (eg visit a person who is seriously ill, seriously injured or whose death is imminent, attend a funeral, provide support to a party or witness to a court case, travel required for a court ordered custody arrangement) - to attend a court case which the person is required to attend as a party or a witness - to attend a job interview or follow up on a job prospect - for clients with a disability, to receive vocational training or disability assistance-dog training not available in New Zealand during the period or periods of absence - for clients with a disability, to travel overseas for the sole or predominant purpose of competing in any overseas multinational or international Special Olympic or Paralympic Games competition - to provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster (flood, earthquake, fire) or similar adverse event (eg house fire) and - Work and Income must be satisfied, when considering the client's reason for travel, that the length of the absence is no longer than necessary for the reason for travel In addition, where the client has already been paid a benefit while absent from New Zealand in the 52 week period Work and Income must be satisfied that either: - the client could not have reasonably foreseen them needing to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in a 52 week period or - the client could not have rearranged their affairs to avoid being absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in a 52 week period and - it would be unreasonable for the benefit not to be paid Note generally we would not pay more than 28 days extra travel per absence. For more information see: - Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason - Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event (within 28 day maximum) - Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days - receive support from family overseas (young partner) — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period where the client is absent from New Zealand. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period where the young partner is travelling to receive support from a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family) who is residing overseas. For more information see: - Definition of 'support' from a family member residing overseas This applies (and is limited to a further 28 days in any 52 week period) when: - the young partner has already been paid a benefit while absent from New Zealand for one or more approved reasons for all or most of 28 days in a 52 week period and - the young partner will be absent from New Zealand for the purpose of obtaining support from a family member residing overseas and - the support that the young partner needs cannot reasonably be provided to the client by one of their family members in New Zealand and - the absence does not prevent the young partner from meeting their youth activity obligations because the absence is at a time when: they are not required to attend education, training or work-based learning (for example, they are exempt from meeting their obligations)they are not yet required to be undertaking education, training or work-based learning because of the age of their youngest child orthey are undertaking education or training but it is semester or term break or they are between academic years) or the course has not yet started andthey are not required to be in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations during the time of the absence (eg they do not need to attend a parenting or budgeting course during the time they will be overseas) - they are not required to attend education, training or work-based learning (for example, they are exempt from meeting their obligations) - they are not yet required to be undertaking education, training or work-based learning because of the age of their youngest child or - they are undertaking education or training but it is semester or term break or they are between academic years) or the course has not yet started and - they are not required to be in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations during the time of the absence (eg they do not need to attend a parenting or budgeting course during the time they will be overseas)

chunks.title: Cannot be paid for more than 28 days for purposes of obtaining support — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: The maximum amount of time a young partner can continue to receive their payment while overseas on the ground that the absence does not prevent them meeting their obligations is 28 days in any 52 week period. Therefore, if a client subject to youth activity obligations has already received their payment for 28 days while they were overseas on a holiday on the grounds that the travel did not prevent them meeting their obligations, they will not be able to travel and continue to receive their payment under the 'obtaining support from a family member' circumstance. For more information see: - Examples of paying for more than 28 days for obtaining family support for young partners

chunks.title: Payment to partners — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Payment to partners
When a couple (with no dependent children) has their Jobseeker Support reduced to the hospital rate, their partner in the community from the same date can:
- have their portion of benefit or pension increased by the difference between the maximum half married, civil union or de facto rate and single rate of that benefit or pension and
- get a Special Disability Allowance
Note that couples with dependent children do not have their rate reduced to the hospital rate.
## Charging income
You need to charge any income the couple receives against the married, civil union or de facto rate before you can determine the amount to pay.
The partner in the community will get the half married, civil union or de facto rate (after charging income) plus the difference between the maximum married, civil union or de facto rate and the single rate.
The client in hospital will get the lesser of the:
- half married, civil union or de facto rate (after charging income) or
- hospital rate of payment

chunks.title: Payment when client or partner absent from New Zealand — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Payment when client or partner absent from New Zealand
There are some situations where the benefit payments will be affected when the client is absent from New Zealand. The action required by Work and Income will depend on the reason the client is absent from New Zealand and whether they are continuing to be paid a benefit.
For more information see:
- Client or partner remains in New Zealand
- Ending payment for partner who can travel for any reason
- Ending payment for client who needs an approved reason for travel
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within a 28 day maximum)
- Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event (within 28 day maximum)
- Child absent

chunks.title: Period over which to charge income — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: Income must be charged against the benefit for the week that it is earned or the period it represents, for example: - a client gets interest payments from their term deposit once every 6 months. This represents the interest earned over the previous 6 months: MSD will charge this payment against their benefit over the previous 6 months that the payment representsif it is an ongoing investment, the payment amount will be added as an ongoing estimated income for the next 6 months - MSD will charge this payment against their benefit over the previous 6 months that the payment represents - if it is an ongoing investment, the payment amount will be added as an ongoing estimated income for the next 6 months - a client works 13 hours every week and gets paid fortnightly. MSD will charge their fortnightly income for each week the wages represent - a client works 2 days a week and gets paid their wages weekly. MSD will charge their income for the week that it is earned - a sole trader who mows lawns invoices their customers monthly. MSD will charge their net profit before tax as income for the actual period it represents If income does not represent a specific period or if MSD cannot determine the actual period it represents, MSD must determine the most appropriate period to charge the income. This may be the week it is received, provided or supplied. In most cases, determining the period will be straightforward. If you are unable to determine the period that the income represents you should discuss the payment with Helpline.

chunks.title: Sole parent and grandparented clients before 30 June 2026 — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: Any income a client receives must be charged against the benefit for the period in which the income was earned or represents. However, sole parent and grandparented Jobseeker Support clients whose benefit commenced (or last commenced) before 1 July 2025 can have their income charged annually until their next 52 week expiry date. This is a transitional arrangement. For clients with annual income charging, MSD will estimate the prospective income that the client is likely to receive over the next 52 weeks and update income from the first available date. If the client declares a change in income, their prospective income should be reviewed. If the client indicates their income is likely to vary week to week and prospective income cannot be estimated, then their income should be charged for the actual period it was earned or represents. For more information see: - Annual income for sole parent and grandparented clients before 30 June 2026 For more information on some specific types of income and how to charge them, see: - Types of income - Income from assets

chunks.title: Overlapping income — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client has income from multiple sources that are paid for the same periods of time, then all of the payments are added together. The total income will be charged against the Jobseeker Support over the period that the income represents. For more information see: - Examples of overlapping income - Income change - Effect of income on Extra help - Net profit

chunks.title: Moving to Australia — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Moving to Australia
If the client is moving to Australia it is important that they are aware that they may not be able to receive a benefit until they have resided in Australia for two years after being granted permanent residence status.
For more information see:
- United Kingdom Reciprocal Agreement Jobseekers Allowance
- Reciprocal Australia Clients going to Australia
- Payments from Overseas

chunks.title: Permitted travel reasons — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Permitted travel reasons
A client or partner not otherwise entitled to be paid their Jobseeker Support while absent from New Zealand may have their payments continue for up to 28 days in any 52 week period, if their travel is for one (or a combination) of, the following permitted travel reasons:
- essential travel - to attend a significant event relating to a family member or a person who fulfils a role in relation to the client that is similar to that of a family member, that the client would reasonably be expected to attend
- to attend a court case which the person is required to attend as a party or a witness - this is to allow clients who are required by law to attend court and supports the maintenance of the law. A client would generally be expected to provide evidence that they are required to attend a court overseas. This would include documents from the court.
- to attend a job interview or follow up on a job prospect
- for clients with a disability, to receive vocational training or disability assistance-dog training not available in New Zealand during the time the client is absent
- for clients with a disability, to travel overseas for the sole or predominant purpose of competing in any overseas multinational or international Special Olympic or Paralympic Games competition
- to provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster (eg flood, earthquake, fire) or similar adverse event (eg house fire)
## Evidence of the client's situation
Although it may not be possible for the client to get proof of their situation, they should make a reasonable effort to do so.
For more information see:
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Definition of family member
- Essential travel
- Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect
- Absences that do not prevent partner from meeting their obligations

chunks.title: Previous tax year — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: A client or their partner may declare income for a period in a previous tax year. There are 3 possible outcomes for the client depending on the amount of income declared and whether any previous income had been charged. These outcomes are: 1. The client is due arrears following a review on their benefit. As the arrears will be issued in the current tax year no adjustment is required to the tax details or 2. The amount of the income declared is under the exemption and the client does not receive any Extra help. The client's SWIFTT record is noted accordingly or 3. A debt will be established and the tax details for this year will need to be adjusted accordingly as in the following example.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: A client's partner phones on Thursday 05/05/2022 to advise that they worked for the week Monday 14/02/2022 to Friday 18/02/2022 and earned $195.54 gross. Manually assess the income deduction: Gross income (excluding cents) $195.00 Less income allowed before benefit is affected $160.00 Equals income $35.00 Amount benefit reduced on account of income (income over $160 reduces benefit by 70 cents per $1.00) ($35 x 0.7) $24.50 To work out the benefit rate payable: Maximum Jobseeker Support couple rate (net, as at 1 July 2021) $453.62 Less reduction due to income $24.50 Benefit rate payable $429.12 ($214.56 each) Once you have calculated the benefit due for this week add the income to INCMA. A backdated review SBDR for both the client and their partner needs to be completed for this week. The following is the process: SBDR $214.56 the week income earned 14/02/2022 to 20/02/2022 LSUM a memo will be produced as a result of the backdated review with details of the debt amount to be added into the appropriate tax year. It is the net amount of debt which is added to SWIFTT SDBTI debt inquiry for the client (F4 for STAXI) STAXI select the appropriate year and DBT which will take you into the SDBTA screen SDBTA add the debt type, add the benefit/pension code, add the debt status and breach type, add the net debt amount, this will also adjust the tax record for the client. Add the period that the debt represents and add any comments where appropriate - remember to commence recovery of the debt via SOFSI

chunks.title: Priority for deductions — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Priority for deductions
Certain forms of deductions take priority over others; the following list gives the order of priority, highest to lowest:
Highest priority
- Child Support deductions made under the Child Support Act 1991
- Inland Revenue tax deductions
- Ministry of Social Development debt repayments including Liable Parent Contributions (LPC), child maintenance debts and Major Repairs Advances (MRA), Student Allowance debt, Student Loan debt converted to Ministry of Social Development debt, Income Related Rent historical Kāinga Ora, Income Related Rent Ministry of Social Development debt
- Attachment orders made under the Family Proceedings Act 1980
- Court attachment orders issued under the Summary Proceedings Act 1957
- Court attachment orders issued under the District Court Act 2016
- Student Loan repayments
Lowest priority
Determining the priority of deductions is necessary where a client has more than one order issued in respect of their benefit. Also each order and deduction notice is subject to its own protected earnings rule.
When you need to reduce deductions you adjust from the lowest priority up to those with a higher priority taking into account the protected earnings rules for each.

chunks.title: Private hospital and homes — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Private hospital and homes
Jobseeker Support can be paid at the full rate regardless of the period of hospitalisation when a client is:
- admitted to a private hospital or
- admitted to a private home that provides residential care disability services
If the client receives Extra help, this will need to be reviewed to see if their costs are continuing.
For more information see:
- Residential Care Subsidy
- Residential Support Subsidy

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Example
An attachment order is received from the Ministry of Justice for $80.00 per week. The order lists the client's protected earnings rate as $286.53 per week.
We need to calculate whether adding the deduction of $80.00 will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate.
Calculate protected earnings rate
Jobseeker Support single person 25+ net rate (as at 1 April 2026)
$372.55
Plus Accommodation Supplement (Area 2)
$105.00
Total net earnings
$477.55
60% of total net earnings (=protected earnings)
$286.53
Calculate if Attachment Order will exceed protected earnings
Total net earnings
$477.55
Less Child Support deduction
$105.00
Less Ministry of Social Development debt
$40.00
Sub total
$332.55
Less Attachment Order
$80.00
Total
$252.55
The attachment order amount of $80.00 takes the client's total net income remaining to $252.55, which is below the protected earnings rate of $286.53.
The attachment order will not operate therefore you must return it to the Ministry of Justice for the order to be amended.

chunks.title: Qualifies for another benefit — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Qualifies for another benefit
A client may qualify for another benefit due to a change in their circumstances. It is also important to determine if the client still qualifies for Jobseeker Support.
For example:
- if a client is aged under 19 years old and they apply to have a child included in their benefit, they would no longer qualify for Jobseeker Support and they would need to apply for Young Parent Payment or
- a client reaches the qualifying age for New Zealand Superannuation
If the client qualifies for more than one benefit they must be told which benefit is the most beneficial for their particular circumstances. You will need to advise them of:
- benefit rates
- the effect of any income they may receive (income reduction and any exemptions) and
- benefit obligations
The client must make the final decision on which benefit they receive after being given all relevant information.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support Qualifications
- Sole Parent Support Qualifications
- Supported Living Payment Qualifications
- Young Parent Payment Qualifications
- New Zealand Superannuation Qualifications
- Processing standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Rate of payment - sole parents — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Rate of payment - sole parents
If payment of Jobseeker Support is to continue while a sole parent client is in prison, you will need to determine the rate to pay to the temporary caregiver.
The Jobseeker Support should generally be paid at the equivalent rate of Unsupported Child's Benefit that would be payable if the caregiver qualified for this, see: Examples - sole parents
However, there is discretion to continue payment at the full sole parent rate.
You can consider including the following costs to calculate the rate to pay the temporary caregiver while the client is in prison:
- rent or outgoings if the children are being cared for in the client's home
- the client's other commitments if these costs are for essential items and they cannot be suspended, such as Child Support payments (when the client does not qualify for an exemption [no link find out why] ) or hire purchase for an essential item
The total amount paid to the temporary caregiver must not exceed the maximum amount of Jobseeker Support payable.
## SWIFTT
The Jobseeker Support, family tax credit and Best Start tax credits should continue in the client's name and be paid to the caregiver as an agent in SWIFTT.
When the temporary caregiver is to be paid less than the maximum rate of Jobseeker Support, you will need to add this as a non-standard rate using the SNSRA screen in SWIFTT.

chunks.title: Applying for Jobseeker Support after finishing employment — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Applying for Jobseeker Support after finishing employment
When a client applies for Jobseeker Support after ceasing employment, the length of time that they have been working will affect the date that their Jobseeker Support can commence.
## In employment less than 26 weeks
No stand-down applies when a client applies for benefit because they have finished employment within 26 weeks of their previous benefit stopping.
Their Jobseeker Support can commence from the entitlement date, which is the day after their employment ceased or the application date of benefit, whichever is the later.
Note some payments a client gets when they finish work affect the date their employment ceased.
For more information see:
- Employment ceased
- No stand-down applies
- Temporary employment
## In employment 26 weeks or more
If the client finishes employment 26 weeks or more after their previous benefit stopped, the usual commencement date and initial stand-down rules apply.
For more information see:
- Commencement date
- Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct

chunks.title: Gets a Student Loan — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Gets a Student Loan
Getting a Student Loan (including the living cost component) does not mean the child is financially independent.
If the child continues to be the client's primary responsibility and maintained as a member of their family and financially dependent (that is the parent is meeting some of the costs for the child) the child can continue to be included in the benefit until the start of the pay period following:
- the date they turn 18 or
- where the child is 18 and continuing in education, the earlier of: the date they are no longer enrolled in school or tertiary education orthe date they are no longer attending school or tertiary education as required orthe date the child is financially independent orthe date the child leaves the parent or caregiver's care or31 December of the year they turn 18
- the date they are no longer enrolled in school or tertiary education or
- the date they are no longer attending school or tertiary education as required or
- the date the child is financially independent or
- the date the child leaves the parent or caregiver's care or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18
Note a parent or caregiver getting a discretionary benefit such as Jobseeker Support on the ground of hardship must complete a review of circumstances when a dependent child turns 18, and when the child is excluded (if they continued to be included in the parent or caregiver's benefit after the child turned 18).

chunks.title: Recording income — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recording income
Any income a client receives, even when the income is less than $160 gross per week, must be added to the client's SWIFTT record on the INCMA screen. This is to ensure any Extra help is reviewed correctly and will create a permanent audit trail of all income details.
If the income is over the benefit cut out point and SWIFTT will not accept this information then a note on CMS should be added.
Ensure the following details are recorded:
- source of income, such as the employer's details
- gross (before tax) amount of income received
- period that the income represents and
- contact details for example phoned in by the client
For more information see:
- Income test
- Charging income

chunks.title: Release from prison — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Release from prison
A client may be entitled to Jobseeker Support when they are released from prison. The date to recommence payment depends on the length of time the client has been in prison.
## Partner
Where the partner of a person in prison has been receiving a benefit, this will need to be reviewed from the date of release.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support Prisoners

chunks.title: Release on bail — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Release on bail
When a client is released on bail, Jobseeker Support can be paid from the date of release providing the client:
- is still able to meet their work obligations
- has been in custody for less than 31 days and
- reapplies for a benefit immediately after their release
If the client has been in custody for more than 31 days an initial stand-down will be imposed.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support Prisoners
- Jobseeker Support Court imposed conditions

chunks.title: Remanded in custody — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Remanded in custody
Generally, when a client is remanded in custody awaiting a further court appearance their benefit should be stopped. However, there is discretion to continue payment of Jobseeker Support after taking the client's financial circumstances and commitments into account.
When deciding whether to continue paying Jobseeker Support for the period for a particular client, consider the following:
- has the client been remanded pending a further court hearing or for sentencing
- does the client have continuing costs that cannot be avoided, such as rent and hire purchase for essential items
- does the client have a partner and or dependent children
Every situation should be considered on a case-by-case basis.
For help contact the Helpline to discuss the circumstances before making a decision.

chunks.title: Residential Parole — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Residential Parole
If a client is released on residential parole they can apply for an exemption from their work obligations.
## Partner
Where the partner of a person in prison has been receiving a benefit, this will need to be reviewed from the date of release.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support Court imposed conditions
- Special Needs Grants Steps to Freedom

chunks.title: Review of Annual Income - sole parents and grandparented clients before 30 June 2026 — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: Sole parent and grandparented Jobseeker Support clients whose benefit commenced (or last commenced) before 1 July 2025 can have their income charged annually until they reach their next 52 week expiry date. This is a transitional arrangement. These clients move to weekly income charging and the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle when they complete the 26 week reapplication process before their final 52 week expiry date. All sole parent and grandparented Jobseeker Support clients will have had their final Review of Annual Income and moved to weekly income charging by 30 June 2026 at the latest.

chunks.title: Review of Annual Income — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: The Review of Annual Income ensures that sole parent and grandparented Jobseeker Support clients, that can have their income charged annually, have received the correct rate of payment for the past 52 weeks. Clients do not have a Review of Annual Income if they have not received any income, or if their benefit has not been abated at any point during the period that income is assessed (the 52 week review period).

chunks.title: Income received during the review period — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: Income received during the 52-week period following the client's commencement date (or last commencement) date, is assessed against the benefit that was paid to the client during that period. Only income that was charged during the current 52 week review period is considered for the Review of Annual Income.

chunks.title: Child Support income for Reviews of Annual Income — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: Non-information share Child Support Non-information share Child Support payments are charged as income using the general charging rules used for most other types of income. Any non-information share Child Support payments charged as income during the current 52 week review period are included in the Review of Annual Income. Information share Child Support Information share Child Support payments are charged forward as income, using defined rules. The income charge is always 4 or 5 weeks from when the client gets the payment regardless of what period the payment related to. Any information share Child Support payments charged as income during the current 52 week review period are included in the Review of Annual Income. Note the amount of information share Child Support payment charged as income may not be the same amount of Child Support a client got in the review period. This could happen if a client gets an information share Child Support payment shortly before the end of the review period. Only the income charged during the review period can be included in the Review of Annual Income. Example Titania is a sole parent getting Jobseeker Support. Her benefit commenced on 6 September 2024, and her expiry date is 6 September 2025. Titania's annual income review period is 6 September 2024 to 5 September 2025. On 21 August 2025 Titania gets an information share Child Support payment. The payment is charged forward for 4 weeks from 18 August 2025 to 14 September 2025. This crosses the end of her annual income review period. Titania has her final Review of Annual Income. The assessment includes the portion of the information share Child Support payment that was charged as income from 18 August 2025 to 5 September 2025. Titania also completes the 26 week reapplication process before her final 52 week expiry date and is regranted Jobseeker Support from 6 September 2025. She moves to weekly income charging and the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle from this date. The rest of the information share Child Support payment that Titania received on 21 August 2025 is charged as weekly income from 6 September 2025 to 14 September 2025.

chunks.title: Verification of Annual Income — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: Depending on the client's circumstances, they will either need to: - provide income verification for the 52 week review period - check if their information is correct. If it is correct, they do not need to do anything. If the client cannot provide verification (for example payslips) MSD can contact the employer and ask them to complete the Employment and earnings information for reviews (V26) form.

chunks.title: Season ends — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Season ends
When the client ceases work at the end of the season they need to re-enrol as a job seeker with Work and Income and reapply for Jobseeker Support.
For more information see:
- Commencement date
- Applying for Jobseeker Support after finishing employment

chunks.title: Seasonal work — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Seasonal work
If a client getting Jobseeker Support commences full-time seasonal work, they will no longer qualify for Jobseeker Support.
If the client has a partner who can meet the qualifications for Jobseeker Support in their own right, the partner can apply for Jobseeker Support as the primary client.
Note there is an exception for some clients, see:
- Temporary employment period for sole parent and grandparented clients before 30 June 2026
- Annual income for sole parent and grandparented clients before 30 June 2026
## Partner
If the person who has commenced seasonal work (either part-time or full-time) is the partner, then the Jobseeker Support can continue with their earnings being charged as income against the benefit.
This is regardless of whether the partner has work obligations.
Note if the partner has full-time work obligations and is working 30 hours per week, or has part-time work obligations and is working 20 hours or more, then they will be meeting their work obligations.
For more information see:
- Assistance during seasonal work
- Charging income
- Employment related income
- Guidelines for suspension or cancellation
- Season ends

chunks.title: Full-time self-employment — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Full-time self-employment
If a client commences full-time self-employment (even if there is no or minimum income being earned) they will no longer qualify for Jobseeker Support.
If the client has a partner who meets the qualifications for Jobseeker Support in their own right, the partner can apply for Jobseeker Support as the primary client.
There is an exception for some clients, see:
- Temporary employment period for sole parent and grandparented clients before 30 June 2026
- Annual income for sole parent and grandparented clients before 30 June 2026
Note Jobseeker Support may be paid to clients investigating self-employment options if they continue to meet the job search requirements and understand that any offer of full time employment takes precedence over any part time activity or employment.
For more information see:
- Clients investigating self-employment options
## Part-time self-employment
If the client starts part-time self-employment, they may still be able to get Jobseeker Support, as long as they continue to meet their job search requirements. Any offer of suitable employment takes precedence over any part-time activity or self-employment that does not meet their work obligations.
For more information see:
- Suitable employment
## Partner
If the person who has commenced self-employment (either part-time or full-time) is the partner, then the Jobseeker Support can continue with their earnings being charged as income against the benefit.
This is regardless of whether the partner has work obligations.
Note if the partner has full-time work obligations and is working 30 hours per week, or has part-time work obligations and is working 20 hours or more, they must be receiving an income from this employment to be meeting their work obligations. If they are not receiving any income from the self-employment, they must still be available for and actively seeking suitable employment.
For more information see:
- Charging income
- Employment related income
- Commission work

chunks.title: Best Start tax credit — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Best Start tax credit
For information on the payment of best start tax credit in shared care situations see:
- Best Start tax credit Shared care
## Winter Energy Payment
For information on the payment of Winter Energy Payment in shared care see:
- Single client shares care of dependent child

chunks.title: Single clients — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Single clients
Generally the Jobseeker Support should be suspended when a single client is imprisoned. This will enable payment to be resumed if the client is only in prison for a short period and reapplies for a benefit following their release.
The Jobseeker Support should be suspended from the day after imprisonment.
Note SWIFTT will automatically cancel the record if it remains suspended for eight weeks.
## Exception
Remanded in custody
Although the Jobseeker Support should generally be stopped for any period during which the client is remanded in custody pending a further court appearance, there is discretion to continue payment of all or part of the benefit.
For more information see:
- Remanded in custody

chunks.title: Sole parents - Hospitalisation — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Sole parents - Hospitalisation
When a sole parent client is admitted to hospital, their benefit can continue at the full rate for the first 13 weeks.
You will need to find out who is caring for the client's child and the length of time the client is likely to be in hospital. If requested, you can pay part of the benefit to the child's caregiver to cover the cost of alternative care or accommodation.
When the child is not going to remain in the care of the client, check what the continuing care arrangements are for the child. If the child is no longer a dependent child you will need to exclude the child and review the client's Jobseeker Support.
## Client in hospital for more than 13 weeks
If the client has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks, their rate of payment will need to be reduced to the hospital rate. You can pay a rate other than the hospital rate where:
- the client's financial circumstances warrant paying a higher rate
If there are no other continuing financial costs and it is likely that the client will remain in hospital long term, consider other means of income support for the children.
For example, the new caregiver may meet the qualifications for Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, or the child may be able to be included as a dependent child if the new caregiver is getting a main benefit.
## Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit
As long as the child continues to be a dependent child, family tax credit and Best Start tax credit payments continue while the client is in hospital.
Note Best Start tax credit cannot be paid past the child's third birthday.

chunks.title: Sole parents imprisoned — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Sole parents imprisoned
Generally, when a sole parent client is imprisoned or detained in custody, they are no longer entitled to Jobseeker Support.
Jobseeker Support should be suspended from the day after imprisonment.
MSD should find out who is caring for the client's dependent children and the length of time the client is likely to be in prison. The length of the time in prison can be found by contacting the prison liaison officer at the Department of Corrections.
Generally, the caregiver will need to apply for financial assistance in their own right.
They may be entitled to:
- have the children included as dependent children in their current benefit
- Unsupported Childs Benefit
- Emergency Benefit Caring responsibilities or
- family tax credit and Best Start tax credit through Inland Revenue
## Exception
There is discretion to pay all or part of the client’s Jobseeker Support to a temporary caregiver caring for the client's dependent children.
There is also discretion to continue payment if the client is remanded in custody pending a further court appearance.

chunks.title: Special Disability Allowance — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Special Disability Allowance
A Special Disability Allowance is paid to the partner of a client who is receiving the hospital rate or Residential Care Subsidy. It is paid to the client in the community to help with the extra costs of their partner's hospitalisation, for example travel costs to visit the patient.
Note that Special Disability Allowance is:
- granted without the client having to apply
- paid separately from Disability Allowance and
- not income or asset tested
Special Disability Allowance can start from the date the client in the community starts receiving a single rate of benefit, and their partner starts receiving a hospital rate of benefit or becomes financially eligible for Residential Care Subsidy.
For more information see:
- Deskfile Special Disability Allowance rates
Special Disability Allowance should be stopped from the first available date if the person receiving it is also admitted to hospital.
## SWIFTT
Grant Special Disability Allowance using code 838 on the SSUPI screen.

chunks.title: Split care — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Split care
Split care is when parents with 2 or more children are living apart and each parent has the care of at least one of their children on a full-time basis.
The child(ren) that is living with the Jobseeker Support client can be included as a dependent child.
Note that in split care situations, generally only one parent can receive Sole Parent Support. The other parent must qualify, in their own right, for another benefit. For more information see: Sole Parent Support Split care

chunks.title: Student Loans repayments — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Student Loans repayments
Clients with a Student Loan must make repayments to Inland Revenue when the income they get is over a pre-determined level. This level is called the 'income threshold'.
A person must make repayments to Inland Revenue when their income is over $464.00 gross per week ($24,128 gross per year) as at 1 April 2026. Note non-taxable Extra help such as family tax credit, Accommodation Supplement and Winter Energy Payment do not count as income for this assessment.
If the client's income is over this income threshold, the Ministry of Social Development can make the required deduction. However, this is only done if the client requests it.
If the client's portion of benefit is below the income threshold, there is no provision to make voluntary repayments through SWIFTT.
The client can make voluntary payments direct to Inland Revenue at any time.
Note the following:
- Student Loan deductions can only be made from taxable benefits
- Student Loan deductions cannot be made if the client's benefit is below the income threshold
- when a client receives a married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit only the client's portion is taken into consideration when assessing Student Loan repayments
- when a client is receiving a reduced rate of payment due to other income, the Student Loan deduction is assessed on the net payment after income deduction
## For more information on Student Loans see:
- Students Student loans
- Deskfile Student Loan Repayment Thresholds

chunks.title: Study — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Study
Clients (and partners) have an obligation to advise Work and Income of any change in their circumstances that may affect their qualification for Jobseeker Support, such as commencing study.
When Jobseeker Support client intends to or has commenced study, you will need to find out:
- the date study starts and
- the type of study, that is part-time or full-time
This will help you decide the appropriate review action required.

chunks.title: SWIFTT process to pay a partner — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## SWIFTT process to pay a partner
When you decide to continue payment of Jobseeker Support to the partner of a client who has been imprisoned, you will need to determine the most appropriate SWIFTT process to enable payment to be made to the partner.
The process for payment will depend on whether the:
- period in prison is in the past
- client is due to be released from prison shortly
- client is likely to be in prison for more than four weeks and
- rate of payment for the partner
Note that there is discretion to pay the full married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit.
## Period in prison has passed or release is imminent
Generally you should use the SBDR screen in SWIFTT to:
- suspend the client's portion of the Jobseeker Support for the period in prison
and
- pay the appropriate rate of Jobseeker Support to the partner
## Period in prison more than 4 weeks
When the Jobseeker Support is to continue, and be paid to the partner you will need to contact Helpline for advice regarding the SWIFTT process to use.
## For more information contact Helpline or see:
- Decision guidelines - clients with a partner

chunks.title: Tax codes — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Tax codes
Jobseeker Support is taxed at the 'M' rate.
Jobseeker Support is always considered the client's primary source of income regardless of the amount paid.
If the client has other income this is always considered the client's secondary income.
Clients can apply to Inland Revenue for a tailored tax code for their other income.

chunks.title: Taxation — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Taxation
Jobseeker Support is a taxable benefit. MSD makes payments to clients at the net rate after the deduction of tax. MSD passes the tax on to Inland Revenue.
Generally, MSD will request clients to give MSD their IRD number or evidence of their IRD number.

chunks.title: Temporary care — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Temporary care
Generally a client will not be considered as the person primarily responsible for the child when the period of care is temporary. Examples of temporary care are:
- school holidays
- Christmas or other public holidays
- during the temporary incapacity of the primary caregiver or
- principal caregiver is in prison, see: Imprisonment

chunks.title: Temporary employment period for sole parent and grandparented clients before 30 June 2026 — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: When a client has commenced full-time employment they will no longer qualify for Jobseeker Support. However, sole parent and grandparented clients whose income is charged annually can work full-time for a temporary period if: - their Jobseeker Support commenced (or last commenced) before 1 July 2025, and - they have not yet completed the 26 week reapplication process before their final 52 week expiry date and moved to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle and - they have not moved to weekly income charging due to a change in circumstances that means they are no longer a sole parent or grandparented client, and - their income, when assessed over 52 weeks, does not fully reduce their benefit. This is a transitional arrangement. For more information see: - Annual income for sole parent and grandparented clients before 30 June 2026

chunks.title: Temporary period is 26 weeks — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: Sole parent and grandparented Jobseeker Support clients who can work for a temporary period, can work full-time for a period of up to 26 weeks. The temporary employment period gives the client a reasonable amount of time to increase their earnings and become independent. The temporary employment period must not exceed 26 weeks.

chunks.title: Supporting the client during the temporary employment period — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: During the temporary employment period MSD should continue to support the client by: - working with them to increase their earnings from the temporary full-time employment - referring them to other offers of suitable employment - referring them to training courses.

chunks.title: Obligations during the temporary period — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: The client will continue to have work obligations during the temporary employment period. The obligation to accept offers of suitable employment still applies. If the client refuses an offer of suitable employment without a good and sufficient reason, they may be subject to an obligations failure. For more information see: - Obligations failures - Suitable employment

chunks.title: Temporary employment period no longer available from 52 week expiry date — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client is still working full-time during a temporary employment period when they reach their final 52 week expiry and reapplication date, their Jobseeker Support cannot be regranted. This is because the temporary employment period is only available to sole parent and grandparented Jobseeker Support clients who have annual income charging, which ends when they reach their final 52 week expiry date. For more information see: - Completing the 26 week reapplication process

chunks.title: At the end of the temporary employment period — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: If the client continues to work full-time at the end of the temporary employment period, their benefit will be cancelled as they will no longer qualify for Jobseeker Support. Example Erin is a grandparented Jobseeker Support client. She advises MSD that she is commencing employment as a ranger with a local nature reserve, and will be working, on average, more than 30 hours per week and will be earning minimum wage. Erin will not be earning enough income to fully reduce her benefit. Erin can continue to get Jobseeker Support and work full-time for up to 26 weeks from the day she commenced full-time employment. At the end of the 26 weeks, Erin continues to work full-time at the nature reserve. Her Jobseeker Support is cancelled as she no longer qualifies for Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: Change in circumstances during the temporary employment period — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text: If the client has a change in circumstances that means they no longer qualify to have their Jobseeker Support continued during the temporary period of full-time employment, their benefit must be stopped. Example Abria is a sole parent client getting Jobseeker Support who is currently working full-time for 15 weeks and having her income charged annually over 52 weeks. In the 13th week of her temporary employment period, Abria's youngest dependent child, Jay, leaves her care. As Abria is no longer getting Jobseeker Support as a sole parent her Jobseeker Support is suspended. Abria's contacts MSD after week 15 when her full-time work ends and her Jobseeker Support is resumed, payable at the appropriate single rate.

chunks.title: Terminal benefit for a single client — main benefits > jobseeker support > changes and reviews jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Terminal benefit for a single client
Generally the Jobseeker Support stops from the date after the date of death for a single client with no children, however, there is some discretion to continue the payment of benefit for up to 28 days. When payment is continued after the date of death, it is referred to as terminal benefit.
Circumstances where you might consider continued payment beyond a single client's date of death include:
- when the deceased client's domestic situation results in a transition cost for a family member, causing hardship
Example: accommodation and other household costs when client has been sharing accommodation
or
- when there are exceptional and justified costs associated with the death of the client
Example: multiple deaths within one family
