The young partner who is youth money managed, has their in-hand allowance of up to $50 and any incentive payments suspended. Their portion of Extra help is not affected. The young partner can continue to get the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment as they are still getting a qualifying benefit.
After 4 weeks
If the young partner has not recomplied within 4 weeks, they will have their portion of the benefit and their portion of Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support and the Winter Energy Payment suspended. Their incentive payments and in-hand allowance will remain suspended.
Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or the payment is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.

chunks.title: Grade 2 sanction — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Grade 2 sanction
The young partner who has met their obligations will continue to have their portion of their assistance (including their incentive payments) paid as usual through the youth money management. The young partner can continue to get their portion of any Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support to which they are entitled. The young partner can get the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment.
If the primary client fails their obligations for the second time, that person's portion of benefit is suspended (along with their portion of any Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support to which they are entitled). Disability Allowance can continue to be paid during a non-entitlement period.
Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or the payment is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.
## Grade 3 sanction
The young partner who has met their obligations is due their portion of their assistance (including their incentive payments) paid as usual. The young partner can also continue to get their portion of any Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support to which they are entitled. The young partner can get the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment.
If the primary client fails their obligations for a third time:
- their portion of the benefit is cancelled immediately
- their portion of Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support and their Winter Energy Payment is cancelled and
- the client subject to a non-entitlement period for 13 weeks from the date of cancellation
The client may get a provisional benefit if they start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities.
If the client does not start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities, they may reapply at the end of their non-entitlement period to get a benefit.
Note Disability Allowance can continue to be paid during a non-entitlement period.

chunks.title: Court imposed conditions — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Court imposed conditions
This exemption may apply to primary clients, partners and sole parents with work or work preparation obligations.
A client serving a sentence of home detention, or who has conditions and requirements of a court sentence or court order that limits their ability to meet all their obligations can be exempt from meeting some or all of their work or work preparation obligations.
This can be a full or partial exemption depending on the conditions imposed by the Courts.
This includes clients who:
- are former prisoners who are subject to probation or parole conditions which means that they cannot meet all their work obligations and
- have work obligations and are required as part of a sentence of the court or other court order to attend programmes or other activities, or have conditions imposed upon them (e.g. bail conditions) which limit their ability to meet all their work obligations
Home detainees or former prisoners are case managed by their probation officer. Part of this case management includes undertaking appropriate job search and activities to improve their prospects of obtaining paid employment.
In all cases, the case manager should contact the probation officer to facilitate any meetings.
Note this can be a full or partial exemption depending on the conditions imposed by the Courts.
## Proof
The client must provide proof from the Ministry of Justice, the Department of Corrections or the Department of Courts stating that they:
- are serving a sentence of Home Detention or
- are subject to probation or parole conditions which limit their ability to meet all their work obligations or
- are required to attend programmes or other activities which limit their ability to meet all their work obligations or
- have conditions imposed (e.g. bail conditions) which limit their ability to meet all their work obligations and
- the length of time the client should be exempt
## Duration
The duration of the exemption can be for up to 12 months or for a period determined by the court order or conditions placed on the person by the Courts, whichever is earliest.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Court Imposed Conditions'.
Note you cannot add an expiry date in SWIFTT, but you must note the duration in CMS.
For more information see:
- Emergency Benefit
- Full or partial exemptions

chunks.title: SWIFTT process — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Court Imposed Conditions'.
Note you cannot add an expiry date in SWIFTT but you must note the duration in CMS.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions (young partners)
For an overview of the exemptions see:
- Table of exemptions for young partners

chunks.title: Criteria for Community Work Experience — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Criteria for Community Work Experience
Clients must meet certain criteria to have Community Work Experience imposed.
A client can only be placed in Community Work Experience if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they have current work obligations, and
- they meet with MSD within the 5-working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure is not disputed and overturned, and
- Community Work Experience is the most appropriate sanction to impose based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or have dependent children.
## Client failed a drug test obligation
Community Work Experience cannot be imposed if a client fails a drug test obligation.
Clients who have failed a drug test obligation may be considered for Money Management if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.
## Client does not have work obligations
Community Work Experience cannot be imposed on a client who only has work-preparation or social obligations.
These clients may be considered for Money Management as an alternative to a financial sanction if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.
## Client fails more than one obligation at the same time
A client may fail more than one obligation on the same day and have multiple failures they need to recomply with.
Community Work Experience cannot be imposed if a client has failed multiple obligations at the same time.
Clients may be considered for Money Management if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.

chunks.title: Criteria for Money Management — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Criteria for Money Management
Clients must meet certain criteria in order for Money Management to be imposed.
A client or their partner can have Money Management imposed if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they meet with MSD within the 5 working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure decision is not disputed or and overturned, and
- Money Management would be the most appropriate sanction to impose based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or they have dependent children
## Client failed a drug test or a social obligation
Money Management may be imposed on clients who have failed a drug test or a social obligation if they meet the above criteria.
Depending on the activity a client fails, they may be able to recomply within 5 working days of the failure instead of imposing Money Management.

chunks.title: Criteria for Report Job Search — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Criteria for Report Job Search
Clients must meet certain criteria to have Report Job Search imposed.
A client can only have Report Job Search imposed if:
- they are in active case management or have dependent children and
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure) and
- they have current work obligations and
- they meet with MSD within the 5-working day notice period and
- the obligation failure is not disputed or overturned and
- Report Job Search is the most appropriate sanction to impose based on their circumstances
## Client failed a drug test obligation
Report Job Search cannot be imposed if a client fails a drug test obligation.
Clients who have failed a drug test obligation may be considered for Money Management if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.
## Client does not have work obligations
Report Job Search cannot be imposed on a client who only has work-preparation or social obligations.
These clients may be considered for Upskilling or Money Management as an alternative to a financial sanction if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.
## Client fails more than one obligation at the same time
A client may fail more than one obligation on the same day and have multiple failures they need to recomply with.
Report Job Search cannot be imposed if a client has failed multiple obligations at the same time.
Clients may be considered for Money Management if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.

chunks.title: Client failed a drug test obligation — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Client failed a drug test obligation
Upskilling cannot be imposed if a client fails a drug test obligation.
Clients who have failed a drug test obligation may be considered for Money Management if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.

chunks.title: Current medical certificates and assessments — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Current medical certificates and assessments
Clients are required to provide a current medical certificate that shows their medical coverage.
Medical certificates need to be current to help MSD determine or review the client's benefit entitlement or capacity to work.
When a client is applying for Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) and the entitlement date is before their application date, MSD may need to ask the client to provide more than 1 medical certificate. This is to ensure the client has sufficient medical coverage.
MSD will advise clients to see their registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) for another medical certificate so they can keep getting Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) if they are still unable to work full-time when their current medical coverage ends.
A client's benefit may stop if a current medical certificate is not provided before their expiry date. However, if a client has a good and sufficient reason for the delay in providing a current medical certificate, MSD may consider applying a discretionary extension to the medical certificate expiry.
## Medical assessment date is different to the medical certificate
The process of getting a medical certificate usually includes a medical assessment by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant).
The medical certificate must be completed when the client attends the assessment with the practitioner. Sometimes a client may request a medical certificate without being assessed.
Generally, MSD will need to get more current information in the following situations:
- at application: when the time between the assessment date and the date the certificate was completed is more than 20 working days or the certificate is more than 20 working days old
- during a medical reassessment: when there is an extended time (e.g. more than 1 week) between the assessment date and the date the medical certificate was completed
MSD should consider:
- the reason for the difference between the assessment date and the date the certificate was completed (e.g. the practitioner was not available to provide a more current assessment) and
- if MSD has information to indicate the impact of the client's impairment or disability is unlikely to have changed
If there is no acceptable reason for the difference between the dates and MSD decides the medical certificate is not current, MSD should ask the client to provide a further medical certificate with a current assessment.

chunks.title: Date job search commenced — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Date job search commenced
In order to accept the date ceased work as the date of event when granting a benefit, you must be satisfied that the applicant has taken reasonable steps to find suitable employment during the period that they ceased work and made representations to apply for benefit.
## Application within 26 weeks of ceasing work
When assessing the entitlement date, if a client applies for Jobseeker Support within 26 weeks of the date they ceased work you can be satisfied that the client has taken reasonable steps to obtain work from the date they ceased employment.
## Application 26 weeks or more after ceasing work
Where the client makes application more than 26 weeks or it is evident at the interview that the client has not taken reasonable steps to obtain work from the date they ceased employment; verification of when they became available for work will need to be provided.
The verification required will vary from case to case and may depend on the length of time that has passed from when the applicant ceased work and when they made representation to Work and Income. Whether any doubt exists as to the extent that an applicant has been searching for employment may also be a factor in what verification is requested.
Possible verification to be requested could include but is not limited to:
- letters of decline from employers
- clippings from newspapers
- diary showing job search
Note if you are still unable to determine the date job search commenced or what verification to request contact Helpline to discuss.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Meeting job search requirements

chunks.title: Date when work obligations apply from (health condition, injury or disability) — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Once you have made a decision about whether the client receiving Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) should have part-time work obligations or work preparation obligations, you will need to determine the date the client's obligations will apply from. The information in the client's Work Capacity Medical Certificate will help you to determine: - work preparation obligations will apply from the date the client has reduced capacity - part-time work obligations apply after a five day notice period from when the client was sent a letter advising them of their part-time work obligations

chunks.title: Clients applying for Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients applying for Jobseeker Support must be given notice in writing that they will have work obligations or work preparation obligations. To do this, you must: - note on the client's obligations section of the application form that you have decided they should have work obligations and - give the client a copy of their obligations from the application form The work obligations will apply from: - the client's commencement date or - the date you grant the benefit in SWIFTT whichever is the later. For more information see: - Informing clients of their obligations

chunks.title: Work obligations - client is already receiving Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients receiving Jobseeker Support will be given a five working day notice period before their work obligations will apply. The five-day notice period begins when a letter is sent to the client advising them of their part-time work obligations. A client cannot be subject to work obligations until they have received notice in writing. The five working days is counted automatically from the date after the letter has been sent. The table below provides an example of how to count the notice period: Case manager enters that the client has part-time capacity to work Day 0 A letter is sent explaining to the client that work obligations will apply from Day 6 Day 1 and 2 Five working day notice period begins Weekend Saturday - Sunday Day 3 - Day 5 Five working day notice period continues Day 6 Work obligations applied in SWIFTT

chunks.title: Applying work obligations from a future date — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: When a client provides a medical certificate prior to their current expiry date in SINCC the client will be sent a letter advising that they will have work obligations (once the medical certificate is processed). The date that the client will be subject to work obligations will be: - the day after the five working day notice period or - the date the medical coverage begins whichever is the later. Note clients cannot be subject to work obligations from a date in the past. For more information see: - Medical review and reassessments

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: A client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date they apply to receive Jobseeker Support. On an on-going basis a client must continue to remain ordinarily resident in New Zealand to get their benefit. Some exceptions occur when the client leaves New Zealand to live overseas permanently in which case they may be eligible for a continuation of their payments under a Social Security Agreement.

chunks.title: Attributes associated with being ordinarily resident — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Ordinarily resident incorporates a number of factors. The key attributes to being ordinarily resident in New Zealand is that a person must have a close and clear connection to New Zealand on the date they apply for Jobseeker Support. Some other key attributes that indicate that a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand include: - their physical presence in New Zealand is other than casually or as a traveller - there is some intention to remain in New Zealand for a settled purpose - despite temporary absences from New Zealand they regularly or customarily live in New Zealand - they prefer residence in New Zealand to any other country (a person cannot be ordinarily resident in 2 countries at the same time) Where it is not clear if a client is ordinarily resident you may need to ask the client further information. Some of the following questions may help to get more information: - if the client is going overseas, what are their intentions towards New Zealand (sighting return air tickets is a good indication) - the length of time they spend in New Zealand compared to their periods of absence and the reasons for the absences - property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans) - where are their cash assets principally held (New Zealand banks or investment entities or overseas based holdings) - is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and are they tax resident in New Zealand - see Inland Revenue Deciding whether you are a resident or non-resident - are they still on an electoral role and vote in central and local body elections - do they have a personal commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in their immediate and extended family community, community events, clubs and other groups) The attributes associated with being ordinarily resident can also be used after Jobseeker Support is granted if there is some indication the client may no longer be ordinarily resident in New Zealand.

chunks.title: How to decide — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Whether a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand is a question of fact and degree. You must consider all the factors of each individual case and decide whether they show a clear and close connection to New Zealand. You may need to ask more questions (or seek clarification of information you have) to get all the relevant information and then you must weigh up all the facts, and make a decision having regard to the attributes associated with a person being ordinarily resident in New Zealand (see above). If, on the balance of facts you are not sure if the client is ordinarily resident in New Zealand ask for advice from Helpline or your manager client service delivery before you make your decision. A determination on whether a person is ordinarily resident is a discretionary legislative provision and the client should be given the benefit of the doubt in situations where their ordinary residence isn't clear.

chunks.title: Non-residentially qualified — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: You should consider other main benefits if a client does not meet the residence requirements for Jobseeker Support. An Emergency Benefit may be granted on the grounds of hardship to a client who does not meet the period of residence requirement. However, the person must generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet the hardship qualifications for Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Deciding work obligations for primary client (health condition, injury or disability) — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Deciding work obligations for primary client (health condition, injury or disability)
Clients getting Jobseeker Support on ground of health condition, injury or disability may have part-time work obligations or work preparation obligations, depending on their capacity to work.
Capacity to work
At least 15 hours per week
Capacity of less than 15 hours per week or no capacity
No capacity
Client's obligations
Part-time work obligations
Work obligations are deferred, client has work preparation obligations
Can apply for an exemption from work preparation obligations in limited circumstances, such as being in hospital
## Factors to consider
Before deciding if the client should have work obligations you need to consider all the information available including:
- the information provided in the Work Capacity Medical Certificate regarding the client's capacity for work
- previous relevant medical or clinical reports
- if required, advice from Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor
- if available, a designated health practitioners report
- if available, Self-Assessment
- if available, structured interview
- if available, relevant Work Ability Assessment

chunks.title: Decision guidelines - clients moving to a limited employment location — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients who move to a limited employment location must continue to meet their work obligations. This includes being available for, and taking reasonable steps to obtain, suitable employment. To meet this obligation, they must demonstrate that they: - have access to reliable transport - are willing to commute to a nearby town or centre where suitable employment is available - are realistically able to commute to a nearby town or centre where suitable employment is available It is up to the client to demonstrate to you how they are meeting their work obligations. If the client is not meeting their work obligations, you must initiate a work obligations failure.

chunks.title: Work obligations failure - recompliance — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Once a work obligations failure has been initiated, the client must show their willingness to meet their work obligations by: - demonstrating they have reliable transport, and are willing and realistically able to commute to a nearby town or centre where employment is available or - moving to a place that is not a limited employment location A client who agrees to recomply by moving to an area that is not a limited employment location will need to show you they have taken steps to move before they can be considered to have recomplied. You will need to keep in regular contact with your client to ensure they are continuing to take steps to move. Where it is not possible to remedy the relevant failure, the client may recomply by completing another activity that is the same or substantially similar to the activity they failed. For more information see: - Obligations failures - Recompliance (Grade 1 and 2) - Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Ongoing work with clients who move to limited employment locations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If your client can demonstrate they will meet their work obligations in a limited employment location, you will need to work closely with them to ensure they actively continue to meet these obligations. Your client should be encouraged to: - keep a verifiable record of what they have been doing each week to find employment and - meet with you on a regular basis For more information see: - Assistance to move back to an area that is not a limited employment location - Clients currently living in limited employment locations - Deskfile Limited employment locations - Employment and Work Readiness Assistance to transition into employment - Meeting job search requirements - Obligations failures - Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period) - Recompliance (Grade 1 and 2) - Why is the client moving to a limited employment location? - Work obligations

chunks.title: Decision Guidelines - part-time students — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Decision Guidelines - part-time students
To see if the client meets the job search requirements consider the following information to make a decision:
- Is the client regarded as full-time or part-time by their place of study?
- If the client is undertaking part-time study are they putting in full-time or part-time hours?
- What fees have been paid by the client?
- Is the course available outside normal hours or by correspondence?
- What other steps has the client taken to find work?
- Is the client restricting their job search to their chosen field of study?

chunks.title: Decision Guidelines - self-employed — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Decision Guidelines - self-employed
The following guidelines can help you decide whether a self-employed client can get Jobseeker Support.
- Can the client participate in full-time employment elsewhere while working part time in their business? If they are working full time in self-employment they cannot get Jobseeker Support.
- What steps has the client taken to find other employment and/or increase their business income? Do they have a business plan, a mentor?
- How much is the client currently earning from self-employment, and what were they earning?
- How did they support themselves during similar periods in the past?
The client needs to provide:
- copies of the latest financial accounts and
- details of ongoing business commitments, for example pricing jobs and availability for other employment and
- records of the number of hours they are working in their business for the 3 months before they applied for Jobseeker Support, and
- details of how the client supported themselves during similar periods in the past and
- an assessment of the expected duration period with no income and
- a statement showing how long the client has been self-employed
To work out whether the client has (or is) working full time in their business you will need to work out the average weekly hours for the 3 months before they applied for benefit.
If a client does not have accounts, they need to be given time to collect the information. It is not the role of MSD to prepare a client's business accounts, however there are ways we can support a client by showing them where to find sources of information and resources that can help them.
Agencies including Business.govt.nz, Citizen's Advice Bureau, Local Government New Zealand, Inland Revenue and Employment New Zealand have a range of advice, support and guidelines for small businesses, including videos and pamphlets that provide step by step instructions on how to prepare accounts as well as guides to business planning, and mentor programmes.
## For specific situations see:
- New business
- Clients investigating self-employment options

chunks.title: Decision Guidelines - students — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Decision Guidelines - students
In addition to job search requirements, consider the following to help you decide if a client is entitled to Jobseeker Support:
- Has the client completed their qualification?
- If not, why are they ending their study now?
- Have they pre-enrolled for any courses next year?
- If they are ending their studies for financial reasons, how have they supported themselves to date?
- Is this support available next year, if not, why not?

chunks.title: Deferrals — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Deferrals
A client can be temporarily deferred from some of their work obligations when they:
- have a health condition, injury or disability, and have no capacity to work, or only the capacity to work for less than 15 hours per week or
- are 27 weeks pregnant or more, or have complications with the pregnancyNote partners who are 27 weeks pregnant or more, or have complications with their pregnancy, may qualify for an exemption from their work obligations. See: Exemptions
Deferrals are considered based on a client's individual circumstances.
The client doesn't have to make an application for a deferral.
A letter will be sent to the client when a deferral is added, advising why the deferral has been granted and the length of time it will be granted for.
Clients who have a health condition, injury or disability will get reminder letters during the 4 weeks before their expiry date, advising of their deferral expiring and what they need to do to extend the deferral or meet the qualifications for Jobseeker Support on grounds of health condition, injury disability

chunks.title: Definite offer of employment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Definite offer of employment
Where the client has stated that they had a definite offer of employment (supplied in writing) to get permanent residence, you must investigate fully what happened to the job offer. This should include contacting the employer.
Where the offer of employment was withdrawn or employment terminated through circumstances beyond the control of the client you may consider granting Jobseeker Support, provided the client meets the two year residence criteria or Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship if they do not meet the two years continuous residence.
Immigration New Zealand will decide on any action to be taken with regard to the client's residence status. In the meantime you need to look at all the circumstances of the client as to whether you can grant benefit assistance.
Note if the client has resided in New Zealand for two years assess the client's entitlement to Jobseeker Support in the usual manner.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Granting on grounds of hardship

chunks.title: Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance school — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance school
For young people studying at Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance school full-time is:
- 4 subjects at NCEA level 1 or
- 3 subjects at NCEA levels 2 and 3

chunks.title: Dependent child — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
A dependent child for Jobseeker Support is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- being maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Jobseeker Support does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 are being made
- child for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
In some situations, a child may not be living at home but is still considered to be a dependent child.
Dependent children are to be included in the benefit.

chunks.title: Designated health practitioner — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Designated health practitioner
Designated health practitioners are:
- vocationally registered medical practitioners or
- nurse practitioners or
- psychologists
with a minimum of 5 years experience in New Zealand and who have demonstrated an ability to work constructively with MSD staff.
Nurse practitioners, medical practitioners and psychologists must apply to become a designated health practitioner. MSD holds a list of all approved designated health practitioners.
## When to refer to a designated health practitioner
MSD can refer a client to a designated health practitioner for the purpose of establishing or reviewing their entitlement to a benefit or capacity to work. MSD will meet the cost of this assessment.
MSD should arrange for the client to be referred to a designated health practitioner when:
- their practitioner indicates on the medical certificate that a second opinion is appropriate or
- benefit eligibility is unclear or
- capacity for work is unclear or
- the Work Readiness Assessment recommends the referral or
- for any other appropriate reason
## Payment for travel
The client may be able to get assistance for the cost of travel when they are required to visit a designated health practitioner if they meet the following criteria:
- the return journey is more than 8 kilometres or
- the client is unable to use public transport because of their illness or disability or
- there is no public transport available and the travel is less than 8 kilometres
Note this assistance is not limited to once every year and is not subject to an income or asset test or emergency criteria.

chunks.title: Determining when a client became non-compliant — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Determining when a client became non-compliant
When a client fails to complete Report Job Search without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must determine from which point the client was non-compliant.
The client's benefit will be suspended or reduced from the first day of the week that MSD determines a client was non-compliant.
The start of each week is based on when Report Job Search was imposed. This means the week may not begin on a Monday.
For example, if a client's Report Job Search is imposed on a Wednesday, the beginning of the week for the sanction will be Wednesday.
## Client engaged initially and then stopped
A client may engage with Report Job Search for a period of time and then fail to meet the requirements before their Report Job Search has ended.
In this case, MSD will consider that a client was non-compliant from first day of the week in which a client stopped meeting the requirements.
## Client does not provide evidence
If a client attends their recompliance appointment and has been reporting on their job-search activities in MyMSD but cannot provide MSD with evidence of this (without a good and sufficient reason), non-compliance should be backdated to the beginning of the week they stopped meeting their sanction requirements.

chunks.title: Determining when a client became non-compliant — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Determining when a client became non-compliant
When a client fails to find or complete Community Work Experience without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must determine from which point the client was non-compliant.
MSD may consider information shared by an organisation when determining if a client has a good and sufficient reason for failing to find or complete Community Work Experience, however MSD must also consider information provided by the client.
The client's benefit will be suspended or reduced from the first day of the week that MSD determines a client was non-compliant.
The start of each week is based on when the Community Work Experience was imposed. This means the week may not begin on a Monday.
For example, if a client's Community Work Experience is imposed on a Wednesday, the beginning of the week for the sanction will be Wednesday.
## Client engaged initially and then stopped
A client may engage with Community Work Experience for a period of time, and then fail to meet the requirements before their Community Work Experience has ended.
In this case, MSD will consider that the client was non-compliant from first day of the week that the client stopped meeting the requirements.
## Client does not make contact
When a client does not provide verification or make contact with MSD at the end of their search period or the end of their position period, they will be considered non-compliant from the first day after the respective period ended.
If a client later makes contact with MSD and has no good and sufficient reason for not meeting their requirements, non-compliance should be backdated to the beginning of the week in which they were no longer complying with the sanction.
## MSD cannot determine when non-compliance occurred
When a client makes contact with MSD, MSD must use the information provided to determine when their non-compliance occurred. If the client does not provide enough information for MSD to determine this, non-compliance must be back-dated to the beginning of the search or position period, depending on which period the client was in when non-compliance occurred.

chunks.title: Determining whether Community Work Experience is appropriate — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Determining whether Community Work Experience is appropriate
MSD must assess whether Community Work Experience is suitable for a client and their circumstances before it may be imposed as a non-financial sanction.
Clients will keep getting their full benefit while in Community Work Experience, instead of a 50% financial sanction.
MSD must consider any relevant factors before choosing to impose Community Work Experience. Examples of some factors to consider are listed below.
## Client's obligations
Clients with work obligations who fail a social obligation may have Community Work Experience imposed. However, it may be more appropriate for a client to recomply with their failure by meeting their social obligations, rather than completing Community Work Experience.
## Skills and experience
Community Work Experience may be best if the client has limited work experience or levels of work readiness.
For example, if a client has significant work history, or tertiary-level qualifications, Community Work Experience may not help them to become more employable.
However, if a client has a large gap in their work history, or no connections in their local community, Community Work Experience may still be suitable, depending on their circumstances.
## Levels of confidence
Community Work Experience is intended to help a client build work-related skills and confidence. However, they may find it overwhelming to approach organisations to find and complete a position for the purpose of a sanction.
Community Work Experience will only be suitable if MSD is reasonably satisfied that a client can find and complete a position.
## Previous experience with community or voluntary work
If a client has previous experience participating in community or voluntary work, it may be more likely that they would commit to carrying out Community Work Experience. This could also help them find a position.
## Local availability
In larger towns or cities, there may be more options for a client to find a suitable position for Community Work Experience. In smaller areas, a client may not be likely to find a position, or MSD may already know there is less availability there.
It would not be reasonable to impose Community Work Experience if it is unlikely that a client would be able to successfully find a position in their area.
## Known risk factors
It would not be appropriate to impose Community Work Experience as a sanction if MSD is aware of something that could be a risk to the client, organisation or other people involved. This can include things like known sex offenders or clients with a history of violence.

chunks.title: Changes in income — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Changes in income
Money Management may not be suitable for clients who frequently have changes in income.
If a client declares a change in their income after their main benefit payment has been issued to their payment card, it may result in an overpayment. If a client is overpaid, a debt will be established as the payment cannot be adjusted.
If a client is underpaid, they will be issued arrears directly into their bank account. This may reduce the effectiveness of the sanction.

chunks.title: Determining whether Report Job Search is appropriate — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: MSD must assess whether Report Job Search is suitable for a client and their circumstances before it may be imposed as a non-financial sanction. Clients will keep getting their full benefit while completing Report Job Search, instead of a 50% financial sanction. MSD must consider any relevant factors before choosing to impose Report Job Search. Examples of some factors to consider are listed below. If Report Job Search is not suitable, a different non-financial sanction may be appropriate.

chunks.title: Client's obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients with work obligations who fail a social obligation may have Report Job Search imposed. However, it may be more appropriate for a client to recomply with their failure by meeting their social obligations, rather than completing Report Job Search. Note if a client doesn't have work obligations they cannot have Report Job Search imposed on them.

chunks.title: What work activities the client has assigned to them — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client is already reporting their job-search activities, as part of an obligation or work-testable activity, it may not be appropriate to impose Report Job Search on them.

chunks.title: Local employment availability — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client lives in a limited employment location, there may be fewer job-search activities available for clients to complete. MSD should consider a client's local labour market when determining if Report Job Search is appropriate. Note clients who live in areas with limited job opportunities must be able to meet their obligations to look for and find suitable work. This can include being willing and realistically able to commute to nearby towns or centres to find employment.

chunks.title: Work readiness — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients with limited skills or work experience (e.g. recent school leavers) need to be looking for any suitable work available in their area. A lack of work history shouldn't prevent a client from being able to complete Report Job Search. However, a client's barriers to employment and personal circumstances should also be considered when deciding if Report Job Search is appropriate.

chunks.title: Accessibility — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients must be able to report their job-search activities on MyMSD. MSD should consider a client's ability to access and report on MyMSD before imposing Report Job Search. For example: - the client must have access to a device they can access the internet on (this can include the kiosks at a service centre) - if the client doesn't have access to a device they can access the internet on, consider their ability to get to a service centre, - the client must have adequate digital literacy skills to report their job-search activities

chunks.title: Developmental activities — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Developmental activities
To provide additional support to the young person, developmental activities may also be included alongside other activities that a young person is undertaking. A young person can undertake other developmental activities and still be considered to be meeting their youth activity obligations as long as:
- they are continuing to participate, or are available to undertake, full-time education, training or work-based learning
- you have assessed that the person needs to address other needs while they undertake full-time education, training or work-based learning and
- the young person agrees to participate
Note a young person can be asked to participate in developmental activities but they cannot be required to. The young person cannot be sanctioned for not agreeing to undertake a developmental activity.
Other developmental activities include (but are not limited to):
- Interpersonal skills - increasing a young person's people or communication skills
- Self-motivation (for example confidence or motivation courses)
- Writing and language - young people who have learned English as their second language may require extra tuition to complement their main education or training activity
- Counselling/family violence related programmes
- Drug and alcohol counselling
- Social rehabilitation programmes
Note the Limited Services Volunteers programme will generally not be appropriate for partners of main beneficiaries unless they are transitioning out of the service and have job seeking as their destination.

chunks.title: Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes when a client is diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence.
Drug addiction or dependence, for the purposes of the drug test requirements, means a person who has been diagnosed with:
- severe substance abuse or
- dependency or drug addiction issues
The client can be asked to provide verification from a registered health practitioner or by a registered AOD practitioner who will have completed a formal assessment and given the diagnosis of drug dependency.
The verification should also state the duration or time that the client will need to address their drug issue dependency.
There is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that MSD can provide to the client.

chunks.title: Disputes and reviews of an obligations failure — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Disputes and reviews of an obligations failure
A client or partner has the right to dispute or review if they disagree with any decision relating to:
- an obligations failure or
- a sanction being imposed or
- the type of sanction being imposed
A client or partner can do this by:
- disputing the decision or
- lodging a formal Review of Decision
- lodging an appeal to the Medical Appeals Board (drug test failure only)
A Review of Decision or appeal to the Medical Appeals Board can be lodged at any stage, within three months of the obligations failure being initiated, or within three months of the sanction being imposed.
If a client or partner disputes their obligations failure or sanction more than 20 working days after it is initiated or imposed, MSD must advise the client or partner to lodge a formal Review of Decision or an appeal to the Medical Appeals Board (drug test failure only) in writing.
For more information see:
- Core policy Medical Appeals Board
- Disputing more than one obligations failure
- The disputes process
- Recording decisions on a dispute
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals

chunks.title: Disputing more than one obligations failure — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Disputing more than one obligations failure
If a client has failed more than one obligation at the same time, they can dispute any of the failed activities by providing a good and sufficient reason for each failure.
## Example 1
A client has failed their social obligations and 2 of their work obligations, and the failures have been initiated on the same day. The client disputes some of these failures as they have good and sufficient reasons. The client also recomplies to 1 of their obligations. The client is not sanctioned but the failure is counted because they recomplied with 1 of the failures.
Obligation
Recompliance
Action
Social obligation - failed to enrol child in ECE
Client must comply with all social obligations
Client disputes failure - has good and sufficient reason
Work obligations - failed to attend interview
Must attend another job interview - or similar activity
Client disputes failure - has good and sufficient reason
Work obligations - refused to take drug test
Must agree to being drug free
Client has no good and sufficient reason for the failure - agrees to recomply
## Example 2
A client has failed their obligations and the failures have been initiated on the same day. The client recomplies for 1 failure but not for the other failure. The sanction remains imposed until the client recomplies.
Obligation
Recompliance
Action
Work obligation - failed to attend a job interview
Client must participate in another job interview - or similar activity
Client has no good and sufficient reason for not attending the interview - the sanction remains imposed until the client recomplies with this activity
Work obligations - failed to attend job seminar
Must attend another job seminar - or similar activity
Client recomplies by attending another job seminar

chunks.title: Drug test job referral not suitable — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Drug test job referral not suitable
There are certain situations where it is not appropriate to refer a client to drug tested jobs as the job is not considered to be suitable. These situations include where a client is:
- taking prescribed medication
- diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- in or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence or
- has a drug issue identified by a provider and is engaging and participating in services and support offered by that provider
These situations are also to be taken into account when deciding whether a client has a good and sufficient reason for failing their drug test requirements. For more information see:
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons
The first time a client presents with one of these situations, you should:
- accept that it is not appropriate to refer the client to drug tested jobs
- add a deferral from drug test obligations for an initial 30 working day period and
- advise the client that if they think they require a deferral from drug test obligations for more than 30 working days, then verification will be required
- there is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to your client
For more information see:
- Drug Test - Referral delay [no link find out why]
Depending on the clients circumstances and the verification provided you can extend the deferral from drug test obligations up to 6 months.
For more information see:
- Taking controlled prescribed medication
- Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence
- Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: Drug test obligation failures - Good and sufficient reasons — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Drug test obligation failures - Good and sufficient reasons
Before you initiate an obligations failure you need to be satisfied that the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their drug test work obligations.
There are certain situations that must be considered to be good and sufficient reasons for drug test obligations failures, these situations include where a client:
- is taking controlled prescribed medication
- is diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- is in or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence or
- has a drug issue identified by the Alcohol Drug Helpline - Work and Income Support Service and is engaging and participating in services and support offered by the 0800 AOD Helpline
## Drug tested job referral not suitable
These situations are also to be taken into account when deciding whether it is appropriate to refer a client to drug tested jobs. If you decide that, due to one of these situations, it is not appropriate to refer a client to further drug tested jobs you must add a drug test referral delay.
For more information see:
- Drug Test - Referral Delay [no link find out why]
The first time a client fails their drug test obligation and provides a good and sufficient reason, you should:
- accept that the client has a good and sufficient reason
- add a deferral from drug test obligations for an initial 30 working day period and
- advise the client that if they think they require a deferral from drug test obligations for more than 30 working days, then verification will be required
- there is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to your client
For more information see:
- Reviewing or disputing the drug test failure
- Taking controlled prescribed medication
- Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence
- Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence
- Referring a client to job not suitable
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures

chunks.title: Drug test obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients receiving Jobseeker Support who have work obligations will be subject to drug test obligations. Clients must undertake and pass drug tests when Work and Income have identified: - a suitable job and pre-employment drug tests are required by a prospective employer or - a suitable course and a pre-course drug test is required as part of the admission process by a training provider A client will fail their drug test work obligations if they have no good and sufficient reason and: - a suitable job is available and they advise they will not apply for the job as they will not pass the pre-employment drug test - they have been referred to or have applied for a suitable job or course and they refuse to take the pre-employment drug test or - they have been referred to a suitable job or course and they fail or refuse a drug test If a client fails their drug test work obligations the same five day notice period and sanctions apply as for any other obligations failure.

chunks.title: Client will not apply as they will not pass the drug test — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: An immediate obligations failure should be initiated if a client, without a good and sufficient reason, has: - been matched to a job opportunity and refuses to apply for it as they advise they will fail the pre-employment drug test or - attended a seminar to discuss a job opportunity and advises they will fail the pre-employment drug test

chunks.title: Client refuses to take the drug test — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: An obligations failure should be initiated if a client without a good and sufficient reason has been referred to a suitable job and refuses to take the pre-employment drug test.

chunks.title: Client fails the drug test — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: An obligations failure should be initiated, if a client, without good and sufficient reason, has: - been referred to a suitable job and the employer advises that they have failed the pre-employment drug test or - been referred to a suitable course and the training provider advises that they have failed the pre-course drug test Note the employer or training provider must confirm that a client has failed the drug test before you initiate the obligations failure.

chunks.title: Client fails pre-employment alcohol test — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Job applicants may be required to be tested for alcohol use prior to being hired. However, the drug test obligation requirements do not include alcohol. If a client failed a test for alcohol use, without a good and sufficient reason, then a work test failure could be initiated because the client has failed to participate in the job interview process. For more information see: - Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements - Drug test job referral not suitable - Client has failed a screening drug test - Informing clients of their obligations - Training providers requiring a drug test - Employers requiring pre-employment drug tests - Types of drug tests and standards

chunks.title: Drug test recompliance count — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Drug test recompliance count
The obligation failure that is initiated or the sanction that is imposed depends on how often the client or partner has failed to comply with their obligations in the previous 24 months while getting a benefit. This is called the 24-month failure count.
The recompliance activity that the client or partner has to complete depends on whether the client or partner has failed their drug test obligation before within the last 24 months.
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation the client or partner must complete a 6-week approved activity.
## Example 2
Obligation / activity failed
Recompliance
24 month failure count
Work obligations - did not attend job interview
Must recomply by completing the same or similar activity eg must attend another job interview
Obligations failure 1 or Grade 1 sanction
Work obligations - refused to apply for a job due to pre-employment drug test requirement
Drugs test recompliance 1
eg must verbally agree to stop using controlled drugs
Obligations failure 2 or Grade 2 sanction
Work obligations - failed pre-employment drug test requirement
Six-week approved activity or programme of activities
Obligations failure 3 or Grade 3 sanction
For more information see:
- Counting previous obligations failures

chunks.title: Earning incentive payments — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Earning incentive payments
Young partners receiving Jobseeker Support can earn the following incentive payments:
- education incentive of $10 a week
- budgeting incentive of $10 a week
- parenting education incentive of $10 a week
## Education incentive
A young partner on Jobseeker Support can earn the education incentive if:
- their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service has confirmed to YSSU that since they started receiving their benefit, they have continuously attended and participated in either education, training or work-based learning for at least 6 calendar months
## Budgeting incentive
A young partner on Jobseeker Support can earn the budgeting incentive if:
- their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service has confirmed to YSSU that since they started receiving their benefit they have attended and participated in discussions on budgeting with the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service provider, for at least 3 calendar months
and
- they have attended and completed a budgeting programme (this can have been completed before the client started getting their benefit)
## Parenting incentive
A young partner with a child on Jobseeker Support can earn the parenting education incentive if:
- the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service has confirmed that, since they started to receive the benefit, they have regularly engaged with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house service' for at least 3 calendar months and
- they have participated in and completed a parenting education programme
- each of their dependent children is enrolled with a primary health organisation
- each of their dependent children aged 5 years or under are up-to-date with their Wellchild checks
- each of their dependent children aged 5 years or under attends an approved early childhood education programme or is placed in other suitable childcare during any time the young person is in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work
Note the earliest date the 3 month period can be calculated from is the date the young partner was granted their Jobseeker Support.
For more information see:
- Removing incentive payments
- Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose
- Incentive payments can continue
- Restoring incentive payments
- Obligations
## Capacity issues prevent a young partner meeting their parenting obligations
Sometimes a young partner may be able to receive a parenting education incentive payment without meeting the criteria.
For more information see:
- Capacity issues prevent a young partner meeting their parenting obligations

chunks.title: Earning the right to receive payment directly — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Earning the right to receive payment directly
Young partners who are subject to youth money management can earn the right to have their portion of main benefit, family tax credit, Best Start tax credit and any extra help paid directly to them.
The young partner can gain control of their payment if:
- they have demonstrated continued compliance with their obligations and
- their service provider or Ministry of Social Development 'in-house' service considers that they are financially competent
A young partner who has earned control over their payment has the choice to have their benefit paid directly to them and they will be responsible for paying their costs.
Note when young partners are sanctioned and they are not subject to youth money management because they have earned the right to manage their own money, they won't be put back on youth money management like those clients on Youth Payment and Young Parent Payment. This ensures the sanctions for clients who aren't subject to youth money management remain graduated through any obligation failures.

chunks.title: Effect of 13 week non-entitlement period for partner — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: When a primary client is subject to a non-entitlement period, their partner may be able to continue to receive financial assistance depending on whether they are eligible for Jobseeker Support. If the partner is eligible for Jobseeker Support, this may affect the sanctioned client's non-entitlement period depending on what obligations they become subject to.

chunks.title: Is partner eligible for Jobseeker Support? — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: In order for a partner to receive financial assistance, they must be eligible for Jobseeker Support in their own right. If they meet the eligibility criteria, they will become the primary recipient of Jobseeker Support, and the original primary client will become the partner. Before the partner and primary status can be changed, it must be confirmed that the client to be the primary would be eligible for Jobseeker Support. They need to: - actively seeking and available for full-time work or - would be but they are limited in their capacity to work full-time because of a health condition, injury or disability or - would be but are temporarily unable to because they qualify for an exemption from their work obligations For more information see: - Qualifications You need to confirm that the client who will be the primary can meet the job search requirements of Jobseeker Support. To help decide if a client is able to meet the job search requirements, you will need to consider the following: 1. If the client had the opportunity, would they: - be available for work for 30 hours or more a week (full-time work obligations) - accept any suitable job offers within their abilitiesNote that this can include weekend work depending on the client's or partner's individual circumstances - not restrict their job search to vacancies within their own trade - not restrict their job search to vacancies in their chosen occupation - not move frequently from one area to another with no intention of getting a job 2. Has the client begun to take steps to find work? For example by: - searching newspapers and other media for vacancies - making applications for suitable jobs - contacting employers about vacancies Have a conversation with the client about what this will mean for their (and their partner's) obligations, and confirm the reasons for the change.

chunks.title: Effect of partner becoming primary on non-entitlement period — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The effect of the partner becoming the primary on the original primary's non-entitlement period depends on what obligations they would now have as the partner. Partners on Jobseeker Support may have work preparation obligations, part-time work obligations, or full-time work obligations, depending on their circumstances. If the reason the original client was subject to a non-entitlement period still applies when they have been assigned obligations as a partner, they will continue to be subject to the non-entitlement period. For example: - If the client subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period becomes the partner and is no longer subject to the type of obligation that they failed then it may be unreasonable for them to complete a recompliance activity. The client's benefit can be resumed and the couple would receive the full married rate of benefit.Note if the client in this scenario was subject to an obligations failure, while they may not have to complete a recompliance activity, their failure count will still include the obligations failure that caused their non-entitlement period. - If the client subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period becomes the partner and now has part-time work obligations, and they were subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period because of a grade three sanction, and they failed to attend an employment seminar, they would be required to complete a 6 week recompliance activity or programme of activities. The primary client would be paid the half married, civil union or de facto rate of Jobseeker Support. - If the client subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period becomes the partner and now has work preparation obligations as they have a child aged under 3 years, and they were subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period because of refusing a suitable employment opportunity of 30 hours per week, it would be unreasonable for them to complete a recompliance activity. The client's benefit can be resumed and the couple would receive the full married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit. For more information see: - Payment when partner becomes primary during non-entitlement period - Effect of sanctions on assistance - Clients with dependent children - 50% protection - Work or work preparation obligations

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction for couples without dependent children — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Grade 3 sanction for couples without dependent children
If one partner of a couple with no dependent children is subject to a grade 3 sanction, this is only applied to half the couple's benefit.
The non-sanctioned partner is entitled to half the couple rate of benefit, with any income reduced at half the rate of the income test that applies.
If both partners of a couple with no dependent children are subject to a grade 3 sanction, the benefit is stopped (as 50% is stopped for each partner who failed).

chunks.title: Effect of certain drugs — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Effect of certain drugs
To fail a drug test a client must have drugs present in their system that reach a certain threshold or cut out level. Passing a drug test does not require a 100% drug free sample.
## Effect of certain drugs
How long certain drugs stay in a person's systems depends on a variety of factors, including (but not limited to) the:
- amount and frequency of use
- persons body mass, age, overall health and
- persons drug tolerance
Below are some examples of drugs and the average 'duration' that they are present in a person's system. This information has been sourced from several publications by experts in this area, however, this must not be considered to be 'absolute' because how drugs affect a person does depend on the factors above.
Drug
Average duration
Amphetamines (including methamphetamine)
1 to 7 days
Ecstasy, Cocaine
2 to 4 days
Benzodiazepines
2 to 10 days
Marijuana / cannabis (including medicinal cannabis)
3 to 30 days
LSD
1 to 3 days
Opioids
Note this covers drugs such as codeine, fentanyl, heroin, oxycodone, morphine and tramadol
1 to 3 days
Cannabis can stay in a person's body for several weeks, particularly if the person is a heavy or regular user. The recompliance period accounts for the general length of time it takes for cannabis to be metabolised out of the body.
Clients have 25 working days to take and pass a drug test and MSD allows an additional 5 working days to receive and process the results from the client.
Clients can consult with their registered health practitioner or the Alcohol Drug Helpline - Work and Income Support Service [no link find out why] for further guidance on how drugs may affect them.

chunks.title: Effect on payments due to not completing the reapplication process — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client does not complete all the required parts of the reapplication before their expiry date, Jobseeker Support cannot be regranted and their benefit will stop.

chunks.title: Clients with a partner — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If the client has a partner included in their benefit, both the client and the partner must complete the relevant parts of the reapplication requirements before the expiry date. If they do not, both the client and the partner's portion of the benefit will stop. This applies even if one person in the couple does complete the reapplication requirements on time. The only exception is when the client (or their partner, if any) qualifies for an extension or is not required to complete the reapplication process.

chunks.title: Example 1 – Client does not complete reapplication before expiry date — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Ahman has been getting Jobseeker Support which commenced on 28 September 2026. Their expiry date is 29 March 2027, which is 26 weeks after their commencement date. On 19 February 2027 they are sent the "initial notice to reapply" letter, advising what they need to do to complete the 26 week reapplication process. They forget to complete their reapplication and do not contact MSD until 14 April 2027, after their benefit stops. Ahman does not qualify for an extension. If they still need Jobseeker Support, they will need to apply for a benefit as a new applicant.

chunks.title: Example 2 – Partner does not complete reapplication — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Indri applies for and is granted Jobseeker Support with her partner Adina included in her benefit. Her Jobseeker Support commenced on 2 March 2026 and their expiry date is 31 August 2026. Indri and Adina both have full-time work obligations. On 27 July 2026, Indri is sent the "initial notice to reapply" letter, advising what she and Adina need to do to complete the 26 week reapplication process. Indri books an appointment for herself and Adina to complete all parts of the reapplication. However, Adina does not attend the appointment. At the appointment, Indri confirms her and Adina's circumstances. MSD books Adina into a work seminar on 26 August 2027 and advises her of this, but she forgets and doesn't attend the seminar either. She does not contact MSD to complete her part of the reapplication. Because Adina has not completed the reapplication before the expiry date, Indri's Jobseeker Support stops. Indri must apply for a benefit as a new applicant if she and Adina still need Jobseeker Support.
