chunks.title: Effect on supplementary assistance - voluntary unemployment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Effect on supplementary assistance - voluntary unemployment
Clients who have a 13 week non-entitlement period because they became voluntarily unemployed cannot get the following during their non-entitlement period:
- Emergency Benefit
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit
Note a client who was getting Accommodation Supplement as a non-beneficiary before applying and being subject to a non-entitlement period upon application, can continue getting Accommodation Supplement during their non-entitlement period.
If eligible, clients can still get:
- Employment and training Assistance to transition into employment
- Disability Allowance

chunks.title: Eligibility part of the 26 week reapplication — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Eligibility part of the 26 week reapplication
All clients must confirm their circumstances so that MSD can ensure they still qualify for Jobseeker Support and are getting the correct rate of payment for their circumstances.
To continue to qualify for Jobseeker Support, the client must meet the qualifications, including being available for, seeking, willing and able to undertake full-time employment, unless they have a health condition, injury or disability that impacts their capacity to work full-time.
To complete the eligibility part of the 26 week reapplication the client and their partner (if any included in their Jobseeker Support) must either:
- complete a specific eligibility engagement in the 13 weeks before their expiry date, or
- confirm their circumstances in the reapplication form.

chunks.title: Who administers the test? — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Who administers the test?
Drug testing is generally provided to individual employers and recruitment agencies by contracted drug test providers. Some large organisations have their own specialised in-house staff, such as nurses, who are accredited in workplace drug testing.
Employment-related drug testing is:
- conducted at a workplace, established testing site or a laboratory and
- through observed collection
For more information see:
- Reimbursement to employers and debt recovery

chunks.title: Employment during stand-down — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Employment during stand-down
If a client gains temporary full-time employment during the initial stand-down period, this may change the date the benefit can start from.
The new entitlement date is the date the temporary employment stops. Reassess the client's initial stand-down period using the income for the 26 and 52 weeks earned immediately before the new entitlement date.

chunks.title: Employment part of the 26 week reapplication — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: As part of the 26 week reapplication, clients and partners (if any included in their Jobseeker Support) must participate in and complete an appropriate employment engagement. An employment engagement helps clients, and their partner, prepare for, find or retain suitable paid employment. The intention is to connect clients to employers, job opportunities, or identify other supports that will help them into employment. The type of employment engagement a client must participate in and complete depends on what obligations they have. Note not all clients and partners need to complete an employment engagement.

chunks.title: Clients and partners with work obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: To satisfy the employment part of the reapplication a client or partner with work obligations (full-time or part-time work obligations) must: - participate in and complete a specific employment engagement in the 13 weeks before their expiry date, or - participate in an engagement that is considered suitable for improving their work readiness, such as discussing their job search activities or help with removing barriers that prevent work readiness, or - confirm they are employed for at least: 15 hours (for a client getting Jobseeker Support on the grounds of a health condition, injury or disability, with part-time work capacity), or20 hours (for a partner with youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years old), or30 hours (for partners with full-time work obligations). - 15 hours (for a client getting Jobseeker Support on the grounds of a health condition, injury or disability, with part-time work capacity), or - 20 hours (for a partner with youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years old), or - 30 hours (for partners with full-time work obligations). Note if a client is in full-time employment they do not qualify for Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: Clients with work-preparation obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients with work preparation obligations who have not completed a specific employment engagement in the 13 weeks before their expiry date, must answer work preparation questions as part of their reapplication to satisfy the employment part of the reapplication. Clients with work preparation obligations may still choose to engage with MSD to discuss what they are doing to prepare for suitable employment, however they do not need to do this as part of their reapplication.

chunks.title: Partners with work-preparation obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Partners with work preparation obligations do not have to complete the employment part of the reapplication. They must still complete the other parts of the 26 week reapplication process.

chunks.title: Clients or partners who are already working — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Part-time employment If a client or their partner has part-time work obligations (either 15 or 20 hours per week) and they are working 15 to 20 hours per week, they are considered to be meeting their work obligations. To satisfy the employment part of their reapplication these clients must engage with MSD during the notice period to confirm their work arrangements. Full-time employment If a partner has full-time work obligations and is working 30 hours or more per week, they are considered to be meeting their work obligations. To satisfy the employment part of their reapplication, partners must engage with MSD during the notice period to confirm their work arrangements. Note if a client is in full-time employment they do not qualify for Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: Employment part of the reapplication not required — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Employment part of the reapplication not required
Generally, all clients and partners with work related obligations are required to complete the employment part of the reapplication. However, some clients and partners may have circumstances that mean they do not need to complete the employment part of the 26 week reapplication.
This is limited to clients in the following circumstances only:
- partners with work preparation obligations or youth activity obligations,
- clients who are getting Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability who are on unpaid sick leave, or working at a reduced capacity, and have a confirmed return to work date,
- clients or partners who have no work or work preparation obligations (i.e. they have a full exemption from their work or work preparation obligations).
If the client or partner is in one of these situations at any point between the date their "initial notice to reapply" letter is sent and their expiry date, they do not need to complete the employment part of the reapplication, even if their circumstances change before their expiry date.

chunks.title: Employment trial period of up to 90 days — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Employment trial period of up to 90 days
When determining if a client qualifies for Jobseeker Support, any employment that has an employment trial period included is assessed the same as any other employment.
Employment agreements, signed by the employer and employee, can include an employment trial period of up to 90 days.
Features of an employment trial:
- an employment trial may be offered by an employer regardless of the number of employees a business has and
- an employer may terminate the employment agreement during a trial at any time before the end of the employment trial period even if the last day of work occurs after the expiry of the employment trial period and
- an employer is not required to provide a reason for ending the employment trial if the notice of termination was given before the employment trial period ended and
- an employee cannot generally bring a personal grievance against the employer in respect of the ending of their employment during the employment trial period
A client can still challenge the ending of their employment agreement including on the grounds of:
- discrimination or
- sexual harassment or
- racial harassment or
- duress imposed by the employer in relation to a client's union affiliations or not as the case may be
For more information about when a client's employment ceases before the end of the employment trial see:

chunks.title: Enrolled in and attending school — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Enrolled in and attending school
A client and their partner (if any) getting Jobseeker Support must take all reasonable steps to ensure their children are enrolled in and attending school from the age of 5 or 6 years old (depending on when they start school).
For more information see:
- Take all reasonable steps
## Age of child
Clients with a dependent child aged 5 or 6 years old (depending on when they start school) to 15 years of age will be required to take all reasonable steps to ensure the child is enrolled in and regularly attending school.
If a child is aged between 5 and 6 years old it is the parent or caregivers choice as to whether they have their child in early childhood education or school.
A child does not legally have to attend school until they are aged 6 years but most children start school at 5 years. A client must meet the early childhood education social obligation if they choose not to enrol their 5 year old in school.
For more information see:
- Early childhood education social obligation
A child can legally leave school when they are 16 years, or at 15 years if they have an early leaving exemption from the Ministry of Education.
A parent or caregiver cannot be asked to comply with the attendance at school social obligation if the child has legally left school or has an early leaving exemption, and is no longer legally required to attend school.
## Verification of child enrolled and attending school
All children aged from 6 to 15 years old are legally required to attend school. In most cases you should take your client's word that they are meeting their social obligations.
However, if you have information that indicates the child may not be attending school you may ask the client to get verification, for example, a letter from the child's school that says the child is enrolled and attending.
There are some situations where a client may be taking all reasonable steps but their child is not attending school.
For more information see:
- Taking all reasonable steps for enrolling in and attending school
- Parent is being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020

chunks.title: Enrolment and attendance at a recognised early childhood education programme — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Enrolment and attendance at a recognised early childhood education programme
A client and their partner (if any) receiving Jobseeker Support must take all reasonable steps to ensure that their child is enrolled in and attending a recognised early childhood education programme from the age of three until they start school. For more information see:
- Take all reasonable steps
Generally, clients should have their children participating in a recognised early childhood education programme for 15 hours a week. This is a target number of hours. If a child is attending less hours this will be acceptable.
Recognised early childhood programmes for the purposes of social obligations include programmes that are:
- Approved early childhood education (ECE) programmes or services
- Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School or
- Other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes
Generally, a place in approved early childhood education (ECE) service should be considered first. Where a place in early childhood education is not available or is not suitable (for example due to hours of operation, distance or family circumstances) then other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes should be considered.

chunks.title: Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits
A young partner must:
- register their child or children with a Well Child or Tamariki Ora provider and
- keep up-to-date with the child's checks
Note a young partner is only required to meet this obligation from the time they begin to receive Jobseeker Support. They will be meeting this obligation if they meet the relevant checks for the child's age from the time they are required to do so.
## Proof of visits
The Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book issued to parents when their child is born is sufficient evidence of the child's attendance at visits.
The Health Book has helpful advice and information about what is happening at different stages in the child's development and has places to record all the Well Child appointments and other special and important things that happen to the child in their first five years.
For more information see:
- Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks

chunks.title: Enrolment with a primary health care provider - young partner — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Enrolment with a primary health care provider - young partner
A young partner must enrol their dependent child or children with a primary health care provider.
This means being enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation.
## Exception
If a client cannot enrol their child with a practitioner or medical practice because of shortages, they can be considered to be meeting this obligation if they have a plan in place to:
- be enrolled with a practice or practitioner when a place becomes available and
- get health care for their child if the child becomes unwell

chunks.title: Enrolment with a primary health care provider — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Enrolment with a primary health care provider
A client and their partner (if any) receiving Jobseeker Support must take all reasonable steps to enrol their child or children with a primary healthcare provider. This means being enrolled with a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation.
Taking all reasonable steps to enrol
If a client cannot register their child at a medical practice or with a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner because of shortages, they can be considered to be meeting this obligation if they have a plan in place to:
- be enrolled with a practice when a place becomes available and
- get health care for their child if the child becomes sick
## Age of child
The primary health care provider obligation applies to parents and caregivers receiving a main benefit:
- with dependent children included in their benefit or
- who are caring for a child that they receive Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for
## Verification
Most children will already be enrolled with a primary health care provider and in most cases MSD should take the client's word that they are meeting this social obligation.
However, if MSD has information that the client may not be taking all reasonable steps to meet this social obligation, MSD may ask the client to get verification.
For example verification could be a letter from their medical centre or their registered practitioner that says they are enrolled (most medical centres will send this when a client is enrolled).

chunks.title: Entering a refuge — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Entering a refuge
When a client is applying for Jobseeker Support after entering a refuge following the break-up of a relationship, the initial stand-down period can be waived.
Generally the client must enter the refuge immediately following the break-up of their relationship. This means entering the refuge within a period similar in duration to the stand-down (that is, within seven to 14 days). Where there is a delay between the separation and the client entering the refuge, general commencement date rules apply.
In this context a refuge is emergency accommodation provided by an agency or organisation. This includes (but is not restricted to) agencies such as Women's Refuge, Home and Family Society, Emergency Housing Trusts, Iwi and cultural organisations, and church organisations.
Note that accommodation provided by family or friends of the client is not considered to be refuge accommodation.
For more information see:
- Commencement date

chunks.title: Entitlement date — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Entitlement date
The entitlement date for Jobseeker Support is usually:
- the day after employment ceased (that is, after any holiday pay, sick pay, etc. has expired)
- the date of incapacity
- the day after separation or financial assistance from partner ceased
- the day after weekly work-related insurance payments ceased
- the day after full-time study or student allowances ceased
- the day after last exam
- the day after school finished (the last day of physical attendance if client has just left school)
- the day after the date the living costs component of Student Loan was paid to
- the date of arrival in New Zealand (if client has returned to New Zealand)
- the date of release from prison or
- the date job search commenced where a client who has been out of the work force for more than 26 weeks decides to recommence job search activity
- the day after (for sole parents) they lost the regular financial support of their partner as they entered prison or remanded in custody
- the day after their partner died
Note when the client has more than one event, you use the later event for their entitlement date.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Keriana is getting Jobseeker Support of $372.55 a week (as at 1 April 2026). She fails an obligation without a good and sufficient reason and her case manager decides to impose Money Management. Her first day of Money Management is Thursday 10 July. Because Keriana's Money Management begins in the middle of the week, only part of her benefit payment for the following week will be under Money Management. This means she will get more than 50% of her benefit into her bank account. Note: the benefit might not divide evenly by 2. When this happens, the higher amount (1 cent more) will be paid to the client's bank account.

chunks.title: How the first week of Money Management is paid — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday Full payment to client's bank account Money Management imposed Client's weekly rate ($372.55) x (number of days that week that Money Management is imposed (4) ÷ 7) = $212.88 50% put onto payment card Total payment onto payment card = $106.45 Remainder paid into client's bank account (weekly benefit amount minus amount paid to payment card) = $372.55 - $106.45 = $266.10 Total payment into client's bank account for the week: $266.10

chunks.title: How the second and third week of Money Management is paid — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday Money Management imposed Client's weekly benefit amount = $372.55 50% put onto payment card Remainder paid into client's bank account (weekly benefit amount minus amount paid to payment card) = $372.55 - $186.28 = $186.27 Total payment into client's bank account for the week: $186.27

chunks.title: How the final week of Money Management is paid — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday Money Management imposed Client's weekly benefit rate ($372.55) x (number of days of week that Money Management is imposed (3) ÷ 7) = $159.66 50% put onto payment card $159.66 x 0.5 = $79.83 Full payment to client's bank account Total payment onto payment card = $79.83 Remainder paid into client's bank account (weekly benefit amount minus amount paid to payment card) = $372.55 - $79.83 = $292.72 Total payment into client's bank account for the week: $292.72

chunks.title: Examples - determining when a client became non-compliant — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Examples - determining when a client became non-compliant
Example 1
Adrian failed a work obligation and MSD imposed Community Work Experience as a non-financial sanction. He contacts MSD at the end of the search period and says he didn't find a position. When MSD asks about what steps he took to find one, Adrian says he contacted a few places in the first week but had no luck, so he gave up trying.
MSD is satisfied that Adrian was complying with the requirements of the search period in week one, but he was no longer compliant in week 2. MSD determines non-compliance from day one of week 2, Thursday 19 June 2025. Adrian's payments are stopped from this date, and he is given a different recompliance activity to complete.

Example 2
Rick had Community Work Experience imposed and found a suitable position working with an environmental organisation cleaning up local rivers.
At the end of his position period, Rick does not provide verification or make contact with MSD. MSD suspends his benefit from the end of his position period.
Rick contacts MSD and asks why his benefit stopped. He is unable to provide any verification of completing his Community Work Experience. MSD also received an email from the organisation advising that Rick had stopped attending.
Because they are unable to confirm exactly when Rick became non-compliant, MSD considers him non-compliant from the beginning of the position period. Because he was not entitled to receive his benefit payments from the beginning of the position period, this results in a debt being established.
MSD then assigns a recompliance activity for Rick to complete to get his payments resumed.

chunks.title: Examples of approved courses — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Examples of approved courses
Examples of approved courses include (but are not limited to):
- Be Your Own Boss training programme
- Drug, alcohol rehabilitation and anger management courses arranged by the Department of Corrections for offenders
- Employment and Work Readiness Work Confidence
- Regional training courses
- Limited Service Volunteers [no link find out why]
- Modularised seminars [no link find out why]
- Outward Bound [no link find out why]
- Skills for Industry [no link find out why]
- Targeted Training [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Examples of when the expiry date is reset — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The expiry date for Jobseeker Support is not reset by any periods of temporary suspension or expiries. The expiry date is only affected if a client: - has their Jobseeker Support cancelled for any reason, or - transfers to another benefit type that is not Jobseeker Support and then transfers back to Jobseeker Support, or - was a partner that has separated from a primary Jobseeker Support client and has been granted Jobseeker Support in their own right. The primary client's expiry date remains the same.

chunks.title: Example 1 - Client's benefit has been suspended — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Rio is getting Jobseeker Support, which commenced on 5 August 2026. His expiry date is 3 February 2027, which is 26 weeks after his benefit commenced. Rio undertakes temporary work for 4 weeks and his benefit is suspended during this time as their income is over the income limit. In this situation, Rio's expiry date does not change when their benefit is resumed and he must reapply before 3 February 2027 if he still needs Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: Example 2 - Client's benefit has been cancelled — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Hafsah's Jobseeker Support commenced on 9 November 2026. Her expiry date is 10 May 2027, which is 26 weeks after her benefit commenced. Hafsah commences full-time employment as a nanny in March 2027. As Hafsah has commenced full-time employment, her benefit is cancelled. The family Hafsah was nannying for is moving overseas, and her employment ceases after 5 months. While Hafsah looks for another job, she applies for and is granted Jobseeker Support which commences on 28 August 2027. Hafsah's expiry date will be 26 February 2028, which is 26 weeks after her new commencement date for Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: Example 3 - Client transfers between benefits — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Neal has been getting Jobseeker Support since 12 November 2025. His expiry date is 13 May 2026, which is 26 weeks after his benefit last commenced. On 21 February 2026, Neal is transferred to Sole Parent Support because he has a 11 year old dependent child come into his care. His new expiry date is 21 February 2027, which is 52 weeks after his Sole Parent Support commenced. After 4 months the child leaves his care and Neal is transferred back to Jobseeker Support on 13 June 2026. In this situation the expiry date will be 12 December 2026, which is 26 weeks from the new Jobseeker Support commencement date.

chunks.title: Example 4 - Partner qualifies for Jobseeker Support in their own right — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Manon has been getting Jobseeker Support, with her partner Dorian and their 16 year old child included in her benefit. Their Jobseeker Support expiry date is 11 August 2027, which is 26 weeks after their benefit commenced on 10 February 2027. On 4 April 2027 Manon and Dorian separate. Manon continues to get Jobseeker Support with her 16 year old child included in her benefit. Her expiry date does not change, and she must reapply before 11 August 2027 if she still needs Jobseeker Support. Dorian applies for and is granted Jobseeker Support in his own right, which commences on 5 April 2027. His expiry date will be 4 October 2027, which is 26 weeks after his Jobseeker Support commencement date.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances for cash assets — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances for cash assets
You can disregard some or all of a client's cash assets when you are looking at granting Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship. You can only do this if you think that there are exceptional circumstances.
Things you need to consider:
- if you refuse to grant Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship to a client, will it have a serious effect on the client's health or welfare
- if you refuse to grant Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship to a client, would the likely alternatives cost the Government more
- can the client realise (that is sell or get access to their cash assets) for more than the appropriate cash asset limit
- is the need for Jobseeker Support temporary
- what is the total amount of the client's assets, including assets that are not cash assets and
- what are the other matters that you would consider relevant to determining whether hardship exists
Every case has to be looked at on its own merits.
If you have a case where you think you can disregard some or all of a client's cash assets, contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances before you make your decision.

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances for reapplication — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances for reapplication
If a client has an exceptional circumstance that affects their ability to reapply or contact MSD before their expiry date, they may be granted an extension on or after the expiry date to complete their reapplication.
An extension may be granted for up to 20 working days starting on their expiry date, on the condition that the client completes their reapplication within the extension period.
A situation or event is considered to be an exceptional circumstance when it:
- is unforeseen, out-of-the ordinary and could not be planned for, and
- is beyond the client's control, and
- sets the client apart from others in a similar situation, and
- happened at any time during the client's notice period
MSD may request evidence of the client's exceptional circumstances. The evidence required depends on the reason of the exceptional circumstance of the client.
If a client does not complete the reapplication process within the extension period or no longer qualifies for Jobseeker Support, their benefit will be cancelled from the expiry date. The amount of benefit (including any Extra Help) that was conditionally paid during the extension period must be established as a debt.
## Exceptional circumstances
The following exceptional circumstances can be accepted:
- Unforeseen hospitalisation
- Seriously sick or injured
- Bereavement of immediate family
- Victim of violent crime (including family violence)
- Other exceptional circumstances
## Applying as a new applicant
If the client does not complete their reapplication within the extension period, or were not granted an extension, they must apply as a new applicant if they still need Jobseeker Support. Their expired benefit must be cancelled from the expiry date before they can be granted Jobseeker Support as a new applicant.
The client will be subject to the usual commencement date rules, including the initial stand-down.
For more information see:
- Commencement date
- Initial stand-down
Note if the client advises they want to apply for Jobseeker Support as a new applicant and completes the reapplication form, MSD can use their reapplication form as their new application.

chunks.title: Exceptions - rate of payment 18 or 19 year olds — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Exceptions - rate of payment 18 or 19 year olds
The full rate can be paid to clients aged 18 or 19 years in the following situations.
## Living in the same house as the parent
The full rate of Jobseeker Support can be paid to 18 or 19 year olds who live in the same house as their parents if:
- the parent is financially dependent on the client
- the client provides accommodation for the parent at their own expense
- the client provides a large amount of care to the parent or
- the home is a hostel, boarding house or similar and the client and the parent each pay their own accommodation costs
## Living on the same property as the parent
If the client lives on the same property as the parent but not in the same house (for example in a caravan or sleep-out), they can receive the full rate of payment if they are paying rent plus their own expenses.

chunks.title: Exemptions — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Exemptions
Exemptions from obligations may apply as there are a number of specific reasons why it is unreasonable to expect a client to meet their work preparation obligations or work obligations for a specified period.
A client can be granted an exemption from some or all of their work preparation or work obligations. Proof may be required before an exemption is granted.
## Clients with a deferral from their work obligations
Clients who have been a deferral from their work obligations, still have work preparation obligations. These clients may also qualify for an exemption from their work preparation obligations if they are unable to plan towards a return to work.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions
If you think the client or partner should be granted a temporary exemption, add the exemption on the SWTDA screen using the appropriate reason code. You must also add an expiry date.
Note a temporary exemption for partners with a health condition, injury or disability is entered in the SINCC screen. This means the partner's medical information is applied the same as if they were a primary client. For more information see:
## Duration of the exemption
Each exemption has a specific duration for which it can be granted. In some instances these can be extended (if appropriate).

chunks.title: Young partners without dependent children — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Young partners without dependent children
Young partners without dependent children can be granted a full or partial exemption from their youth activity obligations for the following reasons:
- Caring for foster child under 12 months old
- Caring full-time for a spouse or partner with a health condition, injury, or disability
- Court imposed conditions
- Family violence (young partners)
- Would qualify for Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability
- Would qualify for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability
## Young partners with dependent children
Young partners with dependent children can be granted a full or partial exemption from their youth activity obligations for the following reasons:
- Caring for a child with special needs
- Caring for foster child under 12 months old
- Caring full-time for a spouse or partner with a health condition, injury, or disability
- Court imposed conditions
- Family violence (young partners)
- Would qualify for Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability
- Would qualify for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability
The young partner can be granted a temporary exemption from some or all of their activity obligations. Proof may be required before an exemption is granted.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions (young partners)
## Processing exemptions
Service centres process exemptions for young partners.
If the young partner is granted an exemption, add the exemption on the SWTDA screen using the appropriate reason code. You must also add an expiry date.

chunks.title: Expiry date — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The expiry date for Jobseeker Support is: - 26 weeks from the date that the client's Jobseeker Support commenced, or last commenced. This is when the client: applies for and is granted Jobseeker Support, orcompletes their reapplication on time and their Jobseeker Support is regranted, oris transferred to Jobseeker Support from any other main benefit. - applies for and is granted Jobseeker Support, or - completes their reapplication on time and their Jobseeker Support is regranted, or - is transferred to Jobseeker Support from any other main benefit. Note if a client's expiry date falls in the week immediately before or including 26 December, their benefit will continue to be paid until the first Monday following 2 January. Their expiry date does not change. For more information see: - Expiry date falls in the week immediately before or including 26 December

chunks.title: Exception — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The expiry date for clients who automatically transfer from Sole Parent Support to Jobseeker Support when their youngest dependent child turns 14 years old is: - 52 weeks from the date the Sole Parent Support last commenced (meaning the Sole Parent Support expiry date is retained), or - 26 weeks from the Jobseeker Support commencement date whichever is earlier. When a client completes their reapplication and is regranted Jobseeker Support, their next expiry date is 26 weeks from the new commencement date. For more information see: - Transfer from Sole Parent Support when youngest child turns 14 years old

chunks.title: Clients who were getting Jobseeker Support before 1 July 2025 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Some clients who were getting Jobseeker Support before 1 July 2025 and are still getting their benefit on 1 July 2025 will retain their current 52 week expiry date. This is a transitional arrangement. This applies to the following clients only: - clients whose Jobseeker Support commenced (or last commenced) before 4 February 2025, or - sole parent or grandparented clients whose Jobseeker Support commenced (or last commenced) before 1 July 2025, or - clients who have an 'in-flight' 52 week reapplication on 1 July 2025. When these clients complete their reapplication process before their final 52 week expiry date and their Jobseeker Support is regranted, they move to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. Note clients whose Jobseeker Support commenced (or last commenced) after 3 February 2025 but before 1 July 2025, had their expiry date adjusted to be 26 weeks from their last commencement date if they were still getting their benefit on 1 July 2025. For more information see: - Expiry date for sole parent and grandparented clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025 - Clients who have an 'in-flight' 52 week reapplication on 1 July 2025 - Completing the 26 week reapplication process - 52 week reapplication process for clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025

chunks.title: Expiry date reset — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The expiry date is not reset by any periods of temporary suspension or expiries. The expiry date is only affected if a client: - has their Jobseeker Support cancelled for any reason, or - transfers to another benefit type that is not Jobseeker Support and then transfers back to Jobseeker Support, or - was a partner and has separated from a primary Jobseeker Support client, and has been granted Jobseeker Support in their own right. The primary client's expiry date remains the same. For more information see: - Examples of when the expiry date is reset

chunks.title: Expiry date falls in the week immediately before or including 26 December — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client's expiry date falls in the week immediately before or including 26 December, their Jobseeker Support can continue to be paid until the first Monday after 2 January. The client must complete the reapplication process before that Monday to continue getting Jobseeker Support. The client's expiry date does not change in this situation. This mean if a client completes the reapplication process and continues to be entitled to get Jobseeker Support, their benefit will be regranted from the expiry date, not from the first Monday after 2 January. Note when a client’s expiry date falls in the week immediately before or including 26 December, the ‘initial notice to reapply’ letter will be sent 25 working days before their expiry date.

chunks.title: Example 1 - Expiry date falls in the week immediately before 26 December — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Zari’s Jobseeker Support expires on 17 December 2025, which falls in the week immediately before 26 December. Her Jobseeker Support will continue to be paid until 5 January 2026, which is the first Monday after 2 January. She must complete the reapplication process before 5 January. Zari completes the reapplication process on time and continues to qualify for Jobseeker Support. Her benefit is regranted from the expiry date, 17 December 2025.

chunks.title: Example 2 - Expiry date falls in the week including 26 December — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Arin’s Jobseeker Support expires on 22 December 2026, which falls in the week of 26 December. His Jobseeker Support will continue to be paid until 4 January 2027, which is the first Monday after 2 January. He must complete the reapplication process before 4 January 2027. Arin completes the reapplication process on time and continues to qualify for Jobseeker Support. His benefit is regranted from the expiry date, 22 December 2026.

chunks.title: Example 3 - Expiry date does not fall within the week immediately before or including 26 December — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Melia's Jobseeker Support expires on 31 December 2027. As the expiry date does not fall within the week immediately before or including 26 December her payments will stop on 31 December 2027, her expiry date. Melia's Jobseeker Support will be cancelled if she does not complete the reapplication process before the expiry date.

chunks.title: Date the payment stops when the expiry date falls in the week before or including 26 December — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Year Week before 26 December Week including 26 December Expiry date range Date payments stop 2025 15 to 21 December 22 to 28 December 15 to 28 December Monday, 5 January 2026 2026 14 to 20 December 21 to 27 December 14 to 27 December Monday, 4 January 2027 2027 13 to 19 December 20 to 26 December 13 to 26 December Monday, 3 January 2028 2028 18 to 24 December 25 to 31 December 18 to 31 December Monday, 8 January 2029

chunks.title: Expiry date for clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Some clients whose benefit commenced (or last commenced) before 1 July 2025 maintain their 52 week expiry date before moving to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. These clients move to the new cycle once they complete the 26 week reapplication process before their final 52 week expiry date. This depends on when their benefit commenced (or last commenced), and applies to the following client groups only: - Clients whose benefit commenced (or last commenced) before 4 February 2025, or - Sole parent or grandparented clients whose Jobseeker Support commenced (or last commenced) before 1 July 2025, or - Clients who have an 'in-flight' 52 week reapplication on 1 July 2025. For information, see: - Clients who have an 'in-flight' 52 week reapplication on 1 July 2025 - Expiry date for sole parent and grandparented clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025

chunks.title: Jobseeker Support commenced before 4 February 2025 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The expiry date for clients whose benefit commenced (or last commenced) before 4 February 2024 and who are still getting Jobseeker Support on 1 July 2025, is 52 weeks from their last commencement date. When these clients complete the 26 week reapplication process at their final 52 week expiry date and are regranted Jobseeker Support, they move to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. Example 1 Nicole's Jobseeker Support commenced on 20 November 2024, with her partner included in her benefit. Her expiry date is 20 November 2025, which is 52 weeks from her commencement date. As Nicole's Jobseeker Support commenced before 4 February 2025, she maintains her expiry date, 20 November 2025. Nicole and her partner complete the 26 week reapplication process before their final 52 week expiry date. She and her partner continue to qualify for and is regranted Jobseeker Support from 20 November 2025. Nicole moves to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. Her new expiry is 21 May 2026, which is 26 weeks from her new commencement date.

chunks.title: Jobseeker Support commenced on or after 4 February 2025 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The expiry date for clients whose benefit commenced (or last commenced) on or after 4 February but before 1 July 2025 is initially set at 52 weeks. On 1 July 2025, the expiry date for these clients was adjusted to be 26 weeks from their last commencement date. Example 1 Hoani has been getting Jobseeker Support which last commenced on 15 May 2025. His expiry date is initially set as 15 May 2026, which is 52 weeks from his last commencement date. Hoani was still getting Jobseeker Support on 1 July 2025 and was moved to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. His expiry date is adjusted to 13 November 2025, which is 26 weeks from his last commencement date, 15 May 2025. Example 2 Noor applies for and is granted Jobseeker Support with her partner and 16 year old dependent child included. Her commencement date is 4 July 2025. As Noor's Jobseeker Support commenced on or after 1 July 2025 her expiry date is 2 January 2026, which is 26 weeks from her commencement date.

chunks.title: Expiry date for sole parent and grandparented clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The expiry date for sole parent and grandparented clients whose benefit commenced (or last commenced) before 1 July 2025 is 52 weeks from their last commencement date. When these clients complete the 26 week reapplication process before their final 52 week expiry date on or after 1 July 2025 and are regranted Jobseeker Support, they move to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. By 30 June 2026 all sole parent and grandparented clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025 will have moved to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle.

chunks.title: Example 1 – commenced before 1 July 2025 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Kahira's Jobseeker Support commenced on 20 September 2024, with her 15 year old dependent child included in her benefit. Her expiry date is 20 September 2025, which is 52 weeks from her commencement date. As a sole parent getting Jobseeker Support, Kahira has her income assessed annually. Because she has income assessed annually and her Jobseeker Support commenced before 1 July 2025, Kahira maintains her expiry date, 20 September 2025. Kahira completes the 26 week reapplication process before her final 52 week expiry date. She continues to be entitled to get Jobseeker Support and it is regranted from 20 September 2025. Kahira moves to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. Her next expiry date is 21 March 2026, which is 26 weeks from her new commencement date.

chunks.title: Example 2 – commenced before 1 July 2025 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Ty's Jobseeker Support commenced on 30 June 2025, with their 16 and 17 year old dependent children included in their benefit. Ty's expiry date is 30 June 2026, which is 52 weeks from their commencement date. As a sole parent getting Jobseeker Support, Ty has their income assessed annually. Because their income is assessed annually and their Jobseeker Support commenced before 1 July 2025, Ty maintains their expiry date, 30 June 2026. Ty is sent their initial notice to reapply letter and must complete the 26 week reapplication process before their final 52 week expiry date if they still need Jobseeker Support. If Ty continues to qualify for and is regranted Jobseeker Support they will move to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. Their next expiry date will be 29 December 2026, which is 26 weeks from their new commencement date (30 June 2026).

chunks.title: Example 3 – last commenced before 1 July 2025 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Suriya was getting Widows Benefit before 15 July 2013 and was transferred to Jobseeker Support. Suriya has continued getting a grandparented rate of Jobseeker Support and her benefit last commenced on 23 July 2024. Suriya’s next expiry date is 23 July 2025, which is 52 weeks from their last commencement date. As a grandparented client getting Jobseeker Support, Suriya has her income assessed annually. Because her income is assessed annually and her Jobseeker Support last commenced before 1 July 2025, Suriya maintains her expiry date, 23 July 2025. On 1 July 2025, Suriya has an 'in-flight' reapplication and completes her final 52 week reapplication process before 23 July 2025. Suriya continues to qualify for and is regranted Jobseeker Support from 23 July 2025. Suriya moves to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. Her next expiry date is 21 January 2026, which is 26 weeks from her new commencement date. For more information see: - Clients who have an 'in-flight' 52 week reapplication on 1 July 2025

chunks.title: Example 4 – commenced on 1 July 2025 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Alex applies for and is granted Jobseeker Support with his 15 year old dependent child included in his benefit. His commencement date is 7 July 2025. As Alex's Jobseeker Support commenced on or after 1 July 2025, the 26 week expiry and reapplication settings apply. Alex's expiry date is 5 January 2026, which is 26 weeks from his commencement date.

chunks.title: Payments that can be redirected — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Payments that can be redirected
Most ongoing extra help payments paid to a young partner are included in the redirection of payment if the young person is under youth money management, for example:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- family tax credit
- Winter Energy Payment
Note because Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support and family tax credit can only be paid to one person, for couples, the person getting the payment is generally responsible for any debt created.
## Payments that are not redirected
The following payments are not included in youth money management and can be paid to the young person, their agent (if authorised) or a supplier (as appropriate):
- Disability Allowance
- Child Disability Allowance
- Flexible Childcare Assistance
- one-off payments of hardship assistance, for example Special Needs Grants for food
- any Advance Payment of Benefits
If the young person qualifies for any of the above payments, MSD will decide who the payment goes to after talking with the young person's youth service provider (if one is assigned to the young person).
## Hardship obligations do not apply to clients who have youth activity obligations
Young partners who are required to get Youth Services will not have hardship obligations if they are accessing Special Needs Grants or Advance Payment of Benefits.
These young people are already working with their service provider or MSD 'in-house' service, on activities that already meet the budgeting activity or reasonable steps hardship obligations.
Generally, all clients and their partners, who apply for Special Needs Grants, Advance Payment of Benefits and Recoverable Assistance Payments, have hardship obligations.
Hardship obligations include:
- a reasonable steps obligation and
- a budgeting activity obligation
Generally, clients must meet their hardship obligations before they get any additional payments.
These obligations do not apply to:
- payments to people in specific circumstance
- young people getting youth support payments (Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment) or have youth activity obligations and are required to get Youth Services

chunks.title: Failing a social obligation — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Failing a social obligation
If a client and their partner have received regular engagement and support, and they are still not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, they still need to attend a final appointment.
A social obligations failure can be initiated when you consider that a client and partner have, without a good and sufficient reason, failed to meet their social obligations by:
- not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations following the process of regular engagement and support (that involves at least 3 contact steps) or
- not attending the final appointment during their regular engagement and support process
Before you initiate an obligations failure for social obligations you must get your manager client service delivery approval. An obligation failure should only be used when all other efforts to encourage engagement and support with the client have been exhausted.

chunks.title: Failing more than one obligation at the same time — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Failing more than one obligation at the same time
If a client fails more than one obligation or activity at the same time and does not have a good and sufficient reason for one or more of the failures, the failures are counted as one failure. However, the client will need to recomply with all the failures before the sanction can be lifted.
Note Money Management is the only non-financial sanction that can be imposed when a client has failed more than one obligation at the same time at grade 1. A client must resolve all of these failures during the 4-week Money Management period in order to recomply.
For grade 1 and 2 failures, if the client successfully disputes one of the failures, the sanction imposed will remain until they recomply with any remaining failures initiated at the same time.
This policy only applies to the first and second time a client or partner fails their obligations in a 24-month period, or 12-month period for a partner if they have youth activity obligations.
For grade 3 failures, a client will need to complete one 6 week approved activity or programme of activities (if they wish to recomply).
Note Disability Allowance can continue to be paid during a non-entitlement period.
## Initiating the failures on the same day
The obligations or activities that a client or their partner has not complied with can be over a recent period (eg within the last five days) or they may not have been complied with all on the same day. However, the client or partner can only be required to recomply with failures that are initiated on the same day.
As soon as MSD is aware that a client or their partner has failed their obligations without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must initiate an obligations failure – it cannot be delayed.
For more information see:
- Work obligations
- Work preparation obligations
- Social obligations
- Drug test obligations
- Recompliance
- Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Failing to complete the 26 week reapplication process — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Failing to complete the 26 week reapplication process
If a client does not complete the 26 week reapplication process before their expiry date, their Jobseeker Support will stop.
Note the benefit will automatically cancel if a client does not complete the reapplication process within 20 working days after the expiry date.
## Client still needs Jobseeker Support
Clients who fail to complete the 26 week reapplication process but still need Jobseeker Support must be advised to apply for a benefit as a new applicant (unless the client is granted an extension). Their expired benefit must be cancelled from the expiry date before they can be granted Jobseeker Support.
The client will be subject to the usual commencement date rules, including the initial stand-down.
Note if the client advises they want to apply for Jobseeker Support as a new applicant, MSD can use their reapplication form as their new application.
## Extra help
If a client does not apply for Jobseeker Support as a new applicant, they may qualify for Extra Help assistance as a non-beneficiary (such as Accommodation Supplement). The client should be advised to apply as a non-beneficiary if they wish to test their entitlement to Extra Help assistance.

chunks.title: Failing the 52 week reapplication process or applying as a new applicant — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Some clients who were getting Jobseeker Support before 1 July 2025 and are still getting their benefit on 1 July 2025 maintain their 52 week expiry date. These clients must complete the 52 week reapplication process before their expiry date. If they complete their reapplication and are regranted Jobseeker Support they will move to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. This applies to the following clients only: - clients who have an 'in-flight' reapplication For more information see: - 52 week reapplication process for clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025 - Expiry date for sole parent and grandparented clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025 - Expiry date for clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025

chunks.title: Failing to compete the 52 week reapplication process — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client does not complete their final 52 week reapplication process before their expiry date, their Jobseeker Support will stop.

chunks.title: Effect on payments due to not completing 52 week reapplication process — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The table below outlines how payments will be impacted if a client and/or their partner (if any) fails to complete the 52 week reapplication process. Clients Partners (if any) (even if the client has completed their requirements) With work obligations With work preparation or no work obligations Effect of not completing the reapplication Full benefit stops Full benefit stops Client and partner portion of benefit stops Effect of not completing the Comprehensive Work Assessment Full benefit stops Obligations failure imposed on the partner's portion of the benefit. (unless there is a good and sufficient reason) N/A Effect of not attending the reapplication appointment Full benefit stops Full benefit stops N/A

chunks.title: Client still needs Jobseeker Support — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients who fail to complete their final 52 week reapplication process, but still need Jobseeker Support must be advised to apply for a benefit as a new applicant (unless the client is granted an extension). Their expired benefit must be cancelled from the expiry date before they can be granted Jobseeker Support. The client will be subject to the usual commencement date rules, including the initial stand-down. Note if the client advises they want to apply for Jobseeker Support as a new applicant and completes the reapplication form, MSD can use their reapplication form as their new application.

chunks.title: Expiry date — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: When a client is granted Jobseeker Support as a new applicant, their expiry date will be 26 weeks from the new commencement date.

chunks.title: Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations
A client and their partner (if any), when required, must:
- attend and participate in interviews with Work and Income to discuss compliance with their social obligations and
- report on compliance with specific social obligations
If during any of the 3 steps of engagement and support, the client does not attend or participate in interviews with Work and Income to discuss compliance with their social obligations or report on compliance with specific social obligations, you should move to the next steps of engagement and support.
For more information on the 3 step process of engagement see:
- Contact steps - social obligations [no link find out why]
- Failure to comply following engagement and support process
- Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Failure to comply following regular engagement and support — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Failure to comply following regular engagement and support
Clients will need to attend a final appointment if they are still not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations after the three step process of regular engagement and support.
A social obligations failure will only be initiated when you consider that a client has, without a good and sufficient reason, failed to meet their social obligations by:
- not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations following the three stage process of regular engagement and support and
- does not attend the final appointment, or attends and is still not meeting their social obligations, following the three stage process engagement and support
Before you initiate an obligations failure for social obligations you must get your Service Centre Manager's approval. A social obligation failure should only be used when all other efforts to encourage engagement and support the client have been exhausted.

chunks.title: Failure within the position period - good and sufficient reason — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Failure within the position period - good and sufficient reason
A client must be able to complete 5 hours of Community Work Experience each week during the 4-week period.
The position duties or conditions may change during this period and make it impossible or unreasonable for the client to complete their Community Work Experience.
A client must inform MSD as soon as possible that they are no longer able to complete their Community Work Experience so that MSD may place them onto an alternative recompliance pathway.
A Grade 1 financial sanction will be imposed from the date MSD has been informed and is satisfied that they are unable to complete their position and a recompliance activity must be arranged for the client to complete as soon as possible.
Example
Marco has had Community Work Experience imposed and is searching for a suitable position. Marco quickly found a suitable position doing odd jobs at his church.
This worked well for the first 2 weeks, but in week 3 there was very little for Marco to do and the church only needed him for 2 hours that week. He contacted MSD to let them know he would not have enough hours for this week.
As this is a change outside Marco's control, MSD informs him that his period of Community Work Experience will be ended, and a financial sanction is imposed from that day. MSD also arranges the first available recompliance activity he can complete, so that Marco can recomply quickly and his payments can return to normal as soon as possible.'
Example
Marcia started a Community Work Experience position with her local sports club. One of the volunteers hears that Marcia is there because she's on a benefit and this position is a sanction for her.
They tell other people who volunteer there and some people start picking on her, making unkind comments about why she's there. Marcia feels very uncomfortable and contacts MSD to let them know what's happening.
MSD decides that the position is no longer appropriate for Marcia to complete, because she's being bullied and feels unsafe. MSD imposes a replacement sanction from that day and arranges for her to do a different recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Failure within the search period - good and sufficient reason — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Failure within the search period - good and sufficient reason
A client may inform MSD at the end of their 2-week search period that they have made a reasonable effort to find a position and have been unsuccessful.
If MSD is satisfied that the client made a reasonable effort to find a position, a Grade 1 financial sanction will be imposed from the day after the search period ends and a recompliance activity must be arranged for the client to complete as soon as possible.
## Client contacts MSD in the middle of the search period
A client may advise MSD before their search period ends that they will be unable to find a suitable position. For example, if a client lives in a small community and has not been able to find a position at any local organisations in the first 10 days.
MSD can consider this a good and sufficient reason if it is satisfied that the client made a reasonable effort and it is unrealistic that the client will find a position by the end of the search period. A Grade 1 financial sanction will be imposed from the date MSD has been informed and determines the client has a good and sufficient reason for failing to find a suitable position.
## Client finds suitable position that does not begin within the first week of position period
If a client finds a suitable position but it does not begin within the first week of the position period, it does not meet the requirements for Community Work Experience.
A client may continue looking for a position during the 2-week search period if it is reasonable for them to do so.
MSD may consider the client to have a good and sufficient reason for failing to find Community Work Experience from the:
- day the position is confirmed to be unsuitable, if it is not reasonable for the client to find another position by the end of the search period or
- day after the 2-week search period ends, if the client makes a reasonable effort to find another position but is unsuccessful.
A Grade 1 financial sanction will be imposed from the date MSD has been informed and determines the client has a good and sufficient reason for failing to find a suitable position.

chunks.title: Family Stream — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Family Stream
The purpose of the Family Stream is to help reunite families in New Zealand by granting residence to the family members of New Zealand citizens and residents. The family member living in New Zealand sponsors the applicant applying for permanent residence.
The Family Stream includes Family categories (Partnership, Parent, Sibling and Adult Child, Dependent Child and Parent Retirement Category).
For clients granted permanent residence under the Family Stream (except the Dependent Child Policy and Parent Retirement Category), the sponsor has signed a declaration they will support the client and their family (if any) for up to 5 years of residence in New Zealand or until they can sustain themselves.
Clients must have 2 years continuous residence in New Zealand to be entitled to Jobseeker Support. Until they have met this requirement Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship may be considered.
Note if a client has permanent residence and already meets the 2 years continuous residence, assess the client for Jobseeker Support in the usual manner.
When assessing the client's entitlement to Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship, the sponsor's financial circumstances are not used in the assessment. However, any assistance given to the client and family (if any) must be used in the assessment.
Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship is both income and asset tested. To assess a client's entitlement to Jobseeker Support confirmation of the client's income and assets declared on the application for permanent residence is required from Immigration New Zealand.
Despite the requirement for immigrants to maintain themselves for a number of years they may still be able to access assistance as non-beneficiaries.
If the client has a change in personal resources, confirmation of that change is required.
For more information see:
- Permanent residence
- Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship
- Change in personal resources

chunks.title: Family tax credit — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Family tax credit
Young partners receiving Jobseeker Support will be paid family tax credit along with their benefit. They cannot receive it from Inland Revenue.
Family tax credit can only be paid to one person in a couple. Generally it is paid to the primary caregiver.
Inland Revenue is responsible for establishing and recovering any debt created.
Note a young partner cannot review the decision on how their portion of Jobseeker Support is paid to them.

chunks.title: Family violence (young partners) — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Family violence (young partners)
A young partner who has left a situation of family violence may be exempt from meeting all of their activity obligations until they have had time to adjust to their new living circumstances. This is a full exemption.
## Definition of family or domestic violence
Family violence is a term used to describe violence within the family and close personal relationships.
Family violence covers a broad range of controlling behaviours which typically involve fear, intimidation and emotional deprivation.
Family violence is defined as:
- physical abuse
- sexual abuse
- psychological abuse including but not limited to intimidation, harassment, damage to property or threats of physical, sexual or psychological abuse
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 3 months.
## Proof
Young people who have recently left situations of family or domestic violence will not have to provide proof.
If a young partner still needs an exemption after 3 months you can ask for proof.
Proof can include statements from:
- their doctor
- their church
- their lawyer
- the police
- Women's Refuge
- any other person or organisation that is able to support the young partner's application
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Family Violence'.

chunks.title: Family violence — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Family violence
This exemption may apply to primary clients, partners and sole parents with work or work preparation obligations.
A client who has left a situation of family violence may be exempt from meeting all their work obligations or work preparation obligations until they have had time to adjust to their new living circumstances. This is a full exemption.
You should talk to the regional Family Violence Response Co-ordinator before granting an exemption. You should also consider:
- Is the client living in temporary refuge accommodation while they seek a permanent home?
- Are they helping children adjust to a new family situation?
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 3 months.
## Proof
Clients who have recently left situations of family violence will not have to provide proof.
If a client still needs an exemption after 3 months you can ask for proof. You should consult the regional Family Violence Response Co-ordinator for advice on the most appropriate way to proceed.
Proof can include statements from:
- their doctor
- their church
- their lawyer
- the police
- Women's Refuge
- any other person or organisation that is able to support the client's application
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Family Violence'.

chunks.title: Exemptions or transfers — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Exemptions or transfers
In some instances it may be appropriate to consider an exemption or a transfer to another benefit that does not have work obligations.
For more information on transfers and exemptions see:
- Jobseeker Support - client has a health condition, injury, or disability
- Exemptions
- Changes and reviews Client qualifies for another benefit
## Special Needs Grants
Clients are not entitled to a Special Needs Grant if a sanction has been imposed, unless they become:
- sick or injured and
- incapable of participating in employment or an approved activity for at least 6 weeks
In this case, the client can get more than one Special Needs Grant, but the amount granted in any one week cannot be more than the combined total of:
- what the client would be entitled to that week if they were entitled to Jobseeker Support and
- the rate of Accommodation Supplement that the applicant would have gotten
For more information see:
- Effect of a non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Assistance when a client is sanctioned
## Recoverable Assistance Payments
Generally clients will not be entitled to Recoverable Assistance Payments when they are subject to a non-entitlement period. This is because they will be contributing to their hardship through not recomplying. The client's first option is to recomply. A Recoverable Assistance Payment cannot be paid when the client has no means of repaying it.
## Advance Payment of Benefit
Generally, clients whose benefit continues to be paid (i.e. clients with dependent children) will not be entitled to an Advance Payment of Benefit when they have a 13 week non-entitlement period imposed. This is because they will be contributing to their hardship through not recomplying. The client's first option to improve their financial situation is to recomply.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Financial support from a sponsor — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Financial support from a sponsor
Where the client was granted permanent residence because a sponsor was to support them for their first two to five years in New Zealand (supplied in writing), you must contact the sponsor to confirm the situation.
Note if the client has resided in New Zealand for 2 years, no contact with the sponsor is required and assess the client's entitlement to Jobseeker Support in the usual manner.
You will also need to obtain information from Immigration New Zealand to confirm the reason for granting permanent residence. Ensure you have the consent of the client before contacting Immigration New Zealand.
Once confirmed, assess Jobseeker Support in the usual manner taking into account all other information provided by Immigration New Zealand.
Generally, where the client elects not to accept support from the sponsor without a valid reason decline the application for Jobseeker Support or grant the Jobseeker Support at a reduced rate.

chunks.title: Five-day verification window — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Five-day verification window
A client must provide MSD with verification of their Community Work Experience before the end of the 2-week search period, and at the end of their position period. This is to verify that they have:
- found a position with an organisation during the 2-week search period, and
- completed all the requirements of their Community Work Experience during the 4-week period.
However, there may be times when MSD is not able to process the information within that same period.
To prevent a client from being disadvantaged due to processing delays, there is a 5-day verification window at the end of the 2-week search period and at the end of the position period. This allows MSD to process information a client has provided and ensures a client's payment will continue.
Note this is not extra time for a client to secure a position or provide verification to MSD. Clients must still complete their search and provide verification before the end of the 2-week search period.
## No action from MSD
The client will be considered non-compliant if, after 5 days:
- MSD has not confirmed if the position is suitable (or unsuitable) for their Community Work Experience, or
- MSD has not been able to confirm if the client has completed their Community Work Experience, or
- the client has not provided the required verification for either their search period or position period.
Their payments will suspend or reduce from the day after the search period or the position period ended, depending on which verification window was in place. This may result in a debt for the client.

chunks.title: Full or partial exemptions — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Full or partial exemptions
A client or partner may be granted a temporary exemption from meeting some or all of their work obligations or work preparation obligations.
Before MSD grants an exemption, it must check if the exemption reason is full or partial (or both).
The client or partner can be granted a partial exemption from their work obligations, if they can still:
- plan for employment and
- undertake some work related activities
If the client or partner is not able to do either of the above they should be granted a full exemption.
A client or partner who has a full exemption from their work obligations may still be required to attend an interview with MSD to discuss their circumstances, and when it might be appropriate for them to start planning towards a return to work.
## Partners with work preparation obligations
Generally, partners with work preparation obligations can only be considered for a full exemption.
Work preparation obligations mean they are required to plan for employment and undertake work preparation activities - the equivalent of a partial exemption.
## Duration
Each exemption has a maximum duration. The period an exemption is granted will depend on the client's circumstances.
At the time of granting the exemption MSD should:
- advise the client or partner of the temporary nature of the exemption and
- schedule a date to review the exemption, if appropriate
At the review MSD should consider the client's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption. MSD can ask the client to provide evidence that their exemption should be extended.
Note the period of an exemption for partners or sole parents with a health condition, injury or disability will be based on the next reassessment date recorded on their medical certificate by their registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant).

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure
You need to be satisfied that the client or partner does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their obligations, based on the information you have, before you initiate an obligations failure.
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'. Having considered the circumstances, was it reasonable for the client or partner not to have met their obligations?
For social obligations you will need to assess whether the client and their partner are taking all reasonable steps to meet all of their social obligations for each dependent child.
Good and sufficient reasons will depend on the obligation the client or partner has failed. For more information see:
- Social obligations All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation
- Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Drug test obligation failures good and sufficient reasons
- Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation
- Good and sufficient reason for failing obligation to work with a contracted service provider
Decide in favour of the client or partner if any doubt remains.
If you are aware that the client or partner has a good and sufficient reason, do not initiate an obligations failure.
If the client or partner does not have a good and sufficient reason, see:
- Effect of sanctions on assistance
- Failing more than one obligation at the same time

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for failure to complete Report Job Search — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: A client may be unable to complete Report Job Search for a good and sufficient reason.
