These reasons may include, but are not limited to, the client: - was unable to complete and/or report on the required number of job-search activities in any one of the four weeks due to reasons outside of their control, for example: there was a death or serious illness in the client's familythey were sick or injured within the sanction period and this impacted their ability to complete the required number of job-search activitiesthey had an unexpected event occur (e.g. they were involved in an accident that affected their ability to complete the required number of job-search activities) - there was a death or serious illness in the client's family - they were sick or injured within the sanction period and this impacted their ability to complete the required number of job-search activities - they had an unexpected event occur (e.g. they were involved in an accident that affected their ability to complete the required number of job-search activities) - faced an unsafe environment while completing their job-search activities - could no longer report and/or complete their job-search activities as the device they were using was unavailable (through loss, damage, or theft) and they were unable to access another device or get to their nearest service centre Note before deciding there was a good and sufficient reason for not completing a job-search activity (e.g. an unsafe environment or their device not being available), MSD should consider if the client could have completed a different activity or used different methods to meet Report Job Search requirements.

chunks.title: Notifying MSD within a reasonable period — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client is delayed in notifying MSD of their good and sufficient reason, the delay must only be for a reasonable period. MSD will determine on a case-by-case basis whether the length of the delay is reasonable or not. If MSD determines that they are unable to complete Report Job Search for a good and sufficient reason, and a client has notified MSD within a reasonable period, MSD must impose a Grade 1 financial sanction. The date the financial sanction is imposed depends on when MSD determines the client has a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete their Report Job Search requirements. MSD must also assign a recompliance activity to the client as soon as possible. Note if a client informs MSD of a good and sufficient reason within a reasonable period, but after the Report Job Search sanction period has ended, a replacement sanction can no longer be imposed. They must be given a different recompliance activity to complete, after which their payments can be increased or resumed.

chunks.title: No good and sufficient reason — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete Report Job Search, or they did not notify MSD within a reasonable period, they will be considered non-compliant.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for failure to find or complete Community Work Experience — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason for failure to find or complete Community Work Experience
A client may be unable to find or complete Community Work Experience for a good and sufficient reason. These reasons may include, but are not limited to:
- a client has made reasonable efforts to find a position but has not found one during the 2-week search period – for example, if a client has contacted many volunteer organisations but they do not have any available positions
- they are unable to complete the required hours in any of the 4 weeks for reasons beyond their control
- the conditions of the organisation and/or requirements of the position make it unsafe for the client to continue
If a client is delayed in notifying MSD of their good and sufficient reason, the delay must only be for a reasonable period. MSD will determine on a case-by-case basis whether the length of the delay is reasonable or not.
If MSD determines that they are unable to complete Community Work Experience for a good and sufficient reason, and a client has notified MSD within a reasonable period, MSD must impose a Grade 1 financial sanction. The date the financial sanction is imposed depends on where the client is in their Community Work Experience period.
When a client is in their search or position period, the Grade 1 financial sanction is imposed from the day a client meets with MSD and MSD is satisfied there is a good and sufficient reason and they have notified MSD within a reasonable period.
When a client's search period has finished and they did not secure a position, the Grade 1 financial sanction is imposed from the day after the search period ended.
MSD must assign a recompliance activity to the client as soon as possible.
If a client does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to find or complete Community Work Experience, or they did not notify MSD within a reasonable period, they will be considered non-compliant.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation
Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting work ability assessment obligations include (but are not limited to) when a client is:
- in hospital
- experiencing an acute mental health episode
For more information see:
- Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting work or work preparation obligations
Note if a client refuses to complete a Self-Assessment or a Work Ability Assessment, and they do not have a good and sufficient reason, they have an obligations failure.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
You need to be satisfied that the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their work or work preparation obligations, based on the information you have, before you initiate an obligations failure.
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'. Having considered the circumstances, was it reasonable for the client not to have met their obligations?
Good and sufficient reasons may include (but are not limited to), that the client:
- was temporarily medically unfit and they have a medical certificate that shows this
- had a death or illness in the immediate family
- could not realistically transport themselves on the day, due to unforeseen circumstances
- had childcare arrangements that fell through on the day, due to unforeseen circumstances
- was dependent on the provision of assistance by Work and Income to complete the activity, and that assistance was not supplied
- had an unexpected event occur on that day, such as providing care for a sick relative
Decide in favour of the client if any doubt remains.
If you are aware that the client has a good and sufficient reason, do not initiate an obligations failure.
If the client does not have a good and sufficient reason, see:
- Effect of sanctions on assistance

chunks.title: Other factors to consider before determining a client has failed to comply — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Other factors to consider before determining a client has failed to comply
You should also consider whether a client has taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligation before deciding that they have failed to comply with their social obligation.
There are also some circumstances where social obligations do not apply. For example, when a child leaves school at age 15 with a Ministry of Education Early Leaving Exemption, the obligation to ensure that child is enrolled in and attending school no longer applies.
Make sure you have provided the client with the appropriate engagement and support before considering that the client has failed their obligation and that this has been recorded in OBMAN.
If the client does not have a good and sufficient reason, see:
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment
You need to consider if there was a good and sufficient reason for the client to stop work.
Examples of good and sufficient reasons for ceasing employment include (but are not limited to) when the client:
- could no longer realistically transport themselves to their employment (e.g. where a client's place of employment has moved)
- had childcare arrangements that were not adequate or fell through
- had an unexpected event occur (e.g. they had to return to the family home in another location to care for a sick relative)
- left the job because the job was outside of their capabilities or the job was not suitable
- had a significant change in conditions of employment that meant the employment was no longer suitable
- needed to take leave without pay to protect their job in the future, eg due to an economic downturn, or an unexpected temporary closure of the premises, as a result of an event such as a fire or flood
- was not able to continue working full-time (and was unable to work reduced hours) as a result of a health condition, illness, or disability and has a medical certificate to show this
Remember you need to consider the circumstances of each case.

chunks.title: Failing 3 obligations in a 24-month period — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Failing 3 obligations in a 24-month period
If a client does not meet their obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, an obligations failure will be initiated and a graduated sanction may be imposed.
The graduated sanction regime applies to all obligations, including social obligations.
If a client fails 3 obligations without a good and sufficient reason in a 24-month period, they are subject to a grade three sanction - 13-week non-entitlement period. This means:
- for clients without dependent children, 3 obligations failures in a 24-month period may result in a benefit cancellation and a 13-week non-entitlement period
- for partnered clients with dependent children, only the partner with a grade 3 failure is affected
- for sole parents with dependent children, 3 obligations failures in a 24-month period will result in a 50% cancellation of benefit for 13 weeks
Note for young partners with youth activity obligations, their obligation failures are only counted for 12 months.
## Job refusal
A client who refuses an offer of suitable employment is subject to a grade 3 sanction, regardless of their failure count in the 24-month period.
Note when an applicant fails their pre-benefit activity to accept an offer of suitable employment, they are not subject to a 13-week non-entitlement period or job refusal failure, as these can only be imposed once a client is getting a main benefit.
For more information see:
- Core policy Pre-benefit requirements
- When the sanction is imposed
- Effect of 13 week non-entitlement period for partner
- Effect of non-entitlement period on financial assistance

chunks.title: Granting on ground of hardship — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Granting on ground of hardship
If a client does not meet the residence qualification of 2 years continuous residence, they must meet the following criteria to be granted Jobseeker Support Hardship:
- they must be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident
- they must be suffering hardship
- they do not qualify for any other benefit and
- they are unable to earn sufficient income to support themselves, their partner and any dependent children
Note the client may qualify for an Emergency Benefit if they:
- cannot meet the job search requirements (caring for an ill or confined partner for example) or
- are under restricted criteria, are in New Zealand on a temporary permit or temporary entry class visa (not a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident)

chunks.title: Hardship criteria — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Hardship criteria
You can consider that a client is in hardship if the client has:
- no other means of supporting themselves and any dependent family
and
- cash assets of or less than: $4,300.00 if the client is single or$7,464.00 if the client is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, or is a sole parent
- $4,300.00 if the client is single or
- $7,464.00 if the client is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, or is a sole parent
See:
- Cash assets
You also need to look at whether the client has recently given any money away or sold any assets.
For more information see:
- Income Sale of assets
There are different criteria for students see:
- Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
In exceptional circumstances you can disregard some of the client's cash assets see:
- Exceptional circumstances for cash assets

chunks.title: Help with paying for the recompliance drug test — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: When a client or partner has failed their drug test obligations the second time, they must agree that they will take and pass a drug test within 25 days of agreeing to do so. Work and Income can help the client meet the full costs of taking the drug test if they cannot meet the cost of the drug test upfront. In this case Work and Income will arrange to cover the cost of the drug test with the provider and then recover the cost from the client by way of debt repayment. In order for Work and Income to help meet the costs of taking the drug test, the client or partner must agree: - to take and pass a drug test within 25 working days - to contact drug test provider and arrange and then take the drug test; and - to provide the results to Work and Income Work and Income will provide the client or partner with names and contact details for drug test providers in the local area. A client or partner can only apply once during the 25 working day period for help with the costs of the recompliance drug test upfront which is then recovered from them. The 25 working days start from the day after the client or partner agrees to recomply. Note that Work and Income has an additional 5 working days to receive the results from the client or partner and to process the information.

chunks.title: Client or partner pays for drug test upfront themselves — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: A client or partner can pay for the recompliance test themselves, if they choose to do this, they must: - take a clean drug test within 25 working days - arrange with a drug test provider to take the drug test and - ensure that they provide Work and Income with the drug test results

chunks.title: Debt recovery and reimbursement to the drug test provider — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Work and Income will arrange with the drug test provider to cover the cost of the drug test. Once the cost of the drug test is reimbursed to the drug test provider it must be established as a debt to the client or partner. The amount of the debt is the same amount that has been repaid to the drug test provider. The recovery rate should be at the appropriate level giving consideration to any other debts the client or partner may have. Debt repayment options must be discussed with the client or partner at the earliest opportunity. This upfront assistance is only available for one recompliance drug test to be undertaken during the 25 working day period. The cost of further tests undertaken within that period will have to be met upfront by the client.

chunks.title: Home schooling — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Home schooling
Clients with dependent children aged five or six years (depending on when they start school) to 16 years of age will be required to take all reasonable steps to ensure the child is enrolled in and attending school. Home schooling meets this obligation in some circumstances.
Clients can home school their children and meet their social obligation if they have a Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School issued by the Ministry of Education.
However, if a client and their partner (if any) have work obligations, generally they won't be able to home school their child as this could impact on their ability to actively seek or be available for work. They may qualify for an exemption from their work obligations to home school their children.
## Certificate of exemption from enrolment at a registered school
A child does not legally have to attend school until they are aged six years (but most children start school at five years). If a child is aged between five and six years it is the parent's or caregiver's choice whether to have their child in early childhood education or school. A Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School issued by the Ministry of Education is not needed while the child is aged five.
Once a child is aged six years a Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School issued by the Ministry of Education is required by law to enable a parent to home school their child.
## Social obligations and work obligations
When a client has work obligations as well as social obligations they must meet both sets of obligations at the same time. If the client is unable to meet their work obligations because they are home schooling a dependent child, you can consider granting an exemption from their work obligations.
The client must meet the additional criteria for the home schooling exemption.
For more information see:
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Home schooling a dependent child (exemptions and deferral JSS)
- Work obligations
- Exemptions

chunks.title: Home schooling a dependent child — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Home schooling a dependent child
This exemption may apply to a partner or sole parent with work obligations.
A client can, in very limited circumstances, be exempt from meeting some of their work obligations:
- if they are home schooling a dependent child or a foster child and
- they have restricted circumstances that make the child's attendance at school unreasonable
Before you grant an exemption you should:
- gather all the proof required
- get the approval of the manager client service delivery to the exemption
This is a partial exemption only.
## Transitional arrangements for a person home schooling a child when they become a beneficiary with work obligations
If a client is home schooling a child before becoming a beneficiary with work obligations, then an exemption can be granted until the end of that school year if they have an exemption certificate from the Ministry of Education.
## Proof
The client must provide:
- proof of the restricted circumstances that makes their child's attendance at school unreasonable and
- if the child is aged 6 years or older, their 'Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School', issued by the Ministry of Education (if it's not a recently issued certificate, the client needs to contact the Ministry of Education to get another certificate)
For an 'Application for exemption from enrolment at a registered school', see the 'Home education application form' link at the bottom of the Home education page (the application form is the same for primary and secondary schooling).
All exemptions for home schooling must be approved by a service centre manager.
For more information see:
- Restricted circumstances guidelines
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for 12 months or the end of the current school year, whichever is earlier.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Home schooling'.

chunks.title: Hours range for suitable employment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients and partners with work obligations must make themselves available for suitable employment of at least: - 30 hours per week for clients with full-time work obligations - 15 hours per week for clients that qualify for Jobseeker Support on the grounds of a health condition, injury, or disability - 20 hours per week for partners with part-time work obligations Although the target to meet work obligations is 15, 20 or 30 hours per week a job can be considered suitable, if the hours of work per week are within the range of hours required to meet their work obligations.

chunks.title: Suitable hours range — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients are expected to apply for, and accept any offers of employment. Client obligations Full-time Part-time (partners) Part-time (HCID) Hours of work required to meet obligations 30 hours 20 hours 15 hours Suitable hours range 20-40 hours 15-25 hours 10-20 hours If a client is offered a job that is within the suitable hours range, but less than their obligations, then they are still expected to be available for other work, training, or other activities until they are meeting their obligations.

chunks.title: Exception — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a position with more hours, but a lower hourly rate, becomes available then this job would only be suitable if the client was financially better off overall. A suitable job would be one with more hours that paid the same or more.

chunks.title: Suitable hours example - full-time work obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: James is a partner with full-time work obligations. A vacancy arises for a forecourt attendant at the petrol station for 25 hours per week. The details of the job suit James circumstances. This job is considered 'suitable employment' and James must apply and accept the job (if it is offered to him) or fail to meet his obligations.

chunks.title: Suitable hours example - part-time obligated partners — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Anna is a partner with a child and has part-time work obligations. She is an experienced hairdresser. A hairdressing vacancy arises for 18 hours per week at the local salon. The details of the job suit Anna's circumstances in all ways, including her caring responsibilities. This job is considered 'suitable employment' and Anna must apply and accept the job (if it is offered to her) or fail to meet her obligations.

chunks.title: Suitable hours example - part-time work obligations because of health condition, injury, or disability — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Alanna has part-time work obligations because she has a health condition that limits her capacity for full-time work. A local factory has an accounts administrator position for 12 hours per week. The details of the job suits Alanna's circumstances. The job is considered 'suitable employment' and Alanna must apply for, and accept the job if it is offered to her, or fail to meet her obligations. For more information see:

chunks.title: Housekeepers Allowance — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Housekeepers Allowance
Housekeepers allowance can be paid to a client if their partner is not receiving a benefit and they have a housekeeper who is:
- caring for the client's home and
- substantially dependent on the client
The rate of allowance payable is the difference between:
- the Jobseeker Support rate payable to the client and
- the married, civil union or de facto rate of Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: Unable to provide visa or permit — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Unable to provide visa or permit
When a client is unable to provide an immigration visa or permit they may provide other Immigration New Zealand documents to verify their immigration status. Work and Income can also undertake an immigration status check directly with Immigration New Zealand.
Note that Immigration New Zealand may be unable to verify immigration status for clients of British nationality who arrived in New Zealand before 2 April 1974 and do not have a passport.
For more information see:
- Two years residence
- Resident in New Zealand
- Refugee or protected person
- Immigration status [no link find out why]
- Immigration Act changes from 29 November 2010 [no link find out why]

chunks.title: In approved full-time training — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## In approved full-time training
This exemption may apply to a partner with work obligations.
A partner can be partially exempt from meeting some of their work obligations if they are engaged in approved full-time training.
Note a client who has started approved training or is about to start an approved training course before they apply for a benefit must still meet all of the qualifications for Jobseeker Support before the benefit can be granted.
Consider whether the training course is the most suitable activity for the client. Also consider if other activities (for example programmes, seminars or work experience) might be a more appropriate option for moving the client towards paid work.
Discuss and take into account the client's career background, including:
- their educational qualifications
- their employment history
- their skills and
- whether training will help them find work at the earliest opportunity
Examples of approved training courses include but are not limited to:
- Limited Service Volunteer
- Skills for Industry
- Targeted Training
- training approved by the regional contracts manager
The approved training must:
- be full time (at least 20 hours a week)
- focus on teaching practical, employment-related skills
- support the client to gain the skills that will help them find work
Approved training does not include a course undertaken by a full-time student, as defined by the Student Allowance Regulations 1998.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months or until the end of the training course, whichever is earlier.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'In approved training'.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions

chunks.title: Duration — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Duration
When an exemption is approved, MSD sets a duration for the exemption.
Generally an exemption can be in place until the earlier of:
- the end of the client's current course of study or
- the end of the current academic year or
- up to 12 months

chunks.title: In approved training (no children or child 14+) — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## In approved training (no children or child 14+)
If a partner is in approved training they must continue to meet their work obligations, including being available for full-time employment, unless they are granted an exemption for approved full-time training.
They are still expected to be available for work or any other activity up to a total of 30 hours each week.
The partner must understand that they have to accept suitable paid work if it becomes available.

chunks.title: In-hand allowance — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## In-hand allowance
When a young partner getting Jobseeker Support is subject to youth money management, they can get an amount of up to $50 a week paid directly to them as an in-hand allowance.
After the young partner's accommodation, service costs and lawful debts are paid by redirection, the balance of payment, if any, is distributed between the young partner's payment card and the in-hand allowance. The maximum amount that can be paid direct to a young partner as an in-hand allowance is $50.
## Altering the distribution of payment for existing clients already subject to youth money management
If, at any time, a Youth Service provider considers that the current distribution of an existing client's payment between the payment card and in-hand allowance is inappropriate for the client's circumstances, they can make a recommendation to YSSU that this distribution be altered.
When determining whether it is appropriate to make a recommendation that a client's payment distribution be altered, providers must take into account a range of factors.
Note a young partner cannot review the decision on how the Jobseeker Support is paid to them.
For more information see:

chunks.title: In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes if a client is in or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence.
Treatment for the purposes of the drug test requirements means any specialist treatment service provided for a person because of a diagnosed drug dependency.
The client can either be participating in or on the waiting list for a specialist treatment service.
Specialist treatment services are services that:
- provide specific medical or psychological interventions with the goal of helping a person to overcome drug dependency
- a client has been referred to following a formal assessment by the Community Alcohol and Drug Service (CADS), a registered health practitioner or by a registered AOD practitioner
The client can be asked to provide verification from the person recommending the treatment or from the treatment service. The verification must state the duration or time that the client will need to address their drug dependency and whether they are participating or on the wait list for treatment.
There is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to your client.

chunks.title: In residential care — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## In residential care
No stand-down applies to clients who:
- are required to pay all or part of a benefit towards the cost of their treatment or care in a residential programme

chunks.title: School and tertiary holidays — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## School and tertiary holidays
Any incentive payments earned by the young person will continue to be paid during any school or tertiary holiday periods while they are receiving Jobseeker Support.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Incentive payments — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Incentive payments
If a young partner is under youth money management, any incentive payments earned are included in the redirection of their payment.
Young partners can earn incentive payments for demonstrating a commitment to their activity obligations.
A young partner getting Jobseeker Support can earn the following incentives:
- budgeting - $10 per week
- education - $10 per week
- parenting - $10 per week
## Review of decision
A young partner cannot review the decision on how their portion of Jobseeker Support is paid to them.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Income criteria — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Income criteria
To meet the income criteria for Jobseeker Support a client must:
- have no income, or
- if they have income it must not reduce the rate of Jobseeker Support to zero.
## Partner in employment
MSD can grant Jobseeker Support at the married, civil union or de facto rate if a client's partner is in employment (full-time or part-time). The partner's income is charged against the benefit.

chunks.title: Income from overseas — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Income from overseas
When a client has been working overseas within the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before their entitlement date you include this in their average weekly income.
If the client cannot provide verification of their earnings, accept the information provided on their application for benefit. For help to convert foreign currency to the equivalent New Zealand dollars see the instructions below.
There is no ability to take higher living costs into account. If the client is in financial hardship during an initial stand-down they may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant.
For more information see:
## Converting foreign currency
To estimate the foreign currency to the equivalent New Zealand dollars use the exchange rate provided in SELXT. The client must be informed that this calculation is not based on the current rate.
To obtain a current exchange rate, contact Westpac bank to request the 'Westpac buys cash' foreign exchange rate. Use the exchange rate as at the date the client returned to New Zealand.
Consideration must be given to the calculation that is in the client's favour. The exchange rate accepted by the client (the estimated rate from SELXT or current rate from bank) should be noted in CMS.

chunks.title: Information from a Self-Assessment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Information from a Self-Assessment
Clients have an obligation to complete a Self-Assessment when asked.
A Self-Assessment is a series of questions that focus on what a person can do and aim to gather information about the person's skills, barriers to employment, and what support would enable them to find and stay in work.
This information, when asked, will be used along with the information on the Work Capacity Medical Certificate to determine benefit eligibility, assign work obligations and to stream people to the appropriate level of service.
Consider whether this, with the other evidence provided, indicates that the client has the capacity to work part-time or not. If so, part-time work obligations must be applied.

chunks.title: Information from a Work Capacity Medical Certificate — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Information from a Work Capacity Medical Certificate
The Work Capacity Medical Certificate provides information to help MSD:
- determine medical eligibility to benefit and
- apply relevant obligations, exemptions and deferrals
Generally, if the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) has indicated on the medical certificate the client has capacity to work at least 15 hours a week, part-time work obligations will be applied.
## Unclear whether a client has the capacity to work
When it is unclear whether the client has capacity for work or whether work obligations should be applied, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor.
## Client does not agree with decision to apply work obligations
Once MSD has decided the client will have part-time work obligations, the client will be sent a letter. The letter advises the client they have a right to review any decisions made relating to medical capacity for work with the Medical Appeals Board.

chunks.title: Informing a client of the drug test obligation failure — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Informing a client of the drug test obligation failure
Once MSD has decided that a client has failed a drug test work obligation, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. The client will then be sent a letter stating that their benefit will be sanctioned and that their benefit will only be increased, restarted, regranted, or continued if they:
- complete a recompliance activity
- dispute the decision to impose the sanction and MSD accepts that they have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting their work obligations or
- lodge a Review of Decision and MSD reconsiders their position and agrees with the client's review
For some clients, if it's their first obligation failure they may be eligible for a non-financial sanction instead of a financial sanction. For more information see: Non-financial sanctions.
## Recompliance for a drug test work obligation failure
Clients may have their benefit increased or restarted from the date they start a drug test failure recompliance activity.
For more information see:
- Obligations failure for clients
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: Informing clients of their obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Informing clients of their obligations
You must ensure that the client understands:
- their obligations
- the consequences of failing to meet those obligations, in particular the sanctions that may be imposed and
- their right to review and dispute any decisions relating to a failure to comply with their obligations
Clients and partners applying for Jobseeker Support must:
- sign their application form and
- be given a copy of their obligations from their application form
Note that work obligations cannot be enforced until the main benefit commencement date.
## Clients transferring between benefits
When a client is receiving a benefit and they have a change in obligations, a letter will be sent advising them what their new obligations are. They do not need to re-sign an obligations form.
This includes where a client is transferring:
- from Sole Parent Support to Jobseeker Support as their youngest dependent child has turned 14 years
- between full-time work obligations and part-time work obligations or work preparation obligations within Jobseeker Support
For more information see:
- Obligations
- Social obligations
- Work or work preparation obligations
- Work preparation obligations
- Work obligations

chunks.title: For more information on the initial stand-down see: — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## For more information on the initial stand-down see:
- Average weekly income
- Number of dependent children
- Employment during stand-down
- Self-imposed stand-down
- Initial stand-down procedure
- Assistance during an initial stand-down
- No stand-down applies
- Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
- Deskfile Initial stand-down

chunks.title: Initial stand-down procedure — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Initial stand-down procedure
Step 1. Find the client's entitlement date.
Step 2. Calculate the client's average weekly income for a 26 and 52 week period.
Step 3. Find out whether the client has or had any dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement date. When determining the correct stand-down period, you must take into account any children that were in the client's care during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to the entitlement date.
Step 4. Using the information from Steps 2 and 3, determine the initial stand-down for the client over a 26 and 52 week period by looking at the Initial stand-down period chart in Deskfile.
Step 5. Use the calculation of average weekly income that gives the client a lesser stand-down period.
Step 6. Apply the initial stand-down from the client's entitlement date to find the commencement date.
Remember if you enter the correct information in SWIFTT it will automatically calculate the initial stand-down and commencement date for you.
Note if the client has had a dependent child (or children) in their care during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement date and the child (or children) is no longer in their care, you will have to use a work around. Contact Helpline for this information.

chunks.title: International/Humanitarian Stream — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## International/Humanitarian Stream
The purpose of the International/Humanitarian stream is to fulfil New Zealand's obligations as a good international citizen. Included in this stream are United Nations mandated refugees who are approved under the annual Refugee Quota and asylum seekers who claim refugee or protection status in New Zealand. The categories in this stream are the:
- Refugee Family Support Category
- Pacific Access Category
- Samoan Quota Scheme
- Victims of Family Violence and
- various other special policies for specific countries
The client usually does not have any assets or income. To assess a client's entitlement to Jobseeker Support confirmation of the client's income declared on the application for permanent residence is required from Immigration New Zealand.
Note if the client has not resided continuously in New Zealand for 2 years since being granted permanent residence, Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship may be considered and assets declared on their application for permanent residence must be included in the assessment.
Once confirmed, assess Jobseeker Support in the usual manner taking into account all other information provided by Immigration New Zealand.

chunks.title: Introduction — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Jobseeker Support is a temporary work-focused benefit, that can be paid for up to 26 weeks while a client looks for work, is in training for work, is unable to work or is working reduced hours due to a health condition, injury or disability.
If clients still require Jobseeker Support after 26 weeks they must complete the 26 week reapplication process.
## For more information on Jobseeker Support for clients see:
- Qualifications
- Obligations
- Commencement date
- Payment
- Changes and reviews
- Reapplication process at 26 weeks

chunks.title: Job-search activities must be reasonable steps towards employment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Job-search activities must be reasonable steps towards employment
As part of completing Report Job Search, clients must do at least 3 job-search activities each week for 4 weeks. Clients also need to report to MSD on all of the job-search activities they complete each week (minimum of 3 per week).
To meet the requirements of Report Job Search, MSD must consider that the client's job-search activities are reasonable steps towards them finding suitable employment.
Factors MSD should consider when determining whether a job-search activity is a reasonable step include (but are not limited to):
- the client's current skills, experience, and employment history
- if the client already has an appropriate CV and cover letter
- if the client has already completed skills-based courses (such as, first aid or barista courses)
- the work-readiness of the client (e.g. work-appropriate clothing, caring responsibilities, access to transport)
Note client's individual circumstances will determine what is considered a reasonable step for them. Each activity should be considered on a case-by-case basis.
Examples of job-search activities that are considered reasonable steps could include (but are not limited to) a client:
- writing different cover letters that focus on the skills for specific job applications
- updating their CV
- attending a CV writing workshop to improve their chances of finding employment
- checking MyMSD for suitable jobs in their area
- calling Job Connect for more details about a specific role
- checking an employment site for suitable roles (e.g. Trade Me, Seek, Indeed)
- visiting local suitable businesses to submit CVs or check for any openings
- attending a skills-based course to improve their chances of securing a suitable role
- taking steps to get suitable clothing for a job interview
- expanding the range of roles they are looking for beyond their employment history
- applying for suitable roles (including if the application is unsuccessful or they don't hear anything back)
- attending an interview (including where the interview is unsuccessful)
- registering with a recruitment agency or career advice service
Note clients are only expected to provide evidence of their job-search activity where it is reasonable for them to get it in their circumstances.

chunks.title: Job search requirements — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Job search requirements
A client granted Jobseeker Support on the ground of being available for, seeking and willing to undertake full-time employment must not be in full-time employment but must be:
- seeking it
- available for it
- willing and able to undertake it and
- taking reasonable steps to find it
To decide if a client meets this qualification, see:
- Clients with specific circumstances
- Meeting job search requirements

chunks.title: Jobseeker Support client with New Zealand Superannuation partner - income assessment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Jobseeker Support client with New Zealand Superannuation partner - income assessment
The gross income of the client and their partner is used to assess the client's rate of Jobseeker Support.
The deduction is half the abatement amount that would be applied if the couple were getting Jobseeker Support - Income test 4.
New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension is not included as income for the income test and is not reduced because of the couple's income.
## Example 1
Client getting Jobseeker Support at the half-married rate.
Partner getting the half-married rate of New Zealand Superannuation.
The couple's weekly income is $275.00 gross a week and no dependent children.
Income weekly
Partner 1 - Jobseeker Support - half couple rate
Partner 2 - New Zealand Superannuation - half couple rate
