Note this example also applies to a Jobseeker Support client with a Veteran's Pension partner.

chunks.title: Limited employment locations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Limited employment locations
These guidelines explain how the limited employment locations policy affects clients in three different situations, outlined below:
## A client living in a limited employment location receiving Jobseeker Support
A client in this situation must continue to meet the work obligations, which include being available for, and taking reasonable steps to obtain, suitable employment. They will not be expected to relocate.
Note this does not include clients who move from one limited employment location to another. In this instance, see:
- Clients moving to a limited employment location
## A person living in a limited employment location applying for Jobseeker Support
A client living in a limited employment location who is applying for Jobseeker Support must meet the Jobseeker Support eligibility criteria.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
## A client receiving Jobseeker Support moves to a limited employment location
A client in this situation must continue to meet the work obligations (if applicable), which include being available for, and taking reasonable steps to obtain, suitable employment.
To meet this obligation, a client who moves to a limited employment location must have access to reliable transport and be willing and realistically able to commute to a nearby town or centre where there is employment available.
For more information see:
- What is a limited employment location?
- Deskfile Limited employment locations
- Clients currently living in a limited employment location
- Clients moving to a limited employment location
- Work obligations

chunks.title: Live organ donors — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Live organ donors
When a client or their partner has decided to donate a kidney or liver tissue, they can keep getting their current benefit.
The client or partner must provide evidence they have been accepted as a live organ donor.
Medical evidence must be signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner.
Note a dentist or midwife cannot provide medical evidence for clients who are live organ donors.
## Change of circumstances
If the client has a change of circumstances and they no longer qualify for their current benefit, they may still need financial assistance from MSD during their recovery time. MSD can consider transferring the client to Emergency Benefit.
For more information see:
- Emergency Benefit Donating a kidney or liver tissue
## Duration
The medical certificate coverage can be the lesser of either:
- a period specified by the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner or
- up to 12 weeks

chunks.title: Lockouts — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Lockouts
A lockout usually involves an employer attempting to force employees to accept conditions of employment, or other demands, before a return to work will be allowed. This can relate to the employee's existing contract or to new terms and conditions in a new contract.
Clients who are 'locked out' cannot receive the Jobseeker Support because they are still in full-time employment. However, they may qualify for an Emergency Benefit.
## Striking employees then 'locked out'
Sometimes employees who have been on strike are then 'locked out' by their employer when they try to return to work. In this situation, the earlier strike is regarded to have ended and replaced by a lockout.
You may consider paying an Emergency Benefit from the date the lockout commenced.
For more information see:
- Emergency Benefit Qualifications

chunks.title: Masters students — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Masters students
Some clients studying toward a Master's degree or a Doctorate may be classified as full-time by education providers. If they are enrolled in a full-time programme, they cannot receive Jobseeker Support. When a student is in hardship between the end of one academic year of a programme and the start of the next, they may be eligible for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
Other clients studying towards a postgraduate degree may be enrolled part-time and genuinely available for and searching for work while studying. These people can receive Jobseeker Support.
MSD should confirm with the students education provider if they are unsure whether the course is full-time.

chunks.title: Medical certificate information about a client's capacity for work — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Medical certificate information about a client's capacity for work
To decide if the client is unable to work full-time (or if they are required to reduce their hours of employment due to a health condition, injury or a disability) MSD should consider all the information provided on the medical certificate. The medical certificate will link the client's condition with their capacity for work.
MSD should consider information on the client's:
- Diagnoses - the client's main health conditions or disabilities, and any relevant secondary health conditions or disabilities
- Prognosis - the likely rate of improvement of the client's condition and its impact on their ability to work. The medical certificate will indicate when and to what extent, the client is capable of undertaking employment or what accommodations, supports or services are required
- Capacity for work - the impact of the condition or disability on the client's capacity for work
- Medical coverage - the recommended period a client's registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) considers a client should have their capacity for work reassessed
When deciding a client's capacity to work, MSD should not consider any restrictions they have to work in a certain job or occupation, as a result of their condition or injury.
Instead, MSD should consider the restrictions the client's health condition or disability may have on the type of work suitable for them. This includes a decision about whether the client should have work obligations, and the appropriate work related activities they should undertake.
If the impact on the client's capacity to work is unclear, questions regarding work capacity are in conflict, or additional support for their health condition or disability could be helpful, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor.

chunks.title: Medical certificates — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients must provide a medical certificate to support their application for Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability). Generally, clients provide a Work Capacity Medical Certificate, however MSD can accept other medical certificates if they contain all the information required. The Work Capacity Medical Certificate provides information to support MSD to: - determine whether the client qualifies for the Jobseeker Support and - determine the services and supports a client needs to work and - apply relevant obligations and exemptions from work obligations A medical certificate for Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) must be completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant). The information required on the medical certificate includes: - a primary diagnosis plus any relevant secondary diagnoses and - the impact of the condition on the client's capacity for work (including whether a client can work part-time for at least 15 hours per week) and - the likely duration of the period of time-off needed and - any other relevant information If the information to determine the client's entitlement to Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability), and the client's capacity for work is unclear, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor.

chunks.title: Incomplete Work Capacity Medical Certificates — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a Work Capacity Medical Certificate is not complete MSD must: - discuss with the client the need for MSD to contact their medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) to request the relevant information or - refer to the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor for advice The Privacy Statement on the application form allows MSD to contact the health practitioner to verify any answers on the Work Capacity Medical Certificate that are unclear or unanswered. Note if MSD can determine the client qualifies for Jobseeker Support on the grounds of a health condition, injury or disability from the information in the medical certificate, MSD can continue with processing the application. This means the client can continue being paid before MSD determines if they should have work obligations.

chunks.title: Consent required when information is additional to information provided — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: MSD must obtain the client's consent before contacting the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) to discuss any information additional to the information already provided on the medical certificate. This includes: - information required to determine whether the client qualifies for the benefit or their capacity to work - obtaining specialist reports held by the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant)

chunks.title: Second opinion — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: In some circumstances MSD may need to refer the client to a designated health practitioner for further assessment. This includes when the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant)indicates on the medical certificate that a second opinion is appropriate. The registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) may also indicate that another person (other than themselves or a designated health practitioner) is best placed to provide the information for the client including a medical specialist or a hospital doctor. When the medical certificate indicates 'other', seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor. If there is likely to be any delay in deciding the client's application for Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury or a disability, MSD may need to consider some other form of financial assistance in the meantime. This could include granting hardship assistance.

chunks.title: Practitioner requests contact to discuss — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The client's registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) may indicate on the medical certificate they would like MSD to contact them to discuss the client's diagnosis and their capacity to work. In this situation, MSD does not need to obtain the client's consent before contacting their practitioner. In most cases they will want to discuss the information they have provided on the medical certificate. Note the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) is required to discuss the information disclosed on the medical certificate when they meet with the client.

chunks.title: Medical review and reassessments — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Medical reassessments determine whether a client's condition or work capacity has changed. A client's registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) will indicate on a medical certificate when they consider a client's capacity for work should next be reassessed (medical coverage). This provides useful information to help MSD work with the client. Generally, MSD will accept the recommended reassessment period made by the client's registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) unless there is any inconsistency. For example, if the information on the client's capacity to work section of the medical certificate indicates the client is available for full-time employment but another question states they are unable to work full-time. If it is past the date the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) assessed that the client is expected to be fit for work, or their capacity to work should be reviewed, there should be a further check on the client's progress. When MSD is uncertain about the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) recommendation for reassessment, MSD should seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor. They may recommend the client is referred to a designated health practitioner for a second opinion.

chunks.title: When medical coverage is for 2 years or longer - assess whether the client qualifies for Supported Living Payment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: A client's medical coverage determined by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner could be 2 years or longer, which may indicate their health condition, injury or disability is permanent. In such cases, MSD should consider whether the client would qualify for the Supported Living Payment. For more information see: - Supported Living Payment Medical qualifications Some clients getting Jobseeker Support because of a permanent health condition, disability or injury will not qualify for a Supported Living Payment because their work capacity is not severely restricted. For example, a client's health condition, injury or disability may be expected to continue for at least 2 years (permanently), but they may not be severely restricted in their capacity for work (i.e. they could regularly work more than 15 hours a week but less than 30 hours a week). In these cases, Jobseeker Support is the correct benefit for a client. Information provided by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner on a medical certificate regarding a client's work capacity should be used to help MSD determine if a client may qualify for Supported Living Payment. MSD can also contact the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor for advice.

chunks.title: Maximum review periods for specific situations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: There are some situations when a maximum review period is applied for clients with specific health conditions.

chunks.title: Medical terms — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Medical terms
Here are some of the medical terms you may find included in your clients' medical reports, assessments or certificates.
## Acute
A condition of recent onset or a severe condition and/or expected to change quickly.
## Benign
Mild and non-progressive condition most frequently used to describe non-cancerous tumour or neoplasm.
## Chronic
A long standing condition - usually existing for longer than 6 weeks.
## Co-morbidity
Existing at the same time as (and usually independently of) another health condition.
## Congenital
Pertaining to a condition present at birth, whether inherited or caused by the environment.
## Diagnosis
The conclusion reached by identifying or determining the nature and cause of a disease or injury.
## Malignant
Severe and progressively worsening condition most frequently used to describe cancer.
## Prognosis
Forecasting the probable course and outcome of a disease including the chances of recovery.

chunks.title: Meeting job search requirements — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Meeting job search requirements
Job search requirements apply to:
- clients and partners with work obligations
To help decide if a client is meeting the job search requirements, you will need to consider the following:
1. If the client (or partner) had the opportunity, would they:
- be available for work of at least 20 hours per week (part-time work obligations)
- be available for work for 30 hours or more a week (full-time work obligations)
- accept any suitable job offers within their abilitiesNote that this can include weekend work depending on the client or partner's individual circumstances
- not restrict their job search to vacancies within their own trade
- not restrict their job search to vacancies in their chosen occupation
- not move frequently from one area to another with no intention of getting a job
2. Has the client (or partner) begun to take steps to find work? For example by:
- searching newspapers and other media for vacancies
- making applications for suitable jobs
- contacting employers about vacancies
For more information see:
- Clients aged 65 years and over

chunks.title: Young person is not subject to youth money management — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Young person is not subject to youth money management
Where a young person is not subject to youth money management they can get their Jobseeker Support, family tax credit, Best Start tax credit and any extra help directly to their bank account.
## Young person is subject to youth money management
Where a young person is subject to youth money management the Jobseeker Support, family tax credit and any extra help (except Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance) is paid via:
- payment directly to supplier (eg a payees redirection for accommodation costs, utility costs and lawful debts)
- in-hand allowance which is paid directly to the young person's bank account
- payment card - the young person is able to purchase goods (such as food and groceries) from approved suppliers
Note Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance is paid directly to the young person's bank account.
## Review of decision
A young person cannot review the decision on how the Jobseeker Support is paid to them.

chunks.title: Situations where the voluntary unemployment 13 week non-entitlement period would apply — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Situations where the voluntary unemployment 13 week non-entitlement period would apply
Situations where a client would be subject to a 13 week non-entitlement include (but are not limited to):
- a previously self-employed client applies for Jobseeker Support because they have closed or sold a viable business without a good and sufficient reason
- a client is applying for Jobseeker Support on the ground of health condition, injury, or disability and is able to work part-time, and left a part-time job without a good and sufficient reason
- a partner who is currently receiving Jobseeker Support has a dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years and therefore has part-time work obligations. The partner has left their part-time job without a good and sufficient reason.
- a client has left a part-time job without a good and sufficient reason, a voluntary unemployment stand-down would apply if the income from the job was sufficient to support the person, and the job was for 13 weeks or more
For more information see:
- Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period
Before applying a 13 week non-entitlement period for misconduct, you should contact both the client and their employer. When you contact the employer ask them to complete the Employment and earnings information for applications (V06) form.
If the employer does not return the form or the reason for termination is not given, no further contact with the employer should be made.
If there is conflicting evidence or the reason for leaving employment is not agreed between the client and the employer, you should give the client the benefit of the doubt.
Each client's circumstances need to be carefully investigated. If you are uncertain whether a voluntary unemployment stand-down should be imposed, discuss the client's circumstances, in the first instance, with a service centre trainer and then with Helpline (if still required).
If you decide to apply a voluntary unemployment stand-down, you will need to:
- advise the client of your decision
- send the client the 'Voluntary Unemployed' letter to confirm your decision. A copy of the letter is available in CMS letter templates
- for couples or sole parents, the client's commencement date letter will confirm your decision and outline their rate of payment
- add the date that a non-entitlement period will apply from and the appropriate VU reason code to the SSTDA screen
- conditionally grant the benefit using code 024 (VU imposed) on the SPGRT screen
- note for sole parents the 13 week non-entitlement period only applies to 50% of the benefit
- make notes in CMS outlining your decision
Ensure the benefit remains conditionally granted. Do not decline the benefit.
For more information see:
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed
- Misconduct
- Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer

chunks.title: Youth money management activity — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Youth money management activity
Young partners who have youth activity obligations are required to co-operate with their service provider or MSD 'in-house' service in managing the spending of their benefit and provide information as required.
The young person must:
- attend and participate in regular one-on-one discussions on budgeting
and provide information on:
- their accommodation costs (for example rent, board) and service costs (for example power, phone)
- any other lawful debts and liabilities (for example court fines, MSD debts, Child Support payments, hire purchase)
- how they spend their in-hand allowance and
- how they spend any money allocated to their payment card
For more information see:
- Youth money management
## Exception
A young partner aged 16 or 17 years (with no children) or 16 to 19 years (with dependent children) will not be subject to youth money management and will have their full payment paid directly to them when they have:
- demonstrated continued compliance with their obligations and been assessed as being financially competent or
- opted out of youth money management because they have turned 18 years (for young partners without dependent children), or 20 years (for young partners with dependent children), and have chosen to stay in the Youth Service and complete their course of study, training or work-based learning

chunks.title: Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes where a client has a drug issue identified by the Alcohol Drug Helpline - Work and Income Support Service and is engaging and participating in services and support offered by the Alcohol Drug Helpline - Work and Income Support Service.
The client can be asked to provide verification from the Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] for beneficiaries. The verification must state the duration or time that the client is receiving support. There is a Drug test obligations Helpline verification form that will be completed by Helpline staff and sent to the client. It is up to the client to provide this form as verification.
The Alcohol Drug Helpline - Work and Income Support Service will offer the following support and services:
- brief interventions (series of telephone contacts)
- brief assessment (brief clinical assessment) or
- referral for a comprehensive face to face AOD assessment and treatment plan or
- referral to other health or social service agencies or
- confirmation of drug treatment details
For more information see:
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: New businesses — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## New businesses
Recently established businesses will not usually have enough money to fall back on during non-productive periods. Consider Jobseeker Support on a short term basis where:
- the client is clearly available for work
- the client meets all of the qualifying criteria and
- there is an expectation that work will be available again
Note there is an exception for some clients, see:
## Example
A client establishes himself as a firewood contractor from February until October. There is no further work available following February. The client is looking for other types of work and has no cash reserves to see them through.
Jobseeker Support could be paid between October and January as there is no ongoing involvement in the business, there has been no opportunity to build up funds, and the client is available to undertake alternative work.

chunks.title: No notice for clients with a grade 3 sanction — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## No notice for clients with a grade 3 sanction
Clients with a partner and single clients with a grade 3 sanction have their benefit cancelled and are subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period. This means they will not be sent the "initial notice to reapply" letter and cannot complete the reapplication process.
If the client still needs Jobseeker Support, they will need to:
- recomply the grade 3 sanction and be granted a provisional benefit while they complete a 6 week recompliance activity or
- wait until the end of the 13 week non-entitlement period and apply for Jobseeker Support as a new applicant.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
Note sole parents with a sanction applied will be sent their "notice to reapply".
For more information see:
- Sole parents with sanction applied

chunks.title: No stand-down applies — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## No stand-down applies
An initial stand-down is not imposed in the following situations:
- Chronic recurring illness
- Client leaves Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre
- Entering a refuge
- In residential care
- Prisoners
- Temporary employment
- Transfer between benefits
When no stand-down applies, the commencement date of the benefit is the later of either:
- the entitlement date or
- the application date
Note when no stand-down applies, the 28-day rule does not apply.

chunks.title: Non-compliance for Community Work Experience — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Non-compliance for Community Work Experience
A client could fail Community Work Experience without a good and sufficient reason at any point. This could occur when:
- a client does not find a position due to making minimal or no effort to search for one, or
- a client does not complete the required hours in any of the 4 weeks of the position period, or
- an organisation advises MSD that a client failed to perform the duties of the position, for example, a client attends the organisation for the hours required but spends most of their time on their phone instead of completing assigned tasks.
MSD may consider information shared by an organisation when determining if a client has a good and sufficient reason for failing to find or complete Community Work Experience, however MSD must also consider information provided by the client.
For example, if an organisation advises MSD that a client did not show up to do their 5 hours that week, MSD must contact the client to see if there was a good and sufficient reason for their absence.
If MSD determines that a client does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to find or complete Community Work Experience, the client is considered non-compliant.
## Clients without dependent children
A client without dependent children will have their benefit suspended from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
Their payments will remain suspended for up to 13 weeks after Community Work Experience was first imposed, unless they recomply.
A client may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be resumed from the date that the client recomplies.
When a client's benefit has remained suspended because they have not recomplied, their benefit will cancel 13 weeks after Community Work Experience was first imposed.
## Clients with dependent children
Clients with dependent children have 50% payment protection.
A client with dependent children will have their payments reduce by 50% from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
A client may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be resumed from the date that the client has recomplied.
These clients will also be contacted after 2 weeks of receiving only 50% of their benefit. For more information see: Effect of financial sanctions on assistance.

chunks.title: Non-compliance for Report Job Search — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Non-compliance for Report Job Search
A client could fail Report Job Search without a good and sufficient reason at any point. This could occur when the client does not:
- complete at least 3 job-search activities within a week or
- report their job-search activities or
- provide sufficient supporting evidence of their job-search activities
If MSD determines that a client does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete Report Job Search, the client is considered non-compliant.
## Clients without dependent children
A client without dependent children will have their benefit suspended from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
Their payments will remain suspended for up to 13 weeks after Report Job Search was first imposed, unless they recomply.
A client may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be resumed from the date that the client recomplies.
When a client's benefit has remained suspended because they have not recomplied, their benefit will cancel 13 weeks after Report Job Search was first imposed.
## Clients with dependent children
Clients with dependent children have 50% payment protection.
A client with dependent children will have their payments reduced by 50% from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
A client may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be increased from the date that the client has recomplied.
These clients will also be contacted after 2 weeks of receiving only 50% of their benefit. For more information see: Effect of financial sanctions on assistance.

chunks.title: Non-entitlement period for 13 weeks — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Non-entitlement period for 13 weeks
A non-entitlement period of 13 weeks is a period where clients are unable to get a benefit because they:
- have become voluntarily unemployed without a good and sufficient reason
- are applying for a benefit because they were dismissed by their employer for misconduct
- have failed their obligations for a third time in the last 24 months (or 12 months for young partners with youth activity obligations) of continuous benefit receipt (as a grade 3 sanction) or
- have refused an offer of suitable employment (if they have work obligations)
## Non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or dismissal
Before imposing a 13-week non-entitlement period, the reason why the client has left employment needs to be carefully investigated to determine whether it is appropriate to apply a 13 week non-entitlement period.
For voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct the 13-week non-entitlement period starts from the day after the date the client's employment ceased.
For more information see:
- Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
## Non-entitlement period for obligations failures
Where a client fails their obligations and has a grade 3 sanction imposed, they will have a 13-week non-entitlement period.
For imposing a grade 3 sanction the 13-week non-entitlement period starts the day after the five working day notice period.
For more information see:
- Grade 3 sanction or job refusal failure non-entitlement period
Also see:
- Effect of 13 week non-entitlement period for partner
- Effect of non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Financial assistance during a non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Non-entitlement period should not be imposed — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Non-entitlement period should not be imposed
MSD may determine that a 13 week non-entitlement period should not be imposed if the client has specific circumstances that are considered to be good and sufficient reasons for leaving employment.
Good and sufficient reasons include where a client has:
- lost their job during an agreed employment trial (except where the employer alleges misconduct)
- recently returned to New Zealand
- taken voluntary redundancy because another employee would lose their job if they remained
- left employment that isn't suitable
- worked for a temporary period.
Note the client will be subject to the usual commencement date and initial stand-down rules.
## Clients who lose their job during an agreed employment trial
Employers can set a trial period when hiring an employee for up to 90 days from the date their employment starts. The employer can dismiss the employee for any reason during the agreed trial period, and they are not required to provide the reason.
To be valid, the trial period must be agreed to by the employer and employee in the employment agreement. The exact period must be stated in the employment agreement.
A 13 week non-entitlement period is not considered if the employment ceased during the agreed notice period.
Note if the employer alleges misconduct by the employee and provides evidence of the misconduct, a non-entitlement period can be considered.
For more information see:
## Clients returning to New Zealand from overseas
A 13 week non-entitlement period does not apply to clients who have returned to New Zealand after working overseas.
## Voluntary redundancy
A 13 week non-entitlement period does not apply to clients who take voluntary redundancy, when staying in their role would mean that another employee may lose their job.

chunks.title: Criteria to receive a non-financial sanction — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Criteria to receive a non-financial sanction
A client or partner can only get a non-financial sanction if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they meet with MSD within the 5 working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure decision is not disputed and overturned, and
- a non-financial sanction would be appropriate for them based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or they have dependent children
MSD must assess a client’s circumstances and determine which non-financial sanction, if any, is most appropriate for the client. Each non-financial sanction has different factors to consider.

chunks.title: Notice to clients with a suspended or expired benefit — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Notice to clients with a suspended or expired benefit
If a client has a suspended (except for a grade 2 sanction) or expired benefit, they will not be sent the 'initial notice to reapply' letter. This is because they are not currently getting a benefit.
If a client's Jobseeker Support is resumed during their notice period, MSD must advise the client about their upcoming expiry date and what they need to do to complete the reapplication process before their expiry date.
MSD should consider whether the client will be able to complete the reapplication process before their expiry date and if an extension may be appropriate.
Note for clients whose benefit is resumed before the 'reminder to reapply' letter is due to be sent, will be sent this letter 10 working days before their expiry date.

chunks.title: Notice to reapply — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients getting a current Jobseeker Support are automatically sent an 'initial notice to reapply' letter 25 working days before the expiry date of their benefit advising the client they need to complete the reapplication process. The notice period allows sufficient time for clients to complete the reapplication process.

chunks.title: 26 weeks reapplication initial notice to reapply — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The initial notice to reapply letter advises the client (and any partner included in their benefit): - that Jobseeker Support is a temporary benefit paid for up to 26 weeks while they prepare for or look for work, and - that if they still need Jobseeker Support, they must complete the 26 week reapplication process before their expiry date, and - what they need to do to complete the 26 week reapplication process. There are no review rights in these letters because it is a requirement for clients to complete the 26 week reapplication process.

chunks.title: Clients getting Jobseeker Support before 1 July 2025 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Some clients already getting Jobseeker Support before 1 July 2025 must complete a 52 week reapplication before their benefit expiry date if they still need it. This is a transitional arrangement. This applies to the following clients only: - Clients who have an 'in-flight' 52 week reapplication on 1 July 2025 These clients will be sent the 'initial notice to reapply' letter 25 working days before their expiry date. The letter advises what they need to do to complete their reapplication, in line with the 52 week reapplication requirements.

chunks.title: 52 week reapplication initial notice to reapply — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The 'initial notice to reapply' letter advises the client (and any partner included in their benefit) that: - their upcoming expiry date is 52 weeks after their benefit was last granted, and - if they still need Jobseeker Support, they must complete the 52 week reapplication process before their expiry date, and - in order to reapply, they will need to attend an appointment with MSD, and - the client and their partner (if any) will need to provide any supporting evidence to determine they are still eligible, and - the client and their partner (if any) will need to complete the reapplication and Comprehensive Work Assessment online before they attend their appointment, and - their Disability Allowance may also be reviewed (if getting it). There are no review rights in these letters because it is a requirement for clients to complete the 52 week reapplication process. For more information see: - 52 week reapplication process for clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025 - Expiry date for sole parent and grandparented clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025 - Expiry date for clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025

chunks.title: Reminder to reapply — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client has not completed the reapplication process a reminder letter will be sent 10 working days before the expiry date.

chunks.title: Jobseeker Support clients getting Disability Allowance — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients getting Jobseeker Support must complete the reapplication process to continue getting their benefit. These clients will have a Mandatory Review for Disability Allowance when they: - are completing the reapplication process for the benefit and - their disability costs have not been reviewed in the last 44 weeks If a client’s disability costs have been reviewed in the last 44 weeks, there will be no Mandatory Review of Disability Allowance. Note the reapplication process is not impacted if a client does not complete their Mandatory Review for Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Number of dependent children — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Number of dependent children
If a client had a dependent child (or children) in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application, the child (or children) must be taken into account when determining the stand-down.
Example if a single client with one dependent child applies for benefit the stand-down period will be based on a single client with one child. However, if this client had 2 dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application, the stand-down period will be based on a single client with two dependent children.
This is regardless of whether the child is still in the client's care at the time of application.

chunks.title: Obligations failures — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client or partner fail to comply with their obligations, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. MSD must be satisfied that the client or partner would have had no good and sufficient reason for their failure based on the information available. For social obligations, MSD must consider whether the client and partner (if any) have taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations and must go through the regular engagement and support process before considering that the client has failed their obligation. For more information see: - Failing more than one obligation at the same time - Work obligations - Work preparation obligations - Social obligations - Social obligations Regular engagement and support process - Social obligations All reasonable steps to meet social obligations - Drug test obligations - Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure - Youth activity obligations failures Note for a client or partner who has full-time or part-time work obligations leaving part-time work averaging less than 20 hours per week, without good and sufficient reason or through misconduct, is also an obligations failure, but may not be specified in the client's work obligations. Once MSD has decided that the client or partner has failed their obligations, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. The client or partner will then be sent a letter stating that their benefit will be sanctioned and that their benefit will only be increased or resumed if they: - complete a recompliance activity - dispute the decision to impose the sanction and MSD accepts that they have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting their obligations - lodge a Review of Decision and MSD reconsiders their position and agree with the client's review or - lodge an appeal to the Medical Appeal Board (drug test work obligations only) Once a client has completed their recompliance activity, their benefit can be increased or resumed from the date MSD is satisfied the client started the activity. For some clients, if it’s their first obligation failure they may be eligible for a non-financial sanction instead of a financial sanction. For more information, see: Non-financial sanctions. All clients have a 5 working day notice period to dispute or recomply before the sanction is imposed. If a client or partner recomplies within the 5 working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the obligations failure is recorded. For more information see: - When the sanction is imposed - Counting previous obligations failures - Failing more than one obligation at the same time

chunks.title: Obligations failures — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients have not failed their obligations if they do not complete or undertake Voluntary Work or Activity in the Community.

chunks.title: Effect on rates payable — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: For financial sanctions, the reduction, suspension and cancellation applies to the main benefit the client or partner is getting. For couples it applies to each person's portion of the married rate of benefit. For young partners, the effect of a sanction on the client's assistance depends on whether the client has children and is youth money managed or not. The effect on extra help depends on the level of sanction imposed, the type of assistance, and whether the client or partner has dependent children. Non-financial sanctions do not affect the rate payable for a client or partner.

chunks.title: Obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Obligations
Clients must:
- advise of any change in circumstances that affect their entitlement or rate of benefit payable
- meet all of their work obligations
- if required, meet their work preparation obligations
- if they have dependent children, take all reasonable steps to meet social obligations that apply for each dependent child in their care
- if required, undertake and pass a pre-employment or pre-course drug test
- if required, participate in a Work Ability Assessment
- if required, work with a contracted service provider
- advise Work and Income if they are intending to travel overseas, before they leave New Zealand
## Partners aged 16 to 19 years old
Young partners (aged 16 to 19 years old) of clients getting Jobseeker Support have youth activity obligations, and not work or work preparation obligations if they are:
- aged 16 to 17 years old without dependent children or
- aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child and
- married to, or in a civil union or de facto relationship with a person getting Jobseeker Support
See:
- Youth activity obligations
Note social obligations do not apply to young partners of Jobseeker Support, as some of their youth activity obligations are similar to social obligations.

chunks.title: On strike — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## On strike
Applications for Jobseeker Support are sometimes received from clients who are on strike from their employment or who have been 'locked out' by their employer.
Jobseeker Support is not paid to clients who are on strike. Before we can decline their application, they must meet the definition of being on strike.
## Partners on strike
If a client applies for Jobseeker Support while their partner is on strike, they must meet all of the qualifications in their own right to be able to receive Jobseeker Support. The partner cannot receive a benefit while on strike and therefore cannot be included in the client's benefit. For information on the rate payable see: Partner not qualified
## Part-time worker on strike
A client who is on strike from their part-time employment cannot generally be granted Jobseeker Support if (as a guide) their employment was sufficient to maintain them for a period of not less than 13 weeks. If Jobseeker Support is granted you can consider that they have deprived themselves of income and pay the client at a reduced rate, by charging their pre-strike earnings.
If a client who is receiving a benefit and working part-time goes on strike, Jobseeker Support can continue to be paid, however, the rate of payment cannot be increased to the full rate as they have deprived themselves of income.
For more information see:
- Strikes
- Lockouts
- Process for investigating industrial disputes
## Extra Help
A client who has been declined a benefit while they are on strike may be able to receive an Accommodation Supplement. If there are dependent children in the family a Special Needs Grant or Temporary Additional Support may be payable.
For more information see:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Special Needs Grants
- Temporary Additional Support

chunks.title: Orphans Benefit/Unsupported Childs Benefit — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Orphans Benefit/Unsupported Childs Benefit
If a client is getting, or has been getting, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for a child in their care, this child is included as a dependent child in the stand-down calculation.
However, the Orphans Benefit/Unsupported Child's Benefit payments are not included as income for determining the average weekly income.

chunks.title: Orphans Benefits or Unsupported Childs Benefit under 3 years — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Orphans Benefits or Unsupported Childs Benefit under 3 years
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
In some cases a client may be caring for a child under 3 years for whom they are receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit.
Clients granted this exemption will be subject to work preparation obligations.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted in SWIFTT for 12 months initially or to when the child turns 3 years old - whichever is earlier.
The exemption can be renewed after 12 months provided the child is still under 3 years and the parent still qualifies for benefit.
## SWIFTT process
Clients who receive Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit for a child under 3 years are not automatically exempt in SWIFTT. You need to add an exemption on the main benefit record via SWTDA in SWIFTT.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions

chunks.title: Other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes
Other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes are programmes that involve parents educating their children at home with external support.
Programmes will need to meet the approval criteria set out in the Ministerial Direction which states the programme must:
- provide early childhood education to children under the age of 6 in their own homes and not to other children
- deliver positive educational outcomes for the children to whom it is provided
- be supervised and have specific early learning outcomes
- be aligned with Government priorities relating to early childhood education (ECE) and vulnerable children
For a list of the approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes for social obligations see:
- Deskfile Social obligations approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes

chunks.title: Other exceptional circumstances — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Other exceptional circumstances
In determining whether a client has any other exceptional circumstance for not completing their reapplication for Jobseeker Support before their expiry date, MSD must consider if they meet the criteria for exceptional circumstances.
The criteria for considering whether a situation or event is an exceptional circumstance, is that it is:
- is unforeseen, out-of-the ordinary and could not be planned for, and
- beyond the client's control, and
- those which set the client apart from others in a similar situation
Also that:
- the exceptional circumstance situation or event happened at any time during the client's notice period, and
- the event has affected their ability to reapply for their benefit
Note other exceptional circumstances may include an emergency or adverse event where no local or national state of emergency has been declared, or where the emergency or adverse event has ended but the client is still affected by the event at the time their "initial notice to reapply" letter is sent.
MSD will need to assess each case on its own merits when determining whether other exceptional circumstances exist.
## Evidence
Clients may be asked to provide evidence. Evidence required will depend on the client's situation, and must be deemed satisfactory by MSD.
For more information see:
- Exceptional circumstances for reapplication

chunks.title: Outcome of designated health practitioner assessment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Outcome of designated health practitioner assessment
Where the designated health practitioner assessment:
- confirms eligibility to Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) MSD should grant or review the client's benefit accordingly
- indicates that the client has or does not have the capacity to work part-time MSD can use this information to make a decision about whether the client should be subject to work obligations
## Permanent and severe
In some cases, the designated health practitioner may provide information that supports eligibility to Supported Living Payment rather than Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability).
In this situation, their application for Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) can be treated as an application for Supported Living Payment.
## No eligibility to Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability)
When the report from the designated health practitioner indicates the client does not qualify for Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability), MSD should consider their eligibility to Jobseeker Support with full-time work obligations.
If MSD declines their application, the client must be advised of the outcome including their right to review the decision. Medical decisions are reviewed by the Medical Appeals Board.
## Cancel Jobseeker Support
If the designated health practitioner indicates the client does not qualify for Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) the client’s eligibility will continue for 28 days beyond the date of the designated health practitioner appointment.
During this period MSD should advise the client they are no longer eligible for Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability), inform them of their right to have this decision reviewed by the Medical Appeals Board and invite them to apply for an alternative benefit.
Any alternative benefit can be granted after the 28 day extension to Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) has expired.
## Part-time capacity to work
If a designated health practitioner indicates the client has or does not have capacity to work part-time this may influence whether the client should be subject to work obligations.
Note this will not have any effect on whether the client is eligible for Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability).

chunks.title: Overview of social obligations according to age of the child — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Overview of social obligations according to age of the child
The table below shows the specific social obligations that apply to the client and their partner (if any) according to the age of their dependent children.
Age of client's or their partner's dependent children
4 weeks - 2 years

Applies for each dependent child

Not applicable

Not applicable

chunks.title: Pacific Access Category — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Pacific Access Category
The Pacific Access Category (PAC) allows for citizens of Tonga, Tuvalu and Kiribati (including their partners and dependent children) to be granted permanent residence in New Zealand.
Clients must have two years continuous residence at any one time since being granted permanent residence in New Zealand to be entitled to Jobseeker Support. Until they have met this requirement Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship may be considered.
To assess a client's entitlement to Jobseeker Support on the grounds of hardship, confirmation of the client's income and assets declared on the application for permanent residence is required from Immigration New Zealand.
Note if a client has permanent residence and already meets the two years continuous residence, assess the client for Jobseeker Support in usual manner.
## Additional requirements for the Pacific access category
Tongan clients
If the client is a citizen of Tonga, the client must normally live in Tonga and actually be in Tonga when they apply for permanent residence under this category. The client must also have been born in Tonga or born overseas to a Tongan citizen who was born in Tonga.
Kiribati clients
If the client is a citizen of Kiribati, the client must normally live in Kiribati and actually be in Kiribati or Fiji when they apply for permanent residence under this category. The client must also have been born in Kiribati or born overseas to a Kiribati citizen who was born in Kiribati.
Tuvalu clients
If the client is a citizen of Tuvalu, the client must normally live in Tuvalu and actually be in Tuvalu or Fiji when applying permanent residence under this category. The client must also have been born in Tuvalu or born overseas to a Tuvalu citizen who was born in Tuvalu.

chunks.title: Parent is being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Parent is being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020
All parents are legally obliged to ensure their children are enrolled in and attending school from the age of 6 to 16 years.
Parents can be prosecuted and fined under Education and Training Act 2020 if their children don't attend school. This can happen when:
- there has been, without explanation, ongoing and irregular attendance by the child at school after support has been offered to the family or
- the parent has made little or no attempt to do anything about ensuring the child attends school
If a parent is in the process of being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020, you must not ask them to comply with this social obligation or initiate an obligations failure for non-attendance.
Note you need to record this as an exception in OBMAN using 'Parent is in prosecution for truant child' as the obligation exception reason.

chunks.title: Parenting obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Parenting obligations
Young partners aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children are required to:
- participate in an approved parenting programme
- enrol their child with a primary health care provider, where a local provider is available
- register their child (if aged under 5 years) with a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and keep up-to-date with their visits and
- ensure the child's attendance at an approved Early Childhood Education programme or in other suitable childcare, while they are in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work
For more information see:
- Approved parenting programme
- Enrolment with a primary health care provider - young partner
- Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits
- Ensuring child attends suitable childcare
- Exemptions for young partners

chunks.title: Part-time students — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Part-time students
Where a client is a part-time student and the hours that the client studies are outside normal working hours, then it is accepted that the client is available for full-time work.
If the client is studying during working hours they must still meet the job search requirements.
If the part-time study is 5 to 8 hours or more each week, you must be satisfied that reasonable job search activity is taking place.
When considering the time available for job search take into consideration the client's study timetable and whether enough blocks or periods of time are available for job search activity.
To help you decide if a part-time student can receive the Jobseeker Support see:
- Decision Guidelines - part-time students

chunks.title: Partner in prison — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: You can pay Jobseeker Support to a client when they have lost the regular support of their partner as their partner: - has been imprisoned or - is subject to release or detention conditions that prevent employment

chunks.title: Impact on benefit — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: When a married, civil union or de facto client is imprisoned, the Jobseeker Support will generally need to be cancelled to enable the partner to be granted a benefit in their own right. The Jobseeker Support should be cancelled from the day after imprisonment. If the primary client is imprisoned, the partner should be invited to apply for an alternative benefit in their own right, for example Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support (where they have dependent children under the age of 14 years). They can be granted a sole parent benefit while their partner is in prison even if they are still in a relationship. If the partner is imprisoned, the Jobseeker Support can continue, provided the primary client is still able to meet their work obligations. The Jobseeker Support will be paid at the single or sole parent rate depending on whether there are dependent children included in the benefit. Where there are dependent children and the primary client is no longer able to meet the eligibility for Jobseeker Support because they are no longer available for and seeking full-time work, they will need to test their eligibility for another benefit, for example Sole Parent Support (where their youngest dependent child is under the age of 14 years).

chunks.title: Exception — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Where a client has a partner and/or dependent children there is discretion to continue payment of the Jobseeker Support for a limited period in some circumstances. There is discretion to pay all or part of the Jobseeker Support to the partner of the person who has been imprisoned. This will depend on the length of time imprisoned - where the length of imprisonment is short, using discretion to continue to pay the benefit would prevent having to re-grant. There is also discretion to continue payment if the client is remanded in custody pending a further court appearance. For example, this may be considered where the client may end up receiving a sentence of home detention and needing to have the benefit re-granted to the couple anyway.

chunks.title: Client's income — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Some income the partner receives while they are in prison is taken into account and charged against the client's Jobseeker Support. For more information see: - Types of income

chunks.title: Benefit eligibility and rate while partner is in prison or home detention — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The rate of Jobseeker Support paid while a client's partner is in prison or on home detention depends on the client's circumstances including whether there are dependent children included in the benefit. For more information see: - Benefit eligibility and rate while partner is in prison - Benefit eligibility and rate while the partner is in home detention

chunks.title: Partner is overseas — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client's partner is overseas and the couple still consider themselves to be in a marriage or civil union type relationship, you must take into consideration the partner's residence status and reasons for the partner being overseas before deciding the rate of payment. Any income received by the partner overseas should be charged against the benefit rate whether or not they are included in the client's benefit. For more information see: - Charging income If the client cannot meet the qualifications for the benefit because the partner is overseas, for example, they cannot meet their work obligations; they may be able to receive an Emergency Benefit. For more information see: - Emergency Benefit

chunks.title: Partner detained overseas or missing — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If the partner intends to live in New Zealand but has not yet arrived, they are not considered ordinarily resident and cannot be included in the client's benefit. Where the client still considers themselves married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, the rate payable to the client is half the married, civil union or de facto rate. A higher married, civil union or de facto rate is payable if the client has a dependent child. For more information see:

chunks.title: Exception — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If the partner cannot get to New Zealand due to circumstances beyond their control (for example they are detained in another country or overseas refugee camp or have applied for a visa that has not been granted) or they are missing or their whereabouts are unknown, the client in New Zealand can be paid the single or sole parent rate depending on their family circumstances.

chunks.title: Partners temporarily overseas — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If the partner was resident in New Zealand but has left the country temporarily, they can be included in the client's benefit at grant, as they are considered ordinarily resident. If the partner included in the benefit does not have work obligations, payment can only continue for the first 28 days from the entitlement date. If the partner included in the benefit does have work obligations, payment can only continue for the first 28 days if they are meeting their work obligations. If you are paying the partner while they are overseas, payment should be stopped from the beginning of the fifth week if the partner has not returned.

chunks.title: Partners overseas long-term — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a partner was resident in New Zealand but has left the country and has no definite plans to return (for example, they have been deported) they are not considered ordinarily resident and cannot be included in the benefit. The rate payable to the client is half the married, civil union or de facto rate. The single or sole parent rate can only be paid where the marriage or civil union no longer exists. A higher married, civil union or de facto rate is payable if the client has a dependent child. See: - Partner not qualified For more information see: - Partner's residence status - Partner not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand - Accommodation Supplement Partner overseas - Accommodation Supplement Partner not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand

chunks.title: Partner made redundant — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partner made redundant
If the partner of a client currently receiving a benefit is made redundant, any redundancy payment received is not treated as income and there is no need to review the initial stand-down.
However, this redundancy payment may affect any supplementary benefit as it may increase the couple's cash assets.

chunks.title: Partner not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partner not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand
You can pay a single or sole parent rate, to a client whose partner is not permanently resident or is unlawfully resident in New Zealand, however you have to take their joint income and assets into account.
There are some exceptions.
For more information see:
- Partner's residence status
Clients who were getting a married or civil union rate of benefit before the 8 August 2001, and have a partner without permanent residence included in their benefit, will continue to be paid at the couple rate until their benefit is cancelled.
To pay the Jobseeker Support at the appropriate single/sole parent rate you need to:
- link the partner and primary through CMS
- do not include the partner in the benefit in SREG
- enter the appropriate rate of payment code in the SDT1A screen
- complete notes in CMS
- contact the Card Centre on the day that the benefit is granted to stop a Community Services Card being issued to the non-resident partner

chunks.title: Voluntary unemployment stand-down, strike or obligations failure — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Voluntary unemployment stand-down, strike or obligations failure
You can pay a special rate equal to half the married, civil union or de facto Jobseeker Support to a client (with or without dependent children) if their partner is:
- subject to a 13 week voluntary unemployment stand-down
- on strike or
- subject to an obligations failure
As at 1 April 2026, the rate payable to the client is:
- $316.97 if they have no dependent children or
- $334.70 if they have dependent children
## Partner's residency status
You can pay a single or sole parent rate to a client whose partner is unlawfully resident or not permanently resident in New Zealand, but you have to take their joint income and assets into account.
There are some exceptions, for more information see: Partner's residence status
A half married rate of Jobseeker Support is payable to a client with dependent children, when their partner:
- cannot be included in the benefit because of their residency status and
- the sole parent rate of payment cannot be paid to the client based on the couple's circumstances
The rate payable to the client is $334.70 as at 1 April 2026.

chunks.title: Partner's residence status — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partner's residence status
When a client has a partner, you must also check the partner's residence status because the rate of benefit payable depends on whether or not the partner is included.
The partner can be included in the benefit if they are:
- a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (ie not in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or
- deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) and
- generally ordinarily resident in New Zealand
For more information see:
- Proof of residence
- Deciding ordinarily resident
If a partner has one of the following, they cannot be included in the benefit:
- a temporary entry visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009
- a temporary permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987 (such as a visitor permit, a work permit, or a student permit)
If the partner does not have a current permit or visa that allows them to remain in New Zealand then they are in New Zealand unlawfully and you cannot include the partner in the benefit, unless one of the exceptions listed below applies.
When the partner is in New Zealand unlawfully or is not a permanent resident, pay the client at a single or sole parent rate taking into consideration all of the couple's income and assets.
Contact the Card Centre when granting the primary benefit to ensure that a Community Services Card is not issued to the non-resident partner.
Encourage the partner to follow up their residence status.
## Exceptions
There are some situations where a partner is exempt and can be included in the benefit without having been granted permanent residence. These are:
- a person lawfully present in New Zealand who is awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protection status in New Zealand or
- a person who has refugee or protection status in New Zealand or
- a person applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 who is compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances

chunks.title: Partners with no children or youngest child 14+ years — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partners with no children or youngest child 14+ years
Full-time work obligations apply to:
- partners with no children and
- partners with a youngest child aged 14 years or over
Partners with full-time work obligations must make themselves available for suitable employment, training or other suitable activities of at least 30 hours or more each week.
If a partner is in employment for less than 30 hours each week, they are still expected to be available for other work, training or other activities up to a total of 30 hours each week. The partner must understand that they are still required to accept suitable full-time work if it becomes available.
For more information see:
- Work obligations
- Hours range for suitable employment
Partners may participate in approved training as long as they continue to meet their work obligations, unless they are granted an exemption for approved full-time training.
For more information see:
- In approved training (no children or child 14+)
- Approved training
- Exemptions - approved full-time training
Partners may undertake volunteer work as long as they continue to meet their work obligations. For more information see:
- Clients undertaking voluntary work
Partners may apply for an exemption from their work obligations. For more information on exemptions see:
- Exemptions
- Table of Exemptions
If a partner fails to comply with their work obligations, their portion of the benefit may be stopped.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Obligations failures
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
## Partners aged 16 to 19 years old
Young partners (aged 16 to 19 years old) of clients receiving Jobseeker Support have youth activity obligations, and not work or work preparation obligations, if they are:
- aged 16 or 17 years old without dependent children or
- aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children and
- married to, in a civil union, or de facto relationship with a person getting Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: Partners with youngest child between 3 and 13 years — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partners with youngest child between 3 and 13 years
Part-time work obligations apply to:
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years
The partner must make themselves available for suitable employment, training or other activities of at least 20 hours a week.
For more information see:
- Work obligations
- Hours range for suitable employment
If a partner is in approved training they must continue to meet their work obligations, including being available for part-time employment, unless they are granted an exemption for approved full-time training. The partner must understand that they have to accept suitable paid work if it becomes available.
Partners may undertake voluntary work but must continue to meet their work obligations.
For more information see:
- Clients undertaking voluntary work
Partners may apply for an exemption from their work obligations. For more information on exemptions see:
- Exemptions
- Table of Exemptions
If a partner fails to comply with their work obligations, their portion of the benefit may be stopped.
For more information see:
- Obligations failures
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
If a partner with part-time obligations is already in employment for 20 hours or more each week, they are meeting their work obligations.
If they are in employment for less than 20 hours each week, they are still expected to be available for other work, training or any other activities.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
## Partners aged 16 to 19 years old
Young partners (aged 16 to 19 years old) of clients getting Jobseeker Support have youth activity obligations, and not work or work preparation obligations, if they are:
- aged 16 or 17 years old without dependent children or
- aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children and
- married to, in a civil union, or de facto relationship with a person getting Jobseeker Support
For more information see:

chunks.title: Partners with youngest dependent child under 3 years — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Partners with youngest dependent child under 3 years
Work preparation obligations apply to:
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
The partner must undertake activities that will prepare them for work in the future.
For more information see:
- Work preparation obligations
Partners may apply for an exemption from their work preparation obligations. Generally, they can only be considered for a full exemption as work preparation obligations mean that they are required to plan for employment and undertake work preparation activities - the equivalent of a partial exemption.
For more information see:
- Exemptions
- Table of Exemptions
If a partner fails to comply with their work preparation obligations, they have an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Obligations failures
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
## Partners aged 16 to 19 years old
Young partners (aged 16 to 19 years old) of clients receiving Jobseeker Support have youth activity obligations and not work or work preparation obligations if they are:
- aged 16 or 17 years old without dependent children or
- aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children and
- married to, or in a civil union, or in a de facto relationship with a person receiving Jobseeker Support
For more information see:

chunks.title: Paying other assistance during a sanction — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Paying other assistance during a sanction
Clients are not entitled to the following forms of assistance when they have had a 100% benefit suspension or cancellation imposed due to an obligations failure:
- Emergency Benefit
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit
## Special Needs Grants
Clients are not entitled to Special Needs Grants if a sanction has been imposed. This applies to both financial and non-financial sanctions.
The only exception to this is if a client or partner is health condition or injured when a grade 3 sanction is imposed and they are incapable of participating in full-time employment or an approved activity for 6 weeks.
For more information see:
- Special Needs Grants Assistance during non-entitlement periods
- Special Needs Grants Assistance when a client is sanctioned
## Advance Payment of Benefits
If a client or partner has a 50% sanction imposed, and the client or partner is experiencing hardship they may apply for an Advance Payment of Benefit. A discussion must be held with the client or partner about recomplying as the reduced rate of benefit will be contributing to their hardship.
Generally clients will not be entitled to advance payments of benefit when they have a 100% sanction imposed. This is because they will be contributing to their hardship through not recomplying. The client's first option to improve their financial situation is to recomply with their obligations and an advance cannot be paid when the client or partner has no means of repaying it.
A client can apply for an Advance Payment of Benefit if they have a non-financial sanction imposed, and may be eligible if they meet all the criteria.
## Assistance to transition into employment
Clients can get assistance to transition into employment if a sanction has been imposed and they meet the qualifications for it.
For more information see:
- Employment and training Assistance to transition into employment
## Young partners
Where a young partner has an obligations failure, the assistance that is available to them depends on the failure number, and whether the young partner is youth money managed or not.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Payment for travel and other associated costs — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Payment for travel and other associated costs
You can pay actual and reasonable costs for travel, accommodation, meals and a support person or where appropriate an attendant carer for clients attending a Work Ability Assessment.
What is reasonable will depend on where the client lives, their family circumstances, and any health condition or disability they have.
For more information see:
- Payment process Work Ability Assessment - Payment for travel and other associated costs [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Payment process for a young partner — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Payment process for a young partner
