The couple's main benefit and any Extra help will be apportioned between the couple.
The young partner who is youth money managed, will have their portion of accommodation, service costs and lawful debts paid direct to a supplier from their portion of their main benefit and any on-going extra help. The balance of payment, if any, is distributed between the young partner's payment card and the in-hand allowance. The maximum amount that can be paid direct to a young partner as an in-hand allowance is $50.
The following process shows how a young partner's portion of benefit assistance is paid when they are subject to youth money management.
## Step 2
Any incentive payments earned is added.
Note to ensure the incentive payment is only paid to the person who earned it, the portion of incentive payment that will automatically be apportioned to the primary client will need to be re-directed back to the young person.
## Step 3
Young partner's portion of extra help, such as Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support and Winter Energy Payment is added.
## Step 6
Disability Allowance is paid directly to the young partner.
## Altering the distribution of payment for existing clients already subject to youth money management
If, at any time, a Youth Service provider considers that the current distribution of an existing client's payment between the payment card and in-hand allowance is inappropriate for the client's circumstances, they can make a recommendation to YSSU that this distribution be altered.
When determining whether it is appropriate to make a recommendation that a client's payment distribution be altered, providers must take into account a range of factors.

chunks.title: Payment when partner becomes primary during non-entitlement period — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Payment when partner becomes primary during non-entitlement period
The rate of payment depends on whether the non-entitlement period still applies to the client once they are no longer the primary on Jobseeker Support.
## Non-entitlement period no longer applies
If the non-entitlement period no longer applies then you can pay the rate of benefit the couple would usually receive, taking into account any income.
## Non-entitlement period still applies
If the non-entitlement period still applies, you can pay the new primary a rate of Jobseeker Support equal to the half married, civil union, or de facto rate of benefit.
## Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit
If there are dependent children, family tax credit and Best Start tax credit is paid at the full rate to the new primary client.
## Supplementary assistance
The partner may receive 50% of any supplementary assistance to which the couple is entitled.
## Income
All income that the couple receive needs to be taken into account. The income should be charged against the full married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit and the remainder divided by two. This is the rate of benefit that you would pay to the partner.
Note calculate the commencement date using the higher income of either the applicant or their partner over the previous 26 or 52 weeks.
For more information see:
- Effect of 13 week non-entitlement period for partner

chunks.title: Payment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Payment
Jobseeker Support is paid weekly on a Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. Payment is from Monday to Sunday and is made one week in arrears.
Generally, payment must be made directly to the client. However, where there is good cause the client's benefit can be paid to another person, agent or institution.
For more information see:
- Core policy Redirection of benefit payment
## Exception for young partners
There are two ways that young partners aged 16 or 17 years (with no children) and 16 to 19 years (with dependent children) can have their portion of their benefit paid to them, depending on whether the young partner is subject to youth money management or not.
## Young partner is not subject to youth money management
When a young partner is not subject to youth money management they can get their portion of their main benefit payment, family tax credit, Best Start tax credit and any extra help paid directly to their bank account.
## Young partner is subject to youth money management
If a young partner is subject to youth money management the young partner's portion of main benefit, family tax credit, Best Start tax credit and any extra help (except Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance) is paid via:
- payment directly to supplier (e.g. a payee redirection for accommodation costs, utility costs and lawful debts)
- in-hand allowance which is paid directly to the young person's bank account
- payment card - the young person is able to purchase goods (such as food and groceries) from approved suppliers
Note Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance is paid directly to the young person's bank account.
For more information see:
- Redirection for young partners
It is a condition of getting a benefit that the client provides a bank account number.
MSD may request the client or their partner to provide an IRD number or evidence of their IRD number.
For more information see:
- IRD number for client or partner who is apportioned assistance
## Rate of payment
The rate of Jobseeker Support that can be paid depends on the client's:
- age
- relationship status
- dependent children
and
for 18 or 19 year olds:
- whether they live at home or not

chunks.title: Payments to the non-sanctioned client — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Payments to the non-sanctioned client
When a client has their portion of the benefit sanctioned, the non-sanctioned client will continue to get:
- their portion of the benefit and
- for a grade 2 or 3 sanction, 50% of the Extra help the couple was entitled to (the couple's Extra help is not affected by a grade 1 sanction) and the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment
MSD should check if the non-sanctioned client has had any changes in their circumstances or their family's situation. The non-sanctioned client should be advised about applying for a benefit in their own right (in this situation the benefit would only be paid at the half-married rate).
For more information see:
- Effect of financial sanctions on assistance
- Financial assistance during non-entitlement period

chunks.title: People in between employment agreements (with same employer) — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## People in between employment agreements (with same employer)
Clients who have an employment agreement which does not include employment over the holiday period can qualify for Jobseeker Support because they only expect to return to that employment (for example Teacher Aides). The employment relationship has ceased for a period and they have no guarantee that they will return to that job. They still have to be:
- seeking other full-time employment
- available for it
- willing and able to undertake it and
- taking reasonable steps to find it
If these clients have been on benefit within the last 26 weeks you can look at waiving the stand-down, as the employment relationship has ceased.
For more information see:
- Initial stand-down

chunks.title: Period of Community Work Experience — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Period of Community Work Experience
Clients who have found a suitable organisation and position for Community Work Experience during their 2-week search period must complete at least 5 hours of work per week over the 4-week period.
## 4-week period
The 4-week period of Community Work Experience generally starts immediately after the 2-week search period ends, unless the client finds and begins a suitable position before the end of the search period.
The 4 weeks must be consecutive. For example, if the position offered is 4 weeks in total, but there is a 1-week break because the organisation is closed that week, the position would not be suitable for Community Work Experience.
## 5 hours per week
A client must complete at least 5 hours per week over 4-week period. A client can choose to do more hours if they wish, however any extra hours must not stop them from meeting their obligations, such as being available for and seeking employment.
Any extra hours a client completes will not count towards their Community Work Experience. The client must complete at least 5 hours each week. Any hours they did the previous week cannot be counted towards their 5 hours for a different week.
## Public holidays
A client does not need to do Community Work Experience on a weekend, public holiday or regional holiday. However, they can choose to do their hours on these days if they want to.
MSD should consider upcoming holidays before imposing Community Work Experience. Many community organisations will be closed on these dates, for example over the Christmas period. If a client is unlikely to complete their required hours due to public holidays, it would not be suitable to impose Community Work Experience.
## Option to secure multiple positions
A client could find more than one suitable organisation and position to help them meet the required number of hours and weeks. This could be:
- finding 2 or more organisations who offer enough hours per week between them, or
- working at 2 or more organisations, who offer back-to-back positions, for example doing the first 2 weeks with one organisation, and the next 2 weeks with a different organisation, or
- a combination of both.
A client can secure more than one position for their Community Work Experience, as long as they are able to meet the requirements of the sanction.
The organisations and positions must all be approved by MSD before they start the community work and before the 5-day verification window has ended.

chunks.title: Period of Money Management — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: When a client fails their obligations, they have 5 working days to dispute the failure before a sanction is imposed. Money Management when imposed starts the day after the 5 working day notice period. Clients are money managed for 4 weeks (28 days). This period includes weekends and public holidays. Money Management will end after 4 weeks and a client’s payments will be made in full to their bank account if they have recomplied with their obligation failure during this time.

chunks.title: Money Management begins in the middle of a pay period — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Money Management will be applied on any weekday, including public holidays. This means that Money Management is likely to begin in the middle of a client’s pay period and will result in partial payments. For more information see:

chunks.title: Benefit stops during Money Management — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: A client’s benefit may stop while they are being money managed, e.g. one week their income was over the income limit. The length of Money Management is not impacted by any breaks in payment, and will always end 4 weeks after it was imposed.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Kale fails their obligation Money Management starts on 14 August. Their last day of Money Management will be 10 September. Kale travels to Australia from 18 August to 25 August for a holiday. They do not inform MSD before their travel and their benefit is stopped from the day after they left New Zealand. Kale’s benefit is resumed from the date they return to New Zealand. Their Money Management continues from 25 August, and will still end on 10 September.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Rahool is getting Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability. He fails a work-preparation obligation on 3 March and is placed onto Money Management on 10 March. His Money Management period will end on 6 April. Rahool’s medical certificate expires on 31 March. His benefit stops until he gets a new medical certificate. He gets a new medical certificate on 10 April, 4 days after his Money Management period has ended. His benefit resumes from 31 March when his medical certificate first expired, and MSD issues arrears of his Jobseeker Support from 31 March to 10 April. Rahool’s arrears for the period of 31 March to 6 April, are subject to Money Management. 50% of those arrears are paid onto his payment card and the remainder to his bank account. The arrears owed after his Money Management ends, from 7 April to 10 April, are also paid directly into Rahool’s bank account.

chunks.title: Period of Report Job Search — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Period of Report Job Search
Clients who have Report Job Search imposed on them must complete at least 3 suitable job-search activities per week over the 4-week period. They must also report to MSD each week on the job-search activities they have completed in that week.
## 3 job-search activities per week
A client must complete and report on at least 3 suitable job-search activities per week over the 4-week period. A client can choose to do and report on more job-search activities if they wish, however any extra job-search activities a client completes can only be counted in the week they completed them. Any extra job-search activities they completed in the previous weeks cannot be counted towards their 3 job-search activities for the current week.
Note MSD must consider a client's job-search activities are reasonable steps towards them finding suitable employment.

chunks.title: Clients without permanent residence or citizenship — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Clients without permanent residence or citizenship
Emergency Benefit may be paid to some categories of migrants who do not have permanent residence or citizenship, eg people waiting for their application for refugee or protection status to be approved.
For more information see:
- Proof of residence
- Emergency Benefit
- Refugee or protected person
Note clients lawfully in New Zealand by virtue of a temporary permit or temporary entry class visa only (ie they do not have permanent residence) are not entitled to any benefit assistance.
To assess a client's entitlement you will generally need to establish exactly what category of migrant they are.
Clients may be granted permanent residence under the following categories:
- Family Stream
- International/Humanitarian Stream
- Skilled/Business Stream
Note if you require further information about a client's application for permanent residence you must get consent from the client to contact Immigration New Zealand or the client should obtain the information themselves. Otherwise the application should be declined. You must not collect or disclose information regarding a client's application without the client's consent.
For more information see:
- Immigration status and supporting documents
- Immigration status [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Personal cash assets — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Personal cash assets
Where the client was granted permanent residence because they had personal cash assets you will need to obtain information from Immigration New Zealand to confirm the reason for granting permanent residence. Ensure you have the consent of the client before contacting Immigration New Zealand.
Once confirmed, assess Jobseeker Support or if the client does not meet the 2 years continuous residence criteria, Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship in the usual manner taking into account all other information provided by Immigration New Zealand.
If there is a significant drop in the client's cash assets declared, confirmation for the following should be requested:
- what cash assets were they referring to and
- what has happened to these cash assets
It is not acceptable for these cash assets to be used to purchase capital items such as a house, furniture or motor vehicle.
Settlement funds can be used to purchase capital items, as these are not the same as cash assets declared as personal resources.
Note if the client has resided in New Zealand for 2 years assess the client's entitlement to the Jobseeker Support in the usual manner.
For more information see:
- Proof of residence
- Qualifications
- Granting on grounds of hardship

chunks.title: Health practitioners that can complete medical certificates — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Health practitioners that can complete medical certificates
A medical certificate for Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) must be signed by a registered:
- medical practitioner or
- dentist (where appropriate) or
- midwife (in respect of a pregnancy, childbirth, or any related conditions) or
- nurse practitioner

chunks.title: Pre-benefit requirements for new applicants — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Pre-benefit requirements for new applicants
Clients who have had their benefit cancelled due to not completing the reapplication process will be subject to the same pre-benefit requirements as other clients applying for Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: Pregnancy — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Pregnancy
A client can only get Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) for pregnancy from the beginning of the 27th week of pregnancy unless they:
- are suffering from an illness or disability other than pregnancy or
- have complications with the pregnancy which prevents the client from being in paid employment
The medical certificate must show the expected date of birth of the child.
Clients without complications who are less than 27 weeks pregnant may be entitled to get Jobseeker Support with full-time work obligations.
If the client does not have a partner, explain to the client that:
- once the child is born they have to let us know of the birth and
- also whether the client intends to keep the baby
For more information about continuing entitlement to Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) when the baby is born, see: Birth of a child
## Overdue pregnancy
You can extend a client's Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) without an additional medical certificate when they have gone past their expected date of the birth.
The client needs to contact their case manager to let them know they are overdue. The Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) can be continued with no further medical verification required.
The benefit can be extended to 4 weeks after the expected due date.

chunks.title: Pregnant 27 weeks or complications — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Pregnant 27 weeks or complications
A client receiving Jobseeker Support can be deferred from their work obligations and be subject to work preparation obligations if they are:
- 27 weeks pregnant or
- earlier if there are complications associated with the pregnancy
Note if a partner is 27 weeks pregnant, or has complications associated with the pregnancy, they may be granted an exemption from their work obligations.
## Evidence
The client must provide evidence from a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or midwife confirming the expected date of birth or the nature of complications if their pregnancy is under 27 weeks.
## Duration
This deferral applies until either:
- the birth of the child or
- the client no longer has complications if they are less than 27 weeks pregnant

chunks.title: Pregnant 27 weeks or earlier if complications — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Pregnant 27 weeks or earlier if complications
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
A partner who is pregnant can be exempt from meeting some of their work obligations from:
- week 27 of the pregnancy or
- earlier if there are complications associated with the pregnancy
Note this is a partial exemption when it is reasonable to plan with the partner.
## Evidence
The partner must provide evidence from a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or midwife confirming the expected date of birth or nature of complications if under 27 weeks.
## Duration
This exemption applies until the birth of the child or for 6 months from the date it was granted, whichever is earlier.

chunks.title: In prison 31 days or more — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## In prison 31 days or more
Clients who have been in prison or on remand for 31 days or more have a stand-down imposed.
These clients have access to a Steps to Freedom Special Needs Grant to assist them during the stand-down. They may also have access to other forms of assistance to help them re-establish themselves in the community.
## Calculating the number of days
When counting the number of days that a client has been in prison or held on remand, you should include the date the client:
- enters the prison or held on remand and
- leaves prison or is released from remand
For more information see:
- Imprisonment Release from prison
- Transfer between benefits

chunks.title: Process for deciding appropriate activities — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Process for deciding appropriate activities
When you and the client are considering appropriate activities for the client to undertake, you should consider the following:
- what needs or barriers to employment is the activity designed to address for the client
- what activities are available to help the client move towards employment
- the Work and Income programmes and services that are available to help the client move towards employment
Examples of appropriate activities include (but are not limited to):
- participating in the Job Search Service
- education or training to improve partners work-readiness or prospects for employment
For more information see:
- Activity Summary
- Informing clients of their obligations

chunks.title: Process for investigating industrial disputes — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Process for investigating industrial disputes
Local decisions are to be made jointly by the regional director and the manager client service delivery.
There must be consultation with your local solicitor on interpretation of the legislation and any applicable employment contracts.
Also consult your local solicitor about any disputes with national implications, for example, the entire freezing industry.
For disputes that cross service centre boundaries, the regional director is to ensure:
- co-ordination of the investigation through one service centre
- other manager client service delivery in the area are fully informed of the dispute and
- other manager client service delivery in the area are informed of the decision when finally reached
## For more information about investigating industrial disputes see:
- Steps for investigating industrial disputes

chunks.title: Proof of residence — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: All documents should be originals. Photocopies and/or documents that have been changed in any way cannot be accepted. Where the client (or partner) cannot provide proof or the proof is unclear, you should ask the client (or partner) to obtain confirmation of their residential status from Immigration New Zealand (for permanent residence) or Internal Affairs (for citizenship). Proof of citizenship and/or permanent residence in New Zealand can be a: - New Zealand birth certificate Generally, a person born in New Zealand is a New Zealand citizen by birth. - New Zealand passport To hold a New Zealand passport you must be a citizen of New Zealand. - Certificate of Registration A child born outside New Zealand (to a parent who is a New Zealand citizen) may be a New Zealand citizen from birth. However, the child must apply for a Certificate of Registration to confirm their New Zealand citizenship. - Grant of Citizenship People who have permanent residence, may (normally after 5 years residence in New Zealand) apply for a Grant of Citizenship. They must meet the conditions of the Grant. - Certificate of Confirmation This is a certificate issued to confirm that the holder is a New Zealand citizen by birth, descent or Grant of Citizenship. British subjects, who immigrated to New Zealand prior to 1948 (and who resided in New Zealand for all of 1948) were made New Zealand citizens in 1949. These people are likely to have a Certificate of Confirmation or a Certificate of Naturalisation. - Certificate of Naturalisation Previously immigrants were naturalised as British Subjects and Citizens of New Zealand. Today they are given a Grant of Citizenship. - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence class visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009 - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987 Note that a visa issued before 29 November 2010 does not allow a person to stay in New Zealand. - Letter of confirmation of permanent residence from Immigration New Zealand - Australian citizens Australian citizens are lawfully allowed in New Zealand as they are deemed to hold a residence class visa here. Their date of entry into New Zealand is generally not recorded. Where possible supporting evidence should be sought, such as, tenancy agreements, bank statements or old utility bills to show that the client has been ordinarily resident for two continuous years. - British nationals

chunks.title: Proof of residence — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients of British nationality who came to New Zealand before 2 April 1974 were automatically allowed to enter New Zealand for residence, and will be unable to provide verification of their residence if they do not have a passport. Immigration New Zealand will have no record of these clients unless the client has contacted them after 2 April 1974. The client should be able to provide New Zealand school, work or tax records to support their claim about when they arrived in New Zealand and the length of time they have lived here. For more information see: - Immigration status and supporting documents

chunks.title: Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Generally, a temporary provisional benefit can be paid to the client or their partner while they are doing an approved activity or programme of activities during their 13 week non-entitlement period (except when the approved activity is full-time employment).

chunks.title: Provisional benefit — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: MSD can grant or increase a provisional benefit from the date the client or partner starts their approved activity or programme of activities. Their benefit will be provisionally paid to them if they are satisfactorily participating in their activity. The provisional payment will continue until: - the 6-week activity period ends or - the 13-week non-entitlement period ends whichever is earlier. Some examples of this: - a client starts their approved activity in the beginning of week 3 of their non-entitlement period. The client does the approved activity for 6 continuous weeks, and the rest of the 13-week non-entitlement period is cancelled. After the follow-up appointment, the client’s benefit is reinstated to their usual benefit, instead of a provisional benefit. - a client starts their approved activity in the beginning of week 10 of the non-entitlement period. The client does the approved activity for the rest of the 13-week non-entitlement period (3 weeks). At the end of the 13-week non-entitlement period, the client’s benefit is reinstated to their usual benefit, instead of a provisional benefit.

chunks.title: End of approved activity or non-entitlement period — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: At the end of the approved activity or programme of activities, a follow-up appointment is required (in approximately 6 weeks' time). At the appointment, MSD should discuss with the client or partner whether they: - have satisfactorily participated in the approved activity, and - can still meet the qualifications and obligations of their benefit. Note if the client or their partner does not recomply, they will have to reapply for their benefit at the end of the 13-week non-entitlement period.

chunks.title: Leaves approved activity or does not satisfactorily participate — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If the client or partner leaves early or does not satisfactorily participate in the approved activity or programme of suitable activities, without a change in their obligations, their provisional benefit must be reduced or stopped from the date it was increased or granted. The benefit amount that was provisionally paid during the 13-week non-entitlement period must be established as a debt and recovered. MSD cannot recover the provisional benefit if they did not complete the approved activity because they: - transferred to a benefit with no work obligations, or - meet the criteria for a full exemption from their work obligations. Only one approved activity or programme can be assigned to a client. MSD cannot give the client a different approved activity if the client fails to satisfactorily complete their approved activity.

chunks.title: Qualifications — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To get Jobseeker Support a client must:
- not be in full-time employment
- be available for and seeking full-time employment
- have taken reasonable steps to find, and be willing and able to undertake employment
or
- not be a full-time student
or
- have a temporary exemption from their work obligations
or
- not be in full-time employment, however are willing to undertake it, but due to a health condition, injury or a disability, are limited in their capacity to seek, undertake, or be available for full-time employment
or
- be in employment, but due to a health condition, injury or a disability is losing earnings because they are not actually working or are working at a reduced level
A client must also:
- be aged 18 years or older if they have no dependent children or20 years or older, if they have dependent children
- 18 years or older if they have no dependent children or
- 20 years or older, if they have dependent children
- have continuously lived in New Zealand for 2 years or more since becoming a New Zealand citizen or residence class visa holder
- complete any pre-benefit requirements, if applicable and
- have no income, or an income of less than the amount that would fully reduce the benefit
## Jobseeker Support on ground of hardship
To get Jobseeker Support on ground of hardship, the client must meet the above qualifications except for the residence criteria.
However they must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or residence class visa holder but have lived in New Zealand for less than 2 years
- be suffering hardship and
- not qualify for any other main benefit.
## For more information on each qualification see:
- Age
- Client has a health condition, injury or disability
- Students
- Dependent child
- Residence
- Income criteria
- Changes and reviews Pre-benefit requirements
- Job search requirements
- Granting on grounds of hardship
- Clients with specific circumstances
- Reapplication process at 26 weeks

chunks.title: Reapplication process — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Jobseeker Support is a temporary work-focused benefit paid for up to 26 weeks while a client looks for work, is in training for work, is unable to work or is working reduced hours due to a health condition, injury or disability. To continue getting Jobseeker Support, a client (and any partner included in their Jobseeker Support) must complete the 26 week reapplication process before their expiry date. The 26 week reapplication process allows MSD to determine if clients still qualify for their benefit. To complete the 26 week reapplication process a client (and any partner included in their Jobseeker Support) must complete the following parts of the reapplication before their expiry date: - an eligibility check and - an appropriate employment engagement and - agree to their obligations and confirm their intention to reapply for Jobseeker Support Note clients getting Emergency Benefit, where the equivalent benefit is Jobseeker Support, are not required to complete the 26 week reapplication process.

chunks.title: Clients getting Jobseeker Support before 1 July 2025 — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients already getting Jobseeker Support before 1 July 2025 must complete either a 26 week or 52 week application before their benefit expiry date if they still need it.

chunks.title: Clients who complete the 26 week reapplication process — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Some clients who were getting Jobseeker Support before 1 July 2025 and are still getting their benefit on 1 July 2025 maintain their 52 week expiry date. To continue getting Jobseeker Support, these clients must complete the 26 week reapplication process before their benefit expiry. This applies to the following clients only: - clients whose Jobseeker Support commenced (or last commenced) before 4 February 2025, and - sole parent or grandparented clients whose Jobseeker Support commenced (or last commenced) before 1 July 2025 When these clients complete the 26 week reapplication process before their final 52 week expiry date and Jobseeker Support is regranted, they move to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle.

chunks.title: Clients who complete the 52 week reapplication process — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Some clients who were getting Jobseeker Support before 1 July 2025 and are still getting their benefit on 1 July 2025 maintain their 52 week expiry date. To continue getting Jobseeker Support, these clients must complete the 52 week reapplication process before their expiry date. This is a transitional arrangement that applies to the following clients only: - clients who have an 'in-flight' 52 week reapplication on 1 July 2025 When these clients complete the 52 week reapplication process before their final 52 week expiry date and Jobseeker Support is regranted, they move to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. By 30 June 2026 all clients will have moved to the 26 week expiry and reapplication cycle. For more information see: - 52 week reapplication process for clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025 - Expiry date for sole parent and grandparented clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025 - Clients who have an 'in-flight' 52 week reapplication on 1 July 2025 - Expiry date for clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025 - Review of Annual Income - sole parent and grandparented clients before 30 June 2026 - Annual income for sole parent and grandparented clients before 30 June 2026

chunks.title: Exceptions — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: There are situations where a client and their partner (if applicable) are not required to complete the reapplication process. See: Client does not need to complete the reapplication process

chunks.title: Reapplication process for clients aged 65 or older — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Reapplication process for clients aged 65 or older
Clients aged 65 years or older who do not qualify for New Zealand Superannuation may get Jobseeker Support if they meet all of the qualifications.
As part of the reapplication process, MSD will discuss with the client about how they are preparing for or looking for employment, for example:
- what steps have they taken to obtain suitable employment
- have they attended any interviews
- what planning for employment have they undertaken
For more information see:
- 52 week reapplication process for clients whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025
- Specific employment engagement
- Employment part of the 26 week reapplication
## Willing and available for work but likelihood of employment low
If the client advises they are willing and available for work, but the likelihood of them gaining employment is low, MSD may consider whether it is appropriate for them to continue getting Jobseeker Support on the ground of being available for full-time work.
To make this decision, MSD will consider the client's situation, including (but not limited to):
- their family circumstances e.g. caring responsibilities
- their job search efforts and the outcome from this
- the local labour market conditions
- their skills and qualifications
- their health and any disabilities they may have.
Consider whether the client is eligible for a deferral from their work obligations or qualifies for another main benefit, such as Supported Living Payment.
## Eligible for Emergency Benefit
If the client does not qualify for Jobseeker Support or any other benefit, Emergency Benefit may be considered in substitution of Jobseeker Support.
The client will need to meet all of the qualifications for Emergency Benefit including the hardship test. This must be decided on a case-by-case basis, taking the client's full circumstances into consideration.
For more information see:
- Emergency Benefit Clients aged 65 years or over
- Emergency Benefit Client in hardship
## Clients with a partner
If the client has a partner, the partner should also be assessed to see if they meet the qualifications for a benefit. If the partner qualifies for a benefit, this should be granted with the client included instead of considering Emergency Benefit.
Note that Emergency Benefit may still be considered for the client if the benefit their partner qualifies for is Supported Living Payment on the ground of caring. This is because the client cannot be included in that benefit, there is no couple rate of payment

chunks.title: Recent bereavement of partner — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recent bereavement of partner
This exemption may apply to clients and sole parents with work or work preparation obligations.
Clients whose partner has recently died can be exempt from meeting all their work or work preparation obligations to allow them time to adjust to their new circumstances. This is a full exemption.
Before granting this exemption you should consider the following factors:
- changes in living circumstances
- changes in childcare responsibilities
- particular religious or cultural beliefs or practices
Note you should consider the client's eligibility for Sole Parent Support.
## Proof
The client needs to provide:
- personal statement
- evidence included in their application for benefit
- a death notice from the newspaper or
- a death certificate
If the client has been granted a Funeral Grant for their partner they should not be asked to provide proof again.
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 3 months from the date of death.
You can extend the exemption. Before you do this you should ask the client to provide information to support the need for the exemption to continue.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Recent bereavement of partner/spouse'.

chunks.title: Recent separation from a partner — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recent separation from a partner
This exemption may apply to clients and sole parents with work or work preparation obligations.
Clients who have recently separated from their partner, can be exempt from meeting all their work or work preparation obligations to allow them time to adjust to their new circumstances. This is a full exemption.
Before granting this exemption you should consider the following factors:
- changes in living circumstances
- changes in childcare responsibilities
## Proof
The client needs to provide:
- a personal statement or
- evidence included in their application for benefit
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 28 days from the date of separation.
You can extend the exemption. Before you do this you should ask the client to provide information to support the need for the exemption to continue.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Recent separation from partner/spouse'.

chunks.title: Reciprocal Agreements — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Reciprocal Agreements
New Zealand has Reciprocal Agreements with some countries. However, only the agreement with the United Kingdom includes Jobseeker Support.
Under that agreement, residence and or periods of insurance contributions in the United Kingdom can be regarded as residence in New Zealand.
- To or from Overseas United Kingdom
For more information about the United Kingdom Agreement contact International Services
## Australian clients
Prior to 1 February 2000, the Australian Reciprocal Agreement allowed Australian residents or holders of an Australian passport to Jobseeker Support after living in New Zealand for 6 months.
From 1 February 2000, Australian residents or holders of an Australian passport have to meet the 2 year continuous residence requirement to receive Jobseeker Support.
For more information about the Australian Reciprocal Agreement contact International Services.

chunks.title: Recompliance — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Recompliance is the activity a client or partner must undertake after they have failed an obligation. They must complete the recompliance activity to have their benefit: - increased or resumed if they have been financially sanctioned or - continued if they have a non-financial sanction imposed Generally, the activities a client or partner need to complete are the same or substantially similar to the obligation that initiated the failure. Clients with an obligations failure initiated who recomply within five working days will not have a sanction imposed, but the obligations failure will be counted. When a client or partner indicates that they want to recomply MSD must make a recompliance activity available for them at the earliest opportunity. An obligations failure that has reduced or stopped their benefit will determine the type of recompliance activity the client or partner will need to undertake. MSD must discuss with the client what activities they need to undertake in order to recomply. For more information see: - Recompliance for work obligation failures - Recompliance for social obligation failures - Recompliance for drug test obligation failures - Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: When to resume or increase a benefit — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The client must have successfully completed the recompliance activity before their benefit is resumed or increased if they have been financially sanctioned. Once completed, the benefit will can be resumed or increased from the date MSD is satisfied the client has started the recompliance activity. Some examples of this: - if the recompliance activity is a one-off, such as attending an interview the benefit would be resumed from the date the client attended and participated in the interview - if the recompliance activity is ongoing, such as a training programme, the client must undertake the training programme to MSD's satisfaction. Once this is complete, the benefit can be resumed from the date the client started the training programme - if the client has multiple recompliance activities to complete (due to more than one failure), the date when they have completed a recompliance activity for the latest failure For what to do if a client cannot recomply, see: - Unable to recomply - Recompliance and change of circumstances

chunks.title: Allocating an extra activity — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Once a client or partner has recomplied and their benefit has been resumed or increased, they may be allocated appropriate additional activities or support. When determining whether to allocate additional activities, the client's individual circumstances must be considered, including: - the type of obligations they have, and - if there are any suitable activities currently available for them If additional activities are assigned to the client or partner, they must complete them. Failure to complete these activities without a good and sufficient reason should be treated as a new obligations failure.

chunks.title: Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period) — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: A client or their partner can complete certain activities to get a temporary provisional benefit if they have a 13-week non-entitlement period because they: - left a job voluntarily - lost a job due to misconduct - have a grade 3 sanction imposed or - refused an offer of suitable employment. If a client or their partner want to recomply, MSD must make a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities available to them at the earliest opportunity. An approved activity can start as soon as a sanction has been imposed, there is no waiting period.

chunks.title: Recompliance activities — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The client or their partner must do the approved activity for 6 continuous weeks, or until their 13-week non-entitlement period ends (whichever is earlier). This can be through: - satisfactory participation in a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities - satisfactory participation in full-time employment or - part-time employment (if they have part-time work obligations). Note clients and partners with full-time work obligations should have a full-time 6-week approved activity. Clients and partners with part-time work obligations should have a part-time 6-week approved activity. Clients and partners with full-time work obligations who are recomplying through approved full-time employment do not get a provisional benefit.

chunks.title: Client does not complete activity — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If a client fails to complete their 6-week activity or programme of activities, and their obligations have not changed, their provisional benefit must be reduced or stopped from the date it was increased or granted. Any provisional benefit the client was paid must be established as a debt. To get a new benefit, the client must wait until the end of the 13-week non-entitlement period to re-apply or to get their full rate of benefit reinstated if the client has dependent children. When a client with dependent children makes contact at the end of the 13 weeks, MSD should review their circumstances to confirm that the client still qualifies and what rate of payment they should get. MSD must determine the appropriate date to increase the rate from, but this cannot be any earlier than the end of the 13-week period. Only one approved activity or programme of activities can be assigned to a client. MSD cannot give a client a different approved activity if they fail to satisfactorily complete the original approved activity.

chunks.title: Recompliance for social obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: If the client or their partner fails their obligations for a third time, and the third failure is a social obligation failure, then their 6 week recompliance activity will be different. In this situation it may not be appropriate to choose an activity focused on work outcomes. A programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate instead.

chunks.title: Recompliance and change of circumstances — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance and change of circumstances
A client who has a failure in progress or a sanction imposed may be unable to recomply because they:
- had a change of circumstances that means they can no longer comply with a social obligation or the social obligation is no longer relevant to them or
- had a change in obligations which means they are no longer required to comply with any activity that is specific to their previous obligations, for example a client moves between work obligations and work preparation obligations
In these situations, a client should not be required to recomply. However, the failure will still be included in the 24-month count.
Note young partners who failed a youth activity obligation will have this counted for 12 months, even if they are no longer subject to youth activity obligations.
Once the client has new obligations, MSD may ask them to complete any activities in relation to their new obligations.
## Examples
Examples of where MSD cannot require the client to complete a recompliance activity:
- where a child leaves care or changes age and the social obligation they had is no longer relevant (for example the client has failed the early childhood education social obligation and the child has now turned 6 years old)
- where a client is subject to work obligations has failed a drug test obligation and is transferred to work preparation obligations
- where a client who has work preparation obligations has failed to undertake planning for employment and is transferred to work obligations
- where a client who has work or work preparation obligations has failed an obligation and has been transferred to Supported Living Payment or Emergency Benefit with no obligations
For more information see:
- Recompliance for work obligation failures
- Recompliance for social obligation failures
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Recomplying more than one failure
- Deactivation, disputes and reviews [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Recompliance and Community Work Experience — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance and Community Work Experience
Community Work Experience is both a sanction for an obligation failure, and a recompliance activity for a client to recomply with their obligations.
This means that a client who is completing Community Work Experience is not required to complete the same or similar activity that they originally failed to do.
If a client completes the requirements of their position and provides verification, they will be considered to have recomplied from the day they complete their Community Work Experience.
Clients who do not complete their Community Work Experience will be considered non-compliant. Their payments will be reduced or stopped, and MSD must assign an alternative recompliance activity as soon as possible.

chunks.title: Recompliance and Report Job Search — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance and Report Job Search
Report Job Search is both a non-financial sanction for an obligation failure, and a recompliance activity for a client to recomply with their obligations.
This means that a client who is completing Report Job Search is not required to complete the same or similar activity that they originally failed to do.
If a client completes the requirements of Report Job Search and provides verification, they will be considered to have recomplied from the day they complete Report Job Search.
Clients who do not complete Report Job Search will be considered non-compliant. Their payments will be reduced or stopped, and MSD must assign an alternative recompliance activity as soon as possible.

chunks.title: Recompliance for drug test obligation failures — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
Clients who have failed their drug test obligations will need to complete a recompliance activity to increase, resume or continue their benefit.
Once a client or partner indicates they want to recomply, MSD must have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply. The grade of the drug test obligation failure will determine the recompliance activity required.
For more information see:
- Recomplying first drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying third drug test obligation failure

chunks.title: Recompliance for social obligation failures — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for social obligation failures
Clients who have failed their social obligations need to meet all their social obligations as part of an activity to increase or continue their benefit.
Once a client or partner indicates they want to recomply, MSD must have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply.
Note when a client has a partner, social obligations apply to both the client and the partner.
For more information see:
- Recompliance social obligations failure (Grade 1 and 2)
- Social obligations recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Client and partner fail their social obligations
- Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Recompliance for work obligation failures — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for work obligation failures
Clients who have failed their work obligations need to recomply to have their benefit:
- increased or resumed if they have been financially sanctioned or
- continued if they have a non-financial sanction imposed
Once a client or partner indicates they want to recomply MSD must have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply.
## Work obligations failure (Grade 1 and 2)
For clients to recomply with a work obligations failure (grade 1 and 2) and have their benefit increased or resumed, the client or partner will need to complete:
• the activity they failed or• an activity that is the same as or substantially similar to the activity they failed
Note for grade 1 failures where a non-financial sanction has been imposed, the recompliance requirements may be different. For more information see:
• Non-financial sanctions
## Work obligations failure or failure to accept an offer of suitable employment (Grade 3)
For clients to recomply to a work obligations failure (grade 3) and be granted a provisional benefit, the client or partner will need to start and complete a 6 week recompliance activity or programme of activities (13 week non-entitlement period) or wait until the end of the 13 week non-entitlement period.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Recompliance for young partners — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for young partners
Young partners with a youth activity obligations failure initiated must recomply within five working days. If they do this no sanction will be imposed but the activity obligations failure will be counted.
If the sanction has been imposed the young partner must recomply to have their benefit increased or resumed.
When a young partner indicates that they want to recomply an appointment must be made for them to discuss recomplying and make a recompliance activity available for them at the earliest opportunity.
## When to resume or increase the benefit
The YSSU will resume or increase the payment from the date the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service are satisfied that the young partner has started the recompliance activity.
Some examples of this:
- if the recompliance activity is a one-off, such as attending an interview with the service provider, the payment would be resumed from the date the young partner attended and participated in the activity
- if the recompliance activity is ongoing, such as attending school or a training programme, the young partner must satisfactorily attend school or the training programme and the payment will be resumed from the date the young partner started to attend
For what to do if a young partner cannot recomply due to health condition see:
- Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption
Also see:

chunks.title: Recompliance programme example — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance programme example
If a client or partner is recomplying through participating in an approved activity, there may not be a single activity long enough to meet the required 6 week period of recompliance. A programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate for the client or partner.
A programme of suitable activities for a client or partner with part-time work obligations should be:
- at least 15 hours per week for clients with limited capacity to work because of health condition, injury, or disability
- at least 20 hours per week for all other clients with part-time work obligations

chunks.title: Full-time employment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Full-time employment
A client or partner, who has a 13-week non-entitlement period and full-time work obligations, can recomply by getting full-time work. This work must last at least 6 continuous weeks.
At the end of these 6 weeks, the 13-week non-entitlement period ends. If the client or partner wants to restart their benefit, they will have to reapply. The benefit is granted from the date their employment ceased.
Note provisional benefit is not paid during the 6 weeks of full-time employment.
## Part-time employment
A client or partner, who has a 13-week non-entitlement period and part-time work obligations, can recomply by getting part-time work. This work must last at least 6 continuous weeks, for an average of 20 hours or more each week.
At the end of 6 weeks, the 13-week non-entitlement period ends. The client or partner’s benefit is reinstated to their usual benefit, instead of a provisional benefit.
If the client or partner leaves the job before the end of the 6 weeks, any provisional benefit paid must be established as a debt and the rest of the non-entitlement period is imposed.
The client or partner can still recomply during the rest of the 13-week non-entitlement period by participating in another approved activity.
Note the income the client gets from their employment is charged against the provisional benefit rate.
For when to grant or increase the benefit, see:
- Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Recompliance when subjected to Money Management — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance when subjected to Money Management
When a client fails an obligation and has Money Management imposed, they still need to recomply with their obligation. They can do this at any point during the 4-week Money Management period, but they need to complete their recompliance activity before their Money Management period ends.
## Client does not recomply
Clients who do not complete their recompliance activity while on Money Management will have their benefit suspended at the end of the 4-week period.
Their benefit can only be resumed when a client has completed their recompliance activity. If a client’s benefit has been suspended following Money Management, their benefit will be automatically cancelled after 9 weeks (13 weeks total). For more information on how non-compliance affects assistance, see:
Clients who have had their benefit cancelled will need to reapply for benefit if they need further support.

chunks.title: Recomplying first drug test obligation failure — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recomplying first drug test obligation failure
To recomply to a first drug test obligation failure a client or partner must verbally agree to stop using controlled drugs.
The day the client or partner agrees to stop taking controlled drugs is the date they can be considered to have recomplied. You must advise the client or partner of the consequences if they fail the drug test obligation again.
For more information see:
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying third drug test obligation failure
- Drug test recompliance count

chunks.title: Client already has a failure in-progress or a sanction imposed — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Client already has a failure in-progress or a sanction imposed
Once failures have been initiated, and the notice letter has been sent, any further failures cannot be initiated until each failure:
- has been recomplied with
- has been successfully disputed because the client provided a good and sufficient reason or reasons or
- is overturned (following a dispute)
These further failures will not be included in the 24-month count (or 12-month count for young partners with youth activity obligations) and the client cannot be required to recomply.
For more information see:
- Recompliance for work obligation failures
- Recompliance for social obligation failures
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Recomplying second drug test obligation failure — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: When a client or partner has failed their drug test obligations the second time, they must agree that they will take and pass a drug test within 25 working days (of the agreement). The benefit can be reinstated from the day the client or partner recomplies, ie the day the client or partner agrees to take the test. The drug test can be either a screening test or an evidential test.

chunks.title: Period to take and provide a drug test — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: A client or partner has 25 working days, from the day after they have agreed to recomply with their second drug test obligations failure, to take and pass a drug test. The client must provide proof of undertaking and passing the drug test, within 30 working days from the day after they have agreed to recomply. A client or partner cannot dispute the 25 working day period to take and pass the drug test. They must take and pass the drug test within that time period or they will fail their obligations for the third time. Work and Income has an additional 5 working days to receive the results from the client or partner and to process the information. Generally, the results of the drug test should be provided to Work and Income within the 25 working days, but they can be accepted in the 5 working day period following. Day 0 A second drug test failure is in-progress and client has agreed to recomply by taking and passing a drug test within 25 working days Recompliance 2 is recorded and automatic count in IT system occurs overnight Client can provide the results of the drug test at any time Day 1 - 25 Letter is sent to the client advising them they have 25 working days to take and pass a drug test Day 26 - 30 Five working days to allow time to receive and process the results of the test starts Day 31 If no "passed" drug test results are received, a work test failure 3 is initiated, and 5 working day notice period, prior to Grade 3 sanction starts They will not be considered to have recomplied until a passed drug test result is received by Work and Income. A client or partner can only access help with the costs of the recompliance drug test once during the 25 working day period. During the 25 working day period a "drug test referral delay" will be automatically added in CMS.

chunks.title: Test not taken — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The client or partner must take and pass the drug test within the 25 working day period. If they do not do this, they will be considered to have failed their work obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, for the third time and a Grade 3 sanction will be imposed.

chunks.title: Verification required — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: In order to make a decision that a client or partner has taken and passed a drug test you must have received written confirmation from the client or partner. The written information that must be provided to Work and Income includes: - the name of the client or partner and the drug test provider and - confirmation of a "passed" test result The Drug test obligations verification [no link find out why] form can be used for this. For more information see: - Help with paying for the recompliance drug test - Recomplying first drug test obligation failure - Recomplying third drug test obligation failure - Drug test recompliance count

chunks.title: Recomplying third drugs test obligation failure — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recomplying third drugs test obligation failure
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation a client or partner must complete a 6 week approved activity and reapply for their benefit. A 6 week approved activity must be completed regardless of the obligation failed or whether the client or partner had failed more than one obligation failure.
## Client or partner fails a third time for another reason during the 25 working day period
A client or partner could fail their other obligations (not drug test obligations) for a third time during the 25 working day period. If this happens the third failure would override the count of the 25 working day period and the client or partner would not have to take and pass a drug test.
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation the client or partner must complete a 6 week approved activity.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Recomplying more than one failure
- Recomplying first drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Drug test recompliance count

chunks.title: Reviews of Decisions and appeals to the Medical Appeals Board for obligations failures — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Reviews of Decisions and appeals to the Medical Appeals Board for obligations failures
Review of Decisions for obligations failures are recorded in HIYA; appeals to the Medical Appeals Board for obligations failures are recorded in the Medical Appeals Database.
However, the outcome of the review or appeal must be recorded in OBMAN. This will ensure that the benefit status can be resumed or re-granted in SWIFTT depending on the outcome of the review or appeal.
Note that if the Review of Decision or Medical Appeals Board process finds that the originally recorded 'upheld' outcome should be changed to overturned, you will need to make this change in OBMAN.
For more information see:
- The disputes process
- Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Core policy Medical Appeals Board

chunks.title: Recurring illness — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Recurring illness
Clients with certain forms of chronic illness can suffer from recurring periods of incapacity. This means they need short periods of time off work to recover. For example haemophiliacs or chronic asthma sufferers.
If a client is reapplying for Jobseeker Support, for the same health condition that they have previously received Jobseeker Support (or Supported Living Payment) for, MSD should ask them to have their registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) include whether this is a chronic illness on their medical certificate.
Where the client's illness has been accepted as chronic and reoccurring, MSD should:
- notify them by letter and ask them to bring the letter with them for subsequent applications and
- accept subsequent applications for Jobseeker Support as a re-application of the initial application
A new application form is not required if the client reapplies within 26 weeks of cancelling their previous benefit. However, a new medical certificate is required.
The initial stand-down only applies for the first application for Jobseeker Support (on the ground of a health condition, injury or a disability), there is no time limit.

chunks.title: Redirection for young partners — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Redirection for young partners
For young partners subject to youth money management the Jobseeker Support, family tax credit and any ongoing extra help must be redirected to pay for:
- the young person's accommodation and service costs, for example rent, board, power, phone
- the young person's lawful debts or other liabilities, for example Child Support payments, Work and Income debts
- food and groceries via a payment card
## Payments that are not redirected
Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance and Flexible Childcare Assistance are not included in youth money management and can be paid directly to the young person, their agent (if authorised) or a supplier (as appropriate).
If the young person qualifies for any of these payments, MSD will decide who the payment goes to after talking with the young person's youth service provider (if one is assigned to the young person).

chunks.title: Referral to a designated health practitioner — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Referral to a designated health practitioner
MSD can require a client to be referred to a designated health practitioner to:
- establish medical eligibility
- confirm ongoing medical eligibility
- decide what work obligations to apply
MSD will meet the cost of the appointment with a designated health practitioner.
## Case manager refers directly to a designated health practitioner
A case manager can refer a client directly to a designated health practitioner when their registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) indicates they are not best placed to provide the medical information and a second opinion is appropriate.
Note the practitioner may indicate that someone else is best placed to provide the information such as a medical specialist or a hospital doctor. If the certificate indicates 'other', the case manager should seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor. [no link find out why]
## Seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor
In all other situations a case manager must seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor before deciding whether the client must be assessed by a designated health practitioner. These situations include:
- diagnosis is unclear
- the medical information provided is ambiguous or conflicting
- a previous MSD medical certificate contains a substantially different diagnosis or recommendation
- the medical certificate appears to be influenced by labour market considerations
- the client is engaged in activities that appear to be at odds with recorded incapacities
## Financial assistance in the interim
When a client is applying for Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) and a referral to a designated health practitioner means there is likely to be a delay in deciding their eligibility, MSD may need to consider another form of financial assistance in the interim such as hardship assistance.
Note if eligibility can be determined from the medical certificate, MSD can continue with processing the application. This means the client can continue to be paid before MSD determines if they should be subject to work obligations.

chunks.title: Referrals to designated health practitioners about capacity to work — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Referrals to designated health practitioners about capacity to work
MSD may require a second opinion from a designated health practitioner before making a decision about whether to apply work obligations.
## Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor assessment
Generally, before a client is referred to a designated health practitioner, MSD’s Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor will assess the case and recommend if the client should be referred for designated health practitioner assessment.
## When to refer to a designated health practitioner
A client should be referred to a designated health practitioner when :
- their capacity for part-time work is unclear or
- their medical certificate indicates they have no capacity to work, but they are currently working (e.g. earnings are being charged against the main benefit) or
- their medical certificate indicates they have capacity to work, but MSD are aware that they do not have capacity (e.g. the medical certificate was based on 1 condition, but the client now has another condition) or
- they are engaged in activities that appear to be at odds with their work capacity information

chunks.title: Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements
When you are referring a client to a drug tested job, you should:
- consider if the job is suitable for the client, regardless of the drug test
- let the client know that the employer may require them to pass a pre-employment drug test
- ask the client if they would pass a pre-employment drug test and
- ensure the client understands the potential consequences of failing a pre-employment drug test
There are certain situations where it is not appropriate to refer a client to drug tested jobs. In these situations you should consider that, because of the drug test requirements, the job is not suitable.
For more information see:
- Drug test job referral not suitable
- Training providers requiring a drug test
- Employers requiring a drug test
- Informing a client of the drug test obligation failure
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons
- Drug test obligation
- Suitable employment
- Types of drug tests and standards
- Drug test obligations

chunks.title: Refugee Family Support Category — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Refugee Family Support Category
The Refugee Family Support Category allows for a quota of refugees' and protected persons' family members to be considered for permanent residence in New Zealand each year. A client may apply for residence under this category if their New Zealand sponsor's registration was selected from the annual ballot.
Clients need to have been living continuously in New Zealand for 2 years to be entitled to Jobseeker Support. However, Jobseeker Support on the ground of hardship may be considered before they meet the 2 year requirement if the client meets all the other eligibility criteria for Jobseeker Support and can meet the relevant obligations.
Jobseeker Support on the ground of hardship is both income and asset tested.
When assessing the client's entitlement to Jobseeker Support on the ground of hardship, the sponsor's financial circumstances are not used in the assessment. However, any financial assistance given to the client and family (if any), from either their sponsor or from another party, must be used in the assessment.
It is important to note that, unlike other visa categories, sponsors under the Refugee Family Support Category have no obligation to financially support their relative.
The only obligation a sponsor under this category has, is to make sure adequate accommodation for their relatives is available during the first 24 months of their relatives residence in New Zealand. Despite this requirement, the client may still be able to get assistance as a non-beneficiary.
If the client has a change in personal resources, confirmation of that change is required to make sure the client is getting the support they're entitled to.

chunks.title: Refugee or protected person — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Refugee or protected person
In general a refugee or protected person cannot receive Jobseeker Support unless they have been granted permanent residence.
If a refugee or a protected person has permanent residence, assess them for Jobseeker Support in the usual manner.
Refugees and protected persons with permanent residence are exempt from meeting the 2 years continuous residence criteria.
Note when a client leaves the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre no stand-down applies to the grant of the benefit.
## Clients without permanent residence
If a client is a refugee or a protected person and has not been granted permanent residence, an Emergency Benefit may be considered.
For more information see:
- Refugee quota
- Emergency Benefit

chunks.title: Refugee quota — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Refugee quota
Refugees with permanent residence are exempt from meeting the 2 years continuous residence criteria, so you should assess the client for Jobseeker Support in the usual manner.
Most refugees accepted as part of the United Nations quota receive permanent residence before arriving in New Zealand or during their period of resettlement at the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre. These clients do not usually have any income or assets.
For more information see:
- Granting on grounds of hardship
- Refugee or protected person
- Qualifications
- No stand-down applies

chunks.title: Regional training courses — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Regional training courses
This is any training approved by the regional contracts manager.
Young people will be meeting their obligations where they are undertaking programmes linked to the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF) credits.
For more information see:
- Employment and training Job search, employment and in-work support services
- Approved training (young partners)

chunks.title: Regular engagement and support process — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Regular engagement and support process
Clients must be contacted at least four times by Work and Income before initiating a failure to meet a social obligation. You must complete the three Contact Steps of regular engagement and support and then make a final appointment. You can only determine that the client has failed to meet their social obligations at the final appointment.
The Contact Steps can be over the phone or face to face.
The aim of this process is to support clients to meet their social obligations or for clients to take all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations.
At the first Contact Step of engagement and support you should discuss with the client and their partner (if any) whether they are meeting their social obligations and, if not, encourage them to do so.
The next two Contact Steps of engagement and support should be focused on encouraging and supporting the client to meet their social obligations, and following up what happened at the previous Contact Steps.
At each of the three Contact Steps you must:
- check that the client is taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, and actively help and encourage the client to meet those obligations
- ensure that the client is connected with local community information
- advise the client of the next stage of engagement and support and contact
- remind the client of their social obligations and consequences of not meeting these
For more information on the three stage process of engagement see:
- Contact steps - social obligations [no link find out why]
Also see:
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Client is meeting their social obligations
- Child changes during engagement and support process
- Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations
- Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation

chunks.title: Rehabilitation — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation is a process aimed at enabling people with ill health and disabled people to reach and maintain their optimal level. It generally has a focus on restoration or improvement of the abilities of the client. Rehabilitation could include services such as re-training a client unable to return to their previous occupation.
As part of the expectation that a client will prepare towards a return to employment, clients with work preparation or work obligations may need support to undertake activities, including rehabilitation.
To improve the client's work-readiness they may be required to undertake activities, including rehabilitation, however this must not include medical treatment.
## Medical treatment
