When a client has satisfied all parts of the reapplication (including where in the 13 weeks before their expiry date, specific engagements for eligibility and employment are completed to satisfy parts of the reapplication) and continues to qualify for Jobseeker Support, their benefit may be regranted automatically.
This applies when all of the following requirements are met:
- a client has confirmed their circumstances for the purposes of an eligibility check, and
- the client has completed an appropriate employment engagement, and
- the client has completed their reapplication, including agreeing to their obligations and their intent to reapply, and
- the outcome is that the client continues to meet the qualifications for Jobseeker Support.
For more information see:
- Completing the 26 week reapplication process
## Example – obligations and intention to reapply completed online and Jobseeker Support automatically regranted
Jholo's Jobseeker Support commenced on 10 November 2025. His expiry date is 11 May 2026.
In March, Jholo applies for Temporary Additional Support which commences on 15 March 2026. He is also granted Course Participation Assistance on 5 April 2026 to attend a short-term employment related training course. As these specific engagements occurred in the 13 weeks before his expiry date, the engagements satisfy both the eligibility and employment parts of the 26 week reapplication.
On 1 April 2026, Jholo is sent a letter advising what he needs to do to complete his reapplication. Jholo only needs to agree to his obligations and confirm his intention to reapply. Jholo completes the reapplication form online and declares he has had no changes in circumstances since he completed the specific engagements.
Jholo's benefit is automatically regranted from 11 May 2026, with a new expiry date of 9 November 2026.

chunks.title: Specific engagements — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Specific engagements
Specific engagements are activities that a client or partner (if any included in their Jobseeker Support) can complete in the 13 weeks before their expiry date that satisfy either the eligibility or employment part of the reapplication process.
A specific engagement may include:
- an interaction with MSD where the client confirms the same circumstances that apply to the Jobseeker Support qualifications, as required for the reapplication, and
- a discussion with MSD about what the client is doing or needs to do to find or prepare for suitable employment
If a client or their partner satisfy the eligibility or employment part of the reapplication process through specific engagements before their expiry date, they do not need to complete those parts of the reapplication again.
They must still complete the outstanding parts of the reapplication when they reapply.
For more information see:
- Specific eligibility engagement
- Specific employment engagement
- Specific engagement completed for both eligibility and employment
## Timeframe for completing specific engagements
Specific engagements can be completed to satisfy the eligibility or employment parts of the reapplication in the 13 weeks before the client’s expiry date.
This means any activities that would be considered a specific engagement, that are completed outside of the 13 weeks before the expiry date, do not count towards the reapplication.

chunks.title: Steps for investigating industrial disputes — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Steps for investigating industrial disputes
1. Find out the following information to help make a decision:
- which parties are directly involved in the dispute
- the sequence of events leading up to the dispute
- the date of stoppage
- the name(s) of the union(s) directly involved in the dispute
- whether any other union(s) are actively supporting the union(s) taking direct action
- whether any employees have been suspended as a result of the industrial action and if so, find out:
a) The date of issue of the suspension notices.
b) The effective date of suspension.
c) The section of the Employment Relations Act 2000 used to suspend the employees (Note this is not required for employees who have been on strike).
d) Which union(s) the suspended employees belong to.
2. Helpful documentation includes:
- newspaper reports about the stoppages
- copies of notices to employees which can confirm events that have taken place
- the employment contract that is in dispute
3. Contact parties by telephone first, to reduce delays, and give them an idea of the information required and why.
4. Follow up immediately in writing. If any of the parties do not provide written comment within a reasonable time, or refuse to comment at all, use only verified details of the dispute when making a decision.
5. Where applications have been received from non-striking employees who have been suspended find out:
- whether the employers have issued notices to individual employees suspending them
- whether such notices have been issued to all members of a particular union at a particular workplace
Then obtain:
- a copy of the notice issued and a list of suspended employees from the employer and
- the employers reason for suspension (this is usually written in the notice)
6. A detailed formal decision must record the relevant factors of the dispute taken into account when reaching the decision. The decision will be recorded as applying to various unions rather than individual applications.
This is not required where all applications can be declined as work resumed during the stand-down period.
7. After a formal decision has been reached, individual applications can be decided.
8. All parties who respond to requests for information about the dispute must be notified in full of the decision reached.
9. All clients must be notified as to the outcome of their individual applications and appeal rights.

chunks.title: Strikes — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Strikes
If a client is on strike, Jobseeker Support is not generally payable.
Examples of strikes include:
- withdrawal of labour where the union/workplace refuses to undertake any further work until their demands are met
- members continue to work but reduce their output below what is usually accepted as normal until such time as demands have been met
Local decisions are to be made jointly by the regional director and the manager client service delivery as to whether the clients are on strike. When the decision is made those union members cannot get Jobseeker Support.
There can be several unions at one workplace with only one union going on strike. Members of the non-striking union, even though they may lose their employment, are not considered to be on strike and can get Jobseeker Support.
If a striker has been suspended or dismissed from their employment, see below:
## Suspension of striking employees
There are many reasons why employers suspend striking employees.
Some examples of these are:
- to avoid paying holiday pay or
- due to misconduct
There is still no eligibility for Jobseeker Support for these clients.
## Strikers dismissed from their employment
Strikers dismissed from their employment can get Jobseeker Support, however they can face a 13 week non-entitlement period for being voluntarily unemployed depending on the circumstances.
For more information see:
- Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
## Suspension of non-striking employees
You can pay the Jobseeker Support to an employee who is not on strike if they are suspended because no work is available as a result of an industrial dispute.
You need to be aware that in some situations, employees who are not on strike may withdraw their labour in sympathy or support. Because they have voluntarily withdrawn their labour, they too are considered on strike and cannot get Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: Students — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Students
Full-time students cannot receive the Jobseeker Support. If MSD is unsure whether a student is full-time or not, they can ask the student to provide verification from their education provider.
## Client has been recently studying
Some students have a financial incentive to apply for Jobseeker Support during the break between the academic years of a programme of study e.g. the summer vacation. This is usually because they do not meet the hardship criteria for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
A client who has been studying can only get Jobseeker Support when they:
- completely withdraw from a course of study during the academic year or after an academic year has finished
- have completed their studies and
- do not intend resuming their studies in the next academic year
The client should be made aware that if they intend to undertake further study they cannot get Jobseeker Support, and it is an offence to misrepresent their intentions.
Clients who have recently finished (within the last 3 months) a course of full-time study, must provide contact details for their parents.
This information is needed in all situations where the client is under the age of 25 years. MSD would only contact the parents where there is doubt about the student's intentions.

chunks.title: Suitability of position and organisation — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: A client is only required to complete the 4-weeks of Community Work Experience if MSD is satisfied the organisation and the position are suitable. Suitability will be different for each client based on their level of capability, however there are general considerations for each position that MSD must take into account.

chunks.title: Organisation — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Suitable organisations can be community or volunteer organisations. These organisations may have existing relationships with MSD, however this is not required. To be suitable, an organisation should: - not be for profit - not be public sector, e.g. central or local government or a Crown entity - have an internal organisation structure, e.g. has defined key functions, roles and responsibilities - be self-governing - the organisation primarily controls its own management and operations - not be something people are required to contribute time to by law, e.g. jury duty. Organisations are not suitable if: - they have previously breached employment law, or - their area of focus would likely be inappropriate or unacceptable to the wider community, or - a client completing Community Work Experience at this organisation is likely to be a reputational risk to MSD. The organisation must be confident they can provide a client with the required hours and 4 consecutive weeks needed to complete their Community Work Experience. If the organisation is unsure, the position would not be suitable for the client. Note clients may secure multiple positions to complete their Community Work Experience. For more information see: Period of Community Work Experience

chunks.title: Position — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: To be suitable, a position should: - be for a role that would otherwise be met by a volunteer, e.g. is not a role that would normally be paid employment - have activities that are reasonable and fair for the client to complete - for example, a position that requires a lot of work on the computer would not be suitable for a client with low computer literacy - not put the personal safety of the client or others at risk - not include activities that could be considered inappropriate or may damage MSD's reputation, e.g. serving alcohol, being involved in gambling, or supporting particular political gain Example Donna has Community Work Experience imposed and is searching for a suitable organisation and position. Donna contacts her local rugby club to see if they have any volunteer positions available that would help her to meet the Community Work Experience requirements. The rugby club can offer Donna at least 5 hours of work for 4 weeks, but tells her they mostly need her help to run the bar. Donna gets in touch with MSD and tells MSD what the position will involve. Although the rugby club is a suitable organisation, it's not appropriate for Donna to be serving alcohol as part of her Community Work Experience, as this could damage MSD's reputation. Donna is advised that the work needed at the rugby club is not suitable for the purpose of the sanction, and to continue looking for a suitable position.

chunks.title: Suitable employment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Suitable employment
Suitable employment varies between clients depending on their individual circumstances.
To meet their work obligations clients and partners need to be available for or take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of at least:
- 30 hours per week for clients with full-time work obligations
- 15 hours per week for clients that qualify for Jobseeker Support on the grounds of a health condition, injury, or disability
- 20 hours per week for all other clients with part-time work obligations
Clients may have pre-benefit obligations to attend an interview or accept an offer of employment. This employment must also be considered suitable.
## Deciding if a job is suitable
When deciding on whether a job is suitable for a client, you need to consider the following (but is not limited to):
- appropriate hours of employment, eg hours are not excessive
- access to childcare
- family commitments
- religious commitments
- jobs which offend strongly held views
- days of the week
- type of employment
- skills required
- experience
- location of the job
- wages
- number of hours is within the appropriate range for the client's obligations
For more information see:
- Hours range for suitable employment
- Meeting job search requirements
- Employment trial period of up to 90 days
- Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements

chunks.title: Suspended/Locked out workers — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Suspended/Locked out workers
Clients who are suspended or locked out from their jobs without pay are not entitled to Jobseeker Support. For benefit purposes they are still employed if their employment contract provides that they would ordinarily work an average of 30 hours or more per week, if they were not suspended or locked out.
You can look at an Emergency Benefit in cases of hardship.
If the client has been suspended because they were or have been on strike see:
- On strike
Also see:
- Emergency Benefit Lockouts

chunks.title: Taking all reasonable steps for enrolling in and attending school — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Taking all reasonable steps for enrolling in and attending school
Reasons to consider a client is taking all reasonable steps to meet this obligation may include (but are not limited to) that:
- the child has a health condition, injury or disability that affects their ability to attend school
- the child is regularly missing classes for no good reason but the Attendance Service is working with the family and the school to get the child attending school again
- the client is actively trying to encourage their child to attend school but the child has behavioural problems and attendance at school is out of the client's control.Note you need to record this as an exception reason in OBMAN using 'Child is not permitted to attend' as the obligation reason.
Note if the parent is in the process of being prosecuted under the Education and Training Act 2020, you must not ask them to comply with this social obligation. You need to record this as an exception reason in OBMAN using 'parent is in prosecution for truant child' as the obligation reason.

chunks.title: Taking all reasonable steps to enrol in an early childhood education programme — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Taking all reasonable steps to enrol in an early childhood education programme
A client could be considered to be taking all reasonable steps to enrol their child in an early childhood education programme for reasons including, (but not limited to) that:
- there are shortages of places or availability issues, and the client has a plan in place or has made a commitment to enrol their child when a place becomes available there are additional costs of participation that may cause financial hardship to the family, including: travel costs oradditional costs associated with attending the early childhood education programme
- travel costs or
- additional costs associated with attending the early childhood education programme
- the child has behavioural problems meaning attendance at an ECE service would be difficult or not possible (for example the child is not currently permitted to attend) (This should be recorded as an exception in OBMAN using "child is not permitted to attend" as the obligation exception reason)
To help clients meet this social obligation you should discuss childcare assistance that may be available to the client.

chunks.title: Taking controlled prescribed medications — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Taking controlled prescribed medications
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes when a client is taking prescription medication correctly.
Not all prescribed medications will affect the results of a drug test. Generally, only controlled prescribed medications do, such as morphine, codeine or medicinal cannabis.
Controlled prescribed medications need to be used correctly to the dose the health practitioner recommends and by the person for whom they are prescribed.
Some controlled prescribed medications may cause a person to be impaired on the job which can cause health and safety issues for employers.
In some situations, screening drug tests can show failed results if controlled prescribed medications have been used.
The client can be asked to provide verification from a registered health practitioner that they are taking a controlled prescribed medication. There is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that MSD can provide to the client.
Note when a client is asked to take a drug test they will be asked to declare any prescribed medications they are taking.

chunks.title: Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School
Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - The Distance School provides an early childhood education programme.
This programme provides learning material and the support of a distance teacher, but is home based and taught by the parent. Parents must meet certain eligibility criteria to enrol their child in the Te Kura Early Childhood Education programme.

chunks.title: Eligibility for Teen Parent Unit — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Eligibility for Teen Parent Unit
Teen Parent Units provide for the educational needs of student who face barriers to learning because of their pregnancy and child rearing responsibilities.
Students who are within the age range to receive free education (that is, up to age 19 years and ending on the first day of January after the student's 19th birthday) are eligible for enrolment.
Where space permits the Teen Parent Unit's school may also enrol students who are over the age of 19. These students are enrolled as adult students.
For more information see:
- Deciding if suitable place at Teen Parent Centre available
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months
- Parenting obligations

chunks.title: Temporary employment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Temporary employment
No stand-down is imposed when a client:
- has been in part-time employment or full-time employment for less than 26 weeks
- was getting a benefit immediately before they were employed
- the benefit was stopped because they returned to work and
- has applied for a benefit after their employment ceased
Temporary employment can include employment during an employment trial period of up to 90 days if the client was getting a benefit and is reapplying for Jobseeker Support as their employment has ceased.
Note the client's average weekly income is not required when the client has been in temporary employment for less than 26 weeks. However, the client's final pay details are required to determine the date of event and entitlement date.
If a client leaves their employment without good and sufficient reason a voluntary unemployment stand-down may be considered.

chunks.title: The disputes process — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The disputes process is a quick process where you must respond to a client or partner's dispute immediately. You must take into account any new information provided by the client or partner, and let the client or partner know your decision straight away. A letter is sent automatically to the client or partner once a decision has been recorded on the dispute. A client or partner can dispute the decision if they believe: - they did not fail their obligations including when they believe they have taken all reasonable steps to meet a social obligation or - that they had a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete the obligation Note if a client or partner has disputed the obligations failure and you have upheld your decision, the client or partner can only dispute it again by following the Review of Decision or Medical Appeal Board appeal (drug test failure only) processes. If a sanction has been imposed you can still use the disputes process. This allows the client or partner an opportunity for a quick resolution to their dispute before proceeding with the Review of Decision process. For more information see: - Recording decisions on a dispute - Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements

chunks.title: Reason for dispute — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The client or partner can dispute the decision if they believe they did not fail their obligations, for one of the following reasons: - an obligations failure was initiated, but the client or partner had undertaken the activity or - an obligations failure was initiated, but the client or partner had a good and sufficient reason for the failure or - undertaking or completing the activity was dependent on the provision of assistance by Work and Income and that assistance was not supplied or - reasonable steps weren't taken by Work and Income to inform a client or partner of the activity that they were required to do Note some clients may fail more than one obligation at the same time. In this case, for the obligation failure not to apply, the client will need to successfully dispute or review all failures in order to not have a sanction imposed. If only one failure is disputed, a sanction may still be imposed for obligation failures that were not disputed, or were disputed and upheld.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for failing — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: You must consider the circumstances of the client or partner, and determine whether it would have been reasonable for the client or partner to have undertaken the activity. Good and sufficient reasons for failing to undertake an activity will depend on the obligation the client or partner has failed. For social obligations you must consider whether the client and partner have taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations. Note that if you are unsure whether a client or partner has a good and sufficient reason then you should seek guidance from your capability developer, Helpline, manager client service operations or manager client service delivery.

chunks.title: Training — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Training
A client who has started training or is about to start an approved training course must still meet all of the qualifications of the Jobseeker Support.
If a client is in approved training they must continue to meet their work obligations, including being available for full-time employment.
If the client has left their employment or has taken leave without pay to attend an approved training course, the client cannot receive the Jobseeker Support.
## Offenders in training
The Department of Corrections may arrange for offenders serving non-custodial sentences to attend courses as part of their sentence, for example, drug or alcohol rehabilitation or anger management courses.
Clients participating in these courses qualify for the Jobseeker Support but are expected to re-arrange the time of these courses if an opportunity of full-time employment becomes available.
For more information see:
- Approved training
- Examples of approved courses

chunks.title: Training providers requiring a drug test — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Training providers requiring a drug test
Some training providers will require potential trainees to pass a drug test as a prerequisite to being accepted on the course.
Training providers will use drug tests where the training programmes have a focus on employment outcomes. This includes training programmes that are:
- non classroom based programmes or on-the-job programmes where the tests are required for health and safely purposes
- classroom based training where the industry would require the trainee to be drug free for health and safety purposes to gain employment
Note a client can only fail the drug test obligations for drug tests that are being taken as prerequisites to being accepted onto a course - not for any other on-going drug tests that a training provider may ask for.
## Verification
In order to make a decision that a client has failed a drug test, without good and sufficient reason, you must have received confirmation from the training provider.
For more information see:
- Types of drug tests
- Client has failed a screening drug test

chunks.title: Transfer between benefits — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: A transfer between benefits can occur when a client qualifies for Jobseeker Support while currently receiving another benefit. There is no stand-down imposed for clients who: - transfer to Jobseeker Support from another benefit type or - are included as a partner in another benefit type and are now applying as the primary client Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Childs Benefit and Orphans Benefit are also a benefit in this situation. Where Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit has been paid and the child now qualifies for Jobseeker Support, no stand-down is imposed.

chunks.title: Partner to be included — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: An initial stand-down is imposed, if a client receiving a benefit is to be included as a partner in a new application for Jobseeker Support. There are situations where a partner can continue to receive payment of Sole Parent Support during the initial stand-down period where they are included as a partner in a new application for Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: Examples — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Generally in the 3 examples below the payment of the Sole Parent Support can be continued up to the actual commencement date of the Jobseeker Support. Example 1A client has been receiving Sole Parent Support and is now to be included in a new application for Jobseeker Support as a partner, an initial stand-down is imposed on the Jobseeker Support. Example 2A client has been in prison or on remand for 31 days or more and has applied for Jobseeker Support. On release, the client moves in with their former partner who was receiving Sole Parent Support. An initial stand-down is imposed on the Jobseeker Support. Example 3A couple with children separated and the mother received Sole Parent Support and the father was working. The father's job ceased and the couple are now living together again. The father applied for Jobseeker Support and an initial stand-down is imposed. If there has been a delay in applying for Jobseeker Support then payment of the Sole Parent Support may be cancelled from the date after the client has reconciled.

chunks.title: Non-beneficiary clients — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: When a non-beneficiary client receiving Extra help such as Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance applies for Jobseeker Support, it is not regarded as a transfer between benefits. An initial stand-down is imposed. For more information see: - No stand-down applies - Processing standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why] - Core policy Relationship status for benefit - Assistance during an initial stand-down

chunks.title: Transfer from Sole Parent Support when youngest child turns 14 years old — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The expiry date for clients who automatically transfer from Sole Parent Support to Jobseeker Support when their youngest dependent child turns 14 years old is either: - 52 weeks from the date the Sole Parent Support last commenced (meaning the Sole Parent Support expiry date is retained), or - 26 weeks from the Jobseeker Support commencement date whichever is earlier. This means clients are never on Jobseeker Support for more than 26 weeks before their benefit expires.

chunks.title: Example 1 - Sole Parent Support expiry date is retained — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Cass's Sole Parent Support commenced on 5 March 2027, with his 13 year old dependent child included in his benefit. His Sole Parent Support expiry date is 5 March 2028, which is 52 weeks from his commencement date. On 6 October 2027 Cass automatically transfers to Jobseeker Support because his youngest dependent child turned 14 years old. In this situation, Cass's Jobseeker Support expiry date remains 5 March 2028, which is 52 weeks from the date his Sole Parent Support commenced. This is because the original Sole Parent Support expiry date is within 26 weeks of the date his Jobseeker Support commenced. Cass completes the 26 week reapplication process before his expiry date. He continues to qualify for and is regranted Jobseeker Support from 5 March 2028. Cass's next expiry date is 3 September 2028, which is 26 weeks from the new commencement date.

chunks.title: Example 2 - Expiry date is 26 weeks from Jobseeker Support commencement date — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Ani's Sole Parent Support commenced on 20 September 2025, with their 13 and 15 year old dependent children included in their benefit. Their Sole Parent Support expiry date is 20 September 2026. On 15 November 2025 Ani automatically transfers to Jobseeker Support because their youngest dependent child turned 14 years old. In this situation, the expiry date of Ani's Jobseeker Support will be 16 May 2026, which is 26 weeks from the date their Jobseeker Support commenced. This is because 16 May 2026 is earlier than their original Sole Parent Support expiry date, which was 20 September 2026. Ani completes the 26 week reapplication process before their expiry date. They continue to qualify for Jobseeker Support and it is regranted from 16 May 2026. Their benefit will continue to expire every 26 weeks.

chunks.title: Client intending to return to the same employer — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Client intending to return to the same employer
If a client has received any sick leave payment they would not be eligible for Jobseeker Support until these payments had stopped. You then assess any initial stand-down.
Clients are not required to use any sick leave they may have if they are intending to return to the same employer.

chunks.title: 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down
When clients in the following circumstances apply for Jobseeker Support within 28 days of their entitlement date, the commencement date rules are different:
- clients who have a health condition, injury or disability
- sole parents
- clients who have lost the financial support of their partner due to: deathseparationending of a de facto relationship orimprisonment
- death
- separation
- ending of a de facto relationship or
- imprisonment
For these clients, the commencement date is the day after the initial stand-down ends.
This means, in some situations, MSD can commence a benefit from a date earlier than the application date.
If the application is not received within 28 days, MSD cannot backdate the commencement date.
Note the 28-day rule only applies to clients who have an initial stand down imposed.

chunks.title: Two-week search period — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Two-week search period
The Community Work Experience sanction begins the day after the 5-working day notice period ends.
A client has 2 weeks from this date to find a suitable organisation and position. MSD can advise a client of local groups that may be willing to provide an opportunity, however this is intended as a starting point only.
If the groups that MSD is aware of are not available or suitable, a client will be expected to make their own enquiries with organisations in their area.
## Verification
A client must provide MSD verification of their position. They can do this anytime during the 2-week search period, but must provide it before the end of that period.
Once a client provides MSD with verification of their position, MSD must confirm whether the organisation and position are suitable before a client can start. MSD has a 5-day verification window to confirm this.
At the end of the 2 weeks, if the client has not provided verification, they will have failed to find or complete their Community Work Experience and be considered non-compliant.

chunks.title: Two years residence — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Two years residence
A client must have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident to qualify for Jobseeker Support.
Note the 2 year period of residence, must be 2 years continuous residence without absence from New Zealand. There are some circumstances however when a client can be absent from New Zealand during this time.
For more information see:
- Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
If the client is not a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident they cannot receive Jobseeker Support, whether or not they have 2 years continuous residence in New Zealand.
They may be eligible for Emergency Benefit.
## Clients who do not meet the 2 years residence criteria
If the client does not meet the 2 year continuous residence requirement they may be able to receive Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship. For more information see:
- Granting on grounds of hardship
For more information about residence see:
- Proof of residence
- Refugee or protected person
- Resident in New Zealand
- Calculating period of residence
- Partner's residence status
- Reciprocal Agreements
- Unlawful residence

chunks.title: Types of drug tests and standards — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: The drug tests a client participates in must comply with the Australian/New Zealand standard - AS/NZS 4308:2008 (the drug test standard). Drug testing detects residues of certain drugs and their metabolites in the body. Each drug has a set threshold or cut-off level for screening and evidential drug tests. To fail a test a person must have drugs present in their system that reach these thresholds or cut out levels. There are two types of tests that measure the presence of drugs, these are: - a screening test which shows whether drugs are or are not present - an evidential test which is completed by an accredited laboratory, which can identify the actual drugs, the drug family and the amount of drugs present In order to test, a urine sample must be provided by the person. Urine testing is the most common and accepted form of drug testing, and meets the drug test standard. To meet the drug test standard drug tests are undertaken by a person who is NZQA accredited for urine specimen collection in the workplace. The standard requires the collection of a sample to follow a process that minimises the chances of a person being able to affect the result of the sample through substitution or adulteration.

chunks.title: Screening tests — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Most employers and training providers will use a screening test as this provides them with enough information to help make the decision to employ a person or not. Screening tests are usually done using on-site urine tests as they provide a simple and cheaper method of detecting a wide range of drugs and can be undertaken outside of a laboratory. Screening tests detect the presence or absence of specific drugs and drug test providers advise that they are up to 98% accurate. Very occasionally they can produce false results, this is usually because: - they have detected some prescribed medicines or - the level of a drug in a person's system is near to the threshold or cut-off points for a particular drug

chunks.title: Evidential tests — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Some employers, particularly larger employers, may require an evidential test and will not conduct screening tests or they may conduct both tests. Generally, evidential tests are used when a screening test is failed. Evidential tests are a more comprehensive and expensive method of detecting drugs. They can detect a wider range of substances and identify the specific substance. This test is also referred to as a confirmation test. Evidential testing is conducted in an accredited laboratory by qualified staff. Samples are sent to the laboratory by drug test providers or specialised staff, or the laboratory will arrange to take the sample themselves. For more information see: - Client fails the screening drug test - Effect of certain drugs

chunks.title: Unable to meet work preparation obligations due to health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Unable to meet work preparation obligations due to health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to:
- clients (who have a deferral from their work obligations and are subject to work preparation obligations) and
- partners with work preparation obligations
A client may be unable to meet their work preparation obligations if their health condition, injury or disability restricts them. For example when a client is:
- in hospital or
- is unable to attend an interview with MSD due to their condition
MSD should consider the information on the client's Work Capacity Medical Certificate to see if the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) has advised of any restrictions to a client's capacity to plan.
This is a full exemption.
## Evidence
To support their exemption, the client must provide a Work Capacity Medical Certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant).
The information required on the medical certificate includes:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to work or to plan for work and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for work or planning for work and
- any other information that is required
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 13 weeks.

chunks.title: Unable to recomply — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Unable to recomply
A client or partner, who is subject to a sanction or a 13 week non-entitlement period, may not need to complete a recompliance activity if:
- they meet the criteria for a full exemption from their work obligations or
- they qualify for a benefit that does not have the obligations to which they must recomply
If a client or partner is subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period, and is unable to complete the 6 week activity or programme of suitable activities, you cannot recover the provisional benefit if they do not complete the activity because they meet the criteria for a full exemption from their work obligations.
## Example
A partner who is subject to a sanction who develops a health condition or becomes injured or disabled, and meets the criteria for the exemption 'would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability'. They are unable to complete a recompliance activity.
In this situation you should add the exemption reason in SWIFTT, and follow the disputes process (so that the benefit can be resumed). Also consider the person's eligibility for Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability.
For details of the requirements for a client or partner who has a health condition, injury or disability, see:
- Paying other assistance during a sanction
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Unclear whether client has the capacity to work — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Unclear whether client has the capacity to work
If it is unclear whether a client, who is receiving Jobseeker Support on the grounds of a health condition, injury, or disability, has the capacity to work at least 15 hours per week in open employment, MSD may:
- ask the client questions to clarify the information
- consult their Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor for clarification of the client's capacity for work and limitations
## Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor
MSD can seek advice from their Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor when:
- a diagnosis is unclear
- assistance is needed to interpret specialist assessments and medical information or reports
- the extent a client's health condition or disability impacts on their ability to work is unclear, for example when the information on the medical certificate is inconsistent with what the client has told MSD
- a referral to a designated health practitioner may be appropriate, for example when the client’s registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) indicates that a second opinion is required
- additional support around their health condition or disability has been suggested by the registered practitioner completing the certificate.
If a decision still cannot be made, MSD may require a second opinion from a designated health practitioner before making a decision about whether to apply part-time work obligations.

chunks.title: Unforeseen hospitalisation — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Unforeseen hospitalisation
In determining whether a client has an exceptional circumstance for not completing their reapplication process before their expiry date on the grounds of unforeseen hospitalisation, the client must have experienced one of the following situations during their notice period:
- an unplanned emergency surgery in a hospital which affected their ability to reapply before their expiry date, or
- unplanned emergency treatment in a hospital which affected their ability to reapply before their expiry date.
## Evidence
MSD may require the client to provide evidence that they were in hospital. This could include:
- admissions or discharge forms
- a medical certificate or medical report
- a letter from their registered medical practitioner.
Note there are some situations where a client does not have to complete the reapplication process.
For more information see:
- Client does not need to complete the reapplication process

chunks.title: Unlawful residence — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Unlawful residence
To reside in New Zealand lawfully the client must either:
- be a New Zealand citizen
- be an Australian citizen
- hold a New Zealand passport
- hold an Australian passport
- hold a visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009
- be deemed to hold a visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents)
- be a British national who arrived in New Zealand prior to 2 April 1974 or
- hold a permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987
If the client does not fulfil one of the above, the client is deemed to be in New Zealand unlawfully.
Any periods of unlawful residence are excluded when calculating the clients' period of residence.
The calculation of the two year period of continuous residence commences from when the client is granted New Zealand citizenship or permanent residence.
For more information see:
- Permanent residence
- Proof of residence
- Calculating the period of residence
- Deciding ordinarily resident

chunks.title: Up to date core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Up to date core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks
A client and their partner (if any) receiving Jobseeker Support must take all reasonable steps to:
- register their child or children with a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and
- keep up-to-date with the child's core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks
Note a client is only required to ensure their child completes core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks to meet this obligation from the time they begin to receive a benefit. For example, a client who starts receiving a benefit when their child is between 3 and 4 months old cannot be failed for not having completed the core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks the child should have had at ages 4 to 6 weeks.
## Verification
Most parents will already have their child or children registered and up to date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks and in most cases you should take the client's word that they are meeting this social obligation.
However, if you have information that indicates the client is not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations you may ask for proof that the checks have been completed, for example by asking to see their Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book.
The Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book is issued to parents when their child is born and is sufficient evidence of the child's attendance. The Health Book has helpful advice and information about what is happening at different stages in the child's development and has places to record all the Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks.
For more information see:
- Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks
- Overview of social obligations according to age of the child
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations

chunks.title: Verification of evidence at end of 4-week period — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Verification of evidence at end of 4-week period
A client must provide MSD with evidence of their job-search activities at the end of the 4-week period. This is to prove that:
- they have completed the required 3 job-search activities per week over the 4-week period and
- their job-search activities are considered reasonable steps towards finding suitable employment
MSD must determine the evidence provided is sufficient and that it matches the reported job-search activity. For example, if a client reports that they have applied for jobs online, they must be able to provide evidence of this.
In some situations, it may not be reasonable for a client to provide evidence for the job-search activity they completed. Clients are not expected to provide evidence that is unreasonable for them to get in their circumstances. For example, if a client reports they have applied for jobs in person, they may not be able to provide evidence of this.
## 5-day verification window
There may be times when MSD is not able to process the information before the end of the 4-week sanction period.
To prevent a client from being disadvantaged due to processing delays, there is a 5-day verification window at the end of the sanction period. This allows MSD to process information a client has provided and ensures a client's payment will continue.
Note this is not extra time for a client to complete their job search activities.
## No action from MSD
The client will be considered non-compliant if, after 5 days:
- MSD has not been able to confirm if the client has completed at least 3 suitable job-search activities per week or
- the client has not provided sufficient evidence of their job-search activities
This may result in a debt for the client.

chunks.title: Victim of violent crime (including family violence) — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Victim of violent crime (including family violence)
In determining whether a client has an exceptional circumstance for not reapplying before their expiry date on the grounds of being a victim of a violent crime, the client must have experienced the following during their notice period:
- been directly affected by a crime committed by another person which affected their ability to reapply before the expiry date and
- suffered physical or emotional harm which affected their ability to reapply before the expiry date
Note if MSD believes a client has been, or is likely to be harmed (physically, emotionally or sexually), they must discuss the situation with a Family Violence Response Co-ordinator.
## Evidence
MSD will consult with the regional Family Violence Response Co-ordinator for advice regarding what evidence should be requested. Evidence could include:
- a personal statement, or
- a statement from a professional (such as the Police or a social worker).
For more information see:
- Family Violence Response Coordinators [no link find out why] Doogle

chunks.title: Victims of family violence — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Victims of family violence
Clients may be granted permanent residence if they have been living in a relationship with a New Zealand citizen or resident that has ended because that person was violent towards the client and they are unable to go back to their home country.
Financial assistance for these clients is decided by Helpline.

chunks.title: Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
A client and their partner (if any) who are applying for Jobseeker Support and have work obligations, can have a 13 week non-entitlement period if they:
- have become voluntarily unemployed without a good and sufficient reason
- are applying for a benefit because they were dismissed by their employer for misconduct
'Becoming voluntarily unemployed' means the client has resigned from, or otherwise left employment without a good and sufficient reason.
'Dismissal as a result of misconduct' means that the client has lost employment as a result of misconduct without a good and sufficient reason.
There are some circumstances where a 13 week non-entitlement period would not be imposed. For more information see:
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed
Note the 50% protection for clients and partners with dependent children applies.

chunks.title: Weekly income example - single clients and couples — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:

chunks.title: Well Child or Tamariki Ora services and checks — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Well Child or Tamariki Ora services and checks
Well Child/Tamariki Ora services are a screening, education and support service offered to all New Zealand children and their families or whānau from birth to 5 years.
The services assist and support families and whānau to improve and protect their children's health. They are provided free to all children under 5 years by registered nurses and community health workers with specific training in child health.
First time parents and families requiring extra support are offered additional visits. Some visits are carried out in the home, and others in clinics or community facilities.
Different providers run the Well Child/Tamariki Ora services, including:
- Plunket
- Māori health providers
- Pacific Island health providers
- Public Health Services - for example, public health nurses, community nurses, community health workers, social workers
## When the checks happen
The Well Child/Tamariki Ora schedule includes 12 health checks (contacts) with 8 of these offered to children aged from 4 to 6 weeks to 5 years.
Only the 8 core Well Child checks are required to meet this social obligation.
## Between 4 weeks and 5 years
The 8 core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks (listed below) for children between the ages of 4 to 6 weeks to 5 years are required to meet social obligations.
These are provided by the Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider when the child is:
- 4 - 6 weeks
- 8 - 10 weeks
- 3 - 4 months
- 5 - 7 months
- 9 - 12 months
- 15 - 18 months
- 2 - 3 years
- 4 - 5 years (this is the before school check, and the final Well Child health check)
For more information see:
- Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits
- Social obligations

chunks.title: Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks
Well Child/Tamariki Ora services are screening, education and support services offered to all New Zealand children and their families or whānau from birth to 5 years.
The services assist and support families and whānau to improve and protect their children's health. They are provided free to all children under 5 years by registered nurses and community health workers with specific training in child health.
First time parents and families requiring extra support are offered additional visits. Some visits are carried out in the home, and others in clinics or community facilities.
Different providers run the Well Child/Tamariki Ora services including:
- Plunket
- Māori health providers
- Pacific Island health providers
- Public Health Services - for example, public health nurses, community nurses, community health workers, social workers
## When do the checks happen
The Well Child/Tamariki Ora schedule includes 12 health checks (contacts) with 8 of these offered to children aged from 4 - 6 weeks to 5 years.
## Between 4 weeks and 5 years
8 more checks are provided by the Well Child provider, at:
- 4 - 6 weeks
- 8 - 10 weeks
- 3 - 4 months
- 5 - 7 months
- 9 - 12 months
- 15 - 18 months
- 2 - 3 years
- 4 - 5 years (this is the before school check, and the final Well Child health check)

chunks.title: What is a limited employment location? — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## What is a limited employment location?
A limited employment location is defined as a place with the following characteristics:
- severely limited availability of work
- local labour market at a low level - therefore having limited job opportunities (if an area has seasonal work available in the coming year, the area is not considered a limited employment location) and
- lack of public transport to take commuters to an area where work is available
The client's residential address is used to decide whether they live in a limited employment location.
For more information see:
- Deskfile Limited employment locations
- Clients currently living in a limited employment location
- Clients moving to a limited employment location

chunks.title: When the sanction is imposed — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## When the sanction is imposed
Sanctions can only be imposed 5 working days after the client has been sent a letter about their obligations failure. This is called the 5 working day notice period.
If a client recomplies within the initial 5 working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the obligations failure is counted.
Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
## How to count the 'five working day notice' period
The 5 working day notice period is counted from the date after the obligations failure letter has been sent to the client, to allow for posting and delivery of the letter.
The 5 working day notice period excludes weekends, public holidays, or the period 25 December to 15 January each year.
The table below provides an example of how to count the notice period.
Day 0
Tuesday
Automatic failure in CMS occurs overnight
Day 0

An obligations failure letter is sent

5 working day notice period begins

5 working day notice period continues
Day 6

chunks.title: Why is the client moving to a limited employment location? — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Why is the client moving to a limited employment location?
You will need to work closely with your client to see if their reasons for wanting to move to a limited employment location can be addressed in a way that alleviates the need to move.
Examples of reasons and possible solutions are as follows:
- a client planning to move to escape a difficult situation in their current location may be encouraged to move to an area where there are employment opportunities available, rather than a limited employment location
- a client moving because they are having difficulty managing high housing costs may also be encouraged to move to a location with low-cost accommodation that is not a limited employment location. Alternatively, you could refer them to an agency offering budgeting advice, or see if they are eligible for Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or social housing
- a client planning to move to take care of a sick relative may be eligible for Supported Living Payment (caring for a person). Clients who receive this or other non work-obligated benefits are not affected by the limited employment locations policy
- a client planning to move for cultural reasons should be assisted as appropriate to work out whether, and how, they can meet their work obligations in that location
Depending on the client's reason for moving, it may be appropriate to assess their eligibility for other forms of assistance that may help them remain in an area where there are employment opportunities available. These may include:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Disability Allowance
- Child Disability Allowance
- Childcare Assistance Programme
- Temporary Additional Support
For more information see:
- Decision guidelines - clients moving to a limited employment location
- Deskfile Limited employment locations
- Supported Living Payment Introduction
- Social housing Assessment of eligibility

chunks.title: Work Ability Assessment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Work Ability Assessment
A Work Ability Assessment is an independent assessment to identify what work a client can do, and the support and services they need to gain and retain work. The assessment will be undertaken by a suitably qualified and registered health practitioner (such as a psychologist or occupational therapist), who is experienced in assisting people into work.
To be considered for a Work Ability Assessment a client must:
- be receiving a benefit and
- have a health condition or disability that stops them from working full-time and
- be actively looking for part-time work (part-time work obligation) or be preparing for work (work preparation obligation) or looking for full-time work with limitations
## Requirements
Before referring a client for a Work Ability Assessment, MSD must have:
- completed a self-assessment with the client and
- been working proactively and intensively with the client to move them into employment and
- completed a structured interview with the client and
- reviewed all relevant information held about the client
MSD should consider if:
- the client is progressing towards employment in line with the existing service plan and the information contained on their Work Capacity Medical Certificates
- previous supports and services have been effective
- more information is needed to match the client to the appropriate employment support and services
Before a referral for a Work Ability Assessment can be made, MSD’s Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor must review the information and documentation held about the client and consider their suitability for a Work Ability Assessment.
If the client is a suitable candidate, the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor will identify the information to be provided as part of the referral and determine the provider or assessor the client will be referred to.
If the client is not a suitable candidate, the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor will recommend alternative options to help the client progress towards employment in line with the existing service plan.

chunks.title: Work ability assessment obligation — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Work ability assessment obligation
Clients getting Jobseeker Support have a work ability assessment obligation that requires them, when asked, to attend and participate in:
- Self-Assessments
- Structured Interview
- Work Ability Assessment
## Purpose of work ability assessment
A work ability assessment will help show what work a person is capable of doing, and what Work and Income can do to help a client find and stay in work.
A work ability assessment will help determine:
- the client's work ability
- what suitable work or work preparation activities are appropriate for the client
- what assistance, services or support Work and Income and/or other agencies should be providing
As a result of a work ability assessment a client's work obligations or benefit entitlement may change.
## Clients required to participate in a work ability assessment
Generally, only clients who have a health condition, injury or disability will be required to undertake or participate in a work ability assessment.
## Failing to comply
If a client does not meet these obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, an obligation failure will be initiated and a sanction may be imposed.

chunks.title: Work obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Full-time work obligations apply to: - primary clients (except those receiving Jobseeker Support on ground of a health condition, injury or disability) - partners with no dependent children and - partners with a youngest dependent child aged 14 years or over Part-time work obligations apply to: - primary clients receiving Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) who have part-time work capacity - partners with a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years Clients (and partners) with work obligations must: - be available for, and take reasonable steps to obtain, suitable employment - accept any offer of suitable employment, including temporary employment or employment that is seasonal or subsidised Note suitable employment can include employment that contains an employment trial. - attend and participate in an interview for any opportunity of suitable employment to which the client is referred - when required to attend and participate in any interview with Work and Income or on behalf of Work and Income - when required to undertake planning for employment - report to Work and Income on progress in meeting their work obligations as often as required and - when required by Work and Income, undertake any activity to improve their work readiness and employment prospects, including: any work assessmentany programme or seminarany work experience or work exploration activityany employment-related trainingrehabilitation (but not medical treatment) - any work assessment - any programme or seminar - any work experience or work exploration activity - any employment-related training - rehabilitation (but not medical treatment)

chunks.title: Partners ages 16 to 19 years old — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Young partners (aged 16 to 19 years old) of clients receiving Jobseeker Support have youth activity obligations, and not work or work preparation obligations, if they are: - aged 16 or 17 years old without dependent children or - aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children and - married to, or in a civil union, or de facto relationship with a person receiving Jobseeker Support For more information see:

chunks.title: Suitable employment — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients with full-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of at least 30 hours or more per week. Clients with part-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of at least: - 15 hours per week, for clients that qualify for Jobseeker Support on the grounds of a health condition, injury, or disability - 20 hours per week for all other clients However, if suitable employment is available for hours other than 15, 20 or 30 hours per week (as applicable), the client or partner can be required to accept an offer of this job. Work obligations can be applied on any day of the week provided it is suitable for the client's circumstances. To help you decide if the job is suitable for the client see: - Suitable employment - Hours range for suitable employment

chunks.title: Failing to comply — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients who fail to comply with their work obligations have an obligations failure. If a client (or partner) does not meet their work obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, you should initiate an obligations failure. You should consider the client's individual circumstances before referring them to a job or an activity, to ensure that they can realistically meet their obligations.

chunks.title: Deferral from work obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients may be able to receive a temporary deferral from their work obligations in specific circumstances. These clients will generally have work preparation obligations for the duration of the deferral. For more information about deferrals, see: - Deferrals

chunks.title: Exemptions from work obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Clients may be able to receive a temporary exemption from their work obligations. For more information about exemptions, see: - Exemptions For more information see: - Meeting job search requirements - Informing clients of their obligations - Setting appropriate activities for clients - Employment trial period of up to 90 days - Drug test obligations - Reporting progress - Rehabilitation - Exemptions - Table of Exemptions - Deferrals - Obligations failures

chunks.title: Work or work preparation obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Work or work preparation obligations
Clients and partners receiving Jobseeker Support have full-time or part-time work obligations, or work preparation obligations.
## Full-time work obligations
Full-time work obligations apply to:
- primary clients (except those receiving Jobseeker Support on ground of a health condition, injury or disability)
- partners with no children and
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged 14 years or over
Clients with full-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of at least 30 hours or more per week.
## Part-time work obligations
Clients with part-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find, suitable employment.
Part time work obligations apply
Part time work is
Primary clients receiving Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) who have part-time work capacity
Employment of at least 15 hours per week
Partners with a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years
Employment of at least 20 hours per week
## Work preparation obligations
Work preparation obligations apply to:
- primary clients receiving Jobseeker Support (health condition, injury or disability) who have a deferral from their work obligations
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
If the partner is receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, these children are not considered dependent children for rates purposes but they are treated as dependent children for setting work or work preparation obligations.
## Partners aged 16 to 19 years old
Young partners (aged 16 to 19 years old) of clients receiving Jobseeker Support have youth activity obligations, and not work or work preparation obligations, if they are:
- aged 16 or 17 years old without dependent children or
- aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children and
- married to, or in a civil union, or de facto relationship with a person receiving Jobseeker Support
For more information see:
- Deciding work obligations for client (health condition, injury or disability)
- Partners with no children or youngest child 14+ years
- Partners with youngest child between 3 and 13 years
- Partners with youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
- Work preparation obligations
- Work obligations
- Youth activity obligations
- Rehabilitation
- Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work or work preparation obligations

- Drug test obligations

chunks.title: Work preparation obligations — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Work preparation obligations
A person with work preparation obligations must take all reasonable steps to prepare for employment. When considering what is reasonable you must consider what is practical for their individual circumstances.
In addition, clients and partners with work preparation obligations must:
- when required to undertake planning for employment
- when required to report to Work and Income on progress in meeting their work preparation obligations as often as required
- when required to attend and participate in any interview with Work and Income or on behalf of Work and Income and
- when required by Work and Income undertake any activity to improve their work readiness and employment prospects, including: any work assessmentany programme or seminarany work experience or work exploration activityany employment related trainingrehabilitation (but not medical treatment)an education programme
- any work assessment
- any programme or seminar
- any work experience or work exploration activity
- any employment related training
- rehabilitation (but not medical treatment)
- an education programme
Work preparation obligations can be applied on any day of the week provided it is suitable for the partner's circumstances.
If a client or partner does not meet their work preparation obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, you should initiate an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Setting appropriate activities for clients
- Reporting progress
- Rehabilitation
- Exemptions
- Table of exemptions
- Deferrals
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Work with a contracted service provider obligation — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Work with a contracted service provider obligation
When required to, certain clients (including partners), may be case managed by a contracted service provider.
When asked, clients have an obligation to co-operate with a contracted service provider and to:
- attend and participate in interviews with them
- report to them on how they are meeting their obligations, this could include their social, work or work preparation obligations and
- when required, complete assessments with the service provider
For more information see:
- Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting obligation to work with a contracted service provider

chunks.title: Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
A client applying for Jobseeker Support can be considered resident and present in New Zealand during periods of overseas employment when their employer (or other relevant person):
- deducted PAYE or source deductions from their wages and
- paid them to Inland Revenue New Zealand
The period overseas that the client was considered resident and present can be used to meet the 2 years residence requirement for Jobseeker Support.
A partner or any dependent child who was with the client while they were working overseas can also be treated as resident and present in New Zealand for the same periods.
If the client has a child born outside of New Zealand during the period they were working overseas, the child is deemed to have been born in New Zealand.
The residential qualifications do not apply to people who are self-employed and working overseas.
Clients should provide evidence of the periods they were employed overseas, and PAYE or source deductions paid to Inland Revenue in New Zealand during these periods.
If the employer (or other relevant person) has deducted the tax but failed to pay it to Inland Revenue New Zealand, and the client did not contribute to the employer's failure to pay the tax, the period of employment overseas can still be regarded as residence and present in New Zealand.
Note if any person leaves New Zealand while getting a benefit and returns to take up ordinary residence in New Zealand at any time within 5 years, they are not required to meet the residential qualifications for the same benefit type.

chunks.title: Workplace/industry training — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Workplace/industry training
Workplace/industry training includes course such as:
- Skills for Industry
These courses are generally less than 13 weeks.
Young people will be meeting their obligations where they are undertaking programmes linked to the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF) credits.
For more information see:
- Employment and training Job search, employment and in-work support services
- Approved training (young partners)

chunks.title: Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
If a partner meets the qualifications for Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their work obligations until their capacity for work improves.
The partner must be limited in their capacity to work because of a health condition, injury or disability and, depending on whether they have part-time or full-time work obligations be:
- unable to look for part-time work of at least 15 hours per week or
- losing earnings because they are unable to work for at least 15 or 30 hours a week
This is a partial exemption and the partner is able to:
- plan for employment and
- undertake certain work related activities
## Evidence
To support their exemption, the client must provide a Work Capacity Medical Certificate completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant).
The information required on the medical certificate is:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to work and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for work planning, training and part-time work and
- any other information that is required
## Duration
The period of an exemption for partners who are limited in their capacity to work because of a health condition, injury or disability is based on the next reassessment date recorded on their medical certificate by their registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant).
This exemption should then be reviewed.
At the review MSD should consider the client's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption. MSD can ask the client to provide evidence that the exemption should be extended.

chunks.title: Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text:
## Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to partners with work or work preparation obligations.
If a partner meets the qualifications for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability or total blindness, they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their work or work preparation obligations.
The partner must be:
- both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, or injury or disability from an accident, or a condition they have had since birth or
- totally blind
Note totally blind and legally blind are not the same.
This can be a full or partial exemption depending on the whether the partner can plan for a return to work.
MSD should discuss with the client whether they can still:
- plan for employment and
- undertake certain work related activities
If it is unclear whether a full or partial exemption should be granted seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor.
Note when appropriate MSD should consider the client's eligibility for Supported Living Payment.
For more information see:
- Supported Living Payment
- Supported Living Payment - Work or work preparation obligations
## Evidence
The client must provide a Work Capacity Medical Certificate or medical information from a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner or psychologist stating:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to work and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for work planning, training and part-time work and
- any other information is required

chunks.title: Young partner with dependent child — main benefits > jobseeker support
chunks.text: Young partners aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children have the following activity obligations.
