chunks.text: A client may be able to get an exemption when they are experiencing an unforeseen event or situation that is beyond their control, and this means they are unable to respond to their Mandatory Review (even if they had more time). The client must let MSD know before their review date to discuss their circumstances. Exemption reasons may include (but are not limited to): - localised natural disaster that affects the client but not the whole region - unexpected serious illness or an accident affecting the client or their immediate family member If MSD determines an exemption applies, the client is not required to complete their Mandatory Review, and the review date is reset to 52 weeks from their current review date. Example Ren is getting New Zealand Superannuation (with a grandparented non-qualified partner included) and has a Mandatory Review due on 15 October 2026. However, Ren and his partner's home is damaged by a landslip, and they cannot return home. Because Ren and his partner have lost all their possessions and are focused on finding accommodation, MSD determines it is not reasonable for Ren to respond to his Mandatory Review by the review date. In this case, MSD grants an exemption. Ren's next Mandatory Review is set for 52 weeks from the original review date.

chunks.title: Charging income — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Charging income
New Zealand Superannuation is income tested when the client has a grandparented non-qualified partner included in their payments. When a partner is not included other income is ignored.
Note overseas benefits or pensions will generally be directly deducted from New Zealand Superannuation. In some cases they will be treated as income.
## Grandparented non-qualified partner included
For a couple with a grandparented non-qualified partner included, income is charged annually and at the following rate:
- the rate of payment is reduced by 70 cents for each $1.00 of income over $160 (before tax) a week
Note income is deducted from the gross rate of New Zealand Superannuation.
For more information see:
- New Zealand Superannuation grandparented non-qualified partner weekly income example
- Core policy Income
- Exemption for severe disablement
- Mandatory Review for New Zealand Superannuation with a grandparented non-qualified partner included
## Overseas benefits or pensions
When a client or their partner is getting an overseas benefit or pension this is generally treated as a direct deduction from the benefit or pension rate. This requires a different calculation to the chargeable income assessment.
For more information see:
- Payments from Overseas Couples getting overseas pensions
Note payments from a Friendly Society or similar organisation of up to $104 a year can be disregarded. Deduct this amount from the client's gross income before charging income.

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Child turns 18
A dependent child must generally be under the age of 18 to be included in their parent or caregiver's single living alone rate of New Zealand Superannuation.
When a child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and must be excluded from their parent or caregiver's New Zealand Superannuation from the start of the pay period following the child's 18th birthday.
However, if the 18-year-old child is continuing in education and is not financially independent, the child may continue to be considered a dependent child and be included in their parent or caregiver's New Zealand Superannuation for a limited period.
In these situations, the child must be excluded from the start of the pay period following:
- the date they no longer meet these criteria or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18
whichever is earlier

chunks.title: Client in hospital — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Client in hospital
A client's rate of payment can be different if they are in hospital when they are granted New Zealand Superannuation.
The rate should be reduced to the hospital rate of payment when the client has been in hospital for 13 weeks (not after receiving a benefit for 13 weeks).

chunks.title: Client meets qualifications while overseas — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Client meets qualifications while overseas
When a client qualifies for New Zealand Superannuation while they are absent from New Zealand, the commencement date is:
- the date of entitlement or
- the date of application
whichever is the later.
A client can be paid for up to the first 26 weeks of their absence if they return to New Zealand within 30 weeks of the New Zealand Superannuation commencement date.
If the client is absent from New Zealand for more than 30 weeks from the New Zealand Superannuation date, and they were not delayed from returning to New Zealand by circumstances outside their control that were reasonably unforeseeable before they left, they cannot get New Zealand Superannuation for the period they were absent.
New Zealand Superannuation can resume from the date the client returns to New Zealand.
## Living in Reciprocal Agreement countries
A client may meet the qualifications for New Zealand Superannuation while living in a country that has a reciprocal agreement with New Zealand.

chunks.title: Clients renting out accommodation — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Clients renting out accommodation
Clients who rent out a flat that is part of their residence can only receive the single living alone rate if the rented out accommodation is fully self-contained ie the client and tenant do not share any rooms (for example the lounge or kitchen).

chunks.title: Clients with a partner — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: If a client has a partner, the rate of payment depends on whether: - both clients can get New Zealand Superannuation in their own right (both meet the age and residency qualifications) and - either client is eligible to get or is getting a deductible overseas benefit or pension and - the partner has a temporary entry visa or is in New Zealand unlawfully Both clients meet the qualifications for New Zealand Superannuation - The couple's income is not taken into consideration when assessing the rate of payment of New Zealand Superannuation - Any overseas benefits or pension either partner may be getting or eligible to get, will only be directly deducted from their individual New Zealand Superannuation payments - A client or partners overseas benefit or pension can still affect the rate of any ongoing financial assistance if there is an excess Only one client qualifies for New Zealand Superannuation - The couple's income is not taken into consideration when assessing the rate of payment of New Zealand Superannuation. New Zealand Superannuation is not income tested. - If the client getting New Zealand Superannuation gets an overseas benefit or pension it is directly deducted from their payments - If the partner is getting an overseas benefit or pension it is not deducted from the client's New Zealand Superannuation payments - A client or partners overseas benefit or pension can still affect the rate of any ongoing financial assistance if there is an excess Only one client qualifies for New Zealand Superannuation and their partner has a temporary entry visa or is in New Zealand unlawfully. - The couple's income is not taken into consideration when assessing the rate of payment of New Zealand Superannuation. New Zealand Superannuation is not income tested. - If the client getting New Zealand Superannuation gets an overseas benefit or pension it is directly deducted from their payments. - If the partner is getting an overseas benefit or pension it is not deducted from clients New Zealand Superannuation payments. - A client or partners overseas benefit or pension can still affect the rate of any ongoing financial assistance if there is an excess. - Pay the client the single rate of New Zealand Superannuation Only one client meets the qualifications for New Zealand Superannuation and the partner is included (grandparented non-qualified partner before 9 November 2020) - Payment is income tested.

chunks.title: Clients with a partner — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: - If the client or partner is getting or entitled to get, an overseas benefit or pension, it is directly deducted from the grandparented non-qualified partner rate of New Zealand Superannuation. The balance is divided equally and paid to the client and partner. - A client or partners overseas benefit or pension can still affect the rate of any ongoing financial assistance if there is an excess. In some situations, clients who are living apart from their partner can get the single sharing accommodation rate or the single living alone rate of New Zealand Superannuation. Note from 9 November 2020, a partner who does not qualify for New Zealand Superannuation cannot be included in the clients New Zealand Superannuation.

chunks.title: Clients with time overseas — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Clients with time overseas
Clients who have spent time overseas, including New Zealand citizens, may need to show that they meet the residency qualification for New Zealand Superannuation.
They may also need to check if they are entitled to a pension from any countries they have lived in.
For help with overseas pensions contact International Services
## Born in the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau
Clients born in the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau before 1 January 2006 are considered New Zealand citizens by birth.
Since 1 January 2006 clients born in the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau are New Zealand citizens by birth, if either parent was a New Zealand citizen or held a resident class visa when the client was born.
Generally, these clients will travel to New Zealand on a New Zealand passport.
People who are not New Zealand citizens by birth and have spent time in the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau must provide a proof of residence document and meet the residency requirements for New Zealand Superannuation.
## Australian citizens and permanent residents
Australian citizens and permanent residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand as they are deemed to hold a residence class visa.
## British nationals
Clients of British nationality who arrived in New Zealand before 2 April 1974 were allowed residence in New Zealand without a visa or a permit.

chunks.title: Commencement date — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
To decide when New Zealand Superannuation can start you must first find the entitlement date.
## Entitlement date
The entitlement date for New Zealand Superannuation is:
- the date the client reaches the qualifying age or
- meets the residency criteria
whichever is the later.
## Commencement date
The commencement date is:
- the date of entitlement or
- the date of application
whichever is the later.
Note applications from the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau do not lapse after 20 days.
There is no provision for any back payment of New Zealand Superannuation.
No stand-down applies to New Zealand Superannuation.

chunks.title: Couple separates or one partner dies — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Couple separates or one partner dies
If a grandparented non-qualified couple separate, or one partner dies, the grandparented non-qualified partner rate will end.
## Couple separate
If the non-qualified partner needs financial assistance they can apply for a main benefit. The qualified partner will not be able to get the non-qualified partner rate again.
## One partner dies
If the non-qualified partner is the surviving partner, they can apply for a main benefit if they need financial assistance. If the qualified partner is the surviving partner, they will not be able to get the non-qualified partner rate again.

chunks.title: Couple's income makes it advantageous to stop the grandparented non-qualified partner rate — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Couple's income makes it advantageous to stop the grandparented non-qualified partner rate
When a couple get the grandparented non-qualified partner rate of New Zealand Superannuation, their combined income above the viability amount of $41,089.49 (as at 1 April 2026) will reduce the rate to less than the amount that would be paid to the qualified partner in their own right.
A decision on whether to continue getting the non-qualified partner rate must be made by the qualifying partner only.
Before a decision is made the qualifying partner must be given the following information to help them decide:
- the couple can continue getting the non-qualified partner rate even though it is less than the qualified partner would get without a partner included. This will keep the partner's grandparented status
- whether the income is likely to reduce below the viability amount in the future - they could continue with the reduced rate until their income reduces
- if the qualified partner chooses to cancel the non-qualified partner rate, they will not be able to apply for it in the future
- the non-qualified partner will only have the option of applying for a main benefit which is paid at a lower amount, is income tested and paid at a half married rate
- the non-qualified partner will not be able to continue using their SuperGold card
- the overseas absence provisions for main benefits are more limited than they are for New Zealand Superannuation
The qualifying partner must make the decision on whether to cancel or continue with the non-qualified partner rate.

chunks.title: Couples who are living apart — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Couples who are living apart
Married, civil union or de facto couples who live apart but still regard themselves as a couple get the married, civil union or de facto rate of payment.
Generally, when a couple is physically living apart only because one partner is in long term care (but they still consider themselves to be in a marriage or civil union) they may be entitled to get the single sharing accommodation or the single living alone rate instead of the married, civil union or de facto rate.

chunks.title: Couples who have separated — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Couples who have separated
When couples have separated, they can be treated as single and can receive the single sharing accommodation or the single living alone rate of New Zealand Superannuation (provided they have not entered into another relationship).
The rate of payment will depend on whether they:
- are sharing their accommodation with any person aged 18 years or over, other than a dependent child, or a visitor who stays more than 13 weeks in any 26 week period or
- meet all the qualifications for the single living alone rate
Note the single sharing accommodation or the single living alone rate can be paid from the date the New Zealand Superannuation commences if the client meets the above criteria at their entitlement date.
For more information about the effective date to review if the client is already receiving New Zealand Superannuation see:
- Effective date of review due to change in relationship
## What determines a separation?
For couples who are married or in a civil union to be separated from their partner there must be a physical separation and an acceptance or recognition by one or both of the partners that the relationship has ended.
For a de facto couple to be separated their relationship must no longer be in the nature of marriage or civil union (a relationship in the nature of marriage or civil union means both a financial interdependence and emotional commitment).

chunks.title: Credit union — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Credit union

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident in New Zealand — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Generally, a client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they apply for New Zealand Superannuation. They must remain ordinarily resident in New Zealand to continue getting New Zealand Superannuation.

chunks.title: Attributes of being ordinarily resident — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: To meet the ordinarily resident qualifications in New Zealand, the client must have a close and clear connection to New Zealand on the date they apply for New Zealand Superannuation. Some of the key attributes that indicate a client is ordinarily resident in New Zealand include: - their physical presence in New Zealand is not casually or as a traveller - they are in New Zealand voluntarily because they want to be - there is some intention to remain in New Zealand for a settled purpose - despite temporary absences from New Zealand, they regularly or customarily live in New Zealand - they prefer residence in New Zealand to any other country (a client cannot be ordinarily resident in 2 countries at the same time) If there is reason to believe the client may no longer be ordinarily resident in New Zealand after New Zealand Superannuation is granted, the key attributes can also be considered at that point

chunks.title: Not clear if the client is ordinarily resident — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: When it is not clear if a client is ordinarily resident in New Zealand, the client may need to be asked for more information. Some of the following considerations may help to make a decision: - if the client is going overseas, what their intentions towards New Zealand are (sighting return air tickets may be a good indication) - the length of time they spend in New Zealand compared to the length of time overseas, and the reasons they are or were overseas - property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (e.g. boats, cars or caravans) - where their cash assets are principally held (New Zealand banks or investment entities or overseas based holdings) - is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and if they are a tax resident in New Zealand - if they are still on an electoral role and vote in central and local body elections, and if they vote anywhere overseas - what their personal commitment to New Zealand is compared to overseas (e.g. their involvement in their immediate and extended family, community, community events, clubs or other groups) If there is reason to believe the client may no longer be ordinarily resident in New Zealand after New Zealand Superannuation is granted, the key attributes of being ordinarily resident can also be considered at that point.

chunks.title: Making a decision — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: To decide if a client is ordinarily resident in New Zealand consideration must be given to all the factors of each case. The client should show a close and clear connection to New Zealand. They should be asked for more information if clarification is needed. If it is still unclear if a client is ordinarily resident in New Zealand, you should seek advice to help you make a decision

chunks.title: Moving overseas — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: When a client leaves New Zealand to live overseas permanently, they may be able to keep getting their New Zealand Superannuation. See: Portability

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident in New Zealand for eligible charitable work overseas — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: For periods of time a client (and partner, if any) were overseas as a full-time voluntary worker to qualify towards being resident and present in New Zealand for applications on or after 9 November 2020 (but can include time worked on or after 1 July 2005) a client (and partner, if any) must have been ordinarily resident before they left for their voluntary work and during the period they worked overseas. Note a client (and partner, if any) must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand at time of application for New Zealand Superannuation. However, it is possible to be both a person undertaking full-time voluntary work overseas and ordinarily resident in New Zealand at the same time. For more information see: - Residency qualifications

chunks.title: Determining ordinarily resident before (and during) a client's full-time voluntary work overseas — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: To determine if a client was ordinarily resident in New Zealand immediately before they started their eligible charitable work, a number of factors must be considered. Some of the key attributes that indicate a client was ordinarily resident in New Zealand before they left (and during the period they were absence) for their voluntary work include: - their physical presence in New Zealand was other than casually or as a traveller - they were in New Zealand because they wanted to be and they were here voluntarily - there was some intention to remain settled in New Zealand for a settled purpose - despite temporary absences from New Zealand they regularly or customarily lived in New Zealand before they left and still considered New Zealand home while they were doing their voluntary work - they preferred residence in New Zealand to any other country (a client cannot be ordinarily resident in 2 countries at the same time)

chunks.title: Not clear if the client is ordinarily resident — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: When it is not clear if a client was ordinarily resident in New Zealand before they left, and during the period they were doing voluntary work overseas, the client may need to be asked for more information. The following could be considered: - when the client was going overseas what were their intentions towards New Zealand, did they intend to return? - what were their ties to other countries at the time? - were there any extended absences from New Zealand leading up to the voluntary work? - the length of time they spend in New Zealand before they left for their eligible charitable work, compared to their periods of absence and the reasons for the absences - property ownership in New Zealand and elsewhere (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (e.g. boats, cars or caravans) - where their cash assets were principally held (New Zealand banks or investment entities or overseas based holdings) - was their income earned in New Zealand or overseas before they left for their voluntary work, and were they tax resident in New Zealand? The client may need to talk to Inland Revenue for this information - were they on an electoral role and voted in central and local body elections before they left for their voluntary work? - did they have a personal commitment to New Zealand (e.g. their involvement in their immediate and extended family, community, community events, clubs and other groups) before they left for their voluntary work. If there is reason to believe a client may no longer be ordinarily resident in New Zealand after New Zealand Superannuation has been granted, the key attributes of being ordinarily resident can also be considered at that point.

chunks.title: Making a decision — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: To decide if a client is ordinarily resident in New Zealand consideration must be given to all factors of each case. The client should show a clear and close connection to New Zealand based on the attributes of being ordinarily resident. They should be asked for more information if clarification is needed. If it is still unclear if a client was ordinarily resident in New Zealand before they left for or during their time doing voluntary work, you should seek advice to help you make a decision.

chunks.title: Missionary postings before 9 November 2020 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Clients who were born overseas and began a missionary posting outside of New Zealand before 9 November 2020 must have been ordinarily resident in New Zealand immediately before they left for missionary work outside of New Zealand. Clients who were born in New Zealand and began a missionary posting outside of New Zealand before 9 November 2020 had no requirement to be ordinarily resident in New Zealand before they left for missionary work overseas.

chunks.title: Missionary postings on or after 9 November 2020 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Clients who began a missionary posting outside of New Zealand from 9 November 2020 must have been ordinarily resident in New Zealand immediately before they left for missionary work overseas. For more information see:

chunks.title: Determining a client was ordinarily resident in New Zealand before they left for missionary work — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: To determine if a client was ordinarily resident in New Zealand immediately before they started their missionary work, a number of factors must be considered. Some of the key attributes indicating a client was ordinarily resident in New Zealand before they left for their missionary work include: - their physical presence in New Zealand was other than casually or as a traveller - they were in New Zealand because they wanted to be - they were here voluntarily - there was some intention to remain in New Zealand for a settled purpose - despite temporary absences from New Zealand they regularly or customarily lived in New Zealand before they left for their missionary work - they preferred residence in New Zealand to any other country (a client cannot be ordinarily resident in 2 countries at the same time) Where it is not clear if a client was ordinarily resident in New Zealand before they left for their missionary work you may need to ask the client for further information. Some of the following questions may help to get more information: - when they client was going overseas what were their intentions towards New Zealand, did they intend to return - the length of time they spend in New Zealand before they left for their missionary work, compared to their periods of absence and the reasons for the absences - property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans) - their cash assets were principally held (New Zealand banks or investment entities or overseas based holdings) - was their income earned in New Zealand or overseas before they left for their missionary work, and were they tax resident in New Zealand (see Inland Revenue New Zealand tax residence guide IR292) - were they on an electoral role and voted in central and local body elections before they left for their missionary work - did they have a personal commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in their immediate and extended family, community, community events, clubs and other groups) before they left for their missionary work

chunks.title: Not clear if the client was ordinarily resident — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: When it is not clear if a client was ordinarily resident in New Zealand before they left for their missionary work, the following could be considered: - when the client was going overseas what were their intentions towards New Zealand, did they intend to return? - what were their ties to other countries at the time? - were there any extended absences from New Zealand leading up to the missionary work? - the length of time they spend in New Zealand before they left for their missionary work, compared to their periods of absence and the reasons for the absences - property ownership in New Zealand and elsewhere (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans) - where their cash assets were principally held (New Zealand banks or investment entities or overseas based holdings) - was their income earned in New Zealand or overseas before they left for their missionary work, and were they tax resident in New Zealand. The client may need to contact Inland Revenue to get this information - were they on an electoral role and voted in central and local body elections before they left for their missionary work? - did they have a personal commitment to New Zealand and elsewhere (e.g. their involvement in their immediate and extended family, community, community events, clubs and other groups) before they left for their missionary work? If there is reason to believe the client may no longer be ordinarily resident in New Zealand after New Zealand Superannuation is granted, the key attributes of being ordinarily resident can also be considered at that point.

chunks.title: Making a decision — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: To decide if a client is ordinarily resident in New Zealand consideration must be given to all the factors of each case. The client should show a close and clear connection to New Zealand based on the attributes of being ordinarily resident. They should be asked for more information if clarification is needed. If it is still unclear if a client was ordinarily resident in New Zealand before they left for their missionary work, you should seek advice to help you make a decision.

chunks.title: Definition of a boarding house — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Definition of a boarding house
A boarding house is a residential premises containing 1 or more boarding rooms along with facilities for communal use by the tenants of the boarding house; and occupied, or intended by the landlord to be occupied, by at least 6 tenants at any one time.
Facilities means the facilities provided by the landlord of a boarding house for the shared use by tenants of the boarding house, such as:
- toilet and bathroom facilities
- cooking facilities
- general living, dining or recreational areas
- laundry facilities
- lifts and stairways
- rubbish storage and rubbish disposal facilities
- appliances for heating or cooling premises
- communication facilities
- lawns, gardens and outhouses
- any land or buildings intended for use for storage space or for the parking of motor vehicles

chunks.title: Definition of living alone — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Definition of living alone
Clients are considered living alone when they are living alone in their principal place of residence. This cannot include sharing their residence with any person aged 18 years or over unless that person is a:
- dependent child who is continuing in education and not financially independent (until the start of the pay period following the date they are no longer in education, are financially independent or 31 December of the year they turn 18) or
- visitor who stays less than 13 weeks in any 26-week period
If a client has a young person under 18 living with them who is in full time employment, the client is still eligible to get the single living alone rate of New Zealand Superannuation.

chunks.title: Dependent child — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
A dependent child for New Zealand Superannuation is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of that client
- maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for New Zealand Superannuation does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
In some situations, a child may not be living at home but is still considered to be a dependent child.

chunks.title: Effect of absence overseas on grandparented couples — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Effect of absence overseas on grandparented couples
Couples getting the grandparented non-qualified partner rate who are both absent from New Zealand at the same time, will keep getting their grandparented rate provided the qualifying partner qualifies to be paid New Zealand Superannuation during the entire period of absence and has returned to New Zealand within 26 weeks.
If the qualifying partner no longer qualifies to be paid New Zealand Superannuation during any part of their absence on or after 9 November 2020, the grandparented non-qualified rate will end and the qualifying partner will not be able to include a non-qualifying partner again.
## Overseas absence where both partners are absent
Period of absence
Is Grandparenting retained?
Absence no more than 26 weeks.
Yes - the qualified partner is entitled for the period of absence.
Absence is more than 26 weeks but does not exceed 30 weeks.
No - from the 27th week of absence, the qualified partner no longer qualifies and neither does the grandparented non-qualified partner. Grandparenting ends from the 27th week of absence.
Absence is more than 30 weeks - whether avoidably or unavoidably delayed in returning.
No - they no longer qualify for the grandparented rate from the day after the date of departure from New Zealand if they were avoidably delayed in returning.
or
They no longer qualify for the grandparented rate from the 27th week of absence if they were unavoidably delayed, but had payment for the first 26 weeks of absence.
Note the above rules apply if:
- the qualified partner is overseas while the grand-parented non-qualified partner is in New Zealand or
- the couple or qualified partner began a period of temporary absence from New Zealand before 9 November 2020, but are still absent on or after 9 November 2020.
## Grand-parented non-qualified partner is absent
Grandparenting is not affected when the grand-parented non-qualified partner is temporarily absent from New Zealand by themselves, as long as the qualified partner in New Zealand still qualifies.
Payments made to the grandparented non-qualified partner during their absence can continue for up to 26 weeks.
If the grandparented non-qualified partner does not qualify for payment for any or all of their absence, this does not affect the grandparented rate when the non-qualified partner's payments are resumed on their return to New Zealand.

chunks.title: Effect of imprisonment on grandparented clients — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Grandparented non-qualified couples may no longer qualify for the grandparented non-qualified partner rate when either the client or partner is: - in prison - in custody on remand or - an escapee from custody There is discretion to continue New Zealand Superannuation for the 2 instalments following imprisonment. Further ongoing payments for the period of imprisonment are also discretionary.

chunks.title: Qualified partner is imprisoned — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: The decision guidelines - married, civil union or de facto clients should be used to decide whether the qualified partners payments continue for the period of imprisonment. If payments will not continue during the period of imprisonment, the grandparented non-qualified partner rate will end, and the qualifying partner will not be able to include a non-qualified partner again. The grandparented non-qualified partner will need to apply for a main benefit.

chunks.title: Grandparented non-qualified partner is imprisoned — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Use the decision guidelines - married, civil union or de facto clients to decide whether the grandparented non-qualified partners payments continue for the period of imprisonment. If payments continue to the grandparented non-qualified partner or the full amount is paid to the partner not in prison, the grandparented non-qualified partner rate continues. If payments to the grandparented non-qualified partner stop, the grandparented non-qualified partner rate can only be paid again on release if the qualifying partner: - continues to qualify for New Zealand Superannuation for the period of imprisonment and - wants to continue getting the grandparented non-qualified partner rate When payments stop for the grandparented non-qualified partner, the qualified partner's payments continue at the same rate paid before their partner's imprisonment. The qualified partner can decide to cancel the grandparented non-qualified partner rate at any time.

chunks.title: Single sharing or single living alone rate for qualified partner — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: The qualified partner may qualify for the single sharing or single living alone rate of New Zealand Superannuation while their grand-parented non-qualified partner is in prison. This must be considered separately based on the client's full circumstances, eg the partner may not intend resuming the relationship when their partner leaves prison, or may end the relationship due to the imprisonment. Note the client should be informed that they will not be eligible for the non-qualified partner rate in the future if they cancel the grandparented non-qualified partner rate, eg because they are treated as single.

chunks.title: Eligible charitable work — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: In certain circumstances, time spent doing eligible charitable work outside New Zealand may be considered as residence and presence in New Zealand to meet the requirements for New Zealand Superannuation. Eligible charitable work is: - full-time voluntary humanitarian work for an entity which had giving aid and assistance to less advantaged communities in one or more countries as its main purpose and - work as a volunteer appointed by Volunteer Services Abroad Incorporated Note voluntary work meant that a client did work for or on behalf of the charitable entity and did not get a salary or wage for doing this work. However, they may have got a small allowance to help with basic living costs. Depending on whether the client applied for New Zealand Superannuation before or after 9 November 2020, the period of absence for eligible charitable work is treated differently for assessing periods of being resident and present to qualify for New Zealand Superannuation.

chunks.title: Applications before 9 November 2020 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: A client who applied for New Zealand Superannuation before 9 November 2020 could only have periods overseas included as a period of being resident and present to qualify for New Zealand Superannuation if they: - were doing work as an accredited volunteer appointed by Volunteer Services Abroad Incorporated and - remained ordinarily resident during their time overseas

chunks.title: Applications on or after 9 November 2020 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: A client who began eligible charitable work outside of New Zealand on or after 9 November 2020 can have it included as a period of residence and presence to qualify for New Zealand Superannuation if they: - were doing work as an accredited volunteer appointed by Volunteer Services Abroad Incorporated and - remained ordinarily resident during their time overseas or - were doing full-time voluntary work that is humanitarian work and - were carrying out the voluntary work for an entity that is affiliated with or closely related to, a charitable entity registered in New Zealand under the Charities Act 2005 and - were carrying out this voluntary work on behalf of a charitable entity which has as its primary function, giving aid and assistance to less advantaged communities and - remained ordinarily resident during their time overseas. Note this also means that only time from when the Charities Act 2005 (1 July 2005) came into force can be counted where a client wants to include work for a charity that is not Volunteer Services Abroad.

chunks.title: Volunteer Services Abroad — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Volunteer Service Abroad (VSA) is a registered charity who appointed accredited volunteers to travel and do voluntary work overseas. They were incorporated under the Incorporated Societies Act 1908 on 8 April 1963. This means that we can only count time from 8 April 1963 for a client who was appointed by VSA, to do voluntary work overseas.

chunks.title: Humanitarian work — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Humanitarian work includes providing help and support to promote human welfare. For an entity providing humanitarian type services, the Charities Act 2005 provides that an entity wanting to register as a charity must have a charitable purpose which covers humanitarian work.

chunks.title: Exemption for severe disablement — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Exemption for severe disablement
As an incentive for the personal effort of a severely disabled person to participate or continue in employment, you can use your discretion to disregard all or part of any income earned from employment as chargeable income for benefit purposes.
Consideration for this special income exemption should be given to clients with a severe disability who are extremely limited in their ability to participate in employment, the community and take care of themselves.
You must first consider whether or not the client is severely disabled. The Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement will help you do this.
Each case should be assessed on an individual basis.
If the client is severely disabled you should consider whether or not to disregard all or part of any income earned by the client. To help you do this, see Amount of income exemption
Note clients who are not severely disabled cannot receive this exemption.

chunks.title: Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit
If a New Zealand Superannuation client has dependent children, family tax credit and Best Start tax credit is paid by Inland Revenue, not through SWIFTT.

chunks.title: Grandparented non-qualified partner with a partner in residential care — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Grandparented non-qualified partner with a partner in residential care
A grandparented non-qualified partner living in the community who has a partner in long-term residential care in a rest home or hospital may get a different rate of payment.
Their rate of payment depends on when they started getting New Zealand Superannuation as a non-qualified partner.
## Partner included on or after 1 October 1991
Clients in the community who started getting New Zealand Superannuation as a grandparented non-qualified partner can get an Emergency Benefit paid at the single rate of Supported Living Payment or Sole Parent rate from the date their partner entered care.
The client in the community will have their income included in their partner's Needs Assessment for Residential Care Subsidy. Any income the partner in the community earns cannot be included as chargeable income against the Emergency Benefit.
Note if the partner does not meet the asset test for Residential Care Subsidy all income is charged against the Emergency Benefit.
## Partner included before 1 October 1991
Clients in the community who started getting New Zealand Superannuation as a grandparented non-qualified partner can get the single sharing accommodation or single living alone rate from the date their partner entered care.
The client in the community will have their income included in their partner's Needs Assessment for Residential Care Subsidy. Any income the partner in the community earns cannot be included as chargeable income against New Zealand Superannuation.
If the partner does not meet the asset test for Residential Care Subsidy all income is charged against the New Zealand Superannuation.
## Special Disability Allowance
Special Disability Allowance can be paid to the client in the community to assist with extra costs due to their partner being in long term residential care, if the partner in care is eligible for Residential Care Subsidy.
## Rate of payment for partner in care
The partner in care will receive the half married, civil union or de facto rate of New Zealand Superannuation.

chunks.title: Grandparenting non-qualified partner couples — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Grandparenting non-qualified partner couples
From 9 November 2020, clients who qualify for New Zealand Superannuation in their own right cannot include their non-qualified partner in their payments. A non-qualified partner can apply for a main benefit in their own right.
To be eligible for the grandparented rate, the client must have chosen to include their non-qualified partner before 9 November 2020 and be entitled to this rate from a date before 9 November 2020.
All existing non-qualified partners that were current, suspended or expired on 8 November 2020 were grandparented from 9 November 2020.
Note couples getting the non-qualified partner rate who temporarily left New Zealand before 26 March 2020 and were not able to return to New Zealand before 9 November 2020 will not be grandparented. Assistance during their absence is covered by the New Zealanders Stranded Overseas Support Programme. Couples who left New Zealand after 26 March 2020 have their absence treated under the usual 26 week absence rules and must be entitled to payment as at 8 November 2020 to be grandparented.
## Client included non-qualified partner at New Zealand Superannuation application
When a person applied for New Zealand Superannuation and included their non-qualified partner in their payments at the same time, the non-qualified partner rate is grandparented if:
- the client was entitled to get New Zealand Superannuation in their own right before 9 November 2020 and
- they applied for the non-qualified rate before 9 November 2020 and
- they were entitled to the non-qualified rate before 9 November 2020

chunks.title: Granny flats — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Granny flats
Granny flats are usually co-sited on one property with the main residential dwelling or house. Generally the main house is occupied by relatives or friends.
Granny flats range from 'outside rooms' to fully self-contained units.
Clients living in a 'granny flat' may receive the single living alone rate if the Granny flat is a house or flat.

chunks.title: Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement
A special income exemption for severe disablement may be given to a client as an incentive for their personal effort to participate or continue in employment.
To help you to decide if a person is severely disabled consider the following:
- Does the client have to put in more effort in order to participate in employment? (for example, they may take a considerably long time to get ready in the morning or a longer time to travel to their place of employment)?
- Is the client's capacity to earn the same wage as a person without a severe disability reduced because of their disability (for example, does the client work reduced hours or receive less money for the job they undertake because of their disability)?
- Does the client have additional expenses to undertake employment (for example additional transport or equipment costs)?
- Does the client have difficulties participating in employment or completing their tasks because of their disability (for example, they may experience difficulties with mobility around the work place, be limited in the tasks they undertake or on occasion may not complete their work duties)?
- Does the client require assistance from another person to carry out some of their daily tasks (for example, washing, dressing or cooking)?
- Does the client require the assistance from another person to travel to work or to ensure their physical safety while at work (for example, does the client have difficulty using public transport)?
- Any other relevant factors that should be considered.
- If the client answers 'yes' to one or more of these questions you will have to decide if the client is severely disabled or if you need further information to make this decision.
Contact Helpline if you need help with the assessment.

chunks.title: Hospitals — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Hospitals
If a single client is in hospital at the time they meet the qualifications for New Zealand Superannuation, they can only receive the single sharing accommodation rate.
When a client is already receiving the single living alone rate of New Zealand Superannuation at the time they are admitted to a public hospital, the single living alone rate continues for the first 13 weeks in hospital. After 13 weeks, the rate of payment may be reduced.
For more information see:
- Changes and reviews Hospitalisation

chunks.title: House or flat — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## House or flat
The principal place of residence occupied by a client is a house, apartment or flat that must:
- be a structure or part of a structure, that is permanently fixed to land
- have, for the exclusive use of the occupant, adequate and distinct areas for day to day living and sleeping whether or not in separate rooms
- have a bathroom with a bath or shower and an adequate supply of hot water
- a sink with a tap connected to an adequate supply of potable water (drinkable)
- have a toilet
- have a kitchen or kitchenette with: adequate space for proper storage of food and utensils (drawers and cupboards or pantry)an adequate means of preparing food, the ability to prepare and cook food, including by boiling or by baking, which as a general rule must contain:- a power source (such as electricity power points, gas or solar power)- a bench space to prepare food and- at least one of the following: a stove top, a microwave or a bench oven
- adequate space for proper storage of food and utensils (drawers and cupboards or pantry)
- an adequate means of preparing food, the ability to prepare and cook food, including by boiling or by baking, which as a general rule must contain:- a power source (such as electricity power points, gas or solar power)- a bench space to prepare food and- at least one of the following: a stove top, a microwave or a bench oven

chunks.title: Immigration status and supporting documents — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Immigration status and supporting documents
Generally, when people born overseas travel to New Zealand they are granted a visa by Immigration New Zealand. The visa shows the conditions under which they are allowed to be in New Zealand, for example temporarily (student, work, visitor) or as a resident.
The type of documents a client may provide to verify their immigration status depends on when they were issued.
From 29 November 2010 clients with an existing visa or permit are 'deemed' to hold the corresponding type of visa under the new Immigration Act 2009. This means that:
- permits continue to be valid until their expiry date. A person does not need to replace a permit in their passport with a new visa until the permit expires
- residents with an existing residence permit may never have this updated as they do not intend to leave New Zealand.
## Documents issued from 29 November 2010
Documents issued from 29 November 2010 include:
- eVisa letter
- Limited visa
- New Zealand Citizenship certificate (issued by Department of Internal Affairs)
- New Zealand Citizen endorsement (in a foreign passport)
- Permanent resident visa
- Resident visa
- Student visa
- Visitor visa
- Work visa
Only the Permanent resident visa, Permanent resident eVisa, Resident visa, and Resident eVisa show a person is a resident.
A visa may be a sticker in the client's passport.
## Documents issued before 29 November 2010
Documents issued before 29 November 2010 that allowed a person to stay in New Zealand included:
- Limited purposes permit
- New Zealand Citizenship certificate (issued by Department of Internal Affairs)
- Residence permit (with or without returning resident's visa)
- Student permit
- Visitor permit
- Work permit
Only the residence permit (with or without returning resident's visa) was issued to residents.
A permit is a sticker in the client's passport.
## Unable to provide visa or permit
When a client is unable to provide an immigration visa or permit, they may provide other Immigration New Zealand documents to verify their immigration status.
With the consent of the client, MSD can undertake an immigration status check directly with Immigration New Zealand
Note Immigration New Zealand may be unable to verify the immigration status for clients of British nationality who arrived in New Zealand before 2 April 1974 and do not have a passport.

chunks.title: Intention to remain permanently — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Intention to remain permanently
When a client has only recently arrived in New Zealand, they may be considered resident in New Zealand if they are able to provide evidence, showing they intend to make their home in New Zealand for the foreseeable future
An application for permanent residence is one way a client can show their intention to make New Zealand their home.
However, a client may be able to demonstrate an intention to make their home in New Zealand at an earlier date, by the date the client:
- arrived lawfully in New Zealand or
- any date between the date of arrival lawfully in New Zealand and permanent residence granted
To determine whether the client intended to make their home in New Zealand at an earlier date, the following could be considered:
- if the client had a return ticket to their country of origin when they arrived in New Zealand
- if the client intended for their time in New Zealand to be temporary, i.e. they intended to return overseas
- the reasons the client decided to come to New Zealand e.g. family ties
- what steps did the client take towards making their home in New Zealand? Such as: if the client bought or own any property or significant assets in New Zealand?if the client moved cash and other assets to New Zealandif the client involved themselves in any New Zealand work, community events, clubs' membership and other groups such as, but not limited to, their local church or school
- if the client bought or own any property or significant assets in New Zealand?
- if the client moved cash and other assets to New Zealand
- if the client involved themselves in any New Zealand work, community events, clubs' membership and other groups such as, but not limited to, their local church or school
- how long after arrival it took the client to apply for permanent residence in New Zealand
- the absences the client had from New Zealand after their arrival in New Zealand: what the reasons were for those absencesif absences were prolonged or repeated
- what the reasons were for those absences
- if absences were prolonged or repeated
The client must be both resident and present in New Zealand at the same time for the period to count when assessing if they meet the residence qualification.

chunks.title: Introduction — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Introduction
New Zealand Superannuation provides a retirement income for clients who have reached 65 years of age.
## For more detailed information on New Zealand Superannuation see:
- Qualifications
- Obligations
- Commencement Date
- Payment
- Changes and Reviews
## Community Services Cards
Community Services Cards are not automatically issued. Clients must make a separate application.
New Zealand Superannuation clients with a partner getting a main benefit are automatically issued a Community Services Card.
For more information see:
- Community Services Card

chunks.title: Kaumatua flats — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Kaumatua flats
Many marae include self-contained kaumatua flats. These flats are usually owned by the Runanga Iwi (Council of people) and are rented to kaumatua (elders).
Kaumatua living alone in one of these flats may receive the single living alone rate if the flat is a house or flat.
Note
Self-contained kaumatua flats will usually meet the definition of flat for the single living alone rate to be paid.
If the Kaumatua flats do not meet the definition of a flat, you need to consider whether they meet the definition of a boarding house.

chunks.title: Living Alone Payment before 2 September 2013 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Living Alone Payment before 2 September 2013
Clients receiving a Living Alone Payment as at 1 September 2013 are entitled to receive the single living alone rate of New Zealand Superannuation, from 2 September 2013.
The single living alone rate can continue to be paid for as long as there is no change in the clients circumstances that affect their entitlement to the living alone payment under the criteria that applied before 2 September 2013.
For example, a client whose principal place of residence had been accepted as a 'licensed boarding-house' for the purpose of being entitled to receive the living alone payment, can receive the single living alone rate even if the premises do not meet the definition of boarding-house that applies from 2 September 2013.

chunks.title: Missionary work — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Missionary work
In certain circumstances, time spent doing missionary work outside New Zealand may be considered as being resident and present in New Zealand to meet the qualification for New Zealand Superannuation.
Missionary work includes the advancement of religion or education and the maintenance, care, or relief, of orphans, or the aged infirm, sick, or needy.
Periods spent overseas at a university or seminary training for example, at a bible or theological college cannot be included as missionary work.
Depending on whether the missionary work was before or from 9 November 2020, the period of absence for missionary work is treated differently for assessing periods of being resident and present in New Zealand to qualify for New Zealand Superannuation.
## Missionary postings before 9 November 2020
A client who began a missionary posting outside of New Zealand before 9 November 2020 can have it included as a period of residence and presence to qualify for New Zealand Superannuation if they:
- were doing missionary work and
- were ordinarily resident in New Zealand immediately before they left for missionary work overseas or
- were born in New Zealand
Note missionary postings that began before 9 November 2020 and continued after that time are covered by these rules.
For more information see:
## Temporary return from posting
A client (and their partner if any) who left for missionary work before 9 November 2020 may return to New Zealand temporarily (after 9 November 2020) during their period of missionary work (e.g. for a holiday or visit family) and then return to their original missionary posting overseas.
A temporary return to New Zealand during the missionary posting period is not seen as disrupting the posting.
## New posting on or after 9 November 2020
A client who began a missionary posting on or after 9 November 2020 can have it included as a period of residence and presence to qualify for New Zealand Superannuation if they:
- were doing missionary work and
- were ordinarily resident in New Zealand immediately before they left for missionary work overseas and
- were carrying out the missionary work for a charitable entity associated with a religious body
If a client has started a new posting on or after 9 November 2020, even if it is with the same missionary entity, the client must meet the requirements for absences that can be considered resident and present that are in place at that time.

chunks.title: Missionary work for charity under the Charities Act 2005 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Missionary work for charity under the Charities Act 2005
For overseas missionary work that began on or after 9 November 2020 to qualify towards being resident and present in New Zealand, the entity the client is doing work for must be registered in New Zealand as a charitable entity in the Charities Act 2005.
If the entity is not a registered charity, the periods spent overseas as a missionary cannot be counted as residence and presence in New Zealand.
Details of when a charity is registered, and any de-registration or periods of de-registration can be found in the Charities Register.
## Client did overseas missionary work and the entity was registered the entire period
A client left New Zealand on 20 November 2020 and worked overseas as a missionary for 5 years and 8 months.
As the missionary entity was registered as a charity in New Zealand for the period of 5 years and 8 months' work, the missionary can be treated as residence and presence in New Zealand for this period (if the client meets the other qualifications).
## Client did overseas missionary work and the entity was not registered for the entire period
A client left New Zealand on 21 December 2020 and worked as a missionary for 9 years.
The missionary entity did not register as a charitable entity under the Charities Act 2005 until the last 3 years of the client's missionary work.
Only the 3 year period during when the entity was registered as a charity can be treated as residence and presence in New Zealand (if the client meets the other qualifications).
Client did overseas missionary work and entity lost registration during the period
A client left New Zealand for missionary work on 30 January 2021 for an entity that was a registered charity under the Charites Act 2005.
The client worked as a missionary for 11 years, but the entity was de-registered from the Charities Register for the last 2 years of the client's missionary work. Only the first 9 years of the client's work can be treated as residence and presence in New Zealand (if the client meets the other qualifications).

chunks.title: Mobile homes — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Mobile homes
From 9 November 2020, the living alone rate of payment can be paid for clients living in a self-contained mobile home.
What is a mobile home?
A mobile home can include a caravan, house bus or self-driven purpose-built mobile home. To be a self-contained mobile home for living alone rate purposes, the mobile home must:
- contain certain features and
- be reasonably habitable.
Features of a mobile home for living alone rate purposes
To be self-contained for living alone rate purposes, a mobile home must have for the exclusive use of the client adequate areas for:
- day to day living
- sleeping
- preparing and cooking food and
- must also contain: a sinka toilet
- a sink
- a toilet
If the mobile home does not have showering or bathing facilities, the client must have access to these facilities e.g. they use public facilities that are readily available to them.
Mobile home must be reasonably habitable
For a mobile home to be reasonably habitable for living alone rate purposes it must have:
- a fresh water tank or tanks; and
- a waste water tank or tanks
The tanks may from time to time be connected for receiving water and removing waste water but do not require a fulltime connection. The water tanks and waste water tanks support the toilet and sink facilities.
Mobile homes must meet all requirements
A client must live in a mobile home that meets all of the requirements to be able to receive the living alone rate.
Mobile homes that do not have all of these facilities including the water and waste water tanks cannot be considered a self-contained mobile home and the living alone rate cannot be paid.
## Start date for clients living in mobile home
A client living alone in a self-contained mobile home can receive the living alone rate from:
- 9 November 2020 or
- the date the client started living alone in a self-contained mobile home
whichever is the later.

chunks.title: Motels and hotels — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Motels and hotels
Clients living alone in a motel unit or hotel room can receive the single living alone rate as long as all other qualifications are met.

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation and ACC weekly earnings-related compensation — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation and ACC weekly earnings-related compensation
There are some limitations on clients receiving both weekly compensation and New Zealand Superannuation. The limitations are contained in the Accident Compensation Act 2001 and administered by ACC.
The limitations which apply are:
## Earnings-related weekly compensation for 24 months before reaching the qualifying age
A client who was entitled to weekly compensation for 24 months, before reaching the qualifying age for New Zealand Superannuation, is only entitled to receive New Zealand Superannuation once they turn 65.
## Earnings-related weekly compensation less than 24 months before reaching the qualifying age
A client who is entitled to weekly compensation, before reaching the qualifying age for New Zealand Superannuation, is entitled to weekly compensation until they reach the qualifying age for New Zealand Superannuation.
After reaching the qualifying age for New Zealand Superannuation, the client may continue getting weekly compensation for up to 24 months from the date they qualified for weekly compensation. The client can get both New Zealand Superannuation and weekly compensation over this period.
## Earnings-related weekly compensation 12 months before or after reaching the qualifying age
A client is entitled to receive both weekly compensation and New Zealand Superannuation for 24 months when ACC weekly compensation entitlement commences:
- within 12 months before their qualifying age for New Zealand Superannuation or
- on or after reaching the qualifying age for New Zealand Superannuation
## Client's paid before the ACC changes on 1 July 2019
Clients who made an election to receive ACC rather than New Zealand Superannuation before 1 July 2019, will still receive only the payment they chose to receive (either New Zealand Superannuation or ACC). There could be clients in this situation up to 30 June 2021.
The weekly compensation payments are treated as income for the purpose of income tested New Zealand Superannuation and Extra Help.

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation grandparented non-qualified partner weekly income example — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation grandparented non-qualified partner weekly income example
Below are examples of calculating the income reduction for weekly income for New Zealand Superannuation clients with a grandparented non-qualified partner.
## Example 1
Weekly gross income
$350.00
Less income allowed before benefit is affected
$160.00
Equals income to calculate reduction with
$190.00
Reduction is 70 cents per $1.00 of income over $160.00 ($190.00 X 0.7)
$133.00 reduction
## Example 2
Weekly gross income
$400.00
Less income allowed before benefit is affected
$160.00
Equals income to calculate reduction with
$240.00
Reduction is 70 cents per $1.00 of income over $160.00 ($240.00 X 0.7)
$168.00 reduction

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation modernisation and simplification changes from 9 November — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation modernisation and simplification changes from 9 November
From 9 November 2020, several changes were made that affect some New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients.
The following changes were effective from 9 November 2020:
- Ending the option to include a non-qualified partner in New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
- Existing couples getting the non-qualified partner rate as at 8 November 2020 are grandparented effective from 9 November 2020
- From 9 November 2020 non-qualified partners who have not been grandparented are able to apply for a main benefit if they need financial assistance
- From 9 November 2020 a non-qualified partner can apply for Emergency Benefit to provide care for their New Zealand Superannuation partner if they would otherwise require hospital care or if they are the principal caregiver of a dependent child under 14
- Extending the Living Alone Rate of Payment to single people who live alone in self-contained mobile homes
- Introducing a new residential concession for people who work overseas as a humanitarian worker for a charitable organisation which allows the periods working overseas to be treated as resident and present in New Zealand
- Amending the residential concession for missionary workers that links the concession to missionary work for organisations that are a New Zealand charity or are closely to aligned to one.
- Exempting the voluntary portion of an overseas pension from the direct deduction policy. The amount of any voluntary portion is treated as income.
- For some couples the excess overseas pension of one partner does not reduce their partner's New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran's Pension and Winter Energy payments.
- Removing deductions for an overseas pension received for a dependent child.
For more information please talk to Helpline.

chunks.title: Obligations — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Obligations
Clients must tell us straight away of any changes in their circumstances or their family's situation that may affect entitlement to New Zealand Superannuation. Clients agree to this by signing the New Zealand Superannuation application form.
Examples of changes and how to deal with these can be found in Changes and Reviews.
## Partners aged 16 to 19 years old
When a young partner (aged 16 to 19 years old) is included as the grandparented non-qualified partner of a client receiving New Zealand Superannuation, they have youth activity obligations.

chunks.title: Partner not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Partner not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand
A client whose partner is not permanently resident or is unlawfully resident in New Zealand can be paid at the single rate of New Zealand Superannuation in some circumstances.
There are some exceptions for more information see:
- Partner's residence status
## Partner lives overseas
If the partner is not in New Zealand and chooses to live overseas with no intention of moving permanently to New Zealand, and the client and partner are still a couple, the client should be paid the married rate of New Zealand Superannuation.

chunks.title: Partner's residence status — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Partner's residence status
When a client has a partner and they do not qualify for New Zealand Superannuation in their own right, their partner's immigration status must be checked as it can affect the client's rate of payment.
When the partner is present in New Zealand unlawfully or is in New Zealand on a temporary entry class visa, the rate of payment for the client is the single rate of New Zealand Superannuation.

chunks.title: Payment — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Payment
New Zealand Superannuation is paid fortnightly on a Tuesday.
In general, payment must be made directly to the client. However, when there is good cause, the client's New Zealand Superannuation can be paid to another person, agent or institution.
For more information see:
- Core policy Redirection of benefit payment
It is a condition of receiving New Zealand Superannuation that the client provides a bank account number.
MSD can request the client or their partner who is included in the New Zealand Superannuation (grandparented non-qualified partner) to provide an IRD number or evidence of their IRD number.
For more information see:
- IRD number for client or partner who is included (grandparented non-qualified partner)
## Rate of payment
The rate of New Zealand Superannuation depends on if the client is:
- single, living alone
- single, living in shared accommodation
- married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, and their partner can receive New Zealand Superannuation in their own right
- married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, and they have a grandparented non-qualified partner included in their payment or
- married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, and they have a non-qualifying partner who is not included in their payment
- eligible to receive or receiving an overseas benefit or pension

chunks.title: Principal place of residence — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Principal place of residence
To get the single living alone rate, the principal place of residence must be a:
- house or flat
- boat or craft moored within New Zealand territory
- hotel room
- motel unit
- room in a boarding house
- unit of accommodation in a caravan park or
- a self-contained mobile home

chunks.title: Proof of absence — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Proof of absence
If the client cannot provide proof of their arrivals and/or departures, you can accept the client's statement where they say they have not been absent from New Zealand since their first date of arrival unless:
- the statement is doubted
- the arrival date affects the date of commencement or
- the referees declaration shows an undeclared absence which would affect the date of commencement

chunks.title: Proof of residence — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: When a client provides proof of residence for their New Zealand Superannuation application. All documents should be originals. Photocopies and/or documents that have been changed in any way cannot be accepted. When the client (or partner) cannot provide proof, or the proof is unclear, they should be asked to get proof of their residential status from Immigration New Zealand (for residence class visa) or the Department of Internal Affairs (for citizenship). Proof of citizenship and/or residence in New Zealand can be: - Australian passportAustralian citizens and permanent residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand as they are deemed to hold a residence class visa. Their date of entry into New Zealand is generally not recorded, but can be requested from Immigration New Zealand / New Zealand Customs by the client. When possible, supporting evidence should be provided, such as tenancy agreements, bank statements or old utility bills, to show that the client is ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date of application. - British nationals (travel information)British nationals who arrived in New Zealand before 2 April 1974, were allowed to enter New Zealand to reside and may be unable to provide proof of their residence information if they do not have a passport.Immigration New Zealand may have travel entries and exits to and from New Zealand for these people from the late 1980s. The client should be able to provide New Zealand school, work, or tax records to support their claim about when they arrived in New Zealand, and the length of time they have lived here. - Certificate of ConfirmationThis is a certificate issued to confirm the holder is a New Zealand citizen by birth, descent, or Grant of Citizenship.British nationals, who immigrated to New Zealand before 1948 (and who resided in New Zealand for all of 1948) were made New Zealand citizens in 1949. These clients are likely to have a Certificate of Confirmation - Certificate of RegistrationA child born outside New Zealand (to a parent who is a New Zealand citizen) may be a New Zealand citizen from birth. However, the child must apply for a Certificate of Registration to confirm their New Zealand citizenship. - Grant of CitizenshipPeople who have permanent residence, may (generally after 5 years residence in New Zealand) apply for a Grant of Citizenship. They must meet the conditions of the Grant. - Letter of confirmation of permanent residence from Immigration New Zealand - Local official confirmation of residence in the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau

chunks.title: Proof of residence — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: - New Zealand birth certificateA person born in New Zealand is only considered a New Zealand citizen by birth if:they were born in New Zealand before 1 January 2006 orafter 1 January 2006 when: one parent is a New Zealand citizen orone parent had a visa allowing them to reside in New Zealand - they were born in New Zealand before 1 January 2006 or - after 1 January 2006 when: one parent is a New Zealand citizen orone parent had a visa allowing them to reside in New Zealand - one parent is a New Zealand citizen or - one parent had a visa allowing them to reside in New Zealand - New Zealand passportTo hold a New Zealand passport, you must be a New Zealand citizen. - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence class visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009 - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987

chunks.title: Qualifications — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
The qualifications for New Zealand Superannuation are age and residency.
For more information on these qualifications see:
- Age
- Residency
In some situations, a client can get New Zealand Superannuation and ACC weekly compensation for up to 24 months, see:
- New Zealand Superannuation and ACC weekly earnings-related compensation

chunks.title: Qualified client with a partner in long-term residential care — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Qualified client with a partner in long-term residential care
A client who is living in the community and whose partner is in long-term residential care in a rest home or hospital, can get the single sharing accommodation or the single living alone rate of New Zealand Superannuation.
The rate of payment will depend on if they:
- share their accommodation with any person aged 18 years or over, other than a dependent child or a visitor who stays more than 13 weeks in any 26 week period or
- meet all the qualifications for the single living alone rate
## Partner is in long-term residential care in a rest home or hospital at the client's entitlement date
The single sharing accommodation or single living alone rate can be paid from the date the New Zealand Superannuation commences when the partner is in long-term residential care in a rest home or hospital at the client's entitlement date.
## Client is already getting New Zealand Superannuation when partner enters long-term residential care in a rest-home or hospital
The single sharing accommodation rate or single living alone rate can be paid from the date the partner enters long-term residential care in a rest home or hospital.
## Special Disability Allowance
Special Disability Allowance can be paid to the client in the community to help with extra costs due to their partner being in long-term residential care and their partner is getting Residential Care Subsidy.
## Rate of payment for partner in care
There is no change to the rate of payment for the partner in care, they continue to get the half married, civil union or de facto rate of New Zealand Superannuation.
