chunks.title: Reciprocal Agreements — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Reciprocal Agreements
New Zealand has social security agreements with several countries.
Under these agreements, residence and/or periods of contributions to their social security schemes in one of the following countries can be regarded as residence and presence in New Zealand

chunks.title: Refugees and protected persons — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: A refugee or a protected person who first became resident and present in New Zealand before the age of 45 will need to meet the standard residence and presence requirement for their date of birth. Refugees or protected persons who first became resident and present in New Zealand from the age of 45 may have a different residence requirement to other New Zealanders. This will depend on their date of birth and the age they first became resident and present in New Zealand. Refugees and protected persons may be able to use periods of residence and presence and/or contributions to a social security scheme in a Reciprocal Agreement country to meet the residence and presence requirement.

chunks.title: Resident and present in New Zealand from the ages of 45 to 54 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: For a refugee or protected person who first became resident and present in New Zealand from the age of 45 to 54 years (inclusive), the total time they will need to meet the residential requirement is determined by the relevant date that applies to them. The relevant date means: - the date the client first became both resident and present in New Zealand, regardless of when they became a recognised refugee or protected person Dual calculations need to be completed to determine the residency requirement that applies. These are: - the difference in days from the relevant date to the date the client turns 65 (both dates inclusive) and - the number of years a client needs to meet the standard residence and presence requirement in New Zealand based on their date of birth The lesser of these 2 calculations will be the total time needed by this client to meet the residence and presence requirement.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Nathan, aged 48 years and 5 months, arrives in New Zealand on 1 March 2016 as a quota refugee. His date of birth is 1 October 1967 and he became a recognised refugee on 1 March 2016. The difference in days from the relevant date to the date Nathan turns 65 The required years Nathan needs to meet the residence and presence in New Zealand based on the date of birth 1 March 2016 to 1 October 2032 = 6,059 days For a person born between 1 July 1967 and 30 June 1969 = 15 years MSD applies the lower time requirement meaning Nathan needs 15 years to meet the residence and presence in New Zealand required based on his date of birth.

chunks.title: Example 2 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Kira, aged 48 years and 2 months, arrives in New Zealand on 1 June 2025, seeking asylum on arrival. Her date of birth is 1 April 1977 and she became a recognised protected person on 1 June 2026. The difference in days from the relevant date to the date Kira turns 65 The required years Kira needs to meet the residence and presence in New Zealand based on the date of birth 1 June 2025 to 1 April 2042 = 6,149 days For a person born between 1 July 1975 and 30 June 1977 = 19 years MSD applies the lower time requirement meaning Kira requires 16.84 years to meet the residence and presence in New Zealand required, based on the difference in days from the relevant date to the date before she turns 65.

chunks.title: Resident and present in New Zealand from the age of 55 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: A refugee or protected person who first became resident and present in New Zealand from 55 years old or over (inclusive) must: - have been resident and present in New Zealand for 10 years from the age of 20 and - have been resident and present in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau or a combination of these, for at least 5 years from the age of 50 and - be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (i.e. not be in New Zealand unlawfully, on a temporary entry visa or a temporary permit) or - be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (e.g. Australian citizens or residents) and - be ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date of application (except when the client is applying from the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau under Special Portability) If a refugee or a protected person does not meet the residency qualifications for New Zealand Superannuation or has not been granted New Zealand residence, they may be able to get a main benefit. If a refugee or a protected person is not able to get another main benefit, an Emergency Benefit may be considered on the grounds of hardship.

chunks.title: Residence class visa — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Residence class visa
Clients need to have a residence class visa or New Zealand citizenship to get New Zealand Superannuation.
A residence class visa is granted by Immigration New Zealand.
Citizenship is granted by the Department of Internal Affairs.
To get New Zealand Superannuation, a client must:
- have or be deemed to hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- have a residence permit under the Immigration Act 1987 or
- be a British national who arrived in New Zealand before 2 April 1974 or
- be a New Zealand citizen
## Clients without a residence class visa or citizenship
Clients without a residence class visa or New Zealand citizenship cannot get New Zealand Superannuation.
An Emergency Benefit may be paid to some clients who do not have a residence class visa or citizenship e.g. people waiting for their application for for refugee or protected person status to be approved.
For more information see:
- Proof of residence
- Emergency Benefit Clients without permanent residence or citizenship
## Additional information needed
If more information about a client's residence status is needed, MSD must get consent from the client to contact Immigration New Zealand or the client should get the information themselves.
If additional information on the client's residence status is not provided the application must be declined.
MSD cannot collect or reveal information about a client's application without their consent.

chunks.title: Residency — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: A client's total residence and presence in New Zealand is used to decide whether they qualify for New Zealand Superannuation. The number of years a client must have lived in New Zealand to qualify for New Zealand Superannuation depends on their date of birth.

chunks.title: Clients who turn 65 before 1 July 2024 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: To qualify for New Zealand Superannuation for people who turn 65 before 1 July 2024, a client must: - have been resident and present in New Zealand for 10 years from the age of 20 and - have been resident and present in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau, or a combination of these, for 5 years from the age of 50 and - be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (i.e. not be in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or - be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (e.g. Australian citizens or residents) and - be ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date of application (except when the client is applying from the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau under Special Portability) Note if a client needs to use residence and presence in New Zealand after age 50 to meet the 10 year requirement, the same residence and presence can also be used to meet the 5 years residence and presence after age 50. For more information see: - Deciding ordinarily resident in New Zealand

chunks.title: Clients who turn 65 from 1 July 2024 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: To qualify for New Zealand Superannuation from 1 July 2024, a client must: - have been resident and present in New Zealand for 10 years from the age of 20 and - have been resident and present in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau, or a combination of these from the age of 20 for an additional period of up to 10 years depending on their birth date, as it is gradually increasing from 10 years to 20 years See: New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension table for the total time required and - have been resident and present in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau, or a combination of these, for 5 years from the age of 50 and - be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (i.e. not be in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or - be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (e.g. Australian citizens or residents) and - be ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date of application (except when the client is applying from the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau under Special Portability)

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Nathan was born on 1 October 1973 in New Zealand and has never left New Zealand. His date of birth means he needs a total of 10 years resident and present in New Zealand from the age of 20 and an additional 8 years residence and presence in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue, and/or Tokelau from the age of 20. Five of the 18 years residence and presence required must be from the age of 50.

chunks.title: Example 2 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Peti was born on 1 August 1971 in New Zealand and moved to the Cook Islands on 1 September 2001 at the age of 30. At the age of 32, she moved to live in the USA and returned to live in New Zealand at the age of 60. She remained a New Zealand citizen. Her date of birth means she needs a total of 10 years residence and presence in New Zealand from the age of 20, and an additional 7 years residence and presence in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue and/or Tokelau from the age of 20. Five of the 17 years residence and presence required must be from the age of 50.

chunks.title: 5 years residence and presence from the age of 50 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Any time a client is resident and present in New Zealand from the age of 50 may be used towards meeting any of the residence and presence requirements. Any time spent in the Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau from the age of 50, may be used towards meeting the additional years of residence and presence requirement. Example Elise was born on 10 August 1966 in New Zealand and moved to Samoa on 10 August 1996 at the age of 30. When he turned 60, he moved to Tokelau for 5 years before returning to New Zealand on 1 September 2031. He remained a New Zealand citizen. His date of birth means he needs a total of 10 years residence and presence in New Zealand from the age of 20, and an additional 4 years residence and presence in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue, and/or Tokelau from the age of 20. The 5 years Elise spent in Tokelau after the age of 50 can be used towards the additional 4 years residence and presence Elise needs to meet the residency requirements. For more information see:

chunks.title: Does not meet residency qualifications — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: If a client does not meet the residency qualifications for New Zealand Superannuation, they may be able to get a main benefit. If a client is not able to get another main benefit, an Emergency Benefit may be considered on the grounds of hardship to a client who does not meet the residency requirements for New Zealand Superannuation.

chunks.title: For more information about residency see: — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: - Clients with time overseas - Refugees and protected persons - Partner's residence status - Intention to remain permanently - Proof of absence - Proof of residence - Resident and present in New Zealand - Reciprocal Agreements

chunks.title: Resident and present in New Zealand — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: To qualify for New Zealand Superannuation a client must be resident and present in New Zealand for certain periods of time.

chunks.title: Resident — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Resident in New Zealand means: - the client must either make their home in New Zealand and have been living in New Zealand on a permanent basis or - if the client has only recently arrived in New Zealand, they must have the intention to make their home in New Zealand for the foreseeable future. Being resident is not the same as being ordinarily resident in New Zealand. For more information see:

chunks.title: Present — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Present in New Zealand means the client must be physically in New Zealand. For more information see: - What is present

chunks.title: Calculating periods of residence and presence — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: A year is regarded as 365 days (including the days a client arrives in and departs from New Zealand) for the calculation of periods of residence and presence in New Zealand. Residence only includes periods of time a client was lawfully resident and present in New Zealand. Any periods of time present but unlawfully resident in New Zealand (i.e. without a valid visa or permit) are not counted in the calculation of residence and presence in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Examples — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Scenario Was client lawfully resident and present in New Zealand Include period of resident and present in New Zealand for assessment? A client comes to NZ on a temporary entry visa for 3 years, with the intention to live permanently in NZ. The client applies for and is granted NZ citizenship in this time Yes the client was lawfully resident and present in NZ for the 3 years prior to being granted NZ citizenship. Yes include the 3 years in the assessment. A client comes to NZ on a temporary entry visa to complete studies for 2 years, with the intention to return to their country of origin. They return to NZ years later to retire. No although the client was lawfully present in NZ, they were only in NZ to complete studies. No do not include the 2 years in the assessment. A client comes to NZ on a temporary entry visa for 5 years with the intent of settling permanently. The client goes through the process of becoming a permanent resident and is granted a residence class visa which replaces the temporary entry visa. Yes the client was lawfully resident and present in NZ for the 5 years while on a temporary visa, as they intended to remain in New Zealand permanently and worked towards this by applying to become a permanent resident. Yes include the 5 years in the assessment, but do not include any period of time the client was absent from NZ. A person is posted in NZ as a Diplomatic Representative (High Commissioner/Ambassador/Consular/Travelling office staff etc) for their country for 4 years and return to their country of origin after this. 10 years later they return to NZ to retire. No although the client was lawfully present in NZ, they were only in NZ for their employment to complete their diplomatic duties for their country of origin. They had no intent to reside in NZ and would not have been in NZ otherwise. No do not include the 4 years in the assessment. A NZ citizen lives overseas and comes to NZ once a year for 5 months only to visit their family and sightsee in NZ with no intention of living in NZ. They continue to do this right up until their retirement. No although the client was lawfully present in NZ, they were only in NZ as a visitor. They had no intent to reside in NZ during these visits. No do not include any time the client was visiting NZ in the assessment. A NZ citizen is overseas for 5 years completing studies at a theological college, with the intention of returning to NZ once this training is completed.

chunks.title: Examples — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: This client is married and has 2 children. The partner and children remain in their home in NZ during the time the client is overseas completing their studies. Each year for 5 years, the client returns to their partner, children and home in NZ for a 2-month break. Yes although the client only spent a short time in NZ during the 5 years, they demonstrated their close connection with NZ and their time in NZ was not in the nature of a traveller/temporary visitor. It was their intention to return to NZ once the training was completed. Yes include all the 2-month breaks during the 5 years study period the client was in NZ. A NZ citizen lives overseas and comes to NZ once a year for 3 months over the summer only to visit their family with no intention of living in NZ. They have no home in NZ and stay with relatives. They continue to do this right up until their retirement. No although the client was lawfully present in NZ, they were only in NZ as a visitor. They had no intent to reside in NZ on an ongoing basis during these visits. No do not include any time the client was visiting NZ in the assessment A NZ citizen works overseas for 5 years as a contractor for a mining company on a fly-in, fly-out basis. They are billeted by their employer while working and have no property overseas. As they are a contractor, tax is not withheld at source on their earnings. They have tax obligations in New Zealand and the country they work in. Every 2 months for the 5 years, they return to their home in NZ for 2 weeks. During the 2 weeks they spend in NZ every 2 months, they live at home with their partner and child, attend the church they are a member of, and play regular pick-up basketball games with their old team at an indoor sports centre near their home. Yes although the client only spent a short time in NZ during the 5 years, they demonstrated a close connection with NZ, and the time they spent in NZ was of the nature of residence while the time overseas was solely to fulfil their contract obligations and had no residential aspect. It was their intention to return to NZ once the contract ended Yes include all the 2 week breaks in NZ, during the 5 years the client was working overseas. A client who is an overseas citizen comes to NZ for 3 months on a temporary visa to stay with her daughter who has a new-born.

chunks.title: Examples — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: The client has no other family, their intention is to settle in NZ to live with their child and grandchild and they have applied for a residence visa. At the end of the 3 months when the temporary visa expires, the client returns to their country of origin and reapplies for a NZ temporary visa. The visa application process always takes 3 months to finalise. As soon as the temporary visa is granted, the client returns to NZ and leaves when the temporary visa expires to reapply again for a NZ temporary visa. While they are away from NZ, they start the process of selling their house and possessions in preparation for their permanent move to NZ. Yes although the client was here on a temporary visa during all their 3 months trips to NZ, the time they spent here was of the nature of residence while the time overseas was solely so they did not overstay in NZ. Their intention is clear to come to NZ on a permanent basis to be around their family. Yes include all the 3 month periods they were in NZ on a temporary visa over the 5 year period.

chunks.title: Periods of residence and presence in Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: Clients can use residence and presence in the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau, or a combination of these to meet the residence and presence required in New Zealand for 5 years from the age of 50. For clients turning 65 on or after 1 July 2024, the number of years residence and presence required will be based on their date of birth. Generally, a minimum of 10 years residence and presence in New Zealand from the age of 20 is required for clients born before 1 July 1959 and a maximum of 20 years of residence and presence is required for clients born after 30 June 1977. Any combination of residence and presence in the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau can be used by clients to meet any additional residence and presence required above the minimum 10 years resident and present in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Rest home complexes — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Rest home complexes
Clients who live alone in a flat or unit that is part of a rest home complex can receive the single living alone rate if the flat or unit is considered a house or flat.
In particular check:
- whether the client owns the flat or has a licence to occupy it and
- that the flat or unit contains adequate and distinct areas for day to day living and sleeping, and a kitchen with facilities for food preparation, storage and cooking and a sink for washing up
Rest home units that provide limited kitchen facilities, for example a jug, sink and microwave can be considered a house or flat and the client can receive the single living alone rate.
Clients living in a rest home complex and receiving a Residential Care Subsidy cannot receive the single living alone rate.

chunks.title: Retirement Villages — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Retirement Villages
Clients living alone in retirement village units can only receive the single living alone rate if the retirement village unit is a house or flat.
In particular check:
- the client owns or rents the unit or has a licence to occupy it and
- the unit contains adequate and distinct areas for day to day living and sleeping, a kitchen with facilities for food storage, preparation and cooking and a sink with a drinkable water supply

chunks.title: Single clients — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Single clients
There are two rates of payment for single clients. This will depend on whether they meet the definition of living alone or share accommodation.
The client's income is not taken into consideration when assessing the rate of payment. However, if a client is eligible to receive or receiving any overseas benefit or pension the gross amount is generally directly deducted from their New Zealand Superannuation.
For more information see:
- Single sharing accommodation rate
- Single living alone rate
- Definition of living alone
- Payments from overseas Overseas pensions

chunks.title: Single living alone rate — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Single living alone rate
Single New Zealand Superannuation clients (or married or civil union clients who are considered single) who meet the definition of living alone can get the single living alone rate. This higher rate recognises the extra costs for clients maintaining a household on their own.
If the client meets the criteria on their entitlement date, the living alone rate is paid from the date New Zealand Superannuation commences.
The single living alone rate is paid to clients who are:
- getting New Zealand Superannuation
- single (or married or civil union clients who are considered single) and
- living alone in their principal place of residence
The following clients cannot get the single living alone rate:
- clients who do not meet the definition of living alone
- clients living in an institution and
- clients paying private board

chunks.title: Single rate for couples — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: In some circumstances a person who qualifies for New Zealand Superannuation in their own right and who is living apart from their partner, can get the single sharing accommodation or the single living alone rate instead of the married, civil union or de facto rate. In some circumstances a grandparented non-qualified partner, who is physically separated from their partner can get the single sharing accommodation rate of New Zealand Superannuation, or a single rate of Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Couples sharing accommodation — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: A client who has a partner can get the single sharing accommodation rate of New Zealand Superannuation if: - they have separated from their partner because their relationship has ended or - their partner is getting the hospital rate of payment because they have or been in hospital for more than 13 weeks or - their partner is in long-term residential care and - they are sharing their accommodation with any person aged 18 years or over, or a visitor who stays more than 13 weeks in any 26 week period Note the single sharing accommodation rate can be paid from the date the New Zealand Superannuation commences if the client meets the above criteria at their entitlement date.

chunks.title: Relationship has ended — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: For a legally married or civil union couple to be separated there must be a physical separation and an acceptance or recognition by one or both of the partners that the relationship has ended. For a de facto couple to be separated their relationship must no longer be in the nature of marriage or civil union (a relationship in the nature of marriage or civil union means both financial interdependence and emotional commitment are evident).

chunks.title: Couples who are living alone — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: A client living in the community who has a partner can get the single living alone rate of New Zealand Superannuation if: - they have separated from their partner because their relationship has ended - their partner is in prison, when the Ministry of Social Development have decided to regard the client as a single person - their partner is receiving the hospital rate of payment because they have been in hospital for more than 13 weeks or - their partner is in long-term residential care and - they are not sharing their accommodation with any person aged 18 years or over other than a dependent child or a visitor who stays less than 13 weeks in any 26 week period - they meet the other qualifications for the single living alone rate Note the single living alone rate can be paid from the date the New Zealand Superannuation commences if the client meets the above criteria at their entitlement date.

chunks.title: Single sharing accommodation rate — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Single sharing accommodation rate
New Zealand Superannuation single clients (or married or civil union clients who are considered single) get the single sharing accommodation rate if they are sharing their accommodation with:
- any person aged 18 years or over, other than a dependent child
- a visitor who stays for more than 13 weeks in any 26 week period or
- they are living overseas and getting payment under a Reciprocal Agreement or the Portability provisions
Note the single sharing accommodation rate can be paid from the date the New Zealand Superannuation is granted if the client meets the above criteria.

chunks.title: Start date for single living alone rate — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Start date for single living alone rate
The single living alone rate can start from:
- the date the client starts living alone or
- the commencement date of the client's New Zealand Superannuation
whichever is the later.
The earliest date the single living alone rate can be paid is from 2 September 2013.

chunks.title: SWIFTT process - Single rate for partner in the community — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## SWIFTT process - Single rate for partner in the community
In order to pay the single sharing accommodation rate of New Zealand Superannuation you will need to:
- add the rate of payment code 52 in the NDTA screen for the client in the community and reassess in the SPBR screen
- issue the client the SWIFTT letter
- complete a client event note (see living alone template)
## Single living alone rate
In order to pay the single living alone rate you will need to:
- go to NDTA screen for the 'In community' partner
- fill in the living alone fields - which are: living alone (Y/N)Effective date DD/MM/YYAccommodation arrangement (code from Codes screen)SPBR (if required)BDR (if required)
- living alone (Y/N)
- Effective date DD/MM/YY
- Accommodation arrangement (code from Codes screen)
- SPBR (if required)
- BDR (if required)
Note that where the client has a partner in hospital (as opposed to residential care) this is an Accommodation Arrangement code in its own right.
- issue the client the SWIFTT letter
- complete client event note (see template)
## Rate of payment for partner in care
There is no change for the partner in care, they continue to receive the half married, civil union or de facto rate of New Zealand Superannuation.

chunks.title: IRD number for client or partner who is included — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: MSD may make a written request for evidence of an IRD number for a client who is being paid New Zealand Superannuation. MSD can also request evidence of an IRD number for a partner who is included in the New Zealand Superannuation payment (grandparented non-qualified partner).

chunks.title: Setting or extending the timeframe for providing evidence — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: MSD must provide the client or grandparented non-qualified partner with a minimum of 10 working days to provide IRD number evidence that has been requested in writing. MSD can extend the 10 working day period (in writing) if the client or partner has a reasonable explanation for requiring more than 10 days to provide evidence of their IRD number. This includes considering factors outside the client or partner’s control that cause delays, including, but not limited to: - client or partner has a family emergency that caused a delay - processing delays with an external agency (e.g., Inland Revenue, Department of Internal Affairs, etc) - client or partner does not speak English as a first language and has difficulty navigating evidence requirements - client or partner has limited access to the internet, a device, or their local service centre - client or partner has a physical or intellectual disability that makes accessing services difficult - client or partner is injured, disabled, or has a medical condition that makes accessing services difficult.

chunks.title: Notice following an unsuccessful match — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a client or partner's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the client or partner (in writing) to provide evidence of their IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include an notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the client or partner a minimum of 10 working days to provide their IRD number evidence or the client's assistance must be suspended. Example Isla is receiving New Zealand Superannuation and MSD holds an IRD number on record. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Isla's IRD number. MSD provides 10 working days in writing, for Isla to provide evidence their IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Isla already having an IRD number - Isla not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD must suspend assistance if evidence of IRD number is not received — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: MSD must suspend all taxable and/or income tested assistance the client is getting, including their New Zealand Superannuation, if evidence of an IRD number is not provided within 10 working days from the written request, or extended period if this has been applied. If the partner has not provided evidence of their IRD number, the partner's taxable and/or income tested assistance must be suspended. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance. Example Koa is receiving New Zealand Superannuation and MSD does not have an IRD number on record for Koa. MSD sends a written request giving 10 working days for Koa to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD receives no response to this request. MSD suspends all of Koa's taxable and/or income tested assistance because Koa has not supplied MSD with evidence of their IRD number within the timeframe provided.

chunks.title: IRD evidence may not be requested in some circumstances — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - significant factors, that are outside the client's or partner's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number (e.g. a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence), and - the client needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided or - there are significant factors related to a health, injury or disability that are outside the client or partner's control that prevent them from providing evidence of an IRD number, and - an agent cannot be appointed to act on the client or partner's behalf. MSD can determine a later point to request the evidence of the IRD number. Example Sienna is 67 and receiving New Zealand Superannuation. Sienna's partner (Sara) is Sienna's agent and acts on Sienna's behalf with MSD. Sara is not a recognised agent for Sienna for Inland Revenue. Sienna has an IRD number that results in a no match when MSD runs the IRD number validation API. MSD requests evidence of Sienna's IRD number. Sienna has a serious head injury, is unconscious and expected to be in hospital for at least 8 weeks. Sienna is not able to give consent to appoint Sara as an agent for Inland Revenue to request IRD number evidence due to their injury. MSD can request this information later when Sienna's situation has changed. Note there is different guidance for requesting an IRD number or evidence of an IRD number when a client is applying for New Zealand Superannuation.

chunks.title: Transfer from another benefit — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Transfer from another benefit
If the client is receiving a benefit, New Zealand Superannuation can start from the day the payment of the previous benefit stops. This will usually be the day the client meets the qualifications for New Zealand Superannuation.
When New Zealand Superannuation is granted, the first payment covers the period from the commencement date to the day payment is made.

chunks.title: Treatment of periods of absence for residential qualification — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Treatment of periods of absence for residential qualification
Some types of absences from New Zealand can be counted as residence and presence in New Zealand for the residency qualification.
The types of absences are:
- special medical or surgical treatment (generally if treatment is necessary and unavailable in New Zealand)
- vocational training (generally only if training is unavailable in New Zealand)
- seamen serving on a ship registered or owned in New Zealand, and engaged in trading to and from New Zealand
- overseas services in forces as a member of the naval, military or air force of any Commonwealth country. This includes war service as a member of any organisation attached to any of these forces, eg, YMCA, church, Red Cross
- full-time voluntary work (humanitarian work) this must be carried out for an entity that is: a charitable entity with its main function the giving of aid and assistance to less advantaged communities in one or more countries) oraffiliated with or closely related to, a charitable entity that has as its main function the giving of aid and assistance to less advantaged communities in one or more countries
- a charitable entity with its main function the giving of aid and assistance to less advantaged communities in one or more countries) or
- affiliated with or closely related to, a charitable entity that has as its main function the giving of aid and assistance to less advantaged communities in one or more countries
- any capacity as an accredited volunteer appointed by Volunteer Service Abroad
- missionary work (defined as including 'the advancement of religion or education and the maintenance, care or relief of orphans, or the aged, infirm, sick or needy')
- when a client has worked overseas, and their New Zealand income tax (PAYE) was paid to Inland Revenue New Zealand (or it was withheld by the employer but failed to pay it to Inland Revenue New Zealand and the client did not contribute to the employer's failure to pay the tax)

chunks.title: Unlawful residence — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Unlawful residence
To reside in New Zealand lawfully the client must either:
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- be an Australian citizen or
- hold a New Zealand passport or
- hold an Australian passport or
- hold a visa issued under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be deemed to hold a visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) or
- be a British national who arrived in New Zealand prior to 2 April 1974 or
- hold a permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987
If the client does not fulfil one of the above, the client is deemed to be in New Zealand unlawfully.
Any periods of unlawful residence are excluded when calculating the clients' period of residence and presence.

chunks.title: Visitors — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Visitors
A client can receive the single living alone rate if they have a temporary visitor who stays less than a total of 13 weeks (91 days) in any 26-week period.
## Note
If the visitor intends to stay for less than 13 weeks, the client can receive the single living alone rate.
If the visitor intends to stay less than 13 weeks, but subsequently changes their mind and stays longer, the rate of payment should be reduced to the single sharing accommodation rate from the beginning of the next pay period at the end of the 13 week period, or the pay period after the client advises that their intention has changed.
If the visitor intends to stay longer than 13 weeks, they are not considered to be a temporary visitor and the client receives the single sharing accommodation rate from the beginning of the pay period after the visitor arrives.
## Visits by the client
If a client receiving single living alone rate goes on holiday or visits another person temporarily, the payment can continue if the client intends to resume living in their principal place of residence on their return.
If the client has moved away from their principal place of residence and is staying with other people for long periods of time or on a permanent basis, they will no longer be entitled to the single living alone rate, if:
- their new residence does not meet the definition of principal place of residence or
- they do not meet the definition of living alone

chunks.title: Voluntary work for charitable entity under the Charities Act 2005 — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Voluntary work for charitable entity under the Charities Act 2005
For any absences overseas for voluntary work on or after 1 July 2005 to be counted for residence and presence in New Zealand, the charitable entity must be registered in New Zealand under the Charities Act 2005.
If the entity is not a registered charity, the periods are not considered qualifying voluntary work and cannot be treated as residence and presence in New Zealand.
Charities can be de-registered from the Charities Act 2005.
Details of when a charity is registered, and any de-registration or periods of de-registration can be found in the Charities Register.

chunks.title: What is present? — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## What is present?
Generally, to be present in New Zealand, the client must be physically in New Zealand, including New Zealand's territorial waters.
The client must be lawfully resident as well as present in New Zealand to meet the residence qualification.
## Period of absence not counted
Generally, any periods of absence from New Zealand are not counted as being present in New Zealand and are excluded in the assessment of the New Zealand Superannuation residency qualifications.
There are exceptions when a period of absence may count as being resident and present in New Zealand.

chunks.title: What is resident? — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## What is resident?
There are certain criteria clients need to meet to be resident for New Zealand Superannuation.
To be resident in New Zealand for New Zealand Superannuation a client must either:
- have made their home in New Zealand and been living in New Zealand on a permanent basis or
- at the time they arrived in New Zealand, it was their intention to make their home in New Zealand
Being resident is not the same as a client's immigration status under the Immigration Act 2009.
## Client makes their home in New Zealand
In many cases, it will be clear that a client was resident in New Zealand as they will have lived in New Zealand on a permanent basis for many years.
When it may not be so clear, the following could be considered:
- the reason the client was in New Zealand
- if the client intended to make their home in New Zealand
- if the client had a fixed abode in New Zealand
- if the client owned property in New Zealand
- if the client had frequent absences from New Zealand: if the absences were prolonged or repeatedwhat the reason were for those absences
- if the absences were prolonged or repeated
- what the reason were for those absences
- what was the client's involvement with New Zealand society, such as (but not limited to): community activitiesemploymentmembership of clubs orlocal churches
- community activities
- employment
- membership of clubs or
- local churches
Residence only includes periods of time when a client was lawfully resident and present in New Zealand.
Any periods of time present but unlawfully resident in New Zealand (i.e. without a valid visa or permit) are not counted in the calculation of the time of being resident and present in New Zealand.

chunks.title: When grandparenting ends — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## When grandparenting ends
Couples getting the New Zealand Superannuation grandparented non-qualified partner rate on or after 9 November 2020 will no longer qualify for the grandparented rate in any of the following situations:
- the non-qualified partner starts getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension in their own right
- the qualified partner chooses not to continue getting the grandparented non-qualified partner rate
- the qualified partner, with or without the non-qualified partner, is absent from New Zealand and no longer qualifies for New Zealand Superannuation on or after 9 November 2020
- the qualified partner is in custody, in prison or on remand on or after 9 November 2020 and does not qualify for ongoing payments of New Zealand Superannuation for the period of imprisonment
Once the grandparented non-qualified partner rate ends, the qualifying partner cannot include a non-qualifying partner again.
Note a client getting the New Zealand Superannuation grandparented non-qualified partner rate can transfer to Veteran's Pension if they qualify and include their grandparented non-qualified partner in their Veteran's Pension payments.
## Client does not respond to Mandatory Review and New Zealand Superannuation is cancelled
If a couple's New Zealand Superannuation (with grandparented non-qualified partner included) is cancelled because the client did not respond to the Mandatory Review, the non-qualified partner can be re-included as a grandparented non-qualified partner if the qualifying partner reapplies for New Zealand Superannuation.

chunks.title: Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings — main benefits > new zealand superannuation
chunks.text:
## Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
A client applying for a benefit including New Zealand Superannuation can be considered resident and present in New Zealand during periods of overseas employment when:
- their employer (or other relevant person) deducted PAYE or source deductions from their wages and
- paid them to Inland Revenue New Zealand
A partner who was with the client while they were working overseas can also be treated as resident and present in New Zealand for the same periods.
The residential concession does not apply to people who are self-employed and working overseas.
Clients should provide proof of the periods they were employed overseas and that PAYE or source deductions were paid to the New Zealand Inland Revenue during these periods.
Note if the employer (or other relevant person) has deducted the tax but failed to pay it to Inland Revenue, and if the client did not contribute to the employer's failure to pay the tax, the period of employment overseas can still be regarded as residence and presence in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Additional care arrangements — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: To get Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit as a either a principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver, the caregiver must have primary responsibility for the day-to-day care of the child, even if they make 'additional care arrangements' for the child. Additional care arrangements are informal and/or voluntary arrangements for someone else to temporarily care for a child. In these situations, the child's main caregiver who is getting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit retains the primary responsibility for the child (including financial support or making contributions towards the child's costs while they are staying with someone else). Additional care arrangements include (but are not limited to): - someone else looking after children for the weekend or school holidays - a child being billeted or hosted by another family or boarding school arrangements - periods of respite care or temporary illness for the ordinary caregiver - additional arrangements to support a caregiver's employment opportunities, such as informal childcare arrangements - family arrangements to look after a child where there has been no breakdown between the child and their caregiver who receives Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit A caregiver who is providing additional care arrangements is not an eligible caregiver, and therefore cannot get Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit for that child. This includes other care situations where the period of care is temporary but Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit qualifications have not been met.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: Kaisa is 8 years old and has been living with Tim and Nina for 2 years. Kaisa’s mother died when she was 6 years old and her dad suffers from a serious illness which means he is unable to care for her. Tim receives Orphans Benefit to support Kaisa as her principal caregiver. Kaisa is best friends with Missy who lives across the road from Tim and Nina. Missy’s family are going to Ūawa/Tolaga Bay for the school holidays at the end of the year and they invited Kaisa to join them. Tim and Nina agree for Kaisa to go with Missy’s family and Kaisa is going to be away for almost 6 weeks. Tim continues to get Orphans Benefit for Kaisa while she is away, as he retains the primary responsibility for her day-to-day care. Missy’s family is providing additional care arrangements for Kaisa, so they would not qualify to get Orphans Benefit for her.

chunks.title: Example 2 — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: Sam is caring for his 7-year-old nephew Tana, who has been living with him for the past month. Tana's mother recently died, and his father is unable to care for him because of a serious long-term disability. Sam is caring for Tana temporarily until the whānau decides who is best placed to raise him. Sam is receiving Orphans Benefit for Tana as he qualifies as his principal temporary caregiver. Every summer Tana goes to stay with his kuia (grandmother), who lives in Ōtepoti/Dunedin. Tana's kuia lives near their marae and it is a good opportunity for Tana to learn about his whakapapa and be immersed in Te Ao Māori. The whānau agrees it would be a good for Tana to visit again this year, so Sam arranges for Tana to stay with his kuia after Christmas for a month. Even though Tana will be away for a month, Sam keeps the primary responsibility for his day-to-day care and continues to get Orphans Benefit for the period Tana is staying with his kuia. Tana's kuia is providing additional care arrangements, so would not qualify for Orphans Benefit.

chunks.title: Age — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Age
To get an Orphans Benefit or an Unsupported Childs Benefit, the caregiver must be aged 18 years or older.
Note all Unsupported Childs Benefit grants must be approved by a manager client service delivery.

chunks.title: Arthur Hall Fletcher Trust — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Arthur Hall Fletcher Trust
This Trust can provide payments for the assistance and advancement of orphaned girls in New Zealand.
When the basic qualification for the Orphans Benefit is met, the case manager must advise the caregiver that this Trust exists.
Payments from the Trust are treated as income for Orphans Benefit purposes.
The caregiver can contact Public Trust - Charitable Services team who administer the Trust for information regarding the types of assistance available under the Trust. They can be contacted by:
- email funding@publictrust.co.nz or
- phone 0800 371 471
Note Arthur Hall Fletcher Trust determines who meets the entry criteria for their services including any specific rules relating to sex or gender.

chunks.title: Bank — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Bank
An appropriate bank is:
- a private savings bank, a trustee savings bank, or The Co-operative Bank Limited (formerly the Public Service Investment Society, or PSIS)
- a registered bank which on the 31st March 1987 was a trading bank or
- any other registered bank or a building society approved by the Minister after consultation with the Minister of Finance
For more information see:
- Processing standards Bank account [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Breakdown in the child's family cannot be established — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Breakdown in the child's family cannot be established
If a breakdown in the child's family cannot be established the caregiver cannot get Unsupported Child's Benefit. The caregiver may wish to:
- ask the child's parent to contribute financially to the care and support of the child
- apply for Child Support through Inland Revenue or
- request the child is included in their benefit
For the child to be included in the caregiver's benefit, the caregiver must meet all of the qualifications and the child must meet the definition of a dependent child.
Generally, periods of temporary care do not meet the definition of dependent child.

chunks.title: Breakdown in the child's family — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: In all cases of Unsupported Child's Benefit MSD must be satisfied that a breakdown in the child's family has occurred. The parents (natural, adoptive and step-parents) have the responsibility to provide care and financially support the child. A family breakdown results in both parents unwilling or unable to provide care and financially support their child. Note 'Child's family' definition refers to immediate family and does not include extended family such as grandparents, uncles and aunts. To determine whether a family breakdown has occurred, MSD must obtain the following information from the applicant: - circumstances of the breakdown between the parents (what happened?) - circumstances of the breakdown between each parent and the child (what happened?) - details of the financial situation of each parent (why are they unable to support their child?) - details about the care arrangement with the caregiver (how long is the child remaining with the caregiver?) - details about on-going contact between each parent and the child (what contact arrangements are there for the child?) It is important that MSD records all the information from the applicant in their own words on the Unsupported Child's Benefit Interview Sheet as this information will assist MSD to determine eligibility.

chunks.title: Care and protection concerns — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: When considering whether a family breakdown has occurred it is important to consider any possible care and protection concerns for a child or young person. If MSD believes any child has been, or is likely to be harmed (physically, emotionally or sexually), ill-treated, abused, neglected, deprived or MSD has concerns about the wellbeing of the child, the case must be referred to Oranga Tamariki. In all other circumstances an applicant must be referred to an Independent Assessment Provider for a family breakdown assessment.

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency involvement — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: At the interview with the caregiver MSD must find out whether there has been any involvement with Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency. MSD can obtain proof of a breakdown from: - a Family Group Conference conducted by Oranga Tamariki (or other authorised agency) or - if there has been no involvement with Oranga Tamariki (or other authorised agency) a family meeting that has been conducted by MSD or Court Order At the interview with the caregiver find out whether there has been any involvement with Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency.

chunks.title: Authorised agency — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: An authorised agency could include, for example: - Barnardos - Ngāpuhi Iwi Social Services - Hauraki Māori Trust Board - The Lifewise Trust - Wesley Wellington Mission - The Mount Cargill Trust - Nelson Marlborough District Health Board - Presbyterian Support Southland If it is unclear whether an agency is an authorised agency, check with the local Oranga Tamariki office.

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency documentation — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: Where there has been Oranga Tamariki involvement and a Family Group Conference held, MSD must obtain copies of the relevant Oranga Tamariki documents from the caregiver. Note the caregiver may not have a copy of the Family Group Conference outcome unless they are directly affected by a Family Group Conference decision or plan, or if the co-ordinator considers that they have a genuine and proper interest in the matter. As an alternative to a Family Group Conference record, there may have been a hui or cultural service meeting that discussed other matters relevant to this child and their family. In these situations, only an extract of the relevant decisions of the hui or meeting is required. The extract will still need to be approved and signed by a social worker or an elder of the iwi or cultural service who attended the meeting. When MSD has proof of a Family Group Conference, a decision must be made based on the information provided. However, just because a Family Group Conference has been completed does not mean a breakdown has occurred.

chunks.title: Caregiver's income — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Caregiver's income
The income and assets of the caregiver do not affect payment of:
- Orphans Benefit
- Unsupported Childs Benefit

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances
Caregivers must tell us straight away of any changes in their circumstances or their family's situation that may affect entitlement to Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit. Caregivers agree to this by signing the Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit application form.
Examples of changes in circumstances and how to deal with these can be found in:
- Changes and Reviews

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
The child (that Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid for) can be temporarily absent from New Zealand and continue to get payment for the first 28 days of an absence if it does not affect the caregiver or child's eligibility for Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit.
When the child remains in New Zealand and the caregiver is temporarily absent from New Zealand, Orphan's Benefit and Unsupported Child's Benefit payments can continue to be paid. The child must continue to meet the definition of dependent child and the caregiver must continue to be the eligible caregiver.
## Exceptions
- When the caregiver qualifies for Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit but they have not been resident and present in New Zealand for a continuous period of 12 months at any time, payment must stop for any period the child is absent from New Zealand.
- When the caregiver and child are going to live or intend to live in a country which New Zealand has a reciprocal agreement with Orphan's Benefit, payments may continue for longer than 28 days. Caregivers have an obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand.
All caregivers getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit must advise MSD before they leave New Zealand. If the caregiver does not advise MSD prior to their and/or the child's (that Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid for) international travel, their benefit payments will stop from the day after they leave New Zealand.
## Mandatory Review while overseas
Caregivers getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit who have temporarily left New Zealand must still respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date.
Temporary absence from New Zealand (e.g. personal travel) does not pause or defer the Mandatory Review.
Caregivers must contact MSD before their review date to talk about their situation if they are unable to respond to their review or if they need more time to do it.

chunks.title: Action on advice of departure — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Action on advice of departure
MSD must look at the circumstances of the absence from and subsequent return to New Zealand to decide when to recommence the benefit and when to treat it as a new application.
When a caregiver contacts MSD to advise that they or the child (that Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid for) intends to travel overseas, MSD should obtain the following information:
- date of departure (flight numbers if possible)
- date of return (flight numbers if possible)
- whether the child is remaining in New Zealand
## Benefit payment to continue
If the child (that the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid for) remains in New Zealand while the caregiver is overseas, benefit payment can continue as long as they continue to meet the qualifications.
If the caregiver or child has not returned on the agreed date, their benefit will stop from the day after their expected date of return.
Where payment of benefit continues for the first 28 days of absence, and the child intends to be absent for more than 28 days, the benefit will stop from the 29th day of absence.
## Benefit payment will not continue
Where payment will not continue for a period of absence, the benefit will stop from the day after departure.

chunks.title: Action on return to New Zealand — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Action on return to New Zealand
MSD needs to look at the circumstances of the caregiver's or the child's (that Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid for) absence from and subsequent return to New Zealand to decide when to recommence their benefit and when to treat it as a new application.
MSD needs to consider the following:
- the caregiver's intention at the time of the departure for example, did they cancel their benefit before leaving New Zealand because they did not intend to return?
- did the caregiver and/or the child remain ordinarily resident during the period of absence?
- the length of time that they have been absent
- the reason for the absence
- have their circumstances changed significantly during their absence?
- is the caregiver eligible to have their benefit backdated to the day after their departure date or date of return?
## Payment can recommence
When a caregiver and/or the child (that Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid for) returns to New Zealand on or before the 29th day (where continued payment of benefit was allowed) their benefit can recommence without any break in payment.
Generally, for other short periods of absence (where continued payment was not approved and the benefit was not paid while the caregiver and/or child was absent) the benefit payments can recommence, if they are eligible, from:
- the date the caregiver and/or child returned to New Zealand as long as they contact MSD within 14 days of their return or
- the date they contacted MSD to advise they and/or the child have returned if more than 14 days after date of return
## New application
In all other circumstances consider whether a new application is needed from the caregiver after reviewing the circumstances above.

chunks.title: Caregiver dies — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Caregiver dies
When a caregiver who was getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit dies, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit can continue to be paid for up to 28 days after the date of death.
MSD will need to find out what care arrangements have been made for the child. The new caregiver may meet the qualifications for Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit, or the child may be able to be included as a dependent child if the new caregiver is getting a main benefit.
## Mandatory Reviews
There are no Mandatory Reviews of Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit when the caregiver has died.
## Child turns 18
When a caregiver has died, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit will not stop when the child turns 18 during the continuation of payment period.

chunks.title: Caregiver or child dies before benefit granted or reviewed — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Caregiver or child dies before benefit granted or reviewed
Where a caregiver or child dies before a decision is made on an application or review for Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit you can continue the application or review process as if the caregiver or child had not died.

chunks.title: Change in age — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Change in age
A child's age may affect:
- the rate of Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit payable and
- whether the child is still a dependent child
Note a change in a child’s age may affect a client's obligations (and those of their partner, if applicable), depending on what other financial assistance they are getting and the obligations that apply.
## Child turns 18
When a child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and can no longer be included in their caregiver's payments unless they are continuing in education and are not financially independent.

chunks.title: Change of address — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Change of address
When a caregiver advises that they have changed their address it is important to check that the move does not affect their entitlement to Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit.
If the caregiver is receiving Extra help or any other benefit this may also need to be reviewed to take into account their new circumstances.
The change of address may also indicate a change in the caregiver's circumstances.
Examples of changes that may affect entitlement are:
- the child or children may have returned to live with their parents
- children have come into or left the client's care

chunks.title: Change of caregiver — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text: To get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit the caregiver must be an eligible caregiver. If the child goes to stay with someone else, MSD needs to establish if the caregiver is still an eligible caregiver, or if the change is an additional care arrangement.

chunks.title: Additional care arrangement — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text: If the change in the caregiver is temporary, for example, school holidays or a short stay in hospital, the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit can continue to be paid to the caregiver, provided contact and support of the child is maintained and the caregiver continues to be the principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver.

chunks.title: Change in care arrangements — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text: If the change of caregiver is long term, and the caregiver no longer meets the definition of principal caregiver or principal temporary caregiver, the benefit should stop. The new caregiver should be invited to apply for Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit in their own right. Note if a caregiver is a principal caregiver (i.e. expected to care for the child for at least 12 months) and the child leaves the caregiver's care before the year, do not take any action to establish a debt. If there is any evidence to suggest that the principal caregiver intended to deliberately defraud MSD, refer the case to your local Fraud Investigation unit for further investigation.

chunks.title: Date of review — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text: Generally, when a dependent child leaves the caregiver's care Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit, and Clothing Allowance for the child should stop from the start of the pay period following the date of event. However, there is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days following the event to allow for a period of financial adjustment, generally to avoid hardship for the client.

chunks.title: Mandatory Reviews — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text: Generally, caregivers getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit must respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date or their payments will suspend. If a child no longer qualifies, but the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit will continue at a different rate because a caregiver gets this payment for more than one child, the caregiver may be able to get an extension if they need more time to respond to the Mandatory Review. If the caregiver is unable to respond to the review (even if they had more time) based on their individual circumstances, they may qualify for an exemption. Generally, when the Mandatory Review is only for Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit and the benefit will stop at the end of the continuation period, and the review is due, an exemption will apply. The caregiver must contact MSD before their review date to discuss their situation if they need an extension or exemption.

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text: Generally, caregivers getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit must respond to their notice before the child's 18th birthday or Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the child will stop. If Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is continuing for up to 28 days because a child no longer qualifies, and that child turns 18 during that period, the caregiver is not required to respond to the notice and Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit will not stop during that period. However, if Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is continuing for up to 28 days because a child no longer qualifies, and a different child in their care (that Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is also paid for) turns 18, the caregiver must respond to the notice or Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the 18-year-old will stop.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
Caregivers have an obligation to advise MSD of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Orphan's Benefit and Unsupported Child's Benefit or the rate of payment.
MSD may also review a benefit at any time to check if the caregiver still meets the qualifications and is getting the correct rate of payment (if applicable).
## Mandatory Review for Orphan's Benefit and Unsupported Child's Benefit
MSD must review a caregiver's Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit within 52-weeks of when the benefit commenced, or within 52-weeks from when the caregiver's last Mandatory Review was completed.
Caregivers must respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date, or their payments will suspend.

chunks.title: Child applies for a benefit in their own right — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Child applies for a benefit in their own right
A dependent child cannot apply for a benefit (in their own right) until they have reached the qualifying age for that benefit. When the benefit is granted they may have an initial stand-down period.
Where a child applies and qualifies for a benefit in their own right, the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit would generally stop from:
- the start of the pay period following the date of event or
- the date the child's benefit is granted
whichever is earlier.
Wherever possible (and in appropriate circumstances) the date the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit stops and the commencement date of the child's benefit should coincide.
Note there are specific rules for deciding whether a child is considered a dependent child when the child turns 18.
There is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days following the event to allow for a period of financial adjustment, generally to avoid hardship for the client.

chunks.title: Child changes — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Child changes
Change to a dependent child's circumstances is generally going to affect the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit.

chunks.title: Child dies — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Child dies
When a child (that Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid for) dies, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit payments can continue for up to 28 days following the date of death.
## Mandatory Reviews
There are no Mandatory Reviews of Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit when the child (that Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid for) has died.
All other Mandatory Reviews, including Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit paid for another child, must still be completed.
The caregiver may be able to get an extension if they need more time to respond to the Mandatory Review. If the caregiver is unable to respond to the review (even if they had more time) based on their individual circumstances, they may qualify for an exemption.
## Child turns 18
When a child (that Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid for) has died, the caregiver is not required to respond to the notice when that child turns 18 and Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit will not stop during the continuation of payment period.
However, if Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is continuing for up to 28 days because a child has died, and a different child in their care (that Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is also paid for) turns 18, the caregiver must respond to the notice or Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the 18-year-old will stop.

chunks.title: Child leaves care — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Child leaves care
Generally, when a dependent child leaves the caregiver's care, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit should stop from the start of the pay period following the date of event.
However, there is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days following the event to allow for a period of financial adjustment, generally to avoid hardship for the client.

chunks.title: Child under the age of 18 years — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Child under the age of 18 years
When a child under the age of 18 years leaves school or tertiary education, MSD can continue to pay Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for that child until the start of the pay period following their 18th birthday as long as the child remains a dependent child.
## Child aged 18 years
When a child aged 18 years leaves school or tertiary education, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the child should stop from the start of the pay period following the date the child left school or tertiary education.
There is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days following the date the child left school or tertiary education to allow for a period of financial adjustment, generally to avoid hardship for the client. MSD needs to consider the activity the child is going to when considering the use of this discretion.

chunks.title: Child starts work — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Child starts work
A child in full-time employment and financially independent is not treated as a dependent child for Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit.
Note a child is still considered a dependent child if they are working full-time during the school holidays and they will be returning to school after the holidays.
For more information see:
- Full-time employment
- Part-time employment
- Childs income
- Income

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Child turns 18
A dependent child must generally be under the age of 18 for a caregiver to get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for them.
When a child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and are not eligible for Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit from the start of the pay period following the child's 18th birthday.
However, if the 18-year-old child is continuing in education and is not financially independent, the child may continue to be considered a dependent child and have Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit paid for them for a limited period.
In these situations, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit must stop from the start of the pay period following:
- the date they no longer meet these criteria or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18
whichever is earlier
However, there is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days following the date the child turns 18 to allow for a period of financial adjustment, generally to avoid hardship for the caregiver.
Note if the caregiver also gets Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for other children, the payments for the other children will not be affected by another child turning 18.

chunks.title: Protected earnings rate — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Protected earnings rate
No attachment order can, whether on its own or when combined with any other attachment order, Child Support deduction, or Ministry of Social Development debt repayment, take a caregiver's total income below the protected earnings rate.
For more information see:
- Protected earnings rate
## Information provided by the Court
The information that will be received from the Ministry of Justice will have:
- the caregiver's name
- the amount to be deducted from the benefit
- the fine's reference number
If a caregiver is suffering undue hardship because of the amount of the attachment order then they should be directed to a Registrar of the District Court for a reassessment of the rate.
For more information see:
- Court request for information
## Transferring or cancelling and re-granting benefits
When transferring or cancelling and re-granting benefits when there are court attachments on the record please email the Central Processing Unit. Include the caregivers name and client number, and a request to review and reload court attachments as necessary.

chunks.title: Court request for information — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit > changes and reviews ob and ucb
chunks.text:
## Court request for information
The Ministry of Justice can request the following information when they are considering either making an attachment order or assessing the caregiver's protected earnings rate under section 87AA of the Summary Proceedings Act 1957:
- the amount of any benefit paid to the caregiver
- the amount of any attachment orders or deduction notices issued under the following Acts: Social Security Act 2018Family Proceedings Act 1980Child Support Act 1991Tax Administration Act 1994
