Consider: - work obligations, sanctions and exemptions available (for example, a caregiver on Sole Parent Support would have part-time work obligations or work preparation obligations, while a caregiver getting Emergency Benefit would have conditions of grant and if these are not met, their entire benefit may be stopped) - ability to study and have access to study assistance such as education and employment-related assistance or Training Incentive Allowance (for example, caregivers getting Sole Parent Support can access this type of assistance, while caregivers on Jobseeker Support or Emergency Benefit cannot) - impact on benefit payments while absent from New Zealand - financial implications for the caregiver - age of the child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid (for example, is the child close to turning 14 years of age) - needs of the child, e.g. whether they need extra care - the number of Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit children for whom they are caring and their ages

chunks.title: Parent applies — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Parent applies
Unsupported Childs Benefit cannot be paid to a parent of the child. This includes a natural (birth) parent, adoptive parent, or step-parent as legislation specifically excludes them.
Orphans Benefit cannot be paid to either a natural (birth) or adoptive parent as the qualifications state.
Note when a child has been legally adopted the birth parents are no longer considered natural parents of that child.
## Step-parent
A step-parent's responsibility in relation to a child are not clearly defined in legislation and each application needs to be considered on a case by case basis taking all the family circumstances into account.
A step-parent can be established by all types of relationships with the child's parent, including marriage, civil union or de facto, and can continue to exist after the breakdown of the relationship.
In most cases it should be clear when a person is a step-parent - when a person has made a clear commitment to the child's day to day care, for example being involved in decisions about their education and wellbeing, and contribution toward costs.
To assist you to determine if an applicant is a step-parent, consider:
- what are their responsibilities for the child's day to day care?
- do they contribute to decisions about the child's education and wellbeing?
- how long was their relationship with the child's parent?
- does the applicant consider the child as their own?
- how does the extended family view the relationship between the child and the step-parent?
It is important to document the reasons for your decision and the factors you have taken into account.
If you need assistance please contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Parent living in the same house — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Parent living in the same house
If a parent is living in the same house as the caregiver, Unsupported Childs Benefit can only be paid when there has been a family breakdown between the parent and child, and the parent is unable to care for or provide fully for the child.
You should consider all the circumstances and discuss cases with your manager client service delivery.
For more information see:
- Parents unable to provide care
If there has been no breakdown, Unsupported Childs Benefit cannot be paid. However, if the caregiver is to raise the child as their own and they are getting a benefit, you can include the child as a dependent child in the caregiver's benefit.

chunks.title: Parents unable to provide care — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Parents unable to provide care
To receive an Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, the child's parents must not be able to provide care.
For more information see:
- Orphans Benefit
- Unsupported Childs Benefit

chunks.title: Paying parent — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Paying parent
A paying parent is a parent defined by Inland Revenue as the person legally responsible for maintaining the child.
It can be:
- the natural parent of the child
- the person named on the birth certificate
- a person legally married to the natural mother of the child at the time of conception or birth
- a person named by Court declaration as the parent of the child
- the adoptive parent
- legal step-parent (if declared by the Family Court) or
- a person who has taken the place of the parent(s) and is now regarded as the parent of the child.For example a person who has been appointed as a guardian under Part 2 of the Care of Children Act 2004.
Note the natural mother may be any gender but must have been pregnant with the child.
## More than 1 paying parent
At times there may be more than 1 paying parent. Each paying parent should be named on a separate application for Child Support for the relevant children.
## Examples
- someone other than the child's legal parents is the carer for the child when both the natural parents would be established as paying parents or
- child has a legal father and also has a step-parent (declared by the Family Court)
Applications need to be made in respect of all paying parents.
## Liability is unclear
When the carer is unclear about whether or not someone is a paying parent, the carer should complete the application form for Child Support, providing full details of the relationship. Inland Revenue will then be able to assess whether someone is a paying parent.
Applications for Child Support must be forwarded to Inland Revenue immediately.

chunks.title: Payment — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Payment
Orphans Benefit and Unsupported Childs Benefit are paid weekly on a Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. Payment is made one week in arrears.
Payment must be made directly to the caregiver.
It is a condition of receiving a benefit that the caregiver provides a:
- tax number and
- bank account number
## Rate of payment
The rates payable depend on the age of the child. For the age groups and rates see:
- Orphans Benefit and Unsupported Childs Benefit
## For clothing allowance rates see:
- Clothing Allowance rates
## Best Start tax credit
Principal caregivers getting a main benefit and Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit for children under the age of three years automatically qualify for Best Start tax credit. The caregiver can choose to get this from the Ministry of Social Development or Inland Revenue.
Principal temporary caregivers getting a main benefit for themselves and Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit for a child in their care under the age of three years do not automatically qualify for Best Start tax credit. They will need to contact Inland Revenue to check if they are eligible.
For more information see:
## To find out how income affects Orphans Benefit and Unsupported Childs Benefit see:
- Caregiver's income
- Child's income
- Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported children

chunks.title: Period of care — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: There is no minimum expected period of care for a caregiver to get Orphan’s Benefit or Unsupported Child’s Benefit. The child's parent must be unable to care, or provide fully, for the child, and the caregiver must have the primary responsibility for the day-to-day care of the child for the time being.

chunks.title: Short-term care arrangements (likely to be less than 12 months) — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: A caregiver can get Orphan’s Benefit or Unsupported Child’s Benefit for a child who is likely to be in their care temporarily or on a short-term basis (i.e. for less than 12 months, or for an unknown or uncertain period) from the date of application. A caregiver who meets the qualifications for Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit and who expects to provide care for less than 12 months is a principal temporary caregiver. Examples of short-term care arrangements include (but are not limited to): - a caregiver who is looking after a dependent child while the child's parent is in prison for less than 12 months and there is no other parent willing or able to provide day-to-day care of the child - a principal caregiver getting an Orphan’s Benefit or Unsupported Child’s Benefit suffers a serious medical event and is unable to provide day-to-day care of the child. While the principal caregiver recovers, the care of the child transfers to another caregiver for a period that is likely to be for less than 12 months - a caregiver who is looking after a dependent child (who meets the qualification criteria for Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit), but the child will stop meeting the definition of dependent child in less than 12 months Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit can still be paid if it is known at the time of application that the child's circumstances may change within the year, for example, the child will turn 18. Caregivers who are providing additional care arrangements are not considered principal caregivers or principal temporary caregivers.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: Debbie is a single mother and has raised 14-year-old Rino on her own. Rino has no relationship with his father and Debbie has had no contact with him since Rino was very young. Debbie has been in trouble with the police and in August is sentenced to four months in prison. She is unable to care for Rino while in prison and he needs to live with Debbie's sister Heather while Debbie serves out her sentence. For the period that Debbie is in prison, Heather will have primary responsibility for the day-to-day care of Rino. Even if Rino stays with someone else temporarily, e.g. if he stays with his grandparents during the school holidays, Heather will keep the primary responsibility for Rino's care. When Debbie re-enters the community, Rino will move back in with his mother. Heather applies for Unsupported Child’s Benefit to support Rino while he is in her care and Heather qualifies because she is Rino's principal temporary caregiver.

chunks.title: Example 2 — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: Sunia is 17 and is living with his 22 year old sister Ilisapeti. Sunia and Ilisapeti's mother died earlier this year, and they have no relationship with their father. Sunia will turn 18 in November and will be in his final year of high school next year. Ilisapeti is financially supporting Sunia while he finishes school, and he plans on living with her until he moves away for university. Ilisapeti applies for Orphan’s Benefit in June with Sunia as her dependent child. Although Sunia turns 18 in November, he will continue to meet the definition of dependent child until the start of the pay period following 31 December of the year he turns 18 as he is financially dependent on her, is continuing in education, and is enrolled in education for the following year. Sunia will stop meeting the definition of dependent child from the start of the first pay period in January onwards. This means that Ilisapeti will be caring for Sunia as her dependent child for a period of less than 12 months. Ilisapeti qualifies for Orphan’s Benefit as Sunia's principal temporary caregiver and is granted Orphan’s Benefit. The Orphan’s Benefit payments will stop in January, when Sunia stops meeting the definition of dependent child.

chunks.title: Long-term care arrangements (likely to be for 12 months or more) — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: A caregiver can get an Orphan’s Benefit or Unsupported Child’s Benefit for a child who is likely to be in their care for at least 12 months from the date of application. A caregiver who meets the qualifications for Orphan’s Benefit or Unsupported Child’s Benefit and who expects to provide care for at least 12 months is a principal caregiver. This does not mean that the minimum period of payment is one year.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: Aleki is a friend of Loimata's aiga (family). He has recently started caring for 14-year-old Loimata after the relationship between Loimata and her father broke down. Loimata's mother has not been involved in her life since Loimata's parents separated when she was a baby. Aleki expects to care for Loimata on a long-term basis, for at least 12 months. Aleki applies for Unsupported Child’s Benefit and meets all the qualification criteria, including the family breakdown criteria. Aleki qualifies as Loimata's principal caregiver.

chunks.title: Process for children in permanency — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Process for children in permanency
The caregiver will generally complete the following steps when they accept the legal custody of a child from Oranga Tamariki.
## Step 1
Each child who is moving into permanency will have a social worker assigned to them from Oranga Tamariki or a contracted agency.
## Step 2
When considering a permanent placement, the caregiver and in some cases the social worker meet with a case manager to discuss any income support that may be available to the caregiver and any supporting documents that may be required.
When applying for Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, caregivers are required to provide verification of the court order. If these documents are unavailable, a letter from the child's social worker and a copy of the application for a court order will be sufficient to allow the application for income support to proceed.
Supporting documents required for Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit include:
- the child's birth certificate
- the caregiver's passport or birth certificate
- a full bank statement for the caregiver
- the caregiver's IR number
- the parenting or guardianship court order or a letter from the child's social worker and a copy of the application for a court order
- the child's parent's names and contact details
- verification of any income the child receives
Generally this meeting will take place before any court orders for financial support from Oranga Tamariki to the caregiver have been made.
## Step 3
When the court hearing to grant parenting or guardianship orders in favour of the caregiver has been held, the caregiver and in some cases, the social worker will meet again with the case manager. During this meeting the caregiver may request and apply for income support.
Caregivers must provide all the correct supporting documentation.
## Step 4
The case manager will determine the caregiver's eligibility for income support and note in CMS any financial assistance ordered by the court to be paid by Oranga Tamariki to the caregiver.
If there are problems in the process you should contact your local permanency liaison person, who will contact Oranga Tamariki.
If you need help to determine whether income should be chargeable for benefit purposes you should contact Helpline or your manager client service delivery who may want to contact Legal Services [no link find out why] .

chunks.title: Proof of paying parent — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Proof of paying parent
It is the carer's responsibility to provide proof of the paying parent. Documents that will provide proof include:
- birth certificateThis will provide proof of the natural mother, and can provide proof of the father of the child.
- paternity orderA paternity order legally establishes who the father of a child is. Generally it needs to be the natural mother of a child who applies for a paternity order.
- declaration of paternityA declaration made by the High Court under section 10 of the Status of Children Act 1969. A declaration may be made when the father of the child cannot be established by a paternity order (for example in some situations when the child is over 6 years old).
- adoption orders
- overseas registration of birth document
- acknowledgement of paternity documentWhere the father of the child wants to acknowledge paternity, Inland Revenue-Child Support (IR-CS) has an Acknowledgement of Paternity form IR106 that should be used. IR-CS does not accept signed statements.
- guardianship orderThe father of a child can establish himself in law as the father by a guardianship order.
- a Family Court step-parent declaration under section 99 of the Child Support Act 1991This can establish a step-parent as the paying parent of the child.
Note the father of a child may be any gender. The natural mother may also be any gender but must have been pregnant with the child.

chunks.title: Qualifications — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: To get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit, the caregiver must: - be an eligible caregiver (which is either the principal caregiver or the principal temporary caregiver) of the child and - be aged 18 years or older and - be a New Zealand citizen or residence class visa holder (i.e. not be in New Zealand unlawfully or here on a temporary entry class visa) In addition, both the caregiver and the child must: - generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and either: the child must be resident and present in New Zealand orthe caregiver must have been resident and present in New Zealand for a continuous period of 12 months at any time - the child must be resident and present in New Zealand or - the caregiver must have been resident and present in New Zealand for a continuous period of 12 months at any time To get Unsupported Child's Benefit, the caregiver must not be the child's natural parent, adoptive parent or step-parent and because of a breakdown in the child's family there is no natural parent, adoptive parent or step-parent able to care for or provide fully for the child. For Orphan's Benefit the caregiver must not be the child's natural or adoptive parent. The child's parents must either be deceased, cannot be found or they suffer from a serious long-term illness or incapacity, which makes them unable to care for their child. If a child has been legally adopted, the birth parents are no longer considered the natural parents of the child.

chunks.title: Establishment Grant — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: When an Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is granted, an Establishment Grant must be considered. This payment must be made for every child included in the caregiver's Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit, if the child qualifies for the Establishment Grant.

chunks.title: School and Year Start-up Payment — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: When an Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is granted between the first Monday, after 10th January and the end of February each year, the caregiver must be advised they may be entitled to a School and Year Start-up Payment and how to apply. This payment must be made for every child included in the caregiver's Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit.

chunks.title: Clothing Allowance for Orphans and Unsupported Children — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: When an Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is granted, a Clothing Allowance is also granted automatically. The Clothing Allowance provides weekly financial assistance for children that Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid for. It is non-taxable and paid at the same rate as the clothing allowance for children in the care of the Chief Executive Oranga Tamariki. Clothing Allowance covers a reasonable range of clothing.

chunks.title: Holiday Allowance and Birthday Allowance — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: The Holiday Allowance and Birthday Allowance are annual, non-taxable payments to caregivers getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit. The Allowances are paid automatically each year at half the weekly rate of Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit. The Holiday Allowance and Birthday Allowance help the caregiver with the costs of preparing a celebration, purchasing gifts, or planning an event or experience for the child, or children in their care.

chunks.title: Getting Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit for a child after the child has been included in a benefit — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Getting Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit for a child after the child has been included in a benefit
A child who has been included in Sole Parent Support can still, at a later date, be a child for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is paid. For example this may occur when the caregiver:
- stops getting a main benefit and applies to get Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit for the child or
- moves to Jobseeker Support where it may be more appropriate to pay Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit

chunks.title: Reciprocal Agreements — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Reciprocal Agreements
New Zealand has Reciprocal Agreements with some countries.
Reciprocal Agreements do not apply to Unsupported Child's Benefit as this is not included in any agreements.
Under these agreements, residence and/or periods of insurance contributions in one of the following countries can be regarded as residence in New Zealand for Orphan's Benefit purposes:
- Hellenic Republic (Greece)
- Ireland
- United Kingdom

chunks.title: Residence — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Residence
To get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit, a caregiver must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit
People who are in New Zealand unlawfully or here on a temporary entry class visa generally do not qualify for a benefit.
The following residence test must also be met:
- both the caregiver and the child must generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and eitherthe child must be resident and present in New Zealand orthe caregiver must have been resident and present in New Zealand for a continuous period of 12 months at any time
- the child must be resident and present in New Zealand or
- the caregiver must have been resident and present in New Zealand for a continuous period of 12 months at any time
In some situations, the child may be living overseas.

chunks.title: Unsupported Childs Benefit — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text:
## Unsupported Childs Benefit
For a caregiver to get an Unsupported Childs Benefit, one or both of the child's natural, adoptive or step-parent must be unable to care for the child or provide fully for the child's support because of:
- a breakdown in the childs family
In situations of 'cultural adoption' (for example tamaiti whāngai children), there must still be a family breakdown before Unsupported Childs Benefit can be paid.
All Unsupported Childs Benefit grants must be approved by a manager client service delivery.

chunks.title: What is a breakdown in the child's family — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: The breakdown of a child's family involves a failure or collapse of the normal family dynamics that results in no natural, adoptive, or step-parent being able to care for or provide fully for their child or children. The child's parents have the legal responsibility to provide care and financially support their child. A family breakdown results in both parents unwilling or unable to provide care and financially support their child. Note 'Child's family' definition refers to immediate family and does not include extended family such as grandparents, uncles and aunts. Not all traumatic events within a family will result in a breakdown of a child's family.

chunks.title: Child's family unable to support them — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: In times of a crisis, a child may not be able to reside with their parents therefore close family members or friends may take over care of the child. The new caregivers should look to the child's parents in the first instance for financial support. The parents could still be able to support the child financially. A crisis does not necessarily mean a breakdown of the child's family. To determine a breakdown in the child's family, you need to consider the circumstances of the breakdown, the financial situation and the care arrangements. Consider the following: - what situation or circumstances has led to the family breakdown between the parents? - what situation or circumstances has led to the family breakdown between each parent and the child? - why is each parent unable to financially support their child? - what is the care arrangement with the caregiver? - how long is the child remaining with the caregiver? - what contact arrangements are there for the child with each parent? It is important that you record all the information from the applicant in their own words on the Unsupported Child's Benefit Interview Sheet as this information will assist you to determine eligibility.

chunks.title: Caregiver would like to be the primary caregiver — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: Where a natural, adoptive or step-parent is able to provide care for their child, then another person (for example a grandparent) who would like to be the child's primary caregiver cannot get Unsupported Childs Benefit for the child, even if they offer to be the principal caregiver or the principal temporary caregiver for the child. Also see: Additional care arrangements

chunks.title: Proof of breakdown in child's family — main benefits > orphans benefit and unsupported childs benefit
chunks.text: Proof of a breakdown in a child's family must be obtained. This may be through documentation already held by the applicant such as court orders or Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency documentation. Unless there has been recent Oranga Tamariki, or other authorised agency involvement, an applicant must be referred to an Independent Assessment Provider for a family breakdown assessment. You should use any available information, including Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency documentation and the Independent Assessment Provider report to assist you to make a decision while considering all relevant information.

chunks.title: Activity Summary — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Activity Summary
After you have discussed with the client the work obligations and activities they are required to complete, you may want to provide the client with an Activity Summary as confirmation of these.
Clients do not sign the Activity Summary and it is not mandatory to provide the Activity Summary to them. You may think it is appropriate to provide the print out or the client may request this.
For more information see:
- Setting appropriate activities for clients

chunks.title: All reasonable steps to meet social obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
There may be some situations where a client can't comply with their social obligations for reasons beyond their control. You can accept that a client has taken all reasonable steps to comply if they:
- have made a commitment to meet their social obligations at a more appropriate time and
- are working towards addressing any barriers they are facing
Every client's situation is different and what may be a barrier to meeting social obligations for one family may not be for another.
The decision about whether a client is taking all reasonable steps to comply lies with Work and Income.
Below are some of the situations you should take into account when considering that the client is taking all reasonable steps:
- Shared care issues in the family or family court proceedings occurring
The parent who is not the principal caregiver does not support their child having to attend recognised early childhood education programmes. It would not be reasonable for the client to be held responsible for the actions of someone else.
- Family violence or safety concerns in the family
A client discloses family violence or they have safety concerns for the child
- Supply or availability issues
A child is on a waiting list for:
- an early childhood education programme or
- a medical centre and the client has a plan or commitment to ensure their child can access primary health care if it is required
- Additional costs of participation or engagement may put the client in hardship
The travel costs or additional early childhood education programme costs associated with attendance would cause hardship to the family.
- The child has a health condition, injury or disability
A child has a health condition, injury or behavioural problems meaning that it would not be reasonable to expect them to participate in an approved programme either temporarily or permanently.
- Family has recently moved to a new area
The family has recently moved and is in the process of establishing networks.
For more information see:
- Social obligations
- Monitoring compliance with social obligations

chunks.title: Amount of income exemption — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Amount of income exemption
When you have determined that a client is severely disabled you must then consider if they should have all or part of their income from employment disregarded for benefit purposes.
The amount of the income exemption depends on the client's individual circumstances after considering the guidelines - exemption for severe disablement and should be:
- a reasonable amount as an incentive to recognise the personal effort that a severely disabled person has made to participate or continue in employment
- any additional costs that a severely disabled person has incurred to participate or continue in employment
- a reasonable amount to ensure that a severely disabled person is not disadvantaged by participating or continuing in employment
Note the client may be entitled to receive other types of assistance, for example Disability Allowance for transport costs to work or employment assistance.
Fully document your decision by recording the reasons and the amount of the exemption in the CMS note template, Income exemption amount.
Contact Helpline if you need help with the assessment.
For more information see:
- Extra Help

chunks.title: Approved early childhood education programmes or service — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Approved early childhood education programmes or service
An approved early childhood education programme or service includes:
- a licensed early childhood education service which includes:
- early childhood education and care centre (eg daycare centre, kōhanga reo, playcentre, kindergarten)
- home-based education and care service
- hospital-based education and care service
- a playgroup that has been certificated by the Ministry of Education (this means a playgroup is funded by the Ministry of Education and will meet certain standards)
- if before 1 December 2014, a licence-exempt early childhood education and care centre funded by the Ministry of Education (this means a playgroup is funded by the Ministry of Education and so meets certain standards)
and
- for which a fee is charged for the children to participate in the programme
Most early childhood education services offer 20 Hours Early Childhood Education. This means that children aged 3, 4 and 5 years old may be able to receive up to 6 hours per day, 20 hours per week of free early childhood education.
To help clients meet this social obligation you should discuss childcare assistance that may be available to the client.

chunks.title: Special Needs Grant — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Special Needs Grant
If a client is suffering hardship they may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant.
For more information see:
- Special Needs Grants Assistance during an Initial stand-down and/or benefit application process

chunks.title: Assistance for the parent not qualified for Sole Parent Support — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Assistance for the parent not qualified for Sole Parent Support
If a sole parent client cannot receive Sole Parent Support because there are no court orders recognising the split care arrangement, you should first consider whether they are entitled to receive any other benefit (for example Jobseeker Support).
To determine whether your client may qualify for a main benefit you should discuss the following:
- are they available for or seeking full-time employment?
- do they suffer from an illness or disability which limits their ability to work (either permanently or temporarily)?
- why are they unable to earn sufficient income to support themselves?
For more information see:
- Court ordered split care arrangements
- No court ordered split care arrangement
- Determining whether a care arrangement is sanctioned by the Family Court
- Privacy Act implications
- When to consider Emergency Maintenance Allowance for split care

chunks.title: Assistance to move back to an area that is not a limited employment location — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Assistance to move back to an area that is not a limited employment location
This applies where a client has moved to a limited employment location and cannot meet their work obligations, and they have decided to move back to an area that is not a limited employment location.
In this situation, the client has put themselves into hardship by moving to a limited employment location where they cannot meet their work obligations. Therefore, we would generally not provide assistance to help them relocate.
However, when hardship is preventing the client from moving to an area that is not a limited employment location, you may look at an Advance Payment of Benefit using the 'other' category. This payment is recoverable and requires a manager client service delivery's approval.

chunks.title: Bank — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Bank
An appropriate bank is:
- a private savings bank, a trustee savings bank or The Co-operative Bank
- a registered bank which on the 31st March 1987 was a trading bank or
- any other registered bank or a building society approved by the Minister after consultation with the Minister of Finance
For more information see:
- Processing standards Bank account [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Bereavement of immediate family — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Bereavement of immediate family
In determining whether a client has an exceptional circumstance for not completing the reapplication process before their expiry date on the grounds of bereavement, the client must have experienced a bereavement of an immediate family member during their notice period which affected their ability to reapply.
Immediate family, for the purposes of exceptional circumstances, are:
- parents (including step-parents and foster parents)
- grandparents (including grandmother and grandfather)
- children (including grandchildren, stepchildren, foster children, mokopuna - those grandchildren who have been raised by the grandparents as the principal caregivers, and whāngai - children who have been raised, normally by a relation or other person within the wider whānau to which the child belongs) and
- siblings (including half siblings and step siblings, but excluding members of organisations/gangs referring to themselves as 'blood brothers and sisters')
## Evidence
MSD may require the client to provide evidence of the bereavement. In most cases the client should just be asked to sign a personal statement.
In some cases clients may also be asked to provide further evidence, this could include:
- a death certificate
- a newspaper notice
- an online obituary which clearly shows the date of death
- birth certificate showing relationship to deceased
- confirmation of the death from the lawyer who is administering the estate or from the minister or funeral director
If the client has been granted a Funeral Grant for their dependent child, they should not be asked to provide evidence again.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Breakdown in the child's family cannot be established — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Breakdown in the child's family cannot be established
If a breakdown in the child's family cannot be established the child cannot be considered dependent for Sole Parent Support purposes.
The client should:
- ask the child's parent to contribute financially to the care and support of the child or
- apply for Child Support or
- have a good and sufficient reason to include the child in their benefit
Note the child must meet the definition of a dependent child to be included in the client's benefit.

chunks.title: Calculating the period of residence — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Calculating the period of residence
A period of residence in New Zealand starts from the date the client was:
- lawfully resident in New Zealand or
- was granted New Zealand citizenship or permanent residence
To be resident at a particular time a client must be lawfully resident, that is, the client must be one of the following:
- a New Zealand citizen
- a permanent resident in New Zealand
- an Australian citizen or passport holder or
- a New Zealand passport holder
For more information see:
- Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
- Permanent residence
- Deciding ordinarily residence
- Unlawful residence

chunks.title: Step 1 — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Step 1
Find out the number of days represented by the payment received. If this is not clearly shown on the 'verification of payments received' provided by the client, use either of the following formula.
Note extra payments paid to the client (for example holiday pay), should not be included in the gross salary figure used to calculate the daily rate of pay. However these payments will be included in the clients' last 26 and 52 weeks gross earnings.
Formula 1
Determine gross salary over last 52 weeks of employment
Divide by 52 weeks = weekly rate of pay
Divide by 5 days = daily rate of pay
Confirm total amount of holiday pay etc
Divide this amount by daily rate of pay = number of days pay
Formula 2
Determine gross salary over last 4 weeks of employment
Divide by 20 (number of working days in 4 weeks) = daily rate of pay
Confirm total amount of holiday pay etc
Divide by daily rate of pay = number of days pay
Note only calculate the period covered by holiday pay using the applicants' last 4 weeks income if it does not disadvantage the client. If the income earned in the last 4 weeks does not reflect what the client normally earned, you may need to request extra weeks or calculate the daily rate of pay using the last 26 weeks gross salary.

chunks.title: Caring for a child or foster child with special needs — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Caring for a child or foster child with special needs
This exemption may apply to clients with work or work preparation obligations.
A client can be exempt from some or all of their work or work preparation obligations if they are the:
- principal caregiver of a dependent child or
- foster parent of a foster child
who has special needs and whose welfare would be unduly harmed if the client attended employment or training, and for whom alternative care arrangements are not available, or are unable to be made.
This means the child must have 1 or more of the following:
- a physical or intellectual disability
- a medical condition
- a chronic or recurring illness
- a learning or behavioural difficulty and
- be unable to attend school on a regular basis or
- be a foster child, aged 3 years or older, who is adjusting to a placement with a new foster carer
Note this can be a full or partial exemption.
## Foster child is under 3 years old
A client may also be exempt from some of their work obligations if they are caring for a foster child under the age of 3 years.
## Evidence
The client must provide written evidence of the child's special needs from a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, psychologist or social worker stating:
- what the child's illness is and its likely duration or
- an assessment of the child's behavioural difficulty or
- the need for full-time care
- the risk to the child if the client has work or work preparation obligations and
- that the child is unable to attend school
Note MSD should also consider eligibility to Child Disability Allowance. However, a child getting Child Disability Allowance does not guarantee the client will meet the criteria for this exemption.

chunks.title: Caring for a child under 3 years who is not their dependent child — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Caring for a child under 3 years who is not their dependent child
This exemption may apply to clients with work obligations.
In some cases a client may be caring for a foster child or children under the age of 3 years old who is in Oranga Tamariki care. Foster children are not considered to be dependent children.
These clients may be exempt from meeting some of their work obligations.
This is a partial exemption only.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted in SWIFTT for 12 months or to when the child turns 3 years old - whichever is earlier.
This exemption can be renewed after 12 months provided the child is still under 3 years old and the parent still qualifies for benefit.

chunks.title: Caring full-time for a person with a health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Caring full-time for a person with a health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to clients with work preparation obligations.
A client may be caring for a person who has a health condition, injury or a disability and who needs to be cared for on a full-time basis.
This can be a full exemption.
Note MSD should consider whether the client should get Supported Living Payment on the ground of caring for a person.
## Evidence
The client must provide a medical certificate from a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner:
- that the person needs the client's full-time care and
- that without that care the person would need hospital care or care of an equivalent kind and
- the length of time the person will need that care

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances
Clients must tell us straight away of any change in their circumstances or their family's situation that may affect their entitlement to Sole Parent Support. Clients agree to this by signing the Sole Parent Support application form.
A change of circumstance may also affect the client's social obligations.
Examples of changes and how to deal with these can be found in Changes and Reviews.
For more information see:
- Child changes and social obligations
- Changes and reviews Child changes

chunks.title: Change in circumstances during Money Management — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances during Money Management
Clients may have a change in circumstances during Money Management, such as a change in income, which may change their rate of benefit.
If a client declares a change in circumstances after their payment has been issued onto the payment card, it may mean this payment is incorrect resulting in a debt being established or arrears due to the client.
Any debt will generally be repaid from their future benefit payments.
If a client is owed arrears, it will be paid directly to their bank account. This is different when a client's benefit stops during Money Management.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
Clients receiving Sole Parent Support must be:
- a sole parent caring for a dependent child aged under 14 years
and
- available for and seeking part-time work or
- taking steps to prepare for part-time work
## Clients with work obligations or work preparation activities generally cannot be absent and continue to receive payment
Generally a client receiving Sole Parent Support cannot continue to receive their payment when they temporarily leave New Zealand if they have:
- work obligations
- work preparation obligations and have had work preparation activities assigned
For more information see:
- Client with work or work preparation obligations or an exemption
- Client with work preparation obligations
## All clients have an obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand
All clients receiving a main benefit must advise Work and Income before they leave New Zealand. If the client does not advise Work and Income prior to their international travel, their benefit payments will stop from the day after they leave New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand
- Permanent absence
## Paying a benefit while a Sole Parent Support client is absent from New Zealand
A client not otherwise entitled to be paid their Sole Parent Support may be able to continue to receive their payments for up to 28 days in a 52 week period, while they are absent from New Zealand for:
- Approved travel reasons
- Overseas for medical treatment
## Payment of benefit while absent for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Absences that do not prevent client from meeting obligations — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Absences that do not prevent client from meeting obligations
Generally, a client receiving Sole Parent Support who has work obligations or work preparation activities assigned cannot be absent from New Zealand and continue to be paid a benefit unless:
- it is for one of the permitted travel reasons or
- they are already meeting their work obligations (by being in employment) or work preparation activities (by participating in employment related training)
and
- the travel will not prevent them continuing to meet these obligations (eg because it is during a period of annual leave or a term or semester break)
For more information see:
- Client meeting their work preparation obligations
- Client meeting their work obligations

chunks.title: Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However, there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
These circumstances are:
- travel is required for an approved reason, and either: it is the client's first absence in 52 weeks and the permitted reason the client needs to be absent from New Zealand necessitates a period longer than 28 days orthe client has had other prior approved absences within the 52 week period and they require further approved absences which will require them to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- it is the client's first absence in 52 weeks and the permitted reason the client needs to be absent from New Zealand necessitates a period longer than 28 days or
- the client has had other prior approved absences within the 52 week period and they require further approved absences which will require them to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- the client is absent from New Zealand for an approved travel reason and their return is prevented by a new circumstances that requires them to be absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period
For more information see:
- Paying more than 28 days for an approved reason
- Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return

chunks.title: Approved travel reasons — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Approved travel reasons
Unless they have an approved reason, a client getting Sole Parent Support is generally not able to continue to get their main benefit payments while they are absent from New Zealand if they have:
- work obligations (including those with an exemption)
- work-preparation obligations and have work preparation activities assigned
Approved travel includes:
- travel for a permitted reason
- travel where the absence does not prevent the client from meeting all of their obligations because the absence is at a time they are not required to attend employment, education or training (whichever applies)
Note clients are not required to meet their job search obligations while absent from New Zealand on approved travel.
For more information see:
- Permitted travel reasons
- Absences that do not prevent client meeting their obligations
## Length of travel for an approved travel reason
Clients can travel for up to 28 days on Sole Parent Support for an approved travel reason. Discuss with the client the amount of time that they need to be absent from New Zealand as a result of the approved reason. The client should explain the length of their intended absence.
Consider:
- the length of time the event or reason for travel will take
- the duties the client will have as part of their reason (eg if they are travelling for a funeral, do they have responsibilities beyond attending the funeral itself such as estate duties or sorting out the possessions of the deceased?)
- flight availability and travel time
Remember to advise clients that generally they are only able to continue to be paid their benefit for up to 28 days in a 52 week period. This should be taken into account when deciding the approved travel period.
## Client travelling for multiple reasons
Some clients may travel overseas for an approved travel reason but elect to stay longer for another reason that is not an approved travel reason. In this case, the client can generally only receive their main benefit payments for the period of time that the approved travel reason applies to.
For more information see:
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy
- Travel notifications made while overseas [no link find out why] process
- Travel notifications made on return to New Zealand [no link find out why] process

chunks.title: Backdating benefit to the day after departure date — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Backdating benefit to the day after departure date
A client who leaves New Zealand without advising Work and Income of their travel can only have their benefit backdated to the day after their departure date if they:
- have a humanitarian reason that justifies their reason for travel and their failure to tell Work and Income before they left and
- contacted Work and Income as soon as they could reasonably have been expected to, given their circumstances after they departed and
- meet the criteria to continue to be paid their benefit while overseas (either because they meet the criteria for approved travel, or the requirement that travel be approved does not apply to them)
For more information see:
- Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure
- Contacting Work and Income as soon as the client reasonably can
- Approved travel reasons
- Paying a benefit when a client has not advised before departure
- Action on return to New Zealand

chunks.title: Birth of a child — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Birth of a child
When a client applies to have their newborn child included in their benefit the following information is required:
- full birth certificate of the child, or confirmation from Internal Affairs that the childs’ birth was registered online and permission was given to share the birth registration with MSD
- written statement from the client requesting inclusion of the child
If a child's birth certificate is not available immediately, you can include the child in the benefit (without delay) when the client can provide:
- Plunket records
- birth notices
- confirmation from the client's midwife or doctor of the date of birth of the new child or
- hospital papers
Note you must follow-up to make sure the client produces a copy of the birth certificate.
## Extra help
If a child is born with a mental or physical disability, needs constant care and attention because of a disability, or is likely to require care for at least 12 months, the client should test their eligibility for Child Disability Allowance.
When a child has on going additional costs because of a disability they may be able to receive a Disability Allowance.
For more information see:
- Date of review (including backdating)
- Dependent child
- Effect on benefit
- Family tax credit
- Best Start tax credit
- Core policy Child Support
- Verification from Internal Affairs

chunks.title: Calculating the period of absence — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Calculating the period of absence
The period of an absence from New Zealand for which payment of Sole Parent Support can continue (if approved) is up to 28 consecutive days, that is, Saturdays and Sundays are included.
In all cases, when assessing the period of absence do not include:
- the date of departure from New Zealand and
- the date of return to New Zealand
If a client is absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period the benefit should be suspended from the 29th day (unless they meet the criteria to pay for longer than 28 days).
Note if a client is leaving New Zealand permanently, the benefit must be cancelled from the day after departure.

chunks.title: Permanent or long term — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Permanent or long term
To include a child as a dependent child, the change of care should be with the intent of permanency or at least capable of being a long-term arrangement.
For more information see:
- Temporary care
- Shared care
- Split care

chunks.title: Change in age — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Change in age
A child's age may affect:
- the family tax credit payable
- the Best Start tax credit payable
- whether the child is still a dependent child
- eligibility for Sole Parent Support and
- the client's obligations
## Child is not dependent
A child is considered a dependent child unless they are:
- in full-time employment
Note generally a child is still a dependent child when they start part-time employment.
- getting a Student Allowance or an Independent Circumstances Allowance
Note getting a Student Loan does not always mean a child is financially independent.
- getting a benefit in their own right or
- financially independent
## Child turns 14
When a client's youngest dependent child turns 14, the client is no longer eligible for Sole Parent Support.
## Best Start child turns 3
A child for who Best Start tax credit is payable will stop being eligible once the child turns 3.
## Under 18 and not attending school
A child does not have to be attending school to remain a dependent child up until the age of 18 years.
## Child turns 18
When a child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and can no longer be included in their parent or caregiver's payments, unless they are continuing in education and are not financially independent.

chunks.title: Change of address — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Change of address
When a client advises that they have changed their address it is important to check that the move does not affect their entitlement to Sole Parent Support.
Note you will need to update the address in CMS.
If the client is receiving Extra help, this will need to be reviewed.
If the client has a portion of their benefit paid to Kāinga Ora or Te Puni Kokiri for accommodation costs this may need to be changed or cancelled.
## Change in circumstances
The change of address may also indicate a change in the client's circumstances.
Examples of changes that may affect the client's entitlement to Sole Parent Support are:
- commencing employment
- commencing study or training
- moving to a remote area where there are few job opportunities
- change of relationship status
- dependent children coming into or leaving care
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Obligations

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client is obliged to advise the Ministry of Social Development of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Sole Parent Support.
You may also review a benefit at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is getting the correct rate of payment.
A change in a client's circumstances may also mean that the client qualifies for another benefit.

chunks.title: Child absent — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Child absent
A dependent child who travels overseas can continue to be included in a benefit as long as they continue to meet the definition of dependent child.
Examples of when a dependent child can be absent from New Zealand are:
- child is overseas on an American Field Scholarship or other student exchange programme
- child is overseas visiting a parent who does not act as caregiver
For more information about the effect of absence from New Zealand for a client receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit see:
- Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit Absence from New Zealand

chunks.title: Child admitted to hospital — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Child admitted to hospital
Where a client's dependent child is admitted to hospital, there is no change to the rate of payment, whilethe child remains in hospital.
Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit payments continue to be paid for a child who is admitted to hospital. If the child turns three while in hospital the best start tax credit payment will stop from the child's third birthday.
Depending on the nature of the child's injury, illness or disability the client may be able to receive Child Disability Allowance.
Child Disability Allowance is a non-taxable allowance paid to the principal caregiver of a child with a serious disability, who is in need of constant care and attention for a period longer than 12 months.
For more information see:
- Child Disability Allowance
- Best Start tax credit Child turns 3

chunks.title: Child applies for a benefit in their own right — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Child applies for a benefit in their own right
Where a child applies for a benefit in their own right, exclude the child from the client's Sole Parent Support from:
- the start of the pay period following the date of event
Note there is discretion to continue payment for one more payday following the event.
or
- the date the child's benefit is granted
whichever is earlier.
Wherever possible (and in appropriate circumstances) the date of exclusion of the child from the client's benefit and the commencement date of the child's benefit should coincide to avoid financial hardship for the family.
Note there are specific rules for deciding whether a child is considered a dependent child when the child turns 18.

chunks.title: Child changes — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Child changes
The number of dependent children in a Sole Parent Support client's care and any change to the circumstance of a child can affect:
- the rate of family tax credit payable
- payment of Best Start tax credit
- the rate of extra help payable
- the client's obligations and
- (in some situations) the client's eligibility to the benefit, for example, last child leaves care
## Including a child in Sole Parent Support
For a child to be included in a client's Sole Parent Support the child must be a dependent child and generally ordinarily resident in New Zealand.
When the child is not the client's natural or adoptive child, the client may be able to get an Unsupported Child's Benefit (instead of having the child included in their Sole Parent Support). This will depend mainly on the care arrangements.
## Changes to a child's circumstances
Change to a dependent child's circumstances is generally going to affect the client's Sole Parent Support.

chunks.title: Child comes into care — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Child comes into care
When a client has made an application to have another child included in their benefit and that child was in the care of another person the following information is required:
- full birth certificate of the childSee: Verification from Internal Affairs
- written statement from the applicant stating they are the principal caregiver and requesting inclusion in the Sole Parent Support
- (where appropriate) letter from previous caregiver confirming that child has left their careNote where the client cannot get written confirmation from the previous caregiver, the new caring arrangement can be confirmed by a referee such as a teacher, Plunket nurse, minister or a Justice of the Peace.
Any benefit payments the previous caregiver was getting for the child must stop.
## Date of review
Include the child in the benefit from:
- the date the child came into the client's care or
- the date the Sole Parent Support was granted
whichever is the later.
## Backdating
Where a client requests the backdated inclusion of a child and the previous caregiver was getting a benefit for the child, you will need to review when the child was excluded from the previous caregivers benefit.
Generally, a child cannot be included in multiple benefits for the same period. In some situations, the previous caregiver may continue to get a benefit in respect of that child for up to 28 days.
Consider all the circumstances and decide whether a debt should be established for the previous caregiver.
If the date you are including the child from is a date in the previous tax year, MSD can only pay arrears of family tax credit and Best Start tax credit from the beginning of the current tax year, that is, 1 April. The client will need to apply for any arrears of tax credits before this date from Inland Revenue.
A review of entitlement needs to be completed to determine the amount of any benefit arrears owed to the client for the backdated period.
For more information see:
- Effect on the benefit
- Child's income
- Carer arrangements
- Discharged from Oranga Tamariki care
- Shared care
- Split care
- Temporary care
- Imprisonment Parent in prison
- Processing standards Child changes [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Personal earnings — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Personal earnings
A dependent child's personal earnings are not charged as income against the Sole Parent Support.
However, a child in full-time employment and financially independent cannot be included as a dependent child in the benefit.
For more information see:
- Child starts work
## Other income
A child may receive other income that is not personal earnings.
For more information about how to treat other forms of child's income see:
- Core Policy Types of income

chunks.title: Child leaves care — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Child leaves care
When a dependent child leaves the client's care, the child should be excluded from the start of the pay period following the date the child leaves care and any extra help the client gets should be reassessed at the appropriate rate where applicable.
If the child is the client's last dependent child aged under 14 years, Sole Parent Support must be cancelled. MSD will need to determine if the client qualifies for another benefit.
Note different rules apply when a child stops being a dependent child of a sole parent client because of a sudden change of circumstances beyond the control of the client.
## Example
A client getting Sole Parent Support has two dependent children included in their benefit, one aged 11 years and the other aged 13 years.
The younger child leaves care to start living with another caregiver as planned and is excluded from the start of the pay period following the date the child left care so the client does not incur a debt.
Six months later the remaining child turns 14.
The client no longer meets the qualification for Sole Parent Support and MSD must determine if the client qualifies for another benefit.

chunks.title: Child leaves care suddenly — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Child leaves care suddenly
When a client getting Sole Parent Support stops caring for a dependent child because of a sudden change of circumstances beyond the control of the client, payment of the benefit may continue at the existing rate for 28 days following the date the child stopped being dependent.
This is to allow a period of transition for the client to adjust to their change in circumstances.
For example when a child suddenly goes into the care of Oranga Tamariki, payment may continue for 28 days from the date the child is no longer dependent on the client.
Extra help payments that can be continued for 28 days are:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Child Disability Allowance
- Disability Allowance
- Temporary Additional Support
- Winter Energy Payment
The exception is Childcare Assistance which must be stopped on the day after the client stopped caring for the dependent child.
During the 28 days continuation of payment, if the client has other changes of circumstances such as a change in income, the rate of main benefit and extra help will need to be reassessed using sole parent threshold rates.
## Child turns 18
Generally, clients getting Sole Parent Support must respond to their notice before the child's 18th birthday or the child will be excluded from their payments.
If Sole Parent Support and any extra help is continuing at the existing rate for up to 28 days because a child has left their care suddenly, and that child turns 18 during that period, the client is not required to respond to the notice and the child will not be excluded during the continuation of payment period.
However, if Sole Parent Support and any extra help is continuing at the existing rate for up to 28 days because a child has left their care suddenly, and a different child in their care turns 18, the client must respond to the notice, or the 18-year-old will be excluded from their payments.

chunks.title: Child under the age of 18 years — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Child under the age of 18 years
When a child under the age of 18 years leaves school or tertiary education, they can continue to be included in the parent or caregiver's Sole Parent Support until the start of the pay period following their 18th birthday as long as the child remains a dependent child.
## Child aged 18 years old
When a child aged 18 years old leaves school or tertiary education, they should be excluded from their parent or caregiver's payment from the start of the pay period following the date the child left school or tertiary education.
## Family tax credit
When a child leaves school or tertiary education, family tax credits should be stopped from the day the child is excluded from the client's Sole Parent Support.

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Child turns 18
A dependent child must generally be under the age of 18 to be included in their parent or caregiver's Sole Parent Support.
When a child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and must be excluded from their parent or caregiver's Sole Parent Support from the start of the pay period following the child's 18th birthday.
However, if the 18-year-old child is continuing in education and is not financially independent, the child may continue to be considered a dependent child and be included in their parent or caregiver's Sole Parent Support for a limited period.
In these situations, the child must be excluded from the start of the pay period following:
- the date they no longer meet these criteria or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18
whichever is earlier

chunks.title: Client applies for assistance from StudyLink — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client applies for assistance from StudyLink
If a client receiving Sole Parent Support advises that they intend to study, and a decision is made that they cannot meet their obligations on Sole Parent Support while they do so. You should explain to the client that they may be sanctioned if they fail one of their obligations as a result of their study commitments.
They can also consider applying for financial assistance support from StudyLink.
If the client is applying for financial support from StudyLink, they can receive Sole Parent Support until they start receiving assistance from StudyLink.
## Applying for Student Allowance, Independent Circumstances Allowance or Student Loan
If the client is applying for a Student Allowance, Independent Circumstances Allowance or Student Loan you will need to:
- add a future suspension to the benefit for the Monday of the week that the client advises they will start receiving a Student Allowance, Independent Circumstances Allowance or Student Loan
For example, the client starts receiving a Student Allowance, Independent Circumstances Allowance, or Student Loan on Wednesday 15 June - add the future suspension for Monday 13 June. Student Allowance or Student Loan living costs (if nominated) will commence on Monday 13 June as these are always paid for the full week
Where there is early approval of Student Allowance, Independent Circumstances Allowance or Student Loan, StudyLink will check the future suspension date on Sole Parent Support and advise the case manager of any correction needed.
When Sole Parent Support has been cancelled from an incorrect date, StudyLink will establish overpayments.
For more information see:
- Students Student Allowance
- Students Student Loan
- Students Independent Circumstances Allowance

chunks.title: Client becomes sick — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client becomes sick
A client with work obligations who has a health condition, injury or disability can be exempt from meeting their work obligations until they are well again.
Where a client's health condition permanently and severely restricts their ability to work, they may be able to receive Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability.
If the client is admitted to hospital it may affect their rate of payment.
For more information see:
- Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
- Hospitalisation

chunks.title: Surviving dependent child — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Surviving dependent child
When a client dies (and there is a surviving dependent child) before a decision is made on an application or review for Sole Parent Support you can continue the application or review process as if the client had not died.
## Funeral Grant
In situations when the decision to grant or review Sole Parent Support is made after the date of death of the client, you decide any Funeral Grant as if the deceased client were receiving Sole Parent Support.

chunks.title: Client does not return — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client does not return
If a client's benefit is suspended because they are absent from New Zealand and they do not return their benefit record will automatically cancel in SWIFTT, 8 weeks after the date of suspension.
Note if the client had been approved continued payment of benefit for the first 28 days of the absence, this is not established as a debt.
For more information see:
- Action on return to New Zealand

chunks.title: Client donates a kidney or liver tissue — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client donates a kidney or liver tissue
When a client is donating a kidney or liver tissue, they can keep getting their Sole Parent Support. Exempt the client from any work obligations during the recovery period.
Grant the exemption 'Would qualify for Jobseeker Support – health condition, injury or disability'.
Add information from the medical certificate in the SINCC screen in SWIFTT.
The exemption starts from the date of their operation and can continue while the client:
- is recovering from their operation and
- they cannot meet their part-time work obligations
This exemption must not be more than 12 weeks.
Do not apply any obligation failures:
- for the maximum period of 12 weeks or
- until the client has recovered from the operation
whichever is earlier.
## Client has an obligation failure
If the client currently has an obligation failure, donating a kidney or liver tissue is a 'good and sufficient reason'. The part-time obligations failure must be overturned.
This will remove the failure from the client’s 12 month obligation failure count and there is no sanction.
## Childcare assistance
Clients may be eligible for Childcare Assistance payments while they are they are recovering.
For more information see:
- Childcare Subsidy Temporary illness
- OSCAR Temporary illness
- Exemptions
- Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability

chunks.title: Examples (but are not limited to) — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Examples (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A client receiving Sole Parent Support was out of New Zealand visiting his father in Australia. His Sole Parent Support was suspended the day after he left New Zealand as it wasn't an approved travel reason.
The client contacts Work and Income three days later to say that his father is in hospital as he has had a heart attack. The client has been paid for five days in the previous 52 weeks while he was absent from New Zealand leaving a balance of 23 days.
The reason for travel now meets the criteria for approved travel. The benefit is resumed from the date the client became eligible to receive the benefit overseas.
The client must contact Work and Income from overseas. The benefit cannot be back-dated if the client advises Work and Income when they return to New Zealand.
A client receiving Sole Parent Support with work preparation but no activities assigned left New Zealand to visit her mother. Two days before she was due to return, her mother's house burnt down.
The client has been paid for 20 days in the previous 52 weeks while she was absent from New Zealand leaving a balance of eight days.
The reason for travel has changed and the client has not been absent from New Zealand for up to 28 days in any 52 week period. The benefit expiry is extended for an additional five days.
This client can travel for any reason. If the client hadn't informed Work and Income, their benefit would continue to be paid up until the 29th day.
Note that where the client has already been absent for 28 days in a 52 week period, consider whether the client meets the criteria for receiving a payment for more than 28 days in any 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Client meeting their work obligations — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client meeting their work obligations
A client receiving Sole Parent Support can continue to be paid a benefit while they are absent from New Zealand for any reason:
- when they are meeting their work obligations by being in paid employment and
- the travel will not prevent them from continuing to meet these work obligations (eg during a period of annual leave from employment)
## Examples (but not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
Client with work obligations on Sole Parent Support with part-time work obligations is in employment for 22 hours per week. They have taken annual leave from their employment to travel to Australia.
The client is already meeting their part-time work obligations by being in suitable employment of over 20 hours per week. Their benefit will continue to be paid for up to 28 days in any 52 week period while they are absent from New Zealand.
Client of a person receiving Sole Parent Support with part-time work obligations is employment for 24 hours per week. They have taken annual leave from their employment to travel to Australia.
The client is already meeting their part-time work obligations by being in suitable employment of over 20 hours per week. Their benefit will continue to be paid for up to 28 days in any 52 week period while they are absent from New Zealand.
## Obligations changes on 1 April 2016
From 1 April 2016, sole parents will need an approved reason for travel if:
- their youngest dependent child is 3 or 4 years old
- they are working between 15 and 20 hours per week
Discretion to continue payments while temporarily overseas is available for clients that:
- will change from work preparation to part-time work obligations on 1 April 2016 because their youngest dependent child is aged 3 or 4 years old or
- will no longer be meeting their part-time work obligations on 1 April 2016 because the definition of part-time work increased from 15 to 20 hours per week and
- book overseas travel before they are aware of the changes to their work obligations that come into effect on 1 April 2016 and
- would continue to receive their payment based on their obligations at the time they booked travel
Note all other absence from New Zealand policy applies when applying this discretion.

chunks.title: Client meeting their work preparation obligations — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client meeting their work preparation obligations
