See your local solicitor if you receive a case in this category. When a child or young person is discharged from the care, custody or sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, always consider including the child in the clients Sole Parent Support or granting Unsupported Childs Benefit. - The legislation referenced above is the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989

chunks.title: Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid
When a client is receiving an Orphans Benefit or an Unsupported Child's Benefit, the child is not treated as a dependent child and is not included in the assessment of Sole Parent Support.
The client's Sole Parent Support is assessed on their family circumstances excluding the child for which Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid.

chunks.title: Part-time employment — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Part-time employment
Part-time employment does not make a child financially independent. Nor do you take the child's earnings into account when assessing the rate of Sole Parent Support payments. For more information on children's income see:
- Child income

chunks.title: Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure
Generally, clients getting a main benefit must advise the Ministry of Social Development of their intention to leave New Zealand before their departure to be eligible to continue to receive their payments.
Only in specific circumstances can a client getting a benefit leave New Zealand without telling us, be able to have their benefit either:
- resumed from the date they notified the Ministry of their absence if their travel is allowed or
- backdated to the day after their departure date
Note this can occur either while the client is overseas or once they have returned.
## Resuming benefit when client failed to advise of absence
If a client contacts the Ministry after they have left New Zealand, and is not eligible to have their payment backdated, their benefit can only be resumed from:
- the date they notified us of their absence and
- only if the travel is allowed (i.e. they meet the criteria to continue to be paid their benefit while overseas either because they meet the criteria for approved travel, or the requirements that travel be approved does not apply to them)
Otherwise, the client cannot have their benefit resumed until they return to New Zealand.

chunks.title: Paying a higher rate — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Paying a higher rate
You can make payment at a rate higher than the hospital rate where the client cannot meet their continuing costs from the hospital rate of payment and any other income they receive.
You will need to take into consideration:
- the client's financial commitments and
- access to other income
When you are considering payment of benefit at a rate higher than the hospital rate, generally you do not take cash assets into account as rates of benefit payment are not subject to an assets test.
If a client is required to make Child Support payments and does not qualify for an exemption from Inland Revenue Child Support, you can increase the hospital rate to include any Child Support payments that are required to be apportioned from the benefit.
For more information about paying at a higher rate see:
- Guidelines for paying a higher rate
## Maximum amount payable
You can pay a rate higher than the hospital rate up to the maximum rate of Sole Parent Support that would otherwise be payable.

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
To pay a benefit more than 28 days during any 52 week period:
- the client must be continuing to receive their benefit while absent from New Zealand because: they have an approved travel reason orthey are not required to have an approved travel reason in order to be paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand
- they have an approved travel reason or
- they are not required to have an approved travel reason in order to be paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand
- the client could not return to New Zealand because of new circumstances that: they could not reasonably foresee at the time when they left New Zealand andthey are out of the client's control
- they could not reasonably foresee at the time when they left New Zealand and
- they are out of the client's control
and
- Work and Income is satisfied that the extension of the absence is no longer than is necessary to address the new circumstances.
## Examples
A client who is absent from New Zealand for an approved reason may be prevented from returning by new unforeseen circumstances which include (but are not limited to):
- travel delays due to unforeseen weather events eg fog, volcano, flooding, earthquakes, terrorism
- travel delays due to transport options being cancelled
- health condition or injury or hospitalisation preventing return

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days for an approved reason — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text: Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. To pay a benefit more than 28 days during any 52 week period of absence from New Zealand, the client must be travelling for one of the following reasons: - essential travel - to attend a significant event relating to a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family), that the client would reasonably be expected to attend (eg visit a person who is seriously ill, seriously injured or whose death is imminent, attend a funeral, provide support to a party or witness to a court case, travel required for a court ordered care arrangement) - to attend a court case which the person is required to attend as a party or a witness - to attend a job interview or follow up on a job prospect - for clients with a disability, to receive vocational training or disability assistance-dog training not available in New Zealand during the period or periods of absence - for clients with a disability, to travel overseas for the sole or predominant purpose of competing in any overseas multinational or international Special Olympic or Paralympic Games competition - to provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster (flood, earthquake, fire) or similar adverse event (eg house fire) and - Work and Income must be satisfied, when considering the client's reason for travel, that the length of the absence is no longer than necessary for the reason for travel. In addition, where the client has already been paid a benefit while absent from New Zealand in the 52 week period Work and Income must be satisfied that either: - the client could not have reasonably foreseen them needing to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in a 52 week period or - the client could not have rearranged their affairs to avoid being absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in a 52 week period and - it would be unreasonable for the benefit not to be paid Note generally we would not pay more than 28 days extra travel per absence. For more information see: - Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason - Client not returned due to an unforeseen circumstance (within 28 days maximum) - Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum) - Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return

chunks.title: Payment when client absent from New Zealand — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Payment when client absent from New Zealand
There are some situations where the benefit payments will be affected when the client is absent from New Zealand. The action required by Work and Income will depend on the reason the client is absent from New Zealand and whether they are continuing to be paid a benefit.
For more information see:
- Ending payment for client who can travel for any reason
- Ending payment for client who needs an approved reason for travel
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum)
- Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event (within 28 day maximum)
- Child absent

chunks.title: Permanent absence — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Permanent absence
If a client is leaving New Zealand permanently, the Sole Parent Support must be cancelled from the day after departure.
If the client is moving to a country that has a reciprocal agreement with New Zealand they may qualify for a benefit or pension in that country.
## Moving to Australia
If the client is moving to Australia it is important that they are aware that they may not be able to receive a benefit until they have resided in Australia for two years after being granted permanent residence status.
## For more information
contact International Services
Also see:
- Reciprocal Agreements

chunks.title: Permitted travel reasons — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Permitted travel reasons
A client not otherwise entitled to be paid their Sole Parent Support while absent from New Zealand may have their payments continue for up to 28 days in any 52 week period, if their travel is for one (or a combination) of, the following permitted travel reasons:
- essential travel - to attend a significant event relating to a family member or a person who fulfils a role in relation to the client that is similar to that of a family member, that the client would reasonably be expected to attend
- to attend a court case which the person is required to attend as a party or a witness - this is to allow clients who are required by law to attend court and supports the maintenance of the law. A client would generally be expected to provide evidence that they are required to attend a court overseas. This would include documents from the court.
- to attend a job interview or follow up on a job prospect
- for clients with a disability, to receive vocational training or disability assistance-dog training not available in New Zealand during the time the client is absent
- for clients with a disability, to travel overseas for the sole or predominant purpose of competing in any overseas multinational or international Special Olympic or Paralympic Games competition
- to provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster (eg flood, earthquake, fire) or similar adverse event (eg house fire)
## Evidence of the client's situation
Although it may not be possible for the client to get proof of their situation, they should make a reasonable effort to do so.
For more information see:
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Definition of family member
- Essential Travel
- Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect
- Absences that do not prevent client meeting their obligations

chunks.title: Private hospital and homes — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Private hospital and homes
Sole Parent Support can be paid at the full rate regardless of the period of hospitalisation when a client is:
- admitted to a private hospital or
- admitted to a private home that provides residential care disability services
If the client is getting Extra help, this will need to be reviewed to see if their costs are continuing.

chunks.title: Protected earnings rate — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Protected earnings rate
Both the District Court Act and the Summary Proceedings Act provide that every Ministry of Justice attachment order must specify a 'protected earnings rate'. The protected earnings rate is usually 60% of the client’s net earnings after PAYE tax has been deducted or withheld.
If the attachment order will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate, then the order will not operate, and you must cancel or return the attachment order to the Ministry of Justice.
Calculating the client's income differs between attachment orders made under the Summary Proceedings Act and the District Court Act, as different benefits are taken into account.
It is important to determine what type of attachment order has been issued.
Summary Proceedings Act 1957
For orders made under the Summary Proceedings Act, the calculation of the client's income does not include Special Benefit, Temporary Additional Support, Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance, Winter Energy Payment, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit
District Court Act 2016
For orders made under the District Court Act, the client's income includes Special Benefit, Temporary Additional Support and Disability Allowance but does not include Child Disability Allowance, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit
## Example
An attachment order is received from the Ministry of Justice for $80.00 per week.
The order lists the protected earning rate as $405.91 per week.
We need to calculate whether adding the deduction of $80.00 will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate:
Calculate protected earnings rate
Sole Parent Support net rate (as at 1 April 2026)
$521.52
Plus Accommodation Supplement
$155.00
Total net earnings
$676.52
60% of total net earnings (= protected earnings)
$405.91
Calculate if Attachment Order will exceed protected earnings
Total net earnings
$676.52
Less Child Support deduction
$125.00
Less Ministry of Social Development debt
$70.00
Sub total
$481.52
Less Attachment Order
$80.00
Total net income remaining for the client per week
$401.52
The Attachment Order amount of $80.00 takes the client's total income remaining to $401.52, which is below the protected earnings rate of $405.91.
The attachment order will not operate, you must return it to the Ministry of Justice for the order to be amended.

chunks.title: Qualifies for another benefit — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Qualifies for another benefit
A client may qualify for another benefit due to a change in their circumstances. It is also important to determine if the client still qualifies for Sole Parent Support.
For example:
- if the client's last child leaves their care they would no longer qualify for Sole Parent Support and they would generally transfer to another benefit or
- a client reaches the qualifying age for New Zealand Superannuation
If the client qualifies for more than one benefit they must be told which benefit is the most beneficial for their particular circumstances. You will need to advise them of:
- benefit rates
- the effect of any income they may receive (income reduction and any exemptions) and
- benefit obligations
The client must make the final decision on which benefit they receive after being given all relevant information.
For more information see:
- Sole Parent Support Qualifications
- Supported Living Payment Qualifications
- Jobseeker Support Qualifications
- New Zealand Superannuation Qualifications
- Processing Standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Rate of payment — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Rate of payment
If payment of Sole Parent Support is to continue while a sole parent client is in prison, you will need to determine the rate to pay to the temporary caregiver.
The Sole Parent Support should generally be paid at the equivalent rate of Unsupported Child's Benefit less the family tax credit and Best Start tax credit that would be payable if the caregiver qualified for this, see: Examples - sole parents
## Exception
However, there is discretion to continue payment at the full sole parent rate.
You can consider including the following costs to calculate the rate to pay the temporary caregiver while the client is in prison:
- rent or outgoings if the children are being cared for in the client's home
- the client's other commitments if these costs are for essential items and they cannot be suspended, such as Child Support payments (where the client does not qualify for an exemption) or a hire purchase for an essential item
Note the total amount paid to the temporary caregiver must not exceed the maximum amount of Sole Parent Support payable. An application for this assistance must be made by the temporary caregiver.
## SWIFTT
The Sole Parent Support, family tax credit and Best Start tax credit rate should continue in the client's name and be paid to the caregiver as an agent in SWIFTT.
When the temporary caregiver is to be paid less than the maximum rate of Sole Parent Support, you will need to add this as a non-standard rate using the SNSRA screen in SWIFTT.
For more information see:
- Examples - sole parents
- Decision guidelines - sole parents
- Remanded in custody
- Temporary caregiver
- Winter Energy Payment - Changes and reviews - imprisonment

chunks.title: Date of review — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Date of review
The child should be excluded from the start of the pay period following the date Student Allowance (or Independent Circumstances Allowance) commences.
Note there are specific rules for deciding whether a child is considered a dependent child when they turn 18 and they are continuing in education.

chunks.title: Gets a Student Loan — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Gets a Student Loan
Getting a Student Loan (including the living cost component) does not mean the child is financially independent.
If the child continues to be the client's primary responsibility and maintained as a member of their family and financially dependent (that is the parent is meeting some of the costs for the child) the child can continue to be included in the benefit until the start of the pay period following:
- the date they turn 18 or
- where the child is 18 and continuing in education, the earlier of: the date they are no longer enrolled in school or tertiary education orthe date they are no longer attending school or tertiary education as required orthe date the child is financially independent orthe date the child leaves the parent or caregiver's care or31 December of the year they turn 18
- the date they are no longer enrolled in school or tertiary education or
- the date they are no longer attending school or tertiary education as required or
- the date the child is financially independent or
- the date the child leaves the parent or caregiver's care or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18
## Extra help
When the dependent child is required to live away from home to undertake their tertiary study, the client may be able to get assistance for accommodation costs.

chunks.title: Release from prison — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Release from prison
A client may be entitled to Sole Parent Support when they are released from prison. The date to recommence payment depends on the length of time the client has been in prison.

chunks.title: Release on bail — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Release on bail
When a client is released on bail, Sole Parent Support can be paid from the date of release providing:
- the client is living apart from their partner and lost the support or being inadequately maintained by the partner
- the client is divorced
- the client is single (never had a partner)
- the client's partner has been imprisoned or released from prison on residential parole or
- the client's partner is deceased
The client must also meet the definition of the parent of 1 or more dependent children.
Note if the client has been in custody for more than 31 days an initial stand-down will be imposed.
For more information see:
- Prisoners no stand-down applies
- Home detention

chunks.title: Remanded in custody — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Remanded in custody
Generally, when a client is remanded in custody awaiting a further court appearance their benefit should be stopped. However, there is discretion to continue payment of Sole Parent Support after taking the client's financial circumstances and commitments into account.
When deciding whether to continue paying Sole Parent Support for the period of remand for a particular client consider the following:
- has the client been remanded pending a further hearing or for sentencing
- does the client have continuing costs that cannot be avoided, such as rent and hire purchase for essential items
- does the client have dependent children
Every situation should be considered on a case-by-case basis.
For help contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances of the client before making a decision.

chunks.title: Review of Annual Income — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text: The Review of Annual Income ensures that clients getting Sole Parent Support have received the correct rate of payment for the past 52 weeks. Clients do not have a Review of Annual Income if their benefit has not been abated at any point during the period that income is assessed (the 52-week review period). Clients who have not received any income during this period will also not have a review.

chunks.title: Income received during the review period — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text: Income received during the 52-week period following the client's commencement date, and each 52 week period thereafter, is assessed against the benefit paid to the client during this time. Most types of income are charged against Sole Parent Support for the review year the income was earned in or the period it relates to. The relevant period may be a period in the past or a future date. Only income charged during the current review period is considered for the Review of Annual Income. If the client has transferred between benefits, but has continuously been getting a benefit that can have income charged annually, the commencement date is the date they first started getting an annual benefit.

chunks.title: Child Support income for Reviews of Annual Income — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text: Non-information share Child Support Non-information share Child Support payments are charged as income using the general charging rules that are used for most other types of income. Any non-information share Child Support payments charged as income during the current review period are included in the Review of Annual Income. Information share Child Support Information share Child Support payments are charged forward as income, using defined rules. The income charge is always for 4 or 5 weeks from when the client gets the payment, regardless of what period the payment relates to. Any information share Child Support payments charged as income during the current review period are included in the Review of Annual Income. Note the amount of information share Child Support payment charged as income may not be the same amount of Child Support a client got in the review period. This could happen if a client gets an information share Child Support payment shortly before the end of the review period. Only the income charged during the review period can be included in the Review of Annual Income. Example Ophelia gets Sole Parent Support and gets information share Child Support payments from her child's other parent. Ophelia's review period for her Review of Annual Income is 6 September to 5 September the following year. Ophelia gets an information share Child Support payment on 21 August. This payment is charged forward for 4 weeks, from the week beginning 19 August. Only the income charged from 19 August to 5 September will be included in this years' Review of Annual Income. The remainder of the 4-week income charge related to that Child Support payment will be included in the following year's review.

chunks.title: Split care — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Split care
Split care is when parents with 2 or more children are living apart and each parent has the care of at least one of their children on a full-time basis.
The child(ren) that is living with the Sole Parent Support client can be included as a dependent child.
Note that in split care situations, generally only one parent can receive Sole Parent Support. The other parent must qualify, in their own right, for another benefit.
For more information see:
- Sole Parent Support Split care

chunks.title: Student Loan repayments — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Student Loan repayments
Clients with a Student Loan must make repayments to Inland Revenue when the income they get is over the repayment threshold. This level is called the 'income threshold'.
A person must make repayments to Inland Revenue when their income is over $464.00 gross per week ($24,128 gross per year) as at 1 April 2026. Note non-taxable Extra help such as family tax credit, Accommodation Supplement and Winter Energy Payment do not count as income in this instance.
If the client's income is over this income threshold, the Ministry of Social Development can make the required deduction. However, this is only done if the client requests it.
If the client's portion of benefit is below the income threshold, there is no provision to make voluntary repayments through SWIFTT. The client can make voluntary payments direct to Inland Revenue at any time.
Note the following:
- Student Loan deductions can only be made from taxable benefits
- Student Loan deductions cannot be made if the client's benefit is below the income threshold
- when a client receives a married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit only the client's portion is taken into consideration when assessing Student Loan repayments
- when a client is receiving a reduced rate of payment due to other income, the Student Loan deduction is assessed on the net payment after income deduction.
For more information on Student Loans see:
- Students Student Loan

chunks.title: Study — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Study
Clients have an obligation to advise Work and Income of any change in their circumstances that may affect their ability to meet their obligations on Sole Parent Support, such as commencing study.
When a Sole Parent Support client intends to or has commenced study, you will need to find out:
- the date study starts and
- the type of study, that is part-time or full-time
This will help you decide the appropriate review action required.
For more information see:
- Studying or training on Sole Parent Support
## Client engaged in study or training
Clients can receive Sole Parent Support and undertake full-time or part-time study, or training as long as either:
- they can meet their work or work preparation obligations at the same time or
- they are eligible for an exemption from their work obligations in order to complete study or training
If a client is not able to study and meet their work or work preparation obligations on Sole Parent Support, and they are not eligible for an exemption, they should consider applying for assistance from StudyLink.
For more information see:
- Studying or training on Sole Parent Support
- Client applies for assistance from StudyLink

chunks.title: Tax codes — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Tax codes
Sole Parent Support is taxed at the 'M' rate.
Sole Parent Support is always considered the client's primary source of income regardless of the amount paid.
If the client has other income this is always considered the client's secondary income. Clients can apply to Inland Revenue for a tailored tax code for other income.

chunks.title: Taxation — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Taxation
Sole Parent Support is a taxable benefit. MSD makes payments to clients at the net rate after the deduction of tax. MSD passes the tax on to Inland Revenue.
Generally MSD will request a client to provide their IRD number.

chunks.title: Extra assistance during temporary care — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Extra assistance during temporary care
Any assistance for additional costs due to temporary care situations should be met, in the first instance, by the principal caregiver. Where this is not available, you can consider Special Needs Grants assistance for the client.

chunks.title: Temporary caregiver — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Temporary caregiver
When a client is imprisoned, you will need to find out who is caring for the client's children and the length of time the client is likely to be in prison. This information can be obtained by contacting the prison liaison officer at the Department of Corrections.
If another person is caring for the client's dependent children, generally the temporary caregiver will need to apply for financial assistance in their own right.
They may be entitled to:
- have the children included as dependent children in their current benefit
- Unsupported Childs Benefit
- Emergency Benefit Single and caring for a child or
- family tax credit and Best Start tax credit through Inland Revenue
## Exception
There is discretion to pay all or part of the Sole Parent Support to a temporary caregiver caring for the client's children.
There is also discretion to continue payment if the client is remanded in custody pending a further court appearance.
For more information to help you decide, see:
- Decision guidelines - sole parents
- Examples - Sole parents
- Rate of payment
- Remanded in custody

chunks.title: Underpaid — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Underpaid
When a client has been underpaid Sole Parent Support and is owed arrears, MSD will work out the amount of tax and pass this on to Inland Revenue.
From 1 April 2024, if an arrears payment relates to a previous tax year, the arrears will not be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment. This means the client will not have to pay any more tax on the payment.
Only arrears payments related to the current tax year will be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment.
Example
A client is paid arrears on 12 June 2026. This payment represents arrears for 25 March 2026 to 8 June 2026.
The arrears for 25 March to 31 March 2026 represent a past tax year, so they will not be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment. The arrears for 1 April to 8 June 2026 represent the current tax year, so they will be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment.
## Overpaid
If a client has been overpaid, the overpayment is always established for the net amount. Inland Revenue will return the tax portion of the overpayment directly to MSD.
The overpayment will reduce the amount(s) of benefit and tax paid in the tax year in which the overpayment was made, that is, the overpayment will directly relate to the tax year(s) in which it occurred.

chunks.title: Verification of annual income — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Verification of annual income
Depending on the client's circumstances, they will either need to:
- provide income verification for the 52 week period
- check if their information is correct. If it is correct, they do not need to do anything. If it is different they will need to provide verification as above.
If the client cannot provide verification (for example payslips) then you can contact the employer and ask them to complete the
- Employment and earnings information for reviews (V26) form
For further details on how to charge income see:
- Core Policy Income

chunks.title: Weekend leave — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Weekend leave
Where the client is receiving the hospital rate and they are on leave for the weekend only, you should pay the appropriate full rate of benefit for the equivalent number of days the client is on leave.
## Example
Client is on leave from Friday to Monday, pay the appropriate full rate of benefit for 4 days. Generally, you will do this by completing a back dated review.
Note the dates of admission and discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital.

chunks.title: Youngest dependent child turns 14 — main benefits > sole parent support > changes and reviews sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Youngest dependent child turns 14
A client's Sole Parent Support expires on the date their youngest dependent child turns 14 years old.

chunks.title: Charging income — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Charging income
SWIFTT will automatically calculate the rate of benefit payable when you add the client's income on the INCMH screen.
## Weekly income
A client who has income charged weekly can receive up to $160 per week before their income will affect their benefit.
For clients who receive over $160 per week:
- income between $160 and $250 per week their benefit is reduced by 30 cents for each $1.00 of income
- income over $250 per week their benefit is reduced by 70 cents for every $1.00 of income
## Annual income
A client who has income charged annually can receive up to $8,320 per year before their income will affect their benefit.
For clients who receive over $8,320:
- income between $8,320 and $13,000 per year their benefit is reduced by 30 cents for each $1.00 of income
- income over $13,000 per year their benefit is reduced by 70 cents for every $1.00 of income
For more details on what is income and how to charge it, see:
- Core policy Income
- Core policy Types of income
- Exemption for severe disablement
- Weekly income example
- Review of Annual Income
## Childcare costs income exemption
If a Sole Parent Support client has to pay childcare costs because they are working they can receive an additional income exemption.
For more information see:
- Childcare cost income exemption

chunks.title: Child changes and social obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Child changes and social obligations
Sometimes a client will have a change in circumstances that may mean the client is no longer required to comply with their social obligations. This includes where:
- a dependent child changes age and the social obligation that applied for the dependent child in their care is no longer relevant or
- child leaves care (for example starts to live with another parent or caregiver or goes into the care of Oranga Tamariki)
For more information see:
- Changes and reviews Child changes
- Child changes during engagement and support process

chunks.title: Child changes during engagement and support process — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Child changes during engagement and support process
A client may have a change of circumstance which means they are no longer subject to a social obligation. These changes may include (but are not limited to):
- a dependent child leaves their care or
- a dependent child changes age and the social obligations that apply for the dependent child in their care are no longer relevant
If this happens during the regular engagement and support process, the client cannot be failed and they are no longer subject to the social obligation.
For more information see:
- Social obligations - actively engaging with clients [no link find out why]
- Overview of social obligations according to the age of the child
- Changes and reviews Child changes

chunks.title: Child not supported — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Child not supported
For Sole Parent Support, you can consider as a dependent child any child whose parents are unable, or in exceptional circumstances, unwilling to support that child.
When a client is caring for a child that is not their own, consider the following:
- Can the client be considered as the parent of the child?
- What are the reasons they are caring for the child?
- What are the parent's circumstances?
- How long does the client expect to care for the child? (the legislation doesn't tell you how long the child is expected to be in the care of the client but it should be expected to be a long term arrangement, not just a few weeks)
- If long term, are more formal arrangements being considered (for example adoption)?
- Do the parents of the child have the ability to contribute to the cost of care?
- Is the child a qualifying child for Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit?
For help to determine whether parents may be unable or unwilling to care for the child, see:
- Determining who is a parent
- Parents unable to care for child
- Parents unwilling to care for child
- Family breakdown

chunks.title: Deciding if a child is financially dependent — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Deciding if a child is financially dependent
When a client states that they are receiving payments for a child's expenses you must decide if the child is a dependent child of the client.
A child does not have to be solely financially dependent on a client to be considered a dependent child. All that is required is that the child is financially dependent on the person to some degree.
However, being financially dependent on a client is only part of the qualifications of a dependent child. The child must still meet all the qualifications to be considered dependent.
If another person or body is paying for the child's expenses, including payments for the care provided, the child is not financially dependent on the client.
If a client is receiving payments toward the expenses of a dependent child this is regarded as income for benefit purposes.
For more information see:
- Charging income
- Dependent child
## Parents unable or unwilling to care for child
For Sole Parent Support, a child whose parents are unable, or in exceptional circumstances, unwilling, may be considered a dependent child.

chunks.title: Childcare cost income exemption — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Childcare cost income exemption
There is an additional $20 per week income exemption for Sole Parent Support clients when they have to pay childcare costs while they are working.
It is not necessary for the child to attend an approved childcare centre, private arrangements can be accepted.
Entitlement to a Childcare Subsidy or OSCAR must be assessed first. If the total cost of childcare is not covered by the subsidy the client can receive the additional income exemption.
The exemption would be the lesser of:
- the amount the client pays for childcare or
- the cost of childcare not covered by a subsidy or
- $20 per week
The exemption only applies for the weeks the sole parent pays for childcare while they are working.

chunks.title: Client accepts the results of a failed screening test — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client accepts the results of a failed screening test
A client will be asked by the employer, training provider or the drug test provider to confirm that they accept the result of the failed screening test. They can accept the result of the failed drug test by:
- signing the Pre-employment Drug Test Result Confirmation Form or
- verbally accepting the result
When a client has accepted the results, this means that they understand:
- there is no requirement to send the failed screening test sample to a laboratory for evidential testing
- this may result in a sanction being imposed and
- they may have to repay Work and Income for the cost of the failed drug test
Before you initiate an obligations failure for a client because they have failed a drugs test, without having a good and sufficient reason, you must receive confirmation from the employer that the client has failed the test.
Once you have received confirmation from the employer or training provider that a client has failed the screening test, and all testing has been completed, an obligations failure should be initiated.
Although the client can still dispute other parts of the decision, by providing a good and sufficient reason for the obligations failure, they cannot dispute the result of the screening drug test because they have already accepted the failed result.
For more information see:
- Informing a client of the drug test obligation failure
- Reimbursement to employers and debt recovery
- Drug test obligation failures - Good and sufficient reasons
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Client does not accept the results of a failed screening drug test

chunks.title: Sample sent for evidential test — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Sample sent for evidential test
Some employers, training providers, or drug test providers, will send all screening test samples for evidential testing, regardless of whether the client accepted the result of the failed screening test or not.
If the client passes the evidential drug test, then the client is not required to repay Work and Income for the cost of either the failed screening drug test or the evidential drug test.
If the client also fails the evidential drug test, the client is required to repay Work and Income for the costs of both the failed tests (screening and evidential).
## Client disputes the results of an evidential drug test
A client can dispute the result of a failed evidential test.
For more information see:
- Disputes and reviews of an obligations failure
- Client has failed a screening drug test
- Informing a client of the drug test obligation failure
- Reimbursement to employers and debt recovery
- Drug test obligation failures - Good and sufficient reasons
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures

chunks.title: Client does not need to complete the reapplication process — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Sole Parent Support clients do not need to complete the 52 week reapplication process where they are, at any time during the notice period, in one of the following circumstances: - in hospital - in residential disability care or rest home care or - living in or visiting a region affected by an emergency or adverse event and they are unable to reasonably leave the area Clients in one of these specific circumstances will have their expiry date reset to the end of the next 52 week period. They will be sent a letter advising that, because of their current situation, they do not need to reapply. The client does not need to complete the reapplication process until their next expiry date, if they still need Sole Parent Support.

chunks.title: Clients in hospital — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: If MSD is aware a client is in hospital when the 'initial notice to reapply' letter is due to be sent, the letter will not be sent. If the client is in hospital at any time during their notice period, they do not need to complete the 52 week reapplication process. MSD will review the client's Sole Parent Support and any Extra Help they get when the client is discharged from hospital. For more information see: - Discharge from hospital

chunks.title: Client in residential disability care or rest home care — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: If MSD is aware a client is in residential disability care or rest home care when the 'initial notice to reapply' is due to be sent, the letter will not be sent. If the client is in residential disability care or rest home care at any time during their notice period, they do not need to complete the 52 week reapplication process. This includes but is not limited to clients in residential disability care or rest home care getting Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy.

chunks.title: Emergency or adverse events — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: It may be determined that a client no longer needs to complete the 52 week reapplication process if they experience an emergency or adverse event which affects their ability to reapply before their expiry date. This is limited to clients who, at any point during their notice period, are: - living in or visiting a region affected by an emergency or adverse event and - they are unable to reasonably leave the area. An area affected by an emergency or adverse event means that: - a local state of emergency or national emergency is in force in the area (e.g. because of a natural disaster such as a flood or earthquake), or - an epidemic notice is in force in the area (i.e. because of an outbreak of a quarantinable disease that is affecting or may affect the area), or - other exceptional circumstances are affecting the area As an emergency or adverse event affects a whole area or region, or is nationwide, it is likely that multiple clients will be affected by the event. Generally, in an emergency or adverse event, MSD will be able to determine which clients have been affected as a result of the emergency or adverse event.

chunks.title: Client has failed a screening drug test — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client has failed a screening drug test
If a client fails a screening drug test with an employer, training provider or drug test provider, they will be advised that they have failed and they will be asked if they:
- accept the results of the screening drug test or
- do not accept the result of the screening drug test
For more information see:
- Informing a client of the drug test obligation failure
- Client accepts the results of a failed screening test
- Client does not accept the results of a failed screening test

chunks.title: Client has recently changed locations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client has recently changed locations
Most clients who have recently changed locations will be able to provide details of a nominated person to verify their relationship status.
However, some clients will be unable to provide the details of a nominated person who has known them for at least 2 years prior to their application, for example because the client has recently returned to New Zealand.
Note it is not necessary for the client and the nominated person to live in the same city or town. A client who has recently moved may still be able to provide the details of a nominated person in the city or town from which they have moved or elsewhere in New Zealand.
In this case, where you have asked the client to get the nominated person to complete a Relationship Status Verification form, you should discuss with the client any issues there might be with getting the form returned in a reasonable time.
If the client is still unable to name a nominated person, Work and Income will consider their application for Sole Parent Support without the details of a nominated person.
For more information see:
- Extending the 20 working day period
- Qualifications
- Relationship Status Verification form contents
- Relationship status verification required
- Who can verify a client's relationship status

chunks.title: Client in hospital — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client in hospital
A client's Sole Parent Support rate of payment can be different if they are in hospital.
The rate is reduced to the hospital rate when the client has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks (not after receiving a benefit for 13 weeks).
The hospital rate allows for the cost of personal items, which patients are expected to provide for themselves.
## Exception
If the client has been in hospital for 13 weeks or more at the commencement date of the benefit, the rate of payment is the hospital rate.
For more information about the hospital rate see:
- Changes and reviews Hospitalisation

chunks.title: Client is experiencing family violence — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client is experiencing family violence
If a client reports that they cannot provide the details of a nominated person because they have just left a situation of family violence, or they are still with a partner and are experiencing family violence, you can consider their application for Sole Parent Support without the details of a nominated person.

chunks.title: Client is meeting their social obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client is meeting their social obligations
If, during any of the three Contact Steps of engagement and support, you consider that the client is meeting their social obligations you will need to let the client know that:
- as they are meeting their social obligations, you do not require any more information or contact from them and
- if they require any support regarding their social obligations they can contact Work and Income at any time
The appropriate outcome for the specific social obligations that apply to each of the client's dependent children needs to be recorded in OBMAN.
For more information on the three step process of engagement see:
- Social obligations - actively engaging with clients [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Client leaves Mangere Resettlement Centre — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client leaves Mangere Resettlement Centre
No stand-down applies to the commencement of a benefit when a client has left the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre.
For more information see:
- Refugees and protected persons
- Commencement date
- No stand-down applies

chunks.title: Client receiving youth support payments — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client receiving youth support payments
A young person who is receiving Young Parent Payment or Youth Payment when they reach the qualifying age for Sole Parent Support can only be granted that benefit if they have been receiving Young Parent Payment or Youth Payment for 6 months.
## Young Parent Payment or Youth Payment was cancelled
Where a young person was previously receiving Young Parent Payment or Youth Payment and this was cancelled because, for example, they moved into employment or went overseas, and they now require financial assistance, the young person can be granted Sole Parent Support if they meet all the qualifications.

chunks.title: Client's job ceases during an employment trial period — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client's job ceases during an employment trial period
Any employment that has an employment trial period included in a client's employment agreement is assessed the same way as any other employment.
A client's job can cease during the employment trial period for any number of reasons, such as:
- the employer not being able to afford the client's wages
- the employer's belief that the client lacks the necessary skills
- misconduct
- any other reason the employer decides to cease the client's employment or
- the client leaving of their own accord
When an employer gives the client notice during the employment trial, they are not required to advise why they have decided to end the client's employment. They are however, required to provide details of their last date of employment and the date they will be paid to.
If the employer gave notice to the client of ending their employment after the employment trial, the employer must provide the client with the reason for ending their employment (ie the employment trial rules do not apply).
To determine the commencement date of the benefit, the client needs to provide evidence and reasons for ceasing their employment, their last day of duty and the last date paid to.
If the client cannot provide this evidence and reason for their employment ceasing, their last day of duty or last date paid to, you can contact the client's employer and ask them to complete the Employment and earnings information for applications (V06) form.
If the client's employer does not provide the reason for the client's employment ceasing during the employment trial, accept the client's reasons for the termination and continue with the application process. However, the employer must complete the date ceased and last pay details.
For more information see:
- Employment trial period of up to 90 days

chunks.title: Client to provide details of a nominated person — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client to provide details of a nominated person
Clients applying for Sole Parent Support are asked on their application form to provide details of a nominated person who has known them for at least 2 years prior to their application and can verify the client's relationship status.
It is not mandatory for a client to provide details of a nominated person on their application form.
If a client is not willing to name a nominated person, you should discuss with the client the reasons why they are unable or unwilling to do so.
From this discussion with the client, you will need to decide if you have enough information to assess whether the client meets the relationship qualification for Sole Parent Support.
In some cases, it is not reasonable for a client not to name a third party.

chunks.title: Clients 65 years or over — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Clients 65 years or over
Clients aged 65 years or older may get Sole Parent Support provided they meet all the qualifications.
These clients must complete the 52 week reapplication process before their expiry date, but eligibility for New Zealand Superannuation must be checked.
For more information see:
- Completing the 52 week reapplication process
- Sole Parent Support Qualifications
- New Zealand Superannuation Qualifications

chunks.title: Cook Island, Niue and Tokelau clients — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Cook Island, Niue and Tokelau clients
Clients born in the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau are automatically New Zealand citizens (by birth). Generally they will travel to New Zealand on a New Zealand passport.
However, they must still have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years at any one time before they can receive the Sole Parent Support.
Other residents of the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau will be required to produce a proof of residence document and meet the 2 years continuous residence requirement in New Zealand.
## Australian clients
Australian citizens are lawfully allowed in New Zealand as they are deemed to hold a residence class visa. However, they must still meet the 2 years residence qualification to qualify for Sole Parent Support.
## British clients
Clients of British nationality who arrived in New Zealand prior to 2 April 1974 were allowed residence in New Zealand without a visa or a permit. However, they must still meet the residence requirement for Sole Parent Support.

chunks.title: Clients moving to a limited employment location — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Clients moving to a limited employment location
If a client is thinking of moving to a limited employment location (or from one limited employment location to another), you must tell them that moving to a limited employment location means they may not be able to meet their work obligations, including to be available for, and take reasonable steps to obtain, suitable employment in that location. This is because of a lack of employment opportunities in that area.
To meet their work obligations, clients moving to a limited employment location must demonstrate that they have access to reliable transport and are willing, and realistically able, to commute to a nearby town or centre where employment is available.
Continued residence in a limited employment location without meeting this requirement could result in an obligations failure being initiated.
Note we do not want clients to put themselves in a situation where they will be unable to continue to meet their work obligations. You need to work with all clients planning to move to a limited employment location, as appropriate, to explore:
- why they want to move
- whether and how the need to move could be alleviated without their having to move to a limited employment location
- how they plan to meet their work obligations should they move to a limited employment location
For more information see:
- Why is the client moving to a limited employment location?
- Decision guidelines - clients moving to a limited employment location
- Deskfile Limited employment locations alert sheet

chunks.title: Clients undertaking voluntary work — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Clients undertaking voluntary work
Sole parents can undertake voluntary work provided they continue to meet their work or work preparation obligations.
Sole parents with work preparation or work obligations may have to give up some or all of their voluntary activities if a work preparation activity is required or if a suitable job becomes available.
For more information see:
- Voluntary Work [no link find out why]
- Suitable employment
- Studying or training on Sole Parent Support

chunks.title: Clients with dependent children - 50% protection — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Sole parents who fail their obligations and have a financial sanction imposed do not have their whole benefit sanctioned. Instead, a maximum sanction of 50% of the total benefit may be imposed. The balance payable is known as 50% protection. Sole parents who are sanctioned can continue to get full Extra help assistance, regardless of the grade of sanction. This includes the Winter Energy Payment. For more information on what a client can continue to get when sanctioned, see: - Paying other assistance during a sanction If the client has not recomplied after 2 weeks, MSD will contact them to discuss financial assistance and recompliance. If the client has still not recomplied at 4 weeks, MSD will send the client a letter advising they need to attend an appointment to discuss ongoing entitlement to benefit. For more information, including treatment of supplementary assistance, see: - Sanction period - Two week intervention [no link find out why] - Sanction period - Four week intervention [no link find out why] Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.

chunks.title: Grade 1 and 2 sanctions — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: For a first and second obligations failure, a sole parent's benefit is reduced by 50% unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed (for a first failure only). They continue to get full Extra help assistance (including the full rate of Winter Energy Payment). For more information on non-financial sanctions see: - Non-financial sanctions If the client does not recomply within 4 weeks, they will have 50% of their benefit suspended. 50% of their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or 50% of their benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks. They continue to get full Extra help (including the full rate of Winter Energy Payment).

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: For a third obligations failure a sole parent is subject to a non-entitlement period for a period of 13 weeks and will have 50% of their benefit cancelled. The sole parent may get a provisional benefit and have their benefit increased to 100% if they start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities. They continue to get full Extra help assistance (including the full rate of the Winter Energy Payment). For more information see: - Recompliance

chunks.title: 50% protection applies during non-entitlement period for other reasons — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: The 50% protection also applies to sole parents if they are subject to a 13-week non-entitlement period for voluntarily leaving employment without a good and sufficient reason, or dismissal due to misconduct, or refusing to accept any offer of suitable employment. For more information see: - Recompliance - Non-entitlement period for 13 weeks [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Clients without permanent residence — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Clients without permanent residence
If a client does not have permanent residence they cannot receive Sole Parent Support (even if they have lived in New Zealand continuously for 2 years). They may be able to receive an Emergency Maintenance Allowance if they:
- are lawfully present in New Zealand and are awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protection status in New Zealand or
- have refugee or protection status in New Zealand or
- are applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 and are compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances
For more information see:
- Refugees and protected persons

chunks.title: Commencement date — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
To decide when Sole Parent Support can start you must first find the entitlement date. This is usually the date that a person no longer has a means of support.
For a list of these dates see:
- Entitlement date
Sole Parent Support is subject to an initial stand-down period of up to a maximum of 2 weeks after the entitlement date.
Generally the commencement date is:
- the day after the initial stand-down ends or
- the application date
whichever is the later.
However, if a client applies for Sole Parent Support within 28 days of their entitlement date the commencement date rules are different. See:
- Twenty-eight day rule

chunks.title: Commencement after 2-week search period — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Commencement after 2-week search period
If a client’s position starts in the first week after the 2-week search period ends, the first day of the position might not be the first day of the week.
If MSD is satisfied the approved position will start within that week, and the client can still complete their required 5 hours, the position period can start from the first day of the week.

chunks.title: Community Work Experience — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Community Work Experience
Community Work Experience is a non-financial sanction that can be imposed on a client instead of a Grade 1 financial sanction. It is intended to help clients build work-related skills and confidence, and also build connections in their community.
A client will work with a community or voluntary organisation, for at least 5 hours a week, for 4 weeks.
A client will have a 2-week search period before their Community Work Experience begins to find a suitable position and organisation.
MSD will need to confirm whether the organisation and position are suitable before the client can begin.
Once a client completes their Community Work Experience, they are considered to have recomplied with their obligation failure and do not need to complete any other recompliance activities.

chunks.title: Completing the 52 week reapplication process — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Completing the 52 week reapplication process
Clients must complete the 52 week reapplication process before their expiry date unless they have exceptional circumstances. If a client does not do this, their Sole Parent Support will stop.
To continue to get their benefit, clients must attend a 52 week reapplication appointment. This can be done either by phone, or face to face at a service centre depending on their circumstances.
To complete the 52 week reapplication process the client must:
- meet the qualifications for Sole Parent Support
- attend the reapplication appointment
- complete the 52 week reapplication form online or during their application appointment
- provide any supporting evidence required
- participate in and complete a Comprehensive Work Assessment
## Actions required at completion
Once MSD is satisfied that the client has completed the 52 week reapplication process for Sole Parent Support, MSD must:
- advise the client that their Sole Parent Support will continue and
- refer the client to suitable work or an appropriate employment related activity
For more information see:

chunks.title: Comprehensive Work Assessment — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Comprehensive Work Assessment
The Comprehensive Work Assessment is a compulsory part of the 52 week reapplication process for Sole Parent Support. It is designed to support in-depth conversations with clients to help them prepare for and find suitable employment.
All Sole Parent Support clients must complete the Comprehensive Work Assessment at their reapplication appointment as part of the 52 week reapplication process.
## Client does not complete Comprehensive Work Assessment
If a client does not complete the Comprehensive Work Assessment before their expiry date, their Sole Parent Support will stop
Clients who fail to complete the 52 week reapplication process but still need Sole Parent Support will need to apply as a new applicant. The client will be subject to the usual commencement date rules, including the initial stand-down.

chunks.title: Contact made but reapplication not completed by expiry date — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Contact made but reapplication not completed by expiry date
Where a client makes contact to complete the 52 week reapplication process before their expiry date but it cannot be completed before their expiry date, through no fault of their own, an extension may be granted.
An extension may be granted for up to 10 working days starting on their expiry date, on the condition that the client complete the reapplication process as soon as possible and within the extension period.
Generally, this extension can be used when:
- a client contacts MSD before their expiry date and there are no available appointments for them or
- there are delays in MSD processing the reapplication or
- a client cannot attend an appointment as the MSD service centre has closed unexpectedly, for example in an emergency
Note if a client is granted an extension and completes the reapplication process within 10 working days of their expiry date, and they still qualify for Sole Parent Support, the benefit must be regranted from their expiry date.
If a client does not complete the 52 week reapplication process within the extension period or no longer qualifies for Sole Parent Support, their benefit will be cancelled from their expiry date. The amount of benefit (including any Extra help) that was conditionally paid during the extension period must be established as a debt.
## Reapplying as a new applicant
If the client does not complete the reapplication process within the extension period or was not granted an extension, they must apply as a new applicant if they still need Sole Parent Support. Their expired benefit must be cancelled from their expiry date before they can be granted Sole Parent Support as a new applicant.
The client will be subject to the usual commencement date rules, including the initial stand-down.
Note if the client advises they want to apply for Sole Parent Support as a new applicant and completes the reapplication form, MSD must use their reapplication form as their new application.
For more information see:
- Commencement date
- Initial stand-down

chunks.title: Counting previous obligations failures — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Counting previous obligations failures
The sanction imposed depends on how often the client has failed to comply with their obligations in the previous 24 months while getting a benefit.
Previous failures are only counted if the failure occurred within the last 24 months while continuously getting a benefit.
The 24-month count starts from the day the obligation failure is imposed. Each obligation failure has its own 24-month count.
Example
A client fails their first obligation on 1 June 2025. They fail another obligation on 1 October 2025, and have an obligation failure count of two. Their obligation failure count is reset to one on 1 June 2027, 24 months after they failed their first obligation.
Their obligation failure count is reset to zero on 1 October 2027, 24 months after the second obligation failure.
## Failure of different obligations add to failure count
The failure count includes all obligation failures. If a client fails a work obligation and then a later failure related to social obligations in a 24-month period, this would be counted as 2 failures.
## Youth clients
When a client transfers from Young Parent Payment or Youth Payment to a benefit without youth activity obligations the count will be zero. This is because the sanction regime is different for young people getting these payments.

chunks.title: Court imposed conditions — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Court imposed conditions
This exemption may apply to clients with work or work preparation obligations.
A client serving a sentence of home detention, or who has conditions and requirements of a court sentence or court order that limits their ability to meet all their obligations can be exempt from meeting some or all of their work or work preparation obligations.
This can be a full or partial exemption depending on the conditions imposed by the Courts.
This includes clients who:
- are former prisoners who are subject to probation or parole conditions which means that they cannot meet all their work obligations and
- have work obligations and are required as part of a sentence of the court or other court order to attend programmes or other activities, or have conditions imposed upon them (e.g. bail conditions) which limit their ability to meet all their work obligations
Home detainees or former prisoners are case managed by their probation officer. Part of this case management includes undertaking appropriate job search and activities to improve their prospects of obtaining paid employment.
In all cases, the case manager should contact the probation officer to facilitate any meetings.
Note this can be a full or partial exemption depending on the conditions imposed by the Court.

chunks.title: Court ordered split care arrangements — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Court ordered split care arrangements
You can only pay Sole Parent Support to one parent, unless, there is a court order awarding split care. A split care order is however, not the only acceptable court order you can consider.
When split care arrangements have the sanction, authority or approval of the Family Court the payment of Sole Parent Support to both sole parents is allowed. This means that we could also accept:
- an order that provides that each parent will have sole care of at least one child
- separate sole orders in respect of each child
- a joint order where the court granted joint care but recognised that each parent would act as the day to day caregiver of at least one child
- a sole order for one child and a joint parenting order for another child where the purpose of making the joint parenting order is to recognise when the other parent is the principal day to day caregiver of the other child
## Joint order
If you are dealing with a joint order, you need to be satisfied that the order recognises that one parent is the principal day to day caregiver of that child. This may be confirmed by either:
- a reference in the order to the role of one parent as day to day caregiver (eg a 70/30 split) or
- the evidence before the court at the time that the order was made, indicates that one parent is the day to day caregiver and the joint parenting order made does not provide otherwise
Note in some cases, parents have made their own arrangements without court involvement. However, to recognise a split care arrangement for benefit purposes, we must see a court parenting order recognising the arrangements. An agreement between the parents is not sufficient, even if this has been formally drafted by a solicitor.
For more information see:
- No court ordered split care arrangement
- Split care
- Determining whether a care arrangement is sanctioned by the Family Court
- Privacy Act implications
- Assistance for the parent not qualified for Sole Parent Support
- When to consider Emergency Maintenance Allowance for split care
