chunks.title: Client does not have work obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client does not have work obligations
Community Work Experience cannot be imposed on a client who only has work-preparation or social obligations.
These clients may be considered for Upskilling or Money Management as an alternative to a financial sanction if they meet the criteria and it is appropriate for their circumstances.

chunks.title: Criteria for Report Job Search — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Criteria for Report Job Search
Clients must meet certain criteria to have Report Job Search imposed.
A client can only have Report Job Search imposed if:
- they are in active case management or have dependent children and
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure) and
- they have current work obligations and
- they meet with MSD within the 5-working day notice period and
- the obligation failure is not disputed and overturned and
- Report Job Search is the most appropriate sanction to impose based on their circumstances

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: A client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date they apply to receive Sole Parent Support. On an ongoing basis a client must continue to remain ordinarily resident in New Zealand to get their benefit. Some exceptions occur when the client leaves New Zealand to live overseas permanently in which case they may be eligible for a continuation of their payments under a Social Security Agreement.

chunks.title: Attributes associated with being ordinarily resident — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Ordinarily resident incorporates a number of factors. The key attributes to being ordinarily resident in New Zealand is that a person must have a close and clear connection to New Zealand on the date they apply for Sole Parent Support. Some other key attributes that indicate that a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand include: - their physical presence in New Zealand is other than casually or as a traveller - there is some intention to remain in New Zealand for a settled purpose - despite temporary absences from New Zealand they regularly or customarily live in New Zealand - they prefer residence in New Zealand to any other country (a person cannot be ordinarily resident in two countries at the same time) Where it is not clear if a client is ordinarily resident you may need to ask the client further information. Some of the following questions may help to get more information: - if the client is going overseas, what are their intentions towards New Zealand (sighting return air tickets is a good indication) - the length of time they spend in New Zealand compared to their periods of absence and the reasons for the absences - property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans) - where are their cash assets principally held (New Zealand banks or investment entities or overseas based holdings) - is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and are they tax resident in New Zealand - see Inland Revenue Deciding whether you are a resident or non-resident - are they still on an electoral role and vote in central and local body elections - do they have a personal commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in their immediate and extended family community, community events, clubs and other groups) The attributes associated with being ordinarily resident can also be used after Sole Parent Support is granted if there is some indication the client may no longer be ordinarily resident in New Zealand.

chunks.title: How to decide — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Whether a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand is a question of fact and degree. You must consider all the factors of each individual case and decide whether they show a clear and close connection to New Zealand. You may need to ask more questions (or seek clarification of information you have) to get all the relevant information and then you must weigh up all the facts and make a decision having regard to the attributes associated with a person being ordinarily resident in New Zealand (see above). If, on the balance of facts you are not sure if the client is ordinarily resident in New Zealand ask for advice from Helpline or your manager client service delivery before you make your decision. A determination on whether a person is ordinarily resident is a discretionary legislative provision, and the client should be given the benefit of the doubt in situations where their ordinary residence isn't clear.

chunks.title: Non-residentially qualified — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: You should consider other main benefits if a client does not meet the residence requirements for Sole Parent Support. An Emergency Benefit may be granted on the grounds of hardship to a client who does not meet the period of residence requirement. However, the person must generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet the hardship qualifications for Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Decision guidelines - clients moving to a limited employment location — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Clients who move to a limited employment location must continue to meet their work obligations. This includes being available for, and taking reasonable steps to obtain, suitable employment. To meet this obligation, they must demonstrate that they: - have access to reliable transport - are willing to commute to a nearby town or centre where suitable employment is available - are realistically able to commute to a nearby town or centre where suitable employment is available It is up to the client to demonstrate to you how they are meeting their work obligations. If the client is not meeting their work obligations, you should initiate an obligations failure.

chunks.title: Obligations failure - recompliance — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Once an obligations failure has been initiated, the client must show their willingness to meet their work obligations by: - demonstrating they have reliable transport, and are willing and realistically able to commute to a nearby town or centre where employment is available or - moving to a place that is not a limited employment location A client who agrees to recomply by moving to an area that is not a limited employment location will need to show you they have taken steps to move before they can be considered to have recomplied. You will need to keep in regular contact with your client to ensure they are continuing to take steps to move. Where it is not possible to remedy the relevant failure, the client may recomply by completing another activity that is the same or substantially similar to the activity they failed. For more information see: - Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work or work preparation obligations - Obligations failures - Recompliance - Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Ongoing work with clients who move to limited employment locations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: If your client can demonstrate they will meet their work obligations in a limited employment location, you will need to work closely with them to ensure they actively continue to meet these obligations. Your client should be encouraged to: - keep a verifiable record of what they have been doing each week to find employment and - meet with you on a regular basis For more information see: - Assistance to move back to an area that is not a limited employment location - Deskfile Limited employment locations alert sheet - Meeting job search requirements - Recompliance - Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period) - Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work or work preparation obligations - Obligations failures - Why is the client moving to a limited employment location? - Work obligations

chunks.title: Decision guidelines for shared care — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Decision guidelines for shared care
The parent with greater responsibility is usually the parent who has the child for most of the time. If a parent has the child for at least 60% of the time they have the primary responsibility.
Where parents have equal time, to help you decide which parent has greater responsibility, consider the following:
- who pays for the child's material support (furniture, clothes etc)
- who decides about the child's daily activities
- who takes them to and from school and supervises leisure activities
- who makes decisions about their education and health
- who pays for which expenses
If it is not clear who has greater responsibility or the parents share the responsibility equally, the parent who was mainly responsible for the day to day care of the child prior to the separation is the person who can receive Sole Parent Support.
If you can't decide who is entitled to Sole Parent Support, the parents must make the decision. Don't include the child in any income support until they have decided.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Dependent child — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
For a client to get Sole Parent Support the child must be a dependent child.
A dependent child for Sole Parent Support is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Sole Parent Support does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- child for whom Orphan's or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
In some situations, a child may not be living at home but is still considered to be a dependent child.
In some situations, a client may not be the natural or adoptive parent of the child but MSD can still regard the child as their own when the child's parents are unable, or in exceptional circumstances unwilling, to look after the child.
## Long term care
The care situation should be permanent or long term. MSD should not grant Sole Parent Support to a client to care for a child who comes to stay with them for a short period such as the school holidays.
All dependent children should be included in the benefit.

chunks.title: Determining eligibility without details of a nominated person — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Determining eligibility without details of a nominated person
To grant Sole Parent Support, you must be satisfied the client meets all the qualifications including their relationship status.
If a client refuses to provide details of a nominated person to verify their relationship status, or is unable to name one, then, based on the available information, you can:
- ask for more information to determine whether the client is eligible for Sole Parent Support, if it is not clear whether the client is eligible
- grant Sole Parent Support if there is enough information to determine that the client is eligible for Sole Parent Support or
- decline Sole Parent Support if the information available indicates that the client is not eligible for Sole Parent Support If this occurs, you should discuss this with the client and determine whether they are eligible for other forms of assistance.
For more information see:
- Examples of using relationship status verification
- No details of a nominated person provided

chunks.title: Determining when a client became non-compliant — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Determining when a client became non-compliant
When a client fails to complete Report Job Search without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must determine from which point the client was non-compliant.
The client's benefit will be reduced from the first day of the week that MSD determines a client was non-compliant.
The start of each week is based on when Report Job Search was imposed. This means the week may not begin on a Monday.
For example, if a client's Report Job Search is imposed on a Wednesday, the beginning of the week for the sanction will be Wednesday.
## Example
Tien failed a work obligation and MSD imposed Report Job Search as a non-financial sanction. He contacts MSD in his third week of Report Job Search and says he did not complete or report on his 3 job-search activities. When MSD asks about why he could not complete his job-search activities he says after week 2 he could not think of another activity to complete.
MSD is satisfied that Tien was complying with the requirements of Report Job Search in week one and 2, but he was no longer compliant in week 3. MSD determines non-compliance from day one of week 3.
Tien's payments are reduced from this date, and he is given a different recompliance activity to complete.
## Example
Dende failed a work obligation and his case manager imposed Report Job Search as a non-financial sanction.
Throughout the 4-week sanction period, Dende reports on 4 job-search activities each week.
At the end of the four-week sanction period, when Dende meets with his case manager, he's unable to provide sufficient supporting evidence of his job-search activities because he forgot this was part of his sanction requirements and so didn't collect evidence throughout.
As he doesn't have a good and sufficient reason for this, MSD determines that he hasn't met the requirements of the sanction.
MSD determines Dende became non-compliant at the beginning of week one of his sanction, as he was unable to provide any supporting evidence of his job-search activities.
His payments are reduced from the beginning of week one and a debt is established.

chunks.title: Determining when a client became non-compliant — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Determining when a client became non-compliant
When a client fails to complete Upskilling without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must determine from which point the client was non-compliant.
The client's benefit will be or reduced from the first day of the week that MSD determines a client was non-compliant.
The start of each week is based on when Upskilling was imposed. This means the week may not begin on a Monday.
For example, if a client's Upskilling is imposed on a Wednesday, the beginning of the week for the sanction will be Wednesday.
## Example
Nami failed a work obligation and MSD imposed Upskilling as a non-financial sanction. In the third week of her sanction period, she does not participate in or report on at least 5 hours of her employment-related training or course. Her benefit is automatically reduced.
She contacts MSD says she did not participate as she forgot to attend the course and report the hours.
MSD is satisfied that Nami was complying with the requirements of Upskilling in weeks 1 and 2, but she was no longer compliant in week 3.
MSD determines non-compliance from day one of week 3. Nami's payments are reduced from this date, and a debt is established. She is given a different recompliance activity to complete.

chunks.title: Determining when a client became non-compliant — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Determining when a client became non-compliant
When a client fails to find or complete Community Work Experience without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must determine from which point the client was non-compliant.
MSD may consider information shared by an organisation when determining if a client has a good and sufficient reason for failing to find or complete Community Work Experience, however MSD must also consider information provided by the client.
The client’s benefit will be reduced from the first day of the week that MSD determines a client was non-compliant.
The start of each week is based on when the Community Work Experience was imposed. This means the week may not begin on a Monday.
For example, if a client’s Community Work Experience is imposed on a Wednesday, the beginning of the week for the sanction will be Wednesday.

chunks.title: Determining whether a care arrangement is sanctioned by the Family Court — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Determining whether a care arrangement is sanctioned by the Family Court
Determine the facts of the care arrangements for the children between the client and the other parent:
- Is there a split care situation - i.e., is each parent the principal caregiver of at least one of their children?
- Are there court order(s) in place to sanction, authorise or approve the split care arrangement?
- Do the orders(s) recognise the care arrangements for both children, not just the care arrangements in respect of one of the children?
- If there is a joint order(s) in place, does the order recognise one parent as the principal caregiver - consider the information that was before the Court when the order was made
It is advisable to consult your local solicitor if the court orders do not clearly establish each parent as the principal caregiver of at least one child.
It may be necessary to interview both parents to ensure they both agree on what is the case. If they do not agree you need to put the case of each to the other and come to a finding on the facts.
For more information see:
- Court ordered split care arrangements
- No court ordered split care arrangement
- Privacy Act implications
- Assistance for the parent not qualified for Sole Parent Support
- When to consider Emergency Maintenance Allowance for split care

chunks.title: Client’s obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client’s obligations
Clients with work obligations who fail a social obligation may have Community Work Experience imposed. However, it may be more appropriate for a client to recomply with their failure by meeting their social obligations, rather than completing Community Work Experience.

chunks.title: Determining who is a parent — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Determining who is a parent
A client applying for Sole Parent Support should be the child's natural or adoptive parent. If the client is not the child's natural or adoptive parent, you can regard the child as their own when:
- the child is being maintained by the client and
- was at any time maintained by the client's partner or
- each of the child's natural or adoptive parents are deceased, cannot be found, or suffers a serious long-term disablement which renders them unable to care for the child or
- due to a breakdown in the child's family no natural, adoptive or step parent is able to care for the child or provide fully to the child's support or
- the child's natural, adoptive or step parents and/or guardians are unwilling to support the child
For more information see:
- Dependent child
- Child not supported
- Parents unable to care for child
- Parents unwilling to care for child
The legislation doesn't tell you how long the child must be maintained by the couple but it should be a reasonable period of time, not just a few weeks.
## Example
A couple takes responsibility for a close relative's child and maintains the child for some years before they separate. This child would be considered as their own child.
For more information see:
- Father of a child

chunks.title: Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes when a client is diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence.
Drug addiction or dependence, for the purposes of the drug test requirements, means a person who has been diagnosed with
- severe substance abuse or
- dependency or drug addiction issues
The client can be asked to provide verification from a health practitioner or by a registered AOD practitioner who will have completed a formal assessment and given the diagnosis of drug dependency. The verification should also state the duration or time that the client will need to address their drug issue dependency. There is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that MSD can provide the client.

chunks.title: Disputes and reviews of an obligations failure — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Disputes and reviews of an obligations failure
A client has the right to dispute or review if they disagree with any decision relating to:
- an obligations failure or
- a sanction being imposed
A client can do this by:
- disputing the decision or
- lodging a formal Review of Decision
- lodging an appeal to the Medical Appeals Board (drug test failure only)
A Review of Decision or appeal to the Medical Appeals Board can be lodged at any stage, within three months of the obligations failure being initiated, or within three months of the sanction being imposed.
If a client disputes their obligations failure or sanction more than 20 working days after it is initiated or imposed, you need to advise the client to lodge a formal Review of Decision or an appeal to the Medical Appeals Board (drug test failure only) in writing.
For more information see:
- Disputing more than one obligations failure
- The disputes process
- Recording decisions on a dispute
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Core policy, Reviews and Appeals Medical Appeals Board

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Example 1
A client has failed their social obligations and 2 of their work obligations, and the failures have been initiated on the same day. The client disputes some of these failures as they have good and sufficient reasons. The client also recomplies to one. The client is not sanctioned but the failure is counted because they recomplied with one of the failures.
Obligation
Recompliance
Action
Social obligation - failed to enrol child in ECE
Client must comply with all social obligations
Client disputes failure - has good and sufficient reason
Work obligations - failed to attend interview
Must attend another job interview - or similar activity
Client disputes failure - has good and sufficient reason
Work obligations - refused to take drug test
Must agree to being drug free
Client has no good and sufficient reason for the failure - agrees to recomply
## Example 2
A client has failed their obligations and the failures have been initiated on the same day. The client recomplies for one failure but not for the other failure. The sanction remains imposed until the client recomplies.
Obligation
Recompliance
Action
Work ability assessment obligation - failed to attend a job interview
Client must attend another job interview - or similar activity
Client has no good and sufficient reason for not participating in the assessment and does not recomply - the sanction remains imposed until the client recomplies with this activity
Work obligations - failed to attend job seminar
Must attend another job seminar - or similar activity
Client recomplies by attending another job seminar

chunks.title: Drug test job referral not suitable — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Drug test job referral not suitable
There are certain situations where it is not appropriate to refer a client to drug tested jobs as the job is not considered to be suitable. These situations include where a client is:
- taking prescribed medication
- diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- in or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence or
- has a drug issue identified by a provider and is engaging and participating in services and support offered by that provider
These situations are also to be taken into account when deciding whether a client has a good and sufficient reason for failing their drug test requirements. For more information see:
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons
The first time a client presents with one of these situations, you should:
- accept that it is not appropriate to refer the client to drug tested jobs
- add a deferral from drug test obligations for an initial 30 working day period and
- advise the client that if they think they require a deferral from drug test obligations for more than 30 working days, then verification will be required
- there is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to your client
For more information see:
- Drug test - Referral delay [no link find out why]
Depending on the clients circumstances and the verification provided you can extend the deferral from drug test obligations up to six months.
For more information see:
- Taking controlled prescribed medication
- Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence
- Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: Drug tested job referral not suitable — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Drug tested job referral not suitable
These situations are also to be taken into account when deciding whether it is appropriate to refer a client to drug tested jobs. If you decide that, due to one of these situations, it is not appropriate to refer a client to further drug tested jobs you must add a drug test obligations deferral.
For more information see
- Drug test - Referral Delay [no link find out why]
## Client provides a good and sufficient reason
The first time a client fails their drug test obligation and provides a good and sufficient reason, you should:
- accept that the client has a good and sufficient reason
- add a deferral from drug test obligations for an initial 30 working day period and
- advise the client that if they think they require a deferral from drug test obligations for more than 30 working days, then verification will be required.
- there is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to your client
For more information see:
- Drug test job referral not suitable
- Taking controlled prescribed medication
- Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence
- Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence
- Reviewing or disputing the drug test failure
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures

chunks.title: Drug test obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Drug test obligations
Clients receiving Sole Parent Support who have work obligations will be subject to drug test obligations.
Clients must undertake and pass drug tests when Work and Income have identified:
- a suitable job and pre-employment drug tests are required by a prospective employer or
- a suitable course and a pre-course drug test is required as part of the admission process by a training provider
A client will fail their drug test work obligations if they have no good and sufficient reason and:
- a suitable job is available and they advise they will not apply for the job as they will not pass the pre-employment drug test
- they have been referred to or have applied for a suitable job or course and they refuse to take the pre-employment drug test or
- they have been referred to a suitable job or course and they fail or refuse a drug test
If a client fails their drug test work obligations the same 5 day notice period and sanctions apply as for any other obligations failure.
## Client refuses to take the drug test
An obligations failure should be initiated if a client without a good and sufficient reason, has been referred to a suitable job and refuses to take the pre-employment drug test.
## Client fails pre-employment alcohol test
Job applicants may be required to be tested for alcohol use prior to being hired. However, the drug test obligation requirements do not include alcohol.
If a client failed a test for alcohol use, without a good and sufficient reason, then a work test failure could be initiated because the client has failed to participate in the job interview process.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements
- Employers requiring pre-employment drug tests
- Training providers requiring a drug test
- Types of drug tests and standards

chunks.title: Drug test recompliance count — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Drug test recompliance count
The obligation failure that is initiated or the sanction that is imposed depends on how often the client has failed to comply with their obligations in the previous 24 months while getting a benefit. This is called the 24 month failure count.
The recompliance activity that the client has to complete depends on if the client has failed their drug test obligation before within the last 24 months.
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation the client must complete a six-week approved activity or programme of activities.

chunks.title: 50% protection for sole parents with dependent children — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## 50% protection for sole parents with dependent children
Sole parents with one or more dependent children, who are subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period do not have their whole benefit affected.
Instead, a maximum sanction of 50% of the main benefit may be imposed. The balance payable is known as 50% protection.
## Effect of on-going Extra help
Sole parents who have a 13 week non-entitlement period because they became voluntarily unemployed can continue to receive full supplementary assistance.
If eligible, clients can also still receive:
- Employment and work readiness Assistance to transition into employment
- Extra help Disability Allowance
For more information see:
- Financial assistance during non-entitlement period [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Effect of sanctions on assistance — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Effect of sanctions on assistance
The tables below give examples of the effect on the benefit and supplementary assistance rates when a client's benefit has been sanctioned due to an obligations failure.
Note for a grade 1 obligation failure if a non-financial sanction is imposed, the client’s rate of payment will not be affected.
See Example 2 for information on how Money Management changes the way payments are made.
## Example 1 - client fails their obligations, has a financial sanction imposed
Main Benefit
Supplementary Assistance(including Winter Energy Payment)
Grade 1 financial sanction
50% reduction
Not affected
Grade 2 financial sanction
50% reduction
Not affected
Grade 3 financial sanction
50% cancellation
Not affected
Note Winter Energy Payment continues when a portion of qualifying benefit is still paid.
## Example 2 - client fails their first obligation, Money Management imposed
Main benefit
Extra help(including Winter Energy Payment)
Grade 1 financial sanction
(Money Management)
50% payment in bank account
50% payment on payment card
Not affected
Note Non-financial sanctions can only be imposed as an alternative to a Grade 1 financial sanction
## Example 3 - client refuses an offer of suitable employment
A client refuses an offer of suitable employment and so is subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period.
Main benefit
Supplementary assistance(including Winter Energy Payment)
50% cancellation
Not affected
Note Winter Energy Payment continues when a portion of qualifying benefit is still paid.

chunks.title: Employment during stand-down — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Employment during stand-down
If a client gains temporary full-time employment during the initial stand-down period, this may change the date the benefit can start from.
## Temporary employment at a disqualifying rate
Where a client has temporary employment during the initial stand-down period and their income is at a disqualifying rate, this may change the date the benefit can start from. The new entitlement date is the date the temporary employment stops. Reassess the client's initial stand-down using the income for the 26 and 52 weeks earned immediately before the new entitlement date.
For more information see:
- Example of employment during stand-down
## Temporary employment at less than a disqualifying rate
Where a client has temporary employment during the initial stand-down period, and their level of income (when charged against the benefit) allows for a part payment of benefit, there is no need to re-assess the client's initial stand-down. For more information see:
- Income less than a disqualifying rate

chunks.title: Employment trial period of up to 90 days — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Employment trial period of up to 90 days
A client may continue to meet their work obligations if their employment agreement includes an employment trial period. This is assessed the same as any other employment.
Employment agreements, signed by the employer and employee, can include an employment trial period of up to 90 days.
Features of an employment trial:
- an employment trial may be offered by an employer regardless of the number of employees a business has and
- an employer may terminate the employment agreement during a trial at any time before the end of the employment trial period even if the last day of work occurs after the expire of the employment trial period and
- an employer is not required to provide a reason for ending the employment trial if the notice of termination was given before the employment trial period ended and
- an employee cannot generally bring a personal grievance against the employer in respect of the ending of their employment during the employment trial period
A client can still challenge the ending of their employment agreement including on the grounds of:
- discrimination or
- sexual harassment or
- racial harassment or
- duress imposed by the employer in relation to a client's union affiliations or not as the case may be
For more information about when a client's employment ceases before the end of the employment trial see:

chunks.title: Ending of Sole Parent Support when youngest child turns 14 — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: A client's Sole Parent Support expires on the date their youngest dependent child turns 14 years old. Generally when the youngest dependent child turns 14 years old, a client getting Sole Parent Support is automatically transferred to Jobseeker Support. Jobseeker Support will commence on the date that the Sole Parent Support expires as if the client had applied for Jobseeker Support. MSD should check if the client has any exemptions in place, and confirm whether these exemptions will end. For more information see: - Exemptions

chunks.title: Information to suggest the client will not qualify for Jobseeker Support — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: If there is information to suggest, on reasonable grounds, that the client would not qualify for Jobseeker Support, the client will not be automatically transferred to Jobseeker Support. MSD will assess whether the client would qualify for other financial assistance. Client in study A client will not qualify for Jobseeker Support if they are in full-time study. If the client wants to continue full-time study, they can check whether they qualify for Student Allowance, Student Loan and/or other tertiary student supports. A client may qualify for Jobseeker Support if they are in part-time study and are able to meet the job search requirements. For more information see: - Client engaged in study - Decision guidelines - part-time students

chunks.title: Client working full-time — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: A client will not qualify for Jobseeker Support if they are in full-time employment. This means that a Sole Parent Support client who is working full-time when their youngest dependent child turns 14 cannot be automatically transferred to Jobseeker Support. For more information see: - Full-time employment

chunks.title: Obligations in place immediately before transfer to Jobseeker Support — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: The following obligations will continue to apply to the client after their transfer to Jobseeker Support: - obligations to work with a contracted service provider - social obligations - work preparation general obligation to take all reasonable steps that are reasonable for their circumstances to prepare for employment - work ability assessment - work obligations

chunks.title: Expiry date for the reapplication process for Jobseeker Support — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: The Jobseeker Support expiry date for clients who are automatically transferred from Sole Parent Support to Jobseeker Support when their youngest dependent child turns 14 years old, is either: - 52 weeks from the date the Sole Parent Support last commenced (meaning the Sole Parent Support expiry date is retained), or - 26 weeks from the Jobseeker Support commencement date whichever is earlier. For more information see: - Transfer from Sole Parent Support when youngest child turns 14 years old

chunks.title: Enrolled in and attending school — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Enrolled in and attending school
Clients getting Sole Parent Support must take all reasonable steps to ensure their children are enrolled in and attending school from the age of 5 or 6 years old (depending on when they start school).
## Age of child
Clients with a dependent child aged 5 or 6 years old (depending on when they start school) to 15 years of age will be required to take all reasonable steps to ensure the child is enrolled in and regularly attending school.
If a child is aged between 5 and 6 years it is the parent or caregiver's choice as to whether they have their child in early childhood education or school. A child does not legally have to attend school until they are aged 6 years (but most children start school at 5 years of age). A client must meet the early childhood education obligation of they choose not to enrol their 5 year old in school.
A child can legally leave school when they are 16 years or at 15 years if they have an early leaving exemption from the Ministry of Education.
A parent or caregiver cannot be asked to comply with the attendance at school social obligation, if the child has legally left school or has an early leaving exemption, and is no longer legally required to attend school.
## Verification of child enrolled and attending school
All children aged from 6 to 15 years old are legally required to attend school. In most cases you should take your clients word that they are meeting their social obligations.
However, if you have information that indicates the child may not be attending school you may ask the client to get verification, for example, a letter from the child's school that says the child is enrolled and attending.
There are some situations where a client may be taking all reasonable steps but their child is not attending school.
For more information see:
- Taking all reasonable steps for enrolling in and attending school

chunks.title: Enrolment and attendance at early childhood programme — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Enrolment and attendance at early childhood programme
Clients receiving Sole Parent Support must take all reasonable steps to ensure that their child is enrolled in and attending a recognised early childhood education programme from the age of three until they start school.
Generally clients should have their children participating in a recognised early childhood education programmes for 15 hours a week. It acceptable for a child to be attending less than this.
Recognised early childhood programmes include programmes that are:
- approved (licensed and certificated under the Education and Training Act 2020) early childhood education programmes
- Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School or
- another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme
Generally, a place in approved early childhood education (ECE) service should be considered first.
When a place in early childhood education is not available or is not suitable (for example due to hours of operation, distance or family circumstances), then other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes should be considered.
## Hours of attendance
Generally you should encourage your clients to take reasonable steps to have their children participating in early childhood programmes for 15 hours a week. It acceptable for a child to be attending less than this.
## Age of child
This obligation only applies to parents of children aged between 3 and 6 years (except where the child has started school at 5 years).
If a child is aged between 5 and 6 years old, the parent or caregiver can choose whether to have their child in a recognised early childhood education programme or school.
A child does not legally have to attend school until they are 6 years (but most children start school at 5 years).
## Verification
In most cases, you should take the client's word that they are meeting this social obligation.
However, where you have information that the client may not be taking all reasonable steps towards this social obligation you can check if a Childcare Subsidy is being paid for the child or may ask the client to provide verification.
For example, if you get information that a child is not attending you can ask the client to get a letter from their childcare provider that confirms the child's attendance. You can also check the client's current Childcare Subsidy information.

chunks.title: Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits
A client receiving Sole Parent Support must take all reasonable steps to:
- register their child or children with a Well-Child/Tamariki Ora provider and
- keep up-to-date with the child's core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks
Note a client is only required to ensure their child completes core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks to meet this obligation from the time they begin to receive a benefit. For example, a client who starts receiving a benefit when their child is between three and 4 months old cannot be failed for not having completed the core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks the child should have had at ages 4 to six weeks.
## Age of child
There are eight core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks that apply to children aged from 4 weeks to 5 years old. There are also three checks that occur shortly after birth. The obligation only applies for the eight core checks that occur from around 4 months through to 5 years of age.
For more information see:
- Well Child or Tamariki Ora services and checks
## Verification
Most parents will already have their child or children registered and up to date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks and in most cases you should take the client's word that they are meeting this social obligation.
However, if you have information that indicates the client is not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations you may ask for proof that the checks have been completed, for example by asking to see their Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book.
The Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book is issued to parents when their child is born and is sufficient evidence of the child's attendance. The Health Book has helpful advice and information about what is happening at different stages in the child's development and has places to record all the Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks.
For more information see:
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Well Child or Tamariki Ora services and checks
- Overview of social obligations according to age of the child

chunks.title: Enrolment with a primary health care provider — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Enrolment with a primary health care provider
A client receiving Sole Parent Support must take all reasonable steps to enrol their child or children with a primary health care provider. This means being enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation.
Taking reasonable steps to enrol
If a client is unable to enrol their child at a practice or with a practitioner due to shortages, they can be considered to be meeting this obligation if they have a plan in place to:
- be enrolled with a practice or practitioner when a place becomes available and
- get health care for their child if the child becomes sick
## Age of child
The primary health care obligation applies in relation to all dependent children in the care of a client getting a main benefit.
Dependent children include:
- children included in the client’s main benefit and
- children the client is getting Orphan’s Benefit or Unsupported Child’s Benefit for
## Verification
Most children will already be enrolled with a primary health care provider and in most cases MSD should take the client's word that they are meeting this social obligation.
However, if MSD has information that the client may not be taking all reasonable steps to meet this social obligation, MSD may ask them to get verification.
For example, verification could be a letter from their medical practice, or registered practitioner that says they are enrolled (most medical practices will send this when a client is enrolled).

chunks.title: Entering a refuge — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Entering a refuge
When a client is applying for Sole Parent Support after entering a refuge following the break-up of a relationship, the initial stand-down period can be waived.
Generally the client must enter the refuge immediately following the break-up of their relationship. This means entering the refuge within a period similar in duration to the stand-down (that is, within 7 to 14 days). Where there is a delay between the separation and the client entering the refuge, general commencement date rules apply, including the twenty-eight day rule.
In this context a refuge is emergency accommodation provided by an agency or organisation. This includes (but is not restricted to) agencies such as Women's Refuge, Home and Family Society, Emergency Housing Trusts, Iwi and cultural organisations, and church organisations.
Note that accommodation provided by family or friends of the client is not considered to be refuge accommodation.
For more information see:
- Commencement date
- Twenty-eight day rule

chunks.title: Entitlement date — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Entitlement date
The entitlement date for Sole Parent Support is usually:
- the day after separation from their partner
- the day after financial assistance from their partner ceased
- the day after their partner was taken into custody
- the day after their employment ceased (that is, after any holiday pay, sick pay, cessation leave, etc. has expired) where the client was earning at a disqualifying rate
- the day after their partner died
- the date of birth of their child (for single clients)
- the date of their arrival in New Zealand (if client has returned to New Zealand) or
- the date of release from prison
Note that when the client has more than one event you use the later event for their entitlement date.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Example 1
A client applying for Sole Parent Support with a 2 year old child states on their application that they have recently separated from their de facto partner. They refuse to provide the details of a nominated person to verify their relationship status.
When they are asked why they won't provide the details of a nominated person, they state that they do not want to as they're not comfortable asking anyone they know to verify their relationship status.
The client's evidence of accommodation costs is a tenancy agreement that shows they moved house a month ago, and they are the sole tenant in a house where they and their child will be the only occupants.
When the case manager asks what the client thinks is the future of the relationship, the client says that they will not ever get back together and gives some personal information about why the relationship ended.
In this circumstance, unless there is something else that leads the case manager to believe the client is still in a relationship, the case manager will have enough information to make the decision to grant Sole Parent Support.
## Example 2
A client applying for Sole Parent Support states that they have recently separated from their partner because they had a big verbal argument. The client explains that the argument wasn't violent but involved a disagreement over what school to send their child to.
The client won't provide the details of a nominated person and, when asked why, states that no one knows that they have separated yet.
When asked about the future of the relationship, the client states that they are hoping to work it out and have not yet decided whether to move out of the home they share with their partner.
In the conversation, the case manager and client both reach the conclusion that the client is still in a relationship. The case manager declines the client's application for Sole Parent Support.

chunks.title: Example 1 - Client wants to do part-time training and the training is not approved — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: A client receiving Sole Parent Support with a child aged 2 years old wishes to take part in full-time training that is not an approved training programme. She advises the case manager that the training is 25 hours per week on site, and that while she attends the training her child would be in early childhood education. The case manager explains that the client would still have to meet their work-preparation obligations while they undertake training. This may mean arranging time to come in for an interview during standard course hours if necessary. However, as the training is employment-focused, the client is encouraged to complete the training as it can be considered part of their efforts to meet their obligation to take steps to improve their work readiness. The conversation is noted in the client's engagement log in CMS.

chunks.title: Example 2 - Client's child is 5 years old, client wants to study full-time on Sole Parent Support — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: A client applying for Sole Parent Support has a 5 year old dependent child and wants to start studying full-time by correspondence. He has three 6 hour shifts during the week while his child attends school, but his income is not enough to make him ineligible for Sole Parent Support. The course he is planning on taking is a Level 2 course. On discussion with his case manager, the client believes he can meet all of his part-time work obligations while studying. He estimates that he will spend 35 hours per week studying, and he will do this at home across the 7 days of the week, including in the evenings. The case manager should grant Sole Parent Support and note all relevant discussions and training details in the engagement log. The case manager should remind the client that his commitments to study will not mean he is exempt from meeting his part-time work obligations. The case manager should also assess the client's entitlement to education and employment-related assistance.

chunks.title: Example 3 - Client's child is 13 years old, client wants to start study — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: A client on Sole Parent Support is considering starting a Certificate in Computing and Business Administration at Te Wānanga o Aotearoa in Auckland to help their long-term employment prospects. This is a full-time National Certificate Level 2 course that lasts for 20 weeks. However, the client's child will turn 14 years old, 2 weeks after the client's proposed start date for the course. The client would not be eligible for Jobseeker Support while they are in full-time study. The case manager recommends that the client considers either: - applying for Student Allowance and Student Loan to support themselves while they study or - consider taking an approved training course while on Jobseeker Support to help them increase their employment prospects The client chooses to apply for student assistance. The case manager confirms the date the client will start studying and adds a future suspension for that date. The case manager then shows the client the StudyLink website and explains that they can apply for student assistance online.

chunks.title: Example 4 - Client in study before subject to work obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: A client has booked an appointment after receiving a letter informing them that they will have part-time work obligations from when their youngest dependent child turns 3 years old in 4 weeks' time. They are worried because they are currently studying full-time, and their course finishes in 6 months' time. The case manager explains that they may be eligible for an exemption from their part-time obligations, but they need to provide evidence that they are enrolled and that they have passed at least 50% of their previous year of study. The client returns for an appointment a week later with the required evidence, and the case manager records an exemption in SWIFTT until their course end date, and notes their discussion in the engagement log in CMS. For more information see: - Studying or training on Sole Parent Support

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances for reapplication — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances for reapplication
If a client has an exceptional circumstance that affects their ability to reapply or contact MSD before their Sole Parent Support expiry date, they may be granted an extension to complete the reapplication process.
An extension may be granted for up to 20 working days starting on their expiry date, on the condition that the client competes the 52 week reappliation process within the extension period.
A situation or event is considered to be an exceptional circumstance when it:
- is unforeseen, out-of-the ordinary and could not be planned for and
- is beyond the client's control and
- sets the client apart from others in a similar situation and
- happened at any time during the client's notice period
Generally, MSD may request evidence of the client's circumstances. The evidence required depends on the reason of the exceptional circumstances of the client.
## Exceptional circumstances reasons
The following exceptional circumstance can be accepted:
## Process for clients with exceptional circumstances
The reapplication must be processed as soon as possible. It can be no later than 20 working days from the expiry date, as the benefit will automatically be cancelled.
Note if a client is granted an extension and completes the reapplication process within the extension period, their Sole Parent Support should be regranted from their expiry date.
If a client does not complete the 52 week reapplication process within the extension period or no longer qualifies for Sole Parent Support, their benefit will be cancelled from their expiry date. The amount of benefit (including any Extra help) that was conditionally paid during the extension period must be established as a debt.
## Reapplying as a new applicant
If the client does not complete their reapplication process within the extension period, or were not granted an extension, they must apply as a new applicant if they still need Sole Parent Support. Their expired benefit must be cancelled from their expiry date before they can be granted Sole Parent Support as a new applicant.
The client will be subject to the usual commencement date rules, including the initial stand-down.
Note if the client advises they want to apply for benefit as a new applicant and completes their reapplication form, MSD must use their reapplication form as their new application.

chunks.title: Exemption for severe disablement — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Exemption for severe disablement
As an incentive for the personal effort of a severely disabled person to participate or continue in employment, you can use your discretion to disregard all or part of any income earned from employment as chargeable income for benefit purposes.
Consideration for this special income exemption should be given to clients with a severe disability who are extremely limited in their ability to participate in employment, the community and take care of themselves.
You must first consider whether or not the client is severely disabled. The Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement will help you do this.
Each case should be assessed on an individual basis.
If the client is severely disabled you should consider whether or not to disregard all or part of any income earned by the client. To help you do this, see: Amount of income exemption
Note clients who are not severely disabled cannot receive this exemption.
For more information see:
- Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement
- Amount of income exemption

chunks.title: Exemptions — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Exemptions
There are several reasons why it may be unreasonable to expect a client to meet their work preparation obligations or work obligations for a specified period.
If a client qualifies they may be granted an exemption from some or all of their work preparation or work obligations. Evidence may be required before an exemption is granted.
## Duration of the exemption
Each exemption has a specific period it can be granted for. In some cases, the exemption can be extended (if appropriate).
The exemption should be reviewed at the end of the exemption period. At the review MSD should discuss the client's circumstances and consider whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption again. MSD can ask the client to provide evidence of the reason to extend the exemption (if appropriate).
Note the duration of an exemption for a client with a health condition, injury or disability is based on the next reassessment date recorded by their registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant).

chunks.title: Expiry date — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: The expiry date for the 52 week reapplication process for Sole Parent Support is 52 weeks from the date that the client's Sole Parent Support commenced or last commenced. This is when a client: - applies for and is granted Sole Parent Support or - completes their reapplication on time and their Sole Parent Support is regranted or - is transferred to Sole Parent Support from another main benefit The expiry date for clients who were automatically transferred to Sole Parent Support on 15 July 2013 is 52 weeks from the date that the previous benefit commenced. This applies to clients who were getting: - Domestic Purposes Benefit - Sole parent or - Widows Benefit Note if a client’s expiry date falls in the week immediately before or including 26 December, their benefit will continue to be paid until the first Monday following 2 January. Their expiry date does not change. For more information, see: - Expiry date falls in the week immediately before or including 26 December

chunks.title: Expiry date reset — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: The expiry date is not reset by any periods of temporary suspension or expiries. The expiry date is only affected if the client: - has their Sole Parent Support cancelled for any reason or - transfers to another benefit type that is not Sole Parent Support and then transfers back to Sole Parent Support

chunks.title: Example - Client's benefit has been suspended — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Nala has been getting Sole Parent Support with her 12 year old dependent child included in her benefit, which commenced on 5 June 2027. Her benefit expiry is 5 June 2028. Nala does temporary full-time temporary employment for 4 weeks and their benefit is suspended during this period as their income is over the income cut-out point. In this situation Nala's expiry date does not change when the benefit is resumed.

chunks.title: Example - Client transfers between benefits — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Poppy has been getting Sole Parent Support with her 7 year old dependent child included in her benefit, which commenced on 16 March 2025. Her benefit expiry is 16 March 2026. Poppy transfers to Jobseeker Support on 11 July 2025 because her dependent child left her care. On 3 September 2025 Poppy transfers back to Sole Parent Support because she resumes care for her 7 year old dependent child. In this situation the expiry date will be 3 September 2026, which is 52 weeks from the new Sole Parent Support commencement date.

chunks.title: Example - Client's benefit has been cancelled — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Fergus has been getting Sole Parent Support with his 9 and 10 year old dependent children included in his benefit, which commenced on 12 February 2026. His expiry date is 12 February 2027. Fergus commences full-time employment in April and his benefit is cancelled. After 8 months, the company Fergus is employed with closes and his employment ends. Fergus applies for and is granted Sole Parent support, which commences on 15 December 2025. In this situation his expiry date will be 15 December 2027, which is 52 weeks from the new commencement date for Sole Parent Support. For more information see:

chunks.title: Expiry date falls in the week immediately before or including 26 December — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: If a client's expiry date falls in the week immediately before or including 26 December, their Sole Parent Support can continue to be paid until the first Monday following 2 January. The client must complete the reapplication process before that Monday to continue getting Sole Parent Support. The client’s expiry date does not change in this situation. This means that if a client completes the reapplication process and continues to qualify for Sole Parent Support their benefit will be regranted from their expiry date, not from the first Monday after 2 January. Note when a client’s expiry date falls in the week immediately before or including 26 December, the ‘initial notice to reapply’ letter will be sent 25 working days before their expiry date.

chunks.title: Example 1 - Expiry date falls in the week immediately before 26 December — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Sol is getting Sole Parent Support with his 8 year old dependent child included in his benefit, which expires on 17 December 2025. Sol's expiry date falls in the week immediately before 26 December. His Sole Parent Support will continue to be paid until 5 January 2026, which is the first Monday after 2 January. He must complete the reapplication process before 5 January 2026. Sol completes the reapplication process on time and continues to qualify for Sole Parent Support. His benefit is regranted from the expiry date, 17 December 2025.

chunks.title: Example 2 - Expiry date falls in the week including 26 December — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Kate is getting Sole Parent Support with her 4 year old dependent child included in her benefit, which expires on 22 December 2026. Kate's expiry date falls in the week of 26 December. Her Sole Parent Support will continue to be paid until 4 January 2027, which is the first Monday after 2 January. She must complete the reapplication process before 4 January 2027. Kate completes the reapplication process on time and continues to qualify for Sole Parent Support. Her benefit is regranted from the expiry date, 22 December 2026.

chunks.title: Example 3 - Expiry date does not fall within the week immediately before or including 26 December — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Bethany is getting Sole Parent Support with her 11 year old dependent child included in her benefit, which expires on 31 December 2027. As the expiry date does not fall within the week immediately before or including 26 December, Bethany's payments will stop on 31 December 2027, which is her expiry date. Bethany's Sole Parent Support will be cancelled if she does not complete the reapplication process before her expiry date.

chunks.title: Extending the 20 working day period — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Extending the 20 working day period
If a client states they are struggling to get the form completed within 20 working days of their date of first contact, you should decide whether to extend the 20 working day period, or to gather other information from the client about their relationship status.
For more information see:
- Determining eligibility without details of a nominated person
- Core policy Requests for financial assistance Extending the 20 day working period

chunks.title: Failing a social obligation — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Failing a social obligation
If a client has received regular engagement and support and they are still not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, they still need to attend a final appointment.
A social obligations failure can be initiated when you consider that a client has, without a good and sufficient reason, failed to meet their social obligations by:
- not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations following the process of regular engagement and support (that involves at least three contact steps) or
- not attending the final appointment during their regular engagement and support process
Before you initiate an obligations failure for social obligations you must get your service centre manager's approval. An obligation failure should only be used when all other efforts to encourage engagement and support with the client have been exhausted.

chunks.title: Failing more than one obligation at the same time — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Failing more than one obligation at the same time
If a client fails more than one obligation or activity at the same time and does not have a good and sufficient reason for one or more of the failures, the failures are counted as one failure. However, the client will need to recomply with all the failures before the sanction can be lifted.
Note Money Management is the only non-financial sanction that can be imposed when a client has failed more than one obligation at the same time at grade 1. A client must resolve all of these failures during the 4-week Money Management period in order to recomply.
For grade 1 and 2 failures, if the client successfully disputes one of the failures, the sanction imposed will remain until they recomply with any remaining failures initiated at the same time.
This policy only applies to the first and second time a client fails their obligations in a 24-month period.
For grade 3 failures, a client will need to complete one six-week approved activity or programme of activities (if they wish to recomply).
## Initiating the failures on the same day
The obligations or activities that the client has not complied with can be over a recent period (eg within the last 5 days) or they may not have been complied with all on the same day. However, the client can only be required to recomply with failures that are initiated on the same day.
As soon as MSD is aware that a client has failed their obligations without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must initiate an obligations failure - it cannot be delayed.
For more information see:
- Work obligations
- Work preparation obligations
- Social obligations
- Drug test obligations
- Recompliance
- Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Failing to complete the 52 week reapplication process for Sole Parent Support — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Failing to complete the 52 week reapplication process for Sole Parent Support
If a client does not complete the 52 week reapplication process before their expiry date, their Sole Parent Support will stop.
Note the benefit will automatically cancel if a client does not complete the reapplication process within 20 working days after the expiry date.
## Client still needs Sole Parent Support
Clients who fail to complete the 52 week reapplication process but still need Sole Parent Support must be advised to apply for a benefit as a new applicant. Their expired benefit must be cancelled from their expiry date before they can be granted Sole Parent Support as a new applicant.
The client will be subject to the usual commencement date rules, including the initial stand-down.
Note if the client advises they want to apply for Sole Parent Support as a new applicant, MSD can use their reapplication form as their application.
If a client does not apply for Sole Parent Support, they may qualify for Extra help as a non beneficiary (such as Accommodation Supplement). The client should be advised to apply as a non-beneficiary if they wish to test their entitlement to Extra help assistance

chunks.title: Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations
A client, when required, must:
- attend and participate in interviews with the Ministry to discuss compliance with their social obligations and
- report on compliance with specific social obligations
If during the three steps of engagement and support, the client does not attend and participate in interviews with the Ministry to discuss compliance with social obligations or report on compliance with specific social obligations you should move to the next steps of engagement and support.

chunks.title: Failure to comply following engagement and support process — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Failure to comply following engagement and support process
Clients will need to attend a final appointment if they are still not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations after the 3 step process of regular engagement and support.
A social obligations failure will only be initiated when you consider that a client has, without a good and sufficient reason, failed to meet their social obligations by:
- not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations following the 3 step process of regular engagement and support or
- does not attend the final appointment, or attends and is still not meeting their social obligations, following the 3 step process engagement and support
Before you initiate an obligations failure for social obligations you must get approval from your manager client service delivery.
A social obligations failure should only be used when all other efforts to encourage engagement and support the client have been exhausted.

chunks.title: Failure within the position period - good and sufficient reason — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Failure within the position period - good and sufficient reason
A client must be able to complete 5 hours of Community Work Experience each week during the 4-week period.
The position duties or conditions may change during this period and make it impossible or unreasonable for the client to complete their Community Work Experience.
A client must inform MSD as soon as possible that they are no longer able to complete their Community Work Experience so that MSD may place them onto an alternative recompliance pathway.
A grade 1 financial sanction will be imposed from the date MSD has been informed and is satisfied that they are unable to complete their position and a recompliance activity must be arranged for the client to complete as soon as possible.

chunks.title: Failure within the search period – good and sufficient reason — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Failure within the search period – good and sufficient reason
A client may inform MSD at the end of their 2-week search period that they have made a reasonable effort to find a position and have been unsuccessful.
If MSD is satisfied that the client made a reasonable effort to find a position, a grade 1 financial sanction will be imposed from the day after the search period ends and a recompliance activity must be arranged for the client to complete as soon as possible.

chunks.title: Family breakdown — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Family breakdown
When including a child as a dependent child as their parents are unable or unwilling to support them, MSD must be satisfied there has been a breakdown in the child's family that will last for a medium to long-term period.
Note for Sole Parent Support, a child's family means their parents (natural, adoptive, or step-parent) and any siblings living with them at the time of the family breakdown.
The applicant must be likely to be the principal caregiver for at least one year. This indicates the breakdown and placement away from the child's family is not a short-term measure.
At the interview with the caregiver check whether there has been any involvement with Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency.
MSD can obtain proof of a breakdown from a:
- Family Group Conference conducted by Oranga Tamariki (or other authorised agency) or
- family meeting conducted by MSD, if there has been no involvement with Oranga Tamariki (or other authorised agency)
## Documentation
Documentation of the Family Group Conference must be approved and signed as a full and correct account of the meeting by a social worker, or an elder of the iwi or cultural service who attended the meeting.
The Family Group Conference may have been a hui or cultural service meeting that discussed other matters not relevant to this child and their family.
In these situations, only an extract of the relevant minutes of the hui or meeting is required. The extract will still need to be approved and signed by a social worker, or an elder of the iwi or cultural service who attended the meeting.
When MSD has proof of a Family Group Conference, a decision must be made on the information provided.
However, just because a Family Group Conference has been completed does not mean a breakdown has occurred.

chunks.title: Family violence — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Family violence
This exemption may apply to clients with either work or work preparation obligations
A client who has left a situation of family violence may be exempt from meeting all their work or work preparation obligations until they have had time to adjust to their new living circumstances. This is a full exemption.
You should talk to the regional Family Violence Response Co-ordinator before granting an exemption. You should also consider:
- Is the client living in temporary refuge accommodation while they seek a permanent home?
- Are they helping children adjust to a new family situation?
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 3 months.
## Proof
Clients who have recently left situations of family or domestic violence will not have to provide proof.
If a client still needs an exemption after three months you can ask for proof. You should consult the regional Family Violence Response Co-ordinator for advice on the most appropriate way to proceed.
Proof can include statements from:
- their doctor
- their church
- their lawyer
- the police
- Women's Refuge
- any other person or organisation that is able to support the client's application
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Family Violence'.

chunks.title: Father of a child — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Father of a child
When the father of a child/ren applies for Sole Parent Support, they must:
- be the natural or adoptive father of the child or
- have care of the child and must have cared for the child with their partner before becoming a sole parent
For more information see:
- Determining who is a parent
## Natural father
A client can be considered the natural father of a child when they:
- were legally married to or in a civil union with to the natural mother at the time of conception or birth
- are named on the birth certificate as the father
- are named in a court declaration or a paternity order as the father of the child
- are a person who has acknowledged that he is the father in a court proceeding and the court has not found to the contrary or
- are appointed as a guardian of the child by reason of being the father of the child
## Adoptive father
A client can be considered the adoptive parent of a child when they have adopted the child under the Adoption Act 1955 or an accepted overseas adoption.
## Carer is required to provide proof
A father is required to provide proof that they are the natural or adoptive father of a child. If there is no proof, you should not grant Sole Parent Support.
You should suggest that the client consult a solicitor in order to apply to the courts for either a declaration of paternity or to be named as a guardian.
Note the father of a child may be any gender. The natural mother may also be any gender but must have been pregnant with the child.

chunks.title: Special Needs Grants — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Special Needs Grants
Clients are not entitled to a Special Needs Grant if a sanction has been imposed, unless they become:
- sick or injured and
- incapable of participating in employment or an approved activity for at least six weeks
In this case, the client can get more than one Special Needs Grant, but the amount granted in any one week cannot be more than the combined total of:
- what the client would be entitled to that week if they were entitled to Sole Parent Support and
- the rate of Accommodation Supplement that the applicant would have gotten
For more information see:
- Effect of a non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Assistance when a client is sanctioned
## Advance Payment of Benefit
Generally, clients whose benefit continues to be paid will not be entitled to an Advance Payment of Benefit when they have a 13-week non-entitlement period imposed. This is because they will be contributing to their hardship through not recomplying. The client's first option to improve their financial situation is to recomply.
For more information see:
## Exemptions or transfers
In some instances it may be appropriate to consider an exemption or a transfer to another benefit that does not have work obligations.
For more information on transfers and exemptions see:
- Exemptions
- Changes and reviews Qualifies for another benefit

chunks.title: Five-day verification window — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Five-day verification window
A client must provide MSD with verification of their Community Work Experience before the end of the 2-week search period, and at the end of their position period. This is to verify that they have:
- found a position with an organisation during the 2-week search period, and
- completed all the requirements of their Community Work Experience during the 4-week period.
However, there may be times when MSD is not able to process the information within that same period.
