To prevent a client from being disadvantaged due to processing delays, there is a 5-day verification window at the end of the 2-week search period and at the end of the position period. This allows MSD to process information a client has provided and ensures a client’s payment will continue.
Note this is not extra time for a client to secure a position or provide verification to MSD. Clients must still complete their search and provide verification before the end of the 2-week search period.
## No action from MSD
The client will be considered non-compliant if, after 5 days:
- MSD has not confirmed if the position is suitable (or unsuitable) for their Community Work Experience, or
- MSD has not been able to confirm if the client has completed their Community Work Experience, or
- the client has not provided the required verification for either their search period or position period.
Their payments will reduce from the day after the search period or the position period ended, depending on which verification window was in place. This may result in a debt for the client.

chunks.title: Full or partial exemptions — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Full or partial exemptions
A client may be granted a temporary exemption from meeting some or all of their work preparation obligations or work obligations.
Before MSD grants an exemption, they must check if the exemption reason is full, partial or both.
The client can be granted a partial exemption from their work obligations if they can still:
- plan for employment and
- undertake some work related activities
If the client is not able to do either of the above they should be granted a full exemption.
A client who has a full exemption from their work obligations may still be required to attend an interview with MSD to discuss their circumstances and when it might be appropriate for them to start planning towards a return to work.
## Clients with work preparation obligations
Generally, clients with work preparation obligations can only be considered for a full exemption.
Work preparation obligations mean they are required to plan for employment and undertake work preparation activities.
## Duration
Each exemption has a maximum duration. The period the exemption is granted for depends on the client's circumstances.
At the time of granting the exemption MSD should:
- advise the client of the temporary nature of the exemption
- schedule a date to review the exemption if appropriate
At the review MSD should consider the client's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption. MSD can ask the client to provide evidence of the reason to extend their exemption.
Note the duration of an exemption for a client with a health condition, injury or disability is based on the next reassessment date recorded by their registered medical practitioner or [MW1] nurse practitioner, (or [MW2] dentist [MW3] or midwife[MW4] where relevant).

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure
You need to be satisfied that the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their obligations, based on the information you have, before you initiate an obligations failure.
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'.
Having considered the circumstances, was it reasonable for the client not to have met their obligations?
For social obligations you will need to assess whether the client is taking all reasonable steps to meet all of their social obligations for each dependent child.
Good and sufficient reasons will depend on the obligation the client has failed.
For more information see:
- Social obligations All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Drug test obligation failures good and sufficient reasons
- Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation
- Good and sufficient reason for failing obligation to work with a contracted service provider
Decide in favour of the client if any doubt remains.
If you are aware that the client has a good and sufficient reason, do not initiate an obligations failure.
If the client does not have a good and sufficient reason, see:
- Effect of sanctions on assistance
- Failing more than one obligation at the same time

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for failure to find or complete Community Work Experience — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason for failure to find or complete Community Work Experience
A client may be unable to find or complete Community Work Experience for a good and sufficient reason. These reasons may include, but are not limited to:
- a client has made reasonable efforts to find a position but has not found one during the 2-week search period – for example, if a client has contacted many volunteer organisations but they do not have any available positions
- they are unable to complete the required hours in any of the 4 weeks for reasons beyond their control
- the conditions of the organisation and/or requirements of the position make it unsafe for the client to continue
If a client is delayed in notifying MSD of their good and sufficient reason, the delay must only be for a reasonable period. MSD will determine on a case-by-case basis whether the length of the delay is reasonable or not.
If MSD determines that they are unable to complete Community Work Experience for a good and sufficient reason, and a client has notified MSD within a reasonable period, MSD must impose a Grade 1 financial sanction. The date the financial sanction is imposed depends on where the client is in their Community Work Experience period.
When a client is in their search or position period, the Grade 1 financial sanction is imposed from the day a client meets with MSD and MSD is satisfied there is a good and sufficient reason and they have notified MSD within a reasonable period.
When a client’s search period has finished and they did not secure a position, the Grade 1 financial sanction is imposed from the day after the search period ended.
MSD must assign a recompliance activity to the client as soon as possible.
If a client does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to find or complete Community Work Experience, or they did not notify MSD within a reasonable period, they will be considered non-compliant.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation
Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting work ability assessment obligations include (but are not limited to) when a client is:
- in hospital
- experiencing an acute mental health episode
For more information see:
- Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work or work preparation obligations
Note if a client refuses to complete a Self-Assessment, Structured Interview or a Work Ability Assessment, and they do not have a good and sufficient reason, they have an obligations failure.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation
Once a client has been through the regular engagement and support process and is not taking all reasonable steps to meet one of their social obligations, you then need to be satisfied that they do not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their social obligation, based on the information you have, before you initiate an obligations failure.
You should also consider whether a client has a good and sufficient reason for failing to comply with their social obligations, if they dispute an obligations failure after it has been initiated.
## Other factors to consider before determining a client has failed to comply
You should also consider whether a client has taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligation before deciding that they have failed to comply with their social obligation.
There are also some circumstances where social obligations do not apply. For example, when a child leaves school at 15 years old with a Ministry of Education Early Leaving Exemption, the obligation to ensure that child is enrolled in and attending school no longer applies.
Make sure you have provided the client with the appropriate engagement and support before considering that the client has failed their obligation and that this has been recorded in OBMAN.
If the client does not have a good and sufficient reason, see:
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment
You need to consider if there was a good and sufficient reason for the client to stop work.
Examples of good and sufficient reasons for ceasing employment include (but are not limited to) when the client:
- could no longer realistically transport themselves to their employment (e.g. where a client's place of employment has moved)
- had childcare arrangements that were not adequate or fell through
- had an unexpected event occur (e.g. they had to return to the family home in another location to care for a sick relative)
- left the job because the job was outside of their capabilities or the job was in an unsuitable business
- had a significant change in conditions of employment that meant the employment was no longer suitable
- needed to take leave without pay to protect their job in the future, e.g. due to an economic downturn, or an unexpected the temporary closure of the premises as a result of an event such as a fire or flood
- was not able to continue working full-time (and was unable to work reduced hours) as a result of a health condition, illness, or disability and has a medical certificate to show this
Remember you will need to consider the circumstances of each case.
For more information see:
- Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed

chunks.title: Failing 3 obligations in a 24 month period — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Failing 3 obligations in a 24 month period
If a client does not meet their obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, an obligations failure will be initiated and a graduated sanction may be imposed.
The graduated sanction regime applies to all obligations, including social obligations.
If a client fails 3 obligations without a good and sufficient reason in a 24-month period, they are subject to a grade three sanction - 13-week non-entitlement period.
This means for sole parents with dependent children, 3 obligations failures in a 24-month period will result in a 50% cancellation of benefit for 13 weeks.
## Job refusal
A client who refuses an offer of suitable employment is subject to a grade 3 sanction, regardless of their failure count in the 24-month period.
Note when an applicant fails their pre-benefit activity to accept an offer of suitable employment, they are not subject to a 13-week non-entitlement period or job refusal failure, as these can only be imposed once a client is getting a main benefit.
For more information see:
- Core policy Pre-benefit requirements
- When the sanction is imposed
- Paying other assistance during a sanction [no link find out why]
- Effect of a non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement
A special income exemption for severe disablement may be given to a client as an incentive for their personal effort to participate or continue in employment.
To help you to decide if a person is severely disabled consider the following:
- Does the client have to put in more effort in order to participate in employment? (for example, they may take a considerably long time to get ready in the morning or a longer time to travel to their place of employment)?
- Is the client's capacity to earn the same wage as a person without a severe disability reduced because of their disability (for example, does the client work reduced hours or receive less money for the job they undertake because of their disability)?
- Does the client have additional expenses to undertake employment (for example additional transport or equipment costs)?
- Does the client have difficulties participating in employment or completing their tasks because of their disability (for example, they may experience difficulties with mobility around the work place, be limited in the tasks they undertake or on occasion may not complete their work duties)?
- Does the client require assistance from another person to carry out some of their daily tasks (for example, washing, dressing or cooking)?
- Does the client require the assistance from another person to travel to work or to ensure their physical safety while at work (for example, does the client have difficulty using public transport)?
- Any other relevant factors that should be considered.
- If the client answers 'yes' to one or more of these questions you will have to decide if the client is severely disabled or if you need more information to make this decision.
Contact Helpline if you need help with the assessment.
For more information see:
- Amount of income exemption
- Exemption for severe disablement

chunks.title: Help with paying for the recompliance drug test — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Help with paying for the recompliance drug test
When a client has failed their drug test obligations the second time, they must agree that they will take and pass a drug test within 25 days of agreeing to do so.
Work and Income can help the client meet the full costs of taking the drug test if they cannot meet the cost of the drug test upfront.
In this case Work and Income will arrange to cover the cost of the drug test with the provider and then recover the cost from the client by way of debt repayment.
In order for Work and Income to help meet the costs of taking the drug test, the client must agree:
- to take and pass a drug test within 25 working days
- to contact drug test provider and arrange and then take the drug test and
- to provide the results to Work and Income
Work and Income will provide the client with names and contact details for drug test providers in the local area.
A client can only apply once during the 25 working day period for help with the costs of the recompliance drug test upfront. The 25 working days start from the day after the client agrees to recomply.
Note that Work and Income has an additional 5 working days to receive the results from the client and to process the information.
## Client pays for drug test upfront themselves
A client can pay for the recompliance test themselves, if they choose to do this, they must:
- take a clean drug test within 25 working days
- arrange with a drug test provider to take the drug test and
- ensure that they provide Work and Income with the drug test results
## Debt recovery and reimbursement to the drug test provider
Work and Income will arrange with the drug test provider to cover the cost of the drug test.
Once the cost of the drug test is reimbursed to the drug test provider it must be established as a debt to the client. The amount of the debt is the same amount that has been repaid to the drug test provider.
The recovery rate should be at the appropriate level giving consideration to any other debts the client may have. Debt repayment options must be discussed with the client at the earliest opportunity.
This assistance is only available for one recompliance drug test to be undertaken during the 25 working day period. The cost of further tests undertaken within that period will have to be met by the client.

chunks.title: Home schooling — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Home schooling
Clients with dependent children aged 5 or 6 years old (depending on when they start school) to 16 years of age will be required to take all reasonable steps to ensure the child is enrolled in and attending school. Home schooling meets this obligation in some circumstances.
Clients can home school their children and meet their social obligation if they have a Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School issued by the Ministry of Education.
However, if a client has work obligations, generally they won't be able to home school their child as this could impact on their ability to actively seek or be available for work. They may qualify for an exemption from their work obligations to home school their children.
## Certificate of exemption from enrolment at a registered school
A child does not legally have to attend school until they are aged 6 years (but most children start school at 5 years). If a child is aged between 5 and 6 years it is the parent's or caregiver's choice whether to have their child in early childhood education or school. They do not need to have a Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School issued by the Ministry of Education while the child is aged 5.
Once a child is aged six years a Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School issued by the Ministry of Education is required by law to enable a parent to home school their child.
## Social obligations and work obligations
When a client has work obligations as well as social obligations they must meet both sets of obligations at the same time. If the client is unable to meet their work obligations because they are home schooling a dependent child, you can consider granting an exemption from their work obligations. The client must meet the additional criteria for the home schooling exemption.
For more information see:
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Home schooling a dependent child
- Work obligations
- Exemptions

chunks.title: Home schooling a dependent child — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Home schooling a dependent child
This exemption may apply to clients with work obligations.
A client can, in very limited circumstances, be exempt from meeting some of their work obligations:
- if they are home schooling a dependent child or a foster child and
- they have restricted circumstances that make the child's attendance at school unreasonable
Before you grant an exemption you should:
- gather all the proof required
- get the approval of the service centre manager to the exemption
This is a partial exemption only.
## Transitional arrangements for a person home schooling a child when they become a beneficiary with work obligations
If a client is home schooling a child before becoming a beneficiary with work obligations then an exemption can be granted until the end of that school year, if they have an exemption certificate from the Ministry of Education.
## Proof
The client must provide:
- proof of the restricted circumstances that makes their child's attendance at school unreasonable and
- if the child is aged 6 years or older, their 'Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School', issued by the Ministry of Education (if it's not a recently issued certificate, the client needs to contact the Ministry of Education to get another certificate)
For an 'Application for exemption from enrolment at a registered school', see the 'Home education application form' link at the bottom of the Home education page (the application form is the same for primary and secondary schooling).
All exemptions for home schooling must be approved by a manager client service delivery.
For more information see:
- Restricted circumstances guidelines
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Home schooling'.

chunks.title: Hours range for suitable employment — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Hours range for suitable employment
Clients with work obligations must make themselves available for suitable employment of:
- at least 20 hours per week
Although the target to meet part-time work obligations is 20 hours per week, a job can be considered suitable if the hours of work per week are around the hours required to meet their work obligations.
## Hours range for clients with part-time work obligations
A person with part-time work obligations could be expected to undertake a job of between 15 and 25 hours per week if all other aspects of the job were suitable.
## Example
Anna is a sole parent and has part-time work obligations. She is an experienced hair dresser. A hairdressing vacancy arises for 18 hours per week at the local salon. The details of the job suit Anna's circumstances in all ways, including her caring responsibilities.
This job is considered 'suitable employment' and Anna must apply and accept the job (if it is offered to her) or fail to meet her obligations. If Anna is offered the job, she would still be expected to be available for other work, training or other activities as she is in employment less than 20 hours per week.
Note if another job with more hours is found for Anna in another salon but the hourly rate is less and overall she would be no better off financially, the job would not be considered suitable. A suitable job would be one that was for more hours that paid the same or greater than what she was earning in her current part-time job.
For more information see:
- Work obligations
- Suitable employment
- Meeting job search requirements

chunks.title: Immigration status and supporting documents — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Immigration status and supporting documents
Generally, when people born overseas travel to New Zealand they are granted a visa by Immigration New Zealand. The visa shows the conditions under which they are allowed to be in New Zealand, for example temporarily (student, work, visitor) or as a resident.
The type of documents a client may provide to verify their immigration status depends on when they were issued.
From 29 November 2010 clients with an existing permit are 'deemed' to hold the corresponding type of visa under the new Immigration Act 2009. This means that:
- permits continue to be valid until their expiry date. A person does not need to replace a permit in their passport with a new visa until the permit expires
- residents with an existing residence permit may never have this updated with a new type of visa
## Unable to provide visa or permit
When a client is unable to provide an immigration visa or permit they may provide other Immigration New Zealand documents to verify their immigration status. Work and Income can also undertake an immigration status check directly with Immigration New Zealand.
Note that Immigration New Zealand may be unable to verify immigration status for clients of British nationality who arrived in New Zealand before 2 April 1974 and do not have a passport.
For more information see:
- Two years residence
- Resident in New Zealand
- Refugees and protected persons
- Immigration status [no link find out why]
- Immigration changes from 29 November 2010 [no link find out why]

chunks.title: In approved full-time training — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## In approved full-time training
This exemption may apply to clients on Sole Parent Support with work obligations.
A client can be partially exempt from meeting some of their work obligations if they are engaged in approved full-time training.
Consider whether the training course is the most suitable activity for the client. Also consider if other activities (for example programmes, seminars or work experience) might be a more appropriate option for moving the client towards paid work.
Discuss and take into account the client's career background, including:
- their educational qualifications
- their employment history
- their skills and
- whether training will help them find work at the earliest opportunity
Examples of approved training courses include but are not limited to:
- Limited Service Volunteer (LSV) [no link find out why]
- Skills for Industry [no link find out why]
- Targeted Training [no link find out why]
- training approved by the regional contracts manager
The approved training must:
- be full time (at least 20 hours a week)
- focus on teaching practical, employment-related skills
- support the client to gain the skills that will help them find work
Approved training does not include a course undertaken by a full-time student, as defined by the Student Allowance Regulations 1998.
## Proof
Generally if a client has been referred to the training, they will not need to provide proof. However, if there is any doubt, you can ask the client to provide a training statement signed by the course provider.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months, or until the end of the training course, whichever is first.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'In approved training'.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions
- Studying or training on Sole Parent Support

chunks.title: In approved study before subject to work obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## In approved study before subject to work obligations
A Sole Parent Support client can be exempt from meeting some or all of their work obligations if they were in MSD approved study when their work obligations started, and they are still in that study.
This happens when a client was partway through a course of study when:
- they became subject to work obligations or
- their youngest dependent child turned 3 years old
When an exemption is approved, MSD may set conditions for the exemption. For example, the client must be passing their course of study.
## Proof
The client must provide proof they are in study, such as enrolment forms or a training statement from their training provider.
## Continuing study
If the client is continuing their study the following year, they must get a new exemption approved.
They must also provide confirmation they passed at least 50% of their course the previous year.

chunks.title: In full-time study at level four or above — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## In full-time study at level four or above
This exemption may apply to clients on Sole Parent Support with work obligations.
A client can be exempt from meeting some of their work obligations if they are engaged in full-time study at level 4 or above. This is a partial exemption.
There are no restrictions on the type of course that a Sole Parent Support client can undertake other than that the course is level 4 or above.
You can check whether study is at level 4 or above on the NZQA qualifications framework. Level 4 courses are courses post-secondary school.
For more information refer to the NZQA website.
You can still require a client to meet with you during the time they are studying. This will allow you to monitor their progress and, plan with them to look for work when their course finished.
Note you should remove the exemption if the client fails their course.
## Proof
The client has to provide evidence of their study such as:
- enrolment forms
- academic transcript
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months or the end of the current academic year, whichever is the earliest. This exemption should be granted each academic year.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason "SPS level 4 study or above".
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions
- Studying or training on Sole Parent Support

chunks.title: In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes where a client is in or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence.
Treatment for the purposes of the drug test requirements means any specialist treatment service provided for a person because of a diagnosed drug dependency.
The client can either be participating in or on the waiting list for a specialist treatment service.
Specialist treatment services are services:
- that provide specific medical or psychological interventions with the goal of helping a person to overcome drug dependency
- that a client has been referred to following a formal assessment by the Community Alcohol and Drug Service (CADS) or by a registered AOD practitioner
The client can be asked to provide verification from the person recommending the treatment or from the treatment service. The verification must state the duration or time that the client will need to address their drug dependency and whether they are participating or on the wait list for treatment. There is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to your client.
For more information see:
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: Income from overseas — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Income from overseas
When a client has been working overseas within the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before their entitlement date you include this in their average weekly income.
If the client cannot provide verification of their earnings, accept the information provided on their application for benefit. For help to convert foreign currency to the equivalent New Zealand dollars see the instructions below.
There is no ability to take higher living costs into account. If the client is in financial hardship during an initial stand-down they can apply for a Special Needs Grant.
## Receiving a benefit from overseas
When a client has been receiving an overseas benefit or pension within the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before their entitlement date you include this in their average weekly wage.
If the overseas benefit or pension payments have stopped and the client cannot provide verification of their payments, accept the information provided on their application for benefit. There is no requirement to obtain verification through International Services
Note when the overseas benefit payments are continuing and the client cannot provide verification, you will need to verify details of these payments. For further assistance contact International Services.

chunks.title: Income less than a disqualifying rate — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Income less than a disqualifying rate
Where Sole Parent Support client starts work during the initial stand-down period, you do not re-assess the client's commencement date when:
- their level of income is less than a disqualifying rate
Where employment continues beyond the commencement date, you charge the clients earnings (income) against their benefit from the commencement date.

chunks.title: Informing a client of the drug test obligation failure — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Informing a client of the drug test obligation failure
Once MSD has decided that a client has failed a drug test work obligation, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. The client will then be sent a letter stating that their benefit will be sanctioned and that their benefit will only be increased if they:
- complete a recompliance activity
- dispute the decision to impose the sanction and MSD accepts that they have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting their work obligations or
- lodge a Review of Decision and MSD reconsiders their position and agrees with the client's review
For some clients, if it's their first obligation failure they may be eligible for a non-financial sanction instead of a financial sanction. For more information see: Non-financial sanctions.
## Recompliance for a drug test work obligation failure
Clients may have their benefit increased or restarted from the date they start a drug test failure recompliance activity.
For more information see:
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Drug test obligation failures - Good and sufficient reasons
- Client has failed a screening drug test

chunks.title: Informing clients of their obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Informing clients of their obligations
You must ensure that the client understands:
- their obligations
- the consequences of failing to meet those obligations, in particular the sanctions that may be imposed and
- their right to review and dispute any decisions relating to a failure to comply with their obligations
Clients applying for Sole Parent Support must:
- sign their application form and
- be given a copy of their obligations from their application form
Note that obligations cannot be enforced until the main benefit commencement date.
## Clients transferring between obligations
When a client is receiving a benefit and they have a change in obligations, a letter will be sent advising them what their new obligations are. They do not need to re-sign an obligations form.
This includes where a client is transferring between having work preparation obligations and then part-time work obligations when their youngest dependent child turns 3 years of age within Sole Parent Support.
For more information see
- Drug test obligations
- Obligations
- Social Obligations
- Work ability assessment obligation
- Work with a contracted service provider obligation
- Work or work preparation obligations

chunks.title: Initial stand-down procedure — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Initial stand-down procedure
Step 1. Find the client's entitlement date.
Step 2. Calculate the client's average weekly income for a 26 and 52 week period.
Step 3. Find out whether the client has or had any dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement date. When determining the correct stand-down period, you must take into account any children that were in the client's care during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to the entitlement date
Step 4. Using the information from Steps 2 and 3, determine the initial stand-down for the client over a 26 and 52 week period by looking at the initial stand-down period chart in Deskfile.
Step 5. Use the calculation of average weekly income that gives the client a lesser stand-down period.
Step 6. Apply the initial stand-down from the client's entitlement date to find the commencement date.
Remember if you enter the correct information into SWIFTT it will automatically calculate the initial stand-down and commencement date for you.
Note if the client has had a dependent child (or children) in their care during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement date and the child (or children) is no longer in their care, you will have to use a work around. Contact Helpline for this information.

chunks.title: Introduction — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Sole Parent Support provides income support for sole parents with one or more dependent children.
For more detailed information on the Sole Parent Support see:
- Qualifications
- Obligations
- Commencement date
- Payment
- Changes and Reviews

chunks.title: Limited employment locations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Limited employment locations
These guidelines explain how the limited employment locations policy affects Sole Parent Support clients who have work obligations.
## Living in a limited employment location
A client living is a limited employment location must continue to meet their work obligations, this includes being available for, and taking reasonable steps to obtain, suitable employment of at least 15 hours per week. They will not be expected to relocate.
Note this does not include clients who move from one limited employment location to another. In this instance, see:
- Clients moving to a limited employment location
## Moving to a limited employment location
If a client is moving to a limited employment location they must be able to show that they can continue to meet their work obligations.
These clients have an obligation to be available for, and taking reasonable steps to obtain suitable employment of at least 15 hours per week.
To meet this obligation, a client who moves to a limited employment location must have access to reliable transport and be willing and realistically able to commute to a nearby town or centre where there is employment available.
For more information see:
- What is a limited employment location?
- Deskfile Limited employment locations alert sheet
- Assistance to move back to an area that is not a limited employment location
- Clients moving to a limited employment location
- Work obligations

chunks.title: Living apart — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Living apart
Generally, if a client is married or in a civil union you can accept that a couple is living apart when it is clear the relationship has ended and they are living in different homes.
However, the term 'living apart' does not mean they must be living in separate homes.
If a client is not married or in a civil union, it is important to establish there is no relationship in the nature of marriage or a civil union before assessing the client's entitlement to Sole Parent Support.
A relationship in the nature of marriage or civil union is determined by showing that a couple:
- is committed to each other emotionally and
- are financially interdependent
## Living in separate homes
When a client advises the relationship with their spouse or civil union partner has ended and they are living in separate homes, you need to consider why they are not living together.
Sometimes couples live apart for reasons other than a breakdown in their relationship or rearrange their circumstances to qualify for a benefit.
This can include (but is not limited to) the following reasons:
- business/employment reasons (e.g. truck driver, shearer etc) or
- health reasons or
- 1 partner lives overseas or
- financial reasons
Sole Parent Support can only be paid when the relationship has ended.

chunks.title: Meeting job search requirements — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Meeting job search requirements
Job search requirements apply to clients with part-time work obligations.
To help decide if a client is meeting the job search requirements, you will need to consider the following:
1. If the client had the opportunity, would they:
- be available for work of at least 20 hours per week
- accept any suitable job offers within their abilitiesNote that this can include weekend work depending on their individual circumstances
- not restrict their job search to vacancies within their own trade
- not restrict their job search to vacancies in their chosen occupation
- not move frequently from one area to another with no intention of getting a job
2. Has the client begun to take steps to find work? For example by:
- searching newspapers and other media for vacancies
- making applications for suitable jobs
- contacting employers about vacancies

chunks.title: Situations where the voluntary unemployment 13 week non-entitlement period would apply — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Situations where the voluntary unemployment 13 week non-entitlement period would apply
Situations where a client would be subject to a 13 week non-entitlement include (but are not limited to):
- a previously self-employed client applies for Sole Parent Support because they have closed or sold a viable business without a good and sufficient reason
- a client who is currently receiving Sole Parent Support has a dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years and therefore has part-time work obligations. The client has left their part-time job without a good and sufficient reason.
For more information see:
- Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period
Before applying a 13 week non-entitlement period for misconduct, you should contact both the client and their employer. When you contact the employer you should give them the Earnings Verification form.
Note if the employer does not return the Earnings Verification form or the reason for termination is not given, no further contact with the employer should be made.
Also note that if there is conflicting evidence or the reason for leaving employment is not agreed between the client and the employer, you should give the client the benefit of the doubt.
Each client's circumstances need to be carefully investigated. If you are uncertain whether a voluntary unemployment 13 week non-entitlement period should be imposed, discuss the client's circumstances, in the first instance, with a service centre trainer and then with Helpline (if still required).
If you decide to apply a voluntary unemployment 13 week non-entitlement period, you will need to:
- advise the client of your decision
- send the client the 'Voluntary Unemployed' letter to confirm your decision. A copy of the letter is available in CMS letter templates
- for sole parents, the client's commencement date letter will confirm your decision and outline their rate of payment
- add the date that a non-entitlement period will apply from and the appropriate VU reason code to the SSTDA screen in SWIFTT
- conditionally grant the benefit using code 024 (VU imposed) on the SPGRT screen on SWIFTT
- note for sole parents the 13 week non-entitlement period only applies to 50% of the benefit
- make notes in CMS outlining your decision
Note ensure the benefit remains conditionally granted. Do not decline the benefit.
For more information see:
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed
- Misconduct
- Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer

chunks.title: Monitoring compliance with social obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Monitoring compliance with social obligations
If you have reasons to be concerned that a client may not be meeting their social obligations you should, in the first instance, discuss and explain their social obligations with them and ensure they understand these obligations. For example when:
- you receive information that a client is not requiring their school age child to attend school
- you receive information that a client's child has not been receiving their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks
In these situations, you should start the regular engagement and support process with the client.
For more information see:
- Regular engagement and support process
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Social obligations

chunks.title: No court ordered split care arrangement — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## No court ordered split care arrangement
To help you decide which parent can get Sole Parent Support, in situations where there is no court ordered split care arrangement, use the following steps:
Step 1
If one parent already receives Sole Parent Support you continue to pay it (the other parent cannot receive Sole Parent Support).
Step 2
If both parents apply for a benefit at the same time the parent who was mainly responsible for the day to day care of the children before the parents separated will get Sole Parent Support.
It may be necessary to interview both parents to ensure that they both agree on what is the case. If they do not agree you need to put the case of each to the other and come to a finding on what are the facts.
Step 3
If it is not clear who was mainly responsible for the day to day care before the separation, the parent who is the principal day to day caregiver of the youngest child will get the Sole Parent Support.
## Exception
If a client with children from a split care situation has a dependent child from another relationship you can pay them Sole Parent Support.
For more information see:
- Court ordered spilt care arrangements
- Split care
- Determining whether a care arrangement is sanctioned by the Family Court
- Privacy Act implications
- Assistance for the parent not qualified for Sole Parent Support
- When to consider Emergency Maintenance Allowance for split care

chunks.title: No details of a nominated person provided — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## No details of a nominated person provided
If a client refuses or is unable to provide the details of a third party, you should talk to the client about why they will not name one. This may include asking the client a series of questions about their relationship status.
You should also consider whether the other information they have provided indicates the client's relationship status. For example, if the client has provided evidence of their bank account number, and this evidence shows that the bank account is a joint bank account number - this might suggest that a client is still in a relationship.
There is a series of follow-up questions you can ask your client to help gather information about their relationship status.
For more information see:
- Examples of using relationship status verification
- Relationship status interview questions

chunks.title: No stand-down applies — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## No stand-down applies
An initial stand-down is not imposed in the following situations:
- Transfer between benefits
- Temporary employment
- Prisoners
- Entering a refuge
- In residential care
- Client leaves Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre
If no stand-down applies, the commencement date of the benefit is the later of either:
- the entitlement date or
- the application date
Note when no stand-down applies, the 28-day rule does not apply.

chunks.title: Nominated person makes contact after completing form — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Nominated person makes contact after completing form
In some cases, a nominated person may complete the Relationship Status Verification form, and then contact Work and Income to state that they want to withdraw or change their statement.
If this occurs, you should consider why the nominated person is retracting their statement, and along with any other information gathered, determine whether the client qualifies for Sole Parent Support.
Note the client must not be told that the nominated person has contacted Work and Income about their statement. You need to make sure you protect the nominated person by thinking carefully about what you note on the client's record. You should follow existing practices for managing allegations if a third party makes contact to change or withdraw statements.
For more information see:
- Relationship Status Verification form received

chunks.title: Clients with dependent children — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Clients with dependent children
Clients with dependent children have 50% payment protection.
A client with dependent children will have their payments reduce by 50% from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
A client may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be resumed from the date that the client has recomplied.
These clients will also be contacted after 2 weeks of receiving only 50% of their benefit.

chunks.title: Clients with dependent children — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Clients with dependent children
Clients with dependent children have 50% payment protection.
A client with dependent children will have their payments reduced by 50% from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
A client may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be increased from the date that the client has recomplied.
These clients will also be contacted after 2 weeks of receiving only 50% of their benefit. For more information see: Effect of sanctions on assistance.

chunks.title: Clients with dependent children — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Clients with dependent children
Clients with dependent children have 50% payment protection.
A client with dependent children will have their payments reduce by 50% from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
A client may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be increased from the date that the client has recomplied.
These clients will also be contacted after 2 weeks of receiving only 50% of their benefit. For more information see: Effect of sanctions on assistance.

chunks.title: Non-entitlement period for 13 weeks — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Non-entitlement period for 13 weeks
A non-entitlement period of 13 weeks is a period where clients are unable to get a benefit because they:
- have become voluntarily unemployed without a good and sufficient reason
- are applying for a benefit because they were dismissed by their employer for misconduct
- have failed their obligations for a third time in the last 24 months of continuous benefit receipt (as a grade 3 sanction) or
- have refused an offer of suitable employment (if they have work obligations)
## Non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or dismissal
Before imposing a 13-week non-entitlement period, the reason why the client has left employment needs to be carefully investigated to determine whether it is appropriate to apply a 13-week non-entitlement period.
For voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct the 13-week non-entitlement period starts from the day after the date the client's employment ceased.
For more information see:
- Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
## Non-entitlement period for obligations failures
Where a client fails their obligations and has a grade 3 sanction imposed, they will have a 13-week non-entitlement period.
For imposing a grade 3 sanction the 13-week non-entitlement period starts the date after the 5 working day notice period.
For more information see:
- Grade 3 sanction or job refusal failure non-entitlement period
- Paying other assistance during a sanction
Also see:
- Effect of non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Financial assistance during non-entitlement period
- Recompliance - 13 week non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Client has left temporary employment — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client has left temporary employment
A 13 week non-entitlement period does not apply when the person was in temporary part-time or full-time employment (employment of less than 26 weeks) and they have applied for a benefit after their employment came to an end. It may be applied if the client voluntarily left their temporary employment before it was due to end.
Temporary employment can include employment during an employment trial period of up to 90 days if the client was receiving a benefit and is reapplying for Sole Parent Support as their employment has ceased.
This also applies when a client has been working more than 30 hours a week on Sole Parent Support and receiving a salary or hourly wage that does not fully reduce the benefit, and they have reached the end of their 26 week temporary period in which this is allowable.
Note the client's average weekly income is not required where the client has been in temporary employment for less than 26 weeks. However, the client's final pay details are required to determine the date of event and entitlement date.
For more information see:
- Qualifications Temporary employment
- Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment
- Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer

chunks.title: Criteria to receive a non-financial sanction — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Criteria to receive a non-financial sanction
A client can only get a non-financial sanction if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they meet with MSD within the 5 working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure decision is not disputed and overturned, and
- a non-financial sanction would be appropriate for them based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or they have dependent children
MSD must assess a client’s circumstances and determine which non-financial sanction, if any, is most appropriate for the client. Each non-financial sanction has different factors to consider.
## Non-financial sanctions, Emergency Housing Grants and Special Needs Grants
Clients who have a non-financial sanction imposed cannot get an Emergency Housing Grant. MSD should take this into consideration before choosing to impose a non-financial sanction.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Not reasonable for a client to provide details of a nominated person — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Not reasonable for a client to provide details of a nominated person
There are some situations where it may not be reasonable for the client to name a nominated person. These include (but are not limited to):
- clients applying because their spouse or partner has died(These clients are not to be asked to provide details of a nominated person)
- Client has recently changed locations
- Client is experiencing family violence
- Partner in prison (These clients are not to be asked to provide details of a nominated person)
Where it is not reasonable for a client to provide details of a nominated person, you still need to be satisfied the client meets the qualifications for Sole Parent Support before granting the benefit.
For more information see:
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Notice to clients with sanctions, suspended or expired benefit — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Notice to clients with sanctions, suspended or expired benefit
If a client has a suspended or expired benefit they will not be sent the 'initial notice to reapply' letter. This is because they are not currently getting a benefit.
If a client's Sole Parent Support is resumed during the notice period, they must be advised about their upcoming expiry date and what they need to do to complete the 52 week reapplication process before the expiry date.
MSD should consider whether the client will be able to complete the reapplication process before their expiry date and if an extension may be appropriate.
For more information see:
- Resuming suspended or expired benefit
- Situations where extensions can be given
Note if the client's benefit is resumed before the 'reminder to reapply' letter is due to be sent, the client will be sent this letter 7 working days before their expiry date.
## Reapplication process for clients with a financial sanction applied
Clients that have a financial sanction imposed will be sent the initial 'notice to reapply' letter and must complete the 52 week reapplication process before their expiry date or their benefit will stop.
This is because when a client getting Sole Parent Support fails their obligations and has a financial sanction imposed, their benefit is current because 50% protection applies.
Clients who have not yet completed a recompliance activity are still able to complete the reapplication process. During the reapplication appointment MSD should also discuss the activity that the client failed to undertake or complete. A client should be encouraged to recomply as soon as possible.
Note if the client completes the reapplication process before their expiry date and their Sole Parent Support is regranted, the sanction will continue to apply to the regranted benefit until they recomply.

chunks.title: Notice to reapply — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Notice to reapply
Clients with a current Sole Parent Support are automatically sent an "initial notice to reapply" letter 25 working days before their expiry date advising them they need to complete the 52 week reapplication process.
A client needs to complete the 52 week reapplication process before their expiry date if they still need Sole Parent Support.
The notice period allows sufficient time for clients to attend an appointment and complete the 52 week reapplication process.
Note the initial notice to reapply letter will not be sent to clients if their benefit is suspended or cancelled.
For more information see:
- Notice to clients with sanctions, suspended or expired benefit
## Initial notice to reapply
The "initial notice to reapply" letter advises the client:
- that if they still need Sole Parent Support they must reapply before their expiry date and
- what they need to do to complete the 52 week reapplication process
There are no review rights in these letters because it is a requirement for clients to complete the 52 week reapplication process.
For information see:
- Review of Decision - 52 week reapplication process
## Sole Parent Support clients getting Disability Allowance
Clients getting Sole Parent Support must complete the reapplication process to continue getting their benefit. These clients will have a Mandatory Review for Disability Allowance when they:
- are completing the reapplication process for the benefit and
- their disability costs have not been reviewed in the last 44 weeks
If a client's disability costs have been reviewed in the last 44 weeks, there will be no Mandatory Review of Disability Allowance.
Note this applies to the Review of Disability Allowance only, it does not apply when the disability is due for medical reassessment.
The reapplication process is not impacted if a client does not complete their Mandatory Review for Disability Allowance.
For more information see:
- Mandatory Review for Disability Allowance
## Reminder to reapply
If a client has not completed the 52 week reapplication process a reminder letter will be sent 7 working days before their expiry date.
## Contact made before notice period
If a client makes contact before their notice period, MSD will schedule an appointment to complete the 52 week reapplication process within their notice period (but before their expiry date).
For more information see:

chunks.title: Number of dependent children — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Number of dependent children
If a client had a dependent child (or children) in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application the child (or children) must be taken into account when determining the stand-down.
For example, if a single client with 1 dependent child applies for benefit the stand-down period will be based on a single client with 1 child. However, if this client had 2 dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application, the stand-down period will be based on a single client with 2 dependent children.
This is regardless of whether the child is still in the client's care at the time of application.
See also:
- Dependent child
- Orphans Benefit/Unsupported Childs Benefit

chunks.title: Obligations failures — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: If a client fails to comply with their obligations, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. MSD must be satisfied that the client would have had no good and sufficient reason for their failure based on the information available. For social obligations, MSD must consider whether the client has taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations and must go through the regular engagement and support process before considering that the client has failed their obligation. For more information see: - Failing more than one obligation at the same time - Work obligations - Work preparation obligations - Social obligations - Social obligations Regular engagement and support process - Social obligations All reasonable steps to meet social obligations - Drug test obligations - Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure Note for a client who has part-time work obligations leaving part-time work averaging less than 20 hours per week, without good and sufficient reason or through misconduct, is also an obligations failure, but may not be specified in the client's work obligations. Once MSD has decided that the client has failed their obligations, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. The client will then be sent a letter stating that their benefit will be sanctioned and that their benefit will only be increased or resumed if they: - complete a recompliance activity - dispute the decision to impose the sanction and MSD accepts that they have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting their obligations - lodge a Review of Decision and MSD reconsiders their position and agree with the client's review or - lodge an appeal to the Medical Appeal Board (drug test failure only) Once a client has completed their recompliance activity, their benefit can be increased or resumed from the date MSD is satisfied the client started the activity. For some clients, if it’s their first obligation failure they may be eligible for a non-financial sanction instead of a financial sanction. For more information, see: - Non-financial sanctions All clients have a 5 working day notice period to dispute or recomply before the sanction is imposed. If a client recomplies within the 5 working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the obligations failure is recorded. For more information see: - When the sanction is imposed - Counting previous obligations failures - Failing more than one obligation at the same time Clients have not failed their obligations if they do not complete or undertake Voluntary Work or Activity in the Community.

chunks.title: Effect on rates payable — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: The reduction, suspension and cancellation applies to 50% of the main benefit the client is getting. The effect on extra help depends on the type of extra help. Non-financial sanctions do not affect the rate payable for a client.

chunks.title: Obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Obligations
Clients getting Sole Parent Support have the following obligations:
- they must advise of any change in circumstances that affect their entitlement or rate of benefit payable
- if they have a youngest dependent child aged under 3 years old, meet work preparation obligations
- if they have a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years, meet part-time work obligations
- if required, undertake and pass a pre-employment or pre-course drug test
- they must take all reasonable steps to meet social obligations that apply for each dependent child in their care
- if required, participate in a Work Ability Assessment
- if required, work with a contracted service provider
- advise Work and Income if they are intending to travel overseas, before they leave New Zealand

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki documentation — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Oranga Tamariki documentation
Where there has been Oranga Tamariki involvement and a Family Group Conference held, you will need to obtain copies of the relevant Oranga Tamariki documents from the client.
If the client cannot show the required "proof" of a breakdown from Oranga Tamariki you will need to hold a Family Meeting.
A supporting letter from Oranga Tamariki (or other authorised agency) alone is not proof of a breakdown but may provide supporting information relevant to a Family Meeting by confirming the continuation of placement with the alternative caregiver.
## Relevant documentation from Oranga Tamariki
Relevant documentation from Oranga Tamariki, obtained via the client, to prove a family breakdown has occurred include:
- a copy of the Family Group Conference outcome
- copies of all current Court Orders in respect of the child
- a copy of the court-approved Plan
These documents confirm current care arrangements and also include future care arrangements, including the reason that the child has come into the client's care.
If the client cannot show Oranga Tamariki documentation, it will be necessary to conduct a Family Meeting.
For more information see:
- Family Meeting

chunks.title: Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit under 3 years — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit under 3 years
This exemption may apply to clients with work obligations.
In some cases a client may be caring for a child under 3 years old for whom they are receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit.
Clients granted this exemption will be subject to work preparation obligations.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted in SWIFTT for 12 months initially or to when the child turns 3 years of age - whichever is earlier.
The exemption can be renewed after 12 months provided the child is still under 3 years old and the parent still qualifies for benefit.
## SWIFTT process
Clients who receive Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit for a child under 3 years old are not automatically exempt in SWIFTT. You need to add an exemption on the main benefit record via SWTDA in SWIFTT.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions

chunks.title: Other exceptional circumstances — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Other exceptional circumstances
In determining whether a client has any other exceptional circumstance for not completing the reapplication process before their expiry date MSD must consider if they meet the criteria for exceptional circumstances.
The criteria for considering whether a situation or event is an exceptional circumstance, is that it is:
- unforeseen, out-of-the ordinary and could not be planned for and
- beyond the client's control and
- those which set the client apart from others in a similar situation
Also that:
- the exceptional circumstance situation or event must have happened at any time during the client's notice period and
- the event has affected their ability to reapply for their benefit
Note other exceptional circumstances may include an emergency or adverse event where no local or national state of emergency has been declared, or where the emergency or adverse event has ended but the client is still affected by the event at the time their "initial notice to reapply" letter is sent.
MSD will need to assess each case on its own merits when determining whether other exceptional circumstances exist.
## Evidence
Clients could be asked to provide evidence. Evidence required will depend on the client's situation, and must be deemed satisfactory by MSD.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Outcome of case — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Outcome of case
Outcomes from mediation are strictly confidential to the parties involved, so any information about the settlement will have to be obtained from the client.
Where a client wins their personal grievance case, and receives a wage settlement for a period during which a benefit with work obligations was paid:
- review the client's entitlement date and non-entitlement period assessments and
- establish any overpayments
If it is determined that the employer was not at fault, then a 13 week non-entitlement period for misconduct can be applied.
If the settlement order states that the payment or part payment is to cover legal or other costs, do not recover benefit received from the payment amount. If it is unclear what the client's settlement is for, contact Helpline for assistance.
If the case is settled but no party is admitting fault, a decision must be made as to whether the voluntary unemployed provisions apply. Use all evidence available but give the benefit of the doubt to the client. Contact your local solicitor for advice.
For more information see:
- Proof client is challenging dismissal
- Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer

chunks.title: Overview of social obligations according to age of the child — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Overview of social obligations according to age of the child
The table below shows the specific social obligations that apply to the client according to the age of their dependent children.
Age of client's dependent children

chunks.title: Parent is being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020 — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Parent is being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020
All parents are legally obliged to ensure their children are enrolled in and attending school from the age of 6 to 16 years.
Parents can be prosecuted and fined under the Education and Training Act 2020 if their children don't attend school. This can happen when:
- there has been, without explanation, ongoing and irregular attendance by the child at school after support has been offered to the family or
- the parent has made little or no attempt to do anything about ensuring the child attends school
If a parent is in the process of being prosecuted under the Education and Training Act 2020, you must not ask them to comply with the social obligation or initiate an obligations failure for non-attendance.
Note you need to record this as an exception in OBMAN using 'Parent is in prosecution for truant child' as the obligation exception reason.

chunks.title: Parents unable to care for child — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Parents unable to care for child
In some situations, a parent may be unable or unwilling to care for their child. In exceptional circumstances a child may be considered as a dependant if the parents are unable to care for the child.
Some examples of when parents are unable to care for their child, include but are not limited to (this is not an exhaustive list):
- are deceased or otherwise cannot be found
- are physically incapable of caring for the child (for example because of a disability, alcohol or other drug dependency etc)
- are emotionally or psychologically unable to care for the child
- are financially unable to care for the child or
- there has been a breakdown in the child's family and the child's parents are unable to care for, or provide fully for the child
## Care and protection concerns
When parents are unable to care for a child, it is important to consider any possible care and protection concerns for a child or young person.
If MSD believes any child has been, or is likely to be harmed (physically, emotionally or sexually), ill-treated, abused, neglected, deprived or MSD has concerns about the wellbeing of the child, the case must be referred to Oranga Tamariki.

chunks.title: Parents unwilling to care for child — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Parents unwilling to care for child
In some situations, a parent may be unable or unwilling to care for their child. In exceptional circumstances a child may be considered as a dependant if the parents are unwilling to care for the child.
To help determine whether the parents have exceptional circumstances and are unwilling to care for the child, consider whether the parents feel that their:
- child would be better cared for in another environment (for example, a child with specific needs who requires full-time attention from their caregiver that they feel they cannot give)
- family is at risk while that child remains in their care (for example, their child has behavioural problems or other issues which could result in other family members being placed at risk should the child remain in their care)
These are examples only, however, and other situations may also fit the criteria of a parent being unable or, in exceptional circumstances, unwilling to care for the child.

chunks.title: Partner in prison — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Partner in prison
You can pay Sole Parent Support to a client when they have lost the regular financial support of their partner as their partner:
- has been imprisoned or
- is subject to release or detention conditions that prevent employment
## Home Detention
Where the client and their partner were receiving a benefit before the partner went into prison (and the partner is eligible to apply for home detention), it is more appropriate to continue to pay all or part of that benefit to the client rather than pay Sole Parent Support. When the partner is approved release under the home detention programme, they may be included in the client's benefit and the partner can apply for an exemption from their work obligations.
Note that when a client has been in receipt of Sole Parent Support and a client's partner is released from prison to the same premises under the home detention programme, the client cannot continue to receive Sole Parent Support. The client or partner (on home detention) can test their eligibility to:
- Jobseeker Support or
- they may be eligible for an Emergency Benefit (if they cannot receive Jobseeker Support)
The partner (on home detention) can apply for an exemption from their work obligations.
When a client's partner is released from prison under the home detention programme but not to the same premises as the client receiving Sole Parent Support, the client can continue to receive Sole Parent Support. The partner released from prison can receive Jobseeker Support at the half married rate.
## Client's income
Some income the partner receives while they are in prison is taken into account and charged against the client's Sole Parent Support.
For more information see:
- Types of income

chunks.title: Paying other assistance during a sanction — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Paying other assistance during a sanction
When sole parents fail their obligations they do not have their whole benefit sanctioned. Instead, a maximum sanction of 50% of the total benefit may be imposed. The balance payable is known as 50% protection.
## On-going Extra help
Sole parents who are sanctioned can continue to get full supplementary assistance. Sole parents can continue to get the following assistance, regardless of the grade of the sanction:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit
## Winter Energy Payment
Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid in situations where a portion of main benefit continues to be paid.
Sole parents have a maximum sanction of 50% of the total benefit imposed but like other supplementary assistance, will continue to get the total amount of the Winter Energy Payment, regardless of the grade of the sanction.
Clients are not entitled to the following forms of assistance when they have had a 50% benefit suspension or cancellation imposed due to an obligations failure:
- Emergency Benefit
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit
## Special Needs Grants
Clients are not entitled to Special Needs Grants if a sanction has been imposed. This applies to both financial and non-financial sanctions.
The only exception to this is if a client has a health condition, injury or disability when a grade 3 sanction is imposed and they are incapable of participating in part-time employment or an approved activity for six weeks.
For more information see:
- Financial assistance during non-entitlement period
- Assistance when a client is sanctioned
## Advance Payment of Benefit
If a client has a 50% sanction imposed, and the client is experiencing hardship they may apply for an advance payment of benefit. A discussion must be held with the client about recomplying as the reduced rate of benefit will be contributing to their hardship.
A client can apply for an Advance Payment of Benefit if they have a non-financial sanction imposed, and may be eligible if they meet all the criteria.
## Assistance to transition into employment
Clients can get assistance to transition into employment if a sanction has been imposed and they meet the qualifications for it.
For more information see:
- Employment and work readiness Assistance to transition into employment
- Clients with dependent children - 50% protection [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Payment — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Payment
Sole Parent Support is paid weekly on a Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. Payment is from Monday to Sunday and is made one week in arrears.
Generally, payment must be made directly to the client. However, where there is good cause, the client's benefit can be paid to another person, agent or institution.
For more information see:
- Core policy Redirection of benefit payment
It is a condition of receiving a benefit that the client provides a bank account number.
MSD can request the client to provide an IRD number or evidence of their IRD number.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Example
Rahool is getting Sole Parent Support with part-time work obligations, however these obligations are deferred on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability.
He fails a work-preparation obligation on 3 March and is placed onto Money Management on 10 March. His Money Management period will end on 6 April.
Rahool’s medical certificate expires on 31 March. His benefit stops until he gets a new medical certificate.
He gets a new medical certificate on 10 April, 4 days after his Money Management period has ended. His benefit resumes from 31 March when his medical certificate first expired, and MSD issues arrears of his Sole Parent Support from 31 March to 10 April.
Rahool’s arrears for the period of 31 March to 6 April, are subject to Money Management. 50% of those arrears are paid onto his payment card and the remainder to his bank account.
The arrears owed after his Money Management ends, from 7 April to 10 April, are also paid directly into Rahool’s bank account.

chunks.title: Clients without permanent residence or citizenship — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Clients without permanent residence or citizenship
Emergency Maintenance Allowance may be paid to some categories of migrants who do not have permanent residence or citizenship eg people waiting for their application for refugee or protection status to be approved.
For more information see:
- Proof of residence
- Emergency Benefit
- Unlawful residence
- Refugees and protected persons
Note clients lawfully in New Zealand by virtue of a temporary permit or temporary entry class visa only (ie they do not have permanent residence) are not entitled to any benefit assistance.
To assess a client's entitlement you will generally need to establish exactly what category of migrant they are.
Clients may be granted permanent residence under the following categories:
- Family Stream
- International/Humanitarian Stream
- Skilled/Business Stream
Note if you require more information about a client's application for permanent residence you must get consent from the client to contact Immigration New Zealand or the client should obtain the information themselves. Otherwise the application should be declined. You must not collect or disclose information regarding a client's application without the client's consent.
For more information see:
- Immigration status [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
