## Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer
A benefit can be conditionally paid if the client challenges the dismissal or loss of employment.
Before the benefit can be paid you must obtain verification that the client is challenging the dismissal or loss of employment.
When a client's former employer confirms the client ceased their employment during their employment trial but does not disclose the reason for the termination, accept the client's reason for the termination and continue with the application process. Contact with the client's former employer is still required to confirm the date ceased and any holiday pay etc.
## Conditions for granting the benefit
The client is only granted their benefit on the condition that:
- they will repay all of the benefit received during the 13 week non-entitlement period if misconduct is proven and
- they may need to repay part or all of the benefit received during the 13 week non-entitlement period if they win wages, damages or other compensation
They will need to sign a statement to this effect.
When you grant a benefit (or pay a full rate of benefit) under these conditions, on the SDT1A screen you must use the 'reason for grant' code (48).
For more information see:
- Proof client is challenging dismissal
- Outcome of case

chunks.title: Pre-benefit activities for new applicants — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Pre-benefit activities for new applicants
Pre-benefit activities are work-related activities that a client may be required to attend and participate in as part of their application for Sole Parent Support.
Clients who have had their benefit cancelled due to the 52 week reapplication process will be subject to the same pre-benefit activities as other clients applying for Sole Parent Support.
## Exception
If a client has a job to go to within 13 weeks, they are not required to undertake pre-benefit activities.
If a client had a sanction imposed, before their benefit was cancelled as a result of the 52 week reapplication process, they should be asked to complete or undertake the activity they failed.
This activity should be assigned as a pre-benefit activity.
The pre-benefit activity must be assigned within 10 working days of the client's date of first contact.
For more information see:
- Core policy Pre-benefit requirements

chunks.title: Pregnant 27 weeks or earlier if complications — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Pregnant 27 weeks or earlier if complications
This exemption may apply to clients on Sole Parent Support with work obligations.
A client who is pregnant can be exempt from meeting some of their work obligations from:
- week 27 of the pregnancy or
- earlier if there are complications associated with the pregnancy
Note this is a partial exemption when it is reasonable to plan with the client.
## Evidence
The client must provide evidence from a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or midwife confirming the expected date of birth or nature of complications if their pregnancy is under 27 weeks.
## Duration
This exemption applies until the earliest date of either:
- the birth of the child or
- within 6 months from the date it was granted

chunks.title: In prison less than 31 days — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## In prison less than 31 days
Clients who have been in prison or on remand for less than 31 days do not have a stand-down imposed if they were receiving a benefit before going into prison.
If the client was not in receipt of benefit prior to being imprisoned or placed on remand, an initial stand-down is imposed.
There is no access to a Steps to Freedom Special Needs Grant for these clients.
## In prison for 31 days or more
Clients who have been in prison or on remand for 31 days or more have a stand-down imposed.
These clients have access to a Steps to Freedom Special Needs Grant to assist them during the stand-down. They may also have access to other forms of assistance to help them re-establish themselves in the community.

chunks.title: Privacy Act implications — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Privacy Act implications
In order to make a decision and give reasons for that decision, it may be necessary to disclose the personal information of one parent to the other parent.
This should be restricted to the information necessary to make an informed decision and comply with the legal requirement to give reasons for that decision.
If you need to interview the other parent, you should take care to inform the parent applying for benefit before contacting the other parent.
For more information see:
- Split care
- Court ordered split care arrangements
- No court ordered split care arrangement
- Determining whether a care arrangement is sanctioned by the Family Court
- Guidelines to the Privacy Act 2020
- When to consider Emergency Maintenance Allowance for split care [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Process for deciding appropriate activities — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Process for deciding appropriate activities
When you and the client are considering appropriate activities for the client to undertake, you should consider the following:
- what needs or barriers to employment is the activity designed to address for the client
- what activities are available to help the client move towards employment
- the Work and Income products that are available to help the client move towards employment
Examples of appropriate activities include (but are not limited to):
- education or training to improve clients work-readiness or prospects for employment
For more information see:
- Activity summary
- Informing clients of their obligations

chunks.title: Proof of residence — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: All documents should be originals. Photocopies and/or documents that have been changed in any way cannot be accepted. Where the client cannot provide proof or the proof is unclear, you should ask the client to obtain confirmation of their residential status from Immigration New Zealand (for permanent residence) or Internal Affairs (for citizenship). Proof of citizenship and/or permanent residence in New Zealand can be a: - New Zealand birth certificate Generally, a person born in New Zealand is a New Zealand citizen by birth. - New Zealand passport To hold a New Zealand passport you must be a citizen of New Zealand. - Certificate of Registration A child born outside New Zealand (to a parent who is a New Zealand citizen) may be a New Zealand citizen from birth. However, the child must apply for a Certificate of Registration to confirm their New Zealand citizenship. - Grant of Citizenship People who have permanent residence, may (normally after 5 years residence in New Zealand) apply for a Grant of Citizenship. They must meet the conditions of the Grant. - Certificate of Confirmation This is a certificate issued to confirm that the holder is a New Zealand citizen by birth, descent or Grant of Citizenship. British subjects, who immigrated to New Zealand prior to 1948 (and who resided in New Zealand for all of 1948) were made New Zealand citizens in 1949. These people are likely to have a Certificate of Confirmation or a Certificate of Naturalisation. - Certificate of Naturalisation Previously immigrants were naturalised as British Subjects and Citizens of New Zealand. Today they are given a Grant of Citizenship - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence class visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009 - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987 Note that a visa issued before 29 November 2010 does not allow a person to stay in New Zealand. - Letter of confirmation of permanent residence from Immigration New Zealand - Australian citizens Australian citizens are lawfully allowed in New Zealand as they are deemed to hold a residence class visa here. Their date of entry into New Zealand is generally not recorded. Where possible, supporting evidence should be sought, such as tenancy agreements, bank statements or old utility bills to show that the client has been ordinarily resident for 2 continuous years. - British nationals

chunks.title: Proof of residence — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Clients of British nationality who came to New Zealand before 2 April 1974 were automatically allowed to enter New Zealand for residence, and will be unable to provide verification of their residence if they do not have a passport. Immigration New Zealand will have no record of these clients unless the client has contacted them after 2 April 1974. The client should be able to provide New Zealand school, work or tax records to support their claim about when they arrived in New Zealand and the length of time they have lived here. For more information see: - Immigration status and supporting documents

chunks.title: Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: A temporary provisional benefit can be paid to the client while they are doing an approved activity or programme of activities during the 13-week non-entitlement period.

chunks.title: Provisional benefit — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: MSD can grant or increase a provisional benefit from the date the client starts the approved activity or programme of suitable activities. Their benefit will be provisionally paid to them if they are satisfactorily participating in their activity. The provisional payment will continue until: - the 6-week activity period ends, or - the 13-week non-entitlement period ends whichever is earlier. Some examples of this: - a client starts their approved activity in the beginning of week 3 of their non-entitlement period. The client participates for 6 continuous weeks, and the rest of the 13-week non-entitlement period is cancelled. After the follow-up appointment, the client’s benefit is reinstated to their usual benefit, instead of a provisional benefit. - a client starts their approved activity in the beginning of week 10 of their non-entitlement period. The client does the approved activity for the rest of the 13-week non-entitlement period (3 weeks). At the end of the 13-week non-entitlement period, the client’s benefit is reinstated to their usual benefit, instead of a provisional benefit.

chunks.title: End of approved activity or non-entitlement period — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: At the end of the approved activity or programme of activities a follow-up appointment is required (in approximately 6 weeks' time). At the appointment, MSD should discuss with the client whether they: - have satisfactorily participated in the approved activity, and - can still meet the qualifications and obligations of their benefit Note if the client does not recomply, they will have to reapply for their benefit at the end of the 13-week non-entitlement period if they wish to get a benefit.

chunks.title: Leaves approved activity or does not satisfactorily participate — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: If a client leaves early or does not satisfactorily participate in the approved activity or programme of suitable activities, change in their obligations, their provisional benefit must be reduced or stopped from the date it was increased or granted. The benefit amount that was provisionally paid during the 13-week non-entitlement period must be established as a debt and recovered. MSD cannot recover the debt if they did not complete the approved activity because they: - transferred to a benefit with no work obligations, or - meet the criteria for a full exemption from their work obligations Only one approved activity or programme can be assigned to a client. MSD cannot give the client a different approved activity if they fail to satisfactorily complete their approved activity. For more information see: - Recompliance - Unable to recomply

chunks.title: Purpose of the meeting — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Purpose of the meeting
The purpose of the family meeting is to find out:
- if a breakdown in the child's family has taken place. This can be found out by asking about the parents' financial and housing situation, or if they have any disabilities (the parents are not expected to provide proof of their financial circumstances)
- whether the parents are able but unwilling to provide full support for the child
- why (due to the breakdown) the child's natural, adoptive or step parent is unable to provide fully for the child
- the period the parent(s) are unable to provide fully for the child
- how long the caregiver is likely to have the child in their care
- what the caregiver's responsibilities are
Note that the meeting is not the time to discuss the best place for the child, resolve family problems or resolve care and protection concerns.
## Information MSD should give at the meeting
- provide the parents and caregiver with the opportunity to consider the information that is given to them in the meeting and decide whether to continue with the application
- explain the alternative to including the child as a dependent child for benefit purposes, (i.e. if they choose to apply for Unsupported Child’s Benefit for that child). This may mean the parents are required to pay Child Support through Inland Revenue
- explain that under family law, the parents keep the legal right to make decisions about their child and the caregiver has the day-to-day care of the child

chunks.title: Qualifications — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
A client applying for Sole Parent Support must have 1 or more dependent children under the age of 14 years, and be one of the following:
- living apart from their partner, and lost the support or being inadequately maintained by their partner
- divorced or had their civil union dissolved
- single (never had a partner)
- has lost the regular support of their partner, as their partner has been imprisoned, or subject to release, or detention conditions that prevent employment or
- their partner has died
To qualify for Sole Parent Support a client must:
- be aged 20 years or older and
- have continuously lived in New Zealand for 2 years or more since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for a benefit
In some situations the client may not be the natural or adoptive parent of the child but Work and Income can still regard the child as their own.
For more information see:
- Determining who is a parent
## Youngest child turns 14 years of age
When the youngest dependent child turns 14 years of age, the client's Sole Parent Support is automatically transferred to Jobseeker Support.
Jobseeker Support will commence on the date that the Sole Parent Support expires as if they had applied for Jobseeker Support, unless there is information to suggest the client will not qualify for Jobseeker Support.
## Verification of relationship status
Generally, clients applying for Sole Parent Support will be asked to provide details of a third party who can verify their relationship status.
For more information see:
- Verification of relationship status
## Pre-benefit requirements
A client applying for Sole Parent Support may be required to complete pre-benefit requirements.
For more information see:
- Core policy Pre-benefit requirements
## For more information on specific situations see:
- Residence
- Two years residence
- Dependent child
- Youngest dependent child turns 14
- Partner in prison
- Shared care
- Split care
- Proof of residence
- Sponsored clients
- Clients without permanent residence
- Residents from other countries
- Client receiving youth support payments
- Core policy Pre-benefit requirements
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit

chunks.title: Reapplication appointment — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Reapplication appointment
Clients must schedule an appointment to complete their 52 week reapplication process before their Sole Parent Support expiry date.
There is a notice period before their expiry date. This gives the client sufficient time to attend the appointment and complete the 52 week reapplication process.
To complete the 52 week reapplication process a client must:
- attend a reapplication appointment and
- complete a 52 week reapplication form and
- provide any supporting evidence required and
- participate in and complete a Comprehensive Work Assessment and
- meet the qualifications for Sole Parent Support
For more information see:
MSD will also check any Extra help the client gets to ensure they are getting their correct entitlement.
## Appointments on or after the expiry date
A client can attend the 52 week reapplication appointment on or after the expiry date in the following situations only:
- where a client makes contact to reapply before their expiry date, but the reapplication process cannot be completed before their expiry date, through no fault of their own or
- where a client has an exceptional circumstance that has affected their ability to reapply or contact MSD before their expiry date
For more information see:
- Contact made but reapplication not completed by expiry date
- Exceptional circumstances for reapplication
- Re-application (within 52 weeks) form

chunks.title: Reapplication process at 52 weeks — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Reapplication process at 52 weeks
Sole Parent Support is paid to help clients support their family while they are looking for or preparing for work. If the client still needs Sole Parent Support after 52 weeks they are required to complete the 52 week reapplication process.
Generally all clients getting Sole Parent Support must reapply and complete a Comprehensive Work Assessment as part of the 52 week reapplication process, regardless of their personal situation or current work obligations.
Note clients getting Emergency Benefit, where the equivalent benefit is Sole Parent Support, are not required to complete the 52 week reapplication process.
## Exceptions
There are situations where a client is not required to complete the reapplication process.
For more information see:
- Client does not need to complete the reapplication process

chunks.title: Recent bereavement of spouse or partner — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Recent bereavement of spouse or partner
This exemption may apply to clients with either work or work preparation obligations.
Clients whose spouse or partner has recently died can be exempt from meeting all their work or work preparation obligations to allow them time to adjust to their new circumstances. This is a full exemption.
Before granting this exemption you should consider the following factors:
- changes in living circumstances
- changes in childcare responsibilities
- particular religious or cultural beliefs or practices
## Proof
The client needs to provide:
- personal statement or
- evidence included in their application for benefit
- a death notice from the newspaper or
- a death certificate
If the client has been granted a Funeral Grant for their spouse or partner they should not be asked to provide proof again.
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to three months from the date of death.
You can extend the exemption. Before you do this you should ask the client to provide information to support the need for the exemption to continue.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Recent bereavement of partner/spouse'.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions

chunks.title: Recent separation from a spouse or partner — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Recent separation from a spouse or partner
This exemption may apply to clients with either work or work preparation obligations.
Clients who have recently separated from their spouse or partner can be exempt from meeting all their work or work preparation obligations to allow them time to adjust to their new circumstances. This is a full exemption.
Before granting this exemption you should consider the following factors:
- changes in living circumstances
- changes in childcare responsibilities
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Recent separation from partner/spouse'.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions

chunks.title: Reciprocal agreements — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Reciprocal agreements
New Zealand has Reciprocal Agreements with some countries.
Under these agreements, residence and or periods of insurance contributions in one of the following countries can be regarded as residence in New Zealand.
- Australia
- Canada
- Denmark
- Hellenic Republic (Greece)
- Ireland
- Jersey and Guernsey
- Malta
- Netherlands
- United Kingdom
For more information about these reciprocal agreements, contact International Services

chunks.title: Recompliance — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Recompliance is the activity a client must undertake after they have failed an obligation. They must complete the recompliance activity to have their benefit: - increased or resumed if they have been financially sanctioned or - continued if they have a non-financial sanction imposed Generally, the activities a client needs to complete are the same as or substantially similar to the obligation that initiated the failure. Clients with an obligations failure initiated who recomply within 5 working days will not have a sanction imposed, but the obligations failure will be counted. When a client indicates that they want to recomply MSD must make a recompliance activity available for them at the earliest opportunity. The obligations failure that has reduced or stopped their benefit will determine the type of recompliance activity the client will need to undertake. MSD must discuss with the client what activities they need to undertake in order to recomply. For more information see: - Recompliance for work obligation failures - Recompliance for social obligation failures - Recompliance for drug test obligation failures - Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: When to resume or increase a benefit — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: A client must have successfully completed the recompliance activity before their benefit is resumed or increased if they have been financially sanctioned. Once completed, the benefit can be resumed or increased from the date you are satisfied the client started the recompliance activity. Some examples of this: - if the recompliance activity is a one-off, such as attending an interview the benefit would be resumed from the date the client attended and participated in the interview - if the recompliance activity is ongoing, such as a training programme, the client must undertake the training programme to MSD’s satisfaction. Once this is complete, the benefit can be resumed from the date the client started the training programme - if the client has multiple recompliance activities to complete (due to more than one failure), the date when they have completed a recompliance activity for the latest failure Once MSD has made the decision to recomply a client through an on-going activity, and the client subsequently does not participate or complete the on-going activity (without a good and sufficient reason), then MSD may initiate another failure from the day they subsequently did not comply. For what to do if a client cannot recomply, see: - Unable to recomply - Recompliance and change of circumstances

chunks.title: Recompliance when a non-financial sanction is imposed — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Non-financial sanctions each have different recompliance requirements that must be met within the sanction period. If the non-financial sanction ends before the client has recomplied, their benefit will be suspended until they recomply. For more information see: - Non-financial sanctions

chunks.title: Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period) — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: A client can complete certain activities to get a temporary provisional benefit if they have a 13-week non-entitlement period because they: - left a job voluntarily - lost a job through misconduct - have a grade 3 sanction imposed or - refused an offer of suitable employment If a client wants to recomply, MSD must make a 6 week approved activity or programme of activities available to them at the earliest opportunity. An approved activity can start as soon as a sanction has been imposed, there is no waiting period.

chunks.title: Recompliance activities — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: The client must do their approved activity for 6 continuous weeks, or until the 13-week non-entitlement period ends (whichever is earlier). This can be through: - satisfactory participation in a 6 week approved activity or programme of activities or - satisfactory participation in part-time employment (if they have part-time work obligations)

chunks.title: Client does not complete activity — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: If the client fails to satisfactorily complete their 6 week activity or programme, and their obligations have not changed, their provisional benefit must be reduced from the date it was increased. The portion of the benefit that the client was paid provisionally must be established as a debt. The client must wait until the end of the 13-week non-entitlement period get their full rate of benefit reinstated. When a client makes contact at the end of the 13 weeks, MSD should review their circumstances to confirm that the client still qualifies and what rate of payment they should get. MSD must determine the appropriate date to increase the rate from, but this cannot be any earlier than the end of the 13-week period. Only one approved activity or programme can be assigned to the client. MSD cannot give the client a different activity if they fail to satisfactorily complete the original approved activity.

chunks.title: Recompliance for social obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: If a client fails their obligations for a third time, and the third failure is a social obligation failure, then their 6 week recompliance activity will be different. In this situation it may not be appropriate to choose an activity focused on work outcomes. A programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate instead. For more information see: - Failing a social obligation

chunks.title: Approved activity examples — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Here are some examples of suitable 6 week approved activities: - Employment and training - [no link find out why] Work experience, Activity in the Community and Voluntary work Note these are examples only. An approved activity or programme should be relevant to the obligation the client failed, and be fair and reasonable.

chunks.title: Programme of suitable activities — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: If there is no appropriate 6 week approved activity available, consider a programme of suitable activities. For more information see: - Recompliance programme example For when to grant or increase the benefit, see: - Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period For what to do if a client cannot recomply see: - Unable to recomply

chunks.title: Recompliance and change of circumstances — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance and change of circumstances
A client who has a failure in progress or a sanction imposed may be unable to recomply because they:
- had a change of circumstances that means they can no longer recomply with a social obligation or the social obligation is no longer relevant to them or
- had a change in obligations which means they are no longer required to comply with any activity that is specific to their previous obligations, for example a client moves between work obligations and work preparation obligations
In these situations, the client should not be required to recomply. However, the failure will still be included in the 24 month count.
Once the client has new obligations, MSD may ask them to complete any activities in relation to their new obligations.
## Examples
Examples of where MSD cannot require your client to complete a recompliance activity:
- where a child leaves care or changes age and the social obligation they had is no longer relevant (for example the client has failed the early childhood education social obligation and the child has now turned 6 years old)
- where a client is subject to work obligations has failed a drug test obligation and is transferred to work preparation obligations
- where a client who has work preparation obligations has failed to undertake planning for employment and is transferred to work obligations
- where a client who has work or work preparation obligations has failed an obligation and has been transferred to Supported Living Payment or Emergency Benefit with no obligations
For more information see:
- Recompliance for work obligation failures
- Recompliance for social obligation failures
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Recompliance and Report Job Search — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance and Report Job Search
Report Job Search is both a non-financial sanction for an obligation failure, and a recompliance activity for a client to recomply with their obligations.
This means that a client who is completing Report Job Search is not required to complete the same or similar activity that they originally failed to do.
If a client completes the requirements of Report Job Search and provides verification, they will be considered to have recomplied from the day they complete Report Job Search.
Clients who do not complete Report Job Search will be considered non-compliant. Their payments will be reduced, and MSD must assign an alternative recompliance activity as soon as possible.

chunks.title: Recompliance and Upskilling — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance and Upskilling
Upskilling is both a sanction for an obligation failure, and a recompliance activity for a client to recomply with their obligations.
This means that a client who is completing Upskilling is not required to complete the same or similar activity that they originally failed to do.
If a client completes the requirements of Upskilling and provides verification, they will be considered to have recomplied from the day they complete Upskilling.
Clients who do not complete Upskilling will be considered non-compliant. Their payments will be reduced, and MSD must assign an alternative recompliance activity as soon as possible.

chunks.title: Recompliance for drug test obligation failures — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
Clients who have failed their drug test obligations will need to complete a recompliance activity to increase or resume their benefit.
Once a client indicates they want to recomply MSD must have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply. The grade of the drug test obligation failure will determine the recompliance activity required.
For more information see:
- Recomplying first drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying third drug test obligation failure

chunks.title: Recompliance for social obligation failures — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for social obligation failures
Clients who have failed their social obligations need to meet all their social obligations as part of an activity to increase their benefit.
Once a client indicates they want to recomply MSD must have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply. The grade of the social obligations failure will determine the recompliance activity required.

chunks.title: Recompliance for work obligation failures — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for work obligation failures
Clients who have failed their work obligations will need to recomply to have their benefit:
- increase or resumed if they have been financially sanctioned or
- continue their benefit if they have a non-financial sanction imposed.
Once a client indicates they want to recomply MSD must have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply.
## Work obligations failure (Grade 1 and 2)
For clients to recomply with a work obligations failure (grade 1 and 2) and have their benefit increased or resumed, the client will need to complete:
- the activity they failed or
- an activity that is the same as or substantially similar to the activity they failed
Note for grade 1 failures where a non-financial sanction has been imposed, the recompliance requirements may be different. For more information see:
- Non-financial sanctions
## Work obligations failure or failure to accept an offer of suitable employment (Grade 3)
For clients to recomply to a work obligations failure (grade 3) and be granted a provisional benefit, the client will need to start and complete a six week recompliance activity or programme of activities (13 week non-entitlement period) or wait until the end of the 13 week non-entitlement period.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Recompliance programme example — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Recompliance programme example
If a client is recomplying through participating in an approved activity, there may not be a single activity long enough to meet the required 6 week period of recompliance. A programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate for the client.
Note a programme of suitable activities for a client with part-time work obligations should be for 15 hours or more each week.

chunks.title: Part-time employment — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Part-time employment
A client with a 13-week non-entitlement period and part-time work obligations can recomply by getting part-time work. This work must last at least 6 continuous weeks, for an average of 20 hours or more each week.
At the end of 6 weeks, the 13-week non-entitlement period ends. The client’s benefit is reinstated to their usual benefit, instead of a provisional benefit.
If the client leaves the job before the end of the 6 weeks, any provisional benefit paid must be established as a debt and the rest of the non-entitlement period is imposed.
The client can still recomply during the rest of the 13-week non-entitlement period by participating in another approved activity.
Note the income the client gets from their part-time employment is charged against the provisional benefit rate.
For when to grant or increase the benefit, see:
- Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Recomplying first drug test obligation failure — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Recomplying first drug test obligation failure
To recomply to a first drug test obligation failure a client must verbally agree to stop using controlled drugs.
The day the client agrees to stop taking controlled drugs is the date they can be considered to have recomplied. You must advise the client of the consequences if they fail the drug test obligation again.
For more information see:
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying third drug test obligation failure
- Drug test recompliance count

chunks.title: Recomplying more than one failure — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Recomplying more than one failure
When more than one obligation failure has been initiated for a client on the same day, to increase, resume or continue getting their full benefit the client needs to successfully dispute or recomply to all the failures.
If the client disputes or recomplies with one obligation, the sanction may still be imposed due to the other obligation failures not being successfully disputed or recomplied.
## Client already has a failure in-progress or a sanction imposed
Once failures have been initiated, and the notice letter has been sent, any further failures cannot be initiated until each failure:
- has been recomplied with
- has been successfully disputed because the client provided a good and sufficient reason or reasons or
- is overturned (following a dispute)
These further failures will not be included in the 24 month count and the client cannot be required to recomply.
For more information see:
- Recompliance for work obligation failures
- Recompliance for social obligation failures
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Recomplying second drug test obligation failure — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: When a client has failed their drug test obligations the second time, they must agree that they will take and pass a drug test within 25 working days (of the agreement). The benefit can be reinstated from the day the client recomplies, ie the day the client agrees to take the test. The drug test can be either a screening test or an evidential test.

chunks.title: Period to take and provide a drug test — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: A client has 25 working days, from the day after they have agreed to recomply with their second drug test obligations failure, to take and pass a drug test. The client must provide proof of undertaking and passing the drug test, within 30 working days from the day after they have agreed to recomply A client cannot dispute the 25 working day period to take and pass the drug test. They must take and pass the drug test within that time period or they will fail their obligations for the third time. Work and Income has an additional 5 working days to receive the results from the client and to process the information. Generally, the results of the drug test should be provided to Work and Income within the 25 working days, but they can be accepted in the 5 working day period following. Day 0 A second drug test failure is in-progress and client has agreed to recomply by taking and passing a drug test within 25 working days Recompliance 2 is recorded and automatic count in IT system occurs overnight Client can provide the results of the drug test at any time Day 1 - 25 Letter is sent to the client advising them they have 25 working days to take and pass a drug test Day 26 - 30 5 working days to allow time to receive and process the results of the test starts Day 31 If no "passed" drug test results are received a work test failure three is initiated and 5 working day notice period prior to Grade 3 sanction starts They will not be considered to have recomplied until a passed drug test result is received by Work and Income. A client can only access help with the costs of the recompliance drug test once during the 25 working day period. During the 25 working day period a "drug test referral delay" will be automatically added in CMS.

chunks.title: Test not taken — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: The client must take and pass the drug test within the 25 working day period. If they do not do this, they will be considered to have failed their work obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, for the third time and a Grade 3 sanction will be imposed.

chunks.title: Verification required — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: In order to make a decision that a client has taken and passed a drug test you must have received written confirmation from the client. The written information that must be provided to Work and Income includes: - the name of the client and the drug test provider and - confirmation of a "passed" test result The Drug test obligations verification [no link find out why] form can be used for this. For more information see: - Help with paying for the recompliance drug test - Recomplying first drug test obligation failure - Recomplying third drug test obligation failure - Drug test recompliance count

chunks.title: Recomplying third drug test obligation failure — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Recomplying third drug test obligation failure
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation a client must complete a 6 week approved activity and reapply for their benefit.
A 6 week approved activity must be completed regardless of the obligation failed or whether the client had failed more than one obligation failure.
## Client fails a third time for another reason during the 25 working day period
A client could fail their other obligations (not drug test obligations) for a third time during the 25 working day period. If this happens the third failure would override the count of the 25 working day period and the client would not have to take and pass a drug test.
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation the client must complete a six week approved activity.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Recomplying more than one failure
- Recomplying first drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Drug test recompliance count

chunks.title: Recording decisions on a dispute — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Recording decisions on a dispute
You must record the outcome of the client's dispute in OBMAN. One of the following outcomes must be recorded for each dispute:
- Upheld - if you believe that the decision relating to an obligations failure or sanction being imposed was correct you must record this as 'dispute upheld'. The obligations failure will be counted.
- Withdrawn - a client may, after disputing the obligations failure, decide to recomply before the sanction is imposed, or may withdraw their dispute and not recomply. In these cases you must record that the dispute has been withdrawn. The obligations failure will be counted.
- Overturned - when you believe that the client had a good and sufficient reason or that they did not fail their obligations you must record this as obligations failure overturned. The obligations failure will not be counted.
In all cases you must advise the client of the outcome of their dispute. A letter is automatically sent to the client.
If the client does not agree with your decision, they can still request a formal Review of Decision or Medical Appeal Board appeal (addiction and dependency only). They must do this in writing. The Review of Decision and Medical Appeal Board process should be followed.
Note if the obligations failure was initiated against the wrong client the status can be changed to 'failed in error' on the same day you initiate the failure. No letter is sent when the status is changed to 'failed in error'.
## Reviews of Decisions and appeals to the Medical Appeals Board for obligations failures
Reviews of Decisions for obligations failures are recorded in HIYA; appeals to the Medical Appeals Board for obligations failures are recorded in the Medical Appeals Database. However, the outcome of the review or appeal must be recorded in OBMAN. This will ensure that the benefit status can be resumed or regranted in SWIFTT depending on the outcome of the review or appeal.
Note that if the Review of Decision or Medical Appeals Board process finds that the originally recorded 'upheld' outcome should be changed to overturned, you will need to make this change in OBMAN.
For more information see:
- The disputes process
- Reviewing or disputing drug test requirements
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Core policy, Reviews and Appeals Medical Appeals Board

chunks.title: Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements
When you are referring a client to a drug tested job, you should:
- consider if the job is suitable for the client, regardless of the drug test
- let the client know that the employer may require them to pass a pre-employment drug test
- ask the client if they would pass a pre-employment drug test and
- ensure the client understands the potential consequences of failing a pre-employment drug test
There are certain situations where it may not be appropriate to refer a client to drug tested jobs. In these situations you should consider that, because of the drug test requirements, the job is not suitable.
For more information see:
- Drug test job referral not suitable
- Training providers requiring a drug test
- Employers requiring pre-employment drug tests
- Informing a client of the drug test obligation failure
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons
- Suitable employment
- Types of drug tests and standards
- Drug test obligations

chunks.title: Refugees and protected persons — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Refugees and protected persons
In general a refugee or a protected person cannot receive Sole Parent Support unless they have been granted permanent residence.
If a refugee or a protected person has permanent residence, assess them for Sole Parent Support in the usual manner. Refugees and protected persons with permanent residence are exempt from meeting the two years continuous residence criteria.
Note when a client leaves the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre no stand-down applies to the grant of the benefit.
## Clients without permanent residence
If a client is a refugee or a protected person and has not been granted permanent residence, Emergency Maintenance Allowance may be considered.
For more information see:
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance

chunks.title: Regular engagement and support process — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Regular engagement and support process
Clients must be contacted at least 4 times by Work and Income before initiating a failure to meet a social obligation. You must complete the three Contact Steps of regular engagement and support and then make a final appointment. You can only determine that the client has failed to meet their social obligations at the final appointment.
The Contact Steps can be over the phone or face to face.
The aim of this process is to support clients to meet their social obligations or for clients to take all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations.
At the first Contact Step of engagement and support you should discuss with the client whether they are meeting their social obligations and, if not, encourage them to do so.
The next 2 Contact Steps of engagement and support should be focused on encouraging and supporting the client to meet their social obligations, and following up on what happened at the previous Contact Steps.
At each of the three contacts you must:
- check that the client is taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, and actively help and encourage the client to meet those obligations
- ensure that the client is connected with local community information
- advise the client of the next stage of engagement and support and contact
- remind the client of their social obligations and consequences of not meeting them
For more information on regular engagement and support see:
- Social obligations - actively engaging with clients [no link find out why]
Also see:
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Client is meeting their social obligations
- Child changes during engagement and support process
- Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations

chunks.title: Rehabilitation — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation is a process aimed at enabling people with ill health and disabled people to reach and maintain their optimal level.
It generally has a focus on restoration or improvement of the abilities of the client. Rehabilitation could include services such as re-training a client unable to return to their previous occupation.
As part of the expectation that a client will prepare towards a return to employment, clients with work or work preparation obligations may need support to undertake activities, including rehabilitation.
To improve the client's work-readiness they may be required to undertake activities, including rehabilitation, however this must not include medical treatment.
## Rehabilitation activities
Requiring clients to undertake rehabilitation activities must be done with care. Generally you would ensure that they are willing and able to undertake activities.
Important before you require the client to undertake a rehabilitation activity you must discuss the situation with your manager client service delivery.
The client must be advised that if they are required to complete a rehabilitation activity and if they fail to do this without a good and sufficient reason a sanction may be imposed.

chunks.title: Reimbursement to employers and debt recovery — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Reimbursement to employers and debt recovery
The potential employer can be reimbursed for a failed drug test for a client only when Work and Income receives confirmation a drug test has been completed that was part of the pre-employment process and the potential employer has completed the claim form for employers, which includes details such as:
- the name of the employer
- the type of test - whether it was a screening or evidential test, or both
- confirmation that the drug test was to the drug test standard
- confirmation of a failed test result and
- the cost of the failed test and the payment rate they are claiming
For more information see:
- Pre-employment drug test claim form for employers
- Reimbursement and claims for employers/drug test agencies [no link find out why]
At the same time that the employer is reimbursed, a debt for the cost of the drug test will be manually added to the clients SWIFTT record by NPCU/NAC.
A training provider cannot be reimbursed for the costs of a failed drug test. In most cases the contract with the provider will have already factored these costs into account.
Although a drug test provider may conduct the testing the employer will be the one to be reimbursed for the costs relating to the failed drug test.
The information provided related to the failed drug tests is not to be shared with other employers, and is only to be used for the purposes of establishing whether a client has failed, without good and sufficient reason, to meet the drug test obligations.
The reimbursement of failed drug tests only apply to jobs where
- the client with work obligations has been referred by Work and Income
- the vacancy is listed with Work and Income and
- the vacancy requires a pre-employment drug test

chunks.title: Relationship status interview questions — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Relationship status interview questions
To help determine whether a client meets the relationship eligibility criteria for Sole Parent Support, a case manager may ask questions including (but not limited to) the following:
- Were you previously in a relationship? How long were you in that relationship?
- What type of relationship were you in?
- Can you tell me anything more about the reason or event in your relationship that resulted in separation? (use the application as a prompt for discussion)
- Can you tell me anything more about your attitude to the relationship, and how you feel about the separation?
- Can you tell me anything more about what you consider the future of the relationship to be? (use the application as a prompt for discussion)
- Is there, or has there been any family violence?
- Do you have any joint financial commitments? Who pays for what?
- Do you support each other financially, if so in what way?
- If your former partner is not the parent of any of the children do they help support the children in any way and act as a parental figure to the children?
- Do you attend any regular social gatherings/activities together? (e.g. clubs, church, or committees, sports played, pubs/bars frequented, holidays you've been on together)
- Do you attend family functions together? (eg weddings, funerals, birthdays, holidays e.g. Christmas)
- Do you attend parent/teacher meetings together or any other school events?
- Do you socialise at home together with friends/family?
Note case managers need to focus on asking questions to determine the client's relationship status based on their financial and emotional commitment to another person.

chunks.title: Relationship Status Verification form contents — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Relationship Status Verification form contents
A Relationship Status Verification form is required to be completed in writing and Work and Income should receive the original form.
It will include the following information:
- a statement confirming that the nominated person meets the criteria listed on the form
- the full name and the birth date of the client whose relationship status the nominated person is verifying
- a statement of what the nominated person considers the applicant's current relationship status to be
- the nominated person's signature
- the date the nominated person signed the statement
- contact details for the nominated person and an indication of whether or not they give permission for Work and Income to contact them
- acknowledgment from the client that the nominated person may be contacted about the client's application directly
For more information see:
- Relationship Status Verification form received
- Nominated person makes contact after completing form
- Who can verify a client's relationship status

chunks.title: Relationship Status Verification form may be required — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Relationship Status Verification form may be required
Clients will be assessed at the point of application to see whether they meet the targeting criteria for needing to provide verification. You must not ask the client for this information. You should look for the information in the application form and the applicant's existing SWIFTT and CMS records.
The targeting criteria are:
- Has the applicant separated and reconciled with a partner in the last 12 months?
- Was the applicant included in a couples' benefit that was cancelled in the last six months?
- Does the applicant have a postal address that is different to their residential address? (not including a PO Box address)
- Has the applicant been included in the Low Trust Client Management [no link find out why] service?
Applicants that have not received a benefit before are unlikely to meet the targeting criteria, as there will be no historical information held in the system. However, the targeting criteria assessment must still be completed.
For information about how to assess whether a client meets the targeting criteria, please see Work and Income procedures.
Clients who meet the targeting criteria need to be asked to get their nominated person to fill in a Relationship Status Verification form.
The client is responsible for getting this form completed by the third party and for returning the form to Work and Income.
The client has 20 working days from their date of first contact to get the form completed and return it to Work and Income.
When a Relationship Status Verification form is required, Work and Income will generally make a decision about whether to grant Sole Parent Support once client has returned the form.
If a client refuses to complete the form, you will need to consider the available information and determine whether the client qualifies for Sole Parent Support.
For more information see:
- Extending the 20 working day period
- Not reasonable for client to provide details of a nominated person
- Relationship Status Verification form contents
- Relationship Status Verification form received

chunks.title: Relationship Status Verification form received — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Relationship Status Verification form received
If you have requested that your client provides a completed Relationship Status Verification form, the client should get this completed and bring it back within 20 working days of the date of their first contact.
When you receive the form, you should consider the form alongside the other information you have about the client to make a decision about whether the client qualifies for Sole Parent Support.
## Relationship Status Verification form does not clearly support application
In some cases the form may not clearly support the client's application for Sole Parent Support. This may include (but is not limited to) when the form:
- appears to have been altered
- is inconsistent with the information the client has provided about their relationship status
- is incomplete
If this occurs, you will need to factor this in to making your decision about whether the client has provided enough information to grant Sole Parent Support.
You may need to ask the client more questions about the form's content to determine whether the form indicates that the client meets the relationship status qualification for Sole Parent Support. For more information see:
- Relationship status interview questions
## Nominated person does not complete form
If the client informs you that their nominated person refuses to complete the verification statement, you can ask them to nominate someone else, or you can ask them more questions to determine whether they meet the relationship status qualification for Sole Parent Support. For more information see:
- Relationship status interview questions
If the client refuses or is unable to get the form completed, you should talk to the client about why they have not provided a completed Relationship Status Verification form.
## Making a decision when a client has been asked to provide the form
Based on the available information, you can:
- ask for more information to determine whether the client is eligible for Sole Parent Support if it is not clear whether the client is eligible
- grant Sole Parent Support if there is enough information to determine that that the client is eligible for Sole Parent Support or
- decline Sole Parent Support if the information available indicates that the client is not eligible for Sole Parent SupportIf this occurs, you need to discuss this with the client and determine whether they are eligible for other forms of assistance.
For more information see:
- Extending the 20 working day period
- Qualifications
- Nominated person makes contact after completing form

chunks.title: Report Job Search — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Report Job Search
Report Job Search is a non-financial sanction that can be imposed on a client instead of a Grade 1 financial sanction. It is intended to help clients actively participate in finding suitable employment.
In a 4-week period, a client must:
- do at least 3 job search activities a week and
- report to MSD on the job-search activities they have done each week and
- provide MSD with evidence of their job-search activities at the end of the 4-week period
MSD must be satisfied the evidence provided is sufficient.
Once a client completes 4 weeks of Report Job Search, they are considered to have recomplied with their obligations and don't need to complete any other recompliance activities.

chunks.title: Reporting progress — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Reporting progress
You can require a client to report on their progress in meeting their work or work preparation obligations.
You must advise the client that if they fail to comply with this obligation, without a good and sufficient reason, they are subject to an obligations failure.
## Clients with work preparation obligations
You can require a client to report on their progress in meeting their work preparation obligations. This may include reporting on progress of any activities they have been required to undertake.
A client can report by either phone, email or in person.
## Example
You have asked a client with a 2 year old child to research childcare options and training options available in their community and to call you in a month to update you on their progress. If the client does not contact you, you should initiate an obligations failure.
## Clients with work obligations
You can require a client with work obligations to report on their job search progress.
A client can report by either phone, email or in person. Generally a client should not be required to report more than once a week.
## Example
You have asked your client to register with various recruitment agencies and call you weekly to update on their job search progress.
If your client does not contact you, you should initiate an obligations failure.

chunks.title: Residence — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Residence
To be granted Sole Parent Support, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (ie not be in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) and
- have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years or more at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
For more information see:
- Permanent residence
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Two years residence
- Proof of residence
- Sponsored clients
- Clients without permanent residence
- Residents from other countries
- Resident in New Zealand
Note clients who are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident but have not lived in New Zealand continuously for 2 years may be eligible for an Emergency Maintenance Allowance.
If a client is from overseas or is a refugee or protected person special provisions may apply, see:
- Clients from overseas
- Refugees and protected persons

chunks.title: Resident in New Zealand — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Resident in New Zealand
To qualify for Sole Parent Support a client must have lived continuously in New Zealand for two years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident.
To be resident in New Zealand at a particular time means that the client either:
- makes their home in New Zealand, that is, they have been living in New Zealand on a permanent basis or
- has an intention to make their home in New Zealand for the foreseeable future
Note 'resident' is not the same as being ordinarily resident.
Remember you must be satisfied that the client has been resident in New Zealand continuously for at least two years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident.
## Client makes their home in New Zealand
A client will be resident in New Zealand if they make their home in New Zealand. You should look for evidence that the client makes their home in New Zealand. Relevant factors you should consider include:
- a fixed abode in New Zealand?
- ownership of property in New Zealand?
- frequent absences from New Zealand, and what is the duration of and reason for those absences?
- involvement with New Zealand society such as (but not limited to):- community activities- employment- membership of clubs and- local churches
For more information see:
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Reciprocal agreements
- Proof of residence
- Calculating the period of residence

chunks.title: Residents from other countries — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Residents from other countries
Sole Parent Support is included in a number of our reciprocal agreements.
For more information see:
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Clients from overseas
- Two years residence
- Reciprocal agreements
- Proof of residence

chunks.title: Restricted circumstances guidelines — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Restricted circumstances guidelines
You must consider the following factors in relation to the restricted circumstances that make the child's attendance at school unreasonable.
It can be unreasonable for that child to attend school:
- if there is no school bus or
- no other suitable transport and
- there is a significant distance between their home and school
It may also be unreasonable for the child to attend the nearest school because the child has particular needs that prevent them from attending the nearest school, for example:
- special needs such as physical/intellectual disability; chronic or recurring illness)
- learning or behavioural difficulties or
- exclusion from the school

chunks.title: Before expiry date — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Before expiry date
If a client has a suspended or expired benefit, they will not be sent the 'initial notice to reapply' letter. This is because they are not currently getting a benefit.
For more information see:
- Notice to clients with sanctions, suspended or expired benefit
If a client's Sole Parent Support is resumed during the notice period MSD must advise the client about their upcoming expiry date and what they need to do to complete the 52 week reapplication before their expiry date.
MSD should consider whether the client will be able to complete the reapplication process before their expiry date and if an extension may be appropriate.
## On or after expiry date
If a client makes contact to have their benefit resumed on or after their expiry date and does not have an exceptional circumstance for not reapplying, their benefit must be manually cancelled from their expiry date. If the client still needs Sole Parent Support, they will need to reapply as a new applicant. The client will be subject to the usual commencement date rules, including the initial stand-down.
Note if the resumption date of the client's benefit would have been before their expiry date, but due to their circumstances the client was unable to complete the 52 week reapplication process before the expiry date, MSD will consider whether the client had exceptional circumstances.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Review of decision - 52 week reapplication process — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Review of decision - 52 week reapplication process
A client cannot review the requirement to complete the 52 week reapplication process for Sole Parent Support as it is a statutory requirement to reapply - rather than a reviewable decision made by MSD.
However a client can apply for a Review of Decision of the 52 week reapplication process when:
- they do not agree with a decision regarding the regrant of their Sole Parent Support, such as the benefit or supplementary assistance being paid at a different rate or being declined or
- they have provided a reason for not reapplying in time which was not deemed by MSD to be an exceptional circumstance
For more information see:
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals

chunks.title: Reviewing or disputing the drug test failure and sanction — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Reviewing or disputing the drug test failure and sanction
A client has the right to dispute or review any decision they disagree with relating to:
- an obligations failure or
- a sanction being imposed
A client can do this by:
- disputing the decision or
- lodging a formal Review of Decision
A Review of Decision can be lodged at any stage within three months of the obligations failure being initiated, or within three months of the sanction being imposed.
If a client disputes their obligations failure or sanction more than 20 working days after it is initiated or imposed, you need to advise the client to lodge a formal Review of Decision in writing.
## Appealing to the Medical Appeal Board
A client can only lodge an appeal to the Medical Appeal Board for a decision relating to a drug test failure when a decision was made that they:
- did not have a good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation and
- the reason given for the failure was that the client was either: addicted to controlled drugs ordependent on controlled drugs
- addicted to controlled drugs or
- dependent on controlled drugs
A client is not required to dispute a decision before lodging a review of decision or appealing to the Medical Appeal Board (drug test failure only).
For more information see:
- The disputes process
- Recording decisions on a dispute
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals

chunks.title: Self-imposed stand-down — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Self-imposed stand-down
Where a client knows they will have a stand-down and delays their application for Sole Parent Support, the commencement date depends on whether the client has applied within 28 days of their entitlement date.
If the application is received within 28 days of the client's entitlement date, the commencement date will be:
- the day after initial stand-down ends
If the application is received 28 days after the client's entitlement date, the commencement date will be:
- the day after initial stand-down ends or
- the application date
whichever is the later.

chunks.title: Seriously sick or injured — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Seriously sick or injured
In determining whether a client has an exceptional circumstance for not completing the reapplication process before their expiry date on the ground of being seriously sick or injured, the client must have experienced serious sickness or an injury during their notice period which affected their ability to reapply before the expiry date.
## Evidence
MSD may require the client to provide evidence that they were seriously sick or injured. This could include a medical certificate or other medical information signed by a health practitioner, stating:
- what the illness or injury was and
- the length of time it affected the client

chunks.title: Setting appropriate activities for clients — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Setting appropriate activities for clients
After a discussion with a client you will need to determine the most appropriate activities for them to undertake. To decide which activities are the most appropriate you should consider:
- the client's individual circumstances
- whether the activity is suitable for the client
- whether the client has work obligations or work preparation obligations
Note you do not need to seek the client's agreement to the activities that you require them to complete.
Once you and the client have discussed which activities will be appropriate include them in the client's Service Plan.
## Types of activities
You should refer the client to appropriate activities to improve their work-readiness or prospects for employment.
Appropriate activities may include (but are not limited to):
Work obligations
Work preparation obligations
A job interview
Contacting employers
Developing or updating a C.V.
Developing or updating a C.V.
Obtaining a driver's licence
Obtaining a driver's licence
Work assessment
Work assessment
Programme or seminar to increase particular skills or enhance motivation
Programme or seminar to increase particular skills or enhance motivation
Work experience or work exploration activity
Work experience or work exploration activity
Employment related training
Employment related training
Completing a high school qualification
Completing further study
Completing further study
Researching childcare options available in the community
Researching childcare options available in the community
You must take reasonable steps to arrange for the client to undertake an activity.
Note a client must not be required to undertake Activity in Community. If a client would like to undertake an Activity in the Community you may include it in their Service Plan. However, if the client fails to complete the activity you must not initiate an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Process for deciding appropriate activities
- Work preparation obligations
- Work obligations
- Rehabilitation
- Activity Summary
- Studying or training on Sole Parent Support

chunks.title: Shared care — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Shared care
Shared care only applies when the parents of a child are living apart, the child lives (for at least 40% of the time) with each parent, and both parents apply for a benefit in respect of that child.
In shared care situations you can only pay a sole parent rate of benefit to the parent that has the greater responsibility.
For more information see:
- Decision guidelines for shared care
Emergency Benefit cannot be paid to the 'other' parent on the basis that they care for the child for part of the time. Parents are expected to arrange care of their children to allow at least 1 parent to work.
Never pay 2 sole parent rates of benefit for the same child (that is 1 child can't be included in two benefits at the same time).
## Only 1 parent applies for benefit
When only 1 parent applies for a benefit for a child in shared care situations, the child still has to be a dependent child before benefit eligibility for that child can be determined.
For more information see:
- Dependent child
## Childcare and OSCAR subsidy
For information on the payment of Childcare and OSCAR subsidy for shared care clients see:
- Childcare subsidy Shared care - principal caregiver
- OSCAR subsidy Shared care - principal caregiver

chunks.title: Situations where extensions can be given — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Situations where extensions can be given
Generally, all clients getting Sole Parent Support need to complete the 52 week reapplication process before their expiry date.
If a client does not complete the reapplication process before their expiry date their Sole Parent Support will stop as they will no longer be entitled to get it.
There are limited situations where a client may complete the reapplication process on or after the expiry date and have their Sole Parent Support regranted, these are:
- where a client makes contact to reapply before their expiry date but the reapplication process cannot be completed before the expiry date through no fault of their own, or
- where a client has an exceptional circumstance that has affected their ability to reapply or contact MSD before their expiry date
For more information see:
If the client does not qualify for an extension but still needs Sole Parent Support, they will need to apply as a new applicant. Their expired benefit must be cancelled from their expiry date before they can be granted Sole Parent Support as a new applicant.
The client will be subject to the usual commencement date rules, including the initial stand-down.
Note if the client advises they want to apply for Sole Parent Support as a new applicant and completes their reapplication form, MSD must use their reapplication form as their new application.

chunks.title: Social obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Social obligations
Clients getting Sole Parent Support have social obligations that apply for each dependent child in their care. This includes a child for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid.
A client must take all reasonable steps to meet all of the social obligations that apply for each child. The social obligations that apply for each child depend on the age of the child.
When required, clients need to take all reasonable steps to meet the following social obligations. The child must be:
- enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation and
- up-to-date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks (for children aged under 5 years) and
- enrolled in and attending 1 of the following from the age of 3 years until they start school: an approved early childhood education programmeTe Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School oranother approved parenting and early childhood home education programme
- an approved early childhood education programme
- Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School or
- another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme
- enrolled in and attending school from the age of 5 or 6 years old (depending on when they start school)
When required a client must:
- attend and participate in interviews with MSD to discuss meeting their social obligations and
- advise on progress where they have not been able to meet their social obligations
A client is only required to meet social obligations from the time they begin getting a benefit.
Clients in the process of applying for Sole Parent Support, or who have a future commencement date of their Sole Parent Support are not required to meet these social obligations. Clients are also not required to meet social obligations that would have been relevant to them before getting a benefit.
For example, a client who starts getting a benefit when their child is between 3 and 4 months old cannot be sanctioned for not having completed the core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks a child should have at ages 4 to 6 weeks.

chunks.title: Social obligations recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period) — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: If a client fails their obligations for a third time, their benefit is reduced or cancelled. For the client to increase their benefit they must undertake a six week recompliance activity or programme of activities and reapply for a benefit. If the third obligation failure is a social obligation failure, the standard six week recompliance activities may not be appropriate as some clients do not have work obligations and cannot work or be in training for a period of 6 weeks. In this situation, a programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate for the client.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Short term approved activities to consider for a Sole Parent Support client with part-time work obligations and social obligations, where the third failure was a social obligations failure. Week 1 Take reasonable steps to talk to providers of appropriate recognised early childhood education programme Week 2 Take reasonable steps to enrol their child in a recognised early childhood education programmes Week 3 CV seminar Week 4 Attend presentation seminar approved by Work and Income Week 5 Attend a local parenting programme that provides support for families Week 6 Meet with case manager to talk about what reasonable steps have been taken to enrol the child in a recognised early childhood education programme and discuss how the other activities went Week 1 Take reasonable steps to talk to providers of appropriate recognised early childhood education programme Week 2 Take reasonable steps to enrol their child in a recognised early childhood education programmes Week 3 CV seminar Week 4 Attend presentation seminar approved by Work and Income Week 5 Attend a local parenting programme that provides support for families Week 6 Meet with case manager to talk about what reasonable steps have been taken to enrol the child in a recognised early childhood education programme and discuss how the other activities went Note a programme of suitable activities for a client with part-time work obligations should be for no more than 20 hours each week.

chunks.title: Example 2 — main benefits > sole parent support
