chunks.text: Example of short term approved activities to consider for a Sole Parent Support client with social obligations, where the third failure was a social obligations failure. Week 1 Make contact with the local Family Start whanau worker and arrange a meeting with them Week 2 Family Start whanau worker visit Week 3 Contact a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and arrange a visit Week 4 Contact the local medical centre to ensure the children are enrolled in primary health care Week 5 Talk to appropriate providers of recognised early childhood education programmesWell Child/Tamariki Ora provider visit Week 6 Meet with a case manager about what steps have been taken Week 1 Make contact with the local Family Start whanau worker and arrange a meeting with them Week 2 Family Start whanau worker visit Week 3 Contact a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and arrange a visit Week 4 Contact the local medical centre to ensure the children are enrolled in primary health care Week 5 Talk to appropriate providers of recognised early childhood education programmes Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider visit Week 6 Meet with a case manager about what steps have been taken

chunks.title: Split care — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Split care
Split care is when parents with 2 or more children are living apart and each parent has the care of at least 1 of their children.
Note when considering the principal caregiver, you should be aware that other terms used by the Family Court are 'day to day care' not 'custody, and 'parenting order' not 'custody order'.
In a split care situation you can only pay Sole Parent Support to one parent unless there is a court order recognising each parent as the principal caregiver of at least one child. When there is a court-ordered spilt care arrangement, both parents can receive Sole Parent Support.
For more information see
- Court ordered split care arrangements
- No court ordered split care arrangement
- Determining whether a care arrangement is sanctioned by the Family Court
- Privacy Act implications
- Assistance for the parent not qualified for Sole Parent Support
- When to consider Emergency Maintenance Allowance for split care

chunks.title: Study or training and transferring to Jobseeker Support — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Study or training and transferring to Jobseeker Support
When discussing study or training options with clients on Sole Parent Support, MSD should take into consideration when the client will transfer from Sole Parent Support to Jobseeker Support.
MSD may need to have a discussion with clients in study or training about how their change of benefit when their youngest child turns 14 will mean that they may not be able to continue their study.
MSD should talk to the client about:
- whether they can finish their course of study or training before they shift to Jobseeker Support
- how they would complete their study or training on Jobseeker Support while still meeting their full-time work obligations
- whether they have considered accessing Student Loan and Student Allowance assistance instead
- whether they can access any other assistance, such as education and employment-related assistance, now, and what assistance they would be able to access on Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: Studying or training on Sole Parent Support — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Studying or training on Sole Parent Support
Clients can get Sole Parent Support and undertake study or training as long as they:
- can meet their work or work preparation obligations at the same time or
- are eligible for an exemption from their work obligations in order to complete study or training
## Exemptions for study and training
Clients on Sole Parent Support may be eligible for one of the following exemptions from their work obligations to study or undertake training:
- in approved full-time training
- in approved study before subject to work obligations
- in full-time study at level 4 or above
For more information about exemptions for study or training see:
- Exemptions
- Work test Exemptions [no link find out why]
## Client is not eligible for an exemption
When discussing study or training with a client on Sole Parent Support, you should consider:
- the requirements of the course of study or training. Is the course part-time or full-time? If the course is full-time, how much of the course work would take place on campus and how much would take place at home?
- whether they have part-time work obligations or work preparation obligations, and what steps they are currently taking to meet these obligations
- the ages of the children in their care
- whether they have an exemption and
- how long their period of study or training would be, and when they will transfer to Jobseeker Support
If the client is not confident that they can study and meet their part-time work obligations or work preparation obligations, you should explain to the client that they may be sanctioned if they fail an obligation as a result of their study commitments.
The client can also consider financial assistance from StudyLink if they do not want to have work or work preparation obligations.

chunks.title: Organisation — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Suitable organisations can be community or volunteer organisations. These organisations may have existing relationships with MSD, however this is not required. To be suitable, an organisation should - not be for profit - not be public sector, e.g. central or local government or a Crown entity - have an internal organisation structure, e.g. has defined key functions, roles and responsibilities - be self-governing – the organisation primarily controls its own management and operations - not be something people are required to contribute time to by law, e.g. jury duty. Organisations are not suitable if: - they have previously breached employment law, or - their area of focus would likely be inappropriate or unacceptable to the wider community, or - a client completing Community Work Experience at this organisation is likely to be a reputational risk to MSD. The organisation must be confident they can provide a client with the required hours and 4 consecutive weeks needed to complete their Community Work Experience. If the organisation is unsure, the position would not be suitable for the client. Note clients may secure multiple positions to complete their Community Work Experience. For more information see: Period of Community Work Experience.

chunks.title: Position — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: To be suitable, a position should: - be for a role that would otherwise be met by a volunteer, e.g. is not a role that would normally be paid employment - have activities that are reasonable and fair for the client to complete – for example, a position that requires a lot of work on the computer would not be suitable for a client with low computer literacy - not put the personal safety of the client or others at risk - not include activities that could be considered inappropriate or may damage MSD’s reputation, e.g. serving alcohol, being involved in gambling, or supporting particular political gain

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Donna has Community Work Experience imposed and is searching for a suitable organisation and position. Donna contacts her local rugby club to see if they have any volunteer positions available that would help her to meet the Community Work Experience requirements. The rugby club can offer Donna at least 5 hours of work for 4 weeks, but tells her they mostly need her help to run the bar. Donna gets in touch with MSD and tells MSD what the position will involve. Although the rugby club is a suitable organisation, it’s not appropriate for Donna to be serving alcohol as part of her Community Work Experience, as this could damage MSD’s reputation. Donna is advised that the work needed at the rugby club is not suitable for the purpose of the sanction, and to continue looking for a suitable position.

chunks.title: Suitable employment — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Suitable employment
Suitable employment varies between clients depending on their individual circumstances.
To meet their work obligations clients need to be available for or take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of:
- at least 20 hours per week
Clients may have pre-benefit obligations to attend an interview or accept an offer of employment. This employment must also be considered suitable.
## Deciding if a job is suitable
When deciding on whether a job is suitable for a client, you need to consider the following (but is not limited to):
- appropriate hours of employment, eg hours are not excessive
- access to childcare
- family commitments
- religious commitments
- jobs which offend strongly held views
- days of the week
- type of employment
- skills required
- experience
- location of the job
- wages
- number of hours per week is between 15 and 25 hours
For more information see:
- Hours range for suitable employment
- Meeting job search requirements
- Employment trial period of up to 90 days
- Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements

chunks.text:

chunks.title: Taking all reasonable steps for enrolling in and attending school — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Taking all reasonable steps for enrolling in and attending school
Reasons to consider a client is taking all reasonable steps to meet this obligation may include (but are not limited to) that:
- the child has a health condition, injury or disability that affects their ability to attend school
- the child is regularly missing classes for no good reason but the Attendance Service is working with the family and the school to get the child attending school again
- the client is actively trying to encourage their child to attend school but the child has behavioural problems and attendance at school is out of their control. Note you need to record this as an exception from the obligation in OBMAN using 'Child is not permitted to attend' as the obligation reason.
Note if the parent is in the process of being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020, you must not ask them to comply with this social obligation.
You need to record this as an exception reason in OBMAN using 'parent is in prosecution for truant child' as the obligation reason.

chunks.title: Taking all reasonable steps to enrol at early childhood programme — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Taking all reasonable steps to enrol at early childhood programme
A client could be considered to be taking all reasonable steps to enrol their child in an early childhood education programme for reasons including (but not limited to) that:
- there are shortages of places or availability issues, and the client has a plan in place or has made a commitment to: enrol their child when a place becomes available orconsider participating in other approved programmes for their child - unless there are cultural or religious reasons for not doing so
- enrol their child when a place becomes available or
- consider participating in other approved programmes for their child - unless there are cultural or religious reasons for not doing so
- there are additional costs of participation that may cause financial hardship to the family, including: travel costs oradditional costs associated with attending the early childhood education programme
- travel costs or
- additional costs associated with attending the early childhood education programme
- the child has behavioural problems meaning attendance at an early childhood education programme would be difficult or not possible (for example the child is not currently permitted to attend). This should be recorded as an exception in OBMAN using "child is not permitted to attend" as the obligation exception reason.
To help clients meet this social obligation you should discuss childcare assistance that may be available to the client.

chunks.title: Taking controlled prescribed medications — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Taking controlled prescribed medications
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes when a client is taking prescription medication correctly.
Not all prescribed medications affect the results of a drug test. Generally, only controlled prescribed medications do, such as morphine, codeine or medicinal cannabis. Controlled prescribed medications need to be used at the dose the health practitioner recommends and by the person for whom they are prescribed.
Some controlled prescribed medications may cause a person to be impaired on the job which can cause health and safety issues for employers.
In some situations, screening drug tests can show failed results where controlled prescribed medications have been used.
The client can be asked to provide verification from a registered health practitioner that they are taking a controlled prescribed medication. There is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that MSD can provide to the client.
Note when a client is asked to take a drug test, they will be asked to declare any prescribed medications they are taking.

chunks.title: Client's IRD number — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: MSD may request evidence of an IRD number for a client who is being paid Sole Parent Support.

chunks.title: Setting or extending the timeframe for providing evidence — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: MSD must provide the client with a minimum of 10 working days to provide IRD number evidence that has been requested in writing. MSD can extend the 10 working day period (in writing) if the client has a reasonable explanation for requiring more than 10 days to provide evidence of their IRD number. This includes considering factors outside the client control that cause delays, including, but not limited to: - the client has a family emergency that caused a delay - processing delays with an external agency (e.g. Inland Revenue, Department of Internal Affairs, etc) - the client does not speak English as a first language and has difficulty navigating evidence requirements - the client has limited access to the internet, a device, or their local service centre - the client has a physical or intellectual disability that makes accessing services difficult - the client is injured, disabled, or has a medical condition that makes accessing services difficult.

chunks.title: Notice following unsuccessful match — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a client's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the client (in writing) to provide evidence of their IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice (adverse action notice) in writing: - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the client a minimum of 10 working days to provide their IRD number evidence or the client's assistance must be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Sole Parent Support and MSD holds an IRD number on record. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Isla's IRD number. MSD provides a notice in writing, giving 10 working days for Isla to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Isla already having an IRD number - Isla not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD must suspend assistance if evidence of IRD number is not received — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: MSD must suspend all taxable and/or income tested assistance the client is getting, including their Sole Parent Support, if evidence of an IRD number is not provided within 10 working days from the written request, or extended period if this has been applied. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance. Example Koa is receiving Sole Parent Support and MSD does not have an IRD number on record. MSD sends a written request giving 10 working days for Koa to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD receives no response to this request. MSD suspends all Koa's taxable and/or income tested assistance because Koa has not supplied MSD with evidence of their IRD number within the timeframe provided.

chunks.title: IRD evidence may not be requested in some circumstances — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - there are significant factors, that are outside the client's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number (e.g. a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence), and - the client needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided or - there are significant factors related to a health, injury or disability that are outside the client's control that prevent them from providing evidence of an IRD number, and - an agent cannot be appointed to act on the client's behalf. MSD can determine a later point to request the evidence of the IRD number. Example Sienna is 23 and receiving Sole Parent Support. Sienna's mother (Sara) is Sienna's agent and acts on Sienna's behalf with MSD. Sienna does not have an IRD number and Sara is not a recognised agent for Sienna for Inland Revenue. Sienna has a serious head injury, is unconscious and expected to be in hospital for at least 8 weeks. Sienna is not able to give consent to appoint Sara as an agent for Inland Revenue to apply for an IRD number due to their injury. MSD can request this information later when Sienna's situation has changed. Note there is different guidance for requesting an IRD number or evidence of an IRD number when a client is applying for Sole Parent Support .

chunks.title: Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School
Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School provides an early childhood education programme.
This programme provides learning material and the support of a distance teacher, but is home based and taught by the parent. Parents must meet certain eligibility criteria to be enrol their child in the Te Kura Early Childhood Education programme.

chunks.title: The disputes process — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## The disputes process
The disputes process is a quick process where you must respond to a client's dispute immediately. You must take into account any new information provided by the client, and let the client know your decision straight away.
A letter is sent automatically to the client once a decision has been recorded on the dispute.
A client can dispute the decision if they believe:
- they did not fail their obligations including when they believe they have taken all reasonable steps to meet a social obligation or
- that they had a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete the obligation
Note if a client has disputed the obligations failure and you have upheld your decision, the client can only dispute it again by following the Review of Decision or Medical Appeal Board appeal (drug test failure only) processes.
If a sanction has been imposed you can still use the disputes process. This allows the client an opportunity for a quick resolution to their dispute before proceeding with the Review of Decision process.
For more information see:
- Recording decisions on a dispute
- Core policy Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements
## Good and sufficient reason for failing
You must consider the circumstances of the client, and determine whether it would have been reasonable for the client to have undertaken the activity.
Good and sufficient reasons for failing to undertake an activity will depend on the obligation the client has failed. For social obligations you must consider whether the client has taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations.
Note that if you are unsure whether a client has a good and sufficient reason then you should seek guidance from your capability developer, Helpline, manager client service operations or manager client service delivery.

chunks.title: Verification — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Verification
In order to make a decision that a client has failed a drug test, without good and sufficient reason, you must have received confirmation from the training provider.
For more information see:
- Types of drug tests and standards
- Client has failed a screening drug test

chunks.title: Transfer between benefits — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Transfer between benefits
A transfer between benefits can occur when a client qualifies for Sole Parent Support while currently receiving another benefit.
There is no stand-down imposed for clients who:
- transfer to Sole Parent Support from another benefit type or
- are included as a partner in another benefit type
Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Childs Benefit and Orphans Benefit are also a benefit in this situation. Where Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit has been paid and the child now qualifies for Sole Parent Support, no stand-down is imposed.
## Non-beneficiary clients
When a non-beneficiary client receiving Extra Help such as Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance applies for Sole Parent Support, it is not regarded as a transfer between benefits. An initial stand-down is imposed.
For more information see:
- Processing standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Client intending to return to the same employer — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Client intending to return to the same employer
If a client has received any sick leave payments they would not be eligible for Sole Parent Support until these payments had stopped. You then assess any initial stand-down.
Clients are not required to use any sick leave they may have if they are intending to return to the same employer.

chunks.title: 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down
When a client applies for Sole Parent Support within 28 days of their entitlement date, the commencement date is the day after the initial stand-down ends.
This means, in some situations, MSD can commence a benefit from a date earlier than the application date.
If the application is not received within 28 days, MSD cannot backdate the commencement date.
Note the 28-day rule only applies to clients who have an initial stand down imposed.

chunks.title: Two years residence — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Two years residence
A client must have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident to qualify for Sole Parent Support.
Note the 2 year period of residence must be 2 years continuous residence without absence from New Zealand. There are some circumstances however when a client can be absent from New Zealand during this time.
For more information see:
- Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
## Clients who do not meet the two years residence criteria
If the client does not meet the 2 year continuous residence requirement they may be able to receive an Emergency Maintenance Allowance.
For more information about residence see:
- Resident in New Zealand
- Calculating the period of residence
- Permanent residence
- Refugees and protected persons
- Reciprocal agreements
- Unlawful residence
- Proof of residence

chunks.title: Evidential tests — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Evidential tests
Some employers, particularly larger employers, may require an evidential test and will not conduct screening tests or they may conduct both tests.
Generally, evidential tests are used when a screening test is failed.
Evidential tests are a more comprehensive and expensive method of detecting drugs. They can detect a wider range of substances and identify the specific substance. This test is also referred to as a confirmation test.
Evidential testing is conducted in an accredited laboratory by qualified staff. Samples are sent to the laboratory by the drug test provider or specialised staff, or the laboratory will arrange to take the sample themselves.
For more information see:
- Client has failed a screening drug test
- Effect of certain drugs

chunks.title: Unable to meet work preparation obligations due to a health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Unable to meet work preparation obligations due to a health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to clients with work preparation obligations. This includes clients who are subject to work preparation obligations as a result of being exempted from work obligations.
A client may be unable to meet their work preparation obligations where their health condition, injury or disability restricts them.
For example, when a client is:
- in hospital or
- is unable to attend an interview with Work and Income due to their condition
MSD should consider the information on the client's Work Capacity Medical Certificate to see if it notes any restrictions to a client's capacity to plan.
This is a full exemption.
## Evidence
To support their exemption, the client must provide a Work Capacity Medical Certificate.
The medical certificate must confirm:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to work or to plan for work and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for work or planning for work and
- any other information that is required
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 13 weeks.

chunks.title: Unable to recomply — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Unable to recomply
A client, who is subject to a sanction or a 13 week non-entitlement period, may not need to complete a recompliance activity if:
- they meet the criteria for a full exemption from their work obligations or
- they qualify for a benefit that does not have the obligations to which they must recomply
If a client is subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period, and is unable to complete the 6 week activity, you cannot recover the provisional benefit if they do not complete the activity or programme of suitable activities because they meet the criteria for a full exemption from their work obligations.

chunks.title: Unforeseen hospitalisation — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Unforeseen hospitalisation
In determining whether a client has an exceptional circumstance for not completing the 52 week reapplication process before their expiry date on the grounds of unforeseen hospitalisation, the client must have experienced one of the following situations during their notice period:
- an unplanned emergency surgery in a hospital which affected their ability to reapply before their expiry date or
- unplanned emergency treatment in a hospital which affected their ability to reapply before their expiry date
## Evidence
MSD may require the client to provide evidence that they were in hospital. This could include:
- admissions or discharge forms
- medical certificate or medical report
- letter from the doctor
If the client is in hospital care during their notice period, they may not need to complete the 52 week reapplication process for Sole Parent Support. If their dependent child is in hospital care, they may qualify for an extension if they need more time to complete the reapplication.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Unlawful residence — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Unlawful residence
To reside in New Zealand lawfully the client must either:
- be a New Zealand citizen
- be an Australian citizen
- hold a New Zealand passport
- hold an Australian passport
- hold a visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009
- be deemed to hold a visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents)
- be a British national who arrived in New Zealand prior to 2 April 1974 or
- hold a permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987
If the client does not fulfil one of the above, the client is deemed to be in New Zealand unlawfully.
Any periods of unlawful residence are excluded when calculating the clients' period of residence.
The calculation of the two year period of continuous residence commences from when the client is granted New Zealand citizenship or permanent residence.
For more information see:
- Calculating the period of residence
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Proof of residence

chunks.title: Upskilling — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Upskilling
Upskilling is a non-financial sanction that can be imposed on a client instead of a Grade 1 financial sanction. It is intended to help clients build work-related skills and confidence.
Each week for 4 weeks, a client must:
- regularly attend and participate in at least one employment-related training or course for at least 5 hours and
- report to MSD on the employment-related training or courses they have participated in
At the end of the 4-week period, a client must provide MSD with evidence of their employment related training or courses. MSD must be satisfied the evidence provided is sufficient.
Once a client completes 4 weeks of Upskilling, they are considered to have recomplied with their obligations and do not need to complete any other recompliance activities.
Note Some employment-related training or courses may be longer than 4 weeks. Clients should be made aware that, if they satisfactorily attend and participate in the training or course, they will be considered to have recomplied after 4 weeks even if the course lasts longer than this.

chunks.title: 5-day verification window — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## 5-day verification window
There may be times when MSD is not able to process the information before the end of the 4-week sanction period.
To prevent a client from being disadvantaged due to processing delays, there is a 5-day verification window at the end of the sanction period. This allows MSD to process information a client has provided and ensures a client’s payment will continue.
Note this is not extra time for a client to complete their job search activities.

chunks.title: Verification of relationship status — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Verification of relationship status
Relationship status is a qualification for Sole Parent Support. Work and Income needs to understand a client's relationship status to ensure that they are receiving the correct benefit. Applicants for Sole Parent Support are asked to provide the details of a nominated person who is willing to verify their relationship status.
Verification of relationship status provided by a nominated person is used to help determine eligibility for Sole Parent Support along with other information about the client.
Note if you determine that a client does not meet the qualifications for Sole Parent Support (including relationship status), you should consider if they meet the qualifications for another benefit.
For more information see:
- Client to provide details of a nominated person
- Determining eligibility without details of a nominated person
- Not reasonable for client to provide details of a nominated person
- Who can verify a client's relationship status

chunks.title: Victim of violent crime (including family violence) — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Victim of violent crime (including family violence)
In determining whether a client has an exceptional circumstance for not reapplying before their expiry date on the grounds of being a victim of a violent crime, the client must have experienced the following during their notice period:
- been directly affected by a crime committed by another person which affected their ability to reapply before the expiry date and
- suffered physical or emotional harm which affected their ability to reapply before the expiry date
Note in all cases if MSD believes that a client has been, or is likely to be harmed (physically, emotionally or sexually) the situation must be discussed with a Family Violence Response Co-ordinator.
## Evidence
MSD will consult with the regional Family Violence Response Co-ordinator for advice regarding what evidence should be required. Evidence could include:
- a personal statement or
- a statement from a professional (such as the Police or a social worker)

chunks.title: Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
A client who is applying for Sole Parent Support and has work obligations, can have a 13 week non-entitlement period if they:
- have become voluntarily unemployed without a good and sufficient reason
- are applying for a benefit because they were dismissed by their employer for misconduct
'Becoming voluntarily unemployed' means the client has resigned from, or otherwise left employment without a good and sufficient reason.
'Dismissal as a result of misconduct' means that the client has lost employment as a result of misconduct without a good and sufficient reason.
There are some circumstances where a 13 week non-entitlement period would not be imposed. For more information see:
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed
Note the 50% protection for clients with dependent children applies.
For more information see:
- Deciding non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or misconduct
- Effect of non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment

chunks.title: Weekly income example — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Weekly income example
Below are examples of calculating the income reduction for weekly income for Sole Parent Support.
## Example 1
Weekly gross income
$350.00

$27.00

## Example 2
Weekly gross income
$400.00
Less income allowed before benefit is affected (as at 1 April 2022)
$160.00

Reduction is 30 cents per $1.00 of income over $160 but not more than $250 ($90 x 0.3 = $27)

chunks.title: Well Child or Tamariki Ora services and checks — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Well Child or Tamariki Ora services and checks
Well Child/Tamariki Ora services are a screening, education and support service offered to all New Zealand children and their families or whānau from birth to 5 years old.
The services assist and support families and whanau to improve and protect their children's health. They are provided free to all children under 5 years of age by registered nurses and community health workers with specific training in child health.
First time parents and families requiring extra support are offered additional visits. Some visits are carried out in the home and others in clinics or community facilities.
Different providers run the Well Child/Tamariki Ora services, including:
- Plunket
- Māori health providers
- Pacific Island health providers
- Public Health Services - for example, public health nurses, community nurses, community health workers, social workers.
## When the checks happen
The Well Child/Tamariki Ora schedule includes 12 health checks (contacts) with 8 of these offered to children aged from, 4 - 6 weeks to 5 years of age.
Only the 8 core Well Child checks are required to meet this social obligation.
## Between 4 weeks and 5 years
The 8 core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks (listed below) for children between the ages of 4 - 6 weeks to 5 years are required to meet social obligations.
These are provided by the Well Child provider when the child is:
- 4 - 6 weeks
- 8 - 10 weeks
- 3 - 4 months
- 5 - 7 months
- 9 - 12 months
- 15 - 18 months
- 2 - 3 years
- 4 - 5 years (this is the before school check, and the final Well Child health check)

chunks.title: What is a breakdown in the child's family — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## What is a breakdown in the child's family
The breakdown of a child's family involves a failure or collapse of the normal family dynamics that results in no natural, adoptive, or step-parent being able to fulfil their role as parents to their child or children.
For Sole Parent Support, a child’s family means their parents (natural, adoptive, or step-parent) and any siblings living with them at the time of the family breakdown.
Note not all traumatic events within a family will result in a breakdown of a child's family.
## Family able to support
In times of a crisis, a child may not be able to reside with their parents. Close family members or friends may take care of the child.
The new caregivers should approach the child's parents in the first instance for financial support.
The parents could still be able to support the child financially.
A crisis does not necessarily mean a breakdown of the child's family. There is also a possibility the child may not be in the applicant's care for at least 1 year.
## Client would like to be the principal caregiver
When a person (for example a grandparent) would like to be the child's principal caregiver but there is a natural, adoptive or step-parent able to provide care for the child, it is not appropriate to consider the child as a dependent child for Sole Parent Support.

chunks.title: What is a limited employment location? — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## What is a limited employment location?
A limited employment location is defined as a place with the following characteristics:
- severely limited availability of work
- local labour market at a low level - therefore having limited job opportunities (if an area has seasonal work available in the coming year, the area is not considered a limited employment location) and
- lack of public transport to take commuters to an area where work is available
The client's residential address is used to decide whether they live in a limited employment location.
For more information see:
- Deskfile Limited employment locations alert sheet
- Clients moving to a limited employment location

chunks.title: When the sanction is imposed — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## When the sanction is imposed
Sanctions can only be imposed 5 working days after the client has been sent a letter about their obligations failure. This is called the 5 working day notice period.
Note that if a client recomplies within the initial 5 working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the obligations failure is counted.
Also note if a client has more than 1 obligation failure initiated on the same day, only 1 sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
## How to count the '5 working day notice' period
The 5 working day notice period is counted from the date after the obligations failure letter has been sent to the client, to allow for posting and delivery of the letter.
The 5 working day notice period excludes weekends, public holidays, or the period 25 December to 15 January each year.
The table below provides an example of how to count the notice period.
Day 0

Automatic failure in CMS occurs overnight
Day 0

An obligations failure letter is sent

5 working day notice period begins

5 working day notice period continues
Day 6

chunks.title: When to consider Emergency Maintenance Allowance for split care — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## When to consider Emergency Maintenance Allowance for split care
You can pay an Emergency Maintenance Allowance where a sole parent:
- is not entitled to any other benefit
- is unable to earn sufficient income for themselves and their family and
- their childcare responsibilities prevent them from earning sufficient income
If the sole parent does not qualify for any other benefit and is unable to earn sufficient income to support themselves because of their current childcare commitments, you can pay an Emergency Maintenance Allowance.
## Reviewing existing clients (not on Sole Parent Support) in split care situations
If you identify an existing sole parent client in a split care situation, or an existing client requests a transfer to the Emergency Maintenance Allowance, you should review their benefit in accordance with the above guidelines.
When a transfer to the Emergency Maintenance Allowance is appropriate, you should review the benefit and all supplementary assistance and transfer them from either:
- the first available date - if there is no financial advantage to the client to transfer from an earlier date and the client is in agreement, review their benefit and transfer them to the Emergency Maintenance Allowance from the first available date
- 12 December 2000 - was the date of an earlier Social Security Appeal Authority decision on this policy issue. This date of review should be used where a client has earnings/other income. They will then receive an increased rate of payment due to the different income tests, and have entitlement to the Emergency Maintenance Allowance from 12 December 2000.
You can review any particular case from an earlier date if you are satisfied that this is more appropriate.
For more information see:
- Court ordered split care arrangements
- No court ordered split care arrangement
- Determining whether a care arrangement is sanctioned by the Family Court
- Privacy Act implications
- Assistance for the parent not qualified for Sole Parent Support

chunks.title: Who can verify a client's relationship status — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Who can verify a client's relationship status
A person nominated by a client applying for Sole Parent Support must meet certain criteria in order to be considered an appropriate nominated person to verify the client's relationship status.
The client is responsible for ensuring their nominated person meets the following criteria:
- be willing to provide the Ministry of Social Development with verification of the client's current relationship status for the client's benefit application
- be aged 18 or over
- knows the client in a personal capacity and has done for at least the 2 years prior to their application
- normally resides in New Zealand
- is not a part of the client's immediate family
A client's immediate family is considered to include their:
- parents (including step-parents and foster parents)
- ex-partner
- former parents in-law or equivalent
- grandparents
- children, grandchildren, stepchildren, and foster children, mokopuna (those grandchildren who have been raised by the grandparents as the principal caregivers) and tamaiti whāngai (children who have been raised, normally by a relation or other person, within the wider whānau to which the child belongs) and
- siblings (including half-siblings)

chunks.title: Why is the client moving to a limited employment location? — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Why is the client moving to a limited employment location?
You will need to work closely with your client to see if their reasons for wanting to move to a limited employment location can be addressed in a way that alleviates the need to move.
Examples of reasons and possible solutions are as follows:
- a client planning to move to escape a difficult situation in their current location may be encouraged to move to an area where there are employment opportunities available, rather than a limited employment location
- a client moving because they are having difficulty managing high housing costs may also be encouraged to move to a location with low-cost accommodation that is not a limited employment location. Alternatively, you could refer them to an agency offering budgeting advice, or see if they are eligible for Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or social housing
- a client planning to move to take care of a sick relative may be eligible for Supported Living Payment - caring for a person. Clients who receive this or other non work-obligated benefits are not affected by the limited employment locations policy
- a client planning to move for cultural reasons should be assisted as appropriate to work out whether, and how, they can meet their work obligations in that location
Depending on the client's reason for moving, it may be appropriate to assess their eligibility for other forms of assistance that may help them remain in an area where there are employment opportunities available. These may include:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Disability Allowance
- Child Disability Allowance
- Childcare Assistance Programme
- Temporary Additional Support
For more information see:
- Decision guidelines - clients moving to a limited employment location
- Deskfile Limited employment locations alert sheet
- Introduction
- Social housing Assessment of eligibility

chunks.title: Work ability assessment obligation — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Work ability assessment obligation
Clients receiving Sole Parent Support have a work ability assessment obligation that requires them, when asked, to attend and participate in:
- Self-Assessments
- Structured Interview
- Work Ability Assessment

chunks.title: Work obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Part-time work obligations apply to clients with a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years. Part-time work is: - work that averages at least 20 hours per week for all other clients with part-time work obligations Clients with work obligations must: - be available for, and take reasonable steps to obtain, suitable employment - accept any offer of suitable employment, including temporary employment or seasonal employment Note suitable employment can include employment that contains an employment trial. - attend and participate in an interview for any opportunity of suitable employment to which the client is referred - when required to attend and participate in any interview with Work and Income or on behalf of Work and Income - when required to undertake planning for employment - report to Work and Income on progress in meeting their work obligations as often as required and - when required by Work and Income, undertake any activity to improve their work readiness and employment prospects, including: any work assessmentany programme or seminarany work experience or work exploration activityany employment related training andrehabilitation (but not medical treatment) - any work assessment - any programme or seminar - any work experience or work exploration activity - any employment related training and - rehabilitation (but not medical treatment)

chunks.title: Suitable employment — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: Clients with part-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find, suitable employment of at least 20 hours per week. However, if suitable employment is available for hours other than 20 hours per week, the client can be required to accept an offer of this job. Work obligations can be applied on any day of the week provided it is suitable for the client's circumstances. To help you decide if the job is suitable for the client see: - Suitable employment - Hours range for suitable employment

chunks.title: Failing to comply — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text: If a client does not meet their work obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, you should initiate an obligations failure. You should consider the client's individual circumstances before referring them to a job or an activity, to ensure that they can realistically meet their obligations. For more information see: - Clients undertaking voluntary work - Drug test obligations - Employment trial period of up to 90 days - Exemptions - Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work or work preparation obligations - Informing clients of their obligations - Limited employment locations - Meeting job search requirements - Obligations failures - Rehabilitation - Reporting progress - Setting appropriate activities for clients - Social obligations - Studying or training on Sole Parent Support - Table of exemptions - Work ability assessment obligations - Absence from New Zealand Client with work obligations - Work with a contracted service provider obligation

chunks.title: Work or work preparation obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Work or work preparation obligations
Sole Parent Support clients have part-time work obligations or work preparation obligations depending on the age of their youngest child.
## Part-time work obligations
Part-time work obligations apply to:
- a sole parent with a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years
Sole parents with part-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of at least 20 hours per week.
## Work preparation obligations
Work preparation obligations apply to:
- a sole parent with a youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
Note that if the client is receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, these children are not considered dependent children for rates purposes but they are treated as dependent children for setting work or work preparation obligations.
For more information see:
- Youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years
- Youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Work preparation obligations
- Work obligations
- Studying or training on Sole Parent Support
- Drug test obligations
- Work ability assessment obligation
- Work with a contracted service provider
- Exemptions
- Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Work preparation obligations — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Work preparation obligations
A person with work preparation obligations must take all reasonable steps to prepare for employment. When considering what is reasonable you must consider what is practical for their individual circumstances.
In addition, Sole Parent Support clients with a youngest dependent child aged under 3 years must:
- when required to undertake planning for employment
- when required to report to Work and Income on progress in meeting their work preparation obligations as often as required
- when required to attend and participate in any interview with Work and Income or on behalf of Work and Income and
- when required by Work and Income undertake any activity to improve their work readiness and employment prospects, including: any work assessmentany programme or seminarany work experience or work exploration activityany employment related trainingrehabilitation (but not medical treatment)an education programme
- any work assessment
- any programme or seminar
- any work experience or work exploration activity
- any employment related training
- rehabilitation (but not medical treatment)
- an education programme
Work preparation obligations can be applied on any day of the week provided it is suitable for the client's circumstances.
If a client does not meet their work preparation obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, you should initiate an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Setting appropriate activities for clients
- Studying or training on Sole Parent Support
- Reporting progress
- Rehabilitation
- Exemptions
- Table of exemptions
- Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Work with a contracted service provider obligation — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Work with a contracted service provider obligation
When required to, certain clients may be case managed by a contracted service provider.
When asked, clients have an obligation to co-operate with a contracted service provider and to:
- attend and participate in interviews with them
- report to them on how they are meeting their obligations, this could include their social, work or work preparation obligations and
- when required, complete assessments with the service provider

chunks.title: Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
A client applying for Sole Parent Support can be considered resident and present in New Zealand during periods of overseas employment when their employer (or other relevant person):
- deducted PAYE or source deductions from their wages and
- paid the deducted amount to Inland Revenue New Zealand
The period overseas that the client was considered resident and present can be used towards the 2 years residence requirement for Sole Parent Support.
A partner or any dependent child who was with the client while they were working overseas can also be treated as resident and present in New Zealand for the same periods.
If the client has a child born outside of New Zealand during the period they were working overseas, the child is deemed to have been born in New Zealand.
The residential qualifications do not apply to people who are self-employed and working overseas.
Clients should provide evidence of the periods they were employed overseas, and PAYE or source deductions paid to Inland Revenue in New Zealand during these periods.
If the employer (or other relevant person) has deducted the tax but failed to pay it to Inland Revenue New Zealand, and the client did not contribute to the employer's failure to pay the tax, the period of employment overseas can still be regarded as residence and present in New Zealand.
Note if any person leaves New Zealand while getting a benefit and returns to take up ordinary residence in New Zealand at any time within 5 years, they are not required to meet the residential qualifications for the same benefit type.

chunks.title: Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to clients with work obligations.
If a client meets the qualifications for Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their work obligations until their capacity for work improves.
The client must be limited in their capacity to work because of a health condition, injury or disability, and be:
- unable to look for part-time work of at least 15 hours per week or
- losing earnings because they are unable to work for at least 15 or 30 hours a week
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support - Qualifications
This is a partial exemption and the client is able to:
- plan for employment and
- undertake certain work related activities
## Evidence
To support their exemption, the client must provide a medical certificate signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant). This is generally a Work Capacity Medical Certificate.
The medical certificate must confirm:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to work and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for work planning, training and part-time work and
- any other information needed
## Duration
The duration of an exemption is based on the reassessment date recorded on the client’s medical certificate (often their Work Capacity Medical Certificate).
This exemption should then be reviewed. At the review MSD should consider the client's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption.
MSD can ask the client to provide evidence of the reason why the exemption should be extended.
## Live Organ Donor
When a Sole Parent Support client is donating a kidney or liver tissue they can continue getting their current benefit. The client must provide evidence they have been accepted as a live organ donor.
Medical evidence must be signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner.
The medical certificate coverage can be the lesser of either:
- the period specified by the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner or
- up to 12 weeks

chunks.title: Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability, or total blindness — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability, or total blindness
This exemption may apply to clients with work or work preparation obligations.
If a client meets the qualifications for Supported Living Payment on the ground of health a condition, injury or disability or total blindness, they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their work obligations.
The client must be:
- both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, or injury or disability, from an accident, or a condition they have had since birth or
- totally blind
Note totally blind and legally blind are not the same.
For more information see:
- Supported Living Payment
Note this can be a full or partial exemption depending on the whether the client can plan for a return to work.
MSD should discuss with the client whether they can still:
- plan for employment and
- undertake certain work related activities
If it is unclear whether a full or partial exemption should be granted, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor.
Note when appropriate MSD should consider the client's eligibility for Supported Living Payment.
## Evidence
To support their exemption, the client must provide a Work Capacity Medical Certificate or medical information signed by a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or psychologist.
The medical certificate or medical information must confirm:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to work and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for work planning, training and part-time work and
- any other information that is required

chunks.title: Youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years
Part-time work obligations apply to:
- sole parents with a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years
The sole parent must make themselves available for suitable employment, training or other activities of at least 20 hours a week.
For more information see:
- Work obligations
Sole parents may do voluntary work but must be available to meet their work obligations. For more information see:
- Clients undertaking voluntary work
Sole parents may apply for an exemption from their work obligations. For more information on exemptions see:
- Exemptions
- Table of Exemptions
If a sole parent fails to comply with their work obligations, they are subject to an obligations failure. For more information see:
- Clients with dependent children - 50% protection [no link find out why]
If a sole parent with part-time obligations is already in employment for 20 hours or more each week, they are meeting their work obligations.
If they are in employment for less than 20 hours each week, they are still expected to be available for other work, training or any other activities.

chunks.title: Youngest dependent child aged under 3 years — main benefits > sole parent support
chunks.text:
## Youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
Work preparation obligations apply to:
- sole parents with a youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
The sole parent must take all reasonable steps to prepare them for work in the future.
For more information see:
- Work preparation obligations
Sole parents may apply for an exemption from their work preparation obligations. Generally, they can only be considered for a full exemption as work preparation obligations mean that they are required to plan for employment and undertake work preparation activities - the equivalent of a partial exemption.
For more information see:
- Exemptions
- Table of exemptions
If a sole parent fails to comply with their work preparation obligations, they are subject to an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures
- Clients with dependent children - 50% protection

chunks.title: Absence during initial stand-down — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Absence during initial stand-down
A client who has applied for and been granted Supported Living Payment may leave New Zealand during the initial stand-down period, provided they are not absent for more than 28 days from the entitlement date.
The absence is calculated from the entitlement date, not the date the client leaves New Zealand, or the date the benefit commences.
## Example
A client applies for Supported Living Payment on 8 July 2013. At the application interview they advise Work and Income that they have a 5 week holiday planned in Australia and are going to leave New Zealand on 13 July 2004.
- their entitlement date is established as 18 July 2013
- a one week stand-down imposed
- their benefit will commence on 22 July 2013
- the calculation of the 28 days starts from the entitlement date, that is, 18 July 2013
If they do not return to New Zealand by 26 August 2013 their benefit should be suspended from that date unless they meet the specific criteria to be paid for more than 28 days. They will need to contact Work and Income on their return.
For more information see:
- Absence from New Zealand
- Entitlement date
- Commencement date

chunks.title: Youth money managed — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Youth money managed
When a young partner is youth money managed and has an obligations failure and has not recomplied within the 5 working day notice period, the effect of the sanction on the client's assistance is the same as for Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Activity Summary — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Activity Summary
After you have discussed with the partner the work obligations and activities they are required to complete, you may want to provide the partner with an Activity Summary as confirmation of these.
Clients do not sign the Activity Summary and it is not mandatory to provide the Activity Summary to them. You may think it is appropriate to provide the print out or the client may request this.
For more information see:
- Setting appropriate activities for clients

chunks.title: Age — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Age
To get Supported Living Payment, the client must be aged:
- 16 years or older if they are permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, injury or disability or total blindness or
- 18 years or older if they are caring for a person and do not have dependent children or
- 20 years or older if they are caring for a person and have a dependent child
If the client is at school or in study and meets the medical qualifications, they can still get Supported Living Payment on ground of health condition, injury or disability.
## Young people who were getting Domestic Purposes Benefit - care of sick or infirm
Young people who were aged 16 to 18 years and getting Domestic Purposes Benefit - care of sick or infirm on 20 August 2012, who were transferred to Supported Living Payment on 15 July 2013, can continue getting Supported Living Payment until they no longer qualify.
## Partners under 18 years
If a client qualifies for Supported Living Payment on the ground of health condition, injury or disability and they have a 16 or 17 year old partner, the partner can be included in the benefit when they are:
- legally married or
- in a civil union or
- in a de facto relationship with Family Court Judge consent

chunks.title: Age of assessment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Age of assessment
Information in existing assessments needs to be current. Generally, in order for existing assessments to be used to decide entitlement to Supported Living Payment the information in your client's assessment needs to:
- be recent, that is written in the last 12 months or
- be within the reports expiry date (if the report has one). That is, your client applies for benefit before the report's next reassessment date or
- contain information on your client's impairment or disability that signals the impact is unlikely to improve (for example, the condition is one they have had since birth)
If you are unsure whether your client's assessment is current, refer to your Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] for advice.

chunks.title: All reasonable steps to meet social obligations — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
There may be some situations where a client or their partner (if any) can't comply with their social obligations for reasons beyond their control. You can accept that a client has taken all reasonable steps to comply if they:
- have made a commitment to meet their social obligations at a more appropriate time and
- are working towards addressing any barriers they are facing
Every client's situation is different and what may be a barrier to meeting social obligations for one family may not be for another.
The decision about whether a client is taking all reasonable steps to comply is made by the Ministry of Social Development.
Below are some of the situations you should take into account when considering that the client is taking all reasonable steps:
- Shared care issues in the family or family court proceedings occurring
The parent who is not the principal caregiver does not support their child having to attend recognised early childhood education programmes. It would not be reasonable for the client to be held responsible for the actions of someone else.
- Family violence or safety concerns in the family
A client discloses family violence or they have safety concerns for the child.
- Supply or availability issues
A child is on a waiting list for:
- an early childhood education programme or
- a medical centre and the client has a plan or commitment to ensure their child can access primary health care if it is required
- Additional costs of participation or engagement may put the client in hardship
The travel costs or additional early childhood education programme costs associated with attendance would cause hardship to the family.
- The child has a health condition, injury or disability
A child has an injury or behavioural problems meaning that it would not be reasonable to expect them to participate in an approved programme either temporarily or permanently.
- Family has recently moved to a new area
The family has recently moved and is in the process of establishing networks.
For more information see:
- Social obligations
- Monitoring compliance with social obligations
- Recognised early childhood education programmes

chunks.title: Approved activity examples — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Approved activity examples
Here are some examples that may be a suitable 6 week approved activity for a partner with work obligations:
- Employment skills programmes
- Employment-related training
- Work experience, Activity in the Community and Voluntary work
Note these are examples only, an approved activity (or programme of suitable activities) should be relevant to the obligations failure and be fair and reasonable.
## Programme of suitable activities
If there is not an appropriate 6 week approved activity available, consider establishing a programme of suitable activities.
For more information see:
- Recompliance programme example
For when to grant or increase the benefit, see:
- Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period
For what to do if a client or partner cannot recomply see:
- Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption

chunks.title: Approved recompliance activities for young partners — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Approved recompliance activities for young partners
Approved recompliance activities for young partners include:
- education, training or work-based learning
- part-time work or work experience (where the young person is not already in part-time work)
- community activities
- any other activity approved by MSD that will enhance skills or motivation
Note the benefit will be resumed or increased from the date the young partner starts the recompliance activity.
For more information see:
- Recompliance for young partners
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Is this the right course? — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Is this the right course?
The course must:
- focus on teaching practical, employment-related skills
- support the partner to find work and
- be less than 12 weeks (other than approved Government sponsored courses)
Some additional things to note are:
- partners applying for courses longer than 12 weeks should be seeking assistance through StudyLink if the course has been approved by the Ministry of Education for Student Loans or Student Allowances and
- if a partner is undergoing pre-employment training under Flexi-Wage [no link find out why] they cannot receive their portion of the benefit as they should be receiving a wage from the employer
For examples of approved courses see:
- Examples of approved courses

chunks.title: Extra Help for young people in approved training — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Extra Help for young people in approved training
The following assistance is available for Young people in approved training:
- Employment and work readiness Education and employment related training
You should also keep in contact with the young partner during their course to ensure that they are regularly attending the training.
For more information see:
- Definition of 'full-time'
- NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification
- Youth activity obligations
- Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months

chunks.title: Assessing capacity for work preparation obligation - primary client — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Assessing capacity for work preparation obligation - primary client
A client receiving Supported Living Payment may be assessed for their capacity to meet the work preparation obligation.
Clients cannot be required to meet the base work preparation obligation to take all reasonable steps to prepare for employment. However, they can, when required, be asked to meet the other work preparation obligations.
Before you require a Supported Living Payment client to meet these work preparation obligations, you must consider their capacity to undertake the work preparation obligations.
## Work preparation obligations cannot be applied
Work preparation obligations will not apply to Supported Living Payment clients who do not have capacity to undertake them.
For more information see:
- Work preparation obligations do not apply - primary client
## Fails to attend interview to discuss capacity
If a Supported Living Payment client does not attend an interview to discuss their capacity to undertake work preparation obligations, you can initiate an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Work preparation obligations - primary client
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Assessment from client's medical specialist — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The client is likely to have been assessed by registered health practitioners, which may include specialists, throughout the duration of their illness or disability. MSD can consider granting Supported Living Payment if it is satisfied the information contained in the assessment from a medical specialist confirms the client meets the medical criteria for Supported Living Payment. Note all medical specialists are registered medical practitioners. The information the client provides needs to be current. In some cases specialist reports will be over 12 months old but they will still be current.

chunks.title: Who will have an existing medical specialist assessment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: A client may have an existing specialist assessment MSD can use to decide their eligibility to Supported Living Payment if they: - are blind - have severe physical disabilities (e.g. tetraplegia, paraplegia, spina bifida, cerebral palsy, stroke) - have long standing, severe ill health (e.g. chronic arthritis, chronic heart failure, cystic fibrosis) - have an intellectual disability - are terminally ill - have a mental health issue (e.g. severe depression, schizophrenia, psychoses) - are deaf This list is not exhaustive and MSD should encourage the client to provide other types of existing assessments if it may avoid further assessment.

chunks.title: Types of medical specialist assessments — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Specialists are registered medical practitioners who concentrate on certain body organ systems, specific age groups or on complex scientific techniques developed to diagnose or treat certain types of disorders. There are many different types of specialists including but not limited to: - addiction medicine specialist (e.g. drug or alcohol addiction) - allergist or immunologist (e.g. asthma, eczema, adverse reactions to drugs, foods and insect stings, immune deficiency diseases) - cardiologist (e.g. heart related conditions) - endocrinologist (e.g. hormonal conditions) - general surgeon (e.g. surgical conditions affecting almost any area of the body) - neurologist (e.g. brain damage arising from a brain tumour, early onset dementia) - oncologist (e.g. cancer) - ophthalmologist (e.g. blindness) - paediatrician (e.g. cares for babies, children and adolescents) - psychiatrist (e.g. schizophrenia, severe depression, psychoses, anxiety disorders, substance abuse disorders, developmental disabilities)respiratory physicians (e.g. diseases and conditions affecting the respiratory system)

chunks.title: What the reports will look like — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The formats of medical specialist assessments are likely to be diverse. They can be provided in the form of a letter from the medical specialist to the client's registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist or could be a written report. The reports and letters will generally be signed by the medical specialist or another registered medical practitioner on their behalf. Although medical specialist assessments are not always signed by a medical specialist, if the client provides a Supported Living Payment medical certificate it must be signed by a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist. Note a psychologist cannot complete a medical certificate for the person who is being cared for when assessing a client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).

chunks.title: Medical specialist reports contain useful information — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Medical specialist reports are particularly useful in establishing the permanency of the client's health condition or disability. All information provided to MSD by the client should be used when deciding whether to approve Supported Living Payment. If it is unclear from the information a client provides that they meet the medical criteria for Supported Living Payment, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] .

chunks.title: At home — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## At home
To get a Supported Living Payment the client must provide full-time care and attention at home. The home can be the client's or the person's home. A client may live in the same house as the person receiving care.
Some carers may receive payment from other funding sources such as the Ministry of Health Funded Family Care programme. These payments are considered income when assessing the rate of benefit.
If the client lives in different accommodation their ability to provide full-time care and attention may be compromised. Consider each case on its merits.

chunks.title: Blind clients subsidy — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Blind clients subsidy
An additional allowance of 25% of their average personal earnings can be paid to a totally blind person who is getting Supported Living Payment on ground of health condition, injury, disability or total blindness. There is a maximum subsidy amount paid on a blind client's earnings.
The subsidy is only assessed on the blind client's personal earnings from actual work they do.
## Change in rate of earnings and review of subsidy
When there has been a clear change in the rate of earnings, review the benefit and subsidy. If there are any small changes, the client's subsidy will be reviewed during their Mandatory Review.
If there has been a clear change in the rate of earnings review the benefit and subsidy from the first available date. Individual cases can only be considered when a retrospective review is requested.
Use the same process if a totally blind person starts working after they have been granted a benefit.
Earnings must be checked every 3 months until the amount earned can be assessed on a real earnings basis.
Ensure the client understands that when a subsidy is granted on likely earnings, the benefit must be assessed by charging probable income from all other sources.
## For help calculating this subsidy see:
- Subsidy Assessment for blind clients
- Mandatory Review for Supported Living Payment
- Outcomes of a Mandatory Review

chunks.title: Calculating the period of residence — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Calculating the period of residence
A period of residence in New Zealand starts from the date the client was:
- lawfully resident in New Zealand or
- was granted New Zealand citizenship or permanent residence
To be resident at a particular time a client must be lawfully resident, that is, the client must be one of the following:
- a New Zealand citizen
- a permanent resident in New Zealand
- an Australian citizen or passport holder or
- a New Zealand passport holder
For more information see:
- Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
- Permanent residence
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Unlawful residence

chunks.title: Step 1 — main benefits > supported living payment
