chunks.text:
## Step 1
Find out the number of days represented by the payment received. If this is not clearly shown on the 'verification of payments received' provided by the client, use either of the following formula.
Note extra payments paid to the client (for example holiday pay), should not be included in the gross salary figure used to calculate the daily rate of pay. However these payments will be included in the clients' last 26 and 52 weeks gross earnings.
Formula 1
Determine gross salary over last 52 weeks of employment
Divide by 52 weeks = weekly rate of pay
Divide by 5 days = daily rate of pay
Confirm total amount of holiday pay etc
Divide this amount by daily rate of pay = number of days pay
Formula 2
Determine gross salary over last 4 weeks of employment
Divide by 20 (number of working days in 4 weeks) = daily rate of pay
Confirm total amount of holiday pay etc
Divide by daily rate of pay = number of days pay
Note only calculate the period covered by holiday pay using the applicants' last four weeks income if it does not disadvantage the client. If the income earned in the last four weeks does not reflect what the client normally earned, you may need to request extra weeks or calculate the daily rate of pay using the last 26 weeks gross salary.

chunks.title: Capacity issues prevent a young partner meeting their parenting obligations — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Capacity issues prevent a young partner meeting their parenting obligations
A young partner may be granted a parenting incentive without meeting the criteria if:
- there are capacity issues preventing a young person from: undertaking a parenting programmeenrolling their dependent child/ren with a primary health organisationkeeping their dependent child/ren aged 5 years or under up-to-date with their Well Child checkshaving their children under five years attends an approved early childhood education programme or being placed in other suitable child care which the young person is in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work
- undertaking a parenting programme
- enrolling their dependent child/ren with a primary health organisation
- keeping their dependent child/ren aged 5 years or under up-to-date with their Well Child checks
- having their children under five years attends an approved early childhood education programme or being placed in other suitable child care which the young person is in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work
and
- the young person has agreed with their service provider or MSD "in-house" service on steps they must take to fulfil these obligations (for example being on a waiting list) and
- the young person has taken the agreed steps to the satisfaction of their service provider or MSD "in-house" service

chunks.title: Carers receiving other income — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Carers receiving other income
Supported Living Payment is paid to support a client while they are providing care. It is not paid to provide a wage.
Where someone is recruited to 'work' for the person getting care, the Employment Relations Act 2000 and various other legislative measures which regulate employment apply (eg the Minimum Wage Act 1983 and the Holidays Act 2003).
A person who needs care may receive funding from another agency such as Accident Compensation Corporation to pay a carer directly. In these cases, the person may employ the client receiving Supported Living Payment to provide care.
While a client who is receiving payment for providing care is not excluded from getting Supported Living Payment any payment they get for providing care is treated as income.

chunks.title: Caring for a child or foster child with special needs — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Caring for a child or foster child with special needs
This exemption may apply to partners with work or work preparation obligations.
A partner can be exempt from some or all of their work or work preparation obligations if they are the:
- principal caregiver of a dependent child or
- foster parent of a foster child
who has special needs and whose welfare would be unduly harmed if the partner attended employment or training, and for whom alternative care arrangements are not available, or are unable to be made.
This means the child must have 1 or more of the following:
- a physical or intellectual disability
- a medical condition
- a chronic or recurring illness
- a learning or behavioural difficulty and
- be unable to attend school on a regular basis
or
- be a foster child, aged 3 years or older, who is adjusting to a placement with a new carer
Note this can be a full or partial exemption.
## Evidence
The partner must provide written evidence from a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, psychologist or social worker stating:
- what the child's illness, disability or medical condition is and its likely duration or
- an assessment of the child's learning or behavioural difficulty or
- the need for full-time care and
- the risk to the child if the partner has work or work preparation obligations and
- that the child is unable to attend school
Note MSD should also consider eligibility to Child Disability Allowance. However, a child getting Child Disability Allowance does not guarantee the partner will meet the criteria for this exemption.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months.
This exemption should then be reviewed.
At the review MSD should consider the partner's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption. MSD can ask the partner to provide evidence the exemption should be extended.

chunks.title: Caring for a child or foster child with special needs (young partners) — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Caring for a child or foster child with special needs (young partners)
A young partner with a dependent child can be exempt from some or all of their activity obligations if they are the:
- principal caregiver of a dependent child or
- foster parent of a foster child
who has special needs and whose welfare would be unduly harmed if the young partner attended education, training or work-based learning and for whom alternative care arrangements are not available, or are unable to be made.
This means the child must have 1 or more of the following:
- a physical or intellectual disability
- a medical condition
- a chronic or recurring illness
- a learning or behavioural difficulty and
- be unable to attend school on a regular basis
or
- be a foster child, aged 1 year or older, who is adjusting to a placement with a new carer
This can be a full or partial exemption.
## Evidence
The young partner must provide written evidence from a registered medical practitioner, or nurse practitioner, psychologist or social worker stating:
- what the child's illness, disability or health condition is and its likely duration or
- an assessment of the child's learning or behavioural difficulty or
- the need for full-time care and
- the risk to the child if the young partner is required to meet their activity obligations and
- that the child is unable to attend school
Note MSD should also consider eligibility to Child Disability Allowance. However, a child getting Child Disability Allowance does not guarantee the partner will meet the criteria for this exemption.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months.
This exemption should then be reviewed.
At the review MSD should consider the young partner's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption. MSD can ask the young partner to provide evidence that their exemption should be extended.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions (young partners)
- Extra help Child Disability Allowance
- Table of exemptions for young partners

chunks.title: Caring for a child under 3 years who is not their dependent child — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Caring for a child under 3 years who is not their dependent child
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
In some cases a partner may be caring for a foster child or children under the age of 3 years who is in Oranga Tamariki care.
Foster children are not considered to be dependent children.
These partners may be exempt from meeting some of their work obligations.
This is a partial exemption only.
## Proof
The partner must provide:
- confirmation of their situation - for example, a letter from Oranga Tamariki
- confirmation of the age of the child
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Caring for a foster child'.

chunks.title: Caring for a person — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Caring for a person
A client applying for Supported Living Payment on ground of caring for a person must provide full-time care and attention to a person (other than their partner), at home who would otherwise need:
- hospital care
- rest home care
- residential disability care
- care of the kind referred to in section 141 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989, which is extended care services provided for severely disabled children and young persons
- care of an equivalent kind
The Supported Living Payment can be paid to a parent who is required to provide full-time care and attention at home, to their dependent child who has a significant disability, and as a result has high care needs of a type listed above.
This is not meant to be paid to parents for children who need only the levels of care required for children typical of their age.
During the assessment process it is important to make sure that the applicant and their family, where appropriate, receive their full and correct entitlement and they are referred to organisations (such as Carers New Zealand) to access all services available. You should consider this when granting, as well as when declining an application.
## Funded Family Care
Funded Family Care is paid to carers aged 16 or over for providing personal care and household management.
From 2 June 2020 partners and carers over the age of 16 can be included as a carer for Funded Family Care.
If a client gets Funded Family Care payments and also qualifies for Supported Living Payment caring for a person, the Funded Family Care payments are treated as income.

chunks.title: Caring for foster child under 12 months old (young partners) — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Caring for foster child under 12 months old (young partners)
In some cases a young partner may be caring for a foster child under the age of 12 months who is in Oranga Tamariki care. Foster children are not considered to be dependent child.
This is a partial exemption only. The young partner can be exempt from meeting their obligation to be in full-time education, training and work-based learning.
The budgeting and parenting obligations, along with the obligation to meet with their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service still apply.

chunks.title: Caring full-time for a partner with a health condition, injury or disability (young partners) — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Caring full-time for a partner with a health condition, injury or disability (young partners)
A young partner may be caring for a partner who has a health condition, injury or disability and who needs to be cared for on a full-time basis.
This can be a full or partial exemption.
## Evidence
The young partner must provide evidence from a registered medical practitioner, or nurse practitioner:
- that their partner needs the young partner's full-time care and
- that without that care their partner would need hospital level care or care of an equivalent kind and
- the length of time their partner will need that care

chunks.title: Caring full-time for person with health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Caring full-time for person with health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to partners with work or work preparation obligations.
A partner may be caring for a person who has a health condition, injury or a disability and who needs to be cared for on a full-time basis.
This can be a full exemption.
MSD should also consider the partner's eligibility to Supported Living Payment on the ground of caring for a person if the person they are caring for is not their partner.
## Evidence
The partner must provide evidence. This should be either a medical certificate signed by a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or other relevant medical assessments that prove:
- the person needs the client's full-time care
- without that care the person would need hospital care or care of an equivalent kind and
- the length of time the person will need that care
Note a psychologist cannot complete a medical certificate for the person who is being cared for when assessing a client';s eligibility to Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months or the length of time they are providing care.
This exemption should then be reviewed.
At the review MSD should consider the client's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption. MSD can ask the client to provide evidence that the exemption should be extended.

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances
Clients must tell us straight away of any change in their circumstances or their family's situation that may affect their entitlement to Supported Living Payment. Clients agree to this by signing the Supported Living Payment application form.
A change of circumstance may also affect the client's social obligations.
Examples of changes and how to deal with these can be found in Changes and reviews.
For more information see:
- Child changes and social obligations
- Changes and reviews Child changes

chunks.title: Change in circumstances during Money Management — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances during Money Management
Clients may have a change in circumstances during Money Management, such as a change in income, which may change their rate of benefit.
If a client declares a change in circumstances after their payment has been issued onto the payment card, it may mean this payment is incorrect resulting in a debt being established or arrears due to the client.
Any debt will generally be repaid from their future benefit payments.
If a client is owed arrears, it will be paid directly to their bank account. This is different when a client’s benefit stops during Money Management. For more information see:
- Period of Money Management

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Clients getting Supported Living Payment must be: - both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, or injury or disability from accident, or totally blind, or a condition they have had since birth or - caring for a person who requires full-time care and attention

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment clients who do not have work preparation activities assigned — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Clients getting Supported Living Payment can continue to get their payment when they temporarily leave New Zealand for a period of up to 28 days in any 52 week period. Note MSD must check that they remain eligible to get Supported Living Payment during any absence. For example, they are taking a short break from caring, and their patient is in respite care.

chunks.title: All clients have an obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: All clients getting a main benefit must advise the MSD before they leave New Zealand. If the client or partner does not advise MSD prior to their international travel, their benefit payments will stop from the day after they leave New Zealand.

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment client has work preparation activities assigned and needs to be absent from New Zealand — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Generally, a client or their partner is not entitled to get Supported Living Payment while absent from New Zealand. However, in limited circumstances, the Supported Living Payment can be paid for up to 28 days in a 52 week period when a client (or their partner) is absent from New Zealand for: - Approved travel reasons - Overseas for medical treatment

chunks.title: Special absence reasons for clients getting Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury, or disability) — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: A client getting Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) may be able to continue getting their payment for more than 28 days in any 52 week period in some circumstances.

chunks.title: Partner absent from New Zealand — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: The partner of a Supported Living Payment client may continue getting their benefit while absent from New Zealand. This depends on their work, or work preparation or youth activity obligations.

chunks.title: Payment of benefit while absent for more than 28 days in any 52 week period — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days absence from New Zealand in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.

chunks.title: Mandatory Review while overseas — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Clients getting Supported Living Payment who have temporarily left New Zealand must still respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date. Temporary absence from New Zealand (e.g. personal travel) does not pause or defer the Mandatory Review. Clients must contact MSD before their review date to talk about their situation if they are unable to respond to their review or if they need more time to do it.

chunks.title: Absences that do not prevent partner from meeting obligations — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Absences that do not prevent partner from meeting obligations
Generally, a client (who has had work preparation obligations assigned) or a partner (who has work obligations or work preparation activities assigned) cannot be absent from New Zealand and continue to be paid a benefit unless:
- it is for one of the permitted travel reasons or
- they are already meeting their work obligations (by being in employment ) or work preparation activities (by participating in employment related training)
and
- the travel will not prevent them continuing to meet these obligations (eg because it is during a period of annual leave or a term or semester break)

chunks.title: Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
These circumstances are:
- travel is required for an approved reason, and either: it is the client's first absence within 52 weeks and the permitted reason the client needs to be absent from New Zealand necessitates a period longer than 28 days orthe client has had other prior approved absences within the 52 week period and they require further approved absences which will require them to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- it is the client's first absence within 52 weeks and the permitted reason the client needs to be absent from New Zealand necessitates a period longer than 28 days or
- the client has had other prior approved absences within the 52 week period and they require further approved absences which will require them to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- the client is absent from New Zealand for an approved travel reason and their return is prevented by a new circumstance that requires them to be absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period
- the client is a young partner of a main beneficiary with youth activity obligations and they are travelling to receive support from a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family) who is residing overseas
For more information see:
- Paying more than 28 days for an approved reason
- Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
- Paying for more than 28 days - receive support from family overseas (young partner)

chunks.title: Action on return to New Zealand — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Action on return to New Zealand
You will need to look at the circumstances of the client's absence from and subsequent return to New Zealand to decide when to recommence their benefit and when to treat it as a new application.
You will need to consider the following:
- the client's intention at the time of their departure for example, did they cancel their benefit before leaving New Zealand because they did not intend to return
- did the client remain ordinarily resident during the period of absence?
- the length of time that they have been absent
- the reason for the absence
- have their circumstances changed significantly during their absence?
- is the client eligible to have their benefit backdated to the day after their departure date or date of return?
For more information see:
- Backdating benefit to day after departure date
## New application
In all other circumstances you may need to consider a new application from the client after reviewing the circumstances above.
For more information see:
- Client does not return

chunks.title: Clients working less than 15 hours — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Clients working less than 15 hours
Clients who are currently working less than 15 hours and are considering increasing their hours may be interested in taking part in the Sustainable Employment Trial. You may like to suggest this option to these clients.
## Clients occasionally working 15 hours or more
In some circumstances, clients may be occasionally working more than 15 hours a week, with the agreement of their Case Manager. It may be appropriate for these arrangements to continue.
These clients are still meeting the Supported Living Payment qualification as they are not regularly working over 15 hours a week. Taking part in a Sustainable Employment Trial is therefore not necessary. However, some clients may want to make their hours of employment more regular and may be interested in the Sustainable Employment Trial process.
For more information see:
- Guidelines for regular employment
- Already in employment - Work and Income not advised

chunks.title: Already in employment - Work and Income not advised — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Already in employment - Work and Income not advised
In some situations, a client may be working more than 15 hours a week and have not informed Work and Income prior to starting the job. You need to consider whether the client still meets the qualifications for the Supported Living Payment.
## Client has recently started working
In many cases, the client may have just started work or has a job offer that starts prior to the time of their appointment with Work and Income. Discuss the option of a Sustainable Employment Trial with them.
If you agree to a Sustainable Employment Trial in these circumstances, the start date of the Sustainable Employment Trial is the date you and the client agree to the Sustainable Employment Trial. Do not backdate the start date to the date the client started employment
## Long delay in informing Work and Income
There may be cases where a client informs Work and Income a considerable time after starting employment. These situations need to be treated on a case-by-case basis. If they have been regularly working over 15 hours you will need to check the client continues to meet the qualifications for the Supported Living Payment. Should you need help in making this decision contact Helpline.
For more information see:
- Start date of Sustainable Employment Trial
- Already in employment - Work and Income advised
- Length of Sustainable Employment Trial
- Guidelines for regular employment
- Inappropriate use of Sustainable Employment Trial

chunks.title: Approved overseas disability forum — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Approved overseas disability forum
A client getting a main benefit, who has a long-term physical, mental, intellectual, or sensory impairment, can travel overseas to attend an approved disability forum (programme or event).
In these cases the client may be able to continue to receive payment of their benefit for up to 12 weeks when they are absent from New Zealand. This absence from New Zealand is not related to any other discretionary 4 week absence they may be allowed in a 52 week period.
This does not apply to a partner with work obligations.
The criteria for continuing payment are:
- the person must have a long-term physical, mental, intellectual, or sensory impairment that, in interaction with various barriers, may hinder the clients participation
and
- the absence from New Zealand must be for the purpose of attending a disability forum approved by the Chief Executive (all applications must be referred to the Principal Disability Advisor)
and
- the approved disability forum must be: a disability programme or event associated with the United Nations or an international disability organisation oranother type of programme or event that the beneficiary is attending to contribute a disability perspective
- a disability programme or event associated with the United Nations or an international disability organisation or
- another type of programme or event that the beneficiary is attending to contribute a disability perspective
## Proof
The client will need to provide proof of the intended attendance at an overseas disability forum.

chunks.title: Approved travel reasons — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Approved travel reasons
Clients receiving Supported Living Payment who have work preparation activities assigned (and partners with work obligations or work preparation activities assigned) are generally not able to continue to receive their main benefit payments while they are absent from New Zealand unless they meet the criteria for approved travel.
Approved travel includes:
- travel for a permitted reason
- travel where the absence does not prevent the partner from meeting all of their obligations because the absence is at a time they are not required to attend employment, education or training (whichever applies)
Note partners with work obligations are not required to meet their job search obligations while absent from New Zealand on approved travel.
For more information see:
- Permitted travel reasons
- Absences that do not prevent client meeting their obligations
## Length of travel for an approved travel reason
Clients who have work preparation activities assigned (or partners with work obligations or work preparation activities assigned) can travel for up to 28 days on Supported Living Payment for an approved travel reason.
Discuss with the client the amount of time that they need to be absent from New Zealand as a result of the approved reason. The client should explain the length of their intended absence.
Consider:
- the length of time the event or reason for travel will take
- the duties the client will have as part of their reason (eg if they are travelling for a funeral, do they have responsibilities beyond attending the funeral itself such as estate duties or sorting out the possessions of the deceased?)
- flight availability and travel time
Remember to advise clients that generally they are only able to continue to be paid their benefit for up to 28 days in a 52 week period. This should be taken into account when deciding the approved travel period.
## Client travelling for multiple reasons
Some clients may travel overseas for an approved travel reason but elect to stay longer for another reason that is not an approved travel reason. In this case, the client can generally only receive their main benefit payments for the period of time that the approved travel reason applies to.
For more information see:
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy
- Permitted travel reasons
- Absences that do not prevent partner from meeting obligations
- Travel notifications made while overseas [no link find out why] procedures
- Travel notifications made on return to New Zealand [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Backdating benefit to day after departure date — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Backdating benefit to day after departure date
A client who leaves New Zealand without advising Work and Income of their travel can only have their benefit backdated to the day after their departure date if they:
- have a humanitarian reason that justifies their reason for travel and their failure to tell Work and Income before they left
- contacted Work and Income as soon as they could reasonably have been expected to, given their circumstances after they departed and
- meet the criteria to continue to be paid their benefit while overseas (either because they meet the criteria for approved travel, or the requirement that travel be approved does not apply to them)
For more information see:
- Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure
- Contacting Work and Income as soon as the client reasonably can
- Approved travel reasons
- Paying a benefit when a client has not advised before departure
- Action on return to New Zealand

chunks.title: Benefit has expired — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Benefit has expired
If your client's benefit has expired before they have been able to provide a Work and Income medical certificate, existing assessments or attend an assessment with a designated health practitioner (or receive an assessment back from the designated health practitioner), you can temporarily continue Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability).
Before temporarily continuing Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) your client needs to advise you of the reason for the delay in providing the information. When they do this you need to:
- consider the reason given for the delay and agree on a reasonable and appropriate period for them to provide the information
- advise your client of the date that they are required to provide the information
- advise them that their benefit will stop from this date if the information isn't provided
Note that if your client is unable to, or it is not reasonable to expect your client or their parent, guardian or agent to obtain existing assessments or reports you can assist them to do this.
For more information see:
- Helping your client obtain existing assessments
## Designated health practitioner assessment
Where it is not reasonable for your client to access the supporting information or where your client is unable to access the supporting information within the timeframe you can refer your client to a designated health practitioner.
For more information see:
- Designated health practitioners
- Outcome of designated health practitioner assessment

chunks.title: Birth of a child — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Birth of a child
When a client applies to have their newborn child included in their benefit, the following information is required:
- full birth certificate of the child, or confirmation from Internal Affairs that the child's birth was registered online, and permission was given to share the birth registration with MSD
- written statement from the client requesting inclusion of the child
If a child's birth certificate is not available immediately, you can include the child in the benefit (without delay) where the client can provide:
- Plunket records
- birth notices
- confirmation from the client's midwife or doctor of the date of birth of the new child or
- hospital papers
You must follow-up to make sure the client produces a copy of the birth certificate.
## Extra help
If a child is born with a mental or physical disability, needs constant care and attention because of a disability, or is likely to require care for at least 12 months, the client should test their eligibility for Child Disability Allowance.
Where a child has ongoing additional costs because of a disability they may be able to receive a Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Calculating the period of absence — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Calculating the period of absence
The period of an absence from New Zealand for which payment of Supported Living Payment can continue (if approved) is up to 28 consecutive days, that is, Saturdays and Sundays are included.
In all cases, when assessing the period of absence do not include:
- the date of departure from New Zealand and
- the date of return to New Zealand
If a client is absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period the benefit should be suspended from the 29th day (unless they meet the criteria to pay for longer than 28 days).
Note if a client is leaving New Zealand permanently, the benefit must be cancelled from the day after departure.
## Calculating 52 week period
When a client is paid a benefit while they are absent from New Zealand, a client can receive a payment for up to 28 days in total in a 52 week period. The 52 week period is counted in the following way:
- identify the day after the client is intending to leave New Zealand
- count back 52 weeks from this date
- identify any periods of paid absence they have used (counting from the day after they have left New Zealand to the day before they returned to New Zealand)
- subtract the number of days absent from New Zealand from 28 days. The remainder is the client's entitlement to be paid a benefit while they are absent from New Zealand
- pay the client the days they have available up to the period of absence. This may not be the whole of the time they intend to be absent from New Zealand depending on how many days of their entitlement they have left.
For more information see:
- Examples of calculating absence from New Zealand
- Client does not return
- Reciprocal Agreements

chunks.title: Caring for a person who requires full-time care — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Caring for a person who requires full-time care
Clients getting Supported Living payment as they are caring for a person who requires full-time care can have their benefit continue for a maximum of 4 weeks, while the patient is in some other person's care, because the client is in hospital.
If the client is in hospital for more than 4 weeks, they will no longer qualify for Supported Living payment. Consider if the client qualifies for another benefit.

chunks.title: Partner's work obligations — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Partner's work obligations
Unless a partner qualifies for an exemption from their obligations, they are required to:
- prepare for work (if required) when the youngest dependent child is under 3 years old
- meet the part-time work obligations when the youngest dependent child turns 3
- meet the full-time work obligations when the youngest dependent child is turns 14

chunks.title: Change of address — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Change of address
When a client advises that they have changed their address it is important to check that the move does not affect their entitlement to Supported Living Payment.
Note you will need to update the address in CMS.
If the client is receiving Extra Help this will also need to be reviewed to take into account their new costs.
If the client has a portion of their benefit paid to Kāinga Ora or Te Puni Kokiri this may need to be changed or cancelled.
The change of address may also indicate a change in the client's circumstances.
Examples of changes that may affect entitlement are:
- client and or partner commencing employment, study or training
- partner with work obligations ceases employment, study or training
- change of relationship status
- dependent children who have come into or left their care

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
Clients have an obligation to advise MSD of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Supported Living Payment or the rate payable. A change in a client's circumstances may mean that the client qualifies for another benefit.
MSD may also review a benefit at any time to check if the client still meets the qualifications and is getting the correct rate of payment (if applicable).
## Mandatory Review for Supported Living Payment
MSD must review a client's Supported Living Payment within 52-weeks of when the benefit commenced, or within 52-weeks from when the client's last Mandatory Review was completed.
Clients must respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date, or their payments will suspend.

chunks.title: Charging income against benefit rate — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Charging income against benefit rate
Clients undertaking a Sustainable Employment Trial and earning income will qualify for a personal earnings exemption. They may also be eligible for a special exemption due to severe disablement.
Any income earned from the Sustainable Employment Trial is to be charged against the benefit, except income to which an exemption applies, with the benefit being reduced under the current charging income rules.
Any income earned by the client may also affect their entitlement to other forms of Extra Help, for example Special Benefit or Temporary Additional Support.
You should provide them with an estimate from DREW of what their benefit and other forms of Extra Help will be after the benefit has been reduced, and the likely gain from employment.
## Client's income fully reduces the benefit
In a situation where the client's income fully reduces their benefit to a nil rate, their benefit will be suspended. You need to discuss with the client what other forms of assistance are available to them as a non-beneficiary, to ensure they are receiving their full and correct entitlement.

chunks.title: Child admitted to hospital — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Child admitted to hospital
Where a client's dependent child is admitted to hospital, there is no change to the rate of payment while the child remains in hospital. Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit payments continue to be paid for a child who is admitted to hospital.
Note Best Start tax credit ends when the child turns three.
Depending on the nature of the child's injury, illness or disability the client may be able to receive Child Disability Allowance
Child Disability Allowance is a non-taxable allowance paid to the principal caregiver of a child with a serious disability, who is in need of constant care and attention for a period longer than 12 months.

chunks.title: Child applies for a benefit in their own right — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Child applies for a benefit in their own right
Where a child applies for a benefit in their own right, exclude the child from the client's Supported Living Payment from:
- the start of the pay period following the date of event
Note there is discretion to continue payment for one more payday following the event.
or
- the date the child's benefit is granted
whichever is earlier.
Wherever possible (and in appropriate circumstances) the date of exclusion of the child from the client's benefit and the commencement date of the child's benefit should coincide to avoid financial hardship for the family.
Note there are specific rules for deciding whether a child is considered a dependent child when the child turns 18.

chunks.title: Child changes — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Child changes
The number of dependent children in a Supported Living Payment client's care and any change to the circumstance of a child can affect:
- the basic rate of benefit payable
- the rate of family tax credit
- payment of Best Start tax credit
- the rate of extra help payable and
- the obligations of the partner (if any)
## Including a child in Supported Living Payment
For a child to be included in a client's Supported Living Payment the child must be a dependent child and generally ordinarily resident in New Zealand.
When the child is not the client's natural or adoptive child, the client may be able to get an Unsupported Childs Benefit (instead of having the child included in their Supported Living Payment). This will mainly depend on the care arrangements.
## Changes to a child's circumstances
Change to a dependent child's circumstances is generally going to affect the client's Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Child comes into care — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Child comes into care
When a client has made an application to have another child included in their benefit and that child was in the care of another person the following information is required:
- full birth certificate of the childSee: Verification from Internal Affairs
- written statement from the applicant stating they are the principal caregiver and requesting inclusion in the Supported Living Payment
- (where appropriate) letter from previous caregiver confirming that child has left their careNote where the client cannot get written confirmation from the previous caregiver, the new caring arrangement can be confirmed by a referee such as a teacher, Plunket nurse, minister or a Justice of the Peace.
Any benefit payments the previous caregiver was getting for the child must stop.
## Date of review
Include the child in the benefit from:
- the date the child came into the client's care or
- the date the Supported Living Payment was granted
whichever is the later.
## Backdating
When a client requests the backdated inclusion of a child and the previous caregiver was getting a benefit for the child, you will need to review when the child was excluded from the previous caregiver's benefit.
Generally, a child cannot be included in multiple benefits for the same period. In some situations, the previous caregiver may continue to get a benefit in respect of that child for up to 28 days.
Consider all the circumstances and decide whether a debt should be established for the previous caregiver.
If the date you are including the child from is a date in the previous tax year, MSD can only pay arrears of family tax credit and Best Start tax credit from the beginning of the current tax year, that is, 1 April. The client will need to apply for any arrears of tax credits before this date from Inland Revenue.
A review of entitlement needs to be completed to determine the amount of any benefit arrears owed to the client for the backdated period.

chunks.title: Personal earnings — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Personal earnings
A dependent child's personal earnings are not charged as income against the Supported Living Payment.
However, a child in full-time employment and financially independent cannot be included as a dependent child in the benefit.

chunks.title: Child leaves care — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Child leaves care
When a dependent child leaves the client's care, the child should be excluded from the start of the pay period following the date the child leaves care. The client's benefit rate and the rates of any extra help the client gets must be reassessed to the appropriate rate where applicable.
Note different rules apply when a child stops being a dependent child of a sole parent client because of a sudden change of circumstances beyond the control of the client.
## Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit
Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit should be stopped from the start of the pay period following the date the event took place to avoid an overpayment with Inland Revenue for the client.

chunks.title: Child under the age of 18 years — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Child under the age of 18 years
When a child under the age of 18 years leaves school or tertiary education, they can continue to be included in the parent or caregiver's Supported Living Payment as long as the child remains a dependent child.
## Child aged 18 years
When a child aged 18 years leaves school or tertiary education, they should be excluded from their parent or caregiver's payment from the start of the pay period following the date the child left school or tertiary education.
## Family tax credit
When a child leaves school or tertiary education, family tax credits should be stopped from the day the child is excluded from the client's Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Child leaves sole parents care suddenly — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: When a child stops being a dependent child of a sole parent because of a sudden change of circumstances beyond the control of the client, payment of the benefit may continue at the existing rate for 28 days following the date the child stopped being dependent. This is to allow a period of transition for the client to adjust to their change in circumstances. For example when a child suddenly goes into the care of Oranga Tamariki, payment may continue for 28 days from the date the child is no longer dependent on the client. Extra help payments that can be continued for 28 days are: - Accommodation Supplement - Child Disability Allowance - Disability Allowance - Temporary Additional Support - Winter Energy Payment The exception is Childcare Assistance which must be stopped on the day after the client stopped caring for the dependent child. During the 28 days continuation of payment, if the client has other changes of circumstances such as a change in income, the rate of main benefit and extra help will need to be reassessed using sole parent threshold rates.

chunks.title: Mandatory Reviews — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Generally, clients getting Supported Living Payment must respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date or their payments will suspend. If a child leaves a sole parent's care suddenly and the client qualifies for Supported Living Payment after the 28-day continuation period, they may be able to get an extension if they need more time to respond to the Mandatory Review. If the client is unable to respond to the review (even if they had more time) based on their individual circumstances, they may qualify for an exemption. Generally, when the Mandatory Review is only for Supported Living Payment and the benefit will stop at the end of the continuation period e.g. if they are over the income limit, and the review is due, an exemption will apply. The client must contact MSD before their review date to discuss their situation if they need an extension or exemption.

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Generally, clients getting Supported Living Payment must respond to their notice before the child's 18th birthday or the child will be excluded from their payments. If Supported Living Payment and any extra help is continuing at the existing rate for up to 28 days because a child has left a sole parent's care suddenly, and that child turns 18 during that period, the client is not required to respond to the notice and the child will not be excluded during the continuation of payment period. However, if Supported Living Payment and any extra help is continuing at the existing rate for up to 28 days because a child has left a sole parent's care suddenly, and a different child in their care turns 18, the client must respond to the notice, or the 18-year-old will be excluded from their payments.

chunks.title: Client doesn't want to include a child — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Client doesn't want to include a child
In cases where the client has genuine concerns about including the child in their benefit (such as concerns about violence from the other parent) advise the client that all information contained in their benefit record is confidential.
If you have any concerns regarding the welfare of a child, the case should be referred to Oranga Tamariki.
## Deciding if a child is financially dependent
When a client states that they are getting payments for a child's expenses you must decide if the child is a dependent child of the client.
A child does not have to be solely financially dependent on a client to be considered a dependent child. All that is required is that the child is financially dependent on the person to some degree.
However, being financially dependent on a client is only part of the qualifications of a dependent child. The child must still meet all the qualifications to be considered dependent.
If another person or body is paying for the child's expenses, including payments for the care provided, the child is not financially dependent on the client.
If a client is receiving payments toward the expenses of a dependent child this is regarded as income for benefit purposes.

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Child turns 18
A dependent child must generally be under the age of 18 to be included in their parent or caregiver's Supported Living Payment.
When a child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and must be excluded from their parent or caregiver's Supported Living Payment from the start of the pay period following the child's 18th birthday.
However, if the 18-year-old child is continuing in education and is not financially independent, the child may continue to be considered a dependent child and be included in their parent or caregiver's Supported Living Payment for a limited period.
In these situations, the child must be excluded from the start of the pay period following:
- the date they no longer meet these criteria or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18
whichever is earlier

chunks.title: Clients caring for a person — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Clients caring for a person
Clients receiving Support Living Payment because they are caring for person who requires full-time care and attention can continue to receive Supported Living Payment for a maximum of 4 weeks while the patient is in some other person's care because the client has a health condition, injury or disability.
If the client's health condition is expected to last for more than 4 weeks, they will no longer qualify for Supported Living Payment - caring for a person. You will need to find out if the client qualifies for another benefit.
## Partner becomes sick
If a partner of someone receiving Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) has work obligations and they themselves have a health condition, an injury or a disability they may be exempt from meeting their work obligations until they are well again.
For more information see:
- Supported living payment Permanently and severely incapacitated for work

chunks.title: Surviving partner or dependent child — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Surviving partner or dependent child
When a client dies (and there is a surviving partner or dependent child) before a decision is made on an application or review for Supported Living Payment you can continue the application or review process as if the client had not died.
## Funeral Grant
In situations when the decision to grant or review Supported Living Payment is made after the date of death of the client, you decide any Funeral Grant as if the deceased client were getting Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Partner with child under 14 years old — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Partner with child under 14 years old
When a client dies and the surviving partner has a youngest dependent child aged under 14 years, the partner may be able to receive Sole Parent Support.
There is no initial stand-down when a partner applies for Jobseeker Support within 28 days of the client's death. When the partner applies 28 days after the death of the client, there will be an initial stand-down.
## Partner with child over 14 years old
If the partner has a dependent child 14 years old or over, they may be able to receive Jobseeker Support, with an exemption from their work obligations to allow them time to adjust to their new circumstances.
There is no initial stand-down when a partner applies for Jobseeker Support within 28 days of the client's death. When the partner applies 28 days after the death of the client, there will be an initial stand-down.
## Delay in granting ACC payments
When the death was the result of an accident, the surviving partner may be able to receive weekly compensation payments from ACC. If there will be a delay in deciding their claim, the partner can apply for a benefit they may qualify for while waiting. The client must acknowledge, in writing, that benefit payments made will be refunded once weekly compensation payments are granted from ACC.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment - caring for a person — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Supported Living Payment - caring for a person
When a client is donating a kidney or liver tissue they cannot keep getting Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).
When a client has been accepted as a kidney or liver tissue donor, transfer them to an Emergency Benefit.
## Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
When a client is donating a kidney or liver tissue they can keep getting their Supported Living Payment as they are permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, injury, disability or total blindness.
## Childcare Assistance
Clients may be eligible for Childcare Assistance payments while they are they are recovering.
For more information see:
- Childcare Subsidy Temporary illness
- OSCAR Temporary illness
Also see:
- Partner donates a kidney or liver tissue

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability)
A Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) client can be a full-time student without it affecting their eligibility for Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) but you must be satisfied that the client still meets the medical qualifications for Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability). See:
- Medical qualifications
If you consider that the client's capacity to undertake full-time study may indicate that the client's health condition has changed you will need to arrange a medical reassessment. See:
- Medical reassessment
## Part-time study
A Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) client can also be a part-time student without it affecting their eligibility for Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) but you must be satisfied that the client still meets the medical qualification for Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability).
If you consider that the client's ability to undertake part-time study may indicate that the client's health condition has changed you will need to arrange a medical reassessment for Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability).
## Supported Living Payment (caring for a person)
When a client starts part-time or full-time study you will need to determine if the client is still able to provide full-time care and attention for the person while undertaking the study. A client can be away from the home for a few hours per week. Provided arrangements for the patient's care have been made, accept that full-time care is being provided. See:
- Full-time care and attention
You will need to find out:
- the number of hours involved in studying (including reading, completion of assignments, exam preparation etc)
- whether the study is by correspondence or on site and
- the frequency and duration of alternative care arrangements
After considering these factors you must be satisfied that the number of hours involved still allows the client to provide full-time care and attention to the patient and may still qualify for Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).

chunks.title: Client is regularly working 15 or more hours a week — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Client is regularly working 15 or more hours a week
If a client is regularly working 15 hours or more a week in open employment they will no longer qualify for Supported Living Payment. The client is not severely restricted in their capacity for work.
## Exceptions
- clients who are totally blind are able to work 15 hours or more a week, without it affecting their qualification for Supported Living Payment
- clients undertaking an Sustainable Employment Trial with the prior agreement of their case manager
These clients can work 15 hours or more a week for an agreed period of up to 26 weeks, without it affecting their qualification for Supported Living Payment during the agreed period.
If a client is regularly working 15 hours or more a week in open employment, and the exceptions above do not apply, you will need to consider if the client qualifies for another benefit or invite the client to apply for non beneficiary assistance, and advise them of possible entitlement to Working for Families Tax Credits through Inland Revenue.
For more information see:
- Unclear if the client is regularly working 15 or more hours a week
- Sustainable Employment Trial
- Guidelines for regular employment
- Deciding entitlement for blind clients

chunks.title: Examples (but are not limited to) — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Examples (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A partner with work obligations on Supported Living Payment was out of New Zealand visiting his father in Australia. His Supported Living Payment was suspended the day after he left New Zealand as it wasn't an approved travel reason. The client contacts Work and Income three days later to say that his father is in hospital as he has had a heart attack. The client has been paid for five days in the previous 52 weeks while he was absent from New Zealand leaving a balance of 23 days.
The reason for travel now meets the criteria for approved travel. The benefit is resumed from the date the client became eligible to receive the benefit overseas. The client must contact Work and Income from overseas. The benefit cannot be back-dated if the client advises Work and Income when they return to New Zealand.
A partner receiving Supported Living Payment with work preparation but no activities assigned left New Zealand to visit her mother. Two days before she was due to return, her mother's house burnt down. The client has been paid for 20 days in the previous 52 weeks while she was absent from New Zealand leaving a balance of eight days.
The reason for travel has changed and the client has not been absent from New Zealand for up to 28 days in any 52 week period. The benefit expiry is extended for an additional five days.
This client can travel for any reason. If the client hadn't informed Work and Income, their benefit would continue to be paid up until the 29th day.
Note that where the client has already been absent for 28 days in a 52 week period, consider whether the client meets the criteria for receiving a payment for more than 28 days in any 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Client no longer entitled (health condition, injury or disability) — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Client no longer entitled (health condition, injury or disability)
Generally, when a client no longer qualifies for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability, their benefit can continue for 28 days.
Note the decision to decline or cancel Supported Living Payment on medical grounds can be appealed to the Medical Appeals Board.
Clients should be invited to apply for an alternative benefit. If the client wants to apply for Jobseeker Support on the ground of health condition, injury or disability, the client's application for Supported Living Payment should be treated as an application for Jobseeker Support.
Any alternative benefit can be granted after the 28-day extension to Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability has expired (that is, grant from the 29th day).
Note during the 28-day continuation of payment, if the client has other changes of circumstances, such as a change in income, the rate of main benefit and extra help will need to be reassessed accordingly.
## Mandatory reviews
Generally, clients getting Supported Living Payment must respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date or their payments will suspend.
However, when the Mandatory Review is only for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability and the benefit will stop at the end of the 28-day continuation period, and the review is due, an exemption will apply.
The client must contact MSD before their review date to discuss their situation if they need an exemption.
## Child turns 18
Generally, clients getting Supported Living Payment must respond to their notice before the child's 18th birthday or the child will be excluded from their payments.
However, when the client no longer qualifies for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability and the benefit will stop at the end of the 28-day continuation period, the client is not required to respond to the notice when a child turns 18 and the child will not be excluded during the continuation of payment period.

chunks.title: Client no longer qualifies — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Client no longer qualifies
Generally, when a client no longer qualifies for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability after a review of their health condition, they can continue to get Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability for 28 days after the decision to cancel Supported Living Payment has been made.
If a client qualifies for another benefit, they should be transferred after the 28 days extension has lapsed.
## Child turns 18
Generally, clients getting Supported Living Payment must respond to their notice before the child's 18th birthday or the child will be excluded from their payments.
However, when the client no longer qualifies for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability and the benefit will stop at the end of the 28-day continuation period, the client is not required to respond to the notice when that child turns 18 and the child will not be excluded during the continuation of payment period.
## Review and appeals
If a client no longer qualifies for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability because they do not meet the medical eligibility criteria they should be advised, including their right to review the decision. Medical decisions are reviewed by the Medical Appeals Board. Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability can continue to be paid for 28 days while the client is awaiting the decision to allow for a period of transition for the client to adjust to their change in circumstances. However, in no circumstances, can the benefit be paid for longer than 28 days.
If the Medical Appeal Board process takes longer than 28 days, where a client meets the eligibility criteria, the client may be granted Jobseeker Support (on the grounds of having a health condition, injury or disability) or another appropriate benefit. If after the appeal they were found to be eligible for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability they will have their benefit reviewed and any arrears paid to them.

chunks.title: Examples include (but are not limited to) — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Examples include (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A partner of someone receiving Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) with work preparation but no activities assigned left New Zealand for a holiday in Australia.
While she was in Australia there was severe flooding which meant she could not return to New Zealand on the day she was meant to return.
She contacts Work and Income. The client has been paid for 20 days in the previous 52 weeks while she was absent from New Zealand, leaving a balance of eight days.
The client cannot return due to circumstances that were not reasonably foreseeable and they were outside the client's control. Work and Income would extend the client's benefit for a reasonable period for her to be able to return.
This client can travel for any reason. If the client hadn't informed Work and Income, their benefit would continue to be paid up until the 29th day.
A client on Supported Living Payment who has work preparation activities assigned has been overseas for five days to attend his father's funeral.
He is delayed in Sydney due to fog. He must remain a further three days.
The client cannot return due to circumstances that were not reasonably foreseeable and they were outside the client's control.
Work and Income would extend the client's benefit for a reasonable period for him to be able to return. Also consider whether there is any grounds to pay for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Client obtains employment overseas — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Client obtains employment overseas
Where the client:
- is successful in their job prospect or job search overseas and
- they are not returning to New Zealand
the Supported Living Payment should be cancelled from the day after the interview or notice of job appointment.
If the client returns to New Zealand for the period between getting the job and actually starting employment, the Supported Living Payment can be continued until they leave the country.
The benefit must be cancelled from the day after they leave New Zealand to commence the job.

chunks.title: Client or partner remains in New Zealand — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Client or partner remains in New Zealand
Qualification for Supported Living Payment may be affected for a married, civil union or de facto couple when one of them remains in New Zealand. This will depend on whether:
- it is the primary client or their partner who remains in New Zealand and
- payment has been approved to continue if it is the primary client overseas
## Client remains in New Zealand
If the primary client remains in New Zealand, they will continue to receive the half married, civil union or de facto rate of Supported Living Payment. If the partner is receiving any income while overseas this must be charged against the benefit.
Note you must continue to treat the couple as married or in a civil union unless they are living apart with the intention of ending their marriage or civil union.
## Partner remains in New Zealand
If the partner remains in New Zealand, they can continue to receive the half married, civil union or de facto rate of Supported Living Payment as long as payment to the primary client has been approved and is continuing to be paid while they are overseas for up to 28 days.
If payment will not continue to the primary client, or has been stopped, the partner will no longer qualify to receive any payment. You will need to determine if the partner qualifies for another benefit in their own right, or they may be able to receive an Emergency Benefit.
For more information see:
- Emergency Benefit
Note the partner can only receive the half married, civil union or de facto rate of Supported Living Payment while the client is overseas, unless the couple are living apart with the intention of ending their marriage or civil union. If the primary client is receiving any income while overseas this must be charged against the benefit.
## Exception
However, there are some situations that allow Supported Living Payment client to be absent from New Zealand and continue to receive payment for a period of absence.
For details of these situations see:
- Approved travel reasons
- Overseas medical treatment

chunks.title: Client with work preparation activities assigned — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Client with work preparation activities assigned
A client receiving Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability) or Supported Living Payment (caring for a person) may have work preparation obligations assigned where they have capacity (excluding the base obligation to be take reasonable steps to prepare for work).
Where a client has work preparation activities assigned, they cannot receive their payment when they temporarily leave New Zealand unless they:
- have an approved travel reason
- are undertaking medical treatment overseas
- are overseas for vocational or disability assistance dog training (Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability only)
- are overseas to participate in the Special Olympics or Paralympics (Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability only)
For more information see:
- Approved travel reasons
- Overseas for medical treatment
- Overseas vocational or disability assistance dog training
- Special Olympics or Paralympics
- Supported Living Payment Work preparation obligations for primary client

chunks.title: Clients undertaking multiple Sustainable Employment Trials — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Clients undertaking multiple Sustainable Employment Trials
Supported Living Payment clients may undertake more than one Sustainable Employment Trial while on benefit, though not more than one Sustainable Employment Trial at the same time. A client may wish to conduct another Sustainable Employment Trial if they were unable to sustain the initial job, for instance:
- the initial job was unsuitable to their individual disability
- the client had a recurrence of an injury or illness requiring a break from employment
In making a decision whether or not to agree to another Sustainable Employment Trial in these circumstances, you must take into account a number of factors, including, if appropriate the reasons why the client ended a previous Sustainable Employment Trial. You should also consider whether the duties in the proposed Sustainable Employment Trial are different to those in the earlier Sustainable Employment Trial.
For more information see:
- Inappropriate use of Sustainable Employment Trial
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Clients who can take part — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Clients who can take part
The option of taking part in a Sustainable Employment Trial is available to any Supported Living Payment client whose benefit will be affected if they regularly work 15 hours or more.
The job must be in open employment, and be more than 15 hours per week. If the employment is for less than 15 hours a week it is not necessary for the client to take part in a Sustainable Employment Trial, as this is allowed under the Supported Living Payment qualifications.
Clients who can take part in a Sustainable Employment Trial include those who are self employed.
There is no restriction on how soon after being granted the Supported Living Payment a client can take part in a Sustainable Employment Trial. For some clients, this may be some time after grant; for others it may be sooner.
The Sustainable Employment Trial does not apply to Supported Living Payment clients if:
- they are not regularly working 15 hours or more per week
their employment does not affect their qualification
- the employment is of a particularly short-term nature
- they are receiving Supported Living Payment on the grounds of being totally blind
(these clients can already regularly work 15 hours or more without losing their entitlement to Supported Living Payment)
- their job is in sheltered employment
if they move into a job in open employment, they can request to take part in a Sustainable Employment Trial
- the position is unpaid (for example voluntary work or work experience)
Note you can only agree to a client's request to take part in a Sustainable Employment Trial once they have a job or a firm offer of employment. However, where appropriate you should still discuss the Sustainable Employment Trial process with the client and invite them to look for employment.
For more information see:
- Already in employment -Work and Income advised
- Already in employment -Work and Income not advised
- Clients undertaking multiple Sustainable Employment Trials
- Inappropriate use of Sustainable Employment Trial
- Suitability of Sustainable Employment Trial
- Start date of Sustainable Employment Trial
- Sheltered employment

chunks.title: Clients who do not have work preparation activities — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Clients who do not have work preparation activities
A client receiving Supported Living Payment can continue to receive their payment when they temporarily leave New Zealand for up to 28 days in any 52 week period if:
- the benefit would continue to be paid except for them having left New Zealand
- the absences do not affect the client's eligibility for the benefit
- they have notified Work and Income in advance of their intention of temporarily leaving New Zealand

chunks.title: Clients with a partner — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Clients with a partner
When a married, civil union or de facto client is imprisoned the Supported Living Payment will generally need to be cancelled. The partner may be granted a benefit in their own right (if required).
The Supported Living Payment should be cancelled from the day following imprisonment.
## Partner of client imprisoned
If the partner of a client is imprisoned the Supported Living Payment can continue provided the primary client continues to meet the eligibility criteria for the benefit. They must either be:
- permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work or
- caring for someone who would otherwise require hospital level care
Depending on the client's family circumstances, they can receive the single or sole parent rate.
## Exception
There is discretion to pay all or part of the Supported Living Payment to the partner of the person who has been imprisoned. This will depend on the length of time imprisoned. Where the length of imprisonment is short, using discretion to continue to pay the benefit prevents having to re-grant the benefit.
There is also discretion to continue payment if the client is remanded in custody pending a further court appearance. For example, this may be considered where the client may end up receiving a sentence of home detention and needing to have the benefit re-granted to the couple anyway.
For more information to help you decide see:
- Decision guidelines - clients with a partner
- Remanded in custody
- Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital

chunks.title: Contacting Work and Income as soon as the client reasonably can — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Contacting Work and Income as soon as the client reasonably can
A client who leaves New Zealand without advising Work and Income of their travel can only have their benefit backdated to the day after their departure date if they contact Work and Income as soon as they could reasonably have been expected to, given the circumstances.
This may be while the client is still absent from New Zealand, or once they have returned.
For more information see:
- Backdating benefit to day after departure date
## Determining reasonable contact time
In order to determine whether a client contacted Work and Income as soon as they could reasonably have been expected to, you need to take into account the circumstances of the client.
