The reason why the client did not contact Work and Income until after returning to New Zealand may be the same reason why they left New Zealand without advising Work and Income of their absence, or a different humanitarian reason.
Reasons for not contacting Work and Income sooner may include (but are not limited to) that the client:
- did not contact Work and Income due to the stress of the event that led to them leaving New Zealand without informing Work and Income
- left with a humanitarian reason, and then could not access the technology to communicate with Work and Income while absent from New Zealand
- left for a humanitarian reason, and then was temporarily medically unfit while overseas and they have a medical certificate that shows this
- left for a humanitarian reason, and then had a death or illness in the immediate family while overseas or on return to New Zealand, and/or
- left for a humanitarian reason, and then experienced an adverse event or natural disaster while overseas or on return to New Zealand that meant they were unable to contact Work and Income
## Contacting Work and Income on return to New Zealand
Generally, it would be reasonable to expect a client to contact Work and Income within 10 working days of returning to New Zealand. However, you should consider whether the client's circumstances meant they were unable to inform Work and Income in this period.
For more information see:
- Approved travel reasons
- Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure
- Clients with work preparation activities assigned
- Partner with work or work preparation obligations or an exemption
- Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy

chunks.title: Date payment should be reduced — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Date payment should be reduced
The hospital rate is paid when the client has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks, not after getting a benefit for 13 weeks. Reduce the client's benefit to the hospital rate or appropriate higher rate from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation.
## SWIFTT
Add the client's admission date on the SHODA screen in SWIFTT.
SWIFTT will automatically reduce the rate of payment to the hospital rate from the beginning of the 14th week after the admission date.
## Client formally discharged
If the client has been formally discharged from the hospital and then re-admitted, the 13 week calculation starts again from the day after they are re-admitted (even if the client has been re-admitted within 28 days of being discharged).

chunks.title: Couples — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Couples
When a dependent child dies, the child should be excluded from a couple's Supported Living Payment from the beginning of the next pay period following the date of the child's death.
## Sole parents
When a dependent child dies they should be excluded from a sole parent's Supported Living Payment 28 days following the date of the child's death.
Payment of the benefit may continue at the existing rate for 28 days following the date the child died. This is to allow a period of transition for the client to adjust to their change in circumstances.
## Mandatory Reviews
Clients must still respond to a Mandatory Review for Supported Living Payment during the 28-day continuation of payment. They may be able to get an extension or an exemption.
Note if the client has other changes of circumstances such as a change of income, the rate of any benefit will need to be reassessed using the sole parent threshold rates.
## Child turns 18
Generally, clients getting Supported Living Payment must respond to their notice before the child's 18th birthday or the child will be excluded from their payments.
If Supported Living Payment and any extra help is continuing at the existing rate for up to 28 days because the sole parent's child has died, and that child turns 18 during that period, the child will not be excluded, and the client is not required to respond to the notice during the continuation of payment period.
However, if Supported Living Payment and any extra help is continuing at the existing rate for up to 28 days because the sole parent's child has died and a different child in their care turns 18, the client must respond to the notice, or the 18-year-old will be excluded from their payments.
## Best Start tax credit
Best Start tax credit is paid for 28 days following the child's date of death.
Note if the child's third birthday is in the 28-day period the Best Start tax credit automatically stops from the date of the child's third birthday.

chunks.title: Mandatory Reviews — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Mandatory Reviews
There are no Mandatory Reviews of Supported Living Payment when the client has died.
## Child turns 18
A child will not be excluded from the parent or caregiver's Supported Living Payment when the child turns 18 during the terminal benefit period.

chunks.title: Death of a client with a partner or child — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Supported Living Payment can continue to be paid for 28 days after the death of a client when there is a surviving partner or child, and the surviving partner is not entitled to a survivor's grant from ACC. Supported Living Payment can also continue to be paid for 28 days after the death of a single client who is a: - liable person and paying Child Support payments or - caregiver getting Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit Continuing payments after the date of death is known as a terminal benefit. When terminal benefit is being paid to a couple, both the deceased person and the surviving person's portion of the benefit continues to be paid. The total benefit, including the surviving person's portion, plus any ongoing extra help continues for 28 days.

chunks.title: Surviving person will get more money on other assistance — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Sometimes the surviving partner or the caregiver of the child would get more money (based on their new circumstances) on: - a new main benefit or - their existing benefit at a higher rate instead of getting their portion of their current assistance for 28 days.

chunks.title: New benefit paid at higher rate — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: If the surviving person's benefit is reviewed and they qualify for a new benefit at a higher rate, they may be granted the new benefit instead of terminal benefit from the day after a client's death. If the deceased person qualified for a terminal benefit their portion will continue to be paid.

chunks.title: Current benefit at a higher rate — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: If the surviving person's current benefit is reviewed and they qualify for a higher rate, their benefit rate increases from the day after their partner's death. MSD pays this instead of their portion of the terminal benefit as they will get more money. If the deceased person qualified for a terminal benefit their portion will continue to be paid.

chunks.title: Surviving person is entitled to survivor's grant from ACC — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: When the death of the person was the result of an accident, entitlement to a survivor's grant from ACC needs to be decided before terminal benefit can be paid. If the surviving person or child is entitled to a survivor's grant from ACC there is no entitlement to terminal benefit. If Supported Living Payment payments have continued after the date of death, an overpayment is established and the debt should be recovered from the estate.

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: A child will not be excluded from the parent or caregiver's Supported Living Payment when the child turns 18 during the 28-day continuation of payment.

chunks.title: Death of a single client — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Death of a single client
When a single client (with no children) dies, benefit payment generally stops from the day after the date of death, but there is some discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days.
Payment should stop from the first available date if we have been notified within 28 days of the date of death. This will avoid creating a debt.
Where there are other circumstances that justify payment of terminal benefit, payment should continue for the full 28 days after death.
Note a single client who is a liable person and paying Child Support payments, or a caregiver getting Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit is regarded as having children.

chunks.title: Deciding if surviving person would be better off getting terminal benefit or a new benefit — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Deciding if surviving person would be better off getting terminal benefit or a new benefit
Terminal benefit is paid for 28 days when a client dies and has a surviving partner and/or children.
When the benefit is being paid to a couple, both the deceased person and the surviving person’s portion of the benefit is paid. Payment is the total benefit including any ongoing Extra help. It does not include family tax credit and Best Start tax credit.
Sometimes the surviving person or the caregiver of the child/children would get more money (based on their new circumstances) on a new benefit or their existing benefit at a higher rate, instead of their portion of their current assistance for 28 days.
Compare the surviving person’s potential new benefit and any ongoing Extra help (from the date after death) against the surviving person’s portion of benefit and ongoing Extra help they were getting before their partner’s death.
Generally, the surviving person will get more money if they change to a single rate of benefit.
If the deceased person qualified for terminal benefit, their portion will continue to be paid to their bank account.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Decision guidelines - clients with a partner — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Decision guidelines - clients with a partner
While Supported Living Payment should generally be stopped when the primary client is imprisoned, there is discretion for payment to be continued and paid to the partner not in prison. This discretion allows payment of all or part of the Supported Living Payment to the partner.
If you feel that payment should be continued, and paid to the partner, this should generally be at the single or sole parent rate. However, you can pay the full married, civil union or de facto rate if you feel this is warranted after having regard to the particular circumstances of the client and their partner.
To help you decide whether it is reasonable to pay the Supported Living Payment to the partner while the client is in prison, and the rate to pay, you should consider the following:
- has the period in prison already passed
- is the client due to be released from prison shortly
- is the likely period in prison less than six months
- does the partner qualify for a statutory benefit in their own right
- do they intend to live together when the partner is released
- has the partner in prison applied for Home Detention
- are there exceptional circumstances that justify paying the full married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit to the partner who is not in prison
For further help you can contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances before you make your decision.

chunks.title: Decision guidelines - sole parents — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Decision guidelines - sole parents
When a sole parent Supported Living Payment client is imprisoned it is important that financial assistance is available to support any dependent children and that the patient is receiving full-time care and attention for Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).
While Supported Living Payment should generally be stopped when the client is imprisoned, there is discretion for payment to be continued and paid to the person who is caring for the client's dependent children and the patient for Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).
To help you decide whether it is reasonable to pay the Supported Living Payment while the client is in prison, you should consider the following:
- has the period in prison already passed
- is the client due to be released from prison shortly
- is the likely period in prison less than twelve months
- will the children return to the client's care on their release from prison
- has the temporary caregiver ceased work to care for the children and patient (for Supported Living Payment - caring for a person)
- has the temporary caregiver lost entitlement to their own benefit due to having to care for the children and patient (for Supported Living Payment - caring for a person)
For further help you can contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances before you make your decision.
For more information see:
- Temporary caregiver
- Rate of payment - sole parents
- Examples - sole parents
- Remanded in custody
- Sole parents

chunks.title: Definition of 'support' from a family member residing overseas — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Definition of 'support' from a family member residing overseas
'Support' means assistance that the young person could not reasonably obtain from a family member in New Zealand, and includes (but are not limited to):
- emotional support
- educational support
- mentoring/guidance
- any other assistance that is beneficial to the welfare of the young person.
Note in assessing whether the young person could not reasonably obtain the support from a family member in New Zealand, you should consider:
- the type and nature of the relationship with the family member residing overseas
- whether there are features of the young person's relationship with that family member that are absent from their relationships with other family members residing in New Zealand (such as shared experiences and the nature of the relationship).

chunks.title: Dependent child — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
A dependent child for Supported Living Payment is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Supported Living Payment does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- child for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
## Primary responsibility
The client must be responsible for the day-to-day care of the child and be the person who makes the major decisions concerning the child's life (for example schooling and health).
There are some situations when the person has principal responsibility of a child is not clear.
## Maintained as a member of the family
The child should be integral part of the family, participating in the usual family activities (for example family outings and holidays).
In some situations, a child may not be living at home but is still considered to be a dependent child.
Dependent children should be included in the assessment of Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Continuing dependent partner's portion of benefit — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: When the partner of a Supported Living Payment client dies, the partner's portion of the benefit is continued for 28 days at the same rate that was being paid on the date their partner died. Benefit payments that continue after the day a client has died are called 'terminal benefit'.

chunks.title: Dependent children — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: When there are dependent children included in the benefit, family tax credit and Best Start tax credit payments should be transferred to the primary client. Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit payments are not part of the terminal benefit. A surviving partner with dependent children, can choose to remain on Supported Living Payment if they can meet the medical qualifications. If they do not meet the medical qualifications they may transfer to Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support, depending on the age of their youngest dependent child. Payment if from the date after the death of their partner. It is important that the different entitlements of Supported Living Payment, Jobseeker Support and Sole Parent Support are explained to the client so they can make the best decision for their circumstances.

chunks.title: No dependent children — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: A surviving client, with no dependent children, can choose to remain on Supported Living Payment if they meet the medical qualifications. If they do not meet the medical qualifications they may need to transfer to Jobseeker Support. Note if a client transfers to Jobseeker Support they can be exempt from meeting their work obligations to allow them time to adjust to their new circumstances.

chunks.title: Date of review — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: When the surviving client remains on Supported Living Payment, review the client's benefit from the date following the death of their partner. You need to: - increase their benefit to the single or sole parent rate and - adjust any Extra help to the single or sole parent rate When the client applies for (and is granted) Sole Parent Support or Jobseeker Support, cancel their Supported Living Payment from the day after the death of their partner. Note when the surviving client decides to receive a new main benefit or their existing benefit at the increased rate, the deceased partner’s portion of the benefit continues for 28 days at the rate being paid at the date of death (if the deceased person qualifies for terminal benefit).

chunks.title: Funeral costs — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: The person responsible for the cost of the funeral may be able to receive a Funeral Grant. For more information see: - Best Start tax credit Main benefit clients dies - Terminal benefit - Deciding if surviving person is better off getting terminal benefit or a new benefit

chunks.title: Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital
When person who has been remanded in custody or is serving a term of imprisonment, is detained in or transferred to a psychiatric hospital you may be able to pay an Emergency Benefit at the hospital rate.
People who are remanded in custody or serving a term of imprisonment who are temporarily hospitalised for treatment of an injury or health condition are still considered to be in prison and the Department of Corrections will meet their costs. An Emergency Benefit or any other financial assistance cannot be paid.
For more information see:
- Emergency Benefit Person serving their sentence of imprisonment in a psychiatric hospital
- Release from prison

chunks.title: Discharged from Oranga Tamariki care — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Discharged from Oranga Tamariki care
Where Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency has care, custody or sole guardianship of the child, and returns the child to the care of the immediate previous caregiver, they do not make payments for the child.
The child is then a dependent child and can be included in the Supported Living Payment.
Where the relationship is not one of care, but more of a boarding arrangement, the young person may be able to receive Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment.
Once a child has been discharged from care the child can be considered a dependent child even when Oranga Tamariki or any other authorised agency involvement continues, for example:
- Additional Guardianship Order
- Support Order or
- Services Order
When there is a Service or Support Order in place, you will need to make sure that the Court's intent allows you to consider the child as a dependent child.
For further details on what discharged from care means see:
- Definition of discharged from Oranga Tamariki care

chunks.title: Effect on benefit — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Effect on benefit
Any inclusion or exclusion of a dependent child from a client's benefit will result in a general review of the client's Supported Living Payment and any extra help they are getting.
You may need to review the following:
- the rate of Supported Living Payment, you will need to review the rate payable if the child being excluded is the client's last or only dependent child
- Supported Living PaymentPartner's obligations may change.
- Accommodation SupplementChanges to the family composition may result in a change to the Accommodation Supplement entry thresholds.
- Non-standard benefit rateWhere a child is added or removed you may need to manually adjust the non-standard rate of payment.
- Special BenefitAny change to family circumstances will result in a review of Special Benefit. A child included or excluded from the Supported Living Payment may result in a change to the allowable costs for Special Benefit.
- Temporary Additional SupportAny change to family circumstances will result in a review of Temporary Additional Support. A child included or excluded from the Supported Living Payment may result in a change to the allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support.
- Disability Allowance

chunks.title: Accommodation Supplement — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Accommodation Supplement
For a single client stop the Accommodation Supplement from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation. Check whether the client still has to meet their continuing accommodation costs. If so, increase the benefit rate above the hospital rate to meet the costs.
For a married, civil union or de facto client (without dependent children) you still treat the couple as married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and take into account the income and assets of both. You can pay the full Accommodation Supplement to the partner not in hospital.
For more information see:
- Accommodation Supplement
## Temporary Additional Support
For a single client stop Temporary Additional Support from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation. Check whether the client still has to meet their continuing costs. If so, increase the benefit rate above the hospital rate to meet the costs.
For a married, civil union or de facto couple Temporary Additional Support must be stopped from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation for the client who is in hospital. From the same date you will need to review Temporary Additional Support and pay the full amount to the partner not in hospital.
No additional costs associated with the hospitalisation should be added to Temporary Additional Support for a married, civil union or de facto client. However you will need to have regard to their individual circumstances taking into consideration that the partner not in hospital is increased to the single rate of payment and can receive Special Disability Allowance to cover any extra costs.
## Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit
As long as the child continues to be a dependent child, family tax credit and best start payments continue to be paid regardless of how long the client is in hospital. Best Start tax credit will stop from the child’s third birthday.

chunks.title: Employment — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Employment
Clients must advise Work and Income of any change in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Supported Living Payment or the rate of benefit, such as commencing employment.
When a client is placed into work or starts working you will need to determine whether they still meet the medical qualification for Supported Living Payment.
If a client is regularly working 15 hours or more a week in open employment they will no longer qualify for Supported Living Payment. The client is not severely restricted in their capacity for work. Open employment is any employment other than sheltered employment.
## Exceptions
- clients who are totally blind are able to work 15 hours or more a week, without it affecting their qualification for Supported Living Payment
- clients undertaking an Sustainable Employment Trial with the prior agreement of their case manager
These clients can work 15 hours or more a week for an agreed period of up to 26 weeks, without it affecting their qualification for Supported Living Payment during the agreed period.
There is no set definition of what is regular but there are guidelines available to help you determine regular employment of 15 hours or more a week.
For help to decide when to cancel the benefit when a client commences regular work of 15 hours or more see:
- Guidelines for regular employment

chunks.title: Employment and training services — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Employment and training services
Open employment for employment programmes and services is different from open employment for Supported Living Payment purposes.
The definition of open employment for employment programmes and services is governed by the Social Security Act 2018. In the context of support for people with ill health and disabilities, open employment is a job available to anyone in the community who has an employment agreement attached as defined in the Employment Relations Act 2000.
This means that a client who is considered to be working in sheltered employment for Supported Living Payment purposes may also be considered to be working in open employment for employment programmes or services assistance.
## Example of a severely disabled client in open employment
A leading NZ freight company has advertised a position for a store person. John, who is severely disabled and was receiving Supported Living Payment, applied for and was successfully appointed as their new store person.
Because of John's disability, his new employer has substantially changed the working conditions to accommodate John.
In this situation, the degree of change to the conditions of John's employment means we can accept employment is sheltered for the purposes of John's entitlement to Supported Living Payment.
In addition, because the position has been advertised in the open market, the job is considered to be open employment. This means Work and Income can also consider programmes and services and financial assistance for clients with severe disabilities to achieve unsubsidised and sustainable employment.
For more information see:
- Deskfile Approved Business Enterprises
- Employment and training Clients who have a health condition, injury or disability
Legislation
- sheltered employment (definition) schedule 2 Social Security Act 2018
- open employment (definition) schedule 2 Social Security Act 2018

chunks.title: End of Sustainable Employment Trial — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## End of Sustainable Employment Trial
The client needs to be informed of the possible outcomes that will be available at the end of the Sustainable Employment Trial period.
At the end of a Sustainable Employment Trial, a number of different outcomes for the client are possible.
These may include the following:
- the client ceases employment
- investigate the reasons the client ceased employment and if there are no obvious barriers then you should consider whether the client still meets the qualifications for Supported Living Payment.
- the client wishes to reduce their hours to below 15 hours a week
eg they cannot sustain the 15 hours or more due to their illness or disability
- the client cannot sustain the job and wishes to try a different job with different duties, either with the same or a new employer
- the client continues to regularly work 15 or more hours a week, therefore they no longer meet the qualifications for Supported Living Payment.
the client's Supported Living Payment should be cancelled; check their eligibility to other assistance. If the client disagrees with your decision to cancel their benefit, they can review the decision.
For more information see:
- Employment and training Employment Transition Assistance

chunks.title: Ending payment for client who can travel for any reason (within 28 day maximum) — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Ending payment for client who can travel for any reason (within 28 day maximum)
Where a client or partner can travel for any reason their payments will suspend automatically on the 29th day in a 52 week period they have been absent from New Zealand and continued to receive a payment.
## Client or partner may need to be absent for more than 28 days
A client or partner may be required to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days.
For more information see:
- Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
- Ending payments for client who needs an approved reason to travel
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Ending payment for client who needs an approved reason to travel (within 28 day maximum) — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Ending payment for client who needs an approved reason to travel (within 28 day maximum)
Where a client (with work preparation activities assigned) or partner (with work obligations or work preparation activities assigned) is receiving their payments while they are absent from New Zealand for an approved reason their payments will suspend automatically on their agreed return date.
For example, a client has been approved travel to attend a job interview in Sydney. They are approved three days. The benefit will suspend automatically on the day they were meant to return.
Where the client or partner is receiving their payments while they are absent from New Zealand because they have an approved travel reason and their return date changes, they must advise Work and Income from overseas, otherwise their payment will be stopped from the day they originally advised they would return to New Zealand.
## Benefit can be backdated once back in New Zealand in very limited circumstances
A client who is continuing to be paid while they are absent from New Zealand for an approved reason may be able to have their benefit backdated if there is an unforeseen reason they cannot notify Work and Income while they are overseas.
For example, a client boards a plane to return home on schedule and the plane is held up due to fog. There is no way the client could notify Work and Income due to an event outside of their control. When the client contacts Work and Income once they are back in New Zealand, their benefit would be resumed from the original date they were due to return (this will be on the itinerary or e-ticket).
For more information see:
- Approved travel reasons
- Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Essential travel — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Essential travel
A client not otherwise entitled to be paid their Supported Living Payment while they are absent from New Zealand may have their payments continue for up to 28 days in any 52 week period if they have to travel outside of New Zealand to attend a significant event relating to a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family).
These events are ones which the client or partner would reasonably be expected to attend. That is, the travel is essential to them and where not attending the event would cause the person emotional distress. This may include, but is not limited to, travel that allows the client to:
- be with a seriously ill or dying person who is a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family)
- attend a funeral or an unveiling in relation to a family member
- pay respect to a family member of the deceased in the event of the client missing the funeral
- attend to legal matters in relation to the affairs of the deceased family member
- attend a birth of a family member or be with a family member around the time of their giving birth
- provide support to a party or witness to a court case
- attend a wedding of a family member - the client does not need to be a member of the bridal party or play a significant part in the wedding in order for the payment of benefit to continue while they are absent from New Zealand
- travel for a court ordered custody arrangement
For more information see:
- Definition of family member
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect
- Permitted travel reasons
- Absences that do not prevent partner meeting their obligations
- Paying benefit when client failed to advise of absence
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within a 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: The following examples show situations where a benefit may be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period (but are not limited to): Client's reason for travelling for 28 days within 52 week period Client's current reason for travel within 52 week period Outcome Essential travel reasons Essential travel reason eg a seriously ill family member Generally consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if reasonable in the circumstances Job interview or job prospect Essential travel reason eg a funeral Generally would consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if reasonable in the circumstances Travelled for a holiday Travel for a holiday This is not an approved reason for paying for more than 28 days in a 52 week period Partners of Supported Living Payment with work obligations, or work-preparation obligations or youth activity obligations to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with these obligations. The client wishes to be absent from New Zealand for another general holiday This is not an approved reason for paying for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. The client would not be able to receive a benefit while absent from New Zealand for this reason even if the travel will not prevent them meeting their obligations (eg even if they had further annual leave from their employment or for partners even if the travel is at a time when they are not required to be in education, training or work-based learning) Partners of Supported Living Payment with work obligations or work-preparation obligations or youth activity obligations to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with these obligations. To provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster or similar adverse event. Generally would allow further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. This is an unforeseen event and it is reasonable for them to help their family member. Partners of Supported Living Payment with work obligations or work-preparation obligations or youth activity obligations to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with these obligations. Essential travel reason Generally would consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if the essential travel reason was unforeseen. Partners of Supported Living Payment with work obligations or work-preparation obligations or youth activity obligations to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with these obligations. Needs to attend a wedding of a family member.

chunks.title: Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Generally would not consider allowing a further period of payment for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. Weddings are usually known about in advance and this should have been planned for when they used the 28 days to go on holiday. However, where the wedding is genuinely unforeseen, consideration could be given to allowing travel for a period of more than 28 days in a 52 week period. Partners of Supported Living Payment with work obligations or work-preparation obligations or youth activity obligations had to spend four days at a funeral overseas. The partner had booked a holiday prior to the attendance at the funeral overseas. This holiday was booked for 28 days because they are able to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with their obligations. The client does not have the full 28 days left Travelling for a general holiday is not an approved reason for paying a benefit for more than 28 days in a 52 week period The benefit will only be paid for the number of days the client has available (that is, 24 days).

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Carlos contacts MSD on 19 November to advise that he has returned from travelling to Malaysia to be with his dying mother. He left in a hurry and didn't contact MSD before his departure. His Supported Living Payment stopped on 4 November, the day after he left the country. He returned to New Zealand on 14 November, but then had to organise a New Zealand-based funeral for his mother, as a large number of people are based in New Zealand. Carlos didn't advise MSD of his travel before leaving New Zealand, but he has a humanitarian reason that justifies his for travel and the reason he didn't contact MSD before he left. Given Carlos' circumstances, he contacted MSD as soon as it would have been reasonable to expect him to and he meets the criteria for an approved travel reason. Carlos' Supported Living Payment can be backdated to 4 November.

chunks.title: Example 2 — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Sanjay left New Zealand for India on 7 December because his father had become suddenly seriously ill and been hospitalised. While in India, Sanjay's father passed away and Sanjay stayed in India for the funeral. Sanjay returned on 16 December, after staying for 2 weeks for the Hindu funeral and mourning period. On 19 December, Sanjay contacts MSD to explain that he has been overseas after learning of his father's sudden illness, and that he stayed for the funeral. On return, Sanjay spent time mourning with his own family and has been distraught. He explains that he only realised on last night that he had not informed MSD of his absence. Sanjay's reason for leaving New Zealand is a humanitarian reason and he meets the criteria for backdating his payment to the day after his departure. Given Sanjay's circumstances, he informed MSD as soon as he reasonably could. Sanjay's Supported Living Payment can be backdated to 8 December, the date it was suspended.

chunks.title: Example 3 — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Tusila is getting Supported Living Payment for caring for a person, On 5 October Tuslia calls MSD to tell them she will leave New Zealand on 7 October to help her sister, who just lost her house in a flood. When asked how long she will be gone for, Tusila says that she hasn't bought a return ticket yet and was considering staying on to catch up with family and see how her sister is going. MSD informs Tusila that she can only keep getting her Supported Living Payment while overseas for 28 days within a 52 week period. Tusila decides she will return on 14 October in order not to use up all of her overseas travel time.

chunks.title: Example 4 — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Tobias left New Zealand on 16 August for a holiday. He returns 20 days later on 5 September. 3 weeks after he returned, on 27 September, Tobias asks MSD why he hasn't been getting his Supported Living Payment. MSD informs him his Supported Living Payment was stopped when he left New Zealand because he did not tell MSD about his travel, and asks if there was a reason why he didn't tell MSD before he left. Tobias says he just hadn't got around to contacting MSD since he got back. MSD restarts Tobias' payment from 27 September, as it is more than 14 days after Tobias' return date.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Example 1
A client applies for benefit to be paid for 10 days when they are going to be absent from New Zealand. In the past 52 weeks the client had 10 days absence from New Zealand and continued being paid their benefit.
Step
Calculation
Identify the day after the client is intending to leave New Zealand.
14 September 2019
Count back 52 weeks from this date.
15 September 2018
Count the number of days the client has continued getting their benefit while they were overseas in this 52 week period.
Days client has continued to receive their benefit while absent from New Zealand between 14 September 2018 and 15 September 2019 = 10 days
Subtract the number of days the client was paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand from 28 days.
28 - 10 days = 18 days available
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay the client for the days they have available.
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay them for the 10 days they are out of the country.
## Example 2
A client applies for benefit to be paid for 10 days when they is going are be absent from New Zealand. In the past 52 weeks the client had 20 days absence from New Zealand and continued being paid their benefit
Step
Calculation
Identify the day after the client is intending to leave New Zealand.
14 September 2019
Count back 52 weeks from this date.
15 September 2018
Count the number of days the client has continued getting their benefit while they were overseas in this 52 week period.
Days client continued getting their benefit while absent from NZ between 14 September 2018 and 15 September 2019 = 20 days
Subtract the number of days the client was paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand from 28 days.
28 - 20 days = 8 days available
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay the client for the days they have available.
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay them for the 8 days they are out of the country. For 2 of the days they are absent from New Zealand they will not get their payments.
Check if the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit for more than 28 days in a 52 week period - if they meet these criteria, they may be able to continue getting their payment for the additional 2 days of absence.

chunks.title: Examples of job interviews and prospects overseas — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: This partner can continue to be paid their Supported Living Payment for the three days while they are absent from New Zealand. A partner advises they are heading to the Gold Coast to 'look for work' and undertake job search. They do not have a job interview or a specific job prospect. Their aim is to undertake general job search and go and see a few employers which they will find when they get there. This provision cannot be used to allow general job search overseas and the client will not be able to continue to receive payment if they are absent from New Zealand for this reason.

chunks.title: Examples of Mandatory Review outcomes — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: MSD must review a client's Supported Living Payment within 52 weeks of the commencement date of their benefit, or 52 weeks from when the client's last Mandatory Review was completed. The Mandatory Review is completed when MSD has determined if the client continues to qualify for Supported Living Payment and the rate payable (if applicable). When a client responds to the review, there are a number of outcomes that can occur. Once MSD has determined if the client qualifies, MSD will either: - continue paying the benefit at the existing rate - adjust the rate of benefit so the client is getting the correct rate - suspend the benefit if there is no rate payable for a period (e.g. partner has variable income) - cancel the benefit if the client no longer qualifies

chunks.title: Examples of outcomes that can occur — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Outcomes of a Mandatory Review Examples Client declares no change (exception doesn't apply) Kevin is getting Supported Living Payment as a sole parent with 1 dependent child. Kevin's Mandatory Review is due on 30 September 2026. Kevin responds to his Mandatory Review on 25 September. Kevin confirms he has had no change in circumstances. Because Kevin has told MSD there has been no change in his circumstances and an exception doesn't apply, MSD must continue Kevin's Supported Living Payment at the same rate. MSD completes Kevin's Mandatory Review on 25 September and sets the next review date for 52 weeks later (24 September 2027). Client declares no change (exception applies) Joshua is getting Supported Living Payment, Accommodation Supplement and Disability Allowance and pays rent of $350.00 per week in Area 1. His Mandatory Review is due on 9 June 2027, and he responds on 7 June 2027 to confirm he has had no change in his circumstances. While his Disability Allowance costs were updated last year, he hasn't declared a change in rent since January 2024. Because Joshua has been getting Accommodation Supplement and declared no change in his accommodation costs for three consecutive years, MSD must consider whether further information is required before completing the Mandatory Review. MSD considers Joshua's circumstances and sees that he hasn't provided verification of his accommodation costs since moving to his current apartment in 2024. Given Joshua lives in an area where rental accommodation is very limited and rents have increased significantly, MSD determines that it is reasonable to request verification of his accommodation costs to confirm that the information is correct before making a decision about his entitlement. Joshua is asked to provide this information before 7 July 2027 (his new deadline for the review) or his Supported Living Payment, Accommodation Supplement and Disability Allowance will stop. Joshua contacts MSD on 1 July 2027 with the evidence requested. MSD determines that Joshua's circumstances have changed as his rent increased in January 2027. MSD adjusts the rate of payment for Accommodation Supplement and exercises discretion to backdate the payment to the date of the increase in costs, and continues Supported Living Payment and Disability Allowance at the same rate. MSD completes Joshua's Mandatory Review on 1 July 2027 and his next Mandatory Review date is set for 52 weeks in the future on 29 June 2028. Client declares a change in circumstances Julie is getting Supported Living Payment as a single person with no dependent children.

chunks.title: Examples of outcomes that can occur — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Julie's Mandatory Review is due on 8 February 2027. Julie responds to the Mandatory Review on 4 February and tells MSD that from 1 February 2027 she has been working part time at 6 hours per week earning $190.00 (before tax). Because Julie is working less than 15 hours per week, and her income is below the income cut-out point, MSD determines that Julie is still eligible for Supported Living Payment. MSD reassesses Julie's benefit and her rate of Supported Living Payment decreases from 1 February 2027. MSD completes the Mandatory Review on 4 February 2027 and sets Julie's next review date for 52 weeks later (3 February 2028). Mandatory Review is not completed, and benefit suspends Chanelle is getting Supported Living Payment as a single person with no dependent children. Chanelle's Mandatory Review is due on 17 May 2027. However, Chanelle does not respond to the Mandatory Review before her review date and her Supported Living Payment suspends on 17 May 2027. Chanelle does not contact MSD or respond to the Mandatory Review for 8 weeks after her Supported Living Payment suspended. Because Chanelle didn't respond during the 8 weeks after her benefit was suspended, her Supported Living Payment is cancelled from 17 May 2027 (the date her benefit originally suspended). Not enough information to complete Mandatory Review Alan is getting Supported Living Payment as a sole parent. Alan's Mandatory Review is due on 16 April 2027. Alan responds to the Mandatory Review on 14 April and tells MSD he is in a de facto relationship and lives with his partner. Alan has declared a change that affects his Supported Living Payment. However, MSD does not have enough information to determine if Alan is getting the right rate of benefit as he has not said when he entered into a relationship or provided any income details for his partner. MSD cannot complete the Mandatory Review without requesting more information from Alan. MSD sets a new reasonable deadline for Alan to provide the information by 23 April 2027. Alan's Supported Living Payment continues to be paid during this time. If Alan does not provide the further information before 23 April, their Supported Living Payment will suspend on this date. Alan does not provide the information requested by MSD before the new deadline and Alan's Supported Living Payment suspends on 23 April.

chunks.title: Examples of outcomes that can occur — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Alan provides the information about his partner on 26 April, confirming that they do not earn any income, and that their relationship started on 12 April. On 26 April MSD includes Alan's partner in his SLP and changes the rate of payment to a de facto couple rate from 12 April. MSD completes the review on 26 April 2027 and sets Alan's next review date for 52 weeks later (24 April 2028). Note when there is a change in circumstances that means a client no longer qualifies for Supported Living Payment, MSD should consider if the client is eligible for other types of assistance.

chunks.title: Young partner of main beneficiary may meet the requirements in some circumstances — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Young partner of main beneficiary may meet the requirements in some circumstances
However, they may be able to be paid their payment for more than 28 days for the purpose of obtaining support from a family member overseas if:
- the support they require can't be given by their partner because the main beneficiary themselves is absent from New Zealand or
- it is support the young partner cannot receive from their partner (for example, it is support from a parent or grandparent or the partner and the young person are having relationship difficulties).

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Example 1
The temporary caregiver is to be paid Supported Living Payment at the equivalent Unsupported Childs Benefit rate while caring for 1 child aged 14 years during the sole parent client's imprisonment.
Unsupported Child's Benefit (as at 1 April 2026)
$350.58
Less family tax credit (as at 1 April 2026)
$151.91
Equals amount to add as a non-standard rate
$198.67
## Example 2
The temporary caregiver is to be paid Supported Living Payment at the equivalent Unsupported Childs Benefit rate while caring for 2 children aged 14 and 10 years during the sole parent client's imprisonment.
Unsupported Childs Benefit (as at 1 April 2026):
- $350.58 for 14-year old and
- $327.16 for 10-year old
$677.74
Less family tax credit (as at 1 April 2026):
- $151.91 for first child and
- $123.78 for second child
$275.69
Equals amount to add as a non-standard rate
$402.05
## Example 3
The temporary caregiver is to be paid Supported Living Payment while caring for 2 children aged 14 and 10 years during the sole parent client's imprisonment. It has been agreed to include the rent of the client's home of $160.00.
Unsupported Childs Benefit (as at 1 April 2026):
- $350.58 for 14-year old and
- $327.16 for 10-year old
$677.74
Plus rent on client's home
$190.00
Sub total
$867.74
Less family tax credit (as at 1 April 2026):
- $151.91 for first child and
- $123.78 for second child
$275.69
Equals calculated amount required to assist the temporary caregiver to care for the client's children (rent included)
$592.05
Maximum Supported Living Payment - Sole parent rate (net as at 1 April 2026)
$581.96
In this case the amount payable is the maximum Supported Living Payment - Sole parent rate of $581.96. You don't need to add a non-standard rate.

chunks.title: Exceptions when a client declares no change in circumstances for Mandatory Review — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: When a client responds to their Mandatory Review and confirms they have no change in circumstances, MSD must generally continue their Supported Living Payment at the same rate. However, there are some exceptions when MSD can request further information from the client to determine if they continue to qualify for Supported Living Payment or that the rate of payment is correct. Exceptions include when, at the time the client responds to their Mandatory Review, they: - have been getting Disability Allowance and have had no change in their disability related costs for three consecutive years or - have been getting Accommodation Supplement and have had no change in their accommodation costs for three consecutive years or - have had no change to their confirmed income amount for three consecutive years If a client has one or more of these exceptions, MSD must consider if further information is required from the client before deciding the outcome of the Mandatory Review.

chunks.title: Further information is needed to complete the Mandatory Review — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: If further information is needed to determine if the client continues to qualify for Supported Living Payment or that the rate of payment is correct, MSD must give a reasonable timeframe for the client to provide it. The date the client is given to provide the information by becomes the client's new deadline to respond to the Mandatory Review. If the client does not provide the information that was asked for, MSD must suspend the Supported Living Payment from the new deadline date. If the client provides the information that was asked for and MSD determines the client continues to qualify for Supported Living Payment (including the rate payable), the future Mandatory Review date is set 52 weeks from the date MSD completed the review.

chunks.title: Further information not needed to complete the Mandatory Review — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: In some situations, there may be good reason for the client having no change in their costs or income, and further information may not be needed for MSD to determine whether they continue to qualify for Supported Living Payment. For example, the client may have provided recent evidence of their costs or income, or they may have recently discussed their circumstances with MSD. If no further information is needed for MSD to determine the client continues to qualify for Supported Living Payment (including the rate payable), the future Mandatory Review date is set 52 weeks from the date MSD completed the review. Example Julius is getting Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability. He works for 10 hours a week as a carpenter with a local employer that specialises in working with disabled people. Julius is paid more than the minimum wage in this role in recognition of his skills and experience. Julius' Mandatory Review for Supported Living Payment is due on 12 February 2027 and he responds on 10 February 2027 to confirm he has had no change in his circumstances. This includes no change in his income (which has remained unchanged since he moved into his current role in 2024). As Julius has been getting Supported Living Payment and declared no change in his income for three consecutive years at the time the mandatory review is returned, MSD must consider whether further information is required before completing the Mandatory Review. MSD considers Julius' circumstances and notes that Julius recently contacted MSD to discuss the Sustainable Employment Trial. However, Julius decided not to increase his hours. As part of that conversation, MSD confirmed Julius' income hadn't changed (as he is paid more than the minimum wage, annual changes to the minimum wage have not impacted his income). MSD determines that no further information is required to determine that Julius continues to qualify for Supported Living Payment. His Supported Living Payment continues at the same rate, and his next review date is set for 52 weeks in the future (9 February 2028).

chunks.title: Date of review — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Date of review
Where a child becomes financially independent it should be excluded from the benefit payment from the start of the next pay period in which the child became financially independent.
There is discretion to continue payment for one payday following the event.
This discretion only applies when the exclusion of the child affects the rate of payment of Supported Living Payment and is generally used when processing deadlines have passed.
## Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit
Stop family tax credit and Best start tax credit payments from the start of the next payday in which the child became financially independent, to avoid an overpayment (with Inland Revenue) for the client.

chunks.title: Date of review — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Date of review
Exclude the child from the Supported Living Payment from the beginning of the next pay period in which the child started work.
## Family tax credit
Family tax credit payments should be stopped from the start of the next pay period in which the child starts full-time employment to avoid an overpayment (with Inland Revenue) for the client.

chunks.title: Guidelines for regular employment — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Guidelines for regular employment
Factors that you may need to consider in making a decision on whether the client is in regular employment of 15 or more hours a week include:
- Is the client able to work 15 or more hours each and every week?
- Is the work permanent, casual or on-call?
- Is there a pattern of the client working 15 or more hours every week?
- Does the client expect to be able to continue working 15 or more hours every week?
- Is it likely that the client's health condition may prevent them from working 15 or more hours some weeks, or in the future?
- Is the client's ability to work 15 or more hours a week due to a temporary improvement in their health condition?
For more information see:
- Unclear if the client is working 15 or more hours a week
- Client is regularly working 15 or more hours a week

chunks.title: Guidelines for sheltered employment — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: Sheltered employment, for Supported Living Payment eligibility purposes is employment that has been designed to cater for the needs of a person who is severely disabled. To determine if a client is working in sheltered employment, you will need to talk with your client and their employer. Your employment co-ordinator may be the most appropriate person to talk to the employer. You must decide whether the client has employment conditions that have been substantially changed to accommodate their disability. Examples of employment conditions may include: - their job content - performance expectations or requirements - environmental changes

chunks.title: What are your client's employment conditions? — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: The following is a list of questions you could ask your client or their employer to help you decide if your client is working in sheltered employment. Note you may need to ask your client or their employer more questions to get all the relevant information. - Does your client need flexibility in working hours because of their impairment or illness? Is this flexibility over and above what the employer would provide for staff without disabilities? - Has the employer allowed the client flexibility in the time taken to complete tasks because of their impairment or illness? Is this flexibility different compared to time taken for staff without disabilities to complete tasks? - Has your client's job been customised to be within their capability (for example, does the client complete a narrower range of tasks than their co-workers, or has their job been created from selected tasks usually done by co-workers)? - Does your client need changes to their work conditions (for example, a place to rest when required)? - Does your client need additional support on an ongoing basis (for example, support from an employment support group over and above what is provided for staff without disabilities, such as regular supervision, job mentoring or coaching)? - Has your client been granted a minimum wage exemption by a labour inspector? If the client answers 'yes' to one of more of the questions outlined above, your client may be in sheltered employment. You need to decide whether the changes in the client's employment conditions are significant enough to establish that the client's employment is sheltered. Note a one-off environmental change is not sheltered employment. For more information see: - One-off environmental change is not sheltered employment

chunks.title: Process for decisions — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: All decisions require comment from your Regional Disability Advisor or Regional Health Advisor. For more information see: - Process for decisions

chunks.title: Contracted vocational services providing employment in business enterprises — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: The Ministry of Social Development contracts with community-based organisations to provide vocational services for people with disabilities. Clients who are employed in a contracted business enterprise (formerly known as approved sheltered workshops) are considered to be working in sheltered employment for Supported Living Payment purposes. For a list of the contracted vocational services providing employment opportunities in business enterprises see: - Deskfile Approved Business Enterprises

chunks.title: Personal earnings exemption and exemption for severe disablement — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: If your client is severely disabled and earning income from employment, whether it is sheltered or open employment, they are entitled to the personal earnings exemption. For more information see: - Personal earnings exemptions - Exemption for severe disablement

chunks.title: Partner — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Partner
When the partner of a person in prison has been receiving a benefit, this will need to be reviewed from the date of release.
For more information see:
- Transfer between benefits
- Release from prison

chunks.title: Hospitalisation — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Hospitalisation
When a Supported Living Payment client (or their partner) is admitted to hospital, the period the Supported Living Payment can continue will depend on the reason for the Supported Living Payment being paid.
## Client in hospital during Mandatory Review
Generally, clients getting Supported Living Payment must respond to the Mandatory Review before their review date, or their payments will suspend.
However, when a client is in hospital (for 13 weeks or less) and needs more time to respond to the review, they may be able to get an extension. If a client is unable to respond to the Mandatory Review, they may be able to get an exemption.
The client must contact MSD before their review date to discuss their situation if they need an extension or exemption.
Note clients who are in hospital for more than 13 weeks do not have a Mandatory Review.

chunks.title: Hours of work — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Hours of work
When the employment position is for less than 15 hours a week there is no need to have a Sustainable Employment Trial.
It is preferable that the number of hours worked is appropriate to the client's circumstances however it is the client's decision. In some cases it may be appropriate for the client to start initially with a lower number of hours and to consider increasing these over time.
## Change in the hours of work
Once the client starts their Sustainable Employment Trial and the client temporarily works less than 15 hours in a week (for example, is on sick leave), the Sustainable Employment Trial should continue. However, if the client ceases work or permanently reduces their hours to below 15 hours a week, the Sustainable Employment Trial should stop.
For more information see:
- Income less than disqualifying rate
- Suitability of Sustainable Employment Trial

chunks.title: Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure
Where a client does not advise of their departure from New Zealand before they go, they may be able to have their benefit paid from the day after their departure date if the client has a humanitarian reason that justifies their reason for travel and their failure to tell Work and Income before they left.
Humanitarian reasons are:
- to provide aid or assistance to a family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member) immediately following a natural disaster (for example, flood, earthquake, bush fires) or similar adverse event (eg house fire)
- to be with a suddenly seriously ill, or dying family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member)
- to attend the sudden funeral of a family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member)
For more information see:
- Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event (within 28 day maximum)
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum)
- Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure
- Backdating benefit to day after departure date

chunks.title: Imprisonment — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Imprisonment
Generally, when a Supported Living Payment client is imprisoned or detained in custody, they are no longer entitled to receive the Supported Living Payment.
Supported Living Payment should stop from the day following the date of imprisonment.
MSD must decide whether to suspend or cancel the benefit after considering the likely period in prison and whether the client has a partner and or dependent children or whether someone else will care for the person temporarily.
In some circumstances Supported Living Payment can continue when the client is imprisoned.

chunks.title: In the care of Oranga Tamariki — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## In the care of Oranga Tamariki
Where a child or young person is in the care, custody or sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, the cost of the child's care is the responsibility of Oranga Tamariki and it is responsible for making payments under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989. The child is not considered a dependent child and Unsupported Childs Benefit cannot be paid.
However, where there is a sole guardianship order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but the child or young person is in the custody of the caregiver, the caregiver may be entitled to Unsupported Childs Benefit if all other criteria are met.
Where Oranga Tamariki is involved, but there are no orders or agreements about care, the child can be considered a dependent child (for example when Oranga Tamariki provides services to family groups under a Family Group Conference plan only).
For information on different orders and whether they mean the child can be considered a dependent child while the order is still in place, see:
- Oranga Tamariki order in place.

chunks.title: Inappropriate use of Sustainable Employment Trial — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Inappropriate use of Sustainable Employment Trial
In some situations, you may become aware of clients who appear to be inappropriately using the Sustainable Employment Trial process. For example, a client who takes up a substantial number of separate Sustainable Employment Trials with no intention to gain and maintain regular employment.
Special care must be taken in these situations and any decision must be on a case-by-case basis; in some cases it may not be appropriate to agree to an additional Employment Trial. If you need help in making this decision, contact Helpline.
If the client has established a pattern of successfully working 15 or more hours per week over a number of Sustainable Employment Trials, the client's benefit entitlement must be reviewed to establish whether they still meet the qualifications for Supported Living Payment. This may include referring the client to a designated health practitioner
. This is not required if the client has a legitimate reason, for example they were not able to sustain their previous jobs.
Where the client no longer meets the qualifications for Supported Living Payment, you should cancel the benefit, and determine the client's eligibility to other forms of assistance such as Jobseeker Support or non-beneficiary assistance.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Designated health practitioners

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Example 1
A client receiving Supported Living Payment has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks. This client has other income which reduces the main benefit rate to $20.00 per week.
In this case we pay the $20.00 per week which is lower than the hospital rate of $58.34 (as at 1 April 2026).
## Example 2
A client receiving Supported Living Payment has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks. This client has other income which reduces the main benefit rate to $70.00 per week.
In this case we pay the hospital rate of $58.34 per week (as at 1 April 2026) which is the lower rate.

chunks.title: IRD number for partner who is not apportioned assistance — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: As part of a review of benefit, MSD may make a written request to the client for evidence of their partner's IRD number when the: - partner is not apportioned the primary client's Supported Living Payment, and - partner's income is relevant to a client's Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Notice following an unsuccessful match — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a partner's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the client (in writing) to provide evidence of their partner's IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the client a minimum of 10 working days to provide their partner's IRD number evidence or the client's assistance may be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Supported Living Payment. Isla's partner, Ariki, has income that is included in MSD's income test to determine eligibility for Supported Living Payment and MSD holds an IRD number for Ariki. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Ariki's IRD number. As part of a review of Isla's benefit, MSD provides a notice in writing, giving 10 working days for Isla to provide evidence of Ariki's IRD number. MSD's decision to give Isla 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Ariki already having an IRD number - Ariki not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD may suspend assistance if evidence is not received — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: MSD may suspend the client's taxable and/or income tested assistance, including Supported Living Payment, if evidence of a partner's IRD number evidence is not provided within a reasonable timeframe (usually 10 working days) or within the extended period if this has been applied. In rare cases, depending on the client's circumstances, MSD may consider cancelling or varying the client's assistance. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance.

chunks.title: IRD number not requested in some circumstances — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - significant factors, that are outside the client's or partner's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number, e.g. a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence, and - the client needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided. A partner's IRD number and evidence of their IRD number does not need to be provided when they are not a New Zealand tax resident. MSD can determine at a later point to request evidence of the IRD number. For more information see: - Non-tax resident partner's IRD number not required Note there is different guidance for requesting evidence of an IRD number for clients and partners apportioned a part of the primary clients Supported Living Payment, or when a client is applying for Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Length of Sustainable Employment Trial — main benefits > supported living payment > changes and reviews supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Length of Sustainable Employment Trial
The length of a Sustainable Employment Trial is for a period agreed with the case manager to establish whether the client can sustain the employment. The agreed period can be for a period up to 26 weeks (6 months) in length.
While the Sustainable Employment Trial cannot be approved for a period greater than this, the job itself may continue past the end of the Sustainable Employment Trial.
## Determining the length
You and the client need to agree to an appropriate period for the Sustainable Employment Trial.
The length of the Sustainable Employment Trial should be driven by what the client believes is a reasonable period for them to establish whether they can regularly maintain their employment. You need to agree that this is reasonable.
When you and the client are determining the length of the Sustainable Employment Trial, the following factors may be considered:
- the expected length of employment
- the period the client suggest they need to establish whether they can sustain the employment
- whether it is appropriate for the Sustainable Employment Trial to be granted for a shorter period of time and then reviewed to consider extending the Employment Trial
Note if the client has completed a Sustainable Employment Trial of 26 weeks, the Sustainable Employment Trial cannot be extended. However, if the agreed period of the client's Sustainable Employment Trial was less than 26 weeks, and their employment is continuing, the client may wish to extend the Sustainable Employment Trial for a further period if they need more time to establish whether they can sustain the employment.
For more information see:
- Stopping the Sustainable Employment Trial early
- End of Sustainable Employment Trial interview
