chunks.title: Criteria for Community Work Experience — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Criteria for Community Work Experience
A client’s partner must meet certain criteria to have Community Work Experience imposed.
A partner can only be placed in Community Work Experience if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they have current work obligations, and
- they meet with MSD within the 5-working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure is not disputed and overturned, and
- Community Work Experience is the most appropriate sanction to impose based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or have dependent children.

chunks.title: Criteria for Money Management — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Criteria for Money Management
Clients must meet certain criteria in order for Money Management to be imposed.
A client or their partner can only have Money Management imposed if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they meet with MSD within the five working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure decision is not disputed and overturned, and
- Money Management would be the most appropriate sanction to impose based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or they have dependent children.

chunks.title: Criteria for Report Job Search — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Criteria for Report Job Search
Partners must meet certain criteria to have Report Job Search imposed.
A partner can only have Report Job Search imposed if:
- they are in active case management or have dependent children and
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure) and
- they have current work obligations and
- they meet with MSD within the 5-working day notice period and
- the obligation failure is not disputed and overturned and
- Report Job Search is the most appropriate sanction to impose based on their circumstances

chunks.title: Current medical assessment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Current medical assessment
If the client is getting a medical certificate from their own registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist, the certificate should be completed when the client attends an appointment with them. Sometimes a client may request a medical certificate without being seen.
Note a psychologist cannot complete a medical certificate for the person who is being cared for when assessing a client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).
MSD may need to get more current information if either the:
- time between the date the client was assessed and the date the certificate was completed is greater than 20 working days or
- certificate is more than 20 working days old
MSD must consider:
- the reason for the difference between the assessment date and the completion date of the medical certificate (e.g. the registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist may not be available to provide a more current assessment)
- if MSD has information to signal that the impact of the client's impairment or disability is unlikely to have changed (e.g. the condition is one they have had since birth) and
- all other health or disability information that MSD have available to decide the client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment
If it is unclear whether the information on the medical certificate is sufficiently up-to-date to decide the client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] . They may recommend the client needs further assessment by a designated health practitioner.
If there is likely to be any delay in deciding the client's eligibility for Supported Living Payment, MSD should consider another form of financial assistance in the interim.
This could include granting Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability or some form of hardship assistance. MSD still needs to be satisfied that there is sufficient evidence before granting.

chunks.title: Deciding amount of income exemption — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The income exemption applies to both open and sheltered employment. When you have decided that your client is severely disabled and the exemption applies, you may exempt all or part of their income (full-time or part-time) earned from personal effort when assessing their benefit entitlement. There is no formula for working out how much of your client's income to exempt. This is a matter of discretion and will depend on your client's individual circumstances. Note the income exemption does not apply to hours of employment. For Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability or total blindness), the hours of employment only apply if your client is regularly working in open employment.

chunks.title: Income exemption providing an incentive for employment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The income exemption is intended to provide an incentive for severely disabled clients to participate in their community by working. Generally, the exemption should help them to be better off financially because they are in employment. These factors may help you to decide the amount of income to exempt: - the additional costs your client has (that a non-disabled person would not incur) due to them participating in employment - any increase in existing cost of services due to changes in income levels from employment - the extra personal effort that is required by your client to participate in employment and a reasonable amount to be an incentive to recognise that personal effort

chunks.title: Additional costs — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: You should consider exempting a level of income equivalent to any direct costs related to the client's participation in employment. For example, if you have worked out that your client has $25 of transport costs to go to employment (that are over and above what a non-disabled person would incur) and this wasn't being reimbursed another way, you would include this amount in the client's income exemption.

chunks.title: Additional costs not included — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: When you are deciding the level of income to exempt you would not include any costs or part costs that are reimbursed through another form of financial assistance (such as Disability Allowance or Total Mobility taxi subsidy).

chunks.title: Increase in existing cost of services — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: You should consider any increase to the cost of existing services for your client due to the change in income level from employment when deciding how much income to exempt. For example, your client lives in a Kāinga Ora or community housing provider rental property and is charged a calculated rate of Income Related Rent. Their rent may increase if their income has increased. Another example, a client may be receiving income tested Home Help provided by the Ministry of Health. If they earn income, they may lose their Home Help.

chunks.title: Extra personal effort to participate in employment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: You can consider exempting a reasonable amount of income as an incentive to recognising your client's personal effort in participating in employment. Extra effort may be signalled by the following situations: - the time required to get your client to work. Your client may need to get up earlier in order to prepare for and travel to work - your client has to organise personal support workers so they can participate in their work - your client needs to organise transport to accommodate their disability to ensure they can get to and from work - any other situation where your client is showing extra effort to participate in their work You will need to use your discretion to decide how much of the client's income to exempt for their personal effort. For more information see: - Review income exemption when client's circumstances change

chunks.title: Process for decisions — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: All decisions require comment from your Regional Disability Advisor or Regional Health Advisor. For more information see: - Process for decisions - Deciding if your client is severely disabled

chunks.title: Deciding entitlement for blind clients — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Deciding entitlement for blind clients
If the client is applying for Supported Living Payment because they are totally blind, they can provide 1 of the following:
- a current assessment from their ophthalmologist or optometrist or
- a medical certificate (usually a Work Capacity Medical Certificate) from their registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist or
- an assessment from a designated health practitioner if they haven't provided sufficient medical information
## Medical criteria for blindness
To qualify for Supported Living Payment due to total blindness, the assessment must identify the client meets one or both of the following criteria:
- the best visual acuity (sharpness), with correcting lenses, does not exceed 3/60 or 1/20 and/or
- state that the visual field is contracted to a maximum of five degrees on either side of the fixation point
MSD must get advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] before making a decision on whether the client's level of vision entitles them to Supported Living Payment under total blindness and whether they can be given simplified access.
## Totally blind
If a client meets the criteria to be considered totally blind, they qualify for Supported Living Payment regardless of the number of hours they can work, and any income they may get from employment.
## Restricted capacity for work due to blindness
If a client does not meet the criteria for total blindness but is both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of their blindness, they can get Supported Living Payment (without simplified access) and be reassessed in 2 years.
## Not granted for blindness
If a client does not qualify for Supported Living Payment under the criteria for total blindness, they cannot get the special earnings exemption (that is, keep their entitlement to Supported Living Payment regardless of the number of hours they are able to work and personal income earned) and Blind subsidy.

chunks.title: Deciding entitlement for terminally ill clients — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: MSD can consider granting Supported Living Payment if MSD are satisfied the client is: - both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, or injury or disability, from an accident, or condition they have had since birth or - totally blind Note totally blind and legally blind are not the same. Permanently means the health condition, injury or disability is expected to continue for at least 2 years, or a terminal illness where the client is not expected to live more than 2 years.

chunks.title: Keep requirement to provide medical evidence to a minimum — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If a client is terminally ill with a life expectancy of less than 2 years, they will be given simplified access to Supported Living Payment and never be medically reassessed. It is important to keep the requirement to provide medical evidence to a minimum. The client may be able to provide: - existing medical specialist assessment or - written confirmation from their registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist or - an MSD medical certificate from their medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist The information needs to be recent. Note if a client is terminally ill and provides a medical certificate, the registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist will generally indicate the client is getting or would qualify for palliative services. Palliative services focus on managing symptoms of a disease rather than seeking a cure (e.g. hospices are an example of a palliative care provider).

chunks.title: Refer to Regional Health Advisor and Regional Disability Advisor for advice — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: MSD should refer to the Regional Health Advisor and Regional Disability Advisor for advice when: - the client may qualify to be given simplified access due to terminal illness - MSD is not satisfied by the information provided that the client meets the medical criteria for Supported Living Payment Note MSD must seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor and Regional Disability Advisor before deciding whether to grant Supported Living Payment giving simplified access.

chunks.title: Decide whether the client is entitled to Supported Living Payment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If the information MSD has confirms the client meets the criteria for Supported Living Payment, MSD can consider granting Supported Living Payment. MSD also needs to decide if the client's eligibility should be reassessed: - in 2 years or - never (if the client qualifies to be given simplified access) Note if the Regional Health Advisor and Regional Disability Advisor determines the information MSD has confirms the client meets the criteria to be given simplified access to Supported Living Payment due to a terminal illness, the client will never be medically reassessed.

chunks.title: Deciding if your client is severely disabled — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: There is no standard medical assessment for deciding if someone is severely disabled for the purposes of this income exemption. You should use all the information you have available to decide if your client is severely disabled.

chunks.title: How do I decide if someone is severely disabled? — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Work, for a client with a severe disability is more complicated and requires additional effort than for a client with mild to moderate disability or a non-disabled person. Your client will be considered severely disabled if the effects of their disability extremely limit their ability to: - participate in employment - take care of themselves and - participate in the community

chunks.title: Indications of severe disablement — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Where the effects of your client's disability are extremely limiting, generally they will require assistance from another person to carry out at least some of the daily routines of life. Consider whether your client: - requires another person to assist them with the daily personal support such as washing, dressing, cooking or eating - is unable to travel without assistance from another person - requires the presence of another person or persons to ensure their safety If one or more of these situations apply your client is likely to be considered severely disabled. You should consider all information available to you to make this decision.

chunks.title: Use all information available to you — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Some of the sources of information that may help you decide if someone is severely disabled are: - recent medical or disability assessments from your client's application or review of Supported Living Payment, Jobseeker Support or Child Disability Allowance - a recent Ongoing Resourcing Scheme assessment (ORS) for a school leaver - your clients NASC assessment For more information see: - NASC (Needs Assessment Service Co-ordination) assessment - Using NASC assessments to decide severe disablement

chunks.title: People likely to be severely disabled — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Not all clients with a disability would be considered severely disabled. However there are some groups where it may be easier to identify that extra personal effort is required for them to participate in their community (including employment). For more information see: - People likely to be severely disabled

chunks.title: May not apply to all Supported Living Payment clients — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The income exemption for severe disablement is not restricted to clients receiving Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability or total blindness) nor does it automatically apply to all Supported Living Payment clients. For example, a client receiving Supported Living Payment may have a condition that severely restricts their ability to regularly work for 15 hours per week but they are able to: - undertake their daily routines - live by themselves or with limited support - participate in their community (for example, by undertaking volunteer work or other activities) and - continue to transport themselves to work and community activities Generally this person would not be considered as being severely disabled for the purposes of deciding the income exemption for severe disablement.

chunks.title: Deciding non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or misconduct — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Deciding non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or misconduct
Before applying a 13 week non-entitlement period, you should consider the partner's individual circumstances to determine whether or not it is appropriate to impose a 13 week non-entitlement period. You should:
- have a conversation with the partner about why they left their employment and consider: if there was a good and sufficient reason for the partner voluntarily stopping workif their employment ceased due to misconduct, what was the misconduct by the employee, and whether there is any evidence of the misconductwhether the misconduct was relatively minor, or whether there are circumstances surrounding their conduct which go a way towards excusing itwhether the partner is challenging their dismissal or loss of employment
- if there was a good and sufficient reason for the partner voluntarily stopping work
- if their employment ceased due to misconduct, what was the misconduct by the employee, and whether there is any evidence of the misconduct
- whether the misconduct was relatively minor, or whether there are circumstances surrounding their conduct which go a way towards excusing it
- whether the partner is challenging their dismissal or loss of employment
- contact the employer to confirm the reason the partner left their employment and ask them to complete the Employment and earnings information for applications (V06) form
if the employer refuses to return the form or provide a reason for the partner's employment having ended, no further contact with the employer should be made - instead ask the partner for a statement of events regarding why they left or were dismissed from employment
- consider whether there is conflicting evidence between what the partner has advised and what the employer has advised
the partner must be advised of the reasons given by the employer if those reasons are the basis of a decision to impose a non-entitlement period
if there is conflicting evidence or the reason for leaving employment is not agreed between the partner and the employer, you should give the partner the benefit of the doubt
- consider whether there are specific circumstances where a non-entitlement period should not be imposed
If you are uncertain whether a voluntary unemployment stand-down should be imposed, discuss the partner's circumstances, in the first instance, with a service centre trainer and then with Helpline (if still required).
For more information see:
- Misconduct
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: A client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date they apply to get a Supported Living Payment. On an ongoing basis a client must continue to remain ordinarily resident in New Zealand to get their benefit. Some exceptions occur when the client leaves New Zealand to live overseas permanently in which case they may be eligible for a continuation of their payments under a Social Security Agreement.

chunks.title: Attributes associated with being ordinarily resident — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Ordinarily resident incorporates a number of factors. The key attributes to being ordinarily resident in New Zealand is that a person must have a close and clear connection to New Zealand on the date they apply for a Supported Living Payment. Some other key attributes that indicate that a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand include: - their physical presence in New Zealand is other than casually or as a traveller - there is some intention to remain in New Zealand for a settled purpose - despite temporary absences from New Zealand they regularly or customarily live in New Zealand - they prefer residence in New Zealand to any other country (a person cannot be ordinarily resident in two countries at the same time) Where it is not clear if a client is ordinarily resident you may need to ask the client further information. Some of the following questions may help to get more information: - if the client is going overseas, what are their intentions towards New Zealand (sighting return air tickets is a good indication) - the length of time they spend in New Zealand compared to their periods of absence and the reasons for the absences - property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans) - where are their cash assets principally held (New Zealand banks or investment entities or overseas based holdings) - is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and are they tax resident in New Zealand - see Inland Revenue New Zealand tax residence guide - IR292 - are they still on an electoral role and vote in central and local body elections - do they have a personal commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in their immediate and extended family community, community events, clubs and other groups) The attributes associated with being ordinarily resident can also be used after Supported Living Payment is granted if there is some indication the client may no longer be ordinarily resident in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Non-residentially qualified — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: You should consider other main benefits if a client does not meet the residence requirements for a Supported Living Payment. An Emergency Benefit may be granted on the grounds of hardship to a client who does not meet the period of residence requirement. However, the person must generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet the hardship qualifications for Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Deciding permanence and severity - existing assessments — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Deciding permanence and severity - existing assessments
In order for you to grant Supported Living Payment you need to be satisfied from the information available to you that your client is:
- both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, or injury or disability, from accident, or condition they have had since birth or
- totally blind
## Permanent
You can determine if your client's illness or impairment is permanent from their diagnosis. Remember not all types of existing assessments will contain information on your client's diagnosis and you should use all information available to you.
Where the assessments signal that your client's condition or disability is permanent you can grant Supported Living Payment. Generally, your client would be considered to have a permanent health condition or disability when:
- they have been accepted for ongoing assistance through the Ongoing Resourcing Schemes (ORS) from Ministry of Education, Special Education (if they are attending or have recently left school) or
- they have a Needs Assessment Service Co-ordination (NASC) assessment or
- an assessment from their specialist has enough information to decide whether their health condition or disability is permanent
If you don't have enough information to decide if your client's condition or disability is permanent, or the information is unclear refer to your Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] for advice.
For more information see:
- Diagnosis not available in existing assessment
## Severe
Existing assessments may not talk directly about the impact of your client's ill health or impairment on their ability to work. Where your client is clearly eligible for Supported Living Payment it is reasonable to translate from the impact on their daily life and decide severity for the purpose of benefit entitlement.
Some existing assessments will have information on how your client's illness or impairment impacts on activities in their everyday life (for example, NASC reports). You can use this information to decide if your client meets the severity criteria.

chunks.title: Permanently restricted — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Permanently restricted
Permanently restricted means the health condition, injury or disability is expected to impact on the client's capacity for work for at least 2 years, or they have been diagnosed with a terminal illness (the client is not expected to live more than 2 years).
MSD should consider information on the client's:
- diagnoses - the client's main health conditions or disabilities and any relevant secondary health conditions or disabilities
- prognosis - the likely rate of improvement of the client's condition and its impact on their capacity for work. The medical certificate will indicate when, and to what extent, the client is capable of undertaking employment or what accommodation, supports or services are required
- indication of permanence - whether the client's incapacity for work will last longer than 2 years. If a person is terminally ill and provides a medical certificate, the registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist will generally indicate the person is receiving or would qualify for palliative services where their life expectancy is less than 2 years. Palliative services focus on managing symptoms of a disease rather than seeking a cure
## Severely restricted
Severely restricted means the client cannot regularly work 15 hours or more per week, in open employment. Open employment is employment other than sheltered employment.

chunks.title: Deciding reassessment from a medical certificate — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Deciding reassessment from a medical certificate
When completing a medical certificate, the registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist will indicate a re-assessment date for clients who have capacity to work regularly in open employment 15 hours a week now, or within the next 2 years.
These clients will not qualify for Supported Living Payment, and MSD can consider Jobseeker Support or Jobseeker Support on ground of health condition or disability.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support - Qualifications
Clients who do not have the capacity to work regularly for 15 hours a week in open employment may not be given a reassessment date on the medical certificate.
## Diagnosis that signals simplified access
MSD must seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor before deciding whether the client's health condition or disability falls into 1 of the specific categories for simplified access. For example, it has been indicated the client is blind, or the client is receiving or would qualify for palliative services.
When MSD determines the client diagnosis meets the criteria for simplified access to Supported Living Payment, the client will never need to be reassessed.
## No simplified access
Clients whose diagnosis does not meet the criteria for simplified access to Supported Living Payment will be reassessed every 2 years.
When simplified access is indicated or MSD are uncertain about which re-assessment period is most appropriate, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] .

chunks.title: Deciding reassessment from an existing assessment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Deciding reassessment from an existing assessment
When you establish that the client meets the criteria for Supported Living Payment you will need to decide if the client will qualify to be given simplified access and never be medically reassessed, or the client's capacity for work needs to be reassessed in 2 years.
This decision needs to be made from the information on the existing assessment and any other relevant information.
If you are uncertain about the medical reassessment period or need to check if your client meets the simplified access criteria, refer to the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] for advice.
For more information see:
- Review of client's health condition
- Medical reassessment for Supported Living Payment
- Supported Living Payment and employment [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Deciding Supported Living Payment from a medical certificate — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The information required on the medical certificate is: - a diagnosis and - the impact of the condition on the client's ability to work and - the likely duration of that effect Note a psychologist cannot complete a medical certificate for the person who is being cared for when assessing a client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment (caring for a person). Generally, the client's registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or psychologist (only accepted for restricted work capacity or blindness) will complete a Work Capacity Medical Certificate. However, MSD can accept other medical certificates or assessments, including: - assessment from client's medical specialist - NASC (Needs Assessment Service Co-ordination) assessment - Special education assessment If the client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment is unclear from the information provided, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor.

chunks.title: Deciding permanence and severity of client's health condition or impairment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: A medical certificate for Supported Living Payment can only be signed by a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist. To grant Supported Living Payment, MSD must be satisfied from the information available that the client is: - both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, or injury or disability, from an accident, or condition they have had since birth or - totally blind Note totally blind and legally blind are not the same.

chunks.title: Incomplete medical certificate — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If a Work Capacity Medical Certificate is not complete, MSD can either: - ask the client to contact their registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist to obtain the information required or - discuss with the client that MSD needs to contact their registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist to request the relevant information Note the Privacy Statement on the application form allows MSD to contact the medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist to verify any answers on the medical certificate that are unclear or unanswered. If a client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment is unclear from the information provided, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor.

chunks.title: Consent — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: MSD will need to obtain the client's consent before contacting their registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist to discuss any information additional to information already provided on the medical certificate. This includes: - information required to determine eligibility or work obligations that has not been disclosed on the medical certificate, including discussing the impacts of a health condition not included on the medical certificate - obtaining specialist reports held by the client's medical specialist or general practitioner

chunks.title: Use all information — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: In addition to a medical certificate, the client may provide existing reports or assessments. MSD should use all information available to decide the client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment. Note If a client provides other medical assessments these can be completed by another registered health practitioner.

chunks.title: Medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist requests contact to discuss — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The client's registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist may indicate on the medical certificate or medical report that they would like MSD to contact them to discuss the client's diagnosis and their capacity for work. In most cases the registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist will want to discuss the information they have provided on the medical certificate. MSD does not need to obtain the client's consent before contacting their medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist in these cases. Note the registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist is required to discuss the information disclosed on the medical certificate at their appointment with the client.

chunks.title: Medical assessment should be current — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: MSD may need to get more current information if either the: - time between the date the client was assessed and the date the certificate was completed is greater than 20 working days or - certificate is more than 20 working days old

chunks.title: Deciding Supported Living Payment using existing assessments — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: For MSD to decide a client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment, the client needs to provide: - a medical certificate from their registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist or - suitable existing medical or disability assessments or - an assessment from a designated health practitioner if they haven't provided sufficient medical information For more information see: - Health practitioners that can complete medical certificates and provide medical information - Deciding Supported Living Payment from a medical certificate MSD can consider granting Supported Living Payment from existing assessments if MSD is satisfied that the information contained in the report or in its records confirms the client meets the medical criteria for Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Deciding permanence and severity of client's illness or impairment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: For MSD to grant Supported Living Payment, MSD needs to be satisfied from the information available that the client is: - both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, or an injury, or a disability, from an accident, or condition they have had since birth or - totally blind Note totally blind and legally blind are not the same. If the information MSD has confirms the client meets the criteria, MSD can consider granting Supported Living Payment. If MSD is not satisfied by the information provided that eligibility is clear, or thinks the client may be given simplified access to Supported Living Payment, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] . For more information see: - Deciding permanence and severity - existing assessments

chunks.title: Who is most likely to have existing assessments? — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Many clients will have been assessed by a range of registered health practitioners throughout the duration of their illness or disability. Using the information already available can make the process of applying for Supported Living Payment easier for the client. Situation Types of Existing Assessments The client is totally blind Specialist report from an ophthalmologist or optometrist The client is terminally ill Specialist report (e.g. oncologist or palliative care physician). Written confirmation from client's registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist (where relevant) The client is deaf or hearing impaired NASC report (Needs Assessment Service Co-ordination report) Specialist reports The client has severe physical disabilities (tetraplegia, paraplegia, spina bifida, cerebral palsy) NASC report Specialist reports The client has long standing, severe ill health (chronic arthritis, stroke, chronic health failure, cystic fibrosis) NASC report Specialist reports The client is 16 years or older and is applying for Supported Living Payment and is still at school or has recently left school Special education reports Child Disability Allowance assessment Specialist report NASC report

chunks.title: Types of existing assessments — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The client might have 1 of the following existing assessments that MSD could use to decide their eligibility to Supported Living Payment: - Assessment from client's medical specialist (e.g. ophthalmologist, optometrist, oncologist, cardiologist etc) - NASC (Needs Assessment Service Co-ordination) assessment - Special education assessment - Ongoing Resourcing Schemes (ORS) - Child Disability Allowance assessment - Other types of assessment These existing assessments are likely to be unformatted, in the form of letters or a written report and may not present advice in a way that allows MSD to easily decide medical eligibility for Supported Living Payment. MSD should consider a range of factors when assessing a client's eligibility for Supported Living Payment, including: - all the information available to MSD - the age of the assessments - if the client will need to be medically reassessed while on Supported Living Payment - if the client needs help obtaining existing assessments

chunks.title: Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance school — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance school
For young people studying at Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance school full-time is:
- four subjects at NCEA level 1 or
- three subjects at NCEA levels 2 and 3

chunks.title: Designated health practitioners — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Designated health practitioners
Designated health practitioners are:
- nurse practitioners or
- vocationally registered medical practitioners or
- psychologists
with a minimum of 5 years' experience in New Zealand and who have demonstrated an ability to work constructively with MSD staff.
Nurse practitioners, medical practitioners and psychologists must apply to become a designated health practitioner. MSD holds a list of all approved designated health practitioners.
## When to refer to a designated health practitioner
Clients can be referred to a designated health practitioner for the purpose of establishing or reviewing their eligibility to Supported Living Payment. MSD will meet the cost of this appointment.
MSD should arrange for the client to be referred to a designated health practitioner when:
- their registered practitioner indicates on the medical certificate that a second opinion is appropriate or
- they are unable or fail to provide existing medical reports, a medical certificate from their own medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist, or other information and MSD holds insufficient information to decide their eligibility or
- benefit eligibility is unclear or
- for any other appropriate reason

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Example
Nami failed a work preparation obligation and MSD imposed Upskilling as a non-financial sanction. In the third week of her sanction period, she does not participate in or report on at least 5 hours of her employment-related training or course. Her benefit is automatically stopped.
She contacts MSD says she did not participate as she forgot to attend the course and report the hours.
MSD is satisfied that Nami was complying with the requirements of Upskilling in weeks 1 and 2, but she was no longer compliant in week 3. MSD determines non-compliance from day one of week 3. Nami's payments are stopped from this date, and a debt is established. She is given a different recompliance activity to complete.

chunks.title: Partner engaged initially and then stopped — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Partner engaged initially and then stopped
A partner may engage with Report Job Search for a period of time, and then fail to meet the requirements before their Report Job Search has ended.
In this case, MSD will consider that a partner was non-compliant from first day of the week in which a partner stopped meeting the requirements.

chunks.title: Determining when a partner became non-compliant — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Determining when a partner became non-compliant
When a partner fails to find or complete Community Work Experience without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must determine from which point the partner was non-compliant.
MSD may consider information shared by an organisation when determining if a partner has a good and sufficient reason for failing to find or complete Community Work Experience, however MSD must also consider information provided by the partner.
The partner’s benefit will be suspended or reduced from the first day of the week that MSD determines a partner was non-compliant.
The start of each week is based on when the Community Work Experience was imposed. This means the week may not begin on a Monday.
For example, if a partner’s Community Work Experience is imposed on a Wednesday, the beginning of the week for the sanction will be Wednesday.

chunks.title: Partner’s obligations — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Partner’s obligations
Partners with work obligations who fail a social obligation may have Community Work Experience imposed. However, it may be more appropriate for a partner to recomply with their failure by meeting their social obligations, rather than completing Community Work Experience.

chunks.title: Redirections and offsets — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Redirections and offsets
Any redirections, offsets, or debt repayments will be deducted from the payment going into a client’s bank account. It may not be possible for a client to make some of these payments while they are on Money Management.
MSD should discuss this with the client before deciding whether to impose Money Management.
## Changes in income
Money Management may not be suitable for clients who frequently have changes in their income.
If a client declares a change in their income after their main benefit payment has been issued to their payment card, it may result in an overpayment. If a client is overpaid, a debt will be established as the payment cannot be adjusted.
If a client is underpaid, they will be issued arrears directly into their bank account. This may reduce the effectiveness of the sanction.

chunks.title: Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes when a partner is diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence.
Drug addiction or dependence, for the purposes of the drug test requirements, means a person who has been diagnosed with:
- severe substance abuse or
- dependency or drug addiction issues
The partner can be asked to provide verification from a registered health practitioner or by a registered AOD practitioner who will have completed a formal assessment and given the diagnosis of drug dependency.
The verification should also state the duration or time that the partner will need to address their drug issue dependency.
There is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that MSD can provide to the partner.

chunks.title: Diagnosis not available in existing assessment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Diagnosis not available in existing assessment
Some types of existing assessments may not contain a diagnosis or the diagnosis might not be clear (for example, Group Special Education reports). In these cases, you can use other types of medical evidence to find the diagnosis. For example you may use:
- previous Child Disability Allowance assessment
- Disability Allowance medical assessment
- another type of existing assessment (for example, a specialist report)
- previous Work and Income medical certificates
Your client, their parent, guardian or agent may also be able to clarify some of the information that you have in the existing assessment.
If you are unsure about your client's diagnosis, refer to your Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] for advice.
For more information see:
- Read codes matrix [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Disputes and reviews of an obligations failure — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Disputes and reviews of an obligations failure
A client or partner has the right to dispute or review if they disagree with any decision relating to:
- an obligations failure or
- a sanction being imposed or
- the type of sanction being imposed
A client or partner can do this by:
- disputing the decision or
- lodging a formal Review of Decision
- lodging an appeal to the Medical Appeals Board (drug test failure only)
A Review of Decision or appeal to the Medical Appeals Board can be lodged at any stage, within three months of the obligations failure being initiated, or within three months of the sanction being imposed.
If a client or partner disputes their obligations failure or sanction more than 20 working days after it is initiated or imposed, MSD must advise the client or partner to lodge a formal Review of Decision or an appeal to the Medical Appeals Board (drug test failure only) in writing.
For more information see:
- The disputes process
- Disputing more than one obligations failure
- Recording decisions on a dispute
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Core policy Medical Appeals Board

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Example
A partner has failed their social obligations and two of their work obligations, and the failures have been initiated on the same day. The partner disputes some of these failures as they have good and sufficient reasons. The partner also recomplies to one. The client is not sanctioned but the failure is counted because they recomplied with one of the failures.
Obligation
Recompliance
Action
Social obligation - failed to enrol child in ECE
Client must comply with all social obligations
Client disputes failure - has good and sufficient reason
Work obligations - failed to attend interview
Must attend another job interview - or similar activity
Client disputes failure - has good and sufficient reason
Work obligations - refused to take drug test
Must agree to being drug free
Client has no good and sufficient reason for the failure - agrees to recomply

chunks.title: District Health Board assistance — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## District Health Board assistance
When a District Health Board Needs Assessor approves Home Support Services to provide relief for a caregiver, it will not affect benefit entitlement unless it means the caregiver is no longer providing full-time care and attention at home.
A person with high needs (assessed as level 4 or 5 care by the District Health Board) may need additional support. This would not affect the full-time caregiver status of the client receiving Supported Living Payment.
When District Health Board assistance reduces the need for care to part-time it would not be appropriate to pay a Supported Living Payment.
Any queries from people about home support services should be referred to the District Health Board.
For more information see:
- Full-time care and attention

chunks.title: Drug test job referral not suitable — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Drug test job referral not suitable
There are certain situations where it is not appropriate to refer a partner to drug tested jobs as the job is not considered to be suitable. These situations include where a partner is:
- taking prescribed medication
- diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- in or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence or
- has a drug issue identified by a provider and is engaging and participating in services and support offered by that provider
These situations are also to be taken into account when deciding whether a partner has a good and sufficient reason for failing their drug test requirements.
For more information see:
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons
The first time a partner presents with one of these situations, you should:
- accept that it is not appropriate to refer the partner to drug tested jobs
- add a deferral from drug test obligations for an initial 30 working day period and
- advise the client that if they think they require a deferral from drug test obligations for more than 30 working days, then verification will be required.
- there is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to the partner
For more information see:
- Drug test - Referral delay [no link find out why]
Depending on the clients circumstances and the verification provided you can extend the deferral from drug test obligations up to 6 months.

chunks.title: Drug tested job referral not suitable — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Drug tested job referral not suitable
These situations are also to be taken into account when deciding whether it is appropriate to refer a partner to drug tested jobs. If you decide that, due to one of these situations, it is not appropriate to refer a partner to further drug tested jobs you must add a drug test obligations deferral.
For more information see:
- Drug Test - Referral Delay [no link find out why] process
## Partner provides a good and sufficient reason
The first time a partner fails the drug test requirements and provides a good and sufficient reason, you should:
- accept that the partner has a good and sufficient reason
- add a deferral from drug test obligations for an initial 30 working day period and
- advise the client that if they think they require a deferral from drug test obligations for more than 30 working days, then verification will be required
- there is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to your client.
For more information see:
- Drug test job referral not suitable
- Taking controlled prescribed medication
- Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence
- Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence
- Reviewing or disputing the drug test failure and sanction
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures

chunks.title: Drug test obligations — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Drug test obligations
Partners of clients receiving Supported Living Payment who have work obligations will be subject to drug test obligations.
Partners must undertake and pass drug tests when Work and Income have identified:
- a suitable job and pre-employment drug tests are required by a prospective employer or
- a suitable course and a pre-course drug test is required as part of the admission process by a training provider
A partner will fail their drug test work obligations if they have no good and sufficient reason and:
- a suitable job is available and they advise they will not apply for the job as they will not pass the pre-employment drug test
- they have been referred to or have applied for a suitable job or course and they refuse to take the pre-employment drug test or
- they have been referred to a suitable job or course and they fail or refuse a drug test
If a partner fails their drug test work obligations the same five day notice period and sanctions apply as for any other obligations failure.
## Partner fails pre-employment alcohol test
Job applicants may be required to be tested for alcohol use prior to being hired. However, the drug test obligation requirements do not include alcohol.
If a partner failed a test for alcohol use, without a good and sufficient reason, then a work test failure could be initiated because the partner has failed to participate in the job interview process.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements
- Employers requiring pre-employment drug tests
- Training providers requiring a drug test
- Types of drug tests and standards

chunks.title: Drug test recompliance count — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Drug test recompliance count
The obligation failure that is initiated or the sanction that is imposed depends on how often the partner has failed to comply with their obligations in the previous 24 months while getting a benefit. This is called the 24-month failure count.
The recompliance activity that the partner has to complete depends on whether the partner has failed their drug test obligation before within the last 24 months.
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation the partner must complete a six-week approved activity.
## Example 2

eg must verbally agree to stop using controlled drugs

Six-week approved activity

For more information see:
- Counting previous obligations failures

chunks.title: Earning incentive payments — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Earning incentive payments
Young partners getting Supported Living Payment can earn the following incentive payments:
- education incentive of $10 a week
- budgeting incentive of $10 a week
- parenting education incentive of $10 a week
## Education incentive
A young partner on Supported Living Payment can earn the education incentive if:
- their service provider or MSD 'in-house' service has confirmed to YSSU that since they started getting their benefit, they have continuously attended and participated in either education, training or work-based learning for at least 6 calendar months
## Budgeting incentive
A young partner on Supported Living Payment can earn the budgeting incentive if:
- their service provider or MSD 'in-house' service has confirmed to YSSU that since they started getting their benefit they have: attended and participated in discussions on budgeting with the service provider or MSD 'in-house' service provider for at least 3 calendar months andattended and completed a budgeting programme
- attended and participated in discussions on budgeting with the service provider or MSD 'in-house' service provider for at least 3 calendar months and
- attended and completed a budgeting programme
## Parenting incentive
A young partner with a child on Supported Living Payment can earn the parenting education incentive if:
- the service provider or MSD 'in-house' service has confirmed that, since they started getting the benefit, they have regularly engaged with their service provider or MSD 'in-house' service for at least 3 calendar months and
- they have participated in and completed a parenting education programme and
- each of their dependent children is enrolled with a primary health organisation and
- each of their dependent children aged 5 years or under are up-to-date with their Well Child checks and
- each of their dependent children aged 5 years or under attends an approved early childhood education programme or is placed in other suitable childcare during any time the young person is in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work
Note the earliest date the 3 month period can be calculated from is the date the young partner was granted their Supported Living Payment.
For more information see:
- Removing incentive payments
- Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose
- Incentive payments can continue
- Restoring incentive payments
- Obligations

chunks.title: Earning the right to receive payment directly — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Earning the right to receive payment directly
Young partners who are subject to youth money management can earn the right to have their portion of main benefit, family tax credit, Best Start tax credit and any extra help paid directly to them.
The young partner can gain control of their payment if:
- they have demonstrated continued compliance with their obligations and
- their service provider or Ministry of Social Development in-house' service considers that they are financially competent
A young partner who has earned control over their payment has the choice to have their benefit paid directly to them and they will be responsible for paying their costs.
Note where young partners are sanctioned and they are not subject to youth money management because they have earned the right to manage their own money, they won't be put back on youth money management like those clients on Youth Payment and Young Parent Payment. This ensures the sanctions for clients who aren't subject to youth money management remain graduated through any obligation failures.

chunks.title: Earnings-related compensation — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Earnings-related compensation
All weekly earnings-related compensation payments received from either Accident Compensation or private insurers are a direct deduction from benefit payments. This is regardless of the reason why the Supported Living Payment was granted.
The Accident Compensation Independence Allowance is not earnings related compensation and is disregarded as income for benefit purposes.
For more information on how earnings related compensation affects benefit entitlement see:
- Types of income Earnings related income

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction for couples without dependent children — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Grade 3 sanction for couples without dependent children
If one partner of a couple with no dependent children is subject to a grade 3 sanction, this is only applied to half the couple's benefit. The non-sanctioned partner is entitled to half the couple rate of benefit, with any income reduced at half the rate of the income test that applies.
If both partners of a couple with no dependent children are subject to a grade 3 sanction, the benefit is stopped (as 50% is stopped for each partner who failed).
For more information see:
- Effect on supplementary assistance - voluntary unemployment
- Effect on supplementary assistance - grade 3 sanction or job refusal
- Financial assistance during non-entitlement period
