chunks.title: Effect on supplementary assistance - voluntary unemployment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Effect on supplementary assistance - voluntary unemployment
Partners who have a 13 week non-entitlement period because they became voluntarily unemployed cannot receive the following during their non-entitlement period:
- Emergency Benefit
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit
Note a partner who was receiving an Accommodation Supplement as a non-beneficiary prior to applying and being subject to a non-entitlement period upon application can continue to get an Accommodation Supplement during their non-entitlement period.
If eligible, partners can still get:
- Employment and work readiness assistance Assistance to transition into employment
- Disability Allowance

chunks.title: Who administers the test? — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Who administers the test?
Drug testing is generally provided to individual employers and recruitment agencies by a contracted drug test provider. Some large organisations have their own specialised in-house staff, such as nurses, who are accredited in workplace drug testing.
Employment-related drug testing is:
- conducted at a workplace, established testing site or a laboratory and
- through observed collection

chunks.title: Temporary employment at a disqualifying rate — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Temporary employment at a disqualifying rate
Where a client has temporary employment during the initial stand-down period and their income is at a disqualifying rate, this may change the date the benefit can start from.
The new entitlement date is the date the temporary employment stops. Reassess the client's initial stand-down using the income for the 26 and 52 weeks earned immediately before the new entitlement date.
For more information see:
- Example of employment during the stand-down
## Temporary employment at less than a disqualifying rate
Where a client has temporary employment during the initial stand-down period, and the level of income (when charged against the benefit) allows for a part payment of benefit, there is no need to re-assess the client's initial stand-down.
For more information see:
- Income less than a disqualifying rate

chunks.title: Employment related compensation — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Employment related compensation
A client can receive Supported Living Payment while ACC or an insurer decides whether earnings related compensation can be paid.
Supported Living Payment is granted on the condition that the benefit will be repaid out of earnings related compensation subsequently received for the same period.
When earnings related compensation is approved, Work and Income is reimbursed for the Supported Living Payment that we have paid to the client. We cannot ask for reimbursement of any supplementary assistance. Any debt that is established for supplementary assistance must be recovered directly from the client.
Do not grant Supported Living Payment if the client can receive earnings related compensation but it is stopped because they have not met their obligations with ACC or an insurer. The most common reason for this would be non-compliance with a rehabilitation programme.
For more information see:
- Claim refund from accident insurer [no link find out why] form
- Core Policy Income

chunks.title: Employment trial period of up to 90 days — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Employment trial period of up to 90 days
A partner may continue to meet their work obligations if their employment agreement includes an employment trial period. This is assessed the same as any other employment.
Employment agreements, signed by the employer and employee, can include an employment trial period of up to 90 days.
Features of an employment trial:
- an employment trial may be offered by an employer regardless of the number of employees a business has and
- an employer may terminate the employment agreement during a trial at any time before the end of the employment trial period even if the last day of work occurs after the expiry of the employment period and
- an employer is not required to provide a reason for ending the employment trial if the notice of termination was given before the employment ended and
- an employee cannot generally bring a personal grievance against the employer in respect of the ending of their employment trial period
A partner can still challenge the ending of their employment agreement including on the grounds of:
- discrimination or
- sexual harassment or
- racial harassment or
- duress imposed by the employer in relation to a partner's union affiliations or not as the case may be
For more information about when a partner's employment ceases before the end of the employment trial see:
- Partner's job ceases during an employment trial period

chunks.title: Enrolled in and attending school — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Enrolled in and attending school
A client and their partner (if any) getting Supported Living Payment must take all reasonable steps to ensure their children are enrolled in and attending school, from the age of 5 or 6 years old (depending on when they start school).
## Age of child
Clients with a dependent child aged 5 or 6 years (depending on when they start school) to 15 years old will be required to take all reasonable steps to ensure the child is enrolled in and regularly attending school.
If a child is aged between 5 and 6 years, it is the parent or caregivers choice as to whether they have their child in early childhood education or school. A child does not legally have to attend school until they are aged 6 years but most children start school at 5 years. A client must meet the early childhood education social obligation if they choose not to enrol their 5 year old in school.
A child can legally leave school when they are 16 years, or at 15 years if they have an early leaving exemption from the Ministry of Education.
A parent or caregiver cannot be asked to comply with the attendance at school social obligation, if the child has legally left school or has an early leaving exemption, and is no longer legally required to attend school.
## Verification of child enrolled and attending school
All children aged from 6 to 15 years old are legally required to attend school. In most cases you should take your client's word that they are meeting their social obligations.
However, if you have information that indicates the child may not be attending school you may ask the client to get verification, for example, a letter from the child's school that says the child is enrolled and attending.
There are some situations where a client may be taking all reasonable steps, but their child is not attending school.
For more information see:
- Taking all reasonable steps for enrolling in and attending school
- Parent is being prosecuted under the Education Act
## Home schooling
A client can home school their children and meet their social obligations.
If the child is aged 6 years or over they will need to have a 'Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School' from the Ministry of Education.
However, if they have work obligations, they are likely to need an exemption from those obligations.

chunks.title: Enrolment and attendance at a recognised early childhood education programme — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Enrolment and attendance at a recognised early childhood education programme
A client and their partner (if any) receiving Supported Living Payment must take all reasonable steps to ensure that their child is enrolled in and attending a recognised early childhood education programme from the age of three until they start school.
Generally, clients should have their children participating in a recognised early childhood education programme for 15 hours a week. This is a target number of hours; if a child is attending less hours this will be acceptable.
Recognised early childhood programmes for the purposes of social obligations include programmes that are:
- approved (licensed and certificated under the Education and Training Act 2020) early childhood education (ECE) programmes
- Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School or
- another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme
Generally, a place in approved early childhood education (ECE) service should be considered first.
When a place in early childhood education is not available or is not suitable (for example due to hours of operation, distance or family circumstances) then other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes should be considered.

chunks.title: Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits
A young partner must:
- register their child or children with a Well Child or Tamariki Ora provider and
- keep up-to-date with the child's checks
Note a young partner is only required to meet this obligation from the time they begin to receive Supported Living Payment. They will be meeting this obligation if they meet the relevant checks for the child's age from the time they are required to do so.

chunks.title: Enrolment with primary health care provider - young partners — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Enrolment with primary health care provider - young partners
A young partner must enrol their dependent child or children at a primary health care provider.
This means being enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or at a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation.
## Exception
If a client cannot enrol their child with a practitioner or medical practice because of shortages, they can be considered to be meeting this obligation if they have a plan in place to:
- be enrolled at a practice or practitioner when a place becomes available and
- get health care for their child if the child becomes sick

chunks.title: Enrolment with primary health care provider — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Enrolment with primary health care provider
A client and their partner (if any) getting Supported Living Payment must take all reasonable steps to enrol their child or children with a primary health care provider. This means being enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation.
Taking all reasonable steps to enrol
If a client cannot register their child at a medical practice, or with a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner because of shortages a client can be considered to be meeting this obligation if they have a plan in place to:
- be enrolled with a practice when a place becomes available and
- get health care for their child if the child becomes sick
## Age of child
The primary health care obligation applies to parents and caregivers getting a main benefit:
- with dependent children included in their benefit or
- who are caring for a child that they get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for
## Verification
Most children will already be enrolled with a primary health care provider and in most cases MSD should take the client's word that they are meeting this social obligation.
However, if MSD has information the client may not be taking all reasonable steps to meet this social obligation, MSD may ask the client to get verification.
For example verification could be a letter from their medical centre or their registered practitioner that says they are enrolled (most medical centres will send this when a client is enrolled).

chunks.title: Entering a refuge — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Entering a refuge
When a client is applying for Supported Living Payment after entering a refuge following the break-up of a relationship, the initial stand-down period can be waived.
Generally the client must enter the refuge immediately following the break-up of their relationship. This means entering the refuge within a period similar in duration to the stand-down (that is, within seven to 14 days). Where there is a delay between the separation and the client entering the refuge, general commencement date rules apply, including the twenty-eight day rule.
In this context a refuge is emergency accommodation provided by an agency or organisation. This includes (but is not restricted to) agencies such as Women's Refuge, Home and Family Society, Emergency Housing Trusts, Iwi and cultural organisations, and church organisations.
Note that accommodation provided by family or friends of the client is not considered to be refuge accommodation.
For more information see:
- Commencement date
- Twenty-eight day rule

chunks.title: Entitlement Date — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Entitlement Date
The entitlement date for Supported Living Payment is usually:
- the date of incapacity
- the day care started
- the day after employment ceased (that is, after any holiday pay, sick pay, etc. has expired) where the client or their partner was earning at a disqualifying rate
- the day after separation or financial assistance from partner ceased
- the day after weekly work-related insurance payments ceased
- the day after full-time study or student allowances ceased
- the day after the date the living costs component of student loan was paid to
- the date of arrival in New Zealand (if client has returned to New Zealand) or
- the date of release from prison
Note where the client has more than one event, you use the later event for their entitlement date.
Also note when an application is lodged due to incapacity and the designated health practitioner medical assessment is set for a future date, you will need to consider any other medical evidence held to determine the actual date of incapacity.

chunks.title: Evidence for ORS — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Your client will need to provide evidence that they were receiving ongoing funding from the ORS scheme. All students accepted to receive ongoing funding from the ORS scheme will be sent a letter from the Manager of Eligibility, Ministry of Education, Special Education. Your client may still have the acceptance letter they received. One assessment may not be sufficient to establish entitlement to Supported Living Payment. Your client's need for ORS is most useful at establishing the severity. You may need to use other assessments or ask your client for information to establish their diagnosis. For more information see: - Use all information available - Diagnosis not available in existing assessment - Helping your client obtain existing assessments If the information you have confirms that your client meets the criteria for Supported Living Payment, you can consider granting Supported Living Payment. You will need to link your client's benefit record to the designated doctor named 'Existing Assessments - Special Education' in the SDOCS screen in SWIFTT. If you are not satisfied by the information provided that your client meets the medical criteria for Supported Living Payment, refer to your Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] for advice.

chunks.title: Client cannot provide evidence of ORS funding — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Your client may have been assessed and granted access to ongoing assistance from the ongoing resources scheme early in their school years. Your client may not still have the verification letter from the Manager of Eligibility, Ministry of Education, Special Education. If your client no longer has a copy of this letter they may be able to get a copy from their school or by contacting Ministry of Education, Special Education directly. If your client is unable to access, or it is not reasonable to expect your client or their parent, guardian or agent to find this information, you can do this for them. If your client asks you to assist them to obtain their medical or disability information from a third party, they must sign the 'Client consent to release of health or disability information form'. For more information see: - Client consent to release of health or disability information [no link find out why] If it is agreed with your client that information from Special Education will best support their application for Supported Living Payment and your client has asked you to assist them to obtain verification, you will need: - a consent form to release health and disability information about your client and - complete the ORS fax sheet For more information about this process and the funding verification fax see: - Ongoing Resourcing Schemes funding assessments [no link find out why] Also see: - Helping your client obtain existing assessments

chunks.title: Single client — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Single client
A single client getting Supported Living Payment on the ground of health condition, injury, disability or total blindness has personal earnings of $2000 (gross) annually.
The Blind Subsidy, which is calculated at 25% of a client's personal earnings from work, is $500.00. The client also has other income of $300.00 (gross) annually.
The annual income limit for a Blind Subsidy to be paid for a single client is $34,175.06 (at 1 April 2026).
The annual income limit for single clients is made up of the Blind Subsidy annual income limit for a married couple of $30,258.44 (at 1 April 2026) and a single supplement amount of $3,916.62 (at 1 April 2026). This equals $34,175.06.
Total income from all sources:
Supported Living Payment - single 18 and over (net at 1 April 2026)
$22,079.20
plus Other income (gross)
$300.00
plus Earnings (gross)
$2,000.00
plus Blind Subsidy (25% of earnings)
$500.00
Total
$24,879.20
As the client's total income is less than $34,175.06 (at 1 April 2026), a Blind Subsidy of $500.00 annually would be granted.

chunks.title: Married client — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Married client
A married Supported Living Payment client (without children) on ground of health condition, injury, disability or total blindness has personal earnings of $9,000.00 (gross) annually.
The Blind Subsidy of 25% based on the client's annual personal earnings would equal $2,250.00. The client also gets Disability Allowance of $25.00 per week or $1,300.00 annually.
The annual income limit (for married clients) for Blind Subsidy to be paid is $30,258.44 (as at 1 April 2026).
## Total income from all sources
Supported Living Payment - clients portion only (net as at 1 April 2026)
$18,757.44
plus Earnings (gross)
$9,000.00
plus Blind Subsidy (25% of earnings)
$2,250.00
plus Disability Allowance
$1,300.00
Total
$31,307.44
As the client's total annual income is more than the annual income limit of $30,258.44 (as at 1 April 2026) we need to calculate whether the client still qualifies for a Blind Subsidy paid at an abated rate.
## Calculation to see if a client qualifies for an abated rate of Blind Subsidy
Total annual income
$31,307.44
Less annual income limit for Blind Subsidy (as at 1 April 2026)
$30,258.44
Equals (income that exceeds the annual income limit)
$1,049.00
Blind Subsidy (25% of earnings, minus the amount of income that exceeds the annual income limit)
$2,250.00 - $1,049.00
Blind Subsidy abated rate (payable to client)
$1,201.00

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Keriana is getting Supported Living Payment of $424.60 a week (as at 1 April 2026). She fails an obligation without a good and sufficient reason and her case manager decides to impose Money Management. Keriana’s first day of Money Management is Thursday 10 July. Because Keriana’s Money Management begins in the middle of the week, only part of her benefit payment for the following week will be under Money Management. This means she will get more than 50% of her benefit into her bank account. Note: the benefit might not divide evenly in 2. If this happens, the higher amount (1 cent more) will be paid to the client’s bank account.

chunks.title: How the first week of Money Management is paid — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday Full payment to client's bank account Money Management imposed Client's weekly rate ($424.60) x (number of days that week that Money Management is imposed (4) ÷ 7) = $242.62 50% put onto payment card Total payment onto payment card = $121.31 Remainder paid into client’s bank account (weekly benefit amount minus amount paid to payment card) = $424.60 - $121.31 = $303.29 Total payment into client’s bank account for the week: $303.29

chunks.title: How the second and third week of Money Management are paid — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday Money Management imposed Client's weekly benefit amount = $424.60 50% put onto payment card Remainder paid into client’s bank account (weekly benefit amount minus amount paid to payment card) = $424.60 - $212.30 = $212.30 Total payment into client’s bank account for the week: $212.30

chunks.title: How the final week of Money Management is paid — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday Money Management imposed Client's weekly benefit rate ($424.60) x (number of days of week that Money Management is imposed (3) ÷ 7) = $181.97 50% put onto payment card $181.97 x 0.5 = $90.98 Full payment to client's bank account Total payment onto payment card = $90.98 Remainder paid into client’s bank account (weekly benefit amount minus amount paid to payment card) = $424.60 - $90.98 = $333.62 Total payment into client’s bank account for the week: $333.62
