Example 2
Rick had Community Work Experience imposed and found a suitable position working with an environmental organisation cleaning up local rivers.
At the end of his position period, Rick does not provide verification or make contact with MSD. MSD suspends his benefit from the end of his position period.
Rick contacts MSD and asks why his benefit stopped. He is unable to provide any verification of completing his Community Work Experience. MSD also received an email from the organisation advising that Rick had stopped attending.
Because they are unable to confirm exactly when Rick became non-compliant, MSD considers him non-compliant from the beginning of the position period. Because he was not entitled to receive his benefit payments from the beginning of the position period, this results in a debt being established.
MSD then assigns a recompliance activity for Rick to complete to get his payments resumed.

chunks.title: Examples of other income - couples caring for a person — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The rates of benefit used in the following examples are as at 1 April 2026.

chunks.title: Example 1 — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Couple (no dependent children), one partner working full-time, and the other partner providing full-time care for a person. The couple's income is $848.00 gross per week. Income deduction 35 cents for every $1.00 earned over $13,000 per year $848.00 gross per week less $250.00 ($13,000 ÷ 52 weeks) $598.00 x 35 cents = $209.30 income deduction Income deduction 15 cents for every $1.00 earned over $8,320 per year but equal to or less than $13,000 per year $250.00 gross per week less $160.00 ($8,320 ÷ 52 weeks) $90.00 x 15 cents = $13.50 income deduction Total income deduction $222.80 client partner maximum benefit payable (no dependent children) $360.72 $360.72 less income deduction $222.80 $222.80 Benefit payable $137.92 plus $137.92 equals $275.84 As $275.84 is less than the maximum rate of Supported Living Payment of $360.72 (as at 1 April 2026) paid to care for a person with no dependent children, you pay the client $275.84 per week.

chunks.title: Example 2 — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Couple (no dependent children), one partner working part-time and the other partner providing full-time care for a person. The couple's income is $370.00 gross per week. Income deduction 35 cents for every $1.00 earned over $13,000 per year $370.00 gross per week less $250.00 ($13,000 ÷ 52 weeks) $120.00 x 35 cents = $42.00 deduction Income deduction 15 cents for every $1.00 earned over $8,320 per year, but equal to or less than $13,000 per year $250.00 gross per week less $160.00 ($8,320 ÷ 52 weeks) $90.00 x 15 cents = $13.50 income deduction Total income deduction $55.50 client partner maximum benefit payable for a couple (no dependent children) $360.72 $360.72 less income deduction $55.50 $55.50 Benefit payable $305.22 $305.22 equals $610.44 As $610.44 is more than the maximum rate of Supported Living Payment of $360.72 (as at 1 April 2026) paid to care for a person, you pay the client $360.72 per week. $360.72 is the maximum Supported Living Payment rate for a client with no dependent children when the partner is working part-time.

chunks.title: Example 3 — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Couple with a dependent child, one partner working part-time, the other partner providing full-time care for a person. The couple's income is $370.00 gross per week. Income deduction 35 cents for every $1.00 earned over $13,000 per year $370.00 gross per week less $250.00 ($13,000 ÷ 52 weeks) $120.00 x 35 cents = $42.00 deduction Income deduction 15 cents for every $1.00 earned over $8,320 per year, but equal to or less than $13,000 per year $250.00 gross per week less $160.00 ($8,320 ÷ 52 weeks) $90.00 x 15 cents = $13.50 income deduction Total income deduction $55.50 client partner maximum benefit payable for a couple (with a dependent child) $378.47 $378.47 less income deduction $55.50 $55.50 Benefit payable $322.97 plus $322.97 equals $645.94 As $645.94 is more than the maximum rate of Supported Living Payment of $378.47 (as at 1 April 2026) paid to care for a person, you pay the client $392.94 per week. The maximum rate for a client with dependent children when the partner is working part-time and not getting a benefit in their own right is $392.94 per week.

chunks.title: Example 4 — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Couple with a dependent child, one partner working full-time and the other partner providing full-time care for a person. The couple's income is $681.00 gross per week. Income deduction 35 cents for every $1.00 earned over $13,000 per year ($681.00 x 52 weeks) $35,412.00 gross annually less $13,000 $22,412 x 35 cents = $7,844.20 ÷ 52 weeks $150.85 deduction Income deduction 15 cents for every $1.00 earned over $8,320 per year but equal to or less than $13,000 per year $250.00 gross per week less $160.00 ($8,320 ÷ 52 weeks) $90.00 x 15 cents = $13.50 income deduction Total income deduction $164.35 client partner maximum benefit payable for a couple (with a dependent child) $378.47 $378.47 less income deduction $164.35 $164.35 Benefit payable $214.12 plus $214.12 equals $428.24 As $428.24 is more than the maximum rate of Supported Living Payment of $378.47 (as at 1 April 2026) generally paid to care for a person, you pay the client $392.94 per week. The maximum Supported Living Payment rate for a client with a dependent child when the partner is working full-time and not getting a benefit in their own right is $392.94 per week.

chunks.title: Exemption for severe disablement — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Exemption for severe disablement
The purpose of the exemption for severe disablement is to provide an incentive for severely disabled clients to work and recognises the personal effort required for them to participate in employment.
If your client is severely disabled, the exemption allows you to disregard all or part of the income they receive from their work when assessing their rate of benefit payment. Generally, the exemption should help them to be better off financially because they are in employment.
Note exemption for severe disablement applies to open and sheltered employment.
## Applied to all benefit types
This income exemption applies to all benefit types and is used in conjunction with other benefit personal earnings exemptions.
Note this income exemption does not apply when assessing income for Special Needs Grant or Recoverable Assistance Payment purposes as these forms of assistance are not defined as benefits.
For more information see:
- Blind clients subsidy
- Deciding entitlement for blind clients
- Personal earnings exemptions
## Hours are not exempt
The exemption for severe disablement applies to the income a client receives from their work. It does not exempt the hours of employment.
If benefit entitlement is based on employment status and your client is working in employment for more than the 'allowed' hours you will need to review entitlement to that benefit.
Note for Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability or total blindness), the hours of employment only apply if your client is regularly working in open employment.
For more information see:
- Sheltered employment
- Guidelines for regular employment
## Deciding if your client is severely disabled
The first step in considering an income exemption is to decide if the person is severely disabled.
For more information see:
- Deciding if your client is severely disabled
- Process for decisions
- People likely to be severely disabled
Note the income exemption can also apply to partners who are severely disabled.
## Amount of income to be exempt
The level of income you may exempt will depend on the circumstances of the individual. There are guidelines to help you make this assessment.
For more information see:
- Deciding amount of income exemption
- Payment process

chunks.title: Exemptions for partners — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Exemptions for partners
Exemptions from obligations recognise there are some specific situations where it may be unreasonable to expect a partner to meet their work preparation or work obligations.
If the partner qualifies, they may be granted an exemption from some or all of their work preparation or work obligations for a specific period. Evidence may be required before an exemption is granted.
## Duration of the exemption
Each exemption has a specific duration for which it can be granted. In some cases, the exemption can be extended (if appropriate).
Note the duration of an exemption for partners because of a health condition, injury or disability is based on the next reassessment date recorded by their registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologists recommendation in the medical certificate or other medical assessments..

chunks.title: Young partners without dependent children — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Young partners without dependent children
Young partners without dependent children can be granted a full or partial exemption from their youth activity obligations for the following reasons:
- Caring for foster child under 12 months old
- Caring full-time for a partner with a health condition, injury or disability (young partners)
- Court imposed conditions
- Family violence (young partners)
- Young partner would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
- Young partner would qualify Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
## Young partners with dependent children
Young partners with dependent children can be granted a full or partial exemption from their youth activity obligations for the following reasons:
- Caring for a child or foster child with special needs (young partners)
- Caring for foster child under 12 months old
- Caring full-time for a partner with a health condition, injury or disability (young partners)
- Court imposed conditions
- Family violence (young partners)
- Young partner would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
- Young partner would qualify Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
The young partner can be granted a temporary exemption from some or all of their activity obligations. Proof may be required before an exemption is granted.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions (young partners)
## Processing exemptions
Service centres process exemptions for young partners.
If the young partner is granted an exemption, add the exemption on the SWTDA screen in SWIFTT using the appropriate reason code. You must also add an expiry date.

chunks.title: Payments that can be redirected — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Payments that can be redirected
Most ongoing extra help payments paid to a young person are included in the redirection of payment if the young person is under youth money management, for example:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- family tax credit
- Winter Energy Payment
Note because Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support and family tax credit can only be paid to one person, for couples, the person getting the payment is generally responsible for any debt created.
## Payments that are not redirected
The following payments are not included in youth money management and can be paid to the young person, their agent (if authorised) or a supplier (as appropriate):
- Disability Allowance
- Child Disability Allowance
- Flexible Childcare Assistance
- Training Incentive Allowance
- one-off payments of hardship assistance, for example Special Needs Grants for food
- any Advance Payment of Benefit
If the young person qualifies for any of the above payments, MSD will decide who the payment goes to after talking with the young person's youth service provider (if one is assigned to the young person).

chunks.title: Failing a social obligation — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Failing a social obligation
If a client and their partner have had regular engagement and support and they are still not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, they still need to attend a final appointment.
A social obligations failure can be initiated when you consider that a client and partner have, without a good and sufficient reason, failed to meet their social obligations by:
- not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations following the process of regular engagement and support (that involves at least 3 stages) or
- not attending the final appointment during their regular engagement and support process
Before you initiate an obligations failure for social obligations you must get your manager client service delivery approval.
An obligation failure should only be used when all other efforts to encourage engagement and support with the client have been exhausted.

chunks.title: Failing more than one obligation at the same time — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Failing more than one obligation at the same time
If a client fails more than one obligation or activity at the same time and does not have a good and sufficient reason for one or more of the failures, the failures are counted as one failure. However, the client will need to recomply with all the failures before the sanction can be lifted.
Note Money Management is the only non-financial sanction that can be imposed when a client has failed more than one obligation at the same time at grade 1. A client must resolve all of these failures during the 4-week Money Management period in order to recomply.
For grade 1 and 2 failures, if the client successfully disputes one of the failures, the sanction imposed will remain until they recomply with any remaining failures initiated at the same time.
This policy only applies to the first and second time a client or partner fails their obligations in a 24-month period.
For grade 3 failures, a client will only need to complete one six-week approved activity or programme of activities (if they wish to recomply).
Note Disability Allowance can continue to be paid during a non-entitlement period.
## Initiating the failures on the same day
The obligations or activities that a client or their partner has not complied with can be over a recent period (eg within the last five days) or they may not have been complied with all on the same day. However, the client or partner can only be required to recomply with failures that are initiated on the same day.
As soon as MSD is aware that a client or their partner has failed their obligations without a good and sufficient reason, MSD must initiate an obligations failure - it cannot be delayed.
For more information see:
- Work or work preparation obligations
- Social Obligations
- Drug test obligations (for partners)
- Work with contracted service provider obligation
- Work ability assessment obligation
- Recompliance
- Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations
A client and their partner (if any), when required, must:
- attend and participate in interviews with Work and Income to discuss compliance with their social obligations and
- report on compliance with specific social obligations
If during any of the three steps of engagement and support, the client does not attend or participate in interviews with Work and Income to discuss compliance with their social obligations or report on compliance with specific social obligations, you should move to the next steps of engagement and support.
For more information on the three steps process of engagement see:
- Contact steps - social obligations [no link find out why]
- Failure to comply following engagement and support process
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Failure to comply following regular engagement and support — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Failure to comply following regular engagement and support
Clients will need to attend a final appointment if they are still not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations after the 3 step process of regular engagement and support.
A social obligations failure will only be initiated when you consider that a client has, without a good and sufficient reason, failed to meet their social obligations by:
- not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations following the 3 stage process of regular engagement and support and
- does not attend the final appointment, or attends and is still not meeting their social obligations, following the three stage process engagement and support
Before you initiate an obligations failure for social obligations you must get your manager client service delivery's approval. A social obligation failure should only be used when all other efforts to encourage engagement and support the client have been exhausted.

chunks.title: Failure within the position period – good and sufficient reason — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Failure within the position period – good and sufficient reason
A partner must be able to complete 5 hours of Community Work Experience each week during the 4-week period.
The position duties or conditions may change during this period and make it impossible or unreasonable for the partner to complete their Community Work Experience.
A partner must inform MSD as soon as possible that they are no longer able to complete their Community Work Experience so that MSD may place them onto an alternative recompliance pathway.
A Grade 1 financial sanction will be imposed from the date MSD has been informed and is satisfied that they are unable to complete their position and a recompliance activity must be arranged for the partner to complete as soon as possible.
Example
Marco has had Community Work Experience imposed and is searching for a suitable position. Marco quickly found a suitable position doing odd jobs at his church.
This worked well for the first 2 weeks, but in week 3 there was very little for Marco to do and the church only needed him for 2 hours that week. He contacted MSD to let them know he would not have enough hours for this week.
As this is a change outside Marco’s control, MSD informs him that his period of Community Work Experience will be ended, and a financial sanction is imposed from that day. MSD also arranges the first available recompliance activity he can complete, so that Marco can recomply quickly and his payments can return to normal as soon as possible.
Example
Marcia started a Community Work Experience position with her local sports club. One of the volunteers hears that Marcia is there because she’s on a benefit and this position is a sanction for her.
They tell other people who volunteer there and some people start picking on her, making unkind comments about why she’s there. Marcia feels very uncomfortable and contacts MSD to let them know what’s happening.
MSD decides that the position is no longer appropriate for Marcia to complete, because she's being bullied and feels unsafe. MSD imposes a replacement sanction from that day and arranges for her to do a different recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit
Young partners getting Supported Living Payment will be paid family tax credit and Best Start tax credit along with their benefit. They cannot receive it from Inland Revenue.
Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit can only be paid to one person in a couple. Generally it is paid to the primary caregiver.
Inland Revenue is responsible for establishing and recovering any debt created.
Note a young partner cannot review the decision on how their portion of Supported Living Payment is paid to them.

chunks.title: Duration — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 3 months.
## Proof
Young people who have recently left situations of family violence will not have to provide proof.
If a young partner still needs an exemption after 3 months you can ask for proof.
Proof can include statements from:
- their doctor
- their church
- their lawyer
- the police
- Women's Refuge
- any other person or organisation that is able to support the young partner's application
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Family Violence'.

chunks.title: Family violence — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Family violence
This exemption may apply to partners with either work or work preparation obligations.
A partner who has left a situation of family violence may be exempt from meeting all their work or work preparation obligations until they have had time to adjust to their new living circumstances. This is a full exemption.
You should talk to the regional Family Violence Response Co-ordinator before granting an exemption. You should also consider:
- Is the partner living in temporary refuge accommodation while they seek a permanent home?
- Are they helping children adjust to a new family situation?
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 3 months.
## Proof
Partners who have recently left situations of family violence will not have to provide proof.
If a partner still needs an exemption after 3 months you can ask for proof. You should consult the regional Family Violence Response Co-ordinator for advice on the most appropriate way to proceed.
Proof can include statements from:
- their doctor
- their church
- their lawyer
- the police
- Women's Refuge
- any other person or organisation that is able to support the partner's application
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Family violence'.

chunks.title: Special Needs Grants — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Special Needs Grants
Clients are not entitled to a Special Needs Grant if a sanction has been imposed, unless they become:
- sick or injured and
- incapable of participating in employment or an approved activity for at least six weeks
In this case, the client can get more than one Special Needs Grant, but the amount granted in any one week cannot be more than the combined total of:
- what the client would be entitled to that week if they were entitled to Supported Living Payment and
- the rate of Accommodation Supplement that the applicant would have gotten
For more information see:
- Effect of a non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Assistance when a client is sanctioned
## Advance Payments of Benefit
Generally, clients whose benefit continues to be paid (i.e. clients with dependent children) will not be entitled to an Advance Payment of Benefit when they have a 13-week non-entitlement period imposed. This is because they will be contributing to their hardship through not recomplying. The client's first option to improve their financial situation is to recomply.
For more information see:
## Exemptions or transfers
In some instances it may be appropriate to consider an exemption or a transfer to another benefit that does not have work obligations.
For more information on transfers and exemptions see:
- Exemptions for partners
- Changes and reviews Qualifies for another benefit

chunks.title: No action from MSD — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## No action from MSD
The partner will be considered non-compliant if, after 5 days:
- MSD has not confirmed if the position is suitable (or unsuitable) for their Community Work Experience, or
- MSD has not been able to confirm if the partner has completed their Community Work Experience, or
- the partner has not provided the required verification for either their search period or position period.
Their payments will suspend or reduce from the day after the search period or the position period ended, depending on which verification window was in place. This may result in a debt for the partner.

chunks.title: Full or partial exemptions — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Full or partial exemptions
A partner may be granted a temporary exemption from meeting some or all of their work obligations, or work preparation obligations.
MSD must check if the exemption reason is full, partial, or both before granting the exemption.
The partner can be granted a partial exemption from their work obligations if they can still:
- plan for employment and
- undertake some work related activities
If the partner is unable to do either of the above they should be granted a full exemption.
A partner who has a full exemption from their work obligations may still be required to attend an interview with MSD to discuss their circumstances and when it might be appropriate for them to start planning towards a return to work.
## Duration
Each exemption has a maximum duration. The period an exemption is granted for depends on the partner's circumstances.
At the time of granting the exemption MSD should:
- advise the partner of the temporary nature of the exemption and
- schedule a date to review the exemption, if appropriate
At the review MSD should consider the partner's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption. MSD can ask the partner to provide evidence that their exemption should be extended.
Note the period of time an exemption for partners or sole parents with a health condition, injury or disability will be based on the next reassessment date recorded by their registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist on their medical certificate or other medical assessments.
Note a psychologist cannot complete a medical certificate for the person who is being cared for when assessing a client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).

chunks.title: Full-time care and attention — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Full-time care and attention
Full-time care and attention means that the person will require 24-hour access to care and attention.
This does not mean the client is expected to give 24-hour care, but they must be available if required.
The level of care and attention must be over and above the ordinary care and attention required by someone of the same age.
A client can be away from the home for a few hours a day and still be considered to be providing full-time care.
Arrangements must be made for the person's care and their safety must not be compromised.
The client's absence could be for a number of reasons including part-time employment or study.
The client must provide the care and support at home. The home can be the client's or the person's home.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure
You need to be satisfied that the client or partner does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their obligations, based on the information you have, before you initiate an obligations failure.
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'. Having considered the circumstances, was it reasonable for the client or partner not to have met their obligations?
Good and sufficient reasons will depend on the obligation the client or partner has failed. For more information see:
- Social obligations All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations (for partners)
- Drug test obligation failures - Good and sufficient reason (for partners)
- Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation
- Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting obligation to work with a contracted service provider
Decide in favour of the client or partner if any doubt remains.
If you are aware that the client or partner has a good and sufficient reason, do not initiate an obligations failure.
If the client or partner does not have a good and sufficient reason, see:
- Effect of sanctions on assistance
- Failing more than one obligation at the same time
- Activity failures for young partners

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for failure to find or complete Community Work Experience — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason for failure to find or complete Community Work Experience
A partner may be unable to find or complete Community Work Experience for a good and sufficient reason. These reasons may include, but are not limited to:
- a partner has made reasonable efforts to find a position but has not found one during the 2-week search period – for example, if a partner has contacted many volunteer organisations but they do not have any available positions
- they are unable to complete the required hours in any of the 4 weeks for reasons beyond their control
- the conditions of the organisation and/or requirements of the position make it unsafe for the partner to continue
If a partner is delayed in notifying MSD of their good and sufficient reason, the delay must only be for a reasonable period. MSD will determine on a case-by-case basis whether the length of the delay is reasonable or not.
If MSD determines that they are unable to complete Community Work Experience for a good and sufficient reason, and a partner has notified MSD within a reasonable period, MSD must impose a Grade 1 financial sanction. The date the financial sanction is imposed depends on where the partner is in their Community Work Experience period.
When a partner is in their search or position period, the Grade 1 financial sanction is imposed from the day a partner meets with MSD and MSD is satisfied there is a good and sufficient reason and they have notified MSD within a reasonable period.
When a partner’s search period has finished and they did not secure a position, the Grade 1 financial sanction is imposed from the day after the search period ended.
MSD must assign a recompliance activity to the partner as soon as possible.
If a partner does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to find or complete Community Work Experience, or they did not notify MSD within a reasonable period, they will be considered non-compliant.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation
Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting work ability assessment obligations include (but are not limited to) when a client is:
- in hospital
- experiencing an acute mental health episode
For more information see:
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
Note if a client refuses to complete a Self-Assessment, Structured Interview or a Work Ability Assessment, and they do not have a good and sufficient reason, they will have an obligations failure.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment
You need to consider if there was a good and sufficient reason for the partner to stop work.
Examples of good and sufficient reasons for ceasing employment include (but are not limited to) when the partner:
- could no longer realistically transport themselves to their employment (e.g. where a partner's place of employment has moved)
- had childcare arrangements that were not adequate or fell through
- had an unexpected event occur (e.g. they had to return to the family home in another location to care for a sick relative)
- left the job because the job was outside of their capabilities or the job was not suitable
- had a significant change in conditions of employment that meant the employment was no longer suitable
- needed to take leave without pay to protect their job in the future, e.g. due to an economic downturn, or an unexpected the temporary closure of the premises as a result of an event such as a fire or flood
- was not able to continue working full-time (and was unable to work reduced hours) as a result of a health condition, illness, or disability and has a medical certificate to show this
Remember you will need to consider the circumstances of each case.
For more information see:
- Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed

chunks.title: Failing 3 obligations in a 24-month period — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Failing 3 obligations in a 24-month period
If a client or partner does not meet their obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, an obligations failure will be initiated and a graduated sanction may be imposed.
The graduated sanction regime applies to all obligations, including social obligations.
If a client or partner fails 3 obligations without a good and sufficient reason in a 24-month period, they are subject to a grade 3 sanction - 13-week non-entitlement period. This means:
- for clients without dependent children, 3 obligations failures in a 24-month period may result in a benefit cancellation and a 13-week non-entitlement period
- for partnered clients with dependent children, only the partner with a grade 3 failure is affected
- for sole parents with dependent children, 3 obligations failures in a 24-month period will result in a 50% cancellation of benefit for 13 weeks.
Note for young partners with youth activity obligations, their obligation failures are only counted for 12 months.
## Job refusal
A partner who refuses an offer of suitable employment is subject to a grade three sanction, regardless of their failure count in the 24-month period.
Note when an applicant fails their pre-benefit activity to accept an offer of suitable employment, they are not subject to a 13-week non-entitlement period or job refusal failure, as these can only be imposed once a client is getting a main benefit.
For more information see:
- Core policy Pre-benefit requirements
- When the sanction is imposed
- Effect of non-entitlement period on financial assistance

chunks.title: Health practitioner recommends a second opinion — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Health practitioner recommends a second opinion
In some circumstances MSD may need to refer the client to a designated health practitioner for further assessment, known as a second opinion.
There may be occasions where the client's registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or psychologist advises on their medical certificate or medical report that a second opinion is useful. This could be because the client:
- is under the care of a specialist
- has a complex condition
- has an unclear outcome from treatment
The client's registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist may indicate who they consider to be the best person to provide the information. They may also recommend that a specialised assessment is required to clarify the diagnosis and help determine the severity and permanency of the client's condition.
The need for a specialised assessment and the type of assessment required will be determined by the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor and endorsed by the Principal Health Advisor or Principal Disability Advisor.
Note if there is likely to be any delay in deciding the client's application for Supported Living Payment, MSD may need to consider if another form of financial assistance could be granted in the interim.
This could include granting Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability or some form of hardship assistance. MSD needs to be satisfied that there is sufficient evidence before granting.

chunks.title: Health practitioners that can complete medical certificates and provide medical information — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Health practitioners that can complete medical certificates and provide medical information
The client must provide evidence for MSD to determine their eligibility for Supported Living Payment. This can be a medical certificate or other medical information and must be signed by a registered health practitioner. Which practitioner depends on whether the client is getting Supported Living Payment because they:
- have restricted work capacity or are totally blind or
- are caring for a person
## Restricted work capacity or total blindness
Clients getting Supported Living Payment for restricted work capacity or total blindness, may be required to get a medical certificate or provide other medical information to support their application.
If a client provides a medical certificate this must be signed by 1 of the following registered health practitioners:
- medical practitioner or
- nurse practitioner or
- psychologist
Note MSD can grant Supported Living Payment for restricted work capacity or total blindness without a medical certificate if the client has sufficient evidence from other medical reports (such as medical assessments and disability assessments). This information must be completed by a registered health practitioner.
Generally, 1 of the above health practitioners will complete a Work Capacity Medical Certificate. However MSD can accept other medical certificates or assessments such as:
- Assessment from client's medical specialist
- NASC (Needs Assessment Service Co-ordination) assessment
- Special education assessment
## The client is caring for a person
When clients apply for Supported Living Payment - caring for another person they must provide a medical certificate for the person being cared for.
The medical certificate must be signed by 1 of the following registered health practitioners:
- medical practitioner or
- nurse practitioner
Note a psychologist cannot complete a medical certificate for the person who is being cared for when assessing a client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).

chunks.title: Help with paying for the recompliance drug test — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Help with paying for the recompliance drug test
When a partner has failed their drug test obligations the second time, they must agree that they will take and pass a drug test within 25 days of agreeing to do so.
Work and Income can help the client meet the full costs of taking the drug test if they cannot meet the cost of the drug test upfront.
In this case Work and Income will arrange to cover the cost of the drug test with the provider and then recover the cost from the client by way of debt repayment.
In order for Work and Income to help meet the costs of taking the drug test, the partner must agree:
- to take and pass a drug test within 25 working days
- to contact drug test provider and arrange and then take the drug test; and
- to provide the results to Work and Income
Work and Income will provide the partner with names and contact details for drug test providers in the local area.
A partner can only apply once during the 25 working day period for upfront help with the costs of the recompliance drug test. The 25 working days start from the day after the client or partner agrees to recomply.
Note that Work and Income has an additional 5 working days to receive the results from the client or partner and to process the information.
## Partner pays for drug test themselves
A partner can pay for the recompliance test upfront themselves, if they choose to do this, they must:
- take and pass a drug test within 25 working days
- arrange with a drug test provider to take the drug test and
- ensure that they provide Work and Income with the drug test results
## Debt recovery and reimbursement to the drug test provider
Work and Income will arrange with the drug test provider to cover the cost of the drug test.
Once the cost of the drug test is reimbursed to the drug test provider it must be established as a debt to the partner. The amount of the debt is the same amount that has been repaid to the drug test provider.
The recovery rate should be at the appropriate level giving consideration to any other debts the partner may have. Debt repayment options must be discussed with the partner at the earliest opportunity.
This assistance is only available for one recompliance drug test to be undertaken during the 25 working day period. The cost of further tests undertaken within that period will have to be met by the client.

chunks.title: Helping your client obtain existing assessments — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Helping your client obtain existing assessments
Generally we expect that your client will have access to existing assessments and will bring these along when they apply for Supported Living Payment.
If your client is unable to, or it is not reasonable to expect your client or their parent, guardian or agent to find this information you can assist them to do this.
## Client consent
The client consent to release of health or disability information process allows us to give assurance to third party holders of medical or disability information that they are able to provide us with this information under the Privacy Act.
If your client asks you to assist them to obtain their medical or disability information from a third party, they must sign the consent form. Third party providers may be more satisfied that they are able to provide the information to us if the provider specific section is completed.
For more information see:
- Evidence for ORS
- Client consent to release of health or disability information [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Home schooling — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Home schooling
Clients with dependent children aged 5 or 6 years (depending on when they start school) to 16 years of age, will be required to take all reasonable steps to ensure the child is enrolled in and attending school.
Home schooling meets this obligation in some circumstances.
Clients can home school their children and meet their social obligation if they have a 'Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School' issued by the Ministry of Education.
However, if a client and their partner (if any) have work obligations, generally they won't be able to home school their child, as this could impact on their ability to actively seek or be available for work. They may qualify for an exemption from their work obligations to home school their children.
## Certificate of exemption from enrolment at a registered school
A child does not legally have to attend school until they are aged 6 years (but most children start school at 5 years). If a child is aged between 5 and 6 years, it is the parent's or caregiver's choice whether to have their child in early childhood education or school.
A 'Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School' issued by the Ministry of Education is not needed while the child is aged 5 years.
Once a child is aged 6 years a 'Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School' issued by the Ministry of Education is required by law to enable a parent to homeschool their child.
## Social obligations cannot be required if child has legally left school
A child can legally leave school when they are 16 years, or at 15 years if they have an early leaving exemption.
A parent or caregiver cannot be asked to comply with the attendance at school social obligation if the child has legally left school or has an early leaving exemption, and is no longer legally required to attend school.
## Social obligations and work obligations
When a client has work obligations as well as social obligations they must meet both sets of obligations at the same time.
If the client is unable to meet their work obligations because they are home schooling a dependent child, you can consider granting an exemption from their work obligations.
The client must meet the additional criteria for the home schooling exemption.

chunks.title: Home schooling a dependent child — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Home schooling a dependent child
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
A partner can, in very limited circumstances, be exempt from meeting some of their work obligations:
- if they are home schooling a dependent child or a foster child and
- they have restricted circumstances that make the child's attendance at school unreasonable
Before you grant an exemption you should:
- gather all the proof required
- get the approval of the manager client service delivery to the exemption
This is a partial exemption only.
## Transitional arrangements for a person home schooling a child when they become a beneficiary with work obligations
If a partner is home schooling a child prior to becoming a beneficiary with work obligations then an exemption can be granted until the end of that school year, if they have an exemption certificate from the Ministry of Education.
## Proof
The partner must provide:
- proof of the restricted circumstances that makes their child's attendance at school unreasonable and
- if the child is aged 6 years or older, their 'Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School', issued by the Ministry of Education (if it's not a recently issued certificate, the client needs to contact the Ministry of Education to get another certificate)
For an 'Application for exemption from enrolment at a registered school', see the 'Home education application form' link at the bottom of the Home education page (the application form is the same for primary and secondary schooling).
All exemptions for home schooling must be approved by a manager client service delivery.
For more information see:
- Restricted circumstances guidelines
## Child is aged 17 or 18 years
If the child being home schooled is aged 17 or 18 years:
- the restricted circumstances criteria still apply
- the partner must complete a personal statement stating that they are home schooling the child and that the child is not attending a registered school
The Ministry of Education issues a 'Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School' only for the years of compulsory schooling.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Home schooling'.

chunks.title: Hours range for suitable employment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Hours range for suitable employment
Partners with work obligations must make themselves available for suitable employment of:
- at least 30 hours a week (partner with full-time work obligations)
- at least 20 hours a week (partner with part-time work obligations)
Although the target to meet work obligations is 20 or 30 hours per week a job can be considered suitable if the hours of work per week are within a range hours required to meet their work obligations.

chunks.title: Unable to provide visa or permit — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Unable to provide visa or permit
When a client is unable to provide an immigration visa or permit they may provide other Immigration New Zealand documents to verify their immigration status. Work and Income can also undertake an immigration status check directly with Immigration New Zealand.
Note that Immigration New Zealand may be unable to verify immigration status for clients of British nationality who arrived in New Zealand before 2 April 1974 and do not have a passport.
For more information see:
- Two years residence
- Resident in New Zealand
- Refugees and protected persons
- Immigration status [no link find out why]
- Immigration Act changes from 29 November 2010 [no link find out why]

chunks.title: In approved full-time training — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## In approved full-time training
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
A partner can be partially exempt from meeting some of their work obligations if they are engaged in approved full-time training.
Consider whether the training course is the most suitable activity for the partner. Also consider if other activities (for example programmes, seminars or work experience) might be a more appropriate option for moving the partner towards paid work.
Discuss and take into account the client's career background, including:
- their educational qualifications
- their employment history
- their skills and
- whether training will help them find work at the earliest opportunity
Examples of approved training courses include but are not limited to:
- Limited Service Volunteer (LSV) [no link find out why]
- Skills for Industry [no link find out why]
- Targeted Training [no link find out why]
- training approved by the regional contracts manager
The approved training must:
- be full time (at least 20 hours a week)
- focus on teaching practical, employment-related skills
- support the client to gain the skills that will help them find work
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months.

chunks.title: In approved study before subject to work obligations — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## In approved study before subject to work obligations
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
A partner with their youngest dependent child aged 3 years or over can be exempt from meeting some or all of their work obligations if they were in approved study at the time they became subject to work obligations.
This would cover situations where a partner was:
- part way through a course of study at the time that they were required to meet work obligations
- part way through a course of study when their youngest dependent child reached the age of 3 years
Note this can be a full or partial exemption.
Also note the partner must be passing the course of study and it must be completed within two years of being required to meet work obligations.
## Proof
The partner has to provide evidence that they are involved in study, such as:
- enrolment forms
- academic transcript, showing that they have passed 50% of their course the previous year
- training statement
## Duration
The exemption can apply for up to 12 months or until their current course of study has finished or the end of the current academic year - whichever is earliest.
The partner has to obtain a new exemption for the following year if the study is continuing and show evidence that they have passed at least 50% of their course the previous year.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'In study before subject to work obligations'.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions

chunks.title: In approved training (no children or child 14+) — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## In approved training (no children or child 14+)
If a partner is in approved training they must continue to meet their work obligations, including being available for full-time employment, unless they are granted an exemption for approved full-time training.
They are still expected to be available for work or any other activity up to a total of 30 hours each week.
The partner must understand that they have to accept suitable paid work if it becomes available.
For more information see:
- Approved training
- Exemptions In approved full-time training

chunks.title: In-hand allowance — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## In-hand allowance
When a young partner getting Supported Living Payment is subject to youth money management, they can get an amount of up to $50 a week paid directly to them as an in-hand allowance.
After the young partner's accommodation, service costs and lawful debts are paid by redirection, the balance of payment, if any, is distributed between the young partner's payment card and the in-hand allowance. The maximum amount that can be paid direct to a young partner as an in-hand allowance is $50.
## Altering the distribution of payment for existing clients already subject to youth money management
If, at any time, a youth service provider considers that the current distribution of an existing client's payment between the payment card and in-hand allowance is inappropriate for the client's circumstances, they can make a recommendation to YSSU that this distribution be altered.
When determining whether it is appropriate to make a recommendation that a client's payment distribution be altered, providers must take into account a range of factors.
Note a young partner cannot review the decision on how the Supported Living Payment is paid to them.
For more information see:

chunks.title: In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes where a partner is in or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence.
Treatment for the purposes of the drug test requirements means any specialist treatment service provided for a person because of a diagnosed drug dependency.
The partner can either be participating in or on the waiting list for a specialist treatment service.
Specialist treatment services are services:
- that provide specific medical or psychological interventions with the goal of helping a person to overcome drug dependency
- that a partner has been referred to following a formal assessment by the Community Alcohol and Drug Service (CADS) or by a registered AOD practitioner
The partner can be asked to provide verification from the person recommending the treatment or from the treatment service. The verification must state the duration or time that the partner will need to address their drug dependency and whether they are participating or on the wait list for treatment. There is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to the partner.
For more information see:
- Drug test obligations failures - Good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: School and tertiary holidays — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## School and tertiary holidays
Any incentive payments earned by the young person will continue to be paid during any school or tertiary holiday periods while they are receiving Supported Living Payment.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Incentive payments — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Incentive payments
If a young partner is under youth money management, any incentive payments earned are included in the redirection of their payment.
Young partners can earn incentive payments for demonstrating a commitment to their activity obligations.
A young partner getting Supported Living Payment can earn the following incentives:
- budgeting - $10 per week
- education - $10 per week
- parenting - $10 per week
## Review of decision
A young partner cannot review the decision on how their portion of Supported Living Payment is paid to them.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Income less than a disqualifying rate — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Income less than a disqualifying rate
Where a Supported Living Payment client starts work during the initial stand-down period, you do not re-assess the client's commencement date when:
- their level of income earned is less than a disqualifying rate
Where employment continues beyond the commencement date, you charge the client's earnings (income) against their benefit from the commencement date.

chunks.title: Informing a partner of the drug test obligation failure — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Informing a partner of the drug test obligation failure
Once MSD has decided that the partner has failed a drug test work obligation, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. The partner will then be sent a letter stating that their benefit will be sanctioned and that their benefit will only be increased, restarted, regranted, or continued if they:
- complete a recompliance activity
- dispute the decision to impose the sanction and MSD accepts that they have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting their work obligations or
- lodge a Review of Decision and MSD reconsiders their position and agrees with the partner's review
For some clients, if it's their first obligation failure they may be eligible for a non-financial sanction instead of a financial sanction. For more information see: Non-financial sanctions.
## Recompliance for a drug test work obligation failure
Partners may have their benefit increased or restarted from the date they start a drug test failure recompliance activity.
For more information see:
- Obligations failures
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Drug test obligations failures - Good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: Informing clients of their obligations — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Informing clients of their obligations
You must ensure that the client understands:
- their obligations
- the consequences of failing to meet those obligations, in particular the sanctions that may be imposed and
- their right to review and dispute any decisions relating to a failure to comply with their obligations
Clients and partners applying for Supported Living Payment must:
- sign their application form and
- be given a copy of their obligations from their application form
Note that work obligations cannot be enforced until the main benefit commencement date.
## Clients transferring to a different benefit or between benefits
When a client is receiving a benefit and they have a change in obligations, a letter will be sent advising them what their new obligations are. They do not need to re-sign an obligations form.
This includes where a partner is transferring between having full-time work obligations, or part-time work obligations or is exempt from work obligations and has work preparation obligations within Supported Living Payment.
For more information see:
- Obligations
- Social Obligations
- Work or work preparation obligations
- Work preparation obligations - primary clients
- Work preparation obligations - partners
- Work obligations - partners
- Drug test obligations

chunks.title: Initial stand-down — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Initial stand-down
This is a period of up to a maximum of 2 weeks where the client cannot get any benefit payment. The length of the stand-down depends on:
- the client's average weekly income (before tax) in the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before the clients entitlement date and
- the number of dependent children in their care at any time during the same period
The initial stand-down starts on the client's entitlement date.
Note clients can choose an income assessment period of either 26 or 52 weeks to calculate their average weekly wage for the initial stand-down.
## For more information on the initial stand-down see:
- Average weekly income
- Number of dependent children
- Employment during stand-down
- Self-imposed stand-down
- Initial stand-down procedure
- Absence during an initial stand-down
- Financial assistance during non-entitlement period
- No stand-down applies
- Deskfile Initial stand-down

chunks.title: Initial stand-down procedure — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Initial stand-down procedure
Step 1. Find the client's entitlement date.
Step 2. Calculate the client's average weekly income for a 26 and 52 week period.
Step 3. Find out whether the client has or had any dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement date. When determining the correct stand-down period, you must take into account any children that were in the client's care during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to the entitlement date.
Step 4. Using the information from Steps 2 and 3, determine the initial stand-down for the client over a 26 and 52 week period by looking at the initial stand-down period chart in Deskfile.
Step 5. Use the calculation of average weekly income that gives the client a lesser stand-down period.
Step 6. Apply the initial stand-down from the client's entitlement date to find the commencement date.
Remember; if you enter the correct information into SWIFTT it will automatically calculate the initial stand-down and commencement date for you.
Note if the client has had a dependent child (or children) in their care during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement date and the child (or children) is no longer in their care, you will have to use a work around. Contact Helpline for this information.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Interpreting NASC assessments — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: You can consider granting Supported Living Payment from a NASC assessment where you are satisfied that the information contained in the assessment confirms that your client is permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work because of a health condition, or injury or disability, from accident, or condition they have had since birth. The main sections within a NASC assessment that you may be able to use to decide eligibility for Supported Living Payment is outlined in the table below:
