chunks.title: Interpreting NASC assessments — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If the information you have confirms that your client meets the criteria for Supported Living Payment, you can consider granting Supported Living Payment. You will need to link your client's benefit record to the designated doctor named "Existing Assessments - NASC" in the SDOCS screen in SWIFTT. Remember the information needs to be current and use all information available to you. For more information see: - Age of assessment - Use all information available If you are not satisfied by the information provided that your client meets the medical criteria for Supported Living Payment, refer to your Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] for advice. For more information see: - Diagnosis not available in existing assessment - Deciding permanence and severity - existing assessments - Helping your client obtain existing assessments

chunks.title: Introduction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Supported Living Payment is for people who are not able to work because they are:
- permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, injury, or disability or totally blind or
- caring for a person who requires full-time care and attention at home
## Simplified Access to Supported Living Payment
Some clients with a specific diagnosis will access Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury, or disability) without having a detailed assessment for their capacity to work.
Generally, the diagnosis and associated information contained in the medical information provided by this group will satisfy Work and Income they are permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work.
For more information see:
- Simplified Access to Supported Living Payment
- Give a person simplified access to Supported Living Payment [no link find out why]
- Guidelines and procedures for Simplified Access [no link find out why]
## Including a partner
A partner can only be included in Supported Living Payment if it is granted on the grounds that the primary client is permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work or totally blind. Partners cannot be included in Supported Living Payment if it is granted on the ground that the client is caring for a person who requires full-time care and attention.
When the primary client is getting Supported Living Payment on the ground that they are caring for a person who requires full-time care and attention, their partner (if any) may be able to get a benefit in their own right.
## For more detailed information see:
- Qualifications
- Obligations
- Commencement date
- Payment
- Changes and reviews
- Employment
- Simplified Access to Supported Living Payment

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Example
Lizzy has told their case manager that they have not updated their CV with their recent employment history. They also noted that they would like to gain employment in the hospitality industry, but they do not have the skills to support this.
Lizzy then fails a work obligation, and their case manager determines that Report Job Search would be the most appropriate non-financial sanction for them. Lizzy's 4-week sanction period comes to an end, and they have a meeting with their case manager to provide evidence and determine whether their job-search activities were reasonable steps towards them finding suitable employment.
The case manager can see that for each of the 4 weeks Lizzy has been updating their CV, attending a barista course, applying for jobs, and had an interview. Lizzy has reported on more than 3 suitable job-search activities per week over the 4-week period.
Their case manager determines that based on their individual circumstances, the job-search activities Lizzy has undertaken are reasonable steps as they align with their skills and experience, developing their capability and help them towards finding suitable employment. As Lizzy has completed the requirements of their sanction, they are considered to have recomplied.
## Job-search activity is not considered a reasonable step
If MSD determines a partner's reported job-search activities are not reasonable steps to find suitable employment, they are considered non-compliant.
MSD may backdate non-compliance to the start of the week that the partner failed to meet the requirements of Report Job Search. This may result in a debt for the partner.
During the appointment, partners will have an opportunity to give a good and sufficient reason why they considered their job-search activity to be a reasonable step.
Examples of job-search activities that are not considered reasonable steps to finding suitable employment could include (but are not limited to), where the partner:
- only looked online for jobs, even though they could have used a variety of methods to look for work
- applied for jobs where it was unreasonable for them to be hired (e.g., applied to be a doctor with no medical training, or applied to be a bus driver with no licence)
- recorded the same job-search activity multiple times where this would be considered unreasonable (e.g., updated their CV three times each week, or contacted the same employer multiple times each week)

chunks.title: List of specialist schools — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## List of specialist schools
Attendance at a specialist school alone does not determine if a client is permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work.
However, many of these students are likely to have received Ongoing Resourcing Schemes funding while attending the specialist school. If a client advises they have been attending a specialist day school or residential school, MSD should determine if they have been getting ongoing assistance from the Ongoing Resource Scheme.
For more information see:
- Ongoing Resourcing Schemes (ORS) assessment
## Day specialist schools
There are day specialist schools throughout New Zealand. Some students stay until they are 21 years old.
For a list of the day specialist schools see:
- Ministry of Education Specialist schools - Day specialist schools
## Residential specialist schools
The following are residential specialist schools in New Zealand.
Residential specialist schools for deaf and hearing-impaired students
- Ko Taku Reo Deaf Education New Zealand (a merger of the Kelston Deaf Education Centre in Auckland and the Van Asch Deaf Education Centre in Christchurch)
Residential specialist school for blind and vision-impaired students
- Blind and Low Vision Education Network NZ or BLENNZ (previously known as Homai National School for the Blind and Vision Impaired)
Residential specialist schools working with students with educational, social and emotional needs, together with an underlying intellectual impairment
- Halswell Residential College for girls and boys, Christchurch
- Salisbury School for girls, Nelson
- Westbridge Residential School Auckland
These schools determine who meets the entry criteria for their services including any specific rules relating to sex or gender.

chunks.title: Medical qualifications — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: To qualify medically for Supported Living Payment the client needs to be either: - both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, or injury or disability, from an accident or condition they have had since birth or - totally blind Note totally blind and legally blind are not the same. Permanent means the health condition, injury or disability the client has is expected to continue for at least 2 years. The client's health condition, injury or disability is also considered permanent when they have been diagnosed with a terminal illness (where the client is not expected to live longer than 2 years). Severely means that the client cannot regularly work 15 hours or more per week in open employment. Open employment is any employment other than sheltered employment. Note the client could be in sheltered employment if the employment conditions need to be specifically designed to cater for their needs for them to work. This applies whether the client is seeking full-time employment, self-employment, supported employment or contract work.

chunks.title: Simplified access to Supported Living Payment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Some clients with a specific diagnosis will access Supported Living Payment without having a detailed assessment of their capacity to work. Clients who have accessed Supported Living Payment through this process will never have their capacity to work reassessed.

chunks.title: Medical and/or disability information — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: When applying for Supported Living Payment, the client can provide either a medical certificate or suitable existing assessments from their registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist. Note a psychologist cannot complete a medical certificate for the person who is being cared for when assessing a client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).

chunks.title: Referral to a second opinion by a designated health practitioner — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The client may be referred to a designated health practitioner when: - their registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist indicates that a second opinion from a designated health practitioner is appropriate or - eligibility to Supported Living Payment is unclear from the medical information they have provided or - they are unable or fail to provide existing medical reports or a medical certificate from their own registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist, and MSD holds insufficient information to decide eligibility or - MSD is concerned the information on the medical certificate and the diagnosis are inconsistent Note if the client is not both permanently and severely restricted for work, they may still be limited in their capacity to work, or be permanently restricted but able to work more than 15 hours. In these cases MSD should consider whether they are eligible to get Jobseeker Support or Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship. If the client meets the medical qualification but they do not meet the residence requirements for Supported Living Payment, they may be able to get an Emergency Benefit, see: Non-residentially qualified.

chunks.title: Medical reassessment for Supported Living Payment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Medical reassessment for Supported Living Payment
When you grant Supported Living Payment you will need to decide if your client's entitlement should be reassessed:
- in 2 years or
- never (if the client qualifies to be given simplified access)
The decision to never reassess a client's capacity to work is based on whether the client has a condition that meets the criteria for them to be given simplified access. This means the client's capacity to work is unlikely to ever improve enough that they could regularly work 15 hours per week or more in open employment.
All other clients will be reassessed in 2 years as their capacity for work could improve enough that they could regularly work 15 hours per week or more in open employment. The reassessment is not reviewing whether the health condition is permanent or not.
For more information see:
- Simplified Access to Supported Living Payment
## Impact of their health condition or disability could improve over time - 2 year reassessment
The 2 year reassessment acknowledges that for some clients it is reasonable to expect the impact of their permanent health condition or disability may change over time and the client's capacity for work may improve. The client's capacity to work may improve over time because the impact of the client's health condition or disability reduces. This could be because:
- their condition improves or
- the client becomes better at managing the impact on their capacity to work over time
## Impact of their health condition or disability is unlikely to improve over time - never reassess
A small number of clients will qualify to be given simplified access because the impact of their health condition or disability on their capacity for work is unlikely to ever improve enough that they could regularly work 15 hours per week or more in open employment and therefore will never require medical reassessment.
## Work and Income can reassess eligibility at any time
Work and Income can continue to reassess a client's medical eligibility at any time if they think that the client's capacity for work has changed.
This includes when it has previously been decided their capacity to work does not need to be reassessed.
## Further advice
If you are uncertain about the medical reassessment period, refer to the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] for advice.

chunks.title: Medical terms — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Medical terms
Here are some of the medical terms you may find included in your clients' reports, assessments or medical certificates.
## Chronic
A long standing condition - usually existing for longer than 6 weeks.

chunks.title: Meeting job search requirements — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Meeting job search requirements
Job search requirements apply to:
- partners with full-time and part-time work obligations
To help decide if a partner is meeting the job search requirements, you will need to consider the following:
1. If the partner had the opportunity, would they:
- be available for work of at least 20 hours per week (part-time work obligations)
- be available for work of at least 30 hours per week (full-time work obligations)
- accept any suitable job offers within their abilitiesNote that this can include weekend work depending on their individual circumstances
- not restrict their job search to vacancies within their own trade
- not restrict their job search to vacancies in their chosen occupation
- not move frequently from one area to another with no intention of getting a job
2. Has the partner begun to take steps to find work? For example by:
- searching newspapers and other media for vacancies
- making applications for suitable jobs
- contacting employers about vacancies

chunks.title: Method of payment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Method of payment
There are two ways that young partners aged 16 or 17 years with no children and 16 to 19 years with dependent children can have their portion of their benefit paid to them depending on whether the young partner is subject to youth money management or not.
## Young person is subject to youth money management
Where a young person is subject to youth money management their Supported Living Payment, family tax credit, Best Start tax credit and any extra help (except Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance) is paid via:
- payment directly to supplier (eg a payees redirection for accommodation costs, utility costs and lawful debts)
- in-hand allowance which is paid directly to the young person's bank account
- payment card - the young person is able to purchase goods (such as food and groceries) from approved suppliers
Note Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance is paid directly to the young person's bank account.
## Review of decision
A young person cannot review the decision on how the Supported Living Payment is paid to them.

chunks.title: Misconduct — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Misconduct
An employer can only terminate a partner's employment on the basis of misconduct if the partner has seriously breached their contract of employment.
This only applies to partners on Supported Living Payment who have work obligations.
Note that if a partner's employment has been terminated during a 90 day employment trial, generally this is not the result of misconduct. An employer is not obligated to give a reason for dismissal during a 90 day employment trial. However, if the employer alleges misconduct by the employee and provides some evidence, misconduct should be investigated in the usual way.
## Situations where the voluntary unemployment 13 week non-entitlement period would apply
Situations where a partner would be subject to a 13 week non-entitlement include (but are not limited to):
- a previously self-employed partner applies for Supported Living Payment and would have work obligations because they have closed or sold a viable business without a good and sufficient reason
- a partner who is currently receiving Supported Living Payment has part-time work obligations. The partner has left their part-time job without a good and sufficient reason.
- a partner has left a part-time job without a good and sufficient reason, a voluntary unemployment stand-down would apply if the income from the job was sufficient to support the person, and the job was for 13 weeks or more
For more information see:
- Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period
Before applying a 13 week non-entitlement period for misconduct, you should contact both the partner and their employer.
Contact the employer and ask them to complete the Employment and earnings information for applications (V06) form.
If the employer does not return the form or the reason for termination is not given, no further contact with the employer should be made.
If there is conflicting evidence or the reason for leaving employment is not agreed between the partner and the employer, you should give the partner the benefit of the doubt.
Each partner's circumstances need to be carefully investigated. If you are uncertain whether a voluntary unemployment stand-down should be imposed, discuss the partner's circumstances, in the first instance, with a service centre trainer and then with Helpline (if still required).
If you decide to apply a voluntary unemployment stand-down, you will need to:
- advise the partner of your decision
- send the partner the 'Voluntary Unemployed' letter to confirm your decision. A copy of the letter is available in CMS letter templates
- the partner's commencement date letter will confirm your decision and outline their rate of payment
- add the date that a non-entitlement period will apply from and the appropriate VU reason code to the SSTDA SWIFTT screen
- conditionally grant the benefit using code 024 (VU imposed) on the SPGRT SWIFTT screen
- make notes in CMS outlining your decision
Ensure the benefit remains conditionally granted. Do not decline the benefit.
For more information see:
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed
- Misconduct
- Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer

chunks.title: Youth money management activity — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Youth money management activity
Young partners who have youth activity obligations are required to co-operate with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service in managing the spending of their benefit and provide information as required.
The young person must:
- attend and participate in regular one-on-one discussions on budgeting
and provide information on:
- their accommodation costs (for example rent, board) and service costs (for example power, phone)
- any other lawful debts and liabilities (for example court fines, Work and Income debts, Child Support payments, hire purchase)
- how they spend their in-hand allowance and
- how they spend any money allocated to their payment card
For more information see:
## Exception
A young partner aged 16 or 17 years (with no children) or 16 to 19 years (with dependent children) will not be subject to youth money management and will have their full payment paid directly to them when they have:
- demonstrated continued compliance with their obligations and been assessed as being financially competent or
- opted out of youth money management when they turned 18 years (for young partners without dependent children), or 20 years (for young partners with dependent children), and have chosen to stay in the Youth Service and complete their course of study, training or work-based learning
For more information see:

chunks.title: More than one caregiver — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## More than one caregiver
Where the person needs 24-hour continuous care it is not reasonable to expect one person to manage. However, there is no provision to pay more than one Supported Living Payment in respect of the same person.
District Health Board assistance may be available when more than one caregiver is needed.
For more information see:
- District Health Board assistance

chunks.title: NASC (Needs Assessment Service Co-ordination) assessment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If your client has a physical, intellectual or sensory impairment they may have a Needs Assessment Service Co-ordination (NASC) assessment which you can use to decide their entitlement to Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Who won't have a NASC assessment? — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Generally people who require an assessment solely as a result of a mental health need, addiction or as a result of a personal health need are not assessed by NASC agencies (unless a District Health Board has contracted this service separately). If your client has a mental health need, addiction or disability as a result of a personal health need they may have been assessed by another part of the health sector. You may be able to use these assessments to decide if your client is entitled to Supported Living Payment. For more information see: - Other types of assessment

chunks.title: What are NASC assessments? — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: NASCs are organisations contracted to the Ministry of Health to work with disabled people to help identify their needs and to outline what disability support services are available. NASC agencies may also contract with other parts of the health system (eg District Health Boards) to provide needs assessments for clients with mental health or addiction issues. The purpose of the NASC assessment is to decide what is needed to maximise a person's independence so they can participate as fully as possible in society. NASC agencies allocate Ministry of Health funded support services and assist with facilitating access to other supports.

chunks.title: Who does NASC assessments? — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: NASC assessments are undertaken by a number of organisations around New Zealand. There are 14 NASC agencies contracted by the Ministry of Health operating around New Zealand. For contact details, see the Ministry of Health website.

chunks.title: What will I see in a NASC assessment? — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: NASC assessments provide a comprehensive needs assessment report. These reports may also include a medical specialist report that confirms the person's diagnosis. All NASC agencies have a standard needs assessment report which covers the following areas: - assessment details (such as date assessment completed, where it was completed and when the person needs to be reassessed) - disability/diagnosis - who was present at the assessment - history/events leading to assessment - present living situation - covers a description of the person's current living situation - current support networks - communication - mobility - covers mobility inside and outside the home, in the community, transfers, transport, driving - sensory function - covers vision, hearing, speech - household management - covers activities such as shopping, meal preparation, housework, finance, home safety etc - personal care - covers ability to get in and out of their bed, bathing/showering, dressing/undressing, dental care, personal hygiene etc - medications and disability related costs - memory behaviour cognition - covers memory, behaviour, delusions/hallucinations, anxiety, supervision etc - other information such as educational/vocational/voluntary work/activities, social recreational, spiritual/cultural, client goals, other information - carer support information - current situation The NASC report may be particularly useful in establishing severity of your client's disability. For more information see: - Age of assessment - Use all information available - Interpreting NASC assessments - Diagnosis not available in existing assessments - Helping your client obtain existing assessments

chunks.title: Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes where a partner has a drug issue identified by the Alcohol Drug Helpline - Work and Income Support Service and is engaging and participating in services and support offered by the Alcohol Drug Helpline - Work and Income Support Service.
The partner can be asked to provide verification from the Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] for beneficiaries. The verification must state the duration or time that the partner is receiving support. There is a Drug test obligations Helpline verification form that will be completed by Helpline staff and sent to the partner. It is up to the partner to provide this form as verification.
The Alcohol Drug Helpline - Work and Income Support Service will offer the following support and services:
- brief interventions (series of telephone contacts)
- brief assessment (brief clinical assessment) or
- referral for a comprehensive face to face AOD assessment and treatment plan or
- referral to other health or social service agencies or
- confirmation of drug treatment details
For more information see:
- Drug test obligations failures - Good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: No stand-down applies — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## No stand-down applies
An initial stand-down is not imposed in the following situations:
- Transfer between benefits
- Temporary employment
- Prisoners
- In residential care
- Applying for Supported Living Payment
- Entering a refuge
- Client leaves Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre
When no stand-down applies, the commencement date of the benefit is the later of either:
- the entitlement date or
- the application date
Note when no stand-down applies, the 28-day rule does not apply.

chunks.title: Clients and partners without dependent children — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Clients and partners without dependent children
A partner without dependent children will have their benefit suspended from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
Their payments will remain suspended for up to 13 weeks after Community Work Experience was first imposed, unless they recomply.
A partner may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be resumed from the date that the partner recomplies.
When a partner’s benefit has remained suspended because they have not recomplied, their benefit will cancel 13 weeks after Community Work Experience was first imposed.
## Clients and partners with dependent children
Clients and partners with dependent children have 50% payment protection.
A partner with dependent children will have their payments reduce by 50% from the first day of the week that they were considered non-compliant.
A partner may complete a recompliance activity during this period that is the same or similar to the activity that they originally failed. Their benefit will be resumed from the date that the partner has recomplied.
These partners will also be contacted after 2 weeks of receiving only 50% of their benefit. For more information see: Effect of sanctions on assistance

chunks.title: Non-entitlement period for 13 weeks — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Non-entitlement period for 13 weeks
A non-entitlement period of 13 weeks is a period where clients are unable to get a benefit because they:
- have become voluntarily unemployed without a good and sufficient reason (partners)
- are applying for a benefit because they were dismissed by their employer for misconduct (partners)
- have failed their obligations for a third time in the last 24 months (or 12 months for young partners with youth activity obligations) of continuous benefit receipt (as a grade 3 sanction) or
- have refused an offer of suitable employment (partners with work obligations)
## Non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or dismissal
This only applies to partners on Supported Living Payment who have full-time or part-time work obligations.
Before imposing a 13-week non-entitlement period, the reason why the partner has left employment needs to be carefully investigated to determine whether it is appropriate to apply a 13-week non-entitlement period.
For voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct the 13-week non-entitlement period starts from the day after the date the partner's employment ceased.
For more information see:
- Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
## Non-entitlement period for obligations failures
Where a client fails their obligations and has a grade 3 sanction imposed, they will have a 13-week non-entitlement period.
For imposing a grade 3 sanction the 13-week non-entitlement period starts the date after the 5 working day notice period.
For more information see:
- Grade 3 sanction or job refusal failure non-entitlement period
Also see:
- Effect of a non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Financial assistance during non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Non-entitlement period should not be imposed — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: There are specific circumstances where a non-entitlement period is not considered, because they are accepted to be good and sufficient reasons for leaving employment, but the initial stand-down must still apply. These situations include where a partner has: - lost their job during a 90 day employment trial (except where the employer alleges misconduct) - recently returned to New Zealand - taken voluntary redundancy because another employee would lose their job if they remained - left work that isn't suitable - worked for a temporary period

chunks.title: Partners who lose their job during a 90 day employment trial — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: An employer may terminate the employee's employment trial for any reason at any time before the end of the employment trial period. An employer is not obliged to give a reason for ceasing the partner's employment during an employment trial. A non-entitlement period is not considered if an employer does not give a reason for ending an employee's employment trial. Note when an employer alleges misconduct by the employee and provides some evidence of the misconduct then a non-entitlement period can be considered and investigated in the usual way.

chunks.title: Clients or partners returning to New Zealand from overseas — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: A non-entitlement period is not considered when a client or partner returns to New Zealand after working overseas. Clients or partners returning to New Zealand after working overseas do not receive a voluntary unemployment stand-down.

chunks.title: Voluntary redundancy — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Where partners have taken voluntary redundancy, they do not receive a voluntary unemployment stand-down if they or another employee must lose their job if the partner remains in that job.

chunks.title: Partner has left temporary employment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: A 13 week non-entitlement period does not apply when the person was in temporary part-time or full-time employment (employment of less than 26 weeks) and they have applied for a benefit after their employment came to an end. It may be applied if the partner voluntarily left their temporary employment before it was due to end. Temporary employment can include employment during an employment trial period of up to 90 days if the partner with work obligations was receiving a benefit and is reapplying for Supported Living Payment as their employment has ceased. This also applies when a partner with work obligations has been working more than 30 hours a week on Supported Living Payment and receiving a salary or hourly wage that does not fully reduce the benefit, and they have reached the end of their 26 week temporary period in which this is allowable. Note the partner's average weekly income is not required where the partner has been in temporary employment for less than 26 weeks. However, the partner's final pay details are required to determine the date of event and entitlement date. For more information see: - Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment - Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer

chunks.title: Criteria to receive a non-financial sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Criteria to receive a non-financial sanction
A client or partner can only get a non-financial sanction if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they meet with MSD within the 5 working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure decision is not disputed and overturned, and
- a non-financial sanction would be appropriate for them based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or they have dependent children
MSD must assess a client's circumstances and determine which non-financial sanction, if any, is most appropriate for the client. Each non-financial sanction has different factors to consider.
Primary Supported Living Payment clients do not have work obligations, although they may have work preparation obligations in some circumstances.
This means it is unlikely they will have an obligation failure, so they would generally not have a sanction imposed.
Partners of a Supported Living Payment client who have work or work preparation obligations are able to have a non-financial sanction imposed if they meet the criteria.
## Client meets with MSD after 5 working days
A non-financial sanction can only be imposed if a client meets with MSD within the 5 working day notice period. This is because a financial sanction will be automatically applied after 5 working days unless MSD has decided to impose a non-financial sanction instead.
If a client meets with MSD after 5 working days, they are not eligible for a non-financial sanction. MSD cannot change ta financial sanction to a non-financial sanction after it has been applied.
## Change in circumstances while subject to a non-financial sanction
A client may have a change in circumstances that means they are no longer required to comply with an obligation they have failed.
In this case, the non-financial sanction no longer applies from the day that a client's circumstances change.
For more information see:
## Non-financial sanctions, Emergency Housing Grants and Special Needs Grants
Clients who have a non-financial sanction imposed cannot get an Emergency Housing Grant or a Special Needs Grant. MSD should take this into consideration before choosing to impose a non-financial sanction.
For more information see:
- Paying other assistance during a sanction

chunks.title: Non residentially qualified — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Non residentially qualified
A client who is permanently and severely restricted for work who does not meet the residence requirements to be granted Supported Living Payment may be eligible for an Emergency Benefit.
Note if a client is not permanently and severely restricted for work, other benefit assistance should be considered, for example Jobseeker Support or Jobseeker Support on grounds of hardship.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Emergency Benefit Non residentially qualified for Supported Living Payment
- Emergency Benefit Unable to earn a sufficient livelihood
- Emergency Benefit Qualifications

chunks.title: Number of dependent children — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Number of dependent children
If a client had a dependent child (or children) in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application the child (or children) must be taken into account when determining the stand-down.
For example, if a single client with one dependent child applies for benefit the stand-down period will be based on a single client with one child. However, if this client had 2 dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application, the stand-down period will be based on a single client with two dependent children.
This is regardless of whether the child is still in the client's care at the time of application.
For more information see:
- Dependent child
- Orphans Benefit/Unsupported Childs Benefit

chunks.title: Obligations failures — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If a client or partner fails to comply with their obligations, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. MSD must be satisfied that the client or partner would have had no good and sufficient reason for their failure based on the information available. For social obligations, MSD must consider whether the client and their partner (if any) have taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, and must go through the regular engagement and support process before considering that the client has failed their obligation. Note primary clients getting Supported Living Payment may have work preparation obligations if they have been assessed as having a capacity for work. Some primary clients getting Supported Living Payment will have no work preparation obligations. Only the partner may have an obligation failure applied for failing to meet their work obligations or drug test obligations. For more information see: - Failing more than one obligation at the same time - Assessing capacity for work preparation obligation - primary client - Work or work preparation obligations - Social Obligations - Social obligations Regular engagement and support process - Social obligations All reasonable steps to meet social obligations - Drug test obligations - Work with contracted service provider obligation - Work ability assessment obligation - Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure - Youth activity obligations failures Note for a partner who has full-time or part-time work obligations leaving part-time work averaging less than 20 hours per week, without good and sufficient reason or through misconduct, is also an obligations failure, but may not be specified in the client's work obligations. Once MSD has decided that the client or partner has failed their obligations, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. The client or partner will then be sent a letter stating that their benefit will be sanctioned and that their benefit will only be increased or resumed if they: - complete a recompliance activity - dispute the decision to impose the sanction and MSD accepts that they have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting their obligations - lodge a Review of Decision and MSD reconsiders their position and agrees with the client's review or - lodge an appeal to the Medical Appeal Board (drug test failure only) Once a client has completed their recompliance activity, their benefit can be increased or resumed from the date MSD is satisfied the client started the activity. For some clients, if it's their first obligation failure they may be eligible for a non-financial sanction instead of a financial sanction. For more information, see: Non-financial sanctions.

chunks.title: Obligations failures — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: All clients have a 5 working day notice period to dispute or recomply before the sanction is imposed. If a client or partner recomplies within the 5 working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the obligations failure is recorded. For more information see: - When the sanction is imposed - Counting previous obligations failures - Failing more than one obligation at the same time Clients have not failed their obligations if they do not complete or undertake Voluntary Work or Activity in the Community.

chunks.title: Effect on rates payable — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: For financial sanctions, the reduction, suspension and cancellation applies to the main benefit the client or partner is getting. For couples it applies to each person's portion of the married rate of benefit. The effect on Extra help depends on the level of sanction imposed, the type of Extra help, and whether the client or partner has dependent children. For young partners, the effect of a sanction on the client's assistance depends on whether the client has children and is youth money managed or not. Non-financial sanctions do not affect the rate payable for a client or partner.

chunks.title: Obligations — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Obligations
Supported Living Payment clients and partners (if any) have the following obligations:
- they must advise of any change in circumstances that affect their entitlement or rate of benefit payable
- if they have dependent children, take all reasonable steps to meet social obligations that apply for each dependent child in their care
- if required, to undertake and pass a pre-employment or pre-course drug test
- if required, participate in a Work Ability Assessment
- if required, work with a contracted service provider
- advise Work and Income if they are intending to travel overseas, before they depart
## Work preparation obligations for primary clients
Primary clients getting Supported Living Payment may have work preparation obligations where they have been assessed as having capacity to prepare for work.
For more information see:
- Assessing capacity for work preparation obligation - primary client
## Work or work preparation obligations for partners
Partners of clients getting Supported Living Payment either have work or work preparation obligations (including drug test work obligations), depending on whether they have children (or not), the age of their youngest dependent child and whether they qualify for an exemption.
For more information see:
- Work or work preparation obligations
- Drug test obligations
## Partners aged 16 to 19 years old
Young partners (aged 16 to 19 years old) of clients getting Supported Living Payment have youth activity obligations and not work or work preparation obligations if they are:
- aged 16 or 17 years old without dependent children or
- aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children and
- married to, or in a civil union or in a de facto relationship with a person getting Supported Living Payment.
For more information see:
- Youth activity obligations
Note social obligations do not apply to young partners of Supported Living Payment as some of their youth activity obligations are similar to social obligations.

chunks.title: Ongoing Resourcing Schemes (ORS) assessment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Ongoing Resourcing Schemes (ORS) assessment
If your client is applying for Supported Living Payment while they are at school or if they have recently left school they may provide you with evidence that they are or have been receiving ongoing funding through the Ongoing Resourcing Schemes (ORS).
## What is ORS?
The ORS scheme provides resources for a very small group of students throughout New Zealand with severe disabilities in the areas of learning, vision, hearing, mobility or language use and social communication. Most of these students have this level of need throughout their school years and are identified early in their development. Many receive a comprehensive early intervention service before they begin school.
There are two resourcing schemes available through Special Education:
Resourcing Scheme - for students who meet the criteria at the time of application but it is unclear whether their needs will remain at the same level throughout their school years. They are reviewed after four years of receiving the funding. After the reviewable period some students then receive support from the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme.
Ongoing Resourcing Scheme - for students verified with very high or high needs at the time of application and where it is clear they will continue to require this high level of specialist support until they leave school.
## Assessing permanent and severe
Your client may meet the medical criteria for Supported Living Payment if:
- they are currently receiving ongoing funding from the ORS scheme or
- they have recently left school and they received ongoing ORS funding from the ORS scheme in the year before they left school
If your client has been assessed as needing ongoing funding through the ORS scheme they need significant assistance to access the education curriculum and this impact is likely to be permanent.
It is reasonable to then translate the impact on accessing the curriculum to the impact on your client's ability to work for the purposes of benefit entitlement.

chunks.title: Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit under 3 years — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit under 3 years
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
In some cases a partner may be caring for a child under 3 years for whom they are receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit.
Partners granted this exemption will be subject to work preparation obligations.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted in SWIFTT for 12 months initially or to when the child turns 3 years old, whichever is earlier.
The exemption can be renewed after 12 months provided the child is still under 3 years and the parent still qualifies for benefit.
## SWIFTT process
Partners who receive Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit for a child under 3 years are not automatically exempt in SWIFTT. You need to add an exemption on the main benefit record via SWTDA in SWIFTT.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions

chunks.title: Other types of assessment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Other types of assessment
Your client may provide another type of assessment that satisfies you that the client is permanently and severely restricted in their ability to work.
One assessment may not be sufficient to establish entitlement to Supported Living Payment. Some assessments are most useful to establish severity. You may need to use other assessments or ask your client for information to establish their diagnosis. For more information see:
- Diagnosis not available in existing assessment
- Use all information available
If the information you have confirms that your client meets the criteria for Supported Living Payment, you can consider granting Supported Living Payment. You will need to link your client's benefit record to the designated doctor named "Existing Assessments - Other" in the SDOCS screen in SWIFTT.
If you are not satisfied by the information provided that your client meets the medical criteria for Supported Living Payment, refer to your Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] for advice.
For more information see:
- Deciding Supported Living Payment from a medical certificate
- Age of assessment
- Deciding permanence and severity - existing assessments
- Helping your client obtain existing assessments
- Child Disability Allowance assessment

chunks.title: Outcome of case — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Outcome of case
Outcomes from mediation are strictly confidential to the parties involved, so any information about the settlement will have to be obtained from the partner.
Where a partner wins their personal grievance case, and receives a wage settlement for a period during which a benefit with work obligations was paid:
- review the partner's entitlement date and non-entitlement period assessments and
- establish any overpayments
If it is determined that the employer was not at fault, then a 13 week non-entitlement period for misconduct can be applied.
If the settlement order states that the payment or part payment is to cover legal or other costs, do not recover benefit received from the payment amount. If it is unclear what the partner's settlement is for, contact Helpline for assistance.
If the case is settled but no party is admitting fault, a decision must be made as to whether the voluntary unemployed provisions apply. Use all evidence available but give the benefit of the doubt to the partner. Contact your local solicitor for advice.
For more information see:
- Proof partner is challenging dismissal
- Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer

chunks.title: Outcome of designated health practitioner assessment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Outcome of designated health practitioner assessment
Where the designated health practitioner assessment confirms your client's entitlement to Supported Living Payment, you should grant the application or, where benefit is current, extend your client's entitlement accordingly.
## No entitlement - application to be declined
When the report from the designated health practitioner indicates that your client does not meet the medical eligibility criteria for Supported Living Payment, you should decline the application and advise the client, including their right to appeal the decision. Medical decisions are appealed to the Medical Appeals Board.
Note that where the medical information indicates that your client meets the medical criteria for Jobseeker Support on the ground of health condition, injury or disability you should discuss with the client whether they would like to apply. If the client does want to apply for Jobseeker Support on the ground of health condition, injury or disability, you should treat the application for Supported Living Payment as an application for Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: Parent is being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020 — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Parent is being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020
All parents are legally obliged to ensure their children are enrolled in and attending school from the age of 6 to 16.
Parents can be prosecuted and fined under the Education and Training Act 2020 if their children don't attend school. This can happen when:
- there has been, without explanation, ongoing and irregular attendance by the child at school after support has been offered to the family or
- the parent has made little or no attempt to do anything about ensuring the child attends school
If a parent is in the process of being prosecuted under the Education and Training Act 2020, you must not ask them to comply with this social obligation, or initiate an obligations failure for non-attendance.
Note you need to record this as an exception in OBMAN using 'Parent is in prosecution for truant child' as the obligation exception reason.

chunks.title: Parenting obligations — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Parenting obligations
Young partners aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children are required to:
- participate in an approved parenting programme
- enrol their child with a Primary Health Organisation, where a local provider is available
- register their child (if aged under 5 years) with a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and keep up-to-date with their visits and
- ensure the child's attendance at an approved Early Childhood Education programme or in other suitable childcare, while they are in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work
For more information see:
- Approved parenting programme
- Enrolment with primary health care provider
- Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits
- Ensuring child attends suitable childcare
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months

chunks.title: Partner accepts the results of a failed screening test — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Partner accepts the results of a failed screening test
A partner will be asked by the employer, training provider or the drug test provider to confirm that they accept the result of the failed screening test. They can accept the result of the failed drug test by:
- signing the Pre-employment Drug Test Result Confirmation Form or
- verbally accepting the result
When a client has accepted the results, this means that they understand:
- there is no requirement to send the failed screening test sample to a laboratory for evidential testing
- this may result in a sanction being imposed and
- they may have to repay Work and Income for the cost of the failed drug test
Before you initiate an obligations failure for a partner because they have failed a drugs test, without having a good and sufficient reason, you must receive confirmation from the employer that the partner has failed the test.
Once you have received confirmation from the employer or training provider that a client has failed the screening test, and all testing has been completed, an obligations failure should be initiated.
Although the partner can still dispute other parts of the decision, by providing a good and sufficient reason for the obligations failure, they cannot dispute the result of the screening drug test because they have already accepted the result.
For more information see:
- Drug test obligations failure
- Informing a partner of the drug test obligation failure
- Reimbursement to employers and debt recovery
- Drug test obligation failures - Good and sufficient reasons
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures

chunks.title: Sample sent for evidential test — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Sample sent for evidential test
Some employers, training providers, or drug test providers, will send all screening test samples for evidential testing, regardless of whether the partner accepted the result of the failed screening test or not.
If the partner passes the evidential drug test, then the partner is not required to repay the Ministry of Social Development for the cost of either the failed screening drug test or the evidential drug test.
If the partner also fails the evidential drug test, the partner is required to repay the Ministry for the costs of both the failed tests (screening and evidential)

chunks.title: Partner is overseas — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If a client's partner is overseas and the couple still consider themselves to be in a marriage or civil union type relationship, you must take into consideration the partner's residence status and reasons for the partner being overseas before deciding the rate of payment. Any income received by the partner overseas should be charged against the benefit rate whether or not they are included in the client's benefit. For more information see: - Charging income If the partner cannot meet the qualifications for the benefit because the client is overseas, for example, they cannot meet their work obligations, they may be able to receive an Emergency Benefit. For more information see: - Emergency Benefit Qualifications

chunks.title: Partner detained overseas or missing — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If the partner intends to live in New Zealand but has not yet arrived, they are not considered ordinarily resident and cannot be included in the client's benefit. Where the client still considers themselves married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, the rate payable to the client is half the married, civil union or de facto rate. A higher married, civil union or de facto rate is payable if the client has a dependent child. See: - Partner not qualified

chunks.title: Partners temporarily overseas — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If the partner was resident in New Zealand but has left the country temporarily, they can be included in the client's benefit at grant, as they are considered ordinarily resident. If the partner included in the benefit does not have work obligations, payment can only continue for the first 28 days from the entitlement date. If the partner included in the benefit does have work obligations, payment cannot continue unless they have an approved travel reason. If you are paying the partner while they are overseas, payment should be stopped from the beginning of the third week if the partner does not have work obligations and has not returned.

chunks.title: Partners overseas long-term — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If a partner was resident in New Zealand but has left the country and has no definite plans to return (for example, they have been deported) they are not considered ordinarily resident and cannot be included in the benefit. The rate payable to the client is half the married, civil union or de facto rate. The single or sole parent rate can only be paid where the marriage, civil union or de facto relationship no longer exists. A higher married, civil union or de facto rate is payable if the client has a dependent child. See: - Partner not qualified For more information see: - Partners residence status - Partner not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand - Accommodation Supplement Partner overseas - Accommodation Supplement Not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand

chunks.title: Partner not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Partner not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand
You can pay a single or sole parent rate to a client whose partner is not a permanent resident or is unlawfully resident in New Zealand; however, you have to take their joint income and assets into account.
There are some exceptions.
For more information see:
- Partner's residence status
Clients who were receiving a married rate of benefit prior to the 8 August 2001 and have a partner/spouse without permanent residence included in their benefit will continue to be paid at the married, civil union or de facto rate until their benefit is cancelled.
To pay the Supported Living Payment at the appropriate single/sole parent rate you need to:
- link the partner and primary through CMS
- do not include the partner in the benefit in SREG
- enter the appropriate rate of payment code in the SDT1A screen
- complete notes in the client event note
- contact the Card Centre on the day that the benefit is granted to stop a Community Services Card being issued to the non-resident partner

chunks.title: Partner not qualified — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Partner not qualified
When a client getting Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury, disability) has a partner who is not granted a main benefit in their own right, then income is charged against the total couple rate of Supported Living Payment:
- 30 cents is taken from the couple rate of benefit for each dollar of income that the client (and their partner) earn over $8,320 per year, but not more than $13,000 per year
- 70 cents for every dollar of income that is more than $13,000 per year
MSD can pay half the couple rate of payment (with or without dependent children) to a client if their partner:
- has a 13-week non-entitlement period
- is on strike or
- has an obligations failure
MSD can pay a single or sole parent rate to a client whose partner is unlawfully resident or is not a permanent resident in New Zealand, but MSD has to take the couple's joint income and assets into account. For the exceptions, see:
- Partners residence status
A higher couple rate of Supported Living Payment is payable to a client with dependent children, when their partner is not getting a main benefit as shown in the table below.
Primary client

- is getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
- does not qualify for a main benefit

- is getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
- does not meet the residency criteria to be included in the benefit, and sole parent rate is not applicable
$392.94 as at 1 April 2026

chunks.title: Partner's job ceases during an employment trial period — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Partner's job ceases during an employment trial period
Any employment that has an employment trial period included in a partner's employment agreement is assessed the same as any other employment.
A partner's job can cease during the employment trial period for any number of reasons, such as:
- the employer not being able to afford the partner's wages
- the employer's belief that the partner lacks the necessary skills
- misconduct
- any other reason the employer decides to cease the partner's employment or
- the partner leaving of their own accord
When an employer gives the partner notice during the employment trial, they are not required to advise why they have decided to end the partner's employment. They are however, required to provide details of their last date of employment and the date they will be paid to.
If the employer gave notice to the partner of ending their employment after the employment trial, the employer must provide the partner with the reason for ending their employment (ie the employment trial rules do not apply).
To determine the commencement date of the benefit, the partner needs to provide evidence and reasons for ceasing their employment, their last day of duty and last date paid to.
If the partner cannot provide this evidence and reason for their employment ceasing, their last day of duty or last date paid to, you can contact the partner's employer and ask them to complete the Employment and earnings information for applications (V06) form.
If the partner's employer does not provide the reason for the partner's employment ceasing during the employment trial, accept the partner's reasons for the termination and continue with the application process. However, the employer must complete the date ceased and last pay details.
For more information see:
- Employment trial period of up to 90 days

chunks.title: Partner's residence status — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: When a client has a partner, you must also check the partner's residence status because the rate of benefit payable depends on whether or not the partner is included. The partner can be included in the benefit if they are: - a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (ie not be in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or - deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) and - generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand Note a partner can only be included in Supported Living Payment if it is granted on the ground that the client is permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work or totally blind. Partners cannot be included in Supported Living Payment if it is granted on the ground that the client is caring for a person who requires full-time care and attention. Where the primary client is receiving Supported Living Payment on the ground that they are caring for a person who requires full-time care and attention, their partner (if any) may be eligible for a benefit in their own right. For more information see: - Proof of residence - Deciding ordinarily resident If a partner has one of the following they cannot be included in the benefit: - a temporary entry visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009 - a temporary permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987 (such as a visitor permit, a work permit or a student permit) If the partner does not have a current permit or visa that allows them to remain in New Zealand then they are in New Zealand unlawfully and you cannot include the partner in the benefit, unless one of the exceptions listed below apply. Where the partner is in New Zealand unlawfully or is not a permanent resident, pay the client at a single or sole parent rate taking into consideration all of the couple's income and assets. Contact the Card Centre when granting the primary benefit to ensure that a Community Services Card is not issued to the non-resident partner. Encourage the partner to follow up their residence status.

chunks.title: Exceptions — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: There are some situations where a partner is exempt and can be included in the benefit without having been granted permanent residence. These are: - a person lawfully present in New Zealand who is awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protection status in New Zealand or - a person who has refugee or protection status in New Zealand or - a person applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 who is compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances or - an Australian citizen or resident as they are lawfully allowed in New Zealand without New Zealand citizenship or permanent residence For more information see: - Immigration status and supporting documents - Partner is overseas - Partner not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand - Permanent resident

chunks.title: Partners getting a benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension in their own right — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Partners getting a benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension in their own right
Income received by a couple, when the partner is getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension in their own right, should be charged against the half married, civil union or de facto rate of Supported Living Payment (health condition, injury or disability).
Note New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension is not included as income for this assessment.
## Partner getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension
Income (including their partner's incomes) is charged annually and at the following rates:
- 15 cents for each dollar of income that the client (and their partner) earn over $8,320 gross per year, but not more than $13,000 gross per year
- 35 cents for every dollar of income that is more than $13,000 gross per year

chunks.title: Partners with no children or youngest child 14+ years — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Partners with no children or youngest child 14+ years
Full-time work obligations apply to:
- partners with no children and
- partners with youngest child aged 14 years or over
Partners with full-time work obligations must make themselves available for suitable employment, training or other suitable activities of at least 30 hours or more each week.
If a partner is in employment for less than 30 hours each week, they are still expected to be available for other work, training or other activities up to a total of 30 hours each week. The partner must understand that they are still required to accept suitable full-time work if it becomes available.
For more information see:
- Work obligations - partners
- Hours range for suitable employment
Partners may participate in approved training as long as they continue to meet their work obligations, unless they are granted an exemption for approved full-time training. For more information see: In approved training (no children or child 14+)
- Approved training
- Exemptions - in approved full-time training
Partners may undertake volunteer work as long as they continue to meet their work obligations. For more information see:
- Voluntary Work [no link find out why]
Partners may apply for an exemption from their work obligations. For more information on exemptions see:
- Exemptions for partners
- Table of Exemptions
If a partner fails to comply with their work obligations, their portion of the benefit may be stopped. For more information see:
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures
## Partners aged 16 to 19 years old
Young partners (aged 16 to 19 years old) of clients receiving Supported Living Payment have youth activity obligations and not work or work preparation obligations if they are:
- aged 16 to 17 years old without dependent children or
- aged 16 to 19 years old with a dependent child or children and
- married to, or in a civil union or in a de facto relationship with a person receiving Supported Living Payment
See:

chunks.title: Partners with youngest child between 3 and 13 years — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Partners with youngest child between 3 and 13 years
Part-time work obligations apply to:
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years
The partner must make themselves available for suitable employment, training or other activities of at least 20 hours a week. For more information see:
- Work obligations - partners
Partners may do voluntary work but must be available to meet their work obligations. For more information see:
- Partners undertaking voluntary work
Partners may apply for an exemption from their work obligations. For more information on exemptions see:
- Exemptions for partners
- Table of Exemptions
If a partner fails to comply with their work obligations, their portion of the benefit may be stopped.
For more information see:
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures
If a partner with part-time obligations is already in employment for 20 hours or more each week, they are meeting their work obligations.
If they are in employment for less than 20 hours each week, they are still expected to be available for other work, training or any other activities.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations

chunks.title: Partners with youngest dependent child aged under 3 years — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Partners with youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
Work preparation obligations apply to:
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
The partner must take all reasonable steps to prepare them for work in the future. For more information see:
- Work preparation obligations - partners
Partners may apply for an exemption from their work preparation obligations. Generally, they can only be considered for a full exemption as work preparation obligations mean that they are required to plan for employment and undertake work preparation activities - the equivalent of a partial exemption. For more information see:
- Exemptions for partners
- Table of Exemptions
If a partner fails to comply with their work preparation obligations, they have an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Special Needs Grants — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Special Needs Grants
Clients are not entitled to Special Needs Grants if a sanction has been imposed. This applies to both financial and non-financial sanctions.
The only exception to this is if a client or partner has a health condition, injury or disability when a grade 3 sanction is imposed and they are incapable of participating in an approved activity for six weeks or programme of activities for 6 weeks. For more information see:
- Assistance during non-entitlement periods
- Assistance when a client is sanctioned
## Advances
If a client or partner has a 50% sanction imposed, and the client or partner is experiencing hardship they may apply for an Advance Payment of benefit. A discussion must be held with the client or partner about recomplying as the reduced rate of benefit will be contributing to their hardship.
Generally clients will not be entitled to advance payments of benefit when they have a 100% sanction imposed. This is because they will be contributing to their hardship through not recomplying. The client's first option to improve their financial situation is to recomply with their obligations and an advance cannot be paid when the client or partner has no means of repaying it.
A client can apply for an Advance Payment of Benefit if they have a non-financial sanction imposed, and may be eligible if they meet all the criteria.
## Assistance to transition into employment
Clients can get assistance to transition into employment if a sanction has been imposed and they meet the qualifications for it.
For more information see:
- Employment and work readiness Assistance to transition into employment

chunks.title: Payment for travel and other associated costs — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Payment for travel and other associated costs
You can pay actual and reasonable costs for travel, accommodation, meals and a support person or where appropriate an attendant carer for clients attending a Work Ability Assessment.
What is reasonable will depend on where the client lives, their family circumstances, and any health condition or disability they have.
For more information see:
- Work Ability Assessment
- Work Ability Assessment - Payment for travel and other associated costs [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Payment process — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Payment process
You will need to manually calculate the rate of benefit you decide to apply the income exemption to a severely disabled person's benefit.
You can contact Helpline if you need help to calculate assistance when disregarding your client's income due to severe disablement.
For more information see:
- Example - Supported Living Payment

chunks.title: Payment process for a young partner — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The couple's main benefit and any supplementary assistance will be apportioned between the couple. The young partner who is youth money managed, will have their portion of accommodation, service costs and lawful debts paid direct to a supplier from their portion of their main benefit and any ongoing extra help. The balance of payment, if any, is distributed between the young partner's payment card and the in-hand allowance. The maximum amount that can be paid direct to a young partner as an in-hand allowance is $50.00. The following process shows how a young partner's portion of benefit assistance is paid when they are subject to youth money management.

chunks.title: In-hand allowance — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: When a young partner is subject to youth money management, they can get an amount of up to $50 a week paid directly to them as an in-hand allowance. After the young partner's portion of accommodation, service costs and lawful debts are paid by redirection from their portion of their main benefit and any ongoing extra help, the balance of payment, if any, is distributed between the young partner's payment card and the in-hand allowance. The maximum amount that can be paid direct to a young partner as an in-hand allowance is $50.00.

chunks.title: Distribution of payment after redirections — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Generally, where there is more than $50.00 available after all of a young partner's redirections have occurred, $50.00 would be paid direct to the young partner and the remainder would be placed on their payment card, unless YSSU is satisfied that another distribution would be more appropriate for the young partner. Youth service providers are responsible for making recommendations to YSSU as to how their client's payments should be distributed between the payment card and in-hand allowance. When making these recommendations to YSSU, providers consider what would be the most appropriate distribution for the young partner, given their individual circumstances. YSSU then makes the final decision as to how the young partner's payment will be distributed, taking into account the information supplied by the young partner's service provider. Example 1 A young partner with a dependent child is renting and has $110.00 left after their accommodation and service costs and any debts have been paid. A maximum of $50.00 could be paid direct to the client. However, the service provider wants to ensure the young person has enough money to purchase a sufficient amount of food for her and her child. The young partner lives close to the school she is attending and the childcare centre her child is attending is also within walking distance. The provider discusses with the young person in their budgeting sessions what their spending habits are and the young partner advises that she goes to the market to get her fruit and vegetables. The provider decides to recommend the young person gets a $50.00 in-hand allowance and will review to see that she is doing this and has enough food with $60.00 on her payment card. YSSU makes a decision to agree with the recommendation and decides to pay the client a $50.00 in-hand allowance, and to put $60.00 on her payment card. Example 2 A young partner with no dependent children in a boarding situation has $80.00 left after her board costs (which include food) and any debts have been paid. The young partner has transport costs to get to school. The young partner must pay for their own lunch everyday as this is not included in the board payment.

chunks.title: Distribution of payment after redirections — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: After discussions with the young person, the provider recommends paying a $40.00 in-hand allowance to the young person and placing $40.00 on the payment card to be used to purchase food for lunches. YSSU decides to agree with the recommendation and decides to pay the client a $40.00 in-hand allowance and to put $40.00 on the payment card.

chunks.title: Payment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Supported Living Payment is paid weekly on a Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. Payment is from Monday to Sunday and is made one week in arrears. Generally, payment must be made directly to the client. However, where there is good cause, the client's benefit can be paid to another person, agent or institution. For more information see: - Core policy Redirection of benefit payment

chunks.title: Exception for young partners — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: There are two ways that young partners aged 16 or 17 (with no children) and 16 to 19 years (with dependent children) can have their portion of their benefit paid to them depending on whether the young partner is subject to youth money management or not.

chunks.title: Young partner is not subject to youth money management — main benefits > supported living payment
