chunks.text: Where a young partner is not subject to youth money management they can get their portion of their main benefit payment, family tax credit, Best Start tax credit and any Extra Help paid directly to their bank account.

chunks.title: Young partner is subject to youth money management — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If a young partner is subject to youth money management the young partner's portion of main benefit, family tax credit, Best Start tax credit and any Extra help (except Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance) is paid via: - payment directly to supplier (e.g. a payee redirection for accommodation costs, utility costs and lawful debts) - in-hand allowance which is paid directly to the young person's bank account - payment card - the young person is able to purchase goods (such as food and groceries) from approved suppliers Note Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance is paid directly to the young person's bank account. For more information see: - Redirection for young partners It is a condition of getting a benefit that the client provides a bank account number. MSD can request the client to provide an IRD number or evidence of their IRD number. For more information see: - IRD number for client or partner who is apportioned assistance - IRD number for partner who is not apportioned assistance

chunks.title: Rate of payment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The rate of Supported Living Payment that can be paid depends on the client's: - age - relationship status - dependent children See: - Deskfile Supported Living Payment rates For more information see: - Blind client's subsidy - Charging income - Client in hospital - Earnings related Accident Compensation - Exemption for severe disablement - Employment and Work Readiness Participation allowance - Personal earnings exemption - Redirection for young partners - Core policy Relationship status for benefit

chunks.title: Money left on payment card when Money Management ends — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Money left on payment card when Money Management ends
A client may have money left on their payment card when Money Management ends. Clients are expected to use this balance as it can continue to be used to buy essential items.
The balance can be transferred to a client's bank account if they ask.
Example
Tayla has been on Money Management for 3 weeks. In her 4th week, she finds full-time employment and cancels her benefit.
She has $220 remaining on her payment card. Tayla requests that this money be transferred to her bank account so that she can use it on work-related expenses.
MSD transfers the payment directly to her bank account.

chunks.title: People likely to be severely disabled — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Not all disabled clients would be considered severely disabled. However there are some groups where it is easily identified that extra personal effort is required for them to participate in their community. The table below outlines situations where your client would be considered to be severely disabled and may qualify for the income exemption for severe disablement. SituationExampleYour client is living in an environment where they need a high level of care and supervision to carry out the daily routines of life.Your client may be in a residential care facility on a long term basis where a Residential Support Subsidy or Residential Care Subsidy is being paid because they require a high level of care and supervision.Your client might be living in a community residential service or supported independent living, or Ministry of Health contracted board arrangement with IHC because they require a high level of care and supervision.Your client who needs a high level of care and supervision may be cared for by a carer who is receiving Supported Living Payment (caring for a person)Your client might be receiving significant personal care support either in their home or at work.Client required significant support to access the education curriculum.Your client has received ongoing assistance from Special Education's Ongoing Resourcing Schemes (ORS). Situation Example Your client is living in an environment where they need a high level of care and supervision to carry out the daily routines of life. Your client may be in a residential care facility on a long term basis where a Residential Support Subsidy or Residential Care Subsidy is being paid because they require a high level of care and supervision. Your client might be living in a community residential service or supported independent living, or Ministry of Health contracted board arrangement with IHC because they require a high level of care and supervision. Your client who needs a high level of care and supervision may be cared for by a carer who is receiving Supported Living Payment (caring for a person) Your client might be receiving significant personal care support either in their home or at work. Client required significant support to access the education curriculum. Your client has received ongoing assistance from Special Education's Ongoing Resourcing Schemes (ORS). Note your client may be severely disabled but their situation is not described above. In these cases you will need to use the indication of severely disablement criteria and all information available to you to decide if your client is severely disabled. For more information see: - Deciding if your client is severely disabled - Process for decisions For more information see: - Deciding amount of income exemption

chunks.title: People likely to be severely disabled — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: - Ongoing Resourcing Schemes (ORS) assessment - Referral to Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Option to secure multiple positions — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Option to secure multiple positions
A partner could find more than one suitable organisation and position to help them meet the required number of hours and weeks. This could be:
- finding 2 or more organisations who offer enough hours per week between them, or
- working at 2 or more organisations, who offer back-to-back positions, for example doing the first 2 weeks with one organisation, and the next 2 weeks with a different organisation, or
- a combination of both.
A partner can secure more than one position for their Community Work Experience, as long as they are able to meet the requirements of the sanction.
The organisations and positions must all be approved by MSD before they start the community work and before the 5-day verification window has ended.

chunks.title: Benefit stops during Money Management — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Benefit stops during Money Management
A client's benefit may stop while they are being money managed, e.g. one week their income was over the income limit. The length of Money Management is not impacted by any breaks in payment, and will always end four weeks after it was imposed.
## Example
Rahool is getting Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability.
He fails a work-preparation obligation on 3 March and is placed onto Money Management on 10 March. His Money Management period will end on 6 April.
Rahool’s medical certificate expires on 31 March. His benefit stops until he gets a new medical certificate.
He gets a new medical certificate on 10 April, 4 days after his Money Management period has ended. His benefit resumes from 31 March when his medical certificate first expired, and MSD issues arrears of his Sole Parent Support from 31 March to 10 April.
Rahool’s arrears for the period of 31 March to 6 April, are subject to Money Management. 50% of those arrears are paid onto his payment card and the remainder to his bank account.
The arrears owed after his Money Management ended, from 7 April to 10 April, are also paid directly into Rahool’s bank account.

chunks.title: Permanent residence — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Permanent residence
Generally migrants need to have permanent residence or New Zealand citizenship to receive benefit assistance. Permanent residence is granted by Immigration New Zealand. Citizenship is granted by the Department of Internal Affairs.
In order to receive a benefit, a client must normally:
- have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 (which can either be a resident visa or a permanent resident visa) or
- have a residence permit under the Immigration Act 1987 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens) or
- be a British national who arrive in New Zealand prior to 2 April 1974 or
- be a New Zealand citizen
## Clients without permanent residence or citizenship
Emergency Benefit may be paid to some categories of migrants who do not have permanent residence or citizenship eg people waiting their application for refugee or protection status to be approved.
For more information see:
- Proof of residence
- Emergency Benefit
Note clients lawfully in New Zealand by virtue of a temporary permit or temporary entry class visa only (ie they do not have permanent residence) are not entitled to any benefit assistance.
To assess a client's entitlement you will generally need to establish exactly what category of migrant they are.
Clients may be granted permanent residence under the following categories:
- Family Stream
- International/Humanitarian Stream
- Skilled/Business Stream
Note if you require further information about a client's application for permanent residence you must get consent from the client to contact Immigration New Zealand or the client should obtain the information themselves. Otherwise the application should be declined. You must not collect or disclose information regarding a client's application without the client's consent.
For more information see:
- Immigration status and supporting documents
- Immigration status [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Personal earnings exemptions — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Personal earnings exemptions
Clients granted Supported Living Payment as they are permanently and severely incapacitated for employment due to a health condition, injury or disability can have a personal earnings exemption.
Note a client getting Supported Living Payment (caring for a person), is not entitled to the personal earnings exemption.
Income earned from the client's personal effort (that is, work completed by the client) qualifies for a personal earnings exemption.
The following are not included as personal earnings:
- Student Allowances
- earnings related Superannuation
- earnings related accident compensation that does not relate to the disability for which Supported Living Payment has been granted
- a partner's income
- other income not earned through personal effort, for example, interest from savings, dividends etc
When assessing income for Supported Living Payment, disregard:
- all personal earnings of a totally blind person
- up to $20 gross a week of personal earnings for all other clients, including partners, who qualify to get Supported Living Payment in their own right
The client may also be entitled to an exemption for severe disablement.
Note the personal earnings exemption applies to Supported Living Payment only. Any income that has been disregarded must be included in the assessment of any Special Benefit or Temporary Additional Support.
## Example 1
Theo is getting Supported Living Payment due to a health condition, injury, or disability.
Theo works part-time and earns income of $400 gross a week.
Theo qualifies for a personal earnings exemption of $20 a week.
Weekly gross income
$400.00
Less personal earnings exemption
$20.00
Less income allowed before benefit is affected
$160.00
Equals income that will affect benefit
$220.00
Reduction is 30 cents per $1 of income over $160 up to $250 ($90 x 0.3)
$27.00
and 70 cents from every $1 of income over $250 ($130 x 0.7)
$91.00
$118.00 reduction
## Example 2
Oscar is getting Supported Living Payment for total blindness.
Oscar works part-time and earns $200 gross per week.
Oscar qualifies to have all their personal earnings disregarded as they are totally blind.
Weekly gross income
$200.00
Less personal earnings exemption
$200.00
Equals income that will affect benefit
Nil

chunks.title: Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer
A benefit can be conditionally paid if the partner with work obligations challenges the dismissal or loss of employment.
Before the benefit can be paid you must obtain verification that the partner is challenging the dismissal or loss of employment.
When a partner's former employer confirms the partner ceased their employment during their employment trial but does not disclose the reason for the termination, accept the partner's reason for the termination and continue with the application process. Contact with the partner's former employer is still required to confirm the date ceased and any holiday pay etc.
## Exception
A partner can challenge their former employer's decision to end their employment and take legal proceedings if the partner thinks their former employer has ceased their employment on grounds of:
- discrimination
- sexual harassment
- racial harassment or
- duress imposed by the employer in relation to partner union affiliations or not as the case may be
Where a partner has lost their job through misconduct, their actions must have seriously breached their contract of employment in order for their employer to be able to terminate their employment.
Partners may choose to follow up their grievance using the Employment Relations Act 2000 or the Human Rights Act 1993. They cannot use both Acts for the same grievance.
## Conditions for granting the benefit
The partner with work obligations is only granted their benefit on the condition that:
- they will repay all of the benefit received during the 13 week non-entitlement period if misconduct is proven and
- they may need to repay part or all of the benefit received during the 13 week non-entitlement period if they win wages, damages or other compensation
They will need to sign a statement to this effect.
When you grant a benefit (or pay a full rate of benefit) under these conditions, on the SDT1A screen you must use the 'reason for grant' code (48).
For more information see:
- Proof partner is challenging dismissal
- Outcome of case

chunks.title: Evidence — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Evidence
The partner must provide evidence from a registered nurse practitioner, medical practitioner or midwife confirming the expected date of birth or nature of complications if their pregnancy is under 27 weeks.
## Duration
This exemption applies from the earliest of either:
- the birth of the child or
- 6 months from the date it was granted

chunks.title: Calculating number of days — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Calculating number of days
When counting the number of days that a client has been in prison or held on remand, you should include the date the client:
- enters prison or held on remand and
- leaves prison or is released from remand
For more information see:
- Imprisonment Release from prison
- Transfer between benefits

chunks.title: Process for deciding appropriate activities — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Process for deciding appropriate activities
When you and the client are considering appropriate activities for the client to undertake, you should consider the following:
- what needs or barriers to employment is the activity designed to address for the client
- what activities are available to help the client move towards employment
- the Work and Income programmes and services that are available to help the client move towards employment
Examples of appropriate activities include (but are not limited to):
- participating in the Job Search Service
- education or training to improve clients work-readiness or prospects for employment
For more information see:
- Activity Summary
- Informing clients of their obligations

chunks.title: Process for decisions — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Process for decisions
Once you have received all the information you require from your client you need to make an assessment and draft your decision. Your case should then be referred to your Regional Disability Advisor or Regional Health Advisor for their comment.
To retain national consistency these should then be referred to the Principal Disability Adviser for their recommendation. The Principal Disability Adviser will send a response to the Regional Disability Advisor or Regional Health Advisor.
When you have received comment from your Regional Disability Advisor or Regional Health Advisor you should finalise your decision and record the information on CMS.
For more information see:
- Payment process

chunks.title: Proof of care — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Proof of care
A medical certificate is needed in every case and must state that the person needs the client's full-time care and attention and without that care the person would be admitted to:
- hospital care or
- rest home care or
- residential disability care or
- care of the kind referred to in section 141 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 which is extended care services provided for severely disabled children and young persons or
- care of an equivalent kind
The medical certificate must be completed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner.
Note a psychologist cannot complete a medical certificate for the person who is being cared for when assessing a client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).
In any situation where the ongoing need for care is in question, MSD can request that the person receiving care be assessed by a designated health practitioner nominated and paid for by MSD.
If the client cannot get a Supported Living Payment because the person's condition does not need hospitalisation, residential care or care of an equivalent kind (as listed above), but the person does need some care, the client may be able to get an Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Proof of residence — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: All documents should be originals. Photocopies and/or documents that have been changed in any way cannot be accepted. Where the client (or partner) cannot provide proof or the proof is unclear, you should ask the client (or partner) to obtain confirmation of their residential status from Immigration New Zealand (for permanent residence) or Internal Affairs (for citizenship). Proof of citizenship and/or permanent residence in New Zealand can be a: - New Zealand birth certificate Generally, a person born in New Zealand is a New Zealand citizen by birth. - New Zealand passport To hold a New Zealand passport you must be a citizen of New Zealand. - Certificate of Registration A child born outside New Zealand (to a parent who is a New Zealand citizen) may be a New Zealand citizen from birth. However, the child must apply for a Certificate of Registration to confirm their New Zealand citizenship. - Grant of Citizenship People, who have permanent residence, may (normally after five years residence in New Zealand) apply for a Grant of Citizenship. They must meet the conditions of the Grant. - Certificate of Confirmation This is a certificate issued to confirm that the holder is a New Zealand citizen by birth, descent or Grant of Citizenship. British subjects, who immigrated to New Zealand prior to 1948 (and who resided in New Zealand for all of 1948) were made New Zealand citizens in 1949. These people are likely to have a Certificate of Confirmation or a Certificate of Naturalisation. - Certificate of Naturalisation Previously immigrants were naturalised as British Subjects and citizens of New Zealand. Today they are given a Grant of Citizenship - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence class visa granted under the immigration Act 2009 - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence permit granted under the immigration Act 1987 Note that a visa issued before 29 November 2010 does not allow a person to stay in New Zealand - Letter of confirmation of permanent residence from Immigration New Zealand - Australian citizens Australian citizens are lawfully allowed in New Zealand as they are deemed to hold a residence class visa here. Their date of entry into New Zealand is generally not recorded. Where possible, supporting evidence should be sought, such as tenancy agreements, bank statements or old utility bills to show that the client has been ordinarily resident for 2 continuous years. - British nationals

chunks.title: Proof of residence — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Clients of British nationality who came to New Zealand before 2 April 1974 were automatically allowed to enter New Zealand for residence, and will be unable to provide verification of their residence if they do not have a passport. Immigration New Zealand will have no record of these clients unless the client has contacted them after 2 April 1974. The client should be able to provide New Zealand school, work or tax records to support their claim about when they arrived in New Zealand and the length of time they have lived here. For more information see: - Immigration status and supporting documents

chunks.title: Proof partner is challenging dismissal — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Proof partner is challenging dismissal
Partners may provide information showing that they are challenging a dismissal. This might be:
- evidence that they have a representative (union, lawyer, community law centre, industrial relations advocate)
- a letter from Mediation Services or the Employment Relations Authority
For more information see:
- Outcome of case
- Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer

chunks.title: Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Generally, a temporary provisional benefit can be paid to the client or their partner while they are doing an approved activity or programme of activities during their 13-week non-entitlement period (except when the approved activity for a partner is full-time employment).

chunks.title: Provisional benefit — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: MSD can grant or increase a provisional benefit from the date the client or partner starts their approved activity or programme of suitable activities. The benefit continues to be provisionally paid while the client or partner is satisfactorily participating in the approved activity. The provisional payment will continue until: - the 6-week activity period ends, or - the 13-week non-entitlement period ends whichever is earlier. Some examples of this: - a client starts their approved activity in the beginning of week 3 of their non-entitlement period. The client participates continuously for 6 weeks, and the rest of the 13-week non-entitlement period is cancelled. After the follow-up appointment, the client’s benefit is reinstated to their usual benefit, instead of a provisional benefit. - a client starts their approved activity in the beginning of week 10 of the non-entitlement period. The client does the approved activity for the rest of the 13-week non-entitlement period (3 weeks). At the end of the 13-week non-entitlement period, the client's benefit is reinstated to their usual benefit, instead of a provisional benefit.

chunks.title: End of approved activity or non-entitlement period — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: At the end of the approved activity or programme of activities a follow-up appointment is required (in approximately 6 weeks' time). At the appointment MSD should discuss with the client or partner whether they: - have satisfactorily participated in the approved activity, and - can still meet the qualifications and obligations of their benefit. Note if the client or their partner does not recomply, they will have to reapply at the end of the 13-week non-entitlement period if they wish to get a benefit.

chunks.title: Leaves approved activity or does not satisfactorily participate — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If a client or partner leaves early or does not satisfactorily participate in the approved activity or programme of suitable activities, without a change in their obligations, their provisional benefit must be reduced or stopped from the date it was increased or granted. The benefit amount that was provisionally paid during the 13-week non-entitlement period must be established as a debt and recovered. MSD cannot recover the provisional benefit if they did not complete the approved activity because they: - transferred to a benefit with no work obligations, or - meet the criteria for a full exemption from their work obligations Only one approved activity or programme can be assigned to a client. MSD cannot give the client a different approved activity if they fail to satisfactorily complete their approved activity. For more information see: - Recompliance - Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption

chunks.title: Qualifications — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To decide if a client can get a Supported Living Payment consider the following:
- Age
- Clients circumstances
- Residence

chunks.title: Applying for Supported Living Payment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Applying for Supported Living Payment
No stand-down is imposed where a client applies for Supported Living Payment and:
- the client meets the medical qualification for Supported Living Payment and
- the client previously received or applied for Supported Living Payment or Invalids Benefit for the same health condition, injury or disability
For more information see:
- Medical qualifications

chunks.title: Recompliance — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Recompliance is the activity a client or partner must undertake after they have failed an obligation. They must complete the recompliance activity to have their benefit: - increased or resumed if they have been financially sanctioned or - continued if they have a non-financial sanction imposed. Generally, the activities a client or partner need to complete are the same as or substantially similar to the obligation that initiated the failure. Clients with an obligations failure initiated who recomply within five working days will not have a sanction imposed, but the obligations failure will be counted. When a client or partner indicates that they want to recomply MSD must make a recompliance activity available for them at the earliest opportunity. The obligations failure that has reduced or stopped their benefit will determine the type of recompliance activity the client or partner will need to undertake. MSD must discuss with the client what activities they need to undertake in order to recomply. For more information see: - Recompliance for work obligation failures for partners - Recompliance for social obligation failures - Recompliance for drug test obligation failures for partners - Recompliance for young partners - Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Allocating a recompliance activity — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: When allocating the recompliance activity, MSD must: - discuss with the client what they need to do to satisfactorily undertake the recompliance activity and the implications of not doing this and - make a note of your discussion in the appropriate system. MSD must decide whether the client has satisfactorily undertaken their recompliance activity. This will be dependent on the client's circumstances and the nature of the recompliance activity.

chunks.title: Same as or substantially similar activity — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If a client is unable to undertake the same activity that they failed to do, they must undertake to MSD's satisfaction another activity that is the same as or substantially similar to the activity they failed to do. The 'same as or substantially similar to' means that MSD must allocate an activity that, as much as possible, requires the same amount of time, effort and commitment as the activity the client failed to complete.

chunks.title: When to resume or increase a benefit — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: A client must have successfully completed the recompliance activity before their benefit is resumed or increased if they have been financially sanctioned. Once completed, the benefit can be resumed or increased from the date MSD is satisfied the client started the recompliance activity. Some examples of this: - if the recompliance activity is a one-off, such as attending an interview the benefit would be resumed from the date the client attended and participated in the interview - if the recompliance activity is ongoing, such as a training programme, the client must undertake the training programme to MSD's satisfaction. Once this is complete, the benefit can be resumed from the date the client started the training programme - if the client has multiple recompliance activities to complete (due to more than one failure), the date when they have completed a recompliance activity for the latest failure For what to do if a client cannot recomply due to a health condition, see: - Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption

chunks.title: Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period) — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: A client or their partner can complete certain activities to get a temporary provisional benefit if they have a 13-week non-entitlement period because: - their partner left a job voluntarily - their partner lost a job through misconduct - they have a grade 3 sanction imposed or - their partner refused an offer of suitable employment. If the client or their partner want to recomply, MSD must make a 6 week approved activity or programme of activities available to them at the earliest opportunity. An approved activity can start as soon as a sanction has been imposed, there is no waiting period.

chunks.title: Recompliance activities — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The client or their partner must do the approved activity for 6 continuous weeks, or until their 13-week non-entitlement period ends (whichever is earlier). This can be through: - satisfactory participation in a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities - satisfactory participation in full-time employment or - part-time employment (if their partner has work obligations) Note partners with full-time work obligations should be given a full-time 6-week approved activity. Partners with part-time work obligations it should be given a part-time 6-week approved activity. Partners with full-time work obligations who are recomplying through approved full-time employment do not get a provisional benefit.

chunks.title: Client does not complete activity — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If a client or their partner fails to satisfactorily complete their 6-week activity or programme of activities, and their obligations have not changed, their provisional benefit must be reduced or stopped from the date it was increased or granted. Any provisional benefit the client was paid must be established as a debt. To get a new benefit, the client must wait until the end of the 13-week non-entitlement period to re-apply or to get their full rate of benefit reinstated if the client has dependent children. When a client with dependent children makes contact at the end of the 13 weeks, MSD should review their circumstances to confirm that the client still qualifies and what rate of payment they should get. MSD must determine the appropriate date to increase the rate from, but this cannot be any earlier than the end of the 13-week period. Only one approved activity or programme of activities can be assigned to a client. MSD cannot give a client a different approved activity if they fail to satisfactorily complete the original approved activity.

chunks.title: Recompliance for social obligations — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If a client or their partner fails their obligations for a third time, and the third failure is a social obligation failure, then their 6-week recompliance activity will be different. In this situation it may not be appropriate to choose an activity focused on work outcomes. A programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate instead. For more information see: - Failing a social obligation - Approved activity examples - Recompliance (13-week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Recompliance and change of circumstances — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Recompliance and change of circumstances
A partner who has a failure in progress or a sanction imposed may be unable to recomply because they:
- had a change of circumstances that means they can no longer comply with an obligation, or the social obligation is no longer relevant to them or
- had a change in obligations which means they are no longer required to comply with any activity that is specific to their previous obligations, for example a partner moves between work obligations and work preparation obligations
In these situations, a partner should not be required to recomply. However, the failure will still be included in the 24-month count.
Note young partners who failed a youth activity obligation will have this counted for 12 months, even if they are no longer subject to youth activity obligations.
Once the partner has new obligations, MSD may ask them to complete any activities in relation to their new obligations.
## Examples
Examples of where MSD cannot require the partner to complete a recompliance activity:
- where a child leaves care or changes age and the social obligation they had is no longer relevant (for example the client has failed the early childhood education social obligation and the child has now turned six years old)
- where a partner who is subject to work obligations has failed a drug test obligation and is transferred to work preparation obligations
- where a client who has work preparation obligations has failed to undertake planning for employment and is transferred to work obligations
- where a partner who has work or work preparation obligations has failed an obligation and has been transferred to Supported Living Payment or Emergency Benefit with no obligations
For more information see:
- Recompliance for social obligation failures
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Recomplying more than one failure
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Work and work preparation obligations [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Recompliance for drug test obligation failures — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
Partners who have failed their drug test obligations will need to complete a recompliance activity to increase, resume or continue their benefit.
Once a partner indicates they want to recomply MSD must have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply. The grade of the drug test obligation failure will determine the recompliance activity required.
For more information see:
- Recomplying first drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying third drug test obligation failure

chunks.title: Recompliance for social obligation failures — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for social obligation failures
Clients who have failed their social obligations need to meet all their social obligations as part of an activity to increase or continue their benefit.
Once a client or partner indicates they want to recomply MSD must have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply.
Note when a client has a partner, social obligations apply to both the client and the partner.
For more information see:
- Recompliance social obligations failure (Grade 1 and 2)
- Social obligations recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Client and partner fail their social obligations
- Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Recompliance for work obligation failures — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for work obligation failures
Partners who have failed their work obligations need to recomply to have their benefit:
- increased or resumed if they have been financially sanctioned or
- continued their benefit if they have a non-financial sanction imposed
Once a partner indicates they want to recomply MSD must have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply.
## Work obligations failure (Grade 1 and 2)
To recomply with a work obligations failure (grade 1 and 2) and have their benefit increased or resumed, the partner will need to complete:
- the activity they failed or
- an activity that is the same as or substantially similar to the activity they failed
Note for grade 1 failures where a non-financial sanction has been imposed, the recompliance requirements may be different. For more information see:
- Non-financial sanctions

chunks.title: When to resume or increase the benefit — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## When to resume or increase the benefit
The YSSU will resume or increase the payment from the date the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service are satisfied that the young partner has started the recompliance activity.
Some examples of this:
- if the recompliance activity is a one-off, such as attending an interview with the service provider, the payment would be resumed from the date the young partner attended and participated in the activity
- if the recompliance activity is ongoing, such as attending school or a training programme, the young partner must satisfactorily attend school or the training programme and the payment will be resumed from the date the young partner started to attend
For what to do if a young partner cannot recomply due to health condition see:
- Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption
Also see:
- Approved recompliance activities for young partners
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Recompliance programme example — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Recompliance programme example
If a client or partner is recomplying through participating in an approved activity, there may not be a single activity long enough to meet the required 6 week period of recompliance. A programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate for the client or partner.
Note a programme of suitable activities for a client or partner with part-time work obligations should be for 20 hours or more each week.
## Example of short term approved activities
This would be appropriate for a partner receiving Supported Living Payment with full-time work obligations.
Week 1
CV Seminar - 20 hours
Week 2
Employment skills programme - 20 hours
Week 3
Employment skills programme - 20 hours
Week 4
Employment skills programme - 20 hours
Week 5
Presentation seminar approved by Work and Income
Week 5
Work experience
Week 6
Work experience
Week 6
Business Plan preparation interview with accountant or local business enterprise centre - 3 hours
Note a programme of short-term suitable activities should be relevant to the obligations failure and be fair and reasonable.
For more information see:
- Recompliance through employment
- Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Recompliance social obligations failure (Grade 1 and 2) — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: When the client or partner fails 1 individual social obligation they need to comply with all other social obligations relevant to the age of their dependent child. MSD should discuss with the client or partner what activities they must undertake to recomply. MSD must be satisfied the client and their partner (if any) have both satisfactorily undertaken their recompliance activity. The benefit will be resumed or increased from the date MSD is satisfied the client or partner has started the recompliance activity. MSD may ask the client or their partner (if any) to get verification, for example: - a letter from their practitioner or medical practice that says they are enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation or - a letter from the child's school that says the child is enrolled and attending or - a letter from their early childhood education provider that says the child is enrolled and attending or - asking to see their Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book

chunks.title: Examples of recompliance — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Example 1 A client has a 3-year-old child. They are required to have their child enrolled in primary health care and attending a recognised early childhood education programme. The child has not been attending an early childhood education programme and the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for this. MSD is unsure that the client enrolled the child in primary health care. The client has failed 1 of their social obligations. To recomply with their social obligations, MSD must be satisfied the client has enrolled their child in primary health care and that they will ensure their child attends an early childhood education programme. MSD asks the client to provide verification of this. The client provides a letter from their medical practice confirming the child is enrolled, and a letter from the early childhood education provider confirming the child is enrolled and attending. MSD is satisfied that the client has recomplied with their social obligations. Example 2 A client has 2 children. The 5-year-old child must be enrolled in primary health care and attending school or an early childhood education programme. The 2-year-old child also needs to be enrolled in primary health care and up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks. Both children are enrolled in primary health care and the 5-year-old child is attending school. However, the 2-year-old child is not up to date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks and the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for this. The client has failed 1 of their social obligations. To recomply with their social obligations, MSD must be satisfied that the 2-year-old child has or will get their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks. MSD asks the client to provide verification of this. The client brings their 2-year-old’s Well child/Tamariki Ora book to MSD which confirms the 2-year-old has upcoming Well child/Tamariki Ora checks booked. MSD is satisfied that the client has recomplied with their social obligations.

chunks.title: Full-time employment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Full-time employment
A partner who has a 13-week non-entitlement period and full-time work obligations can recomply by getting full-time work. This work must last at least 6 continuous weeks.
At the end of the 6 weeks, the 13-week non-entitlement period ends. If the partner wants to restart their benefit, they will have to reapply. The benefit is granted from the date their employment ceased.
Note provisional benefit is not paid during the 6 weeks of full-time employment.
## Part-time employment
A partner who has a 13-week non-entitlement period and part-time work obligations can recomply by getting part-time work. This work must last at least 6 continuous weeks, for an average of 20 hours or more each week.
At the end of 6 weeks, the 13-week non-entitlement period ends. The partner’s benefit is reinstated to their usual benefit, instead of a provisional benefit.
If the partner leaves the job before the end of the 6 weeks, any provisional benefit paid must be established as a debt and the rest of the non-entitlement period is imposed.
The partner can still recomply during the rest of the 13-week non-entitlement period by participating in another approved activity.
Note the income the partner gets from their part-time employment is charged against the provisional benefit rate.
For when to grant or increase the benefit, see:
- Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Client recomplies — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Client recomplies
When a client completes their recompliance activity during their Money Management period, they will be recomplied at the end of the four weeks. Any benefit payments they are entitled to from the day after Money Management ends will go into their bank account.
Money Management will last four weeks regardless of when a client completes their recompliance activity.
## Client does not recomply
Clients who do not complete their recompliance activity while on Money Management will have their benefit suspended at the end of the four-week period.
Their benefit can only be resumed when a client has completed their recompliance activity. If a client’s benefit has been suspended following Money Management, their benefit will be automatically cancelled after 9 weeks (13 weeks total). For more information on how non-compliance affects assistance, see:
Clients who have had their benefit cancelled will need to reapply for the benefit if they need further support.

chunks.title: Recomplying first drug test obligation failure — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Recomplying first drug test obligation failure
To recomply to a first drug test obligation failure a partner must verbally agree to stop using controlled drugs.
The day the partner agrees to stop taking controlled drugs is the date they can be considered to have recomplied. You must advise the client or partner of the consequences if they fail the drug test obligation again.
For more information see:
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying third drug test obligation failure
- Drug test recompliance count

chunks.title: Recomplying more than one failure — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Recomplying more than one failure
When more than one obligation failure has been initiated for a client or partner on the same day, to increase, resume, or continue their full benefit the client or partner needs to dispute or recomply to all the failures.
If the client disputes or recomplies with one obligation, the sanction must still be imposed due the other obligation failures not being successfully disputed or recomplied (within the 5 working day notice period).
## Client already has a failure in-progress or a sanction imposed
Once failures have been initiated, and the notice letter has been sent, any further failures cannot be initiated until each failure:
- has been recomplied with
- has been successfully disputed because the client provided a good and sufficient reason or reasons or
- is overturned (following a dispute)
These further failures will not be included in the 24 month count (or 12 month count for young partners with youth activity obligations) and the client cannot be required to recomply.
For more information see:
- Recompliance for work obligation failures
- Recompliance for social obligation failures
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Recomplying second drug test obligation failure — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
When a partner has failed their drug test obligations the second time, they must agree that they will take and pass a drug test within 25 working days (of the agreement). The benefit can be reinstated from the day the partner recomplies, ie the day the partner agrees to take the test.
The drug test can be either a screening test or an evidential test.
## Period to take and provide a drug test
A partner has 25 working days, from the day after they have agreed to recomply with their second drug test obligations failure, to take and pass a drug test. The partner must provide proof of undertaking and passing the drug test, within 30 working days from the day after they have agreed to recomply.
A partner cannot dispute the 25 working day period to take and pass the drug test. They must take and pass the drug test within that time period or they will fail their obligations for the third time.
Work and Income has an additional 5 working days to receive the results from the partner and to process the information.
Generally, the results of the drug test should be provided to Work and Income within the 25 working days, but they can be accepted in the 5 working day period following.
Day 0
A second drug test failure is in-progress and partner has agreed to recomply by taking and passing a drug test within 25 working days
Recompliance two is recorded and automatic count in IT system occurs overnight
Partner can provide the results of the drug test at any time
Day 1 - 25
Letter is sent to the partner advising them they have 25 working days to take and pass a drug test
Day 26 - 30
5 working days to allow time to receive and process the results of the test starts
Day 31
If no "passed" drug test results are received a work test failure three is initiated and 5 working day notice period prior to Grade 3 sanction starts
They will not be considered to have recomplied until a passed drug test result is received by Work and Income.
A partner can access help with the costs of the recompliance drug test once during the 25 working day period.
During the 25 working day period a "drug test referral delay" will be automatically added in CMS.

chunks.title: Recomplying third drug test obligation failure — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Recomplying third drug test obligation failure
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation a partner must complete a six week approved activity and reapply for their benefit. A six week approved activity must be completed regardless of the obligation failed or whether the partner had failed more than one obligation failure.

chunks.title: Recording decisions on a dispute — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Recording decisions on a dispute
You must record the outcome of the client or partner's dispute in OBMAN. One of the following decisions must be recorded for each dispute:
- Upheld - if you believe that the decision relating to an obligations failure or sanction being imposed was correct you must record this as 'dispute upheld'. The obligations failure will be counted.
- Withdrawn - a client or partner may, after disputing the obligations failure, decide to recomply before the sanction is imposed, or may withdraw their dispute and not recomply. In these cases you must record that the dispute has been withdrawn. The obligations failure will be counted.
- Overturned - when you believe that the client or partner had a good and sufficient reason or that they did not fail their obligations you must record this as obligations failure overturned. The obligations failure will not be counted.
In all cases you must advise the client or partner of the outcome of their dispute. A letter is automatically sent to the client or partner.
If the client or partner does not agree with your decision, they can still request a formal Review of Decision or Medical Appeal Board appeal (drug test failure only). They must do this in writing. The Review of Decision and Medical Appeals Board process should be followed.
Note if the obligations failure was initiated against the wrong client or partner the status can be changed to 'failed in error' on the same day you initiate the failure. No letter is sent when the status is changed to 'failed in error'.
## Reviews of Decisions and appeals to the Medical Appeals Board for obligations failures
Reviews of Decisions for obligations failures are recorded in HIYA; appeals to the Medical Appeals Board for obligations failures are recorded in the Medical Appeals Database. However, the outcome of the review or appeal must be recorded in OBMAN. This will ensure that the benefit status can be resumed or regranted in SWIFTT depending on the outcome of the review or appeal.
Note that if the Review of Decision or Medical Appeals Board process finds that the originally recorded 'upheld' outcome should be changed to overturned, you will need to make this change in OBMAN.
For more information see:
- The disputes process
- Core policy Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Core policy Medical Appeals Board

chunks.title: Redirection for young partners — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection for young partners
For young partners subject to youth money management the Supported Living Payment, family tax credit, Best Start tax credit, and any ongoing extra help must be redirected to pay for:
- the young person's accommodation and service costs, e.g. rent, board, power, phone
- the young person's lawful debts or other liabilities, for example Child Support payments, MSD debts
- food and groceries via a payment card
## Payments that are not redirected
Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance, and Flexible Childcare Assistance can be paid directly to the young partner, their agent (if authorised) or a supplier (as appropriate).
If the young person qualifies for any of these payments, MSD will decide who the payment goes to after talking with the young person's youth service provider.

chunks.title: Referral to a designated health practitioner — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Referral to a designated health practitioner
MSD can require a client to be referred to a designated health practitioner to:
- establish medical eligibility to Supported Living Payment
- confirm ongoing medical eligibility to Supported Living Payment
- decide what work obligations to apply
MSD will meet the cost of the appointment with a designated health practitioner.
## Case manager refers directly to a designated health practitioner
A case manager can refer a client directly to a designated health practitioner when:
- their registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist indicates that they are not best placed to provide the medical information and a second opinion is appropriate or
- they are unable or fail to provide existing reports, a medical certificate from their own medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist , or other information, and MSD holds insufficient information to decide Supported Living Payment eligibility or
- they choose to see a designated health practitioner at their Supported Living Payment medical review
## Seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor
In all other situations a case manager must seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor for advice before deciding whether the client must be assessed by a designated health practitioner, including when:
- a diagnosis is unclear
- there appears to be inadequate information in the medical certificate, existing reports/assessments or MSD records to decide eligibility
- the medical information provided is unclear or conflicting
- a previous MSD medical certificate contains a substantially different diagnosis or recommendation
- the medical certificate appears to be influenced by labour market considerations
- the client is engaged in activities that appear to be at odds with recorded incapacities
## Financial assistance in the interim
If the client is applying for Supported Living Payment and referral to a designated health practitioner means there is likely to be a delay in deciding their eligibility, MSD may need to consider another form of financial assistance in the interim.
This could include granting Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability or some form of hardship assistance. MSD still needs to be satisfied that there is sufficient evidence before granting.
When the Supported Living Payment is current, MSD needs to ensure that payment continues in the interim.

chunks.title: Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements
When you are referring a partner to a drug tested job, you should:
- consider if the job is suitable for the partner, regardless of the drug test
- let the partner know that the employer may require them to pass a pre-employment drug test
- ask the partner if they would pass a pre-employment drug test and
- ensure the partner understands the potential consequences of failing a pre-employment drug test
There are certain situations where it may not be appropriate to refer a partner to drug tested jobs. In these situations you should consider that, because of the drug test requirements, the job is not suitable.
For more information see:
- Drug test job referral not suitable
- Training providers requiring a drug test
- Employers requiring pre-employment drug test
- Informing a partner of the drug test obligation failure
- Drug test obligations failures - Good and sufficient reasons
- Suitable employment
- Types of drug tests and standards
- Drug test obligations

chunks.title: Refugees and protected persons — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Refugees and protected persons
In general a refugee or protected person cannot receive Supported Living Payment unless they have been granted permanent residence.
If a refugee or a protected person has permanent residence, assess them for Supported Living Payment in the usual manner. Refugees and protected persons with permanent residence are exempt from meeting the two years continuous residence criteria.
Note when a client leaves the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre no stand-down applies to the grant of the benefit.
## Clients without permanent residence
If a client is a refugee or a protected person and has not been granted permanent residence, an Emergency Benefit may be considered.
For more information see:
- Emergency Benefit

chunks.title: Regional training courses — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Regional training courses
This is any training approved by the regional contracts manager.
Young people will be meeting their obligations where they are undertaking programmes linked to the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF) credits.
For more information see:
- Approved training (young partners)

chunks.title: Regular engagement and support process — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Regular engagement and support process
Clients must be contacted at least four times by Work and Income before initiating a failure to meet a social obligation. You must complete the three Contact Steps of regular engagement and support and then make a final appointment. You can only determine that the client has failed to meet their social obligations at the final appointment.
The Contact Steps can be over the phone or face to face.
The aim of this process is to support clients to meet their social obligations or for clients to take all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations.
At the first Contact Step of engagement and support you should discuss with the client and their partner (if any) whether they are meeting their social obligations and, if not, encourage them to do so.
The next two Contact Steps of engagement and support should be focused on encouraging and supporting the client to meet their social obligations, and following up what happened at the previous Contact Steps.
At each of the three Contact Steps you must:
- check that the client is taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, and actively help and encourage the client to meet those obligations
- ensure that the client is connected with local community information
- advise the client of the next stage of engagement and support and contact
- remind the client of their social obligations and consequences of not meeting these
For more information on the engagement and support see:
- Social obligations - Actively engaging with clients [no link find out why]
Also see:
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Client is meeting their social obligations
- Clients situation changes during engagement and support process
- Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations

chunks.title: Rehabilitation — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation is a process aimed at enabling people with ill health and disabled people to reach and maintain their optimal level.
It generally has a focus on restoration or improvement of the abilities of the partner. Rehabilitation could include services such as re-training a client unable to return to their previous occupation.
As part of the expectation that a client will prepare towards a return to employment, clients with work preparation or work obligations may need support to undertake activities, including rehabilitation.
To improve the client's work-readiness they may be required to undertake activities, including rehabilitation, however this must not include medical treatment.

chunks.title: Reimbursement to employers and debt recovery — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Reimbursement to employers and debt recovery
The potential employer can be reimbursed for a failed drug test for a client only when Work and Income receives confirmation a drug test has been completed that was part of the pre-employment process and the potential employer has completed the Pre-employment drug test claim form for employers which includes details such as:
- the name of the employer
- the type of test - whether it was a screening or evidential test or both
- confirmation that the drug test was to the drug test standard
- confirmation of a failed test result and
- the cost of the failed test and the payment rate they are claiming
At the same time that the employer is reimbursed, a debt for the cost of the drug test will be manually added to the partners SWIFTT record by NPCU/NAC.
For more information see:
- Reimbursement and claims for Employers/Drug Test Agencies [no link find out why]
A training provider cannot be reimbursed for the costs of a failed drug test. In most cases the contract with the provider will have already factored these costs into account.
Although a drug test provider may conduct the testing the employer will be the one to be reimbursed for the costs relating to the failed drug test.
The information provided related to the failed drug tests is not to be shared with other employers, and is only to be used for the purposes of establishing whether a partner has failed, without good and sufficient reason, to meet the drug test obligations.
The reimbursement of failed drug tests only apply to jobs where
- the partner with work obligations has been referred by Work and Income
- the vacancy is listed with Work and Income and
- the vacancy requires a pre-employment drug test
## Debt recovery
Once the cost of the failed drug test is reimbursed to the employer, it must be established as a debt to the partner. The amount of the debt is the amount that has been reimbursed to the employer.
Debt repayment options must be discussed with the partner giving consideration to any other debts the partner may have. Add notes to the partner's record about the negotiated debt repayment.
For more information see:
- Repayment options available to clients [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Removing incentive payments — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Removing incentive payments
Incentive payments should be removed when the young partner:
- is subject to a grade 1, 2 or 3 sanction
- is in hospital for longer than 13 weeks and they are receiving the hospital rate of payment
- no longer has a dependent child (Parent education incentive only)
- has intentionally acted in a way that is inconsistent with the purpose of the incentives
Note young people can continue to receive their incentive payments once they are earned, if they are granted an exemption from their obligations, unless the reason the exemption is needed is because they have acted in a way that is inconsistent with the purpose of the incentive.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Reporting progress — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Reporting progress
You can require a client to report on their progress in meeting their work or work preparation obligations.
You must advise the client that if they fail to comply with this obligation, without a good and sufficient reason, they have an obligations failure.
## Clients and partners with work preparation obligations
You can require a client or partner to report on their progress in meeting their work preparation obligations. This may include reporting on progress of any activities they have been required to undertake.
A client or partner can report by either phone, email or in person.
## Example
You have asked a partner with a 2 year old child to research childcare options and training options available in their community and to call you in a month to update you on their progress. If the partner does not contact you, you should initiate an obligations failure.

chunks.title: Residence — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Residence
To be granted Supported Living Payment, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (ie not be in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) and
- have lived continuously in New Zealand for two years or more at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
For more information see:
- Deciding ordinarily resident
Note clients who are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident but have not lived in New Zealand continuously for two years may be eligible for an Emergency Benefit.
If a client is from overseas or is a refugee or protected person special provisions may apply, see:
- Clients from overseas
- Refugees and protected persons
## Clients without permanent residence
If a client does not have permanent residence they cannot get Supported Living Payment (even if they have lived in New Zealand continuously for 2 years).
They may be able to get an Emergency Benefit if they:
- are lawfully present in New Zealand and are waiting for the outcome of their application for refugee or protection status in New Zealand or
- are applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act and are compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances

chunks.title: Resident in New Zealand — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Resident in New Zealand
To qualify for Supported Living Payment a client must have lived continuously in New Zealand for two years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident.
To be resident in New Zealand at a particular time means that the client either:
- makes their home in New Zealand, that is, they have been living in New Zealand on a permanent basis or
- has an intention to make their home in New Zealand for the foreseeable future
Note 'resident' is not the same as being ordinarily resident.
Remember you must be satisfied that the client has been resident in New Zealand continuously for at least two years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident.
## Client makes their home in New Zealand
A client will be resident in New Zealand if they make their home in New Zealand. You should look for evidence that the client makes their home in New Zealand. Relevant factors you should consider include:
- a fixed abode in New Zealand?
- ownership of property in New Zealand?
- frequent absences from New Zealand, and what is the duration of and reason for those absences?
- involvement with New Zealand society such as (but not limited to):- community activities- employment- membership of clubs and- local churches
For more information see:
- Calculating the period of residence
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Reciprocal agreements
- Proof of residence

chunks.title: Restricted circumstances guidelines — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Restricted circumstances guidelines
You must consider the following factors in relation to the restricted circumstances that make the child's attendance at school unreasonable.
It can be unreasonable for that child to attend school:
- if there is no school bus or
- no other suitable transport and
- there is a significant distance between their home and school
It may also be unreasonable for the child to attend the nearest school because the child has particular needs that prevent them from attending the nearest school, for example:
- special needs such as physical or intellectual disability; chronic or recurring illness
- learning or behavioural difficulties or
- exclusion from the school

chunks.title: Retrospection when caring for your own child — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: In 2004 the policy intent was clarified and confirmed that Domestic Purposes Benefit - Care of sick or infirm can be paid to a parent who is required to provide full-time care and attention at home to their dependent child who would otherwise need hospital care. Clients can request retrospective consideration of their entitlement to get Domestic Purposes Benefit - Care of sick or infirm and Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).

chunks.title: Retrospection requires an earlier application — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Retrospection can be assessed from a date before 2004 if there is an earlier application for benefit. An earlier application can include: - a previously declined application for Domestic Purposes Benefit - Care of sick or infirm or Supported Living Payment or - an application for some other benefit for the same purpose (e.g. an application for Sole Parent Support and there was sufficient information for this to be treated as an application for Supported Living Payment) or - any verbal application made before 24 September 2007 Where a sole parent was already receiving a benefit, there is no financial advantage in assessing entitlement to Domestic Purposes Benefit - Care of sick or infirm before 1 April 1991. All sole parent benefit rates were the same before this date.

chunks.title: Commencement date for retrospective payment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The commencement date for any retrospective entitlement should be assessed from the date of the earlier application.

chunks.title: Investigating requests for retrospective payment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: When a client requests that their application for Domestic Purposes Benefit - Care of sick or infirm and/or Supported Living Payment be backdated, MSD needs evidence to determine the date they became eligible.

chunks.title: Process for investigating retrospective entitlement — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Step 1. The client needs to complete a Carer Statement [no link find out why] . This statement requires the following information: - the level and type of care provided, the hours of care and details of any additional care provided by any other person or organisation, including care provided during attendance at an early education facility or a primary/secondary school - an indication from the client where they would like MSD to obtain the medical information required to determine entitlement from: existing MSD recordsexisting medical assessments that the client can providea medical certificate that the client will provide ora medical certificate that MSD will obtain - existing MSD records - existing medical assessments that the client can provide - a medical certificate that the client will provide or - a medical certificate that MSD will obtain And where appropriate: - consent from the client (or from the child if they are now an independent adult), to contact the child's health practitioner/specialist - to confirm eligibility for retrospective entitlement to Domestic Purposes Benefit - Care of sick or infirm and Supported Living Payment) and - details of the health practitioner or specialist MSD can contact to request a medical certificate Step 2. MSD should review the information obtained. When MSD records, or existing medical assessments provided by the client are inadequate MSD will need to discuss with the client how additional medical certificates can be obtained. The client can choose to obtain an additional medical certificate themselves or request MSD to obtain a certificate from their health practitioner or specialist. MSD may like to consult the regional solicitor at this point to discuss the level of information MSD has about the date of possible application and medical evidence. If the client requests that MSD obtains a medical certificate on their behalf MSD must contact and advise the medical practice that they will be sending a medical certificate form for completion by the health practitioner or specialist. Inform the medical practice that MSD can pay the fee for this professional service. MSD should also advise the medical practice that this process has been developed specifically to assist those clients who are requesting retrospective entitlement to Domestic Purposes Benefit - Care of sick or infirm and/or Supported Living Payment because they were caring for their own child. Step 3. When MSD has investigated the application for Domestic Purposes Benefit - Care of sick or infirm and/ or Supported Living Payment and obtained sufficient information to make a decision, MSD must contact Helpline to discuss entitlement.

chunks.title: Process for investigating retrospective entitlement — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Step 4. When a decision has been made to grant retrospective entitlement, Helpline will process the application and contact the client. When the decision has been made to decline the retrospective application for Domestic Purposes Benefit - Care of sick or infirm and/ or Supported Living Payment MSD should process this decision in the normal manner, advise the client and provide review and appeal rights.

chunks.title: Example — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: A client is getting Sole Parent Support and Child Disability Allowance for their child. They have recently applied and been granted Supported Living Payment for their child and have asked that this be backdated from the date they were first getting a benefit. The client asks MSD to use the medical information already held about the child's condition to determine eligibility to Supported Living Payment. There is medical evidence that the child has a disability from the first Child Disability Allowance certificate. However, it is not clear how severe their disability was at that time or whether the child required full time care and attention at home and would otherwise have required hospital care. The information MSD currently holds is insufficient to make a decision on eligibility to Supported Living Payment. The client asks MSD to obtain a medical certificate from the child's registered medical practitioner. The registered medical practitioner confirms that the child was severely disabled from that time and required full-time care and attention at home and would otherwise have required hospital care. This evidence, in conjunction with the client's statement, is sufficient to approve Supported Living Payment from that earlier date.

chunks.title: Exception — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Exception
Where young partners are sanctioned and they are not subject to youth money management because they have earned the right to manage their own money, they won't be put back on youth money management like those clients on Youth Payment and Young Parent Payment. This ensures the sanctions for clients who aren't subject to youth money management remain graduated through any obligation failures.

chunks.title: Review income exemption when client's circumstances change — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Review income exemption when client's circumstances change
If your client's circumstances change, you should use your discretion to review the amount of income exemption your client receives. For example:
- a change to their health condition or disability which may affect their costs
- relocates and changes their costs, for example, a change of address may impact on their costs
- employment conditions change and different level of effort is required
For more information see:
- Deciding amount of income exemption

chunks.title: Reviewing or disputing the drug test failure and sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Reviewing or disputing the drug test failure and sanction
A partner has the right to dispute or review any decision they disagree with relating to:
- an obligations failure or
- a sanction being imposed
A partner can do this by:
- disputing the decision or
- lodging a formal Review of Decision
A Review of Decision can be lodged at any stage within three months of the obligations failure being initiated, or within three months of the sanction being imposed.
If a partner disputes their obligations failure or sanction more than 20 working days after it is initiated or imposed, you need to advise the partner to lodge a formal Review of Decision in writing.
## Appealing to the Medical Appeal Board
A client can only lodge an appeal to the Medical Appeal board for a decision relating to a drug test failure when a decision was made that they:
- did not have a good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation, and
- the reason given for the failure was that the client was either addicted to controlled drugs ordependent on controlled drugs
- addicted to controlled drugs or
- dependent on controlled drugs
A partner is not required to dispute a decision before lodging a review of decision or appealing to the Medical Appeal Board (drug test failure only).
For more information see:
- The disputes process
- Recording decisions on a dispute
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Core policy Medical Appeals Board

chunks.title: Sanctions and the 52 week reapplication process — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Sanctions and the 52 week reapplication process
