All clients with grade 1 or 2 sanctions, and clients with dependent children on a grade 3 sanction, can complete the 52 week reapplication process on or before their expiry date in order to continue receiving Supported Living Payment.
Note the reduction or suspension continues to apply to the re-granted benefit.
If a client's benefit has been fully cancelled because of a grade 3 sanction or sanction for refusing an offer of suitable employment, they will not need to complete the 52 week reapplication process.
## Exception
If the grade 3 sanction has not yet been applied to the client's benefit (within the 'five working day notice' period for sanctions), the client can complete the 52 week reapplication process on or before the expiry date, if they have also started their six week approved recompliance activity.
For more information see:
- Effect of sanctions on assistance

chunks.title: Grade 1 sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If both clients fail their obligations for the first time, each person's portion of the benefit is reduced by 50% unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed. The couple will continue to get a maximum of 50% of their married rate of benefit until they recomply. While their benefit is reduced, the couple can continue to get extra help. The couple will continue to get the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment as they are still getting a qualifying benefit. For more information see: - Recompliance - Non-financial sanctions

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If both clients fail their obligations a third time, 50% of the couple's benefit is cancelled. The couple will continue to get a maximum of 50% of their married rate of benefit until they recomply. If both clients are subject to a non-entitlement period for 13 weeks, both clients may get a provisional benefit if they start a six-week approved activity or programme of activities. While part of the benefit is cancelled, the couple gets 50% of any Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support they are entitled to. For more information see: - Recompliance

chunks.title: Processing 50% payments — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: When both clients fail their obligations at the same time and a financial sanction is imposed for each person, the couple must continue to get a maximum of 50% of their married rate of benefit. This must be paid manually, and will depend on which client failed their obligations first. For more information see: - Processing a manual sanction [no link find out why]

chunks.title: One client recomplies first — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If the primary client recomplies first, their portion of benefit and extra help must be resumed or regranted. The primary client will get the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment. The partner's benefit must remain sanctioned until they recomply. If the partner recomplies first, their portion of benefit and supplementary assistance is not able to be resumed or regranted as the primary record is not current. For information on how to process this see: - Processing a manual sanction [no link find out why]

chunks.title: 50% protection and reduction of income — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The 50% protection is applied to half the main benefit rate (eg the married rate) before any reduction of income. Any income will reduce benefit by 35 cents for every $1 of total income over $160 per week (as at 1 April 2022) from the 50% protection payment. For more information see: - Charging income

chunks.title: Client does not recomply — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If either client has not recomplied after 2 weeks, MSD will contact them to discuss financial assistance and recompliance. If they still have not recomplied at 4 weeks MSD will send a letter advising they need to attend an appointment to discuss ongoing entitlement to benefit. For more information on this process see: - Sanction period - Two week intervention [no link find out why] - Sanction period - Four week intervention [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Grade 1 sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If both partners fail their obligations for the first time, each person's portion of the benefit is reduced by 50% unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed. The couple will continue to get a total of 50% of the married rate. For more information on non-financial sanctions see: - Non-financial sanctions While their benefit is reduced, the couple can continue to get supplementary assistance. Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid as the client is still getting a qualifying benefit. If either partner has not recomplied within four weeks, they will have their portion of the benefit and supplementary assistance suspended. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid to the client who has not recomplied as they are not getting a qualifying benefit. Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or their portion of the benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks. Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.

chunks.title: Grade 2 sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If both partners fail their obligations for the second time, each person's portion of the benefit is suspended. While the benefit is suspended, the couple's supplementary assistance is also suspended. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid as they are not getting a qualifying benefit. Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or their portion of the benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks. Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If both partners fail their obligations for a third time, each person's portion of the benefit is cancelled. They are subject to a non-entitlement period for a period of 13 weeks. The client may get a provisional benefit if they start a six-week approved activity or programme of activities. If they have not started a six-week approved activity or programme of activities, they may reapply at the end of the non-entitlement period to get a benefit. When the client's benefit is cancelled, supplementary assistance is also cancelled. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid as they are not getting a qualifying benefit.

chunks.title: Sanctions for couples where one person is youth money managed — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Sanctions for couples where one person is youth money managed
Young partners (16 or 17 with no children and 16 to 19 with children) who are included in a client's Supported Living Payment may be youth money managed.
Sanctions will differ for couples depending on who has failed their obligations.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Grade 1 sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If one partner fails their obligations for the first time, that person's portion of the benefit is reduced by 50% until they recomply, unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed. For more information on non-financial sanctions see: - Non-financial sanctions While the benefit is reduced, the couple can continue to get supplementary assistance. Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid as the client is still getting a qualifying benefit. If the client or partner does not recomply within 4 weeks, they will have their portion of the benefit suspended. While their portion of the benefit is suspended, their portion of Extra help is also suspended. They cannot get their portion of Winter Energy Payment. The other person continues to get their portion of the main benefit and Extra help. The full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment can be paid to the partner who hasn’t failed. Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or their portion of the benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.

chunks.title: Grade 2 sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If one partner fails their obligations a second time, their portion of the benefit is suspended until they recomply. While their portion of the benefit is suspended, their portion of supplementary assistance is also suspended. They cannot get their portion of Winter Energy Payment. The other person continues to get their portion of the main benefit and supplementary assistance. The full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment can be paid to the partner who hasn't failed. Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or their portion of the benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks. Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction will be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply all the obligation failures initiated on the same day. For their partner's entitlements see: - Payments to the non-sanctioned client For more information see: - Recompliance

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If one partner fails their obligations for a third time, their portion of the benefit and supplementary assistance is cancelled. They cannot get their portion of Winter Energy Payment. They are subject to a non-entitlement period for a period of 13 weeks. The client may get a provisional benefit if they start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities. If they have not started a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities, they may reapply at the end of the non-entitlement period to get a benefit. For their partner's entitlements see: - Payments to the non-sanctioned client

chunks.title: Client does not recomply — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If the client has not recomplied after 2 weeks, MSD will contact them to discuss financial assistance and recompliance. If the client has still not recomplied after 4 weeks, MSD will send a letter advising that they need to attend an appointment to discuss ongoing entitlement to benefit. For more information on this process see: - Sanction period - Two week intervention [no link find out why] - Sanction period - Four week intervention [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Grade 1 sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If one partner fails their obligations for the first time, that person's portion of the benefit is reduced by 50%, unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed. For more information on non-financial sanctions see: - Non-financial sanctions While the benefit is reduced, the couple can continue to get supplementary assistance. Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid as the client is still getting a qualifying benefit. If the person being sanctioned has not recomplied within four weeks, they will have their portion of the benefit and supplementary assistance suspended. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid to the client who has failed as they are not getting a qualifying benefit. The full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment can be paid to the partner who hasn't failed. Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or their portion of the benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks. Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.

chunks.title: Grade 2 sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If one partner fails their obligations a second time, their portion of the benefit is suspended. While their portion of the benefit is suspended, their portion of supplementary assistance is also suspended. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid to the client who has failed as they are not getting a qualifying benefit. The full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment can be paid to the partner who hasn't failed. Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or their portion of the benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks. Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If one partner fails their obligations for a third time, their portion of the benefit and supplementary assistance is cancelled. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid to the client who has failed as they are not getting a qualifying benefit. The full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment can be paid to the partner who hasn't failed. They are subject to a non-entitlement period for a period of 13 weeks. They may get a provisional benefit if they start a six-week approved activity or programme of activities. If they have not started a six-week approved activity or programme of activities, they may reapply at the end of the non-entitlement period to get a benefit. For their partner's entitlements see: - Payments to the non-sanctioned client or partner

chunks.title: Young partners — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The effect of a sanction on a young partner's assistance depends on whether the client has children and is youth money managed or not. For more information see: - Sanctions for young partners - Recompliance 13 week non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Grade 1 sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Grade 1 sanction
A first obligations failure means the client's benefit is reduced by 50%, unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed.
For more information on non-financial sanctions see:
- Non-financial sanctions
While their benefit is reduced, the client can continue to get supplementary assistance. Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid as the client is still getting a qualifying benefit.
If the client has not recomplied within four weeks, they will have their benefit suspended along with all supplementary assistance (including Winter Energy Payment).
Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or the payment is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.
Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligations.
## Grade 2 sanction
A second obligations failure means the client's benefit is suspended. When their benefit is suspended, any supplementary assistance the client was getting is also suspended. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid as the client is not getting a qualifying benefit.
Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or the payment is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.
Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligations.
## Grade 3 sanction
A third obligations failure means the client's benefit is cancelled and they are subject to a non-entitlement period for 13 weeks. The client may get a provisional benefit if they start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities.
When the client's benefit is cancelled, supplementary assistance is also cancelled. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid as the client is not getting a qualifying benefit.
If they have not started a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities, they must reapply at the end of the non-entitlement period to get a benefit.
For more information see:
- Recompliance

chunks.title: Sanctions for sole parents — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Sanctions for sole parents
When sole parents fail their obligations and have a financial sanction imposed, they do not have their whole benefit sanctioned. Instead, a maximum sanction of 50% of the total benefit may be imposed. The balance payable is known as 50% protection.
Sole parents who are sanctioned can continue to get full supplementary assistance, regardless of the grade of sanction. This includes the Winter Energy Payment.
For more information on what a client can continue to get when sanctioned, see:
- Paying other assistance during a sanction
If the client has not recomplied after two weeks, MSD will contact them to discuss financial assistance and recompliance. If the client has still not recomplied at four weeks MSD must send the client a letter advising they need to attend an appointment to discuss ongoing entitlement to benefit.
For more information on this process see:
- Sanction period -Two week intervention [no link find out why]
- Sanction period - Four week intervention [no link find out why]
## Grade 1 and 2 sanctions
For a first and second obligations failure, a sole parent's benefit is reduced by 50%, unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed (for a first failure only).
For more information on non-financial sanctions see:
- Non-financial sanctions
If the client does not recomply within 4 weeks, they will have 50% of their benefit suspended.
50% of their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or 50% of their benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.
They continue to get full Extra help (including the full rate of Winter Energy Payment).
Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
## Grade 3 sanction
For a third obligations failure a sole parent is subject to a non-entitlement period for a period of 13 weeks and will have 50% of their benefit cancelled. The sole parent may get a provisional benefit and have their benefit increased to 100% if they start a six-week approved activity or programme of activities.
They continue to get full supplementary assistance (including the full rate of Winter Energy Payment).
For more information see:
- Recompliance

chunks.title: Grade 1 and 2 sanctions — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The client who is not required to get Youth Services and is not youth money managed will continue to get their portion of the assistance. They can continue to get their portion of the Winter Energy Payment. For a client who is required to get Youth Services and is youth money managed, a first or second failure means suspension of the in-hand allowance and any incentive payments, until the client recomplies with the obligation they have failed (or obligations if they have failed to comply with one or more of their obligations). The client can continue to get any Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support to which they are entitled. The young partner can continue to get their portion of the Winter Energy Payment. If the client has not recomplied within 4 weeks the whole of their benefit and any incentive payments are suspended along with any Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Winter Energy Payment the client gets. Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or the payment is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The client who is not required to get Youth Services and is not youth money managed will continue to get their portion of the assistance. The client will get the full couple rate of the Winter Energy Payment. If the person who is required to get Youth Services and is youth money managed fails their obligations for a third time: - their portion of the benefit, and any incentive payments, is cancelled immediately - their portion of Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support and Winter Energy Payment is cancelled and - the young person is subject to a non-entitlement period for 13 weeks from the date of cancellation The client may get a provisional benefit if they start a 6-week approved activity. If the client does not start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities, they may reapply at the end of their non-entitlement period to get a benefit. Note Disability Allowance can continue to be paid during a non-entitlement period. For more information see: - Sanctions for couples where one person is money managed

chunks.title: Client is not youth money managed — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: When a client is not youth money managed, has an obligations failure and has not recomplied within the 5 working day notice period, the effect of the sanction on the client's assistance is the same as for their main benefit except that any incentive payments being paid will also stop, and unlike Youth Payment clients who have earned the right to get their payment directly, a young partner will not be returned to youth money management after they have been sanctioned. For more information see:

chunks.title: Self-imposed stand-down — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Self-imposed stand-down
When a client knows that they will have a stand-down and delays their application for Supported Living Payment, the commencement date depends on whether the client has applied within 28 days of their entitlement date.
If the application is received within 28 days of the client's entitlement date, the commencement date will be:
- the day after initial stand-down ends
If the application is received 28 days after the client's entitlement date, the commencement date will be:
- the day after initial stand-down ends or
- the application date
whichever is the later.

chunks.title: Self-induced incapacity — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Self-induced incapacity
If a client's incapacity was caused by the client's own actions with the intention of receiving Supported Living Payment, they cannot receive Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Setting appropriate activities for clients — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Setting appropriate activities for clients
After a discussion with a client you will need to determine the most appropriate activities for them to undertake. To decide which activities are the most appropriate you should consider:
- the client's individual circumstances
- whether the activity is suitable for the client
- whether the client has work preparation obligations or work obligations
Note you do not need to seek the client's agreement to the activities that you require them to complete.
Once you and the client have discussed which activities will be appropriate include them in the client's Service Plan.
## Types of activities
You should refer the client to appropriate activities to improve their work-readiness or prospects for employment.
Appropriate activities may include (but are not limited to):
Work obligations
Work preparation obligations
A job interview
Contacting employers
Developing or updating a C.V.
Developing or updating a C.V.
Obtaining a driver's licence
Obtaining a driver's licence
Work assessment
Work assessment
Programme or seminar to increase particular skills or enhance motivation
Programme or seminar to increase particular skills or enhance motivation
Work experience or work exploration activity
Work experience or work exploration activity
Employment related training
Employment related training
Completing a high school qualification
Completing further study
Completing further study
Researching childcare options available in the community
Researching childcare options available in the community
You must take reasonable steps to arrange for the client to undertake an activity.
Note a client must not be required to undertake Activity in Community. If a client would like to undertake an Activity in the Community you may include it in their Service Plan. However, if the client fails to complete the activity you must not initiate an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Process for deciding appropriate activities
- Work preparation obligations - primary client
- Work preparation obligations - partners
- Work obligations - partners
- Rehabilitation
- Activity Summary

chunks.title: Several caregivers — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Several caregivers
In some situations more than one caregiver may be needed.
However, there is no provision to pay more than one Supported Living Payment in respect of any one person.

chunks.title: Simplified Access to Supported Living Payment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Simplified Access to Supported Living Payment
Some clients with a specific diagnosis will access Supported Living Payment without having a detailed assessment of their capacity to work.
Generally, the diagnosis and associated information contained in the medical information that is provided by this group will satisfy Work and Income that they are permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work.
Clients who are granted Supported Living Payment through simplified access will never have their capacity to work reassessed.
## Specific diagnosis for simplified access
Diagnosis
Description
Totally blind
Person's best visual acuity (sharpness) with correcting lenses does not exceed 3/60 or 1/20, and/or the person's visual field is contracted to a maximum of five degrees on either side of the fixation point.
Terminally ill
Life expectancy is 24 months or less.
Severe intellectual or cognitive impairment
Supporting Work Capacity Medical Certificate or other assessments indicates an IQ of 45 points or less, or clearly indicates the person has a severe cognitive brain injury
Disorder that has reached a stage of deterioration to extent that condition severely impacts on their ability to function and is unlikely to improve
Generally a person who requires assistance from others for all aspects of their personal care - eg showering, meal preparation, eating, personal hygiene
Note clients who are being granted Supported Living Payment (Caring) will also access Supported Living Payment without having a detailed assessment of their capacity to work.
## Regional Health and Disability Advisor advice required before giving simplified access
When you think your client may qualify to be given simplified access you need to refer to your Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor for advice before deciding whether your client can be given simplified access.
For more information see:
- Deciding Supported Living Payment using existing assessments
- Deciding Supported Living Payment from a medical certificate
- Deciding entitlement for blind clients
- Deciding entitlement for terminally ill clients
- Caring for a person
- Guidelines and procedures for Simplified Access [no link find out why]
- Give a person simplified access to Supported Living Payment [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Social obligations — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Social obligations
A client and their partner (if any) getting Supported Living Payment have social obligations that apply for each dependent child in their care. This includes any children for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid.
A client and their partner (if any) must take all reasonable steps to meet all of the social obligations that apply for each child. The social obligations that apply for each child depend on the age of the child.
Where the client is in a relationship the social obligations apply to both the client and their partner.
When required, clients and their partner (if any) must take all reasonable steps to meet the following social obligations. The child must be:
- enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or at a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation and
- up-to-date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks (for children under 5 years old) and
- enrolled in and attending 1 of the following from 3 years old until they start school: an approved early childhood education programme orTe Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - The Correspondence School orother approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes
- an approved early childhood education programme or
- Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - The Correspondence School or
- other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes
- enrolled in and attending school from 5 or 6 years old (depending on when they start school)
When required, a client and their partner (if any) must:
- attend and participate in interviews with MSD to discuss meeting their social obligations and
- advise on progress where they have not been able to meet their social obligations
A client is only required to meet social obligations from the time they begin to get a benefit. Clients in the process of applying for Supported Living Payment or have a future commencement date of their Supported Living Payment are not required to meet their social obligations. Clients are also not required to meet social obligations that would have been relevant prior to them getting a benefit.
For example a client who starts getting Supported Living Payment when their child is between 3 and 4 months old cannot be sanctioned for not having completed the core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks a child should have at ages 4 to 6 weeks.

chunks.title: Social obligations recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period) — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Social obligations recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
If a client or partner fails their obligations for a third time, their benefit is reduced or cancelled. For the client or partner to increase their benefit they must undertake a six week recompliance activity or programme of activities and reapply for a benefit.
If the third obligation failure is a social obligation failure, the standard six week recompliance activities may not be appropriate as clients receiving Supported Living Payment and some partners do not have work obligations and cannot work or be in training for a period of 6 weeks.
In this situation, a programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate for the client.
## Example 1
Short term approved activities to consider for a partner with part-time work obligations and social obligations, where the third failure was a social obligations failure.
Week 1
Take reasonable steps to talk to providers of an appropriate recognised early childhood education programme
Week 2
Take reasonable steps to enrol their child in a recognised early childhood education programme
Week 3
CV seminar
Week 4
Attend presentation seminar approved by Work and Income
Week 5
Attend a local parenting programme that provides support for families
Week 6
Meet with case manager to talk about what reasonable steps have been taken to enrol the child in a recognised early childhood education programme and discuss how the other activities went
Note a programme of suitable activities for a client with part-time work obligations should be for no more than 15 hours each week.
## Example 2
Example of short term approved activities to consider for a client with social obligations, where the third failure was a social obligations failure.
Week 1
Make contact with the local Family Start whanau worker and arrange a meeting with them
Week 2
Family Start whanau worker visit
Week 3
Contact a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and arrange a visit
Week 4
Contact the local medical centre to ensure the children are enrolled in primary health care
Week 5
Talk to appropriate providers of recognised early childhood education programmes
Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider visit
Week 6
Meet with a case manager about what steps have been taken

chunks.title: Special circumstances justifying delay in activity obligation — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Special circumstances justifying delay in activity obligation
A young partner may have special circumstances that justify not having to attend a Teen Parent Unit when their youngest dependent child is 6 months old even if there is a suitable place available.
Special circumstances include but are not limited to, the:
- young partner's child having an uncontrolled health condition, such as epilepsy, or the child having special needs
- young partner's ability to return to school because of a health condition or disability
- young partner struggling with the challenge of being a new parent (supported by information received from their Well Child/Tamariki Ora or a registered medical practitioner, or nurse practitioner) and returning to education or training being detrimental to them and/or their child
- young partner having difficulty bonding with their child (supported by information received from their Well Child/Tamariki Ora or a registered medical practitioner, or nurse practitioner) and returning to education or training being detrimental to them and/or their child
- dynamics with the other participants of the Teen Parent Unit making the young partner's attendance at the Teen Parent Unit inappropriate
## Special circumstances exist
If the service provider or MSD are satisfied there are special circumstances that justify the delay in the obligation to return to education at the Teen Parent Unit, the obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning would apply from the earliest of either:
- a suitable place becoming available and there are no longer special circumstances that delay the obligation to return to education at the Teen Parent Unit or
- the young partner's youngest child reaching the age of 12 months

chunks.title: Special education assessment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: If the client is a young person, they may have an assessment from the Ministry of Education for special education. MSD can use this to decide the client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment if the young person has: - intellectual disabilities or - severe physical disabilities or - long-standing, severe ill health or - sensory impairments and - they are still at school or - they have recently left school

chunks.title: Special education — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Special education is available for students with physical and/or intellectual impairments, hearing or vision difficulties, students who struggle with learning, communicating or getting along with others, or who have an emotional or behavioural difficulty. Special education is the provision of extra help, adapted programmes, learning environments, or specialised equipment or materials to support students with their learning and help them participate in education.

chunks.title: Special education students that meet the criteria for Supported Living Payment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: There are several different levels of support a student can get from special education, including support for moderate special education needs and high special education needs. Not all students who get special education qualify for Supported Living Payment. However, young people who have received ongoing funding from the Ongoing Resourcing Schemes in their last year at school are likely to qualify for Supported Living Payment. Students getting Ongoing Resourcing Schemes come from many different schooling environments including: - mainstream schools - day specialist schools - residential specialist schools (including those run privately) - correspondence school - home school A young person 16 years or over can get Supported Living Payment and remain a full-time student.

chunks.title: Client who required special education but did not meet qualification for Ongoing Resourcing Schemes — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Clients may have been receiving special education services and not have met the eligibility to Ongoing Resourcing Scheme and still meet the Supported Living Payment criteria. Just because a client didn't receive Ongoing Resourcing Scheme does not mean they won't meet the criteria for Supported Living Payment. In these cases, the client may have an alternative assessment such as an assessment from their medical specialist or a NASC assessment that they could provide. They could also provide a medical certificate from their registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist. Note a psychologist cannot complete a medical certificate for the person who is being cared for when assessing a client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment (caring for a person).

chunks.title: Client who attends or recently attended a special school — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: There are diverse criteria for young people to be granted an exemption to attend special schools. MSD cannot rely on attendance at a special school alone to determine if the client is permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work. However, many of these students are likely to have received Ongoing Resourcing Scheme funding while attending the special school. If the client advises MSD they have been attending a special day school or residential school, MSD should ask them if they have been receiving ongoing assistance from the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme.

chunks.title: Client has an exemption which allows them to attend school up to 21 years — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Some young people with a high level of special education needs may get an exemption which allows them to attend school until they are 21 years old. This is not sufficient on its own to determine if the client is permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work. However, these students are likely to have received Ongoing Resourcing Scheme funding to stay at school. If the client advises they are still at school past 19 years of age, MSD should ask them if they have been getting ongoing assistance from the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme.

chunks.title: Subsidy Assessment for blind clients — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Subsidy Assessment for blind clients
Take the total amount of income from all sources, including:
- Supported Living Payment (net)
- any supplementary assistance
- the additional subsidy (equal to 25% of average gross yearly personal earnings)
- all other income (gross)
To be able to receive a blind subsidy, the total income must not exceed the income limits.
For clients who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, only take into account the primary client's income; disregard the partner's income or benefit.
As at 1 April 2026 these income limits were:
- for clients who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship $30,258.44 a year or $581.89 (gross) per week
- for clients who are single $34,175.06 a year or $657.21 (gross) per week
## SWIFTT process
Pay the blind subsidy through SSUPI using service code 836.
## Examples of assessing blind subsidies
- Example 1 - single client
- Example 2 - married client

chunks.title: Organisation — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Suitable organisations can be community or volunteer organisations. These organisations may have existing relationship with MSD, however this is not required. To be suitable, an organisation should: - not be for profit - not be public sector, e.g. central or local government or a Crown entity - have an internal organisation structure, e.g. has defined key functions, roles and responsibilities - be self-governing – the organisation primarily controls its own management and operations - not be something people are required to contribute time to by law, e.g. jury duty. Organisations are not suitable if: - they have previously breached employment law, or - their area of focus would likely be inappropriate or unacceptable to the wider community, or - a partner completing Community Work Experience at this organisation is likely to be a reputational risk to MSD. The organisation must be confident they can provide a partner with the required hours and 4 consecutive weeks needed to complete their Community Work Experience. If the organisation is unsure, the position would not be suitable for the partner. Note partners may secure multiple positions to complete their Community Work Experience. For more information see: Period of Community Work Experience

chunks.title: Position — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: To be suitable, a position should: - be for a role that would otherwise be met by a volunteer, e.g. is not a role that would normally be paid employment - have activities that are reasonable and fair for the partner to complete – for example, a position that requires a lot of work on the computer would not be suitable for a partner with low computer literacy - not put the personal safety of the partner or others at risk - not include activities that could be considered inappropriate or may damage MSD’s reputation, e.g. serving alcohol, being involved in gambling, or supporting particular political gain Example Donna has Community Work Experience imposed and is searching for a suitable organisation and position. Donna contacts her local rugby club to see if they have any volunteer positions available that would help her to meet the Community Work Experience requirements. The rugby club can offer Donna at least 5 hours of work for 4 weeks, but tells her they mostly need her help to run the bar. Donna gets in touch with MSD and tells MSD what the position will involve. Although the rugby club is a suitable organisation, it’s not appropriate for Donna to be serving alcohol as part of her Community Work Experience, as this could damage MSD’s reputation. Donna is advised that the work needed at the rugby club is not suitable for the purpose of the sanction, and to continue looking for a suitable position.

chunks.title: Suitable employment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Suitable employment
Suitable employment varies between clients depending on their individual circumstances.
To meet their work obligations clients and partners need to be available for or take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of:
- at least 30 hours a week (clients with full-time work obligations)
- at least 20 hours a week (clients with part-time work obligations)
Clients may have pre-benefit obligations to attend an interview or accept an offer of employment. This employment must also be considered suitable.
## Deciding if a job is suitable
When deciding on whether a job is suitable for a client, you need to consider the following (but is not limited to):
- appropriate hours of employment, eg hours are not excessive
- access to childcare
- family commitments
- religious commitments
- jobs which offend strongly held views
- days of the week
- type of employment
- skills required
- experience
- location of the job
- wages
- number of hours per week is within the range for the client's work obligations
For more information see:
- Hours range for suitable employment
- Meeting job search requirements
- Employment trial period of up to 90 days
- Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment (caring for a person) charging income for couples — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Supported Living Payment (caring for a person) charging income for couples
There is no 'married, civil union or de facto' rate of payment for a client getting Supported Living Payment (caring for a person). The client's partner will either qualify for a benefit in their own right or have some other form of income.
However, when you assess the rate of payment for the client you must take both the client's and their partners income into account.
There is no provision for increased benefit for a dependent partner.
Note you do not take into account the patient's income and financial circumstances.
## How to apply the income test
Income is charged annually and at the following rates are:
- 15 cents is taken from the benefit for each dollar of income that the client (and their partner) earns over $8,320 per year, but not more than $13,000 per year
- 35 cents for every dollar of income that is more than $13,000 per year
To assess the rate payable you:
- charge the income as if both the client and their partner qualify for Supported Living Payment in their own right (that is against 2 benefits)
- add the 2 benefit payments together
- compare this total with the maximum rate of Supported Living Payment (caring for a person) payable and pay the lesser amount

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment (caring for person) partner is paid a benefit — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Supported Living Payment (caring for person) partner is paid a benefit
When a client receiving Supported Living Payment (caring for a person) is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, and their partner is paid a benefit in their own right (other than New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension) then income is charged as follows.
For clients who receive over $8,320:
- income between $8,320 and $13,000 per year ($160 - $250 per week) their benefit is reduced by 15 cents from each $1.00 of income (as at 1 April 2022)
- income over $13,000 per year ($250 per week) their benefit is reduced by 35 cents from every $1.00 of income over $13,000 (as at 1 April 2022)
## For more information on income and how to charge it, see:
- Supported Living Payment (caring for a person) charging income for couples
- Core policy Income
- Core policy Types of income
- Exemption for severe disablement
- Weekly income example

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment client with New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension partner - income assessment — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Supported Living Payment client with New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension partner - income assessment
The gross income of the client and their partner is used to assess the client's rate of Supported Living Payment (for health condition, injury or disability).
The reduction is Income test 2 - half the amount of the abatement that would apply if the couple got Supported Living Payment.
New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension is not included as income for the income test and is not reduced because of the couple's income.
Note a client getting Supported Living Payment due to a health condition, injury, or disability, may qualify for a personal earnings exemption. You must consider any personal earnings exemptions when calculating their income.
For more information see:
## Example - Weekly income
Partner 1 is getting Supported Living Payment at the half-married rate.
Partner 2 is getting the half-married rate of New Zealand Superannuation.
The couple's weekly income is $455 gross and they have no dependent children.
Partner 1 qualifies for a personal earnings exemption of $20 a week.
Couple's gross income
$455.00
Less personal earnings exemption
$20.00
Less income allowed before benefit is affected
$160.00
Equals income that will affect benefit
$275.00
Reduction is 15 cents per $1 of income over $160 up to $250 ($90 x 0.15)
$13.50
and 35 cents per $1 of income over $250 ($185 x 0.35)
$64.75
Reduction applied to Partner 1's Supported Living Payment only
$78.25
Note this example also applies to a Supported Living Payment with a Veteran's Pension partner.

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment (health condition) - partners income — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Supported Living Payment (health condition) - partners income
For clients with a partner (with or without dependent children) when the partner is:
- granted any of the main benefits in their own right or
- not entitled to get a benefit because of voluntary unemployment or misconduct or
- on strike or
- not entitled to get a benefit because of a sanction
In these instances income is charged annually at the following rates:
- 15 cents is taken from the half-couple rate of benefit for each $1.00 of their combined income earned over $8,320 per year, but not more than $13,000 per year
- 35 cents for each $1.00 of income over $13,000 per year

chunks.title: Taking all reasonable steps to enrol in a recognised early childhood education programme — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Taking all reasonable steps to enrol in a recognised early childhood education programme
A client could be considered to be taking all reasonable steps to enrol their child in a recognised early childhood education programme for reasons including, (but not limited to) that:
- there are shortages of places or availability issues, and the client has a plan in place or has made a commitment to enrol their child when a place becomes available
- there are additional costs of participation that may cause financial hardship to the family, including:
travel costs or
additional costs associated with attending the early childhood education programme
- the child has behavioural problems meaning attendance at an ECE service would be difficult or not possible (for example the child is not currently permitted to attend) (This should be recorded as an exception in OBMAN using 'child is not permitted to attend' as the obligation exception reason)
Note to help clients meet this social obligation you should discuss childcare assistance that may be available to the client.

chunks.title: Taking controlled prescribed medications — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Taking controlled prescribed medications
A good and sufficient reason for failing a drug test obligation includes when a partner is taking prescription medication correctly.
Not all prescribed medications will affect the results of a drug test. Generally, only controlled prescribed medications do, such as morphine, codeine or medicinal cannabis. Controlled prescribed medications need to be used correctly to the dose the health practitioner recommends and by the person for whom they are prescribed.
Some controlled prescribed medications may cause a person to be impaired on the job which can cause health and safety issues for employers.
In some situations, screening drug tests can show failed results if controlled prescribed medications have been used.
The partner can be asked to provide verification from a registered health practitioner that they are taking a controlled prescribed medication. There is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that MSD can provide to the partner.
Note when a partner is asked to take a drug test they will be asked to declare any prescribed medications they are taking.

chunks.title: IRD number for client or partner who is apportioned assistance — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: MSD may make a written request for evidence of an IRD number for a primary client who is being paid Supported Living Payment. MSD can also request evidence of an IRD number for a partner when they are apportioned a part of the primary client's assistance payment.

chunks.title: Notice following an unsuccessful match — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a client or partner's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the client or partner (in writing) to provide evidence of their IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the client or partner a minimum of 10 working days to provide their IRD number evidence or the client's assistance must be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Supported Living Payment and MSD holds an IRD number on record. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Isla's IRD number. MSD provides a notice in writing, giving 10 working days for Isla to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Isla already having an IRD number - Isla not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD must suspend assistance if evidence of IRD number is not received — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: MSD must suspend all taxable and/or income tested assistance the client is getting, including their Supported Living Payment, if evidence of an IRD number is not provided within 10 working days from the written request, or extended period if this has been applied. If the partner has not provided evidence of their IRD number their taxable and/or income tested assistance must be suspended. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance. Example Koa is receiving Supported Living Payment. MSD does not have an IRD number on file for Koa. MSD sends a written request giving 10 working days for Koa to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD receives no response to this request. MSD suspends all Koa's taxable and/or income tested assistance because Koa has not supplied MSD with evidence of their IRD number within the timeframe provided.

chunks.title: IRD evidence may not be requested in some circumstances — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - there are significant factors, that are outside the client's or partner's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number (e.g. a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence), and - the client needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided or - there are significant factors related to a health, injury or disability that are outside the client or partner's control that prevent them from providing evidence of an IRD number, and - an agent cannot be appointed to act on the client's or partner's behalf. MSD can determine a later point to request the evidence of the IRD number. Example Sienna is 23 and receiving Supported Living Payment. Sienna's mother (Sara) is Sienna's agent and acts on Sienna's behalf with MSD. Sienna does not have an IRD number and Sara is not a recognised agent for Sienna for Inland Revenue. Sienna has a serious head injury, is unconscious and expected to be in hospital for at least 8 weeks. Sienna is not able to give consent to appoint Sara as an agent for Inland Revenue to apply for an IRD number due to their injury. MSD can request this information later when Sienna's situation has changed. Note there is different guidance for requesting an IRD number or evidence of an IRD number for partners who are not apportioned but their income is relevant to a clients Supported Living Payment or when a client is applying for Supported living Payment.

chunks.title: The disputes process — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The disputes process is a quick process where you must respond to a client or partner's dispute immediately. You must take into account any new information provided by the client or partner and let the client or partner know your decision straight away. A letter is sent automatically to the client or partner once a decision has been recorded on the dispute. A client or partner can dispute the decision if they believe: - they did not fail their obligations or - that they had a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete the obligation Note if a client or partner has disputed the obligations failure and you have upheld your decision, the client or partner can only dispute it again by following the Review of Decision or Medical Appeal Board appeal (drug test failure only) processes. If a sanction has been imposed you can still use the disputes process. This allows the client or partner an opportunity for a quick resolution to their dispute before proceeding with the Review of Decision process. For more information see: - Recording decisions on a dispute - Core policy Review of decision for pre-benefit requirements

chunks.title: Reason for dispute — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: The client or partner can dispute the decision if they believe they did not fail their obligations, for one of the following reasons: - an obligations failure was initiated, but the client or partner had undertaken the activity or - an obligations failure was initiated, but the client or partner had a good and sufficient reason for the failure or - undertaking or completing the activity was dependent on the provision of assistance by Work and Income and that assistance was not supplied or - reasonable steps weren't taken by Work and Income to inform a client or partner of the activity that they were required to do - Note some clients or partners may fail more than one obligation at the same time. In this case, for the obligation failure not to apply, the client or partner will need to successfully dispute or review all failures in order to not have a sanction imposed. If only one failure is disputed, a sanction may still be imposed for obligation failures that were not disputed, or were disputed and upheld.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for failing — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: You must consider the circumstances of the client or partner, and determine whether it would have been reasonable for the client or partner to have undertaken the activity. Good and sufficient reasons for failing to undertake an activity will depend on the obligation the client or partner has failed. For social obligations you must consider whether the client and partner have taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations. Note that if you are unsure whether a client or partner has a good and sufficient reason then you should seek guidance from your capability developer, Helpline, manager client service operations, manager client service delivery.

chunks.title: Training providers requiring a drug test — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Training providers requiring a drug test
Some training providers will require potential trainees to pass a drug test as a prerequisite to being accepted on the course.
Training providers will use drug tests where the training programmes have a focus on employment outcomes. This includes training programmes that are:
- non classroom based programmes or on-the-job programmes where the tests are required for health and safely purposes
- classroom based training where the industry would require the trainee to be drug free for health and safety purposes to gain employment
Note a partner can only fail the drug test obligations for drug tests that are being taken as prerequisites to being accepted onto a course - not for any other ongoing drug tests that a training provider may ask for.
## Verification
In order to make a decision that a partner has failed a drug test, without good and sufficient reason, you must have received confirmation from the training provider.

chunks.title: Transfer between benefits — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: A transfer between benefits can occur when a client qualifies for Supported Living Payment while currently receiving another benefit. There is no stand-down imposed for clients who: - transfer to Supported Living Payment from another benefit type or - are included as a partner in another benefit type and are now applying as the primary client Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Childs Benefit and Orphans Benefit are also a benefit in this situation. Where Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit has been paid and the child now qualifies for Supported Living Payment, no stand-down is imposed.

chunks.title: Partner to be included — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: An initial stand-down is imposed, if a client receiving a benefit is to be included as a partner in a new application for Supported Living Payment. There are situations where a partner can continue to receive payment of Sole Parent Support or Jobseeker Support during the initial stand-down period where they are included as a partner in a new application for Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Examples — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: Generally in the 3 examples below the payment of the Sole Parent Support can be continued up to the actual commencement date of the Supported Living Payment. Example 1A client has been receiving Sole Parent Support and is now to be included in a new application for Supported Living Payment as a partner, an initial stand-down is imposed on the Supported Living Payment. Example 2A client has been in prison or on remand for 31 days or more and has applied for Supported Living Payment. On release, the client moves in with their former partner who was receiving Sole Parent Support. An initial stand-down is imposed on the Supported Living Payment. Example 3A couple with children separated and the mother received Sole Parent Support and the father was working. The father's job ceased and the couple are now living together again. The father applied for Supported Living Payment and an initial stand-down is imposed. If there has been a delay in applying for Supported Living Payment then payment of the Sole Parent Support may be cancelled from the date after the client has reconciled.

chunks.title: Non-beneficiary clients — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: When a non-beneficiary client receiving Extra help such as Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance applies for Supported Living Payment, it is not regarded as a transfer between benefits. An initial stand-down is imposed. For more information see: - Financial assistance during non-entitlement period - Core policy Relationship status for benefit - Processing standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Client intending to return to the same employer — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Client intending to return to the same employer
If a client has received any sick leave payments they would not be eligible for Supported Living Payment until these payments had stopped. You then assess any initial stand-down.
Clients are not required to use any sick leave they may have if they are intending to return to the same employer.

chunks.title: 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down
When a client applies for Supported Living Payment within 28 days of the entitlement date, the commencement date is the day after the initial stand-down ends.
This means, in some situations, MSD can commence a benefit from a date earlier than the application date.
If the application is not received within 28 days, MSD cannot backdate the commencement date.
Note the 28-day rule only applies to clients who have an initial stand down imposed.

chunks.title: Verification — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Verification
A partner must provide MSD verification of their position. They can do this anytime during the 2-week search period, but must provide it before the end of that period.
Once a partner provides MSD with verification of their position, MSD must confirm whether the organisation and position are suitable before a partner can start. MSD has a 5-day verification window to confirm this.
At the end of the 2 weeks, if the partner has not provided verification, they will have failed to find or complete their Community Work Experience and be considered non-compliant.

chunks.title: Two years residence — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Two years residence
A client must have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident to qualify for Supported Living Payment.
Note the 2 year period of residence must be 2 years continuous residence without absence from New Zealand. There are some circumstances however when a client can be absent from New Zealand during this time.
For more information see:
- Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
If the client is not a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident they cannot receive Supported Living Payment, whether or not they have 2 years continuous residence in New Zealand. They may be eligible for Emergency Benefit.
## Clients who do not meet the two years residence criteria
If the client does not meet the 2 year continuous residence requirement they may be able to receive an Emergency Benefit.
For more information about residence see:
- Resident in New Zealand
- Proof of residence
- Refugees and protected persons
- Calculating the period of absence
- Partner's residence status
- Reciprocal agreements
- Unlawful residence
- Permanent residence

chunks.title: Types of drug tests and standards — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Types of drug tests and standards
The drug tests a partner participates in must comply with the Australian/New Zealand standard - AS/NZS 4308:2008 (the drug test standard).
Drug testing detects residues of certain drugs and their metabolites in the body. Each drug has a set threshold or cut-off level for screening and evidential drug tests. To fail a test a person must have drugs present in their system that reach these thresholds or cut out levels.
There are two types of tests that measure the presence of drugs, these are:
- a screening test which shows whether drugs are or are not present
- an evidential test which is completed by an accredited laboratory, which can identify the actual drugs, the drug family and the amount of drugs present
In order to test, a urine sample must be provided by the person. Urine testing is the most common and accepted form of drug testing, and meets the drug test standard. To meet the drug test standard drug tests are undertaken by a person who is NZQA accredited for urine specimen collection in the workplace.
The standard requires the collection of a sample to follow a process that minimises the chances of a person being able to affect the result of the sample through substitution or adulteration.

chunks.title: Unable to meet work preparation obligations due to health condition, injury or disability — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Unable to meet work preparation obligations due to health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to partners with work preparation obligations. This includes partners who have work preparation obligations as a result of being exempted from work obligations.
A partner may be unable to meet their work preparation obligations when their health condition, injury or disability restricts them. For example when a partner is:
- in hospital or
- is unable to attend an interview with MSD due to their condition
MSD should consider the information on the partner's Work Capacity Medical Certificate or other medical assessments to see if the registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist has advised of any restrictions to a partner's capacity to plan for their return to work.
This is a full exemption.
## Evidence
To support their exemption, the partner must provide a Work Capacity Medical Certificate or other relevant medical assessments that state:
- a diagnosis (what the illness, injury or disability is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to work or to plan for work and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for work or planning for work and
- any other information that is required
## Duration
The period of an exemption for partners with a health condition, injury or disability is based on the next reassessment date recorded by their registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, or psychologist.

chunks.title: Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption
A client or partner, who is subject to a sanction or a 13 week non-entitlement period, may not need to complete a recompliance activity if:
- they meet the criteria for a full exemption from their obligations or
- they qualify for a benefit that does not have the obligations to which they must recomply
If a client or partner is subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period, and is unable to complete the six week activity or programme of suitable activities, you cannot recover the provisional benefit if they do not complete the activity because they meet the criteria for a full exemption from their work obligations.
## Example
A partner who is subject to a sanction who develops a health condition or becomes, injured or disabled, and meets the criteria for the exemption 'would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability'. They are unable to complete a recompliance activity.
In this situation you should add the exemption reason in SWIFTT, and follow the disputes process (so that the benefit can be resumed). Also consider the person's eligibility for Jobseeker Support on the ground of health condition, injury or disability.
For details of the requirements for a partner who has a health condition, injury or disability, see:
- Paying other assistance during a sanction
- Jobseeker Support Qualifications

chunks.title: Unlawful residence — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Unlawful residence
To reside in New Zealand lawfully the client must either:
- be a New Zealand citizen
- be an Australian citizen
- hold a New Zealand passport
- hold an Australian passport
- hold a visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009
- be deemed to hold a visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens and residents)
- be a British national who arrived in New Zealand prior to 2 April 1974 or
- hold a permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987
If the client does not fulfil one of the above, the client is deemed to be in New Zealand unlawfully.
Any periods of unlawful residence are excluded when calculating the clients' period of residence.
The calculation of the two year period of continuous residence commences from when the client is granted New Zealand citizenship or permanent residence.
For more information see:
- Permanent residence
- Proof of residence
- Calculating the period of residence
- Deciding ordinarily resident

chunks.title: Up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks
A client and their partner (if any) receiving Supported Living Payment must take all reasonable steps to:
- register their child or children with a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and
- keep up-to-date with the child's core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks
Note a client is only required to ensure their child completes core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks to meet this obligation from the time they begin to receive a benefit. For example, a client who starts receiving a benefit when their child is between 3 and 4 months old cannot be failed for not having completed the core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks the child should have had at ages 4 to 6 weeks.

chunks.title: Use all information available — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Use all information available
One form of medical or disability information may not be enough for MSD to decide the client’s eligibility to Supported Living Payment. If the client has additional information, they should bring this to their appointment.
MSD should use all available information about the client including:
- the existing assessment(s)
- information contained in MSD records (e.g. information on Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance)
- previous MSD medical certificates
If the information confirms the client meets the criteria for Supported Living Payment, MSD can consider granting Supported Living Payment.
If it is unclear from the information a client provides that they meet the medical criteria for Supported Living Payment, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor [no link find out why] .
## Example
A client provides an assessment from a specialist that provides a diagnosis and another suitable assessment e.g. NASC or special education report that focuses more on the impact of the person's illness or impairment.
MSD should use the information in both assessments to decide the client's eligibility to Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Using NASC assessment to decide severe disablement — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text: You can consider exempting all or some of your client's income if their disability extremely limits their ability to: - participate in employment - take care of themselves and - participate in the community Severely disabled clients usually need help from another person to carry out at least some of the daily routines of life. Your client's NASC assessment will provide information on the level of assistance they need to carry out their daily routines of life. Clients who need a high level of assistance to carry out their daily routines at home are more likely to require extra effort if they participate in employment. The main sections within a NASC assessment that you may be able to use to help you decide if your client is severely disabled are outlined in the table below. Note if your client has a NASC assessment, it does not necessarily mean that they are severely disabled. For more information see: - Deciding if your client is severely disabled Section of NASC reportThings to considerCurrent living situation(where they are, length of time they have been living there)Consider the person's living situation.Do they live on their own? A person who lives in supported living arrangements or who needs a significant level of assistance to live in their own home would be considered severely disabled.Mobility(covers mobility inside and outside the home, in the community, transfers, transport, driving)Consider your client's mobility needs.Does the person need regular support or assistance in most aspects of mobility?Generally a person who needs a significant level of support from another person to undertake these activities would be considered severely disabled.Personal care(covers ability to get in and out of their bed, bathing/showering, dressing/undressing, dental and personal hygiene etc)Consider your client's personal care needs.Does the person need regular support or assistance in most aspects of their personal care?Generally a person who needs a significant level of support from another person to undertake these activities would be considered severely disabled.Memory, Behaviour, Cognition(covers memory, behaviour, delusions/hallucinations, anxiety, supervision etc)Consider your client's memory, behaviour and cognition assessment domains.Do they have a severe loss of memory for recent and/or remote events?Do they need to be supervised - what is the length of time that the client can be safely left alone?It is likely that a person who has significant issues in these areas would be considered severely disabled. chunks.text: (where they are, length of time they have been living there) Consider the person's living situation. Do they live on their own? A person who lives in supported living arrangements or who needs a significant level of assistance to live in their own home would be considered severely disabled. Mobility (covers mobility inside and outside the home, in the community, transfers, transport, driving) Consider your client's mobility needs. Does the person need regular support or assistance in most aspects of mobility? Generally a person who needs a significant level of support from another person to undertake these activities would be considered severely disabled. It is likely that a person who has significant issues in these areas would be considered severely disabled. If the information you have confirms your client is severely disabled you can consider exempting all or some of their earnings from employment. For more information see: - Deciding amount of income exemption - Exemption for severe disablement - Process for decisions

chunks.title: Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct — main benefits > supported living payment
chunks.text:
## Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
A partner with work obligations applying for Supported Living Payment can have a 13 week non-entitlement period if they:
- have become voluntarily unemployed without a good and sufficient reason
- are applying for a benefit because they were dismissed by their employer for misconduct
'Becoming voluntarily unemployed' means the partner has resigned from, or otherwise left employment without a good and sufficient reason.
'Dismissal as a result of misconduct' means that the partner has lost employment as a result of misconduct without a good and sufficient reason.
There are some circumstances where a 13 week non-entitlement period would not be imposed. For more information see:
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed
Note the 50% protection for clients and partners with dependent children applies.
For more information see:
- Deciding non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or misconduct
- Effect of a non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment

Note a client getting Supported Living Payment (caring for a person), is not entitled to the personal earnings exemption.
For more information see:
## Example 1 - personal earnings exemption
Weekly gross income
