chunks.title: Infirmity - less than 52% — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Infirmity - less than 52%
If a veteran is assessed by Veterans Affairs as having no service related infirmities, or their level of infirmity is assessed as less than 52% whole-person impairment, or they receive a War Disablement Pension under the War Pensions Act 1954 that is less than 70%:
- there is no entitlement to a Lump Sum on Death payment for either the veteran or their surviving spouse or dependant
- the veteran's rate of payment is not reduced if they are hospitalised for more than 13 weeks
- the partner or spouse of the veteran is not entitled to receive Veteran's Pension
- the partner or spouse aged 65 or over has their rate of New Zealand Superannuation reduced to the Hospital rate if they are hospitalised for more than 13 weeks
- the grandparented non-qualified partner or spouse has their rate of Veteran's Pension reduced to the Hospital rate if they are hospitalised for more than 13 weeks
- the surviving partner or spouse is not entitled to continue to receive Veteran's Pension after the veteran dies and must transfer to another benefit or pension
- the partner or spouse is not automatically entitled to a Community Services Card

chunks.title: Infirmity - more than 52% — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Infirmity - more than 52%
If a veteran is getting a disablement pension, independence allowance or a lump sum payment for an impairment of 52% or greater, or is getting a War Disablement Pension under the War Pensions Act 1954 of 70% or more:
- their spouse or partner can also get Veteran's Pension if they qualify for New Zealand Superannuation
- their spouse or partner is eligible to get a Veteran's Pension after the veteran dies
- the surviving spouse or partner or dependent children may qualify for a lump sum payment when the veteran dies
- the veteran and their partner are entitled to Community Services Cards automatically

chunks.title: Intention to remain permanently — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Intention to remain permanently
When a client has only recently arrived in New Zealand, they may be considered resident in New Zealand if they are able to provide evidence, showing they intend to make their home in New Zealand for the foreseeable future.
An application for permanent residence is one way a client can show their intention to make New Zealand their home.
However, a client may be able to demonstrate an intention to make their home in New Zealand at an earlier date, such as the date that the client:
- arrived lawfully in New Zealand or
- any date between the date of arrival lawfully in New Zealand and the date permanent residence is granted
To determine whether the client intended to make their home in New Zealand at an earlier date, the following could be considered:
- if the client had a return ticket to their country of origin when they arrived in New Zealand
- if the client intended for their time in New Zealand to be temporary, i.e. they intended to return overseas
- the reason the client decided to come to New Zealand (e.g. family ties)
- what steps did the client take towards making their home in New Zealand? Such as: if the client bought or own any property or significant assets in New Zealandif the client moved cash and other assets to New Zealandif the client involved themselves in any New Zealand work, community events, clubs' membership and other groups such as, but not limited to, their local church or school
- if the client bought or own any property or significant assets in New Zealand
- if the client moved cash and other assets to New Zealand
- if the client involved themselves in any New Zealand work, community events, clubs' membership and other groups such as, but not limited to, their local church or school
- how long after arrival it took the client to apply for permanent residence in New Zealand
- the absences the client had from New Zealand after their arrival in New Zealand: what the reasons were for those absencesif the absences were prolonged or repeated
- what the reasons were for those absences
- if the absences were prolonged or repeated
The client must be both resident and present in New Zealand at the same time for the period to count when assessing if they meet the residence qualification.

chunks.title: Introduction — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Veteran's Pension provides retirement income for New Zealand veterans who have recognised service and who have reached the qualifying age for New Zealand Superannuation.
A veteran can choose to get either Veteran's Pension or New Zealand Superannuation, but not both.
The Ministry of Social Development is responsible for assessing and paying Veteran's Pension and its associated allowances on behalf of the Secretary for War Pensions (New Zealand Defence Force). The Secretary delegates the administration of Veteran's Pension entitlements to the Ministry under section 160 of the Veterans' Support Act 2014.
Service-related Disablement Pension entitlements are managed by Veterans' Affairs (Veterans Affairs).
## For more detailed information on Veteran's Pension entitlements see:
- Qualifications
- Obligations
- Commencement date
- Payment
- Changes and Reviews
- Community Services Card
- SuperGold Card

chunks.title: Kaumatua flats — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Kaumatua flats
Many marae include self-contained kaumatua flats. These flats are usually owned by the Runanga Iwi (Council of people) and are rented to kaumatua (elders).
Kaumatua living alone in one of these flats may receive the single living alone rate if the flat is a house or flat.
Note self-contained kaumatua flats will usually meet the definition of flat for the single living alone rate to be paid.
If the kaumatua flats do not meet the definition of a flat, you need to consider whether they meet the definition of a boarding house.
For more information see:
- House or flat
- Boarding houses

chunks.title: Missionary work — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: In certain circumstances, time spent doing missionary work outside New Zealand may be considered as being resident and present in New Zealand to meet the qualifications for Veteran's Pension. Missionary work includes the advancement of religion or education and the maintenance, care, or relief, of orphans, or the aged infirm, sick, or needy. Periods spent overseas at a university or seminary training for example, at a bible or theological college cannot be included for missionary work. Depending on whether the missionary work was before or from 9 November 2020, the period of absence for missionary work is treated differently for assessing periods of being resident and present in New Zealand to qualify for Veteran's Pension.

chunks.title: Missionary postings before 9 November 2020 — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: A client who began a missionary posting outside of New Zealand before 9 November 2020 can have it included as a period of residence and presence to qualify for Veteran’s Pension if they: - were doing missionary work and - were ordinarily resident in New Zealand immediately before they left for missionary work overseas or - were born in New Zealand The client’s partner will be able to use the client’s time as a missionary if they were accompanying the client while they were doing missionary work. Note missionary postings that began before 9 November 2020 and continued after that time are covered by these rules. For more information see: - Deciding ordinarily resident in New Zealand before they left for missionary work

chunks.title: Temporary return from posting — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: A client (and their partner if any) who left for missionary work before 9 November 2020 may return to New Zealand temporarily (after 9 November 2020) during their period of missionary work (e.g. for a holiday, or visit family) and then return to their original missionary posting overseas. A temporary return to New Zealand during the missionary posting period is not seen as disrupting the posting.

chunks.title: Missionary postings on or after 9 November 2020 — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: A client who began a missionary posting on or after 9 November 2020 can have it included as a period of residence and presence to qualify for Veteran’s Pension if they: - were doing missionary work and - were ordinarily resident in New Zealand immediately before they left for missionary work overseas and - were carrying out the missionary work for a charitable entity associated with a religious body If a client has started a new posting on or after 9 November 2020, even if it is with the same missionary entity, the client must meet the requirements for absences that can be considered resident and present that are in place at that time.

chunks.title: Missionary work for charity under the Charities Act 2005 — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Missionary work for charity under the Charities Act 2005
For overseas missionary work on or after 9 November 2020 to count as resident and present in New Zealand, the entity the client is doing the work for must be registered in New Zealand under as a charitable entity in the Charities Act 2005.
If the entity is not a registered charity, the periods spent overseas as a missionary cannot be counted as residence and presence in New Zealand.
Details of when a charity is registered, and any de-registration or periods of de-registration can be found in the Charities Register.
Client did overseas missionary work and the entity was registered the entire period
A client left New Zealand on 20 November 2020 and worked overseas as a missionary for 5 years and 8 months.
As the missionary entity was registered as a charity in New Zealand for the period of 5 years and 8 months' work, the missionary can be treated as residence and presence in New Zealand for this period (if the client meets the other qualifications).
Client did overseas missionary work and the entity was not registered for the entire period
A client left New Zealand on 21 December 2020 and worked as a missionary for 9 years.
The missionary entity did not register as a charitable entity under the Charities Act 2005 until the last 3 years of the client's missionary work.
Only the 3 year period during when the entity was registered as a charity can be treated as residence and presence in New Zealand (if the client meets the other qualifications).
Client did overseas missionary work and entity lost registration during the period
A client left New Zealand for missionary work on 30 January 2021 for an entity that was a registered charity under the Charites Act 2005.
The client worked as a missionary for 11 years, but the entity was de-registered from the Charities Register for the last 2 years of the client's missionary work.
Only the first 9 years of the client's work can be treated as residence and presence in New Zealand (if the client meets the other qualifications).

chunks.title: Mobile homes — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Mobile homes
From 9 November 2020, the living alone rate of payment can be paid for clients living in a self-contained mobile home.
## What is a mobile home?
A mobile home can include a caravan, house bus or self-driven purpose-built mobile home. To be a self-contained mobile home for living alone rate purposes, the mobile home must:
- contain certain features and
- be reasonably habitable
## Features of a mobile home for living alone rate purposes
To be self-contained for living alone rate purposes, a mobile home must have for the exclusive use of the client adequate areas for:
- day to day living
- sleeping
- preparing and cooking food and
- must also contain: a sinka toilet
- a sink
- a toilet
If the mobile home does not have showering or bathing facilities, the client must have access to these facilities eg they use public facilities that are readily available to them.
## Mobile home must be reasonably habitable
For a mobile home to be reasonably habitable for living alone rate purposes it must have:
- a fresh water tank or tanks and
- a waste water tank or tanks
The tanks may from time to time be connected for receiving water, and removing waste water but do not require a fulltime connection. The water tanks and waste water tanks support the toilet and sink facilities.
## Mobile homes must meet all requirements
A client must live in a mobile home that meets all of the requirements to be able to receive the living alone rate.
Mobile homes that do not have all of these facilities including the water and waste water tanks cannot be considered a self-contained mobile home, and the living alone rate cannot be paid.

chunks.title: Obligations — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Obligations
Clients must tell us straight away of any changes in their circumstances or their family's situation that may affect entitlement to Veterans Pension. Clients agree to this by signing the Veterans Pension application form.
Examples of changes and how to deal with these can be found in Changes and Reviews
## Partners aged 16 to 19 years old
When a young partner (aged 16 to 19 years old) is included as the grandparented non-qualified partner of a client receiving Veterans Pension, they have youth activity obligations.

chunks.title: Partner not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Partner not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand
A client whose partner is not permanently resident or is unlawfully resident in New Zealand, can be paid at the single rate of Veteran's Pension in some circumstances.
There are some exceptions for more information see:
- Partner's residence status
- Grandparenting non-qualified partner couples
## Partner lives overseas
If the partner is not in New Zealand and chooses to live overseas with no intention of moving permanently to New Zealand, and the client and partner are still a couple, the client should be paid the married rate of Veteran's Pension.

chunks.title: Partner's residence status — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Partner's residence status
When a client has a partner and they do not qualify for Veteran's Pension in their own right, their partner's immigration status must be checked as this can affect the client's rate of payment.
When the partner is present in New Zealand unlawfully or is on a temporary entry class visa, the rate of payment for the client is the single rate of Veterans Pension.

chunks.title: Payment — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Payment
Veteran's Pension is paid fortnightly on a Tuesday.
In general, payment must be made directly to the client. However, where there is good cause, the client's Veteran's Pension can be paid to another person, agent or institution.
For more information see:
- Redirection of benefit payment
It is a condition of receiving Veteran's Pension that the client provides a bank account number.
MSD can request the client or their partner who is included (grandparented non-qualified partner) to provide an IRD number or evidence of their IRD number.
For more information see:
- IRD number for client or partner who is included
## Rate of payment
The rate of Veteran's Pension paid depends on if the client is:
- single, living alone
- single, living in shared accommodation
- married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, and their partner can get New Zealand Superannuation in their own right
- married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, and they have a grandparented non-qualified partner included in their payment or
- married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, and they have a grandparented non-qualified partner who is not included in their payment or
- eligible to receive or receiving an overseas benefit or pension
## Also see:
- Veterans Pension and Accident Compensation
- Payments from overseas Overseas pensions
- Deskfile New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension rates

chunks.title: Principal place of residence — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Principal place of residence
To get the single living alone rate, the principal place of residence must be a:
- house or flat
- boat or craft moored within New Zealand territory
- hotel room
- motel unit
- room in a boarding house
- unit of accommodation in a caravan park or
- a self contained mobile home

chunks.title: Proof of residence — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: When a client provides proof of residence for their Veteran's Pension application all documents should be originals. Photocopies and/or documents that have been changed in any way cannot be accepted. When the client (or partner) cannot provide proof, or the proof is unclear, they should be asked to get proof of their residential status from Immigration New Zealand (for residence class visa) or the Department of Internal Affairs (for citizenship). Proof of citizenship and/or permanent residence in New Zealand can be: - Australian passport Australian citizens and permanent residents are lawfully allowed in New Zealand as they are deemed to hold a residence class visa. Their date of entry into New Zealand is generally not recorded, but can be requested from Immigration New Zealand / New Zealand Customs by the client. When possible, supporting evidence should be provided, such as tenancy agreements, bank statements or old utility bills, to show that the client has been ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date of application. - British nationals (travel information) British nationals who arrived in New Zealand before 2 April 1974, were allowed to enter New Zealand to reside and may be unable to provide proof of their residence if they do not have a passport. Immigration New Zealand may have travel entries and exits to and from New Zealand for these people from the late 1980s. The client should be able to provide New Zealand school, work, or tax records to support their claim about when they arrived in New Zealand, and the length of time they have lived here. - Certificate of Confirmation This is a certificate issued to confirm that the holder is a New Zealand citizen by birth, descent or Grant of Citizenship. British nationals, who immigrated to New Zealand before 1948 (and who resided in New Zealand for all of 1948) were made New Zealand citizens in 1949. These clients are likely to have a Certificate of Confirmation. - Certificate of Registration A child born outside New Zealand (to a parent who is a New Zealand citizen) may be a New Zealand citizen from birth. However, the child must apply for a Certificate of Registration to confirm their New Zealand citizenship. - Grant of Citizenship People who have permanent residence, may (generally after 5 years residence in New Zealand) apply for a Grant of Citizenship. They must meet the conditions of the Grant. - Letter of confirmation of permanent residence from Immigration New Zealand - Local official confirmation of residence in the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau - New Zealand birth certificate

chunks.title: Proof of residence — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: A person born in New Zealand is only considered a New Zealand citizen by birth if: - they were born in New Zealand before 1 January 2006 orafter 1 January 2006: one parent is a New Zealand citizen orone parent had a visa allowing them to reside in New Zealand - they were born in New Zealand before 1 January 2006 or - after 1 January 2006: one parent is a New Zealand citizen orone parent had a visa allowing them to reside in New Zealand - one parent is a New Zealand citizen or - one parent had a visa allowing them to reside in New Zealand - New Zealand passport To hold a New Zealand passport you must be a New Zealand citizen. - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence class visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009 - Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987

chunks.title: Qualifications — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
The qualifications for Veterans' Pensions are service, age, residence and infirmity.
For more information on these qualifications see:
- Service
- Age
- Residency
- Infirmity
Also see:
- Veterans Pension and Accident Compensation

chunks.title: Qualified client with a partner in long term residential care — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Qualified client with a partner in long term residential care
A client who is living in the community and whose partner is in in long-term residential care in a rest home or hospital, can get the single sharing accommodation or the single living alone rate of Veteran's Pension.
The rate of payment will depend on if they:
- share their accommodation with any person aged 18 years or older, other than a dependent child or a visitor who stays more than 13 weeks in any 26 week period, or
- meet all the qualifications for the single living alone rate
## Partner is in long-term residential care in a rest home or hospital at the client's entitlement date
The single sharing accommodation or single living alone rate can be paid from the date the Veteran's Pension commences when the partner is in long-term residential care in a rest home or hospital at the client's entitlement date.
## Client is already getting Veteran's Pension when partner enters long-term residential care in a rest home or hospital
The single sharing accommodation or single living alone rate can be paid from the date the partner enters long-term residential care in a rest home or hospital.
## Special Disability Allowance
Special Disability Allowance can be paid to the client in the community to help with extra costs due to their partner being in long term residential care and their partner is getting Residential Care Subsidy.
## Rate of payment for partner in care
There is no change to the rate of payment for the partner in care, they continue to get the half married, civil union or de facto rate of Veteran's Pension.

chunks.title: Reciprocal Agreements — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Reciprocal Agreements
New Zealand has social security agreements with several countries.
Under these agreements, residence and/or periods of contributions to their social security schemes in one of the following countries can be regarded as residence and presence in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Residency — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: A client's total residence and presence in New Zealand is used to decide whether they qualify for Veteran's Pension. The number of years a client must have lived in New Zealand to qualify for Veteran's Pension is increasing depends on their date of birth.

chunks.title: Clients who turn 65 before 1 July 2024 — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: To qualify for Veteran’s Pension before for people who turn 65 before 1 July 2024, a client must: - have been resident and present in New Zealand for 10 years from the age of 20 and - have been resident and present in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau or a combination of these, for 5 years from the age of 50 and - be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (i.e., not be in New Zealand unlawfully, or on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or - be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (e.g. Australian citizens or residents) and - be ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date of application (except where the client is applying from the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau under Special Portability)

chunks.title: Clients who turn 65 from 1 July 2024 — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: To qualify for Veteran's Pension from 1 July 2024, a client must: - have been resident and present in New Zealand for 10 years from the age of 20 and - have been resident and present in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau or a combination of these from the age of 20 for an additional period of up to 10 years depending on their date of birth, as it is gradually increasing from 10 years to 20 years, see: Residence and presence requirement from 1 July 2024 tables for the total time required and - have been resident and present in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau or a combination of these for 5 years from the age of 50 and - be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (that is, not be in New Zealand unlawfully, or on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or - be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (e.g. Australian citizens or residents) and - be ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date of application (except where the client is applying from the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau under Special Portability) Example Hyrum was born on 1 October 1973 in New Zealand and when he turned 30, he served in the New Zealand army overseas for 20 years. He retired from active service and returned to New Zealand. His date of birth means he needs a total of 10 years resident and present from the age of 20 and an additional 8 years resident and present in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue, and/or Tokelau from the age of 20. Five of the 18 years residence and presence required must be from the age of 50. He can use his time served in the New Zealand army overseas, to count as periods of residence and presence in New Zealand for the residency qualification.

chunks.title: 5 years residence and presence from the age of 50 — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: Any time a client is resident and present in New Zealand from the age of 50 may be used towards meeting any of the residence and presence requirements. Any time spent in the Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau from the age of 50, may be used towards meeting the additional years of residence and presence requirement. Example Jordyn was born on 10 August 1966 in New Zealand and joined the New Zealand Navy at the age of 20. She served overseas from the age of 20 until she medically retired at the age of 30. She moved to American Samoa and lived there for 30 years upon retirement from the Navy. Jordyn at the age of 60 moved to live in the Cook Islands, and stayed there for 5 years before returning to New Zealand on 1 September 2031. Jordyn remained a New Zealand citizen. Her date of birth means she needs a total of 10 years residence and presence in New Zealand from the age of 20, and an additional 4 years residence and presence in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue, and/or Tokelau from the age of 20. She can use her time served in the New Zealand Navy overseas, to count as periods of residence and presence in New Zealand for the residency qualification. The 5 years Jordyn spent in the Cook Islands after the age of 50 can be used towards the additional 4 years residence and presence Jordyn needs to meet the residency requirement. For more information see: - New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pensions: Residence and presence requirement from 1 July 2024 tables - Deciding ordinarily resident in New Zealand

chunks.title: Does not meet residency qualifications — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: If a client does not meet the residency qualifications for Veteran's Pension, they may be able to get a main benefit. If a client is not able to get another main benefit, an Emergency Benefit may be considered on the grounds of hardship to a client who does not meet the period of residence requirement for Veteran's Pension.

chunks.title: For more information about residency see: — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: - Clients 65 years or over - Resident and present in New Zealand - Treatment of periods of absence for residential qualifications - Partner's residence status - Proof of absence - Proof of residence - Reciprocal Agreements - Authenticating procedures [no link find out why] process

chunks.title: Resident and present in New Zealand — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: To qualify for Veteran's Pension a client must be resident and present in New Zealand for certain periods of time.

chunks.title: Resident — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: Resident in New Zealand means that: - the client must either make their home in New Zealand and have been living in New Zealand on a permanent basis or - if the client has only recently arrived in New Zealand, they must have the intention to make their home in New Zealand for the foreseeable future. Resident is not the same as being ordinarily resident in New Zealand. For more information see: - What is resident

chunks.title: Present — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: Present in New Zealand means that the client must physically be in New Zealand. For more information see: - What is present

chunks.title: Calculating periods of residence and presence — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: A year is regarded as 365 days (including the days a client arrives and departs from New Zealand) for the calculation of periods of residence and presence in New Zealand. Residence only includes periods of time a client was lawfully resident and present in New Zealand. Any periods of time present but unlawfully resident in New Zealand (i.e. without a valid visa or permit) are not counted in the calculation of residence and presence in New Zealand. Scenario Was client lawfully resident and present in New Zealand (NZ)? Include period of resident and present in New Zealand (NZ) for assessment? A client comes to NZ on a temporary entry class visa for 3 years, with the intention to live permanently in New Zealand. The client applies for and is granted NZ citizenship. Yes the client was lawfully resident and present in NZ for the 3 years prior to being granted NZ citizenship. Yes include the 3 years in the assessment. A client comes to NZ on a temporary entry class visa to complete studies for 2 years, with the intention to return to their country of origin. They return to NZ years later to retire. No although the client was lawfully present in NZ, they were only in NZ to complete studies. No do not include the 2 years in the assessment. A client comes to NZ on a temporary entry visa for 5 years with the intent of settling here permanently. The client goes through the process of becoming a permanent resident and is granted a residence class visa which replaces the temporary entry visa. The client leaves to live in France and only returns to NZ to retire. Yes the client was lawfully resident and present in NZ for the 5 years while on a temporary visa, as they intended to remain in NZ permanently, and worked towards this by applying to become a permanent resident. Yes include the 5 years in the assessment, but do not include any period of time the client was absent from NZ. A person is posted in NZ as a Diplomatic Representative (High Commissioner/Ambassador/Consular/Travelling office staff etc) for their country for 4 years and return to their country of origin after this. 10 years later they return to NZ to retire. No although the client was lawfully present in NZ, they were only in NZ for their employment to complete their diplomatic duties for their country of origin. They had no intent to reside in NZ and would not have been in NZ otherwise. No do not include the 4 years in the assessment.

chunks.title: Calculating periods of residence and presence — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: A NZ citizen lives overseas and comes to NZ once a year for 5 months only to visit their family and sightsee in NZ with no intention of living in NZ. They continue to do this right up until their retirement. This client decides to retire in NZ and moves to NZ at the age of 65. No although the client was lawfully present in NZ, they were only in NZ as a visitor. They had no intent to reside in NZ during these visits. No do not include any time the client was visiting NZ in the assessment. A NZ citizen is overseas for 5 years completing studies at a theological college, with the intention of returning to NZ one this training is completed. This client is married and has 2 children. The partner and children remain in their home in NZ during the time the client is overseas completing their studies. Each year for 5 years, the client returns to their partner, children and home in NZ for a 2-month break. During these 2 months in NZ, they lived at their home with their partner and children, and attended the church they are a member of, and worked as a volunteer Career Counsellor at the local community college. Yes although the client only spent a short time in NZ during the 5 years, they demonstrated their close connection with NZ and their time in NZ was not in the nature of a traveller/temporary visitor. It was their intention to return to NZ once the training was completed. Yes include all the 2-month breaks during the 5 years study period the client was in NZ. An NZ citizen lives overseas and comes to NZ once a year for 3 months over the summer only to visit their family with no intention of living in NZ. They have no home in NZ and stay with relatives. They continue to do this right up until their retirement. This client decides to retire in NZ and moves to NZ at the age of 65. No although the client was lawfully present in NZ, they were only in NZ as a visitor. They had no intent to reside in NZ on an ongoing basis during these visits. No do not include any time the client was visiting NZ in the assessment.

chunks.title: Calculating periods of residence and presence — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: An NZ citizen works overseas for 5 years as a contractor for a mining company on a fly-in, fly-out basis. They are billeted by their employer while working and have no property overseas. As they are a contractor, tax is not withheld at source on their earnings. They have tax obligations in New Zealand and the country they work in. Every 2 months for the 5 years, they return to their home in NZ for 2 weeks. During the 2 weeks they spend in NZ every 2 months, they live at home with their partner and child, attend the church they are a member of, and play regular pick-up basketball games with their old team at an indoor sports centre near their home. Yes although the client only spent a short time in NZ during the 5 years, they demonstrated a close connection with NZ, and the time they spent in NZ was of the nature of residence while the time overseas was solely to fulfil their contract obligations and had no residential aspect. It was their intention to return to NZ once the contract ended. Yes include all the 2-week breaks in NZ, during the 5 years the client was working overseas. A client who is an overseas citizen comes to NZ for 3 months on a temporary visa to stay with her only child who has a new-born. The client has no other family so, their intention is to settle in NZ to live with their child and grandchild. At the end of the 3 months when the temporary visa expires, the client returns to their country of origin and reapplies for a NZ temporary visa. The visa application process always takes 3 months to finalise. As soon as the temporary visa is granted, the client returns to NZ and leaves when the temporary visa expires to reapply again for a NZ temporary visa. While they are away from NZ, they start the process of selling their house and possessions in preparation for their permanent move to NZ. The client continues this practice for 5 years before they are granted a permanent class visa. Yes although the client was here on a temporary visa during all their 3-month trips to NZ, the time they spent here was of the nature of residence while the time overseas was solely to fulfil the visa obligations and avoid any possible sanctions. Their intention is clear to come to NZ on a permanent basis to be around their family. Yes include all the 3-month periods they were in NZ on a temporary visa over the 5 year period.

chunks.title: Residence and presence in the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: Clients can use residence and presence in the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau, or a combination of these to meet the resident and present required in New Zealand for 5 years from the age of 50. For clients turning 65 on or after 1 July 2024, the number of years residence and presence required will be based on their date of birth. Generally, a minimum of 10 years residence and presence in New Zealand from the age of 20 is required for clients born before 1 July 1959 and a maximum of 20 years of residence and presence is required for clients born after 30 June 1977. Any combination of residence and presence in the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau can be used by client to meet any additional residence and presence required above the minimum 10 years resident and present in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Rest home complexes — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Rest home complexes
Clients who live alone in a flat or unit that is part of a rest home complex can receive the single living alone rate if the flat or unit is considered a house or flat.
In particular check:
- the client owns the flat or has a licence to occupy it and
- that the flat or unit contains adequate and distinct areas for day to day living and sleeping, and a kitchen with facilities for food preparation, storage and cooking and a sink for washing up
Rest home units that provide limited kitchen facilities, for example a jug, sink and microwave can be considered a house or flat and the client can receive the single living alone rate.
Clients living in a rest home complex and receiving a Residential Care Subsidy cannot receive the single living alone rate.
For more information see:
- House or flat
- Residential Care Subsidy

chunks.title: Retirement Villages — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Retirement Villages
Clients living alone in retirement village units can only receive the single living alone rate if the retirement village unit is a house or flat.
In particular check:
- the client owns or rents the unit or has a licence to occupy it and
- the unit contains adequate and distinct areas for day to day living and sleeping, a kitchen with facilities for food storage, preparation and cooking and a sink with a drinkable water supply
For more information see:
- House or flat

chunks.title: Service — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Service
A veteran meets the service qualification for Veteran's Pension if they have qualifying operational service as defined in section 8 of the Veterans' Support Act 2014.
Confirmation of qualifying operational service is always made by Veterans' Affairs.
A decision to decline entitlement to a Veteran's Pension on the basis that the service is not qualifying operational service cannot be reviewed by a Benefits Review Committee or the Social Security Appeal Authority.
Any request for a review of decision must be made to Veterans' Affairs New Zealand.
- Veterans' Affairs List of Qualifying Operational Service
- Veterans' Affairs policies:ReviewsAppealsComplaints
- Reviews
- Appeals
- Complaints

chunks.title: Single clients — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Single clients
There are two rates of payment for single clients, depending on whether they live alone or share accommodation.
The client's income is not taken into consideration when assessing the rate of payment. However, if a client is eligible to receive or receiving any overseas benefit or pension the gross amount is generally directly deducted from their Veteran's Pension.
For more information see:
- Single living alone rate
- Definition of living alone
- Payments from overseas Overseas pensions

chunks.title: Single living alone rate — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Single living alone rate
Single Veteran's Pension clients (or married or civil union clients who are considered single) and who meet the definition of living alone can get the single living alone rate. This higher rate recognises the extra costs for clients maintaining a household on their own.
If the client meets the criteria on their entitlement date, the living alone rate is paid from the date Veteran's Pension commences.
The single living alone rate is paid to clients who are:
- getting Veteran's Pension
- single (or married or civil union clients who are considered single) and
- living alone in their principal place of residence
The following clients cannot get the single living alone rate:
- clients who do not meet the definition of living alone
- clients living in an institution and
- clients paying private board

chunks.title: Single rate for couples — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Single rate for couples
In some circumstances a person who qualifies for Veteran's Pension in their own right and who is living apart from their partner, can get the single sharing accommodation or the single living alone rate instead of the married, civil union or de facto rate.
In some circumstances a grandparented non-qualified partner who is physically separated from their partner can get the single sharing accommodation or single living alone rate of Veteran's Pension.
## Couples sharing accommodation
A client who has a partner can get the single sharing accommodation rate of Veteran's Pension if:
- they have separated from their partner because the relationship has ended or
- the partner of a person in long term residential care (including a rest home) or
- their partner is in long term public hospital care or
- they are legally married or civil union clients living apart with the intention of ending their marriage or civil union
Note the single sharing accommodation can be paid from the date the Veteran's Pension commences if the client meets the above criteria at their entitlement date.
## Relationship had ended
For a legally married or civil union couple to be separated there must be a physical separation, and an acceptance by one or both of the partners that the relationship has ended.
For a de facto couple to be separated their relationship must no longer be in the nature of marriage or civil union. A relationship in the nature of marriage or civil union means both financial interdependence and emotional commitment are evident.
## Couples who are living alone
A client living in the community who has a partner can get the single living alone rate of Veteran's Pension if:
- they have separated from their partner because their relationship has ended or
- their partner is in prison, where the Ministry of Social Development have decided to regard the client as a single person or
- their partner is in long term residential care including a rest home or
- their partner is in long term public hospital care and
- they are not sharing their accommodation with any person aged 18 years or over, other than a dependent child or a visitor who stays less than 13 weeks in any 26 week period
- they meet the other qualifications for the single living alone rate

chunks.title: Single sharing accommodation rate — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Single sharing accommodation rate
Veteran's Pension single clients (or married or civil union clients who are considered single) get the single sharing accommodation rate if they are sharing their accommodation with:
- any person aged 18 years or over, other than a dependent child or
- a visitor who stays for more than 13 weeks in any 26 week period or
- they are living overseas and getting payment under a Reciprocal Agreement or the Portability provisions
Note the single sharing accommodation rate can be paid from the date the Veteran's Pension commences if the client meets the above criteria on the date their Veteran's Pension is granted.

chunks.title: Spouse, civil union or de facto partner - Veteran deceased — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Spouse, civil union or de facto partner - Veteran deceased
A spouse or partner of a deceased veteran is entitled to a Veteran's Pension if:
- they have reached the qualifying age for New Zealand Superannuation and
- they are eligible to receive New Zealand Superannuation and
- the veteran had qualifying operational service and
- if the veteran had not died, they would have been eligible for New Zealand Superannuation and
- the veteran was receiving from Veterans Affairs at the date of their death: a disablement pension oran independence allowance orhad been paid a lump sum payment
- a disablement pension or
- an independence allowance or
- had been paid a lump sum payment
- for whole person impairment of 52% or more ora war disablement pension of 70% or more under the War Pensions Act 1954, if they died before 7 December 2014.
- a war disablement pension of 70% or more under the War Pensions Act 1954, if they died before 7 December 2014.

chunks.title: Start date for single living alone rate — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Start date for single living alone rate
The single living alone rate can start from:
- the date the client starts living alone, or
- the commencement date of the client's Veteran's Pension
whichever is the later.
The earliest date the single living alone rate can be paid is from 2 September 2013.
For more information see:
- Single living alone rate
- Mobile homes
- Effective date of review due to change in relationship

chunks.title: IRD number for client or partner who is included — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: MSD may make a written request a client to provide evidence of an IRD number, for a client who is being paid Veteran's Pension. MSD can also request evidence of an IRD number for a partner who is included in the Veteran's Pension (grandparented non-qualified partner).

chunks.title: Setting or extending the timeframe for providing evidence — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: MSD must provide the client or grandparented non-qualified partner with a minimum of 10 working days to provide IRD number evidence that has been requested in writing. MSD can extend the 10 working day period (in writing) if the client or partner has a reasonable explanation for requiring more than 10 days to provide evidence of their IRD number. This includes considering factors outside of the client or partner's control that cause delays, including, but not limited to: - client or partner has a family emergency that caused a delay - processing delays with an external agency (e.g., Inland Revenue, Department of Internal Affairs, etc) - client or partner does not speak English as a first language and has difficulty navigating evidence requirements - client or partner has limited access to the internet, a device, or their local service centre - client or partner has a physical or intellectual disability that makes accessing services difficult - client or partner is injured, disabled, or has a medical condition that makes accessing services difficult.

chunks.title: Notice following an unsuccessful match — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about IRD a client or partner's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the client or partner (in writing) to provide evidence of their IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the client or partner a minimum of 10 working days to provide their IRD number evidence or the assistance must be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Veteran's Pension and MSD holds an IRD number on record. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Isla's IRD number. MSD provides 10 working days in writing for her to provide evidence their IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Isla already having an IRD number - Isla not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD must suspend Veteran's Pension if evidence of IRD number is not received — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: MSD must suspend all taxable and/or income tested assistance the client is getting, including Veteran's Pension, if evidence of an IRD number is not provided within 10 working days from the written request, or extended period if this has been applied. If the partner has not provided evidence of their IRD number, their taxable and/or income tested assistance must be suspended. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance. Example Koa is receiving Veteran's Pension and MSD does not have an IRD number on record. MSD sends a written request giving 10 working days for them to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD receives no response to this request. MSD suspends Koa's Veteran's Pension because they have not supplied MSD with evidence of their IRD number within the timeframe provided.

chunks.title: IRD evidence may not be required in some circumstances — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text: MSD may not need evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - there are significant factors, that are outside the client's or partner's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number (e.g., a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence), and - the client needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided or - there are significant factors related to a health, injury or disability that are outside the client or partner's control that prevent them from providing evidence of an IRD number, and - an agent cannot be appointed to act on the client or partner's behalf. MSD can determine a later point to request the evidence of the IRD number. Example Sienna is 67 and receiving Veteran's Pension. Sienna's partner (Sara) is an agent with MSD to act on Sienna's behalf. Sara is not a recognised agent for Sienna for Inland Revenue. Sienna has an IRD number that results in a no match when MSD runs the IRD number validation API. MSD requests evidence of Sienna's IRD number. Sienna has a serious head injury, is unconscious and expected to be in hospital for at least 8 weeks. Sienna is not able to give consent to appoint Sara an agent for Inland Revenue to request IRD number evidence due to their injury. MSD can request this information later when Sienna's situation has changed. Note there is different guidance for requesting an IRD number or evidence of an IRD number when a client is applying for Veteran's Pension.

chunks.title: Transfer from another benefit — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Transfer from another benefit
If the client is receiving a benefit, Veteran's Pension can start from the day the payment of the previous benefit stops. This will usually be the day the client meets the qualifications for Veteran's Pension.
When Veteran's Pension is granted, the first payment covers the period from the commencement date to the day payment is made.

chunks.title: Treatment of periods of absence for residential qualification — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Treatment of periods of absence for residential qualification
Some types of absences from New Zealand can be counted as residence and presence in New Zealand for the residency qualification.
The types of absences are:
- special medical or surgical treatment (generally if treatment is necessary and unavailable in New Zealand)
- vocational training (generally if training is unavailable in New Zealand)
- seamen serving on a ship registered or owned in New Zealand and engaged in trading to and from New Zealand
- overseas services in forces as a member of any naval, military or air force of any Commonwealth country. This includes war service as a member of any organisation attached to any of these forces, e.g. YMCA, church, Red Cross
- full-time voluntary work humanitarian work this must be carried out for an entity that is: a charitable entity with its main function the giving of aid and assistance to less advantaged communities in one or more countries oraffiliated with or closely related to a charitable entity that has as its main function the giving of aid and assistance to less advantaged communities in one or more countries
- a charitable entity with its main function the giving of aid and assistance to less advantaged communities in one or more countries or
- affiliated with or closely related to a charitable entity that has as its main function the giving of aid and assistance to less advantaged communities in one or more countries
- any capacity as an accredited volunteer appointed by Volunteer Service Abroad
- missionary work (defined as including 'the advancement of religion or education and the maintenance, care or relief of orphans, or the aged, infirm, sick or needy')
- when a client has worked overseas and their New Zealand income tax (PAYE) was paid to Inland Revenue New Zealand (or it was withheld by the employer but failed to pay it to Inland Revenue New Zealand and the client did not contribute to the employer's failure to pay the tax)

chunks.title: ACC weekly compensation — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## ACC weekly compensation
A veteran may get ACC weekly compensation for an injury that is not related to their service with New Zealand Defence Forces.
There are some limitations on clients receiving both weekly compensation and Veteran's Pension.
The limitations are contained in the Accident Compensation Amendment Act 2019 and administered by ACC.
The limitations which apply are:
## Earnings-related weekly compensation for 24 months before reaching the qualifying age
A client who was entitled to weekly compensation for 24 months, before reaching the qualifying age for Veteran's Pension, is only entitled to get Veteran's Pension once they turn 65.
## Earnings-related weekly compensation for less than 24 months before reaching the qualifying age for Veteran's Pension
A client who is entitled to weekly compensation, before reaching the qualifying age for Veteran's Pension, is entitled to weekly compensation until they reach the qualifying age for Veteran's Pension,
After reaching the qualifying age for Veteran's Pension, the client may continue to receive weekly compensation for up to 24 months from the date they qualified for weekly compensation. The client can receive both Veteran's Pension, and weekly compensation over this period. Once the 24-month period has ended their weekly compensation ceases.
## Earnings-related weekly compensation 12 months before or after reaching the qualifying age
A client is entitled to receive both weekly compensation and Veterans Pension for 24 months where ACC weekly compensation entitlement commences:
- within 12 months before their qualifying age for Veterans Pension or
- on or after reaching the qualifying age for Veterans Pension
## Client's paid before the ACC changes on 1 July 2019
Clients who made an election to receive ACC rather than New Zealand Veterans Pension before 1 July 2019, will still only receive ACC. There could be clients in this situation up to 30 June 2021.
The weekly compensation payments are treated as income for income tested Veterans Pension and extra help.

chunks.title: Veteran's Pension modernisation and simplification changes from 9 November 2020 — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Veteran's Pension modernisation and simplification changes from 9 November 2020
From 9 November 2020, several changes were made that affect some New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension clients.
The following changes were effective from 9 November 2020:
- Ending the option to include a non-qualified partner in New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
- Existing couples getting the non-qualified partner rate as at 8 November 2020 are grandparented effective from 9 November 2020
- From 9 November 2020 non-qualified partners who have not been grandparented are able to apply for a main benefit if they need financial assistance
- From 9 November 2020 a non-qualified partner can apply for Emergency Benefit to provide care for their New Zealand Superannuation partner if they would otherwise require hospital care or if they are the principal caregiver of a dependent child under 14
- Extending the Living Alone Rate of Payment to single people who live alone in self-contained mobile homes
- Introducing a new residential concession for people who work overseas as a humanitarian worker for a charitable organisation which allows the periods working overseas to be treated as resident and present in New Zealand
- Amending the residential concession for missionary workers that links the concession to missionary work for organisations that are a New Zealand charity or are closely to aligned to one.
- Exempting the voluntary portion of an overseas pension from the direct deduction policy. The amount of any voluntary portion is treated as income.
- For some couples the excess overseas pension of one partner does not reduce their partner's New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran's Pension and Winter Energy payments.
- Removing deductions for an overseas pension received for a dependent child.
For more information please talk to Helpline.

chunks.title: Veterans Support Act 2014 Overview — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Veterans Support Act 2014 Overview
The Veterans Support Act 2014 takes effect from 7 December 2014 and replaces the War Pensions Act 1954. The new Act has made significant changes in the provision of support for veterans.
The Ministry of Social Development will continue to administer Veteran's Pension and Lump Sum on Death entitlements that arose prior to 7 December 2014, as well as ongoing Veteran's Pension and Lump Sum on Death entitlements.
All other forms of assistance under the new legislation are administered by Veterans Affairs.
Some entitlements under the former War Pensions Act 1954 have been preserved and will continue to apply, as well as some new transitional provisions to manage veterans' entitlements until December 2015. These mainly apply to assistance administered by Veterans Affairs but are recorded here for your information.
Some of the grand parented and transitional provisions include:
- veterans receiving allowances for attendant services, decorations awarded, and allowances, grants, concessions and loans being received or acquired under the former War Pensions Act will continue as if the War Pensions Act continued to exist
- any reviews or appeals commenced under the former War Pensions Act but not finalised will continue to be finalised under the former provisions of the War Pensions Act.
- any review right that existed under the former War Pensions Act that has not been exercised can be progressed as if the War Pensions Act continued to exist
- a veteran receiving a War Disablement Pension under the War Pensions Act will continue to receive their pension as if it were payable under the Veteran's Support Act 2014
- a spouse or partner of a Veteran receiving a Surviving spouse pension under the former legislation will continue to receive the pension as if it were payable under the Veteran's Support Act 2014
- veterans receiving Veteran's Pension immediately prior to 7 December 2014 are entitled to continue to be paid Veteran's Pension payments at the same rate under the Veteran's Support Act 2014

chunks.title: Veterans under age 65 — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Veterans under age 65
From 7 December 2014 all clients under the age of 65 who receive a current Veteran's Pension under the War Pensions Act 1954 can elect to continue to get Veteran's Pension under the Veteran's Support Act 2014, instead of Weekly Income Compensation from Veterans Affairs.
No new Veteran's Pension applications from veterans under age 65 can be made on the grounds of infirmity not related to service from 7 December 2014.
A veteran who received Weekly Income Compensation cannot elect to receive Veteran's Pension.
Eligible veterans can apply for a Veteran's Pension 2 to 3 weeks before they turn 65 so their payments commence from the date they turn 65.

chunks.title: Voluntary work for charitable entity under the Charities Act 2005 — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Voluntary work for charitable entity under the Charities Act 2005
For any absences overseas for voluntary work on or after 1 July 2005 to be counted for residence and presence in New Zealand, the charitable entity must be registered in New Zealand the Charities Act 2005.
If the entity is not a registered charity, the periods are not considered qualifying voluntary work and cannot be treated as residence and presence in New Zealand.
Charities can be de-registered from the Charities Act 2005. Details of when a charity is registered, and any de-registration or periods of de-registration can be found in the Charities Register.

chunks.title: Period of absence not counted — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Period of absence not counted
Generally, any periods of absence from New Zealand are not counted as being present in New Zealand and are excluded in the assessment of the Veteran's Pension residency qualifications.
There are exceptions when a period of absence may count as being resident and present in New Zealand.

chunks.title: What is resident? — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## What is resident?
There are certain criteria clients need to meet to be resident for Veteran's Pension.
To be resident in New Zealand for Veteran's Pension a client must either:
- have made their home in New Zealand and been living in New Zealand on a permanent basis or
- at the time they arrived in New Zealand, it was their intention to make their home in New Zealand
Being resident is not the same as a client's immigration status under the Immigration Act 2009.
## Client makes their home in New Zealand
In many cases, it will be clear that a client was resident in New Zealand as they will have lived in New Zealand on a permanent basis for many years.
Where it may not be so clear, the following could be considered:
- the reason the client is in New Zealand
- if the client intended to make their home in New Zealand
- if the client had a fixed abode in New Zealand
- if the client owned property in New Zealand
- if the client had frequent absences from New Zealand: if the absences were prolonged or repeatedwhat the reason were for those absences
- if the absences were prolonged or repeated
- what the reason were for those absences
- what was the client's involvement with New Zealand society, such as (but not limited to): community activitiesemploymentmembership of clubs andlocal churches
- community activities
- employment
- membership of clubs and
- local churches
Residence only includes periods of time when a client was lawfully resident and present in New Zealand.
Any periods of time present but unlawfully resident in New Zealand (i.e. without a valid visa or permit) are not counted in the calculation of the time of being resident and present in New Zealand.

chunks.title: When grandparenting ends — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## When grandparenting ends
Couples getting the Veteran's Pension grandparented non-qualified partner rate on or after 9 November 2020 will no longer qualify for the grandparented rate in any of the following situations:
- the non-qualified partner starts getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension in their own right
- the qualified partner chooses not to continue getting the grandparented non-qualified partner rate
- the qualified partner, with or without the non-qualified partner, is absent from New Zealand and no longer qualifies for Veteran's Pension on or after 9 November 2020
- the qualified partner is in custody, in prison or on remand on or after 9 November 2020 and does not qualify for ongoing payments of Veteran’s Pension for the period of imprisonment
Once the grandparented non-qualified partner rate ends, the qualifying partner cannot include a non-qualified partner again.
Note a client getting the Veteran's Pension grandparented non-qualified partner rate can transfer to New Zealand Superannuation if they qualify and include their grandparented non-qualified partner in their New Zealand Superannuation payments.

chunks.title: Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings — main benefits > veterans pension
chunks.text:
## Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
A client applying for a benefit including Veteran’s Pension can be considered resident and present in New Zealand during periods of overseas employment where:
- their employer (or other relevant person) deducted PAYE or source deductions from their wages and
- paid them to Inland Revenue New Zealand.
A partner who was with the client while they were working overseas can also be treated as resident and present in New Zealand for the same periods.
The residential concession does not apply to people who are self-employed and working overseas.
Clients should provide proof of the periods they were employed overseas, and that PAYE or source deductions were paid to the New Zealand Inland Revenue during these periods.
Note if the employer (or other relevant person) has deducted the tax but failed to pay it to Inland Revenue, and if the client did not contribute to the employer's failure to pay the tax, the period of employment overseas can still be regarded as residence and presence in New Zealand.

chunks.title: What's new
chunks.text:
## What's new
4 September 2026
Changes when a child turns 18
From 4 September 2026, when a dependent child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child. This means they will be excluded from their parent or caregiver's payments from the start of the pay period following the child's 18th birthday.
However, if the 18-year-old child is continuing in education and is not financially independent, the child may continue to be considered a dependent child until the start of the pay period following:
- the date they no longer meet these criteria or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18
whichever is earlier.
Note if a parent or caregiver gets a discretionary benefit, they must complete a review of circumstances when a dependent child turns 18, or when the child no longer meets the criteria to be considered a dependent child. If they do not complete the review, their benefit will be suspended.
For more information see:
- Core policy Child turns 18
- Core policy Review of decision when child turns 18
For information relating to specific main benefits or extra help, see the individual Map topics.
