chunks.title: Guidelines — guidelines
chunks.text:
## Guidelines
It is important to know which Act applies when you receive a request for information. This is because the Privacy Act 2020 and the Official Information Act 1982 deal with different types of information.
The following provide some guidance on these Acts:
- Guidelines to the Official Information Act 1982
- Guidelines to the Privacy Act 2020

chunks.title: Administrative reasons — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Administrative reasons
Due to administrative reasons you may not be able to fulfil an official information request. When trying to decide whether to refuse a request based on an administrative reason consider the following:
- Information is or soon will be publicly available
- The document does not exist or cannot be found
- Substantial collation or research is involved
- The request is frivolous or vexatious

chunks.title: Charging fees for providing official information — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Charging fees for providing official information
The Official Information Act 1982 allows us to charge the requester for the reasonable cost of the labour and materials involved in making the information available.
Normally MSD does not charge for Official Information Act requests.
However, if you are considering charging for the request, seek advice from your local solicitor to help decide if it is appropriate.
## Charging for Requests
The suggested charges for requests (as at 18 March 2002) are as follows:
- the first hour is free
- the first 20 pages are free
- $38 is charged for each half hour after the first hour and
- photocopying is charged at 20 cents per copy after the first 20 pages
Note even though MSD has the ability to charge for requests for official information this does not necessarily mean that MSD must charge for all requests for information.

chunks.title: Conclusive reasons — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Conclusive reasons
Information may be withheld where conclusive reasons or grounds apply.
Consider the following situations
- Prejudice the maintenance of the law
- Endanger the safety of any person
- Seriously damage the New Zealand economy
- Damage to the security and defence of New Zealand
Note consult your manager if you are considering withholding information for this reason.

chunks.title: Damage security and defence of New Zealand — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Damage security and defence of New Zealand
Work and Income work is not related to the security and defence of New Zealand.
It is unlikely you will get requests of this kind. However, if you get such a request, seek legal advice.
Example of where this rule applied:
A reporter requested a copy of a report to the Prime Minister on Environmental Damage resulting from French Nuclear Testing.
The report contained detailed policy options in response to the testing.
The information was withheld on the grounds that it could damage our security and defence.
When the requester applied for a review, the Ombudsmen agreed that releasing the report would have been likely to prejudice international relations.
The report was still withheld.

chunks.title: Declining a request for official information — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Declining a request for official information
There are 3 main types of reasons for refusing to supply Official Information:
The 3 categories are:
- Administrative reasons
- Conclusive reasons
- Good reasons
Note each category is a topic on its own.
There is a process you must follow when refusing a request for information.
To refuse a request for official information, you need to:
- notify the requester that the information is being withheld and
- give reasons why it is being withheld and
- inform the requester that they can get this decision reviewed by the Ombudsman
The Ombudsman's postal address is:
Office of the OmbudsmanPO Box 10 152Wellington 6143
or

chunks.title: Defining official information — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Defining official information
Official Information is:
- practically all information held by MSD including personal information
- all information relating to the Department that is held by:
- independent contractors employed by the Department
- any advisory councils or committees relating to the Department
- a Minister of the Crown
- an organisation

chunks.title: Document does not exist or cannot be found — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Document does not exist or cannot be found
The definition of 'document' is very broad as it includes all Work and Income departmental information, including videos, tapes, emails and other forms of media that store information.
Note you must take all reasonable steps to find the information. This means a reasonably systematic search. You must be confident that the document or information could not be found before you can use this reason for refusing a request.

chunks.title: Editing documents — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Editing documents
For requests where there is a good reason for withholding some of the information, but where the rest of the information must be released, you must:
- copy the document
- delete the protected information
- release the rest of the information
Note you must not withhold an entire document based on the need to withhold only part of it.
For example a document is requested from Work and Income. The document contains some personal information about a person other than the requester. Provided there is not a good reason to withhold the rest of the information, the document can be copied, the personal information deleted and the rest of the document released.

chunks.title: Endanger the safety of any person — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Endanger the safety of any person
You can withhold information if you believe its disclosure will put a person's life in danger.
For example: A client is in a refuge and their partner makes a request to Work and Income for the clients contact details. As the client is in a refuge their details should be protected and the information must not be released.

chunks.title: Examples of official information — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Examples of official information
Official information can be:
- a speech made by a work broker to a community organisation
- a set of instructions for staff on how to handle violent people
- the department's performance management system
- materials developed by a training contractor but not yet used within the department
- a case manager's schedule
- the reasons why someone is not entitled to a particular benefit
- a local regional newsletter to Work and Income staff

chunks.title: Good reasons — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Good reasons
When trying to decide if there is a good reason for declining a request for information, consider the following:
- Public interest
- Protecting the privacy of natural persons
- Prejudicing a person's commercial position
- Restricting Work and Income's ability to negotiate
- Maintaining effective conduct of public affairs

chunks.title: Identifiable person — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Identifiable person
A person can be identified through information that is unique to them.
Examples of the type of information that identifies a person are:
- name
- date of birth
- address
Note information which does not identify an individual is not personal information. For example, groups of people or organisations.
## The relationship between Official Information and Personal Information
Personal information is both personal information and official information at the same time.
This is because when the Privacy Act was passed it took over a lot of 'personal information business' from the Official Information Act.
When people make inquiries for personal information, sometimes we use the Official Information Act and sometimes we use the Privacy Act. It depends on who is requesting the information.

chunks.title: Information is or soon will be publicly available — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Information is or soon will be publicly available
You can refuse to supply information if you know that it is 'soon' to be available to the public.
- the difficult word to interpret here is 'soon'. This word means different things to different people. The Ombudsmen suggests that it may be used to decline the release of the text of a ministerial speech before it has been delivered, or to refuse a request for information contained in a readily available publication. Each individual case will be slightly different. Always seek your Service Manager's help
- if the information is already publicly available then you do not have to provide it separately but you may decide to do so anyway
Examples of when you would refuse to supply official information on the basis that the information is or soon will be publicly available.
Situation
Reason for Refusing Request
Someone requests a copy of an annual report which has already been published.
You could refuse to supply this because it is already publicly available. However, it would be courteous to let the Requester know where they could get a copy of the report.
Someone asks for statistics which you release on the 5th of each month - but they want them on the 3rd. There does not seem to be any pressing reason for them to need the statistics on the 3rd.
You could refuse this request on the grounds that the information will soon be publicly available.

chunks.title: Maintaining effective conduct of public affairs — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Maintaining effective conduct of public affairs
Official Information should not be disclosed if it affects the Government's ability to function.
The types of information that would affect the Government's ability to function are:
- inter-departmental minutes
- reports and recommendations
- advice to Ministers
- advice to Cabinet and
- advice to the Governor General
To determine whether disclosing information will affect the function of Government consider the following:
- What does the policy or document say?
- Has a decision been reached?
- Is the issue still being considered?
- What are the risks in revealing information?
- Would revealing information affect the implementation of the decision?
- Is the issue public knowledge?
If you are still unsure of whether revealing official information will affect the conduct of public affairs contact your manager client service delivery or local solicitor.
Note you must still take into consideration whether releasing the information is in the best interests of the public. Even if it disrupts the conduct of public affairs.

chunks.title: Official Information Act 1982 guidelines — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Official Information Act 1982 guidelines
The purpose of the Official Information Act 1982 is to increase the availability of official information in order to:
- enable more effective participation in the making and administration of laws and policies
- promote the accountability of Government Ministers and Officials
- enhance respect for the law and to promote the good government of New Zealand
- protect official information to the extent that it is consistent with the public interest and the preservation of personal privacy

chunks.title: Personal information — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Personal information
Personal information is any information that identifies a person
Note different rules are applied to personal information and protecting a person's privacy.
For more information see:
- Identifiable person
- Requests for personal information

chunks.title: Prejudice the maintenance of the law — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Prejudice the maintenance of the law
You may withhold information if its release is likely to interfere with normal legal processes. The sorts of questions to ask yourself are:
- Would this information stop offences being prevented?
- Would releasing this information stop offences being investigated or detected?
- Would releasing this information interfere with someone's right to a fair trial?
Note if you use these reasons you must be able to explain exactly why you believe the law has been prejudiced. Always contact your local solicitor if you intend to rely on this reason for not releasing information.

chunks.title: Prejudicing a person's commercial position — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Prejudicing a person's commercial position
If you think releasing information, such as disclosing a trade secret, could damage a person's business then you need to consider whether disclosing it is in the interests of the public. If not, then do not disclose the information.
If you are unsure consult your manager client service delivery or local solicitor.

chunks.title: Preventing improper gain or advantage — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Preventing improper gain or advantage
Official information should not be provided if it is going to be used for improper gain or improper advantage.
This may be hard to define but if you are unsure consult your manager client service delivery or local solicitor.
Note it is unlikely that you will get many cases where you will have to decline a request for information to prevent improper gain or advantage.
## Example
A university refused to supply a non-student with course notes and other relevant material.
The university argued that to have access to the information the person should be enrolled and paying a fee like other students.
The Ombudsman agreed that allowing the person access to course materials would lead to improper gain or advantage.
The person was allowed to view the information but could not take them away.

chunks.title: Protecting the privacy of natural persons — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Protecting the privacy of natural persons
This provision includes people who are living and those who are deceased.
Privacy is always an issue when the request is for personal information. You cannot refuse a request just because the information relates to another person. In order to determine whether to release this type of information, the Official Information Act requires you to consider the following:
- what effect the disclosure of the information would have and
- whether the effect is such that it is necessary to withhold the information
Note you can also refer to the Privacy Act as a guide to decide whether the information should be released.
Remember
If you are declining the request in order to protect the privacy of natural persons you are declining it under the Official Information Act 1982.
## Consult the person concerned
Wherever possible, the person (whom the information is about) should be consulted about the information being released.
We should explain to them what personal information is being sought and how their views will be taken into account.
The person should also be told that we cannot guarantee that their information will be withheld because Work and Income may be bound by the Official Information Act 1982 to release the information.
Note Regional Communications staff (only) are authorised to respond to requests from the media. You should refer these types of requests directly to your manager client service delivery.

chunks.title: Providing official information — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Providing official information
A person can make their request for information in any form they choose.
## How information can be made available
Information may be made available by providing the requester with a copy of or allowing inspection of any:
- written information
- film or video
- tape
- photocopy
- transcript
- summary or excerpt
- oral report
The person requesting the information can choose the form in which the information is to be supplied. However, there may be cases where you have to supply the information in a different format.
For more information see:
- Using the right Act
- Requests for personal information
- Requests from another government department
- Timeframe for responding to requests
- Charging fees for providing official information
- Declining a request for Official Information

chunks.title: Public interest — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Public interest
Before you decline a request for information you must consider whether releasing it is in the best interests of the public.
If the benefits to the public outweigh the reason for refusal, then you must release the information.
Note there is a difference between what is 'in the public interest' and what the public is interested in. If you are unsure about deciding what is 'in the public interest', consult your manager client service delivery or local solicitor.

chunks.title: Request is frivolous or vexatious — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Request is frivolous or vexatious
This reason is for rare cases where a person is clearly abusing the rights contained in the Official Information Act 1982, to gain access to information.
Note it is the request that is considered frivolous or vexatious, not the person making the request. Therefore you can only consider the nature of the request and not the requester personally.
In these cases seek advice from your manager client service delivery or local solicitor.

chunks.title: Requests about the reasons for a decision — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Requests about the reasons for a decision
A client has the right to request a written statement containing the reasons for any decision Work and Income may have made about them. Written statements must contain:
- findings on the facts
- an outline of the information that was used to make the decision and
- the reasons for the decision
These types of requests are made under the Official Information Act.
For example, if someone wants to know why we declined their application for a Student Allowance, we would release the information under the Official Information Act 1982.

chunks.title: Requester (or their Agent) makes request for their own personal information — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Requester (or their Agent) makes request for their own personal information
Requests for personal information held by Work and Income are covered under the Privacy Act 1993.
Example
A client asks you when their next benefit payment will be paid.
## Information requested about another person
For personal information requests about another person, (and the requester is not an authorised agent) use the Official Information Act 1982.
Example
A mother wants to know if her son's Student Loan has been granted.

chunks.title: Requests from another government department — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Requests from another government department
If the organisation asking for the information is another government department, do not use the Official Information Act to respond to their request as they are not an individual or body corporate.
Government agencies may use other legislation to request information.
A request for information from another government department should:
- be written on official letterhead
- contain the name of the requester and their position in the agency
- specify what legislation the person is relying on to make the request

chunks.title: Restricting Work and Income's ability to negotiate — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Restricting Work and Income's ability to negotiate
Work and Income carries out negotiations on a daily basis. Any information that is likely to damage negotiations and weaken Work and Income's stance, should not be released.
If you are unsure whether negotiations will be affected by the release of certain information, consult your manager client service delivery or local solicitor.

chunks.title: Seriously damage the New Zealand economy — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Seriously damage the New Zealand economy
Work and Income does not hold a lot of information that could have an impact on New Zealand's economy.
Consult your manager or local solicitor if you get a request of this type.

chunks.title: Substantial collation or research is involved — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Substantial collation or research is involved
The word 'substantial' is open to interpretation. This means a large amount of work rather than an inconvenience.
To help you decide consider the following factors:
- difficulty in locating, researching or collating the information
- the amount of documentation
- the work time involved
- the nature of the resources available
- the effect on the rest of Work and Income if resources (such as people) need to be diverted to meet the request
- that we are able to charge for the collection of information
## Example of when substantial collation or research may apply
You receive a request for information which is held in a certain type of printed document.
You find out where these documents are held, but when you go into the storeroom you find that there are about 500 metres of paper to be searched, with no indexing system.
It would take you a month to go through these documents and sift them for the information needed to answer the question.
## Suggested response to request
- call requester and explain situation
- advise requester of the cost if you are considering charging for the information
- arrange requester to look through information themselves, if this is appropriate
Note phoning the requester in these instances will often save time and extra work for Work and Income and yourself. This also creates an opportunity for you to find out from the requester the exact nature of their request.

chunks.title: Supply the information in a different format — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Supply the information in a different format
If you are unable to provide the information in the format specified (in the request for information) you will need to contact the requester.
Do not provide the information in the format requested if it may:
- impair efficient administration or
- be contrary to a legal duty
Note if you are unsure about providing information in the format requested contact your local solicitor.

chunks.title: Timeframe for responding to requests — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Timeframe for responding to requests
When you receive a request for information, you must either:
- provide the information or
- decline the request as soon as practicable
That means as soon as you can physically do it or within one or two days from the date the request was received.

chunks.title: Timeframes - Upper limits — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Timeframes - Upper limits
A maximum of 20 working days is allowed for:
- deciding whether information will be provided
- informing the requester as to whether the information will be provided or withheld
Note the 20 working days takes effect from the date the request was received.
## Extension of the 20 day period
If you are unable to provide the information within 20 days due to exceptional circumstances, you must contact the requester for an extension of time.
If something unusual happens to stop you providing the information or declining the request straight away, let your requester know.
If the timeframe is likely to be longer than a few days explain this to the requester.
This is all part of good client service.

chunks.title: Transferring requests — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Transferring requests
A request for information not held by MSD should be transferred to the appropriate agency for a response.
A request may be transferred if you believe another department, a Minister, or another organisation is more closely connected to the nature of the request.
For example, if a request for information is about a new policy, this might best be answered by the:
- Labour Market Policy Group, Department of Labour or
- Ministry of Education
Note transfers of requests for information must be made within 10 working days from the time the request was first received.

chunks.title: Using the right Act — guidelines > official information act 1982 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Using the right Act
It is important to know which Act to use when you have received a request for information.
This is because the Official Information Act and the Privacy Act have different processes for reviewing decisions.
Remember that:
- The Ombudsmen reviews requests for information, which have been declined under the Official Information Act
- The Privacy Commissioner reviews requests for information which have been declined under the Privacy Act
To determine which Act to use you have to consider who is making the request.

chunks.title: Authorised agent — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Authorised agent
If a client chooses to appoint an authorised agent to act on their behalf they can do so by completing an agent form or by informing the Ministry of Social Development in writing.
When the agent form or the written request is received, you should do the following:
- check the signatures of the client and agent
- check what information the agent is allowed to access
- check how long the agent has been appointed for
- keep a copy of the written consent or Agent form in the client's file
- make a note on CMS under "Service Details - agents details" with the agent's name and their role as agent
Note before disclosing the client's personal information to an agent you must check that, the agent has authority to obtain the client's personal information.
For more information, see:
- Checking their identity
- Temporary consent

chunks.title: Checking personal information for accuracy — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Checking personal information for accuracy
Before you use or disclose personal information, you must take all reasonable steps to make sure that the information is:
- accurate
- up to date
- complete
- relevant and
- not misleading
To ensure accuracy of personal information, the best source is the clients themselves. If you suspect any part of a client's record is inaccurate or outdated, etc, you should contact the client to check the information with them and then correct their record accordingly.

chunks.title: Checking their identity — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Checking their identity
Checking the identity of the person requesting the information is important before you release any personal information.
## Requests made face to face
1. Check if the Ministry of Social Development has the person requesting information on file.
2. If a file exists, identify the requester by requesting identification and asking questions such as age.
## If the requester does not have a file
1. Ask for a form of photo identification such as a passport.
Note if you have any doubts about the identity of the requester, do not release the information.
## Requests made over the phone
1. If the requester is asking for their own information you can identify them by asking questions and checking the answer from their file.
Note you must ask a minimum of 3 identifying questions.
2. If the requester is asking for someone else's information you must instruct them to make the request in writing. Alternatively, if the requester is another department or company, their request should be made on appropriate letterhead and include the following information:
- their name
- their position
- the information they require
- what authority they are using to ask for the information and
- their contact details
Note if the client is with their agent, we can release the information to the agent if we can identify the client. You must only release the information the client has authorised the agent to get, and only at the time of the conversation, unless the Ministry has recorded the agent has authorised to act.
For more information, see:
- Responding to a request for personal information

chunks.title: Collecting personal information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Collecting personal information
The Ministry of Social Development can only collect personal information that is relevant to its work. That includes using the information to:
- administer benefits
- administer Student Allowances and Student Loans
- provide employment related services
Information that would be considered irrelevant for the Ministry's work would include, for example, a client's eye colour.
For more information see:
- Sources of personal information

chunks.title: Complaints to the Privacy Commissioner — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Complaints to the Privacy Commissioner
If a client believes that the Ministry of Social Development has breached their privacy and is not satisfied with how the Ministry has handled their complaint, they can ask the Privacy Commissioner to investigate. The Privacy Commissioner will:
- decide whether to investigate the complaint
- require Ministry staff members to answer questions and require the Ministry to give information relating to the complaint
- determine whether interference under the Privacy Act 2020 has taken place
- explore the possibility of a settlement
Privacy complaints can go to the Human Rights Review Tribunal for resolution if they cannot be resolved by the Privacy Commissioner. The Human Rights Review Tribunal can award damages of up to $350,000 against the Ministry to the complainant for interfering with their privacy.
For more information, from the Office of the Privacy Commissioner, see:
- Introduction to complaints
- Contact us

chunks.title: Correcting personal information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Correcting personal information
All clients have the right to request their personal records held by the Ministry of Social Development to be corrected. The request must be made by the client themselves or an authorised agent.
If you are unable upon request of a client to correct their personal record for any reason (e.g. the client disagrees with an opinion about them from a third party that has been included in their file, or you do not agree the information the client has provided is correct), the client has a right to provide a statement of correction, which the Ministry must attach to the information in question within the client's record.

chunks.title: Defining personal information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Defining personal information
Personal information means information about an identifiable human being.
A person can be most obviously identified by information such as:
- name
- SWN
- date of birth
- address
The information does not need to name the person directly. If it's possible to tell who the person is from what is said about them, then it is personal information.
For example if we say an unnamed person with green hair in a small town is getting Sole Parent Support, that's quite possibly enough to identify them.
Common examples of personal information that we hold about clients or staff include:
- information about benefits
- employment information
- medical information
- financial information
- a person's ethnicity or iwi affiliation
Information about one person can sometimes also be information about another person - the same information may tell us something about both of them. For example, an opinion may be just as much about the person who holds the opinion as the person they are talking about.

chunks.title: Examples of requests — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Examples of requests
For examples of Privacy Act 2020 requests and Official Information Act 1982 requests, consider the following:
Situation
Act
Someone rings and asks for their entire file.
Privacy Act 2020.
A mother wants information about her daughter who is a Ministry of Social Development client. The mother is not an agent.
And
A landlord wants information about their tenant who is a Ministry client because they have skipped rent.
Official Information Act 1982.
The information may be withheld under the Official information Act 1982 on the grounds that withholding the information is necessary to protect the privacy of natural persons.
Note the information the mother and the landlord want access to in these situations is not about them and, so, they do not have any right to access it under the Privacy Act 2020.
The Police come in and ask for someone's address that they are investigating for an offense.
Privacy Act 2020.
Under the Privacy Act 2020, you may disclose the address to the New Zealand Police so long as you are satisfied that disclosure is necessary for them to conduct their investigation.
Another Act that may apply is the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989. You must disclose information relating to the safety or wellbeing of a child to a Police constable upon request if the information is required to determine whether a child is in need of care or protection.
The Police can also compel the Ministry of Social Development to provide them with information by way of a production order obtained from the Court or by way of some other statutory authority.
See Request for personal information from another government agency for more information.
A client wants to find out the name of the person who made an allegation of fraud against them.
Although it might look like an Official Information Act 1982 request, the person is actually asking for information that is held in their own file, so it should be handled as a Privacy Act 2020 request.
Depending on the circumstances, this information may be withheld under one of several applicable grounds of the Privacy Act 2020.

chunks.title: Informing the client about collecting their personal information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Informing the client about collecting their personal information
When collecting information from a client you must inform them of the following:
- the fact that the information is being collected
- the reason you are collecting the information
- with whom the Ministry intends to share their information
- whether collection of the information is authorised or required under other legislation
- the consequences of not supplying the information
- the client's right to access their information and correct it

chunks.title: Personal information requested is not held by the Ministry — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Personal information requested is not held by the Ministry
If a person makes a request to the Ministry of Social Development for personal information that the Ministry does not hold, one of the following options may apply.
## The information requested does not exist, or cannot be found
The Privacy Act 2020 allows the Ministry to refuse a request if the information requested does not exist or cannot be found. You must take all reasonable steps to find the information. This means a reasonable systematic search. You must be confident that the information could not be found before you can rely on this ground to refuse a request for personal information. See section 53(a) Privacy Act 2020.
## The information is held by another agency
If the information requested is not held by the Ministry but is believed to be held by another agency, or it is more closely connected with the functions or activities of another agency, the Ministry should transfer the request to that agency and inform the requester. If you do not think the requester would want the request to be transferred, check with them, and let them know which agency you would suggest the request should go to. This gives them the choice about what to do.
If you need to transfer the request, it must be done within 10 working days from the date it was received. See section 43 Privacy Act 2020.
See also:
- Reasons for withholding personal information

chunks.title: Purpose — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Purpose
The purpose of the Privacy Act 2020 is to promote and protect individual privacy. It governs how we can collect, use, disclose, store and give access to personal information.
Personal information is information about identifiable, living individuals.
## The information privacy principles
At the heart of the Privacy Act are thirteen information privacy principles. They cover:
- collection of personal information (IPPs 1-4)
- storage and security of personal information (IPP 5)
- requests for access to and correction of personal information (IPPs 6-7 and Part 4 of the Act)
- accuracy of personal information (IPP 8)
- retention of personal information (IPP 9)
- use and disclosure of personal information both within and outside New Zealand (IPPs 10-12) and
- using unique identifiers (IPP 13)
Other laws can override the information privacy principles in certain circumstances.
In addition, the Privacy Act sets out the following:
- the role and functions of the Privacy Commissioner and making complaints
- notifiable privacy breaches
- information sharing between agencies
This section of Map covers the following guidelines pertaining to the Privacy Act 2020:
- Defining personal information
- Requests for personal information
- Privacy Breach
- Collecting personal information
- Source of personal information
- Informing the client about collecting their personal information
- Storing and securing personal information
- Correcting personal information
- Checking personal information for accuracy
- Using personal information
- Complaints to the Privacy Commissioner

chunks.title: Privacy Breach — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: A privacy breach happens when a Ministry of Social Development employee accidentally or without authority, accesses, discloses, alters, loses or destroys a client or staff member's personal information. This can happen for example when: - sending an email or a letter containing personal client information to the wrong person - telling a person who is not a client's authorised agent something about that client - disclosing information about another individual when responding to a Privacy Act request for information - leaving a document containing personal information somewhere others without authorised access can see it - showing a client's record to someone who is not authorised to see it - accessing a client's record for no legitimate business purpose When incidents like this happen, you must report it to the Ministry's Privacy team. The Privacy team is responsible for determining whether a privacy breach has occurred, whether it has caused or may cause serious harm so that it becomes a notifiable breach under Subpart 1-Notifiable privacy breaches Part 6, Privacy Act 2020. Telling the privacy team when a breach occurs is essential. They are there to support you - they can advise you what to do so that you can take steps quickly to protect and contact affected people. The privacy team is also responsible for notifying the Privacy Commissioner about notifiable breaches - if they do not know that a breach has happened, they cannot do this. Failure to notify the Commissioner of a notifiable breach is an offence under the Act and puts the Ministry at risk. Guidance for reporting incidents, together with a link to the Privacy incident online form, can be found at Reporting a Privacy or IT Security Breach [no link find out why] doogle. Once you submit the online form, the Privacy team will get in touch with you to provide advice and support toward full resolution of the incident. Note accidents happen on occasion and are not necessarily a matter for Human Resources. It is important that our staff feel able to tell people when a breach happens so they can get support and we can minimise the possible harm to affected people. However, it may become a Code of Conduct issue if you are blatantly careless with how you treat people's information, or if you ignore guidance and the same or a similar incident happens again. It is also a Code of Conduct issue if you deliberately access or disclose information improperly.

chunks.title: Privacy Breach — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: A person affected by a privacy breach may complain to the Privacy Commissioner if they are not satisfied with how the Ministry has handled it.

chunks.title: Reasons for withholding personal information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: When considering whether personal information requested under the Privacy Act 2020 should be withheld, the following reasons for withholding personal information may apply.

chunks.title: The information is private to someone else — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: If information about another individual is in a requestor's file, such as the requestor's partner or friend, and disclosing the information would unreasonably breach that individual's privacy, you may withhold that information. See section 53(b)(i) or (ii) Privacy Act 2020.

chunks.title: Protecting someone from physical or emotional harm — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: If releasing information would be likely to put the requestor or someone else at risk of physical or emotional harm, the following withholding grounds may apply: - serious threat to life, health or safety of an individual. See section 49(1)(a)(i) Privacy Act 2020. - significant risk of serious harassment of an individual. See section 49(1)(a)(ii) Privacy Act 2020. - disclosing information about a victim of an offence which would cause them distress. See section 49(1)(a)(iii) Privacy Act 2020. - disclosing the information may negatively affect the requester's own physical or mental health. See section 49(1)(b) Privacy Act 2020. - the requester is under 16 years old and disclosing the information may not be in their interests. See section 49(1)(c) Privacy Act 2020.

chunks.title: Disclosing the information would prejudice the maintenance of the law — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: If the person requesting the information is under investigation by the Ministry or the Police, and releasing information to the requestor would be likely to interfere with the investigation, then you may withhold that information. See section 53(c) Privacy Act 2020.

chunks.title: The information is subject to legal professional privilege — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: If the information requested includes advice from a legal representative of the Ministry (e.g. MSD Legal Services), it should be withheld as legally privileged information. Advice from the legal team may have been included in a client's file for example because the client was under investigation for fraud and the Fraud unit needed legal advice to assess whether the Ministry may prosecute the client. See section 53(d) Privacy Act 2020.

chunks.title: Information is evaluative material and is subject to a promise of confidentiality — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: If a staff member requests their HR file, some information may have been provided in confidence (express or implied). A common example is reference checks. If releasing it would breach that confidentiality, the information may be able to be withheld. See section 50(1)(a) Privacy Act 2020.

chunks.title: Where to get advice — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: If you are unsure whether a withholding ground applies, contact the Privacy team at PrivacyOfficer@msd.govt.nz for advice.

chunks.title: Request for personal information from another government agency — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Request for personal information from another government agency
Some government agencies have powers to obtain certain types of information from the Ministry of Social Development by way of a production order obtained from the Court or by way of some other statutory authority. These powers can override the Privacy Act 2020.
A production order is a document the Police or a person authorised under the Search and Surveillance Act 2012 can obtain from the Court. It compels a person, including a person in their role as a representative of the Ministry of Social Development, to give to the Police or authorised person the information they require. Details of the information requested, the grounds on which the order is made and how and when to provide the information must be set out in the production order.
When the Police or another government agency makes a request for information under some other statutory authority, they should provide the following:
- the request in writing, including details of the information they are requesting
- details of the statutory authority they have for obtaining the information, and a description of how their statutory authority applies in the circumstance
- the name, contact details and role of the person in the agency making the request
Common examples of statutory authority are:
- Oranga Tamariki or Police asking for information for child protection purposes under section 66 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- Inland Revenue, under section 17B of the Tax Administration Act 1994
- Ministry of Justice, relating to collection of fines
## Agencies without statutory authority
Debt collectors, landlords and process servers do not usually have any specific statutory authority to obtain information from the Ministry of Social Development.
Requests for information from these agencies should be considered as Official Information Act 1982 requests and assessed on a case by case basis.
If you are unsure about what to do with a request for information from another agency, can contact the Privacy team at PrivacyOfficer@msd.govt.nz for advice.

chunks.title: Requests for personal information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Requests for personal information
An individual has the right under the Privacy Act 2020 to ask for information the Ministry holds about them.
They can ask for it either in writing or verbally. If someone makes a verbal request, make a clear note of that request and when they made it.
They can ask for information to be provided in a particular form (such as a copy). Some people ask for specific things; some want to see everything we hold about them. They do not have to say why they want it.
They can authorise their lawyer, an advocate or someone else (such as a family member or friend) to request and receive their information on their behalf.
When dealing with a request for personal information you must act quickly to ensure it is responded to appropriately and as soon as possible - certainly no later than 20 working days, unless the Act allows us to extend the response time.
There are some exceptions to an individual's right to access their information, such as whether releasing the information may breach someone else's privacy or whether it will cause physical or emotional harm to themselves or someone else. But, generally, we must give them what they ask for.
If someone requests their information, record their request (including their name, contact details and the date requested) and inform your manager client service delivery as soon as possible. You must do this regardless of whether the information is held by your business unit or not, and regardless of whether it is held by the Ministry or not.
You and your manager client service delivery are responsible for making sure it is responded to appropriately.
Note a request must not be returned to the person requesting the information on the basis that the information is not held in the office that received the request.
Example if a person requesting the information makes a request to the Nelson office for their file, but their file is held by the debt unit or StudyLink, or any other part of the Ministry, the Nelson office would be responsible for collecting the information from the other parts of the Ministry and responding to the request.
## For guidance in responding to requests for personal information, see:
- Responding to a request for personal information

chunks.title: 1. Acknowledge the request — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: - Let the requester know you have received their request and that it will be responded to within 20 working days from the date they made it. See Time limits relating to requests for personal information. - If you're not certain what the request is for, or you think the requester may only want specific things rather than their whole file, have a friendly talk to the them to see if they can explain what they want, so we can help them better. Remember though that people are entitled to ask for their whole file if they want to. Make sure you remain helpful and co-operative. - If access to the information requested is restricted to another Ministry of Social Development business unit, you may need to ask that unit to send the information to the requester directly. For guidance on refusing a request if the information does not exist or cannot be found; or transferring a request to another agency if the information is not held by MSD, see: - Personal information requested is not held by the Ministry

chunks.title: 2. Gather the information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: Check everywhere in the Ministry that has information about the requester within the scope of the request. If they are requesting all information held by the Ministry, you must gather all information the Ministry holds about them. Download it, or copy it into a format that will allow you to assess it and withhold any part of it, if required.

chunks.title: 3. Assess the information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: Generally, the requester will be entitled to access their information. But there are good reasons for withholding information, which we need to consider. For guidance on grounds for withholding information, see Reasons for withholding personal information.

chunks.title: 4. Check the information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: Carefully check the copy of information that you propose to send to the requester, to make sure you do not release information that the Ministry should withhold (for instance, information about another person where releasing it would breach that person's privacy).

chunks.title: 5. Release the information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: Send the information with a response letter to the requester. Make sure it is sent safely so that only the requester will see it. The response letter should set out: - the date the request was made and what was requested - what information you have provided - what information you have withheld and your reasons for withholding it - that the requester has a right to complain to the Privacy Commissioner if they are not satisfied with our response The requester should be positively identified before sending the information, so that we can be sure we are sending it to the correct individual. See: - Checking their identity - Authorised agent

chunks.title: 6. Record the request and file it — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: Keep a record of all key documents related to the request in a secure location: - the request letter/email/note - acknowledgement letter, transfer letter, extension letter, or refusal letter - copies of the original file without redactions and the file with redactions - response letter - any other correspondence with the requester

chunks.title: More information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: For more information, see: - Using the right Act - Examples of requests - Request for personal information from another government agency

chunks.title: Source of personal information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Source of personal information
The Privacy Act 2020 states that all personal information should be collected directly from the individual concerned. However, there are certain circumstances when the Ministry of Social Development may use other sources to collect personal information.
This could include:
- the client has consented to the Ministry collecting their information from somewhere else
- the information is publicly available
- the Ministry can access information from anyone under Schedule 6 of the Social Security Act 2018 for specified reasons. You must check with your manager if you need to make a request for information under Schedule 6 as there are specific rules that apply.
If you think there is reason to collect personal information without going to the person first, seek advice before doing so.
For more information see:
- Informing the client about collecting their personal information
- Gathering information - Benefit & Social Housing Fraud [no link find out why] Doogle

chunks.title: Storing and securing personal information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: The Ministry of Social Development has a responsibility to protect and secure all personal information against: - loss - unauthorised access, use, modification and disclosure - other misuse

chunks.title: Examples — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: Situation Response When you are working on a client's file on your computer and you need to leave your desk. You must lock your screen and keep your access card with you so that others cannot access the client's personal information. When you need to send a fax containing personal client information. 1. Always use a cover sheet. 2. Call the recipient to make sure they are there to receive the fax. 3. Check the number before you send it and recheck it on the transmission report after you have sent it. 4. Use speed dial numbers on a fax, if possible. When you need to send an email containing personal client information. 1. Ask the client's permission to send their information via email. 2. Check the email address to ensure it's going to the correct person. 3. Ensure the personal information is contained in a document that can be password encrypted. Do not put personal information into the body of the email. Send the password separately. When you need to send an email to multiple clients. Always use the "Bcc" field so that the recipients cannot see each other's email addresses. Do not put multiple clients' email addresses into the "to" field. When you need to copy personal client information onto a separate document saved on your computer's hard drive or you need to print it out. You must only do this if you have a legitimate business reason to. You must ensure the information is protected at all times against loss and unauthorised misuse, access and disclosure. Once your purpose has been met, you must destroy that information appropriately. When you are collecting a client from the reception area and they start providing you with their personal details before you get to the interview area. You should never discuss personal details with clients when there is a risk you may be overheard. Indicate to the client that you will resume the conversation in the interview area. When you have been told by your manager to destroy a client's personal information. Always put the information in the designated document destruction bins. Do not throw it out with general rubbish. Note be careful when destroying information. It may still be needed or should be archived instead of destroyed. If you are unsure, talk to your manager.

chunks.title: Examples — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text: Remember, failure to protect personal information held by the Ministry against unauthorised or accidental access, disclosure, alteration, loss or destruction is considered a privacy breach. For more information about this, including what to do if a breach occurs, see: - Privacy Breach

chunks.title: Temporary consent — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Temporary consent
A client can give you or an agent temporary consent to act on their behalf as long as proper authorisation is given.
Consider the following examples:
If the client is in front of you and they give you consent to ring the power company for their personal information, you may do so. However, you must make a note on their file that consent has been granted.
- In this case temporary consent has lapsed as soon as the client walks out of the office. You cannot ring the power company again the following week unless the client has explicitly agreed to this.
A client comes in with a cousin to discuss their benefit. The client does not object to their cousin's presence and therefore has consented to the cousin hearing their personal information.
- The next day the cousin rings and asks to find out the client's benefit rate. You must not disclose this information without getting formal consent from the client first.
For more information, see:
- Responding to a request for personal information

chunks.title: Time limits relating to requests for personal information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Time limits relating to requests for personal information
We should respond to requests for information as soon as possible. However, a maximum of 20 working days is allowed to notify the requestor whether the request will be granted (in full or in part). The 20 working days takes effect from the date the request was received.
## Extension of time limits
You can extend the 20 working day period if:
- the request is for a large quantity of information or a search through a large quantity of information is needed, and meeting the original time limit would reasonably interfere with the operations of the Ministry or
- if consultations necessary to make a decision on the request are such that a proper response to the request cannot reasonably be made within the time limit or
- processing the request raises issues of such complexity that more time is needed
The extension period must be reasonable under the circumstances and you must notify the requestor accordingly, including your reason for extending it, within 20 working days from the date the request was received.
If unexpected delays occur, talk to the requestor and explain what is happening and when you expect to be able to provide the information - good communication is part of good client service.

chunks.title: Using personal information — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Using personal information
Personal information must only be used for the purpose it was collected. Using the information for any other purpose may be a breach of the Privacy Act 2020.
There are, however, exceptions to this rule. Consider the following:
- the new use is directly related to the purpose for collecting it
- the information is used in a way where the individual cannot be identified i.e. statistical for research purposes
- the new use is authorised by the individual concerned
- the source of information is publicly available, and it would not be unfair or unreasonable to use it
- it is necessary to use personal information to avoid "prejudice to the maintenance of the law". This includes preventing, detecting, investigating, prosecuting, and punishing offences.
- it is necessary to use the information to prevent or lessen a serious threat to public health, or the life or health of an individual

chunks.title: Using the right Act — guidelines > privacy act 2020 guidelines
chunks.text:
## Using the right Act
Under the Official Information Act 1982 and the Privacy Act 2020, individuals have the right to request information. But the type of information, and who can get access to it can be different under each Act.
## The relationship between official information and personal information
Personal information includes any information about an identifiable individual. See also:
- Defining personal information
Official information is any information held by a public sector agency. All information held by the Ministry of Social Development is official information.
When people make a request for personal information, we must consider whether the Official Information Act 1982 or the Privacy Act 2020 applies. It depends on who has requested the information and what information they have requested.
## Which Act do I use?
The Privacy Act 2020 gives individuals the right to access personal information that the Ministry holds about them.
The Official Information Act 1982 gives anyone the right to ask the Ministry for any other information it holds. This includes information about the Ministry itself or its processes, information about companies, or information about people other than the requester.
Under both these Acts, the Ministry must make available the information requested, unless there's a good reason to withhold it. There are grounds available under both Acts for withholding information.
## Complaints
A person requesting information under these Acts can complain if they are not satisfied with the Ministry's response:
- the Ombudsman investigates complaints related to requests for information made under the Official Information Act 1982
- the Privacy Commissioner investigates complaints related to requests for information made under the Privacy Act 2020
## More information
For examples of requests made under the Privacy Act 2020 and Official Information Act 1982, see:
- Examples of requests
For more information, see:
- Requests for personal information
- Responding to a request for personal information

## Direction on Advance Payments of Instalments of Benefit
Unofficial consolidated version of the Direction on Advance Payments of Instalments of Benefit-- as at 1 April 2026
To: The Chief Executive of the Department of Work and Income
Pursuant to section 5 of the Social Security Act 1964, I, Roger Morrison Sowry, Minister of Social Services, Work and Income, give you the following direction.
This direction is saved by clause 2(1) of Schedule 1 of the Social Security Act 2018 as if it were a direction given to MSD under section 7 of the Act.
This direction replaces and revokes the previous directions relating to Advance Payment of Benefits given to the Director-General of Social Welfare and in force, in relation to you, by virtue of section 10 of the Employment Services and Income Support (Integrated Administration) Act 1998.
This direction applies where a Beneficiary makes application for an advance payment of a Benefit under section 347 of the Social Security Act 2018.
In determining under section 82(6C)(a) of the Social Security Act 1964 whether you are satisfied that an applicant for an advance payment of benefit or an applicant's spouse or partner has failed to take reasonable steps to better manage his or her finances, you must have regard to a failure by that person to comply with a request to undertake a budgeting activity made under clause 9.12 of the Special Needs Grants Programme or clause 9.5 of the Recoverable Assistance Programme.
In considering whether an advance payment of a Benefit would best meet the Immediate Needs of a Beneficiary and in exercising your discretion to make such payment, you are to apply the following provisions.
Dated 25 May 1999
Roger SowryMinister of Social Services, Work and Income
Analysis

3. Determining whether an Advance would Best Meet the Immediate Needs of the Beneficiary
4. Amount of Advance

chunks.title: Clause 2. Identifying Particular Immediate Need — ministerial directions > advance payment of benefits direction
chunks.text:
## Clause 2. Identifying Particular Immediate Need
Unofficial consolidated version of the Direction on Advance Payments of Instalments of Benefit-- as at 1 April 2026
2
Identifying Particular Immediate Need
2.1
To be considered for an Advance, a Beneficiary must be able to identify a Particular Immediate Need.
2.2
In determining if a Particular Immediate Need exists, you are to have regard to the following matters:
(a)
the effect on the Beneficiary or the Beneficiary's Spouse or partner or any Dependent Child if the need is not met:
(b)
when that effect might be expected to impact on that or those persons:
(c)
the Beneficiary's ability to meet the need from the Beneficiary's own resources.
2.3
A Beneficiary can generally be expected to be able to meet a Particular Immediate Need if the Beneficiary and his or her Spouse or partner (if any) has-
(a)
cash Assets to a value of,-
(i)
for a single person, the amount in clause 1 of Schedule 5 of the Act; or
(ii)
for a person who is in a relationship or a sole parent, the amount in clause 2 of that Schedule; or
(b)
income (including any New Zealand superannuation or veteran's pension payable to the Beneficiary and his or her Spouse or partner) in excess of the appropriate amount set out in clause 2.4.
2.4
The appropriate amount of income in subclause 2.3(b) is:
(a)
for a single person aged 16 or 17 years without dependent children, $879.17 per week:
(b)
for any other single person without dependent children, $1,010.41 per week:
(c)
for a person who is in a relationship with or without dependent children, $1,467.61 per week:
(d)
for a sole parent with 1 dependent child, $1,226.09 per week:
(e)
for any other sole parent, $1,291.75 per week.
Consolidation notes
Note discretion in exceptional circumstances in clause 6.2.

chunks.title: Clause 3. Determining whether an Advance would Best Meet the Immediate Needs of the Beneficiary — ministerial directions > advance payment of benefits direction
chunks.text:
## Clause 3. Determining whether an Advance would Best Meet the Immediate Needs of the Beneficiary
Unofficial consolidated version of the Direction on Advance Payments of Instalments of Benefit-- as at 1 April 2026
3
Determining whether an Advance would Best Meet the Immediate Needs of the Beneficiary
In determining if an Advance would best meet the Immediate Needs of a Beneficiary, you are to have regard to:
(a)
the assistance that is or might be available to the Beneficiary from other sources or under the Act to meet the Beneficiary's Particular Immediate Need:
(b)
the Beneficiary's existing level of debt, and whether the rate of repayment of the proposed Advance (as set out in clause 5) from subsequent instalments of the Benefit would be sustainable, having regard to-
(i)
whether the reduction of the amount of Benefit payable to the Beneficiary will leave enough for the Beneficiary's living expenses and any other debt repayments; and
(ii)
the likelihood it would cause the Beneficiary to seek further Advances or other supplementary assistance under the Act:
(c)
whether the Beneficiary is likely to continue to be in receipt of the Benefit for the period over which the Advance would be repayable:
(d)
any other matters put forward by the Beneficiary to justify the Advance.

chunks.title: Clause 4. Amount of Advance — ministerial directions > advance payment of benefits direction
chunks.text:
## Clause 4. Amount of Advance
Unofficial consolidated version of the Direction on Advance Payments of Instalments of Benefit-- as at 1 April 2026
4
Amount of Advance
4.1
The amount of an Advance should be the least amount required to meet the Beneficiary's Particular Immediate Need.
4.1A
If the particular immediate need of the applicant relates to the supply of any goods or services to the applicant or a member of the applicant's family and section 368(1)(a)(iii), (b), and (c) of the Act applies to the applicant, the amount of the advance should be the least amount required under the contract with the preferred supplier under section 366 of the Act to purchase the goods or services from the preferred supplier.
4.2
In no case is the amount of any Advance, or the total of the amount of any Advance and the amount of all prior Advances that have not been repaid, to exceed the instalments of the benefit payable to the beneficiary and his or her spouse or partner (if any) over a period of 6 weeks.
4.3
Clause 4.2 is subject to clause 7.1.
Consolidation notes
Note discretion in exceptional circumstances in clause 6.2.

chunks.title: Clause 5. Repayment of Advance — ministerial directions > advance payment of benefits direction
chunks.text:
## Clause 5. Repayment of Advance
Unofficial consolidated version of the Direction on Advance Payments of Instalments of Benefit-- as at 1 April 2026
5
Repayment of Advance
Subject to clause 7.2.3, every Advance is to be recovered from the Beneficiary at a rate that will ensure the Advance is repaid within 24 months after the making of the Advance.
Consolidation notes
Note discretion in exceptional circumstances in clause 6.2.

chunks.title: Clause 6. Exercise of Discretion — ministerial directions > advance payment of benefits direction
chunks.text: Unofficial consolidated version of the Direction on Advance Payments of Instalments of Benefit-- as at 1 April 2026 6 Exercise of Discretion 6.1 If you determine that a Particular Immediate Need exists, and that an Advance would best meet the Immediate Needs of the Beneficiary, you are to have regard to the matters set out in clause 6.3 in exercising your discretion whether to make an Advance. 6.2 In the exercise of your discretion, if you determine that a Beneficiary has exceptional circumstances, you may, after having regard to the matters set out in clause 6.3- (a) make an Advance where the Beneficiary and his or her Spouse or partner has Cash Assets or Income exceeding the limits set out in clause 2.3; or (b) make an Advance in excess of any limit set out in clause 4 or clause 7.1.3; or (c) recover an Advance at a lower rate than set out in clause 5 or clause 7.2.4. 6.3 The matters referred to in clause 6.1 and 6.2 are- (a) the Beneficiary's ability to repay the Advance; (b) whether the Beneficiary could reasonably have been expected to have made provision for the Particular Immediate Need; (c) the extent to which not making an Advance, or an Advance in excess of the limit, or requiring recovery at the rate set out in clause 5, would- (i) worsen the Beneficiary's position, or (ii) increase or create any risk to the life or welfare of the Beneficiary or the Beneficiary's Spouse or partner or any Dependent Child, or (iii) cause serious hardship to the Beneficiary, or the Beneficiary's Spouse or partner or any Dependent Child, (d) any other matters that you consider to be relevant, in the circumstances of the particular case. 6.4 You may consider that the Beneficiary's application for an advance should be refused if you are satisfied that the Beneficiary (B), or B's spouse or partner (C), has failed- (a) to take reasonable steps to reduce his or her costs or increase his or her income or better manage his or her finances; or (b)

chunks.title: Clause 6. Exercise of Discretion — ministerial directions > advance payment of benefits direction
chunks.text: to take all reasonable steps to obtain any assistance towards his or her costs from any other source from which B or C may be entitled to assistance; or (c) to comply with any requirement of MSD to undertake a budgeting activity under section 348 of the Act.

chunks.title: Clause 7. Advances for Particular Needs — ministerial directions > advance payment of benefits direction
chunks.text: Unofficial consolidated version of the Direction on Advance Payments of Instalments of Benefit-- as at 1 April 2026 7 Advances for Particular Needs 7.1 Essential Home Repairs 7.1.1 You may, subject to the provisions of this direction, make an Advance to any Beneficiary for the following Particular Immediate Need: (a) to carry out essential repairs and maintenance to the Beneficiary's home, or to the paths, fences, or retaining walls of, the property on which that home is located; or (b) to provide essential services to the Beneficiary's home such as sewerage, water, or electricity connection. 7.1.2 No Advance under clause 7.1.1 may be made unless- (a) the Beneficiary provides proof of his or her ownership (or joint ownership) and occupation of the property to which the Advance is to be applied; (b) the work to be done is essential in order to maintain the property in a reasonable living standard; and (c) the Beneficiary shows proof that he or she has unsuccessfully applied for financial assistance for the purpose from any other agencies that provide assistance to Beneficiaries for such purposes. 7.1.3 An Advance under clause 7.1.1 should not exceed an amount of $1,000. Consolidation notes Note discretion in exceptional circumstances in clause 6.2 Consolidation notes 7.2 Safety Footwear 7.2.1 You may, subject to this direction, make an Advance to a Work-tested Beneficiary who- (a) is undertaking, pursuant to section 146(1)(d) of the Act or section 324 of the Act, any activity of a kind referred to in section 146(1)(d) of the Act or activity in the community that involves undertaking work; and (b) is, for the Beneficiary's safety while participating in that activity, required by the provider of the work to wear safety footwear not supplied by that provider, and (c) does not already own suitable safety footwear, and (d) could not participate in the activity without purchasing safety footwear. 7.2.2 A Beneficiary may not be refused an Advance under clause 7.2.1 by reason only of the matters set out in clause 3(b) or (c). 7.2.3

## Explanatory note
Unofficial consolidated version of the Direction setting approval criteria for specified early childhood education programmes for purposes of social obligations under the Social Security Act 2018-- as at 1 April 2026
This note is not part of the direction but is intended to indicate its general effect.
This direction to the chief executive of the Ministry of Social Development under the Social Security Act 1964, which comes into effect on 15 July 2013, sets out approval criteria to which the chief executive must have regard in approving an early childhood education programme as a recognised early childhood education programme for the purpose of the social obligation in section 60RA(3)(a)(i) or (b)(i) of the Social Security Act 1964. This obligation is the obligation that beneficiaries receiving main benefits under the Social Security Act 1964 and their spouses or partners take all reasonable steps to ensure that dependent children aged 3 to 5 are enrolled in and attending a recognised early childhood education programme unless they are attending school or (for 5-year olds in certain circumstances) being actively taught at home.
By way of explanation, a recognised early childhood education programme is defined in section 60RAB(1) of the Social Security Act 1964 as-
- an approved early childhood education programme (as defined in regulations made under section 132AC of the Social Security Act 1964). This refers to a programme of early childhood education provided by a licensed early childhood service, a certificated playgroup, or a licence-exempt early childhood education and care centre (within the meaning in section 309 of the Education Act 1989) that charges a uniform monetary fee for the participation of children in the programme
- an early childhood education programme approved by the chief executive under section 60RAB(1)(b) of the Social Security Act 1964 having regard to approval criteria prescribed by the Minister by direction. This direction prescribes approval criteria for this purpose
- a programme of early childhood education provided by a school designated as a correspondence school under the Education Act 1989.

chunks.text: Unofficial consolidated version of the Ministerial Direction on Debt Recovery-- as at 1 April 2026 6 Deduction notices (1) This clause applies to the issue of a deduction notice to recover a debt. (2) Where it is determined that the method of debt recovery is the issue of a deduction notice, MSD should send a written notice to the debtor, stating that the debt is to be recovered, specifying the amount of the debt, asking the debtor to contact the department so that arrangements for recovery can be made, and advising the debtor of his or her review and appeal rights in respect of the debt. (3) (revoked) (4) If no response satisfactory to MSD is received within two weeks of that notice being sent, MSD should send a further written notice informing the debtor that he or she has 10 days to contact the department and make satisfactory arrangements for the repayment of the debt, and that if he or she does not do so then a deduction notice may be issued. (5) A deduction notice for recovery of debt should be issued to a debtor's employer or any other person who is the provider of payments of income or weekly loss of earnings compensation to the person on a regular or intermittent basis in preference to a bank, unless recovery of the debt from money due to the debtor by a bank is the only realistic option available in the circumstances. Deductions from bank accounts will be lump sum deductions. (6) For any deduction notice issued under section 353(b) of the Act and regulation 217, the amount of the deduction set out in the notice must be based on the amount of the debt, and in determining the amount to be deducted, MSD must take into account the debtor's financial circumstances, the known outgoings of that person (such as essential automatic payments, home mortgage repayments, etc), and the amount that the debtor could reasonably be assumed to require to live on. (6A) Before a deduction notice may be issued to a bank, MSD must check the balances in the debtor's various bank accounts. (7) If a debtor approaches the department claiming that a deduction notice is causing undue hardship, MSD should review the issue of the deduction notice taking into account any alternative method of payment offered by the debtor. (8)

## Explanatory note
Unofficial consolidated version of the Ministerial Direction on Debt Recovery-- as at 1 April 2026
This note is not part of the direction, but is intended to indicate its general effect.
This direction by the Minister of Social Development identifies relevant considerations for determining the rate and method of recovery of debts referred to in section 85A of the Social Security Act 1964. It also identifies relevant circumstances in which the department may defer temporarily the recovery of debts referred to in section 85A of the Social Security Act 1964.
It also identifies relevant considerations for determining the rate and method of recovery and whether to defer temporarily the recovery of debts of the kind set out in section 85A(c) or (d) of the Social Security Act 1964 (debts in respect of any advance payment of a benefit or recoverable assistance under any welfare programme).
Clause 6 replaces the Ministerial direction in relation to the issue of deductions notices and is to the same general effect. Clause 7 consequentially revokes that direction.
This direction comes into force on 7 July 2014.
