chunks.title: Accessibility to alternative housing — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Accessibility to alternative housing
Accessibility considers whether the client's ability to access alternative housing is impacted by:
- discrimination
- lack of cash resources for bond, rent and furniture
- availability of alternative housing in the area where the client currently lives or needs to live
## Reasonable effort to find alternative housing
A client must have made a reasonable effort to find suitable alternative housing.

chunks.title: Additional occupants — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: To be an additional occupant a person must: - be aged 16 years or over - be financially independent - reside (or will reside) in social housing but not be an applicable person ora dependent child of an applicable person - applicable person or - a dependent child of an applicable person

chunks.title: Specific and established ongoing need — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: To be considered as an additional occupant there must be a specific and established ongoing need to have them as part of the household (and not be considered a household in their own right). Generally, there is some form of dependency. The person must also be a full-time member of the household. Bedrooms are allocated for these people as they have an established need to be in the household. If there is no established need for a person to be an additional occupant they will not be included in the application and their housing needs will not be considered (including allocating bedrooms). Bedrooms are also allocated for any dependent children of the additional occupant.

chunks.title: Examples of specific and established ongoing need — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Household members who have an established need to be part of the household as an additional occupant may include (but are not limited to): - elderly parent or grandparent (aged over 65) - non-dependent child (who is 16 years of age or over) or other adult with a physical or mental health disability requiring care and support at home - carer or support person (and any dependent children of the carer or support person) - an adult child when it is reasonable for them to still live with their parentsFor example, it may be reasonable for an adult child to remain living with their parents and be considered an additional occupant if they are getting Student Allowance, working part-time or getting a Student Loan. It may not be reasonable for an adult child to remain living with their parents and considered an additional occupant if they are working full-time. - young person getting Young Parent Payment or Youth Payment living in a stable boarding/family environment - young person getting Young Parent Payment who is living at home with their parents Note this is not a complete list - if assistance is required when considering whether there is an established need for the person to be part of the household, please contact Helpline.

chunks.title: Assessable income and additional occupants — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: When it has been determined a household member is an additional occupant, their income (and any income from their assessable assets) is not considered when assessing Income Related Rent. However, if they are making contributions to applicable persons to live in the house then 62% of those contributions are included in the calculation of Income Related Rent for the household. Note the only people who have security of tenure at the property are the signatories. A person who is an additional occupant will not have any rights to continue the tenancy if the signatory leaves the tenancy.

chunks.title: Adequacy of current housing — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Adequacy of current housing
To assess whether the client's current housing situation is adequate MSD must consider if the client needs accommodation, or needs to move from their current accommodation because they are:
- 'not living in any accommodation' or
- staying in emergency housing or transitional housing for the time being or
- living in accommodation that is not fit to live in, or is in serious state of disrepair that presents a severe and significant health and safety risk to the clients (e.g. no structural integrity or the conditions of the facilities are poor or non-existent) or
- living in accommodation that is overcrowded or
- living in accommodation when they have no, or limited, security of tenure
The overall rating for adequacy will be taken from the highest score across all the criteria.

chunks.title: Affordability of suitable alternative housing — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Affordability of suitable alternative housing
The assessment of affordability measures the client's ability to afford (with any financial assistance to which they may be entitled) suitable alternative housing.
Affordability looks at the client's residual income as a percentage of equivalent benefit to determine if the client can afford alternative housing.

chunks.title: Age — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Age
To qualify for social housing a client must be aged 16 years or over.
## Entering a tenancy agreement
To enter into a tenancy agreement there must be a person who can be a signatory to the tenancy agreement.
To be a signatory, a client must be aged:
- 18 years or over or
- 16 or 17 years and either: be (or have previously been) married or in a civil union orsingle or in a de facto relationship if they have been approved by the Tenancy Tribunal to enter a tenancy agreement for social housing they have been offered
- be (or have previously been) married or in a civil union or
- single or in a de facto relationship if they have been approved by the Tenancy Tribunal to enter a tenancy agreement for social housing they have been offered
## Clients under 18 years
Young people aged 16 or 17 years can qualify for social housing but placement into a property (that is, signing a tenancy agreement) depends on the age restrictions that make a tenancy agreement legally enforceable.
Clients aged 16 or 17 years old cannot sign and enter into a tenancy agreement by themselves unless they are (or have previously been) married or in a civil union.
Clients who are not (or have never been) married or in a civil union
Clients aged 16 and 17 years old who are not (or who have never been) married or in a civil union can obtain approval from the Tenancy Tribunal to enter into a tenancy agreement that is legally enforceable. The social housing provider will discuss this extra process with the young person at the time they are offered a property.
If a young person is unable to enter into a tenancy agreement because of their age they are removed from the register.

chunks.title: Allocating bedrooms for known future household members — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Allocating bedrooms for known future household members
Additional bedrooms can sometimes be approved for household members who are not part of the household at the time of application but it is known they will become part of the household soon. This may be when a signatory, applicable person or additional occupant is:
- pregnant (it is reasonable to expect a newborn child to have their own room)
- having children returning to their care
- reuniting with the household - whether household members have come from overseas or within New Zealand
- requiring a carer for overnight stays
You need to consider whether it is reasonable to include them as a member of the household for bedroom allocation, having regard to the:
- likely date that they will join the household
- length of time that the client is likely to be on the social housing register
The tenant must provide verification the future event will occur before a bedroom can be allocated.
Example:
- client has been assessed as requiring a carer, and the carer is not available for 1 month - include the extra bedroom
- joining household is at the Mangere Refugee Centre - include the family. But if the household is still out of the country working through residency requirements do not include extra bedroom/s
- child is returning to their care as soon as they have a bedroom for them - include the child for bedroom purposes
## Relocation required for children returning from Oranga Tamariki care
A client may need to relocate due to not having enough bedrooms for their children who are returning from Oranga Tamariki care.
When the allocation of bedroom space is the only thing preventing the return of the children from Oranga Tamariki care, a bedroom may be allocated.

chunks.title: Applicable persons — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Applicable persons
An applicable person is:
- a person applying for social housing with the intention of being a signatory to the tenancy agreement and
- any partner of that person
A partner does not have to sign the tenancy agreement however they will be considered when assessing the client's housing need. You will need to inform the partner of the advantages of signing the tenancy agreement (for example rights to the tenancy).
If a partner does not wish to sign the tenancy agreement or cannot as they are not residentially qualified, they will be considered an applicable person when assessing the household's housing need.
## Income and asset details
Applicable persons will have their income and asset details considered during the housing needs assessment and these details are used in the calculation of Income Related Rent.

chunks.title: Assessable income — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Assessable income
Assessable income is the weekly net income used to determine whether the client qualifies for social housing.
MSD uses the same types of assessable income for determining whether a client qualifies for social housing or Income Related Rent.
From 1 July 2023, most types of Child Support are included as assessable income. For more information see: Child Support is assessable income from 1 July 2023

chunks.title: Assessable income for affordability — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Assessable income for affordability
The income used in the assessment of affordability is the income of the applicable persons.
From 1 July 2023, most types of Child Support are included as assessable income for the affordability formula.
For more information on what is considered assessable income, including the 1 July 2023 changes for Child Support, see:
- Income Related Rent Assessable income
- Child Support is assessable income from 1 July 2023

chunks.title: Assessing housing need after declining a social housing property — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Assessing housing need after declining a social housing property
A client who reapplies after previously declining (or failing to accept) a social housing property without a good and sufficient reason in the last 13 weeks must be assessed for eligibility for social housing.
## A client who previously declined a social housing property in the last 13 weeks, may be assessed as eligible
Sometimes other factors will outweigh the client's previous decision to decline or fail to accept a social housing property and using the Social Allocation System (SAS) assessment they will be considered to have a persistent housing need that is serious or severe. This may include:
- when there has been a material change in circumstances since they were last assessed or
- it is clear the client did not fully understand the repercussions of the decline (or failure to accept a property offer by not responding)
In both circumstances the client must be assessed as having a genuine, severe and immediate housing need to be eligible for social housing. They will then be added to the housing register.
## Overall circumstances suggest client's housing need not as urgent, as priority rating suggests
Generally for other cases, a client who has declined or failed to accept a social housing property in the previous 13 weeks suggests the client's housing need is not as urgent as the initial priority rating they have been assigned under the SAS criteria.
In these cases, there is discretion to change the overall priority rating to reflect the client's housing need is not as urgent and the client will be assessed as ineligible for social housing and will not be placed on the housing register.

chunks.title: Assessment for current tenants — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Assessment for current tenants
There are some situations when a current tenant has a change in circumstances that requires their need for social housing to be assessed on their new circumstances.
For more information see:
- Changes to a tenancy agreement
- Death of a client
- Transfers
- Changes and reviews Reviews and Appeals

chunks.title: Assessment of funds available — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Assessment of funds available
The following table shows the definitions of funds available.
## Assessment of funds available
Not available
A client has no funds available
Note for non-beneficiaries over the income limit for Housing Support Products or a Recoverable Assistance Payment this will apply if clients do not have any of their own funds.
Minimal
A client is considered to have minimal funds available for rent, bond and furniture if they have less than 75% of 4 week's lower quartile rent available from savings, a bond that will be returned to them, or Housing Support Products, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment entitlement
Earmarked
A client is considered to have some funds available for rent, bond and furniture if they have more than 75% of 4 week's lower quartile rent available from:
- savings
- a bond that will be returned to them
- Housing Support Products, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment entitlement
but over half of these funds are earmarked for other use, such as power bond, moving costs
Available
A client is considered to have funds available for rent, bond and furniture if they have more than 75% of 4 week's lower quartile rent available from:
- savings
- a bond that will be returned to them
- Housing Support Products, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment entitlement
and less than half of these funds are earmarked for other use, such as power bond, moving costs

chunks.title: Assessment of housing need — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: The client's need for social housing is assessed through the Social Allocation System (SAS) which: - confirms a client's eligibility for social housing - assesses their need for social housing and determines whether their need for social housing is at risk (priority A) or serious (priority B) and - determines their housing needs (housing requirements)

chunks.title: Social Allocation System criteria for assessing housing need — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: There is a set of criteria used to determine the housing need of a household and is based on the household composition, housing circumstances and housing history. The assessment of housing need is used to assess: - housing need (the need to move) of the household which covers the following criteria: adequacy - focuses on whether the client needs accommodation or needs to move from their current accommodation due to: not currently living in any accommodation, or living in emergency housing for the time-beingthe physical condition/structure or lack of basic facilities of the accommodationover-crowding orlack of security of tenure of their current accommodation suitability - focuses on needing to move due to: medical, disability or personal needs orfamily violence or neighbourhood tension (including tension within the household) or other violence relating to the client's current living situation - adequacy - focuses on whether the client needs accommodation or needs to move from their current accommodation due to: not currently living in any accommodation, or living in emergency housing for the time-beingthe physical condition/structure or lack of basic facilities of the accommodationover-crowding orlack of security of tenure of their current accommodation - not currently living in any accommodation, or living in emergency housing for the time-being - the physical condition/structure or lack of basic facilities of the accommodation - over-crowding or - lack of security of tenure of their current accommodation - suitability - focuses on needing to move due to: medical, disability or personal needs orfamily violence or neighbourhood tension (including tension within the household) or other violence relating to the client's current living situation - medical, disability or personal needs or - family violence or neighbourhood tension (including tension within the household) or other violence relating to the client's current living situation - ability to access, afford and sustain alternative housing (that is, the capacity to rent in the private market) which covers the following criteria: affordability - focuses on the ability to afford alternative, suitable housing in the private marketaccessibility - focuses on the ability to access and afford suitable and adequate housing due to discrimination, lack of financial means to move and availability of alternative, affordable suitable housing in the private marketsustainability - focuses on financial management difficulties and difficulties in social functioning and lack of social skills - affordability - focuses on the ability to afford alternative, suitable housing in the private market

chunks.title: Social Allocation System criteria for assessing housing need — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: - accessibility - focuses on the ability to access and afford suitable and adequate housing due to discrimination, lack of financial means to move and availability of alternative, affordable suitable housing in the private market - sustainability - focuses on financial management difficulties and difficulties in social functioning and lack of social skills

chunks.title: Assessment of need for multiple household unit — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Assessment of need for multiple household unit
Sometimes 2 or more families apply for social housing together.
They may do this if they are reuniting through refugee family reunification or one family might need extra support. In other situations it may simply be choice or convenience.
To have a family unit nominated as household number 2, at least one adult member of the second household must agree to sign the tenancy agreement (and a signatory to the tenancy agreement).
The housing need of the household is assessed together.
For more information see:
- Examples of more than one household unit
## Household units are assessed jointly
When 2 household units apply for social housing together an assessment of their housing need is undertaken as one household. The joint assessment will determine whether the household is at risk (priority A) or has a serious housing need (priority B) and eligible for social housing.
Note the assessment to determine the household's housing need across the 5 areas is considered holistically. It is not undertaken separately for each household unit. This includes the income and asset thresholds - these limits do not change even though there is more than one household.
## Multiple households create the need for social housing
In some situations a joint housing application may be the only factor that creates the need for social housing, for example the number of bedrooms needed to house the families makes alternative housing inaccessible.
In this situation, you need to establish whether there is a valid reason for multiple household units to be housed together.
This may be as they have a specific and established need to live together as a household, usually because the households have a dependency on each other. For example:
- elderly parent or grandparent (aged over 65 years)
- non-dependent child or other adult with a physical or mental health disability requiring care and support at home
- carer or support person
If there is a need for them to be housed together, an assessment of their housing need is undertaken as one household. If a need for the two households to live together is not established, they should make separate applications for social housing.
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have received formal notification of (and do not agree with) the outcome of the eligibility assessment.

chunks.title: At risk of rheumatic fever — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## At risk of rheumatic fever
Certain people on the housing register who are at risk of rheumatic fever can be fast-tracked for social housing. This is to target a reduction in the number of hospitalisations for acute rheumatic fever.
If the household meets all the qualifications, they will be fast-tracked for the next available, suitable social housing property, based on matching by the social housing provider, even if there are other households with a higher rating.
This provision only applies to households who meet all of the following qualifications:
- the household must qualify for social housing
and
- have an 'at risk' or 'serious need' for social housing, with an A or B priority rating
and
- the household have more than one child living in that house (does not have to be a dependent child), and at least one of those children is aged 4 to 19 years andhas a child aged 0 - 14 years who has been hospitalised with a qualifying medical condition, while living in their current accommodation or in the past 2 years orhas a child or young person who is getting treatment because of a previous episode of rheumatic fever
- has a child aged 0 - 14 years who has been hospitalised with a qualifying medical condition, while living in their current accommodation or in the past 2 years or
- has a child or young person who is getting treatment because of a previous episode of rheumatic fever
and
- the household is lacking one or more bedrooms, or the household is functionally overcrowded (for example, unable to adequately heat the property and therefore engaging in unsafe sleeping practices)
Note if a household no longer meets the qualifications to be fast tracked, they may still qualify to remain on the social housing register.

chunks.title: Australian clients — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Australian clients
Australian clients must meet the residence requirements for social housing.
Australian clients who have resided continuously in New Zealand for at least 2 years at any one time since coming to New Zealand and are ordinarily resident, qualify for social housing on residency grounds.

chunks.title: Availability of suitable alternative housing in the area — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Availability of suitable alternative housing in the area
The availability of suitable alternative housing in the area where the client currently lives or needs to live can affect the client's ability to access alternative housing.
To consider whether there are accessibility issues due to availability of suitable housing the client must have problems accessing affordable, suitable and adequate housing. They may not be able to find a suitable property due to:
- not being able to find a modified property to suit their disability needs, for example with wheelchair ramps, modified showers, on a flat section
- there are no properties to suit their household size or type, for example there may be high demand or low supply of specific types of properties such as 1 bedroom units or 4 plus bedroom properties
- demand for housing generally is high, for example local real estate agencies have waiting lists for private rental listings.
- an assistance dog is required and is impacting on the client's ability to access alternative housing, for example a companion pet for an elderly person or guide dog or hearing assistance
Note a client must have made a reasonable effort to find suitable alternative housing.
For more information see:
- Accessibility to alternative housing
- Discrimination as a barrier to suitable housing
- Lack of cash resources for bond, rent and furniture
- Risk rating for accessibility
- Reasonable effort to find alternative housing

chunks.title: Bedroom allocation — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Bedroom allocation
Bedrooms are allocated for eligible members of the household. This may include:
- the tenant and their partner (applicable person)
- any dependent children (for eligibility purposes)
- any other person assessed as being an additional occupant and
- any dependent children of an additional occupant
Note the household member must be a full-time member of the household.
## Bedrooms generally allocated based on overcrowding guidelines
The overcrowding guidelines for allocating bedrooms are as follows:
- there should be no more than 2 persons per bedroom
- children aged 10 years or over of the opposite sex should not share a room
- children aged under 18 years of the same sex may reasonably share a bedroom
- single adults and couples should have a separate bedroom
- children should not share a bedroom with their parent(s)
Note for the purposes of allocating bedrooms, an adult is someone aged 18 years or over, or, if aged 16 or 17 years, are (or have been) married or in a civil union.
## Exceptions to bedroom allocation criteria
Generally bedrooms will be allocated based on the overcrowding guidelines however there are some exceptions to this.
For more information see:
- Exceptions to bedroom allocation
## Allocating bedrooms for known future household members
Additional bedrooms can sometimes be approved for household members who are not part of the household at the time of application, but it is known that they will become part of the household soon. For more information see:
- Allocating bedrooms for known future household members

chunks.title: Both carer and client getting care can be signatories — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Both carer and client getting care can be signatories
The carer and the client getting care must decide if both or only one of them will be signatories to the tenancy agreement.
This is an important decision as it can affect their rights to the tenancy at the property. For example, if the person getting care dies, the carer may no longer have a home if they are not on the tenancy agreement.

chunks.title: British clients — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## British clients
British clients must meet the residence requirements for social housing
Note some British citizens who arrived in New Zealand before 1 January 1962 may be deemed to hold a residence class visa,
A British client who has resided continuously in New Zealand since they were granted a residence class visa (when they require one) and who are ordinarily resident qualify for social housing on residency grounds.

chunks.title: Calculating 75% of 4 weeks lower quartile rent — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Calculating 75% of 4 weeks lower quartile rent
The lower quartile rent amount for the area where the client currently lives or needs to live, is available at Tenancy Services.
## Example
Area: Auckland - Waitakere (1 December 2022 - 31 May 2023)
Lower quartile rent for 3 bedroom house
$429 per week
Multiply by 4
$1716
75% of $1716
$1287

chunks.title: Calculation of affordability formula — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Calculation of affordability formula
This formula below is used to determine the client's affordability risk rating.

From 1 July 2023, most types of Child Support are included as assessable income in the client's net weekly income for the affordability formula.
## Consider whether risk rating determined by formula is accurate
MSD will need to consider whether the risk rating determined by the formula accurately reflects the client's level of need.
Sometimes 2 or more families apply for social housing together.

chunks.title: Carer or support person — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Carer or support person
A household member may have a personal care or support person. These carers may or may not live-in permanently and may contribute financially to the household.
A client may require the assistance of a carer or support person because they:
- have a physical, medical or mental health condition that results in them being unable to carry out physical care independently or
- are an elderly person and it is safer to have someone living with them (this person could assist with general housework and cooking meals)
Note if the carer or support person is only providing care during the day, there is no need for a bedroom to be allocated to them, however an extra bedroom may be required to store medical equipment (for example for a dialysis patient).
## Carer or support person lives-in
For social housing purposes, a carer or support person who lives-in:
- is aged 16 years or over
- is financially independent
- has a proven and established need to live with the client and
- may contribute towards the rent
For example, a person who is getting Supported Living Payment - Caring for a person to care for the client:
- is aged over 16 years
- is financially independent and
- has a proven and established need to live with the client
The carer or support person (living-in) can be considered an additional occupant or a signatory.

chunks.title: Carer or support person as additional occupant or signatory — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Carer or support person as additional occupant or signatory
The carer or support person can be considered either an additional occupant or a signatory.
## Carer or support person is an additional occupant
The carer or support person can be considered an additional occupant when:
- they reside permanently with the client and
- they have a specific and on-going need to be part of the household and
- the carer or support person does not want to be a signatory on the tenancy agreement or
- the client does not want the carer or support person included on the tenancy
The carer or support person's income is not considered when assessing the Income Related Rent. However they are an additional occupant and if they are making contributions to applicable persons to live in the house then 62% of those contributions are included in the calculation of Income Related Rent for the household.
## Carer or support person is a signatory
If the carer or support person is a signatory on the tenancy agreement, then they are considered an applicable person and their income is included for Income Related Rent purposes.
For more information see:
- Both carer and client getting care can be signatories
- Additional occupants
- Income Related Rent Income of additional occupants

chunks.title: Cash asset limit — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Cash asset limit
Generally, the cash assets of a client and their partner (if any) must be under the asset limit.
## Asset limit at application
The asset limit is 10% of the national median house sale price.
$42,700
A client with this level of assets or more may be able to use the asset for a deposit for a house in the private market and therefore be able to address their own housing need.
An applicable person (prospective tenant(s) and their partner(s)) must jointly have cash assets under this threshold.

chunks.title: Cash assets for Social Housing — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Cash assets mean assets of the client and their partner (if any) that can easily be converted into cash. For social housing, cash assets include: - bills of exchange or promissory notes - building society shares - money in bank accounts, including fixed and term deposits with any bank, friendly society, credit union, or building society - money invested with or lent to any bank, or other financial institution - money withdrawn from a KiwiSaver scheme - mortgage investments and other long term loans - pre-paid funeral expenses (in some circumstances) - proceeds from the sale of the family home - shares, stocks, debentures, Bonus Bonds and bonds - the client's share in any partnership

chunks.title: Assets not included as cash assets — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Cash assets do not include: - personal effects - motor vehicle principally used by the client for private use - a home property and land on which it is situated - a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2,000 or which is used by the person or a member of their family for day-to-day accommodation - Christchurch mosques attack support payments - Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments - funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts - Māori land when the title is in tribal trust and individual ownership cannot be identified, the client cannot realise or readily convert the land into a cash asset - MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to a system processing error from 1993 to 2014 - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made - specified Ex gratia and compensation payments - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received Note a bank overdraft is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client. Canterbury earthquake related payments Payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client got the payment.

chunks.title: Information share Child Support — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: When a client is getting information share Child Support payments, MSD must determine whether the payments are considered a cash asset or assessable income. The cash asset exemption for the period the information share Child Support is being charged for income-tested financial assistance does not apply to social housing. In most cases, Child Support will be considered assessable income rather than a cash asset because it's paid for an income related purpose, and is likely to be used over the payment period.

chunks.title: Appeals to the Social Security Appeal Authority — assessment of eligibility > changes and reviews assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Appeals to the Social Security Appeal Authority
A client can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority when the Benefits Review Committee has upheld or upheld in part a decision of MSD, including decisions in respect of:
- the assessment or re-assessment of: their eligibility or continued eligibility for social housingtheir housing needs
- their eligibility or continued eligibility for social housing
- their housing needs
- the calculation of the rate of Income Related Rent
- the establishment and recovery of Income Related Rent debt
A client's application for appeal should be sent directly to the Social Security Appeal Authority.
When the Benefits Review Committee has declined to hear an out of time Review of Decision and the client applies for the matter to be heard by the Social Security Appeal Authority, forward the case to the Appeal Authority.
## Outcome
The Social Security Appeal Authority will advise both parties to the appeal (the client and MSD) of the outcome.

chunks.title: Review of decision for Income Related Rent debts — assessment of eligibility > changes and reviews assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Review of decision for Income Related Rent debts
When an application for Review of Decision involves an Income Related Rent debt currently being recovered from the client, it is appropriate to suspend recovery until the review and appeal process is completed.
If the debt is currently being recovered from the client's benefit, the deductions will need to be suspended.
When the client is not getting a benefit you will need to advise Client Support - Debt Management that the client has lodged an application for a Review of Decision in respect of the Income Related Rent debt.
Note you do not refund any payments already deducted until the outcome of the review or appeal is known.

chunks.title: Review of decision - 3 stage process — assessment of eligibility > changes and reviews assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Review of decision - 3 stage process
There are 3 stages to the review and appeal process:
## Stage 1 - Internal review
This is an administrative process only.
When a client applies for a Review of Decision, MSD should check the decision, review any new information, and the information available at the time of the decision, and check the decision was in accordance with legislation.
## Stage 2 - Benefits Review Committee
An application for a Review of Decision is an application for the decision to be heard by the Benefits Review Committee.
Note
- when the internal review outcome is not favourable or only favourable in part for the client, the decision must go before the Benefits Review Committee without any further request from the client and
- the original decision remains in place until the review and appeal process is completed
## Stage 3 - Social Security Appeal Authority hearing
When the original decision is upheld (or partially upheld) by the Benefit Review Committee, the client can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority.

chunks.title: Reviews and Appeals — assessment of eligibility > changes and reviews assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Reviews and Appeals
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have received formal notification of and disagree with a decision, including decisions relating to:
- the assessment or re-assessment of: their eligibility or continued eligibility for social housingtheir housing needs
- their eligibility or continued eligibility for social housing
- their housing needs
- the calculation of the rate of Income Related Rent
- the establishment and recovery of Income Related Rent debt
A client can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority where they do not agree with a decision, which was upheld or upheld in part by the Benefits Review Committee under an application for Review of Decision
## Exceptions
A client has no right of appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority (and therefore no right to apply for a Review of Decision) if they disagree with:
- a decision not to review their housing need
However you will need to ensure that there is a good reason not to undertake a review of their housing needs.
- any decision made by a housing provider regarding tenancy-related matters, such as: the determination of a market rent raterent arrearsdamages debt orwhether someone can join into a tenancy agreement
- the determination of a market rent rate
- rent arrears
- damages debt or
- whether someone can join into a tenancy agreement
The client has the right to apply for a Review of Decision at any time within 3 months of the original decision being advised. When a client has applied for a hearing outside the 3 month time limit the Benefits Review Committee must decide whether or not to accept the application before it considers the decision under review.
A client has the right to have their decision reviewed once. If they wish to have the same decision reviewed again refer the case to Legal Services.

chunks.title: When to advise a client of their right to review — assessment of eligibility > changes and reviews assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## When to advise a client of their right to review
Explain a client's right of review, when you provide formal notification about a decision, including decisions in respect of:
- the assessment or re-assessment of: their eligibility or continued eligibility for social housingtheir housing needs
- their eligibility or continued eligibility for social housing
- their housing needs
- the calculation of the rate of Income Related Rent
- the establishment and recovery of Income Related Rent debt
## Notify decision in full
When you advise a client of a decision, in particular an unfavourable decision, you should explain your decision in full and explain the relevant legislation.
It is not appropriate to just quote a section of the Act verbatim, you should explain the relevant legislation to the client and how it applies to their situation.

chunks.title: Who can apply for a review or appeal — assessment of eligibility > changes and reviews assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Who can apply for a review or appeal
The following people can apply for a Review of Decision:
- the current social housing tenant (that is, a signatory to the tenancy agreement)
- a prospective tenant
- a former tenant or
- an appointed agent or advocate for the tenant
## Joint tenants
When there are joint tenants, each individual tenant can apply for a Review of Decision.
Depending on the decision under review, any response about the decision or the review may be sent to all the joint tenants.
## Persons not able to apply for a review or appeal
A third party, without authorisation, is not able to apply for a Review of Decision.
Example
- the parent or family member of a young person who is or was a tenant or
- an additional occupant

chunks.title: Changes to a tenancy agreement — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Changes to a tenancy agreement
When a client has a change in circumstances it may also require a change to a tenancy agreement.
Situations when this may occur include (but are not limited to):
- an existing tenant requests that a person or household joins in their tenancy
- a client requests to be removed from a joint tenancy

chunks.title: Changing a client's initial priority rating — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Changing a client's initial priority rating
Before confirming the client's priority rating you need to consider if the Social Allocation System (SAS) generated rating reflects the client's entire circumstances.
## Initial priority rating
The client's priority rating is calculated in SAS. There is discretion to change this priority rating when the overall housing need of the client suggests a different priority rating.
## Factors to consider before confirming a client's priority rating
Factors to consider may include (but are not limited to):
- Has the client limited the area they want to live, to high cost areas?
- Has the client reasonably looked for alternative accommodation?
- Has the client limited their income by choice, for example due to work obligations sanctions, or failure to assist child support reduction or not accessing all assistance available to them?
- Has the initial priority rating reflected the client's need to move correctly when considering their whole situation?
- Has the client declined a social housing property (or failed to accept a property offer by not responding to the offer) in the last 13 weeks? When looking at their overall situation and considering their housing need, does it suggest that the clients housing need is not as urgent as the initial property rating they have been assigned under the SAS criteria?
- Are there any other relevant factors that have impacted on a change required to the client's initial priority rating?
Note in the system the changing of a client's initial priority rating up or down is referred to as an over-ride of the priority rating and is undertaken using the over-ride function.

chunks.title: Child Support is assessable income from 1 July 2023 — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: From 1 July 2023, most types of Child Support clients get are included as assessable income for all applicable persons in the household, when determining whether the client qualifies for social housing. Child Support is money paid by parents who do not live with their children, or who share care with someone else. These payments help with the cost of raising a child. Child Support can be paid through Inland Revenue or directly to the client through another payment arrangement. For more information about Child Support Payments see: Child Support Introduction

chunks.title: Information share Child Support — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about Child Support payments clients get. Information share Child Support payments are automatically included as income for clients who get income-tested financial assistance.

chunks.title: Social Housing income assessments — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: However, social housing assessments need to be reviewed manually to include Child Support payments as assessable income at the time of application or at the next review. The information share with Inland Revenue does not include all Child Support payments paid. For more information see: Child Support Income Introduction Note before including information share Child Support as assessable income, MSD must send the client a notice of adverse action. This gives the client 10 working days to tell MSD if the information is incorrect.

chunks.title: Types of Child Support — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: The following types of Child Support are included as assessable income: - Child Support payments paid to a receiving carer from Inland Revenue (formula assessment and voluntary agreement) - Private arrangements for Child Support - Foreign Child Support - Court-ordered lump sums of Child Support (if not considered a cash asset) - Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payments under a voluntary agreement The following types of Child Support are excluded as assessable income: - Offset Child Support payments - Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payments under a formula assessment - Mixed Child Support payments

chunks.title: Child Support is assessable income only for a payment or liability period on or after 1 July 2023 — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Only Child Support that covers a payment or liability period on or after 1 July 2023 is included as assessable income when determining whether the client qualifies for social housing, except when Child Support is the client's sole source of income.

chunks.title: Client gets Child Support through Inland Revenue — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: If the client gets Child Support through Inland Revenue, we only include payments made to them on or after 22 August 2023 as assessable income. This is because Child Support paid by Inland Revenue is paid in arrears. Child Support for the calendar month of July is not paid until 22 August 2023 at the earliest. Any Child Support paid by Inland Revenue before 22 August 2023 covers a liability period before July 2023 and is excluded.

chunks.title: Example — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Saeran applies for social housing on 31 July 2023. He gets Jobseeker Support and Child Support of $375 a month paid under a formula assessment from Inland Revenue. His most recent payment of Child Support was on 21 July 2023. This payment was made for calendar month of June 2023. MSD cannot include his Child Support payments as assessable income when determining whether he qualifies for social housing, as the payments are for a liability period before 1 July 2023. MSD may include Saeran's Child Support as assessable income at a future review (e.g. a review while he is on the social housing register), if his Child Support at time of review is paid for a liability period on or after 1 July 2023.

chunks.title: Client gets Child Support but not through Inland Revenue — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: When a client gets Child Support through another arrangement, e.g. a private arrangement you must determine what period the Child Support is paid for. If it is paid for a period on or after 1 July 2023, it is included as assessable income.

chunks.title: Example — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Lizzie applies for social housing on 3 July 2023. She works full-time and gets Child Support of $150 a week under a private arrangement. Lizzie tells MSD these payments are generally paid for the current week (e.g. not in arrears). Lizzie says the arrangement is intended to last until her children finish primary school next year. MSD includes Lizzie's Child Support as assessable income from 3 July 2023 when determining whether she qualifies for social housing.

chunks.title: Exception - Child Support is client's only income — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: When Child Support is the client's only income it is included as assessable income when calculating the rate of Income Related Rent both before and after 1 July 2023.

chunks.title: Child treated for rheumatic fever — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Child treated for rheumatic fever
A qualifying child for rheumatic fever fast-track includes a person getting treatment for a previous episode of rheumatic fever. Generally, the person will be younger than 25 years but may be older.
To have their circumstances considered for fast-track into public housing, the person getting treatment must be a child or an additional occupant.

chunks.title: Client has difficulty managing their finances — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Client has difficulty managing their finances
Difficulties in managing their finances can impact on the client's ability to sustain alternative housing. To consider whether there are sustainability issues due to financial management the client must have problems keeping affordable, suitable and adequate housing. They may not be able to find a suitable property due to difficulties in financial management caused by:
- community or cultural expectations of financial contribution for example tithing, sending money overseas
- debt due to having to purchase necessities for example washing machine, dryer, fridge, freezer
- cannot afford essential car repairs
- partner has left with their money
- bad investments resulting in debt
- was guarantor for someone who did not repay the debt and now the client is liable
- addiction problem, drug, alcohol or gambling which means the money is not available for essential living expenses
- unable to budget or bad financial management
- change in employment circumstances for example have become unemployed
- not enough money for food after paying essential costs
Difficulties in financial management may lead to the client being unable to cope emotionally or having poor health due to stress. Due to high debt, clients may have insufficient income to meet all their financial commitments.
Note the assessment is of the difficulties the client has in managing their finances. It is not expected that the client addresses their financial issue and therefore reduce their housing risk at this stage of the process.

chunks.title: Client leaves emergency housing for more than 28 days due to exceptional circumstances — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: A client may still qualify for the emergency housing fast-track if: - there were exceptional circumstances that caused them to leave emergency housing for more than 28 days and - they have stayed in emergency housing for at least 12 weeks in the 52-week period before they are assessed for the fast-track Exceptional circumstances are when the client's break from emergency housing: - was an unforeseen event that could not have been planned for and - was out of the client's control and - sets the client apart from others in a similar situation

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances reasons — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: A client may be considered to have exceptional circumstances if they had to leave emergency housing for more than 28 days because: - the client was admitted to hospital or a medical care facility - had safety and welfare concerns that meant they could not stay in emergency housing, for example due to family violence or other serious crime Note the circumstances of the client, their partner and dependent children (if any) need to be considered on a case-by-case basis.

chunks.title: 12 continuous weeks within the last 52-week period — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: The client must be in emergency housing for at least 12 weeks in the 52-week period before the date of assessment for the emergency housing fast-track. Any time spent in emergency housing from more than 52 weeks ago must not be included in the fast-track assessment.

chunks.title: Example 1 — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Matt, his partner, and their 11-year-old twins were in emergency housing in Nelson for 6 months. They had to leave to take 1 of the twins to Starship hospital. Matt and the rest of his family stayed at Ronald McDonald house during that time. The child was hospitalised for 41 days. The family returned to emergency housing 2 weeks ago. Matt meets the exceptional circumstances criteria to have had a break from emergency housing for more than 28 days. The family stayed in emergency housing for over 12 weeks during the 52-week period (6 months + 2 weeks). Matt is added to the fast-track.

chunks.title: Example 2 — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Bri and her 3 dependent children were in emergency housing in Auckland for 3 months. Due to family violence, Bri and her children moved out of emergency housing and stayed at Women's Refuge in Hamilton. They stayed at the Women' Refuge for 1 year and 3 months. Bri and her children returned to Auckland and have been staying in emergency housing for 3 weeks. Although Bri had exceptional circumstances for leaving emergency housing, her first stay in emergency housing was over 52 weeks ago and cannot be included in her 12-week count. This means only her current stay in emergency housing of 3 weeks can be counted towards the 12 weeks. As Bri does not meet the 12 weeks in emergency housing criteria, she does qualify for the emergency housing fast-track yet.

chunks.title: Client qualifies for and getting a main benefit — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Client qualifies for and getting a main benefit
Clients who qualify for, and get 1 of the following main benefits qualify for social housing on residency grounds (if they are ordinarily resident in New Zealand):
- Emergency Benefit (including Emergency Maintenance Allowance)
- Jobseeker Support
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury, disability, or total blindness
- Supported Living Payment - caring for a person
- Youth Payment
- Young Parent Payment

chunks.title: Client recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Client recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand
Some migrants come to New Zealand under the New Zealand Refugee Quota Programme. They are generally known as quota refugees and are recognised as a refugee under the Immigration Act 2002 before they arrive in New Zealand.
Others ask for refugee or protected person status on arrival at the borders of New Zealand (usually international air and seaports), or later, and are known as spontaneous refugees, convention refugees, or asylum seekers. A claim for refugee or protection status can be initiated at any time.
When a person is recognized as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 either through the New Zealand Refugee Quota Programme or through a process on arrival in New Zealand, they will qualify for social housing on residency grounds from the time they get that refugee or protected person status.

chunks.title: Client requests a transfer — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Client requests a transfer
A client in social housing may have a change in circumstances and let us know that the current property no longer meets their housing needs (requirements). The client may request a transfer to a more suitable property.
When a client requests a transfer, the Social Allocation System (SAS) is used to assess their need and priority for 'other' social housing and confirm their housing requirements.
## Outcome of assessment is 'at risk' or' serious housing need'
When a client is assessed as at risk (priority A) or as having a serious housing need (priority B) they will be identified as a transfer client and added to the register. Transfer clients will be matched and referred to suitable properties in the usual manner and according to their priority.
For more information see:
- Register management and referrals
## Outcome of assessment is moderate to low housing need
When a client is assessed as having a moderate (priority C) or low risk (priority D) housing need, you will need to advise them that they do not have a housing need that requires them to move to a different social housing property. Clients with a moderate or low housing need are not placed on the register.
## Offer housing options
If these clients still want to move, they may have entitlement to other assistance to support a move to the private sector. You should consider referring them to the Housing Options seminar.
For more information see:
## Housing provider may be able to move tenant
In some situations, a social housing provider may be able to accommodate the tenant's need to move by transferring them to a more suitable property. The client will need to discuss this with their housing provider.
For more information see:
- Housing provider requires tenant to transfer
## Income Related Rent
The client's change in circumstances may mean their Income Related Rent needs to be reviewed.
## Kāinga Ora tenant with grandparented Income Related Rent
When a Kāinga Ora tenant transfers to a community housing provider, the tenant no longer qualifies to the Income Related Rent grandparenting provisions.
For more information see:
- Social housing Income Related Rent
- Clients getting grandparented rate of Income Related Rent
## Review of decision
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have received formal notification of (and do not agree with) the outcome of assessment of eligibility for 'other' social housing.
- Assessment of eligibility
- Review and Appeals

chunks.title: Clients in specific circumstances — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Clients in specific circumstances
For clients in the following circumstances there are specific things that you need to consider when assessing their eligibility for social housing.

chunks.title: Clients in specific circumstances - Residency — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Clients in specific circumstances - Residency
A client must meet the residency requirements to qualify for social housing.

chunks.title: Clients must choose 3 places where they need to live (letting areas) — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Clients must choose 3 places where they need to live (letting areas)
MSD is responsible for confirming a client's eligibility for social housing and determining their housing needs (housing requirements). Property requirements also include consideration of the specific location needed by the household.
To increase the chances of matching them with a suitable property that meets their housing needs, prospective tenants are required to nominate a minimum of 3 areas where they need to live.
If the prospective tenant cannot nominate 3 areas, and they do not have a good reason for doing so, MSD can use its discretion to add additional suitable letting areas that the client has not nominated.
## Good reasons for not nominating suitable letting areas
Good and sufficient reasons for not selecting 3 letting areas could include:
- good and sufficient reasons similar to those outlined for declining a social housing property
- nominated letting area is already large (e.g. rural locations, postal codes that cover several suburbs already)
## Decline policy applies
If a prospective tenant is offered a property in the additional nominated letting areas but declines it, the declines policy applies and they will be removed from the register if they do not have a good and sufficient reason for declining the property.

chunks.title: Clients 'not living in any accommodation' — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Clients 'not living in any accommodation'
A client who does 'not live in any accommodation' does not have adequate housing.
A client in the following situations would be considered to 'not live in any accommodation':
- rough sleeping, living in a car or other vehicle in the street, or a tent in an area without facilities, or other public space
- living in a shed, garage, or other building that is not intended to be used for human habitation
- living in a tent, caravan, vehicle or other structure (whether permanent or temporary) that is intended to be used as temporary accommodation (eg cabin in a camping ground, marae, caravan at a permanent private dwelling, motel or hotel)
For accommodation to be adequate it must be minimally adequate. A client will not have minimally adequate accommodation if they do not have any accommodation at all, or if they have accommodation that lacks basic features.
Generally, minimally adequate housing is:
- structurally sound and has basic amenities
- intended for residential occupation as a home
- accommodation in which the occupant/s has/have security of tenure (ie legal right to continue to occupy the property)
Clients who are assessed as 'not living in any accommodation' means they have no choice but to live in a situation that lacks basic necessities.

chunks.title: Client's partner is not residentially qualified — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Client's partner is not residentially qualified
When a couple are applying for social housing and one partner does not meet the residence requirements, the partner can still be included in the application for social housing as they do not require a separate bedroom allocation. The non-residentially qualified partner cannot be the applicant and cannot be a signatory to the tenancy agreement.
However, any income the non-residentially qualified partner gets is included in the calculation for the household's Income Related Rent.
For more information see:
- Residence
- Temporary entry class visa - visitors, work and students
- Income Related Rent Household types and income thresholds
- Income Related Rent Assessable income
- Core Policy – Partner’s residence status

chunks.title: Clients getting grandparented rate of Income Related Rent — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Clients getting grandparented rate of Income Related Rent
When Kāinga Ora transfers a client to a community housing provider, the client no longer qualifies for the Income Related Rent grandparenting provisions.
On 1 December 2000, Income Related Rents replaced all accommodation assistance that was paid to Kāinga Ora clients and their partners.
The grand-parenting provision meant that clients living in Kāinga Ora properties at the time did not have a rate of Income Related Rent greater than what they were paying as rent before the change.

chunks.title: Clients suspended from a housing provider — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Clients suspended from a housing provider
Housing providers may suspend tenants who have breached their tenancy agreement. This means that the social housing provider is not willing to accept the client as a tenant.
Clients who are suspended by a housing provider can still request an eligibility assessment to determine if they have a housing need. You should encourage the client to seek a waiver of the suspension from the housing provider if this is available, as this will increase the client's opportunity for a referral to suitable housing.

chunks.title: Condition of facilities in the current house — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Condition of facilities in the current house
When assessing if a client's current accommodation is adequate, the condition of facilities in the house in which the client is living and any associated health and safety risks must be considered.
Note this does not apply to clients who are assessed as 'not living in any accommodation' or living in emergency housing for the time being. These clients have already been rated as 'at risk' (4) for adequacy.
Facilities are the things within the house that are there for a particular purpose and are a standard requirement. They include:
- laundry (wash tub, washing machine, plumbing)
- cooking (oven, cook top, ability to have a refrigerator in the cooking area)
- bathroom (toilet, basins, showers)
- heating (at least power points to be able to use a heater)
The degree of the inadequacies and the effect they are having on the quality of life of the occupants needs to be assessed.
Some factors to consider are:
- lack of cooking, toilet, bathroom and laundry facilities
- facilities not working at all
- the facilities are unsafe and dangerous and the current landlord is reluctant to repair them, for example: exposed electrical wiringgas leakinadequate repairs of essential facilities have been undertakenwindows boarded overdoors tied shut because the lock is broken
- exposed electrical wiring
- gas leak
- inadequate repairs of essential facilities have been undertaken
- windows boarded over
- doors tied shut because the lock is broken

chunks.title: Cook Island, Niue and Tokelau clients — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Cook Island, Niue and Tokelau clients
Clients born in the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau are New Zealand citizens by birth (if they meet the criteria for New Zealand citizenship by birth). Generally they will travel to New Zealand on a New Zealand passport.
To qualify for social housing, clients born in the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Current accommodation becomes unsuitable — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Current accommodation becomes unsuitable
The type, size or design of the client's current accommodation may become unsuitable due to several life events.
For example:
- a marriage, civil union or a de facto relationship may result in the client's current accommodation becoming unsuitable. For example a bed-sit or small apartment may be too small for 2 people
- separation may result in the client's accommodation being too big for their needs
- a large family may have specific needs in terms of the size of accommodation required or a large family may be residing in separate accommodation but want to reunite
- the size of a client's current accommodation may become unsuitable due to household members moving in or out
- the client may need to relocate due to re-unification with children (for example, children who are in Oranga Tamariki care or returning to a parent's care after being with another caregiver)
- a decrease in mobility of a household member, an inability to manage and maintain the section and garden or the inability to make structural modifications to accommodate wheelchairs may make the client's current accommodation unsuitable
- a client's accommodation might be culturally inappropriate, for example the design of the house (toilet is next to the kitchen) or neighbours with conflicting religious beliefs
- the day-to-day management of the current accommodation may become unsuitable for a household member due to an illness or disability. This person may be working full-time and the household may have members who are unable to provide the support necessary to maintain the house and household
- increase in current rental housing costs make the client's current accommodation unsuitable
- primary income earner leaves the home, becomes unemployed or disabled: existing accommodation becomes unaffordableexisting accommodation can no longer be maintained
- existing accommodation becomes unaffordable
- existing accommodation can no longer be maintained

chunks.title: Death of a client — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Death of a client
When a client who is renting a social housing property dies, how you treat the situation depends on whether the client is a sole tenant or a joint tenant.
For more information see:
- Death of a sole tenant
- Death of a joint tenant

chunks.title: Death of a joint tenant — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Death of a joint tenant
Generally, on the death of a joint tenant, the surviving tenant will remain in the property and their Income Related Rent will be reassessed. The client has an obligation to advise of any change to their circumstances that will affect their eligibility for social housing or calculated rate of Income Related Rent. For more information on the impact on the Income Related Rent see:
- Income Related Rent reviews Death of a client
In some cases the death of a joint tenant may:
- lead the surviving tenant to consider that the property is no longer suitable for them
- indicate to the housing provider that the particular social house is no longer suitable for the surviving tenant
In these cases, either the client or the housing provider may request a review of the surviving tenant's housing needs (property requirements).

chunks.title: Death of a sole tenant — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: On the death of a sole tenant under a tenancy agreement (fixed-term or periodic tenancy), the tenancy agreement terminates at the earliest of the following dates: - 21 days after the landlord is given written notice from the tenant's next of kin of the tenant's death - 21 days after the landlord gives the next of kin written notice to vacate the premises that is subject to the tenancy agreement - a date agreed in writing by the landlord with the next of kin - the date determined as the termination date by the Tenancy Tribunal MSD must have confirmation from the social housing provider before MSD can stop paying the Income Related Rent subsidy or calculating the rate of Income Related Rent. For more information about the impact on Income Related Rent see: - Income Related Rent reviews Death of a client

chunks.title: Other family member or additional occupants have no ongoing rights — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: No other party (family member or additional occupant) has ongoing rights to remain in the property after the tenant's death. This includes the partner of the tenant when they are not a signatory to the tenancy agreement. The remaining occupants may be contacted by the social housing provider about: - vacating the premises or - if they are living in a community housing provider property, taking on the tenancy without an Income Related Rent

chunks.title: The next of kin or an additional occupant wants to assess their own eligibility for social housing — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: The next of kin or any other additional occupant may want to test their own eligibility for social housing. In these situations an eligibility assessment for social housing may be undertaken. Note the next of kin or additional occupant may not be allocated the existing social house that they are occupying at the time, even if they qualify for social housing in their own right.

chunks.title: Outcome of review is at risk or in serious housing need — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: If the next of kin or additional occupant is assessed as at risk (priority A) or as having a serious housing need (priority B) they are eligible for social housing and can be placed on the register. Kāinga Ora or a community housing provider will make an offer to the client when they are matched with a suitable property.

chunks.title: Outcome of review is priority is moderate to low housing need — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: When a client is assessed as having a moderate (priority C) or low risk (priority D) housing need, you will need to advise them that they are not eligible for social housing. Do not place them on the register. These clients may be eligible for other assistance through options and advice.

chunks.title: Definition of accommodation — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Definition of accommodation
Accommodation is premises intended for residential occupation as a home, and includes any room or other accommodation intended for occupation as a home, by a boarder.
Accommodation does not include any permanent or temporary building, tent, caravan, vehicle, or other structure, that is:
- not intended to be used for human habitation (e.g. garages shed, barn, or carport)
- intended to be used only as temporary accommodation (e.g. cabin/tent or mobile home in a camping ground, or accommodation at a marae)
- emergency housing (e.g. getting an Emergency Housing Grant to live in commercial accommodation, contracted emergency housing, transitional housing, or other community emergency housing provider)

chunks.title: Definition of lower quartile private rent — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Definition of lower quartile private rent
Lower quartile private rent is the weekly rent at 25% of all market rents when all are placed in order of value.

chunks.title: Dependent child for eligibility purposes — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Dependent child for eligibility purposes
A dependent child for social housing purposes is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- being maintained as a member of that family and
- financially dependent on the client
A child is a single person under the age of 18 years, other than a person who is:
- 16 or 17 and
- financially independent
A child may also include a person who is 18 years old for a limited period if they are:
- continuing in education and
- not financially independent
Note the following children are considered to be a dependent child for eligibility for social housing purposes and would be allocated a bedroom if:
- they are a child for whom the Orphan's Benefit, Unsupported Child's Benefit, or Foster Care Allowance is being paid or
- there is a shared custody arrangement, and the child stays in the house for overnight stays that are equal to or more than six days per fortnight or
- they are a dependent child of an additional occupant
In order to be allocated a bedroom, the child must also be a full-time member of the household.
In some situations, a child may not be living at home, but is still considered to be a dependent child and be allocated a bedroom.
Generally, adult children living with the family would not be considered for bedroom allocation unless they meet the criteria to be an additional occupant. However, they may be considered as an applicable person if they are intending to be a signatory to the tenancy agreement and an assessment of their housing need has been undertaken.

chunks.title: Dependent child for emergency housing fast-track — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Dependent child for emergency housing fast-track
To qualify for the emergency housing fast-track, the client, or their partner, must have at least 1 dependent child.
A dependent child for the emergency housing fast-track is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the person and
- being maintained as a member of that person's family and
- financially dependent on that person
A dependent child (as defined above) includes a child:
- for whom Orphans Benefit or an Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid or
- in the custody of Oranga Tamariki and who has been returned to their parent's care
## Not a dependent child for emergency housing fast-track
A dependent child for the emergency housing fast-track does not include:
- a child or young person (as defined under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989) for whom a Foster Care Allowance is being paid
- a dependent child of an additional occupant for social housing
- a young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child
Note if the young person getting Young Parent Payment qualifies for the emergency housing fast-track in their own right, their child would be considered a dependent child.

chunks.title: Dependent child included in social housing assessment — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Dependent child included in social housing assessment
To qualify for the emergency housing fast-track, the client's dependent child must be included in the client's social housing assessment.
## Shared care arrangement of dependent child
A dependent child who is in a shared care arrangement can only be included in a client's social housing assessment if the child is a full-time member of the client's household.
## Dependent child not staying in emergency housing
A client may have a dependent child who does not stay with them in emergency housing (or who only stays with them some of the time).
Clients in this situation may still qualify for the emergency housing fast-track, as long as their dependent child is included in their social housing assessment.
Example
Taylor is staying in a motel paid for by an Emergency Housing Grant and has been there for 4 months.
Taylor has 2 dependent children, who are staying elsewhere with family members while Taylor is in emergency housing. The children visit him in the motel most weekends.
Taylor's dependent children are included in his social housing assessment, as they will be full-time members of his household when in social housing.
Taylor qualifies for the emergency housing fast-track, even though his dependent children do not stay with him in emergency housing.

chunks.title: Dependent child turns 18 — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Dependent child turns 18
When a dependent child turns 18, they are no longer considered a dependent child for emergency housing fast-track.
If the child turning 18 is the client or their partner's only child, the client will no longer qualify for the emergency housing fast-track.
## Exception - child turns 18 and continues in education
When a dependent child turns 18, they can still be included in the client's emergency housing fast-track for a limited period when the child is:
- continuing in education and
- financially dependent on the client
If they meet the qualifications above, the child can be treated as a dependent child of the client in emergency housing for a limited period.

chunks.title: Determining accessible bedrooms — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Determining accessible bedrooms
The number of bedrooms currently available to the client's household compared with the number of bedrooms required to house them suitably needs to be determined.
Accessible bedrooms, are bedrooms to which the client's household has access.
To work out the number of bedrooms required by the household, see:
- Bedroom allocation
If a client is seeking accommodation because they are currently living in a garage, you need to consider whether there are any other accessible bedrooms available in any dwelling on the same property.
Dwelling
Accessible bedrooms
Living areas
Not considered accessible bedrooms.
Garage
Generally not considered an accessible bedroom.
Where a sleep-out is attached to the garage and separated by a firewall, the sleep-out may be considered 1 bedroom

chunks.title: Determining affordability rating for multiple households — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Determining affordability rating for multiple households
Sometimes 2 or more families apply for social housing together.
