When assessing their affordability rating, use the lower quartile rent for the number of bedrooms required jointly for both households and split the rent between the 2 (or more households) and assess their notional Accommodation Supplement using this split rent figure.
The amount of accommodation income to deduct from the lower quartile rent should be based on the current amounts received from those who are or will be additional occupants for each applicable person in each household.
When determining the rate of unabated main benefit, work out the unabated main benefit for each of the household's household type and then add them together to get the combined residual income for the 2 households.
## Affordability formula for multiple households
Step number
Description
Total $
Step 1
Calculate net weekly income (including family tax credit received) for each applicable person in each household
Total A = income including family tax credit received combined for each household
Step 2
Calculate lower quartile weekly rent in the area the combined household needs to live. Divide this lower quartile weekly rent between the 2 households.
To calculate the accommodation income, use the amount currently received from additional occupants.
To calculate the Accommodation Supplement for each household, divide the lower quartile weekly rent between the 2 households and use this divided figure as the rent for Accommodation Supplement.
Subtract accommodation income currently received from additional occupants and the Accommodation Supplement each household may be able to get from the lower quartile rent.
Total B = lower quartile rent for combined household minus accommodation income currently received from additional occupants and the calculated Accommodation Supplement for each household.
Step 3
Subtract Total B from Total A
Total A - Total B = Total C
Step 4
Work out the unabated main benefit the household are getting or the benefit that each household would get for each of their household type. Add these figures together.
Divide Total C by total unabated main benefit the household is getting or the benefit that they would get for each of the household type (including family tax credit) x 100.
Residual income %
Step 5
Determine risk rating
Risk rating = X
Note
- Accommodation income for Step 2 only includes current amounts received from those who are or will be additional occupants
From 1 July 2023, most types of Child Support are included as assessable income in the client's net weekly income for the affordability formula.

chunks.title: Determining affordability rating for students — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Determining affordability rating for students
If a person getting Student Allowance is applying for social housing, you still assess their affordability rating using Accommodation Supplement based on their household type.
However, like all other situations, you will need to consider whether the risk rating determined by the formula accurately reflects the client's level of need.

chunks.title: Determining history of transience — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Determining history of transience
A client may have difficulty finding a suitable property due to a history of transience.
Only moves when the client was required to move or had an acceptable reason for moving can be taken into account for the assessment of sustainability.
## Acceptable need or requirement to move
An acceptable need or requirement to move may include (but is not limited to):
- client has been asked to leave, evicted or given notice from their accommodation
- client had to leave their accommodation because they could not afford the rent
- property was unfit or lacked essential facilities
- client was in emergency or temporary accommodation
- client was staying with friends on a temporary basis
- client had to leave their accommodation due to a dispute with family members or a relationship breakdown
- client felt unsafe due to violence and threats of violence
- moved to give or receive support
- moved to receive medical or social support not available in the current location
## Moving for reasons that are not considered transience
Some moves are made for the usual reasons that all other members of a community decide to move house. A person moving for these types of reasons would not be considered transient. A move that would not be considered necessary may include (but is not limited to):
- wanted a change of scene
- wanted larger accommodation when overcrowding was not a factor
- wanted better facilities when accommodation met the client's minimum requirements
- landlord and tenant agree to end a fixed-term tenancy at its expiry
- wanted to move closer to family and friends when the move was not required for support
- moved to undertake education
- moved for training or employment reasons including seasonal employment

chunks.title: Difficulty in social functioning, lack of social skills or history of transience — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Difficulty in social functioning, lack of social skills or history of transience
Difficulties in social functioning and a lack of social skills can affect the client's ability to sustain alternative housing.
The client may not be able to find a suitable property due to difficulties in social functioning, lack of social skills or a history of transience caused by:
- a lack of necessary confidence and skills
- a lack of knowledge, for example, does not know who to approach to discuss other housing options
- has only ever had a social housing provider as a landlord
- lacks confidence in private sector or distrusts private landlords
- has a history of transience resulting in reluctance of private sector to rent to them
## History of transience
Only moves where the client was required to move or had an acceptable reason for moving can be taken into account for the assessment of sustainability.
For more information see:
- Determining history of transience
- Risk rating for social functioning and history of transience

chunks.title: Discrimination as a barrier to suitable housing — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Discrimination as a barrier to suitable housing
A client may be having difficulty trying to get suitable alternative housing because of their personal circumstances.
When discussing a client's situation, ask what is making it difficult for them to get alternative housing. The client may identify one or more of the following personal circumstances they consider to be a barrier to them getting alternative housing (clients may have other examples):
- personal appearance: e.g. facial tattoos.
- language barriers e.g. English is not the clients first language, they speak limited English is the reason, or have other communication difficulties
- employment or social factors: e.g. the nature or hours of their employment may be seen as 'anti-social' or the number of vehicles the household owns may deter a property owner
- religion, culture, race, ethnicity, or sexual orientation
- young age: a client says their age is the reason they are unable to get a rental and thinks owners landlords may consider young people may not be responsible tenants
- physical or mental health and/or a disability: a client is having difficulty getting suitable accommodation due to a physical or mental disability, e.g. they need modifications to a property or there is a perception of risk associated with mental health issues
- family size: e.g. number of children or 2 households looking to live together
- credit history: a client says they have a poor or limited credit history (this may include unpaid rent in the past)
- tenancy history: a client says they have a lack of references, limited tenancy history or have been through the Tenancy Tribunal or Court
- criminal record: of the client or their partner
## Options and Advice
You should consider whether any of the barriers can be addressed or reduced.
Examples of this may include (but are not limited to):
- is the client able to get a character reference from an employer or other suitable member of the community?
- budget advice to remedy or demonstrate their ability to pay rent
- rent paid by a redirection of their benefit payment
Some of the barriers faced by clients may be addressed or reduced by providing support or more information.
You should discuss with the client the relevant housing options.

chunks.title: Emergency housing fast-track change in circumstances — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Emergency housing fast-track change in circumstances
A client and their household will be removed from the emergency housing fast-track when 1 or more of the following apply:
- the client left emergency housing for more than 28 days and does not have exceptional circumstances
- the client or their partner no longer has a dependent child
- the client no longer has dependent children included in their social housing assessment
- the client and their household are placed in social housing or alternative housing (e.g. transitional housing)
- the client no longer qualifies for social housing or is no longer on the social housing register
- the client no longer qualifies for emergency housing (including when the client is on an emergency housing non-entitlement period)
Note if a client is no longer fast-tracked, they may still qualify to remain on the social housing register.
## Dependent child leaves care unexpectedly
If a dependent child leaves a client’s care unexpectedly, the client may continue to get payments at the existing rate for 28 days following the date the child left their care if they are getting 1 of the following payments:
- sole parent rate of main benefit or
- Unsupported Childs Benefit or
- Orphans Benefit
However, the client will not remain on the emergency housing fast-track for the additional 28 days. If there are no other dependent children included in their social housing assessment the client will be removed from the emergency housing fast-track.
## Emergency Housing non-entitlement period
If a client on the emergency housing fast track gets an emergency housing non-entitlement period, they must be removed from the emergency housing fast track for their whole 13-week non-entitlement period.
A client who has their non-entitlement period paused because they have been granted an Emergency Housing Grant under limited circumstances must still be removed from the emergency housing fast track.
If the client returns to emergency housing after their 13-week non-entitlement period ends, they will need to be in emergency housing for another 12 weeks or more before they can qualify for emergency housing fast track again.

chunks.title: Example 1 — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: An existing household consists of Paul and Sonya and their 2 daughters living in a 3 bedroom house. Sonya's sister Mary and her 2 children move in with them temporarily (the client household). Bedroom 1 Paul and Sonya Bedroom 2 14 year old daughter Bedroom 3 12 year old daughter Living room Client household (Mary, 10 year old son, 5 year old daughter) If you apply the overcrowding guidelines, the existing household only need 2 bedrooms - Paul and Sonya get their own room and their 2 daughters could reasonably be expected to share, as they are under 18 years and the same sex. In this situation, the client household has 1 accessible bedroom but they require 3 bedrooms (1 bedroom for Mary, 1 bedroom each for the children as one is over 10 years and they are of the opposite sex).

chunks.title: Example 2 — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: An existing household consists of Bryan and Mandy, their 2 daughters and their 18 year old son and his girlfriend. Mandy's sister Justine and her 2 children move in with them temporarily (the client household). The 18 year old son and his girlfriend move into the living room to give their bedroom to Justine and her children. Bedroom 1 Bryan and Mandy Bedroom 2 14 year old daughter 12 year old daughter Bedroom 3 Client household (Justine, 10 year old son, 5 year old daughter) Living room 18 year old son and his girlfriend In this situation, Bryan and Mandy get their own room, the 2 daughters share a room, and the 18 year old son and his girlfriend do not have a bedroom. The existing household requires all 3 bedrooms. Justine and her 2 children have no accessible bedrooms and require 3 bedrooms.

chunks.title: Example 3 — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: An existing household consists of Kelly and her son living in a 2 bedroom property. The client household of Bob, Sandra and their 2 year old son move in. Bedroom 1 Kelly Bedroom 2 7 year old son Living room Client household (Bob, Sandra and 2 year old son) In this situation Kelly has her own room. Her 7 year old son could reasonably be expected to share a room with Bob and Sandra's 2 year old son. The remaining client household members (Bob and Sandra) have no accessible bedroom. The client household has 1 accessible bedroom and requires 2 bedrooms. Note any issues arising from the children sharing a room must be considered under medical, disability and personal needs and supporting verification provided.

chunks.title: Example 4 — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: An existing household consists of Christina and her son living in a 2 bedroom house. The client household consisting of Anna, Doug and 2 children move in. Bedroom 1 Christina Bedroom 2 7 year old son Living room Client household (Anna and Doug, 4 year old son and 6 year old son) In this situation, Christina gets her own room, and her 7-year-old son could share a room with one of the client's children. The client household's remaining members consisting of Anna, Doug and one of their sons, has no accessible bedrooms. Usually this would be recorded as having 1 accessible bedroom and requiring 2 bedrooms. However, when looking at their actual situation, the client household is still 2 bedrooms short as Anna and Doug and their other son still do not have access to a bedroom. The client household has no accessible bedrooms.

chunks.title: Example 1 - eligible — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Example 1 - eligible
Oranga Tamariki has placed a child in the care of the child's grandparents as there were serious concerns about the safety of the child due to family violence.
It is considered a permanent placement (over 12 months) and is in the best interests of the child. The child's grandparents are on the housing register and are now eligible for fast-track.
## Example 2 - eligible
Matthew was placed in the care of his aunty 2 years ago by Oranga Tamariki due to his mother's addiction issues. His mother has recently been proactively engaging with their social worker from Oranga Tamariki and is now in a position to have him return to her care.
Matthew will stay with his mother 5 days a week and the plan is for him to leave the custody of Oranga Tamariki and return to his mother's care full-time in 18 months. Matthew's mother applies for public housing and is eligible for the fast-track provision as Matthew will be placed with his parent.
## Example 3 - not eligible
Oranga Tamariki called a Family Group Conference due to concerns about the safety of a baby. The young mother, wider whānau and Oranga Tamariki agreed that the best solution would be for the grandparents of the baby to take care of them for a few months.
This is a temporary placement, and the intention is not long term. As it is unlikely the child will be in the care of their relative for more than 12 months, the household does not qualify for fast track.

chunks.title: Example 1 — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Jane and Michael live with their 2 sons, 1 daughter and their niece. Jane's brother Doug and his daughter also live in the same house. Doug and his daughter came to live with Jane's family after Doug became a sole parent and stopped working to look after his daughter. The household need of household 1 and household 2 is assessed together and both household signatories are required to sign the tenancy agreement. Household 1 Jane and Michael, their sons aged 12 and 15 years, daughter aged 8 years, and niece aged 8 years Jane and Michael are signatories for this household unit. Their sons, daughter and niece are their dependent children. Household 2 Doug and his daughter aged 7 years Doug is the signatory for the second household unit. His daughter is his dependent child

chunks.title: Example 2 — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Sarah lives with her daughter aged 21 years, and her son aged 15 years. Sarah's sister Fran lives with the family as she needs support from Sarah. There is no obligation for Fran to sign the tenancy agreement as she meets the criteria to be considered an additional occupant. The household decides that Fran does not need to sign the tenancy agreement. Household 1 Sarah, daughter aged 21 years, son aged 15 years Sarah is signatory for the household unit. Her daughter is a non-dependent child is considered an additional occupant as she has an intellectual disability. Sarah's son is a dependent child Additional occupant Fran (Sarah's sister) Fran has been determined as an additional occupant and not a separate household unit. She has a need to remain as part of the household. Her income is not included in the Income Related Rent assessment Sarah and Fran decide that Fran should also sign the tenancy agreement which ensures her security of tenure at the property. Household 1 Sarah, daughter aged 21 years, son aged 15 years Sarah is signatory for this household unit. Daughter is a non-dependent child who is considered an additional occupant as she has an intellectual disability and Sarah's son is a dependent child Household 2 Fran (Sarah's sister) Fran is the signatory for the second household unit. Her income is included in the Income Related Rent assessment

chunks.title: Example 3 — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Jane and Pamela are friends and Jane is supporting Pamela after her rehabilitation for drug and alcohol addiction. They apply for social housing and decide that they will both sign the tenancy agreement. Household 1 Jane Jane is the signatory for herself. Her income is included in the assessment of Income Related Rent Household 2 Pamela Pamela is also a signatory. Her income is included in the assessment of Income Related Rent For more information see: - Assessment of need for multiple household unit

chunks.title: Exception to income and asset limits — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Exception to income and asset limits
Generally a client does not qualify for social housing if they exceed the income or asset limits.
However, there are exceptions that allow you to progress the client's application for social housing when:
- the client's income or assets exceeds the limits and
- they have an urgent social housing need and
- that housing need can be met by the provision of social housing
## Examples
Examples of exceptions include (but are not limited to):
- client has applied for modified housing and it is unlikely that they will be able to fund this modification or have it provided in the private housing market
- application following a breakdown in a relationship when joint property is unable to be realised
- the household requirements mean that there is little likelihood of securing alternative housing options to meet the need, for example a very large family (6 bedrooms or more required and potential discrimination)
Note eligibility for social housing may be reviewed while a client is on the register when there is a change to income or cash assets.

chunks.title: Exceptions to bedroom allocation — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Generally, bedrooms will be allocated based on the overcrowding criteria. However there may be some exceptions to this.

chunks.title: Young people sharing a bedroom — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Generally, it is reasonable that children under the age of 10 years (any sex) and children under the age of 18 years of the same sex should share a bedroom. However there may be good reasons that additional bedrooms would be approved when: - there are health and disability issues that mean sharing is unreasonable - there are health and safety issues for example a child has behavioural problems when the other child is at risk of harm - for example a child has behavioural problems when the other child is at risk of harm - young people are within 6 months of the criteria changing for example a boy aged 9 years is two months away from his 10th birthday and is living in a house with his sister who is aged 7 years - for example a boy aged 9 years is two months away from his 10th birthday and is living in a house with his sister who is aged 7 years - it is unreasonable for the children or young people to share given their gender and privacy needs for example when a young person is gender diverse or when their gender is different from their sex it may be unreasonable for them to share with another young person of the same sex - for example when a young person is gender diverse or when their gender is different from their sex it may be unreasonable for them to share with another young person of the same sex - an age difference in the children means it is unreasonable for them to share a bedroom for example a 17 year old and a 1-year-old have very different developmental needs which might make it unreasonable to expect them to share a bedroom - for example a 17 year old and a 1-year-old have very different developmental needs which might make it unreasonable to expect them to share a bedroom

chunks.title: Unreasonable to share given gender and privacy needs — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: When a household includes 2 or more young people and at least 1 is gender diverse, you will need to discuss what may be an appropriate bedroom arrangement given the genders, ages and privacy needs of the young people. Similarly, clients may also raise concerns about young people allocated to share a room who are the same gender but different sexes. In both scenarios, you will need to consider bedroom allocation on a case-by-case basis and can allocate additional bedrooms as appropriate, given the genders, ages and privacy needs of the young people.

chunks.title: Couples — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Generally a couple would share a bedroom. There may be good reasons that an additional bedroom is required for a couple. This could include: - an extra bedroom is required to store medical equipment (for example for a dialysis patient) - health and safety issues that require 1 of the couple to have their own bedroom For more information see: - Bedroom allocation - Full-time members of the household - Allocating bedrooms for known future household members - Override the bedroom allocation for households with a gender diverse child [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Factors to consider if affordability risk rating accurate — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Factors to consider if affordability risk rating accurate
You need to consider whether the risk rating as determined by the formula represents the client's level of need and whether the client has a high affordability rating due to choice.
The affordability rating may need to be reviewed in the following situations:
- the client is not getting their full entitlement to benefits or family tax credits by choice. The assessed entitlement to benefit and family tax credit should be used as their net income in this situation
- the client has a sanction against their benefit which has reduced their rate paid. The assessed entitlement to benefit should be used as their net income in this situation
- the client is getting Temporary Additional Support to assist with high rent costs and this may lower their affordability rating if it was considered
- the client is a seasonal worker and their income pattern has been assessed as a spike and they are currently on a benefit or lower wage for a short period of time, however the lower quartile rent will be sustainable when they are working or in a normal season
- the client is a student and gets a Student Loan to cover living expenses (a Student Loan is not considered income for the assessment of social housing or Income Related Rent purposes) and if this income was considered it may lower their affordability rating
- the client is a student who gets Student Allowance and Accommodation Benefit and the use of Accommodation Supplement has resulted in a low rating
If you consider a client's initial priority rating needs to be reviewed in any of the above situations, you will need to do this by changing the client's initial priority rating.

chunks.title: Family violence — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Family violence
Family violence covers a broad range of controlling behaviours, commonly of a physical, sexual, and/or psychological nature which typically involve fear, intimidation and emotional deprivation.
It occurs within a variety of close interpersonal relationships, such as between partners, parents and children, siblings, and other relationships where significant others are not part of the physical household but are part of the family and/or are fulfilling the function of family.
Common forms of violence in families/whanau include:
- partner abuse (violence among adult partners)
- child abuse/neglect (abuse/neglect of children by an adult)
- elder abuse/neglect (abuse/neglect of older people aged approximately 65 years and over, by a person with whom they have a relationship of trust)
- parental abuse (violence perpetrated by a child against their parent) and
- sibling abuse (violence among siblings)
## Confirming family violence situation
Generally a client will have been working with police or another agency, and could provide information to confirm their family violence situation from these groups. Clients may have disclosed violence to the following people:
- the client's doctor
- statements from family and friends
- police reports
- community family violence prevention agency (e.g. Women's Refuge)
- court papers
- a social worker
- the client's church
- any other reputable person or organisation to support a client's statement
## Client unable to confirm family violence situation
If the client is unable to provide information to confirm their family violence situation, you should consult with your regional family violence response co-ordinator for advice.

chunks.title: Fast-track no longer applies — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Fast-track no longer applies
Fast-track for households with a specified child or young person in the custody of Oranga Tamariki or in an approved permanent care arrangement will end, unless there is another child or young person who meets fast-track criteria, when:
- the child or young person in care leaves the household or if the child is not already in their care will not be placed with the household
- the custody arrangement with Oranga Tamariki ends, unless the caregiver is granted Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the child or young person
- the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is cancelled, including when the caregiver cancels the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit and includes the child or young person in their main benefit
- the child or young person dies
- the child or young person turns 18, unless the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the child or young person is continuing while they are continuing in education and are not financially independent
A household may still qualify to remain on the social housing register if they are no longer fast-tracked.
## Child or young person leaves care unexpectedly
When the child or young person has left care unexpectedly and Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit continues being paid for 28 days, fast-track ends when the child or young person leaves care and does not continue for the additional 28 days.

chunks.title: Fast-track provision — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Fast-track provision
Fast-track recognises that certain households applying for social housing are at risk of experiencing negative outcomes.
Helping them get into social housing quicker will help improve their long-term outcomes.
If the household meets all the qualifications, they will be fast-tracked for the next available (suitable) social housing property based on matching, by the social housing provider, even if there are other people with a higher priority rating.
## Who can be fast-tracked?
The fast-track policy applies to households in the following circumstances:
- the household has a child at risk of rheumatic fever
- the household has a specified child or young person in the custody of Oranga Tamariki or is in an approved permanent care arrangement
- the household has at least 1 dependent child and has been staying in emergency housing for 12 continuous weeks or more

chunks.title: Financially independent — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Financially independent
To be considered financially independent a person would be aged 16 years or older and:
- in full-time employment (an average of 30 hours or more each week) or
- getting a Student Allowance or
- getting a main benefit in their own right
Full-time employment is paid employment for an average of 30 hours or more each week. This includes temporary or casual work during any week that a person works for 30 hours or more.
Generally a person getting a Student Loan only (including the living cost component) is not financially independent.
For more information see:
- No need established to be an additional occupant
- Additional occupants
- Household composition

chunks.title: Full-time member of the household — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Full-time member of the household
To have a bedroom allocated, a person must be a full-time member of the household.
This means that they stay in the house for overnight stays equal to or more than six days per fortnight. This can be an adult or the child or children of a parent sharing custody.
A child (or person) will meet the overnight stays of 6 days per fortnight or more if they stay in the house for the equivalent of 156 nights a year.
This can be made up of regular overnight stays or for various periods of time, if the total number of overnight stays is equal to or more than 156 nights a year.
For example:
- child stays 2 nights every second weekend plus a minimum of an additional 104 overnight stays during the year
- child stays for all the school holidays (12 weeks = 84 overnight stays per year) plus an additional 72 overnight stays during the year
Note a person or child who stays in the house for overnight stays less than 6 days per fortnight is a part-time member of the household. They are not allocated a bedroom.

chunks.title: Holds a Christchurch Response Visa — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Holds a Christchurch Response Visa
Clients who hold a Christchurch response visa and are ordinarily resident qualify for social housing on residency grounds from the time they are granted the visa. They do not have to reside in New Zealand for 2 years since the visa was granted.
Clients will be granted a Christchurch Response Visa if they were living in New Zealand (held a resident, work or student visa) on 15 March 2019 and:
- were present at the Masjid Al Noor or Linwood Masjid while they were attacked on 15 March 2019 or
- were injured during the attacks or
- are the immediate family member of someone who was present during the attacks that is someone who died or was injured during the attacks or present in one of the mosques

chunks.title: Hospitalised or getting treatment for rheumatic fever — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Hospitalised or getting treatment for rheumatic fever
To be considered for fast-track a household must:
- have a child aged 0 - 14 years who has been hospitalised with a qualifying medical condition while living in their current accommodation or in the last 2 years or
- have a child or young person who is getting treatment because of a previous episode of rheumatic fever
A person getting treatment must be a child or additional occupant to have their circumstances considered.
## Hospitalised
Hospitalised means:
- an admission to Accident and Emergency
- day admission to hospital
- an acute arranged overnight admission to hospital
Verification of the hospital stay, the date of admission and discharge from hospital is required.
## Getting treatment
Getting treatment means getting prescribed treatment for a previous episode of rheumatic fever. The treatment may include prophylactic penicillin (such as getting monthly antibiotic prophylaxis) because of a previous episode of rheumatic fever.
A young person getting treatment will generally be younger than 25 years but may be older. To have their circumstances considered for fast-track into public housing, the person getting treatment must be a child or an additional occupant.

chunks.title: Household composition — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Household composition
Household composition describes the people who will be housed with the client. This may include extended family or additional occupants who are permanent members of the household and provide or receive financial, physical and emotional support.
Some examples of household composition are (but are not limited to):
- single client
- sole parent and dependent child(ren)
- married, de facto or civil union couple with dependent child(ren)
- married, de facto or civil union couple, without dependent children
- caregivers and dependent child(ren)
A household may be made up of the following people:
- applicable persons
- dependent children for eligibility purposes
- additional occupants (who may or may not pay a contribution)
- dependent children of additional occupants
## More than one household unit
A household can also consist of more than one household unit. This could happen when two families might apply for social housing together. They may do this if they are reuniting through refugee reunification or one family might need support. The housing need of the two household units is assessed together.

chunks.title: Households in emergency housing — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Households in emergency housing
The emergency housing fast-track aims to reduce the number of families with dependent children in emergency housing and support them into long-term housing.
The emergency housing fast-track applies when all the following qualifications are met:
- the client qualifies for social housing and
- they have (or their partner has) at least 1 dependent child and
- their dependent child or children qualify for and are included in their social housing assessment and
- the client has been staying in emergency housing for 12 continuous weeks or more at the time MSD assesses them for the fast-track
## Emergency housing
To qualify for the emergency housing fast-track, the client must be staying in:
- accommodation paid for by an Emergency Housing Grant or
- a contracted emergency housing motel.
## Transitional housing not included
Clients staying in transitional housing do not qualify for the emergency housing fast-track.
## Additional occupants for social housing assessment
A client who is an additional occupant can be included in the household being fast-tracked, but they cannot be fast-tracked in their own right.
Any dependent child of an additional occupant is not considered a dependent child for the emergency housing fast-track.
## Client does not qualify for emergency housing fast-track
A client does not qualify for the emergency housing fast-track when 1 or more of the following apply:
- they are not staying in emergency housing at their initial fast-track assessment date
- they have been in emergency housing for less than 12 weeks continuously
- they left emergency housing for more than 28 days and did not have exceptional circumstances
- the client or their partner do not have dependent children
- the client or their partner have a dependent child but they are not included in their social housing assessment
- they do not qualify for social housing or emergency housing
- they are on an emergency housing non-entitlement period
Note the fast track may still apply to a client that leaves emergency housing for more than 28 days due to exceptional circumstances.

chunks.title: Households on the register — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Households on the register
Fast-track will be applied to households already on the social housing register when a caregiver provides a written statement from Oranga Tamariki, an Iwi social service, a cultural social service, or a child and family support service confirming that:
- the household's current accommodation is preventing a specified child or young person in custody under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 or in an approved permanent care arrangement from coming into their care and
- the care arrangement for placement of the child or young person with the household is, or is intended to be, long term (12 months or longer) or permanent
When there is a change in the circumstances of a child or young person in a household on the social housing register that may affect whether the household is fast-tracked, the criteria for fast-track will also be checked to determine if the change means the fast-track should now be applied. These changes include:
- child inclusion
- granting Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit

chunks.title: Housing need priority ratings — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Housing need priority ratings
To qualify for social housing a client must be assessed as having a housing need priority rating of 'at risk' (priority A) or serious (priority B).
Note clients who are assessed as moderate need (priority C) and low or no need (priority D) do not qualify for social housing and are not placed on the register. You will need to discuss other housing options [no link find out why] with these clients as they may qualify for other housing assistance.
The priority ratings for the assessment of housing need as determined by the Social Allocation System (SAS) are:
Risk rating
Short description
Detailed description
A
At risk
The well-being of the household is being severely affected (or is seriously at risk) and there is an immediate need for action due to the unsuitability and/or adequacy of their current housing. Further, the household is unable to access and/or sustain suitable, adequate and affordable alternative housing.
B
Serious housing need
The well-being of the household has been affected in a significant and persistent way due to the unsuitability and/or inadequacy of their current housing. The household is highly unlikely to be able to access and/or sustain suitable, adequate and affordable alternative housing
C
Moderate need
The household is disadvantaged and this is likely to be compounded over time due to the unsuitability and/or inadequacy of their current housing. The household can access and sustain alternative housing with assistance.
D
Low or no need
Households experiencing low housing need for which there are other viable housing options. The household can access and sustain alternative housing without assistance.
The priority rating depends on the level of risk that is calculated under each category.

chunks.title: Housing provider requests needs (requirements) assessment — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Housing provider requests needs (requirements) assessment
When a social housing provider needs to transfer a tenant and a change in housing requirements is identified, the housing provider may request MSD complete a housing needs assessment (for example, the client may require an extra bedroom).
Note the housing requirements assessment is not a full assessment of eligibility. It is a review limited to a current social housing tenant's housing requirements (including bedroom allocation) based on the number of household members and any modifications that are required.
The outcome of this review will give the housing provider confirmation of the client's housing needs and they will take this information into account when allocating a property to the client.
## Review of decision
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have received formal notification of the outcome of the review of their housing needs (property requirements), and they do not agree with it.
For example, when the client has asked to move to a property with more bedrooms and we have determined there is no change in the clients housing needs.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Housing provider requires a tenant to transfer — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Housing provider requires a tenant to transfer
Once a client has been allocated a property, a social housing provider may:
- review a client's requirements to be or continue to be allocated, or rent a particular house
and
- require a client to transfer to a different house belonging to that provider if they consider the transfer is necessary or desirable for any reason and the other housing is appropriate for the tenant's housing needs
This process can be completed by the social housing provider without any review of the client's housing needs by MSD.
## Kāinga Ora moves tenants for business reasons
Currently Kāinga Ora only requires a tenant to transfer for business reasons. As a result of their activities as a landlord or for other business reasons Kāinga Ora may identify that a property needs to be vacated. These reasons may include (but are not limited to) when the property:
- is an earthquake risk
- lease is expiring
- is being re-developed
- can be better utilised
- is going to be sold
Generally Kāinga Ora will transfer the client and their household to another equivalent property. For example, a household currently living in a 3 bedroom property that has been identified as an earthquake risk will be transferred to another 3 bedroom property.
## Review of clients housing needs (requirements)
The housing provider may ask MSD to complete an assessment of housing needs.
For more information see:
## Income Related Rent
When a housing provider requires a tenant to transfer, the client's calculated rate of Income Related Rent remains the same, unless:
- the client has a change of circumstances that changes the rate or
- an annual review of the Income Related Rent is completed or
- the rate of Income Related Rent is higher than the market rent rate

chunks.title: In emergency housing for 12 continuous weeks or more — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## In emergency housing for 12 continuous weeks or more
To qualify for the emergency housing fast-track, the client must be staying in emergency housing for at least 12 continuous weeks at the time of their fast-track assessment.
## Breaks of up to 28 days
The client can leave emergency housing for breaks of up to 28 days without it affecting their 12-week count.
There is no limit to the number of breaks a client can take from emergency housing as long as each break is for 28 days or less.
A break longer than 28 days will reset the client's 12-week count in emergency housing. This means that once the client has left emergency housing for a break of 29 days or more, they will no longer qualify for the fast-track.
Example
Tyson and his 2 dependent children stayed in contracted emergency housing for 8 weeks. They moved out of contracted emergency housing to stay with Tyson's relatives for 21 days over Christmas.
Tyson and his children returned to contracted emergency housing as they were no longer able to stay with Tyson's relatives and had no other options.
Tyson's break from contracted emergency housing was less than 28 days.
Tyson and his children were in emergency housing for another 4 weeks. He meets the 12 week continuous qualification to be added to the emergency housing fast-track (8 weeks initial stay + further 4 weeks).
The break of 21 days does not affect his 12-week count
## Breaks longer than 28 days - exceptional circumstances
If the client left emergency housing for more than 28 days because of exceptional circumstances, MSD may still find the client qualifies for the emergency housing fast-track.
## Break due to emergency housing non-entitlement period
If a client on the emergency housing fast track gets an emergency housing non-entitlement period, they must be removed from the emergency housing fast track for their whole 13-week non-entitlement period. This includes any period where the client has their non-entitlement period paused under limited circumstances.
If the client returns to emergency housing after their 13-week non-entitlement period ends, they will need to be in emergency housing for another 12 weeks or more before they can qualify for the emergency housing fast track again.

chunks.title: Including other person or household unit as a signatory to the tenancy agreement — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Including other person or household unit as a signatory to the tenancy agreement
When an existing tenant requests that another person or household unit be included as a signatory to the tenancy agreement the person or household joining must meet the following qualifications to be allocated social housing:
- age
- residence and
- be earning income at or under the specified limits and
- have assets under the specified limits
In addition, the person or household unit must establish that they qualify to be allocated social housing in their own right (that is they have a need for social housing).
## Assess housing need for person or household unit
When a person or household unit requests to join an existing tenancy a full assessment of the need for social housing must be completed and that person or household must meet the qualifications for social housing.
Note that a full assessment of the need for social housing is not required when a partner requests to be included in the tenancy agreement.
MSD must notify the social housing provider of the outcome of this assessment.
## Future review of eligibility for social housing will be joint
Any future review of the joint tenant's eligibility for social housing will be a joint assessment (that is an assessment of their housing need is undertaken as one household). The combined circumstances of joint tenants may mean that they move into the group identified for Tenancy Review, in particular their combined household income may result in an Income Related Rent equal or near to market rent.
## Reviews of decision
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have received formal notification of (and do not agree with) the outcome of the eligibility review and/or review of their housing needs.

chunks.title: Including partner in tenancy agreement — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Including partner in tenancy agreement
A social housing provider will provide a notice of conditional agreement to MSD when an existing tenant requests that their partner is included in the tenancy agreement.
It needs to be assessed whether the person is eligible for social housing.
## Assessment of eligibility for partners joining a tenancy
To be eligible for social housing and to become a signatory to the tenancy, the person joining the tenancy must meet the following qualifications:
- age
- residence
- be earning income at or under the specified limit and
- have assets under the specified limit
If they do not meet these qualifications, they are not eligible to be allocated social housing and cannot become a signatory to the tenancy agreement. However, they would be considered an applicable person and their income included for the purposes of calculating an Income Related Rent.
The person's need for social housing does not need to be assessed if they are the tenant's partner.
## Assessment of needs (requirements) may be required
If the housing provider has requested an assessment of the persons or households housing needs (requirements), or the person advises that there has been a change, the households new housing requirements may need to be confirmed.
For example, if the partner has a disability they may need a ramp or rails.
Note there are some circumstances when a request to review a client's housing needs (requirements) can be declined if there is reason to believe these have not significantly changed.
When an assessment has been undertaken, MSD must notify the social housing provider of the outcome of this assessment.
## Review of decision
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have had formal notification of (and do not agree with) the outcome of the eligibility review and/or review of their housing needs.

chunks.title: Income limits — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Income limits
Generally to qualify for social housing a client must be earning at or under the income limit for their household type. Assessable income is used to determine eligibility for social housing.
Household type and income limits are:
Client situation
Income limit (net)
Weekly income limit
Single client without a partner, and no dependent children
1.5 x the net weekly living alone rate of New Zealand Superannuation ($555.15 as at 1 April 2026)
$832.72 net
Any other client
1.5 x the net weekly married rate of New Zealand Superannuation ($854.08 as at 1 April 2026)
$1,281.12 net
Note the assessable income details recorded during the assessment of social housing are also used to give an indication of the weekly rate of Income Related Rent.
From 1 July 2023, most types of Child Support are included as assessable income.
For more information see:
- Child Support is assessable income from 1 July 2023

chunks.title: Introduction — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The ability to access suitable, adequate, affordable and sustainable housing can negatively impact on a client's ability to maintain an adequate lifestyle and to meet the basic needs of the household members.
The MSD (the Ministry) is responsible for:
- confirming a client's eligibility for social housing
- assessing their need for social housing
- determining their priority ranking for social housing and
- determining their housing needs (housing requirements)
MSD administers social housing and Income Related Rent.
A client does not have to be getting a benefit to qualify for social housing or Income Related Rent.
When the client is assessed as needing social housing assistance they are referred to a social housing provider, either Kāinga Ora or a Community Housing Provider.
## The Social Allocation System
Clients who are determined at risk (priority A) or in serious housing need (priority B) are eligible for social housing. Housing need is determined as part of the Social Allocation System (SAS).
The Social Allocation System:
- is the assessment tool used to process applications for social housing and
- makes sure social housing is available only to those in the highest need who do not have alternative housing options

chunks.title: Iwi social services, cultural social services and family support services — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Iwi social services, cultural social services and family support services
For fast-track into social housing, a specified child or young person in custody of Oranga Tamariki may be in the care of the following Iwi social services, cultural social services or child and family support services:
- Open Home Foundation
- Barnardos
- Dingwall Trust

chunks.title: Lack of cash resources for bond, rent and furniture — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Lack of cash resources for bond, rent and furniture
A lack of cash resources for bond, rent and furniture can affect a client's ability to access alternative housing.
An assessment of the client's eligibility for Housing Support Product, Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment should be undertaken completed before a rating is given for this criterion.
When assessing a client's eligibility for Housing Support Products, you should consider whether, in the last 52 weeks, the client has received, in the last 52 weeks, more than 2 grants of both of:
- Bond Grants and/or Accommodation Security Costs Cover Grant and/or
- Rent in Advance Grants and/or Accommodation Costs in Advance Grants or
- Rent Arrears Grant and/or Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant or
- Tenancy Costs Cover. Grant in the last 52 weeks
Advance Payments of Benefit and Recoverable Assistance Payments cannot be used for costs that Housing Support Products cover, except for bond top-ups and moving relocatable homes (e.g. cabins, caravans and mobile homes).
For more information see:
- Clients who cannot get a Bond Grant
- Types of moving costs
When assessing the amount of available assistance a client may have to pay for furniture, MSD should:
- consider the total balance of Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment the client has available and
- disregard any other debts the client has
Example
Limit of Advance Payment of Benefit, or Recoverable Assistance Payment (for non-beneficiary)based on Supported Living Payment rate for sole parent
$581.96 net per week x 6 (at 1 April 2026)
$3,491.76
Less Advance Payment of Benefit / Recoverable Assistance Payment debt balance
$950.00
Advance Payment of Benefit / Recoverable Assistance Payment available
$2,541.76
A client can be considered to have a lack of cash resources for bond, rent and furniture if they:
- do not have any appliances or furniture
- have a bad credit history and therefore cannot access store credit
- have a high level of personal debt meaning they do not have any income left after paying debt each week
- have no money for rent in advance or bond or
- have reached their maximum limit for Housing Support Products left to meet their need (for bond or rent) and do not have exceptional circumstances to receive additional payments
- have no Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment provision left to meet their need (for furniture)

chunks.title: Limited data available on lower quartile rent — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Limited data available on lower quartile rent
When deciding the lower quartile rent information, there may be situations where there are limited accommodation options for the location that the client is going to live. In these situations, an alternative property type must be selected from the data that fits the client's bedroom needs in their required location.
For example:
- in Auckland city there may not be any flats and in these cases 'apartment' should be used
- it is unlikely that houses will be available in central city areas and in these cases an apartment with the same number of bedrooms the household needs should be used
For more information see:
- Definition of lower quartile private rent

chunks.title: Location of accommodation — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Location of accommodation
The area used in calculating the affordability risk rating will in most cases, be the area where the client currently lives.
For example, the children may be settled in schools and the client has established local supports networks.
When a client has a need to relocate elsewhere and a proven need to relocate exists, that area will be used in the calculation.

chunks.title: Material change in circumstance — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Material change in circumstance
A material change in circumstance is something important that has changed in the client's need for social housing since the time they declined the social housing property. This may include (but is not limited to):
- child changes - addition or removal of children from the family unit
- health and disability changes - changes to the health or disability of the person or people included in the offer
- change in income - such as ending employment or no longer getting a child support

chunks.title: New Zealand Refugee Quota Programme — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Refugee Quota Programme
Some refugees come to New Zealand under the New Zealand Quota Refugee Programme. They are generally known as quota refugees.
Refugees, including quota refugees, do not have to meet the 2 years continuous residence criteria to qualify for social housing on residency grounds.

chunks.title: No need established to be an additional occupant — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## No need established to be an additional occupant
If there is no ongoing need established for a person to be an additional occupant they will not be considered when assessing housing needs (including allocating bedrooms) during the housing assessment process. This might include:
- a child aged 18 years or older who is working full-time or getting a benefit and is no longer a dependent child or
- a boarder who has lived with the family to bring in extra money but has no real need to be considered part of the household
Note there may be reasons when household members may become a signatory to the tenancy agreement. If so, they are included as household members in the assessment of housing need and their income (including any income from assessable assets) is used in the assessment of Income Related Rent. An assessment of the need for them to be housed together will also need to be completed.

chunks.title: Obligations of a signatory — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Obligations of a signatory
In signing the tenancy agreement as a joint tenant, the person must understand their obligations.
These obligations include that both signatories to the tenancy agreement will be:
- responsible for the tenancy
- liable for any debt incurred
- liable for any damage caused (even if the other joint tenant or third party caused the damage)
- subject to review of their ongoing eligibility for social housing
It is the responsibility of the social housing provider to discuss these obligations with the signatories to the tenancy agreement.

chunks.title: Overall rating for adequacy — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Overall rating for adequacy
The overall risk-rating for adequacy will be taken from the highest score across all of the criteria:
- the client is 'not living in any accommodation' or is living in emergency housing for the time being
- living in accommodation that is not fit for human habitation or is in a serious state of disrepair that presents a severe and significant health and safety risk to the occupants (eg no structural integrity or the condition of the facilities are poor or non-existent)
- whether the client is living in premises that are overcrowded
- whether the client has no, or limited, security of tenure

chunks.title: Overall risk rating for suitability — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Overall risk rating for suitability
The overall rating for suitability will be taken from the highest score across all of the criteria:
- medical, disability or personal issues that requires the household to move from their current accommodation
- family violence or other tension (either within the household or in the neighbourhood), or other violence relating to the client's current living situation that requires them to move from their current accommodation

chunks.title: Overcrowding of current accommodation — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Overcrowding of current accommodation
Overcrowding is measured by the number of bedrooms a client's household has compared to how many bedrooms the household needs.
The guidelines for identifying overcrowding are:
- there should be no more than 2 persons per bedroom
- children 10 years of age or older of the opposite sex should not share a bedroom
- children under 18 years of age and the same sex can reasonably share a bedroom
- single adults, couples and parents should have a separate bedroom
Note adults are considered to be someone aged 18 years or over, or if aged 16 or 17 years are (or have been) married or in a civil union.
## Overcrowding not assessed for clients 'not living in any accommodation' or in emergency housing
You do not need to assess overcrowding for clients who are 'not living in any accommodation' or who are living in emergency housing for the time being. These clients have already been assessed as 'at risk' (4) adequacy.
## Client is illegally sub-letting
If clients are illegally sub-letting, adequacy must be assessed on the number of bedrooms they have access to in the property. The issue of no rights to the tenancy must be considered under the lack of security of tenure.

chunks.title: People holding a temporary visa who are compelled to remain in New Zealand — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## People holding a temporary visa who are compelled to remain in New Zealand
If a client is in New Zealand on a temporary entry class visa, they generally do not qualify for social housing (even if they have lived in New Zealand for 2 years).
However, they may qualify for social housing if they’re getting an Emergency Benefit. Clients who are getting a main benefit qualify for social housing on residency grounds.
## Client does not qualify for an Emergency Benefit
In some cases, the client may be compelled to remain in New Zealand while they apply for a residence class visa, but the person may not qualify for an Emergency Benefit.
This might be because the client is not considered to be in hardship, for example they have other means of support or cash assets over the threshold to receive Emergency Benefit. In these cases, the client does not qualify for social housing.
If this is identified while they are on the Social Housing Register waiting to be matched and placed into a property, the client will be removed from the register.

chunks.title: Person or household wishes to join-in an existing tenancy — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Person or household wishes to join-in an existing tenancy
A join-in is when an existing tenant requests that another person or household unit be added to their tenancy agreement, that is, become a signatory to the tenancy agreement.
A join-in may involve new occupants to the tenancy or an existing household member(s) requesting to be added to the agreement.
## Decision to add someone to the tenancy agreement sits with the social housing provider
An existing tenant must first advise their social housing provider if they want to include another person or household unit in the tenancy agreement. The decision to add a person to a tenancy agreement sits with the social housing provider.
Note a social housing provider would not agree to a join-in when the occupancy limit stated in the tenancy agreement would be breached.
If an existing tenant wishes to include another person or household unit and they would need additional bedrooms:
- a joint assessment to be allocated other social housing (a request for a transfer) would be required
or
- the person or household wanting to join the tenancy could apply and be assessed for their own social housing property
For more information see:
- Social housing provider considerations when adding signatory to tenancy agreement
## Occupants joining the household do not have to become signatories
Occupants joining the household do not have to become signatories to the tenancy agreement.
However, tenants are required to advise us of any changes that may affect their calculated rate of Income Related Rent. For example:
- a tenant who has a partner move in with them must advise of their change in circumstances as the partner's income will be taken into account in calculating Income Related Rent as an applicable person
- a tenant who has someone move in with them as a caregiver could be considered as an additional occupant and depending on whether they are paying a contribution it may affect their Income Related Rent.
Note only the signatories to the tenancy agreement have rights to the tenancy. Partners and additional occupants do not have these rights.
## Must be eligible for social housing
A person or household must be eligible for social housing to be included as a signatory to the tenancy agreement.
MSD will complete the assessment of eligibility.

chunks.title: Property type required for identifying lower quartile rent — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Property type required for identifying lower quartile rent
The lower quartile private rent can be found at Tenancy Services. The type of property required will depend on the household type and their property requirements. The number of bedrooms required is determined by the overcrowding calculation under the suitability criteria. When deciding the most appropriate lower quartile rent, the following property types should be used.
Household type and property required Property type needed Households with dependent children house Elderly (aged over 65 years) house Households with members who have a disability house All other clients flat (if no flat available, use apartment)

Note an apartment is considered to be a residential dwelling, generally in a building greater than three stories high in a commercial residential area.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Qualifications — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To qualify for social housing a client must:
- be aged 16 years or over
- meet the residence requirements
- meet an income and asset test and
- be at risk or in serious housing need (as assessed through the Social Allocation System (SAS))
## Household composition and bedroom allocation
Details of a client's household composition, that is, the number of people needing to be housed, is also required as this determines the number of bedrooms allocated to them in a property.

chunks.title: Qualifying medical conditions for rheumatic fever — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Qualifying medical conditions for rheumatic fever
The qualifying medical conditions for the fast-track rheumatic fever provision are:
- lower respiratory tract infections pneumoniaacute bronchiolitisunspecified lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) and bronchitisbronchiectasis
- pneumonia
- acute bronchiolitis
- unspecified lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) and bronchitis
- bronchiectasis
- meningitis meningococcal diseasebacterial meningitis (including pneumococcal, streptococcal, other)viral meningitismeningitis unspecified
- meningococcal disease
- bacterial meningitis (including pneumococcal, streptococcal, other)
- viral meningitis
- meningitis unspecified
- invasive and post-streptococcal diseases rheumatic feveracute nephritic syndromesepticaemia from group A streptococcus (GAS)
- rheumatic fever
- acute nephritic syndrome
- septicaemia from group A streptococcus (GAS)
## Asthma
Asthma may be a secondary condition to one of the qualifying medical conditions but having asthma alone would not meet the criteria to be fast-tracked under the rheumatic fever provision.
## A child 0 - 14 years must have been hospitalised
A child aged 0 - 14 years must have been hospitalised with a qualifying medical condition to qualify for the rheumatic fever fast-track provision or be a child or young person who is getting treatment because of a previous episode of rheumatic fever.

chunks.title: Reapplying for social housing within 13 weeks of declining a property — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Reapplying for social housing within 13 weeks of declining a property
After being removed from the register, if the client reapplies for social housing within the next 13 weeks, the decline or failure to accept a property offer may affect their eligibility for social housing.
Their decision to decline or fail to accept the property offer by not responding will be considered as a material factor when assessing whether they have a serious or severe housing need.
If they reapply within 13 weeks and their situation has changed, any material change in circumstances will also be considered.
## Access to other financial assistance
A client who is immediately removed from the register for declining (or failing to accept) a property without a good and sufficient reason is still able to access other financial assistance such as extra help and Housing Support Products available to help people access housing in the private market (when they meet the eligibility criteria for assistance).

chunks.title: Reasonable effort to find alternative housing — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Reasonable effort to find alternative housing
A client must have made a reasonable effort to find suitable alternative housing.
This may be through:
- registering and applying for houses through property agencies
- applying for houses advertised in newspapers
- applying for houses advertised on Trade Me
There is no specific number of houses a client must have applied for to meet this criteria as it will depend on the client's circumstances and the rental market in the area.

chunks.title: Release from a joint tenancy agreement — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Release from a joint tenancy agreement
Sometimes a client will contact their social housing provider and advise that they no longer wish to be part of a joint tenancy agreement (but still remain in the property) or leave the property all together.
A client has the right to be removed from a tenancy agreement but the decision to do this should be made by the social housing provider and the tenants jointly.
## One tenant requests a transfer
One client or household unit may request a transfer from a joint tenancy.
The client or household unit will need to apply for an assessment to be allocated other social housing.
If they are qualify, they will be placed on the register.
For more information see:
- Transfers
## No review of eligibility or housing needs required
The review of remaining signatories' eligibility for social housing and their housing needs (requirements) is not required.
## The remaining tenant must advise of change in circumstances
The remaining tenant must advise us of any change in circumstances that might affect their Income Related Rent.
This would include when a joint tenant leaves the tenancy agreement and is either remaining in the property as an additional occupant or leaves the property all together.
The remaining tenant's calculated rate of Income Related Rent will need to be reviewed.

chunks.title: Resided continuously in New Zealand for at least 2 years at any one time since becoming a resident — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Resided continuously in New Zealand for at least 2 years at any one time since becoming a resident
To qualify for social housing clients with a residence class visa must hold a valid resident or permanent resident visa under the Immigration Act 2009. They must also have resided continuously in New Zealand for a period of at least 2 years at any one time after they got their visa.
Continuous residence is defined as 185 days each year. The period of residency in New Zealand must be met by each residence class visa holder who is applying for social housing with the intention of being a signatory to the tenancy agreement.
## Exceptions
The residence status and period of residency in New Zealand does not have to be met by:
- the partner of a person who is applying for social housing, if the partner is not intending to be a signatory to the tenancy agreement
- a dependent child
- an additional occupant
- refugees and protected persons
- those with a Christchurch Response Visa
- people getting Christchurch Mosques Attack payments or
- people getting payments under the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme
New Zealand citizens must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand but do not have to have resided in New Zealand continuously for at least 2 years at any one time.

chunks.title: Residence — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Residence
To qualify for social housing the client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and:
- be a New Zealand citizen or
- hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 and have resided continuously in New Zealand for a period of at least 2 years at any one time after becoming a resident or
- be recognised as a refugee or a protected person in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- hold a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 that is a Christchurch Response Visa or
- qualify for and be getting payments under the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme (for people who have come to New Zealand on a temporary entry class visa with intention of applying for a residence visa under the spouse or de facto partner policy but the relationship has ended due to family violence and they are now living apart from their partner and have lost all financial support) or
- qualify for and be getting a main benefit
## Some groups do not have to have been in New Zealand 2 years continuously
The following groups do not have to meet the 2 year continuous residence in New Zealand criteria to qualify for social housing.
- people recognised as refugees or protected persons under the Immigration Act 2009
- people with a Christchurch Response Visa
- people getting the Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme
## Residence status of other people in the household
The resident status and period of residency in New Zealand does not have to be met by:
- the partner of the person applying for social housing if the partner is not intending to be a signatory to the tenancy agreement
- a dependent child
- an additional occupant
## Does not qualify on residence grounds
Clients who are in New Zealand because they hold a temporary entry class visa(for example student visa, visitor visa, work visa) generally do not qualify for social housing.
However, if they qualify for, and get, an Emergency Benefit or Emergency Maintenance Allowance, they may qualify for social housing on residence grounds (if they are also ordinarily resident in New Zealand).

chunks.title: Reviews and Appeals for fast-track — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Reviews and Appeals for fast-track
An applicant has the right to ask MSD for a review if they disagree with a decision relating to the assessment of their eligibility for social housing.
However, there is no right to appeal a decision relating to the application of fast-track under the Social Security Act 2018 or the Public and Community Housing Management Act 1992.
## When a client does not agree
When a client disagrees with a decision regarding fast-track there is no right of review to a Benefits Review Committee or the Social Security Appeal Authority.
However, when a client does not agree with a fast-track decision, this decision should be reconsidered.
The reconsideration should be based on whether an informed decision was made and should consider the following:
- reasons for the original fast-track decision
- relevant policy and fast-track criteria
- the information provided at the time
- any new information on hand and
- the reason the client disagrees with the decision
Note if the client does not agree with the fast-track decision following it being reconsidered, there are no rights to appeal the decision.
## Specified child or young person in custody of Oranga Tamariki or in approved permanent care
If the client disagrees with the information from Oranga Tamariki, an Iwi social service, a cultural social service or a child and family support service, the client should be directed to discuss this information with the agency that provided the information.

chunks.title: Risk rating for accessibility — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Accessibility measures the client's ability to access suitable alternative housing and considers whether the client's ability to access suitable alternative housing is impacted by: - discrimination - lack of cash resources for bond, rent and furniture - availability of alternative housing in the area where the client currently lives or needs to live

chunks.title: The 4 levels of risk rating for accessibility — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: At risk (4) The client is totally unable to access suitable, affordable and adequate accommodation in the private sector because of discrimination, lack of cash resources for bond, rent or furniture, or no suitable private sector housing is available. For example: - funds are not available for bond, rent in advance or necessary furniture - the client or a household member is experiencing severe and persistent discrimination to the extent they are totally unable to access affordable, adequate, suitable and sustainable accommodation in the private sector - the client or household member is experiencing persistent physical violence due to discrimination - suitable private sector is not available where the client currently lives or needs to live Serious housing need (3) The client would have severe difficulty in accessing suitable, affordable and adequate accommodation in the private sector because of discrimination, or because of a lack of cash resources for bond, rent or furniture. For example: - minimal funds are available which could be used for a proportion of start-up costs (for example can pay one week bond only and has no funds for rent in advance, or furniture, and moving costs) - the client or household member is experiencing discrimination to the extent they would have severe difficulty in accessing affordable, adequate, suitable and sustainable accommodation in the private sector - the client or a household member is experiencing discrimination and physical violence has been threatened Moderate need (2) The client would have difficulty in accessing suitable, affordable and adequate accommodation in the private sector because of discrimination, or because of the lack of cash resources for bond, rent or furniture. For example: - funds are earmarked for other essential expenditure but could be used for start-up costs - the client or a household member is experiencing some discrimination and would have some difficulty in accessing affordable, adequate, suitable and sustainable accommodation in the private sector - the client or household member is experiencing moderate discrimination but is not concerned for their own or the household's health or safety Low or no need (1) There are no (or minimal) accessibility issues. Suitable alternative housing is available. For example: - funds are available for bond, rent and furniture - there is no or very little discrimination and the client could access and sustain their own housing solution - suitable private sector housing is available where the client currently lives or needs to live

chunks.title: Risk rating for affordability — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Risk rating for affordability
The assessment of affordability measures the client's ability to afford (with any financial assistance to which they may be entitled) suitable alternative housing.
## There are four levels of risk rating for affordability
At risk (4)
Residual income when ratio is 35% or less
Serious housing need (3)
Residual income when ratio is between 36% and 55%
Moderate need (2)
Residual income when ratio is between 56% and 69%
Low or no need (1)
Residual income when ratio is 70% or greater

chunks.title: Risk rating for clients 'not living in any accommodation' (including emergency housing or transitional housing) — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: There are only 2 outcomes from the assessment of whether the client is 'not living in any accommodation' or is staying in emergency housing or transitional housing for the time being.
