These are: - at risk (4), or - low or no need (1) Note clients getting an Emergency Housing Grant or who are being housed by a contracted emergency housing or transitional housing provider are at risk and are therefore given a rating of 4. At risk (4) Low or no need (1) A client is at risk if they cannot access adequate housing and are: - not living in any accommodation, examples include: homeless e.g. living in a car, tent, homeless shelter, or public placeliving in accommodation that was only intended to be used as temporary accommodation, e.g. commercial accommodation such as a motel, a hotel, cabins in a caravan park, a marae, a mobile home or caravansquatting in a property - homeless e.g. living in a car, tent, homeless shelter, or public place - living in accommodation that was only intended to be used as temporary accommodation, e.g. commercial accommodation such as a motel, a hotel, cabins in a caravan park, a marae, a mobile home or caravan - squatting in a property - staying in emergency housing or transitional housing for the time being, examples include: getting an Emergency Housing Grantstaying in transitional housing funded by Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - short-term housing where clients have support services providedstaying in contracted emergency housingrefuges such as those provided by Women's Refuge, Home and Family Society, Emergency Housing Trusts, Iwi and cultural organisations, or church organisations - getting an Emergency Housing Grant - staying in transitional housing funded by Ministry of Housing and Urban Development - short-term housing where clients have support services provided - staying in contracted emergency housingrefuges such as those provided by Women's Refuge, Home and Family Society, Emergency Housing Trusts, Iwi and cultural organisations, or church organisations A client is considered to be living in accommodation' and not staying in emergency housing if they are: - boarding - living in a home they and/or their partner owns - living in a private rental - living in social housing - temporarily sharing - staying with friends or family - living in a tent because they are travelling around New Zealand on a holiday - living in a boarding house

chunks.title: Risk rating for clients 'not living in any accommodation' (including emergency housing or transitional housing) — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: - illegally sub-letting a property (how soon the client needs to leave this property is assessed under security of tenure) - living in a garage (the condition of the garage and its facilities are part of the consideration of the adequacy of the current accommodation) - due to leave prison or hospital (how soon the client needs to leave is assessed under security of tenure) - in respite care (how soon the client needs to leave this housing is assessed under security of tenure) - in rehabilitation (how soon the client needs to leave this housing is assessed under security of tenure)

chunks.title: Risk rating for condition of facilities — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Risk rating for condition of facilities
There are only 2 outcomes from the assessment of the condition of the facilities in the client's current house.
Note this does not apply to clients who are assessed as 'not living in any accommodation' or living in emergency housing or transitional housing for the time being. These clients have already been rated as 'at risk' (4) for adequacy.
At risk (4)
Low or no need (1)
When assessing whether the client's house is adequate due to the condition of the facilities in the current house, consider whether the house is:
- fit for habitation or
- in a serious state of disrepair and presents a severe and significant health and safety risk to the client and their family
A house would be considered inadequate if:
- there is no bathroom, toilet or laundry facilities or they are unsafe
- electricity or wiring is unsafe
- there is leaking water or broken pipes or lack of running water in the bathroom, or no shower or bath at all
- there are no cooking or kitchen facilities or they are unsafe
- there is no heating or ventilation (this doesn't have to be installed but there needs to be power points to be able to install these)
- there is only one means of emergency exit and no approved fire scheme in place (multi-blocks only)
A house is considered adequate based on the condition of the facilities in the current house where there may be deficiencies, but these have not been identified as severe or a significant health and safety risk to the client and their family.
For example, the current house has:
- the toilet in the bathroom
- the laundry in the kitchen
- fixtures and fittings that are old but are workable
- doors that stick in extreme temperatures

chunks.title: Risk rating for family violence, tension or other violence — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Risk rating for family violence, tension or other violence
A client may have issues relating to family violence, other tension (either within the household or in the neighbourhood), or other violence relating to the client's current living situation that requires them to move from their current accommodation.
At risk (4)
Need to move from current living situation due to family violence:
- presence of severe persistent family violence or harassment
- household required to move due to potential threat of violence from within the household
- household required to move due to potential threat of violence from outside of the household (eg ex-partner has relocated into the neighbourhood and presents a potential threat to the household)
Need to move from current living situation due to tension, or other violence:
- tension or difficulties exist within the household and immediate relocation is required in order to avoid stress related issues for any household member
- extreme fear of current accommodation or neighbourhood
- current accommodation is unsuitable due to safety and the risk to the client is severe
Serious housing need (3)
Need to move from current living situation due to tension, or other violence:
- tensions or difficulties increasing within the household causing undesirable living environment
- current accommodation is unsuitable due to safety and the risk to the client is serious from someone outside the neighbourhood
- fear of current accommodation
Moderate need (2)
Need to move from current living situation due to tension, or other violence:
- tensions or difficulties within the household causing moderate undesirable living environment
- neighbourhood tension, for example racial tension
- current accommodation is unsuitable due to safety and the risk to the client is moderate
- neighbourhood or racial tension
Low or no need (1)
Need to move from current living situation due to tension, or other violence:
- tension or difficulties within the household exist but no ill effects are being experienced by household member

chunks.title: Risk rating for financial management — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: In determining the risk rating for financial management you are assessing whether the client is having financial difficulties that impact on their ability to sustain suitable alternative housing.

chunks.title: There are four levels of risk rating for financial management — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: At risk (4) The client has a history of, or is experiencing, severe and persistent problems accessing and sustaining alternative housing and requires immediate assistance due to:severe addiction problems (drug, alcohol, gambling) resulting in all or the majority of their income supporting their addictioncomplete inability to budget and manage debt resulting in severe financial issues. For example, repossession of property, court or legal action and continually increasing debt, hire purchase, loansrent arrears are in excess of two months and are mounting on a daily basis causing severe and persistent problems Serious housing need (3) The client has a history of, or is experiencing significant and persistent problems accessing and sustaining alternative housing due to:serious addiction problems resulting in a major portion of income supporting addictionserious inability to budget and manage debt resulting in income being used to pay debt instead of providing for household, for example, inadequate nutrition, clothing, securityrent arrears with no ability to repay debt Moderate need (2) The client is experiencing moderate problems accessing and sustaining alternative housing due to:moderate addiction problem that consumes all discretionary income after minimum commitments met, for example no savingsbudget and debt management are not maintained successfully resulting in a lack of provisions for household Low or no need (1) The client is experiencing low level or no problems accessing and sustaining alternative housing:financial difficulties do not exist or low level inconvenience is sometimes experiencedno evidence of budget or debt management inability At risk (4) The client has a history of, or is experiencing, severe and persistent problems accessing and sustaining alternative housing and requires immediate assistance due to: - severe addiction problems (drug, alcohol, gambling) resulting in all or the majority of their income supporting their addiction - complete inability to budget and manage debt resulting in severe financial issues. For example, repossession of property, court or legal action and continually increasing debt, hire purchase, loans - rent arrears are in excess of two months and are mounting on a daily basis causing severe and persistent problems Serious housing need (3) The client has a history of, or is experiencing significant and persistent problems accessing and sustaining alternative housing due to: - serious addiction problems resulting in a major portion of income supporting addiction - serious inability to budget and manage debt resulting in income being used to pay debt instead of providing for household, for example, inadequate nutrition, clothing, security - rent arrears with no ability to repay debt

chunks.title: There are four levels of risk rating for financial management — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Moderate need (2) The client is experiencing moderate problems accessing and sustaining alternative housing due to: - moderate addiction problem that consumes all discretionary income after minimum commitments met, for example no savings - budget and debt management are not maintained successfully resulting in a lack of provisions for household Low or no need (1) The client is experiencing low level or no problems accessing and sustaining alternative housing: - financial difficulties do not exist or low level inconvenience is sometimes experienced - no evidence of budget or debt management inability Note the assessment is of the difficulties the client has in managing their finances. It is not expected that the client addresses their financial issue and therefore reduce their housing risk at this stage of the process. For more information see: - Client has difficulty managing their finances - Sustainability of alternative housing

chunks.title: Risk rating for lack of security of tenure — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Risk rating for lack of security of tenure
Security of tenure of current accommodation considers how many days before the client must leave their current accommodation. That is, what notice period (whether formal or informal) they have been given?
Note this does not apply to clients who have been assessed as 'not living in any accommodation', or being in emergency housing for the time being. These clients have already been assessed as 'at risk' (4) for adequacy.
## There are 4 levels of risk rating for security of tenure
At risk (4)
Client needs to move within 7 days or less due to:
- notice to vacate current accommodation
- no permanent accommodation and staying as a 'temporary resident' in a permanent private dwelling where they or their families personal health or safety is at risk
- ready to leave institutional accommodation (eg psychiatric hospital, prison, youth justice)
- in a property that has been illegally sublet to the client
Serious housing need (3)
Client needs to move in 8 to 60 days due to:
- notice to vacate current accommodation
- no permanent accommodation and staying as a 'temporary resident' in a permanent private dwelling where the situation is not sustainable (this is their friends or family have asked them to leave)
- ready to leave institutional accommodation (eg psychiatric hospital, prison, youth justice)
- in a property that has been illegally sublet to the client
Moderate need (2)
Client needs to move in 61 to 90 days due to:
- notice to vacate current accommodation
- no permanent accommodation and staying as a 'temporary resident' in permanent private dwelling where the situation is currently sustainable (that is, the people they are staying with haven't asked them to leave)
Low or no need (1)
Client has no specific time to move:
- notice to vacate with no time limit specified
- no requirement to move from current accommodation
## Temporary resident in a private dwelling
A temporary resident in a permanent private dwelling is a person staying in a house, flat, or apartment which may be owned or rented by another person.
Someone is a temporary resident when the:
- expectation is that the living situation will not be long-term and
- the length of stay is ultimately controlled by those who live in the house or flat permanently

chunks.title: Risk rating for medical or disability needs — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: A client may have issues relating to medical or disability needs that require them to move from their current accommodation.

chunks.title: There are 4 levels of risk rating for medical or disability needs — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: At risk (4) At risk due to medical or disability needs includes: - current accommodation is unsuitable due to health and disability, the risk to the client is severe - household member is terminally ill and relocation is required within 7 days or less to enable household members to be together - immediate need to relocate to ensure client can access critical medical care - hospitalisation as a result of a recognised communicable disease, for example, whooping cough, tuberculosis (TB), meningitis, measles, where there is a causal link to the current house - client now has a guide dog and current accommodation is unsuitable for animals Serious housing need (3) Serious housing need due to medical or disability needs includes: - current accommodation is unsuitable due to health or disability and the risk to the client is serious - household member has been diagnosed (or current condition has worsened) with a special need and is hospitalised and the household must be relocated in order to maintain support - mental or physical health has deteriorated or a household member has suffered a permanent disability and a different type of housing is required - current accommodation is no longer suitable due to acute medical condition or worsening of current condition resulting in mobility or access difficulties. For example, household member recently confined to a wheelchair, and current accommodation is two-story, has outside laundry or toilet, external steps or steep paths - a household member requires a separate bedroom due to a serious medical condition - current accommodation is isolated causing difficulties in accessing essential services. For example, unable to get to shops, transport and medical issues (such as depression, anxiety) Moderate need (2) Moderate need due to medical or disability needs includes: - current accommodation is unsuitable due to health or disability and the risk to the client is moderate - household member has been diagnosed (or current condition has worsened) with a special need requiring the household to relocate closer to support services - current accommodation is unsuitable due to a change in living arrangements, for example client may now have another person living with them providing physical or emotional support and therefore another bedroom is required - current accommodation is unsuitable due to change in circumstances. For example, elderly or disabled household member has moved in and cannot access upstairs bedrooms and is sleeping in living areas - current accommodation is isolated and relocation is desirable but no medical or personal issues present Low or no need (1) Low or no need due to medical or disability includes:

chunks.title: There are 4 levels of risk rating for medical or disability needs — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: - household member requires specific medical attention or special support network, but the household can maintain current lifestyle, but relocation would increase convenience - no medical issues present

chunks.title: Risk rating for overcrowding — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Risk rating for overcrowding
Overcrowding is measured by the number of bedrooms a client household has compared to how many bedrooms the household needs.
Note this does not apply to clients who have been assessed as 'not living in any accommodation' or being in emergency housing for the time being. These clients have already been assessed as 'at risk' (4) for adequacy.
## There are 4 levels of risk rating for overcrowding
At risk (4)
The number of bedrooms available for the permanent and eligible household members to be housed is less than the required number of bedrooms by a margin of three or more.
Examples include:
- client is granted 'day to day' care of children creating severe overcrowding
- expected new additions to the household through birth or adoption
- circumstances mean that the family member and their family are required to move into an existing home
Serious housing need (3)
The number of bedrooms available for the permanent and eligible household members to be housed is less than the required number of bedrooms by a margin of two.
Examples include:
- client is granted 'day to day' care of children creating overcrowding
- expected new additions to the household through birth or adoption
- circumstances mean that the family member and their family are required to move into an existing home
Moderate need (2)
The number of bedrooms available for the permanent and eligible household members to be housed is less than the required number of bedrooms by a margin of one.
Examples include:
- client is granted 'day to day' care of children creating overcrowding
- expected new additions to the household through birth or adoption
- circumstances mean that the family member and their family are required to move into an existing home
Low or no need (1)
The current accommodation is not overcrowded. The number of bedrooms available for the permanent and eligible household members is equal to or greater than the number of bedrooms.
For example:
- client has 'day to day' care of child(ren) in the weekends who have no allocated bedroom but there are no overcrowding issues

chunks.title: Risk rating for personal needs — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: A client may have issues relating to personal needs that require them to move from their current accommodation.

chunks.title: There are 4 levels of risk rating for personal needs — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: At risk (4) At risk due to personal needs includes: - employment opportunity exists and the client needs to relocate to commence confirmed employment with start date within 7 days. They can't afford to stay in motels and have no friends and family to stay with - unexpected unemployment with no savings or redundancy payment and cannot meet current rental which is in arrears - primary income earner has left household or has become disabled and remaining income is inadequate to meet current housing cost - current accommodation is culturally inappropriate causing severe stress to the household and immediate relocation is necessary - loss of vital support network and no means to travel to an alternative - the client or a household member is not able to access any funding to modify a private rental property - current housing costs have increased and are now unaffordable, causing severe and persistent problems Serious housing need (3) Serious housing need due to personal needs includes: - employment opportunity exists and client urgently needs to relocate in order to accept job offer. They can't afford motels and have no friends or family to stay with - training opportunity exists in another location with the promise of guaranteed employment on completion of training, and training is not available in current location - unexpected unemployment with minimal savings which will be required to pay for goods and other necessities - primary income earner has left household or has become disabled and remaining income is inadequate to maintain current housing costs but is sustainable for a period of up to 60 days - current accommodation has become culturally inappropriate causing significant and persistent stress to the household, and requiring relocation within 60 days - loss of vital support network and no means of travel to an alternative Moderate need (2) Moderate need due to personal needs includes: - current accommodation is now unsuitable as dependent children, or other occupants, or household members have moved out, and the house or section size is too big - client can no longer maintain the section and garden - fencing has become unsuitable for the safety of children, due to children growing older and needing a safe playing area - car parking remote from accommodation and client has small children or moderate disability - accommodation is now unsuitable due to change in neighbourhood, for example industrial redevelopment - accommodation has lack of storage space, for example bedsit apartment - need to relocate to enhance employment opportunities - newly unemployed with savings - employer has moved premises resulting in increased travel time and costs - primary income earner has left household or has become disabled and remaining income is adequate to maintain current housing costs but will disadvantage some household members

chunks.title: There are 4 levels of risk rating for personal needs — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: - accommodation has become culturally inappropriate causing moderate discomfort to the household and relocation is desirable - a support network has relocated but the household is able to access an alternative provider - the client or a household member is experiencing some difficulty accessing funding to modify a private rental property - large family wish to reunite but accommodation is too small to allow all members to live together - need to relocate to enhance reunification with children - current rental housing costs have increased having a moderate effect on the household Low or no need (1) Low or no need due to personal needs includes: - no ill effects are being experienced by a household member - no social or personal issues present - change of employment but does not disadvantage household - an income earner has left the household or has become disabled but there is little or no effect - accommodation may potentially become inappropriate, for example, conflicting religious organisation has purchased land next door, and a church or other place of worship is proposed to be built on the site - accommodation is culturally appropriate - current rental and housing costs have no effect on the household

chunks.title: Risk rating for social functioning and history of transience — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: To consider whether the client has sustainability issues, they must have problems accessing suitable housing that is affordable and adequate.

chunks.title: There are four levels of risk rating for difficulty in social functioning, lack of social skills and a history of transience — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: At risk (4) The client or a member of the household has severe and persistent level of social dysfunction requiring a high level of support networks (may or may not be associated with mental illness).The result is an inability to function in alternative housing and state housing is required within seven days due to:the client's lack of communication or social skillsthe client's history of high transience resulting in the frequent need for immediate housing - more than eight required moves over the last two years Serious housing need (3) The client or a member of the household has serious and persistent level of social dysfunction requiring a high level of support networks (may or may not be associated with mental illness).The result is an inability to function in the private sector and social housing is urgently required within 60 days due to:the client's limited communication or social skills but their current accommodation is sustainable for a short periodthe client's history of transience resulting in frequent moves - four to eight required moves over the last two years Moderate need (2) The client or member of the household has a moderate level of social dysfunction requiring some support networks (may or may not be associated with mental illness) and experiences some difficulties functioning in the private sector and performing household tasks.the client is experiencing moderate difficulties with day to day functioning and maintaining the household and relocation to alternative accommodation would alleviate the issuesthe client has the necessary skills to be able to secure and sustain housing but lacks motivation to help themselvesthe client has a history of transience which is affecting their ability to secure and sustain suitable accommodation - one to three moves over the last two years Low or no need (1) There is no social dysfunction limiting the client's or any household member's ability to function in the private sector and perform household tasks.the client has the necessary skills to be able to secure and sustain suitable housingthe client has no (or minor) history of transience - no required moves over the last two years At risk (4) The client or a member of the household has severe and persistent level of social dysfunction requiring a high level of support networks (may or may not be associated with mental illness). The result is an inability to function in alternative housing and state housing is required within seven days due to: - the client's lack of communication or social skills - the client's history of high transience resulting in the frequent need for immediate housing - more than eight required moves over the last two years

chunks.title: There are four levels of risk rating for difficulty in social functioning, lack of social skills and a history of transience — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Serious housing need (3) The client or a member of the household has serious and persistent level of social dysfunction requiring a high level of support networks (may or may not be associated with mental illness). The result is an inability to function in the private sector and social housing is urgently required within 60 days due to: - the client's limited communication or social skills but their current accommodation is sustainable for a short period - the client's history of transience resulting in frequent moves - four to eight required moves over the last two years Moderate need (2) The client or member of the household has a moderate level of social dysfunction requiring some support networks (may or may not be associated with mental illness) and experiences some difficulties functioning in the private sector and performing household tasks. - the client is experiencing moderate difficulties with day to day functioning and maintaining the household and relocation to alternative accommodation would alleviate the issues - the client has the necessary skills to be able to secure and sustain housing but lacks motivation to help themselves - the client has a history of transience which is affecting their ability to secure and sustain suitable accommodation - one to three moves over the last two years Low or no need (1) There is no social dysfunction limiting the client's or any household member's ability to function in the private sector and perform household tasks. - the client has the necessary skills to be able to secure and sustain suitable housing - the client has no (or minor) history of transience - no required moves over the last two years For more information see: - Determining history of transience - Difficulty in social functioning and lack of social skills - Sustainability of alternative housing

chunks.title: Risk rating for structural integrity of the house — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Risk rating for structural integrity of the house
There are only 2 outcomes from the assessment of the structural integrity of the client's current house:
At risk (4)
Low or no need (1)
When assessing whether the client's house is adequate due to the structural integrity of the house, consider whether the house is:
- fit for habitation or
- in a serious state of disrepair and presents a severe and significant health and safety risk to the client and their family
A house is considered inadequate if:
- the structure is condemned or has major structural damage and this is confirmed by the Council or other authority
- leaking roof which has damaged wiring
- unsafe foundations
- no flooring or flooring in significant state of disrepair
- no sewer system or sewer system is beyond repair
- excessive dampness or ventilation problems causing serious and persistent health issues
A house is considered adequate when there may be deficiencies, but these have not been identified as severe or a significant health and safety risk to the client and their family.
For example:
- condensation, mould, minor dampness
- minor repairs not undertaken by landlord
- outside steps or paths broken or cracked
- broken or cracked windows
- structural damage to other improvements on the section for example garage, shed or lean-to
Note this does not apply to clients who are assessed as 'not living in any accommodation' or living in emergency housing or transitional housing for the time being. These clients have already been rated as 'at risk' (4) for adequacy.

chunks.title: Signatory — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Signatory
A signatory is a person who signs the tenancy agreement. They are also referred to as the 'tenant'.
The only people who have security of tenure at the property are the signatories. Any other people living at the property have no rights to the tenancy.
For more information see:
- Obligations of a signatory
- Additional occupants
- Household composition

chunks.title: Social housing property changes ownership — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Social housing property changes ownership
A social housing provider may sell or give up a leased property to another social housing provider.
## Client stays in the property
In this situation a review of the client's eligibility or housing needs is not required if the client is staying in the same property.
## Income Related Rent
When a client remains in the property their calculated rate of Income Related Rent remains the same unless:
- the client has a change in circumstances that changes the rate or
- an annual review of the Income Related Rent is completed
## Kāinga Ora tenant with grandparented Income Related Rent
When Kāinga Ora transfers a property to a community housing provider, the client no longer qualifies for the Income Related Rent grandparenting provisions.
For more information see:
- Clients getting grandparented rate of Income Related Rent

chunks.title: Social housing provider considerations when adding signatory to tenancy agreement — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Social housing provider considerations when adding signatory to tenancy agreement
When considering whether to include another person or household unit as a signatory to the tenancy agreement, the social housing provider will consider whether:
- the existing house is suitable for the combined household's needs (for example, the occupancy limit is not breached) and
- the person or family unit joining in, is eligible for social housing
Note MSD will complete the assessment of eligibility for social housing.

chunks.title: Some fast-tracks have priority over another fast-track — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Some fast-tracks have priority over another fast-track
Households on the Oranga Tamariki or rheumatic fever fast-tracks will be prioritised on the register ahead of households on the emergency housing fast-track.
This ensures that priority is given to those most at risk.
## Example
Jason's 12 year-old son is at risk of rheumatic fever and their household are on the rheumatic fever fast-track. Their housing need priority rating is A15.
Another household with dependent children in the same area are staying in emergency housing and are on the emergency housing fast-track. Their housing need priority rating is A20.
Jason's household will be fast-tracked for the next available, suitable social housing property ahead of the household on the emergency housing fast-track.
See:
## More than one fast-track
Clients can be placed on more than one fast-track depending on their circumstances.
Clients may have:
- combined rheumatic fever and emergency housing fast-tracks or
- combined Oranga Tamariki and emergency housing fast-tracks
Note clients who have either the rheumatic fever fast-track or the Oranga Tamariki fast-track will be prioritised ahead of a client with only an emergency housing fast-track.

chunks.title: Specific location requirements — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Specific location requirements
If the client requires a specific location, they must demonstrate an urgent and compelling need to be housed in that location.
Social housing assessment of need ensures that people who are most in need of housing are housed appropriately in a house that meets their property requirements. Property requirements also include consideration of the specific location that is required by the household.
Examples of situations where a specific location requirement might be justified (but not limited to) include:
- where the location of a client's accommodation impacts on the client accessing essential services, amenities, support networks, employment, or special schools, and hospitals
- the household needs to be relocated immediately due to family violence or other violence relating to the client's current living situation
- the household needs to be relocated immediately due to abuse or harassment, or because of neighbourhood tension or tensions within the household relating to the client's current living situation
- client needs to be in a specific location due to a threat to the health and safety of the household members or household members may pose a threat to the community and therefore need to be moved to a different location
For more information see:

chunks.title: Specified child or young person in the custody of Oranga Tamariki or approved permanent care — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Some families in specific circumstances with a child or young person in their care may be able to fast-track into social housing. Fast-track applies when a household applying for social housing includes a child or young person in custody of Oranga Tamariki or is in an approved permanent care arrangement intended to be for 12 months or longer. An application for social housing can be fast-tracked when clients apply for social housing and meet the following criteria: - the household must qualify for social housing - the household must include a specified child or young person who is in the custody of Oranga Tamariki or in an approved permanent care arrangement - the child's placement in the household is intended to be for 12 months or longer, or permanent - placing the household into social housing is needed to help meet the needs of the child, including stability of care and - the specified child or young person is not in the process of leaving care or custody in the next 12 months For more information see:

chunks.title: Leaving care or custody in the next 12 months — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Families with specified children or young people may not be fast-tracked for social housing if they will be leaving care or custody in the next 12 months. The child or young person is considered to have left or be leaving when the custody order (issued by the Family Court) is discharged, lapses, or a care agreement ends or expires.

chunks.title: Clients already registered for social housing — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: There is a different process for households already on the social housing register. For more information see:

chunks.title: Current housing preventing a child coming into care — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: An application can also be fast-tracked if the: - household qualifies for social housing and - household's current accommodation is preventing a specified child or young person in the custody of Oranga Tamariki from coming into their care and - care arrangement is intended to be for 12 months or longer, or is permanent and - specified child or young person are not in the process of leaving care or custody in the next 12 months The client will generally provide a written statement to verify they meet the criteria for fast-track.

chunks.title: Child or young person placed with a parent — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text: Fast-track may still apply when a specified child or young person is, or will be, placed with one or both parent, as long as the child or young person is still in the custody of Oranga Tamariki, or still in approved permanent care.

chunks.title: Specified child or young person — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Specified child or young person
A specified child or young person is under 18 years old and is in custody under the Oranga Tamariki Act or in an approved permanent care arrangement.
This is a child or young person who is:
- in custody under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 (including sole guardianship) of: the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamarikian Iwi social servicea cultural social service ora child and family support service
- the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki
- an Iwi social service
- a cultural social service or
- a child and family support service
or
- is in the care of a person getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for them and was previously in custody under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 (including sole guardianship) of: the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamarikian iwi social servicea cultural social service ora child and family support service
- the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki
- an iwi social service
- a cultural social service or
- a child and family support service
This includes a child or young person being cared for by someone who is an applicant for social housing, or a tenant or an additional occupant in the household.
## Young person aged 18 years
A specified child or young person also includes a person after they turn 18 for a limited period when:
- the carer continues to get an Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the child or young person and
- the child or young person is financially dependent on the carer and
- the child or young person continues in education

chunks.title: Spontaneous or convention refugees or asylum seekers — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Spontaneous or convention refugees or asylum seekers
Some people come to New Zealand under the New Zealand Refugee Quota Programme.
Others apply for refugee or protected person status under the Immigration Act 2009 after they have arrived in New Zealand, and are known as spontaneous refugees, convention refugees or asylum seekers. A claim can be initiated at any time.
## Client may apply for Emergency Benefit while waiting for a decision
When a person is awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protected person status and are lawfully in New Zealand (i.e. they have a valid temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009), they may qualify for Emergency Benefit and Temporary Additional Support.
People who qualify for, and are getting Emergency Benefit can qualify for social housing on residency grounds.
## Residence status reconfirmed regularly while client on register
A client's residence status must be reconfirmed regularly while they are on the register.
This ensures that if a formal offer of housing is made by a social housing provider the client meets the residence requirements.
## Client no longer gets a benefit and doesn't meet the residency qualifications
When a client is declined refugee or protected person status and they are no longer getting a main benefit or do not meet the residence criteria, they will no longer qualify for social housing. If the client is on the Social Housing Register, they will be removed as they no longer qualify for a social housing.

chunks.title: Staying in emergency housing or transitional housing for the time being — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Staying in emergency housing or transitional housing for the time being
Emergency housing and transitional housing provide short-term, temporary accommodation while the client and their immediate family have an immediate housing need because they are unable to access suitable and sustainable housing.
Note for clients in emergency housing, immediate family means the client, their partner, and their dependent children (if any).
Emergency housing and transitional housing are for people who have an immediate need for accommodation because they:
- have no usual place of residence or
- are unable to remain in their usual place of residence (e.g. because of safety concerns)
and
- have no other accommodation that is adequate for their needs
Emergency housing and transitional housing provide a stable place for the individual or family to stay while their needs can be understood and addressed, and a longer-term accommodation solution can be found. The longer-term accommodation solution may include alternative housing (e.g. renting, flatting or boarding in private market), or social housing.
Types of short-term accommodation include:
- emergency housing paid for by an Emergency Housing Grant
- transitional housing funded by Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, which is short-term housing where clients have support services provided
- contracted emergency housing
- refuges such as those provided by Women's Refuge, Home and Family Society, Emergency Housing Trusts, Iwi and cultural organisations, or church organisations
Clients may have found their own temporary accommodation somewhere that is not intended for living in long term (e.g. cabin in a motor camp). MSD considers these clients to 'not be living in any accommodation'.

chunks.title: Structural integrity of the house — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Structural integrity of the house
When you are assessing if a client's current accommodation is adequate, you must consider the structural integrity or the physical condition of the current house and the associated health and safety risks. The degree of the inadequacies and the effect they are having on the quality of life of the occupants needs to be assessed.
Note this does not apply to clients who are assessed as 'not living in any accommodation' or who are living in emergency accommodation for the time being. These clients have already been rated as 'at risk' (4) for adequacy.
Some factors to consider are:
- Is the current house condemned?
- Can vermin enter and breed because of the condition of the house which can cause a health risk? There must be a serious infestation outside the client's control.
- Can the occupants exit the property safely in an emergency? For example, if the doors and windows cannot open, the occupants may be trapped in the event of a fire, intruder or family violence.
- Is the condition of the house causing excessive draughts making heating impossible? Note if there is one living room that can retain heat the house is considered adequate.
- Is the roof leaking and to what extent? Leaking roofs can present problems of dripping water and dampness but over time can also result in more substantial damage, for example, collapsed ceiling.
- Do cracked, broken or overflowing drains present a health risk? Is the private landlord reluctant to complete adequate repairs?
- Are there any other structures on the property that may present a risk to the occupants? For example, the shed or garage may be structurally unsound and could fall on the occupants.

chunks.title: Suitability of current housing — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Suitability of current housing
To assess whether the client's current housing situation is suitable you need to consider whether the client 'needs to move' from where they are currently living because of:
- any medical, disability or personal needs of the client (or a member of their household)
- any threat to the health or safety of the client (or a member of their household): due to family violenceother tension (from within the household or in the neighbourhood) orother violence relating to the client's current living situation
- due to family violence
- other tension (from within the household or in the neighbourhood) or
- other violence relating to the client's current living situation
The overall risk rating for suitability is the highest of the 2 categories.
Changes in the household's circumstances and makeup of a household can also affect the suitability of the client's current accommodation.

chunks.title: Sustainability of alternative housing — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Sustainability of alternative housing
Sustainability considers a client's ability to access or sustain alternative housing. It considers whether the client's ability to sustain alternative housing is impacted by:
- difficulties in financial management
- difficulties in social functioning and lack of social skills (social interaction) or
- a history of transience

chunks.title: Temporary entry class visa - visitors, work and students — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Temporary entry class visa - visitors, work and students
People holding temporary entry class visas do not qualify for social housing unless they:
- are recognised as a refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- qualify for and are getting Special Needs Grant Family Violence Programme or
- qualify for and are getting Emergency Benefit or Emergency Maintenance Allowance
## Exception for New Zealand Superannuation grandparented non-qualified partner
When a client on New Zealand Superannuation has a partner who does not qualify for New Zealand Superannuation in their own right, in exceptional circumstances they may have been included as a grandparented non-qualified partner, even if they had a temporary entry class visa.
This is when the grandparented non-qualified partner is:
- awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protected person status and are lawfully in New Zealand (i.e. they have a valid temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009) or
- a refugee or has protected person status in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or
- applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 and is compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances
If the partner has a temporary entry class visa such as a Visitor's Visa, a Temporary Work Visa, or a Student's Visa, they can only get payment while their visa is current. Therefore they can qualify for social housing while they are on a temporary entry class visa but only while they are getting New Zealand Superannuation.
## Residence status reconfirmed regularly while client on register
A client’s residence status must be reconfirmed regularly while the client is on the register.
This ensures that if a formal offer of housing is made by a social housing provider the client meets the residence requirements.

chunks.title: Transfers — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Transfers
When a client has a change in circumstances that affects their housing needs they may request a transfer to another property that better suits their new circumstances.
A client requesting a transfer to another social housing property will have to be reassessed using the original assessment criteria. This means they must have had a significant change in circumstances, as the client needs to be at risk (priority A) or have a serious housing need (priority B), to be eligible for another property.
If the client has concerns with the existing social housing property they are renting, for example, if it is cold, damp and/or mouldy, or there are concerns with overcrowding or underutilisation in the property, these cases need to be referred to the Housing Processing Hub.
For more information see:
- Social Housing Transfers [no link find out why]
## Housing provider requires transfer
There are also situations when a social housing provider may require a client to move to a different property belonging to that provider.
## Housing needs assessment
When a housing provider requires a tenant to transfer, they may ask MSD to complete a review of the tenant's housing requirements.
For more information see:
## Change in circumstances and effect on tenancy review
All clients in social housing can have their tenancy reviewed. However, these are being targeted to make sure that reviews focus on the people most likely able to sustain alternative housing.
This means when clients tell us about changes in circumstances that effect their continued eligibility or the need for the particular property, their continued eligibility for social housing may not be reviewed straight away.

chunks.title: Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payments — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payments
Unsupported Child's Benefit carers must apply for a formula assessment of Child Support. This rule applies unless they have a voluntary agreement in place before applying for Unsupported Child's Benefit.
For these carers, Inland Revenue keeps Child Support paid by liable parents to help pay for the Unsupported Child's Benefit the child's carer is getting.
When the amount of Child Support paid is more than the rate of Unsupported Child's Benefit, Inland Revenue pays the difference to the receiving carer. This is called an Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payment.
## Types of Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payments
There are 2 types of Unsupported Child's Benefit excess payments:
- formula assessment excess (the most common type)
- voluntary agreement excess
## Formula assessment excess payment
If the formula assessment is higher than the Unsupported Child's Benefit rate, Inland Revenue pays the difference to the receiving carer. This is called a formula assessment excess payment and is not assessable income when determining whether a client qualifies for social housing.
## Voluntary agreement excess payment
If the Unsupported Child's Benefit carer has a voluntary agreement, and the formula assessment is lower than the voluntary agreement amount, Inland Revenue can only keep the amount of the formula assessment. The rest is paid to the receiving carer. This is called a voluntary agreement excess payment and is assessable income when determining whether a client qualifies for social housing.
## Mixed payment not assessable income
In some cases a receiving carer may get an excess payment and another type of Inland Revenue Child Support payment from the same liable parent. This is called a mixed Child Support payment, and is not assessable income for social housing.

chunks.title: What is rheumatic fever? — assessment of eligibility
chunks.text:
## What is rheumatic fever?
Children and young people are most likely to get rheumatic fever. It occurs after a 'strep throat' - a throat infection caused by a group A streptococcus (GAS) bacteria.
In a small number of cases, an untreated strep throat develops into rheumatic fever, where a person's heart, joints, brain and skin becomes inflamed and swollen.
While the symptoms of rheumatic fever may disappear on their own, the inflammation can cause heart disease, when there is scarring on the heart valves.

chunks.title: Change in circumstances for current tenants — duty to advise of changes in circumstances
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances for current tenants
Generally, all social housing tenants have a duty to tell MSD straight away of any changes in their circumstances, and any change in the circumstances of applicable people [no link find out why] , likely to result in them no longer:
- qualifying for social housing or
- in need of the particular property they are renting
Generally, all social housing tenants paying an Income Related Rent also have a duty to advise straight away of any change of circumstances, and any change in the circumstances of applicable people, that may result in them having to pay a higher Income Related Rent.
Generally, all social housing tenants have a duty to tell MSD about any change in their circumstances (or their partner's circumstances, as well as any other tenants circumstances) that may affect eligibility for social housing and the need for the particular property they are renting.
For more information about specific changes in circumstances see:
## Exception – Client’s getting information share Child Support
Clients do not need to tell MSD when they get, or have a change to, information share Child Support payments.
For more information see:
## Clients waiting to be allocated social housing
Generally, clients waiting to be allocated social housing also have a duty to advise MSD of any change in circumstances that may affect their eligibility for social housing or the particular property they need.
For more information see:
- Register management and referrals Change in circumstances.
## Income Related Rent
Generally, clients getting Income Related Rent also have a duty to advise MSD of any changes in circumstances that may affect their calculated rate of Income Related Rent.
For more information see:
- Income Related Rent Change in circumstances
## Change in circumstances and effect on tenancy review
All clients in social housing can have their tenancy reviewed.
However, reviews are being targeted to make sure that initial reviews focus on the people most likely able to sustain alternative housing.
When clients tell MSD about any change in circumstances that may affect whether they still qualify for social housing or the need for the particular property, their situation may not be reviewed straight away.

chunks.title: Change in additional occupant contributions — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text:
## Change in additional occupant contributions
When the client has a change to the additional occupant contributions they get, this may affect their Income Related Rent for social housing, MSD needs to:
- decide whether the change affects the rate of Income Related Rent
- review the rate of Income Related Rent if required
- record the change in the system.
When there are changes to the client's Income Related Rent or an applicant's priority on the social housing register, see:
- Income Related Rent Change in circumstances
- Register management and referrals Change in circumstances.
A client's continued eligibility for social housing will be reviewed when the client is selected for tenancy review.
For more information see:
- Tenancy reviews
## Example
Sandra is getting Sole Parent Support, she has 2 young children. Sandra's brother moves into the property as an additional occupant and pays her a contribution for living there. She is aware of the need to tell MSD about her situation.
Sandra’s brother pays a contribution that means she no longer qualifies for Income Related Rent. Her rent is increased to market rent.
Although they move to the market rent rate, Sandra's continued eligibility for social housing will not be reassessed at this time.
The household needs to be selected for a tenancy review before their continued eligibility is reviewed.

chunks.title: Change in assessable income and assets — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text:
## Change in assessable income and assets
When the client has a change in income or assets, this may affect their continued eligibility for social housing, MSD will need to:
- decide whether the change affects the rate of Income Related Rent
- review the rate of Income Related Rent if required
- record the change in the system.
When there are changes to the client's Income Related Rent or an applicant's priority on the social housing register, see:
- Income Related Rent Change in circumstances
- Register management and referrals Change in circumstances.
A client's continued eligibility for social housing will be reviewed when the client is selected for tenancy review. For more information see:
From 1 July 2023, most types of Child Support are included as assessable income when MSD calculates a clients Income Related Rent or an applicant's priority rating. For more information see:
- Income Related Rent Child Support included in assessable income from 1 July 2023
- Register management and referrals Reviewing clients on the register.
## Example 1
Sandra is getting Sole Parent Support, she has 2 young children. Sandra's new partner moves into the property, and she is aware of the need to tell MSD about her situation.
Her new partner has income and assets greater than the income and asset limits set for social housing eligibility.
Although they move to the market rent rate (and Sandra's benefit is cancelled), Sandra's continued eligibility for social housing will not be reassessed at this time.
The household needs to be selected for a tenancy review before their continued eligibility is reviewed.
## Example 2
Roger has received $60,000 from his late grandmother's estate which he put into a savings account. Roger is currently paying market rent.
Roger has assets greater than the asset limits set for social housing eligibility and is aware he needs to tell MSD about his situation.
Roger's continued eligibility for social housing will not be reassessed at this time.
When Roger is selected for a tenancy review, his continued eligibility will be reviewed.

chunks.title: Change in benefit status affecting residency criteria — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text:
## Change in benefit status affecting residency criteria
When the client has a change in circumstances affecting their residence status, this may affect their continued eligibility for social housing. MSD must:
- decide whether the change affects the rate of Income Related Rent
- review the rate of Income Related Rent if required
When there are changes to the client's Income Related Rent or an applicant's priority on the social housing register see:
- Income Related Rent Change in circumstances
- Register management and referrals Change in circumstances
A client's continued eligibility for social housing will be reviewed when the client is selected for tenancy review.
For more information see:
## Example
Steve is getting Emergency Benefit, he doesn't have a residence class visa, but qualified for social housing because he was getting a main benefit.
Steve has just started full-time work, so he is no longer getting a benefit. He is aware he needs to notify MSD about his situation. Steve's continued eligibility to social housing will not be reassessed at this time.
He will need to be selected for a tenancy review before his continued eligibility is reviewed.

chunks.title: Change in household members — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text:
## Change in household members
When there has been a change in the household members living in a social housing property (e.g. people, children moving in or out of the property), this may affect the client's need for the particular property they are renting.
In these situations, you need to:
- decide whether the change affects the rate of Income Related Rent
- review the rate of Income Related Rent if required and
- record the change in the system
When there are changes to the client's Income Related Rent or an applicant's priority on the social housing register see:
- Income Related Rent Change in circumstances
- Register management and referrals Change in circumstances
A client's need for the particular property they are renting will be reviewed if the client is selected for tenancy review.
For more information see:
The client will need to contact their housing provider to inform them if any other adults or children have moved into or out of the property as it may affect their tenancy agreement.
## Example
Sue works full-time and lives in a 3 bedroom property on her own. Sue's son Shaun has just come back from the United Kingdom and is now living with her. She knows she needs to tell MSD about her situation. Shaun is working and paying a contribution.
Sue's continued eligibility for social housing or the need for the particular property she is renting will not be reassessed at this time. Sue would need to be selected for a tenancy review before her continued eligibility is reviewed.

chunks.title: Change in housing requirements — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text: A client or their partner (if any) may have changes in their circumstances that affect their housing needs (property requirements). A change in housing needs includes when the client: - needs another person to be added or removed from the tenancy agreement or - needs a different property type or - dies When the client has a change in their circumstances affecting the need for the particular property they are renting (e.g. the client or someone else who lives with the client no longer requires the number of bedrooms or modifications such as wheelchair access or wet area shower that are in the property), you will need to: - decide whether the change affects the rate of Income Related Rent - review the rate of Income Related Rent if required - record the change in the system When there are changes to the client's Income Related Rent or an applicant's priority on the social housing register see: - Income Related Rent Change in circumstances - Register management and referrals Change in circumstances A client's continued eligibility for social housing will not be reviewed until they are selected for tenancy review. See:

chunks.title: Example 1 — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text: Nikki and Lua have just separated. They live in a 4 bedroom property with their 3 children. Lua has remained in the property and Nikki and the children have moved out. He knows he needs to tell MSD about the separation. Lua's continued eligibility for social housing and the need for the particular property he is renting will not be reassessed at this time. Lua would need to be selected for a tenancy review before his continued eligibility would be reviewed.

chunks.title: Example 2 — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text: Valerie and her elderly mother live in a 3-bedroom modified property (has wet area shower, wide hallways and a wheelchair ramp). They are both on the tenancy agreement. Valerie's mother has just moved into a rest-home. Valerie knows she needs to tell MSD about her situation. Valerie's continued eligibility for social housing and the need for the particular property she is renting will not be reassessed at this time. When Valerie selected for a tenancy review, her continued eligibility will be reviewed.

chunks.title: Example 3 — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text: Wiremu is a sole parent living in a 2-bedroom unit. He has 3 children but only 1 child in his full-time care. Wiremu confirms that his other 2 children (aged 9 and 11 years old) will be coming back into his full-time care in the coming weeks. He has been in contact with his social worker who has suggested that he applies for a transfer. Wiremu's children should be added into his record when they come into his care. A client initiated transfer needs to be completed and if he is eligible, he will go onto the register. Wiremu needs to be selected for tenancy review before his continued eligibility will be reviewed (for his current tenancy).

chunks.title: Underutilised properties and effect on tenancy reviews — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text: There may be some situations when the client has a change in circumstances which means they have more bedrooms than they need. In these situations, the client is likely to be identified for tenancy review selection sooner than others. One of the focus groups for tenancy review is social housing tenants in underutilised properties.

chunks.title: Transfers — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text: Sometimes, a client may contact MSD to request a transfer to another property that better suits their housing need. For more information see:

chunks.title: Housing needs assessment — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text: When the client has had a significant change in circumstances, you can complete an assessment to identify the client's housing needs (requirements). This isn't a full eligibility assessment, but a review to assess the client's housing needs (e.g. bedroom numbers based on the number of household members). Generally these assessments are only completed when a housing provider requests one. For more information see: A review of housing need may be completed when MSD consider the housing provider should be aware the housing needs of the household have changed significantly (perhaps putting the household in greater risk of overcrowding). Note you must advise the housing provider of the results of any assessment (including on review) of housing needs in relation to one of their tenants. This will give the housing provider confirmation of the tenant's (client's) housing needs so that the housing provider can decide whether any changes to the property are required to suit the tenant or whether the tenant should be transferred to another property.

chunks.title: Requests for disability modifications — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text: If a client or their partner (if any) has a disability and they need modifications made to the property so they can continue to live there, the client must discuss modifications required with their housing provider. When the housing provider cannot make the modifications the client may request a transfer to another more appropriate property.

chunks.title: Change in need for social housing — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text:
## Change in need for social housing
When a client applies for social housing, their circumstances are assessed through the Social Allocation System (SAS) to determine their housing need.
When the client is placed into social housing, their need to move may be resolved. However, the client may still be unable to afford, access and sustain alternative housing (e.g. private rent) so will still have a need for social housing.
Where the client has a change in circumstances affecting the reason why they need housing e.g., health or disability reasons, discrimination, high debt etc, you will need to:
- decide whether the change affects the rate of Income Related Rent
- review the rate of Income Related Rent if required
- record the change in the system
Where there are changes to the client's Income Related Rent or an applicant's priority on the social housing register see:
- Income Related Rent Change in circumstances
- Register management and referrals Change in circumstances
The client's continued eligibility for social housing will be reviewed when the client is selected for tenancy review.

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
Generally, clients should advise MSD within 14 days of any changes in their or their household's circumstances that may affect their continued eligibility for social housing or the need for the particular property they are renting.
## Change in circumstances and effect on tenancy review
All clients in social housing can have their tenancy reviewed. However, initial reviews are targeted to focus on the people most likely able to sustain alternative housing. This means when clients tell MSD about changes in circumstances that affect their continued eligibility or the need for the particular property, their continued eligibility for social housing may not be reviewed straight away.
When there are changes to a client's Income Related Rent or an applicant's priority on the social housing register see:
- Income Related Rent Change in circumstances
- Register management and referrals Change in circumstances.
The client's continued eligibility for social housing or the property they are in, will be reviewed if they meet the selection criteria for tenancy review.

chunks.title: Consequence for tenants not advising of a change in circumstances — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text:
## Consequence for tenants not advising of a change in circumstances
If the client does not advise of any change in their circumstances that may affect their eligibility for Income Related Rent, social housing or their particular social housing property, they may be committing an offence.
MSD may choose to prosecute the client if they have omitted information deliberately to mislead or attempt to mislead MSD to:
- be eligible for social housing or
- continue to be eligible for social housing or
- get a particular social housing property or
- get Income Related Rent or
- get a higher rate of Income Related Rent
The maximum penalty for this type of offending under the Public and Community Housing Management Act 1992 is a term of imprisonment no longer than 12 months or a fine not over $5000, or both.
When the offending has been significant and the circumstances warrant, MSD can file charges of obtaining by deception under the Crimes Act 1961, with a maximum penalty of 7 years imprisonment.
You will need to make sure clients are aware of this penalty when informing them of their duty to advise any change in their circumstances.
## Income Related Rent
Income Related Rent debt is created when a lower Income Related Rent has been calculated for a client than they were entitled to for a past period.
Income Related Rent debt established due to fraud is calculated from:
- when the client first started paying Income Related Rent or
- the date the fraud started to either, the date the fraud ended or the day before the rent effective date (whichever is applicable)

chunks.title: Information share Child Support — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text:
## Information share Child Support
MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about Child Support payments.
These payments are called information share Child Support payments and are automatically included as income for clients who get income tested financial assistance.
However, social housing assessments and Income Related Rent need to be reviewed manually to include information share Child Support payments, as assessable income at the time of application, or at the next review after 22 August 2023.
The information share with Inland Revenue does not include all Child Support payments made. For more information see:
## Declaring information share Child Support
From 1 July 2023, MSD will be notified by Inland Revenue of a change in circumstances regarding a client's information share Child Support. Clients do not need to advise MSD when they get, or have a change to, information share Child Support payments.
## Information share Child Support error
There may be cases when the information share Child Support payment details are incorrect.
Clients must tell MSD when they are notified of the information share Child Support as part of a review, and they know it is incorrect.

chunks.title: Mismatch of additional occupant contributions and accommodation costs — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text: Clients must tell MSD when: - they start getting contributions from additional occupants or - there is a change in the contribution amount they get.

chunks.title: When clients can be matched — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text: When a social housing tenant who pays Income Related Rent gets contributions from a client who lives with them and that client gets Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, and/or Special Benefit, MSD will also check the details match between the two clients.

chunks.title: Step one - Mismatch identified — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text: A mismatch of information will be identified when a clients accommodation type or amount differs from what a client who is a social housing tenant has declared they are getting, or an additional occupant has declared they are paying. MSD must try to contact both clients within one working day of identifying the mismatch to check and confirm the correct details. If one or both clients are uncontactable within one working day, but a message is left for the client/s to make contact, MSD must consider whether it is reasonable to allow the one working day to lapse before moving to the next step in the process. When one or both clients have been contacted, and it is clear the mismatch cannot be resolved within one working day, or one or both clients are uncontactable and a message cannot be left, MSD can continue to the next step in the process. Note the one working day ends on the close of the working day following the day the mismatch is identified. Example Raphael is a tenant in a social housing property and pays Income Related Rent. Donatello boards with him as an additional occupant and gets Accommodation Supplement. On Wednesday 6 May, Donatello contacts MSD to advise of a change in circumstances. He is now paying Raphael $365 a week for board from Monday 4 May, an increase from the $355 he had been paying. The new value differs from what MSD holds in the system for the board Raphael gets from Donatello. Raphael has not yet advised MSD of this change. On Thursday 7 May (within one working day of identifying the payment amount mismatch), MSD contacts Donatello to confirm he intended to declare a change in his board amount. Raphael contacts MSD later that day to advise that Donatello’s board as increased to $365 from Monday. MSD updates the details for both clients’ and the mismatch has been resolved.

chunks.title: Step two - Notification of mismatch — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text: When the mismatch is not resolved within one working day after it was identified, MSD must notify both clients of the mismatch and advise they have 10 working days to resolve it. MSD will also advise if the mismatch is not resolved within 10 working days after the date of notification, any Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, and/or Special Benefit will be suspended from the 11th working day. The client who is a social housing tenant will be notified that the Income Related Rent will be set to market rent if they have not resolved the mismatch within 10 working days after the date of notification. Note the 10 working days starts from the day after the letter is sent.

chunks.title: Step three - Response to the notification of mismatch — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
chunks.text: Contact from client/s and mismatch resolved within 10 working days When the client/s make contact and confirm the correct details within 10 working days, the details should be updated and any assistance reviewed accordingly. This means the mismatch is now resolved. No contact from client/s When one or both clients don’t make contact within 10 working days to confirm their additional occupant contribution payment information, the mismatch is unable to be resolved, and both clients Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, and/or Special Benefit must be suspended. For the client who is a social housing tenant and the mismatch is not resolved, MSD will notify the housing provider that the client’s Income Related Rent must be set to market rent for the property. Community Housing Providers have a discretion not to set the client’s rent to the market rent rate. The standard 60-day notice period will apply. Example Amanda is a social housing tenant and gets Income Related Rent. Bonnie boards with Amanda as an additional occupant and gets Accommodation Supplement. Bonnie gets a mandatory review for her Accommodation Supplement. On Tuesday 9 June, she responds before her review due date confirming that she pays $20 more in board to Amanda. The new amount is different from what MSD holds for Amanda. MSD checks with Bonnie on Wednesday 10 June (within one working day of identifying the mismatch) to see if she advised of the increase in error. She confirms the increase is correct. On Wednesday 10 June, MSD tries contacting Amanda to confirm the new rate, but she doesn’t respond. On Thursday 11 June (after the one working day has lapsed), MSD sends both Amanda and Bonnie notification of the mismatch and provides 10 working days to resolve it and advise MSD. Amanda does not respond to the request for information by close of day Tuesday 23 June (within 10 working days). MSD notifies Amanda’s housing provider that her Income Related Rent needs to increase to market rent. Bonnie’s Accommodation Supplement is suspended from Wednesday 24 June (11th working day) as MSD is unable to confirm the information reported. If Amanda doesn’t respond within 8 weeks, Bonnie’s Accommodation Supplement will be cancelled.

chunks.title: Disputes — duty to advise of changes in circumstances > changes and reviews duty to advise changes of circumstances
