chunks.text:
## Reviews and Appeals
A client can apply for a Review of Decision when they have received formal notification of and disagree with a decision, including decisions relating to:
- the calculation of the rate of Income Related Rent
- the establishment and recovery of Income Related Rent debt
- the assessment or re-assessment of: their eligibility or continued eligibility for social housingtheir housing needs
- their eligibility or continued eligibility for social housing
- their housing needs
A client can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority where they do not agree with a decision, which was upheld or upheld in part by the Benefits Review Committee under an application for Review of Decision
## Exceptions
A client has no right of appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority (and therefore no right to apply for a Review of Decision) if they disagree with:
- a decision not to review their housing need
However you will need to ensure that there is a good reason not to undertake a review of their housing needs.
- any decision made by a housing provider regarding tenancy-related matters, such as: the determination of a market rent raterent arrearsdamages debt orwhether someone can join into a tenancy agreement
- the determination of a market rent rate
- rent arrears
- damages debt or
- whether someone can join into a tenancy agreement
The client has the right to apply for a Review of Decision at any time within 3 months of the original decision being advised. When a client has applied for a hearing outside the three month time limit the Benefits Review Committee must decide whether or not to accept the application before it considers the decision under review.
A client has the right to have their decision reviewed once. If they wish to have the same decision reviewed again refer the case to Legal Services.

chunks.title: Notify decision in full — register management and referrals > changes and reviews register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Notify decision in full
When you advise a client of a decision, in particular an unfavourable decision, you should explain your decision in full and explain the relevant legislation.
Note it is not appropriate to just quote a section of the act verbatim, you should explain the relevant legislation to the client and how it applies to their situation.
For more information see:
- Who can apply for a review or appeal
- Review of Decision [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Client does not respond to offer from social housing provider — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Client does not respond to offer from social housing provider
It is expected a client who has been offered a social housing property will accept or decline the property within the specified time period set by the social housing provider.
This ensures people with a serious and persistent housing need can be housed as quickly as possible into a property that meets their housing requirements.
At the time of being offered the property, a client is advised by the housing provider they are expected to tell the housing provider of whether they will accept or decline the property within the specified time (usually 48 hours).
They will also be advised if they do not contact the social housing provider with their decision within the specified timeframe, they will be considered to have not accepted the property offer.
When a client does not respond to the offer from the social housing provider and the social housing provider has been unable to contact the client themselves to confirm their acceptance or decline of the property offer, the social housing provider will advise MSD the client has not accepted the property offer.
If the client does not accept or declines the property, they will be considered to have not accepted the property and MSD is required to assess whether the client had a good and sufficient reason to not accept the property offered.
If you cannot contact the client to confirm their reasons for not accepting the property, the client will be treated as having declined the property offer with no good and sufficient reason.
The client will no longer be eligible for social housing and will be removed from the register.
If contact is made with the client, you need to decide whether their reason for not accepting the property is good and sufficient.

chunks.title: Client indicates preference for specific provider — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Client indicates preference for specific provider
A client can request to be referred to a specific housing provider because they have a particular need or simply due to preference.
For example, a client may be currently getting other social services from that housing provider.
When possible, clients will be referred to housing providers that provide the best housing services to meet their needs.
For example, some clients may be:
- referred to providers on the basis of their: relationship status
- relationship status
- referred to providers offering specialist services for single parents, vulnerable singles, for example, sole parent or released prisoners disability or health condition
- disability or health condition
- referred to providers offering wrap-around services or tailored services, for example for people with mental illness or physical disabilities age
- age
- referred to housing for older people and kaumatua family status
- family status
- referred to social housing for low-income families
Note these specific housing services are only offered by community housing providers.
When the client's preference significantly restricts their referral opportunities, you will need to explain that this is likely to result in a longer wait period for referral and encourage them to expand their choice of housing providers.
## Clients still may be referred to other housing providers
Clients may still be referred to other housing providers when there is a property available that meets their housing needs. If a client does not accept this property without a good and sufficient reason, it may affect their eligibility to continue to be offered social housing.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Client is suspended by a housing provider — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Client is suspended by a housing provider
A housing provider might suspend a tenant when they have breached their tenancy agreement.
Suspension means the housing provider is not willing to accept the client as a tenant.
Note the decision to suspend a tenant is made solely by the housing provider, not by MSD.
Some providers also have a waiver policy where the client can apply for the suspension to be lifted.
Kāinga Ora has a suspension policy with a waiver provision.
## Effect of a suspension on a client
If a client has been suspended by a particular housing provider they can still:
- apply and be assessed for social housingThe client can apply for a waiver if the housing provider has a waiver policy.
- be referred to other social housing providersFor example, another housing provider may offer specialist support services that would help the person to sustain a social tenancy.
- for clients who are suspended from Kāinga Ora, when the suspension has ended, the client will be eligible for matching to Kāinga Ora properties
## Reasons for suspension
Housing providers can suspend a tenant in line with their own policies.
In general policies will relate to serious or persistent breaches of their tenancy agreement.
Reasons for suspension may include:
- anti-social behaviour
- fraud
- substantial and repeated rent arrears
- wilful damage

chunks.title: Client no longer needs housing — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Client no longer needs housing
Clients may advise they no longer need a house. Where clients identify they no longer have a housing need, they must be removed from the register.
Applications for clients at risk or in serious housing need removed, can be reinstated without the need for a new eligibility assessment if they make contact within 8 weeks.
Note clients who make contact within 8 weeks who are found not to have a good and sufficient reason for declining a property will not have their social housing application reinstated. They will need to re-apply for social housing to determine they have a persistent housing need that is serious or severe.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Client on the register is under investigation — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Client on the register is under investigation
Clients on the register may be under investigation.
The outcome of an investigation can result in a review of the client's eligibility for social housing.
Where the review determines the client is no longer eligible for social housing, they will be removed from the register.
Client Service Integrity will determine the outcome of the investigation and the impact on the client's application.
Note clients under investigation are not removed from the register while the investigation is being completed.
## Review of circumstances
In some cases, the outcome of the investigation may result in a reassessment of eligibility for the client using their correct circumstances.
It may not necessarily mean the client is no longer entitled to social housing. For example, a client may have an undeclared partner but that partner is not working.
## Investigation outcome indicates fraud or client fails to comply with investigation
When the outcome of investigation indicates that the application for social housing is fraudulent, or the client has failed or refused to comply with the investigation, Client Service Integrity will advise whether the client should be removed from the register.
## Under investigation when referred for placement
If a client still under investigation is referred to a housing provider for placement, where possible you should contact Client Service Integrity to confirm:
- the current status of the investigation and
- that it is appropriate for the referral to continue

chunks.title: Clients in specific circumstances — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Clients in specific circumstances
There are specific circumstances that can affect a client's placement on the register.
For more information see:
- Client is suspended by a housing provider
- Client on the register is under investigation
- Emergency housing need
- Grandparented clients
- Warrant to arrest
- Declining offer of a suitable property
Also see:
- Removal from the register
- Reinstatement of application
- Referrals
- Change in circumstances

chunks.title: Declining offer of a suitable property — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Declining offer of a suitable property
Clients can be referred to a social housing provider when the provider has a suitable property available that is likely to meet the client's housing requirements.
The provider will make an offer of a property to the client and arrange for them to view it.
## Advising client of consequences of declining suitable offer
Before you can decide that a client has declined a property without good and sufficient reason, the client must have been advised of the consequences of refusing the offer without a good and sufficient reason. This includes advising how the client's eligibility will be assessed if the client applies for social housing within 13 weeks of declining the offer. The client must be advised that:
- if they decline an offer of a social housing property (or fail to accept a property because of non-response to an offer), without a good and sufficient reason, they will be removed immediately from the housing register and
- their decision to decline (or not accept a property because of a non-response to an offer) without a good and sufficient reason, will be considered a material factor when assessing eligibility for social housing, if they reapply within 13 weeks of declining the offer
## One decline with no good and sufficient reason
If a client declines an offer of a suitable property (or fails to accept a property because of non-response to an offer) without a good and sufficient reason, you must:
- where the client has given reasons, advise the client that your initial view is that the reasons given appear not to be good and sufficient
- give the client a further opportunity to provide alternative and additional reasons for declining (or failing to accept) the property, before a final decision is made
Once you have determined the client did not have a good and sufficient reason to decline (or fail to accept) the property, the client is no longer eligible for social housing and you must remove the client from the register.
Note this also applies to clients who have indicated a preference for a specific housing provider.
For more information see:
## Review rights
A client can review the decision to remove them from the register because they are no longer eligible.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Declining request to review — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Declining request to review
MSD can review the eligibility or continued eligibility or housing needs of a client. A prospective social housing client or current client can also request a review of decisions made about their eligibility or housing needs (property requirements).
There are some circumstances when you can decline a request to review a client's eligibility or housing needs (property requirements) if you have reason to believe that the client's circumstances have not significantly changed while the client on the register.
For example:
- no change in circumstancesthe client is seeking a second opinion about the outcome of their eligibility assessment
- change in circumstances has no impact on housing need or housing needs (property requirements) for example, a child moving in does not have a good reason not to share a bedroom under the bedroom allocation requirements
## Review of decision
A client cannot apply for a Review of Decision if they do not agree with the decision not to review their housing needs.
However, you need to make sure there is good reason not to undertake a review for the client's eligibility, and record the reason in full.

chunks.title: Emergency housing need — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Emergency housing need
Sometimes clients on the register may have an emergency housing need.
Generally, clients can remain on the register while their emergency housing need is responded to, as emergency housing is temporary.
While in emergency housing, you may need to review the client's circumstances to determine if they have changed (in particular their housing needs (requirements)).
For more information see:

chunks.title: Examples of good and sufficient reasons for declining a social housing property — register management and referrals
chunks.text: Suitable offers of social housing should be accepted by the client unless there is a good and sufficient reason why the property does not meet their assessed needs.

chunks.title: Number of bedrooms — register management and referrals
chunks.text: Does the offered property have the correct number of bedrooms for the client, and any other person included in the offer? Examples of reasons considered good and sufficient Examples of reasons unlikely to be considered good and sufficient - The property has fewer bedrooms than the assessed needs. - The property has the correct number of bedrooms for the assessed needs, but the client feels the rooms are too small.

chunks.title: Design and layout — register management and referrals
chunks.text: Does the design and layout cater for the needs of the client, and any other person included in the offer e.g. modified bathrooms, wide enough door-ways, flat section, living area fit for purpose? Examples of reasons considered good and sufficient Examples of reasons unlikely to be considered good and sufficient - The property has no curtains and the housing provider has advised they won't provide them. - Client has an anxiety disorder and cannot live in a shared environment as it would result in isolation and risk to health condition. - The lawn is too big for the client to maintain due to their health condition or disability. - The property has no curtains but the housing provider has advised they will install them; however the client still decides to decline the property. - Client feels the property does not have a big enough living room for their family. - Property does not have a garage. - The property is not suitable for the family pet (where there is no health/disability need). - Client wants a separate shower and the property only has a shower over a bath (no health/disability need for this). - Client simply doesn't want to have to share a lounge area and kitchen on the grounds of them wanting their own space. - The client thinks the lawn is too big and doesn't want to have to mow it themselves (no health condition/disability exists).

chunks.title: Features for clients with specific needs — register management and referrals
chunks.text: Do the features of the property meet the client's (or any other person included in the offer) disability needs, needs of children or specific needs due to being elderly? Examples of reasons considered good and sufficient Examples of reasons unlikely to be considered good and sufficient - The property does not have an outside space which the client requires for a blind or companion dog. - The property has stairs and the client has had a knee replacement surgery which would make it difficult to access the property. - The property does not have enough storage for the client's medical equipment. - The car park is located a distance from the property making the property unsuitable due to the persons health or disability or impact on young children. - Client is not happy with the cosmetic appearance of the property. - Client doesn't want to live in an upstairs property. - The property does not have enough storage for a person's hobby. - Client does not want to live in an apartment. - Client has teenage children who like to play soccer and therefore require a backyard. - The car park is located a distance from the property and there is no identified need for why this is not suitable for the client. - The client wants a standalone property (no medical condition exists to say they specifically require one).

chunks.title: Fencing — register management and referrals
chunks.text: Is the fencing appropriate to meet the needs of the client (and any other person included in the offer)? Examples of reasons considered good and sufficient Examples of reasons unlikely to be considered good and sufficient - The property is unsuitable because they require a secure property for their autistic son, and the provider is unable to fence the property. - Client or other person included in the offer needs fencing due to health condition or disability eg autism, dementia. - Property has no fencing at all and the client has small children. - Property has a fenced play area away from the road and driveway, however the client still chooses to decline. - Client wants fencing because they want privacy and to stop people from walking on their front-lawn (and there is no identified need). - Fencing didn't have locks on the gates as needed for client's child with special needs. Housing provider advises they will add locks, however client still chooses to decline the property.

chunks.title: Proximity to essential services or workplace — register management and referrals
chunks.text: Is the property reasonable when considering the property's proximity and access to essential services or workplace for the client, and any other person included in the offer? Examples of reasons considered good and sufficient Examples of reasons unlikely to be considered good and sufficient - It would be unreasonable for the client to continue to see their current health practitioner but they can't get into another health practitioner closer to the property and they regularly see a health practitioner because of their disability needs. - Client's children are settled in their current school or day-care and accepting the property would mean it isn't reasonable for the child to attend their school e.g. would have to travel on multiple modes of transport to get to the same school or day-care or the only option for the family is walking and this is not practical from the offered property. - Client would have to take two trains and a bus ride to get to work which would result in the client giving up their employment. - There are no health practitioner shortages in the area and the client can change health practitioner. The client doesn't have an ongoing health and disability condition but just doesn't want to change health practitioner. - Client currently drives the children to school and this can continue from the offered property but they would have to travel a little further to the school and the client advises it is too much effort. - There are no health or other reasons why the client cannot catch a train to work but instead chooses to drive. The move would take him further from work and he doesn't want to be stuck in traffic any longer.

chunks.title: Health, well-being or safety of the client — register management and referrals
chunks.text: Will requiring the client to accept the offer (in MSD's opinion) have an adverse effect on the health, well-being or safety of the client (including any other person included in the offer)? Examples of reasons considered good and sufficient Examples of reasons unlikely to be considered good and sufficient - Client has a protection order against someone living in close proximity to the property. - Property has evidence of mould or dampness. - Property is in a gang-affiliated neighbourhood, and the client has been a witness in a police investigation associated with the gang. - Property is in a gang affiliated neighbourhood, and the client fears for the safety of themselves and their children. - Client believes that the property was a previous drug house, and does not want people showing up at the property. - Client is a recovering alcoholic and drug dependent, and the property has neighbours who are known to be "big party people" making offered property an unsafe physical environment. - Client has decided that there are too many of a certain ethnicity in the area, and they will not move there. - The property looked dark and didn't get enough sunshine, but there was no evidence of mould or dampness. - The client advises the street is dangerous as there are boy racers. However, the housing provider advises that there are now speed bumps on the road. - Client doesn't like the area, and doesn't specify a reason.

chunks.title: Court, bail or release conditions — register management and referrals
chunks.text: Is the offered property unsuitable because of any court, bail or release conditions which would prevent the client (including any other person included in the offer) from living in the property? Examples of reasons considered good and sufficient Examples of reasons unlikely to be considered good and sufficient - Known child sex offender is living in the proximity of the offered property, and there will be children living and/or regularly visiting the property. - Property has been offered to a client for whom it would be inappropriate to live there (e.g. probation, child sex offenders, restraining orders against the client). - Known child sex offender is living in the proximity of the offered property, but there will be no children living or regularly visiting the property.

chunks.title: Opportunity to view property interior — register management and referrals
chunks.text: Was the client offered the opportunity to view the interior of the property before deciding whether to accept? Examples of reasons considered good and sufficient Examples of reasons unlikely to be considered good and sufficient - The housing provider was unable to show the client the inside of the property as there were trades people working on the property. - Client refused to look inside the property because they didn't like the outside colour of the property.

chunks.title: Other considerations — register management and referrals
chunks.text: Are there any other reasons the client has given that MSD considers are a good reason to decline the offered property? Examples of reasons considered good and sufficient Examples of reasons unlikely to be considered good and sufficient - Location of property impacts strongly on the beliefs and/or religious views of the client. - Client is vegetarian and feels strongly about living next door to a butchery. - Client feels strongly about living near a cell phone tower or power pylons. Note this list is not exhaustive. If you are unsure whether the client's decline reason is good and sufficient, please contact Helpline for advice.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reasons for declining offer of a property — register management and referrals
chunks.text: To decide if a client has a good and sufficient reason for declining the offer of a property, you need to consider the information provided by the housing provider and the client. Each case should be considered on its merits. Where the information provided or reasons given for declining an offer conflict, or cannot be agreed, the client should generally be given the benefit of the doubt.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reasons — register management and referrals
chunks.text: You need to consider whether the client had a good and sufficient reason to decline the property offer (including any alternative or additional reasons given). You must consider the following: - does the offered property meet the assessed needs (property requirements) of the client (or any other person included in the offer): does the offered property have the correct number of bedrooms for the client?does the design and layout cater for the needs of the client eg modified bathrooms, wide enough doorways, flat section, living area fit for purpose?do the features of the property meet the client's disability needs, needs of children, or specific needs due to being elderly?is the fencing appropriate to meet the needs of the client?is the offered property within reasonable proximity and access to the client's essential services eg medical services, public transport, and where appropriate schools and early childhood centres?is the offered property within reasonable proximity and access to the client's workplace either via private or public transport? - does the offered property have the correct number of bedrooms for the client? - does the design and layout cater for the needs of the client eg modified bathrooms, wide enough doorways, flat section, living area fit for purpose? - do the features of the property meet the client's disability needs, needs of children, or specific needs due to being elderly? - is the fencing appropriate to meet the needs of the client? - is the offered property within reasonable proximity and access to the client's essential services eg medical services, public transport, and where appropriate schools and early childhood centres? - is the offered property within reasonable proximity and access to the client's workplace either via private or public transport? - will requiring the client to accept the offer (in your opinion) have an adverse effect on the health, well-being, or safety of the client? - is the offered property unsuitable because of any court, bail, or release conditions which would prevent the client from living in the property - was the client offered the opportunity to view the interior of the property before deciding whether to accept? - are there any other reasons given by the client that you considered are a good reason to decline the offered property? Note in the above list reference to client includes any other person included in the offer.

chunks.title: Definition of person included in the offer — register management and referrals
chunks.text: Person included in the offer, means a person who, when the offer was made, the agency understood would be living in the offered property with the person to whom the offer was made. The person included in the offer would be: - an applicable person - a dependent child of the client or any person included in the offer - an additional occupant of the offered property

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason is acceptable — register management and referrals
chunks.text: When you are satisfied that the client has a good and sufficient reason, the decline will be recorded as having a good and sufficient reason. This means that the reason for decline does not count against the client. For more information see:

chunks.title: Grandparented clients — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Grandparented clients
From 1 July 2011 clients who are assessed as having a low (priority D) to moderate housing need (priority C) are not eligible for social housing.
A grandparenting provision applies to clients who were assessed as having a low to moderate housing need prior to 1 July 2011. These clients are eligible for social housing and remain on the register until they are placed in a house or request to be removed from the register.
## Change in circumstances
When a grandparented client has a change in circumstances, they remain on the register regardless of any change to their housing need.
Grandparented clients may have changes to their housing need (that is they moved through the four priority ratings) if they have a change in their circumstances. For example, they may move to having a serious housing need but then their circumstances may change again, returning them to a low to moderate need.
These clients can remain on the register until:
- they accept the offer of a suitable property not required by any priority client or
- they request to be removed from the register
## Managing grandparented clients
Grandparented clients have a duty to advise us of any change in circumstances.
Generally clients on a register will have their eligibility proactively reviewed to confirm their eligibility for social housing. The only exception is grandparented clients on a register. These clients will not have their eligibility proactively reviewed while on the register. Their eligibility or housing requirements will only be reviewed when they contact us to advise of a change in their circumstances.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Information given to housing provider at referral — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Information given to housing provider at referral
MSD must give the following information to housing providers to support placement of a client into a suitable property and to enable the provider to make an informed decision about a tenancy:
- the client's contact details
- details of their housing requirements
- any special housing requirements and
- any other information the housing provider reasonably requests to make an informed decision
Note MSD may also include any other information it considers reasonable or necessary, including matters relevant to tenancy sustainability (such as reasons for suspension, if applicable).
## Information not given to provider
MSD should not pass on information to housing providers that has no relevance to making a placement decision, unless MSD considers the provision of the information to be reasonable or necessary. For example, benefit information or details of warrant to arrest.

chunks.title: Introduction — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Clients eligible for social housing are placed on a register according to their priority rating following an eligibility assessment for social housing.
The housing need priority ratings are:
- at risk (priority A)
- serious housing need (priority B)
- moderate need (priority C)
- low or no need (priority D)
Note only clients with a priority rating of A or B are eligible for social housing and will be placed on a register.
## Clients at risk or in serious housing need
Clients who are assessed as at risk (priority A) or as having a serious housing need (priority B) are placed on the register until a suitable house becomes available.
Clients on the register:
- will be contacted on a regular basis to confirm their circumstances (to check they are still eligible for social housing and whether there has been any change to their housing needs) and
- are referred to social housing providers when suitable properties become available
## Clients with low to moderate housing need
Clients who have a low or moderate housing need are not eligible for social housing. They cannot be placed on the register. They may be eligible for other financial assistance and could be referred to an options and advice seminar to assist them with finding alternative housing solutions.
## Exception for grandparented clients
Grandparenting provisions apply to clients who were assessed prior to 2011 as having a low (priority D) to moderate (priority C) housing need. These clients can remain on the register until they are placed in a property or advise that they no longer require social housing and request to be moved from the register.
For more information see:
- Reviewing clients on the register
- Clients in specific circumstances
- Referrals
- Change in circumstances
- Changes and reviews
- Social housing Assessment of eligibility
- Social housing options and advice [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Referrals — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Referrals
Clients can be referred to a social housing provider when the housing provider has an available property that is likely to meet the client's housing requirements.
Clients may be referred individually or on a shortlist.
When a shortlist is provided, clients are ranked in order of need for housing.
Also any reasonable or necessary information we hold about the client is also passed on to the housing provider to help them make an informed decision about allocating a tenancy and the client's ability to sustain the tenancy.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Reinstatement of application — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Reinstatement of application
When a client has been removed from the register because we have not been able to contact them to confirm their eligibility, or they have requested to be removed, their application can be reinstated without the need for a new eligibility assessment, if they make contact within 8 weeks.
The client's current circumstances will need to be confirmed and if appropriate a review of the client's housing need and housing requirements completed.
A new eligibility assessment may be required where another person or household unit wants to join the tenancy.
## Exception
Grandparented clients (clients who were assessed prior to 2011 as having a low (priority C) to moderate (priority D) housing need), who request to be removed from the register cannot be reinstated. Grandparented clients are not at risk or do not have serious housing need.
If a client has been removed from the register because they are not at risk or do not have a serious housing need, they will need to complete a new application for social housing.
## Reapplication for social housing after declining suitable housing without good and sufficient reason
After a client is removed from the register, if they reapply for social housing within the next 13 weeks the decline may affect their eligibility for social housing. Their decision to decline a social housing property will be taken into account as a material factor when assessing whether they have a persistent housing need that is serious or severe.
If they reapply within the 13 weeks and their situation has changed, any material change in circumstances will also be taken into account when assessing whether the person has a housing need that is serious or severe. For more information see:
- Assessment of eligibility Reapplying for social housing within 13 weeks of declining a property
- Assessment of eligibility Material change in circumstances
For more information see:
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Assessment of eligibility Assessment for current tenants

chunks.title: Removal from the register — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Removal from the register
Clients are removed from the register when:
- they are no longer eligible to be allocated social housing
- their need for housing or their housing requirements cannot be confirmed
- they have requested to be removed (including grandparented clients) or
- they have declined an offer of a suitable property without a good and sufficient reason
## Client makes contact within 8 weeks
Some clients removed from the register can have their applications reinstated if they make contact and circumstances can be confirmed within 8 weeks of being removed, or when the client requested to be removed and requests their application be reinstated.
If a grandparented client requests to be removed, their social housing application cannot be reinstated on the register but they can re-apply for social housing.
Note clients who make contact within 8 weeks who are found not to have a good and sufficient reason for declining a property will not have their social housing application reinstated. They will need to re-apply for social housing to determine they have a persistent housing need that is serious or severe.
## Client makes contact after 8 weeks
Clients who make contact after 8 weeks of their application being removed from the register will need to make a new application for social housing.
For more information see:
- Reinstatement of application
- Change in circumstances
- Reviewing clients on the register
- Application status
- Referrals

chunks.title: Reviewing clients on the register — register management and referrals
chunks.text: A client's eligibility for social housing may be reviewed by MSD at any time while they are on the register. This is to make sure clients with the greatest housing need are housed first. Clients on the register are reviewed regularly to: - establish if they still need social housing - determine if their details are current - determine if their circumstances have changed and - promote alternative appropriate housing solutions

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — register management and referrals
chunks.text: If a client has had a change in circumstances likely to affect or alter their priority rating, housing needs (property requirements), or rate of indicative Income Related Rent, their application must be reviewed. The client must be advised if the outcome of the review changes their priority rating or housing needs (requirements). If a client no longer requires social housing, they must be removed from the register.

chunks.title: Child Support is assessable income from 1 July 2023 — register management and referrals
chunks.text: From 1 July 2023, most types of Child Support are included as assessable income when determining whether a client qualifies for social housing. For more information see: Child Support is assessable income from 1 July 2023 For clients on the register, Child Support is included as assessable income at their next review or assessment on or after 1 July 2023. Only Child Support the client gets for a payment or liability period on or after 1 July 2023, is included as assessable income.

chunks.title: Example — register management and referrals
chunks.text: Adrian has been on the register since March 2023 with a priority rating of A20. On 8 August 2023, Adrian contacts MSD as one of his nephews has come into his care on a permanent basis. MSD needs to review Adrian's housing need, including his priority rating and indicative Income Related Rent. As part of this review, MSD asks Adrian about his income, including whether he is getting Child Support. Adrian confirms he is getting Child Support for one of his own children of $45 a week under a private arrangement. The most recent payment he got was on 6 August 2023 and he confirms the arrangement is expected to continue until further notice (a permanent arrangement). As Adrian gets Child Support for a payment period on or after 1 July 2023, MSD needs to include Adrian's Child Support as assessable income for the review of his priority rating and his expected rate of Income Related Rent.

chunks.title: Exception - When Child Support is the client's only income — register management and referrals
chunks.text: When Child Support is the client's only income it is included as assessable income when calculating the rate of Income Related Rent for the time both before and after 1 July 2023.

chunks.title: Client cannot be contacted — register management and referrals
chunks.text: When a client cannot be contacted during an application register review, we do not know if the client is still eligible to be allocated social housing. A client cannot be referred to a housing provider until their circumstances have been confirmed. When a client's eligibility cannot be confirmed, they must be removed from the register.

chunks.title: Shared housing — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Shared housing
Clients may be referred to a housing provider when the provider has an available shared housing property that may meet the client's housing requirements.
The housing provider will let you know what type of household make-up the property is suitable for. For example, the housing provider may have a shared housing property for people over 65 years.
Before referring a client, ensure that the client meets the household make-up for living in the particular shared housing property.
The housing provider is responsible for making sure the shared housing property is suitable and ensuring clients get along with other tenants.
Note that a client declining to live in a property because it is shared housing is not considered to be a good and sufficient reason for declining a property if that is the only reason and there are no circumstances to warrant this (eg medical needs). Clients will still be able to turn down shared accommodation if it is not suitable for their assessed needs. Each case must be considered on its own merits.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Verification of change in circumstances — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Verification of change in circumstances
When a change in circumstances alters or is likely to alter a client's housing need (for example priority rating) or their eligibility for social housing (for example, change in household composition, change in income and assets), the client is required to provide verification.
When a change in circumstances means assessment changes (for example priority changes to C or D), the client is no longer eligible and they must be removed from the register.
However, the client can re-apply to test their eligibility for social housing.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Waiver of suspension — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Waiver of suspension
Housing providers may suspend a tenant who has breached their tenancy agreement. Suspension means that the housing provider is not willing to accept the client as a tenant.
Some housing providers may have a waiver policy where the client can apply for the suspension to be lifted. When a client advises that they have a current suspension from a particular housing provider, you should encourage them to seek a waiver of the suspension if this is available. This will increase the client's opportunity for a referral to suitable housing.
They will need to satisfy the housing provider's waiver requirements. Generally they would need to demonstrate a change in their behaviour which resulted in the suspension.
For more information see:
- Client is suspended by a housing provider
- Assessment of eligibility Clients who are suspended from a housing provider

chunks.title: Warrant to arrest — register management and referrals
chunks.text:
## Warrant to arrest
Clients with a warrant to arrest can be placed on the register as a warrant to arrest does not necessarily affect their eligibility for social housing.
However, in some cases, clients with a warrant to arrest may have an active public risk alert notification. For clients with these notifications, their applications must be placed on hold to eliminate any risk to housing providers.
The reason for being placed on hold is that MSD has limited details about the level of risk the client poses and, as a result, needs to take all necessary precautions to protect housing providers who are part of the public.
Active public risk notifications are high risk alerts issued by the Police Commissioner when clients are considered to be a risk to the public. The suspension eliminates any potential risk to the providers and their staff.
Clients with an active public risk notification can be referred to a housing provider once the public risk alert has been cleared.

chunks.title: Accessibility of alternative housing — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Accessibility of alternative housing
Accessibility considers whether a tenant has access to alternative housing in the area they need to live.
It considers availability of suitable housing in the private market, and whether there are other reasons that a tenant can't access the available houses (for example because of discrimination or lack of financial means to move).
## Reasonable effort to find alternative housing
A tenant must have made a reasonable effort to find suitable alternative housing.
This may be through:
- being engaged in the Independence Planning phase
- registering and applying for houses through property agencies
- investigating home ownership options
- applying for houses advertised in newspapers or
- applying for houses advertised online (for example Trade Me)
There is no specific number of houses a tenant must have applied for to meet this criteria. It depends on their circumstances and the alternative housing options in the area.
## Determining when the accessibility criteria is met
A tenant meets the accessibility criteria when:
- they have made a reasonable effort to find alternative housing and
- there is no suitable alternative housing in the area they need to live or
- there are acceptable reasons that prevent them or their household from accessing these suitable houses due to discrimination, or lack of financial resources for bond, rent, furniture and moving costs
If the tenant and their household can access suitable alternative housing, they will not continue to qualify for social housing.
If the tenant and their household can't access suitable alternative housing, they will continue to qualify for social housing under the accessibility criteria.

chunks.title: Affordability of suitable alternative housing — tenancy reviews
chunks.text: The assessment of affordability measures the tenant’s ability to afford suitable alternative housing (with any financial assistance and resources available to them). Affordability looks at the tenant’s income as a percentage of equivalent benefit to determine if the tenant can afford alternative housing. Generally to be assessed as having continued eligibility for social housing on the affordability criteria, the tenant’s ratio of residual income will need to be less than 55%.

chunks.title: Calculation of affordability formula — tenancy reviews
chunks.text: The formula used to determine whether the household can afford alternative housing. Step number Description Total $ Step 1 Calculate net weekly income (including family tax credit received) Total A = income including family tax credit received Step 2 Calculate lower quartile weekly rent in the area the tenant needs to live minus accommodation income currently received from additional occupants and the Accommodation Supplement the tenant may be able to get Total B = lower quartile rent minus accommodation income currently received from additional occupants and the calculated Accommodation Supplement Step 3 Subtract Total A from Total B Total A - Total B = Total C Step 4 Divide Total C by the full main benefit rate they would get for that household type (including family tax credit) x 100 Residual income % Step 5 Determine whether the client can afford suitable alternative housing. Note - Accommodation income for Step 2 only includes current amounts received from those who are or will be additional occupants.

chunks.title: Consider whether assessment outcome as determined by the formula is accurate — tenancy reviews
chunks.text: MSD will need to consider whether the outcome of the formula accurately reflects the tenant's level of need including whether the tenant has a ratio of residual income under 55% by choice. The affordability outcome may need to be reviewed in the following situations (but is not limited to): - they are not getting their full entitlement to benefits or family tax credit by choice. The assessed entitlement to benefit and family tax credit should be used as their net income in this situation. - they have a sanction against their benefit which has reduced their rate paid. The assessed entitlement to benefit should be used as their net income in this situation. - they are getting Temporary Additional Support to assist with high rent costs and this may increase their level of residual income if it was taken into account - they are a seasonal worker and their income pattern has been assessed as a spike and they are currently on a benefit or lower wage for a short period of time, however the lower quartile rent will be sustainable when they are working or in a normal season - they are a student and get a Student Loan to cover living expenses (a Student Loan is not considered income for the assessment of social housing or Income Related Rent purposes). If the Student Loan was included it may cause an increase in their level of residual income if this income was taken into account and change their affordability rating. - they are a student who gets Student Allowance and Accommodation Benefit, and the use of Accommodation Supplement has resulted in a higher level of residual income

chunks.title: Assessing whether tenant still qualifies for social housing — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Assessing whether tenant still qualifies for social housing
When completing a tenancy review, MSD needs to check if the tenant still qualifies for social housing.
MSD has to consider:
- residence requirements
- income and asset limits
- whether the household has a persistent housing need that is serious or severe and must be addressed immediately as determined by:
- affordability - whether a person can afford (with any financial assistance and resources available to them) suitable alternative housing
- accessibility - whether a person has access to housing other than social housing
- sustainability - the likelihood of a person being able to sustain alternative housing
## Requesting information for social housing criteria
MSD can contact a tenant in writing to ask for information when checking if the tenant still qualifies for social housing.
MSD can also write to any third party (using the Code of Conduct for getting information) to check if the information given by the tenant is correct.

chunks.title: Availability of suitable alternative housing in the area — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Availability of suitable alternative housing in the area
The tenant may not be able to access suitable alternative housing if there is none available in the area where they currently live or need to live.
Note for alternative housing to be considered suitable, it does not have to be assessed against houses available in the lower quartile rent only. If the tenant has an affordability that indicates they have over 55% of their income available, a property might be considered suitable if it is above the lower quartile rent.
MSD would consider the tenant to have problems accessing suitable, alternative housing when:
- they can't find a modified property to suit their disability needs, for example with wheelchair ramps, modified showers, on a flat section
- there are no properties to suit their household size or type, for example there may be high demand or low supply of specific types of properties such as 1 bedroom units or 4 plus bedroom properties
- demand for housing generally is high, for example local real estate agencies have waiting lists for private rental listings and rent auctions are commonplace
- an assistance dog is required and is impacting on the tenant's ability to access alternative housing, for example a companion pet for an elderly person or guide dog for hearing assistance
Note a tenant must have made a reasonable effort to find suitable alternative housing.
## No suitable housing in the area
If there is no suitable alternative housing in the area where the tenant needs to live, they will continue to qualify for social housing.
## Suitable housing available
If there are suitable houses available but the tenant can't access them, MSD needs to consider why.
It may be because of:
- discrimination preventing a tenant accessing these houses
- lack of cash resources for costs to move
Where appropriate MSD should work with the tenant to lessen these barriers.

chunks.title: Change in circumstances during transition period — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances during transition period
When a tenant no longer qualifies for social housing, they are given a 3 month transition period to find alternative housing.
If they have a change in circumstances during the transition period, MSD need to check if they qualify for social housing again.
## The tenant now qualifies for social housing
If a tenant now qualifies for social housing based on their change in circumstances, they can stay in the property they currently live in.
However, the change in circumstances may mean a change to the type of property the tenant needs.
They will remain in the property and MSD will notify their housing provider of any change in their housing needs.
The housing provider will use the information to decide whether to place them in a more suitable, available property (treated as a housing provider-initiated transfer).
## The tenant still does not qualify for social housing
If a tenant doesn't qualify for social housing based on their change in circumstances, they can stay in the property until the end of the transition period.

chunks.title: Change in circumstances once 90 day notice has been given — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances once 90 day notice has been given
When the 3 month transition period ends, MSD will advise the tenant's housing provider that the tenant no longer qualifies for social housing.
The housing provider may give the tenant a 90 day notice period.
Once the 90 day notice period has been given, the tenant may have a change in circumstances and MSD will need to check if they now qualify for social housing.
See:
## The tenant now qualifies for social housing
If a tenant now qualifies for social housing based on their change in circumstances, MSD will ask the social housing provider to revoke the 90 day notice period to vacate the property.
The social housing provider must revoke the notice before the end of the notice period, and they can only do this with the tenant's agreement.
## Social housing provider revokes the 90 day notice
If the notice is revoked, the tenant can stay in the property they currently live in.
However, the change in circumstances may mean a change to the type of property the tenant needs.
They will remain in the current property but MSD will notify their housing provider of the change in their housing needs.
The housing provider will use the information to decide whether to place them in a more suitable available property (treated as a housing provider-initiated transfer).
## Social housing provider does not revoke the 90 day notice
If the notice is not revoked, the tenant will need to vacate the property and be put on the register for social housing.

chunks.title: Changes to household circumstances expected in next 52 weeks — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Changes to household circumstances expected in next 52 weeks
A tenant may know their household circumstances will change in the next 52 weeks which means they won't be able to sustain alternative housing.
If the affordability formula is applied based on the known change, MSD may find the tenant would not be able to stay in alternative housing once the change happens.
This means the tenant still qualifies for social housing.
## Examples of known changes in the next 52 weeks
Examples of known changes include (but are not limited to):
- tenant is on a short-term employment contract and when this ends, they will be unemployed
- tenant has a terminal illness and will need to give up work, or their partner may need to give up work to care for them
- expecting a child which means household earnings will decrease
- additional occupant moving in where the tenant or their partner will need to give up employment to care for this person

chunks.title: Check the tenant's property still meets their needs — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Check the tenant's property still meets their needs
If MSD has determined the tenant still qualifies for social housing, MSD needs to check whether the tenant's current social housing property still meets their needs.
To do this, MSD needs to determine:
- who lives in the household - signatories, applicable people, dependent children, additional occupants
- bedroom allocation - using over-crowding guidelines
- other housing needs, such as: letting area (the area the client needs to live) andother features of the property required by the tenant or their household (e.g. single level, ramps, modified features for health or disability issues or needs of small children)
- letting area (the area the client needs to live) and
- other features of the property required by the tenant or their household (e.g. single level, ramps, modified features for health or disability issues or needs of small children)

chunks.title: Dependent child for exempt tenants — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Dependent child for exempt tenants
A dependent child is either
- a child under 18 who is: the tenant or their partner's responsibilitymaintained as a member of the tenant's family andfinancially dependent on the tenant or their partner
- the tenant or their partner's responsibility
- maintained as a member of the tenant's family and
- financially dependent on the tenant or their partner
The above includes a child under 18 for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid to the tenant or their partner or:
- a child or young person (as defined under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989) who is: placed in the care of the tenant or their partner andfor whom a Foster Care Allowance is paid to the tenant or their partner
- placed in the care of the tenant or their partner and
- for whom a Foster Care Allowance is paid to the tenant or their partner
## Child 16 - 17 years
A child is not a dependent child when they are:
- 16 - 17 and
- financially independent
## Child turns 18
If a dependent child turns 18, they are still considered to be a dependent child for a limited period if they are:
- continuing in education and
- not financially independent

chunks.title: Difficulty in social functioning or lack of social skills — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Difficulty in social functioning or lack of social skills
Difficulties in social functioning and a lack of social skills can mean the tenant can't sustain alternative housing.
The tenant may not be able to find a suitable property due to difficulties in social functioning or lack of social skills caused by:
- a lack of necessary confidence and skills
- a lack of knowledge, for example, does not know who to approach to discuss other housing options
- has only ever had a social housing provider as a landlord
- lacks confidence in private sector or distrusts private landlords
When the tenant has a serious or severe and persistent level of social dysfunction requiring a high level of support, they will continue to qualify for social housing.
## Impact moving properties will have on the tenant's ability to maintain independent living
Sometimes moving properties will have an impact on the tenant's ability to maintain independent living.
MSD will need to consider the level of impact, for example:
- What are the support networks the tenant has in the community they are living in currently? family, neighbours or community organisationsclubs and activities
- family, neighbours or community organisations
- clubs and activities
- Will other accommodation provide the same support or level of support? access to essential services (via proximity or public transport)feelings of security and safety in the homea sense of wellbeing from established community links and knowledge
- access to essential services (via proximity or public transport)
- feelings of security and safety in the home
- a sense of wellbeing from established community links and knowledge
If moving properties will severely impact on the tenant's ability to maintain independent living, they will continue to qualify for social housing.
MSD need to see verification from a third party about the level of impact on the tenant.
## Examples of where moving properties may have an impact on independent living
Examples include (but are not limited to) tenants:
- with a health condition, injury or disability, eg tenants with a terminal illness, who are blind or whose sight is significantly impaired
- at risk tenants, e.g. households who have been subject to family violence and may have a protection order or property order in place
- older tenants

chunks.title: Discrimination preventing household from accessing available houses — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Discrimination preventing household from accessing available houses
A tenant may believe they are being discriminated against when they're trying to access alternative housing. MSD needs to identify the problem and the degree to which this is a barrier for the tenant.
Discrimination may include the following (but is not limited to):
- personal appearance e.g. they have facial tattoos
- language barriers e.g. English is not their first language
- social behaviour e.g. the nature or hours of employment may be seen as 'anti-social' or the number of vehicles the household owns may deter a property owner
- religion or religious beliefs
- sexual orientation
- race
- young age e.g. the tenant believes that property owners may think young people may not be responsible tenants
- physical or mental abilities e.g. the tenant believes the required modifications to a property or a perception of risk associated with mental health issues are not a liability the homeowner is prepared to entertain
- family size e.g. landlords appear to prefer to rent to smaller families with an occupancy level under the maximum
- credit history e.g. a poor credit history which includes unpaid rent in the past
- tenancy history e.g. tenant can't provide a tenancy reference as they have moved frequently or have no previous tenancy history
MSD may need to ask more questions to determine to what degree discrimination is preventing the tenant's access to alternative housing.
Some of the barriers faced by tenants may be addressed or mitigated to some extent, by support or information.

chunks.title: Income and asset thresholds — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Income and asset thresholds
Tenants who are having their tenancy reviewed must meet the income and asset requirements for social housing.
These are the same income and asset requirements they had to meet when they applied for social housing.
The income and assets of all applicable persons are included in the assessment.
If a tenant doesn't meet the income and asset requirements but still has a persistent housing need that is serious or severe, they may still qualify for social housing.
A tenant doesn't qualify for social housing if they:
- no longer meet the income and asset requirements and
- don't have a persistent housing need that is serious or severe

chunks.title: Introduction — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Tenancy reviews check whether tenants still qualify for social housing and whether the property they are in still meets their needs.
Tenancy reviews were paused in March 2020 due to COVID-19, however this pause has been lifted from 25 March 2024.
Tenancy reviews are usually done every 3 years or when a tenant has a change in circumstances.
## Outcome of reviews
If the tenant still qualifies for social housing, and their property meets their needs, they can stay in their current housing.
If their housing needs have changed, the social housing provider may be able to find the tenant another property that meets their needs.
If the tenant no longer qualifies for social housing, MSD can discuss what products and services are available to help them move into private housing. See:
Note some tenants are exempt from the 3 yearly tenancy review.

chunks.title: Lack of cash resources for bond, rent, furniture and moving costs — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Lack of cash resources for bond, rent, furniture and moving costs
A tenant may not be able to access alternative housing if they can't afford to pay for bond, rent, furniture, and moving costs.
## Assess eligibility to other assistance
MSD should check if tenants can get other assistance before deciding whether there is a lack of cash resources for bond, rent and moving costs.
If a tenant can get other assistance but chooses not to, MSD will consider that they can access alternative housing.
For more information see:
## Examples of having a lack of cash resources to move
A tenant can be considered to have a lack of cash resources for bond, rent, furniture and moving costs if they:
- do not have any appliances or furniture
- have a bad credit history and therefore cannot access store credit
- have had to sell basic possessions in order to live
- have a high level of personal debt meaning they do not have any income left after paying debt each week
- do not qualify for a Housing Support Product for bond, rent or moving costs
- do not qualify for an Advance Payment of Benefit or Recoverable Assistance Payment for furniture or
- have no ability to fund moving costs

chunks.title: Tenant does not qualify for social housing — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Tenant does not qualify for social housing
Once a decision has been made that a tenant no longer qualifies for social housing, MSD must notify the housing provider at the end of the 3 month transition period.
When MSD notifies the housing provider, MSD:
- must advise of the results of the review - whether the tenant continues to qualify for social housing or not
- may include any other information MSD considers reasonable or necessary, including matters relevant to tenancy sustainability and
- must include the information requested by the social housing provider so they can make decisions on continuing to allocate and let housing
Note if the tenant applies for a review of decision, it is their responsibility to advise their social housing provider that they have done this.
MSD needs to notify the housing provider of the outcome of the review or appeal.
## Tenant qualifies for social housing
When a tenant continues to qualify for social housing, MSD must notify the housing provider. Generally this will be done straight away.

chunks.title: Outcome of tenancy review — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Outcome of tenancy review
Once MSD has completed a tenancy review there are 3 potential outcomes.
These are:
- the tenant qualifies for social housing and there has been no change to their housing requirements (they are in the best property for their circumstances)
- the tenant qualifies for social housing but there has been a change to their housing requirements (for example their current property is no longer suitable for their assessed needs)
- the tenant no longer qualifies for social housing and they will progress to the 3 month transition period and continue to be supported to find alternative housing

chunks.title: Persistent housing need that is serious or severe — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Persistent housing need that is serious or severe
Tenants can still qualify for social housing if they have a persistent housing need that is serious or severe.
This is based on an assessment of a household's ability to rent in the private market.
It covers the following criteria:
- affordability - whether a person can afford suitable alternative housing (with any financial assistance and resources available to them)
- accessibility - whether a person has access to alternative housing in the area they need to live, whether there is suitable housing available in the private market, and whether there are other reasons a person cannot access these available houses (e.g. because of discrimination or lack of financial means to move)
- sustainability - focuses on the likelihood of a person being able to sustain alternative housing, taking into account a person's financial management, social skills, and other circumstances
MSD does this assessment based on what it considers are the household's property needs.
For example, a tenant currently lives in a 3 bedroom social housing property. When MSD do a formal check to see if the property still meets their needs, they are assessed as only needing a 2 bedroom property.
The tenant may look for alternative 3 bedroom properties as this is what they think they need.
However, they must understand that they will be assessed against the criteria (e.g. for affordability) for 2 bedroom properties.
## Tenant meets criteria for persistent housing need
If a tenant can't afford, access or sustain alternative housing based on their assessed property needs, they are considered to have a persistent housing need that is serious and severe.
This means they will continue to qualify for social housing (if they also continue to meet the other eligibility criteria, e.g. residency requirements).

chunks.title: Requesting information to assess whether tenant still qualifies for social housing — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Requesting information to assess whether tenant still qualifies for social housing
When checking if the tenant still qualifies for social housing, as part of a tenancy review, MSD can contact any person in writing to request information.
MSD can also write to and ask any person to check if the information given by the tenant is correct.
## Timeframe for tenant to provide information
The tenant must provide this information:
- no later than 5 working days after the notice was given and
- in the form that it is asked for (this may be attending a meeting or providing verification in writing)
## Information a person must provide to MSD
A person may be required to provide information to MSD under section 125 of the Public and Community Housing Management Act 1992.
However, there is some information MSD cannot ask for. This includes information protected from disclosure under legal professional privilege (e.g. legal advice).
## Consequences for tenant of not complying
If the tenant doesn't provide the information, or MSD considers they have deliberately given false or misleading information, MSD can check if they qualify for social housing based on the information MSD has about their circumstances.
They will be sent a letter which advises them:
- they need to attend a meeting to discuss whether they still qualify for social housing and
- the consequences if they do not attend

chunks.title: Residence requirements — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Residence requirements
Tenants who are having their tenancy reviewed must meet the residence requirements for social housing.
These are the same residence requirements that they had to meet when they applied for social housing.
If a tenant no longer meets the residence requirements, they will not qualify for social housing. They should be provided with support to find private housing.

chunks.title: Review of Decision — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Review of Decision
A tenant can apply for a Review of Decision when they have received formal notification of and disagree with a decision relating to:
- the assessment or re-assessment of whether: they qualify for social housingtheir current social housing property still meets their needs
- they qualify for social housing
- their current social housing property still meets their needs
- the calculation of their Income Related Rent
- the establishment and recovery of Income Related Rent debt
A tenant can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority when they do not agree with a decision which was upheld by the Benefits Review Committee under an application for Review of Decision.
## Decision not to review their housing needs
A tenant has no right of appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority (and therefore no right to apply for a Review of Decision) if they disagree with:
- a decision not to review their housing needs
However MSD will need to make sure there is a good reason why we would not review their housing needs.
For example, if a housing provider made a decision about tenancy-related matters, such as:
- the determination of a market rent rate or
- rent arrears or
- damages debt or
- whether someone can join into a tenancy agreement
## Tenancy review
A tenant cannot apply for a Review of Decision if they disagree with:
- having a tenancy review because they believe they should be exempt, but do not meet any of the exemption criteria
- the length of the 3 month transition period

chunks.title: Sustainability of alternative housing — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Sustainability of alternative housing
Sustainability measures the likelihood of a tenant being able to sustain alternative housing.
Sustainability takes into account:
- financial management abilities
- any known expected changes in situation in the next 52 weeks
- the impact moving properties might have on the tenant's ability to maintain independent living
- social skills
## Determining when the sustainability criteria is met
A tenant meets the sustainability criteria when:
- they have financial management issues
- known future changes in their financial circumstances will impact on their ability to afford and sustain alternative housing
- they have a high level of social dysfunction requiring a high level of support networks
- moving to alternative housing will severely impact on their ability to maintain their independent living
If a tenant cannot sustain alternative housing, they will continue to qualify for social housing under the sustainability criteria.
If a tenant can sustain alternative housing, they will not continue to qualify for social housing.

chunks.title: Tenancy reviews due to change in tenant's circumstances — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Tenancy reviews due to change in tenant's circumstances
All tenants (including those who are exempt from 3 yearly tenancy reviews) may have their tenancy reviewed when they have a change in their circumstances and the change means:
- they may no longer qualify for social housing or
- the property no longer meets their requirements
Note tenants who have a lifetime tenure will not have their tenancy reviewed even if they have a change in circumstances.
For more information see:
## Finding out about a change in circumstances
MSD may find out about a tenant's change in circumstances in a number of ways.
These include:
- directly from the tenant when they contact us to advise of changes that: might affect their Income Related Rentmay affect whether they still qualify for social housingmean their current property no longer meets their needs (e.g. their housing needs have changed and they may need a bigger house)
- might affect their Income Related Rent
- may affect whether they still qualify for social housing
- mean their current property no longer meets their needs (e.g. their housing needs have changed and they may need a bigger house)
- as part of a review of their housing needs and during this review the tenant provides information that they may no longer qualify for social housing
- when a tenant doesn't advise us of a change in circumstance and MSD have found out through another way (e.g. through a benefit review)
Tenants who have been investigated by MSD may have their tenancy reviewed if investigation indicates the tenant no longer qualifies for social housing.
Anyone on the tenancy agreement and their partners can give us information about a tenant's change in circumstances.
## Changes that mean households no longer qualify for exemption
Some changes in circumstances may mean tenants who have an exemption from 3 yearly tenancy reviews no longer qualify for an exemption.
These changes include:
- change in benefit type e.g. tenant or partner no longer getting Supported Living Payment
- the tenant aged 65 or over dies and there are no other tenants or a partner who qualify for this exemption
- the tenant or their partner no longer have a dependent child
If the tenant no longer qualifies for an exemption, the tenant may be selected for a 3 yearly tenancy review.

chunks.title: Tenancy reviews restart — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Tenancy reviews restart
Tenancy reviews were paused in March 2020 due to COVID-19 and restarted on 25 March 2024.
MSD does tenancy reviews for social housing tenants once every 3 years, or when a tenant has a change in circumstances that may mean they no longer qualify for social housing.
3 yearly tenancy reviews will generally apply to tenants who:
- have held their tenancy for 3 years or more and
- pay market rent and
- are not exempt from 3 yearly tenancy reviews
These tenants are more likely to be able to access and sustain private housing. MSD will still need to consider the tenant's full circumstances to determine whether the household can move into private housing.

chunks.title: Tenant has a property order — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Tenant has a property order
Sometimes a tenant or other person may have a property order for the social housing property.
Property orders, which include occupation or tenancy orders, are granted by the Court under the Family Violence Act 2018.
Under a property order, a tenant or other person living in a social housing property may be granted the right to occupy, or the tenant may have legal right to the tenancy for a specified period.
Orders may be temporary or permanent.
If a tenant (or other person) tells MSD they have a property order for the social housing property, MSD should ask for a copy of the order from the tenant (or other person). Staff should then refer the matter to Helpline. This is to confirm whether or not the tenancy review may continue.

chunks.title: Tenant has difficulty managing their finances — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Tenant has difficulty managing their finances
A tenant may not be able to sustain alternative housing if they have difficulties managing their finances.
To determine if the tenant has difficulties with this, MSD needs to consider:
- their debt levels of all debt not just MSD debt, and the impact this has on being able to use their remaining income for essential expenses
- essential outgoings that impact on the tenant being able to sustain alternative housing (for example unfunded medications)
- level of rent arrears over the last 12 months, for example rent arrears are in excess of 2 months and are mounting on a daily basis or the tenant has rent arrears and no ability to repay debt
