- any health impacts that are due to stress of financial position
- addiction issues - resulting in all or the majority of the tenant's income supporting their addiction
## Examples of difficulties in financial management
A tenant and their household may not be able to find a suitable property due to difficulties in financial management caused by:
- community or cultural expectations of financial contribution, for example tithing, sending money overseas
- debt due to having to purchase necessities, e.g. washing machine, dryer, fridge, freezer
- cannot afford essential car repairs
- partner leaving with their money
- bad investments resulting in debt
- acting as a guarantor for someone who did not repay the debt and now the tenant is liable
- addiction problem e.g. drug, alcohol or gambling which means the money is not available for essential living expenses
- cannot budget or bad financial management
- change in employment circumstances, for example have become unemployed
- not having enough money for food after paying essential costs
If a tenant has difficulties in financial management, it may mean they cannot cope emotionally or have poor health due to stress. If they have high debt, they may not have enough income to meet all their financial commitments.

chunks.title: Tenant is exempt from 3 yearly tenancy reviews — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Tenant is exempt from 3 yearly tenancy reviews
Some tenants are exempt from 3 yearly tenancy reviews.
Tenants are exempt when they or their partner:
- have a dependent child or dependent children in their care or
- are 65 years of age or older or
- get Supported Living Payment
Note a tenant or their partner who gets Supported Living Payment (caring) does not have to be living in the same property as the person they're caring for, to qualify for an exemption.
All tenants (including those exempt from 3 yearly reviews) may still have a tenancy review when:
- they have a change in circumstances that may mean: they no longer qualify for social housing or their property no longer meets their needs (requirements)
- they no longer qualify for social housing or
- their property no longer meets their needs (requirements)
## Lifetime tenure - full exemption from tenancy reviews
Tenants with lifetime tenure are exempt from tenancy reviews even if they have a change in circumstances or no longer qualify for social housing.
Lifetime tenure is when Kāinga Ora has taken over a property from either a local authority, council controlled organisation or a council-controlled trading organisation (as defined in the Local Government Act 2002) and made a commitment to allow the tenant to stay in the property for the rest of the tenant's lifetime.
Kāinga Ora must verify that a tenant has lifetime tenure.

chunks.title: Tenant lodges Review of Decision during transition period — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Tenant lodges Review of Decision during transition period
When a tenant is advised they no longer qualify for social housing and they lodge a review of the decision, the 3 month transition period will continue.
MSD may tell the housing provider the tenant has lodged a review of decision.
MSD will provide a notice to the housing provider to advise the outcome of the review.
If the Review of Decision is over-turned, the tenant will remain in their current property.
If the Review of Decision is up-held, the housing provider may take appropriate action to end the tenancy.
The tenant can appeal to the Social Security Appeal Authority.
If they do appeal, MSD will tell the housing provider.

chunks.title: Tenant no longer qualifies for social housing — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Tenant no longer qualifies for social housing
When a tenant no longer qualifies for social housing, they will be advised and given a 3 month transition period to find alternative housing.
Tenants can apply for a Review of Decision during this time.
At the end of the 3 month transition period, the social housing provider will be advised that the tenant no longer qualifies for social housing. They will also be advised, if applicable, that the tenant has applied for a review or appeal of this decision.
The social housing provider is responsible for administering any termination of tenancy notice required.
## Kāinga Ora tenants
If MSD advises Kāinga Ora that their tenant no longer qualifies for social housing, Kāinga Ora will make a decision whether or not to continue the tenancy.
When the decision is not to continue the tenancy, Kāinga Ora will issue the tenant with a 90 day notice and advise MSD the tenancy has ended.
## Community housing provider tenants
Community housing providers can choose to keep a tenant who no longer qualifies for social housing. If they decide to do this, the housing provider will not get an Income Related Rent Subsidy for the property.
When MSD tells a community housing provider their tenant no longer qualifies for social housing, the housing provider has a maximum of 30 days to decide if their tenant will remain in the property.
When the decision is not to continue the tenancy, community housing providers will issue a 90 day notice and advise MSD the tenancy has ended.
The housing provider must notify the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development if the tenant is going to remain in the property without an Income Related Rent Subsidy for that property.
The Income Related Rent Subsidy will continue to be paid to the community housing provider for the 60 day notice period. This notice period is required for a change in rent to the market rent rate.
## Ending the Income Related Rent
MSD must have confirmation from the housing provider that a tenancy has ended before MSD can stop paying the Income Related Rent Subsidy or calculating the rate of Income Related Rent.
The tenancy will finish at the end of the notice period.
The notice period can be given either:
- by the tenant or
- by the housing provider or
- in a termination order from the Tenancy Tribunal

chunks.title: Tenant still qualifies for social housing — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Tenant still qualifies for social housing
When a tenant qualifies for social housing they either:
- have no change to their housing requirements (they are in the best property for their circumstances)
- have a change to their housing requirements that mean their current property is no longer suitable for their assessed needs and their social housing provider may require them to move to a more suitable one
The tenant won't have another tenancy review for 3 years, unless they have a change in circumstances that means another review is needed.
## No change in housing requirements
If there has been no change to the tenant's housing requirements, they can remain in their current property.
MSD must advise the social housing provider that the tenant still qualifies for social housing and there is no change to their current housing requirements.
## Change in housing requirements
If there has been a change to the tenant's housing requirements that means their current property no longer meets their needs, MSD will advise the social housing provider.
The social housing provider is responsible for deciding whether to act on this information and relocate the client to an available property that meets their new needs.

chunks.title: Timeframe to lodge a review — tenancy reviews
chunks.text:
## Timeframe to lodge a review
The tenant has the right to apply for a Review of Decision at any time within 3 months of the original decision being advised.
When a tenant has applied for a hearing outside the 3 month time limit, the Benefits Review Committee must decide whether to accept the application before it considers the decision under review.
A tenant has the right to have their decision reviewed once.
If they wish to have the same decision reviewed again, refer the case to legal services.

chunks.title: Agent appointed by a Court Order — agents
chunks.text:
## Agent appointed by a Court Order
In certain circumstances, the Courts may appoint an individual to act on behalf of someone who is incapacitated. These Court Orders are made under the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988. The Court Order will list the rights and powers granted to the person named, or any restrictions to these rights and powers.
When a Court Order is provided, you should also request that the 'Appointment of an Agent' form be completed.
This provides us with information which may be used to identify the agent when they contact StudyLink. While it is preferred that this occurs, it cannot be insisted upon.
In these cases, the agent (the person named in the Order) should complete the form, and the student's declaration will be left blank. The agent needs to provide two forms of identification.

chunks.title: Agents — agents
chunks.text:
## Agents
An agent is a person or organisation who acts in the interests of another. A person can be made an agent by:
- consent of both the student and the prospective agent
- way of a Court Order or
- in exceptional circumstances, without a student's consent
'Agency' refers to the relationship that happens when one person is appointed to act as the representative of another.
Granting of agency is not controlled by the Student Allowance Regulations 1998 or the Social Security Act 2018; it is contract-based, and is governed by common law.
## What can an agent do?
The rights and responsibilities an agent has over a student's affairs are determined by the student, and depend on what role the student wishes the agent to have. Generally, anything a person can do for themselves, they may authorise an agent to do.
What an agent can do depends on the role the student wishes them to have. The student must decide exactly what rights and responsibilities they wish to give their agent; the student may also specifically exclude the agent from doing certain things. For example receiving the student's mail.
An agent's power can be limited to cover a specific issue, for example to assist with a Review of Decision, or wider to support a person through all dealings with StudyLink.
When a student appoints an agent, the student still has the right at any time to discuss their circumstances with StudyLink with or without the agent being present.
## Who can be an agent?
A student has the right to appoint any individual or organisation as their agent; however, in certain circumstances StudyLink has the discretion not to deal with an agent of the student's choice.
Generally an agent:
- should be a person of credible reputation and
- will generally be over 18 years of age (an exception to this could be a partner)

chunks.title: Appointing an agent without the student's informed consent — agents
chunks.text:
## Appointing an agent without the student's informed consent
In some situations, an agent may be appointed without the student's consent. This may be relevant, if the student is mentally incapacitated, or physically incapacitated in a way that prevents them from conveying their consent.
If an agent holds "Enduring Power of Attorney" over the student's affairs, the agent is not being appointed without the student's consent as the student has given prior approval.

chunks.title: Contact by telephone — agents
chunks.text:
## Contact by telephone
If contact is by telephone, then you must ask a minimum of 3 identifying questions.
These may include the student's details, such as the student's date of birth.
Alternatively have the representative from the organisation or company supply information that can be used to clearly identify the student.
The agent that has made contact by telephone, may not be the same person who initially completed the 'Agents' form on behalf of the organisation or company.
Any member of the organisation or company should be able to request information on the student's file once you are satisfied that the agent has identified themselves appropriately.

chunks.title: Discretion not to deal with an agent — agents
chunks.text:
## Discretion not to deal with an agent
While a student has the right to appoint any individual or organisation as their agent, in certain circumstances it may be appropriate for StudyLink to not deal with their chosen agent.
The discretion not to deal with a student's chosen agent must be exercised in a reasonable and fair manner, and be for a fully justifiable reason. Examples of where it may be relevant include:
- the agent chosen by the student is their 12 year old child
- the agent has had a trespass notice issued against them, prohibiting them from being present in StudyLink offices
If you decide not to deal with a student's chosen agent, you must inform the student of this. This would preferably occur at the start of the agency, however if you become aware of valid reasons why StudyLink should not deal with the agent after they have already been appointed, it would still be appropriate to inform the student of this.
You will also need to make notes in the student's SAL record, including:
- the name of the agent and
- the reasons why you have determined StudyLink should not deal with the agent
## Letter
You also need to inform the student of your decision in writing.

chunks.title: Enduring Power of Attorney — agents
chunks.text:
## Enduring Power of Attorney
An Enduring Power of Attorney, unlike an ordinary Power of Attorney, comes into affect after the individual becomes mentally incapacitated.
Enduring Powers of Attorney can be made in two forms.
## In relation to personal care and welfare
An Enduring Power of Attorney comes into effect only if and when the individual named becomes mentally incapacitated.
## In relation to personal property
'Property' in this context may include a student's financial affairs, including the ability to act on the student's behalf with StudyLink.
Under this form, the person granting the Power of Attorney can decide when the power may be used: namely, as soon as the Power of Attorney is signed and continuing in the event of mental incapacity, or deferring it until the student becomes mentally incapacitated.
Once this type of Power of Attorney is invoked, the student loses the legal ability to exercise the rights given to the 'attorney'.
Only the Power of Attorney or Enduring Power of Attorney has the ability to sign a document/application on the student's behalf.
## Complete "Appointment of an agent form"
Even when an Enduring Power of Attorney is provided, you should also request that the 'Appointment of an agent form' be completed.
This provides StudyLink with information which may used to identify the agent when they contact StudyLink.
While it is preferable that this occurs, it cannot be insisted upon.
In these cases, the agent (the 'attorney') should complete the form, and the student's declaration will be left blank.
The agent also needs to provide two forms of identification.
For more information see:
## Ending an Enduring Power of Attorney
Once started, an Enduring Power of Attorney will continue to operate unless it is revoked by the student.
This can be done at any time provided they have full capacity, or where this is not the case, by the Court if it is satisfied that termination is in the best interests of the student.

chunks.title: Power of Attorney — agents
chunks.text:
## Power of Attorney
A Power of Attorney is a formal legal document, authorising one person to act on behalf of another person. It can be general, for example, allowing the agent to look after all financial matters, or specific, such as managing a bank account while the student is overseas.
An individual granted a Power of Attorney over the affairs of a student may have the right to act as the student's agent when dealing with StudyLink. In such cases it is important to:
- get the 'attorney' to complete a Certificate of Non-Revocation that certifies that: they have been appointed the student's attorney andto the best of their knowledge the Power of Attorney has not been revoked
- they have been appointed the student's attorney and
- to the best of their knowledge the Power of Attorney has not been revoked
- check what powers are granted by the document
- confirm what these powers will enable the agent to do on the student's behalf, in terms of dealing with StudyLink and
- enter the following details as a 'Must View' note in the student's SAL record: the date the Power of Attorney was signedthe powers granted to the agent
- the date the Power of Attorney was signed
- the powers granted to the agent
If a student wishes to grant an agent the full legal right to make all decisions on their behalf, you should recommend that they arrange for a Power of Attorney between themselves and the agent.
Consult your Ministry of Social Development solicitor if you are unsure of the nature of a Power of Attorney document.
Only a Power of Attorney or enduring Power of Attorney has the ability to sign a document/application on the student's behalf.
## Complete 'Appointment of an agent form'
Even if a Power of Attorney is provided by the student or the agent, you should also request that the "Appointment of an agent form" form be completed.
This provides StudyLink with information which may be used to identify the agent when they contact StudyLink.
While it is preferable that this occurs, it cannot be insisted upon. The agent also needs to provide two forms of identification.

chunks.title: Process for organisations or companies — agents
chunks.text:
## Process for organisations or companies
Ensure that the agency is in the name of the company or firm and not in the name or position of any employee in the organisation.
Whenever a representative from the organisation or company acting as the student's agent makes contact with StudyLink you must always:
- request representative's to confirm their identity
- confirm the representative's link to the organisation or company and
- ensure they exercise only the rights and responsibilities granted by the student (Check the must view note in SAL)
Note StudyLink requires the agency authority in writing. You should encourage the student and the agent to complete the StudyLink 'Appointment of an Agent' form; however, you may accept another form or letter as long as it:
- names both the student and organisation (or the person) being appointed agent
- is signed by both the student and the agent and
- confirms exactly what rights and responsibilities the agent is being granted

chunks.title: When an organisation or company acts as an agent — agents
chunks.text:
## When an organisation or company acts as an agent
A student may ask that an organisation or company be appointed as their agent. This may include but is not limited to, a voluntary organisation or a beneficiary advocacy group.
Any individual member of the organisation can act as the student's agent as long as they continue to work for and on behalf of that organisation.

chunks.title: Activity Summary — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Activity Summary
After you have discussed with the client their work obligations and activities they are required to complete, you may want to provide the client an Activity Summary as confirmation of these.
Clients do not sign the Activity Summary and it is not mandatory to provide the Activity Summary to them. You may think it is appropriate to provide the printout, or a client may request this.
For more information see:
- Setting appropriate activities for clients

chunks.title: Additional hardship criteria — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Additional hardship criteria
Where a client has not been receiving student allowance you may still pay Jobseeker Support Student Hardship if you think hardship is justified after taking the following into account:
- the source of funds for living costs which have been (or are available to the client) to support themselves, including a student loan
- whether it is the clients choice not to access any funds available to them for living costs during the vacation (there is no expectation that students should use student loan funds to support themselves during the vacation period)
- the reasons why the client is not entitled to student allowance
- their parents' financial circumstances (where the client is not to entitled to student allowance because of their parents income)
- the reason the client is suffering hardship (if hardship exists) and how long the hardship will continue
- the nature of the hardship (that is what does the client have to go without)
- the health of the applicant
- ability of the client to improve their financial situation and
- any other relevant matters
For more information see:
- Hardship and student allowance

chunks.title: Age — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Age
To get Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, a client must be aged:
- 18 years or older if they do not have dependent children or
- 20 years or older if they have dependent children or
- 16 or 17 years old (with or without a dependent child) andbe married, in a civil union, or in a de facto relationship with consent orbe single and have a parental support gap
- be married, in a civil union, or in a de facto relationship with consent or
- be single and have a parental support gap
## Partners under 18 years
If a client qualifies for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship and has a 16 or 17 year old partner, the partner can be included in the benefit when they are:
- legally married or
- in a civil union or
- in a de facto relationship with Family Court Judge consent
## Getting Independent Circumstances Allowance
A single student under 18 years with no dependent children will meet the age qualification if:
- they were getting an Independent Circumstances Allowance during the academic year and
- their personal circumstances have not changed
## Getting Student Allowance with a dependent child
A single young parent aged 16 or 17 can get Student Allowance. However, they must have a parental support gap to qualify for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
## Young parent supported by their parents
A single young parent aged 16 or 17 who has been getting Student Allowance cannot get Jobseeker Support Student Hardship if they:
- are living at home or being financially supported by their parents and
- their parents earn less than the family tax credit income limit
These clients must test their eligibility for Young Parent Payment.

chunks.title: Aged 16 or 17 years with a parental support gap — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Aged 16 or 17 years with a parental support gap
A 16 or 17 year old is considered to have a parental support gap when:
- each of their parents (or guardians) is unable to support them financiallyFor example, the young person's parents or guardians may be (but not limited to): deceasedin prisonin hospitaloverseas
- deceased
- in prison
- in hospital
- overseas
- the relationship with their parents (or guardians) has broken down, and none of them is prepared to support the young person financially
- transitioning from care under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989, via an extended care agreement, parenting order
- there is a good and sufficient reason why the young person cannot reasonably expect to be financially dependent on their parents or any other person. For example (but not limited to):the young person has been subject to family violence (physical, psychological, emotional or sexual) in their parent's or guardian's home
A young person is not considered to have a parental support gap if they have the option of living with a parent or guardian, but choose not to and you are satisfied that there are no good and sufficient reasons for the young person not to be living with that parent or guardian.

chunks.title: All reasonable steps to meet social obligations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
There may be some situations where a client or their partner (if any) can't comply with their social obligations for reasons beyond their control. You can accept that a client has taken all reasonable steps to comply if they:
- have made a commitment to meet their social obligation at a more appropriate time and
- are working towards addressing any barriers they are facing
Every client's situation is different and what may be a barrier to meeting social obligations for one family may not be for another.
The decision about whether a client is taking all reasonable steps to comply lies with Work and Income.
Below are some of the situations you should take into account when considering that the client is taking all reasonable steps:
- Shared care/carer issues in the family or family court proceedings occurring
The parent who is not the principal caregiver does not support their child having to attend recognised early childhood education programmes. It would not be reasonable for the client to be held responsible for the actions of someone else.
- Family violence or safety concerns in the family
A client discloses family violence or they have safety concerns for the child.
- Supply or availability issues
A child is on a waiting list for:
- an early childhood education programme or
- a medical centre and the client has a plan or commitment to ensure their child can access primary health care if it is required
- Additional costs of participation or engagement may put the client in hardship
The travel costs or additional early childhood education programme costs associated with attendance would cause hardship to the family.
- The child has a health condition, injury or disability
A child has an injury or behavioural problems meaning that it would not be reasonable to expect them to participate in an approved programme either temporarily or permanently.
- Family has recently moved to a new area
The family has recently moved and is in the process of re-establishing networks.
For more information see:
- Social obligations
- Monitoring compliance with social obligations

chunks.title: Approved early childhood education programmes or services — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Approved early childhood education programmes or services
An approved early childhood education programme or service includes:
- a licensed early childhood education service which includes:
- early childhood education and care centre (eg daycare centre, kōhanga reo, playcentre, kindergarten)
- home-based education and care service
- hospital-based education and care service
- a playgroup that has been certificated by the Ministry of Education (this means a playgroup is funded by the Ministry of Education and will meet certain standards)
- if before 1 December 2014, a licence-exempt early childhood education and care centre funded by the Ministry of Education (this means a playgroup is funded by the Ministry of Education and so meets certain standards)
and
- for which a fee is charged for the children to participate in the programme
Most early childhood education service offer 20 Hours Early Childhood Education. This means that children aged 3, 4 and 5 years old may be able to receive up to 6 hours per day, 20 hours per week of free early childhood education.
To help clients meet this social obligation you should discuss childcare assistance that may be available to the client.

chunks.title: Exception — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Exception
If a client was receiving Accommodation Supplement paid as a non-beneficiary they can continue to receive this during the initial stand-down.
## Special Needs Grants
If a client is suffering hardship they may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant.
For more information see:
- Special Needs Grants Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process

chunks.title: Assistance for student at other times — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Assistance for student at other times
Jobseeker Support Student Hardship can only be paid to clients between the end of 1 academic year of a programme of study and the start of the next year of the same programme.
## Between two programmes of study
When a student has completed one programme of study and enrols or intends to enrol in a new programme, Jobseeker Support Student Hardship cannot be paid during the break between the end of one programme of study and the start of another. The student may qualify for a different benefit.
## Example
Jonah finishes Year 13 of high school and enrols for a Bachelor of Landscape Architecture degree at Lincoln University.
Jonah is not between the academic years of a single programme of study and is not eligible for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship during the period between finishing high school and starting his university studies.
Completing Year 13 was one programme of study, and the degree is a separate programme of study. Jonah may be eligible for an Emergency Benefit or hardship assistance.
If Jonah is in hardship between the end of his first year of his programme of study and the start of the second year, he may be eligible for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship at that point.
## Breaks during the academic year
When a student has a break during the academic year of 3 weeks or less e.g. a semester break, Student Allowance will continue automatically.
When a student has a break during the academic year that is more than 3 weeks, Student Allowance will stop.
## Study overseas
Some clients study overseas, returning to New Zealand for their vacation period. These clients may be able to receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship where they are:
- a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident
- generally ordinarily resident
- a full-time student and
- in between academic years
The client must provide proof of:
- commencement and cessation date of study overseas and
- income received in the last 26 and 52 weeks

chunks.title: Assistance to move back to an area that is not a limited employment location — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Assistance to move back to an area that is not a limited employment location
This applies where a client has moved to a limited employment location and cannot meet the work obligations, and they have decided to move back to an area that is not a limited employment location.
In this situation, the client has put themselves into hardship by moving to a limited employment location where they cannot meet their work obligations. Therefore, we would generally not provide assistance to help them relocate.
However, when hardship is preventing the client from moving to an area that is not a limited employment location, you may look at an Advance Payment of Benefit using the 'other' category. This payment is recoverable and requires manager client service delivery approval.

chunks.title: Break between academic years — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Break between academic years
Jobseeker Support Student Hardship can only be paid during the break between the academic years of a student’s programme of study.
An academic year is the study year of a full-time course that forms part of a recognised programme of study. The break between academic years is the period between the last day of one year of study and the start of the next year of study in that programme.
The break between academic years must be a break in a single programme of study. This means that a student who is going from one completed programme to another is not eligible for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship in the break between the end of one programme and the start of the next.
## Example 1 – break is not between academic years
Jack is enrolled for an 18-week basic computer studies certificate. This certificate is a programme.
Jack decides to enrol in an advanced computer studies certificate in the next semester.
This is a different programme and Jack is not eligible for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship over the break between these two programmes.
## Example 2 – break between academic years
Sione has completed his first year of full-time study at Otago University for a Bachelor of Theology, which is a three year programme. Sione is in hardship and unable to support himself over the summer break between November and February.
Sione may be eligible for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship as he has a break between two of the academic years of his programme of study.
An academic year does not have to align with the calendar year. It can occur at any point during the year depending on the start and end date of a student’s programme of study.
## Example 3 – break does not align with calendar years
Hoani is enrolled in a Bachelor of Nursing degree, the first year runs from August to April. The extended break between the first and second years of Hoani’s degree is from May to July.
Their second year of study commences in August. Hoani may be eligible for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship over their extended break in May to July, as this is the period between the end of one academic year and the start of the next.

chunks.title: Cannot expect financial support from parents — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Cannot expect financial support from parents
To receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship a single young person must meet all of the qualifications and be going through a parental support gap. A 16 or 17 year old is considered to have a parental support gap when:
- they are living independently and
- you are satisfied that they have a good and sufficient reason why they cannot reasonably expect to be financially dependent on their parents or any other person
## When is it reasonable to expect support?
Consider it reasonable to expect financial support from the parents when the parents are willing and able to support the young person.
Ask the young person's parents this information (willingness to support and income details). Note they are not expected to provide proof of their income.
If the young person's parents have been living apart for some time, it is reasonable to ask both parents of the young person if they are willing and able to financially support the young person.
If the parents say they will support the young person, you should work through the details of when payments start and other arrangements for this to take place before declining the benefit.
For more information see:
- When financial support is not expected
- Independent
- Definition of 'parents'
- Unsupported Childs Benefit was paid
- Examples of good and sufficient reason

chunks.title: Caring for a child or foster child with special needs — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Caring for a child or foster child with special needs
This exemption may apply to:
- partners and sole parent clients with work obligations
- all clients with work preparation obligations (including those who have a deferral from their work obligations)
A client can be exempt from some or all of their or work or work preparation obligations if they are the:
- principal caregiver of a dependent child or
- the foster parent of a foster child
who has special needs whose welfare would be unduly harmed if the client attended employment or training, and for whom alternative care arrangements are not available, or are unable to be made.
This means the child must have 1 or more of the following:
- a physical or intellectual disability
- a health condition
- a chronic or recurring illness
- a learning or behavioural difficulty and
- be unable to attend school on a regular basis or
- be a foster child, aged 3 years or older, who is adjusting to a placement with a new foster carer
Note this can be a full or partial exemption.
## Evidence
The client must provide written evidence from a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, psychologist or social worker stating:
- what the child's illness, disability or medical condition is and its likely duration or
- an assessment of the child's learning or behavioural difficulty or
- the need for full-time care and
- the risk to the child if the client has work or work preparation obligations and
- that the child is unable to attend school
Note MSD should also consider eligibility to Child Disability Allowance. However, a child getting Child Disability Allowance does not guarantee the client, or their partner will meet the criteria for this exemption.

chunks.title: Caring full-time for person with health condition, injury or disability — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Caring full-time for person with health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to clients or partners with work preparation obligations, or partners with work obligations.
A client or partner may be caring for a person who has a health condition, injury or a disability and who needs to be cared for on a full-time basis.
This can be a full exemption.
Note you should consider whether the client or partner should transfer to Supported Living Payment on ground of caring for a person.
## Proof
The client or partner must provide proof from a health practitioner:
- that the person needs the client's full-time care
- that without that care the person would need hospital care and
- the length of time the person will need that care
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months.
This exemption should then be reviewed. At the review you should discuss the client's circumstances and consider whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption for a further period. You can ask the client to provide proof that the exemption should be extended.

chunks.title: Cash assets do not include — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Cash assets do not include
- a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2,000, or is used by the client or a member of their family for day to day accommodation
- a home property and land on which it is situated
- a motor vehicle principally used by the client for private use
- Christchurch mosques attack support payments
- Crown funds provided directly to clients to purchase Support Services and Direct Disability Support payments
- funds locked into KiwiSaver and other retirement scheme accounts
- Information share Child Support payments currently being charged as income
- MSD lump sum payments for the first 12 months after payment is made
- Payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to a system processing error from 1993 to 2014 for the first 12 months after payment is made
- Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support for the first 12 months after payment is made
- Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination for the first 12 months after payment is made
- personal effects
- Residential Care Subsidy historic review refunds for the first 12 months after the payment is made
- specified Ex gratia and compensation payments
- FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received
Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a client.
Canterbury earthquake related payments
Payments made by the Crown, Earthquake Commission, insurance companies or the Canterbury Earthquake Commission (Red Cross) relating to the Canterbury earthquake are generally excluded for the first 12 or 24 months following the date the client received the payment.
## For more information see, Types of income:
In exceptional circumstances you can disregard some of the client's cash assets see:
- Exceptional circumstances for cash assets
- Cash assets earmarked for fees

chunks.title: Cash assets earmarked for fees — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Cash assets earmarked for fees
Where a client has cash assets in excess of the hardship criteria but has 'earmarked' the savings to meet their next year's course fees you would generally not concede hardship until the course fees have been paid. However, you would need to consider the following:
- can the client pay for their fees at this time
- what are the financial alternatives for the client to meet their course fees and
- once course fees are paid, would hardship exist (that is would this reduce the clients cash assets to a level which indicates hardship)
Where a student uses their cash assets to pay for next year's fees and then applies (or re-applies) for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship you would generally not consider this deprivation of income or property. In this situation, factors to take into account when exercising the discretion contained in Schedule 3, clause 16(1) of the Social Security Act 2018 are:
- the savings were spent on an essential expense and
- exercising discretion and refusing to grant a benefit in this situation would not encourage students to save for their fees
Note the discretion contained in Schedule 3, clause 16(1) is not limited to the use of cash assets for course fees.
You also need to look at whether the client has recently given any money away or sold any assets.
For more information see:
- Income

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances
Clients must tell us straight away of any change in their circumstances, or their family's situation that may affect their entitlement to Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. Clients agree to this by signing the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship application form.
A change of circumstance may also affect the client's social obligations.
Examples of changes and how to deal with these can be found in Changes and Reviews.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
Jobseeker Support Student Hardship provides income support for a full-time student suffering hardship who does not have full-time employment during vacation periods.
## Jobseeker Support Student Hardship clients generally cannot be absent and continue to receive payment
Clients receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship cannot generally be absent from New Zealand and continue to receive payment of their benefit. The Government's obligation to pay income support usually stops when the client leaves New Zealand.
If a client is intending to travel overseas you will need to check that the client still meets the hardship criteria for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
For more information see:
- Client with work obligations, exemption or deferral
## All clients have an obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand
All clients receiving a main benefit must advise Work and Income before they leave New Zealand. If the client or partner does not advise Work and Income prior to their international travel, their benefit payments will stop from the day after they leave New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand
- Permanent absence
## Paying a benefit while a Jobseeker Support Student Hardship client is absent from New Zealand
A client or partner not otherwise entitled to be paid their Jobseeker Support Student Hardship may be able to continue to receive their payments for up to 28 days in a 52 week period, while they are absent from New Zealand for:
- Approved travel reasons
- Overseas medical treatment
## Partner absent from New Zealand
Whether a partner of a Jobseeker Support Student Hardship client can be absent from New Zealand and continue to receive payment of their benefit depends on their work or work preparation obligations.
For more information see:
- Partner with work or work preparation obligations or an exemption
## Payment of benefit while absent for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Calculating the period of absence
- Permanent absence

chunks.title: Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
These circumstances are:
- travel is required for an approved reason, and either: it is the client's first absence within 52 weeks and the permitted reason the client needs to be absent from New Zealand necessitates a period longer than 28 days orthe client has had other prior approved absences within the 52 week period and they require further approved absences which will require them to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- it is the client's first absence within 52 weeks and the permitted reason the client needs to be absent from New Zealand necessitates a period longer than 28 days or
- the client has had other prior approved absences within the 52 week period and they require further approved absences which will require them to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- the client is absent from New Zealand for an approved travel reason and their return is prevented by a new circumstance that requires them to be absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period
- the client is a young partner of a main beneficiary with youth activity obligations and they are travelling to receive support from a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family) who is residing overseas
For more information see:
- Paying for more than 28 days for an approved reason
- Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
- Paying for more than 28 days - receive support from family overseas (young partner)
- Calculating the period of absence

chunks.title: Action on return to New Zealand — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Action on return to New Zealand
You will need to look at the circumstances of the client's absence from and subsequent return to New Zealand to decide when to recommence their benefit and when to treat it as a new application.
You will need to consider the following:
- the client's intention at the time of their departure for example, did they cancel their benefit before leaving New Zealand because they did not intend to return
- did the client remain ordinarily resident during the period of absence?
- the length of time that they have been absent
- the reason for the absence
- have their circumstances changed significantly during their absence
- is the client eligible to have their benefit backdated to the day after their departure date or date of return?
- For more information see:
- Backdating benefit to the day after departure date

chunks.title: Amount of income exemption — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Amount of income exemption
When you have determined that a client is severely disabled you must then consider if they should have all or part of their income from employment disregarded for benefit purposes.
The amount of the income exemption depends on the client's individual circumstances after considering the guidelines - for severe disablement and should be:
- a reasonable amount as an incentive to recognise the personal effort that a severely disabled person has made to participate or continue in employment
- any additional costs that a severely disabled person has incurred to participate or continue in employment
- a reasonable amount to ensure that a severely disabled person is not disadvantaged by participating or continuing in employment
Note the client may be entitled to receive other types of assistance, for example Disability Allowance for transport costs to work or employment assistance.
Fully document your decision by recording the reasons and the amount of the exemption in the CMS note template, Income exemption S66A.
Contact Helpline if you need help with the assessment.
For more information see:
- Extra Help
- Effect of income on Extra help

chunks.title: Approved travel reasons — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Approved travel reasons
A client receiving Jobseeker Support (and partners with work obligations or work preparation activities assigned) are generally not able to continue to receive their main benefit payments while they are absent from New Zealand unless they meet the criteria for approved travel. Approved travel includes:
- travel for a permitted reason
- travel where the absence does not prevent the partner from meeting all of their obligations because the absence is at a time they are not required to attend employment, education or training (whichever applies)
Note clients with work obligations are not required to meet their job search obligations while absent from New Zealand on approved travel.
For more information see:
- Permitted travel reasons
- Absences that do not prevent partner from meeting obligations
## Length of travel for an approved travel reason
Clients can travel for up to 28 days on Jobseeker Support Student Hardship for an approved travel reason. Discuss with the client the amount of time that they need to be absent from New Zealand as a result of the approved reason. The client should explain the length of their intended absence.
Consider:
- the length of time the event or reason for travel will take
- the duties the client will have as part of their reason (eg if they are travelling for a funeral, do they have responsibilities beyond attending the funeral itself such as estate duties or sorting out the possessions of the deceased?)
- flight availability and travel time
Remember to advise clients that generally they are only able to continue to be paid their benefit for up to 28 days in a 52 week period. This should be taken into account when deciding the approved travel period.
## Client travelling for multiple reasons
Some clients may travel overseas for an approved travel reason but elect to stay longer for another reason that is not an approved travel reason. In this case, the client can generally only receive their main benefit payments for the period of time that the approved travel reason applies to.
For more information see:
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy
- Travel notifications made while overseas [no link find out why] procedures
- Travel notifications made on return to New Zealand [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Assistance during seasonal work — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Assistance during seasonal work
Where Jobseeker Support Student Hardship client is engaged in seasonal work they may be entitled to additional assistance.
For more information see:
- Extra Help
- Working for Families Tax Credits from Inland Revenue
If the client is eligible for non-beneficiary assistance the benefit must be cancelled.
- Employment and training Seasonal Work Assistance
- Transition to Work [no link find out why] procedures
Note if a client is liable to pay Child Support advise them to contact Inland Revenue to make alternative arrangements for payment.

chunks.title: Backdating benefit to the day after departure date — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Backdating benefit to the day after departure date
A client who leaves New Zealand without advising Work and Income of their travel can only have their benefit backdated to the day after their departure date if they
- have a humanitarian reason that justifies their reason for travel and their failure to tell Work and Income before they left
- contacted Work and Income as soon as they could reasonably have been expected to, given their circumstances after they departed and
- meet the criteria to continue to be paid their benefit while overseas (either because they meet the criteria for approved travel, or the requirement that travel be approved does not apply to them)
For more information see:
- Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure
- Contacting Work and Income as soon as the client reasonably can
- Approved travel reasons
- Paying a benefit when a client has not advised before departure
- Action on return to New Zealand

chunks.title: Birth of a child — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Birth of a child
When a client applies to have their newborn child included in their benefit, the following information is required:
- full birth certificate of the child, or confirmation from Internal Affairs that the childs’ birth was registered online, and permission was given to share the birth registration with MSD and
- written statement from the client requesting inclusion of the child
If a child's birth certificate is not available immediately, MSD can include the child in the benefit (without delay) when the client can provide:
- Plunket records or
- birth notices or
- confirmation from the client's midwife or health practitioner of the date of birth of the new child or
- hospital papers
MSD must follow-up to make sure the client produces a copy of the birth certificate.
## Extra help
If a child is born with a physical, sensory, psychiatric or intellectual disability, needs constant care and attention because of a disability, or is likely to require care for at least 12 months, MSD should test if the client qualifies for Child Disability Allowance.
When a child has ongoing additional costs because of a disability they may be able to receive a Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Calculating the period of absence — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Calculating the period of absence
The period of an absence from New Zealand for which payment of Jobseeker Support Student Hardship can continue (if approved) is up to 28 consecutive days, that is, Saturdays and Sundays are included.
In all cases, when assessing the period of absence do not include:
- the date of departure from New Zealand and
- the date of return to New Zealand
If a client is absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period the benefit should be suspended from the 29th day (unless they meet the criteria to pay for longer than 28 days).
Note if a client is leaving New Zealand permanently, the benefit must be cancelled from the day after departure.

chunks.title: Carer arrangements — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Carer arrangements
Where parents of a child live apart and the child comes into the care of the other parent it is important to establish that the arrangements made have been agreed to by both parents before you include the child in the other parents benefit.
In some cases the arrangement between both parents may not be a legal arrangement, but the child has been placed with the other parent by mutual agreement.
## Permanent or long term
To include a child as a dependent child, the change of caregiver should be with the intent of permanency or at least capable of being a long-term arrangement.
For more information see:
- Shared care
- Split care
- Temporary care

chunks.title: Change in age — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Change in age
A child's age may affects:
- the family tax credit payable
- the Best Start tax credit payable
- the partner's obligations and
- whether the child is still a dependent child
## Child turns 18
When a child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and can no longer be included in their parent or caregiver's payments, unless they are continuing in education and are not financially independent. The parent or caregiver must complete a review of circumstances to determine if they continue to qualify for their discretionary benefit such as Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, and the rate payable.

chunks.title: Change of address — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Change of address
When a client advises that they have changed their address it is important to check that the move does not affect their entitlement to Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
Note you will need to update the address in CMS.
If the client is receiving Extra Help, this will need to be reviewed.
If the client has a portion of their benefit paid to Kāinga Ora or Te Puni Kokiri for accommodation costs this may need to be changed or cancelled.
## Change in circumstances
The change of address may also indicate a change in the client's circumstances.
Examples of changes that may affect the client's entitlement to Jobseeker Support Student Hardship are:
- commencing employment
- commencing study or training
- moving to a remote area where there are few job opportunities
- change of relationship status
- dependent children coming into or leaving care
For more information see:
- Meeting job search requirements

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A client is obliged to advise the Ministry of Social Development of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
You may also review a benefit at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is getting the correct rate of payment.
A change in a client's circumstances may also mean that the client qualifies for another benefit.

chunks.title: Child absent — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Child absent
A dependent child who travels overseas can continue to be included in a benefit as long as they continue to meet the definition of dependent child.
Examples of when a dependent child can be absent from New Zealand are:
- child is overseas on an American Field Scholarship or other student exchange programme
- child is overseas visiting a non-custodial parent
For more information about the effect of absence from New Zealand for a client receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit see:
- Orphans and Unsupported Childs Benefit Absence from New Zealand

chunks.title: Child admitted to hospital — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Child admitted to hospital
Where a client's dependent child is admitted to hospital, there is no change to the rate of payment, while child remains in hospital. Family tax credit payments and Best Start tax credits continue to be paid for a child who is admitted to hospital.
Best Start tax credit stops when the child turns three years even if they are in hospital.
Depending on the nature of the child's injury, illness or disability the client may be able to receive Child Disability Allowance.
Child Disability Allowance is a non-taxable allowance paid to the principal caregiver of a child with a serious disability, who is need of constant care and attention for a period longer than 12 months.
For more information see:
- Child Disability Allowance
- Best Start tax credit Child turns 3

chunks.title: Child applies for a benefit in their own right — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Child applies for a benefit in their own right
Where a child applies for a benefit in their own right, exclude the child from the client's Jobseeker Support Student Hardship from:
- the beginning of the next pay period in which the event took placeNote there is discretion to continue payment for one more payday following the event.
or
- the date the child's benefit is granted
whichever is earlier.
Note wherever possible (and in appropriate circumstances) the date of exclusion of the child from the client's benefit and the commencement date of the child's benefit should coincide to avoid financial hardship for the family.
For more information see:
- Processing standards Child exclusions [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Child changes — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Child changes
The number of dependent children in a Jobseeker Support Student Hardship client's care and any change to the circumstance of a child can affect:
- the basic rate of benefit payable
- the rate of family tax credit payable
- payment of Best Start tax credit
- the rate of extra help payable and
- the client's obligations
## Including a child in Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
For a child to be included in a client's Jobseeker Support Student Hardship the child must be a dependent child and generally ordinarily resident in New Zealand.
When the child is not the client's natural or adoptive child, the client may be able to get an Unsupported Child's Benefit (instead of having the child included in their Jobseeker Support Student Hardship). This will mainly depend on the care arrangements.
## Changes to a child's circumstances
Change to a dependent child's circumstances is generally going to affect the client's Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.

chunks.title: Child comes into care — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: When a client has made an application to have another child included in their benefit and that child was in the care of another person the following information is required: - full birth certificate of the childSee: Verification from Internal Affairs - written statement from the applicant stating they are the principal caregiver and requesting inclusion in the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship - (where appropriate) letter from previous caregiver confirming that child has left their careNote where the client cannot get written confirmation from the previous caregiver, the new caring arrangement can be confirmed by a referee such as a teacher, Plunket nurse, minister or a Justice of the Peace. Any benefit payments the previous caregiver was getting for the child must stop.

chunks.title: Single client has child come into care — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: When a single client has a child under the age of 14 years come into their care, the client may be able to get another benefit such as Sole Parent Support. For more information see: - Qualifies for another benefit

chunks.title: Clients aged under 20 years old — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Clients aged under 20 years old who have a child come into their care no longer meet the age qualification for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. For more information see: - Parents aged under 20 years old

chunks.title: Date of review — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Include the child in the benefit from: - the date the child came into the client's care or - the date the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship was granted whichever is the later.

chunks.title: Backdating — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: When a client requests the backdated inclusion of a child and the previous caregiver was getting a benefit for the child, you will need to review when the child was excluded from the previous caregiver's benefit. Generally a child cannot be included in multiple benefits for the same period. In some situations, the previous caregiver may continue to get a benefit in respect of that child for up to 28 days. Consider all the circumstances and decide whether a debt should be established for the previous caregiver. If the date you are including the child from is a date in the previous tax year, MSD can only pay arrears of family tax credit and Best Start tax credit from the beginning of the current tax year, that is, 1 April. The client will need to apply for any arrears of tax credits before this date from Inland Revenue. A review of entitlement needs to be completed to determine the amount of any benefit arrears owed to the client for the backdated period.

chunks.title: Child in care of Oranga Tamariki — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Child in care of Oranga Tamariki
Where a child or young person is in the care, custody or sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, the cost of the child's care is the responsibility of Oranga Tamariki and it is responsible for making payments under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989. The child is not considered a dependent child and Unsupported Childs Benefit cannot be paid.
However, where there is a sole guardianship order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but the child or young person is in the custody of the caregiver, the caregiver may be entitled to Unsupported Childs Benefit if all other criteria are met.
Where Oranga Tamariki is involved, but there are no orders or agreements about care, the child can be considered a dependent child (for example when Oranga Tamariki provides services to family groups under a Family Group Conference plan only).
For information on different orders and whether they mean the child can be considered a dependent child while the order is still in place, see:
- Oranga Tamariki order in place.

chunks.title: Personal earnings — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Personal earnings
A dependent child's personal earnings are not charged as income against the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
However, a child in full-time employment and financially independent cannot be included as a dependent child in the benefit.
For more information see:
- Full-time employment
- Part-time employment

chunks.title: Family tax credit — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Family tax credit
Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit should be stopped from the start of the pay period following the date the event took place to avoid an overpayment with Inland Revenue for the client.

chunks.title: Child under the age of 18 years — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Child under the age of 18 years
When a child under the age of 18 years leaves school or tertiary education, they can continue to be included in the parent or caregiver's Jobseeker Support Student Hardship until the start of the pay period following their 18th birthday as long as the child remains a dependent child.
## Child aged 18 years old
When a child aged 18 years old leaves school or tertiary education, they should be excluded from their parent or caregiver's payment from the start of the pay period following the date the child left school or tertiary education. The parent or caregiver must complete a review of circumstances to determine if they continue to qualify for their discretionary benefit such as Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, and the rate payable.
## Family tax credit
When a child leaves school or tertiary education, family tax credits should be stopped from the day the child is excluded from the parent or caregiver's Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Child turns 18
Generally, clients getting a discretionary benefit such as Jobseeker Support Student Hardship must respond to their notice before the child's 18th birthday or the child will be excluded from their payments. The client must also complete a review of circumstances to determine if they continue to qualify for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship and the rate payable, or their payments will suspend.
If Jobseeker Support Student Hardship and any extra help is continuing at the existing rate for up to 28 days because a child has left a sole parent's care suddenly, and that child turns 18 during that period, the client is not required to complete a review of circumstances.
However, if Jobseeker Support Student Hardship and any extra help is continuing at the existing rate for up to 28 days because a child has left a sole parent's care suddenly, and a different child in their care turns 18, the client must still complete the review of circumstances or their payments will suspend.

chunks.title: Child turns 18 — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Child turns 18
A dependent child must generally be under the age of 18 to be included in their parent or caregiver's Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
When a child turns 18, they are generally no longer considered a dependent child and must be excluded from their parent or caregiver's Jobseeker Support Student Hardship from the start of the pay period following the child's 18th birthday. The parent or caregiver must also complete a review of circumstances to determine if they continue to qualify for their discretionary benefit such as Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, and the rate payable.
However, if the 18-year-old child is continuing in education and is not financially independent, the child may continue to be considered a dependent child and be included in their parent or caregiver's Jobseeker Support Student Hardship for a limited period.
In these situations, the child must be excluded from the start of the pay period following:
- the date they no longer meet these criteria or
- 31 December of the year they turn 18
whichever is earlier
Note a parent or caregiver getting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship must complete a review of circumstances when a dependent child turns 18, and when the child is excluded (if they continued to be included in the parent or caregiver's benefit after the child turned 18). If the parent or caregiver does not complete the review, their Jobseeker Support Student Hardship will be suspended.

chunks.title: Client becomes sick — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Client becomes sick
A client who has a health condition, injury or disability will no longer be able to meet their job search requirements. They may be able to continue to receive a Jobseeker Support Student Hardship with a deferral for temporary illness.
A partner with work obligations who has a health condition, injury or disability can be exempt from meeting their work obligations until they are well again.
Where a client (or partner's) health condition permanently and severely restricts their ability to work, they may be able to receive Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, an injury or a disability.
If the client (or partner) is admitted to hospital it may affect their rate of payment.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Exemptions
- Hospitalisation

chunks.title: Client deferred from their work obligations — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Client deferred from their work obligations
The following clients may have a deferral from their work obligations:
- clients with a health condition, injury or a disability
- clients who are 27 weeks pregnant or more, or have complications with the pregnancy
These clients generally cannot be absent from New Zealand, and keep getting their benefit payments, unless they meet the criteria for approved travel.

chunks.title: Surviving partner or dependent child — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Surviving partner or dependent child
When a client dies (and there is a surviving partner or dependent child) before a decision is made on an application or review for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship you can continue the application or review process as if the client had not died.
## Single client
When there is no surviving partner or dependent children the benefit application should generally be declined. However, if there is a request for the application to be decided or the circumstances of the situation merit it, consult your service manager for a decision.
## Funeral Grant
In situations when the decision to grant or review Jobseeker Support Student Hardship is made after the date of death of the client, you decide any Funeral Grant as if the deceased client were getting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.

chunks.title: Partner with dependent children — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Partner with dependent children
When a client dies and the surviving partner has a youngest dependent child aged under 14 years, the partner may be able to get Sole Parent Support.
For more information see:
- Sole Parent Support
If the partner has a dependent child aged 14 years or over they may be able to receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship with an exemption from their work obligations to allow them time to adjust to their new circumstances.
Note no initial stand-down is imposed when a partner applies for Sole Parent Support within 28 days of the client's death. When the partner delays their application outside 28 days, an initial stand-down will be imposed.
## Partner with no dependent children
When there are no dependent children, the surviving partner must test their entitlement to an appropriate benefit, in their own right.
The surviving partner may be granted a new benefit (instead of terminal benefit) from the day after their partner's death if it is to their financial advantage.
For more information see:
- Terminal benefit rate
## Delay in granting ACC payments
When the death was the result of an accident, the surviving partner may be able to get weekly compensation payments from ACC.
If it is likely there will be a delay in deciding their claim, the partner can apply for a benefit they may qualify for in the interim.
The client must acknowledge, in writing, that benefit payments made will be refunded once weekly compensation payments are granted.

chunks.title: Client engaged in study — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Client engaged in study
A full-time student can receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship between the end of one academic year of a programme of study and the start of the next when they are experiencing hardship and do not have employment during that break.
If MSD is unsure whether a student is full-time or not, they can ask the student to provide verification from their education provider.
The Jobseeker Support Student Hardship should be stopped from the:
- day the client commences full-time study if they are not going to receive Student Allowance or Student Loan living costs or
- Monday of the week the client commences full-time study if they are going to receive Student Allowance or Student Loan living costs (these payments are paid for the full week)
For more information see:
- In approved study before subject to work obligations
## Part-time study
When a client commences part-time study and the hours that they study are outside normal working hours, it is accepted that the client is available for full-time work.
If the part-time study is 8 hours or more each week, MSD must be satisfied that reasonable job search activity is taking place.
When considering the time available for job search MSD should take into consideration the client's study timetable and whether enough blocks or periods of time are available for job search activity.
To help decide if a part-time student can receive the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship see:
- Decision guidelines - part-time student

chunks.title: Examples (but are not limited to) — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Examples (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A primary client on Jobseeker Support Student Hardship was out of New Zealand visiting his father in Australia. His Jobseeker Support Student Hardship was suspended the day after he left New Zealand as it wasn't an approved travel reason. The client contacts Work and Income three days later to say that his father is in hospital as he has had a heart attack. The client has been paid for five days in the previous 52 weeks while he was absent from New Zealand leaving a balance of 23 days.
The reason for travel now meets the criteria for approved travel. The benefit is resumed from the date the client became eligible to receive the benefit overseas. The client must contact Work and Income from overseas. The benefit cannot be back-dated if the client advises Work and Income when they return to New Zealand.
A partner receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship with work preparation but no activities assigned left New Zealand to visit her mother. Two days before she was due to return, her mother's house burnt down. The client has been paid for 20 days in the previous 52 weeks while she was absent from New Zealand leaving a balance of eight days.
The reason for travel has changed and the client has not been absent from New Zealand for up to 28 days in any 52 week period. The benefit expiry is extended for an additional five days.
This client can travel for any reason. If the client hadn't informed Work and Income, their benefit would continue to be paid up until the 29th day.
Note that where the client has already been absent for 28 days in a 52 week period, consider whether the client meets the criteria for receiving a payment for more than 28 days in any 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Examples include (but are not limited to) — jobseeker support student hardship > changes and reviews jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Examples include (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A partner of someone receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship with work preparation but no activities assigned left New Zealand for a holiday in Australia. While she was in Australia there was severe flooding which meant she could not return to New Zealand on the day she was meant to return. She contacts Work and Income. The client has been paid for 20 days in the previous 52 weeks while she was absent from New Zealand, leaving a balance of eight days.
The client cannot return due to circumstances that were not reasonably foreseeable and they were outside the client's control. Work and Income would extend the client's benefit for a reasonable period for her to be able to return.
This client can travel for any reason. If the client hadn't informed Work and Income, their benefit would continue to be paid up until the 29th day.
