- as they are meeting their social obligations, you do not require any more information or contact from them and
- if they require any support regarding their social obligations they can contact Work and Income at any time
The appropriate outcome for the specific social obligations that apply to each of the client's dependent children needs to be recorded in OBMAN.
For more information on the three step process of engagement see:
- Social obligations - actively engaging with clients [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Client's job ceases during an employment trial period — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Client's job ceases during an employment trial period
When determining eligibility for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, any employment that has an employment trial period included in a client's employment agreement is assessed the same as any other employment.
A client's job can cease during the employment trial period for any number of reasons, such as:
- the employer not being able to afford the client's wages
- the employer's belief that the client lacks the necessary skills
- misconduct
- any other reason the employer decides to cease the client's employment or
- the client leaving of their own accord
When a client ceases work during an employment trial period, assess the client's eligibility to Jobseeker Support Student Hardship and commencement date the same as any other employment arrangement.
When an employer gives the client notice during the employment trial, they are not required to advise why they have decided to end the client's employment. They are however, required to provide details of their last date of employment and the date they will be paid to.
If the employer gave notice to the client of ending their employment after the employment trial, the employer must provide the client with the reason for ending their employment (ie the employment trial rules do not apply).
To determine eligibility and commencement date of the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, the client needs to provide evidence and reasons for ceasing their employment, their last day of duty and last date paid to.
If the client cannot provide this evidence and reason for their employment ceasing, their last day of duty or last date paid to, you can contact the client's employer and ask them to complete the Employment and earnings information for applications (V06) form.
If the client's employer does not provide the reason for the client's employment ceasing during the employment trial, accept the client's reasons for the termination and continue with the application process. However, the employer must complete the date ceased and last pay details.
For more information see:
- Employment trial period of up to 90 days
- Clients with specific circumstances
- Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct

chunks.title: Client's situation changes during regular engagement and support process — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Client's situation changes during regular engagement and support process
A client and their partner (if any) may have a change of circumstance which means they can no longer comply with a social obligation. These changes may include (but are not limited to):
- a dependent child leaves their care or
- a dependent child changes age and the social obligations that apply for the dependent child in their care are no longer relevant
If this happens during regular engagement and support, the client cannot be failed and they are no longer subject to the social obligation.
For more information see:
- Social obligations - actively engaging with clients [no link find out why] procedures
- Overview of social obligations according to the age of the child
- Changes and reviews Child changes
- Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation

chunks.title: Clients aged 18 or 19 years — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Clients aged 18 or 19 years
Clients aged 18 or 19 years living at home with their parents are paid a lower rate of Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
Clients must state on the application form if they live at home or away from home. Proof can be requested from the client if doubt exists.
There are certain situations where the lower rate does not apply.

chunks.title: Clients currently living in a limited employment location — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Clients currently living in a limited employment location
This applies to clients who are living in a limited employment location, and are:
- getting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
- transferring from a benefit with no work obligations to Jobseeker Support Student Hardship or
- applying for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
It does not include clients already getting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship who:
- move to a limited employment location or
- move from one limited employment location to another
A client who is living in a limited employment location and applying for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, or transferring from a benefit with no work obligations to Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, must meet the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship eligibility criteria.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
A client who is living in a limited employment location and getting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship through their local service centre must continue to meet the work obligations.
These include being available for, and taking reasonable steps to obtain, suitable employment.
## Assistance to transition into employment
Assistance to transition into employment may be available to help clients, including those living in a limited employment location, with the essential costs of attending a job interview or taking up paid employment.
Note clients who enter temporary employment during breaks between academic years are not eligible for bridging finance.

chunks.title: Clients who have a health condition or are injured or disabled — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Clients who have a health condition or are injured or disabled
A client can be deferred from their work obligations, and be subject to work preparation obligations, when they have a health condition, injury or disability and have:
- no capacity to work or
- capacity to work less than 15 hours per week
## Capacity to work at least 15 hours per week
Clients who have a health condition, injury or disability and have the capacity to work at least 15 hours per week are subject to part-time work obligations.
The information contained in the Work Capacity Medical Certificate will help MSD to determine if the client should be either:
- deferred from work obligations or
- subject to part-time work obligations
## Unable to meet work preparation obligations
Clients who have a health condition, injury or disability may be granted an exemption from their work preparation obligations if it is unrealistic that they be required to plan.
For example, when a client is:
- in hospital or
- is unable to attend an interview with MSD due to their condition
MSD should consider the information on the clients Work Capacity Medical Certificate to see if the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant) has advised of any restrictions to a client's capacity to plan.

chunks.title: Clients with dependent children - 50% protection — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Clients with dependent children - 50% protection
Sanctions are applied differently for:
- sole parent clients who fail their obligations
- couples with dependent children who both fail their obligations
Clients and partners in these situations do not have their whole benefit sanctioned. Instead, a maximum sanction of 50% of the total benefit may be imposed. The balance payable is known as 50% protection.
For more information, including treatment of supplementary assistance, see:
- Sanctions for sole parents
- Sanctions for a couple with dependent children - both fail their obligations
The 50% protection also applies to these two groups if they are subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period for voluntarily leaving employment without a good and sufficient reason, dismissal due to misconduct, or refusing to accept any offer of suitable employment.
Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only 1 sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
For more information see:
- Recompliance

chunks.title: Clients with specific circumstances — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Clients with specific circumstances
A client with specific circumstances may be able to get Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
For more information see:
- Client's job ceases during an employment trial period
- Limited employment locations
- Sole parents whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025

chunks.title: Commencement date — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
To decide when the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship can start you must first find the entitlement date.
This is usually the date that a person no longer has a means of support.
For a list of these dates see:
- Entitlement Date
Jobseeker Support Student Hardship is subject to an initial stand-down period of up to a maximum of two weeks after the entitlement date.
Generally, the commencement date is:
- the day after the initial stand-down ends or
- the application date
whichever is the later.
However, if clients in the following circumstances apply within 28 days of their entitlement date the commencement date rules are different and the twenty-eight day rule can be used:
- clients who have a health condition, injury or disability
- sole parents
- clients who have lost the financial support of their spouse due to death, separation or ending of a de facto relationship or partner going into prison

chunks.title: Commencement after 2-week search period — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Commencement after 2-week search period
If a client's position starts in the first week after the 2-week search period ends, the first day of the position might not be the first day of the week.
If MSD is satisfied the approved position will start within that week, and the client can still complete their required 5 hours, the position period can start from the first day of the week.

chunks.title: Counting previous obligations failures — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Counting previous obligations failures
The sanction imposed depends on how often the client or partner has failed to comply with their obligations in the previous 24 months while getting a benefit.
Previous failures are only counted if the failure occurred within the last 24 months while continuously getting a benefit.
Note this does not apply to young partners who fail their youth activity obligations. These failures are counted for 12 months.
The 24-month count starts from the day the obligation failure is imposed. Each obligation failure has its own 24-month count.
## Transfer between benefits
If a client transfers between benefits, any obligations failures within the previous 24 months are still counted.
Failures on a previous benefit type will count toward the failure count on the new benefit, even if the same obligations do not apply.
Note there are very limited circumstances where a client granted Jobseeker Support Student Hardship would have previous obligations failures still counted.
This could happen with a transfer of benefit, e.g. a client studying full-time no longer qualifies for Sole Parent Support and transfers to Jobseeker Support Student Hardship during the break between academic years, before their Student Allowance begins.
## Failure of different obligations add to failure count
The failure count includes all obligation failures. If a client or partner fails a work obligation and then a later failure related to social obligations in a 24 month period, this would be counted as two failures.
## Youth clients
When a client transfers from Young Parent Payment or Youth Payment to a benefit without youth activity obligations the count will be zero. This is because the sanction regime is different for young people getting these payments.
Note the count does not return to zero when young partners of main beneficiaries with youth activity obligations move to having different obligations.
## Calculating continuous receipt of benefit
To determine whether a client has been in continuous receipt of a main benefit, MSD must disregard any period that the benefit was suspended or cancelled because:
- the client was in employment and
- the employment was less than 10 working days

chunks.title: Criteria for Money Management — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Criteria for Money Management
Clients must meet certain criteria in order for Money Management to be imposed.
A client or their partner can have Money Management imposed if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they meet with MSD within the 5 working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure decision is not disputed and overturned, and
- Money Management would be the most appropriate sanction to impose based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or they have dependent children.

chunks.title: Deciding non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or misconduct — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Deciding non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or misconduct
Before applying a 13 week non-entitlement period, you should consider the client's individual circumstances to determine whether or not it is appropriate to impose a 13 week non-entitlement period. You should:
- have a conversation with the client about why they left their employment and consider: if there was a good and sufficient reason for the client voluntarily stopping workif their employment ceased due to misconduct, what was the misconduct by the employee, and whether there is any evidence of the misconductwhether the misconduct was relatively minor, or whether there are circumstances surrounding their conduct which go a way towards excusing itwhether the client is challenging their dismissal or loss of employment
- if there was a good and sufficient reason for the client voluntarily stopping work
- if their employment ceased due to misconduct, what was the misconduct by the employee, and whether there is any evidence of the misconduct
- whether the misconduct was relatively minor, or whether there are circumstances surrounding their conduct which go a way towards excusing it
- whether the client is challenging their dismissal or loss of employment
- contact the employer to ask them to complete the Employment and earnings information for applications (V06) form
if the employer refuses to return the form or provide a reason for the client's employment having ended, no further contact with the employer should be made - instead ask the client for a statement of events regarding why they left or were dismissed from employment
- consider whether there is conflicting evidence between what the client has advised and what the employer has advised
the client must be advised of the reasons given by the employer if those reasons are the basis of a decision to impose a non-entitlement period
if there is conflicting evidence or the reason for leaving employment is not agreed between the client and the employer, you should give the client the benefit of the doubt
- consider whether there are specific circumstances where a Non-entitlement period should not be imposed
If you are uncertain whether a voluntary unemployment stand-down should be imposed, discuss the client's circumstances, in the first instance, with a service centre trainer and then with Helpline (if still required).
For more information see:
- Misconduct
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: A client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date they apply to get Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. On an ongoing basis a client must continue to remain ordinarily resident in New Zealand to receive their benefit. Some exceptions occur when the client leaves New Zealand to live overseas permanently in which case they may be eligible for a continuation of their payments under a Social Security Agreement.

chunks.title: Attributes associated with being ordinarily resident — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Ordinarily resident incorporates a number of factors. The key attributes to being ordinarily resident in New Zealand is that a person must have a close and clear connection to New Zealand on the date they apply for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. Some other key attributes that indicate that a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand include: - their physical presence in New Zealand is other than casually or as a traveller - there is some intention to remain in New Zealand for a settled purpose - despite temporary absences from New Zealand they regularly or customarily live in New Zealand - they prefer residence in New Zealand to any other country (a person cannot be ordinarily resident in 2 countries at the same time) Where it is not clear if a client is ordinarily resident you may need to ask the client further information. Some of the following questions may help to get more information: - if the client is going overseas, what are their intentions towards New Zealand (sighting return air tickets is a good indication) - the length of time they spend in New Zealand compared to their periods of absence and the reasons for the absences - property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans) - where are their cash assets principally held (New Zealand banks or investment entities or overseas based holdings) - is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and are they tax resident in New Zealand - see Inland Revenue Deciding whether you are a resident or non-resident - are they still on an electoral role and vote in central and local body elections - do they have a personal commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in their immediate and extended family community, community events, clubs and other groups) The attributes associated with being ordinarily resident can also be used after Jobseeker Support Student Hardship is granted if there is some indication the client may no longer be ordinarily resident in New Zealand.

chunks.title: How to decide — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Whether a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand is a question of fact and degree. You must consider all the factors of each individual case and decide whether they show a clear and close connection to New Zealand. You may need to ask more questions (or seek clarification of information you have) to get all the relevant information and then you must weigh up all the facts and make a decision having regard to the attributes associated with a person being ordinarily resident in New Zealand (see above). If, on the balance of facts you are not sure if the client is ordinarily resident in New Zealand ask for advice from Helpline or your manager client service delivery before you make your decision. A determination on whether a person is ordinarily resident is a discretionary legislative provision and the client should be given the benefit of the doubt in situations where their ordinary residence isn't clear.

chunks.title: Non-residentially qualified — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: You should consider other main benefits if a client does not meet the residence requirements for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. An Emergency Benefit may be granted on the grounds of hardship to a client who does not meet the period of residence requirement. However, the person must generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet the hardship qualifications for Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Ongoing work with clients who move to limited employment locations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Ongoing work with clients who move to limited employment locations
If your client can demonstrate they will meet their work obligations in a limited employment location, you will need to work closely with them to ensure they actively continue to meet these obligations.
Your client should be encouraged to:
- keep a verifiable record of what they have been doing each week to find employment and
- meet with you on a regular basis
For more information see:
- Assistance to move back to an area that is not a limited employment location
- Clients currently living in limited employment locations
- Deskfile Limited employment locations
- Meeting job search requirements
- Recompliance (Grade 1 and 2)
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Obligations failures
- Why is the client moving to a limited employment location?
- Employment and work readiness Assistance to transition into employment
- Work obligations

chunks.title: Deferrals — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Deferrals
A client can be temporarily deferred from some of their work obligations when they:
- have a health condition, injury or disability and have no capacity to work or capacity only for work that is less than 15 hours per week or
- are 27 weeks pregnant or more, or have complications with the pregnancyNote partners who are 27 weeks pregnant or more, or have complications with their pregnancy may qualify for an exemption from their work obligations. See: Exemptions
Deferrals are considered based on a client's individual circumstances.
The client doesn't have to make an application for a deferral.
A letter will be sent to the client when a deferral is added, advising why the deferral has been granted and the length of time it will be granted for.
Clients who have a health condition, injury or disability will be reminded 2 weeks before a deferral expiring, about what they need to do to extend the deferral, or meet the eligibility criteria.

chunks.title: Definition of "parents" — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Definition of "parents"
Parents in relation to a young person:
- means the parent or guardians or other person who had the care of the young person most recently before the person turned 16 years and
- includes any other parent, guardian, or former guardian, willing to have financial responsibility for the young person
Where a young person is in the care of Oranga Tamariki or other authorised care agency, the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki or any other body responsible for the care of the young person under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 is not considered to be a parent.

chunks.title: Dependent child — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
A dependent child for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- being maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 are being made
- child for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
In some situations, a child may not be living at home but is still considered to be a dependent child.

chunks.title: Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples
To help you identify when there is a 'dependent child', please see the examples below:
Household
Payments

Parents receiving Jobseeker Support half married rate, young person receiving Young Parent Payment.
Young person is no longer dependent on their parents however the baby is a dependent child of the young person.

chunks.title: Accessibility — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Accessibility
Clients must be able to report their job-search activities on MyMSD. MSD should consider a client's ability to access and report on MyMSD before imposing Report Job Search. For example:
- the client must have access to a device they can access the internet on (this can include the kiosks at a service centre)
- if the client doesn't have access to a device they can access the internet on, consider their ability to get to a service centre
- the client must have adequate digital literacy skills to report their job-search activities

chunks.title: Discharged from care — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Discharged from care
When a 16 or 17 year old has been discharged from the care of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki (or other authorised agency), they can receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship when they are no longer subject to:
- an agreement under section 140 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 or
- an order under section 78, 101 or 283(n) of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 1989 or
- a sole guardianship order under section 110 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
In these cases the young person does not need to prove the relationship breakdown with either their parents or caregivers because it has already been established through Oranga Tamariki.
## Documentation
In all discharge cases, before granting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, make sure that all relevant documentation has been received from Oranga Tamariki confirming orders have been discharged.
Encourage Oranga Tamariki to liaise with you regarding the time of discharge from care to make sure the benefit starts from the correct date.

chunks.title: Example — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Example
A client has failed their social obligations and 2 of their work obligations, and the failures have been initiated on the same day. The client disputes some of these failures as they have good and sufficient reasons. The client also recomplies to 1. The client is not sanctioned but the failure is counted because they recomplied with 1 of the failures.
Obligation
Recompliance
Action
Social obligation - failed to enrol child in ECE
Client must comply with all social obligations
Client disputes failure - has good and sufficient reason
Work obligations - failed to attend interview
Must attend another job interview - or similar activity
Client disputes failure - has good and sufficient reason
Work obligations - refused to take drug test
Must agree to being drug free
Client has no good and sufficient reason for the failure - agrees to recomply
## Example
Client recomplies for 1 failure but not for the other - failure is counted and sanction imposed.
A client has failed their obligations and the failures have been initiated on the same day. The client recomplies for one failure but not for the other failure. The sanction remains imposed until the client recomplies.
Obligation
Recompliance
Action
Work ability assessment obligation - failed to participate in a job interview
Client must participate in another job interview - or similar activity
Client has no good and sufficient reason for not participating in the assessment and does not recomply - the sanction remains imposed until the client recomplies with this activity
Work obligations - failed to attend job seminar
Must attend another job seminar - or similar activity
Client recomplies by attending another job seminar

chunks.title: Drug test job referral not suitable — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Drug test job referral not suitable
There are certain situations where it is not appropriate to refer a client to drug tested jobs as the job is not considered to be suitable. These situations include where a client is:
- taking prescribed medication
- diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- in or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence or
- has a drug issue identified by a provider and is engaging and participating in services and support offered by that provider
These situations are also to be taken into account when deciding whether a client has a good and sufficient reason for failing their drug test requirements. For more information see:
- Drug test obligations failures - Good and sufficient reasons
The first time a client presents with one of these situations, you should:
- accept that it is not appropriate to refer the client to drug tested jobs
- add a deferral from drug test obligations for an initial 30 working day period and
- advise the client that if they think they require a deferral from drug test obligations for more than 30 working days, then verification will be required
- there is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to your client
For more information see:
- Drug test - Referral delay [no link find out why]
Depending on the clients circumstances and the verification provided you can extend the deferral from drug test obligations up to six months.
For more information see:
- Taking controlled prescribed medications
- Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence
- Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: Drug tested job referral not suitable — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Drug tested job referral not suitable
These situations are also to be taken into account when deciding whether it is appropriate to refer a client to drug tested jobs. If you decide that, due to one of these situations, it is not appropriate to refer a client to further drug tested jobs you must add a Drug test obligations deferral.
For more information see:
- Drug Test - Referral Delay [no link find out why] procedure
## Client provides a good and sufficient reason
The first time a client fails the drug test obligation and provides a good and sufficient reason, you should:
- accept that the client has a good and sufficient reason
- add a deferral from drug test obligations for an initial 30 working day period and
- advise the client that if they think they require a deferral from drug test obligations for more than 30 working days, then verification will be required
- there is a Drug test obligations verification form [no link find out why] that you can provide to your client
For more information see
- Drug test job referral not suitable
- Taking controlled prescribed medication
- Diagnosed with a drug addiction or dependence
- In or awaiting treatment for a drug addiction or dependence
- Needs help to stop or undiagnosed drug dependence
- Reviewing or disputing the drug test failure
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures

chunks.title: Drug test obligations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Drug test obligations
Clients receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship who have work obligations will be subject to drug test obligations.
Clients must undertake and pass drug tests when Work and Income have identified:
- a suitable job and pre-employment drug tests are required by a prospective employer or
- a suitable course and a pre-course drug test is required as part of the admission process by a training provider
A client will fail their drug test work obligations if they have no good and sufficient reason and:
- a suitable job is available and they advise they will not apply for the job as they will not pass the pre-employment drug test
- they have been referred to or have applied for a suitable job or course and they refuse to take the pre-employment drug test or
- they have been referred to a suitable job or course and they fail or refuse a drug test
If a client fails their drug test work obligations the same five day notice period and sanctions apply as for any other obligations failure.
## Client fails pre-employment alcohol test
Job applicants may be required to be tested for alcohol use prior to being hired. However, the drug test obligation requirements do not include alcohol.
If a client failed a test for alcohol use, without a good and sufficient reason, then a work test failure could be initiated because the client has failed to participate in the job interview process.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements
- Employers requiring pre-employment drug tests
- Training providers requiring a drug test
- Types of drug tests and standards
- Client has failed a screening drug test

chunks.title: Drug test recompliance count — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Drug test recompliance count
The obligation failure that is initiated or the sanction that is imposed depends on how often the client or partner has failed to comply with their obligations in the previous 24 months while getting a benefit. This is called the 24 month failure count.
The recompliance activity that the client or partner has to complete depends on whether the client or partner has failed their drug test obligation before within the last 24 months.
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation the client or partner must complete a 6-week approved activity.

chunks.title: Is partner eligible for Jobseeker Support? — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: In order for a partner to receive financial assistance, they must be eligible for Jobseeker Support in their own right. If they meet the eligibility criteria, they will become the primary recipient of Jobseeker Support, and the original primary client will become the partner. Before the partner and primary status can be changed, it must be confirmed that the client to be the primary would be eligible for Jobseeker Support. They need to: - actively seeking and available for full-time work or - would be but they are limited in their capacity to work full-time because of a health condition, injury or disability or - would be but are temporarily unable to because they qualify for an exemption from their work obligations For more information see: - Qualifications You need to confirm that the client who will be the primary can meet the job search requirements of Jobseeker Support. To help decide if a client is able to meet the job search requirements, you will need to consider the following: - If the client had the opportunity, would they: be available for work for 30 hours or more a week (full-time work obligations)accept any suitable job offers within their abilities- which can include weekend work depending on the client's or partner's individual circumstancesnot restrict their job search to vacancies within their own tradenot restrict their job search to vacancies in their chosen occupationnot move frequently from one area to another with no intention of getting a job - be available for work for 30 hours or more a week (full-time work obligations) - accept any suitable job offers within their abilities- which can include weekend work depending on the client's or partner's individual circumstances - not restrict their job search to vacancies within their own trade - not restrict their job search to vacancies in their chosen occupation - not move frequently from one area to another with no intention of getting a job - Has the client begun to take steps to find work? For example by: searching newspapers and other media for vacanciesmaking applications for suitable jobscontacting employers about vacancies - searching newspapers and other media for vacancies - making applications for suitable jobs - contacting employers about vacancies Have a conversation with the client about what this will mean for their (and their partner's) obligations, and confirm the reasons for the change.

chunks.title: Effect of partner becoming primary on non-entitlement period — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: The effect of the partner becoming the primary on the original primary's non-entitlement period depends on what obligations they would now have as the partner. Partners on Jobseeker Support may have work preparation obligations, part-time work obligations, or full-time work obligations, depending on their circumstances. If the reason the original client was subject to a non-entitlement period still applies when they have been assigned obligations as a partner, they will continue to be subject to the non-entitlement period. For example: - If the client subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period becomes the partner and is no longer subject to the type of obligation that they failed then it may be unreasonable for them to complete a recompliance activity. The client's benefit can be resumed and the couple would receive the full married rate of benefit.Note if the client in this scenario was subject to an obligations failure, while they may not have to complete a recompliance activity, their failure count will still include the obligations failure that caused their non-entitlement period. - If the client subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period becomes the partner and now has part-time work obligations, and they were subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period because of a grade three sanction, and they failed to attend an employment seminar, they would be required to complete a six week recompliance activity or programme of activities. The primary client would be paid the half married, civil union or de facto rate of Jobseeker Support. - If the client subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period becomes the partner and now has work preparation obligations as they have a child aged under 3 years, and they were subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period because of refusing a suitable employment opportunity of 30 hours per week, it would be unreasonable for them to complete a recompliance activity. The client's benefit can be resumed and the couple would receive the full married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit. For more information see: - Payment when partner becomes primary during non-entitlement period - Effect of sanctions on assistance - Clients with dependent children - 50% protection - Work or work preparation obligations

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction for couples without dependent children — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Grade 3 sanction for couples without dependent children
If one partner of a couple with no dependent children is subject to a grade 3 sanction, this is only applied to half the couple's benefit. The non-sanctioned partner is entitled to half the couple rate of benefit, with any income reduced at half the rate of the income test that applies.
If both partners of a couple with no dependent children are subject to a grade 3 sanction the benefit is stopped (as 50% is stopped for each partner who failed).
For more information see:
- Effect on supplementary assistance - voluntary unemployment
- Effect on supplementary assistance - grade 3 sanction or job refusal
- Financial assistance during a non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Effect on supplementary assistance - voluntary unemployment — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Effect on supplementary assistance - voluntary unemployment
Clients who have a 13 week non-entitlement period because they became voluntarily unemployed cannot receive the following during their non-entitlement period:
- Emergency Benefit
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit
Note a client who was receiving an Accommodation Supplement as a non-beneficiary prior to applying and being subject to a non-entitlement period upon application, can continue to receive an Accommodation Supplement during their non-entitlement period.
If eligible, clients can still receive:
- Employment and Work Readiness Assistance to transition into employment
- Disability Allowance
For more information see:
- Financial assistance during a non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Employment during stand-down — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Employment during stand-down
If a client gains temporary full-time employment during the initial stand-down period, this may change the date the benefit can start from.
The new entitlement date is the date the temporary employment stops. Reassess the client's initial stand-down period using the income for the 26 and 52 weeks earned immediately before the new entitlement date.
For more information see:
- Example of employment during the stand-down

chunks.title: Employment trial period of up to 90 days — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Employment trial period of up to 90 days
When determining if a client qualifies for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, any employment that has an employment trial period included is assessed the same as any other employment.
Employment agreements, signed by the employer and employee, can include an employment trial period of up to 90 days.
Features of an employment trial are:
- an employment trial may be offered by an employer regardless of the number of employees a business has and
- an employer may terminate the employment agreement during a trial at any time before the end of the employment trial period even if the last day of work occurs after the expiry of the employment trial period and
- an employer is not required to provide a reason for ending the employment trial if the notice of termination was given before the employment trial period ended and
- an employee cannot generally bring a personal grievance against the employer in respect of the ending of their employment during the employment trial period
A client can still challenge the ending of their employment agreement including on the grounds of:
- discrimination or
- sexual harassment or
- racial harassment or
- duress imposed by the employer in relation to a client's union affiliations or not as the case may be
For more information about when a client's employment ceases before the end of the employment trial see:

chunks.title: Enrolled in and attending school — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Enrolled in and attending school
A client and their partner (if any) getting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship must take all reasonable steps to ensure their children are enrolled in and attending school from the age of 5 or 6 (depending on when they start school).
## Age of child
Clients with a dependent child aged 5 or 6 years old (depending on when they start school) to 15 years of age will be required to take all reasonable steps to ensure the child is enrolled in and regularly attending school.
If a child is aged between 5 and 6 years old it is the parent or caregivers choice as to whether they have their child in early childhood education or school. A child does not legally have to attend school until they are aged 6 years but most children start school at 5 years old. A client must meet the early childhood education social obligation if they choose not to enrol their 5 year old in school.
A child can legally leave school when they are 16 years or at 15 years old if they have an early leaving exemption from the Ministry of Education. A parent or caregiver cannot be asked to comply with the attendance at school social obligation if the child has legally left school or has an early leaving exemption and is no longer legally required to attend school.
## Home schooling
A client can home school their children and meet their social obligations.
If the child is aged 6 years old or over they will need to have a Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School issued by the Ministry of Education.
However, if they have work obligations, they are likely to need an exemption from those obligations.

chunks.title: Enrolment and attendance at recognised early childhood education programme — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Enrolment and attendance at recognised early childhood education programme
A client and their partner (if any) getting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, must take all reasonable steps to ensure their child is enrolled in, and attending a recognised early childhood education programme from the age of 3 until they start school.
Generally, clients should have their children participating in a recognised early childhood education programme for 15 hours a week. This is a target number of hours. It is acceptable for a child to be attending for less than this.
Recognised early childhood programmes to meet social obligations, include programmes that are:
- approved (licensed and certificated under the Education and Training Act 2020) early childhood education (ECE) programmes
- Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School or
- other approved parenting and early childhood home education programme
Generally, a place in approved early childhood education (ECE) service should be considered first.
When a place in early childhood education is not available or is not suitable (for example due to hours of operation, distance or family circumstances), then other approved parenting and early childhood home education programmes should be considered.
This is a target number of hours. It is acceptable for a child to be attending for less than this.
## Hours of attendance
Generally you should encourage your clients to take reasonable steps to have their children participating in early childhood programmes for 15 hours a week.
## Age of child
This obligation only applies to parents of children aged between 3 and 6 years (except where the child has started school at 5 years).
If a child is aged between 5 and 6 years, the parent or caregiver can choose whether to have their child in a recognised early childhood programme or school.
A child does not legally have to attend school until they are 6 years (but most children start school at 5 years old).

chunks.title: Enrolment with a primary health care provider — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Enrolment with a primary health care provider
A client and their partner (if any) getting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship must take all reasonable steps to enrol their child or children with a primary health care provider. This means being enrolled with a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation.
Taking all reasonable steps to enrol
If a client is unable to enrol their child at a practice or with a practitioner due to shortages they can be considered to be meeting this obligation if they have a plan in place to:
- be enrolled with a practice or practitioner when a place becomes available and
- get health care for their child if the child becomes sick
Note the client must provide evidence if the medical practice cannot enrol the child because of shortages.
## Age of child
The primary health care obligation applies in relation to all dependent children in the care of a client and their partner getting a main benefit. Dependent children include:
- children included in the client or their partner’s main benefit or
- children the client or partner is getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for
## Verification
Most children will already be enrolled with a primary health care provider and in most cases MSD should take the client's word that they are meeting this social obligation.
However, if MSD has information that the client may not be taking reasonable steps to meet this social obligation, MSD may ask them to get verification.
For example verification could be a letter from their medical practice or registered practitioner that says they are enrolled (most medical practices will send this when a client is enrolled).

chunks.title: Entering a refuge — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Entering a refuge
When a client is applying for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship after entering a refuge following the break-up of a relationship, the initial stand-down period can be waived.
Generally the client must enter the refuge immediately following the break-up of their relationship. This means entering the refuge within a period similar in duration to the stand-down (that is, within seven to 14 days). Where there is a delay between the separation and the client entering the refuge, general commencement date rules apply.
In this context a refuge is emergency accommodation provided by an agency or organisation. This includes (but is not restricted to) agencies such as Women's Refuge, Home and Family Society, Emergency Housing Trusts, Iwi and cultural organisations, and church organisations.
Note that accommodation provided by family or friends of the client is not considered to be refuge accommodation.
For more information see:
- Commencement date

chunks.title: Entitlement Date — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Entitlement Date
The entitlement date for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship is usually:
- the day after the completion of examinations
- the day after the last day of required attendance for the term (where the student has no exams to sit)
- the day after student allowance ceased
- the day after the date the living costs component of student loan was paid to
- the day after the end of the school year (in the case of a secondary school student)
- the day after employment ceased (that is, after any holiday pay, sick pay, cessation leave, etc. has expired)
- the date job search commenced
Note a client must be seeking full-time work. MSD can assume that job search started straight after one of the above dates unless there is any proof that it didn't.
Where the client has more than one event, MSD must use the later event for their entitlement date.

chunks.title: Example — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Keriana is getting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship of $361.32 a week (as at 1 April 2025). She fails an obligation without a good and sufficient reason and her case manager decides to impose Money Management. Her first day of Money Management is Thursday 10 July. Because Keriana’s Money Management begins in the middle of the week, only part of her benefit payment for the following week will be under Money Management. This means she will get more than 50% of her benefit into her bank account. Note: the benefit might not divide evenly by 2. When this happens, the higher amount (1 cent more) will be paid to the client’s bank account.

chunks.title: Examples of good and sufficient reason — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Examples of good and sufficient reason
Examples of a good and sufficient reason include:
- the young person's parents have moved to an area where there is low employment or employment related training prospects and the parents are unable to financially support the young person
- a serious relationship breakdown has taken place between the young person and a member of the family and someone is now at risk
- the young person has been orphaned and is living independently
- the young person was living with a partner and has now separated
- the young person has had professional advice for good reasons (for example on advice from their health practitioner) to live away from other members of the family and their parents are unable to financially support them
- the young person has been removed from home on advice from the Police that they were at risk and the young person is unable to be financially supported by their parents
The following reasons alone are not considered to be 'good and sufficient' reasons:
- the young person's parents can no longer afford to keep the young person
- the parent's house is too small
- the young person has finished a training course
- the young person is a full-time student who does not qualify for a Student Allowance because of high parental income or failure of previous studies

chunks.title: Exceptional circumstances for cash assets — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Exceptional circumstances for cash assets
You can disregard some or all of a client's cash assets when you are looking at granting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship on grounds of hardship. You can only do this if you think that there are exceptional circumstances.
Things you need to consider:
- if you refuse to grant Jobseeker Support Student Hardship on grounds of hardship to a client, will it have a serious effect on the client's health or welfare
- if you refuse to grant Jobseeker Support Student Hardship on grounds of hardship to a client, would the likely alternatives cost the Government more
- can the client realise (that is sell or get access to their cash assets) for more than the appropriate cash asset limit
- is the need for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship temporary
- what is the total amount of the client's assets, including assets that are not cash assets and
- what are the other matters that you would consider relevant to determining whether hardship exists
Note where a student has put money aside during the year for next year's school fees we would not generally disregard this. Meeting their current living costs would be seen as a priority.
For more information see:
- Cash assets marked for fees

chunks.title: Living in the same house as the parent — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Living in the same house as the parent
The full rate of Jobseeker Support Student Hardship can be paid to 18 or 19 year olds who live in the same house as their parents if:
- the parent is financially dependent on the client
- the client provides accommodation for the parent at their own expense
- the client provides a large amount of care to the parent or
- the home is a hostel, boarding house or similar, and the client and the parent each pay their own accommodation costs

chunks.title: Exemptions — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Exemptions
Exemptions from obligations recognise there are some specific situations where it may be unreasonable to expect a client to meet their work preparation obligations or work obligations..
If a client qualifies, they may be granted an exemption from some or all of their work preparation or work obligations for a specific period. Evidence may be required before an exemption is granted.
## Duration of the exemption
Each exemption has a specific period it can be granted for. In some cases, the exemption can be extended (if appropriate).
The exemption should be reviewed at the end of the exemption period. At the review MSD should discuss the client's circumstances and consider whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption again. MSD can ask the client to provide evidence of the reason to extend the exemption (if appropriate).
Note the duration of an exemption for a client due to a health condition, injury or disability is based on the next reassessment date recorded by their registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant)
## Clients with a deferral from their work obligations
Clients who have a deferral from their work obligations are subject to work preparation obligations. These clients may also qualify for an exemption from their work preparation obligations if they are unable to plan towards a return to work.

chunks.title: Failing a social obligation — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Failing a social obligation
If a client and their partner has received regular engagement and support and they are still not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, they still need to attend a final appointment.
A social obligations failure can be initiated when you consider that a client and partner have, without a good and sufficient reason, failed to meet their social obligations by:
- not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations following the process of regular engagement and support (that involves at least 3 contact steps) or
- not attending the final appointment during their regular engagement and support process
Before you initiate an obligations failure for social obligations you must get approval from your manager client service delivery. An obligation failure should only be used when all other efforts to encourage engagement and support with the client have been exhausted.

chunks.title: Failing more than one obligation at the same time — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Failing more than one obligation at the same time
If a client fails more than one obligation or activity at the same time and does not have a good and sufficient reason for one or more of the failures, the failures are counted as one failure. However, the client will need to recomply with all the failures before the sanction can be lifted.
Note Money Management is the only non-financial sanction that can be imposed when a client has failed more than one obligation at the same time at grade 1. A client must resolve all of these failures during the 4-week Money Management period in order to recomply.
For grade 1 and 2 failures, if the client successfully disputes one of the failures, the sanction imposed will remain until they recomply with any remaining failures initiated at the same time.
This policy only applies to the first and second time a client or partner fails their obligations in a 24-month period.
For grade 3 failures, a client will need to complete one six-week approved activity or programme of activities (if they wish to recomply).

chunks.title: Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations
A client and their partner (if any), when required, must:
- attend and participate in interviews with Work and Income to discuss compliance with their social obligations and
- report on compliance with specific social obligations
If during any of the three steps of engagement and support, the client does not attend or participate in interviews with Work and Income to discuss compliance with their social obligations or report on compliance with specific social obligations, you should move to the next steps of engagement and support.
For more information on the three step process of engagement see:
- Failure to comply following regular engagement and support process
- Obligations failures
- Social obligations - actively engaging with clients [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Failure to comply following regular engagement and support process — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Failure to comply following regular engagement and support process
Clients will need to attend a final appointment if they are still not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations after the 3 step process of regular engagement and support.
A social obligations failure will only be initiated when you consider that a client has, without a good and sufficient reason, failed to meet their social obligations by:
- not taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations following the 3 step process of regular engagement and support or
- does not attend the final appointment, or attends and is still not meeting their social obligations, following the 3 stage process engagement and support
Before you initiate an obligations failure for social obligations, you must get your manager client service delivery's approval.
A social obligation failure should only be used when all other efforts to encourage engagement and support the client have been exhausted.

chunks.title: Family breakdown — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Family breakdown
To receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship a single young person must meet all of the qualifications and going through a parental support gap. A 16 or 17 year old is considered to have a parental support gap when:
- their relationship with their parents (or guardians) has broken down and
- none of them is prepared to support the young person financially
It is important that the relationship breakdown must be serious. Serious situations include:
- issues of health and safety
- sexual, physical or emotional abuse
- situations where the young person would be at risk if they were to return home
Exception when a young person has been discharged from Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency care they are considered to be going through a parental support gap. The relationship breakdown has already been established by Oranga Tamariki.
For more information see:
- Aged 16 or 17 years with a parental support gap
- Discharged from care
- Unable to receive financial support from parents
- Definition of 'parents'
- Family Violence Intervention Programme [no link find out why] Doogle

chunks.title: Family violence — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Family violence
This exemption may apply to primary clients, partners and sole parents with work or work preparation obligations.
A client who has left a situation of family violence may be exempt from meeting all of their work obligations or work preparation obligations until they have had time to adjust to their new living circumstances.
This is a full exemption.
MSD should talk to the regional Family Violence Response Co-ordinator before granting an exemption. MSD should also consider:
- Is the client living in temporary refuge accommodation while they seek a permanent home?
- Are they helping children adjust to a new family situation?
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 3 months.
## Evidence
Clients who have recently left situations of family violence will not have to provide evidence.
If a client still needs an exemption after 3 months MSD can ask for evidence. MSD should consult the regional Family Violence Response Co-ordinator for advice on the most appropriate way to proceed.
Evidence can include statements from:
- their registered health practitioner
- their church
- their lawyer
- the police
- Women's Refuge
- any other person or organisation that is able to support the client's application

chunks.title: Special Needs Grants — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Special Needs Grants
Clients are not entitled to a Special Needs Grant if a sanction has been imposed, unless they become:
- sick or injured and
- incapable of participating in employment or an approved activity for at least 6 weeks
In this case, the client can get more than one Special Needs Grant, but the amount granted in any 1 week cannot be more than the combined total of:
- what the client would be entitled to that week if they were entitled to Jobseeker Support and
- the rate of Accommodation Supplement that the applicant would have gotten
For more information see:
- Effect of a non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Assistance when a client is sanctioned
## Advance Payments of Benefit
Generally, clients whose benefit continues to be paid (i.e. clients with dependent children) will not be entitled to an Advance Payment of Benefit when they have a 13-week non-entitlement period imposed. This is because they will be contributing to their hardship through not recomplying. The client's first option to improve their financial situation is to recomply.
For more information see:
- Recompliance - 13-week non-entitlement period
## Exemptions or transfers
In some instances it may be appropriate to consider an exemption or a transfer to another benefit that does not have work obligations.
For more information on transfers and exemptions see:
- Client has a health condition, injury, or disability
- Exemptions
- Changes and reviews Client qualifies for another benefit

chunks.title: Full or partial exemptions — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Full or partial exemptions
A client or partner may be granted a temporary exemption from meeting some or all of their work obligations or work preparation obligations.
Before MSD grants an exemption, it must check if the exemption reason is full, partial or both.
The client or partner can be granted a partial exemption from their work obligations they can still:
- plan for employment and
- undertake some work related activities
If the client or partner is not able to do either of the above they should be granted a full exemption.
A client or partner who has a full exemption from their work obligations may still be required to attend an interview with MSD to discuss their circumstances, and when it might be appropriate for them to start planning towards a return to work.
## Duration
Each exemption has a maximum duration. The period the exemption is granted for depends on the client's circumstances.
At the time of granting the exemption MSD should:
- advise the client or partner of the temporary nature of the exemption
- schedule a date to review the exemption if appropriate
At the review MSD should consider the client's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption. MSD can ask the client to provide evidence of the reason to extend their exemption.
Note the duration of an exemption for a client or partner due to a health condition, injury or disability is based on the next reassessment date recorded on their medical certificate by their registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner, (or dentist or midwife where relevant).
## For more information on the exemptions available to clients see:
- Table of Exemptions
- Exemptions [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Full-time study — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Full-time study
To get Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, a client must be undertaking a full-time course of study at one of the following institutions in the next academic year:
- Agricultural College
- Community College
- Secondary School
- Teachers College
- Technical Institute (Polytechnic)
- University
- Wānanga
- Private Training Establishments (PTE's)

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure
You need to be satisfied that the client or partner does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their obligations, based on the information you have, before you initiate an obligations failure.
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'.
Having considered the circumstances, was it reasonable for the client or partner not to have met their obligations?
For social obligations you will need to assess whether the client is taking all reasonable steps to meet all of their social obligations for each dependent child.
Good and sufficient reasons will depend on the obligation the client or partner has failed.
For more information see:
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Drug test obligation failures good and sufficient reasons
- Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation
- Good and sufficient reason for failing obligation to work with a contracted service provider (link to Jobseeker Support)
- Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation
Decide in favour of the client or partner if any doubt remains.
If you are aware that the client or partner has a good and sufficient reason, do not initiate an obligations failure.
If the client or partner does not have a good and sufficient reason, see:
- Effect of sanctions on assistance
- Failing more than one obligation at the same time
## Disputing the obligations failure
A client or partner can dispute the decision to initiate the obligations failure or the sanction.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason for not meeting work ability assessment obligation
Good and sufficient reasons for not meeting work ability assessment obligations include (but are not limited to) when a partner is:
- in hospital
- experiencing an acute mental health episode
Note if a partner refuses to complete a Self-Assessment or a Work Ability Assessment, and they do not have a good and sufficient reason, they will be subject to an obligations failure.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation
Once a client has been through the regular engagement and support process, and is not taking all reasonable steps to meet one of their social obligations, you then need to be satisfied that they do not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their social obligation, based on the information you have, before you initiate an obligations failure.
You should also consider whether a client has a good and sufficient reason for failing to comply with their social obligations, if they dispute an obligations failure after it has been initiated.
## Good and Sufficient reasons
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'. Having considered the circumstances, was it reasonable for the client not to have met their obligations?
Good and sufficient reasons for failing to comply with a social obligation may include (but are not limited to) when a client:
- is in hospital
- has a death or illness in the immediate family
- is experiencing family violence
- experiences an emergency or adverse event
- was dependent on the provision of assistance by the Ministry of Social Development to complete the activity, and that assistance was not supplied
- is being prosecuted under the Education and Training Act 2020
Decide in favour of the client if any doubt remains.
If you are aware that the client has a good and sufficient reason, do not initiate an obligations failure.
Note when a client has a partner, social obligations apply to both. If a client has a good and sufficient reason for failing a social obligation, talk with them to find out whether their good and sufficient reason also applies to their partner. In most cases, it is likely that if the client has a good and sufficient reason this reason will also apply to their partner.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment
You need to consider if there was a good and sufficient reason for the client to stop work.
Examples of good and sufficient reasons for ceasing employment include (but are not limited to) when the client:
- could no longer realistically transport themselves to their employment (eg where a client's place of employment has moved)
- had childcare arrangements that were not adequate or fell through
- had an unexpected event occur (eg they had to return to the family home in another location to care for a sick relative)
- left the job because the job was outside of their capabilities or the job was not suitable
- had a significant change in conditions of employment that meant the employment was no longer suitable
- needed to take leave without pay to protect their job in the future, e.g. due to an economic downturn, or an unexpected the temporary closure of the premises as a result of an event such as a fire or flood
- was not able to continue working full-time (and was unable to work reduced hours) as a result of a health condition, illness, or disability and has a medical certificate to show this
Remember you will need to consider the circumstances of each case.
For more information see:
- Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed

chunks.title: Failing 3 obligations in a 24 month period — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Failing 3 obligations in a 24 month period
If a client does not meet their obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, an obligations failure will be initiated and a graduated sanction may be imposed.
The graduated sanction regime applies to all obligations, including social obligations.
If a client fails 3 obligations without a good and sufficient reason in a 24 month period, they are subject to a grade 3 sanction - 13-week non-entitlement period.
This means:
- for clients without dependent children, 3 obligations failures in a 24 month period may result in a benefit cancellation and a 13-week non-entitlement period
- for partnered clients with dependent children, only the partner with a Grade 3 failure is affected
- for sole parents with dependent children, 3 obligations failures in a 24 month period will result in a 50% cancellation of benefit for 13-weeks
## Job refusal
A client who refuses an offer of suitable employment is subject to a grade three sanction, regardless of their failure count in the 24 month period.
Note when an applicant fails their pre-benefit activity to accept an offer of suitable employment, they are not subject to a 13-week non-entitlement period or job refusal failure, as these can only be imposed once a client is getting a main benefit.
For more information see:
- Core policy Pre-benefit requirements
- When the sanction is imposed
- Effect of 13-week non-entitlement period for partner
- Effect of non-entitlement period on financial assistance

chunks.title: Granting on grounds of hardship — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Granting on grounds of hardship
If a client does not meet the residence qualification of 2 years continuous residence, they must meet the following criteria to be granted Jobseeker Support Student Hardship:
- they must be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident
- they must be suffering hardship
- they do not qualify for any other benefit and
- they are unable to earn sufficient income to support themselves, their partner and any dependent children
Note the client may qualify for an Emergency Benefit if they:
- cannot meet the job search requirements (caring for an ill or confined partner for example) or
- are under restricted criteria, are in New Zealand on a temporary permit or temporary entry class visa (not a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident)
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support Refugee or Protected Person
To decide if a client is suffering hardship see:
- Hardship criteria

chunks.title: Hardship and student allowance — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Hardship and student allowance
One aspect of the hardship criteria is that a client:
- has been receiving a Student Allowance during the academic year of a programme of study or
- at the time of application, is entitled to a Student Allowance (or would be if their course of study had started)
In linking a client's ability to receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship to their entitlement to Student Allowance we are saying that if a person received a Student Allowance, this indicates that a level of hardship exists.
## Student Allowance subject to parental income test
For clients under 24 years of age entitlement to a Student Allowance is linked to their parents' income.
Where a client didn't receive a Student Allowance (on account of parental income) hardship may not exist. The client's parents are likely to be in a position to support them.
## Exception
Where the student did not receive (or would not receive) Student Allowance for another reason, for example they have used up their 200 weeks entitlement, you may be able to pay Jobseeker Support Student Hardship where you decide that hardship is justified, provided they meet the other criteria.
## Use of Student Loan funds
As part of the process to decide whether or not hardship exists the Ministerial Direction states that MSD should consider the source of funding the student has used throughout the academic year, including Student Loan. However there is generally no expectation that a client should use Student Loan funds to support themselves in between academic years.

chunks.title: Hardship criteria — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Hardship criteria
You can consider that a client is in hardship if:
- the client has no other means of supporting themselves and any dependent family
and
- the client has cash assets of or less than: $4,300.00 if the client is single or$7,464.00 if the client is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, or is a sole parent
- $4,300.00 if the client is single or
- $7,464.00 if the client is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, or is a sole parent
and
- the client: has been receiving a Student Allowance during the academic year of a programme of study orat the time of application, is entitled to a Student Allowance or would be entitled to a student allowance if their course of study had started
- has been receiving a Student Allowance during the academic year of a programme of study or
- at the time of application, is entitled to a Student Allowance or would be entitled to a student allowance if their course of study had started
It is important to ensure that the client is entitled to Student Allowance at the time of application and not at some future date.
Example
Emma is not entitled to Student Allowance because of their parent's income. Emma is going to turn 24 years old before the next academic year starts (and would no longer be subject to the parental income test).
Emma is not entitled to Student Allowance at the time of application for a Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
Emma may not be eligible for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, but may be eligible under other hardship criteria.
## Exception
When a client has not been getting Student Allowance (or at the time of application, is not entitled to Student Allowance) you may still consider Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.

chunks.title: Help with paying for the recompliance drug test — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Help with paying for the recompliance drug test
When a client or partner has failed their drug test obligations the second time, they must agree that they will take and pass a drug test within 25 days of agreeing to do so.
Work and Income can help the client meet the full costs of taking the drug test if they cannot meet the cost of the drug test upfront.
In this case Work and Income will arrange to cover the cost of the drug test with the provider and then recover the cost from the client by way of debt repayment.
In order for Work and Income to help meet the costs of taking the drug test, the client or partner must agree:
- to take and pass a drug test within 25 working days
- to contact drug test provider and arrange and then take the drug test; and
- to provide the results to Work and Income
Work and Income will provide the client or partner with names and contact details for drug test providers in the local area.
A client or partner can only apply once during the 25 working day period for help with the costs of the recompliance drug test upfront. The 25 working days start from the day after the client or partner agrees to recomply.
Note that Work and Income has an additional five working days to receive the results from the client or partner and to process the information.
