## Debt recovery and reimbursement to the drug test provider
Work and Income will arrange with the drug test provider to cover the cost of the drug test.
Once the cost of the drug test is reimbursed to the drug test provider it must be established as a debt to the client or partner. The amount of the debt is the same amount that has been repaid to the drug test provider.
The recovery rate should be at the appropriate level giving consideration to any other debts the client or partner may have. Debt repayment options must be discussed with the client or partner at the earliest opportunity.
This upfront assistance is only available for one recompliance drug test to be undertaken during the 25 working day period but this is recovered from the client. The cost of further tests undertaken within that period will have to be met by the client with no upfront assistance (recoverable).

chunks.title: Home schooling — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Home schooling
Clients with dependent children aged 5 or 6 years (depending on when they start school) to 16 years of age, will be required to take all reasonable steps to ensure the child is enrolled in and, attending school. Home schooling meets this obligation in some circumstances.
Clients can home school their children and meet their social obligation if they have a Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School issued by the Ministry of Education.
However, if a client and their partner (if any) have work obligations, generally they won't be able to home school their child as this could impact on their ability to actively seek or be available for work. They may qualify for an exemption from their work obligations to home school their children.
## Certificate of exemption from enrolment at a registered school
A child does not legally have to attend school until they are aged 6 years (but most children start school at 5 years old). If a child is aged between 5 and 6 years it is the parent's or caregiver's choice whether to have their child in early childhood education or school. A Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School issued by the Ministry of Education is not needed while the child is aged 5.
Once a child is aged 6 years a Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School issued by the Ministry of Education is required by law to enable a parent to home school their child.
## Social obligations cannot be required if child has legally left school
A child can legally leave school when they are 16 years, or at 15 years old if they have an early leaving exemption. A parent or caregiver cannot be asked to comply with the attendance at school social obligation if the child has legally left school or has an early leaving exemption and is no longer legally required to attend school.

chunks.title: Home schooling a dependent child — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Home schooling a dependent child
This exemption may apply to a partner or sole parent with work obligations.
A client can, in very limited circumstances, be exempt from meeting some of their work obligations:
- if they are home schooling a dependent child or a foster child and
- they have restricted circumstances that make the child's attendance at school unreasonable
Before you grant an exemption you should:
- gather all the proof required
- get the approval of the service centre manager to the exemption
This is a partial exemption only.
## Proof
The client must provide:
- proof of the restricted circumstances that makes their child's attendance at school unreasonable and
- if the child is aged 6 years or older, their 'Certificate of Exemption from Enrolment at a Registered School', issued by the Ministry of Education (if it's not a recently issued certificate, the client needs to contact the Ministry of Education to get another certificate)
For an "Application for exemption from enrolment at a registered school", see the "Home education application form" link at the bottom of the Home education page (the application form is the same for primary and secondary schooling).
All exemptions for home schooling must be approved by a service centre manager.
For more information see:
- Restricted circumstances guidelines
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Home schooling'.

chunks.title: Hours range for suitable employment — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Clients and partners with work obligations must make themselves available for suitable employment of at least: - 30 hours per week for clients with full-time work obligations - 15 hours per week, for clients that qualify for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship on the grounds of a health condition, injury, or disability - 20 hours per week for partners with part-time work obligations Although the target to meet work obligations is 15, 20 or 30 hours per week, a job can be considered suitable if the hours of work per week are within the range of hours required to meet their work obligations.

chunks.title: Suitable hours range — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Clients are expected to apply for, and accept any offers of, suitable employment. If a client is offered a job that is within the suitable hours range, but less than their obligations, then they are still expected to be available for other work, training, or other activities until they are meeting their obligations.

chunks.title: Example — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: If the client has then the client is obligated to work and the suitable hours of range is Example Full-time work obligations 30 hours per week 20-40 hours per week James is a partner with full-time work obligations. A vacancy arises for a forecourt attendant at the petrol station for 25 hours per week. The details of the job suit James' circumstances. This job is considered "suitable employment" and James must apply and accept the job, if it is offered to him, or fail to meet his obligations. Part-time work obligations 20 hours per week 15-25 hours per week Anna is a partner with a child and has part-time work obligations. She is an experienced hair dresser. A hairdressing vacancy arises for 18 hours per week at the local salon. The details of the job suit Anna's circumstances in all ways, including her caring responsibilities. This job is considered "suitable employment" and Anna must apply and accept the job, if it is offered to her, or fail to meet her obligations. Part-time work obligations 15 hours per week 10-20 hours per week Alanna has part-time work obligations because she has a health condition that limits her capacity for full-time work. A local factory has an accounts administrator position for 12 hours per week. The details of the job suits Alanna's circumstances. The job is considered "suitable employment" and Alanna must apply for, and accept the job if it is offered to her, or fail to meet her obligations. Clients are expected to apply for and accept any offers of suitable employment. If a client is offered a job that is within the suitable hours range, but less than their obligations, then they are still expected to be available for other work, training, or other activities until they are meeting their obligations. For more information see: - Work obligations - Suitable employment - Meeting job search requirements

chunks.title: Housekeepers Allowance — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Housekeepers Allowance
Housekeepers allowance can be paid to a client if their partner is not receiving a benefit and they have a housekeeper who is:
- caring for the client's home and
- substantially dependent on the client
The rate of allowance payable is the difference between:
- the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship rate payable to the client and
- the married, civil union or de facto rate of Jobseeker Support Student Hardship

chunks.title: Unable to provide visa or permit — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Unable to provide visa or permit
When a client is unable to provide an immigration visa or permit they may provide other Immigration New Zealand documents to verify their immigration status. The Ministry of Social Development can also undertake an immigration status check directly with Immigration New Zealand.
Note that Immigration New Zealand may be unable to verify immigration status for clients of British nationality who arrived in New Zealand before 2 April 1974 and do not have a passport.
For more information see:
- Permanent residence
- Immigration Act changes from 29 November 2010 [no link find out why] procedures
- Immigration status [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: In approved full-time training — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## In approved full-time training
This exemption may apply to a partner with work obligations.
A client can be partially exempt from meeting some of their work obligations if they are engaged in approved full-time training.
Consider whether the training course is the most suitable activity for the client.
Also consider if other activities (for example programmes, seminars or work experience) might be a more appropriate option for moving the client towards paid work.
Discuss and take into account the client's career background, including:
- their educational qualifications
- their employment history
- their skills and
- whether training will help them find work at the earliest opportunity
Examples of approved training courses include but are not limited to:
- Limited Service Volunteers
- Skills for Industry
- Targeted Training
- training approved by the regional contracts manager
The approved training must:
- be full-time (at least 20 hours a week)
- focus on teaching practical, employment-related skills
- support the client to gain the skills that will help them find work
Approved training does not include a course undertaken by a full-time student, as defined by the Student Allowance Regulations 1998.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted for up to 12 months or the end of the training course, whichever is earlier.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'In approved training'.

chunks.title: In approved training (no children or child 14+) — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## In approved training (no children or child 14+)
If a partner is in approved training they must continue to meet their work obligations, including being available for full-time employment, unless they are granted an exception for approved full-time training.
They are still expected to be available for work or any other activity up to a total of 30 hours each week.
The partner must understand that they have to accept suitable paid work if it becomes available.

chunks.title: Income criteria — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Income criteria
To meet the income criteria for Jobseeker Support a client must:
- have no income or
- if they have income it must not reduce the rate of Jobseeker Support Student Hardship to zero
## Partner in employment
MSD can grant Jobseeker Support Student Hardship at the married, civil union or de facto rate if a client's partner is in employment (full-time or part-time). The partner's income is charged against the benefit.

chunks.title: Income from overseas — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Income from overseas
When a client has been working overseas within the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before their entitlement date you include this in their average weekly income.
If the client cannot provide verification of their earnings, accept the information provided on their application for benefit. For help to convert foreign currency to the equivalent New Zealand dollars see the instructions below.
There is no ability to take higher living costs into account. If the client is in financial hardship during an initial stand-down they may be able to receive a Special Needs Grant.

chunks.title: Independent — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Independent
Single young people must be independent and responsible for:
- meeting their personal expenses and
- making their own decisions on such things as schooling, job seeking, medical treatment and budgeting
If the young person is sharing accommodation with another person or people, the living arrangement must be one of boarding or renting rather than being "in care".
Where the young person is not independent, the caregiver may be able to receive an Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit
## In Oranga Tamariki care
Young people who are in the care, custody or sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki cannot receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship as the cost of the young person's care is the responsibility of Oranga Tamariki.
The young person is not seen as independent.
When a young person has been discharged from Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency care they would be considered to have a parental support gap and may receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
For more information see:
- Discharged from care

chunks.title: Informing a client of the drug test obligation failure — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Informing a client of the drug test obligation failure
Once MSD has decided that a client has failed a drug test work obligation, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. The client will then be sent a letter stating that their benefit will be sanctioned and that their benefit will only be increased, restarted, regranted or continued if they:
- complete a recompliance activity
- dispute the decision to impose the sanction and MSD accepts that they have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting their work obligations or
- lodge a Review of Decision and MSD reconsiders their position and agrees with the client's review
For some clients, if it's their first obligation failure they may be eligible for a non-financial sanction instead of a financial sanction. For more information see: Non-financial sanctions.
## Recompliance for a drug test work obligation failure
Clients may have their benefit increased or restarted from the date they start a drug test failure recompliance activity.
For more information see:
- Drug test obligations failure
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons

chunks.title: Informing clients of their obligations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Informing clients of their obligations
You must ensure that the client understands:
- their obligations
- the consequences of failing to meet those obligations, in particular the sanctions that may be imposed and
- their right to review and dispute any decisions relating to a failure to comply with their obligations
Clients and partners applying for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship must:
- sign their application form and
- be given a copy of their obligations from their application form
Note that work obligations cannot be enforced until the main benefit commencement date.
## Clients transferring to a different benefit or between benefits
When a client is receiving a benefit and they have a change in obligations, a letter will be sent advising them what their new obligations are. They do not need to re-sign an obligations form.
This includes where a client is transferring:
- from Sole Parent Support to Jobseeker Support Student Hardship as their youngest dependent child has turned 14 years
- between full-time work obligations and part-time work obligations or work preparation obligations within Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
For more information see
- Obligations
- Social obligations
- Work or work preparation obligations
- Work preparation obligations
- Work obligations

chunks.title: Initial stand-down — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Initial stand-down
This is a period of up to a maximum of 2 weeks when the client cannot receive any benefit payment. The length of the stand-down depends on:
- the client's average weekly income (before tax) in the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before the clients entitlement date and
- the number of dependent children in their care at any time during the same period
The initial stand-down starts on the client's entitlement date.
Note clients can choose an income assessment period of either 26 or 52 weeks to calculate their average weekly wage for the stand-down.
For more information on the initial stand-down see:
- Average weekly income
- Number of dependent children
- Employment during stand-down
- Self-imposed stand-down
- Initial stand-down procedure
- Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process
- No stand-down applies
- Voluntary unemployment stand-down
- Deskfile Initial stand-down

chunks.title: Introduction — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Jobseeker Support Student Hardship provides income support for a full-time student who is experiencing hardship during the break between the academic years of their programme of study.
An academic year is the study year of a full-time course that forms part of a recognised programme of study.
This means that the client must have been a full-time student before they apply for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship and must be enrolled or intending to enrol in the same programme of study for the next academic year.
## For more information for clients looking for work see:
- Qualifications
- Break between academic years
- Obligations
- Commencement Date
- Payment
- Changes and Reviews

chunks.title: Job search requirements — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Job search requirements
A client for the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship must not be in full-time employment but must be:
- seeking it
- available for it
- willing and able to undertake it and
- taking reasonable steps to find it

chunks.title: A client living in a limited employment location receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## A client living in a limited employment location receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
A client in this situation must continue to meet the work obligations, which include being available for, and taking reasonable steps to obtain, suitable employment. They will not be expected to relocate.
Note this does not include clients who move from one limited employment location to another. In this instance, see:
- Clients moving to a limited employment location
## A person living in a limited employment location applying for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship
A client living in a limited employment location who is applying for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship must meet the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship eligibility criteria.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
## A client receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship moves to a limited employment location
A client in this situation must continue to meet the work obligations, which include being available for, and taking reasonable steps to obtain, suitable employment.
To meet this obligation, a client who moves to a limited employment location must have access to reliable transport and be willing and realistically able to commute to a nearby town or centre where there is employment available.
For more information see:
- What is a limited employment location?
- Deskfile Limited employment locations
- Clients currently living in a limited employment location
- Clients moving to a limited employment location
- Work obligations

chunks.title: Meeting job search requirements — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Meeting job search requirements
To help decide if a client is meeting the job search requirements, you will need to consider the following:
1 If the client (or partner) had the opportunity, would they:
- be available for work for 30 hours or more a week
- accept any suitable job offers within their abilities Note that this can include weekend work depending on the client or partner's individual circumstances
- not restrict their job search to vacancies within their own trade
- not restrict their job search to vacancies in their chosen occupation
- not move frequently from one area to another with no intention of getting a job
2 Has the client (or partner) begun to take steps to find work? For example by:
- searching newspapers and other media for vacancies
- making applications for suitable jobs
- contacting employers about vacancies
For more information see:
- Clients with specific circumstances

chunks.title: Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Misconduct applying a 13 week non-entitlement period
Before applying a 13 week non-entitlement period for misconduct, you should contact both the client and their employer.
Contact the employer and ask them to complete the Employment and earnings information for applications (V06) form.
If the employer does not return the form or the reason for termination is not given, no further contact with the employer should be made.
If there is conflicting evidence or the reason for leaving employment is not agreed between the client and the employer, you should give the client the benefit of the doubt.
Each client's circumstances need to be carefully investigated. If you are uncertain whether a voluntary unemployment stand-down should be imposed, discuss the client's circumstances, in the first instance, with a service centre trainer and then with Helpline (if still required).
If you decide to apply a voluntary unemployment stand-down, you will need to:
- advise the client of your decision
- send the client the 'Voluntary Unemployed' letter to confirm your decision. A copy of the letter is available in CMS letter templates
- for couples or sole parents, the client's commencement date letter will confirm your decision and outline their rate of payment
- add the date that a non-entitlement period will apply from and the appropriate VU reason code to the SSTDA screen
- conditionally grant the benefit using code 024 (VU imposed) on the SPGRT screen
- note for sole parents the 13 week non-entitlement period only applies to 50% of the benefit
- make notes in CMS outlining your decision
Ensure the benefit remains conditionally granted. Do not decline the benefit.
For more information see:
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed
- Misconduct
- Personal grievance or legal proceedings against employer

chunks.title: No stand-down applies — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## No stand-down applies
An initial stand-down is not imposed in the following situations:
- Transfer between benefits
- Temporary employment
- Prisoners
- Entering a refuge
When no stand-down applies, the commencement date of the benefit is the later of either:
- the entitlement date or
- the application date
Note when no stand-down applies, the 28-day rule does not apply.

chunks.title: Non-entitlement period for obligations failures — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Non-entitlement period for obligations failures
Where a client fails their obligations and has a grade 3 sanction imposed, they will have a 13-week non-entitlement period.
For imposing a grade 3 sanction the 13-week non-entitlement period starts the date after the 5 working day notice period.
For more information see:
- Grade 3 sanction or job refusal failure non-entitlement period
Also see:
- Effect of 13-week non-entitlement period for partner
- Effect of non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Financial assistance during a non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Non-entitlement period should not be imposed — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Non-entitlement period should not be imposed
MSD may determine that a 13 week non-entitlement period should not be imposed if the client has specific circumstances that are considered to be good and sufficient reason for leaving employment.
Specific circumstances include where a client has:
- lost their job during an employment trial period of up to 90 days (except where the employer alleges misconduct)
- recently returned to New Zealand
- taken voluntary redundancy because another employee may lose their job if they remained
- left employment that isn't suitable
Note the client will be subject to the normal commencement date rules and the initial stand-down.
## Clients who lose their job during an employment trial period of up to 90 days
Employers can set a trial period when hiring an employee for up to 90 days from the date their employment starts. The employer can dismiss the employee for any reason during the agreed trial period, and they are not required to provide the reason.
To be valid, the trial period must be agreed to by the employer and employee in the employment agreement. The exact period must be stated in the employment agreement.
A 13 week non-entitlement period is not considered if the employment ceased during the agreed notice period and no reason is provided by the employer.
Note if the employer alleges misconduct by the employee and provides evidence of the misconduct, a non-entitlement period can be considered.
For more information see:
- Client's job ceases during an employment trial period

chunks.title: Criteria to receive a non-financial sanction — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Criteria to receive a non-financial sanction
A client or partner can only get a non-financial sanction if:
- they have no other current obligation failures (i.e. this is their first obligation failure), and
- they meet with MSD within the 5 working day notice period, and
- the obligation failure decision is not disputed or and overturned, and
- a non-financial sanction would be appropriate for them based on their circumstances, and
- they are in active case management or they have dependent children
MSD must assess a client’s circumstances and determine which non-financial sanction, if any, is most appropriate for the client. Each non-financial sanction has different factors to consider.
## Non-financial sanctions, Emergency Housing Grants and Special Needs Grants
Clients who have a non-financial sanction imposed cannot get an Emergency Housing Grant or Special Needs Grant. MSD should take this into consideration before choosing to impose a non-financial sanction.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Number of dependent children — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Number of dependent children
If a client had a dependent child (or children) in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application the child (or children) must be taken into account when determining the stand-down.
For example, if a single client with one dependent child applies for benefit the stand-down period will be based on a single client with one child. However, if this client had two dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application, the stand-down period will be based on a single client with two dependent children.
This is regardless of whether the child is still in the client's care at the time of application.
See also:
- Dependent child
- Orphans Benefit/Unsupported Childs Benefit

chunks.title: Obligations failures — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: If a client or partner fails to comply with their obligations, MSD must initiate an obligations failure. MSD must be satisfied that the client or partner would have had no good and sufficient reason for their failure based on the information you have. For social obligations, MSD must consider whether the client and partner (if any) have taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations and must go through the regular engagement and support process before considering that the client has failed their obligation. For more information see: - Good and sufficient reason before initiating an obligations failure - Failing more than one obligation at the same time - Work obligations - Work preparation obligations - Social obligations - Regular engagement and support process - All reasonable steps to meet social obligations - Drug test obligations Note for a client or partner who has full-time or part-time work obligations leaving part-time work averaging less than 15 or 20 hours per week (as appropriate), without good and sufficient reason or through misconduct, is also an obligations failure, but may not be specified in the client's work obligations. Once MSD has decided that the client or partner has failed their obligations, you should initiate an obligations failure. The client or partner will then be sent a letter stating that their benefit will be sanctioned and that their benefit will only be increased or resumed if they: - complete a recompliance activity - dispute the decision to impose the sanction and MSD accepts that they have a good and sufficient reason for not meeting their obligations - lodge a Review of Decision and MSD reconsiders their position and agrees with the client's review or - lodge an appeal to the Medical Appeal Board (drug test failure only) Once a client has completed their recompliance activity, their benefit can be increased or resumed from the date MSD is satisfied the client started the activity. For some clients, if it’s their first obligation failure they may be eligible for a non-financial sanction instead of a financial sanction. For more information, see: Non-financial sanctions All clients have a 5 working day notice period to dispute or recomply before the sanction is imposed. If a client or partner recomplies within the 5 working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the obligations failure is recorded. For more information see: - When the sanction is imposed - Counting previous obligations failures - Failing more than one obligation at the same time

chunks.title: Obligations failures — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Clients have not failed their obligations if they do not complete or undertake Voluntary Work or Activity in the Community.

chunks.title: Effect on rates payable — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: For financial sanctions, the reduction, suspension and cancellation applies to the main benefit the client or partner is getting. For couples it applies to each person's portion of the married rate of benefit. The effect on supplementary assistance depends on the level of sanction imposed, the type of supplementary assistance, and whether the client or partner has dependent children. Non-financial sanctions do not affect the rate payable for a client or partner. For more information see: - Disputes and reviews of an obligations failure - Effect of sanctions on assistance - Recompliance for drug test obligation failures - Recompliance for social obligations failures - Recompliance work obligations failure - Setting appropriate activities for clients

chunks.title: Obligations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Obligations
Clients must:
- advise of any change in circumstances that affect their entitlement, or rate of benefit payable
- meet all of their work obligations
- if they are required to, meet their work preparation obligations
- if they have dependent children, take all reasonable steps to meet social obligations that apply for each dependent child in their care
- if required, undertake and pass a pre-employment or pre-course drug test
- if required, participate in a Work Ability Assessment
- if required, work with a contracted service provider
- advise the MSD if they are intending to travel overseas, before they depart
## Partners aged 16 to 18 years old
Young partners (aged 16 to 18 years old) of clients getting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship have youth activity obligations. Partners over 18 years old have different work and work preparation obligations than younger clients. See:
- Youth activity obligations
Note social obligations do not apply to young partners of Jobseeker Support Student Hardship as they have youth activity obligations, some of these are similar to social obligations.

chunks.title: Overview of social obligations according to age of the child — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Overview of social obligations according to age of the child
The table below shows the specific social obligations that apply to the client and their partner (if any) according to the age of their dependent children.
Age of client's or their partner's dependent children
4 weeks - 2 years
3 and 4 years
5 years
6 - 15 years
16 - 18 years
Core Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider visits
Applies for each dependent child
Not applicable
Enrolled in and attending recognised early childhood education programmes
Not applicable
Applies for each dependent child
Applies for each dependent child where they are not in school
Not applicable
Enrolled in and attending school
Not applicable
Applies for each dependent child (except where child is aged between 5 and 6 years and is enrolled in and attending a recognised early childhood programme)
Not applicable
Enrolled in primary health care
Applies for each dependent child

chunks.title: Parent is being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020 — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Parent is being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020
All parents are legally obliged to ensure their children are enrolled in and attending school from the age of 6 to 16 years of age.
Parents can be prosecuted and fined under Education and Training Act 2020 if their children don't attend school.
This can happen when:
- there has been, without explanation, ongoing and irregular attendance by the child at school after support has been offered to the family or
- the parent has made little or no attempt to do anything about ensuring the child attends school
If a parent is in the process of being prosecuted under Education and Training Act 2020, you must not ask them to comply with this social obligation or initiate an obligations failure for non-attendance.
Note you need to record this as an exception in OBMAN using 'Parent is in prosecution for truant child' as the obligation exception reason.

chunks.title: Parents overseas — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Parents overseas
If the young person's parents are overseas the responsibility to support the young person should remain with the parents if:
- there has been no family breakdown and
- the decision to move overseas and leave the young person in New Zealand is planned and agreed between the young person and their parents or
- the decision to send the young person to New Zealand for education, or job prospects and the like, is planned and agreed between the young person and their parents
If the situation results in a family breakdown the young person may be able to receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
For more information see:
- Family breakdown
- What is financial support?
- Independent

chunks.title: Partner detained overseas or missing — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Partner detained overseas or missing
If the partner intends to live in New Zealand but has not yet arrived, they are not considered ordinarily resident and cannot be included in the client's benefit.
When the client still considers themselves married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, the rate payable to the client is half the married, civil union or de facto rate.
A higher married, civil union or de facto rate is payable if the client has a dependent child. See:
- Partner not qualified
## Exception
If the partner cannot get to New Zealand due to circumstances beyond their control (for example they are detained in another country or overseas refugee camp, or have applied for a visa that has not been granted) or they are missing or their whereabouts are unknown, the client in New Zealand can be paid the single or sole parent rate depending on their family circumstances.
## Partners overseas long-term
If a partner was resident in New Zealand but has left the country and has no definite plans to return (for example, they have been deported) they are not considered ordinarily resident and cannot be included in the benefit. The rate payable to the client is half the married, civil union or de facto rate.
The single or sole parent rate can only be paid where the marriage or civil union no longer exists.
A higher married, civil union or de facto rate is payable if the client has a dependent child. See:
- Partner not qualified

chunks.title: Partner not qualified — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Partner not qualified
You can pay a special rate equal to half the married, civil union or de facto rate with no dependent children to a client (with or without dependent children) if their partner is:
- subject to a 13 week voluntary unemployment stand-down
- on strike or
- subject to an obligations failure
You can pay a single or sole parent rate to a client whose partner is unlawfully resident or not permanently resident in New Zealand but you have to take the joint income and assets into account. There are some exceptions. See: Partner's residence status
For more information see:
- Cash assets
- Charging income
- Permanent residence
- Partner is overseas
- Partner's residence status
- Accommodation Supplement Partners not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand

chunks.title: Partner's residence status — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Partner's residence status
When a client has a partner, you must also check the partner's residence status because the rate of benefit payable depends on whether or not the partner is included.
The partner can be included in the benefit if they are:
- a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (ie not in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or
- deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) and
- generally ordinarily resident in New Zealand
For more information see:
- Proof of residence
- Deciding ordinarily resident
If a partner has one of the following, they cannot be included in the benefit:
- a temporary entry visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009
- a temporary permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987 (such as a visitor permit, a work permit, or a student permit)
If the partner does not have a current permit or visa that allows them to remain in New Zealand then they are in New Zealand unlawfully and you cannot include the partner in the benefit, unless one of the exceptions listed below applies.
Where the partner is in New Zealand unlawfully or is not a permanent resident, pay the client at a single or sole parent rate taking into consideration all of the couple's income and assets.
Contact the Card Centre when granting the primary benefit to ensure that a Community Services Card is not issued to the non-resident partner.
Encourage the partner to follow up their residence status.
## Exceptions
There are some situations where a partner is exempt and can be included in the benefit without having been granted permanent residence. These are:
- a person lawfully present in New Zealand who is awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protection status in New Zealand or
- a person who has refugee or protection status in New Zealand or
- a person applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 who is compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances
For more information see:
- Immigration status and supporting documents
- Cash Assets
- Charging income
- Partner is overseas

chunks.title: Partners with no children or youngest child 14+ years — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Partners with no children or youngest child 14+ years
Full-time work obligations apply to:
- partners with no children and
- partners with a youngest child aged 14 years or over
Partners with full-time work obligations must make themselves available for suitable employment, training or other suitable activities of at least 30 hours or more each week.
If a partner is in employment for less than 30 hours each week, they are still expected to be available for other work, training or other activities up to a total of 30 hours each week. The partner must understand that they are still required to accept suitable full-time work if it becomes available.
For more information see:
- Work obligations
- Hours range for suitable employment
Partners may participate in approved training as long as they continue to meet their work obligations, unless they are granted an exception for approved full-time training.
For more information see:
- In approved training (no children or child 14+)
- Approved training
- Exemptions In approved full-time training
Partners may undertake volunteer work as long as they continue to meet their work obligations. For more information see:
- Clients undertaking voluntary work
Partners may apply for an exemption from their work obligations. For more information on exemptions see:
- Exemptions
- Table of Exemptions
If a partner fails to comply with their work obligations, their portion of the benefit may be stopped. For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Partners with youngest child between 3 and 13 years — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Partners with youngest child between 3 and 13 years
Part-time work obligations apply to:
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years
The partner must make themselves available for suitable employment, training or other activities of at least 20 hours a week.
For more information see:
- Work obligations
- Hours range for suitable employment
If a partner is in approved training they must continue to meet their work obligations, including being available for part-time employment, unless they are granted an exception for approved full-time training. For more information see:
Partners may undertake voluntary work but must continue to meet their work obligations. For more information see:
- Clients undertaking voluntary work
Partners may apply for an exemption from their work obligations. For more information on exemptions see:
- Exemptions
- Table of Exemptions
If a partner fails to comply with their work obligations, their portion of the benefit may be stopped.
For more information see:
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures
If a partner with part-time obligations is already in employment for 20 hours or more each week, they are meeting their work obligations.
If they are in employment for less than 20 hours each week, they are still expected to be available for other work, training or any other activities.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations

chunks.title: Partners with youngest dependent child under 3 years — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Partners with youngest dependent child under 3 years
Work preparation obligations apply to:
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
The partner must undertake activities that will prepare them for work in the future. For more information see:
- Work preparation obligations
Partners may apply for an exemption from their work preparation obligations. Generally, they can only be considered for a full exemption as work preparation obligations mean that they are required to plan for employment and undertake work preparation activities - the equivalent of a partial exemption. For more information see:
- Exemptions
- Table of Exemptions
If a partner fails to comply with their work preparation obligations, they are subject to an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Special Needs Grants — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Special Needs Grants
Clients are not entitled to Special Needs Grants if a sanction has been imposed. This applies to both financial and non-financial sanctions.
The only exception to this is if a client or partner has a health condition, injury or disability when a grade 3 sanction is imposed and they are incapable of participating in full-time employment or an approved activity for 6 weeks.
For more information see:
- Assistance during non-entitlement periods
- Assistance when a client is sanctioned

chunks.title: Family Tax Credit and Best Start tax credit — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Family Tax Credit and Best Start tax credit
If there are dependent children, family tax credit and Best Start tax credit is paid at the full rate to the new primary.

chunks.title: Payment — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Payment
Jobseeker Support Student Hardship is paid weekly on a Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. Payment is from Monday to Sunday and is made 1 week in arrears.
Generally, payment must be made directly to the client. However, where there is good cause the client's benefit can be paid to another person, agent or institution.
For more information see:
- Redirection of benefit payment
## Exception for young partners
Young partners can choose to have their benefit payment redirected; they are not required to meet the 'good cause' criteria.
For more information see:
- Redirection of benefit for young partners
It is a condition of getting a benefit that the client provides a bank account number.
MSD may request the client or their partner to provide an IRD number or evidence of their IRD number.
For more information see:
- IRD number for client or partner who is apportioned assistance
## Rate of payment
The rate of Jobseeker Support Student Hardship that can be paid depends on the client's:
- age
- relationship status
- dependent children
and for clients aged 18 or 19 year olds:
- whether they live at home or not
To help you decide the rate of payment for 16 or 17 year olds, see:
- Rate of payment for 16 and 17 year olds

chunks.title: Payments to the non-sanctioned client — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Payments to the non-sanctioned client
When a client has their portion of the benefit sanctioned, the non-sanctioned client will continue to get:
- their portion of the benefit and
- for a grade 2 or 3 sanction, 50% of the supplementary assistance the couple was entitled to (the couple's supplementary assistance is not affected by a grade 1 sanction)
MSD must check if the non-sanctioned client has had any changes in their circumstances or their family's situation. The non-sanctioned client should be advised about applying for a benefit in their own right (in this situation the benefit would only be paid at the half-married rate).
For more information see:
- Financial assistance during non-entitlement period
- Effect of financial sanctions on assistance

chunks.title: Benefit stops during Money Management — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Benefit stops during Money Management
A client’s benefit may stop while they are being money managed, e.g. one week their income was over the income limit. . The length of Money Management is not impacted by any breaks in payment, and will always end 4 weeks after it was imposed.
## Example
Kale fails their obligation, Money Management starts on 14 August. Their last day of Money Management will be 10 September.
Kale travels to Australia from 18 August to 25 August for a holiday. They do not inform MSD before their travel and their benefit is stopped from the day after they left New Zealand.
Kale’s benefit is resumed from the date they return to New Zealand. Their Money Management continues from 25 August, and will still end on 10 September.

chunks.title: Option to attend multiple training courses — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Option to attend multiple training courses
A client could attend and participate in more than one suitable employment-related training or course to help them meet the required number of hours and weeks. This could be:
- finding 2 or more courses that offer enough hours per week between them or
- completing 2 or more courses back-to-back or
- a combination of both.
A client can attend and participate in more than one course for Upskilling, as long as they are able to meet the requirements of the sanction.

chunks.title: Permanent residence — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Permanent residence
Generally migrants need to have permanent residence or New Zealand citizenship to receive benefit assistance. Permanent residence is granted by Immigration New Zealand. Citizenship is granted by the Department of Internal Affairs.
In order to receive a benefit, a client must normally:
- have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 (which can either be a resident visa or a permanent resident visa) or
- have a residence permit under the Immigration Act 1987 or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents)
- be a British national who arrived in New Zealand prior to 2 April 1974 or
- be a New Zealand citizen
## Clients without permanent residence or citizenship
Emergency Benefit may be paid to some categories of migrants who do not have permanent residence or citizenship, eg people waiting for their application for refugee or protection status to be approved.
For more information see:
- Proof of residence
- Emergency Benefit
Note clients lawfully in New Zealand by virtue of a temporary permit or temporary entry class visa only (ie they do not have permanent residence) are not entitled to any benefit assistance.
For more information see:
- Immigration status and supporting documents
- Immigration status [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Evidence — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Evidence
The client must provide evidence from a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or midwife confirming the expected date of birth or nature of complications if their pregnancy is under 27 weeks.
## Duration
This deferral applies until either the:
- birth of the child or
- client no longer has complications if they are less than 27 weeks pregnant

chunks.title: Evidence — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Evidence
The partner must provide evidence from a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner, or midwife confirming the expected date of birth or nature of complications if their pregnancy is under 27 weeks.

chunks.title: Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Generally, a temporary provisional benefit can be paid to the client or their partner while they are doing an approved activity or programme of approved activities, during their 13 week non-entitlement period (except when the approved activity is full-time employment).

chunks.title: Provisional benefit — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: MSD can grant or increase a provisional benefit from the date the client or partner starts the approved activity or programme. Their benefit will be provisionally paid to them if they are satisfactorily participating in their activity. The provisional payment will continue until: - the 6-week activity period ends, or - the 13-week non-entitlement period ends whichever is earlier. Some examples of this: - a client starts their approved activity in the beginning of week 3 of their non-entitlement period. The client participates for 6 continuous weeks, and the rest of the 13-week non-entitlement period is cancelled. After the follow-up appointment, the client’s benefit is reinstated to their usual benefit, instead of a provisional benefit. - a client starts their approved activity in the beginning of week 10 of the non-entitlement period. The client does the approved activity for the rest of the 13-week non-entitlement period (3 weeks). At the end of the 13-week non-entitlement period, the client’s benefit is reinstated to their usual benefit, instead of a provisional benefit.

chunks.title: End of approved activity or non-entitlement period — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: At the end of the approved activity or programme of activities a follow-up appointment is required (in approximately 6 weeks' time). At the appointment, MSD should discuss with the client or partner whether they: - have satisfactorily participated in the approved activity, and - can still meet the qualifications and obligations of their benefit. Note if the client or their partner does not recomply, they will have to reapply for their benefit at the end of the 13 week non-entitlement period if they wish to get a benefit.

chunks.title: Leaves approved activity or does not satisfactorily participate — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: If a client or partner leaves early or does not satisfactorily participate in the approved activity or programme of suitable activities, without a change [no link find out why] in their obligations, their provisional benefit must be reduced or stopped from the date it was increased or granted. The benefit amount that was provisionally paid during the 13-week non-entitlement period must be established as a debt and recovered. MSD cannot recover the provisional benefit if they did not complete the approved activity because they: - transferred to a benefit with no work obligations, or - meet the criteria for a full exemption from their work obligations Only one approved activity or programme can be assigned to a client. MSD cannot give the client a different approved activity if they fail to satisfactorily complete their approved activity. For more information see: - Recompliance - Unable to recomply - Good and sufficient reason before

chunks.title: Qualifications — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
To get Jobseeker Support Student Hardship a client must:
- meet an age qualification
- be a New Zealand citizen or residence class visa holder
- have little or no income
- be in the break between two academic years of a programme of study
- complete any pre-benefit requirements, if applicable
- be available for and actively seeking full-time work and
- be suffering hardship
## Clients already getting a benefit
When a client who is already getting a benefit advises MSD that they intend to study full-time, they will stay on that benefit until they start their full-time study. To keep getting their current benefit they must continue to meet the qualifications and their obligations. They should not be transferred to Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
Jobseeker Support Student Hardship can only be paid to clients during the break between academic years of their programme of study.
A client may be able to get other financial assistance if they cannot get Jobseeker Support Student Hardship when their break is during the academic year, or if they are between 2 programmes of study.
For more information see:
- Assistance for students at other times

chunks.title: Rate of payment for 16 and 17 year olds — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Rate of payment for 16 and 17 year olds
To receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, young people aged 16 and 17 years old must:
- be married, in a civil union or in a de facto relationship or
- single and have exceptional circumstances and
- have been receiving Independent Circumstances Allowance or Student Allowance during the semester
## Single, no dependent children, living at home
These clients do not meet the qualifications for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
## Single, no dependent children, living away from home
These clients are paid the 18 to 19 away from home rate of Jobseeker Support.
## Single, dependent children, living away from home
These clients are paid the sole parent rate of Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
## Married, in a civil union or de facto relationship
These clients are paid the married, civil union or de facto couple (with or without dependent children) rate of Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.
For more information see:
- Deskfile Jobseeker Support Student Hardship rates
- Payment

chunks.title: Recent bereavement of spouse or partner — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Recent bereavement of spouse or partner
This exemption may apply to clients and sole parents with work or work preparation obligations.
Clients whose spouse or partner has recently died can be exempt from meeting all their work or work preparation obligations to allow them time to adjust to their new circumstances. This is a full exemption.
Before granting this exemption you should consider the following factors:
- changes in living circumstances
- changes in childcare responsibilities
- particular religious or cultural beliefs or practices
Note you should consider the client's eligibility for Sole Parent Support.

chunks.title: Recent separation from a spouse or partner — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Recent separation from a spouse or partner
This exemption may apply to clients and sole parents with work or work preparation obligations.
Clients who have recently separated from their spouse or partner can be exempt from meeting all their work or work preparation obligations to allow them time to adjust to their new circumstances. This is a full exemption.
Before granting this exemption you should consider the following factors:
- changes in living circumstances
- changes in childcare responsibilities

chunks.title: Recompliance — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Recompliance
Recompliance is the activity a client or partner must undertake after they have failed an obligation. They must complete the recompliance activity to have their benefit:
- increased or resumed if they have been financially sanctioned or
- continued if they have a non-financial sanction imposed
Generally, the activities a client or partner need to complete are the same as or substantially similar to the obligation that initiated the failure.
Clients with an obligations failure initiated who recomply within five working days will not have a sanction imposed, but the obligations failure will be counted.
When a client or partner indicates that they want to recomply MSD must make a recompliance activity available for them at the earliest opportunity.
The obligations failure that has reduced or stopped their benefit will determine the type of recompliance activity the client or partner will need to undertake. MSD should discuss what activities they need to undertake in order to recomply.
For more information see:
- Recompliance for work obligation failures
- Recompliance for social obligation failures
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Recomplying more than one failure
## When to resume or increase a benefit
A client must have successfully completed the recompliance activity before their benefit is resumed or increased if they have been financially sanctioned. Once completed, the benefit can be resumed or increased from the date MSD is satisfied the client started the recompliance activity.
Some examples of this:
- if the recompliance activity is a one-off, such as attending an interview the benefit would be resumed from the date the client attended and participated in the interview
- if the recompliance activity is ongoing, such as a training programme, the client must undertake the training programme to MSD's satisfaction. Once this is complete, the benefit can be resumed from the date the client started the training programme
- if the client has multiple recompliance activities to complete (due to more than one failure), the date when they have completed a recompliance activity for the latest failure
## For what to do if a client cannot recomply, see:
- Unable to recomply
- Recompliance and change of circumstances

chunks.title: Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period) — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: A client or their partner can complete certain activities to get a temporary provisional benefit if they have a 13 week non-entitlement period because they: - left a job voluntarily - lost a job through misconduct - have a grade 3 sanction imposed or - refused an offer of suitable employment If a client or partner wants to recomply, MSD must make a 6 week approved activity or programme of activities available to them at the earliest opportunity. An approved activity can start as soon as a sanction has been imposed, there is no waiting period.

chunks.title: Recompliance activities — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: The client or partner their must do the approved activity for 6 continuous weeks, or until their 13 week non-entitlement period ends (whichever is earlier). This can be through: - satisfactory participation in a 6 week approved activity or programme of activities - satisfactory participation in full-time employment or - part-time employment (if they have part-time work obligations) Note clients and partners with full-time work obligations should have a full-time 6 week approved activity. Clients and partners with part-time work obligations should have a part-time 6-week approved activity. Clients and partners with full-time work obligations who are recomplying through approved full-time employment do not get a provisional benefit.

chunks.title: Client does not complete activity — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: If a client fails to satisfactorily complete their 6-week activity or programme of activities , and their obligations have not changed, their provisional benefit must be reduced or stopped from the date it was increased or granted. Any provisional benefit the client was paid must be established as a debt. To get a new benefit, the client must wait until the end of the 13-week non-entitlement period to re-apply or to get their full rate of benefit reinstated if the client has dependent children. When a client with dependent children makes contact at the end of the 13 weeks, MSD should review their circumstances to confirm that the client still qualifies and what rate of payment they should get. MSD must determine the appropriate date to increase the rate from, but this cannot be any earlier than the end of the 13-week period. Only one approved activity or programme can be assigned to a client. MSD cannot give the client a different approved activity if they fail to satisfactorily complete the original approved activity.

chunks.title: Recompliance for social obligations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: If the client or their partner fails their obligations for a third time, and the third failure is a social obligation failure, then their 6 week recompliance activity MSD will be different. In this situation it may not be appropriate to choose and activity focused on work outcomes. A programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate instead. For more information see: - Failing a social obligation

chunks.title: Approved activity examples — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Here are some examples that may be a suitable 6-week approved activity for the client or partner: - Work experience, Activity in the Community and Voluntary work Note this list is an example only. An approved activity (or programme of suitable activities) should be relevant to the obligation the client failed, and be fair and reasonable.

chunks.title: Programme of suitable activities — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: If there is not an appropriate 6 week approved activity available, consider a programme of suitable activities. For more information see: - Recompliance programme example For when to grant or increase the benefit, see: - Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period For what to do if a client or partner cannot recomply, see: - Unable to recomply

chunks.title: Recompliance and change of circumstances — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Recompliance and change of circumstances
A client who has a failure in progress or a sanction imposed may be unable to recomply because they:
- had a change of circumstances that means they can no longer comply with a social obligation, or the social obligation is no longer relevant to them or
- had a change in obligations which means they are no longer required to comply with any activity that is specific to their previous obligations, for example a client moves between work obligations and work preparation obligations
In these situations, the client should not be required to recomply. However, the failure will still be included in the 24 month count.
Once the client has new obligations, MSD may ask them to complete any activities in relation to their new obligations.
## Examples
Examples of where MSD cannot require the client to complete a recompliance activity:
- where a child leaves care or changes age and the social obligation they had is no longer relevant (for example the client has failed the early childhood education social obligation and the child has now turned six years old)
- where a client is subject to work obligations has failed a drug test obligation and is transferred to work preparation obligations
- where a client who has work preparation obligations has failed to undertake planning for employment and is transferred to work obligations
- where a client who has work or work preparation obligations has failed an obligation and has been transferred to Supported Living Payment or Emergency Benefit with no obligations
For more information see:
- Recompliance for work obligation failures
- Recompliance for social obligation failures
- Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
- Recomplying more than one failure
- Recompliance [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Recompliance for drug test obligation failures — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for drug test obligation failures
Clients who have failed their drug test obligations will need to complete a recompliance activity to increase or resume their benefit.
Once a client or partner indicates they want to recomply MSD must have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply. The grade of the drug test obligation failure will determine the recompliance activity required.
For more information see:
- Recomplying first drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying third drug test obligation failure
- Help with paying for the recompliance drug test
- Drug test recompliance count

chunks.title: Recompliance for social obligation failures — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Recompliance for social obligation failures
Clients who have failed their social obligations need to meet all their social obligations as part of an activity to increase their benefit.
Once a client or partner indicates they want to recomply MSD must have a discussion with them about what they need to do to recomply.
Note when a client has a partner, social obligations apply to both the client and the partner.

chunks.title: Work obligations failure (Grade 1 and 2) — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Work obligations failure (Grade 1 and 2)
For clients to recomply with a work obligations failure (grade 1 and 2) and have their benefit increased or resumed, the client or partner will need to complete:
- the activity they failed or
- an activity that is the same or substantially similar to the activity they failed
Note for grade 1 failures where a non-financial sanction has been imposed, the recompliance requirements may be different. For more information see:
- Non-financial sanctions
## Work obligations failure or failure to accept an offer of suitable employment (Grade 3)
For clients to recomply to a work obligations failure (grade 3) and be granted a provisional benefit, the client or partner will need to:
- start and complete a six week recompliance activity or programme of activities (13 week non-entitlement period) or
- wait until the end of the 13 week non-entitlement period
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Recomplying more than one failure

chunks.title: Recompliance programme example — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Recompliance programme example
If a client or partner is recomplying through participating in an approved activity, there may not be a single activity long enough to meet the required 6 week period of recompliance. A programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate for the client or partner.
Note a programme of suitable activities for a client or partner with part-time work obligations should be:
- at least 15 hours per week for primary clients that qualify for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship on the grounds of a health condition, injury or disability
- at least 20 hours per week for partners with part-time work obligations

chunks.title: Recompliance social obligations failure (Grade 1 and 2) — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: When the client or partner fails 1 individual social obligation they need to comply with all other social obligations relevant to the age of their dependent child. MSD should discuss with the client or partner what activities they need to do to recomply. MSD must be satisfied the client and their partner (if any) have both satisfactorily undertaken their recompliance activity. The benefit will be resumed or increased from the date MSD is satisfied the client or partner has started the recompliance activity. In some situations, MSD may ask the client or their partner (if any) to get verification, for example: - a letter from their practitioner or medical practice that says they are enrolled with a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation or - a letter from the child's school that says the child is enrolled and attending or - a letter from their early childhood education provider that says the child is enrolled and attending or - asking to see their Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book

chunks.title: Examples of recompliance — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Example 1 A client has a 3-year-old child. They are required to have their child enrolled in primary health care and attending a recognised early childhood education programme. The child has not been attending an early childhood education programme and the client does not have a good and sufficient reason for this. MSD is unsure if the child is enrolled in primary health care. The client has failed 1 of their social obligations. To recomply with their social obligations, MSD must be satisfied the client has enrolled their child in primary health care and that they will ensure their child attends an early childhood education programme. MSD asks the client to provide verification of this. The client provides a letter from their medical practice confirming the child is enrolled, and a letter from the early childhood education provider stating the child is enrolled and attending. MSD is satisfied the client has recomplied with their social obligations. Example 2 A client has 2 children. The 5-year-old child must be enrolled in primary health care and attending school or an early childhood education programme. The 2-year-old child also needs to be enrolled in primary health care and up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks. Both children are enrolled in primary health care and the 5-year-old child is attending school. However, the 2-year-old child is not up to date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks and the client doesn’t have a good and sufficient reason for this. MSD needs to be satisfied that 2-year-old child has or will be receiving the core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks. MSD asks the client to provide verification of this . The client brings their 2-year-old’s Well child/Tamariki Ora book to MSD which confirms the 2-year-old has upcoming Well child/Tamariki Ora checks booked. MSD is satisfied the client has recomplied with their social obligations.

chunks.title: Full-time employment — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Full-time employment
A client or partner who has a 13-week non-entitlement period and full-time work obligations can recomply by getting full-time work. This work must last at least 6 continuous weeks.
At the end of these 6 weeks, the 13-week non-entitlement period ends. If the client or partner wants to restart their benefit, they will have to reapply. The benefit is granted from the date their employment ceased.
Note provisional benefit is not paid during the 6 weeks of full-time employment.
## Part-time employment
A client or partner who has a 13-week non-entitlement period and part-time work obligations can recomply by getting part-time work. This work must last at least 6 continuous weeks, for an average of 20 hours or more each week.
At the end of 6 weeks, the 13-week non-entitlement period ends. The client’s benefit is reinstated to their usual benefit, instead of a provisional benefit.
If the client or partner leaves the job before the end of the 6 weeks, any provisional benefit paid must be established as a debt and the rest of the non-entitlement period is imposed.
The client or partner can still recomply during the rest of the 13-week non-entitlement period by participating in another approved activity.
Note the income the client gets from their employment is charged against the provisional benefit rate.
For when to grant or increase the benefit, see:
- Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Client does not recomply — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Client does not recomply
Clients who do not complete their recompliance activity while on Money Management will have their benefit suspended at the end of the 4-week period.
Their benefit can only be resumed when a client has completed their recompliance activity. If a client’s benefit has been suspended following Money Management, their benefit will be automatically cancelled after 9 weeks (13 weeks total).
For more information on how non-compliance affects assistance, see:
Clients who have their benefit cancelled will need to reapply for benefit if they need further support.

chunks.title: Recomplying first drug test obligation failure — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Recomplying first drug test obligation failure
To recomply to a first drug test obligation failure a client or partner must verbally agree to stop using controlled drugs.
The day the client or partner agrees to stop taking controlled drugs is the date they can be considered to have recomplied. You must advise the client or partner of the consequences if they fail the drug test obligation again.
For more information see:
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying third drug test obligation failure
- Drug test recompliance count
- Help with paying for the recompliance drug test

chunks.title: Period to take and provide a drug test — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: A client or partner has 25 working days, from the day after they have agreed to recomply with their second drug test obligations failure, to take and pass a drug test. The client must provide proof of undertaking and passing the drug test, within 30 working days from the day after they have agreed to recomply. A client or partner cannot dispute the 25 working day period to take and pass the drug test. They must take and pass the drug test within that time period or they will fail their obligations for the third time. Work and Income has an additional 5 working days to receive the results from the client or partner and to process the information. Generally, the results of the drug test should be provided to Work and Income within the 25 working days, but they can be accepted in the 5 working day period following. Day 0 A second drug test failure is in-progress and client has agreed to recomply by taking and passing a drug test within 25 working days. Recompliance 2 is recorded and automatic count in IT system occurs overnight. Client can provide the results of the drug test at any time Day 1 - 25 Letter is sent to the client advising them they have 25 working days to take and pass a drug test. Day 26 - 30 5 working days to allow time to receive and process the results of the test starts. Day 31 If no "passed" drug test results are received a work test failure three is initiated and 5 working day notice period prior to Grade 3 sanction starts. They will not be considered to have recomplied until a passed drug test result is received by Work and Income. A client or partner can only access recoverable help with the costs of the recompliance drug test once during the 25 working day period. During the 25 working day period a "drug test referral delay" will be automatically added in CMS.

chunks.title: Verification required — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: In order to make a decision that a client or partner has taken and passed a drug test you must have received written confirmation from the client or partner. The written information that must be provided to Work and Income includes: - the name of the client or partner and the drug test provider and - confirmation of a "passed" test result The Drug test obligations verification [no link find out why] form can be used for this. For more information see: - Drug test recompliance count - Help with paying for the recompliance drug test - Recomplying first drug test obligation failure - Recomplying third drug test obligation failure

chunks.title: Recomplying third drug test obligation failure — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Recomplying third drug test obligation failure
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation a client or partner must complete a 6 week approved activity and reapply for their benefit. A 6 week approved activity must be completed regardless of the obligation failed or whether the client or partner had failed more than one obligation failure.
## Client or partner fails a third time for another reason during the 25 working day period
A client or partner could fail their other obligations (not drug test obligations) for a third time during the 25 working day period. If this happens the third failure would override the count of the 25 working day period and the client or partner would not have to take and pass a drug test.
To recomply with a third failure of any obligation the client or partner must complete a 6 week approved activity.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Recomplying more than one failure
- Recomplying first drug test obligation failure
- Recomplying second drug test obligation failure
- Drug test recompliance count
- Help with paying for the recompliance drug test

chunks.title: Recording decisions on a dispute — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Recording decisions on a dispute
You must record the outcome of the client or partner's dispute in OBMAN. One of the following outcomes must be recorded for each dispute:
- Upheld - if you believe that the decision relating to an obligations failure or sanction being imposed was correct you must record this as 'dispute upheld'. The obligations failure will be counted.
