- Withdrawn - a client or partner may, after disputing the obligations failure, decide to recomply before the sanction is imposed, or may withdraw their dispute and not recomply. In these cases you must record that the dispute has been withdrawn. The obligations failure will be counted.
- Overturned - when you believe that the client or partner had a good and sufficient reason or that they did not fail their obligations you must record this as obligations failure overturned. The obligations failure will not be counted.
In all cases you must advise the client or partner of the outcome of their dispute. A letter is automatically sent to the client or partner.
If the client or partner does not agree with your decision, they can still request a formal Review of Decision or Medical Appeal Board appeal (drug test failure only). They must do this in writing. The Review of Decision and Medical Appeals Board process should be followed.
Note if the obligations failure was initiated against the wrong client or partner the status can be changed to 'failed in error' on the same day you initiate the failure. No letter is sent when the status is changed to 'failed in error'.
## Reviews of Decisions and appeals to the Medical Appeals Board for obligations failures
Reviews of Decisions for obligations failures are recorded in HIYA; appeals to the Medical Appeals Board for obligations failures are recorded in the Medical Appeals Database. However, the outcome of the review or appeal must be recorded in OBMAN. This will ensure that the benefit status can be resumed or regranted in SWIFTT depending on the outcome of the review or appeal.
Note that if the Review of Decision or Medical Appeals Board process finds that the originally recorded 'upheld' outcome should be changed to overturned, you will need to make this change in OBMAN.
For more information see:
- The disputes process
- Core policy Reviews and Appeals
- Core policy Medical Appeal Board

chunks.title: Redirection of benefit for young partners — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Redirection of benefit for young partners
Young partners can choose to have their benefit payment redirected and do not have to meet the 'good cause' criteria.
This applies to young partners:
- aged 16 and 17 years old without dependent children
- aged 16 to 18 years with a dependent child or children
The young partners benefit payment and any ongoing Extra help can be redirected to pay for their:
- accommodation and service costs, for example rent, board, power, phone and
- lawful debts or other liabilities, for example Child Support payments, Work and Income debts
Note Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance cannot be redirected and are paid directly to the young partner.
## Opting out of redirection
Young partners can opt out of redirection of their payment at any time.
For more information see:
- Payment

chunks.title: Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements
When you are referring a client to a drug tested job, you should:
- consider if the job is suitable for the client, regardless of the drug test
- let the client know that the employer may require them to pass a pre-employment drug test
- ask the client if they would pass a pre-employment drug test and
- ensure the client understands the potential consequences of failing a pre-employment drug test
There are certain situations where it is not appropriate to refer a client to drug tested jobs. In these situations you should consider that, because of the drug test requirements, the job is not suitable.
For more information see:
- Drug test job referral not suitable
- Training providers requiring a drug test
- Employers requiring a pre-employment drug test
- Informing a client of the drug test obligation failure
- Drug test obligations failures - good and sufficient reasons
- Suitable employment
- Types of drug tests and standards
- Drug test obligations

chunks.title: Regular engagement and support process — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Regular engagement and support process
Clients must be contacted at least four times by Work and Income before initiating a failure to meet a social obligation. You must complete the three Contact Steps of regular engagement and support and then make a final appointment. You can only determine that the client has failed to meet their social obligations at the final appointment.
The Contact Steps can be over the phone or face to face.
The aim of this process is to support clients to meet their social obligations or for clients to take all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations.
At the first Contact Step of engagement and support you should discuss with the client and their partner (if any) whether they are meeting their social obligations and, if not, encourage them to do so.
The next two Contact Steps of engagement and support should be focused on encouraging and supporting the client to meet their social obligations, and following up what happened at the previous Contact Steps.
At each of the three Contact Steps you must:
- check that the client is taking all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations, and actively help and encourage the client to meet those obligations
- ensure that the client is connected with local community information
- advise the client of the next stage of engagement and support and contact
- remind the client of their social obligations and consequences of not meeting these
For more information on the engagement and support process, see:
- Social obligations - actively engaging with clients [no link find out why] procedures
Also see:
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations
- Client is meeting their social obligations
- Child changes during engagement and support process
- Failure to attend interviews or make contact about social obligations

chunks.title: Reimbursement to employers and debt recovery — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: The potential employer can be reimbursed for a failed drug test for a client only when Work and Income receives confirmation a drug test has been completed that was part of the pre-employment process and the potential employer has completed the Pre-employment drug test claim form for employers which includes details such as: - the name of the employer - the type of test - whether it was a screening or evidential test - confirmation that the drug test was to the drug test standard - confirmation of a failed test result and - the cost of the failed test and the payment rate they are claiming At the same time that the employer is reimbursed, a debt for the cost of the drug test will be manually added to the clients SWIFTT record by NPCU/NAC. For more information see: - Reimbursement and claims for Employers/Drug Test Agencies [no link find out why] A training provider cannot be reimbursed for the costs of a failed drug test. In most cases the contract with the provider will have already factored these costs into account. Although a drug test provider may conduct the testing the employer will be the one to be reimbursed for the costs relating to the failed drug test. The information provided related to the failed drug tests is not to be shared with other employers, and is only to be used for the purposes of establishing whether a client has failed, without good and sufficient reason, to meet the drug test obligations. The reimbursement of failed drug tests only apply to jobs where: - the client with work obligations has been referred by Work and Income - the vacancy is listed with Work and Income and - the vacancy requires a pre-employment drug test

chunks.title: Standard rates that can be reimbursed for failed drug tests — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: There are standard rates that can be reimbursed to the potential employer for a failed drug test. These amounts only cover the actual and reasonable costs of the tests. The standard rate of payment will be paid to the employer regardless of the amount that they charge (ie regardless of whether the amount is higher or lower). For recompliance drug testing, the full cost can be paid. Standard rate of payment for screening tests In-house testing When an employer has staff on their premises that have been trained to the New Zealand Drug Testing Standard, and have attained the relevant NZQA unit standards $30 External agency testing Where employers contract a drug testing company to do pre-employment drug testing procedures on their behalf $70 Standard rate of payment for evidential tests Evidential testing When an employer sends samples to a laboratory for evidential testing, the cost associated with this type of testing is significantly higher than a screening test $120 Standard rate of payment for recompliance Screening or evidential tests Actual and reasonable costs - generally this should be the same as the standard rates of payment The costs for alcohol testing cannot be reimbursed as this type of test is not included as a drug test.

chunks.title: Reporting progress — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Reporting progress
You can require your client to report on their job search progress in meeting their work or work preparation obligations.
You must advise the client that if they fail to comply with this obligation without a good and sufficient reason, they are subject to an obligations failure.
## Example
You have asked a partner with a 2 year old child to research childcare options and training options available in their community and to call you in a month to update you on their progress. If the client does not contact you, you should initiate an obligations failure.
## Clients and partners with work obligations
You can require a client with work obligations to report on their job search progress.
A client can report by either phone, email or in person. Generally, a client should not be required to report more than once a week.

chunks.title: Residence — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Residence
To be granted Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (ie not be in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) and
- have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years or more at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
For more information see:
- Deciding ordinarily resident
Note clients who are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident but have not lived in New Zealand continuously for 2 years may be eligible for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship on grounds of hardship.
If a client is from overseas or is a refugee or protected person special provisions may apply, see:
- Jobseeker Support Refugee or protected person
## Sponsored clients
Some clients have been granted permanent residence on condition that they will be supported by a New Zealand sponsor. Before a decision can be made about the client's application for benefit, any reasons why their sponsor can no longer support the client must first be determined and verified.
For more information see:
- Authenticating [no link find out why] procedures
## Clients without permanent residence
If a client does not have permanent residence they cannot receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship or Jobseeker Support Student Hardship on the grounds of hardship (even if they have lived in New Zealand continuously for 2 years). They may be able to receive an Emergency Benefit if they:
- are lawfully present in New Zealand and are awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protection status in New Zealand or
- are applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act and are compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances
For more information see:
- Permanent residence
- Proof of residence
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Partner's residence status
- Granting on grounds of hardship

chunks.title: Reviewing or disputing the drug test failure and sanction — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Reviewing or disputing the drug test failure and sanction
A client has the right to dispute or review any decision they disagree with relating to:
- an obligations failure or
- a sanction being imposed
A client can do this by:
- disputing the decision or
- lodging a formal Review of Decision
A Review of Decision can be lodged at any stage within three months of the obligations failure being initiated, or within 3 months of the sanction being imposed.
If a client disputes their obligations failure or sanction more than 20 working days after it is initiated or imposed, you need to advise the client to lodge a formal Review of Decision in writing.

chunks.title: Sanctions for a couple with dependent children - both fail their obligations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Couples with dependent children who both fail their obligations at the same time do not have their whole benefit sanctioned. Instead, a maximum financial sanction of 50% of the total benefit may be imposed. The balance of the benefit payable is known as 50% protection. Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.

chunks.title: Grade 1 sanction — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: If both clients fail their obligations for the first time, each person's portion of the benefit is reduced by 50% until they recomply, unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed. The couple will continue to get a maximum of 50% of their married rate of benefit. While their benefit is reduced, the couple can continue to get Extra help. The couple will continue to get the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment as they are still getting a qualifying benefit. For more information see: - Recompliance - Non-financial sanctions

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: If both clients fail their obligations a third time, 50% of the couple's benefit is cancelled. The couple will continue to get a maximum of 50% of their married rate of benefit until they recomply. If both clients are subject to a non-entitlement period for 13 weeks, both clients may get a provisional benefit if they start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities. While part of the benefit is cancelled, the couple gets 50% of any extra help they are entitled to. However, they can get the full rate of the Winter Energy Payment as they are still getting a qualifying benefit. For more information see: - Recompliance 13 week non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Processing 50% payments — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: When both clients fail their obligations at the same time the couple must continue to get a maximum of 50% of their married rate of benefit unless one of the couple has a non-financial sanction imposed. This must be paid manually, and will depend on which client failed their obligations first. For more information see: - Sanctions [no link find out why] process

chunks.title: One client recomplies first — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: If the primary client recomplies first, their portion of benefit and supplementary assistance must be resumed or regranted. The partner's benefit must remain sanctioned until they recomply. If the partner recomplies first, their portion of benefit and extra help is not able to be resumed or regranted as the primary record is not current. For information on how to process this see: - Recompliance [no link find out why] process

chunks.title: 50% protection and reduction of income — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: The 50% protection is applied to half the main benefit rate (eg the married rate) before any reduction of income. Any income will reduce benefit by 35 cents for every $1.00 of total income over $160.00 per week from the 50% protection payment. For more information see: - Charging income

chunks.title: Grade 1 sanction — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Grade 1 sanction
If both partners fail their obligations for the first time, each person's portion of the benefit is reduced by 50%. The couple will continue to get a total of 50% of the married rate unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed.
For more information on non-financial sanctions see:
- Non-financial sanctions
While their benefit is reduced, the couple can continue to get Extra help. Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid as the client is still getting a qualifying benefit.
If either partner has not recomplied within 4 weeks, they will have their portion of the benefit and Extra help suspended. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid to the client who has not recomplied as they are not getting a qualifying benefit.
Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or their portion of the benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.
Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
## Grade 3 sanction
If both partners fail their obligations for a third time, each person's portion of the benefit is cancelled. They are subject to a non-entitlement period for a period of 13 weeks. The client may get a provisional benefit if they start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities.
If they have not started a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities, they may reapply at the end of the non-entitlement period to get a benefit.
When the client's benefit is cancelled, supplementary assistance is also cancelled. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid as they are not getting a qualifying benefit.
For more information see:
- Recompliance

chunks.title: Grade 2 sanction — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Grade 2 sanction
If one partner fails their obligations a second time, their portion of the benefit is suspended until they recomply. While their portion of the benefit is suspended, their portion of Extra help is also suspended. They cannot get their portion of Winter Energy Payment. The other person continues to get their portion of the main benefit and Extra help. The full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment can be paid to the partner who hasn't failed.
Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
For their partner's entitlements see:
- Payments to the non-sanctioned client
For more information see:
- Recompliance
## Grade 3 sanction
If one partner fails their obligations for a third time, their portion of the benefit and extra help is cancelled. They are subject to a non-entitlement period for a period of 13 weeks. The client may get a provisional benefit if they start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities.
If they have not started a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities, they may reapply at the end of the non-entitlement period to get a benefit.
For their partner's entitlements see:
- Payments to the non-sanctioned client
For more information see:
- Recompliance

chunks.title: Grade 1 sanction — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Grade 1 sanction
If one partner fails their obligations for the first time, that person's portion of the benefit is reduced by 50%, unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed. While the benefit is reduced, the couple can continue to get supplementary assistance.
For more information on non-financial sanctions see:
- Non-financial sanctions
While the benefit is reduced, the couple can continue to get Extra help. Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid as the client is still getting a qualifying benefit.
If the person being sanctioned has not recomplied within 4 weeks, they will have their portion of the benefit and Extra help suspended. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid to the client who has failed as they are not getting a qualifying benefit. The full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment can be paid to the partner who hasn’t failed.
Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or their portion of the benefit is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.
Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
## Grade 3 sanction
If one partner fails their obligations for a third time, their portion of the benefit and Extra help is cancelled. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid to the client who has failed as they are not getting a qualifying benefit. The full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment can be paid to the partner who hasn’t failed.
They are subject to a non-entitlement period for a period of 13 weeks. They may get a provisional benefit if they start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities
If they have not started a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities, they may reapply at the end of the non-entitlement period to get a benefit.
For their partner's entitlements see:
- Payments to the non-sanctioned client or partner
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Grade 1 sanction — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Grade 1 sanction
A first obligations failure means the client's benefit is reduced by 50% until the client recomplies, unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed.
For more information on non-financial sanctions see:
- Non-financial sanctions
While their benefit is reduced, the client can continue getting Extra help. Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid as the client is still getting a qualifying benefit.
If the client has not recomplied within 4 weeks, they will have their benefit suspended along with all Extra help (including Winter Energy Payment).
Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or the payment is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.
Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
## Grade 2 sanction
A second obligations failure means the client's benefit is suspended. When their benefit is suspended, any Extra help the client was getting is also suspended. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid as the client is not getting a qualifying benefit.
Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or the payment is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.
Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
## Grade 3 sanction
A third obligations failure means the client's benefit is cancelled and they are subject to a non-entitlement period for 13 weeks. The client may get a provisional benefit if they start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities.
When the client's benefit is cancelled, Extra help is also cancelled. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid as the client is not getting a qualifying benefit.
If they have not started a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities, they may reapply at the end of the non-entitlement period to get a benefit.
For more information see:
- Recompliance

chunks.title: Sanctions for sole parents — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Sanctions for sole parents
When sole parents fail their obligations and have a financial sanction imposed, they do not have their whole benefit sanctioned. Instead, a maximum sanction of 50% of the total benefit may be imposed. The balance payable is known as 50% protection.
Sole parents who are sanctioned can continue to get full supplementary assistance, regardless of the grade of sanction. This includes the Winter Energy Payment.
For more information on what a client can continue to get when sanctioned, see:
- Paying other assistance during a sanction
If the client has not recomplied after 2 weeks, MSD will contact them to discuss financial assistance and recompliance. If the client has still not recomplied at 4 weeks MSD will need to send the client a letter advising they need to attend an appointment to discuss ongoing entitlement to benefit.
For more information on this process see:
- Sanction period - Two week intervention [no link find out why]
- Sanction period - Four week intervention [no link find out why]
## Grade 1 and 2 sanctions
For a first and second obligations failure, a sole parent's benefit is reduced by 50% until they recomply, unless they have a non-financial sanction imposed (for a first failure only).
For more information on non-financial sanctions see:
- Non-financial sanctions
They continue to get full supplementary assistance.
Note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must successfully dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
## Grade 3 sanction
For a third obligations failure a sole parent is subject to a non-entitlement period for a period of 13 weeks and will have 50% of their benefit cancelled. The sole parent may get a provisional benefit and have their benefit increased to 100% if they start a 6-week approved activity or programme of activities.
They continue to get full supplementary assistance (including the full rate of Winter Energy Payment).
For more information see:
- Recompliance

chunks.title: Setting appropriate activities for clients — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Setting appropriate activities for clients
After a discussion with a client, you will need to determine the most appropriate activities for them to undertake. To decide what activities are most appropriate, you should consider:
- client's individual circumstances
- whether the activity is suitable for the client
Note you do not need to seek the client's or partner's agreement to the activities that you require them to complete.
Once you and the client have discussed what activities will be appropriate, include them in the client's Service Plan.

chunks.title: Social obligations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Social obligations
A client and their partner (if any) getting Jobseeker Support Student Hardship have social obligations that apply for each dependent child in their care.
This includes any children for whom Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid.
A client and their partner (if any) must take all reasonable steps to meet all of the social obligations that apply for each child. The social obligations that apply for each child depend on the age of the child.
When the client is in a relationship, the social obligations apply to both the client and their partner.
When required, clients and their partner (if any) must take all reasonable steps to meet the following social obligations.
The child must be:
- enrolled with a medical practitioner or nurse practitioner, or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation and
- up-to-date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks (for children under 5 years old) and
- enrolled in and attending 1 of the following from the age of 3 years old until they start school: an approved early childhood education programme orTe Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School oranother approved parenting and early childhood home education programme
- an approved early childhood education programme or
- Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - Distance School or
- another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme
- enrolled in and attending school from the age of 5 or 6 years old (depending on when they start school)
When required, a client and their partner (if any) must:
- attend and participate in interviews with MSD to discuss meeting their social obligations and
- advise on progress where they have not been able to meet their social obligations
A client is only required to meet social obligations from the time they begin to receive a benefit.
Clients in the process of applying for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship or who have future commencement date of their Jobseeker Support Student Hardship are not required to meet these social obligations.
Clients are also not required to meet social obligations that would have been relevant they started getting a benefit.
For example, a client who starts receiving Jobseeker Support when their child is between 3 and 4 months old cannot be sanctioned for not having completed the core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks a child should have at ages 4 to 6 weeks.

chunks.title: Social obligations recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period) — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Social obligations recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
If a client or partner fails their obligations for a third time, their benefit is reduced or cancelled. For the client or partner to increase their benefit they must undertake a 6 week recompliance activity or programme of activities and reapply for a benefit.
If the third obligation failure is a social obligation failure, the standard 6 week recompliance activities may not be appropriate as some partners do not have work obligations and cannot work or be in training for a period of 6 weeks.
In this situation, a programme of short-term approved activities may be more appropriate for the client.
## Example 1
Short term approved activities to consider for a Jobseeker Support Student Hardship client with part-time work obligations and social obligations, where the third failure was a social obligations failure.
Week 1
Take reasonable steps to talk to providers of appropriate recognised early childhood education programme
Week 2
Take reasonable steps to enrol their child in a recognised early childhood education programmes
Week 3
CV seminar
Week 4
Attend presentation seminar approved by Work and Income
Week 5
Attend a local parenting programme that provides support for families
Week 6
Meet with case manager to talk about what reasonable steps have been taken to enrol the child in a recognised early childhood education programme and discuss how the other activities went
Note a programme of suitable activities for a client with part-time work obligations should be:
- for no more than 15 hours each week for primary clients that qualify for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship on the grounds of a health condition, injury or disability
- for no more than 20 hours each week for partners with part-time work obligations
## Example 2
Example of short term approved activities to consider for a Jobseeker Support Student Hardship client with social obligations, where the third failure was a social obligations failure.
Week 1
Make contact with the local Family Start whanau worker and arrange a meeting with them
Week 2
Family Start whanau worker visit
Week 3
Contact a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and arrange a visit
Week 4
Contact the local medical centre to ensure the children are enrolled in primary health care
Week 5
Talk to appropriate providers of recognised early childhood education programmes
Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider visit
Week 6
Meet with a case manager about what steps have been taken

chunks.title: Sole parents whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025 — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Sole parents whose benefit commenced before 1 July 2025
Sole parents whose Jobseeker Support Student Hardship commenced before 1 July 2025 can have their income charged annually, until their benefit is cancelled. When a sole parent with annual income charging declares a change in income, this should be updated from the first available date.
Sole parents whose Jobseeker Support Student Hardship commences on or after 1 July 2025 are subject to weekly income charging. They must have their income charged for the week in which the income is earned or the period it represents.
## Annual income charge
Clients with annual income charging whose annual income is over $8,320 gross will have their benefit reduced by:
- 30 cents for each $1.00 of income that is between $8,320 and $13,000 gross per year
- 70 cents for every $1.00 of income that is over $13,000 gross per year.

chunks.title: Suitability of employment-related training or course — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Suitability of employment-related training or course
The employment-related training and courses a client must attend and participate in as part of their Upskilling sanction will generally be online.
In some instances, an in-person employment-related training or course can be recommended or approved if MSD staff consider it suitable for the client's circumstances.
Suitability is based on a client's level of expertise and skills.
There are some general factors that should be considered when determining if a training or course is suitable for a client. For example:
- where a client lives (e.g. the distance the client has to travel to get to the training or course)
- a client's age and family situation (e.g. caretaking responsibilities at certain times)
- any previous job experience and education
- any specific barriers to employment that an employment-related training or course may address, (e.g. a health condition or disability, or caring responsibilities)
- if a client has already participated in other employment-related training or courses, or any of MSD's other employment programmes or services.
Note a client's individual circumstances will determine what is considered suitable. Each activity should be considered on a case-by-case basis.

chunks.title: Organisation — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Organisation
Suitable organisations can be community or volunteer organisations. These organisations may have existing relationship with MSD, however this is not required.
To be suitable, an organisation should:
- not be for profit
- not be public sector, e.g. central or local government or a Crown entity
- have an internal organisation structure, e.g. has defined key functions, roles and responsibilities
- be self-governing - the organisation primarily controls its own management and operations
- not be something people are required to contribute time to by law, e.g. jury duty.
Organisations are not suitable if:
- they have previously breached employment law, or
- their area of focus would likely be inappropriate or unacceptable to the wider community, or
- a client completing Community Work Experience at this organisation is likely to be a reputational risk to MSD.
The organisation must be confident they can provide a client with the required hours and 4 consecutive weeks needed to complete their Community Work Experience. If the organisation is unsure, the position would not be suitable for the client.
Note clients may secure multiple positions to complete their Community Work Experience. For more information see: Period of Community Work Experience

chunks.title: Suitable employment — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Suitable employment
Suitable employment varies between clients depending on their individual circumstances.
To meet their work obligations clients and partners need to be available for, and take reasonable steps to find, suitable employment of at least:
- 30 hours per week for clients with full-time work obligations
- 15 hours per week, for clients receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship (health condition, injury or disability) who have part-time work capacity
- 20 hours per week for all other clients with part-time work obligations
Clients may have pre-benefit obligations to attend an interview or accept an offer of employment. This employment must also be considered suitable.
## Deciding if a job is suitable
When deciding on whether a job is suitable for a client, you need to consider the following (but is not limited to):
- appropriate hours of employment, eg hours are not excessive
- access to childcare
- family commitments
- religious commitments
- jobs which offend strongly held views
- days of the week
- type of employment
- skills required
- experience
- location of the job
- wages
- number of hours per week is within the suitable range for the client's obligations
For more information see:
- Hours range for suitable employment
- Meeting job search requirements
- Employment trial period of up to 90 days
- Referrals to jobs with drug test requirements

chunks.title: Taking all reasonable steps to enrol in a recognised early childhood education programme — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Taking all reasonable steps to enrol in a recognised early childhood education programme
A client could be considered to be taking all reasonable steps to enrol their child in an early childhood education programme for reasons including, (but not limited to) that:
- there are shortages of places or availability issues, and the client has a plan in place or has made a commitment to enrol their child when a place becomes available
- there are additional costs of participation that may cause financial hardship to the family, including: travel costs oradditional costs associated with attending the early childhood education programme
- travel costs or
- additional costs associated with attending the early childhood education programme
- the child has behavioural problems meaning attendance at an ECE service would be difficult or not possible (for example the child is not currently permitted to attend). This should be recorded as an exception in OBMAN using 'child is not permitted to attend' as the obligation exception reason.
To help clients meet this social obligation you should discuss childcare assistance that may be available to the client.

chunks.title: IRD number for client or partner who is apportioned assistance — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: MSD may request a client's for evidence of an IRD number for a primary client who is being paid Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. MSD can also request evidence of an IRD number for a partner when they are apportioned a part of the primary client's assistance.

chunks.title: Notice following an unsuccessful match — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a client or their partner's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the client or partner (in writing) to provide evidence of their IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the client or partner a minimum of 10 working days to provide their IRD number evidence or their assistance must be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship and MSD holds an IRD number on record. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Isla's IRD number. MSD provides a notice in writing, giving 10 working days for Isla to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Isla already having an IRD number - Isla not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD must suspend assistance if evidence of IRD number is not received — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: MSD must suspend all taxable and/or income tested assistance the client is getting, including their Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, if evidence of an IRD number is not provided within 10 working days from the written request, or extended period if this has been applied. If the partner has not provided evidence of their IRD number, the partner's taxable and/or income tested assistance must be suspended. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance. Example Koa is receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship and MSD does not have an IRD number on record. MSD sends a written request giving 10 working days for Koa to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD receives no response to this request. MSD suspends Koa's taxable and/or income tested assistance because Koa has not supplied MSD with evidence of their IRD number within the timeframe provided.

chunks.title: IRD number evidence may not be requested in some circumstances — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - there are significant factors, that are outside the client's or partner's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number (e.g. a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence), and - the client needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided or - there are significant factors related to a health, injury or disability that are outside the client or partner's control that prevent them from providing evidence of an IRD number, and - an agent cannot be appointed to act on the client or partner's behalf. MSD can determine a later point to request the evidence of the IRD number. Example Sienna is 23 and receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. Sienna's mother (Sara) is Sienna's agent and acts on Sienna's behalf with MSD. Sienna does not have an IRD number and Sara is not a recognised agent for Sienna for Inland Revenue. Sienna has a serious head injury, is unconscious and expected to be in hospital for at least 8 weeks. Sienna is not able to give consent to appoint Sara as an agent for Inland Revenue to apply for an IRD number due to their injury. MSD can request this information later when Sienna's situation has changed. Note there is different guidance for requesting an IRD number or evidence of an IRD number for partners who are not apportioned but their income is relevant to a clients Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, or when a client is applying for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.

chunks.title: Temporary employment — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Temporary employment
No stand-down is imposed when a client:
- has been in part-time employment or full-time employment for less than 26 weeks
- was receiving a benefit immediately before they were employed
- the benefit was stopped because they returned to work and
- has applied for a benefit after their employment ceased
Temporary employment can include employment during an employment trial period of up to 90 days if the client was getting a benefit and is reapplying for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship as their employment has ceased.
Note the client's average weekly income is not required where the client has been in temporary employment for less than 26 weeks. However, the client's final pay details are required to determine the date of event and entitlement date.
If a client leaves their employment without good and sufficient reason a voluntary unemployment stand-down may be considered.
For more information see:
- Commencement date
- No stand-down applies
- Employment trial period of up to 90 days

chunks.title: The disputes process — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## The disputes process
The disputes process is a quick process where you must respond to a client's dispute immediately. You must take into account any new information provided by the client or partner and let the client or partner know your decision straight away. A letter is sent automatically to the client or partner once a decision has been recorded on the dispute.
A client or partner can dispute the decision if they believe:
- they did not fail their obligations including when they believe they have taken all reasonable steps to meet a social obligation or
- that they had a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete the obligation
Note if a client or partner has disputed the obligations failure and you have upheld your decision, the client or partner can only dispute it again by following the Review of Decision or Medical Appeal Board appeal (drug test failure only) processes.
If a sanction has been imposed you can still use the disputes process. This allows the client or partner an opportunity for a quick resolution to their dispute before proceeding with the Review of Decision process.
For more information see:
- Recording decisions on a dispute
## Good and sufficient reason for failing
You must consider the circumstances of the client or partner, and determine whether it would have been reasonable for the client or partner to have undertaken the activity.
Good and sufficient reasons for failing to undertake an activity will depend on the obligation the client and partner have failed. For social obligations you must consider whether the client has taken all reasonable steps to meet their social obligations.
Note that if you are unsure as to whether a client or partner has a good and sufficient reason then you should seek guidance from your capability developer, Helpline, manager client service operations or manager client service delivery.

chunks.title: Training providers requiring a drug test — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Training providers requiring a drug test
Some training providers will require potential trainees to pass a drug test as a prerequisite to being accepted on the course.
Training providers will use drug tests where the training programmes have a focus on employment outcomes. This includes training programmes that are:
- non classroom based programmes or on-the-job programmes where the tests are required for health and safely purposes
- classroom based training where the industry would require the trainee to be drug free for health and safety purposes to gain employment
Note a client can only fail the drug test obligations for drug tests that are being taken as prerequisites to being accepted onto a course - not for any other ongoing drug tests that a training provider may ask for.
## Verification
In order to make a decision that a client has failed a drug test, without good and sufficient reason, you must have received confirmation from the training provider.

chunks.title: Transfer between benefits — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: A transfer between benefits can occur when a client qualifies for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship while currently receiving another benefit. There is no stand-down imposed for clients who: - transfer to Jobseeker Support Student Hardship from another benefit type or - are included as a partner in another benefit type and are now applying as the primary client Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Childs Benefit and Orphans Benefit are also a benefit in this situation. Where Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit has been paid and the child now qualifies for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, no stand-down is imposed.

chunks.title: Partner to be included — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: An initial stand-down is imposed, if a client receiving a benefit is to be included as a partner in a new application for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. There are situations where a partner can continue to receive payment of Sole Parent Support during the initial stand-down period where they are included as a partner in a new application for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship.

chunks.title: Examples — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Generally in the 3 examples below the payment of the Sole Parent Support can be continued up to the actual commencement date of the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. Example 1A client has been receiving a Sole Parent Support and is now to be included in a new application for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship as a partner an initial stand-down is imposed on the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. Example 2A client has been in prison or on remand for 31 days or more and has applied for a Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. On release, the client moves in with their former partner who was receiving Sole Parent Support. An initial stand-down is imposed on the Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. Example 3A couple with children separated and the mother received Sole Parent Support and the father was working. The father's job ceased and the couple are now living together again. The father applied for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship and an initial stand-down is imposed. If there has been a delay in applying for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship then payment of the Sole Parent Support may be cancelled from the date after the client has reconciled.

chunks.title: Non-beneficiary clients — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: When a non-beneficiary client receiving Extra help such as Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance applies for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship, it is not regarded as a transfer between benefits. An initial stand-down is imposed. For more information see: - No stand-down applies - Processing standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why] - Core policy Relationship status for benefit - Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process

chunks.title: Client intending to return to the same employer — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Client intending to return to the same employer
If a client has received any sick leave payment they would not be eligible for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship until these payments had stopped. You then assess any initial stand-down.
Clients are not required to use any sick leave they may have if they are intending to return to the same employer.

chunks.title: 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down
When clients in the following circumstances apply for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship within 28 days of their entitlement date, the commencement date rules are different:
- clients who have a health condition, injury or disability
- sole parents
- clients who have lost the financial support of their spouse due to: deathseparationending of a de facto relationship orimprisonment
- death
- separation
- ending of a de facto relationship or
- imprisonment
For these clients, the commencement date is the day after the initial stand-down ends.
This means, in some situations, MSD can commence a benefit from a date earlier than the application date.
If the application is not received within 28 days, MSD cannot backdate the commencement date.
Note the 28-day rule only applies to clients who have an initial stand down imposed.

chunks.title: Evidential tests — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Evidential tests
Some employers, particularly larger employers, may require an evidential test and will not conduct screening tests or they may conduct both tests.
Generally, evidential tests are used when a screening test is failed.
Evidential tests are a more comprehensive and expensive method of detecting drugs. They can detect a wider range of substances and identify the specific substance. This test is also referred to as a confirmation test.
Evidential testing is conducted in an accredited laboratory by qualified staff. Samples are sent to the laboratory by drug test providers or specialised staff, or the laboratory will arrange to take the sample themselves.
For more information see:
- Client has failed a screening drug test
- Effect of certain drugs

chunks.title: Unable to meet work preparation obligations due to health condition, injury or disability — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Unable to meet work preparation obligations due to health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to:
- clients (who have a deferral from their work obligations, but have work preparation obligations) and
- partners with work preparation obligations
A client may be unable to meet their work preparation obligations when their health condition, injury or disability restricts them. For example when a client is:
- in hospital or
- is unable to attend an interview with MSD due to their condition
MSD should consider the information on the client's Work Capacity Medical Certificate to see if the registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner, (or dentist or midwife where relevant) has advised of any restrictions to a client's capacity to plan.
This is a full exemption.
## Evidence
To support their exemption, the client must provide a Work Capacity Medical Certificate. The certificate should be completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant).
The information required on the medical certificate includes:
- a diagnosis (what the illness, disability or health condition is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to work or to plan for work and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for work or planning for work and
- any other information needed
## Duration
The period of an exemption is based on the reassessment date recorded on the medical certificate by a client's health practitioner.
This exemption should then be reviewed.
At the review MSD should consider the client's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption.
MSD can ask the client to provide evidence of the reason why the exemption should be extended.

chunks.title: Unable to receive financial support from parents — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Unable to receive financial support from parents
To receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship a single young person must be going through a parental support gap. A 16 or 17 year old is considered have a parental support gap when their parents (or guardians) are unable to support them financially because they are:
- deceased
- in prison
- in hospital or
- overseas
You will need to find out:
- what the period of absence is and what provisions have been made for the young person's support
- if the parents are overseas, ask if it is temporary or permanent, and why the young person has not gone as well. See: Parents overseas
- if the parents are living apart, ask the young person what involvement they have with the other parent and whether they have considered living with them and
- whether the young person is living in a 'care' arrangement as opposed to an independent situation
For more information see:
- What is financial support?
- Independent
- Parents overseas
- Discharged from care
- Definition of parents

chunks.title: Example — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Example
A partner who is subject to a sanction who develops a health condition or becomes, injured or disabled, and meets the criteria for the exemption 'would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability'. They are unable to complete a recompliance activity.
In this situation you should add the exemption reason in SWIFTT, and follow the disputes process (so that the benefit can be resumed). Also consider the person's eligibility for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship on the ground of a health condition, injury or a disability.
For details of the requirements for a client or partner who has a health condition, injury or disability see:
- Paying other assistance during a sanction
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Under 3 years - Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Under 3 years - Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit
This exemption may apply to partners with work obligations.
In some cases a client may be caring for a child under 3 years for whom they are receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit.
Clients granted this exemption will be subject to work preparation obligations.
## Duration
This exemption can be granted in SWIFTT for 12 months initially or to when the child turns 3 years old - whichever is earlier.
The exemption can be renewed after 12 months provided the child is still under five and the parent still qualifies for benefit.

chunks.title: Unsupported Childs Benefit was paid — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Unsupported Childs Benefit was paid
If the young person has been living with a caregiver who was receiving Unsupported Childs Benefit for the young person, the young person can only receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship if:
- the young person has stopped living with the caregiver and
- there has been a relationship breakdown between the young person and caregiver
This is because caregivers who receive Unsupported Childs Benefit for a dependent person are considered parents.

chunks.title: Up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks
A client and their partner (if any) receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship must take all reasonable steps to:
- register their child or children with a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and
- keep up-to-date with the child's core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks
Note a client is only required to ensure their child completes core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks to meet this obligation from the time they begin to receive a benefit. For example, a client who starts receiving a benefit when their child is between three and four months old cannot be failed for not having completed the core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks the child should have had at ages four to six weeks.
## Age of child
There are eight core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks that apply to children aged from 4 weeks to 5 years old. There are also 3 checks that occur shortly after birth. The obligation only applies for the 8 core checks that occur from around 4 months through to 5 years of age.
For more information see:
- Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks
## Verification
Most parents will already have their child or children registered and up to date with their core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks and in most cases you should take the client's word that they are meeting this social obligation.
However, if you have information that indicates the client is not taking reasonable all steps to meet their social obligations, for example you may ask for proof that the checks have been completed by asking to see their Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book.
The Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book is issued to parents when their child is born and is sufficient evidence of the child's attendance. The Health Book has helpful advice and information about what is happening at different stages in the child's development and has places to record all the Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks.
For more information see:
- Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks
- Overview of social obligations according to age of the child
- All reasonable steps to meet social obligations

chunks.title: Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Voluntary unemployment or dismissal for misconduct
A client and their partner (if any) who are applying for Jobseeker Support and have work obligations, can have a 13 week non-entitlement period if they:
- have become voluntarily unemployed without a good and sufficient reason
- are applying for a benefit because they were dismissed by their employer for misconduct
'Becoming voluntarily unemployed' means the client has resigned from, or otherwise left employment without a good and sufficient reason.
'Dismissal as a result of misconduct' means that the client has lost employment as a result of misconduct without a good and sufficient reason.
There are some circumstances where a 13 week non-entitlement period would not be imposed. For more information see:
- Non-entitlement period should not be imposed
Note the 50% protection for clients and partners with dependent children applies.
For more information see:
- Deciding non-entitlement period for voluntary unemployment or misconduct
- Effect of 13 week non-entitlement period for partner
- Effect of non-entitlement period on financial assistance
- Good and sufficient reasons for voluntary unemployment

chunks.title: Charging income example - single clients and couples — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Charging income example - single clients and couples
Below are examples of calculating the income reduction for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship - single clients and couples.

## Example 2

chunks.title: Charging income example - sole parents — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Charging income example - sole parents
Below are examples of calculating the income reduction for Jobseeker Support Student Hardship - sole parents.
## Example 1
Weekly gross income
$350.00
Less income allowed before benefit is affected (as at 1 April 2022)

chunks.title: Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks
Well Child /Tamariki Ora services are a screening, education and support service offered to all New Zealand children and their families or whānau from birth to 5 years old.
The services assist and support families and whānau to improve and protect their children's health. They are provided free to all children under 5 years old by registered nurses and community health workers with specific training in child health.
First time parents and families requiring extra support are offered additional visits. Some visits are carried out in the home and others in clinics or community facilities.
Different providers run the Well-Child/Tamariki Ora services, including:
- Plunket
- Māori health providers
- Pacific Island health providers
- Public Health Services - for example, public health nurses, community nurses, community health workers, social workers.
## When do the checks happen?
The Well Child/Tamariki Ora schedule includes 12 health checks (contacts) with 8 of these offered to children aged from 4 to 6 weeks to 5 years.
Only the 8 core Well Child checks are required to meet this social obligation.
## Between birth and 4 weeks
Four checks are provided by a midwife, health practitioner or obstetrician:
- soon after birth
- 24 hours after birth
- during the first week of baby's life
- between 2 and 4 weeks
Note the birth to 4 weeks checks listed above do not apply for social obligations purposes.
## Between 4 weeks and 5 years
The 8 core Well-Child/Tamariki Ora checks (listed below) for children between the ages of 4 - 6 weeks to 5 years are required to meet social obligations.
These are provided by the Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider when the child is:
- 4 - 6 weeks
- 8 - 10 weeks
- 3 - 4 months
- 5 - 7 months
- 9 - 12 months
- 15 - 18 months
- 2 - 3 years
- 4 - 5 years (this is the before school check, and the final Well Child health check)

chunks.title: What is financial support? — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## What is financial support?
Consider a young person to be financially supported by their parents when payments received are:
- long-term
- ongoing
- regular and
- at least equal to or higher than the benefit rate payableIf a young person receives a lesser amount of support from their parents (or a one-off payment), they may still receive Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. Any support received would be charged as income.
Any financial support the young person receives must be given without any conditions for payment.
For more information see:
- Unable to receive financial support from parents
- Independent

chunks.title: When financial support is not expected — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## When financial support is not expected
Parents will not be expected to financially support the young person if:
- the young person is, or has been married
- the young person, is in, or has been in, a civil union
- the young person is, or has been, living in a de facto relationship that is in the nature of marriage or civil union (as determined by StudyLink) or
- the young person has been discharged from the care of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, and is not dependent on a caregiver
For more information see:
- De facto relationship (definition)
- Discharged from care
- Unsupported Childs benefit was paid

chunks.title: When the sanction is imposed — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## When the sanction is imposed
Sanctions can only be imposed 5 working days after the client has been sent a letter about their obligations failure. This is called the 5 working day notice period.
Note that if a client recomplies within the initial 5 working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the obligations failure is counted.
Also note if a client has more than one obligation failure initiated on the same day, only one sanction can be imposed on the client. For the sanction to be lifted, the client must dispute or recomply with all the obligation failures.
## How to count the '5 working day notice' period
The 5 working day notice period is counted from the date after the obligations failure letter has been sent to the client, to allow for posting and delivery of the letter.
The 5 working day notice period excludes weekends, public holidays, or the period 25 December to 15 January each year.
The table below provides an example of how to count the notice period.
Day 0

Day 0

Day 1Day 2

Five working day notice period begins

Five working day notice period continues
Day 6

chunks.title: Why is the client moving to a limited employment location? — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Why is the client moving to a limited employment location?
You will need to work closely with your client to see if their reasons for wanting to move to a limited employment location can be addressed in a way that alleviates the need to move.
Examples of reasons and possible solutions are as follows:
- a client planning to move to escape a difficult situation in their current location may be encouraged to move to an area where there are employment opportunities available, rather than a limited employment location
- a client moving because they are having difficulty managing high housing costs may also be encouraged to move to a location with low-cost accommodation that is not a limited employment location. Alternatively, you could refer them to an agency offering budgeting advice, or see if they are eligible for Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or social housing
- a client planning to move to take care of a sick relative may be eligible for Supported Living Payment (caring for a person) Clients who receive this or other non work-obligated benefits are not affected by the limited employment locations policy
- a client planning to move for cultural reasons should be assisted as appropriate to work out whether, and how, they can meet their work obligations in that location
Depending on the client's reason for moving, it may be appropriate to assess their eligibility for other forms of assistance that may help them remain in an area where there are employment opportunities available. These may include:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Disability Allowance
- Child Disability Allowance
- Childcare Assistance Programme
- Temporary Additional Support

chunks.title: Work ability assessment obligation — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Work ability assessment obligation
Partners receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship have a work ability assessment obligation that requires them, when asked, to attend and participate in:
- Self-Assessments
- Structured Interview
- Work Ability Assessments
## Reason for work ability assessment
A work ability assessment will help show what work a partner is capable of doing and what Work and Income can do to help a partner with their return to work.
A work ability assessment will help determine:
- the client's work ability
- what suitable work or work preparation activities are appropriate for the partner
- what assistance, services or support Work and Income and/or other agencies should be providing
As a result of a work ability assessment, a client's work obligations, or benefit entitlement may change.
## Partners required to participate in a work ability assessment
Generally only partners who have a health condition, injury or disability will be required to undertake or participate in a Work Ability Assessment.
## Failing to comply
If a partner does not meet these obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, an obligation failure will be initiated and a sanction may be imposed.

chunks.title: Work obligations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Full-time work obligations apply to: - primary clients (except those receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship on ground of a health condition, injury or disability) - partners with no dependent children and - partners with a youngest dependent child aged 14 years or over Part-time work obligations apply to: - primary clients receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship (health condition, injury or disability) who have part-time work capacity - partners with a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years Clients (and partners) with work obligations must: - be available for, and take reasonable steps to obtain, suitable employment - accept any offer of suitable employment, including temporary employment or employment that is seasonal or subsidised Note suitable employment can include employment that contains an employment trial. - attend and participate in an interview for any opportunity of suitable employment to which the client is referred - when required to attend and participate in any interview with Work and Income or on behalf of Work and Income - when required to undertake planning for employment - report to Work and Income on progress in meeting their work obligations as often as required and - when required by Work and Income, undertake any activity to improve their work readiness and employment prospects, including: any work assessmentany programme or seminarany work experience or work exploration activityany employment-related trainingrehabilitation (but not medical treatment) - any work assessment - any programme or seminar - any work experience or work exploration activity - any employment-related training - rehabilitation (but not medical treatment)

chunks.title: Suitable employment — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Clients with full-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of at least 30 hours or more per week. Clients with part-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of at least: - 15 hours per week, for clients receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship (health condition, injury or disability) who have part-time work capacity - 20 hours per week for all other clients However, if suitable employment is available for hours other than 15, 20 or 30 hours per week (as applicable), the client or partner can be required to accept an offer of this job. Work obligations can be applied on any day of the week provided it is suitable for the client's circumstances. To help you decide if the job is suitable for the client see: - Suitable employment - Hours range for suitable employment

chunks.title: Failing to comply — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Clients who fail to comply with their work obligations are subject to an obligations failure. If a client (or partner) does not meet their work obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, you should initiate an obligations failure. You should consider the client's individual circumstances before referring them to a job or an activity, to ensure that they can realistically meet their obligations.

chunks.title: Deferrals from work obligations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Clients may be able to receive a temporary deferral from their work obligations in specific circumstances. These clients will generally work preparation obligations for the duration of the deferral. For more information about deferrals, see: - Deferrals

chunks.title: Exemptions from work obligations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text: Clients may be able to receive a temporary exemption from their work obligations. For more information about exemptions, see: - Exemptions For more information see: - Meeting job search requirements - Informing clients of their obligations - Setting appropriate activities for clients - Employment trial period of up to 90 days - Drug test obligations - Reporting progress - Rehabilitation - Exemptions - Deferrals - Table of Exemptions - Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations - Obligations failures

chunks.title: Work or work preparation obligations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Work or work preparation obligations
Clients and partners receiving Jobseeker Support Student Hardship have full-time or part-time work obligations or work preparation obligations.
## Full-time work obligations
Full-time work obligations apply to:
- primary clients
- partners with no children and
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged 14 years or over
Clients with full-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of at least 30 hours or more per week.
## Part-time work obligations
Part-time work obligations apply to:
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged between 3 and 13 years
Clients with part-time work obligations must be available for, and take reasonable steps to find suitable employment of at least 20 hours per week.
## Work preparation obligations
Work preparation obligations apply to:
- partners with a youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
Note that if the partner is receiving Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit, these children are not considered dependent children for rates purposes but they are treated as dependent children for setting work or work preparation obligations.
For more information see:
- Partners with no children or youngest child 14+ years
- Partner with youngest child between 3 and 13 years
- Partner with youngest dependent child aged under 3 years
- Work preparation obligations
- Work obligations
- Rehabilitation
- Work ability assessment obligation
- Working with contracted service provider obligation
- Drug test obligations
- Limited employment locations
- Exemptions
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Work preparation obligations — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Work preparation obligations
A person with work preparation obligations must take all reasonable steps to prepare for employment. When considering what is reasonable you must consider what is practical for their individual circumstances.
In addition, clients and partners with work preparation obligations must:
- when required to undertake planning for employment
- when required to report to Work and Income on progress in meeting their work preparation obligations as often as required
- when required to attend and participate in any interview with Work and Income or on behalf of Work and Income and
- when required by Work and Income undertake any activity to improve their work readiness and employment prospects, including: any work assessmentany programme or seminarany work experience or work exploration activityany employment related trainingrehabilitation (but not medical treatment)an education programme
- any work assessment
- any programme or seminar
- any work experience or work exploration activity
- any employment related training
- rehabilitation (but not medical treatment)
- an education programme
Work preparation obligations can be applied on any day of the week provided it is suitable for the partner's circumstances.
If a client or partner does not meet their work preparation obligations, without a good and sufficient reason, you should initiate an obligations failure.
For more information see:
- Informing clients of their obligations
- Setting appropriate activities for clients
- Reporting progress
- Rehabilitation
- Exemptions
- Table of exemptions
- Good and sufficient reason not meeting work or work preparation obligations
- Obligations failures

chunks.title: Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to a client or partner with work obligations.
If a client meets the qualifications for Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury, or disability they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their work obligations until their capacity for work improves.
The client must be limited in their capacity to work because of a health condition, injury or disability and, depending on whether they have part-time or full-time work obligations be:
- unable to look for part-time work of at least 15 hours per week or
- losing earnings because they are unable to work for at least 15 or 30 hours a week
This is a partial exemption and the client is able to:
- plan for employment and
- undertake certain work related activities
## Evidence
To support their exemption, the client is required to provide a Work Capacity Medical Certificate.
The medical certificate should be completed and signed by a registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner, (or dentist or midwife where relevant).
The information required on the medical certificate is:
- a diagnosis (what the illness, disability or health condition is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to work and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for work planning, training and part-time work and
- any other information that is required
## Duration
The period of time for an exemption is based on the reassessment date recorded on their medical certificate by their registered medical practitioner or nurse practitioner (or dentist or midwife where relevant).
This exemption should then be reviewed.
