At the review MSD should consider the client's circumstances and whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption. MSD can ask the client to provide evidence of the reason why the exemption should be extended.

chunks.title: Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability — jobseeker support student hardship
chunks.text:
## Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
This exemption may apply to partners with work or work preparation obligations.
If a partner meets the qualifications for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability or total blindness, they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their work or work preparation obligations.
The partner must be
- both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for work because of a health condition, or injury or disability from an accident, or a condition they have had since birth or
- totally blind
Note totally blind and legally blind are not the same.
This can be a full or partial exemption depending on the whether the client can plan for a return to work.
MSD should discuss with the client whether they can still:
- plan for employment and
- undertake certain work related activities
If it is unclear whether a full or partial exemption should be granted, seek advice from the Regional Health Advisor or Regional Disability Advisor.
Note when appropriate MSD should consider the client's eligibility for Supported Living Payment.
## Evidence
The client is required to provide a Work Capacity Medical Certificate or medical information from a registered medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or psychologist stating:
- a diagnosis (what the illness, disability or health condition is) and
- the impact of the condition on their ability to work and
- the likely duration of the impact and
- their capacity for work planning, training and part-time work and
- any other information is required

chunks.title: Eligibility — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Eligibility
An Accommodation Benefit is payable to eligible students getting a Student Allowance.
## Students not eligible for Accommodation Benefit
The following groups of students are not eligible for Accommodation Benefit:
- students who are living with a parent in the parental home unless: they or their partner have a supported child
- they or their partner have a supported child
- students who are not living with a parent, but who are living in a home maintained or provided by their parents, unless: they are paying market rent for the area of the home occupied by the student orthey are responsible for the payment of the outgoings for the area of the home occupied by the student orthey or their partner have a supported childA parent may be providing a home for a student even if they do not legally own the property, e.g. a parent who is a settlor/trustee of a trust which owns property where a student is living can be considered to be providing a home for that student:
- they are paying market rent for the area of the home occupied by the student or
- they are responsible for the payment of the outgoings for the area of the home occupied by the student or
- they or their partner have a supported childA parent may be providing a home for a student even if they do not legally own the property, e.g. a parent who is a settlor/trustee of a trust which owns property where a student is living can be considered to be providing a home for that student:
- students, their spouse or partner, who have a tenancy agreement with a social housing providerThe definition of spouse or partner in this situation is the definition in the Public and Community Housing Management Act 1992. This means that a student who is generally considered to be single for Student Allowance purposes, has a spouse or partner in this situation.
- students who have a partner and their combined income is more than the combined income threshold unless: they are living away from their partnerIn some cases a student, or their partner may be eligible for an Accommodation Supplement.
- they are living away from their partnerIn some cases a student, or their partner may be eligible for an Accommodation Supplement.
## Accommodation Benefit rates
There are 2 types of Accommodation Benefit rates, the:
- sole parent rate and
- standard rates for all other students

chunks.title: Administrative reviews — student allowance
chunks.text: Students are entitled to review certain decisions MSD makes about their Student Allowance, Independent Circumstances Allowance or Accommodation Benefit. These reviews are called statutory reviews and are provided for in clause 5, Schedule 10 of the Education and Training Act 2020. For more information see: Statutory reviews Sometimes, a student's reason for review may not be covered in clause 5 of the Act. In such cases, an administrative review can be used.

chunks.title: What is an administrative review? — student allowance
chunks.text: Administrative reviews are used when a student disagrees with an action by MSD but the student does not have the right to review that action under a statutory review. Administrative reviews are not included in legislation, but they follow a similar process to statutory reviews. Administrative reviews give a student the opportunity to be heard and for MSD to complete a full review of the student’s file when a statutory review is not possible.

chunks.title: When an administrative review is used — student allowance
chunks.text: Administrative reviews are generally used to review whether: - a debt should be established or - the student needs to repay the debt (e.g. whether the debt meets the criteria for a debt write off) The reason why the debt was created should be assessed to see if it can be reviewed as a statutory review.

chunks.title: Example — student allowance
chunks.text: Kiriana contacts MSD to apply for a Student Allowance and is advised incorrectly she does not need to notify MSD if she changes her address while getting a Student Allowance. Kiriana moves to a new flat 6 months after she starts getting her Student Allowance and does not tell MSD. MSD later becomes aware of Kiriana's change of address, and determines she got paid the incorrect rate of Accommodation Benefit for the period she was in the new address. MSD creates a debt for the overpaid amount of Accommodation Benefit. Kiriana accepts she was paid the incorrect rate of Accommodation Benefit. However, she doesn't believe she should have to repay the debt as she was not at fault. She asks MSD to review the debt. This would be an administrative review.

chunks.title: Student disagrees with outcome of the administrative review — student allowance
chunks.text: A student cannot appeal MSD's decision from an administrative review to the Student Allowance Appeal Authority. A student who disagrees with the outcome of the review and thinks they have been unfairly treated can raise their concerns with the Office of the Ombudsman.

chunks.title: When it's unclear if the student has statutory or administrative review rights — student allowance
chunks.text: A statutory review generally should be provided if MSD cannot determine whether the student has statutory or administrative review rights. In some cases, the Student Allowance Appeal Authority may need to determine if the review is statutory or administrative before they can consider the situation the student is disputing.

chunks.title: Age — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Age
A student must be at least 16 years of age and (for study starting on or after 1 January 2014) under 65 years of age at study start date to get Student Allowance.
Generally students can only receive a maximum of:
- 92 weeks of entitlement for secondary study
- 120 weeks of entitlement for tertiary study if aged 40 and over (at study start date)
- 200 weeks of entitlement for tertiary study if under the age of 40 (at study start date)
For more information see:
- Age restriction - 65 years
- The 92 week limit for secondary school study
- The 120/200 week limit for tertiary study
The age categories that determine whether a Student Allowance is parentally income tested are:
- Students aged 16-23 years
- Students aged 24 years old and over
Students who qualify for an Independent Circumstances Allowance do not have their Student Allowance parentally income tested.
For more information see:
- Independent Circumstances Allowance
The age categories that determine how Student Allowance eligibility is assessed for secondary students are:
- Secondary students aged 16 or 17 years old
- Secondary students aged 18 years and over

chunks.title: Aged 65 and over — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Aged 65 and over
For study starting on or after 1 January 2014, students aged 65 and over are not eligible for a Student Allowance.
This means that:
If a student is aged 65 or over at the date they start study, they will not be eligible for a Student Allowance.
If a student is aged 64 years at the date they start study, and they turn 65 during that period of study, they are assessed under the 120-week limit for the duration of that period of study.
Students, whose study started in 2013 and carries over into 2014 are assessed under the 200 week limit for the duration of that period of study.
The period of study referred to above is the period of study covered by the student's application.
Note the age restriction for Student Allowances eligibility is linked to the age of eligibility for New Zealand Superannuation as specified in section 7(1) of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001.
## Grand-parenting provision
Students, who studied and received a Student Allowance in 2013, are entitled to receive a Student Allowance up until 31 December 2014, or until they reach their 200-week limit to a Student Allowance, whichever comes first.
The study in 2014 does not need to be towards the same qualification as the study in 2013.
There are no other 'transitional' provisions, including any form of discretion, available to vary the 65 year age limit from 1 January 2014.
## Important reminders
Students who apply for an extension to the 200 week limit prior to 1 January 2014 that is approved will continue to be entitled to that extension after 1 January 2014.
For applications for an extension under the 'special circumstances' provision, special circumstances do not exist as a result of the age restriction.
If a student applies for an extension after 1 January 2014, the approval of an extension is not restricted by the fact that the student may reach age 65 during the period of the requested extension.

chunks.title: Appeals — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Appeals
If a student disagrees with a decision made as the result of a statutory review, they have the right to lodge an appeal with the Student Allowance Appeal Authority (the Authority).
The Authority is a Tribunal supported by the Ministry of Justice.
The student must lodge an appeal with the Authority in writing within 21 days after the decision. The Authority has discretion to accept appeals received outside that timeframe.
The Authority will make a decision after considering any submissions by the student and MSD.
The Notice of Appeal form is on the Ministry of Justice website. See: Student Allowance Appeal Authority
Any appeals received by MSD must be forwarded immediately to the Ministry of Justice.
## Student Allowance Appeal Authority
The Authority considers the appeal and any submissions it receives. It determines the relevant issues, questions and circumstances, and either confirms the decision, or makes a different decision that the Chief Executive may have made.
The Authority can refuse to consider any part of an appeal. This includes situations where it considers an appeal:
- could not reasonably succeed or
- is likely to cause prejudice or delay or
- is frivolous or designed to annoy MSD or the Authority or
- would be an abuse of the appeal process
The Authority can issue practice notes as a guide for the Authority and those involved in appeals heard by the Authority. Any practice notes must be consistent with provisions of the Education and Training Act 2020 and the Student Allowances Regulations 1998. The Authority has not issued any practice notes since this provision was enacted in late 2018.
The Ministry of Justice provides administrative support to the Authority to enable it to carry out its functions.
The Ministry of Justice must publish information on a website about:
- the purpose of the Authority and
- how to make an appeal and
- how to find out about the progress of an appeal and when a decision may be expected
In addition, the Ministry of Justice must publish all written decisions of the Authority on a website, unless there is good reason not to.

chunks.title: Initial application — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Initial application
Recipients of NZQA Scholarship Monetary Awards are determined by the New Zealand Qualifications Authority (NZQA). Recipients are notified by NZQA of their award.
This notification includes information about the awards, requests further information from the recipient. For selected recipients, this includes an invitation to an award ceremony held in Wellington.
NZQA forwards information about the recipients to StudyLink. StudyLink sends each recipient a form to sign (to confirm their personal details) and return to StudyLink. Forms are usually sent out to students in March or April each year.
## Confirmation of study
StudyLink will confirm with the student's education provider that the student is studying an approved programme of study.
## Continuing eligibility for the award
Some NZQA Scholarship Monetary Awards are paid for more than one year.
Subsequent years of payment
Students who have been awarded an NZQA Scholarship Monetary Award that is for more than one year do not have to re-apply each year for the award. They continue to be entitled to payment of the Award provided they:
- complete and return their renewal form to StudyLink each year and
- have an entitlement to a further year of the award and
- for students who received their initial payment in 2006 or later, maintain a minimum of a B Grade average for each year of their course or
- for students who received their initial payment in 2005, pass over half of their study each year
StudyLink will send the student a renewal form in October prior to the next year of payment. The student needs to check the form, confirm or correct the information on the form, sign it and return it. Where required, the student also needs to send evidence of their results for the course just ended/about to end.

chunks.title: Applications — student allowance
chunks.text: A student must make an application to be eligible and entitled to receive a Student Allowance. The application must be on a form approved for the purpose and submitted to MSD. An application establishes the intent to apply for a Student Allowance. Seeking information about eligibility or entitlement, including completing the online eligibility tool, is not making an application. MSD can require an applicant to provide information or evidence necessary to establish eligibility and entitlement. If an applicant does not provide any necessary information the application remains incomplete and then lapses at the end of the study period, or at the end of any further time granted to provide the information. An application that lapses is not declined as no decisions have been made on the eligibility or entitlement of the applicant. There is no right of review or appeal in relation to an application that has lapsed. When an application has lapsed or been declined, and the student subsequently wants to test their eligibility or entitlement for a period of study covered by the lapsed or declined application, or any later period of study, they must make a new application. For more information see:

chunks.title: Date of application — student allowance
chunks.text: The date of application for a Student Allowance is the date the application is received by MSD. Students are encouraged to submit their applications well before the start date of their course or when they would otherwise become eligible and/or entitled, even if they do not have all the required information or evidence available.

chunks.title: Date entitlement begins — student allowance
chunks.text: The date entitlement begins is the Monday of the week that a student's course starts when an application has been received in that week or before that week. When an application is received after that week, entitlement begins from the Monday of the week in which it is received. The date of entitlement for a change in circumstances begins from the Monday of the week in which the students' circumstances change.

chunks.title: Date entitlement ends — student allowance
chunks.text: The date entitlement ends (if not lost earlier) is either: - on the Sunday of the last week in which the last examination of that course is held or - on the Sunday of the week during which the study ends, if that study ends without an examination

chunks.title: Late applications — student allowance
chunks.text: A late application is generally only paid from the Monday of the week it was received. However, payment may be made from an earlier date provided there are special circumstances that warrant an extension of time for making an application. If special circumstances exist, the revised entitlement date will be the Monday of the week that the application would have been received. This date cannot be any earlier than the Monday of the week in which the course of study commenced.

chunks.title: Special circumstances — student allowance
chunks.text: The special circumstances exception is an exercise of discretion. Special circumstances may include: - Did MSD significantly contribute to the delay or the reason for not making an application? Do notes or correspondence indicate that the student was misinformed, or was there an unacceptable delay in providing information, advice or material to the student. Has the student been on a benefit or Student Loan living costs and not been advised that they should have been on Student Allowance? - Was there a significant event that has contributed to the delay in not making an application? Medical - accident or health issues Family - family breakdown or illness in the family Civil Emergency - Does the student have a significant psychological, physical or intellectual impairment that has contributed to the delay? - Does the student have a significant language barrier that has contributed to the delay? Special circumstances are situations that are beyond the student's control. Each case must be considered on its merits. For more information see: - Payments - Obligations, offences and penalties

chunks.title: Providing information or evidence — student allowance
chunks.text: Any information or evidence required as part of an application must be provided before the end date of the course of study to which the application relates, unless there are special circumstances that justify a delay in providing the information. A later date must be specified and advised to the student. A decision to allow further time to provide information or evidence must include a new deadline for providing the information or evidence. Agreeing that special circumstances exist is an exercise of discretion. An applicant must not be awarded a Student Allowance if they do not provide the required information or evidence, or they provide it after the required date.

chunks.title: Signatures — student allowance
chunks.text: The requirement for an applicant to sign their application fulfils two purposes: - it assists in ensuring MSD can identify who is making the application and - it is part of the declaration by the applicant that they have read and understood the information on the form, including any obligations they have agreed to, and the information they have provided is to the best of their knowledge, true and correct In some cases MSD also requires signatures from partners, parents and/or witnesses.

chunks.title: Online applications and electronic signatures — student allowance
chunks.text: When a student submits an application online, they are undertaking an electronic transaction using an electronic signature. RealMe is a digital signature. It is a type of electronic signature that provides MSD with certainty the person using the digital signature is who they say they are. It is also part of the declaration by the applicant that they have read and understood the information on the form, including any obligations they have agreed to, and the information they have provided is to the best of their knowledge, true and correct.

chunks.title: Assessing employment pay periods — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Assessing employment pay periods
Student Allowance is paid for a Monday to Sunday period. Employment earnings that are for the period Monday to Sunday should be assessed against the Student Allowance for that week.
Fortnightly earning periods require assessment as follows:
- where the earnings for each individual week can be identified those earnings should be assessed to the week earned
- where the earnings for each individual week cannot be identified (e.g. the employer does not hold a weekly breakdown of earnings), then the earnings are averaged (divided equally) over the fortnight
Earning periods that cross calendar weeks should be assessed as follows:
- where the weekly hours of earnings are identifiable, those earnings should be assigned to the week earned
- where the weekly hours of work and hourly/daily payment cannot be identified then the earnings are divided by the number of days in the pay period and charged to each Student Allowance week appropriately

chunks.title: The parental income test — student allowance
chunks.text: Entitlement to Student Allowances for students who are under 24 years old with no supported children, is assessed on their parents' income.

chunks.title: Definition of parental income — student allowance
chunks.text: The definition of parental income for Student Allowances purposes is largely taken from the 'family scheme income' definition for Working for Families Tax Credits under the Income Tax Act 2007. Parental income assessments are based on the parents' combined income for the relevant tax year. The assessment uses the current income for the period of time the student will be studying. For more information see:

chunks.title: Parental income abatement - how it works — student allowance
chunks.text: The amount of parental income over the threshold (the lower limit) abates or reduces the gross rate of Student Allowance. The cut-out points are the upper parental income limits at which the amount of parental income will reduce the gross rate of Student Allowance payable to zero. The rate of abatement of the net rate Student Allowance where the parental income is over the threshold (the lower limit) is 25%. For more information see:

chunks.title: Parental income - change in income — student allowance
chunks.text: When the parental income amount increases (due to a change in income) after the initial assessment, there is no obligation on the parents or the student to advise MSD the change. Therefore, there is no requirement to review the student's entitlement where the parental income increases after the initial assessment. When information is received that the parental income has increased, that information should be recorded. When the parental income amount decreases by at least 25% (due to a change in income) the parents can apply for a Reassessment of Parental Income (RPI).

chunks.title: Parental income - a change in circumstances — student allowance
chunks.text: When the parental income increases after the initial assessment due to a change in circumstances (e.g. a parent enters into a new relationship) there is no obligation on the parents or the student to advise MSD of the change. Therefore, there is no requirement to review the student's entitlement where the parental income increases after the initial assessment. When information is received that the parental income has increased, that information should be recorded. When the parental income reduces after the initial assessment due a change in circumstances (e.g. a parent dies), there is no obligation on the parents or the student to advise MSD of the change. Therefore, there is no requirement to review the student's entitlement where the parental income decreases after the initial assessment. When information is received that the parental income has reduced, that information should be recorded.

chunks.title: Entitlement may be reviewed — student allowance
chunks.text: While there is no requirement to review the student's entitlement where there has been a change in circumstances, a student's entitlement may be reviewed if in all the circumstances it would be appropriate. Note when a change in circumstances leads to a reduction of the parental income, the reduction does not need to be by at least 25%. For more information see:

chunks.title: A student has more than 2 parents — student allowance
chunks.text: If a student has more than 2 parents, the student must nominate the 2 parents who are the major contributors to the student's support. The combined parental incomes of these 2 contributors is the parental income of the student. MSD does not have to accept the nomination, if there is information that confirms the nominated parents' are not the major contributors to the student's support.

chunks.title: Parents unable to determine their current annual income — student allowance
chunks.text: Parents whose annual income cannot be determined until the end of the tax year (e.g. they are self-employed), can declare an estimate of their income.

chunks.title: Historic roles and responsibilities — student allowance
chunks.text: Between 1992 and 1998 the following organisations were responsible for different aspects of the Student Allowances Scheme: - the Ministry of Education: the government's lead advisor on education policy (including Student Allowances)the delivery and administration of the scheme (including the payment of all Student Allowances) andthe approval of tertiary education providers and qualifications or programmes for access to Student Allowances (and Student Loans) - the government's lead advisor on education policy (including Student Allowances) - the delivery and administration of the scheme (including the payment of all Student Allowances) and - the approval of tertiary education providers and qualifications or programmes for access to Student Allowances (and Student Loans) - tertiary education providers (other than private tertiary establishments) - the assessment of Student Allowances applications from their students - Eduserve (Christchurch Polytechnic) - from 1995 the processing of Student Allowance applications from students attending secondary schools and private tertiary establishments (under an agreement with the Ministry of Education) - the New Zealand Vice-Chancellors Committee - the quality assurance of New Zealand University qualifications or programmes - New Zealand Qualifications Authority - the quality assurance of non-University qualifications or programmes Any queries in relation to Student Allowances for study from the beginning of 1992 to the end of 1998 are not the responsibility of MSD. MSD does not hold any Student Allowances information in relation to study, applications or payments during those years. If students raise questions relating to Student Allowances paid during those years, they should be referred to their Education Provider. However, their Education Provider may no longer hold any relevant records as they are not required to keep records indefinitely. If their Education Provider no longer exists and they have a complaint, they can raise it with the Ministry of Education. Note the Ministry of Education no longer holds any individual Student Allowances records for those years.

chunks.title: Current roles and responsibilities — student allowance
chunks.text: In December 1997, the government decided MSD would take over responsibility for the delivery of the assessment and payment of Student Allowances for study starting on or after 1 January 1999. This decision recognised the benefits that would flow from an integrated approach to the assessment and payment of financial support to students, including the delivery of the Student Loan Scheme. Since 1 January 1999, the following organisations have been responsible for different aspects of the Student Allowances Scheme: - MSD (via StudyLink) - the assessment and payment of Student Allowances to eligible students - the Ministry of Education - the government's lead advisor on education policy (including Student Allowances) - tertiary education providers and secondary schools - the supply of enrolment information to StudyLink - the Tertiary Education Commission - since its creation in 2002, the approval of tertiary education providers and qualifications or programmes for access to Student Allowances (and Student Loans) - New Zealand Vice-Chancellors Committee - the quality assurance of New Zealand University qualifications or programmes - New Zealand Qualifications Authority - the quality assurance of non-university qualifications or programmes on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework - Statistics New Zealand - the management of the Integrated Data Infrastructure, including Student Allowances (and Student Loan) data supplied by MSD

chunks.title: Cross-agency work — student allowance
chunks.text: Given the individual roles and shared responsibilities for different aspects of the Student Allowances Scheme, regular joint meetings of the respective agencies are held to consider and co-ordinate work related to the scheme.

chunks.title: Breaks in tuition of 3 weeks or less — student allowance
chunks.text: An eligible student who is not on study leave and is not studying due to a break in tuition at their education provider, can continue getting Student Allowance when the break in tuition is for 3 weeks or less. A student must be eligible for a Student Allowance directly before, and directly after the break in tuition to get payments for the period of the break in tuition. A student who loses entitlement, but not eligibility, to a Student Allowance due to personal and/or spousal income directly before or directly after a break in tuition of 3 weeks or less, can get payments for the period of the break in tuition.

chunks.title: Breaks in tuition longer than 3 weeks — student allowance
chunks.text: When the break in tuition is longer than 3 weeks, the payment of any Student Allowances must be suspended unless discretion is used to permit it to continue. The use of discretion to continue payments is intended when there are unforeseen or unusual circumstances only, e.g. extreme weather conditions, interruptions to essential services, non-controlled health and safety issues, or civil defence emergencies. You must consider the specific circumstances of each student before deciding if their payments can be continued. Breaks in tuition due to COVID-19 Discretion may be used to continue payment of Student Allowances for a study break of longer than 3 weeks due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Breaks in tuition due to the impacts of Cyclone Gabrielle Discretion may be used to continue payment of Student Allowances between 6 March and 1 May 2023 for up to another 8 weeks if a student has a break in tuition because their education provider temporarily cannot deliver their course(s) due to the impacts of Cyclone Gabrielle (the cyclone). This includes breaks in tuition starting at any time from 6 March to 1 May 2023 due to subsequent weather events that worsen the impacts of the cyclone. Breaks in tuition do not need to be consecutive. A student must remain enrolled in full-time study to receive payments for the period of the break. Students who cannot get continued payments Student Allowance payments cannot continue if a student's education provider can deliver their course(s), but the student cannot study because of the impacts of Cyclone Gabrielle. E.g. they have no internet access because their internet connection was damaged in the cyclone. In this situation you should consider if the student qualifies for other financial assistance. You should also advise the student to contact their education provider to discuss any other supports that may be available.

chunks.title: Business income — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Business income
When a student or their partner receives income from business activities, including where they are self-employed, this income is included in the definition of 'personal' or 'partner' income for Student Allowance purposes.
The definition of income for Student Allowance purposes is wider than the definition of income used for PAYE tax purposes. This reflects the different objectives and purposes of the Student Allowances Scheme from the purposes and objectives of PAYE taxation.
Where they own a business, their income for Student Allowance purposes is the higher of either the net profit or drawings they receive from the business. A copy of the business accounts may be required to correctly identify any income received as it may depend on how the accounts are structured and how particular 'income' transactions are recorded.
It is also important to look for any possible deprivation of income.
Where they have multiple forms of income, a loss from one form of income cannot be offset against other forms of income.
A loss is effectively nil income for Student Allowance purposes.

chunks.title: Caregivers and legal guardians — student allowance
chunks.text: The term caregiver covers a range of caring arrangements from emergency and respite care through to permanent care. A caregiver can be a person with or without legal orders for the child, such as guardianship orders or parenting orders. A legal guardian is a natural parent (a natural guardian), a person appointed as a guardian by the Family Court (a court-appointed guardian), or a person appointed as a testamentary guardian by the child's natural parent. The Family Court or High Court can also appoint themselves as a guardian. In these cases the court often appoints Oranga Tamariki to act on the court’s behalf. This is known as Guardianship of the Court, or Ward of the State.

chunks.title: Some caregivers and legal guardians are not parents — student allowance
chunks.text: A caregiver or legal guardian is not a parent for the Student Allowance parental income test if they are: - receiving or have received a Foster Care Allowance, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the student - providing or have provided a transition support living arrangement for the student under section 386AAD of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 If a caregiver or legal guardian is not excluded from the definition of parent for the above reasons, MSD must consider if they are acting in place of a parent of the student.

chunks.title: Permanent caregivers — student allowance
chunks.text: Permanent caregiver is a term used by Oranga Tamariki to describe a person who is providing a permanent care arrangement for a child. This is usually a court-appointed guardian, but it can include a caregiver who does not have legal orders. A permanent caregiver is defined as a: - special guardian who is appointed by the Family Court to provide a long term, safe and stable care arrangement - person who has legal orders under the Care of Children Act 2004 in substitution for a section 140 agreement under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 - person who provides a permanent living arrangement without having legal orders, after custody orders in favour of the chief executive of Oranga Tamariki have been discharged. This is sanctioned through a family group conference. Most permanent caregivers will receive Foster Care Allowance, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the student at some point. This means they are not considered parents for Student Allowance. If a permanent caregiver has not received one of these payments, MSD must consider if they are acting in place of a parent of the student. Permanent caregivers may also receive financial assistance through the Permanent Caregiver Support Service. This service provides financial and non-financial assistance to permanent caregivers to support the needs of the children in their care. The service is provided through a non-Government organisation on behalf of Oranga Tamariki. Generally financial assistance provided through the service is for one off or short term needs and is not regular or ongoing. This means a permanent caregiver who has received financial assistance from the service is still likely to have overall financial responsibility for the student.

chunks.title: Court-appointed guardians — student allowance
chunks.text: The Family Court can appoint someone who is not already a natural guardian of a child to be that child’s guardian. A court-appointed guardian can be a joint guardian along with any other guardians, or a sole guardian of the child. If a court-appointed guardian is not excluded from the definition of parent, MSD must consider if they are acting in place of a parent.

chunks.title: Testamentary guardians — student allowance
chunks.text: A parent can name a person in their will to be their child's testamentary guardian if the parent dies. Their role is like other guardians, but they do not have rights to the day to day care of the child. A testamentary guardian can apply to the Family Court for a parenting order to gain these rights, and may also get Foster Care Allowance, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the child. Testamentary guardians who do not have a parenting order cannot be considered as acting in place of a parent of the student.

chunks.title: Change of course — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Change of course
Students (tertiary or secondary) who start a second or further recognised course at the same, or a different education provider, before completing any other recognised course can continue to get a Student Allowance.
The student will need to produce evidence from the Head of the Department or Faculty of the new programme of study certifying that they will be capable of succeeding in their intended programme of study. The student must also be otherwise eligible and entitled to the Student Allowance.
This provision applies where the student's allowance is not already suspended for any of the following reasons:
- imprisonment
- failure to attend or perform
- failure of a full-time course
- the tertiary provider loses accreditation
- suspension due to injury, health condition or holidays
## Applying this provision
This provision will generally be applied where the student:
- switches from one approved course to another approved course (both similar in nature and where cross-crediting is possible)
- the study dates of both courses will generally be for the same period and
- the education provider accepts the student into the new course on the basis of an academic decision that they are capable of passing it. This may be because they are starting some parts of the new course late and will have to catch up.
This provision would not generally apply to someone dropping out of one course and taking a completely new course with a different course code and different study dates. In this case the allowance should be suspended for failing to pass more than half of the first course. It is not intended to allow someone to avoid suspension when they withdraw from one course and start a different one at a later date.
## Other situations where this provision may apply
This provision could also apply in cases where a tertiary student who is in their final year of 1 recognised programme of study, wishes to commence another recognised programme during that same year.
For example, where a student has 1 or 2 papers remaining to complete a Bachelor of Arts degree, but wishes to undertake a Bachelor of Science degree, their course can be recognised as full-time for Student Allowance purposes under this provision.

chunks.title: Clinical placements or block courses - Accommodation Benefit — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Clinical placements or block courses - Accommodation Benefit
Eligible students who move to a new location for clinical placements, work experience, or to attend a block course as a requirement of their course of study, can have their rate of Accommodation Benefit changed to the applicable standard rate of Accommodation Benefit for the new location, while they are living there.
Example
Lagi is an extramural student at UCOL studying Early Childhood Education.
Lagi lives in Waipukurau and gets the Waipukurau standard rate of Accommodation Benefit.
As part of her course, Lagi is required to do a teaching placement in Palmerston North for 8 weeks.
Lagi moves to Palmerston North temporarily for her placement, and her rate of Accommodation Benefit is changed to the Palmerston North Accommodation Benefit rate until she moves back to Waipukurau.

chunks.title: Commission — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Commission
Commission payments are personal income for Student Allowance purposes.
Personal income (whether weekly, fortnightly, monthly or other) must be assessed on a week by week basis. In cases where the amount of the commission is not known by the time the allowance is due to be paid, an amount should be estimated for that period, and then reassessed when the actual income is known.
In some cases you may be unable to determine a weekly amount of income altogether. In these cases you may calculate weekly income by taking the commission earned over a longer period and averaging this over the number of weeks.
## Example
A student (or partner) is a real estate agent and receives a commission of $15,000 for their sales over a 9 week period.
This is then averaged against the Student Allowance over the 9 weeks it is earned.

chunks.title: 16 and 17 year old students — student allowance
chunks.text: Student Allowances are available to 16 and 17 year olds in tertiary study provided they meet the usual eligibility and entitlement criteria, and they have: - completed year 13 study or - obtained, at level 3 of the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA), 42 credits or more If a student doesn't meet these additional criteria, they may still be eligible for a Student Allowance if they have: - gained other equivalent qualifications or - been accepted into a course that has equivalent Academic Entry Requirements Where a student has not completed year 13 or obtained at level 3 NCEA (42 credits or more), they can complete and gain level 3 NCEA (with 42 credits or more) by undertaking tertiary study and gaining credits on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF). This is effectively an alternative to gaining other equivalent qualifications - as described below. Any student who believes that they have gained level 3 NCEA with 42 credits by undertaking tertiary study can apply for and receive their level 3 NCEA Certificate from NZQA. They can then be assessed for eligibility for a Student Allowance from the point they attained level 3 NCEA with 42 credits or more.

chunks.title: Equivalent qualifications — student allowance
chunks.text: Where a student has not completed year 13 or gained at level 3 NCEA, with 42 credits or more, they can still be eligible for a Student Allowance if they have gained other qualifications that are equivalent (such as an overseas qualification or other qualifications on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework - NZQF). If a student gains another qualification on the NZQF they will need to have gained at least 42 NZQF credits, at level 4 to meet the "equivalent" qualification requirement. Once a 16 or 17 year old student has gained at least 42 level 4 credits on the NZQF, they can access a Student Allowance from that point. This may be at the end of the semester, completion of the programme or a point in time during the programme of study where the student has been awarded the required credits at level 4. The New Zealand Qualifications Authority (NZQA) determines an assessment of the 'equivalence' of tertiary qualifications in relation to the NZQF. NZQA does not assess the "equivalent" status of secondary school qualifications. A student will need to obtain the required assessment from a suitably qualified and independent person. This person could be an academic or other educational professional who has the relevant skills and expertise.

chunks.title: Equivalent Academic Entry Requirements — student allowance
chunks.text: Where a student has not completed year 13 nor gained level 3 NCEA, with 42 credits or more, they can still be eligible for a Student Allowance if they have been accepted into a fulltime tertiary course that has Academic Entry Requirements equivalent to or greater than level 3 NCEA with 42 credits.

chunks.title: Single students who are 'dependent children' for other forms of financial support — student allowance
chunks.text: For single 16 and 17 year old students entitlement to a Student Allowance is subject to the level of their parents' combined income. Parents of 16 and 17 year old single students who get a Student Allowance will not be eligible to get: - Working for Families Tax Credits for that student as they are no longer a dependent child or - any other assistance available under the Social Security Act 2018 for that student as a dependent child

chunks.title: Continuation periods — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Continuation periods
When a current study application ends and the student is on a grandparented standard rate of Accommodation Benefit, the higher value of the 2 rates the student is eligible for on either side of the break in tuition will be paid until the next semester begins.

chunks.title: Courses spanning two calendar years — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Courses spanning two calendar years
If a course spans 2 calendar years, payments of Student Allowance may continue over the Christmas/New Year period, providing the break between the 2 periods of full-time study does not exceed 3 weeks.

chunks.title: What is a de facto relationship? — student allowance
chunks.text: A de facto relationship is when two people, both aged 16 years or older, live together as a couple in a relationship in the nature of marriage or civil union. Where a relationship exists, and one or both of the couple are 16 or 17 years old, before you can accept that the relationship is a de facto relationship, they must provide an order from a Family Court Judge giving consent for the de facto relationship. For more information see: - Ministry of Justice Get consent to marry if you're aged 16 or 17 This requirement exists because court consent is required for a marriage or civil union of people aged 16 and 17 years old. As a de facto relationship is a relationship in the nature of marriage, 16 and 17 year old students have a similar requirement. It is illegal to engage in sexual conduct with a young person who is under the age of 16. If information is received that suggests this is occurring (or has occurred), seek advice from your manager on the appropriate action to take. Whether a de facto relationship exists can sometimes be unclear and will require consideration of all the circumstances of the relationship. To determine whether a de facto relationship exists requires the exercise of discretion.

chunks.title: Characteristics of a de facto relationship — student allowance
chunks.text: For a de facto relationship to exist the student and the other person must be living together in a relationship in the nature of marriage or civil union. There are two characteristics used to help determine whether the relationship is in the nature of marriage - emotional commitment and financial interdependence. The absence of either of these two characteristics means the student is not in a de facto relationship.

chunks.title: Emotional commitment — student allowance
chunks.text: When considering if a student is in a de facto relationship with another person, you need to determine whether they have an emotional commitment to each other. The relationship must demonstrate a degree of companionship and a level of ongoing emotional commitment. Every relationship is different. Possible indicators are listed below. Not all relationships will have all these indicators: - student perception - the student and the other person see their relationship as a relationship in the nature of marriage or civil union; they consider the relationship is exclusive and likely to continue - public perception - they are viewed as a couple by their community (this may include their family, local church, sports club etc) - history - the length of time the student and the other person have known each other and/or have resided at the same address, if they have shared children - extent to which their lives are merged - socialising together and how often this occurs; going out as a family; belonging to and attending the same clubs/sports teams or interest groups together; having meals together as a couple/family; their sleeping and sexual relationships - shared responsibilities - arrangements for domestic duties such as gardening, cleaning, cooking; the caring arrangements for any children including when children are sick; joint decision making and plans together - support - the emotional support that the student and the other person provide to each other; the nature of any companionship and support that the student and the other person provide to each other When considering if a student is in a relationship and the student indicates they are a victim of family violence, extra care must be taken when determining if the required level of emotional commitment and financial interdependence exists.

chunks.title: Financial interdependence — student allowance
chunks.text: When considering if a student is in a de facto relationship, you also need to determine if the student and the other person are financially interdependent. This includes the sense of at least a willingness to support the other person if that person cannot support themselves. This does not necessarily mean that the financial support already exists, but that it would if needed. Financial interdependence exists when the student and the other person have a mutual commitment and understanding over their support for each other that goes beyond sharing living expenses. It is a willingness to support and be supported. Every relationship is different. Possible indicators are listed below. Not all relationships will have all these indicators: - joint bank accounts, assets, or joint loans/credit - joint ownership of real estate or other major assets and any joint liabilities e.g. both the student and the other adult own a rental property - significant pooling of financial resources especially in relation to major financial commitments e.g. saving for a house, car or holiday - legal obligation owed by one person in respect of the other person e.g. the other adult is the guarantor for a TV hire purchase - joint ownership of a car. Do they both use it? - items or services the other adult pays for, if any, e.g. SKY television rental, internet broadband - arrangements for paying bills or groceries - the sharing of day to day household expenses

chunks.title: Debt recovery — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Debt recovery
MSD is entitled to recover a debt to the Crown established as a result of a payment to any person, including a third party, of a Student Allowance or Student Loan to which they are no longer entitled in the following ways.
## Student Allowance debt
MSD is entitled to recover a Student Allowance debt by:
- deduction from any subsequent Student Allowance payments or
- deduction from any subsequent benefit payments made under the Social Security Act 2018 or
- deduction notice under section 217 of the Social Security Act 2018 or
- civil suit through the Court
For more information see:
## Student Loan debt
When any Student Loan payments have been converted into MSD debt, MSD is entitled to recover the debt by:
- deduction from any subsequent Student Allowance payments or
- deduction from any subsequent benefit payments made under the Social Security Act 2018 or
- deduction notice under regulation 217 of the Social Security Regulations 2018 or
- civil suit through the Court
For more information see:
- Converting all or part of a Student Loan into an MSD debt
## Benefit debt
MSD is entitled to recover a benefit debt by deduction from any subsequent Student Allowance payment.
## Income Related Rent debt
MSD is entitled to recover Income Related Rent debt by deduction from any subsequent Student Allowance payment.

chunks.title: Do grounds exist for debt write-off — student allowance
chunks.text: Once a debt is established, it is important to consider whether any grounds exist to write-off the debt before recovery commences.

chunks.title: Authority to write-off debt — student allowance
chunks.text: Joint Ministers have delegated to MSD's Chief Executive the authority to write-off Crown assets in certain circumstances, including debts under a certain value. This debt write-off delegation encompasses several categories of debt write-off, together with conditions. It includes debt that cannot be recovered as MSD made the payment (or payments) in error. This category used to be known as estoppal, as set out in section 94B of the Judicature Act 1908. This Act was repealed in March 2017. The provision became section 74B of the Property Law Act 2007, and therefore only relates to property as defined in that Act.

chunks.title: Debt that cannot be recovered as payment was made in error — student allowance
chunks.text: Deciding whether MSD made any payment in error involves the use of discretion. The reasons and circumstances that led to any payments being made, including why the student was not entitled to them, need to be confirmed. A debt for any payments made in error can be written-off when the following criteria are met: - the payment(s) resulted wholly or partly from a mistake or error by MSD in relation to the law and/or the facts of the case - the student received the payment(s) in good faith Did they reasonably believe when they received them that they were entitled to them? - the student changed their position believing they were entitled to the payment(s)Did they make different decisions to those they would have otherwise made, because they believed they were entitled to the payment(s)? - considering all the circumstances, including the student's financial situation and the implications for any other person, it would be inequitable to recover the debt

chunks.title: Legal advice required for debt of $5000 or more — student allowance
chunks.text: When the value of the debt is $5000 or more, legal advice is required to confirm that the above criteria have been met. This requirement only applies to any recommendation to write-off debt for any payments made in error.

chunks.title: Other categories of debt write-off — student allowance
chunks.text: Other categories of debt write-off that may need to be considered are listed below. Some also involve the use of discretion.

chunks.title: The debtor is insolvent — student allowance
chunks.text: The debt cannot be recovered because: - the debtor has been adjudicated bankrupt and - the debtor has been automatically discharged from bankruptcy after 3 years, or has been granted a discharge from bankruptcy by the High Court, and that discharge has not been reversed and - the Official Assignee has confirmed that the debtor's bankruptcy has been discharged and that discharge has not been reversed The debt cannot be recovered because: - the debtor has been admitted to the No Asset Procedure under section 363 of the Insolvency Act 2006 and - the debtor has been discharged from the No Asset Procedure under section 377 of the Insolvency Act 2006 and - the Official Assignee has confirmed the debtor has been discharged from the No Asset Procedure These provisions do not apply to any debt established due to fraud, apart from fraud balances included in the No Asset Procedure before 10 March 2009.

chunks.title: Agent insolvent — student allowance
chunks.text: An agent of the Crown was paid the funds to be used for repayment of the debt, but has since become insolvent.

chunks.title: Debtor is deceased — student allowance
chunks.text: The debtor is deceased and the debt cannot be recovered, or it is uneconomic to recover.

chunks.title: The debt or the identity of the debtor cannot be proven — student allowance
chunks.text: Insufficient information exists to accurately establish the amount of the debt, and legal advice is received that MSD would be unable to prove the amount of the debt to the satisfaction of a Court. Insufficient information exists to identify the debtor or legal advice has been received that confirms the alleged debtor cannot be lawfully identified with the debt.

chunks.title: The debt cannot be proved to the Court's satisfaction — student allowance
chunks.text: - civil proceedings have been issued and - the Court finds that the full amount of the debt is not proven and - legal advice has been received that confirms the balance of the debt must be written off

chunks.title: Foreign exchange balances — student allowance
chunks.text: The debt arises from the conversion of a foreign currency and it does not exceed $1000.

chunks.title: The debt has become statute barred — student allowance
chunks.text: - the debt has been established for more than 6 years and - there has been no acknowledgement of the debt from the debtor for more than 6 years and - the debtor has never agreed in writing, to owing the debt or entered into any repayment arrangement, or made any repayments during the preceding 6 years and - there is no possibility of a deduction notice being issued in respect of the debt, including a deduction from benefit or allowance payment

chunks.title: The debtor is a participant in a Witness Protection or Relocation programme. — student allowance
chunks.text: Advice is received from Data Integrity that the debtor is a participant in a witness protection or relocation programme, and debt recovery should not take place.

chunks.title: All economic avenues of collection have been exhausted and the debt is less than $20,000 — student allowance
chunks.text: 1. Debt $50 or less - automatic write-off after 70 calendar days The debtor owes between $0.01 and $50.00 (in total) and there have been no repayments during the previous 70 calendar days. 2. Debt less than $200 The debtor owes between $50.01 and $199.99 (in total) and there have been no repayments during the previous 6 months for innocent debts, or during the previous 12 months for fraudulent debts. 3. Debt less than $1000 The debtor owes between $200.00 and $999.99 (in total) and there have been no repayments during the previous 12 months for innocent debts, or during the previous 2 years for fraudulent debts. 4. Debt less than $2000 - the debtor owes less than $2000 and there have been no repayments during the preceding 2 years for innocent debts, or during the previous 4 years for fraudulent debts and - it is established that the debtor does not reside at the last known address or no longer works at the last known place of employment and - current debtor records do not appear on any MSD databases and - current debtor records do not appear on any public databases e.g. credit reference checks, internet searches, and - current debtor records do not appear in any information matching exercises with other government agencies e.g. IRD, ACC, Customs and - exhaustive searches are completed with utility companies e.g. power companies, electronic white pages and banks 5. Innocent breach debt of $2000 or more: - there has been no ability to gain repayment or communicate with the debtor for at least 6 years and - current debtor records do not appear on any MSD databases and - current debtor records do not appear on any public databases e.g. credit reference checks, internet search and - current debtor records do not appear in any information matching exercises with other government agencies e.g. IRD, ACC, Customs and - exhaustive searches are completed with utility companies e.g. power companies, electronic white pages and banks 6. Fraudulent breach debt of $2000 or more and less than $20,000: - there has been no ability to gain repayment or communicate with the debtor for at least 10 years and - current debtor records do not appear on any MSD databases and

chunks.title: All economic avenues of collection have been exhausted and the debt is less than $20,000 — student allowance
chunks.text: - current debtor records do not appear on any public databases e.g. credit reference checks, internet search and - current debtor records do not appear in any information matching exercises with other government agencies e.g. IRD, ACC, Customs and - exhaustive searches are completed with utility companies e.g. power companies, electronic white pages and banks

chunks.title: The debtors assets have been seized by the police and sold — student allowance
chunks.text: - the debtors assets have been seized under the Proceeds of Crime Act 1991 or the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009 and - the net amount realised through sale of the seized assets, after deductions required under section 82 of the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009 have been made, is equal to or greater than the debt that will be written-off

chunks.title: External deductions — student allowance
chunks.text: MSD must comply with any formal notice to make a deduction from a client's Student Allowance when this is provided for in legislation.

chunks.title: Required deductions — student allowance
chunks.text: Currently, the following deductions are provided for in legislation, and therefore when a deduction notice is received, it must be followed - subject to the 'protected earnings' provisions described below: - Child Support - section 154 Child Support Act 1991 - Income Tax Arrears - section 157 Tax Administration Act 1994 These deductions are over and above the standard tax deductions required from taxable Student Allowance payments.

chunks.title: Deductions not required — student allowance
chunks.text: MSD is not required by legislation, and therefore does not make the following types of deduction: - a Debt Repayment Order made under section 344 Insolvency Act 2006 - the Ministry is not an 'employer' for Student Allowances purposes under that provision - a civil debt established as an Attachment Order under section 155 District Court Act 2016 - a court fine established as an Attachment Order under section 155 District Court Act 2016 In addition, when a student asks MSD to deduct an amount from their Student Allowance and pay it to a third party (and MSD is not required by legislation to make that deduction), they should be advised to arrange this payment through their bank.

chunks.title: Protected earnings — student allowance
chunks.text: Deductions sometimes include what are known as a 'protected earnings' requirement. Protected earnings are the portion of the payment that is protected from any deduction. This mechanism is used to ensure the recipient of the payment is not unfairly disadvantaged by a deduction. This will be either be specified in legislation or detailed in the policies of the relevant agency.

chunks.title: Ministry debts — student allowance
chunks.text: MSD has both the legislative authority and obligation to recover debts incurred by clients while receiving payments from MSD. For more information see:

chunks.title: Priority of deductions — student allowance
chunks.text: Certain forms of deductions take priority over others. The following list sets out the order of priority, highest to lowest: - Child Support under section 157 Child Support Act 1991 - Inland Revenue deduction notices - all MSD debt repayments (with Student Allowance and then Student Loan MSD debt having the highest priority within this category)

chunks.title: For more information on Student Loan MSD debts see: — student allowance
chunks.text: - Converting all or part of a loan into an MSD debt Determining the priority of deductions is necessary when a client has more than one order issued in respect of their Student Allowance. If the deduction amount needs to be reduced, then deductions will be made in order of priority from the lowest to highest priority deduction, taking into account the protected earnings rules for each type. For example, when a client has both Child Support and MSD debt deductions, when MSD debt deduction would reduce the Student Allowance payment to below the Child Support protected earnings amount, the Ministry deduction would be reduced, not the Child Support deduction. This is because Child Support deductions take priority over MSD debt deductions.

chunks.title: Definition — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Definition
The definition of a student's parent for the Student Allowance parental income test includes:
- a natural or adoptive parent
- a step-parent - a person who is married to, in a civil union or, a de facto relationship with, the student's parent
- any person acting in place of a parent of the student
A parent does not include a caregiver or legal guardian, or their partner, who is:
- getting or has received a Foster Care Allowance, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the student
- providing or has provided a transition support living arrangement for the student under section 386AAD of Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
A transition support living arrangement is where a young person stays or returns to living with a caregiver up to the age of 21.
## More than 2 parents
If a student has more than 2 parents, they must nominate the 2 parents who are the major contributors to their support.
The combined parental income of these 2 parents is the parental income of the student.
MSD does not have to accept the nomination of the student if there is information to suggest the nominated parents are not the major contributors to the student's support.

chunks.title: Deprivation of income — student allowance
chunks.text: Student Allowance is a targeted form of financial assistance. The respective income tests reflect the shared responsibility for funding study between the student, the government, their partner, or their parents.

chunks.title: Deprivation of income — student allowance
chunks.text: If a student, (and, from 1 January 2012, a student's parent or partner) directly or indirectly deprives themselves of income resulting in the student getting a Student Allowance, an Independent Circumstances Allowance or payment at a higher rate (as applicable), that deprived income may be included in their income assessment. In general, if deprivation of income has occurred, it should be included back in their income assessment unless there are good reasons not to. There are three essential questions that assist in deciding whether to include deprived income in an income assessment: - Has the person (directly or indirectly) deprived himself/herself of income? - Would the deprivation result in the student becoming entitled for an allowance or for payment at an increased rate? - Exercise discretion: Having regard to all relevant circumstances, is it fair and appropriate to cancel or reduce the allowance? It is recommended that advice is sought from the Business Support team or Legal Services before any decisions are made, including the best approach to take in any particular case. It is important that a consistent approach is taken.

chunks.title: Has the person (directly or indirectly) deprived himself/herself of income — student allowance
chunks.text: Deprivation of income involves deliberately giving up or foregoing income. This can be by an act or by omission (eg, choosing not to do something) as long as a "deliberate choice" has been made. Some examples of deprivation include where: - the person re-arranges their financial circumstances which reduces their income - the person makes a significant interest free loan - the person makes a gift of cash or property that could otherwise have been used to generate income - the person owns a rental property but does not collect rent from the property - the person has invested in Bonus Bonds instead of an interest-bearing account or term deposit - an income stream from an estate or trust is stopped or not accessed at the person's request Generally deprivation of income will not have occurred in the following situations: - the person chooses to reduce their work hours during their study period - the person sells, purchases or exchanges items for their normal value - the person has a loss or reduction of income that was outside of their control - for example the investment marker return is under performing - the person is not renting out a room in the home where the student lives - the person chose to take a conservative approach to financial decisions

chunks.title: Trust income — student allowance
chunks.text: Deprivation of income can occur in respect of a trust that an applicant, their partner or their parent has a responsibility to administer, manage or has some other form of relationship with (e.g. a beneficiary). Listed below are some examples of how deprivation may occur in relation to a trust: - a loan made to a trust without the requirement for the payment of interest - investments within a trust which are designed for capital gain rather than earning income - making a decision to not receive income as a beneficiary of a trust

chunks.title: Notional interest rate — student allowance
chunks.text: Where deprivation occurs due to an investment that could have been made, the deprived income is calculated using a notional interest rate. In some cases, this rate may be easily determinable (for example interest at 7% that has been waived resulting in deprivation). In other cases the appropriate rate may not be clear. Generally, in these instances, it is the Reserve Bank six month term deposit rate that should be used.

chunks.title: Did that person's deprivation of income result in the student becoming entitled for an allowance or for payment at an increased rate? — student allowance
chunks.text: It is not necessary to show that the purpose of the deprivation was to allow a student to get a Student Allowance - it is sufficient that the effect of the deprivation would result in the payment of the allowance or payment at an increased rate.

chunks.title: Exercising discretion — student allowance
chunks.text: The decision as to whether to include deprived income in an income assessment involves the exercise of discretion. You must take into account the individual circumstances of the situation and decide whether it is fair and appropriate to include the deprived income. Generally, the following matters should be taken into consideration: - At what point were the decisions made for the student to undertake study? - Has the student already been advised of the outcome of their application? - Does the person have any right to access income from either an estate or trust or other agreement? - What are the terms of the person's investments and when were the investments established? - Is it possible for the person to rearrange their finances to restore the deprived income? - Has the person recently rearranged the investment from previously high return to low return? - Would the person be put into serious financial hardship if the deprived income were included? - Are there any other individual factors which are relevant? Note it may be appropriate to give the person a reasonable opportunity to rearrange their finances to restore the income that they've deprived themselves of, eg, allow a period of time before the deprived income is included back in their income assessment.

chunks.title: Stopping payments — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Stopping payments
A student may postpone their course without suspending their entitlement to Student Allowance.
Payments of any allowance must cease from the date of postponement.
If a student postpones their study and there is a possibility that they may not resume study, you need to advise them of the consequences of not returning to complete their course.
## Resuming payments
A student may postpone their course without suspending their entitlement to student allowances. Allowance payments may only be resumed when they resume their study.
Resuming payments of any allowance will be subject to eligibility and entitlement in the year in which the study recommences.

chunks.title: Withdrawal or reduction to part-time study — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Withdrawal or reduction to part-time study
If a student withdraws from study or reduces to part-time study, they may lose their future Student Allowance entitlement for failing to pass more than half of their study.
If a student indicates that they are intending to withdraw or reduce their study to part-time, you must advise them of the possible consequences.
## Full year study reduced to 1 semester
If a student enrols in a full year course with semester 1 and 2 papers but then decides to withdraw before receiving any semester 2 payments (including any continuation period payments), they will become a 'semester' student.
As a 'semester' student they will need to pass more than half of their semester 1 study to retain their future entitlement to a Student Allowance.
## Full-time study reduced to part-time
Where a student or the tertiary provider is considering reducing the student's study from full-time to part-time, the student may no longer be eligible to continue to receive Student Allowance for that study. The student may seek approval for a Student Allowance under Limited full-time study.
Limited full-time study is assessed on the student's personal circumstances. The tertiary provider may need to seek approval from the Tertiary Education Commission for any planned change to the course or programme. The course or programme may no longer be approved for Student Allowances due to the planned change.

chunks.title: Eligibility — student allowance
chunks.text: To be eligible for a Student Allowance a student must make an application and meet the following eligibility criteria: - be aged 18 (some exceptions apply for 16 and 17 year old's) and less than 65 years of age at study start date and - be a New Zealand citizen or be ordinarily resident and entitled to reside indefinitely in New Zealand or meet a specific residency requirement and - be studying a recognised programme either full-time or (with our approval) limited full-time at an approved tertiary provider or secondary school and - not be getting a benefit, New Zealand Superannuation, Veterans Pension or a youth payment and - not be getting similar government study assistance without MSD approval If a student meets these eligibility requirements they are also assessed to establish their entitlement to an allowance.

chunks.title: Entitlement — student allowance
chunks.text: To be entitled to a Student Allowance, a student must meet the following entitlement criteria: - a parental income assessment (if under 24) and - a personal income assessment or - a combined income assessment (if in a recognised relationship) For a tertiary student to continue to be entitled to a Student Allowance they must: - pass more than half the work of a full-time or approved limited full-time course, meet course requirements, (some exceptions apply) and - not exceed the maximum of 120 weeks of entitlement for tertiary education if aged 40 or over at study start date (some exceptions apply) or - not exceed the maximum of 200 weeks of entitlement for tertiary education if under the age of 40 at study start date (some exceptions apply) and - not be undertaking paid practical work, which is recognised as fulfilling part of the requirements of their programme and - meet particular criteria, if completing a period of study overseas at a campus or delivery site of a New Zealand tertiary provider, meet particular criteria and - be a New Zealand residence class visa holder, be studying in a country they are not familiar with, and enrolled as an intramural (face to face study) student, if completing a period of study overseas For a secondary school student to continue to be entitled to an allowance they must: - not exceed the maximum of 92 weeks entitlement for secondary school education (some exceptions apply)

chunks.title: Entitlement to payments — student allowance
chunks.text: A student is only entitled to payments between the start and finish date of their study. Their education provider advises these dates as part of the Verification of Study (VoS) process. A student must be enrolled and be accepted onto a course of study for their education provider to confirm their study start and end dates. A student's study start and end dates may subsequently change if their enrolment changes or the delivery of one or more of the papers or courses they are undertaking changes.

chunks.title: Entitlement is reduced, refused or exhausted — student allowance
chunks.text: If a full-time (or approved limited full-time) student has earned sufficient income to reduce their allowance entitlement to nil, or a student chooses not to get a Student Allowance, or the student has exhausted their weeks of entitlement, the student is still considered to be eligible (because they have met the eligibility criteria). The student is however not entitled to an allowance. From 1 January 2011, no student is entitled to get a Student Allowance, while that student or student's partner is getting either New Zealand Superannuation (under the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001) or a Veteran's Pension (under the Veterans' Support Act 2014).

chunks.title: Suspension of allowance due to failure — student allowance
chunks.text: Students who have had their allowance suspended due to failure and subsequently continue to study full-time, are still considered to be eligible (because they have met the eligibility criteria) for the Student Allowance, however, their entitlement to an allowance has been suspended.

chunks.title: Extension of payment period — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Extension of payment period
Payments are generally made for the length of the student's enrolment on an approved course of study.
Courses of study, programmes or qualifications are assessed and approved by Tertiary Education Commission using both gross weeks and teaching weeks per year.
Gross weeks include semester breaks or time spent on research, field work, or practical work that are requirements of the course or programme. The teaching weeks are the weeks of the course or programme where teaching occurs.
For example, a course may be approved for 40 gross weeks and 37 teaching weeks; this is to allow for the 3 week break between semesters.
Education Providers advise the study start and end dates and any breaks for individual students using the Verification of Study (VoS) process.
An enrolment can be extended beyond the gross weeks initially advised. An education provider will advise any changes using the Verification of Study (VoS) process.
MSD are only able to extend the payment period if the LET calculation for the extended study period confirms it is full-time study.
