For example, if the course has 0.5 EFTS, the maximum period that Student Allowances and living costs will be paid for is 20 weeks from the beginning of the course.
Students who are approved for limited full-time study are also treated as being full-time for any approved extension.

chunks.title: Extra assistance for students — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Extra assistance for students
Students may qualify for additional assistance such as:
- Accommodation Supplement
In some cases students or their partners may be able to receive an Accommodation Supplement paid as a non-beneficiary
- Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit
Students with children need to apply to Inland Revenue for family tax credit and Best Start tax credit. It is not paid with Student Allowance.
- Extra help
Students or their partners may qualify for Extra help as a non-beneficiary, such as:
Disability Allowance
Temporary Additional Support
Childcare Assistance Programme
- Community Services Card
Students receiving Student Allowance automatically get sent a Community Services Card. However, students who receive a lower rate of Student Allowance because their partner is earning must apply for a Community Services Card.

chunks.title: Extramural study — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Extramural study
Extramural students who meet all the eligibility and entitlement requirements can access a Student Allowance.
This includes studying extramurally overseas or in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Previous study performance — student allowance
chunks.text: Generally a tertiary student will not be entitled to a Student Allowance if they failed to pass more than half the work of a full-time tertiary course in the last course they received a Student Allowance for.

chunks.title: Reasons beyond a student's control — student allowance
chunks.text: The 'failure for reasons beyond a student's control' exception provides discretion to make an entitlement decision based on the intent and wording of the regulation, and the facts of the particular situation. A student may qualify for this exception if: - they failed to pass more than half of a full-time course because of reasons beyond their control or - they were unable to complete a Master's Degree due to reasons beyond the student's control 'Reasons beyond their control' may include but are not limited to: - medical, social or psychological reasons which prevented the student passing their course - in the case of continuing illness or other reasons, evidence should also be obtained that the student is now capable of undertaking their study - course cancellation - where the education provider has cancelled or changed the course or withdrawn tuition Financial hardship is not in itself an acceptable circumstance. Where an exception under 'reasons beyond a student's control' is approved, the student must be advised of the consequences of further failure for the same reasons for their future entitlement. In particular, that ongoing failure will more likely than not result in a further application being declined.

chunks.title: Acceptable evidence of reasons beyond a student's control — student allowance
chunks.text: Acceptable evidence of reasons beyond a student's control may include: - a medical certificate specifically stating the effect of the illness on the student's study. Where the illness is on-going, it needs to include confirmation that the student is now capable of successfully undertaking their study - statement from a solicitor, minister of religion, social worker etc, setting out details of the family circumstances that have adversely affected the student's study. Where this reason is ongoing, it needs to include confirmation that the student is now capable of successfully undertaking their study. - a statement by their education provider advising of a change in the course, withdrawal of tuition etc. which was not initiated by the student and which made it impossible for them to complete the course

chunks.title: On-going failure for reasons beyond a student's control — student allowance
chunks.text: It is not appropriate to continue to allow a student to access a Student Allowance where it is evident that they are continuing to fail more than half of their study, even if this is for reasons that are beyond the student's control. The performance test is designed to ensure only students who succeed in their study can continue to access a Student Allowance. If a student is repeatedly failing to meet the performance requirement, even for reasons beyond their control, further investigation is required. This investigation may include, but is not limited to, consideration of whether: - a reduction in study is likely to improve the student's performance. If this means the student reduces their study to less than full-time, a limited full-time approval may be appropriate - the student is receiving their full and correct entitlement. A student who is not succeeding may be under financial pressure due to unanticipated costs associated with their situation. They may also have difficulty in accessing the services they need if there is a cost involved In some cases, it may be prudent to suspend access to a Student Allowance until a decision is made.

chunks.title: Regaining access to a Student Allowance — student allowance
chunks.text: If the performance requirement set out above is not met, access to a Student Allowances can be regained by studying and passing more than half the work of a Student Allowance approved full-time course at their own expense.

chunks.title: Extending entitlement — student allowance
chunks.text: If a 'failure for reasons beyond a student's control' exception is approved, you may also consider extending a student's entitlement to the Student Allowance beyond the 120 or 200 week limit. An extension granted under this provision would need to relate to the reasons beyond the students control. The decision to grant an extension needs to clearly explain why the number of weeks was approved. A reasonable decision needs to be made that ensures the student is not disadvantaged due to their failure for reasons beyond their control. In addition, there may be situations where a tertiary student has been granted an extension under the special circumstances provision, but has subsequently failed for reasons beyond the student's control. They can be granted a further extension under the 'reasons beyond their control' provision, provided they relate to the study undertaken during their extension period. Students granted extensions due to 'reasons beyond their control' are subject to the age limitation when the student reaches 65 years of age. For study starting on or after 1 January 2013, Student Allowance eligibility for all NZQF (New Zealand Qualifications Framework) level 8 and above postgraduate certificates, diplomas, master's degrees, and doctorates were removed. There was a transitional provision for some students affected by this policy change.

chunks.title: Failure to attend because of injury or sickness — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Failure to attend because of injury or sickness
Where a student is absent because of injury or sickness for a period exceeding 2 weeks, their entitlement to a Student Allowance may be suspended, until they resume meeting the requirements of their course.
Several factors need to be considered before making a decision to suspend entitlement, including:
- The nature of the injury or sickness and whether it is likely to continue and for how long?
- Is the absence affecting the student's ability to meet their course requirements?
- What is their provider's view?
- Is the student entitled to another form of financial support (e.g. a main benefit or ACC)?

chunks.title: Family breakdown — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Family breakdown
A family breakdown can include the following situations:
- the applicant has been subject to severe mental cruelty by parent(s) or
- the applicant is estranged from their parents to the extent that contact would have a detrimental psychological effect on them or their parent(s) or
- the applicant has a parent who is in prison or in a psychiatric hospital and is unable to take responsibility for them or contribute towards their support and they are unable to live with or depend on their other parent or
- the applicant has been subject to physical or sexual abuse by their parent(s) or
- it is clearly detrimental for the applicant to live with or depend on their parents for financial support
Evidence of these matters can include a recommendation from a certified psychologist or counsellor who is aware of the applicant's circumstances.
## Important points to consider when assessing a family breakdown
- The applicant is not expected to live with, or be dependent on, the other parent in the same household if it is established that there is physical or sexual abuse caused by a parent. However, where parents are separated, applicants are normally expected to depend on the other parent for financial support.
- When the applicant is subjected to, or at risk of, physical or sexual abuse from some other person (i.e. not a parent), this will not normally amount to exceptional circumstances making it unreasonable for the parents to provide financial assistance. In this case the applicant may live away from the parental home but the parents are still expected to support the applicant financially.
- An applicant who has been subjected to physical or sexual abuse in the past may have recently resumed contact with the parent responsible for the abuse. In this situation, the applicant is not expected to live with or depend on that parent for support, if evidence shows that the applicant's dependence on the parent would harm their new relationship.
- If the applicant is not living with their parents you must check that there is no one 'acting in place of a parent'.
- When an applicant has a sibling who has had an Independent Circumstances Allowance application, it is still necessary to confirm the nature of the applicant's own relationship with their parents. This means that siblings have to individually provide evidence of their circumstances.
- When an applicant has lived away from their parents for some time simply because of a desire to be independent, that will not on its own meet the criteria for Independent Circumstances Allowance.

chunks.title: Family member of someone affected by Christchurch the mosques attack — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Family member of someone affected by Christchurch the mosques attack
Some students who came to support their family members following the Christchurch mosques attack on 15 March 2019, may not have been living in New Zealand for 3 years when they apply for Student Allowance.
The requirement to have lived and been entitled to live indefinitely in New Zealand for 3 years has been waived for these students.
This waiver only applies to study starting on or after 1 January 2024.
To qualify for the 3-year residency waiver the student must:
- have been granted a Residence Class Visa between 15 March 2019 and 31 December 2024.
and
- have a family member (affected person) who they are related to by birth, marriage, or adoption
## Family members (affected person) must meet specific requirements
To qualify for the residency waiver the student applying, and their family member (affected person) must have a specific relationship.
The family member (affected person) must be alive at the time the student applies for the residency waiver. The family member (affected person) does not need to be living in New Zealand.
The family member (affected person) must also meet 1 of the following criteria:
- have a Christchurch Response Visa
or
- qualified for a Christchurch Response Visa, held a Resident Visa on 15 March 2019, and currently holds a Residence Class Visa or is a New Zealand citizen
or
- would have qualified for a Christchurch Response Visa but already had a Permanent Resident Visa or New Zealand citizenship on 15 March 2019
or
- was granted New Zealand citizenship after holding a Christchurch Response Visa

chunks.title: Free accommodation in lieu of income — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Free accommodation in lieu of income
If a student receives free accommodation or meals in lieu of income, then the value of the accommodation or meals should be treated as personal income for Student Allowance purposes.
## Example
A student manages a hostel and in lieu of wages receives free accommodation and/or meals.
However, this may not apply to accommodation and meals provided by the student's parent or caregiver, if the student is single and younger than 24.

chunks.title: Full-time secondary school — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Full-time secondary school
To be eligible for a Student Allowance, a student must be a full-time student, or with the approval of MSD, a part-time student. See:
- Limited full-time study
For a secondary school student a full-time course is defined as:
- 20 class contact hours a week
The full-time course definition for students studying at a distance school is:
- four subjects - NCEA level 1 or
- three subjects - NCEA level 2 and 3
MSD will request a Verification of Study (VoS) from the education provider where the student is studying.
Home schooling is not included in the definition of a secondary school for Student Allowance purposes. Students who are home schooled are not eligible for a Student Allowance.

chunks.title: Full-time study — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Full-time study
To be eligible for Student Allowances, a student must be:
- a full-time student or
- a part-time student with the approval of StudyLink, see Limited full-time study
A student can be full-time at secondary school or a tertiary education provider.

chunks.title: Full-time tertiary — student allowance
chunks.text: To be eligible for a Student Allowance, a student must be a full-time student, or separately approved for study on a 'Limited full-time' basis. Tertiary programmes have an Equivalent Full-Time Student (EFTS) value assigned to them. The EFTS value determines if a course of study is full-time or not. The Verification of Study (VoS) process is used to confirm the EFTS of a student's course of study. To be full-time, a student must be studying the minimum EFTS in regards to weeks, as outlined in the LET table below.

chunks.title: Loan Entry Threshold (LET) table — student allowance
chunks.text: Number of weeks (gross weeks) EFTS Number of weeks (gross weeks) EFTS 12 0.3 23 0.575 13 0.3 24 0.6 14 0.3 25 0.625 15 0.3 26 0.65 16 0.4 27 0.675 17 0.4 28 0.7 18 0.4 29 0.725 19 0.4 30 0.75 20 0.5 31 0.775 21 0.525 32-52 0.8 22 0.55 53 or more 1.0 A student may have a period of study which is less than 12 weeks (for example some trimester 3 study). If this is the case, a student is considered to be undertaking full-time study if they are studying at least 0.025 EFTS per teaching week.

chunks.title: Full-time - trimester 3 (summer school) study — student allowance
chunks.text: Students who are undertaking study in trimester 3 (i.e. study that is undertaken over the summer period) need to meet all general Student Allowance eligibility and entitlement criteria, to qualify for a Student Allowance. If the trimester 3 study on its own is less than full-time, then the student is not eligible for that period of study. If the trimester 3 study is attached to their existing or subsequent study programme the student can be eligible for any part of the combined study that is full-time.

chunks.title: Full year courses that are not full-time for the whole year — student allowance
chunks.text: Students undertaking full-year courses that are not full-time for the whole year can be eligible for any periods of study they are full-time. This can occur where there are combinations of full-year and part-year study within the overall study programme.

chunks.title: Combining periods of study — student allowance
chunks.text: For Student Allowance purposes, 2 normally unrelated periods of part-time study cannot be combined together as full-time study except where they are conjoint or concurrent study.

chunks.title: Grandparented Accommodation Benefit payments — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Grandparented Accommodation Benefit payments
The change to the calculation of the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit means some students will get less Accommodation Benefit on 1 January 2023.
Students will be grandparented their current rate of Accommodation Benefit if they will get a lower standard rate of Accommodation Benefit from 1 January 2023 compared to 31 December 2022 (within a current study application). The grandparented rate will end when the current study application period ends, or they have a change in circumstances which ends their eligibility.
This will affect students who:
- are getting, or were eligible to get, the maximum rate of $60 on 31 December 2022, but their new Territorial Authority rate is less than the maximum rate from 1 January 2023 or
- move to a lower standard rate of Accommodation Benefit due to their SAL regions splitting into different Territorial Authorities on 1 January 2023
## Example - New Territorial Authority rate is less than the student's current rate of Accommodation Benefit
Rawiri is an extramural student at Waikato University.
Rawiri's study application period is 11 July 2022 to 9 April 2023, he is getting a Student Allowance and, based on his rural residential address, a standard rate of Accommodation Benefit paid at the rural rate.
On 1 January 2023 the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit is mapped to Territorial Authorities.
Rawiri's residential address now comes under the Opotiki District Territorial Authority, and the rate of Accommodation Benefit is now lower.
However, as Rawiri is within the same study application, he will get the grandparented rate for his residential address until he has a change in circumstances or his current application ends (whichever is first).

chunks.title: Grandparented - late applications for study assistance — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Grandparented - late applications for study assistance
There may be some students who start studying before 1 January 2023, but don't apply for Student Allowance (and Accommodation Benefit) until after 1 January 2023.
If there are special circumstances and the student was eligible for a higher rate before 1 January 2023 than the rate after 1 January 2023, the higher rate will be grandparented.
When there are no special circumstances for the delay in the student's application, grandparenting would not be considered and they would be paid at the current Territorial Authority rate at the time the application was received
## Example
Conrad lives rurally and is an extramural student at Massey University. Before 1 January 2023, Conrad was eligible for the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit based on his rural residential address.
From 1 January 2023, Conrad's address will come under the Territorial Authority for Ōpōtiki District, and the Territorial Authority rate payable will be less than the previous rural rate for his residential address before 1 January 2023.
Conrad doesn't apply for assistance until after 1 January 2023 as he was admitted to hospital in mid-December.
Conrad's study application period is from 5 December 2022 to 6 September 2023.
As Conrad submitted his application late, MSD can use our discretion for special circumstances and pay Conrad the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit from the day his study period started.
As his study period started before 1 January 2023, Conrad gets the grandparented rate of Accommodation Benefit for his rural residential address.
Conrad's next semester of study starts on 7 September 2023, and he submits another application for assistance. As this is a new study application period, Conrad's grandparenting ends and he gets the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit based on the Ōpōtiki District Territorial Authority.

chunks.title: Grandparenting ends - Accommodation Benefit standard rates — student allowance
chunks.text: The higher standard rate of Accommodation Benefit will be grandparented for any eligible student until one of the following occurs: - the student's application on which they are getting the grandparented rate ends or - the student has a change in circumstances and they are no longer eligible for the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit, this is when the student: starts living in the same home as a parent ormoves into a home maintained by, or provided by a parents ormoves into social housing - starts living in the same home as a parent or - moves into a home maintained by, or provided by a parents or - moves into social housing - the student has a change in course which results in a new application or - the student becomes eligible for a higher rate than the grandparented Accommodation Benefit rate while under the same application, due to a change in the student's: address (extramural study only) orcampus location (intramural study only) or - address (extramural study only) or - campus location (intramural study only) or - the student has a child enter their care and they qualify for the Sole Parent Accommodation Benefit rate under the same application

chunks.title: Current study application period ends — student allowance
chunks.text: Grandparenting of the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit can only be paid to students on their current study application. When the current study application period ends, so will the grandparenting.

chunks.title: Change in circumstances that end grandparenting eligibility — student allowance
chunks.text: The grandparented standard rate of Accommodation Benefit will end if the student: - moves back into their parental home or - moves to a home maintained by, or provided by their parents or - moves into social housing

chunks.title: Change in course resulting in a new application — student allowance
chunks.text: Grandparented standard rates of Accommodation Benefit only apply for the current study application a student is enrolled in. Where a student decides to change their course, a new application will be started and grandparenting will end when the original application ends.

chunks.title: Student is eligible for a higher rate than the grandparented rate — student allowance
chunks.text: If a student is on a grandparented standard rate of Accommodation Benefit and has a change in circumstances making them eligible for a higher rate of Accommodation Benefit than the grandparented rate, grandparenting will end.

chunks.title: Dependent child enters the student's care — student allowance
chunks.text: Students who are getting a standard rate of Accommodation Benefit and have a dependent child enter their care, will be transferred to the sole parent rate of Accommodation Benefit. Once this happens, any grandparented standard rate of Accommodation Benefit will stop. Note sole parents who do not qualify for a sole parent rate of Accommodation Benefit are not eligible for the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit.

chunks.title: Is holiday pay classed as income? — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Is holiday pay classed as income?
Holiday pay is classed as income for Student Allowance purposes as it is part of employment earnings.
Holiday pay can be paid out in a number of different ways, which will determine how the payment is assessed.
## Holiday pay that is paid with the weekly earnings
The total earnings for that week including the holiday pay, is counted as personal income and assessed accordingly.
## Holiday pay that is paid as a lump sum with a final pay or pre-annual leave pay
The holiday pay is added to the final pay and the total is counted as personal income for the week it is received.
## Holiday pay that is paid per week of annual leave
This holiday pay is personal income for each of the weeks of annual leave.
## Holiday pay paid after employment ceases
Any holiday pay that is paid as a lump sum, after employment has ceased, will be counted as personal income for the week it is received.
Any holiday pay that is received outside the study period has no effect on the Student Allowance.

chunks.title: Hostel - Accommodation Benefit — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Hostel - Accommodation Benefit
Eligible students who live in a recognised student hostel or boarding school get the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit applicable to that hostel, up to the maximum rate payable of $60.
Note the change to the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit calculation from 1 January 2023, does not affect hostel-based accommodation rates.
Example
Elizabeth is an intramural student at the University of Canterbury in Christchurch and lives in Christchurch City at a recognised student hostel.
Christchurch City has a standard Accommodation Benefit rate, however Elizabeth gets the rate for the specific hostel she stays at, even though it is lower than the standard Accommodation Benefit rate for Christchurch.

chunks.title: The calculation — student allowance
chunks.text: Tertiary courses have an Equivalent Full Time Student (EFTS) value assigned to them that measures the amount of study they cover. Many education providers divide their courses into papers and assign an EFTS value to each paper. The EFTS value is also used to determine whether a tertiary course is full-time, based on the total length of the course. To be full-time, a course must meet the minimum EFTS value required for a course of that length. For information on the minimum EFTS values see: - Full time tertiary A student must pass more than half of the work of a Student Allowance approved full-time course of study. This means a student needs to pass more than half of the EFTS of a full-time course of that length. When Limited full-time (LFT) study has been approved, a student must pass more than half of the EFTS of the course they are undertaking. For more information on Limited full-time study see: - Limited full-time study When a student undertakes study with an EFTS value greater than the minimum amount required for a full-time course, they are only required to pass more than half the work of a full-time course.

chunks.title: Some examples — student allowance
chunks.text: Example 1 A student taking a full year course of at least 0.8 EFTS, needs to pass more than 0.4 EFTS. Example 2 A student taking a single semester course of 18 weeks of at least 0.4 EFTS, needs to pass more than 0.2 EFTS. Example 3 A student approved to study 0.2 EFTS on a Limited full-time basis, needs to pass more than 0.1 EFTS. Example 4 A student who does not pass more than half of a full-year course can have their entitlement to a Student Allowance reinstated, by passing more than half of the work of a full-time semester of study. This means they can be approved a Student Allowance in the second semester of a full-time course if they pass more than half the work of the first semester. Example 5 A student enrolled in a 25 week course must be studying at least 0.625 EFTS to be considered full-time. Therefore they need to pass more than half of 0.625 EFTS, i.e. they need to pass more than 0.3125 EFTS.

chunks.title: Results of Study datamatch — student allowance
chunks.text: The Results of Study (RoS) datamatch provides the information MSD uses to confirm the amount of EFTS that a student has passed.

chunks.title: Suspension — student allowance
chunks.text: Suspension for failure to pass more than half of a full-time course applies regardless of when the failure occurred. For example, if a student failed to pass more than half of a full-time course 10 years ago for which they received a Student Allowance, and they have not received a Student Allowance since then, the suspension still applies and the student needs to meet the reinstatement criteria to receive a Student Allowance again. Some older courses may not have an EFTS value. To calculate failure to pass more than half for these courses, you should use the method or calculation used by the education provider to determine failure. If a student received a Student Allowance for only part of a failed course, the suspension still applies.

chunks.title: Illness of the student — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Illness of the student
When a student is unable to study full-time because of a medical condition, they can apply for approval to study on a Limited full-time basis.
MSD needs written confirmation from a registered medical practitioner of the details of the medical condition, as well as advice that confirms why it prevents the student from studying full-time and how long this situation is likely to continue (where this is appropriate).
A student is required to apply for limited full-time for each new application period.

chunks.title: Income test — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Income test
Student Allowance is an income tested payment. The rate of allowance paid can depend:
- the student's income (personal income)
- the combined income of the student and their partner (combined income) and
- for most single students under 24, their parents' income (parental income)
For Student Allowance, a partner or spouse is someone who the student is in a recognised relationship with.
For more information see:
## Single students under 24 with no children
For students under 24 with no children the rate of allowance will depend on both parent(s) and personal income.
The Student Allowance rate is assessed on the students parental income, and then reduced by any personal income the student earns over the personal income threshold.
## Single students under 24 with children
For single students under 24 with children, the rate of allowance will depend on personal income only.
## Single students 24 or over (with or without children)
For single students, who are 24 or over, with or without children, the rate of allowance will depend on personal income only.
## Students in a recognised relationship
For students in a recognised relationship, the rate of allowance will depend on both personal and combined income.
The Student Allowance rate is assessed on their combined income, and then reduced by any personal income the student earns over the personal income threshold.

chunks.title: Income from a trust — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Income from a trust
Generally, a payment that a student derives from a trust will be personal income for Student Allowance purposes.
Example a student who is the beneficiary of a family trust, receives a payment of $2,600 for a certain period from the trust for study, training or any other general purpose. This income should be charged against the student's Student Allowance over the period to which it relates.
Note payments received from a trust that are intended as payment of tuition fees for a Student Allowance approved course are not personal income for Student Allowance purposes.

chunks.title: Income from boarders — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Income from boarders
If a student or their partner receives income from boarders the profit is treated as personal income for Student Allowance purposes.
"Profit" means the total board charged (for all boarders) less reasonable expenses, for example, expense incurred as a direct result of having a boarder.

chunks.title: Personal income — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Personal income
If a student's income is more than $284.70 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026) their gross Student Allowance will reduce by the equivalent amount of income received over this figure.
Example if a student receives $295.00 gross per week, their Student Allowance rate will reduce by $10.30.
## Parental income
For students under 24, the full Student Allowance rate begins to abate when the combined parental income exceeds $72,108.92 gross annually (at 1 April 2026).
The cut-off points for parents' combined taxable income (as at 1 April 2026) are:
- $131,670.35 gross annually if the student lives at home or
- $141,451.55 gross annually if the student lives away from home
Note parents' combined taxable income is adjusted to take into account:
- an exemption of $7,000 for each additional student in the family (who is not younger than 16 on the 31st December the year before the application, and is not older than 23 on 1 January in the year of the application) who are also studying full-time at either secondary or tertiary level and
- an exemption of $3,400 for parents who live in separate households
## Combined income
A higher rate of Student Allowance will be paid if the couple's combined income is $569.40 gross or less per week (at 1 April 2026).
If the couple's combined income is more than $569.40 but less than $1,185.75 gross per week (at 1 April 2026), Student Allowance will be paid at a lower rate.
In any week that their income is $1,185.75 gross or more (at 1 April 2026), there will be no entitlement to Student Allowance.
Note the personal income assessment limit noted above still applies to the student.

chunks.title: Income that is not parental income — student allowance
chunks.text: Some types of payments are not parental income for Student Allowances and are not included in a parental income assessment.

chunks.title: Payments not included as parental income — student allowance
chunks.text: Parental income does not include: - a Christchurch mosques attack support payment, and any income earned from the investment of it (for study starting on or after 1 January 2021) - a loan under ordinary commercial conditions - a monetary benefit under the Social Security Act 2018 defined as exempt income under the Income Tax Act 2007, i.e. supplementary beneficiary assistance payments made under the Social Security Act 2018 - a Student Loan under the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011 - a payment made to relieve the adverse effects of a declared emergency event, (including payments made between 1 April 2011 and 3 September 2011 (inclusive) to relieve the adverse effects of the Canterbury earthquake of 4 September 2010, and payments made between 1 April 2011 and 21 February 2012 (inclusive) to relieve the adverse effects of the Canterbury earthquake 22 February 2011). - a payment of a foster care allowance under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 - a pension or allowance under the Veterans' Support Act 2014 defined as exempt income under the Income Tax Act 2007 - a participation allowance payment under the Social Security Act 2018 - an amount derived by a trustee of: a Trust for the benefit of persons harmed by thalidomide orNew Zealand Agent Orange Trust oror a distribution to a beneficiary of those trusts - a Trust for the benefit of persons harmed by thalidomide or - New Zealand Agent Orange Trust or - or a distribution to a beneficiary of those trusts - an educational scholarship or bursary - any Child Support or maintenance payments - any payment the Governor General declares not to be income under section 418 of the Social Security Act 2018 - any resident passive income a parent's dependent child receives (whether the applicant or other dependent children) - compensation for a loss other than a loss of income - distributions from a charity registered under the Charities Act 2005 - forgiveness of debt by a public authority (e.g. Student Loan interest write-offs) - grants for the payment of expenses relating to medical treatment or a funeral - lump sum compensation under the Accident Compensation Act 2001 - Kāinga Ora energy subsidy - payments of Accommodation Supplement arrears due to a system processing error from 1993 to 2014 (and any interest earned on the payment), for the first 12 months from when the payment is received - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support and income earned on the arrears for the first 12 months after the payment is made

chunks.title: Payments not included as parental income — student allowance
chunks.text: - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after the payment is made - payments on behalf of the parent by a local authority or a public authority (e.g. rates, rebates, or health or education subsidies) - payments under an insurance contract, other than a payment for the loss of income - proceeds from the disposal of property except where those proceeds have already been included in a parent's taxable income - severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment) - Working for Families Tax Credits paid under the Income Tax Act 2007 - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received The following types of payments are not parental income for Student Allowance purposes, and are not included in a parental income assessment: - money won gambling or from a New Zealand lottery, as those terms are used in the Gambling Act 2003 - payment from a deceased estate - payment, other than a payment by a trustee, from the person's ownership of an investment activity or business, when the payment: is received on the capital account andis not a loan - is received on the capital account and - is not a loan - refund of a payment, including a refund of any overpaid tax, Student Loan payments, or Child Support payments - repayment of a loan, or a mistaken or misdirected payment

chunks.title: These include — student allowance
chunks.text: - a Christchurch mosques attack support payment (for study starting on or after 1 January 2021) - a Student Loan under the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011 - Accommodation Supplement arrears received in a lump sum on or after 1 November 2016 (and any interest earned) due to a system processing error from 1993 to 2014, for the first 12 months after payment is made - assistance from parents or caregivers for single students under the age of 24 years without children - ACC payments made: for a sensitive claim (except for any payments paid as weekly compensation for loss of earnings or potential earnings)to replace the income of a former parent of the supported child of a student (or their partner)under schedule 1 of the Accident Compensation Act 2001 as a lump sum for impairmentfor the death of a parent to a single student, without children, under 24 years of age - under schedule 1 of the Accident Compensation Act 2001 as a lump sum for impairment - for the death of a parent to a single student, without children, under 24 years of age - an ex-gratia payment made by the Crown, in particular by MSD - any benefit, grant, allowance, bursary or payment received under the Veterans' Support Act 2014 - any benefit or earnings received before starting the course - any loans with ordinary commercial conditions - any money the student earns during vacation periods when they are not getting a Student Allowance - family tax credits, including Best Start tax credits paid under the Income Tax Act 2007 - for study starting on or after 1 January 2019, disability support payments made directly: by or on behalf of the Crownto a student or their partner (or a person on the student or their partner's behalf)for the purpose of purchasing or obtaining Disability Support Services - by or on behalf of the Crown - to a student or their partner (or a person on the student or their partner's behalf) - for the purpose of purchasing or obtaining Disability Support Services - income or interest generated by a superannuation scheme when the superannuation scheme has a lock-in clause - income received from work that is a prerequisite to the course - lump sum payments (not including scholarships, grants and bursaries) - Kāinga Ora energy subsidy

chunks.title: These include — student allowance
chunks.text: - one-off gifts, winnings or prizes - payments intended as payment of tuition fees for a Student Allowance approved course - proceeds from the sale of a capital asset - e.g. the sale of a house - Payments of arrears to Special Benefit clients better off on Temporary Additional Support and income earned on the arrears for the first 12 months after the payment is made - Payments to clients whose Kāinga Ora tenancy was terminated due to methamphetamine contamination and income earned on the payment for the first 12 months after the payment is made - reimbursements received for work related expenses; e.g. an employer may reimburse an employee for such things as, meal and clothing expenses the employee incurs as part of their employment - severe weather event payments for the first 12 months from when payment is received (and any interest earned on the payment) - supplementary beneficiary assistance payments made under the Social Security Act 2018 - Temporary Accommodation Assistance lump sum or weekly payments (ended 30 June 2025) - Temporary GST Assistance paid to Student Allowance recipients between 1 October 2010 and 1 April 2011 - the following payments made under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989Home for lifeCaregiver allowancesTransition Support Service - Home for life - Caregiver allowances - Transition Support Service - the following scholarships: TeachNZ scholarships (except the living cost portion of the Career-Changer Scholarship)Tulī Takes Flight: Career changer scholarshipsNZQA Scholarship Monetary AwardsBonded Merit Scholarship (no longer available)Step up Scholarship (no longer available)Canterbury Earthquake Scholarships (no longer available) - TeachNZ scholarships (except the living cost portion of the Career-Changer Scholarship) - Tulī Takes Flight: Career changer scholarships - NZQA Scholarship Monetary Awards - Bonded Merit Scholarship (no longer available) - Step up Scholarship (no longer available) - Canterbury Earthquake Scholarships (no longer available) - the amount of a scholarship that is paid for tuition fees, under the terms and conditions of that scholarship - FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received

chunks.title: Income that is parental income — student allowance
chunks.text: The following sections provide advice on income that is included in a parental income assessment.

chunks.title: Taxable income — student allowance
chunks.text: Any payment or money received that is taxable (i.e. a parent is liable to pay tax on it) is parental income for Student Allowances.

chunks.title: Wages and salary — student allowance
chunks.text: The gross amount of any wages or salary a parent receives is parental income (whether taxable or not). Wages and salary includes paid parental leave, weekly accident insurance payments and overseas wages and salaries. Allowances paid to parents by an employer are only considered income where taxable.

chunks.title: Benefit income — student allowance
chunks.text: The gross amount of any income received from an income tested benefit is parental income. This is for main benefits only, not extra help.

chunks.title: Dividends — student allowance
chunks.text: Dividends are part of a company's profits that is passed on to its shareholders. Company profits are paid to shareholders according to the proportion of the company they own.

chunks.title: Business income — student allowance
chunks.text: Business income in general terms is the income that owners of a business get from that business. From a technical or legal perspective, for the purposes of Family Scheme Income under the Income Tax Act 2007, business income is defined as the net income of the business. Net income is the annual gross income less any permitted deductions. - if, for a tax year, a person's annual gross income is more than their annual total deduction, the difference is their net income for the year - if, for a tax year, a person's annual gross income equals their annual total deduction, their net income for the year is zero - if, for a tax year, a person's annual total deduction is more than their annual gross income, the difference is their net loss for the year, and their net income for the year is zero The 'net income' amount is before any business (or tax) losses are included in order to determine a person's taxable income. Business (or tax) losses include losses brought forward. For income tax, an individual may offset any business (or tax) losses against their other taxable income. But, for parental income, when a business loss occurs, generally it is ignored and therefore cannot be offset against other forms of income. If a parent has separate business or investment activities which are normally carried out in association with each other, a loss can be off-set from one business or investment activity against another. When deciding if this provision applies, firstly it needs to be confirmed that both activities are active through the same legal personality (i.e. a trust cannot have its loss offset against a partnership or a company as they would be owned by separate legal personalities). Secondly, it would need to be confirmed that the activities are normally carried on in association with each other. Associated business activities are ones that are connected, joint or combined in relation to the activities themselves, not the ownership structure. For this association to be confirmed, the activities must only operate in association with each other and not have any other business activities occurring.

chunks.title: Business income — student allowance
chunks.text: For example, a parent has a loss from their landscaping partnership of $7,500. They have also made a profit from a lawn-mowing partnership of $50,000. These 2 partnerships only operate in conjunction with each other. The activities are owned by the same legal personality and are carried out in association with each other, so the $7,500 loss can be off-set against the $50,000 profit. The legal authority for determining whether separate businesses or investment activities "...are of the kind that are normally carried on in association with each other" is given to the Commissioner of Inland Revenue under section MB 3(3) of the Income Tax Act 2007. If there is doubt in a particular case, the case or situation can be raised with Inland Revenue for a decision. If a decision is made by Inland Revenue in a specific case, then that decision is generally not covered by the review and appeal provisions under the Education and Training Act 2020.

chunks.title: Drawings — student allowance
chunks.text: Drawings is the term used in financial accounts to describe money withdrawn from a business or a company by the owners or shareholders. Drawings cannot be taken from a trust. Payments of this type are either a beneficiary distribution, a trustee loan or a tax free distribution which is used for private living expenses. Drawings are by definition not money intended to be used for the use of the 'business' it is drawn from, so should generally be included as income for the purposes of calculating parental income for Student Allowances. In some cases it would be more accurate to categorise these payment(s) as either a shareholder wage or salary, or a dividend payment. Accountants may not always label drawings in an easily identifiable way (e.g. they could be described as a donation, taxation or insurance payments). Generally it is the purpose or intended use of the money (i.e. the substance of the transaction) that will determine whether it is parental income for Student Allowances. Firstly it needs to be determined whether the drawings payments are some form of income, dividend or salary that has been miscoded in financial statements. Secondly, it should be determined if the drawings fall under any of the exemptions as outlined in Income that is not parental income. Some examples of types of drawings that are considered parental income based on the purposes or intended use include: - where a payment is 'coded' in the business accounts of a parent as 'drawings' where it should be (based on its source and use) categorised as a payment of shareholder salary, a dividend payment, a loan (other than a loan made on ordinary commercial terms and conditions which is not parental income) or in the case of a trust a beneficiary distribution or loan - where a capital contribution is made to a business entity. Subsequently a drawing is made that is described as being a drawing down of all or part of that capital amount, but it is for personal use (i.e. income related) - where the payment(s) meet the definition of 'Payments for income related purposes where the total exceeds $5000 a year' In respect of the capital contribution described above, from the 2015/2016 tax year and onwards payments from a parent's capital ownership of an investment activity or business that: - are not payments by a trustee and - are received on capital account and - are not a loan are not parental income.

chunks.title: Drawings — student allowance
chunks.text: As this applies from the 2015/2016 tax year and onwards, it means any assessments of the parental income where the relevant tax year is 1 April 2015 - 31 March 2016 (or a later tax year) must apply the new policy. These payments are in effect reducing an asset. E.g. taking money from a savings account. The Student Allowance parental income test is not an asset test.

chunks.title: Retirement savings income — student allowance
chunks.text: Payments received from retirement savings are generally parental income for Student Allowances. See below for a description of different types of retirement savings income and advice on when this should be included as parental income. Income, pensions or annuities from a life insurance policy or private superannuation fund Half of any payment received in the form of a pension/annuity from a private superannuation fund or a pension/annuity under a life insurance policy is parental income for Student Allowances. New Zealand Superannuation is not a private superannuation scheme and therefore all the income received for New Zealand Superannuation is parental income for Student Allowances. When the pension or annuity is a regular ongoing payment, i.e. unless it represents a regular ongoing payment, a lump sum payment is not generally considered to be parental income, but may fall into the 'Distribution from superannuation schemes' or 'Distributions from retirement savings schemes' categories described below. The Government Superannuation Fund (GSF) was established in 1948 to provide a way for state sector employees to save for their retirement. GSF is a private superannuation fund and therefore half of any payments received from this fund are parental income for Student Allowance purposes. The fund was closed to new members in 1992. Distributions from superannuation schemes The amount of any distribution received by a parent from a superannuation scheme will be included as parental income if: - an employer of the parent has made contributions to the scheme in the income year in which the distribution was received or the 2 years immediately prior and - the parent continues to work for the employer for 1 month or more after the date of the distribution Only the employer contributions received are assessed as parental income (not the returned contributions that the parent made as a member of the scheme). The employer contributions are divided into the years that the contributions were made and, for assessment purposes, allocated to those years. Where the distribution is allocated to the relevant tax year, the income is included as parental income for that tax year. Distributions from KiwiSaver schemes or a complying superannuation fund are not included as parental income for Student Allowance purposes unless the next paragraph applies.

chunks.title: Retirement savings income — student allowance
chunks.text: If the parent receives a pension or annuity from a superannuation scheme as a result of or after their retirement from employment from the employer, (who contributed to the scheme), half of the pension or annuity is included under the category 'Income from a life insurance policy or private superannuation fund' (see above). Distributions from retirement savings schemes The amount of any distribution received by a parent from a retirement savings scheme will be included as parental income for Student Allowances if: - retirement savings scheme contribution tax was not paid by the contributor when the contributions were made and - at the time of the distribution, the parent is not eligible for New Zealand Superannuation The amount to be assessed as parental income is the amount distributed to the parent.

chunks.title: Overseas pensions — student allowance
chunks.text: The amount of any overseas pension (taxable and non-taxable) received by a parent is parental income for Student Allowances.

chunks.title: Income of major shareholders in a closely held company — student allowance
chunks.text: From the 2014/2015 tax year onwards, if a parent is a major shareholder in a closely held company the amount of income that is parental income for Student Allowances is the greater of either zero or the amount calculated using the following formula. For the purpose of this formula, the following definitions apply: parent's interest is the percentage voting interests for the company held, on the last day of the company's income year, by the parent income is the net income of the company for the company's income year dividends is the total dividends paid by the company for the company's income year Attributed interest is calculated using the following formula: For the purposes of this second formula, the following definitions apply: dependent child interest is the total percentage voting interests for the company held, on the last day of the company's income year, by: - the person's dependent children (as the term is defined in the Income Tax Act 2007) and - dependent children of the person's spouse, civil union partner or de facto partner relevant major shareholders is the total number of the following people who are major shareholders of the company on the last day of the company's income year: - the person - the person's spouse, civil union partner or de facto partner - principal caregivers of the dependent children described above This policy allocates any shares held by dependent children to the parents, for the purposes of apportioning any income that may be earned from them to the parents. It is designed to prevent a parent artificially reducing their income by the mechanism of allocating shares to a dependent child.

chunks.title: Attributable trustee income — student allowance
chunks.text: For a settlor of a trust, attributable trustee income is all income for the year of a trust that has not been distributed as beneficiary income. It includes income from trading and investment activities and the net income of any companies controlled by the trust. Attributable trustee income that a parent receives from a trust, as a settlor of the trust, is parental income for Student Allowances, unless: - the trustee of the trust is registered as a charitable entity under the Charities Act 2005 - the trust is solely for the benefit of a local authority - the interest and dividends derived is for funeral costs - the trust is a superannuation fund - the parent (or a member of their family) is not permitted to benefit from the trust except under an order of a court In determining attributable trustee income, this may require confirmation of who the settlors of the trust are. This may be required to determine: - whether the parents are the settlors of the trust and - how the attributable trustee income should be apportioned including where there are other settlors in addition to any parents From the 2014/2015 tax year onwards, the attribution of trust income to settlors can only occur in relation to settlors that are alive in the income year.

chunks.title: Attributable fringe benefits received by shareholder employees — student allowance
chunks.text: Where a parent who is a shareholding employee of a company and holds: - voting interests of 50% or more and/or - market value interests of 50% or more (if market value circumstances exist) the taxable value of any fringe benefits received is parental income for Student Allowances.

chunks.title: Portfolio Investment Entity (PIE) income that is not 'locked in' — student allowance
chunks.text: Any amount of income that is included in a tax return by a Portfolio Investment Entity to a parent, is parental income for Student Allowances, unless it is a 'locked in' superannuation fund or a retirement savings scheme. If the income is from a superannuation fund or a retirement savings scheme, the Superannuation Scheme and Retirement schemes rules apply as noted above.

chunks.title: Tax exempt income — student allowance
chunks.text: When a parent (who is a New Zealand tax resident) receives income that is exempt from tax in New Zealand, that income is parental income for Student Allowances purposes. This includes: - salary and wages that are exempt from income tax under specific international agreements in New Zealand - employees of international organisations such as the United Nations or the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), or under the Diplomatic Privileges and Immunities Act 1968

chunks.title: Income equalisation scheme deposits and withdrawals — student allowance
chunks.text: Main income equalisation schemes Deposits made into a main income equalisation scheme are parental income for Student Allowance purposes. Any withdrawals from the scheme are not parental income (however any interest earned on the deposit is parental income once withdrawn). For income tax purposes all deposits to all schemes are ignored and the withdrawals are taxable. Adverse events and forestry thinning operations income equalisations schemes Withdrawals from adverse events income equalisation schemes and forestry thinning operations income equalisation schemes are parental income as they are taxable. Deposits are not parental income.

chunks.title: Income from board — student allowance
chunks.text: Any taxable income that a parent receives from board payments is parental income for Student Allowance purposes. A parent is required to declare any taxable income they receive from boarders to Inland Revenue. The Inland Revenue website outlines what amount of any declared boarding payments are deemed to be taxable. This amount will depend on the costs they incur and the boarding payments they receive. Information on when a person is required to pay tax on income from boarders is available from Inland Revenue

chunks.title: Income from rental properties — student allowance
chunks.text: Income from rental properties that are part of a Business or Trust, must be included in any Business or Family Trust income declared. Income from rental properties not part of a Business or Trust must be declared to Inland Revenue. This income will be included in any taxable income declared.

chunks.title: Motor vehicle — student allowance
chunks.text: From the 2014/2015 tax year onwards, if a parent agrees to a lower salary in exchange for use of a company motor vehicle, the amount of reduction in the salary is parental income.

chunks.title: Employer-provided short-term charge facility — student allowance
chunks.text: From the 2014/2015 tax year onwards, if an employer provides a parent with a short-term charge facility, (e.g. vouchers) the amount may be considered parental income. Where the charge facility is already included in the taxable income of the parent, it should not be counted twice. If the parent is required to pay all the costs associated with the purchase, including any interest and fees, the amounts would not be parental income. The value of the benefit received, less any amounts that are paid towards the benefit by the employee, are parental income, if the total sum of short-term charge facilities paid to the parent in the tax year exceeds either: - 5% of the parents salary and wages or - $1,200 A parent can apply the maximum fringe benefit tax rate (49.25%) when declaring their short-term charge facilities as income, if their employer does not or is not able to provide the actual fringe benefit tax rate that was used. This provision does not apply where the 'Attributable fringe benefits received by shareholder employees' section applies as described above.

chunks.title: Payments for income related purposes where the combined total exceeds $5,000 a year — student allowance
chunks.text: The combined total value of all payments paid or provided to a parent from any source is parental income for Student Allowance purposes if the payments: - are used by the parent to replace lost or diminished income of the parent or the parent's family or - are used to meet usual living expenses of the parent or the parent's family and - the total payments for that particular financial year are more than $5000 - are not in any of the exclusions listed under Income that is not parental income This can include shareholders drawings. The origins of any funds introduced to the business by the shareholder, as well as the nature of the use of any drawings by the shareholder must be confirmed as part of any decision to include drawings as parental income. This may require further requests for information from the parent(s). Drawings are not included in parental income where they have already been included under another category (e.g. if the money has already been included in company income as a salary then it would not also be included as drawings under this category).

chunks.title: Parent is not or was not a resident in New Zealand — student allowance
chunks.text: When a parent is not or was not a tax resident in New Zealand, the parent's income for that period is every foreign sourced amount, when a form of tax is payable on the amount derived.

chunks.title: Income that is personal income — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Income that is personal income
Personal income for Student Allowances is personal income received or obtained by a student in New Zealand or overseas, whether it is taxable or not.
The definition of personal income is not the definition of income used by Inland Revenue for income tax purposes.
It is deliberately a wider definition of income that is closer to the definition of income for benefit purposes. This reflects the different objectives and purposes of the Student Allowances Scheme from the purposes and objectives of income tax.
Personal income generally has 3 broad characteristics:
- it is received or obtained by a student - being either money or something that can be sold or exchanged for money and
- it is periodic, recurring or regular and
- it has the character or nature of money in the hands of a student
Personal income will generally be intended for general living purposes. It includes such things as:
- money received which is not a one-off capital paymentFor example: wages, salary, commission or Parental Leave payments
- the value of any interest (before tax) acquired which is not a one-off capital payment
- payments, or the value of credits or services received periodically that are made and used for an income-related purpose
- an income-related insurance payment e.g. an income protection insurance payment
- Accident Compensation Payments to replace lost income
Personal income does not include payments excluded under the definition of 'personal income' in the Student Allowance Regulations 1998.
For more information see:
- Income that is not personal income
Important reminders
- a student must advise of any income they receive that may affect their entitlement to a Student Allowance
- the gross amount of income (before tax) is used in the personal income test
- where the income of the student is negative, it must be treated as nil
- financial assistance from parents or caregivers for single students without children and under the age of 24 years is not personal income
- it is also important to look for any deprivation of income
## Common types of income
Below is a list of the more common types of personal income:
- Salary or wages
- Income related insurance payments
- Accident compensation payments to replace lost income
- Child Support - whether via Inland Revenue or a private arrangement
- Other government assistance
- Income from boarders
- Business income
- Rental property income
- Commission
- Free accommodation in lieu of income
- Holiday pay
- Superannuation funds
- Investments
- Income from a trust
- Scholarships
- Redundancy payments

chunks.title: Parental income test — student allowance
chunks.text: For students who are under 24, without children, entitlement to a Student Allowance is normally subject to both their parents' income. The Independent Circumstances Allowance is available for students who are not living in the parental home or receiving financial assistance from either parent, and there are exceptional circumstances that mean it would be unreasonable for them to: - live with their parents and - receive financial support from their parents

chunks.title: Exercise of discretion — student allowance
chunks.text: A decision to grant an Independent Circumstances Allowance involves the exercise of discretion to make an entitlement decision based on the purpose and intent of the regulation, the limitations of the wording of the regulation, and the facts of the particular situation. This will require an assessment of the nature and extent of the relationship between any parents and the student. This will involve making a judgement on the relevant facts in relation to the purpose and intent of the policy. Each case needs to be considered on its merit.

chunks.title: Definition of 'exceptional circumstances' — student allowance
chunks.text: Exceptional circumstances’ means circumstances that are far beyond what is ordinary. Normally, these circumstances will need to be beyond the student's control. For example, if a student chooses to live and study in a different city/town from their parents, this would not meet the threshold of ‘exceptional circumstances’. It is important to remember that while it is not uncommon for young people to have disagreements, arguments or ‘problems’ with their parents, to meet the threshold of ‘exceptional circumstances’, it must be far beyond what is ordinary and mean that it is both: - unreasonable to expect the student to live with either parent and - unreasonable for the student to receive financial assistance from either parent

chunks.title: Breakdown in family relationships — student allowance
chunks.text: An Independent Circumstances Allowance application can often involve a student describing a breakdown in family relationships, in particular with their parents. For more information see:

chunks.title: Important considerations — student allowance
chunks.text: An applicant must not be getting financial assistance from any parent (or any other person acting in place of a parent). If an applicant receives financial assistance from any parent, the student is not eligible to get an Independent Circumstances Allowance. An applicant must be independent from all parents. If the applicant is independent from only one parent, an Independent Circumstances Allowance cannot be approved. For example, an applicant's parents may have separated and remarried. In many cases only one parent or one step-parent may be the cause for an application for an Independent Circumstances Allowance. The applicant must be independent from all parents and any step-parents before the criteria for an Independent Circumstances Allowance can be met. The following situations are not considered to be exceptional circumstances for the purposes of an Independent Circumstances Allowance: - financial hardship of parents – where they consider they cannot afford to financially support the student - the refusal of the parents to provide financial support for the student

chunks.title: Other eligibility and entitlement criteria still relevant — student allowance
chunks.text: Applicants for an Independent Circumstances Allowance must still meet the standard eligibility and entitlement criteria for a Student Allowance.

chunks.title: Continuation of an Independent Circumstances Allowance — student allowance
chunks.text: If a student has received an Independent Circumstances Allowance in the study period immediately prior to their application for an allowance, they can effectively apply for their Independent Circumstances Allowance to be 'continued'. This means, their personal situation does not have to be fully verified as long as the student declares and confirms that their circumstances have not changed. However, if a student indicates that their circumstances have changed you will need to review their continued eligibility and make a new assessment.

chunks.title: Parents have no right of review — student allowance
chunks.text: Third parties, including a parent, do not have a right of review in relation to an application for an Independent Circumstances Allowance. The application is the student's application. In addition, MSD do not have the authority or right to disclose to a third party, including a parent, any matters relating to an application - unless the student has authorised it. If a third party, including a parent, wishes to act on behalf of a student then they must become an agent for the student. An agent's powers may be limited to a specific issue, for example to assist with a Review of Decision application. If a third party applies to act on behalf of a student in relation to their Independent Circumstances Allowance application, MSD need to ensure they are not 'acting in place of a parent' for that student.

chunks.title: Introduction — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The Student Allowances Scheme provides targeted financial assistance, in the form of grants (Student Allowances), to assist New Zealanders who undertake secondary and tertiary education.
Student Allowances are designed to assist students with their living costs while they study.
Eligible students must generally be undertaking full-time study, and they must be enrolled in a recognised course of study or programme at an approved education provider.
Together with the Student Loan Scheme, Student Allowances are the main components of the Student Support system that provides funding directly to students. The government funds education providers through the Tertiary Education Commission.
Students getting a Student Allowance are not dependent children for the purposes of; Child Support, family tax credits, and both the Orphans Benefit and the Unsupported Childs Benefit.
For more background information see:

chunks.title: Investments — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Investments
When a student has investments that generate income, that income is generally considered to be personal income for Student Allowances purposes.
This includes, but is not limited to, interest on savings accounts and term deposits, and the income derived from other forms of investments, such as; bonds, equity, trusts and shares.
If a student reinvests the income back into the fund, or into another fund or account that pays a lower rate of interest, then you need to consider whether this is a case of deprivation of income.
For more information on Deprivation of income see:
- Deprivation of income

chunks.title: Eligibility and entitlement policies — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Eligibility and entitlement policies
The eligibility and entitlement policies of the Student Allowances Scheme are made by government, and set out in legislation.
## Statutes
There are a number of statutes that provide legal authority for aspects of the Student Allowances Scheme.
For a brief description see:
## Student Allowances Regulations 1998
The Student Allowances Regulations 1998 are provided for under the Education and Training Act 2020.
They contain the detailed eligibility and entitlement provisions of the scheme.
The previous 1998 Regulations replaced the 1991 Regulations when the administration of the scheme was transferred from the Ministry of Education to the (then) Department of Work and Income from 1999.
## Annual General Adjustment (AGA)
The Annual General Adjustment (AGA) is the annual increase of the rates and some thresholds of various financial assistance payments, including Student Allowances.
Changes to Student Allowances take effect from 1 April each year, reflecting any upward movement in the Consumers Price Index CPI.
Increases affect the rate of:
- basic grants and independence circumstances grants
- personal and couple income thresholds and
- parental income thresholds
The Annual General Adjustment does not affect the maximum standard rate of Accommodation Benefit.

chunks.title: Full-time study - Eligibility — student allowance
chunks.text: To be eligible for a Student Allowance or Student Loan Living Cost and Course-Related Costs components a student must normally be studying full-time. The exception to this requirement is when they apply and receive approval to study part-time under the Limited full-time provisions set out below. The Limited full-time exceptions provide discretion to make an entitlement decision based on the intent of the regulation, the limitations of the wording of the regulation, and the facts of the particular situation.

chunks.title: When can Limited full-time study be approved? — student allowance
chunks.text: A student may receive approval to study on a Limited full-time basis if it is considered appropriate because of one of the following: - Illness of the student - There is 'sufficient cause that is outside the student's control' - The course of study is 'in the student's academic best interests' - The student will complete a recognised programme that they previously commenced but did not complete and they are undertaking 'more than half of a full-time course' Approval would not be appropriate where a student is studying part-time because the course or programme is designed and/or delivered on a part-time basis for all the students undertaking it. This is because it is part-time study, not full-time study that is being undertaken on a part-time basis because of the exceptions described above. Further, a course or programme that is designed and/or delivered on a part-time basis for all students undertaking it, would not normally be approved for access to Student Allowances and/or Student Loans by the Tertiary Education Commission. Any examples that are identified should be raised with the Tertiary Education Commission. For more information see: Any approval of Limited full-time status for illness of the student, sufficient cause that is outside of the student's control or academic best interests, must be on the advice of the relevant tertiary provider or secondary school principal. This advice must provide evidence or arguments that confirm the student's application for Limited full-time approval is supported because of one of the exceptions described above.

chunks.title: Implications for the 92/120/200 week limit — student allowance
chunks.text: A student who is undertaking a reduced course or programme because of one of the 'limited full-time' provisions, can apply for assistance beyond the 92/120/200 week limit. For more information see:

chunks.title: Poor academic performance — student allowance
chunks.text: Poor academic performance does not generally on its own justify approving an application for Limited full-time status. It may be a symptom of one of the 4 exceptions described above.

chunks.title: Suspension and reinstatement — student allowance
chunks.text: If a student's Limited full-time entitlement is suspended due to not meeting attendance and/or work requirements, or for not passing more than half the work of their limited full-time workload, they would need to meet the 'Reinstatement' criteria to be eligible for further entitlement to allowances. For more information see: - Performance requirements - passing more than half - Meeting course requirements

chunks.title: Single students not living in the parental home — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Single students not living in the parental home
A living away from home rate of Student Allowance is payable to a single student who is not living with a parent in the parental home.
## Students sharing accommodation with a parent
A single student can receive the living away from home rate of Student Allowance where they are sharing accommodation with a parent, as the property is not the parental home.
Whether a student is sharing accommodation with a parent, as opposed to living with the parent in the parental home, will depend on the facts of the situation. Some situations will not be clear without further investigation.
The definition of parental home sets out several factors that need to be considered. In particular, any recent or planned change in the student's living situation need to be carefully considered, as it may suggest the student is attempting to organise their living arrangements to qualify for a higher rate of Student Allowance.
It is the reality of their living situation that needs to be established to determine the correct rate of Student Allowance.
## Self-contained residence on parent's property
When a single student is living on the same property as a parent, but in a self-contained residence, the student can get the living away from home rate of Student Allowance, as living in a self-contained residence is in effect the same as living away from home.
## Student not living in the same home as their partner
A student who is in a recognised relationship and is eligible for the 'couple with a combined weekly income between $569.40 and $1,185.75 rate' (as at 1 April 2026) of Student Allowance, can only get the 'away from home' rate if they are not living in the same home as their partner.
## Accommodation Benefit
The definition of 'parental home' used to assess eligibility to an Accommodation Benefit, includes the additional criteria where a student is not living with a parent, but is living in a home provided or maintained by a parent.

chunks.title: Living with a parent — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Living with a parent
Living with a parent means a student is living in the same home as a parent.
For Student Allowance purposes living with a parent does not include situations where:
- the parent is financially dependent on the student or
- the student, at their own expense, provides accommodation for the parent in the home or
- the student provides a substantial degree of care to the parent or
- the home is a hostel, boarding house or similar lodging and the student and the parent pay for accommodation in it

chunks.title: Eligibility — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Eligibility
An eligible student will receive an Accommodation Benefit if they are not living with a parent in the parental home.
When a student is not living with a parent in the parental home, but is living in a home provided or maintained by a parent, they are only eligible for an Accommodation Benefit if:
- they pay the market rent for the area of the home they occupy or
- they are responsible for the payment of the outgoings for the area of the home they occupy
A home provided by a parent can include a self-contained residence on the property of a parent.
## Market rent
A student is considered to be paying market rent if they are responsible for paying what is considered the market rent for the area of the home they occupy.
Example if a student occupies 1 bedroom of a house, and the market rent for that 1 bedroom is $100 per week, the student must be paying close to or more than $100 per week to qualify as paying market rent.
A parent must not be contributing to the payment of the area of the home they occupy.
