## Outgoings
A student is considered to be responsible for paying the outgoings in respect of a home if they are responsible for the payment of the outgoings for the area of the home they occupy.
Outgoings include:
- local authority rates (including water rates charged by a local authority, regardless of how the rates are calculated)
- mortgage payments (when there is a mortgage on the property)
- house insurance premiums, excluding contents insurance (when the house is insured)
- essential repairs and maintenance
An example
The outgoings in respect of a home provided by a student's parents are the mortgage, rates, house insurance, essential repairs and maintenance totalling $400 per week. The student lives in the home with 2 other flatmate's. The student would need to be responsible for the payment of the outgoings for the area of the home they occupy.
The student occupies a bedroom and shared living spaces, therefore it would be reasonable to expect the student to pay a third of these payments, $133.33 per week.
A parent must not be contributing to the payment of the area occupied by the student.

chunks.title: Student requirements — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Student requirements
Students are generally required to:
- attend classes, lectures or tutorials and/or
- submit work for assessment
In order to meet course requirements and complete and pass their course of study.
If a student fails to do any of these things, their Student Allowance may be suspended.
Before suspending access to a Student Allowance, consideration must be given to the circumstances of the case, including whether the student's situation is ongoing or whether it is a one-off occurrence.
## Reinstatement
If allowance payments are suspended for failing to meet course requirements, the allowance payments may be reinstated if the student resumes attending classes and/or meeting their work requirements.
Generally, this would be from the Monday of the week in which they resume meeting the attendance and/or work requirements of their course.
## Cancellation of enrolment by a provider
Not meeting course requirements is an entitlement issue. It is different to a cancellation of enrolment. If a student's enrolment is cancelled, their Student Allowance eligibility ceases from the date their enrolment is cancelled.

chunks.title: Merit grants — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Merit grants
The Ministry of Education may declare a grant or other award to be a ‘merit grant’. A merit grant is awarded based on academic merit.
A merit grant is not personal income for Student Allowance purposes up to a total value of $750. When a student gets more than $750 under a merit grant, the amount over $750 is personal income.
The only merit grant the Ministry of Education has previously approved is the University Junior Scholarship. However, this scholarship no longer exists.

chunks.title: Non completion of postponed part of course — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Non completion of postponed part of course
A student who postpones a course cannot receive assistance for another course until they have completed the portion of the course that was postponed or they have withdrawn from it completely.
A student who does not complete a postponed course will place their Student Allowance under suspension if they have not passed more than half of the recognised full-time course.

chunks.title: NZQA Scholarship Monetary Awards — student allowance
chunks.text:
## NZQA Scholarship Monetary Awards
The NZQA Scholarship Monetary Awards (originally called the Top Scholar Awards) replaced the University Bursary awards from 2004. They recognise and reward achievement and excellence of secondary school students in the New Zealand Scholarship Examinations.
The NZQA Scholarship Monetary Awards are the overall responsibility of New Zealand Qualifications Authority (including the award decisions). StudyLink is only responsible for confirming whether the successful student meets the study criteria for an award and making payment of the award to the student.

chunks.title: Obligations, offences and penalties — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Obligations, offences and penalties
A student, education provider or any other third party is required to provide complete and accurate information and advice, and in some cases, papers, documents, records or other things relevant to the determination of a student's eligibility or entitlement to a Student Allowance.
Failure or refusal to comply with a lawful request to supply information or documents or answer questions may result in the suspension of entitlement or the refusal to grant entitlement to a Student Allowance.
Education providers are also required to keep, maintain and provide MSD with access to enrolment records, when necessary to assess and determine eligibility or entitlement to a Student Allowance.
In some situations, it is an offence not to comply with these obligations and there are penalties relating to these offences.
For an offence to be proven, it must be prosecuted in a court of law. It is the court that decides whether to impose a penalty, and the amount of any penalty.
If there is information that suggests a student, education provider or third party has committed an offence, inform your manager.

chunks.title: Offences and penalties — student allowance
chunks.text: A student, education provider or other third party commits an offence, and is liable to a penalty, fine or imprisonment under the Education and Training Act 2020 in the following circumstances.

chunks.title: Student offences and penalties — student allowance
chunks.text: As part of an application and when subsequently providing information If a student: - knowingly makes a false or misleading statement in an application or - knowingly makes a false or misleading statement in a notification of a change of their circumstances that materially affects or may affect their entitlement to a Student Allowance or rate of entitlement to a Student Allowance or - wilfully fails to notify MSD of any change in their circumstances that materially affects or may affect their entitlement to Student Allowance or the rate of Student Allowance they receive they commit an offence and are liable to a term of imprisonment (not exceeding 12 months) or a fine (not exceeding $5,000). Charges must be filed within 12 months of the date on which MSD becomes aware of the offence. During an investigation If a student when asked a question, or when they are required to provide information or documents necessary to establish entitlement: - knowingly makes a false or misleading statement or - knowingly makes a statement from which any material matter has been omitted or - knowingly provides any false or misleading paper, document, or record or - knowingly provides a paper, document, or record from which any material matter has been omitted or - refuses to answer a question during an investigation they commit an offence and are liable to a fine not exceeding $2,000. Charges must be filed within 12 months of the date on which MSD becomes aware of the offence.

chunks.title: Education provider offences and penalties — student allowance
chunks.text: if an education provider, when required to provide information necessary to establish entitlement, intentionally: - makes a false or misleading statement or - makes a statement from which any material matter has been omitted or - provides a false or misleading paper, document, or record or - provides a paper, document, or record from which any material matter has been omitted or - fails or refuses to provide requested information as soon as possible after a time requested by us they commit an offence and are liable to a fine not exceeding $5,000 (or when the offence is a continuing one, a fine not exceeding $500 for each day the offence continues). For offences committed on or after 1 August 2020, charges must be filed within 12 months of the date on which MSD becomes aware of the offence. For offences committed before 1 August 2020, charges must be laid within 6 months after the date on which the offence was committed.

chunks.title: Additional offences and penalties for private training establishments — student allowance
chunks.text: If a private training establishment fails, without reasonable excuse, to: - keep accurate enrolment and academic records or - ensure that the enrolment records are readily available, upon request, to MSD, among others they commit an offence and are liable to a fine not exceeding $10,000. Charges must be filed within 12 months after the date on which the offence was committed. The provisions covering these offences and penalties are the responsibility of the New Zealand Qualifications Authority.

chunks.title: Third party offences and penalties — student allowance
chunks.text: During the course of an investigation, MSD may ask a third party questions. They must answer these questions. When they refuse to answer a question, they commit an offence and are liable to a fine not exceeding $2,000. Charges must be filed within 12 months of the date on which MSD becomes aware of the offence.

chunks.title: Suspicion of offence — student allowance
chunks.text: If there is information that suggests a student, education provider or third party has committed an offence as outlined above, you should inform your manager.

chunks.title: Parental income test — student allowance
chunks.text: For students under 24 without children, the rate of Student Allowance is normally subject to both their parents' income. The 'one parent application' is for situations where the student is considered to be 'independent' from one parent, and therefore only the income of the other parent will be assessed. A one parent application can only be approved where the two parents are not living together. A one parent application should generally not be approved if: - the parent states they have a new partner or - the parent is not the only person responsible for the student's well-being or financial support In these cases, you need to determine whether the other person should be considered to be a 'parent'. If the new partner states that they do not support the student, this does not exclude the new partner's income from the parental income test, as refusal to provide support is not by itself a reason to exclude them.

chunks.title: Exercise of discretion — student allowance
chunks.text: A decision to grant a One Parent Application involves the exercise of discretion to make an entitlement decision based on the purpose and intent of the regulation, the limitations of the wording of the regulation, and the facts of the particular situation.

chunks.title: Criteria — student allowance
chunks.text: A student may have only one parent's income assessed if the parents are not living together and the student is considered to be 'independent' of the other parent. A student will only be considered to be 'independent' from the other parent if: - the student is estranged from that other parent to the extent that contact now would have a detrimental psychological effect on either the student or the parent - the student is or has been subject to severe mental cruelty by their parent or - the other parent (or their spouse) has physically or sexually abused the student or - the other parent is serving a sentence of imprisonment or is otherwise remanded or detained in a prison and therefore is unable to be responsible for the student or contribute towards the student's support or - the other parent is under an inpatient order under the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992, and therefore is unable to be responsible for the student or contribute towards the student's support or - by reasons of other special circumstances the relationship has broken down to such an extent that the student should be considered independent from the other parent If only one parent is living or one parent's whereabouts are unknown, e.g. one parent is in a "politically unstable" country and no contact or financial support is possible, then a one parent application can be approved. A one parent application form must be completed in addition to a Student Allowance application form. If a one parent application is approved, the parental income assessment will usually remain in place for at least that period of study. If however, circumstances change before the start of the student's course so that the circumstances under which the one parent application was approved no longer apply, then the application must be reassessed. The following situations do not demonstrate a student's 'independence' from a parent: - the parent is overseas - the refusal of the parent to provide financial support for the student - Relationship Property Settlements where it has been agreed that one parent is not responsible for financially supporting the student

chunks.title: Does an Independent Circumstances Allowance need to be considered? — student allowance
chunks.text: It is important to consider entitlement to a Student Allowance irrespective of what is actually applied for, as an application may not reflect the actual entitlement that exists, depending on the understanding of the applicant. Therefore, when assessing a one parent application, it may become apparent that it would be more appropriate to test the student's eligibility to an Independent Circumstances Allowance given the student's circumstances.

chunks.title: Other eligibility and entitlement criteria still relevant — student allowance
chunks.text: Students applying for a Student Allowance under a one parent application must still meet the standard eligibility and entitlement criteria for a Student Allowance.

chunks.title: Continuation of a 'one parent' situation — student allowance
chunks.text: If a student has previously had a 'one parent' application approved, they can effectively apply for their approval to be 'continued'. This means, their personal situation does not have to be fully verified as long as the student declares and confirms that their circumstances have not changed. However, if a student indicates that their circumstances have changed you will need to review their continued eligibility and make a new assessment.

chunks.title: Parents have no right of review — student allowance
chunks.text: Third parties, including a parent, do not have a right of review in relation to a 'one parent' application. The application is the student's application. MSD does not have the authority or right to disclose to a third party, including a parent, any matters relating to an application - unless the student has authorised it. If a third party, including a parent, wishes to act on behalf of a student then they must become an agent for the student. An agent's powers may be limited to a specific issue, for example to assist with a Review of Decision application. If a third party applies to act on behalf of a student in relation to their one parent application, MSD needs to ensure they are not acting in place of a second parent for the student.

chunks.title: Getting a benefit or pension — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Getting a benefit or pension
If a student or their partner are getting any of the following benefits they are not eligible to get a Student Allowance.
- Emergency Benefit
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance
- Jobseeker Support
- New Zealand Superannuation
- Sole Parent Support
- Supported Living Payment
- Veterans Pension
- Young Parent Payment
- Youth Payment
If a student has a partner but they are not in a recognised relationship, the partner of the student may qualify and get a benefit in their own right. For benefit purposes the student's Student Allowance will be counted as income against the partner's benefit.
For more information see:
- Student with a partner
## Other government study assistance
Students may not be granted a Student Allowance if they receive a bursary, scholarship, or award (or similar) from money appropriated by Parliament for study at a secondary school or a tertiary provider, without our approval.
There is discretion to award a Student Allowance despite a student being in receipt of a bursary, scholarship or award (or similar), subject to any conditions that may be determined in any particular case or class of case.
Students may receive a Student Allowance despite receiving other government study assistance on the condition that, the amount of that Allowance and the term for which it is payable may be less than the student would otherwise receive.
If you are unsure about a particular case or scenario, seek further advice from your manager.
Medical Trainee Intern Grant
The Medical Trainee Intern Grant (TIG) is a stipend payable to domestic sixth-year medical trainee interns. The grant is paid to the University of Auckland and the University of Otago by the Tertiary Education Commission, who then pay it to eligible sixth-year medical students.
The grant is paid to students in two ways. Most students will receive their grant in monthly instalments during the year. Those eligible students who study medicine after having completed a degree (graduate entry students), can receive their grant in a lump sum payment.
For more information on graduate entry students see:
- Student Loans The 7 EFTS lifetime limit
The Medical Trainee Intern Grant is not a bursary, scholarship or award for the purposes of the other government study assistance provision set out in Regulation 14.
It is personal income, but not a scholarship, for Student Allowances, except when it is used to pay fees or course-related costs.

chunks.title: Overseas income — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Overseas income
If parents receive income that was not subject to tax in New Zealand, this income must be converted to New Zealand currency before it can be used in the parental income test to determine eligibility for Student Allowances.
## New Zealand currency
The Cook Islands, Niue, and the Tokelau Islands use New Zealand currency.
Islands that fall into these groups are:
Cook Islands
Aitutaki, Atiu, Mangaia, Manihiki, Manuae, Ma'uke, Mitiaro, Nassau, Palmerston Island, Penrhyn Island, Pukapuka, Rakahanga, Rarotonga, Suwarrow, Takutea
Niue
Tokelau Islands
Atafu, Fakaofo, Nukunonu
## Converting overseas currency
For information and guidance on converting overseas currency to New Zealand dollars refer to the relevant training material.

chunks.title: Overseas study - Accommodation Benefit — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Overseas study - Accommodation Benefit
Eligible students who are studying overseas get the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit for the New Zealand location of their education provider.
Example
Anastasia attends University of Auckland and gets the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit for Auckland.
Anastasia is currently on a student exchange, studying in France for 1 year and is eligible to get her Student Allowance while she is away. Anastasia gets the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit for Auckland during her overseas study period.

chunks.title: Paid practical work — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Paid practical work
Students who undertake paid employment, which is recognised as fulfilling part of the requirements of their programme (known as paid practical work), are not entitled to any Student Allowance payments during the period of paid employment.

chunks.title: The parental income test — student allowance
chunks.text:
## The parental income test
Entitlement to Student Allowances for students who are under 24 years old with no supported children, is assessed on their parents' income.
Parental income is assessed over the relevant tax year.
## Definition
Parental income is the income that the parents' of a student have access to in order to support themselves and their family.
In Budget 2010, the Government made a number of decisions designed to improve the integrity of the social assistance system.
This included expanding the 'taxable income' definition used for the parental income test for Student Allowances to align with the definition of Family Scheme Income in the Income Tax Act 2007 (with some differences, parental income does not include Child Support payments, amounts derived by dependent children, or foreign sourced income for a parent's partner).
This definition of parental income for Student Allowances purposes applies to study starting on or after 1 January 2012.
For information on types of income included as parental income see:
- Income that is parental income
For information on types of income not included as parental income see:
- Income that is not parental income
## Parental income information is confidential
Parental income information belongs to the parents, not to the student. Some parents do not want the student to know any details of their income.

chunks.title: Parents living in separate households — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Parents living in separate households
When the student's parents are living in separate households (either in New Zealand or overseas) the parents' total combined income can be reduced by $3,400. This reduction takes into account the extra costs these parents have running two separate households.
The 'separate households' reduction is in addition to the reduction for parents supporting other students.
Living in separate households means living at different addresses for the majority of the week.
Note the $3,400 deduction can only be considered where a student has two parents that are being parentally income tested.

chunks.title: Parents supporting other dependent students — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Parents supporting other dependent students
For the purposes of the parental income test, there is a provision that where one or both of the parents of a student, who has applied for a Student Allowance, has more than one dependent student, the parent's combined income is reduced by $7,000 for each additional dependent student.
## Definition of dependent student
The additional dependent student must:
- be a child of the parent(s) (this includes a step-child or a relationship where the parent has an on-going responsibility for that child's well-being and financial support) and
be a child of the parent(s) (this includes a step-child or a relationship where the parent has an on-going responsibility for that child's well-being and financial support) and
- the student must not be younger than 16 on 31 December in the year prior to the application and not older than 23 on 1 January in the year of the application and
the student must not be younger than 16 on 31 December in the year prior to the application and not older than 23 on 1 January in the year of the application and
- be attending a full-time course at a tertiary provider or secondary school and
be attending a full-time course at a tertiary provider or secondary school and
- not be studying overseas unless they are undertaking a recognised exchange programme and
- not have been awarded an Independent Circumstances Allowance and
- be financially supported by the parent(s) who must not be receiving an Unsupported Childs Benefit or Orphans Benefit for the student
Note to be attending a full-time course at a tertiary provider or secondary school means they are enrolled, whether or not classes have commenced for the year.
## Additional dependent student is no longer a full-time student
If an additional dependent student has a change in circumstances after the parental income adjustment has been made, and they are no longer a full-time student, the parental income adjustment remains at the initially assessed level for the rest of the application period. It does not need to be reassessed.
## Separated parents
A parent can include an additional dependent student who is living separately with another parent if the criteria are met.

chunks.title: Students under 24 with no children — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Students under 24 with no children
Students who are under 24, with no children, who are getting a benefit as part of a couple, can apply for a Student Allowance in their own right. If eligible and entitled the student will be granted a Student Allowance at a single rate. This is because they are not in a recognised relationship for Student Allowance purposes
Their student's partner may still be eligible to get a benefit.
The Student Allowance is charged against the half married rate of benefit payable to the partner.
The implications of getting a Student Allowance must be discussed with the couple.
## Student in a recognised relationship
There is no provision to pay a 'half-couple' rate of Student Allowance.
Therefore, a student in a recognised relationship for Student Allowance purposes, is not eligible for a Student Allowance if their partner is getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension.
## Student under 24 with children
Students who are under 24, with children, who are getting a benefit as part of a couple, can apply for a Student Allowance, as part of a couple in a recognised relationship for Student Allowance purposes.
If the partner is a not a student, and not eligible and entitled to a Student Allowance in their own right they will be included in the student's couple rate of Student Allowance.
The implications of getting a Student Allowance must be discussed with the couple.
## Students and partner 24 and over
Students who are over 24, who are getting a benefit paid as a partner can apply for a Student Allowance, as part of a couple in a recognised relationship for Student Allowance purposes.
If the partner is a not a student, and not eligible and entitled to a Student Allowance in their own right, they will be included in the student's couple rate of Student Allowance.
The implications of getting a Student Allowance must be discussed with the couple.

chunks.title: Partner's income — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Partner's income
The definition of partner's income, is the same as the definition of personal income for Student Allowance purposes.
A student's partner is required to advise StudyLink of any income they get that may affect the student's entitlement to a Student Allowance.
## Common types of income
The following link provides advice on the inclusion of the more common types of income for Student Allowances.
There may be other types of 'personal income' that also need to be included.
- Income that is personal income

chunks.title: Partner studying — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Partner studying
If a student's partner is studying, the partner must complete their own Student Allowance application.
Even if the partner states that they do not study more than half of a full-time course or that they are not studying a recognised programme, it is important to check the EFTS value of the partner's enrolment.
The EFTS value of the partner's enrolment will determine the student's allowance rate, or if each student can establish their own entitlement to a Student Allowance. Where a course has no EFTS value other forms of determining the quantity of study will need to be undertaken.
Any consequences for payment as a result of a change in eligibility or entitlement must be discussed with the couple.

chunks.title: First Year payments — student allowance
chunks.text:
## First Year payments
The top performing students are invited to attend a ceremony in Wellington, where they are presented with their award by the Governor General.
All students receive their payments directly into their nominated bank account. Payments that are ready to be made are released on the day after the ceremony.
The date of the awards ceremony (and therefore the date the awards will be paid) is usually in May each year. The date is dependant on the availability of the Governor General, who presides over the ceremony.
## Subsequent year payments
StudyLink will confirm with the student's education provider that the student is continuing to study an approved programme.
When StudyLink receives these study details, the award payment will be paid into the student's nominated bank account. The earliest that this payment can occur is 1 January each year.

chunks.title: Entitlement — student allowance
chunks.text: Payment commences from the later of: - the beginning of the week in which a student starts studying or - the beginning of the week of the date of application A student's study start date is the later of either the date the student's course of study commenced or the date they commenced the course. A student's study end date is the last date the student is enrolled in a course of study. As long as a student maintains eligibility and entitlement, payments will continue through to the later of: - the end of the week in which either the work for the course of study ceases or - the final examination is held A student is entitled to payment for the whole week, starting on Monday, through to and including Sunday, except in relation to the initial payment of an increase in the rate that occurs as a result of the Annual General Adjustment (AGA). When 1 April falls on a day other than Monday, the increase in rate will apply from the day on which 1 April falls (from 1 April 2018). Where an Accommodation Benefit is payable in addition to the initial payment of an increase in Student Allowance rate as a result of the AGA, and there is an increase in the Accommodation Benefit payable, the increase in the rate will also apply from the day on which 1 April falls, if this is not a Monday. For more information on the AGA see: - Legal framework - Student Allowances Scheme If a student is receiving a main benefit immediately before starting study, their benefit eligibility ceases from the beginning of the week they became eligible for a Student Allowance. Any benefit payments made for any period they were studying and eligible for a Student Allowance (and therefore not eligible for a benefit) need to be recovered. For more information see: - Applications

chunks.title: Pay day — student allowance
chunks.text: Student Allowances are paid weekly on Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. The day is allocated based on a student's birth month. Payments are made in arrears and by direct credit.

chunks.title: Rates — student allowance
chunks.text: The types and rates of Student Allowance payable vary according to a student's age, living situation, marital status and whether they have any supported children. For the rates of Student Allowance see:

chunks.title: Minimum payment — student allowance
chunks.text: The minimum weekly amount payable is $2.00 per week. Student Allowances cannot be paid if the rate payable is less than $2.00 per week (including any Accommodation Benefit).

chunks.title: Bank account — student allowance
chunks.text: Student Allowances are paid into the student's nominated bank account. The account will normally be in the name of the student (single or joint account). However, Student Allowances can also be paid into an account that is not in the name of the student.

chunks.title: Performance requirement - passing more than half — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Performance requirement - passing more than half
Access to a Student Allowance must be suspended if a student failed to pass the equivalent of more than half the work of a full-time course in the last tertiary course they received a Student Allowance for.
Where the failure was for reasons beyond the student's control, their access to a Student Allowance may not be suspended.
A limited full-time student only needs to pass more than half of the course that they were undertaking.
The 'passing more than half' requirement does not apply to secondary school study.

chunks.title: Person acting in place of a parent — student allowance
chunks.text: A person is acting in place of a parent if they have financial responsibility for the student. This can include but is not limited to: - whāngai and other cultural adoption carers - relatives e.g. grandparents - caregivers and legal guardians not excluded from the definition of a parent

chunks.title: Factors to consider — student allowance
chunks.text: MSD must consider a range of factors when deciding if a person is acting in place of a parent. This includes: - whether the person provides, or has provided, financial support to the student - whether the person made a deliberate decision to take on financial support of the student, including whether they intended to provide for basic needs until the student was independent, or intended to fully support the student including their future financial decisions e.g. tertiary study - whether the person provides accommodation to the student and if so, whether the student must pay for it, and whether the person would continue to provide it if the student was unable to pay - whether the person would provide support to the student if they had financial or other problems - whether the person has, or had, legal guardianship of the student Generally there won't be one single factor that means a person is or isn't acting in place of a parent of the student. MSD must consider the person's full situation when making this decision.

chunks.title: Financial support — student allowance
chunks.text: Students may get a range of financial support from different people throughout their study for various reasons. This could include payments made towards the student’s day to day living. When considering whether a person is acting in place of a parent of the student, determine the extent, nature and frequency of any financial support first. For example: - whether it is or was temporary or long term - whether the student is expected to repay it Financial support provided in a parental type relationship would generally be regular ongoing financial support that the student is not required to repay. One off payments e.g. a gift of money or a loan to buy a luxury item would not generally be considered financial support for this purpose.

chunks.title: Non-financial support — student allowance
chunks.text: There may be other factors not outlined above that are relevant to whether a person is acting in place of a parent such as non-financial support that relates to family life in general. In these cases, financial support must be the primary focus.

chunks.title: People who are not parents — student allowance
chunks.text: A person is not acting in place of a parent if they are or were a caregiver or legal guardian of the student who is: - getting or has received a Foster Care Allowance, Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for the student - providing or has provided a transition support living arrangement for the student under section 386AAD of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989

chunks.title: Definition — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Definition
A student may postpone their course without suspending their entitlement to Student Allowances. The decision to postpone a course rests with individual tertiary education providers.
This means that it is up to each education provider to decide whether the postponement procedures can be exercised within the limits of their programme structures. Based on information from the education provider, StudyLink will make a decision regarding Student Allowance entitlement.
## Situations where postponement may be considered
Students may apply to postpone completion of their course provided that they ceased studying at a recognised interval that is the end of a semester or term in the academic year of their provider.
There is no provision (under the regulations) for students to postpone retrospectively. In other words, applications should only be considered when the student actually ceases study.
## Approval for postponement will be subject to
- the student having successfully completed (by examination or assessment) more than half of the work of their full-time course when they postponed. For example, at the end of the first term this would equal more than one half of that term's work. At the end of the second term it would equal more than one half of the work of the 2 terms and
- it being possible for the student to resume study at approximately the same point at a subsequent time
## Effect on 92/120/200-week limit
The period of study before study was postponed and the period after it recommenced count as 1 year of the student's 92/120/200 week entitlement, or the normal number of weeks for a course if less than 1 year.

chunks.title: Previous study assistance — student allowance
chunks.text: If a student received a Student Allowance for tertiary study before 1 January 1999 (when MSD took over the delivery of Student Allowances), then this is included in the 120/200 week limit. The lifetime limit was part of the Student Allowances Scheme from its inception in 1992. Under the previous 1991 Regulations the limit was 5 years. When the Regulations were re-written in 1998, the limit of 5 years was replaced with the 200 week limit. For study before 1 January 1999, the following rules are used to convert years of study into weeks of study: - any course of 37 weeks or more must be treated as 40 weeks - any course of less than 37 weeks is treated as the number of actual weeks the student was paid the allowance The 120 week limit for those aged 40 and over was introduced for study starting on or after 1 January 2014. Other Government assistance received by the student currently or in previous years may also count towards the 120/200 weeks.

chunks.title: Other Government study assistance — student allowance
chunks.text: Other study assistance provided by the government, in the form of allowances or salary for full-time tertiary study, may also count towards the 120/200 weeks, including: All Public Service, Railways, and Post Office full-time study awards before 1966 National Library Studentship Armed Forces Officer Cadetship Nursing Bursary Bilateral Aid (Colombo Plan) Occupational Therapy Bursary Boarding Bursary Ordinary National Bursary Bursary in Agriculture Pharmacy Bursary Bursary in Architecture Physiotherapy Bursary (at a Polytechnic) Bursary in Engineering Post Primary or Secondary Teacher Bursary Bursary in Fine Arts Post Primary or Secondary Teacher Studentship (old conditions) Bursary in Home Science Public Service, Railways and Post Office full-time study awards after 1965 (full or part salary) Bursary in Science Rehabilitation Bursary (old scheme) Dental Bursary Rural-Field Cadetship Dietetic Bursary Social Science Bursary Fees and Allowances Bursary Standard Tertiary Bursary Full-time Bursary Teachers College Studentship Guidance Counsellor Study Award Teachers Study Award Iwi Transition Awards Teachers University Studentship Māori or Polynesian Scholarship Technical Institute Bursary Medical Bursary Tertiary Study Grant Mining Bursary War Bursary National Boarding Bursary If, in any particular case, it is unclear whether and/or how to include other government assistance in a student's maximum entitlement, contact the Operational Policy and Practice Team in National Office.

chunks.title: Programmes not recognised — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Programmes not recognised
To be eligible for a Student Allowance a student must meet a number of criteria. One requirement is that the student must be studying a full-time recognised programme at an approved tertiary provider or secondary school.
## Postgraduate qualifications
For study starting on or after 1 January 2013, Student Allowance eligibility for all NZQF (New Zealand Qualifications Framework) level 8 and above postgraduate certificates, diplomas, master's degrees, and doctorates was removed.
All Bachelor degrees with Honours retained eligibility, as they are considered to be an undergraduate qualification for the purposes of this policy.
## Transitional provision until December 2013
Students studying NZQF level 8 and above postgraduate certificates, diplomas, master's degrees and doctorates, who were in a recognised relationship and/or had a supported child or supported children and who also:
- had an allowance approved for study at NZQF level 8 or above in 2012 and
- were continuing to study the same qualification in 2013 and
- retained eligibility in all other respects
were able to continue to be eligible for a Student Allowance until 31 December 2013.
These (grand-parented) students lost their entitlement to this "transitional provision" if they:
- ceased to be in a recognised relationship or
- ceased to have a supported child or supported children or
- reached their 200 week entitlement limit (unless they are eligible for an extension)
## Home schooling
Home education, sometimes called home schooling, is an option in New Zealand for parents or caregivers who are approved by their local Ministry of Education office.
Approved home educators are eligible for the home education supervision allowance through the Ministry of Education.
Home schooling is not included in the definition of a secondary school for Student Allowance purposes. Students who are home schooled are not eligible for a Student Allowance.
For more information see:
- Ministry of Education Home education (homeschooling)
## Other government programmes
Clients who are engaged in employment and training opportunities, and might be getting a main benefit, are not considered to be studying a recognised programme for Student Allowance purposes. These clients are not eligible for a Student Allowance. See:
- Training and work experience

chunks.title: Protected person — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Protected person
A protected person is a person recognised under sections 130 and 131 of the Immigration Act 2009 when there are substantial grounds for believing they would be in danger of:
- being tortured if deported from New Zealand or
- arbitrary deprivation of life or cruel treatment if deported from New Zealand.
Once they are granted protected person status, a protected person needs to apply for a residence class visa to be entitled to reside indefinitely in New Zealand.
They meet the residency criteria for a Student Allowance from the date they are granted a residence class visa.
However, for study starting on or after 1 May 2022, a protected person meets the residency criteria for a Student Allowance from the date they are granted protected person status. They are not required to have a residence class visa, but are required to hold a valid temporary entry class visa.

chunks.title: Reasons beyond student's control — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Reasons beyond student's control
Reasons beyond the student's control means the student should not have any choice or influence on the situation.
Reasons include:
- medical, social or psychological reasons which affected the student's ability to carry out their studiesIn cases of continuing illness (for example psychological problems), or where the student is seeking continuation for a second or subsequent time, evidence should also be obtained that the student is now capable of undertaking and successfully completing full-time study.
- family breakdown or illness in the family
- civil emergency such as flooding, earthquake or similar
- course cancellation - where the education provider has cancelled or changed the course or withdrawn tuition
Note financial hardship alone is not normally an acceptable reason.
Students who believe that their situation was beyond their control will need to supply a written statement and, in most situations, evidence of their circumstances (such as a medical certificate, letter from a counsellor or letter from their education provider).

chunks.title: Reassessing parental income — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Reassessing parental income
Entitlement to Student Allowances for students who are under 24 years old with no supported children is assessed on their parents' income.
If, after the approval of a Student Allowance, but during the student's course of study, there is a reduction of at least 25% in the parents combined income, the parental income amount can be reassessed.
Note when parental income has increased a reassessment is not required.
## Calculation
The parents' income must reduce by a minimum of 25% to qualify for a reassessment.
The reduction is the difference between the most recently approved parental income assessment (either the original assessment, or, if applicable, the most recently approved reassessment) and the new reduced income assessment.
A Reassessment of Parental Income application can include a confirmed change that is yet to occur.
If the parents income reduces further, then another Reassessment of Parental Income can occur if the income decreases by at least 25%.
For more information see:
## Date of new rate of Student Allowance
The new rate of Student Allowance will apply from the date the reduction in parental income occurs.
## Timeframe for receiving an application
Applications for the Reassessment of Parental income must be received by the end of the period of study for which the Student Allowance has been applied for, unless special circumstances exist.
Note the use of discretion is required when determining whether special circumstances exist.
## Siblings also getting a Student Allowance
When the student has one or more siblings also getting a Student Allowance with the same nominated parents, a parental income reassessment also needs to be completed for the siblings.

chunks.title: Recognised Long Programmes — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Recognised Long Programmes
For study starting on or after 1 January 2013, the provision for extensions to the 200 week limit for Recognised Long Programmes was removed from the Student Allowances Regulations 1998.
Students who had received approval for a Recognised Long Programme extension before 1 January 2013, retained their eligibility to the extension after 1 January 2013.
A student could not receive an extension beyond the 200 week limit if they have also received a Student Allowance for a programme other than the Recognised Long Programme.
Recognised Long Programmes included programmes and combinations of qualifications that required more than 200 weeks to complete. For example; a Bachelor of Veterinary Science required 219 weeks of study, or a combination of Bachelor/Master of Social Work required up to 250 weeks of study.
In addition, an individual student could seek approval from the Ministry of Education for approval of their course as an equivalent Long Programme.
Recognised Long Programmes were approved by the Minister for Tertiary Education, on the recommendation of the Tertiary Education Commission.

chunks.title: Eligibility — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Eligibility
To be eligible for a Student Allowance, a student must be enrolled and accepted into an approved course of study which leads to the completion of a recognised programme.
The Tertiary Education Commission is responsible for the approval of recognised programmes for Student Allowance purposes.
Approved programmes may include conjoint or concurrent study.
Students enrolled in full-time study can apply for a Student Allowance if the course is a recognised programme at the following education providers:
- an approved tertiary education provider
- secondary school
Students undertaking a Youth Guarantee course or programme will be eligible for a Student Allowance if the course is either approved as a Recognised Programme, or leads to the completion of a Recognised Programme, and they meet all other eligibility and entitlement criteria.
For more information see:
- Programmes not recognised
## Removal of programme recognition
From time to time the Tertiary Education Commission reviews education providers funding. As part of that process, the approval of the provider and/or their programmes for Student Allowance purposes are also considered.
When a review results in a provider having their approval for Student Allowances purposes removed (i.e. recognised programme approval is withdrawn), payments of Student Allowances to students undertaking programmes where approval has been withdrawn are to be suspended from the first available date.
Payments are to be reinstated if the approval is reinstated before the end of the same academic year, or earlier at the discretion of StudyLink.
In practice this means a decision would need to be made for each programme of study, when and if reinstatement of suspended Student Allowances payments would occur. A decision would be made by StudyLink in conjunction with TEC and other relevant agencies and advised to staff.
In addition, StudyLink has the discretion to not suspend Student Allowance payments in any individual case, depending on the circumstances of the student, including the circumstances of the withdrawal of programme approval.
This broad discretion needs to be exercised carefully to ensure consistency of approach. Any cases that arise where you consider this discretion might be exercised should be referred to your manager for consideration alongside other known cases and within the context of the decision by TEC to withdraw programme approval.

chunks.title: Recognised relationship changes — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Recognised relationship changes
A number of changes in circumstances can lead to a change in whether, a couple is in a recognised relationship for Student Allowances.
## Student aged 16-23 with a supported child
If a couple cease to have a supported child in their care, this may affect their relationship status for Student Allowances.
If one or both of the partners is under 24 and there is no other child in their care, they will no longer be considered to be in a recognised relationship for Student Allowances.
## Student or partner turns 24
If the student or their partner turns 24, and their partner is 24 or over, they must have their entitlement to a Student Allowance reassessed, because the student is no longer entitled to a single rate of Student Allowance.
Any partner income needs to be included from the date the student turns 24, so that the appropriate rate of Student Allowance is paid.
## Child comes into the care of a student
If a student who is single for Student Allowance purposes has a child come into their care (a supported child), they must have their entitlement to a Student Allowance reassessed because the rate of Student Allowance that they are entitled to will change to either a 'single student with supported child' or a 'couple with supported child' rate.
If the student has a partner and is under 24 years old at the time that the child comes into care, they are no longer treated as single but are in a recognised relationship for Student Allowance purposes.
They need to be assessed as a couple to determine the correct rate of Student Allowance to be paid.
## Entitlement changes
Any entitlement change generally occurs from the Monday of the week the change in circumstances occurs.
MSD has discretion to make the change from a later date, if in all the circumstances it would be reasonable to do so.

chunks.title: Redundancy payments — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Redundancy payments
Redundancy payments are treated as personal income for Student Allowance purposes and should be included as income in the week that they are received.

chunks.title: Mandate or quota refugees — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Mandate or quota refugees
Refugees who come to New Zealand under the refugee quota system are known as mandate or quota refugees.
They are normally granted a residence class visa automatically with their refugee status, before their arrival in New Zealand. They are entitled to reside indefinitely in New Zealand from the date they are granted that visa.
They meet the residency criteria for a Student Allowance from the date they are granted a residence class visa.
## Convention or asylum refugees
Refugees who are granted refugee status under the Refugee Convention are known as convention or asylum refugees. They apply for refugee status under the Immigration Act 2009 after they have arrived in New Zealand.
Once they are granted refugee status, they need to apply for a residence class visa to be entitled to reside indefinitely in New Zealand.
They meet the residency criteria for a Student Allowance from the date they are granted a residence class visa.
However, for study starting on or after 1 May 2022, a student who has refugee status meets the residency criteria for a Student Allowance from the date they are granted refugee status under the Immigration Act 2009. They are not required to hold a residence class visa, but are required to hold a valid temporary entry class visa.

chunks.title: Refund of payments after withdrawal — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Refund of payments after withdrawal
Generally, any study for which a student receives a Student Allowance is included in the count towards their 120/200 week (for tertiary study) or 92 week (for secondary study) maximum entitlement.
## Criteria for exclusion of payments received from the maximum entitlement
A student is deemed not to have received any Student Allowance payments, and therefore will not have the weeks for which they received a Student Allowance counted towards the 120/200 week or 92 week maximum entitlement, if they:
- pay back the total after-tax amount of Student Allowance payments and
- make that payment within 12 months of the start of the course (where the course duration was one full academic year), or before the end of the course in every other case and
- officially withdraw from the course before the final examination period begins
## Repayment by instalment
Repayment of any Student Allowance payments received can be made by instalment, as long as the requirements outlined above are met. Any agreement to repay by instalment must be confirmed by a signed written agreement that stipulates all the conditions of the agreement and the consequences of any failure to meet those conditions.
Once a signed written agreement is in place, a student is deemed to have met the repayment criteria set out above.
## Failure to meet the repayment criteria
If a student fails to repay all the Student Allowances payments received within the required timeframe, then all assistance received by them to the nearest week, must be included in their 92/120/200 week maximum entitlement, and any money they have refunded must be returned to them.
However, any minor or inconsequential failure to meet the required repayment timeframe can be accepted, if in all the circumstances it would be reasonable to do so.
## Passing more than half requirement
A tertiary student who meets the criteria outlined above does not need to meet the 'passing more than half' requirements for that course of study, as they are deemed not to have received those Student Allowance payments.
A tertiary student who withdraws from part of a course in any year, and remains enrolled in study on a part-time basis, and who meets the criteria outlined above, does not need to meet the ‘passing more than half’ requirements for that course of study, as they are deemed not to have received those Student Allowance payments.

chunks.title: Reinstatement — student allowance
chunks.text: When a student has failed to pass more than half the work of a full-time tertiary course, their entitlement may be reinstated if they meet the reinstatement criteria.

chunks.title: Criteria — student allowance
chunks.text: A student whose Student Allowance is suspended for failing to pass more than half the work of the last tertiary course they received an allowance for, may have their entitlement reinstated if, since the suspension, they pass more than half the work of a Student Allowance approved full-time course, at their own expense (for example, using a Student Loan).

chunks.title: Part-year or full-year study — student allowance
chunks.text: It does not matter whether the student is enrolled in a part-year or full-year course, as long as they pass more than half of the work of a Student Allowance approved full-time course, their entitlement can be reinstated. For example a student: - enrolled part-time over a full year, (not eligible for Limited full-time) needs to pass at least 0.4001 EFTS or - enrolled part-time on a 12 week course needs to pass at least 0.15001 EFTS For more information about EFTS see: - Full-time tertiary

chunks.title: Semester-based study — student allowance
chunks.text: A student who passes more than half the work of a Student Allowance approved full-time course in the first semester, whether or not they are enrolled on a semester or full year basis, can use that study to reinstate their entitlement to a Student Allowance for the second semester. A standard full-time course in semester one is generally 15 weeks long. To reinstate their entitlement to a Student Allowance, they must pass at least 0.15001 EFTS of a 15 week first semester full-time course.

chunks.title: Study that is not semester-based — student allowance
chunks.text: A student who passes more than half the work of a Student Allowance approved full-time course in the first part of their study that is not semester based, can use that study to reinstate their entitlement to a Student Allowance for the later part of that study. The reinstatement calculation will depend on the length and EFTS value of their study, including any of its component parts, and determining at what point they passed more than half of a full-time course. For more information about EFTS see: - Full-time tertiary

chunks.title: Study overseas — student allowance
chunks.text: When a student has undertaken tertiary level study at an overseas tertiary provider, that study can be used for reinstatement purposes when the study is a recognised programme, or the New Zealand tertiary provider recognises that study as part of the student's recognised programme.

chunks.title: Course now 'recognised' since suspension — student allowance
chunks.text: A student may have passed more than half of a full-time course which was not recognised at the time as an approved course but has since been recognised for Student Allowance purposes. This situation needs to be considered on its merits. Seek advice if you are unsure.

chunks.title: Secondary school study — student allowance
chunks.text: A Student Allowance for tertiary study that has been suspended cannot be reinstated by the completion of any secondary school study.

chunks.title: Limited full-time study — student allowance
chunks.text: The reinstatement requirements also apply to Limited full-time students. Example A student is approved to study 0.2 EFTS Limited full-time. This student would need to pass more than half of the 0.2 EFTS (i.e. more than 0.1 EFTS) to have their Student Allowance entitlement reinstated.

chunks.title: Relationship changes — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Relationship changes
When it is unclear whether a recognised de facto relationship exists, it may be because the relationship has yet to reach the point where it can be categorised as a de facto relationship.
Relationships evolve, and therefore it is possible that a relationship exists but it is not yet a de facto relationship.
In addition, relationships cease or end. A marriage, civil union or a de facto relationship ceases when the relationship has genuinely ceased to exist.
A student who is married or in a civil union may be considered to be single when:
- they are estranged from their partner and
- they live apart from their partner
Also, when there are relationship difficulties, tensions or problems, there can be trial or temporary separations before the relationship finally ceases to exist.
When a relationship change does occur, consideration must be given to any eligibility or entitlement change that may have resulted from the relationship change.
## Entitlement changes
Any entitlement change generally occurs from the Monday of the week the relationship change occurred.
MSD has discretion to make the change from a later date, if in all the circumstances it would be reasonable to do so.

chunks.title: Assessable income — student allowance
chunks.text: Generally, the assessable income from a rental property is the difference between the actual rent the client receives and the allowable expenses.

chunks.title: Allowable expenses — student allowance
chunks.text: When someone has a rental property and you are determining income the following expenses are considered allowable income and can be deducted from the rental income: - interest payments on money borrowed for the purchase of the rental property, but not capital instalments for the reduction of mortgage - rates - house insurance - agent fees and commission if a property manager or agent is used - repairs and maintenance - other fees - for example, bank administration fees for the mortgage, tenancy agreement costs, any valuation required for mortgage purposes, accounting fees, etc When a client rents out part of their property, only expenses attributable to the rented portion of the home can be deducted. To determine the expenses for the portion of the home rented out, calculate the area of the rental portion as a percentage of the total home. The rental area is the area of the home that is used only by the tenant and does not include any common areas that are used by the client and tenant.

chunks.title: Depreciation — student allowance
chunks.text: Depreciation is an on-paper deduction for wear and tear on a fixed asset. It is usually claimed as part of an income tax return at the end of a financial year. Depreciation cannot be deducted to assess the net weekly income from properties to be treated as personal income for Student Allowance purposes. Please see below for more information about the costs that can be included for repairs and maintenance.

chunks.title: Essential repairs — student allowance
chunks.text: Repairs to existing essential services that may be considered allowable expenses include: - water - gas - power - sewerage services (including showers, toilets, sinks and the drains attached to them) Other repairs can be considered if they are essential to: - the structural stability of the house or property (repairs to buildings or sheds on the property that are not used for accommodation purposes are not to be considered) - wiring and light fittings - septic tanks (provided repairs have not been paid as a non-recoverable Special Needs Grant) - any repairs required to meet building regulations

chunks.title: Major appliance repairs — student allowance
chunks.text: Repairs to any major appliance that helps maintain the house in a habitable state can be included, such as: - gas or electric stove and - hot water cylinder The cost of repairs or replacement of household contents is not considered an allowable expense, for example: - microwaves - furnishings - fridges and - washing machines Note if the washing machine or fridge is included in the tenancy agreement, then repairs or replacement may be included. Repairs that are allowable expenses can only be included in the rental income assessment if the bills are incurred while the Student Allowance is being received.

chunks.title: Maintenance expenses — student allowance
chunks.text: Maintenance expenses that may be considered an allowable expense include any reasonable maintenance carried out on the house or grounds, which is necessary to prevent damage or substantial deterioration to the house. This may include but is not limited to: - clearing chimneys - replacing broken windows - removing trees (when necessary) - painting (internal and external) if required Painting expenses can be considered an allowable expense only if the costs are incurred while receiving a Student Allowance. Maintenance costs do not include such things as: - mowing the lawns - work carried out for cosmetic purposes
