chunks.title: Resuming grandparenting in the same study application period — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Resuming grandparenting in the same study application period
If a grandparented standard rate of Accommodation Benefit has been stopped, the grandparented rate may be resumed if it is within the same study application, and the student:
- has a dependent child enter and then leave their care or
- becomes eligible for a higher standard rate of Accommodation Benefit and then moves back to the Territorial Authority where they were previously getting the grandparented rate
## Student has a dependent child enter and then leave their care
Students who have a dependent child enter their care, will be transferred to the Sole Parent rate of Accommodation Benefit and their grandparented rate will stop.
If the dependent child leaves the student's care within the same study application, then the grandparented standard rate of Accommodation Benefit can be resumed for the remainder of the application period.
For more information see:
## Change in address for extramural students
If an extramural student gets a grandparented standard rate of Accommodation Benefit, a change of address may affect their grandparenting arrangements when they move to a Territorial Authority with a higher rate of Accommodation Benefit than the grandparented rate.
## Student Allowance has stopped due to excess income
Student Allowance is an income tested payment and the rate of allowance paid can depend on any personal income a student earns (and any income of a spouse, partner or parent).
If a student's income is more than the gross threshold per week, their Student Allowance will abate by the equivalent amount of income received over this figure until their entitlement reaches nil.
When Student Allowance stops, so does the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit.
When the student's weekly income goes under the income threshold again, Student Allowance will be re-started as well as any grandparented rate of Accommodation Benefit providing it is within the same study application period.
## Change in campus but same provider
An intramural student may have their grandparented rate end if they have a change in campus and are eligible for a higher rate at the new campus.
The grandparented rate can resume if the student returns to the campus in the Territorial Authority where they received the grandparented rate while they are under the current study application.

chunks.title: Retraining for employment in programmes of national interest — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Retraining for employment in programmes of national interest
For study starting on or after 1 January 2013, the provision for extensions to the 200 week limit for retraining for employment in programmes of national interest was removed from the Regulations.
Students who received approval for an extension to undertake retraining for employment in programmes of national interest for study before 1 January 2013 retained their eligibility to the extension after 1 January 2013.
The only programmes approved by Ministry of Education were teacher training (early childhood education, primary or secondary) that after completion would enable a student to register as a teacher.

chunks.title: Reviewing entitlement — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Reviewing entitlement
A student's entitlement to a Student Allowance may be reviewed at any time to determine if the student was or is entitled to receive any payments.
This may result in a Student Allowance payment being suspended, declined, or the rate of payment being varied.
This involves the use of discretion, including whether to review entitlement, and if a review is undertaken, from what date any change is made, and if applicable, whether a debt should be established.
When a review results in a change in payment, this will generally occur from the Monday of the week that the entitlement changed.
## Making the change from a later date
It may be appropriate to make the change from a later date if the circumstances suggest it would be reasonable to do so.
When a student's circumstances have changed, there may be a valid reason MSD was not notified of the change immediately.
This includes the death of a student or a family member.
## Payment of arrears
If it is determined that a student has not received their full entitlement, then any arrears owing must be paid to the student.
## Debt establishment
If it is determined that a student received a payment that they were not entitled to, the students' circumstances need to be considered and confirmed to determine if a debt should be established.
A debt should be established if all the facts confirm one or more payments have been received where there was no (or less) entitlement, and it would be reasonable, considering all the circumstances, to do so.
There may be circumstances where establishing a debt would not be appropriate, including when a student who is not entitled to a Student Allowance due to exhausting their 200 week entitlement, may gain access to Student Allowance payments due to the establishment of a debt.
For example, if a debt of $200 is created, it would result in the student being entitled to a further week of Student Allowance payment in the future.
Due to the small amount, and the fact that the student has already had use of the money, the cost of recovering the debt would be more than the cost of the debt itself.
If a decision is made to establish a debt, debt write-off should be considered before recovery commences.

chunks.title: Informal review of a decision — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Informal review of a decision
A student may not agree with or understand a decision that has been made on their application.
A decision is the outcome of an assessment of an application where eligibility and entitlement are determined.
An informal review of a decision is designed to both assist students to understand the basis or reason for any decision MSD have made, and provide us with an opportunity to re-check the decision.
An important part of this process involves confirming what specific aspect of the decision might be unclear or disputed and why.
MSD needs to be satisfied that the decision correctly reflects the student's circumstances, the applicable policy, and the law.
An initial informal review is an opportunity to identify and rectify any errors or mistakes that may have been made during the processing of a student's application.
If after completing an informal review, the student does not agree with a decision, they can seek a formal review of the decision.
For more information see:
## Formal review of a decision
There are two different types of formal reviews:
- Statutory review - this is a review of a decision set out in clause 5(1) of Schedule 10 of the Education and Training Act 2020. This provision sets out which decisions have statutory review rights, and subsequently statutory appeal rights, and the requirements that must be followed
- Administrative review - this is a review of decisions not covered by clause 5(1) of Schedule 10 of the Education and Training Act 2020. These decisions are reviewed using an administrative process that is consistent with the purpose and intent of the statutory review process.
All reviews must be conducted in a transparent way, i.e. carried out by an independent person who has had no prior involvement in the case, and follow the principles of natural justice. This involves:
- avoiding any suggestion of bias, whether actual or apparent, in both the decision-making process and by the decision-maker and
- ensuring the student receives a fair hearing, including: being advised of and having adequate opportunity to consider the reasons for the decisionhaving the opportunity to give their views and other relevant informationbeing able to ask any questions they may havereceiving full and complete answers to their questions
- being advised of and having adequate opportunity to consider the reasons for the decision
- having the opportunity to give their views and other relevant information
- being able to ask any questions they may have
- receiving full and complete answers to their questions

chunks.title: When a scholarship is personal income — student allowance
chunks.text:
## When a scholarship is personal income
Students may get an educational scholarship payment to help fund their study and associated costs. Scholarships are considered personal income for Student Allowance, unless they are specifically paid for tuition fees, or are exempt from the personal income test.
## Scholarships paid for tuition fees
Tuition fees are the fees a student must pay to the tertiary education provider for an enrolment in an approved programme. This includes tuition fees, examination fees and student levies.
Some scholarship agreements have an amount that is set aside for tuition fees, which the student must use to pay their fees. This amount is not personal income for Student Allowance. This is because the student cannot use that portion to support themselves or their family.
Any part of the scholarship paid to the student to use as they choose, or for costs other than tuition fees (e.g. course-related costs or general living costs), is included as personal income for Student Allowance.
When a scholarship agreement does not specify an amount to be paid for tuition fees, any part of the scholarship the student chooses to pay towards their tuition fees is still considered personal income for their Student Allowance.
## Scholarships exempt from the personal income test
The following scholarships are exempt from the income test and are not personal income:
- NZQA Scholarship Monetary Awards
- TeachNZ scholarships (except the living costs portion of the Career-Changer Scholarship)
- Tulī Takes Flight: Career changer scholarships
- Bonded Merit Scholarship (no longer available)
- Canterbury Earthquake Scholarships (no longer available)
- Step up Scholarship (no longer available)
## Charging scholarship income
When determining how to charge income from a scholarship, MSD must consider the student's situation using the following 2 principles:
- a scholarship paid in lump sums is charged weekly from the date the scholarship was awarded as this is the date the student became entitled to it
- a scholarship awarded for study in a particular year or years is charged for that study period
The following situations affect the way the 2 principles are applied:
- a scholarship awarded before or after the study year it relates to is charged from the date study starts, not from the date the award is made
- a scholarship awarded in instalments due to academic or study requirements is charged for the whole study period, not from the date the instalment is paid

chunks.title: Secondary students aged 16 or 17 years — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Secondary students aged 16 or 17 years
A secondary student aged 16 or 17 years old can qualify for a Student Allowance if they meet the standard Student Allowance eligibility criteria and:
- they have a partner and
- have a supported child
Note secondary school students aged 16 or 17 years cannot receive an Independent Circumstances Allowance, but may qualify for Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment.
For more information see:
- Completed year 13 or attained at level 3 NCEA, 42 credits or more
- Eligibility and Entitlement
- Secondary students aged 18 years and over
- Sole parents
- Students aged 16 -23 years
- Youth Service Young Parent Payment
- Youth Service Youth Payment

chunks.title: Secondary students aged 18 years and over — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Secondary students aged 18 years and over
A secondary student aged 18 years and over can qualify for a Student Allowance if they meet the standard Student Allowance eligibility criteria.
For more information see:
- Eligibility and Entitlement

chunks.title: Sole parent rate of Accommodation Benefit — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Sole parent rate of Accommodation Benefit
Eligible sole parents get the sole parent rate of Accommodation Benefit.
They are the same as the Accommodation Supplement rates payable to eligible recipients of Sole Parent Support. They are calculated in exactly the same way using the same policy and methodology.
The sole parent rate of Accommodation Benefit was first payable for study starting on or after 1 July 2015.
Sole parents who are not eligible for a sole parent rate of Accommodation Benefit, are not eligible for a standard rate of Accommodation Benefit.
## Overseas study
Eligible sole parent students who are studying overseas get the sole parent rate of Accommodation Benefit for the New Zealand location of their education provider.
## Extramural study
Eligible sole parent students who are studying extramurally get the sole parent rate Accommodation Benefit for the region where they live.
## Calculating the sole parent Accommodation Benefit rate
Eligibility
The sole parent rate of Accommodation Benefit is only payable to eligible students who have a supported child or children.
Cash assets
A sole parent student must not have cash assets that exceed:
- $16,200
For more information see:
- Accommodation Supplement Cash assets
Weekly qualifying accommodation costs
The sole parent rate of Accommodation Supplement is assessed using a client’s weekly qualifying accommodation costs. This is calculated by reducing the accommodation costs (rent, board or home ownership) by the cost of any part of the property not lived in and any accommodation income they get.
For more information see:
- Accommodation Supplement Accommodation costs
- Accommodation Supplement Weekly qualifying accommodation costs
Entry threshold
The type of accommodation cost a sole parent has will determine the minimum entry threshold to be eligible for a sole parent rate of Accommodation Benefit.
An eligible sole parent must have weekly qualifying accommodation costs that meet or exceed the minimum entry threshold for the applicable accommodation cost.
Minimum entry threshold rates as at 1 April 2026:
- rent or board $168.00
- mortgage $202.00
Area and Maximum rates
The rate of sole parent Accommodation Benefit depends on what 'area' the sole parent lives in. New Zealand has been divided into 4 areas, each with its own maximum rate.
The maximum rate for each area is also dependent on the amount of the sole parent's accommodation costs and whether they have 1 child, or 2 or more children.
If a sole parent's accommodation costs exceed the maximum rate for the area they live in, they can only get the maximum rate for that area.
For more information see:
- Calculating rate – general formula

chunks.title: Sole parents — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Sole parents
Students who are single and have a supported child (or children) are eligible for a Student Allowance if they are either:
- tertiary students aged at least 16 years old or
- secondary students aged at least 18 years
Their rate of Student Allowance is not dependent on their parents' income, however the personal income limit applies.
Note some sole parents may be able to remain on a main benefit and study. For more information please refer to the relevant main benefit.
For more information see:
- Main benefits
- Supported child
- Eligibility and Entitlement

chunks.title: Extending the 92/120/200 week limit — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Extending the 92/120/200 week limit
For some students there are special circumstances that justify an extension to the 92/120/200 week limit for Student Allowance.
The 'special circumstances' exception provides discretion to make an entitlement decision based on the intent of the regulation, the limitations of the wording of the regulation, and the facts of the particular situation.
When assessing whether or not special circumstances exist, it is important to ensure that the circumstances relate to the student's individual situation and that supporting evidence is provided.
Special circumstances are very limited in scope and normally only apply to situations where personal circumstances do not allow a student to complete their study within the 92/120/200 week limit. These personal circumstances would generally not be able to be anticipated by the student and would be beyond their control. For example there has been an illness, injury, accident, bereavement, or personal difficulty that has prevented the student completing their study programme within the 92/120/200 week limit.
For study starting on or after 1 January 2013, this provision was narrowed to exclude any changes to the Student Allowances Regulations from being included as a special circumstance.
Students approved an extension under the special circumstances provision for study prior to 1 January 2013 retained their eligibility to the extension after 1 January 2013.
Students granted an extension under the special circumstances provision are not subject to the aged 40 and over restriction that applies to the 120/200 week limits, or the aged 65 and over restriction. This means that an extension can be approved beyond those restrictions.
## Further extensions
There may be situations when for example a student has been granted an extension because of failure for reasons beyond their control, and then subsequently they need a further extension due to special circumstances that affected their ability to study during the extension period.
A student can be granted a further extension under the 'special circumstances' provision provided the special circumstances relate to the study undertaken during the extension period.

chunks.title: Standard rates of Accommodation Benefit — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Standard rates of Accommodation Benefit
The standard rate of Accommodation Benefit is paid to all eligible students who get Student Allowance.
The standard rates of Accommodation Benefit are updated each year on 1 January.
The new standard rates are calculated using the last 12 months of Ministry of Business and Innovation (MBIE) data for Territorial Authorities.
Note this excludes the sole parent rate of Accommodation Benefit as these rates are calculated in the same way as the Accommodation Supplement rates payable to clients getting Sole Parent Support.
## Maximum amount payable
The maximum amount of Accommodation Benefit payable per week to eligible students is $60 (at 1 April 2026).
## Calculating the standard rates of Accommodation Benefit
From 1 January 2023, the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit will be replaced by Territorial Authority rates. These rates are based on data provided by Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment.
The Territorial Authority rate is found by:
- subtracting $40 from the average of the mean weekly room rate for the Territorial Authority (using the last 12 months data provided by Ministry of Business Innovation and Employment) then
- multiplying by 0.5
This calculation reflects that the standard rate of Accommodation Benefit is a 50% subsidy on any accommodation costs over $40.
For more information see:
## Intramural and extramural students
The standard rate of Accommodation Benefit a student will get depends on if they are an intramural student or an extramural student.
## Chatham Islands
Extramural students who live in the Chatham Islands will have their standard rate of Accommodation Benefit paid at $60 per week.
Other students living on islands not captured by Territorial Authorities will get the same rate of Accommodation Benefit as students living on the Chatham Islands.
## Grandparenting standard rates of Accommodation Benefit
Some students getting the standard Accommodation Benefit rate before 1 January 2023 may get less Accommodation Benefit from 1 January 2023.
If calculations show the student's rate will be lower on 1 January 2023 than what they were getting or eligible to get within the same study application period on 31 December 2022, their original higher rate will be grandparented for the student.

chunks.title: Statutes — student allowance
chunks.text: The Education and Training Act 2020 is the primary legislation for the Student Allowances Scheme. The detailed eligibility and entitlement criteria are provided in the Student Allowances Regulations 1998. The following statutes provide the legal authority for the administration of the Student Allowances Scheme.

chunks.title: Education and Training Act 2020 — student allowance
chunks.text: Part 4, Part 6, Schedule 9 and Schedule 10 contain the provisions that provide the statutory authority for the Student Allowances Scheme and for MSD to administer it. This includes (but is not limited to): - authority for the Student Allowances Regulations 1998 - the authority to require applicants to provide information necessary to establish eligibility and/or entitlement - the Results of Study (ROS) data-match - the Student Allowance Appeal Authority - offences and penalties in relation to students, education providers or third parties - the use of information obtained under the Social Security Act 2018 - the use of information obtained under Part 9 of the Public and Community Housing Management Act 1992 - the recovery of debts - the Annual General Adjustment (AGA) as it relates to Student Allowances - Verification of Study (VOS) data-match

chunks.title: Income Tax Act 2007 — student allowance
chunks.text: Since 1 January 2012, parental income has been defined by the definition of family scheme income in section MB of the Income Tax Act 2007, except for: - any exempt income described in section CW 32 of the Act - any income referred to in section MB 12 of the Act derived by any dependent child (under section YA 1 of the Act) - any income referred to in section MB 12 of the Act

chunks.title: Privacy Act 2020 — student allowance
chunks.text: Purpose and application The purpose of the Privacy Act 2020 is to promote and protect individual privacy. It governs how agencies can collect, use, disclose, store and give access to personal information. For more information about the Privacy Act, including guidelines for collecting, using, storing and giving access to personal information and for privacy breaches, see: - Privacy Act 2020 guidelines Information matching Subpart 4-Authorised information matching programmes of Part 7 of the Privacy Act 2020 governs how agencies can compare personal information in accordance with an authorised information matching programme. Both Verification of Study (VoS) and Results of Study (RoS) are authorised information matching programmes under the Privacy Act 2020. They are authorised by clauses 7 and 8 of Schedule 9 of the Education and Training Act 2020, and must comply with the requirements set out in Subpart 4 of Part 7, and Schedule 6 of the Privacy Act 2020. Privacy Commissioner The Privacy Act 2020 also sets out the role and functions of the Privacy Commissioner. For more information about the Privacy Commissioner, including how individuals can make a complaint if they feel their privacy has been breached, see: - Office of the Privacy Commissioner

chunks.title: Social Security Act 2018 — student allowance
chunks.text: Calculation of the Accommodation Benefit paid to sole parents under Regulation 9 of the Student Allowances Regulations 1998, is provided for in section 65 of the Social Security Act 2018, and Part 2, Subpart 5 of the Social Security Regulations 2018. Assessments for this assistance includes: - a cash asset test - an income test and - weekly qualifying accommodation costs

chunks.title: What is a statutory review? — student allowance
chunks.text: A statutory review is the statutory right to review a decision set out in clause 5(1) of Schedule 10 of the Education and Training Act 2020. The person undertaking a statutory review of a decision has been delegated authority by the Chief Executive of MSD to undertake the review. They must not have had any involvement in the original decision.

chunks.title: Timeframe for requesting a statutory review — student allowance
chunks.text: When a student makes an application for a statutory review of a decision, the application must be received by MSD within 3 months of the student receiving notification of the decision. An application made outside of the 3 month timeframe may be allowed if there is a good reason for the application not being made within the 3 month timeframe. When a request is made outside the 3 month timeframe, but prior to lodging or finalising an application for a statutory review of a decision, the person who considers the request needs to advise what further time will be allowed to make or finalise the application. In making a decision to extend the timeframe for applying for a statutory review of a decision, the person uses the discretion provided in clause 5(3)b of Schedule 10 of the Education and Training Act 2020.

chunks.title: Student Allowance Review Panel — student allowance
chunks.text: The person undertaking the statutory review either does this : - alone or - if the student requests, as part of a Student Allowance Review Panel Where a Student Allowance Review Panel is requested, a hearing is conducted where the student can be heard in person. The Student Allowance Review Panel is not provided for in legislation. It was established to provide students who request a statutory review of a decision, an opportunity to state their case in a hearing, similar to a Benefit Review Committee hearing under the Social Security Act 2018. The Student Allowance Review Panel is made up of: - the person undertaking the statutory review - a Ministry advisor - an advisor from the New Zealand Union of Students' Associations The person undertaking the statutory review is solely responsible for making the decision to either confirm the original decision or substitute a different decision. The two advisors provide advice. The consent of the student is required to enable the advisor from the New Zealand Union of Students Associations who sits on the review panel to have access to any personal information regarding the student.

chunks.title: Decisions that have a statutory right of review — student allowance
chunks.text: Decisions that have a statutory right of review are set out in clause 5(1) of Schedule 10 of the Education and Training Act 2020. They include: Types of decisions (a) Fixing the amount of an allowance Decisions which determine the rate of Student Allowance. (b) Declining to award an allowance to a person Decisions to decline a Student Allowance. (c) Approving as a full-time programme for a person in any year a specified part of a course of study Decisions to approve Limited Full-Time status (this does not include decisions by other agencies in relation to programmes and their status for Student Allowance purposes). (d) Refusing to approve as a full-time programme in any year a part of a course of study for a person Decisions to decline Limited Full-Time status (this does not include decisions by other agencies in relation to programmes and their status for Student Allowance). (e) Refusing to extend the period for which any person may receive payments under an allowance Decisions to refuse an extension of the period for which an allowance can be received. (f) Refusing to recognise the amount of work passed in any year by a person as being sufficient to entitle the person to the reinstatement of an allowance Decisions to refuse a reinstatement application. (g) Refusing to recognise any qualification or amount of work gained or passed by a person as being equivalent to any other qualification or amount of work Some decisions to decline an application on the basis of not passing more than half of a full-time course.

chunks.title: When there is no agreement whether a statutory right of review exists — student allowance
chunks.text: When there is doubt whether a decision is subject to a statutory right of review, or a student disputes whether a decision is subject to a statutory right of review, it would generally be appropriate to provide a statutory right of review. In some circumstances it may be necessary for the Student Allowance Appeal Authority to make a determination whether a statutory right of review exists before considering the substantive matter under dispute. Where this occurs, a legal submission will be required on the question of whether a statutory right of review exists. For more detailed information on the types of decision that are subject to the statutory review process see:

chunks.title: When there is no agreement whether a statutory right of review exists — student allowance
chunks.text: When there is doubt whether a decision is subject to a statutory right of review, or a student disputes whether a decision is subject to a statutory right of review, then it would generally be appropriate to provide a statutory review. In some circumstances it may be necessary for the Student Allowance Appeal Authority to make a determination whether a statutory right of review exists, before considering the substantive matter under dispute. Where this occurs, a legal submission will be required on the question of whether a statutory right of review exists.

chunks.title: Student Allowances may not be assigned — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Student Allowances may not be assigned
A student getting a Student Allowance may not:
- assign it to another person or organisation or
- allow it to be the subject of a charge
Where either of the above occurs, discretion is available to terminate the Student Allowance or reduce the amount of the allowance.
This action should only be taken after a full consideration of the issues, discussion with the student, and an appropriate warning given to the student that this may occur if the assignment or charge is not removed.
If you are unsure about a particular case or scenario, seek further advice from your manager.

chunks.title: Student couple - both eligible — student allowance
chunks.text: Where 2 students are considered a couple for Student Allowance and they are both eligible, they both need to submit an application to determine their eligibility and entitlement to a Student Allowance. If one student chooses not to apply, receive or applies late for the Student Allowance they are eligible for, the other student is still assessed at a 'both eligible' rate of Student Allowance. This is because a 'both eligible' rate correctly reflects their circumstances and therefore the rate payable. The rate of Student Allowance payable due to one student choosing not to apply or receive a Student Allowance or applying late for a Student Allowance needs to be made clear to the couple. For student couples where both students are eligible for and receive a Student Allowance, the following apply: - each eligible student may earn personal income up to $284.70 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026). In any week this is exceeded, abatement will occur - if the couple's total combined income is more than $569.40 but less than $1,185.75 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026), each eligible student is paid the applicable rate - in any week that the couple's total combined income is $1,185.75 gross or more per week (as at 1 April 2026), there is no entitlement to Student Allowance The personal income abatement reduces the gross weekly rate of Student Allowance by the equivalent amount received by the eligible student over $284.70 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026) until entitlement is nil. Example if a student gets $290.00 gross per week, their gross Student Allowance will reduce by $5.30 (as at 1 April 2026). If 2 students who are considered to be a couple for Student Allowance purposes are living apart while studying (but who are not separated), each will be eligible for an Accommodation Benefit at the rate applicable to the area where each is living. Both partners are required to advise of any income they receive that would affect any entitlement to a Student Allowance. The 'both eligible' rates are payable to both partners if they are both entitled. The combined net amount is equal to the net rate payable where only one partner is a student. This payment rate reflects that the couple has committed to full-time study and therefore, they have a limited earning capacity.

chunks.title: Student couple - both eligible — student allowance
chunks.text: Where only one student is entitled and therefore receives payment, the rate reflects the fact that both eligibility and entitlement need to be determined in order to pay the correct rate to a student.

chunks.title: Student couple earning between $569.40 and $1,185.75 per week — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Student couple earning between $569.40 and $1,185.75 per week
When 2 people are considered a couple for Student Allowance purposes, and
- one is not a student, or is a student enrolled in half or less than half of a full-time course and
- the couple's total combined income is more than $569.40 but less than $1,185.75 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026)
the student receives the applicable rate of Student Allowance.
However, when the couple are both eligible students, and the above criteria are met, each student is entitled to the applicable rate.
In any week that the couple's total combined income is $1,185.75 or more gross per week (as at 1 April 2026), there is no entitlement to Student Allowance.
For the student, the personal income abatement reduces the gross weekly rate of Student Allowance by the equivalent amount received by the student over $284.70 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026) until entitlement is nil.
Example if a student receives $290.00 gross per week, their gross Student Allowance will reduce by $5.30 (as at 1 April 2026).
## Living with their partner
A lower rate is payable if the student is living with their partner. They are not eligible for an Accommodation Benefit in this situation.

chunks.title: Student couple earning not more than $569.40 per week — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Student couple earning not more than $569.40 per week
When 2 people are considered a couple for Student Allowance purposes and one of them is:
- not a student themselves or
- is a student enrolled in half or less than half of a full-time course and
- their combined income not more than $569.40 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026)
The student will receive Student Allowance paid at the applicable rate and an Accommodation Benefit.
The partner may be eligible for an Accommodation Supplement payable as a non-beneficiary.
The student may earn personal income up to $284.70 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026). In any week this is exceeded, abatement will occur.
For the student, the personal income abatement reduces the gross weekly rate of Student Allowance by the equivalent amount received by the student, over $284.70 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026), until entitlement is nil.
Example if a student receives $290.00 gross per week, their gross Student Allowance will reduce by $5.30 (as at 1 April 2026).
The partner does not have to live with the student to be considered a partner.
Both the student and their partner are required to advise of any income they get that would affect any entitlement to Student Allowance.

chunks.title: Student couple - one eligible — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Student couple - one eligible
When 2 students are considered a couple for Student Allowance purposes and only one of them is eligible for a Student Allowance, the following apply:
- the eligible student may earn personal income up to $284.70 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026). In any week this is exceeded, abatement will occur
- if the couple's total combined income is more than $569.40 but less than $1,185.75 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026), the eligible student is paid the applicable rate
- in any week that the couple's total combined income is $1,185.75 gross or more per week (as at 1 April 2026), there is no entitlement to Student Allowance
The personal income abatement reduces the gross weekly rate of Student Allowance by the equivalent amount received by the eligible student over $284.70 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026) until entitlement is nil.
Example if a student gets $290 gross per week, their gross Student Allowance will reduce by $5.30 (as at 1 April 2026).
A student enrolled in more than half of a full-time course whether a recognised programme or not, but who is not eligible or entitled to a Student Allowance in their own right, cannot be paid as though they were eligible.
The eligible student will get a 'one eligible' rate of Student Allowance and an Accommodation Benefit. This rate will increase if the couple have a supported child or children.
The partner does not have to live with the student to be considered a partner.
Both the eligible student and their partner are required to advise of any income they get that would affect any entitlement to a Student Allowance.
When the non-eligible student undertakes study that is not full-time (but more than half of full-time) whether it is a recognised programme or not, the rate payable is reduced as a Student Allowance is not generally paid for part-time study.
Where the non-eligible partner undertakes study that is full-time, but they are not eligible, the rate payable is also reduced, as a Student Allowance is not payable to a non-eligible student.

chunks.title: Obligations — student allowance
chunks.text: Students, education providers and other third parties all have obligations, both to provide information, and to respond to requests for information.

chunks.title: Student obligations — student allowance
chunks.text: Application and subsequent advice A student must provide complete and accurate information when completing an application and when advising of a change in circumstances. A student must advise of any change in circumstances that would materially affect their entitlement to a Student Allowance. Written request to a student At any time, by written notice to any student, MSD can require the student to provide any papers, documents, records, information or other things that are in the student's possession or under the student's control that are required to determine their entitlement to or rate of entitlement to a Student Allowance. The authority also allows MSD to make copies of any such papers, documents or records that MSD receives in case MSD needs to retain the documents for any future assessments that may occur. Investigation At any time MSD may investigate a student's circumstances in order to determine whether or not a student is or was entitled to get a Student Allowance payment. A student, who is asked questions during this investigation, must answer those questions.

chunks.title: Education provider obligations — student allowance
chunks.text: Education providers are obliged to provide MSD with information and details that MSD reasonably require in order to determine a student's entitlement to a Student Allowance. The mechanism for requesting this information is the Verification of Study (VoS) process and the procedures that surround it. The Verification of Study (VoS) process may include follow up questions.

chunks.title: Private Training Establishment obligations — student allowance
chunks.text: Private training establishments are also required to: - keep accurate enrolment and academic records for each student enrolled in a programme or training scheme and - ensure that the enrolment records are readily available, upon request, to MSD among others This provision is specific to private training establishments as they are not public institutions and therefore are not subject to the provisions of the Public Records Act 2005.

chunks.title: Third party obligations — student allowance
chunks.text: At any time MSD may investigate a student's circumstances in order to determine whether or not a student is or was entitled to get a Student Allowance. In the course of this investigation, MSD may ask a third party questions. The third party must answer these questions. MSD can ask the third party for documents supporting the answers to these questions, they are not required to provide any documents.

chunks.title: Suspension or refusal to grant entitlement — student allowance
chunks.text: When MSD are satisfied that a student or third party has, without reasonable cause, failed or refused to comply with a request to supply information or documents or answer questions, MSD may suspend or refuse to grant entitlement. A student must be warned of the consequence of failure or refusal to comply with a request, and given the opportunity to either explain their refusal or comply. When a third party fails to comply with a request for information or documents or answer questions, MSD must, before taking action to suspend or refuse to grant entitlement, provide the student with the opportunity to provide the information.

chunks.title: Student, partner or supported child dies — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Student, partner or supported child dies
When a student, their partner, or their supported child dies, generally the student's Student Allowance entitlement must be reassessed from the week after the date of death.
Discretion is available to make this change from a later date if there are circumstances that suggest it is reasonable to do so.
A debt should be created for any payments or parts of any payments incorrectly paid.
Arrears must be paid where they have not received their full entitlement.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Who is a partner? — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Who is a partner?
For Student Allowance purposes, a partner is someone who the student is in a recognised relationship with.
## Recognised relationships
A recognised relationship is when the student and their partner are both 24 and over, or 1 or both of them are under 24 and there is a supported child, regardless of the sex or gender of either partner.
From 1 January 2009 the age test for a recognised relationship changed from 25 years to 24 years.
The following relationship types are recognised relationships for Student Allowances purposes:
- marriage - a legally recognised union between 2 people for the purpose of: the formation of a family unit; social stability; education and development of offspring; economic stability; security; companionship or various combinations of these purposes
- civil union - a legally recognised union equivalent to marriage that provides couples with rights, benefits and responsibilities equal to those enjoyed by married couples
- de facto relationships - a de facto relationship exists when 2 people live together as if they were married but they have not been legally married or entered into a civil union
## Living separately
Some couples, who are in a recognised relationship, live in separate homes.
This may be for a number of reasons, including (but not limited to):
- their financial circumstances
- their health
- their work and or business responsibilities
- one of them lives overseas
- the student's partner is in prison
They will no longer be in a recognised relationship if their relationship has genuinely ended.
A students partner does not have to meet the residency requirements for them to be considered a couple in a recognised relationship.
The partner is required to advise of any income they get that will affect their entitlement to a Student Allowance.
There is no provision to pay a 'half-couple' rate of Student Allowance. Therefore, a student in a recognised relationship is not eligible for a Student Allowance if their partner is getting a main benefit, New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension.

chunks.title: Aged 16-23 years — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Aged 16-23 years
A student's age and whether the student has a partner and/or supported child(ren), determines what other criteria need to be met (for example parents' income, partner's income) and what rate of Student Allowance (if any) the student will be paid.
The parental income test applies to students aged 16-23 years, unless they have a supported child(ren) or have been granted an Independent Circumstances Allowance.
## Tertiary students aged 16 or 17 years
A tertiary student aged 16 or 17 years can qualify for a Student Allowance if the student meets the standard Student Allowance eligibility criteria and:
- has a supported child or
- qualifies for Independent Circumstances Allowance or
- has completed year 13 or attained at level 3 NCEA, 42 credits or more
For more information see:
- Students who are independent of their parents
Note parents of 16 or 17 year old students may be eligible to get an Away from Home Allowance for their child's accommodation costs.
Also see:
- Away from Home Allowance
## Tertiary and secondary students aged 16 to 23 years with children
Students aged 16 to 23 with children, do not have their Student Allowance parentally income tested.

chunks.title: Students aged 24 years and over — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Students aged 24 years and over
Parental income is not considered for students over the age of 24 years.
If they meet all the other essential eligibility and entitlement criteria for a Student Allowance of:
- citizenship/residency
- attending a recognised course
- income
- passing more than half the work of a full-time course they last received a Student Allowance for
- maximum 200 weeks entitlement if under the age of 40 at study start date
- maximum 120 weeks entitlement if over the age of 40 at study start date
- under the age of 65 years at study start date
they can qualify for a Student Allowance.
A student may become entitled to a Student Allowance when they turn 24 years of age. If they have not already done so, they will need to complete an application.

chunks.title: Students in prison — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Students in prison
Students who are imprisoned or detained in prison under a sentence of imprisonment or preventative detention, are not entitled to a Student Allowance or an Accommodation Benefit during any period of detention or imprisonment.
## Short periods of custody
A student detained in custody for a short period of time can continue to qualify and retain their entitlement for a Student Allowance for that period as long as it does not affect their ability to meet their minimum attendance and/or work requirements.
## Students on home detention
Students who are on home detention may qualify and be entitled to a Student Allowance at the same rate as other students.
The student's residential arrangements are relevant to the rate of pay and in the case of a student on home detention there may be no other form of income available to them.
## Public Protection Orders
A student subject to a Public Protection Order is not "imprisoned or detained in prison under a sentence of imprisonment or preventative detention" and therefore may be entitled to a Student Allowance.

chunks.title: Students who are independent of their parents — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Students who are independent of their parents
Students under 24 are generally subject to the parental income test.
Students are treated as being independent of their parents, between the ages of 16-23 if they have:
- a supported child or
- they meet the Independent Circumstances Allowance criteria
Entitlement to a Student Allowance for these students is not based on their parents' income.
For more information see:
- Sole parents

chunks.title: Study and residency criteria — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Study and residency criteria
To be awarded a NZQA Scholarship Monetary Award a student must be:
- enrolled at a New Zealand tertiary education provider in a course recognised for Student Loan and/or Student Allowance purposes in New Zealand and
- enrolled in more than 0.4 EFTS
The requirement to be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident was removed from 2009. The change applies to students sitting the examinations from the end of 2009 and means that international students can now qualify for these awards, provided they meet the general eligibility criteria.

chunks.title: Study overseas — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Study overseas
Tertiary and secondary students who meet all the eligibility and entitlement requirements, and are studying overseas as part of their approved programme in New Zealand, can access Student Allowances.
## Tertiary study at an overseas campus or delivery site
For study starting on or after 1 January 2017 tertiary students (only) who are studying at an overseas campus or delivery site must be:
- studying part of their course of study or programme overseas
- studying in an approved specified country
- enrolled in intramural (face to face) study
- enrolled in a course of study or programme of level 7 on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework, or a Bachelor Honours Degree
An overseas campus or delivery site is where a New Zealand tertiary education provider delivers, or has an agreement with another institution to deliver, their recognised course(s) of study overseas.
For more information see:
- Deskfile Overseas study - regions and specified countries
## Residence class visa holders
Tertiary students who hold a residence class visa, and are studying overseas, must be enrolled in face to face study, and only be studying in a country they are not familiar with (from 1 January 2017).
'Not familiar with' means the student:
- has never been to that country or
- has been to that country but has spent less than 6 months in total there in the 5 years before the date their study overseas begins
The above rules for residence class visa holders also apply to tertiary students studying overseas who are a refugee or protected person, hold a valid temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 and whose study started on or after 1 May 2022.
## Immediate family member of refugee or protected person
A student who is an immediate family member of a refugee or protected person, and who holds a temporary entry class visa, is not eligible to get a Student Allowance for study overseas.
This is because they must reside (be present) in New Zealand to meet the residency criteria for Student Allowance.

chunks.title: Superannuation funds — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Superannuation funds
Income or positive returns that are locked into a superannuation scheme registered as a managed investment scheme under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 will not be considered personal income for Student Allowance purposes.
A qualifying lock-in clause prevents a member of the scheme from receiving a withdrawal from the scheme until the member:
- reaches the stated time of retirement or
- leaves the employment which established the scheme
## Example
Income earned in a KiwiSaver account will not be considered personal income while the funds are locked in.
When a student or their partner reaches the age of 65 they may be able to withdraw their funds from their KiwiSaver account.
At that point any income from the scheme should be included as personal income; including interest generated from funds invested.
## Significant lump sums deposited in a superannuation scheme account
Depositing significant lump sum funds into a superannuation scheme may be considered deprivation of income.
This depends on factors such as the size and frequency of those deposits and the individual circumstances of the client.
Deprivation will affect entitlement to Student Allowances if MSD considers that these sums were deposited into a superannuation scheme in order to qualify for a Student Allowance or a higher rate of allowance.
Each case needs to be considered on its merits and you should seek advice from the StudyLink Business Support team or Legal Services before any decisions are made.
## For more information about Deprivation of Income see:
- Deprivation of income

chunks.title: Definition — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Definition
A supported child, in relation to a student applying for a Student Allowance, is a person younger than 24:
- whose well-being and financial support are the responsibility of the student applicant and
- who lives with the student at least half of the time and
who is not getting:
- Student Allowance or
- Jobseeker Support, Sole Parent Support, Emergency Benefit, or Supported Living Payment or
- New Zealand Superannuation or a Veteran's Pension or
- payments under any government assisted scheme (other than the Student Loan Scheme) which, in the opinion of the chief executive, is similar to a benefit under the Social Security Act 2018 or
- income before tax from employment or self-employment which exceeds $80 per week and
- in respect of whom no Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is payable
## Student Allowance rates
Student couples with a supported child or children will be entitled to an allowance equivalent to the relevant rate of Jobseeker Support plus an Accommodation Benefit, subject to the personal and couple income limits.
The allowance rate varies depending on whether the student is a sole parent, is married to, in a civil union or de facto relationship with another student, or has a combined income of not more than $569.40 per week (as at 1 April 2026).
A single student with a supported child or children is treated as being independent from their parents and will be entitled to the 'with supported child' rate of Student Allowance plus any Accommodation Benefit - sole parents payable, even if the student is living in a parental home.
## Shared care-Student Allowance
The same child can be included in 2 parents' Student Allowance as a supported child if:
- the child spends 50% of the time with each parent and
- both parents share responsibility for the well-being and financial support of the child
The supported child may also be included in a Student Allowance and a benefit at the same time. The case manager will need to confirm if the child can be included in the benefit.
The definition of "shared care" for Student Allowances is not the same as the definition of shared care for beneficiaries.
Note a student may qualify for Accommodation Benefit - sole parents via the Student Allowance scheme, but due to their 'shared care' arrangements they may not be able to have their child or children included in their main benefit or Accommodation Supplement application.

chunks.title: Tax codes — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Tax codes
A student must choose and advise MSD of a tax code appropriate to their circumstances. A student can change their tax code at any time.
All queries about the correct tax code for a student must be referred to Inland Revenue.
In general terms:
- where the Student Allowance payment is the client's highest or only source of income, the 'M' tax code should be used
- where the Student Allowance is not the student's main source of income a secondary or 'S' tax code should be used
- students with a Student Loan must use a tax code with the Student Loan (SL) repayment code
## Tailored tax codes
It may be appropriate for a student to have a tailored tax code that enables their tax to be deducted at a different rate to the 'standard' rates.
All queries about tailored tax codes must be referred to Inland Revenue.
## Special deduction rate and repayment deduction exemption
if a student needs to reduce their Student Loan repayment deductions they can apply for a 'special deduction rate' on their secondary earnings or a 'repayment deduction exemption' if they are studying full-time.
All queries about a 'special deduction rate' or a 'repayment exemption' must be referred to Inland Revenue.
## Students who want to pay off their Student Loan faster
If a student wants to pay off their Student Loan faster they can make extra repayments to Inland Revenue, or they can ask their employer to make extra Student Loan repayments through their salary or wages.

chunks.title: The 120/200 week limit for tertiary study — student allowance
chunks.text: A student usually has a maximum of 200 weeks entitlement to a Student Allowance for tertiary study, or if aged 40 or over at the date they start study, a maximum of 120 weeks entitlement. Weeks that do not count towards the 120/200 week limit include: - study at a secondary school - transition courses - weeks where the payments received have been refunded in accordance with the refund of payments after withdrawal requirements

chunks.title: Extension to the 120/200 week limit — student allowance
chunks.text: A student may receive an extension to their 120/200 week limit when there are special circumstances. Students, who have been approved to study less than full-time under the 'limited full-time' provisions, can receive an extension beyond the 120/200 week limit, provided there are special circumstances.

chunks.title: 120 week limit for students aged 40 years or over — student allowance
chunks.text: For study starting on or after 1 January 2014, students aged 40 years or over at their study start date, have a maximum of 120 weeks entitlement. This means that: - if a student is aged 40 or over at the date they start study, and they have already used 120 or more weeks of Student Allowance, they will not be entitled to a Student Allowance - if a student is aged 40 or over at the date they start study, and they have used less than 120 weeks of Student Allowance, they will be able to receive up to a maximum of 120 weeks of Student Allowance - if a student is 39 years of age at the date they start a course of study, and they turn 40 years old during that course of study, they are assessed under the 200 week limit for the duration of that course of study Those students whose course of study started in 2013 and carried over into 2014 had an entitlement of up to 200 weeks limit for the duration of that course of study. The course of study referred to above is the period of study covered by the student's application.

chunks.title: Grand-parenting provision — student allowance
chunks.text: Students who studied and received a Student Allowance in 2013 were entitled to receive a Student Allowance up until 31 December 2014, or until they reached their 200 week limit to a Student Allowance, whichever came first. The study in 2014 did not need to be towards the same qualification as the study in 2013. There are no other 'transitional' provisions, including any form of discretion, available to vary the maximum entitlement to 120 weeks for students aged 40 years or over.

chunks.title: Important reminders — student allowance
chunks.text: Students who had an extension to the 200 week limit approved before 1 January 2014 continued to be eligible for the extension after 1 January 2014. Applications for an extension under the 'special circumstances' provision on or after 1 January 2014 cannot be approved if they only want to avoid the change to the maximum entitlement under the Regulations.

chunks.title: Transition courses — student allowance
chunks.text: For study starting on or after 1 January 2011, the transition course provision in regulation 20 was removed. The Minister of Tertiary Education had previously only recognised the University of Otago, Foundation Studies Certificate, (PC code OO0372) as a transition course.

chunks.title: Removal of Recognised Long Programmes and retraining for employment provisions — student allowance
chunks.text: For study starting on or after 1 January 2013, extensions are not available for Recognised Long Programmes, study that is equivalent to a Recognised Long Programme and retraining for employment in a programme of national interest. Students who had an extension approved for study before 1 January 2013 for a Recognised Long Programme, a programme equivalent to a Recognised Long Programme or retraining for employment in a programme of national interest, retained their eligibility to the exemption after 1 January 2013.

chunks.title: The 92 week limit for secondary school study — student allowance
chunks.text:
## The 92 week limit for secondary school study
A student usually has a lifetime maximum of 92 weeks entitlement to a Student Allowance for secondary school study.
Once a student has used up their 92 weeks, they will cease to be entitled to a Student Allowance.
Weeks that do not count towards the 92 week limit include:
- weeks paid for secondary school level study before 1 January 1999
- weeks paid for tertiary level study
- weeks paid in excess of the 92 week limit for secondary school level study before 1 January 2011
- weeks when the payments received have been refunded in accordance with the 'refund of payments after withdrawal' requirements
## Extension to the 92 week limit
A student may get an extension to their 92 week limit if there are special circumstances.
Students, who have been approved to study less than full-time under the 'limited full-time' provisions, can get an extension beyond the 92 week limit provided there are special circumstances.

chunks.title: Academic best interests — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Academic best interests
For study starting on or after 1 January 2013 the 'best interest' category of LFT was narrowed to the student's 'academic best interests'.
Academic best interests is defined as: that the student would be likely to fail their current course of study, for academic reasons, if they undertook a full-time course but would be likely to pass more than half of the course if they studied part-time.
Academic reasons are reasons that relate directly and only to the student's cognitive ability to successfully undertake the course of study.
When considering these applications, MSD needs to use the advice provided by the student and the education provider to determine whether the student meets the definition of 'academic best interests'.
The student's education provider needs to confirm that the student is likely to succeed in completing the course, if given the opportunity to study on a part-time basis. They should also indicate whether they believe the student is likely to need to continue study on a part-time basis beyond the current enrolment period, and why.
Each case must be considered on its merits.
## 'Best interests' applications before 1 January 2013
Students who have received approval to study part-time under the 'best interests' category prior to 1 January 2013, can continue to study under that approval until the earlier of 31 December 2014 or until the programme is completed, as long as they continue to be eligible in all other respects.

chunks.title: Criteria — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Criteria
Where a student is enrolled in more than half of a full-time course, but not in a full-time course and they have completed part of that course previously, and they will complete a recognised programme when they complete that course, they may be eligible for Limited-full-time status.
If a student subsequently makes an application for the same course of study (after it should have been completed), MSD needs to consider the situation carefully.
To approve a further period of study for the same course, there needs to be good reason why the course was not completed as originally intended.
## Situations where a student may qualify under this provision
The following are examples where a student may qualify under this provision:
Recognition of prior learning
- a student who is studying less than full-time due to the recognition of prior learning and
- will complete a recognised programme they have previously commenced but did not complete and
- is studying more than half a full-time course
Part-time study
- a student who is undertaking a programme of study that usually involves up to 1 year of study, but it takes longer than a year and
- they are completing a recognised programme which they previously commenced but did not complete and
- is studying more than half of a full-time course
Repeating papers due to failure
- a student who is repeating papers due to an earlier failure and
- who will complete a recognised programme they have previously commenced but did not complete and
- is studying more than half of a full-time course
The requirement to maintain an acceptable level of academic performance is managed by the 'passing more than half' provision.
## Changes made from 1 January 2013
For study starting on or after 1 January 2013 the Regulation covering this Limited full-time provision was clarified by including the requirement that the student must, on completing that course, be completing a recognised programme.
## Changes made from 1 July 2015
For study starting on or after 1 July 2015 the Regulation covering this Limited full-time provision was clarified by including the requirement that a student must have previously completed part of the course of study they are now undertaking.
Any cases, reviews or appeals dealing with eligibility or entitlement prior to these changes will need to take into account the law and approach in place at that time.

chunks.title: Situations outside the student's control — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Situations outside the student's control
There will be situations that are outside a student's control that are sufficient to prevent them from undertaking full-time study. In these situations a student can apply for approval to study on a Limited full-time basis.
This may include, but is not limited to:
- family circumstances or responsibilities or
- a disability or
- significant administrative changes made by the education provider to a student's proposed course of study
Each case must be considered on its merits.
## Recognition of prior learning
A student may be studying less than full-time due to the 'recognition of prior learning'. This may include cross-crediting of previous study or recognition of relevant work experience.
The 'recognition of prior learning' is not on its own a sufficient cause that is outside of the students' control. This is because it is not unusual nor something that either necessarily prevents a student undertaking full-time study, or justifies payment of a Student Allowance for undertaking part-time study. Rather, it simply means that a student does not need to undertake full-time study to meet the minimum requirements of the particular programme or qualification they are undertaking.
## Disabled students
Where an education provider substitutes other relevant study, for work that the student cannot complete because of a disability, this information should be included on the application form, including:
- an outline of the proposed course or programme and
- the length of time in which the student should complete the course or programme
A student who is undertaking a changed course or programme because of a disability can apply for assistance beyond the 120/200 week limit for tertiary study.
Students with a disability may be eligible for other types of assistance, such as Supported Living Payment or Disability Allowance. Students receiving Supported Living Payment are not eligible to receive a Student Allowance at the same time.

chunks.title: Three years living in New Zealand — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Three years living in New Zealand
Three years living in New Zealand can be either a continuous period, or several periods added together to make 3 years.
Periods when a student has lived in New Zealand while on a temporary entry class visa (e.g. a work visa, visitor's visa or a student visa), can be included.
Time living overseas in the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau cannot be included.

chunks.title: Transferring students — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Transferring students
Students can transfer between education providers providing they are undertaking the same course at the second education provider that they were undertaking at the first.
Student Allowance can be continued for students transferring education providers, though still undertaking the same programme.
Note the student will need to reapply for their Student Allowance so that the second education providers information is recorded in our records.

chunks.title: Transitioning from Youth Payment — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Transitioning from Youth Payment
A student who has been receiving Youth Payment, who then applies for an Independent Circumstances Allowance may not have to provide evidence of their circumstances, if they have previously done so as part of their application for Youth Payment.
However, the criteria for Independent Circumstances Allowance and Youth Payment are not identical. There may be instances where a student who has been receiving Youth Payment will need to verify their circumstances when applying for an Independent Circumstances Allowance.
For those applicants who have been receiving Youth Payment you will need to request a copy of the Independent Assessment Provider's report completed for the Youth Payment application from the Youth Service Support Unit (YSSU).
Where this report contains sufficient information to confirm the applicant meets the criteria set for Independent Circumstances Allowance then the application can be approved.
Note an Independent Assessment Provider's report is not required from every application for Youth Payment.
If the application for Independent Circumstances Allowance is made more than 52 weeks after the student last received Youth Payment, then it may be necessary to gather further information from the student before a final decision can be made.
## Young Person on Youth Guarantee Course
A young person can continue to receive Youth Payment when they participate in Youth Guarantee courses. They do not have to apply for a Student Allowance or Independent Circumstances Allowance.

chunks.title: Trimester 3 (summer school) study — student allowance
chunks.text:
## Trimester 3 (summer school) study
Students who are undertaking study in Trimester 3 (study that is undertaken over the summer period) need to meet all general Student Allowance eligibility and entitlement criteria, like any other applicant, to qualify for a Student Allowance.
If the trimester 3 study on its own is less than full-time, the student is not eligible for a Student Allowance for this period unless:
- the study can be included in their existing or planned study programme. In which case, the student must be enrolled, and be full-time for the whole period of study

chunks.title: Withdrawals — student allowance
chunks.text: If a student withdraws from their study, and does not intend to return to study, they will not be eligible for any further award payments.

chunks.title: Postponements — student allowance
chunks.text: Students who have not received their initial payment can apply to the New Zealand Qualifications Authority (NZQA) to postpone commencing tertiary study for one academic year only. A postponement for NZQA Scholarship Monetary Award students is a period of one year between their secondary and tertiary study. This means that students who continue to study at secondary school level may have a postponement period of longer than one year. Example where a student who excelled in the 2008 exams is awarded a NZQA Scholarship Monetary Award, the initial payment would normally be in 2009. If the student continues to study at secondary school in 2009 the initial payment of an award would be in 2010. The student is still entitled to a one year postponement in 2010 before beginning tertiary study. Once a student has received their initial award payment they are able to postpone for any period for any logical reason. They will not receive the award payment for the years that they are not studying, but will be able to receive the award when they return to study. The student will need to supply a written statement to StudyLink confirming that they wish to postpone their payments.

chunks.title: Failure — student allowance
chunks.text: Students who received their initial award payment in 2006 or later, need to maintain a minimum of a B-grade average each year to continue to receive the award. Students, who received their initial payment in 2005, need to pass more than half of their course each year. If a student does not maintain a B-grade average or pass more than half due to reasons beyond their control, they continue to be entitled to the NZQA Scholarship Monetary Award. If a student does not maintain a B-grade average or pass over half for reasons within their control, they are not entitled to any further award payments.

chunks.title: Transfers — student allowance
chunks.text: Recipients may change the course or programme that they are studying, and continue to receive their award provided they maintain the required academic performance and continue to meet the study and residency criteria.

chunks.title: Part-time study — student allowance
chunks.text: To be eligible for an award a student needs to be enrolled in more than 0.4 EFTS regardless of the length of their course. Students who study 0.4 EFTS or less and wish to receive the award payment will need to apply for Limited Full-time Status. The limited full-time status criteria for NZQA Scholarship Monetary Award recipients, is the same as the existing criteria for Student Allowance and Student Loan limited full-time status. This means that the one form can be used for all products.

chunks.title: Accepting a Student Loan contract after withdrawal or the study end date — student loan
chunks.text:
## Accepting a Student Loan contract after withdrawal or the study end date
The Student Loan Contract is a contract between the student and the Crown.
The contract is not completed, until the student has returned the signed contract or accepted it online. Because Student Loans are provided to enable students to study, this should be done before their withdrawal from study, or study end date.
If the contract is not signed and returned, or accepted online until after their withdrawal from study or study end date, MSD should not process the contract, as the reason for seeking financial support provided by the Student Loan Scheme, to enable study, no longer exists. In effect the application will remain uncompleted.
If there has been an error by MSD that prevented the contract acceptance process from being completed, or there is another reason beyond the student's control that prevented the contract acceptance process from being completed, MSD needs to consider whether there is a good reason (consistent with the purpose of the Student Loan Scheme) to process the acceptance of the contract.

chunks.title: Age limits — student loan
chunks.text:
## Age limits
There is no lower age limit for a student to apply for a Student Loan to undertake tertiary study.
Students under the age of 18 without dependent children are generally required to have parental consent to be able to get a Student Loan.
There are some situations where parental consent is not required for students under the age of 18 years, including where:
- students under 18 have dependent child(ren) or
- students who have or would qualify for Independent Circumstances Allowance
For more information see:
- Parental consent
## Student Loan contract enforceable against a minor
Young people under the age of 18 are usually treated as a minor in relation to contracts.
Accordingly, when a minor enters into a contract, under the Contract and Commercial Law Act 2017, a contract is not usually enforceable against them.
For Student Loan purposes, under the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011, when a student is under the age of 18 and enters into a Student Loan contract they must be treated, for the purposes of the Contract and Commercial Law Act 2017, as if they are 18 years of age.
## Students aged 55 years or older
For study starting on or after 1 January 2013 students aged 55 or over at study start date are not entitled to the Course-Related Costs or Living Costs components of the Student Loan.

chunks.title: Applications — student loan
chunks.text: A student must make an application to be eligible and entitled to get a Student Loan. The application must be on a form approved for the purpose and submitted to MSD. An application establishes the intent to apply for a Student Loan. Seeking information about eligibility or entitlement, including completing the online eligibility tool, is not making an application. MSD can require an applicant to provide information or evidence necessary to establish eligibility and entitlement. If an applicant refuses to provide any necessary information the application remains incomplete and then lapses at the end of the study period. When an application has lapsed or been declined, and the student subsequently wants to test their eligibility or entitlement for a period of study covered by the lapsed or declined application, or any later period of study, they must make a new application. For more information see:

chunks.title: Date of application — student loan
chunks.text: The date of application for a Student Loan is the date the application is received by MSD. Students are encouraged to submit their applications well before the start date of their course or when they would otherwise become eligible and/or entitled, even if they do not have all the required information or evidence available.

chunks.title: Date entitlement begins — student loan
chunks.text: For Living Costs, the date entitlement begins is the Monday of the week that a student's course starts when an application has been received in that week or before that week. When an application is received after that week, entitlement begins from the Monday of the week in which it is received. For Living Costs, the date of entitlement for a change in circumstances begins from the Monday of the week in which the students' circumstances change. For Compulsory Fees, entitlement can begin before the course start date if all the Loan Contract requirements have been met. For Course Related Costs, entitlement can begin before the course start date if all requirements have been met.

chunks.title: Date entitlement ends — student loan
chunks.text: For Living Costs, the date entitlement ends (if not lost earlier) is either: - on the Sunday of the last week in which the last examination of that course is held or - on the Sunday of the week during which the study ends, if that study ends without an examination For more information see: For Compulsory Fees, entitlement to a payment generally ends after the course end date. However, payment can occur after the course end date if in all the circumstances of a particular case it would be reasonable. For Course Related Costs, entitlement to payment generally ends after the course end date. However, payment can occur after the course end date if in all the circumstances of a particular case it would be reasonable.

chunks.title: Late applications — student loan
chunks.text: Where an application is received after the week in which the course start date occurs, Living Costs are generally only paid from the Monday of the week the application was received. However payment may be made from an earlier date provided there are special circumstances that warrant an extension of the time for making an application. If special circumstances exist, the revised entitlement date will be the Monday of the week that the application would have been received. This date cannot be any earlier than the Monday of the week in which the course of study commenced. For Compulsory Fees and Course Related Costs, entitlement and therefore payments are for the period of study the application relates to. An application received after the course end date should be declined, unless special circumstances exist.

chunks.title: Special circumstances — student loan
chunks.text: The special circumstances exception is an exercise of discretion. Special circumstances may include: - Did MSD significantly contribute to the delay or reason for not making an application?
