Do notes or correspondence indicate that the student was misinformed, or was there an unacceptable delay in providing information, advice or material to the student. - Was there a significant event that contributed to the delay in not making an application? Medical - accident or health issues Family - family breakdown or illness in the family Civil Emergency - Does the student have a significant psychological, physical or intellectual impairment that contributed to the delay? - Does the student have a significant language barrier that contributed to the delay? Special circumstances are situations that are beyond the student's control. Each case must be considered on its merits. For more information see:

chunks.title: Providing information or evidence — student loan
chunks.text: Any information or evidence required as part of an application must be provided before the end date of the course of study to which the application relates, unless there are special circumstances that justify a delay in providing the information. A later date must be specified and advised to the student. A decision to allow further time to provide information or evidence must include a new deadline for providing the information or evidence. Agreeing that special circumstances exist is an exercise of discretion. An applicant must not be awarded a Student Loan if they do not provide the required information or evidence, or they provide it after the required date.

chunks.title: Signatures — student loan
chunks.text: The requirement for an applicant to sign their application fulfils two purposes: - it assists in ensuring MSD can identify who is making the application and - it is part of the declaration by the applicant that they have read and understood the information on the form, including any obligations they have agreed to, and the information they have provided is to the best of their knowledge, true and correct

chunks.title: Online applications and electronic signatures — student loan
chunks.text: When a student submits an application online, they are undertaking an electronic transaction using an electronic signature. RealMe is a digital signature. It is a type of electronic signature that provides MSD with certainty the person using the digital signature is who they say they are. It is also part of the declaration by the applicant that they have read and understood the information on the form, including any obligations they have agreed to, and that the information they have provided is to the best of their knowledge, true and correct.

chunks.title: Fees and charges — student loan
chunks.text: Where a Student Loan account is established and activated there are fees and charges that apply.

chunks.title: Enrolling in an approved programme — student loan
chunks.text: A Student Loan may be approved if a student is enrolled in an approved programme. An approved programme for Student Loan purposes is one which: - is offered by a tertiary education provider - is approved for Student Component funding (Government funding) by the Tertiary Education Commission (from 1 January 2007) - is listed by PC code in Tertiary Education Commission's Which Course Where - leads to a recognised award or qualification - is a full-time programme or a part-time programme of at least 32 weeks or a part-time part-year programme of at least 0.25 EFTS (fees only) The following programmes are not approved for Student Loan purposes: - training and work experience programmes offered by MSD - STAR (Secondary Tertiary Alignment Resource) programmes, which are provided for secondary school students and fully funded by the Ministry of Education Students under the age of 18 at study start date who are undertaking a Youth Guarantee course or a fees-free level 1-2 course or programme are not eligible for a Student Loan, as the course is fully funded by the Government. For more information see: The number of students on a programme who can access a Student Loan is not limited to the number of Ministry of Education funded places.

chunks.title: Tertiary Education Commission role — student loan
chunks.text: The Tertiary Education Commission (TEC) formally approves education providers, and programmes, or qualifications for access to Student Allowances and/or Student Loans, as part of its primary role of approving government funding for tertiary education providers. In order for a Student Allowance or Student Loan application to be approved, the programme or qualification the applicant is intending to study (and the education provider who will be delivering it) must be approved by TEC. It forms part of the eligibility criteria for both Student Allowances and Student Loans. The TEC approval of funding and access to Student Allowance and/or Student Loans can only occur after the provider has obtained the necessary quality assurance from the appropriate quality assurance body under the Education and Training Act 2020. When TEC approve the funding of a particular qualification and access to Student Loans and/or Student Allowances, they: - verify the level of the qualification on the qualification register - confirm EFTS value allocated to the qualification - confirm the course classification and funding category of the qualification and - ensure the qualification and the provider meet the eligibility requirements of the Funding Guide All approved providers and qualifications are subject to review by TEC to ensure that they continue to meet the requirements of the Funding Guide, including where changes have occurred to the qualification, the financial viability of the provider, any contractual arrangements for the delivery of the qualification, and (for PTEs) the ownership or governance of the provider. It is the responsibility of education providers to deliver a programme or qualifications with the approvals that have been given. A Verification of Study (VoS) response for a student may include different information (eg EFTS value or study period) from what was approved by TEC. This can occur as the VoS response relates to the study being undertaken by that student, which may differ from the standard programme or qualification approved by TEC. It should be consistent with that approval, therefore where it is significantly different, MSD may decide to raise this difference with either the education provider or TEC. If you have any concerns about a VoS response being different from the TEC approval you should raise them with your manager. The Tertiary Education Commission has more information about its role and responsibilities.

chunks.title: Historic roles and responsibilities — student loan
chunks.text: Between 1992 and 1999 the following organisations were responsible for different aspects of the Student Loan Scheme: - the Ministry of Education - the government's lead advisor on education policy (including Student Loans)the delivery and administration of the scheme andthe approval of tertiary education providers and qualifications or programmes for access to Student Loans (and Student Allowances) - the government's lead advisor on education policy (including Student Loans) - the delivery and administration of the scheme and - the approval of tertiary education providers and qualifications or programmes for access to Student Loans (and Student Allowances) - tertiary education providers (other than private training establishments) - assessment of Student Loan applications from their students (under contract to the Ministry of Education) - Eduserve (Christchurch Polytechnic) - from 1995 the assessment of Student Loan applications from students attending private training establishments (under an agreement with the Ministry of Education) - the Student Loan Accounts Manager (EDS (NZ) Ltd) - the processing of all Student Loan applications from tertiary providers and Eduserve, including all payments and the management of all loan accounts - New Zealand Vice-Chancellors Committee - the quality assurance of New Zealand University qualifications or programmes - New Zealand Qualifications Authority - the quality assurance of all non-University qualifications or programmes - the Treasury - the government's lead advisor on economic, financial and regulatory policy, including the value and sustainability of the Student Loan Scheme - Inland Revenue - managed and recovered student loan debt under the Student Loan Scheme Act 1992 Any queries in relation to Student Loans from the beginning of 1992 to the end of 1999 are not the responsibility of MSD. MSD does not hold any Student Loans information in relation to those years. Any Student Loan queries for those years should be referred to Inland Revenue as they hold the records created by the Student Loan Accounts Manager, as well as their own records for those Student Loans.

chunks.title: Current roles and responsibilities — student loan
chunks.text: In December 1997, the government decided that MSD would take over responsibility for the delivery of the "front end" of the Student Loan Scheme from 1 January 2000. This decision recognised the benefits that would flow from an integrated approach to the delivery of financial support to students. Since 1 January 2000, the following organisations have been responsible for different aspects of the Student Loan Scheme: - MSD (via StudyLink) - the assessment and payment of Student Loans to eligible students - the Ministry of Education - the government's lead advisor on education policy (including Student Loans) - tertiary education providers - the supply of enrolment information to MSD (via StudyLink) - Inland Revenue - the management and recovery of Student Loan debt under the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011 - the Tertiary Education Commission - since its creation in 2002, the approval of tertiary education providers and qualifications or programmes for access to Student Loans (and Student Allowances) - New Zealand Vice-Chancellors Committee - the quality assurance of New Zealand University qualifications or programmes - New Zealand Qualifications Authority - the quality assurance of non-University qualifications or programmes on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework - the Treasury - the government's lead advisor on economic, financial and regulatory policy, including the value and sustainability of the Student Loan Scheme - Statistics New Zealand - the management of the Integrated Data Infrastructure, including Student Loan (and Student Allowances) data supplied by MSD

chunks.title: Cross-agency work — student loan
chunks.text: Given the individual roles and shared responsibilities for different aspects of the Student Loan Scheme, regular joint meetings of the respective agencies are held to consider and co-ordinate work related to the scheme.

chunks.title: Being adjudged bankrupt — student loan
chunks.text:
## Being adjudged bankrupt
If a student is declared bankrupt they are not eligible for a Student Loan until they have received a Certificate of Discharge from the Official Assignee, or seek approval from the High Court for an early discharge.
A bankruptcy generally lasts 3 years from the date of filing, but may last longer if all the requirements have not been met.
Clients who are discharged early can have conditions imposed by the court that restrict their ability to incur further debt. When conditions are attached to a discharge which affect a student's entitlement to any or all components of a Student Loan, appropriate action must be taken to ensure those conditions are adhered to.
If a student borrower is declared bankrupt (while studying and getting a Student Loan), StudyLink will close the loan account.
## Inland Revenue and the administration of the bankruptcy
Inland Revenue will prepare and lodge a proof of debt with the Official Assignee for the total Student Loan debt up to the date of bankruptcy.
The Official Assignee is responsible for the administration of the bankruptcy and alternatives to bankruptcy. Alternatives to bankruptcy are the No Asset Procedure and Debt Repayment Orders.
## Drawing down on a loan after the date of bankruptcy
Note if a student has drawn down from their loan after the date of bankruptcy, these amounts will not be included in the proof of debt and will not be written off.
This may occur if the bankruptcy is applied retrospectively due to a delay in notification and in this case the bankruptcy notice does not cover any amounts drawn down after the date of bankruptcy.
These amounts are treated as a debt to the Crown and transferred to MSD debt to be recovered accordingly.

chunks.title: Borrowing limit - pilot training — student loan
chunks.text:
## Borrowing limit - pilot training
For study starting on or after 1 January 2013 there is a limit on borrowing for compulsory fees for pilot training. The maximum that may be borrowed is $35,000 per 1 EFTS.
This means the amount a student can borrow is proportional to the EFTS of their programme. For example, if a student is enrolled in 0.5 EFTS the maximum amount they can borrow for compulsory fees is $17,500.
## Transitional provision
For study starting on or after 1 January 2018, fees-free eligible students continue to be covered by the borrowing limit set out above.

chunks.title: Breaks in tuition of 3 weeks or less — student loan
chunks.text:
## Breaks in tuition of 3 weeks or less
A student who is not on study leave and not studying due to a break in tuition at their education provider can continue getting Living Costs payments, when the break in tuition is for 3 weeks or less.
A student must be entitled to, and have nominated Living Costs, for the period directly before and directly after the break in tuition to get any payments for the period of the break in tuition.
## Breaks in tuition longer than 3 weeks
When the break in tuition is longer than 3 weeks, the payment of any Living Costs must be suspended, unless the break is due to a COVID-19 outbreak.
If the break in tuition is due to a COVID-19 outbreak, payment of Living Costs can continue for up to 8 weeks or the impacts of Cyclone Gabrielle (2023).
COVID-19 outbreak
If the break in tuition is due to a COVID-19 outbreak, payment of Living Costs can continue for up to 8 weeks.
Impacts of Cyclone Gabrielle
Between 6 March and 1 May 2023, payment of Living Costs can continue for up to another 8 weeks if a student has a break in tuition because their education provider temporarily cannot deliver their course(s) due to the impacts of Cyclone Gabrielle (the cyclone).
This includes breaks in tuition starting at any time from 6 March to 1 May 2023 due to subsequent weather events that worsen the impacts of the cyclone.
Breaks in tuition do not need to be consecutive.
A student must remain enrolled in study to continue getting payments, for the period of the break in tuition, for up to 8 weeks.
Living Costs cannot continue for a student from 1 May 2023 unless their study has resumed.
Students who cannot get continued payments
Living Costs payments cannot continue if a student's education provider can deliver their course(s), but the student cannot study because of the impacts of Cyclone Gabrielle. E.g. they have no internet access because their internet connection was damaged in the cyclone.
In this situation you should consider if the student is eligible for other financial assistance.
You should also advise the student to contact their education provider to discuss any other supports that may be available.

chunks.title: How to cancel a Student Loan — student loan
chunks.text:
## How to cancel a Student Loan
A student may cancel their loan contract within 7 working days after the date the initial Loan Entitlement Advice (LEA) was issued by notifying MSD in writing.
If a student does not cancel their loan in writing within this timeframe they are considered to have accepted their loan contract.
The student may verbally request their loan contract be cancelled, however, once an initial LEA has been issued, they must confirm their request to cancel their loan contract in writing.
If a student has already used any component of their Student Loan they will have to pay back the money they have borrowed.
## Waiving the Establishment Fee
The Establishment Fee is waived if a student pays back any money they have borrowed, no later than the end of the 7th working day, after the date the initial LEA was issued.
## How to stop a Student Loan
If a student wishes to 'stop' their Student Loan more than 7 working days after the date the initial LEA was issued, their loan can be closed. The loan is not cancelled as it is considered they have already accepted their loan contract.
A student can also stop drawing down any money from their loan account and make any repayments to Inland Revenue when they are due or, pay off the total outstanding balance to Inland Revenue to clear the loan balance.
## Fee refunds
Any fee refunds owing to the student must be returned by the education provider. MSD will reconcile their loan account with Inland Revenue.

chunks.title: Benefit ceases — student loan
chunks.text:
## Benefit ceases
If a student's benefit ceases during their programme they will be eligible to get living costs from the date the benefit ceased, provided they are studying full-time on an approved programme.
## Granted benefit
If a student is granted a benefit or becomes the spouse or partner of a beneficiary during their programme their living costs entitlement will cease from the date the benefit is granted.
Full-time students are not eligible for a main benefit but clients receiving a main benefit may study part-time provided they continue to meet the conditions of those benefits.

chunks.title: Closure of a loan account — student loan
chunks.text:
## Closure of a loan account
A loan account is closed when all borrowing activity has ceased or when circumstances require it, including when a student:
- has completed all study included in that loan account and no more study will be added
- dies
- is adjudged bankrupt
- has engaged in proven fraud or other unacceptable behaviour
Once a loan account is closed it should not be accessed unless a correction is required to any transactions contained within it.
## Death of a borrower
If a student dies before repaying their loan to Inland Revenue, the balance of the debt will generally be written off by Inland Revenue.
If a death certificate is available it should be obtained. If not, details of the date and place of death should be obtained.
The loan account will be closed and any details of the death MSD holds will be sent to Inland Revenue.
When a payment has been made from the loan account after the date of the death of a student, an MSD debt may be established for recovery from the student's estate.
## Fee refunds
Any fee refunds due from a provider must be repaid to a student's loan account if they were paid from the student's loan account.
In the event of the death of a student, fee refunds must not be paid by the provider to the student's estate.

chunks.title: Payments — student loan
chunks.text:
## Payments
Compulsory fees are paid from the students loan account to their tertiary education provider's nominated bank account.
Students authorise this on their loan application form.
## Increase in fees
If fees increase due to a change of programme, students have the option of paying the increase or borrowing it.
If the student has authorised the direct transfer of their fees on their Student Loan application, this is sufficient to authorise the payment of additional tuition fees that are incurred.
The tertiary provider must send StudyLink a Verification of Study (VoS) detailing the additional fees.
When the Verification of Study (VoS) has been received a subsequent LEA will be issued to the student advising them of their new entitlement.
## Refunds
Where a student qualifies for a full or partial fee refund due to a change of programme or a withdrawal, the tertiary education provider must pay back to StudyLink any amount that has been directly transferred from the student's loan account.
Different tertiary education providers have different policies about fee refunds. If a student thinks that a refund is due they should discuss this with their education provider.
In signing the contract, the student is authorising the repayment of fee refunds by direct credit from the tertiary education provider to StudyLink under the Student Loan Contract terms and conditions.
## Reference
- Refer to the relevant loan contract for the year in question. These can be found on SLKBase under "Student Loan, Terms and Conditions "

chunks.title: What is a compulsory fee? — student loan
chunks.text:
## What is a compulsory fee?
The Compulsory Fee component of the Student Loan can be used to pay all or part of the fees the student must pay to the tertiary education provider for an enrolment in an approved programme. This includes:
- tuition fees
- examination fees
- student levies
It does not include charges such as:
- external fees or costs (e.g. teacher registration fees, costs of practising certificates for lawyers)
- penalty fees for late enrolment/registration
- other administration fees such as instalments charges - that is, special charges which would not normally be incurred by every student enrolling or registering in the same programme
- student association fees (from 1 January 2012)
Since 1 January 2012 membership of a student association has been voluntary.
## Part-time part-year students
Part-time part-year students must be studying 0.25 EFTS or more to access the compulsory fee component of the Student Loan.
Students studying on a part-time, part-year basis are only entitled to the compulsory fees component, unless they are approved as being Limited Full-Time (LFT), then they are considered to be studying full-time.
## Students changing from part-time to full-time
Part-time students, who increase their study (EFTS) to be full-time during the year, may be entitled to all components of a Student Loan.
## Beneficiaries
Students receiving a benefit (including New Zealand Superannuation) can borrow the compulsory fee component of the loan, provided they are otherwise eligible.
Students who are granted employment and training related assistance for course fees (e.g. Training Incentive Allowance), can only borrow the Compulsory Fee component for any remaining fees not covered by the employment and training related assistance.
## Fees Free tertiary study
The first-year Fees Free policy for new tertiary students applied to first time students starting on or after 1 January 2018. The first-year Fees Free scheme ended on 31 December 2024 and was replaced by final-year Fees Free from 1 January 2025.
Students who used first-year Fees Free in 2024 may have some remaining entitlement to first-year Fees Free in 2025. If a student can use their remaining first-year Fees Free entitlement in 2025, they will not need to access a Student Loan for their compulsory course fees unless their fees exceed their Fees Free entitlement.

chunks.title: Contact person — student loan
chunks.text:
## Contact person
To be eligible for a Student Loan, all students applying for a Student Loan for study starting on or after 1 January 2013 will be required to provide details of a New Zealand-based contact person.
A contact person can be anyone the student wishes to use as a contact person to enable Inland Revenue to get hold of them.
A contact person can be, but is not limited to, a parent, guardian, other relative or friend.
MSD will pass the details provided about the contact person to Inland Revenue as part of the regular transfer of borrower information.
MSD have agreed with Inland Revenue that the following contact person details must be provided by an applicant:
- name
- postal address
- telephone number (mobile or landline)
MSD have agreed with Inland Revenue that the following contact details will be optional:
- email address (if the person has one)
- Inland Revenue number
- date of birth

chunks.title: Reviewing entitlement — student loan
chunks.text:
## Reviewing entitlement
Once a Student Loan has been approved, if it is identified that a borrower was not entitled to all or part of their Loan, an MSD debt may be created for those parts.
Changes to entitlement can include (but are not limited to) situations where a student:
- does not meet the performance requirement
- is declared bankrupt
- receives another form of study related government assistance
- is in prison
- receives living costs while in part-time study
- starts or ceases to receive a benefit
- does not meet their obligations under the Student Loan contract
For more information about eligibility and entitlement see:
- Eligibility and entitlement criteria for a Student Loan
- Applications
## Debt establishment
A student's circumstances need to be considered to determine if a MSD debt should be established. The student's study details and all relevant circumstances need to be confirmed.
MSD debt should be established if all the facts confirm money has been received when there is no entitlement and it would be reasonable, considering all the circumstances, to do so.
For information on whether to include the establishment fee or any interest charged prior to April 2012 in MSD debt, refer to Knowledge Base.
If MSD debt is established, the possibility of a debt write-off should be considered before recovery commences.
## Debt recovery
MSD is entitled to recover a debt to the Crown established as a result of a payment to any person, including a third party, to which they were not entitled to.
When a Student Loan payment has been converted into MSD debt, MSD is entitled to recover the debt by:
- deduction from any subsequent Student Allowance payments or
- deduction from any subsequent payments made to them of a benefit under the Social Security Act 2018 or
- deduction notice under regulation 217 of the Social Security Regulations 2018 or
- civil suit through the Courts

chunks.title: What is a Course-Related Cost? — student loan
chunks.text:
## What is a Course-Related Cost?
The Course-Related Costs (CRC) component of a Student Loan is provided to cover non-compulsory Course-Related Costs such as textbooks, course equipment, non-compulsory fees and levies, and costs such as study related travel, and childcare.
Evidence of Course-Related Costs may be requested. When this evidence is insufficient or when costs claimed are not considered to be course-related, the application may be declined.
## How much can be borrowed?
The Course-Related Costs component provides a maximum of $1000 per loan account.
A loan account is usually established for a period of 52 weeks. It can be longer if a student is studying an approved programme that is longer than 52 weeks.
A student is therefore entitled to a maximum of $1000 for each loan account. When the loan account is longer than 52 weeks the student has entitlement to a maximum of $1000.
## Overlapping periods of study
When there are overlapping periods of study, make sure the cumulative Course-Related Costs entitlement does not exceed the maximum of $1000 for a loan account. A loan account generally covers a 52 week period (or longer for programmes longer than 52 weeks).
This is a cumulative assessment and therefore you need to consider entitlement over the entire study period.

chunks.title: Debt Repayment Orders — student loan
chunks.text:
## Debt Repayment Orders
A Debt Repayment Order sets out how and when a debtor must repay some or all of their debts.
The Official Assignee is responsible for the administration of Debt Repayment Orders. For more information about Debt Repayment Orders, see: New Zealand Insolvency and Trustee Service
## Student Loan debt and Debt Repayment Orders
Student Loan debt is not included in Debt Repayment Orders. Students must continue paying off their Student Loan as well as any payments under a Debt Repayment Order.
## Currently getting or applying for a Student Loan
Students with a current Debt Repayment Order may still qualify for a Student Loan.
However they must tell MSD they have a Debt Repayment Order by:
- declaring it in their Student Loan application or
- completing a Change of Circumstances form (if the student is currently getting a Student Loan when they get a Debt Repayment Order)
Failure to tell MSD about a Debt Repayment Order is a breach of the loan contract and may be an offence under the Insolvency Act 2006.
Note Debt Repayment Orders used to be called Summary Instalment Orders.

chunks.title: Authority to write-off debt — student loan
chunks.text: Joint Ministers have delegated to MSD’s Chief Executive the authority to write-off Crown assets in certain circumstances, including debts under a certain value. This debt write-off delegation encompasses several categories of debt write-off, together with conditions. It includes debt that cannot be recovered as MSD made the payment (or payments) in error. This category used to be known as ‘estoppel’, as set out in section 94B of the Judicature Act 1908. This Act was repealed in March 2017. The provision became section 74B of the Property Law Act 2007, and therefore only relates to property as defined in that Act.

chunks.title: Debt that cannot be recovered as payment was made in error — student loan
chunks.text: Deciding whether MSD made any payment in error involves the use of discretion. The reasons and circumstances that led to any payments being made, including why the student was not entitled to them, need to be confirmed. A debt for any payments made in error can be written-off when the following criteria are met: - the payment(s) resulted wholly or partly from a mistake or error by MSD in relation to the law and/or the facts of the case - the student received the payment(s) in good faith Did they reasonably believe when they received them that they were entitled to them? - the student changed their position believing they were entitled to the payment(s)Did they make different decisions to those they would have otherwise made, because they believed they were entitled to the payment(s)? - considering all the circumstances, including the student's financial situation and any implications for any other persons, it would be inequitable to recover the debt

chunks.title: Other categories of debt write-off — student loan
chunks.text: The other categories of debt write-off that may need to be considered are listed below. Some of them also involve the use of discretion.

chunks.title: All economic avenues of collection have been exhausted and the debt is less than $20,000 — student loan
chunks.text: 1. Debt $50 or less - automatic write-off after 70 calendar days when: The debtor owes between $0.01 and $50.00 (in total) and there have been no repayments during the previous 70 calendar days. 2. Debt less than $200 The debtor owes between $50.01 and $199.99 (in total), and there have been no repayments during the previous 6 months for innocent debts, or during the previous 12 months for fraudulent debts. 3. Debt less than $1000 The debtor owes between $200.00 and $999.99 (in total) and there have been no repayments during the previous 12 months for innocent debts, or during the previous 2 years for fraudulent debts. 4. Debt less than $2000 - the debtor owes less than $2000 and there have been no repayments during the preceding 2 years for innocent debts, or during the previous 4 years for fraudulent debts and - it is established that the debtor does not reside at the last known address or no longer works at the last known place of employment and - current debtor records do not appear on any MSD databases and - current debtor records do not appear on any public databases e.g. credit reference checks, internet searches and - current debtor records do not appear in any information matching exercises with other government agencies e.g. IRD, ACC, Customs and - exhaustive searches are completed with utility companies e.g. power companies, electronic white pages and banks 5. Innocent breach debt of $2000 or more - there has been no ability to gain repayment or communicate with the debtor for at least 6 years and - current debtor records do not appear on any MSD databases and - current debtor records do not appear on any public databases e.g. credit reference checks, internet search and - current debtor records do not appear in any information matching exercises with other government agencies e.g. IRD, ACC, Customs and - exhaustive searches are completed with utility companies e.g. power companies, electronic white pages and banks 6. Fraudulent breach debt of $2000 or more and less than $20,000 - there has been no ability to gain repayment or communicate with the debtor for at least 10 years and - current debtor records do not appear on any MSD databases and

chunks.title: All economic avenues of collection have been exhausted and the debt is less than $20,000 — student loan
chunks.text: - current debtor records do not appear on any public databases e.g. credit reference checks, internet search and - current debtor records do not appear in any information matching exercises with other government agencies e.g. IRD, ACC, Customs and - exhaustive searches are completed with utility companies e.g. power companies, electronic white pages and banks

chunks.title: The debtors assets have been seized by the police and sold — student loan
chunks.text: - the debtors assets have been seized under the Proceeds of Crime Act 1991 or the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009 and - the net amount realised through sale of the seized assets, after deductions required under section 82 of the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act have been made, is equal to or greater than the debt that will be written-off For the operational processes that must be followed for all categories of debt write-off refer to Knowledge Base.

chunks.title: Including a child in a benefit — student loan
chunks.text:
## Including a child in a benefit
A child can be included in a Social Security Act benefit if they are a dependent child.
A dependent child is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- child for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
## Child living at home or away from home
Where the child lives (at home or away from home) may help determine if the client is a dependent child.
MSD should consider the following:
- why the child is living at/away from home and
- how permanent the arrangement is and
- what payments the client makes towards the child's care and everyday living expenses

chunks.title: Eligibility — student loan
chunks.text:
## Eligibility
To be eligible for a Student Loan a student must make an application and meet the following eligibility criteria.
A student must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or be ordinarily resident and entitled to reside indefinitely in New Zealand or meet a specific residency requirement and
- be studying an approved programme at an approved tertiary provider and
- meet the performance requirement and
- provide details of a New Zealand based contact person and
- not be bankrupt and
- not have an overdue Student Loan repayment obligation with Inland Revenue
For more information about eligibility, see:
- Approved programme
- Applications
- Bankruptcy
- Contact person
- Overdue repayment obligation
- Performance requirement - passing at least half
## Entitlement
7 EFTS Lifetime limit students generally have a 7 EFTS lifetime limit of entitlement to a Student Loan (some exceptions apply).
Entitlement to the different components of the Student Loan can depend on the amount of study being undertaken, and the student's age at study start date.
Compulsory Fees generally a student is entitled to claim the compulsory fees they are charged by their provider. There are 2 exceptions, either:
- when they are studying on a part-time, part-year basis they must be studying at least 0.25 EFTS or
- when they are pilot training there is a $35,000 per EFTS limit
Living Costs to be entitled to Living Costs a student must be studying full-time (or approved Limited full-time), and under the age of 55 at study start date and not subject to a period of imprisonment.
Course-Related Costs to be entitled to Course-Related Costs a student must be studying full-time (or approved Limited full-time), and under the age of 55 at study start date.
2 EFTS limit borrowing is limited to a maximum of 2 EFTS per loan account.
Overseas study for study starting on or after 1 January 2017, students studying at an overseas campus or delivery site of a New Zealand provider must meet particular criteria.
Also, for study starting on or after 1 January 2017, students who are New Zealand permanent residents must be studying in a country they are not familiar with, and enrolled as an intramural (face to face study) student.

chunks.title: Residency and residence class visas — student loan
chunks.text:
## Residency and residence class visas
To be entitled to reside indefinitely in New Zealand, a student who is not a New Zealand citizen must hold a residence class visa. This includes a Christchurch Response Visa.
## New Zealand residency documentation
Documents that provide evidence of citizenship and/or entitlement to reside indefinitely in New Zealand include a:
- New Zealand birth certificate
Generally, a person born in New Zealand before 1 January 2006 is a New Zealand citizen by birth. A person born in New Zealand after 1 January 2006 must be born to at least 1 parent who is a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident to qualify as a New Zealand citizen by birth.
- New Zealand passport
To hold a New Zealand passport you must be a New Zealand citizen.
- Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence class visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009
- Certificate of Registration
A child born outside New Zealand (to a parent who is a New Zealand citizen) may be a New Zealand citizen from birth. However, the child must apply for a Certificate of Registration to confirm their New Zealand citizenship.
- Grant of Citizenship
People, who are entitled to reside in New Zealand indefinitely under the relevant Immigration Act, may (normally after 5 years residence in New Zealand) apply for a Grant of Citizenship. They must meet the conditions of the Grant.
- Certificate of Confirmation
This is a certificate issued to confirm that the holder is a New Zealand citizen by birth, descent or Grant of Citizenship.
British subjects, who immigrated to New Zealand before 1948 (and who resided in New Zealand for all of 1948) were made New Zealand citizens in 1949. These people are likely to have a Certificate of Confirmation or a Certificate of Naturalisation.
- Certificate of Naturalisation
Previously immigrants were naturalised as British subjects and citizens of New Zealand. Today they are given a Grant of Citizenship.
- Letter of confirmation of residence from Immigration New Zealand
## Australian citizens and permanent residents
Australian citizens and permanent residents are entitled to reside indefinitely in New Zealand.
## United Kingdom citizens
United Kingdom immigrants had unrestricted access to New Zealand and weren't required to apply to live and stay in New Zealand before 4 April 1974.
They were automatically entitled to reside indefinitely in New Zealand.
Therefore, they are not required to provide evidence to show that they are entitled to reside indefinitely in New Zealand.
However, MSD can ask for evidence to show that the student arrived in New Zealand before 4 April 1974.

chunks.title: Establishment Fee — student loan
chunks.text:
## Establishment Fee
Student Loan borrowers are expected to make a contribution toward the administration cost of their loans.
For study starting on or after 1 January 2011, all loan accounts established incur a $60 Establishment Fee.
The fee will be added to the principal balance of the account when the account is activated (by fees being paid to the student's education provider or course-related costs or living costs being paid to the student's nominated bank account).
The Establishment Fee is charged once for each loan account used. If the student finishes the year without having used the account there is no charge.
The Establishment Fee is repayable under the same terms and conditions as the rest of the Student Loan.
Note for study commencing prior to 1 January 2011 an Administration Fee of $50 was charged.
## Administration Fee - Inland Revenue
A $40 Administration Fee is charged by Inland Revenue on outstanding loan balances for each tax year.
No administration fee may be charged to a borrower for a tax year if that borrower was charged an Establishment Fee in that tax year.
The Administration Fee was first charged for the 2011-2012 tax year.

chunks.title: How long can Living Costs be paid for? — student loan
chunks.text:
## How long can Living Costs be paid for?
Living Costs payments (when nominated) are generally paid for the length of the student's enrolment on an approved course of study.
Courses of study, programmes or qualifications are assessed and approved by Tertiary Education Commission using both gross weeks and teaching weeks per year.
Gross weeks includes semester breaks or time spent on research, field work, or practical work that are requirements of the course or programme. Teaching weeks are the weeks of the course or programme where teaching occurs.
For example, a course may be approved for 40 gross weeks and 37 teaching weeks; this is to allow for the 3 week break between semesters.
## Extending the period that Living Costs can be paid
Education providers advise the study start and end dates, and any breaks, for individual students using the Verification of Study (VoS) process.
An enrolment can be extended beyond the gross weeks initially advised. An education provider will advise any changes using the Verification of Study (VoS) process.
MSD are only able to extend the payment period if the LET calculation for the extended study period confirms it is full-time study.
For example, if the course has 0.5 EFTS, the maximum period that the Student Loan Living Costs will be paid for is 20 weeks from the beginning of the course.
Students who are approved for limited full time study are also treated as being full-time for any approved extension.

chunks.title: Extramural study — student loan
chunks.text:
## Extramural study
Extramural students who meet all the eligibility and entitlement requirements can access a Student Loan.
This includes studying overseas and in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Family member of someone affected by the Christchurch mosques attack — student loan
chunks.text:
## Family member of someone affected by the Christchurch mosques attack
Some students who came to support their family members following the Christchurch mosques attack on 15 March 2019, may not have been living in New Zealand for 3 years when they apply for Student Loan.
The requirement to have lived and been entitled to live indefinitely in New Zealand for 3 years has been waived for these students.
This waiver only applies to study starting on or after 1 January 2024.
To qualify for the 3-year residency waiver the student must:
- have been granted a Residence Class Visa between 15 March 2019 and 31 December 2024.
and
- have a family member (affected person) who they are related to by birth, marriage, or adoption

chunks.title: Age — student loan
chunks.text:
## Age
For study starting on or after 1 January 2014, students under the age of 18 at study start date, who undertake fees-free study at level 1 or 2 on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework, are not eligible for any component of a Student Loan.
Students who reach the age of 18 during that period of study will not be able to access a Student Loan for that level 1 or 2 course during that period of study.
## Grandparenting
Those students under the age of 18 years whose fees-free level 1 or 2 study started in 2013 and carried over into 2014 were able to access Course-Related Costs and Living Costs, if eligible.
The period of study referred to above is the period of study covered by the student's application.
## Fees-free provision extended
For study starting on or after 1 January 2014, the level 1 and 2 fees-free provision was extended to include students up to the age of 24 years, and to level 3 study.
Also, if eligible, students who are 18 years of age or over at study start date, are able to borrow Living Costs and/or Course-Related Costs.
## Important reminders
From 1 January 2013, all students undertaking fees-free study at level 1 or 2 (and from 1 January 2014, all students undertaking fees-free study at level 3) on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework have not been able to access the compulsory fee component of a Student Loan.
For Student Loan purposes, a student can be studying a combination of level 1-3 fees-free programmes and other programmes that are not fees-free. Therefore, they may be eligible for a Student Loan to pay fees for any study that is not fees-free.

chunks.title: Full-time study — student loan
chunks.text:
## Full-time study
To be entitled to Living Costs or Course-Related Costs, a student must be a full-time student, or separately approved to study on a Limited full-time basis.
Tertiary programmes have an Equivalent Full-Time Student (EFTS) value assigned to them.
The EFTS value determines if a course of study is full-time or not.
The Verification of Study (VoS) process is used to confirm the EFTS of a student's course of study.
To be full-time, a student must be studying the minimum EFTS in regards to weeks, as outlined in the LET table below.
## Full-time - trimester 3 (summer school) study
Students who are undertaking study in trimester 3 (i.e. study that is undertaken over the summer period) need to meet all general Student Loan eligibility and entitlement criteria (like any other applicant), to qualify for a Student Loan.
If the trimester 3 is attached to their existing or subsequent study programme the student can be eligible for any part of the combined study that is full-time.
## Full year courses not full-time for the whole year
Students undertaking full-year courses that are not full-time for the whole year can be eligible for Living Costs and Course-Related Costs for any periods of study they are full-time.
This can occur where there are combinations of full-year and part-year study within the overall study programme.

chunks.title: Ordinarily resident — student loan
chunks.text: "Ordinarily resident" means someone who is normally and lawfully in New Zealand and intends to stay here. That is, they consider New Zealand to be their home. For the purposes of 'ordinarily resident', New Zealand does not include the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau. A determination of whether a student is ordinarily resident involves the exercise of discretion.

chunks.title: Being ordinarily resident — student loan
chunks.text: Being ordinarily resident in New Zealand means a student must have a close and clear connection to New Zealand. Some of the important things that indicate a student is ordinarily resident in New Zealand include: - their physical presence in New Zealand other than casually or as a traveller - they are in New Zealand because they want to be - they are here voluntarily - there is some intention to remain in New Zealand for a settled purpose - despite temporary absences from New Zealand they regularly or customarily live in New Zealand - they prefer residence in New Zealand to any other country A student cannot be ordinarily resident in 2 countries at the same time. Where it is not clear if a student is ordinarily resident, consider the following: - their intentions toward New Zealand (that is, the reasons for their absence from New Zealand and the reasons for their return). Are they going overseas for a holiday or are they intending to live overseas permanently (sighting return air tickets is a good indication)? - the length of time they spend in New Zealand compared to their periods of absence and the reasons for the absences. - property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans). - where are their cash assets principally held? (New Zealand banks or investment entities, or overseas based holdings). - is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and do they pay New Zealand taxes? - ae they on the electoral role and do they vote (or are they eligible to vote) in local body or general elections? - their commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in the community, community events, clubs and other groups)?

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — student loan
chunks.text: Whether a student is ordinarily resident is a question of both fact and degree. Their intention during any period of absence is the most important factor. You must consider all the factors of each individual case and decide whether they show a clear and close connection to New Zealand.

chunks.title: Short absences from New Zealand — student loan
chunks.text: Short absences from New Zealand (for holidays or visiting relatives etc) do not generally mean that the student is not ordinarily resident in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Interest rate — student loan
chunks.text:
## Interest rate
The interest rate is reviewed annually and is generally adjusted on 1 April each year.
The base interest rate from 1 April 2026 is 5.6%.
## Full interest write-off
A New Zealand based borrower may qualify for a full interest write-off.
To be considered a New Zealand based borrower the student will need to be physically in New Zealand for a period of 183 consecutive days (some exemptions apply).
Students with questions about the full interest write-off and exemptions should contact Inland Revenue. See:
- Inland Revenue Contact us
## Reference - Charging interest
Since 1 April 2012 the administration and charging of any interest has been the responsibility of Inland Revenue.
Before 1 April 2012 MSD charged interest on Student Loans.
- refer to the relevant loan contract for the year in question

chunks.title: Introduction — student loan
chunks.text:
## Introduction
The Student Loan Scheme provides financial support to New Zealanders to undertake tertiary education.
Eligible students must be enrolled in a recognised course of study or programme at an approved education provider.
Student Loans are delivered via a contract between the student and the Crown.
Student Loans must be repaid when a borrower earns over the applicable repayment threshold. Student Loan debt and repayments are administered by Inland Revenue.
Together with the Student Allowances Scheme, Student Loans are the main components of the Student Support system that provides funding directly to students. The government funds education providers through the Tertiary Education Commission.
For background information see:
- Background
- Legal framework - Student Loan Scheme

chunks.title: Eligibility and entitlement policies — student loan
chunks.text: The eligibility and entitlement policies of the Student Loan Scheme are not all contained within legislation. There are a number of components to the legal framework of the Student Loan Scheme.

chunks.title: Statutes — student loan
chunks.text: There are also a number of statutes that provide legal authority for some aspects of the Student Loan Scheme. For a brief description of these see: - Statutes

chunks.title: Cabinet decisions — student loan
chunks.text: The policy decisions (as agreed to by Cabinet and recorded in Cabinet Minutes) set out the eligibility and entitlement "rules" - who can access a Student Loan and on what basis. The Student Loan Scheme was introduced in 1992. The Government did not introduce legislation to provide a statutory basis for the policies on who could take out a Student Loan and how much they could borrow. It decided that as long as the Crown reserved the right to change the loan contract, contract law would suffice and therefore legislation was not required. These policy decisions are recorded as decisions of Cabinet in various Cabinet Minutes. They are described and explained in this Student Loan manual.

chunks.title: Regulations under the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011 — student loan
chunks.text: Student Loan Scheme (Details of Borrower's Contact Person) Regulations 2012 - these regulations specify what details can be collected about the borrower's contact person. Student Loan Scheme (Repayment Percentage) Regulations 2012 - these regulations specify the repayment percentage deduction, currently 12% for each dollar of income over the repayment threshold. Student Loan Scheme (Repayment Threshold) Regulations 2020 - these regulations specify the annual repayment threshold from 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2024. A repayment deduction of 12% is made for each dollar of income over the repayment threshold. Student Loan Scheme (Repayment Threshold for 2024-2025 Tax Year and Subsequent Tax Years) Regulations 2023 – these regulations specify the annual repayment threshold starting from 1 April 2024.

chunks.title: Student Loan contract — student loan
chunks.text: The Student Loan contract is a contract between the student and the lender (the Crown). The loan contract, in accordance with the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011, sets out the terms and conditions for accessing the Student Loan Scheme including, eligibility and the collection by Inland Revenue of money borrowed under the scheme. Section 13 of the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011 sets out what information must (as a minimum) be disclosed in the contract. If there is any conflict between the Student Loan contract and any legislation about Student Loans, such as the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011, the legislation will prevail. For more information see: - Student Loan Contract

chunks.title: Loan entitlement advice — student loan
chunks.text: A contract exists when: - the offer of something of value by one party is accepted by the other party - there is an intention to create a legal relationship and - there is certainty over the terms of the legal agreement The Loan Entitlement Advice (LEA) letter is both the offer of something of value and further details of the terms of the agreement. A student is considered to have accepted the offer, including the terms, if the Student Loan is not cancelled within 7 working days after the date the initial LEA letter was issued. For more information see: - Loan Accounts

chunks.title: Annual General Adjustment (AGA) — student loan
chunks.text: The Annual General Adjustment (AGA) is the name given to the annual increase in the rates and some thresholds of various social assistance payments (including Student Loan Living Costs). Any changes to the Student Loans Living Costs take effect from 1 April each year, reflecting any upward movement in the Consumers Price Index (CPI).

chunks.title: Limited full-time applications — student loan
chunks.text:
## Limited full-time applications
To be eligible for the living costs component of a Student Loan, a student must normally be studying full-time.
The exception to this requirement is when they apply and get approval to study part-time under the Limited full-time provisions.
The Limited full-time study policy for Student Loans is the same policy used to assess eligibility to Limited full-time study for a Student Allowance, follow the links below for the categories of Limited full-time study:
- Student Allowance Illness of the student
- Student Allowance There is sufficient cause that is outside the student's control
- Student Allowance The course of study is in the students academic best interests
- Student Allowance The student will complete a recognised programme that they previously commenced but did not complete and they are undertaking 'more than half of a full-time course'

chunks.title: Eligibility and Entitlement — student loan
chunks.text: A Student Loan for Living Costs provides assistance towards students' day to day living expenses. It is available for full-time (or approved Limited Full-Time) students who are taking an approved course or programme. A student must meet the standard Student Loan eligibility and entitlement criteria to qualify for Living Costs. A student can get Living Costs along with the other components of the loan, when: - the student is still included in their parent or caregiver's benefit or - their caregivers get an Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for them For more information see:

chunks.title: Who cannot get Living Costs? — student loan
chunks.text: The Living Costs component of the Student Loan is not available to: - part-time students (i.e. not approved as Limited Full-Time) - students taking a programme not recognised for Student Loan - students getting a main benefit - students getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veterans Pension or are a grandparented non-qualified partner - prisoners (Living Costs may be paid to prisoners on Home Detention) - students aged 55 and over at study start date - students under 18 at study start date enrolled in fees-free study at levels 1-3 - students under 18 at study start date enrolled in a Youth Guarantee programme

chunks.title: Maximum amount of Living Costs — student loan
chunks.text: The weekly maximum is: - $333.48 (as at 1 April 2026) less the net amount of any Student Allowance the student is getting Students can change their nominated amount of Living Costs to an amount equal to or less than their maximum entitlement. For more information see:

chunks.title: Payment of Living Costs — student loan
chunks.text: Living Costs are paid weekly in arrears, on a Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday, by direct credit to the student's nominated bank account. Living Costs are paid for the whole week, starting on Monday, through to and including Sunday. The maximum weekly amount for Living Costs is usually increased each year as part of the Annual General Adjustment on 1 April. If the 1 April falls on a day other than Monday, any increase in the weekly rate will apply from that day. For example, if 1 April is a Wednesday, any increase in the payment will apply from the Wednesday. If a student is getting a main benefit immediately before starting study, they will no longer qualify for a benefit and this will end from the Sunday before the beginning of the week they became a full-time student and became entitled to Living Costs. If a full-time student does not apply for a Student Loan before starting study, any benefit payments made for a period they did not qualify for a benefit, will need to be recovered.

chunks.title: Entitlement not claimed is lost — student loan
chunks.text: A student who doesn't apply for a Student Loan until after their study start date cannot be paid Living Costs for the period before the loan application. Students who increase their nominated amount of living costs cannot access any difference between their previous nominated amount and the new nominated amount before the change. A part week is counted as 1 week. A week runs from Monday through to and including Sunday. If a study programme starts on a Wednesday, Living Costs will be paid for the full week. Payments are made from the later of: - the study start date or - the Living Costs start date or - the date of application through to the end of the student's study programme, as long as they still qualify for Living Costs. When programmes overlap, students only get one payment for Living Costs per week.

chunks.title: Students aged under 18 enrolled in fees-free level 1-3 study — student loan
chunks.text: Students under the age of 18 at study start date, who undertake fees-free study at level 1-3 on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework, do not qualify for Living Costs. Students who become 18 years of age during a period of study are not able to get Living Costs for a level 1-3 course during their period of study.

chunks.title: Youth Guarantee 18 - 24-year-olds — student loan
chunks.text: Youth Guarantee is provided to help young people access foundation learning (NCEA levels 1-3) without paying course fees. The courses are level 1-3 on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF). The courses provide students with knowledge and information on vocational pathways, and contain a mix of practical, specific and general skill development. Students aged 18 - 24 years old can apply for a Student Loan for Living Costs while they are getting Youth Guarantee assistance. Students must have reached the age of 18 before the date their study starts to qualify for Living Costs. When a student turns 18 during a period of study, they can only get Living Costs from their next period of study. The 'period of study' referred to above is the period covered by the student's study application.

chunks.title: Students under 18 paying fees for some study — student loan
chunks.text: Students under 18 may be studying a combination of a level 1-3 fees-free Youth Guarantee course, and another programme that is not fees-free. These students may be eligible for Living Costs for any study not fees-free.

chunks.title: Definition and use of a Student Loan Account — student loan
chunks.text:
## Definition and use of a Student Loan Account
A Loan Account is the administrative mechanism used to record and manage borrowing by a student from the Student Loan Scheme. It holds all the borrowing transactions related to a particular period of study, usually a maximum of 52 weeks, including; the payment of tuition fees, course-related costs and living costs, as well as the establishment fee and any refunds from providers.
A Loan Account can be longer than 52 weeks if a student is studying an approved programme that is longer than 52 weeks.
Loan Accounts have not included interest from 1 April 2012. Any interest that may be charged is charged by Inland Revenue after the loan balance has been transferred to them for collection.
The Loan Account records the amounts transferred to Inland Revenue for collection. From 1 April 2012, this has occurred on a daily basis.
When students apply for a Student Loan, a Loan Account is established. They are not obliged to use their Student Loan. There is no charge or penalty if it is not used.
## Overlapping periods of study
When there are overlapping periods of study, make sure the cumulative Course-Related Costs entitlement does not exceed the maximum of $1000.
A Loan Account generally covers a 52 week period (or longer for programmes longer than 52 weeks).
This is a cumulative assessment and therefore will require consideration of the total entitlement over the entire study period.

chunks.title: Loan repayments — student loan
chunks.text:
## Loan repayments
Loan repayments can be made at any time to Inland Revenue.
From 1 April 2012 once a Student Loan borrower earns income in excess of the relevant pay period repayment threshold they are required to make Student Loan repayments (their repayment obligation) to Inland Revenue, unless Inland Revenue approve an exception, in which case the annual repayment threshold will apply.
Prior to 1 April 2012 a Student Loan borrower was only required to make Student Loan repayments (their repayment obligation) to Inland Revenue once they earned income in excess of the annual repayment threshold.
For more information see:
- Deskfile Repayment thresholds (current)
Students who wish to make voluntary payments or enquire about interest, or their repayment obligations should contact Inland Revenue. See:
- Inland Revenue Contact us
To ensure the Student Loan repayments are paid at the correct rate a student must use the correct tax code.

chunks.title: Loan statements — student loan
chunks.text:
## Loan statements
Student Loan statements provide the borrower with a breakdown of their loan account transactions for a particular period.
From 1 January 2012 Inland Revenue has been responsible for issuing Student Loan statements to borrowers.
Prior to 1 January 2012 StudyLink was responsible for issuing Student Loan statements to students covering transactions that occurred prior to their loan account being transferred to Inland Revenue.
StudyLink sent the final Student Loan statements on the 31 December 2011 with projected interest calculated to 28 February 2012.
## Requests for statements
From 1 January 2012 students can request a statement at any time by contacting Inland Revenue or requesting a statement via their 'myIR' account. See:
- Inland Revenue Contact us
- Inland Revenue myIR Secure Online Services

chunks.title: What is the No Asset Procedure? — student loan
chunks.text:
## What is the No Asset Procedure?
No Asset Procedure is an alternative to bankruptcy. It is for debtors who have no means of repaying their debts. This procedure lasts for 12 months instead of the normal 3 year term for bankruptcy.
To enter into a No Asset Procedure the student must have:
- no realisable assets
- unsecured debts between $1,000 and $50,000
and not have:
- previously been through a No Asset Procedure
- previously been bankrupt
- the means of repaying any amount towards the debt
- a creditors petition outstanding against them
Students accepted into a No Asset Procedure on or after 03 December 2007 remain eligible for the Student Loan for study from that date and the Student Loan debt is not dischargeable.
When a student has entered into a No Asset Procedure, they must declare it in their Student Loan application or complete a Change of Circumstances form if the student is currently getting a Student Loan. Failure to advise is both a breach of the loan contract and an offence under the Insolvency Act 2006.
The Official Assignee will be responsible for the administration of bankruptcy and alternatives to bankruptcy including the No Asset Procedure and Debt Repayment Orders.

chunks.title: Students not entitled to the compulsory fee component — student loan
chunks.text:
## Students not entitled to the compulsory fee component
The compulsory fee component is not available to:
- students who do not authorise payment of their fees from their loan account to their tertiary education provider
- students undertaking a qualification at levels 1-3 on the New Zealand Qualifications and Credentials Framework where the fees for the qualification are fully funded by the government a student should be referred to their education provider if they are unsure whether their qualification is fully funded by the government
- a student should be referred to their education provider if they are unsure whether their qualification is fully funded by the government
- part-time part-year students who are studying less than 0.25 EFTSif a part-time part-year student studying less than 0.25 EFTS subsequently enrols in another programme they may become entitled
- if a part-time part-year student studying less than 0.25 EFTS subsequently enrols in another programme they may become entitled
- students enrolled in a Youth Guarantee programme when the fees for the qualification are fully funded by the government
- students who can use their remaining first-year Fees Free entitlement in 2025, unless they have compulsory fees that are higher than their remaining entitlement if this is the case, the student is still entitled to the compulsory fee component of a Student Loan to cover fees not covered by Fees Free entitlement
- if this is the case, the student is still entitled to the compulsory fee component of a Student Loan to cover fees not covered by Fees Free entitlement
## Important reminders
Students may study a combination of government funded Youth Guarantee programmes and other non-funded programmes.
These students may be eligible for the compulsory fee component of the Student Loan to pay fees for study that is not funded through Youth Guarantee.
Students who pay all or part of their fees from their own resources, or have them paid by a third party, cannot access the compulsory fee component of the loan for that portion of their compulsory fees.

chunks.title: Objecting to details of a Student Loan — student loan
chunks.text:
## Objecting to details of a Student Loan
If a borrower wishes to object to the details of a loan advance made or charged to them, as set out in a notification they receive, they must write to the Loan Manager.
A borrower may only object if they reasonably believe those details are incorrect.
Any objection must:
- state the reasons for the objection
- include a copy of the notification given to the borrower
- be received by the Loan Manager within 31 days of the date of the notification
Note the Loan Manager may extend the time within which the objection must be received if it would be reasonable to do so.
The Loan Manager will then consider any objections, and as soon as is practicable, write to the borrower and advise them of their decision.
The Loan Manager must also advise Inland Revenue of any decisions made in respect of an objection.
## Objections not allowed by the Loan Manager
If an objection is not wholly allowed by the Loan Manager, the borrower may require that the objection be determined by MSD.
The borrower has 21 days from the date the Loan Manager notifies them of the decision, to formally notify MSD.
Note MSD may extend the time within which the borrower must notify MSD, if it would be reasonable to do so.
MSD will then consider any objections, and as soon as is practicable, write to the borrower and the Loan Manager and advise them of their decision, and the reason(s) for it.
The Loan Manager must advise Inland Revenue of any decision(s) made by MSD.
## Objections to Disputes Tribunal and District Court
If an objection is not wholly allowed by the Chief Executive, the borrower may apply to the Disputes Tribunal for a determination of the dispute if the amount in dispute is within the financial jurisdiction of the Disputes Tribunal.
Alternatively, the borrower may apply to the District Court for a determination of the dispute.
The borrower has 30 days from the date the Chief Executive notified them of their decision to make an application.
Note a Referee of a Disputes Tribunal or a District Court Judge may extend the time within which the borrower must make an application, if it would be reasonable to do so.
The Loan Manager must then advise Inland Revenue of any decision(s) made by the Disputes Tribunal or the District Court.

chunks.title: Obligations, offences and penalties — student loan
chunks.text:
## Obligations, offences and penalties
A student, education provider or any other third party is required to provide complete and accurate information and advice, and in some cases, papers, documents, records or other things relevant to the determination of a student's eligibility or entitlement to a Student Loan.
Failure or refusal to comply with a request to supply information or documents or answer questions may result in the suspension of entitlement or the refusal to grant entitlement to a Student Loan.
Education providers are also required to keep, maintain and provide MSD with access to enrolment records, when necessary to assess and determine eligibility or entitlement to a Student Loan.
In some situations, it is an offence not to comply with these obligations and there are penalties relating to these offences.
For an offence to be proven, it must be prosecuted in a court of law. The court decides whether to impose a penalty, and the amount of any penalty.
If there is information that suggests a student, education provider or other third party has committed an offence, you should inform your manager.

chunks.title: Student offences and penalties — student loan
chunks.text: As part of an application and when subsequently providing information If a student: - knowingly makes a false or misleading statement in an application or - knowingly makes a false or misleading statement in a notification of a change of their circumstances that effects their entitlement to a Student Loan or particular amount of a Student Loan or - wilfully fails to notify MSD of any change in their circumstances that materially affects their entitlement to Student Loan they commit an offence and are liable to a term of imprisonment (not exceeding 12 months) or a fine (not exceeding $5,000). Charges must be filed within 12 months of the date on which MSD becomes aware of the offence. During an investigation If a student, when asked a question, or when they are required to provide information or documents necessary to determine entitlement: - knowingly makes a false or misleading statement or - knowingly makes a statement from which any material matter has been omitted or - knowingly provides any false or misleading paper, document or record or - knowingly provides, a paper, document, or record from which any material matter has been omitted or - refuses to answer a question during an investigation they commit an offence and are liable to a fine not exceeding $2,000. Charges must be filed within 12 months of the date on which MSD becomes aware of the offence.

chunks.title: Education provider offences and penalties — student loan
chunks.text: If an education provider, when required to provide information necessary to establish entitlement, intentionally: - makes a false or misleading statement or - makes a statement from which any material matter has been omitted or - provides a false or misleading paper, document, or record or - provides a paper, document, or record from which any material matter has been omitted or - fails or refuses to provide requested information as soon as possible after a time requested by MSD they commit an offence and are liable to a fine not exceeding $5,000 (or when the offence is a continuing one, a fine not exceeding $500 for each day the offence continues). For offences committed on or after 1 August 2020, charges must be filed within 12 months of the date on which MSD becomes aware of the offence. For offences committed before 1 August 2020, charges must be filed within 6 months after the date on which the offence was committed.

chunks.title: Third party offences and penalties — student loan
chunks.text: During the course of an investigation, MSD may ask a third party questions. They must answer these questions. When they refuse to answer a question, they commit an offence and are liable to a fine not exceeding $2000. Charges must be filed within 12 months of the date on which MSD becomes aware of the offence.

chunks.title: Suspicion of offence — student loan
chunks.text: If there is information that suggests a student, education provider, or third party has committed an offence as outlined above, you should inform your manager.

chunks.title: Other assistance — student loan
chunks.text:
## Other assistance
The following forms of assistance do not affect students' entitlement to a Student Loan:
- Accident Rehabilitation and Compensation Insurance (ACC)
- Accident insurance in general, including that paid by private insurers
- Working for Families Tax Credits (including family tax credit)
- Child Support
- study leave on pay (teachers, public servants etc)
- research grants
- scholarships (including grants offered by the Careers Service, Tertiary Education Commission (TEC) and Māori Education Trust Scholarships)
- training grants paid to 6th year medical students
- assistance offered by Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade

chunks.title: Overdue repayment obligation — student loan
chunks.text:
## Overdue repayment obligation
Students, who have an overdue repayment obligation with Inland Revenue of $500 or more, where some or all of it has been overdue for a year or more, are not eligible for further Student Loans while their overdue repayment obligation remains at $500 or more.
This policy was introduced for all new applications from 7 February 2013.
The SAL system confirms information on overdue loan repayments with Inland Revenue through the Business to Business (B2B) online data exchange.

chunks.title: Parental consent definition — student loan
chunks.text:
## Parental consent definition
If a student is under 18 years of age when they sign their loan contract, then one of their parents will generally also have to give their consent for the student to enter into the loan contract.
Only one parent's consent is required.
By giving parental consent they are giving the student permission to access all components of the Student Loan (fees, course-related costs and living costs).
By giving their consent, the parent is not guaranteeing the loan. The only person responsible for repayment of any loan debt is the student.
The parent cannot subsequently withdraw their consent. They agree to this when they sign the parental consent.
The parental consent is an administrative provision only. It is not part of the contract and therefore does not affect the operation of the contract, including the terms and conditions, and the enforceability of it.
Once the contract is agreed, this administrative provision is completed.
Note under the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011, students under the age of 18 must be treated as if they are 18 years of age for the purposes of the Contract and Commercial Law Act 2017.
## Parent definition for Student Loans
A parent includes a:
- step-parent
- guardian
- caregiver or
- any person 'acting in place of a parent'
A person is considered to be acting in place of a parent if they have been, or are, responsible for the student's wellbeing and/or financial support. This can include grandparents, other relatives (including whāngai) and foster parents if they are acting in place of a student's parent(s).
## Parental consent is not required
Students under 18 years of age can only sign the loan contract without providing parental consent if they:
- have one or more dependent children
- are married
- are in a civil union or
- have had a Student Allowance ICA application approved in the current or a previous year
Some students under 18 years of age may face difficulties in getting parental consent. If a student has circumstances that demonstrate the required level of independence, for example; the student would meet the 'ICA independence test' (if they applied), then parental consent is not required.

chunks.title: Payment of Course-Related Costs — student loan
chunks.text:
## Payment of Course-Related Costs
Students must claim their Course-Related Costs up to the $1000 maximum, either by applying online or completing a Course-Related Costs claim form.
After a claim has been made and approved, the money is paid by direct credit into the student's nominated bank account.
All claims must be made by the end date of the student's course.

chunks.title: Previous study performance — student loan
chunks.text: Generally, to access a Student Loan, a student will need to have passed at least half the EFTS of their previous study. This requirement applies to all study commencing on or after 1 January 2011. Tertiary qualifications have an Equivalent Full-Time Student (EFTS) value assigned to them. Where a qualification is divided into papers or modules, the EFTS are disaggregated. That is, each paper or module is assigned a certain number of the EFTS of the whole qualification.

chunks.title: When will a student's performance be assessed? — student loan
