chunks.text: A student's performance will be assessed when: - they apply for a Student Loan for study starting on 1 January 2011 or later and - they have studied at least 1.6 EFTS or more since accessing any part of a Student Loan for courses of study ending in 2009 or later

chunks.title: Which EFTS are counted — student loan
chunks.text: The EFTS count commences (at the earliest) with the student's first course with an end date in 2009 (or later) and for which the student used one or more parts of the Student Loan (eg living costs, course fees, or course-related costs). The EFTS for all tertiary study is counted, regardless of whether the student has used a Student Loan for that study or not, unless following the provision applies.

chunks.title: Period over which performance is assessed — student loan
chunks.text: Performance is only assessed over a 5 year rolling cycle; this means after 5 years, the first year of the original 5 year assessment is disregarded. This cycle continues. This ensures that earlier failure does not continue to adversely affect a student but more recent failure does. Example A student whose EFTS count includes a course with an end date of 15 June 2009 will have the EFTS for that course counted for any Student Loan application they make for any course with a start date from 1 January 2011 to 15 June 2014. The EFTS for that course will not be included in the performance assessment for study starting on or after 16 June 2014. When a student withdraws from study, the course end date is the date the student withdrew from study.

chunks.title: The performance calculation — student loan
chunks.text: Of all the EFTS that are counted in the previous 5 years, the EFTS passed need to be equal to, or exceed the EFTS failed. The EFTS value of papers or modules in a course can vary. This means that the number of papers a student passes and fails may not be the same proportion of the course as the number of EFTS that a student has passed or failed.

chunks.title: Which EFTS are not counted — student loan
chunks.text: In the following situations EFTS will not be counted: - if the student has failed to pass at least half of a course for reasons beyond their control - if the course end date is more than 5 years before - if the course has not ended before the new course starts and the student has not withdrawn - if the student has formally withdrawn from a course and received a full refund of their tuition fees - if the student has received a partial refund of their tuition fees for 2020 study due to the COVID-19 pandemic

chunks.title: Full fees refund — student loan
chunks.text: If a student withdraws from a course and receives a full fees refund, the student is considered not to have studied for that course and therefore the enrolment is not included in the performance requirement EFTS count. An education provider may charge a fee for the withdrawal. The payment of this fee from the fee refund does not prevent the refund from being a full fees refund. When there were no fees drawn from a student's loan account, there cannot be a 'full fees refund' when that student withdraws from that course of study. In these situations, the student can have the relevant EFTS for that study excluded if MSD considers they have effectively not undertaken that study based on the new EFTS value received as part of the withdrawal advice from their provider. This provision applies to both withdrawals from an entire study programme and to part withdrawals, for example, on a paper or semester basis. The EFTS that are excluded are the EFTS which have been refunded.

chunks.title: Partial fee refund due to the COVID-19 pandemic — student loan
chunks.text: When a partial fee refund occurs for study in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the EFTS value of the course or papers covered by the partial fee refund is not counted. The EFTS calculation for the performance requirement is different to the EFTS calculation for the lifetime limit. For more information see: - The 7 EFTS lifetime limit

chunks.title: Overlapping courses — student loan
chunks.text: Only the EFTS of completed courses are counted. For the purposes of the Student Loans performance requirement a course is completed when the end date has passed or the student has withdrawn (whether formally or not) from the course, whichever occurs first. This means that a student who applies for a Student Loan for a new course will not have the EFTS for their previous course included in the performance assessment for their new course in cases where the new course has a start date earlier than the end (or withdrawal) date of their previous course.

chunks.title: Failure for reasons beyond a student's control — student loan
chunks.text: The 'failure for reasons beyond a student's control' exception provides discretion to make an eligibility decision based on policy intent, the wording of the Cabinet decision and the facts of the particular situation. Generally a student will not be eligible for a Student Loan if they have failed to pass at least half of the EFTS of their study in the previous 5 years. If a student's failure to pass at least half of the EFTS of a particular course or courses was for reasons beyond their control, they can have the EFTS for those courses excluded. The student must provide evidence of those reasons, except in cases that are self-evident or where MSD already holds that evidence. Reasons beyond the student's control may include, but are not limited to: - medical, social or psychological reasons which affected the student's performance - course cancellation - where the education provider cancelled or changed the course or withdrew tuition Financial hardship is not, in itself, an acceptable circumstance. When an exemption for 'reasons beyond a student's control' is approved, the student must be advised of the consequences of further failure, for the same reasons for future entitlement. In particular, that ongoing failure will more likely than not result in a further application being declined.

chunks.title: Acceptable evidence of reasons beyond a student's control — student loan
chunks.text: Acceptable evidence of reasons beyond the student's control may include: - a medical certificate specifically stating the effect of the illness on the student's study. When the illness is ongoing, it needs to include confirmation that the student is now capable of successfully undertaking their study - a statement from a solicitor, minister of religion, social worker, etc, setting out details of family circumstances that have adversely affected the student's study. Where this reason is ongoing, it needs to include confirmation that the student is now capable of successfully undertaking their study. - a statement by their education provider advising of a change in the course, withdrawal of tuition etc, which was not initiated by the student and which made it impossible for them to complete the course

chunks.title: Ongoing failure for reasons beyond a student's control — student loan
chunks.text: It is not appropriate to continue to allow a student to access a Student Loan where it is evident that they are persistently failing to pass at least half of their study, even if this is for reasons that are beyond the student's control. The performance test is designed to ensure only students who succeed in their study can continue to access a Student Loan. If a student is repeatedly failing to meet the performance requirement, even for reasons beyond their control, further investigation will be required. This investigation may include, but is not limited to, consideration of whether: - a reduction in study is likely to improve the student's performance. If this means the student reduces their study to less than full-time, limited full-time approval may be appropriate. - the student is receiving their 'full and correct entitlement'. A student who is not succeeding be under financial pressure due to unanticipated costs associated with their situation. They may also have difficulty in accessing the services they need if there is a cost involved. In some cases, it may be prudent to suspend access to a Student Loan until a decision is made.

chunks.title: Regaining access to a Student Loan — student loan
chunks.text: If the performance requirement set out above is not met, access to a Student Loan can be regained by studying and passing enough EFTS so that the total number of EFTS passed in the last 5 years is at least equal to the number of EFTS not passed.

chunks.title: Protected person — student loan
chunks.text:
## Protected person
A protected person is a person recognised under sections 130 and 131 of the Immigration Act 2009 when there are substantial grounds for believing they would be in danger of:
- being tortured if deported from New Zealand or
- arbitrary deprivation of life or cruel treatment if deported from New Zealand
Once they are granted protected person status under the Immigration Act 2009, a protected person needs to apply for a Residence Class Visa to be entitled to reside indefinitely in New Zealand.
They meet the residency criteria for a Student Loan from the date they are granted a Residence Class Visa.
However, for study starting on or after 1 May 2022, a protected person meets the residency criteria for a Student Loan from the date they are granted protected person status under the Immigration Act 2009.
They are not required to hold a Residence Class Visa, but are required to hold a valid Temporary Entry Visa.

chunks.title: Mandate or quota refugees — student loan
chunks.text:
## Mandate or quota refugees
Refugees who come to New Zealand under the refugee quota system are known as mandate or quota refugees.
They are normally granted a Residence Class Visa automatically with their refugee status, before their arrival in New Zealand.
They are entitled to reside indefinitely in New Zealand from the date they are granted that visa.
They meet the residency criteria for a Student Loan from the date they are granted a Residence Class Visa.
## Convention or asylum refugees
Refugees who are granted refugee status under the Refugee Convention are known as convention or asylum refugees. They apply for refugee status under the Immigration Act 2009 after they have arrived in New Zealand.
Once they are granted refugee status, they need to apply for a Residence Class Visa to be entitled to reside indefinitely in New Zealand.
They meet the residency criteria for a Student Loan from the date they are granted a Residence Class Visa.
However, for study starting on or after 1 May 2022, a student who has refugee status meets the residency criteria for a Student Loan from the date they are granted refugee status under the Immigration Act 2009.
They are not required to hold a Residence Class Visa, but are required to hold a valid Temporary Entry Visa.

chunks.title: Refusing or suspending access — student loan
chunks.text: The reasons a Student Loan is refused or suspended can vary. Some examples are: - not meeting the performance requirement - passing at least half their courses - misuse of payments or - attempted fraud Refusal of a Student Loan, or suspension of access to a Student Loan may be temporary, or for a longer period of time, depending on the student's circumstances. Note for more information regarding the legislative basis for eligibility and entitlement to a Student Loan, see:

chunks.title: Questions to consider — student loan
chunks.text: When considering whether to refuse or suspend access to a Student Loan, all the relevant information, including the student's circumstances, need to be confirmed. Questions you may need to ask include, (but are not limited to): 1. Does the student have very high debt levels in relation to the type of course they want to study or their particular situation? - high debt on its own may not be a problem as high levels of debt resulting from high cost courses may not lead to poor outcomes for students 2. Has the student repeatedly failed a course (e.g. 2 or more times) and is therefore unlikely to succeed or complete their qualification? - if a student is continually failing a course or has excessive debt levels, a discussion could be arranged between the student, the education provider and if the student's under 18 years, their parents to discuss our concerns 3. Is there suspicion of fraud or misuse of the Student Loan Scheme? - is the student using the scheme primarily as a form of income support (as opposed to providing support for gaining a qualification)? For example, it is clear a student has only applied for the Student Loan scheme as a means of support as they do not qualify for a main benefit under the Social Security Act 2018, or a student is applying for and accessing multiple Student Loan course-related cost entitlements for costs not related to their course. 4. Is there ongoing use of a Student Loan that is more than is considered reasonable for achieving the intended qualification? For example by applying for and/or accessing multiple course-related costs for similar items. 5. Is the intended study appropriate given the student's personal circumstances? - the student may have a medical or other condition that would make it inappropriate for them to undertake certain types of study or certain areas of study

chunks.title: Suspension of a Student Loan account — student loan
chunks.text: When suspending access to a Student Loan account you must consider: - why the suspension is required - what components of the Student Loan account are being suspended - what date the suspension is effective from - what actions are required (by both StudyLink and the student) for the Student Loan account to be reactivated - if reactivated, the date the Student Loan account should be reactivated It is important to gather all the relevant information to correctly make an assessment of a student's circumstances.

chunks.title: Residency — student loan
chunks.text: A student is eligible to get a Student Loan if: - the student is a New Zealand citizen or - the student is ordinarily resident in New Zealand and - has lived in New Zealand for at least 3 years and - has been entitled under the Immigration Act 2009 to live indefinitely in New Zealand for at least 3 years or - the student is a refugee or protected person and is entitled to live indefinitely in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 or - for study starting from 1 May 2022, the student is a refugee or protected person and holds a valid temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 or - for study starting from 1 May 2022, the student is an immediate family member of a refugee or protected person and is either: living in New Zealand on a valid Temporary Entry Visa, and eligible to transition to a Residence Class Visa with the refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009 orthe holder of a Residence Class Visa, the student transitioned to with the refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009 - living in New Zealand on a valid Temporary Entry Visa, and eligible to transition to a Residence Class Visa with the refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009 or - the holder of a Residence Class Visa, the student transitioned to with the refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009 or - the student is entitled to live indefinitely in New Zealand, and was sponsored into New Zealand by a family member, who at the time the student entered New Zealand, was recognised as a refugee or a protected person, and held a Residence Class Visa under the Immigration Act 2009 or - the student holds a Christchurch Response Visa under the Immigration Act 2009 or - the student holds a Residence Class Visa under the Immigration Act 2009, and would have been eligible for a Christchurch Response Visa if they did not already hold a Residence Class Visa or - for study starting from 1 January 2024, the student was granted a Residence Class Visa between 15 March 2019 and 31 December 2024 and is a family member of someone who: has a Christchurch Response Visa orwas eligible for a Christchurch Response Visa, held a Resident Visa on 15 March 2019, and currently holds a Residence Class Visa or is a New Zealand citizen orwould have been eligible for a Christchurch Response Visa but already had a Permanent Resident Visa or New Zealand citizenship on 15 March 2019 orwas granted New Zealand citizenship after holding a Christchurch Response Visa - has a Christchurch Response Visa or

chunks.title: Residency — student loan
chunks.text: - was eligible for a Christchurch Response Visa, held a Resident Visa on 15 March 2019, and currently holds a Residence Class Visa or is a New Zealand citizen or - would have been eligible for a Christchurch Response Visa but already had a Permanent Resident Visa or New Zealand citizenship on 15 March 2019 or - was granted New Zealand citizenship after holding a Christchurch Response Visa or - the student is an Afghan national, or a member of that person's family, who is ordinarily resident in New Zealand and has been granted residency. They were granted residency as part of a specific group of Afghan nationals who arrived in New Zealand in April 2013 and are exempt from the residency stand-down or - for study starting on or after 1 January 2022, the student holds an Afghan Emergency Resettlement Residency Visa under the Immigration Act 2009

chunks.title: Reviewing entitlement to a Student Loan — student loan
chunks.text:
## Reviewing entitlement to a Student Loan
A student's entitlement to a Student Loan may be reviewed by StudyLink at any time to determine if the student was or is entitled to receive payment(s). A review may result in a change in the student's entitlement.
When a review results in a change in living costs payment, this will generally occur from the Monday of the week that the entitlement changed.
It may be appropriate to make the change from a later date if the circumstances suggest it would be reasonable to do so. There may be a reason a student did not notify StudyLink of their change of circumstances. This may include a situation where a death of a family member changed entitlement, but the situation was traumatic and therefore notification did not occur immediately. Each case needs to be considered on its merits.
Note a review may identify that a student has not received their full entitlement. If this occurs, back payment of arrears should be considered and discussed with the student as they may decide not to incur further debt.
If it is determined that a student received a payment that they were not entitled to, the students' circumstances need to be considered and confirmed to determine if a debt should be established.
When a student gets a living costs payment that they were not entitled to, and subsequently becomes approved for a Student Allowance or Benefit for the same period, the Benefit or Student Allowance arrears should be initially used to pay back the Student Loan MSD debt.
## For more information on reviewing entitlement see:
- Converting all or part of a Loan into an MSD debt
- Refusing or suspending access to a Student Loan

chunks.title: Statutes — student loan
chunks.text: The Student Loan Scheme Act 2011 is the primary legislation for the Student Loan Scheme. It provides the legal framework for the collection of Student Loan debt by Inland Revenue, core aspects of the Student Loan contract, and the administrative arrangements that exist between Inland Revenue and MSD. The following statutes provide the legal authority for the administration of the Student Loan Scheme.

chunks.title: Student Loan Scheme Act 2011 — student loan
chunks.text: This Act provides for: The establishment of a Student Loan, including: - the exchange of information about loan applicants between MSD and Inland Revenue - information that must be disclosed in the loan contract and the provision of the loan contract to borrowers - the establishment fee - the right to cancel a loan contract - the transfer of loan balances to Inland Revenue, (including the associated objection process) - that Student Loan contracts are enforceable against a minor - the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011 applies despite anything to the contrary in any Student Loan contract if a Student Loan contract cannot be interpreted in a manner that is consistent with the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011, then the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011 prevails over the terms of the Student Loan contract - if a Student Loan contract cannot be interpreted in a manner that is consistent with the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011, then the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011 prevails over the terms of the Student Loan contract The Student Loan recovery responsibilities of Inland Revenue including: - the calculation of the repayment obligations of borrowers - the administration fee - the calculation of interest - the collection of repayment obligations from borrowers - offences and penalties - dispute procedures and rights to challenge - hardship relief - the statutory authority for Regulations including: the repayment thresholds and approval of charitable organisations in relation to working overseas and obtain an interest write-off

chunks.title: Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act 2003 — student loan
chunks.text: The Student Loan contract is not a consumer credit contract, as stated in section 15(1)(ca) of the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act 2003 (CCCFA), and section 206 of the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011. When the government agreed to remove the Student Loan contract from the definition of consumer credit contracts under the CCCFA it was noted the government would adhere to the spirit and intent of the CCCFA.

chunks.title: Education and Training Act 2020 — student loan
chunks.text: Part 4, Part 6, Schedule 9 and Schedule 10 contain the empowering provisions that provide the statutory authority for MSD to administer the Student Loan Scheme. This includes (but is not limited to): - the authority to require applicants to provide information necessary to establish eligibility and/or entitlement - the Results of Study (ROS) data-match - offences and penalties in relation to students, education providers or third parties - the use of information obtained under the Social Security Act 2018 - the use of information obtained under Part 9 of the Public and Community Housing Management Act 1992 - the recovery of debts, other than valid Student Loan debt which is recovered by Inland Revenue through the PAYE system - the Verification of Study (VoS) data-match

chunks.title: How Living Cost entitlement is affected by Student Allowance entitlement — student loan
chunks.text:
## How Living Cost entitlement is affected by Student Allowance entitlement
Entitlement to Living Costs is reduced by deducting the Student Allowances entitlement (not including Accommodation Benefit).
This is calculated on a weekly basis and may result in a student receiving less than their nominated amount of Living Costs.
## Student does not apply for Student Allowance
If a student does not apply, and therefore does not get a Student Allowance, they can get the maximum rate of Living Costs.
## Subsequent entitlement to Student Allowance
If a student is subsequently assessed to have entitlement to a Student Allowance, their Living Costs entitlement for any overlapping period must be adjusted accordingly.
This means, that where a Student Allowance back-payment covers a period where they have received Living Costs, the amount of the back-payment for that period is used to repay that Student Loan debt.
A student is not entitled to be paid twice (Student Allowance and Living Costs) for the same period.
## Legal authority to adjust Living Cost entitlement when Student Allowance entitlement is subsequently established
The Education and Training Act 2020 gives authority for the recovery of Student Loan debt from a Student Allowance payment, when Living Costs have already been paid for that period.

chunks.title: Obligations — student loan
chunks.text: Students, education providers and other third parties all have important obligations, both to provide information, and to respond to requests for information.

chunks.title: Student obligations — student loan
chunks.text: Application and subsequent advice A student must provide complete and accurate information when completing an application and when advising of a change in circumstances. A student must advise of any change in circumstances that would affect their entitlement to a Student Loan. Written request to a student At any time, by written notice to any student, MSD can require the student to provide any papers, documents, records, information or other things that are in the student's possession or under the student's control that are required to determine a student's entitlement to a Student Loan. The authority also allows MSD to make copies of any such papers, documents or records, in case MSD needs to retain the documents for any future assessments that may occur. Investigation of entitlement At any time MSD may investigate a student's circumstances in order to determine whether or not a student is or was entitled to receive any component of the Student Loan. A student, who is asked questions during this investigation, must answer those questions.

chunks.title: Education provider obligations — student loan
chunks.text: Education providers are obliged to provide MSD with information and details that MSD reasonably requires in order to determine a student's entitlement to a Student Loan. The mechanism for requesting this information is the Verification of Study (VoS) process and the procedures that surround it. The Verification of Study (VOS) process may include follow up questions.

chunks.title: Private training establishment — student loan
chunks.text: Private training establishments are also required to: - keep accurate enrolment and academic records for each student enrolled in a programme or training scheme and - ensure that the enrolment records are readily available, upon request, to MSD, among others This provision is specific to private training establishments as they are not public institutions and therefore are not subject to the provisions of the Public Records Act 2005.

chunks.title: Third party obligations — student loan
chunks.text: At any time MSD may investigate a student's circumstances in order to determine whether or not a student is or was entitled to receive any component of a Student Loan. In the course of this investigation, MSD may ask a third party questions. The third party must answer these questions. MSD can ask the third party for documents supporting the answers to these questions, but they are not required to provide any documents.

chunks.title: Suspension or refusal to grant entitlement — student loan
chunks.text: When MSD are satisfied that a student or third party has, without reasonable cause, failed or refused to comply with a request to supply information, or documents, or answer questions, MSD may suspend or refuse to grant entitlement. A student must be warned of the consequence of failure or refusal to comply with a request, and given the opportunity to either explain their refusal or comply. When a third party fails to comply with a request for information or documents or answer questions, MSD must, before taking action to suspend or refuse to grant entitlement, provide the student with the opportunity to provide the information.

chunks.title: Entering into a Student Loan Contract — student loan
chunks.text: Students applying for a Student Loan must sign a Student Loan Contract. This is a contract with the Crown. This means either signing a paper Student Loan Contract, or 'accepting' a Student Loan Contract online.

chunks.title: Parental consent — student loan
chunks.text: For students under 18 years of age, a parent must generally provide parental consent. Students under the age of 18 cannot accept a Student Loan Contract online, as a parent is generally required to provide parental consent. Parental consent is an administrative requirement and therefore is not part of a Student Loan Contract.

chunks.title: Enforceability where student is under 18 years of age (a minor) — student loan
chunks.text: Under the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011, students under the age of 18 (a minor) must be treated, for the purposes of the Contract and Commercial Law Act 2017, as if they are 18 years of age.

chunks.title: What is in the Student Loan Contract? — student loan
chunks.text: The contract sets out the terms and conditions of a Student Loan, including: - the current interest rate and when interest is charged - the annual repayment threshold - the repayment rate - the student's obligation to provide the information to MSD or Inland Revenue necessary for the management of their Student Loan - the establishment and administration fees - the student's right to cancel the loan contract within 7 working days of the date of the initial Loan Entitlement Advice (LEA) - changes to eligibility - the transfer of loan debt to Inland Revenue for collection - the right to object to any amount borrowed and transferred to Inland Revenue for collection - the parts of a Student Loan - repaying a Student Loan - notices - who is responsible for the Student Loan - the applicable law and that in the event of a conflict between the contract and the Student Loan Scheme Act 2011, the Act applies - offences MSD has a responsibility to ensure that students who ask, are given correct and complete information about the Student Loan Contract and the obligations it contains.

chunks.title: What is a contract? — student loan
chunks.text: A contract exists when: - the offer of something of value by one party is accepted by the other party - there is an intention to create a legal relationship and - there is certainty over the terms of the legal agreement When any of these things are missing or in doubt, the court, if asked to rule on the existence or enforceability of a contract, may determine that there is no contract, and therefore the contract obligations cannot be enforced.

chunks.title: Situations that may arise regarding the enforceability of a Student Loan Contract — student loan
chunks.text: Situation Requirement There is doubt about the capacity of a student to fully understand the contract - in particular, applicants who may have an intellectual disability It will depend on the facts of the case. Seek further advice, including legal advice The student has used a preferred name rather than their legal name on their contract Their legal name must be used to avoid uncertainty and therefore legal risk The student has not signed the contract The contract must be signed by the student The student's name has been misspelled on the contract A minor misspelling of the student's name is unlikely to invalidate the contract Parental consent is either missing or has been completed by someone other than a parent As the parental consent is an administrative requirement, the contract is still valid and enforceable

chunks.title: Student getting a main benefit — student loan
chunks.text: Students getting a main benefit can borrow money under the Student Loan Scheme for: - compulsory fees and - course-related costs Students getting a main benefit cannot borrow the living costs component of a Student Loan. This is because their main benefit provides financial assistance towards their day to day living costs. Some students may not be eligible to continue receiving their main benefit if they are in full-time study. For example, see: - Jobseeker Support - Client engaged in study Note young people getting Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment and on a Youth Guarantee course cannot get a Student Loan.

chunks.title: Student's partner getting a main benefit — student loan
chunks.text: If a student's partner is granted a 'half couple rate' of main benefit, the student may borrow: - compulsory fees and - course-related costs and - living costs Half couple rate When only one partner in a couple qualifies for a main benefit, that partner gets paid their main benefit at a 'half couple rate'. For more information see: - New Zealand Superannuation Study

chunks.title: Student getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension — student loan
chunks.text: Students getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veterans Pension or who are a grandparented non-qualified partner cannot borrow the living costs component of a Student Loan. This is because their New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension provides financial assistance towards their day to day living costs. Students getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension can borrow for compulsory fees but cannot borrow course-related costs.

chunks.title: Student's partner getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension — student loan
chunks.text: If a student's partner is getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension, but the student does not, the student can borrow the living costs component of a Student Loan (if they meet the usual loan qualifications and are not getting a main benefit). The student can borrow for compulsory fees and if they are aged under 55 years old at study start date they can also borrow course-related costs. For more information see: - Age - Eligibility and entitlement criteria for a Student Loan

chunks.title: Student getting Extra help only — student loan
chunks.text: A student who only gets Extra Help from MSD may borrow Student Loan: - compulsory fees and - course-related costs and - living costs

chunks.title: Student getting Training Incentive Allowance — student loan
chunks.text: A Training Incentive Allowance is paid to help students getting a specified main benefit to take up education or training. Students getting a Training Incentive Allowance may still be able to get a Student Loan for compulsory fees and course-related costs in some situations. They cannot get Student Loan living costs. This is because they are getting a main benefit that provides financial assistance towards their day to day living costs. For more information see: - Training Incentive Allowance and Student Loan

chunks.title: Student getting education and employment-related training payment for course costs — student loan
chunks.text: Some students getting a main benefit may be granted education and employment-related training payments to help meet their tuition fees or other course costs. These payments are made under the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme. Students getting education and employment-related training payments for course costs can only borrow the course-related costs component of the Student Loan remaining (if any) after the education and employment-related training entitlement to course costs has been deducted. If the student gets payments under the Employment and Work Readiness Assistance Programme to help with: - care for another person or - childcare, transport or disability related costs these payments do not affect their Student Loan entitlement to course-related costs (no deduction is made). For more information see: Work readiness assistance

chunks.title: Inclusion of a child in a benefit when the child gets Student Loan living costs — student loan
chunks.text: A child who gets Student Loan living costs can still be included in a parent or caregiver's benefit if they are a dependent child for that benefit. Note parents of a 16 or 17 year old student may qualify for an Away from Home Allowance for their child's accommodation costs.

chunks.title: Eligibility — student loan
chunks.text:
## Eligibility
For Student Loan purposes, a prisoner is someone who is imprisoned or detained in prison under a sentence of imprisonment or preventative detention.
Prisoners may only access the Fees and Course-Related Costs components of a Student Loan.
For a prisoner to qualify for a Student Loan, they must:
- meet all of the qualifications for a Student Loan and
- obtain approval to study from the appropriate person at the prison
Prisoners who want to claim Course-Related Costs will be sent a claim form to complete and the prison to endorse. The prison endorses the claim to ensure the items meet prison requirements, including any security restrictions.
Students who are on home detention may be entitled to Fees, Course-Related Costs and Living Costs as long as they meet the other qualifications and for Student Loans.
## Short periods of custody
A student detained in custody for a short period of time can continue to qualify and their entitlement to Living Costs for this period as long as the imprisonment does not affect their ability to meet their minimum attendance and/or work requirements.
## Public Protection Order
A student subject to a Public Protection Order is not 'imprisoned or detained in prison under a sentence of imprisonment or preventative detention' and therefore may be entitled to all components of a Student Loan.
## Prisoners released from prison
If a student who is studying full-time leaves prison and requests Living Costs from their Student Loan, they will need to provide evidence that they are no longer in prison, for example a Steps to Freedom form.

chunks.title: Part-time students — student loan
chunks.text:
## Part-time students
The Course-Related Costs component is not available for part-time part-year students.
For study starting on or after 1 January 2012, Course-Related Costs have not been available to part-time full-year students.
If a part-time student subsequently enrols in another course or programme in the same study period and becomes full-time, they can be entitled to Course-Related Costs.
## Students aged 55 years and over
Course-Related Costs are not available to people aged 55 years and over (for study that starts on or after 1 January 2013).
Transitional provision
Students who were over 55 on 19 May 2011 (the date the policy change was announced), or who reached 55 before 1 January 2013 were entitled to Course-Related Costs for the qualification they were enrolled in on 19 May 2011, until they completed that qualification or 1 January 2015, whichever came first.
## Students aged under 18 enrolled in Youth Guarantee and fees-free level 1 and 2 study
Students under the age of 18 at study start date, who undertake other fees-free study at level 1 or 2 on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework or Youth Guarantee programmes, are not eligible for the Course-Related Costs component of the Student Loan (for study that starts on or after 1 January 2014).
Transitional provisions
Students under the age of 18 years whose fees-free level 1 or 2 study started in 2013 and carried over into 2014 were able to access the Course-Related Costs component of the Student Loan for that application.
Students who reach the age of 18 during the period of study cannot access the Course-Related Costs component of the Student Loan during that period of study.
## Important reminder
For Student Loans a student under the age of 18 may be studying a combination of level 1 or 2 fees-free/Youth Guarantee, and other programme(s) that are not fees-free. They may be eligible for the Course-Related Costs component of Student Loan for the non fees-free programme only.
## Reference
- Refer to the relevant loan contract for the year in question. These can be found on SLKBase under "Student Loan T&Cs"

chunks.title: Signing the contract — student loan
chunks.text:
## Signing the contract
A student wishing to access a Student Loan is normally required to sign and date the Student Loan Contract as a Student Loan is provided via a contract between the student and the Crown.
## Temporary inability to sign the contract
If the student is temporarily unable to sign and date the contract it can be deferred until they are able to do so.
However if deferral prevents them from commencing study, the Student Loan Contract may be completed by a third party on the applicant's behalf, using the agents form.
## Permanent inability to sign the contract
If a student is permanently unable to sign and date the contract the Student Loan Contract may be completed by a third party on the applicant's behalf, using the agents form. This would generally apply in situations where a student has a physical or intellectual incapacity to complete the contract themselves.
For more information see:
## Mental incapacity
For students, whose mental incapacity means they are unable to make decisions and manage their own property affairs, an agent can act as a property manager under part 4 of the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988, or as an attorney in relation to property, acting under an enduring power of attorney under Part 9 of that Act.
## MSD responsibilities
MSD are responsible for ensuring we address any questions or issues we are aware of that suggest a student may not have the necessary understanding to enter into a Student Loan Contract.
If a question about the capability or understanding of a student about the nature, implications and obligations of a Student Loan Contract were to be tested in court, a contract may be determined to be unenforceable.
If you have any concerns or questions about a student's understanding of the terms of the contract, or the activities or role of an agent, seek advice from your manager.

chunks.title: Study overseas — student loan
chunks.text:
## Study overseas
Tertiary students who meet all the eligibility and entitlement requirements and are studying overseas as part of their approved programme in New Zealand, can access Student Loans.
## Study at an overseas campus or delivery site
For study starting on or after 1 January 2017, tertiary students who are studying at an overseas campus or delivery site must be:
- studying part of their course of study or programme overseas
- studying in an approved specified country
- enrolled in intramural (face to face) study
- enrolled in a course of study or programme level 7 or above on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework
An overseas campus or delivery site is where a New Zealand tertiary education provider delivers, or has an agreement with another institution to deliver, their recognised course(s) of study overseas.
For more information see:
- Deskfile Overseas study - regions and specified countries
## Residence class visa holders
Tertiary students who hold a residence class visa, and are studying overseas, must be enrolled in face to face study, and only be studying in a country they are not familiar with (from 1 January 2017).
'Not familiar with' means the student:
- has never been to that country or
- has been to that country but has spent less than 6 months in total in the 5 years before the date on which their overseas study begins
The above rules for residence class visa holders also apply to tertiary students studying overseas who are a refugee or protected person, hold a valid temporary entry class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 and whose study started on or after 1 May 2022.
## Immediate family member of refugee or protected person
A student who is an immediate family member of a refugee or protected person, and who holds a temporary entry visa, is not eligible to get a Student Loan for study overseas.
This is because they must reside (be present) in New Zealand to meet the residency criteria for Student Loan.

chunks.title: Temporary performance requirement exemption for study between 2009 - 2010 — student loan
chunks.text:
## Temporary performance requirement exemption for study between 2009 - 2010
If a student had failed the Student Loan performance requirement but could have demonstrated they had made a very significant improvement in their study ending in 2010 as compared to study undertaken in 2009, (i.e. by passing more than 70% of their EFTS) they may have been able to retain Student Loan eligibility.
This was a transition measure and only available to students who had studied full-time in 2009 and 2010 and who were having their performance assessed in 2011.
This exemption does not apply to study starting on or after 1 January 2012.

chunks.title: The lifetime limit and eligibility — student loan
chunks.text: Students generally have a lifetime limit of 7 EFTS entitlement to a Student Loan. The EFTS count includes all courses starting on or after 1 January 2010 that a student accessed any part of a Student Loan for. Some students are entitled to more than 7 EFTS. This is when the student has: - nearly completed 7 EFTS - already completed 7 EFTS (in specific situations detailed below)

chunks.title: Nearly completed 7 EFTS of study — student loan
chunks.text: A student who has used less than 7 EFTS can get another Student Loan, even if their next course or paper will take them over the 7 EFTS limit. For example, they have studied 6.5 EFTS and have enrolled for another course which is 1 EFTS. They can get a Student Loan for the extra 1 EFTS.

chunks.title: Already completed 7 EFTS of study — student loan
chunks.text: A student who has completed 7 EFTS of study, or more if their previous study took them over the 7 EFTS limit, can get extra EFTS in the following situations. Situations when students can access additional EFTS as they have already completed 7 EFTS of study How many extra EFTS they can get? Completing a postgraduate qualification (i.e. they are finishing off the qualification they started but did not finish before they reached their 7 EFTS limit) Note a student cannot access this extension by transferring credits or points gained before they reached their 7 EFTS limit to a different qualification they intend to complete after they reached their 7 EFTS limit. Students can get up to an extra 1 EFTS. If a student has already used the extra 1 EFTS for completing an undergraduate qualification from 2016-2018, they can't also get the extra 1 EFTS for completing a postgraduate qualification. Studying one of these long undergraduate qualifications: - Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (AU0386) at University of Auckland - Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (OO0033) at University of Otago - Bachelor of Optometry (AU000112) at University of Auckland - Bachelor of Veterinary Science (MY0108) at Massey University - Bachelor of Dental Surgery (OO0056) at University of Otago From 2019, studying the following postgraduate qualification: - Bachelor of Dental Surgery with Honours (OO0489) at University of Otago 2019 onwards From 2019, students can get up to an extra 3 EFTS (including if they start study in late 2018). The EFTS will be reduced by the number of extra EFTS they've already used for either: - completing a postgraduate qualification or - studying a long undergraduate qualification between 2016-2018 2016 - 2018 From 2016 - 2018 graduate-entry students could get up to an extra 1 EFTS (including if they started study in late 2015). If a student has already used the extra 1 EFTS for completing a postgraduate qualification, they can't also get the extra 1 EFTS for studying a long undergraduate qualification. Doctoral study Students can get up to an extra 3 EFTS. The EFTS will be reduced by the number of extra EFTS they've already used for either: - completing a postgraduate qualification or - studying a long undergraduate qualification

chunks.title: Limits to accessing extra EFTS — student loan
chunks.text: Students can only get up to a maximum of 10 EFTS (plus any previous study that took them over the 7 EFTS limit). A student can only access each of the additional entitlements (above) once.

chunks.title: Withdrawal from study - EFTS that are not counted — student loan
chunks.text: When a student formally withdraws from a course or paper, and the education provider has given a full fee refund (less any withdrawal fee charged), the EFTS aren't counted. If no fees were charged (eg fees-free study), the EFTS aren't counted as long as the education provider: - confirms a student has formally withdrawn from the course and - advises a new EFTS value that confirms the student did not do the course or paper

chunks.title: Partial fee refunds for study in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic — student loan
chunks.text: When a student receives a partial fee refund for study in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the EFTS value for the course or papers covered by the partial fee refund is not counted.

chunks.title: EFTS calculation — student loan
chunks.text: The EFTS calculation for the lifetime limit is different to the EFTS calculation for the performance requirement.

chunks.title: Three years living in New Zealand — student loan
chunks.text:
## Three years living in New Zealand
Three years living in New Zealand can be either a continuous period or several periods added together to make 3 years.
Periods when a student has lived in New Zealand while on a temporary visa (eg a work visa, visitor's visa or a student visa), can be included.
Time living overseas in the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau cannot be included.

chunks.title: Transfer of Loan Balances to Inland Revenue — student loan
chunks.text:
## Transfer of Loan Balances to Inland Revenue
Student Loan accounts contain all the borrower transactions for a particular period of study.
Inland Revenue will provide the student, notice of the transfer of borrowings within 6 months of it being received. This notification can be used by the student to lodge objections (if any) with the loan manager.
From 1 January 2012, borrower loan balances have been transferred to Inland Revenue daily.
Before 1 January 2012, borrower loan balances were transferred to Inland Revenue yearly.
All loan accounts which closed on or before 31 December 2011 were transferred to Inland Revenue on 28 February 2012. This was the final yearly transfer of loan accounts.
## Reference
- Refer to the loan contract for the relevant year

chunks.title: Two EFTS limit — student loan
chunks.text:
## Two EFTS limit
For study starting on or after 1 January 2013 there is a limit on Student Loan borrowing of 2 EFTS per loan account.
An application for study that exceeds the 2 EFTS limit per loan account cannot be approved.

chunks.title: Youth Guarantee — student loan
chunks.text:
## Youth Guarantee
Youth Guarantee is provided to help young people access foundation learning (NCEA levels 1-3) without paying course fees.
The courses are level 1-3 on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF).
The courses provide students with knowledge and information on vocational pathways, and contain a mix of practical, specific and general skill development.
## Under 18 year olds
Students who are under the age of 18 on the date their study application period starts and are undertaking a Youth Guarantee course or programme, are not eligible for a Student Loan, as the course is fully funded by the government.
When a student reaches the age of 18 during a period of study, they can access Living Costs when they begin their next period of study.
The period of study referred to above is the period covered by the student's study application.
## 18 - 24-year-olds
From 1 January 2023, clients up to 24 years old can participate in Youth Guarantee.
From 1 January 2014 until 31 December 2022, the maximum student age for the Youth Guarantee scheme was 19 years.
18 - 24 year old students can only access Living Costs and Course-Related Costs components of a Student Loan, as Youth Guarantee courses are fees-free.

chunks.title: Accident compensation — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## Accident compensation
When a client is getting accident compensation payments from overseas, the payments are treated in the same way as New Zealand earnings related compensation payments.
You need to convert the rate of the overseas compensation to New Zealand dollars using the current exchange rate. This can be found using the SELXT screen in SWIFTT.
Note to calculate the NZ dollar amount you will need to multiply the overseas currency by the exchange rate. For more information see: Exchange rates
If the particular country is not available, or you are unsure how the calculation works, you should contact International services

chunks.title: Example 1 - Client is getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension or a main benefit — payments from overseas
chunks.text: Alberto is a single person aged 65 years. They live alone and pay rent of $225.00 (Area 1). They get an overseas pension of $650.00 (NZ$) gross per week. Alberto meets all the qualifications for New Zealand Superannuation but their overseas pension is more than the New Zealand Superannuation rate payable. New Zealand Superannuation - single living alone rate (at 1 April 2026) $647.37 gross Accommodation Supplement - calculated as follows: $62.20 Rent $225.00 Less: New Zealand Superannuation - single living alone entry threshold (at 1 April 2026) $139.00 Equals $86.00 Accommodation Supplement (multiplied by 0.70 and rounded up) $61.00 Total New Zealand benefit (New Zealand Superannuation plus Accommodation Supplement) $708.37 Less overseas pension $650.00 Accommodation Supplement payable $58.37

chunks.title: Example 2 – Client is not getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension or a main benefit — payments from overseas
chunks.text: Anna is aged 55 years. She lives in her own home and has accommodation costs (mortgage) of $184.44 per week. (Area 1). She gets wages of $750.00 gross per week plus an overseas pension of $14.61 (NZ$) gross per week. Anna does not currently qualify for New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran's Pension, or a main benefit. She is assessed as a non-beneficiary. Assessment of Accommodation Supplement for a non-beneficiary Accommodation costs Less entry threshold - non-beneficiary (at 1 April 2026) Equals Accommodation Supplement before income reduction (multiplied by 0.70 cents) $184.44 $112.00 $72.44 $50.70 Calculating Accommodation Supplement reduction due to income Client's income before tax Less: income threshold - non-beneficiary (at 1 April 2026) Equals Reduction due to income for Accommodation Supplement($57.00 multiplied by 0.25) $750.00 $693.00 $57.00 $14.25 Full rate of Accommodation Supplement Less reduction due to income Equals $50.70 $14.25 $36.45 Equals (rounded up) $37.00 Less overseas pension $14.61 Accommodation Supplement payable $22.39

chunks.title: Couples getting overseas pensions — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## Couples getting overseas pensions
From 9 November 2020, the process for deducting an overseas pension changed for couples where either one of them, or both get an overseas pension depending on the benefit or pension they get.
If a client or partner get an overseas pension, that pension cannot reduce the amount of their partner’s rate of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension including Winter Energy Payment.
The changes apply in the following client situations:
- couples where both clients qualify for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension in their own right, and either the client or their partner has an overseas pension which they get in excess
- New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client whose partner does not get any benefit and, either client has an overseas pension which they get in excess
- New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client whose partner gets a main benefit and, either client has an overseas pension which they get in excess
There is no change to the way overseas pensions are deducted for the following client situations:
- couples both qualified for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension in their own right but whose overseas pensions do not result in an excess
- single clients getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
- couples getting a main benefit
- grandparented non-qualified partner rates of New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: Direct deductions of overseas pensions — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## Direct deductions of overseas pensions
When a client is eligible to get or is getting any overseas benefit or pension the gross amount is generally directly deducted from their New Zealand benefit.
The overseas benefit or pension is deducted from:
- the gross rate of New Zealand Superannuation or Veterans Pension and
- the net rate of any other New Zealand benefit (eg Accommodation Supplement)
- when an overseas pension is considered to be in the nature of a Disability Allowance, it will be directly deducted from any New Zealand Disability Allowance but not any other New Zealand benefit
Note to calculate the NZ dollar amount you will need to multiply the overseas currency by the exchange rate held on SELXT [no link find out why] . If the client wants you to take into account bank fees you should contact International Services for advice.
For more information see: Couples getting overseas pensions
When a client is already getting a New Zealand benefit or pension at the time the overseas benefit or pension is granted, the deduction will be processed by Senior Services - international.
The following information should be sent to International Services:
- verification of the rate
- type of overseas pension
- the grant date and
- the name of the organisation making the payment. If you are unsure whether an overseas pension is deductible, you should check the direct deduction list and contact International Services for advice
- If the client is already getting an overseas benefit or pension at the time a New Zealand benefit or pension is being granted the direct deduction should be added by International Services
## Review of New Zealand benefits or pensions
International Services must be advised of all clients who are getting an overseas benefit or pension. International Services will complete all New Zealand benefit or pension reviews when the overseas benefit or pension deduction is being updated or reviewed.
Any other reviews of the client's New Zealand benefit, such as a change of relationship status or a change of chargeable income, should be completed by the Work and Income service centre.

chunks.text:

chunks.title: Exchange rates — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## Exchange rates
SELXT contains exchange rates for all the countries listed and can be used to convert the value of an overseas currency into New Zealand dollars. The exchange rates are average exchange rates for all countries that are notified to MSD, by its nominated bank for the period of the 16th of one month to the 15th of the following month.
There are social security agencies in 4 countries which independently notify MSD of the exchange rates used to pay their pensions into New Zealand. These exchanges rates are compared to the average exchange rates supplied by the nominated bank for the same country and the most advantageous rate for the client is entered into SELXT.
To convert overseas currency to New Zealand currency, take the foreign currency and multiply it by the New Zealand exchange rate.
## Example - SWIFTT exchange rate
A client is receiving weekly payments of £150.00 per week in pounds sterling. The exchange rate for the United Kingdom pound showing in SELXT screen is 1.8564 (as at 20 March 2018).
- 150.00 (sterling) x 1.85640 (NZ) = $278.46 (NZ)
## Banks exchange rate
Clients may query the exchange rate as banks express their rates in a different way than SWIFTT does. The bank would express 1.85640 as 0.53870. This is calculated by dividing 1 by 1.85640 = 0.53870.
The bank calculates the exchange rate for overseas currency by dividing the overseas pension amount by the exchange rate, instead of multiplying it, as in the SWIFTT example above. When comparing the calculations using the two exchange rates there may be a small difference in the NZ dollar amounts.
## Example - Bank exchange rate
- £150.00 (sterling) divided by 0.53870 = $278.45 (NZ)
In these examples the difference in the exchange rate is one cent.

chunks.title: Accommodation Supplement — payments from overseas
chunks.text: When a client is applying for Accommodation Supplement, how their overseas pension affects it depends on other assistance the client is getting. The overseas pension is treated differently depending on whether the client applying for Accommodation Supplement is: - getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension, or a main benefit or - not getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension, or a main benefit

chunks.title: Clients getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension or a main benefit — payments from overseas
chunks.text: When a client is getting an overseas pension that is more than the New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension, or main benefit rate, the excess amount above the rate is directly deducted from any: - Accommodation Supplement and - other benefits they are getting MSD will calculate the amount of New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension or main benefit the client is entitled to get and the rate of Accommodation Supplement payable with their benefit or pension. When deducting an overseas pension, MSD must first calculate the total New Zealand benefit amount the client is entitled to (including Accommodation Supplement). For example, New Zealand Superannuation plus Accommodation Supplement. The overseas pension is then deducted from the total amount of Accommodation Supplement plus New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension, or main benefit. The balance left is the actual rate of Accommodation Supplement payable.

chunks.title: Clients not getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension or a main benefit — payments from overseas
chunks.text: When a client is getting an overseas pension and they are not getting New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran’s Pension, or a main benefit their overseas pension is directly deducted from any Accommodation Supplement they may get. MSD will calculate the rate of Accommodation Supplement payable alongside the client’s overseas pension. The overseas pension is deducted from the Accommodation Supplement, and the balance left is the actual rate of Accommodation Supplement payable. For more information see: - Accommodation Supplement - examples

chunks.title: Disability Allowance — payments from overseas
chunks.text: When a client is getting an overseas pension that has the nature of a Disability Allowance, it will be directly deducted from any Disability Allowance, but not any other benefit they may get.

chunks.title: Winter Energy Payment — payments from overseas
chunks.text: If a client is entitled to get or is getting an overseas pension the overseas pension should be directly deducted from the client’s Winter Energy Payment. There are certain circumstances when an overseas pension should not be directly deducted from a client’s Winter Energy Payment. Their overseas pension must not be directly deducted from their Winter Energy Payment if: - the client is entitled to get, or is getting, Winter Energy Payment because they qualify for New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension. and - the client is entitled to get, or is getting, the overseas pension in respect of their partner or dependant or - the client’s partner or dependant is entitled to get, or is getting, the overseas pension Note if the client’s New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran’s Pension is not payable because of an overseas pension deduction, the Winter Energy Payment will not be payable to them.

chunks.title: Government occupational pensions — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## Government occupational pensions
Government occupational pensions are private pension plans for former government employees or those who have had a period of Government service.
Government occupational pensions are
- paid in addition to any pension or benefit paid through the public system and
- generally charged as income for benefit and pension purposes
When a client is getting an overseas pension which they claim is a government occupational pension it is important to obtain further information. This will help you decide whether the payments can be treated as a government occupational pension.
You will need to find out the following:
- a general summary of the paying country's pension system and
- whether the pension is paid in addition to benefits and pensions available to the general population
or
- whether it is offered as an alternative to the public system
## Not a government occupational pension
If the pension is paid as an alternative to benefits and pensions paid through the public system then it is generally not a government occupational pension. That is, the client can't get benefits or pensions through both schemes.
This pension would be treated as a direct deduction from the New Zealand benefit or pension.
The pensions have to be 'similar', start at the same times (eg the same age or at retirement), and the amount payable is not hugely different.

chunks.title: Grandparented New Zealand Superannuation non-qualified partner included and New Zealand Superannuation with main benefit partner — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## Grandparented New Zealand Superannuation non-qualified partner included and New Zealand Superannuation with main benefit partner
From 9 November 2020, there is no change to the way an overseas pension is deducted for couples that are getting the non-qualified couple rate of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension through grandparenting provisions.
An overseas benefit or pension will be deducted from the married, civil union or de facto rate and the balance is split equally between each partner.
Melissa gets New Zealand Superannuation and included Sam as her non-qualified partner. Melissa also gets an overseas pension which reduces the rate of their combined rate of New Zealand Superannuation.
For more information on how to calculate:
Example - New Zealand Superannuation paid at the grandparented non-qualified rate

chunks.text:

chunks.title: Introduction — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## Introduction
A client must provide information about any overseas pension they get, including the payment rate. If they do not comply, their New Zealand benefit or pension can be refused or payment suspended.
When a client advises they are receiving payments from overseas you need to find out the type of payment so you can determine the effect it will have on the clients New Zealand benefit or pension.
It is important the information is obtained as quickly as possible to enable the client's correct entitlement to be assessed.
If the client is unable to provide full documentation of the payments you will need to have the client complete an Information Release Authority form and forward the form to International Services.
This will enable International Services to obtain and verify the following information:
- rate of payment in the overseas currency and whether it includes any amount in respect of the clients partner and any dependent children
- reason for the grant, such as age, widowhood, disablement, or war service
- the name of the organisation or authority that is making the payment
- verification of any portion of an overseas pension which came from voluntary contributions
- ensure the client is receiving their correct entitlement

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension both qualify — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension both qualify
Any deductible overseas pension payments a client is getting will be deducted from their own New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension.
If either client gets an overseas pension payment it will only affect their own rate of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension and not their partner's rate of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension.
If either client gets ongoing financial assistance such as Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit then any excess of their overseas pension will reduce these as well (excluding Winter Energy Payment).
## Example
Ihno and Margaret both get New Zealand Superannuation in their own right. Margaret also gets Accommodation Supplement paid to her.
Ihno gets an overseas pension and this does not affect Margaret's rate of New Zealand Superannuation, but any excess of his overseas pension is applied to and will reduce Margaret's Accommodation Supplement.
For more information on how to calculate:
- Example - New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension both qualify

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension with a partner getting a main benefit — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension with a partner getting a main benefit
Any deductible overseas pension payments a client is getting will be deducted from their own New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension.
However, any excess of the client's overseas pension can affect the partner's main benefit.
## Client on New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension is getting the overseas pension
When a client getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension has an overseas pension which exceeds their rate of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension, their partner's main benefit will be reduced.
If either client gets ongoing financial assistance such as Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit then any excess of their overseas pension will reduce these as well (excluding Winter Energy Payment).
## Example
Maia gets New Zealand Superannuation as well as an overseas pension, and her partner Ben gets Supported Living Payment and Accommodation Supplement.
If Maia's overseas pension is more than her rate of New Zealand Superannuation, this excess will be deducted from Ben's rate of Supported Living Payment.
Any further excess over the rate of Supported Living Payment is deducted from his rate of Accommodation Supplement.
For more information on how to calculate see:
- Example - New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension with a partner getting a main benefit
## Partner on main benefit is getting the overseas pension
Any deductible overseas pension payments a partner of the New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension client is getting will be deducted from their own main benefit.
However, any excess of the partner's overseas pension will not affect the client's New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension.
If either client gets ongoing financial assistance such as Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit any excess of their overseas pension will reduce these as well (excluding Winter Energy Payment).
## Example
Nikau gets New Zealand Superannuation as well as an overseas pension and his partner Jessica gets Jobseeker Support as well as Accommodation Supplement.
Any excess of overseas pension will reduce Jessica's rate of Jobseeker Support.
Any further excess over the rate of Jobseeker Support will be deducted from the rate of Accommodation Supplement.
For more information on how to calculate see:
- Example - New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension with a partner getting a main benefit

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension with a partner not getting a benefit — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension with a partner not getting a benefit
Any deductible overseas pension payments a client is getting will be deducted from their own New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension.
If either client gets ongoing financial assistance such as Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit then any excess of their overseas pension will reduce these as well (excluding Winter Energy Payment).
Partner gets an overseas pension
If the client’s partner does not get a benefit but gets an overseas pension, this does not affect the client’s New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension payments.
## Example
Jacob gets New Zealand Superannuation and his partner Ancelin does not get a benefit, but she does get an overseas pension. Jacob's New Zealand Superannuation is not affected by Ancelin's overseas pension, but his Accommodation Supplement will be reduced by the amount of Ancelin's overseas pension.
If the amount of his Accommodation Supplement is less than her amount of overseas pension, this will reduce to nil and he will no longer be eligible to get it.
For more information on how to calculate:
- Example - New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension with a partner not getting a benefit
Example - New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension with a partner not getting a benefit

chunks.title: Other payments — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## Other payments
When a client is getting other payments, such as interest or rent from investments or properties they own overseas, the payments will be treated in the same way as income earned in New Zealand.
You need to convert the income to New Zealand dollars using the current exchange rate. This can be found using the SELXT screen in SWIFTT.
Note to calculate the NZ dollar amount you will need to multiply the overseas currency by the exchange rate. For more information see: Exchange rates
If the particular country is not available, or you are unsure how the calculation works you should contact International services

chunks.title: Overseas pensions for dependants — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## Overseas pensions for dependants
An overseas pension payable for a dependent child may be deducted depending on:
- the nature and purpose for which the pension is paid and
- if it is paid by or on behalf of the Government of the overseas paying authority.
If you are unsure whether the child’s overseas pension should be deducted contact International Services.
When a child’s overseas pension is not deducted
A child’s overseas pension is not deducted from the following clients:
- Single clients getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
- Couples getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension including couples getting the grandparented non-qualified partner rate
- A couple where one partner gets either New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension and their partner does not get any other benefit payments.
The Winter Energy payment paid to these clients is not affected if they get an overseas pension for a dependent child.
When a child’s overseas pension is deducted
A child’s overseas pension that meets the requirements for a deductible pension will be deducted from benefit payments for:
- Single clients getting a main benefit
- Couples getting a main benefit
- Couples where one partner receives New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension and their partner receives a main benefit
- Non beneficiary assistance
A deduction will also apply to any on going supplementary beneficiary assistance payments. This excludes Winter Energy Payment.

chunks.title: Overseas pensions — payments from overseas
chunks.text: Most countries have social security legislation that provides pensions for old age, disability, or death of a spouse. A client getting an overseas pension will have their pension directly deducted from their New Zealand benefit or pension if that overseas pension is: - part of a programme that provides benefits, pensions and periodical allowances for the same circumstances for which a New Zealand benefit or pension would be made and - administered by or on behalf of the government of the overseas country. Overseas pensions are treated as income for other income tested assistance. Note the portion of an overseas pension that comes from voluntary contributions to a country's pension scheme is not deducted from New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran's Pension or other benefits. Overseas pensions are treated as income for other income tested assistance. You need to be aware: - in most instances the amount to deduct is the gross (before tax) amount converted to New Zealand dollars - when a client is getting a pension from a country that has a Reciprocal Agreement with New Zealand you need to check the agreement of that country as special provisions may apply (eg Netherlands and Denmark have specific provisions) - overseas pensions are directly deducted from all benefits types, including New Zealand Superannuation, Veteran's Pension and Accommodation Supplement - when the overseas pension is more than the main benefit rate, the amount over the main benefit rate is also directly deducted from any Accommodation Supplement the client or partner is getting - when an overseas pension is considered to be in the nature of a disability allowance, it will be directly deducted from any New Zealand Disability Allowance, but not from any other New Zealand benefit - if the client has a partner the deduction is applied differently depending on whether: both partners are getting a New Zealand benefit or pension in their own right orone partner was included as a non-qualified partner (before 9 November 2020) oronly one client is getting a New Zealand benefit or pension, see: Couples getting overseas pensionsthe couple are getting a main benefit - both partners are getting a New Zealand benefit or pension in their own right or - one partner was included as a non-qualified partner (before 9 November 2020) or - only one client is getting a New Zealand benefit or pension, see: Couples getting overseas pensions - the couple are getting a main benefit - some overseas pensions, or parts of these pensions, are not counted in the assessment of any benefit paid in New Zealand, and some are charged as income

chunks.title: Overseas pensions — payments from overseas
chunks.text: - if the client has entitlement to an overseas pension but has not claimed it, this can also affect their New Zealand benefit or pension, see: Possible overseas pension entitlement International Services must be told of all clients who are getting an overseas benefit or pension as it is their responsibility to carry out New Zealand benefit or pension reviews when the overseas benefit or pension deduction needs up-dating or reviewing. If you are unsure whether all, or part of the overseas pension should be directly deducted from the New Zealand benefit or pension, you should contact International Services

chunks.title: Possible overseas pension entitlement — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## Possible overseas pension entitlement
A client may be entitled to receive an overseas benefit or pension if they were born or have lived or worked overseas.
Clients are expected to test their entitlement to any overseas benefit or pension they may be entitled to.
You should ensure clients complete the overseas residence details section of their application form and enter these details into CMS.
These details are automatically transferred to International Services to identify people who may have overseas pension entitlements.
International Services will:
- send the appropriate forms to the client to complete or
- provide the client with the address to write to, about their entitlement and
- follow up any entitlement to an overseas benefit or pension
You need to tell the client they are required to take all reasonable steps to test their entitlement to an overseas pension or their New Zealand benefit or pension could be suspended or cancelled.
Note when the partner of a client says they have overseas residence that may give them entitlement to an overseas pension, you should ask the partner to test their entitlement to the overseas pension. This is regardless of whether they are getting a New Zealand benefit or pension or not.

chunks.title: Reciprocal Agreements — payments from overseas
chunks.text:
## Reciprocal Agreements
New Zealand has Reciprocal Agreements with a number of countries.
For more information regarding payments from these countries see:
- Australia
- Canada
