When a young parent is donating a kidney or liver tissue, they can keep getting their Young Parent Payment. Exempt the young parent from undertaking, or being available to participate in, education, training or work-based learning during the recovery period.
Grant the exemption 'Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability'.
Add the exemption in the SWTDA screen.
The exemption starts from the date of the operation and can continue while the young parent:
- is recovering from their operation and
- they cannot undertake or be available to participate in education, training or work-based learning
The exemption must not be more than 12 weeks.
Do not apply any obligations failures:
- for the maximum period of 12 weeks or
- until the young person has recovered from the operation
whichever is earlier.
## Young parent has an obligation failure
If the young parent currently has an activity obligation failure, donating a kidney or liver tissue is a 'good and sufficient reason'.
The activity obligations failure must be overturned in OBMAN. This will remove the failure from the client's 12 month obligation failure count and there is no sanction.
For more information see:
- Exemptions from activity obligations

chunks.title: Being paid a benefit for an approved travel period — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Being paid a benefit for an approved travel period
Where the client has already left New Zealand for an approved travel period, they may be able to receive their payment for longer (where they have sufficient days left from their 28 days within a 52 week period).
## Examples (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A client receiving Young Parent Payment who was enrolled in secondary school was out of New Zealand visiting his father in Australia. His Young Parent Payment was suspended the day after he left New Zealand as it wasn't an approved travel reason. This is because the travel took place in the middle of the school term and therefore it prevented the client from meeting his obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning.
The client contacts Work and Income three days later to say that his father is in hospital as he has had a heart attack. The client has been paid for five days in the previous 52 weeks while he was absent from New Zealand leaving a balance of 23 days.
The reason for travel now meets the criteria for approved travel. The benefit is resumed from the date the client became eligible to receive the benefit overseas. The client must contact Work and Income from overseas.
The benefit cannot be back-dated if the client advises Work and Income when they return to New Zealand.
A client receiving Young Parent Payment who is attending a full-time training course left New Zealand to visit her mother during the term break. The client continued to receive her payment while overseas on the grounds that the travel did not prevent her from meeting her obligations. Two days before she was due to return, her mother's house burnt down. The client has been paid for 20 days in the previous 52 weeks while she was absent from New Zealand leaving a balance of eight days.
The reason for travel has changed and the client has not been absent from New Zealand for up to 28 days in any 52 week period. The benefit expiry is extended for an additional five days.
Note that where the client has already been absent for 28 days in a 52 week period, consider whether the client meets the criteria for receiving a payment for more than 28 days in any 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Client meeting their youth activity obligations — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Client meeting their youth activity obligations
A client receiving Young Parent Payment can continue to be paid a benefit while they are absent from New Zealand for any reason if:
- the travel will not prevent them from continuing to meet their youth activity obligations (eg because they are attending school and the travel is during the school holidays or they are attending a training course and the travel is during a term or semester break, and they do not need to be in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations during the travel period)
## Examples include (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A young person is meeting their education obligation by attending secondary school and they wish to holiday in Australia during the school holidays. The client is not required by their Service Provider to undertake a parenting or budgeting course or attend any meetings with them during the period they wish to travel.
The travel will not prevent the client from meeting any of their youth activity obligations so it will be approved. The young person can be absent from New Zealand and continue to receive their payment for up to 28 days in any 52 week period.
A young person is meeting their education obligation by participating in a full time training course and decides to take time off from the course in the middle of the term so that they can holiday in Australia.
The travel will not be approved as it will prevent the young person from meeting their obligation to be in full-time education or training.
A young person is enrolled in a full-time training course, however, the course has not yet started, and the young person wishes to travel to the United States for a holiday before the course commencement date. The young person does not have to be in New Zealand to meet any other obligations during the travel period (eg they do not have to attend a budgeting or parenting course during the time of the travel)
The travel will not prevent the client from meeting any of their youth activity obligations so it will be approved. The young person can continue to receive their payment for up to 28 days in any 52 week period while they are absent from New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Young people who are exempt from their youth activity obligations

chunks.title: Examples include (but are not limited to) — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Examples include (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A client receiving Young Parent Payment left New Zealand for a holiday in Australia, and is continuing to receive their payment on the grounds that the travel is not preventing them from meeting their obligations. While the client was in Australia there was severe flooding which meant they could not return to New Zealand on the day they were meant to return. The client contacts Work and Income. The client has been paid for 20 days in the previous 52 weeks while she was absent from New Zealand, leaving a balance of eight days.
The client cannot return due to circumstances that were not reasonably foreseeable and that were outside the client's control. Work and Income would extend the client's benefit for a reasonable period to allow the client to return.
Also consider whether there is any grounds to pay for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
A client receiving Young Parent Payment has been overseas for five days to attend his father's funeral. He is delayed in Sydney due to fog. He must remain a further three days.
The client cannot return due to circumstances that were not reasonably foreseeable and that were outside his control. Work and Income would extend the client's benefit for a reasonable period for him to be able to return. Also consider whether there is any grounds to pay for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Client obtains employment overseas — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Client obtains employment overseas
Where the client:
- is successful in their job prospect or job search overseas and
- they are not returning to New Zealand
the Young Parent Payment should be cancelled from the day after the notice of job appointment.
If the client returns to New Zealand for the period between getting the job and actually starting employment, the Young Parent Payment can be continued until they leave the country. The benefit must be cancelled from the day after they leave New Zealand to commence the job.

chunks.title: Client with youth activity obligations — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Client with youth activity obligations
A client receiving Young Parent Payment cannot continue to receive their payment when they temporarily leave New Zealand unless they meet the criteria for approved travel.
Where they meet the criteria for approved travel they can continue to receive their payment for a period of up to 28 days in any 52 week period if:
- the benefit would continue to be paid except for them having left New Zealand
- the absences do not affect the client's eligibility for the benefit
- they have notified Work and Income of their intention to temporarily leave New Zealand
For more information see:
- Client meeting their youth activity obligations
- Young people who are exempt from their youth activity obligations
- Approved travel reasons

chunks.title: Clients with a partner — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Clients with a partner
When a married, civil union or de facto client is imprisoned their Young Parent Payment will generally need to be cancelled.
Note clients who are married, in a civil union or in a de facto relationship qualify for Young Parent Payment in their own right. If either of the couple is imprisoned, the other person can continue to receive their own Young Parent Payment.
The Young Parent Payment of the client in prison should be cancelled from the day after imprisonment.
Where there are dependent children, the person who is not imprisoned can receive the sole parent rate of Young Parent Payment where they are no longer in a relationship.
## Exception
Where a client is imprisoned and they have a partner and/or dependent children, there is discretion to continue payment of the client's Young Parent Payment in some circumstances.
There is discretion to pay all or part of the imprisoned client's Young Parent Payment to the person who has not been imprisoned. This will depend on the length of time imprisoned.
There is also discretion to continue payment if the client is remanded in custody pending a further court appearance.
For more information to help you make a decision see:
- Youth activity obligations
- Decision guidelines - clients with a partner
- SWIFTT process to pay a partner
- Remanded in custody

chunks.title: Contacting Work and Income as soon as the client reasonably could — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Contacting Work and Income as soon as the client reasonably could
A client who leaves New Zealand without advising Work and Income of their travel can only have their benefit backdated to the day after their departure date if they contact Work and Income as soon as they reasonably could have been expected to, given their circumstances.
This may be while the client is still absent from New Zealand, or once they have returned.
For more information see:
- Backdating benefit to day after departure date
## Determining reasonable contact time
To determine whether a client contacted Work and Income as soon as they could reasonably have been expected to, you need to take into account the circumstances of the client.
The reason why the client did not contact Work and Income until after returning to New Zealand, may be the same reason why they left New Zealand without advising Work and Income of their absence, or a different humanitarian reason.
Reasons for not contacting Work and Income sooner may include (but are not limited to) that the client:
- did not contact Work and Income due to the stress of the event that led to them leaving New Zealand without informing Work and Income
- left with a humanitarian reason, and then could not access the technology to communicate with Work and Income while absent from New Zealand
- left for a humanitarian reason, and then was temporarily medically unfit while overseas and they have a medical certificate that shows this
- left for a humanitarian reason, and then had a death or illness in the immediate family while overseas or on return to New Zealand, and/or
- left for a humanitarian reason, and then experienced an adverse event or natural disaster while overseas or on return to New Zealand that meant they were unable to contact Work and Income
## Contacting Work and Income on return to New Zealand
Generally, it would be reasonable to expect a client to contact Work and Income within 10 working days of returning to New Zealand.
However, you should consider whether the client's circumstances meant they were unable to inform Work and Income in this period.
For more information see:
- Approved travel reasons
- Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure
- Clients with youth activity obligations
- Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy

chunks.title: Transferring or cancelling and re-granting benefits — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Transferring or cancelling and re-granting benefits
When transferring or cancelling and re-granting benefits when there are court attachments on the record please email the Central Processing Unit. Include the client's name and client number, and a request to review and reload court attachments as necessary.

chunks.title: Backdating — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Backdating
Where a client requests the backdated inclusion of a child and the previous caregiver was in receipt of a benefit for the child, you will need to review when the child was excluded from the previous caregivers benefit.
Note a child cannot be included in two benefits for the same period.
Have regard to all the circumstances and decide whether a debt should be established for the previous caregiver.
If the date that the child is being included from is a date in the previous tax year, SWIFTT will only pay arrears of family tax credit and best start tax credit from the beginning of the current tax year, that is, 1 April. The client must be advised that any arrears of family tax credit and best start tax credit prior to this date will need to be claimed by them from Inland Revenue.
YSSU will need to do a backdated review in the SBDR screen to pay any benefit arrears to the client for the previous tax year. A backdated review may be required for the current year if other rate changes have occurred - check the SRAUI screen for details.
For more information see:
- Processing standards Child changes [no link find out why]
- Family tax credit
- Best Start tax credit

chunks.title: Death of a child — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Death of a child
When a dependent child dies, the child should be excluded from Young Parent Payment 28 days following the date of the child's death.
Payment of the benefit should continue at the existing rate for 28 days following the date the child died.
This provides a transition period for the client to adjust to their change in circumstances.
## Childcare assistance
Childcare assistance, including Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment paid for the child must be stopped on the day after the child died.
## Family tax credit
Family tax credits should be stopped from the start of the pay period following the date the child dies, to avoid an overpayment with Inland Revenue for the client.
## Best Start tax credit
Best Start tax credit differs from family tax credit and is continued for 28 days from the date of death of the child.
Note If the child's third birthday falls due in the 28-day period payment will stop from the deceased's child's third birthday.

chunks.title: Death of a client — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Death of a client
The date benefit payment stops following the death of a client depends on whether the client has a dependent partner.

chunks.title: Death of a client with a partner or child — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Death of a client with a partner or child
Young Parent Payment can continue to be paid for 28 days following the death of a client when there is a surviving:
- partner and/or
- child or children
This includes the death of a single client who is a:
- liable person and paying Child Support payments or
- principal caregiver receiving Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit
The continuation of payment beyond the date of death is referred to as terminal benefit.
When the benefit is being paid to a couple, both the deceased person and the surviving person's portion continues to be paid.
The total benefit, including the surviving person's portion, plus any extra help continues for 28 days.
## There are 3 exceptions
- If the surviving person's benefit is reviewed and they qualify for a higher rate on a new benefit, they may be granted that new benefit instead of terminal benefit from the day after a client's death. We do this because it is to the client's financial advantage.
or
- If the surviving person's current benefit is reviewed and they qualify for a higher rate, their benefit rate increases from the day after their partner's death, we pay this instead of terminal benefit. We do this because it is to the client's financial advantage.
or
- When the death of a person was the result of an accident, entitlement to a survivor's grant from ACC needs to be decided before terminal benefit can be paid.
If the partner or child is entitled to a survivors grant from ACC there is no entitlement to terminal benefit beyond the date of death.
In the situation where benefit payment has continued beyond the date of death, an overpayment is established and the debt should be recovered from the estate.

chunks.title: Arrears — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Arrears
When a client has arrears owing to them at the time of their death and they have an outstanding debt balance, the debt should be recovered in full from the arrears, from the final payment.
## Terminal benefit
Do not recover debts from terminal benefit payments.

chunks.title: Decision guidelines - clients with a partner — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Decision guidelines - clients with a partner
While Young Parent Payment should generally be stopped when the client is imprisoned, there is discretion for their payment to be continued and paid to the partner not in prison. This discretion allows payment of all or part of the client's Young Parent Payment to their partner.
When considering if payment should be continued, and paid to the partner, this should generally be at the sole parent rate. However, the full married, civil union or de facto rate can be paid if this is warranted after having regard to the particular circumstances of the client and their partner.
To help decide whether it is reasonable to pay the client's Young Parent Payment to the partner while the client is in prison, and the rate to pay, consider the following:
- has the period in prison already passed
- is the client due to be released from prison shortly
- is the likely period in prison less than six months
- do they intend to live together when the partner is released
- has the partner in prison applied for Home Detention
- are there exceptional circumstances that warrant paying the full married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit to the partner who is not in prison
For further help contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances before you make your decision.
For more information see:
- SWIFTT process to pay a partner

chunks.title: Decision guidelines for shared care — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Decision guidelines for shared care
The parent with greater responsibility is usually the parent who has the child for most of the time. If a parent has the child for at least 60% of the time they have the primary responsibility.
Where parents have equal time, to help you decide which parent has greater responsibility, consider the following:
- who pays for the child's material support (furniture, clothes etc)
- who decides about the child's daily activities
- who takes them to and from school and supervises leisure activities
- who makes decisions about their education and health
- who pays for which expenses
If it is not clear who has greater responsibility or the parents share the responsibility equally, the parent who was mainly responsible for the day-to-day care of the child prior to the separation is the person who can have the child included.
If a decision can't be made on who is entitled to have the child included, the parents must make the decision. Don't include the child in any income support until they have decided.

chunks.title: Decision guidelines - sole parents — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Decision guidelines - sole parents
When a sole parent Young Parent Payment client is imprisoned it is important that financial assistance is available to support any dependent children.
While the Young Parent Payment should generally be stopped when the client is imprisoned, there is discretion for payment to be continued and paid to the person who is caring for the dependent children.
To help you decide whether it is reasonable to pay the Young Parent Payment while the client is in prison, consider the following:
- has the period in prison already passed
- is the client due to be released from prison shortly
- is the likely period in prison less than twelve months
- will the children return to the client's care on their release from prison
- has the caregiver ceased work to care for the children
- has the caregiver lost entitlement to their own benefit due to having children in their care
For further help contact the Helpline to discuss the circumstances before making a decision.
For more information see:
- Rate of payment - sole parents
- Examples - sole parents
- Remanded in custody
- Sole parents

chunks.title: Deductions — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Deductions
In certain circumstances Work and Income can be required to pay part of a client's benefit to another party.
Work and Income is legally required to make such deductions when served with a properly issued Deduction Notice or Attachment Order. In these cases, the consent of the client is not required.
Deductions are different to the redirection of a young person's payments when they are subject to money management.
Certain forms of deductions take priority over others.

chunks.title: Dependent child — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
A dependent child for Young Parent Payment is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Young Parent Payment does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- child for whom Orphan's or Unsupported Child's Benefit is being paid and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
## Maintained as a member of the family
The child should be an integral part of the family, participating in the usual family activities (for example outings and annual holidays).
Dependent children should be included in the assessment of Young Parent Payment.
In some situations, a child may not be living at home but is still considered to be a dependent child.

chunks.title: Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital
When person who has been remanded in custody or is serving a term of imprisonment, is detained in or transferred to a psychiatric hospital you may be able to pay an Emergency Benefit at the hospital rate.
People who are remanded in custody or serving a term of imprisonment who are temporarily hospitalised for treatment of an injury or health condition are still considered to be in prison and the Department of Corrections will meet their costs. Therefore an Emergency Benefit or any other financial assistance cannot be paid.
For more information see:
- Emergency Benefit Person serving their sentence of imprisonment in a psychiatric hospital
- Release from prison

chunks.title: Discharge from hospital — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Discharge from hospital
When a client is getting hospital rate and they are discharged from hospital:
- increase their benefit to the appropriate full rate from the date of discharge and
- review any Extra help from the same date
Note the dates of admission and discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital.

chunks.title: Discharged from Oranga Tamariki care — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Discharged from Oranga Tamariki care
Where Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency has care, custody or sole guardianship of the child, and returns the child to the care of the immediate previous caregiver, they do not make payments for the child.
The child is then a dependent child and can be included in the Young Parent Payment.
Where the relationship is not one of care, but more of a boarding arrangement, the young person may be able to receive Youth Payment.
Once a child has been discharged from care the child can be considered a dependent child even when Oranga Tamariki or any other authorised agency involvement continues, for example:
- Additional Guardianship Order
- Support Order or
- Services Order
When there is a Service or Support Order in place, staff need to make sure that the Court's intent allows consideration of the child as a dependent child.
For further details on what discharged from care means see:
- Definition of discharged from Oranga Tamariki care

chunks.title: Effect of income on Extra help — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Effect of income on Extra help
When income is added or changed you will also need to review any Extra help the client may be receiving.
Some Extra help is not income tested such as Child Disability Allowance, Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment and Winter Energy Payment. It is the client's obligation to advise Work and Income of any changes in their circumstances.
Income is charged against Temporary Additional Support and Childcare Subsidy.
For more information see:
- Income change
- Childcare Subsidy Chargeable income
- Temporary Additional Support Chargeable income
- Extra help

chunks.title: Effect on benefit — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Effect on benefit
Any inclusion or exclusion of a dependent child from a client's benefit will result in a general review of the client's Young Parent Payment and any Extra help they are getting.
YSSU may need to review the following:
- Accommodation SupplementChanges to the family composition may result in a change to the Accommodation Supplement entry thresholds.
- Non-standard benefit rateWhere a child is added or removed the non-standard rate of payment may have to be manually adjusted.
- Temporary Additional SupportAny change to family circumstances will result in a review of Temporary Additional Support. A child included or excluded from the Young Parent Payment may result in a change to the allowable costs for Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Effect on Extra Help — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Effect on Extra Help
Extra help can continue being paid to the client for the first 13 weeks they are in hospital. When Young Parent Payment is reduced to the hospital rate, any Extra help they get will need to be reviewed.
## Accommodation Supplement
Stop the Accommodation Supplement from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation. Check whether the client still has to pay their ongoing accommodation costs. If so, increase the benefit rate above the hospital rate to meet the costs.
## Temporary Additional Support
Stop Temporary Additional Support from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation. Check whether the client still has to pay their ongoing costs. If so, increase the Young Parent Payment rate above the hospital rate to meet the costs.
## Disability Allowance
Cancel the client's Disability Allowance from the date Young Parent Payment is reduced to the hospital rate. All costs associated with the client's disability are the responsibility of the hospital.
## Winter Energy Payment
A client who has had their Young Parent Payment reduced to the hospital rate can only get the Winter Energy Payment if they still need help with their energy costs during the winter period.

chunks.title: Ending payment for client who needs an approved reason to travel (within 28 day maximum) — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Ending payment for client who needs an approved reason to travel (within 28 day maximum)
Where the client is receiving their payments while they are absent from New Zealand because they have an approved travel reason and their return date changes, they must advise Work and Income from overseas, otherwise their payment will be stopped from the day they originally advised they would return to New Zealand.
They may be able to have their benefit backdated if there is an unforeseen reason they cannot notify us.
For example, a client boards a plane to return home on schedule and the plane is held up due to fog. There is no way the client could notify Work and Income due to an event outside of their control. The benefit would be resumed from the original date the client was due to return (this will be on the itinerary or e-ticket).
For more information see:
- Approved travel reasons
- Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Essential travel — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Essential travel
Clients will sometimes have to travel outside of New Zealand to attend a significant event relating to a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family).
These events are ones which the client would reasonably be expected to attend. That is, the travel is essential to them and where not attending the event would cause the person emotional distress. This may include, but is not limited to, travel that allows the client to:
- be with a seriously ill or dying person who is a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family)
- attend a funeral or an unveiling in relation to a family member
- pay respect to a family member of the deceased in the event of the client missing the funeral
- attend to legal matters in relation to the affairs of the deceased family member
- attend a birth of a family member or be with a family member around the time of their giving birth
- provide support to a party or witness to a court case
- attend a wedding of a family member - the client does not need to be a member of the bridal party or play a significant part in the wedding in order for the payment of benefit to continue while they are absent from New Zealand
- travel for a court ordered custody arrangement
For more information see:
- Definition of family member
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect
- Permitted travel reasons
- Absences that do not prevent the client meeting their obligations
- Paying benefit when client failed to advise of absence
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within a 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Estimated income — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Estimated income
Clients must advise Work and Income of any change in their circumstances that affects their entitlement or rate of Young Parent Payment, such as commencing employment.
Where the client has one-off, fluctuating or casual income, it may be necessary to estimate their earnings to prevent a debt.
When the client under or over estimates their income they should confirm the actual amount earned as soon as possible.
If the actual income is different this should be charged against the Young Parent Payment for the week it was earned or the period that it represents.
This may result in arrears or a debt for the client.
For more information about income see:
- Income change
- Calculating the benefit rate
- Income for a past period
For information about debt recovery, see:
- Debt treatment [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: The following examples show situations where we may pay a benefit for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. Please note this list is not exhaustive. Client's reason for travelling for 28 days within 52 week period Client's current reason for travel within 52 week period Outcome Essential travel reasons Essential travel reason eg a seriously ill family member Generally consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if reasonable in the circumstances Job interview or job prospect Essential travel reason eg a funeral Generally would consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if reasonable in the circumstances Young Parent Payment client to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with their youth activity obligations. The client wishes to be absent from New Zealand for another general holiday This is not an approved reason for paying for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. The client would not be able to receive a benefit while absent from New Zealand for this reason even if the travel will not prevent them meeting their obligations (eg the travel is at a time when they are not required to be in education, training or work-based learning or in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations) Young Parent Payment client to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with their youth activity obligations. To provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster or similar adverse event. Generally would allow further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. This is an unforeseen event and it is reasonable for them to help their family member. Young Parent Payment client to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with their youth activity obligations. Essential travel reason Generally would consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if the essential travel reason was unforeseen. Young Parent Payment client to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with their youth activity obligations. Needs to attend a wedding of a family member. Generally would not consider allowing a further period of payment for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. Weddings are usually known about in advance and this should have been planned for when they used the 28 days to go on holiday. However, where the wedding is genuinely unforeseen, consideration could be given to allowing travel for a period of more than 28 days in a 52 week period.

chunks.title: Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: Young Parent Payment client had to spend four days at a funeral overseas. The client had booked a holiday prior to the attendance at the funeral overseas. This holiday was booked for 28 days because they are able travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with their obligations. The client does not have the full 28 days left Travelling for a general holiday is not an approved reason for paying a benefit for more than 28 days in a 52 week period The benefit will only be paid for the number of days the client has available (that is, 24 days).

chunks.title: Example 1 — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: Carlos contacts MSD on 19 November to advise he has returned from travelling to Malaysia to be with his dying mother. He left in a hurry and didn't contact MSD before his departure. His Young Parent Payment stopped on 4 November, the day after he left the country. He returned to New Zealand on 14 November, but then had to organise a New Zealand-based funeral for his mother, as a large number of people are based in New Zealand. Carlos didn't advise MSD of his travel before leaving New Zealand, but he has a humanitarian reason that justifies his travel and the reason he didn't contact MSD before he left. Given Carlos' circumstances, he contacted MSD as soon as it would have been reasonable to expect him to and he meets the criteria for an approved travel reason. Carlos' Young Parent Payment can be backdated to 4 November.

chunks.title: Example 2 — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: Sanjay left New Zealand for India on Saturday 7 December because his father had become suddenly seriously ill and been hospitalised. While in India, Sanjay's father passed away and Sanjay stayed in India for the funeral. Sanjay returned on 16 December, after staying for 2 weeks for the Hindu funeral and mourning period. On 19 December, Sanjay contacts MSD to explain he has been overseas after learning of his father's illness, and that he stayed for the funeral. On return, Sanjay spent time mourning with his own family and has been distraught. He explains that he only realised last night that he had not informed MSD or his Youth Service provider of his absence. Sanjay's reason for leaving New Zealand is a humanitarian reason and he meets the criteria for backdating his payment to the day after his departure. Given Sanjay's circumstances, he informed MSD as soon as he reasonably could. Sanjay's Young Parent Payment can be backdated to 8 December, the date it was suspended.

chunks.title: Example 3 — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: Tusila calls MSD on 5 October to tell them she will leave New Zealand on 7 October to help her sister, who just lost her house in a flood. When asked how long she will be gone for, Tusila says that she has not bought a return ticket yet and was considering staying on to catch up with family and see how her sister is going. MSD informs Tusila that she can only keep getting her Young Parent Payment if she is absent for essential travel.. Helping her sister after a flood is considered essential travel, however if she is going to stay longer for a holiday, she will not be able to get her Young Parent Payment during the time she is on holiday. Tusila returns to MSD the next day with an airline quote showing that the cheapest return flight is on 14 October. She thinks it will take her a week to ensure her sister has sorted out insurance, medium-term accommodation, and access to basic goods like clothing and food. She has decided not to stay on for the holiday. MSD agrees this is reasonable and tells Tusila that she can keep getting Young Parent Payment from 7 to 14 October, while she is overseas helping her sister.

chunks.title: Example 4 — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: Christy is getting Young Parent Payment and contacts MSD to advise her sister is getting married in Australia on 8 September. Christy is going to Australia to her sister's wedding but intends to stay on for a further 2 weeks to visit other family. Her stay is not during a study break and she will have to miss some of her course. Christy is leaving New Zealand on 4 September as she has to help her sister prepare. She will stay until 10 September. Christy then begins the holiday part of her trip, returning to New Zealand on 25 September. Christy's travel is divided as follows: - 5 September to 10 September period meets the essential travel criteria - 11 September to 24 September period is considered other travel (holiday), is not during Christy's school holidays, and does not meet the essential travel criteria Christy's Young Parent Payment can only be paid until 10 September, for the period that meets the essential travel criteria.

chunks.title: Example 5 — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: Bill left New Zealand on 10 October during the school term to help his brother in Palmerston, a remote island in the Cook Islands, after his brother lost his house in a fire. He returns to New Zealand on 31 October. A week later, on 7 November he attends an appointment and asks his Youth Service provider why his Young Parent Payments have stopped. His Youth Service provider informs him that his payments stopped when he left the country and asks why he didn't contact MSD or the provider sooner. Bill explains that he left in a hurry and he wasn't able to contact MSD while away as he couldn't access a computer. When he got back he started going to school again but forgot about contacting MSD. He only remembered when his landlord asked him about rent. His provider tells him that, because he didn't contact MSD or his provider as soon as he reasonably could have been expected to (i.e. once he had helped his brother), his payment can only be backdated to 31 October, the date he got back to New Zealand.

chunks.title: Example 1 — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Example 1
A client applies for benefit to be paid for 10 days when they are going to be absent from New Zealand. In the past 52 weeks the client had 10 days absence from New Zealand and continued to be paid their benefit.
Step
Calculation
Identify the day after the client is intending to leave New Zealand.
14 September 2019
Count back 52 weeks from this date.
15 September 2018
Count the number of days the client has continued getting their benefit while they were overseas in this 52 week period.
Days client has continued getting their benefit while absent from New Zealand between 14 September 2018 and 15 September 2019 = 10 days
Subtract the number of days the client has been paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand from 28 days.
28 - 10 days = 18 days available
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay the client for the days they have available.
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay them for the 10 days they are out of the country.
## Example 2
A client applies for benefit to be paid for 10 days when they are going to be absent from New Zealand. In the past 52 weeks the client had 20 days absence from New Zealand and continued being paid their benefit.
Step
Calculation
Identify the day after the client is intending to leave New Zealand.
14 September 2019
Count back 52 weeks from this date.
15 September 2018
Count the number of days the client has continued getting their benefit while they were overseas in this 52 week period.
Days client continued getting their benefit while absent from New Zealand between 14 September 2018 and 15 September 2019 = 20 days
Subtract the number of days the client was paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand from 28 days.
28 - 20 days = 8 days available
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay the client for the days they have available.
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay them for the 8 days they are out of the country. For 2 of the days they are absent from New Zealand they will not get their payments.
Check if the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit for more than 28 days in a 52 week period - if they meet these criteria, they may be able to continue being paid for the additional 2 days of absence.

chunks.title: Examples of paying for more than 28 days for obtaining family support — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period where the client is travelling to receive support from a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family) who is residing overseas.

chunks.title: Examples (but are not limited to) — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: Client's previous reason for travel 28 days of travel within the 52 week period Client's current reason for travel within 52 week period Outcome A Young Parent Payment client who is attending school continued to receive their payment while they went to Australia for a 2 week holiday during the school holidays on the grounds that this travel did not prevent them from meeting their obligations. Following this, they continued to receive their payment while they travelled to Australia in the same year for a further 2 weeks to visit their uncle while he was seriously ill and to attend his funeral. As a result, the young person has already received their payment while travelling overseas for 28 days in a 52 week period. The young person's relationship with their parents has broken down. The young person has an aunt is the United States whom they are very close to and who provides them with guidance and support. The young person does not have any family members in New Zealand that provide them with the type of support they can obtain from their aunt. The young person wishes to travel to the United States during the school holidays to visit their aunt. The travel is during a time when the young person is not required to be in New Zealand to meet any other obligations (e.g. it is at a time when they are not required to attend a budgeting or parenting course). Generally would consider allowing the young person to receive their payment for a maximum of 2 weeks while they travel overseas to visit their aunt. The maximum amount of time that a young person can receive their payment on the grounds that the travel will not prevent them from meeting their obligations is 28 days. Therefore, the maximum amount of time this young person can continue to receive their payment while they visit their aunty to obtain support is 2 weeks as they have already received their payment for 2 weeks when they went to Australia for a holiday earlier in the year. A Young Parent Payment client who is attending a training course continued to receive their payments while they travelled to Australia to holiday with friends for 28 days, on the grounds that this travel did not prevent them from meeting their obligations. The young person wishes to travel to Australia for a week during the semester break to visit their grandmother who provides them with support and guidance. The young person's grandmother is their closest relative and they do not have any family members in New Zealand who can offer them the type of support they get from their grandmother.

chunks.title: Examples (but are not limited to) — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: The travel will be during a time when the young person is not required to be in New Zealand to meet any other obligations (e.g. it is at a time when they are not required to attend a budgeting or parenting course). The young person has already received their payment while they travelled overseas for a total of 28 days in a 52 week period on the grounds that the travel did not prevent them from meeting their obligations. As a result, they are not permitted to get their payment for a further period of overseas travel to obtain support from a family member residing overseas. They would only be permitted to receive their payment for a further period of overseas travel if they met one of the other circumstances for paying a benefit from more than 28 days in 52 weeks. A Young Parent Payment client continued to get their payments while they travelled overseas to attend the funeral of a family member, the wedding of another family member and a court case that they were required to attend as a witness. The total period of time the young person has received their payments while they travelled overseas for these reasons is 28 days in a 52 week period. The young person has a brother in Australia whom they are very close to and who provides them with support and mentoring. The young person does not have any family members is New Zealand who can offer them the type of support that they get from their brother. The young person is attending a training course and wishes to travel to Australia to visit their brother during the semester break. The travel will be during a time when the young person is not required to be in New Zealand to meet any other obligations (e.g. it is at a time when they are not required to attend a budgeting or parenting course). Generally would consider paying the young person while they travel to visit their brother to obtain support for a maximum of 28 days. This is because the young person has not yet travelled in the last 52 weeks on the grounds that the travel did not prevent them from meeting their obligations.

chunks.title: Exemption for severe disablement — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Exemption for severe disablement
As an incentive for the personal effort of a severely disabled person to participate or continue in employment, discretion can be used to disregard all or part of any income earned from employment as chargeable income for benefit purposes.
Consideration for this special income exemption should be given to clients with a severe disability who are extremely limited in their ability to participate in employment, the community and take care of themselves.
Consider whether or not the client is severely disabled. The Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement will help.
Each case should be assessed on an individual basis.
If the client is severely disabled consider whether or not to disregard all or part of any income earned by the client. To help with this, see Amount of income exemption.
Clients who are not severely disabled cannot receive this exemption.
For more information see:
- Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement
- Amount of income exemption

chunks.title: Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement
A special income exemption for severe disablement may be given to a client as an incentive for their personal effort to participate or continue in employment.
To help decide if a person is severely disabled consider the following:
- Does the client have to put in more effort in order to participate in employment? (for example, they may take a considerably long time to get ready in the morning or a longer time to travel to their place of employment)?
- Is the client's capacity to earn the same wage as a person without a severe disability reduced because of their disability (for example, does the client work reduced hours or receive less money for the job they undertake because of their disability)?
- Does the client have additional expenses to undertake employment (for example additional transport or equipment costs)?
- Does the client have difficulties participating in employment or completing their tasks because of their disability (for example, they may experience difficulties with mobility around the work place, be limited in the tasks they undertake or on occasion may not complete their work duties)?
- Does the client require assistance from another person to carry out some of their daily tasks (for example, washing, dressing or cooking)?
- Does the client require the assistance from another person to travel to work or to ensure their physical safety while at work (for example, does the client have difficulty using public transport)?
- Any other relevant factors that should be considered.
- If the client answers 'yes' to one or more of these questions you will have to decide if the client is severely disabled or if you need further information to make this decision.
Contact Helpline if you need help with the assessment.
For more information see:
- Amount of income exemption
- Exemption for severe disablement

chunks.title: Guidelines for paying a higher rate — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Guidelines for paying a higher rate
Payment can be increased above the hospital rate to a rate that (together with the client's other income) will be sufficient to meet the client's continuing commitments.
Use the following guidelines to assess whether the client's rate should be higher.
1. Have the client complete an Increased payment while you are in hospital form.
2. Accept stated expenses where they appear reasonable but ask for proof if there is doubt.
3. Check that all possible action has been taken to reduce expenses. For example, giving up the lease on a flat where the hospital stay is indefinite.
4. If the increase in payment request is for one-off items such as clothing, YSSU can pay the increase by:
- a backdated review of the benefit rate to create a lump sum payment or
- increasing the benefit rate for a limited time
## Example
Continuing commitments per week
$55.00
less other weekly income (bank interest)
$5.00
rate of increase
$50.00
plus hospital rate (net, at 1 April 2026)
$58.34
rate of benefit payable
$108.34
YSSU will add the rate payable as a non-standard rate on the SNSRA screen.
A parent benefit reassessment SPBR may also be required.

chunks.title: Home Detention — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Home Detention
A client may be in prison for a short time before being released on home detention.
Home detainees can apply for an exemption from their youth activity obligations. Young people on home detention should be encouraged to undertake education and training options suitable to their circumstances.
## Period in prison more than 31 days
If the period in prison is thirty-one days or more, an initial stand-down will be imposed and the client will also have access to a Steps to Freedom Special Needs Grant to assist them during the stand-down.
## Partner
When the partner of a person in prison has been receiving a benefit, this will be reviewed from the date of release.

chunks.title: Hospitalisation — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Hospitalisation
When a sole parent client getting Young Parent Payment is admitted to hospital, their benefit can continue at the full rate for the first 13 weeks. The rate of payment will need to be reduced to the hospital rate after the client has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks (not after receiving a benefit for 13 weeks).
If a client is in hospital they may be exempt from meeting their youth activity obligations.
## Care of the child
You will need to find out who is caring for the client's child and the length of time the client is likely to be in hospital.
If the child is being cared for by someone else temporarily, YSSU can pay part of the client's Young Parent Payment to the caregiver to help with the cost of care.
If the child is not staying in the client's care long term and is no longer a dependent child, YSSU will need to stop the client's benefit. The client may need to transfer to another benefit.
The new caregiver may be able to get Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit or include the child as a dependent child if they are getting a main benefit.
## Hospital rate
The hospital rate allows for the cost of personal items, which patients are expected to provide for themselves.
The net weekly hospital rate is $58.34 (as at 1 April 2026).
YSSU can pay an amount above the hospital rate when there are financial circumstances to warrant paying at a higher rate.
Note you cannot pay an amount less than the hospital rate.

chunks.title: Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Humanitarian reasons for backdating to day after departure
Where a client does not advise of their departure from New Zealand before they go, they may be able to have their benefit paid from the day after their departure date if the client has a humanitarian reason that justifies their reason for travel and their failure to tell Work and Income before they left.
Humanitarian reasons are:
- to provide aid or assistance to a family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member) immediately following a natural disaster (for example, flood, earthquake, bush fires) or similar adverse event (eg house fire)
- to be with a suddenly seriously ill, or dying family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member)
- to attend the sudden funeral of a family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member)
For more information see:
- Client not returned due to unforeseen circumstances (within 28 day maximum)
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Imprisonment — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Imprisonment
Generally, when a Young Parent Payment client is imprisoned or detained in custody, they are no longer entitled to receive Young Parent Payment.
Young Parent Payment should stop from the day following the date of imprisonment.
The Youth Service Support Unit (YSSU) must decide whether to suspend or cancel the benefit after considering the likely period in prison and whether the client has a partner and/or dependent children.
In some circumstances Young Parent Payment can continue when the client is imprisoned.

chunks.title: Example 1 — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Example 1
A client getting Young Parent Payment has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks.
This client has other income which reduces the main benefit rate to $20 per week. In this case pay the rate of $20 per week which is lower than the hospital rate of $58.34 (as at 1 April 2026).
## Example 2
A client getting Young Parent Payment has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks.
This client has other income which reduces the main benefit rate to $70 per week. In this case pay the hospital rate of $58.34 per week (as at 1 April 2026) which is the lower rate.

chunks.title: Income change — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Income change
Clients must tell MSD if they have any change in circumstances that affects their entitlement or rate of benefit payable, such as when they earn and receive income.
Any income the Young Parent Payment client (or their partner) gets should be charged against the benefit for the week(s) in which the income was earned or represents.
When a client has fluctuating or casual income, income is charged on a week-by-week basis. Income is charged for the week they work, and for the week without work 'nil' income is charged.
In all cases the client must still qualify for Young Parent Payment.
Any Extra help the client is getting must also be reassessed each time there is a change in the client's income.
## Deductions or redirections
When adding income to a client's record, check there is enough benefit to cover any deductions or redirections. Any deductions or redirections may need to be reduced depending on the amount of benefit payable.

chunks.title: Income for a past period — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Income for a past period
Where a client declares income for a past period and there is either no income or a different amount entered on INCMH, the client's Young Parent Payment must be reviewed.
Income must be charged against the Young Parent Payment for the week in which the income is earned or the period that it represents.
## Example
A client phones on 22/04/2015 and advises that they received $220 gross income for one week's work for the period 06/04/2015 to 12/04/2015.
The client has been overpaid their Young Parent Payment as there is no income on their SWIFTT record. A debt must be established for the overpayment of benefit for the week 06/04/2015 to 12/04/2015.
The following is the process:
INCMA
add 00.00 effective from Monday 13/04/2015
INCMA
add $220 effective from Monday 06/04/2015 - a backdated review will be required
SBDR
complete a back dated review using the abated benefit rate for the week 06/04/2015 to 12/04/2015
SWIFTT
debt established for the period 06/04/2015 to 12/04/2015
## Backdated review required
In some cases when income has been added SWIFTT will give a message that a backdated review SBDR is required.
This warning message occurs because the effective date (when adding the income) is prior to the current pay period. SWIFTT reads the benefit rate record SRAUI and can only automatically pay any arrears or establish any debt from the date of the last benefit rate review. Therefore you need to tell SWIFTT how much benefit the client should have been paid and over what period, by entering the abated benefit rate in SBDR.
As with all income recorded on a client's record any Extra help must also be reviewed.
- Income change
- Previous tax year
- Effect of income on Extra help
- Income from employment

chunks.title: Income from employment — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Income from employment
Clients must advise their service provider or Work and Income of any change in their circumstances that affects their entitlement or rate of Young Parent Payment, such as commencing employment.
## Full-time employment
If the client has commenced full-time employment, the Young Parent Payment must be stopped from the date the client commences work as they will no longer be entitled to receive the Young Parent Payment because they will not be able to meet their youth activity obligations.
If the partner has commenced full-time employment, then their Young Parent Payment must be stopped from the date they commenced work. They will no longer be entitled to receive the Young Parent Payment because they will not be able to meet their youth activity obligations.
## Part-time employment
A young person can receive Young Parent Payment while they are working part-time as long as they can meet:
- the qualification of being in, or available for, full-time education, approved training or approved work-based learning and
- other qualifications
The income from part-time employment will be charged against the benefit for the week in which the income was earned or represents.
However, if the earnings from the part-time or casual employment reduce the Young Parent Payment to a 'nil' rate of payment, when charged against the benefit then the benefit must be suspended.
For more information see:
- Income reduces the benefit to a nil rate
## Weekend work
If a client (or partner) is working weekends regularly, casually or 'one-off' then the income is charged against the benefit from the previous Monday.
For more information see:
- Estimated income
- Youth activity obligations

chunks.title: Income reduces the benefit to a 'nil' rate — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Income reduces the benefit to a 'nil' rate
If the client has earnings or income for a period that will reduce the Young Parent Payment payable to a 'nil' rate of payment, then the Young Parent Payment will need to be suspended or cancelled.
Although the main benefit may be stopped a client may still qualify for Extra help.
For more information see:
- Effect of income on Extra help
- Income from employment
- Income change
Note clients will not qualify to receive the Winter Energy Payment where their income reduces their benefit payment to nil.

chunks.title: Income stops — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Income stops
When a Young Parent Payment client advises that income has stopped you must review their Young Parent Payment and any Extra help they may be receiving, from the day after the income ceased.
You will need to determine why the income has stopped for example, a client may advise that the interest payments from their investment have ceased. You need to find out what the client has done with the money that was invested.
## Discretion
There is discretion to reduce or decline a benefit (or Extra help) where clients have deprived themselves of income or assets.
For more information see:
- Core Policy Definition of income
- Types of income
## Stops work
When a Young Parent Payment client stops work you need to decide when to commence or review their Young Parent Payment from.
You will need to find out:
- the date they ceased work
- the reason they ceased work
- final pay details (including any holiday pay, redundancy etc)
Note if the client currently getting Young Parent Payment receives any holiday pay charge the holiday pay as ongoing income over the period it represents.
## Example
Client has been earning $250 gross per week and ceases work 1 April 2026 getting $500 in holiday pay.
This is the equivalent of 2 weeks holiday pay. Continue to charge $250 per week for the period 1 April 2026 to 14 April 2026.
You can use DREW to help with this calculation.

chunks.title: Income test — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Income test
Young parents can earn up to $284.70 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026) before it will affect their benefit.
Income is charged weekly as it is earned and at the following rates:
For a sole parent:
- $1.00 is taken from the benefit for each $1.00 of income over $284.70 (before tax) a week until they earn $334.70 (as at 1 April 2026)
For clients who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and both are getting Young Parent Payment then the rate is:
- 50 cents is taken from each of their benefits for each $1.00 of combined income of the young person and their partner over $284.70 (before tax) a week until they earn $384.70 (as at 1 April 2026)
For a client who is married, in a civil union or in a de facto relationship where their partner is not getting Young Parent Payment then the rate is:
- $1.00 is taken from the benefit for each $1.00 of combined income of the client and their partner over $284.70 (before tax) a week until they earn $384.70 (as at 1 April 2026)

chunks.title: Client chooses to be absent for longer than reasonably necessary — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Client chooses to be absent for longer than reasonably necessary
Where a client chooses to be absent for longer than is reasonably necessary to attend the job interview or investigate a potential job prospect, their benefit will not continue to be paid for those extra days.
For more information see:
- Examples of job interview or job prospects overseas
- Client obtains employment overseas

chunks.title: Must receive payment for six months — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Must receive payment for six months
A young person who has been granted Young Parent Payment who has not been receiving the payment for six months cannot qualify for a main benefit when they turn 20 years. They must complete a minimum period of six months receiving Young Parent Payment first.
This ensures that the young person is able to have a reasonable chance to move towards a qualification by participating in education, training or work-based learning and undertaking other youth activity obligations before they focus on obligations attached to other main benefits.
For example, a young person is granted Young Parent Payment at the age of 19 years and 8 months old. When they turn 20 years old they will need to continue to receive Young Parent Payment for another two months to complete the six month minimum period. They can then be assessed for entitlement to other main benefits.
## Exception
A young person, who is receiving Young Parent Payment and then meets the criteria for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability, can be granted this benefit instead of Young Parent Payment without completing the minimum six months.
For more information see:
- Chooses to remain on Young Parent Payment past 20 years of age
- Age
- Qualifies for another benefit

chunks.title: Information Sharing Agreement with New Zealand Customs Service — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Information Sharing Agreement with New Zealand Customs Service
The Ministry of Social Development has an Approved Information Sharing Agreement with New Zealand Customs Service that identifies clients getting a benefit who have left New Zealand.
Once identified, the client's eligibility to keep getting their benefit payments while they are absent from New Zealand is automatically determined by Ministry systems.
## Does not advise of departure
If the client did not tell the Ministry they were leaving New Zealand their benefit will be suspended immediately from the day after they left New Zealand.
The Integrity Intervention Centre will determine if there has been an overpayment, establish any debt, and advise the client.
If a client challenges the information match refer them to the Integrity Intervention Centre.
For more information see:
- Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure
- Approved travel reasons
- Backdating benefit to day after departure date
- Action on return to New Zealand
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy

chunks.title: Ongoing assistance for surviving partner — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Ongoing assistance for surviving partner
When the partner of a Young Parent Payment client dies the partner's benefit is continued for 28 days at the rate that is payable at the date of death.
The continuation of payment beyond the date of death is referred to as terminal benefit.
## Client's benefit options
A surviving client can remain on Young Parent Payment as long as they continue to meet the qualifications.
## Date of review
When the surviving client remains on Young Parent Payment review the client's benefit from the date following the death of their partner and:
- adjust any extra help to the single rate

chunks.title: On leave for 28 days or less — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## On leave for 28 days or less
When a client getting the hospital rate is on leave from hospital for 28 days or less:
- increase their benefit to the appropriate full rate from the date of discharge on leave and
- review any Extra help from the same date
On re-admission to hospital:
- reduce the benefit to the rate paid before the period of leave and
- review any Extra help from the same date
Note the dates of admission and discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital.

chunks.title: On leave for more than 28 days — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## On leave for more than 28 days
When a client getting the hospital rate is on leave from hospital for more than 28 days:
- increase their benefit to the appropriate full rate from the date of discharge on leave and
- review any Extra help
On re-admission to hospital continue to pay the full rate of benefit and any Extra help for another 13 weeks of hospitalisation.
Note calculation of the 13 week period in hospital begins again after the client has been re-admitted when on leave for more than 28 days.

chunks.title: On leave from hospital — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## On leave from hospital
Young Parent Payment is paid at the full rate for any period of leave from hospital. Where the client has been receiving the hospital rate increase their benefit for any period they are on leave.
The benefit action to take, on the client's re-admission to hospital, will depend on how long they were on leave.

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki order in place — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: The following table identifies when a child can be considered a dependent child and when it can't, depending on the type of order that is in place and section of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 that applies. When to include as a dependent child When not to include as a dependent child section 139: Agreements for temporary care of child or young person by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 140: Agreements for extended care of child or young person by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 78: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, pending determination of court proceedings. If Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki has returned the child or young person into the care of the immediate previous caregiver. section 78: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, pending determination of court proceedings. section 101: Custody order in favour of principal caregiver. Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki under section 110. section 101: Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 102: Interim Custody Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 110(2)a: Sole Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. Section 101 Custody Order in favour of principal caregiver and other dependent child criteria are met. Please refer case to your local solicitor for consideration. section 110(2)a: Sole Guardianship Order in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 110(2)b: Additional Guardianship Order, to any other guardian in favour of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 112: Guardianship Order in favour of Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki for a specific purpose. Please refer case to your local solicitor for consideration. section 86: Services Orders that provide for particular services and assistance required by the child or young person (e.g. counselling fees, special education costs). section 86: Services Orders that provide for general financial support to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. section 91: Support Orders. The child may be considered a dependent child where the documentation states that specific financial support is to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki.

chunks.title: Oranga Tamariki order in place — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: section 91: Support Orders. The child cannot be considered a dependent child where the documentation states that general financial support is to be provided by the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki. See your local solicitor if you receive a case in this category. When a child or young person is discharged from the care, custody or sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, always consider including the child in the clients Young Parent Payment or granting Unsupported Childs Benefit. - The legislation referenced above is the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989

chunks.title: Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Orphans or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid
When a client is receiving an Orphans Benefit or an Unsupported Child's Benefit, the child is not treated as a dependent child and is not included in the assessment of Young Parent Payment.
The client's Young Parent Payment is assessed on their family circumstances excluding the child for which Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit is being paid.

chunks.title: Partner's IRD number — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: As part of a review of Young Parent Payment, MSD may make a written request to the young person for evidence of a partner's IRD number when the partner's income is relevant to a young parent's Young Parent Payment.

chunks.title: Setting or extending the period for providing evidence — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: MSD can request a young parent to provide evidence of their partner's IRD number within a reasonable time period (usually 10 working days). MSD can set a different period or extend the period to provide evidence of an IRD number when it is expected to take longer to get the evidence. This includes considering factors outside of the young parent or partner's control that may cause delays, including, but not limited to: - the young person has a family emergency that caused a delay - processing delays with an external agency (e.g., Inland Revenue, Department of Internal Affairs, etc) - the young person or their partner does not speak English as a first language and has difficulty navigating evidence requirements - the young person or their partner has limited access to the internet, a device, or their local service centre - the young person or their partner has a physical or intellectual disability that makes accessing services difficult.

chunks.title: Notice following unsuccessful match — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a young person or their partner's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the young person (in writing) to provide evidence of their partner's IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the client a minimum of 10 working days to provide their partner's IRD number evidence or the young person's assistance may be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Young Parent Payment. Isla's partner, Ariki, has income that is included in MSD's income test to determine eligibility for Young Parent Payment and MSD holds an IRD number for Ariki.
