The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Ariki's IRD number. As part of a review of Isla's assistance, MSD provides a notice in writing giving 10 working days for Isla to provide evidence of Ariki's IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Ariki already having an IRD number - Ariki not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD may suspend assistance if evidence is not received — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: If a partner's IRD number evidence is not provided within a reasonable timeframe (usually 10 working days) or within the extended period if this has been applied, the young parent's assistance may be suspended. In rare cases the young parent's assistance may be cancelled or the rate of payment varied. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance.

chunks.title: IRD number not requested in some circumstances — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - significant factors, that are outside the young person or partner's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number, (e.g. a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence), and - the young person needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided. A partner's IRD number or evidence of their IRD number does not need to be provided when they are not a New Zealand tax resident. MSD can determine a later point to request the evidence of the IRD number. For more information see: - Non-tax resident partner's IRD number not required Note there is different guidance for requesting evidence of an IRD number for a young person or when a young person is applying for Young Parent Payment.

chunks.title: Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure
Generally, clients receiving a main benefit must advise Work and Income of their intention to leave New Zealand prior to their departure to be eligible to continue to receive their payments.
Only in specific circumstance can a client receiving a benefit who leaves New Zealand without telling us be able to have their benefit either:
- resumed from the date they notified Work and Income of their absence if their travel is allowed or
- backdated to the day after their departure date
Note this can occur either while the client is still overseas or once they have returned.
## Paying benefit when client failed to advise of absence
If a client contacts Work and Income after they have left New Zealand and is not eligible to have their benefit backdated, their benefit can only be resumed from:
- the date that they notified us of their absence and
- only if the travel is allowed (ie they meet the criteria to continue to be paid their benefit while overseas either because they meet the criteria for approved travel, or the requirement that travel can be approved does not apply to them)
Otherwise, the client cannot have their benefit resumed until they return to New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Backdating benefit to day after departure
- Action on return to New Zealand
- Approved travel reasons
- Payment when client absent from New Zealand
- Exampled of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy

chunks.title: Paying a higher rate — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Paying a higher rate
YSSU can make payment at a rate higher than the hospital rate where the client cannot meet their continuing costs from the hospital rate of payment and any other income they receive.
Take into consideration:
- the client's financial commitments and
- access to other income
Note when considering payment of benefit at a rate higher than the hospital rate; generally do not take cash assets into account as rates of benefit payment are not subject to an assets test.
For more information about paying at a higher rate see:
- Guidelines for paying a higher rate
## Maximum amount payable
YSSU can pay a rate higher than the hospital rate up to the maximum rate of Young Parent Payment that would otherwise be payable.
## When not to pay a higher rate
A client cannot be paid a higher rate of benefit (because of hospitalisation) than they would otherwise receive. Where their usual benefit payment is less than the hospital rate, don't increase their benefit to the hospital rate (or any other higher rate).
A benefit may be paid at less than the hospital rate because of:
- the client's income (if it continues while in hospital)
- maintenance deductions or
- overseas pension deductions

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
To pay a benefit more than 28 days during any 52 week period:
- the client must be continuing to receive their benefit while absent from New Zealand because: they have an approved travel reason orthey are not required to have an approved travel reason in order to be paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand
- they have an approved travel reason or
- they are not required to have an approved travel reason in order to be paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand
- the client could not return to New Zealand because of new circumstances that: they could not reasonably foresee at the time when they left New Zealand andthat are outside of the client's control
- they could not reasonably foresee at the time when they left New Zealand and
- that are outside of the client's control
and
- Work and Income is satisfied that the extension of the absence is no longer than is necessary to address the new circumstances

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days for an approved reason — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period when the client is absent from New Zealand. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. To pay a benefit more than 28 days during any 52 week period of absence from New Zealand, the client must be travelling for one of the following reasons: - essential travel - to attend a significant event relating to a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family), that the client would reasonably be expected to attend (eg to visit a person who is seriously ill, seriously injured or whose death is imminent, to attend a funeral, to provide support to a party or witness to a court case, travel required for a court ordered custody arrangement) - to attend a court case which the person is required to attend as a party or a witness - to attend a job interview or follow up on a job prospect - for clients with a disability, to receive vocational training or disability assistance-dog training not available in New Zealand during the period or periods of absence - for clients with a disability, to travel overseas for the sole or predominant purpose of competing in any overseas multinational or international Special Olympic or Paralympic Games competition - to provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster (flood, earthquake, fire) or similar adverse event (eg house fire) and - Work and Income must be satisfied, when considering the client's reason for travel, that the length of the absence is no longer than necessary for the reason for travel In addition, where the client has already been paid a benefit while absent from New Zealand in the 52 week period Work and Income must be satisfied that either: - the client could not have reasonably foreseen them needing to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, or - the client could not have rearranged their affairs to avoid being absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, and - it would be unreasonable for the benefit not to be paid Note generally we would not pay more than 28 days extra travel per absence. For more information see: - Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason - Client not returned due to unforeseeable event (within 28 days maximum) - Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days - receive support from family member residing overseas — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period where the client is travelling to receive support from a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family) who is residing overseas. For more information see: - Definition of 'support' from a family member residing overseas This applies (and is limited to a further 28 days in any 52 week period) when: - the young person has already been paid a benefit while absent from New Zealand for one or more approved reasons for all or most of 28 days in a 52 week period and - the young person will be absent from New Zealand for the purpose of obtaining support from a family member residing overseas (while still meeting the eligibility criteria for Young Parent Payment if receiving it due to a family breakdown) and - the support that the client needs cannot reasonably be provided to the client by one of their family members in New Zealand and - the absence will not prevent the young person from continuing to meet their youth activity obligations because the absence is at a time when: they are not required to attend education, training or work-based learning (for example, they are exempt from meeting their obligations) orthey are meeting their obligation to be in, or available for, education, training or work-based learning but it is the school holidays or the semester/term break or they are between academic years or the course/school has not started yet andthey are not required to be in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations during the time of the absence (eg they do not need to attend a parenting or budgeting course during the time they will be overseas) - they are not required to attend education, training or work-based learning (for example, they are exempt from meeting their obligations) or - they are meeting their obligation to be in, or available for, education, training or work-based learning but it is the school holidays or the semester/term break or they are between academic years or the course/school has not started yet and - they are not required to be in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations during the time of the absence (eg they do not need to attend a parenting or budgeting course during the time they will be overseas)

chunks.title: Cannot be paid for more than 28 days for purposes of obtaining support — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: The maximum amount of time that a client receiving Young Parent Payment can continue to receive their payment while overseas due to the absence not preventing them meeting their obligations is 28 days in any 52 week period. Therefore, if a client subject to youth activity obligations has already received their payment for 28 days in a 52 week period while they were overseas on a holiday on the grounds that the travel did not prevent them meeting their obligations, they will not be able to continue to receive their payment for a further period of overseas absence in the same 52 week period under the 'obtaining support from a family member' circumstance. For more information see: - Examples of paying for more than 28 days for obtaining family support

chunks.title: Period over which to charge income — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Period over which to charge income
Income should be charged against the benefit for the week it is earned or the period it represents for example:
For example:
- an interest payment is received once every 6 months representing the previous 6 months
1. This payment should be charged against the benefit over the previous 6 months the payment represents.
2. If it is an ongoing investment you would then add it on as estimated income for the next 6 months.
- a client gets wages for working a fortnight. Income should be charged each week representing the wages paid for that week.
- a client works for 2 days of the week. Income should be charged in the week it is earned.
For more information on charging weekend work see: Income from employment
In most cases, determining the period will be straightforward. For more information on some specific types of income and how to charge them, see:
- Core Policy Types of income
If the period of when the income was earned, or the period it represents is still unable to be determined, discuss the payment with Helpline.
## Overlapping income
Where a client has income from several sources paid for the same periods of time, then all of the payments are added together.
This total income will be charged against the Young Parent Payment over the period the income represents.

chunks.title: Permanent absence — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Permanent absence
If a client is leaving New Zealand permanently, the Youth Payment must be cancelled from the day after departure.
If the client is moving to a country that has a Reciprocal agreement with New Zealand they may qualify for a benefit or pension in that country.
## Moving to Australia
If the client is moving to Australia it is important that they are aware that they may not be able to receive a benefit until they have resided in Australia for two years after being granted permanent residence status.
For more information see:
- To or from overseas Reciprocal Agreements

chunks.title: Permitted travel reasons — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Permitted travel reasons
A client not otherwise entitled to be paid their Young Parent Payment while absent from New Zealand may have their payments continue for up to 28 days in any 52 week period, if their travel is for one (or a combination of), of the following permitted travel reasons:
- essential travel - to attend a significant event relating to a family member or a person who fulfils a role in relation to the client that is similar to that of a family member, that the client would reasonably be expected to attend
- to attend a court case which the person is required to attend as a party or a witness - this is to allow clients who are required by law to attend court and supports the maintenance of the law. A client would generally be expected to provide evidence that they are required to attend a court overseas. This would include documents from the court.
- to attend a job interview or follow up on a job prospect
- for clients with a disability, to receive vocational training or disability assistance-dog training not available in New Zealand during the time the client is absent
- for clients with a disability, to travel overseas for the sole or predominant purpose of competing in any overseas multinational or international Special Olympic or Paralympic Games competition
- to provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster (eg flood, earthquake, fire) or similar adverse event (eg house fire)

chunks.title: Previous tax year — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: A sole parent client may declare income for a period in a previous tax year. There are three possible outcomes for the client depending on the amount of income declared and whether any previous income had been charged. These outcomes are: 1. The client is due arrears following a review on their benefit. As the arrears will be issued in the current tax year no adjustment is required to the tax details or 2. The amount of the income declared is under the exemption and the client does not receive any Extra help. The client's SWIFTT record is noted accordingly or 3. A debt will be established and the tax details for this year will need to be adjusted accordingly as in the following example.

chunks.title: Example — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: A client phoned on 02/04/2022 and advises they worked for the week 24/01/2022 to 30/01/2022 and earned $250.54 gross. Manually assess the income deduction: Gross income (excluding cents) $250.00 Less income allowed before benefit is affected (as at 1 July 2021) $227.18 equals income $22.82 Amount benefit reduced on account of income (income over $227.18 reduces benefit by $1.00 per $1.00) $22.00 To work out the benefit rate payable: Maximum benefit (as at 1 July 2021) $406.78 Less reduction due to income $22.00 Benefit rate payable $384.78 Once you have calculated the benefit due for this week add the income to INCMA. A backdated review SBDR needs to be completed for this week. The following is the process: SBDR $384.78 for the week 24/01/2022 to 30/01/2022 LSUM a memo will be produced as a result of the backdated review with details of the debt amount to be added into the appropriate tax year. It is the net amount of debt which is added to SWIFTT SDBTI debt inquiry for the client (F4 for STAXI) STAXI select the appropriate year and DBT which will take you into the SDBTA screen SDBTA add the debt type, add the benefit/pension code, add the debt status and breach type, add the net debt amount, this will also adjust the tax record for the client. Add the period that the debt represents and add any comments where appropriate - remember to commence recovery of the debt via SOFSI

chunks.title: Priority for deductions — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Priority for deductions
Certain forms of deductions take priority over others; the following list gives the order of priority, from highest to lowest:
Highest priority
- Child Support deductions made under the Child Support Act 1991
- Inland Revenue tax deductions
- Ministry of Social Development debt repayments including Liable Parent Contributions (LPC), child maintenance debts and Major Repairs Advances (MRA), Student Allowance debt, Student Loan debt converted to Ministry of Social Development debt, Income Related Rent historical Kāinga Ora (previously Housing NZ) debt, Income Related Rent Ministry of Social Development debt
- attachment orders made under the Family Proceedings Act 1980
- court attachment orders issued under the Summary Proceedings Act 1957
- court attachment orders issued under the District Court Act 2016
- Student Loan repayments
Lowest priority
Determining the priority of deductions is necessary when a client has more than one order issued in respect of their benefit. Also each order and deduction notice is subject to its own protected earnings rule.
When deductions need to be reduced adjust from the lowest priority up to those with a higher priority taking into account the protected earnings rules for each.

chunks.title: Private hospital and homes — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Private hospital and homes
Young Parent Payment can be paid at the full rate regardless of the period of hospitalisation when a client is:
- admitted to a private hospital or
- admitted to a private home that provides residential care disability services
If the client receives Extra Help, this will need to be reviewed to see if their costs are continuing.
For more information see:
- Residential Support Subsidy

chunks.title: Protected earnings rate — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: Both the District Court Act and the Summary Proceedings Act provide that every Ministry of Justice attachment order must specify a 'protected earnings rate'. The protected earnings rate is usually 60% of the client's net earnings after PAYE tax has been deducted or withheld. The protected earnings rate is usually 60% of the client's net earnings after PAYE tax has been deducted or withheld. If the attachment order will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate, then the order will not operate, and you must cancel or return the attachment order to the Ministry of Justice. Calculating the client's income differs between attachment orders made under the Summary Proceedings Act and the District Court Act, in that different benefits are taken into account. Therefore, it is important to determine what type of attachment order has been issued. Summary Proceedings Act 1957 For orders made under the Summary Proceedings Act, the calculation of the client's income does not include Special Benefit, Temporary Additional Support, Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance, Winter Energy Payment, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit. District Court Act 2016 For orders made under the District Court Act, the client's income includes Special Benefit, Temporary Additional Support and Disability Allowance but does not include Child Disability Allowance, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit.

chunks.title: Example — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: An attachment order is received from the Ministry of Justice for $80.00 per week. The order lists the client's protected earnings rate as $375.91 per week. We need to calculate whether adding the deduction of $80.00 will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate. Calculate protected earnings rate: Young Parent Payment - sole parent net rate (as at 1 April 2026) $521.52 Plus Accommodation Supplement $105.00 Total net income $626.52 60% of total net earnings (= protected earnings) $375.91 Calculate if Attachment Order will exceed protected earnings Total net earnings $626.52 Less Child Support deduction $135.00 Less Ministry of Social Development debt $40.00 Sub total $451.52 Less Attachment Order $80.00 Total $371.52 The attachment order amount of $80.00 takes the client's total net income remaining to $371.52, which is below the protected earnings rate of $375.91 per week. The attachment order will not operate, you must return it to the Ministry of Justice for the order to be amended.

chunks.title: Qualifies for another benefit — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Qualifies for another benefit
A young person may qualify for another benefit due to a change in their circumstances. It is also important to determine if the young person still qualifies for Young Parent Payment.
For example, if a young person turns 20 they would no longer qualify for Young Parent Payment and would generally transfer to Sole Parent Support.
Note when a young person turns 20 years old the Young Parent Payment should stop. However in some circumstances the benefit may continue. See: Change in age
If the young person qualifies for more than one benefit they must be told which benefit is the most beneficial for their particular circumstances. They will need to be advised of:
- benefit rates
- the effect of any income they may receive (income reduction and any exemptions) and
- benefit obligations
The young person must make the final decision on which benefit they receive after being given all relevant information.
For more information see:
- Qualifications Young person turns 20 years old
- Change in age
- Sole Parent Payment Qualifications
- Jobseeker Support Qualifications
- Processing standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Rate of payment - sole parents — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Rate of payment - sole parents
If payment of Young Parent Payment is to continue while a sole parent client is in prison, YSSU will need to determine the rate to pay to the temporary caregiver.
The Young Parent Payment should generally be paid at the equivalent rate of Unsupported Child's Benefit that would be payable if the caregiver qualified for this, see: Examples - sole parents
However, there is discretion to continue payment at the full sole parent rate.
Consider including the following costs to calculate the rate to pay the temporary caregiver while the client is in prison:
- rent or outgoings if the children are being cared for in the client's home
- the client's other commitments if these costs are for essential items and they cannot be suspended, such as Child Support payments (where the client does not qualify for an exemption) or hire purchase for an essential item
The total amount paid to the temporary caregiver must not exceed the maximum amount of Young Parent Payment payable.
## SWIFTT
The Young Parent Payment and family tax credit should continue in the client's name and be paid to the caregiver as an agent in SWIFTT.
When the temporary caregiver is to be paid less than the maximum rate of Young Parent Payment, YSSU will need to add this as a non-standard rate using the SNSRA screen in SWIFTT.
For more information see:
- Examples - sole parents
- Decision guidelines - sole parents
- Sole parents

chunks.title: Reapplication for Young Parent Payment — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Reapplication for Young Parent Payment
When a young person reapplies for Young Parent Payment, they must complete the application process as if they are applying for the first time.
## Previous Independent Assessment report
Where a young person was receiving Young Parent Payment due to a relationship breakdown or another good and sufficient reason and an Independent Assessment Provider report was completed, YSSU will need to:
- retrieve the original Independent Assessment Provider report
- ask the young person what circumstances have changed that has led to another application for Young Parent Payment
- decide whether it is appropriate to send the young person for another assessment with the Independent Assessment Provider In some cases it may be helpful to speak with the Independent Assessment Provider before doing so.
If the young person's circumstances are the same as their previous application, you do not need to request another assessment from the Independent Assessment Provider.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Family breakdown
- Independent Assessment Provider

chunks.title: Recording income — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Recording income
Any income a client receives, even when the income is less than $284.70 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026), must be added to the client's SWIFTT record on the INCMA screen.
This is to ensure any Extra help is reviewed correctly and will create a permanent audit trail of all income details.
If the income is over the benefit cut-out point, and SWIFTT will not accept this information then a note on CMS should be added.
Ensure the following details are recorded:
- source of income, such as the employer's details
- gross (before tax) amount of income received
- period that the income represents
- how the income was advised, for example, phoned in by the client

chunks.title: Release from prison — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Release from prison
A client may be entitled to Young Parent Payment when they are released from prison. The date to recommence payment depends on the length of time the client has been in prison.
## Period in prison is more than 31 days
If the period in prison is thirty-one days or more, an initial stand-down will be imposed and the client will also have access to a Steps to Freedom Special Needs Grant to assist them during the stand-down.
## Partner
When the partner of a person in prison has been receiving a benefit, this will need to be reviewed from the date of release.
For more information see:
- Young Parent Payment Prisoners

chunks.title: Release on bail — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Release on bail
When a client is released on bail, Young Parent Payment can be paid from the date of release providing the client:
- is still able to meet their youth activity obligations
- has been in custody for less than 31 days and
- reapplies for a benefit immediately after their release
If the client has been in custody for more than 31 days an initial stand-down will be imposed.
For more information see:
- Young Parent Payment Prisoners
- Exemptions Court imposed conditions

chunks.title: Remanded in custody — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Remanded in custody
Generally, when a client is remanded in custody awaiting a further court appearance the benefit should be stopped. However, there is discretion to continue payment of Young Parent Payment after taking the client's financial circumstances and commitments into account.
When deciding whether to continue paying Young Parent Payment for the period for a particular client, consider the following:
- has the client been remanded pending a further court hearing or for sentencing
- does the client have continuing costs that cannot be avoided, such as rent and hire purchase for essential items
- does the client have a partner and or dependent children
Every situation should be considered on a case-by-case basis.
For help contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances before making a decision.

chunks.title: Residential Parole — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Residential Parole
If a client is released on residential parole they can apply for an exemption from their youth activity obligations.
## Partner
Where the partner of a person in prison has been receiving a benefit, this will need to be reviewed from the date of release.
For more information see:
- Young Parent Payment Court imposed conditions
- Special Needs Grants Steps to Freedom

chunks.title: Returns to live with parents — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Returns to live with parents
When young person who is 16 or 17 years old is receiving Young Parent Payment because of exceptional circumstances returns to live with their parents or begins to be financially supported by them or someone else, they are no longer entitled to receive the payment.
The Young Parent Payment should be cancelled from the date of their return home.
## Exception
If the young person is receiving Young Parent Payment because their parent's income is less than the Family Tax Credit cut-off point they can receive Young Parent Payment when they are living at home with their parents.
YSSU will need to review their Young Parent Payment and any Extra Help to ensure the young person is receiving the correct rate of payment.
For more information see:
- Deskfile Young Parent Payment rates

chunks.title: Sole parents — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Sole parents
When a sole parent client is imprisoned they will no longer be entitled to Young Parent Payment.
The Young Parent Payment should be suspended from the day after imprisonment.
The service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service may need to find out who is caring for the client's children and the length of time the client is likely to be in prison. This information can be obtained by contacting the prison liaison officer at the Department of Corrections.
Generally, the caregiver will need to apply for financial assistance in their own right.
They may be entitled to:
- have the children included as dependent children in their current benefit
- Unsupported Childs Benefit
- Emergency Benefit Caring for a child who is not their own or
- family tax credit and Best Start tax credit through Inland Revenue
## Exception
There is discretion to pay all or part of the Young Parent Payment to a temporary caregiver caring for the client's children.
There is also discretion to continue payment if the client is remanded in custody pending a further court appearance.
For more information see:
- Decision guidelines - sole parents
- Rate of payment - sole parents
- Examples - sole parents
- Remanded in custody

chunks.title: Split care — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Split care
Split care is when parents with two or more children are living apart and each parent has the care of at least one of their children on a full-time basis.
The child(ren) that is living with the Young Parent Payment client can be included as a dependent child.
Note in split care situations, generally only one parent can receive Sole Parent Support. The other parent must qualify, in their own right, for another benefit.
For more information see:
- Sole Parent Support Split care

chunks.title: Student Loans — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Student Loans
Clients with a Student Loan must make repayments to Inland Revenue when the income they receive exceeds a pre-determined level. This level is called the 'income threshold'.
A person must make repayments to Inland Revenue when their income exceeds $464.00 gross per week ($24,128 gross per year) as at 1 April 2026. Note non-taxable Extra help such as family tax credit, Best Start tax credit, Accommodation Supplement and Winter Energy Payment do not count as income in this instance.
If the client's income is over this income threshold, MSD can make the required deduction. However, this is only done if the client requests it.
If the client's portion of benefit is below the income threshold, there is no provision to make voluntary repayments through SWIFTT. The client can make voluntary payments direct to Inland Revenue at any time.
Note the following:
- Student Loan deductions can only be made from taxable benefits
- Student Loan deductions cannot be made if the client's benefit is below the income threshold
- when a client is getting a married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit only the client's portion is taken into consideration when assessing Student Loan repayments
- when a client is getting a reduced rate of payment due to other income, the Student Loan deduction is assessed on the net payment after income deduction

chunks.title: SWIFTT process to pay a partner — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## SWIFTT process to pay a partner
When YSSU decide to continue payment of the client's Young Parent Payment to the partner, they will need to determine the most appropriate SWIFTT process to enable payment to be made to the partner.
The process for payment will depend on whether the:
- period in prison is in the past
- client is due to be released from prison shortly
- client is likely to be in prison for more than four weeks and
- rate of payment for the partner
Note that there is discretion to pay the full married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit.
## Period in prison has passed or release is imminent
Generally, use the SBDR screen in SWIFTT to:
- suspend the client's Young Parent Payment for the period in prison
and
- pay the appropriate rate to the partner (that is, sole parent rate or married rate)
## Period in prison exceeds four weeks
When the client's Young Parent Payment is to continue, and be paid to the partner YSSU will need to contact Helpline for advice regarding the SWIFTT process to use.
For more information contact Helpline or see:
- Decision guidelines - clients with a partner

chunks.title: Tax codes — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Tax codes
Young Parent Payment is taxed at the 'M' rate.
Young Parent Payment is always considered the client's primary source of income regardless of the amount paid. If the client has other income this is always considered the client's secondary income.
Clients can apply to Inland Revenue for a tailored tax code for their other income.

chunks.title: Taxation — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Taxation
Young Parent Payment is a taxable benefit. MSD makes payments to clients at the net rate after the deduction of tax. MSD passes the tax on to Inland Revenue.
Generally, MSD will request a young person to give MSD their IRD number or evidence of their IRD number.

chunks.title: Temporary care — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Temporary care
Generally a client will not be considered as the person principally responsible for the child when the period of care is temporary. Examples of temporary care are:
- school holidays
- Christmas or other public holidays
- during the temporary incapacity of the primary caregiver or
- principal caregiver is in prison
## Extra assistance during temporary care
Any assistance for additional costs due to temporary care situations should be met, in the first instance, by the principal caregiver. Where this is not available, you can consider Special Needs Grants assistance for the client.
For more information see:
- Imprisonment
- Extra help Special Needs Grants

chunks.title: Terminal benefit rate — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: The provision to continue the benefit payment for 28 days following the date of death is referred to as terminal benefit. Benefit payment is continued at the rate which was payable to the client and partner (if any) at the date of death and includes any extra help payments. A terminal benefit includes extra help being paid (for up to 28 days following the date of death).

chunks.title: Benefit paid at a reduced rate — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: When the client's benefit was paid at a reduced rate at the date of death, terminal benefit is paid at the reduced rate. Benefit payments may have been reduced because of: - hospitalisation the deceased client's benefit is reduced as they were in hospital for more than 13 weeks - the deceased client's benefit is reduced as they were in hospital for more than 13 weeks - income - debt repayments when benefit arrears are due at the date of death attempt to recover the debt payment in full from the final benefit paymentdo not recover debts, in full, from terminal benefit payments - when benefit arrears are due at the date of death attempt to recover the debt payment in full from the final benefit payment - do not recover debts, in full, from terminal benefit payments - Child Support if a client had an information share Child Support payment being charged as income at their date of death, they may have been getting a reduced rate of benefit. The effect of the income charge for the information share Child Support will continue for the duration of the terminal benefit, as the rate payable cannot be reviewedChild Support liability ends when the liable person dies; however, MSD cannot remove a Child Support deduction from a benefit record without the authorisation of Inland Revenuewhen a surviving partner or family member makes enquiries, refer them to Inland Revenue - if a client had an information share Child Support payment being charged as income at their date of death, they may have been getting a reduced rate of benefit. The effect of the income charge for the information share Child Support will continue for the duration of the terminal benefit, as the rate payable cannot be reviewed - Child Support liability ends when the liable person dies; however, MSD cannot remove a Child Support deduction from a benefit record without the authorisation of Inland Revenue - when a surviving partner or family member makes enquiries, refer them to Inland Revenue - redirection to Kāinga Ora or a community housing provider when the accommodation is being retained by a surviving partner or family member, continue the redirection to Kāinga Ora or the community housing provider. For more information see: Social housing, Assessment of eligibility Death of a client - when the accommodation is being retained by a surviving partner or family member, continue the redirection to Kāinga Ora or the community housing provider. For more information see: Social housing, Assessment of eligibility Death of a client - court attachment orders

chunks.title: Benefit paid at a reduced rate — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text: Note all of the above deductions will continue to be made from the terminal benefit payments unless they are manually stopped before cancellation.

chunks.title: Treatment of income — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Treatment of income
When a client (or their partner) is receiving Young Parent Payment and declares any income, the following information is required:
- determine the source and the amount of income
- check the client still qualifies for Young Parent Payment and meets the youth activity obligations
- check the client's income is below the cut-out point
- check the period over which to charge income
- review the rate of payment, see Income test and Income change
- review any Extra help Effect of income on Extra help
- check any Exemption for severe disablement
For information on how to charge specific types of income for example, Accident Compensation Payments and employment related income see: Types of income
When a client (or their partner) advises that they have commenced employment, you will need to find out more specific information about their employment. See: Income from employment
## Benefit stopped, suspended or expired
Where a benefit is stopped (suspended or expired) and the client has declared income for a period where no benefit has been paid, determine the client's entitlement to benefit first and then charge the income accordingly.
For more information see:
- Calculating the benefit rate
- Processing standards Income and asset details [no link find out why]
- To or from overseas Payments from Overseas

chunks.title: Underpaid — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Underpaid
When a client has been underpaid Young Parent Payment and is owed arrears, MSD will work out the amount of tax and pass this on to Inland Revenue.
From 1 April 2024, if an arrears payment relates to a previous tax year, the arrears will not be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment. This means the client will not have to pay any more tax on the payment.
Only arrears payments related to the current tax year will be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment.
Example
A client is paid arrears on 12 June 2026. This payment represents arrears for 25 March 2026 to 8 June 2026.
The arrears for 25 March to 31 March 2026 represent a past tax year, so they will not be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment. The arrears for 1 April to 8 June 2026 represent the current tax year, so they will be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment.

chunks.title: Verification — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Verification
Staff must be satisfied that they can accurately identify the deceased client's benefit record.
Generally verbal notification of a client's death is acceptable. This advice can be acted on when the relationship of the caller to the deceased client is determined and sufficient information is obtained to provide confirmation of the deceased's identity.
Follow-up verification should generally be requested. A copy of the death certificate or a copy of the death notice is acceptable supporting documentation.

chunks.title: Weekend leave — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Weekend leave
Where the client is receiving the hospital rate and they are on leave for the weekend only, the appropriate full rate of benefit should be paid for the equivalent number of days the client is on leave.
Example
Client is on leave from Friday to Monday; pay the appropriate full rate of benefit for 4 days. Generally, this is done by completing a back dated review.
Note the dates of admission and discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital.

chunks.title: Young people not yet subject to obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Young people not yet subject to obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning
A young person who is not yet subject to the obligation to be in education, training or work based learning can continue to be paid a benefit while they are absent from New Zealand for any reason if the:
- travel will not prevent them from continuing to meet their youth activity obligations (eg because they are attending school and the travel is during the school holidays or they are attending a training course and the travel is during a term or semester break, and they do not need to be in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations during the travel period)
## Example (but not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A young person who is not yet subject to the education obligation as their youngest dependent child is less than 12 months (and there is no Teen Parent Unit place available for them) wishes to holiday in Australia.
As long as the travel will not prevent the young person from meeting their other obligations (eg their budgeting obligations) it will be approved. The young person can continue to receive their benefit while they are overseas for up to 28 days in any 52 week period.

chunks.title: Young people who are exempt from their youth activity obligations — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Young people who are exempt from their youth activity obligations
A young person who is exempt from all of their youth activity obligations can continue to be paid a benefit for up to 28 days in any 52 week period while they are absent from New Zealand for any reason.
A young person who is exempt from some of their youth activity obligations can continue to receive their payment for any reason for up to 28 days in any 52 week period if the travel will not prevent them from continuing to meet their youth activity obligations.

chunks.title: Young person with a health condition — young parent payment > changes and reviews young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Young person with a health condition
If a young person meets the medical qualifications for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability (except for their age) they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their youth activity obligations until their capacity to undertake education, training and work-based learning improves.
The young person must be limited in their capacity to undertake activities because of health condition, injury or disability.
Where a young person's health condition permanently and severely restricts their ability to undertake education, training or work-based learning, they may be able to receive a Supported Living Payment.
If the young person is admitted to hospital it may affect their rate of payment.
For more information see:
- Exemptions from activity obligations
- Supported Living Payment
- Hospitalisation

chunks.title: Charging income — young parent payment
chunks.text: The abatement rules for Young Parent Payment are different based on the type of income young parents are getting.

chunks.title: General abatement rules — young parent payment
chunks.text: Young people who get most types of income (i.e., income from salary, wages or non-information share Child Support payments) can only get a limited amount of income before their Young Parent Payment will stop. Note these rules do not apply to information share Child Support payments. Young parents (and their partner if any) can get up to $284.70 gross income per week (as at 1 April 2026) before it will affect their benefit. If a young person (and their partner if any) is only getting other income (i.e. not getting information share Child Support payments), the abatement rules are: For a young parent who is single: - their benefit will reduce by $1.00 for every $1.00 of income over $284.70 gross a week until their income is $334.70 (as at 1 April 2026) - if their income is more than $334.70 per week their benefit will stop For young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and both are getting Young Parent Payment in their own right: - each of their benefits will reduce by 50 cents for every $1.00 of the combined income of the young person and their partner over $284.70 gross a week until their combined income is $384.70 (as at 1 April 2026) - if their combined income is more than $384.70 per week their benefits will stop For young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and only one of them is getting Young Parent Payment: - the Young Parent Payment will reduce by 50 cents for every $1.00 of the combined income of the young person and their partner over $284.70 gross a week until their income is $384.70 (as at 1 April 2026) - if their combined income is more than $384.70 per week the Young Parent Payment will stop For an example of an income assessment, see: When a young person is applying for Young Parent Payment and declares any income you need to: - determine the source and the amount of income - check the young person qualifies for the Young Parent Payment and is meeting the youth activity obligations For information on how to charge specific types of income for example, Accident Compensation Payments see: Types of income Also see: - Processing standards Income and asset details [no link find out why] - Changes and reviews Treatment of income

chunks.title: Income period — young parent payment
chunks.text: It is important to distinguish between income a client gets for a period before the entitlement date of benefit and income that is ongoing after a client's benefit has commenced. Income received before the entitlement date of benefit must be considered when calculating the Initial stand-down period. Income received for a period after commencement, must be charged against their ongoing Young Parent Payment. When a young person works during an initial stand-down period the commencement date of their Young Parent Payment will need to be reassessed, see: Employment during stand-down Note information share Child Support payments have different income charging rules.

chunks.title: Income from overseas pensions — young parent payment
chunks.text: Income from overseas pensions is generally treated as a direct deduction from the benefit rate and requires a separate calculation to charging other types of income. For more information see: - To or from overseas Payments from overseas

chunks.title: Childcare costs exemption — young parent payment
chunks.text: If a young person getting Young Parent Payment has to pay childcare costs because they are working they can get an additional income exemption.

chunks.title: Charging information share Child Support payments as income — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Charging information share Child Support payments as income
The abatement rules for Young Parent Payment are different based on the type of income young parents are getting.
If a young person gets information share Child Support payments, any other types of income they get are counted first.
If their other income is below the income cut-out point, income from information share Child Support payments will gradually reduce their benefit until the rate of payment is zero.
Young parents (and their partner if any) can get up to $284.70 gross income per week (as at 1 April 2026) before it will affect their benefit.
If a young person (and their partner if any) is getting information share Child Support payments, the abatement rules are:
For a young parent who is single:
- if their other income is below $334.70, their benefit will reduce by $1.00 for every $1.00 of total income (including information share Child Support payments) over $284.70 gross per week until their benefit is reduced to zero (as at 1 April 2026)
- if their other income is more than $334.70 gross per week their benefit stops
For young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and both are getting Young Parent Payment in their own right:
- if their combined other income is below $384.70, each of their benefits will reduce by 50 cents for every $1.00 of combined total income (including information share Child Support payments) of the young person and their partner over $284.70 gross per week until their benefit is reduced to zero (as at 1 April 2026)
- if their combined other income is more than $384.70 gross per week their benefits stop
For young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and only one of them is getting Young Parent Payment:
- when their combined other income is below $384.70, their Young Parent Payment will reduce by 50 cents for every $1.00 of combined total income (including information share Child Support payments) of the young person and their partner over $284.70 gross per week until their benefit is reduced to zero
- if their combined other income is more than $384.70 gross per week their benefit will stop

chunks.title: Child not living at home — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Child not living at home
The child doesn't have to be living with the young person to be a dependent child. To help you decide consider the following:
- why the child is living away from home
- how permanent the arrangement is and
- what payments the young person makes towards the child's care
For more information see:
- Child to be included

chunks.title: Child to be included — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Child to be included
A young person is obliged to tell us of all their circumstances including the number of children in their care.
If a child is considered to be dependent that child is to be included in the carer's benefit.
## Deciding if a child is financially dependent
When a client states that they are receiving payments for a child's expenses you must decide if the child is a dependent child of the client.
A child does not have to be solely financially dependent on a client to be considered a dependent child. All that is required is that the child is financially dependent on the person to some degree.
However, being financially dependent on a client is only part of the qualifications of a dependent child. The child must still meet all the qualifications to be considered dependent.
If another person or body is paying for the child's expenses, including payments for the care provided, the child is not financially dependent on the client.
If a client is receiving payments toward the expenses of a dependent child, this is regarded as income for benefit purposes.

chunks.title: Childcare cost income exemption — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Childcare cost income exemption
There is an additional $20 per week income exemption (as at 1 April 2026) for all young people getting Young Parent Payment when they have to pay childcare costs while they are working. It is not limited to sole parent clients.
It is not necessary for the child to attend an approved childcare centre, private arrangements can be accepted.
However, eligibility to Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment, Childcare Subsidy or OSCAR must be assessed first. If the total cost of childcare is not covered by the subsidy the client can receive the additional income exemption.
The exemption would be the lesser of:
- $20 per week or
- the cost of childcare not covered by a subsidy
The exemption only applies for the weeks the young person pays for childcare while they are working.

chunks.title: Chooses to remain on Young Parent Payment past 20 years of age — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Chooses to remain on Young Parent Payment past 20 years of age
Generally, when a young person turns 20 years old the Young Parent Payment should stop.
However, to give a young person a chance to complete the qualification they have started while on Young Parent Payment, a young person can choose to continue to receive Young Parent Payment after they turn 20 years of age until their course ends if they remain in education, training or work-based learning.
## Attending secondary education
When a young person reaches the age of 20 years and is attending secondary school they may continue in the Youth Service until the following 31 March.
For example a young person attending school who turns 20 years old in June can continue in the Youth Service until the following 31 March.
## Attending tertiary education, training or work-based learning
When a young person is attending tertiary education, training or work-based learning and they turn 20 years old, they may continue in the Youth Service until their course finishes, unless their course ends in December. If their course ends in December, they may remain in the Youth Service until 31 March the following year.
Examples:
A client is part way through a training course when they turn 20 years old. The training course finishes on 20 November. The young person will be exited from the Youth Service on 21 November.
A client is part way through a training course when they turn 20 years old. The training course finishes on 20 December. The young person can remain in the Youth Service until the following 31 March.
For more information see:
- Must receive payment for six months

chunks.title: Cook Island, Niue and Tokelau clients — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Cook Island, Niue and Tokelau clients
Clients born in the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau are automatically New Zealand citizens (by birth). Generally they will travel to New Zealand on a New Zealand passport.
However, they must still have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years at any one time before they can receive Young Parent Payment.
Other residents of the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau will be required to produce a proof of residence document and meet the 2 years continuous residence requirement in New Zealand.
## Australian clients
Australian citizens are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they are deemed to hold a residence class visa. However, they must still meet the 2 years residence qualification to qualify for Young Parent Payment.
Note clients who are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident, but have not lived in New Zealand continuously for 2 years, may be eligible for Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship.

chunks.title: Commencement date — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
To decide when the Young Parent Payment can start you must first find the entitlement date.
This is usually the date that a person no longer has a means of support.
For a list of these dates see:
- Entitlement date
Note young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship must qualify for the Young Parent Payment in their own right. For more information see:
- Calculating the commencement date for couples
Generally, the Young Parent Payment is subject to an initial stand-down of up to a maximum of 2 weeks after the entitlement date.
The commencement date is the:
- day after the initial stand down ends or
- application date
whichever is the later.
## Exception
Applicants for the Young Parent Payment who are enrolled full-time in a course of secondary education or employment-related training or other training course approved by the Ministry are not subject to initial stand-down periods. Therefore, the commencement date is the:
- entitlement date or
- application date
whichever is the later.
## Twenty-eight day rule
If a young person applies for Young Parent Payment within 28 days of their entitlement date, the commencement date rules are different. See: Twenty-eight day rule

chunks.title: Continued compliance with their obligations — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Continued compliance with their obligations
Generally a young person will be considered to have demonstrated continued compliance with their obligations when:
- they have earned all of the incentives that are available to them or
- where a young person has a full or partial exemption, the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service is satisfied that the young person is engaging with the provider as is required and
- the young person has not had an activity obligations failure in the last six months
Note after a sanction has been imposed, the young person will be returned to youth money management. To earn the right to manage their money again, the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service will need to be satisfied that the young person has been demonstrating a continued compliance with their obligations.
## Earning all of the incentives available to them
For young people getting Young Parent Payment to have the option of not being subject to youth money management they would need to earn the following incentive payments:
- budgeting
- education and
- parenting
A young person who has a full or partial exemption for their activity obligations is only be able to earn those incentive payments which apply to their current obligations.
For more information see:
- Returned to youth money management
- Youth money management
- Obligations Removing incentive payments

chunks.title: Counting previous activity obligations failures — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Counting previous activity obligations failures
The sanction imposed depends on how often the young person has failed to comply with their activity obligations in the previous 12 months while continuously getting Young Parent Payment.
For Young Parent Payment previous failures are only counted if the failure occurred within the last 12 months while continuously getting Young Parent Payment where the young person had activity obligations.
The 12-month count starts from the day the obligation failure is imposed. Each obligation failure has its own 12-month count.
## Example
A client fails their first obligation on 1 June 2025. They fail another obligation on 1 October 2025, and have an obligation failure count of two. Their obligation failure count is reset to one on 1 June 2026, 12 months after they failed their first obligation.
Their obligation failure count will be reset to zero on 1 October 2026, 12 months after the second obligation failure.
## Young person transfers between benefits
If a young person transfers between benefits where they have activity obligations (for example Youth Payment to Young Parent Payment) any activity obligations failures within the previous 12 months are still counted.
The count of activity obligations failures within 12 months will reset to zero for young people transferring to a benefit with or without activity obligations (for example Young Parent Payment to Jobseeker Support).
For more information see:
- Examples of transfers between benefits

chunks.title: Couple - both failed, one recomplies first — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Couple - both failed, one recomplies first
Where a married, civil union or de facto couple both have a grade 3 sanction imposed and one person recomplies first, their Young Parent Payment and their portion of the supplementary assistance must be resumed or regranted.
The non-complying partner's benefit must remain sanctioned until they recomply.
Note Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support can only be paid to one person. The YSSU will need to regrant Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support to the young person who has recomplied and pay them 50% of the rate the couple received prior to the sanctions being imposed.
If the other sanctioned person recomplies, increase this rate to 100% from the date that this young person recomplies.
For more information see:
- Paying other assistance during an activity obligations sanction
- Returning incentive payments after a sanction
- Sanctions and youth money management

chunks.title: Court imposed conditions — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Court imposed conditions
A young person serving a sentence of home detention, or who has conditions and requirements of a court sentence or court order that limits their ability to meet their obligations can be exempt from meeting some or all of their activity obligations.
This can be a full or partial exemption depending on the conditions imposed by the Courts.
This includes young people who are:
- former prisoners who are subject to probation or parole conditions which means that they cannot meet all their activity obligations and
- required as part of a sentence of the court or other court order to attend programmes or other activities, or have conditions imposed upon them (eg bail conditions) which limit their ability to meet all their activity obligations
Home detainees or former prisoners are case managed by their probation officer. Part of this case management includes undertaking appropriate activities to improve their prospects of obtaining paid employment (which may include education, training or work-based learning).
In all cases, the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service should contact the probation officer to facilitate any meetings for that young person.
## Proof
The young person must provide proof from the Ministry of Justice, the Department of Corrections or the Department of Courts stating that they:
- are serving a sentence of Home Detention or
- are subject to probation or parole conditions which limit their ability to meet all their activity obligations or
- are required to attend programmes or other activities which limit their ability to meet all their activity obligations or
- have conditions imposed (eg bail conditions) which limit their ability to meet all their activity obligations and
- the length of time the young person should be exempt
## Duration
The duration of the exemption can be for up to 12 months or for a period determined by the court order or conditions placed on the young person by the Courts, whichever is earliest.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Court imposed conditions'.
Note you cannot add an expiry date in SWIFTT but you must note the duration in CMS.
## Receiving an incentive payment
If the young person is receiving an incentive payment and then qualifies for an exemption you will need to decide if they can continue to receive it.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemption
- Obligations Incentive payments can continue

chunks.text:
