chunks.title: Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities
After a discussion with the young person, you will need to determine the most appropriate education, training or work-based learning activity for them to undertake. To decide what activities are most appropriate, you should consider:
- the young person's individual circumstances
- whether the activity is suitable for the young person
- other information already held about the young person (for example a plan may have been established by Oranga Tamariki)
- information provided by Independent Assessment Provider
- the young person's overall future goals and needs
A young person must undertake education, training or work-based learning to receive Young Parent Payment, unless they qualify for an exemption, or the obligation to be in education or training doesn't apply because their youngest dependent child is under six months (where they are the principal caregiver).
Where the youngest dependent child is aged between 6 and 12 months, the young person may be required to attend a Teen Parent Unit if a suitable place is available. For more information see:
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months
You do not need the young person's agreement to the activities you set for them.
## When education or training will be most appropriate
The first approved activity to consider for young people is secondary education.
You will need to assess whether the young person should continue to attend, or return to secondary education.
There may be reasons why secondary education will not be appropriate for the young person. These include (but are not limited to) where the young person:
- has been expelled and not able to attend another school
- has experienced severe bullying
- leaves school in October and turns 18 in November
In situations where a young person cannot return to secondary education, the next option to consider is approved training or work-based learning.
For more information see:
- Secondary education
- Tertiary education
- Approved training
- Work-based learning
## When developmental activities will be appropriate
A young person may require other support and services to successfully participate in or achieve their activity obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning as well as gain and retain sustainable employment in the future.
For more information see:
- Secondary education
- Tertiary education
- Approved training
- Work-based learning
- Developmental activities

chunks.title: Deciding if suitable place at Teen Parent Unit available — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Deciding if suitable place at Teen Parent Unit available
Where there is a Teen Parent Unit in the area, generally the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service will investigate this education option first for a young person receiving Young Parent Payment.
A place in the Teen Parent Unit is considered suitable if:
- the Teen Parent Unit and approved Early Childhood Education or other suitable childcare is a reasonable travel distance for the young person taking into account their transport options
- there is a suitable approved Early Childhood Education place available or other suitable childcare that meets the child's needs
- the Teen Parent Unit is considered the best learning option for the young person and
- there is a place available for the young person
## Suitable place available but young person does not want to attend
If there is a suitable place available, and the young person has reasons for not wanting to attend the Teen Parent Unit, you must consider whether special circumstances exist that justify the young person not being subject to the obligation to be education, training or work-based learning until a later date.
Where there are no special circumstances that justify the delay in the obligation for the young person to return to education at a Teen Parent Unit, the young person will be required to attend.
## No suitable place available
If there is no suitable place available in the Teen Parent Unit, the obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning applies from when:
- a suitable place becomes available
- the young person's youngest dependent child reaches the age of 12 months
whichever is earlier.
For more information see:
- Special circumstances justifying delay in activity obligation
- Teen Parent Unit

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — young parent payment
chunks.text: A client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date they apply to get a Young Parent Payment. On an ongoing basis a client must continue to remain ordinarily resident in New Zealand to get their benefit. Some exceptions occur when the client leaves New Zealand to live overseas permanently, in which case they may be eligible for a continuation of their payments under a Social Security Agreement.

chunks.title: Attributes associated with being ordinarily resident — young parent payment
chunks.text: Ordinarily resident incorporates a number of factors. The key attributes to being ordinarily resident in New Zealand is that a person must have a close and clear connection to New Zealand on the date they apply for a Young Parent Payment. Some other key attributes that indicate that a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand include: - their physical presence in New Zealand is other than casually or as a traveller - there is some intention to remain in New Zealand for a settled purpose - despite temporary absences from New Zealand they regularly or customarily live in New Zealand - they prefer residence in New Zealand to any other country (a person cannot be ordinarily resident in 2 countries at the same time) Where it is not clear if a client is ordinarily resident you may need to ask the client further information. Some of the following questions may help to get more information: - if the client is going overseas, what are their intentions towards New Zealand (sighting return air tickets is a good indication) - the length of time they spend in New Zealand compared to their periods of absence and the reasons for the absences - property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans) - where are their cash assets principally held (New Zealand banks or investment entities or overseas based holdings) - is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and are they tax resident in New Zealand (see Inland Revenue New Zealand tax residence guide IR292) - are they still on an electoral role and vote in central and local body elections - do they have a personal commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in their immediate and extended family community, community events, clubs and other groups) The attributes associated with being ordinarily resident can also be used after a Young Parent Payment is granted if there is some indication the client may no longer be ordinarily resident in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Non-residentially qualified — young parent payment
chunks.text: You should consider other main benefits if a client does not meet the residence requirements for a Young Parent Payment. An Emergency Benefit may be granted on the grounds of hardship to a client who does not meet the period of residence requirement. However, the person must generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet the hardship qualifications for Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Deducting debt from the funds — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Deducting debt from the funds
When a young person applies for the money left on their payment card, the money must first be used to pay any debts to the Ministry established while the young person was required to have their money managed. Except when the young person has their debt recovery suspended because they are cancelling their benefit for employment, in these instances no debt deduction will be made.
In some cases, the amount of debt owing could be more than the remaining money on the payment card, meaning the young person won’t get any money paid to them.
## Debt after youth money management has ended
Debts created before the young person was required to have their money managed or after youth money management has ended, must not be deducted from the funds. However, a young person may choose to use the money to reduce any outstanding debt.
## Young person requests debt recovery suspension and applies for funds on payment card
If a young person requests debt recovery suspension and applies for the money left on their payment card at the same time, the Ministry must manage the debt recovery suspension first before making the payment to the young person.

chunks.title: Definite offer of employment — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Definite offer of employment
Where the client has stated that they had a definite offer of employment (supplied in writing) to get permanent residence, you must investigate fully what happened to the job offer. This should include contacting the employer.
Where the offer of employment was withdrawn or employment terminated through circumstances beyond the control of the client you may consider granting Young Parent Payment provided the client meets the two year residence criteria or Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship if they do not meet the two years continuous residence.
Immigration New Zealand will decide on any action to be taken with regard to the client's residence status. In the meantime you need to look at all the circumstances of the client as to whether you can grant benefit assistance.
Note if the client has resided in New Zealand for two years assess the client's entitlement to Young Parent Payment in the usual manner.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Granting on grounds of hardship

chunks.title: Definition of 'full-time' — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Definition of 'full-time'
Young people must be in or available for full-time:
- secondary or tertiary education
- approved training or
- work-based learning
## Te Kura - Distance school
For young people studying at Te Kura - Distance school full-time is:
- 4 subjects at NCEA level 1 or
- 3 subjects at NCEA levels 2 and 3
## Tertiary education
Tertiary programmes have an equivalent full-time student (EFTS) value assigned to them. The EFTS value determines if the course of study is full-time or not. To be full-time, a young person must be studying the minimum EFTS in regards to weeks, as used for assessing full-time for Student Allowance purposes.
For more information see:
- Table of weeks for EFTS
## Work-based learning and other approved training
For work-based learning and all other types of training, full-time means the young person must be engaged for 30-40 hours.
For more information see:
- NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification

chunks.title: Definition of "parents" — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Definition of "parents"
For the purposes of Young Parent Payment, parents in relation to a young person:
- means the parent or guardians or other person who had the care of the young person most recently before the young person turned 16 years and
- includes any other parent, guardian, or former guardian, willing to have financial responsibility for the young person
When a young person is in the care of Oranga Tamariki or other authorised care agency, the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki or any other body responsible for the care of the young person under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 is act is not considered to be a parent.
If a young person is in approved Supported Housing for Vulnerable Teen Parents and has written verification from Oranga Tamariki confirming that they have been referred by them, the young person does not require an Independent Assessment.
For more information see:
- Approved Supported Housing for Vulnerable Teen Parents

chunks.title: Definition of second and third failures — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Definition of second and third failures
For Young Parent Payment purposes:
## Second failure
A 'second failure' means a failure that occurs after the young person has satisfied the obligation to which a first failure related.
## Third failure
A 'third failure' means a failure that occurs after the young person has satisfied the obligation to which a second failure related.
## Example
A young person fails to attend school without a good and sufficient reason. Activity obligation failure is initiated. Young person's in-hand allowance and any incentive payments are cancelled.
A second activity obligation failure cannot be initiated until the young person recomplies with the first obligation they failed.

chunks.title: Delayed retirement payments — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Delayed retirement payments
If the young person has been granted a benefit and then receives a retirement payment within 52 weeks after the date the young person's employment ceased, the benefit stand-down and date employment ceased must be reassessed.
To review the initial stand-down:
- divide the redundancy payment by 26 weeks (and 52 weeks if the young person's entitlement date to benefit is on or after 1 May 2005). Add the appropriate weekly redundancy amount to the young person's average weekly income received before employment ceased.
- re-assess the length of the initial stand-down period to determine a new commencement date. (Remember to use the calculation that provides the young person with the lesser stand-down period).
and
- establish an overpayment for any monies paid to the young person prior to the reassessed commencement date
## Payments received more than 52 weeks after retirement
If the young person receives a retirement payment more than 52 weeks after the date the date the young person's employment ceased, the payment is treated as a capital payment. The young person's entitlement to any Extra help must also be reassessed.
Any interest received from the investment of any lump sum must be charged as income.

chunks.title: Dependent child — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Dependent child
A dependent child for Young Parent Payment is a child who is:
- primarily the responsibility of the client
- being maintained as a member of that family
- financially dependent on that client
- in the custody of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki but has been returned to their parent's care
A dependent child for Young Parent Payment does not include a:
- child getting payments under section 363 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- child for whom Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit is paid and
- young person getting a Young Parent Payment and their child (see Dependent children, young parents and the child's parent or step parent examples)
For Young Parent Payment purposes, a dependent child of a young person who is married, in a civil union or in a de facto relationship must also be treated as a dependent child of the young person's spouse or partner.
In some situations, a child may not be living at home but is still considered to be a dependent child.
## Long term care
The care situation should be permanent or long term. MSD should not grant a Young Parent Payment to a young person to care for a child who comes to stay with them for a short period such as the school holidays.
All dependent children should be included in the benefit.

chunks.title: Developmental activities — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Developmental activities
To provide additional support to the young person, developmental activities may also be included alongside other activities that a young person is undertaking. A young person can undertake other developmental activities and still be considered to be meeting their youth activity obligations as long as:
- they are continuing to participate, or are available to undertake, full-time education, training or work-based learning
- you have assessed that the young person needs to address other needs while they undertake full-time education, training or work-based learning and
- the young person agrees to participate
Note a young person can be asked to participate in developmental activities but they cannot be required to. The young person cannot be sanctioned for not agreeing to undertake a developmental activity.
Other developmental activities include (but are not limited to):
- Interpersonal skills - increasing a young person's people or communication skills
- Self motivation (eg confidence or motivation courses)
- Writing and language - young people who have learned English as their second language may require extra tuition to complement their main education or training activity
- Counselling/family violence related programmes
- Drug and alcohol counselling
- Social rehabilitation programmes
Note the Limited Services Volunteers programme will generally not be appropriate for young people receiving Young Parent Payment unless they are transitioning out of the service and have job seeking as their destination.

chunks.title: Discharged from care — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Discharged from care
When a 16 or 17 year old young person has been discharged from the care of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki (or other authorised agency), they can receive Young Parent Payment when they are no longer subject to:
- an agreement under section 140 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- an order under section 78, 101 or 283(n) of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 or
- a sole guardianship order under section 110 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
When a young person has been discharged from Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency care they do not require an Independent Assessment. This is because being discharged from Oranga Tamariki care is considered to have a parental support gap.
If a young person is in approved Supported Housing for Vulnerable Teen Parents and has written verification confirming that they have been referred there by Oranga Tamariki, the young person does not require an Independent Assessment.
For more information see:
- Approved Supported Housing for Vulnerable Teen Parents
## Documentation
In all discharge cases, before granting Young Parent Payment, make sure that all relevant documentation has been received from Oranga Tamariki confirming orders have been discharged.
Encourage Oranga Tamariki to liaise with you regarding the time of discharge from care to make sure the benefit starts from the correct date.
For more information see:
- Discharged from Oranga Tamariki care

chunks.title: Disputes and reviews of an activity obligations failure — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Disputes and reviews of an activity obligations failure
A young person has the right to dispute or review if they disagree with any decision relating to:
- an activity obligations failure or
- a sanction being imposed
A young person can do this by:
- disputing the decision or
- lodging a formal Review of Decision
A Review of Decision can be lodged at any stage, within three months of the activity obligations failure being initiated, or within three months of the sanction being imposed.
If a young person disputes their activity obligations failure or sanction more than 20 working days after it is initiated or imposed, you need to advise the young person to lodge a formal Review of Decision in writing.
For more information see:
- The disputes process
- Recording decisions on a dispute

chunks.title: Earning incentive payments — young parent payment
chunks.text: Young people receiving Young Parent Payment can earn the following incentive payments: - education incentive of $10 a week - budgeting incentive of $10 a week - parenting education incentive of $10 a week

chunks.title: Education incentive — young parent payment
chunks.text: A young person on the Young Parent Payment can earn the education incentive if: - their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service has confirmed to YSSU that since they started receiving the Young Parent Payment they have continuously attended and participated in either education, training or work-based learning for at least 6 calendar months

chunks.title: Budgeting incentive — young parent payment
chunks.text: A young person on the Young Parent Payment can earn the budgeting incentive if: - their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service has confirmed to YSSU that since they started receiving the Young Parent Payment they have attended and participated in discussions on budgeting with the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service provider for at least 3 calendar months and - they have attended and completed a budgeting programme (this can have been completed before the client started getting their benefit)

chunks.title: Parenting incentive — young parent payment
chunks.text: A young person on the Young Parent Payment can earn the parenting education incentive if: - the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service has confirmed that, since they started to receive the Young Parent Payment they have regularly engaged with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house service' for at least 3 calendar months and - they have participated in and completed a parenting education programme - each of their dependent children is enrolled with a primary health organisation - each of their dependent children aged 5 years or under are up-to-date with their Wellchild checks - each of their dependent children aged 5 years or under attends an approved early childhood education programme or is placed in other suitable childcare during any time the young person is in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work The earliest date the 3 month period can be calculated from is the date the young person was granted Young Parent Payment.

chunks.title: Capacity issues prevent a young person meeting their parenting obligations — young parent payment
chunks.text: Sometimes a young person may be able to receive a parenting education incentive payment without meeting the criteria. For more information see: - Capacity issues prevent a young person meeting their parenting obligations

chunks.title: Incentive payments for couples — young parent payment
chunks.text: For couples, each person must earn their incentive payments in their own right. For example if one young parent attends a parenting programme, then only they can receive the parenting education incentive. If both young parents meet the obligation, they can both receive the incentive. Incentive payments are non-taxable allowances and are not considered chargeable income for Extra help and hardship assistance. For more information see: - Removing incentive payments - Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose - Incentive payments can continue - Restoring incentive payments - Obligations

chunks.title: Earning the right to receive payment directly — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Earning the right to receive payment directly
Young people who are subject to youth money management can earn the right to have their Young Parent Payment, incentives, Family Tax Credit and any Extra Help paid directly to them.
The young person can gain control of their payment if:
- they have demonstrated continued compliance with their obligations and
- their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service considers that they are financially competent
A young person who has earned control over their payment has the choice to have their benefit paid directly to them and they will be responsible for paying their costs.
## Young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship
For young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, both young people must meet the criteria in order for each of them to manage their own payment.
## Young people aged 20 years
Young people who have turned 20 years old and have chosen to stay on Young Parent Payment to complete their course of study, training or work-based learning, can opt out of youth money management (unless they are subject to a sanction). This applies even if they haven't been getting Young Parent Payment long enough to earn all their incentive payments.
For more information see:
- Continued compliance with their obligations
- Assessed as financially competent
- Opting out of youth money management

chunks.title: Employment during stand-down — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Employment during stand-down
If a young person gains temporary full-time employment during the initial stand-down period, this may change the date the benefit can start from.
## Temporary employment at a disqualifying rate
Where a young person has temporary employment during the initial stand-down period and their income is at a disqualifying rate, this may change the date the benefit can start from.
The new entitlement date is the date the temporary employment stops. Reassess the young person's initial stand-down using the income for the 26 and 52 weeks earned immediately before the new entitlement date.
For more information see:
- Example of employment during the stand-down
## Temporary employment at less than a disqualifying rate
Where a young person has temporary employment during the initial stand-down period, and their level of income (when charged against the benefit) allows for a part payment of benefit, there is no need to re-assess the young person's initial stand-down.
For more information see:
- Changes and reviews Income reduces the benefit to a 'nil' rate

chunks.title: Enrolled in secondary education — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Enrolled in secondary education
Young people applying for Young Parent Payment who are enrolled full-time in a course of secondary education do not have an initial stand-down imposed.
For more information see:
- No stand-down applies

chunks.title: Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits
A young person receiving Young Parent Payment must:
- register their child or children with a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and
- keep up-to-date with the child's core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks
Note a young person is only required to meet this obligation from the time they begin to receive Young Parent Payment. They will be meeting this obligation if they meet the relevant checks for the child's age from the time they are required to do so.
## Proof of visits
The Well Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book issued to parents when their child is born is sufficient evidence of the child's attendance at visits.
The Health Book has helpful advice and information about what is happening at different stages in the child's development and has places to record all the Well Child/Tamariki Ora appointments and other special and important things that happen to the child in their first 5 years.
For more information see:
- Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks

chunks.title: Enrolment with a primary health care provider — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Enrolment with a primary health care provider
A young person getting Young Parent Payment must enrol their dependent child or children with a primary health care provider. This means being enrolled with a general practitioner (GP), nurse practitioner, or a medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation (PHO).
## Exception
Where there are shortages of places at a medical practice, a young person can be considered to be meeting this obligation if they have a plan in place to:
- be enrolled with a practice when a place becomes available
- get health care for their child if the child becomes unwell
For more information see:
- Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits

chunks.title: Ensuring child attends suitable childcare — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Ensuring child attends suitable childcare
A young person is required to ensure their child's attendance at an approved early childhood education programme or other suitable childcare while they are in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work.

chunks.title: Entering a refuge — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Entering a refuge
When a young person is applying for Young Parent Payment after entering a refuge following the break-up of a relationship, the initial stand-down period can be waived.
Generally the young person must enter the refuge immediately following the break-up of their relationship. This means entering the refuge within a period similar in duration to the stand-down (that is, within 7 to 14 days). When there is a delay between the separation and the young person entering the refuge, general commencement date rules apply.
In this context a refuge is emergency accommodation provided by an agency or organisation. This includes (but is not restricted to) agencies such as Women's Refuge, Home and Family Society, Emergency Housing Trusts, Iwi and cultural organisations, and church organisations.
Note that accommodation provided by family or friends of the young person is not considered to be refuge accommodation.
For more information see:
- Commencement date

chunks.title: Entitlement date — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Entitlement date
The entitlement date for the Young Parent Payment is usually:
- the day after employment ceased (that is, after any holiday pay, sick pay, etc. has expired)
- the day after separation or financial assistance from their partner ceased
- the day after weekly work-related insurance payments ceased
- the day after full-time study or student allowances ceased
- the day after last exam
- the day after school finished (if young person has just left school)
- the day they enrolled in full-time secondary or tertiary education or other training course approved by the Ministry
- the day after the date the living costs component of student loan was paid to
- the date of arrival in New Zealand (if young person has returned to New Zealand)
- date of incapacity
- day after moved out of parent's home
- the date of release from prison or
- the day after discharged from the care of Oranga Tamariki
Where the young person has more than one event, you use the later event for their entitlement date.

chunks.title: Example couple - one gets Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support, and the other family tax credit — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Example couple - one gets Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support, and the other family tax credit
The following example shows how to pay a couple (with 1 child) where one of them is getting Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support and the other is getting family tax credit.
Note the couple is subject to youth money management.
Step 1
Add up costs
$40.00 car repayment$20.00 hire purchase$400.00 rent (Area 2)
Total costs: $460.00
Step 2
Deduct the Extra Help from total costs
$460.00
- $144.00 Accommodation Supplement
- $49.80 Temporary Additional Support
- $151.91 family tax credit (1 April 2026)
Total costs not getting assistance for: $114.29
Step 3
Divide by 2
$114.29 ÷ 2
Amount each partner must contribute: $57.14
Step 4
Partner 1 getting family tax credit only
Must contribute $209.05 ($57.14 + $151.91 family tax credit) towards the redirection of costs (this will be taken off the highest cost).
Set up the following redirection:
- $209.05 towards rent
Step 5
Partner 2 getting Extra help - Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support
Must contribute $250.94 ($57.14 + $144.00 AS + $49.80 TAS) towards everything else.
Set up the following redirections:
- $194.75 for rent ($400 - partner 1, rent contribution)
- $40.00 for car repayments
- $20.00 for hire purchase
After the above is complete, process the in-hand allowance for each young person on the balance remaining of their individual payment.
Note a young person cannot review the decision on how the Young Parent Payment is paid to them.

chunks.title: Example couple with one child — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Example couple with one child
The following example shows how to pay a couple (with one child) getting Young Parent Payment who is subject to youth money management.
Step 1
Add up costs
$40.00 car repayment$20.00 hire purchase$400.00 rent (Area 2)
Total costs: $460.00
Step 2
Deduct Extra Help from total costs
$460.00
- $144.00 Accommodation Supplement
- $49.80 TAS
- $151.91 family tax credit (at 1 April 2026)
Total costs not getting assistance for: $114.29
Step 3
Divide by 2
$114.29 ÷ 2
Amount each partner must contribute: $57.14
Step 4
Partner 1 not getting any Extra help
Must contribute $57.14 towards the redirection of costs (this will be taken off the highest cost). Set up the following redirection:
- $57.14 towards rent
Step 5
Partner 2 getting Extra help and family tax credit
Must contribute $402.85 ($57.14 + $144.00 AS + $49.80 TAS + $151.91 FTC) towards everything else. Set up the following redirections:
- $339.05 for rent ($400 - partner 1 rent contribution)
- $40.00 for car repayments
- $20.00 for hire purchase
After the above is complete, process the in-hand allowance for each young person on the balance remaining of their individual payment.
Note a young person cannot review the decision on how the Young Parent Payment is paid to them.

chunks.title: Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose
Incentive payments can be removed where the young person has acted on purpose in a way that is inconsistent with the reason the incentive is being paid.
Acting in a way that is inconsistent with an incentive includes (but is not limited to):
Education incentiveBudgeting incentiveHave conditions imposed by the court which impact on them attending activitiesContinuous unexplained absences from the school or training programmeDidn't pay core costs (rent, power etc) without a good reasonSuspended from schoolPurchased an unnecessary item on credit and this has put them in hardshipBeing disruptive or not completing assignmentsNot appropriate choices for their situation when spending their payment card or their in-hand allowance

For more information see:
- Restoring incentive payments
- Incentive payments can continue

chunks.title: Examples of good and sufficient reason — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Examples of good and sufficient reason
Examples of a good and sufficient reason include:
- the young person's parents have moved to an area where there is low employment or employment-related training prospects and the parents are unable to financially support the young person
- a serious relationship breakdown has taken place between the young person and a member of the family and someone is now at risk
- the young person has been orphaned and is living independently
- the young person has had professional advice for good reasons (for example on advice from their doctor) to live away from other members of the family and their parents are unable to financially support them
- the young person has been removed from home on advice from the Police that they were at risk and the young person is unable to be financially supported by their parents
You must send the young person to an Independent Assessment Provider for an assessment and recommendation before granting a Young Parent Payment.
The following reasons alone are not considered to be 'good and sufficient' reasons:
- the young person's parents can no longer afford to keep the young person
- the parent's house is too small
- the young person has finished a training course
- the young person is a full-time student who does not qualify for a Student Allowance because of high parental income or failure of previous studies

chunks.title: Exemptions from activity obligations — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Exemptions from activity obligations
Exemptions from activity obligations recognise that there are a number of common reasons why it is unreasonable to expect a young person to meet their activity obligations for a specified period.
Young people getting Young Parent Payment can be granted a full or partial exemption from their activity obligations for the following reasons on the recommendation from their service provider or Ministry of Social Development 'in-house' service:
- Caring for a child with special needs
- Caring for foster child under 12 months old
- Caring full-time for a partner with a health condition, injury or disability
- Court imposed conditions
- Family violence
- Recent bereavement of their partner
- Recent separation from their partner
- Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
- Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
The young person can be granted a temporary exemption from some or all of their activity obligations. Proof may be required before an exemption is granted.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions
## YSSU role in exemptions
The YSSU will make the decision to decline or approve any exemption.
## Duration of the exemption
Each exemption has a specific period of time it can be granted for. In some cases these can be extended if appropriate.
For an overview of the exemptions see:
- Table of exemptions
Note the maximum duration for a young person who has an exemption due to a health condition, injury or disability is based on a health practitioner’s recommendation in the medical certificate of when they should next be medically reassessed.
## Getting an incentive payment
If the young person is getting an incentive payment, and then qualifies for an exemption you will need to decide if they can continue to get the payment.

chunks.title: Payments that can be redirected — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Payments that can be redirected
Most ongoing extra help payments paid to a young person are included in the redirection of payment if the young person is under youth money management, for example:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit
- Winter Energy Payment
Note because Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, family tax credit and Best Start tax credit can only be paid to one person, for couples, the person getting them is generally responsible for any debt created.
## Payments that are not redirected
The following payments are not included in youth money management and can be paid to the young person, their agent (if authorised) or a supplier (as appropriate):
- Disability Allowance
- Child Disability Allowance
- Flexible Childcare Assistance
- Training Incentive Allowance
- one-off payments of hardship assistance, for example Special Needs Grant for food
- any Advance Payment of Benefit
If the young person qualifies for any of the above payments, MSD will decide who the payment goes to after talking with the young person's youth service provider (if one is assigned to the young person).
## Flexible Childcare Assistance
Flexible Childcare Assistance must be used to pay for costs associated with informal childcare. This means that any amount of Flexible Childcare Assistance a young person gets cannot be used to pay for other essential costs.
Note as Flexible Childcare Assistance is only a contribution towards informal childcare costs, the young person is required to pay any remaining costs from their in-hand allowance or other resources (e.g. if their Flexible Childcare Assistance does not cover their informal childcare cost in full).

chunks.title: Factors to consider when recommending payment distribution between payment cards and in-hand allowance — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Factors to consider when recommending payment distribution between payment cards and in-hand allowance
When making a recommendation as to how a young person's payment should be distributed between the in-hand allowance and the payment card, the Service Provider will consider the young person's circumstances, including (but not limited to) the following:
- what level of need does the client have for costs that can be met through the payment card, eg if they are boarding and their food is covered they may not need as much money on the payment card as most of their main meals will be covered
- what essential costs does the client need to meet from their in-hand allowance eg do they have clear essential needs such as travel costs on which they need to spend their in-hand allowance, or do they have access to a food supplier (eg fruit and vegetable market) where it would be more cost effective for them to shop, however that supplier does not accept the payment card
- does the client have sufficient budgeting skills to ensure their in-hand allowance is prioritised to meet essential costs, such as food and groceries, where necessary
- has the client demonstrated poor budgeting skills in relation to the way they have been using their current distribution of payment eg has the client failed to provide food or other essentials for their children out their in-hand allowance, where this has been necessary due to them not having enough credit on their payment card
YSSU makes the final decision as to how the young person's payment will be distributed between the payment card and in-hand allowance, taking into account the information supplied by the young person's Service Provider.
When making this decision, YSSU must be satisfied that the distribution between the two payment methods is reasonable given the client's individual circumstances.
For more information see:
- Redirection of Young Parent Payment
- Method of payment
- Incentive payments

chunks.title: Family breakdown — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Family breakdown
To receive a Young Parent Payment a single young person must meet all of the qualifications and have a parental support gap. A 16 or 17 year old is considered to have a parental support gap when:
- their relationship with their parents (or guardians) has broken down and
- none of them is prepared to support the young person financially
It is important that the relationship breakdown must be serious. Serious situations include:
- issues of health and safety
- sexual, physical or emotional abuse
- situations where the young person or their family would be at risk if they were to return home
Young people must be sent for an assessment with the Independent Assessment Provider to help you determine whether there has been a serious breakdown in the young person's relationship with their parents. For more information see:
- Independent Assessment Provider
Exception when a young person has been discharged from Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency care they do not require an Independent Assessment. This is because the relationship breakdown has already been established by Oranga Tamariki.
If a young person is in approved Supported Housing for Vulnerable Teen Parents and has written verification from Oranga Tamariki confirming that they have been referred by them, the young person does not require an Independent Assessment. See:
- Approved Supported Housing for Vulnerable Teen Parents
For more information see:
- Parental support gap
- Discharged from care
- Unable to receive financial support from parents
- Definition of 'parents'
- Family Violence Intervention Programme [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Family Stream — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Family Stream
The purpose of the Family Stream is to help reunite families in New Zealand by granting residence to the family members of New Zealand citizens and residents. The family member living in New Zealand sponsors the applicant applying for permanent residence.
The Family Stream includes family categories (Partnership, Parent, Sibling and Adult Child, Dependent Child and Parent Retirement Category).
For clients granted permanent residence under the Family Stream (except the Dependent Child Category and the Parent Retirement Category), the sponsor has signed a declaration they will support the client and their family (if any) for up to 5 years of residence in New Zealand or until they can sustain themselves.
Clients must have 2 years (24 months) continuous residence in New Zealand to be entitled to Young Parent Payment. Until they have met this requirement Young Parent Payment on the ground of hardship may be considered.
Note if a client has permanent residence and already meets the 2 years continuous residence, assess the client for Young Parent Payment in the usual manner.
When assessing the client's entitlement to Young Parent Payment on the ground of hardship, the sponsor's financial circumstances is not used in the assessment. However, any assistance given to the client and family (if any) must be used in the assessment.
Young Parent Payment on the ground of hardship is both income and asset tested. To assess a client's entitlement to Young Parent Payment on the ground of hardship confirmation of the client's income and assets declared on the application for permanent residence are required from Immigration New Zealand.
Despite the requirement for immigrants to maintain themselves for a number of years, they may still be able to access assistance as a non-beneficiary.
If the client has a change in personal resources, confirmation of that change is required.
For more information see:
- Permanent residence
- Granting on grounds of hardship
- Change in personal resources

chunks.title: Family Tax Credit — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Family Tax Credit
Young people getting Young Parent Payment will be paid family tax credit and Best Start tax credit along with their benefit. They cannot get it from Inland Revenue.
Family tax credit can only be paid to one person in a couple. Generally it is paid to the principal caregiver.
Inland Revenue is responsible for establishing and recovering any debt created.
Note a young person cannot review the decision on how the Young Parent Payment is paid to them.

chunks.title: Family violence — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Family violence
A young person may be exempt from meeting all of their activity obligations when their living circumstances have changed because of family violence. This is a full exemption.
## Proof
Young people who have recently left situations of family violence will not have to provide proof.
If a young person still needs an exemption after 3 months you can ask for proof.
Proof can include statements from:
- their doctor
- their church
- their lawyer
- the police
- Women's Refuge
- any other person or organisation that is able to support the young person's application
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 3 months.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Family Violence'.
## Receiving an incentive payment
If the young person is receiving an incentive payment and then qualifies for an exemption you will need to decide if they can continue to receive it.

chunks.title: Financial support from a sponsor — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Financial support from a sponsor
Where the client was granted permanent residence because a sponsor was to support them for their first 2 to 5 years in New Zealand (supplied in writing), you must contact the sponsor to confirm the situation.
Note if the client has resided in New Zealand for 2 years no contact with the sponsor is required and assess the client's entitlement to Young Parent Payment in the usual manner.
You will also need to obtain information from the Immigration New Zealand to confirm the reason for granting permanent residence. Ensure you have the consent of the client before contacting Immigration New Zealand.
Once confirmed, assess Young Parent Payment in the usual manner taking into account all other information provided by Immigration New Zealand.
Generally, where the client elects not to accept support from the sponsor without a valid reason decline the application for Young Parent Payment or grant the Young Parent Payment at a reduced rate.
## Family sponsorship before February 1997
Where a client applied for permanent residence under family sponsorship (other than family of refugees) before February 1997, their sponsor only agreed to ensure adequate accommodation for up to 12 months from the immigrant's arrival in New Zealand. The sponsor was not usually expected to provide any other financial support.
For more information see:
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Full or partial exemptions — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Full or partial exemptions
Full and partial exemptions are temporary.
A young person may be granted a full or partial exemption from meeting some or all of their activity obligations with a recommendation from their service provider or Ministry of Social Development 'in-house' service.
The YSSU will make the decision to decline or approve any exemption.
Before you grant an exemption, check if the exemption reason is full or partial, (or both).
## Full exemptions
A full exemption means the young person is exempt from all activities that are part of their obligations. They may be granted a full exemption if they are unable to meet any of their activity obligations.
A young person who has a full exemption from their activity obligations may still be required to attend an interview to discuss their circumstances and when it might be appropriate for them to start to plan towards a return to education, training or work-based learning.
## Partial exemptions
The young person can be granted a partial exemption from their activities when they can participate in some, but not all, of their activity obligations.
For example, a young person granted a partial exemption from education, training or work-based learning, may still be required to:
- attend a budgeting programme
- attend a parenting programme and undertake other parenting activities and
- meet with their service provider or Ministry 'in-house' service
## Duration
Each exemption has a maximum duration. The period the exemption is granted for depends on the young person's circumstances.
At the time of granting the exemption the young person should be:
- advised of the temporary nature of the exemption and
- if appropriate, a date scheduled to review the exemption
At the review you should discuss the young person's circumstances and consider whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption for a further period. You can ask the young person to provide proof that their exemption should be extended.
Note the period of an exemption for a young person due to a health condition, injury or disability is based on the next reassessment date recorded by the health practitioner's recommendation in the medical certificate.
## For an overview of the exemptions see:
- Table of exemptions

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason before initiating an activity obligations failure — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason before initiating an activity obligations failure
You need to be satisfied that the young person does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their activity obligations, based on the information you have, before you initiate an activity obligations failure.
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'. Having considered the circumstances, was it reasonable for the young person not to have met their obligations?
Good and sufficient reasons may include (but are not limited to), that the young person:
- was temporarily medically unfit and they have a medical certificate that shows this
- had a death or illness in the immediate family
- could not realistically transport themselves on the day, due to unforeseen circumstances
- was dependent on the provision of assistance by Work and Income 'in-house' service or the service provider to complete the activity, and that assistance was not supplied
- had an unexpected event occur on that day, such as providing care for a sick relative
Decide in favour of the young person if any doubt remains.
If you are aware that the young person has a good and sufficient reason, do not initiate an activity obligations failure.
Note the Youth Service Support Unit (YSSU) makes the final decision to apply an activity obligations failure.
If the young person does not have a good and sufficient reason, see:
- Sanctions for sole parents
- Sanctions for couples - one person fails
- Sanctions for couples - both fail
## Disputing the activity obligations failure
A young person can dispute the decision to initiate the activity obligations failure or the sanction. For more information see:
- Disputes and reviews of an activity obligations failure

chunks.title: Granting on grounds of hardship — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Granting on grounds of hardship
If a young person does not meet the residence qualification of 2 years continuous residence, they must meet the following criteria to be granted Young Parent Payment:
- they must be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident
- they must be suffering hardship
- they do not qualify for any other benefit and
- they are unable to earn sufficient income to support themselves, their partner and any dependent children
Note the young person may qualify for an Emergency Benefit if they:
- are under restricted criteria
- are in New Zealand on a temporary permit or temporary entry class visa (not a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident)
For more information see:
- Refugees and protected persons
## SWIFTT
To identify young people granted Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship; enter entitlement code 11 - hardship and relevant reason for emergency code in SDT1A screen.
To decide if a young person is suffering hardship see:
- Hardship criteria

chunks.title: Hardship criteria — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Hardship criteria
You can consider that a young person is in hardship if the young person has:
- no other means of supporting themselves and any dependent family
and
- cash assets of or less than: $4,300.00 if the young person is single or$7,464.00 if the young person is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, or is a sole parent
- $4,300.00 if the young person is single or
- $7,464.00 if the young person is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, or is a sole parent
You also need to look at whether the young person has recently given any money away or sold any assets. For more information see:
- Income Sale of assets
In exceptional circumstances you can disregard some of the young person's cash assets see:
- Hardship exceptional circumstances

chunks.title: Hardship exceptional circumstances — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Hardship exceptional circumstances
You can disregard some or all of a young person's cash assets when you are looking at granting Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship. You can only do this if you think that there are exceptional circumstances.
Things you need to consider:
- if you refuse to grant Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship to a young person, will it have a serious effect on the young person's health or welfare
- if you refuse to grant Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship to a young person, would the likely alternatives cost the Government more
- can the young person realise (that is sell or get access to their cash assets) for more than the appropriate cash asset limit
- is the need for Young Parent Payment temporary
- what is the total amount of the young person's assets, including assets that are not cash assets and
- what are the other matters that you would consider relevant to determining whether hardship exists
Every case has to be looked at on its own merits.
If you have a case where you think you can disregard some or all of a young person's cash assets, contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances before you make your decision.

chunks.title: Immigration status and supporting documents — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Immigration status and supporting documents
Generally, when people born overseas travel to New Zealand they are granted a visa by Immigration New Zealand. The visa shows the conditions under which they are allowed to be in New Zealand, for example temporarily (student, work, visitor) or as a resident.
The type of documents a client may provide to verify their immigration status depends on when they were issued.
From 29 November 2010 clients with an existing permit are "deemed" to hold the corresponding type of visa under the Immigration Act 2009. This means that:
- permits continue to be valid until their expiry date. A person does not need to replace a permit in their passport with a new visa until the permit expires
- residents with an existing residence permit may never have this updated with a new type of visa
## Documents issued from 29 November 2010
Documents issued from 29 November 2010 include:
- New Zealand citizenship certificate (issued by Internal Affairs)
- New Zealand citizen endorsement (in a foreign passport)
- Permanent resident visa
- Resident visa
- Visitor visa
- Work visa
- Student visa
- Limited visa
Only the permanent resident visa and the resident visa show the person is a resident.
A visa is a sticker in the client's passport.
## Documents issued before 29 November 2010
Documents issued before 29 November 2010 that allow a person to stay in New Zealand include:
- New Zealand citizenship certificate (issued by Internal Affairs)
- Residence permit (with or without returning resident's visa)
- Visitor permit
- Work permit
- Student permit
- Limited purpose permit
Only the residence permit (with or without returning resident's visa) was granted to residents.
Note that a visa issued before 29 November 2010 does not allow a person to stay in New Zealand.
A permit is a sticker in the client's passport.
## Unable to provide a visa or permit
When a client is unable to provide an immigration visa or permit they may provide other Immigration New Zealand documents to verify their immigration status. Work and Income can also undertake an immigration status check directly with Immigration New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Two years residence
- Resident in New Zealand
- Refugees and protected persons
- Immigration status [no link find out why]
- Immigration changes from 29 November 2010 [no link find out why]

chunks.title: In a training course approved by the Ministry — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## In a training course approved by the Ministry
Young people participating in a training programme that MSD has approved do not have an initial stand-down imposed.
A training course approved for the purposes of assessing whether to waive an initial stand-down for Young Parent Payment is:
- employment-related training or
- tertiary study
Note this differs from the definition of approved training for the purpose of assessing the qualification for Young Parent Payment. Approved training for qualifications is employment-related training only.
For more information see:
- Qualifications In or available for approved training

chunks.title: In-hand allowance — young parent payment
chunks.text: When a young person getting Young Parent Payment is subject to youth money management, they can get an amount of up to $50 a week paid directly to them as an in-hand allowance. After the young person's accommodation, service costs and lawful debts are paid by redirection, the balance of payment, if any, is distributed between the young person's payment card and the in-hand allowance. The maximum amount that can be paid direct to a young person as an in-hand allowance is $50.

chunks.title: Distribution of payment after redirections — young parent payment
chunks.text: Generally, where there is more than $50 available after all of a young person's redirections have occurred, $50 would be paid direct to the young person and the remainder would be placed on their payment card, unless YSSU is satisfied that another distribution would be more appropriate for the young person. Youth Service providers are responsible for making recommendations to YSSU as to how their clients' payments should be distributed between the payment card and in-hand allowance. When making these recommendations to YSSU, providers consider what would be the most appropriate distribution for the young person, given their individual circumstances. YSSU then makes the final decision as to how the young person's payment will be distributed, taking into account the information supplied by the young person's service provider.

chunks.title: Example 1 — young parent payment
chunks.text: A sole parent renting has $110 left after their accommodation and service costs and any debts have been paid. A maximum of $50 could be paid direct to the client. However, the service provider wants to ensure the young person has enough money to purchase a sufficient amount of food for herself and her toddler. The young parent lives close to the school she is attending and the childcare centre her child is attending is also within walking distance. The provider discusses with the young person in their budgeting sessions what their spending habits are and the young person advises that she goes to the market to get her fruit and vegetables. The provider decides to recommend the young person gets a $50 in-hand allowance and will review to see that she is doing this and has enough food with $60 on her payment card. YSSU makes a decision to agree with the recommendation, and decides to pay the client a $50 in-hand allowance, and to put $60 on her payment card.

chunks.title: Example 2 — young parent payment
chunks.text: A young parent with a toddler in a boarding situation has $80 left after her board costs (which include food) and any debts have been paid. The young parent has transport costs to get to and from school and must use public transport to drop her child off at day-care. The young person must pay for the child's nappies and formula from the supermarket herself. After discussions with the young person, the provider recommends paying a $40 in-hand allowance to the young person and placing $40 on the payment card to be used to purchase nappies, wipes and formula. YSSU decides to agree with the recommendation and decides to pay the client a $40 in-hand allowance and to put $40 on the payment card.

chunks.title: Altering the distribution of payment for existing clients already subject to youth money management — young parent payment
chunks.text: If, at any time, a Youth Service provider considers that the current distribution of an existing client's payment between the payment card and in-hand allowance is inappropriate for the client's circumstances, they can make a recommendation to YSSU that this distribution be altered. When determining whether it is appropriate to make a recommendation that a client's payment distribution be altered, providers must take into account a range of factors. Note a young person cannot review the decision on how the Young Parent Payment is paid to them. For more information see: - Factors to consider when recommending payment distribution between payment cards and in-hand allowance - Redirection of Young Parent Payment - Method of payment - Incentive payments

chunks.title: In or available for approved training — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## In or available for approved training
A young person can receive Young Parent Payment if they are available for or enrolled full-time in an approved training programme and meet the other qualifications.
For youth activity obligations purposes approved training is defined as employment-related training.
Generally the training will lead to a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or other higher qualification.
While in approved training and receiving Young Parent Payment, the young person has activity obligations, including regularly attending the programme.
In SWIFTT the Young Parent Payment activity should be recorded as 'Approved training'. An expiry date should be added for the end of the training course. At this time you should reassess the Young Parent Payment, for example, check with the young person if they intend to undertake another training course.
For more information see:
- Obligations
- Obligations Approved training
- Obligations NCEA Level 2 or equivalent qualification

chunks.title: In or available for secondary education — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## In or available for secondary education
A young person can receive Young Parent Payment if they are enrolled in or available for a full-time course of secondary education, and meet the other qualifications. Secondary education includes composite schools, correspondence schools, and secondary school.
Generally they will be working towards a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification.
Young people in secondary education do not qualify for the Young Parent Payment if they have moved from their parents' home to improve their educational prospects, for example if they have moved to another town to a more prestigious school.
While in school and receiving Young Parent Payment, the young person has activity obligations, including regularly attending classes and completing assignments. For more information see:
- Obligations
- Obligations Secondary education
In SWIFTT the Young Parent Payment activity should be recorded as 'Enrolled in Secondary Education'. The payment will automatically expire at the end of the school year. At this time you should reassess the Young Parent Payment, for example, check with the young person if they are intending to return to school.
## School holidays
Young people intending to return to secondary education in the next academic year can be paid Young Parent Payment during the summer holidays. Any incentive payments earned will continue to be paid over this period.
Note a service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service may require a young person to undertake other activities that work towards NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualifications during the summer break.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Young person turns 20 years old
- Obligations NCEA Level 2 or equivalent qualification

chunks.title: In or available for tertiary education — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## In or available for tertiary education
A young person can receive Young Parent Payment if they are enrolled in or available for a full-time course of tertiary education, and meet the other qualifications. Tertiary education includes study at universities and polytechnics.
Generally the course of study will lead to a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or other higher qualification.
While in tertiary education and receiving Young Parent Payment, the young person has activity obligations, including regularly attending lectures and completing assignments.
In SWIFTT the Young Parent Payment activity should be recorded as 'Approved Training'. An expiry date should be added for the earlier of the end of the academic year or the last exam (if the course finishes half-way through the year). At this time you should reassess the Young Parent Payment, for example, check with the young person if they intend to continue studying.
## School holidays
Young people intending to return to tertiary education in the next academic year can be paid Young Parent Payment during the summer holidays. Any incentive payments earned will continue to be paid over this period.
Note a service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service may require a young person to undertake other activities that work towards NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualifications during the summer break.
For more information see:
- Obligations
- Obligations Tertiary education
- Obligations NCEA Level 2 or equivalent qualification

chunks.title: In or available for work-based learning — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## In or available for work-based learning
A young person can receive Young Parent Payment if they are in or available for, full-time approved work-based learning and meet the other qualifications.
Generally the work-based learning will lead to a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification.
In SWIFTT the Young Parent Payment activity should be recorded as 'work-based learning'. An expiry date should be added for the course end date. At this time you should reassess the Young Parent Payment, for example, check with the young person if they intend to undertake another training course.
For more information see:
- Obligations
- Obligations Work-based learning
- Obligations NCEA Level 2 or equivalent qualification

chunks.title: Incentive payments — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Incentive payments
If a young person is under youth money management, any incentive payments earned are included in the redirection of their payment.
Young people can earn incentive payments for demonstrating a commitment to their activity obligations.
A young person getting Young Parent Payment can earn the following incentives:
- budgeting - $10.00 a week
- education - $10.00 a week
- parenting - $10.00 a week
## Young person not under youth money management
When a young person is not under youth money management, incentive payments are paid directly to them.
For more information see:
- Payment process for single people
- Payment process for couples
- Obligations Earning incentive payments

chunks.title: Incentive payments can continue — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Incentive payments can continue
Generally, the incentive payment will continue if a young person has earned them and then is exempt from their activity obligations.
Where a young person is granted an exemption from their activity obligations, continued eligibility for the incentive payment needs to be assessed. Where a person has acted in a way that is inconsistent with the purpose of the incentive, all of or some of the incentives may be removed, for example, when an exemption is required due to court imposed conditions.
## School and tertiary holidays
Any incentive payments earned by the young person will continue to be paid during any school or tertiary holiday periods while they are receiving Young Parent Payment.
For more information see:
- Removing incentive payments
- Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose
- Payment Incentive payments

chunks.title: Income abatement and 50% protection — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Income abatement and 50% protection
The 50% protection is applied to half of the young person's Young Parent Payment before any reduction of income.
Any income will reduce the 50% protected rate of Young Parent Payment by:
- $1.00 for $1.00 of total income over $284.70 (before tax) per week up to $334.70 (before tax) for a sole parent (at 1 April 2026)
- 50 cents each person for every $1.00 of total income over $284.70 (before tax) per week up to $384.70 (before tax) for a couple (at 1 April 2026)
Note income from information share Child Support payments continues to abate the 50% protected rate of Young Parent Payment until the rate of payment is zero.

chunks.title: Income criteria — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Income criteria
A young person applying for the Young Parent Payment must have:
- no income or
- if they have income it must not fully abate Young Parent Payment
## Partner in employment
If a young person qualifies for Young Parent Payment and they have a partner who is in employment (full-time or part-time), the partner's income is charged against the benefit rate. For more information on charging income see:
- Charging income

chunks.title: Income from overseas — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Income from overseas
When a young person has been working overseas within the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before their entitlement date you include this in their average weekly income.
If the young person cannot provide verification of their earnings, accept the information provided on their application for benefit. For help to convert foreign currency to the equivalent New Zealand dollars see the instructions below.
There is no ability to take higher living costs into account. If the young person is in financial hardship during an initial stand-down they can apply for a Special Needs Grant.
For more information see:
- Assistance during an Initial stand down and/or benefit application process
## Receiving a benefit from overseas
When a young person has been receiving an overseas benefit or pension within the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before their entitlement date, you include this in their average weekly wage.
If the overseas benefit or pension payments have stopped and the young person cannot provide verification of their payments, accept the information provided on their application for benefit. There is no requirement to obtain verification through International Services.
Note when the overseas benefit or pension payments are continuing and the young person cannot provide verification, you will need to verify details of these payments. For further assistance contact International Services.
## Converting foreign currency
To estimate the foreign currency to the equivalent New Zealand dollars use the exchange rate provided in the SELXT screen in SWIFTT. The young person must be informed that this calculation is not based on the current rate.
To obtain a current exchange rate, contact Westpac bank to request the 'Westpac buys cash' foreign exchange rate. Use the exchange rate as at the date the young person returned to New Zealand.
Consideration must be given to the calculation that is in the young person's favour. The exchange rate accepted by the young person, (the estimated rate from SELXT or current rate from bank) should be noted in CMS.

chunks.title: Independent — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Independent
Single young people must be independent and responsible for:
- meeting their personal expenses and
- making their own decisions on such things as schooling, job seeking, medical treatment and budgeting
If the young person is sharing accommodation with another person or people, the living arrangement must be one of boarding or renting rather than being 'in care'.
Where the young person is not independent, the caregiver may be able to receive an Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit
## In Oranga Tamariki care
Young people who are in the care or sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki cannot receive Young Parent Payment as the cost of the young person's care is the responsibility of Oranga Tamariki.
The young person is not seen as independent.
When a young person has been discharged from Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency care they do not require an Independent Assessment. This is because the relationship breakdown has already been established by Oranga Tamariki.
If a young person is in approved Supported Housing for Vulnerable Teen Parents and has written verification confirming that they have been referred there by Oranga Tamariki, the young person does not require an Independent Assessment. See:
- Approved Supported Housing for Vulnerable Teen Parents
For more information see:
- Discharged from care

chunks.title: Independent Assessment Provider — young parent payment
chunks.text: The Independent Assessment Provider is required to provide an assessment and recommendation to MSD for young people who have applied for Young Parent Payment because of: - a family breakdown or - other situations where the young person cannot expect financial support from parents due to another good and sufficient reason (where appropriate) - unable to get financial support (where appropriate) from parents

chunks.title: Involving parents — young parent payment
chunks.text: In all cases the Independent Assessment Provider will invite the parents/caregivers to discuss the application. Consent is not required from the applicant as the Social Security Act 2018 allows MSD to investigate a claim for benefit. If the applicant refuses to allow their parents to be interviewed without a satisfactory reason and there is not sufficient information to grant the benefit, MSD must decline the application. The parent's invitation can be made by phone but must be followed up with a letter. When the parents/caregivers cannot be reached and do not make contact a further attempt must be made. Where the parents/caregivers still do not make contact or refuse to participate in the assessment other significant family members, adults or community groups (for example school counsellors) will be contacted. The Independent Assessment Provider will detail all contact and attempts at contact in the Young Parent Payment assessment report. Exception where the young person's parents are absent or there are care and protection concerns an assessment is not required. When a young person has been discharged from Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency care they do not require an Independent Assessment. This is because the relationship breakdown has already been established by Oranga Tamariki.

chunks.title: Disputes about recommendations made by the Independent Assessment Provider — young parent payment
chunks.text: MSD determines eligibility for Young Parent Payment using information in the assessment report and the recommendation of the Independent Assessment Provider. If MSD has concerns about the recommendations made by the Independent Assessment Provider, these should be discussed with them.

chunks.title: Request to access the Young Parent Payment assessment report: Independent Assessment Provider — young parent payment
chunks.text: The Young Parent Payment assessment report generally contains sensitive information that has been shared by the parties in confidence. If one of those parties (i.e., a parent or guardian) requests a copy of the report, they may be able to access information about themselves in the report. MSD should take care to protect the other parties, particularly the young person who the report is about, and in some circumstances, it may be appropriate to withhold the information requested. If it is unclear whether to withhold some or all of the report, contact the Information Privacy and Sharing team [no link find out why] .

chunks.title: Inform young person of their activity obligations — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Inform young person of their activity obligations
Before granting Young Parent Payment, a young person must be advised of their activity obligations arising from payment of the benefit.
Once the benefit has been granted, and the activity has been set for the young person, they must be advised of:
- the activity obligations they are required to meet and the specific activities that have been set for them (eg school, training, work-based learning, parenting, budgeting)
- the consequences of failing to comply with their activity obligations without a good and sufficient reason, in particular the sanctions that will be imposed and
- their right to review and dispute any decisions relating to a failure to comply with their activity obligations
The activity obligations cannot be enforced until the commencement date of Young Parent Payment.
Note the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service is responsible for informing young people of their activity obligations.
For more information see:
- Obligations
- Youth activity obligations
- Activity obligations failures

chunks.title: Initial stand-down — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Initial stand-down
This is a period of up to a maximum of 2 weeks where the young person cannot get any benefit payment. The length of the stand-down depends on:
- the young person's average weekly income (before tax) in the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before the young persons entitlement date and
