- the number of dependent children in their care at any time during the same period
The initial stand-down starts on the young person's entitlement date.
Young people can choose an income assessment period of either 26 or 52 weeks to calculate their average weekly wage for the initial stand-down.
## For more information on the initial stand-down see:
- Average weekly income
- Employment during stand-down
- Self-imposed stand-down
- Initial stand-down procedure
- Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process
- No stand-down applies
- Deskfile Initial stand-down

chunks.title: Initial stand-down procedure — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Initial stand-down procedure
Step 1 Find the young person's entitlement date.
Step 2 Calculate the young person's average weekly income for a 26 and 52 week period.
Step 3 Find out whether the young person has or had any dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement to determine the correct "family circumstances" to use to determine the stand-down period.
Step 4 Using the information from Steps 2 and 3, determine the initial stand-down for the young person over a 26 and 52 week period by looking at the Initial stand-down period chart in Deskfile.
Step 5 Use the calculation of average weekly income that gives the young person a lesser stand-down period.
Step 6 Apply the initial stand-down from the young person's entitlement date to find the commencement date.
Remember if you enter the correct information into SWIFTT it will automatically calculate the initial stand-down and commencement date for you.
Note if the young person has had a dependent child (or children) in their care during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement date you will need to use a work around. Contact Helpline for this information.

chunks.title: International/Humanitarian Stream — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## International/Humanitarian Stream
The purpose of the International/Humanitarian stream is to fulfil New Zealand's obligations as a good international citizen. Included in this stream are United Nations mandated refugees who are approved under the annual Refugee Quota and asylum seekers who claim refugee or protection status in New Zealand. The categories in this stream are the:
- Refugee Family Support Category
- Pacific Access Category
- Samoan Quota Scheme
- Victims of family violence or
- various other special policies for specific countries
The client does not usually have any assets or income. To assess a client's entitlement to Young Parent Payment confirmation of the client's income declared on the application for permanent residence is required from Immigration New Zealand.
Note if the client has not resided continuously in New Zealand for two years since being granted permanent residence, Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship may be considered and assets declared on their application for permanent residence must be included in the assessment.
Once confirmed, assess Young Parent Payment in the usual manner taking into account all other information provided by Immigration New Zealand.

chunks.title: Introduction — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Young Parent Payment is for 16 to 19 year old young people who:
- have a dependent child or children and
- are single or
- are, or have been, married, in a civil union, or in a de facto relationship
The Youth Service Support Unit (YSSU) is responsible for making decisions on behalf of Work and Income and for the general administration of the Young Parent Payment.
While a young person is receiving Young Parent Payment, they are case managed by a service provider (if one is assigned to them), or the Work and Income 'in-house' service. The service provider or the Work and Income 'in-house' service work closely with the YSSU and will make recommendations to assist the YSSU to make decisions.

chunks.title: Method of payment — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Method of payment
There are several ways that Young Parent Payment can be paid depending on whether the young person is subject to youth money management or not.
## Young person is not subject to youth money management
Where a young person is not subject to youth money management they can get their Young Parent Payment, family tax credit and any Extra Help paid directly to their bank account.
## Young person is subject to youth money management
If a young person is subject to youth money management the Young Parent Payment, family tax credit and any Extra Help (except Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance) is paid via:
- payment directly to supplier (eg a payee redirection for accommodation costs, utility costs and lawful debts)
- in-hand allowance which is paid directly to the young person's bank account
- payment card - the young person is able to purchase goods (such as food and groceries) from approved suppliers
Note Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance is paid direct to the young person's bank account.
## Review of decision
A young person cannot review the decision on how the Young Parent Payment is paid to them.

chunks.title: Money left on payment card after youth money management ends — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Money left on payment card after youth money management ends
When youth money management ends for young people, they can still use any funds left on their payment card for approved suppliers, or they can apply for the money to be paid to them directly.
## Applying for direct payment of money
The young person (or Youth Coach, or their agent on their behalf) can make an application to have any money left on their payment card paid directly to them. This can be done verbally or in writing and can be made at any time after youth money management ends.
Note applications and payment can be made several years after the young person leaves Youth Service. There is no time limit.

chunks.title: Youth money management — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Youth money management
Youth money management is where a young person being paid a Young Parent Payment can get an in-hand allowance of up to $50 a week, with most of their payment being redirected to pay for their everyday living costs and any lawful debts. Any remainder is placed onto their payment card.
Young people will not be subject to youth money management and will have their full payment paid directly to them when they have:
- demonstrated continued compliance with their obligations and been assessed as being financially competent or
- opted out of youth money management because they have turned 20 years old and have chosen to stay on Young Parent Payment and complete their course of study, training or work-based learning

chunks.title: Youth money management activity — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Youth money management activity
Young people are required to co-operate with their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service in managing the spending of their Young Parent Payment and provide information as required.
The young person must
- attend and participate in regular one-on-one discussions on budgeting
and provide information on:
- their accommodation costs (for example rent, board) and service costs (for example power, phone)
- any other lawful debts and liabilities (for example court fines, Work and Income debts, Child Support payments, hire purchase)
- how they spend their in-hand allowance and
- how they spend any money allocated to their payment card
For more information see:
- Payment Youth money management
Young people will not be subject to youth money management and will have their full payment paid directly to their bank account when they have:
- been assessed as being financially competent or
- turned 20 years old and have chosen to stay on Young Parent Payment and continue their course of study
For more information see:
- Payment Youth money management
- Payment Assessed as financially competent
- Qualifications Young person turns 20 years old

chunks.title: Must receive payment for six months — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Must receive payment for six months
A young person who has been granted Young Parent Payment who has not been receiving the payment for 6 months cannot qualify for a main benefit when they turn 20 years. They must complete a minimum period of 6 months receiving Young Parent Payment first.
This ensures that the young person is able to have a reasonable chance to move towards a qualification by participating in education, training or work-based learning and undertaking other youth activity obligations before they focus on obligations attached to other main benefits.
For example, a young person is granted Young Parent Payment at the age of 19 years and 8 months old. When they turn 20 years old they will need to continue to receive Young Parent Payment for another 2 months to complete the 6 month minimum period. They can then be assessed for entitlement to other main benefits.
## Exception
A young person, who is receiving Young Parent Payment and then meets the criteria for Supported Living Payment on the ground of having a health condition, injury or disability, can be granted this benefit instead of Young Parent Payment without completing the minimum 6 months.
For more information see:
- Chooses to remain on Young Parent Payment past 20 years of age
- Age

chunks.title: NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification
In order to meet the obligation to be in full-time education, training, or work-based learning the young person should generally be working towards NCEA level 2 or an equivalent or higher qualification.
An equivalent qualification to NCEA level 2 would be any qualification at level 2 on the New Zealand Qualification Framework.
## Meeting education obligations
A young person is meeting their education obligations if they are in (or available for) full-time education, training or work-based learning, working towards a qualification registered at:
- level 2 on the New Zealand Qualification Framework (which includes NCEA Level 2)
- level 3 or higher on the New Zealand Qualification Framework (NZQF)
Note young people undertaking courses at level 1 on the New Zealand Qualification Framework are considered to be meeting their obligations as long as it is a qualification which will build towards a level 2 NZQF qualification.

chunks.title: No stand-down applies — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## No stand-down applies
An initial stand-down is not imposed in the following situations:
- Enrolled in secondary education
- In a training course approved by the Ministry
- Temporary employment
- Transfer between benefits
- Prisoners
- Entering a refuge
- Young person leaves Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre
When no stand-down applies, the commencement date of the benefit is the later of either:
- the entitlement date or
- the application date
Note when no stand-down applies, the 28-day rule does not apply.

chunks.title: Number of dependent children — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Number of dependent children
If a young person had a dependent child (or children) in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application the child (or children) must be taken into account when determining the stand-down.
For example if a young person with one dependent child applies for benefit the stand-down period will be based on a single person with one child. However, if this client had two dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application, the stand-down period will be based on a single client with two dependent children.
This is regardless of whether the child is still in the young person's care at the time of application.
For more information see:
- Dependent child
- Orphans Benefit and Unsupported Childs Benefit

chunks.title: Obligations — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Obligations
Young people getting Young Parent Payment have the following obligations.
They must:
- advise the Ministry of Social Development of any change in circumstances that affect their entitlement or rate of benefit payable
- meet all of their activity obligations
Note young people may be able to get an exemption from some, or all of their obligations when it is unreasonable to expect them to meet their obligations for a specified period.

chunks.title: Opting out of youth money management — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Opting out of youth money management
Young people who are not subject to a sanction will be able to get their full payment directly, when they have:
- turned 20 years old
- chosen to stay on Young Parent Payment to complete their course of study, training or work-based learning and
- provided written notice to their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service that they opt out of money management
This applies even if they haven't been getting Young Parent Payment long enough to have earned all the incentives available to them.
For more information see:
- Method of payment
- Payment

chunks.title: Orphans Benefit and Unsupported Childs Benefit — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Orphans Benefit and Unsupported Childs Benefit
If a young person is getting, or has been getting, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Childs Benefit for a child in their care, this child is included as a dependent child in the stand-down calculation.
However, the Orphans Benefit/Unsupported Child's Benefit payments are not included as income for determining the average weekly income.

chunks.title: Pacific Access Category — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Pacific Access Category
The Pacific Access Category (PAC) allows for citizens of Tonga, Tuvalu and Kiribati (including their partners and dependent children) to be granted permanent residence in New Zealand.
Clients must have two years continuous residence at any one time since being granted permanent residence in New Zealand to be entitled to Young Parent Payment. Until they have met this requirement Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship may be considered.
To assess a client's entitlement to Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship, confirmation of the client's income and assets declared on the application for permanent residence is required from Immigration New Zealand.
Note if a client has permanent residence and already meets the two years continuous residence, assess the client for Young Parent Payment in the usual manner.
## Additional requirements for the Pacific Access Category
Tongan clients
If the client is a citizen of Tonga, the client must normally live in Tonga and actually be in Tonga when they apply for permanent residence under this category. The client must also have been born in Tonga or born overseas to a Tongan citizen who was born in Tonga.
Kiribati clients
If the client is a citizen of Kiribati, the client must normally live in Kiribati and actually be in Kiribati or Fiji when they apply for permanent residence under this category. The client must also have been born in Kiribati or born overseas to a Kiribati citizen who was born in Kiribati.
Tuvalu clients
If the client is a citizen of Tuvalu, the client must normally live in Tuvalu and actually be in Tuvalu or Fiji when applying permanent residence under this category. The client must also have been born in Tuvalu or born overseas to a Tuvalu citizen who was born in Tuvalu.
For more information see:
- Granting on grounds of hardship
- Samoan Quota Scheme

chunks.title: Parental support gap — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Parental support gap
To get a Young Parent Payment a single young person aged 16 or 17 years old must:
- meet all of the qualifications
- not be living with their parents or guardians and
- have a parental support gap
A 16 or 17 year old is considered to have a parental support gap when:
- each of their parents (or guardians) is unable to support them financiallyfor example, the young person's parents or guardians may be (but not limited to): deceasedin prisonin hospitaloverseas
- deceased
- in prison
- in hospital
- overseas
- the relationship with their parents (or guardians) has broken down, and none of them is prepared to support the young person financially
- transitioning from care under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989, via an extended care agreement, parenting order or guardianship order
- there is a good and sufficient reason why the young person cannot reasonably expect to be financially dependent on their parents or any other person− for example (but not limited to): the young person has been subject to family violence (physical, psychological, emotional or sexual) in their parent's or guardian's home
- the young person has been subject to family violence (physical, psychological, emotional or sexual) in their parent's or guardian's home
A young person is not considered to have a parental support gap if they have the option of living with a parent or guardian but chooses not to, and you are satisfied that there are no good and sufficient reasons for the young person not to be living with that parent or guardian.
You should use any Oranga Tamariki or other agency documentation or the Independent Assessment Provider report to assist you to make a decision while considering all the relevant information.
If a young person is in approved Supported Housing for Vulnerable Teen Parents and has written verification from Oranga Tamariki confirming that they have been referred by them, the young person does not require an Independent Assessment. See:
- Approved Supported Housing for Vulnerable Teen Parents
If a young person is married, in a civil union or considered to be in a de facto relationship, they do not have to meet the parental support gap qualification to receive a Young Parent Payment.

chunks.title: Parenting obligations — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Parenting obligations
Young people getting Young Parent Payment are required to:
- participate in an approved parenting programme
- enrol their child with a general practitioner (GP), nurse practitioner, or medical practice that is part of a Primary Health Organisation (PHO), where a local provider is available
- register their child (if aged under 5 years) with a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider and keep up-to-date with their visits and
- ensure the child's attendance at an approved Early Childhood Education programme or in other suitable childcare, while they are in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work
## Parenting incentive payment
After 3 months of working with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service and satisfactorily meeting these parenting requirements, the young person can earn their parenting incentive payment.
For more information see:
- Approved parenting programme
- Enrolment with a primary health care provider
- Enrolment and attendance at Well Child visits
- Ensuring child attends suitable childcare
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months
- Earning incentive payments

chunks.title: Parents earn less than Family Tax Credit cut-off point — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Parents earn less than Family Tax Credit cut-off point
A single young person aged 16 or 17 years old can receive Young Parent Payment when they are:
- living at home with, or being financially supported by their parents or guardians and
- their parents or guardians earn less than the Family Tax Credit income cut-out point
Note young people whose parents or guardians earn less than the Family Tax Credit cut-off point do not have to meet the exceptional circumstances qualification.
## Calculating family tax credit
If the parent or guardian who the young person is living with is not entitled to family tax credit because they do not have a dependent child (for example the young person is no longer considered a dependent child under that Act), their entitlement to family tax credit must be calculated as if they would still be entitled.
For more information see:
- Extra help Family tax credit
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Parents overseas — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Parents overseas
If the young person's parents are overseas the responsibility to support the young person should remain with the parents if:
- there has been no family breakdown and
- the decision to move overseas and leave the young person in New Zealand is planned and agreed between the young person and their parents or
- the decision to send the young person to New Zealand for education, or job prospects and the like, is planned and agreed between the young person and their parents
If the situation results in a family breakdown the young person may be able to receive a Young Parent Payment.
For more information see:
- Family breakdown
- What is financial support
- Independent

chunks.title: Partner made redundant — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Partner made redundant
If the partner of a young person currently receiving a benefit is made redundant, any redundancy payment received is not treated as income and there is no need to review the initial stand-down.
However, this redundancy payment may affect any supplementary benefit as it may increase the couple's cash assets.
## Interest received
Also, any interest (before tax) paid on any lump sum received is treated as income and charged against the benefit.
To decide whether or not the young person is in a de facto relationship see:
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit

chunks.title: Paying money left on the payment card — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Paying money left on the payment card
The money left on the payment card is paid as a lump sum directly to the young person.
## Twelve-month asset and income exemption
For the first 12 months, the lump sum payment is not chargeable income or a cash asset when assessing qualifications for other benefit assistance under the Social Security Act 2018.
After 12 months any money left is treated as a cash asset, and any interest generated by the cash asset is treated as chargeable income.

chunks.title: Paying other assistance during an activity obligations sanction — young parent payment
chunks.text: Young people are not entitled to the Emergency Benefit when a 50% cancellation due to a grade 3 sanction has been imposed.

chunks.title: Supplementary assistance — young parent payment
chunks.text: Sole parents who are sanctioned can continue to get full supplementary assistance, regardless of the grade of sanction. Married, civil union or de facto couples who have a grade 3 sanction imposed can get 50% of their entitlement to the following supplementary assistance: - Accommodation Supplement - Temporary Additional Support Note when one person fails, the 50% of the couple's entitlement is paid to non-sanctioned partner. When both fail, 25% of the couple's entitlement is paid to each person.

chunks.title: Winter Energy Payment — young parent payment
chunks.text: The Winter Energy Payment is treated slightly different to other Supplementary Assistance. Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid in situations where a portion of main benefit continues to be paid. In some cases it can continue to be paid at the full couple rate in cases where one client has been fully sanctioned. Clients who have a dependent child, and who are getting Winter Energy Payment who are subject to a 100% suspension or cancellation have a maximum sanction of 50% of the total benefit imposed (including other supplementary assistance). However, the full rate of Winter Energy Payment should continue to be paid. Sole parents also have a maximum sanction of 50% of the total benefit imposed but like other supplementary assistance, will continue to get the total amount of the Winter Energy Payment, regardless of the grade of the sanction.

chunks.title: Ongoing Extra help — young parent payment
chunks.text: The following Extra help can continue be paid if the young person is eligible: - Disability Allowance - Child Disability Allowance - Childcare Assistance, including Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment - family tax credit and Best Start tax credit Note Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment could not continue if the failure reason was for not meeting their education, training or work-based learning obligation.

chunks.title: Special Needs Grants — young parent payment
chunks.text: Young people are not entitled to Special Needs Grants if an activity obligations failure has been imposed. The only exception to this is if a young person is sick or injured when a grade three sanction is imposed and they are incapable of participating in full-time employment or an approved activity for six weeks. For more information see: - Assistance during a non-entitlement period - Assistance when a client is sanctioned

chunks.title: Advances — young parent payment
chunks.text: If a young person has a 50% sanction imposed, and they are experiencing hardship, they may apply for an advance payment of benefit. The service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service must discuss recompliance with the young person as the reduced rate of payment will be contributing to their hardship.

chunks.title: Assistance to transition into employment — young parent payment
chunks.text: Young people may get assistance to transition into employment if a sanction has been imposed and they meet the qualifications for it. For more information see: - Employment and work readiness Assistance to transition into employment

chunks.title: Payment process for couples — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Payment process for couples
Young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship are granted Young Parent Payment in their own right. Young Parent Payment is not apportioned as are other benefits paid to people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, for example Jobseeker Support.
Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit can only be granted to one of the young people in the couple.
The redirections need to be allocated equally because of the way the in-hand allowance and remainder are paid.
The following process shows how Young Parent Payment is paid when a couple is subject to youth money management:
## Step 1
Add up the costs and work out eligibility for Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support based on the couple's costs.
## Step 2
Deduct the Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit from the total costs. This leaves the amount for which they do not get any assistance.
## Step 3
Divide this in half to find out what each person is responsible for contributing.
## Step 4
The partner who is getting Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit must contribute the amount they are getting for each of these, plus half of the amount from step 3.
Note because Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, Family tax credit and Best Start tax credit can only be paid to one person, the person getting them is generally responsible for any debt created. Debts cannot be created for family tax credit and best start tax credit.
## Step 5
The partner not getting any Extra Help must contribute their half share of step 3. This amount will go to offset the highest cost.
Note a young person cannot review the decision on how the Young Parent Payment is paid to them.
For more information see:
- Family tax credit
- Best Start tax credit
- Example couple with one child
- Example couple - one gets AS and TAS and the other gets FTC

chunks.title: Payment process for single people — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Payment process for single people
The following process shows how Young Parent Payment is paid when a young person is subject to youth money management:
## Step 1
Young Parent Payment rate (minus any abatement or sanction) is established.
## Step 2
Family tax credit, Best Start tax credit and any incentive payments earned are added.
## Step 3
Extra Help, such as Accommodation Supplement, Winter Energy Payment and Temporary Additional Support is added.
## Step 4
Redirection of accommodation, service costs and lawful debts occurs by adding payees.
## Step 5
In-hand Allowance (if any) is paid directly to the young person and the remainder is redirected to the payment card.
## Step 6
Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance is paid directly to the young person.
## Review of decision
A young person cannot review the decision on how the Young Parent Payment is paid to them.
For more information see:
- Payment process for couples
- Obligations Youth money management activity

chunks.title: Payment to the non-sanctioned partner — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Payment to the non-sanctioned partner
For married, civil union or de facto couples getting Young Parent Payment, their benefit is not apportioned.
When a young person has their Young Parent Payment sanctioned, the non-sanctioned partner will continue to get:
- their full Young Parent Payment and any incentive payments they have earned and
- where the other young person is subject to a grade 3 sanction, 50% of the supplementary assistance the couple was entitled and the full rate of Winter Energy Payment
Note this may or may not be paid under youth money management.
Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Assistance can only be paid to one person. The YSSU will need to:
- regrant supplementary assistance to the non-sanctioned young person and pay at 50% of the rate the couple were getting prior to the sanction being imposed
- review each of the young persons' redirections
Where the non-sanctioned young person is already getting the supplementary assistance, the YSSU will need to reduce the amount they are getting by 50% and review the non-sanctioned young person's redirections.
For more information see:
- Paying other assistance during an activity obligations sanction

chunks.title: Payment — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Payment
Young Parent Payment is paid weekly on a Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. Payment is from Monday to Sunday and is made one week in arrears.
Most young people getting Young Parent Payment will be under youth money management. This is when the young person gets an in-hand allowance of up to $50 a week, with the majority of their payment being redirected to pay for their everyday living costs and lawful debts. For more information about how this is paid see:
- Youth money management
For young people who are not subject to youth money management, payment must be made directly to the young person.
It is a condition of getting a benefit that the young person provides a bank account number. MSD can request the young person to provide an IRD number or evidence of their IRD number.
For more information see:
- Young person's IRD number
## Rate of payment
For the rate of Young Parent Payment that can be paid see:
- Deskfile Young Parent Payment rates

chunks.title: Clients without permanent residence or citizenship — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Clients without permanent residence or citizenship
Emergency Benefit may be paid to some categories of migrants who do not have permanent residence or citizenship eg people waiting for their application for refugee or protected person status to be approved.
For more information see:
- Proof of residence
- Emergency Benefit
- Refugees and protected persons
Note clients lawfully in New Zealand by virtue of a temporary permit or a temporary entry class visa only (ie they do not have permanent residence) are not entitled to any benefit assistance.
To assess a client's entitlement you will generally need to establish exactly what category of migrant they are.
Clients may be granted permanent residence under the following categories:
- Family Stream
- International/Humanitarian Stream
- Skilled/Business Stream
Note if you require further information about a client's application for permanent residence you must get consent from the client to contact Immigration New Zealand or the client should obtain the information themselves. Otherwise the application should be declined. You must not collect or disclose information regarding a client's application without the client's consent.
For more information see:
- Immigration status [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Personal cash assets — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Personal cash assets
Where the client was granted permanent residence because they had personal cash assets you will need to obtain information from the Immigration New Zealand to confirm the reason for granting permanent residence. Ensure you have the consent of the client before contacting the Immigration New Zealand.
Once confirmed, assess Young Parent Payment or, if the client does not meet the two years continuous residence criteria, Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship in the usual manner taking into account all other information provided by Immigration New Zealand.
If there is a significant drop in the client's cash assets declared, confirmation for the following should be requested:
- what cash assets were they referring to and
- what has happened to these cash assets
It is not acceptable for these cash assets to be used to purchase capital items such as a house, furniture or motor vehicle.
Settlement funds can be used to purchase capital items, as these are not the same as cash assets declared as personal resources.
Note if the client has resided in New Zealand for two years assess the client's entitlement to the Young Parent Payment in the usual manner.
For more information see:
- Proof of residence
- Qualifications
- Granting on grounds of hardship

chunks.title: In prison less than 31 days — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## In prison less than 31 days
Young people who have been in prison or on remand for less than 31 days do not have a stand-down imposed if they were receiving a benefit before going into prison and apply for a benefit immediately following their release.
If the young person was not in receipt of benefit prior to being imprisoned or placed on remand, a stand-down is imposed.
There is no access to Steps to Freedom Special Needs Grant for these young people.
## In prison 31 days or more
Young people who have been in prison or on remand for 31 days or more have a stand-down imposed.
These young people have access to a Steps to Freedom Special Needs Grant to assist them during the stand-down. They may also have access to other categories of special needs grants to help them re-establish themselves in the community.
## Calculating number of days
When counting the number of days that a young person has been in prison or held on remand, you should include the date the young person:
- enters prison or held on remand and
- leaves prison or is released from remand
For more information see:
- Imprisonment Release from prison

chunks.title: Proof of residence — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Proof of residence
All documents should be originals. Photocopies and/or documents that have been changed in any way cannot be accepted.
Where the client cannot provide proof or the proof is unclear, you should ask the client to obtain confirmation of their residential status from Immigration New Zealand (for permanent residence) or Internal Affairs (for citizenship).
Proof of citizenship and/or permanent residence in New Zealand can be a:
- New Zealand birth certificate
Generally, a person born in New Zealand is a New Zealand citizen by birth.
- New Zealand passport
To hold a New Zealand passport you must be a citizen of New Zealand.
- Certificate of Registration
A child born outside New Zealand (to a parent who is a New Zealand citizen) may be a New Zealand citizen from birth. However, the child must apply for a Certificate of Registration to confirm their New Zealand citizenship.
- Grant of Citizenship
People who have permanent residence may (normally after 5 years residence in New Zealand) apply for a Grant of Citizenship. They must meet the conditions of the Grant.
- Certificate of Confirmation
This is a certificate issued to confirm that the holder is a New Zealand citizen by birth, descent or Grant of Citizenship.
British subjects, who immigrated to New Zealand prior to 1948 (and who resided in New Zealand for all of 1948) were made New Zealand citizens in 1949. These people are likely to have a Certificate of Confirmation or a Certificate of Naturalisation.
- Certificate of Naturalisation
Previously immigrants were naturalised as British subjects and citizens of New Zealand. Today they are given a Grant of Citizenship
- Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence class visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009
- Passport (other than a New Zealand passport) containing a residence permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987
Note that a visa issued before 29 November 2010 does not allow a person to stay in New Zealand
- Letter of confirmation of permanent residence from Immigration New Zealand
- Australian citizens
Australian citizens are lawfully allowed in New Zealand as they are deemed to hold a residence class visa here. Their date of entry into New Zealand is generally not recorded. Where possible supporting evidence should be sought such as, tenancy agreements, bank statements or old utility bills to show that the client has been ordinarily resident for two continuous years.
For more information see:
- Immigration status and supporting documents

chunks.title: Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period — young parent payment
chunks.text: A provisional benefit can be paid to the young person when they are undertaking an approved activity during the 13 week non-entitlement period.

chunks.title: Provisional benefit — young parent payment
chunks.text: You can grant or increase a provisional benefit from the date the young person starts the approved activity. The benefit continues to be provisionally paid while the young person is satisfactorily participating in the approved activity. Payment continues until: - the six week activity period ends or - the 13 week non-entitlement period ends whichever is earlier.

chunks.title: Example 1 — young parent payment
chunks.text: A young person participates in an approved activity from the beginning of week three of the non-entitlement period. The young person participates for a continuous period of 6 weeks and the remaining period of the 13 week non-entitlement is cancelled. After the follow up appointment with the young person the benefit ceases to be paid on a provisional basis.

chunks.title: Example 2 — young parent payment
chunks.text: A young person participates in an approved activity from the beginning of week 10 of the non-entitlement period. The young person participates in the approved activity for the remainder of the 13 week non-entitlement period (for 3 weeks). At the end of the 13 week non-entitlement period, the young person's benefit ceases to be paid on a provisional basis.

chunks.title: End of approved activity or non-entitlement period — young parent payment
chunks.text: The service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service should discuss with the young person whether they: - have satisfactorily participated in the approved activity and - can still meet the qualifications and obligations of the benefit Note that if the young person does not recomply, they must reapply at the end of the 13 week non-entitlement period to receive a benefit.

chunks.title: Leaves or has not satisfactorily participated in an approved activity — young parent payment
chunks.text: If a young person leaves early or does not satisfactorily participate in the approved activity, without a good and sufficient reason, their provisional benefit must be reduced or stopped from the date it was increased or granted. The amount of benefit that was provisionally paid during the 13 week non-entitlement period must be established as a debt and recovered. You cannot recover the provisional benefit if the young person does not complete the approved activity because they: - transferred to a benefit with no work or activity obligations or - meet the criteria for an exemption from their activity obligations For more information see: - Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Qualifications — young parent payment
chunks.text: A young person applying for Young Parent Payment must be a parent or step-parent to a dependent child or children and be either: - single or - married, in a civil union or in a de facto relationship, and not married to, in a civil union, or in a de facto relationship with a specified beneficiary Note for Young Parent Payment purposes, a dependent child of a young person who is married, in a civil union or in a de facto relationship must also be treated as a dependent child of the young person's spouse or partner. To qualify for the Young Parent Payment the young person must be: - aged 16 to 19 years old - undertaking or is available for a full-time course of secondary or tertiary education, approved training or approved work-based learning leading to NCEA level 2, an equivalent qualification (in the opinion of MSD) or a higher qualification or - would be available but: the young person is in a situation that would qualify them for an exemption from the obligation to undertake education or training or work-based learning orthe obligation to be in full-time education, training or work-based learning does not apply to them because their youngest child is: aged under 6 months oraged between 6 and 12 months and there is no suitable place available in a Teen Parent Unit or there is a suitable place available but there are special circumstances to justify the obligation applying later - the young person is in a situation that would qualify them for an exemption from the obligation to undertake education or training or work-based learning or - the obligation to be in full-time education, training or work-based learning does not apply to them because their youngest child is: aged under 6 months oraged between 6 and 12 months and there is no suitable place available in a Teen Parent Unit or there is a suitable place available but there are special circumstances to justify the obligation applying later - aged under 6 months or - aged between 6 and 12 months and there is no suitable place available in a Teen Parent Unit or there is a suitable place available but there are special circumstances to justify the obligation applying later - have continuously lived in New Zealand for 2 years or more at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident and - have no income or an income of less than the amount that would fully abate the benefit To receive Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship, the young person must meet the above qualifications except for the residence criteria. However they must:

chunks.title: Qualifications — young parent payment
chunks.text: - be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident but have lived in New Zealand for less than 2 years - be suffering hardship and - not qualify for any other benefit For more information see: - Age - Dependent child - Parental support gap - Single young people - Young people who are in a relationship - Residence - Two years residence - Income criteria - Activity requirements - Granting on grounds of hardship - Exemptions from activity obligations

chunks.title: Recent bereavement of their partner — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Recent bereavement of their partner
A young person whose partner has recently died, can be exempt from meeting all their activity obligations to allow them time to adjust to their new circumstances. This is a full exemption.
Before granting this exemption you should consider the following factors:
- changes in living circumstances
- changes in childcare responsibilities
- particular religious or cultural beliefs or practices
## Proof
The young person needs to provide:
- a personal statement
- evidence included in their application for benefit
- a death notice from the newspaper or
- a death certificate
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 3 months from the date of death.
You can extend the exemption. Before you do this you should ask the young person to provide information to support the exemption continuing.

chunks.title: Recent separation from their partner — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Recent separation from their partner
A young person who has recently separated from their partner, can be exempt from meeting all their activity obligations to allow them time to adjust to their new circumstances. This is a full exemption.
Before granting this exemption you should consider the following factors:
- changes in living circumstances
- changes in childcare responsibilities
## Proof
The young person needs to provide:
- a personal statement or
- evidence included in their application for benefit
## Duration
The duration of an exemption is based on the reassessment date recorded on the medical certificate by the young person’s health practitioner.
You can extend the exemption. Before you do this you should ask the young person to provide information to support the exemption continuing.
## Getting an incentive payment
If the young person is getting an incentive payment and then qualifies for an exemption you will need to decide if they can continue to get the payment.

chunks.title: Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period) — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
A young person can complete certain activities to get a provisional benefit if they are subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period due to having a grade 3 sanction imposed for failing to meet their activity obligations.
If a young person wants to recomply, you must make an approved activity available to them at the earliest opportunity.
There is no waiting period before an approved activity can start after a sanction has been imposed.
The young person must undertake an approved activity for a continuous period of 6 weeks or until the 13 week non-entitlement period ends (whichever is the earlier).
## Approved activity examples
Here are some examples that may be a suitable 6 week approved activity for a young person:
- secondary education
- approved training
- work-based learning
- budgeting activity
- parenting activity
- community activities
- part-time work or work experience (where they are not already in part-time work)
- a combination of any of the above
Note this list is an example only, an approved activity (or programme of suitable activities) should be relevant to the activity obligations failure and be fair and reasonable.
For when to grant or increase the benefit, see:
- Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period
For what to do when a young person cannot recomply due to health condition, see:
- Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption
Also see:
- Couple - both failed, one recomplies first
- Returning incentive payments after a sanction
- Sanctions and youth money management

chunks.title: Recompliance (Grade 1 and 2) — young parent payment
chunks.text: Young people with an activity obligations failure initiated must recomply within 5 working days. If they do this no sanction will be imposed but the activity obligations failure will be counted. If the sanction has been imposed the young person must recomply to have their benefit increased or resumed. When a young person indicates that they want to recomply an appointment must be made for them to discuss recomplying and make a recompliance activity available for them at the earliest opportunity.

chunks.title: Service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service role in recompliance — young parent payment
chunks.text: The service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service will need to discuss with the young person the activities they need to undertake to recomply. To recomply they must: - undertake the original activity (or activities if they have failed more than one obligation) if it is still available or - if the original activity (or activities if they have failed more than one obligation) is not available, undertake another activity, to the satisfaction of MSD, that is the same as or substantially similar to the activity the young person failed to do When a recompliance activity is allocated, MSD must: - discuss with the young person what they need to do to satisfactorily undertake the recompliance activity and the implications of not doing this and - make a note of the discussion

chunks.title: Same or substantially similar activity — young parent payment
chunks.text: If the young person is unable to undertake the same activity that they failed to do, they must undertake to the satisfaction of MSD another activity that is the same as or substantially similar to the activity they failed to do. The 'same or substantially similar to' means that any recompliance activity should, as much as possible, require the same amount of time, effort and commitment as that which the young person failed to complete.

chunks.title: YSSU role in recompliance — young parent payment
chunks.text: The YSSU must decide whether the young person has satisfactorily undertaken their recompliance activity based on the recommendation from the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service. This will depend on the young person's circumstances and the nature of the recompliance activity.

chunks.title: When to resume or increase the benefit — young parent payment
chunks.text: The YSSU will resume or increase the payment from the date the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service are satisfied that the young person has started the recompliance activity. Some examples of this: - if the recompliance activity is a one-off, such as attending an interview with the service provider, the payment would be resumed from the date the young person attended and participated in the activity - if the recompliance activity is ongoing, such as attending school or a training programme, the young person must satisfactorily attend school or the training programme and the payment will be resumed from the date the young person started to attend For what to do if a young person cannot recomply due to a health condition see: - Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption

chunks.title: Recording decisions on a dispute — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Recording decisions on a dispute
You must record the decision in OBMAN that you have made as a 'Case Managers Review'. The following decisions must be recorded:
- Upheld - if you believe that the decision relating to an activity obligations failure or sanction being imposed was correct you must record this as 'dispute upheld'. The activity obligations failure will be counted.
- Withdrawn - a young person may, after disputing the activity obligations failure, decide to recomply before the sanction is imposed, or may withdraw their dispute and not recomply. In these cases you must record that the dispute has been withdrawn. The activity obligations failure will be counted.
- Overturned - when you believe that the young person had a good and sufficient reason or that they did not fail their activity obligations you must record this as activity obligations failure overturned. The activity obligations failure will not be counted.
In all cases you must advise the young people of the outcome of their dispute. A letter is automatically sent to the young person.
If the young person does not agree with your decision, they can still request a formal Review of Decision. They must do this in writing. The Review of Decision process should be followed.
Note if the activity obligations failure was initiated against the wrong person the status can be changed to 'activity obligations failure in error'. No letter is sent when the obligations status is changed to 'activity obligations failure in error'.
## Reviews of Decisions for activity obligations failures
Review of Decisions for activity obligations failures are recorded in HIYA. However, the outcome of the review must be recorded in OBMAN. This will ensure that the benefit status can be resumed or regranted in SWIFTT, depending on the outcome of the review.
Note that if the Review of Decision process finds that the originally recorded 'upheld' outcome should be changed to overturned, you will need to make this change in OBMAN.
For more information see:
- The disputes process
- Disputes and reviews of an activity obligations failure

chunks.title: Redirection of Young Parent Payment — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection of Young Parent Payment
For young people subject to youth money management the Young Parent Payment, family tax credit, Best Start tax credit and any ongoing Extra help must be redirected to pay for:
- the young person's accommodation and service costs, for example rent, board, power, phone
- the young person's lawful debts or other liabilities, for example Child Support payments, MSD debts
- food and groceries via a payment card
Note Disability Allowance and Child Disability Allowance are paid directly to the young person.

chunks.title: Delayed redundancy payments — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Delayed redundancy payments
If the young person has been granted a benefit and then receives a redundancy payment within 52 weeks after the date the young person's employment ceased, the benefit stand-down and date employment ceased must be reassessed.
To review the initial stand-down:
- divide the redundancy payment by 26 weeks (and 52 weeks if the young person's entitlement date to benefit is on or after 1 May 2005). Add the appropriate weekly redundancy amount to the young person's average weekly income received before employment ceased.
- re-assess the length of the initial stand-down period to determine a new commencement date. Remember to use the calculation that provides the young person with the lesser stand-down period.
and
- establish an overpayment for any monies paid to the young person prior to the reassessed commencement date
## Payments received more than 52 weeks after redundancy
If the young person receives a redundancy payment more than 52 weeks after the date the young person's employment ceased, the payment is treated as a capital payment. The young person's entitlement to any Extra Help must also be reassessed.

chunks.title: Refugee Family Support Category — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Refugee Family Support Category
The Refugee Family Support Category allows for a quota of refugees' and protected persons' family members to be considered for permanent residence in New Zealand each year. A client may apply for residence under this category if their New Zealand sponsor's registration was selected from the annual ballot.
Clients need to have been living continuously in New Zealand for 2 years to be entitled to Young Parent Payment. However, Young Parent Payment on the ground of hardship may be considered before they meet the 2 year requirement if the client meets all the other eligibility criteria for Jobseeker Support and can meet the relevant obligations.
Jobseeker Support on the ground of hardship is both income and asset tested.
When assessing the client's entitlement to Young Parent Payment on the ground of hardship, the sponsor's financial circumstances is not used in the assessment. However, any financial assistance given to the client and family (if any) from either their sponsor or from another party, must be used in the assessment.
It is important to note that, unlike other visa categories sponsors, under the Refugee Family Support Category have no obligation to financially support their relative.
The only obligation a sponsor under this category has is to make sure adequate accommodation for their relatives is available during the first 24 months of their relative's residence in New Zealand. Despite this requirement, the client may still be able to get assistance as a non-beneficiary.
If the client has a change in personal resources, confirmation of that change is required to make sure the client is getting the support they are entitled to.

chunks.title: Refugee quota — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Refugee quota
Refugees with permanent residence are exempt from meeting the 2 years continuous residence criteria, so you should assess the client for Young Parent Payment in the usual manner.
Most refugees accepted as part of the United Nations quota receive permanent residence prior to arriving in New Zealand or during their period of resettlement at the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre. These clients do not usually have any income or assets.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Refugees and protected persons
- No stand-down applies

chunks.title: Refugees and protected persons — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Refugees and protected persons
In general a refugee or protected person cannot receive Young Parent Payment unless they have been granted permanent residence.
If a refugee or a protected person has permanent residence, assess them for Young Parent Payment in the usual manner. Refugees and protected persons with permanent residence are exempt from meeting the two years continuous residence criteria.
Note when a client leaves the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre no stand-down applies to the grant of the benefit.
## Clients without permanent residence
If a client is a refugee or protected person and has not been granted permanent residence, an Emergency Benefit may be considered.
For more information see:
- Refugee quota
- Emergency Benefit
- No stand-down applies

chunks.title: Removing incentive payments — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Removing incentive payments
Incentive payments should be removed when the young person:
- is subject to a grade 1, 2 or 3 sanction
- is in hospital for longer than 13 weeks and they are receiving the hospital rate of payment
- moves from Young Parent Payment to Youth Payment because they no longer have a dependent child (Parent education incentive only)
- moves from Young Parent Payment onto a main benefit
- has intentionally acted in a way that is inconsistent with the purpose of the incentives
Note young people can continue to receive their incentive payments once they are earned if they are granted an exemption from their obligations, unless the reason the exemption is needed is because they have acted in a way that is inconsistent with the purpose of the incentive.
For more information see:
- Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose
- Incentive payments can continue
- Restoring incentive payments

chunks.title: Report to service provider or Work and Income on progress — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Report to service provider or Work and Income on progress
A young person receiving Young Parent Payment is required to report to their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service on how they are satisfactorily meeting their obligation to be:
- in education, training or work-based learning
- participating in a budgeting programme and
- participating in a parenting education programme and other parenting obligations
A service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service can ask a young person to report to them by either phone, email or in person and will determine how often the young person must report.
The frequency of reporting must be reasonable and take into account:
- the length of the activity
- how often the young person is required to attend
- whether a young person has failed to comply with their obligations in the past
Generally a young person should not be required to report more than once a week.
Example
The service provider sets an activity for a young person to attend a budgeting programme and asks that they report on their progress when they commence the programme and when they attend each week.
A young person undertakes the budgeting programme. They phone their service provider when they commence the programme and report in each week of the programme to confirm their attendance.
For more information see:
- Obligations

chunks.title: Residence — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Residence
To be granted Young Parent Payment, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (ie not be in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) and
- have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years or more at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
For more information see:
- Deciding ordinarily resident
Note clients who are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident, but have not lived in New Zealand continuously for 2 years, may be eligible for Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship.
If a client is from overseas or is a refugee or protected person special provisions may apply, see:
- Clients from overseas
- Refugees and protected persons
## Sponsored clients
Some clients have been granted permanent residence under the Immigration New Zealand sponsorship policy.
Before a decision can be made about the client's application for benefit, any reasons why their sponsor can no longer support the client must first be determined and verified.
For more information see:
- Authenticating [no link find out why]
## Clients without permanent residence
If a client does not have permanent residence they cannot receive a Young Parent Payment (even if they have lived in New Zealand continuously for 2 years). They may be able to receive an Emergency Benefit if they:
- are lawfully present in New Zealand and are awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protection status in New Zealand or
- are applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act and are compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances
For more information see:
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Clients from overseas
- Two years residence
- Proof of residence
- Granting on grounds of hardship
- Payments from Overseas Reciprocal Agreements

chunks.title: Resident in New Zealand — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Resident in New Zealand
To qualify for Young Parent Payment a client must have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident.
To be resident in New Zealand at a particular time means that the client either:
- makes their home in New Zealand, that is, they have been living in New Zealand on a permanent basis or
- has an intention to make their home in New Zealand for the foreseeable future
Note "resident" is not the same as being ordinarily resident.
Remember you must be satisfied that the client has been resident in New Zealand continuously for at least 2 years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident.
## Client makes their home in New Zealand
A client will be resident in New Zealand if they make their home in New Zealand. You should look for evidence that the client makes their home in New Zealand. Relevant factors you should consider include:
- a fixed abode in New Zealand?
- ownership of property in New Zealand?
- frequent absences from New Zealand, and what is the duration of and reason for those absences?
- involvement with New Zealand society such as (but not limited to): community activitiesemploymentmembership of clubs andlocal churches
- community activities
- employment
- membership of clubs and
- local churches
For more information see:
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Reciprocal Agreements
- Proof of residence

chunks.title: Restoring incentive payments — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Restoring incentive payments
The service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service can recommend that an incentive payment be returned to the young person, if they are satisfied that the young person is now acting in a way that is consistent with the aims of the incentive payment.
When the incentives will be returned depends on:
- the reason that the incentive was removed
- whether the young person has undertaken or completed steps to address their actions
- whether the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service is satisfied that the young person is now acting in a way that is consistent with the aims of the incentive payment
For more information see:
- Removing incentive payments
- Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose
- Payment Incentive payments

chunks.title: How retirement payments affect benefit payments — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## How retirement payments affect benefit payments
Retirement payments can be paid in one or more lump sums or on a periodical basis.
Payment received before a benefit is granted
Retirement payments are included in the assessment of a person's last 26 or 52 weeks' income to determine the length of their initial stand-down).
Retirement payments do affect the date employment ceased.
Payment received after a benefit is granted
When a young person receiving a benefit has been working and having their earnings charged then receives a retirement payment, this payment is not regarded as income for benefit purposes.
However, it will be regarded as a cash asset and may affect any Extra Help the young person is receiving.
Different rules apply for retirement payments received more than 52 weeks after the person's employment ceased. For more information see:
- Delayed retirement payments

chunks.title: Returned to youth money management — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Returned to youth money management
A young person can be returned to youth money management for the following reasons:
- they are subject to a grade 1, 2 or 3 sanction or
- they are demonstrating poor financial judgement
## Sanction has been imposed
After a sanction has been imposed, the young person will be returned to youth money management when they recomply.
To earn the right to manage their money again, the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service will need to be satisfied that the young person has been demonstrating a continued compliance with their obligations.
## Poor financial judgement
Generally a young person may be considered to have poor financial judgement if they have:
- sought or accessed hardship assistance without a good and sufficient reason, or where they could have avoided the application(for example, they did not pay their power account, but spent the money on clothes)
- purchased an unnecessary item on credit
- spent their in-hand allowance on items that are inappropriate for their situation (for example, alcohol and cigarettes and had no money to buy their weekly bus pass)
- increased their costs unnecessarily (for example, moved into more expensive accommodation)
- not used their part-time earnings in a way that is appropriate for their situation (for example, bought very expensive clothing items when they should have saved for their car registration)
- entered a relationship with a coercive partner, who is starting to control their money or are being unduly influenced by peer pressure
## In-hand allowance and incentives
When a young person is returned to youth money management because they have demonstrated poor financial judgement, they will retain their in-hand allowance and any incentives earned.
For more information see:
- Assessed as financially competent
- Continued compliance with their obligations
- Earning the right to receive payment directly
- Youth money management
- Obligations Removing incentive payments

chunks.title: Grade 1 and 2 sanctions — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Grade 1 and 2 sanctions
Incentive payments can be returned from the date MSD is satisfied the young person has started their recompliance activity.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (Grade 1 and 2)
## Grade 3 sanction
Failure to comply with education obligation
Where the failure that led to the cancellation of the Young Parent Payment was due to failing to comply with their obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning, the education incentive cannot be regranted if Young Parent Payment is regranted.
The young person must earn this incentive again by completing another 6 months commitment to education, training or work-based learning.
Example
A young person fails their activity obligations for a third time because they did not go to school. They are getting incentive payments for education and budgeting. When they undertake a 6-week approved activity their Young Parent Payment is restarted and their budgeting incentive is returned at the same time. The education incentive is not returned and the young person must re-earn this incentive by completing a further 6 months of education or training.
Failure for other reason
For any other failure reason, the incentive payment for budgeting, parenting and education can be regranted when the young person recomplies.
Example
A young person has earned the budgeting, parenting and education incentives. They fail activity obligations for a third time for refusing to attend their budgeting discussions with their service provider. The young person undertakes a six-week approved activity and their Young Parent Payment is restarted and all of their incentives are returned at the same time.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Obligations Earning incentive payments
- Sanctions and youth money management

chunks.title: Samoan Quota Scheme — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Samoan Quota Scheme
This category is run by ballot and is available to Samoan citizens. Either the principal applicant or their partner must have an offer of employment in New Zealand.
Where the offer of employment was withdrawn or employment terminated through circumstances beyond the control of the client, you may consider granting Young Parent Payment where the client meets the two year residence criteria.
If you find that there was no job or that the job fell through you need to advise Immigration New Zealand after consulting with Legal Services regarding any privacy law implications with doing this.
Immigration New Zealand will decide on any action to be taken with regard to the client's residence status. In the meantime you need to look at all the circumstances of the client as to whether you can grant benefit assistance.
Note if the client has permanent residence and has lived continuously in New Zealand for two years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident, assess the client's entitlement to Young Parent Payment in the usual manner.
Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship is both income and asset tested. To assess a client's entitlement confirmation of the client's income and assets declared on the application for permanent residence is required from Immigration New Zealand. The client's current income and assets is also required.
Once confirmed, assess Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship in the usual manner taking into account all other information provided by Immigration New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Definite offer of employment
- Granting on grounds of hardship
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Sanctions - 50% protection — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Sanctions - 50% protection
Sanctions are applied differently for sole parents and married, civil union or de facto couples with dependent children who receive Young Parent Payment.
These young people do not have their whole payment sanctioned. Instead, a maximum sanction of 50% of their total Young Parent Payment may be imposed. The balance payable is known as 50% protection.
For more information, including treatment of supplementary assistance, see:
- Sanctions for sole parents
- Sanctions for couples - one person fails
- Sanctions for couples - both fail
Also see:
- Income abatement and 50% protection

chunks.title: Sanctions and youth money management — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Sanctions and youth money management
Where a young person was not subject to youth money management before a first, second or third activity obligations failure, they will be returned to youth money management when they recomply.
For more information see:
- Payment Youth money management

chunks.title: Sanctions for couples - both fail — young parent payment
chunks.text: Married, civil union or de facto couples with dependent children who both fail to meet their activity obligations at the same time do have their whole payment sanctioned. A maximum sanction of 50% of the total Young Parent Payment may be imposed. The balance payable is known as 50% protection.

chunks.title: Grade 1 and 2 sanctions — young parent payment
chunks.text: If both people in a married, civil union or de facto couple fail their activity obligations for the first or second time, each person's in-hand allowance (or $50 for those who are not subject to youth money management before the failure) and any incentive payments are suspended until they recomply with the obligation(s) they have failed. The couple can continue to get any Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support and Winter Energy Payment to which they are entitled.

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction — young parent payment
chunks.text: If both people in a married, civil union or de facto couple fails their activity obligations for a third time: - 50% each person's Young Parent Payment, and all of their incentive payments, is cancelled immediately - 50% Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support is cancelled and - they are both subject to a non-entitlement period for 13 weeks from the date of cancellation They can continue to get the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment as they are still getting a qualifying benefit. Both young people may get a provisional benefit and have their payment increased to 100% if they start a six-week approved activity. If the young person does not start a 6-week approved activity, they must reapply at the end of their non-entitlement period to get a benefit. Note Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance and Childcare Assistance (including Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment) can continue to be paid during a non-entitlement period. For more information see: - Definition of second and third failures - Effect of sanctions on assistance

chunks.title: Young person does not recomply — young parent payment
chunks.text: If the young person has not recomplied within 2 weeks, the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service will need to contact the young person to discuss financial assistance and recompliance. If they have not recomplied at 4 weeks, a letter will need to be sent requesting the young person attends an interview to discuss ongoing entitlement to Young Parent Payment. For more information see: - Recompliance (Grade 1 and 2) - Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)

chunks.title: Sanctions for couples - one person fails — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Sanctions for couples - one person fails
When one person in a married, civil union or de facto couple with dependent children fails to meet their activity obligations, they do not have their whole payment sanctioned.
Instead a maximum sanction of 50% of the total Young Parent Payment may be imposed on the person who failed. The balance payable is known as 50% protection.
## Grade 1 and 2 sanctions
If one person in a married, civil union or de facto couple fails the activity obligations for the first or second time, that person's in-hand allowance (or $50 for those who are not subject to youth money management before the failure) and any incentive payments are suspended until they recomply with the obligation(s) they have failed.
The couple can continue to get any Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support to which they are entitled, as well as the full rate of Winter Energy Payment.
## Grade 3 sanction
If one person in a married, civil union or de facto couple fails their activity obligations for a third time:
- 50% of their Young Parent Payment, and all of their incentive payments, is cancelled immediately
- their portion of Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support and Winter Energy Payment is cancelled and
- the young person is subject to a non-entitlement period period for 13 weeks from the date of cancellation
The young person may get a provisional benefit and have their payment increased to 100% if they start a six-week approved activity.
If the young person does not start a 6-week approved activity, they must reapply at the end of their non-entitlement period to get a benefit.
Note Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance and Childcare Assistance (including Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment) can continue to be paid during a non-entitlement period.
For more information see:
- Effect of sanctions on assistance
- Definition of second and third failures
- Payment to the non-sanctioned partner

chunks.title: Sanctions for sole parents — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Sanctions for sole parents
When sole parents fail to meet their activity obligations they do not have their whole payment sanctioned. Instead, a maximum sanction of 50% of the total Young Parent Payment may be imposed. The balance payable is known as 50% protection.
Sole parents who are sanctioned can continue to get full supplementary assistance, regardless of the grade of sanction. This includes the Winter Energy Payment.
## Grade 1 and 2 sanctions
A first or second activity obligations failure means suspension of the in-hand allowance (or $50 for those who are not subject to youth money management before the failure) and any incentive payments, until the young person recompiles with the obligation(s) they have failed.
The young person can continue to get any Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support to which they are entitled, as well as the full rate of Winter Energy Payment.
## Grade 3 sanction
For a third activity obligations failure a sole parent is no longer entitled to get Young Parent Payment and the payment is cancelled. However they can get 50% of the sole parent rate of Young Parent Payment. They continue getting the full rate of Winter Energy Payment.
The young person may get a provisional benefit and have their payment increased to 100% if they start a 6-week approved activity.
For more information see:
- Definition of second and third failures
- Effect of sanctions on assistance

chunks.title: Secondary education — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Secondary education
Participating in secondary education is the preferred way for a young person receiving Young Parent Payment to meet their activity obligation of being in or available for full-time secondary or tertiary education, approved training or work-based learning.
Generally they should be working towards a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification.
A young person enrolled in secondary education (including composite schools, correspondence schools, and secondary schools) must:
- regularly attend classes
- compete assignments and
- complete other course requirements
## School holidays
Young people intending to return to secondary education in the next academic year can be paid Young Parent Payment during the summer holidays. Any incentive payments earned will continue over this period also.
