Note you may also require a young person to undertake other activities that work towards NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualifications during the summer holidays.
## Incentive payments
Young people receiving Young Parent Payment can earn incentive payments for education and budgeting obligations if they meet certain criteria.
For more information see:
- Definition of 'full-time'
- NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification
- Qualifications In or available for secondary education
- Earning incentive payments
- Obligations
- Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months

chunks.title: Self-imposed stand-down — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Self-imposed stand-down
Where a young person knows that they will have a stand-down and delays their application, the commencement date will be:
- the day after initial stand-down ends or
- the application date
whichever is the later.

chunks.title: Make-up of a severance agreement — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Make-up of a severance agreement
Depending on the circumstances, a severance agreement can include payments for more than one reason. Payments may include:
- an extension of the required period of notice in the employment agreement
- contractual entitlements that have not yet accrued such as long service leave
- compensation for loss of future earnings for a specified period
- compensation for hurt and humiliation
- a contribution towards legal fees
- reimbursement for other costs incurred such as medical costs, relocation, career services, retraining
The make-up of a severance agreement is usually specified in the terms of settlement or other formal severance agreement documentation.
However, some agreements are subject to a confidentiality or non-disclosure clause which means the young person will not be able to tell us about the details of their severance package.

chunks.title: Aged 16 or 17 years old — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Aged 16 or 17 years old
To receive Young Parent Payment a single young person aged 16 or 17 years old must meet all of the qualifications and be one of the following:
- not living with their parents or guardians and have a parental support gap or
- living at home with, or being financially supported by their parents or guardians who earn less than the Family Tax Credit income cut-off point or
- single because they are divorced, dissolved civil union or separated from their de facto partner
Note young people who are single because they are divorced, have a dissolved civil union or are separated from their de facto partner do not have to have a parental support gap to qualify and get a Young Parent Payment.
## Aged 18 or 19 years old
Single young people aged 18 or 19 years do not have to meet the parental support gap criteria to receive Young Parent Payment.
Note if a young person is married, in a civil union or in a de facto relationship, they do not have to meet the parental support gap qualification to receive Young Parent Payment. See:
- Young people who are in a relationship
For more information see:
- Parental support gap
- Parents earn less than Family Tax Credit cut-out point
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Skilled/Business Stream — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Skilled/Business Stream
The purpose of the Skilled/Business stream is to help talented and entrepreneurial migrants gain residence in New Zealand. The categories in this stream are the:
- Skilled Migrant Category
- Business Categories (Long term Business, Migrant investment, Entrepreneur, Entrepreneur Plus, Employees of Relocating Businesses) and
- Residence from Work Categories (Talent (Accredited Employers), Talent (Arts, Culture, and Sports), and Long Term Skill Shortage List instructions)
For clients granted permanent residence under the Skilled/Business Stream the client has signed a Declaration of Personal Resources statement they have funds to support themselves and family (if any) for the first 2 years residence in New Zealand.
Generally the client would have had a work/study visa for at least 2 years before permanent residence was granted.
## Exception
Clients granted permanent residence under the Skilled Migrant Category should already have had employment for their first year of residence in New Zealand.
Clients must have 2 years continuous residence in New Zealand to be entitled to Young Parent Payment. Until they have met this requirement Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship may be considered.
Note if a client has permanent residence and already meets the 2 years continuous residence, assess the client for Young Parent Payment in usual manner.
Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship is both income and asset tested. To assess a client's entitlement to Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship confirmation of the client's income and assets declared on the application for permanent residence is required from the Immigration New Zealand.
If the client has a change in personal resources, confirmation of that change is required.
For more information see:
- Granting on grounds of hardship
- Change in personal resources

chunks.title: Social rehabilitation programmes — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Social rehabilitation programmes
Examples of social rehabilitation programmes include (but are not limited to):
- social rehabilitation for drug, alcohol or mental health
- social rehabilitation for pregnant single women and abuse victims
- social rehabilitation for repeat offenders
A social rehabilitation provider can include (but are not limited to):
- Salvation Army
- Anglican Social Services
- Arohanui Christian Trust
For more information see:
- Extra help Social Rehabilitation Assistance

chunks.title: Special circumstances justifying delay in activity obligation — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Special circumstances justifying delay in activity obligation
A young person may have special circumstances that justify not having to attend a Teen Parent Unit when their youngest dependent child is 6 months old even if there is a suitable place available.
Special circumstances include, but are not limited to:
- the young person's child has an uncontrolled health condition, such as asthma, or the child has special needs
- an illness or post natal depression affecting the young person's ability to return to school
- the young person is struggling with the challenge of being a new parent (supported by information received from their Well Child/Tamariki Ora or health practitioner) and returning to education or training will be detrimental to the young person and/or their child
- the young person is having difficulty bonding with their child (supported by information received from their Well Child/Tamariki Ora or health practitioner) and returning to education or training will be detrimental to the young person and/or their child
- the dynamics of the other participants of the Teen Parent Unit makes the young person's attendance at the Teen Parent Unit inappropriate
## Special circumstances exist
Where the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service are satisfied that there are special circumstances that justify the delay in the obligation to return to education at the Teen Parent Unit, the obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning would apply from when:
- a suitable place becomes available
- there are no longer special circumstances that delay the obligation to return to education at the Teen Parent Unit
- the young person's youngest dependent child reaches the age of 12 months
whichever is earlier.
## No special circumstances exist
Where there are no special circumstances that justify the delay in obligations for the young person to return to education at a Teen Parent Unit, the young person must attend.
For more information see:
- Deciding if suitable place at Teen Parent Centre available

chunks.title: Special regional training courses — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Special regional training courses
This is any training approved by the regional contracts manager.
Young people will be meeting their obligations where they are undertaking programmes linked to the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF) credits.
For more information see:
- Approved training

chunks.title: Temporary employment — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Temporary employment
No stand-down is imposed where a young person:
- has been in part-time employment or full-time employment for less than 26 weeks
- was receiving a benefit immediately before they were employed
- the benefit was stopped because they returned to work and
- has applied for a benefit after their employment ceased
Tthe young person's average weekly income is not required where the young person has been in temporary employment for less than 26 weeks. However, the young person's final pay details are required to determine the date of event and entitlement date.

chunks.title: Tertiary education — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Tertiary education
A young person receiving Young Parent Payment can meet their activity obligation by studying full-time at a university or polytechnic.
Generally they should be working towards a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification.
A young person enrolled in full-time tertiary education must:
- be enrolled in a course considered to be 'full-time'
- regularly attend classes
- complete assignments and
- complete other course requirements
Note a young person does not have to move to Independent Circumstances Allowance if they qualify for this payment.
## Tertiary holidays
Young people intending to return to tertiary education in the next academic year can be paid Young Parent Payment during the summer holidays. Any incentive payments earned will continue over this period also.
Note you may also require a young person to undertake other activities that work towards NCEA level 2 or an equivalent or higher qualifications during the summer holidays.
## Incentive payments
Young people receiving Young Parent Payment can earn incentive payments for education and budgeting obligations if they meet certain criteria.
For more information see:
- Definition of 'full-time'
- NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification
- Earning incentive payments
- Qualifications In or available for tertiary education
- Obligations
- Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months

chunks.title: The disputes process — young parent payment
chunks.text: The disputes process is a quick process where MSD must respond to a young person's dispute immediately. MSD must take into account any new information provided by the young person and let them know the decision straight away. A letter is sent automatically to the young person once a decision has been recorded on the dispute. A young person can dispute the decision if they believe: - they did not fail their activity obligations or - that they had a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete the activity obligation Note if a young person has disputed the activity obligations failure and MSD has upheld the decision, the young person can only dispute it again if they provide new information. If new information is not provided, the young person will need to follow the Review of Decision process. If a sanction has been imposed MSD can still use the disputes process. This allows the young person an opportunity for a quick resolution to their dispute before proceeding with the Review of Decision process. For more information see: - Recording decisions on a dispute - Disputes and reviews of an activity obligations failure

chunks.title: Reason for dispute — young parent payment
chunks.text: The young person can dispute the decision if they believe they did not fail their activity obligations, for 1 of the following reasons: - an activity obligations failure was initiated, but the young person had undertaken the activity or - undertaking or completing the activity was dependent on the provision of assistance by the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service and that assistance was not supplied or - reasonable steps weren't taken by the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service to inform a young person of the activity that they were required to do Note a young person cannot appeal the decision to be paid under youth money management.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for failing — young parent payment
chunks.text: MSD must consider the circumstances of the young person, and determine whether it would have been reasonable for the young person to have undertaken the activity. Good and sufficient reasons for failing to undertake an activity include (but are not limited to): - the young person was temporarily medically unfit or injured - there was death or illness in the family - due to unforeseen circumstances the young person could not realistically transport themselves on the day - an unexpected event occurred on the day, eg the young person had to provide care for a sick family member or relative Note if you are unsure whether a young person has a good and sufficient reason then you should seek guidance from your capability developer, manager client service operations, manager client service delivery.

chunks.title: Third party application for funds — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Third party application for funds
A third party can only make an application for the remaining money on a payment card if they have the power to act for the young person. This could be their appointed agent, or the executor of their estate if the young person has died.
The Ministry of Social Development must be sure that a third party has the appropriate authority to act on behalf of the young person.
## Young person has died
When a young person dies, the executor of their estate may apply for the money left on the payment card, if there is no executor of their estate, their next of kin can apply.
Note any money left on the payment card that has been paid out to the young person's estate will generally be part of the assessable estate when assessing qualifications for a Funeral Grant. Funds that remain on the payment card are generally impractical to realise and therefore may be excluded from the assessable estate.

chunks.title: Transfer between benefits — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Transfer between benefits
A transfer between benefits can occur when a young person qualifies for Young Parent Payment while currently receiving another benefit.
There is no stand-down imposed for young people who:
- transfer to Young Parent Payment from another benefit type or
- are included as a partner in another benefit type
Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Child's Benefit and Orphan's Benefit are also a benefit in this situation. Where Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit has been paid and the child now qualifies for Young Parent Payment, no stand-down is imposed.
## Non-beneficiary clients
When a non-beneficiary client receiving Extra help such as Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance applies for Young Parent Payment, it is not regarded as a transfer between benefits. An initial stand-down is imposed.
For more information see:
- Processing standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Young person intending to return to the same employer — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Young person intending to return to the same employer
If a young person has received any sick leave payments they would not be eligible for Young Parent Payment until these payments had stopped. You then assess any initial stand-down.
Young people are not required to use any sick leave they may have if they are intending to return to the same employer.
## Annual leave entitlement
Young people are not required to use up their annual leave entitlement if they are intending to return to the same employer.

chunks.title: 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down
When a young person applies for Young Parent Payment within 28 days of their entitlement date, the commencement date is the day after the initial stand-down ends.
This means, in some situations, MSD can commence a benefit from a date earlier than the application date.
If the application is not received within 28 days, MSD cannot backdate the commencement date.
Note the 28-day rule only applies to clients who have an initial stand down imposed.

chunks.title: Two years residence — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Two years residence
A client must have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident to qualify for Young Parent Payment.
Note the 2 year period of residence must be 2 years continuous residence without absence from New Zealand. There are some circumstances however when a client can be absent from New Zealand during this time.
For more information see:
- Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
If the client is not a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident they cannot receive Young Parent Payment, whether or not they have 2 years continuous residence in New Zealand. They may be eligible for an Emergency Benefit.
## Clients who do not meet the 2 years residence criteria
If the client is a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident and does not meet the 2 year continuous residence requirement they may be able to receive Young Parent Payment on grounds of hardship. See:
- Granting on grounds of hardship
For more information about residence see:
- Proof of residence
- Permanent residence
- Refugees and protected persons
- Resident in New Zealand
- Calculating period of residence
- Unlawful residence
- Reciprocal Agreements

chunks.title: Unable to receive financial support from parents — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Unable to receive financial support from parents
To receive a Young Parent Payment, a single young person must have a parental support gap.
A 16 or 17 year old is considered to have a parental support gap when their parents (or guardians) are unable to support them financially because they are:
- deceased
- in prison
- in hospital or
- overseas
You will need to find out:
- what the period of absence is and what provisions have been made for the young person's support
- if the parents are overseas, ask if it is temporary or permanent, and why the young person has not gone as well. See: Parents overseas
- if the parents are living apart, ask the young person what involvement they have with the other parent and whether they have considered living with them and
- whether the young person is living in a 'care' arrangement as opposed to an independent situation
For more information see:
- What is financial support?
- Independent
- Parents overseas
- Discharged from care
- Definition of parents

chunks.title: Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption
A young person, who is subject to a sanction or a 13 week non-entitlement period, may not need to complete a recompliance activity if they meet the criteria for an exemption from their activity obligations (this may be a full or partial exemption).
If a young person is subject to a 13 week non-entitlement period, and is unable to complete the six week activity, you cannot recover the provisional benefit if they do not complete the activity because they meet the criteria for an exemption from their activity obligations.
## Example - young person develops a health condition, injury or disability
A young person who is subject to a sanction develops a health condition, injury or disability, and meets the criteria for the exemption "would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury, disability". They are unable to complete a recompliance activity.
In this situation you should add the exemption reason in SWIFTT (medical incapacity), and follow the disputes process so that the benefit can be resumed.
## Proof
To support their exemption, the young person is required to provide a medical certificate. The information required on the medical certificate is:
- a diagnosis (what the health condition is)
- the impact of the condition on their ability to undertake activity obligations
- the likely duration of the impact
- their capacity for education, training and work-based learning and
- any other information that is required
For more information see:
- Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
- Exemptions from activity obligations

chunks.title: Unlawful residence — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Unlawful residence
To reside in New Zealand lawfully the client must either:
- be a New Zealand citizen
- an Australian citizen
- hold a New Zealand passport
- hold an Australian passport
- hold a visa granted under the Immigration Act 2009
- be deemed to hold a visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) or
- hold a permit granted under the Immigration Act 1987
If the client does not fulfil one of the above, the client is deemed to be in New Zealand unlawfully.
Any periods of unlawful residence are excluded when calculating the clients' period of residence.
The calculation of the two year period of continuous residence commences from when the client is granted New Zealand citizenship or permanent residence.
For more information see:
- Permanent residence
- Proof of residence
- Calculating the period of residence
- Deciding ordinarily resident

chunks.title: Unsupported Childs Benefit was paid — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Unsupported Childs Benefit was paid
If the young person has been living with a caregiver who was getting Unsupported Childs Benefit for the young person, the young person can only get Young Parent Payment if:
- the young person has stopped living with the caregiver and
- there has been a relationship breakdown between the young person and caregiver
This is because caregivers who get Unsupported Childs Benefit for a dependent person are considered parents.
The Independent Assessment Provider report will assist you in determining relationship breakdown.
For more information see:
- Independent Assessment Provider

chunks.title: Weekly income example — young parent payment
chunks.text: Below are examples of calculating the income deduction for weekly income for Young Parent Payment.

chunks.title: Example 1 - Single young person getting Young Parent Payment — young parent payment
chunks.text: Weekly gross income from wages $290.00 Less income allowed before Young Parent Payment is affected (As of 1 April 2026) $284.70 Equals income that will reduce the Young Parent Payment $5.30 Amount to deduct (rounded down) $5.00 Deduction will be $1.00 per $1.00 of income over $284.70 until they reach $334.70 per week (at 1 April 2026). When income is over $334.70 (at 1 April 2026) Young Parent Payment is no longer payable.

chunks.title: Example 2 - Couple, both getting Young Parent Payment — young parent payment
chunks.text: Weekly gross income from wages (one partner earns $125 and the other $200) $325.00 Less income allowed before Young Parent Payment is affected (As of 1 April 2026) $284.70 Equals income that will reduce the Young Parent Payment $40.30 Amount to deduct (rounded down) $40.00 in total or $20.00 each The deduction will be 50 cents per $1.00 of the couple's combined income over $284.70 gross per week (at 1 April 2026) until their income reaches $384.70 per week (at 1 April 2026). When income is over $384.70 (at 1 April 2026) Young Parent Payment is no longer payable.

chunks.title: Example 3 - Couple, 1 getting Young Parent Payment — young parent payment
chunks.text: Weekly gross income from wages (partner not getting Young Parent Payment $287.00 Less income allowed before Young Parent Payment is affected (As at 1 April 2026) $284.70 Equals income that will reduce the Young Parent Payment $2.30 Amount of deduction (rounded down) $2.00 The deduction will be 50 cents per $1.00 of the couple's combined income over $284.70 gross until their income reaches $384.70 per week (at 1 April 2026). When income is over $384.70 (at 1 April 2026) Young Parent Payment is no longer payable.

chunks.title: Example 4 - Sole parent getting Young Parent Payment, getting other income and information share Child Support payments — young parent payment
chunks.text: Weekly gross income from wages $300.00 Information share Child Support payment weekly income $100.00 Less income allowed before Young Parent Payment is affected (As of 1 April 2026) $284.70 Equals income that will reduce the Young Parent Payment $115.30 Amount to deduct (rounded down) $115.00 This example shows a young person getting information share Child Support income and other income (wages). The young person's other income is less than the income cut-out of $334.70 (as at 1 April 2026). Deduction will be $1.00 per $1.00 of total income over $284.70 until their benefit is reduced to $0.00.

chunks.title: Example 5 - Couple, both getting Young Parent Payment and information share Child Support payments only — young parent payment
chunks.text: Information share Child Support payment weekly income $400.00 Less income allowed before Young Parent Payment is affected (As of 1 April 2026) $284.70 Equals income that will reduce the Young Parent Payment $115.30 Amount of deduction (rounded down) $115.00 in total or $57.50 This example shows a young couple getting income from information share Child Support payments. Deduction is 50 cents per $1.00 of total income over $284.70 (as at 1 April 2026) until their benefit is reduced to $0.00.

chunks.title: Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Well Child/Tamariki Ora services and checks
Well Child/Tamariki Ora services are a screening, education and support service offered to all New Zealand children and their families or whanau from birth to 5 years old.
The services assist and support families and whanau to improve and protect their children's health. They are provided free to all children under 5 years by registered nurses and community health workers with specific training in child health.
First time parents and families requiring extra support are offered additional visits. Some visits are carried out in the home and others in clinics or community facilities.
Different providers run the Well Child/Tamariki Ora services, including:
- Plunket
- Maori health providers
- Pacific Island health providers
- Public Health Services - for example, public health nurses, community nurses, community health workers, social workers
## When do the checks happen?
The current Well Child/Tamariki Ora schedule includes 12 health checks (contacts) with 8 of these offered to children aged from 4 - 6 weeks to 5 years old.
## Between birth and 4 weeks old
Three checks are provided by a midwife, general practitioner or obstetrician:
- soon after birth
- during the first week of baby's life
- between 2 and 4 weeks old
## Between 4 weeks and 4 years old
Eight more checks are provided by the Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider, at:
- 4 - 6 weeks
- 8 - 10 weeks
- 3 - 4 months
- 5 - 7 months
- 9 - 12 months
- 15 - 18 months
- 2 - 3 years
- 4 - 5 years (this is the before school check, and the final Well Child/Tamariki Ora health check)
For more information see:
- Parenting obligations

chunks.title: What is financial support? — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## What is financial support?
Consider a young person to be financially supported by their parents when payments received are:
- long term
- ongoing
- regular and
- at least equal to or higher than the benefit rate payableIf a young person receives a lesser amount of support from their parents (or a one-off payment), they may still receive Young Parent Payment. Any support received would be charged as income.
Any financial support the young person receives must be given without any conditions for payment.
For more information see:
- Unable to receive financial support from parents
- Independent

chunks.title: When financial support is not expected — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## When financial support is not expected
Parents are not be expected to financially support the young person if:
- the young person is, or has been married
- the young person, is in, or has been in, a civil union
- the young person is, or has been, living in a de facto relationship that is in the nature of marriage or civil union (as determined by Work and Income) or
- the young person has been discharged from the care of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, and is not dependent on a caregiver
In all other circumstances an Independent Assessment Provider report will assist you to consider whether financial support should be expected or not.
For more information see:
- Young people who are, or have been, in a relationship
- De facto relationship (definition)
- Discharged from care
- Unsupported Childs Benefit was paid

chunks.title: When the sanction is imposed — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## When the sanction is imposed
Sanctions can only be imposed five working days after the young person has been notified by text message (where they have consented to receive information from us in this way) or in a letter about their activity obligations failure. This is called the 5 working day notice period.
Note that if a young person recomplies within the initial 5 working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the activity obligations failure is counted.
## How to count the '5 working day notice' period
The 5 working day notice period is counted from the date after the activity obligations text message (where the young person has consented to receive information from us in this way) or letter has been sent to the young person, to allow for posting and delivery of the letter.
The five working day notice period excludes weekends, public holidays, or the period 25 December to 15 January each year.
The tables below provide an example of how to count the notice period.
Day 0

Day 0

chunks.title: Work-based learning — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Work-based learning
A young person receiving Young Parent Payment can meet their education activity obligation by being in work-based learning.
Work-based learning includes courses that offer more practical, hands-on learning than the school environment.
For a young person to be considered to be in work-based learning they must be:
- employed and undertaking on-the-job learning and
- undertaking a course or programme that is relevant to their employment
While the young person is in paid work, all usual workplace conditions, including the applicable minimum wage, will apply to the work element of work-based learning in the same way that they apply to all other forms of employment.
Note if the young person earns more than the cut-out point for Young Parent Payment, they will no longer be able to receive it.
Programmes that contain elements of work-based learning include:
- Youth Guarantee programmes and
- part-time industry partnerships
## Incentive payments
Young people receiving Young Parent Payment can earn incentive payments for education and budgeting obligations if they meet certain criteria.
For more information see:
- Definition of 'full-time'
- NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification
- Earning incentive payments
- Qualifications In or available for work-based learning
- Obligations
- Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities
- Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months

chunks.title: Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
A client applying for Youth Parent Payment can be considered resident and present in New Zealand during periods of overseas employment when their employer (or other relevant person):
- deducted PAYE or source deductions from their wages and
- paid the deducted amount to Inland Revenue New Zealand
The period overseas that the client was considered resident and present can be used towards the 2 years residence requirement for Youth Parent Payment.
A partner or any dependent child who was with the client while they were working overseas can also be treated as resident and present in New Zealand for the same periods.
If the client has a child born outside of New Zealand during the period they were working overseas the child is deemed to have been born in New Zealand.
The residential qualifications do not apply to people who are self-employed and working overseas.
Clients should provide evidence of the periods they were employed overseas and that PAYE or source deductions were paid to Inland Revenue in New Zealand during these periods.
If the employer (or other relevant person) has deducted the tax but failed to pay it to the Commissioner of Inland Revenue New Zealand and the client did not contribute to the employer's failure to pay the tax, the period of employment overseas can still be regarded as residence and present in New Zealand.
If any person leaves New Zealand while getting a benefit and returns to take up ordinary residence in New Zealand at any time within 5 years are not required to meet the residential qualifications for the same benefit type.

chunks.title: Working part-time — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Working part-time
Participating in education, training or work-based learning is the focus for young people receiving Young Parent Payment. It is not a requirement that they seek part-time employment.
However, if they wish to they can work part-time and still receive Young Parent Payment as long as they can meet the qualification to be in, or available for, full-time education, approved training or approved work-based learning.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- In or available for secondary education
- In or available for tertiary education
- In or available for approved training
- In or available for work-based learning

chunks.title: Workplace/industry training — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Workplace/industry training
Workplace/industry training includes courses such as:
- Skills for Industry [no link find out why]
These courses are generally less than 13 weeks.
Young people will be meeting their obligations where they are undertaking programmes linked to the New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF) credits.
For more information see:
- Approved training

chunks.title: Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
If a young person meets the qualifications for Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability (but for their age) they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their activity obligations, until their capacity for education, training and work-based learning improves.
This can be a full or partial exemption.
The young person must be limited in their capacity to undertake activities because of a health condition, injury or disability.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support Client has a health condition, injury or disability
If the young person is partially exempt they are able to:
- plan for education, training or work-based learning and
- undertake other activities such as budgeting
If a young person qualifies for a full exemption this means they are unable to meet any of their activity obligations, including planning.
## Proof
To support their exemption, the young person is required to provide a medical certificate. The information required on the medical certificate is:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is)
- the impact of the condition on their ability to undertake activity obligations
- the likely duration of the impact
- their capacity for education, training and work-based learning and
- any other information that is required
## Duration
The duration of an exemption is based on the reassessment date recorded on the medical certificate by the young person's health practitioner.
This exemption is initially granted for up to 13 weeks or the next reassessment date recorded by the health practitioner on the medical certificate - whichever is earlier.
This exemption should then be reviewed. At the review you should discuss the young person's circumstances and consider whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption for a further period. You can ask the young person to provide proof that their exemption should be extended.

chunks.title: Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
If a young person meets the qualifications for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability or total blindness, they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their activity obligations. The young person must be both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for education, training and work-based learning because of a health condition, injury, disability, total blindness or a condition they have had since birth.
For more information see:
- Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
This can be a full or partial exemption depending on whether the young person can plan for a return to education, training or work-based learning.
You should discuss with the young person whether they can still:
- plan for education, training or work-based learning and
- undertake other activities such as budgeting
If you are unsure about whether a full or partial exemption should be granted discuss with your regional health or regional disability advisor.
Note in all cases you should consider the young person's eligibility for Supported Living Payment.
Note use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Would qualify for Supported Living Payment Health condition/Injured/Disabled'
## Proof
The young person must provide either a medical certificate or medical information from a health professional stating:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is)
- the impact of the condition on their ability to undertake activities
- the likely duration of the impact
- their capacity for planning and undertaking activities part-time and
- any other information that is required
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Would qualify for SLP Health condition/Injured/Disabled'.
## Receiving an incentive payment
If the young person is receiving an incentive payment and then qualifies for an exemption you will need to decide if they can continue to receive it.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemption
- Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
- Obligations Incentive payments can continue

chunks.title: Young people who are in a relationship — young parent payment
chunks.text: When a young parent is in a relationship, their eligibility for Young Parent Payment depends on their partner's age and whether they get a main benefit. A relationship means the couple are: - legally married - in a civil union - in a de facto relationship with Family Court Judge consent

chunks.title: Both partners aged 16 to 19 years old — young parent payment
chunks.text: When a young parent in a relationship applies for Young Parent Payment and both partners are aged 16 to 19 years old, each partner must qualify in their own right. They do not need to have a parental support gap. These couples cannot get any other main benefit, except when the partner qualifies for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury, or disability. In this situation, the young parent can be included in their partner's Supported Living Payment.

chunks.title: Partner is aged 20 years or older — young parent payment
chunks.text: A young parent cannot get Young Parent Payment if their partner is aged 20 years or older and is getting one of the following benefits: - Emergency Benefit - Jobseeker Support - Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury, or disability In these situations, the young parent can be included in their partner's main benefit. Note if the partner is getting Supported Living Payment - caring for a person, the young parent can get Young Parent Payment in their own right.

chunks.title: Partner is not getting a main benefit — young parent payment
chunks.text: If the partner is not getting a benefit, e.g. because they are working or are subject to a non-entitlement period, the young parent can get Young Parent Payment in their own right.

chunks.title: Partner is not permanently or lawfully resident in New Zealand — young parent payment
chunks.text: If the partner does not have a current permit or visa that allows them to remain in New Zealand then they are in New Zealand unlawfully and you cannot include the partner in the benefit, unless one of the exceptions listed below applies. When the partner is in New Zealand unlawfully or is not a permanent resident, pay the client at a single or sole parent rate taking into consideration all of the couple's income and assets. Contact the Card Centre when granting the primary benefit to ensure that a Community Services Card is not issued to the non-resident partner. Encourage the partner to follow up their residence status. Exceptions There are some situations where a partner is exempt and can be included in the benefit without having been granted permanent residence. These are: - a person lawfully present in New Zealand who is awaiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protection status in New Zealand or - a person who has refugee or protection status in New Zealand or - a person applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 who is compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances

chunks.title: Young person in hospital — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Young person in hospital
The rate of payment for a young person getting Young Parent Payment can be different if they are in hospital.
The rate is reduced to the hospital rate when the young person has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks (not after getting a benefit for 13 weeks).
The hospital rate is paid directly to the young person and allows for the cost of personal items, which patients are expected to provide for themselves.
A young person on the hospital rate is not subject to youth money management.
## Exception
If the young person has been in hospital for 13 weeks or more at the commencement date of the benefit, the rate of payment is the hospital rate.
For more information about the hospital rate see:
- Changes and reviews Hospitalisation
- Youth money management

chunks.title: Young person leaves Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Young person leaves Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre
No stand-down applies to the commencement of a benefit when a young person has left the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre.
For more information see:
- Refugees and protected persons
- Commencement date
- No stand-down applies

chunks.title: Young person turns 20 years old — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Young person turns 20 years old
Generally when a young person turns 20 years old the Young Parent Payment should stop. However there are 2 situations where the payment can continue to be paid after they turn 20 years old. These are where a young person:
- must receive Young Parent Payment for a minimum of 6 months and cannot receive another main benefit (excluding Supported Living Payment on the ground of having a health condition, injury or disability) until after this period
- chooses to continue to receive Young Parent Payment if they remain in education, training, or work-based learning
For more information see:
- Must receive payment for six months
- Chooses to remain on Young Parent Payment past 20 years of age

chunks.title: Young person's IRD number — young parent payment
chunks.text: MSD may make a written request for evidence of an IRD number for a young person who is being paid Young Parent Payment.

chunks.title: Setting or extending the timeframe for providing evidence — young parent payment
chunks.text: MSD must provide the young person with a minimum of 10 working days to provide IRD number evidence that has been requested in writing. MSD can extend the 10 working day period (in writing) if the young person has a reasonable explanation for requiring more than 10 days to provide evidence of their IRD number. This includes considering factors outside the young parent's control that cause delays, including, but not limited to: - young person has a family emergency that caused a delay - processing delays with an external agency (e.g. Inland Revenue, Department of Internal Affairs, etc) - young person does not speak English as a first language and has difficulty navigating evidence requirements - young person has limited access to the internet, a device, or their local service centre - young person has a physical or intellectual disability that makes accessing services difficult - young person is injured, disabled, or has a medical condition that makes accessing services difficult.

chunks.title: Notice following unsuccessful match — young parent payment
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a young person's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the young person (in writing) to provide evidence of their IRD number. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the young person a minimum of 10 working days to provide their IRD number evidence or their assistance must be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Young Parent Payment and MSD holds an IRD number on record. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Isla's IRD number. MSD provides 10 working days in writing, for Isla to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Isla already having an IRD number - Isla not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD must suspend assistance if evidence of IRD number is not received — young parent payment
chunks.text: MSD must suspend all taxable and/or income tested assistance the young person is getting, including their Young Parent Payment if evidence of an IRD number is not provided within 10 working days from the written request, or extended period if this has been applied. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance. Example Koa is receiving Young Parent Payment and MSD does not have an IRD number on record. MSD sends a written request giving 10 working days for Koa to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD receives no response to this request. MSD suspends all Koa's taxable and/or income tested assistance because Koa has not supplied MSD with evidence of their IRD number within the timeframe provided.

chunks.title: IRD evidence may not be requested in some circumstances — young parent payment
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - significant factors, that are outside the young person's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number (e.g. a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence), and - the young person needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided or - significant factors related to a health, injury or disability that are outside the young person's control that prevents them from providing evidence of an IRD number, and - an agent cannot be appointed to act on the young parent's behalf. MSD can determine at a later point to request evidence of the IRD number. Example Sienna is 18 and receiving Young Parent Payment. Sienna's mother (Sara) is Sienna's agent and acts on Sienna's behalf with MSD. Sienna does not have an IRD number and Sara is not a recognised agent for Sienna for Inland Revenue. Sienna has a serious head injury, is unconscious and expected to be in hospital for at least 8 weeks. Due to their injury, Sienna is not able to give consent to appoint Sara as an agent for Inland Revenue to apply for an IRD number. MSD can request this information later when Sienna's situation has changed. Note there is different guidance for requesting evidence of an IRD number for partner's whose income is relevant to a young parent's Young Parent Payment or when a young parent is applying for Young Parent Payment.

chunks.title: Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Youngest dependent child is aged under 12 months
Young Parent Payment obligations apply from the time it is first paid except where the young person is caring for their youngest dependent child who is aged less than 12 months. In these cases, the obligation to be in or available for full-time education, training or work-based learning applies on the earlier of:
- the day the child becomes 6 months old if there is a suitable place available for the young person in a teen parent unit andMSD is satisfied that there are no special circumstances justifying the obligation starting at a later date
- if there is a suitable place available for the young person in a teen parent unit and
- MSD is satisfied that there are no special circumstances justifying the obligation starting at a later date
or
- the day on which the child becomes 12 months old
## Young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship
For young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and who are receiving Young Parent Payment the delay in the obligation to be in full-time education, training or work-based learning only applies to the principal caregiver. The obligation applies immediately to the other parent unless they qualify for an exemption on other grounds.
For more information see:
- Parenting obligations
- Deciding if suitable place at Teen Parent Unit available
- Special circumstances justifying delay in activity obligation
- Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities
- Exemptions from activity obligations

chunks.title: Youth activity obligations — young parent payment
chunks.text: Young people getting Young Parent Payment have the following activity obligations. They must: - be enrolled in and undertaking, or be available for, a full-time course of secondary or tertiary education, or approved training or work-based learning leading to a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification - when required to, participate in and complete an approved budgeting programme - when required to, participate satisfactorily in an approved parenting education programme - report to their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service on progress in meeting their education, parenting and budgeting obligations (above) as often as required - when required to, attend and participate in any interview with their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service and - when asked, provide within 20 working days, to their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service, details of the young person's accommodation costs, service costs and lawful debts or other liabilities - co-operate with their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service in managing the spending of their Young Parent Payment andattend and participate in regular discussions on budgetingat any discussion, or when asked, provide details of:- accommodation costs and service costs such as power and phone- lawful debts and liabilities- how they spent any in-hand allowance and any money credited to their payment or any other device - attend and participate in regular discussions on budgeting - at any discussion, or when asked, provide details of:- accommodation costs and service costs such as power and phone- lawful debts and liabilities- how they spent any in-hand allowance and any money credited to their payment or any other device A young person getting Young Parent Payment is also subject to the following obligations. They must: - enrol their child with a Primary Health Organisation, where a local provider is available - keep their child or children under the age of 5 years up-to-date with their Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks - ensure their child's attendance at an approved Early Childhood Education (ECE) programme or other suitable childcare, while they are participating in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work All obligations apply from the time Young Parent Payment is first paid except where the young person is caring for a child aged less than 12 months of age the obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning may apply from a later date.

chunks.title: Youth activity obligations — young parent payment
chunks.text: For more information see: - Youngest dependent child is under 12 months Young people who fail without good and sufficient reason to comply with their activity obligations may be sanctioned.

chunks.title: Incentive payments — young parent payment
chunks.text: Young people getting Young Parent Payment can earn incentive payments for education, parenting and budgeting obligations if they meet certain criteria. For more information see: - Deciding education, training or work-based learning activities - Approved budgeting programme activity - Report to service provider or Work and Income on progress - Parenting obligations - Earning incentive payments - Youth money management activity - Activity obligations failures

chunks.title: Youth Guarantee courses — young parent payment
chunks.text:
## Youth Guarantee courses
Young people attending and participating in Youth Guarantee courses can receive Young Parent Payment as these courses are considered to be employment-related training.
## Student Allowance and Student Loan
A young person can continue to receive Young Parent Payment when they participate in Youth Guarantee courses. They do not have to apply for a Student Allowance or Independent Circumstances Allowance.
Young people on a Youth Guarantee course are not eligible for a Student Loan.
For more information see:
- Tertiary Education Commission Youth Guarantee
- Approved training

chunks.title: Activity obligations failures — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Activity obligations failures
If a young person fails to comply with their activity obligations, an activity obligations failure needs to be considered.
The service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service:
- must be satisfied that the young person did not have a good and sufficient reason for their failure and
- if the young person did not have a good and sufficient reason, recommend an activity obligations failure be imposed
The Youth Service Support Unit (YSSU):
- makes the decision to apply a sanction, based on the recommendation of the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service and
- initiates the activity obligations failure in the system
For more information see:
- Obligations
- Good and sufficient reason for failing activity obligations
If it is decided that the young person has failed their activity obligations, the YSSU will initiate an activity obligations failure. The young person will then be notified by text message or letter that
- an obligations failure has occurred and
- they have 5 working days to recomply otherwise a sanction will be imposed
All young people have a five working day notice period to dispute or recomply before the sanction is imposed. If a young person recomplies within the 5 working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the activity obligations failure is recorded. For more information see:
- When the sanction is imposed
- Counting previous activity obligations failures
For more information, see:
- Disputes or reviews of an activity obligations failure
- Recompliance Grade 1 and 2
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Effect of sanctions on assistance

chunks.title: Activity requirements — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Activity requirements
A young person applying for Youth Payment must be undertaking or available for a full-time course of:
- secondary education
- tertiary education
- approved training
- approved work-based learning
Generally the activity will lead to a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification.
Note if a young person would be available for these activities but qualifies for an exemption, the exemption can apply from the start of the Youth Payment.
For more information see:
- In or available for secondary education
- In or available for tertiary education
- In or available for approved training
- In or available for work-based learning
- Working part-time
- Exemptions from activity obligations
- Obligations NCEA level 2 or equivalent qualification or higher qualification

chunks.title: Age — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Age
Young people applying for Youth Payment must be aged:
- 16 or 17 years old
When a young person turns 18 years old the Youth Payment should stop, however in some circumstances Youth Payment can continue to be paid after the young person has turned 18 years old.
For more information see:
- Young person turns 18 years old

chunks.title: Approved budgeting programme activity — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Approved budgeting programme activity
Young people receiving Youth Payment are required to participate in and complete an approved budgeting programme.
The budgeting programme aims to provide young people with skills to help them competently manage their finances. It is expected that budgeting courses delivered as part of the Youth Service will generally meet the Ministry's guideline for an approved budgeting programme.
Young people must be referred to a provider from the list of authorised course providers contracted by the Ministry of Social Development.
The providers of the budgeting programme will provide a programme that is in line with the Youth Services Guidelines for the content of the approved budgeting programme.
In areas where there are no contracted budgeting providers, the Youth Service provider is expected to deliver the budgeting programme to the young people in their service.
Young people receiving Youth Payment are not subject to hardship obligations if they are accessing Special Needs Grants or Advance Payment of Benefit.
## Recognition of prior learning
Prior learning can be recognised for clients who have previously completed budgeting programmes.
The client can be assessed as having met the requirement to participate in an approved budgeting programme if they have completed at least 2 unit standards in financial literacy.
Applicable unit standards
The following unit standards can be considered for prior learning:
Level
Unit standard
1
24709 - Produce a balanced budget to manage personal finances
28088 - Demonstrate understanding of credit and debt on personal finances
2
28094 - Produce a balanced household budget and adjust the budget to reflect changing financial circumstances
28096 - Demonstrate understanding of insurance products for personal financial capability
3
28099 - Analyse credit options and select strategies to manage personal finances
28100 - Develop a plan to achieve a long-term personal financial goal(s)
This list is not exhaustive. Other unit standards in financial literacy can also be considered.
Providers can consult the NZQA website to confirm if a young person has completed an appropriate unit standard in Financial Capability
## Incentive payments
Young people receiving Youth Payment can earn incentive payments for education and budgeting obligations if they meet certain criteria.
- Earning incentive payments
- Obligations

chunks.title: Approved training — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Approved training
In a situation where a young person cannot return to secondary education, the next appropriate activity to consider is approved training.
For youth obligations purposes approved training is defined as employment-related training.
Generally they should be working towards a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification.
Approved training must:
- be reputable and likely to teach the young person skills that will help them find work
- have an emphasis on training rather than study
- offer full-time training (at least 30 hours per week) and
- offer NCEA or New Zealand Qualification Framework (NZQF) credits
When advising a young person of approved training you need to consider their future goals and aspirations. You should try and match types of training that would be suitable for the young person and their career path.
A young person in full-time approved training must:
- regularly attend the programme
- complete assignments and
- complete other course requirements
## Employment-related training
Employment-related training includes (but is not limited to):
- Special regional training courses
- Workplace/industry training
- Youth Guarantee courses
## Incentive payments
Young people receiving Youth Payment can earn incentive payments for education and budgeting obligations if they meet certain criteria.
For more information see:
- Definition of 'full-time'
- NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification
- Earning incentive payments
- Qualifications In or available for approved training
- Obligations
- Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities

chunks.title: Assessed as financially competent — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Assessed as financially competent
A young person is generally considered to be financially competent where they have:
- earned their budgeting incentive and
- shown consistent, sound financial judgement which may include: the young person is spending their in-hand allowance on items that are appropriate for their situationany hardship assistance is justifiedthe young person has lowered their coststhe young person has found a part-time job and is managing the money they receive from that in a way that is appropriate for their situation
- the young person is spending their in-hand allowance on items that are appropriate for their situation
- any hardship assistance is justified
- the young person has lowered their costs
- the young person has found a part-time job and is managing the money they receive from that in a way that is appropriate for their situation
For more information see:
- Earning right to receive payment directly
- Continued compliance with their obligations

chunks.title: Recompliance assistance — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Recompliance assistance
If a young person undertakes a recompliance activity their benefit payment will be resumed from the date they start the activity.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (Grade 1 and 2)
Provisional Benefit
During a 13 week non-entitlement period a young person may be able to receive a provisional Youth Payment while they undertake an approved activity.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
## Transfers and exemptions
In some instances it may be appropriate to consider an exemption from the activity obligations or transfer to another benefit.
For more information on transfers and exemptions see:
- Exemptions from activity obligations
- Main benefits Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
Also see:
- Assistance for partners
- Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption
- Special Needs Grant Assistance during a non-entitlement period

chunks.title: Assistance for partners — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Assistance for partners
The partner of a young person who has a non-entitlement period of 13 weeks can receive Youth Payment in their own right, but must meet all of the qualifications (age, residence and activity).
To decide whether or not the young person is in a de facto relationship see:
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit
## If the partner has income
If the partner qualifies for the Youth Payment and either partner has income, the income is charged against the benefit at the following rate:
- 50 cents is taken from the benefit for each $1.00 of the combined income of the young person and their partner over $284.70 (before tax) a week (as at 1 April 2026)

chunks.title: Calculating the commencement date for couples — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Calculating the commencement date for couples
Young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship must qualify for Youth Payment in their own right.
When working out the commencement date of the payment, you must calculate the entitlement date and initial stand-down for each person using their individual circumstances.
## Example
A young couple apply for Youth Payment. Jane is attending college full-time. James left school six months ago, he has been doing casual work for his uncle but this has finished.
You can waive the stand down for Jane as she is still at school.
You impose a one week stand down for James.
For more information see:
- Entitlement date
- Twenty-eight day rule
- Initial stand-down
- No stand-down applies

chunks.title: Step one — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Step one
Find out the number of days represented by the payment received. If this is not clearly shown on the 'verification of payments received' provided by the young person, use either of the following formula.
Note extra payments paid to the young person for example holiday pay, should not be included in the gross salary figure used to calculate the daily rate of pay. However these payments will be included in the young persons' last 26 and 52 weeks gross earnings.
Formula 1
Determine gross salary over last 52 weeks of employment
Divide by 52 weeks = weekly rate of pay
Divide by 5 days = daily rate of pay
Confirm total amount of holiday pay etc
Divide this amount by daily rate of pay = number of days pay
Formula 2
Determine gross salary over last 4 weeks of employment
Divide by 20 (number of working days in 4 weeks) = daily rate of pay
Confirm total amount of holiday pay etc
Divide by daily rate of pay = number of days pay
Note only calculate the period covered by holiday pay using the applicants' last four weeks income if it does not disadvantage the young person. If the income earned in the last four weeks does not reflect what the young person normally earned, you may need to request extra weeks or calculate the daily rate of pay using the last 26 weeks gross salary.
## Step two
Add the number of days pay to the last day the young person worked.
This is the date that employment ceased.
Remember do not count Saturdays and Sundays - use Monday to Friday weekdays only. For example, if a young person stopped work on a Friday, add the days from the following Monday.
## Step three
The entitlement date is the day after this date. The stand-down commences from the entitlement date.

chunks.title: Cannot expect financial support from parents — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Cannot expect financial support from parents
To receive a Youth Payment a single young person must meet all of the qualifications and have a parental support gap. A 16 or 17 year old is considered to have a parental support gap when:
- they are living independently and
- you are satisfied that they have a good and sufficient reason why they cannot reasonably expect to be financially dependent on their parents or any other person
You must send the young person to an Independent Assessment Provider for an assessment and recommendation before granting Youth Payment.
If you are granting a young person Youth Payment due to other 'good and sufficient' reasons, add the reason in the Youth Payment comments field in the SDT1A screen in SWIFTT.
## When is it reasonable to expect support?
Consider it reasonable to expect financial support from the parents when the parents are willing and able to support the young person.
Ask the young person's parents this information (willingness to support and income details). Note they are not expected to provide proof of their income.
If the young person's parents have been living apart for some time, it is reasonable to ask both parents if they are willing and able to financially support the young person.
If the parents say they will support the young person, you should work through the details of when payments start and other arrangements for this to take place before declining the benefit.
For more information see:
- When financial support is not expected
- Independent
- Definition of 'parents'
- Unsupported Childs Benefit was paid
- Examples of good and sufficient reason
- Independent Assessment Provider

chunks.title: Caring full-time for a partner with a health condition, injury or disability (young partners) — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Caring full-time for a partner with a health condition, injury or disability (young partners)
A young person may be caring for a spouse or partner who has a health condition, injury or disability and who needs to be cared for on a full-time basis.
This can be a full or partial exemption.

chunks.title: Cash assets do not include — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Cash assets do not include
- a home property and the land on which it is situated
- a caravan, boat or other vehicle with a net equity less than $2,000, or is used by the young person or a member of their family for day to day accommodation
- motor vehicle principally used by the young person for private use
- personal effects
- FamilyBoost Tax Credit payments for the first 12 months after payment is received
Note a bank overdraft facility is not considered a cash asset or resource available to a young person.
Generally, ex gratia payments and compensation payments made by the Crown are excluded for the first 12 months following the date the young person received the payment. For more information see:
- Core Policy Ex gratia and Compensation payments
In exceptional circumstances you can disregard some of the young person's cash assets see:
- Hardship exceptional circumstances

chunks.title: Change in circumstances — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Change in circumstances
Young people must tell their service provider or Work and Income straight away of any changes in their circumstances or their family's situation that may affect their entitlement to Youth Payment. Young people are made aware of their obligations by:
- signing the Youth Payment application form or
- selecting that they agree to the obligations when they submit the online application form for Youth Payment
Examples of changes and how to deal with these can be found in Changes and reviews.

chunks.title: Change in personal resources — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Change in personal resources
Immigration New Zealand requires applicants to sign a Declaration of Personal Resources when applying for permanent residence under the following categories:
- Skilled/Business Stream and
- Family Stream
Note people do not have to sign a declaration if they are granted permanent residence under the categories of International/Humanitarian Stream which includes the:
- Refugee Family Support Category
- Pacific Access Category
- Samoan Quota Scheme
- Victims of family violence or
- various other special policies for specific countries
By signing the Declaration of Personal Resources, the client declares they are able to support themselves and family (if any) for the first two years residence in New Zealand.
The requirement for an immigrant to maintain themselves for the first two years does not mean they cannot access benefit assistance as a non-beneficiary. However, the client may not have entitlement to non-beneficiary assistance due to those resources.
For the above categories a client's permanent residence has been assessed on the following resources:
- a definite offer of employment (supported in writing)
- financial support from family members in New Zealand (supported in writing) and/or
- personal cash assets
Youth Payment on grounds of hardship is income and asset tested. To assess a client's entitlement to Youth Payment on grounds of hardship confirmation of the client's income and assets declared on application for permanent residence is required from the Immigration New Zealand. Confirmation of the client's current income and assets is also required. If there is a change in financial circumstances further investigation will need to be done to establish the client's entitlement to benefit assistance.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Absence from New Zealand
Clients receiving Youth Payment must either be:
- single or
- married, in a civil union or in a de facto relationship and not be married to or in a civil union or in a de facto relationship with a specified beneficiary
and
- undertaking youth activity obligations
## Youth Payment clients generally cannot be absent and continue to receive payment
Clients receiving Youth Payment cannot generally be absent from New Zealand and continue to receive payment of their benefit. The Government's obligation to pay income support usually stops when the client leaves New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Client with youth activity obligations or an exemption
- Permanent absence
## All clients have an obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand
All clients receiving a main benefit must advise Work and Income of any travel plans they may have before they leave New Zealand. If the client or partner does not advise Work and Income prior to their international travel, their benefit payments will stop from the day after they leave New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Obligation to advise of departure from New Zealand
## Paying a benefit while a Youth Payment client is absent from New Zealand
A client not otherwise entitled to be paid their Youth Payment may be able to continue to receive their payments for up to 28 days in a 52 week period, while they are absent from New Zealand for:
- Approved travel reasons
- Overseas for medical treatment
## Payment of benefit while absent for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Absent for more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Absences that do not prevent client from meeting obligations — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Absences that do not prevent client from meeting obligations
Generally, a client receiving Youth Payment who has youth activity obligations cannot be absent from New Zealand and continue to be paid a benefit unless:
- it is for one of (or a combination of) the permitted travel reasons or
- the travel will not prevent them from continuing to meet their youth activity obligations (eg because they are attending school and the travel is during the school holidays or they are attending a training course and the travel is during a term or semester break, and they do not need to be in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations during the travel period)
Note the Youth Service Support Unit will determine whether the young person meets the criteria to continue to be paid their benefit while they are absent from New Zealand based on a recommendation from the young person's service provider.
## Can be paid a benefit for a maximum of 28 days for reason of 'meeting obligations'
Young people receiving Youth Payment can continue to be paid a benefit for a maximum of up to 28 days in any 52 week period while they are absent from New Zealand on the grounds that the travel will not prevent them from meeting their obligations.
For example, if a Youth Payment client has already received their payment for two weeks while they were overseas because the travel did not prevent them from meeting their obligations, they will only be able to continue to receive their payment for this reason, for two additional weeks in the same 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Client meeting their youth activity obligations
- Young people who are exempt from their youth activity obligations

chunks.title: Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
These circumstances are:
- travel is required for an approved reason and, either: it is the client's first absence within 52 weeks and the permitted reason the client needs to be absent from New Zealand necessitates a period longer than 28 days orthe client has had other prior approved absences within the 52 week period and they require further approved absences which will require them to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- it is the client's first absence within 52 weeks and the permitted reason the client needs to be absent from New Zealand necessitates a period longer than 28 days or
- the client has had other prior approved absences within the 52 week period and they require further approved absences which will require them to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- the client is absent from New Zealand for an approved travel reason and their return is prevented by a new circumstance which will require them to be absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period or
- the client is travelling to receive support from a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family) who is residing overseas
For more information see:
- Paying more than 28 days for an approved reason
- Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
- Paying for more than 28 days - receive support from family member residing overseas

chunks.title: Action on return to New Zealand — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Action on return to New Zealand
You will need to look at the circumstances of the client's absence from and subsequent return to New Zealand to decide when to recommence their benefit and when to treat it as a new application.
You will need to consider the following:
- the client's intention at the time of their departure for example, did they cancel their benefit before leaving New Zealand because they did not intend to return
- did the client remain ordinarily resident during the period of absence?
- the length of time that they have been absent
- the reason for the absence
- have their circumstances changed significantly during their absence

chunks.title: Amount of income exemption — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Amount of income exemption
