When it is determined that a client is severely disabled consider if they should have all or part of their income from employment disregarded for benefit purposes.
The amount of the income exemption depends on the client's individual circumstances after considering the guidelines - for severe disablement and should be:
- a reasonable amount as an incentive to recognise the personal effort that a severely disabled person has made to participate or continue in employment
- any additional costs that a severely disabled person has incurred to participate or continue in employment
- a reasonable amount to ensure that a severely disabled person is not disadvantaged by participating or continuing in employment
Note the client may be entitled to receive other types of assistance, for example Disability Allowance for transport costs to work or employment assistance.
Fully document the decision by recording the reasons and the amount of the exemption in the CMS note template, Income exemption.
Contact Helpline if help is needed with the assessment.
For more information see:
- Effect of income on Extra Help
- Extra help

chunks.title: Approved travel reasons — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Approved travel reasons
A client receiving Youth Payment is generally not able to continue to receive their main benefit payments while they are absent from New Zealand unless they meet the criteria for approved travel. Approved travel includes:
- travel for a permitted reason
- travel where the absence will not prevent the client from continuing to meet all of their youth activity obligations
Note clients are not required to meet their youth activity obligations while absent from New Zealand for approved travel.
## Length of travel for an approved reason
Clients can travel for up to 28 days on Youth Payment for an approved travel reason. Discuss with the client the amount of time that they need to be absent from New Zealand as a result of the approved reason. The client should explain the length of their intended absence.
Consider:
- the length of time the event or reason for travel will take and
- flight availability and travel time
Remember to advise clients that generally they are only able to continue to be paid their benefit for up to 28 days in a 52 week period. This should be taken into account when deciding the approved travel period.
## Client travelling for multiple reasons
Some clients may travel overseas for an approved travel reason but elect to stay longer for another reason that does not an approved travel reason. In this case, the client can generally only receive their main benefit payments for the period of time that the approved travel reason applies to.
For more information see:
- Permitted travel reasons
- Absences that do not prevent client meeting their obligations
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy
- Travel notifications made while overseas [no link find out why] procedures
- Travel notifications made on return to New Zealand [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Avoiding a debt — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Avoiding a debt
When a single client (with no children) dies, payment generally stops from the day after the date of death. All possible steps must be taken to stop payments from this date.
When payment cannot be stopped from the day after the date of death there is discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days after the date of death. This discretion can be used to stop payment from the first available date, that is, the earliest date that payments can be stopped from after death so that no overpayment is established.
When there has been a deliberate intent to delay advising Work and Income of the client's death, payments should be stopped from the day after the date of death and an overpayment established.
Note under no circumstances can payment continue for more than 28 days after the date of death.
If the period between the date of death and the first available date to cancel payment from (to avoid creating a debt) is more than 28 days, an overpayment should be established from the 29th day after death.
## SWIFTT
Payments should be cancelled from the earliest possible date (but not more than 28 days after the date of death) in SBFTZ. However, the date of death entered in CMS must be the client's actual date of death. Full notes must be made in CMS of the actions taken.
Wherever possible the next of kin or the executor of the deceased's estate should be entered into SWIFTT.
For more information see:
- Terminal benefit for a single client

chunks.title: Backdating benefit to departure date (while still absent from New Zealand) — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Backdating benefit to departure date (while still absent from New Zealand)
A client who leave New Zealand without advising Work and Income of their travel overseas can only have their benefit backdated to the day after their departure date if they:
- have a humanitarian reason that justifies their reason for travel and their failure to tell Work and Income before they left
- contacted Work and Income as soon as they reasonably could after they departed (taking into account the circumstances of the client) and
- they meet the criteria to continue to be paid their benefit while overseas (either because they meet the criteria for approved travel, or the requirement that travel be approved does not apply to them)
For more information see:
- Humanitarian reasons for backdating to departure
- Contacting Work and Income as soon as the client reasonably can
- Approved travel reasons
- Paying a benefit when a client has not advised before departure
- Action on return to New Zealand

chunks.title: Calculating the benefit rate — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Calculating the benefit rate
SWIFTT will automatically calculate the rate of benefit payable when the client's income is added on the INCMA screen.
If income is declared late it may be appropriate to complete a back dated review SBDR. SWIFTT will prompt staff when a back dated review is required. Check SRAUI to determine the period the review is required for.
The Income Assessment tab in DREW can be used to estimate the benefit rate with income for the client.
Note income must be rounded down to the nearest dollar.
For more information see:
- Example of income assessment
- Recording income
- Income for a past period

chunks.title: Calculating the period of absence — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Calculating the period of absence
The period of an absence from New Zealand for which payment of Youth Payment can continue (if approved) is up to 28 consecutive days, that is, Saturdays and Sundays are included.
In all cases, when assessing the period of absence do not include:
- the date of departure from New Zealand and
- the date of return to New Zealand
If a client is absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period the benefit should be suspended from the 29th day (unless they meet the criteria to pay for longer than 28 days).
Note if a client is leaving New Zealand permanently, the benefit must be cancelled from the day after departure.

chunks.title: Change in age — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Change in age
Generally when a young person turns 18 years old the Youth Payment should stop. However there are 2 situations where the payment can continue to be paid after they turn 18 years old. These are where a young person:
- must receive Youth Payment for a minimum of 6 months and cannot receive another main benefit (excluding Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability) until after this period
- chooses to continue to receive Youth Payment if they remain in education, training, or work-based learning
For more information see:
- Must receive payment for six months
- Chooses to remain on Youth Payment past 18 years of age

chunks.title: Change of activity — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Change of activity
If a Youth Payment client has changed their education, training or work-based learning activity it is important to update their record in both SWIFTT, and ART.
The activity code in SDT1A must be updated with the new activity code to reflect the activity that the young person is undertaking:
- Training
- Enrolled secondary education
- Enrolled in tertiary education
- Work-based learning
When you change the activity code in the SDT1A screen in SWIFTT you must also complete a benefit reassessment using the SPBR screen with the reason for reassessment code 340.
Note that if you do not complete the reassessment using the reason code 340, the benefit will expire from the beginning of the next pay period.
If the client has stopped doing an activity then you need to consider whether a sanction should be imposed.
## Example
A client was granted Youth Payment because they were enrolled full time in a course of secondary education. They have since left school and are now participating in a training course.
You will need to complete the following actions in SWIFTT:
- change the activity code in the SDT1A screen from 3 to 2 and add the course end date and add details into the 'training course type' field
- complete a benefit reassessment in the SPBR screen using the reason for reassessment code 340
For more information see:
- Youth activity obligations
- Activity obligations failures

chunks.title: Change of address — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Change of address
When a client advises that they have changed their address it is important to check that the move does not affect their entitlement to Youth Payment.
You will need to check the reasons for the move and ensure that they are still meeting all the qualifications for Youth Payment, and their youth activity obligations.
## Young person returns to live with their parents
If a single young person has returned to live with their parents they will no longer be entitled to Youth Payment and it should be cancelled.
Note the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service will need to update the address in ART and YSSU will need to update the address in CMS.
If the client is receiving Extra Help, this will also need to be reviewed by YSSU.
For more information see:
- Change of activity
- Returns to live with parents
- Core policy Relationship status for benefit

chunks.title: Changes and reviews — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Changes and reviews
A young person is obliged to advise their service provider or Work and Income of any changes in their circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Youth Payment.
A benefit may also be reviewed at any time to ensure that the client still meets the qualifications and is receiving the correct rate of payment.
A change in a client's circumstances may also mean that the client qualifies for another benefit.
## Youth Service Support Unit (YSSU) role
The Youth Service Support Unit (YSSU) is responsible for making decisions on behalf of Work and Income and for the general administration of the Youth Payment.
## Service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service role
The service provider or the Work and Income 'in-house' service work closely with the YSSU and will make recommendations to assist the YSSU to make decisions by:
- keeping the young person's information up to date in the Activity Reporting Tool (ART)
- notifying YSSU immediately of any change in the young person's circumstances that may affect their entitlement to Youth Payment or any Extra Help

chunks.title: Chooses to remain on Youth Payment past 18 years of age — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Chooses to remain on Youth Payment past 18 years of age
Generally, when a young person turns 18 years old the Youth Payment should stop. However, to give a young person a chance to complete the qualification they have started while on Youth Payment, a young person can choose to continue to receive Youth Payment after they turn 18 years of age if they remain in education, training or work-based learning.
## Attending secondary education
When a young person reaches the age of 18 years and is attending secondary school their Youth Payment will continue to be paid until the following 31 March. For example a young person attending school who turns 18 years old in June will continue in the Youth Service until the following 31 March.
## Attending tertiary education, training or work-based learning
When a young person is attending tertiary education, training or work-based learning and they turn 18 years old, their Youth Payment may continue to be paid until their course finishes, unless their course ends in December. If their course ends in December, their Youth Payment will continue to be paid until 31 March the following year.
Examples:
- a young person is part way through a training course when they turn 18 years old. The training course finishes on 20 November. The young person will be exited from the Youth Service on 21 November.
- a young person is part way through a training course when they turn 18 years old. The training course finishes on 20 December. The young person will continue to receive their Youth Payment and remain in the Youth Service until the following 31 March.
For more information see:
- Must receive payment for six months

chunks.title: Surviving partner — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Surviving partner
When a client dies (and there is a surviving partner) before a decision is made on an application or review for Youth Payment, the application or review process can be continued as if the client had not died.
## Single client
When there is no surviving partner the benefit application should generally be declined. However, if there is a request for the application to be decided or the circumstances of the situation merit it, consult your manager client service delivery for a decision.
## Funeral Grant
In situations when the decision to grant or review Youth Payment is made after the date of death of the client, any Funeral Grant can be decided as if the deceased client were getting a Youth Payment.

chunks.title: Client donates a kidney or liver tissue — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Client donates a kidney or liver tissue
When a young person is donating a kidney or liver tissue they can keep getting their Youth Payments.
Exempt the young person from undertaking or being available for education, training or work-based learning during their recovery period.
Grant the exemption 'Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability'.
The exemption should be entered in the SWTDA screen.
The exemption starts from the date of the operation and can continue while the young person:
- is recovering from their operation and
- they cannot meet their obligation to attend education, training or work-based learning full-time
This exemption must not be for more than 12 weeks.
## Young person has an obligations failure
If the young person currently has an activity obligation in progress or 'fails their activity obligations', donating a kidney or liver tissue is a 'good and sufficient reason'.
Overturn the activity obligations failure in OBMAN. This will remove the failure from the client’s 12 month obligation failure count and there is no sanction.
For more information see:

chunks.title: Examples (but are not limited to) — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Examples (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A client receiving Youth Payment who was enrolled in secondary school was out of New Zealand visiting his father in Australia. His Youth Payment was suspended the day after he left New Zealand as it wasn't an approved travel reason. This is because the travel took place in the middle of the school term and therefore it prevented the client from meeting his obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning.
The client contacts Work and Income three days later to say that his father is in hospital as he has had a heart attack. The client has been paid for five days in the previous 52 weeks while he was absent from New Zealand leaving a balance of 23 days.
The reason for travel now meets the criteria for approved travel. The benefit is resumed from the date the client became eligible to receive the benefit overseas. The client must contact Work and Income from overseas. The benefit cannot be back-dated if the client advises Work and Income when they return to New Zealand.
A client receiving Youth Payment who is attending a full-time training course left New Zealand to visit her mother during the term break.
The client continued to receive her payment while overseas on the grounds that the travel did not prevent her from meeting her obligations. Two days before she was due to return, her mother's house burnt down. The client has been paid for 20 days in the previous 52 weeks while she was absent from New Zealand leaving a balance of eight days.
The reason for travel has changed and the client has not been absent from New Zealand for up to 28 days in any 52 week period. The benefit expiry is extended for an additional five days.
Note that where the client has already been absent for 28 days in a 52 week period, consider whether the client meets the criteria for receiving a payment for more than 28 days in any 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Client meeting their youth activity obligations — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Client meeting their youth activity obligations
A client receiving Youth Payment can continue to be paid a benefit while they are absent from New Zealand for any reason if:
- the travel will not prevent them from continuing to meet their youth activity obligations (eg because they are attending school and the travel is during the school holidays or they are attending a training course and the travel is during a term or semester break, and they do not need to be in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations during the travel period)
## Examples include (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A young person is meeting their education obligation by attending secondary school and they wish to holiday in Australia during the school holidays. The client is not required by their Service Provider to undertake a budgeting course or attend any meetings with them during the period they wish to travel.
The travel will not prevent the client from meeting any of their youth activity obligations so it will be approved. The young person can be absent from New Zealand and continue to receive their payment for up to 28 days in any 52 week period.
A young person is meeting their education obligation by participating in a full time training course and decides to take time off from the course in the middle of the term so that they can holiday in Australia.
The travel will not be approved as it will prevent the young person from meeting their obligation to be in full-time education or training.
A young person is enrolled in a full-time training course, however, the course has not yet started, and the young person wishes to travel to the United States for a holiday before the course commencement date. The young person does not have to be in New Zealand to meet any other obligations during the travel period (eg they do not have to attend a budgeting course during the time of the travel)
The travel will not prevent the client from meeting any of their youth activity obligations so it will be approved. The young person can continue to receive their payment for up to 28 days in any 52 week period while they are absent from New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Young people who are exempt from their youth activity obligations

chunks.title: Examples include (but are not limited to) — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Examples include (but are not limited to)
Client situation
Outcome
A client receiving Youth Payment left New Zealand for a holiday in Australia, and is continuing to receive their payment on the grounds that the travel is not preventing them from meeting their obligations.
While the client was in Australia there was severe flooding which meant they could not return to New Zealand on the day they were meant to return.
The client contacts Work and Income. The client has been paid for 20 days in the previous 52 weeks while she was absent from New Zealand, leaving a balance of eight days.
The client cannot return due to circumstances that were not reasonably foreseeable and that were outside the client's control. Work and Income would extend the client's benefit for a reasonable period to allow the client to return.
Also consider whether there is any grounds to pay for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
A client receiving Youth Payment has been overseas for five days to attend his father's funeral. He is delayed in Sydney due to fog. He must remain a further three days.
The client cannot return due to circumstances that were not reasonably foreseeable and that were outside his control.
Work and Income would extend the client's benefit for a reasonable period for him to be able to return. Also consider whether there is any grounds to pay for more than 28 days in a 52 week period.
For more information see:
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period

chunks.title: Client obtains employment overseas — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Client obtains employment overseas
Where the client:
- is successful in their job prospect or job search overseas and
- they are not returning to New Zealand
the Youth Payment should be cancelled from the day after the notice of job appointment.
If the client returns to New Zealand for the period between getting the job and actually starting employment, the Youth Payment can be continued until they leave the country. The benefit must be cancelled from the day after they leave New Zealand to commence the job.

chunks.title: Client with youth activity obligations — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Client with youth activity obligations
A client receiving Youth Payment cannot continue to receive their payment when they temporarily leave New Zealand unless they meet the criteria for approved travel.
Where they meet the criteria for approved travel they can continue to receive their payment for a period of up to 28 days in any 52 week period if:
- the benefit would continue to be paid except for them having left New Zealand
- the absences do not affect the client's eligibility for the benefit
- they have notified Work and Income of their intention to temporarily leave New Zealand
For more information see:
- Client meeting their youth activity obligations
- Young people who are exempt from their youth activity obligations
- Approved travel reasons

chunks.title: Clients with a partner — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Clients with a partner
When a married, civil union or de facto client is imprisoned their Youth Payment will generally need to be cancelled.
Note clients who are married, in a civil union or in a de facto relationship qualify for Youth Payment in their own right. If either of the couple is imprisoned, the other person can continue to receive their own Youth Payment.
The Youth Payment of the client in prison should be cancelled from the day after imprisonment.
## Exception
Where a client is imprisoned and they have a partner, there is discretion to continue payment of the client's Youth Payment in some circumstances.
There is discretion to pay all or part of the imprisoned client's Youth Payment to the person who has not been imprisoned. This will depend on the length of time imprisoned.
There is also discretion to continue payment if the client is remanded in custody pending a further court appearance.
For more information to help you decide these cases see:
- Youth activity obligations
- Decision guidelines - clients with a partner
- SWIFTT process to pay a partner
- Remanded in custody

chunks.title: Contacting Work and Income as soon as the client reasonably can — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Contacting Work and Income as soon as the client reasonably can
A client who leaves New Zealand without advising Work and Income of their travel can only have their benefit backdated to the day after their departure date if they contact Work and Income as soon as they reasonably could have been expected to, given their circumstances.
This may be while the client is still absent from New Zealand, or once they have returned.
For more information see:
- Backdating benefit to departure date

chunks.title: Death of a client — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Death of a client
The date benefit payment stops following the death of a client, depends on whether the client has a dependent partner.
Note when a client has a Community Services or SuperGold Card, the card must be manually cancelled and death details added to the Person Details latch in CMS.
Contact the Card Centre on 0800 999 999 or email to request cancellation of the card.

chunks.title: Death of a married, civil union or de facto client — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Death of a married, civil union or de facto client
Continue to pay Youth Payment for 28 days following the death of a client when there is a surviving partner.
The continuation of payment beyond the date of death is referred to as Terminal Benefit. Where the benefit is being paid to a couple, both the deceased client and the surviving partner's portion of the benefit should be paid. The total benefit, including the partner's portion and any Extra help can continue for 28 days.
## Exception
When the death of the client was the result of an accident, entitlement to a lump sum Accident Compensation payment needs to be decided before terminal benefit can be paid.
If the partner is entitled to a survivors grant from the Accident Compensation Corporation there is no entitlement to Youth Payment beyond the date of death.
When benefit payment has continued beyond the date of death, an overpayment should be established and recovery of the debt should be sought from the estate.

chunks.title: Death of a single client — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Death of a single client
When a single client (with no children) dies, payment generally stops from the day after the date of death, but there is some discretion to continue payment for up to 28 days.
Payment should stop from the first available date if we have been notified within 28 days of the date of death. This will avoid creating a debt.
When there are other circumstances that justify payment of terminal benefit, payment should continue for the full 28 days after death.
For more information see:
- Avoiding a debt
- Terminal benefit for a single client

chunks.title: Decision guidelines - clients with a partner — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Decision guidelines - clients with a partner
While Youth Payment should generally be stopped when the client is imprisoned, there is discretion for their payment to be continued and paid to the partner not in prison.
This discretion allows payment of all or part of the client's Youth Payment to their partner.
The full married, civil union or de facto rate can be paid if this is warranted after having regard to the particular circumstances of the client and their partner.
To help decide whether it is reasonable to pay the client's Youth Payment to the partner while the client is in prison, and the rate to pay, consider the following:
- has the period in prison already passed
- is the client due to be released from prison shortly
- is the likely period in prison less than 6 months
- do they intend to live together when the partner is released
- has the partner in prison applied for Home Detention
- are there exceptional circumstances that warrant paying the full married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit to the partner who is not in prison
For further help contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances before you make your decision.
For more information see:
- SWIFTT process to pay a partner

chunks.title: Definition of 'support' from a family member residing overseas — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Definition of 'support' from a family member residing overseas
'Support' means assistance that the young person could not reasonably obtain from a family member in New Zealand, and includes (but is not limited to):
- emotional support
- educational support
- mentoring/guidance
- any other assistance that is beneficial to the welfare of the young person
Note in assessing whether the young person could not reasonably obtain the support from a family member in New Zealand, you should consider:
- the type and nature of the relationship with the family member residing overseas
- whether there are features of the young person's relationship with that family member that are absent from their relationships with other family members residing in New Zealand (such as shared experiences and the nature of the relationship).

chunks.title: Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital
When person who has been remanded in custody, or is serving a term of imprisonment is detained in or transferred to a psychiatric hospital you may be able to pay an Emergency Benefit at the hospital rate.
People who are remanded in custody or serving a term of imprisonment who are temporarily hospitalised for treatment of an injury or illness are still considered to be in prison and the Department of Corrections will meet their costs. An Emergency Benefit or any other financial assistance cannot be paid.
For more information see:
- Emergency Benefit Person serving their sentence of imprisonment in a psychiatric hospital
- Release from prison

chunks.title: Discharge from hospital — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Discharge from hospital
Where a client is receiving the hospital rate and they are discharged from hospital:
- increase their benefit to the appropriate full rate from the date of discharge
- for married, civil union or de facto clients (where appropriate) reduce the partner's benefit to the half married, civil union or de facto rate and suspend Special Disability Allowance and
- review any Extra Help from the same date
Note the dates of admission and discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital.

chunks.title: Effect of income on Extra help — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Effect of income on Extra help
When income is added or changed you will also need to review any Extra help the client may be receiving.
Some Extra help is not income tested such as Child Disability Allowance, Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment or Winter Energy Payment. It is the client's obligation to advise Work and Income of any changes in their circumstances.
Income is charged against Temporary Additional Support and Childcare Subsidy.
For more information see:
- Income change
- Childcare Subsidy Chargeable income
- Temporary Additional Support Chargeable income
- Extra help

chunks.title: Accommodation Supplement — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Accommodation Supplement
For a single client stop the Accommodation Supplement from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation. Check whether the client still has to meet their continuing accommodation costs. If so, increase the benefit rate above the hospital rate to meet the costs.
For a married, civil union or de facto client (without dependent children), still treat the couple as married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and take into account the income and assets of both. The full Accommodation Supplement can be paid to the partner not in hospital.
For more information see:
- Accommodation Supplement
## Temporary Additional Support
For a single client stop Temporary Additional Support from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation. Check whether the client still has to meet their continuing costs. If so, increase the benefit rate above the hospital rate to meet the costs.
For a married, civil union or de facto couple Temporary Additional Support must be stopped from the beginning of the 14th week of hospitalisation for the client who is in hospital. From the same date YSSU will need to review Temporary Additional Support and pay the full amount to the partner not in hospital.
No additional costs associated with the hospitalisation should be added to Temporary Additional Support for a married, civil union or de facto client. However, have regard to their individual circumstances taking into consideration that the partner not in hospital is increased to the single rate of payment and can receive Special Disability Allowance to cover any extra costs.
## Winter Energy Payment
For a single client who is getting the Winter Energy Payment and who has had their main benefit reduced to the hospital rate, they can only get the Winter Energy Payment if they still require assistance with their energy costs.
Where a partner is in hospital (no dependent children) the client who is still living in the community can receive the full couple rate of the Winter Energy Payment.
For more information see:
- Winter Energy Payment Hospitalisation

chunks.title: Essential travel — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Essential travel
Clients will sometimes have to travel outside of New Zealand to attend a significant event relating to a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family).
These events are ones which the client would reasonably be expected to attend. That is, the travel is essential to them and where not attending the event would cause the person emotional distress. This may include, but is not limited to, travel that allows the client to:
- be with a seriously ill or dying person who is a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family)
- attend a funeral or an unveiling in relation to a family member
- pay respect to a family member of the deceased in the event of the client missing the funeral
- attend to legal matters in relation to the affairs of the deceased family member
- attend a birth of a family member or be with a family member around the time of their giving birth
- provide support to a party or witness to a court case
- attend a wedding of a family member - the client does not need to be a member of the bridal party or play a significant part in the wedding in order for the payment of benefit to continue while they are absent from New Zealand
- travel for a court ordered custody arrangement
For more information see:
- Absent from New Zealand more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Definition of family member
- Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect
- Permitted travel reasons
- Absences that do not prevent the client meeting their obligations
- Paying benefit when client failed to advise of absence
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within a 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Estimated income — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Estimated income
Clients must advise Work and Income of any change in their circumstances that affects their entitlement or rate of Youth Payment, such as commencing employment.
Where the client has one-off, fluctuating or casual income, it may be necessary to estimate their earnings to prevent a debt. When the client under or over estimates their income they should confirm the actual amount earned as soon as possible.
If the actual income is different this should be charged against the Youth Payment for the week it was earned or the period that it represents.
This may result in arrears or a debt for the client.
For more information about income, see:
- Income change
- Calculating the benefit rate
- Income for a past period
For information about debt recovery, see:
- Debt treatment [no link find out why] procedures

chunks.title: Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: The following examples show situations where we may pay a benefit for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. Please note this list is not exhaustive. Client's reason for travelling for 28 days within 52 week period Client's current reason for travel within 52 week period Outcome Essential travel reasons Essential travel reason eg a seriously ill family member Generally consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if reasonable in the circumstances Job interview or job prospect Essential travel reason eg a funeral Generally would consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if reasonable in the circumstances Youth Payment client to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with their youth activity obligations. The client wishes to be absent from New Zealand for another general holiday This is not an approved reason for paying for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. The client would not be able to receive a benefit while absent from New Zealand for this reason even if the travel will not prevent them meeting their obligations (eg the travel is at a time when they are not required to be in education, training or work-based learning or in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations) Youth Payment client to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with their youth activity obligations. To provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster or similar adverse event. Generally would allow further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. This is an unforeseen event and it is reasonable for them to help their family member. Youth Payment client to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with their youth activity obligations. Essential travel reason Generally would consider allowing further period of payment while absent for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, if the essential travel reason was unforeseen. Youth Payment client to travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with their youth activity obligations. Needs to attend a wedding of a family member. Generally would not consider allowing a further period of payment for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. Weddings are usually known about in advance and this should have been planned for when they used the 28 days to go on holiday. However, where the wedding is genuinely unforeseen, consideration could be given to allowing travel for a period of more than 28 days in a 52 week period.

chunks.title: Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: Youth Payment client had to spend four days at a funeral overseas. The client had booked a holiday prior to the attendance at the funeral overseas. This holiday was booked for 28 days because they are able travel for any reason if the travel will not interfere with their obligations. The client does not have the full 28 days left Travelling for a general holiday is not an approved reason for paying a benefit for more than 28 days in a 52 week period The benefit will only be paid for the number of days the client has available (that is, 24 days).

chunks.title: Example 1 — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: Carlos contacts MSD on 19 November to advise that he has returned from travelling to Malaysia to be with his dying mother. He left in a hurry and didn't contact MSD before his departure. His Youth Payment stopped on 4 November, the day after he left the country. He returned to New Zealand on 14 November, but then had to organise a New Zealand-based funeral for his mother, as a large number of people are based in New Zealand. Carlos didn't advise MSD of his travel before leaving New Zealand, but he has a humanitarian reason that justifies his travel and the reason he didn't contact MSD before he left. Given Carlos' circumstances, he contacted MSD as soon as it would have been reasonable to expect him to and he meets the criteria for an approved travel reason. Carlos' Youth Payment can be backdated to 4 November.

chunks.title: Example 2 — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: Sanjay left New Zealand for India on 7 December because his father had become suddenly seriously ill and been hospitalised. While in India, Sanjay's father passed away and Sanjay stayed in India for the funeral. Sanjay returned on 16 December, after staying for 2 weeks for the Hindu funeral and mourning period. On 19 December, Sanjay contacts MSD to explain that he has been overseas after learning of his father's illness, and that he stayed for the funeral. On return, Sanjay spent time mourning with his own family and has been distraught. He explains that he only realised last night that he had not informed MSD or his Youth Service provider of his absence. Sanjay's reason for leaving New Zealand is a humanitarian reason and he meets the criteria for backdating his payment to the day after his departure. Given Sanjay's circumstances, he informed MSD as soon as he reasonably could. Sanjay's Youth Payment can be backdated to 8 December, the date it was suspended.

chunks.title: Example 3 — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: Tuslia calls MSD on 5 October to tell them she will leave New Zealand on 7 October to help her sister, who just lost her house in a flood. When asked how long she will be gone for, Tusila says that she hasn't bought a return ticket yet and was considering staying on to catch up with family and see how her sister is going. MSD informs Tusila that she can only keep getting her Youth Payment if she is absent for essential travel. Helping her sister after a flood is considered essential travel, however if she is going to stay longer for a holiday, she won't be able to get Youth Payment during the time she is on holiday. Tusila returns to MSD the next day with an airline quote showing that the cheapest return flight is on 14 October. She thinks it will take her a week to ensure her sister has sorted out insurance, medium-term accommodation, and access to basic goods like clothing and food. She has decided not to stay on for the holiday. MSD agrees this is reasonable and tells Tusila that she can keep getting Youth Payment from 7 to 14 October while she is overseas helping her sister.

chunks.title: Example 4 — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: Christy is getting Youth Payment and contacts MSD to advise that her sister is getting married in Australia on 8 September. Christy is going to Australia to her sister's wedding but intends to stay on for a further 2 weeks to visit other family. Her stay isn't during a study break and she will have to miss some of her course. Christy is leaving New Zealand on 4 September as she has to help her sister prepare. She will stay until10 September. Christy then begins the holiday leg of her trip, returning to New Zealand on 25 September. Christy's travel is divided as follows: - 5 September to 10 September period meets the essential travel criteria - 11 September to 24 September period is considered other travel (holiday), is not during Christy's school holidays, and does not meet the essential travel criteria. Christy's Youth Payment can only be paid until 10 September, for the period that meets the essential travel criteria.

chunks.title: Example 5 — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: Bill left New Zealand on 10 October during the school term to help his brother in Palmerston, a remote island in the Cook Islands, after his brother lost his house in a fire. He returns to New Zealand on 31 October. A week later, on 7 November he attends an appointment and asks his Youth Service provider why his Youth Payments have stopped. His Youth Service provider informs him his payments stopped when he left the country and asks why he didn't contact MSD or the provider sooner. Bill explains that he left in a hurry and he wasn't able to contact MSD while away as he couldn't access a computer. When he got back he started going to school again but forgot about contacting MSD. He only remembered when his landlord asked him about rent. His provider tells him that because he didn't contact MSD or his provider as soon as he reasonably could have been expected to (i.e. once he had helped his brother), his payment can only be backdated to 31 October, the date he got back to New Zealand.

chunks.title: Example 1 — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Example 1
A client applies for 10 days to be absent from New Zealand. In the past 52 weeks the client had 10 days absence from New Zealand and continued being paid their benefit.
Step
Calculation
Identify the day after the client is intending to leave New Zealand.
14 September 2019
Count back 52 weeks from this date.
15 September 2018
Count the number of days the client continued getting their benefit while they were overseas in this 52 week period.
Days client has continued to receive their benefit while absent from NZ between 14 September 2018 and 15 September 2019 = 10 days.
Subtract the number of days the client was paid their benefit while absent from New Zealand from 28 days.
28 - 10 days = 18 days available.
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay the client for the days they have available.
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay them for the 10 days they are out of the country.
## Example 2
A client applies for 10 days to be absent from New Zealand. In the past 52 weeks the client had 20 days absence from New Zealand and continued being paid their benefit.
Step
Calculation
Identify the day after the client is intending to leave New Zealand.
14 September 2019
Count back 52 weeks from this date.
15 September 2018
Count the number of days the client has continued to receive their benefit while they were overseas in this 52 week period.
Days client continued getting their benefit while absent from New Zealand between 14 September 2018 and 15 September 2019 = 20 days.
Subtract the number of days the client has received their benefit while absent from New Zealand from 28 days.
28 - 20 days = 8 days available.
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay the client for the days they have available.
If the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit while overseas, pay them for the 8 days they are out of the country. For 2 of the days they are absent from New Zealand they will not get their payments.
Check if the client meets the criteria to be paid their benefit for more than 28 days in a 52 week period - if they meet these criteria, they may be able to continue being paid for the additional 2 days of absence.

chunks.title: Examples of job interviews and prospects overseas — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: A client advises they are heading to the Gold Coast to 'look for work' and undertake job search. They do not have a job interview or a specific job prospect they are following up on. Their aim is to undertake general job search and go and see a few employers which they will find when they get there. The provision cannot be used to allow general job search overseas. The client will not be able to continue to receive payment if they are absent from New Zealand for this reason.

chunks.title: Examples (but are not limited to) — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: Client's previous reason for travel 28 days of travel within the 52 week period Client's current reason for travel within 52 week period Outcome A Youth Payment client who is attending school continued to receive their payment while they went to Australia for a two week holiday during the school holidays on the grounds that this travel did not prevent them from meeting their obligations. Following this, they continued to receive their payment while they travelled to Australia in the same year for a further two weeks to visit their uncle while he was seriously ill and to attend his funeral. As a result, the young person has already received their payment while travelling overseas for 28 days in a 52 week period. The young person's relationship with their parents has broken down. The young person has an aunt is the United States whom they are very close to and who provides them with guidance and support. The young person does not have any family members in New Zealand that provide them with the type of support they can obtain from their aunt. The young person wishes to travel to the United States during the school holidays to visit their aunt. The travel is during a time when the young person is not required to be in New Zealand to meet any other obligations (e.g. it is at a time when they are not required to attend a budgeting course). Generally would consider allowing the young person to receive their payment for a maximum of two weeks while they travel overseas to visit their aunt. The maximum amount of time that a young person can receive their payment on the grounds that the travel will not prevent them from meeting their obligations is 28 days. Therefore, the maximum amount of time this young person can continue to receive their payment while they visit their aunty to obtain support is two weeks as they have already received their payment for two weeks when they went to Australia for a holiday earlier in the year. A Youth Payment client who is attending a training course continued to receive their payments while they travelled to Australia to holiday with friends for 28 days, on the grounds that this travel did not prevent them from meeting their obligations. The young person wishes to travel to Australia for a week during the semester break to visit their grandmother who provides them with support and guidance. The young person's grandmother is their closest relative and they do not have any family members in New Zealand who can offer them the type of support they get from their grandmother.

chunks.title: Examples (but are not limited to) — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: The travel will be during a time when the young person is not required to be in New Zealand to meet any other obligations (e.g. it is at a time when they are not required to attend a budgeting course). The young person has already received their payment while they travelled overseas for a total of 28 days in a 52 week period on the grounds that the travel did not prevent them from meeting their obligations. As a result, they are not permitted to receive their payment for a further period of overseas travel to obtain support from a family member residing overseas. They would only be permitted to receive their payment for a further period of overseas travel if they met one of the other circumstances for paying a benefit from more than 28 days in 52 weeks. A Youth Payment client continued to receive their payments while they travelled overseas to attend the funeral of a family member, the wedding of another family member and a court case that they were required to attend as a witness. The total period of time the young person has received their payments while they travelled overseas for these reasons is 28 days in a 52 week period. The young person has a brother in Australia whom they are very close to and who provides them with support and mentoring. The young person does not have any family members is New Zealand who can offer them the type of support that they get from their brother. The young person is attending a training course and wishes to travel to Australia to visit their brother during the semester break. The travel will be during a time when the young person is not required to be in New Zealand to meet any other obligations (e.g. it is at a time when they are not required to attend a budgeting course). Generally would consider paying the young person while they travel to visit their brother to obtain support for a maximum of 28 days. This is because the young person has not yet travelled in the last 52 weeks on the grounds that the travel did not prevent them from meeting their obligations.

chunks.title: Exemption for severe disablement — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Exemption for severe disablement
As an incentive for the personal effort of a severely disabled person to participate or continue in employment, discretion can be used to disregard all or part of any income earned from employment as chargeable income for benefit purposes.
Consideration for this special income exemption should be given to clients with a severe disability who are extremely limited in their ability to participate in employment, the community and take care of themselves.
Consider whether or not the client is severely disabled. The Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement will help.
Each case should be assessed on an individual basis.
If the client is severely disabled consider whether or not to disregard all or part of any income earned by the client. To help with this, see: Amount of income exemption.
Note clients who are not severely disabled cannot receive this exemption.
For more information see:
- Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement
- Amount of income exemption

chunks.title: Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Guidelines - exemption for severe disablement
A special income exemption for severe disablement may be given to a client as an incentive for their personal effort to participate or continue in employment.
To help decide if a person is severely disabled consider the following:
- Does the client have to put in more effort in order to participate in employment? (for example, they may take a considerably long time to get ready in the morning or a longer time to travel to their place of employment)?
- Is the client's capacity to earn the same wage as a person without a severe disability reduced because of their disability (for example, does the client work reduced hours or receive less money for the job they undertake because of their disability)?
- Does the client have additional expenses to undertake employment (for example additional transport or equipment costs)?
- Does the client have difficulties participating in employment or completing their tasks because of their disability (for example, they may experience difficulties with mobility around the work place, be limited in the tasks they undertake or on occasion may not complete their work duties)?
- Does the client require assistance from another person to carry out some of their daily tasks (for example, washing, dressing or cooking)?
- Does the client require the assistance from another person to travel to work or to ensure their physical safety while at work (for example, does the client have difficulty using public transport)?
- Any other relevant factors that should be considered.
If the client answers 'yes' to one or more of these questions you will have to decide if the client is severely disabled or if you need further information to make this decision.
Contact Helpline if you need help with the assessment.
For more information see:
- Amount of income exemption
- Exemption for severe disablement

chunks.title: Guidelines for paying a higher rate — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Guidelines for paying a higher rate
Payment can be increased above the hospital rate to a rate that (together with the client's other income) will be sufficient to meet the client's continuing commitments.
Use the following guidelines to assess whether the client's rate should be higher.
1. Have the client complete an Increased payment while you are in hospital form.
2. Accept stated expenses where they appear reasonable, but ask for proof if there is doubt.
3. If a client is married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, do not include home outgoings or accommodation expenses. These are the responsibility of the partner not in hospital. (The partner may qualify for Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support.)
4. Check that all possible action has been taken to reduce expenses. For example, giving up the lease on a flat where the hospital stay is indefinite.
5. If the increase in payment request is for one-off items such as clothing, you can pay the increase by:
- a backdated review of the benefit rate to create a lump sum payment or
- increasing the benefit rate for a limited time

chunks.title: Partner — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Partner
When the partner of a person in prison has been receiving a benefit, this will be reviewed from the date of release.
For more information see:
- Youth Payment Court imposed conditions
- Youth Payment Transfer between benefits
- Release from prison

chunks.title: Hospitalisation — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Hospitalisation
When a client getting Youth Payment is admitted to hospital, their benefit can continue at the full rate for the first 13 weeks.
The rate of payment will need to be reduced to the hospital rate after the client has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks (not after getting a benefit for 13 weeks).
If a client is in hospital they may be exempt from meeting their youth activity obligations.
## Hospital rate
The hospital rate allows for the cost of personal items, which patients are expected to provide for themselves. The weekly hospital rate is $58.34 net (as at 1 April 2026).
YSSU can pay an amount above the hospital rate where there are financial circumstances to warrant paying at a higher rate.
Note you cannot pay an amount less than the hospital rate.

chunks.title: Humanitarian reasons for backdating to departure — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Humanitarian reasons for backdating to departure
Where a client does not advise of their departure from New Zealand before they go, they may be able to have their benefit paid from the day after their departure date if the client has a humanitarian reason that justifies their reason for travel and their failure to tell Work and Income before they left.
Humanitarian reasons are:
- to provide aid or assistance to a family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member) immediately following a natural disaster (for example, flood, earthquake, bush fires) or similar adverse event (eg house fire)
- to be with a suddenly seriously ill, or dying family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member)
- to attend the sudden funeral of a family member (or a person to whom they have a relationship similar to a family member)
For more information see:
- Client not returned due to unforeseeable event (within 28 day maximum)
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Imprisonment — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Imprisonment
When a Youth Payment client is imprisoned or detained in custody they are no longer entitled to receive Youth Payment.
The Youth Payment should stop from the day following the date of imprisonment.
YSSU will need to decide whether to suspend or cancel the benefit after having regard to the likely period in prison and whether the client has a partner and/or dependent children.
If the period in prison has already passed, and the client is still meeting their youth activity obligations, the Youth Payment can be suspended for the period in prison using the SBDR screen in SWIFTT.
For more information see:
- Youth activity obligations
- Definition of imprisonment
- Single clients
- Clients with a partner
- Home detention
- Release from prison
- Release on bail
- Remanded in custody
- Detention in or transfer to a psychiatric hospital

chunks.title: Example 1 — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Example 1
A client getting Youth Payment has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks.
This client has other income which reduces the main benefit rate to $20 per week.
In this case pay the $20.00 per week rate, which is lower than the hospital rate of $58.34 (as at 1 April 2026).
## Example 2
A client getting Youth Payment has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks.
This client has other income which reduces the main benefit rate to $70 per week.
In this case pay the hospital rate of $58.34 per week (as at 1 April 2026) which is the lower rate.

chunks.title: Income change — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Income change
Clients must advise of any change in circumstances that affects their entitlement or rate of benefit payable, such as when they earn and receive income. Any income the Youth Payment client (or their partner) receives should be charged against the benefit for the week(s) in which the income was earned or represents.
Where a client has fluctuating or casual income, income is charged on a week by week basis. For the week they work income is charged, and for the week without work 'nil' income is charged.
In all cases the client must still qualify for Youth Payment. Any Extra help the client receives must also be reassessed each time there is a change in the client's income.
## Deductions or redirections
When adding income to a client's record, check that there is enough benefit to cover any deductions or redirections. Any deductions or redirections may need to be reduced depending on the amount of benefit due.
For more information see:
- Deductions
When adding income to a client's record, consider:
- if the client has estimated income
- the period over which to charge income
- income from employment
- if the income is for a past period
- if the income is for a previous tax year
- if the client's income stops
- if the income reduces the benefit to a nil rate

chunks.title: Income for a past period — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Income for a past period
Where a client declares income for a past period and there is either no income or a different amount entered on INCMH, the client's Youth Payment must be reviewed.
Income must be charged against the Youth Payment for the week in which the income is earned or the period that it represents.
## Example
A client phones on 22/04/2015 and advises that they received $220 gross income for one week's work for the period 06/04/2015 to 12/04/2015.
The client has been overpaid their Youth Payment as there is no income on their SWIFTT record. A debt must be established for the overpayment of benefit for the week 06/04/2015 to 12/04/2015.
The following is the process:
INCMA
add 00.00 effective from Monday 13/04/2015
INCMA
add $220.00 effective from Monday 06/04/2015 - a backdated review will be required
SBDR
complete a back dated review using the abated benefit rate for the week 06/04/2015 to 12/04/2015
SWIFTT
debt established for the period 06/04/2015 to 12/04/2015

chunks.title: Income from employment — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Income from employment
Clients must advise their service provider or Work and Income of any change in their circumstances that affects their entitlement or rate of Youth Payment, such as commencing employment.
## Full-time employment
If the client has commenced full-time employment, the Youth Payment must be stopped from the date the client commences work as they will no longer be entitled to receive the Youth Payment because they will not be able to meet their youth activity obligations.
If the partner has commenced full-time employment, then their Youth Payment must be stopped from the date they commenced work. They will no longer be entitled to receive the Youth Payment because they will not be able to meet their youth activity obligations.
## Part-time employment
A young person can receive Youth Payment while they are working part-time as long as they can meet:
- the qualification of being in, or available for, full-time education, approved training or approved work-based learning and
- other qualifications
The income from part-time employment will be charged against the benefit for the week in which the income was earned or represents.
However, if the earnings from the part-time or casual employment reduce the Youth Payment to a 'nil' rate of payment when charged against the benefit, then the benefit must be suspended.
For more information see: Income reduces the benefit

chunks.title: Income reduces the benefit to a 'nil' rate — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Income reduces the benefit to a 'nil' rate
If the client has earnings or income for a period that will reduce the Youth Payment payable to a 'nil' rate of payment, then the Youth Payment will need to be suspended or cancelled.
Although the main benefit may be stopped a client may still qualify for Extra help.
For more information see:
- Effect of income on Extra help
- Income from employment
- Income change
Note clients will not qualify to receive the Winter Energy Payment where their income reduces their benefit payment to nil.

chunks.title: Income stops — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Income stops
When a Youth Payment client advises that income has stopped you must review their Youth Payment and any Extra help they may be getting from the day after the income ceased.
You will need to determine why the income has stopped for example, a client may advise that the interest payments from their investment have ceased.
You need to find out what the client has done with the money that was invested.
## Stops work
When a Youth Payment client stops work you need to decide when to commence or review their Youth Payment from. You will need to find out:
- the date they ceased work
- the reason they ceased work
- final pay details (including any holiday pay, redundancy etc)
Note if the client currently getting Youth Payment receives any holiday pay, charge the holiday pay as ongoing income over the period it represents.
## Example
Client has been earning $250.00 gross per week and stops work 1 April 2026 getting $500 in holiday pay.
This is the equivalent of 2 weeks holiday pay. Continue to charge $250.00 per week for the period 1 April 2026 to 14 April 2026.
You can use DREW to help with this calculation.

chunks.title: Income test — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Income test
Young people can earn up to $284.70 gross per week before it will affect their benefit.
Income is charged weekly as it is earned and at the following rates:
For a single client:
- $1.00 is taken from the benefit for each $1.00 of income over $284.70 (before tax) a week until they earn $334.70 (as at 1 April 2026)
For clients who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and both are getting Youth Payment then the rate is:
- 50 cents is taken from each of their benefits for each $1.00 of the combined income of the young person and their partner over $284.70 (before tax) a week until they earn $384.70 (as at 1 April 2026)
For a client who is married, in a civil union or in a de facto relationship where their partner is not getting Youth Payment then the rate is:
- $1.00 is taken from the benefit for each $1.00 of combined income of the client and their partner over $284.70 (before tax) a week until they earn $384.70 (as at 1 April 2026)

chunks.title: Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Job interviews or follow up on a job prospect
A client can continue to receive payment of their benefit for an absence from New Zealand if it can be confirmed that the travel is to:
- attend a job interview or
- follow up a definite job prospect
Benefit payments cannot continue if the client is leaving New Zealand to carry out general job search, that is, to 'have a look' for a job.
You will need to treat each case on its merits and take the following into account:
- does the client have proof of the interview or specific job prospect?
They will need to provide the employer's name and phone number and the date of the interview or meeting with the employer
- is it a realistic job opportunity for the client? That is, does it match the skills and qualifications of the client
- how long are they going for?
Consider what would be a reasonable time period for the client to complete the trip, for example, x number of days to get there, 1 day for the interview, x number of days to return home and frequency of flights to and from the destination
- what arrangements have they made for the continuing care of their children and accommodation while they are absent?

chunks.title: Must receive payment for six months — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Must receive payment for six months
A young person who has been granted Youth Payment who has not been receiving the payment for six months cannot qualify for a main benefit when they turn 18 years. They must complete a minimum period of six months receiving Youth Payment first.
This ensures that the young person is able to have a reasonable chance to move towards a qualification by participating in education, training or work-based learning and undertaking other youth activity obligations before they focus on obligations attached to other main benefits.
For example, a young person is granted Youth Payment at the age of 17 years and 8 months old. When they turn 18 years old they will need to continue to receive Youth Payment for another two months to complete the six month minimum period. They can then be assessed for entitlement to other main benefits.
## Exception
A young person, who is receiving Youth Payment and then meets the criteria for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability, can be granted this benefit instead of Youth Payment without completing the minimum six months.
For more information see:
- Chooses to remain on Youth Payment past 18 years of age
- Age
- Qualifies for another benefit

chunks.title: Does not advise of departure — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Does not advise of departure
If the client did not tell the Ministry they were leaving New Zealand their benefit will be suspended immediately from the day after they left New Zealand.
The Integrity Intervention Centre will determine if there has been an overpayment, establish any debt, and advise the client.
If a client challenges the information match refer them to the Integrity Intervention Centre.
For more information see:
- Paying a benefit when the client has not advised before departure
- Approved travel reasons
- Backdating benefit to the day after departure date
- Action on return to New Zealand
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy

chunks.title: Ongoing assistance for surviving partner — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Ongoing assistance for surviving partner
When the partner of a Youth Payment client dies the partner's benefit is continued for 28 days at the rate that is payable at the date of death.
The continuation of payment beyond the date of death is referred to as terminal benefit.
## Client's benefit options
A surviving client can remain on Youth Payment as long as they continue to meet the qualifications.
## Date of review
When the surviving client remains on Youth Payment review the client's benefit from the date following the death of their partner and:
- adjust any extra help to the single rate

chunks.title: On leave for 28 days or less — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## On leave for 28 days or less
Where a client who is receiving the hospital rate is on leave from hospital for 28 days or less:
- increase their benefit to the appropriate full rate from the date of discharge on leave
- for married, civil union or de facto clients (where appropriate) reduce the partner's benefit to the half married, civil union or de facto rate and suspend Special Disability Allowance and
- review any Extra help from the same date
On re-admission to hospital:
- reduce the benefit to the rate payable prior to the period of leave
- for married, civil union or de facto clients (where appropriate) increase the partner's benefit to the single rate and resume Special Disability Allowance and
- review any Extra help from the same date
Note the dates of admission and discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital.

chunks.title: On leave for more than 28 days — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## On leave for more than 28 days
Where a client who is receiving the hospital rate is on leave from hospital for more than 28 days:
- increase their benefit to the appropriate full rate from the date of discharge on leave
- for married, civil union or de facto clients (where appropriate) reduce the partner's benefit to the half married, civil union or de facto rate and suspend Special Disability Allowance and
- review any Extra Help
On re-admission to hospital continue to pay the full rate of benefit and any Extra Help for a further 13 weeks of hospitalisation.
Note calculation of the 13 week period in hospital begins again after the client has been re-admitted when on leave for more than 28 days.
The dates of admission and discharge are not regarded as days spent in hospital.
For more information see:
- Effect on Extra help

chunks.title: On leave from hospital — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## On leave from hospital
Youth Payment is paid at the full rate for any period of leave from hospital. Where the client has been receiving the hospital rate increase their benefit for any period they are on leave.
The benefit action to take, on the client's re-admission to hospital, will depend on how long they were on leave.

chunks.title: Partner's IRD number — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: As part of a review of Youth Payment, MSD may make a written request to the client for evidence of a partner's IRD number when the partner's income is relevant to a client's Youth Payment.

chunks.title: Setting or extending the period for providing evidence — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: MSD can request a client to provide evidence of their partner's IRD number within a reasonable time period (usually 10 working days). MSD can set a different period or extend the period to provide evidence of an IRD number when it is expected to take longer to get the evidence. This includes considering factors outside the client or partner's control that may cause delays, including, but not limited to: - the client or partner has a family emergency that caused a delay - processing delays with an external agency (e.g., Inland Revenue, Department of Internal Affairs, etc) - the client or partner does not speak English as a first language and has difficulty navigating evidence requirements - the client or partner has limited access to the internet, a device, or their local service centre - the client or partner has a physical or intellectual disability that makes accessing services difficult.

chunks.title: Notice following an unsuccessful match — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about IRD numbers. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the client (in writing) to provide evidence of their partner's IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving the client a minimum of 10 working days to provide their partner's IRD number evidence or the client's assistance may be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Youth Payment. Isla's partner, Ariki, has income that is included in MSD's income test to determine eligibility for Youth Payment and MSD holds an IRD number for Ariki. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Ariki's IRD number. As part of a review of Isla's assistance, MSD provides a notice in writing, giving 10 working days for Isla to provide evidence of Ariki's IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Ariki already having an IRD number - Ariki not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD may suspend assistance if evidence is not received — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: If a partner's IRD number evidence is not provided within a reasonable timeframe (usually 10 working days) or within the extended period if this has been applied, the client's assistance may be suspended. In rare cases the client's assistance may be cancelled or the rate of payment varied. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance.

chunks.title: IRD number not requested in some circumstances — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - there are significant factors, that are outside the client or partner's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number, (e.g. a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence), and - the client needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided. A partner's IRD number or evidence of their IRD number does not need to be provided when they are not a New Zealand tax resident. MSD can determine a later point to request the evidence of the IRD number. For more information see: - Non-tax resident partner's IRD number not required Note there is different guidance for requesting evidence of an IRD number for clients or when a client is applying for Youth Payment.

chunks.title: Paying benefit when the client failed to advise of absence — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Paying benefit when the client failed to advise of absence
