If a client contacts Work and Income after they have left New Zealand, and is not eligible to have their payment backdated, their benefit can only be resumed from:
- the date that they notified us of their absence and
- only if the travel is allowed (ie they meet the criteria to continue to be paid their benefit while overseas either because they meet the criteria for approved travel, or the requirement that travel be approved does not apply to them)
Otherwise, the client cannot have their benefit resumed until they return to New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Backdating benefit to the day after departure date
- Action on return to New Zealand
- Approved travel reasons
- Payment when client or partner absent from New Zealand
- Examples of applying the Absence from New Zealand policy

chunks.title: Maximum amount payable — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Maximum amount payable
YSSU can pay a rate higher than the hospital rate up to the maximum rate of Youth Payment that would otherwise be payable.

chunks.title: Examples — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Examples
A client who is absent from New Zealand for an approved reason may be prevented from returning by new unforeseen circumstances which could include (but are not limited to):
- travel delays due to unforeseen weather events eg fog, volcano, flooding, earthquakes, terrorism
- travel delays due to transport options being cancelled
- health condition or injury or hospitalisation preventing return
For more information see:
- Overseas for medical treatment
- Absent from NZ more than 28 days in any 52 week period
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days for an approved reason — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period. To pay a benefit more than 28 days during any 52 week period of absence from New Zealand, the client must be travelling for one of the following reasons: - essential travel - to attend a significant event relating to a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family), that the client would reasonably be expected to attend (eg to visit a person who is seriously ill, seriously injured or whose death is imminent, to attend a funeral, to provide support to a party or witness to a court case, travel required for a court ordered custody arrangement) - to attend a court case which the person is required to attend as a party or a witness - to attend a job interview or follow up on a job prospect - for clients with a disability, to receive vocational training or disability assistance-dog training not available in New Zealand during the period or periods of absence - for clients with a disability, to travel overseas for the sole or predominant purpose of competing in any overseas multinational or international Special Olympic or Paralympic Games competition - to provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster (flood, earthquake, fire) or similar adverse event (eg house fire) and - Work and Income must be satisfied, when considering the client's reason for travel, that the length of the absence is no longer than necessary for the reason for travel In addition, where the client has already been paid a benefit while absent from New Zealand in the 52 week period Work and Income must be satisfied that either: - the client could not have reasonably foreseen them needing to be absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, or - the client could not have rearranged their affairs to avoid being absent from New Zealand for more than 28 days in a 52 week period, and - it would be unreasonable for the benefit not to be paid Note generally we would not pay more than 28 days extra travel per absence. For more information see: - Examples for paying more than 28 days for an approved reason - Client not returned due to unforeseeable event (within 28 days maximum) - Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum) - Paying for more than 28 days - delayed return

chunks.title: Paying for more than 28 days - receive support from family member residing overseas — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: Generally, a benefit cannot be paid for more than 28 days in any 52 week period. However there are limited circumstances where a benefit can be paid for more than 28 days in a 52 week period where the client is travelling to receive support from a family member (including other person who is treated by the client as a member of the client's family) who is residing overseas. For more information see: - Definition of 'support' from a family member residing overseas This applies (and is limited to a further 28 days in any 52 week period) when: - the young person has already been paid a benefit while absent from New Zealand for one or more approved reasons for all or most of 28 days in a 52 week period and - the young person will be absent from New Zealand for the purpose of obtaining support from a family member residing overseas (while still meeting the eligibility criteria for Youth Payment if receiving it due to a family breakdown) and - the support that the client needs cannot reasonably be provided to the client in New Zealand and - the absence will not prevent the young person from continuing to meet their youth activity obligations because the absence is at a time when: they are not required to attend education, training or work-based learning (for example, they are exempt from meeting their obligations)they are meeting their obligation to be in, or available for, education, training or work-based learning but it is the school holidays or the semester/term break or they are between academic years or the course/school has not started yet andthey are not required to be in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations during the time of the absence (eg they do not need to attend a budgeting course during the time they will be overseas) - they are not required to attend education, training or work-based learning (for example, they are exempt from meeting their obligations) - they are meeting their obligation to be in, or available for, education, training or work-based learning but it is the school holidays or the semester/term break or they are between academic years or the course/school has not started yet and - they are not required to be in New Zealand to meet any of their other obligations during the time of the absence (eg they do not need to attend a budgeting course during the time they will be overseas)

chunks.title: Cannot be paid for more than 28 days for purposes of obtaining support — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: The maximum amount of time that a client receiving Youth Payment can continue to receive their payment while overseas due to the absence not preventing them meeting their obligations is 28 days in any 52 week period. Therefore, if a client subject to youth activity obligations has already received their payment for 28 days in a 52 week period while they were overseas on a holiday on the grounds that the travel did not prevent them meeting their obligations, they will not be able to continue to receive their payment for a further period of overseas absence in the same 52 week period under the 'obtaining support from a family member' circumstance. For more information see: - Examples of paying for more than 28 days for obtaining family support

chunks.title: Payment to partners — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Payment to partners
When a client with a partner has their Youth Payment reduced to the hospital rate, and their partner is getting a benefit or pension (other than Youth Payment) in their own right, the partner from the same date can:
- have their benefit or pension increased by the difference between the maximum half married, civil union or de facto rate and single rate of that benefit or pension and
- get a Special Disability Allowance
Note if the partner is getting Youth Payment there is only one rate of payment and they cannot get Special Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Payment when client absent from New Zealand — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Payment when client absent from New Zealand
There are some situations where the benefit payments will be affected when the client is absent from New Zealand. The action required by Work and Income will depend on the reason the client is absent from New Zealand and whether they are continuing to be paid a benefit.
For more information see:
- Ending payment for client who needs an approved reason for travel
- Client left New Zealand and reason for travel changes (within 28 day maximum)
- Client not returned due to an unforeseeable event (within 28 day maximum)

chunks.title: Period over which to charge income — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Period over which to charge income
Income should be charged against the benefit for the week that it is earned or the period it represents for example:
- an interest payment is received once every six months representing the previous six months
1. This payment should be charged against the benefit over the previous six months that the payment represents.
2. If it is an ongoing investment you would then add it on as estimated income for the next six months.
- a client receives wages for working a fortnight. Income should be charged each week representing the wages that are paid for that week.
- a client works for two days of the week. Income should be charged in the week that it is earned.
For more information on charging weekend work see: Income from employment
In most cases, determining the period will be straightforward. For more information on some specific types of income and how to charge them, see:
- Core Policy Types of income
If the period of when the income was earned, or the period that it represents is still unable to be determined, discuss the payment with Helpline.
## Overlapping income
Where a client has income from a number of sources paid for the same periods of time, then all of the payments are added together. This total income will be charged against the Youth Payment over the period that the income represents.
For more information see:
- Example of overlapping income
- Income change
- Effect of income on Extra help
- Income for a past period

chunks.title: Moving to Australia — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Moving to Australia
If the client is moving to Australia it is important that they are aware that they may not be able to receive a benefit until they have resided in Australia for two years after being granted permanent residence status.
For more information see:
- Reciprocal Agreements

chunks.title: Permitted travel reasons — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Permitted travel reasons
A client not otherwise entitled to be paid their Youth Payment while absent from New Zealand may have their payments continue for up to 28 days in any 52 week period, if their travel is for one (or a combination of), of the following permitted travel reasons:
- essential travel - to attend a significant event relating to a family member or a person who fulfils a role in relation to the client that is similar to that of a family member, that the client would reasonably be expected to attend
- to attend a court case which the person is required to attend as a party or a witness - this is to allow clients who are required by law to attend court and supports the maintenance of the law. A client would generally be expected to provide evidence that they are required to attend a court overseas. This would include documents from the court.
- to attend a job interview or follow up on a job prospect
- for clients with a disability, to receive vocational training or disability assistance-dog training not available in New Zealand during the time the client is absent
- for clients with a disability, to travel overseas for the sole or predominant purpose of competing in any overseas multinational or international Special Olympic or Paralympic Games competition
- to provide aid or assistance to a family member immediately following a natural disaster (eg flood, earthquake, fire) or similar adverse event (eg house fire)

chunks.title: Previous tax year — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: A single client may declare income for a period in a previous tax year. There are 3 possible outcomes for the client depending on the amount of income declared and whether any previous income had been charged. These outcomes are: 1. The client is due arrears following a review on their benefit. As the arrears will be issued in the current tax year no adjustment is required to the tax details or 2. The amount of the income declared is under the exemption and the client does not receive any Extra help. The client's SWIFTT record is noted accordingly or 3. A debt will be established and the tax details for this year will need to be adjusted accordingly as in the following example.

chunks.title: Example — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: A client phoned on 02/04/2022 and advises they worked for the week 24/01/2022 to 30/01/2022 and earned $250.54 gross. Manually assess the income deduction Gross income (excluding cents) $250.00 Less income allowed before benefit is affected (as at 1 July 2021) $227.18 equals income $22.82 Amount benefit reduced on account of income (income over $227.18 reduces benefit by $1.00 per $1.00) $22.00 To work out the benefit rate payable: Maximum Youth Payment (as at 1 July 2021) $239.70 Less reduction due to income $22.00 Benefit rate payable $217.70 Once you have calculated the new benefit rate for the period 24/01/2022 to 30/01/2022 add the income to INCMA. A backdated review 'SBDR' still needs to be completed for this week. The following is the process: SBDR $217.70 for the week 24/01/2022 to 30/01/2022 LSUM a memo will be produced as a result of the backdated review with details of the debt amount to be added into the appropriate tax year. It is the net amount of debt which is added to SWIFTT SDBTI debt inquiry for the client (F4 for STAXI) STAXI select the appropriate year and DBT which will take you into the SDBTA screen SDBTA add the debt type, add the benefit/pension code, add the debt status and breach type, add the net debt amount, this will also adjust the tax record for the client. Add the period that the debt represents and add any comments where appropriate - remember to commence recovery of the debt via SOFSI

chunks.title: Priority for deductions — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Priority for deductions
Certain forms of deductions take priority over others; the following list gives the order of priority, from highest to lowest:
Highest priority
- Child Support deductions made under the Child Support Act 1991
- Inland Revenue tax deductions (including Student Loan repayments)
- Ministry of Social Development debt repayments including: Liable Parent Contributions (LPC)child maintenance debts and Major Repairs Advances (MRA)Student Allowance debtStudent Loan debt converted to Ministry of Social Development debt orIncome Related Rent historical Kāinga Ora debtIncome Related Rent Ministry of Social Development debt
- Liable Parent Contributions (LPC)
- child maintenance debts and Major Repairs Advances (MRA)
- Student Allowance debt
- Student Loan debt converted to Ministry of Social Development debt or
- Income Related Rent historical Kāinga Ora debt
- Income Related Rent Ministry of Social Development debt
- attachment orders made under the Family Proceedings Act 1980
- court attachment orders issued under the Summary Proceedings Act 1957
- court attachment orders issued under the District Court Act 2016
- Student Loan repayments
Lowest priority
Determining the priority of deductions is necessary when a client has more than one order issued in respect of their benefit. Also each order and deduction notice is subject to its own protected earnings rule.
When deductions need to be reduced adjust from the lowest priority up to those with a higher priority taking into account the protected earnings rules for each.

chunks.title: Private hospital and homes — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Private hospital and homes
Youth Payment can be paid at the full rate regardless of the period of hospitalisation when a client is:
- admitted to a private hospital or
- admitted to a private home that provides residential care disability services
If the client receives Extra Help, this will need to be reviewed to see if their costs are continuing.
For more information see:
- Extra help Residential Support Subsidy

chunks.title: Protected earnings rate — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Protected earnings rate
Both the District Court Act and the Summary Proceedings Act provide that every Ministry of Justice attachment order must specify a 'protected earnings rate'.
If the attachment order will reduce the client's income below the protected earnings rate, then the order will not operate, and you must cancel or return the attachment order to the Ministry of Justice.
Calculating the client's income differs between attachment orders made under the Summary Proceedings Act and the District Court Act, as different benefits are taken into account. Therefore, it is important to determine what type of attachment order has been issued.
Summary Proceedings Act 1957
For orders made under the Summary Proceedings Act, the calculation of the client's income does not include Special Benefit, Temporary Additional Support, Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance, Winter Energy Payment, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit.
District Court Act 2016
For orders made under the District Court Act, the client's income includes Special Benefit, Temporary Additional Support and Disability Allowance but does not include Child Disability Allowance, Orphans Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit.
## Example
An attachment order is received from the Ministry of Justice for $60.00 per week. The order lists the protected income as $257.70 per week:
Youth Payment rate (net as at 1 April 2026)
$324.50
Plus Accommodation Supplement (Area 2)
$105.00
Total net earnings
$429.50
60% of total net earnings (=protected earnings)
$257.70
Net earnings: Less Child Support deduction
$70.00
$359.50
Less MSD debt
$45.00
Sub total
$314.50
Less Court Order
$60.00
Total
$254.50
The court order takes the client's income to $254.50, which is below the protected income rate of $257.70.
The attachment order will not operate, you must return it to the Ministry of Justice for the order to be amended.

chunks.title: Qualifies for another benefit — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Qualifies for another benefit
A young person may qualify for another benefit due to a change in their circumstances. It is also important to determine if the young person still qualifies for Youth Payment.
For example, if a young person turns 18 they would no longer qualify for Youth Payment and would generally transfer to Jobseeker Support.
Note when a young person turns 18 years old the Youth Payment should stop. However in some circumstances the benefit may continue. See: Change in age
If the young person qualifies for more than one benefit they must be told which benefit is the most beneficial for their particular circumstances. They will need to be advised of:
- benefit rates
- the effect of any income they may receive (income reduction and any exemptions) and
- benefit obligations
The young person must make the final decision on which benefit they receive after being given all relevant information.
For more information see:
- Qualifications Young person turns 18 years old
- Change in age
- Jobseeker Support Qualifications
- Processing standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Reapplication for Youth Payment — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Reapplication for Youth Payment
When a young person reapplies for Youth Payment, they must complete the application process as if they are applying for the first time.
## Previous Independent Assessment report
Where a young person was receiving Youth Payment due to a relationship breakdown or another good and sufficient reason and an Independent Assessment Provider report was completed, YSSU will need to:
- retrieve the original Independent Assessment Provider report
- ask the young person what circumstances have changed that has led to another application for Youth Payment
- decide whether it is appropriate to send the young person for another assessment with the Independent Assessment ProviderIn some cases it may be helpful to speak with the Independent Assessment Provider before doing so.
If the young person's circumstances are the same as their previous application, you do not need to request another assessment from the Independent Assessment Provider.
For more information see:
- Youth Payment Qualifications
- Youth Payment Family breakdown
- Youth Payment Independent Assessment Provider

chunks.title: Recording income — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Recording income
Any income a client receives, even when the income is less than $284.70 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026), must be added to the client's SWIFTT record on the INCMA screen.
This is to make sure any Extra help is reviewed correctly and will create a permanent audit trail of all income details.
If the income is over the benefit cut-out point, and SWIFTT will not accept this information then a note on CMS should be added.
Ensure the following details are recorded:
- source of income, such as the employer's details
- gross (before tax) amount of income received
- period that the income represents
- how the income was advised, for example, phoned in by the client

chunks.title: Release from prison — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Release from prison
A client may be entitled to Youth Payment when they are released from prison. The date to recommence payment depends on the length of time the client has been in prison.
## Partner
When the partner of a person in prison has been receiving a benefit, this will need to be reviewed from the date of release.
For more information see:
- Youth Payment Prisoners

chunks.title: Release on bail — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Release on bail
When a client is released on bail, Youth Payment can be paid from the date of release providing the client:
- is still able to meet their youth activity obligations
- has been in custody for less than 31 days and
- reapplies for a benefit immediately after their release
If the client has been in custody for more than 31 days an initial stand-down will be imposed.
For more information see:
- Youth Payment Prisoners
- Exemptions Court imposed conditions

chunks.title: Remanded in custody — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Remanded in custody
Generally, when a client is remanded in custody awaiting a further court appearance the benefit should be stopped. However, there is discretion to continue payment of Youth Payment after taking the client's financial circumstances and commitments into account.
When considering continuing payment of the Youth Payment for the period for a particular client, consider the following:
- has the client been remanded pending a further court hearing or for sentencing
- does the client have continuing costs that cannot be avoided, such as rent and hire purchase for essential items
- does the client have a partner and or dependent children
Every case should be looked at on its own merits.
For further help contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances before making a decision.

chunks.title: Partner — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Partner
Where the partner of a person in prison has been receiving a benefit, this will need to be reviewed from the date of release.
For more information see:
- Youth Payment Court imposed conditions
- Special Needs Grants Steps to Freedom

chunks.title: Returns to live with parents — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Returns to live with parents
When a young person, who is 16 or 17 years old and receiving Youth Payment because of a parental support gap, returns to live with their parents, or begins to be financially supported by them or someone else, they are no longer entitled to receive the payment.
The Youth Payment should be cancelled from the date of their return home.

chunks.title: Single clients — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Single clients
Generally the Youth Payment should be suspended when a single client is imprisoned. This will enable payment to be resumed if the client is only in prison for a short period and reapplies for a benefit following their release.
The Youth Payment should be suspended from the day after imprisonment.
Note SWIFTT will automatically cancel the record if it remains suspended for 8 weeks.
## Exception - Remand in custody
Although the Youth Payment should generally be stopped for any period during which the client is remanded in custody pending a further court appearance, there is discretion to continue payment of all or part of the benefit.

chunks.title: Special Disability Allowance — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Special Disability Allowance
A Special Disability Allowance is paid to the partner (who receives a benefit other than Youth Payment in their own right) of a client who is receiving the hospital rate. It is paid to the person not in hospital to help with the extra costs of their partner's hospitalisation, for example travel costs to visit the patient.
Note that Special Disability Allowance is:
- granted without the client having to apply
- paid separately from Disability Allowance and
- not income or asset tested
Special Disability Allowance can start from when the patient's benefit is reduced to the hospital rate.
Special Disability Allowance should be stopped from the first available date if the person receiving it is also admitted to hospital.
## SWIFTT
Grant Special Disability Allowance using code 838 on the SSUPI screen.
For more information see:
- Extra help Special Disability Allowance
- Deskfile Rates of Special Disability Allowance

chunks.title: Student Loans — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Student Loans
Clients with a Student Loan must make repayments to Inland Revenue when the income they get exceeds a pre-determined level. This level is called the 'income threshold'.
A person must make repayments to Inland Revenue when their income exceeds $464 gross per week ($24,128 gross per year) as at 1 April 2026.
Note non-taxable Extra help such as family tax credit, Best Start tax credit, Accommodation Supplement and Winter Energy Payment do not count as income in this instance.
If the client's income is over this income threshold, MSD can make the required deduction. However, this is only done if the client requests it.
If the client's portion of benefit is below the income threshold, there is no provision to make voluntary repayments through SWIFTT. The client can make voluntary payments direct to Inland Revenue at any time.
Note the following:
- Student Loan deductions can only be made from taxable benefits
- Student Loan deductions cannot be made if the client's benefit is below the income threshold
- when a client is getting a married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit, only the client's portion is taken into consideration when assessing Student Loan repayments
- when a client is getting a reduced rate of payment due to other income, the Student Loan deduction is assessed on the net payment after income deduction

chunks.title: SWIFTT process to pay a partner — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## SWIFTT process to pay a partner
When YSSU decide to continue payment of the client's Youth Payment to the partner, they will need to determine the most appropriate SWIFTT process to enable payment to be made to the partner.
The process for payment will depend on whether the:
- period in prison is in the past
- client is due to be released from prison shortly
- client is likely to be in prison for more than four weeks and
- rate of payment for the partner
Note that there is discretion to pay the full married, civil union or de facto rate of benefit.
## Period in prison has passed or release is imminent
Generally, use the SBDR screen in SWIFTT to:
- suspend the client's Youth Payment for the period in prison
and
- pay the appropriate rate to the partner (that is, the married rate)
## Period in prison exceeds 4 weeks
When the client's Youth Payment is to continue, and be paid to the partner YSSU will need to contact Helpline for advice regarding the SWIFTT process to use.

chunks.title: Tax codes — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Tax codes
Youth Payment is taxed at the 'M' rate.
Youth Payment is always considered the client's primary source of income regardless of the amount paid. If the client has other income this is always considered the client's secondary income.
Clients can apply to Inland Revenue for a tailored tax code for other income.

chunks.title: Taxation — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Taxation
Youth Payment is a taxable benefit. MSD makes payments to clients at the net rate after the deduction of tax. MSD passes the tax on to Inland Revenue.
Generally, MSD will request a young person to provide MSD with their IRD number or evidence of their IRD number.

chunks.title: Terminal benefit for a single client — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Terminal benefit for a single client
Generally the Youth Payment stops from the date following the death of a single client with no children; however, there is some discretion to continue the payment of benefit for up to 28 days. When payment is continued after the date of death, it is referred to as terminal benefit.
Circumstances where continued benefit payment might be considered beyond a single client's date of death include:
- when the deceased client's domestic situation results in a transition cost for a family member, causing hardshipExample: accommodation and other household costs when client has been sharing accommodation
or
- when there are exceptional and justified costs associated with the death of the clientExample: multiple deaths within one family
Payment should not continue for 28 days following the death of a single client to meet funeral expenses. A Funeral Grant may be available for this purpose.
## SWIFTT
When paying terminal benefit for a single client manually calculate entitlement and make an adhoc payment.
There is no automatic provision for the payment of terminal benefit (for a single client) on SWIFTT.
Wherever possible the next of kin or the executor of the deceased's estate should be added to SWIFTT.

chunks.title: Terminal benefit rate — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: The provision to continue the benefit payment for 28 days following the date of death is referred to as terminal benefit. Benefit payment is continued at the rate which was payable to the client and partner (if any) at the date of death. A terminal benefit includes extra help being paid (for up to 28 days following the date of death).

chunks.title: Benefit paid at a reduced rate — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text: When the client's benefit was paid at a reduced rate at the date of death, the terminal benefit is also paid at the reduced rate. Benefit payments may have been reduced due to: - hospitalisation the deceased client's benefit was reduced as they were in hospital for more than 13 weeks - the deceased client's benefit was reduced as they were in hospital for more than 13 weeks - income - debt repayments when benefit arrears are due at the date of death, attempt to recover the debt payment in full from the final benefit paymentdo not recover debts, in full, from terminal benefit payments - when benefit arrears are due at the date of death, attempt to recover the debt payment in full from the final benefit payment - do not recover debts, in full, from terminal benefit payments - Child Support if a client had an information share Child Support payment being charged as income at their date of death, they may have been getting a reduced rate of benefit. In this situation, the effect of the income charge for the information share Child Support will continue for the duration of the terminal benefit, as the rate payable cannot be reviewedChild Support liability ends when the liable person dies; however MSD cannot remove a Child Support deduction from a benefit record without the authorisation of Inland Revenuewhen a surviving partner or family member makes enquiries, refer them to Inland Revenue - if a client had an information share Child Support payment being charged as income at their date of death, they may have been getting a reduced rate of benefit. In this situation, the effect of the income charge for the information share Child Support will continue for the duration of the terminal benefit, as the rate payable cannot be reviewed - Child Support liability ends when the liable person dies; however MSD cannot remove a Child Support deduction from a benefit record without the authorisation of Inland Revenue - when a surviving partner or family member makes enquiries, refer them to Inland Revenue - redirection to Kāinga Ora or a community housing providerWhen the accommodation is being retained by a surviving partner or family member, continue the redirection to Kāinga Ora or the community housing provider. For more information see: Social housing, Assessment of eligibility Death of a client - court attachment orders Note all of the above deductions will continue to be made from the terminal benefit payments unless they are manually stopped before cancellation.

chunks.title: Treatment of income — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Treatment of income
When a client (or their partner) is receiving Youth Payment and declares any income, the following information is required:
- determine the source and the amount of income
- check the client still qualifies for Youth Payment and meets the youth activity obligations
- check the client's income is below the cut-out point
- check the period over which to charge income
- review the rate of payment, see Income test and Income change
- review any Extra help Effect of income on Extra help
- check any Exemption for severe disablement
For information on how to charge specific types of income for example, Accident Compensation Payments and employment related income see: Types of income
When a client (or their partner) advises that they have commenced employment, you will need to find out more specific information about their employment. See: Income from employment
## Benefit stopped, suspended or expired
Where a benefit is stopped (suspended or expired) and the client has declared income for a period where no benefit has been paid, determine the client's entitlement to benefit first and then charge the income accordingly.

chunks.title: Underpaid — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Underpaid
When a client has been underpaid Youth Payment and is owed arrears, MSD will work out the amount of tax and pass this on to Inland Revenue.
From 1 April 2024, if an arrears payment relates to a previous tax year, the arrears will not be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment. This means the client will not have to pay any more tax on the payment.
Only arrears payments related to the current tax year will be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment.
Example
A client is paid arrears on 12 June 2026. This payment represents arrears for 25 March 2026 to 8 June 2026.
The arrears for 25 March to 31 March 2026 represent a past tax year, so they will not be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment. The arrears for 1 April to 8 June 2026 represent the current tax year, so they will be included in the client's end-of-year tax assessment.

chunks.title: Young person with a health condition — youth payment > changes and reviews youth payment
chunks.text:
## Young person with a health condition
If a young person meets the medical qualifications for Jobseeker Support (except for their age) they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their youth activity obligations until their capacity to undertake education, training and work-based learning improves.
The young person must be limited in their capacity to undertake activities because of health condition, injury or disability.
Where a young person's health condition permanently and severely restricts their ability to undertake education, training or work-based learning, they may be able to receive a Supported Living Payment.
If the young person is admitted to hospital it may affect their rate of payment.

chunks.title: Charging income — youth payment
chunks.text: The abatement rules for Youth Payment are different based on the type of income a young person is getting.

chunks.title: General abatement rules — youth payment
chunks.text: Young people who get most types of income (i.e. income from salary, wages, or non-information share Child Support payments) can only get a limited amount of income before their Youth Payment will stop. Note these rules do not apply to information share Child Support payments. Young people (and partner if any) can earn up to $284.70 gross per week (as at 1 April 2026) before it will reduce their benefit. If a young person (and their partner if any) is only getting other types of income (but not getting information share Child Support payments), the following applies: For a young person who is single: - their benefit will reduce by $1.00 for every $1.00 of income over $284.70 gross per week until their income is $334.70 (as at 1 April 2026) - if their income is more than $334.70 their benefit will stop For young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, and both getting Youth Payment in their own right: - each of their benefits will reduce by 50 cents for every $1.00 of combined income of the young person and their partner over $284.70 gross per week until their combined income is $384.70 (as at 1 April 2026) - if their combined income is more than $384.70 per week their benefits will stop For young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, and only one of them is getting Youth Payment: - the Youth Payment will reduce by 50 cents for every $1.00 of the combined income of the young person and their partner over $284.70 gross per week until they earn $384.70 (as at 1 April 2026) - if their combined income is more than $384.70 per week the Youth Payment will stop For an example of an income assessment, see: - Weekly income example When a young person is applying for Youth Payment and declares any income you need to: - determine the source and the amount of income - check the young person qualifies for Youth Payment and is still meeting their youth activity obligations For information on how to charge specific types of income for example, Accident Compensation Payments, see: Types of income Also see: - Processing standards Income and asset details [no link find out why] - Changes and reviews Treatment of income

chunks.title: Income period — youth payment
chunks.text: It is important to distinguish between income a client gets for a period before the entitlement date of benefit and income that is ongoing after a client's benefit has commenced. Income received before the entitlement date of benefit must be considered when calculating the Initial stand-down period. Income received for a period after commencement must be charged against their ongoing Youth Payment. When a young person works during an initial stand-down period the commencement date of their Youth Payment will need to be reassessed, see: Employment during stand-down Note information share Child Support payments have different income charging rules. For more information see:

chunks.title: Charging information share Child Support payments as income — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Charging information share Child Support payments as income
The abatement rules for Young Parent Payment are different based on the type of income a young person is getting.
If a young person gets information share Child Support payments, any other types of income they get are counted first.
If their other income is below the income cut-out point, income from information share Child Support payments will gradually reduce their benefit until the rate of payment is zero.
Young parents (and their partner if any) can get up to $284.70 gross income per week (as at 1 April 2026) before other income will affect their benefit.
If a young person (and their partner if any) is getting information share Child Support payments, the abatement rules are:
For a young parent who is single:
- if their other income is below $334.70, their benefit will reduce by $1.00 for every $1.00 of total income (including information share Child Support payments) over $284.70 gross per week until their benefit is reduced to zero (as at 1 April 2026)
- if their other income is more than $334.70 gross per week their benefit stops
For young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and both are getting Youth Payment in their own right:
- if their combined other income is below $384.70, each of their benefits will reduce by 50 cents for every $1.00 of combined total income (including information share Child Support payments) of the young person and their partner over $284.70 gross per week until their benefit is reduced to zero (as at 1 April 2026)
- if their combined other income is more than $384.70 gross per week their benefits stop
For young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and only one of them is getting Youth Payment:
- when their combined other income is below $384.70, their Youth Payment will reduce by 50 cents for every $1.00 of combined total income (including information share Child Support payments) of the young person and their partner over $284.70 gross per week until their benefit is reduced to zero
- if their combined other income is more than $384.70 gross per week their benefit will stop

chunks.title: Chooses to remain on Youth Payment past 18 years of age — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Chooses to remain on Youth Payment past 18 years of age
Generally, when a young person turns 18 years old the Youth Payment should stop. However, to give a young person a chance to complete the qualification they have started while on Youth Payment, a young person can choose to continue to receive Youth Payment after they turn 18 if they remain in education, training or work-based learning.

chunks.title: Cook Island, Niue and Tokelau clients — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Cook Island, Niue and Tokelau clients
Clients born in the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau are automatically New Zealand citizens (by birth). Generally they will travel to New Zealand on a New Zealand passport.
However, they must still have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years at any one time before they can receive Youth Payment.
Other residents of the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau will be required to produce a proof of residence document and meet the 2 years continuous residence requirement in New Zealand.
## Australian clients
Australian citizens are lawfully allowed in New Zealand, as they are deemed to hold a residence class visa. However, they must still meet the 2 years residence qualification to qualify for Youth Payment.
Note clients who are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident, but have not lived in New Zealand continuously for 2 years, may be eligible for Youth Payment on grounds of hardship.

chunks.title: Commencement date — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Commencement date
To decide when the Youth Payment can start you must first find the entitlement date.
This is usually the date that a person no longer has a means of support.
For a list of these dates see:
- Entitlement date
Note young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship must qualify for the Youth Payment in their own right. For more information see:
- Calculating the commencement date for couples
Generally, the Youth Payment is subject to an initial stand-down of up to a maximum of 2 weeks after the entitlement date.
The commencement date is the:
- day after the initial stand down ends or
- application date
whichever is the later.
## Exception
Applicants for the Youth Payment who are enrolled full-time in a course of secondary education or are in employment-related training or other training course approved by the Ministry are not subject to initial stand-down periods. Therefore, the commencement date is the:
- entitlement date or
- application date
whichever is the later.
## Twenty-eight day rule
If a young person applies for Youth Payment within 28 days of their entitlement date, the commencement date rules are different. See: Twenty-eight day rule

chunks.title: Earning all of the incentives available to them — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Earning all of the incentives available to them
For young people getting Youth Payment to have the option of not being subject to youth money management they would need to earn the following incentive payments:
- budgeting
- education
A young person who has a full or partial exemption for their activity obligations is only be able to earn those incentive payments which apply to their current obligations.
For more information see:
- Returned to youth money management
- Youth money management
- Obligations Removing incentive payments

chunks.title: Counting previous activity obligations failures — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Counting previous activity obligations failures
The sanction imposed depends on how often the young person has failed to comply with their activity obligations in the previous 12 months while continuously getting Youth Payment.
For Youth Payment previous failures are only counted, if the failure occurred within the last 12 months, while continuously getting Youth Payment where the young person had activity obligations.
The 12-month count starts from the day the obligation failure is imposed. Each obligation failure has its own 12-month count.
Example
A client fails their first obligation on 1 June 2025. They fail another obligation on 1 October 2025, and have an obligation failure count of two. Their obligation failure count is reset to one on 1 June 2026, 12 months after they failed their first obligation. Their obligation failure count will be reset to zero on 1 October 2026, 12 months after the second obligation failure.
## Young person transfers between benefits
If a young person transfers between benefits where they have activity obligations (for example Youth Payment to Young Parent Payment) any activity obligations failures within the previous 12 months are still counted.
The count of activity obligations failures within 12 months will reset to zero for young people transferring to a benefit with or without activity obligations (for example Youth Payment to Jobseeker Support).
For more information see:
- Examples of transfers between benefits

chunks.title: Couple - both failed, one recomplies first — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Couple - both failed, one recomplies first
Where a married, civil union or de facto couple are both on a 100% suspension (this could be a grade 3 sanction or a suspension after 4 weeks) and one person recomplies first, their Youth Payment and their portion of the supplementary assistance must be resumed or regranted.
The non-complying partner's benefit must remain sanctioned until they recomply.
Note Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support can only be paid to one person. The YSSU will need to regrant Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support to the young person who has recomplied and pay them 50% of the rate the couple got prior to the sanction being imposed. The full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment can also be paid to the young person who has recomplied.
If the other sanctioned person recomplies, increase this rate to 100% from the date that this young person recomplies.
For more information see:
- Paying other assistance during an activity obligations sanction
- Returning incentive payments after a sanction
- Sanctions and youth money management

chunks.title: Credit union — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Credit union

chunks.title: Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities
After a discussion with the young person, you will need to determine the most appropriate education, training or work-based learning activity for them to undertake. To decide what activities are most appropriate, you should consider:
- the young person's individual circumstances
- whether the activity is suitable for the young person
- other information already held about the young person (for example a plan may have been established by Oranga Tamariki)
- information provided by Independent Assessment Provider
- the young person's overall future goals and needs
A young person must undertake education, training or work-based learning to receive Youth Payment, unless they qualify for an exemption. You do not need the young person's agreement to the activities you set for them.

chunks.title: Deciding ordinarily resident — youth payment
chunks.text: A client must be ordinarily resident in New Zealand on the date they apply to get a Youth Payment. On an ongoing basis a client must continue to remain ordinarily resident in New Zealand to receive their benefit. Some exceptions occur when the client leaves New Zealand to live overseas permanently in which case they may be eligible for a continuation of their payments under a Social Security Agreement.

chunks.title: Attributes associated with being ordinarily resident — youth payment
chunks.text: Ordinarily resident incorporates a number of factors. The key attributes to being ordinarily resident in New Zealand is that a person must have a close and clear connection to New Zealand on the date they apply for a Youth Payment. Some other key attributes that indicate that a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand include: - their physical presence in New Zealand is other than casually or as a traveller - there is some intention to remain in New Zealand for a settled purpose - despite temporary absences from New Zealand they regularly or customarily live in New Zealand - they prefer residence in New Zealand to any other country (a person cannot be ordinarily resident in 2 countries at the same time) Where it is not clear if a client is ordinarily resident you may need to ask the client further information. Some of the following questions may help to get more information: - if the client is going overseas, what are their intentions towards New Zealand (sighting return air tickets is a good indication) - the length of time they spend in New Zealand compared to their periods of absence and the reasons for the absences - property ownership (as this tends to suggest permanent ties with a place), including other asset ownership (for example boats, cars or caravans) - where are their cash assets principally held (New Zealand banks or investment entities or overseas based holdings) - is their income earned in New Zealand or overseas, and are they tax resident in New Zealand (see Inland Revenue New Zealand tax residence guide IR292) - are they still on an electoral role and vote in central and local body elections - do they have a personal commitment to New Zealand (for example their involvement in their immediate and extended family community, community events, clubs and other groups) The attributes associated with being ordinarily resident can also be used after a Youth Payment is granted if there is some indication the client may no longer be ordinarily resident in New Zealand.

chunks.title: How to decide — youth payment
chunks.text: Whether a person is ordinarily resident in New Zealand is a question of fact and degree. You must consider all the factors of each individual case and decide whether they show a clear and close connection to New Zealand. You may need to ask more questions (or seek clarification of information you have) to get all the relevant information and then you must weigh up all the facts, and make a decision having regard to the attributes associated with a person being ordinarily resident in New Zealand (see above). If, on the balance of facts you are not sure if the client is ordinarily resident in New Zealand ask for advice from Helpline or your manager client service delivery before you make your decision. A determination on whether a person is ordinarily resident is a discretionary legislative provision, and the client should be given the benefit of the doubt in situations where their ordinary residence isn't clear.

chunks.title: Non-residentially qualified — youth payment
chunks.text: You should consider other main benefits if a client does not meet the residence requirements for a Youth Payment. An Emergency Benefit may be granted on the grounds of hardship to a client who does not meet the period of residence requirement. However, the person must generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and meet the hardship qualifications for Emergency Benefit.

chunks.title: Definite offer of employment — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Definite offer of employment
Where the client has stated that they had a definite offer of employment (supplied in writing) to get permanent residence, you must investigate fully what happened to the job offer. This should include contacting the employer.
Where the offer of employment was withdrawn or employment terminated through circumstances beyond the control of the client you may consider granting Youth Payment provided the client meets the two year residence criteria or Youth Payment on grounds of hardship if they do not meet the two years continuous residence.
Immigration New Zealand will decide on any action to be taken with regard to the client's residence status. In the meantime you need to look at all the circumstances of the client as to whether you can grant benefit assistance.
Note if the client has resided in New Zealand for two years assess the client's entitlement to Youth Payment in the usual manner.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Granting on grounds of hardship

chunks.title: Te Kura o Te Aho Pounamu - Distance school — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Te Kura o Te Aho Pounamu - Distance school
For young people studying at Te Kura - Distance school full-time is:
- 4 subjects at NCEA level 1 or
- 3 subjects at NCEA levels 2 and 3
## Work-based learning and other approved training
For work-based learning and all other types of training, full-time means the young person must be engaged for 30-40 hours.

chunks.title: Definition of "parents" — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Definition of "parents"
For the purposes of Youth Payment, parents in relation to a young person:
- means the parent or guardians or other person who had the care of the young person most recently before the young person turned 16 years and
- includes any other parent, guardian, or former guardian, willing to have financial responsibility for the young person
When a young person is in the care of Oranga Tamariki or other authorised care agency, the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki or any other body responsible for the care of the young person under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 is not considered to be a parent.

chunks.title: Developmental activities — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Developmental activities
To provide additional support to the young person, developmental activities may also be included alongside other activities that a young person is undertaking. A young person can undertake other developmental activities and still be considered to be meeting their youth activity obligations as long as:
- they are continuing to participate, or are available to undertake, full-time education, training or work-based learning
- you have assessed that the young person needs to address other needs while they undertake full-time education, training or work-based learning and
- the young person agrees to participate
Note a young person can be asked to participate in developmental activities but they cannot be required to. The young person cannot be sanctioned for not agreeing to undertake a developmental activity.
Other developmental activities include (but are not limited to):
- Interpersonal skills - increasing a young persons people or communication skills
- Self-motivation (eg confidence or motivation courses)
- Writing and language - young people who have learned English as their second language may require extra tuition to complement their main education or training activity
- Counselling/family violence related programmes
- Drug and alcohol counselling
- Social rehabilitation programmes
Note the Limited Services Volunteers programme will generally not be appropriate for young people receiving Youth Payment unless they are transitioning out of the service and have job seeking as their destination.

chunks.title: Discharged from care — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Discharged from care
When a 16 or 17 year old young person has been discharged from the care of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki (or other authorised agency), they can receive Youth Payment when they are no longer subject to:
- an agreement under section 140 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
- an order under section 78, section 101 or section 283(n) of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 or
- a sole guardianship order under section 110 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989
In these cases the young person does not need to prove the relationship breakdown with either their parents or caregivers because it has already been established through Oranga Tamariki. An Independent Assessment Provider report is not required.
## Documentation
In all discharge cases, before granting Youth Payment, make sure that all relevant documentation has been received from Oranga Tamariki confirming orders have been discharged.
Encourage Oranga Tamariki to liaise with you regarding the time of discharge from care to make sure the benefit starts from the correct date.

chunks.title: Earning incentive payments — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Earning incentive payments
Young people receiving Youth Payment can earn the following incentive payments:
- education incentive of $10 a week
- budgeting incentive of $10 a week
## Education incentive
A young person on the Youth Payment can earn the education incentive if:
- their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service have confirmed to YSSU that since they started receiving the Youth Payment they have continuously attended and participated in either education, training or work-based learning for at least 6 calendar months
## Budgeting incentive
A young person on the Youth Payment can earn the budgeting incentive if:
- their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service have confirmed to YSSU that since they started receiving the Youth Payment they have attended and participated in discussions on budgeting with the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service provider for at least 3 calendar months
and
- they have attended and completed a budgeting programme (this can have completed before the client started getting their benefit)
A young person can earn the budgeting incentive after 3 months of satisfactorily meeting their budgeting requirements.
Incentive payments are non-taxable allowances and are not considered chargeable income for Extra help and hardship assistance.
For more information see:
- Removing incentive payments
- Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose
- Incentive payments can continue
- Restoring incentive payments
- Obligations

chunks.title: Earning the right to receive payment directly — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Earning the right to receive payment directly
Young people who are subject to youth money management can earn the right to have their Young Parent Payment, incentives, family tax credit, best start tax credit and any Extra Help paid directly to them.
The young person can gain control of their payment if:
- they have demonstrated continued compliance with their obligations and
- their service provider or Ministry of Social Development 'in-house' service considers that they are financially competent
A young person who has earned control over their payment has the choice to have their benefit paid directly to them and they will be responsible for paying their costs.
## Young people aged 18 years
Young people who have turned 18 years and have chosen to stay on Youth Payment to complete their course of study, training or work-based learning, can opt out of youth money management (unless they are subject to a sanction). This applies even if they haven't been getting Youth Payment long enough to earn all their incentive payments.
For more information see:
- Continued compliance with their obligations
- Assessed as financially competent
- Opting out of youth money management

chunks.title: Temporary employment at less than a disqualifying rate — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Temporary employment at less than a disqualifying rate
Where a young person has temporary employment during the initial stand-down period, and their level of income (when charged against the benefit) allows for a part payment of benefit, there is no need to re-assess the young person's initial stand-down.
For more information see:
- Changes and reviews, Treatment of income Income reduces the benefit to a 'nil' rate

chunks.title: Enrolled in secondary education — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Enrolled in secondary education
Young people applying for the Youth Payment who are enrolled full-time in a course of secondary education do not have an initial stand-down imposed.
For more information see:
- No stand-down applies

chunks.title: Entering a refuge — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Entering a refuge
When a young person is applying for Youth Payment after entering a refuge following the break-up of a relationship, the initial stand-down period can be waived.
Generally the young person must enter the refuge immediately following the break-up of their relationship. This means entering the refuge within a period similar in duration to the stand-down (that is, within seven to 14 days). Where there is a delay between the separation and the young person entering the refuge, general commencement date rules apply.
In this context a refuge is emergency accommodation provided by an agency or organisation. This includes (but is not restricted to) agencies such as Women's Refuge, Home and Family Society, Emergency Housing Trusts, Iwi and cultural organisations, and church organisations.
Note that accommodation provided by family or friends of the young person is not considered to be refuge accommodation.
For more information see:
- Commencement date

chunks.title: Entitlement date — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Entitlement date
The entitlement date for the Youth Payment is usually:
- the day after employment ceased (that is, after any holiday pay, sick pay, etc. has expired)
- the day after separation or financial assistance from their partner ceased
- the day after weekly work-related insurance payments ceased
- the day after full-time study or student allowances ceased
- the day after last exam
- the day after school finished (if young person has just left school)
- the day they enrolled in full-time secondary or tertiary education or other training course approved by the Ministry
- the day after the date the living costs component of student loan was paid to
- the date of arrival in New Zealand (if young person has returned to New Zealand)
- date of incapacity
- day after moved out of parent's home
- the date of release from prison or
- the day after discharged from Oranga Tamariki care
Where the young person has more than one event, you use the later event for their entitlement date.

chunks.title: Example couple getting Youth Payment — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Example couple getting Youth Payment
The following example shows how to pay a couple getting Youth Payment who is subject to youth money management.
Step 1
Add up costs
$400.00 rent$40.00 car repayment$20.00 hire purchase
Total costs: $460
Step 2
Deduct Extra Help from total costs
$460.00
less: $150.00Accommodation Supplement
less: $80.00Temporary Additional Support
equals $230
Total costs not getting assistance for: $230.00
Step 3
Divide by 2
$230 divided by 2equals $115
Amount each partner must contribute: $115
Step 4
Partner 1 not getting any Extra Help
Must contribute $115 towards the redirection of costs (this will be taken of the highest cost). Set up the following redirection:
$115.00 towards rent
Step 5
Partner 2 getting Extra Help
Must contribute $345.00 ($115 + $150 Accommodation Supplement + $80 Temporary Additional Support) towards everything else. Set up the following redirections:
$285.00 for rent$40.00 for car repayments$20 for hire purchase
After the above is complete, process the in-hand allowance for each young person on the balance remaining of their individual payment.
Note a young person cannot review the decision on how the Youth Payment is paid to them.

chunks.title: Examples of good and sufficient reason — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Examples of good and sufficient reason
Examples of a good and sufficient reason include:
- the young person's parents have moved to an area where there is low employment or employment related training prospects and the parents are unable to financially support the young person
- a serious relationship breakdown has taken place between the young person and a member of the family and someone is now at risk
- the young person has been orphaned and is living independently
- the young person has had professional advice for good reasons (for example on advice from their health practitioner) to live away from other members of the family and their parents are unable to financially support them
- the young person has been removed from home on advice from the Police that they were at risk and the young person is unable to be financially supported by their parents
You must send the young person to an Independent Assessment Provider for an assessment and recommendation before granting a Youth Payment.
The following reasons alone are not considered to be 'good and sufficient' reasons:
- the young person's parents can no longer afford to keep the young person
- the parent's house is too small
- the young person has finished a training course
- the young person is a full-time student who does not qualify for a Student Allowance because of high parental income or failure of previous studies

chunks.title: Exemptions from activity obligations — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Exemptions from activity obligations
Exemptions from activity obligations recognise that there are a number of common reasons why it is unreasonable to expect a young person to meet their activity obligations for a specified period.
Young people getting Youth Payment can be granted a full or partial exemption from their activity obligations for the following reasons on the recommendation from their service provider or Ministry of Social Development 'in-house' service:
- Caring full-time for a partner with a health condition, injury or disability
- Court imposed conditions
- Family violence
- Recent bereavement of partner
- Recent separation from partner
- Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
- Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
The young person can be granted a temporary exemption from some or all of their activity obligations. Proof may be required before an exemption is granted.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions
## YSSU role in exemptions
The YSSU will make the final decision to decline or approve any exemption.
## Duration of the exemption
Each exemption has a specific duration for which it can be granted. In some cases these can be extended if appropriate.
Note the duration of an exemption for a young person with a health condition, injury or disability will be based on the next reassessment date recorded on the medical certificate by their health practitioner.
For an overview of the exemptions see:
- Table of exemptions
## Getting an incentive payment
If the young person is getting an incentive payment and then qualifies for an exemption, you will need to decide if they can continue getting the payment.

chunks.title: Payments that can be redirected — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Payments that can be redirected
Any ongoing Extra help (except Disability Allowance) paid to a young person are included in the redirection of payment if the young person is under youth money management, for example:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- Winter Energy Payment
Note because Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support can only be paid to one person, for couples, the person getting them is generally responsible for any debt created.
## Payments that are not redirected
The following payments are not redirected and can be paid to the young person or a supplier (as appropriate):
- Disability Allowance
- one-off payments of hardship assistance, for example Special Needs Grant for food
- any Advance Payment of Benefit

chunks.title: Factors to consider when recommending payment distribution between payment cards and in-hand allowance — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Factors to consider when recommending payment distribution between payment cards and in-hand allowance
When making a recommendation as to how a young person's payment should be distributed between the in-hand allowance and the payment card, the Service Provider will consider the young person's circumstances, including (but not limited to) the following:
- what level of need does the client have for costs that can be met through the payment card eg if they are boarding and their food is covered they may not need as much money on the payment card as most of their main meals will be covered
- what essential costs does the client need to meet from their in-hand allowance eg do they have clear essential needs such as travel costs on which they need to spend their in-hand allowance, or do they have access to a food supplier (eg fruit and vegetable market) where it would be more cost effective for them to shop, however that supplier does not accept the payment card
- does the client have sufficient budgeting skills to ensure their in-hand allowance is prioritised to meet essential costs, such as food and groceries, where necessary
- has the client demonstrated poor budgeting skills in relation to the way they have been using their current distribution of payment eg has the client failed to provide food or other essentials for their children out their in-hand allowance, where this has been necessary due to them not having enough credit on their payment card
YSSU makes the final decision as to how the young person's payment will be distributed between the payment card and in-hand allowance, taking into account the information supplied by the young person's Service Provider.
When making this decision, YSSU must be satisfied that the distribution between the two payment methods is reasonable given the client's individual circumstances.
For more information see:
- Redirection of Youth Payment
- Method of payment
- Incentive payments

chunks.title: Family breakdown — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Family breakdown
To receive a Youth Payment a single young person must meet all of the qualifications and have a parental support gap.
A 16 or 17 year old is considered to have a parental support gap when:
- their relationship with their parents (or guardians) has broken down and
- none of them is prepared to support the young person financially
It is important that the relationship breakdown must be serious.
Serious situations include:
- issues of health and safety
- sexual, physical or emotional abuse
- situations where the young person or their family would be at risk if they were to return home
Young people must be sent for an assessment with the Independent Assessment Provider to help you determine whether there has been a serious breakdown in the young person's relationship with their parents.
For more information see:
- Independent Assessment Provider
Exception when a young person has been discharged from Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency care they do not require an Independent Assessment. This is because the relationship breakdown has already been established by Oranga Tamariki.

chunks.title: Family Stream — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Family Stream
The purpose of the Family Stream is to help reunite families in New Zealand by granting residence to the family members of New Zealand citizens and residents. The family member living in New Zealand sponsors the applicant applying for permanent residence.
The Family Stream includes Family categories (Partnership, Parent, Sibling and Adult Child, Dependent Child and Parent Retirement Category).
For clients granted permanent residence under the Family Stream (except the Dependent Child Category and the Parent Retirement Category), the sponsor has signed a declaration they will support the client and their family (if any) for up to five years of residence in New Zealand or until they can sustain themselves.
Clients must have 2 years (24 months) continuous residence in New Zealand to be entitled to Youth Payment. Until they have met this requirement Youth Payment on grounds of hardship may be considered.
Note if a client has permanent residence and already meets the two years continuous residence, assess the client for Youth Payment in the usual manner.
When assessing the client's entitlement to Youth Payment on grounds of hardship, the sponsor's financial circumstances is not used in the assessment. However, any assistance given to the client and family (if any) must be used in the assessment.
Youth Payment on grounds of hardship is both income and asset tested. To assess a client's entitlement to Youth Payment on grounds of hardship confirmation of the client's income and assets declared on the application for permanent residence are required from Immigration New Zealand.
Despite the requirement for immigrants to maintain themselves for a number of years, they may still be able to access assistance as a non-beneficiary.
If the client has a change in personal resources, confirmation of that change is required.
For more information see:
- Permanent residence
- Granting on grounds of hardship
- Change in personal resources

chunks.title: Family violence — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Family violence
A young person may be exempt from meeting all of their activity obligations where their living circumstances have changed because of family violence. This is a full exemption.
## Definition of family violence
Family violence is a terms used to describe violence within the family and close personal relationships.
Family violence covers a broad range of controlling behaviours which typically involve fear, intimidation and emotional deprivation.
Family violence is defined as:
- physical abuse
- sexual abuse
- psychological abuse including but not limited to intimidation, harassment, damage to property or threats of physical, sexual or psychological abuse
## Proof
Young people who have recently left situations of family or domestic violence will not have to provide proof.
If a young person still needs an exemption after 3 months you can ask for proof.
Proof can include statements from:
- their doctor
- their church
- their lawyer
- the police
- Women's Refuge
- any other person or organisation that is able to support the young person's application
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 3 months.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'family violence'.
## Receiving an incentive payment
If the young person is receiving an incentive payment and then qualifies for an exemption, you will need to decide if they can continue to receive it.

chunks.title: Financial support from a sponsor — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Financial support from a sponsor
Where the client was granted permanent residence because a sponsor was to support them for their first 2 to 5 years in New Zealand (supplied in writing), you must contact the sponsor to confirm the situation.
Note if the client has resided in New Zealand for 2 years, no contact with the sponsor is required, and assess the client's entitlement to Youth Payment in the usual manner.
You will also need to obtain information from the Immigration New Zealand to confirm the reason for granting permanent residence. Ensure you have the consent of the client before contacting Immigration New Zealand.
Once confirmed, assess Youth Payment in the usual manner taking into account all other information provided by Immigration New Zealand.
Generally, where the client elects not to accept support from the sponsor without a valid reason decline the application for Youth Payment or grant the Youth Payment at a reduced rate.

chunks.title: Full or partial exemptions — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Full or partial exemptions
Exemptions are temporary. A young person may be granted a full or partial exemption from meeting some or all of their activity obligations on the recommendation from their service provider or Ministry of Social Development 'in-house' service.
The YSSU will make the final decision to decline or approve any exemption.
Before you grant an exemption, check if the exemption reason is full or partial (or both).
## Partial exemptions
The young person can be granted a partial exemption from their activities when they can participate in some, but not all, of their activity obligations.
For example, a young person granted a partial exemption from education, training or work-based learning, may still be required to:
- attend a budgeting programme and
- meet with their service provider or Ministry 'in-house' service
## Duration
Each exemption has a maximum duration. The period the exemption is granted for depends on the young person's circumstances.
At the time of granting the exemption the young person should be:
- advised of the temporary nature of the exemption and
- if appropriate, a date scheduled to review the exemption
