At the review you should discuss the young person's circumstances and consider whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption for a further period. You can ask the young person to provide proof that their exemption should be extended.
Note the maximum duration of an exemption for a young person due to a health condition, injury or disability is based on the next reassessment date recorded by their health practitioner in the medical certificate
## For an overview of the exemptions see:
- Table of exemptions

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason before initiating an activity obligations failure — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Good and sufficient reason before initiating an activity obligations failure
You need to be satisfied that the young person does not have a good and sufficient reason for failing to meet their activity obligations, based on the information you have, before you initiate an activity obligations failure.
The guiding principle in determining 'good and sufficient' reason is one of 'reasonableness'. Having considered the circumstances, was it reasonable for the young person not to have met their obligations?
Good and sufficient reasons may include (but are not limited to), that the young person:
- was temporarily medically unfit and they have a medical certificate that shows this
- had a death or illness in the immediate family
- could not realistically transport themselves on the day, due to unforeseen circumstances
- was dependent on the provision of assistance by Work and Income "in-house" service or the service provider to complete the activity, and that assistance was not supplied
- had an unexpected event occur on that day, such as providing care for a sick relative
Decide in favour of the young person if any doubt remains.
If you are aware that the young person has a good and sufficient reason, do not initiate an activity obligations failure.
Note the Youth Service Support Unit (YSSU) makes the decision to apply an activity obligations failure.
If the young person does not have a good and sufficient reason, see:
- Sanctions for single people
- Sanctions for couples - one person fails
- Sanctions for couples - both fail

chunks.title: Granting on grounds of hardship — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Granting on grounds of hardship
If a young person does not meet the residence qualification of 2 years continuous residence, they must meet the following criteria to be granted Youth Payment:
- they must be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident
- they must be suffering hardship
- they do not qualify for any other benefit and
- they are unable to earn sufficient income to support themselves or their partner
Note the young person may qualify for an Emergency Benefit if they:
- are under restricted criteria
- are in New Zealand on a temporary permit or temporary entry class visa (not a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident)
For more information see:
- Refugees and protected persons
## SWIFTT
To identify young people granted Youth Payment on grounds of hardship; enter entitlement code 11 - hardship and relevant reason for emergency code in SDT1A screen.
To decide if a young person is suffering hardship see:
- Hardship criteria

chunks.title: Hardship exceptional circumstances — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Hardship exceptional circumstances
You can disregard some or all of a young person's cash assets when you are looking at granting Youth Payment on grounds of hardship. You can only do this if you think that there are exceptional circumstances.
Things you need to consider:
- if you refuse to grant Youth Payment on grounds of hardship to a young person, will it have a serious effect on the young person's health or welfare
- if you refuse to grant Youth Payment on grounds of hardship to a young person, would the likely alternatives cost the Government more
- can the young person realise (that is sell or get access to their cash assets) for more than the appropriate cash asset limit
- is the need for Youth Payment temporary
- what is the total amount of the young person's assets, including assets that are not cash assets and
- what are the other matters that you would consider relevant to determining whether hardship exists
Every case has to be looked at on its own merits.
If you have a case where you think you can disregard some or all of a young person's cash assets, contact Helpline to discuss the circumstances before you make your decision.

chunks.title: In a training course approved by the Ministry — youth payment
chunks.text:
## In a training course approved by the Ministry
Young people participating in a training programme that the Chief Executive has approved do not have an initial stand-down imposed.
A training course approved for the purposes of assessing whether to waive an initial stand-down for Youth Payment is:
- employment-related training or
- tertiary study
Note this differs from the definition of approved training for the purpose of assessing the qualification for Youth Payment. Approved training for qualifications is employment-related training only.
For more information see:
- Qualifications In or available for work based training
- Qualifications In or available for tertiary education

chunks.title: In-hand allowance — youth payment
chunks.text: When a young person is getting Youth Payment with youth money management, they can get up to $50 a week paid directly to them as an in-hand allowance. After the young person's accommodation, service costs and lawful debts are paid by redirection, the balance of payment, if any, is divided between the young person's payment card and their in-hand allowance. The maximum amount that can be paid direct to a young person as an in-hand allowance is $50.

chunks.title: Distribution of payment after redirections — youth payment
chunks.text: Generally, when there is more than $50 available after all of a young person's redirections have been taken out, $50 is paid directly to the young person and the remainder is placed on their payment card. This is unless YSSU thinks that another distribution would be more appropriate for the young person. Youth Service providers are responsible for making recommendations to YSSU on how their clients' payments should be divided between the payment card and the in-hand allowance. When doing this, providers consider what would be the best distribution for the young person, given their individual circumstances. YSSU then makes the final decision on how the young person's payment will be distributed, taking into account the information supplied by the young person's service provider.

chunks.title: Example 1 — youth payment
chunks.text: A young person renting has $85 left after their accommodation and service costs and any debts have been paid. A maximum of $50 can be paid directly to the young person. However, the service provider wants to make sure the young person has money to buy enough food for themselves. The young person lives within walking distance of the school they are attending and does not have transport costs to get there. The provider discusses with the young person in their budgeting sessions what their spending habits are, and the young person advises them they go to the market to get fruit and vegetables. The provider decides to recommend the young person gets a $25 in-hand allowance and will check with them that they are still going to the market and have enough food with $60 on their payment card. YSSU agrees with the recommendation and pays the client a $25 in-hand allowance, and puts $60 on the payment card.

chunks.title: Example 2 — youth payment
chunks.text: A young person in a boarding situation has $70 left after their board costs (which include food) and any debts have been paid. The young person has transport costs to get to school. The young person buys their own personal toiletry items from the supermarket. After discussions with the young person, the provider recommends paying a $50 in-hand allowance to the young person and placing $20 on the payment card to be used to purchase their personal toiletry items. YSSU agrees with the recommendation and pays the client a $50 in-hand allowance and puts $20 on the payment card.

chunks.title: Altering the distribution of payment for existing clients already subject to youth money management — youth payment
chunks.text: If, at any time, a Youth Service provider considers that the current distribution of an existing client's payment between the payment card and in-hand allowance is inappropriate for the client's circumstances, they can recommend to YSSU that the distribution be altered. When determining whether it is appropriate to recommend a client's payment distribution be altered, providers must take into account a range of factors. Note a young person cannot review the decision on how the Youth Payment is paid to them.

chunks.title: In or available for approved training — youth payment
chunks.text:
## In or available for approved training
A young person can receive Youth Payment if they are available for or enrolled full-time in an approved training programme and meet the other qualifications.
For youth activity obligations purposes approved training is defined as employment-related training.
Generally the training will lead to a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or other higher qualification.
While in approved training and receiving Youth Payment, the young person has activity obligations, including regularly attending the programme.
In SWIFTT the Youth Payment activity should be recorded as 'Approved training'. An expiry date should be added for the end of the training course. At this time you should reassess the Youth Payment, for example, check with the young person if they intend to undertake another training course.
For more information see:
- Obligations
- Obligations Approved training
- Obligations NCEA Level 2 or equivalent qualification
- Young person turns 18 years old

chunks.title: In or available for secondary education — youth payment
chunks.text:
## In or available for secondary education
A young person can receive Youth Payment if they are enrolled in or available for a full-time course of secondary education, and meet the other qualifications. Secondary education includes composite schools, correspondence schools, and secondary school.
Generally they will be working towards a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification.
Young people in secondary education do not qualify for the Youth Payment if they have moved from their parents home to improve their educational prospects, for example if they have moved to another town to a more prestigious school.
While in school and receiving Youth Payment, the young person has activity obligations, including regularly attending classes and completing assignments. For more information see:
- Obligations
- Obligations Secondary education
In SWIFTT the Youth Payment activity should be recorded as 'Enrolled in Secondary Education'. The payment will automatically expire at the end of the school year. At this time you should reassess the Youth Payment, for example, check with the young person if they are intending to return to school.
## School holidays
Young people intending to return to secondary education in the next academic year can be paid Youth Payment during the summer holidays. Any incentive payments earned will continue to be paid over this period.
Note a service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service may require a young person to undertake other activities that work towards NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualifications during the summer break.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Young person turns 18 years old
- Obligations NCEA Level 2 or equivalent qualification or higher qualification

chunks.title: In or available for tertiary education — youth payment
chunks.text:
## In or available for tertiary education
A young person can receive Youth Payment if they are enrolled in or available for a full-time course of tertiary education, and meet the other qualifications. Tertiary education includes study at universities and polytechnics.
Generally the course of study will lead to a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or other higher qualification.
While in tertiary education and receiving Youth Payment, the young person has activity obligations, including regularly attending lectures and completing assignments.
In SWIFTT the Youth Payment activity should be recorded as 'Approved Training'. An expiry date should be added for the earlier of the end of the academic year or the last exam (if the course finishes half-way through the year). At this time you should reassess the Youth Payment, for example, check with the young person if they intend to continue studying.
## School holidays
Young people intending to return to tertiary education in the next academic year can be paid Youth Payment during the summer holidays. Any incentive payments earned will continue to be paid over this period.
Note a service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service may require a young person to undertake other activities that work towards NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualifications during the summer break.
For more information see:
- Obligations
- Obligations Tertiary education
- Obligations NCEA Level 2 or equivalent qualification or higher qualification
- Young person turns 18 years old

chunks.title: In or available for work-based learning — youth payment
chunks.text:
## In or available for work-based learning
A young person can receive Youth Payment if they are in or available for, full-time approved work-based learning and meet the other qualifications.
Generally the work-based learning will lead to a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification.
In SWIFTT the Youth Payment activity should be recorded as 'work-based learning'. An expiry date should be added for the course end date. At this time you should reassess the Youth Payment, for example, check with the young person if they intend to undertake another training course.
For more information see:
- Obligations
- Obligations Work-based learning
- Obligations NCEA Level 2 or equivalent qualification or higher qualification
- Young person turns 18 years old

chunks.title: Incentive payments — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Incentive payments
If a young person is under youth money management, any incentive payments earned are included in the redirection of their payment.
Young people can earn incentive payments for demonstrating a commitment to their activity obligations.
A young person getting Youth Payment can earn the following incentives:
- budgeting - $10 a week
- education - $10 a week

chunks.title: School and tertiary holidays — youth payment
chunks.text:
## School and tertiary holidays
Any incentive payments earned by the young person will continue to be paid during any school or tertiary holiday periods while they are receiving Youth Payment.
For more information see:
- Removing incentive payments
- Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose
- Payment Incentive payments

chunks.title: Income criteria — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Income criteria
A young person applying for the Youth Payment must have:
- no income or
- if they have income it must not fully abate the Youth Payment
## Partner in employment
If a young person qualifies for Youth Payment and they have a partner who is in employment (full-time or part-time), the partner's income is charged against the benefit rate.
For more information on charging income see:
- Charging income

chunks.title: Income from overseas — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Income from overseas
When a young person has been working overseas within the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before their entitlement date you include this in their average weekly income.
If the young person cannot provide verification of their earnings, accept the information provided on their application for benefit. For help to convert foreign currency to the equivalent New Zealand dollars see the instructions below.
There is no ability to take higher living costs into account. If the young person is in financial hardship during an initial stand-down they can apply for a Special Needs Grant. For more information see: Assistance during an Initial stand down and/or benefit application process
## Receiving a benefit from overseas
When a young person has been receiving an overseas benefit or pension within the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before their entitlement date you include this in their average weekly wage.
If the overseas benefit or pension payments have stopped and the young person cannot provide verification of their payments, accept the information provided on their application for benefit. There is no requirement to obtain verification through International Services.
Note when the overseas benefit or pension payments are continuing and the young person cannot provide verification, you will need to verify details of these payments. For further assistance contact International Services

chunks.title: In Oranga Tamariki care — youth payment
chunks.text:
## In Oranga Tamariki care
Young people who are in the care or sole guardianship of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki cannot receive Youth Payment as the cost of the young person's care is the responsibility of Oranga Tamariki.
The young person is not seen as independent.
When a young person has been discharged from Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency care they do not require an Independent Assessment. This is because the relationship breakdown has already been established by Oranga Tamariki.
For more information see:
- Discharged from care

chunks.title: Independent Assessment Provider — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Independent Assessment Provider
The Independent Assessment Provider is required to provide an assessment and recommendation to MSD for young people who have applied for Youth Payment because of:
- a family breakdown or
- another good and sufficient reason (where appropriate)
## Involving parents
In all cases the Independent Assessment Provider will invite the parents/caregivers to discuss the application. Consent is not required from the applicant as schedule 6 of the Social Security Act 2018 allows MSD to investigate a claim for benefit.
If the applicant refuses to allow their parents to be interviewed without a satisfactory reason and there is not sufficient information to grant the benefit, MSD must decline the application.
The parent's invitation can be made by phone but must be followed up with a letter. When the parents/caregivers cannot be reached and do not make contact a further attempt must be made. Where the parents/caregivers still do not make contact or refuse to participate in the assessment other significant family members, adults or community groups (for example school counsellors) will be contacted.
The Independent Assessment Provider will detail all contact and attempts at contact in the Youth Payment assessment report.
Exception where the young person's parents are absent or there are care and protection concerns an assessment is not required. When a young person has been discharged from Oranga Tamariki or other authorised agency care they do not require an Independent Assessment. This is because the relationship breakdown has already been established by Oranga Tamariki.
## Disputes about recommendations made by the Independent Assessment Provider
MSD decides who can get a Youth Payment using information gotten in the assessment report and the recommendation of the Independent Assessment Provider.
If MSD have concerns about the recommendations made by the Independent Assessment Provider, these should be discussed with them.
## Request to access the Youth Payment assessment report
The Youth Payment assessment report generally contains sensitive information that has been shared by the parties in confidence.
If one of those parties (i.e., a parent or guardian) requests a copy of the report, they may be able to access information about themselves in the report. MSD should take care to protect the other parties, particularly the young person who the report is about, and in some circumstances it may be appropriate to withhold the information requested.

chunks.title: Inform young person of their activity obligations — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Inform young person of their activity obligations
Before granting Youth Payment, a young person must be advised of their activity obligations arising from payment of the benefit.
Once the benefit has been granted, and the activity has been set for the young person, they must be advised of:
- the activity obligations they are required to meet and the specific activities that have been set for them (eg school, training, work-based learning, budgeting)
- the consequences of failing to comply with their activity obligations, in particular the sanctions that may be imposed and
- their right to review and dispute any decisions relating to a failure to comply with their activity obligations
The activity obligations cannot be enforced until the commencement date of Youth Payment.
Note the service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service is responsible for informing young people of their activity obligations.
For more information see:
- Obligations
- Youth activity obligations
- Activity obligations failures

chunks.title: Initial stand-down — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Initial stand-down
This is a period of up to a maximum of 2 weeks where the young person cannot get any benefit payment. The length of the stand-down depends on:
- the young person's average weekly income (before tax) in the 26 or 52 weeks immediately before the young persons entitlement date and
- the number of dependent children in their care at any time during the same period
The initial stand-down starts on the young person's entitlement date.
Note young people can choose an income assessment period of either 26 or 52 weeks to calculate their average weekly wage for the initial stand-down.
## For more information on the initial stand-down see:
- Average weekly income
- Previous dependent children
- Employment during stand-down
- Self-imposed stand-down
- Initial stand-down procedure
- Assistance during an initial stand-down and/or benefit application process
- No stand-down applies
- Deskfile Initial stand-down

chunks.title: Initial stand-down procedure — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Initial stand-down procedure
Step 1. Find the young person's entitlement date.
Step 2. Calculate the young person's average weekly income for a 26 and 52 week period.
Step 3. Find out whether the young person previously had any dependent children in their care at any time during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement to determine the correct 'family circumstances' to use to determine the stand-down period.
Step 4. Using the information from Steps 2 and 3, determine the initial stand-down for the young person over a 26 and 52 week period by looking at the Initial stand-down period chart in Deskfile.
Step 5. Use the calculation of average weekly income that gives the young person a lesser stand-down period.
Step 6. Apply the initial stand-down from the young person's entitlement date to find the commencement date.
Remember if you enter the correct information into SWIFTT it will automatically calculate the initial stand-down and commencement date for you.
Note if the young person previously had a dependent child (or children) in their care during the 26 and 52 weeks prior to their entitlement date you will need to use a work around. Contact Helpline for this information.

chunks.title: International or Humanitarian Stream — youth payment
chunks.text:
## International or Humanitarian Stream
The purpose of the International/Humanitarian stream is to fulfil New Zealand's obligations as a good international citizen. Included in this stream are United Nations mandated refugees who are approved under the annual Refugee Quota and asylum seekers who claim refugee or protection status in New Zealand.
The categories in this stream are the:
- Refugee Family Support Category
- Pacific Access Category
- Samoan Quota Scheme
- Victims of family violence or
- various other special policies for specific countries
The client does not usually have any assets or income. To assess a client's entitlement to Youth Payment confirmation of the client's income declared on the application for permanent residence is required from Immigration New Zealand.
Note if the client has not resided continuously in New Zealand for 2 years since being granted permanent residence, Youth Payment on grounds of hardship may be considered and assets declared on their application for permanent residence must be included in the assessment.
Once confirmed, assess Youth Payment in the usual manner taking into account all other information provided by Immigration New Zealand.

chunks.title: Introduction — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Introduction
Youth Payment is for 16 and 17 year old young people who:
- have no dependent children and
- are not being supported by their parents or
- are, or have been, married, in a civil union, or in a de facto relationship
The Youth Service Support Unit (YSSU) is responsible for making decisions on behalf of Work and Income and for the general administration of the Youth Payment.
While a young person is receiving Youth Payment they are case managed by a service provider (if one is assigned to them) or the Work and Income 'in-house' service. The service provider or the Work and Income 'in-house' service work closely with the YSSU and will make recommendations to assist the YSSU to make decisions.

chunks.title: Method of payment — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Method of payment
There are several ways that Youth Payment can be paid depending on whether the young person is subject to youth money management or not.
## Young person is not subject to youth money management
Where a young person is not subject to youth money management they can get their Youth Payment and any Extra Help paid directly to their bank account.
## Young person is subject to youth money management
If a young person is subject to youth money management the Youth Payment and any Extra help (except Disability Allowance) is paid via:
- payment directly to supplier (eg a payee redirection for accommodation costs, utility costs and lawful debts)
- in-hand allowance which is paid directly to the young person's bank account
- payment card - the young person is able to purchase food and groceries from approved suppliers
Note Disability Allowance is paid direct to the young person's bank account.
## Review of decision
A young person cannot review the decision on how the Youth Payment is paid to them.

chunks.title: Youth money management — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Youth money management
Youth money management is when a young person being paid a Youth Payment gets an in-hand allowance of up to $50 a week, with most of their payment being redirected to pay for their everyday living costs and any lawful debts. Any remainder is placed onto their payment card.
Young people will not be subject to youth money management and will have their full payment paid directly to them when they have:
- demonstrated continued compliance with their obligations and been assessed as being financially competent or
- opted out of youth money management because they have turned 18 years and have chosen to stay on Youth Payment and complete their course of study, training or work-based learning

chunks.title: Youth money management activity — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Youth money management activity
Young people are required to co-operate with their service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service in managing the spending of their Youth Payment and provide information as required.
The young person must
- attend and participate in regular one-on-one discussions on budgeting
and provide information on:
- their accommodation costs (for example rent, board) and service costs (for example power, phone)
- any other lawful debts and liabilities (for example court fines, Work and Income debts, Child Support payments, hire purchase)
- how they spend their in-hand allowance and
- how they spend any money allocated to their payment card
For more information see:
- Payment Youth money management
Young people will not be subject to youth money management and will have their full payment paid directly to their bank account when they have:
- been assessed as being financially competent or
- turned 18 years and have chosen to stay on Youth Payment and continue their course of study
For more information see:
- Payment Youth money management
- Payment Assessed as financially competent
- Qualifications Young person turns 18 years old

chunks.title: Must receive payment for six months — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Must receive payment for six months
A young person who has been granted Youth Payment who has not been receiving the payment for 6 months cannot qualify for a main benefit even if they turn 18 years. They must complete a minimum period of 6 months receiving Youth Payment before they can receive another main benefit.
This ensures that the young person is able to have a reasonable chance to move towards a qualification by participating in education, training or work-based learning and other youth activity obligations before they focus on obligations attached to other main benefits.
Example
A young person is granted Youth Payment at the age of 17 years and 8 months old.
When they turn 18 years old they will need to continue to receive Youth Payment for another 2 months to complete the 6 month minimum period. They can then be assessed for entitlement to other main benefits.
## Exception
A young person, who is receiving Youth Payment and then meets the criteria for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability, can be granted this benefit instead of Youth Payment without completing the minimum 6 months.
For more information see:
- Chooses to remain on Youth Payment past 18 years of age
- Age

chunks.title: Meeting education obligations — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Meeting education obligations
A young person is meeting their education obligations if they are in (or available for) full-time education, training or work-based learning, working towards a qualification registered at:
- level 2 on the New Zealand Qualification Framework (NZQF) (which includes NCEA Level 2)
- level 3 or higher on the New Zealand Qualification Framework
Note young people undertaking courses at level 1 on the New Zealand Qualification Framework are considered to be meeting their obligations as long as it is a qualification which will build towards a level 2 NZQF qualification.

chunks.title: Obligations — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Obligations
Young people receiving Youth Payment have the following obligations. They must:
- advise of any change in circumstances that affect their entitlement or rate of benefit payable and
- meet all of their activity obligations
Note young people may be able to get an exemption from some or all of their obligations where it is unreasonable to expect them to meet their obligations for a specified period.
For more information see:
- Change in circumstances
- Inform young person of their activity obligations
- Youth activity obligations
- Exemptions from activity obligations
- Activity obligations failures

chunks.title: Opting out of youth money management — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Opting out of youth money management
Young people who are not subject to a sanction will be able to get their full payment directly when they have:
- turned 18 years
- chosen to stay on Youth Payment to complete their course of study, training or work-based learning and
- provided written notice to their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service that they opt out of youth money management
This applies even if they haven't been getting Youth Payment long enough to have earned all the incentives available to them.
For more information see:
- Method of payment
- Payment

chunks.title: Pacific Access Category — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Pacific Access Category
The Pacific Access Category (PAC) allows for citizens of Tonga, Tuvalu and Kiribati (including their partners and dependent children) to be granted permanent residence in New Zealand.
Clients must have 2 years continuous residence at any one time since being granted permanent residence in New Zealand to be entitled to Youth Payment. Until they have met this requirement Youth Payment on grounds of hardship may be considered.
To assess a client's entitlement to Youth Payment on grounds of hardship, confirmation of the client's income and assets declared on the application for permanent residence is required from Immigration New Zealand.
Note if a client has permanent residence and already meets the 2 years continuous residence, assess the client for Youth Payment in the usual manner.

chunks.title: Parental support gap — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Parental support gap
A single young person must meet all of the qualifications and have a parental support gap to get a Youth Payment.
A 16 or 17 year old is considered to have a parental support gap when:
- each of their parents (or guardians) is unable to support them financially− for example, the young person's parents or guardians may be (but not limited to): deceasedin prisonin hospitaloverseas
- deceased
- in prison
- in hospital
- overseas
- the relationship with their parents (or guardians) has broken down, and none of them is prepared to support the young person financially
- transitioning from care under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989, via an extended care agreement, parenting order or guardianship order
- there is a good and sufficient reason why the young person cannot reasonably expect to be financially dependent on their parents or any other person− for example (but not limited to): the young person has been subject to family violence (physical, psychological, emotional or sexual) in their parent's or guardian's home
- the young person has been subject to family violence (physical, psychological, emotional or sexual) in their parent's or guardian's home
A young person is not considered to have a parental support gap if they are not in one of the circumstances outlined above, and have the option of living with a parent or guardian but choose not to.
You should use any Oranga Tamariki or other agency documentation or the Independent Assessment Provider report to assist you to make a decision while considering all the relevant information.
When a young person has been discharged from care, or other authorised agency care, they do not require an Independent Assessment. This is because being discharged from Oranga Tamariki care is considered to be an exceptional circumstance.
If a young person is married, in a civil union or considered to be in a de facto relationship, they do not have to have a parental support gap to qualify to get a Youth Payment.

chunks.title: Parents overseas — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Parents overseas
If the young person's parents are overseas the responsibility to support the young person should remain with the parents if:
- there has been no family breakdown and
- the decision to move overseas and leave the young person in New Zealand is planned and agreed between the young person and their parents or
- the decision to send the young person to New Zealand for education, or job prospects and the like, is planned and agreed between the young person and their parents
If the situation results in a family breakdown the young person may be able to receive a Youth Payment.
For more information see:
- Family breakdown
- What is financial support
- Independent

chunks.title: Paying other assistance during an activity obligations sanction — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Paying other assistance during an activity obligations sanction
Young people are not entitled to the following forms of assistance when a cancellation due to a grade 3 sanction has been imposed:
- Emergency Benefit
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
## Winter Energy Payment
The Winter Energy Payment is treated slightly different to other Extra help.
Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid in situations where a portion of main benefit continues to be paid. In some cases it can continue to be paid at the full couple rate in cases where one client has been fully sanctioned.
## Special Needs Grants
Young people are not entitled to Special Needs Grants if an activity obligations failure has been imposed.
The only exception to this is if a young person is sick or injured when a grade 3 sanction is imposed and they are incapable of participating in full-time employment or an approved activity for 6 weeks.
For more information see:
- Assistance during a non-entitlement period
- Assistance when a client is sanctioned
## Advance Payment of Benefit
Generally young people will not be entitled to advance payments of benefit when they have a 100% sanction imposed. This is because they will be contributing to their hardship through not recomplying.
The young person's first option to improve their financial situation is to recomply with their obligations and an advance cannot be paid when the young person has no means of repaying it.
## Assistance to transition into employment
Young people can get assistance to transition into employment if a sanction has been imposed and they meet the qualifications for it.
For more information see:
- Employment and work readiness Assistance to transition into employment

chunks.title: Payment process for couples — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Payment process for couples
Young people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship are granted Youth Payment in their own right. Youth Payment is not apportioned as are other benefits paid to people who are married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, for example Jobseeker Support.
Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support can only be granted to one of the young people in the couple.
The redirections need to be allocated equally because of the way the in-hand allowance and remainder are paid.
The following process shows how Youth Payment is paid when a couple is subject to youth money management:
## Step 2
Deduct the Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support from the total costs. This leaves the amount for which they do not get any assistance.
## Step 4
The partner who is getting Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support must contribute the amount they are receiving for each of these, plus half of the amount from step 3.
Note because Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support can only be paid to one person, the person getting them is generally responsible for any debt created.
## Step 5
The partner not getting any Extra help must contribute their half share of step 3. This amount will go to offset the highest cost.
Note a young person cannot review the decision on how the Youth Payment is paid to them.
For more information see:
- Example couple receiving Youth Payment

chunks.title: Payment process for single people — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Payment process for single people
The following process shows how Youth Payment is paid when a young person is subject to youth money management:
## Step 1
Youth Payment rate (minus any abatement or sanction) is established.
## Step 2
Any incentive payments earned is added.
## Step 3
Extra Help, such as Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support and Winter Energy Payment is added.
## Step 6
Disability Allowance is paid directly to the young person.
## Review of decision
A young person cannot review the decision on how the Youth Payment is paid to them.
For more information see:
- Payment process for couples
- Obligations Youth money management activity

chunks.title: Payment to the non-sanctioned partner — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Payment to the non-sanctioned partner
For married, civil union or de facto couples getting Youth Payment, their benefit is not apportioned.
When a young person has their Youth Payment sanctioned, the non-sanctioned partner will continue to get:
- their full Youth Payment and any incentive payments they have earned and
- where the other young person is subject to 100% suspension, 50% of the supplementary assistance the couple was entitled and the full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment
Note this may or may not be paid under youth money management.
Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Assistance can only be paid to one person. The YSSU will need to:
- regrant supplementary assistance to the non-sanctioned young person and pay at 50% of the rate the couple were getting prior to the sanction being imposed
- review each of the young persons' redirections
Where the non-sanctioned young person is already receiving the supplementary assistance, the YSSU will need to reduce the amount they are getting by 50% and review the non-sanctioned young person's redirections.
For more information see:
- Paying other assistance during an activity obligations sanction

chunks.title: Payment — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Payment
Youth Payment is paid weekly on a Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. Payment is from Monday to Sunday and is made one week in arrears.
Most young people getting Youth Payment will be under youth money management. This is when the young person gets an in-hand allowance of up to $50 a week, with the majority of their payment being redirected to pay for their everyday living costs and lawful debts.
For more information about how this is paid see:
- Youth money management
For young people who are not subject to youth money management, payment must be made directly to the young person.
It is a condition of getting a benefit that the young person provides a bank account number.
MSD can request the young person to provide an IRD number or evidence of their IRD number.
## Rate of payment
For the rate of Youth Payment that can be paid see:
- Deskfile Youth Payment rates

chunks.title: Clients without permanent residence or citizenship — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Clients without permanent residence or citizenship
Emergency Benefit may be paid to some categories of migrants who do not have permanent residence or citizenship eg people waiting for their application for refugee or protected person status to be approved.
For more information see:
- Proof of residence
- Emergency Benefit
- Refugees and protected persons
Note clients lawfully in New Zealand by virtue of a temporary permit or a temporary entry class visa only (ie they do not have permanent residence) are not entitled to any benefit assistance.
To assess a client's entitlement you will generally need to establish exactly what category of migrant they are.
Clients may be granted permanent residence under the following categories:
- Family Stream
- International/Humanitarian Stream
- Skilled/Business Stream
Note if you require further information about a client's application for permanent residence you must get consent from the client to contact Immigration New Zealand or the client should obtain the information themselves. Otherwise the application should be declined. You must not collect or disclose information regarding a client's application without the client's consent.
For more information see:
- Immigration status and supporting documents
- Immigration status [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Personal cash assets — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Personal cash assets
Where the client was granted permanent residence because they had personal cash assets you will need to obtain information from the Immigration New Zealand to confirm the reason for granting permanent residence. Ensure you have the consent of the client before contacting the Immigration New Zealand.
Once confirmed, assess Youth Payment or, if the client does not meet the 2 years continuous residence criteria, Youth Payment on grounds of hardship in the usual manner taking into account all other information provided by Immigration New Zealand.
If there is a significant drop in the client's cash assets declared, confirmation for the following should be requested:
- what cash assets were they referring to and
- what has happened to these cash assets
It is not acceptable for these cash assets to be used to purchase capital items such as a house, furniture or motor vehicle.
Settlement funds can be used to purchase capital items, as these are not the same as cash assets declared as personal resources.
Note if the client has resided in New Zealand for 2 years assess the client's entitlement to the Youth Payment in the usual manner.
For more information see:
- Proof of residence
- Qualifications
- Granting on grounds of hardship

chunks.title: Previous dependent children — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Previous dependent children
If a young person has previously had a dependent child (or children) in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application the child (or children) must be taken into account when determining the stand-down.
Note to qualify for Youth Payment the applicant cannot currently have any dependent children in their care.
For example a young person previously had a dependent child in their care at any time during the 26 or 52 weeks before application, the stand-down period will be based on a single person with one dependent child.
This is regardless of whether the child is still in the young person's care at the time of application.
For more information see:
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Calculating number of days — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Calculating number of days
When counting the number of days that a young person has been in prison or held on remand, you should include the date the young person:
- enters prison or held on remand and
- leaves prison or is released from remand
For more information see:
- Changes and reviews, Imprisonment Release from prison

chunks.title: Example one — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Example one
A young person participates in an approved activity from the beginning of week three of the non-entitlement period. The young person participates for a continuous period of six weeks and the remaining period of the 13 week non-entitlement is cancelled. After the follow up appointment with the young person the benefit ceases to be paid on a provisional basis.
## Example two
A young person participates in an approved activity from the beginning of week ten of the non-entitlement period. The young person participates in the approved activity for the remainder of the 13 week non-entitlement period (for three weeks). At the end of the 13 week non-entitlement period, the young person's benefit ceases to be paid on a provisional basis.

chunks.title: Qualifications — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Qualifications
A young person applying for Youth Payment must have no dependent children and be one of the following:
- single and in exceptional circumstances or
- single because they are divorced, have a dissolved civil union or are separated from their de facto partner or
- married, in a civil union or de facto relationship and not be married to, or in a civil union or de facto relationship with a specified beneficiary
To qualify for the Youth Payment the young person must be:
- aged 16 or 17 years old
- undertaking or is available for a full-time course of secondary or tertiary education, approved training or approved work-based learning leading to NCEA level 2, or an equivalent qualification (in the opinion of the Chief Executive) or a higher qualification
or
- would be available but the young person is in a situation that would qualify them for an exemption from the obligation to undertake education or training or work-based learning
- have continuously lived in New Zealand for 2 years or more at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident and
- have no income, or an income of less than the amount that would fully abate the benefit
To get Youth Payment on grounds of hardship, the young person must meet the above qualifications except for the residence criteria. However they must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident but have lived in New Zealand for less than 2 years
- be suffering hardship and
- not qualify for any other benefit

chunks.title: Getting an incentive payment — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Getting an incentive payment
If the young person is getting an incentive payment, and then qualifies for an exemption you will need to decide if they can continue getting it.

chunks.title: Duration — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Duration
This exemption is initially given for up to 28 days from the date of separation.
You can extend the exemption. Before you do this you should ask the young person to provide information to support the exemption continuing.
## Getting an incentive payment
If the young person is getting an incentive payment, and then qualifies for an exemption you will need to decide if they can continue getting the incentive payment.

chunks.title: Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period) — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
A young person can complete certain activities to get a provisional benefit if they are subject to a 13-week non-entitlement period due to having a grade three sanction imposed for failing to meet their activity obligations.
If a young person wants to recomply, MSD must make an approved activity available to them at the earliest opportunity.
There is no waiting period before an approved activity can start after a sanction has been imposed.
The young person must undertake an approved activity for a continuous period of six weeks or until the 13-week non-entitlement period ends (whichever is the earlier).
## Approved activity examples
Here are some examples that may be a suitable six-week approved activity for a young person:
- secondary education
- approved training
- work-based learning
- budgeting activity
- community activities
- part-time work or work experience (where they are not already in part-time work)
- a combination of any of the above
Note this list is an example only, an approved activity (or programme of suitable activities) should be relevant to the activity obligations failure and be fair and reasonable.
For when to grant or increase the benefit, see:
- Provisional benefit and end of non-entitlement period
For what to do when a young person cannot recomply due to sickness, see:
- Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption
Also see:
- Couple - both failed, one recomplies first
- Returning incentive payments after a sanction
- Sanctions and youth money management

chunks.title: Service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service role in recompliance — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service role in recompliance
The service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service will need to discuss with the young person the activities they need to undertake in order to recomply. To recomply they must:
- undertake the original activity (or activities if they have failed more than one obligation) if it is still available or
- if the original activity (or activities if they have failed more than one obligation) is not available, undertake another activity, to our satisfaction, that is the same as or substantially similar to the activity the young person failed to do
When a recompliance activity is allocated, MSD must:
- discuss with the young person what they need to do to satisfactorily undertake the recompliance activity and the implications of not doing this and
- make a note of the discussion
## Same or substantially similar activity
If the young person is unable to undertake the same activity that they failed to do, they must undertake to your satisfaction another activity that is the same as or substantially similar to the activity they failed to do.
The 'same or substantially similar to' means that any recompliance activity should, as much as possible, require the same amount of time, effort and commitment as that which the young person failed to complete.
## When to resume or increase the benefit
The YSSU will resume or increase the payment from the date the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service are satisfied that the young person has started the recompliance activity.
Some examples of this:
- if the recompliance activity is a one-off, such as attending an interview with the service provider, the payment would be resumed from the date the young person attended and participated in the activity
- if the recompliance activity is ongoing, such as attending school or a training programme, the young person must satisfactorily attend school or the training programme and the payment will be resumed from the date the young person started to attend
For what to do if a young person cannot recomply due to sickness see:
- Unable to recomply due to meeting the criteria for an exemption
Also see:
- Couple - both failed, one recomplies first
- Returning incentive payments after a sanction
- Sanctions and youth money management

chunks.title: Redirection of Youth Payment — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Redirection of Youth Payment
For young people subject to youth money management the Youth Payment and any ongoing Extra help must be redirected to pay for:
- the young person's accommodation and service costs, for example rent, board, power, phone
- the young person's lawful debts or other liabilities, for example Child Support payments, Work and Income debts
- food and groceries via a payment card
Note Disability Allowance is paid directly to the young person.
For more information see:
- Method of payment
- Extra help
- Payment process for single people
- Payment process for couples

chunks.title: Refugee Family Support Category — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Refugee Family Support Category
The Refugee Family Support Category allows for a quota of refugees' and protected persons' family members to be considered for permanent residence in New Zealand each year. A client may lodge an application for residence under this category if their New Zealand sponsor's registration was selected from the annual ballot.
Clients need to have been living continuously in New Zealand for 2 years to be entitled to Youth Payment. However, Youth Payment on the ground of hardship may be considered before they meet the 2 year requirement if the client meets all the other eligibility criteria for Jobseeker Support and can meet the relevant obligations.
Jobseeker Support on the ground of hardship is both income and asset tested.
When assessing the client's entitlement to Youth Payment on the ground of hardship, the sponsor's financial circumstances is not used in the assessment. However, any financial assistance given to the client and family (if any) from either their sponsor or from another party, must be used in the assessment.
It is important to note that, unlike other visa categories sponsors, under the Refugee Family Support Category have no obligation to financially support their relative.
The only obligation a sponsor under this category has is to make sure adequate accommodation for their relatives is available during the first 24 months of their relative's residence in New Zealand. Despite this requirement, the client may still be able to get assistance as a non-beneficiary.
If the client has a change in personal resources, confirmation of that change is required.

chunks.title: Refugee quota — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Refugee quota
Refugees with permanent residence are exempt from meeting the two years continuous residence criteria, so you should assess the client for Youth Payment in the usual manner.
Most refugees accepted as part of the United Nations quota receive permanent residence prior to arriving in New Zealand or during their period of resettlement at the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre. These clients do not usually have any income or assets.
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- Refugees and protected persons
- No stand-down applies

chunks.title: Refugees and protected persons — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Refugees and protected persons
In general a refugee or protected person cannot receive Youth Payment unless they have been granted permanent residence.
If a refugee or a protected person has permanent residence, assess them for Youth Payment in the usual manner. Refugees and protected persons with permanent residence are exempt from meeting the two years continuous residence criteria.
Note when a client leaves the Mangere Refugee Resettlement Centre no stand-down applies to the grant of the benefit.

chunks.title: Removing incentive payments — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Removing incentive payments
Incentive payments should be removed when the young person:
- is subject to a grade 1, 2 or 3 sanction
- is in hospital for longer than 13 weeks and they are receiving the hospital rate of payment
- moves from Young Parent Payment to Youth Payment because they no longer have a dependent child (Parent education incentive only)
- moves from Youth Payment onto a main benefit
- has intentionally acted in a way that is inconsistent with the purpose of the incentives
For more information see:
- Examples of actions inconsistent with purpose
- Incentive payments can continue
- Restoring incentive payments

chunks.title: Report to service provider or Work and Income on progress — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Report to service provider or Work and Income on progress
A young person receiving Youth Payment is required to report to their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service on how they are satisfactorily meeting their obligation to be:
- in education, training, or work-based learning and
- participating in a budgeting programme
A service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service can ask a young person to report to them by either phone, email or in person and will determine how often the young person must report.
The frequency of reporting must be reasonable and take into account:
- the length of the activity
- how often the young person is required to attend
- whether a young person has failed to comply with their obligations in the past
Generally a young person should not be required to report more than once a week.
Example
The service provider sets an activity for a young person to attend a budgeting programme and asks that they report on their progress when they commence the programme and when they attend each week.
A young person undertakes the budgeting programme. They phone their service provider when they commence the programme and report in each week of the programme to confirm their attendance.
For more information see:
- Obligations

chunks.title: Residence — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Residence
To be granted Youth Payment, a client must:
- be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (ie not be in New Zealand unlawfully, here on a temporary entry class visa or a temporary permit) or
- be deemed to hold a residence class visa in New Zealand under the Immigration Act 2009 (eg Australian citizens or residents) and
- have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years or more at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they first apply for benefit and
- generally be ordinarily resident in New Zealand
For more information see:
- Deciding ordinarily resident
Note clients who are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident, but have not lived in New Zealand continuously for 2 years, may be eligible for Youth Payment on grounds of hardship.
If a client is from overseas or is a refugee or protected person special provisions may apply, see:
- Clients from overseas
- Refugees and protected persons
## Clients without permanent residence
If a client does not have permanent residence they cannot receive a Youth Payment (even if they have lived in New Zealand continuously for 2 years). They may be able to receive an Emergency Benefit if they:
- are lawfully present in New Zealand and are waiting the outcome of their application for refugee or protection status in New Zealand or
- are applying for a residence class visa under the Immigration Act and are compelled to remain in New Zealand through unforeseen circumstances
For more information see:
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Clients from overseas
- Two years residence
- Proof of residence
- Reciprocal Agreements
- Granting on grounds of hardship

chunks.title: Resident in New Zealand — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Resident in New Zealand
To qualify for Youth Payment a client must have lived continuously in New Zealand for 2 years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident.
To be resident in New Zealand at a particular time means that the client either:
- makes their home in New Zealand, that is, they have been living in New Zealand on a permanent basis or
- has an intention to make their home in New Zealand for the foreseeable future
Note 'resident' is not the same as being ordinarily resident.
Remember you must be satisfied that the client has been resident in New Zealand continuously for at least two years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident.
## Client makes their home in New Zealand
A client will be resident in New Zealand if they make their home in New Zealand. You should look for evidence that the client makes their home in New Zealand. Relevant factors you should consider include:
- a fixed abode in New Zealand?
- ownership of property in New Zealand?
- frequent absences from New Zealand, and what is the duration of and reason for those absences?
- involvement with New Zealand society such as (but not limited to): - community activities - employment - membership of clubs and - local churches
For more information see:
- Calculating the period of residence
- Deciding ordinarily resident
- Reciprocal Agreements
- Proof of residence

chunks.title: Returned to youth money management — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Returned to youth money management
A young person can be returned to youuth money management for the following reasons:
- they are subject to a grade 1, 2 or 3 sanction or
- they are demonstrating poor financial judgement
## In-hand allowance and incentives
When a young person is returned to youth money management because they have demonstrated poor financial judgement, they will retain their in-hand allowance and any incentives earned.
For more information see:
- Assessed as financially competent
- Continued compliance with their obligations
- Youth money management
- Obligations Removing incentive payments

chunks.title: Grade 3 sanction — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Grade 3 sanction
Failure to comply with education obligation
Where the failure that led to the cancellation of the Youth Payment was due to failing to comply with their obligation to be in education, training or work-based learning, the education incentive cannot be regranted if Youth Payment is regranted.
The young person must earn this incentive again by completing another six months commitment to education, training or work-based learning.
Example
A young person fails their activity obligations for a third time because they did not go to school. They are getting incentive payments for education and budgeting. When they undertake a six-week approved activity their Youth Payment is restarted and their budgeting incentive is returned at the same time. The education incentive is not returned and the young person must re-earn this incentive by completing a further six months of education or training.
Failure for other reason
For any other failure reason, the incentive payment for budgeting and education can be regranted when the young person recomplies.
Example
A young person has earned the budgeting and education incentives. They fail activity obligations for a third time for refusing to attend their budgeting discussions with their service provider. The young person undertakes a six-week approved activity and their Youth Payment is restarted and both the budgeting and education incentives are returned at the same time.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Obligations Earning incentive payments
- Sanctions and youth money management

chunks.title: Samoan Quota Scheme — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Samoan Quota Scheme
This category is run by ballot and is available to Samoan citizens. Either the principal applicant or their partner must have an offer of employment in New Zealand.
Where the offer of employment was withdrawn or employment terminated through circumstances beyond the control of the client, you may consider granting Youth Payment where the client meets the two year residence criteria.
If you find that there was no job or that the job fell through you need to advise Immigration New Zealand after consulting with Legal Services regarding any privacy law implications with doing this.
Immigration New Zealand will decide on any action to be taken with regard to the client's residence status. In the meantime you need to look at all the circumstances of the client as to whether you can grant benefit assistance.
Note if the client has permanent residence and has lived continuously in New Zealand for two years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident, assess the client's entitlement to Youth Payment in the usual manner.
Youth Payment on grounds of hardship is both income and asset tested. To assess a client's entitlement confirmation of the client's income and assets declared on the application for permanent residence is required from Immigration New Zealand. The client's current income and assets is also required.
Once confirmed, assess Youth Payment on grounds of hardship in the usual manner taking into account all other information provided by Immigration New Zealand.
For more information see:
- Definite offer of employment
- Granting on grounds of hardship
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Sanctions and youth money management — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Sanctions and youth money management
Where a young person was not subject to youth money management before a first, second or third activity obligation failure, they will be returned to youth money management when they recomply.
For more information see:
- Payment Youth money management

chunks.title: Grade 1 and 2 sanctions — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Grade 1 and 2 sanctions
If both people in a married, civil union or de facto couple fail their activity obligations for the first or second time, each person's in-hand allowance (or $50 for those who are not subject to youth money management before the failure) and any incentive payments are suspended until they recomply with the obligation they have failed (or obligations if they have failed to comply with one or more of their obligations).
The couple can continue to get any Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support to which they are entitled. They continue to get the full couple rate of the Winter Energy Payment as they are still getting a qualifying benefit.
If either young person has not recomplied within four weeks, they will both have their Youth Payments, incentives and supplementary assistance (including Winter Energy Payment) suspended.
Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or the payment is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (Grade 1 and 2)
## Grade 3 sanction
If both people in a married, civil union or de facto couple fails their activity obligations for a third time:
- each person's Youth Payment, and any incentive payments, is cancelled immediately
- Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support is cancelled and
- they are both subject to a non-entitlement period for 13 weeks from the date of cancellation
Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid as they are not getting a qualifying benefit.
The young person may get a provisional benefit if they start a six-week approved activity.
If the young person does not start a six-week approved activity, they must reapply at the end of their non-entitlement period to get a benefit.
Note Disability Allowance can continue to be paid during a non-entitlement period.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Definition of second and third failures
- Effect of sanctions on assistance

chunks.title: Grade 1 and 2 sanctions — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Grade 1 and 2 sanctions
If one person in a married, civil union or de facto couple fails the activity obligations for the first or second time, that person's in-hand allowance (or $50 for those who are not subject to youth money management before the failure) and any incentive payments are suspended until they recomply with the obligation they have failed (or obligations if they have failed to comply with one or more of their obligations).
The couple can continue to get any Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support and portion of Winter Energy Payment to which they are entitled.
If the person being sanctioned has not recomplied within four weeks, they will have their Youth Payment, incentives and their portion of Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support suspended. They cannot get their portion of Winter Energy Payment. The full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment can be paid to the partner who hasn’t failed.
Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or the payment is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (Grade 1 and 2)
## Grade 3 sanction
If one person in a married, civil union or de facto couple fails their activity obligations for a third time:
- their Youth Payment, and any incentive payments, is cancelled immediately
- their portion of Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support and Winter Energy Payment is cancelled and
- the young person is subject to a non-entitlement period for 13 weeks from the date of cancellation
Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid to the client who has failed as they are not getting a qualifying benefit. The full couple rate of Winter Energy Payment can be paid to the partner who hasn't failed.
The young person may get a provisional benefit if they start a six-week approved activity.
If the young person does not start a six-week approved activity, they must reapply at the end of their non-entitlement period to get a benefit.
Note Disability Allowance can continue to be paid during a non-entitlement period.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Payment to the non-sanctioned partner
- Effect of sanctions on assistance
- Definition of second and third failures

chunks.title: Grade 1 and 2 sanctions — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Grade 1 and 2 sanctions
A first or second failure means suspension of the in-hand allowance (or $50 for those who are not subject to youth money management before the failure) and any incentive payments, until the young person recomplies with the obligation they have failed (or obligations if they have failed to comply with one or more of their obligations).
The young person can continue to get any Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support to which they are entitled. Winter Energy Payment can continue to be paid as the client is still getting a qualifying benefit.
If the young person has not recomplied within four weeks the whole of their Youth Payment and any incentive payments is suspended along with any Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Winter Energy Payment the young person gets. Winter Energy Payment cannot continue to be paid as the client is not receiving a qualifying benefit.
Their benefit will remain suspended until they recomply or the payment is automatically cancelled after 13 weeks.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (Grade 1 and 2)
## Grade 3
A third activity failure means:
- the Youth Payment, and any incentive payments, is cancelled immediately
- Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support and Winter Energy Payment is cancelled and
- the young person is subject to a non-entitlement period for 13 weeks from the date of cancellation
The young person may get a provisional benefit if they start a six-week approved activity.
If the young person does not start a six-week approved activity, they must reapply at the end of their non-entitlement period to get a benefit.
Note Disability Allowance can continue to be paid during a non-entitlement period however these may need to be granted as a non-beneficiary.
For more information see:
- Recompliance (13 week non-entitlement period)
- Definition of second and third failures
- Effect of sanctions on assistance

chunks.title: Secondary education — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Secondary education
Participating in secondary education is the preferred way for a young person receiving Youth Payment to meet their activity obligation of being in or available for full-time secondary or tertiary education, approved training or work-based learning.
Generally they should be working towards a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification.
A young person enrolled in secondary education (including composite schools, correspondence schools, and secondary schools) must:
- regularly attend classes
- compete assignments and
- complete other course requirements
## School holidays
Young people intending to return to secondary education in the next academic year can be paid Youth Payment during the summer holidays. Any incentive payments earned will continue over this period also.
Note you may also require a young person to undertake other activities that work towards NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualifications during the summer holidays.
## Incentive payments
Young people receiving Youth Payment can earn incentive payments for education and budgeting obligations if they meet certain criteria.
For more information see:
- Definition of 'full-time'
- NCEA level 2 or equivalent or higher qualification
- Qualifications In or available for secondary education
- Earning incentive payments
- Obligations
- Deciding education, training and work-based learning activities

chunks.title: Single young people — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Single young people
To receive Youth Payment a single young person must:
- meet all of the qualifications and
- be in exceptional circumstances or
single because they are divorced, have a dissolved civil union or are separated from their de facto partner
Note young people who are single because they are divorced, have a dissolved civil union or are separated from their de facto partner do not have to meet the exceptional circumstances qualification to receive Youth Payment.
## Young people who are in a relationship
If a young person is married, in a civil union or in a de facto relationship, they do not have to meet the exceptional circumstances qualification to receive Youth Payment. See:
- Young people who are in a relationship
For more information see:
- Parental support gap
- Qualifications

chunks.title: Skilled/Business Stream — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Skilled/Business Stream
The purpose of the Skilled/Business stream is to help talented and entrepreneurial migrants gain residence in New Zealand. The categories in this stream are the:
- Skilled Migrant Category
- Business Categories (Long term Business, Migrant investment, Entrepreneur, Entrepreneur Plus, Employees of Relocating Businesses) and
- Residence from Work Categories (Talent (Accredited Employers), Talent (Arts, Culture, and Sports), and Long Term Skill Shortage List instructions)
For clients granted permanent residence under the Skilled/Business Stream the client has signed a Declaration of Personal Resources statement they have funds to support themselves and family (if any) for the first two years residence in New Zealand. Generally the client would have had a work/study visa for at least two years before permanent residence was granted.
## Exception
Client granted permanent residence under the Skilled Migrant Category should already have had employment for their first year of residence in New Zealand.
Clients must have two years continuous residence in New Zealand to be entitled to Youth Payment. Until they have met this requirement Youth Payment on grounds of hardship may be considered.
Note if a client has permanent residence and already meets the two years continuous residence, assess the client for Youth Payment in usual manner.
Youth Payment on grounds of hardship is both income and asset tested. To assess a client's entitlement to Youth Payment on grounds of hardship confirmation of the client's income and assets declared on the application for permanent residence is required from the Immigration New Zealand.
If the client has a change in personal resources, confirmation of that change is required.
For more information see:
- Granting on grounds of hardship
- Change in personal resources

chunks.title: Special regional training courses — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Special regional training courses
This is any training approved by the regional contracts manager.
Young people will be meeting their obligations where they are undertaking programmes linked to New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF) credits.
For more information see:
- Approved training

chunks.text:
