chunks.title: Temporary employment — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Temporary employment
No stand-down is imposed where a young person:
- has been in part-time employment or full-time employment for less than 26 weeks
- was receiving a benefit immediately before they were employed
- the benefit was stopped because they returned to work and
- has applied for a benefit after their employment ceased
Note the young person's average weekly income is not required where the young person has been in temporary employment for less than 26 weeks. However, the young person's final pay details are required to determine the date of event and entitlement date.

chunks.title: Tertiary education — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Tertiary education
A young person getting Youth Payment can meet their activity obligation by studying full-time at a tertiary provider.
Generally they should be working towards a NCEA level 2 qualification, or an equivalent or higher qualification.
A young person enrolled in full-time tertiary education must:
- be enrolled in a course considered to be 'full-time'
- regularly attend classes
- complete assignments and
- complete other course requirements
Note a young person does not have to move to Independent Circumstances Allowance if they qualify for this payment.
## Tertiary holidays
Young people intending to return to tertiary education in the next academic year can be paid Youth Payment during the summer holidays. Any incentive payments earned will continue over this period also.
Note you may also require a young person to undertake other activities that work towards NCEA level 2 or an equivalent or higher qualifications during the summer holidays.
## Incentive payments
Young people receiving Youth Payment can earn incentive payments for education and budgeting obligations if they meet certain criteria.

chunks.title: The disputes process — youth payment
chunks.text: The disputes process is a quick process where MSD must respond to a young person's dispute immediately. MSD must take into account any new information provided by the young person and advise the young person of any decision straight away. A letter is sent automatically to the young person once a decision has been recorded on the dispute. A young person can dispute the decision if they believe: - they did not fail their activity obligations or - that they had a good and sufficient reason for failing to complete the activity obligation Note if a young person has disputed the activity obligations failure and MSD has upheld the decision, the young person can only dispute it again if they provide new information. If new information is not provided, the young person will need to follow the Review of Decision process. If a sanction has been imposed, MSD can still use the disputes process. This allows the young person an opportunity for a quick resolution to their dispute before proceeding with the Review of Decision process. For more information see: - Recording decisions on a dispute - Disputes and reviews of an activity obligations failure

chunks.title: Reason for dispute — youth payment
chunks.text: The young person can dispute the decision if they believe they did not fail their activity obligations, for one of the following reasons: - an activity obligations failure was initiated, but the young person had undertaken the activity or - undertaking or completing the activity was dependent on the provision of assistance by the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service, and that assistance was not supplied or - reasonable steps weren't taken by the service provider or Work and Income 'in-house' service to inform a young person of the activity that they were required to do Note a young person cannot appeal the decision to be paid under youth money management.

chunks.title: Good and sufficient reason for failing — youth payment
chunks.text: MSD must consider the circumstances of the young person, and determine whether it would have been reasonable for the young person to have undertaken the activity. Good and sufficient reasons for failing to undertake an activity include (but are not limited to): - the young person was temporarily medically unfit or injured - there was death or illness in the family - due to unforeseen circumstances the young person could not realistically transport themselves on the day - an unexpected event occurred on the day, eg the young person had to provide care for a sick family member or relative Note if you are unsure as to whether a young person has a good and sufficient reason then you should seek guidance from your capability developer, manager client service operations or manager client service delivery.

chunks.title: Transfer between benefits — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Transfer between benefits
A transfer between benefits can occur when a young person qualifies for Youth Payment while currently receiving another benefit.
There is no stand-down imposed for young people who:
- transfer to Youth Payment from another benefit type or
- are included as a partner in another benefit type
Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Child's Benefit and Orphan's Benefit are also a benefit in this situation. Where Child Disability Allowance, Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit has been paid and the child now qualifies for Youth Payment, no stand-down is imposed.
## Non-beneficiary clients
When a non-beneficiary client receiving Extra help such as Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance applies for Youth Payment, it is not regarded as a transfer between benefits. An initial stand-down is imposed.
For more information see:
- Processing standards Client transfers to another benefit type [no link find out why]

chunks.title: Young person intending to return to the same employer — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Young person intending to return to the same employer
If a young person has received any sick leave payments they would not be eligible for Youth Payment until these payments had stopped. You then assess any initial stand-down.
Young people are not required to use any sick leave they may have if they are intending to return to the same employer.

chunks.title: 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down — youth payment
chunks.text:
## 28-day rule for clients with an initial stand down
When a young person applies for Youth Payment within 28 days of their entitlement date, the commencement date is the day after the initial stand-down ends.
This means, in some situations, MSD can commence a benefit from a date earlier than the application date.
If the application is not received within 28 days, MSD cannot backdate the commencement date.
Note the 28-day rule only applies to clients who have an initial stand down imposed.

chunks.title: Two years residence — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Two years residence
A client must have lived continuously in New Zealand for two years at any one time since becoming a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident to qualify for Youth Payment.
Note the two year period of residence must be two years continuous residence without absence from New Zealand. There are some circumstances however when a client can be absent from New Zealand during this time.
For more information see:
- Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
If the client is not a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident they cannot receive Youth Payment, whether or not they have two years continuous residence in New Zealand. They may be eligible for an Emergency Benefit.
## Clients who do not meet the two years residence criteria
If the client is a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident and does not meet the two year continuous residence requirement they may be able to receive Youth Payment on grounds of hardship. See:
- Granting on grounds of hardship
For more information about residence see:
- Proof of residence
- Permanent residence
- Refugees and protected persons
- Resident in New Zealand
- Calculating the period of residence
- Unlawful residence
- Reciprocal Agreements

chunks.title: Unable to receive financial support from parents — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Unable to receive financial support from parents
To receive a Youth Payment, a single young person must be in exceptional circumstances. A 16 or 17 year old is considered to have a parental support gap when their parents (or guardians) are unable to support them financially because they are:
- deceased
- in prison
- in hospital or
- overseas
You will need to find out:
- what the period of absence is and what provisions have been made for the young person's support
- if the parents are overseas, ask if it is temporary or permanent, and why the young person has not gone as well. See: Parents overseas
- if the parents are living apart, ask the young person what involvement they have with the other parent and whether they have considered living with them and
- whether the young person is living in a 'care' arrangement as opposed to an independent situation
For more information see:
- What is financial support?
- Independent
- Parents overseas
- Discharged from care
- Definition of parents

chunks.title: Example - young person develops a health condition, injury or disability — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Example - young person develops a health condition, injury or disability
A young person who is subject to a sanction develops a health condition, injury or disability, and meets the criteria for the exemption "would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability". They are unable to complete a recompliance activity.
In this situation you should add the exemption reason in SWIFTT (medical incapacity), and follow the disputes process so that the benefit can be resumed.
## Proof
To support their exemption, the young person is required to provide a medical certificate. The information required on the medical certificate is:
- a diagnosis (what the illness is)
- the impact of the condition on their ability to undertake activity obligations
- the likely duration of the impact
- their capacity for education, training and work-based learning and
- any other information that is required
For more information see:
- Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
- Exemptions from activity obligations

chunks.title: Unsupported Childs Benefit was paid — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Unsupported Childs Benefit was paid
If the young person has been living with a caregiver who was receiving Unsupported Childs Benefit for the young person, the young person can only receive Youth Payment if:
- the young person has stopped living with the caregiver and
- there has been a relationship breakdown between the young person and caregiver
This is because caregivers who receive Unsupported Childs Benefit for a dependent person are considered parents.
The Independent Assessment Provider report will assist you in determining relationship breakdown.
For more information see:
- Independent Assessment Provider

chunks.title: Victims of family violence — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Victims of family violence
Clients may be granted permanent residence if they have been living in a relationship with a New Zealand citizen or resident that has ended because that person was violent towards the client, and they are unable to go back to their home country.
Financial assistance for these clients is decided by Helpline.

When income is over $334.70 (at 1 April 2026) Youth Payment is no longer payable.

When income is over $384.70 (at 1 April 2026) Youth Payment is no longer payable.

When income is over $384.70 (at 1 April 2026) Youth Payment is no longer payable.

chunks.title: Example 4 - Single young person getting Youth , earning income from a part-time job, and getting information share Child Support payments — youth payment

The young person's information share Child Support income is charged against their benefit. The deduction is $1.00 per $1.00 of total income over $284.70 (as at 1 April 2026) until their benefit is reduced to $0.00.

chunks.title: What is financial support? — youth payment
chunks.text:
## What is financial support?
Consider a young person to be financially supported by their parents when payments received are:
- long term
- ongoing
- regular and
- at least equal to or higher than the benefit rate payable If a young person receives a lesser amount of support from their parents (or a one off payment), they may still receive Youth Payment. Any support received would be charged as income.
Any financial support the young person receives must be given without any conditions for payment.
For more information see:
- Unable to receive financial support from parents
- Independent

chunks.title: When financial support is not expected — youth payment
chunks.text:
## When financial support is not expected
Parents will not be expected to financially support the young person if:
- the young person is, or has been married
- the young person, is in, or has been in, a civil union
- the young person is, or has been, living in a de facto relationship that is in the nature of marriage or civil union (as determined by Work and Income) or
- the young person has been discharged from the care of the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki, and is not dependent on a caregiver
In all other circumstances an Independent Assessment Provider report will assist you to consider whether financial support should be expected or not.
For more information see:
- Young people who are in a relationship
- De facto relationship (definition)
- Discharged from care
- Unsupported Childs benefit was paid

chunks.title: When the sanction is imposed — youth payment
chunks.text:
## When the sanction is imposed
Sanctions can only be imposed five working days after the young person has been notified by text message (where they have consented to receive information from us in this way) or in a letter about their activity obligations failure. This is called the five working day notice period.
Note that if a young person recomplies within the initial five working day notice period their benefit is not sanctioned but the activity obligations failure is counted.
## How to count the 'five working day notice' period
The five working day notice period is counted from the date after the activity obligations text message (where the young person has consented to receive information from us in this way) or letter has been sent to the young person, to allow for posting and delivery of the letter.
The five working day notice period excludes weekends, public holidays, or the period 25 December to 15 January each year.
The tables below provide an example of how to count the notice period.
Day 0
Tuesday
Automatic failure in CMS occurs overnight
Day 0
Wednesday
An activity obligations failure text message or letter is sent
Day 1 Day 2
Thursday Friday
Five working days' notice period begins
Weekend
Saturday-Sunday
Day 3 Day 4 Day 5
Monday Tuesday Wednesday
Five working days' notice period continues
Day 6
Thursday
Benefit sanction occurs in SWIFTT

chunks.title: Work-based learning — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Work-based learning
A young person receiving Youth Payment can meet their education activity obligation by being in work-based learning.
Work-based learning includes courses that offer more practical, hands-on learning than the school environment.
For a young person to be considered to be in work-based learning they must be:
- employed and undertaking on-the-job learning and
- undertaking a course or programme that is relevant to their employment
While the young person is in paid work, all usual workplace conditions, including the applicable minimum wage, will apply to the work element of work-based learning in the same way that they apply to all other forms of employment.
Note if the young person earns more than the cut-out point for Youth Payment, they will no longer be able to receive it.
Programmes that contain elements of work-based learning include:
- Youth Guarantee programmes and
- part-time industry partnerships

chunks.title: Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Working overseas and paying New Zealand tax on earnings
A client applying for Youth Payment can be considered resident and present in New Zealand during periods of overseas employment when their employer (or other relevant person):
- deducted PAYE or source deductions from their wages and
- paid the deducted amount to Inland Revenue New Zealand
The period overseas that the client was considered resident and present can be used towards the two years residence requirement for Youth Payment.
A partner or any dependent child who was with the client while they were working overseas can also be treated as resident and present in New Zealand for the same periods.
If the client has a child born outside of New Zealand during the period they were working overseas, the child is deemed to have been born in New Zealand.
The residential qualifications do not apply to people who are self-employed and working overseas.
Clients should provide evidence of the periods they were employed overseas and that PAYE or source deductions were paid to Inland Revenue in New Zealand during these periods.
If the employer (or other relevant person) has deducted the tax but failed to pay it to the Commissioner of Inland Revenue New Zealand and the client did not contribute to the employer's failure to pay the tax, the period of employment overseas can still be regarded as residence and present in New Zealand.
Note if any person leaves New Zealand while getting a benefit and returns to take up ordinary residence in New Zealand at any time within 5 years are not required to meet the residential qualifications for the same benefit type.

chunks.title: Working part-time — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Working part-time
Participating in education, training or work-based learning is the focus for young people receiving Youth Payment. It is not a requirement that they seek part-time employment. However if they wish to they can work part-time and still receive Youth Payment as long as they can meet the qualification to be in, or available for, full-time education, approved training or approved work-based learning
For more information see:
- Qualifications
- In or available for secondary education
- In or available for tertiary education
- In or available for approved training
- In or available for work-based learning

chunks.title: Workplace/industry training — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Workplace/industry training
Workplace/industry training includes course such as:
- Skills for Industry [no link find out why]
These courses are generally less than 13 weeks.
Young people will be meeting their obligations where they are undertaking programmes linked to New Zealand Qualifications Framework (NZQF) credits.
For more information see:
- Approved training

chunks.title: Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Would qualify for Jobseeker Support - health condition, injury or disability
If a young person meets the qualifications for Jobseeker Support on the ground of a health condition, injury or disability (but for their age) they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their activity obligations until their capacity for education, training and work-based learning improves.
This can be a full or partial exemption.
The young person must be limited in their capacity to undertake activities because of a health condition, injury or disability.
For more information see:
- Jobseeker Support - client has a health condition, injury or disability
- Exemptions [no link find out why]
## Full or partial exemption
If the young person is partially exempt they are able to:
- plan for education, training or work-based learning and
- undertake other activities such as budgeting
If a young person qualifies for a full exemption this means they are unable to meet any of their activity obligations, including planning.
## Duration
The duration of an exemption is based on the reassessment date recorded on the medical certificate by the young person’s health practitioner.
This exemption should then be reviewed. At the review you should discuss the young person's circumstances and consider whether it is appropriate to extend the exemption for a further period. You can ask the young person to provide proof that their exemption should be extended.
## Getting an incentive payment
If the young person is getting an incentive payment and then qualifies for an exemption, you will need to decide if they can continue to get the payment.

chunks.title: Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Would qualify for Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
If a young person meets the qualifications for Supported Living Payment on the ground of a health condition, injury, disability or total blindness, they can be exempt from meeting some or all of their activity obligations. The young person must be both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity for education, training, and work-based learning because of a health condition, injury, disability, total blindness or a condition they have had since birth.
For more information see:
- Supported Living Payment
This can be a full or partial exemption depending on whether the young person can plan for a return to education, training or work-based learning.
You should discuss with the young person whether they can still:
- plan for education, training or work-based learning and
- undertake other activities such as budgeting
If you are unsure about whether a full or partial exemption should be granted discuss with your regional health or regional disability advisor.
Note in all cases you should consider the young person's eligibility for Supported Living Payment.
## SWIFTT process
Use SWIFTT exemption reason 'Would qualify for SLP Sick/Injured/Disabled'.
## Receiving an incentive payment
If the young person is receiving an incentive payment and then qualifies for an exemption, you will need to decide if they can continue to receive it.
For more information see:
- Full or partial exemptions
- Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability
- Obligations Incentive payments can continue

chunks.title: Young people who are in a relationship — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Young people who are in a relationship
When a young person is in a relationship, their eligibility for Youth Payment depends on their partner's age and whether they get a main benefit. A relationship means the couple are:
- legally married
- in a civil union
- in a de facto relationship with Family Court Judge consent
## Both partners aged 16 or 17 years old
When a young person in a relationship applies for Youth Payment and both partners are aged 16 or 17 years old, each partner must qualify in their own right. They do not need to have a parental support gap.
These couples cannot get any other main benefit, except when the partner qualifies for Supported Living Payment – health condition, injury, or disability. In this situation, the young person can be included in their partner's Supported Living Payment.
## Partner is aged 18 years or older
A young person cannot get Youth Payment if their partner is aged 18 years or older and is getting one of the following benefits:
- Emergency Benefit
- Jobseeker Support
- Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury, or disability
In these situations, the young person can be included in their partner's main benefit.
Note if the partner is getting Supported Living Payment - caring for a person, the young person can get Youth Payment in their own right.
## Partner is not getting a main benefit
If the partner is not getting a benefit, e.g. because they are working or are subject to a non-entitlement period, the young person can get Youth Payment in their own right.

chunks.title: Young person in hospital — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Young person in hospital
The rate of payment for a young person getting Youth Payment can be different if they are in hospital.
The rate is reduced to the hospital rate when the young person has been in hospital for more than 13 weeks (not after getting a benefit for 13 weeks).
The hospital rate is paid directly to the young person and allows for the cost of personal items, which patients are expected to provide for themselves.
A young person on the hospital rate is not subject to youth money management.
## Exception
If the young person has been in hospital for 13 weeks or more at the commencement date of the benefit, the rate of payment is the hospital rate.
## Incentive payments
When a young person is getting the hospital rate of payment, any incentive payments should be removed.
For more information about the hospital rate see:
- Changes and reviews Hospitalisation
- Youth money management

chunks.title: Young person turns 18 years old — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Young person turns 18 years old
Generally, when a young person turns 18 years old the Youth Payment should stop. However there are two situations where the payment can continue to be paid after they turn 18 years old.
These are where a young person:
- must receive Youth Payment for a minimum of six months and cannot receive another main benefit (excluding Supported Living Payment - health condition, injury or disability) until after this period
- chooses to continue to receive Youth Payment if they remain in education, training or work-based learning
For more information see
- Must receive payment for six months
- Chooses to remain on Youth Payment past 18 years of age

chunks.title: Young person's IRD number — youth payment
chunks.text: MSD may make a written request for evidence of an IRD number for a client who is being paid Youth Payment.

chunks.title: Setting or extending the timeframe for providing evidence — youth payment
chunks.text: MSD must provide the client with a minimum of 10 working days to provide IRD number evidence that has been requested in writing. MSD can extend the 10 working day period (in writing) if the client has a reasonable explanation for requiring more than 10 days to provide evidence of their IRD number. This includes considering factors outside the client's control that cause delays, including, but not limited to: - client has a family emergency that caused a delay - processing delays with an external agency (e.g., Inland Revenue, Department of Internal Affairs, etc) - client does not speak English as a first language and has difficulty navigating evidence requirements - client has limited access to the internet, a device, or their local service centre - client has a physical or intellectual disability that makes accessing services difficult - client is injured, disabled, or has a medical condition that makes accessing services difficult.

chunks.title: Notice following an unsuccessful match — youth payment
chunks.text: MSD has an agreement with Inland Revenue to share information about a client's IRD number. When the IRD number information MSD holds does not match Inland Revenue's information, or there's an error, MSD should ask the client (in writing) to provide evidence of their IRD number, unless there are significant barriers to providing this. In the written request for evidence of the IRD number, MSD must include a notice in writing (adverse action notice): - advising that MSD has shared information (including IRD number and some personal details) with Inland Revenue, and the match was unsuccessful, and - giving a minimum of 10 working days to provide their IRD number evidence or the client's assistance must be suspended. Example Isla is receiving Youth Payment and MSD holds an IRD number on record. The IRD number validation results in a No Match for Isla's IRD number. MSD provides a notice in writing, giving 10 working days in writing, for Isla to provide evidence their IRD number. MSD's decision to give 10 working days to provide evidence is based on: - Isla already having an IRD number - Isla not having any significant barriers to getting evidence of their IRD number - MSD's obligation to provide a minimum of 10 working days to provide the information.

chunks.title: MSD must suspend assistance if evidence of IRD number is not received — youth payment
chunks.text: MSD must suspend all taxable and/or income tested assistance the client is getting, including their Youth Payment, if evidence of an IRD number is not provided within 10 working days from the written request, or extended period if this has been applied. Note suspension does not apply to Childcare Assistance. Example Koa is receiving Youth Payment and MSD does not have an IRD number on record. MSD sends a written request giving 10 working days for Koa to provide evidence of their IRD number. MSD receives no response to this request. MSD suspends all Koa's taxable and/or income tested assistance because Koa has not supplied MSD with evidence of their IRD number within the timeframe provided.

chunks.title: IRD evidence may not be requested in some circumstances — youth payment
chunks.text: MSD may not ask for evidence of an IRD number when there are significant barriers to providing the evidence, including, but not limited to: - significant factors, that are outside the client's control, that would substantially delay providing evidence of their IRD number (e.g., a national emergency affecting Inland Revenue's ability to provide IRD number evidence), and - the client needs assistance to continue, before the evidence can be provided or - significant factors related to a health, injury or disability that are outside the client's control that prevent them from providing evidence of an IRD number, and - an agent cannot be appointed to act on the client or partner's behalf. MSD can determine a later point to request the evidence of the IRD number. Example Sienna is 16 and receiving Youth Payment. Sienna's mother (Sara) is Sienna's agent and acts on Sienna's behalf with MSD. Sienna does not have an IRD number and Sara is not a recognised agent for Sienna for Inland Revenue. Sienna has a serious head injury, is unconscious and expected to be in hospital for at least 8 weeks. Sienna is not able to give consent to appoint Sara as an agent for Inland Revenue to apply for an IRD number due to their injury. MSD can request this information later when Sienna's situation has changed. Note there is different guidance for requesting an IRD number or evidence of an IRD number for partners or when a client is applying for Youth Payment.

chunks.title: Youth activity obligations — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Youth activity obligations
Young people getting Youth Payment have the following activity obligations. They must:
- be enrolled in and undertaking, or be available for, a full-time course of secondary or tertiary education, or approved training or work-based learning leading to a NCEA level 2 qualification or an equivalent or higher qualification
- when required to, participate in and complete an approved budgeting programme
- report to their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service on progress in meeting their education and budgeting obligations (above) as often as required
- when required to, attend and participate in any interview with their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service and
- when asked, provide within 20 working days, to their service provider or Work and Income “in-house” service, details of the young person’s accommodation costs, service costs and lawful debts or other liabilities
- co-operate with their service provider or Work and Income "in-house" service in managing the spending of their Youth Payment and
- attend and participate in regular discussions on budgeting at any discussion, or when asked, provide details of: accommodation costs and service costs such as power and phonelawful debts and liabilitieshow they spent any in-hand allowance and any money credited to their payment card or any other device
- accommodation costs and service costs such as power and phone
- lawful debts and liabilities
- how they spent any in-hand allowance and any money credited to their payment card or any other device
Young people who fail without good and sufficient reason to comply with their activity obligations may be sanctioned.
## Incentive payments
Young people getting Youth Payment can earn incentive payments for education and budgeting obligations if they meet certain criteria.
For more information see:
- Deciding education, training or work-based learning activities
- Approved budgeting programme activity
- Report to service provider or Work and Income on progress
- Earning incentive payments
- Youth money management activity
- Activity obligations failures

chunks.title: Youth Guarantee courses — youth payment
chunks.text:
## Youth Guarantee courses
Young people attending and participating in Youth Guarantee courses can get Youth Payments, as these courses are considered to be employment-related training.
## Student Allowance and Student Loan
A young person can continue to receive Youth Payment when they participate in Youth Guarantee courses. They do not have to apply for a Student Allowance or Independent Circumstances Allowance.
Young people on a Youth Guarantee course are not eligible for a Student Loan.

chunks.title: Introduction — youth service information sharing
chunks.text:
## Introduction
MSD may contract with service providers to provide the following services:
- services to encourage and help young persons to move into education, training, and employment rather than receiving financial support from Work and Income
- services to provide wrap around support to young people receiving a benefit
These services are called Youth Service (NEET) and Youth Service (Payment). In order to provide a service to young people and to administer payments information relevant to the young person's participating in the service needs to be shared.
These guidelines outline the circumstances when information can be shared.
For more information see:
- Youth Service (NEET) provider sharing information with Work and Income
- Work and Income information sharing with Youth Service (NEET) provider
- Work and Income sharing information with Youth Service (Payment) provider
- Youth Service (Payment) provider sharing information with Work and Income
- Third party sharing information about a young person to youth service provider
## Youth service
- Young Parent Payment
- Youth Payment

chunks.title: List of third party agencies or organisations covered by information sharing — youth service information sharing
chunks.text:
## List of third party agencies or organisations covered by information sharing
Where the service provider has not been able to get the information about a young person that is relevant to the service they are providing for the young person directly from the young person, they can ask the following agencies for this information:
- WellChild or Tamariki Ora provider
- any primary health organisation
- health practitioners providing health services to young people under the Integrated Family Health Centre Framework
- independent health practitioners who are not part of a primary health organisation
- any organisation employing or contracting individuals to provide health services to young people in schools
- any organisation providing mental health services to young people (including services provided in relation to drug or alcohol abuse)
- any organisation providing services to young people as 'Youth One Stop Shops'
- any organisation employing or contracting individuals as socials workers to provide services to young people in secondary and primary schools
- any state school established as a secondary school, intermediate school, primary school including designated as Kura Kaupapa Māori under the Education Act 1989
- tertiary education and training providers
- any organisation contracted to provide training and placements under the programme known as the Youth Guarantee
- any organisation providing an approved early childhood education programme (including Kōhanga Reo) regulated by the Education Act 1989
- New Zealand Qualifications Authority
- any organisation employing or contracting individuals as youth workers to provide services to young people in schools
- New Zealand Police
- Department of Corrections
- any organisation providing placements for alternative education funded by the Ministry of Education or approved by the New Zealand Qualifications Authority
- any organisation providing alternative education training for the purposes of the New Zealand Qualifications Framework
- any organisation providing services under the Family Start or Early Learning programme
Note an agency must be covered by the list above to be covered by the information sharing legislation.

chunks.title: Third party sharing information about a young person to youth service provider — youth service information sharing
chunks.text:
## Third party sharing information about a young person to youth service provider
Generally, when a service provider requires information from a young person, the young person should be asked for the information themselves as a first step. Asking third party agencies for the information should only be done if the young person cannot or will not provide the information the provider needs to carry out their role. The young person also must either give their consent to the service provider seeking their information from a third party, or be notified of the collection of information.
## Young person refuses or information not accurate
If the young person refuses to give the information or the provider considers the information they are providing is not accurate, the service provider can make requests to other agencies who they think will hold this information. There are two ways that a provider can request this information depending on whether the agency is listed as an authorised agency.
## Authorised agencies
An authorised agency may share any information about a young person to the Ministry of Social Development if they are satisfied that the young person:
- has applied for or is gettng Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment or
- is subject to youth activity obligations (young people aged 16 or 17 or parents aged 16-18 who are partners of a main beneficiary) and
- has left or finished education, and is not or may not be in employment or training
- has left or finished training, and is not or may not be in employment and
- the information will help the service provider to provide the services they have been contracted to provide
The information requested must be about the young person. The service provider cannot request information about family members of the young person.
When making requested to agencies, it is the responsibility of the service provider to provide enough information about their role and the purpose of the request for the third party agency to be satisfied of the above points.
For more information see:
- List of third party agencies or organisations covered by information sharing
## Not an authorised agency
When an agency or service provider wants to request information from an organisation that is not an authorised agency, they can still request the information they need, but the agency disclosing the information will need to comply with the Privacy Act. There is no other authority for the agency to rely on in disclosing the information.
## Complaints to the Privacy Commissioner
A young person may complain to the Privacy Commissioner if personal information relating to the person has been disclosed in breach of the Privacy Act or Social Security Act authorisations outlined above.

chunks.title: Work and Income information sharing with Youth Service (NEET) provider — youth service information sharing
chunks.text:
## Work and Income information sharing with Youth Service (NEET) provider
Work and Income may share personal information about a young person with a Youth Service (NEET) provider in the following circumstances:
- when a young person is identified as not in education, employment or training, or at risk of becoming not in education, employment or training so that the service provider can contact the young person to offer services
- when a young person consents to participate in the service, provided that: the information is requested by the Youth Service (NEET) provider andthe information is relevant to the young person's involvement in the service including benefit information
- the information is requested by the Youth Service (NEET) provider and

In order to provide Youth Service (Payment) a service provider and Work and Income need to share relevant personal information about a young person. Work and Income also need information from service providers to administer the benefit payments for a young person.
## When Work and Income can share information with provider
Work and Income can share personal information about the young person with the service provider where it is necessary for the service provider to be able to deliver the young person with the service they are contracted to provide. The personal information may include, but is not limited to:
- the young person's contact details
- relevant information about the young person's previous involvement with Oranga Tamariki
- relevant information about the young person's involvement with Work and Income
Where a service provider or Work and Income are satisfied on reasonable grounds that the sharing of information meets the situations outlined above, they may share the information with each other.
A service provider includes an employee of the service provider. A volunteer working for the service provider is also considered an employee.

## Youth Service (NEET) provider sharing information with Work and Income
In order to provide the Youth Service (NEET) a service provider and Work and Income need to share relevant personal information about young person.
A NEET youth service provider and its employees can share personal information with Work and Income in the following circumstances:
- when Work and Income requires the service provider to provide a report on the: enrolment of the young person in the serviceprogress of a young person against specified milestones (eg whether they are in education or training)payment of a success fee for the service provider (when they have achieved NCEA level 2 or are not on benefit three months after they have reached the age of 18 years)
- enrolment of the young person in the service
- progress of a young person against specified milestones (eg whether they are in education or training)
- payment of a success fee for the service provider (when they have achieved NCEA level 2 or are not on benefit three months after they have reached the age of 18 years)
- when a young person transfers from the service provider to another, so that Work and Income may share relevant information about the young person to the new provider
- when the youth service provider is no longer contracted to provide the service to the young person Work and Income may share relevant information about the young person to a new provider or Work and Income may use the information to provide the service
Where a service provider or Work and Income are satisfied on reasonable grounds that the sharing of information meets the situations outlined above, they may share the information with each other.
Note a service provider includes an employee of the service provider. A volunteer working for the service provider is also considered an employee.
## Complaints to the Privacy Commissioner
A young person may complain to the Privacy Commissioner if personal information relating to the person has been disclosed in breach of the Privacy Act or Social Security Act 2018 authorisations outlined above.

## When a service provider can share information with Work and Income
A Youth Service (Payment) provider can share personal information necessary for Work and Income to administer the young persons benefit entitlement and obligations and any other power under the Social Security Act.
The personal information of a young person includes but is not limited to information:
- for assisting a young person to apply for any benefit or financial assistance available from Work and Income
- about a young person's accommodation costs, services costs and lawful debts an liabilities
- about a young person's compliance with their obligations for receiving a payment and managing their payments (including information about reasons for non-compliance)
- about a young persons ability to manage their money
- about changes in the circumstances of a young person that affect the young person's eligibility or rate of payment
The information also includes information contained in a report by the Youth Service (Payment) provider to Work and Income required under their contract relating to:
- the enrolment of a young person in the service
- the progress of a young person against their milestones (eg attending a budgeting, being in education or training, and for parents attending a parenting programme)

- the reason the young person has exited the service (including whether the young person or partner has given birth to a child)

chunks.title: 2020 COVID-19 Wage Subsidy
chunks.text:
## 2020 COVID-19 Wage Subsidy
The 2020 COVID-19 Wage Subsidy was to help businesses pay staff impacted by COVID-19. It was available from 17 March 2020 to 9 June 2020.
The 2020 COVID-19 Wage Subsidy was support for businesses to pay 12 weeks of wages for their employees. It was to continue support for businesses affected by changes to COVID-19 alert levels and lockdowns.
The information on this page is a summary of the key details about this payment. Detailed information can be found in the declarations at the bottom of this page.
## Who could get it
This payment was available to employers, including self-employed people, whose employees could not work and had a 30% decline in revenue:
- over the period of any month being applied for, when compared to the same month in 2019; andthat loss was attributable to the COVID-19 outbreak.
- State Sector organisations were generally not eligible to get the 2020 COVID-19 Wage Subsidy, however some may have been granted an exception.
## Payment rates
The 2020 COVID-19 Wage Subsidy was paid at a flat rate of:
- $585.80 for full-time employees 20 hours or more a week (full-time rate)
- $350.00 for part-time employees less than 20 hours per week (part-time rate).
If the employee's usual wages were less than the subsidy rate, any difference should have been used to pay wages of other affected staff. If there were no other affected staff, the remaining amount must be repaid.
## Paying your staff
The business must have tried their hardest to pay the employee at least 80% of their usual wages while getting the 2020 COVID-19 Wage Subsidy for them. If that wasn't possible, the employee must have been paid at least the subsidy payment rate.
## Declaration
The declaration contains the full eligibility criteria, obligations and repayment responsibilities for the 2020 COVID-19 Wage Subsidy.

Declaration for 2020 COVID-19 Wage Subsidy before 4pm 27 Mar 2020
## For applications made after 4pm on 27 March 2020

chunks.title: ACC payments
chunks.text: If you get certain types of payments from ACC you need to let us know. The amount and type of payment you get may affect your benefit or payment. If you don't tell us we may not pay you enough. Or we may pay you too much and you'll have to pay the debt back.

chunks.title: Payments you need to tell us about
chunks.text: You have to tell us about these ACC payments as they could affect your benefit: - weekly compensation - survivor's grant (regular or one-off) - childcare - ACC payments from private insurers - payments for attendant care, home help and rehabilitation services - independence allowance - lump sum payments for impairment. If you're getting ACC payments because of a sensitive claim, you need to tell us as it may affect your benefit entitlement. You do not need to tell us why you are getting this payment.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: The easiest way to tell us about your ACC payments is online, using MyMSD. - If you've already told us about your ACC payments, they will show in MyMSD and you can change this from the home screen. - If you haven't told us about them yet, you need to select 'Declare wages' and then 'Change other income'. You need to tell us: - how much the payment is before tax - when you're paid - how often you get this payment. The amount you declare will continue every week until you let us know it has stopped or changed.

chunks.title: If you can't use MyMSD
chunks.text: If you can't use MyMSD you can call us or come into one of our service centres. If you’re declaring income from self-employment, make sure you mention you're self-employed. Phone us Find a service centre

chunks.title: Keep us up to date
chunks.text: If you don't tell us, we'll keep paying you the same benefit week after week. This could be too little or too much, and you could get into debt.

chunks.title: Main benefit
chunks.text: Most payments from ACC will affect your main benefit. In most cases we’ll deduct $1 for every $1 you get from ACC. It depends on the type of payment and the reason you’re getting it. Main benefit

chunks.title: Other payments
chunks.text: If you're getting an ongoing payment such as Accommodation Supplement, most ACC payments will be included as income when assessing your rate of payment. It depends on the type of payment and the reason you’re getting it. Contact us for more information. Phone us

chunks.title: Backdated ACC weekly compensation payments
chunks.text: If ACC approves weekly compensation for a period in the past, we need to review any benefits or extra help you received for that same time. This is to make sure you got the right amount of financial support. Backdated ACC weekly compensation payments

chunks.title: Contact
chunks.text: If you need more information or want to discuss this in more detail contact us. Phone us

chunks.title: Accepting a public housing offer
chunks.text:
## Accepting a public housing offer
If a housing provider makes you an offer for a property and it suits your needs, you can accept this by signing the tenancy agreement.
The housing provider will contact you and invite you to view the property.
## If you accept the offer
If you're happy with it, you'll sign a tenancy agreement with the housing provider. They'll then become your landlord.
The tenancy agreement sets out:
- your rights and responsibilities
- the landlord’s rights and responsibilities.
## Living in public housing
Once you're living in public housing:
- we'll work out how much rent you need to pay
- you'll need to let us know about any changes in your or your partner's situation, and
- you can stay for as long as you qualify. We may review your tenancy from time to time while you're living there.
Living in public housing
## If you don't accept the offer
If an offer for a property comes up, you can choose not to accept it if you have a good reason. For example, there are stairs which you find hard to climb because you've had a knee replacement.
If you don't accept the offer and don’t have a good reason, we'll check that you still qualify for public housing. This means you must still have a serious and immediate housing need. If you don't, you may be taken off the social housing register.
If you reapply for public housing within 13 weeks, we'll look at your decision to decline the offer when checking if you meet the criteria.

chunks.title: Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant
chunks.text: If you're worried you'll lose your housing because you owe accommodation costs, you may be able to get an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. This type of payment can also be called Rent Arrears Grant. It will be called this if you're in a tenancy that the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA) applies to, i.e. you have a tenancy agreement. - You don't have to be on a benefit to get this payment. - You'll need to pay the money back. We'll put a repayment plan in place to suit your financial circumstances. If you're having trouble paying rent on an on-going basis, you may be able to get an Accommodation Supplement. This is a weekly payment which helps people with their rent, board or the cost of owning a home. Accommodation Supplement

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant if you: - have an accommodation agreement, e.g. with your landlord or head tenant - have overdue accommodation costs you need to pay, e.g. rent, board or cabin hire, and - may be evicted because you haven't paid your accommodation costs. We'll also take into account other factors, such as: - your situation - if you can afford to keep paying accommodation costs once the arrears are paid - if this is the best payment for you - what other help is available to you. There are also residency and income criteria you need to meet.

chunks.title: Residency criteria
chunks.text: You must be either: - getting a main benefit, NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, or - ordinarily resident in New Zealand and either: a New Zealand citizen have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 recognised as a refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009, or getting a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your New Zealand partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence. - a New Zealand citizen - have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 - recognised as a refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009, or - getting a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your New Zealand partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence. Main benefit Ordinarily resident

chunks.title: Income criteria
chunks.text: Getting an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have.

chunks.title: Weekly income (before tax) is less than:
chunks.text: Single $1,353 Couple without children $2,006 Couple with children $2,337 Sole parent, 1 child $1,846 Sole parent, 2+ children $2,126

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: Your assets need to be under a certain limit. Assets include money in the bank, or things like a caravan or second property. They don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, e.g. your home or your car.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: How much you get depends on the amount of accommodation costs you owe. The most you can get is 4 weeks accommodation costs and you'll need to pay it back. You can only get this payment twice in 12 months, unless there's an exceptional situation outside your control, for example: - you haven't been able to work, or earn your usual income, due to an unforeseen serious sickness or injury, or - you're in a family violence situation.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Call us on 0800 559 009 If you get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, call Senior Services on 0800 552 002 We may need to book you an appointment either to come in and see us, or a phone appointment. We'll let you know if this is the case. You'll need to provide proof of the amount of accommodation costs arrears. This could be a letter or notice showing how much overdue accommodation costs you need to pay, from either: - your accommodation supplier, e.g. your landlord or head tenant - the Disputes Tribunal - a Court - the Tenancy Tribunal, or - Tenancy Services.

chunks.title: If you have a shared tenancy
chunks.text: If you share your tenancy with: - your partner, you can apply for your portion and your partner's portion of the accommodation costs arrears. Or your partner can apply separately for their portion. - someone else, you can only apply for your portion of the accommodation costs arrears. The other person will need to apply separately for their portion.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: If your application’s approved, we’ll pay the accommodation costs arrears directly to the accommodation supplier. We’ll check if they are already a supplier with us. If they’re not, we’ll ask them to register as a supplier by completing a ‘Supplier Registration Form’. This is so we can make the payment to them. Register as a Work and Income supplier

chunks.title: Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant
chunks.text: If you need to pay accommodation costs before moving in and don't have enough money, we may be able to help pay for this. This type of payment can also be called Rent in Advance Grant. It will be called this if you're in a tenancy that the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA) applies to, i.e. you have a tenancy agreement. - You don't need to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. - You'll need to pay the money back. We'll put a repayment plan in place to suit your financial circumstances.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant if: - you have accommodation costs in advance you need to pay, e.g. rent, board or cabin hire - the supplier (e.g. your landlord or head tenant) has agreed you can move into the accommodation if you pay the accommodation costs in advance, and - you need the grant to pay the accommodation costs in advance. We'll also take into account other factors, such as: - your situation - if you can afford to stay in the accommodation long-term - how long you’ll be living in your accommodation (generally this needs to be at least 28 days) - if this is the best payment for you - what other help is available to you. There are also residency and income criteria you need to meet.

chunks.title: Income criteria
chunks.text: Getting an Accommodation Costs in Advance Grant also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have.

chunks.title: Income limits
chunks.text: If you're: Weekly income (before tax) is less than: Single, 16+ years $1,353 Couple without children $2,006 Couple with children $2,337 Sole parent 1 child $1,846 Sole parent 2+ children $2,126

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: Assets include money in the bank, or things like a caravan or second property. Assets don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, like the home where you live or your car. If you're: Your assets are worth less than: Single $8,100 Couple (with or without children) or sole parent $16,200

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: How much you get depends on the amount of accommodation costs in advance you have to pay. The most you can get is 2 weeks of accommodation costs and you'll need to pay it back. You can only get this payment twice in 12 months, unless there's an exceptional situation outside your control, for example: - you need to move unexpectedly through no fault of your own, or - you're in a family violence situation.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Call us on 0800 559 009 If you get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, call Senior Services on 0800 552 002 We may need to book you an appointment either to come in and see us, or a phone appointment. We'll let you know if this is the case. You'll need to provide proof of the amount of accommodation costs in advance. This will be an agreement signed by you and the accommodation supplier, e.g: - a tenancy agreement, or - an accommodation agreement.

chunks.title: If you share your tenancy
chunks.text: If you share your tenancy with: - your partner, you can apply for your portion and your partner's portion of the accommodation costs in advance. Or your partner can apply separately for their portion. - someone else, you can only apply for your portion of the accommodation costs in advance. The other person will need to apply separately for their portion.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: If your application's approved, we'll pay the accommodation costs in advance directly to the accommodation supplier. We'll check if they are already a supplier with us. If they're not, we'll ask them to register as a supplier by completing a 'Supplier Registration Form'. This is so we can make the payment to them.

chunks.title: Accommodation Supplement
chunks.text: Accommodation Supplement is a weekly payment which helps people with their rent, board or the cost of owning a home.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get an Accommodation Supplement if you: - have accommodation costs (you must be paying a minimum amount) - are 16 or older - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - are not paying rent for a public (social) housing property. Public housing properties are provided by: Kāinga Ora (used to be Housing New Zealand), and approved community housing providers. - Kāinga Ora (used to be Housing New Zealand), and - approved community housing providers. It also depends on: - how much income you and your partner get - any money or assets you and your partner have - any payments you get from boarders or renters.

chunks.title: Minimum accommodation costs
chunks.text: You need to be paying a minimum amount of accommodation costs each week. This is called an Accommodation Supplement entry threshold. Accommodation Supplement entry thresholds

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: This cash asset limit may increase if: - you get paid a lump sum under the Accident Compensation Act 2001, or - you get a lump sum payment of an Independence Allowance under the Accident Insurance Act 1998.

chunks.title: Check if you can get Accommodation Supplement
chunks.text: To find out if you could get Accommodation Supplement and what else you might qualify for, use our 'Check what you might get' tool.

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: How much you get depends on: - your income - your assets - your accommodation costs - your family circumstances - where you live. Definitions of areasexternal Depending on your situation and where you live, the most you can get is: Accommodation Supplement is not taxed. Use our 'Check what you might get' tool to work out how much Accommodation Supplement you might be able to get.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: What application form you fill out depends on what payments you're getting from us. We can grant you the financial assistance you're entitled to from the date you first contact us if you complete your application within 20 working days of that date.

chunks.title: New client or only getting childcare payments
chunks.text: If you're not getting any payments from us, or only getting childcare payments, you can either: - apply online through MyMSD, or - fill out an Extra Help application form. If you can't apply online or fill out the form, call us. Phone us

chunks.title: Apply online
chunks.text: Apply online through MyMSD. We'll check if you can get any other payments at the same time and tell you what else you need to do. Apply online

chunks.title: Fill out paper application form
chunks.text: You can fill out the Extra Help application form. You'll also need to provide proof of your costs. You can get your application form and proof of costs to us by either: - dropping them in to your nearest service centre - posting them to your nearest service centre, or - uploading them to MyMSD (you'll need to call us first). Find a service centre Upload your documents to MyMSD After you've applied you may need to call us to book an appointment. This could be a phone appointment or a face-to-face appointment. If this is your first time applying for a benefit or ongoing payment, you need to bring your ID into a service centre so we can verify it. Verify your identity at a service centre

chunks.title: Existing client
chunks.text: If you're already getting payments from us, e.g. a benefit or Disability Allowance, you can complete an Accommodation Supplement application form. You'll also need to provide proof of your costs. You can get your application form and proof of costs to us by either: - dropping them in to your nearest service centre - posting them to your nearest service centre, or - uploading them to MyMSD (you'll need to call us first). Find a service centre Upload your documents to MyMSD After you've applied we may book an appointment with you if we need more information. This could be a phone appointment or a face-to-face appointment. If you can't fill out the form, call us on 0800 559 009. If you're a student, you can apply through the StudyLink website: StudyLinkexternal

chunks.title: Already getting Accommodation Supplement and costs change
chunks.text: If you're already getting Accommodation Supplement and your accommodation costs or circumstances change, you need to let us know. Tell us about your change of accommodation costs If you're not sure what costs are included in your Accommodation Supplement, you can check in MyMSD. Find out about MyMSD

chunks.title: Confirming your circumstances
chunks.text: If you get an Accommodation Supplement, we must review your circumstances at least once every 52 weeks (one year). This is to make sure you are getting the correct assistance and amount. As part of this, we might ask you to fill out a Confirming your Circumstances form. It's important to fill out the form and return it promptly. If you don't respond to the form before the due date, Accommodation Supplement payments will stop. Confirming your circumstances

chunks.title: Accommodation Supplement (area you live in) payment error
chunks.text: We've found an error where some peoples Accommodation Supplement was being paid incorrectly for the area they were living in. This means we owe some people money.

chunks.title: Who's affected by this error
chunks.text: You may be affected if you: - got Accommodation Supplement before April 2018, and - were paid incorrectly for the area you were living in.

chunks.title: Check if you or someone else is owed money
chunks.text: We're contacting and paying all our current clients affected by this error. If you used to get payments from us, you can use the 'Payment errors enquiry' form to check if you're owed money. Our staff can't tell you if you're owed money or how much it is. You can also use the 'Payment errors enquiry' form to enquire for someone else if: - they're not a current client - a person has died. Information to make an enquiry for someone elseInformation to make an enquiry for someone who has died The form will check if you (or the person you're enquiring for) are owed money. It won't say how much you're owed. We'll write to tell you that. Payment errors enquiry form

chunks.title: Using the enquiry form overseas
chunks.text: At this stage the enquiry tool can only be accessed from Australia and New Zealand.

chunks.title: How this payment affects your benefit or allowance
chunks.text: If you're getting a benefit or allowance from us, they won't be affected for 12 months from when we pay you the money we owe. If you: - still have this money after 12 months, you'll need to tell us and it will be counted for any benefits or payments that are asset tested - invest the money you get and earn interest, after 12 months you'll need to tell us and this will be counted as income.

chunks.title: Getting Working for Families
chunks.text: Your payment won't affect your Working for Families payment because Accommodation Supplement payments aren't counted as income for Working for Families.

chunks.title: Impact on your taxes
chunks.text: You won't have to pay tax on this payment because Accommodation Supplement payments aren't taxable. Any income you earn on it (for example, interest) will be taxable.

chunks.title: Review rights
chunks.text: If you don't understand or agree with a decision we've made, please talk with us so we can explain it. You have the right to ask us to review a decision you think is wrong. You can use the application form on our website, or write to us. We need to get your request within 3 months. If you have a good reason why you can't ask us to review a decision within 3 months, get in touch. We may still be able to review the decision. You can find out more on the review of a decision page of our website, or you can give us a call on 0800 559 009 Get a decision reviewed

chunks.title: Accommodation Supplement obligations
chunks.text: There are things you and your partner need to do when you're getting an Accommodation Supplement If you don't do them, your payment could reduce or stop.

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: You and your partner must tell us (or your Youth Service Provider if you have one assigned to you) immediately if you: - have a change in your work situation, e.g. starting part-time, casual or full-time work (paid or unpaid) - become self-employed or start a business - have changes to your income or financial circumstances - have a boarder or renter that moves in or out, or the payments you get from them change - plan to travel overseas - start or finish study - part-time or full-time - have a change to your personal details, e.g: name address bank account number - name - address - bank account number - have a change to your living situation, e.g: marriage or separation starting or ending a civil union starting or ending a de facto relationship change in the number of children you support - marriage or separation - starting or ending a civil union - starting or ending a de facto relationship - change in the number of children you support - have a change in your accommodation costs - are imprisoned or held in custody on remand - are admitted to or discharged from hospital - are granted an overseas pension - have any other change that may affect your entitlement or rate.

chunks.title: If you don't meet your obligations
chunks.text: If there's any reason why you or your partner can't meet your obligations, talk to us straight away. Contact us If you or your partner don't tell us about changes in your life that might affect your payment entitlement, or rate, then: - your payment may be reviewed and cancelled - you may have to pay back the total amount of any overpayment that you've received - we may impose a penalty (up to 3 times the value of the overpayment) - you may be prosecuted and fined and/or imprisoned.

chunks.title: Going overseas
chunks.text: If you or your partner intend to travel overseas and don't let us know before you leave New Zealand, your payment will be stopped the day after you leave New Zealand.

chunks.title: Other things we may ask you to do
chunks.text: We must review Accommodation Supplement payments regularly. This means we may also ask you to fill out a Confirming your Circumstances form. This information helps us make sure you are getting the correct assistance and amount. If you don't respond to the form before the due date, your Accommodation Supplement payments will stop. Confirming your circumstances

chunks.title: Accommodation Supplement (type of accommodation) payment error
chunks.text:
## Accommodation Supplement (type of accommodation) payment error
We've found an error where some people's Accommodation Supplement was paid incorrectly when they moved between renting, boarding and living in their own home. This means we owe some people money and others were overpaid.
## Who's affected by this error
You may be affected if you:
- got Accommodation Supplement from us before December 2014, and
- moved between renting, boarding and living in your own home.
If you've been overpaid you don't have to pay the money back because it was our mistake. Our error will not affect any future payments you might get from us.
## Check if you or someone else is owed money
If you:
- currently get payments from us and were owed money because of this error, you were paid automatically in November 2016.
- used to get payments from us, you can use the payment errors enquiry form to check if you're owed money. Our staff can't tell you if you're owed money or how much it is.
You can also use the 'Payment errors enquiry' form to enquire for someone else if:
- they're not a current client
- a person has died.
Information to make an enquiry for someone elseInformation to make an enquiry for someone who has died
The form will check if you (or the person you're enquiring for) are owed money. It won't say how much you're owed. We'll write to tell you that.
Payment errors enquiry form
