chunks.title: Changes to your address, housing or accommodation costs
chunks.text: If your address or housing costs change, you need to tell us right away as it could affect how much you're paid.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: Call us to tell us if you have changes to your: Phone us - address - rent costs - board costs - homeownership costs - other accommodation costs (including water rates) - board or rent payments you get.

chunks.title: Getting Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment
chunks.text: If you get Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment, you also need to contact your Youth Service provider directly to tell them about your changes. Find your nearest provider (Youth Service)external

chunks.title: Changed address
chunks.text: If you've moved or have a new postal address you'll need to tell us: - your new address - your new postal address - the date you moved.

chunks.title: Rent or board costs
chunks.text: If your rent or board costs have changed, you'll need to tell us: - who you live with - how much you're now paying - when the costs changed. We'll let you know if you need to do anything else like providing proof of costs.

chunks.title: Own your own property
chunks.text: You need to tell us of any changes to your: - mortgage - if it's with Kāinga Ora (used to be Housing New Zealand) you'll need the current interest rate - council rates - house insurance - mortgage protection insurance - water rates - grounds lease or body corporate fees - costs for essential repairs and maintenance in the last 12 months. We'll need to know: - who you pay - how often you make payments - how much you pay - the date when the costs changed. We'll let you know if you need to do anything else like providing proof of costs.

chunks.title: Rent or board payments you get
chunks.text: You need to tell us if the amount of board or rent you get has changed if you are getting: - an income-tested benefit (e.g. Jobseeker Support, Supported Living Payment), or - a housing subsidy (e.g. Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support, Away from Home Allowance), or - Income Related Rent. You need to tell us: - the address - details of the person paying you board or rent - how much the board or rent is - when you get paid, and how often. You can tell us this in MyMSD, by selecting 'Declare boarders and renters' on the home page. If you can’t use MyMSD, you can complete the Board and rent information form instead: You can get this to us by bringing it into any Work and Income service centre (you don’t need an appointment for this), or posting it to us. Find a service centre We'll let you know if you need to do anything else, like providing proof of costs.

chunks.title: We're paying your rent directly to your landlord
chunks.text: If you have a rent redirection set up (where we pay your rent directly to your landlord) and you get a new landlord, you will need to set up a new redirection. You don't need to do this if you're living in public housing as we'll organise your rent payments with Kāinga Ora (used to be Housing New Zealand). To set this up for a new private landlord you need to: - complete a Redirection of Benefit Payment form - provide proof: to support your application of your new landlord's bank account - to support your application - of your new landlord's bank account - ask your new landlord to sign the bottom of page 3 of the application form. Talk to us about how to get this information to us.

chunks.title: What your landlord needs to do
chunks.text: Your landlord will need to register with us as a supplier, if they haven't already. Register as a Work and Income supplier

chunks.title: Checking your board or rent details
chunks.text: When people tell us about their accommodation costs, we ask them: - if they pay rent, board or homeownership costs, and if they get rent or board payments - who they pay it to, or are paid by - how much and how often those payments are. If both the boarder/renter and the person they pay board or rent to (e.g. their landlord or the head tenant) are getting either a housing subsidy or are living in public housing, we need to independently check this information with each of them. If it doesn't match, we need to contact both these people to get the correct details. This is part of meeting their obligations. We'll try calling them first. If we can’t contact them by phone, we'll send them a letter giving them 10 working days to confirm the correct details. We'll also send them a MyMSD notification, where they can confirm the details. If they don't confirm or still don't agree, after the 10 working days: - if they get a housing subsidy, this will stop on day 11 - if they are an public housing tenant, we will notify the housing provider and their rent may go up to market rent.

chunks.title: Advance Payment of Benefit
chunks.text: An Advance Payment of Benefit is a one-off payment to help you pay an essential or emergency cost if you can't pay it another way. To qualify for this payment you need to be getting a main benefit (e.g., Jobseeker Support), a pension or Orphan's or Unsupported Child's Benefit and you will have to pay the money back.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get an Advance Payment of Benefit if you: - are getting a main benefit (e.g., Jobseeker Support), Orphan's or Unsupported Child's Benefit, NZ Super or Veteran's Pension - have an essential or emergency cost you can't pay for. It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have.

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: These don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, e.g. your home, car, and some payments after a severe weather event. They do include things like money in the bank, or a second property.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: How much you get depends on your situation and what you need help with. Examples of costs we can help with are: - ambulance subscription fees - appliances and furniture - attendance at funerals and tangihanga - bedding - beds, chairs and tables - car repairs - child carseat - clothing - costs to end your tenancy early, or sublet or assign your tenancy - dental treatment - dentures and hearing aids - electricity, gas and water - essential home repairs - fire loss or burglary - fridges, freezers and washing machines - glasses - laser therapy to remove birthmarks - safety footwear - school costs - school stationery - school uniforms - tenancy tribunal fees - travel if you're stranded. We may be able to help with other costs, it depends on your situation. If you're not sure whether we can help, talk with us about your situation.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: If your application is approved, we'll give you a payment card (if you don't already have one) and load the money onto it. We'll talk to you about how we get this to you. You have 7 days to spend the money before it expires.

chunks.title: Using your payment card
chunks.text: A payment card is like an Eftpos card and you can use it at any supermarket or store that accepts them. Food grant suppliers (Manuals and Procedures)external Information about Payment Cards You can login to MyMSD to see how much you have left on your payment card and when it expires. Once you've used your payment card, keep it. You can use it again if you need help from us in the future.

chunks.title: Contact
chunks.text: This information is a guide only. Contact us to talk about your individual circumstances. - Phone us

chunks.title: After the Limited Service Volunteer course
chunks.text: Graduate from the Limited Service Volunteer (LSV) course with the skills to find a job and the confidence and support to keep moving forward. At the end of the 6-week LSV course, there is a graduation ceremony. You can invite your family and friends to celebrate your achievements and see how far you've come. After the course, we give you a reference and help you find work, or get into training or study. We can also help you pay for things you need to start work, like getting a driver licence or equipment. You get regular support from your Work and Income representative. They help you continue to meet the goals you set for yourself during the course. This could be help to find somewhere new to live, sticking to your routine or mental health support. If you get the chance, take it. It’s hard and you will want to quit but it helps so much. You learn so much and the bonds you make will last forever. – Trainee Duncan

chunks.title: Graduating from LSV
chunks.text: At the end of your 6-week Limited Service Volunteer course, you graduate from LSV. This is a chance for you as a group to celebrate your achievements, and for you to show the people who mean the most to you how far you've come and feel proud of you. There are 2 parts to graduation – a formal dinner and a parade. - The graduation dinner is with your fellow LSV trainees and the NZ Defence Force staff. You are served a 3-course meal, with awards and speeches from NZ Defence Force staff. - The graduation parade is held on the last day of the course, and your family and friends can attend, with an invitation. The parade includes a pōwhiri, and then the trainees perform marching displays. There are awards presented to LSV trainees, a speech from your commanding officer and the LSV haka. Photos are taken at both events, which are shared on the camp's Facebook page.

chunks.title: Support after the course
chunks.text: By the end of the LSV course, you have: - the determination to change your life - new skills and new friends - motivation and confidence to find a job - made yourself and others proud. After the course, we regularly check how you're doing and talk about what we can do to help you reach your goals. We also help you carry on meeting the goals you set for yourself during the course. We can help you find somewhere new to live, stick to your routine or offer encouragement and mental health support. You can also keep in touch with other people from the course and see how you're all doing.

chunks.title: Finding a job or training
chunks.text: When you leave LSV, you: - have a CV, with a reference from Work and Income - know how to write a cover letter - have NZQA credits and a first aid certificate - know how to talk to employers and have job interviews - have the kind of skills and qualities that employers look for, like reliability and positivity - can look forward to getting a job. During the course, you meet different employers. Some of them may offer you a job when you leave LSV. A lot of employers know about LSV and really value the personal qualities young people develop during this course. You can also talk to us if there's a certain job you want to do or a specific place you want to work. If you want to do training or study, we talk to you about what you want to do and help you apply. We make sure you have what you need to start work. We can help with things like: - getting a driver licence - paying for gear or equipment - helping you move to somewhere closer to work. Find jobs Do it! You will meet a lot of new people and they will become your new family for the next 6 weeks. And remember you haven’t come this far to only come this far. – Trainee Aumua

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Contact the Veteran's Pension Centre to talk about your circumstances and they'll explain how to apply. Veteran's Pension Centre

chunks.title: 20 working days to complete your application
chunks.text: You have 20 working days from the date you first contact us to complete the application process. You'll also need to provide any supporting documents within this time. If you don't do this, you may have to reapply. If you can't complete your application within 20 working days for any reason, contact the Veteran's Pension Centre Veteran's Pension Centre

chunks.title: Supporting documents you need to provide
chunks.text: You'll need to provide the following supporting documents: - proof of your residence in NZ - this could be a: NZ birth certificate current NZ passport other country passport with residence class visa or residence permit, or NZ Citizenship Certificate - NZ birth certificate - current NZ passport - other country passport with residence class visa or residence permit, or - NZ Citizenship Certificate - 2 or more documents as proof of your identity (one of these must be at least 2 years old) - these could be: a marriage certificate a driver's licence, or bank statements - a marriage certificate - a driver's licence, or - bank statements - proof of name change - this could be: a marriage certificate a Civil Union certificate, or deed poll papers - a marriage certificate - a Civil Union certificate, or - deed poll papers - proof of bank account number - this could be a: bank statement screenshot of your online banking (showing your name, account number and bank logo), or deposit slip - bank statement - screenshot of your online banking (showing your name, account number and bank logo), or - deposit slip - proof of any overseas pension you get - this could be a: letter showing your payments statement showing your payments, or payslip showing your payments - letter showing your payments - statement showing your payments, or - payslip showing your payments - proof of the medical condition that stops you working (if you're under 65) - this could be: an application form with the medical part filled in by your doctor. - an application form with the medical part filled in by your doctor.

chunks.title: Community Services Card
chunks.text: If you get the Veteran's Pension, you're automatically entitled to a Community Services Card. We'll send one out to you once your application for Veteran's Pension is approved. Community Services Card

chunks.title: Veteran SuperGold Card
chunks.text: Once your Veteran's Pension is approved, we'll automatically send you a Veteran SuperGold Card. SuperGold Card

chunks.title: Apply for emergency housing
chunks.text: Find out how to apply for emergency housing. When you apply, we'll ask you about other housing options you might have, including: - staying with family or friends - accommodation options you can afford (including temporary accommodation) - help if you're behind in your accommodation costs - help if you need bond or accommodation costs for a new property - help with moving and travel costs to shift to another suitable placenegotiating with landlords. We'll look at other housing options first, before we pay for emergency housing. Emergency housing is short-term accommodation. If you qualify for emergency housing, you could stay in places like a boarding house, backpackers, or motel. It depends on your situation and what's available.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: If you don't have other housing options (listed above), follow the steps below to apply for emergency housing. It's important you do not book or pay for accommodation until you've talked to us.

chunks.title: Step 1 - Call us
chunks.text: - If you're 65 and over, call 0800 552 002 - If you're under 65, call 0800 559 009 - If you get Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment, call your youth coach. If you don't know how to contact your youth coach, call your Youth Service provider and ask for your youth coach. You can find the contact details for your Youth Service provider on the Youth Services website. If your youth coach isn't available, call us on 0800 559 009 Youth Services external

chunks.title: Step 2 - We'll discuss your housing options
chunks.text: We'll talk with you about your situation and what housing options you might have. For example, staying with family or friends. If we think you qualify for emergency housing, we'll book an appointment for you. You may need to provide supporting documents. If so, we'll let you know what these are.

chunks.title: We'll confirm whether you qualify for emergency housing.
chunks.text: As part of this discussion, we'll check there are no other housing options available to you.

chunks.title: We'll check if transitional housing is available
chunks.text: This is funded by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). If there's a space in transitional housing, you can stay there for a few months while you find a more permanent home. If there are no spaces in transitional housing, we'll look at emergency housing options. Transitional housing (Ministry for Cities,Environment,Regions & Transport)external

chunks.title: We'll look at emergency housing options
chunks.text: We'll try to find somewhere for you to stay. We have a set of standards that emergency housing suppliers need to meet. You can stay with a supplier who has opted in to our standards. If they haven't opted in, you may still be able to stay with them, but only in certain situations. Read our supplier standards What happens if a supplier is not opted in to our standards To find a place, we may contact these places to check if there's anything available. We may ask you to contact some of these places too. We'll try to keep you in the same area but it will depend on what's available. Ideally, emergency housing will be available on the same day, but there may be a wait. Once a place has been confirmed, you can go there as soon as it's available.

chunks.title: We'll tell you about your rights and responsibilities
chunks.text: You'll have rights and responsibilities while staying in emergency housing. We'll talk to you about these, including: - a security deposit, if the supplier requires one - your rights - what you're expected to do - if you have concerns or want to make a complaint, and - your responsibilities from the 8th night (if you're still in emergency housing after 7 nights) and what will happen if you don’t meet them.

chunks.title: Step 4 - Follow up appointment
chunks.text: Emergency housing is short-term accommodation. We'll approve it for a certain period of time (usually 7 nights). If you still need emergency housing after this time, we'll book another appointment with you. At this appointment, we'll: - check if you still qualify for emergency housing - check there are no other housing options available to you - confirm you understand and agree to your responsibilities and what activities you need to do to meet them - check if the accommodation you're staying in still meets your needs, and - check if you qualify for public housing. Your responsibilities in emergency housing Who can get public housing We'll also check we have your correct contact details. This is so we can get in touch with you again when we need to.

chunks.title: Apply for public housing
chunks.text: Find out how to apply for public (social) housing. If you’re in urgent housing need and have nowhere to live now or in the next 7 days, call: - Work and Income on 0800 559 009 or - Senior Services on 0800 552 002 if you get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension.

chunks.title: Step 1 - Call us
chunks.text: Call us on 0800 559 009 If you get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, call Senior Services on 0800 552 002

chunks.title: Step 2 - Discuss your situation
chunks.text: We'll talk with you about your situation and look at ways we can help you. This includes checking what support you might be able to get to move into private housing, for example, help with rent or bond. If we think you may qualify for public housing, we’ll book a housing assessment interview for you. This is usually done over the phone but you can come in and see us if you'd prefer. Who can get public housing

chunks.title: Support person or interpreter
chunks.text: If you want a support person at your interview, you can organise to have one with you. If you can't speak English, you can bring someone to interpret for you. Or we can find an interpreter for you, just let us know so we can organise this.

chunks.title: Step 3 - Attend an interview
chunks.text: The interview will take about an hour. We’ll: - talk with you about your situation and the type of housing you need - confirm you meet the criteria for public housing. You'll need to tell us at least 3 areas where you could live so you can be matched to a suitable property.

chunks.title: Documents you need to provide
chunks.text: We'll also ask you to gather some documents and drop them off to one of our service centres. We'll let you know what documents you need to get. These could be: - proof of who you are, such as your birth certificate, passport or driver licence - proof of any income (after tax) you've got in the last 52 weeks, such as wages, holiday pay, family tax credits and any other income - proof of any assets you have and their value - your business accounts, if you have your own business - trust documents, if you're involved in a trust, such as trust deed, deed of debt, gift statements, or accounts - full birth certificates for each dependent child in your care. We may ask you to bring the same documents for other members of your household who are moving with you. Household members are people who permanently live with you.

chunks.title: Step 4 - Wait for a property
chunks.text: If you qualify for public housing, you’ll go on the social housing register. The register has details of people who need public housing and the type of property they need. We'll pass the register onto housing providers who will let you know when a suitable property becomes available. There are some things you'll need to do while you're waiting to get into a public house. Waiting for public housing

chunks.title: Step 5 - Accept a public housing offer
chunks.text: If a housing provider makes you an offer for a property and it suits your needs, you can accept this by signing the tenancy agreement. Accepting a public housing offer

chunks.title: Apply for the Limited Service Volunteer course
chunks.text: Who can apply for a Limited Service Volunteer (LSV) course and what you need to include. Check the application process and what happens after you apply for a Limited Service Volunteer course. The free voluntary Limited Service Volunteer (LSV) course is for young people who are not: - working - in education or training.

chunks.title: Who can apply for LSV
chunks.text: To apply for LSV, you must be: - between 18 and 24 years old - in good health so you can take part in outdoor activities. You can be male, female or gender-diverse. If you're gender-diverse, we'll talk with you about how we can make sure you're comfortable and safe throughout the course. If you're 17, you can still apply and we'll consider your application. You don't have to be: - getting payments from Work and Income to apply - fit already.

chunks.title: Criminal convictions
chunks.text: If you have a criminal conviction, you may still be able to attend LSV. When you apply, we complete a police vetting check so it's best to be honest if you have any convictions. We look at each application on a case-by-case basis. If you're on probation or waiting for a court hearing, your probation officer or lawyer needs to write a letter of support to go with your LSV application. I wanted to enhance my leadership skills and make a new family. I wanted to become drug-free in order to transition into work. – Trainee Reynolds

chunks.title: Before you apply
chunks.text: The New Zealand Defence Force can accept applications at any time. But the earlier you apply and get accepted, the more time you have to get ready.

chunks.title: Information you need to apply
chunks.text: To apply, you need to give us: - your personal details, like your name, address and date of birth - contact details of someone we can contact in an emergency - proof of your identity, like a driver licence, birth certificate or passport. - reasons you want to join an LSV course. If you have any of the following, you also need to include details of your: - Work and Income client number - Community Services Card - driver licence - special food needs. If you're on probation or waiting to appear in court, you also need a letter of support from your probation officer or lawyer.

chunks.title: How to apply for LSV
chunks.text: You need to fill in an application form and pass a medical check to make sure you can take safely part in outdoor activities. The application form includes a police vetting form.

chunks.title: Help to fill in the application form
chunks.text: Give your name and contact details in the 'Enquire about LSV' form and someone will give you a call.

chunks.title: After you apply
chunks.text: We'll call you within the next day or so between 9am and 5pm to talk about: - the LSV programme - the application process - any questions you have.

chunks.title: Medical check
chunks.text: You need to get a medical check as part of your application. This is a basic health check to make sure you can take part in outdoor activities and help keep you safe on the LSV course. If you have asthma, allergies, past injuries or poor mental health, this doesn't stop you from going on an LSV course. We talk to you about the medical check and we also pay for it. You visit a GP or registered nurse practitioner, who fills in a form with your medical details. I wanted to boost up my motivation to work and to do things that were out of my comfort zone. I also came here to get healthy and to start a new journey of getting fit and staying fit. – Trainee Leota

chunks.title: Getting a decision
chunks.text: It can take up to 6 weeks to get the final decision about your application for an LSV course. The New Zealand Defence Force decides if you're accepted on the course. Before the final decision, we keep in touch with you to let you know how things are going. We may need more information from you, especially if you have a criminal record, are on probation or something comes up in your medical check. We regularly speak with you on Zoom video-calls before the course starts. Before you start the Limited Service Volunteer course

chunks.title: Relationships and payments
chunks.text: The type of payment you get from us and how much you get depends on a few things, including if you're in a relationship. Here are some things you need to know about relationships, including how we determine if you're in one. You need to tell us straight away if you start or end a relationship, or if you're in a relationship you haven't told us about before. We need to know this so we can make sure you’re paid the right amount and don’t miss out on any extra payments or get into debt.

chunks.title: What we mean by being in a relationship
chunks.text: When we look at what benefits you can get, we consider you to be in a relationship if you are: - married - in a civil union, or - in a de facto relationship. This means you and your partner have a degree of companionship that includes being: - emotionally committed to each other for the foreseeable future, and - financially interdependent. To give you a better idea of what we mean by this, think about whether your relationship includes some of these things: - you live together at the same address most of the time - you share responsibilities, eg bringing up children (if any) - you socialise and holiday together - you share money, bank accounts or credit cards - you share household bills - you have a sexual relationship - people think of you as a couple - you give each other emotional support and companionship - your partner would be willing to financially support you if needed. If you or your partner are 16 or 17, a Family Court Judge must consent to your relationship. If you're unsure about whether we would consider you to be in a relationship, contact us. Phone us Relationship changes

chunks.title: If you're in a violent relationship
chunks.text: If you're in a violent relationship, or thinking of leaving one, we may be able to give you extra financial help. We may also be able to offer advice on where you can go for other support. Please talk with us about it. The Police can also help you get protection, shelter and support.

chunks.title: Make sure you tell us everything
chunks.text: When you get payments from us, you need to tell us everything about your personal situation that might affect your entitlement. For example, if you're working or in a relationship. It's also important you honestly answer any questions we may ask about your personal situation. If your situation changes in any way that may affect your entitlement, you must tell us straight away. Call us if there's anything you're uncertain about, we're happy to answer your questions. Phone us

chunks.title: What happens if you don't tell us
chunks.text: If we find out later that any information you give us is not true, or that you knew information you should have told us and did not tell us, we may stop your payments. You might need to pay money back, we may impose a penalty, and you could be prosecuted.

chunks.title: How benefit payments are affected
chunks.text: If you or your partner have an uncleared warrant for criminal matters, you'll be told that unless it's cleared, or you've taken reasonable steps to try and clear it, your benefit will either: - stop, if you don't have dependent children, or - reduce by up to half, if you have dependent children. If it hasn't been cleared within 28 days after its issued, you'll get a letter advising you to clear it within 10 working days. If the warrant is not cleared within 10 working days, your benefit payment will be affected. If you have an arrest warrant and the New Zealand Police considers you to be a risk to public safety, your benefit can be stopped or reduced immediately, without telling you first.

chunks.title: What you need to do
chunks.text: Only a court can issue and clear warrants to arrest. To clear your warrant to arrest you need to: - go to the criminal counter at a courthouse. It's best to go to the court where the warrant was issued, but it can be done at any courthouse. You can't clear a warrant over the phone - tell them you want to make a voluntary appearance to clear your warrant - try to arrive early in the day. If you leave it too late you may not be able to clear the warrant that day. try to arrive early in the day. If you leave it too late you may not be able to clear the warrant that day. You can go to a police station to start the process of clearing your warrant if you can't get to a court.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: The court will let you know if the warrant can be cleared straight away or if a Judge needs to make the decision. - If the warrant can be cleared straight away, the court will give you a Notice of bail.The Ministry of Justice lets Work and Income know when this has been done.You only have to bring the Notice of bail into your local Work and Income service centre if your benefit has already been stopped or reduced. - If the decision has to be made by a Judge you'll be given a Notice of hearing to withdraw an outstanding warrant to arrest. You'll then be given a new court date.You need to bring your "Notice of hearing" into your local Work and Income service centre.

chunks.title: More information
chunks.text: For all questions about your warrant and to check the courts opening hours, please contact the Ministry of Justice: - call 0800 268 787 - visit the criminal counter at your local court, or Ministry of Justiceexternal

chunks.title: How to get your benefit payments restarted
chunks.text: Benefit payments will only be restarted from the date your warrant is cleared and any missed payments won't be backdated. Other payments from us may also be affected. If the warrant can be cleared straight away, the court will give you a 'Notice of bail'. The Ministry of Justice will let us know when this has been done. You'll need to bring the 'Notice of bail' into your local Work and Income service centre. If the decision has to be made by a Judge, you'll be given a 'Notice of hearing to withdraw an outstanding warrant to arrest'. You'll then be given a new court date. You'll need to bring the "Notice of hearing' into your local Work and Income service centre.

chunks.title: Social Security Agreement with Australia
chunks.text:
## Social Security Agreement with Australia
New Zealand (NZ) has an agreement with Australia to share responsibility for social security coverage.
This agreement generally allows you to apply for certain NZ payments (paid by us) or Australian payments (paid by Centrelink).
NZ payments covered by this agreement are:
- New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super)
- Veteran's Pension
- Supported Living Payment, where you have a health condition, injury or disability.
Australian payments covered by this agreement are:
- Australian Age Pension
- Disability Support Pension
- Carer Payment.
It also allows you to add together your periods of residence in either country so you can meet certain criteria for these payments.
## Living in Australia
If you've lived in New Zealand and now live in Australia, you may be able to get some payments.
Social Security Agreement with Australia - living in Australia
## Living in New Zealand
If you've lived in Australia and now live in New Zealand, you may be able to get some payments.
Social Security Agreement with Australia - living in New Zealand

chunks.text:
## Away from Home Allowance
Away from Home Allowance is a weekly payment which helps carers with the living costs for 16 or 17 year olds who are living away from home while on a tertiary or training course. We pay the allowance to the carer of the young person.
## Who can get it
You may get an Away from Home Allowance if:
- you are the main carer of a 16 or 17 year-old young person
- you are eligible for a family tax credit for the young person
- the young person is dependent on you
- the young person is living away from home while on a tertiary course or approved employment related training.
## How much you can get
This depends on your and the young person's circumstances.

chunks.title: Backdated ACC weekly compensation payments
chunks.text: What happens if you get backdated ACC weekly compensation payments for the time you were getting a benefit. If ACC approves weekly compensation for a period in the past, we need to review any benefits or extra help you received for that same time. This is to make sure you got the right amount of financial support.

chunks.title: How backdated ACC payments affect payments from us
chunks.text: People get two types of payments from us. Weekly compensation payments from ACC affects your main benefit payments and any extra help payments. - Main benefits are payments like Jobseeker Support, Sole Parent Support or Supported Living Payment – including Winter Energy Payment when it’s paid. - Extra help are payments like Accommodation Supplement, Disability Allowance or Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Main benefit payments
chunks.text: If you are entitled to backdated ACC Weekly Compensation for a period when you were receiving a main benefit, we may determine that a benefit should not have been paid. This would result in a debt with us because you can’t get both for the same time. This debt must be repaid from your backdated ACC payment by law, then any remaining amount is paid to you.

chunks.title: Extra help payments
chunks.text: ACC Weekly Compensation is treated as income, so you may still be entitled to some or all of the extra help payments you received. We will work this out and if you have a debt, you will need to repay us. If a debt is created, this needs to repaid in one of the following ways: - We can deduct the debt from your backdated ACC payment before it’s paid to you, or - You can make an arrangement with us to pay it back .

chunks.title: What happens during the review
chunks.text: ACC and MSD work together and share the information for the assessment the law allows them to. There’s nothing you need to do at this stage. The process works like this: - ACC asks us to confirm whether you received benefits and extra help during the period covered by your weekly compensation entitlement. - We identify any benefits that may need to be reviewed and advise ACC. - If you’re moving from a benefit to ACC payments, we provide a handover date so there is no gap in your payments and it's a smooth transition. - ACC provides us with weekly compensation rates and dates for the assessment. - We start the assessment and may contact you to let you know your case has been assigned for processing. - We review your entitlement and determine whether any debt has been created.

chunks.title: Keeping you informed
chunks.text: Most assessments take around 6 to 8 weeks. More complex cases can take longer. We’ll keep you informed throughout the process, including: - when the assessment starts and is completed - what the outcome is - any repayment options that may apply.

chunks.title: How you’ll find out the result
chunks.text: Once the assessment is finished, we will contact you to explain the outcome. We also provide the final payment information to ACC. Debts on your main benefit will be paid by ACC from your backdated ACC payment before you get it. ACC will pay any tax to Inland Revenue. If a debt has been identified on your extra help payments, we will talk to you about your repayment options. If we can’t reach you, you will receive a letter explaining: - the assessment outcome - any debt that has been identified - how you can choose to repay the extra help debt. If you get a letter asking you to reply, you need to do this within 10 business days. If we don’t hear from you, our Collections Team will contact you.

chunks.title: More information
chunks.text: Find out more about ACC payments and benefits and how we protect your privacy. - ACC payments - Our privacy notice

chunks.title: Change your bank account
chunks.text:
## Change your bank account
If you want to change your bank account, you need to let us know as soon as possible. Don't close your old bank account until you've received a payment into your new account.
It takes 5 working days for your account details to be changed. If you've already closed your old account, call us.
Phone us
## Before you start
If you’re only changing the last 2 numbers of your account (the suffix), call us. We'll update this over the phone.
## Step 1 - Get proof of your account
First you need to get proof of your new bank account number. This could be a:
- bank statement
- bank print-out stamped by the bank
- letter from the bank
- print-out from an ATM
- print-out of your internet banking which shows the web address, or
- photo or screenshot of your online banking.
Bank account evidence must show the:
- bank logo
- bank account number (does not have to show suffix), and
- account name(s).
## Step 2 - Tell us about the change
You can either:
- upload your document to MyMSD (you need to call us on 0800 559 009 first), or
- complete the Change of bank account form. You can drop this and your evidence into, or post it to, your nearest service centre
Upload your document to MyMSD
Find a service centre
## Getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
If your payments go to an overseas bank account, or you want your payments to go to an overseas bank account, contact contact International Services.
International Services.
## Getting Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment
If you get Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment, you also need to contact your Youth Service provider directly to tell them about your change in circumstances.
Contact ( Youth Service)external

chunks.title: Bereavement
chunks.text: You may be able to get help to pay for funeral expenses or travel to a funeral or tangi. When a client dies, we need to know. Please call us to let us know. Phone us If they were getting NZ Super or Veteran's Pension you can tell us by filling out our online form. Online formexternal

chunks.title: Funeral expenses
chunks.text: We may be able to help you pay for some funeral expenses if the person who had died has little or no money to pay for this. You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for a Funeral Grant and you don't have to pay the money back.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: We may be able to pay a Funeral Grant of up to $2,697.43 if the estate of the person who has died can't pay. This money can be used for costs such as: - professional services for preparing the body for cremation or burial (e.g. embalming) - the cost of a casket - newspaper death notice costs - hearse fees - compulsory fees for buying a burial plot - cremation fees. Funeral Grant

chunks.title: If the person died from an injury or accident
chunks.text: If someone close to you has died from an injury or accident, ACC may be able to give you financial support. They can help with funeral or memorial costs, one-off payments and loss of income. Financial support if someone has died from an injury (ACC)external

chunks.title: Travel to a funeral or tangi
chunks.text: We may be able to help you if you can't afford to travel to a funeral or tangi. You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for help and you may have to pay the money back depending on your situation. How much you get depends on your situation. You may be able to get help with your travel costs if someone has died and you are either their: - Partner (if you were living together at the time of their death) - child (including step-children, foster children and whāngai) - grandchild or mokopuna - sibling (including half-siblings and step-siblings) - parent (including step-parents and foster parents) - grandparent.

chunks.title: If you're on a benefit
chunks.text: Advance Payment of Benefit You may be able to get an Advance Payment of Benefit to help with your travel costs.

chunks.title: If you're not on a benefit
chunks.text: Recoverable Assistance Payment You may be able to get a Recoverable Assistance Payment to help with your travel costs.

chunks.title: Bond Grant
chunks.text: If you don't have enough money to pay bond to your landlord, you may be able to get a Bond Grant. - You don't need to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. - You'll need to pay the money back. We'll put a repayment plan in place to suit your financial circumstances.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Bond Grant if you need to pay bond because you're entering a tenancy that the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA) applies to, for example a tenancy agreement. You can also apply if your existing bond is being increased because of a rent increase. You can apply for a bond grant for a General Bond or a Pet Bond. We'll also take into account other factors, such as: - your situation - if you can afford to stay in the accommodation long-term. - how long you’ll be living in your accommodation (generally this needs to be at least 28 days) - if this is the best payment for you - what other help is available to you. There are also residency and income criteria you need to meet. If you're not entering a tenancy under the RTA, we may still be able to help. You may be able to get an Accommodation Security Cover Grant to help with outstanding costs when you leave your accommodation. Accommodation Security Cover Grant

chunks.title: Income criteria
chunks.text: Getting a Bond Grant also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have.

chunks.title: Weekly income (before tax) is less than:
chunks.text: Single, 16+ years $1,353 Couple without children $2,006 Couple with children $2,337 Sole parent, 1 child $1,846 Sole parent, 2+ children $2,126

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: Assets include money in the bank, or things like a caravan or second property. Assets don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, like the home where you live or your car.

chunks.title: Your assets are worth less than:
chunks.text: Single $8,100 Married, civil union or de facto couple (with or without children) or sole parent $16,200

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: The Bond Grant is to help pay the cost of your bond, including an increase to an existing bond due to a rent increase, even if you have more than one bond. For example you may have to pay for a General Bond and a Pet Bond. We pay for whichever is the lowest of: - 4 weeks rent, or - the amount your landlord asks for, or - your share of the bond. The most you can get is 4 weeks rent. If your bond is being increased, the grant can cover the increase up to these same limits. You need to pay the Bond Grant back. The Bond Grant and Accommodation Security Cover Grant are paid for similar reasons. This means you can only get these payments a total of twice in 52 weeks (i.e. 1 year). So within 52 weeks, you could get either: - 2 Bond Grants - 2 Accommodation Security Cover Grants, or - 1 Bond Grant and 1 Accommodation Security Cover Grant. You may be able to get another grant if there's an exceptional situation outside your control, for example: - you need to move unexpectedly through no fault of your own, or - you're in a family violence situation.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Call us on 0800 559 009 If you get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, call Senior Services on 0800 552 002 We may need to book you an appointment either to come in and see us, or a phone appointment. We'll let you know if this is the case. You'll need to provide proof of the amount of bond, for example a: - tenancy agreement, or - bond form which is signed by the landlord, or - written notice from your landlord showing the bond increase due to a rent increase.

chunks.title: If you have a shared tenancy
chunks.text: If you share your tenancy with: - your partner, you can apply for your portion and your partner's portion of the bond. Or your partner can apply separately for their portion. - someone else, you can only apply for your portion of the bond. The other person will need to apply separately for their portion of the bond. If your bond is being increased due to a rent increase, you can only apply for your portion of the increase. Anyone else who needs to pay (e.g. your partner or flatmates) must apply separately for their own portions.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: If your application's approved, we'll pay the bond directly to the landlord. We'll check if your landlord's already a supplier with us. If they're not, we'll ask them to register as a supplier by completing a 'Supplier Registration Form'. This is so we can make the payment to them. Register as a supplier

chunks.title: Budgeting
chunks.text: We can provide support and practical information to help you budget. Budgeting gives you control of your money – and your life. It helps you to - see how much money you have - look at what you spend your money on, and - think about ways to make your money go further. Thinking carefully about where your money goes also gives you opportunities to explore ways to improve your situation. By budgeting, you can: - pay off your debts faster - keep up with your bills - save for the things you want - be more prepared for unplanned expenses.

chunks.title: Work out if you need a budget
chunks.text: To work out if you need to budget, ask yourself: - do I worry about money? - do I often have no money to pay my bills? - does talking about money with my family cause arguments? - am I unable to afford the things I want? - am I always in debt? - have my costs increased for some reason? - have I given up hope of having money for holidays or retirement? If your answer is YES to any of these, it may be a good idea to start budgeting.

chunks.title: Ideas to pay off debt or save
chunks.text: Here are some ideas on how you could help to pay off your debt, or save some money.

chunks.title: Open a separate bank account for savings
chunks.text: Open a separate bank account and make an automatic payment into it every time you get paid. This can be your savings account and you can see it build up over time. You can ask your bank about setting up an automatic payment.

chunks.title: Put some money towards your debt every time you get paid
chunks.text: Pay off your debts as soon as you can. The longer you have a debt, the more interest you're charged and the more money you owe. An easy way to pay off a debt is to put a bit towards it every time you get paid (but only after you've paid your bills). You can organise to pay it straight from your bank account so you don't have to think about it. Then you're not tempted to use the money for other things. Ask your bank about setting up an automatic payment. Only buy the things you need if you really want to pay off your debts and get closer to reaching your goals.

chunks.title: Plan a budget
chunks.text: Putting together and planning a budget helps you understand more about how to manage your money. Everyone can benefit from managing their money better and it's a good idea to do a budget plan, or redo the one you have, to make sure it's still helping you. There are 3 steps listed below to help you make your plan, with a separate worksheet for each step. You can print these off and use them to make your plan. You should do them one-by-one to build your plan over time.

chunks.title: Step 1 - Your money
chunks.text: Budgeting is not just about how much money you spend, it's also about where you spend your money. You can use this to write down the money you get. This can help you to set goals to see if there are any ways to reduce your costs and money you owe. It also helps you think of ways to start saving.

chunks.title: Step 2 - Your goals
chunks.text: Setting goals is a good way to start helping you decide how you spend your money in the future. It is about changing the way you manage your money to see if there are any ways to spend less and increase the money you get.

chunks.title: Step 3 - Managing your money
chunks.text: A budget plan needs to change when something different happens in your life. You might move house and have to pay more or less than you were paying before. Or you might get part-time work which means you have more money now. Your budget plan should show any new income or costs for you and your family/whānau. You might need to set some new goals so you keep planning ahead for you and your family/whānau.

chunks.title: Budget worksheet
chunks.text: Enter your income and expenses into this budget worksheet to get you started. Budget worksheet

chunks.title: Business Training and Advice Grant
chunks.text: If you're starting your own business, we may be able to help with developing a business plan, training in business skills, advice and project reports.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Business Training and Advice Grant if you’re: - out of work, and - aged 16 or older and not qualified to receive NZ Super, and - disadvantaged in the local labour market, and - at risk of likelihood of long-term benefit dependency (this usually means you are getting a benefit or you qualify for one), and - able to meet the residency criteria. To meet the residency criteria you need to be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and either: - a New Zealand citizen - a resident with a residence class visa - recognised as a refugee or protected person, or - have a temporary visa that allows you to work in New Zealand and either: have applied to be recognised as a refugee or protected person and are waiting on the outcome, or have applied for a residence class visa and are compelled to stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances. - have applied to be recognised as a refugee or protected person and are waiting on the outcome, or - have applied for a residence class visa and are compelled to stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances. Disadvantaged in the labour market means you have, or are expected to have, difficulty in getting or keeping a job. For example, you might have barriers to employment such as lack of education and training. You also need to be: - planning to start a new business and - getting help from us to start that business and - intending to get Flexi-wage Self Employment for that same business. If you're not sure whether you qualify, contact us. Phone us

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: We'll pay an expert who will help you with things like: - business skills training - developing a business plan - business advice before and when starting your business - independent vetting report - mid-project financial report. You can apply more than once, but the total amount cannot be more than $5,000 in a 52 week period

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us. You'll need to: - write a brief summary about your business - provide information about what course or service you want the grant for.

chunks.title: Calculating your rent payments
chunks.text: When you live in public (social) housing, the amount of rent you pay is based on your income, and the income of people you live with. This is called Income Related Rent. Income Related Rent means: - you pay some of the rent - the government pays some of the rent. We'll generally pay your rent directly to your landlord if you get either: - a main benefit, for example Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support - NZ Super, or - Veteran's Pension. Otherwise you'll need to arrange to pay it to your landlord.

chunks.title: Step 1 - Work out your weekly household income
chunks.text: We work out what your total weekly household income is after tax. This includes any income that you, your partner, anyone else on the tenancy agreement and their partners, get. Income can include: - a benefit from Work and Income - NZ Super or Veteran's Pension - Student Allowance - wages - salary - commission - parental leave payments - most child support payments - income from assets (e.g. income from a rental property you own, or interest on savings) - minimum family tax credits. If your income changes often, we may work out your weekly income in a different way.

chunks.title: Your income changes often
chunks.text: If your income changes often (e.g. you work casual hours, or are self-employed), we look at your total income over a longer period of time (at least 4 weeks). We then work out your average weekly income based on this. For example, you earn the following amounts (after tax) over 4 weeks: - Week 1: $400 - Week 2: $300 - Week 3: $700 - Week 4: $420 Altogether this comes to $1,820 after tax. We divide this by the number of weeks it covers (4). This would make your average weekly income $455 after tax.

chunks.title: Step 2 - Check your income threshold
chunks.text: We find out what your living situation is. Then, using the table below, we check what your income threshold is. For example, if you're single and living by yourself, your weekly income threshold (after tax) is $555.15.

chunks.title: Step 3 - Calculate your rent payment
chunks.text: We check if your total weekly household income (after tax) is higher or lower than your income threshold.

chunks.title: Income is higher than your income threshold
chunks.text: If your total weekly household income (after tax) is higher than your income threshold, first we: - take your income threshold, and - calculate 25% of it. Then we: - take your total weekly household income (after tax) - work out how much is over the income threshold - calculate 50% of this amount. Then we add these two amounts together to work out your rent payment.

chunks.title: For example:
chunks.text: - Your income threshold is $854.08. - 25% of that threshold is $213.52. Then: - Your income is $890 (after tax) a week. - This is $35.92 over the income threshold. - 50% of $35.92 is $17.96. We add $213.52 and $17.96 together, which makes your rent $231.48 per week.

chunks.title: Income is lower than your income threshold
chunks.text: If your total weekly household income (after tax) is lower than your income threshold, we: - take your total weekly household income (after tax) - calculate 25% of it.

chunks.title: For example:
chunks.text: - Your total household income is $650 (after tax) a week (your income threshold is $854.08). - 25% of your income is $162.50. This makes your rent $162.50 per week.

chunks.title: Step 4 - Family tax credits
chunks.text: If you get family tax credits (not including Best Start, In-Work and Minimum family tax credits), we work out the lowest amount of either: - 25% of your weekly family tax credit payment, or - $36.07 (25% of the first or only child weekly family tax credit payment). We then add the lower amount to your rent payment.

chunks.title: Step 5 - Income from boarders
chunks.text: A boarder is any person, who is not a tenant, who pays you to live in that home – regardless of whether the payment includes other costs like food. If you get payments for board, 62% of the board payment will be added to your rent payment.

chunks.title: Step 6 - Finalise your rent payment
chunks.text: Once we've worked out your rent payment, we round it down to the nearest dollar.

chunks.title: Step 7 - Check against market rent or minimum rent required
chunks.text: If you're not sure what the market rent price is for your property, you can find this out from your property provider or landlord.

chunks.title: Rent calculation is more than market rent
chunks.text: If the rent payment we've worked out for you is more than the actual market rent price for the property, you'll only pay the market rent amount.

chunks.title: Rent payment is lower than the minimum amount required
chunks.text: There is a minimum amount of rent you have to pay, depending on your circumstances. This amount is the lowest rent that a public housing provider can charge. If the rent amount we've calculated for you is lower than the minimum amount, you'll need to pay the minimum amount instead. The table below shows the minimum rent payment for each circumstance.

chunks.title: Sole parent
chunks.text: Julie is a sole parent with an 8 year old son. She gets a Sole Parent Support payment of $521.52 a week. Her living situation is single with children. - Her total household income is $521.52 a week (after tax). - Her income threshold is $854.08. Because Julie’s total household income ($521.52) is lower than her income threshold ($854.08), we calculate 25% of her household income. - 25% of $521.52 is $130.38. - Julie also gets family tax credits of $151.91 per week. We work out 25% of $151.91, which comes to $37.97. We then add $130.38 and $37.97 together (and round it down to the nearest dollar). This makes Julie’s rent $168 a week.

chunks.title: Couple with children
chunks.text: Sam and Jo live with their 2 year old daughter and 6 year old son. They both work part-time, and are paid $450 (after tax) each. - Their total household income is $900 (after tax) a week. - Their income threshold is $854.08. Because Sam and Jo’s income is higher than their income threshold, we: - take their income threshold ($854.08) - calculate 25% of it, which is $213.52. Then we: - take their total household income ($900) - work out how much is over the income threshold, which is $45.92 - calculate 50% of this amount, which is $22.96. We then add $213.52 and $22.96 together, which is $236.48. They also get a family tax credit payment of $275.69 per week. This means we work out the lowest amount of either: - 25% of $275.69 which is $68.92, or - $37.97 of their weekly family tax credit payment. We then add $236.48 and $37.97 together (and round down to the nearest dollar). This makes Sam and Jo’s rent $274 per week.

chunks.title: Single, living on your own
chunks.text: Barry is single and living on his own. He does casual work, and his hours change from week to week. For the past 4 weeks, Barry has earned the following amounts: - Week 1: $600 (after tax) - Week 2: $500 (after tax) - Week 3: $700 (after tax) - Week 4: $450 (after tax) Altogether this comes to $2,250 (after tax). We divide this by the number of weeks this covers (4), which makes Barry’s average weekly income $562.50. - His total household income is $562.50 (after tax) a week. - His income threshold is $555.15. Because Barry's income is higher than his income threshold, we: - take his income threshold ($555.15). - calculate 25% of it, which is $138.78. Then we: - take his total household income ($562.50) - work out how much is over the income threshold, which is $7.35 - calculate 50% of this amount, which is $3.67. We then add $138.78 and $3.67 together (and round it down to the nearest dollar). This makes Barry’s rent $142 per week.

chunks.title: Disagree with rent amount
chunks.text: If you disagree with a decision about your rent, talk to us. We may be able to solve the problem or explain the decision. If you still disagree, you can apply for a review of decision. Making a complaint

chunks.title: Social Security Agreement with Canada
chunks.text:
## Social Security Agreement with Canada
New Zealand (NZ) has an agreement with Canada to share responsibility for social security coverage.
This agreement generally allows you to apply for certain NZ payments (paid by us) or Canadian payments (paid by Service Canada).
NZ payments covered by this agreement are:
- New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super)
- Veteran's Pension
- Supported Living Payment, where you have a health condition, injury or disability
- Sole Parent Support for widows and widowers.
Canadian payments covered by this agreement are:
- Old Age Security Pension
- Canada Pension Plan (if you get the Quebec Pension Plan, this is not covered by the agreement).
It also allows you to add together your periods of residence in either country so you can meet certain criteria for these payments.
## Living in Canada
If you've lived in New Zealand and now live in Canada, you may be able to get some payments.
Social Security Agreement with Canada - living in Canada
## Living in New Zealand
If you've lived in Canada and now live in New Zealand, you may be able to get some payments.
Social Security Agreement with Canada - living in New Zealand

chunks.text:
## Car repairs
If your car needs to be fixed, we may be able to help.
- You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for this help.
- You'll have to pay the money back.
## Who can get it
You may get help if:
- you're 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services)
- you're a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident
- you normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here
- you have an immediate or essential need
- you need the car for you, your partner or children
- you need the car because of either: a health condition disability employment lack of access to public transport
- a health condition
- disability
- employment
- lack of access to public transport
- you or your partner own the car, i.e., you bought the car or were gifted it.
It also depends on:
- how much you and your partner earn
- any money or assets you and your partner have.
Youth Servicesexternal
## What you can get
Generally we can pay up to $400 to help with some car repairs.
We don't usually pay for standard car costs, e.g.:
- fuel
- warrant of fitness
- car insurance
- car registration
- regular servicing costs.

chunks.text:
## Caring for a child with a health condition or disability
If you're caring for a child with a health condition or disability, we may be able to help.
## Child has a serious disability or health condition
Your dependent child needs constant care and attention, over and above what a child or young person of the same age would need, because of a serious disability or health condition.
Child Disability Allowance
If you get the Child Disability Allowance, we may be able to help with extra childcare assistance.
Childcare
A Community Services Card can help with the costs of healthcare. You'll pay less for some health services simply by showing your card. Most people who are on a benefit automatically get one of these cards. If you're on a low income you can also apply for one.
Community Services Card

You need help to cover the ongoing costs of your child's disability.
Disability Allowance
## Caring for someone else's child
If you're caring for someone else's child there are also other kinds of help you may be able to get.
Caring for someone else's child
## Unsure of what you'll be able to get
You may also be able to get a benefit or help with other expenses, eg living expenses. Use "Check what you might get" to find out what help you could qualify for.

chunks.title: Caring for someone with a health condition, injury or disability
chunks.text:
## Caring for someone with a health condition, injury or disability
If the person you're caring for would need hospital, rest home or residential care without you, we may be able to help.
## Caring for someone ill or disabled
You may be able to get a Supported Living Payment if you're caring for a person at home who would otherwise need hospital-level, rest home or residential care (or the equivalent). This includes caring for your own child but not your partner.
The person you're caring for can also apply for a Supported Living Payment.
We'll need to see a medical certificate for the person you're caring for. It needs to be completed by their health practitioner.
Supported Living Payment
## Supported Living Payment
If you're caring for your partner at home and they would otherwise need hospital-level care or residential care (or the equivalent), they may be able to get a Supported Living Payment. They will need to apply for this benefit and you can be included in it. We'll need to see a medical certificate from their health practitioner.
Supported Living Payment
## Special Disability Allowance
If you're getting a benefit and your partner is in residential care, or has been in a public hospital for over 13 weeks, you may be able to get a Special Disability Allowance.
Special Disability Allowance
## Guide for carers
There is help available from other government agencies and organisations.
A guide to services and support available for carers (Ministry of Social Development)external
## Applying on someone else's behalf
You can apply for help from us on someone else's behalf, but only if they've filled out a form to appoint you as their agent.
Having someone act on your behalf

chunks.title: Caring for someone else's child
chunks.text: If you're caring for someone else's child, we may be able to help. What you get will depend on both your and the child's circumstances.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Unsupported Child’s Benefit A weekly payment that helps carers supporting a child or young person whose parents can't care for them because of a family breakdown. Orphan’s Benefit A weekly payment that helps carers supporting a child or young person whose parents have died or can't be found, or can't look after them because they have a serious long-term health condition or incapacity. Sole Parent Support A benefit that helps single parents and caregivers of dependent children under 14 get ready for future work, supports them to find part or full-time work and provides financial help through a weekly payment. Away from Home Allowance A weekly payment which helps carers with the living costs for 16 or 17 year olds who are living away from home while on a tertiary or training course. We pay the allowance to the carer of the young person. There are other types of help you may be able to get, it depends on your situation. Use "Check what you might get" to find out what help you could qualify for.

chunks.title: Getting Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit
chunks.text: Clothing Allowance If you get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit, you'll also automatically get a Clothing Allowance for children in your care, to help you pay for their clothing. Establishment grant Establishment grant is paid automatically when you first get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit. This is a once only payment of $350 for each child you're caring for. This money helps you buy things like a bed, bedding and clothing. You won't be taxed on this money, and you won't have to pay it back. Holiday and Birthday Allowance You automatically get the Holiday and Birthday Allowance if you already get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit. Use these payments to celebrate important events in the child’s life, like their birthday or Christmas. School and Year Start-up Payments Help with the costs that mostly happen at the beginning of the year, in particular pre-school and school-related costs, eg clothing, school fees and stationery. Extraordinary Care Fund This fund helps support children to develop their skills and talents. It can also help children who are experiencing difficulties that are significantly impacting on their development.

chunks.title: On a benefit
chunks.text: If a child comes into your care while you're on a benefit, you may have a change in obligations or your benefit could be affected.

chunks.title: Getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: It's different for people getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension - your payments stay the same whether or not you include the child in your payments. You may qualify for Working for Families Tax Credits from Inland Revenue, depending on your income. You'll need to apply by calling 0800 227 773 or visiting www.ird.govt.nzexternal Remember, any extra income you get can affect your other payments. It's probably better for you to get the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit if you qualify. Contact Work and Income to find out which is the best option for you.

chunks.title: Wages from casual work
chunks.text:
## Wages from casual work
If you do a one-off job and get paid, you need to let us know. The amount you earn may affect your benefit and any other payments you get from us.
If you don't tell us we may not pay you enough. Or we may pay you too much and you'll have to pay the debt back.
Do you need to declare income?
## Tell us before you get paid
You need let us know the week you earn the money, not when you've been paid. We need to know by Friday 6pm. If you're working the weekend, include this time too.
The amount you declare will continue every week until you let us know it has stopped or changed.
## Make an estimate
If you don't know what you'll earn tell us what you think it will probably be.
## What we need to know:
- the amount before tax (gross) or estimate for the work, or the hourly rate
- the number of hours you worked.
## How to tell us
The easiest way to tell us about your earnings is to use MyMSD.
You'll need your client number to register then follow a few simple steps.
About MyMSD
## If you can't use MyMSD
Call us or come into one of our service centres.
If you're declaring income from self-employment, make sure you mention you're self-employed.
Phone us
Find a service centre
## How your main benefit will be affected
Other payments from us such as Accommodation Supplement, may also be affected.
Income deduction tables
## Made a mistake or need to change your estimate?
If you think the amount you entered in our online services isn't right, correct this as soon as you can by logging back in.
If you need to change your estimate after 6pm on Friday, call us before midday on the following Monday.

## Change in your circumstances
If you get a Childcare Subsidy or before, after-school or holiday care for your child, you need to tell us straight away if something changes in your life as it can affect how much childcare we pay.
## What you need to tell us about
We need to know if:
- your income or your partner's income changes
- the number of hours you or your partner work, train or study each week changes
- your child stops attending childcare
- your child moves to another childcare provider
- there's a change to the number of hours your child attends childcare
- your relationship status changes, eg you become single or are now in a relationship
- you have another child
- a child is no longer in your care
- the reason why your payments change, eg your health improves or you stop working or studying
- your child now needs before, after-school or holiday care
- your child is going to a cohort entry school
- your child starts or stops receiving 20 Hours ECE
- you want to have another child in childcare.

chunks.title: Change of costs for Disability Allowance
chunks.text:
## Change of costs for Disability Allowance
If you're getting a Disability Allowance and you have a new cost that you need help with, or a cost has changed, you need to let us know straight away.
If you're not sure what costs are included in your Disability Allowance, you can check in MyMSD.
Find out about MyMSD
## A new cost
If you have another cost that you want the Disability Allowance to help with and you're getting less than the maximum amount of $82.85 a week, we may be able to help.
- Your health practitioner needs to complete a Disability Certificate form
- You need to get proof of the new cost.
Call us to talk about how to get these to us.
Contact us
If the cost is approved, we'll include it in your Disability Allowance from the date the cost started.
Disability Allowance - Types of costs (Maps and Procedures)external
If you're already getting the maximum amount of Disability Allowance, we may still be able to help. Call us to talk about this.
Contact us
## Cost has increased
If a cost you're getting Disability Allowance for has increased, you need to let us know.
You need to get proof of the change of cost. Call us to talk about how to get this to us.
Contact us
If the cost is approved, we'll reassess your Disability Allowance from the date the cost increased.
## Cost has stopped or decreased
If a cost you're getting Disability Allowance for has stopped or decreased, you need to let us know straight away.
Call us and tell us:
- the date the cost stopped or decreased
- how much the cost has decreased to (if the cost decreased).
We'll reassess your Disability Allowance from the date you call us.
Contact us
If you don't tell us straight away, we'll reassess your Disability Allowance from the date the cost stopped or decreased. This means you may get a debt.

Allowable costs (Manuals and Procedures)external

Find out about MyMSD

You can tell us about this in MyMSD, or you can call us.
Phone us
Find out about MyMSD
## You need to provide proof
You'll need to provide proof of:
- the amount of the new cost or change in cost, and
- the date the cost started or changed.
You'll be able to upload this proof in MyMSD as you go. If you call us, we'll let you know how you can get it to us.
If your cost is formula assessed child support through Inland Revenue, you can give consent in MyMSD for IR to share this information with us.
## If your application is approved
If it's approved, we'll reassess your Temporary Additional Support from either:
- the date you tell us about the new cost, or
- the date an existing cost changed.
## Cost has stopped or decreased
If a cost you're getting Temporary Additional Support for has stopped or decreased, you need to let us know straight away.
You can tell us about this in MyMSD, or you can call us.
Phone us
Find out about MyMSD
We'll need to know:
- the date the cost stopped or decreased, and how much the cost has decreased to (if the cost decreased).
- the date the cost stopped or decreased, and
- how much the cost has decreased to (if the cost decreased).
We'll reassess your Temporary Additional Support from the date you tell us. If you don't tell us straight away, you may get a debt.

chunks.title: Changing your tax code for NZ Super and Veteran's Pension
chunks.text:
## Changing your tax code for NZ Super and Veteran's Pension
Tell us straight away if you need to change your tax code, eg, if you stop working, so we can pay you the right amount of NZ Super or Veteran's Pension.
## Find out your tax code
If you don't know what tax code you should be on, go to Inland Revenue's website.
Tax codes and tax rates for individuals (Inland Revenue)external
## How to change your tax code
Select the 'Change tax code' button above to complete the 'Change tax code' form.
## What you'll need
You'll need the following information to complete the form:
- client number
- name
- IRD number
- current tax code
- new tax code.
## What happens next
We'll change your tax code and send you a letter to let you know how it affects your payments.
## Tailored tax code
If you have a tailored tax code, you need to renew it with Inland Revenue at the end of each financial year. If you don't renew your tailored tax code, you need to change it to a standard tax code and let us know.
If you don't renew or change your tailored tax code before the end of the financial year, your tax rate will default to 45% on 1 April.
What is a tailored tax code? (Inland Revenue)external
## If you use myIR
When it's time to renew your tailored tax code, Inland Revenue will send you a letter through myIR, and you'll be able to complete the form online.
Inland Revenue will let us know what your tax code is.
Apply for a tailored tax code (Inland Revenue)external
## If you don't use myIR
When it's time to renew your tailored tax code, Inland Revenue will send you a renewal form. You need to fill it out and send it back to them.
Inland Revenue will let us know what your tax code is.
## How to change to a standard tax code
To change your tailored tax code to a standard tax code, you need to complete the 'Change tax code' form.
