chunks.title: Reviewing Childcare Subsidy payments
chunks.text:
## Reviewing Childcare Subsidy payments
If you're getting childcare payments for your child and they haven't started school yet, your payments are reviewed every 52 weeks.
## Why payments are reviewed
We'll check if:
- you still need childcare
- your circumstances have changed
- the correct childcare rate is being paid.
Your childcare payments may stop if you don't confirm this with us.
## What you need to do
We'll send you a review form a few weeks before the review is due.
- Complete the review form - even if you've updated your details for childcare recently.
- You'll also be sent a verification form - get the supervisor at your child's childcare provider to sign.
- You may need to provide proof of any income you have - the form will tell you what to provide.
- Post the completed form to us (you'll find the address on the form) or you can email paperwork to us at Centralised_childcare_reviews@msd.govt.nz
Find your nearest service centre
## What happens next
We'll let you know if your payments will continue for the next year. Or we may need to talk to you about your circumstances and changing your payments.
## Contact
Contact us if you need help or more information.
- Phone us

chunks.title: Confirm OSCAR Subsidy payments every term
chunks.text:
## Confirm OSCAR Subsidy payments every term
If you want to keep getting childcare payments for before, after school and holiday care for your child, you need to confirm that with us every term.
## How to tell us
We'll send you an Out of School Care and Recreation (OSCAR) declaration form to complete about a month before the school term ends. Or you can download the form.
The form asks you to confirm your childcare arrangements, or let us know about any changes, eg, your child goes to after school care but now needs care in the holidays.
- Download the OSCAR declaration form
- Print the form and get your childcare provider to complete and sign the 'OSCAR Programme Supervisor to complete' section.
- Post the completed form to your local service centre or you can email paperwork to us at Centralised_childcare_reviews@msd.govt.nz.
If you can't print the form, contact us and we'll send one to you.
Find your nearest service centre
If your child is in more than one programme, you need to complete a declaration form for each.
## When you need to reapply
If it's been more than 8 weeks since you got the OSCAR Subsidy for before, after school or holiday care you'll need to apply again.
OSCAR Subsidy
You will also need to reapply if:
- you want to enrol an additional child
- your before, after school or holiday care payments have been cancelled.
## Contact
Contact us if you need help or more information.

## Contraception
If you need contraception, there are a number of options available to you.
Your decision whether to use contraceptives or not, and the type to use, is an entirely personal one made in consultation with a health practitioner, e.g. a doctor.
You can talk to a health practitioner, e.g. your doctor, about what options are available.
You can also get contraception at a lower cost or for free through some funded services.

chunks.title: Cost of emergency housing
chunks.text: In most cases we'll cover the cost of your accommodation for the first 7 nights if you qualify. Then you'll have to start paying for some of the accommodation costs. This is called an Emergency Housing Contribution. In most cases we'll cover the cost of your accommodation for the first 7 nights if either: - it's your first time in emergency housing, or - it's been a while since you've needed emergency housing and there's a new reason you need it again.From the 8th night, you'll pay an Emergency Housing Contribution. If the emergency housing supplier also needs a security deposit, we can help with this. Security deposit for emergency housing

chunks.title: How much you have to pay
chunks.text: After 7 nights, you'll start to pay an Emergency Housing Contribution. You will need to pay the higher amount of either: - 25% of your and your partner's (if you have one) weekly income (after tax), or - 25% of the Jobseeker Support benefit rate you and your partner (if you have one) would qualify for (if you're not already getting it). Income may include payments from us, wages, salary or other income, or family tax credits. We'll let you know exactly how much your Emergency Housing Contribution will be and when you need to pay it by.

chunks.title: How to pay for it
chunks.text: If you get a main benefit, NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, it will automatically come out of your payment. Main benefit If you don't get a main benefit, NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, you can either: - set up an automatic payment (in the reference field put the letter 'E' followed by your 9 digit client number) - make a one-off payment to pay your contribution in full. There are different ways to do this, e.g. online or internet banking. See our Pay debt in NZ page for options of how to pay your contribution in full, or - pay the contribution directly from your wages - call our Client Support Debt Management team on 0800 558 0008 or email Client_Support_Debt_Management@msd.govt.nz How to repay debt from New Zealand

chunks.title: What happens if you don't pay it
chunks.text: You must pay your Emergency Housing Contribution on time. This is one of your responsibilities while in emergency housing. If you haven't paid it on time and you don't have a good reason, then either: - you'll get a warning, or - if you've had 2 warnings, your emergency housing grant will be declined and you won't be able to get it for 13 weeks. Your responsibilities while in emergency housing

chunks.title: Counselling
chunks.text: If you need help with counselling fees or transport to counselling, we may be able to pay this as part of a Disability Allowance. - You can get a Disability Allowance for a number of different things, including counselling. The maximum you can get for a Disability Allowance is $82.85 a week. - You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for a Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You can apply for a Disability Allowance for you, your partner or a child. The person who needs counselling must: - have a health condition or disability that's likely to last at least 6 months from when they were diagnosed - need counselling because of the health condition or disability - have regular, ongoing counselling costs that are not fully covered by another agency (e.g. Oranga Tamariki, ACC). They also need to be seeing either: - a counsellor who is a member of: Psychotherapists Board of Aotearoa New Zealand NZ Association of Counsellors (NZAC) NZ Christian Counsellors Association The Social Workers Registration Board (SWRB) Australian, New Zealand and Asian Creative Arts Therapy Association (ANZACATA) - previously known as the Australian and New Zealand Arts Therapy Association (ANZATA) Drug and Alcohol Practitioners Association of Aotearoa New Zealand (DAPAANZ). This only includes Registered Competent Practitioners and Associate Practitioners. It does not include a support worker - Psychotherapists Board of Aotearoa New Zealand - NZ Association of Counsellors (NZAC) - NZ Christian Counsellors Association - The Social Workers Registration Board (SWRB) - Australian, New Zealand and Asian Creative Arts Therapy Association (ANZACATA) - previously known as the Australian and New Zealand Arts Therapy Association (ANZATA) - Drug and Alcohol Practitioners Association of Aotearoa New Zealand (DAPAANZ). This only includes Registered Competent Practitioners and Associate Practitioners. It does not include a support worker - a psychologist who: holds a current practising certificate is registered with the Psychologists Board. - holds a current practising certificate - is registered with the Psychologists Board. To apply, you need to be: - 16 and older - a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident. It also depends on how much you and your partner earn.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: We pay up to a maximum of $82.85 a week for Disability Allowance. How much you get for counselling depends on your situation. If this is the first time you're applying for counselling, you can get up to 10 sessions. You can apply for more if a health practitioner, for example your doctor, recommends them.

chunks.title: We don't pay for:
chunks.text: - counselling not directly related to your disability or health condition, e.g. relationship counselling - counselling provided through hospitals (for example drug and alcohol), where no charge is made for these services (although we can pay for transport to these sessions) - the costs of childcare while you go to counselling.

chunks.title: Already getting payments from us (e.g. a benefit or Accommodation Supplement) but not Disability Allowance
chunks.text: - Complete a Disability Application for existing clients form. Your health practitioner (e.g. your doctor) will need to complete the Disability Certificate inside this form. - You need to complete a Disability Certificate - Counselling form. This needs to be completed by you, your health practitioner and your counsellor. Drop these documents off at one of our service centres, or post them to us: Find a service centre

chunks.title: Already getting Disability Allowance
chunks.text: You need to complete a Disability Certificate - Counselling form. This needs to be completed by you, your health practitioner and your counsellor. Drop these documents off at one of our service centres, or post them to us: Find a service centre We'll include the cost of counselling in your Disability Allowance from the date the cost started.

chunks.title: Not getting any payments from us
chunks.text: You can apply online. Apply online You'll also need to complete a Disability Certificate - Counselling form. This needs to be completed by you, your health practitioner and your counsellor. Drop these documents off at one of our service centres, or post them to us: Find a service centre

chunks.title: More than 10 sessions
chunks.text: We'll send you a letter when your 10 sessions are finished. If your health practitioner recommends you need more sessions: - You need to complete another Disability Certificate - Counselling form. This needs to be completed by you, your health practitioner and your counsellor. - you'll need to get your record of attendance (a form that your counsellor will get you to sign). Drop these documents off at one of our service centres, or post them to us: Find a service centre

chunks.title: Applying on behalf of someone else
chunks.text: You can apply for Disability Allowance on someone else's behalf, but only if they've filled out a form to appoint you as their agent. Having someone act on your behalf

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: It's your responsibility to agree with your counsellor on: - what you hope to get from the counselling - how many counselling sessions you'll need - how much you'll pay and how you'll pay for them. You'll have to pay for your counselling sessions directly to your counsellor or the organisation you're getting counselling through. To show us you've been going to the sessions, we may ask you for receipts and your record of attendance (your counsellor will complete that for you). Your counsellor will also get you to sign a form that lets them tell Work and Income about your attendance, and if you don't turn up for appointments or your counselling has ended.

chunks.title: Course Participation Assistance
chunks.text:
## Course Participation Assistance
We may be able to help with the costs of going to a short-term course or programme that helps you gain specific employment skills.
## Who can get it
To get Course Participation Assistance, you need to:
- be on a benefit or stand-down for a benefit
- be attending a short-term employment related course or programme that's 12 weeks or less
- have specific costs because of your participation in a course or programme.
It may also depend on:
- how much you and your partner earn
- any money or assets you and your partner have.
Courses must be 12 weeks or less. They need to be either:
- supplied by a provider who has a contract with Work and Income
- approved by Work and Income
- matched to a specific vacancy
- specifically recognised alongside a Skills for Industry initiative, or
- an Intensive Literacy and Numeracy programme or Targeted ESOL programme contracted by the Tertiary Education Commission.
## How much you can get
We can pay up to a maximum of $1,000 for:
- course tuition and enrolment fees
- transport to/from your course or programme
- specific clothing required for your course or programme, and
- care costs.
How much you get depends on your circumstances.
## How to apply
Once you’re clear about your career goal and what course you can take to help you get there, make an appointment with one of our case managers.
Call us on 0800 559 009
We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us.
You also need to fill out this form. We'll discuss the best way to get the completed form to us.
## Contact
This information is a guide only.
Please contact us to talk about your individual circumstances.
- Phone us

chunks.title: Payments to victims of crime
chunks.text:
## Payments to victims of crime
Lump-sum payments for victims of crimes don't need to be declared as income. But if you get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit you do need to tell us about it.
## What is it?
This is paid by Victim Support if you or your family are a victim of crime. This could be money to attend court, travel to court, or help with on-going or one-off expenses.
## How it affects your benefit and allowances
You have to tell us about this payment if you:
- get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit
- invest the money you get and earn interest, after 12 months this will be counted as income.

chunks.title: Imprisoned or held in custody on remand
chunks.text:
## Imprisoned or held in custody on remand
If you're imprisoned or held in custody on remand you need to tell us.
## How to tell us
You, or someone you've appointed to act on your behalf, need to call us as soon as you can. If you don't, we may pay you too much and you'll have to pay this back.
Phone us
## Payments while you're in custody or remand
Your payments from us will stop the day after you enter custody – either sentenced or on remand.
We'll send a letter to your home address and the prison you are being held at to confirm exactly what will happen to your payments and the date the payment will stop.
## Still need payments while you're in custody
Your payments may be able to continue while you're in custody. This depends on your costs and circumstances, for example if you have:
- a partner or dependent children
- costs you must keep paying, like rent or hire purchase bills for essential items.
If you still need your payments while you're in custody, contact us to talk about this. Your letter from us will tell you how to contact us.
## Having someone act on your behalf
While you're in prison or custody, you can appoint an agent to act on your behalf.
How to choose someone to act on your behalf

chunks.title: CVs and cover letters
chunks.text:
## CVs and cover letters
Take the hard work out of writing your CV and cover letter. Get advice about what to write, support to show you what to do, and free templates you can use.
When you apply for a job, employers will look at your:
- CV, to see your skills, any qualifications, and your work history
- cover letter, to find out what kind of person you are and why you want this job.
They'll use this to decide if they want to interview you, so it's really important to make a good impression.
## 'Build my CV' service
A free service to help you write your CV and cover letter. It's run by the Auckland Business Chamber, and it's available online throughout New Zealand.
You can get this if you're getting Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support.
To sign up for ‘Build my CV’, call our Job Search line on 0800 779 009 or talk to your local service centre.
## Te Heke Mai CV builder
An app to help when you're looking for work, including help to create a professional, polished CV.
Te Heke Mai uses a fast and simple 7 step CV builder. You can also get personalised support and feedback.
It's open to anyone in New Zealand.
Find out more about Te Heke Maiexternal
## How to write a cover letter
Careers.govt.nz has great advice about:
- what your cover letter needs
- how to make it look good
- templates you can use.
How to write a cover letter (tahatu.govt.nz)external

chunks.title: Your debt with us
chunks.text: We can help you manage any money you owe to Work and Income. When a debt is created, we'll check to see if this happened because of an error we made. If it's because of an error we made, we'll check against a list of criteria to see if we can write it off. If it wasn't because of an error we made, or we can't write it off, we'll send you a letter to let you know about it.

chunks.title: How we can help with your debt
chunks.text: If you have a debt with us, we're here to help. We can help with: - a breakdown of your debt, if you want one - debt repayments - what to do if you don't agree with your debt, and - support for managing your debt.

chunks.title: When you could get a debt
chunks.text: There are 2 common ways to get into debt with us: - We paid you too much money (an overpayment). This could happen if you didn't tell us: your correct income before we paid you about a change in your circumstances - your correct income before we paid you - about a change in your circumstances - We paid you money for something which you agreed to pay back. This is usually for something you really needed and couldn't afford at the time, e.g. a: washing machine, school uniform, or rent payment. - washing machine, - school uniform, or - rent payment.

chunks.title: Get a breakdown of your debt
chunks.text: If you want to get a breakdown of your debt, you can. How you get the breakdown depends on whether you get a benefit from us or not. - If you get a benefit from us, you'll be able to see a breakdown of your debt in MyMSD from 2018 onwards. If you want details of your debt from before 2018, you'll need to contact us. MyMSD login - If you don't get a benefit from us, you can contact us for a debt breakdown. If the debt breakdown is quite complex, it might take a few days to get this for you. It may be best for us to give it to you in writing as well. If this is the case, we'll let you know when you contact us.

chunks.title: How to contact us
chunks.text: If you're getting payments from us, call us on 0800 559 009 If you're not getting payments from us, contact our Client Support Debt Management Team. Client Support Debt Management Team Our staff will talk you through the debt and how it was created, and give you a breakdown of it.

chunks.title: Debt repayments
chunks.text: How much you repay and how you pay your debt back depends on whether you get one of these payments from us: - a main benefit - NZ Super or Veteran's pension, or - Accommodation Supplement. Repaying debt while getting one of these payments Repaying debt if you're not getting one of these payments

chunks.title: Disagree with your debt
chunks.text: If you think we've made a mistake with your debt, you can contact our Client Support - Debt Management Team. Client Support - Debt Management Team They can: - explain why you have a debt - consider any new information you give us - start a review of the decision if you ask them to. Review of a decision

chunks.title: Support for managing your debt
chunks.text: We have support to help you budget, deal with debt and manage your money. This includes information about: - budgeting support - MoneyTalks - a free financial helpline - joining a MoneyMates support group, and - talking to a financial mentor. Managing your money

chunks.title: Want someone else to talk with us about your debt
chunks.text: If you want someone else to talk with us about your debt, you need to fill out a form to nominate them as your agent. Having someone act on your behalf

chunks.title: If someone has died and had a debt with us
chunks.text: The debt becomes part of the person's estate, which is what a person owns and owes at the time they die. The debt won't be transferred or inherited by children, siblings, parents or any other relatives or friends. In most cases, the debt is not transferred to a surviving partner. The person's partner would only be liable if some of the debt was a shared debt from benefit fraud. We'll send a letter with information about the money owed to us. This letter is sent to the address of the person who died, or to whoever is settling their estate (if we know who it is). The letter will explain what to do. If there is money to pay it back from the person's estate, the letter will tell you how to pay this. If the estate doesn't have enough money to pay it, we may be able to write it off. If you want to get in touch about debt after death, please contact our Client Support Debt Management team: - phone 0800 558 008, or - email Client_Support_Debt_Management@msd.govt.nz

chunks.title: Social Security Agreement with Denmark
chunks.text:
## Social Security Agreement with Denmark
New Zealand (NZ) has an agreement with Denmark to share responsibility for social security coverage.
This agreement generally allows you to apply for certain NZ payments (paid by us) or Danish payments (paid by Udbetaling Danmark).
NZ payments covered by this agreement are:
- New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super)
- Veteran's Pension
- Supported Living Payment, where you have a health condition, injury or disability
- Sole Parent Support for widows and widowers.
Danish payments covered by this agreement are:
- Old Age Security Pension
- Anticipatory Pension
- Disability Benefit
- Labour Market Supplementary Pension.
It also allows you to add together your periods of residence in either country so you can meet certain criteria for these payments.
## Living in Denmark
If you've lived in New Zealand and now live in Denmark, you may be able to get some payments.
Social Security Agreement with Denmark - living in Denmark
## Living in New Zealand
If you've lived in Denmark and now live in New Zealand, you may be able to get some payments.
Social Security Agreement with Denmark - living in New Zealand

chunks.title: Dental treatment
chunks.text: If you're on a low income or benefit, we may be able to help you pay for immediate and essential dental treatment. Immediate and essential dental treatment includes treatment such as fillings and extractions, but not periodic cleaning or check-ups. See more examples in the 'What you can get' section. You can apply for up to $1,000 a year (any 52-week period), to help with immediate and essential dental treatment. You don't have to pay this back. We may still be able to help if the cost of your dental treatment is more than $1,000. You may need to pay some of this back, depending on your situation. Talk to us about how we can help. Phone us You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get help for dental treatment for yourself or a child, if immediate and essential work needs to be done. To apply, you need to: - be 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services) Youth Servicesexternal - be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - have an immediate and essential need. It also depends on: - how much you (and your partner) earn - any money or assets you (and your partner) have. Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of income or benefit you receive. The following income and asset limits apply:

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: We can help pay for immediate and essential treatment, which can include: - extractions - fillings for tooth restoration – not for cosmetic or for non-oral health issues - root canal treatment (except molars) - treatment of infection. It does not include: - regular dental check-ups - cosmetic treatment - scale and polish, and teeth cleaning (unless this treatment is required because of gum infection) - cast restorations - orthodontic treatment - molar root canal treatment - dentures. If you need help with dentures, there are other ways we can help, such as recoverable assistance or an advance payment of benefit. Talk to us about how we can help. Recoverable assistance Advance payment of benefit Phone us You can apply more than once a year (any 52-week period), up to a total of $1,000 for the period. You don't have to apply for all the assistance at once. You don't have to pay this money back.

chunks.title: Payments over $1,000
chunks.text: If you need help with immediate and essential dental treatment that's over $1,000, or that will bring your total payments within a 52-week period to over $1,000, we still may be able to help you meet this cost. You may need to pay some of this back. Talk to us about the options available to you. Phone us

chunks.title: Examples of how much we can pay
chunks.text: If you haven't had help from us for dental treatment in the last 52 weeks, we could pay up to $1,000 towards immediate and essential treatment. If you got $1,000 for dental treatment on 12 December 2024, you wouldn't have any dental treatment funds available until 12 December 2025. If you need more treatment talk to us, we may still be able to help you.

chunks.title: More than one payment in a year
chunks.text: If you got $300 for dental treatment on 1 July 2024, and you need more treatment 6 months later, you still have up to $700 available to you. From 1 July 2025, the $300 that was used on 1 July 2024, would again be available. If no other payments had been made in that period, then you would have a total of $1,000 available for immediate and essential dental treatment.

chunks.title: Step 1: Get a Dental Treatment information form
chunks.text: Your dentist or health agency needs to complete a Dental Treatment information form. They will already have this form and will fill it in when they examine you. The form will tell us: - what dental treatment you need - the cost of the treatment - who is providing the treatment, and - any other information that will help us assess your application. We can only make payments to dentists or health agencies who are registered suppliers with us. You can ask them if they are registered with us.

chunks.title: You're a client with us
chunks.text: The easiest way to apply is in MyMSD under 'One-off cost'. You can upload the Dental Treatment Information form during the application. Once you've completed the application, you'll need to check MyMSD again to see if it's been approved. This can take up to 1 working day. Otherwise you can either: - call us to apply over the phone. You'll need to upload the form through MyMSD (we can help you do this), or - drop or post the form to a service centre. Then call us so we can process this on the phone. Please allow enough time for us to get the form and add it to your file before calling. Phone us Find a service centre

chunks.title: You're not a client with us
chunks.text: You can either: - call us to apply over the phone. We'll set you up with a MyMSD login and help you upload the form through MyMSD, or - drop or post the form to a service centre. Then call us so we can process this on the phone. Please allow enough time for us to get the form and add it to your Phone us Find a service centre Phone us Find a service centre

chunks.title: Step 3: Get a payment card
chunks.text: If your application is approved, we'll load the money onto your Work and Income Payment Card. If you don't already have a Payment Card, you can pick one up from a service centre. You'll pay the dentist with your Payment Card (like an Eftpos card). In some cases, we may pay it directly to the dentist or health agency. You have 7 working days to pay your dentist or health agency before it expires. If you need more time, call us before the 7 day period has ended. You can also pay your dentist or health agency before you get the treatment, if you can't get an appointment within 7 days. You can login to MyMSD to see how much you have left on your payment card and when the payment expires.

chunks.title: Community Services Card
chunks.text: If you have a Community Services Card, you may be able to get dental treatment through your local hospital. Talk to a health practitioner, e.g. your doctor or dentist, about this. Community Services Card

chunks.title: ACC
chunks.text: ACC may be able to cover dental injuries caused by accidents, sports injuries, or as a result of medical or dental treatment. Injuries ACC covers (ACC)external

chunks.title: Health New Zealand
chunks.text: Health New Zealand has advice about emergency dental care, including how to find an after-hours dentist or how your local hospital can help. Dentists and emergency dental care (Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora)external You may be able to get publicly funded dental care if you're under 18 years of age, or have a Community Services Card, or have a disability or medical condition. Dentists (Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora)external

chunks.title: Information for dental providers
chunks.text: If you have a patient who needs help to pay for immediate and essential dental treatment, they may apply for financial support through Work and Income. You'll need to: - be registered as a supplier with Work and Income - complete a Work and Income Dental Treatment Information form. Register as a Work and Income supplier Dental treatment - information for dentists and health agencies

chunks.title: Deported to New Zealand
chunks.text:
## Deported to New Zealand
If you've been sent back to New Zealand from another country, there's a range of support you may be able to get to help you get on your feet.
It's important you contact us right away as there may be a stand-down period before you get the first payment of any benefit.
## You've been in prison
You may be able to get help with initial set up costs if you've:
- been in prison or remand for 31 days or more
- been sent back to New Zealand straight after your release.
It can help with things like:
- housing
- living expenses, eg power, a phone connection or food
- other essential costs, eg bedding, clothing, appliances or toiletry items.
Steps to Freedom grant
## Haven't lived in New Zealand for 2 years
If you've got New Zealand residency or citizenship but haven't lived in New Zealand for 2 years, we may still be able to help, depending on your circumstances.
Call us to discuss your situation.
Phone us
## Need money while you look for work
You're looking for full-time work and need help to pay day-to-day living expenses until you find a job.
Jobseeker Support
When you apply for Jobseeker Support, there may be some things you need to do before you can get it.
Online application process
## Ability to work affected because of a health condition or disability
You'll need a medical certificate from your health practitioner, eg, your doctor, to tell us how your health condition or disability affects your ability to work.
Ability to work affected because of a health condition or disability

chunks.title: Direct Career Service
chunks.text:
## Direct Career Service
Get free advice from qualified career practitioners. Whether you’re looking for work, thinking about a change or unsure where to start, a career practitioner can give you clear guidance and practical support.
## What you can get
You can get one-on-one help to understand your skills and explore new career opportunities. This can include:
- planning your next steps into work or training
- understanding your skills and how you can use them in a new job
- looking for a new direction or exploring training options and more.
This service will not affect the support you get from us.
## Who can use this
This service is available to all New Zealand residents who are 17 or older and want support to plan their career. You can also use this service if you are 16 years old and you’re not in school, training or work. It’s especially helpful if you’re:
- unemployed
- at risk of losing your job
- looking for support to return to the workforce.
## How to get started
Request an appointment by:
- calling 0800 222 733
- emailing direct_careers@msd.govt.nz
- asking your case manager or work broker.
We will ask you some questions to check if you’re eligible. After this, we will pass on your details to a career practitioner, who will contact you to schedule an appointment.
You can meet with a career practitioner:
- in person at a Work and Income site
- by phone
- online through Zoom or other platforms.
Find a service centre
## How it works
During the appointment, the career practitioner will talk with you about your situation, skills, interests, and goals. Together, you will create a personalised career action plan, which can include advise and practical steps on:
- planning and developing your career
- study and training options
- skills you can use in your career
- job applications
- understanding the labour market
- understanding employment rights and conditions.
You can talk to your career practitioner about what you would like your plan to look like.
Your career practitioner may also book some future appointments to work with you on your progress. When you feel you no longer need their help, you can stop the service any time.

chunks.title: Disability Allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance is a weekly payment for people who have regular, ongoing costs because of a disability. These could be visits to the doctor or hospital, medicines, extra clothing or travel. You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for a Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get a Disability Allowance if you: - have a disability that is likely to last at least 6 months - have regular, ongoing costs because of your disability that are not fully covered by another agency - aren't getting a Residential Care Subsidy - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here. Residential Care Subsidy It also depends on how much you and your partner earn. The income limits for Disability Allowance are:

chunks.title: Your child has a disability
chunks.text: You can apply on behalf of a child if they're 18 or under and financially dependent on you. If you're applying on behalf of a child: - your child needs to meet the above criteria (under 'Who can get it'), except the income limits, and - your income needs to be under the income limits. You may be able to get both the Disability Allowance and the Child Disability Allowance for the same child. Child Disability Allowance You can't get a Disability Allowance if you get Board payments from Oranga Tamariki for the child. The information provided in this page is a guide only. Contact us to talk about your individual circumstances. Phone us

chunks.title: Types of costs that can be included
chunks.text: Regular, ongoing disability-related costs that can be included are: - Alternative treatment - Ambulance fees and subscriptions - Authorised consumables - Clothing - Counselling - Day care for the elderly disabled - Gardening, lawns and outside window cleaning - Gym and swimming pool fees - Medical alarms - MedicAlert costs - Medical fees - Nicotine replacement products - Prescription fees, subsidised and unsubsidised - Power, gas and heating - Rental equipment - Residential care services - Rest home costs for a private paying patient - Special foods - Phone - Travel to counselling - Travel because of your disability - Vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals. Your health practitioner must confirm you need these costs. You need to provide proof of your costs when you apply. Contact us to talk about your individual circumstances. Phone us

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: You can get up to $82.85 a week for Disability Allowance. How much you get depends on the extra costs you have.. This payment is not taxed and you don’t have to pay it back.

chunks.title: How it's paid
chunks.text: The Disability Allowance is paid straight into your bank account, on the same day as any other payments you get from us.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: We can grant you the financial assistance you’re entitled to from the date you first contact us if you complete your application within 20 working days of that date.

chunks.title: Step 1: Fill in application form
chunks.text: What application form you fill out depends on whether you’re already getting payments from us. If you’re already getting payments from us, fill in the Disability Allowance application form: If you’re not getting payments from us, or only getting childcare payments You can either: - apply online through MyMSD, or - fill out a paper Extra Help application form. MyMSDexternal

chunks.title: Step 2: Visit your health practitioner
chunks.text: Ask your health practitioner (e.g. your doctor) to complete a Disability Certificate for you. This will confirm that the disability is ongoing and also verify what extra costs can be included. They will give this back to you, so you can bring it to us.

chunks.title: Step 3: Gather your proof of your costs
chunks.text: You need to provide proof of any costs you’re claiming for, so we know how much to pay you. This needs to show: - what it’s for and - how much it costs (or enough information that we can work this out ourselves). Some examples of you can provide are:

chunks.title: Proof you'll need to provide
chunks.text: Doctor's, specialist's and hospital fees (That aren't already subsidised) Receipts or print-outs from your medical practitioner showing the date, cost, and reason for your visit. Travel costs Prescription fees Your doctor needs to complete the 'Disability Allowance Medical Assessment for Medical Alarm' form. You'll also need to provide the contract or receipt for the installation/rental of the medical alarm. You, your doctor and counsellor also need to complete a Counselling form. Disability Certificate - Counselling formexternal Special food costs You can use the special foods information form to help you work out your extra costs. Disability Allowance – special foods information formexternal

chunks.title: Step 4: Get your documents to us
chunks.text: You can get your proof of costs and form (if you applied using a paper form) to us by either: - dropping it in to your nearest service centre - posting it to your nearest service centreexternal, or - uploading it to MyMSD (you'll need to call us first). Find a service centre MyMSDexternal If this is your first time applying for a benefit or ongoing payment, you’ll need to bring your ID and any other supporting documents listed in your application form, such as documents relating to your back account, income and residency into a service centre so we can check it.

chunks.title: Step 5: You may need an appointment
chunks.text: After you've applied we may ask you to call us to book an appointment. This could be a phone appointment or a face-to-face appointment.

chunks.title: If your costs or circumstances change
chunks.text: If you're getting Disability Allowance and your disability costs or circumstances change, let us know. This includes new, increased, stopped, or decreased costs. For any new or increased costs, you'll need to provide a medical certificate and proof of the costs. Tell us about your change of costsexternal If you're not sure what costs are included in your Disability Allowance, you can check MyMSD.

chunks.title: Renew your medical certificate
chunks.text: You may need to get your health practitioner to complete another Disability Certificate. We’ll let you know when you need to renew this. Renew your medical certificate or information

chunks.title: Confirming your circumstances
chunks.text: If you get a Disability Allowance, we will review your circumstances at least once every 52 weeks (one year) to make sure you are getting the correct assistance and amount. As part of this, we might ask you to fill out a Confirming your Circumstances form. Confirming your circumstances

chunks.title: Disability Allowance obligations
chunks.text:
## Disability Allowance obligations
There are things you and your partner need to do when you're getting a Disability Allowance. If you don't do them, your payment could reduce or stop.
## Tell us if something changes
You and your partner must tell us (or your Youth Service Provider if you have one assigned to you) immediately if you:
- have a change in work situation, e.g. starting part-time, casual or full-time work (paid or unpaid)
- have a change to your disability costs
- become self-employed or start a business
- have changes to your income or financial circumstances
- have a boarder or renter that moves in or out, or the payments you get from them change
- plan to travel overseas
- start or finish study - part-time or full-time
- have changes to your personal details, e.g: name address bank account number
- name
- address
- bank account number
- have changes to their living situation, e.g: marriage or separation starting or ending a civil union starting or ending a de facto relationship change in the number of children you support
- marriage or separation
- starting or ending a civil union
- starting or ending a de facto relationship
- change in the number of children you support
- have a change in accommodation costs
- are imprisoned or held in custody on remand
- are admitted to or discharged from hospital
- are granted an overseas pension
- have any other change that may affect your entitlement or rate.
## Other things we may ask you to do
We must review Disability Allowance payments regularly. This means we may also ask you to fill out a Confirming your Circumstances form.
This information helps us make sure you are getting the correct assistance and amount.
If you don’t respond to the form before the due date, your Disability Allowance payments will stop.

chunks.title: Doing seasonal work
chunks.text:
## Doing seasonal work
You may be able to get help to pay for things like clothes, gear or temporarily moving home. There's also help if you can't work due to bad weather.
## Who can get these
You need to have recently started a seasonal job and stopped your benefit.
## When you start work
If you're starting seasonal horticulture or viticulture work, the New Zealand Seasonal Work Scheme can help with:
- costs like transport, gear and clothing
- an accommodation costs payment
- an incentive payment.
Talk to us about New Zealand Seasonal Work Scheme before you start the job.
Find out the full details of who can get this and what you can get:
New Zealand Seasonal Work Scheme
## Can't work due to bad weather
Seasonal Work Assistance is a payment to help if you've:
- lost wages because of work missed due to bad weather, and
- stopped getting a benefit to do this job.
Find out the full details of who can get this and what you can get:
Seasonal Work Assistance
## Planning your next job
Most seasonal jobs are temporary, so you need to plan what job you'll do next.
Seasonal jobs are available all year in New Zealand. We have information about finding seasonal work and how to plan out where you can work and when:
Finding seasonal work
If you'd like to try a different type of job, or just want to see what's out there, you can see jobs available now:
Where to look for jobs
## When your seasonal work ends
When your contract ends we may be able to help with:
- money while you look for work
- finding a new job.

chunks.title: Dress for Success
chunks.text:
## Dress for Success
Support and practical help for women looking for work. You can get help to feel more confident when you're going to job interviews or starting a new job.
Dress for Success is a worldwide organisation which supports women to find and keep work. They provide clothing suitable for your job interview and work, job-seeking advice and skills, and ongoing employment support.
## Who can get it
To get the Dress for Success service you need to qualify for a Transition to Work Grant from us. This covers the cost of the service.
Check the Transition to Work Grant page on our website to find out who can get this and how to apply:
Transition to Work Grant
## What you can get
Dress for Success offers:
- clothing and styling services, and
- careers services
The costs are covered by Transition to Work Grant. You don't have to pay the money back.
Transition to Work Grant
## Clothing and Styling Services
You can get clothing suitable for an interview or work experience. They'll adjust the styling to the type of job you're applying for. You can then get a mix-and-match wardrobe once you're successful in finding a job. This will include shoes and other accessories.
## Careers services
You can get practical skills and advice to improve your chances of getting and keeping a job. You'll get help to prepare your CV and job interview material, get more skilled in doing job interviews, and learn how to plan your career. These services might be one-on-one, or with a group of women in workshops and seminars.
## Locations
These services can change depending on what the Dress for Success closest to you can offer, you can find their addresses on their websites:
Auckland - Dress for Successexternal
Bay of Plenty - Dress for Successexternal
Christchurch - Dress for Successexternal
Hamilton - Dress for Successexternal
Hawkes Bay - Dress for Successexternal
Northland - Dress for Successexternal
Palmerston North - Dress for Successexternal
Wellington - Dress for Successexternal
## How to apply
Call us on 0800 559 009 to apply for a Transition to Work Grant.
We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us.

chunks.title: Early Learning Payment
chunks.text:
## Early Learning Payment
The Early Learning Payment helps pay the costs of Early Childhood Education for children aged 18 months to 3 years. These children need to be from families enrolled in selected Family Start or Early Start Programmes.
If you're enrolled in a Family Start or Early Start programme, you'll be assigned a family/whānau worker who'll contact us for you.
## Who can get it
You may be able to get the Early Learning Payment if:
- you're enrolled in a Family Start or Early Start programme
- your child is aged 18 months to 3 years.
This can be paid for your child to attend an approved early childhood service for up to 20 hours a week.
Families getting Childcare Subsidy or Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment (GCAP) can't get Early Learning Payment for the same hours.
## Leaving Family Start or Early Start
From 1 October 2017, if your family leaves Family Start or Early Start, you may be able to continue getting the payments.
Your child must be:
- the child that the Early Learning Payment was being paid for when your family left Family Start or Early Start
- aged between 18 months to 3 years
- a dependent child and
- attending an approved early childhood service.
## How to apply
You need to call us on 0800 559 009
We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us.
You'll need to fill out the 'Early Learning Payment application form'. We'll discuss the best way to get the completed form to us.

chunks.title: Emergency Benefit obligations
chunks.text: There are things your partner needs to do when you're getting an Emergency Benefit. If they don't do them, your benefit could reduce or stop.

chunks.title: Overview of your obligations
chunks.text: - You have an obligation to tell us if something changes. - If you're taking care of dependent children, you have social obligations. - If we ask you to, you have an obligation to take part in a Work Ability Assessment or to work with a contracted service provider. You may also have an obligation to find or prepare for work. If so, your case manager would have discussed this with you when you applied for the benefit. These obligations are detailed on this page below. If you have a partner, there are things they'll need to do as well. Emergency Benefit obligations for partners

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: You must tell us (or your Youth Service Provider if you have one assigned to you) immediately if you: - have a change in your work situation, e.g. starting part-time, casual or full-time work (paid or unpaid) - become self-employed or start a business - have changes to your income or financial circumstances - have a boarder or renter that moves in or out, or the payments you get from them change - plan to travel overseas - start or finish study - part-time or full-time - have changes to your personal details, e.g: name address bank account - name - address - bank account - have changes to your living situation, e.g: marriage or separation starting or ending a civil union starting or ending a de facto relationship change in the number of children you support - marriage or separation - starting or ending a civil union - starting or ending a de facto relationship - change in the number of children you support - have a change in accommodation costs - are imprisoned or held in custody on remand - are admitted to or discharged from hospital - are granted an overseas pension - have any other changes that may affect your benefit entitlement or rate.

chunks.title: When taking care of dependent children (social obligations)
chunks.text: You’re expected to take reasonable steps to meet social obligations as a parent or a caregiver. These obligations are to help ensure children get a good start. You must ensure your dependent child(ren) (including any child you get Orphan’s or Unsupported Child’s Benefit for) are: - enrolled with a general practitioner (GP) or a medical practice that’s part of a Primary Health Organisation (PHO) - enrolled in and attending one of the following from the age of 3 until they start school: an approved early childhood education programme, eg, Kohanga Reo, Punanga Reo, Aoga and other programmes with a language and culture focus parenting and early childhood home education programmes kindergartens preschools childcare centres playcentres home-based care services, or Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu – The Correspondence School, or another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme - an approved early childhood education programme, eg, Kohanga Reo, Punanga Reo, Aoga and other programmes with a language and culture focus parenting and early childhood home education programmes kindergartens preschools childcare centres playcentres home-based care services, or - Kohanga Reo, Punanga Reo, Aoga and other programmes with a language and culture focus - parenting and early childhood home education programmes - kindergartens - preschools - childcare centres - playcentres - home-based care services, or - Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu – The Correspondence School, or - another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme - up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks if aged under 5, at a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider, eg: Plunket Maori health provider Pacific health provider - Plunket - Maori health provider - Pacific health provider - enrolled in and attending school from the age of 5 or 6 (depending on when they start school). We understand there could be some situations outside of your control that mean you may not be able to meet an obligation right now. For example: - your child is on a waiting list for a GP, or - there aren’t any available places in your nearby childcare centre. You may be required to meet with us to discuss how you’re meeting your obligations as a parent or a caregiver.

chunks.title: Take part in Work Ability Assessments
chunks.text: When it has been agreed, you have an obligation to attend and participate in a Work Ability Assessment.

chunks.title: Take part in activities with our service providers
chunks.text: When it has been agreed that you will work with a Contracted Service Provider, you have an obligation to co-operate with them and to: - attend and participate in any interview with them - report to them on how you're meeting your obligations - complete assessments with them.

chunks.title: Full-time work obligations
chunks.text: You'll generally be expected to look for work of at least 30 hours a week, unless you have a health condition or disability that means you can't work full-time. If you have full-time work obligations, you need to: - be available for and take reasonable steps to get a suitable job - take any offer of suitable full-time, part-time or temporary work, or work that is seasonal or subsidised - attend and take part in any suitable job interviews we ask you to - take and pass any drug test potential employers or training providers require - attend and take part in interviews with Work and Income as required - work with us to plan how you'll find a suitable job - take part in any other activities we refer you to that will improve your work readiness or help you get work, such as: job training courses work experience, or work assessments (including rehabilitation, but not medical treatment) - job training courses - work experience, or - work assessments (including rehabilitation, but not medical treatment) - let us know how you're meeting your work obligations as often as we reasonably require.

chunks.title: Part-time work obligations
chunks.text: If you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you can only work part-time, you'll need to look for work of at least 15 hours a week. If you have part-time work obligations, you need to: - be available for and take reasonable steps to get a suitable part-time job - take any offer of suitable part-time or temporary work, or work that is seasonal or subsidised - attend and take part in any suitable job interviews we ask you to - take and pass any drug test potential employers or training providers require - attend and take part in interviews with us as required - work with us to plan how you'll find a suitable job - take part in any other activities that we refer you to, such as attend any job training courses, seminars, work experience or work assessments (including rehabilitation, but not medical treatment) that will improve your work readiness or help you get work - let us know how you're meeting your work obligations as often as we reasonably require.

chunks.title: Work preparation obligations
chunks.text: If you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you're unable to work, or can only work fewer than 15 hours a week, you won't be asked to meet work obligations until your situation changes. In the meantime, you have the following work preparation obligations to: - take reasonable steps to prepare and plan for work - attend and take part in work preparation interviews, where we ask you to - attend and take part in work related activities or programmes such as a work assessment, a programme or seminar to increase particular skills or enhance motivation where we ask you to - attend and take part in any other activity that we require you to (including rehabilitation but not medical treatment, voluntary work or activity in the community).

chunks.title: If you don't meet your obligations
chunks.text: If there's any reason why you can't meet your obligations, talk to us straight away. If you don't meet your obligations without good and sufficient reason, your benefit could be reduced or stopped. Contact us To find out what happens if you don't meet your obligation for telling us if something changes, go to the 'When you don't meet your obligations' page. When you don't meet your obligations We have a traffic light colour system to help you stay on track with your work-related and social obligations (if you have these). It lets you know where you're at and what you need to do. Go to the 'Traffic light system' page to find out what happens if you don't meet the following obligations: - find or prepare for work - take part in Work Ability Assessments - take part in activities with our service providers - social obligations (when taking care of dependent children). Traffic light system

chunks.title: Other things we may ask you to do
chunks.text: We must review Emergency Benefit payments regularly. This means we may also ask you to fill out a Confirming your Circumstances form. This information helps us make sure you are getting the correct assistance and amount. If you don't respond to the form before the due date, your Emergency Benefit payments will stop. Confirming your circumstances

chunks.title: Emergency Benefit obligations for partners
chunks.text: There are things your partner needs to do when you're getting an Emergency Benefit. If they don't do them, your benefit could reduce or stop.

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: Your partner must tell us (or their Youth Service Provider if they have one assigned to them) immediately if they: - have a change in work situation, e.g. starting part-time, casual or full-time work (paid or unpaid) - become self-employed or start a business - have changes to their income or financial circumstances - have a boarder or renter that moves in or out, or the payments you get from them change - plan to travel overseas - start or finish study - part-time or full-time - have changes to their personal details, e.g: name address contact details bank account number - name - address - contact details - bank account number - have changes to their living situation, e.g: marriage or separation starting or ending a civil union starting or ending a de facto relationship change in the number of children they support - marriage or separation - starting or ending a civil union - starting or ending a de facto relationship - change in the number of children they support - have a change of accommodation costs - are imprisoned or held in custody on remand - are admitted to or discharged from hospital - are granted an overseas pension - have any other change that may affect your benefit entitlement or rate.

chunks.title: Full-time work obligations
chunks.text: If your partner is in employment for less than 30 hours each week, they are still expected to be available for other work, training or other activities up to a total of 30 hours each week. Your partner must understand that they are still required to accept suitable full-time work if it becomes available. Your partner will generally be expected to look for full-time work of at least 30 hours a week if they're either: - 18 or over with no dependent children, or - 19 or over with no dependent children under 14 (including any child they get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit for). They have the following full-time work obligations to: - be available for and take reasonable steps to get a suitable job - take any offer of suitable full-time, part-time or temporary work, or work that is seasonal or subsidised - attend and take part in any suitable job interviews we ask them to - take and pass any drug test potential employers or training providers require - attend and take part in interviews with Work and Income as required - work with us to plan how they'll find a suitable job - take part in any other activities that we refer them to, such as attend any job training courses, seminars, work experience or work assessments (including rehabilitation, but not medical treatment) that will improve their work readiness or help them get work - let us know how they're meeting their work obligations as often as we reasonably require.

chunks.title: Part-time work obligations
chunks.text: Your partner will generally be expected to look for part-time work of at least 20 hours a week if they're 19 or over and their youngest child is aged 3-13. They have the following part-time work obligations to: - be available for and take reasonable steps to get a suitable part-time job - take any offer of suitable part-time or temporary work, or work that is seasonal or subsidised - attend and take part in any suitable job interviews we ask them to - take and pass any drug test potential employers or training providers require - attend and take part in interviews with us as required - work with us to plan how they'll find a suitable job - take part in any other activities that we refer them to, such as attend any job training courses, seminars, work experience or work assessments (including rehabilitation, but not medical treatment) that will improve their work readiness or help them get work - let us know how they're meeting their work obligations as often as we reasonably require.

chunks.title: Work preparation obligations
chunks.text: Your partner will be expected to prepare for work if they're 19 or over and their youngest child is under 3 (including any child they get Orphan's or Unsupported Child's Benefit for). They have the following work preparation obligations to: - take reasonable steps to prepare and plan for work - attend and take part in work preparation interviews, where we ask them to - attend and take part in work related activities or programmes such as a work assessment, a programme or seminar to increase particular skills or enhance motivation where we ask them to - attend and take part in any other activity that we require them to (including rehabilitation but not medical treatment, voluntary work or activity in the community).

chunks.title: Take part in Work Ability Assessments
chunks.text: When it has been agreed, your partner has an obligation to attend and participate in a Work Ability Assessment.

chunks.title: Take part in activities with our service providers
chunks.text: When it has been agreed that your partner will work with a Contracted Service Provider, they have an obligation to co-operate with them and to: - attend and participate in any interview with them - report to them on how they're meeting their obligations - complete assessments with them.

chunks.title: When taking care of dependent children (social obligations)
chunks.text: Your partner's expected to take reasonable steps to meet social obligations as a parent or a caregiver. These obligations are to help ensure children get a good start. They must ensure their dependent child(ren) (including any child they get Orphan's or Unsupported Child's Benefit for) are: - enrolled with a health practitioner or a medical practice that's part of a Primary Health Organisation (PHO) - enrolled in and attending one of the following from the age of 3 until they start school: an approved early childhood education programme, eg, Kohanga Reo, Punanga Reo, Aoga and other programmes with a language and culture focus parenting and early childhood home education programmes kindergartens preschools childcare centres playcentres home-based care services, or Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - The Correspondence School, or another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme - an approved early childhood education programme, eg, Kohanga Reo, Punanga Reo, Aoga and other programmes with a language and culture focus parenting and early childhood home education programmes kindergartens preschools childcare centres playcentres home-based care services, or - Kohanga Reo, Punanga Reo, Aoga and other programmes with a language and culture focus - parenting and early childhood home education programmes - kindergartens - preschools - childcare centres - playcentres - home-based care services, or - Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - The Correspondence School, or - another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme - up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks if aged under 5, at a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider, eg: Plunket Maori health provider Pacific health provider - Plunket - Maori health provider - Pacific health provider - enrolled in and attending school from the age of 5 or 6 (depending on when they start school). We understand there could be some situations outside of their control that mean they may not be able to meet an obligation right now. For example: - their child is on a waiting list for a GP, or - there aren’t any available places in their nearby childcare centre. They may be required to meet with us to discuss how they're meeting their obligations as a parent or a caregiver.

chunks.title: No children
chunks.text: If your partner is 16 or 17 with no children, they have the following youth activity obligations: - be enrolled in and satisfactorily undertaking, or be available for a full-time course of secondary school or tertiary education or approved training or work-based learning leading to: NCEA Level 2 or an equivalent qualification or a higher qualification - NCEA Level 2 or - an equivalent qualification or - a higher qualification - when it has been agreed, participate in and complete a budgeting programme - when it has been agreed, and in the manner required, report to us or their Youth Service Provider (where they have one assigned to them) on how they're meeting the obligations above - when it has been agreed, attend and participate in regular budgeting discussions with us or their Youth Service Provider (where they have one assigned to them) - when it has been agreed, attend and participate in any interview with us or their Youth Service Provider (where they have one assigned to them).

chunks.title: 1 or more children
chunks.text: If your partner is 16-19 and has 1 or more dependent children, they have the following activity obligations: - when it has been agreed, participate in and complete a budgeting programme - when it has been agreed, participate satisfactorily in an approved parenting education programme - enrol their child(ren): with a Primary Health Organisation, where local provider capacity allows under the age of 5 years, with a WellChild/Tamariki Ora provider and keep up to date with their visits - with a Primary Health Organisation, where local provider capacity allows - under the age of 5 years, with a WellChild/Tamariki Ora provider and keep up to date with their visits - ensure their child(ren) are attending an Early Childhood Education Programme or other suitable childcare, while they're participating in education, training, work-based learning or part-time work - when it has been agreed, and in the manner reasonably required, report to us or their Youth Service Provider (where they have one assigned to them) on how they're meeting the obligations above - when it has been agreed, attend and participate in regular budgeting discussions with us or their Youth Service Provider (where they have one assigned to them) - when it has been agreed, attend and participate in any interview with us or their Youth Service Provider (where they have one assigned to them). When their youngest dependent child is 12 months or over (or is over 6 months and a suitable place becomes available in a Teen Parent Unit) and there are no special circumstances, or they're not the primary caregiver, they also have the following activity obligations: - be enrolled in and satisfactorily undertaking, or be available for a full-time course of secondary school or tertiary education or approved training or work-based learning leading to: NCEA Level 2 or an equivalent qualification or a higher qualification. - NCEA Level 2 or - an equivalent qualification or - a higher qualification.

chunks.title: If they don't meet their obligations
chunks.text: If there's any reason why your partner can't meet their obligations, talk to us straight away. If they don't meet their obligations without good and sufficient reason, your benefit could be reduced or stopped. Contact us We have a traffic light colour system to help your partner stay on track with their work-related and social obligations. It lets them know where they’re at and what they need to do. Go to the 'Traffic light system' page to find out what happens if your partner doesn’t meet the following obligations: Traffic light system - find or prepare for work - take part in Work Ability Assessments - take part in activities with our service providers - social obligations (when taking care of dependent children). Go to the 'When you don't meet your obligations' page to find out what happens if they don't meet their other obligations. When you don't meet your obligations

chunks.title: Emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Emergency housing
If you have nowhere to stay tonight or in the next 7 nights, we may be able to pay for you to stay in emergency housing.
Emergency housing is short-term accommodation for people who need it because:
- they can’t stay where they are, and
- they have nowhere else to go.
## Who can get emergency housing
If you need emergency housing, you must meet certain criteria.
Who can get emergency housing
## Apply for emergency housing
Find out how to apply for emergency housing.
Apply for emergency housing
## Cost of emergency housing
In most cases we'll cover the cost of your accommodation for the first 7 nights if you qualify. Then you'll have to start paying for some of the accommodation costs. This is called an Emergency Housing Contribution.
Cost of emergency housing
## Security deposit
If you're going to stay in emergency housing, your housing supplier may ask for a security deposit.
Security deposit for emergency housing
## Staying in emergency housing
If you're staying in emergency housing, you can find information about:
- your rights
- what we expect you to do
- your responsibilities
- what to do if you have concerns or want to make a complaint
- what to do when you leave.
Staying in emergency housing

## Emergency Maintenance Allowance
Emergency Maintenance Allowance is assistance that may be paid to sole parents who do not qualify for any other payments.
There are certain criteria you'll need to meet. Please call us on 0800 559 009 so we can discuss your situation.

chunks.title: Emergency Maintenance Allowance obligations

You may also have an obligation to find or prepare for work. If so, your case manager would have discussed this with you when you applied for the benefit. These obligations are detailed on this page below.

chunks.text: If your youngest child is aged 3 to 13 (including any child you get Orphan's or Unsupported Child's Benefit for), you have the following part-time work obligations: - be available for and take reasonable steps to get a suitable part-time job - take any offer of suitable part-time or temporary work, or work that is seasonal or subsidised - attend and take part in any suitable job interviews we ask you to - take and pass any drug test potential employers or training providers require - attend and take part in interviews with us as required - work with us to plan how you'll find a suitable job - take part in any other activities that we refer you to, such as attend any job training courses, seminars, work experience or work assessments (including rehabilitation, but not medical treatment) that will improve your work readiness or help you get work - let us know how you’re meeting your work obligations as often as we reasonably require.

chunks.title: Employer help if you have a health condition, injury or disability
chunks.text:
## Employer help if you have a health condition, injury or disability
Help from your employers because of a health condition, injury or disability doesn't need to be declared as income. But if you get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit you do need to tell us about it.
## What is this?
This includes any payment or service you get so you can keep working eg transport to and from your job.
## How it affects your benefit and allowances
You have to tell us about this payment if you:
- get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit
- invest the money you get and earn interest, this will be counted as income.

chunks.title: How to see your employment plan
chunks.text: If you have an employment plan in MyMSD, you can see it by going to 'My employment plan' on the home screen. MyMSD

chunks.title: Can't use MyMSD
chunks.text: If you can’t use MyMSD, your case manager will print the plan with your activities and when they need to be done by.

chunks.title: Your activities
chunks.text: Your case manager will talk to you about your employment needs. They'll tailor the activities based on your conversations. Together you will agree on a due date for each activity. Activities could be things like: - creating a CV - updating your Jobseeker profile on MyMSD, or - applying for suitable jobs. You may have to apply for jobs as one of your activities. If you apply for a job, record this activity in your employment plan in MyMSD. You don't need to tell your case manager about it. When you complete any other activity, you need to contact your case manager. They can then mark that activity as complete in your plan. If there's any reason why you can't complete an activity by the due date, contact your case manager straight away.

chunks.title: Help with your activities
chunks.text: If you're unsure what you need to do or need help with your activities, the best thing to do is contact your case manager. They'll be able to talk you through it.

chunks.title: What happens if you don't complete your activities
chunks.text: These activities are part of your obligation to find or prepare for work. If you don’t do an activity, it means you’re not meeting your obligations. If you don't meet your obligations without good and sufficient reason, your benefit could be reduced or stopped. If there's any reason why you can't complete an activity by the due date, contact your case manager straight away. We have a traffic light colour system to help you stay on track with your work obligations. Traffic light system

chunks.title: Employment service for people with a disability or health condition
chunks.text:
## Employment service for people with a disability or health condition
If you have a disability or health condition, including a mental health condition or neurodiversity, you can get one-on-one help to find work, support during your first year of employment, and as needed while you're in employment.
We have contracted experienced Employment Service providers who can work with you to prepare you for work, and help you find an ongoing job. The provider will also support you while you're in work.
Our providers are experts in preparing people for work and finding job opportunities. They specialise in helping people who have a disability, health condition, mental health condition, or are neurodiverse move into work.
## Who can get it
You can use Employment Service if:
- you have a disability or health condition, including a mental health condition or neurodiversity, and this is likely to continue for six months or more, and
- your disability or health condition affects your ability to find work, and
- you're ready to go into work, and
- you're currently living in New Zealand, and
- you're a New Zealand citizen or a permanent resident, and
- you're aged between 16 and 64, and
- you've left school.
You don't need to be getting a benefit to use Employment Service.
## What you can get
Employment Service providers can help with:
- career planning
- preparation for employment, e.g. help writing a CV, techniques for interviews, etc.
- job searching and matching
- employment placement
- negotiations of any flexible working arrangements
- talking with your employer about how they can best support you while you're working.
Once you're in work, they can provide ongoing support to you and, if needed, your employer, for up to one year.
## How to apply
You'll need to contact an Employment Service provider. If you're getting a benefit from us, you may already have an Employment Service provider. If you don't already have a provider, you can choose from a list of providers in your area:
Our Employment Service providers
Your provider will let you know how they'll work with you and help you develop a plan for your employment future.
