chunks.title: Employment service for secondary school students with a disability or health condition
chunks.text: Employment Service in Schools is for secondary school students who have a disability or health condition, including mental health condition or neurodiversity. This pilot service helps the students, their family or whānau, and school plan for their future and explore job and career opportunities. Working with the Ministry of Education, we have contracted providers in Otago-Southland, Canterbury, Wellington, Waikato, and parts of Auckland. These providers are experts in preparing people for work and finding job opportunities. Their focus is on preparing students for employment through skill development and work experience or job trials. This service is a pilot and will be available until 30 June 2026.

chunks.title: Who can take part
chunks.text: You can take part in Employment Service in Schools if you: - have a disability or health condition, including a mental health condition or neurodiversity, which: is likely to continue for six months or more, and may mean you have trouble getting into or finding work - is likely to continue for six months or more, and - may mean you have trouble getting into or finding work and you are: - a student aged 14 to 21 enrolled in English or Māori medium secondary school or kura, and you plan to leave school in the next two years, and - finding out what job or type of work you would like - living in Otago-Southland, Canterbury, Wellington, Waikato, or parts of Auckland, and - a New Zealand citizen or a permanent resident. You don't need to be getting a benefit to use Employment Service in Schools. You won't be able to take part in the service if you: - can get funding from ACC to transition from school, or - are currently getting funding from us through Transition Services. If you're already getting help through our Transition Service, and would like to move to Employment Service in Schools, please email us at Employment_Service_in_Schools@msd.govt.nz If you're not living in an area with Employment Service in Schools please see the information about other support available at the bottom of this page or you can email us at Employment_Service_in_Schools@msd.govt.nz

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: With Employment Service in Schools, you'll work with a provider in your area to get ready for when you leave school and go into a job or training for a job. Our providers are experts in preparing people for work and finding job opportunities. You'll get help with things like: - identifying what types of jobs you could do when you leave school - finding information to help you make decisions - finding out what job of type of work you would like - creating your CV - getting ready for interviews - work experience - getting a part-time job while you're at school. Our providers specialise in helping people who have a disability or health condition, including a mental health condition or neurodiversity. They'll work with you, your family or whānau, school and other networks to help you plan your future.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Talk to your teacher, your teaching support, or your careers advisor about Employment Service in Schools. They'll let you know which providers are in your area, and help you and your family or whānau choose the right one. You'll need to complete the form (linked below) to apply, and get your parents/whānau, your school and the provider you've chosen to fill in the sections marked for them. Once you've completed this form give it to the provider you've chosen. There are several providers available in each region. You and your family or whānau can choose the provider you want to work with.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: We'll process your application, this usually takes 2-3 working days. Your provider will tell you if your application is accepted or not. If your application is accepted, your provider will contact you to organise a meeting. This will be with you and your parents or whānau. You'll work together to find out what kind of employment future you'd like, and what needs to happen for this. You'll get Employment Service in Schools until you leave school or when the pilot ends (30 June 2026), even if you start a job while you're still at school.

chunks.title: Other support available
chunks.text: There's other support available if you're not able to get Employment Service in Schools, or if you were getting this and it's now finished. You can contact your school about these: - Transition Service, for students who are verified on the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme (ORS) and are in their last year of school. - Mana Whaikaha, a disability support system offering disabled people and whānau more choice and control over their supports. - Vocational support through your school, such as career support, Gateway or Vocational Pathways. - Funding for students with very high needs, who are verified on the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme, and are leaving school. Mana Whaikaha (Disability Support Services)external, We may also be able to help you with: - Employment Service, similar to Employment Service in Schools and available when you leave school. Employment Service - Mainstream programmes, to help you get paid work experience and a long-term job. Mainstream programmes

chunks.title: Employment Transition Assistance
chunks.text:
## Employment Transition Assistance
Employment Transition Assistance is a weekly payment you can get if you've completed a Supported Living Payment Employment Trial.
## Who can get it
You may get an Employment Transition Assistance if you:
- have completed a Supported Living Payment Employment Trial
- can no longer get a Supported Living Payment
- are earning less than the Supported Living Payment after completing the trial
- regularly work 15 hours or more per week (not in sheltered employment)
- can’t carry on working these hours without this payment.
It also depends on how much you and your partner earn.
## How much you can get
This depends on your living situation and age. You can see the rates for Employment Transition Assistance here:
View our maximum current rates (Manuals and Procedures)external
## How to apply
Call us on 0800 559 009.
We'll book an appointment for you to meet with us. When you book the appointment, we'll let you know what information you need to provide.

chunks.title: Child turning 18
chunks.text: If a child in your care is turning 18 and there is a change in their circumstances, your payments can be affected. Find out what you need to do to keep getting the right support, and when you need to tell us you’re no longer supporting them.

chunks.title: When a child can stay included in your payments
chunks.text: When a child turns 18, we usually stop including them in payments. However, if the child in your care has their 18th birthday on or after 4 September 2026, they can continue to be included in your payments if they: - are enrolled and attending school or tertiary education, and - still depend on you for financial support.

chunks.title: Tell us before they turn 18
chunks.text: You need to tell us if the child in your care is still meeting these requirements to stay included in your payments before they turn 18. You can tell us through this form: Child turning 18external If you don't let us know, your payments may reduce. If a child in your care has finished or left education before they turn 18, but they are still financially dependent on you, they can be included in your payments until they turn 18. If the child in your care is no longer financially dependent on you, please contact us. Phone us If you are receiving one of these payments, you need to get in touch with us before your child turns 18 or your payments will stop: - Emergency Benefit - Emergency Maintenance Allowance - Jobseeker Support on ground of hardship - Jobseeker Support Student Hardship - Special Benefit - Community Costs.

chunks.title: No longer supporting your 16-17 year old
chunks.text: We can only include your 16 or 17 year old in your payments if you're supporting them. If you're not supporting them at the moment, you need to tell us. Supporting a child means you take the main responsibility for them, and: - they're part of your family - they depend on you financially - they're not in paid full time work (30 hours or more a week) - you're not getting payments from Oranga Tamariki on behalf of them. If you support your 16 or 17 year old at the moment, you don't need to do anything. Your payments will continue even if they are not in education.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: If you're not supporting your 16 or 17 year old at the moment, you need to contact us. Phone us

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: We'll send you a letter to let you know if there are any changes to your payment.

chunks.title: Your child's studying
chunks.text: If your child wants to study next year, they may be able to get a Student Allowance from StudyLink. Student Allowanceexternal

chunks.title: Automated decision-making
chunks.text: Please let us know before a child in your care turns 18 if they are still financially dependent on you, and still attending either school or tertiary education. This is so that they can continue to be included in your benefit. If we do not hear from you, we will use automated decision-making to automatically remove them from your benefit from the beginning of the next pay period after their 18th birthday. This means your payments from us may change or stop. We’ll always let you know when we’ve used automated decision-making to make a decision that affects you. More information about how we use automated decision-making can be found here: Automated decision-making

chunks.title: Enhanced Taskforce Green
chunks.text: If there's been an emergency event that's caused significant damage, the Government may approve an Enhanced Taskforce Green (ETFG) work programme to help with clean-up and recovery. The Ministry of Social Development will work with a range of agencies in the impacted area to determine what support is needed. If required we will contract a local provider to employ workers to help with clean-up activities. These workers could be job seekers or workers at risk of losing their employment because of the emergency.

chunks.title: What costs will be covered by ETFG
chunks.text: ETFG assistance may cover the costs of: - wages for workers - wages for supervisors - purchasing personal safety gear - hiring light equipment and transport, for example: chainsaws vans four-wheel-drive vehicles - chainsaws - vans - four-wheel-drive vehicles - a start-up grant for local authorities to assist with administration costs. ETFG does not cover the cost of hiring heavy machinery.

chunks.title: Work and Income's role
chunks.text: Work and Income is responsible for: - liaising with affected councils and the Ministry for Primary Industries - contracting a suitably qualified provider to complete the clean-up work required - identifying suitable workers and profiling them to the provider - providing identified workers with financial assistance (including Working for Families Assistance information).

chunks.title: The contracted provider's role
chunks.text: The contracted provider will: - organise Site Safe Certificate training for each ETFG worker - pay ETFG workers and supervisors - purchase and/or hire safety gear and equipment, including: boots gloves overalls hi-visibility vests helmets earmuffs protective eye wear chaps wet weather gear - boots - gloves - overalls - hi-visibility vests - helmets - earmuffs - protective eye wear - chaps - wet weather gear - oversee the day-to-day management of the work programme - transport workers to and from the areas of work. Relevant programme costs will be covered by an upfront lump sum payment, by way of a contract with the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: ETFG workers
chunks.text: Each ETFG work crew will be accompanied by a supervisor. Crews will assist with clean-up activities, for example: - fence clearance and repair - tree and debris removal on: farms marae orchards parks reserves. - farms - marae - orchards - parks - reserves. ETFG crew workers are paid the living wage for a 40 hour week. ETFG supervisors are paid at a higher hourly rate.

chunks.title: Employment disputes
chunks.text: Anyone who expresses concerns regarding the conduct of ETFG workers should be directed to their relevant council for resolution as the council is the employer.

chunks.title: Establishment Grant
chunks.text:
## Establishment Grant
The Establishment Grant is a one-off payment to carers of someone else's child to help with the costs when a child first comes into their care, eg a bed, bedding and clothing.
You'll automatically receive an Establishment Grant when you get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit.
## Who can get it
You'll automatically receive an Establishment Grant when you get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit.
The Establishment Grant is not available to carers who:
- applied for the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit before 13 January 2014. However, you'll be able to apply every year for the School and Year Start-up Payment to help with costs that come at the beginning of the year such as pre-school or school-related costs.
- received (or have been approved to receive) an upfront payment for the child as part of the Child, Youth and Family Home for Life support package.
School and Year Start-up Payment
A carer will only be paid the Establishment Grant once for the child. If the child leaves the person's care (resulting in the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit being stopped) and then returns after a period of time, the Establishment Grant won't be paid to that carer again.
## How much you get
You'll receive a one-off payment of $350 for each child.
You won't be taxed on this money and you won't have to pay it back.
## How to apply
You'll automatically get this payment when you get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit. You don't have to apply for it.
If you're granted the Orphan's or Unsupported Child's Benefit for more than one child on or after the 13 January 2014, you'll automatically get the Establishment Grant for each child.
## Contact
You may be able to receive other financial help with your costs even if you get this payment.
The best thing to do is call us to talk about your situation.

chunks.title: Ex gratia and compensation payments
chunks.text: Most ex gratia and compensation payments are not considered as income or cash assets. You'll need to let us know if you get one of these payments, so we can check if it will affect your payments from us.

chunks.title: About these payments
chunks.text: You may get an ex gratia payment if you've been harmed in some way. An ex gratia payment means there's no legal requirement to pay you or accept blame. Compensation payments are also made because of harm done, or to settle a claim of harm. They are sometimes ordered by a court or tribunal, but can also be made through a settlement outside court.

chunks.title: Lake Alice payments
chunks.text: This includes: - ex gratia or compensation payments for people who were patients at the Lake Alice Hospital - ex gratia payments as part of the redress package for survivors of the Lake Alice Child and Adolescent Unit.

chunks.title: When these payments count as income or a cash asset
chunks.text: An ex gratia or compensation payment may not count as income and/or a cash asset if it is paid for a case of harm. These payments are usually made by: - the Government - agencies who provide services on behalf of the Government, or - charities, incorporated societies, and faith-based institutions such as churches. It can be counted as income or a cash asset if it's paid for other things like: - a loss e.g. involving money, land, an asset or goods and services you've provided - a personal grievance at work. Some ex gratia and compensation payments may not count as income or a cash asset for the first 12 months after they're paid. Others, e.g. Lake Alice payments, may not be counted as income or a cash asset permanently. The amount of time a payment is not counted as income or a cash asset depends on who makes the payment to you and why. It's best to talk to us so we can make sure your payments are right.

chunks.title: How your payments from us could be affected
chunks.text: You need to tell us about any ex gratia or compensation payment you get. If we decide that an ex gratia or compensation payment does count as income or a cash asset, it may affect your payments from us if: - you get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit - you save or invest the payment and earn interest or other income from it.

chunks.title: What we expect you to do when in emergency housing
chunks.text:
## What we expect you to do when in emergency housing
When you’re staying in emergency housing, there are things we expect you to do.
## We expect you to:
- understand the security deposit responsibilities and conditions of payment
- understand and follow the supplier's rules and not do anything that will result in being asked to leave
- understand what will happen if you cause or contribute to your emergency housing need
- be responsible for your actions and those of your guests. For example, if you or one of your guests has damaged property, you'll need to pay for it
- accept offers of housing if it meets the needs of you and your whānau, including temporary options like transitional housing
- let us know if things change, including if: you leave your emergency housing your or your partner's income changes the make-up of your household changes (for example, if your relationship changes or the number of children in your care changes)
- you leave your emergency housing
- your or your partner's income changes
- the make-up of your household changes (for example, if your relationship changes or the number of children in your care changes)
- do all you need to do to meet any benefit obligations you may have, such as searching for or getting ready to work.
## Your responsibilities after 7 nights
If you're in emergency housing for more than 7 nights, there are also responsibilities you have to meet from the 8th night. Find out what these are and what happens if you don't meet them.
Your responsibilities in emergency housing

chunks.title: Extending childcare when your child turns 5
chunks.text:
## Extending childcare when your child turns 5
If your child's going to a school where children start when they turn 5, but they can't start straight away, we may be able to pay for an extra 4 weeks of childcare.
## Who can extend their childcare payments
There could be a number of reasons why your child can't start school straight away, eg, the school's closed because it's the middle of the school/Christmas holidays.
Whatever your situation, we may be able to pay an extra 4 weeks of childcare if:
- you're getting Childcare Subsidy
- your child's going to a school where children start when they turn 5, instead of a cohort entry school (where new entrants start after they turn 5)
- your child can't start school straight away
- you continue to meet the criteria for Childcare Subsidy until your child starts school.
Childcare Subsidy
## How to apply
Call us on 0800 559 009 and tell us why your childcare payments need to be extended.
## Getting Child Disability Allowance
If you get Child Disability Allowance for your child and they're not starting school yet, we may be able to keep paying your childcare until they start - up until they turn 6.
Call us on 0800 559 009 to discuss your situation.

chunks.title: Extraordinary Care Fund
chunks.text: You can apply if a child you care for shows promise in a skill or talent, or because they are experiencing difficulties and need extra support. To qualify you need to get the Orphan’s Benefit or Unsupported Child’s Benefit. You can apply for one grant of up to $2,000 each year. If you're caring for more than one child, you can apply for each child.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: The Extraordinary Care Fund helps pay for extra costs you have because a child you care for: - shows promise in an ability, skill, or talent, for example in school, sports, dance, or music - is experiencing difficulties that impact their development, for example learning or behavioural difficulties You can apply if you get the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit. Grants are made based on your child's needs and the documents that support this, not your family’s financial situation.

chunks.title: Showing promise
chunks.text: Examples of costs we can help with: - Participating in a national Kapa Haka competition - Attending a science academic programme or event - Competing in a national sports competition - Coaching, tutoring or mentoring - Private music lessons and instrument hire or purchase

chunks.title: Experiencing difficulties
chunks.text: Examples include: - courses or activities to: develop self-esteem, physical capability, or social skills for example YMCA programmes improve their ability to learn if they have learning difficulties swimming lessons (if they haven't learnt to swim at school) - develop self-esteem, physical capability, or social skills for example YMCA programmes - improve their ability to learn if they have learning difficulties - swimming lessons (if they haven't learnt to swim at school) - orthodontic work that isn’t funded by the Ministry of Health - counselling You can apply for other costs we haven't mentioned here.

chunks.title: We can’t help to pay for:
chunks.text: - costs covered by an Establishment Grant or School and Year Start-up Payment - health and medical costs, for example: doctor's visits medication - doctor's visits - medication - everyday costs, for example: school trips vehicles (this includes any repairs, warrants, registration, and any fuel costs to and from events) legal costs childcare - school trips - vehicles (this includes any repairs, warrants, registration, and any fuel costs to and from events) - legal costs - childcare - overseas travel and related costs, for example: hotels overseas courses - hotels - overseas courses - teacher aides - school uniforms.

chunks.title: How much can you get
chunks.text: Between 1 July to 30 June each year you can get one grant of up to $2,000 for each child you care for. This table is a guide to how much we can help with: Cost type Technology: LaptopsTablets/iPads Secondary school level: up to $1,400 Intermediate school level: up to $1,200 Primary school level: up to $750 Primary school level to secondary school level all $600 Under 5 years: $600 by exception only You can apply for help with technology every two years unless there are exceptional circumstances. Counselling Psychological fees/services Development programmes e.g. Speech development, YMCA programmes Initial assessment $125 to $180 per hour. $45 to $130 per session

chunks.title: Step 1: Fill out an application form
chunks.text: Print and fill out the Extraordinary Care Fund Grant application form. If you can't print the form, call us and we'll post one to you. Phone us

chunks.title: Step 2: Gather your documents
chunks.text: You'll need to provide: - Proof of the cost you're applying for, for example: A quote The receipt A letter from an organiser asking for payment. - A quote - The receipt - A letter from an organiser asking for payment. - Letters of support. There may be other documents you need to provide if you're applying for help with technology, costs over $2000, orthodontic treatment, extra tuition or eyewear.

chunks.title: Letters of support
chunks.text: A letter of support explains how your child is showing promise or how they're experiencing difficulty. If you're applying for a cost that's: - under $500, you need one letter of support - $500 or more, you need 2 letters of support The letter needs to be from an independent person, for example: - A teacher - Coach - Other person of standing in the community

chunks.title: Technology
chunks.text: If you're applying for help with technology, you need to provide documents: - from the school with their recommended item, especially if they have a 'bring your own device' (BYOD) programme - for anything that's significantly more expensive than what the school recommends, your letter of support will need to outline why it's needed. You can apply for help with tablets/iPads/laptops every two years unless there are exceptional circumstances.

chunks.title: Applying for costs over $2,000
chunks.text: If you're applying for a cost that's more than $2,000, you need to confirm how you can pay for the rest of the cost.

chunks.title: Orthodontic treatment
chunks.text: If you're applying for help with orthodontic treatment, for example braces, you need to provide documents from the orthodontist with: - the proposed treatment - how long the treatment will take - confirmation of any payments made so far and the balance owing.

chunks.title: Progress report for extra tuition
chunks.text: If you're applying for extra tuition, you need to provide a progress report for your 2nd application, and any further applications after this. The report must detail how your child has progressed with their extra tuition over the previous 12 months.

chunks.title: Eyewear over $300
chunks.text: If you're applying for eyewear that costs more than $300, you need to provide documents from an optometrist which specify that the child needs specialised lenses or frames.

chunks.title: Step 3: Submit your application
chunks.text: You can get your completed form and documents to us by either: - dropping these into your nearest service centre - posting these to your nearest service centre. Find a service centre

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: Our panel assesses each application. They meet 4 times a year, but you can apply at any time. We'll send you a letter telling you the outcome of your application. If you apply before: You will hear back from us after: 24 July 2026 By 16 September 2026 23 October 2026 By 16 December 2026 4 February 2027 By 24 March 2027 20 April 2027 By 23 June 2027

chunks.title: Other payments
chunks.text: If you get the Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit, you can apply for the School and Year Start-up Payment. This payment helps you with the costs that are mostly at the start of the year. These costs are usually things children need for school or pre-school, like pre-school and school-related costs such as clothing, school fees and stationery. School and Year Start-up Payments

chunks.title: Family breakdown
chunks.text:
## Family breakdown
If you're under 19 and have had a family breakdown, we may be able to help.
## Who can get help
If you're under 19 and can't live with your parents or guardians, we may be able to help. You may be in one of these situations:
- you've left the care of Oranga Tamariki - Ministry for Children, or an agency approved by Oranga Tamariki - Ministry for Children, eg, Iwi Social Services or Cultural Social Services
- your relationship with your parents or guardians has broken down and they're not prepared to financially support you
- your parents or guardians can't support you financially, eg: they've gone to prison they've moved overseas they're in hospital long term they've died.
- they've gone to prison
- they've moved overseas
- they're in hospital long term
- they've died.
## Under 16
If you're under 16, your guardian should talk to us about what help is available.
They can call us on 0800 559 009
## 16-17
If you're 16 or 17 and your relationship with your parents or guardians has broken down and they can't support you, you may be able to get a Youth Payment.
Youth Payment
## Teen parent
If you're a 16-19 year old parent, you may be able to get a Young Parent Payment.
Young Parent Payment
## Getting Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment
If you get Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment, a Youth Service provider will work with you to:
- get the correct financial support
- ensure you're in either education training or work-based learning
- manage your money well, including helping you with budgeting
- make sure you are living somewhere reasonable and affordable
- talk about other services you might need.
Youth Serviceexternal
## 18+
If you're 18 years or older, we may be able to help in a number of ways.
Use "Check what you might get" to find out what help you could qualify for.
## Call us
Call us if you're unsure of what you can get and you want to discuss your situation.
Phone us

chunks.title: Housing when escaping family violence
chunks.text:
## Housing when escaping family violence
If you need to leave home because of family violence, we may be able to help you find somewhere to go.
If you're in immediate danger, dial 111 and ask for the Police.
## Women's Refuge
If you’re a woman in a family violence situation, call the Women’s Refuge free Crisisline on 0800 733 843 (0800 REFUGE).
There are many ways they can help, including a safe house if you need accommodation urgently. Their safe houses are in secret locations and you can come to them in a crisis, day or night.
Women's Refugeexternal
## Family violence information and services
The 'Are You Ok' website has information for people experiencing family violence:
www.areyouok.org.nzexternal
You can also call the 24/7 helpline on 0800 456 450. Trained counsellors can provide support and connect you with support services in your area.
## Emergency housing
If you have nowhere to stay tonight or in the next 7 days, you may be able to apply for emergency housing.
Emergency housing
## Public housing
We may be able to help with public housing.

chunks.title: FamilyBoost payment
chunks.text:
## FamilyBoost payment
If you get a FamilyBoost payment from Inland Revenue, it is not counted as income. If you keep it (or part of it) for 12 months or more, or get interest from the payment, you need to tell us.
## About FamilyBoost
FamilyBoost is a childcare payment to help households pay for the cost of early childhood education (ECE). It's administered by Inland Revenue.
FamilyBoost (Inland Revenue)external
## How it affects your payments from us
You have to tell us if you:
- keep the money you get (or part of it) for 12 months or more - this will be counted as a cash asset
- get interest from the payment - the interest will be counted as income.
If you're applying for a one-off hardship payment (e.g. food), we’ll consider FamilyBoost payments as part of your available resources.

chunks.title: Feeling anxious about work
chunks.text: Getting a job and going to work doesn't have to be hard. These services can make life easier and give you confidence. These support services are designed to help you mentally prepare yourself to get into work. They can help you with: - building your confidence - working through your worries - overcoming obstacles. All these services are free.

chunks.title: Te Heke Mai
chunks.text: An app to help when you're looking for work or starting training or a new job. Te Heke Mai offers: - a digital coach and real-life mentors - personalised support and feedback - quick and easy chats. It's open to anyone in New Zealand. Te Heke Maiexternal

chunks.title: Here Toitū
chunks.text: Get a dedicated support team working with you and your health provider. They'll help you set goals and plan how to reach them. You can get this if you: - get a main benefit (e.g. Supported Living Payment or Jobseeker Support), or - have a job but can't work right now due to a health condition, injury or disability. Your doctor must also be registered with either: - THINK Hauora in MidCentral - Pegasus Health in Christchurch - ProCare in Auckland - National Hauora Coalition in Auckland. To join Here Toitū, contact one of these health providers, or talk to your doctor.

chunks.title: Individual Placement and Support
chunks.text: You can get this if you get mental health support from Te Whatu Ora (Health New Zealand) in: - Auckland, - Counties Manukau, or - Waitematā. You'll get an employment consultant, who will work with you and your mental health support team. Together you'll make a plan to help you get a job. Contact your Mental Health Key Worker to apply for this.

chunks.title: E Ara E
chunks.text: A counselling and mental health service helping young Aucklanders with work or study. It's run by Odyssey Auckland. You can join if you're 18-24, getting a benefit, and live in Auckland region. Visit the E Ara E page on the Odyssey website or talk to a case manager. Work and study support for ages 18-24 (Odyssey)external

chunks.title: Take Charge
chunks.text: A counselling and mental health service for young people in Canterbury. You can get help to work or study, and manage your wellbeing. It's run by Odyssey House. You can join if you're 18-24, getting a benefit, and live in Canterbury. Visit the Take Charge page on the Odyssey House website, or talk to a case manager. Supporting youth mental health and employment (Odyssey)external

chunks.title: Final work payments
chunks.text: We’ve found an error in the way we treated some payments people received at the end of their employment. This meant the start date of benefit payments was incorrect and we owe some people money.

chunks.title: Who's affected by this error
chunks.text: You may be affected if you: - received payments, such as holiday pay or pay in lieu of notice, at the end of your employment, and - your benefit was granted on or after 23 March 2020, but before 8 June 2020.

chunks.title: Check if you or someone else is owed money
chunks.text: We’re contacting and paying all our current clients affected by this error. If you used to get payments from us, you can use the ‘Payment errors enquiry’ form to check if you’re owed money. Our staff can’t tell you if you’re owed money or how much it is. You can also use the ‘Payment errors enquiry’ form to enquire for someone else if: - they’re not a current client with us - a person has died. The form will check if you (or the person you’re enquiring for) are owed money. It won’t say how much you’re owed, we’ll send you a letter to let you know this. Payment errors enquiry form external

chunks.title: Using the enquiry form overseas
chunks.text: At this stage the enquiry tool can only be assessed from Australia and New Zealand.

chunks.title: Checking payment errors for someone else
chunks.text: You can also use the payment errors enquiry form to check to see if we owe someone else money when: - they're not a current client - a person has died. Information to make an enquiry for someone else The form will tell you if the person you're making an enquiry for is on the list of clients who may be affected and you can apply for them. It won't say how much they may be owed.

chunks.title: How this payment affects your benefit or allowance
chunks.text: If you're getting a benefit or allowance from us, it won't be affected for 12 months from when we pay you the money we owe. If you: - still have this money after 12 months, you'll need to tell us and it will be counted for any benefits or payments that are asset tested - invest the money you get and earn interest, after 12 months you'll need to tell us and this will be counted as income.

chunks.title: Review rights
chunks.text: If you don't understand or agree with a decision we've made, please talk with us so we can explain it. You have the right to ask us to review a decision you think is wrong. You can use the application form on our website, or write to us. We need to get your request within three months. If you have a good reason why you can't ask us to review a decision within three months, get in touch. We may still be able to review the decision. You can find out more on the review of a decision page of our website, or you can give us a call on 0800 559 009. Get a decision reviewed

chunks.title: Find a house
chunks.text:
## Find a house
If you need to find a place to live, we may be able to help. You may be able to apply for public (social) housing or get some ideas on where to look for private housing.
If you have nowhere to stay right now, we may be able to help you find somewhere until you can get something longer-term.
Nowhere to stay
## Public housing
If you can't afford a private rental, you may be able to live in a public house where the Government pays part of the rent. These are houses that are rented out by Kāinga Ora (used to be Housing New Zealand) and other Community Housing Providers.
You need to meet certain criteria to qualify for public housing. If you apply, you may have to wait for a while until a suitable property becomes available.
- Who can get public housing Find out if you can get public housing.

Find out if you can get public housing.

There are lots of websites where you can look for private housing. It depends if you want to find your own place or flat with others.
It’s a good idea to check the market rent in the suburbs where you want to live. Then you can see roughly how much you'll need to pay. Market rent is how much most people are paying for rental properties in each area.

chunks.text: There are lots of jobs to choose from across New Zealand. Find out what's available, which job is right for you and how you can plan your career.

chunks.text: Find websites to help you search for jobs. - How to choose the right job Explore your options and choose a job that's right for you.

chunks.text: Find job events, training opportunities and chat to us directly about work on our Job Connect Facebook page. Job Connect on Facebookexternal

chunks.title: Finding seasonal work
chunks.text: Seasonal jobs are available all year, in places like orchards, farms, forests, or tourist hotspots. Doing a seasonal job can help you: - learn new skills and get work experience - earn good money, sometimes more than $700 a week - be active and fit - meet new people - gain confidence. Seasonal jobs can last from a few weeks up to 6 months. You may be offered a permanent job, or you can use your new skills and experience for a similar job.

chunks.title: How much it pays
chunks.text: Employers rely on seasonal workers and will pay good money for a good worker. For example, if you worked 30 hours a week picking fruit or vegetables you could earn around $700 before tax a week, or more. Exactly how much depends on the employer and the job. Some jobs are paid by the hour and others by a contract rate, e.g. if you’re picking apples you might get a set amount for each bin you fill.

chunks.title: Where to work and when
chunks.text: The work changes with the seasons, so the type of jobs needed and available change too. You can use this table to see what type of work is available, and when, so you can plan ahead. chunks.title: When you start work
chunks.text: You may be able to get help from us for costs like accommodation, gear and clothing for when you start work, and regular bills like travel and childcare. Doing seasonal work

chunks.title: Can’t work because of bad weather
chunks.text: If bad weather means you can't do your horticulture or viticulture job, and you stopped getting a benefit to do this job, we may be able to help. Seasonal Work Assistance is a payment that helps you pay for costs while you're not working. Seasonal Work Assistance

chunks.title: When you stop work
chunks.text: We can help you find a new job quickly, and make sure you have everything you need to start your new job. Finishing seasonal work

chunks.title: Fire or theft
chunks.text:
## Fire or theft
If you need help replacing essential items after a fire or theft and can't pay for these any other way, we may be able to help.
- You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for this help.
- You may have to pay the money back depending your situation.
## Who can get it
We may be able to help if you:
- are 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services)
- have urgent and necessary costs
- have no other way to meet these costs
- are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident
- normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here.
It also depends on:
- how much you and your partner earn
- any money or assets you and your partner have.
Youth Servicesexternal
Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income and asset limits apply:
## What you can get
We may be able to pay up to $1000 to help with costs such as:
- whiteware (e.g., fridge, freezer, washing machine)
- bed
- couch.
## How to apply
You need to call us on 0800 559 009
We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us.
You may need to send us a police or fire report.

chunks.title: Fired for misconduct or left voluntarily
chunks.text:
## Fired for misconduct or left voluntarily
If you've been fired for misconduct or left your job without a good reason there may be a number of ways we can help you, but you won't be paid right away.
It's important you contact us right away as you may need to wait up to 13 weeks before your payments start. It depends on why you've been fired or left your job.
How payments work and when your payments start
## Stopped working during a trial period of up to 90 days
If you've stopped working during, or at the end of, a trial period of up to 90 days, you may be able to apply for Jobseeker Support.
You may have a shorter stand-down period if you're in this situation.
Jobseeker Support
Information about trial periodsexternal
When you apply for Jobseeker Support, there may be some things you need to do before you can get it.
The online application process
## Ability to work affected because of a health condition or disability
You have a health condition or disability that affects your ability to work. This means that you have to reduce your hours or stop work for a while. We may still be able to help if you have a job to go back to.
You'll need a medical certificate from your health practitioner, eg, your doctor, to tell us how your health condition or disability affects your ability to work.
Jobseeker Support
## Sole parent with children under 14 to support
Sole Parent Support
## Need money and your partner works
You're down to one wage and you need help to pay day-to-day expenses while you look for work.

chunks.title: Flexi-wage
chunks.text:
## Flexi-wage
Support to hire staff, get the skills you need to do a job, or start your own business.
Flexi-wage is one of the ways we're supporting more New Zealanders into work. You can get help to hire staff, get the skills you need to do a job, or start your own business.
## How Flexi-wage can help
There's a wage contribution to help employers pay wages, as well as training and ongoing support for employees if it's needed. Find out more below.
- Employers
## Employers

## Self-employed
If you're an employer, contact us about Flexi-wage before making jobs redundant. Flexi-wage can help with:
- support to retrain your employee to do a different job in your business
- support for another business where the employee can work in a temporary, fixed-term job. Once their normal job is stable they can return to that role.

chunks.title: Flexi-wage – job seeker information
chunks.text: Flexi-wage is one of the ways we're supporting more New Zealanders into work, by helping you get the skills you need for the job, and supporting more employers to hire staff. Flexi-wage can support you if you need some extra help to get started and learn the skills you need for a job.

chunks.title: What's Flexi-wage
chunks.text: Flexi-wage can help you get the skills you need to meet the entry-level requirements for a job. You can get training and ongoing support if you need it, and your employer can get a wage contribution to help them pay your wages. The job must continue after the Flexi-wage has finished.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get Flexi-wage if you: - are likely to need a benefit for a long time if you don’t get this assistance, and - haven't worked for a long time, and - need training to meet the entry-level requirements for the job and/or - have difficulty getting or keeping a job. For example, you might have barriers to finding a job because you need education or training, or your current job may be at risk. Flexi-wage can help you get the skills you need to do a job, which might be with: - an employer who wants to hire you, or - an employer you're already working for who needs to move you into a different role that requires further training and more hours, rather than making you redundant.The employer also needs to meet the 'Who can get it' criteria outlined in Flexi-wage - employer information. Flexi-wage - employer information The job must: - pay at least the minimum wage - have the minimum number of hours to meet any work obligations Work obligations and be either: - ongoing, continuing after Flexi-wage has finished, or - a fixed-term project that benefits the community or environment and will help you gain the skills needed to get into work once it's finished.

chunks.title: What support you can get
chunks.text: Support from us can include: - a contribution to your wages - we'll pay this to your employer - training - ongoing support. We'll talk to your employer about what you need and how we can help.

chunks.title: How to find out more
chunks.text: If you're already talking to us about finding or getting ready for work, ask about Flexi-wage. Otherwise, call us on 0800 559 009 to book an appointment to talk about Flexi-wage and how we can help you into work. You’ll need a client number to book an appointment – if you don’t already have one, you can request a client number here. How to get a client number

chunks.title: Flexi-wage for self-employment
chunks.text: Flexi-wage is one of the ways we're supporting more New Zealanders into work. We may be able to help you start your own business and help with costs while you get started.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: To get Flexi-wage self-employment there's basic criteria you and your intended business need to meet. Additional criteria will also apply - we can talk to you about this when you contact us to find out more about Flexi-wage self-employment.

chunks.title: Criteria your business needs to meet
chunks.text: You need: - to be in the early stages of developing a business and unable to be self-sufficient - an in-depth understanding of all aspects of your proposed business idea - a business plan – find out how to write this here: How to write a business plan (Business.govt.nz)external We must be satisfied your business idea is viable before we can consider any assistance.

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet:
chunks.text: You need to be: - out of work, and - 18 years or older and not able to get NZ Super, and - having difficulty getting or keeping a job (for example you might have barriers to finding a job because you need training, or your current job may be at risk). You must also be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and either: - a New Zealand citizen, or - a resident with a residence class visa, or - recognised as a refugee or protected person, or - have a temporary visa that allows you to work in New Zealand and either: have applied to be recognised as a refugee or protected person and are waiting on the outcome, or have applied for a residence class visa and are compelled to stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances. - have applied to be recognised as a refugee or protected person and are waiting on the outcome, or - have applied for a residence class visa and are compelled to stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances.

chunks.title: Who can't get it
chunks.text: You can't get Flexi-wage for self-employment if you're: - re-starting a business that you've owned before, or - already running an established business that is struggling financially, or - currently bankrupt.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You can only get Flexi-Wage for self-employment if you meet the eligibility criteria and we are convinced your business idea is viable. To do this, we'll meet with you and get you to give us details of your business idea so we can assess it in detail.

chunks.title: Step 1: Appointment for initial eligibility
chunks.text: Call us on 0800 559 009 to book an appointment. At the appointment we will: - check if you and your business meet the eligibility criteria - discuss how your job search is going - talk about your business idea, your needs and what type of help we may be able to offer. We may ask if you have a business plan, and if you're already operating any other businesses.

chunks.title: Step 2: Give us details of your business
chunks.text: After your appointment you need to give details of your business idea. This includes details about: - your business plan - any relevant skills and experience - market research - marketing and competition - finance and operations - compliance and risk planning. We'll tell you how you can send this information to us. We may also ask for your findings and proof of research for these things.

chunks.title: Step 3: Appointment for business plan
chunks.text: If we're satisfied with the information you have provided, we'll book an appointment with you go through your business details and discuss your business idea in full. We'll also talk about developing your business plan, and whether a Business Training and Advice Grant could help.

chunks.title: Step 4: Assessing your business idea
chunks.text: To make sure your business idea is viable, we'll send your business plan to be independently assessed. If it's approved you'll be granted Flexi-Wage for self-employment. We'll then send you a contract, which you need to complete and email back to us with evidence of your bank account number.

chunks.title: If you get the subsidy
chunks.text: We'll: - contact you regularly to see how things are going - send you 4-weekly claim forms for the Flexi-wage subsidy over the period of the contract. We'll make sure you know how to make a claim every 4 weeks.

chunks.title: Mid-project financial report
chunks.text: You'll need to provide a mid-project financial report within the first 12-20 weeks. The report needs to outline things like: - productivity levels (for example, the amount of work or items manufactured) - actual cash flow - a comparison of performance against the original business plan - cash flow expectations for at least the next 6 months. We'll let you know when we need this and who to send it to. The report will be reviewed by an independent person, and we'll let you know the outcome of this review.

chunks.title: Business Training and Advice Grant
chunks.text: You may be able to get up to $5,000 to help you develop a business plan and/or train in business skills, advice and project reports. Business Training and Advice Grant

chunks.title: Self-Employment start up payment
chunks.text: You may also be able to get help with essential start-up costs, for example furniture or the first lot of stock. Self-Employment start up payment

chunks.title: Flexible Childcare Assistance
chunks.text: We may be able to help with the costs of informal childcare e.g. a babysitter, if you can't access formal childcare programmes while you're at work or in employment-related study or training.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get Flexible Childcare Assistance if you: - are the principal caregiver of a dependent child or young person - have informal childcare costs because you’re unable to access formal childcare - are in or starting an employment-related activity and need childcare because of this - likely to need a benefit for a long time if you don’t get this assistance, and - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (you may be able to get this payment if you have a temporary entry class visa that allows you to work in New Zealand). Principal caregiver

chunks.title: Employment-related activity
chunks.text: You need to be participating in the employment-related activity for at least 3 hours a week, during times you need informal childcare. This can include: - paid employment - employment-related study, or - employment-related training. If you're working and won't be getting a main benefit, your job must be expected to last at least 13 weeks. Main benefit If you're in training or study, you must be doing a specific type of course, and it will depend on how long you’ll be taking part. If your course is: - 12 weeks or less, the course can be at any level and does not need to be NZQA certified - 13 weeks or more, the course must be Level 3 or below on the NZQA framework, which means it is certificate level study.

chunks.title: The child or young person
chunks.text: The child or young person must be: - 13 years or younger, or - 14 to 18 years but can’t safely be left home alone, e.g. because they need special help.

chunks.title: Other parent or caregiver
chunks.text: You may not be able to get this payment if the child's other parent or caregiver can take care of them.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: You can get a weekly rate of: - $64.02 for one child - $32.01 for each additional child. The maximum amount you can get is $192.06 a week. You can get the payment for up to 52 weeks. The payment is to help pay for your informal childcare costs, e.g: - paying the person who’s caring for your child, which could be a: family member trusted friend neighbour child-minder - family member - trusted friend - neighbour - child-minder - food - activities - travel. You need to pay the person caring for the child or young person yourself.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 to book an appointment. In most cases, we’ll need you to come in for a face-to-face appointment. However, there may be times we’ll be able to support you over the phone. Find a service centre The information we need from you is listed in our pdf form. You can print and fill out the form yourself, or we can help you fill it in at your appointment. We’ll also need you to provide documents showing your: - employment details e.g. name of the company, your position, and start date - employment-related training details, or - employment-related education details. Types of documents we accept If this is your first time applying for a benefit or ongoing payment, you need to bring your original government-issued ID into a service centre so we can check it. Verify your identity at a service centre

chunks.title: Organising childcare
chunks.text: You’re responsible for choosing and organising appropriate care for your children. When you’re looking at options for childcare, there are a number of things you may like to consider or do, so that you know your children will be safe and well cared for. These could include: - asking the person for references, then contacting their referees and talking to them - asking to see a copy of the person’s criminal record they can get this from the Ministry of Justice - they can get this from the Ministry of Justice - thinking about the environment where your children will be cared for, e.g: fencing for pools and balconies who else will be there safety around animals - fencing for pools and balconies - who else will be there - safety around animals - checking if the child will be travelling in the person’s car, e.g: do they have a driver licence is the vehicle safe do they need car seats - do they have a driver licence - is the vehicle safe - do they need car seats - talking to the person about how you want your child looked after, e.g: types of food and activities behaviour expectations special needs or medication they need to be aware of. - types of food and activities - behaviour expectations - special needs or medication they need to be aware of. You can leave a child under 14 at home or in another place if you’ve made reasonable provisions to have them supervised and cared for safely, and they’re not left for a long time.

chunks.title: Reviews and changes
chunks.text: You must also tell us straight away about any changes in your circumstances that could affect your payments, e.g. if your child leaves your care. Phone us

chunks.title: Paying for formal childcare
chunks.text: If you get Flexible Childcare Assistance, you can still apply for OSCAR or Childcare subsidy to help with childcare costs during the times you're able to access formal childcare programmes. OSCAR or Childcare subsidy

chunks.title: Food
chunks.text: We may be able to help you pay for food if you’re on a low income or a benefit. - You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. - You don't have to pay the money back.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You could find yourself in a situation where you've had to pay for an essential cost that means you don’t have enough money to pay for food. Maybe you’ve paid for: - doctors visits - dental treatment - clothing for a job interview - school clothes or materials for your child. You may also find that you have less income this week because: - you’ve been off work due to sickness but you’re not eligible for sick pay - your hours are reduced unexpectedly. Whatever your situation, we may be able to help if you: - are 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services) Youth Servicesexternal - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - have an urgent and immediate need to buy food - have no other way to pay for food (e.g., no money in the bank and no other cash assets). Definition of cash assets It also depends on how much you and your partner if you have one) earn. Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income limits usually apply:

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: How much you get depends on your situation. You can only use the money for food and essential grocery items, e.g., toiletries. You can’t buy other things, e.g., alcohol, cigarettes, gift cards, vouchers, etc.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: If you are a current client, you may be able to apply using MyMSD. If you are a new client or unable to use MyMSD, you’ll need to call us. We’ll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help, and let you know if you need to do anything else. Phone us

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: If your application is approved, we’ll give you a payment card (if you don’t already have one) and load the money onto it. We’ll talk to you about how we'll get this card to you. You have 7 days to spend the money before it expires. A payment card is like an Eftpos card and you can use it at any supermarket or store that accepts them. Find out where payment cards are acceptedexternal You can also login to MyMSD to see how much you have left on your payment card and when it expires. Once you've used your payment card, keep it. You can use it again if you need help from us in the future.

chunks.title: Fraud and investigations
chunks.text: Information about fraud, how to avoid it, our fraud investigations and your rights. Fraud is where you have intentionally misled us to receive money you are not entitled to. It's not fraud if you have received money from us that you were not entitled to, but did not intentionally mislead us.

chunks.title: Talk to us
chunks.text: You need to tell us everything about your situation so we can work out the correct amount you're entitled to. It's important to tell us about changes that affect your entitlement. If you don't, you could find yourself in the situation of being investigated for fraud. Don't take the risk. Call us if there's anything you'd like to know more about. We're always happy to answer your questions and there is no need to identify who you are. You can call us free on 0800 559 009 or if you are a student call 0800 889 900 Your obligations while getting payments from us

chunks.title: How we find fraud
chunks.text: We find benefit fraud in lots of different ways, including: - through members of the public - sharing information with other government agencies - our own internal sources, and - regular entitlement reviews. Sharing your information Report a suspected fraud

chunks.title: How we investigate fraud
chunks.text: If we have information that suggests you may be involved in benefit or housing fraud, our investigators need to gather evidence. Evidence helps us determine if you: - received money you weren't entitled to, and - misled us to receive it. Our investigators will talk to you as well as other people. They'll decide on a case-by-case basis whether to talk to you first or go to a third party. They will also make sure the right amount of information is collected.

chunks.title: We will talk to you in most cases
chunks.text: In most cases our investigators will contact you first to request more information about your situation and talk to you about our concerns. If they want to talk to you about your entitlement or an investigation, they'll meet you at a time that suits you. You can choose whether or not you want to be interviewed. You can also get legal advice if you want to. You may wish to seek advice about this from an advocate or legal representative. If you want legal advice and don’t already have a lawyer, you can contact: - your local Community Law Centre, or - Citizens Advice Bureau. Community Lawexternal Citizens Advice Bureauexternal If you choose to be interviewed, they'll give you an opportunity to tell us: - your side of the story, and - about any changes in your circumstances. They'll also go through the information we have and there'll be opportunities for you to ask questions. If you need to, they can make a further appointment to discuss your entitlement in more detail. You can bring a support person or advocate with you to the interview. For example, you could bring a lawyer, family member, friend, an interpreter or benefit advocate. Please tell us if you want an interpreter and we can arrange one for you. Having someone act on your behalf What you say in an interview can be used as evidence in a criminal prosecution. Because of this, you have rights which we'll remind you of at the interview. - You don't have to answer all our questions and you can stop the interview at any time - You can leave the interview at any time - You can speak with a lawyer or support person at any time in private.

chunks.title: We may talk to a third party
chunks.text: Our investigators may request information from others before they talk with you. This can include: - financial institutions - employers - property managers, and - other government agencies. They may also contact other organisations or talk to people in the community. When we have to approach others for information directly, we can use powers under the Social Security Act 2018 and the Public and Community Housing Management Act 1992. These powers to collect information are controlled by Codes of Conduct with rules about what information we can request and the process we must follow. Read the Codes of Conductexternal We'll only gather information that is relevant and necessary for our investigation.

chunks.title: We may use publicly available information
chunks.text: We may also access information that's publicly available, including: - newspapers and media - using internet search engines - looking up public lists and registers, and - social media (we won't interact with you or private groups you're part of). We have a policy that allows us to use publicly available information for this purpose.

chunks.title: How to make a complaint about the investigation
chunks.text: If you believe we have collected information we weren't entitled to, or breached the Codes of Conduct, you can email our privacy team. They will look into your complaint and be in touch with you as soon as they can. Email the Privacy Team

chunks.title: Complaint to Privacy Commissioner
chunks.text: If you're not happy with our response, you can also make a complaint to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner. Make a complaint to the Office of the Privacy Commissionerexternal

chunks.title: Formal review
chunks.text: If you believe there was a breach of your privacy that affected a decision we made on your entitlements, you can ask for a formal review. You can use the review of decision form on our website or you can write to us. You need to do this within 3 months. If it’s after that, please get in touch anyway. If you have a good reason why you couldn’t ask us earlier, we may still be able to review the decision for you. Visit our 'Review of decision' page for more information. Review of a decision

chunks.title: Legal advice
chunks.text: You may wish to seek advice about this from an advocate or legal representative. If you want legal advice and don’t already have a lawyer, you can contact: - your local Community Law Centre, or - Citizens Advice Bureau. Community Lawexternal Citizens Advice Bureauexternal

chunks.title: Accessing information about the investigation
chunks.text: To protect your privacy, only authorised people can access detailed information about our benefit and housing fraud investigations. This includes only a few MSD people who need it for their work. Case managers, contact centres and most other people working at MSD don’t have access to this level of detail. However they may be able to see some information, such as letters we’ve sent to you. If you want a copy of your records that we hold, you can ask us for this. Request a copy of your recordsexternal If you have any questions about the information in your file, or want to correct something, we can work with you to do this.

chunks.title: If you were investigated before 2018
chunks.text: If you were investigated before 2018 and want to know more about the information gathered about you, email privacyofficer@msd.govt.nz. We'll get back to you as soon as we can.

chunks.title: What happens if you're found to have committed fraud
chunks.text: Fraud is taken very seriously and can have severe consequences, e.g. you may: - be restricted from using our phone and online channels - have a decrease in the amount you get from us - have to pay back any money you weren’t entitled to - face criminal prosecution – this can mean a fine or being sentenced to community service, home detention or imprisonment (on top of having to pay back any money you owe us). A conviction for fraud is very serious and can affect your: - job or future job prospects - ability to travel overseas, and - ability to get a loan, credit or insurance.

chunks.title: Privacy Commissioner's 2019 inquiry
chunks.text: From 2012 until 2018, for the most serious fraud allegations, we went to third parties for information without going to the client first. In 2019, an Office of the Privacy Commissioner inquiry found we had been acting inconsistently with our legal obligations for some fraud investigations.

chunks.title: We accepted this finding
chunks.text: We accepted all 5 recommendations made by the Privacy Commissioner and made changes to the way we do investigations. We also undertook an independent review of our fraud investigation practices and policies and made more improvements in line with that. Our investigators now decide on a case-by-case basis whether to go first to the client, or third party, and to make sure the right amount of information is collected. MSD accepts Privacy Commissioner's recommendations (Ministry of Social Development)external

chunks.title: If you were investigated before 2018
chunks.text: If you were investigated before 2018 and want to know more about the information gathered about you, email privacyofficer@msd.govt.nz We'll get back to you as soon as we can.

chunks.title: Funeral Grant
chunks.text: A Funeral Grant can help with some of the funeral costs of someone who has died. A Funeral Grant can only be used towards reasonable funeral expenses. Some examples of reasonable funeral expenses are: - any professional services fees charged by a funeral director - the cost of a casket - death certificate - newspaper notice costs - hearse fees - burial costs (including plot and interment) - cremation fees - venue hire - food and catering including kai for a tangihanga - flowers - celebrant, minister or clergy fees - a slideshow or photo tribute. You do not have to pay back a Funeral Grant if all the criteria are met (under 'Who can get it'). If we can't confirm income or asset amounts when you apply, we may still pay a Funeral Grant and confirm the amounts later. If the income or asset criteria is not met later, you will have to pay the money back.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Funeral Grant if the person who's died is: - your partner - your parent or guardian - your child (if they're under 18), or - someone over 18 and single (with or without children) who you're arranging a funeral for. In all cases, the person who died must have normally lived in New Zealand. If the person who's died is your partner or child, it will also depend on your income. We'll also make sure the reasonable funeral expenses cannot be met by: - the assets of the deceased person, and - your assets, if the person who died was your partner or child.

chunks.title: Income limits
chunks.text: If the person who's died is your partner or child, your income needs to be under a certain limit. Definition of Income (MAP)external

chunks.title: When you can't get a Funeral Grant
chunks.text: If there's other help with costs available to you, you may not be able to get a Funeral Grant. Other help could be that funeral costs are covered by: - another organisation, e.g. ACC or Veteran's Affairs - prepaid funeral cover. ACCexternal Veteran's Affairsexternal

chunks.title: If the person who died is not your partner or child
chunks.text: If the person who died has assets, we'll count the total amount of their assets. We'll then deduct this from the total funeral expenses. We'll then pay the lesser amount of either the: - maximum Funeral Grant, or - balance of the reasonable funeral expenses.

chunks.title: What's counted as assets
chunks.text: Find out what's counted as assets (Manuals and Procedures)external If we've kept their payments going for 28 days, this is also counted as an asset. Payments when a client dies

chunks.title: If the person who died is your partner or child
chunks.text: We'll count: - some of your assets (we won't count the first $2,351.46 of your assets), and - the total amount of the deceased person's assets. We'll deduct the total amount of assets from the total amount of reasonable funeral expenses. We'll then pay the lesser amount of either the: - maximum Funeral Grant, or - balance of the reasonable funeral expenses.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: The person applying for a Funeral Grant must be able to provide estate details or other information about the person who has died (including details about any children they are responsible for).

chunks.title: Step 2: Gather your documents
chunks.text: You will need to provide: - confirmation of death (if you don’t have this, please tell us as we may be able to get this information), for example: a death certificate (you can order this online here) funeral director confirmation, or a newspaper death notice. - a death certificate (you can order this online here) - funeral director confirmation, or - a newspaper death notice. - details of the funeral expenses: the itemised funeral account, and if it's already paid, the original receipt and proof of a bank account number for the person who paid it. - the itemised funeral account, and - if it's already paid, the original receipt and proof of a bank account number for the person who paid it. - proof of who you are, for example your: driver's licence passport, or business card if you're applying on behalf of a funeral home. - driver's licence - passport, or - business card if you're applying on behalf of a funeral home. Order certificates (NZ Government)external You may also need to provide details about assets and income.

chunks.title: Step 3: Send in your documents
chunks.text: Drop the completed form and your documents off at one of our service centres, or you can post it in to us. Find your nearest service centre
