chunks.title: Getting a payment card
chunks.text: Payment cards are used to buy one-off costs, for example food, groceries, glasses or dental treatment. Find out how we can help with these costs, how to apply and how to get a payment card. You must have set a personalised PIN on your payment card before you can use it. Setting your PIN If you're a young person in Youth Service getting payments, there are a few differences in getting and using your payment card. Find out more on the Youth Service website: Payments (Youth Service)external

chunks.title: How to apply for help with a cost
chunks.text: If you need help with an urgent, unexpected or one-off essential cost, you can find out how we can help here: Urgent or unexpected costs Help with living expenses The links above will also tell you how to apply for these costs. If your application is approved, we'll check how we can pay this. Some costs will not need a payment card – we'll let you know if this is the case. If we need to put this onto a payment card for you, we'll check if you already have a card. If you don't, you'll need to pick up a card from your local service centre - see below to find out how to do this.

chunks.title: Step 1:
chunks.text: Once your application is approved, pick up a payment card from any of our service centres. There's a list of their locations here: Find a service centre

chunks.title: Step 2:
chunks.text: Go to reception and ask for a payment card. You need to have: - your client number - a government issued identity document (for example a driver licence, birth certificate, or passport). You don't need an appointment for this.

chunks.title: Step 3:
chunks.text: Our staff will finish your application and load the money onto your card. They will tell you: - how much money is on the card - you can also check this online in MyMSDexternal - which shops you can use it at - what you can buy with it - how long the money will stay on the card for.

chunks.title: Step 4:
chunks.text: You need to set a PIN on your card before you can use it. The easiest way is to do it online: - Log in to MyMSDexternal. - Go to 'My payment cards'. - Select the card you want to add a PIN for. - Enter a 4-digit PIN - don't use a PIN that is consecutive, easily associated with you (like birthdays), or the numbers on your card. - Re-enter your PIN to confirm. - Done! Your PIN is now ready to go. Other ways to set your PIN: - call us and say "set my card PIN" - register your voice so you can set your PIN by calling us at any time without waiting to talk to a person - our staff in our service centres can help set your PIN in MyMSD - we have other ways you can contact us if you're deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech impairment.

chunks.title: Step 5:
chunks.text: Sign the back of your card. When you use the card you will need to sign your receipt, and the shop staff will check this matches the signature on your card. Keep your payment card in a safe place. If you need further payments, we can load them onto this card, so you don't need to go to a service centre to get another one.

chunks.title: Getting a Notice of Credit letter instead of a payment card
chunks.text: There are times when we need to give you a Notice of Credit letter instead of a payment card. This can happen when: - the EFTPOS network or our internal systems are down - there's a state of emergency or natural disaster - you're unable to use a payment card. When you call us to apply, we'll talk about whether you need this letter.

chunks.title: Getting a Support Person or Job Coach
chunks.text: Job and Training Support Funds can help you pay for a support person or job coach. Find out how you can get someone to help you at work or training. Before you get a support person or job coach, you need to have an assessment done. This will identify the level of support you need. You can request this assessment when you apply for Job or Training Support Funds. You can also email us at support_funds@msd.govt.nz or call us on 0800 551 001.

chunks.title: Choosing a support person or job coach
chunks.text: It's your choice who you would like to be your support person or job coach. They can be someone you know, or a person found through an agency. When you hire a job coach you should talk to your employer before making your choice. This will help you find someone suitable to help with your job. Once you have chosen someone you should discuss with them: - the tasks they will do - their hours and pay rate - signing an agreement between you as confirmation. It's up to you to manage your relationship with your support person or job coach. This includes making sure the support you get meets your needs.

chunks.title: What a support person does
chunks.text: A support person is someone you who will help you at work or during training. This could include a: - reader/writer - New Zealand Sign-language interpreter - driver. You may be able to get funding for more than one support person if they're doing different tasks, e.g. a driver and a New Zealand Sign-language interpreter. You can't get funding for 100% of your working hours. If your support person is driving you, they must have a full New Zealand drivers licence. Your employer or training provider may be a Contracted Supported Employment provider with us. If they are, they may already provide some of the support you would get from a support person. When you apply we'll work with you to understand if you need any extra support on top of this, and if we can cover it.

chunks.title: What a job coach does
chunks.text: A job coach is someone who gives you short-term coaching to help you if: - you start a new job - your job description changes - your job requires new or different skills - your disability changes, which affects your ability to do your normal job. You can get help to pay for a job coach for up to 6 weeks. You can't get help to pay for a job coach if: - your employer already provides employment coaching for you - you're getting help to pay for training through Skills for Industry. When you apply you'll need to tell us how many hours you'll need the job coach for, and what tasks they'll need to do.

chunks.title: What you need to do
chunks.text: You must record and send us the information we need to make sure your support person or job coach gets paid. This information includes: - a supplier registration form - timesheets and invoices. This must be done by you and your support person or job coach.

chunks.title: Supplier registration
chunks.text: Your support person or job coach needs to register as a supplier with us. To do this they must print and fill in a Retailer/Supplier/Payee Details PDF form: Once they've completed the form, they need to scan or take a photo of it and email this to support_funds@msd.govt.nz

chunks.title: Timesheets and invoices
chunks.text: Your support person or job coach must give you a timesheet and invoice every 2 weeks. This shows the hours they have worked. Make sure the invoice is not more than the number of hours we have agreed to fund. You both need to agree to and sign the timesheet. Email the signed timesheet and your invoice to us at support_funds@msd.govt.nz. We will use these to pay the support person or job coach their approved hours on your behalf. There's more information about invoices on Inland Revenue's website: How taxable supply information for GST work (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: Other things you need to do
chunks.text: You and your support person or job coach also need to take care of your other obligations. These includes things like income tax, GST, ACC levies and other legal matters.

chunks.title: Gifts - one-off
chunks.text:
## Gifts - one-off
We don't treat one-off gifts as income but if you earn interest, dividends or rent from the gift, you will need to tell us about it. But if you get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit you do need to tell us about the gift.
## What is this?
A one-off gift of cash, rental property or personal property won't affect your benefit.
## Example
You get some cash and vouchers for your birthday. You usually don't need to tell us about them.
## How it affects your benefit and allowances
You have to tell us about this payment if you:
- get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit
- invest the money you get and earn interest, dividends or rent, this will be counted as income. You can check how your income will affect your benefit using the income deduction tables.
Income deduction tables

chunks.title: Gifts that provide a regular income
chunks.text:
## Gifts that provide a regular income
If you get regular payments from money or assets you've received as a gift you need to let us know. The amount you get will affect your benefit. If you don't tell us we may not pay you enough. Or we may pay you too much and you'll have to pay the debt back.
## Payment details
A one-off gift of cash, rental property or personal property won't affect your benefit. But if you get regular gifts of cash, goods or services then we'll treat this as income and your benefit will be affected.
## Example
You are given $100 a week by a family member to help out with food and bills. As this is a regular payment you need to tell us about it.
If you hold onto the cash gift and you are getting extra help from us, this may be affected. Extra help includes:
- Accommodation Supplement
- Temporary Additional Support
- Special Benefit.
If you invest the money and earn interest, this will be counted as income and you have to tell us about it.
## How to tell us
You need to contact us

chunks.title: Glasses
chunks.text: If you're on a low income or benefit we may be able to help you with the cost of eye tests and glasses. - You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. - You'll have to pay the money back. - You don't have to get a quote before you see us.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get help if you: - are 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services) - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - have an immediate and essential need. Youth Servicesexternal It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have. Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income and asset limits apply:

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: We can pay $280 for: - an eye test - lenses, including: single vision bifocals, or standard progressives - single vision - bifocals, or - standard progressives - frames - prescription sunglasses, if they're part of an in-store special that includes glasses and sunglasses for under $280 - a fitting service - repairs - a cleaning cloth and case - a 2 year warranty on defective parts. You'll have to pay this money back.

chunks.title: What's not included
chunks.text: We don't pay for: - high end, expensive frames - extras you may want, eg tinting - lens coatings or glasses specifically for Irlen Syndrome. You also can't 'top up' or 'up-grade' with your own money so you can obtain costlier items or extras.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us. Phone us We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us.

chunks.title: Choose a supplier
chunks.text: We'll ask you what supplier you want to use. We have an arrangement with certain optometrists and opticians to provide optical services. Here's a list of our preferred suppliers for glasses in your area. You can choose which one to go to. Preferred suppliers for glasses If there's no preferred supplier in your area, we may still be able to help. Talk to us about your situation.

chunks.title: Step 1 - We'll give you a payment card
chunks.text: If your application's approved, we'll give you a payment card (if you don't already have one) and load the money onto it. We'll talk to you about the best way to get this to you. You'll pay the supplier with your payment card (much like an Eftpos card). You have 21 days to spend the money before it expires.

chunks.title: Step 2 - Book an appointment with the supplier
chunks.text: You need to book an appointment with the optometrist or optician that you've chosen. Take your payment card to the appointment. They'll give you an eye examination and then advise you what you'll need. Use your payment card to pay for the frames you choose.

chunks.title: Assessed as having high clinical needs
chunks.text: We may be able to pay more than $280 if the optometrist or optician assesses you as having high clinical needs. If this happens, you need to get evidence of the amount you need to pay and call us. Phone us

chunks.title: Repairs
chunks.text: Your glasses are covered by a 2 year warranty. If they're faulty, contact the optometrist or optician and they will exchange or repair them. If you break your glasses, the optometrist or optician won't replace them or refund money to you. If you need another pair of glasses you'll need to apply for hardship assistance again.

chunks.title: Social Security Agreement with Greece
chunks.text:
## Social Security Agreement with Greece
New Zealand (NZ) has an agreement with Greece to share responsibility for social security coverage.
This agreement generally allows you to apply for certain NZ payments (paid by us) or Greek payments (paid by the Greek Social Security Institute).
NZ payments covered by this agreement are:
- New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super)
- Veteran's Pension
- Supported Living Payment, where you have a health condition, injury or disability
- Sole Parent Support for widows and widowers
- Orphan's Benefit
- Funeral Grant.
Greek payments covered by this agreement are:
- Old Age Benefit
- Invalidity Benefit
- Survivors Benefit
- Funeral Grants.
It also allows you to add together your periods of residence in either country so you can meet certain criteria for these payments.
## Living in Greece
If you've lived in New Zealand and now live in Greece, you may be able to get some payments.
Social Security Agreement with Greece - living in Greece
## Living in New Zealand
If you've lived in Greece and now live in New Zealand, you may be able to get some payments.
Social Security Agreement with Greece - living in New Zealand

chunks.title: Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment
chunks.text: If you're under 20 and in full-time education, training or work-based learning, you may be able to get the Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment (GCAP) to assist with the cost of childcare.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get GCAP if you're: - getting a Young Parent Payment (or 16–19 and included as a partner of a specified beneficiary) Specified beneficiary - in full-time education, training or work-based learning - the main caregiver for a child aged either: under 5, or over 5 if the school has advised they can't start until the beginning of the term straight after their fifth birthday. - under 5, or - over 5 if the school has advised they can't start until the beginning of the term straight after their fifth birthday. Or, if you're not on a benefit, and: - under 18 - attending secondary school full-time - the main caregiver for a child aged either: under 5, or over 5 if the school has advised they can't start until the beginning of the term straight after their fifth birthday - under 5, or - over 5 if the school has advised they can't start until the beginning of the term straight after their fifth birthday - either living with, and supported by your parents or guardian, or married or in a civil union or de facto relationship. If you have a partner, in order to receive GCAP there needs to be a good reason why your partner can’t provide childcare. For example, your partner is studying, working or actively seeking work.

chunks.title: Check if you can get GCAP
chunks.text: To find out if you could get Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment and what else you might qualify for, use our 'Check what you might get' tool.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: GCAP covers the actual childcare service costs, up to $6.38 an hour and up to 50 hours a week for each child and can be paid for the hours you're: - in full-time education, training or work-based learning (including travel time) - working part-time (for up to 15 hours a week) - meeting your youth activity obligations, if you have them (eg attending a parenting course). Young Parent Payment activity obligationsexternal GCAP is usually paid straight to the early childhood centre or service. You can't get both GCAP and the Childcare Subsidy for the same child. GCAP can't be paid for an informal carer. If you need help with the costs of informal childcare, check to see if you can get Flexible Childcare Assistance: Flexible Childcare Assistance

chunks.title: 20 Hours Early Childhood Education
chunks.text: You can only get GCAP for the same hours you're getting 20 Hours Early Childhood Education (ECE) if: - your child is at a home-based educator, and - the home-based educator is charging a top up payment for the same hours as 20 Hours ECE. Home-based educators may charge you a top up payment to cover the difference between their normal hourly rate and the 20 Hours ECE. 20 Hours ECE - Ministry of Educationexternal

chunks.title: Term breaks (including Christmas holidays)
chunks.text: If you are still eligible for GCAP after a term break, it can be paid to ensure your child retains their place at the childcare centre.

chunks.title: Absences
chunks.text: GCAP will continue to be paid (if an absence fee is charged) if you or your child is temporarily sick or away.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: How you apply depends on what payments you’re already getting from us. If you need help, talk to your Youth Service provider if you have one, or contact us. Find a Youth Service providerexternal Contact us We can grant you the financial assistance you’re entitled to from the date you first contact us if you complete your application within 20 working days of that date.

chunks.title: You’re not getting any payments from us
chunks.text: If you're not getting any payments from us, you can either: - apply online through MyMSD, or - fill out a paper application form.

chunks.title: Apply online
chunks.text: You can apply online through MyMSD. We'll also check to see if you can get any other help from us based on the answers you give in your application. Apply online

chunks.title: Fill out paper application form
chunks.text: If you can’t print out the form we can send one to you, or you can complete it when you come in to see us. You can get your application form and supporting documents to us by either: - dropping them in to your nearest service centre - posting them to your nearest service centre, or - uploading them to MyMSD (you'll need to call us first). Find a service centre Types of documents we accept

chunks.title: Already getting payments from us
chunks.text: If you're already getting payments from us, eg, Young Parent Payment, you can complete a paper application form. If you can’t print out the form we can send one to you, or you can complete it when you come in to see us. You can get your application form and supporting documents to us by either: - dropping them in to your nearest service centre - posting them to your nearest service centre, or - uploading them to MyMSD (you'll need to call us first). Find a service centre Types of documents we accept

chunks.title: Contact
chunks.text: This information is a guide only. Contact your Youth Service provider if you have one, otherwise contact us to talk about your individual circumstances. - Youth Service provider (MSD) external - Phone us

chunks.title: Social Security Agreement with Guernsey
chunks.text:
## Social Security Agreement with Guernsey
New Zealand (NZ) has an agreement with Guernsey to share responsibility for social security coverage.
This agreement generally allows you to apply for certain NZ payments (paid by us) or Guernsey payments (paid by the Guernsey Social Security Department).
NZ payments covered by this agreement are:
- New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super)
- Veteran's Pension
- Supported Living Payment, where you have a health condition, injury or disability
- Sole Parent Support for widows and widowers.
Guernsey payments covered by this agreement are:
- Old Age Pension
- Sickness Benefit
- Bereavement Allowance (formerly Widow's Benefit)
- Industrial Injury Benefit
- Industrial Disablement Benefit
- Invalidity Benefit.
It also allows you to add together your periods of residence in either country so you can meet certain criteria for these payments.
## Living in Guernsey
If you've lived in New Zealand and now live in Guernsey, you may be able to get some payments.
Social Security Agreement with Guernsey - living in Guernsey
## Living in New Zealand

## Having another child
If you have another child or another child comes into your care, you must tell us as soon as possible as it could affect how much we pay for your childcare

chunks.title: Having a baby
chunks.text: We may be able to help during your pregnancy and after your baby is born.

chunks.title: Pregnant
chunks.text: Go online with SmartStart and get step-by-step information and support to help you access the right services for you and your baby. SmartStartexternal If you're pregnant, it's important that you get a midwife and access maternity services. Talk to your doctor, or the local hospital maternity services, to find out what's available in your area.

chunks.title: Getting a benefit
chunks.text: If you're pregnant and getting a benefit, you may have a change in obligations. Having a baby while you're on a benefit

chunks.title: Unable to work
chunks.text: You may be able to get Jobseeker Support if your health practitioner (eg, your midwife or doctor) says you're unable to work because of your pregnancy. You'll need a medical certificate from your health practitioner. Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: Getting a benefit
chunks.text: Having a baby while you're on a benefit If you're having a baby and getting a benefit, you may have a change in obligations or your payments could be affected. There are also other types of support that you may be able to get.

chunks.title: Working for families
chunks.text: Best Start tax credit (BSTC) is a payment to help families with costs in a child's first 3 years. If you're getting a Work and Income benefit, we'll pay you the Best Start tax credit with your payments. You'll need to apply through Inland Revenue (IR) if you don't get a benefit from Work and Income. It is also available to caregivers getting either: - Orphan's Benefit - Unsupported Child's Benefit, or - Foster Care Allowance. Eligibility and how to apply for the Best Start tax credit (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: Paid parental leave
chunks.text: If you're getting paid parental leave, you can't get the Best Start tax credit until your paid parental leave ends.

chunks.title: Helping with living costs
chunks.text: Help with living expenses If you're struggling financially or have had an unexpected bill, we might be able to help you, even if you're working.

chunks.title: Help with costs for the baby
chunks.text: We may be able to help with costs for the baby if it's an essential or emergency cost you can't pay for another way, eg: - car seats - cots - buggies - clothes. Advance Payment of Benefit If you're getting a benefit, we may be able to help with an advance payment. Recoverable Assistance Payment If you're not getting a benefit, we may be able to help with a recoverable payment.

chunks.title: Breast pumps
chunks.text: Special Needs Grant Help with a breast pump if you can't breastfeed because you or your baby have health issues. Finding or starting work – help with costs Help with a breast pump if you can't breastfeed because you're returning to work. Disability Allowance Help with a breast pump if you or your baby have an ongoing disability.

chunks.title: Sole parent support
chunks.text: Sole Parent Support You might be able to get Sole Parent Support, a payment that will help you get ready for future work and supports you to find part or full-time work.

chunks.title: Teen parent
chunks.text: Young Parent Payment If you're 16-19, you might be able to get a Young Parent Payment from us.

chunks.title: Multiple birth - Need help
chunks.text: Home Help We may be able to help you with the cost of home help when you've had a multiple birth.

chunks.title: Your baby is sick and needs ongoing medical care
chunks.text: Caring for a child with a health condition or disability If you need additional help with medical expenses we may be able to help.

chunks.title: Having a baby while you're on a benefit
chunks.text: If you're having a baby while you're on a benefit, you need to let us know as it could affect your payments and whether you need to look for work.

chunks.title: Unable to work
chunks.text: You may be getting a benefit that requires you to look for work. If your health practitioner, eg, your doctor or midwife, says you're unable to work because of your pregnancy, we may be able to help. We'll need to see a medical certificate from your health practitioner. Some health practitioners send us medical certificates electronically. If you already have a Work and Income client number, make sure they include that on the certificate. If they don't send your medical certificate electronically, or you want to send something else as proof, call us to talk about how to get this information to us. Phone us

chunks.title: 27 weeks pregnant
chunks.text: You may be getting a benefit that requires you to look for work. You don't have to meet this requirement if you're at least 27 weeks pregnant. We'll need to see proof of your child's expected date of birth (eg. a medical certificate). Your health practitioner or midwife can complete a medical certificate for you. Most health practitioners send us medical certificates electronically. If you already have a Work and Income client number, make sure they include that on the certificate. If they don't send your medical certificate electronically, or you want to send something else as proof, call us to talk about how to get this information to us. Phone us

chunks.title: Tell us once you have the baby
chunks.text: If you've had a baby you need to tell us right away. You may also need to apply for child support. We'll talk to you about this when you come to see us. To tell us you can either: - Register the birth with SmartStartwhen you register your child's birth with Department of Internal Affairs (DIA), using SmartStart, agree to share this information with the Ministry of Social Development (MSD). You won't have to purchase a physical birth certificate. SmartStartexternal We'll then: - work out if the change affects what you're getting from us - send you a letter to let you know the outcome. If you need to do anything else, we'll book a phone appointment for you and include the details in your letter. or - Call us to book an appointmentYou need to call us on 0800 559 009. We'll let you know what information we'll need from you.

chunks.title: Having another child and your work obligations
chunks.text: If you're on a benefit which requires you to look or prepare for work and you have a child, you will be expected to prepare for work until your youngest child turns 3 years old. If your youngest child is: - between 3 and 13, you'll be expected to actively seek part-time work of at least 20 hours a week and accept any suitable job - 14 or older, you'll be expected to actively seek full-time work of at least 30 hours a week and accept any suitable job.

chunks.title: Helping you get back into work
chunks.text: We can help you access training and a range of other support to help you get ready to move into work. You may be able to get assistance with the cost of childcare while you're working, attending training or doing some other activity that will help you move into work. The Childcare Subsidy is for preschool children and the Out of School Care and Recreation (OSCAR) Subsidy is for before and after school care and holiday programmes for children aged 5-13. For more information, read: Childcare Work This information is a guide only. Contact us to talk about your individual circumstances. Phone us

chunks.title: A child has come into your care
chunks.text: If a child has come into your care, you need to let us know as it could affect your payments and whether you need to look for work. A child enters or leaves your care

chunks.title: Having someone act on your behalf
chunks.text: You can choose to have someone else act on your behalf in your dealings with us. We call them an agent. You may be able to verbally agree to have an agent for one meeting, or you can fill out a form to have an agent for longer. In most cases, we'll only let someone represent you if you agree to it. Agents must always act in the best interests of the person they represent and treat our staff respectfully.

chunks.title: Why have an agent
chunks.text: You can have an agent for any reason. This may be because: - you're overseas - you have mobility issues that makes it physically hard to go to our offices - you're sick or unwell - you're living in residential care or an institution - you want help or advice with a decision we've made - you've been served a trespass notice which says you cannot enter our offices. If you're having difficulty communicating in English, you can talk to us in another language using our free translation services. You can still use these services with or without appointing an agent. We speak other languages

chunks.title: Who can be your agent
chunks.text: Your agent can be a person or an organisation. They generally need to be 18 or older. They may be able to be an agent if they're under 18, e.g. if they're your partner. You can give your agent a lot of power over your affairs. You can also give them a lot of access to your personal information. It is important to be careful who you choose as an agent and what you allow them to do. Your agent should be someone you trust. They can be someone like: - a family member - a person or an organisation that cares for you (but not your Youth Service provider if you have one) - a lawyer - an advocate.

chunks.title: How to find an advocate
chunks.text: There are advocate groups who may be able to help you with an independent advocate who has experience in dealing with us. A good advocate can: - help you if you don't understand or disagree with a decision we made - work with us to make sure you get all the support you're entitled to - help explain your situation in meetings with us or in a review or appeal process. You can find an advocate through the Citizens Advice Bureau or Community Law. Citizens Advice Bureauexternal Community Lawexternal

chunks.title: When an agent is appointed for you
chunks.text: There may be cases where an agent is appointed for you, for example: - a court may appoint someone as your agent. The court will state what rights and responsibilities they have. - if someone has your power of attorney or enduring power of attorney. If the court has appointed someone to help you, usually you cannot change or cancel their authorisation. Only the court can do that. You can change or cancel someone's power of attorney but not someone's enduring power of attorney. In exceptional circumstances, we may allow someone to act as your agent without any legal document. For example this might be if you're in a coma and need help from us and there isn't time to get a court order. We would normally need proof that you cannot act for yourself temporarily, e.g. a medical certificate.

chunks.title: What your agent can do
chunks.text: You're responsible for deciding what your agent can and cannot do. You can allow your agent to do things like: - get personal information we hold about you - tell us information on your behalf, e.g. change of address or income - get your mail from us - complete and sign application forms on your behalf - have authority over your affairs, as granted by a current Power of Attorney - be paid part or all of your benefit on your behalf if there's a good reason, e.g. you're sick or unwell and cannot physically withdraw money or manage your finances you're living in residential care or an institution you're misusing your benefit payment and the wellbeing of your family is put at risk. - you're sick or unwell and cannot physically withdraw money or manage your finances - you're living in residential care or an institution - you're misusing your benefit payment and the wellbeing of your family is put at risk. You can have more than one agent and they can do different things. For example, you may have: - a family member who fills in forms for you, and - an advocate who represents you in a dispute with us. Agents cannot access or use your MyMSD account. You can still talk to us and act for yourself when you have an agent. You can choose to remove your agent or change what they're allowed to do at any time.

chunks.title: Court Order or Power of Attorney
chunks.text: If your agent has been appointed by a court order, the court determines what they can and cannot do on your behalf. If your agent holds an Enduring Power of Attorney, they will have authority over your affairs.

chunks.title: How to appoint an agent
chunks.text: You can verbally agree for someone to act on your behalf when you meet with us or call us, which will only last for that meeting. If you want someone to be your agent for longer, you'll need to fill out an 'Appointment of Agent' form. You can use the form below or you can have one sent to you by calling 0800 559 009. This will: - name you and your agent - show exactly what rights and responsibilities you want your agent to have - be signed by both you and your agent. Please complete this form if you would like an agent to act on your behalf. You or your agent can bring the completed form into a service centre. You can just drop it off, you don't need an appointment. Your agent needs to bring their original government-issued identity document (ID) with them. Find a service centre If you or your agent can’t bring the form into a service centre, call us to find out how to get it to us. Phone us If this is your first time applying for a benefit or ongoing payment, you or your agent needs to bring your original government-issued ID into a service centre so we can check it. Checking ID in person helps us make sure we give support to the right person and protect your identity. Types of documents we accept

chunks.title: Paying your benefit to an agent
chunks.text: If you want your payments to go to your agent, you'll also need to fill in a 'Redirection of benefit payment' form with them. - why you need your payments to go to your agent - what other ways you've tried to organise your payments - how much of your payments you want to go to your agent. Your agent will need to show us proof of their bank account details, e.g. a bank statement or a deposit slip. chunks.title: Stopping work because of health condition or disability
chunks.text:
## Stopping work because of health condition or disability
If you have to stop work because of a health condition, injury or disability we may be able to help you.
## Talk to your health practitioner
You'll need a medical certificate from your health practitioner, eg your doctor, to tell us how your health condition or disability affects your ability to work.
Some health practitioners send us medical certificates electronically. If you already have a Work and Income client number, make sure they include that on the certificate.
If your health practitioner doesn't send your medical certificate electronically, you'll need to send it to us.
## Have to stop work for a while or reduce hours
You have a health condition or disability that affects your ability to work. This means that you have to reduce your hours or stop work for a while. We may still be able to help if you have a job to go back to.
Jobseeker Support
## Sole parent
You're a sole parent with children under 14 and have a health condition or disability that affects your ability to work.
Sole Parent Support
## Permanently unable to work
You're permanently and severely restricted in your ability to work because of a health condition, injury or disability, or are legally blind.
Supported Living Payment
## You've had to stop work and your partner is working
You're down to one wage and you need help to pay day-to-day expenses while you look for work.
## Working and have no sick leave or paid leave
You're not on a benefit anymore and you can't work because of sickness or a breakdown in childcare arrangements. You don't have any sick leave or paid leave available.
New Employment Transition Grant
You can't work for a while because you have a health condition or disability which affects your ability to work, and you have no sick pay available.
Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: Power, gas, water bills or heating
chunks.text: We may be able to help you with an urgent power, gas or water bill, heating costs or water tank refill if you have no other way to pay. - You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. - You may have to pay the money back depending on your situation.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You could find yourself in a situation where you have an outstanding power, gas or water bill that you can't pay. You need to talk to the power or water company first to see if you can make a payment arrangement with them. If this is not possible, we may be able to help if you: - are 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services) - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - have an immediate and essential need. Youth Servicesexternal It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have. Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income and asset limits apply:

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Generally, we can pay up to $200 to help with: - an outstanding power, gas or water bill - reconnecting your electricity, gas or water supply.

chunks.title: Water tank refill
chunks.text: We may be able to help you pay to get your personal water tank refilled and delivered. You need to be living in either: - a property you own - a property you're renting and you're responsible for refilling the water tank. You can get up to $500 to pay for refill and delivery. You can generally get one payment for water tank refill every 12 months.

## Help to get a driver licence
Need help to get your driver licence? We can help you get the support you need.

We'll talk to you about getting your licence, and we'll check what help is available.

If you're not a client with us, use the Family Services Directory to find a provider near you, and contact them about help to get your driver licence:

chunks.title: Holiday and Birthday Allowance
chunks.text:
## Holiday and Birthday Allowance
You automatically get the Holiday and Birthday Allowance if you already get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit. Use these payments to celebrate important events in the child’s life, like their birthday or Christmas.
If you get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit for a child you’re caring for, use the Holiday and Birthday Allowance to help pay for the costs of making the child feel special.
Celebrating important events in a child’s life helps them feel valued, part of the family and more secure and happy. Being the centre of an enjoyable event helps the child’s emotional and mental health.
You get this payment two times each year. If you don’t celebrate birthdays or Christmas, use the money to do something fun that makes the child feel special.
Holiday and Birthday Allowance payments don’t:
- affect other payments you may get from us
- count as income for tax purposes.
## Who can get it
You automatically get the Birthday and Holiday Allowance if you get Unsupported Child’s Benefit or Orphan’s Benefit.
## How much you get
How much money you get depends on the age of the child you're looking after.
You don't have to let us know when the child's age changes. We update the payment automatically.
## How to apply
You don't need to apply for the Holiday and Birthday Allowance. You get this payment automatically when you get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit.
## How you’re paid
We pay you the Holiday and Birthday Allowance with your Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit.
Each year, you get the:
- Birthday Allowance around 2 weeks before the child’s birthday
- Holiday Allowance around 2 weeks before 25 December.
When you stop getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit, the allowance also stops.

## Home equity conversion scheme lump sum
Lump sum payments from a home equity conversion scheme don't need to be declared as income. But if you get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit you do need to tell us about it.
## What is this?
A one-off payment (also known as a reverse mortgage) that lets you borrow against your home to pay for major expenses, for example:
- a new car
- house repairs or maintenance
- a holiday
- a medical operation.
## How it affects your benefit and allowances
You have to tell us about this payment if you:
- get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit
- invest the money you get and earn interest, this will be counted as income
- don't use the payment for major expenses, but everyday goods and services
- get regular home equity conversion payments.

chunks.title: Home Help
chunks.text:
## Home Help
If you're a parent or carer we may be able to help you with the cost of home help to complete household tasks or training in parenting skills.
## Who can get it
You may get Home Help if:
- you're either a: New Zealand citizen permanent resident
- New Zealand citizen
- permanent resident
- you normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here
- you either have a multiple birth from the same pregnancy adopt 2 or more children from the same pregnancy have a domestic emergency (a sudden change of circumstances that creates a crisis situation) need domestic support.
- have a multiple birth from the same pregnancy
- adopt 2 or more children from the same pregnancy
- have a domestic emergency (a sudden change of circumstances that creates a crisis situation)
- need domestic support.
If you have or adopt twins, you must already have another child under 5.
## Domestic emergencies and Home Help
You can get Home Help for a domestic emergency, but you must have:
- no immediate family or anyone else living with you who can help
- a current Community Services Card, or your partner must have one.
Domestic emergency Home Help is also based on any money or assets you and your partner have.
## How much you can get
This depends on your current circumstances.
View our maximum current hourly rates (Map)external
## How to apply
You need to call us on 0800 559 009.
We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us.
We'll ask you to complete a 'Home Help Payments' form and discuss the best way to get this to us.
## What happens next
If your application's approved, you and your home helper need to complete a timesheet for each week you get the home help.
There's a section on the timesheet for you to fill in and a section for your home helper to fill in. Both of you will need to sign and date the timesheet.
Call us to talk about the best way to get the completed timesheet to us.
Phone us

chunks.title: Payments may be affected
chunks.text: Your benefit or payment will keep being paid for the first 13 weeks you're in hospital. Then your payments will change to our hospital rate of $58.34 a week (after tax), unless you either: - have a partner and a child, or - are a veteran. The hospital rate covers the cost of personal items you need to get while you're in hospital.

chunks.title: Get Supported Living Payment
chunks.text: You may get the Supported Living Payment because you're caring for someone. If you, or the person you're caring for, is in hospital, your benefit will keep being paid for the first 4 weeks. Then it will stop. If you're in hospital for longer than 4 weeks, we'll need to check if there are other payments you could qualify for.

chunks.title: You have a partner and no child
chunks.text: Once you get the hospital rate, we'll review any benefit or payment your partner gets from us. This is so we can make sure they're getting all the help they qualify for while you're in hospital. They may also be able to get a Special Disability Allowance to help cover the costs of visiting you in hospital. If they qualify for this, we'll pay it to them automatically once you start getting the hospital rate.

chunks.title: Hospital rate won't cover costs
chunks.text: If the hospital rate isn't enough to cover your costs, we may be able to pay more. This will depend on what expenses and income you have while you're in hospital.

chunks.title: What you need to do
chunks.text: You need to fill out an 'Increased payment while you're in hospital' form. You can drop it off to one of our service centres, or post it to us. Find a service centre If you can't download and print the form, ask the hospital. They may have some on site. The hospital staff may also be able to help you fill it out and send it.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: Once we've processed your form, we'll send you a letter and give you a call to let you know if it's approved.

chunks.title: Home repairs and maintenance
chunks.text:
## Home repairs and maintenance
If you need money for essential repairs or maintenance for your home and you're on a benefit, we may be able to help.
You may have to pay the money back depending on your situation.
## Who can get it
You may be able to get help if:
- you’re receiving a benefit, pension or NZ Superannuation
- you have an immediate and essential need
- the repairs or maintenance are needed to keep your home to a reasonable living standard
- you’ve been to your bank or another provider but they weren’t able to help you.
It also depends on:
- how much you and your partner earn
- any money or assets you and your partner have.
Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income and asset limits usually apply:
## Not on a benefit
If you’re not on a benefit and need help urgently, e.g., with a sewage treatment system, we may still be able to help. Call us on 0800 559 009 to discuss your situation.
## What you can get
Generally you can get up to $1,000 depending on your situation.
## What you get it for
You can get help with essential repairs and maintenance for your home, e.g.:
- roof
- hot water cylinder
- paths
- fences
- retaining walls.
You may also be able to get help with essential services such as:
- sewerage (e.g., sinks, toilet, shower, drains)
- water
- electricity connection.
## How to apply
Call us to book an appointment with us.
Our phone numbers
During your appointment, we’ll need to understand your situation and how we can help, and let you know what information you need to provide. This will include:
- evidence that you own your home (or have joint ownership)
- evidence that you live in your home
- evidence that you went to your bank or another provider for help but your application was unsuccessful
- evidence of the costs you're applying for, e.g., quotes or a link to a cost on the supplier's website. You'll need to check with the store or supplier to see if they can accept our payment.

chunks.text: If you're renting, it's the landlord’s responsibility to repair and maintain the house. So, if something breaks down or goes wrong, tell the landlord straight away. chunks.title: How board and rent affect your payments
chunks.text: You need to tell us if you're getting board or rent payments or paying board or rent to someone else. Board or rent payments you get may affect how much help you get for accommodation costs, how much Income Related Rent you pay, and they may count as income. You need to tell us about any board and rent payments you get or pay. This is part of meeting your obligations when you get payments from us. Your obligations while getting payments from us

chunks.title: What is board
chunks.text: A boarder is someone who pays for accommodation and food in another person's home, and their food costs can't be easily separated out from the amount they pay. Their board payment may also cover other service costs, e.g. internet or power. If you're living in public housing, and the person living with you is not on the tenancy agreement, they will be considered a boarder. If you're getting payments from a boarder, it can affect: - any housing subsidies (e.g. Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support) for your own accommodation costs - how much Income Related Rent you pay if you're living in public housing - income-tested payments from us in some cases. If you're paying board to someone, we will ask for details of who you're paying this to and how much. If you're flatting, and all household members share the responsibility to cover the accommodation cost for the property, you do not need to declare your flatmates as boarders or renters. The amount you pay as a flatmate is usually considered rent.

chunks.title: What is rent
chunks.text: A renter is someone whose accommodation costs cover the room or property they stay in. This may also include service costs (e.g. gardening). If you're getting payments from a renter, it can affect: - any housing subsidies you get (e.g. Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support) for your own accommodation costs - any income-tested payments from us in some cases. If you're paying rent to someone, we will ask for details of who you're paying this to and how much. If you're flatting, and all household members share the responsibility to cover the accommodation cost for the property, you do not need to declare your flatmates as boarders or renters. The amount you pay as a flatmate is usually considered rent.

chunks.title: How board or rent affects housing subsidies
chunks.text: Housing subsidies include: - Accommodation Supplement - Temporary Additional Support and Special Benefit - Away from Home Allowance. How much housing subsidy you can get depends on how much your accommodation costs are.

chunks.title: How board affects housing subsidies
chunks.text: If you're getting board payments, some of those payments will already cover part of your accommodation costs. To work out how much your accommodation costs are, we: - look at how much board you are paid - work out 62% of this, which is the accommodation portion of the board (the other 38% is for food and other services) - reduce your accommodation costs by that amount. Your total accommodation costs are used to work out how much housing subsidy we will pay you.

chunks.title: How rent affects housing subsidies
chunks.text: How much housing subsidy you can get depends on how much your accommodation costs are and whether you live in the same property as your renter. If you're getting rent payments for part of the same property you live in, those payments will not be included in your personal accommodation costs. This includes when you rent out: - a self-contained portion of the property (e.g. granny flat), - non-accommodation rentals (e.g. garage being used as storage). For these types of rent payments, we work out the portion/percentage of the property you live in, not including the area used by someone else. The non-accommodation rental payments are treated as income, but will not affect your accommodation costs for a housing subsidy. If you're paid rent by someone who doesn't live with you (e.g. they live in a separate property), we treat the whole payment you get from them as income, but it will not affect your accommodation costs for a housing subsidy. To work out how much your accommodation costs are, we: - look at how much rent you are paid - reduce your accommodation costs by the full rent payment amount. If you rent out a self-contained portion of your home, we work out your personal accommodation costs based on the portion/percentage of the property you live in - this does not include the area used by someone else.

chunks.title: How board affects Income Related Rent
chunks.text: If you live in public housing, Income Related Rent is the amount of rent you pay. When we calculate your Income Related Rent, we add on 62% of any board payments you get. If you're living in public housing, and the person living with you is not on the tenancy agreement, they will always be considered a boarder. You can read about the full calculation here: Calculating your rent payments This change took effect on 2 March 2026. This means 62% of the board payments will be added to your Income Related Rent rate from: - your next annual rent review, or - when you next tell us about a change in circumstances.

chunks.title: How board and rent payments affect income-tested payments
chunks.text: The money you get from board or rent can affect other payments you get from us, so you need to tell us if you're getting board or rent payments. Not all the money you get from board or rent payments counts as income – only the amount that is more than either: - your accommodation costs, or - the market rent for your home if you're living in public housing, or - the full amount of the rent payment if they don't live on the same property as you. To work out how much of your board or rent payments count as income, we: - calculate how much of the payment we need to count – for board this is 62%, and for rent 100% - then we compare this amount to your accommodation costs, or market rent if you're in public housing. If this amount is higher than your accommodation costs or market rent, we work out the difference – that difference counts as income. If this amount is lower than your accommodation costs or market rent, your board or rent payments do not count as income. You can check how your income will affect your benefit using the income deduction tables: Income deduction tables

chunks.title: How to tell us you're getting board or rent payments
chunks.text: The easiest way to tell us is online in MyMSD. Once you’ve logged in, select 'Declare boarders and renters'. You need to tell us: - the address - details of the person paying you board or rent - how much the board or rent is - when you get paid, and how often. We will continue to use this amount every week, so make sure you let us know if it stops or changes. If you can't use MyMSD, you can also fill out our PDF form: You need to print this form, complete it, and either post it to us or bring it into one of our services centres. You can also pick one up from any of our service centres. Find a service centre

chunks.title: Checking your board or rent details
chunks.text: When people tell us about their accommodation costs, we ask them: - if they pay board or rent, or get paid board or rent - who they pay it to, or are paid by - how much and how often those payments are. If both the boarder/renter and the person they pay board or rent to (e.g. their landlord or the head tenant) are getting either a housing subsidy or are living in public housing, we need to independently check this information with each of them. If it doesn't match, we need to contact both these people to get the correct details. This is part of meeting their obligations. We'll try calling them first. If we can't contact them by phone, we'll send them a letter giving them 10 working days to confirm the correct details. We'll also send them a MyMSD notification, where they can confirm the details. - If they don't confirm or still don't agree, after the 10 working days: - if they get a housing subsidy, this will stop on day 11 - if they are a public housing tenant, we will notify the housing provider and their rent may go up to market rent.

chunks.title: How income affects your payments
chunks.text: Getting a job doesn't always mean your payments will stop. We're still here to help even when you're working. Your payments may be able to continue, and there may be other ways we can help out too.

chunks.title: Let us know you’re starting a job
chunks.text: Starting a new job is a great achievement, but it can be scary. We want to help you as much as we can, and make it easy for you to get off to a great start. Get in touch with us before you start your new job. We'll sort out your payments from us and make sure you're getting everything you're entitled to. We'll also check if there's anything else we can do to help while you're starting out. Call us on 0800 559 009 before you start your new job.

chunks.title: How much you can earn
chunks.text: You may be able to keep getting your benefit or payment even if you're working. This depends on: - which benefit or payment you're getting, and - how much you get paid for your job. Our income deduction tables show how much income you can get before your benefit is affected: Income deduction tables

chunks.title: Declare your income while you’re working
chunks.text: If you're getting payments from us while you're working, you need to declare your income so we can pay you the correct amount. We need to know by Friday 6pm the week you earn the money (not the week you've been paid). If you're working the weekend, include the hours you think you’ll work. You can change it later if your hours change. If your income and hours are the same every week, you only need to tell us once. The amount you declare will continue every week until you let us know it has stopped or changed. The easiest way to tell us your income is through MyMSD: Find out more about declaring wages, how to do this, and what happens after you've declared them: Wages

chunks.title: If you can't use MyMSD
chunks.text: If you can't use MyMSD you can call us or come into one of our service centres. If you’re declaring income from self-employment, make sure you mention you're self-employed. Phone usFind a service centre

chunks.title: Help while you're working
chunks.text: As well as checking whether your existing payments can continue, we may also be able to help with: - paying for work costs like training or equipment - managing your money - budgeting - managing your debt with us.

chunks.title: How much you can get for NZ Super
chunks.text: New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super) is paid fortnightly on a Tuesday. How much you get depends on your situation and what tax code you use. Payment rates may be different if: - you live overseas, or - your partner is included in your payment. You live overseas Your partner is included in your payment If you get an overseas pension, this could affect your NZ Super payments. Talk to us about how this could affect your payments. Overseas pensions Phone us If you or your partner get other income as well as NZ Super, it may change the tax code you use. This means you could get less for your NZ Super payments, it depends what tax code you're on.

chunks.title: Increases to NZ Super
chunks.text: NZ Super rates increase every year on 1 April to adjust to changes in the average wage. Any information about this increase, or any other changes to our payment rates, will always be communicated here on the Work and Income website.

chunks.title: Your tax code
chunks.text: NZ Super is a taxable payment. The amount of tax you pay depends on the tax code you use. If you only get NZ Super, your tax code will probably be 'M'. If you get other income as well, it may be a different tax code. If you need help working out what tax code you should use, go to the Inland Revenue website to look at what tax code you should use. What tax code should I use? (Inland Revenue)external If you've changed your tax code, you need to let us know. You can do this by filling out our 'Change tax code' form online. Change of tax code form

chunks.title: Payment rate if you're single
chunks.text: How much you get depends on your living situation and what tax code you use. Payments are fortnightly. Live alone or with a dependent child Live with someone who's either: - 18 or older (unless they're a dependent child who's 18), or - visiting and staying more than 13 weeks in any 26 week period. Definition of dependent child

chunks.title: Payment rate if you have a partner
chunks.text: How much you get depends on who meets the criteria for NZ Super and what tax code you use. Payments are fortnightly. Both you and your partner meet the criteria for NZ Super If you don't see your situation in the table, there are non-standard rates under the heading 'NZ Super and Veteran's Pension' on our page: Benefit rates at 1 April 2026

chunks.title: How much you can get for Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: Veteran's Pension is paid fortnightly on a Tuesday. How much you get depends on your situation and what tax code you use. Payment rates may be different if: - you get other income - you live overseas, or - your partner is included in your payment. If you get an overseas pension this could affect your Veteran's Pension payments. Talk to us about how this could affect your payments. Phone us

chunks.title: Increases to Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: Veteran's Pension rates increase every year on 1 April to adjust to changes in the average wage. Any information about this increase, or any other changes to our payment rates, will always be communicated here on the Work and Income website.

chunks.title: Your tax code
chunks.text: Veteran's Pension is a taxable payment. The amount of tax you pay depends on the tax code you use. If you only get Veteran's Pension, your tax code will probably be 'M'. If you get other income as well, it may be a different tax code. If you need help working out what tax code you should use, go to the Inland Revenue website to look at what tax code you should use. What tax code should I use?external If you've changed your tax code, you need to let us know. You can do this by filling out our 'Change tax code' form online. Change your tax code

chunks.title: Payment rate if you're single
chunks.text: How much you get depends on your living situation and what tax code you use. Payments are fortnightly. Live with someone who's either: - 18 or older (unless they're a dependent child who's 18), or - visiting and staying more than 13 weeks in any 26 week period. Definition of dependent child

chunks.title: Payment rate if you have a partner
chunks.text: How much you get depends on who meets the criteria for Veteran's Pension and what tax code you use. Payments are fortnightly. Who can get Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: If you get other income
chunks.text: If you get other income, it will affect your Veteran's Pension payments if: - you're under 65 - you were getting a Veteran's Pension on 7 December 2014, when the War Pensions Act 1954 was replaced by the Veterans' Support Act 2014, and - you've chosen to get Veteran's Pension instead of weekly income compensation from Veteran's Affairs. Other income will also affect your Veteran's Pension when: - you're 65 or older, and - you have included your partner in your Veteran's Pension payments.

chunks.title: How other income will affect your payment
chunks.text: You and your partner can earn up to $160 a week (before tax) in total before it affects your payment.

chunks.title: Then, if you're under 65
chunks.text: Once you and your partner earn over $160 (before tax) a week: - any income you get between $160 and $250 a week (before tax) will reduce your payment by 30 cents for each $1 of income - any income you get over $250 a week (before tax) will reduce your payment by 70 cents for every $1 of income.

chunks.title: Or, if you're 65 or older
chunks.text: Once you and your partner earn over $160 (before tax), your payment reduces by 70 cents for every extra $1 of income you earn.

chunks.title: How payments work
chunks.text: Information about when your payments start, pay days and when you get your first and last payment.

chunks.title: When your payments start
chunks.text: If you've applied for a benefit, you may have a stand-down of 1 or 2 weeks. Your payments will start after your stand-down finishes. If you've been working recently, your payments may take longer to start. Stand-down periods

chunks.title: You've been working recently
chunks.text: Your payments can take up to 3 months (13 weeks) to start if you've recently been in work and: - left your job without a good reason, or - lost your job because of misconduct

chunks.title: Other payments you get from work
chunks.text: You may get other payments from work, eg: - holiday pay - sick pay - pay in lieu of notice - retirement payments If you get one of these, your payments from us will start once they're finished. For example, you get 3 weeks worth of holiday pay. This means your payments from us will start 3 weeks after your stand-down finishes.

chunks.title: Redundancy pay
chunks.text: If you’re made redundant and get redundancy pay, you’ll have a stand-down of 1 or 2 weeks. It depends how much your redundancy pay is. The stand-down period for redundancy pay has changed over time. If you’ve had a redundancy payment, you can ask us to check if we treated this correctly when working out your stand-down period.

chunks.title: Weekly payments
chunks.text: Once your payments start, you won't get any money in the first week. This is because we pay you for the week that's just been. This means you're on a benefit for one week and get paid for that benefit in the next week. This is also called arrears. For example: - Your payments start on Monday - you won't get any money in this week - Your first weekly payment is paid in the next week, on your pay day

chunks.title: Approved part-way through the week
chunks.text: If your payments start part-way through the week, your first payment will be less than what you would normally get. For example: - Your payments start on Wednesday - Your first weekly payment: is paid in the next week, on your pay day, and will be for 5 days (Wednesday - Sunday). - is paid in the next week, on your pay day, and - will be for 5 days (Wednesday - Sunday).

chunks.title: NZ Super and Veteran's payments
chunks.text: New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension are paid every fortnight on a Tuesday. These are set pay dates. NZ Super payment dates Once your payments start, you'll get your first payment of NZ Super or Veteran's Pension on the next set pay date. In most cases if you apply: - before your 65th birthday, your payments will start from your birthday - after your 65th birthday, your payments will start from the date you apply. These payments are paid in arrears, so it includes the previous 13 days and the pay day. For example, the pay day Tuesday 25 June will cover the period from Wednesday 12 June to (and including) Tuesday 25 June. If your payments start part-way through the pay period, your first payment will be less than what you would normally get. Examples Your application is approved on Friday 12 January 2018, your first payment: - is paid on Tuesday 23 January - will be for 12 days (Friday 12 January - Tuesday 23 January). Your application is approved on Friday 26 October 2018, your first payment: - is paid on Tuesday 30 October - will be for 5 days (Friday 26 October - Tuesday 30 October)

chunks.title: Child Disability Allowance
chunks.text: Child Disability Allowance is paid every fortnight on a Tuesday. These are set pay dates (the opposite fortnights to NZ Super and Veteran's Pension payments). Once your application is approved, you'll get your first payment of Child Disability Allowance on the next set pay date. If your application is approved part-way through the pay period, your first payment will be less than what you would normally get.

chunks.title: Weekly payments
chunks.text: Most benefits and payments are paid weekly. If you get a weekly payment, your official pay day is either: - Tuesday - Wednesday, or - Thursday Once you have a pay day, it will never change. Even if you get another benefit or payment from us later on. You might see your payment in your account the night before, it depends on who you bank with.

chunks.title: Fortnightly payments
chunks.text: There are 3 payments that are paid fortnightly. These are: - New Zealand Superannuation - Veteran's Pension - Child Disability Allowance New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension are paid every fortnight on a Tuesday. If you get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, most other payments you get from us, eg Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance, will also be paid fortnightly. Child Disability Allowance is paid every fortnight on a Tuesday (the opposite fortnight to NZ Super and Veteran's Pension). You might see your payment in your account the night before, it depends on who you bank with. NZ Super payment dates

chunks.title: Find out your pay day
chunks.text: Once your application is approved, we'll send you a letter letting you know the date of your first payment. You can also check what your pay day is in MyMSD. Find out more about MyMSD

chunks.title: Weekly payments
chunks.text: If your benefit or payment stops, you'll get your last payment a week after the date it stops. This is because we pay you for the week that's just been. This means you're on a benefit for one week and get paid for that benefit in the next week. This is also called arrears.

chunks.title: Stops part-way through the week
chunks.text: If your benefit or payment stops part-way through the week, your last payment will be less than what you would normally get. For example: - Your benefit stops on Wednesday - Your last weekly payment: is paid in the next week, on your pay day, and will be for 2 days (Monday - Tuesday) - is paid in the next week, on your pay day, and - will be for 2 days (Monday - Tuesday)

chunks.title: Pay days on public holidays
chunks.text: Sometimes your regular pay day will fall on a public holiday. When this happens, we'll always make sure you get your payments either the day before or on your regular pay day. For example, if you're usually paid on Wednesdays, and Wednesday is a public holiday, your payment will be available from Tuesday.

chunks.title: Regional anniversary holidays
chunks.text: If your regular pay day falls on a regional anniversary (eg Wellington or Auckland anniversary), you will still be paid on your usual pay day. This is because pay dates only change when there is a national holiday for the whole country.

chunks.title: How to choose the right job
chunks.text: Tools and experts to help you find out what you're good at and what job suits you. Knowing what kind of job you want will make searching and applying for jobs easier. You can do this by figuring out your skills, planning your career and finding a job that fits your life.

chunks.title: Discover your skills and what employers value
chunks.text: Use Tahatū’s resources to learn about your skills, what matters to you at work, and explore career ideas. Know your skills (Tahatu Career Navigator)external

chunks.title: Not sure what you're good at
chunks.text: The Interest quiz suggests job ideas matched to your interests. You can also learn about the pay, skills and qualifications for your job matches. Interest quiz (Tahatu Career Navigator)external

chunks.title: Flexi-wage
chunks.text: Help to get started and learn the skills you need for a job. We'll find you a job where you can get paid while you learn, with an employer who will help you towards long-term work. You'll also get ongoing support from us and your employer. Flexi-wage - job seeker information

chunks.title: Mana in Mahi
chunks.text: Get paid while you train towards a career you love. We'll find a job for you in an industry that interests you. You'll get started on an apprenticeship or industry qualification. Mana in Mahi - Strength in work

chunks.title: Community Job Coaching
chunks.text: A job coach can help you prepare for and find work. This is for 18 to 24 year olds in some regions, who have been getting Jobseeker Support for at least 3 months. Community Job Coaching

chunks.title: Family-friendly jobs
chunks.text: The Jobs for Mums website lists jobs in 30+ career fields that meet the needs of families. They have flexible job opportunities in your area or remote work. Jobs for Mumsexternal

chunks.title: If you're disabled or have a health condition
chunks.text: We can help you get a job and set up your career if you're disabled or have a health condition. This includes mental health conditions or neurodiversity. - Employment Service: Get an employment provider who will help you prepare for work, find a job that's right for you and make sure you have everything you need. Employment service for people with a disability or health condition - Employment Service in Schools: For secondary school students. An employment provider will work with you, your family and your school to help you plan your future and explore job and career opportunities. Employment Service in Schools - Mainstream Programmes: Get a work placement, on-the-job training, and a long-term job. There's different programmes for your situation and goals. Mainstream Programmes

chunks.title: In-Work Support
chunks.text:
## In-Work Support
If you've come off your benefit to start work, we can offer ongoing support and advice to help you manage any challenges that come up.
Starting a new job can be a challenge, especially if you haven't worked for a while. We want to do everything we can to help you succeed in your new job.
## What we can help with
We can help with many things, including:
- ensuring you get any support from us that you qualify for, e.g. help with: Accommodation Supplement Working for Families childcare costs, including Flexible Childcare Assistance disability costs
- Accommodation Supplement
- Working for Families
- childcare costs, including Flexible Childcare Assistance
- disability costs
Flexible Childcare Assistance
- regular check-ins to see how things are going for you at home or at work
- advice on talking to your employer about things like: working arrangements learning your new job training and mentoring
- working arrangements
- learning your new job
- training and mentoring
- advice on how to manage a disability or health condition while working, e.g: structuring your day workplace modifications
- structuring your day
- workplace modifications
- information about other services you could get, e.g: additional tax credits from Inland Revenue budgeting relationship services.
- additional tax credits from Inland Revenue
- budgeting
- relationship services.
## How to get in-work support
If you'd like to take part in the in-work support service, call us on 0800 559 497 when you start work.
We can contact you by phone or email regularly, so you won't have to take time off to meet with us.

chunks.title: Income from boarders
chunks.text: If you have other people sharing your home and paying you to live there, you need to tell us about it as it could affect your payments.

chunks.title: What is board
chunks.text: Board is the amount paid by someone (called a boarder) who pays for accommodation and food in another person's home, and their food costs can't be easily separated out from the amount they pay. Their board payment may also cover other service costs, e.g. internet or power. If you're living in public housing, and the person living with you is not on the tenancy agreement, they will be considered a boarder.

chunks.title: How board payments can affect payments from us
chunks.text: The money you get from your boarders can affect any income-tested payments you get from us. You need to tell us if you're getting board payments. Not all the money you get from board payments counts as income – only the amount that is more than either: - your accommodation costs, or - the market rent for your home if you're living in public housing. To work out how much of your board payments count as income, we: - look at how much board you are paid and work out 62% of this - compare this amount to your accommodation costs, or market rent if you're in public housing. If the 62% is lower than your accommodation costs or market rent, your board payments do not count as income. However, it will affect the amount of housing subsidy you can get from us. If the 62% is higher than your accommodation costs or market rent, we work out the difference – that difference counts as income. You can check how this affects your payments using the income deduction tables: Income deduction tables

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: The easiest way to tell us is online in MyMSD. Once you’ve logged in, select ‘Declare boarders and renters’. You need to tell us: - the address - details of the person paying you board - how much the board is - when you get paid, and how often. We will continue to use this amount every week, so make sure you let us know if it stops or changes. If you can't use MyMSD, you can also fill out our PDF form: You need to print this form, complete it, and either post it to us or bring it into one of our services centres. You can also pick one up from any of our service centres. Find a service centre

chunks.title: Income Related Rent reassessment issue
chunks.text:
## Income Related Rent reassessment issue
We've found we incorrectly reassessed some people's Income Related Rent.
This only affects you if you have an Income Related Rent debt because you were investigated for benefit fraud. The investigation must have happened between 14 April 2014 and 21 December 2016. All Income Related Rent debt established since then has been calculated correctly.
We'll contact you to let you know if you're affected. You don't need to do anything.
If you are affected, your Income Related Rent debt will decrease. This means your overall debt with us will also decrease.
