chunks.title: New Zealand Seasonal Work Scheme
chunks.text: Get help with costs like travel, clothing or temporarily moving home, when you're starting seasonal horticulture or viticulture work.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: The Seasonal Work Scheme is made up of 3 types of support: - Support with costs - Accommodation costs payment - Incentive payment.

chunks.title: Support with costs
chunks.text: To help pay for: - daily transport to work - clothing and work gear - moving home if you have to move to take up seasonal horticulture or viticulture work - training for the job. We can't pay for any costs that you've already paid for.

chunks.title: Accommodation costs payment
chunks.text: - You can get up to $200 a week for accommodation costs, for up to 26 weeks. - To help pay for temporary accommodation if you've had to move somewhere closer to work, and still have to pay your normal accommodation costs at the place you usually live. - You can get up to $5200 in a 52 week period.

chunks.title: Incentive payment
chunks.text: - $500 paid halfway through your work, and $500 paid when your work ends. - You can get up to $1000 in a 52 week period.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: To qualify for the scheme you must meet the general criteria for: - work - age, and - residency. These criteria are detailed below. We'll also take your situation into account. If you want to get the Accommodation costs payment or Incentive payment, there are extra criteria you need to meet.

chunks.title: Work criteria
chunks.text: You'll need to talk to us about this when you have a job starting soon, or you’ve recently started in a job. - The job must last for at least 6 weeks - You need to be working at least 30 hours a week. - You need to show us proof of the job, for example, emails from your employer, or your employment contract. The work must be seasonal work in either a horticulture or viticulture role, doing either: - packing - picking - planting - pruning - plant maintenance - thinning. Any horticulture or viticulture roles not listed above can't get New Zealand Seasonal Work Scheme because they are Essential Skills roles. For example, the New Zealand Seasonal Work Scheme cannot be paid for a Winery Cellar Hand. This is because the role's main tasks are operating machines and making and bottling wine - not packing, picking, planting, pruning, plant maintenance or thinning. We'll also take into account your: - work history - work experience - level of skills and qualifications. There must be a risk that you could be unemployed for a long time. For example, if you're a student and have a short gap between study, you are not likely to qualify for the scheme.

chunks.title: Age criteria
chunks.text: You need to be aged either: - 16-64, or - 65 or older and you don't qualify for NZ Super.

chunks.title: Residency criteria
chunks.text: You need to: - be an NZ citizen - be a resident with a residence class visa - be recognised as a refugee or protected person, or - have a temporary visa that allows you to work in New Zealand and either: have applied to be recognised as a refugee or protected person and are waiting on the outcome, or have applied for a residence class visa and are compelled to stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances. - have applied to be recognised as a refugee or protected person and are waiting on the outcome, or - have applied for a residence class visa and are compelled to stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances. You also need to be ordinarily resident in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Accommodation costs payment criteria
chunks.text: To get the accommodation costs payment you need to: - meet the general criteria for the scheme above - be taking up seasonal horticulture or viticulture work for 6 weeks or more, at 30 hours or more a week (this can be for more than one job) - temporarily move to start seasonal horticulture or viticulture work because travel between your home and your workplace is unreasonable or not possible - have accommodation costs in the place you're moving to, and - still be paying accommodation costs for your home.

chunks.title: Incentive payment criteria
chunks.text: To qualify for the incentive payment, you need to: - meet the general criteria for the scheme above - be taking up seasonal horticulture or viticulture work for 6 weeks or more, at 30 hours or more a week - temporarily move to start seasonal horticulture or viticulture work because travel between your home and your workplace is unreasonable or not possible, and - work the period agreed between you and your employer.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: To apply for any part of the NZ Seasonal Work Scheme, you can either: - call us on 0800 779 009 or - come in and see us. We'll talk to you about: - what types of support you qualify for, and - what area you're looking to work in. Find your nearest Work and Income office

## Going overseas for NZ Super or Veteran's Pension
If you get NZ Superannuation or Veteran's Pension and go overseas, you may still be able to be paid. It depends if you're going overseas for a holiday or going to live overseas.

## Going to live overseas
If you get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension and plan to live overseas, you must apply to keep these payments going.
You need to meet certain criteria and how much you get depends on which country you're going to live in.

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension obligations
chunks.text: There are things you need to do when you're getting New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super) or Veteran's Pension. If you don't do them, your payment could reduce or stop.

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: You must tell us if you: - have changes to personal details, eg: contact details address bank account number name - contact details - address - bank account number - name - have changes to your living situation, eg: marriage or separation enter or end a civil union start or end a de facto relationship start or stop living alone - marriage or separation - enter or end a civil union - start or end a de facto relationship - start or stop living alone - intend to live overseas - intend to travel overseas for longer than 26 weeks - are admitted to or discharged from hospital - have been granted an overseas benefit or pension - are imprisoned / held in custody on remand - have any other change that may affect your NZ Super or Veteran's Pension entitlement or rate.

chunks.title: If your partner is included in your NZ Super or Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: You also need to tell us if either your partner or yourself - have a change in work situation, e.g. starting paid part-time, casual or full-time work - have become self employed or start a business - have a boarder or renter that moves in or out, or the payments you get from them change - have other changes to you or your partner's income or financial circumstances. If you included your partner in your payments before 9 November 2020, your partner also needs to tell us about changes. Obligations for partners included in NZ Super or Veteran’s Pension

chunks.title: Getting other payments from us
chunks.text: If you're getting other payments from us, eg Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance, or your partner is getting a benefit, there are other obligations you need to meet as well, eg you need to tell us if you intend to travel overseas for any length of time. Obligations if you're getting other payments from us

chunks.title: If you don't meet your obligations
chunks.text: If you don't tell us about changes in your life that might affect your NZ Super or Veteran's Pension entitlement, then: - your NZ Super or Veteran's Pension may be reviewed and stopped - you may have to pay back the total amount of any overpayment that you've received - we may impose a penalty (up to 3 times the value of the overpayment) - you may be prosecuted and fined and/or imprisoned.

chunks.title: Obligations for partners included in NZ Super and Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: There are things your partner needs to do when they're included in your NZ Super or Veteran's Pension. If they don't do them, your payment could reduce or stop.

chunks.title: What your partner needs to do
chunks.text: These obligations are only for partners who are included in your NZ Super or Veteran's Pension payments. Before 9 November 2020, you could include your partner in your NZ Super or Veteran's Pension payments. You could do this if you qualified for NZ Super or Veteran's Pension but your partner didn't (e.g. they were under 65).

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: Your partner must tell us if they: - have changes to personal details, e.g. their: contact details address bank account number name - contact details - address - bank account number - name - have changes to their living situation, e.g: marriage or separation enter or end a civil union start or end a de facto relationship start or stop living alone - marriage or separation - enter or end a civil union - start or end a de facto relationship - start or stop living alone - become self-employed or start a business - have other changes to their income or financial circumstances - have a change in work situation, e.g. starting paid part-time, casual or full-time work - plan to live overseas - plan to travel overseas for longer than 26 weeks - are admitted to or discharged from hospital - are granted an overseas benefit or pension - are imprisoned or held in custody on remand - have any other change that may affect your NZ Super or Veteran's Pension entitlement or rate. Note: some of these changes may mean you can no longer get the non-qualified partner payment. In these cases, you can't restart the non-qualified partner payment in the future.

chunks.title: If they don't meet their obligations
chunks.text: If your partner doesn't tell us about changes in their life that might affect your NZ Super or Veteran's Pension entitlement, then: - your NZ Super or Veteran's Pension may be reviewed and stopped - you may have to pay back the total amount of any overpayment that you've received - we may impose a penalty (up to 3 times the value of the overpayment) - you may be prosecuted and fined and/or imprisoned.

chunks.title: Contact

chunks.title: Change to residence criteria for NZ Super and Veteran's Pension
chunks.text:
## Change to residence criteria for NZ Super and Veteran's Pension
The new residence criteria for New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super) and Veteran's Pension affect people turning 65 from 1 July 2024.
If you're getting NZ Super or Veteran's Pension before 1 July 2024, these changes won't affect you.
## New residence criteria
To get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension you must have lived in NZ for a certain amount of time. This is gradually increasing from 10 years to 20 years.
The number of years you must have lived in NZ since you turned 20 is based on your date of birth. You still need to have lived in NZ for at least 5 years since you turned 50.
These years (including the 5 years from age 50) do not need to be consecutive.
Use the table below to work this out:
## Number of years you must have lived in NZ since you turned 20
If you haven't lived in NZ the whole time, you may be able to use another country to meet the residency criteria if:
- it is a country that has a Social Security Agreement (SSA) with NZ, or
- it is a NZ Realm country (the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau).
If you're recognised as a refugee or protected person, the number of years you need is worked out differently.
## Other criteria you need to meet
As well as meeting the residence criteria, you also need to:
- be 65 or older
- either: be a New Zealand (NZ) citizen be a permanent resident, or hold a residence class visa, and
- be a New Zealand (NZ) citizen
- be a permanent resident, or
- hold a residence class visa, and
- be ordinarily resident in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau when you apply.
You can find the full criteria for getting NZ Super or Veteran’s Pension here:
Who can get NZ Super
Who can get Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: Jobseeker Support obligations
chunks.text: There are things you need to do when you're getting a Jobseeker Support benefit. These are called obligations. If you don't do them, your benefit could reduce or stop.

chunks.title: Overview of your obligations
chunks.text: - You have an obligation to find or prepare for work – this means you must: look for full-time work, or look for part-time work, if you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you can only work part-time, or prepare for work, if you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you can’t work or can only work less than 15 hours a week. - look for full-time work, or - look for part-time work, if you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you can only work part-time, or - prepare for work, if you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you can’t work or can only work less than 15 hours a week. - You have an obligation to tell us if something changes. - If you're taking care of dependent children, you have social obligations. - If we ask you to, you have an obligation to take part in a Work Ability Assessment or to work with a contracted service provider. These obligations are detailed on this page below. If you have a partner there are things they'll need to do as well. Jobseeker Support obligations for partners

chunks.title: Full-time work obligations
chunks.text: You'll generally be expected to look for work of at least 30 hours a week, unless you have a health condition or disability that means you can't work full-time. If you have full-time work obligations, you need to: - be available for and take reasonable steps to get a suitable job - take any offer of suitable full-time, part-time or temporary work, or work that is seasonal or subsidised - attend and take part in any suitable job interviews we ask you to - take and pass any drug test potential employers or training providers require - attend and take part in interviews with Work and Income as required - work with us to plan how you'll find a suitable job - take part in any other activities we refer you to that will improve your work readiness or help you get work, such as: creating a Jobseeker profile, and keeping this up to date job training courses Kōrero Mahi work seminars work experience work assessments (including rehabilitation, but not medical treatment) - creating a Jobseeker profile, and keeping this up to date - job training courses - Kōrero Mahi work seminars - work experience - work assessments (including rehabilitation, but not medical treatment) - let us know how you're meeting your work obligations as often as we reasonably require.

chunks.title: Part-time work obligations
chunks.text: If you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you can only work part-time, you'll need to look for work of at least 15 hours a week. If you have part-time work obligations, you need to: - be available for and take reasonable steps to get a suitable part-time job - take any offer of suitable part-time or temporary work, or work that is seasonal or subsidised - attend and take part in any suitable job interviews we ask you to - take and pass any drug test potential employers or training providers require - attend and take part in interviews with us as required - work with us to plan how you'll find a suitable job - take part in any other activities that we refer you to, such as creating a Jobseeker profile and keeping it up to date, and attending any job training courses, seminars, work experience or work assessments (including rehabilitation, but not medical treatment) that will improve your work readiness or help you get work - let us know how you're meeting your work obligations as often as we reasonably require.

chunks.title: Work preparation obligations
chunks.text: If you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you're unable to work, or can only work fewer than 15 hours a week, you won't be asked to meet work obligations until your situation changes. In the meantime, you have the following work preparation obligations to: - take reasonable steps to prepare and plan for work - attend and take part in work preparation interviews, where we ask you to - attend and take part in work related activities or programmes such as a creating a Jobseeker Profile and keeping it up to date, work assessment, a programme or seminar to increase particular skills or enhance motivation where we ask you to - attend and take part in any other activity that we require you to (including rehabilitation but not medical treatment, voluntary work or activity in the community).

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: You must tell us immediately if you: - have a change in your work situation, e.g. start part-time, casual or full-time work (paid or unpaid) - become self-employed or start a business - plan to travel overseas - start or finish study - part-time or full-time - have a boarder or renter that moves in or out, or the payments you get from them change - have a change of personal details, e.g. your: name address contact details bank account number - name - address - contact details - bank account number - have changes to your living situation, e.g: marriage or separation starting or ending a civil union starting or ending a de facto relationship change in the number of children you support - marriage or separation - starting or ending a civil union - starting or ending a de facto relationship - change in the number of children you support - have a change in accommodation costs - are imprisoned or held in custody on remand - are admitted to or discharged from hospital - are granted an overseas pension - have any other change that may affect your benefit entitlement or rate.

chunks.title: When taking care of dependent children (social obligations)
chunks.text: You're expected to take reasonable steps to meet social obligations as a parent or a caregiver. These obligations are to help ensure children get a good start. You must ensure your dependent child(ren) (including any child you get Orphan's or Unsupported Child's Benefit for) are: - enrolled with a health practitioner or a medical practice that's part of a Primary Health Organisation (PHO) - enrolled in and attending one of the following from the age of 3 until they start school: an approved early childhood education programme, eg, Kohanga Reo, Punanga Reo, Aoga and other programmes with a language and culture focus parenting and early childhood home education programmes kindergartens preschools childcare centres playcentres home-based care services, or Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - The Correspondence School, or another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme - an approved early childhood education programme, eg, Kohanga Reo, Punanga Reo, Aoga and other programmes with a language and culture focus parenting and early childhood home education programmes kindergartens preschools childcare centres playcentres home-based care services, or - Kohanga Reo, Punanga Reo, Aoga and other programmes with a language and culture focus - parenting and early childhood home education programmes - kindergartens - preschools - childcare centres - playcentres - home-based care services, or - Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu - The Correspondence School, or - another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme - up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks if aged under 5, at a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider, eg: Plunket Maori health provider Pacific health provider - Plunket - Maori health provider - Pacific health provider - enrolled in and attending school from the age of 5 or 6 (depending on when they start school). We understand there could be some situations outside of your control that mean you may not be able to meet an obligation right now. For example: - your child is on a waiting list for a GP, or - there aren’t any available places in your nearby childcare centre. You may be required to meet with us to discuss how you're meeting your obligations as a parent or a caregiver.

chunks.title: One-off or lump sum payments
chunks.text:
## One-off or lump sum payments
Some one-off or lump sum payments don't count as income if you're getting a payment from us. Find out what kind of payments you need to tell us about and how they might affect your payments.
## Whether you need to tell us
If you get Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support, you need to tell us about any one-off or lump sum payments.
If you're getting a benefit (but not Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support), you may need to tell us about your one-off or lump sum payments. This depends on whether you get any income from it and what it's for - you can check this in the list below.
## Types of one-off or lump sum payments
Find the type of one-off or lump sum you were paid to check if this will affect your payments from us:
- Compassionate grants
- Employer help if you have a sickness, injury or disability
- Ex gratia and compensation payments
- FamilyBoost payment
- Gifts - one-off
- Home equity conversion scheme lump sum
- Lottery prize money or gambling winnings
- Lump sum payment from a will or estate
- Payments relating to a severe weather event
- Payments to victims of crime
- Sale of assets
- Settlement payments for sleepover shifts
## Getting income from one-off or lump sum payments
If you're getting income from your one-off or lump sum payment, e.g. interest or dividends, you need to tell us. This income may affect your payments from us.
You can tell us about this income using MyMSD:
If you can't use MyMSD you can call us or come into one of our service centres.
Call us
Find a service centre
## Income from severe weather event payments
If you got a one-off or lump sum payment due to a severe weather event, is it not counted as income for 12 months from the day it was paid to you. However you still need to let us know about this income. Find out what happens to this income and how to tell us about it here:
Payments relating to a severe weather event
## Contact
If you're not sure, contact us.
Phone us

chunks.title: Ordinarily resident in SSA country when you apply for NZ Super or Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: You may be ordinarily resident in a country NZ has a Social Security Agreement (SSA) with when you apply. If so, there are extra criteria you need to meet to get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension. SSA countries are: Australia, Canada, Denmark, Greece, Ireland, Jersey, Guernsey, Malta, the Netherlands, South Korea and the United Kingdom.

chunks.title: Definition of ordinarily resident
chunks.text: Ordinarily resident means you: - are normally and lawfully in an SSA country - intend to stay in that SSA country, and - consider that SSA country to be your home. How we decide if someone is ordinarily resident

chunks.title: Living in Australia but not ordinarily resident
chunks.text: If you're living in Australia but not ordinarily resident there, you may still qualify. You need to meet the extra criteria (listed further down the page), and either: - have been physically present in Australia for at least 26 weeks, or - intend to remain physically present in Australia for 1 year from when you apply.

chunks.title: Ordinarily resident in the UK
chunks.text: If you're ordinarily resident in the UK when you apply, you cannot get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension. You may be able to get a UK benefit or pension instead under the UK Social Security Agreement Social Security Agreement with the United Kingdom

chunks.title: Extra criteria you need to meet
chunks.text: Select the SSA country you're ordinarily resident in to find out what extra criteria you need to meet. If you want to talk about your situation, contact our International Services team.

chunks.title: Australia
chunks.text: You need to: - meet the criteria for Australian Age Pension (this includes the age criteria which is age 67) - be either: an NZ citizen and have a Special Category visa an Australian citizen, or an Australian permanent resident - an NZ citizen and have a Special Category visa - an Australian citizen, or - an Australian permanent resident - be in Australia when you apply, and - have been resident in New Zealand for at least 1 year continuously from age 20. Who can get Australian Age Pension (Services Australia)external

chunks.title: What we mean by 'resident in New Zealand'
chunks.text: When we say 'resident in NZ', we mean you permanently made your home in NZ. This definition is part of the definition of 'have lived in NZ'. Definition of 'have lived in NZ' for NZ Super and Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: Canada
chunks.text: You need to: - be in Canada or New Zealand when you apply - intend to remain ordinarily resident in Canada for at least 26 weeks from when you apply, and - have been resident in New Zealand for at least 1 year continuously from age 20.

chunks.title: Denmark
chunks.text: You need to: - be in Denmark or New Zealand when you apply - intend to remain ordinarily resident in Denmark for at least 26 weeks from when you apply, and - have been resident in New Zealand for at least 1 year continuously from age 20.

chunks.title: Greece
chunks.text: You need to: - intend to live in Greece for more than 26 weeks, and - have been resident in New Zealand for at least 1 year from age 20.

chunks.title: Ireland
chunks.text: You need to: - be in Ireland or New Zealand when you apply - intend to remain ordinarily resident in Ireland for at least 26 weeks from when you apply, and - have been resident in New Zealand for at least 1 year continuously from age 20.

chunks.title: Jersey/Guernsey
chunks.text: You need to: - intend to live in Jersey or Guernsey for more than 26 weeks, and - have been resident in New Zealand for at least 1 year from age 20.

chunks.title: Malta
chunks.text: You need to: - be in Malta or New Zealand when you apply - intend to live in Malta for at least 26 weeks from when you apply, and - have been resident in New Zealand for at least 1 year continuously between ages 20 and 65.

chunks.title: Netherlands
chunks.text: You need to: - be in the Netherlands or New Zealand when you apply - intend to remain ordinarily resident in the Netherlands for at least 26 weeks from when you apply, and - have been resident in New Zealand for at least 1 year continuously from age 20.

chunks.title: South Korea
chunks.text: You need to: - be in South Korea or New Zealand when you apply - intend to live in South Korea for at least 26 weeks from when you apply, and - have been resident in New Zealand for at least 1 year continuously between ages 20 and 65.

chunks.title: Orphan's Benefit obligations
chunks.text:
## Orphan's Benefit obligations
There are things you need to do when you're getting an Orphan's Benefit. If you don't do them your benefit could reduce or stop.
## Tell us if something changes
You must tell Work and Income or your contracted service provider (where one is assigned to you) immediately if:
- the care and/or support arrangements for the child change
- the financial circumstances of the child change
- either you or the child intend to travel overseas
- you or the child have changes to personal details, eg: name address bank account number
- name
- address
- bank account number
- either you or the child have any other change that may affect your benefit entitlement or rate
## If you don't meet your obligations
If there's any reason why you can't meet your obligations, talk to us straight away.
Contact us
If you don't tell us about changes in your life that might affect your benefit entitlement, or rate, then:
- your benefit may be reviewed and cancelled
- you may have to pay back the total amount of any overpayment that you receive
- we may impose a penalty (up to 3 times the value of the overpayment)
- you may be prosecuted and fined, or imprisoned.
You have the right to review or dispute any decision to reduce or stop your benefit.

chunks.title: Orphan's Benefit
chunks.text: Orphan's Benefit is a weekly payment which helps carers supporting a child or young person whose parents have died or can't be found, or can't look after them because they have a serious long-term health condition or incapacity.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get the Orphan's Benefit if the child or young person you care for is: - 18 years old or younger - single, and - financially dependent on you. You must also: - be 18 or older and the main carer of the child or young person - have primary responsibility for the day-to-day care of the child - be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - not be the child or young person's natural or adoptive parent, and - be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when you apply. Ordinarily resident You or the child or young person must normally live in New Zealand. If you're working and are granted the Orphans Benefit, you may also qualify for the In-work tax credit from Inland Revenue. In-work tax credit (Inland Revenue)external This benefit is not based on your income or any money the child gets from working after school or in the holidays. But other income the child gets such as from a family trust, ACC, investments or their parents' estate could affect whether you qualify and the amount you can get. You won't be able to get the Orphan's Benefit at the same time as Board payments from Child, Youth and Family or Working for Families Tax Credits from Inland Revenue (expect In-work tax credit) for the same child.

chunks.title: Child is 16 or 17
chunks.text: In some cases, a child may qualify for their own income support. To find out more call us or your local Youth Service provider. Call us Youth Service providerexternal

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: How much you get depends on how old the child is and any income they have. View our maximum current rates (Manuals and Procedures)external You will also be able to get a Clothing Allowance. This is paid automatically when you get an Orphan's Benefit. Clothing Allowance

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Talk to us about your circumstances. We'll explain how to apply, and what documents you'll need to provide. Contact us You'll usually need to provide: - full birth certificate for the child - copy of the custody or guardianship agreement - details about the child's income - copies of the parents' death certificates (if this applies). You can order this online here. Order certificates (New Zealand Government)external If you don't have these documents or find it hard to get these, please talk to us.

chunks.title: How long do I have to complete my application?
chunks.text: You have 20 working days from when you first contacted us. If we ask for any supporting documents, you'll need to provide them within this time. If you can't complete your application within 20 working days for any reason, please let us know when you talk with us.

chunks.title: When do payments start?
chunks.text: If your application is approved, you'll usually receive your first payment 2 to 4 weeks from the date you apply or start looking after the child (whichever is later). You'll need to apply as soon as you become the child's main caregiver as we can't backdate payments.

chunks.title: Other payments
chunks.text: If you get the Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit you may be able to get help with other expenses.

chunks.title: Holiday and Birthday Allowance
chunks.text: You automatically get these two payments each year if you already get Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit for a child in your care. Use these payments to celebrate important events in the child’s life, like their birthday or Christmas. Holiday and Birthday Allowance

chunks.title: Establishment Grant
chunks.text: Establishment grant is paid automatically when you first get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit. This is a once only payment of $350 for each child you're caring for. This money helps you buy things like a bed, bedding and clothing. You won't be taxed on this money, and you won't have to pay it back. Establishment Grant

chunks.title: School and Year Start-up Payment
chunks.text: Help with the costs that mostly happen at the beginning of the year, in particular pre-school and school-related costs such as clothing, school fees and stationery. School and Year Start-up Payment

chunks.title: Extraordinary Care Fund
chunks.text: This fund helps support children to develop their skills and talents. It can also help children who are experiencing difficulties that are significantly impacting on their development. Extraordinary Care Fund

chunks.title: Income rules for Orphan's Benefit/Unsupported Child Benefit
chunks.text:
## Income rules for Orphan's Benefit/Unsupported Child Benefit
You only have to tell us about any income if you get another benefit as well as Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child Benefit. If the child has an income you have to contact us.
## Do you get any other benefits?
If you only get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child Benefit you don't have to tell us about any regular income, one-off payments or any assets you have.
If you get any other benefits or extra help, check the income rules for them to find out if you need to tell us about your income and one-off payments.
However, if the child has an income you need to contact us.
Phone us

chunks.title: Out of School Care and Recreation (OSCAR) Subsidy
chunks.text: Out of School Care and Recreation (OSCAR) Subsidy is a payment which helps families with the costs of before and after school care for up to 20 hours a week, and school holiday programmes for up to 50 hours a week.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get an OSCAR Subsidy if: - you're the principal caregiver of a dependent child - you're a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - your family is on a low or middle income. You also need to be in one of these situations: - working, studying or on an approved training course - involved in an activity that Work and Income has asked you to do - a shift worker who works nights - seriously ill or disabled - caring for a child in hospital or for a child you get the Child Disability Allowance for. Principal caregiver You can't get the OSCAR Subsidy if the child's other parent or caregiver can take care of the child. It also depends on how much you and your partner earn. To receive your OSCAR subsidy from the day your child starts the programme, you need to submit your application to us before your child's first day. This is especially important at school holidays. The child or young person must: - normally live in New Zealand - be at school - be under 14 (or under 18 if you get a Child Disability Allowance for them) - be attending an approved OSCAR programme for at least 3 hours a week, which includes: before school after school holiday programmes and camps. - before school - after school - holiday programmes and camps. Find an OSCAR provider

chunks.title: Check if you can get OSCAR Subsidy
chunks.text: To find out if you could get OSCAR Subsidy and what else you might qualify for, use our 'Check what you might get' tool.

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: How much you get depends on the size of your family, your income and how many hours a week your child goes to the childcare provider. If you don't know how many hours of care you'll need each week (because you're a casual or on-call worker for instance) we'll talk with you about your options when you apply for a subsidy. All subsidies are paid directly to the childcare provider. View our current ratesexternal

chunks.title: When payments start from
chunks.text: Childcare assistance starts from the date the care starts (or from the date you apply if you apply after it starts).

chunks.title: Benefits of choosing an OSCAR approved programme
chunks.text: The OSCAR Standards provide reassurance to parents and caregivers that a programme is properly run and takes place in a safe environment for children. In addition, parents and caregivers may qualify for an OSCAR Subsidy. Parents of children attending unapproved programmes cannot receive an OSCAR Subsidy.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: We suggest you apply at least 3 to 4 weeks before you need your subsidy to start. We can grant you the financial assistance you're entitled to from the date you first contact us, or the date your childcare started, whichever is later, if you complete your application within 20 working days of that date. If you're a Youth Service client, you need to talk to your Youth Service provider.

chunks.title: Apply for OSCAR Subsidy only
chunks.text: - You and your partner (if you have one) need to complete the Childcare Assistance application form. - Your childcare provider also needs to complete the supervisor's section inside this form. - You'll need to email the application form, and any other documents we've asked you to get to Centralised_childcare_reviews@msd.govt.nz or you can ask your childcare provider to send this to us on your behalf.

chunks.title: Apply for OSCAR Subsidy and other payments
chunks.text: You can apply online through MyMSD. We'll also check to see if you can get any other help from us based on the answers you give in your application. Apply online Once you've applied online, we'll tell you what you need to do. This will include having to get your childcare provider to complete the supervisor's section of the Childcare Assistance application form.

chunks.title: Reviews and changes
chunks.text: Childcare assistance is reviewed regularly. It also usually stops or is reviewed: - the day after your job or course ends - after 12 weeks if you stop work because you have a health condition or are injured - when your child reaches the age limit for the subsidy - when your child leaves the pre-school facility or OSCAR programme - if the child leaves your care.

chunks.title: Changes in your circumstances
chunks.text: You must also tell us straight away about any changes in your circumstances that could affect your payments, for example: - if you or your partner's income changes - if your child stops going or moves to another early childhood programme or OSCAR programme - if there's a change in your child's attendance - if the number of hours you (or your partner) work or study each week changes - if the reason why you get a subsidy changes, e.g. your health improves or your child leaves hospital - your child starts or stops receiving 20 Hours ECE. Manage your childcare payments

chunks.title: Other payments for seniors
chunks.text:
## Other payments for seniors
When you turn 65, NZ Superannuation and Veteran's Pension are the main payments you may qualify for. There are also other payments you may be able to get.
You can use our 'Check What You Might Get' tool to find out what payments you may be able to get and how to apply for them.
This includes common payments like:
- Accommodation Supplement - if you need help with your rent, board, or cost of owning your own home
- Disability Allowance - if you have regular, ongoing costs because of a disability
- Temporary Additional Support - if you don't have enough money to cover your essential living costs, and
- Community Services Card - use this card to pay less on health care and public transport.
## Residential Care Subsidy
If you need long-term residential care in a hospital or rest home, you may be able to get a Residential Care Subsidy.
Residential Care Subsidy
## Residential Care Loan
If you're going into residential care and want to keep your home for a while, you may be able to get a Residential Care Loan.
Residential Care Loan
## Disability Allowance
If some of your care is being paid for by a Residential Care Loan or a Residential Support Subsidy, you may also be able to get a Disability Allowance. This will help to help cover costs such as medical fees, prescriptions, etc.
Disability Allowance
## Special Disability Allowance
If you're getting a benefit and your partner is in residential care,or has been in a public hospital for over 13 weeks, you may be able to get a Special Disability Allowance. This can help with the extra costs of your partner being in care.
Special Disability Allowance
## Caring for someone with a health condition, injury or disability
If the person you're caring for would need hospital, rest home or residential care without you, we may be able to help.
Caring for someone with a health condition, injury or disability

## Types of regular income
- Income from bank interest or investments
- Gifts that provide a regular income
- Rental income

chunks.title: Overseas pensions
chunks.text: You or your partner may qualify for a pension from another country - this is called an overseas pension. If you or your partner do qualify for an overseas pension, it may affect payments you get from us. If you or your partner qualify for an overseas pension, you must apply for that overseas pension.

chunks.title: What's counted as an overseas pension
chunks.text: An overseas pension is a benefit, pension or allowance that is: - paid for the same types of circumstances as New Zealand benefits, pensions or allowances, and - administered by, or on behalf of, another country’s government.

chunks.title: Voluntary contributions
chunks.text: Voluntary contributions are extra payments you make into a country's pension scheme. If you make voluntary contributions, the voluntary amount is not counted as part of an overseas pension.

chunks.title: How overseas pensions affect your payments
chunks.text: For every one dollar you get from an overseas pension, your New Zealand (NZ) payment is reduced by one dollar. If your overseas pension amount is more than your NZ payment, you will only get the overseas pension. We'll convert the amount of your overseas pension to NZ dollars and take that off your NZ payment. This is done using the gross (before tax) rate. Ben gets NZ Super of $647.37 gross a week. He also gets an Australian pension of AUD$5,642.12 a year. - We convert his Australian pension to NZ dollars using the exchange rate: $5,642.12 x 1.20 (exchange rate) = $6,770.54 a year. - We work out the weekly amount: $6,770.54 divided by 52 (weeks) = $130.20 - We deduct the Australian pension from the NZ payment: $647.37 minus $130.20 = $517.17 gross a week. Carl and Andrea are married and both get NZ Super of $492.14 gross each a week. Carl also gets a UK pension of £46.82 a week. - We convert Carl's UK pension to NZ dollars using the exchange rate: £46.82 x 2.30 (exchange rate) = $107.68 a week. - We deduct the UK pension from Carl's NZ payment: $492.14 minus $107.68 = $384.46 gross a week. For most countries we use an average exchange rate from the 16th of one month to the 15th of the next. To work this out, we look at an average exchange rate between: - the overseas currency, and - the New Zealand dollar. Some countries tell us the actual exchange rate. In this case, we'll compare this with the exchange rate that Westpac provides us. We'll use the one that is best for you. Some countries use more than one exchange rate. If this happens, we'll use either: - the actual exchange rate, or - the average of the exchange rates for the month, whatever is best for you. Your partner’s overseas pension will only affect your payments from us if: - either of you get a benefit (eg. Jobseeker Support or Supported Living Payment), or

chunks.title: How overseas pensions affect your payments
chunks.text: - your partner is included in your NZ Super or Veteran’s Pension as a non-qualified partner.­­­ Your payments will not be affected if you only get NZ Super or Veteran’s Pension. If you’re getting a benefit from us: If your partner’s overseas pension is equal to, or less than, their rate of NZ Super it will not affect your benefit payments. If your partner’s overseas pension is more than their rate of NZ Super, your benefit will be reduced by the excess amount. If your partner is included in your NZ Super or Veteran’s Pension as a non-qualified partner: This means your partner does not qualify for NZ Super or Veteran’s Pension themselves, and you included them in your payments before 9 November 2020. In this case any overseas pension will be equally deducted from both your payments. If you're getting extra help from us: If you get any other payments from us that are income tested (e.g. a Disability Allowance), your partner's overseas pension may affect those payments.

chunks.title: How your overseas pension can be paid
chunks.text: Generally the overseas agency pays your overseas pension directly into your bank account. This is called the 'Direct Payment Option'. Using the Direct Payment Option means: - you’ll get 2 separate payments: your overseas pension from the overseas agency (based on their payment cycle), and your NZ payment from Work and Income (either weekly or fortnightly) - your overseas pension from the overseas agency (based on their payment cycle), and - your NZ payment from Work and Income (either weekly or fortnightly) - your overseas pension payments will vary as the exchange rates change - you're responsible for paying New Zealand tax on your overseas pension if you're getting NZ Super or Veteran's Pension. Your overseas pension will be paid using the Direct Payment Option unless you tell us you want the Special Banking Option. You can choose to use a Special Banking Option if you get an overseas pension from: - Australia - Guernsey - Ireland - Jersey - the Netherlands, or - United Kingdom. Using the Special Banking Option means: - you receive 1 payment from Work and Income that is the total amount you’re entitled to - changes in the exchange rate will not affect your overseas pension payments - New Zealand tax on your overseas pension is already deducted.

chunks.title: Why overseas pensions affect your payments
chunks.text: The policy is there to ensure that people who have lived overseas and in NZ get the same amount of help as people who have only lived in NZ. This is outlined under sections 187-191 in the Social Security Act 2018.

chunks.title: Going overseas
chunks.text:
## Going overseas
If you get any payments from us, you may need to tell us about your travel plans before you leave New Zealand. It depends what payments you get from us. Going overseas may also affect your payments.
## Getting NZ Super or Veteran's Pension

Examples of other payments are:
