chunks.title: Public transport fares
chunks.text: You can get a 50% discount on single-trip adult fares on public transport if you have a Community Services Card. This discount is part of the Community Connect programme. You need to apply for the discount through your local transport provider. Check with your local public transport provider what discounts are available and which ones are the best for you.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You can get the Community Connect discount if you have a Community Services Card (CSC). More information on who can get a CSC is on our page:

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: First, you need to apply for a Community Services Card if you don't already have one. Once you have a Community Services Card, you can apply for the Community Connect discount through your local transport provider. Visit your local transport provider's website to find out how to apply. We've listed some of them in the table below. You can get a free travel card when you apply for Community Connect. You may need to load a minimum of $5 onto the new card. Check with your local transport provider for more information.

chunks.title: Transport provider information
chunks.text: Community Connect - AT HOPexternal Christchurch:Community Connect - Metro/Christchurchexternal Timaru:Community Connect - Metro/Timaruexternal Metlink - Concessionsexternal Northland,Waikato,Bay of Plenty,Gisborne,Taranaki,Manawatū-Whanganui,Hawkes Bay,Nelson,Otago,Invercargill

chunks.title: SuperGold card and the Community Services Card
chunks.text: If you have a SuperGold card you can already travel for free on public transport at off-peak times. If you have a Community Services Card (CSC) as well as a SuperGold card, or a combo card, you can apply for a 50% discount at peak travel-times as well. SuperGold Card In most cases, you need one travel card for each discount. If you want discounted travel during on- and off-peak times, you may need two travel cards.You could have the: - SuperGold discount, for free off-peak travel on one card, and - Community Connect discount on a second travel card. See your local public transport provider’s website for more information and how to apply.

chunks.title: Letting us know your public transport costs have changed
chunks.text: If you have public transport included as a cost for payments such as Disability Allowance or Temporary Additional Support, please tell us your new costs when you start using the Community Connect discount. This may affect the amount you get for these types of payments.

chunks.title: Re-apply, review or renew
chunks.text: You may have to re-apply for a benefit or payment, review your circumstances or income, or renew a medical certificate.

chunks.title: Re-apply for a benefit or payment
chunks.text: There are certain benefits or payments that you may have to re-apply for after a certain period of time. - Reapply for Jobseeker Support Re-apply for Jobseeker Support every 26 weeks.

chunks.title: Reapply for Jobseeker Support
chunks.text: Re-apply for Jobseeker Support every 26 weeks. - Reapply for Sole Parent Support Re-apply for Sole Parent Support every 52 weeks.

chunks.title: Reapply for Sole Parent Support
chunks.text: Re-apply for Sole Parent Support every 52 weeks. - Reapply for Temporary Additional Support (TAS) Re-apply for Temporary Additional Support every 13 weeks.

chunks.title: Other payments
chunks.text: If you get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit, you need to re-apply for this payment every year between mid-January and the end of February. - School and Year Start-up Payment Re-apply each year to keep getting the School and Year Start-up Payment.

chunks.title: School and Year Start-up Payment
chunks.text: Re-apply each year to keep getting the School and Year Start-up Payment. - Extraordinary Care Fund Re-apply during the approved dates to keep getting this payment.

chunks.title: Renew your medical certificate or information
chunks.text: You may need to renew your medical certificate or medical information at certain times. It depends what payment you get as to what you have to do. - Renew your medical certificate or information Find out when you need to renew your medical information.

chunks.title: Re-confirm your details
chunks.text: If you get a benefit or payment, there are some situations where you have to re-confirm your details.

chunks.title: Child turning 18
chunks.text: We can only include your 18-year-old in your payments if they are still in education and financially dependent on you. The easiest way to do this is to fill out a Child turning 18 online form. Child turning 18 formexternal If you're not supporting them at the moment, you need to get in touch with us. Phone us - Child turning 18 Find out what you need to do when a child in your care turns 18.

chunks.title: Child turning 18
chunks.text: Find out what you need to do when a child in your care turns 18.

chunks.title: Review of circumstances and annual income
chunks.text: You may have to confirm your circumstances or review your income every year. It depends on what payment you get. This is to make sure you're getting everything you're entitled to and that we're paying you the right amount. - Confirming your circumstances Confirm your circumstances to make sure you're getting the right support.

chunks.title: Confirming your circumstances
chunks.text: Confirm your circumstances to make sure you're getting the right support. - Review of annual income Review your income to make sure you're being paid the right amount.

chunks.title: Reapply for Temporary Additional Support (TAS)
chunks.text: If you're getting Temporary Additional Support and you still need it after 13 weeks, you have to re-apply. You need to do this before your payment stops.

chunks.title: Who can reapply
chunks.text: You can reapply for Temporary Additional Support if you still meet the criteria. Temporary Additional Support You must also have taken: - all necessary steps to try and pay your expenses another way, e.g.: if your circumstances have changed, use our 'Check what you might get' tool to see if there's any other payments you could get if you're working, check if you can get Working for Families payments from Inland Revenue - if your circumstances have changed, use our 'Check what you might get' tool to see if there's any other payments you could get - if you're working, check if you can get Working for Families payments from Inland Revenue - reasonable steps to increase your income and reduce your costs, e.g.: getting budgeting advice stopping paid subscriptions, e.g. Netflix, Sky, Spotify looking for paid work or increasing your hours of work. - getting budgeting advice - stopping paid subscriptions, e.g. Netflix, Sky, Spotify - looking for paid work or increasing your hours of work.

chunks.title: How to reapply
chunks.text: You'll get a letter (with a re-application form), as well as a notification in MyMSD, at least 4 weeks before you need to re-apply for Temporary Additional Support. You need to re-apply before your Temporary Additional Support stops. If you don't, we can only start it again from the date you re-apply. This may mean you have a gap in your payments.

chunks.title: Reapply in MyMSD
chunks.text: To re-apply in MyMSD you need to: - log in to MyMSD - select re-apply - complete the online form - upload any documents, if required - submit the online form. If there's been a change to your partner or child details, you'll need to talk with us. MyMSD will let you know if you need to do this. myMSD login

chunks.title: Can't use MyMSD
chunks.text: If you can't use MyMSD, you can either: - call us and say "Temporary Additional Support" and we may be able to help you re-apply over the phone, or - complete the re-application form we sent you and drop it off to your local service centre We'll let you know if there are any documents you need to provide. You'll need to drop these off to your local service centre. Local service centre

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: Once your online form has been processed, we'll send you a letter to let you know the outcome.

chunks.title: Re-establishment grant
chunks.text: The Re-establishment grant is a payment to help people in specific circumstances re-establish themselves in the community. A re-establishment grant can pay for things like: - accommodation, including bond and rent in advance - beds, bedding and essential appliances - a fridge, freezer or washing machine - connecting electricity, gas and telephone - clothing - cost of attending English language classes, including transport costs - translation costs for work-related documents.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You must meet the qualifications for a Special Needs Grant. If you're an Afghan evacuee and have an Afghan Emergency Resettlement Visa, you don't need to meet the residency criteria for a Special Needs Grant. You also need to be re-establishing yourself in the community and be in one of the following situations: - you're a refugee who isn't entitled to other forms of government assistance for refugees - you're a sole parent who: is a victim of family violence is being assisted by a social service agency (e.g. Women's Refuge) to relocate after the initial separation, and has no other resources - is a victim of family violence - is being assisted by a social service agency (e.g. Women's Refuge) to relocate after the initial separation, and - has no other resources - you're a patient in hospital or a residential home for more than 6 months - you've just been released from a custody period of 31 days or more - you're an Afghan interpreter who has a residence class visa - you're an Afghan evacuee who either: is a New Zealand citizen has a residence class visa (including an Afghan Emergency Resettlement Visa), or has applied for an Afghan Emergency Resettlement Visa, or - is a New Zealand citizen - has a residence class visa (including an Afghan Emergency Resettlement Visa), or - has applied for an Afghan Emergency Resettlement Visa, or - you're in a 'Transition from Care to Independence' initiative with Oranga Tamariki and: 16 or older have been in supported care under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 leaving supported care to live independently have a letter from your personal advisor verifying that you're participating in this initiative and have a youth transition payment. - 16 or older - have been in supported care under the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 - leaving supported care to live independently - have a letter from your personal advisor verifying that you're participating in this initiative and - have a youth transition payment. Re-establishment grants are considered on a case-by-case basis.

chunks.title: Sole parent and victim of family violence
chunks.text: You can get up to $800 for accommodation costs but you have to pay this back. You can get up to $600 for other costs and you don't have to pay this back.

chunks.title: Long-term hospital or residential home
chunks.text: You can get up to $800 for accommodation costs but you have to pay this back. You can get up to $1,200 for other costs and you don't have to pay this back.

chunks.title: Refugee, Afghan interpreter or Afghan evacuee
chunks.text: You can get up to a total of $5,000. Of that $5,000, you can get up to $3,500 for accommodation costs. You don't have to pay back any of the $5,000.

chunks.title: Released from custody
chunks.text: You can get up to $350 for all costs and you don't have to pay this back.

chunks.title: Transition from care to independence initiative
chunks.text: You can get up to $800 for accommodation costs but you have to pay this back. You can get up to $1,200 for other costs and you don't have to pay this back.

chunks.title: You're a refugee, Aghan interpreter or Afghan evacuee
chunks.text: You need to apply within the first year of your arrival in New Zealand. If you're applying for help with English language classes, you can apply within the first 2 years of your arrival in NZ.

chunks.title: Using NZ Realm countries to meet residence criteria for NZ Super and Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: You need to have lived in New Zealand for a certain amount of time to get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension. If you haven't, you may be able to use time you've lived in NZ Realm countries to meet this criteria. NZ Realm countries are the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau.

chunks.title: Residence criteria
chunks.text: You must have lived in NZ for a certain number of years from age 20. This must include 5 years from age 50. The total number of years you need is based on your date of birth. If you're a refugee or protected person, this may be different depending on the age you started living in NZ. These years (including the 5 years from age 50) do not need to be consecutive. Work out how many years you need

chunks.title: Residence criteria in other languages
chunks.text: You can read the residence criteria in Cook Island Māori, Niuean or Tokelauan. Residence criteria in other languages

chunks.title: Using a NZ Realm country to meet residence criteria
chunks.text: Of the total number of years, you need to have lived in NZ for at least 10 years from age 20. For the rest of the years, you can include time you've spent living in NZ, the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau (or a combination of these). When we say 'have lived in a NZ realm country', we mean you were 'resident' and 'physically present' in the realm country at the same time.

chunks.title: How to meet the residence criteria
chunks.text: Add together your time in: - NZ from age 20 (must be at least 10 years), and - the NZ Realm country (or countries) from age 20. This needs to add up to the total number of years you need to meet the residence criteria. The total must include 5 years from age 50 (you can use your time in the NZ Realm country, or countries, for the 5 years too). If you want to talk about your situation, contact our International Services team. International Services

chunks.title: If you don't meet residence criteria using NZ Realm countries
chunks.text: You may have spent time living in, or contributing to the pension scheme of, a Social Security Agreement (SSA) country. If so, you may be able to use this time to meet the residence criteria as well. If you're ordinarily resident in a NZ Realm country when you apply for NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, you usually cannot use time from an SSA country. You may be able to use time from some SSA countries (Australia, Canada, Denmark, Ireland, Malta and the Netherlands) if you meet certain criteria. If you want to talk about your situation, contact our International Services team. Contact International Services team Using SSA countries to meet residence criteria for NZ Super

chunks.title: Resident in a realm country
chunks.text: Being resident in a realm country means you permanently made your home in the realm country. In most cases, you'll be resident in a realm country if you lived there on a permanent basis for the required number of years. In other cases, we may need to consider other things to work out if you've been resident in a realm country. To do this, we'll look at your involvement in the realm country's society, e.g. your: - employment - community activities - club memberships, and - local churches.

chunks.title: Physically present in a realm country
chunks.text: To work this out, we'll look at if you were physically in the realm country for the required number of years. If you left the realm country, you weren't physically present in that realm country for that period of time. For example, if you went on holiday for: - 25 days, you weren't physically present in the realm country for 25 days. This means you would need to have lived in the realm country for an extra 25 days to make up what is required - 14 days every year for 10 years, that's 140 days in total. This means you weren't physically present in the realm country for 140 days. So you would need to have lived in the realm country for an extra 140 days to make up what is required.

chunks.title: Examples
chunks.text: You were born in NZ on 12 May 1978. At age 25 you moved to the Cook Islands and you still live there. You apply for NZ Super (from the Cook Islands) when you turn 65. Based on your date of birth, you must have lived in NZ for at least 20 years from age 20. The 20 years must include 5 years from age 50. To meet the residence criteria, you can use the time you've lived in the Cook Islands. Of the 20 years, you must have lived: - at least 10 years in NZ, and - the rest of the years in NZ or the Cook Islands. In this example, you have: - 5 years living in NZ from age 20-25 - 40 years living in the Cook Islands from age 25-65. You would not meet the residence criteria as you have only lived in NZ for 5 years from age 20. You were born in NZ on 12 May 1963. You moved to Tokelau at age 30. You move back to NZ at age 65 and apply for NZ Super. Based on your date of birth, you must have lived in NZ for at least 12 years from age 20. The 12 years must include 5 years from age 50. To meet the residence criteria, you can use the time you've lived in Tokelau. Of the 12 years you must have lived: - at least 10 years in NZ - the rest of the years in NZ or Tokelau. In this example, you have: - 10 years living in NZ from age 20-30, and - 35 years living in Tokelau from age 30-65. This means you meet the residence criteria for NZ Super because you have: - 10 years living in NZ and - the rest of the years living in Tokelau. This includes the 5 years over 50. You were born in NZ on 1 February 1979. You moved to Niue at age 60. You apply for NZ Super from Niue when you turn 65. Based on your date of birth, you must have lived in NZ for at least 20 years from age 20. The 20 years must include 5 years from age 50. To meet the residence criteria, you can use the time you've lived in Niue. These 20 years must be made up of: - at least 10 years living in NZ - the other 10 years living in NZ or Niue. In this example, you have:

chunks.title: Examples
chunks.text: - 40 years living in NZ from age 20-60, and - 5 years living in Niue from age 60-65. This means you meet the residence criteria for NZ Super because you have: - 10 years living in NZ and - the rest of the years living in NZ and Niue. This includes the 5 years over 50.

chunks.title: Recoverable Assistance Payment
chunks.text: A Recoverable Assistance Payment is a one-off payment to help you pay an essential or emergency cost if you can't pay it another way. You don't qualify for this payment if you're on a benefit. You have to pay the money back.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Recoverable Assistance Payment if you: - don't get a benefit from us - have an essential or emergency cost you can't pay for - have no other way to pay for this cost - are either a: New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - New Zealand citizen or - permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here. It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have.

chunks.title: Current income limits
chunks.text: Single and 16 to 17 years old $45,716.84 Single and 18 years old or over $52,541.32 Couple (with or without children) $76,315.72 Sole parent with 1 child $63,756.68 Sole parent with 2 or more children $67,171

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: How much you get depends on your situation and what you need help with. Examples of costs we can help with are: - ambulance subscription fees - attendance at funerals and tangihanga - beds, chairs and tables - car repairs - child car seat - clothing - costs to end your tenancy early, or sublet or assign your tenancy - dentures and hearing aids - driver licence - electricity, gas or water - fire loss or burglary - fridges, freezes and washing machines - glasses - school costs - school stationery - school uniforms - tenancy tribunal fees - travel if you're stranded. We may be able to help with other costs, it depends on your situation. If you're not sure whether we can help, talk with us about your situation.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: If your application is approved, we'll give you a payment card (if you don't already have one) and load the money onto it. We'll talk to you about how to get this to you. You have 7 days to spend the money before it expires.

chunks.title: Using your payment card
chunks.text: A payment card is like an Eftpos card and you can use it at any supermarket or store that accepts them. Information about Payment Cards You can login to MyMSD to see how much you have left on your payment card and when it expires. Find out more about MyMSD Once you've used your payment card, keep it. You can use it again if you need help from us in the future.

chunks.title: Refugees or protected persons residence criteria to get NZ Super and Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: You need to have lived in New Zealand for a certain amount of time to get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension. Find out how we work this out if you're recognised as a refugee or protected person. You must have lived in NZ for a certain number of years from age 20. This must include 5 years from age 50. These years (including the 5 years from age 50) do not need to be consecutive.

chunks.title: Find out how many years you need
chunks.text: Select the age you were when you started living in NZ to find out how many years you need. In each of these situations, you still need to have lived in New Zealand for at least 5 years since you turned 50. If you want to talk about your situation, contact our International Services team. International Services

chunks.title: Before age 45
chunks.text: How many years you need is based on your date of birth. Use the table on the 'Who can get NZ Super' page to find out how many years you need based on your date of birth. Who can get NZ Super

chunks.title: Example - started living in New Zealand at age 40
chunks.text: You started living in New Zealand as a refugee at age 40. You apply for NZ Super when you turn 65. You were born on 15 February 1980 so you must have lived in New Zealand for at least 20 years. The 20 years must include 5 years since you turned 50. You have lived in New Zealand for 25 years, including 5 years since you turned 50. This means you meet the residence criteria for NZ Super.

chunks.title: From age 45 to 54
chunks.text: You need the shorter time of either: - the number of years between when you started living in New Zealand and your 65th birthday, or - between 10 and 20 years - use the table on the 'Who can get NZ Super' page to find out how many years you need based on your date of birth. Who can get NZ Super

chunks.title: Example - started living in New Zealand at age 50
chunks.text: You started living in New Zealand as a refugee at age 50. You apply for NZ Super when you turn 65. Your date of birth is 10 September 1978. The total number of years you must have lived in New Zealand is the shorter time of either: - the 15 years between when you started living in New Zealand and your 65th birthday, or - 20 years (based on your date of birth). The shorter of these is 15 years, so this is the number of years you would need. The 15 years must include 5 years since you turned 50. This means you would meet the residence criteria for NZ Super.

chunks.title: Example - started living in New Zealand at age 60
chunks.text: You started living in New Zealand as a refugee at age 60. You apply for NZ Super when you turn 65. You've only lived in New Zealand for 5 years, from 60-65. This means you won't meet the residence criteria for NZ Super until you turn 70.

chunks.title: Don't meet the required years
chunks.text: You may be able to use other countries to meet this residence criteria if: - they are a country that has a Social Security Agreement with New Zealand, or - they are a New Zealand realm country (the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau). Using SSA countries to meet residence criteria for NZ Super Using NZ Realm countries to meet residence criteria for NZ Super

chunks.title: Relocate for Work Support
chunks.text: We may be able to help with travel and moving costs if you're relocating for a new job. You must apply for this payment before you move for your new job.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You need to meet the criteria below for: - yourself, and - your new job.

chunks.title: Criteria for yourself
chunks.text: You must: - be getting a main benefit (e.g. Jobseeker Support) - agree to cancel your main benefit from when you start your new job - be aged either: 8-64 years old, or 65 or older and don't qualify for NZ Super or Veteran's Pension - 8-64 years old, or - 65 or older and don't qualify for NZ Super or Veteran's Pension - be likely to need a main benefit for a long time if you don't get this job - have organised a new place to live near your new job that's suitable for you and your family - have been unable to get a job in your current location - have not received any other payments from us for relocating for the same job, and - have applied for this payment before moving for your new job. We'll also look at: - any cash assets you or your partner have - whether you or your partner have been paid 'Relocate for Work Support' or '$5k to Work' in the last 52 weeks.

chunks.title: Criteria for your new job
chunks.text: You must have accepted an offer for a job in New Zealand, which must: - be either: 30 hours or more a week, or less than 30 hours a week if your pay is at least the same as 30 hours a week at minimum wage, or 20 hours a week if you're a sole parent and you only have part-time work obligations - 30 hours or more a week, or - less than 30 hours a week if your pay is at least the same as 30 hours a week at minimum wage, or - 20 hours a week if you're a sole parent and you only have part-time work obligations - pay at least minimum wage - be permanent, or fixed term, for at least 12 months - be too far away to commute from where you live now, and - be suitable for your skills, abilities and situation.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Relocate for Work can help to pay towards: - travel expenses, and - the cost of moving your possessions, if needed. For example, you need to hire a truck or trailer because you can't fit them in your car.

chunks.title: Travel expenses
chunks.text: The maximum amount you can get depends on the method of transport and how many people in your family are moving. - If you're travelling by land, and air or sea, you will only get the amount for air or sea. - If you're travelling by one method and your family is travelling by another, you will only get the amount for air or sea.

chunks.title: Moving your possessions
chunks.text: You can only get this cost if you need it. The maximum amount you can get depends on how far you're moving and how many people in your family are moving.

chunks.title: Step 1 - Complete the application form
chunks.text: You need to complete the PDF application form. You can download and print it. If you can't print it, you can call us to get one posted to you, or you can pick up one from our service centres. Alternatively, you can arrive early for your appointment (see step 3) to complete the form in the service centre.

chunks.title: Step 2 - Gather your documents
chunks.text: You need to bring to your appointment: - proof of your new job offer, with the start date, number of hours, and duration of the contract - proof of what you did to try find work in your current area, e.g. job applications submitted or rejection letters, and - proof you have new accommodation arranged, e.g. a tenancy agreement or confirmation from family or friends you'll be staying with them.

chunks.title: Step 3 - Call us to book an appointment
chunks.text: Call us on 0800 559 009 to book an appointment at your local service centre.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: We’ll usually grant or decline your application at your appointment. If your application's approved, we'll pay the money into your bank account. You may need to pay the money back if one of these things happens (unless there's a good reason): - you don't use the money for what it's intended for - you don't relocate within 28 days of getting the payment, or - you re-apply for a main benefit or Student Allowance within 6 months (182 days) of the date you're due to start your new job.

chunks.title: Renew your medical certificate or information
chunks.text: You may need to renew your medical certificate or medical information at certain times. It depends what payment you get as to what you have to do.

chunks.title: Jobseeker Support
chunks.text: If you have a health condition, injury or disability that impacts your ability to work, you would have provided a medical certificate. The medical certificate will show your medical coverage. This is a period of time where your health practitioner has determined that you can't work due to your health condition, injury or disability.

chunks.title: Medical coverage is due to expire
chunks.text: If your medical coverage is due to expire while you're getting Jobseeker Support, you'll need to provide another medical certificate. We'll write to you 4 weeks before your coverage expires asking you to either: - renew your medical certificate, or - tell us you're ready to look for work. If you're going to renew your medical certificate, you must do this before your medical coverage expires. If you can't renew it before the expiry date, contact us as soon as you can.

chunks.title: Find out when your medical coverage expires
chunks.text: You can use MyMSD to find out when your medical coverage expires. It's listed in the 'My Profile' section. You can also call us on 0800 559 009. MyMSD

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment
chunks.text: When you applied, you would have provided information that confirms your condition and the impact it has on your ability to work. Every 2 years we may ask you for updated medical information. We may ask for this even if your health condition or disability is permanent or hasn’t changed. This is to check how your health condition or disability currently impacts on your capacity to work. This will help us understand what support you need from us, and whether you’re able to work right now or in the future.

chunks.title: If you need to complete a review
chunks.text: We’ll write to you if you need to complete a Supported Living Payment review. We’ll ask you to show us a recently completed Work Capacity Medical Certificate completed by a health practitioner. If we need further information, we’ll let you know. If you can’t provide this information, or you want to see one of our designated doctors, call us to let us know.

chunks.title: Situations when you won't need to complete a review
chunks.text: We won't ask you to complete a Supported Living Payment review if you: - are totally blind - are terminally ill - have a severe intellectual or cognitive impairment - have a disorder that severely impacts on your ability to function and care for yourself and is unlikely to improve. How to tell us if something changes

chunks.title: Disability Allowance
chunks.text: You would have provided a Disability Certificate when you applied for Disability Allowance. The Disability Certificate shows the expected duration of the disability. This is how long your health practitioner has determined that you may have the disability for. Once you're getting a Disability Allowance, we may do a full review of this payment if: - your Disability Allowance has not been reviewed in the last 44 weeks or, - your medical condition or disability is due for reassessment. If we do a full review, we'll send you a 'Confirming your Circumstances' form. You have 25 working days to complete and sign the form and provide any relevant verification. This may include a Disability Certificate which you need to get your health practitioner to complete.

chunks.title: If the review is for your child
chunks.text: If the review is for your child, you'll need to get their health practitioner to complete the Disability Certificate. If you're also getting Child Disability Allowance for your child, this will be a separate review.

chunks.title: Child Disability Allowance
chunks.text: When you applied, your child's health practitioner would have completed a Medical Certificate. They would have let us know on the Medical Certificate when they think the child should next be reassessed for the Child Disability Allowance. We'll send you a letter 6 weeks before the reassessment date and then we'll send you a medical review form. You'll need to get the child's health practitioner to complete the medical review form. Then you'll need to send this back to us.

chunks.title: Rental income
chunks.text: You need to let us know if you get any type of rental income. This could be from someone renting a room, whole house, self-contained property or a non-accommodation property. If you don't tell us about rental income we may not pay you enough, or we may pay you too much and you'll have to pay the debt back.

chunks.title: What is rent
chunks.text: A renter is someone whose accommodation costs cover the room or property they stay in or use. This may also include services costs (e.g. gardening).

chunks.title: How much of your rent payments count as income
chunks.text: How much of a rent payment counts as income depends on the type of rent you're being paid for.

chunks.title: Rent payments from someone who lives with you
chunks.text: If someone lives with you and is paying you rent, we work out the income from this by: - looking at how much rent you are paid - comparing this to your accommodation costs If the rent payment is higher than your accommodation costs, we work out the difference – that difference counts as income. If the rent payment is lower than your accommodation costs, the rent payment does not count as income. However, it will affect the amount of any housing subsidy you get from us.

chunks.title: Rent payments for a property you don't live in
chunks.text: If someone is renting a property from you that you own but do not live in, some of the rent money can be used for certain expenses without it affecting your benefit. These expenses include: - interest payments earned on the money borrowed to buy the property - rates - house insurance - fees and commission if a property manager or agent is used - repairs and maintenance - other fees e.g. bank administration fees for the mortgage, tenancy agreement costs, any valuation required by your bank, accounting fees. Any rent payments you receive after these costs are paid is considered income.

chunks.title: Rent payments for a self-contained part of the property
chunks.text: If the self-contained part of the property is a granny flat or unit, it must have a kitchen or kitchenette and a bathroom. If it's a mobile home it needs to have facilities for: - day-to-day living - sleeping - preparing and cooking food. It must also have a: - sink - toilet - fresh water tank - waste water tank. To work out how much of the self-contained property's rent payments count as income, we: - look at the accommodation costs for the whole property - look at what proportion of the whole property is self-contained, to work out the percentage that you live in - reduce the accommodation costs for the whole property to the percentage that is self-contained - the final amount is your personal accommodation costs. If that final amount is lower than the rent payment for the self-contained dwelling, these rent payments do not count as income. If that final amount is higher than the rent payment for the self-contained dwelling, we work out the difference – that difference counts as income.

chunks.title: Rent payments for non-accommodation property
chunks.text: Non-accommodation property is when someone rents an area of your property, but they do not live there, e.g. a garage used for storage. All the rent payment you receive for this type of rent is considered income.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: The easiest way to tell us is online in MyMSD. Once you've logged in, select: - 'Declare boarders and renters' to let us know about rent payments from people who live with you, or - 'Declare wages' to let us know about any other payments you get for a rental property. When you 'Declare boarders and renters' in MyMSD, you need to tell us: - the address - details of the person paying you rent - how much the rent is - when you get paid, and how often. We will continue to use this amount every week, so make sure you let us know if it stops or changes. If you can't use MyMSD to tell us about renters who live with you, you can also fill out our PDF form: You need to print this form, complete it, and either post it to us or bring it into one of our services centres. You can also pick one up from any of our service centres. Find a service centre If you need to tell us about other payments you get for a rental property and you can't use MyMSD, you can call us. Phone us

chunks.title: Repaying debt if you're not getting a benefit or pension
chunks.text: If you're not getting a main benefit, NZ Super, Veteran's Pension, or Accommodation Supplement you can set up a repayment arrangement to pay off your debt. We can work with you on a repayment plan that suits you. Go to the page 'Your debt with us' if you want information about: - how to get a breakdown of your debt - what to do if you don't agree with your debt - support for managing your debt - if someone has died and had a debt with us. Your debt with us

chunks.title: Debt repayment information
chunks.text: If you're getting a main benefit, NZ Super, Veteran's Pension or Accommodation Supplement, there's a different process for your debt repayments. What we mean by 'main benefit' Repaying debt while getting a benefit or pension

chunks.title: Help with your debt
chunks.text: If you need help with your debt or want to talk about it, you can contact our Client Support Debt Management team. Phone us

chunks.title: Debt repayment amount
chunks.text: Below is a guide of how much you could repay. This is just a guide, it depends how much you can afford. When deciding how much your repayments should be, you'll need to think of things like: - your budget - your upcoming expenses - any other debts you may have - how long you want to be repaying the money. You need to contact our Client Support Debt Management team about your repayment amount. They'll work with you on a repayment plan based on what you can afford. Phone us When you call, they'll ask you: - your contact details, e.g. address, phone and email - about your income - about your expenses - if you have any dependent children. You may be asked to provide proof.

chunks.title: Setting up debt repayments
chunks.text: We want to help you repay your debt in a way that best suits your situation. We have a range of repayment options available, it depends if you're making payments from New Zealand or overseas. How to repay debt from New Zealand How to repay debt from overseas

chunks.title: While repaying your debt - tell us about any changes
chunks.text: If you have a change in circumstances while repaying your debt, you need to contact our Client Support Debt Management team. Phone us This could be changes for: - your address - your contact details - if you go overseas. If you get a new job, let our Client Support Debt Management team know before you start. Then they can arrange for repayments to be deducted from your wages with your new employer.

chunks.title: If you miss a debt repayment
chunks.text: If you miss a repayment, we'll send you a reminder letter. We don't charge penalties or interest. If you're having trouble repaying your debt, contact our Client Support Debt Management team. They can work with you on a repayment plan that suits you. Phone us

chunks.title: If you don't repay your debt
chunks.text: We understand that it can be hard to stretch your budget to include debt repayments. If you're struggling to repay your debt, contact our Client Support Debt Management team. They can work with you on a repayment plan based on what you can afford. Phone us We won't charge interest or impose penalties on your debt. We'll try to contact you several times about your debt. If you don't respond, we'll seek to get the money back in other ways. To find out your current circumstances, we compare information with other government agencies, e.g. Inland Revenue. There are legal steps we can take which allow us to recover your debt without your consent, such as: - making deductions from your wages, or - making deductions from your bank account. If you don't pay back your debt, it could affect what financial help you can get from us in the future.

chunks.title: Repaying debt while getting a benefit or pension
chunks.text: If you're getting a main benefit, NZ Super, Veteran's Pension or Accommodation Supplement, we'll work with you on a repayment plan that suits you. You can also set up a separate repayment arrangement if you want to. Go to the page 'Your debt with us' if you want information about: - how to get a breakdown of your debt - what to do if you don't agree with your debt - support for managing your debt. Your debt with us

chunks.title: Debt repayment information
chunks.text: If you're not getting a main benefit, NZ Super, Veteran's Pension or Accommodation Supplement, there's a different process for your debt repayments. What we mean by 'main benefit' Repaying debt if you're not getting a benefit or pension

chunks.title: Debt repayment amount
chunks.text: We'll set up a repayment amount depending on your circumstances. We want to make sure this is affordable for you. When deciding how much your repayments should be, you'll need to think of things like: - your budget - your upcoming expenses - any other debts you may have - how long you want to be repaying the money. Call us on 0800 559 009 to: - discuss debt repayments - set up a time to talk to your case manager, if you want to - talk to us about any questions you have about your debt.

chunks.title: Setting up debt repayments
chunks.text: Call us on 0800 559 009 to set up debt repayments. We'll set these up so they come out of your benefit, pension or Accommodation Supplement. If you want to pay the debt off faster you can make extra repayments at any time. You can also set up a separate repayment arrangement via internet or telephone banking if you want to. If you're getting a Student Allowance, you need to contact StudyLink. Contact us (Studylink)external

chunks.title: Set up repayment via internet or telephone banking
chunks.text: You can make a one-off payment or set up regular payments using internet or telephone banking. Your bank may charge you for these services. To set up the payments you'll need the account number: 03-0049-0006243-025. If your bank only needs a 2 digit suffix, use 25 instead of 025. Once you enter the account number, your bank may match it to the account name it uses for us. If your bank doesn't match it, you can use the account name 'Work and Income Debt Management'. In the reference field, you need to put the letter 'S', followed by your 9 digit client number.

chunks.title: If your benefit, pension or Accommodation Supplement is about to stop
chunks.text: If you owe us money and your benefit, pension or Accommodation Supplement is about to stop, you need to call us on 0800 559 009 to: - let us know when your payment needs to stop - arrange an exit interview with us where we can discuss your repayment options. You'll be able to pay your debt off either: - in a lump sum, or - each week at an amount you can afford.

chunks.title: If you're going into full-time work
chunks.text: If you’re going into full-time work and can get Assistance to Transition into Employment, you may be able to stop repaying your debt for 3 months. This is called a 3 month debt recovery suspension. This is to help you pay for work related costs. Talk to us at your exit interview about whether you qualify for this payment.

chunks.title: Repaying a previous COVID-19 payment
chunks.text:
## Repaying a previous COVID-19 payment
Find out when you need to repay a previous COVID-19 payment and how to repay it.
Businesses could apply for a COVID-19 payment to help to pay their employees, including self-employed people. This includes the COVID-19 Wage Subsidies, the Leave Support Scheme and the Short-Term Absence Payment.
## When you need to repay
You need to repay some or all of a COVID-19 payment if you or your employee were not eligible for it during the payment timeframe. This could be because something changed later on.
You may have to make a repayment if:
- you no longer meet the criteria for the payment
- you did not use the payment to keep or pay your staff
- you provided false or misleading information in your application
- your employee has resigned, been dismissed, or no longer meets the criteria for the payment (you can use the money to pay other affected employees, or repay it)
- your employee has been made redundant or their contract finished (you need to repay the remaining amount after you've paid them their wage)
- your business has closed
- you applied for the wrong payment rate (e.g. you applied for a full-time rate when you only need the part-time rate)
- you're self-employed and your regular business income is less than the COVID-19 payment (you need to repay the surplus)
- you're a state sector organisation who didn't have an exception approved, oryour business got a payment it is not entitled to due to a Ministry of Social Development error.
## How to make a repayment
You can make a repayment by filling out our online 'Repayment request' form:
You'll need to tell us your:
- business name
- IRD number
- New Zealand Business Number (NZBN), if you have one
- phone number
- email address
- postal address, and
- the amount you need to repay.
Repayment requestexternal
Once we process the form, we'll be in touch to confirm how to make the repayment.

chunks.title: Residential care
chunks.text: If you need full-time care in a hospital, rest home or residential treatment programme, you may be able to get help to pay for some of the cost of your care.

chunks.title: Your situation
chunks.text: The information here is just a guide. What payment you qualify for will depend on your individual circumstances.

chunks.title: 65 and over, need to be in a rest home or private hospital indefinitely
chunks.text: Residential Care Subsidy If you need to be in a rest home or private hospital indefinitely, a Residential Care Subsidy may be able to pay for some of your care. It will depend on your and your partner's assets and income. Residential Care Loan If you need to be in a rest home or private hospital indefinitely and want to keep your own home, a Residential Care Loan may be able to pay for some of your care.

chunks.title: Under 65, need to be in a rest home or private hospital
chunks.text: Residential Support Subsidy If you're under 65 and need to be in residential care, a private hospital or disability residential services, a Residential Support Subsidy may be able to pay for some of your care. Residential Care Subsidy If you're 50-64 and need to be in a rest home or private hospital indefinitely, a Residential Care Subsidy may be able to pay for some of your care instead of a Residential Support Subsidy. It depends on your situation. Community Costs Payment You may be able to get a Community Costs Payment if you: - are getting a Residential Support Subsidy - need to be in a residential treatment programme for less than 39 weeks - still have costs such as rent and childcare to pay.

chunks.title: Getting a Residential Care Loan or Residential Support Subsidy
chunks.text: If some of your care is being paid for by a Residential Care Loan or a Residential Support Subsidy, you may also be able to get a Disability Allowance to help cover costs such as medical fees, prescriptions, etc. Disability Allowance

chunks.title: Partner in care
chunks.text: If you're getting a benefit and your partner is in residential care, or has been in a public hospital for over 13 weeks, you may be able to get a Special Disability Allowance to help with the extra costs of your partner being in care. Special Disability Allowance

chunks.title: Coming out of care
chunks.text: If you've lived in a private hospital or residential home for 6 months or more, and are now setting yourself up independently in the community, you may be able to get a Re-establishment Grant. Re-establishment Grant

chunks.title: More information
chunks.text: Call us to talk about your situation - 0800 999 727 - if you need to be in a rest home or private hospital indefinitely. - 0800 999 779 - if you need care for rehabilitation, mental health, an intellectual disability or chronic health condition.

chunks.title: Residential Care Loan
chunks.text: If you’re going into residential care and want to keep your home for a while, you may not be able to pay for the cost of your care. You may be able to get a Residential Care Loan to help pay for this. We look at each loan application on a case-by-case basis. There is no obligation to approve a loan. Before you apply for a Residential Care Loan, check if you qualify for a Residential Care Subsidy. This a subsidy that will help pay for your care and you don't have to pay it back. Residential Care Subsidy

chunks.title: What is a Residential Care Loan
chunks.text: A Residential Care Loan is an agreement with the Crown to provide a loan for the cost of your care. It's secured by placing a caveat over your home. It's an interest-free loan paid directly to the rest home. It's usually repaid when you pass away or your home's sold, whichever happens first. The Ministry of Health pays for the loan. We do things like: - prepare loan agreements and other documents - a financial means assessment - handle settlements.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Residential Care Loan if: - you still own the home you lived in before going into residential care - your home is worth more than $300,811 in assets (if it's less, you may qualify for a Residential Care Subsidy) - the total of any other assets you own is less than $15,000 if you're single, or $30,000 if you have a partner. To approve your application, we'll also check that: - it fits within the loan scheme - we can secure the loan with a caveat over your home - you'll be able to repay the loan and meet your obligations under the loan agreement.

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: If you get a Residential Care Loan, it will be paid directly to the rest home to help pay for your care. How much you can get depends on the rest home fees and where you live. We call this the 'maximum contribution'. The loan amount covers the ‘maximum contribution’ minus ‘your contribution’.

chunks.title: Your contribution and personal allowance
chunks.text: If you get a benefit or pension, most of it will also go to the rest home. This is your contribution. If you're getting NZ Super, the current contribution rate is $454.11 per week. You'll keep $58.34 a week (after tax on an M tax code). This is called a personal allowance.

chunks.title: Example
chunks.text: If you live in Auckland City and the rest home fee is $1,511.09 a week, the maximum loan you can get is: $1,511.09 - $454.11 (rest home fee minus your contribution) = $1,056.98

chunks.title: Step 1 - Contact a Needs Assessor
chunks.text: You need to get in touch with a Needs Assessor in your area. They will: - assess your residential care needs and - give you a ‘Residential Care Subsidy Application’ form. For contact details of a Needs Assessor in your area, call the health Seniorline on 0800 725 463.

chunks.title: Step 2 - Fill out an application form
chunks.text: The 'Residential Care Loan' application is also in the form the Needs Assessor gives you. You need to complete the entire form.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: First, we'll check your assets to see how much they're worth. If they're worth less than $300,811, you may qualify for a Residential Care Subsidy instead of a loan. It can take 6-8 weeks to process your application. You may need to pay for the full cost of your residential care while we process it. It's best to talk with your care provider about this. You need to pay for any costs that come with the loan application, e.g. registration of the caveat. These costs are not covered by the loan.

chunks.title: If we approve your loan
chunks.text: We'll send a loan agreement to your solicitor. You, or your power of attorney, need to sign the agreement and send it back to us. You also need to send us confirmation that: - the rates for your home are paid up to date - your home is insured. Then we'll register a caveat over your home. This will remain in place until the loan is repaid.

chunks.title: Payments
chunks.text: The Ministry of Health will pay the loan directly to the rest home. They will start the payments when all documentation is complete.

chunks.title: Transfer to Residential Care Subsidy
chunks.text: One of the criteria to get a Residential Care Loan is if your home and other assets are worth more than $300,811. Once your loan balance reduces your assets to less than $300,811, you may qualify for a Residential Care Subsidy instead.

chunks.title: How to transfer to a Residential Care Subsidy
chunks.text: The Ministry of Health will send you loan statements every 4 months. They'll let you know when you may be able to get a Residential Care Subsidy. You'll need to fill out a 'Financial means assessment' form so your assets can be reviewed. To get one of these forms, contact our Residential Subsidy Unit on 0800 999 727.

chunks.title: If a Residential Care Subsidy is approved
chunks.text: If a Residential Care Subsidy is approved, the Residential Care Loan will stop. We'll let you know the outstanding balance.

chunks.title: Repayment of the loan
chunks.text: The loan needs to be repaid when your home's sold or within 12 months of the date you pass away, whichever happens first. If there's a late repayment, interest may be charged at 10% a year, calculated on a daily basis.

chunks.title: Selling your home
chunks.text: Once your home's sold, we'll confirm the amount that needs to be repaid. It could be less than what we told you to start with. This is because we will deduct certain fees for example: - real estate agency fees - solicitor fees - protected equity - funeral allowance.

chunks.title: Can't repay within 12 months
chunks.text: There may be some situations where you can't repay the loan within 12 months. In these cases you may be able to defer the loan instead. How to defer your loanexternal

chunks.title: Residential Care Subsidy
chunks.text: If you need long-term residential care in a hospital or rest home, you may be able to get a Residential Care Subsidy from Health New Zealand - Te WhatuOra. This subsidy helps with the cost of care. It's paid directly to the hospital or rest home by Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Residential Care Subsidy if you: - are aged either: 65 or older, or 50-64 and single with no dependent children - 65 or older, or - 50-64 and single with no dependent children - are assessed as needing long-term residential care in a hospital or rest home - need this care for an indefinite length of time - are receiving contracted care services. It may also depend on: - any money or assets you and your partner (if you have one) have - how much you and your partner (if you have one) earn.

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: If you're 50-64 and single with no dependent children, you'll automatically meet the asset test. If you're 65 or older and: - single, your total assets must be $300,811 or less. - have a partner who is in long-term residential care, you and your partner's total assets must be $300,811 or less. If you're 65 or older and have a partner who's not in long-term residential care, you can choose whether to include the value of your family home and car in your assets. Your assets must be: - $164,731 or less, if you do not want to include the value of your family home and car, or - $300,811 or less, if you do want to include the value of your family home and car.

chunks.title: Family home
chunks.text: A 'family home' is the main place where your partner or dependent child lives. It can be: - a residential property - a property occupied under a Licence to Occupy (LTO) or an Occupation Right Agreement (ORA) - a life interest in a property owned by a family trust or an estate - an apartment - a granny flat - a motor home, or - a boat. If you choose to include the value of your family home in your assets, you need to find out its value. This is usually the net equity you or your partner have in the family home, minus any debts owing on it. The value of a Licence to Occupy unit or Occupation Right Agreement is different. It will be the surrender value (if any) that would be paid to you or your partner under the licence or agreement.

chunks.title: Income limits
chunks.text: We'll check to make sure your income is below the required limits. How we work this out is different for each type of income.

chunks.title: When you don't qualify
chunks.text: You won't qualify for Residential Care Subsidy if you're either: - under 50, or - 50-64, in a relationship and have dependent children. You'll need to contact Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora for assistance.

chunks.title: Step 1 - Book a needs assessment
chunks.text: Book an appointment with a Needs Assessment Service Coordination (NASC) agency funded by Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora. You can do this by visiting the NASCA website to find your local NASC. NASCAexternal They will: - check you meet Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora's criteria - determine what level of care you need - complete a Needs Assessment Certificate. If you're under 65 and have a partner, this is all you need to do, as we won't look at your assets or income. A Needs Assessment Certificate will be sent to Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora, who will organise payment for your care.

chunks.title: Complete a financial means assessment form
chunks.text: If we need to assess your assets or income, you will be given a 'Residential Care Subsidy application for Financial Means Assessment' form at your appointment. You need to: - fill out the form - gather your supporting documents (these are listed on the form) - return the form and your supporting documents to us as soon as you can. Call us to talk about the best way to do this. if you're 65 or over, you'll need to return them within 90 days of the date you want the subsidy to start. - if you're 65 or over, you'll need to return them within 90 days of the date you want the subsidy to start. Phone us

chunks.title: Step 2 - We'll check what assets you have
chunks.text: We'll check to make sure your assets are below the required limits. This is the first part of what we call a 'Financial means assessment'.

chunks.title: What's included as an asset
chunks.text: Assets may include but are not limited to: - cash or savings - bonus bonds - investments or shares - life insurance policies with a surrender or cash asset value - loans made to other people (including family trusts) - boats, caravans and campervans - investment properties - an apartment or property you own through a: license to occupy (LTO) occupational right agreement - license to occupy (LTO) - occupational right agreement - refundable accommodation deposits or bonds.

chunks.title: Family home and personal vehicle
chunks.text: Your family home and personal vehicle are included as assets if either: - you don't have a partner - both you and your partner are in long-term residential care, or - your partner is not in long-term residential care but you have chosen to have your assets assessed against the $300,811 asset threshold.

chunks.title: What's not included as an asset
chunks.text: Assets that aren't included are: - pre-paid funeral expenses for you and your partner of up to $10,000 each, if they're held in a recognised funeral plan - personal belongings such as clothing and jewellery - household furniture and effects.

chunks.title: Assets are above the limit
chunks.text: If you're 65 or over and your assets are above the threshold because you own your own home, you may be able to get a Residential Care Loan. This will help with the cost of your care. Residential Care Loan

chunks.title: Step 3 - We'll check what assets you've gifted or sold
chunks.text: If you or your partner have gifted assets, there's a certain portion that won't be included as an asset. The amount depends if you've gifted the assets: - in the last 5 years (from when you apply for the subsidy), or - longer than 5 years ago (from when you apply for the subsidy). If you sold an asset in the last five years we will check that it was sold for fair value. We might ask you some more questions if you sold an asset for less than fair value or if you sold it in exchange for a debt.

chunks.title: Gifted assets in the last 5 years
chunks.text: We won't count up to $8,500 of assets you've gifted each year in the last 5 years (from when you apply for the subsidy). This is a total of $42,500 of any assets you and your partner (even if they've died) have gifted in the last 5 years. If your partner applies at the same time, this amount will double to $85,000 (but we won't count $42,500 each if you apply at different times). This amount includes any assets you've gifted to someone in recognition of care. If your partner applies, it will not double if you've gifted assets to someone in recognition of care.

chunks.title: Gifting assets in recognition of care
chunks.text: We may not count assets you've gifted to someone who's provided you with a high level of care if you've: - received care for at least 12 continuous months in the last 5 years - gifted these assets to the carer in the last 12 months (from when you apply for the subsidy) - lived in the same home as the person providing the care - not received any funding for home-based disability support from the Ministry of Health, e.g., Home Support, meals on wheels - been able to stay in your home because you received care which meant you didn't need to get this payment. Also: - the person providing the care cannot be your partner or dependent child - the type of care needs to be necessary to help you around the home, e.g. help with bathing or toileting. Your gifts in recognition of care cannot be more than $42,500, when combined with other allowable gifting in the last 5 years (from when you apply for the subsidy).

chunks.title: Gifted assets longer than 5 years ago
chunks.text: We won't count up to $27,000 a year of any assets you've gifted longer than 5 years ago (from when you apply for the subsidy). $27,000 is the total amount between you and your partner (even if they've died).

chunks.title: Sold assets in exchange for a debt
chunks.text: We won't count assets that you have sold in your means assessment. This is because you no longer own the asset. However, if you sold your assets in exchange for a debt then the outstanding debt that is owed to you will be considered an asset.

chunks.title: Step 4 - We'll check your income
chunks.text: If your assets are below the required asset limits, the next thing we'll do is complete an income assessment. This is the last part of the financial means assessment.

chunks.title: What's included as income
chunks.text: - NZ Super, Veteran's Pension or any other benefit. - 50% of private superannuation payments. - 50% of life insurance annuities. - Overseas Government pensions. - Contributions from relatives. - Earnings from interest and bank accounts. - Investments, business or employment. - Income or payments from a trust or estate. We'll need more information if you or your partner have ever: - transferred assets to a trust - been the settlor, trustee or beneficiary of a trust or estate.

chunks.title: What's not included as income
chunks.text: - Any money your partner has earned through work. - Income from assets when the income is under: $1,267 a year for single people $2,534 a year for a couple when both have been assessed as needing care $3,801 a year for a couple where one partner has been assessed as needing care. - $1,267 a year for single people - $2,534 a year for a couple when both have been assessed as needing care - $3,801 a year for a couple where one partner has been assessed as needing care. - A War Disablement Pension from New Zealand or any other Commonwealth country.

chunks.title: Step 5 - We'll work out when the subsidy is paid from
chunks.text: You may qualify for the Residential Care Subsidy earlier than when you applied, which means it may be paid from an earlier date.

chunks.title: 50-64 years old
chunks.text: If you're 50-64 and single with no dependent children, it can be paid from either: - the date you were assessed as needing care, or - the date you entered care. It will be paid from whichever date is later.

chunks.title: 65 or older
chunks.text: If you're 65 or older, it can be paid from up to 90 days before we got your application. It depends on when you qualified from. For example, if we received your application on 1 May but you qualified for the subsidy earlier than this, it can be paid from when you qualified (but only as far back as 1 February).

chunks.title: Step 6 - We'll advise the outcome
chunks.text: We'll let these people know the outcome of your financial means assessment: - you - Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora, and - your rest home or hospital.

chunks.title: How the subsidy is paid
chunks.text: The Residential Care Subsidy is paid directly to the rest home or hospital by Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora.

chunks.title: How much the subsidy is
chunks.text: - We'll work out how much you should contribute to your care, based on your income assessment (generally we calculate this using your annual income at the time you applied). - Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora will look at how much your care costs. - The amount of the subsidy is the difference between these 2 amounts. For example: - We've worked out that you should contribute $300 a week to your care. - Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora has confirmed that your care costs $900 a week. - Your subsidy will be $600 a week.

chunks.title: What's included in cost of care
chunks.text: Some things are not included in the cost of your care, for example a Premium Room Charge because you pay for it privately. If you don't know what's included in the cost of your care, you should talk with your rest home or hospital.

chunks.title: Getting a benefit, NZ Super or Veterans Pension
chunks.text: If you get NZ Super, Veteran's Pension or any other benefit, most of this will go towards your care. - You'll keep a personal allowance of $58.34 a week. - You'll also receive a clothing allowance of $365.92 a year. You must continue to pay for your care until your application for Residential Care Subsidy has been approved.

chunks.title: If you have a partner living at home
chunks.text: Your partner may: - be able to get the Special Disability Allowance of $51.67 a week to help with extra costs - get an increase in their payment, if they get a benefit - qualify for a single rate of payment, if they get a NZ Super or Veteran's Pension - qualify for other payments after you go into care, if they aren't getting any payments from us.

chunks.title: Contact
chunks.text: If you have any questions, contact the Residential Subsidy Unit by: - calling 0800 999 727 - email msd_rcs@msd.govt.nz

chunks.title: Residential Support Subsidy
chunks.text: Residential Support Subsidy is a payment that helps with the cost of residential support. The Residential Support Subsidy is paid to the residential service provider by the Health New Zealand. This is to help with the cost of residential care.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get a Residential Support Subsidy if you're assessed as needing residential care due to: - drug and alcohol rehabilitation - an intellectual disability - a psychiatric disability - a physical or sensory disability, or - long term support - chronic health conditions. For age-related residential care, visit our page Residential Care Subsidy. Residential Care Subsidy

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: Health New Zealand pays most of the care costs to the residential service provider. While in residential care, you have an obligation to pay towards these costs. Most of your benefit or pension goes to the care provider. We call this a 'benefit contribution'. You keep a personal allowance. The rate is set by Health New Zealand. These rates are reviewed on 1 April every year.

chunks.title: Step 1: You're assessed
chunks.text: A contracted Needs Assessment Service Co-ordinator (NASC) service completes a ‘needs assessment’. The assessment is to see if you're eligible for residential care (see 'Who can get it' section). Needs Assessment Service Co-ordinator (NASC)external

chunks.title: Step 2: You enter residential care
chunks.text: If you're eligible, the needs assessor places you into full-time residential care. This will be with a Health New Zealand-contracted residential service provider.

chunks.title: Step 3: Filling out all relevant forms
chunks.text: You and the residential service provider both complete the Residential Support Subsidy application and authorisation form. The residential service provider submits the form(s) and all supporting documents to Work and Income.

chunks.title: Check what you might get
chunks.text: If you don't get a main benefit or NZ Super, it's a good idea to apply. Use Check what you might get to see what other support could be available to you. Paper application forms can be submitted at the same time as the Residential Support Subsidy application and authorisation form. Check what you might get Paper application forms

chunks.title: Step 4: Residential Support Subsidy starts
chunks.text: Health New Zealand start to pay Residential Support Subsidy to the residential service provider. Your benefit contributions that you've authorised (step 3) will also start. You may choose to: - redirect the contribution to the service provider through Work and Income, or - pay this to the service provider directly yourself.

chunks.title: Having someone act on your behalf
chunks.text: You may need help from an agent. An agent is a person or organisation that acts on your behalf with Work and Income. For more information on agents see our page: Having someone act on your behalf The Residential Support Subsidy application and authorisation form asks if you: - already have an agent - whether you want to appoint your residential service provider to be your agent temporarily for the time you're in care. If someone helps you to complete the form, there's a section about this too.

chunks.title: Changes in your circumstances
chunks.text: You must let Work and Income know about any changes in your circumstances. This can include changes in your income, relationship status, or address. Let us know by calling us. Contact us

chunks.title: Your responsibilities in emergency housing
chunks.text: If you're in emergency housing for more than 7 nights, there are responsibilities you have to meet from the 8th night. Find out what these are and what happens if you don't meet them. Your responsibilities are: - make a good effort to find other housing by doing things like: looking for rentals getting help to pay for private accommodation, or staying with whānau or friends - looking for rentals - getting help to pay for private accommodation, or - staying with whānau or friends - engage with support services like a housing broker or navigator, or budget or employment advisors. These will be either services we refer you to, or services you're already working with, and - pay your emergency housing contribution on time. We'll let you know about these responsibilities when you apply for emergency housing. You won't need to meet them until you've been in emergency housing for more than 7 nights.

chunks.title: How to meet your responsibilities
chunks.text: From night 8, you'll need to complete activities to help you meet your responsibilities. Your case manager will discuss and agree with you what activities you'll need to do. Activities will be tailored to your circumstances and be achievable. They will be things which will help you to get a home, for example: - meeting with a housing broker - attending a Ready to Rent course - working with budget advisors, or - looking for a private rental. You'll get a letter listing your agreed activities, and who to contact if you need help. At each re-grant appointment, we'll check you've done the activities you agreed to. We'll also talk with you about any activities you'll need to do to get your next grant.

chunks.title: What happens if you don't meet your responsibilities
chunks.text: If you don't meet your responsibilities and do what we've agreed, we'll want to understand why. If you don't meet your responsibilities without a good reason for the: - first time - you'll get a written warning. - second time - you'll get another written warning. - third time, then: we'll decline your next emergency housing application you won't be able to get emergency housing for 13 weeks (this is called a 'non-entitlement period'), and you can't be included as a partner on someone else's emergency housing application. - we'll decline your next emergency housing application - you won't be able to get emergency housing for 13 weeks (this is called a 'non-entitlement period'), and - you can't be included as a partner on someone else's emergency housing application. If you get a written warning, we'll give you a letter with this warning. If you still need emergency housing during the 13 weeks, you may be able to get it if you meet certain criteria. Contact us to talk about your situation. Phone us

chunks.title: COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy
chunks.text:
## COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy
The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy was to help businesses pay their staff affected by COVID-19. It was available from 21 August 2020 to 3 September 2020.
The information on this page is a summary of the key details about this payment. Detailed information can be found in the declaration at the bottom of this page.
## Who could get it
This payment was available to employers and self-employed people. Their business must have had at least a 40% drop in revenue because of COVID-19 over a 14 day period between 12 August and 10 September 2020, compared to a similar period in 2019.
State Sector organisations were generally not eligible to get the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy, however some may have been granted an exception.
## Payment rates
The COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy was for 2 weeks from the day an application was submitted. It was paid as a lump-sum of either:
- $585.80 for full-time employees (20 hours or more a week), or
- $350.00 for part-time employees (less than 20 hours a week).
If the employee's usual wages were were less than the subsidy rate, any difference should have been used to pay the wages of other affected staff. If there were no other employees to use the subsidy for affected staff, the remaining amount must have been repaid back.
## Paying your staff
The business must have made an effort to pay the employee named in the application at least 80% of their usual wages while getting the wage subsidy for them. If that wasn't possible, at least the subsidy rate needed to be paid.
## Declaration
The declaration contains the full eligibility criteria, obligations and repayment responsibilities for the COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy.
Declaration for COVID-19 Resurgence Wage Subsidy
