chunks.title: Review of annual income
chunks.text: If you're getting certain payments from us, we review your annual income each year to check if anything has changed. That way we can make sure you're still getting paid the right amount.

chunks.title: When we confirm your annual income
chunks.text: We'll confirm your annual income each year if you're getting: - Sole Parent Support - Supported Living Payment - NZ Super or Veteran's Pension at the non-qualified rate - Emergency Maintenance Allowance - Emergency Benefit (if you can't get Sole Parent Support or Supported Living Payment in some circumstances). We'll look at your income details for the last 52 weeks (year) and compare this with the payments we've made to you. We do this to check we've paid you the right amount over the last year.

chunks.title: If you're getting Jobseeker Support and it started before 1 July 2025
chunks.text: We'll also confirm your annual income if your Jobseeker Support started before 1 July 2025 and: - you're a sole parent, or - you: were getting Domestic Purposes Benefit - Woman Alone or Widow's Benefit before 15 July 2023, and transferred to Jobseeker Support on 15 July 2013 and have remained on this benefit since then. - were getting Domestic Purposes Benefit - Woman Alone or Widow's Benefit before 15 July 2023, and - transferred to Jobseeker Support on 15 July 2013 and have remained on this benefit since then. If you're in this situation, your annual income review will change to a weekly income assessment when you next reapply (at 52 weeks). Reapply for Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: What you need to do
chunks.text: We'll send you a letter which will ask you to either: - confirm your income details, or - provide proof of your income details.

chunks.title: If you need to confirm your income details
chunks.text: The letter will have details of your income for the last 12 months (that we have on your record). If these income details are: - correct, you don't need to do anything. - not correct, you need to call us and let us know. If your income details are not correct, we may ask you to provide proof of your income. We'll let you know what to provide and how to do this when you call us.

chunks.title: If you need to provide proof of your income
chunks.text: The letter will ask you to provide proof of your income for the last 12 months. Examples of documents you can provide are: - payslips from your employer, if you get wages or salary - bank statements, if you get interest payments - a letter from ACC, if you get ACC payments. You can drop the documents into your local service centre, or post them to us at the address provided in the letter. The letter will also let you know the date you have to provide these documents to us.

chunks.title: Confirming your circumstances
chunks.text: For certain payments, we must review your circumstances at least once every 52 weeks (one year). This helps us make sure you're getting the correct assistance and amount. We'll confirm your circumstances each year if you're getting: - Supported Living Payment - Emergency Maintenance Allowance (that expires in 52 weeks or more, or has no expiry date) - Emergency Benefit (that expires in 52 weeks or more, or has no expiry date) - New Zealand Superannuation (if you have a partner included in your payment who does not qualify to get it) - Accommodation Supplement (except people also getting the Youth Payment and Young Parent Payment) - Disability Allowance - Orphan's Benefit - Unsupported Child's Benefit. As part of this review, we might send you a Confirming your Circumstances form. This will cover information about your:family (if you have a partner or children), work, income, assets, accommodation, costs, and living arrangements. It's important you fill in and return the form promptly, even if nothing has changed. If you don't respond to the form before the due date, your payments will stop. In some limited situations, we may be able to give you more time to complete your form or give you an exemption. You need to contact us before it's due, because payments will automatically stop on the due date. We may also ask you to provide proof of your costs or income, and attend an appointment with us.

chunks.title: Step 1 - Complete the form
chunks.text: The form will be sent either online in MyMSD or in the post, if you still get paper letters from us. The form will be pre-filled with some information we already hold about you. You'll need to: - check the information on the form - update any information that's changed or new - return the completed form to us before the due date. If you get your form in MyMSD, you can complete and submit it in MyMSD. If you get your form in the post, you can still complete and submit it online if you have a MyMSD account. Or you can complete the paper form and return it to the address that's on the form or take it into one of our service centres. MyMSD is a fast and secure way to get the form back to us. If you submit your form online and have declared a change, you will be directed to the next steps page and may have the option to upload documents (evidence) or make an appointment.

chunks.title: The form will be processed
chunks.text: If you submit the form in MyMSD and your circumstances have not changed, your form will be processed using Automated Decision-Making. Automated decision-making If you return a paper form, our staff will manually process it. If your circumstances have changed, our staff will process your form and let you know what will happen next.

chunks.title: Step 2 - Provide more information, if needed
chunks.text: We will call you or send you a letter if you need to provide more details or proof for the information in your form. You can: - upload your documents in MyMSD - post your documents to us, or - drop your documents into a service centre. Sometimes, we may book you an appointment as well. If we do, you can bring your documents with you to your appointment.

chunks.title: Step 3 - Attend an appointment, if needed
chunks.text: Some changes may require you to attend an appointment. For example: - if you have entered a relationship or left one, or - if a child has come into your care, or left your care - if you get Supported Living Payment to care for someone, but you're no longer caring for that person. If you need an appointment, we'll book one for you. Then we will call you or send you a letter to let you know the details of the appointment.

chunks.title: Reviews of Residential Care Subsidy assessments
chunks.text: Anyone who had a financial means assessment for a Residential Care Subsidy before 3 December 2019 can ask for their assessment to be reviewed, based on a Court of Appeal decision in May 2019.

chunks.title: Chance to ask for a review
chunks.text: Anyone applying for a Residential Care Subsidy has to have a financial means assessment. We’ve realised the way we’ve been doing these assessments for some people is wrong. We’re offering people who may be affected by this the opportunity to ask for a review. Since December 2019 we have adjusted our assessments based on the Court of Appeal decision for new and existing clients to make sure they are paying the right amount going forward. We’re now at the stage of looking back at Residential Care Subsidy financial means assessments in the past.

chunks.title: Why we're offering reviews
chunks.text: On 31 May 2019, the Court of Appeal issued a decision clarifying how the Ministry of Social Development can exercise discretion for people applying for a Residential Care Subsidy who may have deprived themselves of assets and/or income (called ‘deprivation’ – see separate section below). The Court of Appeal found that our interpretation of the relevant law was wrong. This specifically included when and how we identified and included deprivation in your assessment.

chunks.title: Who can ask for a review
chunks.text: We’re writing to clients who we think have been impacted by the Court of Appeal’s decision. If your financial means assessment didn’t include deprived assets or deprived income, a review may not change your situation. You can refer to your past financial means assessment to check if this applies to you. Anyone who applied for a Residential Care Subsidy can ask for a review. You can also apply for a review on behalf of someone who has died if you are the executors or administrators of their estate.

chunks.title: Having someone help you with your review
chunks.text: If you decide to request a review, you can have someone help you fill in the form. If someone else is requesting the review on your behalf, they’ll need to have authority such as an MSD agent, Enduring Power of Attorney for Property or a property manager. Having someone act on your behalf

chunks.title: What is deprivation
chunks.text: Deprivation takes many forms, but the most common examples are when you or your partner: - have given away more than the allowable amounts, more than five years before your financial means assessment - have sold an asset for less than its value - haven’t charged interest on past or current debts owed to you - do not generate reasonable income from your current assets. The Ministry of Social Development has the discretion to include any deprived assets or income in your financial means assessment for Residential Care Subsidy. If you’re the beneficiary of an estate or trust, MSD will generally assume those resources are available to help pay for your care. If you don’t think this is right, you’ll need to share information about the trust or estate to show that they are not.

chunks.title: Request a review
chunks.text: To fill in our paper form select the link below to download and print the form. If you don’t have a printer call us on 0800 752 101 and we’ll post a form to you. Download the form

chunks.title: After you have requested a review
chunks.text: In some circumstances we’ll need to ask you for more information. We’ll be in touch if we have any questions, and you can phone us for an update. We’ll only ask you for more information if it’s essential. We’ll write to you with the outcome of your review.

chunks.title: Reviewing rent payments
chunks.text: When you live in public (social) housing, we'll review your rent payments. This is so we can make sure you're paying the right amount of rent. We'll review your rent every 12 months, or sooner if you or someone in your household tells us about a change in circumstances. For example, this could be a change to your income or relationship status. As part of your rent review we'll check your income details with you. This includes any child support you get from Inland Revenue (IR). If your rent payment changes, we'll send you a letter to tell you how much it will be.

chunks.title: 12 months since last review
chunks.text: If we haven’t reviewed your rent for 12 months, we'll send you a letter to check if your situation has changed. This includes things like income changes, or if anyone has moved out or moved in. If there are changes, it may affect how much rent you pay. You need to check the information in the letter to see if it's still correct. If your situation: - has changed, you need to tell us You may need to provide proof of these changes - if so, we'll tell you what documents you need to provide. - You may need to provide proof of these changes - if so, we'll tell you what documents you need to provide. - has not changed, sign the form and return it to us by the date in your letter.

chunks.title: If there's a change to your income
chunks.text: Your rent is based on your household income. You need to tell us as soon as you can if you or someone in your household has a change in income. Some changes are only temporary, e.g: - your hours change each week, or - you're temporarily sick and can’t work. You still need to tell us if this happens, but we'll check if this change is permanent before we review your rent. A permanent change to income means any changes that last, or are likely to last, longer than 8 weeks. These could be things like: - starting or stopping work - going onto a benefit - getting a pay rise - getting board payments from someone living with you - getting child support payments.

chunks.title: If you get child support through Inland Revenue
chunks.text: Inland Revenue (IR) will share your child support payment information with us every time they pay you child support. We'll use the shared information from IR and treat this as income if you get one of these payments from us: - a main benefit, e.g. Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support - NZ Superannuation or Veteran's Pension and you have a partner who doesn't qualify for this but is included in your payments - Veteran's Pension and you're under 65 - Accommodation Supplement - Disability Allowance - Temporary Additional Support - Special Benefit - Childcare Subsidy - OSCAR Subsidy, or - Employment Transition Assistance. If you get one of these payments, you don't need to tell us about most types of IR child support payments. The only type of child support paid by IR you need to tell us about is if you're getting Court Ordered lump sum child support payments. If you don't get one of the payments in the above bulleted list, you need to tell us about your IR child support payments. You also need to tell us about any other child support payments you get.

chunks.title: We'll send you a letter confirming your IR child support details
chunks.text: Before we review rent payments, we'll send you a letter to let you know the amount of child support IR has shared with us. If you think there's an error with the child support information, you have 10 working days to let us know. We may need to contact IR to confirm your information.

chunks.title: What happens after we've reviewed your rent
chunks.text: Once we've worked out how much rent you should be paying, we check how much it will increase or decrease by. If your rent review is based on a change in circumstances, we’ll only change your rent when there is either: - an increase of $5 or more per week, or - a decrease of $1 or more per week If your rent review is a 12 month review, we'll only change your rent when there is either: - an increase of $1 or more per week, or - a decrease of more than $1 per week. If your rent payment does change, we‘ll send you a letter to tell you how much this is. Your landlord will also send you a letter, to tell you when you need to start paying the new rent amount.

chunks.title: Your rights while in emergency housing
chunks.text: Find out your rights while staying in emergency housing. You can expect certain things from your emergency housing supplier in regards to: - check in information - your room, and - what your supplier will do. We will also make sure we support you while you're staying there.

chunks.title: Check in information
chunks.text: When you check in, you can expect information about: - the facilities and services available (for example, room cleaning, changing linen, laundry facilities) - the 'rules of stay' for guests - contacting the supplier about issues and concerns, during or outside of business hours - how to check out.

chunks.title: Your room
chunks.text: You can expect your room to be: - clean, warm and dry - suitable for you and your whānau, including being accessible and the right size - safe and secure.

chunks.title: What your supplier will do
chunks.text: You can expect your emergency housing supplier to: - treat you the same as any other paying guest, with fairness and respect - allow you to use facilities other guests use, like the laundry if there is one - have clear information available about what to do in an emergency - repair or replace damaged or broken fixtures or fittings as soon as possible - respond to any concerns you have as soon as possible. The supplier will also tell us about any issues to do with your stay, or if their rules aren't being followed.

chunks.title: How we will support you
chunks.text: We will support you by: - assigning you a case manager or youth coach while you're staying in emergency housing - getting to know you, your situation and your needs and will: make sure you get all the help you're eligible for, including financial help and other support services help you find housing, including transitional and public housing work with you to achieve your goals, such as finding work or training - make sure you get all the help you're eligible for, including financial help and other support services - help you find housing, including transitional and public housing - work with you to achieve your goals, such as finding work or training - making sure the emergency housing meets the needs of you and your whānau - letting you know your rights while in emergency housing - letting you know about your responsibilities while in emergency housing and what happens if you don't meet these - respecting your privacy and being clear about how we use your information and who we share it with.If you've agreed to a security deposit, we may pay for loss or damage to the supplier on your behalf. Your responsibilities in emergency housing Security deposit for emergency housing

chunks.title: Rural Assistance Payments
chunks.text: Rural Assistance Payments can help farmers during or after an adverse event, such as a flood or drought. Rural Assistance Payments are not currently available.

chunks.title: About Rural Assistance Payments
chunks.text: Rural Assistance Payments are paid during or after an adverse event. They're paid to help farmers with essential living costs.

chunks.title: Adverse events
chunks.text: Adverse events are climatic events, natural disasters or biosecurity issues. The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) classifies these as either localised events, or medium- or large- scale events. If it's a medium or large scale event, the Government then decides what sort of assistance will be provided. Find out how adverse events are classified on the Ministry for Primary Industries' website: How we classify adverse events (Ministry for Primary Industries)external

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Rural Assistance Payment if: - you're finding it difficult to meet your essential living costs through your farming business because of an adverse event. - your farm is your main source of income, e.g: meat or poultry farming wool dairy products arable farming aquaculture sharemilking an orchard bee-keeping herb or flower growing a market garden. - meat or poultry farming - wool - dairy products - arable farming - aquaculture - sharemilking - an orchard - bee-keeping - herb or flower growing - a market garden. It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn (not including your farming business), and - any money or off-farm assets you and your partner have.

chunks.title: Income limits
chunks.text: If you have other income other than your farming business, this may affect how much Rural Assistance Payment you get. You and your partner can earn up to $160 a week (before tax) combined before this affects your payments. If you earn more than this, you may still get a Rural Assistance Payment, but at a lower rate.

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: To get this payment, any cash or off-farm assets you have must be under a certain amount. This doesn't include farm or orchard assets, such as shares in dairy, meat or fertiliser companies. If you are: Your assets must be less than: single $1,411.22 a couple (with or without children) or a sole parent $2,351.46

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Payments are equivalent to the current rate of the Jobseeker Support benefit at the time of the event. Benefit rates You or your partner can earn up to $160 per week (before tax) before your Rural Assistance Payments are affected. If you're earning more than this, you may still be able to get Rural Assistance Payments at a reduced rate, which will be paid weekly. Tax is automatically deducted at 'M' rate.

chunks.title: How long you can get it for
chunks.text: Rural Assistance Payments are generally paid in a lump sum covering 4 weeks. If you need the payment for longer than this, you'll need to reapply every 4 weeks. You can apply for Rural Assistance Payments for: - up to one year from the date you apply, or - a set length of time, which is approved by the Minister for Social Development. You'll get paid for whichever is the shortest of these options.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to: 1. Fill out the 'Rural Assistance Payment Application' form: 2. Get the declaration part of the form signed by either: - an Agri-recovery Facilitator, or - a Rural Support Trust coordinator 3. Contact either us or the Rural Support Trust to submit your application: - to contact us (Ministry of Social Development), call 0800 559 009 - to contact your local Rural Support Trust, go to www.rural-support.org.nzexternal Whoever you contact will tell you how to get the application form to us, and if need to provide any documents.

chunks.title: How to re-apply (every 4 weeks)
chunks.text: Rural Assistance Payments are generally paid in a lump sum covering 4 weeks. If you need the payment for longer than this, you'll need to reapply every 4 weeks. To re-apply, fill out the 'Rural Assistance Payment continuation' form: Then you can either: - send it to your local Rural Support Trust (go to their website to find an Agri-recovery Facilitator near you), or - drop it into your nearest service centre. Help and Support (Rural Support)external Find a service centre

chunks.title: Other support from us
chunks.text: We may be able to help you in other ways, for example if you've had to stop work or need help to pay unexpected costs. You can use our online tool to find out what support you might be eligible for, and how to apply for this.

chunks.title: Sale of assets
chunks.text:
## Sale of assets
Asset sales don't need to be declared as income. But if you get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit you do need to tell us about it.
## What is this?
The money you get from the sale of an asset does not affect your benefit. Assets include:
- a property
- a business
- a car
- a boat.

chunks.title: School and Year Start-up Payment
chunks.text: If you're caring for someone else's child and need help with pre-school or school-related costs at the beginning of the year, you may be able to get the School and Year Start-up Payment. This is a once-a-year payment. For 2026, you need to apply between Monday 12 January and Friday 28 February.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You can get a School and Year Start-up Payment if you're getting Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit. You can get the payment for every child that you get these benefits for.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: This payment is to help with the costs that mostly happen at the beginning of the year, in particular pre-school and school-related costs, e.g. clothing, school fees and stationery. How much you get is based on the age of the child at the end of February each year. You won't be taxed on this money and you won't have to pay it back.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: For 2026, applications are open from Monday 12 January, to Friday 28 February. Applications are open during this time because a lot of costs associated with raising a child can come at the beginning of the year, such as pre-school or school-related costs like fees, clothing and stationery. This payment is to help take the pressure off carers at this time of the year. You don't need to show us any receipts or quotes to get the School and Year Start-up Payment. However, it is expected that the payment will go towards covering the child's school-related costs, or costs arising at the start of the year.

chunks.title: Can't apply when applications are open
chunks.text: If you have a good reason for not being able to apply between mid-January and the end of February (e.g. being in hospital), talk to us about your situation as we may still be able to make this payment to you.

chunks.title: Other payments
chunks.text: Extraordinary Care Fund If you get the Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit, you can apply for extra financial help in special cases. The Extraordinary Care Fund helps you with extra costs if the child you care for is either having difficulties that affect their development or showing special talent.

chunks.title: Related links
chunks.text: - Caring for someone else's child - Orphan's Benefit - Unsupported Child's Benefit - School costs

chunks.title: School costs
chunks.text: We may be able to help you pay for school uniforms, stationery, and childcare costs if you're on a low income or a benefit and struggling to pay school costs.

chunks.title: Uniforms and stationery
chunks.text: We may be able to help pay for school uniforms and stationery if you're on a low income or a benefit. You will need to pay this money back. School uniforms and stationery Apply through MyMSD or call us. MyMSDexternal Phone us

chunks.title: School fees and activities
chunks.text: We may be able to help with the costs of some school fees and activities if there is an immediate and essential need for them. You will need to pay this money back. These costs could be: - exam fees - attendance dues. Some schools may ask that students have computing equipment, e.g. an iPad, laptop or tablet. If you can't afford to buy these we may be able to help, but you need to talk to the school first to see what options are available.

chunks.title: If you're on a benefit
chunks.text: You may be able to get an Advance Payment of Benefit. Advance Payment of Benefit

chunks.title: Childcare assistance
chunks.text: If you need help with childcare costs, like before or after school care, we may be able to help: Childcare If you’re already getting childcare payments, find out what you need to do to keep getting these: Getting childcare payments If you get an OSCAR Subsidy and want it to continue in the new school term, you'll need to let us know: Continuing childcare when your child's at school

chunks.title: Uniforms, stationery and school fees
chunks.text: If you're getting Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit, you can get the School and Year Start-up Payment. This is to help pay for uniforms, stationery or school fees. You don't need to pay this back. School and Year Start Up Payment

chunks.title: Child is having difficulties at school or showing promise
chunks.text: Extraordinary Care Fund is for children who are either: - having difficulties at school that are significantly impacting on their development - showing promise through high achievement in a particular area, e.g. music or sport. You need to be getting Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit to apply for this. Extraordinary Care Fund

chunks.title: Support in your community
chunks.text: There may be other supports available in your local community. Check what's available by searching in the Family Services Directory for help with things like school items or costs. You can also find other services like financial planning, childcare and finding a local food bank.

chunks.title: School uniforms and stationery
chunks.text: We may be able to help you pay for school uniforms and stationery if you're on a low income or a benefit. You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. You'll have to pay the money back.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get help if you: - are 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services) - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - have an immediate and essential need. Youth Servicesexternal It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have. Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income limits apply:

chunks.title: Bring your own device
chunks.text: If you need help to buy computing equipment for your child to take to school, e.g. iPad, laptop or tablet, we may be able to help. You need to talk to the school first to see what options are available.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: If you are a current client, you may be able to apply using MyMSD. MyMSD will tell you what information we need and if you need to talk with us. Find out about MyMSD If you are a new client or can't use MyMSD, call us. We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help, and let you know if you need to do anything else. Phone us

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: If your application's approved, we'll give you a payment card (if you don't already have one) and load the money onto it. We'll talk to you about how to get this to you. You have 7 days to spend the money before it expires. You can pay for school uniforms and stationery with your payment card at any store that accepts them (much like an EFTPOS card). You'll need to check with the store first to see if they accept them. You can login to MyMSD to see how much you have left on your payment card and when it expires. Sign up or log in to MyMSDexternal

chunks.title: If your supplier doesn't accept payment card
chunks.text: If your uniform or stationary supplier doesn't accept our payment card, we will organise a direct payment to them, and provide confirmation of payment for when you pick up the items. Make sure you get a reference number or quote from the supplier, and give this to us.

chunks.title: If you're getting Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit
chunks.text: If you get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit, you may also be able to get a School and Year Start-up Payment. This helps with pre-school or school-related costs at the beginning of the year. It can pay for things like clothing, school fees and stationery and you don't have to pay it back. School and Year Start-up Payment

chunks.title: Seasonal worker
chunks.text:
## Seasonal worker
If you're a seasonal worker (e.g. fruit and vegetable production) and have lost wages because of bad weather, or your contract has finished, we may be able to help.
## What is seasonal work
Seasonal work could be:
- fruit and vegetable picking, packing, processing and pruning
- vineyards
- forestry
- dairy industry
- freezing works, meat processing
- lambing and shearing gang work
- fisheries/seafood
- ski-related work on ski fields and in local towns
- tourism work - everything from waiting tables to being a tour guide.
## Lost wages because of bad weather
If you work in the horticulture industry and you've lost wages because of bad weather, you may be able to get help from us, depending on your circumstances.
You need to be working in one of these industries:
- berry fruit growing
- citrus fruit growing
- grape and olive
- growing cut flower and flower seed
- hop, tobacco and hemp growing
- kiwifruit growing
- pip fruit growing
- plant nurseries
- stone fruit growing
- vegetable growing.
Seasonal Work Assistance
## Your contract has ended
If you're working in any seasonal industry and your contract has finished, we may be able to help depending on your circumstances.
## Sole parent with children under 14 to support
Sole Parent Support
## Need money but your partner works
You're down to one wage and you need help to pay day-to-day expenses while you look for work.

chunks.title: Seasonal Work Assistance
chunks.text:
## Seasonal Work Assistance
Assistance for seasonal workers who are no longer getting a benefit and have lost wages because of work missed due to bad weather.
## Who can get it
You may get Seasonal Work Assistance if you:
- stopped getting a benefit within the last 26 weeks to go into seasonal horticultural or viticultural work
- have lost wages because you could not work due to bad weather, and
- are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident.
It also depends on:
- how much you and your spouse or partner earn
- any money or assets you and your spouse or partner have.
You should also normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here.
## How much you can get
The amount of Seasonal Work Assistance you can get depends on how many hours of work you lost in that week.
The maximum amount you can be paid in a 26-week period is $2,754.

chunks.title: Accommodation Security Cover Grant
chunks.text: You may find accommodation where your supplier needs assurance that costs can be paid for if you leave. If so, we may be able to provide that assurance. The Accommodation Security Cover Grant can pay for costs a bond would usually cover, like: - unpaid accommodation costs - damages to property or chattels - missing chattels - rubbish removal or cleaning costs the accommodation provider has had to pay for - change of locks or replacement keys (if you've lost the keys) - any costs included in a Disputes Tribunal, Tenancy Tribunal, or court order. Apply once you've found accommodation. We'll give you a 'Letter of assurance' you can show to your supplier, e.g. your head tenant. It will assure them we can cover any costs you have when you leave, if you leave within 1 year. If you need to pay costs when you leave, you can make a claim to get the grant paid. If you don't agree to the costs, your accommodation supplier can make a claim. If you're going to stay there for longer than 1 year, you can apply for another grant after the 1 year period has ended. If you or your accommodation supplier make a claim, you'll need to pay the money back. We'll put a repayment plan in place to suit your financial circumstances.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get an Accommodation Security Cover Grant if: - your accommodation supplier needs assurance that costs you may have at the end of your stay can be paid for - when you claim, you: need the grant to pay for any costs you may have, and have left your accommodation within 1 year. - need the grant to pay for any costs you may have, and - have left your accommodation within 1 year. We'll also take into account other factors, such as: - your situation - if you can afford to stay in your accommodation long-term - how long you'll be living in your accommodation (generally this needs to be at least 28 days) - if this is the best payment for you - what other help is available to you. There are also residency and income criteria you need to meet.

chunks.title: Residency criteria
chunks.text: You must be either: - getting a main benefit, NZ Super or Veteran’s Pension, or - ordinarily resident in New Zealand and either: a New Zealand citizen have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 recognised as a refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009, or getting a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your New Zealand partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence. - a New Zealand citizen - have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 - recognised as a refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009, or - getting a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your New Zealand partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence. Main benefit Ordinarily resident

chunks.title: Income criteria
chunks.text: Getting an Accommodation Security Cover Grant also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have.

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: Assets include money in the bank, or things like a caravan or second property. Assets don’t include the things you need for day-to-day living, like the home where you live or your car.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: You'll get the lesser amount of: - the actual amount of accommodation costs you owe at the end of your accommodation agreement, or - 4 weeks accommodation costs.

chunks.title: How many grants you can get
chunks.text: The Accommodation Security Cover Grant and Bond Grant are paid for similar reasons. This means you can only get these payments a total of twice in 52 weeks (i.e. 1 year). So within 52 weeks, you could get either: - 2 Accommodation Security Cover Grants - 2 Bond Grants, or - 1 Accommodation Security Cover Grant and 1 Bond Grant. You may be able to get another grant if there's an exceptional situation outside your control, for example: - you unexpectedly need to move through no fault of your own, or - you're in a family violence situation.

chunks.title: Step 1 - Call us
chunks.text: Call us on: - 0800 559 009 or - 0800 552 002 if you get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension. We'll book you an appointment to come in and see us. You'll need to bring: - a copy of your accommodation agreement, and - a letter from your accommodation supplier confirming that they need this security cover.

chunks.title: Step 2 - Go to an appointment
chunks.text: At your appointment, we'll: - check if you qualify for an Accommodation Security Cover Grant, and - give you an application form to fill out. We'll process your application and let you know if it's approved or not.

chunks.title: Step 3 - Get a Letter of assurance
chunks.text: If your application's approved, we'll give you a letter of assurance. You'll need to give this letter to your accommodation supplier. This letter will explain: - what the Accommodation Security Cover Grant is - the conditions of the grant - how you can claim for the grant - what evidence you'll need to provide for costs that need to be paid, and - how we'll pay the accommodation supplier.

chunks.title: Making a claim
chunks.text: You can make a claim if: - your accommodation agreement ends within 1 year - you have costs to pay for, and - you agree to the costs. The claim needs to be lodged within 3 months after your accommodation agreement ends. If you don't agree to the costs, your accommodation supplier can make a claim. They'll need to provide a Disputes Tribunal Order or court order.

chunks.title: How to make a claim
chunks.text: You can make a claim by showing us evidence of the costs you need to pay, e.g: - invoices for damage, or - bank statements showing accommodation costs owing. You can bring these documents into your local service centre or post them to us. Find a service centre

chunks.title: If the claim is approved
chunks.text: If the claim is approved, we'll pay the money directly to your accommodation supplier. We'll check if they are already a supplier with us. If they're not, we'll ask them to register as a supplier by completing a 'Supplier Registration Form'. This is so we can make the payment to them. Register as a Work and Income supplier

chunks.title: Security deposit for emergency housing
chunks.text: If you're going to stay in emergency housing, your housing supplier may ask for a security deposit. The security deposit can help to cover certain types of losses or damages that you, or people staying with you, are responsible for. For example, damage to, or replacement of: - curtains, carpet or furniture - kitchen appliances (toaster, jug, etc) - walls, doors - locks or keys/key cards - any other spaces or shared spaces, such as a laundry room, hallway or play area.

chunks.title: How it works
chunks.text: If your supplier asks for a security deposit, talk to us about this when you apply for emergency housing. We'll approve a security deposit at the start of your stay, but we won't pay the supplier then. We'll usually approve up to 7 nights' of the accommodation cost. We'll discuss the amount with you before we approve it and check you agree with it. If there are any losses or damages during your stay or when you leave, your supplier can make a claim to get the deposit paid.

chunks.title: Making a claim
chunks.text: We'll only pay the security deposit on your behalf if: - there are losses or damages that you, or someone staying with you, were responsible for - there are unpaid costs, and - the supplier has made a claim.

chunks.title: The supplier must claim within 3 months
chunks.text: Your housing supplier will need to claim any losses or damages from us within 3 months of when you leave.

chunks.title: You will need to pay it back to us
chunks.text: If you get a main benefit, NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, it will automatically come out of this payment. If you don't, we'll let you know how you can pay us back. Main benefit

chunks.title: If you don't agree to the loss or damage
chunks.text: If the supplier tells us you don't agree that you or your whānau are responsible for the loss or damage, we won't pay the security deposit. We will pay it once you have agreed on an outcome with the supplier. If you don't agree on an outcome, it may go to a Tribunal or court. If you didn't check out of your accommodation, we will still pay it regardless. You'll need to talk to the emergency housing supplier and resolve it with them.

chunks.title: Costs not covered by security deposit
chunks.text: There are standard costs that are not covered by the security deposit. If you have these costs, you will need to pay the bill yourself. This could include things like: - phone - internet pre-pay television charges - storage - laundry services - car-parking - utilities - meal charges.

chunks.title: Self-Assessment
chunks.text: A self-assessment is a questionnaire that you fill out to explain the sort of work you think you can do now or in the future, and what support you might need to find and stay in work. We'll let you know if you need to complete one.

chunks.title: Who needs to complete a Self-Assessment
chunks.text: You may need to complete a Self-Assessment if you: - have a health condition or disability that affects your ability to work - need support or services to help you prepare for, find and stay in work. You won't need to complete a Self-Assessment if you've got either: - a job to return to within 13 weeks of when you applied for a benefit - a medical certificate or other appropriate assessments which tells us that you: are more than 27 weeks pregnant are totally blind have a terminal illness have a severe intellectual or cognitive impairment have a condition which means you can no longer work and it's unlikely that this will change. - are more than 27 weeks pregnant - are totally blind - have a terminal illness - have a severe intellectual or cognitive impairment - have a condition which means you can no longer work and it's unlikely that this will change. If you're unsure whether you need to complete one, contact us. Phone us

chunks.title: Completing a Self-Assessment
chunks.text: The Self-Assessment is available in different formats. Use the format that suits you best. You can ask someone else to help you complete the Self-Assessment, or your case manager can help you. When you meet with your case manager to discuss your Self-Assessment, you can use an interpreter. Contact us to arrange this. Phone us

chunks.title: Paper form
chunks.text: You can either: - print the Self-Assessment below - pick one up from one of our offices - call us and we'll post one out to you. You'll need to bring this completed form with you when you meet with us. Find a service centre Call us Self-Assessment questionnaire (PDF 204 KB)

chunks.title: Easy Read
chunks.text: You can read and answer the questions using the Easy Read version. Easy Read uses pictures and short sentences to make it easier for people with learning disabilities or English as a second language. You can either: - print the Easy Read form below - pick one up from one of our offices - call us and we'll post one out to you. Find a service centre Call us Easy Read (PDF 1.9 MB)

chunks.title: New Zealand Sign Language
chunks.text: You can watch a video of a person signing the Self-Assessment questions (Easy Read version). These videos aren't covered by Cheap as data. Cheap as data You then need to either: - answer the questions using one of the other formats, - call us to arrange a sign language translator for when you meet with your case manager. Phone us

chunks.title: Braille
chunks.text: We can arrange for a copy of the Self-Assessment in braille to be sent to you. Please contact us to ask for this. Contact us

chunks.title: Self-employed, sole trader or business income
chunks.text: If you're getting a benefit or payment from us and you earn income, you need to let us know. The amount you earn will affect how much we pay you. You need let us know the week you earn the money, not when you've been paid. We need to know by Friday 6pm. If you're working the weekend, include this time too. If you don't tell us, we'll keep paying you the same amount week after week. This could be too little or too much, and you could get into debt. Tell us every time your income changes.

chunks.title: Work out your income
chunks.text: We need to know the following: - your total income before tax or any other deductions - any business expenses you want to deduct from your income - the number of hours you worked that week - your hourly rate (if applicable) - when you earned the income (not when you were paid). Please note, the expenses you can deduct from your income can be different for benefit purposes than it is for tax purposes. We'll discuss this with you during your appointment (see below section ‘How to tell us’ under ‘step 2’).

chunks.title: Make an estimate
chunks.text: If you don't know what you'll earn, tell us what you think it will probably be. For example, you may need to do this if you work on the weekend. We may still pay you too much or too little. But your debt will usually be less than if you don’t declare any income.

chunks.title: Starting a new job
chunks.text: If you start a new job we also need to know: - who you work for (this could be more than one employer or yourself) - when you started work.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: We need to know your income the week you earn it, even if you’re paid: - fortnightly - monthly, or - on an irregular basis.

chunks.title: MyMSD
chunks.text: Select 'Declare wages' and then 'Self-employed’ for self-employed, sole trader or business income. For anything else (eg interest and investments), or if you're unsure, choose 'Change other income'. About MyMSD

chunks.title: If you can't use MyMSD
chunks.text: If you can't use MyMSD you can call us or come into one of our service centres. If you’re declaring income from self-employment, make sure you mention you're self-employed. Call us Find a service centre

chunks.title: Step 2 - We’ll contact you
chunks.text: We’ll contact you and explain if there’s anything more you need to do. If we have everything we need, we may be able to help you over the phone. However, there may be times we need you to come in for a face-to-face appointment. Find a service centre

chunks.title: Documents we need
chunks.text: You'll need to provide either a: - IR3 – Individual tax return, or - profit and loss account and either a - IR3B – Schedule of business income, or - IR10 – a financial statements summary. We’ll tell you the best way to get your documents to us when we talk to you (see 'How to tell us'). If you don't have these forms, or we need more information, we may ask you to provide: - your full set of accounts, or - a personal declaration. Types of documents we accept

chunks.title: Help to prepare your accounts
chunks.text: It’s important we have the correct income information. If you need help preparing this, support is available online and in the community. The Inland Revenue website is a helpful place to start. Self-employed (Inland Revenue)external Record keeping (Inland Revenue)external For help in the community, see the Family Services Directory. Budgeting/Financial Capability (Family Services Directory)external

chunks.title: How your benefit or payment will be affected
chunks.text: You can check how your income will affect your benefit using the income deduction tables. Income deduction tables

chunks.title: Want to check or change your income?
chunks.text: If you've already told us about your income, it will show in MyMSD. If you think the amount you entered isn't correct, please change this as soon as you can by logging back into MyMSD. If you need to change your income after 6pm on Friday, call us before midday on the following Monday. Phone us

chunks.title: Self-employment start up payment
chunks.text: If you're starting a business and need help with essential start up costs, eg furniture or the first lot of stock, we may be able to help. If you don't have a business planexternal, we can talk with you about how to create one. We need to make sure that your business is viable before we can approve the payment.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Self-employment start up payment if you’re: - out of work, and - aged 16 or older and not qualified to receive NZ Super, and - disadvantaged in the local labour market, and - at risk of likelihood of long-term benefit dependency (this usually means you are getting a benefit or you qualify for one), and - able to meet the residency criteria. To meet the residency criteria you need to be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and either: - a New Zealand citizen - a resident with a residence class visa - recognised as a refugee or protected person, or - have a temporary visa that allows you to work in New Zealand and either: have applied to be recognised as a refugee or protected person and are waiting on the outcome, or have applied for a residence class visa and are compelled to stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances. - have applied to be recognised as a refugee or protected person and are waiting on the outcome, or - have applied for a residence class visa and are compelled to stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances. Disadvantaged in the labour market means you have, or are expected to have, difficulty in getting or keeping a job. For example, you might have barriers to employment such as lack of education and training. You also need to: - be starting a new business and - have essential start-up costs that you need help with.

chunks.title: Who can't get it
chunks.text: You can't get the Self-employment start up payment if: - you're currently bankrupt - you're re-starting a business you've owned before.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: How much you get depends on your situation. We can pay for things like: - equipment required for the business - initial start-up stock for the business - materials required to produce goods for the business - renovation of premises to facilitate start of business or - one-off start-up costs, for example: connection fees, such as power, phone or internet first month's lease and bond legal costs associated with establishing the business insurance start-up costs for advertising/marketing printing business cards or flyers - connection fees, such as power, phone or internet - first month's lease and bond - legal costs associated with establishing the business - insurance - start-up costs for advertising/marketing - printing business cards or flyers - setting up a basic website.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009. We'll: - ask you about your business - talk with you about: your business plan, if you already have one how to create a business plan, if you don't already have one a Business Training and Advice Grant and how this may be able to help. - your business plan, if you already have one - how to create a business plan, if you don't already have one - a Business Training and Advice Grant and how this may be able to help. Business Training and Advice Grant You'll need to send your business plan to us and we'll send it away to be independently assessed to make sure it's viable.

chunks.title: COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment
chunks.text:
## COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment
The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment was to help businesses pay their employees while they waited for PCR test results. It was available between 9 February 2021 and 17 October 2022.
The information on this page is a summary of the key details about this payment. Detailed information can be found in the declarations at the bottom of this page.
## Who could get it
This payment was available to help businesses pay employees waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result.
The application for the person who took the COVID-19 PCR test must have been for either:
- an employee
- someone who was a dependant of an employee, or
- someone who was self-employed.
They must have been unable to work from home while they waited for the results.
Also, during the period applied for:
- the business must have been registered with the New Zealand Companies Office (except for self-employed people) and operating in New Zealand.
- self-employed people must have been physically located and legally working in New Zealand, along with other requirements, e.g. having an IRD number.
- State Sector organisations were generally not eligible for COVID-19 payments, however some may have been granted an exception. This could be because they had an exception for a previous COVID-19 payment, or the organisation was a State-Owned Enterprise or Mixed Ownership Model company.
The full eligibility criteria is listed in the declarations.
## Payment amount
The payment amount was a one-off payment of $359 for each eligible employee. This was regardless of whether they were working full or part-time.
## Declarations
There are different declarations depending on when you applied for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment. Your obligations and repayment responsibilities are in the declaration you agreed to when you applied.

## Skills for Industry
You may be able to get short-term job-focused training to help you get a job.
Skills for Industry programmes are entry-level industry training programmes to help you get and keep a job. We've partnered with employers and training providers to create these.
Programmes usually include:
- entry-level training, e.g. workplace safety training
- industry-specific training
- help to get a job
- on-the-job training once you start work
- help to get a qualification to advance in the industry.
Skills for Industry programmes are available in industries offering entry-level employment with a career pathway. Their goal is to help you find meaningful work.
If there’s an industry you’d like to work in, ask your local Work and Income service centre staff about Skills for Industry, or call us on 0800 559 009.

## Who can get it

If you are getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension it also depends on how much you and your spouse or partner earn.
If you are going into a social rehabilitation programme but are not getting a benefit, contact us to find out if you qualify for one.

chunks.title: Reapply for Sole Parent Support
chunks.text:
## Reapply for Sole Parent Support
If you're getting Sole Parent Support and you still need it after 52 weeks, you have to reapply. The easiest way to do this is online.
## How to reapply
You'll get a letter and notification in MyMSD 4 weeks before you need to reapply for Sole Parent Support.
You need to:
- log in to MyMSD
- select the notification
- complete the online reapplication form.
You may need to talk with us. MyMSD will let you know if you need to do this.
MyMSDlogin
If you can't use MyMSD, call us and we'll:
- book an appointment for you
- complete the reapplication form with you at your appointment
- let you know if there are any other documents you need to provide.
Call us
## What happens next
Once you submit your form, you'll get a page that confirms your reapplication has been submitted successfully. It also tells you:
- to book an appointment, if you haven't already
- what supporting documents you'll need to provide.
If we need any supporting documents, e.g. proof of your income, you'll need to either:
- drop them off to your local service centre, or
- upload or email them, contact us to find out how to do this, or
- bring them with you to your appointment, if it's at a service centre.
Local service centre
Contact us
## Your appointment
During your appointment we'll talk with you about:
- work you've done before what you enjoyed what you didn't enjoy
- what you enjoyed
- what you didn't enjoy
- the types of jobs or training you're interested in
- other skills or experience you have
- what you've done to look for work
- how we can help you look for work.

chunks.title: Sole parent support - deduction tables
chunks.text:
## Sole parent support - deduction tables
Use this table to estimate how much will be deducted from your Sole Parent Support benefit payment if you earn income.
## Your deductions
If you're a sole parent, you can earn up to $160 a week (before tax), before your benefit is affected. Once you earn over $160 a week (before tax):
- any income you get between $160 and $250 a week (before tax) will reduce your benefit by 30 cents for each $1 of income
- any income you get over $250 a week (before tax) will reduce your benefit by 70 cents for every $1 of income.
We calculate this by:
- We take the income you get between $160 and $250 (maximum will be $90) and multiply by 0.3.
- If your income is over $250, we take your total income and minus $250, then multiply by 0.7.
- Then we add these two amounts together.
If you're paying for childcare, you may be able to earn up to $180 a week (before tax), before your payment is affected. This depends on the amount you're paying for childcare while you're working. It can include private childcare arrangements and childcare costs not covered by a Childcare or OSCAR Subsidy.
Any other payments you get, e.g. Accommodation Supplement, may also be affected.
If you earn over a certain amount, you won't qualify for Sole Parent Support. We call this the 'Gross weekly income cut-out point'.

chunks.title: Sole Parent Support
chunks.text: Sole Parent Support is a weekly payment that helps single parents find part-time work or get ready for future work. This benefit: - helps you get ready for future work (if your youngest child is under 3) - supports you to find part-time work (if your youngest child is aged 3-13) - may mean you can get help with education and training. Only one parent or caregiver can get Sole Parent Support. Shared care of your child could affect your payments.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get Sole Parent Support if you: - are aged 20 or older (if you're 19 or younger, you may be able to get a Young Parent Payment) - are a single parent or caregiver - have one or more dependent children under 14 - are not in a relationship, and - do not have adequate financial support. Young Parent Payment You also need to: - be either: a New Zealand citizen a permanent resident, or have a residence visa under the Immigration Act 2009 - a New Zealand citizen - a permanent resident, or - have a residence visa under the Immigration Act 2009 - have lived continuously in NZ for at least 2 years since either: becoming a NZ citizen becoming a permanent resident, or getting a residence class visa - becoming a NZ citizen - becoming a permanent resident, or - getting a residence class visa - be ordinarily resident in NZ, and - be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when you apply. Ordinarily resident If you meet all the above criteria except for the one about how long you've lived in New Zealand, talk to us. Phone us This information is a guide only. For more detail about who can get it, read: Sole Parent Support qualification criteria (Manuals and Procedures)external

chunks.title: Check if you can get Sole Parent Support
chunks.text: To find out if you could get Sole Parent Support and what else you might qualify for, use our 'Check what you might get' tool.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Sole Parent Support is paid weekly. How much you get depends on your situation and how much you earn. Sole Parent Support rates and income limits (Map)external Income deduction tables If you get Sole Parent Support, you'll also automatically get a Winter Energy Payment. This is paid during the Winter months. Winter Energy Paymentexternal

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You can apply online through MyMSD. We'll also check to see if you can get any other help from us, based on the answers you give in your application. If you want to get child support through Inland Revenue, you can apply through us when you complete your online application. Or you can apply through Inland Revenue. Any child support payments you get will be counted as income for your benefit. Apply online Child support

chunks.title: Complete your next steps in MyMSD
chunks.text: Once you've submitted your online form, you need to complete your next steps in MyMSD. - Complete a Jobseeker profile. - Read and agree to your obligations. - Provide your documents. - Verify your identity. - Book an appointment. Apply online - Complete your next steps in MyMSD

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: Once you've submitted your online form, we'll call you if there's anything else you need to do.

chunks.title: If your application's approved
chunks.text: - We'll let you know when your payments will start. - We'll send you a Community Services Card to help with the costs of healthcare and public transport. - You may get a family tax credit. This can be paid with your benefit or from Inland Revenue (it depends what option you chose when you applied for your benefit). Community Services Card Family tax credit (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: While you're getting Sole Parent Support
chunks.text: There are things you need to do when you're getting a Sole Parent Support benefit. If you don't do them, your benefit could reduce or stop. This includes things like: - telling us if something changes - finding or preparing for work - taking part in work ability assessments. Sole Parent Support obligations

chunks.title: Getting Sole Parent Support for more than 12 months
chunks.text: If you're getting Sole Parent Support and you still need it after a year, you have to re-apply. Re-apply for Sole Parent Support

chunks.title: Once your youngest child turns 14
chunks.text: Once your youngest child turns 14, you are no longer able to get Sole Parent Support. We may transfer you from Sole Parent Support to Jobseeker Support. Find out when you'll transfer and what you'll need to do differently when you're on Jobseeker Support. Transfer from Sole Parent Support to Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: When someone getting Veteran's Pension dies
chunks.text: If someone getting Veteran's Pension dies, the surviving partner or dependent child may be able to get extra help from us. You need to let us know they've passed away. You can do this by completing our online form. Register a senior's death with usexternal We'll contact you to discuss what extra help you may be able to get.

chunks.title: Lump sum payment
chunks.text: There are 2 lump sum payments available. Which payment you may be able to get depends on whether the person who's died is a veteran or not.

chunks.title: Person who died is a veteran
chunks.text: If you're the surviving partner or dependent child of a veteran who's died, you may be able to get a lump sum payment. This is $7,580.60 and not taxed. It's to help with funeral costs. You may be able to get this lump sum payment if the veteran who died: - was getting Veteran's Pension when they died - had either a war disablement pension of 70% or more under the War Pensions Act 1954, or disablement pension of 52% or more under the Veterans' Support Act 2014, and - war disablement pension of 70% or more under the War Pensions Act 1954, or - disablement pension of 52% or more under the Veterans' Support Act 2014, and - was ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they died. The surviving partner will get the full amount of the lump sum payment. If there is no surviving partner, the lump sum payment will be split between any dependent children.

chunks.title: Person who died is not a veteran
chunks.text: If your partner dies, you may be able to get a lump sum payment of $5,780.43. This is not taxed and is to help with funeral costs. You can get this lump sum payment if your partner: - was getting Veteran's Pension when they died, and - was ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they died.

chunks.title: Veteran's Pension payments continue for 28 days
chunks.text: As well as a lump sum payment, we may also be able to keep payments going for 28 days into the person's account who's died. Or pay it into the surviving partner's account instead. If this happens, the amount we pay over 28 days will be deducted from any lump sum payment you receive.

chunks.title: Ongoing payments
chunks.text: What type of ongoing payments you can get from us depends on whether you're the surviving partner or dependent child.

chunks.title: Surviving partner
chunks.text: If you're the surviving partner of a veteran who's died, we'll look to see if you: - meet the criteria for Veteran's Pension, or - were included as a partner in their Veteran's Pension payments. If you meet the criteria for Veteran's Pension, we'll reassess your Veteran's Pension payment. This is so we can make sure you're now getting the correct amount. You may be better off getting a different payment from us, for example NZ Super. We'll contact you to discuss your options. If you were included as a partner in their Veteran's Pension payments, your Veteran's Pension payments may stop. It depends on your situation. We'll contact you to discuss your options.

chunks.title: Surviving dependent child
chunks.text: There may be a surviving dependent child of a veteran who's died, who's going to be cared for by a person who's not their parent. If so, the caregiver may be able to get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit. Orphan's Benefit Unsupported Child's Benefit The dependent child may also qualify for a Children's Pension from Veteran's Affairs. Veterans' Affairs websiteexternal

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: While you're living in public (social) housing, you need to let us know straight away about any changes in your or your partner's situation You need to tell us no matter how much rent you pay. This could be changes to: - income - assets - people moving in or out of the property - children in your care, for example having a child or changing custody arrangements. Changes may affect: - the amount of rent you pay - whether you still qualify for public housing, or - whether the property you're in is still suitable for you. If you don't let us know, you could end up paying the wrong amount of rent and may have a debt to pay back. Or you may only get a few weeks' notice before your rent goes up.

chunks.title: If you get child support through Inland Revenue
chunks.text: Inland Revenue (IR) will share your child support payment information with us every time they pay you child support. We'll use the shared information from IR and treat this as income if you get one of these payments from us: - a main benefit, e.g. Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support - NZ Super or Veteran's Pension and you have a partner who doesn't qualify for this but is included in your payments - Veteran's Pension and you're under 65 - Accommodation Supplement - Disability Allowance - Temporary Additional Support - Special Benefit - Childcare Subsidy - OSCAR Subsidy, or - Employment Transition Assistance. If you get one of these payments from us, you don't need to tell us about most types of IR child support payments. The only type you need to tell us about is if you're getting Court Ordered lump sum child support payments. If you don't get one of the payments in the above bulleted list, you need to tell us about your IR child support payments. You also need to tell us about any other child support payments you get.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: You need to call us. Who you call depends on your situation. If you get: - a benefit or extra help payments from us, call us on 0800 559 009 - NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, call Senior Services on 0800 552 002 - no payments from us or Senior Services, call Housing Unit on 0800 673 468.

chunks.title: Tenancy reviews
chunks.text: As well as telling us about any changes, your tenancy may be reviewed from time to time. Tenancy reviews

chunks.title: Social Security Agreement with South Korea
chunks.text:
## Social Security Agreement with South Korea
New Zealand (NZ) has an agreement with South Korea to share responsibility for social security coverage.
This agreement generally allows you to apply for certain NZ payments (paid by us) or South Korean payments (paid by the South Korean National Pension Service).
NZ payments covered by this agreement are:
- New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super)
- Veteran's Pension
The only South Korean payment covered by this agreement is the Old-age Pension.
It also allows you to add together your periods of residence in either country so you can meet certain criteria for these payments.
## Living in South Korea
If you've lived in New Zealand and now live in South Korea, you may be able to get some payments.
Social Security Agreement with South Korea - living in South Korea
## Living in New Zealand
If you've lived in South Korea and now live in New Zealand, you may be able to get some payments.
Social Security Agreement with South Korea - living in New Zealand

chunks.title: Special Banking Option
chunks.text: If you get an overseas pension and a payment from us, you may be able to use the Special Banking Option. There are 2 methods of payment for overseas pensions: - Direct Payment Option, and - Special Banking Option. Your overseas pension will be paid using the Direct Payment Option unless you tell us you want the Special Banking Option.

chunks.title: Direct Payment Option
chunks.text: Usually when you get an overseas pension, the overseas agency pays this directly into your bank account. This means: - you'll get separate payments: your overseas pension from the overseas agency and your NZ payment from us - your overseas pension from the overseas agency and - your NZ payment from us - your NZ payment will be reduced dollar-for-dollar by the amount of your overseas pension - your NZ payment and overseas pension payments will vary as the exchange rates go up and down - you're responsible for paying tax on your overseas pension.

chunks.title: Special Banking Option
chunks.text: In some cases, you can choose to have the overseas agency pay your overseas pension into a Special Banking Option bank account in NZ. This bank account is in your name but can only be accessed by Work and Income. The account doesn't incur bank fees and it doesn't earn any interest. Using the Special Banking Option (SBO) means: - you'll get a payment from Work and Income that is your NZ payment - any payments paid into the SBO account will not be passed on to you, except in specific circumstances. If the payment is passed on to you, it may affect your NZ payment amount. If the payment is not passed on to you, your NZ payment won't be affected (including when the exchange rate for the overseas payment changes) - If the payment is passed on to you, it may affect your NZ payment amount. - If the payment is not passed on to you, your NZ payment won't be affected (including when the exchange rate for the overseas payment changes) - you don't need to pay NZ tax on payments that are in the SBO account, unless they are passed onto you. If the payment in the SBO account is passed on to you, we'll let you know. If the total amount of your overseas pensions is more than your NZ payment, you may be better off using the Direct Payment Option.

chunks.title: If you get a Netherlands pension
chunks.text: If your Netherlands pension is paid into the SBO account, we'll pay your holiday pay to you shortly after it's received. You may have paid voluntary contributions towards your Netherlands pension. If you did, and your pension is paid into the SBO account, we'll pay the voluntary portion to you shortly after it's received. This means you'll get an extra: - monthly payment from us with your voluntary portion of your Netherlands payment - yearly payment (in June) from us with your holiday pay portion. You may have to pay tax on these payments.

chunks.title: Who can use the Special Banking Option
chunks.text: You can choose to use the Special Banking Option if: - you get an overseas pension from either: Australia Guernsey Ireland Jersey the Netherlands, or United Kingdom, and - Australia - Guernsey - Ireland - Jersey - the Netherlands, or - United Kingdom, and - you don't have a non-deductible component in your pension (e.g. voluntary contributions), except if it's a Netherlands pension. If you choose to use the Special Banking Option and have a partner who also gets an overseas pension from the same country, they must choose the Special Banking Option as well. Once you've chosen the Special Banking Option, you can switch to the Direct Payment Option. But you can't switch back to the Special Banking Option again.

chunks.title: When you can't use it
chunks.text: You can't use the Special Banking Option when: - you're going overseas for more than 26 weeks - you're un-discharged bankrupt - you have an overseas pension debt with the overseas agency - you have more than one overseas pension and you can't get a NZ payment because one of your pensions is too much - you have a voluntary or non-deductible component to your overseas pension (except if it's a Netherlands pension).

chunks.title: Apply for Special Banking Option
chunks.text: To apply for the Special Banking Option, you need to complete 3 forms: - Information release form - Bank account application form, and - Special Banking Option Offer form. To find the forms you need, select the country you get your overseas pensions from below. Once you've filled the forms out, you can either: - scan and email them to us at international_services@msd.govt.nz - drop them off to one of our service centres or - post them to our International Services team.

chunks.title: Special Benefit issue
chunks.text: We found some people would have been better off financially if they'd moved from Special Benefit to Temporary Additional Support after 1 April 2006. We thought Special Benefit clients couldn't move to Temporary Additional Support. We got this wrong. We're sorry for this and we're fixing it. We want all our clients to get all the help they need.

chunks.title: If you're still getting Special Benefit
chunks.text: We'll arrange to meet with you if you're still getting Special Benefit and might be better off moving to Temporary Additional Support. We'll talk about your situation and help you work out what's best for you. You can bring a family member, friend or advocate with you, and take some time before you decide if you want to stay on Special benefit or move to Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: If you used to get Special Benefit check if you're owed money
chunks.text: If you used to get Special Benefit, you can use the payment errors enquiry form to see if you're owed money. It won't say how much you're owed. If you're owed money you can use the form to submit your enquiry. We can process it and pay the money we owe you. Unfortunately, our staff can't tell you if you're owed money or how much it is. Payment errors enquiry form The payment errors enquiry form will tell you if you're owed money - it won't say how much you're owed. We'll write to you to confirm your payment. The payment errors enquiry form will also let you know if we owe you money for the Accommodation Supplement error. More information on errors with Accommodation Supplement areasMore information on errors with Accommodation Supplement accommodation types

chunks.title: Checking payment errors for someone else
chunks.text: You can also use the payment errors enquiry form to check to see if we owe someone else money when: - they're not a current client - a person has died. Information to make an enquiry for someone elseInformation to make an enquiry for someone who has died The form will tell you if the person you're making an enquiry for is on the list of clients who may be affected and you can apply for them. It won't say how much they may be owed.

chunks.title: How payments may affect your benefit or allowance
chunks.text: If you're getting a benefit or allowance from us, it won't be affected for 12 months from the date we make any payment to you because of the Special Benefit issue. If you: - still have this money after 12 months, you'll need to tell us and it will be counted for any benefits or payments that are asset tested - invest the money you get and earn interest, after 12 months you'll need to tell us and this will be counted as income.

chunks.title: Working for Families and Special Benefit payment
chunks.text: Your payment won't affect your Working for Families payment because Special Benefit payments aren't counted as income for Working for Families.

chunks.title: Impact on your taxes
chunks.text: You won't have to pay tax on this payment because Special Benefit payments aren't taxable. Any income you earn on it (for example interest) will be taxable.

chunks.title: Income rules for Special Benefit
chunks.text:
## Income rules for Special Benefit
If you're getting Special Benefit you have to tell us about any income, one-off payments or assets you, or your partner, get.
## How it works
If you get Special Benefit as part of the benefits you're paid you have to tell us about any other regular payments, assets or one-off payments you, or your partner, get.
Declare income
## Changes to your other payments
If your other payments from us change, it could affect how much you get for your Special benefit. This includes main benefits (e.g. Jobseeker Support or Supported Living Payment), and extra help payments (e.g. Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance).
If your main benefit payment goes up, your Special Benefit payment may go down. If your main benefit goes down, your Special Benefit may go up. Main benefits are reviewed every year on 1 April, and they usually go up from this date.
If you're getting extra help, your Special Benefit may change if your extra help payment changes. If your costs go down (e.g. your prescriptions), your Special Benefit payment may go down, because you're paying less. If your costs go up (e.g. your rent), your Special benefit may go up, because you're paying more.

## Who can get it

- you are getting a benefit or pension
- your spouse or partner is in residential care, or has been in a public hospital for over 13 weeks.

You do not need to apply if you've told us about your partner going into hospital or a rest home.
Contact the Residential Subsidy Unit on 0800 999 727 to talk about your circumstances.
