chunks.title: Other urgent or unexpected costs
chunks.text: If you have a cost that's urgent or unexpected and not listed here, eg, clothing or bedding, we may still be able to help. We may be able to give you a one-off payment. What payment you may be able to get depends on if you're getting a benefit or not, and what cost you have.

chunks.title: If you're already getting a benefit
chunks.text: You may be able to get either Special Needs Grant or Advance Payment of Benefit. Special Needs Grant Advance Payment of Benefit Each payment covers lots of different costs. If you get stuck, give us a call on 0800 559 009 and talk with us about your situation.

chunks.title: If you're not getting a benefit
chunks.text: You may be able to get either: - Special Needs Grant or - Recoverable Assistance Payment. Special Needs Grant Recoverable Assistance Payment Each payment covers lots of different costs. If you get stuck, give us a call on 0800 559 009 and talk with us about your situation.

chunks.title: Using a payment card
chunks.text: How to use your payment card, where you can use it and what you can buy. Make sure you: - set a personalised PIN before you use it - sign the back of your card - spend the money within 7 days from when it's loaded onto the card (for glasses you have up to 28 days) - use the card at shops that are registered with us and accept payment cards - only spend up to the amount of money on your card. How to set your PIN

chunks.title: Setting your PIN
chunks.text: You need to set a personalised PIN to use your payment card. If you haven't set your own PIN the card won't work. If you have more than one card, you need to set a PIN for each card.

chunks.title: How to set your PIN:
chunks.text: - Log in to MyMSD. - Go to 'My payment cards'. - Select the card you want to add a PIN for. - Enter a 4-digit PIN - don't use a PIN that is consecutive, easily associated with you (like birthdays), or the numbers on your card. - Re-enter your PIN to confirm. - Done! Your PIN is now ready to go. MyMSD Loginexternal Other ways to set your PIN: - call us and say "set my card PIN" - register your voice so you can set your PIN by calling us at any time without waiting to talk to a person - our staff in our service centres can help set your PIN in MyMSD - we have other ways you can contact us if you're deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech impairment.

chunks.title: How to use the card
chunks.text: - At the checkout, swipe the payment card through the EFTPOS terminal. - Select the CHQ option. - Enter your personalised PIN. Make sure no one can see you PIN when enter it. - Sign your receipt – the shop staff will check this matches your signature on the back of your card. Find out how to set your PIN Don't throw the card away after you've used up the balance. Keep it so we can use it again if you need more help.

chunks.title: What you can buy
chunks.text: You can only use your payment card to buy the essential items you applied for. These are things like: - food and groceries - clothes - dental treatment. You can't buy non-essential items like: - alcohol - cigarettes, tobacco or vaping products - gift cards or vouchers (except for phone top-ups) - lotto tickets - non-essential appliances or electronics (such as an air fryer or gaming console). If you're a young person in Youth Service on Money management, there's a few different rules about what you can get: Money management - Youth Service - ratonga taiohiexternal

chunks.title: Keeping your PIN and card safe
chunks.text: Your PIN is a security measure to make sure no one else can use your payment card. Do not write your PIN down, and do not tell anyone else your PIN. This includes police, family members and Ministry of Social Development staff. If you think someone else knows your PIN, reset it or call us. Keep your payment card in a safe place. If you need further payments, we can load them onto this card, so you don't need to go to a service centre to get another one. Never let anyone else use your payment card.

chunks.title: Where you can use it
chunks.text: You can only use payment cards in shops that are registered with us and accept our cards. When you apply we'll talk with you about what help you need, how much money has been granted and which shops you can go to. You can check which shop your payment is for in MyMSD. MyMSDexternal. You may be able to use the card in more than one registered shop, depending on what you've applied for. For example, you can use food grant payments in more than one grocery or food shop.

chunks.title: Money leftover
chunks.text: You can check how much money you've spent and how much is left online in MyMSD. MyMSDexternal. You may have money leftover if you: - haven't spent all the money yet because you're planning to spend it at more than one shop - didn't need to spend all the money. Any money you don't need will stay on the payment card until the 7 days is up. After the 7 days is up it will expire. If the money is for glasses you have up to 28 days to spend it. If you don't spend the full amount on your card, you can't get cash out for the rest. You also can't get vouchers or gift cards for the rest.

chunks.title: Vasectomies
chunks.text:
## Vasectomies
If you're on a benefit or a low income and want a vasectomy, we may be able to help with the cost of travel, accommodation and surgery.
- The decision whether to get a vasectomy or not is an entirely personal decision made in consultation with a health practitioner, e.g., a doctor.
- You don't have to pay the money back.
## Who can get it
You may be able to get help if:
- assistance is not available from your District Health Board
- only partial funding is available from your District Health Board
District Health Board - Ministry of Health websiteexternal
- you need to travel away from home or pay private fees.
You also need to:
- be 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Service)
Youth Serviceexternal
- be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident
- normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here
- have no other way to meet these costs.
It also depends on:
- how much you and your partner earn
- any money or assets you and your partner have.
Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income and asset limits apply:
## What you can get
We can pay up to $300 for:
- travel
- accommodation
- surgery.
How much you get depends on your situation. You don't have to pay the money back.
## How to apply
You need to call us on 0800 559 009
We'll book you an appointment to come in and see us. We'll let you know what you need to bring.

chunks.title: Violent relationships
chunks.text:
## Violent relationships
If your relationship has ended because of family violence, there are a number of ways we may be able to help you.
If you're in immediate danger, dial 111 and ask for the Police.
Family violence help and support (NZ Police)external
The 'Are you OK' website also has information and services that can help you. You can call them on 0800 456 450.
Are You OK (Family Violence Information and Support)external
## How we can help
If you are living in or leaving a violent relationship you can talk to Work and Income about how we can help you. We have specialist staff in each region who will help you access the right support services, including financial help from us, depending on your need.
This could include:
- financial help to get back on your feet - including benefit payments, help with accommodation costs, special needs grants and other assistance
- help to find somewhere to live - including information on housing options in your area and, if need be, an assessment for social housing
- referring you to other support services and agencies able to help you.
We'll also support you to build a better future for you and your family by helping you prepare or look for suitable work. We'll take into account your particular circumstances and what's appropriate for you.
Work and Income case managers have been trained to identify and respond appropriately to people who are living in or leaving violent family situations. Talk to us about your situation. The more we understand what is happening for you, the better we can help you.
Call us on 0800 559 009 to make an appointment and say "Appointment".

chunks.title: COVID-19 Wage Subsidy August 2021
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Wage Subsidies August 2021 were a series of 8 payments. These were to help businesses pay employees and protect jobs affected by COVID-19 alert level changes. They were available from 20 August 2021 to 9 December 2021 and are now closed. The COVID-19 Wage Subsidies August 2021 were support for businesses to pay 2 weeks of wages (per application) for their employees. It was to continue support for businesses affected by changes to COVID-19 alert levels and lockdowns. The information on this page is a summary of the key details about these payments. Detailed information can be found in the declarations at the bottom of this page.

chunks.title: Who could get it
chunks.text: These payments were available to employers, including self-employed people, whose employees could not work during the COVID-19 alert level changes. The alert level changes lasted from 17 August 2021 until 2 December 2021, when New Zealand moved to the COVID-19 Protection Framework. Employers and self-employed people could apply on behalf of their employees. To get a payment, a business must have: - had at least a 40% decline in revenue over a certain timeframe (this timeframe depended on the time of application, there’s more detail about this in the declarations below) - been registered with the New Zealand Companies Office (except for self-employed people) and operating in New Zealand - physically located and legally working in New Zealand (for self-employed people). State Sector organisations were generally not eligible for COVID-19 payments, however some may have been granted an exception. This could be because they had an exception for a previous COVID-19 payment, or the organisation was a State-Owned Enterprise or Mixed Ownership Model company. The full eligibility criteria is listed in the declarations.

chunks.title: Payment amount
chunks.text: These payments were paid as a 2-week lump sum of: - $600 a week for each full-time employee (20 hours a week or more) - $359 a week for each part-time employee (less than 20 hours a week).

chunks.title: Declarations
chunks.text: The declarations contain the full eligibility criteria, obligations and repayment responsibilities for each of the Wage Subsidy August 2021 payments. Each Wage Subsidy had its own declaration. Wage Subsidy 1 declaration: from 9am 20 Aug 2021 to 7am 3 Sep 2021Wage Subsidy 2 declaration: from 9am 3 Sep 2021 to 11:59pm 16 Sep 2021Wage Subsidy 3 declaration: from 9am 17 Sep 2021 to 11:59pm 30 Sep 2021Wage Subsidy 4 declaration: from 9am 1 Oct 2021 to 11:59pm 14 Oct 2021Wage Subsidy 5 declaration: from 9am 15 Oct 2021 to 11:59pm 28 Oct 2021Wage Subsidy 6 declaration: from 9am 29 Oct 2021 to 11:59pm 11 Nov 2021Wage Subsidy 7 declaration: from 9am 12 Nov 2021 to 11:59pm 25 Nov 2021Wage Subsidy 8 declaration; from 9am 26 Nov 2021 to 11:59pm 9 Dec 2021

chunks.title: COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Extension
chunks.text:
## COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Extension
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Extension was to help businesses pay staff impacted by COVID-19. It was available from 10 June 2020 to 1 September 2020.
The Wage Subsidy Extension was support for businesses to pay 8 weeks of wages for their employees. It was to continue support for businesses affected by changes to COVID-19 alert levels and lockdowns.
The information on this page is a summary of the key details about this payment. Detailed information can be found in the declaration at the bottom of this page.
## Who could get it
This payment was available to employers, including self-employed people, whose employees could not work. The business must also have had a 40% decline in revenue:
over the period of any month being applied for, when compared to the same month in 2019, andthat loss was attributable to the COVID-19 outbreak.State Sector organisations were generally not eligible to get the Wage Subsidy Extension, however some may have been granted an exception.
## Payment rates
The subsidy was paid at a flat rate of:
$585.80 for full-time employees (20 hours or more a week)$350.00 for part-time employees (less than 20 hours a week).If the employee's usual wages were less than the subsidy rate, any difference should have been used to pay wages of other affected staff. If there were no other affected staff, the remaining amount must be repaid.
## Paying your staff
The business must have tried their hardest to pay the employee at least 80% of their usual wages while getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Extension for them. If that wasn't possible, the employee must have been paid at least the subsidy payment rate.
## Declaration
The declaration contains the full eligibility criteria, obligations and repayment responsibilities for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Extension.

chunks.title: COVID-19 Wage Subsidy March 2021
chunks.text:
## COVID-19 Wage Subsidy March 2021
The Wage Subsidy March 2021 was to help businesses pay staff affected by COVID-19 alert level changes. It was available from 1pm on 4 March 2021 to 11:59pm on 21 March 2021.
The information on this page is a summary of the key details about this payment. Detailed information can be found in the declaration at the bottom of this page.
## Who could get it
This payment was available to employers or self-employed people. Their business must have had or expected to have had a 40% decline in revenue over 14 consecutive days between 28 February and 21 March, compared to a typical 14-day period between 4 January and 14 February 2021.
Businesses with highly seasonal revenue could compare their decline in revenue to the same period in 2019.
State Sector organisations were generally not eligible to get the Wage Subsidy, however some may have been granted an exception.
## Payment rates
The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy March 2021 was paid as a 2-week lump sum of either:
- $585.80 a week for full-time employees (20 hours a week or more)
- $350 a week for part-time employees (less than 20 hours a week).
## Paying your staff
The business must have tried their hardest to pay their employees at least 80% of their usual wages while getting the wage subsidy for them. If that wasn't possible, at least the subsidy rate needed to be paid.
## Declarations
The declaration contains the full eligibility criteria, obligations and repayment responsibilities for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy March 2021.

chunks.title: Waiting for public housing
chunks.text:
## Waiting for public housing
Once you apply for public housing, you'll need to wait until a suitable property becomes available. You'll also need to tell us if your situation changes while you're waiting.
## How long you have to wait
The length of time you have to wait depends on:
- how urgently you need a property
- how quickly a suitable property becomes available
- what your needs are
- the number of other people waiting with urgent needs.
People with the greatest needs are placed first, when suitable properties become available. A suitable property is one that meets your housing needs as agreed during your interview.
While waiting for a property, it’s important to keep looking for other options, like rental properties in the private market.
Find private housing
## Tell us if something changes
While you're waiting to get into a public house, you must let us know straight away about any changes in your and your partner’s (if you have one) circumstances.
This could be changes to your:
- address and phone number
- income or financial circumstances
- family or household arrangements.
If you don’t let us know, you might not be able to get a property that best meets your needs, or you may no longer qualify for public housing.
## How to tell us
Call us on 0800 673 468
## Confirm your circumstances
We may contact you and ask you to confirm your circumstances. This is so we can make sure your situation hasn't changed.
We will either:
- call you and ask you to confirm over the phone, or
- text you and ask you to confirm in MyMSD.
MyMSD is our online service where you can apply and manage your information online.
About MyMSD
If we contact you, it's important you confirm your circumstances. Otherwise we may think you no longer need public housing and cancel your application.

- Accepting a public housing offer
- Living in public housing
- Find a house

We've found an error where some people's benefits were stopped or reduced too early when they had a Warrant to Arrest. This means we owe some people money.

- you had an arrest warrant before July 2016, and
- your payments were stopped or reduced because of this.
## If we owe you money
We're contacting and paying all our current clients.
We aren't currently making payments to former clients affected by this error. We want to make sure these payments won't affect other payments people may be getting, eg Working for Families.

chunks.title: What happens to your benefit while you train or study
chunks.text: Find out if your benefit will change while you're training or studying, and what other help you might be able to get. To keep getting your benefit while you train or study, you need to make sure you still meet your benefit obligations. - Obligations are things you need to do when you get a payment from us. - If you don't do them, your payments could reduce or stop. Select a benefit below to find out what kind of training or study you can do while getting that benefit.

chunks.title: Jobseeker Support
chunks.text: To get Jobseeker Support while you train or study, you need to meet your work obligations. Jobseeker Support has 3 types of work obligations: - full-time work obligations - part-time work obligations - work preparation obligations.

chunks.title: Full-time work obligations
chunks.text: This means you need to be available and looking for full-time work, which is at least 30 hours a week. If you're studying or training: - part-time, you can get Jobseeker Support if you're still available and looking for full-time work - full-time, you can't get Jobseeker Support, as you won't be available for full-time work. You may be able to get payments from StudyLink instead. Studylinkexternal If you're not sure if a course is part-time or full-time, check with your education provider.

chunks.title: Part-time work obligations
chunks.text: If you have a health condition, injury or disability, you will have part-time work obligations. This means you need to be available and looking for part-time work, which is at least 15 hours a week. If you're studying or training part-time, you can get Jobseeker Support if you're still available and looking for part-time work.

chunks.title: Work preparation obligations
chunks.text: If you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you can't work or can only work less than 15 hours a week, you will have work preparation obligations. This means you need to do a number of things to prepare and plan for work. If you're studying or training part-time, you can get Jobseeker Support if you can still meet this work obligation. You can read the full list of Jobseeker Support obligations to check all the obligations. Jobseeker Support obligations

chunks.title: Your youngest child is under 3
chunks.text: To get Sole Parent Support while you train or study: - you need to meet your work preparation obligations - your course must help you to find work in the future.

chunks.title: Your youngest child is 3 to 13
chunks.text: You can get Sole Parent Support if you're available, and looking, for part-time work of at least 20 hours a week. You may not have to do this if you're either: - already doing a course when your part-time work obligations started (e.g. when your Sole Parent Support started), or - studying at NZQA Level 4 or higher. You must pass at least half of your training or study. Sole Parent Support obligations You can read the full list of Sole Parent Support obligations to check all the obligations and make sure you're meeting those as well. Sole Parent Support obligations

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment
chunks.text: You can still get a Supported Living Payment while you train or study. This includes people getting Supported Living Payment as a carer. Your payment amounts won't change.

chunks.title: Young Parent and Youth Parent Payments
chunks.text: You can study full-time while getting these payments. Your payment amounts won't change. You may be able to get help from StudyLink as well. Contact your Youth Service provider so they can help you to work out which type of support is best for you.

chunks.title: If your benefit stops
chunks.text: If your benefit stops because your training or study means you can't meet your obligations, you might be able to get a different payment instead. Check if you can get help from StudyLink, including a Student loan or Student Allowance. Use their eligibility test to find out what you can get: Eligibility test (StudyLink)external

chunks.title: What you do on the Limited Service Volunteer course
chunks.text: What you do during the Limited Service Volunteer (LSV) course, where it's located, course dates, what you get, and paying for costs. At LSV, you do activities every day to learn new skills and improve yourself. You stay on a NZ Defence Force base in Auckland, Wellington or Christchurch. Your accommodation, food, clothing and travel are all free. If you need medical care, like seeing a dentist or physio, this is free as well. To get the most out of the course, you need to put in as much effort as you can, and push yourself to your limits. This will help you discover your strengths and how you can use these in future. You do this as part of a team. You are also supported by NZ Defence Force staff, a Work and Income staff member, and a social worker. Read more about LSV on this page, or if you're ready to apply, you can do this on the Applying for LSV page. Apply for the Limited Service Volunteer course

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: There's no other course like this that I'm aware of. You know, these guys come here, everyone's got an equal chance here to prove themselves and to learn. We always tell them, once you get used to the routine, you'll honestly love the course. And the last month will change your life. Move! Get your bags! Shoulders back. Heads up. That's the one. Be proud. Focus. One! I'm going to give you fifteen seconds. Move! The first day of LSV is really loud and aggressive. I think from a trainee's perspective, coming in, it can be quite overwhelming and quite scary. But knowing that there's a purpose behind everything we do, it sets up the rest of the six week. Get it in your mind that's going to be your clothing for the next six weeks. Make sure when you do this, your head is looking up, your shoulders are back, and you are proud to be here. We always say the first two weeks is the hardest, but if you're here at LSV you're pushed outside of your comfort zone. And when you're outside of your comfort zone you grow as a person, and it shows you what you're able to do as well. Get out any drugs, alcohol, knives, lighters, cell phones, MP3 players, aerosol cans, food, or jewellery, and this includes makeup, okay? This is the stuff we'll be taking from you for safe keeping. You'll get it back at the end. And you'll get it back when you need it. Before this course, I've been waking up at like, three or four PM. But I'm hoping to get, like, a routine from this. Just get up, get out and do things. And not just sit in my bed all day. Don't look at me. Look straight ahead. Stay in this position. I will be back with you. I want to change my life, and just make everyone proud. Especially my mum, because that's like the main person I'm trying to make myself proud to. Because she was a police officer. So I want to carry on the path that she took.

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: I can handle discipline, most of the time. And I've done camps and stuff before but not anything this intense. I'm finding it a bit strict, but in a good way. Like, this is the kind of strictness I need right now. Corridor! The first thing about us is that we're military. And you have come to us to learn, okay? So we come across as strict, stern, and we enforce standards. The reason for that is because we get you here, and we want to give you back to society here. Okay? So, we need to hold you accountable for your actions and at all times hold you to the standard that we expect of ourselves. So just because we're holding you accountable, and we're holding you quite strictly to these standards that we give out, doesn't mean that we don't care, doesn't mean that we don't like you. Understand that? Yes Staff. I feel like our 17 to 25 years olds, at that time of their life, their decisions that they make really impact them. So being here at a six-week residential live-in programme, it is tough. It is confronting. It is challenging. But that's the whole point of it, is to get people outside of their comfort zone so the real work can happen. One foot in front of the other. Five, four, three, two, one. It's not about your weaknesses. It's about your strengths. The longest day. The longest day. That massive, massive day. Beast of a day. We woke up at four o'clock. And then from there on, pretty much hell started. So the longest day is a real long day of team building activities. There's a lot of thinking involved. There's a lot of fitness. A lot of mental push, that we try to push them to create new limits in their lives. That way, the next time they find hardship in their lives, they understand that they can push through things that they never knew they could. It was quite difficult for me. I haven't done that much fitness ever. I just wanted to stop, walk away and just go home. But I just thought about the feeling of graduating. I'd feel pretty crap if I did all this and then just left. It was kind of just pushing through, and not giving up, for me.

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: [Clapping game] I thought that I would give up at some point. But then I actually pushed myself and tried to remind myself, like, my purpose of why I'm here, why I'm doing this, who I'm doing this for. The challenges I had was really pushing my mental strength. No matter how many times my brain says "no, stop, stop, stop, stop" because I'm not going to stop. I'm going to push through it. I feel like I've actually achieved something. I feel like I can say to my dad "I did this, and this, and this". He's going to be incredibly proud. I've learned that my mind's a lot stronger than I realised. So instead of just dwelling in the negative, we're focusing on the positive. And that's the cool thing about here, is that they push forward the positive. So, I never give up. It was pretty intense but the good thing about it was just, like, all the support, encouragement. Everyone that's, like, been pushing everyone to, like, try their best. I got used to being a leader, stepping out of my comfort zone, trying to, like, push everyone to come together. If I can just do my best for this small portion of my life, I could probably change my whole life. It's probably the greatest second chance I've ever been given, coming to LSV. As a platoon, and for myself, we've grown to be pretty good 2.0 versions of ourselves. So, we've raised the bar quite a lot through these six weeks. I'm happy. I'm proud of myself and how far I came, because I'm leading my team. Getting the trainees through to the end of the six weeks is a big achievement on its own. Graduation day could be the most proudest day of their life. I thought this was like a six-week bootcamp but it's not like that at all. It's getting them ready for a job, making them employment ready.

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: The job opportunities that the trainees have available to them post-course, they're a whole lot bigger than what they were prior. The skills and attributes that they've developed - things like work ethic, being on time, and being prepared to do any sort of task that they are given - they can actually show the employers that they are capable. That's what this course does. It not only gets you out of your shell a bit, it makes you accept you for who you are, and also others. And it gives you those skills so that you can go out, back into your everyday life and be independent. Each and every one of us has grown and developed skills that we wouldn't have known in the big wide world. So once again, I'd like to thank and congratulate you all for making it this far. You can take a man out of Three Platoon, but you cannot take Three Platoon out of the man. Thank you. Teamwork's probably the most essential part of this course, because you're working with people who have completely different backgrounds to you. You make good friends that you wouldn't have actually thought you would have. I was just happy with the way I sort of learned to work with people. And that's just something I can take into, sort of, any area of my life. I'm more out there now. I can stand up and take charge. I'm actually proud of myself. I'm the leader of the haka. I'm one of the kotiros. And I never seen myself as that. So, I feel really great and honoured to do that. It's a big change for me. The significance of the graduation parade is huge for the trainees. It's the culmination of all of the successes, all of the hardships, all of the experiences that they've had to bond together. And to see that transformation, that different person marching out in that crisply ironed uniform is basically their way of saying "Yep, this is me now. This is who I am. This is who I believe in. And who I'm proud to be." I'm really grateful that I decided to take this course. It was very challenging at first. But taking big challenges that I never thought I could achieve, it changed me a lot, actually.

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: The LSV course is a live-in, 6-week course. The course is free, and if you're getting a benefit your payments will keep going while you're on the course. You: - stay in army barracks for 6 weeks - get 3 meals a day - get gear to wear while you're on the course - do fitness training and team work - learn life skills to help you look after yourself - talk with employers about how to get a job you like, and what they look for when they hire people. Fitness training is a regular activity, and it's designed for all fitness levels. It starts off easy and gradually builds up to be more challenging. Everyone is at a different fitness level but, as a team, you support and encourage each other through the activities.

chunks.title: An average day at LSV
chunks.text: I am most proud of completing every task that was thrown at me. Every mountain that had to be climbed, I climbed. The early wake-ups, the discipline, the mahi – everything about LSV has made me a proud individual. – Trainee Rimene-Macrae

chunks.title: What you get
chunks.text: At an LSV course, you get: - clothes, food and accommodation - any gear you need for the course - free transport to and from camp - free medical care, like dental care - practical and personal support to overcome challenges. You save money while you're at LSV because you don't need to pay for costs like food or power. If you're getting a benefit, your payments keep going while you're on the course. At the end of the course, you: - know how to take care of yourself - have new life skills, like managing your time and money - are fitter and healthier - know how to talk to employers and get a job - have more confidence and are proud of yourself.

chunks.title: Where you stay
chunks.text: There are 3 LSV camps: - Whenuapai Base, in Auckland - Trentham Base, in Wellington - Burnham Base, in Christchurch. Most of the time you go to the base closest to where you live.

chunks.title: Living on the base
chunks.text: You live on the base for 6 weeks and sleep in the barracks on the base. There could be up to 8 trainees in a room and the rooms are divided into men-only and women-only. You must stay at the base for the whole 6 weeks. NZ Defence Force are responsible for you and your safety while you're at the base, and there are strict rules about who can go in or out. This means you can't go home for things like family celebrations or during the weekend. You also can't have visitors during the course, except for your graduation at the end. If there's an emergency, you can leave the base. An emergency includes when a family or whānau member is very unwell or has a bad accident, or if there's a death. You might leave the course for a few days, or you can leave the course altogether. We'll keep in touch and continue to support you, and you may be able to do the course again later. Just do it! The only person that can change you is yourself. You can’t rely on others to make that decision. What I can say is it will be the best decision you’ve ever made in your life. – Trainee Reynolds

chunks.title: Cell phones
chunks.text: You can bring a cell phone or mobile device with you, but you won't be able to use this all the time. This helps you focus on the course, so you can get the most out of it. If you bring your phone, it's collected and stored safely when you arrive at the base. You can only use it a few times during the 6 weeks. If there's an emergency, you are given the phone to contact home. You can write letters while you're on the course and post these from the camp. People can also write letters back to you. Before you start, you can give your family or friends the emergency contact details for the camp, so they can contact you in case of emergency.

chunks.title: Hair and jewellery
chunks.text: You can choose if you want to get your hair cut or not. Long hair needs to be tied up. You must remove face and body piercings during the course. You can still wear some other jewellery, like necklaces. Tidy hair and less jewellery protects your health and safety. Your commanding officer tells you what you can and can't wear.

chunks.title: Leaving the course early
chunks.text: If you want to leave early, you can talk to the NZ Defence Force and the Work and Income staff at the base. They listen and support you, and organise support for you after you leave. If you get very sick or are injured, you may need to leave the course early. You discuss this with staff at the base. You may be able to start the course again later, after you've recovered.

chunks.title: Whiteware
chunks.text: We may be able to help you buy a new fridge, freezer, combined fridge-freezer or washing machine if you’re on a low income or a benefit. We may also be able to help you pay for repairs to your current appliance. - You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. - You don't have to get a quote. - You'll have to pay the money back. - You should only buy an approved whiteware appliance with this assistance. If you need help with other essential items, please talk with us.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get help if you: - are 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services) - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - have an immediate or essential need. Youth Servicesexternal It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have. Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income and asset limits usually apply:

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: You can apply for an advance or recoverable assistance payment to buy a: - fridge - freezer - combined fridge-freezer - washing machine. Advance Payment of Benefit Recoverable Assistance Payment If your application is approved, you'll be able to buy your appliance from one of the suppliers we have an arrangement with. They will: - provide a minimum 2-year warranty - deliver and install the appliance - remove your old appliance (if it's clean and empty). The appliance will also be covered under the Consumer Guarantees Act. Consumer Guarantees Actexternal You only need to pay back the money you spend. Any money left on your payment card will automatically return to us, and you won't have to pay it back.

chunks.title: Where you can get it from
chunks.text: We have an arrangement with 4 suppliers for whiteware for you to choose from. They have a range of appliances, models and brands available at MSD prices. These suppliers are: - Big Save - Noel Leeming - Trade Depot - Fisher & Paykel and Haier (through 100% Home, Appliance Plus, Harvey Norman and Heathcotes - these retailers offer only Fisher & Paykel/Haier whiteware through this arrangement). You can go to any of these stores to buy the appliance you've been approved for. Once you're in store, tell the staff you're paying with a Work and Income payment card. They will show you the approved range of appliances and tell you the MSD prices. If an appliance in the approved range is on sale, the sale price is also available to you. The sale price won’t include the cost of delivery, installation, and removal of packaging and the old appliance, so that would be added. You should pay the lowest overall price, whether it’s the MSD price or a sale one (plus delivery, installation, and removal charges). Click on the links below to see the appliances and price ranges for MSD clients: - Big Saveexternal - Fisher & Paykel/Haierexternal - Noel Leemingexternal - Trade Depotexternal The specific MSD prices for individual appliances aren't available online.

chunks.title: Step 1: Call us
chunks.text: You need to call us. Phone us We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us. You do not need to provide quotes.

chunks.title: Step 2: Get a payment card
chunks.text: If your application is approved, we'll load the money onto a payment card for you. If you don't already have one of these, you'll need to visit a service centre to get one, and set a pin on it before you use it. Find a service centre Set a PIN Find out more about payment cards

chunks.title: Step 3: Choose where you'll buy your appliance from
chunks.text: We have an arrangement with 4 suppliers for whiteware for you to choose from. They have a range of different appliances, models and brands available at MSD prices. These suppliers are: - Big Save - Noel Leeming - Trade Depot - Fisher & Paykel and Haier (through 100% Home, Appliance Plus, Harvey Norman and Heathcotes - these retailers offer only Fisher & Paykel/Haier whiteware through this arrangement). You can go to any of these stores to buy the appliance you've been approved for. Tell the staff you're paying with a Work and Income payment card. They will show you the approved range of appliances and tell you the MSD prices. Click on the links below to see the appliances and price ranges for MSD clients: - Big Saveexternal - Fisher & Paykel/Haierexternal - Noel Leemingexternal - Trade Depotexternal The specific MSD prices for individual appliances aren't available online. You can't top up the money available on your payment card with your own funds.

chunks.title: Step 4: Buy the appliance
chunks.text: You'll need to buy your appliance at the store using your payment card. Let the staff know you're an MSD client and are here for an appliance with an MSD price. You can't use your payment card online. If you can't get to a store, tell us when you call to apply. You should only buy the appliance you have approval for. For example, if you get assistance to buy an approved fridge, you can’t buy other items such as an air fryer or a microwave. If you need help with other essential items, please talk with us. If you have been approved to buy multiple items on your payment card, for example a fridge-freezer and bedding, you need to pay for these in separate transactions – even if it’s from the same store. If you're not sure how to use your payment card, you can find out how to do this here: Using a payment card Our whiteware retailers tell us about payment card transactions, including the payment card number used. We use this information to make sure clients are using the assistance for the purpose we've discussed with them.

chunks.title: Step 5: Arrange delivery
chunks.text: The store will work with you to arrange for the appliance to be delivered to your home and installed. They will also remove the packaging and take away your old appliance (if it's clean and empty). These services are included in the MSD price. You can't take the appliance away after you buy it. It has to be delivered and installed by the store. If you need to make any changes to your order, get in touch with the store. If there is a refund, the money will be returned to us, not your payment card.

chunks.title: Appliances purchased on or after 3 September 2025
chunks.text: If you need help with your appliance, contact the store you bought it from. They will talk to you about what needs to be done, and if needed arrange for a service technician to come look at it. If the fault with your appliance isn't covered by the warranty, we may be able to help you pay for servicing and repairs. Call us to apply. Phone us

chunks.title: Appliances purchased before 3 September 2025
chunks.text: If you need help with your appliance purchased from Fisher & Paykel before 3 September 2025, call Fisher & Paykel on 0800 673 424. Discuss the fault and, if needed, arrange a repair service. If the fault with your appliance isn't covered by the warranty, we may be able to help you pay for servicing and repairs. Call us to apply. Phone us

chunks.title: Who can get NZ Super
chunks.text: If you want to apply for New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super), you need to meet certain criteria. Use our step-by-step guide to find out if you may meet the criteria for NZ Super. Find out if you can get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet
chunks.text: You may qualify for NZ Super if you: - are 65 or older - either: are a New Zealand (NZ) citizen are an NZ permanent resident, or hold an NZ residence class visa - are a New Zealand (NZ) citizen - are an NZ permanent resident, or - hold an NZ residence class visa - are ordinarily resident in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau when you apply, and - have lived in New Zealand for a certain amount of time. Definition of 'ordinarily resident' Ordinarily resident in SSA country when you apply

chunks.title: If you're working
chunks.text: You can still get NZ Super while you're working. However if you have to change your tax code, your NZ Super payments may be less after tax. If you get any other payments from us, like Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance, any income you earn will affect them.

chunks.title: Overseas pensions
chunks.text: If you or your partner qualify for an overseas pension, you must apply for it. This could affect your NZ Super payments. Overseas pensions

chunks.title: You must have lived in NZ
chunks.text: You must have lived in New Zealand for a certain number of years from age 20. This must include 5 years from age 50. The total number of years you need is based on your date of birth. These years (including the 5 years from age 50) do not need to be consecutive. Work out how many years you must have lived in NZ Haven't lived in NZ for required years

chunks.title: What we mean by 'have lived in NZ'
chunks.text: When we say 'have lived in NZ', we mean you were 'resident' and 'physically present' in NZ at the same time. If you left NZ to travel overseas, this period may not be counted as having lived in NZ. Read the definition to find out more. Definition of 'have lived in NZ'

chunks.title: You're a refugee or protected person
chunks.text: If you're recognised as a refugee or protected person, the number of years may be worked out differently. It depends on the age you started living in NZ. Refugees and protected persons

chunks.title: Work out how many years you need
chunks.text: Use the table below to work out how many years you must have lived in NZ.

chunks.title: Example - born in 1961
chunks.text: Your date of birth is 28 March 1961. You must have lived in NZ for at least 11 years from age 20. The 11 years must include 5 years from age 50. The 11 years (including the 5 years from age 50) do not need to be consecutive.

chunks.title: Haven't lived in NZ for required years
chunks.text: If you haven't lived in NZ the whole time, you may be able to use another country to meet this criteria if: - it is a country that has a Social Security Agreement (SSA) with NZ, or - it is a NZ realm country (the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau). SSA countries are: Australia, Canada, Denmark, Greece, Ireland, Jersey, Guernsey, Malta, the Netherlands, South Korea and United Kingdom. Using SSA countries to meet residence criteria for NZ Super Using NZ Realm countries to meet residence criteria for NZ Super

chunks.title: Wait until you meet the residence criteria
chunks.text: If you don't meet the residence criteria when you're 65, you can wait until either: - you've lived in NZ for the required number of years, or - you can use another country to meet this criteria. Then you can apply for NZ Super (as long as you meet all the other criteria).

chunks.title: Who can get emergency housing
chunks.text:
## Who can get emergency housing
If you need emergency housing, you must meet certain criteria.
## Criteria you need to meet
You may qualify for emergency housing if you:
- have nowhere to stay tonight or in the next 7 nights, and
- agree to meet your responsibilities from the 8th night (if you're in emergency housing for more than 7 nights).
You must also meet the residency criteria. This means you need to be either:
- getting a main benefit, NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, or
- ordinarily resident in New Zealand and either: a New Zealand citizen have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 recognised as a refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009, or getting a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your New Zealand partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence.
- a New Zealand citizen
- have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009
- recognised as a refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009, or
- getting a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your New Zealand partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence.
Main benefit
Ordinarily resident
It also depends on your income and any assets you have.
We may also look at whether you've caused or contributed to your need for emergency housing. For example:
- you moved out of your accommodation without a good reason and didn't have another place to move into, or
- you had to move out of your accommodation because you: damaged the property, or didn't follow the supplier's rules of stay.
- damaged the property, or
- didn't follow the supplier's rules of stay.
## If you're getting a main benefit
We'll look at the status of your benefit. You can't get emergency housing if it's been suspended, reduced for a certain reason, or cancelled for 13 weeks.
## Income
Generally you need to have income under these limits. However, if your income is over these limits, you may still qualify. Contact us to talk about your situation.
Phone us
## Cash assets
Generally you need to have cash assets under these limits. However, if they're over these limits, you may still qualify. Contact us to talk about your situation.
Phone us

chunks.title: Who can get Veteran's Pension
chunks.text:
## Who can get Veteran's Pension
If you want to apply for Veteran's Pension, you need to meet certain criteria.
Use our step-by-step guide to find out if you may meet the criteria for Veteran's Pension.
Find out if you can get Veteran's Pension
## Criteria you need to meet
You may qualify for Veteran's Pension if you:
- have served in the New Zealand Armed Forces on Qualifying Operational Service
- are 65 or older
- either: are a New Zealand (NZ) citizen are an NZ permanent resident, or hold an NZ residence class visa
- are a New Zealand (NZ) citizen
- are an NZ permanent resident, or
- hold an NZ residence class visa
- are ordinarily resident in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau when you apply, and
- have lived in New Zealand for a certain amount of time.
If you are ordinarily resident in a country NZ has a Social Security Agreement (SSA) with when you apply for Veteran's Pension, you may still qualify. There may be additional criteria you need to meet, it depends on your situation.
If you get other income, it may affect your Veteran's Pension payments.
Definition of 'ordinarily resident
Ordinarily resident in SSA country when you apply
If you get other income
## If you get other income
If you get other income, it may affect your Veteran's Pension payments.
Getting other income may also mean the tax code you use could change. This means you could get less for your Veteran's Pension payments, it depends what tax code you're on.
If you get an overseas pension, you can still get Veteran's Pension. However this could affect your Veteran's Pension payment.
Overseas pension

chunks.title: Who can get public housing
chunks.text: If you want to apply to live in public (social) housing, you need to meet certain criteria.

chunks.title: Residency
chunks.text: If you're getting a main benefit from us (e.g. Jobseeker Support), you meet the residency criteria. If you don't get a main benefit from us, you need to meet one of these residency criteria: - you're a New Zealand citizen - you have a resident visa or permanent resident visa and have lived in NZ continuously for at least 2 years since getting it - you're recognised as a refugee by Immigration New Zealand - you're recognised as a protected person by Immigration New Zealand, or - you either: have a Christchurch Response Visa, or get a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your NZ partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence. - have a Christchurch Response Visa, or - get a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your NZ partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence.

chunks.title: Serious housing need
chunks.text: You must have a serious housing need. This means we'll look at things like: - your current housing situation, including: the property's physical condition if the property has basic living facilities over-crowding how secure your tenancy is - the property's physical condition - if the property has basic living facilities - over-crowding - how secure your tenancy is - whether your current property or area is safe for you and suitable for your medical or physical needs - whether you could afford to rent privately - how difficult it is to find a private rental that meets your needs - whether you could manage long term in a private rental.

chunks.title: Income and assets
chunks.text: Generally you need to have: - income under: $832.72 a week (after tax) if you're single with no children $1,281.12 a week (after tax) if you have a partner or children - $832.72 a week (after tax) if you're single with no children - $1,281.12 a week (after tax) if you have a partner or children - cash assets worth less than $42,700. If you have income or assets worth more than this, you may still qualify for public housing. It depends on your situation.

chunks.title: Lump sum payment from a will or estate
chunks.text:
## Lump sum payment from a will or estate
Lump-sum payments from wills don't need to be declared as income. But if you get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit you do need to tell us about it.
## What is this?
This is a one-off payment when someone dies and leaves you money or you get some money when their property is sold.
## How it affects your benefit and allowances
You have to tell us about this payment if you:
- get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit
- invest the money you get and earn interest, this will be counted as income
- get this money as regular payments.

chunks.title: Winter Energy Payment
chunks.text: The Winter Energy Payment is an extra payment to help with the cost of heating your home over the winter months. You must be getting a main benefit, pension or Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. You don't need to apply for the Winter Energy Payment. If you meet the criteria, it's paid automatically from 1 May to 1 October every year. The Winter Energy Payment for 2026 ends on 1 October 2026.

chunks.title: Your last 2026 payment
chunks.text: Find out when your last Winter Energy Payment will be paid for 2026. If you're paid weekly: - Your last full Winter Energy Payment will be paid in the week starting 28 September. - You'll get a part Winter Energy Payment (4 days’ worth) in the week starting 5 October. - Your first payment without Winter Energy Payment will be in the week starting 12 October. If you're getting NZ Super or Veteran's Pension: - You'll get a part Winter Energy Payment (9 days’ worth) in the week starting 5 October. - Your first payment without Winter Energy Payment will be in the week starting 19 October.

chunks.title: Power redirections
chunks.text: If you have a redirection of your benefit set up to pay for power costs, you may want to review your redirection if your usage changes as winter eases. Contact us if you need to change this.

chunks.title: Need some extra help?
chunks.text: We know this can be a tough time. If you're worried about how you'll manage after the Winter Energy Payment ends, these things may be able to help: Check What You Might Getexternal - an online tool to help you check if you can get other help from us Managing your money - help manage your money, including budgeting support and financial mentors.

chunks.title: Who can get the Winter Energy Payment
chunks.text: You'll only get the Winter Energy Payment if you get one of these payments from us: - NZ Super - Veteran's Pension - Jobseeker Support - Jobseeker Support Student Hardship - Sole Parent Support - Supported Living Payment - Young Parent Payment - Youth Payment - Emergency Benefit - Emergency Maintenance Allowance. You also cannot be: - getting Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy - living overseas, or - getting an overseas pension which means you don't get any NZ Super or Veteran's Pension.

chunks.title: Winter Energy Payment rates
chunks.text: Single people with no dependent children $20.46 a week Couples, and people with dependent children $31.82 a week You'll get the Winter Energy Payment automatically, along with your other regular payments from us (either weekly or fortnightly). The Winter Energy Payment: - doesn't affect your other payments from us, or your Income Related Rent - is a non-taxable payment - can't be paid as a lump sum.

chunks.title: Couples getting NZ Super or Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: Couples are paid $31.82, whether you live together or separately. It's paid to one person in the couple. The system we use for payments can't split it to pay into 2 separate accounts. Generally, we'll pay it into the bank account of the person in the couple who has the lowest client number. You can find your client number on your Community Services Card, SuperGold Card or letters from us. If you'd like to switch the payment to the other person's account, please call us. Phone us

chunks.title: Overseas travel when you're getting NZ Super or Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: If you're heading away from New Zealand over the winter months, we can keep paying your Winter Energy Payment for up to 28 days. Tell us if you plan to leave New Zealand for more than 28 days, otherwise we might pay you too much and have to ask for some money back. The easiest way to let us know is to either: - fill out and submit the overseas travel dates online formexternal - call us on our Seniors line, 0800 552 002

chunks.title: When you return to New Zealand
chunks.text: If you return to New Zealand: - before 1 October, you need to contact us so we can start your Winter Energy Payment again. Call our Seniors line on 0800 552 002 - after 1 October, your Winter Energy Payment will automatically start again next year, as long as you still qualify.

chunks.title: Overseas travel and getting a benefit
chunks.text: You need to let us know your travel plans, the reasons for travelling, and for how long. Going overseas If you're able to keep getting your benefit when you're overseas, we'll also keep paying your Winter Energy Payment for up to 28 days.

chunks.title: When you return to New Zealand
chunks.text: If you return to New Zealand: - before 1 October, you need to contact us so we can start your Winter Energy Payment again. Call us on 0800 559 009 - after 1 October, your Winter Energy Payment will automatically start again next year, as long as you still qualify.

chunks.title: Opt out of the payment
chunks.text: If you meet the criteria, the Winter Energy Payment is paid automatically from 1 May to 1 October. It's paid with your main benefit, pension or Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. If you do not want the Winter Energy Payment, you can opt out of getting it by either: - completing the 'Stop or restart Winter Energy Payment' form, or - contacting us. Phone us We won't re-start it for you (even in future years) unless you ask us to.

chunks.title: Fill in the form
chunks.text: You can only fill in this form if you meet the criteria for Winter Energy Payment. This means you must be getting a main benefit, pension or Jobseeker Support Student Hardship. If you get Special Benefit or Temporary Additional Support - please call us instead of filling out this form. Phone us You'll need the following information to complete the form: - client number - name and date of birth - email address and contact number. If you have a partner, the payment can only be started or stopped as a couple. The form will ask you to confirm you both agree to this. Stop or restart Winter Energy Payment

chunks.title: If you've opted out, you can opt back in
chunks.text: Once you've opted out, we won't re-start it for you (even in future years) unless you ask us to. If you want to re-start it, you need to fill out the same form, or contact us.

chunks.title: Work Bonus
chunks.text:
## Work Bonus
If you're on a benefit and choose to work even though you don't have work obligations, you may be able to get a Work Bonus.
## Who can get it
You may be able to get Work Bonus if you're getting either:
- Sole Parent Support, and your youngest child is under 3
- Emergency Maintenance Allowance, and your youngest child is under 3
- Supported Living Payment, because you've got a health condition, injury or disability, or
- Emergency Benefit instead of Supported Living Payment because you don't have New Zealand residency.
You also need to:
- be coming off one of these benefits to start work
- be starting work in New Zealand
- tell us you want to stop your benefit within 14 days of starting work.
## Who can't get Work Bonus
You can't get Work Bonus if:
- you're coming off your benefit to start self-employed work, or
- you have work obligations while you're on your benefit.
## What you can get
Work Bonus is paid weekly. The first week's payment will be at the full rate of the benefit you're on. This doesn't include any other payments you get, e.g. Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance. It then reduces by $100 a week until it runs out.
You can only get one Work Bonus a year.
It's not counted as income (including for Working for Families Tax Credits) or as an asset.
## How to apply
Call us on 0800 559 009 to let us know you've found a job. If you qualify for Work Bonus, we'll pay this to you automatically. It will start the week after you get your last benefit payment.

chunks.title: Kōrero Mahi work seminars
chunks.text: At our Kōrero Mahi work seminars you'll get support to get ready to work. We'll explain how we can help you find work, and get you set up to start applying for jobs. Work seminars are in-person seminars held at your local Work and Income office. The seminars take about 1 hour. Narrator [00:00:02]: Here's a bit about what to expect at our Kōrero Mahi work seminars. These seminars are to support you to get ready for work. They are held at your local Work and Income service centre. [Man smiles and raises his hand in a wave. chunks.title: Kōrero Mahi work seminars
chunks.text: Narrator [00:00"42]: If you have to look for or prepare for work to meet your benefit obligations, then you'll need to come to a Kōrero Mahi seminar. [Woman sits at a desk in a Work and Income office and talks to someone. The screen transitions to an outline of a cellphone with the words 'Kōrero Mahi seminar' and a notification email] Man: And just know that we are here to help you along the way. [Man sits at a table in an office. The MSD logo, Work and Income logo and URL 'www.workandincome.govt.nz' appear on the screen.]

chunks.title: Who the seminars are for
chunks.text: You have to go to a seminar if: - you've applied for Jobseeker Support for the first time, and - and you have full-time or part-time work obligations. If you've reapplied for Jobseeker Support at 26 weeks (6 months), you may have to go to a seminar. Find out more on the Reapply for Jobseeker Support page. Reapply for Jobseeker Support You don't have to go if you're getting any other benefit, or if you're getting Jobseeker Support and only have work preparation obligations.

chunks.title: Which seminar you need to go to
chunks.text: If you have full-time work obligations, you need to go to: - 'Kōrero Mahi - Let's talk work' within 2 weeks of starting Jobseeker Support. If you have part-time work obligations, you need to go to: - 'Kōrero Mahi - Into work' within 2 weeks of starting Jobseeker Support. Use the links below to find out what happens at each seminar:

chunks.title: Kōrero Mahi - Let's talk work
chunks.text: You need to go to this seminar if you have full-time work obligations. You need to go within 2 weeks of starting Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: About the seminar
chunks.text: At the seminar we'll tell you about: - what you have to do while you're getting Jobseeker Support - how we can help you get ready for work - where to look for jobs and what help you can get. We'll also talk with you one-on-one about: - what you've been doing to find work - what kind of work you can do - what support you need to get a job, like a CV, training, work gear or clothes - what your next step is to get into work.

chunks.title: Booking a seminar
chunks.text: We'll book you in for a seminar after you apply for Jobseeker Support. We'll do this when you come to your first appointment.

chunks.title: If you can't make it to your seminar
chunks.text: You can rebook in MyMSD if it's the first time you can't make it. Just open your appointment from the home screen and select 'I can't make it'. You can rebook for a date up to 4 weeks in the future. If you can't use MyMSD, call us on 0800 559 009. MyMSDexternal If you can't make it a second time, let us know as soon as possible by calling 0800 559 009. If you have a good reason, we can rebook you again for another date.

chunks.title: Kōrero Mahi - Into work
chunks.text: You need to go to this seminar if you have part-time work obligations because of your health condition or disability. You need to go within 2 weeks of starting Jobseeker Support.

chunks.title: About the seminar
chunks.text: This seminar is to help you prepare and find work that's suitable for you. We want to understand how you're doing and how we can help you. At the seminar we'll talk about: - how we'll work with you - what support we can offer - getting yourself ready to work, finding jobs and ongoing support while you're working - what you have to do while you're getting Jobseeker Support. We'll also talk with you one-on-one about: - your individual situation, so we can understand what's important to you - what kind of work you can do - what we can do to help you find the right job. Seminars are held in a private room at your local Work and Income office, with a small group of people. We won't discuss your personal situation in a group setting.

chunks.title: Booking a Kōrero Mahi - Into work seminar
chunks.text: You need to come to a seminar within 2 weeks of starting Jobseeker Support. We'll book the seminar for you, and let you know when and where it is.

chunks.title: After your seminar
chunks.text: By the end of the seminar you'll know what you need to do to get yourself ready to work, and where to look for jobs. If there’s something you need specific help with that we talked about at your seminar, we’ll be in touch to sort this out. These things can also help: - Get ready to work – specialised help with CVs, cover letters, or job interviews. - Feeling anxious about work – talk to someone if you need support or you’re feeling anxious. - Find jobs – places you can look for jobs and find the right job for you. - Where to look for jobs – job-search websites where you can find something that works for you. - How to choose the right job – tools and experts to help you find out what you're good at and what job suits you.

chunks.title: What happens if you don't go to the seminar
chunks.text: Attending the 'Kōrero Mahi - Let's talk work' and 'Kōrero Mahi - Into work' seminars is part of your obligations to look for or prepare for work. If you don't attend (and you haven’t rebooked), you need to have a good reason why you couldn't come. Otherwise your Jobseeker Support could reduce or stop.

chunks.title: Working for Families
chunks.text: Working for Families is help from Work and Income and Inland Revenue (IR) to make it easier to work and raise a family.

chunks.title: What Work and Income help with
chunks.text: Work and Income help with: - childcare costs for pre-school care - childcare costs for before and after school care - accommodation costs with the Accommodation Supplement You can use our 'Check what you might get' tool to find out what Work and Income payments you might qualify for and how much you might be able to get. Childcare Subsidy Out of School Care and Recreation (OSCAR) Subsidy Accommodation Supplement

chunks.title: What Inland Revenue help with
chunks.text: Inland Revenue (IR) can help you with Working for Families Tax Credits. Apply for Working for Families (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: Family tax credit
chunks.text: This payment provides ongoing financial support for families. The amount you receive depends on your family situation. If you're on a Work and Income benefit you can get us to pay your family tax credit with your other payments. Inland Revenue pay the family tax credit to you if you're not getting a benefit payment from us. Family tax credit (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: Best Start tax credit
chunks.text: Best Start tax credit (BSTC) is a payment to help families with the costs in a child's first three years. If you're getting a Work and Income benefit, we'll pay you the Best Start tax credit with your payments. You'll need to apply through IR if you don't get a benefit from Work and Income. Best Start (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: In-work tax credit
chunks.text: In-work tax credit (IWTC) is an entitlement from Inland Revenue for people in paid work with families. In-work tax credit (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: Minimum family tax credit
chunks.text: Minimum family tax credit (MFTC) is a payment made by Inland Revenue to families with dependent children, so there is a minimum income each week after tax. Minimum family tax credit (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: Work out your tax credits
chunks.text: Working for Families payments are based on your family income and the number of children in your care. Use Inland Revenue's calculator to estimate how much your Working for Families payments could be. Can you get Working for Families? (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: Worried about losing your job
chunks.text: If you're struggling at work or worried you might lose your job, we can help. Tell us what's going on and we'll create a tailored plan to help you. Things don't always go to plan, but that's OK. We have a dedicated team who can help you keep your job or find a new one. We can help if: - you're worried you might lose your job, for any reason - you're struggling to do your job - you're finding work hard - your contract is about to end. Contact us early so we can help you right away, even if no decisions have been made yet. We'll do our best to help you keep your current job. If that's not possible, we'll help you get a new job as soon as possible.

chunks.title: How we can help
chunks.text: We may be able to help you and your employer to avoid making your job redundant. Talk to us as early as possible, even if you're not sure if you'll lose your job. We'll talk about your situation right now, and how we can help. We can do things like: - check how we can help your employer keep your job going - figure out what your options are and talk through these with you - find training options that can help you do your job - help you upskill into a new job. You don't have to be getting a benefit for this. If you've already lost your job, or it's about to finish, we can still help. We'll help you get a new job as soon as possible, and support you between jobs: Redundancy support

chunks.title: How to contact us
chunks.text: Email our team at RedeploymentSupport@msd.govt.nz In your email tell us: - your name - your contact details - how your job is going and what's worrying you. We'll connect you to someone in your area who will talk to you directly to understand what's going on and what you need.

chunks.title: Help for your job
chunks.text: As well as talking to us, there are also other things we can do to help you with your current job.

chunks.title: Feeling anxious about work
chunks.text: It can be hard to do your job if you're worried or anxious about work. These services are specifically designed to help people with their jobs, or help them get a job: Feeling anxious about work

chunks.title: Seasonal work
chunks.text: If your seasonal job is finishing soon, we can help you get set to find a new one. Finished seasonal work

chunks.title: Costs while you're working
chunks.text: We may be able to help you pay an unexpected cost, or pay your bills, even if you've got a job. Help while you’re working

chunks.title: Paying for work costs
chunks.text: Get help from us to pay for things you need to do your job like training, transport, gear or clothing. Payments to help you at work

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get the Young Parent Payment if you: - are 16-19 years old - have a dependent child or children - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here. You must also: - be in, or available for, full time education, training or work-based learning leading towards an NCEA level 2 qualification, or an equivalent or higher qualification - be in a teen parent unit if your child is one year old, or from six months old if there is a place available for you - work with a Youth Service provider who will help you manage your money - attend a budgeting course - attend a parenting course to develop your parenting skills - enrol your child (or children) at a medical centre or with a doctor - register your children under 5 with a WellChild provider, like Plunket, and make sure they have regular checkups with this provider - have your child (or children) attend Early Childhood Education or other suitable childcare when you are in education, training or work-based learning or part-time work.

chunks.title: You're single
chunks.text: If you're single and 16 or 17, you may only get Young Parent Payment if you either: - have a parental support gap - are living at home with, or being financially supported by, your parents or guardians and they earn less than the Family Tax Credit income cut-off point, or - are divorced, your civil union has been dissolved, or you have separated from your de-facto partner. You are considered to have a parental support gap if either: - you have left the care of Oranga Tamariki - Ministry for Children, or - your parents or guardian can't support you. This could be because they are in prison, in hospital, deceased, or overseas, or - your relationship with your parents or guardians has broken down and no one can support you financially, or - there is a good reason why you can no longer live with your parents or guardian, or be supported by them or anyone else. You would not be considered to have a parental support gap if you have the option of living with a parent or guardian but choose not to without a good and sufficient reason.

chunks.title: You're in a relationship
chunks.text: If you're married, in a civil union or de facto relationship, you may get Young Parent Payment as long as you're not in a relationship with a specified beneficiary If you or your partner are 16 or 17, a Family Court Judge must consent to your relationship. You'll need to show us the court order from the Family Court Judge. Before 14 August 2018, we accepted written consent from the parents of the 16-17 year old. If you've already given the parents' consent to us before then, we can still use it. You don't need to get consent from a Family Court Judge.

chunks.title: Check if you can get Young Parent Payment
chunks.text: To find out if you could get Young Parent Payment and what else you might qualify for, use our 'Check what you might get' tool.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You can apply online through MyMSD. We'll also check to see if you can get any other help from us based on the answers you give in your application. If you want to get child support through Inland Revenue, you can apply through us when you complete your online application. Or you can apply through Inland Revenue. Any child support payments you get will be counted as income for your benefit. Child Support

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: Once you've submitted your online form, we'll call if there's anything else you need to do.

chunks.title: Parent/caregiver involvement
chunks.text: When you apply for a Young Parent Payment, we usually discuss your situation with your parents or caregivers. There are some circumstances when this won't happen, for example, if you're married or in a civil union. Information for parents/caregivers

chunks.title: Education and Training
chunks.text: Most young people are better off if they finish their education or are in training for future work. When you apply, we'll call you to talk about what education or training you'll return to, start or continue doing.

chunks.title: Your rights at work and advice
chunks.text:
## Your rights at work and advice
Work can be a stressful place, and sometimes things don't go to plan. You can get help to make your job easier, understand your rights and resolve problems at work.
## Feeling anxious
It can be hard to do your job if you're feeling worried or anxious. These coaching and mental health services are designed to help you keep your job or find a new one:
Feeling anxious about work
## Managing challenges at work
If you've come off your benefit for this job, you can get ongoing support and advice to help you manage any challenges. This is called In-Work Support.
In-Work Support
## Leave and holidays
Employment New Zealand has information about the types of leave you can get and what you need to do to get this.
Leave and holidays - Employment New Zealandexternal
## How to talk to your employer
Employment New Zealand has advice on the best ways to prevent and resolve relationship problems between you and your employer.
Resolving problems - Employment New Zealandexternal

chunks.text:
## Income rules for Youth Payment and Young Parent Payment
If you're getting a youth payment, you need to let us or your Youth Service provider know about any income you or your partner get. Depending on what extra help you get, you may need to tell us about one-off payments or any assets you have.
Find your nearest provider (Youth Service)external
## No
You need to tell us or your Youth Service provider about any income you get and some one-off payments. You don't have to tell us about any assets you have.
